title: Man City's leaky defence highlights Donnarumma & Guehi struggles
description: Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season comes to an abrupt end against Aston Villa - leaving Enzo Maresca with glaring defensive issues to resolve.
body: Since the start of last season, only eight players have made more errors leading to Premier League goals than Gianluigi Donnarumma and Marc Guehi Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season came to an abrupt end against Aston Villa - leaving Enzo Maresca with glaring defensive issues to resolve. Nicolas Jackson's double in a 2-1 home win for Villa means City have now managed only one clean sheet in their past six games and the form of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma and defender Marc Guehi is of concern. Since the start of last season, only eight players have made more errors leading to Premier League goals than Donnarumma and Guehi with three each. City's most recent shutout came in their impressive victory at Liverpool two weeks ago but, around that game, City have conceded against teams ranging from Champions League holders Paris St-Germain to top-flight strugglers Sunderland. Maresca was forced to try different combinations at the back against Villa, but as the legendary Sir Alex Ferguson once said, "attack wins you games, defence wins you titles". Though still early days in the campaign and guaranteed to be in the top two come the end of the weekend, City need to shore up their backline if they are to make a realistic title challenge this season. Asked if the two goals were avoidable, Maresca told TNT Sports: "Absolutely, both. "Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances, but we created a lot of chances. "We played most of the game in their box but you have to be clinical and avoid mistakes like the two goals we conceded." Jackson stars with two goals - player ratings for Aston Villa v Man City Jackson double for Villa ends Man City's 100% start This video can not be played City 'deserved more' from 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa - Maresca City were undone by goals in each half from the brilliant Jackson at a raucous Villa Park to end their streak of seven straight wins at the start of this campaign. Maresca's team started the season by conceding eight goals in their first nine games but that has seen a dramatic downturn, with nine goals hitting the back of their net in the past four matches. The signing of Donnarumma last summer was heralded as the acquisition of one of the best goalkeepers in the world to replace Ederson. The Brazilian changed the face of English football with his footwork, spraying short and long passes across the pitch, and there are few keepers who can come close to matching that. But Italy captain Donnarumma struggles with the ball at his feet and often puts his team-mates in trouble with passes out from the back. On Saturday, City captain Ruben Dias gesticulated to his team-mate to send the ball up the pitch after the Portuguese failed to control a difficult pass. Maresca decided to sell James Trafford to Leeds for £45m in the summer, and the England international has been impressive at Elland Road. Trafford has made more passes than Donnarumma this season, has a slightly better rate at preventing goals and has come out to sweep the ball 11 times compared with Donnarumma's one. Though Donnarumma could do little about Jackson's thumping finish for the opening goal, he should have done better for the second as a low shot seemed to squirm under him. Former City defender Steph Houghton said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think Villa really utilised keeping the ball and being a real threat to Manchester City. Donnarumma, especially with the second goal, could probably have done a little bit better. "But I don't want to take anything away from Villa. I think they performed really, really well and the gameplan was spot on, just to nullify City as much as possible." Centre-back Guehi's £20m arrival from Crystal Palace in January was considered a bargain. But it was his loose pass at Everton late last season which cost City dearly in the title race, drawing that game and losing the impetus to eventual champions Arsenal. This season has been a struggle for the England defender, culpable for both goals scored by Ipswich last weekend and being picked off by John McGinn deep in his own half for Villa's first goal. Later in the half, he hauled down Jackson on the edge of the box before being shown a yellow card, and was put out of his misery by being taken off at half-time. City sources had said they were targeting signing a right-back in the summer before pivoting elsewhere, saying Abdukodir Khusanov can provide back-up should Matheus Nunes not be available. Khusanov started out wide but struggled before being moved inside in place of Guehi, while Rico Lewis was brought to fill the gap, with Maresca acknowledging afterwards he needs to "find that balance" in defence. Villa supporters provided constant reminders to the travelling fans of their side being "cheats", and the vitriol faced following the guilty verdict of the financial charges may be beginning to weigh on the players' minds. Asked by BBC Sport if Guehi's form is a worry, Maresca said: "No, I'm not worried about Marc at all. "I know he is playing every minute since the season started with us and the national team, so it's not easy but the change was also because he was on a yellow card. "The way we want to be aggressive sometimes, to have one yellow card can be dangerous but I am not worried at all." Maresca, though, should be concerned by coming up against Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring Brighton twice next week - in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, and Premier League on Saturday. The Italian needs to fix the defensive leaks before they become something more serious. title: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis
description: The ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr, with whom she shares five children, announced in May that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer.
body: Vanessa Trump and her 19-year-old daughter Kai Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year. Trump, 48, who has five children with President Donald Trump's eldest son, shared in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free". The video, posted on Friday, teases the release of a longer YouTube video to come on Saturday, in which Vanessa and Kai Trump will discuss breast cancer awareness and prevention, Kai wrote in the caption. Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods. "October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram. "I sat down with my mom and Dr. Nicole Saphier to talk about my mom's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection," she continued. Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from American singer and media personality Mary Millben. In Friday's video, Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team. According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, according to the group. Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some disease remains, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk. Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy. title: 'My daughter's bed was propped up on books,' says mum amid child poverty fears
description: Sarah Ruscoe, a single mum out of work due to health issues, worried her daughter’s bed would collapse at night.
body: Sarah Ruscoe's daughter Sabrina is among Wales' one-third of children living in relative poverty "I was sleeping on the sofa, she had a bed that was propped up on books. One of the legs had fallen off completely." Sarah Ruscoe, a single mum out of work because of a health condition, said she had worried her daughter's bed would collapse in the night after finding herself in a "dire" financial situation. A food bank user, Ruscoe said "every year seems to be getting worse" as she struggled to make her benefits cover essentials. A charity eventually paid for a new bed for daughter Sabrina, 11. But MPs heard this week that the general picture of one in three children living in relative poverty in Wales had not changed in 20 years, with a think tank saying the problem was becoming entrenched. 'There's so much I want to give my daughter - poverty means I can't' £10-a-week child poverty payment plans faces obstacles, says expert On Wednesday MPs at the UK Parliament's Welsh Affairs Committee opened an inquiry on ending child poverty in Wales. The country has the highest child poverty rate of any UK nation, with 32% of children living in relative poverty after housing costs, according to the latest official statistics. A child is considered to be in relative poverty if the income of the household they live in is below 60% of the UK median. Evidence was given by charities including Action for Children, who paid for Sabrina's new bed and provides financial support to thousands of low income families in Wales each year. Ruscoe, from Barry, told BBC Wales that three years ago she struggled to afford to replace her daughter's "ropey" bed which had been "second or third hand". "It was getting a bit distressing," she said, and both mother and daughter had worried it might collapse in the night when Sabrina moved. "I was having difficulty finding somewhere where I could afford one, and also not having the greatest credit rating in the world meant that you had to pay like two or three times what you would have done if you'd just gone into a shop and bought it outright." The new bed meant Sabrina had "somewhere safe" to sleep, her mother says The cabin bunk and a mattress purchased by Action for Children made a "massive difference", she said. "It meant she had somewhere safe. It's a little nest now. We decorated it," Ruscoe said. "Nobody else has slept in it. It's something that's new for her. "Up until that point it was worry and trying to work out, maybe if I didn't pay this bill maybe I could save some money here, what could I go without, trying to work out which company had the smallest APR on an item that I could afford. "There's not that much out there, especially when they hear you're on benefits." One year the charity also helped the family with a gift card for local supermarkets before Christmas. Ruscoe, who used to work in a job centre, said her chronic pain condition fibromyalgia had left her feeling fatigued and in pain and, when it had flared up, unable to move. "I don't work due to my disabilities so it's a case of benefits, and that's how we survive, and this year seems to be worse than last year. Every year seems to be getting worse. "Last year I managed to put money away over the course of the year for Christmas and this year I haven't been able to at all. Everything has gone up. "There's only so much penny pinching you can do on everything and then realise that every penny you've pinched is still not covering all your bills and your outgoings." The mother and daughter are just one of hundreds of families who have received financial help from Action for Children Ruscoe warned that anyone could find themselves in a crisis situation because of ill-health or an unexpected life event. Laurie Ryall, Wales director at Action for Children, gave evidence to MPs on the first day of their inquiry in Westminster, and said the absence of a single point of access for support had often left families experiencing child poverty feeling overwhelmed. "They don't always know what they're entitled to or where to go, it's confusing, it's a minefield," Ryall said. Mabli Jones from the Bevan Foundation think tank told MPs that although child poverty had remained at the same level for two decades "what's been happening under the surface is that poverty has got deeper". "Almost half - 47% - of people in Wales who live in poverty live in what's classed as very deep poverty - that's an income that is at or below 40% of the median," she said. "Families who are experiencing that kind of poverty are likely to be going without many of the basics." A UK government spokesperson said: "We're determined to turn the tide on poverty, and our landmark child poverty strategy will lift 550,000 children out of poverty in the final year of this parliament - the largest reduction in child poverty since records began." They said abolishing the two-child limit would benefit an estimated 69,000 children in Wales, and a temporary cut to electricity bills and raising the National Living Wage had contributed to a fall in food bank usage. A Welsh government spokesperson said it had "inherited a damning legacy of stubbornly high levels of child poverty". It said it was helping families through the first phase of its offer of 12.5 hours of free childcare to all two-year-olds and extending free school meals. They also said the government was seeking assurance from the UK government that a proposed pilot scheme for £10 a week to each child to support low-income families would not affect families' benefit payments. "We continue to call on the UK government to use all the levers at its disposal, including those on welfare, to make a lasting difference to families in Wales," they said. title: Jackson stars with two goals - player ratings for Aston Villa v Man City
description: How Aston Villa and Man City players rated following their Premier League match.
body: Nicolas Jackson scored twice for Aston Villa Nicolas Jackson scored twice as Aston Villa ended Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season. Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players. What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? Zion Suzuki: Good in the air, decent distribution and made three important stops to deny Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Josko Gvardiol with a brilliant, fingertip save. 7 Matty Cash: Battled all game with Jeremy Doku and though he was booked for a push on the Belgian, he managed more tackles than any other player. 7 Victor Lindelof: Threw his body at everything that came his way but outmuscled for Haaland's goal. 6 Pau Torres: Calming presence at the back without being too ruffled. 6 Ian Maatsen: Could have scored early on but blazed a volley over. Vital header away to deny Erling Haaland's goalbound header late on. 6 John McGinn: Picked off Marc Guehi to lay on the opening goal and created more chances than anyone else on the pitch. 7 Boubacar Kamara: At the heart of everything good from the home side, sniffing out the danger. 7 Joao Gomes: Mucked in alongside Kamara by keeping the ball ticking and contributing three interceptions. 6 Alysson: The 20-year-old Brazilian impressed against Viking in the Champions League and showed why he was given a start again with another eye-catching performance. 7 Johan Manzambi: Switzerland international displayed sparks of his undoubted talent and could have had a penalty in the first half. 6 Nicolas Jackson: Brimming with confidence. Took the opening goal brilliantly, firing high into the roof of the net, before stroking in a second. 9 Ibrahim Mbaye (on 58, Alysson) Instant impact after coming on, providing a low cross for Jackson to finish. 7 Emiliano Buendia (on 66, Manzambi) 6 Ross Barkley (on 66, McGinn) 6 Brian Madjo (on 82, Jackson) 6 Leon Goretzka (on 82, Gomes) 6 Subs not used: Marco Bizot, Tyrone Mings, Lamare Bogarde, George Hemmings. Gianluigi Donnarumma: Conceded an early corner after taking too long over a goal-kick, poor kicking often put team-mates in trouble and should have done better for the second goal. 5 Abdukodir Khusanov: Shaky at right-back before being moved into central defence for the second half. 6 Ruben Dias: Rattled by Jackson in the first half but made a good block to deny Alysson a certain goal. 5 Marc Guehi: Another shocker. Culpable for both of Ipswich's goals last weekend and made another poor error which led to Villa's opener. Booked for hauling down Jackson on the edge of the box before being taken off at half-time. 4 Josko Gvardiol: Given a difficult time by Alysson throughout but came close to scoring in the second half. 5 Elliot Anderson: Struggled to impose himself in the game and was shown a yellow card for a mis-timed challenge on Gomes. 6 Enzo Fernandez: Always available for the ball but lost the midfield battle. 6 Iliman Ndiaye: City's liveliest player. Showed quick footwork to force Suzuki into a decent save, clipped the post with another similar effort and provided the cross for Haaland's equaliser. 8 Jeremy Doku: Looked to create openings with his box of tricks but often wasteful. 6 Rayan Cherki: Often crowded out by Villa's midfield and booked for a frustrated tug on Manzambi. Subbed at half-time. 5 Erling Haaland: Quiet in the first half but came to life in the second with a towering header to draw his side level. 7 Phil Foden (on 46, Cherki) Had little impact after Tuesday's Champions League hat-trick. 6 Rico Lewis (on 46, Guehi) Pushed forward but unable to make a meaningful contribution. 6 Ryan McAidoo (on 69, Ndiaye) 6 Subs not used: Geronimo Rulli, Mateo Kovacic, Rayan Ait-Nouri, Vitor Reis, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Nico O'Reilly. After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: 68-point swing and a Tonga win - how England avoid World Cup exit
description: England need a few things to go their way next weekend to stay in the Men's Rugby League World Cup - but they have at least given themselves a chance.
body: This video can not be played England crush France 82-0 to stay in World Cup contention Sixty-eight. That is the magic number for England. For Brian McDermott's side to reach the semi-finals of the Rugby League World Cup, a specific series of events needs to happen next weekend. On the backfoot since being humbled 30-12 by Tonga in their opening game, England responded with a crushing 82-0 victory over France to keep their dreams alive. It means England need to beat co-hosts Papua New Guinea in their final group match in Wollongong next Friday – then hope Tonga beat Samoa, two days later in Sydney. If Samoa win, England will be eliminated because of their inferior head-to-head record against Tonga. But if Tonga win, it comes down to points difference between England and Samoa. England's difference, after the Tonga loss and France win, is +64. Samoa, following hefty victories over the French and PNG, is +132 – which is 68 better than England. So, 68 is the number to remember. If England beat PNG by 68 points or more, then any Tongan win is good enough for McDermott's men. Less than 68, and they must hope Tonga are really inspired by Pacific rivalry to put one over their island neighbours. England hope the numbers go in their favour to avoid an unwanted first. In 16 previous Rugby League World Cups, staged in varying formats, neither England nor Great Britain have ever finished outside the top four. And every time the format has included semi-finals, they have got there. Fri, 30 Oct: England v Papua New Guinea: Wollongong, 09:05 GMT Sun, 1 Nov: Lebanon v France: Parramatta, Sydney: 06:40 GMT Sun, 1 Nov: Tonga v Samoa: Parramatta, Sydney: 09:05 GMT Tonga and Samoa are both above England in Group B-C with two wins from two "What we have done today is enormous, given the context," McDermott told his post-match media conference in Perth. "Knowing we had to win big - and we have had candid conversations about that this week - we have done that without getting hot. Everything was measured and planned. "Whatever the results next week, we have to finish strong - if we go home next week, we will be disappointed, but I'm not sure what else we could have done." McDermott's final comments may allude to the controversial format of this men's World Cup, which features an unbalanced group stage that has not helped England's prospects. Pool A has four teams - Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands - fighting for two semi-final places in a round-robin format. Simple enough. But Pools B and C are combined into one six-team league, from which only the top two will make the semi-finals. England, drawn in Pool B, play the three Pool C teams - Tonga, France and Papua New Guinea. It means while England are competing with Samoa for a semi-final place, they will not actually play each other. It also means that while New Zealand lost their opening fixture against Australia, their path to the semis remains simple – win their final two group games. England too had to win their last two pool matches but also needed snookers. There is some reason behind the maddening format, introduced after France – who were supposed to host a 16-team men's World Cup last summer – pulled out because of money troubles. Australia stepped in with New Zealand and Papua New Guinea, with the number of teams involved shrunk from 16 to 10 to cut costs. This format also means every team plays three group games, there are no fallow weekends and the whole tournament can be done in a relatively tight five weeks. England thrash France to keep alive World Cup hopes 'We had to change after Vegas' - but England suffer another humbling George Williams has captained England in their opening two matches in Perth But it is unquestionably harder on sides in Groups B and C. The fact Australia and New Zealand are in Group A won't help the perception of the tournament being skewed towards the southern hemisphere giants. "We were the best we could be," England captain George Williams said of the France win. "The situation has been difficult, but we have given ourselves half a chance." It also leaves England fans with a nagging feeling their side are only producing their best when they are already halfway home. After a sluggish, disconnected showing against Tonga, England were slow starting against France before finding their mojo - no tries until the 23rd minute; by the final whistle they had run in 14. England's UK based players took nearly 48 hours to travel out to Perth. BBC Sport understands that the tournament organiser planned England's travel itinerary for the World Cup. The convoluted route featured a bus journey to London, then flights via Singapore and Sydney rather than straight to Perth, where they played their first two games. McDermott's side did not play a warm-up fixture and completed just two full training sessions before taking on Tonga. "We have been together for only five field sessions; we are building something here," said McDermott. "The tries we scored before half time were what we are chasing. "With a long build up, we could have achieved some special things." Ifs, buts and maybes. All England can do now is aim for 68 points, and hope. title: Met Police says letter with claims about Meghan's father not shared with other law enforcement
description: The Met said it passed information to the duchess but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
body: Meghan says she was informed of "disturbing allegations" about her father via a letter A letter making a "number of claims" relating to the Duchess of Sussex's father was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, Scotland Yard has confirmed. The Met said it passed the information relating to allegations outside the UK to the office of the Duke and Duchess but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies. It was reported on Friday that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle, 82, had been found in his former home in the Philippines. Markle, who is based in the US, denies possessing any such images. On Friday, Meghan said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018. The Met said it was reviewing the matter and deciding whether to refer itself to the police watchdog. Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father Responding to Saturday's developments dating the letter to 2019, a spokesman for the duchess said "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time". The claims were first carried by the Sun newspaper, which later said that the letter made direct allegations of child sex abuse against Markle. In a statement, Scotland Yard said: "Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. "It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. "The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies. "The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach." Undated image shows Thomas Markle with Meghan Markle Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes. He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025. Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported. He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July. In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated". Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children". Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father. The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force. Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination. Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland. He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged. The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals. They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away. title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of tour
description: The Geordie singer says on Instagram he is "not happy" with the reported ticket prices.
body: Sam Fender said prices for his 2027 stadium tour would be lowered Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost. The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027. While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices. The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs". Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday. But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices. "They're getting changed," he said on Instagram. "It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on." The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front. "The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said. "I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour." He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing. Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive. The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future. title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
description: The slowed Starlink connections had affected the Ukraine's military and drone operations for a week.
body: Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network. Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it. This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back". Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored. "This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday. Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war. Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied. Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues. Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea. Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike. Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours. They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday. This video can not be played Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? title: Rising demand from families needing Christmas help
description: Charlotte Riley says more families are reaching out for help for a variety of reasons.
body: Charlotte Riley has been collecting and distributing Christmas gifts for families in need since 2024 The number of families asking for help to afford Christmas presents is rising, according to the organiser of a charitable cause. For the past two years Charlotte Riley has collected and distributed donated gifts voluntarily as part of Christmas Kindness Appeal Jersey which she organises through Facebook. The gifts are given to families for children aged up to 18. Riley said: "What we are seeing is that each year we're getting more and more numbers coming through." She said the donated gifts helped to "take the pressure off" families in need of support. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Riley said when she first started the appeal in 2024 she "didn't expect the response from the community". She said: "I knew there were people in need. "I didn't quite know how many people that would be." She said the reasons people might reach out to the appeal included unemployment, ill health and the general high cost of living. Along with more demand, Riley said there were also increasing numbers of people offering to help. "It wouldn't be done without those other people helping," she said. "We have people doing deliveries, we have people doing pickups... we have people that have accessed this and got gifts in previous years that are now saying 'I want to give back' so they will go and do collections for us as well." Riley said there was a three-week window for donations which can include clothes, food and essentials as well as gifts. Donations can be made before 14 November. "People are very complimentary and very thankful," Riley said. She said she wanted parents to feel part of the process so they were also given wrapping paper and labels. "It's the small simple things as well that make that big difference," she said. Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test
description: The prime minister might be dreaming of gold medals in 2040, but he must first navigate the difficult years in between, writes Laura Kuenssberg.
body: Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test Giving the north of England a crack at hosting the globe's biggest sports event might seem about as Brand Burnham as it gets. Seven million pounds of taxpayers' cash is a teeny drop in the context of the overall Budget, to pay for the government to take a closer look at possible plans. But the idea is sure to get tongues wagging - and headline writers scribbling. A "Northern Games" in 2040 or beyond just might create a massive sense of national feel-good, jobs and development, as the Olympics in east London did more than a decade ago. But it's a promise of a possibility at least a decade away. And what could be more in tune with the Manchester-loving prime minister and his proud Yorkshireman chancellor than a sporting plan fixed firmly on the top geographical chunk of the country? Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget It's Brand Burnham alright, popular with most of the Labour backbenches, just add the Twiglets and the pint in the stands. The prime minister and his team are proud of a distinct feature of their government so far, focusing on small things that might make a big difference: fines for blaring out music on your phone on the bus, cracking down on "rip-off" parking charges, investing a small amount of cash in a big ambition for a sporting event in future. It's what some ministers call "the politics of trying" – putting time and effort into ideas that you don't pretend are revolutionary, but give direction, and a sense of sympathy to the public. It's an echo, deliberate or not, of another Labour Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, who sent memos to his cabinet in 1974 demanding "little things that mean a lot". He ended up with a list of plans including nationalising small breweries to stop them being gulped up by big firms (paging Andy Burnham), freezing phone installation charges for pensioners, and plans for empty office blocks. But the next few days could bring an end to that "politics of trying" phase, with one senior official describing the coming Budget as "the first proper moment for the government, which will then be in the pipeline for the 10-year plan, then a very difficult spending review". What is the Budget and what could be in it? An influential Labour MP told me: "The Budget has to be the beginning of the future story." A fancy way of saying, beyond the short-term announcements and clear long-term aspirations, what is this government actually going to do? "Steady as she goes," is what one well-connected senior MP predicts, and how expectations of the Budget are being managed across Westminster. They tell me: "Not doing a lot might be more reassuring to people than promising the earth with whose money?" The boss of one well-known high street business told me they are even hoping there won't be any big bazookas. "Just do no harm," they implored the Chancellor John Healey. "The hole is too big that they are trying to fill, so my view is don't try and do anything big to help because you don't have the money, but don't do anything to harm us either." After all, the chancellor is bound by Labour's manifesto promises not to fiddle with the main taxes – income tax, VAT, National Insurance for workers. And you don't need me to remind you that public spending, borrowing and tax are all at historic highs. Chuck in prices jacking up again because of war in the Middle East and there isn't much money to spray around. In fact, some big cuts to public spending are already pencilled in for the later years of this parliament. The chancellor and prime minister face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending But the widespread suggestion that you'll be able to blink and miss the Budget has got some hackles up in the Treasury. A budget, by its very nature, can never be a small event - it sets billions upon billions of taxes and spending decisions. And there are likely to be extra taxes on banks, vows to sweep away some business regulation, particularly for small business, more powers passing to local leaders under the guise of devolution and more action on energy bills which are heading back up again. John Healey has made it clear publicly and to staff, that he wants to encourage people with the guts and drive to start a business. One source said: "If you are taking on John's mantra about talking up Britain then you can't say, 'Nothing to see here'." Whatever else the chancellor brings to Parliament in his red box, do not expect him to arrive with all the solutions to the country's very well-documented problems, whether that's getting the economy growing more convincingly, sorting out gaps in defence cash, welfare, social care, or new ways to pay off the country's groaning debts more quickly. One former minister suggests even if Healey and Burnham had stumbled upon all the answers in a few months, it's just not possible to fix everything at the same time because of the constraints on the economy. They wondered: "Is he going to invest in growth? Is he going to put everything he has into the challenges people will face this winter? Is he going to throw it at defence? There is just not enough to tackle all these problems simultaneously - ministers are going to be exposed to the cold light of day." Burnham and Healey have to find a way of maintaining the balance in an unusually happy Labour Party. MPs talk of ministers and Burnham himself being more visible and approachable in Parliament, knocking around with colleagues in the evening, fewer "golden slips" doled out when ministers were excused from voting alongside colleagues so they could get on with their important jobs. One minister told me they'd had to tell their private office not to arrange for them to be "slipped" , from going to the Commons in the evening to see

title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
description: The full feasibility study will look in detail at how hosting the Games in northern England could work.
body: Team GB at the opening ceremony of the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris A £7m fund to explore how the Olympics could be brought to northern England will be announced in John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, the BBC has learned. The chancellor plans to allocate the money for a full feasibility study on the possibility for a bid for a "Northern Games". If successful, it could see the games held in the North in the 2040s. The last time the UK hosted the Olympics was London 2012. A UK Trade and Investment (UKTI) department report estimated in 2013 it boosted the economy by £9.9bn, although the amount was met with some scepticism. Olympians join mayors to back northern Olympic bid Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC: "Few things bring a country together quite like the Olympics. I want people to feel that sense of excitement again, and to experience it in their own towns and communities, not just watch it on the telly. "The Games would unlock opportunity across our towns and cities for the whole country. From north to south, it would be something everyone could get behind and be proud of. "We know we can put on the greatest show on earth. Now we want to explore how we can do it again, with the whole country behind it." In May the government asked UK Sport to carry out an initial assessment of the idea, looking at the possible cost and benefit of a bid to hold the Olympics across the North. The idea had been put forward by Northern Mayors and backed by a group of former Olympians including Dame Laura Kenny and Dame Sarah Storey. As part of next week's Budget the government will announce the next step - a "full feasibility study". Chancellor John Healey will present his first Budget on Wednesday The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work. It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit. Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost £8.9bn. A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a £9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments. But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR). The new feasability study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations. Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable. "Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost." News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport. "We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement. "Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements." title: Infantino tells BBC Sport he is backed by 'vast majority' of world football
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino laughs off questions about whether he considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.
body: This video can not be played Infantino laughs off resignation questions Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle. In a rare interview, he struck a defiant tone to BBC Sport about his own position in the wake of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and said it was not always easy to bring different points of view "under one roof". "There is nothing bad in disagreeing," he said. "We see it every day in so many countries in the world. It's OK to disagree. It's OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on." Two months ago, Infantino was facing mounting calls to stand down as president of the organisation he has led since 2016. The heads of European football's governing body Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception". Last week Uefa demanded that Fifa release all key documents relating to FFE by 2 November, with Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis saying that the organisation had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions". Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of competitions run by football's world governing body would have been sold to a private investment firm. Since the delivery of the letter, Infantino has been travelling the world, appearing in Morocco, the Dominican Republic, Cape Verde, and Japan, managing to shore up support to the point where his re-election as president for a fourth term next year now looks inevitable. He has also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn). During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries". But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE. He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE. Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it". "We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said. Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good". He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship. Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world. "I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view. "But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority. "I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football] countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world." He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run." The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed. Infantino re-election hopes boosted by Asia support after U-turn Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents Infantino arrived in Baku on Friday for the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival, which is being held in Azerbaijan and features teams from 189 member associations. England, Spain, France, Argentina and Brazil are all taking part. Russia have also sent a team, marking the country's first appearance in a Fifa-sanctioned tournament since the world governing body, and Uefa, suspended Russian teams from international competitions in February 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine. This tournament is only for boys, with next year's tournament being girls only, and then from 2028 Fifa's plan is to have boys and girls competing in the tournament annually. Matches are played in an 8v8 format, on smaller pitches and with 20-minute halves. "It's just beautiful to bring the world together at such a young age to create something like this," Infantino said. "When some of these boys participate in a World Cup 10 years, 20 years from now, they will all remember that their first World Cup was here." title: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany's recovery will take 'weeks' after collapse
description: Vincent Kompany remains stable in hospital as doctors run tests following his collapse on Friday, says Bayern Munich director Max Eberl.
body: Bayern Munich are joint top of the Bundesliga after four wins from their opening six games as Vincent Kompany attempts to lead them to a third consecutive title Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany needs "protecting from himself" and will take weeks to recover after collapsing at the club's training ground on Friday, said the club's director of sport Max Eberl. Former Manchester City and Belgium defender Kompany, 40, remains in a "stable" condition in hospital and "examinations were continuing". Eberl added that Bayern had considered asking for Sunday's Bundesliga game at Freiburg to be postponed, but believed the best tonic for Kompany would be to "play and be successful". "Vinnie will be given all the time he needs. We're not starting to put together any timeframes," said Eberl. "We need to firstly figure out what it is and then we'll discuss calmly what the recovery time is to be. We won't be talking about days, but weeks. We need to all be clear on that." Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing at training Rice scores late as Arsenal draw with Bayern Kane scores 150th Bayern goal in win over Elversberg Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train. He had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday for Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal. Kompany was on the touchline for Wednesday's match and Eberl questioned whether he "should have put the brakes on him earlier". "The fact is, we protect our coach wherever we can," he said. "If a coach says he feels ready to do something, then we're not going to say 'we won't allow that' if we don't know what's going on. "It's also everyone's own responsibility to say, 'I can't carry on now'. "Vinnie's a hard worker. If you don't listen to the subtle signals your body sends, eventually it will scream out in pain. "Vinnie will be given that time [now], and we'll continue to try, even more than before, to protect him from himself." Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups, before going into management with Burnley. After guiding them to the 2022-23 Championship title, Kompany was unable to keep the Clarets in the Premier League. He left to take over at Bayern in May 2024 and has led them to successive Bundesliga titles. Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks has spoken with the Bayern boss in hospital. "I explained to him that we would be having no football conversations," said Danks. "It was just checking in on his health and making sure he's OK. "All the football operations are in our hands and we'll work together as a team to keep the club moving forward." title: England thrash France to keep alive World Cup hopes
description: England beat France 82-0 to maintain their hopes of reaching the Men's Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.
body: Herbie Farnworth scored England's first World Cup hat-trick since Tommy Makinson against Papua New Guinea in 2022 Tries: Farnworth 3, Young 3, Lewis 2, Ashton, Williams, Radley, Litten, Welsby, Brimson Goals: Savala 13 After losing their opener, then watching Tonga and Samoa rack up huge victories, England knew only a massive win over France in Perth would keep alive their World Cup dreams. Mission accomplished: 82-0. But they still require a lot of work and a pinch of luck to reach the semi-finals. England needed this margin of victory following their 30-12 defeat by Tonga last Saturday. They must do the same against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on Friday - then hope Tonga beat Samoa next Sunday. After a nervy opening quarter, in which England looked weighed down by expectations and permutations, they finally got going with three tries in four first-half minutes. By half-time, England had six converted tries on the board including a Herbie Farnworth hat-trick. Come full time, Dom Young also bagged a treble and England had 14. Dom Young (centre) scored England's opening try after a scoreless first quarter After 23 minutes, England found their breakthrough as captain George Williams - overwhelmed by Tonga last week and initially nervy here - broke the line before a clever behind-the-back pass set up Young to score in the corner. England had, belatedly, arrived at this World Cup as a force to be reckoned with. Soon after, full-back AJ Brimson - whose direct runs pierced France time and again - led a breakaway before finding Matty Ashton. The wing had knocked on over the try line early on to spill a seemingly certain England opener, but made no mistake here for his seventh try in six Tests. Harry Smith spotted the gap before setting up Farnworth for his first try on 27 minutes. And after a period of defence against a France side - who threatened sporadically but made too many simple mistakes - Farnworth scored again nine minutes later. Williams powered over under the posts for 30-0, and then came England's best move of the World Cup just before the break - slick through the hands to the right before Young set Farnworth back in for his third. Eight minutes after the break, Young chased down a grubber kick to bring up 40 points - before Jez Litten and Williams cut through a tiring defence and Victor Radley scored unopposed. England needed to repel another French siege, before overpowering at the other end for Litten - who impressed as an interchange - to score. Another Brimson surge led the way for try number 10, scored by Mikey Lewis. A dreadful short kick-off was caught by Young, who raced through for his hat-trick. Jack Welsby got on the act for try 12, a third score in four minutes, as the French surrendered. The 13th try - scored by Lewis who broke through two weak tackles - ensured England surpassed Samoa's 74-point winning margin against the French. After a frustrating few minutes where they had to defend deep for their clean sheet, England finally reached 80 as Brimson scored a deserved try. Hugo Savala was also a key figure with superb kicking. He only missed one goal from 14 attempts, adding 26 points. England are far from perfect. They made six errors in the opening 20 minutes - and a better side than France, who haven't reached the semi-finals since 1992, would have taken advantage. But it all comes down to points on the scoreboard - and England must hope they have enough. After Samoa thrashed Papua New Guinea 62-6 earlier, England were a massive 150 behind the Samoans on points difference - which, if Tonga beat Samoa next weekend, would be the deciding factor between the teams as to who reaches the semis. A hefty win here helps the English cause, but they still need work and luck to avoid missing the World Cup last four for the first time ever. There was a moment in this game where AJ Brimson had just crashed through two would-be tacklers and completely split France wide open, and his England team mate Max King gave him a look of admiration. This was a full-back doing the hard yards for his team - and the paceman appreciated it. His fingerprints were all over this win. The little man was a menace throughout with ball in hand and defused much of France's threat at the other end. His yardage was immense, line breaks frequent and finishing touches to release team-mates crucial, and he even grabbed a score of his own. The standard has been set and Brimson a big part of it. title: Charity expects demand for Christmas present campaign
description: The campaign, run by Little Stars, is running from today until 4 December.
body: The Santa's Little Stars campaign started in 2020 A Shropshire charity has said it expects demand to be high this year for its campaign which provides Christmas presents to struggling families. Little Stars, which gives away free essentials to families in need, has launched Santa's Little Stars, which runs from Saturday 24 October to Friday 4 December. The public is asked to donate new, unwrapped toys and gifts to donation points in Shrewsbury's Darwin shopping centre. Donations are wrapped and given to children from birth to age 17, as well as pregnant women who are referred to the charity. Little Stars said 2025 was its biggest campaign year to date, and it expected demand to continue to be high due to many families continuing to face financial pressures. The charity launched Santa's Little Stars in 2020 and has given out more than 8,000 presents in that time, supporting more than 2,100 children. It added that donations could be taken to collection points outside the Collective, The Entertainer, Home Bargains and Clarks Shoes. title: Mum dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea
description: The children were subsequently rescued from the water, police say.
body: The two children were rescued from the water, police in the Bahamas said A woman has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas. The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday. The force said they believed the woman - believed to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away. In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water. In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock. "Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life. "Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away. "In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away. "She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. "Foul play is not suspected at this time. "An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death." A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas. "We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family." title: Seven missing after multi-storey building collapses in Kenya's capital
description: Rescue efforts are under way to find people trapped under the block, which was still under construction when it buckled.
body: A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi. Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets. Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building. The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya. The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors. Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening. Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath. Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed Rescue efforts have been complicated by concerns that excavation using diggers could limit the supply of air to those trapped, prompting emergency responders to cease using them, according to the Daily Nation newspaper. Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations. Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday. Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied. He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards". Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors. title: Three released without charge after fatal arson attack in Ireland
description: Three people - two women and one man - have been released, and one person remains in custody, gardaí say.
body: Flowers have been left at the home where four people died after an arson attack in Waterford Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaí (Irish police) have said. Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month. A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack. On Saturday, gardaí said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge. A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody. title: No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning
description: A 2-0 series defeat for the Red Roses, their record 39-match winning streak and 41-match unbeaten run ended, and consecutive losses for the first time since 2016 - England are not invincible.
body: This video can not be played Back-to-back losses for Red Roses against Canada Before England's three-match series against Canada, few would have predicted this outcome. A 2-0 series defeat for the Red Roses; their record 39-match winning streak and 41-match unbeaten run – stretching back nearly four years – ended; and consecutive losses for the first time since 2016. Over the past 13 months, Canada have turned a 33-13 defeat in the World Cup final into a statement 31-22 win in Ottawa. And three years out from the 2029 World Cup, they have laid down an early marker of their title credentials. More than that, they have proved England are not invincible – a reality which should hearten New Zealand and perennial Women's Six Nations bridesmaids France because both have beaten giant-killers Canada in the past 12 months. For the second time in eight days, England captain Meg Jones has been called upon to take stock of a defeat. Once again, she opted for a message of defiance. "It was a hell of a contest. We're not broken, we just need to grow," said Jones. "Do it together, use the lessons. We're playing the best teams, getting the best punches thrown at us. "I genuinely believe we've got the best players in the world. When we're firing, generally we're unstoppable. We don't dwell on the past, we're not anxious about the future, we're focused on the present." Canada inflict back-to-back losses on England How have Canada closed gap to world champions England? It's true, this is far from panic stations. In 2016, England were the defending world champions when they lost to France and beaten finalists Canada. Since then, they've been imperious, winning a second World Cup, reaching the final in 2017 and 2022, and lifting nine of the past 10 Six Nations titles. This is only their third defeat in 74 matches, so perspective is required. But England's performances throughout the WXV Global Series highlighted areas for improvement. They have lacked their usual clinical edge in attack. In Ottawa, Sarah Bern was held up over the line and England conceded a turnover less than five metres out as they failed to make their dominance pay before the break. Tellingly, they opted to kick a penalty early in the second half to close the deficit – perhaps a lesson learned from last month's 26-26 draw in Exeter, where they turned down a shot at goal to snatch the win in the dying moments. In defence, they have conceded 18 tries across their past five matches in the WXV, compared to eight in six at the World Cup. They have trailed at the break three times, something they hadn't experienced since 2020. Last week, ill-discipline repeatedly gifted Canada field position before a late handling error, which put a clearing kick under pressure, opened the door for the hosts' winning try. On Friday night, Gabrielle Senft picked off a bouncing ball from a missed pass to set up Canada's second try. Minutes later, England were lucky not to concede a similar try when a pass bisected Jess Breach and Jones, who pounced on the ball just before Lizzie Gibson got to it. "We were riding the waves, building phases, scrum, set piece, we were very strong. Sometimes it's the bounce of the ball or it doesn't swing your way. We couldn't execute when we got in their 22, that's a big one to reflect on for sure," said Jones. Six Canadians started the PWR final for champions Saracens in July Canada does not have a professional women's domestic league and their players had to launch a crowd-funding campaign before the last World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps. It's unsurprising, therefore, that many of Canada's top talents play domestically in England's Premiership Women's Rugby, which offers a level of training and match experience they cannot find elsewhere. Twenty-five Canadian players are contracted for the 2026-27 season, with 11 featuring in July's PWR final between Saracens and Trailfinders. Three Canadian coaches, including head coach Kevin Rouet at Saracens, are also involved in English domestic rugby. PWR squads must have a minimum of 13 England qualified players in a matchday squad. But England head coach John Mitchell has warned that too many overseas players in the PWR could be detrimental for future Red Roses sides. "I think it's necessary to make sure that young English girls are getting enough PWR time," Mitchell said. "It's a critical pathway because Sevens is definitely gone. For players aged between 19 and 23, it's critical. "We're just going to make sure we don't erode our depth as a result of [overseas involvement]. It's not so much about now. It will be the future that will suffer if we're not smart in that area." Mitchell has been forced to call upon England's squad depth on multiple occasions in 2026 with Abby Dow and Emily Scarratt retiring after the World Cup, four players absent through pregnancy, and several big names – including Hannah Botterman, Alex Matthews, and Amy Cokayne – spending time on the sidelines because of injury. He's handed out more than half a dozen debuts this year, with hooker Bryony Field particularly impressing during September's home internationals, played the likes of Abi Burton and Ellie Kildunne out of position, and brought Liz Crake back into the fold after several years away. title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
description: Around 200 emergency personnel are deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
body: The Eagle's Nest was still on fire early on Saturday Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest. Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames. Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries. The Nazi dictator used the retreat, which lies above the town of Berchtesgaden, as a part-time seat of government and met commanders there to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941. Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature. A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire. The Eagle's Nest (file photo) Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945. Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn. It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website, external. During World War Two, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death. There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler. While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists. In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site. Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war. And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station. title: Smith v Puello world title fight predictions
description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's light-welterweight title fight between WBC champion Dalton Smith and Alberto Puello.
body: WBC light-welterweight champion Dalton Smith (left) has won all 19 pro fights with 14 stoppages Dalton Smith will make the first defence of his WBC light-welterweight title on home soil when he faces former champion Alberto Puello in Sheffield on Saturday. Unbeaten Smith, 29, returns to the ring for the first time since becoming world champion with a stunning knockout of Subriel Matias in New York in January. Dominican Republic fighter Puello, 32, is aiming to become a three-time world champion, having lost his WBC belt to Matias on points last year. Smith will have the backing of his home crowd at the Utilita Arena. Can he keep his dream of fighting at Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough stadium alive with another win? Or will the tricky and experienced southpaw Puello, who has lost just once in 26 professional fights, ruin the homecoming? BBC Sport spoke to figures from across the boxing world to get their predictions on who will come out on top. Smith v Puello - all you need to know How world champion Smith can become a mainstream star "I think it's going to be a great fight, I think there will be a lot of close rounds, but I'm going for a majority decision win for Smith in a really tough fight." "What a brilliant fight this is. It's such a terrific match-up with contrasting styles. You have a slick southpaw in Puello and the tough, rugged, well-schooled Smith. Puello being a southpaw will suit Dalton who throws a fantastic right hand. "This is fine margins - high-level chess. I think Dalton will come through via decision, or perhaps a late stoppage, and he will have produced two back-to-back victories to cement his place in the top 15 pound-for-pound rankings." "I think this will be an interesting fight. Both guys have a similar sort of style. Puello is a boxer-puncher who goes really well to the body. He throws that loopy left hand shot quite well that Dalton will have to be quite careful of. "It will be cagey at the start and I think Puello will fall behind a little bit. Dalton is a better boxer than him and better at his game. Puello will then have to come forward and I think that will suit Dalton. "So I see Dalton winning quite a wide points decision." "It's a good fight and I think Puello is a good fighter but I'm Team Smith. He boxes well and his style has matured. Puello has fast hands and is good in close but Smith can find a way to beat him. If he knocks him out then it's a big statement, but I'll go for a Smith win on points." "This is a harder fight for Smith than Matias. Matias was a monster, while Puello is a clever boxer who sits on the back foot and punches nice and long. He's southpaw which makes it awkward to adjust your feet and stance. "Ultimately, I think the angles of attack will be the difference for Smith. I think it might be a bit of a frustrating night for him but I think he comes out on top on points. "It will be relatively entertaining - not as exciting as the win over Matias, perhaps - but a good homecoming for the champion." "I'm backing Dalton, he's been my guy since we were 12 years old. He was my roomate at every tournament and now is his time as WBC world champion." "I'm backing Dalton Smith to beat Alberto Puello and retain his world title. Smith's power, accuracy and impressive stoppage win over Subriel Matias make him a dangerous opponent. "Although Puello's experience and awkward southpaw style could make it a tough fight, I think Smith's power and work-rate will prove too much. Smith to win by unanimous decision." "Puello can be awkward and disrupt rhythm as he did in wins over guys like now WBA champion Gary Antuanne Russell, but Dalton's a big light-welterweight and his boxing is on point as well as intelligent decision-making. "His stoppage win over Subriel Matias was impressive but I see Dalton winning this one on points. Puello will complicate things in some moments, but Smith wins a comfortable decision." "It's a big fight. I think the Utilita Arena - pound-for-pound - is the noisiest venue in the country. To use a football analogy, I think it will have to be a 12th man for Dalton. "I think he's up against it. Puello is a very special talent, as is Dalton who put on a performance of a lifetime in January. "Dalton has a lot of the advantages but Puello comes here with experience at the highest level at this division. He wants the belt back, which he thinks was robbed from him in his loss to Matias. "I do edge towards the current champion because of home advantage, but I wouldn't be shocked if Puello walks away with the belt." "Dalton is a real hero in Sheffield but Puello is very dangerous. He's a southpaw and a former two-time world champion. "It's a very tough first defence but Dalton has home advantage, the age and the unbeaten record. He probably has plans A, B, C and D. He's a very clever boxer whose background has been perfect - an excellent amateur and a solid professional." "I expect him to come through a very tough test." "I think Dalton will stop him late on - round nine or 10. Dalton is just too good for Puello, he'll try to put pressure on but Dalton will just have his number." "Dalton will have a little bit too much speed and a little bit too much flair. The one thing that Dalton has to watch out for is he cannot afford to slow it down to Puello's pace. He's decent with his jab, he likes his opponent to stand in front, he doesn't like it when they move. "If Dalton is in and out with his feet, plays it tricky, he'll be able to beat him fairly comfortably as long as he doesn't stand and trade." "I've got Dalton winning on points. I think it will be a competitive fight but Dalton will edge it."
