title: The convicted £33m tax fraudster evading justice and living it up in Dubai
description: Arif Patel "should not be beyond the reach of the justice system," says the PM’s anti-corruption champion.
body: Arif Patel, who masterminded a massive VAT carousel fraud, remains on the run One of the UK's most prolific fraudsters, described by a judge as a "breathtakingly arrogant" and "totally dishonest" man, remains on the run in Dubai after stealing more than £33m of public money. Arif Patel, from Preston in Lancashire, was exposed following a complex investigation spanning years, led by His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), which established that he had tried to steal as much as £90m. Patel, who skipped the UK in 2011 never to return, was eventually convicted in his absence and in 2023 was handed a 20-year prison sentence. BBC File on 4 Investigates has been on the trail of the man who stole from all of us - and seemingly got away with it. The fugitive fraudster who stole from you "Al Capone was brought down by the taxman. This is the same situation and 20 years was more than a satisfying result," said Rod Stone, a veteran investigator of large-scale tax fraud, of Patel's conviction and custodial sentence. The judge at Patel's sentencing hearing described him as the leader of a "fraternal organised crime group" with his brothers Munaf and Faisal who were "truly high-level criminals". The fact that Arif Patel has not served a single day of his 20-year prison sentence clearly rankles with Stone. For him and the dozens of others who were involved in bringing Patel down, there remains a strong sense that justice has only been served on paper. Former HMRC assistant director Rod Stone specialised in the detection of fraud and organised crime In the early part of the millennium, Arif Patel appeared to be a businessman very much on the up. His company, Faisaltex, headquartered in his home city of Preston, was known for manufacturing textiles, such as socks and nighties, which it supplied to retailers. Patel was a fixture in the Sunday Times Rich List with his wealth in 2006 estimated to be £105m. He was also investing heavily in property across the city and beyond. In 2007, his teenage son bought a minority stake in Preston North End Football Club. There was even a plan to build a £100m, 19-storey tower block - complete with botanical gardens and restaurant - in the centre of the city. Behind the facade, though, something very different was going on. In the early 2000s, organised crime groups had turned to large-scale attacks on the tax system through what became known as carousel fraud. Chains of fake business transactions are created as a way of stealing VAT repayments from HMRC. Goods move between different companies, into and out of the country, to generate false tax refunds. The same shipments of goods are often moved around repeatedly, hence the name carousel fraud. This type of fraud was costing taxpayers billions of pounds a year and experts like Stone were at the vanguard of the fightback. This is how Patel's textiles empire appeared on his radar. "When we started to look at them we did notice some very strange shipments of goods - a container load of hats to Switzerland seemed odd because they were actually Swiss hats," he said. The fake clothes the gang were selling would have been worth up to £50m had they have been genuine Most carousel fraudsters dealt in high-value, high-volume items like mobile phones or computer chips, for which investigators were on the lookout. But Patel's enterprise had predominantly been dealing in textiles, making the scam harder to spot. The team of investigators discovered Patel had successfully stolen more than £33m of taxpayers' money before HMRC cottoned on to what he was doing. In total, he tried to steal more than £90m of public money - the rest of the payments were stopped. Teams of investigators spent years working through vast chains of transactions until they were ready to make their move. Patel was charged with a range of offences including conspiracies to cheat the taxman, money-laundering, false accounting and selling counterfeit goods. But when he appeared at Bolton Crown Court in 2011, Patel asked the judge for permission to travel to Dubai on bail. The judge agreed to this request and Patel left the UK, never to return. In Dubai, he joined his brothers Munaf and Faisal, who had already left the country before they could be charged for their part in the conspiracy. Over the next three years, 24 members of Patel's gang were convicted. Collectively, they were jailed for more than 116 years. A judge ordered Patel's Ferrari Superamerica to be auctioned off Efforts to have Arif Patel extradited back to the UK failed and he remained a free man in Dubai. The BBC has heard claims he had been actively seeking to strike a deal with the UK authorities to settle the case against him. "In my opinion, he thought he was above justice," said Graham Honey, another former HMRC investigator. In 2020, he was working in the private sector when he said he was approached by Patel's representatives. Honey said he was asked to open up a channel of communication with HMRC and the Crown Prosecution Service because Patel wanted to make a deal. It soon became clear, however, that there would be a sticking point. "It started to become apparent to me that Patel was not willing to come back," said Honey. "He just thought he could get an agreement, pay some money, and this would all go away." Honey claimed that while Patel was willing to admit his guilt and repay money, he was not prepared to face a criminal trial or the prospect of time behind bars. He claimed it was not the first time that Patel had attempted to strike such a deal. Honey said: "One of the officers told me that he had said 'I'm a tiger, not a caged tiger' meaning he was a big man, he'd done what he'd done, but in essence, he wasn't prepared to go to prison for it." HMRC said it had seized more than £78m of the gang's UK assets In 2023, Patel's trial got under way without him, something which is highly unusual and only

title: Project to restore rare native trees with DNA testing
description: Conservation groups say black poplars are endangered due to felling, land drainage and habitat loss.
body: Conservation groups say England's black poplar trees are on the verge of extinction A project is aiming to help restore one of the UK's rare native trees across the Thames Valley using DNA testing. Conservation groups have warned numbers of black poplar trees have fallen due to decades of felling, land drainage and habitat loss. The Swindon to Oxford: Regenerating the Thames and Tributaries nature recovery programme is working with local conservation groups to regenerate the population along the River Thames and its flood plain. Catrina Bass, from the Long Mead Foundation in Swindon, is involved in the project and said while the trees were "extraordinary survivors", there were just 50 recorded in Oxfordshire currently. Describing black poplars as "Lord of the Rings" looking trees with "great gnarled trunks", she said they support other wildlife, including the poplar hornet moth. The project secured initial funding from West Oxfordshire District Council and the Vale of White Horse Council but is now aiming to raise £20,000 for the work, which involves DNA analysis of existing trees, propagating new cuttings and planting them in suitable sites. Oxfordshire County Council's Local Nature Recovery Strategy has committed to match fund the fundraiser up to £10,000. Also involved in the project is the Trust for Oxfordshire's Environment, which works with community groups to fund local environmental projects. Chief executive Benjamin Heaven Taylor said black poplars play an important role in reducing flood risk, by lining rivers and floodplains, holding water back. He said the population that remained was "extremely fragmented", adding that it "needs a helping hand to recover". title: Historic swimming pond to be restored
description: Specialists are looking at how to clear the Cornwall bath house pond and understand the tidal inlet.
body: The aim is to create "a welcoming community resource" Plans have been made for a historic swimming pond to be restored. A new partnership between the Carew Pole Garden Trust, Torpoint Artists Collective and Rooted Futures said it was "taking the first steps" towards restoring a historic bath house swimming pond on the Antony Estate, in Cornwall, funded through the National Lottery Community Fund. It said it hoped it would bring it into community use and improve access to nature. In a joint statement, the partners said specialists at the garden trust had started to look at how the bath house pond "could be cleared, identify tree maintenance needs and better understand the tidal inlet and the movement of water through the site". More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall The bath pond and bathing house were built in the late 18th Century after being designed by Thomas Parlby. Reginald Pole Carew, who had inherited Antony, wanted somewhere to swim in the stretch of woodland on the bank of the tidal River Lynher. Sir Tremayne Carew Pole, who currently resides on the estate, said, when it was first built, it was used to swim in and the bath house, where the ladies would swim, had a sunken pool fed by the pond. He said, over the years, it started to be used as a decorative pond for the garden as surrounding trees shed leaves into the pond and humus (soil organic matter) and mud formed at the bottom, making it not a great place to swim. "I've always wanted to restore it to be swimmable and to share the benefits with those in the local community," he said. In the statement, the organisations said this would help shape the next steps of restoration and it aimed to "create a welcoming community resource where people can connect with green and blue space, discover the natural environment and contribute to the long-term care of a valued local landscape". It added "education, creativity and community participation" would be central to the project. It said Torpoint Artists Collective would develop a programme of artist-led workshops including wildlife recording, photography and nature journalling. Open-water swimmers, nature lovers and anyone interested in the pond's future have been invited to share feedback and volunteer by emailing Antony Woodland Garden. The partners said a Friends of the Pond group would be set up to "help shape the next steps, bringing together local knowledge, practical skills and ideas for the site's long-term care and use". title: Why Tottenham v Arsenal could define their seasons - live on BBC One
description: With Tottenham stuttering and Arsenal floundering, these fierce rivals both need a victory in Saturday's showdown, live on BBC One.
body: Arsenal's Alessia Russo has scored more goals against Tottenham than any other opponent - but has only one league goal so far in 2026-27 Arsenal have scored five goals in six Women's Super League (WSL) games this season - the joint-second lowest tally in the division. They might well be grateful, then, to be facing a team on Saturday that have conceded 12 goals in their past two matches. It just so happens that team is fierce rivals Tottenham. But Spurs have their own fires to fight, given their decent start to the WSL campaign has gone up in flames. This is a north London derby that could define both teams' seasons. Saturday, 24 October, 12:45 BST Since Renee Slegers was appointed initially as interim head coach in October 2024, her WSL win percentage of 65.2% is bettered only by Chelsea (76%) and Manchester City (73.1%) The first six games have been galling for under-pressure Arsenal boss Renee Slegers, particularly given pre-season talk of a serious title push. The facts do not make for pleasant reading for Arsenal and their fans: No victory since the opening day at Brighton Toothless home draws with promoted Birmingham and Crystal Palace Defeats at pre-season title rivals Chelsea and Manchester City mean they are nine points off Champions League qualification Eighth in the table on the same tally as West Ham, Aston Villa and Palace That said, on one level Slegers can feel hard done by. After all, Arsenal have hit the woodwork more times than anyone else (five), had the joint-most touches in the opposition box (283) and created the third-highest number of chances (93). However, their shot conversion rate of 5.9% is comfortably the worst in the division, with leaders Manchester City's at 16.7%. The statistic is more staggering given the quality they possess in Alessia Russo, Stina Blackstenius and Olivia Smith among others. "You can't question the commitment of the players, but they are trying to walk it in," England's record goalscorer Ellen White told the BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast. "They are creating opportunities but look a little lost, a bit desperate. "It's going to be a very uncomfortable day. I don't think a draw is enough." Slegers has been searching for solutions to the lack of goals, retaining the same front four in her starting XI just once in all competitions She has made more substitutions than any other manager too, including using her full complement of five in all but one match. But to little avail. Where to use last season's top scorer Russo is a conundrum, given she has yet to ignite either as a central striker or in the number 10 role. Losing team heartbeat Mariona Caldentey for up to 10 weeks with a hamstring issue has been another disruption. "We all know they have the individual quality, but for whatever reason it's not clicking," said former England captain Steph Houghton. This video can not be played 'Even more pressure on Arsenal in North London Derby' In some respects, Tottenham are perfect opponents for Arsenal. While Martin Ho has helped Spurs ascend the table since his arrival at the start of last season, they still only have one win in 13 WSL matches against the Gunners - although they did hold them to a goalless draw at home last season. Ten points from their opening four games with just two goals conceded was a terrific start to 2026-27, but 6-1 and 6-2 defeats by London City Lionesses and Chelsea respectively have provided a thumping reality check. Even though Spurs flirted with the top three for much of last season, Ho believes his side are not ready for that step. "We're not at that level yet. People don't like to hear it but it's the honest truth," he said. "We need to understand and accept that because if we don't, we're putting unrealistic expectations on ourselves." Prior to those losses, it was looking promising at Tottenham, who have picked up their own share of big wins against Crystal Palace (7-0) and Aston Villa (4-0) and demonstrated the clinical edge so lacking in their north London neighbours. Attackers Signe Gaupset, Olivia Holdt and Kirsty Hanson have all scored two or more in the WSL already this season while five-goal Victoria Pelova has been the standout player. Given she arrived in the summer from Tottenham's north London rivals - and has scored as many by herself as the entire Arsenal team - she will have her own motivation to pile more misery onto her former employers. "I didn't get a lot of minutes last year with Arsenal," Pelova told BBC Sport. "I get more freedom here and I feel full trust from my team-mates and the staff. "We have to beat them." Denmark playmaker Holdt, who scored a hat-trick against Crystal Palace in September, told BBC Radio 5 Live Drive that hosting the derby at the men's stadium could be an advantage. "It's amazing we have the possibility to play there," she said. "We'll feel it in the game with all the fans supporting us and not Arsenal. "It's an opportunity for us to play some good football." At this early stage, Manchester City, Chelsea and London City have put daylight between themselves and the rest. That leaves both Spurs and Arsenal needing wins to realistically stand any chance of overhauling them in the race for Champions League football next season - starting at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday. title: Parents call for tougher measures in schools to tackle allergies
description: At present, the onus is mainly on parents and individual schools to ensure safety measures for pupils are in place.
body: Stephanie Kerr is one of a number of parents calling for new mandatory measures For Stephanie Kerr's five-year-old son Caolán many foods come with a serious risk. "Caolan's allergic to milk, egg, wheat, oat, cumin, tuna, strawberry," she said. "We have a running joke that it would be quicker listing what he's not allergic to so that's just some of them." Kerr is one of a number of parents calling for new mandatory measures in schools to keep pupils like Caolán safe. In England, Benedict's law came into force in September, requiring all schools to follow strengthened allergy guidelines including training for staff and storing equipment like life-saving allergy pens. It was named after Benedict Blythe, who died aged five after accidental exposure to cow's milk protein while at Barnack Primary School, near Peterborough, in December 2021. The Education Minister, Paul Givan, has committed to a consultation on a similar change in Northern Ireland to introduce stronger allergy guidance for Northern Ireland schools. At present though, the onus is mainly on parents and individual schools to ensure safety measures for pupils are in place. Stephanie Kerr was one of several parents and experts in Regent House School in Newtownards on Friday training teachers about safety for pupils with severe allergies. And that meant confronting some fears. "I find it difficult as well sometimes talking about the reactions that Caolan has had in the past and what could potentially happen in the future," she said. But she was not alone. Niamh Kennedy's three children have allergies Niamh Kennedy has three children who have food allergies and she is the chair of Food Allergy NI, the voluntary group who organised the training. "Our eldest is the most severe. He's had anaphylaxis in the past," she said. "We're very reliant here at the moment on goodwill, individual school policies and individual awareness so it's very much left to up to the school to initiate and to design what works for them. "But the problem with that is that there's huge variation." She estimates that about two children in every class could have a food allergy and said that, aside from school canteens and packed lunches, risks could lurk in expected places. "One of the things that we experience as a campaigning group is that most people understand that food allergies need to be considered at mealtimes, but it can be the other moments in the day that can sort of be underestimated," she said. "Things like making cakes or buns or using crafts. "There can be quite a lot of allergens in some of the craft materials, there can be allergens in simple things like hand soaps. "This is a potentially life-threatening medical condition." Tracey Dunn said some of the most common foods that can trigger anaphylaxis are milk, fish and eggs That point was reinforced by Tracey Dunn, from the Allergy UK incorporating Anaphylaxis UK organisation, who also spoke to teachers at Regent House School. "Anaphylaxis is the most serious form of an allergic reaction that can be fatal," she said. "During anaphylaxis the airways are closing and blood pressure is dropping and that leads a person to have symptoms where they are unable to breathe or have noisy breathing or they develop a persistent cough where their voice changes. "But they can also have, related to the blood pressure, circulatory difficulties where they feel cold, pale clammy or they may feel faint, dizzy." While most people may be aware of nut allergies or the risk of shock from insect stings, other common foods can also pose a risk to some people. "Some of the most common foods that can trigger anaphylaxis are things like milk and fish and eggs," Dunn said. The consultation on changes to how pupils with severe allergies are supported in schools in Northern Ireland is due to take place before the end of 2026. title: The people on standby when a storm strikes
description: While most people are preparing to stay indoors as another storm approaches, others are getting ready to head straight into it.
body: Tree surgeon Callum Kirk said preparing for severe weather involves checking and sharpening equipment While most people are preparing to stay indoors as another storm approaches, others are getting ready to head straight into it. Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and disruption to parts of Northern Ireland this weekend. For those tasked with keeping people safe and dealing with the damage, severe weather can bring long hours, dangerous conditions and calls for help at any moment. In preparation for the storm, the Department for Infrastructure said their teams have been checking and clearing road gullies, monitoring river levels and tidal surges, and deploying a portion of temporary flood defences. "Regional Community Resilience Groups have also been advised of weather patterns and to make appropriate preparations," a spokesperson said. From rescue volunteers to tradespeople, being on standby means preparing for situations they cannot always predict. With equipment checked and vehicles ready, they are prepared to respond whenever their help is needed. The Belfast area commander for the Community Rescue Service said: "Don't underestimate the weather" Darren Harper is the Belfast area commander for the Community Rescue Service, whose volunteers are preparing to respond to emergencies. He said severe weather can bring heavy rainfall, rising water levels and flooding, with volunteers placed on standby to respond if needed. "Our main concern is the safety of the public," he said. Harper explained that preparations involve checking vehicles and equipment to ensure volunteers are ready for any call out. "Being on standby, our volunteers are ready to mobilise at a short notice," he said. "They're checking over vehicles, checking over equipment and they're ready to assist their partner agencies and emergency services as and when the call comes." He said the risks associated with severe weather should not be underestimated, particularly around rivers and areas prone to flooding. "Take weather warnings seriously, avoid flooded roads and paths. Stay away from swollen rivers and never put yourself at risk by entering any flood water," he said. "Don't underestimate the weather - and stay away from riverbanks," he added. Harper said taking simple precautions could prevent people from getting into dangerous situations. Charles Howard advised homeowners to inspect their roofs before and after storms, particularly for loose or damaged tiles For roofer Charles Howard, storms can bring an overwhelming number of calls from people needing emergency repairs. "Normally years ago you would have loved the storms, because obviously you got the influx of work," he said. "But now because the storms are so regular, I kind of hate it." During a storm early last year, Howard said he received about 800 messages from people seeking help. "It's hard to actually keep control of it," he said. He explained that preparing for particularly bad weather usually involves stocking his van with spare roof tiles and clearing his schedule to deal with emergency calls. "If it's going to be a bad, bad storm, you just pretty much go and load the van up with all the salvage tiles and stuff like that," he said. He said his work can begin even before the worst of a storm arrives, with strong winds already causing damage to roofs, advising homeowners to inspect their homes before and after storms, particularly for loose or damaged tiles. He added that dislodged ridge tiles can fall onto driveways and gardens, potentially damaging vehicles. Tree surgeon Callum Kirk, who works in the Newtownabbey area and covers much of Belfast, said storms bring a different kind of working day. Instead of scheduled jobs, he must be prepared to respond to fallen trees and potentially dangerous situations. "Whenever there's a storm, we have to be on standby for any trees that could come down over someone's driveway or their property," he said. He said preparing for severe weather involves checking and sharpening equipment, even when there is no guarantee of being called out. "You haven't got planned work, you don't know, it's sort of a surprise, you're just more or less going to help people," he said. Kirk explained that much of his work comes after the worst of the weather has passed, when fallen trees need to be removed from roofs, garages and other properties. He said that work can be particularly hazardous. "If you see a tree that looks like it's going to fall, get in contact with someone before it's too late." He encouraged homeowners to keep an eye on potentially unstable trees throughout the year, particularly as the storm season approaches. title: Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief tells BBC
description: Greg Bovino was the public face of the controversial immigration enforcement operation in the city earlier this year.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Trump's ex-border patrol chief challenged over Minneapolis operation The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration. Greg Bovino also told the BBC that he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time". Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January. The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. US President Donald Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city. Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters. One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence". Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter". A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless". This video can not be played Watch: Renee Good's partner speaks publicly for first time since her death Speaking in Detroit, where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill". He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens". Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against". Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents. "The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said. Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake". The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan. When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that." Bovino recently addressed a rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed Kristi Noem, who was Homeland Security secretary at the time of the operation, was fired by Trump in March. Bovino has since retired from the US border patrol. He has become known for his hardline stance on immigration, often going further in his statements than Trump's own officials and claiming without evidence that 100 million people are illegally in the US and should be deported. He has called for "total spectrum immigration enforcement" with support from the US military involving "cruise ships packed to the gills, cars, planes, trains, automobiles, all headed out of the United States packed with illegal aliens". Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials The ICE raids are over, but some Minnesotans say they still live in fear Analysing the Minneapolis shooting frame by frame Newly released video undermines ICE account of Minneapolis migrant shooting When asked about Bovino's comments about Minneapolis, a White House spokesperson said "the president has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history". "He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," they said. Bovino has also floated "exploring" a presidential run in 2028. "If politicians aren't going to step up and do their job then you might see something happen," he told the BBC when asked about his intentions. Bovino recently addressed a far-right rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Abdul El-Sayed, a US citizen and Democratic candidate running in the state's tightly fought race for a Senate seat. American-born Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate if he wins the seat against Republican Mike Rogers. title: How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race
description: Calls for change present a challenge to President Lula in the second round of the election on Sunday.
body: A student at a rally for President Lula da Silva In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley." The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president. Like many of Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried. He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up. "We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers. "Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built." The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies. Tairine says high prices are a problem for her "He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022. Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new. One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco. Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine. Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again. Flávio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes. For his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president. But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments. "There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered. Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro Richard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio's father and Brazil's president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil. But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success." Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the UN's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" in which people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high. Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him. But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending. "Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says. In some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998. In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people – particularly students – on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in São Paulo attracted about a million people. "A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things." Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times. The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral. Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail. title: Met investigates reports of letter detailing claims about Meghan's father
description: Scotland Yard opens an inquiry after the Duchess of Sussex said she was sent a letter containing "disturbing allegations".
body: Meghan says she was informed of allegations about her father in a letter in 2018 The Metropolitan Police says it is investigating reports that a letter was sent to one of its specialist units in 2018 containing allegations about Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex. Meghan released a statement saying that a letter was sent to the force containing "disturbing allegations" about the behaviour of her estranged father, and subsequently shared with her. On Friday, it was reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle, 82, were found in his former home in the Philippines. The Sun newspaper, which first carried the claims, external, later said that the letter made direct allegations of child sex abuse against him. UK police are not investigating Thomas Markle, who is based in the US and strenuously denies the allegations made against him. Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018 Instead, Scotland Yard has opened an inquiry to confirm the claim that the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess eight years ago. According to the Sun, the letter was sent to a Met Police unit tasked with dealing with individuals posing a threat to Royals and politicians - the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre. A Met spokesperson said: "We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018. "We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this." Thomas Markle moved to the Philippines in 2025 after a series of strokes. He is reportedly now living in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again, after having a leg amputated during surgery in December 2025. In her statement on Friday, Meghan said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father in 2018, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated". Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun that he had allegedly found child abuse images at his father's home in the Philippines and reported it to the police. The Undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC that "the matter is currently being investigated" by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force in Cebu. Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately told the BBC that national police had secured Thomas Markle Snr's computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Investigators there are currently analysing the data to determine the full scope and extent of his alleged criminal activities, with the minister saying it would take one week to get the forensic results. The US Federal Bureau of Investigations said it was "aware of the allegations", adding it would "provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities". The FBI's statement continued: "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law." Meghan is the only child of Thomas Markle's marriage to her mother, Doria Ragland, but he has two other children - Samantha and Thomas Markle Jr - from an earlier marriage. The relationship between Meghan and her father, a former TV lighting director, broke down in the run-up to her wedding in 2018. At the time, Thomas Markle was found to have colluded with photographers, accepting payment to stage photographs of him preparing for the wedding. It is understood that Meghan first learnt about the allegations against her father shortly after she married the Duke of Sussex Prince Harry. Sources close to the Sussexes said Meghan could not speak publicly about the allegations when she first learned of them, in order to avoid jeopardising any future investigation. Speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her, the sources said. Undated image shows Thomas Markle with Meghan Markle In her statement released on Friday, Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children". This was "to protect them", Meghan said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families". "I am deeply distressed", she said. "My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed". She described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children". The BBC has contacted Thomas Markle for additional comment. title: Tory activist in 'contract killing broker' claim had worked for party HQ
description: Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.
body: Jack Ross (pictured) held the post of Chief Operations Officer at Turning Point UK, an offshoot of the US organisation A former Tory activist who appeared to offer to "broker" the hiring of contract killers in an undercover film report previously worked for Conservative headquarters. Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told. It comes after Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch referred to them as "shocking allegations", adding that she did not "believe that person is a member anymore". A Conservative spokesman said Ross's party membership had "been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". It has reported that Ross said his words were not meant to be taken seriously. Ross was paid to provide social media advice to the party for a brief period, the BBC has been told. He was never an employee or Conservative Campaign Headquarters pass holder. However, he met Badenoch on several occasions as part of his role as chief executive of Turning Point UK, an offshoot of a right-wing American organisation. Ross has also met several other right-wing politicians including the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader. In undercover filming broadcast this week by Al Jazeera, Ross appears to offer to "broker" the services of contract killers. The Al Jazeera report said its undercover journalist approached Ross in 2022 with a fictitious situation of a family business at risk of being taken over by a criminal gang. Ross is alleged to have asked the undercover reporter what was needed from him, and listed violent options that could be bought including stabbing, shooting and killing. Al Jazeera said Ross denied the finding "completely" and claimed everything he said to the reporter was not meant seriously. Turning Point UK has been approached for comment. title: Second storm to hit UK with more wind and rain as thousands remain without power
description: An amber weather warning has been issued for much of Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and northern England, as Storm Boelo approaches.
body: Rough sea along the Dorset coastline on Friday A second storm in as many days is set to batter parts of the UK, as thousands of homes remain without power following powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday. Storm Boelo is forecast to hit on Saturday, with an amber weather warning issued from 21:00 BST across much of Scotland as well as parts of Northern Ireland and northern England where gusts of up to 80mph (128km/h) could lash exposed areas. Travel chaos, power cuts and localised flooding are all possible as the storm sweeps in on Saturday. The warning comes just one day after Storm Austen unleashed wind gusts in excess of 75mph, resulting in toppled trees, transport disruption and thousands of power outages. Trains cancelled and roads warnings as Scotland prepares for Storm Boelo Storm Austen brings power cuts and travel disruption as more wind and rain forecast Strong winds and heavy rain will persist over the weekend as Storm Boelo moves across parts of the country. An amber weather warning for wind has been issued for across much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England from 21:00 BST on Saturday to 21:00 BST on Sunday. Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph. The Central Lowlands could also experience periods of disruption as strong winds funnel through the region. Travel disruption is expected - with ScotRail has confirming that some train services will be cancelled after 21:00 on Saturday - while damage caused by the winds could lead to additional power cuts. An amber wind warning for Saturday covers much of Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England. The second bout of bad weather comes after Austen, the first named storm of the season, brought strong wind gusts to large parts of southern England and Wales throughout Friday. Bad weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads. In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea. The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began - but more than 10,000 homes were still without power on Friday evening. Storm Boelo is forecast to bring widespread heavy rain and gales across the UK Yellow weather warnings for wind on Saturday cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England. Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph. While the worst of Saturday's weather is forecast to be felt in areas covered by warnings, heavy and persistent rain is expected across larger parts of the UK. Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding. Strong winds are forecast to continue into Sunday, although rain should gradually ease across most of the country. Sunny spells and blustery showers are expected elsewhere, while north-east Scotland is likely to see the most persistent rainfall. This video can not be played Watch: Homes without power as Storm Austen batters Britain Once the weekend's stormy weather has passed, forecasts suggest another area of low pressure will develop over the Atlantic before deepening as it approaches the UK from the south-west. This could bring a further spell of wet and potentially very windy weather to much of the country on Monday and into Tuesday. Whether the system will be strong enough to be named remains uncertain. Later in the week, high pressure is expected to build over the near continent, bringing a return to drier, calmer and more settled conditions. Part of Brighton's iconic West Pier collapses BBC presenter battles strong winds as Storm Austen hits Newquay It is not unusual for storms to arrive one after another – in fact, they often develop in clusters, particularly during periods of unsettled weather across the Atlantic. A strong jet stream is needed to help rapidly develop powerful windstorms. The process involves warmer air being pushed northwards and colder air moving southwards across large areas of the Atlantic, creating a sharp contrast in temperatures. These temperature differences provide favourable conditions for new low-pressure systems to form and strengthen. If these systems are then steered beneath a developing, powerful jet stream, they can intensify rapidly, potentially becoming named storms capable of bringing damaging winds, heavy rain and widespread disruption as they move towards the UK. title: Australian MP's condition improves after alleged car attack
description: The Independent MP is now in a serious but stable condition, according to the Melbourne hospital.
body: Helen Haines had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable. The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday. In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there. Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges. The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape". This video can not be played Shock and disbelief: How the attack on an Australian MP unfolded in a small rural town Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder. His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail. Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident. Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines. Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia. Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife. title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
description: Do British pensioners have it better or worse than those in other countries?
body: Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic. The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011. But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade. Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people. And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while. Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term. But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries? One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate. The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place. On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries. And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes. If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries. Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care State pension likely to top £13,000 a year What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it? But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows. However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere. So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK? Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund. But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country. But there are two issues to consider. Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare. And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes). Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing. As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform. So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap. The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income. It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men. But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021. Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark. So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere. But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action. The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving. That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late. title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
description: The chancellor will unveil AI spending aimed at shoring up the UK's defences in Wednesday's Budget.
body: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats. As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms. The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats. "AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said. "I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI. "One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country." The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge. But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops. "That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said. "By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country." The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models. What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it? Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI). Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing. The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development. It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre. This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy. It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language. Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks. There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far. But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI. title: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
description: She was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
body: Travellers are subject to temperature checks at Kenyan border crossing-points Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease. A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said. Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added. All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said. More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease. Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said. The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later. Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner. The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert. Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding. The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way. With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread. Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic. Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival. Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases. Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital. It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people. Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed? Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat 'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya. Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way. He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus. "We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said. Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month. Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep your house warmer for longer
description: Make draught excluders from socks, leave your oven door open after cooking and opt for lots of thin layers of clothing to stay warm.
body: Cora Harrison says she saves money by only turning on heating in rooms her family is using As the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all. But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run. Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health. To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective. When it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body. The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in. Natalie, 29, says she's replaced some of the clothes she wears round the house with supermarket thermal leggings and tops and says "it's made such a difference". Amber Waring, 27, from Devon, says she eats warm meals like stews and pasta bakes, and dances round the kitchen with her toddler while they cook to help keep warm. Amber Waring turns to warming meals such as pasta bake, fish pie and stew With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in. So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under £20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher. But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet. You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin. Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years. Keep doors closed to trap heat in the room you're in. You can place curtains or blankets over your doors for extra insulation. Embrace the daylight. "If it's sunny outside, open the curtains so the sun heats the room, then shut them when the sun sets to keep the heat in," says Rebecca. Sunlight can help keep rooms comfortable for longer before you need to switch the heating on "If you're using a hot appliance, let the heat into the room," says Lianne Macfarlane, 40, from Cheshire. She recommends leaving your oven door open after using it to help warm your kitchen, though this isn't advised if you have small children who could injure themselves. As well as curtains, other soft furnishings like rugs can help keep a room warm, says Seymour. Elin Davis fires up her log burner when it gets cold If you have a fireplace, lighting a fire to warm the room you're in can be cheaper than turning on the central heating for your whole house. Elin Davis, 30, from South Wales, says her log burner is more economical than turning her heating on - though she added that "logs can cost quite a bit these days". Gaps around doors can cause heat to escape, so place draught excluders around your door frames. You don't need to buy them - you can use towels or stuff socks into a pair of tights. When it's a windy day, Seymour recommends looking for other draughts in your house and either finding ways to seal these spots yourself or calling in a professional to help. These include using foam strips, sealant and specialist chimney draught excluders if you don't use your fireplace. Things such as extractor fans and purpose-built ventilation shouldn't be blocked, she adds. If your windows are single-glazed, then Sophie Burr of charity National Energy Action suggests looking at secondary glazing or investing in thermal curtains to help keep the heat in. Or for a cheaper option, some people suggest placing bubble wrap on your windows. Even though it may be tempting, don't keep your windows closed all the time. Seymour notes that it's important to allow some ventilation in your house to prevent damp. If you're after cheap insulation, especially if your window panes are single-glazed, then placing bubble wrap on them might help "I wouldn't recommend not having your heating on at all," says Seymour, pointing to both the health issues this can cause as well as how pipes can freeze over. But there are ways you can use heating wisely. These include checking whether your energy supplier offers cheaper prices at off-peak times, bleeding your radiators so that they're more efficient, and turning your heating up in small increments until you reach the right temperature. If you have furniture in front of your radiator, then try moving it to avoid blocking the heat. You can also buy dedicated radiator foil or make your own with kitchen foil to reflect the heat back into the room rather than losing it through the walls, says Burr. She points out that about 35% of heat that comes from radiators is lost through walls. Cora Harrison, 34, from Wakefield, says that she only turns the radiators on in the rooms her family

title: Leclerc fastest from Antonelli in US GP practice
description: Ferrari's Charles Leclerc leads Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in Friday practice at the United States Grand Prix.
body: Charles Leclerc topped both practice sessions in Austin on Friday Ferrari's Charles Leclerc led Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in Friday practice at the United States Grand Prix - but Max Verstappen left the strongest impression in his Red Bull. Leclerc, who topped both sessions, was 0.042 seconds ahead of the Italian, who has a mathematical chance of tying up his first world title this weekend. Antonelli will win the championship in Austin only if he wins the race and team-mate George Russell finishes below eighth and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton below fourth. Verstappen was third fastest, 0.189secs back, ahead of Hamilton, although the seven-time champion was 0.615secs off the pace. Russell was fifth ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson. Verstappen appeared fastest on the race-simulation runs later in the session, which often provide a more accurate read of overall competitiveness than the single laps. The Dutchman could be compared directly only with the Ferrari drivers, as all were running the soft-compound tyres on their long runs. Verstappen was marginally faster than Leclerc on average but the consistency of his pace suggested he was in the best shape, at least on Friday. Hamilton appeared to be struggling for pace compared with Leclerc whether on short runs or long. Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live and 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app Ferrari have an upgrade on their car this weekend, focused on a new floor, but Leclerc was downplaying expectations. "It felt good but it is not the gain I have seen or heard about," Leclerc said. "It is small gains but we could still see them on the car. It is a small step forward and we started the weekend on the right foot with a good balance and that is the outstanding thing with this Friday. "It has been a very clean Friday for me, but the others seem to be gaining more than us from Friday to Saturday and seeing the little gap there is, it is not going to be so easy tomorrow." Leclerc picked up on Verstappen's complaints about the track surface on Thursday by saying: "It was very poor. The first sector is particularly poor and very bumpy." McLaren's Lando Norris was seventh fastest, although the world champion did not set a time on his qualifying simulation run on soft tyres after making a mistake at Turn 16. Norris was the fastest on the long runs, at about 0.2secs on average faster than Verstappen, but cannot be compared as he was running the hard tyre. McLaren have introduced the first of three consecutive planned upgrades this weekend, but he was not happy with his performance. "Difficult," Norris said. "The pace is not bad. We seem a step away from Red Bull and Ferrari, probably Mercedes as well, but the car is very difficult to drive, too difficult to be consistent and get a nice feeling consistently. "To get the car be quick we just have to try so hard to be perfect and you can't be perfect. I am sure everyone has similar problems in a way but we are just not quick enough yet to be there consistently enough." McLaren's Oscar Piastri was eighth quickest, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar and Haas driver Oliver Bearman. Kimi Antonelli leads Mercedes team-mate George Russell by 102 points in the drivers' championship Mercedes have reverted both their cars to the upgraded specification that was introduced in Malaysia two races ago but about which there remain questions over its relative performance. The team believe that the upgrade has more performance within it, but that they have not yet found the appropriate set-up to maximise it. They hope a full, 'normal' weekend with three practice sessions will enable them to hone it. "Having both cars on the same package helps because we can try lots of different stuff and we have a better understanding of this package," Antonelli said. "However, we are still trying to get the car in the right window." Three drivers have grid penalties for using more than the permitted number of engine parts - Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad will go back five places, Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto 20 and Alpine's Franco Colapinto 10.
