title: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?
description: Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have split opinion but are getting into the groove, critics say.
body: Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman's "keep dancing" move for three Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove. Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park. And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more. Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow. Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV. Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics. Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine. The new hosts joined the judges on the dance floor when the series began After they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as, external "TV's most awkward ménage à trois". The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared, external that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding". Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express, external. And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said, external Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve". She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem. "He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News. "I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works." Widdicombe has been at the centre of comic sketches with the other hosts and judges The problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous. "They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in. "Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse." She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him". "But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says. Emma Willis has hosted shows including Big Brother and The Voice Radio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in. "I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles." When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less. "They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds. "It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly. "Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous." One episode featured Widdicombe and Willis in a Mary Poppins-inspired sketch Frost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects. The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests. "Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically." Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter". Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere". Radebe has already gained a reputation for his flamboyant fashion But while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed. Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain. "JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast. "He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. title: Are California voters about to impose world's first 'tax on billionaires'?
description: Voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.
body: Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions and being home to many rich and famous. Now voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them - names that include media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare. Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires. There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted". What are the US midterms? A simple guide But the vote is also offering regular everyday residents a voice on an issue that has riled politics for decades. "I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap. The state has the largest economy in the country - and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the whole of the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the globe. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps. Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system. Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill. "If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she told the BBC. While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external. California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue. A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided. The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents. California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year. While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs. Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue, she said. In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax. They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey. Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax. "I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he added, saying the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if

title: Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests
description: Younger Limoges residents see the destruction of their town hall as unfortunate collateral damage in a wider movement. For others, the fire was an unacceptable tragedy.
body: This video can not be played A town in mourning: One week after protests left historic French town hall in ruins "It is a historical tragedy for France, not just Limoges". Just six months into his mayoral term, it is hard to imagine Guillaume Guérin having a more momentous week. We talk next to what became the defining image of last week's nationwide protests: the still impressive, yet fragile exterior of his town's 19th-Century town hall, charred from a fire. The sight of its wooden clock tower collapsing into the flames drew widespread shock and anger, and Guérin, who was in tears when he first saw the scale of the damage this week, believes the reaction is "legitimate and completely understandable". This video can not be played Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protests Limoges city hall was set on fire last weekend with its wooden clock tower collapsing on Saturday What is apparent from the array of flowers and sombre onlookers gathered at the hall's entrance, is that this is a town mourning the loss, or at the least the harm inflicted on its most iconic and, frankly, most beautiful building. Guérin blames the damage on the French hard left, "supported by rioters". Two men have been arrested, a 66-year-old, as well as another suspect who is 34. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks". Limoges' conservative mayor claims he has received a message of support from US Vice President JD Vance, but not Emmanual Macron, his own, outgoing president. "What happened here will have an influence on the upcoming presidential election. This country is not doing well at all," he says. Two men have been arrested in connection with the fire. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks" For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become. In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time. In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening. Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre. Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone. Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask. Jade, a 19-year-old medical student, says she has to get by on €300 per month and is frustrated by French politics "Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24. It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend. I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument? "For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits. Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests." She complains of having to live on €300 per month. "I feel we are not respected as young adults." Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower. This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget. In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century. "It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us." Jean Roger Faucher got married in Limoges town hall. He says he cannot accept protests when they put people's lives at risk Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that. "On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds. Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease. "Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork. Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily. Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement. In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history wil

title: The artist dropping her debut album after a billion streams
description: Irish DJ Jazzy came up on the Dublin club scene and has worked with industry heavyweights like Calvin Harris.
body: Irish DJ Jazzy is best known for tracks like No Bad Vibes and Somedays Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides. The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris. If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin. For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send. She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work. "It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat. "That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment." The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks. Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally. It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night. But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles. Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music". "When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album. "I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me." Jazzy says releasing her debut album feels "surreal" Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city. But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline. "When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says. "There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad. "There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure." Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic. "I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland. "We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going." Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd. Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date". While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work. She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track". "I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well. "So there's a little message from me in each song." Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
description: The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests to form the biggest challenge to Vučić's rule.
body: The Student List is Number 3 on Serbia's ballot paper, so the figure seen being hugged by this supporter has become a symbol of the movement's fight for change If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race. Ilija Srdanović appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans. He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to Vučić since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012. The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad. What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list. "It is absolutely normal to stand with my students to help them in their fair struggle," Srdanović told the BBC. Ilija Srdanović tops the Student List's 250 candidates but would not necessarily lead Serbia if they won The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister. Whatever Vučić's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge – an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media. He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure. Vučić has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally. Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history. Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote. A reported 150,000 supporters turned out for the final Student List rally in Belgrade's Slavija Square on Thursday night Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won. Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time." The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness. "We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name. "All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds. The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage. At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources". The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response. Vučić continues to command strong support among sections of Serbia's population For the past 18 months, there has also been a full-time, pro-SNS camp in the small park between the National Assembly and the Presidency building in the centre of Belgrade. Its residents have repeatedly attacked journalists and made the park a no-go zone for local people. Vučić has called the camp "a symbol of resistance" against those who "cannot stand different opinions". But his major challenge remains what happened outside Novi Sad railway station two years ago. The station's renovation was a key part of his signature infrastructure project – the high-speed line linking Belgrade and Budapest. So it has been difficult for Vučić to distance himself from the disaster. Aleksandar Vučić stepped down as president last month with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands". "This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED. "Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy." On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act. Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia. Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power. "When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but n

title: The Papers: 'Meghan warned over father' and 'Don't risk Truss-style budget'
description: Meghan Markle's responds to allegations over her father and PM warned to not risk 'Truss-style' budget leads Saturday's papers.
body: Nearly all the front pages feature the Duchess of Sussex's response to the allegations made about her estranged father, Thomas Markle, after it was reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to him were found at his former home in the Philippines. "Meghan warned over father 8 years ago," says the Daily Telegraph, with Markle sharing on Friday that she received a letter containing "troubling and disturbing allegations" about her father in 2018. Thomas Markle, who is 82 and based in the US, denies possessing any such images. "Met hunt for Markle letter" is the Daily Mail's headline, saying that Scotland Yard was "scrambling" to find the correspondence sent to the Duchess of Sussex in 2018. Sources stressed the Metropolitan Police "never investigated Mr Markle", the paper adds. The Daily Star says the "Duchess heard 'disturbing' claims soon after wedding", when she married the Duke of Sussex. The Daily Express writes that Meghan Markle's "half-brother Thomas Markle Jr reportedly alerted police" about the allegations. "Meghan's anguish" is the Daily Mirror's headline. The Independent's headline is "Meghan 'distressed' over abuse images claim against father". Elsewhere, it reports that Scotland is braced for Storm Boleo after Storm Austen caused disruption in south-west England on Friday. Its photo shows part of Brighton's historic West Pier that has collapsed after 100mph winds hit. As the Autumn Budget looms, the papers are in full swing speculating what Chancellor John Healey will hand down on Wednesday. The Times carries a warning from former chief economist at the Bank of England Andy Haldane, telling the Prime Minister Andy Burnham not to "risk a Truss-style budget crisis", referencing the mini-budget of former Prime Minister Liz Truss which contained unfunded spending pledges, including major tax cuts, precipitating the sacking of ex-chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng, the collapse of the bond markets, and resignation of Truss. Speaking to the paper, Haldane qualifies by saying unfunded spending measures could "crater" the economy, urging Burnham to "take the knife" to public spending. The FT Weekend says Healey is planning a "£20bn lending boost" for the "state's business leaders and infrastructure bank" in the budget. The move requires the chancellor to "flex fiscal rules", according to the paper, with Treasury arguing "it would create and support 100,000 jobs in sectors including AI, defence and green energy by 2035". The Guardian says "online safety laws have failed to protect children", quoting the UK's online safety regulator. It reports that Ofcom's verdict from the first nine months "after the children's safety duties came into force in July 2025" is that "children have been fed an almost unchanged diet of unsafe content that has often left them frightened, confused and upset". "UK Cabinet spilt on whether to rejoin EU" and whether to hold a new "Brexit referendum" is the i Weekend's splash, reporting there is a 15-13 divide between ministers in favour and those opposed or undecided. "They are also torn on whether to call a new referendum on rejoining" the European bloc, writes the paper. Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Britain's posh schools are heading to India for students and profits
description: Half a dozen elite British schools are chasing growth in India amid a boom in its wealthy population.
body: At Harrow's Bengaluru campus, students wear the traditional Harrow hats and uniforms On the outskirts of Chandigarh city in India's north-western Punjab state, a 473-year-old legacy British public school opened its first all-girls international campus earlier this year. In contrast to the prominent Gothic-style central building on the school grounds in Bedfordshire, England, the Indian premises are more modern, with purpose-built academic blocks. But a conspicuous red-brick clock tower bears the imprint of the school's British heritage. The Bedford School, Mohali, is the newest in at least half a dozen British public schools (elite, fee-paying private schools with a long history), including three of the country's oldest, that have set up shop across the length and breadth of India. Their expansion comes amid tighter market conditions in China and the introduction of VAT on private school fees in Britain from 1 January 2025. Since 2023, Bengaluru - India's Silicon Valley and a hub of software and start-up companies - has been home to the prestigious Harrow School, alma mater of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Shrewsbury School has a campus in Bhopal in central India, while Wellington College has chosen to set up base in Pune, a western city that calls itself the "Oxford of the East" for its well-regarded universities and colleges. Millfield, Queen Elizabeth's School and a few others are reportedly on their way with satellite campuses in the coming years. For decades, India has been home to well-established local boarding schools modelled on the colonial British public-school system, serving elite, aristocratic families. But this market has rapidly expanded with newly wealthy Indian families increasingly aspiring to give their children more global exposure. "Our international curriculum is quite a driver for many of them," Caroline Pascoe, head of school at Harrow in Bengaluru, told the BBC. Harrow and Bedford are among the few schools in India that follow an all-through Cambridge curriculum - a global education framework recognised at 10,000 schools worldwide - from primary through to A-levels. Bedford School is the latest in at least half a dozen British public schools that have entered India Harsimran Singh Kocchar, whose own extended family runs a chain of schools across India, says he decided to send his five-year old daughter Parineet to Bedford Mohali because of the "holistic focus of the school on character development, confidence and not merely academics". He said he was also drawn to the fact the school did not have a "VIP culture" unlike many Indian equivalents. "All kids are treated the same. Children of ministers and bureaucrats don't get greater privileges," said Singh. Beyond the growing ranks of well-heeled local families, non-resident Indians who have either returned home after long stints abroad, or those still in the UK or Middle East wanting their children to connect to their roots, are also a significant market for these schools, says Pascoe. Sixty per cent of Harrow's staff in Bengaluru are international and, like the others, it has imported its unique traditions to its Bengaluru campus: teachers are called Beaks, and students wear the traditional Harrow hats and uniform and take part in The Long Ducker - a cross-country race that happens across its schools globally. There is also a house system - a hallmark of traditional British education. These quintessentially parochial quirks are blended with local customs such as singing the Indian national anthem every morning or celebrating Ganesh Chaturthi, a major Hindu festival. Schools such as Harrow in Bengaluru promote extracurricular activities like music and drama While India's growing economic credentials and burgeoning population of newly minted millionaires are a natural tailwind for expansion, this growth is partly being driven by a slowdown in China. Much of the expansion of British public schools abroad in the past decade was driven by China and Hong Kong - half of the 151 satellite campuses operated by 50 UK schools are situated in these countries. But that growth has slowed following changes in regulation, and "increased scrutiny, and even resistance, from national governments", according to a 2025 study by the UK-based Private Education Policy Forum (PEPF, external) think tank. A new 2024 Chinese law that required schools to integrate patriotic education into all subjects further challenged expansion and even led to planned campuses being cancelled, prompting these schools to consider other locations like India and Vietnam, according to PEPF. Moreover, in the 2024 Autumn Budget, Britain introduced a 20% VAT on private school fees. Naomi Atkins, founding principal at Bedford School Mohali, says this has forced many private schools to look overseas. "They are in a desperate situation. Even those that hadn't previously looked for international expansion are now suddenly active in India," she told the BBC. Well-heeled local families and non-resident Indians are a major target market for British schools in India But India has not been an easy market, she admits. Most of these schools are set up in partnership with local investors or operators. While in the past schools in other countries might have been able to do deals at 10% of revenue - the fee that they would charge the local partner-investor - margins in India may have shrunk to as low as 1% in some cases, says Atikins. There has also been some over-estimation of the size of the market, she says. Even though India has nearly 250 million children enrolled in schools, English education is deeply entrenched in the country and competition from local players is much more intense compared with other non-English speaking countries like China, Korea or Vietnam. India's per capita income is also far lower and the high price-points of the British schools - which can charge up to £15,000 or more

title: The gang murder and the women who went to the White House looking for answers
description: The fallout of the murder of 33-year-old Robert McCartney, a father-of-two, reverberated around the world - forcing the IRA to acknowledge several of its members were involved.
body: Robert McCartney's sisters from left, Catherine, Donna, Paula, Claire and Gemma with his partner Bridgeen Hagans (seated, centre) have long campaigned for justice over his murder It is a Sunday night in the pub. There is football on the TV and people packed around the bar - then suddenly, violence erupts. Bottles are smashed and broken glass is slashed across the throat of one of the biggest men in the bar. The melee spills out into the street, where the injured man says out loud the name of the man he believes attacked him. There is, he says later, an immediate reaction with hostile men in the crowd around him saying: "You're getting it, you're getting it." A knife flashes and two friends are left bleeding heavily on the pavement. One of them is dying. Robert McCartney, an engaged father-of-two, took no part in the violence, according to the few available accounts of what happened that night in January 2005. But the 33-year-old ended up losing his life, and no one has ever been held to account for his murder – an outcome that reverberated across the world and is now the subject of a documentary series, Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice. Robert McCartney was engaged when he was killed in January 2005 The failure to secure convictions can be linked to the organisation which exercised power over many of those present. Even while Robert McCartney was being treated by paramedics on the street, his killers' tracks were being covered. Back in Magennis's bar, right behind the Royal Courts of Justice in central Belfast, the pub's CCTV tape was snatched and the bar was cleaned with bleach. "It wasn't their first rodeo," said David Lowans, a former Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) detective who worked on the case. "They were experienced in clearing themselves forensically." The bar was a popular venue in central Belfast, which backed on to a series of smaller streets The series, made by BBC Northern Ireland in association with Irish broadcaster RTÉ, obtained crime scene video and photos showing the aftermath of the incident. The clean-up wasn't complete and police were able to find some blood stains in parts of the bar. But substantial evidence seemed to have gone. The knife used in the murder was never found and reportedly destroyed. Crucially, witnesses appear to have been silenced. "Out of the 70 people who were in the bar, we got no information from anybody to say the detail of what happened," said Lowans. "We either got: 'I was in the toilet' or 'I didn't see anything', which is unbelievable. "Whenever this altercation took place there were lots of people there." David Lowans was a PSNI detective for more than 15 years In the days after the murder, Robert's five grieving sisters and his devastated fiancée, Bridgeen Hagans, had even less information about the murder than the police. "We were still completely in the dark as to what had happened," said his sister Paula McCartney. "Didn't know where it had happened, how it had happened, who'd done it. Nothing." But they soon began to hear rumours. "It was just people coming in and telling what they'd heard in the street and 'such and such was in the bar that night'," said another sister, Catherine McCartney. "All the talk about who'd done it, who was involved." The information they were receiving explained why some witnesses weren't talking. The killers were said to be members of the Provisional IRA. The IRA had waged a campaign of violence for 30 years. In 2005, as Northern Ireland's peace process was being cemented, the group was observing a ceasefire. It issued a statement denying involvement in McCartney's murder, but that didn't convince witnesses who feared deadly consequences if they named IRA members to the police. Robert McCartney and another man were attacked in Market Street after leaving the bar "I've been about these areas enough to know how dangerous this organisation can be when they want to be," said Ed Gowdy. He was McCartney's friend and one of the witnesses telling his story on television for the first time. "I do know exactly the treatment informers get throughout the years. "If I tell what happened, am I an informer? "My mate's dead, heartbreaking. But I had to survive what had happened here." Gowdy was one of several witnesses who were then questioned by the IRA, conducting its own secret investigation running parallel to police inquiries. Another witness, who was also interrogated by the IRA, gives for the first time on TV a personal account of what happened in the bar. The McCartney sisters, meanwhile, found themselves fronting a campaign for justice that increasingly drew attention to the case. All five sisters were interviewed for the series. "It was my brother, and I just felt the world needs know... what has happened to him," said Paula. Catherine (left) and Paula McCartney, speaking at a press conference in Belfast in January 2006 "I think [it was] the way we came across on TV, down to earth, working-class women, standing up for justice," said Gemma McCartney, the eldest sister. "And doing something, breaking away from the old custom of not reporting these things to the police." Their campaign produced some extraordinary results, forcing the IRA to acknowledge several of its members were involved in the murder – though it said the killing was not done on behalf of the IRA. The IRA said three members were expelled from the organisation. It even claimed it offered to kill them – although the McCartney sisters say that offer was never made. (L-R) Bridgeen Hagans, the partner of Robert McCartney, walks with his sisters; Donna, Paula, Claire, Gemma, and Catherine outside the White House The sisters' campaign caught the attention of America's then Special Envoy to Northern Ireland, Mitchell Reiss. He recognised an opportunity to put pressure on the IRA to make mov

title: Celebrity Traitors left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
description: A newly earned special power left one contestant with a big decision to make in Friday's episode.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Celebrity traitors' unlikely daytime reunion Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hurrah! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week. And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast. When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife as to whodunnit and why? The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before. "I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense." Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried. "I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable. Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally. "Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again". Miranda was gutted to leave but delighted to have played the game With Miss Marple now out of the picture, James A told viewers that two of the remaining traitor hunters, James Blunt and Michael Sheen are like "Holmes and Watson". "Luckily they're completely looking in all the wrong places," he added. Leigh-Anne, having lost her new Big Mix dance partner from episode six, said she was now praying that the heat on her would now cool down. While Miranda was being murdered on Thursday night, out in the real world another Little Mix star Jade Thirlwell told BBC News - at the Mercury prize ceremony - that her groupmate was a real life "faithful through and through". Those kind words would be worth little if the now nicely positioned traitors kept going at this rate, however. "This is actually embarrassing," declared comedian Romesh at breakfast. "We are getting battered," a sneaky Maya agreed. "This is just getting harder and harder by the second." Breaking character in the safety of the diary room, the Gentleman actress and presenter admitted: "I'm not gonna lie, I feel terrible about Miranda, I really do and she will be sorely missed. "But with great honour comes great pressure, and here I am, "OG Traits", still flying it up." Joanne had earlier joked that Maya would not be killed or banished as "she's too hot. The hot ones always survive." "The trustworthy trio" - Kenny, Maya and James A - kept their scarecrow pumpkin heads while all around were losing theirs After breakfast, James B, who has been pretty consistently wrong with his theories throughout the series, continued his fine form, saying of Maya and Kenny: "I think they are the two most innocent." He joked (it was a joke, right?): "Watching me in this castle must be like watching Sherlock at work." With less heat on her than Christmas Day in Blackpool, Maya started planting a seed that roundtable "chief investigator" Michael Sheen might be up to something. "How has that guy not been killed?" asked Romesh. "It's like not getting rid of [Hercule] Poirot," he added, as the literary detective references kept coming. Michael and Sharon - fast becoming a dark horse with her theory about Ross Kemp having been killed with perfume - said she was determined to catch a traitor and would "not be taking any prisoners". On to Friday's mission, as the dwindling group arrived in a "field of screams", as presenter Claudia Winkleman aptly put it, full of scary-looking scarecrows. "This is like the Wickerman," said Joanne. "A solo scarecrow is sinister enough. A gaggle of scarecrows is terrifying." The task involved them attempting to retrieve bags of gold from inside the straw men with a pitchfork, in a bid to add thousands of pounds to the charity prize pot. Joanne's knot-tying badge she claimed to have been awarded in her youth didn't seem to help her much, though, as she struggled initially to grab any gold. "I have a newfound respect for the farming community," she declared. But it wasn't only gold on offer, it transpired. An as-yet unrevealed game-changing power would be bestowed upon one player, but only after they had to blow up the proxy pumpkin scarecrow heads of all but three of the most trustworthy contestants. Things got a bit awkward when poor Sharon "got so mad at the boys" - James B, Michael and Kenny - over which heads should roll. In the most remarkably stupid moment of the series since Richard E Grant told everyone he was a traitor, the group chose to preserve the heads belonging to Maya, James A and Kenny. "I had to hold in my laughter," said Maya, privately afterwards. "Of all people, you saved us. I just thought, 'oh my gosh, have we completed this game already? We are trusting. We are unsuspecting. We are killing you all'." With the others en route back to the castle, Winkleman quipped to the traitors: "This is like an outdoor turret." The special power was revealed to be a double dagger en

title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish over children he couldn't save
description: Kaylub Giamanco, has been hailed as a hero for killing a teenager who fatally shot three children and a teacher.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Bystander who stopped Oregon school shooter describes how he approached gunman A father who shot dead a gunman at his two daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described "hearing children pleading for their lives" and his anguish over those he could not save. Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by parent Kaylub Giamanco. "I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save." Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them". He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life. "I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said. The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was also killed, another child and a teacher were wounded. Giamanco told OPB the day of the attack began with breakfast and packed lunches. He and his wife spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day. The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began. He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school. Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services. "I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" he told the broadcaster. He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building. "I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said. Three schoolchildren and a teacher were killed in the shooting Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was struggling with the gunman. He opened the door and fired. Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared. He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman and said he "was supposed to be there" that day. Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened. "Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said. Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation. Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed". The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, 5. His father said the family was "broken and lost". Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job". "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said. The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request. The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door. Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in US school shooting before suspect shot by bystander Teacher in Oregon shooting said she pretended to be dead to survive Giamanco's name became public less than a day after the shooting. His mother, Kenda Freeman, read a family statement saying he was not seeking recognition and asking for privacy. Shortly after the attack, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised his intervention while acknowledging its emotional cost. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said. Giamanco told OPB he now lies awake after his family goes to bed, replaying the attack. "I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams." title: Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?
description: President Zelensky says limits to the technology continue to affect Ukrainian forces, while US officials and Elon Musk offer conflicting accounts of who controls it.
body: This video can not be played Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky says unexplained limits on Starlink and Starshield services continue to affect Ukrainian forces, while US officials and Elon Musk offer conflicting accounts of who controls the restrictions. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. The BBC's Washington correspondent Daniel Bush looks at what officials have said about the technology. Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? title: Fitness became an addiction that left me anxious and sleep deprived
description: Wayne Davies was left "constantly worrying" about race times, comparing himself to other runners on social media.
body: Wayne Davies says he became obsessed with fitness, training plans and data A runner says he became so consumed by a fitness addiction that he spiralled into anxiety and became sleep deprived. Wayne Davies said he was left "constantly worrying" about race times, training plans and fitness data and comparing himself to other runners on social media. The 40-year-old said it felt like the "rug was being pulled from under my feet", before he was signposted to NHS Wales where he was able to regain control. An expert said she had seen an increase in search traffic for fitness addiction in recent months as society talks more honestly about these behaviours. Wayne, from Newtown in Powys, began running about 10 years ago as a way of keeping fit but said he reached a "real low point" at the height of his addiction as his sleep suffered, concentration declined and anxiety began to affect other areas of his life. After starting with casual jogs he quickly progressed to marathons, before taking on ultra-distance races including a gruelling 75 miles (120km) around the Llŷn Peninsula in Gwynedd. "I became obsessed with trying to do longer and longer distances," he said, "then I started focusing on times." "I was never happy, and always chasing the next challenge or trying to get a better time." To Wayne, it felt like the "end of the world" if he didn't succeed. "I never stopped to appreciate what I'd achieved," he said. Wayne said it felt like the "end of the world" if he did not hit his target He said his struggle intensified following a heart scare during a training run, which led to him being diagnosed with atrial fibrillation - a heart rhythm condition. Although he returned to running after treatment, he constantly worried the condition would recur, and realised it was becoming an obsession. Wayne said he never realised a fitness addiction existed until he spoke up about it, adding that he was just trying to "get better all the time." "Since I shared the story I've had a a lot of people saying they can relate to it," he said. "I probably wasn't open about it before because you feel like you're going to get judged." His friends and family encouraged him to seek help through his GP, who signposted him to the Powys-based charity, Ponthafren. "A lot of men think talking about how they feel is a sign of weakness, and I admit I did feel a bit ashamed at first," he said. "But taking that first step was probably the best thing I ever did." After enrolling on the NHS Wales SilverCloud Space from Anxiety programme, he worked through a 12-week course, learning "how to manage my thoughts and let things go". He said: "I don't tend to look at the data as much anymore. I just accept it for what it is." He sometimes uses his watch as a guideline when running, but no longer "obsesses over it", adding that he "goes by how I feel on the day". Wayne wants to encourage others to seek help if fitness is having a negative effect on their lives He has been in training for the The Marathon Eryri, formerly the Snowdonia Marathon, but with a very different outlook. "I'm not worried about times anymore," he said. "I just want to do the best I can on the day and enjoy it." Wayne believes more men should feel comfortable reaching out for support when they need it. "People do want to listen and there are tools out there that can help. It's not as scary as you think." The inaugural Marathon Eryri was held in 1982 Zaheen Ahmed, head of therapy at UK Addiction Treatment Centre, said she has seen an increase of fitness addiction cases, with more than 57,000 people seeking help from their exercise addiction page in the past six months. "Typically this stems from clients embarking on sobriety and cross-addicting into fitness, to the point where that in itself then becomes the problem instead of substances," she said. She said fitness apps have added a competitive element to "inform and advise" people in a way that could not be done a decade ago, but this can lead to compulsive behaviour disorder. "If fitness has overtaken your daily joy sources, then it's likely a problem has developed," she added. Zaheen said she did not think addictions were changing, but instead "we just have the means and desire to talk more openly and honestly about these behaviours". "As life evolves and as a society we're exposed to more things to do, more ways to be engaged, there are more opportunities for unhealthy relationships develop." Dafydd Judd is a personal trainer in Cardiff Dafydd Judd, a personal trainer in Cardiff, said he felt the "lines are blurring" between fitness and technology addiction. He said calorie counting apps can become "highly addictive" if you are weighing, measuring and adjusting your calorie intake. "There's way more food to track than there is with exercise, so I can see how that can get extremely obsessive," he added. Dafydd encouraged people to seek help if its starts to become an unhealthy relationship to ensure you are "channelling your energy in the right way". He also advised people to be wary when seeing fitness records posted online as there are an increasing number of people "fudging the numbers and lying to to create this illusion that they're better than they are". He described social media as a "double-edged sword" when helping people to stay fit. "Companies are tapping into social media to help promote their business, but on the flip side, it creates these communities," he said, adding that "healthy competition" online can spur people on. Fionnuala Clayton, project manager of NHS Wales' Online Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Service, said they were "grateful that Wayne reached out during a "challenging time in his life". Clayton said that while exercise has mood-boosting benefits, "too much can can have negative impacts on both mental and physical health". She said it was important to reach out for support if a routine starts to dominate other areas of yo

title: Argentina drops investigation into President Milei over crypto fraud
description: Javier Milei had denied acting fraudulently when a cryptocurrency nosedived after he deleted a social media post about it.
body: Javier Milei had denied crypto fraud allegations A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped. The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show. The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra , which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025. He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped. Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category", and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven. Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups. The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it. But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money. It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales. The Argentinian president, though, insisted: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it" in an interview with local media Todo Noticias'. The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine if the president had acted improperly. Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it". And, in a TV interview, he insisted that those who invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks. title: Wade equals Prem record as Newcastle beat Sale
description: Christian Wade equals Chris Ashton's Prem try-scoring record with a 101st score as Newcastle post their first league win of their season against Sale.
body: Newcastle winger Christian Wade equalled Chris Ashton's Prem try-scoring record against Sale Tries: Wade, McGuigan Cons: Hodge 2 Pen: Hodge Christian Wade equalled Chris Ashton's Prem try-scoring record with a 101st score as Newcastle Red Bulls posted their first league win of their season against Sale Sharks. On a blustery night dominated by kicking, penalties and stubborn defence delivered a 17-3 win and the try that Kingston Park wanted, with Wade going over in the right corner to draw level with Ashton nine minutes into the second period. A second eluded Wade in a game of few chances but George McGuigan did smuggle the ball over at the back of a maul as Newcastle stretched clear to post only a fifth win in four Prem seasons. Despite Wade's milestone, the match was far from a thrilling spectacle However, Newcastle coach Dan McFarland will be keen now to build on this first step against a side who had been unbeaten in their previous two league outings and among the names in the title conversation before the start of the season. Newcastle: Hodge; Wade, Harris, Rigg, Kok; Connon, Benitez Cruz; Rakete-Stones, McGuigan, Millar Mills, Usher, Tuima, Hicks, Christie, Sotutu. Replacements: Togiatama, West, Moreno, Baker, Leatherbarrow, Graham, Elliott, Henry. Sale: Carpenter; Roebuck, Marchant, Maasi-White, O'Flaherty; Ford, Hanson; N Smith, Cowan-Dickie, Francis, Van Rhyn, Bamber, Tshiunza, B Curry, T Curry. Replacements: Jibulu, McIntyre, Opoku-Fordjour, Canakaivata, Dugdale, Lozowski, Louw, Reed. title: White House says the US is lifting tariffs on some Canadian goods
description: Susan Collins, a Republican in a tight race to keep her senate seat in next month's elections, said she had been working with the White House on tariff relief.
body: The US is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with the White House saying on Friday it was working to "protect the economic prosperity and national security of the American people". The exemptions could also boost Republican candidates in the midterms elections on 3 November, as many US voters list affordability and economic pressures as top issues. Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race in Maine to keep her seat in the election, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry. After trade talks collapsed this summer, the US and Canada started an escalating tariff war that has affected both sides of the border. Senator Susan Collins said she had worked with the administration to secure "tariff relief" The White House, in a statement, said that starting 30 October the US would remove certain products from the list of Canadian goods it taxes, such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes. It added those items would be replaced with certain valves, carpets, waste products, among others. The White House said the action reflects President Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade", as well as "offsetting the burden and disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada's discriminatory treatment". The BBC has contacted the White House, US commerce department and trade representative for further comment. Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said that Canada is "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal, but is willing to wait it out. "We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said, according to CBC. Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met with members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada. So far, Canada has not commented on the White House's announcement. LeBlanc's office did not immediately respond on Friday to the BBC's request for comment. The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts The Wall Street Journal had reported that the exemptions, largely focused on Canadian agricultural and forestry, were made in a bid to help Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. The reductions could be offset by raising levies on ​other Canadian goods, the Journal reported. In a statement Collins put out before the White House announcement, the incumbent lawmaker, who is trying to clinch her sixth term, said she had "secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers". "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she posted on X. Collins said she has asked US officials and senior administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada. ​Maine's economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the month-long trade war. Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state. title: Man dies after car crashes into Lidl supermarket
description: West Midlands Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene with others requiring treatment.
body: A blue car crashed through the entrance of the store in Finchfield, Wolverhampton A man in his 30s has died after a car crashed through the entrance of a Lidl shop in Wolverhampton. Police were called to the supermarket in Finchfield Hill shortly before 18:00 BST on Friday. West Midlands Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and a number of other people were treated for injuries. West Midlands Fire Service said it dispatched four crews to the incident at 17:51 BST with two crews still at the scene at 20:05 BST. The car had crashed through the entrance of the shop, smashing the glass, and remained just inside the doors on Friday night as emergency services remained at the scene. Tina Bonev, who witnessed the crash, said it was "absolutely terrifying" and there had been "shock and confusion" in the aftermath. Police were called to the scene shortly before 18:00 BST on Friday Police have cordoned off Finchfield Road West and Finchfield Hill and a fire engine was parked outside the supermarket. Police said the roads were expected to remain closed for some time and advised drivers to find alternative routes. Cars remained in the Lidl car park and the shop's entrance appeared to be damaged. "The man's death is not being treated as suspicious and our thoughts are with his family at this sad time. Officers remain at the scene to help fire and ambulance colleagues carry out their enquiries," a police spokesperson said.
