title: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
description: Ukrainians held alongside the American say they witnessed beatings and sexual humiliation by Russian guards during his detention.
body: Stephen Hubbard (second from left in the first row) was flown back home on a US plane earlier this week Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention. Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022. "We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days." Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers. "It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read." Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner. He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial. Ihor Shyshko alleges that Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of Russian prison staff Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun. "They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold. "He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'." Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff. Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison. The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine. Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine. US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before. Dmytro Khyliuk says Hubbard was hidden in a Russian prison to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv. He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor. Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth. "It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said. Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened. "There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said. "Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move." They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions. "There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said. Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors. "I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said. The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue." Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange. He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. "Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners". Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US. "I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said. But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress". Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice. "Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that". Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024, accused of serving in a defence unit in eastern Ukraine US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin Be

title: Trains cancelled and roads warnings as Scotland prepares for Storm Boelo
description: Heavy rain and strong winds are expected during the second named storm to hit in two days, with gusts of up to 80mph forecast.
body: Some train services will be cancelled during Storm Boelo Train services have been cancelled and police have warned against unnecessary road journeys as Scotland prepares for the arrival of Storm Boelo. Heavy rain and strong winds are expected during the second named storm to hit in two days, with gusts of up to 80mph forecast. Most of the country is covered by a yellow Met Office warning from midday on Saturday, while a more severe amber alert takes effect from 21:00 on Saturday until 21:00 on Sunday, covering the mainland and Western Isles. Forecasters say the storm, which is the second named storm in two days, could result in injury, flying debris, power cuts and damage to trees and buildings. Scotland to be hit with 80mph wind gusts as Storm Boelo alert upgraded to amber Major travel disruption and thousands without power as Storm Austen hits UK Although the 24-hour amber warning is not unprecedented, it is unusual because of the length of time it will be in place over such a wide geographical area. On Friday the forecast triggered a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience room which ensures the country is prepared for severe weather events. The amber warning takes effect from 21:00 on Saturday Storm Boelo will bring very strong westerly winds with widespread gusts of 60-70mph (96.6-112.7km/h), and gusts up to 80mph (128.7km/h) in exposed coastal areas. The strongest winds will initially affect western Scotland and the far north of Northern Ireland on Saturday evening and then spread eastwards overnight and through Sunday. This will be accompanied by periods of heavy rain and frequent showers. Forecasters warned that flying debris could cause injuries and danger to life, with a good chance of power cuts and an impact on phone coverage. The Met Office also warned of damage to trees and buildings, bridge closures and transport disruption. Winds will gradually ease from the west through Sunday. Public transport is still running, though ScotRail has confirmed that some train services will be cancelled: Glasgow Central – Ayr line will close between Kilwinning and Ayr from 21:00 on Saturday Glasgow Queen Street – Oban / Mallaig line will close between Fort William and Mallaig and between Crianlarich and Oban from around 22:00 Inverness – Kyle of Lochalsh line will close between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach from the start of service on Sunday Inverness – Wick / Thurso line will close between Helmsdale and Wick / Thurso from the start of service on Sunday Network Rail said trains will also run at reduced speeds across large parts of Scotland from Saturday night into Sunday. Passengers are advised to expect significant disruption and longer journeys, and are should check services before they travel. Supt Andy Barclay, deputy head of road policing for Police Scotland, warned drivers that conditions may be hazardous and urged them to consider whether journeys were "really necessary" over the weekend. Stopping distances can be at least double on wet roads compared to dry conditions, and spray can reduce driver visibility HGV and bus drivers should drive with extreme caution and be aware you may be asked to park at a suitable position by the police If you need to travel, please drive to the conditions and allow extra time for your journey Stay tuned to media outlets for further updates and consult the Traffic Scotland website and social media channels for information relating to affected roads As for coastal areas, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) said that weather conditions pose a safety risk to visitors and advised "extreme caution" if people are near the shoreline, especially along exposed cliffs, seafronts and piers. The charity's water safety lead, Michael Avril, urged people to keep a safe distance from the water as conditions "could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea". CalMac cancelled a number of sailings on Friday and has amended the Saturday timetable for MV Isle of Mull - which runs between the mainland, South Uist and Barra. This video can not be played Storm Boelo expected to have widespread impact on Scotland - Kirsteen MacDonald has the forecast. It may be that some events are postponed during stormy conditions. Friday's Scottish Cup tie between Penicuik Athletic and Clyde was among the first to be delayed because of heavy rain. Western Isles Council said events including church services should be aware of strong winds throughout Sunday and advised they "plan accordingly". Paisley's popular Halloween festival is due to take place this weekend, which includes a parade, street theatre and outdoor light installations. Renfrewshire Council said Friday's programme would go ahead as planned, but that an update on Saturday's events would be provided closer to the time. And a Halloween family fun day at Dean Park Castle and Country Park in Kilmarnock, scheduled for Sunday, has been postponed due to the weather warning. title: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment
description: The doctor says she faced a brutal investigation after she passed on complaints brought to her by other doctors.
body: Dr Sarah Redvers brought a claim of constructive dismissal A doctor who raised concerns about the treatment of children questioning their gender has told the BBC she was accused of transphobia, bullied and harassed out of her child protection job in the NHS. Dr Sarah Redvers, who was a named safeguarding GP, said she faced a brutal investigation after she passed on complaints brought to her by other doctors. Speaking publicly for the first time, Redvers said she felt she was "silenced" for doing her job after questioning whether another GP was appropriately assessing the needs of young people who were distressed about their gender identity. She has brought a claim of constructive dismissal against the NHS Sussex Integrated Care Board (ICB), which managed health services in the county, and Adam Doyle, who was the ICB's chief executive until 2025. Redvers told a three-week employment tribunal hearing that she felt the focus on investigating her meant issues of patient safety had been sidelined. Dozens of children put at risk after gender care failures at GP clinic, inquiry finds Unacceptable waits for adult gender clinic appointments, review says "I was just bewildered really that the medical and safeguarding issues were completely lost," she said. "It's really risky," she told the BBC. NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently." They have apologised to Redvers. In June 2026, nearly six years after she first raised concerns, a separate NHS safety investigation found that dozens of children, some as young as 13, had been inappropriately prescribed drugs at the WellBN practice, the clinic where the other doctor worked. The report said 78 children had potentially been harmed after puberty-blocking drugs and cross sex hormones were prescribed to them without proper checks. The report said it was in response to a drug review carried out in autumn 2024, not to the concerns first raised by Redvers years earlier. NHS England said: "It is totally unacceptable young people were put at risk of harm because some practitioners at the WellBN practice provided care they were not commissioned to deliver by the NHS." "To read about a medical scandal knowing it could have been stopped was upsetting," said Redvers, "because concerns were raised appropriately and leaders knew about it". Redvers, who has many years of experience working with vulnerable groups, was a named safeguarding GP for Sussex, which meant other doctors who had safety concerns about patients could turn to her for advice and help. The tribunal heard that in July 2020, a doctor got in touch because she was worried about a patient who had gone to an online clinic which was registered overseas. It wanted the GP to take over prescribing testosterone to a vulnerable 18-year-old female, who was distressed about her gender. The doctor was also given advice on such prescriptions by a Brighton GP, Dr Sam Hall. "The concerns to me were that Hall was recommending treatment for patients that he hadn't assessed, that he hadn't met, and that other GPs were uncomfortable with prescribing," Redvers said. Redvers spoke to NHS England (NHSE) and was advised to make the complaint as a whistleblower. It was investigated and NHSE said it was satisfied with Hall's practice. Over the following months several other GPs voiced their concerns to Redvers about the quality of assessments, the prescription of puberty blocking drugs and cross sex hormones, and the lack of specialist supervision at the WellBN clinic, where Hall was based. Again, the NHS investigated her concerns. She said she was also told by the investigator that there was a "general worry" that there "would be allegations of transphobia." Hall, who is a trans man and was born female, qualified as a GP in 2019 and is known as a campaigner for transgender rights in Brighton. Publicly, he had said that his own pain had shown him the importance of "affirmative care" - support for a patient in a way which accepts rather than challenges their preferred gender and treatment decisions follow from that. He was also working with the NHS locally on setting up a Trans Health hub and with a Brighton trans support charity called The Clare Project. The second NHS investigation considered "the full scope" of Hall's work and concluded there was no cause for concern. It also said there was "one colleague whose persistent interest in the issue appeared disproportionate." Redvers took that to mean her. The concerns she said she and others were raising were about the quality of care being provided, and whether it had the necessary medical evidence to underpin it, not her views on gender. "It's about medical assessment and treatment of patients, which is something we have to get right, particularly in this complex group of vulnerable patients," she said. She said she viewed any suggestion of transphobia as "appalling," and it was "dangerous" that such claims were obscuring the medical and safeguarding issues she was raising. In 2021, whilst waiting for the outcome of the second investigation and prompted by a concern raised by local mental health services about the care of a vulnerable 15-year-old, Redvers referred Hall to the medical regulator, the GMC. Hall emailed Adam Doyle, then CEO of NHS Sussex, directly to complain. "I am being victimised here, and I need proper protection from this individual and their repeated attempts to disrupt my career" he said. Adam Doyle, was chief executive of the NHS Sussex Integrated Care Board until 2025 Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP. The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator. title: Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election
description: The justice department has filed a lawsuit arguing that the inclusion of two candidates named Dan Sullivan could confuse voters.
body: Senator Dan Sullivan, right, is in a tight race with Democratic contender Mary Peltola. The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters. The justice department said in a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday that the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate. Polls suggest the race between Senator Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote. The US government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan. "I'm the one that said do it," US President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday. Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it. The retired teacher previously denied his candidacy had an ulterior motive. Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court. For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box. In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan". The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year. In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator. "Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued. Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign. He said separately to Courthouse News that it was his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but, ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running". In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot. Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit. The Senate race in Alaska - which Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections. The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran. GUIDE: What are the US midterms? title: Storm Austen brings power cuts and travel disruption as more wind and rain forecast
description: Millions remain under yellow weather warnings for wind and rain, with a second storm expected to hit Scotland and parts of northern England on Saturday.
body: Choppy seas led to a dramatic display at Newhaven, East Sussex More than 15,000 homes are without power as Storm Austen continues to batter southern England and Wales, with more bad weather expected this weekend. The first named storm of the season brought gusts of up to 84mph (135km/h) to Jersey, while in southern England the wild weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads. In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea. On Saturday, Storm Boelo is forecast to bring more strong winds and heavy rain. The Met Office has put in place an amber warning for wind on Saturday and Sunday to cover parts of Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland. Austen made landfall in the south-west overnight and tracked eastwards throughout the day. All schools on Jersey and Guernsey closed for the day and some in Cornwall were closed or started later than normal. Ahead of the worst of the storm on Thursday afternoon, families were evacuated from a holiday park in Perranporth, Cornwall. Among them was Hannah Dawson-Turk, who told the BBC "the night before last, it sounded like our caravan was going to be ripped apart". "The storm is very loud outside now, and the waves look huge from our windows," she said from a nearby hotel. The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began. Some ferry services between the UK and France were cancelled, while National Rail advised many routes were travelling at slower speeds. In Brighton, onlookers filmed as a section of the West Pier fell into the sea as it was pummeled by large waves. Stephen Royle, who lives opposite, said the waves rolling in were "enormous" and he is "shocked" by how much of the pier ended up in the sea. The pier closed to the public in 1975 and fell into disrepair, but the ruined structure became a symbol of Brighton for some. This video can not be played Part of Brighton's iconic West Pier collapses On the Channel Islands, fresh food shortages are expected in the coming days due to a lack of ferry services, according to the boss of the Co-op there. "It's rare we get this level of disruption to storms backing up so quickly and probably a little bit more heavier than what we've had to deal with in the past," Mark Cox said. Paul Aked, head of Jersey Met, said there were gusts in Guernsey up to 76mph (122km/h), equivalent to a severe gale, force nine. Residents told BBC Radio Guernsey that they could hear the wind rattling through their homes. Jersey Airport said flights won't be running "until at least 17:00" while Cornwall Airport Newquay is warning passengers to check with their airline before travel. Departure boards at Exeter airport were showing multiple cancellations. Train operators across the country have warned that services are likely to be disrupted over the weekend. A car in Horsham was badly damaged after a tree fell onto it, however the driver was unharmed The UK will continue to be battered by strong winds and heavy rain over the weekend as Storm Boelo follows on the heels of Storm Austen. The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for wind for much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England. Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph. The Central Lowlands could also experience disruption as strong winds funnel through the region. Damage caused by strong winds could lead to further power cuts, while travel disruption is also predicted. Yellow wind warnings also cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England. Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph. Alongside the strong winds, heavy and persistent rain is forecast across the UK on Saturday. Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding. The Met Office has advised the public to drive cautiously in strong wind, and to secure loose items outside their homes such as bins and trampolines. People living or working in coastal areas were advised to take extra care during windy or stormy weather, including staying indoors as much as possible. A collapsed tree in the Jersey town of Gorey The storm came as the government released general advice for households to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies. The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "It's not about panic buying... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation." Last month, the National Audit Office warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis. It said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience. title: Bodycam clip released in fatal police shooting of Mississippi one-year-old
description: The family lawyer says an allegation of shoplifting "does not warrant the death" of a child.
body: This video can not be played Mississippi releases footage of police shooting that killed infant Mississippi authorities have released body camera footage showing how a toddler was fatally shot by a police officer responding to a report of shoplifting in a Walmart car park. Kohen Wiley, aged one, was on his mother's lap in a moving car when officers surrounded the vehicle in the city of Senatobia on 14 June. The state's attorney general found the policeman was justified in using force, and the officer's lawyer argued in a statement to the BBC that the driver was attempting to kill law enforcement. The child's family disputes that the shooting was justified. Their lawyer, Ben Crump, has called the police response "excessive from the very start". Crump said an allegation of shoplifting "does not warrant the death" of a child. Kohen Wiley was riding in the vehicle with his mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and another woman at the time of the incident. Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed to the BBC's US partner CBS that Hunter Foster, the officer who opened fire, had resigned. The Senatobia Police Department did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for confirmation. The footage released by Mississippi authorities on Thursday shows a first-person perspective of the officer who opened fire. After being told by a staff member that suspected shoplifters were getting away, five law enforcement officers run towards the car with guns drawn. The vehicle reverses, crashing into a parked car, before pulling forwards. The officer wearing the body camera raises his gun and aims it at the moving vehicle as he runs closer, shouting: "Stop!" As the car closely passes the officer, he fires his gun, shattering the passenger-side window. Four gunshots can be heard, as police command the driver to stop. The car continues to drive off slowly through the car park. CCTV video from the storefront appears to show that at the moment the policeman opens fire, another officer is standing near the front of the moving vehicle. "The driver of the vehicle was attempting to kill those 5 officers," Martin Zummach, an attorney representing the officer, said in a statement to the BBC, adding that his client "had no choice but to discharge his weapon". "We are very sad for the loss of life," Zummach said. "But the outcome of the investigation was not only expected, but it was overdue." The child's mother, Wiley, has denied she and her friend stole nappies from the store. No charges have been filed against them. The boy's death has sparked protests and vigils in Mississippi. At a news conference, relatives demanded accountability. "After what I've seen today, I'm having a difficult time understanding the word, 'justified,' said LaSandra Williams, Kohen Wiley's grandmother. title: Watch: Prince William on how he once dreamed of becoming 'DJ Xara'
description: The Prince of Wales made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.
body: This video can not be played The Prince of Wales has revealed he once dreamed of becoming a policeman or a DJ. Speaking on BBC One's The Graham Norton Show, Prince William said he thought being a policeman was "quite cool," before going through a phase where he wanted to be a DJ. Billing himself as "DJ Xara" - with an X - he told the host he "wasn't very good", falling short of the calibre needed to play school parties. The Prince made a surprise appearance on the show which airs on Friday evening, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize, an initiative he set up in 2020 to tackle global environmental issues. He was joined on the sofa by Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize. Read more about the prince's appearance here. title: Celebrated Irish musician Dónal Lunny dies aged 79
description: A founding member of three renowned bands - The Bothy Band, Planxty and Moving Hearts - he was widely credited for the revival and growth of Irish traditional music.
body: Lunny formed some of the most influential musical groups in the Irish music scene One of Ireland's most-celebrated traditional musicians and multi-instrumentalists, Dónal Lunny, has died aged 79. A founding member of three renowned bands - The Bothy Band, Planxty and Moving Hearts - he was widely credited for the revival and growth of Irish traditional music. He also composed and wrote scores for a wide range of projects including TV dramas, documentaries and films. In recent years he worked with contemporary artists such as Kate Bush, Rod Stewart, Elvis Costello, Clannad and Dire Straits frontman Mark Knopfler. He is noted for having left a lasting impact on the music scene in Ireland and was once described by U2's Bono as the island's "answer to Quincy Jones". Born in Tullamore, County Offaly, in 1947, Lunny moved to Newbridge in County Kildare when he was five years old and he said, from childhood, music was always an enjoyable part of his life. Irish folk group Planxty, pictured in London in January 1973, left to right: Christy Moore, Liam O'Flynn, Andy Irvine and Donal Lunny He first met a young Christy Moore in 1959, according to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, and the two school friends recognised a musical connection between them that would last for many decades. A founding member of Planxty with Moore, Liam O'Flynn and Andy Irvine, Lunny helped redefine traditional Irish music. The group recorded three albums between 1971 and 1973, with Lunny playing bouzouki, guitar, keyboards and bodhrán throughout. In 1973, he set up the label Mulligan Records and went on to produce 17 albums, with the label publishing music from a range of artists including Boomtown Rats, The Radiators and Agnes Bernell. Lunny joined The Bothy Band in 1975, helping push the boundaries of traditional Irish music alongside Matt Molloy, Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill, Kevin Burke, Paddy Glackin and Paddy Keenan. The Irish Traditional Music Archive said Lunny's influence on Irish music was "immense" In 1981, Ireland hosted the Eurovision Song Contest. For the interval act, Dónal Lunny and Bill Whelan composed a three-part suite of baroque-influenced traditional music called Timedance, recorded and performed live by Planxty. When Whelan was commissioned to orchestrate the interval for the 1994 competition, again hosted in Ireland, he built on the foundation established by himself and Lunny. That interval act was later developed into the full-scale production Riverdance - composed by Whelan and starring Michael Flately - which went on to become one of the most successful touring stage shows in the world. "It was no mistake of mine to call it Riverdance because it connected absolutely to Timedance," Whelan told author Leagues O'Toole in his 2006 book The Humours of Planxty. In 1992, Lunny produced and served as musical director of the acclaimed TV series Bringing It All Back Home, beginning a long creative partnership with producer Philip King. He also composed film scores, including for This Is My Father, starring Aidan Quinn and James Caan. Following a successful, decades-long career, Lunny was presented a lifetime achievement award at the BBC Radio 2 Folk Awards in 2018. Last year, he was awarded a lifetime achievement award at the RTÉ Radio 1 Irish Folk Awards. One of his last public appearances was in August, when he performed at the Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann [All-Ireland Fleadh] in Belfast. Musician and composer Neil Martin, who had collaborated with Lunny throughout his career described the loss as "huge" and said he was an "extraordinary figure". "Since the mid-60s nearly anything that was of significant movement within the traditional music world, Dónal was at the epicentral to it," he told BBC's Evening Extra programme. Speaking of a time he shared with Dónal 18 months ago, when they sat over a drink, Neil recalled thinking "Lunny's back again" and said, although the musician had been unwell for some time, the news of his death came as "a bit of a shock". He told the programme he was "delighted" that his last memory with Dónal is a "happy one". "All the musicians in Ireland will have nodded to him at some stage," he added. Renowned Irish musician Dónal Lunny dies aged 79 Musician and composer Neil Martin on the life of the renowned Irish musician Donal Lunny who has died aged 79. In a statement, The Irish Traditional Music Archive (ITMA) said Lunny's influence on Irish music was "immense" and he "opened new harmonic and rhythmic possibilities". Crediting the work he produced in his bands, they said "his imagination shaped the sound of Irish music" and his career was described as being built on "creativity, friendship and collaboration." "Dónal leaves behind an extraordinary body of work. His artistry, generosity and influence are woven deeply into the living tradition and into the lives of so many who knew him, were inspired by him, or had the privilege of playing and working alongside him," ITMA added. Lunny is survived by his family including his children Oisin, Cora Venus, and Sora Chan, as well as his partner Una O'Boyle. His brother, Manus, is also a noted musician and producer. He had a brief relationship with his musical collaborator Sinéad O'Connor in the early 2000s and they welcomed a son, Shane, in 2004. Shane died in 2022 at the age of 17, followed by his mother in 2023. title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
description: Green leaders have been given until Sunday to disown their party's "Zionism is racism" conference vote.
body: Green leader Zack Polanski has faced criticism over his response to the Zionism motion Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism. The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power. Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end. But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse. The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made. These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition. The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council. In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum. In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it. But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party. In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio. Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded. The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first. Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford. Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum. Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023. The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy. The "Zionism is racism" motion was passed by members of the Green Party of England and Wales at its annual conference in Brighton last month. The policy motion adopted by members said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians. It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs. Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future. Labour councillors require the approval of the party's NEC before entering into local tie-ups. According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power-sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office. By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally. A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong. "Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic." Additional reporting by Victoria Walton, Jennie Aitken, Hannah Miller, Vikki Irwin, Emily Hudson, Lucinda Adam. title: Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father
description: Today, without exactly using the word, Meghan claimed vindication.
body: Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father. Quite when the duchess last saw her father Thomas isn't clear. By the time her engagement was announced in 2017, a once-close relationship had cooled. He had moved to Mexico following his retirement in the US and then, as he spoke freely to the media before and after her 2018 wedding, the relationship went into the deep freeze. He said she barely called as he underwent heart surgery, the duchess's people briefed that she had. Then they went silent as he complained in interview after interview that he no longer saw his daughter, had never met Harry nor, later, his grandchildren. Now Meghan has told us why. Thomas Markle gave the first, very large, hint that things would be different within weeks of the announcement of Meghan and Harry's wedding. Instead of accepting the embrace of the Palace - and the media silence that involves - he happily went rogue, giving comments, sometimes commentary, to various media outlets. He had what appeared to be a paid photoshoot whilst claiming that he was being harassed by the media, withdrawing from the wedding just days beforehand as he underwent heart surgery. There was no lack of drama. The interviews and comments never really stopped. Markle was a regular on some broadcast outlets, often complaining that he had no contact with his daughter and son-in-law or, later, his grandchildren. From Meghan came neither comment nor guidance as to why she had cut contact with the father with whom she had once been so close. And into that vacuum rushed theory and supposition - that Meghan was embarrassed by her father, that she and Harry felt their privacy had been compromised by him and so would no longer give him material to recycle, that the old man who was so close to the popular news outlets that tormented them was no longer part of the life they wanted to lead. Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018 Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family Those theories became part of the case against Meghan; that she would sacrifice anyone and anything - even her father - to protect her position and save herself from any embarrassment. That must have stung. Because today, without exactly using the word, she claimed vindication. "I hope it can now be understood" she wrote. "That, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them." Meghan says she was informed of the allegations back in 2018. It is understood that it was after her marriage to Harry in May that year. Since then there has only been very limited contact between Meghan and her father - she wrote to him after he underwent surgery in the Philippines late last year. How much all of this changes the perception of Meghan is difficult to tell. Many people have made their minds up about Meghan and the saga with her father is only part of the tangled story of the duchess and the rest of the royal family. But her supporters will see vindication in the allegations - which have been denied by Thomas Markle - and the response that Meghan says she made when she first learned of them. title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
description: The US president has praised Burnham after the government allowed gas drilling in the North Sea's Jackdaw field.
body: Donald Trump said Andy Burnham's decision on Jackdaw would "make the UK a very rich country" US President Donald Trump has praised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the UK government's decision to approve production from the North Sea's Jackdaw gas field. He said he had spoken with Burnham, telling reporters on Friday that the decision would "make the UK a very rich country". Trump said: "The other prime minister, the previous man, Starmer. He's a very nice man, but he never got it done, and this one is getting it." The decision had been subject to intense debate around its environment and economic impact and came after years of legal challenges. The Jackdaw platform is located east of Aberdeen Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week. Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund. Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security. Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036. Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years. Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas. He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years." Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country." In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw. The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read. It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power". Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK. Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world". A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed. However, Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision by not giving any regard to climate obligations - things he said "have to be considered in the round". Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month, but that it would not lower energy bills this winter. She said the decision was "compatible" with legally binding climate commitments, adding: "We remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050." Environmental groups have criticised the Jackdaw approval. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said it was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Meanwhile, Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments". During their Friday talks, Trump and Burnham spoke about the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between British and Israeli companies. In September, the Argentinian government threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands, and earlier this month, it began legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields. Burnham raised the "economic consequences of Argentina's coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the Islanders' right to develop their natural resources", Downing Street said. The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, with the prime minister underlining the importance for Ukraine "to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", according to Number 10. Starlink technology is a satellite system owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company which Ukraine has relied upon during the war. In recent days, Ukraine has been recording issues with the network, according to sources within the defence ministry. This has affected the country's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations. The Downing Street statement added: "The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners to bring an end to the bloodshed." title: Babydoll singer gives Wales its first UK number one in 15 years
description: Jamie Miller is the first Welsh artist since 2011 to earn a UK Number 1 single - after Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.
body: Jamie Miller is now also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the Singles Chart for Babydoll Jamie Miller has become the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with his viral TikTok hit, Babydoll. Miller, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, narrowly beat Tate McRae and her single Housewife to claim the top spot on the UK Number 1 on Friday, according to the Official Charts Company. The achievement means Miller is the first Welsh artist since 2011 to earn a UK Number 1 single - after Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder. Miller, 29, told Charts: "I don't even know what to say other than thank you so much for getting me Number 1, this is the biggest thing that's ever happened to me in my life, I love you guys." He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone. Babydoll was released on 7 August - months after Miller considered quitting music - and exploded after actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos which featured the track. This video can not be played Babydoll singer Jamie Miller on 'the craziest journey' It sparked a TikTok dance trend and hit number one on the US iTunes pop chart, and earned Miller his first appearance on the US Billboard Hot 100. Babydoll narrowly missed out on the top spot last week. Jamie Miller and Off Campus star Antonio Cipriano (right) recorded a version of Babydoll together after a joke on social media Miller, who previously told BBC Wales his dad is an Uber driver in Cardiff, launched his career nearly a decade ago as a 19-year-old, after coming third on the sixth season of The Voice UK. Miller has also recorded a separate version of Babydoll with Off Campus star Antonio Cipriano, after initially joking about the idea on social media. Cipriano told BBC Wales last week that Miller was "one of the best vocalists I've ever heard", adding he had been a fan of Miller's voice "for years". Miller previously said his love for music began accidentally, after becoming "hooked" on singing following an audition for a primary school show. He said he was "proud" of his new music and was excited to share his latest album with the world and to tour it – in particular, he said, to bring it to Wales. Jamie Miller, from Cardiff, said he considered quitting his music career at the start of 2026 The singles chart top five was completed by Olivia Rodrigo's remixed version of Expectations with Chappell Roan and Ashe's Stop The Wedding at number four. Meanwhile, the albums chart saw Irish band Fontaines DC score their second number one album with Dopamine Chamber. The record marked the third biggest opening week for an album in 2026, and is also the fastest-selling Irish studio LP in 15 years since Snow Patrol's 2011 Fallen Empires. title: Police yet to receive £2m after A66 crash, says commissioner
description: Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey says it has been nearly two months since force was promised the cash.
body: Seven people including two police officers were killed in the crash on the A66 in the early hours of 22 August A police force has still not received the £2m it was promised by the government in the wake of a car crash that led to the deaths of seven people, including two police officers, the local police and crime commissioner (PCC) says. Cleveland PCC Matt Storey said Cleveland Police was still waiting for the extra funding promised by the home secretary in August. Shabana Mahmood pledged the cash in light of challenges faced by the force following the deaths, which followed a pursuit on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed. The Home Office said the force would receive the £2m it had been promised by the end of November. During the fatal crash, a Volkswagen Passat in which the five young men were travelling hit an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the dual carriageway near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST. Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene. The occupants of the VW Passat, which was travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy - were also killed. On the morning of the crash, Cleveland Police said it received several reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 had been seen ramming properties. Further arrests were subsequently made in connection with organised crime, including the following weekend after another vehicle ramming. PCC Matt Storey called for the £2m to be released immediately Storey called for the immediate release of the £2m but also said policing costs linked to the crash, which had led to the arrests of 50 people so far, were now forecast to exceed £5m. "These are exceptional and unavoidable costs arising from utterly tragic and devastating circumstances," he said. "They are not costs that should be borne locally or met from existing policing budgets." The PCC also criticised the lack of a "substantive" communication from the government about Cleveland Police's long-term funding. Storey said the current police funding model, which Mahmood had previously committed to reviewing, disadvantaged the Teesside force. He said the upcoming Budget was a chance to "align resources more fairly with demand" and "place Cleveland on a sustainable footing". PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in the crash in August The 50 arrests have come as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash. Fifteen people have been charged - 13 men and two women ranging in age from 19-45. title: Bayern Munich manager Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing at training
description: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany is taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.
body: Kompany was appointed Bayern Munich manager in May 2024 Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday. The 40-year-old had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday prior to Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal. The former Manchester City and Belgium defender was subsequently on the touchline for the match on Wednesday. Reports in Germany say Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital. "Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during an FC Bayern reserve team training session on Friday," said a statement from the Bundesliga club., external "The first-team head coach was watching the second string's session. "Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations in hospital and will remain under medical care. "His coaching staff will oversee training and match activities until further notice." Bayern's next game is against Freiburg in the German top flight on Sunday. "Vincent Kompany's health is our top priority. We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure his speedy recovery," said Bayern sporting director Max Eberl. "Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and all the time he needs. "His coaching team, in whom we have complete confidence, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery." Aaron Danks, one of Kompany's assistants, took the pre-match news conference for Bayern before the Arsenal game. German football journalist Taufig Khalil told BBC Radio 5 Live that Kompany had been "suffering with the virus for about a week". He added: "The thing started last weekend on Saturday against Leipzig, and that's the first time we saw Vincent Kompany [when] he didn't look very well. "He didn't do the press conference after, and Max Eberl told us that he's suffering with a virus. "Everybody was really surprised that Vincent Kompany was standing there with his black jacket in the pouring rain of Munich on Wednesday night against Arsenal. Everybody expected Aaron Danks to be there. "The problem was that maybe you couldn't bench Vincent Kompany, the game was too important for him. "Bayern Munich just told us that he's in stable conditions. There was a helicopter involved in the whole thing, which landed on the training ground at Bayern Munich, but he was not brought into the hospital by helicopter. They brought him with a medical car and he will be now there." Kompany left his role as Burnley manager to take over at Bayern in May 2024, succeeding current England manager Thomas Tuchel. He had won the Championship with Burnley in 2022-23 and, despite the Clarets being relegated from the Premier League under him the following season, Kompany was appointed by the Bundesliga club. He has led Bayern to the German top-flight title in the past two seasons and reached the 2025-26 Champions League semi-finals before being beaten by eventual winners Paris St-Germain. Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups. "Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and club legend, Vincent Kompany," said City in a post on social media. "Get well soon, Vinny." "Everyone here at Burnley FC sends our best wishes to Vincent and we wish him a speedy recovery," said a Burnley statement. title: Andrew can be called to give evidence in High Court fraud trial
description: The High Court trial involves allegations of fraud made by a wealthy Turkish woman against her former adviser.
body: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor can be called to give evidence in a High Court trial involving allegations of fraud against a Turkish businessman, a judge has ruled. Nebahat Isbilen, a Turkish national, alleges that Selman Turk, her former adviser, misled her over a £750,000 payment made to Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019. The judge agreed to allow Turk, who denies dishonesty, to seek to call evidence from Mountbatten-Windsor in a trial in London expected to begin in November. Mountbatten-Windsor repaid the money, and there was no suggestion of wrongdoing by the former Duke of York. Ahead of the trial, Turk made a bid to be allowed to call Mountbatten-Windsor to give evidence. In a judgment on Friday, Justice Adam Johnson agreed, allowing Turk to rely on a witness summary and seek to call evidence from the former duke. Johnson said: "Given the seriousness of the allegations, both on their own terms and in light of their wider impact, fairness requires that Mr Turk should be afforded an opportunity of putting forward his own case, using the evidence he considers relevant and material." The judge later said that his decision meant Turk could call evidence from the former duke, but that a witness summons "will likely" be needed to compel Mountbatten-Windsor to give evidence. Johnson added: "It is highly unlikely that a person in the position of Mr Mountbatten-Windsor would wish voluntarily to provide a witness statement and give evidence at a trial in public proceedings involving payments made by the wife of a person said to be a political prisoner in Turkey, in connection with a dispute about the reason the payments were made." Isbilen, who in 2022 was 77 years old, is from a wealthy family, but when her politician husband was jailed she wanted help moving her assets out of Turkey. Lawyers for Isbilen previously told the court that tens of millions of her funds had been misappropriated, with Turk failing to explain where the money had gone. In Friday's ruling, Johnson said it "has long been Mr Turk's case" that the £750,000 payment was made on Isbilen's own accord as she believed Mountbatten-Windsor could help with her husband. title: Deadly shooting near Paris investigated as 'crime of terrorism', minister says
description: One person is killed and five wounded in a series of attacks and the suspected gunman has been apprehended.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Emergency services at the scene of shooting near Paris One person has been killed and five others wounded - three seriously - in a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which authorities are investigating as "terrorism". Several drive-by shootings took place on Friday - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière. The rampage lasted almost 15 minutes, said Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. A12-year-old girl is among the wounded. The suspected attacker has been arrested. The motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise". Nuñez told reporters in Trappes: "It's clearly a terrorist crime, that's what [the prosecutor] has said." The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning. The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said. The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La Verrière. A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La Verrière on the main N10 road that runs through the town. French police inspect the scene of the shooting in Trappes, near Paris French firefighters and police were seen at a petrol station in the area Asked what the motive for the shootings may have been, the mayor of Trappes said that the victim who had died was of African origin and one of those in a critical condition was of North African descent. The attack had a "racist, probably Islamophobic overtone", he said. In its own statement, the anti-terror prosecutor called for caution regarding the identity of the victims. However, among the alleged offences covered by the investigation, the prosecutor listed "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise" with the aggravated circumstance of acts committed because of "real or perceived membership of a particular race, ethnicity, nation or religion". The mother of the injured 12-year-old told French broadcaster RTL her daughter suffered eight gunshot wounds and needed surgery. "How could anyone do this to a child?" she asked. The mother said her daughter had been wearing a headscarf and questioned whether this was why she was attacked. "She's a child who was born in France, in Trappes. She has the right to live in France, to make her life in France," she added. The attacker reportedly travelled down a main road, shooting intermittently out of his car window. A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon" with bursts of fire. Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two. Rabeh said the shooter had hit a health centre, a petrol station and several vehicles during the spree. The suspected attacker was then arrested at the nearby town of Coignières, local media report. The interior minister said the motive of the attacker remained unclear. The suspect, a 39-year-old, was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV. PNAT said its investigation also includes "possession of a Category A weapon" - which includes military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts. The anti-terrorist office also said its investigation is looking into "conspiracy with a terrorist group for the purpose of preparing crimes against persons". title: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
description: Another 34 people are injured in the southern Karak governorate, and a manhunt is now under way.
body: Between 150 and 200 people were in the church at the time of the shooting, according to one witness Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, after gunmen opened fire on a church, officials have said. At least 34 others were injured in the church in the village of Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday. The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing, in what government spokesperson Dr al-Momani Mohammad described as a "heinous attack". Jordan's King Abdullah II said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties." Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV. He said two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes. In a news conference, Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya described the incident as a "terrorist" act carried out by a "group of extremists" and said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators. He added that the incident was "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan". No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack. Security officials and members of the public gathered outside the Greek Orthodox church on Friday Initial reports from Jordanian officials indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven. CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church. Two of the attackers are seen making their way onto what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns. Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes. This video can not be played Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed. In his post on X, King Abdullah II offered his condolences to the families of the victims, writing: "Whoever imagines that the bullets of treachery can divide the ranks of Jordanians will fail in his endeavour before our steadfastness and unity." Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media. Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan. Such violence is rare in Jordan, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the country in the past. Additional reporting by Husam Assal, BBC Arabic. title: Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen at site of Jordan shooting
description: Dozens of people had been inside the church for a funeral when the shooting began, local media report.
body: This video can not be played Six people were killed when gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, a government spokesperson has said. Another 28 people were injured in the church in the Karak governorate on Friday. The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car and began shooting inside the church before fleeing the scene. Security forces have been deployed to the area after the "heinous" attack, government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said. Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church in Jordan. title: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
description: Ukraine and Russia confirm the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.
body: These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said. The statement said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" would begin on 29 October. "Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," it added. Ukraine and Russia later confirmed the ceasefire was agreed. Oleshky, in the Kherson region, was seized by Russian forces during the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Remaining residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive. This video can not be played Trump: First lady's 'initiative' led to truce for Ukraine city The White House statement said Melania Trump and her representative had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire". "Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible". The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for. Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future". "To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said. In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed the truce had been agreed. "The military is currently working to coordinate the timings of a ceasefire," Dmitry Peskov said. "Those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement." Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water. They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education. Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations. The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months. The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv. Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces. The city was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children. While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war. In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide". Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children. In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa. Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July. According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace. "I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year. "And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home'." title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets
description: Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when the 2024 general election would be held.
body: Anthony Lee and his wife Laura pleaded guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have received suspended prison sentences after they admitted to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election. Anthony Lee used "inside information" emerging from a private meeting called by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to bet on the general election date months before it took place, Southwark Crown Court heard. Lee and his wife Laura stood to win more than £23,000 had their cheating not been uncovered, the court heard. Lee was sentenced to 10 months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, while his wife was sentenced to four months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for a year. Amy Hind, a former Tory party employee who was working as an NHS business support manager, was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment, suspended for a year, after previously pleading guilty to cheating on the date of the election. Judge Tony Baumgartner, sentencing the three of them, said their conduct "risked undermining" the confidence the public has in the Conservative Party "as an institution", "undermining trust in the democratic process" and the "integrity of the gambling system". The trio were among several people charged with betting offences by the Gambling Commission. The trials of other defendants will take place next year and in 2028. Former Conservative MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.
