title: Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
description: Satellite images show oil spreading for miles along the coastline, threatening local marine wildlife
body: An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas. Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran. The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed. UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black. The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts". Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage. Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October. But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR. Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish. They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce. Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation. But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish. The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory. BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2. Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished. Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship. Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea. The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media. All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October. Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October. Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane. Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries. Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities. title: Trial set for men accused of synagogue bomb plot
description: The Iranian men are alleged to have identified Heaton Park Synagogue and the Jewish Museum as targets.
body: Salam Ahmadyan and Rahman Salehi are accused of plotting to target the Jewish community in Manchester Two Iranian men have appeared in court over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade bomb. Salam Ahmadyan, 36, of Liverpool, and Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, are accused of conducting hostile reconnaissance at Heaton Park Synagogue, which was subject to a fatal attack last year, along with the Jewish Museum in Cheetham Hill. The pair, who arrived illegally into the UK on boats, are charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts on or before 20 September. They deny the charges. They appeared via videolink at the Old Bailey and a trial date was set at Manchester Crown Court for 15 June 2027. It is alleged Ahmadyan and Salehi were in contact with an Iranian national who directed and co-ordinated the planned attack, with the third party most likely operating within Iran. The men are accused of getting instructions to make a chlorine bomb and acquiring liquids, components and equipment required in order to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps of potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack. The pair deny the charges against them. The trial is estimated to last five weeks. The next court hearing is due to take place on 16 April next year. Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, drove into the gates of Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue on 2 October last year, and began a knife attack while wearing a fake suicide belt. title: Civil servant who juggled five jobs says he was 'surprised' to be charged with fraud
description: Kashim Chowdhury denied being dishonest when not telling employers he had other jobs.
body: Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraududlently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public sector jobs. A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple government jobs says he was ''surprised'' to have been charged with fraud. Kashim Chowdhury told the jury at Southwark Crown Court he had not been dishonest in failing to tell his employers he had other government jobs. "At that time I was just on auto pilot, I was like a robot, I was not thinking clearly," he said. Chowdhury, 55, from east London, is accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight overlapping public sector jobs. He was contractually obliged to work full time and was paid a full-time salary by each organisation. He is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000. In March 2023 Chowdhury began working for the Home Office despite being under contract to work full time at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency. The court was told he started the Home Office job while on sick leave from three of his other jobs. Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ asked him: "If you were really sick for work, how were you able to start your work at the Home Office?" Chowdhury said: "I did not want this job at the Home Office, I was told there would be adequate support and I could work whatever hours I wanted to work." Organ also asked why he did not submit a sick note to the Home Office "You were using these sick notes to be able to cope. It was all too much wasn't it?" Chowdhury rejected the suggestion, adding: "I wanted to carry on working." In May 2023, Chowdhury was contracted to work 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days. He told the jury he agreed with his employers to work flexibly and that his work was project or output based. He said this was agreed "informally" via text messages but the phones used to send the texts had gone missing when his house was searched by investigators. He said that to cope with the workload he would work from 07:00 on Saturdays and Sundays and not finish until 20:00 or 21:00. Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs Organ asked him: "Wasn't that a bit much for you?" "I was house bound, I was looking after my mum," he said. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity". His line manager at the UKHSA, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023 to discuss his sick leave. She previously told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin. She told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck." But Chowdhury denied having worn make-up at the meeting ''That's a smear, I've never worn make-up in my life. At that particular time, I was suffering from anxiety and depression. I had already submitted my sick note, there was no need to put on make-up.'' title: US justice department investigating Corey Lewandowski over DHS role
description: Trump's former campaign manager is reportedly being investigated for allegedly using his role at the Department of Homeland for financial gain.
body: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating whether Corey Lewandowski, who was a top aide to former Department ⁠of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, personally profited from his role, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. Lewandowski worked closely with Noem as a special government employee until March, when the two were both ousted after a series of controversies, including the fatal shootings of US citizens by immigration officers. The probe is related to contracts the agency signed under Noem's leadership, a source told CBS. The BBC has contacted Lewandowski's attorney, who told CBS his client denies any wrongdoing. "Mr Lewandowski has not been contacted by the justice department regarding any investigation," his attorney, Adam Trigg, said. Asked about the investigation on Thursday, President Donald Trump told reporters he had heard about it but did not know the details, adding, "I want my people to be honest". "And if they're not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted," he said. Lewandowski served as a campaign manager to Trump during his first presidential run in 2016 and helped advise his 2024 campaign. DHS officials told Reuters that Lewandowski had approved some DHS contracts despite not having the legal authority to do so as a special government employee. He also allegedly put certain grants and contracts on hold, including some involving the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the officials told Reuters. Special government employees serve as temporary advisers to federal agencies and are given strict limits on how much they can work and what they can do. The justice department took on the investigation after receiving a referral from the DHS inspector general's office, which is made up of lawyers charged with monitoring the agency's conduct and operations. At DHS, Lewandowski served as Noem's de facto chief of staff. Noem also faced a contract controversy. Shortly before she left office, lawmakers pressed her about the process she had used to award a $220m (£164m) advertising contract to two companies with ties to her and people in her inner circle. The Wall Street Journal has reported, external that Lewandowski also allegedly tried to use his role at DHS for financial gain by asking Middle Eastern countries to hire him on the side to help with visa and other DHS issues. title: Poulter leaves LIV as exodus of big names continues
description: Ian Poulter wants to help his sons become professional golfers and develop his YouTube channel as he announces his exit from LIV Golf.
body: Ian Poulter was co-captain of the Majesticks team alongside Lee Westwood Ryder Cup legend Ian Poulter has become the latest star name to confirm he is quitting LIV Golf - leaving the breakaway tour's future looking increasingly uncertain. The 50-year-old Englishman was among a plethora of stars lured by LIV when the Saudi Arabia-backed project was launched in 2022 and was a staunch defender of the circuit when it was criticised. But Poulter has followed the likes of major champions Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen in announcing his departure. He has said he wants to help his two sons, Luke and Joshua, pursue professional careers, as well as develop his YouTube channel. Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month. It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed to the proposed competition in 2027. "I wanted everyone to hear it direct from me that I have decided to not move forward with being part of LIV 2.0," Poulter wrote on his social media channels. "Needless to say, it was a tough decision and one I thought about and discussed at length with my family and team. "Ultimately, the opportunity to spend more time at home with my family, reduce international travel, focus on senior golf and have the opportunity to pursue other interests was something that I felt was right for me at this stage of my life and career." Former Open champion Oosthuizen quits LIV Golf Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV Golf LIV Golf secures potential $300m investment Former world number five Poulter was co-captain of the Majesticks team alongside fellow Englishman and Ryder Cup icon Lee Westwood. Westwood's future plans remain unclear. Poulter's decision to leave comes in the same week as 2010 Open champion Oosthuizen, who captained the Southern Guards GC team and said quitting was the "hardest decision" of his career. Last week, two-time major winner Rahm gave up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV after reaching a separation agreement. Abraham Ancer and David Puig are also leaving while Sergio Garcia, Thomas Pieters, Tom McKibbin, Laurie Canter and Adrian Meronk appear unlikely to stay with LIV. Richard Bland, Cameron Tringale and Brendan Steele are three of the few players to commit to the second phase of the breakaway circuit. LIV's future could hinge on whether it can secure the signature of American superstar Bryson DeChambeau, who ESPN reported earlier this week "remains committed" to the league. In his statement, Poulter acknowledged LIV has "clearly divided opinion", but said he will be "forever proud" to be part of its founding group. "Change is never easy and it's fair to say professional golf has experienced plenty of it over the last few years," he added. "But I've always believed that change can create opportunity and ultimately lead to positive outcomes. "There will undoubtedly be more changes ahead, but I am confident the game will continue to grow, evolve, and deliver the very best for golf fans around the world." title: Glasgow museums remove mummified remains from public view over ethical concerns
description: Kelvingrove Museum and The Hunterian say they have removed human remains from display because of ethical concerns.
body: Lady Shep-En-Hor's sarcophagus on display at The Hunterian Museum in Glasgow Two museums in Glasgow have removed the remains of Egyptian mummies from display over ethical concerns. The mummified corpse of the priest Nekht was taken out of public view at Kelvingrove Gallery, while The Hunterian Museum has covered Lady Shep-En-Hor's body in a specially designed textile to protect it from being seen by visitors. The institutions said the decisions followed a reassessment of their duty of care towards the deceased. It comes after the International Council of Museums (Icom) revised its code of ethics, recommending that the "inherent dignity" of human remains be upheld. Both museums said they would consider repatriation of the remains should they receive an approach from a country or institution. Despite the new code of ethics, there is no uniform approach across Scotland's museum sector with different institutions given leeway on how to implement it. A spokesperson for National Museums Scotland (NMS) said it was not considering any changes to the display of human remains in its collection. NMS has a large collection of Scottish archaeological remains, external as well as mummified people from Egypt and Peru. The Hunterian Museum said the decision to remove the sarcophagus followed a reassessment of their duty of care towards the deceased Glasgow Life, which manages Kelvingrove, said it had taken the decision to remove the painted coffin containing the remains of Nekht in the "absence of consent from the deceased individual or their ancestors". Nekht is thought to have lived at some point between 1985 and 1797 BC and was excavated at Beni Hasan in Middle Egypt during digs carried out in the early 20th century. The remains were donated to the city of Glasgow in 1923. Is it ever ethical for museums to display human remains? Glasgow university returns human remains to South Africa A spokesperson for Glasgow Life said the withdrawal of the remains "reflected contemporary museum practice". They added a new draft human remains policy proposed that they were only displayed "where there is documented and informed consent from the deceased individual or, in appropriate circumstances, their descendants". They said a parliamentary group on African repatriation had highlighted "ethical concerns" over the display of such remains due to the "constant disregard" of potential wishes and intentions of ancestors who buried them. A mummified male head, right foot and a right hand recovered from the Valley of the Kings in Luxor were also taken out of public view. The spokesperson added: "We believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." Kelvingrove Museum removed mummified Egyptian remains from its display because it was not possible to obtain consent from the deceased or their family Meanwhile, The Hunterian said it had sought advice from Egyptologists before protecting Lady Shep-En-Hor's remains as part of a "commitment to becoming a more ethical institution". A spokesperson for the museum, managed by the University of Glasgow, said the conclusion of that consultation led to the view Lady Shep-En-Hor "deserved privacy in death". Her ornate sarcophagus, which has been on display almost continuously since 1820, will remain on public view as a "fine work of late period ancient Egyptian funerary art". Lady Shep-En-Hor has never been removed from the coffin, but has been X-rayed and CT scanned in the last 50 years. In the 1970s, several theories were put forward questioning whether the remains in the coffin were actually those of Lady Shep-En-Hor. The Hunterian said excavators in the 19th century occasionally swapped over remains from different coffins, with better preserved specimens placed in the most intact or ornate sarcophagi. The Icom code, which was revised in June, states museums should "uphold the inherent dignity of human remains and promote respect for their significance". It adds: "Decisions about these items and collections should be made in collaboration with descendants or communities from which they originate, if known." Prof Steph Scholten, who sits on the Icom ethics committee, said the code was intended as guidance and the final decision ultimately rested with each individual institution. He added: "What the code of ethics puts forward is that these topics need careful consideration and decision making, they do not suggest one fixed outcome. "Kelvingrove and The Hunterian have come to slightly different outcomes about our displays. "The code of ethics does not prescribe that all human remains should be taken of display." title: PSG v Lyon moved as Paris prepares for more protests
description: Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon at the Parc des Princes is pushed back 24 hours as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests.
body: Paris St-Germain fans celebrated winning the Champions League near the Eiffel Tower in May 2026 Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon has been pushed back 24 hours to Monday as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests. The fixture at the Parc des Princes in Paris had been scheduled to kick off at 19:45 GMT on Sunday but will instead take place at 20:30 on Monday. The Ligue de Football Professionnel (LFP) announced the postponement in a statement, external on Friday after French police prohibited the fixture from taking place on its original date. French authorities are preparing a major security operation for demonstrations planned for Saturday. Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations last Saturday to protest rising fuel prices, education standards and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests. Marches took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions and student groups, and were marred by some incidents of violence, looting and destruction. The security challenge is further complicated by Sunday's NFL match between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France, an event expected to require a significant police deployment. The game will be played in Saint-Denis, about 10km from Place de la Bastille, where the protests are expected to begin. The disruptions have already affected France's domestic football schedule with Toulouse's Ligue 1 home game against Troyes moved from Saturday to Sunday at the request of authorities. Reigning French and European champions PSG are second in the standings after seven matches, while Lyon lead the table on 14 points, ahead of the holders on goal difference. The match will also now be played on the same day as the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London. Injured PSG pair Ousmane Dembele, the 2025 winner, and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are among the contenders for the award. PSG on different level - but where do they rank against other great sides? title: PM defends Gogglebox appearance after Badenoch criticism
description: Burnham says he "makes no apology" for the move as Kemi Badenoch says she is "amazed" he has time.
body: Burnham will appear on the show with his friend Steve Rotheram, the Labour mayor of the Liverpool City Region Prime Minister Andy Burnham has defended his decision to appear on a celebrity episode of Channel 4 hit show Gogglebox after opposition leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "amazed" he had time to do it. Badenoch told BBC Breakfast that "even as a junior minister or as a secretary of state, I never had time to go on Gogglebox" and it "takes hours to do". The Conservative leader was responding after Burnham was revealed in the line-up of a celebrity episode of the show in aid of Stand Up To Cancer - which will air later. "I'm proud to support Stand Up To Cancer. I make no apology for trying to lead with a bit of lightness and at times a bit of humour, that's the way I go at things," Burnham said. The former Greater Manchester mayor will appear on the programme alongside friend Steve Rotheram, the Labour mayor of the Liverpool City Region. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Burnham continued: "It is always a moment in the annual calendar where we support Stand Up To Cancer through Gogglebox," Burnham said of the recurring charity special. "Steve and I are proud to do it. "I'm trying to give the country a lift - trying to give the county some hope. "That's always my approach and it's what I'm trying to do. "It may not appeal to everybody when it comes to Gogglebox. "It's Stand Up To Cancer night and I've always been somebody who puts my shoulder behind the fight against cancer." Kemi Bademnoch questioned how the prime minister could have time to appear on the programme However, Badenoch said appearing on the programme was "not my thing". "What I'm amazed at is that Andy Burnham has got time to go on Gogglebox," she said. "When you get a new job in politics it's so difficult. "There's so much to do and it's like drinking from a fire hose. "Even as a junior minister or as a secretary of state I never had time to go on Gogglebox - I just don't know how he's got the time. "Gogglebox takes hours to do." Describing Burnham as "on social media all day", she said she could do the same but "I wouldn't actually be able to do my job as leader of the opposition". "My job is to hold him to account and I've seen a lot of prime ministers up close and I've never seen a prime minister have the time to do this much Goggleboxing, social media and Lad Bible," she added. The special Gogglebox edition airs on Channel 4 at 21:05 BST. title: Arsenal fear Saka could be out for two months
description: Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka could be sidelined for up to eight weeks with the quadriceps injury he suffered against Bayern Munich.
body: Bukayo Saka was substituted early in Wednesday's Champions League group game against Bayern Munich Arsenal fear Bukayo Saka could miss a minimum of six weeks with the quadriceps injury he sustained in their Champions League tie against Bayern Munich. The 25-year-old will undergo an MRI scan on Friday afternoon to better assess the problem, which forced him off in Wednesday's 2-2 draw at the Allianz Arena. Fluid around the affected muscle has made diagnosing the injury difficult, but club medics are estimating, after early examinations, Saka will miss a minimum of six weeks and it could be even longer. If those early concerns are realised, he will miss a clutch of key games for the Gunners, as well as England's forthcoming Uefa Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain. "We need a few more scans and opinions from the specialists," said Arsenal head coach Mikel Arteta. "When a player has to walk off the pitch, he is struggling to walk without any pain, and is restricted to movement; it is not a good sign. Let's be a little bit patient so we can give a definitive assessment. "He's got another MRI as there was quite a lot of fluid in the area so it was quite difficult to understand the extent of the injury. We will know more tomorrow." Saka will miss Saturday's home Premier League match against Everton, where second-placed Arsenal will hope to close a three-point gap on leaders Manchester City. The Arsenal academy product has had fitness issues in recent months and his game time was managed at the end of last season, as well as with England at the World Cup, because of an Achilles injury he suffered in March. He missed the March international break and seven games for the Gunners, but returned to help them lift the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years. Saka started the Champions League final defeat by Paris St-Germain but was substituted after 54 minutes, and only started three of England's eight games at the World Cup - scoring a hat-trick in the 6-4 third-place win over France. The forward also had surgery on a hamstring injury he picked up in December 2024, which kept him out for 101 days in the 2024-25 campaign. He made 49 appearances as Arsenal won the title last term, despite a stop-start season. As well as the Achilles issue, Saka pulled out of a game in January against Leeds with a hip injury in the warm-up, while a hamstring problem also kept him out for about four weeks. The fact Saka needs follow-up scans and is likely to be out for up to eight weeks is a major blow for Arteta and Arsenal. The Gunners boss had been speaking about how the player had been adapting his positioning to be more of a regular goalscorer for the club in recent weeks and the winger has scored four goals in 11 appearances so far this season. But now Saka has gone down with another muscle injury there are questions about whether he still has the robustness that made him a certain starter in the Arsenal team. The 25-year-old had Achilles, hip and hamstring problems last season and underwent surgery on a hamstring injury in the previous season which kept him out for 101 days. He also had his game time managed at the World Cup in the summer with England and Arteta acknowledged Saka's robustness and availability has "certainly been different in the last year or so". Arsenal tried to sign a world-class forward to level up their frontline in the summer but were unable to do so, with unsuccessful pursuits of Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez. They did bring in Greece international Christos Tzolis, but he is currently injured too. That has left them with Noni Madueke, Eberechi Eze and 16-year-old Max Dowman as alternative wing options. Teenager Dowman has had limited minutes this season but Arteta spoke glowingly of his talent and ability to impact matches. Saka injury 'does not look good' - how will Arsenal cope? title: Smith partnership & Saracens spice - Furbank on life at Quins
description: George Furbank traded champions Northampton for struggling Harlequins - and the early signs of synergy with Marcus Smith are promising.
body: Furbank arrived at the Stoop in the summer after a decade in the senior Northampton squad In the 10 years he spent in the Franklin's Gardens dressing rooms, George Furbank sang the line plenty of times. "Big city lights don't bother me," goes Northampton's victory song,, external a version of local anthem The Fields Are Green. "Northampton Saints I'd rather be." Had Northampton offered him a longer contract at the end of last season, Furbank may still have been with the champions. They didn't though, and Harlequins did. And suddenly those big city lights beckoned. "Yeah, the big city lights are a change, but a change I'm enjoying," says Furbank. "There is just stuff on your doorstep which is unreal - great food spots, good coffee spots. I feel like within 10 minutes I can walk to get anything I need." The 30-year-old, who grew up in Cambridgeshire, has opted to live nearer to central London, rather than right by Quins' Guildford training base. After a decade up the line in Northampton, Furbank is now closer to his partner and old school friends. On the pitch, the move has brought him into tandem with Marcus Smith. A twin playmaker axis made up of two of England's most extravagantly talented footballers was the concept. After a Smith-less Quins were thrashed 48-0 by Gloucester on Furbank's debut, some questioned whether such notions were a luxury, given the Londoners' under-powered pack. But, once they got to play together, the duo's attack has been their defence. After two minutes against Sale, Smith pulled the ball out the back to Furbank, whose long pass allowed hooker Sam Riley to trundle in. After eight minutes, Furbank's blurringly fast hands set up a try for Smith. After 19 minutes, the pair were part of a blindside pod of runners that barged through for another score. Harlequins ultimately lost the game 28-24, but Furbank and Smith pulled strings effectively again the following week in a resounding Challenge Cup victory over French strugglers Vannes. "He's a one-of-a-kind player," said Furbank of Smith. "I think people take him for granted sometimes in terms of the player he can be. The things he can do on a rugby pitch - I don't think many others many others can do "He's obviously a massive threat with ball in hand and has a great passing game as well, so it's just about trying to understand what he's going to do in certain moments then making my move off that." Furbank and Smith start together for the third game in succession for Sunday's Prem game against Saracens Team-mates have described how riffing off Smith's brilliance is different to playing alongside fly-halves that play more conventionally and to more predictable patterns. So far for Harlequins though, there have been some promising signs of harmony. This Sunday will be a chance to see how Furbank and Smith's partnership stands up to the noisy neighbours from north of the river. Saracens have stoked their rivalry with their trademark social media spikiness, labelling the meeting at the Stoop as Quins' 'cup final', external on X. Harlequins have certainly risen to the occasion in recent meetings. A 20-14 home win in a feisty encounter last season was a rare highpoint in a difficult campaign. A similarly dogged display carried the day in the same fixture in 2024. With prop Fin Baxter back after 10 months out to steel Harlequins pack, the hosts are hoping to snap a streak of three straight league losses by completing the hat-trick. For Furbank it will be a different flavour of fire on the Prem's 'derby weekend'. "I obviously experienced quite a few East Midlands derbies and they were unbelievable days," he added. "I'm expecting no different from the London derby to be honest." England's training squad to prepare for the Nations Championships will be announced in the hours after the final whistle. Furbank, who missed England's summer campaign after an appendicitis added to a long run of injuries, says he is "chomping at the bit" to be involved. First though, he has club business to take care of. "We're chasing a performance and if we start performing consistently for 80 minutes, we feel the wins will come," he says. Sunday and Saracens would be a perfect place to start. title: Man Utd manager Carrick refuses to rule out dropping Fernandes in emotional address
description: Michael Carrick speaks for five uninterrupted minutes at media briefing to outline what Manchester United means to him, then refuses to rule out dropping Bruno Fernandes.
body: This video can not be played Man Utd boss Carrick responds to criticism Under-pressure Manchester United boss Michael Carrick delivered a passionate and emotional address lasting five minutes and 30 seconds as he battles to save his job. And he refused to rule out dropping skipper Bruno Fernandes for Sunday's Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Old Trafford. Instead of taking his seat and answering questions as normal in Friday's scheduled pre-match media conference at Carrington, Carrick said he wanted to start himself. It was a strategy former boss Sir Alex Ferguson used, although the legendary Scot rarely spoke at such length. After a run of seven games without a win, culminating in Wednesday's shocking 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como, and attacks on the club's hierarchy by defender Lisandro Martinez and then Fernandes' condemnation of his own tactics in Italy, Carrick wanted to reaffirm his view of what United stood for. "Recently we haven't had a good time, I think that's pretty obvious," he said. "Wednesday was a bad night, and it hurt me to see us play like that. It was unacceptable. "My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club, and the supporters, and they can be proud of in the identity we show. We have gone away from that recently. It's important we all recognise that. "The foundation and values of this football club have been etched for many years. I totally understand and get every single one of them. "There's a resilience about this football club that runs very deep. I've seen it with my own eyes, I've felt it, I'm know some of the individuals closely who have been a big part of that history. "Entitlement cannot be at this football club. "It was based on being humble, having humility, and hard work. We can never lose that, and I won't let us lose that." Asked about Fernandes and whether he has considered dropping him, a defiant Carrick added: "The most important thing for me is the team, the squad and dynamics in the squad. "It's about the football club. I'll always do what is best for the football club." Conte plays down 'unfounded' Man Utd speculation Should Man Utd boss Carrick drop captain Fernandes? Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club? Manchester United won 12 of their 17 games under Michael Carrick last season Club sources said on Thursday Fernandes would not have the captaincy taken away or be fined for his post-match observations following the Como defeat. In a further interview on Wednesday night with Sky Italia, the Portugal international referred to Manchester United's storied history. "At this club, there's too much focus on what's been done in the past," said Fernandes. "But we're not those people anymore. The club and the players need to understand that. "Unfortunately for us - especially when it comes to the players - those who join expect to win trophies, win games, and reach the highest level, that's been very difficult at this club in recent years." Whether Carrick was aware of Fernandes' comments about United's history before he spoke was uncertain. When asked again if he would take the captaincy away from the 32-year-old midfielder, Carrick repeated: "I will always do what is best for the football club." He then refused to say whether he had spoken to Fernandes about his conduct, adding: "I don't think this is the time to go into too much detail." Despite the challenge to his authority, Carrick said the United dressing room was not divided. "No, it's not," he added. "We just need to get back to doing what we do best." Carrick also said the club were 'doing everything' to support Fernandes and his family, whose Cheshire home was burgled on Wednesday. "Thankfully they weren't directly affected even though it is an awful situation." Carrick named legendary United figures such as Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney and Ferguson as examples of the humility, sacrifice and hard work expected of United players. That was at odds with his post-match criticism on Wednesday, when he said if you don't run forward or back properly, you will not win games. Asked how he would persuade his current squad to adhere to the values expected and he demanded, Carrick added: "It's clear as day. "I'm not telling you anything new. I haven't invented that. That's the make-up of any good football team. You have to earn the right to be better than your opponent. That never changes. "What we look like as a group is my responsibility. That's the privileged position I am in. I'll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and everyone else to stay dry. "[Wednesday] hurts an awful lot, but that doesn't stop me. That hurt is used as pure motivation and inspiration to want more, expect more and get us going in a different direction." title: Woman at centre of Cornell University rape inquiry in 'constant fear', lawyer says
description: The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, alleged she was drugged and raped by several men on Cornell's campus.
body: The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her lawyer has said. Speaking to the BBC ahead of a hearing in the civil case on Friday in New York, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said: "She feels under fire." The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over the alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. When the case went viral, a series of "I am Jane Doe" solidarity posts appeared, but there was a separate campaign aimed at unmasking her and defending the men, who have all denied any wrongdoing. The men, who are also being sued by the woman, have not been charged with any crimes. "I am Jane Doe" placards were seen being held during a rally in Manhattan against sexual violence on 8 October With initial proceedings now under way in the civil case, Giuffra told the BBC that these last few weeks have been "a very hard time" for his client, who isn't doing a lot beyond "surviving". Her decision to sue was rooted in a desire for closure and to take power back, he said. Giufrra visited Jane Doe this week and found that she hadn't been sleeping well – relying on medication to get rest. Now in trauma therapy, he says she doesn't feel safe in her own home following malicious threats that were directed at her and her family. After her address was published online without her consent, someone called in a fake emergency that led to police in full tactical gear drawing assault rifles on her father, her friend and her brother at their family home. "It's just constant fear," he said. He added that despite this her resolve hadn't been shaken and she remains determined to overhaul the university system at Cornell, and across the country, to protect survivors. Cornell University, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of Jane Doe's case. After facing intense pressure, the college's president announced that fraternity parties would be suspended until the end of the academic year to allow for a thorough review to determine whether and how they can safely continue. The school also said it would add sexual assault investigators to its police force. Giuffra, however, says he is surprised that Cornell has not reached out to him and believes they have been focused solely on "damage control". He says any agreement with Cornell to resolve the civil lawsuit will need to include "steps to ensure there are no more Jane Does" and if there are, that they are going to be supported. The BBC contacted Cornell for comment who directed us to the university's previous statements and comments on its internal investigation in 2024. New York's governor Kathy Hochul appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted. Giuffra expects it will take a long time to do a proper investigation but is concerned that they will be going after evidence that is now "stale". "A lot of the communication was on Snapchat, Snapchat goes away," he told the BBC. "The best time to get evidence is around the time of the crime and that just didn't happen." However, Giuffra believes he can win the civil case against the university, the men and others, where the burden of proof is lower than a criminal case. Civil cases require a preponderance of the evidence, that it's more likely than not it happened, while criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Recent high profile cases have shown the way juries evaluate consent can be unpredictable. "I wouldn't have taken the case if I didn't think it was a strong case that I could win and get her some closure." title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?
description: The UK government has warned households to have three days of essential supplies on hand.
body: Do you have three days' worth of food and water in your home? That is what the government has told all of us to have on hand to get through a national emergency, as well as some other basic items. Its "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days. On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments". As one expert warns the UK is "light years" behind our neighbours when it comes to preparing for major disruption, we've drilled down into what you need and why. The government recommends having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods. Wet wipes, a torch and cash are also recommended - you can scroll through below to see the full list. Disaster planning expert Professor Lucy Easthope said the goal of asking household to prepare is to make it easier for emergency service to cope in the event of a national emergency. For example, the government says people who need medication should have an extra supply just in case. Prof Easthope says: "If people have got their heart pills for an extra for an extra 48 hours, it stops [response crews] from having to immediately find an emergency pharmacist." While the latest government campaign only launched on Thursday, some people are well ahead of the game. Speaking to Radio 5 Live, Bridgette Clamp, who lives in near Penzance in Cornwall, said she has stocked up on "lots of tinned goods" as well as "flour, yeast and everything to bake bread". "We're rocking and rolling," she says. Bridgette says she also bought generators and water pumps following Storm Goretti earlier this year One woman, who spoke to 5 Live anonymously, said she bought "loads and loads" of emergency food - but ended up eating it before it was strictly necessary. Like others, she wondered if the government was "scaremongering", adding: "I don't know but I've certainly bought into it." Rob, who lives off-grid in north Wales, told the programme he has stocked up on so many supplies he "wouldn't even notice" if a disaster struck. But he said he still felt there was "a bit of scaremongering" going on and wondered if he would ever need it all. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the advice - which is similar to guidance issued by the previous government - was not triggered by any "particular piece of intelligence", but rather about improving "national resilience" more generally. The government's announcement focused on extreme weather events, which are becoming more frequent because of man-made climate change - but Streeting also referred to the threat of "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, and supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists". Prof Easthope said she has been lobbying the government to launch this sort of campaign for "about 16 years". She said successive governments have been hesitant of "putting out information that might cause tension" - and speculated that this advice may have been "rushed" out ahead of Storm Austen hitting the UK. Expert Prof Lucy Easthope says the UK is playing "massive catch up" to other nations in disaster preparedness While many of us will already have a stash of tinned food in the cupboards, fewer homes are likely to have a store of bottled water. Paul from Torquay, Devon, said to Radio 5 Live: "Who on earth carries three day supply of water?" He added: "I think they've made it our responsibility, rather than their responsibility." Prof Easthope described the UK as "light years" behind neighbouring countries when it comes to preparedness. "Countries like Scandinavia, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, they've been good at this for years," she said. France advises people to store 72-hours' worth of food, while the German government says homes should have enough supplies to last for a 10-day period. "This is one area where I'm very comfortable saying we are playing massive catch-up," added Easthope. Awareness campaigns such as "think 72 hours" make a big difference in the US, Australia and "all around Europe", she said. However, in the UK, she said disaster messaging often gets parodied, or governments are accused of "panic-mongering". "We have seen the pendulum shift" in recent years, she adds, saying that "we are now seeing people recognise this" as an issue that needs tackling. title: Military base asylum plans challenged at High Court
description: Campaigners are asking for a judicial review into Home Office plans for MoD Bicester.
body: The government plans to provide accommodation for up to 1,256 men at the site near Bicester Campaigners against government plans to house asylum seekers at a former Ministry of Defence (MoD) site have taken their complaints to the High Court. The group Wrong Plan Wrong Site is appealing for a judicial review into Home Office proposals for the former MoD Bicester site in Oxfordshire. The plans, which the government is trying to fast-track using an Urgent Crown Development application, could see up to 1,256 men housed. But they have prompted a backlash locally, with Wrong Plan Wrong Site the first to submit an official legal challenge. In August, the government concluded an environmental assessment was unnecessary for the proposed development. But campaigners are now challenging that decision, with the group saying there were "credible concerns about potential significant environmental effects". The complaint was lodged with the High Court on Friday, and is backed by Cherwell District Council. The campaigners behind Wrong Plan Wrong Site have taken their complaints to the High Court The Home Office first made an Urgent Crown Development application regarding the site in July. The special procedure is used to fast-track applications deemed to be of "national importance", and involves an expedited consultation process on behalf of the Secretary of State. It later agreed to hold a short public consultation on the proposals, which local MP Calum Miller hailed at the time as a "win for democracy". But campaigners said in "rushing" the plans through, the government had "failed to consider the potential environmental effects of the development". "We are not asking for special treatment," a spokesperson for the group said. "We are asking the government to demonstrate that it has followed the law and properly assessed the environmental consequences of a development of this scale and in this environmentally-sensitive location. "There are legitimate questions about its potential environmental impact, and those questions deserve clear, evidence-based answers, not a rushed job." Wrong Plan Wrong Site's legal submission comes a month after the village of Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the MoD Bicester proposals. The Home Office declined to comment on the legal challenge, but previously said it was "closing every asylum hotel, saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support since the election". It added: "We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites which are designed to be self-contained to reduce impact on the local community." title: Watch: Moment part of Brighton's historic West Pier collapses
description: Footage taken during Storm Austen shows a section of the famous landmark battered by large waves and collapsing into the water.
body: This video can not be played A section of Brighton's historic West Pier has collapsed into the sea during the wet and windy weather brought by Storm Austen. In footage obtained by the BBC, one side of the famous landmark in the East Sussex city can be seen falling into the water as it is battered by large waves. The pier - which first opened in 1866 - attracted two million visitors at its peak, though its popularity declined after World War Two. While it was closed to the public in 1975, the increasingly ruined structure has become a symbol of Brighton for some. Major sections fell into the sea during storms in late 2002, while two separate fires the following year destroyed most of what remained. Subsequent storms have destroyed its iron frame even further. title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
description: The prime ministers says unexpected events seem to be becoming more common and it was wise to prepare.
body: This video can not be played 'Be prepared': PM Andy Burnham suggests stocking up on basic food items The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies. With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common". The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster. Burnham added: "It's not about panic buying... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation." At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine. She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while." Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work. "But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup. "I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those." Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience. The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system". Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common. "Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now. "It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience." Why should I stockpile and what will I need? Military aircraft to help get UK 'on front foot' to fight wildfires, Burnham says Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns A checklist drawn up by the government recommends having nine litres of water per person – enough for three days – along with non-perishable food such as tinned meat and vegetables or dried fruit. The government suggests having an FM radio, either battery or wind-up. During a national crisis, the BBC would prioritise broadcasting news, as well as health and safety information. In the event of a severe power cut, FM radio will be the best way to receive these updates. The list also suggests hand sanitiser, wet wipes and toiletries, food for any pets, supplies for any babies, a torch, blankets, a charged power bank for devices, cash in case payment systems collapse, a first aid kit and copies of important documents. Earlier, Treasury minister James Murray told BBC Breakfast he has not yet followed the government's guidance on stockpiling supplies to prepare for a crisis. He said he had a stockpile of coffee, but pointed out that neighbouring countries including Ireland, France and the Netherlands had given the same guidance "for quite a long time". He added: "I'm not going to pretend I've followed all that advice myself yet." Speaking on the same programme, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "stocked up for the week at any time". She said the previous Conservative government had issued similar advice on preparing for emergencies, but added: "What I'm more concerned about is that it doesn't look like [the government] are explaining what the risks we are under are, and what they are doing about the big things. "Families can stock up but what's going on with defence, the cyber attacks, the hybrid warfare? The money to look after the country has not been forthcoming." title: October's full Hunter's Moon to light up night sky this weekend
description: October's full Moon, known as the Hunter's Moon, will rise on Sunday night. Will the weather be in your favour?
body: October's full Moon, nicknamed the Hunter's Moon, is set to light up the night sky this weekend. It will be visible in the UK from Sunday 25 October into the morning of Monday 26 October. Marking the 11th full Moon of 13 in 2026, it is the final one before a run of four consecutive supermoons, external. If you want to catch a glimpse, keep an eye on the forecast to see if the weather will allow a clear view. The Moon will rise in the east at just after 16:00 GMT on Sunday and set towards the west between 07:00 and 08:00 GMT on Monday - times vary across the UK. The Moon will be officially full at 04:11 GMT on Monday. This is the moment of "syzygy" when the Sun and Moon will be aligned either side of the Earth. However, the Moon will appear full on both Sunday and Monday nights, giving skygazers two chances to spot it. During a full Moon, the whole of the Earth-facing side of the Moon is illuminated by the Sun. A full Moon occurs every 29.5 days - the length of the lunar cycle You may notice an orange or reddish hue to the Moon when it is low in the sky due to the scattering of short wavelength blue light as it passes through a large depth of the atmosphere. The longer wavelength red and orange colours are not scattered as readily so pass through to our eyes. The Moon may also appear larger in the sky near moonrise and moonset - something called the "Moon Illusion". This is when our brain makes us think the Moon looks bigger because it is viewed alongside objects on the horizon such as buildings and trees. As well as looking out for the full Moon, there is also a chance to spot some shooting stars, with the Orionid meteor shower just past its peak. The extra lunar light, however, may obscure some of the meteors, so be patient and leave time for your eyes to adjust. The Hunter's Moon may appear large and reddish in colour when it is near the horizon Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature. Different cultures use different names for the 12 or 13 full Moons across the lunar calendar, but many of the common ones we use today originate from Native American cultures. In October, the term Hunter's Moon comes from the time of year hunters would have been most active, preparing for the colder and darker winter months ahead. The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies. Sunday night's moon viewing prospects Storm Boelo will continue to bring rain and very strong winds to northern Scotland early on Sunday night, but prospects of seeing the Moon increases as the night wears on. There will be plenty of blustery showers in west Scotland and north-west England - any gaps between these could give a brief chance to view. For the rest of the UK prospects are better, especially early in the night with clearer skies, before cloud tends to spread in from the south-west later. If the weather fails to cooperate where you live, the next chance to see a full Moon will be on 24 November as the Beaver Supermoon. This will be followed by a Christmas Eve Cold Supermoon on 24 December. The succession of supermoons will then continue into 2027, with January and February's full Moons both set to be supermoons too. title: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn
description: Once the world's largest producer of mink pelts, the nation's industry has declined in recent years.
body: Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice. Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population. The ban is due to come into effect on 7 August next year, and is followed by a two-year transition period to phase out the practice. Danish Nature Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said the government had chosen animal welfare. "A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time. It should also make sense for society, for the economy and for the animals," he said. The Danish government had initially sought an exemption for its mink industry when the EU added the mammal to its list of invasive species in 2025, prohibiting people from keeping them. However, the current coalition government, elected in June, reversed this decision and decided not to proceed with the application on Friday. Social Democrat MP Brigitte Vind said it was "a good day for animal welfare". "It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said. The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment. Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments. However, its production has slipped behind that of other countries, such as Poland and China, in recent years. The industry faced a crisis during the coronavirus pandemic, when the government ordered a mass cull of mink after a mutated strain of Covid-19 was found in the animals. Approximately 15 million were killed. At the time, the country had huge export markets to China and Hong Kong. The government later admitted it had no legal basis for the culling. There are now approximately 15,000 mink left in Denmark. No costs have yet been determined for closing Denmark's seven remaining mink farms, but an animal welfare spokesperson for one of the governing coalition parties previously estimated it would be around 14m Danish krone (£1.56m), local media report, but the final amount could be higher. The wearing of fur is a controversial subject within fashion circles, with publications and fashion brands choosing not to use or promote it several years ago. But it re-entered the spotlight last year, with celebrities and fashionistas wearing both vintage and so-called faux fur. title: Conte plays down 'unfounded' Man Utd speculation
description: Antonio Conte says he is not in advanced talks with any club, in response to speculation he has held talks with Manchester United.
body: Antonio Conte won the Premier League with Chelsea in 2017 Antonio Conte has said he is not in "advanced negotiations" with any club in response to reports he has held talks with Manchester United. Italian newspaper La Repubblica, external claimed on Thursday that Conte had held talks with United's board about replacing Michael Carrick following the 4-1 defeat against Como on Wednesday. The report said the former Chelsea manager had demanded full control of United's transfer policy and stated his intention to appoint his own staff at Old Trafford. But, while BBC Sport understands Conte is keen on the job, the Italian says he is not in "advanced" talks with any club. "My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage," Conte wrote on Instagram. "I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my "strong personality". These reports are unfounded. "Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties' needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager." Carrick's future at Old Trafford is uncertain after a humiliating defeat to Cesc Fabregas' Como in the Champions League earlier this week. Although Carrick is set to remain in charge for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth, sources have told BBC Sport that United have begun the process of identifying possible replacements. Former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe, Conte and ex-Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann are all understood to have their eyes on the job. Conte, who played for Juventus and Italy in a stellar career, is a free agent after leaving Napoli at the end of last season. He won the Serie A title during his first season in Naples, before a Supercoppa Italiana victory in his final campaign. The 57-year-old won the Premier League with Chelsea during his debut campaign at Stamford Bridge in 2016-17 and beat Manchester United in the FA Cup final the following season. He returned to the Premier League in 2021 when he replaced Jose Mourinho at Tottenham Hotspur. Conte's time in north London lasted just 16 months though, with the Italian leaving in March 2023 after criticising "selfish" players and the club's culture in a remarkable news conference. Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler has distanced himself from links to Old Trafford. The German has been touted as a possible successor to Carrick given his free-scoring Brighton side are sitting third in the Premier League. Hurzeler has a contract with the Seagulls until 2029 and says he is happy at the club. "I am really focused on my job here. I have no time to think about these rumours because we play every three days," said Hurzeler. "I have a lot of respect for Michael Carrick. He is a great human being, he is a great personality. Every time we meet each other, we have a really good relationship." title: 'Sexually obsessed' stepdad jailed for murdering student
description: Nathan Owens had a "longstanding sexual obsession" with his stepdaughter Carla Georgescu, a judge says.
body: Nathan Owens was "sexually obsessed" with his stepdaughter, police said This article contains distressing details. A man who was "sexually obsessed" with his stepdaughter has been jailed for a minimum of 35 years for murdering her at her university flat on her 20th birthday. Nathan Owens, 34, from Hartlepool, killed Carla Georgescu in her room at the University of Lancashire property in Preston in February and then staged the scene to make it look like she had taken her own life. Judge Jacobs said Carla had been described as polite, kind, intelligent and articulate with "a very gentle way" but she had suffered "a horrific brutal attack". He said Owens had a "longstanding sexual obsession with Carla" that was hidden from her and her mother. This video can not be played Moment stepdad arrested for murdering student The second-year student suffered knife wounds, including injuries where she tried to defend herself, internal injuries from a sexual assault and two "powerful blows to the head", the judge said. Owens also attempted to strangle her, the court heard. Nicholas Lumley KC, for the prosecution, told Preston Crown Court Carla was "thriving" at the University of Lancashire, and had planned to continue her studies at a high level, "working towards a doctorate". He said she was "excitedly looking forward" to travelling to her home country of Romania to meet up with her first boyfriend. Carla Georgescu was found dead in her student flat in February Owens had pleaded guilty shortly before the trial to making and possessing indecent images of Carla when she was between the ages of two and four by superimposing her image on to sexualised pictures. Lumley said Owens' offending was "pre-meditated, non consensual, violent and sustained" and that Carla would have been in "very great pain" when he sexually assaulted her. The judge said he was "sure" that fatal violence was "part of the plan" if Carla were to resist the sexual attack that Owens had decided to carry out. He said "the last 90 minutes of Carla's life are too horrendous to think about" but he said "it is likely and indeed to be hoped that at some point she became unconscious and so was not aware of everything that happened to her". Owens had not shown any remorse, he said, and had denied injuring Carla in any way. The judge said he had "taken victim blaming to its limit" by suggesting she may have taken her own life. CCTV footage of Carla letting Owens in to her flat was the last time she was seen alive, Lancashire Police said Carla's body was found in her room at the university's Ribble Hall on 5 February. The trial saw CCTV footage of Owens having a meal with Carla and her mother in the days before she died and him going to her flat in the early hours of 4 February wrapped in a blanket. Carla let him into the building at about 04:00 GMT after he lied about picking something up and he left an hour-and-a-half later, the court heard. That CCTV footage of Carla letting Owens in was the last time she was seen alive, Lancashire Police said. Owens subjected his stepdaughter to a violent and sexual assault as he strangled her. He then staged the scene to look as if Carla had taken her own life and returned home as though nothing had happened, disposing of evidence on his route. Detectives arrested him soon afterwards but he denied any involvement in Carla's death. Owens chose not to give evidence at his trial. Det Insp Pete Macdonald said: "Owens has taken Carla's life, but he has also changed her mum's completely. "He has torn apart the family he was trusted to love. title: Holiday balcony inquest hears engineer may not have known he was falling to his death
description: A post-mortem examination found a "substantial level" of alcohol in Kieran Hughes blood.
body: Kieran Hughes died in the early hours of 11 July 2025 A software engineer may not have known he was falling to his death from a balcony, an inquest has heard. Kieran Hughes, 25, from Nant Gwynant, Gwynedd, died in the early hours of 11 July, 2025, while on holiday in Malta with three friends. A post-mortem examination by Maltese authorities found there was a "substantial level" of alcohol in his blood. The inquest at Caernarfon Coroner's Court heard there was no evidence of third-party involvement, and coroner Elizabeth Dudley-Jones concluded his death was an accident. His dad, Alan, said the family endured "heartache all day, every day". Hughes' friends said he had been a high achiever, "a legend and a genius". In July 2025, Hughes and his friends went to St Julian's in Malta and stayed at the Cavalieri Art Hotel. On 10 July, the court was told, they left the hotel at about 19:00 BST, went to dinner, a casino and elsewhere, drinking beer, cocktails and limoncello. At about 04:15 on 11 July, a member of the public went into the hotel to say a man was lying on the ground outside. Police were called and found a man "in a pool of blood" who looked "lifeless". Police went to room 603, above where Hughes' body was found, and tried to wake his friend, Osian Jones, who was asleep in a "state of intoxication" and smelled of alcohol. The pair had been sharing a room, while the other two friends were in a different room. The inquest heard Jones did not wake up until about 06:30, but after investigations there were no indications of third-party involvement in Hughes' death. There was no disarray in room 603, the inquest heard, and CCTV showed the pair returning to their room holding on to each other. "It does not seem that there was any animosity between Kieran and Mr Jones," Dudley-Jones said. There were no reports of shouting or arguing. CCTV captured Hughes' fall about 48 minutes after he returned to his room. An autopsy concluded he died from multiple injuries following blunt force trauma due to a fall from height. No apparent resistance injuries were found, indicating it was possible "he was not even aware he was falling from the balcony". The inquest heard it was probable Hughes and his friend went to sleep, and Hughes, in a state of "severe drunkenness" went outside - possibly because he felt unwell or wanted air. Dudley-Jones told Hughes' family, who attended the hearing, his death was a "complete tragedy" and he was "an amazing man". She added: "I have not enjoyed this inquest... this one, I have to say, it is very moving." In a statement read to the inquest by the coroner, Hughes' father Alan said the family encountered "hurdle after hurdle" in dealing with the Maltese authorities and said they experienced "heartache all day, every day". title: World champion Jepchirchir fails drugs test
description: Reigning world women's marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir is provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after a sample tests positive for EPO.
body: Peres Jepchirchir won the 2026 Sydney marathon by three minutes and 40 seconds Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO. Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026. The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney. EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells. If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream. Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025. She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020. In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024. Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai. She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race. title: 'It's been relentless': IT workers scramble to fix PHP flaw described as worst crisis in years
description: IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours to update their systems.
body: This video can not be played How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time". Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks". Other IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours, whose stories give us an insight into what it is like at the coalface of a major cyber emergency. But also highlight how misinformation and panic has made things a lot worse. "It's been relentless," says UK-based system administrator Adam Mudd. He said he had never had so many messages from people who were worried about their websites. "The biggest challenge has been juggling clients who want their sites taken offline as a precaution, while trying to coordinate updates and fixes across countless different setups," he said. "Sometimes it takes me longer to take a website down than to fix the PHP problem." PHP is a very popular programming language which powers millions of websites. But two critical flaws were found with the system that led to the emergency response, with national cyber-security authorities urging IT teams to download a security fix urgently or take websites and servers offline. Mudd says since then he has been under enormous pressure and has lost a huge amount of sleep - working early and not finishing until 22:30 BST to secure his customers' systems. In Mauritius, IT administrator Loganaden Velvindron said he too was flat out since his team realised just how much software relies on PHP. "Many versions of php running are completely end-of-life, so we are having to rebuilding web apps and change code in some cases," he said. He said part of the problem was the announcement about the security vulnerabilities in PHP came as a surprise, without much time to prepare for action. Jon Jones, Technical director for a digital advertising company, was also spurred into action by the alerts. "Seeing the warning drop was definitely eye-opening and a new experience we've not dealt with before," he said. "But, in a way, it was exciting feeling like a bit of a Hollywood action scene." The PHP Foundation, which manages the programming language, released its software fix and there was a scramble for people to download it. Jones said it felt like "the race was on" when the patch launched at 15:00 BST on Wednesday. "It was also a bit nerve-racking as anyone who has applied software updates before would know, there's always a chance than an update can cause other issues," he said. The rush came as someone had leaked details of the PHP flaw early - and it was heavily rumoured that cyber-criminals were already trying to carry out attacks. But cyber experts are also now questioning whether or not those rumours were real. "We were flooded with rubbish intel about hackers being out there actively with working Proof of Concept (PoC) methods," said UK cyber expert Daniel Card. He said he also been flat out since Tuesday when the rumours of PHP hacks began circulating. "This isn't the first time we've had a situation like this but it feels like it's been on another dimension," he said. He agreed that on paper the PHP vulnerabilities were very serious and should be taken seriously, but he and many others are frustrated with the misinformation about hackers being on the loose. As well as the alerts from government agencies - even the Prime Minister of Japan - cyber-security companies also made errors which didn't help. One major firm in this space issued warnings saying hackers had a working PoC - only to have to retract it. In spite of warnings from Cloudflare and AWS that "millions of hacking attempts" had been made every hour, there is also no evidence of large scale data breaches or cyber-attacks. It is true that hackers have been seen to use AI to attempt to build attack methods, but none of them seem to be working at scale at the moment - something that may well change soon. AI was also used to find the PHP flaws which had been hidden from human researchers for decades. The IT workers we spoke to all agreed that these kinds of serious flaws were going to be uncovered more frequently now that AI tools had become so good at hacking. But some in the industry are concerned about how people were told about the critical vulnerabilities in PHP, as they fear improvements in AI will throw up more incidents like it. "We're going to find scary vulnerabilities with the amazing capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are bringing online, but we need to calibrate the messaging," posted Mark Maunder, founder of Wordfence - a Wordpress security tool. He said there was a risk of "alert fatigue" which could be a big problem if a fully exploitable and serious vulnerability arose. What is AI and how does it work?
