title: Island inflation rate rises to 3%, figures show
description: The rising cost of food and alcohol drives an increase in the inflation rate, figures show.
body: Alcohol and food drove the biggest increase in the inflation rate, statisticians said The annual rate of inflation in Jersey rose to 3% in September, according to new figures. Jersey's retail price index (RPI) rose 0.2 percentage points since June when it was 2.8%. Statistics Jersey said increases in the cost of household services, alcoholic drinks and food made the most notable contributions to annual rate of inflation. It said there were also "substantial increases" in the price of some fuels, with heating oil and other fuels increasing by 47.7% across the year, while petrol and oil increased by 22.7%. It said food prices increased by 3.5% and housing costs by 0.2%. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Statistics Jersey said this quarter the island's headline inflation rate was 0.6 percentage points lower than the UK's CPIH, a measure of inflation that includes housing costs, which stood at 3.6%. It said housing costs made the largest contribution to the RPI - this group includes public and private rentals, as well as mortgage interest payments, parish rates and maintenance and repair costs. Statisticians said global energy markets remained affected by conflict in the Middle East. Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Denmark nurdles may be from Tyne spill, agency says
description: The Danish Environment Protection Agency says nurdles it has tested are similar to the Tyne pellets.
body: The Danish Environment Protection Agency said the pellets along the Wadden Sea coast looked similar to those from the Tyne spill Nurdles found along the Danish coast are likely to originate from the spill in north-east England, according to the country's environment agency. Masses of plastic pellets were found along the western coast of Denmark in September. The Danish Environment Protection Agency has now confirmed tests carried out on the microplastics suggest they originated from the River Tyne spill in July. It said the nurdles had the same characteristics as the one billion which had been spilled in north-east England and their arrival in Denmark in late September and early October - about 390 miles (630km) away - was consistent with "current patterns and circulation in the North Sea". Signe Simonsen, the head of startup Race for Oceans Technology, first spotted the nurdles on the island of Mandø in Denmark on 26 September. "There were just so many milk white plastic pellets," she said. "So many that I've never seen before in this area." Signe Simonsen said the nurdle discovery had saddened her Simonsen said the discovery of the nurdles had made her "really sad" considering the "pristine" nature of the Wadden Sea. Simonsen then said she drove along the coast of several nearby islands which are roughly on the same latitude as Newcastle. She said there were nurdles "all over" where the tide had washed up. Simonsen said she had collected nurdles from 10 different spots along the Danish coast and Sylt in Germany. Simonsen, whose firm aims to detect microplastic pollution from drone images, then passed on some of her samples to the Danish Environment Protection Agency. The agency, which tested the pellets alongside Aarhus University, said another factor which suggested the Danish nurdles were the same as those spilled in the River Tyne was the fact there were no other recorded spills in the area that could explain their presence. Nurdles from the spill have washed up along the coast of north-east England including Teesside and Durham. As of September, about 28% of the nurdles are believed to have been recovered. title: Doctors tell the BBC about the targeting of Sudanese hospitals by paramilitary fighters
description: A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system.
body: This video can not be played A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago. UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing". Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict. The health minister of the group's civilian-affiliated government, Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, dismissed the allegations as propaganda. The BBC's Africa correspondent Barbara Plett Usher speaks to two doctors who support the claims of systemic targeting of hospitals. title: Man charged over Belfast knife attack pleads not guilty
description: A man charged in connection with a knife attack in north Belfast, that sparked serious disorder in the city, pleads not guilty to attempted murder.
body: An artist's impression of Alodid at an earlier court appearance A man charged in connection with a knife attack in north Belfast that sparked serious disorder in the city has pleaded not guilty to attempted murder. Hadi Alodid, 31, of Duncairn Avenue in Belfast, has also denied possessing a bladed weapon and a charge of threatening or abusive behaviour. Alodid is accused of carrying out the attack on Stephen Ogilvie in June. Stephen Ogilvie, who is in his 40s, lost his left eye in the incident and sustained damage to his right. Alodid, who has been in custody since the attack, was led into the dock in handcuffs at Belfast Crown Court, where three charges were put to him. Dressed in a grey prison tracksuit, Alodid stood with his arms folded as an Arabic interpreter translated the proceedings for him. He responded to all three charges in English with the words "not guilty". A date was set for his trial in early February. A number of review hearings will be held prior to that. The attack, which the court heard took place in the vicinity of Kinnaird Avenue in north Belfast, happened on June 8. Videos circulating online at the time showed a number of people, including one wielding a hurling stick, confronting the apparent attacker until police arrived. Alodid was arrested at the scene and remanded into custody. Following the attack, violence erupted across Belfast, which saw homes and vehicles set alight. title: Wales plans to ban steel pylons as government launches consultation
description: The Welsh government says it is consulting on an "undergrounding-first approach" to electricity lines.
body: Building pylons in Wales could be a thing of the past, with the country's ministers instead wanting to bury energy cables underground The Welsh government has announced plans to ban the use of traditional steel pylons to support electricity lines over which it has control. Plaid Cymru ministers favour burying cables underground instead. Plans for a network of pylons in the Towy Valley have faced a fierce local backlash with local Plaid politicians speaking out against the proposals. The company behind the plans, Green Gen Cymru, has been asked to comment but had previously said that undergrounding cables would be significantly more expensive than running them overhead. Prohibiting the use of large steel lattice pylons for new lines up 132 kilovolts was a Plaid Cymru manifesto pledge before May's Senedd election. Launching a consultation on its policy on Friday, the Welsh government said undergrounding electricity circuits could "reduce the visual impact of electricity infrastructure, helping to protect landscapes and local amenity". It also said that burying cables could make them less vulnerable to severe weather and could reduce the potential impact on birds and other wildlife. However, the consultation document also acknowledges that undergrounding is "generally considered more expensive to install and maintain and could create construction impacts during installation". The government's policy would allow for wooden poles or "equivalent, less intrusive infrastructure" to be used to support overhead cables where certain planning tests are met. Farmers 'vindicated' after judge's ruling on pylon firm accessing land Energy firm unveils new slimline pylons designed 'with Welsh landscape in mind' after backlash Green Gen hoped to build three major power line routes connecting onshore wind farms planned by its sister company Bute Energy with the wider grid network. It said it would invest nearly £1bn by 2030, with proposals affecting parts of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Powys and Shropshire. But it had faced considerable opposition in certain communities, with groups representing hundreds of landowners taking the company to court last year. In a bid to address concerns, Green Gen recently unveiled a "slim and compact" 22 metre (72ft) pylon, designed "with the Welsh landscape in mind". The company has consistently said that undergrounding its cables would cost on average 4.5 times more, external than running them overhead. That would mean an extra cost of £500m for the Towy Usk project between Carmarthenshire and Powys, according to Green Gen. Green Gen Cymru had previously proposed three pylon routes from mid Wales across to Shropshire, south-west Wales to Ceredigion, and one from the same point to Powys Welsh Energy Minister Adam Price said: "We know the necessary changes in the way energy is generated and used in Wales will require new grid infrastructure, however, we also know that new infrastructure can impact on the communities and the environment that hosts it. "We want to see infrastructure that is sensitively designed to minimise impacts on the environment and the communities that host them, while offering the maximum benefits for Wales." The consultation, external will run until 15 January 2027. title: Mum pleads guilty to killing her three children
description: Yasmeen Ali, 44, admits the manslaughter of her children at their family home.
body: Fares, Joury and Mohammed were found dead at their home in Sea Mills A mother who admitted killing her three children at their home wept in court as details of their deaths were read out. The bodies of Fares Bash, seven, Joury Bash, three, and nine-month-old Mohammed Bash were discovered on Blaise Walk in Sea Mills, Bristol, on 18 February 2024. Appearing at Bristol Crown Court earlier, Yasmeen Ali, 44, admitted three charges of manslaughter, before her defence team said she was suffering from an "acute psychosis". She is due to be sentenced later. An inquest into the deaths was previously told the three children died of knife wounds, with injuries to their chests and necks. Fares Bash also showed possible signs of asphyxia. Ali, speaking through an interpreter, appeared in court wearing a purple coat and a black head scarf. Only six people were allowed into the courtroom to minimise the impact on her mental health. Police cordons were put in place after the bodies were discovered Her defence team told the court she suffered from an "acute psychosis". The court also heard Ali had been discharged from mental health services on 12 February - just six days before the killings. The incident began with a three-minute phone call to 999, in which Ali sounded out of breath, was speaking in Arabic, and told police she was "going to God". When officers arrived, they discovered the children dead and found Ali with self-inflicted wounds to her neck. The house was described as "dirty and chaotic". Ali, who previously worked as a nurse in Sudan, wept in the dock as her children's fatal injuries were read out. Their father Alfil Bash left the room. Police found the children's bodies while responding to a welfare call Avon and Somerset Police said Ali was detained under the Mental Health Act after being assessed by medical experts at the scene after the children's bodies were discovered. She was later discharged from Southmead Hospital after being treated for her injuries, and is now living in a secure psychiatric hospital. The force referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) due to prior contact with the family, but the watchdog said no investigation was required. A social worker described the defendant as a "very loving" mother who had never caused concerns. The children's father previously spoke of his devastation at the loss of his children, saying he "could not get his head around what had happened". In a victim impact statement, Bash described the children as "his whole world", adding it was hard to accept the "size of the betrayal" from their mother. "No words can describe the pain I am going through. Part of me has died," he said. "My children were innocent human beings. They were precious and deserved long happy lives, to make friends and make their own families one day. "I'll spend the rest of my life grieving for my children." After the children's deaths, the community held vigils in their memory. Sian Randall, headteacher at Sea Mills Primary School, where the two eldest children were pupils, said there were "no words that display the depth of sorrow". "We will miss them dearly, they were integral to us. Their absence will always be felt," she added. Andrew Langdon KC, defending, said two separate doctors at the secure psychiatric unit believed Ali was suffering from schizoaffective disorder. This combines symptoms of schizophrenia - such as hallucinations or delusions -with symptoms of a mood disorder, such as depression or bipolar disorder. Langdon argued Ali was in the "grip of delusions which she acted on", and "was unable to understand the nature of what she was doing". "She didn't realise her children were dead or that she had killed them - the horror when she was told can only be imagined," he said. "It was her illness that made it happen. "On an instinctive emotional level from a mother, the horror never dissipates - she will have to live with this for the rest of her life." Judge Justice Linden added: "What has happened is a tragedy, from which neither of you will recover and causes both of you unimaginable pain in your daily lives." title: Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
description: The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed loans for those buying new-builds in England.
body: The government is expected to allow households earning up to £110,000 to apply for its new loan scheme to help first-time buyers in England. As first reported by The Times, external, a higher earnings limit of £140,000 is expected to apply to those purchasing properties in London. The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed equity loans worth 20% of new-build properties purchased from participating developers. The loans, which will also be subject to an initial interest-free period, are designed to help people buy a home with deposits as low as 2.5%. Previous schemes to help first-time buyers did not restrict eligibility by income but faced criticism for stoking house prices by allowing relatively wealthy households to borrow more. Unveiling the Your First Home Scheme at last month's Labour conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it would focus on those who "really need support". Details of the changes, including salary caps, are due to be confirmed at next week's Budget. The Times reported that ministers had initially decided to set the earnings limits at £90,000 for homes outside outside London and £110,000 in the capital, before concluding this would deny access to too many middle-earning couples, such as teachers and nurses. The government has also argued that the scheme will help to boost housebuilding, after ministers conceded they are set to miss a target to build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election. Labour has said the scheme will be funded by within existing government budgets, but is yet to provide details of which other areas will see their spending cut. Developers taking part in the scheme will also be asked to contribute towards running costs. Like the Help to Buy scheme launched under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, the scheme will use equity loans, which are linked to changes in the value of properties they are used to purchase. That scheme, which initially ran between 2013 and 2021, enabled all home purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home worth up to £600,000. Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years. A second version of that scheme, which ran from 2021 to 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties could be bought under the programme. title: Malawi opposition demands answers over president's prolonged stay abroad
description: This is President Peter Mutharika's fifth visit to South Africa this year.
body: This is President Peter Mutharika's fifth visit to South Africa this year Malawi's opposition has demanded an explanation for President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, power cuts and economic difficulties. The 86-year-old Mutharika left Malawi on 6 October, for what officials described as a private visit. This is his fifth visit this year, with limited information made public on each of these trips. "Malawi is at a critical moment, and there is a need for decisive action," the opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) said. Information Minister Shadric Namalomba has denied that Mutharika's absence had created a leadership vacuum. The professor who beat fraud allegations to become Malawi's president…again Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera. He previously governed Malawi between 2014 and 2020. His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa. On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges. He said that Malawians deserved to know who was managing the country's affairs. "The issue is not that the president has traveled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge." He called on the government to explain how it intended to address persistent fuel shortages, frequent electricity blackouts, shortage of essential medicines in public hospitals and difficulties accessing foreign currency. The information minister responded by telling local media that "a state president is always in charge at any time, anywhere," insisting that the president remained firmly in control of government affairs. Asked about the purpose of the visit, the minister said: "A private trip is private." He accused the opposition of attempting to exploit problems he said had developed under its previous administration. "That is why Malawians voted us into government, not them. May I request them to seal their mouths as we address the problems they miserably created and failed to solve," he added. On Thursday, Mutharika delegated the trade minister to lead Malawi's delegation to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) summit in Zimbabwe. Earlier this month, officials dismissed reports on social media that Mutharika had travelled from South Africa to India for medical treatment. Chief Secretary to the Government Justin Saidi said the president remained in South Africa and urged the public not to spread unverified information. Mutharika has previously dismissed speculation about his health, describing such claims as "silly and laughable" and insisting that he was well. Malawi faces a severe shortage of foreign currency, which has disrupted fuel imports and contributed to rising transport costs. Long queues have formed at petrol stations, while unreliable electricity supplies and shortages of medicines have added to public frustration. title: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
description: The attack comes at a time of heightened tensions in the West Bank and four days before Israel's general election.
body: Photos of one of the suspected attackers were shared by AFP news agency Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say. Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron. In response, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had ordered the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday. The attack comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time. The two injured Israelis are in critical condition, according to Israel's ambulance service. The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there. Unverified CCTV footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire. The Israeli military said it had begun raids on the homes of the attackers, while far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said he had ordered the demolition of several Palestinian buildings adjacent to the site of the attack. It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis. Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security for Israelis, said that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning. The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media. At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN. Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says. title: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
description: The Duchess of Sussex issues a statement following reports her father Thomas Markle is being investigated over child sex abuse images in the Philippines.
body: The Duchess of Sussex has said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018. In a statement, Meghan said a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle was sent to the Metropolitan Police that year and subsequently shared with her. Her comments come after reports that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to her father had been found at his former home in the Philippines, which she said were "deeply" distressing. In an interview with the Daily Mail, Thomas Markle denied possessing child sex images, calling the accusations "sick lies". The duchess said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed." She said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated". She added she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children". This was "to protect them", she said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families". Meghan described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children". title: Boulter into Japan semi-finals and back as British No 1
description: Katie Boulter reclaims the British number one ranking after fighting back to beat Antonia Ruzic in three sets in the quarter-finals of the Japan Open.
body: Katie Boulter is through to her third WTA semi-final of the 2026 season Katie Boulter has reclaimed the British number one ranking after fighting back to beat Antonia Ruzic in three sets in the quarter-finals of the Japan Open. The 30-year-old was dethroned on Monday following Sonay Kartal's run to the final in Wuhan but knew she could overturn the 55-point deficit by reaching the last four in Osaka. Eighth seed Boulter trailed world number 91 Ruzic by a set and a break but recovered to win 3-6 6-3 6-3 in two hours to reach her first semi-final since Queen's in June. She will face Czech Katerina Siniakova in the last four and whatever the result will climb above Kartal and back into the world's top 50 when the WTA rankings are updated on Monday. "[Ruzic] is a really good player, full credit to her," said Boulter. "I tried to hang tough and find a way. I was a bit lucky in the middle of the second [set] but I feel I did really well to stay there." On facing Siniakova for a spot in the final, she added: "She's one hell of a player, extremely dangerous. It's going to be who gets the first strike in. "I've got nothing to lose. She's been building extremely well this week, so I'm going to have to come prepared." Inside British number one Kartal's remarkable comeback Boulter struggled on serve in the opening two sets, winning just 60% points behind her first serve, hitting four double faults, and facing seven break points, but grew into the match, finding success when stepping inside the baseline to put pressure on the 23-year-old Croat. Broken in her opening service game, Boulter was gifted a route back into the first set at 4-2 when Ruzic double-faulted on break point. However, Ruzic immediately hit back, winning the next four games. Boulter wrested back control in an increasingly scrappy second set, saving two break points in the third game to avoid going a double-break down before coming up with a crucial hold in the seventh after the pair had exchanged three successive breaks. That hold proved the second of eight straight games for Boulter, who raced into a 4-0 lead in the decider. Although she failed to serve out the match at 5-2, she broke her opponent to love to wrap up the win. The immense pride which Kartal felt about becoming the British number one came shining through, describing it as being "up there" in her career achievements. While she will only initially hold the status for a week, Kartal's impressive comeback and Boulter's decent run creates a fascinating subplot for the leading British women in the final throes of the season - and the start of 2027. Boulter will have the chance to further improve her ranking when she plays in Tokyo and Hong Kong in the coming weeks, with Kartal's plans for the rest of the season still uncertain as she sensibly manages her workload. And don't forget about Emma Raducanu. It seems increasingly unlikely she will play again this season because of the shin injury which ruled her out of Wimbledon, but is clearly too good a player not to be pushing back into the top 50 when she does return. When all three are back competing on the WTA Tour at the same time, it promises to be an interesting tussle between them in the rankings. Boulter and Raducanu both insisted they were not transfixed by the British number one spot when they exchanged positions in 2025, instead preferring to focus on their own career paths and the bigger picture of the world rankings. But there is no doubt that Boulter, in particular, could see the opportunity to cement her place as the nation's best player as an extra incentive to continue finishing 2026 strongly. title: Fund to help businesses switch to green vehicles
description: Council leader Stephen Place says it will help businesses counter the rising cost of fuel.
body: The Zero Emission Grant Programme is being targeted at small businesses A £2m fund has been launched to help businesses switch their vehicles to greener vehicles, Bradford Council has announced. Reform UK council leader Stephen Place said it would help businesses counter the rising cost of petrol and diesel as well as modernise their fleets. The funding is part of Bradford Council's Clean Air programme, which will allow businesses to apply for up to £16,000 in support. Announcing the fund at the Scale Up Bradford event on Tuesday, Place said it would help businesses invest in cleaner, more efficient technology to "future proof their operations for years to come". Earlier this month, Place said he was committed to scrapping Clean Air Zone (CAZ) charges as it had a negative impact on businesses. He accepted the move would have "quite a lot of legalities surrounding it" but said the council would "work to run it out naturally". Stephen Place, Reform leader of Bradford Council, said his party planned to get rid of the CAZ charge, but keep the zone Funded by the Labour government, the Zero Emission Grant Programme will be targeted at small businesses, charities and organisations, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service. Businesses will be able to apply for up to £16,000 to improve heavy-duty vehicles and £4,500 for light-duty vehicles. Bradford Council said the fund would provide practical support to help businesses remain competitive while adapting to new vehicle technologies. "We want to help organisations to upgrade their fleets and position themselves for future success," said Place. "I hope that this will appeal to tradies, they are the people out there every day keeping the nation moving." Petrol and diesel prices have risen significantly since the US-Israel war with Iran. Currently the average price of petrol in the UK is 173.2p per litre, while diesel costs 199.9p per litre. Mark Casci, of West Yorkshire Chamber of Commerce, welcomed the plans and said a lot of businesses were looking to "decarbonise" their vehicles. "Every large business with a fleet is looking at this issue very carefully, it is very much on their agenda," said Casci. "It is the right thing to do and what customers want. It is driven by customer demand as well as moral responsibility." Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. title: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
description: Questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers, were raised earlier this month.
body: Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich - his lawyers have said he denies concealing his fortune Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax. Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ). A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit. Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws". The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering. The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed. Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation. A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months. When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved." He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated." Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune Watch now on BBC iPlayer Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible. The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts. Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over €25m in unpaid VAT. Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it. title: Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat
description: Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed any symptoms, Swiss officials say.
body: This is the first case of Ebola in Nigeria in more than a decade Switzerland's foreign ministry has confirmed that the woman who has tested positive for Ebola in Nigeria is the wife of a Swiss diplomat. The woman, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born national who lives in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, tested positive for the virus on 20 October, becoming the country's first confirmed Ebola patient in more than a decade. They both travelled to Uganda earlier this month. Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed any symptoms, according to the Swiss foreign ministry. The ministry told the BBC that all 25 staff at its embassy in Nigeria were in good health and did not need to isolate. The ministry said the woman had spent about a week at a private clinic in Abuja with symptoms before her diagnosis. It believes she contracted the virus while travelling in Uganda, although health authorities have yet to establish the source of her infection. Uganda borders Democratic Republic of Congo, where some 4,600 have died in the country's most deadly outbreak of Ebola. Two people died in Uganda shortly after the outbreak began in May but it has been declared free of Ebola since August. The ministry said the decision not to isolate the embassy's eight Swiss and 17 local employees was taken in consultation with Nigeria's Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization (WHO). It added that the embassy remained open and operational, with health and safety measures in place. The woman is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the WHO. She returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda. The patient did ​not travel to DR Congo, the Swiss ‌government told Reuters news agency on Friday, contradicting accounts from Uganda. She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October. Health officials are now investigating whether she may have crossed paths with a Kenyan man who died from Ebola and had travelled through Uganda's main airport on the same day. Investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday. Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established. "One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," he told journalists. The Kenyan man had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He died shortly afterwards, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death. Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed? What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? Kenya has since confirmed nine infections, including the fatal case. Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact. Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source. The WHO said it was too early to determine where the woman in Nigeria became infected. "The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official. He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital. Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help establish whether her infection is linked to other cases. "The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria. Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business. However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country. Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there. Meanwhile, Nigerian authorities are tracing more people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially identified. Kenya's Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission. He urged the public to remain vigilant and not panic but warned: "We are not out of the woods". He said the remaining eight patients were still in isolation and responding well to treatment. The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands cross daily for trade, work and family visits. Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points. The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers. Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu. The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infec

title: Man, 61, in court charged with murder of 'stabbed' woman who died after crash
description: Clifford Foster, 61, from Bridgend, appeared at Newport Magistrates' Court on Friday morning.
body: Clifford Foster was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of the murder of Eleanor Barnfield A 61-year-old man has appeared in court charged with the murder of a woman who suffered "stab wounds" and died following a crash. Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to a crash on Coity Road in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision". The BBC understands they were sustained in a stabbing. Clifford Foster, of Ger-y-Nant, was arrested on Tuesday at the Ger-y-Nant retirement housing complex, close to where the crash happened, where Eleanor worked. Speaking only to confirm his name, age and address, Foster appeared at Newport Magistrates' Court on Friday, wearing a grey tracksuit and using a crutch to support himself. Police say Eleanor Barnfield "sustained puncture wounds unrelated to the collision" in Bridgend on Monday The incident led to a significant police operation, with specially trained firearm officers involved in a "stand off" at the retirement complex which lasted 12 hours, before an arrest at 01:00 BST on Tuesday. Reports in some media had claimed Eleanor had crashed her car while driving herself to hospital. On Thursday, the Welsh Ambulance Service (WAS) denied Eleanor was driving because of ambulance wait times, saying it was aware of "misleading rumours" circulating online. It said medics were called to the crash on Coity Road at about 12:44 and a response unit arrived seven minutes later, adding two emergency ambulances then arrived to provide additional support at 13:07 and 13:13. It described the rumours on social media as "contradictory" and "factually untrue". "We would encourage members of the public not to speculate," the service said. Ger-y-Nant, a sheltered housing retirement complex, where a man was arrested In a statement on Thursday, WAS said initial investigations were "unable to identify" any calls from Eleanor's phone numbers. It said enquiries were ongoing to "establish if any calls were received by other means". In a tribute, Eleanor was described by her family as the "kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world". "She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock," they added. The police confirmed the murder was not being investigated as a domestic incident, and encouraged the public "to not speculate about the circumstances" as court proceedings were now active. Foster remains remanded in custody and will appear at Cardiff Crown Court on 26 October. title: Final James Bond screen tests to take place this weekend, reports say
description: Callum Turner and Jack Lowden "appear to be in the mix" of actors doing screen tests for the role.
body: Callum Turner and Jack Lowden are both thought to be part of the final auditions to play James Bond Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor are among the actors thought to be taking part in final auditions to play James Bond, according to reports. Screen tests are said to be taking place this weekend, possibly as early as Friday, according to the Hollywood Reporter, external, with between three and five actors understood to have reached the last stages of the process. The finalists are said to be taking part in auditions with three components - stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Deadline reported the screen tests, external had been due take place in early October, but had been delayed by scheduling conflicts, while Variety said Turner and Lowden, external "appear to be in the mix" to replace Daniel Craig. British actors Aaron Taylor-Johnson and James Norton were previously connected to the role, while Irish actor Paul Mescal's name had also been thrown into the mix. Other actors now appear to be in the frame, but reports on the current casting situation vary. Variety suggested Slow Horses star Lowden may now be edging ahead, while Masters of the Air star Turner was speculated about earlier this year, with some fans suggesting his wife Dua Lipa could sing the Bond theme song. Sources told Deadline that at least four final screen test offers have been made, and while unconfirmed, "three of the four expected to test are Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor". O'Connor is best known for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and for starring in 2025's Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, with Craig. Jack O'Connell had been thought to be in the mix, but sources said this may no longer be the case, while Euphoria and Wuthering Heights Star Jacob Elordi is not thought to be testing. Other stars who were previously linked with the role include The King's Man star Harris Dickinson, along with SAS: Rogue Heroes' Jack Barton. Deadline said: "Even with the tests wrapping next week, there is no timeline for when a final decision will be made." Daniel Craig served as James Bond across 15 years and five films Amazon MGM Studios, who now control the Bond franchise, announced in May, external that the casting process was under way, but had no further comment at the time. In August, Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, told Deadline, external the "end of the year is a good bet" for possible news on who would be playing Bond. "We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow," she said. "And it's got to be something really different that is a stirring and exciting and different." The BBC's Lizo Mzimba reported in September that "for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen". He added: "As the 007 team themselves have explained, external in the past: 'Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors'." The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered Search for new James Bond officially kicks off as auditions begin Writer Steven Knight said in September the first draft of the Bond script was done Only six actors have ever played novelist Ian Fleming's British Secret Service agent 007 in the official film series - Sean Connery, Roger Moore, George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig. The last announcement of a new Bond was in 2005 with Craig, who last starred in the role in 2021's No Time to Die, directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga. During the equivalent stage of the audition process two decades ago, Superman actor Henry Cavill was widely thought to have also been in the running. "They told me I was close," Cavill told the Happy Sad Confused podcast in 2022. "They told me it was ultimately down to, and this is what I've been told, it was just down to me and Daniel, and I was the younger option. "They obviously went with Daniel and I think it was an amazing choice to go with Daniel," he said. "I probably wasn't ready at the time and I think Daniel did an incredible job over the past movies, so I'm happy they made that choice." The forthcoming film, reportedly out in 2028, will be directed by Dune's Denis Villeneuve, with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight writing the script. Knight told Zoe Ball on Greatest Hits Radio, external in September that the first draft of the script was completed. Amazon bought MGM for $8.5bn (£6.3bn) in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond, and they are reported to have paid at least $20m (£14.9m) more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future. Pascal and David Heyman are producing the film, while Tanya Lapointe is executive producer. Knight's final words on the film were about how much he was enjoying working on it. He told Ball:, external "I'm absolutely loving doing it. It's an honour to be asked. And believe it's going to be so good. I really do believe it's going to be amazing." title: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning
description: Recent polls suggest the president is facing challenging headwinds in the state ahead of the midterms.
body: Father Roy Snipes is known locally as the Cowboy Priest - he resisted plans to seize chapel land to build Trump's border wall It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel. The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself. As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest. "I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname. In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys. During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the US president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). "There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers. Donald Trump campaigning in Texas earlier this month - the close Senate race is being hotly contested Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state - according to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project. "They said we're gonna seek out, capture, detain and deport the worst of the worst," Snipes said in his sermon. "Well, we're here on the border and the cartel is the worst-of-the-worst. So we thought, well, that's a good thing. "But it turned out, you can hear almost every day, some poor guy going to work and they stop him and detain him and start a big fight." After the service, two members of the congregation stopped to chat. "We're educators, and we have a lot of students that are having to go back because their parents are getting deported," one said. "The cruelty that we're seeing - I think that's turning the tide, at least I hope so," their friend added. Turning the tide politically is what Democrats are hoping they can do in Texas in the midterm elections on 3 November. But that will not be easy. This stretch of the Rio Grande was once one of the busiest crossing points on the US-Mexico border. Under former President Joe Biden, hundreds of thousands of migrants came through here, with more than two and a half million apprehensions recorded in a single year. Trump promised to stop these illegal crossings during his 2024 election campaign, and in large parts he has delivered. Border crossings are now at their lowest level in decades. And it was that promise which in part drove Trump's astonishingly high level of support in the state, taking around 55% of Hispanic votes in Texas alone - a record for a Republican presidential candidate. Javier Villalobos is the Republican Mayor of McAllen, one of the biggest cities in the Rio Grande Valley. He expects Republicans will find it tough this time around, but credits the Trump administration with stemming the border problem. "I remember I put out a video… thanking the administration for immediately securing the border. That was great," he said. "And I think generally most people are okay with the deportation of criminals, violent people, or people that really are not productive at all." But if you start deporting people that are productive and law-abiding, that is where the problem is, he added. Mario Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November Recent polls suggest much of Trump's support among Hispanic voters has ebbed away since 2024. Surveys taken since late summer indicate a majority of Texan Hispanic voters disapprove of the president. They also suggest Hispanic voters are favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin. "When I voted for President Trump, I voted for him because we saw an influx of immigration during the Biden administration," said Mario Guerrero, a young Mexican-American businessman who leads the South Texas Builders Association. It needed to be fixed, he said. "We thought that we were in the right by voting for Trump, and that he was going to do what was best in order to fix the crisis on the border. "And I think to myself, we were really not told the extreme that they were willing to go to make a point," he added, before referencing recent shootings involving ICE agents in US cities. Guerrero is a reminder that, for many who live and work close to the US-Mexico border, security and immigration enforcement are two distinct issues. A voter here may be supportive of securing the border and stopping illegal crossings, but oppose the actions of ICE and how the administration is enforcing its crackdown on undocumented migration. Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November, in part due to his unease with that crackdown. "There's a man that I know that… last year, had 35 workers that were working for him every day," he said. "Right now, he just told me two days ago that he would be lucky if he would get four to six guys to show up to work." Even though Guerrero plans to vote Democrat, he describes himself as neither Democrat nor Republican. And that, according to Mike Madrid, a leading Republican consultant and expert on Hispanic voters, is key to understanding the largest ethnic demographic voting group in the country. "Latinos are more likely than any other racial or ethnic group to identify as independents rather than Republicans or Democrats," he said. G

title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
description: One person has died after being swept away by waves in Taiwan's Liuqiu island, authorities say.
body: Taiwan is bracing for Champi's worst effects on Saturday Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast. Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday. One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate. Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far. On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) . After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island. Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan. However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches. Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said. Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains. Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island. Taiwan's $5tn (£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather. Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual. In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company. More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines. Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan. Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties. Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane. While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea. This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms. The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El Niño - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons. title: Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pushed a business and energy agenda over diplomacy on his second trip to India this year.
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in India this week The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit. So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi? The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions – or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs. Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani. It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations. The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies. With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets. And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation. The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now. Rubio (left) held talks with foreign minister S Jaishankar (right) in Mumbai Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties. The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic. "Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital. "This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai." The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works. But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip. Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms". Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website. It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets. During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani. The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products. Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil. "They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters. Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East. Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer. Rubio's visit to the Jamnagar refinery was closed to the media, with images released afterwards by the Reliance Group Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil. India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022. Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude. In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties. India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority. Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel. title: Watch: BBC presenter battles strong winds as storm hits Newquay
description: BBC lead weather presenter Simon King is in Newquay as the "full force" of the storm arrives.
body: This video can not be played Power cuts are affecting more than 9,000 homes in Cornwall and Devon as Storm Austen hits parts of the UK. A red warning is in place for Guernsey and Jersey, while Cornwall and parts of Devon are under an amber weather warning for strong winds. A yellow rain warning is also in place in parts of Scotland, including the Lothian Borders. The storm is expected to affect millions more this morning as a yellow warning kicks in across the South East and North West of England, the East Midlands and Wales. BBC lead weather presenter Simon King is in Newquay as the "full force" of the storm arrives. Simon is reporting from a safe, sheltered area away from the coastline. title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
description: Indian workers are being paid to film themselves at work and the footage is used to train AI.
body: Mohammed Ashim is paid to film his hands at work Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru. But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work. The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out. "The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working." He wears the camera for five or six hours a day. "It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim. He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities. Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work. That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world. Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data. "Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig. His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work. "For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says. Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says. "We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off." But his customers are getting more demanding. "Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands. "Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people." And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year. Shahil Baig expects dozens more firms to start collecting video of workers Why is such data so important? If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data. Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact. "Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says. And until recently, that data was not available. "There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco. At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia. Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients. "You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US." This video can not be played The factory workers teaching robots how to work like humans But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs? At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai. For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says. The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about. "By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says. Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI. "AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence." Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development. Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day. Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years. "Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says. He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work. "For me, it's simple. This is survival. I have a family back home in Bihar

title: Personalised skin cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial
description: The scientists involved say the results could mark a turning point in cancer treatment, bringing personalised medicine a step closer.
body: Tony Chapman, 75, from Corby in the East Midlands was one of the 1,100 melanoma patients enrolled on the vaccine trial A new personalised cancer vaccine given alongside a widely used immunotherapy drug has cut the risk of patients dying or their skin cancer returning by 42% in a major clinical trial. The researchers involved say the results could mark a turning point in cancer treatment, bringing personalised medicine a step closer. The trial also found that the new drug combination reduced the risk of melanoma, a type of skin cancer, spreading by 38% over two years compared to immunotherapy alone. The drug manufacturers MSD and Moderna say the same approach is already being tested against other tumours, including kidney, bladder and lung cancer. Independent cancer experts described the results as impressive but said longer-term studies were still needed to establish whether the treatment really helps most patients live longer, on average. The new approach is aimed at cancer patients who have already had their tumour removed through surgery. In the trial, 1,137 adults were given Keytruda, an established immunotherapy drug which helps the body's immune system find and attack cancer cells. About two-thirds also received an experimental vaccine with the rest being given a placebo or dummy drug. The vaccine, called Intismeran, uses the same mRNA technology as some Covid jabs. It is personalised to each patient, using information from their own tumour to help train their immune system to recognise cancer cells and target them if they return. Two years after starting the treatment, the patients who received the jab were far less likely to have had melanoma come back or see it spread across the body. "Personalisation is the next step up and it's really exciting, it's a fabulous technology," says Prof Pippa Corrie, a consultant medical oncologist who helped run part of the study with patients at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. "The question is how much can we really demonstrate it's worth and this trial was the first proof of principle." The latest checks show that Tony Chapman is cancer free three years after he was first told melanoma skin cancer had spread to his lymph nodes Prof Corrie worked with patients enrolled in the trial including 75-year old Tony Chapman, who was diagnosed with melanoma in 2019. He had the tumour removed from his chest but a lump later appeared under his arm. He was told his cancer had returned and he needed a second operation. He then volunteered to take part in the study but, like all the other participants, he still doesn't know whether he was given the experimental vaccine or a placebo alongside his immunotherapy treatment. "This just seemed like a really good example of moving science forward, as well as getting some benefit for yourself, so what's to lose?" Tony said. Three years on he is now having checks every six months and remains cancer-free. Shares in the drugmakers MSD (known as Merck in the US) and Moderna have surged since both companies first hinted at the success of the vaccine in the summer. But investors sold off stock on Thursday after financial analysts said the results were not quite as strong as those seen in an earlier, much smaller trial. Both companies said they were now "engaging with authorities" suggesting they could file for approval from medicine regulators as soon as next year. Widespread NHS use will also depend on cost, given that each individual patient will need to have their tumour genetically analysed and a personalised vaccine made for them. The trial will continue so that the patients involved can be monitored – both to see if the cancer returns over time and to assess whether the drug ultimately helps them live longer. Professor Alan Melcher from the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn't involved in the research, described the results as "very impressive". "It is an important proof of principle for the field, although we shouldn't get ahead of the evidence," he said. "We can't assume from one melanoma trial that the same approach will work across all cancers, and longer follow-up will be important to understand the effect on overall survival." The full trial results are due to be presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) cancer conference in Madrid on Saturday. They have yet to be published in a peer-reviewed medical journal, where they can be scrutinised by independent experts. title: Infantino re-election hopes boosted by Asia support after u-turn
description: Gianni Infantino's hopes of being re-elected Fifa president are enhanced by an endorsement from the Asian Football Confederation.
body: Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (left) had previously criticised Gianni Infantino over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme Gianni Infantino's hopes of being re-elected Fifa president have been given a major boost by an endorsement from the head of the Asian Football Confederation. President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa told the confederation's Congress in Tokyo - which was attended by Infantino - that "we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you as you seek a new mandate as president". Sheikh Salman's backing represents a significant u-turn just two months after he signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf criticising Infantino over his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. At the time the three confederations accused him of breaking trust "through deception" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, and "a profound failure of judgement...these are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership." But in what appears to be a blow to the rebellion against Infantino, Sheikh Salman told the meeting in Japan it was time "to move forward". "I've spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear," he added. "Yes, we had some issues, we spoke about them in the past, but let's not relate the two things together... "As one Asian family, we are ready to move forward, united in your support, Gianni." Alongside Infantino's power base in Africa and South America, Sheikh Salman's endorsement could be crucial in ensuring the Fifa president secures a fourth and final term. At the election in Rabat in March, Uefa will have 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10. Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency? The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed. Potential rivals such as Victor Montagliani, the president of Concacaf, and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders. "You've been doing a fantastic job in AFC in the last 13 years, my dear Salman," Infantino said in an address to the confederation's delegates. "You will do fantastically as well for the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of Fifa, because we have seen what we have been doing in the last years." Asked later about Sheikh Salman's comments, Infantino said: "I feel great about the AFC's support." At a meeting of Fifa's Council last week, Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan, but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised. He also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn). Uefa has since told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by 2 November.
