title: What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas for England
description: England face Australia at the Women's Rugby League World Cup on Saturday determined to show they have moved on from the nightmare of their last meeting in Las Vegas 19 months ago.
body: England will face Australia for the first time since a 90-4 loss in March 2025 Mention of Las Vegas is enough to send a shiver down the spine of any England women's rugby league supporter. Not because of lost life savings on the slot machines or undercooked food at the buffet, but because England fell to a record 90-4 defeat by Australia at the Allegiant Stadium in Nevada. The meeting between England and Australia in March 2025 had been touted as the first in a three-match Test series. It was meant to be the beginning of a regular Women's Ashes competition between two historic rivals and form a large part of world rugby league's charm offensive in the US. Instead it served up a sobering reminder of the gulf between the Jillaroos - the winners of the previous three World Cups - and England, who shipped 17 tries in a lopsided affair. The sight of Georgia Roche, who scored England's only try, in tears at the final whistle and being consoled by her opponents only added to the suffering of English fans who made the trip. The outcome also led many to believe the game in the northern hemisphere had reached a new nadir - with England's World Cup prospects almost dismissed out of hand as a result. However, it has also delivered a seismic shift in England head coach Stuart Barrow's thinking. Few of those selected for this tournament bear the scars of that encounter, with a youthful and dynamic squad featuring only six of the team from the Sin City debacle. And Barrow says excitement, not trepidation, is the feeling in the England camp as they get ready to face the World Cup co-hosts in Perth on Saturday (10:05 BST). "The youngsters coming in think that they can do better than what we did last time and I fully back that and believe them as well," Barrow said. "I don't think they've [Australia] been beaten internationally for a long time, but that's exciting. "If you're a young player coming into this group and coming to represent your country in a World Cup on the other side of the world, you want to play the best. "People were saying, 'do we want to avoid teams?' When you come all this way, you want to pit yourself as an athlete against the best. So there is excitement among the group but they're all very aware and very respectful of who we're playing." Rugby League World Cup: Australia v England Saturday, 24 October: 10:05 BST Listen to live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app. Stuart Barrow was appointed as England women's head coach in November 2022 While England thrashed Wales 70-6 in their World Cup opener, Barrow acknowledged their preparations to face Australia were dealt a "devastating blow" when Jasmin Strange picked up a serious knee injury in training on Tuesday, ruling her out of the rest of the tournament. The absence of the Sydney Roosters second-row forward will be sharply felt by Barrow's squad as they take on opponents who have lost just once since 2016 and remain the benchmark at international level. And Barrow insists that while their most recent encounter is "buried" and "in the past", he is using the chastening loss to help ensure England's readiness for this competition. "We learned a lot from it," he added. "We've built on that through all our training over the last 18 months. "We've got some senior players who were in that group at the time and it allows them to talk about what happened in that game to our young group. It allows them to talk about the difficulties, challenges and we can draw on the experience mainly from player to player." With Australia opening their campaign with a 40-0 win over Samoa, Barrow says his side will have to step things up from last weekend. "We came up with some unforced handling errors on first. We weren't at such a high completion rate but our skill with the ball let us get away with that," Barrow added. "You don't get that opportunity when you play the world champions. If you're giving cheap ball away, then you're defending. "We've done a lot of work about keeping possession and respecting the ball, but I also think we've got some exciting football in us when we get to the right end of the field to challenge them, so that's our aim." Meanwhile, Australia hooker Keeley Nizza has made it clear they will not take England lightly. "We definitely know about the rivalry," Nizza said. "Last year we played them in Vegas and there was a big score, but I think England are a very different team now." This video can not be played She ran the length of the field! Watch Amelia Brown's 100-metre-plus try Along with heritage player Hope Millard, Barrow's new-look squad contains centre Connie Boyd, who crossed for a hat-trick on her debut. They also have Super League's Woman of Steel Jenna Foubister, 19, and her highly-rated Wigan team-mate Isabel Rowe, who kicked nine conversions alongside a couple of tries to record the highest points tally (26) in a single game by a female England player at a World Cup. Barrow, who has previously called Rowe and Foubister's partnership in the halves "telepathic" also has Huddersfield Giants winger Amelia Brown among his new group. The 22-year-old - a dog groomer by trade - scored two tries against Wales, the second of which went viral on social media after she ran 107 metres to score it. "My phone's been popping off, so it just feels good," Brown said. "Some of my family don't really understand social media. So they're like: What does this mean? What does that mean? But they're all really happy for me and really proud of me." Barrow added: "You don't get many international tries that look like that, so to do that on your World Cup debut is outstanding. "We want moments like that in our sport and especially the women's game because the one million views [it has had] puts us on the map and hopefull

title: A Ballon d'Or campaign as fierce off the pitch as on it
description: The Ballon d'Or is football's greatest individual accolade - and the thirst to win it has grown in recent years.
body: Ousmane Dembele won the Ballon d"Or in 2025 and is one of 10 PSG players listed for it this year An emotional Ousmane Dembele had barely settled back into his chair at Paris' historic Theatre du Chatelet last September, gold-dipped orb in hand, when campaigns for this year's men's Ballon d'Or prize began to whirr into action. Entourages roused their candidates, media revelled in the hype. Who deserved the award in 2026? A World Cup year, no less, in which the narrative occasionally became not just which players could lead their country to glory, but how doing so would help them secure football's biggest individual accolade. "The Ballon d'Or has been discussed every single day," said European football expert Guillem Balague on BBC Sport's Euro Leagues podcast. "Quite clearly it follows the pattern of society, where it puts a lot of emphasis on the individual - it's harder to understand why a collective works, it becomes very easy to understand why one dribbles or doesn't dribble." Clamour for the spotlight only increased as the red-carpet ceremony neared. "You can't underestimate the PR machine that some clubs and some players are going to use," added French football journalist Julien Laurens. Managers and sporting directors talked up their charges, and questioned why others on their squad did not make the 30-man shortlist. Deco branded it a "huge scandal" that Barcelona pair Raphinha and Pedri missed out, but backed Lamine Yamal as overwhelming favourite to win it. Not, he says, because he is also a Barca player, but "because I like football". Star names have appeared frequently in the media. Lamine Yamal himself insisted he will not "beg for anything" - after last year saying he dreamed of "winning many" - but suggested the prize should not merely go to the top goalscorer. Paris St-Germain manager Luis Enrique confessed he is "bored of the Ballon d’Or" - although with a record 10 PSG players on the shortlist, perhaps he wishes to keep out of the debate. Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia talked each other up to BBC Sport. "We can cut it in two," joked Dembele. "Honestly, he deserves it, the season he had was exceptional." Kvaratskhelia responded: "Of course it's him!" A 'Kvara d'Or' campaign in Georgia celebrated the country's favourite fleet-footed son. "I think for the big nations it's really difficult to understand what [winning] would mean for the small country," the winger explained. Kylian Mbappe, who Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho compared to the original Ronaldo, was less subtle than most in his pitch to win the award for the first time. "I always think I'm the best but everyone has their own opinion," professed the Frenchman, now the all-time World Cup top goalscorer. "Of course, this year could be good for me to win the Ballon d'Or - but journalists vote." Indeed - since a short spell of national team captains and managers also voting ended in 2015 - the 30-player shortlist drawn up by the publications France Football and L'Equipe has been voted on by one journalist from each of the top 100 Fifa-ranked nations. The deadline has passed. The winner has already been chosen. This video can not be played What does it mean to win the Ballon d'Or? James Kirkham, a sports brand strategist who has worked with top clubs and players, including Harry Kane, says the build-up has had an election feel. "You're going out, canvassing, getting your vote and making sure you shore up certain blocks from certain countries, and why wouldn't you?" adds Kirkham. The lobbying is not for everyone. Max Eberl, Bayern Munich's board member for sport, championed Kane and Michael Olise but said the best players, external "are the ones who don't need to run a campaign". Mbappe's compatriot, Jean-Pierre Papin, winner of the award in 1991, meanwhile told French TV:, external "I like Kylian a lot, he's a record-breaker. However, there comes a point when it's all about me, me, me and me." Mbappe did make an interesting observation, alluding to the dominance of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo - the pair won a combined 13 in a 15-year period between 2008 and 2023. "My idea of the Ballon d'Or comes from the Messi and Ronaldo era - you don't give it to ordinary players, you give it ​to players who are different," explained Mbappe. AC Milan's Kaka was the last recipient before Messi and Ronaldo's tug-of-war began, the Brazilian pipping the young pair to the prize in 2007. That was a year after fledgling social media platforms Facebook and Twitter launched to the public. Nokia dominated mobile phone markets, people took digital cameras on nights out. The world had changed immeasurably by the time Messi won for an eighth time in 2023. "Today everything moves at the speed of light," explains former AC Milan chief executive and sporting director Ariedo Braida, who witnessed the club land seven awards, from Ruud Gullit to Marco van Basten's treble, George Weah, Andriy Shevchenko and Kaka. "Fans follow individuals - the players - rather than the club themselves. It's a widespread phenomenon, which we see, for example, in politics too. "Once upon a time, you'd be a Milan fan and go to watch Milan. Today, everything is live and with the Champions League you always get to see all the great stars straight away. "I must say this makes me feel a bit nostalgic, because the event is always immediate. Anticipation creates that sense of longing which has now disappeared." Are fans now more invested in star names than clubs? Messi and Ronaldo's brilliance, and often tribal online following, has also driven an increased emphasis on individual records - among fans, media and the players who grew up dreaming of emulating them. "You could argue we are in a more interesting time because for basically 15 years it was Messi v Ronaldo and it certainly feels more open.

title: The World Treadmill Championship - pitching elite runners against amateurs
description: Everyday runners are being given the chance to compete alongside elite athletes in the first World Treadmill Championship, a new global 5km competition.
body: This video can not be played Treadmill World Championship - what are they and how to compete? For decades, treadmill running has been viewed as little more than a training tool for outdoor runners. But that could be about to change, with the launch of the World Treadmill Championship. In this new World Athletics-sanctioned competition, runners around the world log 5km on a treadmill and compete for a prize pool of $100,000 and the title of world champion. Known as Run X, it pitches everyday runners against elite athletes. BBC Sport was invited along to a qualification event at a gym in Southampton to observe runners logging their times on the global virtual leaderboard. The finals for the first ever Treadmill World Championship will take place in Italy in March Among them is British marathon runner Charlotte Purdue. "I think it's good to get people into running. 5km is obviously not too far so people can have a shot at it, there's no pressure," she tells BBC Sport. Purdue, who holds the third fastest British female marathon time, believes the treadmill has been long misunderstood. "I personally love the treadmill and I've always used it in my training. We've got one at home and I find it easy at home and I really enjoy it." But does she think she's got what it takes to be the first ever treadmill world champion? "It's definitely added motivation," she adds. "But I wish it was a marathon on the treadmill, I think I'd have a better chance!" Elite marathon runner Charlotte Purdue logged her 5km time at 18 minutes 15 seconds Runners have until 24 January to complete 5km, for free, at an official Run X centre. They can make multiple attempts, but only their best time will count. There is no official 5km treadmill world record recognised by World Athletics. The men's 5,000m track record is 12 minutes, 35.36 seconds, while the women's is 13:58.06 The men's road record for the distance stands at 12:49, with the women's at 13:54. The top 25% of runners in age categories from 18 to 75+ will represent their nation at the regionals, before the 10 best men and women in each category advance to the world finals in Italy next March. The $100,000 prize pool is split between the men's and women's overall podiums, across seven age-group categories. The exact distribution has not been published. There are currently 20 countries taking part and the list of elite runners registered has not yet been disclosed. Organisers hope to entice more participants with wildcard entries to events like the 2027 World Road Running Championships in China. Despite the treadmill sometimes being referred to anecdotally as the 'dreadmill' due to the repetitive and monotonous nature of indoor running, World Athletics president Lord Coe told BBC Sport it's a "great opportunity" to introduce a new audience to running. "It's across a whole range of age groups. It's very important that we continue to innovate and it's really important that when we innovate, we use technology that attracts more young people into our sport," he says. The ambition for treadmill running doesn't stop there, with hopes the discipline can also be included in Esport competitions in the next five years. "We know there are a lot of long-distance challenges but nothing at that 5km mark which is more accessible and that's the real big starting point," Luke Townsend, education manager at Technogym UK, the co-organisers of the competition, tells BBC Sport. Alongside professionals like Purdue on the treadmills in Southampton were members of the 'She Strides' run club. They usually opt to run together outdoors but wanted to take part in Run X to highlight how important treadmill running is from a safety point of view. "Unfortunately, so many women in the winter have to change their routines of running outside because they don't feel safe," says Hollie Thackway, founder of She Strides. With the clocks going back this weekend, many runners will soon be spending more of their training time in the dark. Thackway added: "By being able to run inside on a treadmill, it means you don't have to stop your training, you can still be on a programme, achieve your goals and not stop running altogether through the winter, so I think this event is great to highlight that." title: Have Manchester United become the unmanageable club?
description: The cycle of doom that has engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip, writes Phil McNulty.
body: Manchester United are without a win in seven games in all competitions The cycle of doom that has ultimately engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has the hapless Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip. Carrick recreated a familiar scene - the same one acted out by predecessor Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after a 4-1 loss at Watford in November 2021 cost him his job - by raising his hands in apology to supporters who had just seen United humiliated by the same scoreline at Como in the Champions League. Carrick is the seventh full-time manager since Ferguson stepped down in 2013 after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge. Since then there have been days of success under Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho and Erik ten Hag, and moments of hope, but the final outcome is always the same - dismissal. Carrick will need something miraculous to change that storyline, with results poor and revolt within the dressing room as defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid, while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the tactics in Como. It hints at something rotten in the state of United. So should it really be crestfallen managers standing in front of those disappointed supporters? Can it really be United's managers every time? Should not even more scrutiny now be aimed at those who appointed them, then decided the direction of the club? Have United effectively, through years of decay, decline and appalling decision-making, become the unmanageable club? There have been those seven full-time managers - David Moyes, Van Gaal, Mourinho, Solskjaer, Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick. There have also been spells as interims for others such as Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher. United's leaders, from former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward to the ruling Glazer family and now part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, have effectively tried every trick in the book to recreate the Ferguson era. Moyes, an ill-starred appointment led by Ferguson, found the job too big for him after leaving Everton. Van Gaal and Mourinho were tried and trusted operators with stellar track records of success at Europe's superpowers. Solskjaer was effectively the anti-Mourinho without any sort of managerial track record that suggested he would succeed at United, but appointed after a successful spell in temporary charge. Ten Hag got the job on the back of leading a superb young Ajax side to the Champions League semi-final. Amorim was regarded as European coaching's hottest young property when he was lured from Sporting in Lisbon. All ended up sacked. All eventually found the unwieldy beast that is United impossible to tame. Van Gaal won the FA Cup in 2016. Mourinho won the League Cup and the Europa League in 2017. Ten Hag won the FA Cup in 2024 with a landmark win against Manchester City. Slim pickings compared to previous glories. United, however, have not become a bad or dysfunctional club overnight. They have been heading towards this point ever since the succession plan to Ferguson - not easy, admittedly - was botched so badly. Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp all felt able to resist the lure of Old Trafford, leading to what should have been red faces all round in December 2019, when they were all managing within 35 miles of each other in the north-west but none were at United. Ancelotti was at Everton, Guardiola was at Manchester City. Klopp was at Liverpool. United had Solskjaer, an over-sentimental choice made on the back of a feelgood interim spell. He lasted less than three years. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer adopts a similar pose to Carrick after his final game in charge in 2021 With every passing day, Carrick looks like Solskjaer Mark II. Carrick is a former fan favourite who did well in temporary charge, but whose previous managerial career was a sacking at Championship club Middlesbrough. Solskjaer shared that same unwanted distinction, sacked by Cardiff City in September 2014 after only nine months in charge as they struggled in the Championship. It has all brought United to the point where the question must be asked. Since Ferguson's departure, has it ever been worse than it is now? In recent times, has there ever been less hope than there is now? Has morale ever been lower than it is now? United will always find a manager should they require one, but their current parlous circumstances mean they are no longer the attraction they once were. They will not have the pick of the globe's finest. They will need to persuade someone that there is a future at Old Trafford that contains something other than future dismissal, a sobering state of affairs for the self-styled "biggest club in the world". Given the current state of United's squad, there is no guarantee a manager with a high-class track record would have a quick fix, or any fix at all, without huge investment. Carrick is front of house and, on current evidence, will pay the price for United's failings. He is a repeat of the Solskjaer mistake, an easy choice made after taking them back into the Champions League, a comfort blanket with supporters that has now been torn away by poor results. Manchester United part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in heated discussion with director of football Jason Wilcox - with CEO Omar Berrada in between - at Wolves in December 2025 There are significant culprits elsewhere, led by Ratcliffe. United fans have held regular protests against the Glazers since they took control in 2005, their leveraged purchase loading debt on to the club. They have remained majority owners, despite the level of angered aimed towards them from supporters, unmoved by years of ill feeling. In turn, Ratcliffe's move into part-ownership alongside the Glazer family has meant fans turned on him for his association and business partnership with the hugely unpopular Americans. title: 'I live in the dark': How rising bills are shaping daily life
description: Errol McGuiness says he has changed his daily routine to cope with higher household bills.
body: Errol McGuiness says he has changed his daily routine to cope with higher household bills As evenings grow colder and household budgets come under renewed pressure, 79-year-old grandad Errol McGuiness has developed a routine to keep costs down. The pensioner collects rainwater, spends much of his time in a single room and piles on extra layers rather than turning up the heating. "I keep lots of clothes on, but don't tell my daughter," he said. His most striking money-saving measure comes when night falls. "I live in the dark. "You don't need a light on to watch telly. You don't need a light on when you go to bed. You know the way to the toilet and the kitchen, so you don't need a light on." Errol admits he has a health condition and says his daughter regularly reminds him to switch the heating on. But he is far from alone in trying to cut household costs. New figures published this week showed inflation rose to 3.5% in September, its highest level for almost a year, while higher fuel prices have pushed up living costs for many households. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised measures aimed at easing pressure on household finances, including removing standing charges from gas bills. Four years into the cost-of-living crisis, almost two-thirds of low-income families say they struggle to afford essentials such as food, heating and clothing, according to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. Almost half said they had skipped meals or reduced portion sizes to save money. Melissa Baydilly says many people seeking help are struggling with the rising cost of essentials Among them is 83-year-old widower Bryan, who says he now lives largely in a single room to keep bills down. "I put a cardigan on and whatever it is you put on to keep yourself warm, shut the door, put the fan heater on to warm the house up," he said. "When you see the price keep going up, I think,' well, I'm sitting in one room'." At Affordable Foods in Blurton, Stoke-on-Trent, centre manager Melissa Baydilly says stories like Errol's and Bryan's are becoming increasingly common. The organisation runs a food bank, social supermarket and outreach service helping people with debt, benefits and employment issues. "Every supermarket you go into, everything's gone up," she said. "There isn't a place where you would go now and not say there's at least a 25% to 30% hike on prices." She believes pensioners are among those feeling the strain most acutely. "I don't believe, in this day and age, our seniors of the city should go to the supermarket, look at the fruit and veg and think, 'I can't have apples and oranges this week, I've got to pick'. "Should they be doing that in their 60s and 70s, when they've worked all their life?" title: Slade star Dave Hill's debut album honours city
description: Slade legend Dave Hill's first solo album celebrates Wolverhampton roots and personal stories.
body: Dave Hill, the lead guitarist for Slade, has named his album after a lane near his childhood home Slade star Dave Hill is set to release his debut solo album, paying homage to some of his old haunts in Wolverhampton. Named Dirty Foot Lane, the 10-track album was named after a road near his childhood home and not far from where he lives today. He collaborated with Noddy Holder's son, Django Holder, on the project, his first since the break-up of the band behind hits such as Merry Xmas Everybody. "It's got a lot of depth to it, every one of those tracks is a true story about someone close or someone I've lost," he told BBC Radio WM. Hill teamed up with Noddy Holder's son Django who produced the album The album blends rock, blues and folk, capturing the energy of Hill's live-performance roots alongside his personal journey, including struggles with mental health and the impact of the Covid-19 lockdowns. "When I started to write, I knew when something was good - it would almost make me cry," the 80-year-old added. He continued: "I was talking to Noddy Holder, [who is] probably one of my best friends in life, and he encouraged me to write my own music. "Wolverhampton was where I lived. [I remember] the council estate and the cinema and growing up in the days when Doris Day was in the charts. I loved her. I used to watch Flash Gordon at the cinema." Hill also teamed up with American country music star John Berry for the album. He also told BBC Radio WM that he has plans to release two further albums in the future. title: Matilda celebrates 15 years as West End success story
description: The musical is seen by more than 12 million people worldwide after starting in Stratford-upon-Avon.
body: Matilda The Musical is celebrating 15 years since its debut in London A musical that began life as a Christmas production in Stratford-upon-Avon has become one of the biggest theatre successes of the century as it celebrates 15 years in London's West End. Matilda The Musical, which is now the 10th longest-running musical in West End history, has been seen by more than 12 million people around the world, staged more than 10,000 performances and played in more than 100 cities. Composer and lyricist Tim Minchin said he was still amazed by the show's success. "Probably the biggest family musical of this century is written by [us] couple of idiots," he joked. Based on Roald Dahl's classic children's novel, the production premiered at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon in 2010 before transferring to the West End the following year. Composer Tim Minchin and writer Dennis Kelly said they never expected the show's global success Written by Dennis Kelly, with music and lyrics by Minchin, the musical has gone on to win more than 100 international awards, including 25 for best musical. Kelly said neither of them expected the production to become a global phenomenon. "If we'd made a successful show at Stratford, we'd have been delighted," he said. "I just remember the first night... the audience going crazy and I just wasn't ready for it all. "I was standing at the back, I wasn't even sitting in a seat and I just wasn't ready for it and I just thought, 'This is weird'." Roald Dahl's larger-than-life characters continue to entertain audiences around the world Minchin said the scale of the show's success became apparent when he and Kelly watched an early preview in Stratford. "We saw it on stage at the first preview in Stratford and we thought, 'Ah, hold on a minute'," he said. "We thought at that point that we might have a real crack at getting to the West End - but the bonus 15 and a half years. It's mad." He attributed part of the show's enduring popularity to its message. "It says to kids, stand up for what's right. Be brave, reading and stories are freedom, your family is where you find it, love conquers all, little girls are powerful. It's hard to feel cynical about it." Jacqui O'Hanlon said nobody involved in the original production expected its lasting success Jacqui O'Hanlon, deputy executive director of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said nobody involved in the original production could have predicted its longevity. "None of us could have guessed that it would be the global phenomenon that 16 years later we're still talking about," she said. "We started the run of the show with ticket discounts in place for the previews, because there were seating gaps and by the end of it, tickets were being sold on eBay for hundreds of pounds, so it was that quick." What started as a Christmas production has become one of theatre's biggest success stories The show is currently touring the UK and Ireland while continuing its West End run, with tickets on sale in London until January 2027. title: Pupils pen special song to give classmates a voice
description: Many pupils at Mitchell House Special School in east Belfast are non-verbal but that does not mean they cannot communicate.
body: Gemma she said that she wanted people to be more aware that not everyone communicates the same way It is a special song for young people who struggle to speak. Many pupils at Mitchell House Special School in east Belfast are non-verbal but that does not mean they cannot communicate. And to get that message across they have written and recorded a song called My Voice. It aims to educate people about alternative communication like Makaton, eye gaze and electronic devices and those who use them. The lyrics and music to My Voice were written by the "Moon" Class in Mitchell House School, made up of pupils from 11 to 13 years-old. "Sometimes my voice is confident, sometimes my voice is calm, sometimes I use my talker, to tell you who I am," one of the verses goes. Katie-Louise said the class are celebrating how they all communicate differently Gemma,12, was one of those behind the song and she said that she wanted people to be more aware that not everyone communicates the same way. "The meaning of the song is that we wanted to tell you that no matter how you use your voice, it's still important and that's really the school motto that we wanted to embody," she said. "And it's really important to me personally being friends with a lot of people who are non-verbal that people understand that they're not actually non-verbal. "It's people who don't understand them that think they're non-verbal." Caelainn is the school's deputy head pupil Katie-Louise, 11, used an electronic communication device to take part. "We're celebrating how we all communicate differently," she told BBC News NI. "This month we wrote a song with our teacher Miss Ryan to show how we all communicate differently and that our voices matter." Matthew operates an electronic communication device with his eyes The school's deputy head pupil Matthew uses eye gaze to communicate with his friend, the head pupil Caelainn. Eye gaze lets people operate a computer or tablet to communicate using their eye movement, or communicate with the use of cards as visual cues. "Matthew usually uses cards for yes or no questions," Caelainn said. But Matthew also operates an electronic communication device with his eyes. "So if Matthew looks whatever way it picks up on his eye," Caelainn explained. "It's been a privilege to be here for 16 years, it's been amazing and all the kids are amazing, they're so friendly, they're so respectful to people and they're good with other people's needs." Principal of Mitchell House Miriam Donnan said that they were proud to share the different ways their pupils communicated Due to its work, Mitchell House has been accredited as a Communication Friendly Setting by Elklan, a UK-wide organisation supporting children's speech, language and communication. It is one of only two schools in Northern Ireland to achieve the accreditation for its work using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC). Principal Miriam Donnan said that they were proud to share the different ways their pupils communicated. "We want to tell the world that communication is not just about speech," she said. "We work really closely with our speech and language therapy department here in school to really promote lots of different ways of communicating and we wanted to celebrate that and share that with everybody. "So the class themselves came up with the idea for the song and the words are all their own that they came up with their teacher Miss Ryan and it's really a lovely celebration of everybody's voice matters." And Gemma wants everyone to know that sometimes a little patience and consideration might be required. "It's really important that people understand that you have to take time and be patient to understand how other people communicate," she said. title: Could experts have a solution to toxic algae?
description: Experts from the University of Bath are testing out a new invention at a lake in Wiltshire.
body: Blue-green algae - or cyanobacteria - has been a persistent problem in hot weather in Warminster Experts are testing out a new method that could see a way to tackle blue-green algae blooms. The toxic algae is actually cyanobacteria rather than a true algae and can increase dramatically in heat, making people and animals sick when ingested. Dr Sanjay Nagarajan, from the Institute for Sustainability and Climate Change at the University of Bath, took his child to the Warminster Pleasure Grounds in Wiltshire when he saw the lake there closed because of the bloom. He and colleagues have since created a machine to help eliminate it from the water which he hopes he can make bigger and loan to councils. Children's cancer unit gets £500K upgrade Search for 'suspicious men' in dog walker's murder 'Shock' as new ornamental bench vandalised From January to October this year alone there have been more than 168,000 visits to the park in Warminster. People would usually be able to take boats out onto the lake and an active model boat club is in the area. However, while it tends to die off in wintry weather, the algae has been causing problems over summers and this year it has been closed to activities for several months, with warning signs up round it. The bloom has meant the lake has been inaccessible over summer "Every year it gets worse and worse with climate change," said Kevin Whitehorn, the estates manager for Warminster Town Council. "Water levels in the lake have gone down which meant the blue-green algae has grown even more than it has done in the previous years," he added. Nagarajan, a chemical engineer, visited the park with his child and emailed the council saying he wanted to test something. Dr. Madhubalaji Chegu Krishnamurthi (left) has studied algae for ten years and Dr Sanjay Nagarajan (right) is a chemical engineer His colleague, Dr Madhubalaji Chegu Krishnamurthi, has been studying algae for a decade and said "there many good algae as well as bad algae". "Whenever the bad algae grows more, because of the nutrients in the lakes, it will release the various toxins that are very harmful for humans." Nagarajan, with colleagues and a PhD student, have put together a machine with a reactor that uses bubbles to get rid of the algae. The type of reactor is not new, but its use like this is. The invention involves pumping water through a small box which is actually a reactor As with many new inventions, in order to get the water in and out of the reactor, they have had to improvise. This devices uses a generator and equipment usually used for home beer brewing. A small box at the side does a lot of the work - Nagarajan explained that it is the reactor. "If you take a small drinks can, fill it up with some water, heat it up and then invert it into an ice bath, it gets crushed. That's exactly what happens inside the reactor and we call it cavitation. "Whenever we are able to manipulate the conditions to produce these cavitation bubbles, these bubbles will actually be crushed or imploding. "Once the implosion happens those effects will help in destroying the bloom." The lake and park is a popular local attraction Nagarajan said they have had positive results: "We've seen up to 20% degradation in terms of toxins and we've also seen a lot of the algal cells being destroyed because of the effect of cavitation." The next stage is to get their results published and apply for funding to create a bigger machine they can loan out to councils. title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
description: The quake hit a mountainous, sparsely-populated area in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region.
body: This video can not be played Watch: CCTV vision shows moment quake strikes in Tibet A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens, according to Chinese state media. The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau. The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km (250 miles) north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa. Authorities have declared the incident an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 65 others have been injured, including 11 people with severe injuries. The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas. Local media said more than 12,400 people had been relocated following the earthquake. Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas. The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km. Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes. This video can not be played Rescuers search through rubble after Tibet earthquake Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape. Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu told Tibet Daily that she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, her "legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home. Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us". Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet. Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks had been registered since the quake occurred. China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media. Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude, around 4,800m (15,750ft), and prone to aftershocks. The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations. Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (£5.6m; $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet. Firefighters are seen helping residents injured by the quake in Baqên, Tibet Videos on social media of the moment the quake struck show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark. These have not been independently verified. The region is prone to devastating seismic activity. In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China. Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing. Despite the region presenting some of the most challenging rescue conditions, rescue teams on the Tibetan plateau are highly experienced and have shown an ability to mobilise quickly. In January 2025, military personnel, firefighters, police and specialist rescue teams were in the area within hours after a powerful eartquake struck the Shigatse region of Tibet. The Chinese military also have drones to help survey the area. Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China. With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen. title: 'Wildly unfair that my husband and I pay £4k a year for ADHD treatment'
description: Northern Ireland is the only part of the UK without a formally commissioned, publicly-funded adult service for ADHD.
body: Rebecca and her husband, who also has ADHD, both pay for regular private psychiatric reviews, GP prescriptions and medication Adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are demanding urgent action over a lack of funded services in Northern Ireland, with some revealing they pay thousands of pounds a year for private treatment. Northern Ireland doesn't have a formally commissioned, publicly funded adult ADHD pathway like in other parts of the UK. One woman has described the situation as "wildly unfair and inhumane", saying she and her husband spend about £4,000 a year on private treatment and care. The Department of Health acknowledges increasing demand but said decisions must be taken in the context of overall affordability. Rebecca Bryson owns three businesses, which helps to cover the cost of her ADHD, external treatment and follow up care. Her husband, Colum Coyle, also has ADHD, and both pay for regular private psychiatric reviews, prescriptions and medication. Their combined costs of staying on treatment are about £4,000 a year. "It's a tonne of money that most people don't have, and I'm in a position where we do have it because I work multiple jobs," she said. She said the situation felt "wildly unfair and kind of inhumane". "If I had another medical condition like cancer or a broken bone, and I asked for medical treatment, they wouldn't turn me away." Bryson said there needed to be a clear route to diagnosis for adults with ADHD in Northern Ireland. "You can get a diagnosis as a child, but once you turn 18, you're on your own. It's bananas." Northern Ireland: Remains without a formally-commissioned ADHD service. Trusts manage referrals within existing resources, leading to long waiting lists. England: A legal right to choose exists in areas within England. If a local wait is long, a GP can refer a patient to another NHS-approved provider. Scotland: There is no single commissioned service for ADHD, as local statutory partners have responsibility for planning, designing and delivering services to meet the neurodevelopmental support needs locally, including services commissioned from the third sector where appropriate. Wales: ADHD services are commissioned locally by health boards. The Welsh government is working through its Neurodiverse Improvement Programme to increase capacity, improve assessment pathways and reduce long waiting lists. Dr Allen McCullough said ADHD diagnoses has become an "evolving picture" Dr Allen McCullough has worked as a GP for 35 years. He said he understands the difficulties with those seeking ADHD diagnoses and it has become an "evolving picture". "I can refer to an adult ADHD service within my local area, but that's in the full knowledge that there isn't anybody there to receive it," he said. McCullough says some GPs have concerns issuing medication for those looking shared-care arrangements, where a consultant and GP collaborate to manage and prescribe specialist medications. "Some of these patients are attending privately, and we don't get any notification of who they're seeing or the qualification of the person who's doing the diagnosis. So, I'm not saying it isn't a stand over diagnosis, but if we're not getting the information, we're definitely not going to get involved or cannot get involved. "When you prescribe it, you're responsible." 28-year-old Jordan says he struggled to get access to ADHD services here after concerns from family members. Jordan Young, 28, said he struggled to get access to ADHD services, which typically include assessments, medication and follow-ups. "I tried so many different places. I was basically told that the doors were closed, they weren't taking anyone else on," he said. He went to England to get diagnosed. "If it wasn't for my granny, I wouldn't have gone over and gone private to be honest. She put me through her private health insurance." Young said more needed to be done to improve access to ADHD services in Northern Ireland. "I want to see where the health minister actually comes to some sort of agreement that he will put a budget [in] for people with ADHD or people that looking to be diagnosed with ADHD and treat it like it is a serious matter." Alliance MLA Peter McReynolds said adults with ADHD had been "completely forgotten about" Alliance MLA Peter McReynolds said adults with ADHD had been "completely forgotten about" by the Department of Health. He said he had been pushing for a commissioned service since 2024 and had met three health ministers, who he said had taken a similar approach. "I think we should be a hell of a lot further [on] in terms of commissioning that service because it would be transformative for the people of Northern Ireland and it would save us money in the longer term as well." A Department of Health spokesperson said health trusts "manage referrals within existing resources and demand continues to exceed available capacity, resulting in long waiting times which has led to people seeking a private diagnosis". "Significant work has been undertaken to better understand the level of need for ADHD services," he said. "Any future commissioning decisions must be taken in the context of overall affordability, at a time when we face significant funding constraints across health and social care." title: We'll dress women for court to empower them on their darkest days
description: A new campaign will help women feel confident to give evidence in sexual assault trials.
body: Sarah Lee was worried how she would be perceived as a witness Walking into a witness box to give evidence is one of the most daunting things a person can do. Giving evidence as a victim of a sexual assault case is even more challenging. That's something rape survivor Sarah Lee knows too well. Fears about being judged on her appearance added to that pressure. "Should I wear this? How will that look? How am I going to be perceived? Will I be judged?," she told BBC Scotland News. "Should I wear something that's closed? Should I wear something that's open? "There's just all these questions, how will my hair look? You're anticipating that people... are going to put you on trial." Sarah, 39, describes the trial as one of the darkest periods of her life. She was terrified that attention would focus on her appearance rather than her evidence. This video can not be played 'You know walking into a trial that you're on trial too' That anxiety motivated Sarah Lee and Kayla Poulton, who has also been through the court process, to do something that might help to remove some of the stress for others in a similar position. They've set up a new campaign called CourtRobe which asks high street department stores in Scotland to donate vouchers or clothing and give staff specialist training to help women dress for court. The women are working with the Emma Ritch Law Clinic at the University of Glasgow to develop the project. For them, it's about empowerment. Kayla, 36, said: "For me it was, do I wear a dress? If I wear a dress, do I look too provocative? Do I wear heels? Then I got suit trousers and a blouse and then I was so worried that the blouse was going to be see-through. "You just overthink. You don't want people to think, oh, she deserved that. Oh, if she dressed like that, then, well, she deserved it. "That's a really scary part and that's where we want to empower women and for them to just feel confident enough to go in and be who they are." Kayla Poulton says women often feel stigma when giving evidence in sexual assault trials Sarah said: "It's not like you can turn up in a situation like this in your leggings and a hoodie. It's just not the way that women want to portray themselves." CourtRobe aims to provide support to women who need it and who are looking to find confidence at an incredibly difficult time. The project is aimed specifically at those on limited incomes. The women believe it will help others be more prepared and feel less intimidated. Shop staff involved in the programme will be given trauma informed training and will offer survivors free personal shopper sessions to choose clothes they feel comfortable in. Women will have access to clothing and a shop stylist to help them dress confidently for the courtroom Kayla hopes the project can remove some of the stigma she feels women face when attending sexual assault trials. She said: "You're just so worried about what the jury are thinking about you as a person and not the person that's on trial. "CourtRobe is about empowering women at a time where they feel really vulnerable." Rape Crisis Scotland points to research which suggests that image can, in fact, have an impact in sexual assault trials. Spokeswoman Nicola Love said it shouldn't be surprising that women are "disproportionately worried about how they're perceived" when they go to give evidence. "We've seen research, we've seen evidence from juries that if it's deemed to be a revealing piece of clothing or a provocative piece of clothing, they find that witness less credible." She added that Rape Crisis Scotland was also fully behind Sarah and Kayla's plans. "Whether or not you're wearing the right outfit should be the last thing you're thinking about. Going to court is really costly. We don't have that conversation enough. "Having a service that is able to take that stress away is incredibly important and would make an incredibly distressing, stressful experience, feel significantly less stressful." title: What books had people turning pages and turning up the volume this year?
description: Thrillers, self-help books and Harry Potter were the big winners for readers from Libraries NI data.
body: Books with "short chapters" and include "catchy, racy" themes seem to be most popular Thrillers, self-help books and Harry Potter were among the favourites for readers in Northern Ireland this year, according to Libraries NI. For those who prefered to listen to their fiction, Freida McFadden had eight of her titles featuring in the top 10 adult fiction audiobooks borrowed. Jillian McFrederick from Libraries NI said books with "short chapters" and "catchy, racy" themes seemed to be most popular. But when it came to younger readers, there was little change with Harry Potter continuing to be popular - almost 30 years after the release of the first book. This week marks Book Week - a joint initiative between BBC NI and Libraries NI and celebrates books, reading and libraries and everything that they make possible. The data provided by Libraries NI covers a 12-month period from 1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026. Jillian McFrederick from Libraries NI said books with "short chapters" seem to be most popular Audiobooks led the way this year with more downloads than physical book loans. The Housemaid by McFadden was the most listened to, with only Romantasy favourite Fourth Wing by Rebecca Yarros and The Pumpkin Spiced Café by Laurie Gilmore breaking McFadden's hold on the chart. This video can not be played The figures come from Libraries NI as part of Book Week NI 2026 When it came to non-fiction, those listening seem focused on personal development. A best-selling title by Mark Manson, The Subtle Art of not Giving a ... (Google the rest if you wish), topped the non-fiction section, while Atomic Habits and 101 Essays That Will Change the Way You Think followed closely behind. Meanwhile, for younger listeners, the Harry Potter series remained the standout success with all seven books from the series making it into the top 10. Other favourites included classic titles such as Matilda by Roald Dahl, and Diary of a Wimpy Kid by Jeff Kinney. Freida McFadden has released 36 books since her first publication in 2013 The Housemaid also topped the charts when it came to physical loans, with the title being borrowed more than 3,000 times. McFrederick said the release of the movie adaptation, starring Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfield in 2025, had brought a whole new audience to McFadden's work. Niall Williams' historical fiction book based in 1960s Ireland, Time of the Child, came close to beating McFadden with only 15 loans behind. When it came to non-fiction, global best-seller, The Let Them Theory by Mel Robbins came first, slightly ahead of Nobody's Girl by Virginia Roberts Giuffre. The wider top five reflected variety from self improvement to baking, including Mary Berry's very best recipes. Variety continued for junior readers. A Belfast Fairytale led the fiction category with nearly 3,000 loans and the Guinness World Records 2026 took the lead in non-fiction. Ebooks showed library users were split between very different reading habits over the last year. In fiction, readers gravitated towards page turners from authors like Virginia Evans with The Correspondent claiming top spot. Richard Osman showed a true favourite with three of the top 10 being written by him. Andy Weir's Project Hail Mary also proved popular following a movie adaption earlier this year. For non-fiction, self-help was a clear winner. Again, Mel Robbin's The Let Them Theory came first, with more than 2,000 loans. McFrederick said the book "struck a chord with people because they're all so stressed and so anxious". Mel Robbin's The Let Them Theory had more than 2,000 ebook loans Other popular self-help books were also in the top five including The Psychology of Money and The Courage to be Disliked. Among younger readers, the magic around the Harry Potter series continued with more than 1,500 loans in fiction. Junior non-fiction interests ranged from The Wimpy Kid Movie Diary, Historical Royal Palaces: Ghost in the Walls and 101 Amazing Harry Potter Facts among the most borrowed eBooks. title: Monk on Caldey Island gave naked photos of himself to visitors
description: The monk denies sexually assaulting a visitor, who says he also gave her naked photos of himself.
body: Brother Titus denies sexually assaulting a visitor, who says he also gave her naked photos of himself A woman has spoken out for the first time about an alleged sexual assault by a monk who lived on a private island off the coast of west Wales. Brother Titus Keet, 78, has also been accused of sexually harassing and sexually assaulting a former Caldey Island employee as well as giving women naked photos of himself. He denied the allegations saying "a woman who feels rejected can become very vicious" and said the pictures were not sexual, but he would reflect on his behaviour. The claims, revealed in a new BBC podcast Dark Island, were investigated by Dyfed-Powys Police but there was no further action. Caldey Island is off the coast of Tenby, Pembrokeshire, and is owned by a group of Cistercian monks. Single mum Natalie Roberts was a regular visitor from the early 2000s and would spend holidays there with her two sons. She told the Dark Island podcast that Keet would give her photos of himself posing naked on beaches on Caldey, often accompanied by a poem. He shared photos with other women too. An island of dreams for some, a place to hide for others. Investigative journalist India Pollock uncovers the disturbing secrets beneath the tranquil image of Caldey Island. In 2016, Natalie went for a walk from Caldey to nearby St Margaret's Island with her sons and a friend. She did not know Keet would be there. The walk is quite dangerous and you have to scramble across slippery rocks to get from one island to the other. Natalie claims it was then, when Keet was walking behind her, he repeatedly sexually assaulted her over her clothes. She said she was horrified, adding: "I was so angry because I knew this was an absolute violation. "You know, this wasn't spiritual. This was his opportunity just to do that." Brother Titus Keet would take naked photos of himself at different places around Caldey Island She said she was stunned but did not say anything to Keet because she thought he would deny it and she might be asked to leave the island. Natalie said: "I think the worst thing it did, if I'm completely honest, it took away my whole spiritual belief in Catholicism." But Keet claimed she turned "wickedly against him" after he rejected her attempts to seduce him. It is also claimed Keet made several unwelcome sexual advances towards an employee of the abbey. Allegedly, he touched her breasts and bottom, commented on her body and referred to her genitals, despite being asked not to. Other allegations included making sexualised comments while showing nude photos of himself and pictures of naked women. It is claimed Keet was confronted at the time but said UK law did not apply to him as he was a Dutch citizen, that he could do as he liked as he was on a private island and allegedly, he called the employee "too sensitive". He is also accused of saying the woman was lucky to receive sexual attention from him and "women welcomed male attention". It is also claimed the monk told her she would lose her job if she complained. Keet said the allegations were false and quoted The Bible in his statement to the podcast: "To all who are pure themselves, everything is pure; but to those who have been corrupted and lack faith, nothing can be pure [Letter to Titus 1,15]." He said the employee had made up the allegations in the hope the monastery would pay her money and that she was paid to "keep quiet". "If it was not so sad, it would be laughable, how she could make up so many allegations spread out over three years, in which we had co-operated so pleasantly together. Very sad," he added. Brother Titus Keet would write letters or poems to accompany his naked photographs In response to the allegation from Natalie, he said: "This is a classic example of a woman who felt frustrated in her advances, disappointed in her expectations, feeling rejected and then turns against the other in a very vicious way." Natalie denied that claim and said he was in a position of "significant power" and she was in a position of vulnerability. She added he used victim-blaming language and had attempted to discredit her. The abbot of Caldey Abbey, Father Jan Rossey, said they referred complaints in line with their safeguarding procedures. He said in 2024, Keet was "required to leave" Caldey Island and will not be allowed back. This was years after the employee made a complaint of sexual assault. Keet has moved to another monastery. About 50,000 day trippers catch the boat from the popular seaside resort of Tenby to visit Caldey island every year. It is owned by the order of monks that live there, and is only 1.5 miles (2.4km) long and a mile (1.6km) wide. Visitors who stay overnight can do so in the guesthouse or other properties the monks own. There are also about 30 lay people who live there. Caldey Abbey has been home to Cistercian monks since a group moved from Scourmont Abbey in Belgium in 1929 Caldey Island was once known for being "crime free", but in 2017, six women settled a civil claim against the abbey. They had been sexually abused as children by the monk Thaddeus Kotik. The former abbot Robert O'Brien knew about the abuse but did not report it. An independent review, published in 2024, found that victims were treated in a heartless, hostile and cruel way. It said frequent allegations of abuse were made, but not followed up on or reported to police, and the lack of challenge had enabled Kotik to abuse children over four decades "in plain sight". Other offenders have also stayed on the island, including a man who was wanted by police and lived under an alias for seven years before being jailed for 30 months for possessing child abuse images. The abuse by Kotik was investigated by the police in 2014 and 2017, but officers concluded there was little they could do as he died in 1992. title: 'Shock' of first England farmer hit by bird flu this season
description: The first farmer in England hit by bird flu this season tells of the "emotional roller coaster" of losing 32,000 hens.
body: Catherine Armstrong says the outbreak of bird flu is all her worst fears realised A farmer hit by England's first outbreak of avian flu this season has said the loss of 32,000 egg-laying birds is likely to cost her business more than £100,000. Catherine Armstrong, who has a free-range farm near Belford, Northumberland, told the BBC of the "shock" of her worst fears coming true when she found "a carpet of dead birds" in her barns this week. The outbreak's source is not yet known but the virus is thought to have been brought onto the site, which has strict biosecurity measures, by wild birds. The farm's remaining poultry were culled. The Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) has put control measures in place to contain the outbreak, external but warned cases were likely to rise. Strict controls have been placed around the farm to contain the outbreak of avian influenza, Armstrong says So far, there has been one other case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in the UK, external, on the Isle of Lewis, Scotland. Armstrong said her birds, which normally produce 28,500 eggs a day, which are then supplied to a range of UK supermarkets, began to die a week ago. "At this age of the flock, you would tend to see the odd death but on the Friday my lady who works in the shed messaged me at night to say that 39 had died," she explained. During the weekend, the virus spread rapidly, with more than 1,000 birds dead by Sunday night. The APHA was contacted and a vet came out to carry out tests but Armstrong said she knew it would be bird flu: "In my heart of hearts, when you are shovelling dead birds out of a shed, you feel... well, I didn't need the results. I knew what the results would be." By Tuesday, the virus had been confirmed, with thousands of birds dead. Within two days, all the remaining birds had been culled to control the virus' spread. "All your worst fears, I suppose, are realised then. It is an emotional roller coaster. I mean, for instance, on the Sunday, I just felt numb. On the Monday, just a bit like 'Why me?'. Angry, cross, upset. "On the Tuesday, it's a bit matter of fact. It's like, 'Right, we've got to do this. I've got to do that'. And on Wednesday, I was just desperately sad. "Normally, you'd open up a hen shed door and there'd be 16,000 birds looking at you but to see them all lying dead, just a carpet of dead birds, is quite shocking. "As a poultry keeper, it's a horrible shock." Armstrong praised the APHA staff for their work and the wider industry for its support. She said despite the high cost of the outbreak - which she estimated would be more than £100,000 - she was "not going to sit back and let it beat us". Gary Ford, of the British Free Range Egg Producers' Association (Bfrepa), said the farm had high standards of biosecurity but "sadly, as was the case here, that does not always prevent infection as free-range hens come into regular contact with wild birds, which spread this dreadful disease". He added the association would be calling on the government to bring in a regional housing order to protect "those poultry farms close to coastal areas and known flight paths of migratory wild birds". Meanwhile, farmers are still waiting for the results of a recent government trial of a bird flu vaccine in turkeys. A spokesman for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said that, while the trial concluded in August, results would not be available until the end of the year and vaccination would not be an option for this bird flu season. Meanwhile, an APHA spokesperson said it expected colder temperatures and the arrival of migratory birds "to see a rise in infection cases, which is why it is so important that bird keepers have robust biosecurity measures in place to limit the spread of this devastating disease". The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the risk to the general public's health posed by avian influenza remained very low while the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said it posed a very low food safety risk, with properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, safe to eat. title: Blue Planet III: Moment octopus escapes death after hunt gone wrong
description: The sequence is part of the latest Blue Planet series from Sir David Attenborough.
body: This video can not be played Filmmakers have captured an octopus's lucky escape after venturing from her normal underwater habitat. The sequence is part of the latest Blue Planet series from Sir David Attenborough, who has continued to produce nature documentaries into his 101st year. In the third instalment, viewers are taken around the world - from icy polar waters to the tropics, and out into the open oceans. For UK audience, Blue Planet III starts on Sunday 1st November, 8pm, BBC One and iPlayer. For those outside the UK, Blue Planet III will launch from November into 2027 across the world. title: Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says
description: Kanishka Narayan tells the BBC that dealing with the technology requires not only regulation, but "building capability and capacity".
body: This video can not be played AI minister: "500 new vulnerabilities" previously found by AI in government systems Britain cannot let aritificial intelligence be ruled by "tech bros and oligarchs", the AI minister has said. Kanishka Narayan told the BBC's Political Thinking podcast that dealing with the technology requires not only regulation, but "building capability and capacity in the state" too. He compared AI to the Victorian-era Industrial Revolution, but said the country needed to transition better than it did back then. His comments were recorded the day before Barclays banking group announced it was cutting 5,000 jobs in an AI-led efficiency drive. He was also speaking before another major AI-related development - the discovery of a cyber-security flaw affecting millions of websites, which was found with the help of AI. Narayan, who became the UK's first cabinet minister for AI when he was appointed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July, said the scale of the technological change was "something that we haven't seen for decades and decades". "It is comparable and in some ways exceeds the Industrial Revolution," he said, referencing the shift from a predominantly agricultural economy to industrial and manufacturing sectors between about 1750 and 1900. The Labour MP told the BBC's Nick Robinson that Britain needed to avoid what happened in the Industrial Revolution where "the outcome as a whole was good for the country, but the transition was extremely painful for too many people". "The fundamental thing is that the British public and democracy has to assert power rather than leave it to tech bros and oligarchs," he added. He did not name any specific companies or tech bosses. AI minister Kanishka Narayan: The challenge and opportunity of AI Political Thinking with Nick Robinson As well as "pulling the lever of regulation", the country needs to build AI in Britain "so you can shape the working conditions" and avoid it all being developed abroad, he said. "We need to build technology to defend ourselves and to grow ourselves so we have leverage internationally - we're now currently totally reliant on other countries for essential bits of technology," he added. Pointing to the capabilities of AI, he said the government recently used frontier AI models, external in Whitehall to check for cybersecurity issues. "We only spent £13,000 on it - we discovered 500 new vulnerabilities. These are novel vulnerabilities that we discovered in significant areas of the public sector," Narayan said, without detailing what they were. He also said his conversations with Chancellor John Healey had hinted at a potential AI announcement in next week's Budget, though he did not say what this was. Narayan rejected the notion that the US and China were the only powers that matter for AI, saying the UK's AI Security Institute had seen "every US lab...coming to us" asking it to test models before deployment. Earlier this month, Narayan warned it was likely the UK's cyber defences will at some point be breached, after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June. He has made a series of interventions in recent weeks after an AI safety researcher went public with claims that people building the technology believed it could destroy humanity. title: Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m
description: Ministers say the changes in regulations will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy.
body: John Healey becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to cut red tape for businesses ahead of his first Budget The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m. Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations, announced ahead of John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses. The move is part of a broader effort in the Budget to offer households and businesses more support amid rising costs. In response to the announcement, the Conservatives said Labour had only made problems worse for businesses. "Labour have finally admitted that endless red tape is hammering businesses and killing jobs across the country," shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said. Healey acknowledged British firms are "fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork" eating into time and money that would be more valuable invested into their businesses. He becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to slash red tape, which he said will allow businesses more "breathing space" to invest and create good jobs. The changes should make compliance guidance easier, and simplify the reporting rules firms have to follow, the Treasury said. Ministers have claimed this will save almost £800m in administrative and tariff costs. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey are expected to meet some business leaders on Friday at No 10 North. Burnham said that it's unfair "pointless bureaucracy gets in the way" of hard-working people building their businesses. "If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms," Burnham said. The government has set itself a target of cutting regulation by 25% by the end of the current Parliament. The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Chief Executive Rain Newton Smith has welcomed the plans, but said the test would be in delivering reform. Meanwhile, the shadow chancellor argued that the employment act had only made "the situation worse and has created a youth jobs emergency". "John Healey must get a grip in his Budget next week. He must back our Conservative plans to cut welfare and cut taxes so we can get Britain working again," he said. Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story? title: Watch: Met chief Rowley not fit for job, says detective raped by colleague
description: Det Con Linda Williams, a victim of serial abuser David Carrick, says she has no faith in the system.
body: This video can not be played A Met Police detective who was raped by a fellow officer has said the force's handling of her case was "like being raped all over again". Det Con Linda Williams was attacked in 2004 by PC David Carrick - who was jailed for life in 2023 for sexual offences against her and 11 others. Linda sought damages from the Met for failing to protect her from Carrick and said the process left her feeling suicidal. She now wants Met Commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, to resign because he has failed to change police culture as promised. Investigations correspondent Daniel De Simone reports.
