title: Detective raped by colleague says Met handling of case 'like being raped again'
description: Linda Williams was attacked by David Carrick, who was jailed in 2023 for sexual offences against 12 women.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Met chief Rowley not fit for job, says Linda Williams A Metropolitan Police detective, who was raped by a fellow officer, has told the BBC that Scotland Yard's handling of her case was "like being raped all over again". Det Con Linda Williams was attacked in 2004 by PC David Carrick - a serial abuser jailed for life in 2023 for sexual offences against her and 11 other women. Linda has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because of the attack and sought damages from the Met for failing to protect her from Carrick. The lengthy civil case left her feeling suicidal, she says. The "worst thing", she says, was when lawyers acting for the Met commissioner challenged the severity of her PTSD on the basis that she had been raped only once. The Met has told the BBC it "tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams' welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible". "We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer," the force added. "Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable." Linda, who has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak to the BBC, has settled her civil case and the Met has now paid her compensation without acceptance of liability. In an unprecedented move for a serving officer, she is now calling publicly for Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley to resign. She believes he has failed to change police culture as promised and she still does not trust her own force to handle cases like hers. When he took on the most important job in UK policing in 2022, Sir Mark pledged to change the Met. At the time, the force was viewed as being in crisis - following Sarah Everard's murder by a serving officer and other scandals including officers sharing photos of murdered sisters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman. Met Police commissioner Sir Mark Rowley has promised to get rid of officers unfit to serve After Carrick was jailed in January 2023, Sir Mark praised the victims and said: "We have failed and I'm sorry. He should not have been a police officer." Two months later, in an official report by Baroness Casey, the Met was described as a "boys' club", that was institutionally misogynistic and had failed women. Linda contacted the BBC, after seeing Panorama's report last year into a hidden culture of misogyny and racism inside the Met. Since reporting the rape by Carrick in 2021, Linda says it has been "horrific" and she would not report a rape to the Met today "because I don't trust the police and I don't think they deal with it correctly". Carrick was brought to justice by Hertfordshire Police, which investigated the rape of Linda. She reported it to the force after seeing media coverage of the news that Carrick had been charged with raping another woman. Linda was herself a rape investigation officer in the early 2000s. "I supported victims through rape but didn't report myself. I think that says loads. "I'm asking members of the public to report, and I'm there to support them, but I wouldn't do it myself and I didn't do it." She says if a similar attack happened to her tomorrow, she would not report it to the Met, because she has "no faith" that the force would deal with it correctly. Carrick raped her while she was on a three-month attachment with him in south London - miles from where she was normally based. One night, Linda says, Carrick suggested she should stay at his home, so she did not have to drive far late at night only to return early the next morning. When Linda told him no, she says Carrick replied: "It's what I do. I'm going to carry on." She knew that if she fought back then Carrick was going to get violent, she says. Linda has been a Met Police officer for 27 years Afterwards, Linda says she "never told a soul". She says she felt unable to report the rape then, or for years afterwards, because of the culture in the Met. Reporting the rape "would have been the end of my career", she says, because Carrick would not have been charged and she would have been shunned. "I would imagine that if Carrick had been arrested, he probably would have been interviewed and then no further action. So then mud sticks, doesn't it? "Then I'd be the officer that alleges rape, and who's going to want to work with me?" The "very sexist" culture she says she experienced included having her forehead stamped with the words "Property of the Met" and being locked in the boot of a police car for the duration of a shift. Linda, now 60, says the mental and emotional impact of the rape has been vast. She has led a lonely life, she says, focused primarily on her work and pets. She has not had a relationship with a man since the day she was attacked and says she has missed out on having a family. "I still don't feel I could have any relationship," she adds. She feels guilty at not having come forward earlier to report Carrick, she says. Since his conviction, she says the Met's culture has not changed as much as it should have done. "We've not moved on enough in the police to really give victims of domestic violence, sexual offences any [of the] support they really need." Her PTSD after the attack is "90% down to the Met Police, 10% to Carrick", she says. Carrick used his police role as a tool of coercion, raping and controlling his victims Linda brought a civil case against the Met seeking damages on the basis the force failed to protect her from him and that she felt she had been unable to report the rape. During the four-year case, she says the Met's legal team questioned the severity of her PTSD diagnosis. title: The Papers: 'Prepare for the worst' and 'Covid report fallout'
description: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting's national campaign on preparedness for cyber or climate emergencies dominates today's papers.
body: Spoiler warning: This review reveals details from the latest episodes of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has made headlines in today's papers after launching a national campaign on public preparedness for disruption caused by natural disasters and cyber attacks. The Daily Telegraph reports on Britons being asked to make "Be ready" kits for emergencies, "including three days' worth of non-perishable food and bottled water, an FM radio and blankets". Meanwhile, the Metro warns readers to "prepare for the worst" after websites around the world were taken offline after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a globally-used programming language, PHP. "In the UK, 32 government services were down", the paper reports, before asking the question "are you emergency ready?" The Independent leads on Streeting's messaging for Britons to be prepared in case "'state-sponsored terrorism' disrupts everyday life". The government's campaign comes as global security flaw knocked dozens of government services offline, the paper says. Similarly, the Guardian leads on UK households being urged to stockpile enough food and water to "survive 72 hours in a crisis", the Guardian reports. The new guidance from the government follows concerns on "climate change, technological dependency and hostile state threats", the paper says. Streeting "issues checklist for coping after catastrophe" and to "be prepared with 3 days of supplies", the Times reports. Elsewhere British singer Raye is pictured singing on stage as a "golden wonder" following her Mercury Prize win. "Don't Panic!" the Daily Mail instructs after ministers were "accused of lecturing families" to stockpile "in case of a national emergency". Elsewhere on the page, Catherine, Princess of Wales, is pictured with her son Prince George, who she is said to be missing while he is at Eton. Former Health Secretary Matt Hancock has been heavily criticised after another Covid inquiry over "untested patients being discharged into care homes where tens of thousands of residents died", the Daily Mirror reports. "Bereaved families are calling for Hancock to be stripped of his Right Honourable title" following his handling of Covid, the paper says. Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its workforce, the Financial Times reports. Support roles are predicted to bear the brunt as "AI makes our people more productive", the bank said, according to the paper. It comes as chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver his Budget next week that is likely to tax banks. A landmark report proposing to create career plans for 14-year-olds and above to help them with their future employment, is the lead of the i Paper. The plan aims to tackle the high number of young people not in education, employment or training once they leave school, the paper explains. The Daily Star splashes on The Celebrity Traitors and how one contestant admitted their experience was "harder than any war zone". The Sun reports that Thomas Markle, the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is being investigated by police, after a "huge stash" of child sex abuse images were allegedly found at his home in the Philippines. The paper reports that the discovery was made by the 82-year-old's son, Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Junior. It says he told detectives that "hundreds, if not thousands" of pictures and videos of young girls were "mixed up with innocent family mementos" in four large boxes. There is no response from Thomas Markle Senior. And the Daily Express headlines on victims of "shocking" attacks wanting tougher sentences for offenders to try to stop records levels of violence against women. title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
description: The pop star beat artists like Paul McCartney, Suede and Jade Thirlwall to lift the £25,000 prize.
body: Raye is the 35th winner of the Mercury Prize, which was established to recognise albums that push the boundaries of music Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope. A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize. "I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry." It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994. Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband? "I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old. "Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist." Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient. Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians. This video can not be played Raye wins 2026 Mercury Prize Released in March, the album went straight to the top of the UK charts and won glowing reviews from critics. Rolling Stone magazine praised its "old-school show-tune razzle-dazzle [and] big-band swing frills", while the NME raved that, "Raye's agile voice has never sounded so good, and her pen has never been so strong". In the BBC's own review, it was described as an "eccentric, kitsch and dramatic" record where Raye "unapologetically goes for broke". Raye comes out swinging on her new album, This Music May Contain Hope But the album almost never happened. Two years ago this week, the singer's car was stolen, along with all of her songwriting notebooks and demos. Although they were eventually recovered, it delayed work on This Music May Contain Hope by almost a year. Looking back, she was philosophical about the delay. "I was distraught. I was very worried, but you know, it all turned out great. "Every little slip, every little accident, every little thing, it creates the path that you take. "And it's easy to spend time wishing things were the other way. But right now, I certainly do not." The star performed the big band number I Hate The Way I Look Today during the Mercury Prize ceremony Established in 1992, the Mercury Prize was envisaged as an antidote to the commercially-focused Brit Awards, recognising albums that moved music forwards, without recourse to fashion or trends. Of the last 35 winners, 20 have been debut albums - from artists including Arctic Monkeys, Suede and Franz Ferdinand. Many people have mistakenly assumed it is a prize for first albums - but this year's shortlist included only two: Dove Ellis's heartfelt and delicate Blizzard, and Jade's That's Showbiz, Baby. This video can not be played 'I'm speechless': Olivia Dean on making UK chart history In the run-up to this year's ceremony, Olivia Dean had been the bookmakers' favourite for her second album, The Art of Loving. An easy-going, soulful collection of love songs, it had already been named album of the year at the Brit Awards and the Mobos, and is widely expected to earn the singer a Grammy nomination in the same category next month. Speaking backstage, the singer said she was overwhelmed by the success. "I don't think I've processed it yet, to be honest," she said. "I feel like I'm still in this crazy whirlwind of it all. "And maybe, when I take a break over Christmas, I'll reflect on the sofa." Other nominees included the rapper Kojey Radical, Geordie jazz act Knats, and former Little Mix star Jade - who was the first ever X Factor winner to receive a Mercury nomination. The shortlist also included the charity compilation album Help (2), recorded in aid of Warchild, which featured new music and cover versions by artists such as Olivia Rodrigo, Damon Albarn, Depeche Mode and The Last Dinner Party. The tracklist also included nine former Mercury Prize winners: Arctic Monkeys, Young Fathers, Wolf Alice, Pulp, Sampha, Portishead's Beth Gibbons, Arlo Parks, English Teacher and Ezra Collective. Last year, the prize was won by Newcastle singer-songwriter Sam Fender, who donated his £25,000 winnings to grassroots music venues, helping to support up-and-coming songwriters around the UK. title: Amber warning in place as Storm Austen hits parts of UK
description: Disruption to travel is likely as the season's first named storm brings a swathe of powerful winds to south-west England on Friday.
body: An amber weather warning has come into force in parts of the UK as Storm Austen brings a swathe of powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday. South West England is forecast to be worst hit by the storm which the Met Office warns could bring travel disruption, power cuts and a possible danger to life. Wind gusts of 60-70mph, with 80mph in exposed locations, are forecast across Cornwall and parts of Devon, where the Met Office warning is in force until 10:00 BST. Wind gust of 45-60mph are forecast more widely across most of England and Wales, where two less severe yellow warnings will be in force throughout Friday. A separate yellow warning will also cover part of Scotland, including Glasgow and Edinburgh, from 06:00 BST. Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts. Winds of this strength will blow some trees over while buildings could also potentially be damaged, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm. A number of schools are closed in the impacted areas with many others opening later than usual to avoid the strongest winds. Train cancellations and speed restrictions are possible because of the increased danger of branches and trees blocking railways. A number of ferry sailings have also been cancelled, including crossings between Pembrokeshire and Ireland. Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places. As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre. That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph. The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph. All schools in Jersey have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen. Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday. Wind warnings have been issued ahead of Storm Austen's arrival on Friday Closely following Storm Austen will be Storm Boelo, named by the Met Office on Thursday and set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend. Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways. The Met Office has issued yellow wind warnings for Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, valid on Saturday and lasting most of Sunday. Gusts are forecast to reach 50-65mph widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations. There could be some localised disruption with strong winds funnelling through the Central Lowlands for a time. Transport disruption is expected and there may be some power cuts. Following recent spells of wet weather, there is an additional risk of some localised flooding. Yellow wind warnings have been issued ahead of Storm Boelo's arrival over the weekend It is not unusual to get storms one after another - in fact they quite often arrive in clusters. A strong jet stream is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process involved in creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic. These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds. The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer. May is the only month with no named storms in the 11 years that storms have been named in the UK. The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months. This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year. In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November. title: Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past
description: The attack on Shroff has revived memories of the 1990s, when gangsters wielded influence over the industry.
body: Actor Tiger Shroff, who made his debut in 2014, is known for his action roles On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor. Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt. Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies. Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers. The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years. Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why. The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history. During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip. Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again? This video can not be played Watch: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting attempt in Mumbai Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest. D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution. In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt. Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision. Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle. But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad. "This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else." Gangster Lawrence Bishnoi has been locked up in prison since 2015 That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online. Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing. Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety. Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it." Bishnoi's gang claime

title: Call of Duty promises a return to form - but can it compete with GTA?
description: Modern Warfare 4 faces an uphill battle after last year's Call of Duty missed the mark with fans.
body: Modern Warfare 4 is released on Friday after its predecessor "missed the mark" last year Call of Duty is back - and it's got a lot to prove. Last year was a low point for the video game juggernaut, with poor reviews for its single-player campaign mode and multiplayer fans defecting to rival titles. So for latest instalment, Modern Warfare 4, publisher Activision is pulling out all the stops to bring fans back on board. But with increasing competition for fans' time and attention, and the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 just weeks away, can Call of Duty still cut through? BBC Newsbeat spoke to some of those behind the game to find out, and why they see the upcoming release of GTA 6 as an "opportunity". Since 2009, Call of Duty has been at the top - or a close second-place - in the US video game sales charts every year. But 2025's edition, Black Ops 7, dropped to seventh place in America, according to data from analytics firm Circana. In the UK, it was the eighth best-selling game, external. It’s thought the game’s inclusion on Xbox’s Game Pass subscription service, where it won’t appear on release this year, hit sales. But competition from long-running rival Battlefield 6 and new release Arc Raiders - a surprise success from Swedish studio Embark - put the behemoth on the back foot. Fans also complained about the inclusion of novelty skins, which change the appearance of characters during multiplayer games, based on cartoons, external and other pop culture crossovers. Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, admits it was a tough year for the series. "I think we missed expectations with our community last year," he tells BBC Newsbeat. "So we took a step back, we listened to them." Players now have the ability to switch off controversial cosmetic changes, and Bahl says Modern Warfare 4 is a "return to form". It's a message they've been keen to get out. The game locates players in a war between North and South Korea Newsbeat meets Bahl in a corner of Shoreditch, London, that's been turned into a convincing replica of a South Korean street complete with noodle bars and convenience stores. A similar installation to promote Modern Warfare 4 has been built in downtown LA - but it's far from the only extravagant promotional attempt to generate buzz around the game. Back in July, Activision recruited Obsession star Inde Navaratte - who streamed Call of Duty on Twitch before becoming one of Hollywood's hottest young stars - to publicise the game at sports convention Fanatics Fest, external. It's also struck a sponsorship deal with six-a-side football championship Baller League and worked with world's biggest YouTuber Mr Beast to showcase the game's new DMZ multiplayer mode, external. Bahl says the events and collabs are designed to demonstrate Call of Duty's "stature, swagger and scale" - something he admits does not come cheap. He says he's always thinking of ways for Call of Duty to leverage its position and "show up in culture in a really big and innovative way" to reach "as many people as possible". Call of Duty does have some strong competition in that space, however. This year it's launching just weeks before GTA 6 - arguably the most anticipated video game of the decade. Despite rising console prices, there's hope that the massive interest in Rockstar Games' ultra-blockbuster will convince people to buy a new console or return to the hobby. Bahl says GTA 6 and Call of Duty are "the two biggest games of the year" but they're not necessarily in direct competition. "More people dusting off their Xbox or their PlayStation, starting to play for the first time it gives an opportunity for more gamers to come in and play both of the games," says Bahl. GTA 6 will only be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles at first, and multiplayer modes won't be available at launch. "So we feel like this is differentiated enough to really stand out," says Bahl. The game itself sells for about £70 in the UK, but Bahl points out it can be a year-round hangout space for many fans. "The number one reason people come to Call of Duty is not just for the combat or the gunplay, but it's actually because their friends are there, right? "And so that social connection is so powerful." The game's makers have splashed out promoting the new release One of the biggest criticisms of last year's Call of Duty was its single-player campaign mode. The short, cinematic adventures are rarely the main reason players pick up the latest title, but are nevertheless popular. Alternating titles in the series follow different storylines, and the Modern Warfare strand has produced some of Call of Duty's most beloved characters. Activision has said Modern Warfare 4 is the "epic conclusion" to the story of fan favourite Capt John Price, played by British actor Barry Sloane. "It's a lot of surprises, a culmination of all those pieces that we've been putting together coming together," he says. Sloane tells Newsbeat he's not too intimidated by the weight of expectation. "I've been greeted with love from the fan base since the get-go," he says. María Elisa Camargo, who returns to the series as cartel leader Valeria Garza, admits the fanbase is "a tough crowd". "They're very smart, very story-driven, and they're not just loving anyone," she says. Actor Mads Mikkelsen, known for appearances in films such as Casino Royale and TV show Hannibal, plays mysterious enemy The Archer. He says there's at least one player who'll be there to play through the campaign. "I know for sure my son will try to kill me again and again. title: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok
description: Grandma Droniak, Nonna Gracie, Viv Truran and Barbara Costello have all found fame on social media in their later years.
body: Grandma Droniak pays for her care home fees with the money she makes from brand deals on social media Ninety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties. The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks. With 15 million followers, Droniak has turned her personality into a lucrative business, earning enough from social media to cover her nursing home fees of $12,000 (£9,000) a month. The Connecticut grandma is one of many older women finding unexpected fame online, with most of their audiences often young enough to be their grandchildren. From fashion and food to dating and homemaking, they are finding new audiences and, in some cases, a new lease of life. "I always knew I had it in me to be famous, I just didn't think it would happen in my 90s," Droniak tells me, explaining that her grandson began helping her post videos in 2020, initially out of boredom. She believes her appeal lies in showing younger people that life doesn't stop as you get older. "They think old people just sit and stare at a wall but I'm showing it's not that bad to get old. We embrace it, can still have fun and I'm still partying and going out sometimes." Her grandson edits her sponsored content, which includes partnerships with food and beauty brands. As well as paying for her nursing home fees, the money also goes towards a college fund for her great-grandchildren. Despite being recognised by fans in public, she says her fame feels different at the retirement home. "They don't get it as they don't go on TikTok." On the other side of the Atlantic, there's Viv Truran, an equally cheeky and cheery 82-year-old from Cardiff. She started posting on Instagram after losing her husband and her neighbour suggested filming her colourful outfits. Viv Truran shares her colourful outfits with her more than 800,000 followers Now she makes two videos a day from her bedroom-turned-studio, showing off her clothes, 22 pairs of glasses and two drawers of scarves. "I get up in the morning, I never come downstairs until I've done my morning video and I'm very strict about that." She also keeps a notebook tracking her followers and views – and is now on book five. Truran is regularly stopped by strangers, many of them women in their 20s and 30s, who tell her they are "frightened of getting old" and she shows them "it's not that bad". Brands have taken notice too and Truran says she'd "be stupid" not to do deals but is selective. She does a couple of sponsored posts a month, prioritising local brands and charities like Age UK who paid her several thousand for a recent campaign. "I've turned down some big deals because it's not my thing. I'm very picky about who I work with, I have to really love the brand." Naomi Baker from influencer marketing agency We Are Social says older creators are attractive to brands as they often have "deeply established, highly loyal" communities with greater purchasing power, which "carries a massive premium". Nonna Gracie has been dubbed "the internet's Italian grandma" Grace Geramita, 85, has millions of followers who watch her cook recipes she has made for decades. Known as Nonna Gracie, she moved from Italy to the US when she was 18 and worked multiple jobs at once to provide for her two daughters. Now, she earns more than she ever made in a previous job. Her grandson Matthew suggested they start filming her cooking six years ago but Geramita wasn't keen as she knew nothing about social media and doesn't "speak very good English", but the videos took off. "I always cry when people send me messages from all around the world," she says. Much of her content is about more than food – she says she wants to pass on the "tradition of bringing family together around the table". Baker from We Are Social says this is part of the appeal of TikTok grannies as they "offer comfort in an uncertain world". Their wholesome content can also act as a "virtual grandma" for followers, she says. Barbara Costello says many people see her as the mother or grandmother they never had That's certainly the case for Barbara Costello. The 77-year-old former teacher now shares videos about cooking, cleaning and homemaking skills on her Brunch with Babs accounts. Her followers tell her she reminds them of their own mothers and grandmothers, with some calling her "the mom I never had". "Recently, a university student approached me in a restaurant to tell me my cookbook had helped her through her first year living independently and I was so happy." Costello works with brands but says she has to think carefully about if it's something she wants to put her name on. She says the best part of being a creator is seeing former pupils at her book signings with their own children. "It's a full circle moment. I really can't believe this is my life." title: I thought I was dying but it was health anxiety - here's how to recognise the signs
description: Hollie Sharman shares her experience of health anxiety and a doctor advises on how to manage symptoms.
body: Hollie Sharman spent hours searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated Hollie Sharman was convinced she was dying. She would go to hospital "four to five times a week" complaining of excruciating chest pain. "I think the longest I spent in A&E was 13 hours," says the 25-year-old. But despite numerous tests, doctors could never find anything wrong. Sharman says she had "always worried" about her health as a child and remembers "making up any excuse" to get sent home from school and get into bed. Her 22nd birthday meal was spent in the restaurant toilets "having the worst panic attack I've ever had". That triggered years of health anxiety, with hours spent searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated. "I was constantly Googling and using ChatGPT, every source I could get that could tell me what was wrong," she says. "I spent so long in the hospital. They'd tell me it's nothing, they'd check everything. "I'd go home, but then my legs would feel weak, so I'd Google that and then it would say it's a sign of heart failure. So I'd go back, it was literally a constant cycle." At its worst, she "completely disconnected from everyone" and wouldn't reply to messages from family to avoid repetitive conversations. Sharman says her health anxiety also had an extreme affect on her relationship. "It got to the point that nothing he said would be the right thing. "I would get upset because he didn't understand what was going on inside my own head. How can you tell someone everything's fine when I think I'm actually dying?" Dr Schnack says health anxiety is an "obsessional worry" about being seriously ill Clinical psychologist Dr Kirren Schnack says health anxiety is "a constant worry about being seriously ill or becoming seriously ill when you are not". Key signs can be "checking" behaviours, such as frequently examining your body, taking your temperature, blood pressure or researching symptoms online. Another is constantly asking the internet, friends or family for reassurance that you are safe and healthy, she tells Complex with Kimberley Wilson. Others may experience "avoidance" - not looking at their body or going to doctors appointments because they fear "the worst". Some may "take on the persona of somebody who has an illness", she adds. "You may slow down your movements and stop exercising, you're treating yourself and your body and mind as if you are already ill." Sharman says her parents understand her condition more after watching the videos she makes about health anxiety on TikTok Sharman was eventually diagnosed with health anxiety and health-related obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD). She says her family and partner have been "incredibly supportive" and have helped her get to a "better place" with techniques to manage her anxiety. "I'd write down my symptoms like 'chest pain, excruciating'. And then at the end of the day, I'd write that I was fine. "And then next time I'd have it, I'd have something to read and I'd be like, but I thought I was dying then and I wasn't." Sharman says her health anxiety "doesn't control her life any more". "You need to push yourself and do things when you're anxious, don't put your life on hold because I did for so many years." How to deal with health anxiety. Listen now. Dr Schnack says if you have a symptom that is "new, concerning or doesn't go away", it is "responsible health behaviour" to check the NHS website. If a symptom has not gone away within two weeks, she advises making a GP appointment. Here's when to call 111, 999 or go to A&E. And here are some tips from Dr Schnack that might help: Challenge worst-case thinking - give your brain other explanations for physical sensations; a stiff back might be poor posture rather than a serious illness. Limit reassurance-seeking - set rules and time limits on how often you ask friends or family about symptoms, and stick to them. Burn off anxious energy - take quick bursts of movement, like jumping jacks, to help process adrenaline and cortisol. Ground yourself - use strong sensory experiences such as holding an ice cube or tasting something sour or spicy. Breathing techniques - take a long breath through your nose, add a second inhale at the top and release it with a long sigh through your mouth. title: Private care home investors a risk to public sector, regulator says
description: US investors are buying up UK care homes - a situation regulators say they are "watching carefully" in case it threatens plans for a National Care Service.
body: Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's ambition to create a universal care service, the regulator says. The Care Quality Commission's annual report, external highlights how an increasing share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest have increased their share of the market by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors. Between them they own around one in seven homes. While there could be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in the quality of care - something the CQC says needs to be monitored. Meanwhile, home care, providing support to help people wash and dress in their own home, has become more fragmented, with a greater number of smaller providers. The CQC says this could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people. In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care. Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter. The CQC says the funding system remains fragile – people using care services either self-fund or, for the poorest, the state helps to pay for their costs. And in some areas, providers are increasingly turning to self-funders, making it more difficult for councils to buy the care they need for those relying on state help. CQC chief inspector of adult social care, Chris Badger, said the reshaping of the market was happening "largely by accident rather than design", driven by a combination of economic pressure and the problems some councils were having in buying services for those relying on state-funded care. He said this government's renewed focus on social care – Andy Burnham made it one of his key priorities when he became prime minister – was welcome. But he said it was important the market was "shaped around what's best for people". "A clearer vision is needed," he added. Hugh Alderwick, of the Health Foundation think-tank, said the report by the CQC "lays bare the massive challenges" facing the government. "The prime minister's commitment to reforming the sector provides an opportunity to fundamentally redraw the state's offer on social care. "But change is needed now to strengthen the fundamentals of the system. "Councils need enough funding, the right skills and strong leadership to shape services around people's needs." Prof Martin Green, of Care England, which represents care providers, said: "If the government and regulators are concerned by consolidation in the care sector, they need to take some clear and tangible action to support smaller care home providers." He said changes to employer national insurance contributions, inflation and the rising cost of energy was making smaller homes unviable. "Unless we get some real progress in a funding settlement, the trend of smaller homes closing will be a trend that will continue." The Department of Health and Social Care said the report demonstrated the "scale of the challenge this government inherited", but said it was committed to overhauling social care. title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
description: Officials compare working in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to the Cold War era.
body: Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre Lévy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC. US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War. But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year. The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion. They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials. Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed. Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia. "There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty." The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls. Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023 Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater. "Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow. Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission. The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution". Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials. One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy. Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect They fled Russia, but the West sent them back Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police. One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear. Not everyone can deal with the pressure. One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months. In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre Lévy. He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be. The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible. And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies. Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country. But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning. Pierre Lévy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024 After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Еven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers. One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'." Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses. A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase. "It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour." A wooden replica of the Great Seal of the US was given to the American ambassador to Russia as a gift in 1945 - it was later found to contain a listening device Russian officials make little secret of

title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
description: The UN human rights chief Volker Türk says the multiple attacks may amount to war crimes.
body: Medics at el-Fasher's Saudi Hospital performed a Caesarean by phone light on the day it was bombed A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago. UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings. The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation. Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times. Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict. The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted. "The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC. "The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned." The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military. Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities. In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility. But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query. UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city. The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city. A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023. Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city. Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies. The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher. In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city. The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman. The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says. On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added. The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist. But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office. They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs. "There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners. Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead. "They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me." That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said. The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated. Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base. According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy". In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim. He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters. Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war. The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Dar

title: Give more people weight-loss jabs on the NHS, say MPs
description: Current plans for 6% of eligible patients to get Mounjaro by 2028 unambitious, say MPs.
body: Hundreds of thousands more people should be given access to the weight-loss injection Mounjaro on the NHS in England, a cross-party group of MPs says. The Health Committee said the current plan for 220,000 people to have this jab for free on prescription in 2028 was a "woefully small number" and "unambitious". This represents only around 6% of eligible people and is a key reason why more than a million have been paying privately for weight-loss injections, including Mounjaro and Wegovy. The committee says a two-tier system is emerging in which only the wealthy can get good access to the medication that curbs appetite. Due to costs, the NHS is currently working on a 12-year rollout for Mounjaro - although this is being reviewed. It is estimated that if all 2.8 million people eligible for the drug were given it immediately, it would cost the NHS £15.2 billion over five years. Some of that expense is linked to the NHS relying heavily on GPs to oversee the prescribing and monitoring. MPs say the NHS must learn from private providers who often use digital platforms to do some of this work. The MPs said streamlining the process of support for patients could reduce that bill – and they said it also made financial sense because of the overall cost of obesity to the economy – estimated to be around £75 billion a year. Another weight-loss injection, Wegovy, is available on the NHS, but only through specialist weight management services. The committee also called for a crackdown on the black market for weight-loss drugs, saying the lack of availability on the NHS had driven people to buy unlicenced products online. It wants a public awareness campaign to warn about the dangers, along with a review to look at how better to regulate online advertising. The MPs also criticised the wider system of weight-loss services, saying they were poorly designed and resourced. They want people to have better access to diet and lifestyle courses and bariatric (obesity) surgery. Moran said obesity should be treated as a serious health condition, like diabetes. "People can spend their entire lives battling with their weight. We say the NHS should provide effective, structured support to beat obesity for all those who seek it. Instead, those people are repeatedly failed," she said. Jack Doughty, of the Obesity Health Alliance, said people living with obesity were being "let down by a fragmented and overstretched treatment system". "The reality is that the existing treatment services, from behavioural support to weight-loss medications and bariatric surgery, remain patchy and unequal." NHS England said it was looking at ways to accelerate roll out weight-loss drugs, but was currently “rightly prioritising these treatments for those with the most severe and complex needs“. title: Grid operator says lights will stay on this winter after concerns
description: The assurance from the National Energy System Operator comes amid concern from its engineers about their ability to ensure adequate supply.
body: The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers. The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months. However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation. NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days". It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine. "While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO. In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables. The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears. The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations. Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas. However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator. Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced. It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult". The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership. Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said. The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run". One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June. This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation. Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right". Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them". "I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added. title: Haematology centre for cancer patients at risk over 'disgraceful' funds move
description: The Department of Health has decided to take back £1.5m from the project, Belfast Trust officials have told a Stormont committee.
body: The health committee was told there were concerns about the lack of isolation for haemotology patients who are being treated for cancer A plan to build a haematology centre in Belfast for cancer patients has been put at risk after the Department of Health (DoH) withdrew funding, the chief executive of the Belfast Trust has said. The move was described as "disgraceful" during Thursday's session of Stormont's health committee after trust officials said the department had now decided to take back £1.5m from the project. Belfast Health Trust had planned to move 80 staff out of an area of Belfast City Hospital to make way for the new unit, but having reviewed the proposal the DoH withdrew related funding. The project is now a year behind its planned opening date, which is currently put back to March 2031. Belfast Trust Chief Executive Jennifer Welsh said: "The relocation of approximately 80 staff remains a challenge. "The Department of Health was not satisfied with the trust's options' appraisal and has challenged the robustness of the capital cost estimate, resulting in £1.5m of funding having been withdrawn from the decant allocation." 'Dangerously long cancer waits have me constantly on a knife-edge' 'It was awful waiting on my diagnosis': NI cancer cases hit record high Bowel cancer screening expanded - but 50 year olds face five year wait "I will be clear with members that this is a significant issue for us, which potentially poses a substantial risk to this project," Welsh added. She said the trust was exploring ways to fund the movement of the 80 staff out of the area within the city hospital and the issue was "being escalated to the permanent secretary" at the DoH. The trust planned to relocate 80 of its staff at Belfast City Hospital to make room for the proposed haematology centre Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member Diane Dodds said the public would be very concerned about the trust's report on the haematology unit. "They are very worried about the conditions that haematology patients currently have within the city hospital and the lack of isolation for patients whose systems are very, very vulnerable," she told the committee. "This was seen as something of significant hope for cancer patients in Northern Ireland. "This is something that needs addressed as quickly as possible without any delay, because delaying this is really putting very vulnerable people at risk." Alliance assembly member Nuala McAllister said the move by the department to remove the funding was "disgraceful". "We are talking about patients who are undergoing some quite intense treatment, and with very specialised staff," she said. "We are talking about very vulnerable patients - severely immuno-compromised... and the department who receives over half of the executive's budget has decided that £1.5m cannot move ahead for a new cancer unit for some of our most immuno-compromised cancer patients." The Department of Health has been approached for a response. title: O'Neill bemoans marginal moments but are Celtic just not good enough?
description: Martin O'Neill spoke of refereeing decisions and near misses after the Europa League defeat against Celta Vigo. But is the reality more concerning?
body: Three Europa League games. Three defeats for Celtic. They are 35th of 36 teams in the competition after another European collapse, this time against Celta Vigo. Only Ararat-Armenia and their inferior goal difference keeps the Scottish champions from propping up the table. Off the back of Sunday's 7-1 drubbing of Hearts, there was hope Martin O'Neill's team had turned a corner. Instead, the disparity between their domestic dominance and European shortcomings was laid bare once more. After Mika Baur swept Celtic in front on 47 minutes, they went into their shells and succumbed to a timid 2-1 defeat as Javi Rodriguez struck twice in three minutes. O'Neill bemoaned refereeing decisions and marginal moments that went against his team, but are Celtic simply "not good enough" to compete in Europe? That was the verdict of former Scotland attacker James McFadden after a Celtic collapse that is becoming all too familiar. "The performances at this level haven't been good enough," he said on Sportsound. "Celtic are way short." Celtic suffer third Europa League defeat in row after Celta Vigo turnaround Latest Celtic news, analysis and fan views Celtic looked nailed on for the Champions League this season when they went into a 4-0 aggregate lead against Austrian champions LASK in the play-off round, before shipping five goals in 77 minutes to drop into the Europa League. O'Neill's side have now lost their last four European matches, conceding 14 goals in the process. Only once before had they done so in the same season - in the 2017-18 Champions League. "It seems as though Celtic struggle when there's a bit of adversity," McFadden added. "If something goes against them, the confidence drops, their heads drop, they stop playing forward. "The ball goes back and across, inviting pressure, and there's no way they take the pressure off. That has been a theme." This video can not be played "A bit of adversity and the lights go out" After another disappointing night, O'Neill focused on moments that went against his team - a free-kick not given before Celta's equaliser and a Liam Scales header that flicked the top of the bar at 1-0. "We conceded a free-kick and I thought a second before that we should have had a foul for us," O'Neill said. "They score from the free-kick and it knocks us a little bit. It gave them a bit of momentum. "I think if [Liam] Scales' header goes in to make it 2-0, we get the three points. We've lost three matches now, remarkably we're still in with a chance [of progressing]. We've got to win here and got to win away from home. "We take the lead in the game, if we get the second goal we win the match and it changes the whole dynamic. It didn't happen, that's it - we need to try to find a way to win European games." This video can not be played 'We have what we have' - O'Neill speaks after Celta Vigo collapse Centre-back Liam Scales had by far the most touches of any Celtic player with 121, well ahead of left-back Kieran Tierney (79) and goalkeeper Sam Johnstone (69). Goalscorer Baur admitted they did not do enough to win and was at a loss when asked what needs to change. "How we played second half, last 30 minutes, we deserved it in the end," Baur said. When asked if he knew why his team collapsed in such a manner, he responded: "I cannot tell you, sorry. "It can happen that you get a goal, they can score too, good team - you should then get control back, hold the ball a bit longer to take the momentum away from them. You should break that." Celtic did not get control back, did not break Celta's momentum and ultimately paid the price. "I don't think Celtic are good enough, individually and collectively, to take on a team that's eighth in La Liga," former Celtic goalkeeper Pat Bonner said on Sportsound. "They moved the ball really well and Celtic couldn't get close to them. "They are not good enough at this level. Celtic are paying big money for some players because the fans are demanding it and then they come in and aren't good enough." Their next European outing comes on 5 November as they host Besiktas, trying to reverse their continental woes. Whether they can or not is another matter. title: Celebrity Traitors - paranoia deepens as traitor behaviour splits opinion
description: The murder in plain sight victim was revealed ahead of another difficult round table.
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traitors. So it was a relief to be put out of our misery as last Friday's literal yawn-fest came to its slow-burning conclusion; the traitorous trio eventually succeeding in their mission to kill in plain sight. The snoozefest - which involved reluctant traitor James Acaster making faithful Ross Kemp yawn by boring him to tears - meant the paranoid EastEnders star was finally put out of his misery. On learning his fate, the actor turned to Shakespeare - who else? "To thine own self be true," he declared, quoting Polonius from Hamlet. As usual at breakfast, the faithfuls seated early mused over who may have been murdered overnight: "If Jerry's not here, I don't think I can handle it," Romesh Ranganathan confessed. Jerry Hall was charmingly late to the party. After everyone had discussed Ross's demise, she piped up in her famous Texan drawl: "Is Ross gone?" As the typical off-the-wall theories began to swirl, Jerry later told Miranda Hart she suspected fellow faithful James Blunt - for the very plausible reason that "his face is redder than a fox's ass at gooseberry time". It's as good a reason as any proffered so far this series. This video can not be played Watch: The traitors were given a special task to complete in the latest episode of Celebrity Traitors Once the croissant crumbs had been cleared, it was time for a mission that threw the cat among the pigeons - not least because the traitor's lair it took place in "smelled like a litter tray", according to Jerry. Miranda felt there were more complex olfactory notes at play: "A mix of salmon, cheap cologne and crotch." Delightful. The mission involved each player having to build a shield on a plinth in front of them out of 3D jigsaw-type pieces which were buried in troughs in sawdust. Think Krypton Factor meets lucky dip. At three intervals, a bell would ring, and the players all had to stop and put on blindfolds for a few minutes. The traitors could then remove theirs and go about sabotaging the handiwork of anyone they fancied. And while James A revealed he was "starting to have more fun" after murdering poor Ross, if there was a prize for the worst traitor of all time, he would still smash it. He was too scared to take off his blindfold and remove any shield pieces from the faithfuls, leaving the dirty work - and all the risk - to fellow traitors Maya Jama and King Kenny. Suffice to say, they were not impressed. "He didn't even lift the blindfold off - I'm speechless," said Maya. James A knew he was in trouble: "I'm aware I'll get a dressing down in the turret but I am the one who killed Grant Mitchell." He wasn't wrong about the telling off. And the fact he completed his own puzzle, earning himself a shield, must have really riled his co-conspirators. To be fair, you could argue he's playing a blinder - there's been very little suspicion of him so far. Three other celebrities also managed to complete their shield puzzles - James B, Joanne McNall and Michael Sheen - but no money was banked after Maya and Kenny panicked and didn't remove any pieces at their last opportunity. But the task at least threw up another bunch of mad theories for the faithfuls to chew over, as they tried to unsuccessfully guess where the floorboard creaking was coming from as two of the traitors tried to creep around the room. It was good news for Romesh at least, whose hay fever saved the day - Sharon Rooney could hear him sniffing constantly next to her so knew he couldn't have been a traitor. Maybe the tickly moustache isn't helping his allergies - and combing it won't make much difference. Romesh combing his moustache - as you do Ahead of the round table, self-styled "Poundland Poirot" Sharon was living up to her nickname with a red herring theory about a perfume bottle being used to kill someone in plain sight. Ross's murder and the disorienting mission ultimately confused everyone, with the round table being the most random of the series so far. Leigh-Ann Pinnock, Bash Croft, Joanne and Jerry were among the accused, with Jerry - having survived murder overnight - banished for being "a professional pot stirrer. She's "planted more seeds than a farmer's market" – or at least that was Joanne's reasoning. Romesh's deadpan excuse was better: "I've long suspected she preferred Rob (his comedy partner and former contestant Rob Beckett) to me." Once again, the faithfuls were left to rue losing one of their own, with Jerry chastising them as she made her grand exit: "I told you so!" Leigh-Ann still had heat on her after Jerry's banishment, with her bright red - blood red? - leather-look long gloves drawing attention in the kitchen. "I said they looked traitorous and villainous," she bemoaned. Back in the turret, as James A predicted, Maya and Kenny were not happy about his lack of action at the mission. "You hung us out to dry!" Maya chastised him. But he redeemed himself somewhat by declaring that he had finally got a taste for villainy. "When I killed Ross Kemp in plain sight, I loved it!" James A told a delighted Maya and Kenny. It's only taken him three-quarters of the series to get there but better late than never.
