title: Austin track bumps out of control - Verstappen
description: Max Verstappen says the bumps on the track that hosts this weekend's United States Grand Prix are "unacceptable" and "out of control".
body: Max Verstappen has won the past two grands prix, in Malaysia and Singapore Max Verstappen says the bumps on the track that hosts this weekend's United States Grand Prix are "unacceptable" and "out of control". The Dutchman said drivers had complained about the condition of the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, and attempts by the organisers to resolve it had not worked. Red Bull's Verstappen said: "I love this track, I love this place. It's one of the best layouts ever and it's one of the best venues, best city to be at. "But for me the bumps are unacceptable. Over time they've been grinding a little bit here and there but it's just putting a plaster on the big problem. "But that of course means you need to really fully open up the track. That costs a lot of money and time but that's the only way to get rid of it because these bumps are not natural and they are out of control." Antonelli to 'just have fun' as he aims for title Approach African GP with humility, says Hamilton The track is built on former marshland and that has made it difficult for organisers to keep it in good condition, but the four-time champion rejected that as a reason not to try to solve the issue. "You can use the excuse that the soil is the problem but then you should have known that and you need to make sure that you reinforce it more," Verstappen said. "Last year, for example, you pull around 5-6G in a corner, but I had some impacts, vertical load, which was over 9G on my spine, which I can tell you is really not fun, and especially the older you get, you think about that more and more." Verstappen said the problem was likely to be exacerbated this year because although the cars from 2022-25 had lower ride-heights overall, the way the cars are run under the latest regulations means they are running lower in corners than last season. That's because of the switch between having the front and rear wings open in drag-reduction mode on the straights and closing in corners means the cars drop down towards the ground when they brake. "You bottom out way harder, because when the wings close and the ride-height comes down, under braking is actually a very stressful moment, and I know around here in some places, it's very bumpy under braking," he said. "Especially when it's like these kind of awkward bumps, not just bumps from the track getting older, but the surface underneath the soil just moving up and down, sometimes (it's) very hard to expect, or if you're like a tiny bit offline, you don't know what is there, because no-one really drives here sometimes. "I can tell you from the checks that I've done from my spine, the bottom end doesn't look that great. "I know that's part of racing. I know that can be part of sport, but it's also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years. "And now if we continue with finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer with that much more." Verstappen won last year in Austin while Lando Norris finished second World champion Lando Norris, of McLaren, backed Verstappen's opinion, saying: "The regulation of building a new track, the tolerances you have to be within are pretty small. It certainly doesn't fit anywhere close to what those regulations are now. "It's an old track, not a new track so it's pretty bad. There's a lot of places I need to take headache tablets before I go out simply because it's so bumpy and you're hitting your head pretty hard against the headrest and things because of the bumps so it's certainly not a nice thing. There's not much we can do. I mean, we complain about it so it's stuff we've brought up many, many times but there's only so much we can complain about things. But he's right." But Mercedes driver George Russell said: "It's bumpy, but I think it's just part of racing. I'd say my general view is F1 tracks probably need to be repaved every couple of years just to make it a bit more consistent. Because we're going to tracks now where Tarmac's coming up, it's falling apart, it's causing more issues than not. "Not ideal, but not much we can do." title: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skin care sales
description: The beauty giant's CEO says the use of GLP-1s is "a very important phenomenon for us".
body: The use of weight loss drugs, known as GLP-1s, has increased in popularity in recent years Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skin care sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side effects of rapid weight loss. The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context, and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us". He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular". L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations. The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite. While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side effect of loose skin - including around the face. Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss. L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December. Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters. Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler. Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance. Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs. title: Heavy rain warning as Storm Austen sweeps across Scotland
description: The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for rain across most of central and eastern Scotland on Friday.
body: Scotland is braced for a wet and windy weekend as two named storms hit in two days. Storm Austen is the first to sweep across the country, with the Met Office issuing a a yellow warning for rain, external in central and eastern areas from 06:00 on Friday until midnight. Forecasters say some places could experience 60-80 mm of rain, with a risk of flooding and travel disruption. Storm Boelo will follow hard on its heels on Saturday, with another yellow weather warning issued, this time for high winds, for the whole of mainland Scotland, the Western Isles and Orkney. Two storms in two days as Austen and Boelo target UK The wind warning will come into force from 18:00 on Saturday and last until 21:00 on Sunday. The wind speeds are expected build on Saturday afternoon, reaching a peak overnight. Gusts of 50-65mph are forecast widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations. The storm will also bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways. Yellow wind warnings have been issued ahead of Storm Boelo's arrival over the weekend Network Rail Scotland said that trains on Friday will be slowed down to keep people safe in the areas expected to see the heaviest rain. Speed restrictions will be in place on parts of the West Coast Main Line and East Coast Main Line, as well as routes across southern and eastern Scotland. It said some journeys would take longer as a result, but that the restrictions meant trains could continue running through areas where the weather is at its worst. Speed restrictions for trains are also expected in some areas as the second storm moves across the country over the weekend. Craig Gorman, head of operational weather strategy at Network Rail Scotland, said: "We can't control the weather, but we can make sure we're as ready as possible for whatever it brings. "We know any disruption from these storms will be frustrating, particularly as it's the weekend, but we'll do everything we can to keep people moving wherever it's safe to do so." Mark Ilderton, ScotRail service delivery director, said: "Safety is always our top priority and with weather warnings in place as Storm Austen and Storm Boelo bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Scotland this weekend, there is an increased risk of flooding and disruption on the railway." He advised customers to check services before they travel. Power cuts are possible, which could also affect mobile phone coverage and other services. There is a small risk of damage to buildings, including roof tiles being blown off, while flying debris could pose a danger to the public. title: Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network, Trump says
description: Ukraine relies on Starlink for a range of military uses - its owner Elon Musk has repeatedly denied restricting access.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access after row Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces. Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored. Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia and protect itself from attacks. Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but when asked about it he said: "Bottom line, he put it back." The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access. The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. A Ukrainian soldier using a Starlink satellite internet terminal which connects to thousands of SpaceX satellites Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields. Modern warfare often relies on the use of high-speed internet to effectively operate drones. Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully. Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it." He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so." The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink. The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials. The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks. The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation. BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation. Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October. Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted. title: UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says
description: The prime minister is hosting the UK's first wildfire summit to prepare for future blazes after a record summer 2026.
body: RAF A400M planes will be able to fight wildfires if fire crews request them Military planes and helicopters will be drafted in to tackle wildfires, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to tell the UK's first summit on the issue. Civilian fire services in all four nations will be able to request the support of the Royal Air Force's Chinook helicopters and A400M planes to fight wildfires on tough terrain such as remote moorland and steep hillsides. Burnham said the measures were needed because "we cannot put people through another summer like this one". The government will host its first "wildfire resilience summit" on Friday to discuss how to prevent, respond to and recover from such blazes after a record-breaking summer 2026. There have been 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales this year, an all-time high and up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024, according to figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council. Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025 - but the UK's Climate Change Committee has warned the risk will rise in the coming decades. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said this was the first time the RAF's Chinooks and the four-engine A400Ms were being equipped to tackle wildfires. Some areas struggled with no air assistance in the summer. Chinooks have practised picking up and dropping water from firefighting buckets in Portland harbour, UK RAF Chinook crews have already helped respond, external to wildfires in Cyprus. In addition to military aircraft, the government said it would also spend £45m on wildfire-specific personal protective equipment for firefighters on the ground. It is lighter than current firefighting equipment which is designed for fires in buildings and not meant to be worn for a long time, the government added. Ministers are also pledging a £25m scheme from April 2027 to April 2029 to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they are natural firebreaks, and financial support for farmers to fireproof their land such as by digging ponds. "The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high," a briefing ahead of the summit said, following a temporary ban on disposable BBQs. Burnham will meet fire chiefs, local leaders and experts from tech companies at the summit. "I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything," he said on Thursday, recounting the night of a wildfire that destroyed 19 homes in the West Midlands in August. "I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn't have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs." Earlier this month, MPs on the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said there were weaknesses in the UK's wildfire preparedness, including access to aerial firefighting resources, securing water supplies during major incidents and coordinating resources at a national level. Firefighters tackled wildfires across the UK over the summer, including here in Ebbw Vale, Wales MPs said the current system for obtaining aerial firefighting support was "no longer fit for purpose". At the summit, a "Wildfires AI Unit" will be announced to combine universities, tech firms and officials on the Cobra emergency committee, along with Met Office wildfire forecasts and closer work with devolved governments. In August, the government convened a Cobra meeting before sending an emergency alert to millions of phones across England and Wales - which sparked a backlash from some. Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to the Met Office. In a study on how this summer was impacted by human-induced climate change, it said the heat experienced was made 130 times more likely. "The wildfires that tore through our countryside this summer showed the urgent need to adapt to our changing climate," Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said ahead of the summit. "Nature is our greatest ally in preventing wildfires starting in the first place," she added. Major incidents were declared for wildfires this year in areas such as Dunwich Heath and RSPB Minsmere in Suffolk, the Cairngorms, Hampshire and Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire. title: Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power
description: Bournemouth's 3-0 win against AC Milan further illustrated the dominance of Premier League sides against their European counterparts.
body: Bournemouth have beaten Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now AC Milan in the Europa League At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation. That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time continental champions AC Milan 3-0 in only their third-ever European fixture. Justin Kluivert scored the opener at Vitality Stadium, 31 years after his father, Patrick, scored the winning goal for Ajax against Milan in the Champions League final. Having seen their club narrowly avoid the jaws of liquidation in 2008, not many Bournemouth fans would have dreamed that famous name would one day appear on their shirts. "It's mega. In terms of the story of the club it's ridiculous. Someone told me today, 15 years ago today we were 17th in League One, so it's pretty incredible," Bournemouth midfielder Ryan Christie told TNT Sports. "So many of these fans have been here for this journey so to have nights like this and win as well is special." To add to the peculiarity of the situation, Milan fielded more English players in their starting XI (three) than the hosts (two). While the sending off of Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan killed the contest after 27 minutes, Bournemouth were by far the better side up until that point. In truth, that didn't come as a surprise, even though Bournemouth have won just six points from seven league games this term while Milan are fourth in Serie A. The three sides they have beaten this season - Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now Milan - have all competed in the Champions League inside the past three years. For them it's a fairytale, but for the rest of Europe, is it a Premier League-induced nightmare? Five months after a missed Arsenal penalty denied a Premier League clean sweep in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, is this yet another sign of English club dominance? Bournemouth sweep aside 10-man Milan in Europa League English clubs played nine games in Europe this week, losing just once. In fact, Premier League clubs have lost just four of 26 games played across the three continental competitions so far this season. Manchester United are responsible for two of them. In the five seasons since the Conference League was introduced, no league has yet won all three, but in three different seasons Premier League clubs have won two of them. Over the past two seasons, Premier League clubs have played 21 knockout ties against European opposition in the Conference League and Europa League - and won all 21. The only two ties they have lost have been to other English teams. But, despite such dominance, the Champions League still remains elusive for most, with only Manchester City lifting the trophy over the past five years. So, why are English clubs so dominant in Europe's secondary competitions - and why hasn't this transferred to consistent Champions League glory? Fifteen of last season's 20 Premier League teams featured in the top 30 of Deloitte's 2026 Money List. It is easy to see why then English clubs appear to be head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to the Europa League and the Conference League. Premier League clubs earn more than £1.37bn per season in television rights, a figure La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 could only match combined. Brighton are easily the richest club in the Conference League this season, while Bournemouth and Crystal Palace both appear in last season's top 30. Last season Aston Villa beat Freiburg comfortably in the Europa League final, with a revenue more than double the Germans'. Crystal Palace won the Conference League with a revenue of almost four times more than Rayo Vallecano, the side they saw off in the final. In 2025, Tottenham beat Manchester United in the Europa League final. In the Premier League, they finished 17th and 15th respectively. In 2022-23, West Ham finished 14th and won the Conference League. All the evidence points to the Premier League's collective strength. Take away Europe's richest and England dominates. The summer transfer window was further evidence of Europe's struggles against the Premier League, with the latter again setting a new transfer spend record of £3.49bn to dwarf their rival leagues. Of the 20 most expensive transfers completed in the summer only six were not to clubs in the English top flight. You now have Premier League clubs - away from the traditional big six - beating other top European sides to signings. Premier League wages are generally higher and the league is increasingly seen as the place to be for a lot of European talent. "With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," football finance expert Kieran Maguire said in August. "A significant proportion of overseas players are now choosing to play in England than elsewhere in Europe because of the wages on offer." Despite the success of Premier League sides in the Europa League and Conference League, the Champions League is a harder nut to crack. While Barcelona, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich all lost to English teams in last season's elongated Champions League league stage, it has been a very different story when it really mattered. Over the past two campaigns, eight of nine English teams have been knocked out by one of the Deloitte Money League's big four, according to the last report produced in January 2026. Chelsea, Manchester City, Newcastle and Liverpool were eliminated by an aggregate score of 25-6 last season. No English club appeared in the top four of Deloitte's Money List, with Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain leading the way. Three of those have won the Champions League five times between them in the last seven years. English clubs are certainly very much in the mix for the Champions League, with Ar

title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
description: The Prince of Wales was marking his Earthshot Prize, to which all of Norton's guests were linked.
body: The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize. During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize. As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa. They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet". The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films. William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely. There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m. The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November. Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro. The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability. At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible". The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday. title: US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in Picket Fences, Mash and Alien, dies aged 93
description: The actor died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said.
body: US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in the TV series Picket Fences and the films Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93, his family says. Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said: "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives." In a six-decade career, he took on film and TV roles, appearing in the film Mash, A River Runs Through It and Ted. He also co-founded TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support next-generation filmmakers and storytellers. His family said he will be remembered "for his belief that stories can help people heal, find purpose, and create change". The moustachioed star of several 20th century hit films was born in 1933 in Detroit, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career that boasted several military roles. He made his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford ​in War Hunt and years later re-teamed with Redford in the 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It, which starred Brad Pitt. Skerritt's breakthrough role came when he played US army surgeon Duke Forrest in the 1970 Korean War comedy Mash, which also starred Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman. The hit film, which was released amid unrest over the Vietnam War, was nominated for five Academy Awards and was adapted for television two years later. He also starred alongside Sigourney Weaver in the 1979 sci-fi film Alien, which earned two Oscar nominations, and led to three sequels and several crossover projects. "It is spontaneity and impulse ​that make the difference, and that is ⁠what I felt we had with 'Alien,'" Skerritt said in a 2019 interview, according to Reuters news agency. "Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other." Skerritt said that one of the things he liked most when he first read the script was that "the woman becomes a hero", referring to Weaver's character, Ripley. During his career, he starred opposite several strong female leads. He appeared with Shirley MacLaine in the 1977 film Turning Point and played Sally Field's husband in 1989's Steel Magnolias. As Commander Mike "Viper" Metcalf in the 1986 classic Top Gun, the versatile actor appeared alongside a young Tom Cruise in the blockbuster. On television, he won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his role as Sheriff Jimmy Brock in David E Kelley's drama Picket Fences. The quirky procedural's ensemble cast was nominated for SAG Awards in 1995 and 1996, and he received a nod for male actor in a drama series in 1995. Picket Fences star Lauren Holly, who played Skerritt's deputy on Picket Fences, described him in a tribute as "our leader". "His example made those years such a joy and we all loved and respected him so much," Holly wrote, adding: "He cared deeply for his family-both the one at home and the one at work. He cared deeply for his planet, and all of its inhabitants. He had a huge impact on my life, and so many memories I have of him include sharing fits of crippling laughter." Skerritt also had guest roles on the small screen in The West Wing, Madam Secretary, Law & Order: SVU and Huff. He reteamed with Field as the family patriarch, William Walker, in the drama Brothers & Sisters from 2007-09. He had a six-episode stint on Cheers playing Rebecca Howe's crush-worthy boss Evan Drake. In a statement, Skerritt's family said that he leaves behind a "legacy that reaches far beyond the screen". A deep believer in the power of storytelling, Skerritt helped found the TheFilmSchool in Seattle and co-founded the Red Badge Project, which helps veterans work through PTSD, anxiety and depression by writing and sharing their experiences. Inspired in part by his experience filming A River Runs Through It, he also believed in protecting the natural world. He created the documentary series Reflections of the River about America's rivers and supported river conservation. Skerrit is survived by his third wife Julie, five children and several grandchildren. title: Items recovered in search for missing fishing boat and crew
description: Tam Murray, 40 and Murdo Morrison, 23 remain missing after their vessel disappeared off Lewis and the body of crewmate Douglas Craigie was found at sea.
body: Douglas Craigie, Murdo Morrison and Norman Murray had been fishing off the north coast of Lewis Items belonging to a fishing boat that vanished off the north coast of the Isle of Lewis last week have been recovered as the search for the vessel and two missing crew members continues. Norman "Tam" Murray, 40 and Murdo Morrison, 23, were on board the Kilda when it disappeared on 13 October. The body of crewmate Douglas Craigie, 49, was recovered from the sea in the early hours of the following morning by rescuers. On Thursday, police confirmed that items belonging to the vessel had been recovered from what was described as "an area of interest" off the coast near Port of Ness. The search was carried out by Police Scotland's marine and dive unit and partners. A Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone has been in place for divers and vessels in an area between the Butt of Lewis and Port of Ness, but this will be lifted from 23:59 on Thursday. Insp Neil Taylor, local area inspector for the Western Isles, said the search was a "complex operation" and asked for officers to be given "time and space" to carry out inquiries. He said: "Efforts are continuing to work with partners and we are doing everything we can to get answers. "While the Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone will be lifted tonight, we would urge people not to put themselves at any risk. "Please do not attempt to carry out searches in areas which put you at risk of harm." A GoFundMe for the families affected by the event has raised more than £148,000, against a target of £110,000. title: Watch: 'It's part of the culture' - New York bans horse-drawn carriages after more than 160 years
description: The BBC's Madeline Halpert spoke to city tourists, residents and horse carriage workers about the industry and their opinion on the ban.
body: This video can not be played The New York City Council has passed a ban on the city's well-know horse-drawn carriages starting in June 2028, a proposal backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. While animal rights activists and officials have pushed for the ban for years, the final catalyst was the death of a 18-year-old earlier this year, who died after a carriage horse bolted and caused a fatal fall. The BBC's Madeline Halpert spoke New York City tourists, residents and horse carriage workers to get their perspectives on the industry and the ban. title: Could rebel knight Roger Casement be exhumed for a second time?
description: In 1965, his remains were exhumed and brought to Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin. But a commemoration society in his name, who have lodged the application, has said it wants to "fulfil his wish" to be buried in County Antrim.
body: Roger Casement was executed in 1916 for his part in an Irish rebellion An application has been lodged to have the remains of a knight of the realm turned Easter Rising conspirator, Roger Casement, moved to Northern Ireland. If successful, it would be the second time Casement will have been exhumed and reburied. Casement was originally interred in the grounds of Pentonville Prison in London, where he was hanged in 1916 after being discovered returning to Ireland aboard a U-boat following a trip to Germany to secure arms for Irish nationalists. In 1965, his remains were exhumed and brought to Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin. But a commemoration society in his name, who have lodged the application, has said it wants to "fulfil his wish" of being buried in County Antrim. The Roger Casement Commemoration and Re-interment Association has applied for an exhumation licence from Dublin City Council and Glasnevin Cemetery. Specifically, they want to transfer Casement's remains from the Irish capital to Murlough Bay in County Antrim - where, they said, a man called Patrick McCarry has agreed to allow the reburial on his ground. In a letter on 25 July 1916, just more than a week before his death, Casement wrote: "Don't let my body lie here - get me back to the green hill at Murlough, by the McGarry's house, looking down on the Moyle, that's where I'd like to be now, and there's where I'd like to lie." A ceremony was held at Glasnevin Cemetery in 2001 when nine men executed during Ireland's war of independence were reburied, showing the graveyard's links with Irish Republicanism In a statement, the association said its plans have the support of Casement's family - namely James Casement from Arizona in the United States. On Thursday night, the association and McCarry gathered at the Casement Social Club in Belfast alongside their legal team, Phoenix Law solicitors, and O'Neill's Funeral Directors. Association chairperson Alan Daly said: "After many months of preparation, we have formally applied for the exhumation of Roger Casement to bring him home." The Roger Casement Commemoration and Re-interment Association was formed over a decade ago with the aim of getting Casement's remains moved to Antrim He said "Casement always wanted to return home" and that it was "historic to be co-signing this application with Roger's direct and surviving relative, James Casement". "It pulls the heart strings. Not only do we want to right a wrong here, we want to fulfil a dying man's wish," he told BBC News NI. "We're going to see that it's granted - his wish that he's laid to rest in Murlough Bay," added Daly. The Mystery of Casement, Rebel Knight Episode 1 - Searching for his place in the world Roger Casement became a household name in Britain and Ireland in the early 20th century. But his childhood gives no hint of what is to come. The association has claimed that "exhumations are regularly granted across the island of Ireland". However, obtaining an exhumation licence in Northern Ireland, external or the Republic of Ireland (ROI), external involves a highly regulated process, primarily due to the strict legal, ethical, and public health safeguards surrounding human remains. When it was suggested Casement's bones should be repatriated to Northern Ireland from Pentonville in 1965, Prime Minister Harold Wilson's government forbade it, insisting it would stir up political tensions. It is unclear how Casement's complex legacy will influence this most recent attempt to bring him to County Antrim. Those unfamiliar with the life and times of Roger Casement might still recognise his name from the sports stadium at the heart of one of Northern Ireland's most enduring modern political rows - Casement Park. But while it is not unusual for a GAA stadium to be called after a perceived Irish republican martyr, it is much less common for a pitch to be named after a British knight. And before being stripped of his knighthood at the end of his life, Casement had been both. In 1911, Casement was knighted by King George V for his humanitarian work - which took him from central Africa to some of the poorest parts of South America. But on his travels Casement - who considered himself a Protestant most his life - eventually became disillusioned with colonialism, retired from diplomacy and dedicated himself to the Irish nationalist cause by joining the Irish Volunteer Force. With World War One raging, Casement became attracted by the potential of an Irish-German alliance as a way of securing full Irish independence. As the secret military council of the Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB) planned the Easter Rising, Casement agreed to travel to Germany, where he would attempt to raise a brigade by recruiting Irish soldiers who had fought for Britain and been captured by Germany. Soon after arriving on the continent, it became clear than the German promises of soldiers and 200,000 rifles were not going to be fulfilled. Returning on a German U-boat to County Kerry in April 1916, Casement was intercepted and arrested by British authorities. As Pádraig Pearse read the proclamation on the steps of the Dublin's General Post Office, Casement was locked in the Tower of London awaiting trial for treason. On 29 June 1916 Casement was found guilty of high treason and sentenced to death. A campaign for a reprieve was supported by leading political and literary figures, including W B Yeats and George Bernard Shaw, but ultimately failed. Casement was executed on 3 August 1916. Part of what hampered his chances of a reprieve were extracts from his diaries which were widely circulated, publicly outing him as a homosexual. title: 'Difficult decision' to close Samaritans branch after more than 50 years
description: "Sadly, and due to circumstances beyond anyone's control, the difficult decision was reached to close the branch," they charity says.
body: Samaritans charity estimates it answers a call for help every 10 seconds An elected representative has called for "answers" after the closure of the Omagh, County Tyrone, branch of the Samaritans charity. Founded in 1953, the Samaritans focus on preventing suicides by connecting trained volunteers with people who are struggling. The charity estimates it answers a call for help every 10 seconds. The Omagh branch, which had been part of the community for more than 50 years, had about 20 'active' volunteers, the charity said. In a statement, the charity said "due to circumstances beyond anyone's control" a "difficult decision" was reached to close the branch. Last year, the BBC learned that dozens of branches had voiced concerns over the plan to close more than 100 branches across the UK and Ireland. At the time, the Samaritans said that having more than 200 branches "is not sustainable" and hindered them from providing the best service. On Thursday, a Samaritans spokesperson told BBC News NI the closure of the branch "is not related to Samaritans future-proofing programme, which is not currently looking at services in Northern Ireland". Samaritans of Omagh had not been open for face-to-face support with members of the public since March 2020, when all branches reduced services due to Covid-19 restrictions. BBC News NI spoke to a former Omagh team member, who shared the volunteers' concerns about their future. The branch covered counties Fermanagh and Tyrone, with volunteers making lengthy journeys for shifts, and they they said volunteers are conscious that the distance between other branches in Northern Ireland may be unattainable. It is understood that the news of the closure came via email and those without email addresses were left unaware. Sinn Féin councillor Barry McElduff is calling for a meeting between the Samaritans and the council Speaking to BBC News NI, Sinn Féin councillor Barry McElduff said he intends to propose an "informal meeting" between Fermanagh and Omagh District Council and the charity "to explore the issues which have arisen and contributed to the closure". "There is a lot of uncertainty as to the reasons that this has happened. We need answers," he said. "There are a significant number of volunteers in the Omagh area, as I understand it, and there is a great need for this service." A spokesperson for the charity said the Omagh branch "has been a valued part of Samaritans for more than 50 years" and they "recognise the contribution made" by successive trustees, directors, leaders and all volunteers. "Sadly, and due to circumstances beyond anyone's control, the difficult decision was reached to close the branch," they said. "Samaritans operates a national listening service, so people in Tyrone and across Northern Ireland will be unaffected and will remain able to access help from Samaritans at any time, day or night, 365 days a year on 116 123 or at samaritans.org. "All volunteers in the branch have been offered support, as well as receiving one to one phone calls offering support and guidance around relocation. Support meetings have also been offered. "Some volunteers have already begun the process of transferring to other locations." The charity said any proceeds from future property sales will be reinvested into running Samaritans services across the UK and Ireland. If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line. title: See the Pokémon cards that made a retired decorator a millionaire
description: A man from Surrey is now a millionaire after selling a collection of Pokémon cards at auction.
body: This video can not be played A collection of Pokémon cards stored in a retired decorator's attic for 15 years has sold for £1.56m at auction. The seller, from Woking, said he realised the cards were valuable after reading about a single card fetching more than £6,000 in his local newspaper. His collection was auctioned off at Ewbank's in Surrey on Wednesday. The auction house claims it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever. The BBC's Duncan Kennedy visited Ewbank's to see the collection in person. Find out more about the collection, and how much the most valuable cards sold for, here. title: Trump says NBA star LeBron James disrespected US anthem and demands apology
description: The basketball star recently appeared to be practising a golf swing and basketball shots while the national anthem was performed.
body: President Donald Trump has said basketball star LeBron James disrespected the US by not being still while the national anthem was sung. James, who now plays for the Philadelphia 76ers, appeared to be practising a golf swing and basketball shots as the anthem was being performed ahead of the season-opening match against the New York Knicks on Wednesday. "While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country!," Trump posted on social media. "LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag." James has not responded to the president's latest comments but the pair have criticised each other in the past. James can be seen in a video making the motion of a golf swing as a performer sings the Star-Spangled Banner at New York's Madison Square Garden. His teammates, who are lined up next to him on the court, mostly remain standing with minimal movement. "I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE," Trump added, referring to James. "LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!" The BBC has contacted James for a response through the 76ers and has also asked the team to comment. The US anthem is played or performed at the start of most professional sports games. Players and spectators are expected to stand for it, if they can, and refrain from moving around. Some people sing along. This tradition has become a political flash-point before. In 2016, former American football player Colin Kaepernick sat down and later knelt on one knee during the anthem as a demonstration against police brutality and racism in the US. Trump criticised Kaepernick and later took credit when the athlete could not find a team to play for. Years later, he softened his stance saying Kaepernick should "get another shot" to play in the NFL. The president has had a longstanding feud with James, who has publicly endorsed or campaigned for Trump's political opponents since the 2016 presidential election In 2018, Trump suggested James was not intelligent after the athlete said he "would never sit across" from him. That same year, James accused Trump of giving racists "an opportunity to be out and outspoken without fear". He has also suggested that Trump's rhetoric led to a mob storming the US Capitol in 2021 to stop the certification of the result of the 2020 election, which former President Joe Biden won. James had endorsed Biden. In July, when asked to choose between James and Michael Jordan as the all-time greatest basketball player in history, Trump said he preferred Jordan. "I only like people that like me," Trump said. James, 41, is the highest point scorer in the history of the National Basketball Association league with more than 40,000 points. He has had a long career and has won the NBA championship with every team he has played for. In July,⁠ he signed a two-year contract with Philadelphia which is widely expected to be his last as a professional player. title: Woman charged after police officer injured in shooting
description: The officer was injured after approaching two people at a bus stop in Nottingham city centre.
body: Nottinghamshire Police said the officer approached two people in Angel Row before being shot in the foot A 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre. Nottinghamshire Police said the officer was shot in the foot after he approached a man and a woman at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday. The male officer remains in hospital receiving treatment, the force added. Aisha Zaman, of Collison Street, Hyson Green, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence. Police said the charge came after "consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service". Zaman has been remanded into custody and will appear before Nottingham Magistrates' Court on Friday, police added. Several other people have been arrested in connection with the incident, including two men, 24 and 30, and two women, 25 and 21, who have been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender. A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both remain in police custody. Det Ch Supt Rich Bull, who is leading the investigation, said the "outpouring of support" for the officer had been "greatly appreciated". "We would just like to take this moment to thank the public", he added. "We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation." He said officers were "still following a number of lines of inquiry", and anyone with information has been asked to contact the force. title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother
description: Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy is airing the ad featuring her mother, whose husband was charged with sexual abuse in her childhood.
body: Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable". Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done". In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody. The ad set off a storm of criticism from members of both parties. On Thursday, President Donald Trump sought to defend it and Ramaswamy on social media. Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election. In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down. "I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening. "You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad. The last time Acton saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted, according to Acton's campaign. Arthur's husband fled the state before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004. Arthur left with him. In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point". Trump, who has endorsed Ramaswamy, blamed the press for the negative reaction to the ad, in a long post where he also commended Arthur and Ramaswamy. Trump blasted DeWine, as well. He urged Ramaswamy to keep up his attacks and "let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" "I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse," Trump also posted. In the ad, Arthur repeatedly says Acton lies and asserts she "needs help", but does not discuss anything related to cheating or stealing. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it. Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state. The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling". On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor. "And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well." MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election. Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party. David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads are not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense". He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour. A poll by VoteHub, external released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad. If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades. GUIDE: What are the US midterms? title: Lockerbie bombing accused loses bid to have case thrown out
description: Abu Agila Mas'ud al-Marimi had claimed he was victim of an illegal rendition when he was transferred into US custody.
body: Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has been in custody since December 2022 A Libyan man accused of building the bomb that brought down an American airliner over Lockerbie nearly 38 years ago has lost his bid to have the case thrown out of court. Abu Agila Mas'ud al-Marimi had claimed he was the victim of an illegal rendition when he was transferred into US custody from Libya in 2022. A US district court judge has ruled that the manner of his removal should not prevent his trial going ahead in Washington in January. Marimi has denied playing a key role in the attack on Pan Am 103, which killed 270 people on 21 December 1988. Hundreds of people died when Pan Am Flight 103 exploded over Lockerbie in December 1988 His attempt to have the case dismissed was made public through documents lodged with the court in Washington. Marimi's lawyers said he was violently abducted from his home in Tripoli in 2022 by armed members of a militia, "in a cloak and dagger operation conducted in the middle of the night". They alleged that weeks later, after being held without access to lawyers in a detention centre, he was handed over to FBI agents at an airport in Misrata and flown to the United States. Marimi argued the case should be dismissed because the United States had invaded his constitutional rights and violated extradition agreements between the US and Libya. Court transcripts obtained by BBC Scotland News have revealed that trial judge Dabney Friedrich rejected the defence motion. She referred to a longstanding American legal doctrine, which stipulates that a court's right to hold a trial is not impaired if the suspect has been the subject of a forceful abduction. "This rule rests on the principle that due process of law is satisfied when one present in court is convicted of a crime after a fair trial and in accordance with constitutional procedural safeguards," said the judge. "Put differently, there's nothing in the Constitution that requires a court to permit a guilty person rightfully convicted to escape justice because he was brought to trial against his will." In her ruling, the judge said there were two exceptions to that doctrine. One would apply if Marimi had been brought before the court through the US government's "deliberate, unnecessary and unreasonable invasion" of his constitutional rights. For that exception to be triggered, the challenged conduct had to be carried out by, or at the direction of, US officials. The judge said Marimi's allegations "at best suggest that US government officials exerted pressure on Libyan officials to facilitate a rendition, not that US government officials directed or controlled the challenged conduct." The second exception to the doctrine would apply if the US government had violated an extradition agreement which was the only way a suspect could be transferred between the two countries. The judge said the US government had invoked two conventions to secure Marimi's appearance in a US court. On 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing? "Neither the Montreal Convention nor the Terrorists Bombing Convention provides that it is the only way by which one country may gain custody of a national of another country for the purposes of prosecution," she said. "Accordingly, Libya was free to transfer Mr Al-Marimi to the United States using any method it chose." The defence and prosecution have fought a series of legal battles in the approach to Marimi's trial, which is now scheduled to get underway on 19 January after three postponements. In another ruling, the judge rejected a defence motion to suppress a confession alleged to have been made by Marimi when he was in custody in Libya in 2012. According to the FBI, Marimi admitted building the bomb which destroyed Pan Am 103 in an operation carried out by the Libyan intelligence service. Marimi has claimed the confession was false and was made under duress. The only previous criminal trial related to the Lockerbie bombing took place between May 2000 and January 2001, when three Scottish judges convicted Libyan intelligence agent Abdulbasset al-Megrahi of playing a key role in the plot. Megrahi was jailed for life but released on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government in 2009 after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer. He died three years later at home in Tripoli. title: Bruno Fernandes has home burgled while in Italy with Man Utd
description: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes had his home burgled on Wednesday while he was in Italy for his club's Champions League game against Como.
body: Bruno Fernandes joined Manchester United in January 2020 Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes had his home burgled on Wednesday while he was in Italy for his club's Champions League game against Como. It is understood Fernandes' family were not in the house in Cheshire when it was broken into and that the intruders were inside for less than five minutes before police arrived. United are understood to be supporting the 32-year-old following the break-in. BBC Sport has contacted Cheshire Police about the incident. He is the latest player to have his family home burgled while playing for his team. Manchester City player Ruben Dias and former girlfriend Maya Jama also had their Cheshire home burgled in similar circumstances to Fernandes. Dias was at City's Champions League game against Galatasaray when his home was targeted in January. Previous victims in the same area include footballers Jack Grealish, Raheem Sterling and Riyad Mahrez. Portugal midfielder Fernandes has been with Manchester United since joining from Sporting in January 2020. United were beaten 4-1 by Como and, following the match, Fernandes criticised his manager Michael Carrick's tactics. However, he will remain as the club's captain and will not be disciplined for his comments. title: Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists
description: Energy secretary says she "didn't get it right" over comments she made about a TV interview.
body: Miatta Fahnbulleh initially did not explicitly back the government's proposals The energy minister has insisted she backs Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's immigration reforms after she made what she described as a "light-hearted remark". Miatta Fahnbulleh was repeatedly asked in an interview on Wednesday whether she supported the government's plans to increase the time it takes for migrants to gain permanent UK residency, but refused to. Referring to that exchange, she joked to reporters on Thursday that she did not explicitly answer the question because she had told herself she would "never lie". In a later statement, she said: "Today I made what was meant to be a light-hearted self-deprecating remark. I didn't get it right and it hasn't come off as I intended." She added: "I fully support our home secretary and the government's position on migration reform." Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years. Mahmood told Labour Party conference in September the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country". But a significant number of Labour MPs and trade unions want her to water down the proposed policy. Downing Street has repeatedly insisted that Mahmood is considering responses to a consultation exercise before finalising the reforms. On Wednesday, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to make sure we get this right." Asked earlier on the same day on Sky News, whether she backed the proposed reforms, Fahnbulleh said: "We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution." She was pressed several more times on the issue, saying the government was consulting on the proposals and would "will come out with the measures that we take forward". At a lunch with political reporters on Thursday, Fahnbulleh said: "I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge [on Sky] yesterday, but nevermind." In her later statement, she said this was a joke and suggested it was not intended to show she did not support Mahmood's reforms. "As I said earlier this week, it's absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship," Fahnbulleh said. It comes after another Cabinet minister, Angela Rayner, criticised the proposed changes ahead of Labour's conference in Liverpool. Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules. She later denied there was a split within the heart of government over the issue. title: Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in remarkable defeat
description: Once the disappointment of defeat dissipates, Harry Brook can reflect on another starring role with the bat which underlines his status as the world's best all-format batter, says Stephan Shemilt.
body: Harry Brook hit the fastest 200 in the history of one-day internationals Just under a year ago, Harry Brook was left wondering if he would be sacked as England white-ball captain and what damage he had done to his international career. What a turnaround in 12 months. From whacked in Wellington to the run-fest in Rawalpindi, Brook is undeniably England's most important cricketer and probably the best multi-format batter in the world. Brook's 202 in England's defeat against Sri Lanka was an astonishing display of stroke-making. There can be no higher praise than to compare Brook's dismantling of the Sri Lankan attack to the sort of innings once played by South African genius AB de Villiers. It was the first double hundred scored by an Englishman in an ODI, passing England's previous best individual score of 182 by Ben Stokes against New Zealand in 2023. In reaching 200 in 114 balls, Brook registered the fastest double ton by anyone in an ODI, bettering the 117 deliveries of India's Shubman Gill against West Indies only last month. Brook has joined one of international cricket's most exclusive clubs. In completing the set of a hundred in a T20, double hundred in an ODI and triple century in a Test, Brook has matched the previously unique treble of West Indies' legend Chris Gayle. In the moment, the collection of another landmark might not mean a great deal to Brook. Despite his efforts, his team were beaten as the spirited Sri Lankans pulled off the second-highest run-chase in history in one of the most astonishing ODIs ever played. For a man who has previously spoken about prioritising match-winning contributions over individual achievements, Brook the captain was left dejected that his innings ultimately counted for nothing. He is the first man to make a double ton in an ODI and end up on the losing side. Still, it further underlined his status as the premier run-getter across all kinds of international cricket. Perhaps only Australia's Travis Head can challenge Brook for the crown. Ranked by the International Cricket Council as the best Test batter in the world, Brook averages 53.08 in the longer format of the game. No England player with a minimum of 20 innings since 1968 has a better average than Brook – he stands above Joe Root, Alastair Cook, Geoffrey Boycott, Graham Gooch and everyone else to have batted for England in the past seven decades. In T20 internationals, Brook averages 36.21 at a strike-rate of 164.92. No batter to have played at least 20 innings for a major nation averages more at a better strike-rate. Brook is learning to play List A cricket in one-day internationals. Sri Lanka was his 61st List A match, 45 of which have been ODIs. After a slow start to his international 50-over career, Brook averages just under 50 in his past 29 matches and almost 57 in 2026. The responsibility of captaincy suits him. In ODIs, Brook averages 31 runs more as captain compared to when not. In T20s, his average jumps 19 runs when wearing the metaphorical armband. This video can not be played 'That's life' - captain Brook on England defeat Brook's workload is an issue, the Yorkshireman having played in every England fixture since being rested for a T20 series in Ireland last September and, fitness permitting, he will be the only man to play in every game this winter – that's five tours to four countries across three continents. He left home last week and will not again see his own bed until mid-January. He says his time to rest is during the Indian Premier League, the riches of which he has turned down in order to focus his energy on England. Brook probably does not get enough credit for making such a decision. There is the question of how good Brook could become. Ben Stokes revealed that, at the end of the Ashes, he took Brook to one side to say he should be averaging 60 or more in Test cricket. Speaking to the BBC in August, Brook admitted to not being the "finished article". "I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games," he said. In terms of improvement, Brook has already shown a willingness to do the hard yards to become a better cricketer. As a youngster, he struggled with his fitness, but has worked hard to become one of the best athletes in the England team. He has spoken at length about being better able to run twos – he is one of the best runners between the wickets in the world. Brook has also turned himself into one of England's most reliable catchers. As for the batting, well-qualified judges don't hold back in their praise. Last month, Stokes said Brook may have more talent than Kevin Pietersen. In 2024, James Anderson said Brook could surpass Root as England's highest Test run-scorer. Just last week, Chris Woakes labelled Brook as "next level". Harry Brook hit 21 fours and 10 sixes against Sri Lanka The missing achievement is a starring role in winning a major series or tournament. Brook's magnificent century should have been enough for England to win the fifth Test against India at The Oval last year, only for him to throw away his wicket with victory in sight. He has not made a century in 10 Ashes Tests against Australia and was only a bit-part player as part of the England team that won the T20 World Cup in 2022. Maybe his moment is approaching. Next summer is a home Ashes, followed by the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. Brook will be 28 and at the peak of his powers. There is the chance to play a major part in regaining the urn and to become one of the few British athletes to lift a World Cup in any sport. To do that, he will have to iron out the flaws that have arisen in England's one-day cricket across the first two matches of the tri-series in Pakistan. In the opening match, against Pakistan, dropped catches and poor strokes left them well beaten in a contest they could have won. Against Sri Lanka, England somehow lost from what

title: Watch: Ukraine hit by strikes after Russia agrees to new peace talks
description: The three waves of Russian missiles were launched at hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks with the US and Ukraine.
body: This video can not be played Kyiv has been hit by another round of missile strikes hours after Russia agreed to resume peace talks on Wednesday. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the three waves of missiles were launched by "Russian humanitarians". This comes after US envoy Steve Witkoff called Russia's President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" following a meeting in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks with the US and Ukraine. The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from the scene of a destroyed retail park. title: 'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
description: The influencer, whose real name is Braden Peters, is accused of sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl in 2025.
body: Clavicular, a social media influencer who promotes the "looksmaxxing" trend of young men maximising their attractiveness, has pleaded not guilty to criminal charges including rape. The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged in September with felony rape, drugging an individual for sexual intercourse and procuring alcohol for someone under the age of 21. The charges stem from an incident in 2025 when he is accused of assaulting a 17-year-old girl at his family's Massachusetts home. Peters has denied the allegations and said the encounter was consensual. On Thursday, he was granted $10,000 bail, ordered not to contact or post about his accuser, and to surrender his passport. Clavicular walks a runway at Paris Fashion Week in June 2026 A woman told police that on 23 May 2025, Peters ordered her an Uber to his family's house in Chatham where they were drinking alcohol while filming a livestream before he allegedly raped her, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News. The police officer who took the report said he believed she was unable to consent due to her age and the level of intoxication she exhibited in the livestream, CBS reported. Clavicular has more than a million followers on TikTok and Instagram and has garnered media attention for extreme measures he has taken for "looksmaxxing". He has admitted to using a hammer on his face and jawline and taking a number of steroids, injections, and other drugs to achieve bodily perfection. He also gives advice on appearing masculine and performs stunts to shock followers. In Florida earlier this year, he was charged after filming himself shooting at what appeared to be a dead alligator. He pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public. In March, he was arrested on suspicion of battery after authorities suspected him of instigating a fight between two women. Authorities said in July that they did not intend to file charges. After Thursday's hearing, Peters posted a photo of himself in the black suit and black tie he wore to court, while holding his dog which he also brought to court. His next hearing will be on 24 November, when the judge will decide if there is enough evidence for the case to move forward. title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
description: Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave in 2021.
body: A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December. Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021. Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period, during which both sides are legally required to exchange information with each other on their case. Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia. In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings. The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended. Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place. On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida. In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action." Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021. The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action". The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US. In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters. Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary". Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present. Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials. In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions.
