title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
description: Websites were taken offline after the developers of programming language PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" had been discovered.
body: This video can not be played How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP. Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades. Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution. There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent. Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out. "The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords. She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied". The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected. A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue". "But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added. Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented". "It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One. But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers. He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on. Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date. "Hacking has been around for many years," he said. "The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point." Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online. He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long. "MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said. He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers. PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor. It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit. When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read. It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today. PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks. According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it. The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP. Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems. Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added. Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal. Cyber researchers at Calif and Wiz unearthed the php2shell flaw, theorised by the PHP Foundation in 2024, in part using OpenAI tools While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday. The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday. But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required. In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes. According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally. title: Germany target of 'intensive' espionage, Merz says after suspected Russian spy arrest
description: A Ukrainian man was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia - one of several such cases in Germany this year.
body: Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Russian intelligence activity in Germany remains 'at a consistently high level' Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said after a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Officials said the suspect, named as Vadym Y., had allegedly collected military-related intelligence from Germany. Merz called the uncovering of the case a "success", but warned "let us not delude ourselves - the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level". Several people alleged to be acting on behalf of Russia and other foreign powers have been arrested in Germany this year. Germany has been one of the leading European suppliers of weapons to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. The German Federal Prosecutor General's Office said on Thursday that Vadym Y., as he was identified under German privacy law, had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025. It also said the Ukrainian man had collected information including "on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives". He is due to appear before an investigating judge on Friday. In January, a woman was arrested in Berlin suspected of gathering information for an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy. Other arrests this year included a Romanian woman and a Ukrainian man accused of spying on an individual supplying drones from Germany to Ukraine, according to the prosecutor's office. UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid And, the former German spy chief August Hanning was arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power earlier this month. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved. Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant. Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D and accused him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents in exchange for money. Speaking at the sidelines of a conference in Montenegro on Thursday, Merz said: "We will likely see more such cases in the coming months and years." Merz reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier this month, including tackling hybrid attacks and hostile activity. The talks between the two leaders came after Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport in September. Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Russia. title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
description: The Brazilian president accuses the tech firm of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro, which it denies.
body: Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro in the second round of voting on Sunday Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta. In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign. In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp. The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally. It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms. A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election. It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts". "Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read. Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally. Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted. Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula. Pro-Lula supporters gathered outside Meta's office in São Paulo on Monday, accusing the company of interference in the Brazilian electoral process Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office. Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright. On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network". The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election. Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power". He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes. Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes. title: UK needs to be ready for emergencies and hostile acts, warns Streeting
description: The defence secretary warned the public and businesses needed to think about how they would cope with natural disasters and cyber attacks.
body: Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says. Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them. He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies. Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean. Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households. He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and with flooding expected this winter. Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists". "How would we cope if the payment systems at the local supermarket went down?" he said. "Those are the sorts of everyday challenges and threats that we could well face. And it's right that we ask the country to be ready for those things and to ask everyone to do their bit." The defence secretary on Thursday spoke at the opening of the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford, Shropshire The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as severe weather, which it says can affect services like power, water, phones and the internet. The "Be Ready" campaign encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items. It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news. Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation". It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added. Last month, Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the powerful natural climate phenomenon El Niño will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient. Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather. The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden. title: Sri Lanka make 430 to beat England after Brook's 202
description: Harry Brook’s first double century by an England batter in a one-day international is not enough to prevent his team being stunned by Sri Lanka, who pull off a remarkable chase of 430 in Rawalpindi.
body: Brook's previous highest score in ODIs was 136 not out, also against Sri Lanka England 429-4 (50 overs): Brook 202, Root 69, Jacks 66* Sri Lanka 430-8 (49.5 overs): Rathnayake 130, Avishka 97, Shanaka 97 Sri Lanka won by two wickets Harry Brook's first double century by an England batter in a one-day international was not enough to prevent his team being stunned by Sri Lanka, who pulled off a remarkable chase of 430 in Rawalpindi. Brook passed Ben Stokes' previous England best score of 182 and posted the fastest ODI double hundred, off 114 balls, in his astonishing 202. In clobbering the 14th double-hundred in a men's one-day international and the 12th highest individual score, Brook lifted England to 429-4 – at halfway the highest total made in a one-day international in Pakistan. But Sri Lanka, who chose to bat second, were not deterred, even when they were reduced to 24-2. They set about completing the second-highest successful chase in ODI history. Pavan Rathnayake made a sublime 130, while Aviksha Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both added 97. With Jofra Archer rested for the tri-series and leg-spinner Adil Rashid left out of this match for tactical reasons, England's bowling was woeful. Sam Curran conceded 103 runs from his nine overs. Up with the required rate throughout their innings, Sri Lanka needed 109 from the final 10 overs and were able to absorb the losses of Rathnayake and Shanaka. Sri Lanka needed eight off the final over, sent down by Josh Tongue, who was pinpoint with his accuracy to bowl Dinuth Wellalage and Eshan Malinga with successive deliveries. But in a sensational finish, Janith Liyanage, the man bowling when Brook reached 200, would not be denied. With six needed from two balls, Liyanage pummelled Tongue's penultimate delivery of the match down the ground for a match-winning maximum, sparking joyous of celebrations by the Sri Lankans. One of the most incredible one-day internationals ever played ended with an aggregate of 847 runs, behind only a match total of 872 when South Africa chased 435 to beat Australia in 2006. The total of 123 boundaries across both innings - 93 fours and 30 sixes - is also a record in ODIs. How did England lose this game? At halfway, when Brook left the field arm-in-arm with Will Jacks, the thought of Sri Lanka even getting close to their target seemed highly fanciful. Yet, Sri Lankan captain Kusal Mendis' decision to chase proved inspired, despite the way his team were dismantled by Brook. Ultimately, Sri Lanka put the conditions – and Brook's knock – into context, helped by an England team who wilted under the pressure. They were hampered by the dew, another factor in Sri Lanka's decision to bat second. England made mistakes in the field and their bowlers struggled to grip the ball. Without Archer, they lacked a death bowler. And, with less then a year to go until the World Cup, England showed no composure as the game began to run away from them. For as well as Brook batted, his tactics will come into question. Too much faith was placed in Curran, whose 103-2 are the most expensive figures returned by an England bowler in an ODI. Gus Atkinson opened the bowling and sent down just seven overs of his allotted 10 and Tongue, who almost rescued the game, was only into his ninth. This tri-series is designed to replicate the tournament conditions England will face at the World Cup in southern Africa. Two games in they are without a win and facing the prospect of needing to beat Pakistan in Lahore on Sunday to stay in the competition. title: Map thief leads 'merry dance' with return promises
description: The 1684 world map, cut from an atlas at the National Maritime Museum’s library, has not been found.
body: Melvin West has been sentenced to three years in jail A man who used a Stanley knife to cut a rare 17th Century world map out of an atlas at a museum library has been jailed for three years. Melvin West, 70, sliced the map from a 1684 atlas by Dutch cartographer Frederik de Wit while viewing it at the Caird Library, part of the National Maritime Museum in Greenwich, in February 2025. The map has never been found, and a judge at Woolwich Crown Court said West had led the court, police and museum a "merry dance" over where it was. The Metropolitan Police has appealed for anyone who knows where it is to come forward. This video can not be played Man sentenced for stealing antique map from museum in Greenwich The double hemisphere world map, known as Nova Orbis Tabula, was one of 12 in the atlas, and is studied by scholars around the world. The court heard West, from Chingford in east London, had viewed the atlas on 19 and 20 December 2024 and again on the day before the theft. Staff called police after finding a knife on the floor of the viewing room where he had been looking at the atlas. They then discovered the map had been cut out. West was arrested at his home in March 2025, but the map was not there. He pleaded guilty at Bromley Magistrates' Court in May to theft, criminal damage and possession of a bladed article. Prosecution barrister Damian Warburton said the complete atlas had been worth about £50,000 and the map alone could fetch £6,000 on the black market. The atlas is now valued at £20,000, but he told the court the "cultural loss far outweighs the financial loss". The stolen map, like the one pictured, was a double hemisphere Defence barrister Jessica Flain said West had partly paid a man to restore the map, but he would not hand it back until the full fee was settled. She asked for sentencing to be adjourned for seven days so a friend could pay the balance and West could take the map to Charing Cross Police Station. Judge Charlotte Welsh refused, saying she did "not believe a word of it". She said West had told the court in June that he could return the map within seven days, and in August that it was with a friend and he would retrieve it once he had recovered from heart surgery. "Again, that appears to have been a lie," she said. "You were charged in February. You have had eight months to return the map." The judge said she believed West had a buyer in mind and had stolen the map "to order". The court heard he had 27 convictions for 107 offences in the UK and abroad, mostly for dishonesty and including 41 thefts. They included a burglary conviction in Hungary in 2011 and a theft conviction in France in 2013, and he had also been convicted under various identities. Flain said West, a father of two, was "ashamed and embarrassed" and had been in debt and unable to meet basic living costs. She described the offence as "a short-term, pressured decision by an elderly man living in difficult circumstances". Judge Welsh said the map was of "international cultural significance" and the damage had "permanently diminished what can be learned from it". The court was told the two digital copies of the atlas are incomplete. West was jailed for three years for criminal damage, with concurrent sentences of 16 months for theft and six months for possessing a bladed article. The judge refused to suspend the sentence, saying immediate custody was needed "to deter other people from doing precisely what you have". title: The rising French star whose dad won Rugby World Cup with England
description: Felix Balshaw is the son of an English Rugby World Cup winner - but is representing France as he climbs the world tennis rankings.
body: Felix Balshaw has climbed more than 500 places in the ATP rankings since the start of 2026 Accents quickly reveal a lot about a person. So speaking to Leeds-born Felix Balshaw - the 20-year-old son of England Rugby World Cup winner Iain - it quickly becomes clear why he is representing France on his climb up the professional tennis ladder. There is no mistaking a strong Gallic twang as Balshaw, who celebrated the first ATP Tour victory of his career this week, discusses his journey. Balshaw was born in West Yorkshire while his father played for Premiership club Leeds Tykes, before the family moved to Biarritz when Iain - an electrifying full-back/wing who scored three tries in England's iconic 2003 campaign - joined the cross-channel exodus to the French Top 14. The Balshaws have remained in the luxurious Basque coastal city, known for its Belle Epoque architecture, Atlantic seafront casinos and world-class surfing. "We came down in Biarritz in 2009 and we just loved the place," said Felix, who broke into the world's top 200 last month for the first time. "I grew up in France and, as each day went by, I felt more and more French. "Since I've been little, from when I started playing in Tennis Europe juniors, I have always had the French flag by my name." Vickery's journey from World Cup winner to bodybuilder at 50 Balshaw pledging allegiance to his adopted country is understandable given his limited contact with his birthland. Trips back across the English Channel have been "very rare" for the Balshaw children, largely restricted to Christmas family gatherings. Their maternal grandmother lives in Bath, although Felix has never visited his father's hometown of Blackburn. But the world number 178 is fully aware his dad will forever be ingrained in the fabric of English sporting history. The then Bath player scored three tries during England's historic 2003 World Cup campaign, helping secure a 20-17 victory over Australia in the final when he came on as a second-half substitute. On the eve of the biggest match of his career - facing fellow Frenchman Corentin Moutet in the Lyon Open second round - Felix tried to draw inspiration from watching highlights of his father playing in 2003. "I just had a massive smile [watching] because I can say 'this is my dad'," he said. "When he was at Biarritz I was always stood in a little corner in the stands with the rugby gang. It was very, very inspirational to watch him. "As a father he's tough, but it's always important that he has a lot of experience in rugby, so he's got a lot of stuff to teach me. "He's always been a great, great part of my life. He's always had my back." Iain Balshaw scored three tries for England during the pool stage of their 2003 World Cup campaign Balshaw started playing tennis at the age of four, but unsurprisingly also had a talent for rugby. At 13, he needed to make a choice about which sport he wanted to pursue more seriously with the prospect of a professional career looming. "When I was little, and your father is a rugby champion, of course you always want to follow in his steps and do the same journey as him," Balshaw said. "But I just felt that rugby was not going to be my sport. "Tennis, I guess, is more difficult for me than rugby because it's an individual sport, but there was a little more fire in me [playing tennis]. "That meant it was the right choice to choose tennis." Balshaw is essentially an inverted Arthur Fery - the French-born British number one who became a household name with a stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July. The pair actually met for the first time at this week's ATP 250 event in Lyon, where Balshaw beat Portuguese world number 56 Jaime Faria for his maiden win at tour level. Possessing a Roger Federer-style one-handed backhand, and a Thor-inspired hammer celebration, Balshaw announced his arrival in some style. Next week Balshaw will rise into the world's top 180, having starting the 2026 season ranked 718th. His success will also attract interest among Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) chiefs, who are desperate to increase the pool of British players at the elite level. Was Balshaw ever approached by the LTA to represent the country of his birth? And was there ever a conversation with his parents about who he should represent? "Maybe my parents are hiding stuff and I don't know, but I have never been personally contacted by the LTA," Felix said. "I think for [my parents] the most important thing is if I'm happy, they'll be happy as well." title: Fernandes to remain Man Utd captain despite outburst
description: Bruno Fernandes will remain as Manchester United captain and will not be disciplined for his post-match criticism of Michael Carrick after the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.
body: Fernandes criticised Carrick's tactics in the defeat by Como on Wednesday Bruno Fernandes will remain as Manchester United captain and will not be disciplined for his post-match criticism of Michael Carrick after the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como. The United skipper criticised Carrick's tactics for the game, then said it was up to the United head coach and his backroom team, not the players, to spot any issues and change them. It was seen by many externally as a challenge to Carrick's authority, just eight days after United defender Lisandro Martinez criticised director of football Jason Wilcox and the club's summer recruitment. Inside Old Trafford, there is sympathy for Fernandes for the position he found himself in. The Portugal midfielder did 10 post-match interviews in Como, despite being replaced by Joshua Zirkzee midway through the second half. While there is disappointment at some of his comments, it is acknowledged Fernandes' annoyance was understandable given the manner of the loss, which was one of the worst in United's European history. It remains to be seen whether Fernandes will be picked for Sunday's Premier League encounter with Bournemouth at Old Trafford. Carrick will be asked about the situation when he holds his pre-game news conference at 13:30 BST on Friday. title: Meta strikes deal to stop Mark Zuckerberg leaving California over billionaire tax
description: The Meta boss had said he would exit the state over a wealth tax that has not yet come into force.
body: Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg Meta has agreed a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to stop the Facebook co-founder from leaving California after he threatened to move from the state because of a proposed tax on billionaires. The agreement allows Zuckerberg - reportedly one of the world's richest people - to sell shares in Meta without losing control of the Californian-based company if he needs to pay a large tax bill. The measure, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on state residents with a net worth of more than $1bn (£750m), is yet to pass. Californian residents will vote on 3 November. Nevertheless, Zuckerberg secured a deal with a special committee at Meta after "robust", and "at several points, contentious" negotiations. California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group. Zuckerberg - who has a $226bn fortune according to Forbes' billionaires tracker - had told Meta's board that it was his intention to remain with the firm for "the foreseeable future". However, he said he was evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and, if he listed his home on the real estate market, it "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees". This, he told the board, "would raise questions for management of the company going forward". A special committee within Meta decided it was "critically important" to keep Zuckerberg in a leadership role and in California to manage the firm from its headquarters "during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry". Tech companies in the US and globally are spending billions of dollars on developing artificial intelligence and the infrastructure around it. Meta said the share deal was appropriate to ensure Zuckerberg "remains working closely" with the company's AI at its headquarters. It said his "talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the special committee wants that to continue". title: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
description: The attack on the unidentified victim follows a wave of anti-migrants protests in South Africa this year.
body: Anti-migrant protesters in South Africa demand that all undocumented foreign nationals leave the country A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say. According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established. The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg. Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified. 'We have to prioritise South Africans': Anti-migrant movement blocks foreigners from healthcare The uniformed group targeting foreigners in South Africa The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year. One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa. Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries. These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence. Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month. Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals. His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated. One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic. "We can't be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic," she told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme. South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals. The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce. Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence. Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities. title: BBC Inside Science
description: A Japanese spacecraft could become the first ever to bring Martian samples back to Earth.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·22 Oct 2026,·28 mins The first ever spacecraft to bring Martian samples back to Earth has launched from Japan. However, before the spacecraft returns from Phobos in 2031 there are many complex challenges that lie ahead, leaving an anxious 5 year wait for the scientists involved. To help us understand just how ambitious a feat of engineering the Mars Moons eXploration mission is Tom Whipple is joined by Naomi Murdoch, research director at ISAE-SUPAERO. What is it like to carry out scientific research when your work might lead to you being publicly cancelled or reviled? For the next few weeks, we are going to be hearing from finalists of Sense about Science’s John Maddox Prize, this week neuropsychologist Professor Sallie Baxendale discusses what it is like to continue their scientific endeavours despite being met with hostility. Plus managing editor of New Scientist Penny Sarchet brings Tom a round-up of the science news you might have missed. Produced in partnership with The Open University. Presenter: Tom Whipple Producer: Alex Mansfield, Keiran Manetta-Jones Editor: Martin Smith

title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
description: Raghad and Raad's family had to flee their home on foot because of the fighting between pro-government forces and the Houthis.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war rages From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival. They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces. When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets. What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden. The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden "It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused." As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse." By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs. Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured. Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk. The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet. More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed. The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer. Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz. The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices. The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes. Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away. Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018. "I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself." Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred. "I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]." Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space. Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing." Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut. There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment. That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor. "It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says. "We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them." A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line. Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year. Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon. "Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again." They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics. "Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital." She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them. Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the street Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood. As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there. So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation. Ad

title: UK plans emergency powers to protect undersea cables
description: Ministers are set to gain powers over telecoms companies during national security emergencies.
body: The UK has accused the Yantar, operated by Russia's Ministry of Defence, of mapping underwater infrastructure The government has outlined new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables amid increased fears of Russian interference. Ministers are set to gain powers to order telecom companies to remove or disable services during national security emergencies, as well as granting officials access to sites including cable landing stations. The government has also outlined plans for stronger criminal penalties for those convicted of tampering with either undersea internet cables or energy pipelines. The new powers would be backed up with prison sentences of up to 14 years for intentional conduct, 10 years for reckless conduct and two years for grossly negligent conduct, alongside unlimited fines. It comes amid growing fears of suspicious activity in UK waters, and concerns that legal powers over the network have not kept pace with its growing importance to national security. An extensive network of undersea cables and pipelines owned and operated primarily by the private sector are thought to carry almost all the UK's international data traffic and three-quarters of its gas supplies. The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report last year, external to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems. The UK and its Nato allies are concerned about the risk Russia poses to offshore infrastructure. In April, the government accused Russian submarines of conducting a covert operation over cables and pipelines in waters north of the UK. The UK has also accused Russia of mapping undersea infrastructure using spy ships. Last year, it revealed the Royal Navy had tracked one such suspected ship, the Yantar, after it passed near UK waters. Russia has denied the claims, and accused the UK of stirring up tensions through "anti-Russian alarmism". In a policy paper on Thursday, the government said it currently lacked emergency powers to deal with incidents affecting undersea infrastructure. It added there were currently no equivalent powers to measures that allow intervention in the water and air traffic sectors, whilst broader powers for national emergencies could prove too slow to exercise during a crisis. It is now proposing new powers that would allow it to force telecoms companies to hand over information or modify or disable services in connection with specific threats or incidents. The changes will require new legislation, to be set out after a consultation with industry closing in January. Companies that refused to comply with the orders could be fined up to £17m or 10% of global turnover. The orders would typically be published, but could be made secret on national security grounds, it added. The proposed powers are not intended to apply to companies operating energy infrastructure, although the document added that new powers in this area were being considered separately. Ministers said they hoped the new powers would apply across the "full extent" of undersea services, including outside the UK's territorial waters, which extend up to 12 nautical miles from the coast. However, the document concedes this is likely to require co-ordination with other countries, adding that the government was considering how its proposals compare to equivalent regimes internationally. It was also uncertain that existing laws on undersea infrastructure, dating from the Victorian period and designed for telegraphic cables, could be used for breaches of modern fibre-optic cables, the document added. title: Council vows support for 'Toxic Town' public inquiry
description: Martin Griffiths, Reform-UK Leader of North Northants Council, says: "We have nothing to hide."
body: The steelworks in Corby, pictured, closed in 1981 A council leader says he will support a public inquiry into contaminated land in a town, following a report published last week that revealed it could pose a risk to human health. The charity Earthwatch Europe says trained citizen scientists have found potentially harmful levels of metal or metalloid at 52 freshwater sites across Corby. Children in Corby have been born with birth defects, believed to have been caused when steelworks were demolished in the 1980s. As first reported in the NN Journal, Martin Griffiths, Reform-UK Leader of North Northamptonshire Council said: "We have nothing to hide." He added: "We would welcome a genuinely independent examination of the historic events and the questions that remain unanswered, and we would cooperate fully with any inquiry established by the government." Griffiths challenged the Labour MP for Corby and East Northamptonshire, Lee Barron, to take his longstanding calls for a public inquiry directly to the Labour government. "If Lee Barron and his Government believe a public inquiry is necessary, we are ready to support his efforts to secure one," added Griffiths. In response, Lee Barron said it was "baffling" the council would ask for a public inquiry. He said the authority needed to immediately publish a plan to investigate and clean up any contaminated land. Barron said: "It is important that North Northamptonshire Council investigate the [Earthwatch] report. "People deserve answers and it is the role of the council to provide them." Earthwatch Europe said volunteers found the chemical element cadmium in six freshwater samples in July Earlier this week, Barron wrote to both the leader of North Northamptonshire Council and the Health Secretary Yvette Cooper. In his letters, seen by the BBC, he said the findings from the environmental charity "need to be investigated as a matter of urgency". He has also called on the health secretary to "ensure North Northamptonshire Council take immediate action to clean up any contaminated land". Parents are calling for more transparency around issues they believe are causing illnesses Earlier this year, a number of families gathered outside North Northamptonshire's Corby headquarters calling for a public inquiry to clarify the situation. Des Collins, the solicitor who represented families affected by the town's toxic waste scandal, said: "We welcome the leader's announcement, which finally admits what we have been telling his council for the past year - our clients need, and deserve, a public inquiry as it is the only feasible way of getting to the truth behind the disposal of toxic waste around Corby. "We look forward to Lee Barron MP and North Northamptonshire Council working together to encourage the Cabinet Office to authorise the Inquiry without further delay. "Quite literally, local lives depend on it." The government has been approached for comment. Do you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? Contact us below. title: Four London councils challenge funding reforms
description: Three Tory and one Liberal Democrat-led councils are officially challenging government funding changes.
body: The councils' leaders say services will be hit due to funding cuts Four London council leaders have formally submitted a challenge to government reforms that are set to see their central funding slashed by up to 58%. The leaders of Wandsworth, Richmond, Westminster and Kensington and Chelsea councils delivered revised funding proposals to the Treasury on Thursday urging the government to rethink its overhaul of local authority funding rules. Among those councils, the leaders said the reforms would result in funding cuts ranging from 40% to 58% by 2029. The government said the "outdated" local authority funding model was being reformed to ensure "money goes where it is most needed". The changes, known as the Fair Funding Review 2.0, aim to shift more cash towards areas with higher deprivation. Wandsworth's Conservative administration said the reforms would cut funding by 40% and force it to slash services and raise council tax. The authority is proposing to raise council tax by 94% from April, in addition to making sweeping cuts – including shutting its cost-of-living reserve with £6.2m of unspent funds, replacing Labour's Access for All with a much smaller concessionary scheme, cancelling its Borough of Sanctuary status and suspending voluntary sector grants for four years. Kensington and Chelsea is set to lose £108m, or more than 40% of its central funding over the next four years under the reforms, while Westminster is due to see these resources drop by around £100m (46%). Richmond is set to be stripped of £26m (58%) of its core funding. The councils have now formally submitted their revised funding proposals, under the Sustainable Communities Act, asking the government to reconsider its decision. Wandsworth Council leader Robert Morritt, who heads a Conservative minority administration, said: "Residents should not have to pick up the bill for changes imposed by Whitehall. This proposal takes our case directly to government. "We are using every route available to fight for a fairer deal and protect Wandsworth taxpayers." London councils face £5bn gap by 2030, group warns Westminster council cuts 520 jobs in savings plan Mixed council verdicts on new 'fair funding' plan Lib Dem Richmond council leader Gareth Roberts said the cuts risked "pushing this council towards a financial cliff edge". He said: "We will not stand by while Whitehall forces our residents to pay the price for a deeply flawed formula." Tory Kensington and Chelsea council leader Elizabeth Campbell said: "I will use every tool at my disposal to fight these cuts, stand up for our residents and secure the fair deal our borough deserves." A Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson previously said: "We have consulted extensively on reforming the outdated council funding system to ensure money goes where it is most needed, following on from a longstanding consensus. "We're also protecting councils through transitional arrangements so no area faces a cliff edge." title: Caroline Flack's brother 'never recovered' from her death, inquest hears
description: Paul Flack was "everyone's favourite person" but this "took its toll", an inquest hears.
body: Paul Flack was Caroline's older brother. They both grew up in Norfolk The brother of TV presenter Caroline Flack took his own life having "never recovered" after his sister's death, an inquest heard. Paul Flack, 55, was found unresponsive at his home in Sandringham Road, Norwich, on 21 June, and died later in hospital. His partner told Norfolk Coroner's Court how he had struggled with his father developing dementia and his younger sister's death in 2020. Area Coroner Johanna Thompson gave a narrative conclusion, stating Paul Flack died while under the influence of alcohol and that his "intent in doing so is unknown". He was described as "everyone's favourite person" by his partner Joanna Millington, but she said this "took its toll". His sister, the ex-Love Island and X Factor host, was found dead at her home in Stoke Newington, east London, on 15 February 2020. "We then went into lockdown for Covid," said Millington, who provided a written statement to the court. "I do not think Paul ever recovered from this." An inquest later established Caroline Flack took her own life, aged 40, having feared press intrusion ahead of her trial accused of assaulting her boyfriend. Earlier, the inquest heard Paul Flack sought help for low mood from his GP in August 2020, but he did not attend follow-up appointments or counselling. The self-employed graphic designer also struggled to find work as the "industry had begun to decline", which "contributed to his sadness", his partner of 32 years said. His father Ian developed dementia in his early 70s in recent years, and died at the beginning of this year. Millington added: "[Paul] was a lovely person, he took a lot on from everyone. "There was no suggestion he would ever harm himself, he said he never would." Paul Flack died at his home in Norwich in June this year On the day of Paul Flack's death - which was Father's Day - the inquest heard he and Millington enjoyed some time together as a family. At 18:30 BST, his daughter offered him a cup of tea and a slice of cake she had made. He declined and instead went to the shop and bought four beers and spent the rest of the evening in the garden listening to music while his partner and daughter watched a film inside. Will Caroline Flack's death be a turning point? Before going to bed at about 22:20, his daughter found he was no longer in the hammock outside. She screamed when she then found him unresponsive. A neighbour attempted CPR and another neighbour called an ambulance. The coroner heard Millington told a neighbour he had been in a "bad mood all day" and that it may be because they were celebrating Father's Day so soon after his dad's death. He was pronounced dead at Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital at 23:45. A toxicology report found he had a blood alcohol level four times over the legal alcohol limit to drive. Paul Flack was born in Enfield in north London, but his family later moved to Norwich, where he lived much of his life. He had two children. No family members were present at the inquest If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this article, help is available through the BBC Action Line Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? title: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron
description: Some cities including Lyon and Nice have banned all protests, and the French president said only authorised demos would be allowed.
body: The tourism office in Lyon was set on fire during protests last weekend, the city has banned all demonstrations this Saturday Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend. Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected. Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed. Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest. France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise. Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court. Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper. Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday. "The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned." He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic". Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm. The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned. In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations. "In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the Rhône prefecture said in a statement. Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east. Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds. Unrest spread across several French cities last weekend, including the capital Paris Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests. Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction. Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests. Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the office, housed in a 19th-Century building, was "a tragedy". In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday. A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started. The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc. Following the unrest, France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez tendered his resignation, which was rejected by President Macron. The Élysée Palace asked him instead to look at how to make France's streets safer and bring rioters to justice. Nuñez said his teams had forecast 200,000 demonstrators, a figure much lower than the 550,000 estimated to have gathered. The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year. title: Weather warning in place ahead of Storm Boelo
description: A Met Office weather warning is in place from 18:00 BST on Saturday until 15:00 GMT on Sunday.
body: Coastal areas could be particularly vulnerable, with large waves and beach material potentially being thrown onto seafronts Strong winds of up to 75mph could cause disruption across parts of Northern Ireland this weekend as Storm Boelo moves in. A Met Office weather warning has been issued from 18:00 BST on Saturday until 15:00 GMT on Sunday. Strong westerly winds are expected to become widespread on Saturday evening, with very windy conditions continuing overnight and through much of Sunday. Gusts up to 60mph (96kph) are forecast widely, while coastal and exposed areas could have gusts reaching up to 75mph (120kph). The strong winds will come with heavy, blustery showers at times. Conditions are expected to gradually improve from the southwest during Sunday afternoon as the strongest winds begin to ease. In light of the warning, Causeway Coast and Glens Borough Council has cancelled its fireworks display at Ballymoney on Saturday. In statement, the council said: "We understand how disappointing this will be, but the decision has been taken with the safety of visitors, staff and event personnel as the priority." The Met Office has warned that strong winds could cause disruption to transport networks and essential services. Power cuts are possible, which could also affect mobile phone coverage and other services. There is a small risk of damage to buildings, including roof tiles being blown off, while flying debris could pose a danger to the public. Road, rail, air and ferry passengers could face longer journey times or cancellations, with some roads and bridges potentially closing. Coastal areas could be particularly vulnerable, with large waves and beach material potentially being thrown onto seafronts, coastal roads and nearby properties. The arrival of Storm Boelo comes just a day after Storm Austen is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Ireland. Storm Austen is forecast to track towards the south coast of Ireland on Thursday evening and into Friday morning, bringing the risk of flooding and travel disruption. Irish weather service Met Éireann has issued an orange rain warning - the second highest level - for six counties in the Republic of Ireland, including Cork, Dublin, Kerry, Waterford, Wexford and Wicklow. The Irish weather service has warned of possible flooding, public transport disruption and very difficult driving conditions. A nationwide yellow warning for rain and wind is also in place from 19:00 on Thursday until 10:00 on Friday. Although no weather warnings have been issued for Northern Ireland in connection with Storm Austen, widespread rain is expected on Thursday night before clearing eastwards on Friday morning. title: Civil servant who juggled five jobs 'wasn't thinking straight', court hears
description: Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently juggling multiple public sector jobs.
body: Kashim Chowdhury wears dark sunglasses, a hat, hoody and gloves as he arrives at court. His face is largely obscured. A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple public sector jobs has told the court he "wasn't thinking straight" when he allegedly misled future bosses about his employment status. Kashim Chowdhury said he was "in a panic" when he applied for a job at the Department of Health (DHSC), failing to declare he was already working at the Department for the Environment (Defra). The prosecution said he already had three full-time jobs at the time, including roles at the London Borough of Tower Hamlets and East London NHS Trust. The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. Chowdhury said he was "in a panic'' because he feared losing his Defra job and was uncertain about his future. He told the jury he was "not paying attention, I was not thinking straight',' when filling out the application. The prosecution said Chowdhury held five jobs on full-time salaries at the height of the alleged deceit. Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023. Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work-from-home culture which began during the Covid-19 pandemic to hide his multiple jobs and took sick leave from some employers to manage the workload. But Chowdhury told the court he had not wanted the jobs at the DHSC, Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. He told the jury: ''I sent out a flurry of these applications. The offers for these jobs came all at once. I had discussions with my line managers saying that I did not want these jobs and explained my circumstances. These were all short term and probationary and my priority was to look after my mother.'' He added that around May and June 2022, his mother's health "deteriorated". He said: "That overwhelmed me at the time. It just destroyed me." Chowdhury described the jobs as his "lifeline at the time". "They gave me a link to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time." The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity". title: Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Badenoch
description: The Tory leader calls for more support for police officers and the public when they step in to help.
body: Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch speaking at the Police Federation conference in London Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised punishments for people who intervene to "do the right thing" in a speech at the Police Federation conference. Telling delegates she was "not scared to wade in", she called for more support for members of the public as well as police officers who step in to stop wrongdoing. Badenoch also criticised Labour for failing to send a minister to the conference for two years in a row. The prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman rejected the claims, stating the police have the government's "full backing" and are benefitting from investment. The BBC has contacted the Home Office for comment on ministerial attendance at the police conference. In a speech at the conference, Badenoch said: "Too often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service. "Whether it's hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they're in trouble themselves. "It's no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police." The Conservative leader listed police officers who have been killed in the line of duty, such as PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough who died in the Cleveland A66 crash, and PC Andrew Harper, killed investigating a quad bike theft. She also attacked police being investigated following controversial cases, including the case of 24-year-old Chris Kaba, who was shot by Sgt Matthew Blake in 2022 after he tried to ram his way past police cars. The police officer was put on trial for murder before being cleared, with Badenoch saying his "job was made harder because he didn't get the backing he deserved". Badenoch also attacked Labour, saying: "I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour Government has not sent anyone to address this conference – not the policing minister, not the Home Secretary. "You are the ones who enforce the law. You are the ones who ensure there are consequences for bad behaviour. That's why, if we want law and order back in our country, back on our streets, we need to back the police." Responding, the prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman said: "I would reject those claims. "The police have the government's full backing and as you will have seen from various reports this morning, we are continuing to invest in our police and we are bringing forward reforms following the Bernard Hogan Howe report in due course." The Home Office has been contacted for comment about ministerial attendance at the conference and whether the government is still planning to recruit 13,000 police officers. title: Tommy Robinson hired detectives to find journalists, court told
description: The political activist cries in court while on trial accused of harassing Daily Mail journalists.
body: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, has been giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court Political activist Tommy Robinson has told a court he hired private detectives to track down and photograph two reporters to "put pressure" on them. The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, told Southwark Crown Court he was "shocked and scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed". He has denied two charges of harassment causing fear of violence to reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after the 2024 Southport attacks. Robinson is accused of writing posts on X, sending direct messages and making phone calls that made the two journalists fear the risk of vigilante attacks. He denied wanting to expose the journalists to threats of violence, and said he felt his actions were "totally reasonable... under the circumstances". Robinson wiped tears from his eyes as he gave evidence in the dock about events in August 2024 In early August 2024, he was on holiday at the Atlantica Mare resort in Cyprus, as riots took place in England following the murders of three girls in Southport. Robinson was on holiday with "my ex-wife, my three children and three other families and their children", he told the jury. He said he had managed to keep her and children out of sight "for 17 years -and that meant travelling in separate cars". In the witness stand, he claimed he had not "stoked" the riots, but tried to "calm" things. When the Daily Mail published an article online, he said he was "shocked". "I'm scared because the Mail Online is the biggest publication in the world." He said the original article allowed people to quickly work out where he was holidaying, and included an image of his wife. He panicked, thinking it would "change her life forever", he said. Robinson struggled to answer a question about how his children were affected by the story, as he took tissues and wiped tears from his eyes. He replied that he left the hotel after the story was published, and that his family moved to a different location within the hotel following advice from security. Robinson told the jury his 12-year-old daughter had received rape threats, and his ex-wife had previously been threatened with an acid attack. He said he tried to call the editor-in-chief of the Daily Mail, but he would not answer. "They could have run the story without giving my location," he said. "They shouldn't have done that and this is not journalism, this is endangering us." Tommy Robinson denies the charges of harassment causing fear of violence against two Daily Mail journalists The court heard how Robinson used private investigators to obtain telephone numbers and emails for the journalists. He phoned Andrew Young, the Daily Mail reporter who had tracked him down in Cyprus. "I wanted my ex-wife's picture removed from the publication," he said. "I said: 'You're not going to get away from this problem...You've endangered my children'." He told jurors he wanted to "find the journalists" and ask them "on camera" to explain how he was "stoking race riots". Robinson said he had asked the private investigators to try to get pictures of the journalists and their family members. Young said he had to use private security after the defendant posted pictures on X of his wife and daughter near their home, with their faces cropped off. And Dirnhuber said in a statement read to the jury that he left his home for a week after Robinson published a picture of him outside his house on X. He said he feared the risk of a "vigilante attack". Under cross examination from prosecutor Ben Holt, Robinson said he did not publish details of their exact address or images that showed the journalists' family members' faces. He said he was trying to "bring the Daily Mail to the table" and did not know the reporters were "in fear". "That wasn't my intention at all," he said. Holt responded: "They're scared of you Mr Lennon." "They're not scared of physical violence, they're scared of humiliation," Robinson replied. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks?
