title: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
description: After two years of student protests, Serbians vote on Sunday in elections that could bring down the ruling party.
body: Young Serbians have been the driving force behind the movement, but none of the candidates are students Rallies have been taking place across Serbia on Thursday, the final day of campaigning ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future. After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power. The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote. They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia. The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable." It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people. The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project. The canopy over the front of the station in Novi Sad collapsed without warning on 1 November 2024 What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges. The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by Vučić, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums. At the last election in 2023, Vučić's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties. Anger lingers in Serbia after train station tragedy Vučić has been prime minister or president since 2014, and was deputy prime minister for two years before that Vučić has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017. The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities. Vučić has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladić, prompting EU anger at his "glorification". Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is Vučić's biggest challenge since he came to power. "He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President Vučić isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade. Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation. Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday. There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for. Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote. Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List. Ilija Srdanović (in yellow) tops the list of Student List candidates Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists. They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija Srdanović is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir Stanić and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić. Under an 11-point programme, external, the student movement wants to: eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media. European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere". Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned of a campaign that has seen threats and physical violence, external, and opposition activists subjected to surveillance. title: Big Brother fans still not happy as housemate called out on behaviour
description: Ofcom received thousands of complaints related to Omar El Mayer's behaviour in the Big Brother house.
body: Big Brother contestants Omar El Mayer and Rhianna Collins have had a turbulent romance in the house A Big Brother housemate who prompted more than 7,000 complaints has been spoken to about his on-screen behaviour - but some fans say the show's not doing enough. Viewers and women's safety charities had been calling on ITV to intervene in Omar El Mayer and Rhianna Collins' relationship after several heated exchanges between the pair. He was called into Big Brother's Diary Room during Wednesday's episode and told his language and behaviour "could cause offence". He denied dismissing Rhianna's feelings. ITV has been contacted for comment. The broadcaster previously said "welfare and safeguarding are prioritised throughout the production". Big Brother contestants live together for 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with almost everything they do captured on camera. The popular reality show format sees divides form and tensions build as housemates try to avoid being eliminated in weekly votes. Collins and El Mayer struck up a relationship after entering the Big Brother house but concerns about his alleged "toxic" behaviour had grown among fans. Monday's episode, which showed a heated exchange between the pair, generated 7,138 complaints, according to broadcast watchdog Ofcom. Viewers saw Collins break off the relationship before being called to the Diary Room, where she told Big Brother she and El Mayer "have not been good over the last few days". "Sometimes I don't like the way he speaks to me." Later, Collins was seen telling El Mayer she didn't want to argue, to which he replied: "Then don't say mad things that you don't mean. It's not fair... sort it out, get it together." Both Women's Aid and Refuge allege the 21-year-old behaviour towards Collins is concerning and say ITV should do more to protect contestants. Following the backlash, EL Mayer was called to the Diary Room during Wednesday's episode. Big Brother told him: "At times it appears that you are dismissing your fellow housemates' feelings and experiences". "Some of the language used on more than one occasion and the behaviour you have exhibited could cause offence to your housemates or the viewing public." El Mayer said he "fully understood" the allegations but denied dismissing Collins' feelings. He said he would challenge people if he disagreed with them, but said he did not believe he had told anyone they weren't entitled to feel however they wanted to. "Let's be honest here, we're not just talking about housemates, we're talking about my conversations with me and Rhianna," he continued. He said he'd "done nothing but look out for her" and "didn't walk in with any bad intentions or any malice". "I've acknowledged my housemate's feelings." Fans were quick to complain on social media, saying Big Brother should have been firmer and El Mayer should have received a formal warning for his behaviour. One viewer described it as "a soft talking to" but another said Big Brother made "it clear that his behaviour has not gone unnoticed". Ofcom said it was assessing the complaints and had not yet decided whether to investigate. A spokesperson for ITV said earlier this week that housemates receive "respect and inclusion training" and an "extensive briefing" from the show's team on how to prepare for living in the house and to "set out Big Brother's expectations for appropriate behaviour and language". They said housemates are monitored 24 hours a day and "any instances of inappropriate behaviour are responded to appropriately". A welfare team is also available to support housemates, the statement added. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: Mystery of man found dead in wetsuit deepens as inquest questions ethnicity
description: An international appeal was launched after the man's body was discovered in a reservoir two years ago.
body: Specialists used photographs, dental records and CT scans to digitally recreate the man's face An unidentified man whose body was discovered in a reservoir in mid Wales two years ago may not have been of white ethnicity as previously thought, an inquest heard. The body of the man, who was wearing an open water swimming wetsuit, was found by a dogwalker at the Claerwen Reservoir near Rhayader, Powys, in October 2024. Despite a major international police appeal and the use of ground-breaking facial reimaging techniques, his identity and the cause of his death remain a mystery. Coroner Patricia Morgan told detectives to analyse a liver sample given to the police two years ago which was never tested, adding she wanted to explore "this further line of inquiry" before reaching a conclusion. The inquest heard the man's remains could have been in the water for more than three months before they were found. Claerwen Reservoir is in a remote location Tests could determine if he had died before or after he entered the water. It also emerged that although the force ran the man's DNA through police databases, they did not use commercial DNA sites which are commonly used by people investigating their family history and trying to make connections with long-lost relations. Det Insp Anthea Ponting told the inquest via videolink that the force considered using such sites at the time but was told it could involve significant resources. "We were advised we could have results into the thousands. The NCA (National Crime Agency) said they could filter them," she said. The Claerwen Reservoir in mid Wales helps provide drinking water to Birmingham and the West Midlands "But it could still lead to a large number of results and a large number of officer hours to work through," Ponting said. "We wanted to get an ID as soon as possible. We felt that facial recognition might trigger a more far-reaching response." Initial enquiries gave officers a general idea of the man's age, height and build as between 30 and 60 years old, around 6ft (1.83m), weighing between 202lbs and 220lbs (91.5kg to 99.5kg), and of white European descent. Police have put out an appeal for information about a man found dead in Claerwen Reservoir wearing a wetsuit usually used by triathletes and open water swimmers But in written evidence, forensic orthodontist Dr Sally Andrew said from her examination of his teeth and jaw her finding was that the man "may not have been of white ethnicity". The hearing was also told an examination of a tag on the wetsuit found marks which could possibly have been a name, but scientific support officers were unable to enhance those marks. The inquest was adjourned until the test on the liver sample has been carried out. title: Teacher in Oregon shooting said she pretended to be dead to survive
description: The teacher said she could not help children because she was badly injured by the attacker.
body: This video can not be played Watch: "It's really hard to believe" - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded Some readers may find this article distressing. A 54-year-old teacher who survived a mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school said she pretended to be dead so the gunman would not shoot her again. Becky Drury, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, said in a statement shared with US media that as she tried to shut her classroom door, the gunman shot her and she fell to the floor. "I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again," Drury said. The attacker - who has been identified as a 16-year-old former student at the school - killed three students and a teacher before a parent from the school fatally shot him. In her first remarks since the 15 October shooting in Bend, Oregon, Drury said that she went to see what was happening outside the special-education classroom, and after spotting the shooter, she tried to shut the door. The attacker still managed to shoot her, so she could not help any of the children in the classroom. "Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she said. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else." Drury suffered serious but not life-threatening harm from the shooting, which killed five-year-old Rhoam Summer, an eight and eleven-year-old, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert. Police have said another teacher - who has not been named - attempted to disarm the gunman by throwing her mobile phone. She was not injured. A father of two other children who had followed the suspect into the school then shot and killed the attacker, who officials named as Griffin J John II. Reports had emerged that another teacher threw herself on top of a student to protect the child during the shooting, but Drury said she wanted to clear the record about what happened on 15 October. "I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she said in her statement. Police have not yet shared a motive for the suspect, who officials say was a special-education needs student at Silver Rail. Drury said what happened in the classroom was "unimaginable". "[L]ike so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy," she said. title: YouTuber arrested after popular Indian finance influencer's suicide
description: V Harish, who ran the hugely popular Instagram account "Finance with Harish", was found dead on Tuesday.
body: V Harish ran a hugely popular Instagram handle called "Finance with Harish" A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give financial advice to investors. V Harish - who ran a hugely popular Instagram account called "Finance with Harish" - was found dead on Tuesday morning at his home near Chennai, capital of the southern state of Tamil Nadu. His suicide came just weeks after his account was disabled by Meta after complaints of irregularities. In a complaint lodged with the police, his father J Vinayagam has alleged that his son took his life because of online harassment by Jason Samuel, a YouTuber and CEO of tech-centric venture studio Zemuria. Police arrested Samuel on Thursday under suspicion of trying to "extort money from Harish" and posting "defamatory videos against him on social media". BBC Tamil has not been able to reach him for comment. Earlier, he denied wrongdoing in a post on X. The case has brought into focus the growing influence of financial content creators in India, where millions of first-time investors increasingly turn to social media for market advice. Harish began posting videos about finance and investing around five years ago, building a substantial online following. Over the years, he published more than 1,500 videos and amassed more than 1.3 million Instagram followers. He described himself as a financial adviser to "millionaires" and "high-net-worth individuals". He often used music, film clips and photos of global political leaders to make dramatic videos while talking about the rise and fall of the share market and prices of gold and silver. The videos, which broke down financial issues in simple terms, became hugely popular as they coincided with a rapid expansion in India's retail investor base, especially since the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic. The country's largest stock exchange, the National Stock Exchange, said earlier this year it now had more than 130 million unique investors registered with it as opposed to under 30 million in 2019. But in September, Meta took down Harish's Instagram page after receiving complaints he was not registered with Indian market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) - which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios. A back-up account, which gained over 60,000 followers in a short time, was also subsequently taken down, external following complaints from social media users and others. A few other accounts in his name remain on Instagram, though with much smaller followings - and it's not clear who runs them. According to Harish's friends and family, he recorded a video message before his death in which he said that "five years of hard work has been stolen" from him, news channel NDTV reported, external. The video, which has also been shared widely on social media, shows him speaking in Tamil and then switching to English to say "I'm very sorry" to his parents, sister, friends and followers. Meta took down Harish's account after complaints that he was not registered with Sebi, which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios. Police say Harish's father J Vinayagam has blamed "cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his channels" for his son's suicide and named Jason Samuel in his complaint registered at Kanathur police station near Chennai. Samuel had posted a video on his YouTube channel on 18 October questioning Harish's credentials since he did not have Sebi or Amfi (Association of Mutual Funds in India) registrations. In it, he mentioned that Harish's Instagram account had been disabled following complaints. This, Vinayagam says, triggered severe online harassment and led to pressures that drove his son to take his own life. "We demand that a proper investigation be conducted and legal action be taken against Jason Samuel and his accomplices, who spread defamation on social media and caused mental distress through cyberbullying," his complaint states. A police statement says Vinayagam's complaint was registered under "abetment to suicide" and preliminary investigations found Samuel had a "role in this case". "[Samuel] will be produced before court and sent to judicial custody," it says. Samuel has defended the video in which he flagged Harish's lack of credentials saying he was acting in the consumer interest. In a statement on X, Samuel said he was "deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life". He however, rejected allegations of "cyber-bullying" Harish. "I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of licence and authority, misrepresentation of licence and fraud... his illegal activity. "I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper Sebi licence. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss," he wrote. If you're having thoughts of suicide, or know someone that might be, you can find support lines in India via the AASRA website, external or globally via Befrienders Worldwide, external. In the UK you can call the Samaritans Helpline on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org, external. title: Prime Minister swaps dispatch box for Gogglebox
description: Andy Burnham is taking part in a Stand Up To Cancer Gogglebox special with his friend Steve Rotheram.
body: Andy Burnham is joined by Liverpool City Region mayor Steve Rotheram on the show Andy Burnham is to appear in a special edition of Channel 4 hit show Gogglebox. The prime minister will be joined by Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram for a celebrity edition of the programme in support of Stand Up To Cancer, the campaign the broadcaster runs with charity Cancer Research UK. Rotheram said he was a huge supporter of the cause, but had also agreed to take part because he did not want his friend to end up looking like "Billy No-Mates" on the Downing Street sofa alone. The special Gogglebox edition airs on Channel 4 at 21:05 BST on Friday. The long-running TV series, narrated by The Royle Family's Craig Cash, has viewers watching other viewers watching the week's telly, often to comic and heartwarming effect. The celebrity version of the show has previously featured the likes of musician Ed Sheeran, actress Joanna Lumley and presenter Maya Jama. New faces join Channel 4's Gogglebox line-up Gogglebox is a gift Caroline left me, Cash says Appearing on the edition with the prime minister will be comedian Joe Lycett and Sugababes singers Mutya Buena, Keisha Buchanan and Siobhan Donaghy. A Channel 4 spokesperson said nothing would be "off limits as Gogglebox continues to celebrate the simple joy of watching television together". "They'll be sharing hilarious, honest and often unexpected reactions to the week's biggest television moments as well as poignant stories all in aid of Stand Up To Cancer," they added. Burnham and Rotheram have been friends for many years, serving together as Labour MPs before they both left Parliament to become regional mayors in 2017. They remained close allies, writing a book together on their vision for Britain's future, and Rotheram was a visible supporter of Burnham's successful campaign to become the MP for Makerfield in June. The Liverpool City Region mayor said while filming their contributions, he and Burnham had struggled with one particularly cerebral TV quiz show and found themselves flummoxed by its music round. "We're both big into our music but we couldn't get it," he said. He added that while their television tastes were largely similar, he and the prime minister disagreed over what snacks to eat while watching. "I'm more of a cheesy puffs-type guy, but he's more into the hard, crunchy stuff," he said. title: Katie Price's ex not guilty of raping girl, 13
description: Kieran Hayler had denied rape, sexual assault and sexual activity with a child at his trial.
body: Kieran Hayler has been acquitted of raping a 13-year-old girl Katie Price's ex-husband, Kieran Hayler, has been found not guilty of raping a 13-year-old girl. Hayler, 39, has been on trial accused of rape and sexual assault against the girl in West Sussex in 2016, when he was married to the media personality. In total he was acquitted of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault at Lewes Crown Court. Hayler had also faced four alternative counts of sexual activity with a child, for which he was also found not guilty. In a statement outside court, Hayler thanked the jury, as well as his friends and family "who have stood by me for five years of absolute hell". He added: "I would like to be left in peace now to rebuild my life and spend time with my family." He had denied the allegations, telling the jury that he believed them to be fabricated. Price and Hayler separated in 2018, and later divorced in 2021. Hayler had told the court that Price had "launched a campaign" against him after their marriage broke down, and that the allegations formed part of it. Katie Price arriving at Lewes Crown Court during the trial He told the trial that "trust had gone on both sides" of his marriage to Price by mid-2013, and he admitted affairs with three other women during their relationship. Giving evidence, Price denied being "angry and vengeful" towards her ex-husband. It can now be reported that Hayler's lawyers had applied for the jury to be discharged after Price's first day of evidence. It was argued that some of Price's testimony had resulted in an "overwhelming tsunami of prejudice" and was a "premeditated attempt to bring down this trial". Judge Mark van der Zwart dismissed the legal bid but warned the jury to disregard a portion of the testimony. He described Price as "what barristers of a previous generation would have called a dangerous witness", with a personal agenda in proceedings, and who was "liable to say something prejudicial given half a chance". The jury, made up of four men and six women, acquitted Hayler after 14 hours and 55 minutes of deliberations. Hayler was emotional and bent over as he was discharged and told he could leave the dock. title: Ten councillors quit after leader's fraud conviction
description: Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of defrauding the county council out of thousands of pounds.
body: Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion Ten Ashfield Independent councillors have quit the party this week following the former leader's fraud conviction. Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion last month He resigned as leader of Ashfield District Council the following day, but was later given a seat on the authority's planning committee. As of Thursday, 13 councillors are sitting as non-aligned independents, while 18 Ashfield Independents remain, meaning the party is one councillor away from losing its majority. Zadrozny was accused of setting up a fake heritage group to defraud Nottinghamshire County Council out of thousands of pounds. Prosecutors also alleged that he had failed to pay tax on four rental properties. The 46-year-old, who served as an Ashfield Independents councillor on the county council, was told by the judge he would be sentenced on 27 November, and was "at risk of an immediate custodial sentence". The Ashfield Independents now have a majority of one Councillors Warren Nuttall and Kier Barsby had quit the Ashfield Independents group prior to this week. One of the 10 members to quit this week is John Wilmott, a cabinet member who is also a Nottinghamshire county councillor for Hucknall North. Another is the chairman of the council, Dale Grounds. Councillor Matt Relf, executive lead member for growth, regeneration and local planning, said quitting the party was an "enormously upsetting" decision. "The understandable controversy around Jason's conviction and the choices he made that led to that have upset and surprised a lot of people in the group," he said. "With the election of a new leader we hoped that would put everything behind us, but unfortunately the decision to appoint Jason back on to the planning committee was just a step too far. "That decision was made with no consultation with the broader group. "To stay true to our principles of integrity and democratic accountability I was left with no option but to leave, and I think others have reached the same conclusion." Hucknall Central councillor Lee Waters, who was another one of the councillors to quit this week, said his decision "follows a period of reflection, and I believe the time is right to move on". "Throughout my time as a councillor, my priority has been to listen to residents, address their concerns and work hard on the issues that matter to our community. That remains unchanged," he added. "I will continue carrying out my council responsibilities and dealing with ongoing casework with the same commitment and dedication as always." Lee Anderson, the MP for Ashfield, posted on Facebook to warn that former Ashfield Independent councillors would not be accepted into Reform UK. He said there would be "no deals" between the parties. Samantha Deakin has taken over as leader of the council, but has so far declined the BBC's request for an interview. Fiona Fillingham attended the demonstration on Thursday A demonstration was held outside the council house on Thursday in protest at Zadrozny being able to remain as a council. Protesters told the BBC they had been "let down" by the authority. John Green, of the Ashfield Community Action Group, said: "We are disgusted that the Ashfield Independents have voted a convicted fraudster onto the planning a committee." Tim Curtis, who also attended the demonstration, said: "There's no mechanism to get him out. He should stand down from the council and not be anywhere near making any decisions." Fiona Fillingham, a local business owner, added: "If I got done for fraud I am sure I wouldn't get my job back. "It seems backhanded, shoddy, unfair and unrealistic. They can't keep getting away with it." title: Michael Carrick carrying on but senior Man Utd figures concerned by poor performances
description: While head coach Michael Carrick is expected to be in charge for Sunday's match against Bournemouth, Manchester United begin the process of identifying possible replacements.
body: Michael Carrick apologises to Manchester United's 700 travelling fans after the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como Michael Carrick is set to remain in charge of Manchester United for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth, but senior figures are concerned about performances and results. Carrick is said to be carrying on as normal and has not been made aware of any imminent change following Wednesday's humiliating 4-1 defeat by Italian side Como. But some at Old Trafford believe the squad should be doing much better, with one source telling BBC Sport: "We need to work hard to get through it." Another accepted the level of current injuries "doesn't help, but no excuse", claiming effort levels were "concerning". "We have a Champions League squad and need to be playing at that level," the source said. Despite concern at the performances, some in the United hierachy are of the view chopping and changing mangers so regularly in recent years has failed to arrest United's decline, and Carrick has been let down by players who are under-performing. While club sources say Carrick will remain in charge for Sunday's match, United have already begun the process of identifying possible replacements. Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Nagelsmann are understood to have their eyes on the Old Trafford job. After Wednesday's match - United's seventh in a row without a win - captain Bruno Fernandes questioned Carrick's tactics. The players were given Thursday off but will be back at Carrington on Friday when Carrick will hold his news conference to preview the Bournemouth match at 1330 BST. While there remains major uncertainty over Carrick future, there is also an appreciation in some quarters of the progress he and his squad made last season, and a view he should be given more time to turn things around. For weeks, managers - in and out of work - have grown aware the United job may become available. Howe, for example, is available and would be considered. Sources have indicated the former Newcastle boss is open to returning to management with United after leaving St James' Park in the close season. Former Chelsea boss Conte and ex-Germany manager Naglesmann, who are also out of work, are also interested. Aston Villa head coach Unai Emery and Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler's stock is high with those in the corridors of power at United - but extracting them from their respective clubs would be difficult. 'Not what a captain should be' - the debate around Fernandes' outburst Breaking down Man Utd's tactics after Fernandes' criticism Man Utd humbling by Como leaves Carrick job in danger For the third year in a row, United have publicly and financially backed a manager in the summer, but positive results have not followed. Ruben Amorim staggered on to January, but the shock League Cup defeat at League Two side Grimsby last August and the awful performance at Brentford less than a month later stripped away his safety net and gave United's hierarchy nowhere to go when he attacked their influence. United looked extensively at other candidates, including Thomas Tuchel and Roberto de Zerbi, in the summer of 2024 before deciding to stick with Erik ten Hag. The Dutchman was dismissed in the October. There were dissenting voices when he was appointed on a permanent basis in May, but the majority of supporters felt 12 wins from 17 in interim charge and a place in the Champions League after a two-year absence meant the 45-year-old former United midfielder deserved a crack at the job. But, as ever, results shape everything. There are numerous reasons behind the club's poor form this season and blame can be apportioned across a variety of departments and to the very top of the club. However, the brutal truth is two wins from 11 games, and none in seven, their worst run since 2015-16 when eight matches without a win took Louis van Gaal to the brink of dismissal, is simply not good enough. And as head coach, Carrick bears significant responsibility for that. Accusations of a lack of passion, desire and intensity have dogged United all season, having won just two of their matches in all competitions. The team have also been hampered by injuries and players failing to reach the level anticipated. While they have struggled in attack, they have also only kept a single clean sheet all season as form, results and confidence have all dipped. Mixed into that negativity has come explosive post-match comments from experienced defender Lisandro Martinez, attacking the recruitment, and Fernandes, attacking Carrick and his tactics. In between was the interview in the Athletic with Ten Hag when he spoke of 'broken promises' and a 'toxic culture'. It all smacks of a club lacking control, discipline and a clear forward-looking strategy. There is certainly a view from senior figures around the club that while overall recruitment can be questioned - specifically strengthening midfield in the summer at the expense of bringing in striking support for Benjamin Sesko or competition at left-back - the players have to take a significant amount of responsibility. Whether that helps Carrick is another matter. The proximity of United's next Premier League game does not make immediate change straightforward, even if that was the thinking. Following Amorim's dismissal in January, former United midfielder Darren Fletcher took over as interim manager for two games. Fletcher subsequently returned to his role as Under-18 coach, but two of the coaches who helped him, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, stayed with the senior set-up as part of Carrick's team. United have a clear midweek coming up following their EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, who came back from two down to win at Old Trafford last month. That, in theory, would allow time to take stock without the immediate pressure a match can bring. Bournemouth secured their firs

title: Tank barrel production returns to UK after 20 years
description: The defence secretary says the UK is "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces.
body: Rheinmetall said the facility had created 100 jobs and it would look to expand its workforce in the future The production of gun barrels to be used on tanks has returned to the UK for the first time in 20 years with the opening of a new manufacturing facility. The UK Gun Hall in Telford, run by German defence firm Rheinmetall, has supported 100 jobs and will make barrels and breaches for large calibre weapons. Defence secretary, Wes Streeting, attended the opening ceremony on Thursday and said Britain was "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces. "From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action," he said. "One hundred skilled jobs in world class manufacturing and the return of large calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in 20 years - this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like," Streeting added. The barrels and breaches will be made for both 120m and 155mm weapon systems, including for the RCH 155 and future artillery platforms, according to Rheinmetall. The firm is already involved in the UK's Boxer combat vehicle programme and is upgrading the country's Challenger tanks. Wes Streeting said the opening of the facility would be a boost to Britain's defence capabilities Specialist workers from Telford have been recruited and the firm said it would expand its workforce as production ramped up. Ahead of the factory's opening, staff spent time at a Rheinmetall facility in Germany where they were trained in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production. Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall, said the gun hall was an "important milestone" that would strengthen the country's industrial base "for decades to come". "We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future," he added. Papperger told BBC Radio Shropshire it was a significant investment in Telford, adding that the firm only had one similar production line in Germany. "At the moment, we have a lot of orders and we need the capacity. Telford has very well-educated people, highly-motivated people," he added. Papperger said the company currently had 1,300 employees in the UK but was looking to build up that number. During his speech at the event, Streeting described Telford as being "synonymous with engineering and manufacturing". "Today is a vote of confidence in our country," he continued, "a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country." title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
description: The congresswoman said federal agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of a federal investigation.
body: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid. "With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MS NOW, external. In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation. The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation". The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya. More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized. Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS NOW, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out." Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed. "We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre". The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way". Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one. She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s. The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS. Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating. Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies". Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling". Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia. He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me". At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster." The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it". "You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported." title: Activists celebrate as land given protected status
description: Volunteers say they have been campaigning for 30 years to keep a wild space free from development.
body: The Harding's Pits Community Association Group campaigned for three decades to keep it as a wild leisure space Campaigners who have been trying to stop the development of a town's green space have celebrated it being given "village green status" by a council. Harding's Pits, seven acres of land beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, had previously been earmarked for a housing development and a supermarket before the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk applied to Norfolk County Council for the status. The Harding's Pits Community Association Group has campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as a leisure space. Rick Morrish, 64, the director of the group, said it was a "really great decision... we've struggled to get the village green status for 30 years". The application was considered by Norfolk County Council's Planning (Regulatory) Committee on Tuesday. Morrish told Chris Goreham on BBC Radio Norfolk that "this year's administration got right behind" the cause and it would "give more legal status to protect the site... we're safeguarding it as a public open space". Alexandra Kemp and campaigners have been working together to attain protected status for the area Alexandra Kemp, an Independent councillor at the borough council, said she has held nine public events in favour of keeping Harding's Pits as a space for nature. "After the long campaign that we fought since 2017 with residents to stop the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk putting traffic on Harding's Way, the borough council's support is very important and now protects all of Harding's Pits west of Harding's Way," she said. Kemp also campaigned with residents in July against a new car park that the borough council sought to build next to Harding's Pits. Visitors can see a whale sculpture in one section of Harding's Pits Morrish said the Harding's Pits Association Group was formed in 2004, adding that the green space was originally a clay pit in the 19th Century, before being used as a landfill site. "There is actually rubbish underneath the site," he added. Harding's Pits was then turned into a public space in the early 1960s. The Harding's Pits is located alongside the River Great Ouse and has cut through routes to King's Lynn town centre The site is currently used for dog walking, accessing King's Lynn town centre, picking fruit such as blackberries and for bird and wildlife spotting, Morrish said. He told the BBC that "a hundred species of birds" had been recorded there and it was home to "three or four regular reptile residents, including a lot of lizards" who had enjoyed the warm temperatures this year. "Within the town, this is quite a rare asset to have and that's why we think it's so important," he added. He said the site has grown over the years, with a new community orchard and a national art project, where artists have planted a circle of oak trees. Michael de Whalley said the village green status is very welcome news for South Lynn Michael de Whalley, the cabinet member for climate change and biodiversity on Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk, said: "This is very welcome news for South Lynn and an important final step in a journey that the community has been pursuing for at least 30 years." He added that local people valued and enjoyed places such as Harding's Pits and surrounding green spaces, where habitats could flourish. Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. title: The Briefing Room
description: After mass protests and violence, what will persuade the French to accept economic reform?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·22 Oct 2026,·28 mins Available for over a year Will the French accept that changes need to be made to fix their ailing economy? Political paralysis and a debt crisis has led to 5 prime ministers in the last two years. Every attempt at fixing the economic problems is met with outrage and protest. Saturday 17th October 2026 saw some of the worst protests in years, with peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living and school funding descending into an 'apocalyptic hell'. 500 police officers were injured in the violence, 1,500 shops were damaged and an historic 19th century city hall was burnt to the ground in the mass disorder that ensued. But there are some serious economic issues that must be faced head on. France's borrowing costs have just hit a 26 year high, signalling they are not trusted to manage their growing debt. Public spending in France is higher than in many other European countries and a big part of that bill is pensions. Raising the pension age would save the state much needed money but proposals to do so were met with outrage and put on hold. So, has France become ungovernable? Guests: Sophie Pedder, Paris bureau chief, The Economist Victor Mallet, Financial Times, author of Far-Right France: Le Pen, Bardella and the Future of Europe Agnes Poiriet, UK editor, L'Express Producers: Ben Carter, Phoebe Keane, Kirsteen Knight

title: Former Scotland rugby international to go on trial charged with rape
description: Tim Visser is accused of controlling and abusive behaviour against a woman over a a 14-year period in Edinburgh and elsewhere.
body: A hearing took place at the High Court in Glasgow A former Scotland rugby international is to go on trial accused of controlling, abusing and raping a woman. The charges against Tim Visser span a 14-year period and are alleged to have happened in Edinburgh and elsewhere between 2010 and 2024. Two of the four charges state that the 39 year-old, who has been capped 33 times by Scotland, raped the woman on various occasions. These include claims he had sex with her after consent had been withdrawn. A separate charge alleges that the ex-Newcastle Falcons, Edinburgh and Harlequins player repeatedly behaved in a threatening and abusive manner towards the woman. Among the accusations are that Visser "took intimate images" of her without her consent. He was said to have been aggressive, sent her unwanted calls and texts, demanded to know where she was and controlled her appearance, finances and what she wore and ate. Prosecutors further claim Visser, from Milton Bridge, Midlothian, isolated the woman from family and friends and was physically violent. A fourth charge says he engaged in a course of abusive behaviour against the woman on various occasions. The accusation lists a total of 26 different claims. A number of them are similar to the threatening behaviour allegation, but also include a string of sexual matters. One is that he sent an intimate image of the woman to someone else. The indictment goes on to state that the prosecution may present evidence about other matters dating back to 2004, but these are not formal charges at this stage. They feature claims of physical and sexual incidents, threats and controlling behaviour. At the High Court in Glasgow, Ian Duguid, defending, said: "It is a plea of not guilty to the indictment." A trial was set for 12 January 2028 in Edinburgh. The ex-rugby star was born in the Netherlands, but opted not to play for his home nation. Instead he represented Scotland as a winger between 2012 and 2017 before he retired from the sport two years later. title: AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened
description: The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy explains how it happened, and what it means for you.
body: This video can not be played Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers. Developers of the PHP platform - which powers more than 70% of websites, including Wikipedia and digital shopping sites - rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. Cyber-security firm Wiz described the issue as the "most severe" ever detected, while OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". But how did AI discover a massive cyber-security risk in the internet, and what does it mean for you? The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy reports. Read more on the cyber-security threat here. title: Grandparent hugging consent ad pulled after criticism
description: Jim O'Callaghan described the video as "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents".
body: The ad depicts two grandparents enthusiastically hugging a young boy The Irish minister for justice has criticised an advertisement produced by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) promoting consent, calling it "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents". The ad depicts two grandparents enthusiastically hugging a young boy, but when they approach their granddaughter she appears unhappy about the exchange. It includes the message "not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them". The ad, which has since been removed, has attracted criticism and and also received international coverage in publications such as the New York Post. Fianna Fáil politician Jim O'Callaghan, whose department funds the campaign, said the the video has since been removed following engagement with the DRCC. He said the video "does not represent the views of the Government". "It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them. "While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive." The video was part of a campaign titled 'We-Consent', which is led by the DRCC. In a statement to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, the DRCC said: "We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland. "We created three videos premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too. "We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have." As well as the Department of Justice, the 'We-Consent' campaign is also supported by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, and CUAN (the Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Agency). All three have been approached for comment. Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill said the video was a waste of resources. "What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which at best has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," he said. "The issue of consent is a very serious one and I acknowledge the important work the Rape Crisis Centre and other agencies do every day to advocate for all victims of rape and sexual violence, including children. "But this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark." He added: "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?" A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said: "'We-Consent' is a programme created and developed by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, aimed at informing, educating, and engaging the public about all forms of consent. "Social media videos shared recently as part of this programme were produced by DRCC at a low-cost using volunteers and are not part of a Government advertising campaign. "The Department understands that DRCC intends to review these videos. They are being removed from their social media channels to enable this review." title: Senior detective accused of using AI for decisions
description: It is alleged the officer used the technology "inappropriately during criminal investigations".
body: The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) launched an investigation into the officer in August A senior detective is being investigated over alleged artificial intelligence (AI)-related gross misconduct. The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it launched an investigation into the officer in August after they were referred to the watchdog by Derbyshire Police following an "internal review" of their use of AI. Derbyshire Police said it made a voluntary referral to the IOPC on 23 June. On Thursday, the IOPC said it was alleged the officer used AI to "create policy decisions, assess and manage risk, justify decision-making, and input sensitive operational and personal case data". The IOPC said the force was concerned the senior detective's use of AI "may not have been in line with guidance and conditions issued by the force". It said it assessed the detail contained in the referral and decided to carry out an independent investigation. The officer has been served notice advising they are being investigated for alleged gross misconduct. Emily Barry, IOPC director of engagement, said: "These are serious allegations and it's right they are investigated thoroughly and independently. "We understand Derbyshire Constabulary authorised the use of Microsoft Copilot for officers in May 2025, with guidance on how it could be used to aid productivity in drafting reports and summarising information. There were conditions on its use, including that no operational, sensitive or personal data should be inputted to AI. "Our investigation will analyse the officer's use of Copilot between May last year and June this year and assess if there are any potential breaches of police professional standards." title: At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
description: The deaths include two women found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.
body: A car lies abandoned after severe rainfall in Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts, near Marseille At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam. The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport. The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region. Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death. In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area. Roads and train lines ‌in ⁠the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post ​on X. "The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday. Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues." A local resident shows her house which has been flooded following severe rainfall in Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts, near Marseille More severe weather is forecast in France, with Storm Austen - a newly named weather system moving in from the Atlantic - expected to reach the country's north-west. France's weather service, Météo-France, has issued an orange-level wind warning for five western departments from Thursday evening into Friday. The alert covers Côtes-d'Armor, Finistère, Morbihan, Ille-et-Vilaine and Manche. Heavy rainfall that began on 19 October caused significant flooding in south-eastern France Storm Adam had already brought severe flooding to eastern Spain, where at least three people were killed. Several towns along the Mediterranean coast were cut off by floodwaters, while helicopters were deployed to rescue people stranded on rooftops. Members of the Military Emergencies Unit found the body of a woman in the town of Oliva, Valencia, during rescue operations on Monday. Two other women were confirmed dead over ⁠the weekend. One woman's body was washed up on a beach in Sagunto, in the eastern region of Valencia, and another was swept away by floodwaters in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a promise that the national government would provide resources to help in reconstruction during a visit to the Valencia region on Tuesday. The Valencian government approved on Tuesday an aid package of €23.5m (£20m) for those affected by Storm Adam. title: Project aims to protect rare arctic-alpine plants
description: The three year scheme is awarded £65,000 to collect seeds and plant them in the fells.
body: A pot of £65,000 has been awarded for a three-year project to protect rare plants A project aiming to help protect rare arctic-alpine plants is set to launch. Teesdale Special Flora Research and Conservation Trust has been given a £65,000 grant for a three-year scheme. It will see volunteers work with the trust to collect seeds and put them on the fells of Upper Teesdale. The trust's founder, Dr Margaret Bradshaw, said the group wanted to raise awareness of the fragility of special flora in the area. "This project is crucial to support the ongoing research and conservation of these rare species," she said. The trust is also raising £15,000 to help support the project. The North Pennines National Landscape awarded £65,000 to the trust from the government's Farming in Protected Landscapes programme. The organisation said Upper Teesdale had an "unusually large number of rare plant species", including the Teesdale Assemblage. This is a "unique community" of 20 rare and endangered arctic-alpine plants believed to have "survived continuously since shortly after the last glaciation", between 10,000 and 12,000 years ago, a spokesman said. The programme manager for natural heritage at the North Pennines National Landscape, Sarah Tooze, said: "We are looking forward to working with local farmers on ways to support these fragile species." title: Moment man rescued from sinking car by Australian TV reporter
description: Journalist Will Murray describes how he and a bystander saved an SUV driver from his vehicle.
body: This video can not be played A man in a sinking car has been saved by a TV journalist after driving into deep flood water. Will Murray was at the scene reporting for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in Morayfield, Queensland, when he saw a vehicle drive past him into the water. Murray, and a bystander, rushed to help the driver as the SUV sank. Murray says when it became clear the car was sinking very fast "there was no thinking involved", because the man might have drowned. "Better that you jump in and give it a crack", Murray tells BBC News. Moment man rescued from sinking car by Australian TV reporter. title: First human case of Shamonda virus detected in France, officials say
description: The disease, which usually affects cattle, has been identified in a patient who died in early October.
body: Shamonda virus mostly affects livestock, in whom it can cause fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production The first known human case of the Shamonda virus (Shav) has been detected in a patient who died in early October, French authorities have said. Health officials said it was an "exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient" and there was currently no risk to the public. Shav is a disease that primarily affects cattle and can be spread by infected midges. Cases have also occurred in sheep, goats, alpacas and horses, but infections in people were previously unheard of. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was monitoring the situation and officials were still investigating how the virus had spread to a human. It is currently thought the patient contracted Shav through a midge bite in eastern France, the country's health and agriculture ministries said on Thursday, where cases were first identified in animals in the spring. They said the patient was being treated for a serious illness in a Lyon hospital and experienced neurological complications thought to have been "very likely linked" to the virus, based on initial findings. The statement stressed that their immune system was weakened, leaving them more vulnerable to getting ill. "Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans," it noted, having only been identified in animals "despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia". Dairy herds that catch Shav from bites can experience fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production. The ECDC said it was working with French and European partners to investigate the "potential public health implications" of the infection. The first cases of the virus in Europe were identified in late July, the agency said. It has since been detected in farm animals in several countries, including Ireland, Germany, Italy and Spain, as well as in Jersey. The case has also been reported to the World Health Organization. title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
description: The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand says she said he was "quite aggressive".
body: Warning - this report contains graphic content The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt". The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show. She said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants. The witness said Brand had sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead. She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset". "He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her. "He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt". The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started. You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts She said the woman replied "lots of times". "She told me that she was in a lot of pain" and that "she couldn't sit down". Another friend of the same complainant also gave evidence to the court. From the witness box, she told the jury her friend had told her that she had told him to stop during the alleged rape. She said her friend had said the worst moment had been after the act, and "she said that Brand told her she'd been dirty and had to clean up her mess". "She said he was quite cold and keen to get her gone". The witness said she had given her friend advice after she had confided in her. "I told her that she should go and get checked out because she had anal tears and a lot of discomfort and to seek guidance from her parents and to go to the police. "She just wasn't sure - it was all a bit chaotic in her head. She felt like it wasn't worth it." title: 'Not what a captain should be' - the debate around Fernandes' outburst
description: Bruno Fernandes' comments after Manchester United's humbling by Como have got fans and pundits talking - but what now for the captain?
body: This video can not be played Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on Carrick Bruno Fernandes' comments after Manchester United's humbling by Como have got fans and pundits talking - but what now for the captain? United's 4-1 Champions League defeat in Italy was the result of a wretched performance and Fernandes questioned boss Michael Carrick's tactics. "It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," said the Portugal attacking midfielder on TNT Sports. Asked if Carrick got his tactics wrong, the 32-year-old continued: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me." Are these the actions of a captain? Fernandes rounds on Carrick after Man Utd humiliation Man Utd humbling by Como leaves Carrick job in danger Not according to former Liverpool vice-captain Jamie Carragher, working as a summariser, on CBS Sports. "He's reacted like that because he's been embarrassed by the manager [who] brought him off," said the ex-England defender. "And when he talks about pressing, whether it's man-to-man or zonal, for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd. "He runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard for the supporters. They all think he's working hard. He's not. He's killing the rest of the team doing it." He added: "Watching him throw his arms up every week in a game is an absolute disgrace [and] calling the manager out considering how he's performed this season on the pitch. "[It's an] awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be." Fernandes' comments come a week after defender Lisandro Martinez made similar headlines following United's previous Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid. The Argentine said he expected more investment in the squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]". He later apologised. And while Martinez's outburst sparked debate, Fernandes' comments could have even larger repercussions. Carrick, who was under huge pressure already following a terrible start to the season, said in reply: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win." United have not won in their past seven games since beating Champions League minnows Sabah. They have just one win in their seven Premier League games this season. This video can not be played 'Simply not good enough - Warnock on Man Utd's Como display Not many people have defended Fernandes' public questioning of the tactics. But some do understand his frustrations. Former Leicester and Celtic keeper Kasper Schmeichel, whose dad Peter won the Champions League, five Premier League titles and three FA Cups as a United player, said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Given last week and what's happened, he probably should not be saying these things because it's only going to add to the problems. "With experience you learn that you need to keep these things in-house. It's a problem, with everything that happened during the week. "Michael Carrick didn't need this, the club didn't need this. It's exposing all of the issues that are at Manchester United. "It's very plain to see that there are loads of issues but you need to be fixing them, you need to be having meetings within the club, which I'm sure that they are, but it's obviously not resolved. It's just translating on to the pitch." The issue that most pundits have is not that Fernandes has these opinions - but that he has let the world know them. Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock, speaking on BBC Match of the Day, said: "I think there will be ex-players now from Manchester United saying, 'why are you letting this get out, this should be a collective in the changing room where we come together'. "Whether you like the manager or not, you've got to come together and say 'OK how do we correct this?' "Senior players go to the manager and say 'listen we didn't agree with the tactics, we didn't think we got it right, how do we go about this, how do we move forward', because you start airing it in public and it doesn't end well for anyone." Former Chelsea midfielder Joe Cole on TNT Sports called it "sacrilege". "I've played for managers where I don't agree with the tactics but you might say that to your mate or to your wife. You don't come out as captain of the club and question the manager," he said. This video can not be played Man Utd fans on if Carrick should stay Andy Mitten, editor of United We Stand, told BBC 5 Live Breakfast that Fernandes has "thrown his coach under the bus". "It's a terrible look," he continued. "And Manchester United fans are divided as to whether he should or should not do that. Last week, Martinez was also critical. A lot of Manchester United fans agreed with him. "Again, there's mitigation, he wants a new contract. That's because he's not been playing enough, because he's been injured. And injuries are a real problem for Manchester United. There's no recognised centre-forward. So it is a really difficult time for United." Former United midfielder Carrick, who took over in January initially as caretaker manager, seemed to blank his players at full-time before heading over to the United fans. "I don't blame him for ignoring the players," said Mitten. "He went to the fans and he held his hands up and he said, 'I'm sorry'. "You can tell he's hurting. He's a Manchester United fan himself. He was a season ticket holder only a year ago before he took the job. I think he's trying his be

title: Retired decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m after years in attic
description: He says he found treasure in his attic where the collection had been stored for 15 years.
body: The auctioneer said there had been an "incredible" buzz before the sale A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of Pokémon cards at auction. The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than £6,000. His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for £1.56m. The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record. "I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified. "When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school. "I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment. "He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say." Pokémon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series. The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay. One set which cost him £300 at the time went for £75,000 at Wednesday's auction. The cards, all filed into bespoke Pokémon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the Japanese gaming and film franchise. Ewbank's said "jaws hit the floor" when the man presented his 42 sets of cards to them. "When we saw what he had – all in mint condition – we couldn't believe it," said James Spooner, its head of trading cards. The auction house added the sale had been their most successful in more than 30 years in business. Its top lot was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set, including a Charizard card in near-mint condition. It had been pitched at £15,000-£20,000 but bagged £100,000. The auctioneer said the "buzz was incredible" Andrew Ewbank, who runs Ewbank's and conducted the sale from the rostrum himself, told bidders he was "going for a lie down" afterwards. "The build-up to this... has been phenomenal, and on the day it did not disappoint," he added later. "We had bidders from all over the world. "The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was – extensive, untouched, complete, and with just about every rarity you could hope for." The record sum for the collection beat the previous best, set only on 9 October in London, when a sale at Stanley Gibbons declared a sale total of £872,000, according to Ewbank's.
