title: Devon and Cornwall battening down the hatches ahead of Storm Austen
description: Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are forecast to bring disruption across the South West.
body: Staff at Perranporth's Watering Hole bar have secured parts of the building before Storm Austen Extra safety measures have been set up by people and businesses as they prepare for the UK's first named storm of the season. Storm Austen is forecast to bring gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) and heavy rain across parts of Cornwall and Devon from Thursday night, according to the Met Office. The conditions, which are also set to affect parts of Wales, England's south coast, Wiltshire and Somerset, have led to weather warnings being issued, external for Friday. Bosses at The Watering Hole bar on Perranporth Beach in Cornwall said they were taking extra precautions after the venue suffered damage during Storm Goretti in January. Jamie-Lee Job said the bar lost several glass panels during that storm as the wind physically lifted them up and sent them crashing through a roof canopy. Ahead of Storm Austen, staff at the bar have been fixing parts of the building down to make them more secure. "It was quite scary, we've survived a lot of storms but that particular storm we underestimated how bad it was going to be," Job said. "It is a reminder to us all to best err on the side of caution. "So for this one we are doing everything we can do to make sure everything is secure and hopefully the roof stays on for this one." Jamie-Lee Job said The Watering Hole lost a lot of glass panelling during Storm Goretti in January The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind on Friday from 00:00 until 17:00 BST. It covers Devon, Cornwall, south Wales, England's south coast, Wiltshire and Somerset, with "transport disruption likely and possible damaging winds in some areas". From 01:00 until 10:00 this warning is increased to amber for Cornwall, with power cuts and building damage listed among possible consequences. A separate yellow warning for wind covering other parts of England and Wales including the Midlands, Essex, Manchester and Anglesey has also been issued from 10:00 to 21:00. The Met Office is advising people, external to make preparations to protect their property and other people from injury. It recommends checking for loose items outside homes and making plans to secure them, including bins, garden furniture, trampolines, tents, sheds and fences. The Watering Hole was badly damaged by a storm in January Other people in Perranporth said they had stocked up on supplies in case they lost power during Storm Austen. Chris Eves said: "We've got loads of torches and candles and lots of flasks so we should be OK." Another woman who was walking along the town's beach said she was preparing to "hunker down". She added: "I've got lots of candles, we've got a rechargeable radio, rechargeable lights, a gas-fired pizza oven and I am thinking about buying a primus stove as well. "I am also thinking I won't have anything expensive in my freezer, so if there's a power cut I won't lose too much." Cornwall Council has issued a warning urging people to prepare before the storm hits and to avoid exposed coastal areas on Thursday evening and Friday. "Strong winds and large waves could make conditions extremely dangerous," the council said. The authority added schools across the county could be closed during the storm. Camborne Rugby Club said it would be closing its club grounds for at least 24 hours from 15:00 on Thursday, while its clubhouse would be shut from about 22:00. Meanwhile, Newquay Business Improvement District said it had cancelled Saturday's Zombie Crawl parade due to the weather forecast. Josie Tennant said the Pebbleridge Kitchen in Devon had a plan in place for the high winds In Devon, storm preparation at the Pebbleridge Kitchen near Northern Burrows Country Park is a "well-versed process" after the last winter. Josie Tennant, operations manager across the Royal George Group, which runs the cafe, said: "We're super exposed here so we make sure all the furniture is against the building so that anything moving around is not moving too far so it can't hurt anyone. "We also make sure all the shutters are down so the rain is not being driven into the building and then we are looking out for red alerts as well." She added: "The manager Sam here knows exactly what to do to keep the building safe to keep the staff safe and to keep our customers safe as well." RNLI Coxswain Simon McCarthy said his crew was ready to go out at any time The RNLI has reminded those along the coast to exercise "extreme caution if visiting the shoreline, especially along exposed cliffs and seafronts". Appledore RNLI Coxswain Simon McCarthy said his crew was ready to go out "at any time" and was securing its boats with extra lashings while monitoring the storm. "With the amber warning, it means the all-weather lifeboats are more called upon," McCarthy explained. "The inshore boats have got their limitations, so we have to make sure we have crew available." He added: "We really do want people to be sensible. The sea will always win." Devon County Council said it would have extra staff on hand in its Network Operations Control Centre to monitor conditions and co-ordinate responses to any weather-related incidents. Councillor Dan Thomas, cabinet member for highways, said: "We're preparing for a spell of unsettled weather and would encourage everyone travelling around Devon to keep an eye on the forecast and plan ahead. "With many trees still in leaf following the dry weather, there is a risk of fallen trees and branches on our roads." Great Western Railway said its long-distance services would be running from London Paddington to Plymouth rather than Penzance. It added local trains would provide a shuttle service between Penzance and Plymouth and some early morning services on Saturday could also be cancelled while its teams assess any damage. Dartmouth Food Festival has also been impacted by the storm with organisers pushing some events planned for Friday ba

title: Claims 'stabbed' woman tried to drive to hospital because of ambulance wait time denied
description: Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to a crash in Bridgend on Monday.
body: Police say Eleanor Barnfield "sustained puncture wounds unrelated to the collision" in Bridgend on Monday The Welsh Ambulance Service has denied that a woman who died after crashing a car into a wall after suffering "stab wounds" was driving because of ambulance wait times. Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing. A 61-year-old man from Bridgend, who has been arrested on suspicion of murder, remains in custody. The ambulance service said it was aware of "misleading rumours" circulating online but said medics were called to the crash in Coity Road at about 12:44 BST and a response unit arrived seven minutes later. Flowers left in tribute to Eleanor Barnfield who died earlier this week In a statement, it said two emergency ambulances then later arrived to provide additional support at 13:07 and 13:13. It described the rumours on social media as "contradictory" and "factually untrue". "We would encourage members of the public not to speculate," the service said. It also confirmed that "advanced critical care" was delivered by the emergency medical retrieval and transfer service, which arrived by helicopter, before the patient was driven to hospital. South Wales Police said it made the arrest on Tuesday after undergoing a "significant" police operation at a retirement housing complex, Ger-y-Nant, near the crash. Eleanor worked for the housing association Valleys to Coast, which runs the complex that provides accommodation for over-60s and consists of 13 flats. Ger-y-Nant, a sheltered housing retirement complex, where a man was arrested In a family tribute on Wednesday, Eleanor was described by her family as the "kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world". "She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock," the tribute added. Jo Oak, chief executive of Valleys to Coast, said Eleanor was a "much-valued member" of the team and they were "devastated" by her loss. Oak added the organisation would "continue to cooperate fully with South Wales Police". Police have thanked the patience and support of residents and said communities may notice an "increased police presence" as the investigation continues. title: Two storms in two days as Austen and Boelo head for UK
description: The Met Office have named a new storm, Boelo, which is set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend.
body: The Met Office have named a new storm, Boelo, which is set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend. Storm Boelo will be hot on the heels of Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season. Storm Austen is expected to bring strong winds to south-west England during Friday morning. The Met Office has issued an amber wind warning for Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly, Plymouth and parts of Devon valid between 1am and 10am on Friday. Gusts of wind will widely reach 60-70mph, and perhaps 80mph in exposed locations. Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts. Some buildings could potentially be damaged by the strongest winds, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm. Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places. As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre. That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph. The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph forecast, and some ferry services have already been cancelled. Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday. Wind warnings have been issued ahead of storm Austen's arrival on Friday Storm Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways. The strongest winds will move into Scotland on Saturday afternoon, reaching a peak overnight. The Met Office have also issued yellow wind warnings for Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England valid on Saturday and lasting most of Sunday. Gusts are forecast to reach 50-65mph widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations. There could be some localised disruption with strong winds funnelling through the Central Lowlands for a time. Transport disruption is expected and there may be some power cuts. Following recent spells of wet weather, there is an additional risk of some localised flooding. Wind warnings have been issued ahead of storm Boelo's arrival over the weekend It's not unusual to get storms so close together, in fact they quite often arrive in clusters. A strong jet stream is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process involved in creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic. These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds. Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer. The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May. The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months. This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year. In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November. title: Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
description: The aid workers from Switzerland and Austria are due to fly home on Thursday, reports say.
body: Eva Greztmacher, 76, had spent many years in Niger as an aid worker Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi. Austrian national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Swiss Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year. No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed. Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed. Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker. Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release. Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez. A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported. Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi. It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah. Under Gaddafi, many ethnic Tuaregs from Mali and Niger were recruited to join armed groups loyal to him in Libya. After he was killed, many went home. Analysts say this has been a major factor in the spread of instability in the Sahel region. Niger and its neighbours have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State. The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum. title: Legendary video game studio BioWare closed after 31 years
description: The influential studio that made Mass Effect and Dragon Age announces it is closing its doors.
body: BioWare developed Mass Effect, the influential sci-fi role-playing game BioWare, the video game studio behind sci-fi epic Mass Effect and fantasy saga Dragon Age, has been closed down. The Canadian developer specialising in role-playing games was founded in 1995 and found millions of fans with its complex, branching narratives. Its last two releases, however, did not meet sales expectations, and parent company Electronic Arts (EA) announced it had decided to close the studio as it cut 400 jobs across the business. In its own statement, BioWare, which was working on a new Mass Effect game, thanked players for "being the most important part of the story" during its 31-year history. The developer's first big taste of success came in 1998 when it released role-playing game Baldur's Gate, based on Dungeons and Dragons rules. It became renowned for the quality of its games and in the late 2000s had twin successes with the Mass Effect trilogy and several Dragon Age games. Mass Effect in particular is regarded as having a long-lasting influence on the video game industry thanks to its ambitious narrative and inclusion of same-sex relationships. As industry trends changed, BioWare pivoted from single player to multiplayer games with the release of Anthem in 2019 - which disappointed fans and critics. It followed up with Dragon Age: The Veilguard, the fourth game in the series, in 2024. The game's protracted development cycle was blamed for its lukewarm reviews - particularly from long-time series fans, who complained it lacked the complex moral choices of its prequels. BioWare's most recent release, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, did not meet EA's expectations Despite BioWare's recent performance, there was a huge response to the news. Actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, who voiced female and male versions of Mass Effect's main character Commander Shepherd, reacted via a livestream on Instagram., external Addressing fans, Hale said the community that had formed around the game would keep it alive. "BioWare lives on. Mass Effect lives on. We live on," she said. The pair closed the livestream by delivering Shepherd's famous line: "I should go on." Fellow industry figures also showed their support for BioWare. Michał Nowakowski, co-CEO of The Witcher developer CD Projekt Red, said BioWare had been "a massive part" of the Polish studio's history, "sharing their wisdom" since working to release Baldur's Gate in Eastern Europe. "Not a great day in the games industry," he wrote, external. BioWare project director Mike Gamble thanked fans and colleagues for the "words of support for the studio, the legacy, and the impact that BioWare has had on you". "It means so much to us," he added, external. BioWare also released fondly remembered Star Wars RPG Knights of the Old Republic in 2003 The studio's closure comes months after EA - the video game giant responsible for series including EA FC, The Sims and Battlefield - was bought for $55bn by a Saudi Arabia-led group of investors. As part of the deal, EA took on $20bn in debt, which the company will have to pay back. In a message to staff, since published on its website, external, the company said it had taken a "hard look" at its business and chosen to focus on key titles and series. This meant working on "fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects in the action-adventure space", it said, confirming that a new Iron Man game and a Star Wars Jedi title were being worked on. The company said it had two projects in development under its EA Sports banner, including a "social-first" American Football game code-named "Project Gridiron", and that it was in the early stages of resurrecting boxing simulator Fight Night. EA also said it was committed to the long-term success of skateboarding simulator Skate, and The Sims. However, it did announce the cancellation of one new Sims project, and said there would be job cuts at Skate developer Full Circle. The company said BioWare was "a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly". title: El Salvador's president threatens Haitian gangs over military hostages
description: Four members of the so-called Gang Suppression Force have been missing since Sunday.
body: El Salvador's president has said he has launched a military operation to rescue four air force personnel who have been missing in Haiti since Sunday. Threatening further action, Nayib Bukele said that Wednesday's attack was "nothing" compared with what would happen if all the hostages - who he said were not combatants - were not returned alive. They went missing after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups," El Salvador's armed forces said. The ambush occurred in Croix-des-Bouquets, an area controlled by armed groups. They were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), approved by the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, to tackle escalating gang violence in Haiti. According to an X post from Bukele, the mission consisted of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary jobs were to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war". His post said the Salvadoran military operation's single objective was to bring the four men back home alive. He added that if all four were returned alive, without being harmed, "everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping". Bukele added they were kidnapped "in a cowardly manner" while returning after buying food at a market in the area. A statement released by the Armed Forces of El Salvador on Sunday said the group was ambushed while travelling back to its camp in an armoured vehicle, which caught fire after being hit by explosives. So far, no gang has claimed responsibility for the attack. Salvadoran helicopters were deployed to assist, with multiple attempts to make an approach by land and air hampered by fighting and local security conditions, the armed forces said. On Wednesday, before Bukele announced the launch of the military operation, the GSF said it was searching for the four missing personnel following the attack. It added that it had "engaged armed gang elements, with helicopter support" and that early reports had indicated that several gang members were killed. Earlier this week, the UN warned that Haiti's armed gangs were adapting to intensified security conditions, saying that they were "stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas". Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and two weeks ago postponed presidential and legislative elections - scheduled for 13 December - indefinitely. The country has been wracked by economic chaos, a political vacuum and increasingly violent gang warfare since its president was assassinated in 2021. More than 5,500 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti in 2024. Armed gangs currently control about 85% of the capital, Port-au-Prince. title: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb
description: It has been a dramatic, public and global response, but the cyber event hasn't happened yet.
body: Cyber-security flaws were recently identified in the popular PHP programming language, which is used on a vast number of websites across the world I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built. We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed during the construction. In the end, there were none, but procedures were put in place as a precaution and we all had to practice filing into designated safe zones inside our building. The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb - I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet. There has been no painful attack like the ransomware we saw knock out M&S and JLR in 2025. But the potential threat is so serious that websites around the world have been taken down as a precaution. Less than two months ago, 100 tech companies wrote an open letter warning the world to adopt a new level of cyber resilience in the age of AI. It turns out we didn't have to wait very long to find out what they meant. The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit. One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult. However, things that are very difficult for humans are increasingly very little trouble for AI. The tech is getting a lot of credit here for assisting researchers in finding the bugs, and the PHP foundation, which oversees the programming language, was on the case and issued a fix. It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites - but the news was leaked. From that point the clock started ticking. As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site. "There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University. "How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers? "Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out." But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made. We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either. As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success. Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, described this as a good news story. "We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," she told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4. "We have enormous capability to handle these risks." But the baddies can use AI too, and those same tools are probably churning away right now trying to get in. Cyber security authorities are warning website owners to fix the weaknesses immediately, but the patch only works on the latest version of PHP, so older sites will need to upgrade first. For many it may be a significant repair job, so if there's a web developer in your life you may want to send them thoughts, prayers and maybe a strong coffee. title: Celebrity shark guided out of South Korea canal refuses to swim out to sea
description: Bukangi the shark became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted in a canal in Busan weeks ago.
body: This video can not be played Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canal A famed dusky shark in South Korea is still lingering near a canal that it was guided out of on Wednesday. The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month. For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get it back to the open sea using large nets. On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and has been circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway. Its rescue prompted mixed reactions in Busan, where some said the shark should stay while others felt it was better for it to go. In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour. Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark. But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities. For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal. Rescuers freed it by removing the outer layer, and have since fortified the remaining layer of nets to prevent it from going back in. Since then, authorities said, Bukangi has been swimming further out but keeps circling back. A government official told the BBC on Thursday afternoon that rescuers had concluded their operations to free the shark. Authorities had attempted to lead the shark out of the canal It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future. In the month that she has been in the canal, Bukangi had already attracted more than 1.6 million visitors. Its popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city embraced it as an unofficial mascot. But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as it appeared to be injured and was not eating. Social media users have been circulating videos of Bukangi swimming in the canal with what appears to be a bloodied snout. There were concerns the shark would be further weakened by falling water temperatures. Before this week's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets. Some in Busan felt it was safer for the shark to remain in the canal. The BBC saw two people holding up cardboard signs protesting against Bukangi's eviction. One of them was Cho Hannah, who had travelled for two hours from her home in North Gyeongsang province to see the shark. Bukangi, she insisted, was "a rare gift" to Busan. "This shark has made this canal her home, and we are kicking her out unnecessarily. I am afraid the shark might die tangled with the net, or die out at sea," she said. But others like Yoon In-taek said it was only right that Bukangi left. "Bukangi seemed much larger when I first saw her on 18 September, when she first got here. Now she seems gaunt. I'm worried for her health if she stays," he said. "It doesn't sit right with me that she keeps returning here. It will be best if Bukangi leaves, doesn't come back, and lives and feeds freely in the open sea. I'd love to see her find a healthy, free life out there," said Shin Seungmin. Bukangi has "brought so much joy to us", he said, adding that he was sad to see her leave. "But she should go and live her normal shark life." Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi. title: NI secretary arrives at Stormont ahead of budget meetings
description: The Stormont executive maintains it cannot balance the books without more support from London.
body: Sir Chris has insisted there is no more money available The Northern Ireland secretary will be in Northern Ireland later for further talks with executive parties to try to break the budget deadlock. Sir Chris Bryant, who has insisted there is no more money available beyond the £1.5bn the government has already offered, has accused executive ministers of being financially "irresponsible". He held brief virtual discussions with parties last Friday, but it is understood that Thursday's discussions will involve a series of meetings between Sir Chris and party leaders. The executive has maintained it cannot balance its books without more support from London. The current package would be split into three tranches with £525m available this year, but the Stormont parties said that still falls short of what they require. Without an agreed budget, public sector workers in Northern Ireland cannot receive long-awaited pay awards that they are entitled to, in line with their counterparts in other parts of the UK. Health workers run out of patience with Stormont budget delay Divided executive 'speaking as one' on budget, says finance minister PM tells Stormont parties to be 'realistic' in budget negotiations Hospital doctors have announced they will strike next month over the issue, while the Royal College of Nursing is also balloting for industrial action. At Stormont's finance committee on Wednesday, the Department of Finance's top civil servant Neil Gibson confirmed that it is now too late for any civil service pay settlement before Christmas because of the ongoing lack of a budget. "We're too late in the year for Christmas for the sector I'm in," he told assembly members. Sir Chris has suggested the absolute deadline for reaching a deal is January because at that point the money available to departments to spend under emergency arrangements will run out. Stormont departments are facing a shortfall of up to £1.6bn, according to a spending watchdog. Last month, Sir Chris made an offer of a financial package worth about £1.5bn over the next three years. But executive parties said that did not go far enough and they have argued that significant gaps remain before they can agree to a deal that would allow them to set a budget. With no agreed budget, public services have been operating under contingency arrangements allowing departments to spend up to 95% of last year's funding. SDLP assembly member Matthew O'Toole said more than 20,000 civil servants have no prospect of seeing a pay increase in their Christmas pay packet On Wednesday, the secretary of state told the House of Commons there had to be "political accountability for finances", and that he wanted to be able to settle the issue with the executive. The government is due to publish its own budget next week, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham previously saying the executive needed to be "realistic" about what more Westminster could do, given some Whitehall departments are being asked to make in-year cuts. SDLP Leader of the Opposition Matthew O'Toole, who chairs the finance committee, said "ordinary workers are paying the price" for the executive's failure, referencing a row between Sinn Féin and the DUP at another committee over tensions linked to the Drumcree dispute. "Today's scenes exposed everything that's wrong with this Executive," O'Toole said in a statement on Wednesday. "While the two largest parties were busy attacking each other, more than 20,000 civil servants learned they have no prospect of seeing a pay increase in their Christmas pay packet," he said. "The mudslinging and manufactured outrage won't hide the fact that this Executive has failed to agree a budget." Robert Murtagh from the FDA union, which represents senior civil servants, said it is "deeply frustrating" that formal negations over civil servant pay have not begun. Civil service pay is aligned with the budget period, he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme. "As far away from the budget we are... we're also away from civil service pay." Murtagh added that officials and civil servants are "collateral damage" however he welcomed that the finance minister said it is a "day one issue" once a budget is agreed. He said civil service unions "stand ready" to engage in negations "as soon as possible". title: Woman 'scared to turn heating on' due to oil cost
description: Roslynn Garner-Gatley uses a hot water bottle bed socks and earlier bedtimes to stay warm.
body: This video can not be played A woman has said she is frightened to put her heating on because the cost of domestic oil has nearly doubled. Roslynn Garner-Gatley, 76, lives in a three-bedroom semi-detached cottage in Yealmpton, south Devon, with no gas supply and relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water. She said her oil tank held 1,000 litres (220 gallons). About six months earlier, she bought 500 litres (110 gallons) for £317 plus VAT but, when she contacted her supplier for a current quote, she was told the same amount would cost £600 plus VAT. title: Police investigate Married at First Sight Australia after 'inappropriate' allegations
description: New South Wales Police say inquiries took place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".
body: Married at First Sight Australia is facing fresh controversy after police launched an investigation into the hit reality TV show. New South Wales told BBC News that inquiries had taken place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared". Channel Nine, which broadcasts Married at First Sight Australia, confirmed that it was "aware of a police investigation" involving the show's production company. It is the latest blow for the show, after a BBC News investigation earlier this year into MAFS Australia revealed cast members said they had not been told their partners had previous drug and violence convictions. Those revelations led to a warning from Australia's media watchdog, which called them "serious and disturbing". The British version of Married at First Sight, known to many as MAFS UK, was separately plunged into crisis in May after BBC Panorama reported rape allegations from two female cast members - allegations the men involved have denied. MAFS UK is made by a different production company to the Australian version. The Dark Side of Married at First Sight Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm. Married at First Sight shows single people agreeing to "marry" total strangers after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings. The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on "honeymoons", before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day. According to industry news website TV Blackbox, external, a male cast member on the current series of MAFS Australia made a formal complaint to the police after producers allegedly shared private information about him with his on-screen bride. Married at First Sight Australia stars not told partners had drug and violence convictions Married at First Sight Australia allegations 'disturbing', says country's watchdog Married at First Sight UK brides tell BBC they were raped by on-screen husbands A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commenced an investigation following a report of inappropriate content being shared. "Following inquiries, the matter will be referred to WA [Western Australia] Police Force." BBC News has approached WA Police Force, who said the referral has not yet been received. A spokesperson for Channel Nine said: "We are aware of a police investigation involving Endemol Shine Australia and all enquiries should be directed to them." Endemol Shine Australia, which makes MAFS Australia, has not responded to multiple requests for comment over the latest developments. In June, a BBC News investigation heard from nine former cast members from MAFS Australia, who urged the show to improve its background checks and to stop allowing individuals with previous convictions or allegations on the show. One woman from last year's Australian series told us she was not told the man she had been matched with had a previous drug conviction and only found out after the show ended. "There should be informed consent," she told us. Responding to those claims at the time, Channel 9 and Endemol Shine Australia said they had "strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing". As well as being a huge hit in Australia, the show is popular in the UK and is shown on Channel 4. The broadcaster pulled all the UK episodes of MAFS from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation in May, but MAFS Australia remains available to watch. In July, BBC News revealed that a cast member from MAFS UK had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme. The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law. The media regulator Ofcom has also launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 show. The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million. The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report. Channel 4's chief executive previously said the review was due back in the summer, but it has not yet been published. Speaking to MPs earlier this week, Ofcom boss Dame Melanie Dawes said the report was due back "any day now". BBC News has approached Channel 4 for a response. Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading. title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
description: The bank says it is using more AI leading to a 5% reduction in its workforce.
body: Barclays is cutting its staff by around 5,000 as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes. The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce. The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall. Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy. The banking group is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected. Barclays also revealed it made £2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast. Economists have been watching companies' results carefully for signs that investment in new technology, and AI specifically, is making a difference in their day-to-day operations, leading to greater efficiency and lower employment. Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business. "AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future. "We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake. "Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI." Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers. Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Barclays was "reaching for the AI lever, expecting to cut a decent chunk of its workforce as it expands the use of artificial intelligence", but had failed to match expectations with its financial results. Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years". "Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said. Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further £1.1bn of savings in 2027. How has AI changed your job or the type of work your do? title: MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years, newly released files show
description: He came to its attention in the 1930s when he was considered a left-wing firebrand.
body: Papers show Aneurin Bevan first came to the attention of the security service in the 1930s NHS founder Aneurin "Nye" Bevan was spied on by MI5 for more than 20 years, according to newly released files. Papers given to the National Archives show he first came to the attention of the security service in the 1930s when he was considered a firebrand left-winger linked to prominent communists. Monitoring continued after Bevan, from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, became a minister in the post-war Labour government when he drove through the creation of the NHS in the face of opposition from doctors. At one stage the then MI5 director general became so concerned about his links to a Russian spy that he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee in No 10 to warn him. But some in the service questioned why it was taking an interest in him, given everything he did was in the open. After his death in 1960, one MI5 officer called the content of the file "remarkably tame". The papers show MI5 first opened a file on Bevan when he was backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in 1933. One of the first reports included an account of an anti-Nazi rally in Montreal, Canada, which Bevan addressed in 1934. "Bevan has inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the Communist cause," it said. In 1943, Roger Hollis, future director general, summarised what they knew of Bevan's activities. In 1933 he said the MP had been "in close touch" with Communist Party of Great Britain general secretary Harry Pollitt and party members who backed his plan to organise "workers' freedom groups" to defend against "capitalists". Although there was nothing in the files to indicate MI5 tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, some wondered why they were watching him at all. One MI5 director general was so worried about Bevan's links to a Russian spy he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee (left) about it "I do not think that Bevan's activities are a matter in which we, the security service, should be involved," one officer wrote in 1943. "In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently." The reporting continued after the war when Bevan was made health minister in Attlee's government. In 1949 MI5 became increasingly concerned about Bevan's friendship with Wilfred Macartney, "an unsavoury, unscrupulous character" convicted of spying for Russia in 1928. Recordings of conversations suggested he was passing information obtained by Bevan to Communist Party leader Pollitt. That May MI5 chief Sir Percy Sillitoe took evidence to Attlee, who dismissed Macartney's claims as a "tissue of lies" but agreed to warn Bevan about him. One of the final reports dates from 1954 when Bevan, now back in opposition, was invited to meet the Soviet ambassador, Yakov Malik, at London's Polish embassy. The event "went off very badly", partly because the Russian had difficulty in understanding Bevan's accent, which led to misunderstanding. "The party broke up in a none too friendly atmosphere," the report said. The file was not closed until 1975 - 15 years after Bevan died. title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
description: Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.
body: Current polling suggests Gadi Eisenkot (left) is in a tight race with incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu (right) to become Israel's prime minister Israel's general election takes place on Tuesday 27 October. It's the first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel and its subsequent conflicts in Gaza and with Iran, Hezbollah and the Houthis. Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications. Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister. Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year. He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October. Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government. Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory. There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them. Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters Israel's parliament - known as the Knesset - has 120 seats, meaning a government must hold 61 seats to command a majority. Israel uses a proportional representation voting system, meaning governments have always been coalitions of multiple parties. This means that after election day, it may take weeks or even months before the next government is formed - with different parties wrangling for concessions and deals being struck. If no bloc can form a majority, it is possible a minority government could take power. The dominating topic has been security - with the challengers to Netanyahu all heavily criticising the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken back to Gaza as hostages. Nevertheless, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security", pointing to strategic victories in Israel's wars since 2023. Conscription is also a major topic. Historically, ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in full-time religious study have been exempt from military service, but since war broke out this has become an increasingly divisive policy. Judicial reform has also featured heavily during the campaign. Netanyahu's government is still pursuing contentious plans for reforms to the judicial system, which led to mass protests before 7 October. Critics say the plans would compromise the independence of the judiciary and threaten democracy. As in many countries, cost of living is another key issue. Food and housing costs have grown steadily in recent years. A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it. More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding. So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives. On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary. In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion. Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers. For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it. title: Two killed in attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
description: It is the latest in a series of attacks by the Houthi movement which have targeted airports and other sites in the kingdom.
body: Dammam is the largest city in Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says. Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals. The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles. On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said. The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze. It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal. Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen. US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities. One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis' military spokesman said on Wednesday that they had targeted military equipment at an airport in the southern Yemeni city of al-Mukalla, which it said had been transported by Saudi Arabia for use by pro-government forces. Meanwhile, Houthi-run media reported that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours. According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago. The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period. The UN says more than 256,000 people have also been displaced. The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran. Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support. However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces. title: Some New Yorkers back ban on horse-drawn carriages, but drivers fear for incomes
description: As councillors prepare to banish the vehicles, views in Central Park are divided over the 160-year-old tradition.
body: Drivers of horse-drawn carriages in Central Park are concerned for their future - while animal activists see the ban as a victory After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked. She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horse, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried. "What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old, who has been driving in the park for six years. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?" Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity. On Thursday, New York City Council is expected to vote to pass a ban on the carriages that would start in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry. But several drivers who spoke to the BBC said they did not want new jobs, and disputed claims their horses are mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban. Horse-drawn carriages in New York City expected to be outlawed "There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing." Since 1982, 40 horses working in Central Park have died, according to the Manhattan Borough President's office, which blames issues including overheating and collisions. New York leaders previously sought a ban, under pressure from animal-rights activists, but faced pushback from city council members and unions representing the workers. But the ban movement found new momentum this summer after the death of a teenager. In June, Romanch Mahajan, a tourist visiting New York with his family from India, was in a carriage when the horse bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall out and die. The planned ban - named Romanch's Law after the teen - also follows the death this year of a carriage horse, Deniz, who ate a toxic plant in Central Park. Several Central Park horse carriage drivers who spoke to the BBC said they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk. Lawson, who was nearby on the day Mahajan fell to his death, called the deadly incident "extremely tragic". But she said if the city was really worried about the safety of the horse-drawn carriages, it would outlaw them immediately - not in two years' time. The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the carriage ban, said that over the past 13 months alone, there had been seven "horse-related incidents". In May, a driver was taken to the hospital after a spooked horse hit another carriage, causing it to tip over. In January, another horse, named Destiny, ran into traffic near the park, causing a multi-car collision. Lawson, who owns six horses, pointed out that New York City carriages were the most regulated in the country and said horses enjoyed the stimulation. "They look at an animal in harness and they see a trap," Lawson said of officials pushing for the ban. "They see a job as something that's terrible. Horses are working animals." Lawson says she feels very attached to her horse - and to her business as a carriage driver Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, feels similarly attached to his horse, calling allegations of mistreatment a joke. "I spend more time with my horses than my wife and my kids," he said. "They're telling me I'm abusing my horse? No way." Fidan said he was angry, and that officials were passing a ban without talking in-person to drivers and others in the industry. "If you don't listen to me, how can you come and kill my business, destroy my family's, my livelihood?" he asked. The city council held a hearing in July, inviting community members, including horse-carriage drivers, to comment. The legislation to end horse-drawn carriages proposes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counselling, and financial compensation for those in the business. A spokesperson for Mamdani said his office was involved in planning to find new jobs for these workers - who make around $60,000 (£ 44,000) to $70,000 a year, according to drivers who spoke at the city council hearing. But the Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, said the plan did not include guarantees - including compensation - and that the workers would be "economically wiped out". The union also raised concerns about a lack of funding for individuals and organisations who eventually take in the horses. It argued that thousands end up at slaughter auctions each year. The bill forbids selling horses for slaughter or for similar work. Chris Koenigs thinks the horses are "wonderful", but too much of a risk for public safety Though carriage drivers say they are committed to the health of their horses, concerns over the animals' well-being have been raised in the city for decades. The carriages have been opposed by animal-rights groups, including one that was founded in response to New York's industry. In 1866, after Henry Bergh witnessed the brutal beating of a carriage horse, he established the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) to protest horses' treatment and other instances of animal abuse. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) and a coalition of organisations supporting the horse-carriage ban also oppose the carriages. Horses can work up to nine hours a day. They are currently restricted to certain entrances of the park, where they stand

title: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
description: Governments and companies are scrambling to protect their websites, as Amazon says it experienced attacks before the warning was made public.
body: The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites. Governments and some of the world's biggest companies are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws. The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them. A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a statement., external Amazon said its threat intelligence system identified it was targeted on Saturday. It added there were further "exploitation attempts" once the embargo on the flaw warning was lifted. The company said it "automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability." PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs. When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web. Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites. As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like." "They can steal data , they can go to other parts of your network. All sort of things like that - even plant a backdoor to get in later on, so it's pretty serious," Woodward told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. This video can not be played Why have websites around the world been taken down? BBC explains Cyber security researcher Ryan Austin, who has been researching PHP security for the last 20 years, said he discovered the flaw in the programming language. He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI". Austin described PHP as "one of the first web languages that powered the early internet". "It's in a lot of places that you wouldn't expect to be that are basically very core to how the internet runs in a lot of ways. It's like all the old things that are in a house that you know keeps it [running] but you don't really think about," the PHP researcher said. But Austin said this incident is not necessarily bad news because organisations would now "run and patch PHP immediately" if they haven't already. Listen to BBC Radio 4 Today programme on BBC Sounds Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October. In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said. The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said. While the PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch", details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday. In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said. The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning. The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added. The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days". She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said. The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade. Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure. The websites for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors are currently inaccessible. They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it had followed guidance to take its website offline, "in view of the critical security issues affecting PHP". Edinburgh and Oxford council websites also went offline on Wednesday, but are now accessible. What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble? The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website. This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed. The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database". It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update. title: Children in care to get £10 a week savings
description: Eligible people in the care system will be able to access the savings once they turn 18.
body: The States of Guernsey said about 40 people in care will be eligible for the scheme. A new government savings scheme will set aside £10 a week for children in care for them to access when they turn 18. Established by the States' Children and Family Community Services and Guernsey Community Savings, it is designed to give young people a financial foundation when becoming an adult. The States said the scheme will apply to children from entry into the care system and 40 will benefit immediately. Associate director of children services Lucy Cook said the savings accounts would support young people by "helping them to access opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach." The States of Guernsey said the transition to independent living for people in care can bring "significant financial pressures, from setting up a home to managing everyday living costs". "Having savings of their own can offer greater choice, security and confidence as they take this important step," it said. The States will pay a one-off fee to allpay, a payment services company, to establish the scheme. The charity Guernsey Community Savings will then open and manage the accounts, and work with each young person and their social worker as they approach their 18th birthday. At 18 years old, they will have the choice of opening an account with Guernsey Community Savings or transferring their savings to an account of their choice. Cook said children in care deserve the opportunity to "look ahead with confidence and hope for their future". "This initiative is about giving our care-experienced young people a stronger foundation and recognising our commitment to them as corporate parents. "We want every child in care to know that they are valued, supported and encouraged to achieve their full potential." More news stories for Guernsey Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Chief executive of Guernsey Community Savings Joe Brown said children from care are "particularly vulnerable to financial exclusion when they reach adulthood". "Giving them the opportunity to build up savings, and the financial security that comes with this, can make a real difference as they take their first steps towards independence." title: Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't do a play, a film or read any more'
description: The actress tells BBC Radio 4's Today programme about how her eye condition has affected her life.
body: This video can not be played Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't be on stage, I can't do a film, I can't read anymore' Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench says her eye condition has left her unable to perform on stage or read, more than a decade after she was diagnosed. Dame Judi was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012, a condition that affects her vision and has made it incredibly difficult to even recognise faces. Speaking to Emma Barnett on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she said: "I can't be on stage. I can't do a play any more. I can't do a film any more. I can't read any more." She also revealed how her condition can lead to awkward encounters, saying she sometimes approaches the wrong people "and give them an almost hug" before realising her mistake. When asked about ageing, Dame Judi, who's 91, replied: "There's nothing to say for it at all. [I] don't think about it too much." Dame Judi Dench made her debut as "M" in GoldenEye in 1995 She has enjoyed a career spanning more than seven decades and is one of Britain's most celebrated actors, with a body of work across theatre, television and film. Dame Judi won an Academy Award for best supporting actress for playing Queen Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love in 1999, and became internationally recognised for her portrayal of "M", James Bond's boss. She made her debut as the character in GoldenEye in 1995, becoming the first woman to play the role. But her sight loss has increasingly affected her ability to work, with the actress previously speaking about struggling to see on film sets and having difficulty learning scripts. Despite her condition, she has continued to make public appearances and speak openly about adapting to life with deteriorating vision, stating that "the radio has always been important to me". She was speaking to the BBC ahead of the release of her memoir, called Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, which was written alongside theatre director Brendan O'Hea. Watch the full interview with Dame Judi Dench Emma Barnett speaks to Dame Judi about her sight loss, her career and some memorable moments from her life During the interview, Dame Judi recalled being invited to lunch by former MI6 chief Sir David Spedding, describing the experience as "very exciting". When she asked where her driver should drop her off, she was told: "No, no, we'll send a car to you, we'll come and pick you up." However, she arrived about 20 minutes late after the driver struggled to find her house. "I said, 'I'm sorry for being so late because your driver couldn't find my house.' I loved it." Asked if she had any views on who should play the next Bond, she simply replied: "No." She won an Academy Award for best supporting actress for playing Queen Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love in 1999 Dame Judi also discussed meeting US actor Sidney Poitier, who became the first black man to win the Academy Award for best actor in 1964. She was appearing in Amy's View in New York when Poitier came backstage after a performance. She recalled that director Richard Eyre was in her dressing room, giving her notes, when there was a knock at the door. She said she felt as if she were in a wind tunnel when Poitier walked in, adding: "It was thrilling." Asked what she had said to him, Dame Judi replied: "Not much, a bit of an open mouth. So charming. Very tall." The conversation then turned to her love of Shakespeare. She recalled watching her brother play King Duncan in Macbeth when she was nine. "He walked on and he said, 'What bloody man is that?' I thought, 'Oh my God, this is for me'. He said 'bloody', did you hear that?" She also admitted to being "besotted" by Shakespeare's sonnets: "I just love them." "It's the rhythm of it. It's the rhythm of your heart," she added. "It's the way he's summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything."
