title: What is PHP and why did it spark an international cyber-security alert?
description: AI uncovered long-hidden programming flaws, triggering a rare global cyber-security response.
body: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily. Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs. When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide. The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on Wednesday A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said. Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms. The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker". Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP "We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X. "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said. Tech companies are also racing to secure their systems. E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability. The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz. The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can. "Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said. "The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said. Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale. The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post. The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure. "Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre. Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP. The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said. The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors. title: Is the UK set to green-light a huge untapped oil field in the North Atlantic?
description: Scotland editor James Cook visits Rosebank - the UK's largest known untapped oilfield - in the North Atlantic.
body: This video can not be played The Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea has been allowed to start production after years of debates and legal wrangling - but a decision is yet to be taken on the Rosebank oil field in the North Atlantic. Industry bodies argue that the sites could provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply. However, environmentalists insist that more drilling would hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect billions across the globe. BBC Scotland editor James Cook is at Rosebank, which is scheduled to be up and running by 2027 if approved by the government. Is the UK set to green-light a huge untapped oil field? title: Leicester hit their lowest ebb - but is Martin turning things around?
description: Leicester are 10th in League One, 10 years after winning the Premier League. After hitting their lowest ebb, are there now grounds for optimism?
body: Russell Martin was appointed Leicester boss on a three-year deal in June Leicester are at one of the lowest points in their history. Sitting 10th in League One, it has been a spectacular decline. A decade ago, they were reigning 5,000-1 Premier League champions and the toast of the world. Five years ago, the Foxes lifted the FA Cup for the first time and were challenging for Champions League qualification. Since then they have fallen fast with financial problems, points deductions and the drop to the third tier, leaving the club up for sale. But back-to-back wins this week - for the first time since last November - have shown the shoots of recovery after a stuttering start. This summer was a hard reset and, after three relegations in four years, have the Foxes found a way to recover under head coach Russell Martin? Tuesday's 4-0 thumping of Bromley followed the 2-1 win over Doncaster which dampened the external noise. Martin - a sometimes polarising personality with fans who have criticised his style and ability following a 17-game spell at Rangers last season - had been the target of anger following two wins in eight which left them 17th in League One and a point above the relegation zone. Home defeats by Burton, Oxford and Peterborough were a world away from the Champions League quarter-final against Atletico Madrid in 2017. That has little bearing internally at the club and BBC Sport can reveal the Foxes were working under a transfer embargo for five weeks in the summer. It related to the EFL's Salary Cost Management Protocol (SCMP) with an independent Club Financial Review Panel agreeing future Premier League distributions within Leicester's SCMP calculation could not be used to increase their spending capacity. It meant the club could not sign players until they brought money in, although it only disrupted the order of summer business. Jeremy Monga and Abdul Fatawu were not sold until the middle of July and only after Monga left for Manchester City on 11 July were the Foxes able to bring in Conor Chaplin and Alex McCarthy five days later. Four of the starting XI on Tuesday signed on deadline day and 66% of the players joined after the season started. Leicester missed out on targets who were not willing to wait but Chaplin, McCarthy and Wes Burns were just three who were prepared to hold on to join Martin. It is the relationships the head coach has built and something which has started to turn the tide at Seagrave. Martin inherited a broken, expensive squad, which had lost the faith and connection with supporters and a dressing room which let egos get in the way and lacked work ethic. In a different financial reality, it needed to be stripped back and, including loans and academy exits, 34 players left the club in the summer and 16 arrived. Sources have told BBC Sport the atmosphere at the club has now markedly improved. The £100m training ground is one of the best in the country - with a herb garden and golf course - but has been seen as part of the problem over the decline in standards. Players have been allowed to become too comfortable but Martin has worked hard to change the culture and behaviours. There is a blanket ban on mobile phones in the canteen and anyone breaking the rules is not fined, they run. Players - and staff - have to run the length of the pitch and back in 35 seconds three times, with a 35-second break in between. The same punishment is handed out for lateness, with Martin and his senior staff also adhering to it to set the standards. Earlier this season players left tape and drinks at the swimming pool and were shown a picture the next day. The punishment was the same. Run. King Power bought Leicester in 2010 from Milan Mandaric for £35m There is an acute acceptance the club needs to show and not tell fans about progress. Yet there is calm and a focus behind the scenes with the appointment of James McCarron as sporting director and Martin viewed as giving the club a strong leadership. McCarron watches training most days and has a close working relationship with Martin. Although, despite the positives, it is hard to ignore fan feeling towards the club and chief football officer Jon Rudkin in particular. The frustration towards Rudkin, who has been at the club since 1998, has been constant for years. His relationship with former chief executive Susan Whelan had broken down long before her departure a year ago. Rudkin's policy of also not talking to the media - until this month - has been criticised. He remained quiet during their plunge to League One and while that has been consistent - having not spoken to the press when Leicester were winning the Premier League - it has left an information vacuum and the club being unable to communicate efficiently to supporters. That he finally addressed the fans in an interview with BBC Radio Leicester before defeat to Peterborough speaks volumes of the realisation and determination from the club to try to change - and the dire situation. It was a positive step forward and internally there is a hope it will lead to more appearances, although there needs to be more substance. "We do have to remember he saw us through the good times as well. He was in when it was all going fantastically," Foxes Trust co-chair Lynn Wyeth told BBC Sport. "But do we know what he does all day, do we know if it's all his fault? That's a good question. "It's all very well the fans targeting Russell and Jon but this all goes down to Top (Aiyawatt Srivaddhanaprabha, owner) "It's pretty clear that Rudkin has had his time and since the end of last season and it being put up for sale we've seen more people coming round to the idea King Power and Top needs to go as well." Midfielder John Lundstram is seen as a key architect for Leicester's style Everything has led to a massive fan disconnect with supporters disengaged from the senior leadership. title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
description: Disaffection has often driven down turnout among Arab Israelis, but there is a strong push to get rid of the right-wing governing coalition.
body: Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's election At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power. Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. "I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future." All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab parties Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority. If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists. A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values. Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority. Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis "After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza." Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending. There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis. Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank. How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders? The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government". To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders. Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab parties At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party. I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties. "In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel." Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings. These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas. United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence" While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Abbas has had a taste of power. title: Woman 'scared to turn heating on' due to oil cost
description: Roslynn Garner-Gatley starts using a hot water bottle, bed socks and earlier bedtimes to stay warm.
body: Roslynn Garner-Gatley says she relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water A woman has said she is frightened to put her heating on because the cost of domestic oil has nearly doubled. Roslynn Garner-Gatley, 76, lives in a three-bedroom semi-detached cottage in Yealmpton, south Devon, with no gas supply and relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water. She said her oil tank held 1,000 litres (220 gallons). About six months earlier, she bought 500 litres (110 gallons) for £317 plus VAT but, when she contacted her supplier for a current quote, she was told the same amount would cost £600 plus VAT. Garner-Gatley said: "I did not expect at my age after working for 50 years to be in a situation where I am terrified of putting on the heating because of the price of it." The cost of filling her heating oil tank has nearly doubled Garner-Gatley said she had started going to bed earlier to keep warm while watching television and had recently begun using a hot water bottle and bed socks as evening temperatures dropped. She said instead of keeping hot water on a timer, she only switched it on when she needed it for washing, cooking or bathing before turning it off again. She added that people living in rural areas who depended on oil had "no choice" but to buy it. She said: "After working all my life I didn't expect to be constantly worrying about how to keep warm at my age. It is really quite frightening." Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, according to Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington. Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector. Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong. Minimum order levels set for some customers would also be reviewed, they added. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, said: "We have pledged £53m in support for vulnerable households on heating oil, while helping people switch to clean heat with Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants worth £9,000. "We are also reforming the heating oil sector, holding suppliers to account and giving consumers confidence that they will get a fair deal." Cornwall Council and Devon County Council have money available for households struggling with increasing heating oil costs from their crisis resilience funds, which are provided by the government. Cornwall Council said it had issued payments of £300 to 1,386 households, a total spend of £415,800, which would double after a decision was made to award a further £300 to the same households. The Devon fund, worth about £8.4m a year, is available through district councils, and is targeted at low‑income households facing an "essential cost they cannot afford". Plymouth City Council and Torbay Council also have their own crisis resilience funds. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? title: 'I can't afford to heat my home on my pension'
description: Teresa Goubert says heating is "very expensive" and she was struggling on her pension.
body: Teresa Goubert said the cost of heating had become so expensive that she could not afford to heat her home this winter Some pensioners say they are going to bed early, wearing extra layers and using hot water bottles because they cannot afford to heat their homes this winter. Teresa Goubert, from Guernsey, who uses electric and oil heating, said: "I'm trying to keep it off as long as possible because it's got very expensive and I just can't afford to do it [heat home] on my pension." The States has proposed a 19% increase in the means-tested winter fuel allowance to £50.48 a week. It will be debated in November. Tina Bury, Employment and Social Security President, said: "The fuel allowance is quite a broad brush approach and obviously everyone's needs are different in this area." More news stories for Guernsey Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Ms Goubert, who receives the allowance, said: "The first £70 of it is standing charges, so you're only getting sort of £100... just over £100 for your month, which is nothing at the moment." "I'm putting blankets on me and then if I get too cold, I go up to bed, you know, just put more blankets on up there. That's the only solution." Islander Katina Jones, who lives with her husband, said they waited as long as they could before turning the heating on. "Once I make a cup of tea, I use the extra hot water in a hot water bottle to use just to keep us warm." Sheila Cornelius, who lives in an over-55 housing development in the island, said: "It's not very good because I don't believe in being cold so of course all my money, most of it goes on there. "Luckily I've got some nice thick clothes that I can wear instead of having the heating on full, you know, [I] can't afford it." Gareth Wordingham, from Guernsey Electricity, said: "The standing charges this year only went up by 3% so it wasn't a large proportion of the increase itself. "We buy our electricity in international markets, years in advance, so that smooths the price that we pay or our customers' pay. "We have to balance between the smaller customers and also those larger customers who might be equally vulnerable, a family with children, could be equally strapped for money." Nick Crolla, head of marketing for fuel suppliers, Rubis Channel Islands, said: "Since August, we've seen prices increase by up to 30%. "We are really seeing that we're not shielded from the volatile international market. "If customers are concerned about the cost of heating oil, the best thing is to come speak to us, we have payment options to help the customer ease the volatility of the oil prices." Bury, said the committee could respond if heating oil prices increased sharply over winter. "Should we get to the depths of winter and there's a massive spike in costs of oil, for example, we do have the ability to react to that," she added. title: 'An £8k service charge left me unable to pay bills'
description: Housing association Curo defends large increases to leaseholder bills.
body: Callum Maddern says he is still straddled with debt after facing a huge increase in his bills A housing association has defended the charges faced by its leaseholders after many complained of huge bill increases to pay for maintenance. Callum Maddern, who lives in Bath, said he had seen his service charge increase six-fold to more than £8,000 per year after Curo said vital work needed doing on his accommodation block. "I didn't have enough money to put the heating on," he said. "I had water on my sink and coffee tables that was freezing. I'd be lying in bed and I could see my breath." Curo, which says it does not make any money from the contributions, said it was "trying to work with residents to prepare them for these bills". Man jailed for 'cruel' attack that killed pensioner Community ownership could restore city landmark Student who murdered uni housemate jailed for life When Maddern bought his flat in 2023, the annual service charge was about £1,300 per year. He was told there was £5,000 in what is known as a sinking fund to cover any necessary works. But the following year, he received a bill for £8,000 to go towards fire safety work and new windows. "Originally I thought there was some kind of mistake," he said. But when he queried the charge, Curo confirmed it was accurate. Maddern describes "constant delays" in his attempts to reach out to Curo and negotiate. "They were totally uncaring," he said, adding he was told he could sell his property and pay the fee that way. Maddern said he ended up selling possessions and taking out loans to pay for the work. While he said he knew that as a leaseholder he had a responsibility to contribute towards maintenance costs, he questioned why everything suddenly had to be done in a three-year period. "If new windows are needed, absolutely that must be scheduled in. But to have everything in the space of three years, surely that is not a good approach," he added. Andrew Snee, director of housing and support at Curo, acknowledged the way charges had been communicated could have been better and said he wanted to apologise "if our correspondence has caused any concern or upset". But Snee denied the company could have managed the costs better, describing the situation as a "perfect storm". "The cost of living is increasing, the cost of contracts is increasing, at the same time we've got increased legislation around property safety and fire safety, which has to be a good thing but it does come at a cost," he said. "We are being as honest and transparent as we can to deliver these costs in as caring a way as we can. Keep talking to us." Ken Pearson says Curo have a responsibility to prepare leaseholders for large bills Ken Pearson owns his flat in a different block elsewhere in Bath. He says his sinking fund contributions dropped to £124 per year when Curo took over his building, but then increased dramatically to £1,767 when a new roof was needed. "We were only being prepared for the new roof when it was a matter of urgency because two flats upstairs had leaks," he said. "We should have paid over a longer period." Pearson took Curo to a tribunal over the sinking fund increases and lost his case, but now believes there needs to be a change in the law to ensure that landlords prepare leaseholders better for expected works. "Curo have failed us and need to be held to account," he said. "They have not picked up that there was this financial catastrophe coming along." In response, Snee said: "I think sinking funds have been managed as well as we can in today's world with all of the pressures on costs and contracts." He added: "If you've been building a sinking fund up and decoration has taken place, that would have potentially drawn quite a lot out. "Then if you're looking at a roof replacement in four to five years' time, not only are you looking at paying for that you're also starting from zero." The government is working on a new law that would ban the use of leasehold for most new flats and create a new right for leaseholders to request improvements. title: Vickery's journey from World Cup winner to bodybuilder at 50
description: Why England Rugby World Cup winner Phil Vickery has started entering bodybuilding competitions at the age of 50.
body: This video can not be played Vickery's journey from Rugby World Cup winner to bodybuilder It could have been deep in the bowels of English rugby's national stadium in Twickenham. Instead, Phil Vickery was backstage at the Physical Culture Show in Hull, waiting for his moment - but this time as a bodybuilder. However, the feeling was familiar. "It reminded me of being in the changing room before the big game, your nerves - are you going to be sick, you're happy, you're not happy, I can do this, this is raw," he said, adding that just recalling that moment earlier this month makes his hair stand on end. "That nervous energy and waiting and then, oh, it's just a horrific feeling. All the girls and boys can relate to that, because that's the same at whatever level of sport you play. "I'm questioning myself, should I even be there? But then you go, actually, do you know what? I've done the work. I've done the graft." What started as an ambition to get fit has ignited a passion for mental and physical fitness, and for Vickery being the best version of himself. It's 23 years since Phil Vickery was part of the England team that won the Rugby World Cup final in Australia Then came a challenge from his friend Lee Powell and, with support from his physical trainer Dave Campbell, Vickery entering bodybuilding competitions at the age of 50. Posing to the strains of the familiar World Cup anthem World in Union. "What it probably did for me is ignite that ex-pro rugby player in me of detail, discipline, turning up when it's dark and dingy and cold, competing, and we went from there," Vickery said. "What I've fallen in love with, with the bodybuilding, it's a very singular, isolated sport, because it is you against you. It's not about anyone else. "There is no out. You can't hide behind a keyboard. You are stood on stage. Your physique and what you look like is a direct reflection of your effort and what you have done, and that is quite scary." The former Gloucester and Wasps prop won 73 caps for England, five more for the British and Irish Lions. Victory at the 2003 Rugby World Cup in Australia was a sporting zenith in a career that includes being a businessman and a Celebrity MasterChef winner. But personal struggles and a diagnosis for probable CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy), for which Vickery is part of a continuing litigation battle, means he has had to manage his mental health. "We all deal with things differently," he said. "I think having the gym and having that space to be able to work is really important for my mental health, but also for my body physically, because it is broken, so I use it in that sense. "I think the one thing I really struggled with when I finished playing is I trained to play and I couldn't find that reason to train afterwards. "And although you should train for yourself or your wellbeing, it probably took a low point or something to actually trigger it. "But, probably, the bodybuilding - or doing the show or doing the original transformation - I have to close the circle. You know, you have a plan, you make a plan, you implement it, you commit to it, see it through, and then it's over and it's done. And then you move on." Vickery won 73 caps for England and five for the British and Irish Lions as a prop forward When Vickery took to the stage in Hull, he says he weighed about 99kg. More defined, but lighter than his playing days when he said his weight would range between 118kg and 135kg. "[On stage] you look the best version of you that you could look, but you feel the worst. It's kind of a silly sport but it's amazing what the human body can do. "Age, for me, doesn't bother me at all. I still think I'm 27. My body tells me different." Training now involves three or four weight sessions a week, combined with daily walks (fasting cardio) and a protein-rich diet. He hopes more shows will follow in the future. "I can't do what I used to do and I think the battle for me, certainly when I finished [playing] and even to this day, is you cannot get back those feelings that you had when you used to do what you do," he said. "I think doing things which can get you outside, test you physically and mentally, and put you in those uncomfortable positions. It's repurposing the skills that you've learned. You've just got to use them in a different way." Vickery is known for his openness. He posts regularly on his social media channels about his health and fitness. But he's not comfortable with being labelled as an "influencer". "We are all influencers," he said. "I don't think everyone should go bodybuilding. My message is trying to be positive. Get out, do something, make a plan." "I know I will never be a top bodybuilder. But it doesn't stop me, it doesn't stop me having a go and being the best version of me that I can be." title: Women targeted by police who 'abused the badge'
description: Two women preyed upon by serving police officers describe their ordeals and why they are speaking out.
body: Catherine and Naomi were both targeted by serving police officers Two women who were preyed upon by serving police officers they trusted have described their ordeals and why they decided to speak out. Naomi Meadows was raped by a detective she met online in Devon, while Catherine Dobson was subjected to years of coercive and controlling behaviour by a Lancashire police officer who worked in a sexual offences unit. Catherine said: "He used his job, he used his power and he abused the badge. Whatever his motives were, I will never understand." The women waived their right to anonymity to tell their harrowing stories as part of a BBC investigation that uncovered more than 1,200 domestic abuse allegations made in three years against police officers and special constables across England and Wales. Professional standards investigations were opened into allegations including rape, sexual assault, grievous bodily harm, stalking and serious violence. Most cases were discontinued, subjected to no further action or dropped because of a lack of evidence or victims withdrawing their complaints. Campaigners say more needs to be done to tackle police-perpetrated abuse despite repeated warnings about failures to identify and remove dangerous officers in the wake of the 2021 murder of Sarah Everard in London by serving Metropolitan Police officer Wayne Couzens. Catherine said she had no reason to disbelieve the lies told by her abuser Catherine Dobson, from Rawtenstall in Lancashire, said she was asked out for a drink by Michael Harvey after a chance meeting in a supermarket. "The only reason I trusted him was because he told me he was a detective in the police," she said. "We got on really well: this was a man who was paid to look after the most vulnerable in society - women and children who'd been abused - so that made me feel safe." What Catherine did not realise was that Harvey had already accessed police computer systems to obtain her address and phone number. Cracks appeared early on in their relationship. Catherine grew suspicious that Harvey had not introduced her to his children and would not let her post pictures of them together online. When she discovered Harvey had been texting other women, she was told they were victims of sexual offences he was investigating. Catherine said she had no reason to disbelieve him. "At the time I backed off because who am I to stop a victim of a crime like that from being supported by the officer?" It was when she tried to end the relationship that the psychological abuse escalated. Catherine said he told her he had been abused as a child and later made unfounded claims he had been tested for cancer. "I believed him," she said. "I felt responsible for keeping him well." Catherine believes it was part of a pattern of emotional manipulation designed to stop her leaving. She said Harvey threatened to take his own life on several occasions if she left him, including once during a phone call while she was at work. "I called the police immediately, then I drove back to the house and I was in bits," she said. "I honestly thought I'd open the door and find him dead. "The police were there and they were just about to bash the door in when he calmly opened it wrapped in a towel and he said, 'What's the problem officer? I've just been in the shower'. "I felt like this hysterical mess who'd made the whole thing up. But when you're in it, you're not thinking straight." During years of emotional blackmail, Catherine described how Harvey had faked an anaphylactic shock and threatened to jump out of a moving car. She eventually left him, but it was another six years before she filed a police report. Explaining her hesitation, she said: "Who is going to believe me over a detective on the sex offenders' unit?" Harvey was arrested in 2023 and was jailed earlier this year. He was sentenced to two-and-a-half years after admitting coercive and controlling behaviour and the unauthorised use of police computers. He was cleared of three counts of rape. Lancashire Constabulary described Harvey's behaviour as "abhorrent" and said it had "no place in policing". The force said it remained committed to protecting women and girls. The BBC understands another woman complained to the force about Harvey before he met Catherine but was told he had not committed an offence. Lancashire Constabulary declined to comment, citing an ongoing complaints process. Catherine believes Harvey subjected her to a pattern of emotional manipulation designed to stop her leaving Harvey's case was not an isolated incident. The BBC sent Freedom of Information requests to 45 police forces across England and Wales, asking for details of domestic abuse allegations involving police officers. Just over half responded, disclosing a total of 1,280 cases investigated by professional standards departments in the three years to January. The allegations included rape, sexual assault, coercive control, stalking and non-fatal strangulation. Former Merseyside PC Ryan Theaker was jailed earlier this month for 11 years. A court heard his victim had told him to "get off me" more than 300 times as he subjected her to an 82-minute ordeal in a Liverpool hotel room. Theaker was one of few convicted of a criminal offence, however. Most concluded cases resulted in no further action, including 96% in the North West. Nearly half of the 1,280 cases in England and Wales disclosed to the BBC were recorded by the largest force, the Metropolitan Police. Dozens of its officers were accused of rape or other sexual offences. Former Merseyside Police constable Ryan Theaker was jailed earlier this month for 11 years Devon and Cornwall PC Stuart Mines was convicted last year of rape. He met Naomi Meadows on a dating website before they agreed to meet in person. Naomi told the BBC: "You kind of have a childlike trust because they're the police - they're honest, trustworthy." title: NI risks missing 2030 energy goals, says Stormont committee
description: A committee hears that Northern Ireland could lose out on economic opportunities if action is not accelerated.
body: Daniel McCrossan is the chair of the Public Accounts Committee Time is running out to meet key targets within Stormont's energy strategy by 2030, a committee has said. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) report followed an inquiry into the Department for the Economy's (DfE) delivery of the net zero strategy. The PAC heard that Northern Ireland could lose out on significant economic opportunities if action was not speeded up. Committee chair Daniel McCrossan said the government had a "responsibility to create the conditions needed for investment to proceed, otherwise there is a real risk it will go elsewhere". During its inquiry, the PAC heard from business and energy sector representatives that uncertainty around future policies and delivery timescales was affecting investment decisions. It heard investment could be diverted to Great Britain, Ireland and other European markets where existing factors were seen as more certain. PAC members said it was unacceptable that delays were affecting projects which could support economic growth, create jobs and strengthen energy security. Stormont's strategy aims at achieving net zero emissions by 2050 and ensuring at least 80% of electricity consumption comes from renewable sources Published in 2021, the NI energy strategy included a plan to fully decarbonise by 2050 and ensure that at least 80% of electricity consumption comes from renewable sources. McCrossan, said that despite the strategy presenting a major economic opportunity for Northern Ireland, the evidence heard "pointed to growing frustration among businesses and investors over delays, policy uncertainty and a lack of clarity around delivery". The PAC chair added: "Our message is clear - there can be no further delays. We want to see barriers removed so that delivery can be accelerated. "Almost £124m of public money has been spent on energy-related programmes, since 2020. We need assurances that Northern Ireland is on track." The PAC heard that uncertainty around future energy policies and delivery timescales was affecting external investment decisions He said that despite the DfE "consulting widely" during the development of the strategy, the PAC found "that significant weaknesses had undermined its implementation". PAC deputy chair Tom Buchanan said: "The next four years are critical. We need to see decisive action, stronger oversight and a clear focus on results. "Our report makes 11 recommendations, including the publication and regular updating of the department's Energy Policy Statement. Funded plans must also be brought forward to address grid, infrastructure and energy storage constraints." While the committee noted the department's confidence in achieving the strategy's ambition of a £2bn green economy, members said the challenge was turning ambition into results so that Northern Ireland could realise the investment, jobs and wider benefits promised by the transition to net zero. title: Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't be on stage, I can't do a film, I can't read anymore'
description: The actress sat down with her friend and fellow actor Brendan O'Hea to talk to the BBC's Emma Barnett ahead of the launch of her memoir.
body: This video can not be played Actress Dame Judi Dench opened up about her struggle with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), telling the BBC she can longer "be on stage, do a film and read anymore". "They said this summer was absolutely sensational with bluebells, I couldn't see one," she told BBC's Emma Barnett. Dench is releasing her memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? written with fellow actor Brendan O'Hea at the end of October in the UK. The Oscar-winning star revealed she was diagnosed with AMD back in 2012, which left her struggling to read scripts and recognise faces. title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?
description: How fair are AI recruitment tools that help decide our future, and what happens when we click "apply"?
body: Sheeraz Gulsher says there are "huge worries" about AI I have lost track of the number of people who have told me they have applied for hundreds of jobs, only to be met with rejection after rejection. Often, they said it felt like a human had not even looked at their applications. There are lots of different types of recruitment tools. Some match candidates to jobs, others grade and screen CVs. Employers use them to save time sifting through applications, but there are growing concerns that these tools could be biased. I want to find out how fair AI recruitment tools being used to help decide our futures really are - and what happens when we click "apply". There are concerns about the increasing use of AI in recruitment A London-based non-profit organisation, People Like Us, is raising awareness of people's legal right to challenge automated decisions when they disagree with the outcome. A survey conducted by Censuswide among 2,000 UK workers who had applied for at least one job in the past 24 months found that 75% were unaware of their right to challenge an automated rejection. Sheeraz Gulsher, CEO of People Like Us, is leading the campaign called Reject the Rejections, which calls on employers to improve transparency and accountability in the use of AI and automated recruitment systems. He describes the current situation as an "AI war", with candidates "resorting to AI to bolster their applications" while "employers are dealing with huge amounts of applications". Gulsher said: "We can't say for certain that every company is operating its automated or AI systems without bias. That's why we're calling for companies to audit these systems, publish the results and have them independently assessed. "In our research, we found guidance from the Information Commissioner's Office, external stating that people subject to certain automated decisions have the right to request a human review. We're trying to remind people of that right, as many simply aren't aware of it." The research also found 70% of ethnically diverse jobseekers had altered or concealed information on their CVs, including their country of origin, religion or name, out of fear that recruitment software or AI tools would reject their applications. This compares with 57% of white candidates. Vivi says she needs feedback as a jobseeker Business consultant Vivi, who lives in Lewisham, was made redundant earlier this year. She says she has applied for so many jobs that she's given up and started her own company. "There's one instance where applications closed on Friday and I got a reply on a Saturday morning basically saying that I should work on my skills and come back in six months. But it was so obvious that nobody had assessed my skills." If she had known she could ask for a human to review her application, she might have done things differently. "I would definitely go back and ask for a human to look at my application and if it is a 'no', that's fine, but feedback helps me as a jobseeker." Hema was made redundant in June Hema, 49, from Surrey, is an HR and talent professional who has worked internationally across multiple sectors. She was made redundant in June and has since tracked more than 100 job applications and recruitment opportunities. "A lot of them have been automatically rejected within 24 to 36 hours." She added: "I've always landed a job in 10 applications, so to be nearing 100 is completely out of this world." While she is "hesitant" about asking for a human review in case she jeopardises her application, she believes "a human recruiter can see the fuller picture". "If you've got an in-house recruitment team, they know the culture, they can see the type of language that you're using in your CV, in your cover letter, during a phone screen." Of the 425 recruiters CV Library spoke to, about 90 said they used AI in the CV screening stage. Alec Stanwell, director of marketing, believes there is a "perception gap". "Candidates almost universally believe that employers are using AI to screen their CVs, filter them and to screen them as they go through the process and that is happening but nowhere near as much as candidates think it is. "That perception gap is a problem because candidates are now writing their CVs, and applications, through the lens of 'an AI bot is going to be reviewing this rather than a human'. He adds this is a problem because recruiters are seeing all CVs look the same because "they're all written by AI, or polished by AI". He says this creates a "perfect storm" because AI is then more likely to be used to filter through a large volume of applications. "We're going to end up with computers hiring computers, but we're actually in the world of hiring people." In the four years to December 2022, Stanford researchers analysed four million job applications processed by an AI hiring tool, external. Some candidates were rejected from multiple roles more often than would have been expected if they had been assessed by each employer independently. The analysis also indicated black and Asian applicants were recommended for jobs at lower rates. But the evidence is limited. They only looked at one AI hiring tool, and other factors such as education and immigration status could have also played a role. The hiring tool assessed did not respond to our requests for comment. The people I have interviewed are not talking about any company in particular, but concerns over AI used in recruitment are also playing out in the courts. One company, Workday, is facing legal claims, external in the US, alleging that its tools discriminated against job applicants. The case is ongoing, but Workday denies the claims and says its tools do not make hiring decisions. More generally, it says its tools "support rather than replace human judgement". title: No order, no seat: Starbucks China rolls out new store policy
description: Starbucks says it is improving customers' in-store experience as it competes with homegrown rivals.
body: "Purchase to sit" signs are popping up in Starbucks stores around China Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there. A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes. Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee. Starbucks stores around the world have also been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers. In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores, after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow. In North America, Starbucks reversed its open-door policy which for years allowed people to use their seats and toilets without buying anything, saying that it wanted to "prioritise" paying customers. Starbucks China is now following suit. Ahead of the official announcement on Wednesday, reports of the new seating policy at China's Starbucks stores had been circulating this week - along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores. Many on Chinese social media welcomed the new policy. "Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit," "There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented. Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying. Since opening its first store there in 1999, China has become Starbucks' second-largest market. But it has faced stiff competition in recent years from Luckin and other local brands that offer cheaper products. Luckin also offers a robust app-based ordering system that prioritises grab-and-go transactions, challenging Starbucks' model of a full cafe experience where people can sit down and enjoy their food and drinks. In 2023, Luckin overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain. Starbucks said last year it would sell 60% stake of its business in China as part of a $4bn (£3.04bn) deal with investment firm Boyu Capital. In another statement on Wednesday, Starbucks China said it was planning to increase staffing and improve digital systems at its stores, among other investments to "ensure customers receive timely and warm service even during peak hours". title: US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the claim, noting that US initiated trade actions against Canada.
body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, right, and Ontario Premier Doug Ford deny that their country is interfering in the US midterm elections The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms. The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over "potential interference", and that ministers and premiers "openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances". Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Relations between the North American neighbours have hardened during the second Trump administration. The midterms will determine which political party controls both branches of the US Congress, which could have a significant impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The fact sheet released by the US Embassy on Wednesday alleges the Canadian government "brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances". It cites comments and actions, like meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US. For example, it says that when Industry Minister Mélanie Joly was asked what she expected regarding tariffs if Democrats were to win midterm elections, she responded, "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates." Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed Canada's federal government, it states, to consider additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from "politically significant states to the current administration's base of support". Asked on Wednesday about the allegations, Carney noted that it was the US that first initiated trade actions against Canada. "We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said. He said his government's response has been "in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy". Carney, who was announcing a nearly C$9bn ($6.2bn) aid package in response to US tariffs, was accompanied by both Joly and Ford. Ford said that he has "no interest at all" in interfering in US elections. "I'll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability," Ford said, adding that he will focus on Ontario and Canada. "The people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms," he said. Last week, Minister Joly denied Canadian interference and said that Canadians "never accept that also being done to us in Canada", according to CBC. She said that her recent visits to the US were "to attract investments" from American companies, which she plans to continue. What are the US midterms? A simple guide Washington and Ottawa have argued for months over tariffs and trade, which once flowed freely across their borders, and the effects of Canada's counter measures. Earlier this month, US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra warned that US officials are "closely watching" Canada's politicians for signs of election interference. Trump administration officials have also been accused of making inappropriate remarks about the separation referendum in the province of Alberta this week. A petition calling for Hoekstra's removal from his post for "undermining the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relations" has received more than 280,000 signatures. title: UK's gaps in Arctic defence leave it open to Russian attacks, committee warns
description: A report by MPs urges the UK to address capability gaps including a lack of Royal Navy warships and submarines, as Russia seeks to dominate the region.
body: A UK carrier conducts operations in the High North and Arctic The UK has "glaring gaps" in its ability to defend the Arctic region, leaving it vulnerable to potential Russian attacks, a report by MPs has warned. The Commons Defence Committee said a shortage of Royal Navy warships and submarines was leaving the country's critical infrastructure in the High North, including undersea cables and energy supplies, exposed. In the event of a conflict, the report added that Russia could threaten the UK's population, civilian and military infrastructure and vital supply routes across the Atlantic from the US. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said it is "clear-eyed about the threat Russia posed" and is investing heavily to protect Britain's undersea cables. Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer previously warned that Russia could attack Nato by the end of the decade. The High North - which includes the Arctic circle and areas adjacent to it - has become central to the UK's defence concerns in recent years. Earlier this year, the MoD said Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic is now back to the same levels as the Cold War era. In the new report, MPs highlighted a "shockingly low availability" of submarines and said there was a temporary loss in ability to operate them beneath Arctic ice. "Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening Nato sea lanes, UK critical infrastructure and the UK's nuclear deterrent," it added. Chair of the Defence Committee, Tan Dhesi, said: "This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage." The work to address these gaps "cannot start soon enough," he added. In light of uncertainty over US support for Nato, the report said the UK should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (Jef), a UK-led military coalition of northern European nations, should focus more on the High North. An MoD spokesperson said the Jef was already "strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats". Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said: "If Nato could be at war with Russia as soon as 2030, as the former prime minister warned, that means time is just as important as money. "To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it's too late". title: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits
description: Judges will be given new powers to impose tougher prison punishments on offenders who refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing.
body: The new measures given to judges could see offenders confined to cells for up to three weeks Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing. The tougher sanctions, due to come into effect next year, build on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years for contempt of court. The move is the latest bid to push killers to attend court, with the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) acknowledging that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter them if they are already behind bars. "Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said. "Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences", she added. The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, social visits could be banned for nearly a month and any prison privileges revoked for longer. Judges will also being able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for almost three months for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing. For criminals aged 18-20, judges will be able to impose similar restrictions but for shorter periods of time, the MoJ said. However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions. But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves". The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa, law graduate Zara Aleena and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa have previously advocated for changes to the laws. All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings. Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court. Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman OBE, said the announcement follows "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice". She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve". title: US State Department orders some staff to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate
description: The warning to US officials comes as at least three people die in the latest strikes at an airport and an oil field.
body: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis also attacked the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh earlier this month The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country. Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month. The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years. This video can not be played Watch: Who are the Houthis, and why are they so hard to fight? "The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement. "Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added. The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly". In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said. No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces. The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule. An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks Who are the Houthis and what do they want? title: The Papers: 'Drill, Andy Drill!' and a Budget for 'bloody-minded entrepreneurs'
description: Several of today's papers continue to follow the "storm" surrounding Andy Burnham's decision to approve a new gas field and what that will mean for future ones.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is "facing a storm" for approving drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which the Metro has headlined as "Drill, Andy, Drill!" The move has been praised by US President Donald Trump, the paper says, but not by those concerned about the project's environmental and economic impact. Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh could reject a giant Rosebank oil field, sources have told the Guardian, after the approval of the Jackdaw gas field on Wednesday. According to officials, Fahnbulleh is considering "blocking what would be one of the biggest oil fields in the North Sea", the paper says. "Pathetic" reads the Daily Mail headline about the Foreign Secretary Ed "Miliband's Net Zero madness" on potentially rejecting the Rosebank oil field. The Daily Mail calls Labour's approval of the Jackdaw gas field as a "rare outbreak of common sense". The upcoming Budget will cut regulations and "back business in Britain making a profit", the chancellor has told the Times, in a move that will be for "bloody-minded entrepreneurs". The Telegraph has been analysing Russian fishing vessels above critical UK undersea cables and suggests the Kremlin is using the fleet to "spy on Britain". The paper found "more than 500 incidents in which Russian trawlers loitered above vital communications cables". Headteachers have spoken to the i Paper over fears their schools will have to find money for a national 3.5% teacher pay rise, "despite claims it would be 'fully funded'". The UK government has denied that the education secretary said the pay rise would be fully funded, the paper reports. The Financial Times leads on the richest man in the world, Elon Musk, as he considers merging his two companies SpaceX and Tesla into a "sprawling conglomerate spanning rockets, satellites, social media, robots and cars". Investors are welcoming the idea, the paper reports, and shares in SpaceX surged on Wednesday. "Britain must be ready" the Daily Express reports, amid growing threats of war. Senior Conservatives are urging Burnham to increase spending on defence to combat a rise in Russian threats, the paper says. The Sun splashes on a picture of former Manchester City player Kyle Walker's "4 In A Row" leg tattoo that he said he will have removed if the club are stripped of its titles for breaching financial rules. The club was found guilty by an independent commission of more than 100 charges. City has denied any wrongdoing and has appealed the ruling. The Prince of Wales faces off the Duke of Sussex on the front page of the Daily Mirror above the headline "Ruled Out". According to a royal insider, Prince William has "no intention" of engaging with Prince Harry, the paper reports, after the younger brother called for a reconciliation. The Daily Star leads on TV personality and presenter Ryan Clark who said he "carpeted for missing work because of an air traffic strike" at the BBC. And Donald Trump is the lead image on the Independent after he apparently "lashed out" at reporter Andrew Feinberg. The Independent reporter asked the president about fraud tip-off payments, which reportedly "triggered Trump". Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: The real reasons US politicians are getting older
description: No country for young men and women: why do older politicians seem to have such a tight grip on the US political system?
body: The real reasons US politicians are getting older Not many US politicians have endured for as long as Hal Rogers, who will go into November's midterm elections seeking his 24th term in the House of Representatives. The 88-year-old Republican has represented Kentucky's 5th congressional district since 1981, making him the longest serving member of the House of Representatives. He was elected on the same night Ronald Reagan won his first presidential term under the slogan "Let's make America great again", a phrase later revived by Donald Trump. Among the challengers Rogers beat to win the nomination this year was one 60 years his junior. But Rogers, born in the 1930s, is far from the only senior US politician to have stuck at the job into their 80s. Others to have done so include US President Donald Trump, 80; Trump's predecessor Joe Biden, who left office at 82; and Nancy Pelosi, who stepped down as the Democratic leader in the House at the same age. Chuck Grassley, 93, is still a senator. He entered politics in 1958, before Alaska and Hawaii were even US states. Hal Rogers, far left, with Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, centre, in 1996 The age and health of some politicians has raised widespread concern within both Republican and Democratic circles, however, reigniting questions about whether age limits or health checks should be imposed. The US is well known for its "gerontocracy", a government ruled by people who are significantly older than most of the adult population. At the other end of the age spectrum, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under the age of 45 among comparable democracies, according to research from the Inter-Parliamentary Union. So why are so few young people becoming politicians? And for those who do enter politics, can they make a success of it? Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November. Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters. When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream. The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans. Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates. Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website. Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says. The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56. In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington Mitch McConnell's recent long spell of absence has raised questions But the median age of Congress members has ticked upwards over time. Congressional records show that the lowest median ages in the House and Senate were both recorded in the early 1980s - at 48 and 52 respectively. The average ages of a House member and a senator at the start of the current Congress were 58 and 65 respectively, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center. The median age of a US citizen is 39. There is now also a sharper focus on the health and acuity of some of the nation's oldest politicians. Joe Biden's age became a major issue while he was in office. To a lesser extent Trump has faced questions too. So too has Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, with increasing regularity, after a months-long absence from Congress to undergo medical treatment. Meanwhile, on the Democratic side, Maxine Waters, 88, faces a leadership challenge as the lead Democrat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee, with her age considered by some to be a factor counting against her. Some of the most vocal critics of this so-called gerontocracy have been candidates who identify as democratic socialists, meaning that their political views are further to the left than those of the Democratic Party mainstream. These candidates tend to campaign heavily on the cost of living and other issues that cut through to Millennials and Gen Z, and their supporters skew younger too. The demographic profile of people who vote tends to skew older, like the elected officials themselves. Pew research highlights that the proportion of non-voters who are young (aged 18 to 29) has been increasing. In the 2020 US election, 25% of non-voters belonged to that age category, according to Pew. Four years later,

title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
description: For the first time, the Treasury calculates how much the UK could have raised by investing North Sea proceeds.
body: The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea. After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund. Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund. A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks. It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go? It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time. "The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said. "If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds." On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth. The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's. "Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me. It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said. Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era. The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories. Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996. The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s. I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund. Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic. It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future. While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance. UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits. Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that. Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past? How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?
