title: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroad
description: With graduate jobs hard to come by, more young adults are reported to be considering emigrating.
body: Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseas Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place. "I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails." More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey, external of 15,000 final year university students. Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high. UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report, external. For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading? While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show., external In addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme,, external British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years. Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than London Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for insurance giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First. She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London. Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched. "People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life." Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures, external from the UK's Office for National Statistics. It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived. After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US. Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunities Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University. West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching. "I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live. "In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences." The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult. One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends. Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from Finland This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design. Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020. "Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently." Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon. "To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities." Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas. "When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational." Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London. "I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better." title: Goal, assist... goal-kick - Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials
description: Why Declan Rice backs his England team-mate Harry Kane to win the Ballon d'Or after Arsenal's draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League.
body: This video can not be played Is it 'phenomenal' Kane's year to lift the Ballon d'Or? Even by Harry Kane's remarkable standards, this was mightily impressive. There were fewer than 25 minutes on the clock during Bayern Munich's thrilling 2-2 draw with Arsenal in the Champions League when the forward took matters into his own hands in a bid to break the deadlock. As the Premier League champions prepared to defend a Bayern goal-kick, Kane seized the initiative by launching his side up the pitch with a raking 80-yard pass. It was a moment of remarkable ingenuity from the England international, one that almost ended with Bayern taking the lead. "Under Vincent Kompany, he has been given a level of trust that he has probably never had before under any other manager," former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport. "For all the things we've seen him do and the positions we've seen him roam into, nobody has seen him take a goal-kick before. "But even someone like Manuel Neuer, who is his senior and has been at Bayern for a large part of his career, sees Harry Kane put the ball down and thinks, 'OK, sure'. He lets Harry go for it because he thinks whatever he sees is going to be correct. "At the same time, there were Bayern players running forward because they knew that the ball could come. "For him to be taking a goal-kick is not something you may want to see very often. You don't necessarily want your number nine to be THAT deep, but the nature of his game when he is playing for Bayern is to roam, and today it was a huge benefit to the team." Although Kane was denied the opportunity to add another outstanding assist to his already impressive catalogue, he did not have to wait long to make another decisive contribution. After Eberechi Eze had put Arsenal ahead, Kane helped Bayern restore parity, bending a sumptuous pass around Jurrien Timber for Alphonso Davies to finish. The England captain then fired the hosts in front from the penalty spot midway through the second half, taking his career tally of goals against Arsenal to 16. But Declan Rice struck late on to earn Arsenal a share of the spoils. Kane recorded 40 touches in Wednesday's 2-2 draw with Arsenal For Kane, it was another mesmerising performance that underlined his credentials as the frontrunner for the 2026 Ballon d'Or. The former Tottenham Hotspur captain, 33, could become the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the prestigious individual award, with Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Paris St-Germain forward and current holder Ousmane Dembele among the favourites. Kane was named on the 30-man shortlist in September, with the winner due to be announced on Monday following a vote by an international jury of 100 journalists. "He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves. The year he has had has been remarkable," Arsenal and England midfielder Declan Rice told TNT Sports. "When you play with him, you realise how good he is, and when you play against him, you see how much of a pain it is. "He is ridiculous, such a good player, and I am lucky I can play with him, not so lucky I have to play against him." By scoring against Arsenal on Wednesday night, Kane became only the second player in Champions League history to find the net in 10 consecutive matches. The only other player to achieve the feat was five-time Ballon d'Or winner Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored in 11 successive matches for Real Madrid between June 2017 and April 2018. "Kane certainly looks at home at Bayern. He understands the team and its system, and they all understand him. They know that when he gets the ball at his feet, wherever that may be, something good can happen," Onuoha added. "I think all the Bayern players are really playing into that, but then Harry steps up and scores a penalty as well. "Having freedom is probably the best way to describe what he has got playing for Bayern, because he will work hard defensively, which allows him the freedom to be creative when he is in attack. For now, he certainly is thriving." Kane's goal against Arsenal took his tally to 156 in 158 appearances since joining Bayern Munich from Tottenham in 2023. It was another night to remember for the England captain, but the best could yet be to come, with the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London looming. "It would be amazing to win," said Kane afterwards. "The voting closed a long time ago so there's nothing I can do, just wait and see what happens." This video can not be played Is Kane too 'low-key' to win the Ballon d'Or? title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
description: With immigration curbs and tech firms cutting foreign hiring, US residency is becoming a distant dream for many Indians.
body: Indian tech workers are facing growing uncertainty amid US immigration curbs For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country. But that may end soon. Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway. New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship. The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say. Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally. "Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds. Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers. A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26. BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered. Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them. But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business. Vice President JD Vance's remarks on H-1B workers added to concerns over US immigration policy A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level. "A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said. Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders. Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets. While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants". While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation. Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs. Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all. Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible. While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation". Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs. Indians dominate the US employment green card backlog The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher. But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process. Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises. Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next." While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest. Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP). Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category. title: 'Betrayed by my body': The taboo health issue women are talking about on social media
description: Women are sharing their experiences with chronic urinary tract infections on social media in an effort to break the stigma surrounding UTIs.
body: Adrianne says her chronic UTI has impacted her physically and mentally "The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells her roughly 8,000 followers in a video on TikTok. For nearly five years, Adrianne has lived with a chronic urinary tract infection (UTI) - a condition it took her two years to get a diagnosis for. In that time she was wrongly told it was colon cancer, Crohn's disease or even that her partner must have been cheating and had given her a sexually transmitted infection. What started as one UTI in 2022 became a debilitating cycle. "It has completely stripped me of everything: being able to work properly, my relationships, my friendships, going out, being able to have a normal social life," says Adrianne, who works in digital marketing in London. The 29-year-old was eventually diagnosed privately with a chronic UTI - something experts estimate could affect up to 1.7 million women in the UK, external. Men and children are also affected. Adrianne is not alone in sharing her story and coping mechanisms on social media to fight the stigma surrounding UTIs. A quick search on Tiktok or Instagram shows hundreds of posts of women of all ages talking about the reality of living with recurrent and chronic UTIs. "I felt incredibly nervous to put myself out there, but there's now this community of people who can share tips with each other, and understand each other," said Adrianne, saying her posts have had a "really positive response". This video can not be played Like ‘weeing lava’: Living with chronic UTIs A chronic UTI, which has no official medical definition, is an infection with persistent symptoms - even after a standard course of antibiotics. It can be caused by bacteria entering the lining of your bladder. The condition can be unpredictable, but at its worst is "completely debilitating", says Adrianne, describing "the most excruciating abdominal pain, like shooting, spasming pain." "You need a wee all the time, but it's like weeing lava." "It's a very claustrophobic feeling, of I'm trapped in this body that is betraying me and is in pain," she adds. Even on a good day she struggles to leave the house as she worries about having a flare-up. While sending a urine sample to the lab remains the gold standard to diagnose a UTI, "false negatives" can often occur, says Professor Chris Harding, a consultant urologist at Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. Another hurdle is the significant crossover between chronic UTIs and other conditions such as painful bladder syndrome, chronic pelvic pain and endometriosis, says Magda Kujawa, a consultant urologist at Stockport NHS Foundation Trust. Adrianne says she felt "dismissed" by doctors while trying to get a diagnosis, and frustrated at repeatedly being given advice around hygiene and hydration, while her symptoms persisted. Both experts say health professionals should listen to the patient's story to understand whether symptoms amount to a recurrent or chronic condition or something else entirely. Since she started posting online, Adrianne has received messages from other young women who worry they are "dirty" and "not taking care of themselves" or that there is "something wrong with them". "There's definitely still a lot of stigma around why people get them (UTIs), and it all just comes back to education. We're not taught about them at school," she adds. Laura says not knowing when or how she would get better left her feeling "hopeless" Laura Von Müllen, 26, has also been diagnosed with a chronic UTI and documents her experience on TikTok. She says her symptoms "really badly" impacted university, and became particularly difficult to manage when she started working. She now works remotely from Kent doing social media management. As well as urinary symptoms, Laura says she also experiences heart palpitations and panic attacks. "People don't understand, they think it's just a UTI and that it'll clear within three days, but I've still got mine two years later," she says. Laura also feels there is still a lot of misconception around UTIs. "People have said to me: who have you been sleeping with then? When that's not the case." Adrianne and Laura hope more women sharing their experience will help demystify the condition. Harding agrees. adding that "the more we can talk about these conditions, the more people will present to appropriate specialists and get the right treatment." But both Harding and Kujawa warn that while social media can be a useful resource, there is the risk of coming across misinformation and harmful advice, including "hacks" that could cause more harm. "I've seen women on social media sitting in baths of disinfectant, all because they were convinced that that they were dirty, and that's why they were getting infections. And actually, that just made things ten times worse," Kujawa says. While Adrianne and Laura's symptoms are showing improvements, they say it's a "long road to recovery". title: Only one female scientist named in GCSEs, research finds
description: A new study finds Rosalind Franklin is the only woman named in Key Stage 4 science specifications.
body: Franklin was a British chemist and crystallographer, whose X-ray diffraction work helped discover the structure of DNA Rosalind Franklin is the only female scientist named in GCSE and National 5 science exam specifications in the UK, according to new research. A Cambridge study found that of the 86 scientists named by UK exam boards, the English chemist, whose work in the 1950s helped reveal the structure of DNA, was the only woman. Exam specifications set out the skills and knowledge students are expected to have gained by the end of their course and how they will be assessed. Exam boards said there was "a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications". Academics from the University of Cambridge, along with institutions in the US and Australia, examined how many women were mentioned in specifications for biology, chemistry, physics, environmental science, geology and astronomy. Their work, published in the British Educational Research Journal, looked at six exam boards in the UK: At Key Stage 4 and equivalent, including GCSEs and National 5s in Scotland, Franklin was the only woman among the 86 scientists mentioned. She was also one of three women mentioned at Key Stage 5 and equivalent - including A-levels, AS-levels, National Highers and National Advanced Highers - out of a total of 181 scientists. Marie Tharp, an American cartographer who created the first map of the floor of the Atlantic ocean in the 1950s, and Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist who discovered the existence of the Earth's inner core in the 1930s, both feature in the Cambridge OCR's A-­level Geology. Franklin, who was named in Cambridge OCR's GCSE Biology and Scottish Highers Biology, produced a famous DNA image known as Photograph 51. Cambridge scientists Francis Crick and James Watson used the image to work out the following year that DNA has a double-helix structure. Watson, Crick and Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery. Franklin had died four years earlier. Academics who wrote the paper found that "several major scientific breakthroughs" in specifications were made by women, but they were not explicitly mentioned. The paper said: "Many of the scientific discoveries and explanations were developed in the 1800s and early 1900s, a period when scientific and mathematical practice was largely, but not solely, dominated by men. "Our findings confirm that the UK science specifications reflect this historical imbalance: although women made significant contributions to major scientific breakthroughs, this fact is rarely acknowledged." The academics recommended that Franklin should be included "in all specifications when teaching DNA structure". They also said specifications should refer to Marie Curie, who discovered radium and polonium and coined the term radioactivity, and nuclear physicist Lise Meitner, who discovered nuclear fission, among others. Stephanie Buttigieg, one of the authors, said: "Relatable role models can help keep more girls in STEM by strengthening their sense of belonging in science and fostering positive attitudes towards scientific careers." A spokeswoman for the Joint Council for Qualifications, which represents AQA, Cambridge OCR, CCEA, WJEC and Pearson, said: "Exam boards recognise that there is a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications, and this is an area they will be focusing on as these qualifications are reformed." Qualifications Scotland said the Curriculum Improvement Cycle offered "an opportunity to consider gender representation within our future qualifications and assessments". The Department for Education in England said "girls should see the contribution women have made in STEM", adding it was "committed to improving the school curriculum over the coming years, and as part of that will make sure every girl can see where their learning can take them". The Scottish Government said it was "committed to closing the gender gap in STEM and will carefully consider the findings of this research". title: Four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029
description: The winner, announced in early 2027, will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural activities.
body: Blackpool is one of four shortlisted locations to be the next UK City of Culture Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029. The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford. A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid. The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories". Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps". Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon. What is it known for? Its landmark Blackpool Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations. It also hosts a major dance festival and an annual visit from Strictly Come Dancing. The Showtown museum celebrates Blackpool's history as a showbiz and comedy hotspot. What have they said? Lynn Williams, leader of Blackpool Council, said: "Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of." She added: "Blackpool has never been a town that stands still. It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen." What is it known for? Constructed in the 1960s and 70s, Milton Keynes is known for its US-style grid road system and numerous roundabouts. It is home to historic World War II codebreaking centre Bletchley Park, now a museum, and the National Bowl, an amphitheatre that has hosted concerts by Oasis, Queen and David Bowie. What have they said? Milton Keynes' bid described it as "a city built on imagination – a place where innovation, diversity and creativity thrive side by side". Councillor Jane Carr, leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "We're now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond." What is it known for? The traditional centre of steel and cutlery manufacturing, Sheffield has since become known for musical exports like the Arctic Monkeys and Pulp, for its annual documentary film festival, and for the Crucible - one of the leading theatres outside London. What have they said? The city's bid put its spotlight on Sheffield's "world-renowned creative heritage, as well as our ambitious future plans". Celebrating its place on the shortlist, councillor Fran Belbin, leader of the city council, said: "Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit... Culture is part of who we are." What is it known for? North Wales's largest city was a powerhouse of the industrial revolution, and most recently hit the headlines when its historic football club Wrexham AFC was bought by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney. What have they said? The bid said: "Our ambition is simple but bold: to make Wrexham the world's most playful place." Joanna Knight OBE, chair of the Wrexham bid, styled as Wrecsam2029, explained: "There's a real sense that something very special is happening here. Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean... the opportunities are enormous." title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study
description: Drugs will be tested simultaneously, which it's hoped will speed up the process of finding new treatments for this common type of dementia.
body: A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease. It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life. Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART. "We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC. "My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life. "But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me." Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something". "Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back." Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose father died from Alzheimer's last month, said he knew how it felt to lose a loved one to dementia, and had seen first-hand the devastating impact of the disease on families. "That's why I'm proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible," he said. The AD-SMART study is what's known as a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial where several treatments are tested simultaneously, with the results compared with one group of participants taking a placebo or dummy. This means those involved have a higher likelihood of getting an active treatment than in a traditional trial. If any drug isn't showing benefit it can be dropped quickly and a new treatment added in its place - the approach has been used successfully in cancer and motor neurone disease. The two initial drugs being tested are metformin, used to treat type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, for ADHD, which were selected by an international panel of experts. Both drugs may help reduce brain inflammation, which is a driver of neurodegeneration, said chief investigator Prof Paresh Malhotra, group leader at the UK Dementia Research Institute Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London. "For too long, Alzheimer's research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer - sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we've found something that works," he told the BBC. "We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer's disease." For the drugs to be successful, the study has to show that they have beneficial effects on thinking and the ability to carry out everyday activities. "That's what patients and their carers care about," said Prof Malhotra. Some 1,200 participants with mild to moderate Alzheimer's will be recruited at more than 30 sites across the UK. Sites in Cambridgeshire, Surrey, London, Southampton and Edinburgh are already open. Scientists expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030 and, in that time, additional treatments are likely to be added. All the participants will have regular health checks including cognitive tests, which will help researchers assess how effective the treatments are. Angela Bucksey's husband Steve, who is her study partner, told the BBC: "Joining the trial has brought us back from the despair of a diagnosis which everybody recognises is non-recoverable. "People who know we are on a drug trial understand that we're doing something about it and, rather than be sorry for us, they can be encouraging." Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer's Research UK said "time is precious" for people living with Alzheimer's disease and more treatment options are urgently needed. People with a confirmed Alzheimer's diagnosis who would like to take part can register their interest on the AD-SMART website, external. The trial is being led by the UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer's Research UK. Partners include the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Medical Research Council and Health Data Research UK, with funding by UK government. title: Daughter of woman killed by partner 'refuses to be another victim'
description: Keeley McKee's mother Leanne was killed by her partner in 2003, weeks before the couple were due to marry.
body: Keeley McKee only learned the full details of her mum's death when she turned 18 A woman who was three years old when her mother was killed by her partner is speaking out about the damage caused by domestic abuse. Keeley McKee only learned the full details of her mum Leanne's murder when she turned 18. She is now channelling her pain into highlighting domestic abuse and the lasting impact it can have on those left behind, determined to turn her own experiences into something positive. "I'm not being a victim of this story. I am going to do something about it," she said. Warning: This story contains distressing details Leanne McKee was killed by her partner in 2003 Leanne McKee was killed by her partner in March 2003, weeks before the couple were due to marry. He then took his own life. Keeley was staying with her grandmother that night and expected her mother to collect her the following day. Her family protected her from the full circumstances of her mother's death as she grew up. She said when she found out, it contributed to her spiralling out of control and abusing drugs and alcohol. As a young child, Keeley remembers her mother telling her to hide in a bedroom and not come out until she was called. "There was someone trying to get in, and I believe it was that partner that she was frightened of," Keeley told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme. At 18, she found a news report online about her mother's death and confronted what had happened. "I had an idea but I think I was in denial. I didn't want to believe it and I didn't want to face it. I had googled it and saw a news article… I read it in the most brutal way you could probably read something like that. "I think from that time then, I just ran away from grieving." Keeley said she felt angry and confused, struggling to process the trauma. She said her mental health deteriorated, she withdrew from friends and family, experienced suicidal thoughts and attempted to take her own life on multiple occasions. She also struggled with drug and alcohol misuse and said the consequences of her mother's murder shaped how she viewed love and relationships. "I was scared to fully love in case that was taken from me again," she added. "For a while there, I didn't trust, but at the same time I've a lot of love to give. "And I believe the right day God is going to put someone on my path, and I am going to build that strong family unit. "And they're going to know nothing but love." Keeley credits her faith with helping her confront the past after taking part in a Christian discipleship programme. She said it allowed her to face the experiences she spent years avoiding. "It gave me the fuel, it gave me the fight to say: 'I'm not being a victim of this anymore. My mum was a victim. I'm not being a victim of this story. I am going to do something about it'." Keeley as a baby with her mum Leanne For Keeley, speaking up against domestic abuse is a way of living with her grief and seeking justice. "My mum was robbed from me. The life that I had with my mum was taken from me by the evil acts of a man, who I won't name because I don't believe he deserves me to speak his name." She added that she believes that violence has become normalised in society and said more needs to be done to tackle it. She said she also wants greater recognition of the lasting impact domestic abuse has on the children and families left behind, saying they can be left struggling with trauma. Keeley was brought up by her great-aunt and great-uncle, who took her into their home while they were grieving for Leanne themselves. She said their support helped her through some of the most difficult periods of her life. Now, she hopes her story will encourage people experiencing abuse to seek help and consider the impact on their children. "Think about your future and your kids' future. What image is that giving them? You're bringing them up in an environment that they will see as normal and maybe they potentially treat their future partner the same way "It's just going to go from generation to generation." If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line. Does NI need a minister for women's safety and health? title: Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad
description: The ad by Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy features his Democratic rival's estranged mother, who she has not seen since her stepfather was charged with sexual abuse in her childhood.
body: This video can not be played Watch: In response to the BBC, Vice President Vance says he's 'disgusted' some Republicans are 'whining' about Ramaswamy ad US Vice-President JD Vance has urged fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about a controversial attack ad that featured a Democratic candidate's estranged mother calling her a liar. While campaigning in Ohio for Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, Vance said he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party. In the ad, Donna Arthur, the mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, said her daughter "lied her entire life". It does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child. The Ramaswamy campaign have claimed credit for the ad, and have paid millions to have it advertised around the state. Acton's brother is among those who have condemned the ad, saying turning alleged sexual assault into "a political talking point" was a "despicable low". Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged in 1978. That is when she last spoke to her mother, Acton said in an interview with The Vindicator, an Ohio news outlet. The Arthurs fled Ohio and Cledith Arthur was never prosecuted on the rape charge. He died in 2004. Amy Acton is the former head of the Ohio Department of Health When the ad featuring Donna Arthur was initially released to social media on Monday evening, it did not say who the video was paid for or authorised by. Ramaswamy confirmed on Tuesday that it came from his campaign, and he later pledged to spend $4m (£2.9m) to further air it. The move has drawn a bipartisan backlash. Former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for president in 2024, said "he's a bad guy. It's a shame he continues to get away with it". Vance, when asked by BBC News if he thought the ad was appropriate, answered: "It's not really my concern." "What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government." He also said he was "a little bit disgusted" by members of his own party who "are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America". Vance, a former Ohio senator, later defended the ad at a rally for Ramaswamy, saying: "Now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar." Vivek Ramaswamy is an ally of President Donald Trump When asked about Ramaswamy's ad on Wednesday, Trump said: "I know nothing about it. I heard the mother went very rogue on the daughter." He added: "It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much. But I dont think that has anything to do with Vivek." Acton's team released its own campaign ad on Tuesday, a video featuring her brother, Philip Stearns, recounting childhood abuse and saying "Amy always got the worst of it". "Shame on Vivek," he says in the 30-second clip. "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio." Other Republicans, including ones running for statewide office, have now criticised the ad. Ohio Senator John Husted, who is up for re-election, told the Associated Press: "I would not have run that ad." Ohio Secretary of Frank LaRose, who is running to be state auditor, was another Republican coming out against the ad. "I will say that, you know, candidates will answer for their own ads, that, you know, I probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision," he told WSYX-TV, external in the city of Columbus. Political attack ads are not a new feature of US politics, but David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that "they have become more intense, and the boundaries have stretched in terms of what one attacks about". Lublin said it was not new for relatives to be used against a political opponent, mentioning family members who testified against Robert F Kennedy Jr before he was confirmed as health secretary. "But this is of a different order," he said. "They're estranged not over policy but over a rape allegation." Lublin believes President Donald Trump's rhetoric and campaigns have helped act as a catalyst for the coarsening of American political discourse - mentioning the time Trump mocked a reporter in Ohio who had a disability. "We live in an age where certainly many candidates can appear mean and even inappropriate at times," Lublin said, adding: "The key purpose of attack ads isn't necessarily to convert the followers of your opponent, but more to depress their turnout." He expects the Ramaswamy attack ad to backfire, saying it could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour in the increasingly competitive race for Ohio governor - even though a Democrat has not been elected governor there in over two decades. Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has moved the Ohio governor's race from "leans Republican" to "toss up", meaning neither candidate has a clear advantage. title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
description: The updated policy will apply to all reservations booked on the accommodation site on or after 20 November.
body: Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to do Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning. The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests. Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds. The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace. "House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC. "So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises." According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes". The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions. A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders. Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules. While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said. If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree. Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees. TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail. One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place. They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts. title: Saka injury 'does not look good' - how will Arsenal cope?
description: Mikel Arteta says the quadriceps injury Arsenal's Bukayo Saka picked up in the Champions League draw with Bayern Munich "does not look good at all".
body: Bukayo Saka was withdrawn after just 10 minutes with a quad injury Mikel Arteta says the quadriceps injury Arsenal's Bukayo Saka picked up in the 2-2 Champions League draw against Bayern Munich "does not look good at all". The 25-year-old winger went down in the 10th minute at Allianz Arena - attempting to play a pass with nobody around him - and had to be replaced by Eberechi Eze, who went on to score the opening goal. "They are a bit concerned. A player who has to come off with a really sharp pain is never good news but we have to wait and see," Arteta told TNT Sports. Saka has had fitness issues in recent months and his game time was managed at the end of last season, as well as with England at the World Cup, because of an Achilles injury he picked up in March. He missed the March international break and seven games for the Gunners, but returned to help them lift the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years. Saka started the Champions League final defeat by Paris St-Germain but was substituted after 54 minutes, and only started three of England's eight games at the World Cup - scoring a hat-trick in the 6-4 third-place win over France. The forward also had surgery on a hamstring injury he picked up in December 2024, which kept him out for 101 days in the 2024-25 season. He made 49 appearances as Arsenal won the title last term, despite a stop-start season - as well as the Achilles issue, he pulled out of the warm-up against Leeds with a hip injury in January and a hamstring problem kept him out for about four weeks. But he remains vital to the Gunners, whose win percentage is notably more impressive with him in the team. This video can not be played Rice strikes to earn Arsenal draw at Bayern Rice scores late as Arsenal draw with Bayern Despite the loss of Saka early on in the game, Arsenal still produced a good performance and could have won the match late on after Declan Rice's late equaliser. "The only negative is seeing one of their star players, Saka, having to pull up with an injury early in the first half," said Champions League Match of the Day pundit Nedum Onuoha. "He was lying on the floor with his hand up and he knew he was in a bit of trouble, so now the concern will be how long he is out for. "It's not necessarily something that means the team will struggle heavily, but there is a reason why he is regarded as one of the best players in this Arsenal team and is seen as being important for them." After Saka's withdrawal Noni Madueke, who had started on the left wing, switched to the right and looked bright, while Eze scored the opening goal from the left after coming off the bench. "This is one of the reasons their squad has been built the way it has been and I think Madueke and Eze did well on the wings today after Saka came off," added Onuoha. "In terms of options, at this moment in time for Arsenal, it is not going to be an issue - they will miss the star power that he has, they still have plenty of other wide players who can step up and do the job while they wait for him to come back." This video can not be played 'This could be a real problem for Arsenal tonight and going forward' Arsenal's style of play has been criticised this season but, even before Saka's withdrawal, the Gunners played on the front foot and enjoyed more possession than their German opponents. Losing Saka, who has scored four goals in 11 appearances in all competitions, will be tough to deal with. But the Gunners have invested heavily in their squad over the past two summer transfer windows and have options. Madueke can play on both wings, while summer signing Christos Tzolis - although currently out with a hamstring injury - has started the season well. The Gunners also have 16-year-old Max Dowman as an attacking option, and the youngster has already shown that he can have an impact for the senior side after scoring in the Premier League last season. Arteta, who was asked what the rest of the forward line will need to do in Saka's absence, said he was pleased with what he saw against Bayern. "I think Ebs [Eze] had a great game. Not only the ball, but the actions. His overall performance, I think his commitment without the ball as well," he said. "And when the other ones come in, I think they really contributed to this. First of all, the energy. "And then to bring different tools that the team needed in that moment to get something out of the game. So, very pleased again." title: New Mexico sues Epstein lawyer and accountant, accusing them of hiding his sex crimes
description: Both men have denied having any knowledge of Epstein's crimes and their attorney rejected the lawsuit as "categorically false".
body: Prosecutors say Epstein abused victims at his Zorro Ranch in New Mexico with the help of key aides Prosecutors in the US state of New Mexico have filed a civil lawsuit against two longtime aides of Jeffrey Epstein, accusing the men of profiting from the late financier's sex trafficking ring. Lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn are the sole executors of Epstein's estate, controlling all his wealth and possessions. They have denied any role in his crimes. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez says they played a key role in concealing abuse at Epstein's remote Zorro Ranch near the city of Santa Fe, and that they continue to earn money while victims seek accountability. The lawsuit is separate to the state's ongoing criminal probe into Epstein, which was re-launched in February. An attorney representing both Indyke and Kahn told the BBC that they "emphatically reject" the claims in the lawsuit. The lawsuit was filed in New Mexico on Wednesday under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act and New Mexico Racketeering Act. During a news conference, Torrez argued that the two men are blocking efforts by Epstein's victims to seek compensation from his fortune, estimated at roughly $635m (£474m) at the time of his death. "Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors - there should be no distribution of Mr Epstein's remaining assets to people like Mr Indyke and Mr Kahn for participation in what I think is one of the most horrific criminal enterprises in modern America," he said. Both men worked with Epstein for decades, and have previously testified to Congress that they were unaware of the crimes he committed alongside accomplice Ghislane Maxwell. Their attorney Daniel Weiner said in a statement to the BBC that, "they are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them". "Both Mr Indyke and Mr Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him," Weiner said. He added that the New Mexico prosecutor never asked to speak to either man "before filing this baseless lawsuit", and that they both have "cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so". Jeffrey Epstein had two key aides - why do they still control his money and secrets? Epstein tried to buy a palace in Morocco days before his arrest in 2019 The two aides were named as co-executors in August 2019 by Epstein, just two days before he killed himself in jail while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges. He revised his will to transfer all his wealth into a trust named after the year of his birth, which the lawyer and accountant would administer. In their role as executors, Indyke and Kahn agreed to fund compensation packages for survivors that included conditions that prevented survivors who accepted funds from taking further legal action against them personally. Other claims are still outstanding. As beneficiaries of the trust, the men could also be paid tens of millions of dollars each from whatever remains when the claims are settled. In his remarks, Torrez alleged that Epstein's crimes were "made possible by handlers, by lawyers, by accountants, by others who have yet to face real consequence". "Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," he said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences," he added. title: My dying daughter gasped in pain while medics argued at her bedside
description: Families have raised concerns over palliative care at Edinburgh's children's hospital.
body: Stephanie Kent and Jamie Gentleman raised a complaint about the care given to their daughter Flora in the days before her death In the days before her death, six-year-old Flora Gentleman was in pain and visibly distressed. But because she was autistic and non-verbal, she could not tell her parents what was wrong. After four years of living with neuroblastoma, an aggressive form of cancer, Flora had stopped responding to treatment. By December 2024 she was receiving palliative care at Edinburgh's Royal Hospital for Children and Young People. Despite being given the highest possible dose of pain relief, her mother, Stephanie Kent, said she could see her daughter "gasping and wincing in pain". According to Stephanie, disagreements between medical teams over how best to manage Flora's symptoms erupted into a heated discussion at her daughter's bedside. The oncology team said the kindest route was to sedate Flora, but the palliative care team wanted to give the pain relief more time to take effect. Stephanie said the conversation became so "insensitive" that the group of medics had to leave the room. "It was barbaric," said Stephanie. "It felt like we were going in circles, right next to Flora's bed. The level of unprofessionalism was diabolical." After Flora's death, Stephanie complained to NHS Lothian about the care she had received. The health board upheld the complaint, partly because of the distress the family had felt as a result of divisions between medical teams. BBC Scotland has spoken to several families who have raised concerns over palliative care at the hospital. One family described the treatment they received as "unprofessional" while another said "it feels like they are not taking the concerns of parents seriously." NHS Lothian said it had carried out a full investigation into Flora's care, and that recommendations had been acted upon and communicated to her family. More broadly, it said its complaints process involves "thorough and robust" investigations with clinical teams. Flora was cared for at the Royal Hospital for Children and Young People In her complaint, Stephanie said that members of the oncology and palliative care teams began arguing by Flora's bedside while she was in distress. She said a member of the palliative care team made a number of upsetting remarks, which included "Flora is on such a high dose of pain relief that it would knock an elephant out", and that this medication would "chill her out". "I felt like I was going crazy, saying 'I know something's not right here' and you feel like you are not being taken seriously," said Stephanie. "As if watching your child die isn't traumatising enough, you also have to watch her suffer while these two teams that should be helping ease her pain can't even see eye to eye." After medical staff left the room, Stephanie said she had to leave Flora's bedside for 45 minutes to continue the conversation about her care. "Anything could have happened in that time," she said. "She was only six years old, lying there in pain all she wanted was her mum and dad." Following the argument, the lead oncologist took over Flora's care. Within 24 hours, Stephanie said Flora was peaceful and able to sleep. She died two days later. Flora was neurodivergent and non-verbal NHS Lothian upheld Stephanie's complaint on the grounds that the family were left out of decision making and had experienced distress due to "visible" divisions between clinical teams. In an official response to the complaint, seen by BBC News, the health board acknowledged Flora's family was affected by comments made by the palliative care team that were perceived as "insensitive". It also acknowledged that it was inappropriate for the meeting to have taken place beside Flora's bed and said a further conversation took place outside her room. The staff member alleged to have made the two inappropriate comments said they did not recall making the remark about pain relief dosage, but acknowledged that if they had, it would have come across as insensitive or unprofessional. In reference to the second comment, they said it was never meant to cause offence. NHS Lothian has identified eight "major learning outcomes" following a review of Flora's care. They include the need to better coordinate working between teams, greater consideration of how Flora's neurodiversity affected her acre and concerns that aspects of staff communication caused distress to the family. Stephanie said this was a starting point but wider improvements could be made to end-of-life care for children in Scotland. These include specific wards for children's palliative care. Over 70% of children and young people with serious health conditions or receiving palliative care in Scotland die in a hospital setting, according to Public Health Scotland. BBC Scotland also spoke to Jamie Walker whose 17-year-old daughter Sophie died in the same ward in July 2024. The family submitted a complaint in January 2026. NHS Lothian initially said it would investigate and respond to seven points raised under stage two of its complaints procedure within two weeks. However, 11 days later, the family received another letter saying they had been given multiple opportunities to complain within the relevant timeframe. The complaint was then closed. Sophie died on 6 July, 2024 The family referred the matter to the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO), which is investigating. There is also a separate investigation by the Scottish Fatalities Investigation Unit into Sophie's death. Jamie said NHS Lothian underestimated how difficult it could be for bereaved parents to navigate the complaints process. "It is so hard. You are sitting there and reliving the worst thing that has ever happened to you, word by word," he said. "It feels like they are not taking the concerns of parents seriously."
