title: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
description: Hotel chaos, transport mishaps and diplomatic blunders cast a spotlight on organisers and the firm hired to deliver the games.
body: From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems. There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation". Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected. "If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned. The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements. Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation. Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds". Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap. The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000. Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation". Container units were used to host some participants as organisers opted not to build a traditional athletes' village This was just the start of the problems. Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event. In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved. Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations. "Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said. "During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures." Organisers acknowledged major challenges and said athletes from some delegations had been inconvenienced As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events. GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction. A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers. Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged. But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games". "We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC. Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given. "Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added. GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment. Volunteers were told they could attend the closing ceremony for free, before an organiser said that decision hadn't been approved Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event. It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase. Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation. But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit. "This achievement does not come without the bes

title: Firefighters and public 'knowingly put at risk' during summer wildfires
description: Crews and control centre staff say the fires were relentless with many firefighters still off work injured.
body: Firefighters said this summer's wildfires were the worst they had experienced Firefighters and the public were knowingly put at risk during this year's wildfires due to chronic underfunding, a union has said. Those working on the ground and in the South Wales control centre said the fires were relentless with injuries "commonplace" for crews. The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) said firefighters were climbing hills in unsuitable boots and non-breathable layers used for house fires due to not having enough kit, and there is a "real risk to the public" if immediate action isn't taken. The Welsh government said it doesn't provide the core funding but "recognise the concerns raised and are clear that we need to do all we can to reduce the risk of wildfires". Sean says some injured firefighters from the wildfires are still not back at work Sean Cayford, a firefighter in Bridgend, said crews were told in mid August that there were no pumps or fire appliances available across the brigade's entire region. "I've never heard that before but that was heard again later in the wildfire season. That was startling," he said. "One particular day we were at an incident on top of Tredegar mountain and as we looked around the landscape we could see in the region of six or seven other category three wildfires, the most serious type of wildfires, on the horizon in every direction you looked." Sean said even with help from other brigades from all over the UK, they "still didn't have enough" firefighters. "We were stretched so thinly," he said. "It has an increasingly destructive affect on the morale of our firefighters. "It's very difficult to be at a wildfire incident in excess for eight or 10 or 12 hours and not get injured to some degree." He said colleagues sustained lower limb injuries and heat illness, with many still unable to work. Gemma Thomas says control room staff were exhausted Gemma Thomas, who works in the control centre, said the average number of calls is usually 200-300 but on their busiest day this summer they had almost 2,000. "It was just relentless in there," she said. "There were times where we were unable to fulfil the requests that were coming from the incidents. "We are the first point of contact for somebody who is having potentially the worst day of their life. "It was so stressful, mentally draining, that you're getting home from work absolutely shattered to think right I've got to back and do it all again tomorrow." Gemma said there were times when staff needed to take breaks "one at a time for 10 minutes just to get people out of the room". "People were getting to the point where they were just shattered in work, shattered at home," she said, adding there was no work-life balance because they needed to use free time to rest. Gemma says the support from management within the team was "phenomenal" and "even the firefighters on the ground were understanding how stretched we were in the control room". But she doesn't believe they could sustain it long term and wants to see an increase in numbers of firefighters. A wildfire above Cwm, Ebbw Vale, in August First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth is hosting a climate change and resilience summit in Merthyr Tydfil on Thursday, which will "bring key partners together to develop future actions". It will host representatives from the fire services and police, local government, farmers and climate change organisations. "There was poor preparation," said Gareth Tovey, executive council member for Wales, explaining they redirected specialist crews such as water teams to the wildfires. "At some stages there was zero crew back up for vast parts of south Wales," he said. "Firefighters were injured because they didn't have the right kit to fight wildfires." The FBU says there's a shortfall of 400 firefighters in Wales. Tovey said the union had been warning "for years" that authorities needed to do something and there was a "real risk to the public" if immediate action isn't taken. Tovey said bringing in the army, while helpful, "is not a silver bullet" as they do not have the firefighting skills needed. An FBU survey following the fires found 69% of firefighters felt significantly under-equipped, with just 8% feeling fully equipped. Nearly half reported welfare facilities during wildfire deployment were insufficient. Firefighters are funded by the public but through a levy decided by the local authority for the area. This is part of their budget, which is in turn set by the Welsh government. North Wales Fire and Rescue Service is applying to the Welsh government's emergency assistance scheme to cover the additional £500,000 the wildfires this summer cost. At one point firefighters in north Wales were managing six wildfires at once - more than ever before. It comes as a new report from the UK's Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said the wildfires left firefighters working in extreme conditions and exposed weaknesses in the UK's resilience and preparation. They called for a UK government-funded "national wildfire prevention campaign" with clear and consistent messaging, along with wildfire risk indicators in weather forecasts. The Welsh government said individual fire and rescue authorities determine how many firefighters they need and set their budgets accordingly. "They should take this summer's wildfires into account when doing so," a spokesperson said. Ahead of the summit, ap Iorwerth said: "What we saw this summer was much more dangerous than fires in other years. "While we cannot reverse climate change, we can take practical steps to keep the risk of wildfire as low as possible and ensure a swift and effective response to incidents." South Wales Fire and Rescue Service said: "We are incredibly proud of the professionalism, resilience and commitment shown by our firefighters, control colleagues and everyone who supported the response, often in extremely cha

title: Angry scenes and protests at Senedd as Reform call for ban on Muslim face coverings
description: It is the latest heated debate in the Senedd on a Wednesday prompted by Reform MSs.
body: After the debate a number of Plaid Cymru and Labour politicians took part in a protest on the Senedd steps - with Safa Elhassan addressing those gathered There were bad-tempered and dramatic exchanges in the Senedd on Wednesday night as members of Reform called for Muslim religious face coverings, such as the burka, to be banned. Politicians from the party said they were "anti-British", allowed Muslim women to hide their identities, and suggested they represented an "alien culture". Plaid Cymru and Labour politicians responded with disdain - deputy first minister Sioned Williams raised the Nuremberg Laws of 1930s Germany and how they led to the extermination of Jews. The Muslim Council of Wales described "disturbingly authoritarian attitudes" - Reform's Jason O'Connell accused the group of trying to "silence" the debate. There was no vote on the topic. The Senedd would have no power to ban face coverings. A protest, including some MSs, took place on the Senedd steps. It is the latest heated debate in the Senedd on a Wednesday prompted by Reform MSs - previous include a discussion about the Nation of Sanctuary and calls for foreign nationals to be banned from house shares. A niqab is a form of a veil used by Muslim women Reform UK has previously said it would ban face coverings in public places, including burkas and balaclavas, if it won power at the next Westminster election. Opening the debate to a nearly full chamber, Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, Jason O'Connell, began by speaking about young men wearing balaclavas. "From Newport to Rhyl, balaclava-clad young men, often dangerously riding illegal e-bikes, have been fuelling anti-social behaviour and making our streets feel unsafe," he said. "For these individuals, face coverings are a way to conceal their identity, to make it harder for authorities to hold them accountable. "And while governments across the UK turn a blind eye to this, Reform says enough is enough now, face coverings have no place in British and Welsh society." Turning to the burka, O'Connell, who called Wednesday's debate, said: "We have no issue or problem with Islam or Muslims." With opposing members heckling as he spoke, he added: "We do have an issue with people living amongst our communities hiding their identities. "We say the same thing to protesters that cover their face, whatever their political persuasion." Jason O'Connell called the short debate on face coverings late on Wednesday night Amid frequent interruptions, fellow Reform MS Francesca O'Brien told the Senedd that face coverings, including the burka, were "anti-British". "Not all cultures are equal," she said, "we cannot continue to import alien cultures into this country and expect integration." "Oppressive beliefs are totally at odds with our history and culture. "Banning these coverings is simple, common sense." Reform MS Joe Martin said the burka and niqab were "two of the many ways in which fundamentalist Islam is uniquely incompatible with Western civilization". "We can't even see the faces of thousands of people who've moved here. If two Muslim women live in the same street and they both wear burkas, how are we meant to tell them apart? "Assimilation means losing religious face coverings and to encourage that they should be banned." The burka is a veil worn by some Muslim women that covers the face and body, often leaving a mesh screen to see through. It covers more of the face than a niqab, a veil that leaves the area around the eyes clear. In comparison, a hijab is a headscarf that in the West most commonly covers the head and neck but leaves the face clear. A protest took place on the steps of the Senedd before the debate on Wednesday Sioned Williams, deputy first minister, said the debate was a "shameful" end to a "sad day" that began with the commemoration of the Aberfan disaster. Looking at the Reform members, she accused them of "conflating the intimidating behaviour of thugs and those whose protest can descend into disorder and violence, often in demonstrations directed against migrants or Muslims, with the very people who are targeted by that intimidating behaviour". "I do not accept that a face covering worn by an individual for religious reasons means they don't share British or Welsh values," she said. "Nor should we suggest that someone belongs any less, because their religious practice differs from that of others." Williams added: "The Jewish people of 1930s Germany were subject to the Nuremberg Laws, which stated they were no longer German, laws which led to their persecution and extermination by the state that stripped them of the Germaness. "Who decides that a woman who [has] a face covering is less British or less Welsh?" The comments led to angry protests and finger-pointing from the Reform benches. A point of order was raised by a member of the party asking the presiding officer if the comments were appropriate. The presiding officer Huw Irranca-Davies said he was "always happy" to review the record of proceedings, but did not make a ruling. Williams said she was making a "statement of fact". Carrie Harper, Plaid MS for Fflint Wrecsam, told Reform: "How on earth can you claim to stand up for women when you are trying to dictate what Muslim women can and cannot wear?" Plaid MS Kiera Marshall, for Caerdydd Penarth, said a Muslim woman in her constituency was subject to a "physical, violent attack in broad daylight". "The attacker shouted at her about removing her headscarf and continued to do exactly this while physically assaulting her," she said. "This is just one example of an increasingly common occurrence when Muslim women are being targeted. "This is exactly what the rhetoric that Reform is peddling is doing." Labour's Huw Thomas said he had not heard Reform condemn "the masked mobs who stormed RNLI stations across of South Coast, last month". A lifeboat station in Portsmouth went out of service in Sept

title: Attempted murder arrests after boy, 16, attacked
description: Two boys aged 15 and 16 were being questioned after the teenager was found injured in Everton, Liverpool.
body: Road closures were put place in the local area Two boys aged 15 and 16 have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a 16-year-old was seriously assaulted in Liverpool, police have said. Officers were called to The Lutine Bell pub on Breck Road in Everton at about 14:15 BST following reports of a boy being assaulted nearby. He was taken to hospital with head and chest injuries where he remains in a serious condition. A 37-year-old man and a 41-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender. All four remain in custody, Merseyside Police said. Det Ch Insp Paula Jones said: "We are continuing to appeal for anyone who was in the area of Breck Road shortly after 14:00 and saw, heard or captured anything to please get in touch." Jones added: "You may also live or work nearby and witnessed people running off at the time. Pass on all information and we will make the assessment." title: New lab to become centre for investigating uplands
description: The research facility in Penrith will also help train the next generation of environmental scientists.
body: It is the hoped the lab will become a hub for upland research A new, purpose-built laboratory will serve as a base for scientists, universities and students to investigate Cumbria's upland landscapes, and how they respond to nature recovery. It is hoped the research facility at RSPB Wild Haweswater, in Penrith, will become a hub for upland science, bringing researchers and conservationists together to carry out fieldwork, share expertise, and develop new collaborations. The lab was funded by the estate of the late ornithologist Denis Summers-Smith. "We want to build on Denis's commitment to field ecology and conservation research, creating a lasting legacy that will benefit both science and nature recovery in Cumbria and beyond," said RSPB's Will Peach. The new lab will support current research through Cumbria Connect, whose work and scientific monitoring spans Wild Haweswater, the Lowther estate and the Lowther Valley. Dr Mo Verhoeven, conservation scientist at Cumbria Connect, explained how the region's landscape is made up of a number of distinctive environments, including peatlands and rainforest, which play a key role in storing carbon and managing water. "Cumbria's uplands are incredibly important for nature recovery," he said. "We hope this laboratory will give researchers, students and conservationists a place to work together and build the evidence needed to guide restoration, both here in Cumbria and in upland landscapes further afield. "It's about making Cumbria a much stronger base for upland science." "Just as importantly, it will help train the next generation of environmental scientists," he said. Cumbria Connect is part of a scheme paid for by the Arcadia Fund which was co-founded by one of the heirs to the Tetra Pak fortune. title: Ex-prosecutor charged with treason in Mexico over US drug raid
description: César Jáuregui Moreno is accused of allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April.
body: César Jáuregui Moreno (pictured) was arrested over the weekend Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation. César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year. The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers. Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations. The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday. A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports. Jáuregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country. She has been adamant that foreign officials can only operate on Mexican soil if given prior clearance by the federal government, and has insisted the Latin American nation's sovereignty should not be breached. The crash occurred on 19 April, when a convoy returning from an operation targeting suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area veered off the road and plunged into a ravine. Two members of the Chihuahua State Investigation Agency were killed along with the Americans, officials said. At the time, in his capacity as state attorney general, Jáuregui told a news conference that the Americans had been "instructor officers" from the US embassy engaged in "training work as part of the general and normal exchange we have with the US authorities". US media have reported that the two individuals worked for the CIA as part of an expanded effort to combat narcotics trafficking in the region. title: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
description: Test results have confirmed his diagnosis as a lung adenocarcinoma that was localised.
body: Pope Leo returned to St Peter's Square on Wednesday for his weekly general audience Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said. Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican. "A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added. The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds. It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday. The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung. He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage". Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar. On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace". The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday. Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November. title: Fernandes rounds on Carrick after Man Utd humiliation
description: Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes has blamed head coach Michael Carrick for the tactics that led to an embarrassing 4-1 defeat by Como in the Champions League.
body: This video can not be played Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on Carrick Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history. A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future. He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later. However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly as he understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards. "It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said. Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable." Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win." Man Utd embarrassment in Como leaves Carrick job in danger This video can not be played Carrick 'bitterly disappointed' by Man Utd peformance Carrick also refused to answer questions about his own future. Instead, he described his own feelings about United's performance and focused on taking responsibility. "I have to apologise to the supporters," said the former player. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more, with the position that I'm in and what I value this football club. For us to play in that way is not acceptable. "I always go over to the fans anyway, regardless, so it wasn't a particularly different kind of reason why I went over. "It's the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they've gone through and have done over a period of a few weeks now. As I said, I was one of them. "I'm feeling the same as them. We've got a lot of values in this football club; what we represent and how we want to go about it. We might win, we might lose, but the way we went about it tonight wasn't acceptable. I just wanted to let the fans know that I feel for them. "Listen. I've not given my own position any thought - this is for the supporters - I was one of them watching that and I wasn't happy all." Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick acknowledges the club's fans after the 4-1 defeat by Como After winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season to guide United back into the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick was given a two-year contract. However, as happened with Solskjaer five years ago, the new campaign has unravelled spectacularly and they are 13th in the Premier League, three points clear of bottom club Sunderland. Although they recovered from their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull by coming from behind to beat Ipswich the following week, United have not won in the Premier League since. Their only other success in 11 games in all competitions came against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. Their latest loss meant they have now gone seven games without a win, their worst run since they went eight without a victory under Louis van Gaal between 25 November and 28 December 2015. Only Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time consolation prevented United suffering their joint second-worst European defeat of all time. The embarrassment was heightened by the knowledge that when they were last crowned European champions in 2008, Como were playing semi-professional football in front of a couple of hundred spectators in Serie D. It is a basic reality that if Como's star man Nico Paz, who opened the scoring after 118 seconds, created the second and added a third goal, said he wanted to leave Como, virtually every big club in Europe would want to sign him and United's chances would be virtually non-existent. They entertain 15th-placed Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday knowing that prior to last season's amazing 4-4 draw, the Cherries recorded 3-0 wins on their previous two visits to Old Trafford. United flew straight back to Manchester after the game. It remains to be seen whether the position around Carrick changes before the Bournemouth game. However, United supporters sang against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the shambolic evening unravelled. Both Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox have been absolved of partial blame for the club's plight by some; Carrick because he was let down badly in the summer transfer window, when the club signed three midfielders, but failed to bring in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back and Benjamin Sesko in attack. Wilcox too, because he had to work to a budget set by those above him, including chief executive Omar Berrada. "There was a lot going through my mind watching that," admitted Carrick, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League during his United playing career. "It was tough to watch. "It wasn't just the goals, if I'm totally honest. It was was the manner and way we played at times. "I'm giving my absolute best all the time, I care about it. My whole life is wrapped around it. It might go well, it might not go so well, but I I genuinely give everything that I possibly can." This video can not be played Man Utd fans on if Carric

title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
description: Russia's President Putin does not feel under pressure right now to end the war.
body: Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L) After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending? "Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives. In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting. But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow. The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level. In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..." Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks. Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv". The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard. "In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov. Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace. "I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction." It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war. He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain. He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission. He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow. Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky. That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader. "Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says. "Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?" A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent. But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit. Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe. "Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China." After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics. title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
description: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
body: Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this year Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices. A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data. "The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices". Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful. The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety. New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal. That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time. New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added. Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been. They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday. "Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable." The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter. He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order. While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine. It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices. New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children. The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children". California and several other states had collectively sued Meta over similar issues. They reached a mutual settlement deal to end that case only a few days into what was expected to be a multi-week trial. title: 'Playing for their careers' - Australia reeling after extraordinary day
description: Australia are facing defeat in the second Test against South Africa with careers on the line after their shambolic performance on day four.
body: Australia had South Africa 110-6 on day three but are now facing defeat Second Test, Gqeberha (day four of five) South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81 Australia 99 & 156-4: Head 87*; Rabada 2-30 Australia trail by 170 runs Not since the Nottingham Ashes Test in 2005, Shane Warne's spin and watching Ashley Giles' leg glance from behind a cushion, had Australia been asked to follow-on in an away Test. It had only happened to them on one other occasion anywhere in the world in 38 years. But by being bowled out for 99 by South Africa in their first innings of the second Test, Australia matched those lows and handed their hosts an unlikely route to winning this Test and leveling the series. Travis Head remains on 87 not out, but this was a calamitous day for the tourists as they conceded their biggest first-innings lead since 1984, before failing for the second time in the same day's play. At 156-4 in their second innings they are still 170 runs behind and the Proteas now look likely winners with a day to go. "There are a number of players playing for their careers in this innings," said former Australia opener Simon Katich, Australia's highest scorer from that Trent Bridge Test 21 years ago, on SEN Radio. For some, it might even be too late... If Katich's words seem strong for a side 1-0 up in the series, this South African subsidence was the latest example of an Australian batting line-up only consistent for its inconsistency. Bowled out for 132 in the first Test of the Ashes last winter, they piled up 511 in Brisbane in the next. They scored 567 at the end of the Ashes, but were bundled out for 198 by Bangladesh in their next Test en route to a shock defeat. Even the highs of Matt Renshaw's 190 in the first-Test win in Durban were countered by the fact no other Australian made 50. And after another failure, Marnus Labuschagne appears the most at risk. He will not get another chance to bat for his place before Cape Town hosts the third Test from 27 October. After edging a drive to third slip for 14 off Anrich Nortje in the morning, he gave it away by hitting spinner Simon Harmer to long-on after tea for 39 - his third dismissal in the thirties in the series. It was made worse by the fact he had only survived an lbw decision on review just three runs earlier. It is now 47 innings since the 32-year-old, once the leading batter in the world, has made a Test century. "Only he knows what was going through his mind when he tried to take Harmer down the ground, against the breeze, when Australia are trying to play for a draw," added Katich. "How will the Australian selectors view that dismissal? "He's been given plenty of rope over the past few years, when plenty of others haven't, but he has." Australia head coach Andrew McDonald said he was "disappointed" with Labuschagne's dismissal. "You saw what we saw," he said. "For me, the option is there if the ball is the right area. It is a strength of this, but in that scenario there probably are some shots that players would take back. "He did a lot of hard work once again. I feel like I am on repeat around the amount of 30s that he has got. That has become a danger period for him. "We had a good partnership going and were starting to claw ourselves back into the game, albeit a long way behind. "When you do that hard work you've got to cash in and unfortunately that wasn't to be the case for Marn. We were disappointed and he will be too." Opener Nic Maddinson is another who must simply await his fate. He was not involved in the Wednesday-morning collapse, but only because he had already edged Kagiso Rabada to slip the night before. Opening the batting against Rabada and Marco Jansen would be feverishly difficult for a regular opener, never mind a batter more used to the middle order. It is because of that very fact Maddinson has chased balls outside off stump in both innings, leaving the left-hander with two ducks to go with scores of eight and 48 since his surprise recall aged 34. As he watched on, Sam Konstas, once seen as Australia's next opener, made 151 not out for New South Wales back home. Credit must also go to left-armer Jansen, who was superb in taking 5-33 in Australia's first innings. He was in full flow when dismissing Renshaw, Alex Carey and Beau Webster to rip out the middle order - all three were caught between wicketkeeper and gully. Renshaw and wicketkeeper Carey have credit in the bank, but Webster, who became the day's 13th wicket when he was pinned lbw by Harmer in the final 20 minutes, will be another looking over his shoulder. An admirable cricketer, he averages 34.13 with the bat and 28.75 with the ball in his 11 completed Tests. But he has also now gone seven innings without a 50 since the Ashes and yet to reach three figures. McDonald said Australia know they are not the "perfect batting unit" and he could not defend some of the dismissals. "We've had some of these moments across the journey," he said. "The pitch didn't play too many tricks either, there was a bit of bounce. "You do have to give some credit to the South Africans, they exposed some of our deficiencies, but there was some batter error there. "I think we are better than that but as we sit here now, I can't defend that." Crucially, Head remains, having been dropped on five at gully by Jansen. It was a sharp catch as Head cut, and shelling it was the only thing the towering 6ft 8in seamer did wrong all day. Intrigue is added by the delayed entrance to the second innings of Steve Smith. He survived longer than anyone else in the first innings - 88 balls for 28 runs - but was given treatment for a neck issue throughout and remained in the dressing room as evening wickets fell. McDonald said Smith will bat on Thursday, meaning South Africa still have work to do but - after the first two days were almost entirely wiped out by rain - they have a real chance to comp

title: Pupils who designed a badge sent to space meet NASA astronaut
description: Frank Rubio is set to be in the crew for the Artemis III mission and previously spent a year in space.
body: Pupils at the school in Cemaes got the chance to ask question to a NASA astronaut Pupils at a school on Anglesey were "very excited" when they met virtually with a NASA astronaut. Students at Ysgol Cemaes were able to put their questions to Frank Rubio on Wednesday, who is set to be part of the crew for the Artemis III mission. Rubio also spent more than a year aboard the International Space Station (ISS) after a fault with the spacecraft that was due to bring him and his fellow astronauts back to Earth. During the virtual session, pupils asked him about his experiences of living and working in space, as well as the challenges and excitement of space travel. Astronaut Frank Rubio was stranded on the ISS for 371 days This is not the first time pupils at the primary school have had the chance to speak with astronauts. Earlier this year, they took part in a project to design a badge that was sent into space, later seeing it float in zero gravity aboard the ISS. The opportunity was made possible by former pupil Dr Melanie Coathup, a scientist who works closely with astronauts and has helped inspire the school's growing links with the space industry. Guto Rhys, acting headteacher, said the students were "extremely excited" ahead of the meeting, and had "been looking at videos of life on the ISS and life in space". The school's headteacher says the pupils were very excited to talk to an astronaut The pupils had prepared many questions to ask Rubio. Harry, 9 and his friend Sofia, 8, were among those listening to the astronaut talk about his experiences. Harry said: "The most interesting thing I've done today is learning about NASA and Frank Rubio." The pupils had been busy preparing in the classroom ahead of the meeting, according to Sofia. She said: "In the school today, we've been learning about Frank Rubio. We learned that if you're sick in space, there are medical kits to help. "We've been watching some videos about how to brush your teeth and sleep in space." Harry and Sofia were both delighted to meet Frank Rubio Lola, 9, was also in the hall for the talk on Wednesday. She was delighted to see Rubio holding a badge that one of the pupils at the school had designed. "We've been learning about Frank Rubio and that he was supposed to stay in space for six months, but he ended up staying there for a year," she said. "We got to design a badge to go up to space and it was my cousin who won and her badge got to go up to space." Lola and Ruby say they're lucky to be able to have such a close connection with NASA as a school Speaking to a real astronaut was "very cool" according to Ruby, 10, "because no other schools in Wales will get that experience". "The most interesting thing that I learned today was that there is a space station up in space," she said. The school plans to design a new badge very soon, with the plan to send another one up to space next year. title: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
description: The wife of a diplomat based in Abuja travelled to Kampala for a vacation.
body: There are no quick Ebola tests available to check travellers, so officials rely on monitoring temperatures Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC. The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return. "She's stable, she's improving," Muhammad Ali Pate said. The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said. "Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC. Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed? What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? None of the contacts, who are now in isolation, are known to have developed symptoms, including the person the patient travelled with, the health minister said, adding that the woman had not travelled outside Abuja since landing. Kaseya explained that the woman had first developed symptoms on 6 October when she had sought medical help. "She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th," he told the BBC's Newshour programme. Malaria is endemic in Nigeria and its symptoms - a high temperature, headaches, muscle aches, vomiting and or diarrhoea - are similar to those of Ebola. After her condition failed to improve, public health authorities were alerted on Monday 19 October, Pate said. Her diagnosis was confirmed the next day following three laboratory tests, he said. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding. The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external. Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged. There have been conflicting accounts about the patient in Nigeria and her movements. Pate and Kaseya's comments contradict a statement issued earlier by the Ugandan ministry of health, which described the woman as a Nigerian national who had gone to eastern DR Congo for business, only transiting through Uganda. It insisted there were currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country and that the woman's passage through Uganda did not mean she had contracted the virus there. Nigeria's health minister and the Africa CDC chief have sought to play down any tension. Pate said Nigerian officials were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the full facts. "We respect our sister nation of Uganda," he said. "We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together." Kaseya also urged African countries to share information, saying this would help investigators trace the woman's movements and establish where she might have contracted the virus. And he encouraged Western countries not to impose travel restrictions, saying "collaboration and solidarity" were the way to help stop the current outbreak. The disease recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections. On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country. In 2014, Nigeria successfully contained an Ebola outbreak, which had resulted in 20 confirmed cases and eight deaths. Pate expressed confidence in the country's ability to repeat that success, citing strengthened disease surveillance, laboratories and thousands of trained epidemiologists. "Nigeria has muscle memory that has been activated, but we are not fighting the past outbreak in the exactly the same way. We have to be vigilant," he said. The outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way. title: MP harassed for 'being English' by man who took axe to pub
description: Michael Glover left a note on MP Henry Tufnell's office door and claimed he knew where he lived.
body: Henry Tufnell MP says he now worries about his family when he works away, following the incident A man who harassed a Labour MP for being "English", and claimed he knew where he lived, has been given a suspended jail sentence. Michael Glover, 59, left a note on Mid and South Pembrokeshire MP Henry Tufnell's office door in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, on 10 March, and carried an axe to the pub the following day. In the letter, which he signed, he also wrote that he had taken "a look around" Tufnell's family home and had "left some presents". The MP said he felt "uneasy" that the defendant said he knew where he lived with his family, including his newborn baby. Swansea Crown Court heard Glover, who is a wheelchair user and has "complex mental health difficulties", was "frustrated" because of a delay in his application for a blue badge. The court heard that CCTV captured the defendant taping a bag, which contained the letter, to the front door of Tufnell's office. He then made "gestures" to the camera before driving away. On 11 March, he carried an axe in a plastic bag to a local pub, and picked it up in front of a member of the public. Glover was arrested that day, and later pleaded guilty to both charges at the magistrates' court. Regan Walters, prosecuting, read a victim personal statement by Tufnell, who said the incident made him feel "uncomfortable". "Knowing that Glover knows where I live with my wife and young child has made me rethink things, such as the security of my address," the politician said. He said he had to be mindful that his "panic alarms and CCTV cameras are working" and that, when he worked away, he felt "on edge, wondering if [his family] are safe". Joseph Hocquard, representing Glover, said his client had been in custody for the past four months for breaching a probation order, which he said had been "incredibly challenging" because of his mental health and disabilities. Glover appeared via video link with his barrister in the cells at Swansea Crown Court because of a "technical issue" with the lift in the building. Judge Mark Powell KC told him "members of parliament are there to advocate for their constituents". He said: "They are entitled to go about their business, without being subject to the sort of threats and harassment that you carried out… regardless of if they are English or not English." He also said that brandishing an axe in public would have been "extremely frightening for those around" but that he "didn't intend to harm anyone". The judge told the court that it was "frustration" and a "deterioration in his mental state" that led to Glover committing the offence. He said he was satisfied the defendant had shown remorse for both offences, and that he needed support and medication for his "complex mental health" needs. Judge Powell gave him a six-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, as well as a five-year restraining order. He was also ordered to pay a victim surcharge of £154. title: Fuel leak which killed fish in River Taff stopped
description: GE Aerospace previously confirmed fuel got into the river while repair work took place nearby.
body: NRW said it had found the source of the pollution on Friday night A fuel leak in the River Taff which killed fish and sparked a warning for people to shut their windows has now stopped, official have said. Officers from Natural Resources Wales (NRW) on Wedneaday the source of the pollution affecting the Taff in places such as Nantgarw, Treforest and Taffs Well since 16 October over. GE Aerospace previously confirmed fuel got into the river while repair work took place at its site nearby, but NRW said it was working to determine how fuel entered the drainage system and reached the river. NRW added it had found fewer than 10 dead fish and impacts to aquatic invertebrates as a result of the leak. NRW said the source was identified at 19:30 BST on Friday, after kerosene spread down almost 2.5 miles (4km) of the river. It added evidence was being compiled and reviewed as part of the ongoing investigation. The environmental body also received reports of pollution affecting the Taff in Glan Y Llyn, Gwaelod-y-garth and Tongwynlais. Residents said the area began to smell "like a petrol station" on Friday In an update on Sunday evening, NRW said due to the nature of the incident, identifying how the fuel entered the drainage system was difficult as it involved underground systems. Specialist drainage and containment contractors had been sent to the site and were removing the fuel. Eurig Thomas, a resident in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cyon Taff, told the BBC on Sunday: "It smelt like a petrol station, it hit you as soon as you came out." title: India 'cockroach' leaders who called on election chief to quit are freed from jail
description: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were accused of breaking into an unauthorised protest venue in Delhi.
body: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka have spent a week in jail after being accused of trespassing Two leaders of the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been freed from jail a week after they were arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka walked out of Tihar jail hours after a magistrate ordered their release. They had been detained by police and jailed after they crossed barricades and climbed over the locked gate at Jantar Mantar. The historic venue was recently removed from a list of designated protest sites. The men, who denied wrongdoing, have been calling on India's chief election commissioner to resign. Critics accuse the commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit India's governing party, charges the commission rejects. A special executive magistrate court in Delhi, passed their release order, legal news website Bar and Bench reported. After bail was granted, Das told reporters from a police van: "Truth alone triumphs. Long live the revolution." Das and Ranka are key leaders of the CJP, which began as an internet joke in May after India's top judge compared unemployed young people to "cockroaches". CJP members were detained by police after unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans at Jantar Mantar The CJP is not a registered political party, but a collective which began by mobilising thousands of young people to protest over leaked exam papers. By July it had emerged as a major force. A march towards parliament that month ended in clashes with police, drawing wider attention to the movement and increasing pressure on the government. The unrest eventually led to the resignation of India's education minister. The CJP has since shifted its focus to India's electoral system. Along with opposition parties, students and other critics of the government, it accuses Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of revising electoral rolls, an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the allegation. The SIR exercise has resulted in around 130 million names being removed from voter lists since last year. Critics warn that the process could also exclude eligible voters, potentially denying them their right to vote, while the Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove ineligible, dead and duplicate entries. title: 'Targeted' attack on much-loved MP leaves Australian town heartbroken
description: Locals describe the MP, who had to have both legs amputated, as a genuinely kind person who fought for the community.
body: Wangaratta locals have described their disbelief at the alleged attack on local MP Helen Haines Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing through on their way to regional wineries, or music lovers visiting its annual jazz and blues festival. Instead, locals are fielding endless questions about their MP - and having to explain to strangers what it all means for the town's nearly 30,000 people. They are clearly in shock about what police say was a targeted and deliberate attack on Helen Haines on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a car just outside her office. "People are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy," Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who represents King Charles, said at a press conference on Wednesday. The independent federal MP had to have both legs amputated after she was airlifted to Melbourne. But the "two most important parts of Helen", her heart and her mind, were in "good shape", her husband Phil Haines said. The MP isn't a divisive figure, locals tell the BBC, and no one can understand why she was allegedly targeted. "Everyone knows Helen," says Jane Hill, who owns a giftware shop a few hundred metres down the town's main street from where Haines was hit. "She is a such a good person in our community. She'd go to everything - celebrations, funerals, she's one of those genuinely kind people - and so are her family." Local man Brendan Nugent, whose father has been good friends with Haines for decades, faces at least three charges over the alleged attack including intentionally causing harm and appeared in court on Wednesday. Police say they are considering further charges, including attempted murder. Wangaratta Mayor Irene Grant says Helen Haines is a "cheerful" and "committed" MP First elected to parliament in 2019, Haines is best known for her years-long efforts to establish a national anti-corruption commission. She was spurred by on a series of major political scandals which, in her words, saw "public money spent for political gain", disproportionate spending on "shiny infrastructure projects" in marginal seats and decisions benefitting big donors over ordinary people. The commission finally opened in 2023 under Anthony Albanese's Labor government. Haines has also helped to secure funds for housebuilding, railway improvements and health infrastructure in her region, which she argues has long been sidelined by policies favouring cities. On a spring afternoon in Wangaratta, nobody seemed to have a bad word to say about the former nurse and midwife turned politician. Local Mayor Irene Grant described her as "warm", "cheerful" and "committed", and pointed to her record on climate action and Indigenous rights. In a police update on Wednesday, Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said she'd given "wonderful support" to local police when two officers were shot dead in the nearby town of Porepunkah last year. Bystanders who came to Haines' aid recalled how she thanked them even as she lay severely injured. "It was incredible," Jacklyn Black told Nine Network's Today show. "We were having conversations, she was telling me about her grandkids." "To be in that situation and be as calm as she could be in the moment, but also thankful to the aid that the community had given her... I could [not] speak any more highly of her in a moment like that," Cody Lepoidevin added. Bystanders Jacob Evans, Cody Lepoidevin and Jacklyn Black said Haines thanked them for rushing to her aid There's a large print-out of Helen Haines plastered onto the window of her office - anyone delivering flowers for her gets a big smile back as they look up and walk away. Across the road on Tuesday, a man waved an Australian flag. On his T-shirt were the words "Wangaratta - this is not us!!" It's clear that many feel that way in this friendly community where people look out for each other. Next door to Haines' office is RickyChops barbershop, owned by Ricky Jefferies. When he heard the chaos unfolding outside, he rushed to help, pinning down the suspect. "I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him, and I told him that he can't leave," he explained after the incident. "I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way." Some clearly disagree with Ricky. By Tuesday afternoon, he too had received a bouquet of flowers tied to his shop's door, and a small balloon with the words "thank you". Floral tributes to Helen Haines have mounted up outside her office Down the road at the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral, a vigil was held, attended by a couple of hundred people lining up to light a candle for Haines. Some hugged the clergy, while others wore campaign T-shirts carrying the words "Team Helen Haines". Her husband Phil said he had received "thousands upon thousands" of messages of love and support. "I can only say how much of a difference that makes to all of us," he said. "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter." "Whether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community at heart so that's all you can really ask for; a politician that represents your community," said Austin Longfield who lives in nearby Albury. "It's just something that you wouldn't expect in our community," he added. "You see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here." title: Radio presenter's 'wobbles' over Children in Need cycling challenge
description: Owain Wyn Evans says the 400-mile challenge doesn't "feel like a thing I'm able to do".
body: BBC Radio 2 host Owain Wyn Evans will ride through the UK's four nations Radio presenter Owain Wyn Evans has voiced fears about his upcoming challenge to cycle through all four UK nations for Children in Need. The host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show admitted he has had "wobbles", adding: "I just don't feel like it's a thing I'm able to do." It will see him travel almost 400 miles (643km), setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff, and is the greatest distance anyone has covered in a Radio 2 fundraising challenge. With just 19 days to go before he is due to set off, he told colleague Sara Cox on the BBC Radio 2 Breakfast Show on Wednesday he was "so not ready". Sports scientist Prof Greg Whyte has been supporting him on the run-up to the bike ride. He also helped Cox on her Great Northern Marathon Challenge in 2025. Radio 2 presenter Sara Cox took on a 135-mile (217km) journey for Children in Need last year Evans, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, said: "When I think about what I need to do, you know, 400 miles, four nations over the space of four or five days, I just don't feel like it's a thing I'm able to do." Cox recommended he take it a day at a time, but warned the weather had "taken a slight turn". Evans said: "It's been pouring down here and also quite cold to be honest, quite chilly. So that's the thing that I know it was the same with your challenge, Sara, right? "You try and get as ready as you can and there are certain things you can control, but the weather certainly isn't something we can control." After riding through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales, Evans' journey will end in central Cardiff on 13 November. Cox said: "Just keep pedalling, that's all you've got to do, and you will do it." title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
description: The prime minister provided little detail, and there are questions over shifting the fees onto unit costs.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used. Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill. But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill. During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills". He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity". No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate, external, so people pay for what they use. This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more. For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges. Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers. Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas. When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills. Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure. The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households. Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, but Citizens Advice has warned, external about the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers. Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised. But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices." Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy prices forecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January. In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament". Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries. title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy
description: Number 10 North deputy director Duncan Parish has told a conference he is still facing "institutional barriers".
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened Number 10 North in July A "mindset shift" is needed across the UK's central government to help Number 10 North deliver its objectives, its deputy director has said. Duncan Parish told a conference in Lincolnshire on Wednesday there were "institutional challenges" within government that needed to be overcome to deliver change. The Manchester office of Number 10 North - sister to London's Downing Street - was set up by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July. Burnham's political opponents have called the office a "gimmick" and raised transparency concerns about the costs involved. Speaking to the Great Exhibition conference of local political and business leaders, Parish said his career in the civil service to date had "not been without its frustrations" and there can be "friction" between different parts of government which have "similar but ever so slightly competing objectives". Parish, a civil servant in Whitehall before moving to Manchester four years ago, said Number 10 North staff were "delivering outcomes at a national level across a huge range of areas" including health, transport, education and social care. "But we continually need to work to overcome those institutional challenges," he added. He said one priority of Number 10 North was to "shift power and accountability" closer to local areas, but acknowledged "that means reforming the civil service as well" - by not viewing national, regional and local government as separate. Duncan Parish spoke to local political and business leaders in Lincolnshire, in an event chaired by regional mayor Dame Andrea Jenkyns Describing Number 10 North's second focus of growth, Parish told local leaders: "We're here to unblock issues that may have become stalled or where boundaries within government end up being a hindrance." He said that "too often, working within government or departments can be perceived as either difficult or slow". "But to deliver that change, requires us all to change - and part of that change is a mindset shift within central government," he said. "We need to focus on the whole country and work across those boundaries, bringing in mayoral strategic authorities like Greater Lincolnshire into discussions that previously they may not have been part of - working bottom-up, rather than top-down." His comments come as the government continues to face questions about the cost to the taxpayer of the new headquarters. In September, Conservative shadow minister Mike Wood raised concerns about "little information and so little transparency" surrounding Number 10 North which he described as a "gimmick". "The minister either doesn't know or won't tell us how much No 10 North will cost, how many people work there or how many of them actually turn up to work - it's almost as though this hasn't been properly thought through," he told a House of Commons debate. He called for the annual budget, staff levels and office attendance statistics to be published. Current staffing levels have also not yet been clarified. Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said last week that the government did not know how much has been spent on hotels for No 10 North staff, ministers and special advisers travelling between London and Manchester since it opened. The cost is "not centrally collated" but is "being met within existing departmental budgets", Jameson said in response to a parliamentary question. Number 10 North's latest summit of regional mayors, held in its "situation room", will take place on Thursday. Burnham has previously indicated he will work there at least once a week, and hosted the Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in September. Parish added in his speech: "How will we know if Number 10 North is working? "Ultimately, success will be in people in the UK feeling the difference in their communities, with greater opportunities, improved living standards, faster decisions...more joined up services and a stronger voices in the future of their place." title: Tributes paid to 'bravest' woman who died of 'stab wounds' after crash
description: It is understood Eleanor Barnfield, from Bridgend, had been stabbed before the crash.
body: Police say Eleanor Barnfield "sustained puncture wounds unrelated to the collision" in Bridgend Tributes have been paid to a woman who crashed a car into a wall after allegedly being stabbed. Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing. A 61-year-old man from Bridgend has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a "significant" police operation at a retirement housing complex, and remains in custody. Eleanor, who worked for housing association Valleys to Coast which runs the complex, has been described by her family as the "kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world". South Wales Police said Eleanor was taken to hospital after officers were called to the crash on Coity Road at about 12:40 BST on Monday, but later died. Police were also called to nearby sheltered housing retirement complex, Ger-y-Nant, where the man was arrested. Describing Eleanor, from North Cornelly, Bridgend, her family said: "She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock." Jo Oak, chief executive of Valleys to Coast, added the organisation was "devastated by the tragic death of our colleague". "Eleanor was a much-valued member of the Valleys to Coast team, and her loss has been deeply felt by everyone who knew and worked alongside her," she said. "She made an important contribution to our organisation and to the communities we serve, and she will be remembered with great warmth and affection by her colleagues. "Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Eleanor's family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time." Oak said the organisation would "continue to cooperate fully with South Wales Police". Ch Supt Jason Rees said: "Our thoughts remain firmly with Eleanor's family. I want to assure the community that teams of detectives and specialist staff are investigating. "We appreciate the patience and support of residents, especially those displaced following the incident. Local communities may notice an increased police presence as our investigation continues."
