title: Chip muffin? Bacon and egg soda? How Just Eat's AI struggled to depict Britain's regional dishes
description: A spokesperson said it was removing inaccurate AI images and pausing the rollout of the tool.
body: A chip muffin and bacon and egg soda - menu items well known in parts of the UK, but not to the AI which made this Just Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items. The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned. Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins. A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed. Salt and pepper chips usually involves frying chips with onions, garlic and chillies - a little bit more exciting than this suggests "We work with tens of thousands of small restaurants on their food imagery, including funding professional local photographers," the spokesperson told the BBC. "We've been trialling AI-enhanced images, and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time." What some parts of Manchester call a "chip muffin" - also known as a chip butty - causing the AI to invent a dish which seemingly involved baking potato into bread The incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context. Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items. Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus. A "cheese roll" was inexplicably turned into sushi A Belfast cafe, meanwhile, had its bacon and egg soda bread dish represented as a glass of fizzy drink with a cooked egg and bacon floating in it. Spelling mistakes on menu items have sometimes added to the confusion, with the Instagram account @uknewestfoods posting a picture of garlic bread in the shape of a plane - presumably because of a misspelling of the word "plain". Meanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll. While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet". Meanwhile, one person on Instagram, external questioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing. "I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said. "These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like." Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. title: Hull MP has the Labour whip restored
description: Karl Turner is back in the parliamentary party after his suspension for criticising the government.
body: Hull East MP Karl Turner was suspended from the parliamentary party in March Karl Turner has had the Labour whip restored on a "probationary basis". The Hull East MP was suspended from the parliamentary party in March after publicly criticising government policy – in particular the plan to restrict jury trials. In an "agreed" statement, Turner said: "I want to take this opportunity to apologise and reflect on the offence I may have caused colleagues in recent months." He added: "With the party under new leadership and a renewed approach to managing differences of opinion, I am keen to move forward positively and draw a line under this episode." Turner had been critical of Sir Keir Starmer's leadership, saying the Gorton and Denton parliamentary by-election defeat to the Greens was "catastrophic", and blaming that loss on the decision to block now-Prime Minister Andy Burnham from running for the seat. In his statement, Turner said his concerns over plans to limit jury trials in England and Wales had been "sincerely held" and reflected his "long-standing commitment to justice and the rule of law". He added: "However, I acknowledge that, in advancing those arguments, my approach was sometimes overly robust and that my words or actions caused offence to colleagues." A Labour Party spokesperson said: "Following discussions with the government chief whip, Karl Turner MP has had the Labour whip restored on a probationary basis. "The chief whip welcomes Karl Turner's constructive engagement and his acknowledgement that aspects of his behaviour, actions and public comments fell short of the standards expected of Labour MPs. "We welcome his public apology and the undertakings he has given regarding his future conduct. "We now look forward to moving ahead positively, with Karl Turner continuing to contribute as a Labour MP." title: Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
description: The announcement came after Russian President Vladimir Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
body: The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St Petersburg Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said. Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and its European allies have been pressing Moscow for an immediate resumption of the talks suspended in February, and Ushakov said a new round could be held next month, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Russia has for months refused talks as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks. Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland on Monday in Oslo. Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful". Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The talks, however, were put on hold, with the Kremlin blaming last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes on Russia during its general elections for their disruption. Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict." A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine". "This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative". Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front. The talks in Oslo and St Petersburg were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US. Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine". Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran. European leaders have expressed concern about recent US statements towards Russia. title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
description: The vulnerabilities with PHP, a programming language widely used across the internet, have been described as the most significant ever found by AI.
body: International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet. The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon. Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline. The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape. Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities. The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix. "These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote. Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue. And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP. The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities. "We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said. That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday. Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors. They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment. Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance, external" without specifying the reason. The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. They used state-of-the art AI, made by OpenAI, to find the flaws. OpenAI said in a blog post, external it was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". According to the firms, they had gone undetected for more than a decade. "Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post. It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure. The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website. Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note, external. Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning, external. "PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said. Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers. The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said. "The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said. He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold". The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution". Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites. Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was, external "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up". The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP". It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004. The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade. PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites. Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet. title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
description: Kashim Chowdhury was contracted for 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days.
body: Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by working multiple full-time public sector jobs The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent". Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood. He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021. The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs. He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had jobs elsewhere. At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector. In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023. Chowdhury said the jobs were a "lifeline" during a time his mother's health had declined. Asked by defence barrister Pieter Briegel what extent stress in his life was due to the number of jobs, he replied: "The jobs at the time were my lifeline at the time, that was what I survived on at that particular moment. "And they gave me a link to the outside, they were the only thing I had to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time," he told the court. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity". A succession of Chowdhury's line managers have told the jury that he performed poorly in his roles. Abigail Mounde, who was Chowdhury's line manager at the Department for Business and Trade previously told the court: ''Any basic tasks I asked him to do he either did late or not to the standard I would have expected." Chowdhury was asked whether he accepted the criticism of his performance, including the allegation he failed to deliver work on time. He replied: "I reject them all." The prosecution also alleges Chowdhury used sick notes from his doctor as part of the cover-up. But the prosecution said while he was telling some employers he was sick and unfit to work because of "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" he was not giving sick notes to other employers. The prosecution said this ''underlines the dishonesty involved in the whole affair". His line manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, arranged a video call in May 2023, to support him returning to work after a period of absence. In previous evidence she told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin. She told the court that as the call went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck." Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ told the court: ''This almost laughable incident demonstrates quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit.'' title: Aberfan disaster 'most tragic of days imaginable' says King on 60th anniversary
description: In total 116 children and 28 adults were killed when a colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.
body: King Charles paid tribute to the Aberfan community's strength, resilience and "unconquerable spirit" on the disaster's 60th anniversary The King has described the Aberfan disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults as the "most tragic of days imaginable" on its 60th anniversary. Pantglas Junior School and a number of nearby houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966. King Charles III, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales joined survivors and bereaved families on Wednesday and laid wreaths and a posy with the last surviving teacher in the Aberfan Memorial Garden, located on the site of the school. The King also paid tribute to the community's strength, resilience and "unconquerable spirit". Warning: This story contains upsetting details that some may find distressing About half the children from the school died when excavated mining debris from the Merthyr Vale Colliery was dislodged, and 150,000 tonnes of coal waste came thundering down the hillside. Emergency services, miners and people who rushed to the village began an around-the-clock battle to dig out those trapped by the debris. This video can not be played Aberfan falls silent to mark disaster anniversary An official inquiry found the National Coal Board was responsible for the disaster, but no-one has ever been prosecuted. On Friday morning a minute's silence was held at 09:15 BST to mark the moment the coal spoil struck the village, and church bells rang 144 times for each child and adult who died. Pupils at Ynysowen Community Primary School, which was built to carry on the legacy of Pantglas, also gathered to pay their respects. Coal slurry crashed into Pantglas Junior School in Aberfan when a colliery waste tip collapsed in 1966 The royals joined survivors, bereaved parents and members of the community in the memorial garden to pay tribute to all those who lost their lives, followed by a visit to the nearby Aberfan and Merthyr Vale Community Centre. First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth also greeted crowds of people in Aberfan, with flowers that Aberfan victims would have seen in their gardens chosen for the wreaths laid in the garden. The coal waste had been piled high on the side of Mynydd Merthyr – above Aberfan – for years, even though there were numerous underground springs below. An official inquiry in 1967 found the National Coal Board was responsible for the Aberfan disaster, but survivors and bereaved families have long pointed to a litany of injustices. Money was taken from the public disaster fund to help pay for the removal of remaining coal tips above the village, while compensation payments were limited and survivors had to undergo repeated assessments. Support to help deal with their trauma was also minimal. Professor Iain McLean, the co-author of Aberfan - Government and Disaster, has questioned why nobody was ever prosecuted for the Aberfan disaster. Speaking on the BBC Radio Wales Phone In on Wednesday, he said: "And so one of the other failures of the government of the day is their, to me, incomprehensible failure to sack Lord Robens and his senior directors." Robens was the chairman of the National Coal Board at the time, and had faced numerous complaints about the dangers that loomed a quarter of a mile high above the village. One of these included a petition from Pantglas school in 1963, three years before the disaster. In 1997, McLean met three of the counsels who had appeared before the 1967 tribunal and asked why no legal action was taken. "They all said 'nobody thought of it at the time'," he said. Flowers that Aberfan victims would have seen in their gardens were chosen for wreaths to be laid at the memorial garden A school choir performed at Aberfan and Merthyr Vale Community Centre, King Charles met members of the local community at Aberfan and Merthyr Vale Community Centre Ynysowen School pupil's held a minute's silence The First Minister of Wales, Rhun ap Iorwerth, greeted members of the public The wreath laid by the Prince William at Aberfan Memorial Garden The King met Marilyn Brown, one of the few surviving parents of children who died Prince William revealed a plaque during his visit to Ynysowen Community Primary School to unveil the Aberfan Memorial Tree On Wednesday the royal party met retired members of the emergency services at the community centre who helped in the hours and days after the disaster. They then spent time with survivors, bereaved parents, and siblings of those who died. In a speech to those in the community centre, King Charles said the disaster "was and always will be, the saddest and most tragic of days imaginable". He said: "Over the years, as once again today, it has been profoundly humbling to hear the testimonies of survivors of relatives who lost their loved ones, and of rescuers who fought so hard to save others during this appalling tragedy." "Today in our nation and across the world, thoughts will turn to you in Aberfan, hearts far from this valley will ache with yours." This video can not be played Prince William speaks to survivors of the Aberfan disaster King Charles added: "Throughout all this, and through all the years, your unconquerable spirit has shone all the more brightly for the darkness which it has overcome. "No one should ever have to bear what you, as a community, have endured, but no one could have borne it with greater strength, resilience, or hope. "Please know how deeply we feel with your sorrow, how greatly we admire your strength, and how you will, always, be in our hearts." Jeff Edwards, who survived the disaster as an eight-year-old pupil, said in a speech that October 21 1966 was "forever etched into our memory, a day of unimaginable tragedy and loss that changed the lives of families and the community forever". title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military
description: The BBC speaks to several current and former Google DeepMind employees about their concerns with AI use on the battlefield.
body: DeepMind is Google's AI company Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use. The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts. Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so. "Realising my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity. Sofia Liguori resigned from Google, saying the company's push for more AI technology in the military made her feel "ashamed" to work there In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles." "We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind." Google is one of several tech companies that signed contracts with the US military earlier this year to deploy AI across classified military environments. The US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has made integrating AI into the armed forces a key priority, saying the Trump administration will become an "AI-first warfighting force". But AI technology is evolving rapidly, and critics question whether it is reliable enough to be used in warfare without more testing, stronger guardrails and human oversight. After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said. Those values, according to Google's AI Principles, external, include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights". But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said in January that the US "will become an 'AI-first' warfighting force" The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for. Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns. Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future." "Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added. Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch does not think current AI models are "robust enough" for military use In the past few years, the US military has deployed multiple AI-enabled technologies to help advance its warfighting abilities. The most prominent example of this is Maven Smart Systems, the Pentagon's main software platform for organising intelligence and data. Developed by US defence company Palantir, it uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Palantir has integrated the technology from several leading AI companies into Maven, and it has enabled some processes to be significantly speeded up. Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, who is the former director of Project Maven, said the "philosophy" seems to be: "Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation." However, the Pentagon has maintained that adopting AI technologies is essential for winning wars. "Speed defines victory in the AI era," said Emil Michael, an under secretary in the US Department of Defense, in a statement earlier this year. Google's contract with the Pentagon, which was signed earlier this year, allows its AI technology to be used for classified military work. The agreement says Google's AI models can be used for "any lawful government purpose" and "should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons (including target selection) without appropriate human oversight and control". Google's AI Principles include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning with "international law and human rights" Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations. As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war. "AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team. "When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors." Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company. title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
description: The UK government says the field, which is opposed by environmental campaigners, could be producing gas by the end of this month.
body: Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact. Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund. But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision. Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand. The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter. She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear". "The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said. The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects. At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision. She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences. "We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said. The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up". He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round". Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills. The Jackdaw platform is located east of Aberdeen Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland. "It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader. He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland". Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail." Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision. This video can not be played Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial? But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism". He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now." Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify". The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank. Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989. The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit. Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production. But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully. The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate chan

title: Anderson, 44, not offered new Lancashire contract
description: James Anderson’s legendary career could be over after Lancashire opt against offering England’s all-time leading wicket-taker a new deal.
body: James Anderson is England's all-time leading Test wicket-taker with 704 dismissals James Anderson's legendary career could be over after Lancashire opted against offering England's all-time leading wicket-taker a new contract. Anderson, 44, chose to continue playing with Lancashire after England forced him into international retirement in 2024. He captained Lancashire in the County Championship last season but the Red Rose endured a poor campaign, finishing next to bottom of Division Two. Now, as first reported by the Times, Anderson will not be given the opportunity to play at Old Trafford in 2027 - the summer when he will turn 45. It is not known whether Anderson will retire or look to extend his 26-year professional career with another county. Anderson first played top-level cricket as a 17-year-old for Lancashire Cricket Board in 2000, then made his Lancashire debut the following year. His exit from the Red Rose comes at a time of upheaval at Old Trafford. The county are undergoing a review of their cricket operations, led by interim chair Dame Sarah Storey and new chief executive Richard Kenyon. Paul Farbrace was appointed as Lancashire's director of cricket earlier this month. Although Anderson is in his mid-40s, he has remained in supreme form in a struggling team. He took 50 wickets in the County Championship in 2026, a tally bettered by only six other bowlers in Division Two. Anderson was named Lancashire's Championship player of the year. Overall, 443 of Anderson's 1,193 first-class wickets came for Lancashire, to go with 83 List A wickets and 50 T20 wickets for the county. In a 23-year international career, Anderson took 991 wickets across formats for England. Only spinners Muttiah Muralitharan of Sri Lanka and Australia's Shane Warne have more in international cricket. In 2024, Anderson became the third bowler in Test history, after Muralitharan and Warne, to reach 700 wickets. He remains third on the all-time list with 704, a record for a pace bowler that is unlikely to be broken. Later that year, Anderson was asked to call time on his international career by England's then hierarchy of coach Brendon McCullum, captain Ben Stokes and director of cricket Rob Key. He played his 188th and final Test against West Indies at Lord's before embarking on a short spell as England's bowling consultant. In 2025, Anderson signed a new deal with Lancashire and suggested he could play county cricket for three more seasons. In April of that year, he was knighted for services to cricket. Anderson stood in as Lancashire captain during the 2025 season and was given the job full-time for 2026. He was understood to be enjoying the role and, at the end of the this summer, there was no suggestion Anderson would end his career. On Wednesday, as reports of his exit from Old Trafford began to emerge, those close to Anderson were unaware of the situation. Lancashire have not commented. title: Glastonbury coach tickets oversold in admin error
description: Bookings will automatically be converted into a general admission ticket and coach fare refunded.
body: Bookings will automatically be converted into a general admission ticket and the coach fare will be refunded An administrative error resulted in coach journeys to the Glastonbury Festival being oversold through its official ticketing partner. More coach package tickets were sold for certain departures than there are seats available, according to an email See Tickets sent to customers. Those affected will not lose their tickets however. Instead, their booking will automatically be converted into a general admission ticket and the coach fare will be refunded. The ticketing agency declined to comment further, but the BBC understands Glastonbury Festival was not responsible for the error. Glastonbury coach ticket prices range from £26 to £185 - on top of general admission - depending on the departure town or city and whether it is a single or return journey. What to do if you missed out on Glastonbury tickets Glastonbury founder on hosting his first festival at Worthy Farm Top tips for taking kids to Glastonbury Festival 'We want to give you best seat in house for Glasto' Affected customers have been told that unless they opt to keep their coach seat by 31 October 2026, their booking will automatically be converted to general admission. The coach fare will then be refunded to the card used for the original booking. See Tickets' customer services department assured customers the error will not affect festival deposits, and ticket holders will be able to pay the remaining balance for their tickets as normal in April. The agency apologised and thanked customers for their understanding, adding: "We're looking forward to welcoming you to the festival in June." The first batch of tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in less than 30 minutes For some the news is welcome, as it provides more flexibility with travel arrangements. Glastonbury Festival requires those who bought a coach ticket to to board their designated coach for the initial journey to the festival, or entry could be denied. It is part of the festival's Green Travel Initiatives, external, where they encourage revellers to use public transportation in a bid to reduce the environmental impact. Laura Brooks, based in Birmingham, says she and her friends bought the coach package because "we had failed so often getting [general admission] tickets". She had planned to meet them in London to travel to Somerset together, but can now arrange simpler and shorter journeys from their own respective homes. "I don't mind the admin error, they're clearly dealing with it sooner than later. These things happen," she said. "I'm just glad we've not lost our tickets altogether." title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
description: Education Secretary Lucy Powell has stressed the importance of reminding new generations of the horrors of the Holocaust.
body: Education Secretary Lucy Powell says the government will "update and strengthen" Holocaust education within schools after a major review highlighted the "shocking scale" of antisemitism in British society. Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it. It means anti-Jewish hatred will be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying. The government has accepted all of the 27 recommendations made in the government-commissioned review including dedicated training for teachers and more consistent recording of incidents. Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday. Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent". She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges. "I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next – that is the job of education – to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world." Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have. The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers. Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics. The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed. Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws. The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse. It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters. The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism. Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations. He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries." Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism. Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role. "When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said. "We think about it a lot." In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory. The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities. However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial. The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism". In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability." Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism". They said: "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition." Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day". "Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged." "One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust." The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition. It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza". The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised". Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents

title: Andrews died of tear in artery around heart - autopsy
description: Former Sale player Hyron Andrews - who was found dead at his new team's hotel base before a Champions Cup match - died of natural causes, an autopsy finds.
body: Hyron Andrews joined Sale midway through the 2023-24 season Hyron Andrews - the former Sale second row found dead at his new team's hotel base before a Champions Cup match in France on Saturday - died of natural causes, an autopsy has found. The 31-year-old, who joined the Johannesburg-based Lions this summer, suffered a tear in the aorta, an artery which carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body. The rupture led to blood filling the muscle sac surrounding his heart. Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle, with investigators working on the theory that he had either suffered a fall, a heart attack or, as transpired, an aneurysm, where a bulging blood vessel breaks. A tear in the aorta is a rare and dangerous medical condition, which can be caused by undetected high blood pressure or a birth defect. His body is yet to be returned to his native South Africa. Andrews' wife Maighlin, with whom he had two young sons, has asked for "respect, privacy and patience during this difficult time as the repatriation process begins", according to a statement from the Lions., external His team-mates went ahead with their game against La Rochelle on Saturday in his honour. The visitors were applauded into the Stade Marcel-Deflandre by home fans,, external while several of the Lions players were in tears during a minute's silence before kick-off. Sale, with whom Andrews spent two and half seasons, also paid tribute, with director of rugby Alex Sanderson saying that his team "to a man, loved playing with Hyron and being around him". title: Don't Stop Believin'! - high school musical Glee set for reboot
description: Ryan Murphy's popular musical comedy-drama is set to return on Hulu and Disney+ after a decade away.
body: Left to right: Jenna Ushkowitz, Chris Colfer, Kevin McHale, Amber Riley and Lea Michele in Glee We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return. Ryan Murphy's series, which chronicled the highs and lows of choir members from Ohio, premiered on Fox in 2009 and ran for six seasons until 2015. The original cast included Lea Michele, Amber Riley, the late Cory Monteith, Jane Lynch and Matthew Morrison as Will Schuester, the optimistic teacher leading the fictional McKinley High's glee club. The reboot was announced, external by Disney and Hulu via the show's social media team on Wednesday. The show was a huge hit first time around, known for its big laughs and big heart, tackling topics such as sexuality, race, disability and mental health. In the series, glee club New Directions helped misfit students find their voices through song and dance. Lynch served as the club's main antagonist, the villainous cheerleading coach Sue Sylvester. The choir's covers of Don't Stop Believin', River Deep, Mountain High and Smooth Criminal also brought older hit songs to the attention of younger audiences. In 2010, the show was adapted for a concert tour in which was captured on film. Around the same time, the cast overtook The Beatles as the non-solo act with the most Billboard Hot 100 appearances. On Wednesday, the Wanted singer Max George told BBC Scotland that appearing in the show's sixth season was "an amazing experience", adding that he'd "love to do it again". "I messaged the casting director from it, just with wide eyes from the announcement," he said. Asked if it makes sense for the series to come back, he said: "I think so… It's been over 10 years, so I think that's a nice break. "I think it was probably coming towards the end in terms of the storylines and everything, but 10 years has gone by, and Ryan Murphy will probably come up with something genius. So I'm expecting big things." In a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight, co-creator Murphy confirmed he had written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan. He also said he had "been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members". "It's very sweet, they all had a lot of questions but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea," he said. "Nobody's read it, so we'll see." He added: "I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, because we were very close when we were making it." It came after Michelle, who played Rachel Berry, the ambitious singer at the centre of the club, had told E! News that she - like Lynch - would be more than happy to return. "I will always love Glee," she said. "I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me... I will follow Ryan wherever he goes." Speaking to Bustle recently, another star of the show, Chris Colfer, admitted that any such reboot would be difficult following the death of Naya Rivera, who played Glee club favourite Santana Lopez. "It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya is gone," said Colfer, who portrayed Kurt Hummel - the flamboyant singer and original choir member who faces bullying at the school. "But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don't know, but hopefully I'll have more information and I can actually think about it." Rivera died in 2020 at the age of 33 in an accidental drowning. Hers was the third death among the Glee cast. Monteith, who played football star turned singer Finn Hudson, died in 2013 at the age of 31 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin. Mark Salling, another Glee cast member, took his own life in 2018 at the age of 35 while awaiting sentencing on child pornography charges. A mini Glee reunion occurred on Sunday at London's Royal Albert Hall, when Darren Criss, aka Glee's Blaine Anderson, brought out Colfer for a duet of the song Baby It's Cold Outside. Earlier this month, former Glee co-stars Harry Shum Jr and Amber Riley reunited on Dancing with the Stars. title: Jailed former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson being investigated over alleged rape inside Parliament
description: While not naming the disgraced former MP, the Metropolitan Police has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.
body: Donaldson appearing at a previous court appearance in June 2026 Jailed former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated by London police about an alleged rape of a woman inside the Houses of Parliament, the BBC can reveal. The disgraced former MP has been accused of raping the woman in Parliament in 2016, at the very heart of the political establishment. Last week Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions. It is understood the woman has been interviewed by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers. The PSNI has now shared her claims with the Metropolitan Police, as the alleged incident happened in London. While not naming the former DUP leader, the Met has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated. It said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report referred to us by the Police Service of Northern Ireland relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63. "The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers. "The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing." In July, the Belfast Telegraph first reported that a woman from Northern Ireland alleged she had been sexually assaulted by Donaldson in the DUP offices at Parliament in 2016. She claimed that he attempted to get her to drink vodka shots in his office, before trying to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt. On Saturday, the newspaper further reported that the Met was set to investigate and interview Donaldson about these accusations. But in response to BBC questions it has now emerged the same woman has also alleged Donaldson raped her. Concerns about the ex-DUP MP's behaviour in London was raised in a BBC NI Spotlight film, earlier this year. A former senior PSNI detective told the programme he had seen Donaldson drunk in the Houses of Parliament. Two other former senior PSNI detectives also reported seeing him going into a gay sauna not far from Parliament in 2006, the same year in which Donaldson described homosexuality as "sinful". title: Belfast comedian criticised for rape 'joke' about assault victim
description: Vittorio Angelone referred to content creator Rebecca Goodwin in a remark about rape.
body: Vittorio Angelone has faced criticism for his remarks A Belfast comedian has been criticised for making a rape "joke" about a woman who had recently spoken publicly about being the victim of a sexual assault. Vittorio Angelone, who has since apologised on social media, referred to content creator Rebecca Goodwin in a remark about rape which he made in a podcast episode in 2025. Goodwin, who had previously reported a rape to police, said it will "forever live with me that it was allowed for my name to be used as the punchline of a malicious 'joke' about such a serious issue". Angelone said he has reached out to Goodwin and apologised directly. Goodwin had claimed that Angelone posted videos of the "joke" on his social media accounts in recent days. Rape Crisis Northern Ireland and Dublin Rape Crisis Centre have both criticised the remarks. The makers of the podcast have been contacted for comment. During a 2025 episode of the 'Have a Word' podcast, Angelone asked of fellow comedian Freddy Quinne "if you're here, who's raping Rebecca Goodwin?". British OnlyFans creator Rebecca Goodwin had previously spoken publicly about being the victim of sexual assault. The comments were made during a "roast" episode of the podcast posted in December 2025. The episode, which Goodwin was not involved in, contained comedians taking turns insulting each other in front of an audience. In a post on Facebook, Goodwin said the episode was recorded "in September/October of 2025 and has been behind a paywall for a year before being published to social media". She reported a rape to police in July 2025 and had spoken publicly about her experience. Goodwin said she only became aware of the comments when clips were posted to social media in recent days. "I am grateful I never saw it sooner because it would've been just weeks after [the assault] happened and I was in a different mental state to what I am now," she said. At that time, Goodwin said that "no contact or apology has been attempted" by Angelone, but that he had "removed the joke from his own social media, again, over a year after it was made, edited, clipped, captioned and posted with my full name included". The comments have not been edited out of the paywalled episode of the podcast. Goodwin said: "We are facing a global crisis of violence against women and girls, and we are begging for our safety and experiences to be taken seriously." She added that Freddy Quinne, as well as a number of other comedians who were part of the podcast episode, had since apologised to her. However, Goodwin said that she did not accept the apologies as they "only came a year after the joke was made and nobody had my back in that room at the time, up until I made a social media post about it". Quinne has been approached for comment. In a statement on Instagram, Angelone said he let his "need for validation supersede my own standards and morals". "It's completely pathetic and I'm ashamed to realise that about myself," he said. Angelone will feature in his first major acting role in upcoming BBC sitcom Rewarding, which is set to air this autumn. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are aware of the concerns that have been raised and are actively considering them, recognising their seriousness and the sensitivities involved." Rape Crisis Northern Ireland said they were "very disappointed to hear of the comments made by Vittorio Angelone which contribute to a culture in which rape and sexual violence can be trivialised". "When rape becomes a punchline and sexual violence is treated as entertainment, it becomes easier to dismiss its impact and harder for survivors to speak out." It continued: "Those with a public platform and an audience have a responsibility to consider the impact of the language they use and the attitudes they help to normalise. "Rape jokes might seem far removed from an act of sexual violence, but they sit within that same culture of minimising and trivialising it." They added "survivors should never be left feeling that what happened to them is something that could be laughed at, minimised or dismissed". Chief Executive of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, Rachel Morrogh, said: "For survivors, hearing rape treated as a punchline can be deeply hurtful, and it reinforces the attitudes that discourage people from coming forward. "Anyone with a public platform, including performers, promoters and venues, has a responsibility to consider who is listening and the harm this kind of material can do. To treat sexual violence as a joke betrays a deep lack of understanding of what survivors have lived through." If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line. title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
description: The comment is an apparent swipe at Benjamin Netanyahu and Donald Trump, who both face elections in coming weeks.
body: Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the country French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes. Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests. Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic". It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month. Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots. Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice. Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media. The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools. Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble. Clean up begins after French riots but police remain Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them In pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders... "We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false." On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam". He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added. Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France. "When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country." "Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron. Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections Pink Panther rioting in France is actually AI According to a report in the UK's Financial Times newspaper, external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states. It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds. David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives". France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year. BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka. The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24. The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics. Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website. The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image. It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened. While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views. Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated. title: Why do Man City fans boo pre-match anthems?
description: The cacophony of boos that greet the Premier League and Champions League anthems before kick-off have now become a fixture at Etihad Stadium.
body: Manchester City fans held up literal 'boos' during a Champions League game at Sevilla in 2015 The cacophony of boos that greet the Premier League and Champions League anthems before kick-off have now become a fixture at Etihad Stadium. The jeers from Manchester City fans were turned up a notch against Ipswich last Saturday when the side played their first home game since being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules. "I can't remember a Premier League or Champions League home game where the anthems haven't been booed," City season-ticket holder Dave Wilson told BBC Sport. The pre-match dissatisfaction towards top-flight chiefs can likely be traced back to February 2023, when the 115 charges for breaching the rules were first announced. Later that same year, Everton had 10 points - reduced to six on appeal - deducted after being found to have broken profit and sustainability rules. In their first game back after the sanction, Toffees fans displayed their ire at Goodison Park by loudly booing the league's pre-match anthem as well as holding up red cards with the word 'corrupt' printed underneath the Premier League logo. Though City supporters did not organise a similar display, their anger was clear. "The Premier League anthem has been booed by City fans for many years," said Wilson. "It was probably heightened on Saturday because it was the first home game since the [guilty verdict] announcement. "There hasn't been much love lost between City and the Premier League for a long time. For certain games it will be louder than others, it definitely wasn't co-ordinated for that [Ipswich] game but a symptom of everything coming together." There was audible booing before Tuesday's Champions League fixture against AEK Athens too. No Haaland, no problem - can Foden be Man City's alternative goalscorer? Everton fans held up cards with the word 'corrupt' printed underneath the Premier League logo and booed during the top-flight anthem in November 2023 City fans' displeasure towards Uefa goes back even further, there being a litany of disputes with Europe's top brass. In 2012, Porto were handed a fine, external of around £17,000 by Uefa after City made a complaint of racial abuse towards striker Mario Balotelli to the organising body. In that same season, City were given a fine, external of around £24,000 for being one minute late back on to the pitch for the second half of a game against Sporting. In 2014, Uefa fined City £49m and capped their squad size for the Champions League after they failed Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules. Six years later, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned City's two-year ban from European club competitions after clearing them of "disguising equity funds as sponsorship contributions" - Uefa initially ruled City had committed "serious breaches" of FFP regulations between 2012 and 2016. Wilson adds: "City fans generally feel there is a conspiracy against them, like the booing of the Uefa anthem too. There is a feeling of being targeted, rightly or wrongly. "City fans just don't seem to like the competitions we play in!" City and their supporters are currently in limbo as they await the outcome of the appeal and any potential sanctions. The side are currently top of the table having won all seven league games so far and that 100% record will be given a stern examination with a difficult trip to Aston Villa on Saturday (kick-off 12:30 BST). Nick Clarke is interim chair of The Citizens Trust - Manchester City supporters' union, a member-led trust that was set up earlier this year at a time when the "potential biggest issue affecting City fans in the club's history" had transpired. Though it has been a "difficult time", fans are "completely behind the team" and he says his job is to ensure their views are heard amid the external noise. "The booing of the anthem on Saturday was totally organic," says Clarke. "Whereas the bananas at Liverpool was a fan-led initiative co-ordinated by the 1894 atmosphere group and they did great work handing those out before the game. "Even though there are fans who are conflicted about what has happened with the club, there is still a general feeling among the majority [of City fans] that the Premier League is not fit for purpose in regulating itself and how it is ran." Whatever the outcome of the appeal, City fans are likely to continue making their feelings clear before kick-off. title: Woman told Russell Brand he 'treated her like an animal', court hears
description: The comedian and actor is on trial for charges including rape and sexual assault, which he denies.
body: Warning - this report contains graphic content One of the women who claims Russell Brand raped her later told him he had "treated her like an animal", a court has heard. The comedian's trial at Southwark Crown Court in London has been hearing recorded police interviews with a female complainant, who claims she did not consent to anal sex with him at his house in 2009. Brand, 51, denies three charges of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one charge of indecent assault. He has said he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity. The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants. On Wednesday, the jury heard an interview with a woman who says she first met Brand at one of his comedy shows at Hammersmith Apollo in 2009. She said she had a boyfriend at the time but went to his dressing room, where she performed a sex act on him. The woman said it was during their next meeting at his house when the sex was not consensual and she had only agreed to vaginal sex. Asked by the detective in the interview whether there was ever a conversation about anal sex, she replied: "No." She said she was surprised to receive a "random" text message from Brand six months later, saying he wanted to "push her further". She said she replied asking: "Why are you even messaging me?" "I remember his response, saying, 'Because you're dirty and I want to push you further'." The jury heard that the woman did not respond straight away because she was upset, but then replied saying: "I think you've pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal." The woman added: "I do remember his response was immediate. He said, 'I'm sorry'." You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts During cross-examination, the woman was asked by defence barrister Ian Winter KC about her decision to meet Brand. "You made it clear that you went to his house to have sex with him, knowing his reputation," he said. She said that was "correct", adding: "I want to flag that I wanted to go there, I take ownership." The woman said she had a couple of glasses of alcohol while getting ready at home and another glass while waiting in a restaurant for Brand's driver to pick her up on the day of the alleged rape. The court heard he made her shower and brush her teeth before they had sex. Winter suggested that Brand asked her to do so because he did not like the smell of alcohol "because of his soberism", but the woman said it was because "he didn't like the smell of my hair". When questioning her about the alleged rape, Winter put to the female complainant: "You had vaginal sex with a condom on and then it finished with you agreeing to anal sex." The woman replied: "I did not consent to that at that time. "We're not here to discuss my morality. We're here to discuss criminality. I thought I was going to have penetrative vaginal sex. "He acted like nothing happened." She broke down in tears at the end of giving her evidence. title: Kildunne drops to bench as England ring changes
description: Star full-back Ellie Kildunne is dropped to the bench as England shake up selection in response to a first defeat in four years.
body: Kildunne made more metres (149) and clean breaks (two) and beat more defenders (six) than any other England player in defeat by Canada England head coach John Mitchell says Ellie Kildunne needs to show greater consistency after dropping his star full-back to the bench in the wake of the Red Roses' first defeat in four years. Kildunne was part of the starting XV that lost 24-21 to Canada last Friday in Toronto as England's unbeaten streak ended at 41 matches. "It is undisputed that she adds huge value," said Mitchell of the 27-year-old. "She's just going through a difficult period at the moment, and it's important for us to to help her through that. "She wants to become consistent as well and she'll get back. "It's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game and that goes for everyone." This video can not be played Late Canada fightback ends Red Roses' unbeaten streak Emma Sing comes in at full-back in Kildunne's place for Saturday's rematch (00:10 BST) against Canada in Ottawa, while Tatyana Heard and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald - backline starters in the defeat - drop out of the matchday squad entirely. Helena Rowland and Mia Venner replace Heard and Moloney-MacDonald at inside centre and wing respectively. In the fourth change to the starting line-up, Sadia Kabeya, who appeared off the bench last week on her comeback from a leg injury, starts with Alex Matthews, two-time Rugby World Cup winner, dropping to the bench. Exeter's Flo Robinson and Sale's Hollie Aitchison are included on the bench as a new-look set of half-back replacements. Sing, a rangy runner who can also kick goals, started two matches at full-back during England's Six Nations campaign, with Kildunne switching to a different position on the wing on each occasion. Sing's Gloucester-Hartpury team-mate Venner made her England debut in 2020 aged just 17. Venner has won only another four caps since but was putting pressure on England's more established back three at the start of this year, appearing in wins over Scotland and Italy. The 24-year-old finished as the PWR's joint top try-scorer last season, crossing 12 times. Moloney-MacDonald cost her side an early try in the defeat by Canada when, after doing superbly to pick Jess Breach's pass off her toes, she spilled the ball over the line in the sixth minute. "Last Friday, we lost sight of what we could control when it mattered most. That's on us to fix," added Mitchell. "This week is about getting back to who we are - hungry, accountable to each other and demanding more of ourselves than anyone outside this group ever could."We've earned a strong period but nothing about it is owed to us going forward. "Friday [Saturday 00:10 BST] is an opportunity to apply sustained pressure, learn from what we missed and come out the other side better than we went in."
