title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case linked to East Africa
description: The female patient, who sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian, is in isolation and in an Abuja hospital.
body: Medics across Africa, including these nurses pictured during a training drill in Kenya, have been on high alert since May Nigeria has recorded a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda in East Africa to Abuja, capital of the West African state. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the diagnosis had been confirmed by laboratory tests. The patient, who health sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian and is the wife of a diplomat, is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja. She developed symptoms on Wednesday 7 October, four days after arriving in the country, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Health authorities have begun contact-tracing to prevent further spread, with 44 close contacts of the woman identified. Nigeria, the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East Africa, successfully stopped a previous outbreak in 2014. Uganda's Ministry of Health has stressed there are currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country. "We urge the public to remain calm, vigilant and to practice regular handwashing and sanitising," it said. Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed? What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding. The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external. It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way. Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged. Following the latest case in Nigeria, Uganda's health ministry said preliminary information indicated that the patient had transited through Uganda without symptoms. In a statement on X, Uganda's Director General of Health Services Charles Olaro said the woman had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October. He said her symptoms had only developed after arriving in Nigeria. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The woman's exact travel history - key to tracing contacts - appears to be unclear at the moment. "The location of exposure remains under investigation. The government of Nigeria is yet to provide detailed information on her travel itinerary and clinical history which will guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing," Olaro said. Nigeria's health minister confirmed the woman had had no symptoms when she arrived in Nigeria, but he said the patient had not confirmed travel to DR Congo. "We presume that it was likely picked in Uganda," Pate told the national broadcaster Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) on Tuesday evening. Her travel documents will be used to trace contacts and the authorities have urged the public to co-operate with health officials carrying out contact tracing. The disease has also recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections. On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country. Since the outbreak, Nigeria has stepped up disease surveillance, with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control issuing public health advice to travellers. The agency says travellers from countries with active or relevant Ebola transmission may be required to complete a health declaration form. Those arriving from other countries are currently exempt. It has also urged travellers to remain vigilant and seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms of Ebola. In 2014, Nigeria managed to beat an outbreak of Ebola which caused at least eight deaths. title: How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?
description: BBC Verify looks at what the Jackdaw decision means for bills, energy security and the environment.
body: The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks. BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment. Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor. The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036. Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years. Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines. Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines. But a higher share of the UK's gas imports now come in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) compared with 20 years ago. This is natural gas which is extracted, turned into liquid form and then transported by ship to the country which buys it, where it is turned back into gas form to be used as an energy source. And the UK increasingly relies on shipments of LNG from the US, which accounted for a quarter of all natural gas imports in 2025, external. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has said the gas from Jackdaw "won't lower energy bills this winter". And most energy analysts do not expect the additional gas production from Jackdaw to have a significant, direct impact on households' energy bills, either. This is because of the way natural gas markets work. Great Britain is integrated with wider European gas markets and physically linked to the continent through undersea pipelines. Gas prices faced by British households and businesses are effectively set at a pan-European level and determined by the price customers across Europe are prepared to pay for the energy. People across the continent have seen their energy bills rise significantly in recent years, fuelled by the wars in Ukraine and Iran affecting gas and oil supplies. But the additional gas being pumped into the UK's system from Jackdaw will still be relatively small, and unlikely to significantly move the European price paid by British firms and households. "Essentially, producing more British energy doesn't necessarily mean cheaper British energy," Karl Matikonis, professor of taxation at University College Dublin, told BBC Verify. "North Sea oil and gas are sold at market prices rather than reserved for British consumers at a discount." However, the additional production of gas from Jackdaw could result in more corporation tax revenues for the UK government, because any profits made by the owner would be taxable. As part of its Jackdaw announcement, external, the government said it was setting up a new energy wealth fund, using tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas to invest in green energy projects. It said this would "help get bills down for good in the long term" by reducing the UK's reliance on gas for electricity production. The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said, external the tax revenue from Jackdaw "could be used to bring down energy bills" more directly by taking costs of households' bills directly. However, both proposals depend on the future profits of the owner of Jackdaw, which cannot be forecast with certainty. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said opening the gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs" and the move has been welcomed by unions. The owner of Jackdaw has also estimated, external it will help support around 500 jobs, including roles on nearby production hubs, but only 27 direct roles on the Jackdaw gas extraction platform in the North Sea. One of the key arguments put forward in favour of developing Jackdaw is that it would improve the UK's national energy security. Energy experts take different views on this. Some suggest, external that if, for some reason, foreign LNG shipments were not able to reach the UK, having additional North Sea gas from Jackdaw available and delivered through a pipeline that the UK controls might prove valuable. They argue that the reliability of the US as a source of energy has been put into question by Donald Trump's recent comments that he was considering banning exports of US diesel , externalto European countries. However, others are not convinced Jackdaw would make a significant difference to national energy security because the UK would remain heavily reliant on natural gas imports even when the field is up and running. The enviromental impact of Jackdaw has also been a significant point of contention. Advocates argue the gas field would be beneficial because the carbon emissions arising from production from the the UK's own North Sea field will be lower than those arising from the production of US LNG. The North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the sector, has estimated the emissions arising from the production, delivery and processing of US LNG are around three times higher than from the production of North Sea natural gas. That is because the process of liquefying, shipping and then turning LNG back in to natural gas on arrival is extremely energy intensive, compared with pumping it ashore by a pipeline, creating higher carbon emissions. title: Astronaut surprise video leaves pupils starstruck
description: The surprise came after a teacher's father met Peake while working on a cruise ship.
body: Tim Peake told pupils: "Stay curious. Keep looking up at the stars" Primary school children have been left amazed after receiving a personal video message from British astronaut Tim Peake. Pupils at Thornbury Primary School in Plymouth, Devon, were sent the message after teacher Emily Trevarthen's father met Peake while working on a cruise ship over the summer. Trevarthen explained that her father and the astronaut got chatting and her father mentioned she was a teacher. "We didn't expect to get what we got really," she said. Peake told pupils, external: "I hear you've been studying all about space, a subject very close to my heart, something I love, so I'm very pleased that you enjoy it too. Stay curious. Keep looking up at the stars." Trevarthen said that some children had previously assumed all astronauts were American, but learning about a British astronaut had helped them see that such ambitions were possible. Tim Peake visited the space station in 2015 The video was kept secret until World Space Week, external, when staff revealed it during a celebration assembly. Trevarthen said the children were "so excited" when they saw the video, with some initially wondered whether the message had been created using artificial intelligence before realising it was genuine. She said: "The children absolutely loved it. The standout moment was learning that Tim Peake had run a marathon on the International Space Station. They couldn't believe it." Teacher Joanna Stelmaszczyk said there was "so much excitement" when the video was shown and recalled similar enthusiasm when pupils watched Peake's historic arrival at the International Space Station in 2015. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she said. "I was teaching Year 1 at the time, and the buzz and excitement in the classroom was something I will never forget." title: F1 races to return to standard distance in 2028
description: Formula 1 grands prix will return to their standard distance in 2028 after the maximum length was shortened for next season.
body: The maximum distance of a Formula 1 race will be reduced by 15km in 2027 Formula 1 grands prix will return to their standard distance in 2028 after the maximum length was shortened for next season. The maximum distance of a race was cut by 15km from 305km (189.5 miles) to 290km (180.2 miles) for the 2027 season. That reduction was introduced because of a quirk of the situation surrounding changes to the engine rules for next year. The new hybrid engines introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have been criticised for reducing the impact of driver skill. The power split will be changed, in two steps, to 60-40 by 2028, enabling drivers to have maximum power for longer. This means the cars will use more fuel - and that became a concern when it emerged some teams wanted to carry their chassis over into next year to save money. As the fuel tank is within the chassis and therefore its size could not be changed, this meant those teams might not have been able to finish grands prix with their existing fuel tanks. The change affects only a handful of races where fuel consumption is heaviest. The sport's governing body, the FIA, published the 2027 rules this week and these included a section on changes for 2028 in which there is a clause that removes the reduction and reinstates the 305km maximum distance. Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton had previously objected to the shortening of race distances. Britain's Hamilton, 41, said: "The races should be longer because the races are physically easier than ever before. So shortening, I don't think, makes much sense. "This is supposed to be the sport that's the most physically demanding - mentally and physically. There are some that are just so hot and ultimately you are on the edge. Like Singapore is incredibly hot and demanding. "But that's where I think you want to see athletes - just right on the edge, right? Right at the edge of their performance, having to actually push their bodies further because that's what this sport is about - pushing, pushing the levels and pushing the boundaries." title: Residents report Bayeux Tapestry ticket issues
description: The British Museum says residents were offered tickets on a "first come, first served" basis.
body: The British Museum says residents were offered tickets on a "first come, first served" basis Residents in and around Hastings who had been assured of tickets to see the Bayeux Tapestry say they have had "considerable difficulty" obtaining the tickets. The British Museum said that while residents were offered the chance to secure tickets before wider release, these were on a "first come, first served basis". Hastings and Rye MP Helena Dollimore told BBC Radio Sussex that the process has been "shambolic" and that the British Museum should put aside a batch of tickets for locals. A British Museum spokesperson said: "All residents are still able to book tickets as part of the general sale on the 21 October." The spokesperson added there will be a third opportunity when the next round of tickets are released in the new year. Jenny, from St Leonards, told BBC Radio Sussex: "I phoned the number at 10:00 BST on Monday when they went on sale but it was engaged. "When I managed to get through after an hour, I was on hold for two hours then cut off. "I can't believe we had to phone up - it's such a shame, I'd have loved to have got priority tickets but now I'll have to try and get tickets like everyone else." Dollimore added: "Residents were unable to get through or on hold for hours, trying to secure tickets only to be cut off before getting through to the box office. "Why is it so hard for local residents of 1066 Country to get tickets, but so easy for billionaires to get exclusive private viewings? "As a publicly funded museum, the British Museum has a responsibility to make sure the arts is for the many, not the few." The British Museum said it is not financially feasible to set up an online platform for residents and it may exclude people, as well as the codes being vulnerable to be shared further. body: This video can not be played Four people who were children at the time of the Aberfan disaster recall the moment when a coal waste tip collapsed on schools and homes 60 years ago. title: Women welcome annual check for debilitating condition
description: Women with PMOS say too often they are diagnosed and left to manage the condition on their own.
body: Neelam Heera-Shergill founded charity Cysters to provide support she felt was missing after her diagnosis When Neelam Heera-Shergill was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) at the age of 18, she feared it could one day stop her becoming a mother. "I'm never going to have children. That's it, my life is over," she said. The condition affects about one in eight women in the UK, yet despite its broad impact on health and wellbeing, Neelam, from Birmingham, said she was left with little understanding of what her diagnosis really meant. It is one of the reasons she supports the decision to rename PCOS to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) earlier this year, alongside a recommendation for annual health checks to improve diagnosis and long-term care. The NHS said PMOS, which affects millions of women, was a health condition that could affect hair growth, periods, fertility and mood, external. Cysters, based in Birmingham, holds monthly events to support women with the condition For Neelam, finding out she had the condition sent her into what she described as a "rabbit hole" of fear and uncertainty. Not long after beginning university, she started experiencing irregular and painful periods, thinning hair, weight gain and exhaustion. "My periods were so irregular but when I had them they were extremely painful, massively fatigued," she said. "I kept going back and forth to the GP... I went quite a number of times because it was affecting me going into lectures and things because I was exhausted." Neelam described how she was advised to exercise more and lose weight, but her symptoms soon began affecting her studies, causing her to miss lectures and re-sit exams. She was eventually diagnosed with PCOS, having "never heard" of the condition before. "It was the comment of 'it'll be difficult for you to have children, but we'll cross that bridge when we come to it'," she explained. "It was just dropped in a conversation and I was kind of left to figure it all out by myself." Neelam was inspired to set up Birmingham-based charity Cysters to help tackle inequalities in menstrual, maternal and menopausal health. She later went on to have a daughter, which she said was a "really big surprise". The charity founder said the renaming of the condition, which supporters said was "more representative" of how it affected the whole body, could help improve understanding, but there was still a "long way to go". "PCOS itself wasn't even understood. So PMOS is also something that's going to be really misunderstood as well," she said. "If that name change means those conversations come more to light, then I'm all for it." Rochelle Lewis said years of symptoms and appointments left her feeling unheard For many years, Rochelle Lewis, from Wolverhampton, struggled with facial hair growth, painful periods and anxiety. "I've always struggled with a lot of facial hair growing up, it was something I was really bullied about, so I tried to do absolutely everything I could to try and get rid of it," she explained. "One of my mum's friends, she was like, 'oh, maybe she's got PCOS'. So that was the first time I'd ever even heard of it, and I was probably about 16." Rochelle said she first raised concerns about PCOS as a teenager, but felt they were dismissed. "So I went to the doctors and they literally just brushed it off and were like, 'no, we don't think you've got PCOS'," she said. The 31-year-old was finally diagnosed with the condition in 2025, a process she described as "frustrating". "It was emotionally draining, not to be listened to, not to be heard," she said. Now a mother to a seven-month-old son, she said too often women were diagnosed and then left to navigate the condition alone. The name change alone wasn't enough, she added. "So you get told, you get given your diagnosis and that's it... we're just left to it," she said. "We need to have processes put in place to actually help us." Annual health checks would have helped manage the condition, Rochelle said In July, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) published draft guidance for the NHS, recommending an annual review for women with PMOS, to help monitor symptoms, treatment and longer-term health risks. "Recommending a simple annual review is an important step towards ensuring people get the ongoing care and monitoring they need," said Marie Anne Ledingham, consultant clinical adviser for women's and reproductive health at NICE. The health watchdog said, external the advice aimed to improve consistency of care, increase awareness and support earlier diagnosis and management, with the final guideline due to be published on 27 January. Dr Rima Smith, from Birmingham Women's Hospital, said PMOS was a "multi-organ, lifelong whole body condition" Dr Rima Smith, clinical associate professor of reproductive medicine at Birmingham Women's Hospital, said PMOS was "so much more than an ovarian or gynaecological condition". "It's a cardiometabolic condition," she explained. "PCOS never accurately represented the condition in so many ways. It had never captured the complexity and the fact it is a multi-organ, lifelong whole-body condition." She added that women with PMOS were often cared for through fragmented services and that annual health checks could involve diabetes, thyroid and menstrual function checks, alongside making sure any treatment was working. "We know a large proportion of women with PMOS have a healthy weight so it's not entirely weight-driven," she said. "It should be a holistic approach." Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) Annual reviews are the sort of follow-up both women said was missing after their diagnosis. title: Masked teenager found guilty of trying to murder 15-year-old schoolgirl
description: The school went into lockdown and parents gathered at the gates as they waited for news about their children.
body: A photo taken from within a classroom showed an armed police officer at the scene A masked teenager who was captured on CCTV stabbing a girl at his school has been found guilty of attempted murder. Armed police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on Wednesday 11 March following reports a 15-year-old had been stabbed in the back. Her attacker brought a knife to school, was dressed in black, was wearing a face mask and had written notes saying he hated women, the trial at King's Lynn Crown Court heard. The defendant, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, will be sentenced on 18 December. Jurors deliberated for three hours and 54 minutes before delivering a majority verdict in the two-week trial. The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said. The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury. Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School at 10:24 GMT that Wednesday CCTV footage captured the moment the girl was stabbed in the back, before her attacker ran off while "pursued by a teacher". The victim described to the jury how, in the aftermath of the attack, she had told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed". In a police interview played to the court, the girl said she was in "panic mode" and felt numb and weak. Chris Paxton KC, prosecuting, said it was "sheer good fortune" the "defenceless and vulnerable" pupil was not seriously hurt. "This was a knife strike delivered, we the prosecution say, as an attempt to kill," he added. The boy, who was 15 at the time, had previously pleaded guilty to possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent. He messaged his mother to say "I'm sorry" shortly after the attack, jurors heard. "I was in complete shock," she told the court. Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. title: Student who murdered uni housemate jailed for life
description: Jamie Collins, 21, was ambushed and killed in the garden of the home he shared with his killer.
body: Jamie Collins (pictured) was ambushed and killed after returning home from university A student has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 28 years for murdering his university housemate after laying in wait and stabbing him 30 times. Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home near Bristol on 8 April. Coughlan left his victim dying in an alleyway as he cycled away to dispose of bloodstained evidence. He called police eight hours later. Coughlan had denied murder and a trial was under way at Bristol Crown Court but he changed his plea to guilty on Tuesday. Both men were final-year University of the West of England students. title: Hackers steal children's data after company used 'Password1' to protect old account
description: The data watchdog reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited and Data Cymru after the 2024 ransomware attack.
body: Hackers stole information from Data Cymru's systems in 2024 which exposed the personal information of 3,300 people A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024. The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second. ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists. The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them". Data Cymru has been approached for comment. Both organisations were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective. During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families. David Doodson, head of investigations at the Information Commission's Office, said: "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands." Doodson added the responsibility for "these failures did not sit with one organisation alone". According to the watchdog, ONL created a test account in 2012 and used the password "Password1" to protect it, failing to audit it or remove it for more than 12 years. It also did not review local administrator accounts after they were first deployed, with accounts on three affected systems using the same password, for the same period of time. The watchdog said Data Cymru failed to put a data protection agreement in place with ONL, and that there was a gap in responsibility between the two organisations. It also said Data Cymru failed to ensure the dormant test account was identified and removed, or updated to meet stronger password requirements. The ICO added it was a lesson for every organisation to "use strong passwords, protect remote access with multi-factor authentication, regularly review every user account, and be completely clear about who is responsible for cyber-security when services are outsourced". Following the cyber-attack, both organisations introduced stronger security measures. ONL introduced a process prompting customers to review active accounts periodically and providing recommendations about accounts that should be removed, the ICO said. It also strengthened its account access controls, including the use of multi-factor authentication. On 30 April 2025, Data Cymru and ONL entered into a legally compliant data processing contract. Data Cymru also introduced periodic account reviews and strengthened account access controls, including using multi-factor authentication. A spokesperson for ONL said: "Within a week of the attack, we'd worked with Data Cymru to check every account on its network and switched off the ones it no longer needed that same day. "We also brought in independent cyber-security specialists to investigate." They added: "Since then, we've protected remote access with multi-factor authentication and introduced regular account reviews for the customers whose networks we look after, so accounts that aren't needed are found and removed. "This was limited to the server we hosted for Data Cymru. title: Allen reveals mental health clinic stay before return
description: Mark Allen says he is working to "turn things around" and reveals he spent time in a mental health clinic before returning to snooker.
body: Allen returned to snooker after a five-month absence on Tuesday Mark Allen says he is working to "turn things around" and revealed he spent time in a mental health clinic before returning to snooker. The former world number one lost to friend Jordan Brown in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open on Tuesday after five months away from the sport. Speaking after the match, an emotional Allen said he was in a "bad place at the minute" and considering retirement. "Everything I said in that interview was true. However, rest assured I'm doing my best to turn things round," Northern Ireland's Allen said in a statement on X on Wednesday. He said he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic and discharged himself so he could prepare for Tuesday's match against Brown, adding that he plans to continue his treatment. "I owed that to my family, in particular my daughter, to see me play for what could be the last time. I also owed it to the fans who have supported me throughout my 21 years on tour," added the 40-year-old. "I also owed that to World Snooker who have been amazing from day one in all this, in particular Simon Brownell [CEO] and Neil Tomkins [World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association COO] who have remained in touch regularly, even Simon paying me a visit in the clinic itself." Allen considers retirement after NI Open exit Allen's 21-year professional career includes 12 ranking titles - including the 2022 UK Championship - and a stint at the top of the world rankings in 2024. In his last tournament before this week's Northern Ireland Open, Allen missed a match-winning black off its spot in the World Championship semi-final against eventual champion Wu Yize. On Tuesday, Allen was visibly emotional as he admitted he "probably" would not have played had he not been drawn against his friend Brown. "I'm not OK, but I'm OK in that itself. I've been much worse in the last few months than you saw yesterday. "My daughter kept me going, the therapists, staff and all the other patients were amazing and helped me through some really dark days." He added: "I also know it won't happen overnight. I'm a work in progress! "My fight and determination on the table has always been there for ones to see. I need to show those same fighting qualities off it now for a while." Allen also praised Brown for handling Tuesday's match with "grace and skill", adding he is "proud to call him a friend". He also thanked those who have sent him messages of support and added: "This is only the beginning of my new journey." title: Amber warning issued as Storm Austen threatens UK with strong winds and heavy rain
description: The deep area of low pressure is expected to move close to the south of the UK early on Friday with south-west England set to bear the brunt.
body: The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for strong winds as Storm Austen is forecast to sweep across parts of the UK. The warning - the second-highest tier that the Met Office issues - is valid for Cornwall and parts of west Devon from 03:00 until 10:00 BST on Friday. Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are expected around exposed coasts, with 60-70mph gusts elsewhere. Flying debris could lead to injuries or a danger to life, with the risk of power cuts and damage to buildings. A broader yellow Met Office wind warning covers large swathes of southern England and south Wales with some travel disruption possible. Southern and eastern Scotland is also covered by a Met Office yellow warning - this one for heavy rain which could bring the risk of flooding. Storm Austen - an area of low pressure - is currently developing in the Atlantic and will continue to deepen as it approaches the UK. It will move close to south-west England on Thursday night with the strongest winds expected to arrive early on Friday morning. The very windiest conditions are expected on coastal headlands in north and west Cornwall - exposed to the north-westerly gales - but gusts of up to 70mph could occur even in inland areas. Gusts of 60-70mph are expected across the amber warning area, with 80mph gusts possible in exposed areas. According to the Met Office there is a high risk of 'significant' disruption with possible delays to road and rail transport. Air and ferry services could also be affected. Injuries and danger to life are likely from flying debris and large waves along the coast. Some power cuts are also possible. The centre of Storm Austen is then forecast to move through the English Channel which could mean the Channel Islands - which are not covered by the Met Office warning system - are hit by damaging winds. Gusts in excess of 80mph are possible. Strong winds will spread across many other southern parts of the UK during Friday with a Met Office yellow warning covering the rest of south-west England, the English Channel coast, and the south of Wales. 50-60mph gusts are likely in these areas, with 70mph gusts in exposed spots, bringing the threat of travel disruption, power cuts and damage. As strong winds batter parts of southern England and Wales, heavy rain will also fall - especially in southern and eastern Scotland. Heavy rain will also sweep across the country with almost all areas seeing some wet weather - much needed in those southern areas where severe drought has been declared. However the most persistent downpours are expected to affect southern and eastern Scotland - where a Met Office yellow warning for rain has been issued. 20-40mm of rain is likely to fall across the warning area, with up to 80mm in a few places, bringing the risk of flooding and travel disruption. It is even possible that some snow could fall over the mountains, above 600m elevation, as cold air interacts with the wet weather. Austen is the first named storm of the 2026/2027 season. It is being propelled towards the UK by a powerful jet stream which is blowing across the Atlantic, high in the atmosphere, with top speeds expected to touch around 200mph in the core of the jet. The jet stream will continue to blow in our direction, delivering another deep area of low pressure over the weekend. This second low has not, so far, been named but it could bring a spell of gales - particularly for the northern half of the UK. Computer models suggest that western Scotland could see gusts of 80mph or more so some further disruption is possible. Heavy rain is also likely across many parts of the country. More areas of low pressure are expected to move in from the Atlantic next week meaning spells of wind and rain, interspersed with drier interludes. Beyond that, there are signs that high pressure could bring somewhat calmer weather into the start of November, especially in the south of the UK - but there is a good deal of uncertainty at this range. title: US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia and 'on his way home', Trump says
description: The former teacher has been released without any "swap" required, according to the president.
body: Stephen Hubbard pictured in a Moscow courtroom as he was sentenced in 2024 Russia has agreed to release a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine. Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, according to state media. President Trump said Hubbard was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary for this release". Hubbard, a former teacher originally from Michigan, was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024. Prosecutors had accused him of serving in a defence unit in the eastern city of Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine two years earlier. Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week. "There was no "swap" necessary for this release," Trump said. The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard as "wrongfully detained" and Trump had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent. "Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused ⁠on ​Hubbard". CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment. President Putin and Witkoff met at the Constantine Palace on Wednesday morning Russian state media reported that Witkoff had thanked Putin for Hubbard's release and, on Trump's behalf, for the deal struck with Washington earlier this month to import Russian diesel. The first shipment under the agreement will leave Russia "in two to three days", Putin said during the meeting, as quoted by state news agency TASS. The diesel deal infuriated Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and triggered a tumultuous few weeks of deteriorating relations, during which Trump suspended several Russian sanctions and said it was time for Ukraine to elect a new leader. Kyiv meanwhile accused Washington of halting intelligence sharing on deadly Russian strikes, causing Ukrainians to lose their lives - an allegation Washington rejected as "scandalous". The Ukrainian president said on Tuesday that such information sharing had resumed, following talks with Witkoff in Oslo described by the US as "positive". During Wednesday's meeting in St Petersburg, Witkoff was filmed by Russian TV saying the diesel deal was an example to Ukraine of what could be achieved by working together. "Your decision to remove export controls on diesel oil from Russia, not just to the US but also to the world at large in the midst of an economic shock, I think that was really important that that happened," he told Putin. "I know [President Trump] is deeply grateful for it." title: Author Helen Fielding launches award to find the next Bridget Jones's Diary
description: The Bridget Jones Prize will go to the author of the funniest 1,000-word diary-style piece of writing.
body: Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding (right) alongside film star Renée Zellweger Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven". West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North. The award will go to the person who submits the funniest 1,000-word piece of first-person writing. Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up." The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North. Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996. It spawned several sequels and hit movie adaptations starring Renée Zellweger as the endearingly chaotic and lovelorn thirty-something diarist. In a statement announcing the prize, external, Fielding noted how the "comedy heart" of Bridget's story came from the "everyday humour of people around me when growing up in Yorkshire: laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth". "There are lots of famous northern comics," said the writer, whose own work was inspired by the likes of Victoria Wood, Alan Bennett and Morecambe and Wise. "But this prize is for the comic voices of people who aren't famous: just living their lives being quietly hilarious." The Bridget Jones Prize will be awarded to an unpublished writer, without an agent, based in the north of England as part of New Writing North's Northern Writers' Awards. Submissions will be open from 23 November 2026 to 1 February 2027. The winner will be announced at the Northern Writers' Awards ceremony in Newcastle next summer, and will be presented with the award by Fielding. Will Mackie from New Writing North said: "This is the first time the Northern Writers' Awards have featured an award exclusively for comedy writing. "There is no-one more fitting to identify an original comedy voice than Helen, who created one of the nation's most beloved comic characters of the last 30 years." title: MNEK cancels tour over lack of ticket sales and high production costs
description: The Grammy-nominated artist was due to start a run of shows for his latest album Bulldozer!! next month.
body: MNEK has worked with major artists including Beyoncé and Zara Larsson MNEK has cancelled his upcoming tour due to a lack of ticket sales and the show not being "ready to the standard" he wanted. The Grammy-nominated artist, who has worked with the likes of Beyoncé, Zara Larsson and Madonna, was due to start a run of shows for his latest album Bulldozer!! next month. In a statement shared on Instagram, the 31-year-old said he joins other artists who have cancelled shows recently as a result of "high production costs" and "over-ambitious planning". Earlier this year, The Pussycat Dolls called off almost the entire US leg of their reunion tour following poor ticket sales. The singer, whose real name is Uzoechi Emenike, said he had been "really looking forward" to performing his new album but had "no interest in doing this tour if I can't do it right". He thanked fans who had bought tickets and said they would be refunded soon. The artist also said he would try to tour the album when he could put on a show which fans "deserve". Pop star Larsson, whose hit album Midnight Sun was executive produced by MNEK, was among those who offered their support to the artist in the comments. Little Mix star Leigh-Anne Pinnock also sent him love, while singer Becky Hill encouraged him, saying: "Touring is devastatingly expensive but you'll find a way". The artist has been nominated for two Grammy Awards A growing number of artists have reported struggling with a "cost of touring crisis" due to rising prices. Earlier this year, the chair of the Featured Artists Coalition and Blur drummer David Rowntree told the BBC is was "virtually impossible now to make touring pay for itself". MNEK had been due to play dates across the UK and Europe, with tickets starting from about £30. Born in south-east London, he became a professional songwriter at the age of 14 when he signed his first publishing deal. He went on to co-write for British acts such as The Saturdays and Little Mix and later earned credits on tracks for global stars like Madonna, Kylie Minogue and Christina Aguilera. His first Grammy nomination came in 2014 for his collaboration track, Need U (100%), with Duke Dumont and A*M*E. He was also nominated earlier this year for best dance pop recording for his work on Midnight Sun. After years as a featured artist, he broke out in his own right to release his debut studio album Language in 2018. Fans have had to wait eight years for the follow-up, with his second album Bulldozer!! finally released last month. Touring is a costly struggle for bands like us. title: Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
description: The economic figures released on Wednesday show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his Budget.
body: The Chancellor was on a early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped. From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms. The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures. The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months. Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase. These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week. On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures. The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs. While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased. From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year. The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month. The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output. The latest inflation figure also applies as the uprating to tens of billions in welfare payments next April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation. The figure also confirms that the Triple Lock will see the State Pension increase by 3.9% next April. There is one form of relief here - food price inflation remains largely unaffected by the energy shock. While higher inflation at a time of frozen tax thresholds will raise more tax in cash terms, it will also increase the cost of public services, including likely union pay demands. All the while, UK borrowing costs have risen alongside most of the advanced world as the US-Israel war against Iran has intensified. The Jackdaw gas field decision is seen as the start of a run of "pro growth" pre-Budget announcements. It sends a directional message, but will not fundamentally change the trade off between cost of living breathing space, and delivering a Budget that convinces the markets and investors. The fact the borrowing costs gap has narrowed a bit with other G7 nations, and the IMF praised pencilled-in plans to shrink borrowing, provided a platform for the chancellor's Budget. The latest economic numbers amply illustrate the challenge of actually delivering them. title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
description: Inflation accelerated to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
body: UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week. The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices. The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running £6bn above official forecasts. Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules. Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September. It is the highest inflation has been since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed. The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre. Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures. ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year. As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said. September's inflation figure is also important because it suggests how benefits will increase next April. It means the state pension will most likely rise by 3.9%, in line with average wage rises from May to July, due to the triple lock. The inflation figure for September also dictates how other benefits will rise in April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation. With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide." He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field. The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space". But the inflation figure came as the ONS said the government borrowed £24.5bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs. The overshoot means, cumulatively, the government has borrowed £6bn more this year than the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which scores government spending plans, had forecast. Despite overall debt topping £3tn for the first time, debt as a proportion of the UK's economic output - the measure used by the government to judge whether it is in line with its fiscal rules - fell. Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge The Conservatives said higher inflation and borrowing showed Labour had "lost control of the economy". Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith called for Healey to use his Budget to "tackle the deficit, and reduce the red tape and net zero costs that are driving up the cost of living for families". He added that the Conservatives would cut taxes, the costs of benefits and "wasteful" spending to "make our country prosperous again". Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the borrowing figures "painted a dismal picture" ahead of Healey's Budget. She said the amount borrowed in September was higher than analyst expectations as well as spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)'s forecast. "This reinforces our view that the Chancellor will deliver a cautious Budget on 28 October that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year," she said. title: Storm Austen to batter Wales coast with 70mph winds
description: Gusts of wind about 50 to 60mph are likely to hit large parts of south Wales on Friday.
body: Delays and cancellations to public transport are likely, the Met Office said Travel disruption and damage to buildings are expected when Storm Austen, the first named storm of the autumn, hits south Wales later this week. The Met Office said the storm will bring a spell of strong winds up to 70mph (112km/h) overnight on Thursday and into Friday, mainly in coastal areas. The yellow warning, external for Wales was issued on Wednesday morning, with periods of heavy rain also expected. The Met Office said injuries and danger to life from flying debris are possible. Some roads and bridges may close, and longer journey times and cancellations to public transport are possible. The weather warning is in place between 00:00 and 14:00 BST on Friday. The Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) has urged anyone visiting the coast in south Wales to "to stay vigilant and not take unnecessary risks". The Met Office yellow weather warning for wind is in place for much of south Wales overnight on Thursday and into Friday afternoon Gusts of wind about 50 to 60mph are likely to hit areas such as Cardiff, Swansea and Merthyr Tydfil. Some coastal or exposed areas could see about 70mph gusts of wind, the Met Office said, adding winds will slowly ease during Friday afternoon. The regions affected in Wales are: The RNLI is urging people to stay safe while visiting the coast in south Wales Ross Macleod, RNLI water safety manager, said: "If you plan to visit the coast or a waterside location, we urge you stay a safe distance from the water as conditions could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea." MacLeod said anyone in trouble in the water should "lie back in the water with your head so far back that your ears are wet, extend your arms and legs and try to relax as best as you can until you get control of your breathing before then calling for help or swimming to safety". He added if anyone sees someone in danger, throw them something buoyant into the water and call 999 or 112 and ask for the coastguard. 60 years on: The Aberfan disaster through the eyes of those who survived Decision to delay council tax shake-up in Wales is 'absurd', says IFS The Trip's Rob Brydon originally against playing fictional version of himself Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC UK government approves drilling in Jackdaw gas field with production to start this month US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia and 'on his way home', Trump says Aberfan stops to remember 60 years since coal tip collapsed, killing 116 children and 28 adults Tighter rules planned to protect people from cosmetic surgery that goes badly wrong Where to spot brilliant colours after 'false autumn' spoils some leaf displays I left state secrets on the train - I'm proof you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life Ali G is back. title: Who is London’s Batman? Is it Niko Omilana?
description: A mysterious caped figure has been helping the people of London. Some are convinced it is Niko Omilana disguised as Batman - but where is the proof?
body: Part of Other Side of the Story Did Bruce Wayne ever have it this bad? A mysterious caped figure has been helping the people of London. Not dealing with the criminal hi-jinks of The Joker or Catwoman (thankfully), instead doing good deeds for others: paying for fuel at petrol stations, helping people across busy roads and even filling in potholes. These may not be the type of do-gooder acts that sell comic books, but London's Batman, as they are known, has already got 297k followers on TikTok and their posts have had more 2m likes since they first appeared at the end of September. Despite the capital’s hero doing their best to make people’s days a little brighter, one question keeps hounding them: who are they? Can they be like Bruce and keep their identity secret, or will they soon be unmasked? Socials are awash with the theory that London's Batman is none other than Niko Omilana, known for posting prank videos on socials and as a contestant on the first series of The Celebrity Traitors. Niko appears to be the most popular candidate for London Batman’s secret identity as he has a reputation for pranks which take a lot of organisation and can involve handing out goods to people. In 2021, he opened a fake store in the city and gave away free smartphones to the public as his comment on what he saw as the high price of technology. Niko posted a short video of himself on TikTok showing he was in the heart of New York, a move some people interpreted as him trying to prove he is not London’s Batman. That hasn’t stopped others trying to prove otherwise. Comments on the post suggest it could have been pre-recorded as the theatre advertisements behind him don’t reflect the ones playing in the city at the moment, although this hasn’t been verified. TikTok user officialroyce1 posted that Niko’s video was meaningless as he could have flown to New York and back in the same day to cover his tracks. At the moment, there are lots of theories but absolutely no evidence that Niko is dressing up as a superhero and helping out in the community. A similar situation happened earlier this year when some posters on socials were convinced that the Liverpool rapper EsDeeKid was really the actor Timothee Chalamet in disguise. This was later disproved after the theory went viral. When you see stories like this online it's always important to check your facts before repeating or reposting the information, to prevent false information from spreading. Until London’s Batman pulls back their mask to reveal their secret identity, we can’t say for sure. But we can use the same kind of critical thinking which has saved Gotham City countless times. And how many of us wouldn’t want to be more like Batman? This article was published in October 2026 Not sure if the news you’re seeing on social media is true or false? title: Man charged after three Jewish women assaulted
description: The women suffered minor injuries when they were assaulted at Clapton Common, police say.
body: Police were called to the Clapton Common area on Monday afternoon A 33-year-old man has been charged after three Jewish women were assaulted in Hackney, east London. Police were called to Clapton Common at about 13:40 BST on Monday following reports that a man had been detained by Shomrim, a Jewish neighbourhood watch group, after assaulting the women. The victims suffered minor injuries. The Metropolitan Police said it was treating the incident as a hate crime. Abdisamad Siad, of Pilgrims Way, Islington, has been charged with three counts of assault by beating. He is due to appear at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court later. CCTV posted online by Shomrim appears to show a man running up to a woman before pausing briefly and then punching her twice. The group said on X that it had already been called because another "visibly Jewish" woman had reported being punched in the face on Clapton Common on Monday. The Met Police said it had increased its patrols in the local area since the incident. The force said it was also working with Jewish community leaders to provide "further reassurance" to those living nearby. Siad has also been charged with grievous bodily harm with intent over an unrelated attack on a woman, who is believed to be known to him, in the Islington area on 16 October. title: Farmer lost out by minutes in race for wildlife funding
description: Richard Peace is among thousands of farmers who missed out as funding was snapped up in hours.
body: Richard Peace wanted funding for work aimed at encouraging the barn owls already thriving on his farm The barn owls have become one of Richard Peace's favourite sights on the farm. As dusk falls near the woods edging his land outside Nuneaton in Warwickshire, the birds emerge to hunt over fields he has spent years managing. This year he wanted to do more to help them thrive. To encourage the owls, Richard planned to leave some crops unharvested near the woodland where they live. "Obviously that will bring some of the wildlife out of the woods, like voles and mice, and I was hoping that the barn owls would then thrive even more than they are already," he said. But leaving part of a crop in the ground comes at a cost. The government offers support to farmers carrying out environmental work through schemes that pay for so-called public goods, from improving habitats to boosting biodiversity. Richard said technical difficulties and the speed at which applications were processed left him missing out on funding For Richard, accessing some of the £310m funding from the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) scheme seemed straightforward enough. All he had to do was submit an application. What he did not realise was that he was entering a race against thousands of other farmers for that limited pot of cash. "We looked at 8am and it wasn't live. I had things to do so I went to work on the farm," he said. "Checked again at lunchtime, it was live and I started. We had a few errors but I did get to the end of the form and submitted it. "I was minutes too late and the scheme had been subscribed. The money pot was exhausted." Richard is among thousands of farmers who missed out after funding was snapped up within hours. He believes smaller family farms may have been at a disadvantage. While some larger businesses could dedicate staff to monitoring the application process, Richard spent the morning carrying out day-to-day work on the farm before returning to complete his submission. The National Farmers' Union (NFU) had already warned that demand could outstrip the available funding. Helen Fisher, who farms near Atherstone and is deputy regional chair of the NFU Midlands, said: "The scheme opened and closed in six hours. Nobody had anticipated that level of demand. "We had been warning Defra there would be high demand and 12,000 farmers just couldn't get their applications in in time." Helen Fisher says the NFU warned ministers there would be strong demand for the scheme Richard believes a first-come, first-served system is the wrong way to allocate support. "It should be available to everybody, those applications should then be evaluated," he said. "If the scheme is oversubscribed the larger payments should be scaled back so that smaller farmers can get a slice of the larger pot." Farmers in the Midlands often operate on a smaller scale than elsewhere in England, although regional data showing who ultimately benefited from the scheme is not publicly available. Stories like Richard's have become increasingly familiar, and ministers have acknowledged concerns about the way applications were handled. Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said: "I know some farmers who wanted to join SFI26 will be deeply disappointed not to have secured an agreement during Window 2, particularly given the challenges the sector has faced this year. "I have heard those concerns and am determined to work closely with farmers as we learn lessons from this year and shape SFI27, including exploring alternatives to a first-come, first-served application process." For Richard, the hope is that by next year the system will be fairer and allow more farmers to access support for projects that benefit wildlife. If that happens, the barn owls he enjoys watching over his farm may have an even better chance of thriving. title: PSG's Kvaratskhelia to have surgery on ruptured ACL
description: Paris St-Germain winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia will undergo surgery after suffering a knee injury during his side's 4-2 win over Barcelona on Tuesday.
body: Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was making his first start of the season in the Champions League Paris St-Germain winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia will undergo knee surgery after rupturing his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) during his side's 4-2 win over Barcelona on Tuesday. Kvaratskhelia sustained the injury during a challenge with Xavi Espart and was unable to put weight on his right leg as he was substituted in the 59th minute of the Champions League tie. PSG have not put a timeline on his return to action. Kvaratskhelia, 25, helped PSG win back-to-back Champions League titles following his move to the French capital from Napoli in January 2025. The Georgia international has featured 11 times for PSG this season. The club also confirmed Ousmane Dembele and Marquinhos will be absent for a "few weeks". Dembele limped off with a left thigh injury while Marquinhos injured his right thigh. PSG and Barcelona were level at 2-2 heading into the final 10 minute at Parc des Princes before the hosts scored twice late on to maintain their winning start to their Champions League defence. They sit top of the table with three wins from three matches. title: 'Lessons need to be learnt' as report into care homes during Covid published
description: An inquiry found that Government failings in care settings allowed the spread of Covid.
body: Martina Ferguson said the report has "reopened, wounds for many families here in Northern Ireland" Lessons need to be learnt after an inquiry found that government failings in care settings allowed the spread of Covid, a woman whose mother died during the pandemic has said. The sixth report from the Covid inquiry, which was published on Tuesday, said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time. There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022. Martina Ferguson, whose mother Ursula Derry died during the coronavirus pandemic, said "we need to learn from what's happened". She said the report has "reopened, wounds for many families here in Northern Ireland". "Many families in our bereaved group were prevented from being with loved ones when they were at their most vulnerable, you know, they stood outside windows trying to communicate through a glass. "I did that for nine months when my mummy was in her care home." There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022 About 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit. Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said. Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme, Ferguson said: "Years later, families are still carrying deep feelings of guilt and, despite having done absolutely nothing wrong, but they wonder whether their loved one felt, abandoned, frightened, or alone." Ferguson has created Ursula's Law, a proposed legislative campaign in Northern Ireland that is named in her mum's memory, which aims to establish a statutory right for patients to designate a care partner across all health and social care settings. Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says Covid inquiry PPE report - key findings In 2016, Prof Raphael Bengoa published a review, external that was supposed to change the way Northern Ireland does healthcare. Ferguson makes reference to the report and said that "when you look at what happened, bereaved families and other families during the pandemic, guidance completely failed us during the pandemic". "If we face another health crisis or a pandemic, we face, in my opinion, utter chaos in healthcare settings because the trust is totally broken and people simply won't comply," she added. She said if Stormont is serious about Bengoa's report and improving the health care system they "must enshrine this absolute right in law" for patients to designate an essential family carer. IHCP Chief Executive Pauline Shepherd said the "government's response to COVID in care homes was much too little, too late" The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of personal protective equipment for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes. It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves. Pauline Shepherd, chief executive of Independent Health & Care Providers, said the "government's response to Covid in care homes was much too little, too late". "It was a horrific time for people living in the care homes, their families and the staff that were caring for them." A decade after a critical health service review, has there been any change? title: Actor Noel Clarke pleads not guilty to sexual offence charges
description: The former Doctor Who and Kidulthood star appeared at Westminster Magistrates Court on Wednesday.
body: Noel Clarke attended the hearing appeared at Westminster Magistrates Court Actor Noel Clarke has pleaded not guilty to sexual offences including sexual assault, voyeurism and exposure. The former Doctor Who and Kidulthood star appeared at Westminster Magistrates Court in London on Wednesday on two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. He pleaded not guilty to all the charges, which relate to alleged offences against five women between 2007 and 2016. The 50-year-old, from Kensington, west London, will next appear at Southwark Crown Court on 18 November. Clarke found fame playing Mickey Smith in Doctor Who between 2005 and 2010, and went on to become a successful actor, writer, producer and director. title: Why Eze is struggling to find his form at Arsenal
description: Eberechi Eze has been struggling for form this season for Arsenal, but there could be hope that the forward turns it around.
body: Eberechi Eze has scored one goal in nine appearances in all competitions for Arsenal The sound of fans being wowed by his football is something that has followed Eberechi Eze wherever he has played. The Arsenal forward is known for his off-the-cuff skill, maverick nature and entertaining style. But lately, those familiar elements of Eze have been missing. Sunday's 1-0 win over Nottingham Forest was Eze's first Premier League start of the season. But replaced at half-time, having completed just nine passes and 22 touches of the ball, many have started to question whether he can reproduce the performances he was once known for. Arsenal criticism from very small minority - Arteta Madueke's 'anger and conviction' shows he's more than a 'finisher' This is not the first time Eze's role in the squad has been called into question. He switched off when Matty Cash scored Aston Villa's opener in their 2-1 defeat in December 2025 and, despite starting the following game, was left on the substitute's bench for the next four league matches. And while the 28-year-old is a much-loved character around both the Arsenal and England squads, even Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel referenced how Eze was "coming back to his true shape and form" in training during the last international break - hinting that he has not been at his best so far this season. The reason Eze's performance is coming under scrutiny now is that the Gunners failed to land a new world-class attacker in the transfer window, despite being heavily interested in Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr and Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez. Arsenal signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge in the summer and the Greek international had been the first-choice winger for Mikel Arteta this season, until he picked up a hamstring injury on international duty. Tzolis being out of action presented an opportunity for Eze to break into the squad again, scoring in a start on the left wing against Lille in the Champions League - but he was unable to follow that up against Forest. "I think that finding his role and position has been challenging," former Arsenal and England defender Matt Upson said. "And when you come to a club with the stature and the quality of Arsenal, if you're not showing that you're nailing down a certain role, I think it's very very hard to maintain a position in the team. "He's now filling in a bit on the left-hand side, which I don't think particularly suits him, but he's had to. "He doesn't play like a wide player for me and I think just knowing your role when you're at a club like Arsenal is so important." Eze scored some spectacular goals in big moments when he was at Crystal Palace, including the winner in the FA Cup final against Manchester City in 2025. "I think all the high-end stuff that we saw from him which made him a player that Arsenal were going to go and target, that's the icing on the cake," said Upson. "So when the foundation's not quite there in terms of the situations you're getting in and how quickly you get into the ball, where you are on the field, where your headspace is at about what your role is and what you've got to do, then it's hard to produce those moments that make you the top player." Eze shone from the left at Palace, but in his final two seasons in south London he operated from a narrower number 10 role. But with captain Martin Odegaard the first choice in that position at Arsenal and Arteta unlikely to start the pair regularly with the options he has available in the middle of the pitch, it means Eze's route into the team is limited. Upson believes Eze must understand what is wanted from him. "It's almost a process for him if he wants to kind of grow into starting more matches for Arsenal," he said. "I think figuring that out is really important and having that level of intensity, which I think has been an adjustment for him from where he's come from - into a big club, with a manager that they don't come more intense than really." There's an argument that Eze does not get a run in one position or a run of games to build momentum, but the stats show he gets a substantial amount of game time. The Gunners played 63 matches last season and Eze started 36 of those (57%). Since his debut for Arsenal in August 2025 he has started in 56% of games (40 out of 72). His 11 goals in 61 appearances have been scored across just eight games. And he has delivered some huge moments in an Arsenal shirt, scoring five against rivals Tottenham Hotspur across two Premier League matches, with a hat-trick in the home fixture - while he also scored winners against Newcastle and former club Crystal Palace as the Gunners won the title. Encouragingly for Eze and Arsenal fans, there are signs it still could click this season. Although the sample size is a lot smaller, Eze's numbers per 90 minutes this season are higher in assists (0.25), goals and assists combined (0.50), shots on target (0.74), dribbles completed (1.98) and touches in the opposition box (5.95) than the previous campaign. "We have some really good players and the expectations are so big for all of them," Arteta said. "And we want more from everybody. That is the mindset. "That is what is going to make us better individually and as a team. I hope that continues as it is going to push all of us to reach different kind of levels and develop."
