title: Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
description: Jackdaw and Rosebank are case studies in the slow motion awkwardness the UK has over energy.
body: The decision to grant approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea and the further delay in a decision about the Rosebank oil field, also in the North Sea, are case studies in the slow-motion awkwardness the UK has collectively had, over years, about energy. At the heart of that awkwardness, these questions: where should our energy come from, and with what costs and consequences, for the customer and for the environment? Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has talked about a desire to be "pragmatic" about the North Sea as he puts it, which is why this decision about Jackdaw isn't a surprise. In fact it felt near inevitable after President Trump blurted out – after his first phone call with Burnham in the summer – that the prime minister had told him he would "open up the North Sea". Burnham acknowledged the two leaders had discussed the issue, arguing: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that." What we now know is the government is approving drilling of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen. A decision on Rosebank, an oil field about 80 miles north east of Shetland, is expected to take a bit longer. UK government approves Jackdaw gas field and says production will start this month The city caught in the middle of the big energy shift debate What is happening with the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields? The timeline of back and forth about both projects is worth revisiting. Jackdaw was first approved four years ago, Rosebank three years ago. But after a legal challenge by environmental campaigners, it was ruled that consent had been granted unlawfully and there needed to be a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact. And then, of course – there is politics, international and domestic, between parties and within parties. Debate about energy security and spiralling prices, given the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the environmental impact, carbon emissions and the message new drilling sends to the wider world. But others point to the extra carbon emissions when energy is imported, the tax revenues generated from domestic energy and the social and economic consequences of the British oil and gas sector deindustrialising too quickly and, in particular, the impact on cities such as Aberdeen. Then, for the government, there are the promises the Labour Party made when it was seeking your support at the general election in 2024. Page 52 of Labour's manifesto reads like a rhetorical twister – a paragraph of promises seeking to stretch in multiple directions at the same time, trying to keep a breadth of people happy simultaneously, or perhaps not annoy too many people too much. "Labour will not revoke existing licences and we will partner with business and workers to manage our existing fields for the entirety of their lifespan. Crucially, oil and gas production in the North Sea will be with us for decades to come, and the North Sea will be managed in a way that does not jeopardise jobs," it reads. "And our offshore workers will lead the world in the industries of the future. We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis," it adds. Crucially, the Jackdaw and Rosebank licences had already been issued, leaving political wriggle room on these two outstanding and high profile decisions the Labour government inherited on taking office. But the multiple trade-offs, of course, remain very real, including for some of the key individuals involved. Miatta Fahnbulleh took over from Ed Miliband as energy secretary earlier this yer Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who used to be the energy secretary, has long been vocal about what he sees as the need to move away from fossil fuels. His successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who has announced this decision, previously wrote, external that "to have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can't have any new oil or gas fields," adding "it's irresponsible and short sighted to be funding new fossil fuels when we need to get to Net Zero fast." Fahnbulleh has today told BBC Radio Scotland gas from Jackdaw will be "in our homes and businesses this month" but acknowledged that it "won't lower our energy bills this winter". Instead, she is grounding her argument for approving this in energy security and saying the tax revenue generated will go into an "Energy Wealth Fund" to pay for "low carbon and renewable projects". Rosebank, she added, was a "different proposition" as its oil would be exported, but she will "look at it". Politically, the decision on Jackdaw is considerably easier for the government than the decision on Rosebank. Broadly speaking, most Labour MPs are comfortable with endorsing Jackdaw. It is also a project backed by the Conservatives and Reform (who argue a decision should have been taken much sooner) and the Scottish National Party and the Liberal Democrats. The Green Party of England and Wales are opposed. On Rosebank, the argument is much more contentious within the Labour Party. Some, who can see the rationale for Jackdaw cannot see it for Rosebank. Bluntly, it is a much more difficult decision, as Fahnbulleh has acknowledged. What we can expect in the coming hours and days - as it has started already - is a resumption of all the arguments these projects have already provoked, with some saying approval should have happened ages ago, alongside plenty more. And others arguing the announcement is utterly irresponsible. Do you have questions or comments about this? title: Gambia to pay victims of Yahya Jammeh's rule from proceeds of his seized US mansion
description: The Gambia has confirmed receiving $2.5m from the sale of the house in Maryland.
body: Jammeh, who is now living in exile in Equatorial Guinea, ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years The Gambia will use funds received from the US from the forfeiture of long-time ruler Yahya Jammeh's property to pay victims of his rule, authorities have said. The Gambia's Reparations Commission said it received $2.5m (£1.86m) from the sale of a mansion in Maryland owned by former leader of the West African nation. The US had in 2022 secured the right to sell the property on grounds that it was acquired through "criminal proceeds and misappropriated Gambian public funds". Jammeh ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years after taking over in a coup in 1994 - a time marked by allegations of human rights abuses forced disappearances and extrajudicial killings. How US mansion of Gambia's ex-president was seized Profile: Former Gambian President Yahya Jammeh On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property. It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors". Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results. He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure. Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office. In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea. A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts. There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m. Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture. A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents". title: Family of prison officer shot dead by IRA to get state apology
description: Brian Stack was crossing a street in Dublin in 1983 when he was shot in the back of the neck and died 18 months later.
body: Brian Stack was shot in the back of the neck as he left a boxing match in 1983 The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA is to receive a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing. Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck. Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49. There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing. On Wednesday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin will offer an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the Dáil (Irish parliament). Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us". "It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the missions that happened," he said. He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions". "So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report. "And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it." Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family. "My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said. "He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name." Prior to the Dáil proceedings, the Stack family will hold a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan. The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn Fein's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander. Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing. A Sinn Féin spokesperson said that "in a 2013 statement, a former IRA leader acknowledged that IRA volunteers were responsible for Brian Stack's killing". "The statement said the shooting had not been authorised by the IRA leadership, accepted IRA responsibility for his death, said it should not have happened and expressed sorrow for the pain and hurt suffered by the family." The spokesperson added: "As republicans, we acknowledge the hurt caused by republican actions. That suffering cannot be disowned. We are sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception." In 2019, the family received an apology from then garda commissioner Drew Harris in relation to the handling of the investigation into the murder. In 2023, gardaí told the family that the file on the case - which was with the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) - was being sent back to police for further investigation. Stack was the only prisoner officer in the state killed by violence related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland. title: Huge crowds watch attempt to save shark stranded in South Korean canal
description: A third attempt has been made to guide the 9ft 10in (3m) shark back to the open sea.
body: This video can not be played Huge crowds have flocked to a canal in South Korea to watch a stranded shark. The 9ft 10in (3m) shark, nicknamed Bukangi, was first spotted in the waterway last month in the south-eastern city of Busan. Now a third attempt has been made to rescue the female using nets to guide her back to the open sea. It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish. The BBC's Seoul correspondent Jake Kwon goes to Busan to follow the latest attempt to rescue Bukangi. Huge crowds watch attempt to save shark stranded in South Korean canal. title: Boulter wins in under an hour to reach quarters
description: Katie Boulter moves into the quarter-finals of the Japan Open after she beat Viktorija Golubic in less than an hour.
body: Katie Boulter is British number two after Sonny Kartal replaced her at the top of the rankings on Monday Katie Boulter moved into the quarter-finals of the Japan Open after she beat Viktorija Golubic in less than an hour. The British number two defeated her Swiss opponent 6-2 6-1 in Osaka and will face either Croatia's Antonia Ruzic or American Kayla Day in the next round. Boulter saved a break point in the opening game but dominated from 2-2 in the first set, winning nine games in a row before Golubic took the penultimate game of the match. The 30-year-old lost the British number one spot to Sonny Kartal on Monday, but is set to retake the position following her run this week. Boulter, who is seeded eighth in the competition, said she was pleased with how she handled "difficult conditions", with a strong wind affecting play. "I think one of the biggest things for me is staying patient in the wind," she said. "Sometimes I can get a little frustrated, and I'm very pleased that I didn't allow that to affect me today and I think I ended up playing some really good tennis in the second set. I'm really pleased with the performance." title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
description: Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'Her heart and her mind are in good shape', husband of Helen Haines says Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed. Phil Haines said the "horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive". The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday. Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne. Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated. "She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for." He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund. "Please keep sending Helen your love," he added. Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder. Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance. He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis. This video can not be played Watch: BBC inside court with man charged with Australian MP attack In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail. The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord. Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. "His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush. "Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court." Phil and Helen Haines have been married for nearly 40 years - next month is their anniversary Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said. Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines. Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable". The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him. Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured. "Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun. "She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme. Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs. Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters. The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare. Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers. Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident. In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape. There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said. Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs. Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing. Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said. Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better". "We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says. "Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency." title: What is happening with the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields?
description: The UK government has moved a step closer to making a decision on whether to approve further drilling.
body: Those against further oil and gas exploration have turned the heat on the new prime minister The Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea has been allowed to start production after years of debates and legal wrangling - but a decision is yet to be taken on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland. Industry bodies argue that the sites could provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply. Environmentalists insist that more drilling would be unconscionable, hampering efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect billions across the globe. They also say starting production would not protect energy security and that transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs. Jackdaw is a gas field located about 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen. The UK government, which has now given permission for production to begin, says it will be able to start to supplying gas from the end of this month. Rosebank, about 80 miles (128km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas. It would take longer than Jackdaw to become operational, but is scheduled to be up and running by 2027 if approved. Licences for the fields were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 - sparking legal challenges from environmental groups. The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites. A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published. These updated estimates were put out for consultation. The UK government then had to decide whether to re-approve the fields, with input from industry regulators. Prime Minister Andy Burnham had previously said he would stick to Labour's promise not to issue new oil and gas licences while honouring existing ones. While Jackdaw has now been approved, the BBC understands that the Rosebank decision is still with the regulator and has not yet been passed to the energy secretary. The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North Sea If approved, Rosebank is expected to fill up to 500 million barrels of oil over its 25-year lifetime. But that increased supply does not necessarily guarantee cheaper energy bills for people in the UK. Prices are determined by international markets which are vulnerable to shocks such as the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran. Most of the oil produced from Rosebank would be sent to the Netherlands because the UK's remaining refineries are not equipped to process the heavier type of crude oil extracted from the North Sea. If any of the refined products - such as diesel or jet fuel - were to be used in the UK, they would then to be reimported. When plans for Jackdaw were unveiled in 2022, developers said it would produce enough gas to power 1.4 million homes. It would be a relatively simple process to connect Jackdaw to the UK energy system, meaning gas could be quickly pumped to the mainland. Announcing that the project would go ahead, the UK government said it was expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6% at its peak. It said that over its 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would protect hundreds of jobs and add an estimated £2.9bn to the UK economy. Backers say opening the fields would improve the UK's energy security. Yet Fatih Birol, a leading energy economist at the International Energy Agency, told The Guardian, external earlier this year that new drilling in the North Sea "would not change much for the UK's energy security" or bring down energy bills. He said that the UK would still be reliant on oil and gas imports, with prices set internationally. Workers on the Jackdaw gas platform, which could be up and running within months Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Norwegian company Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank. It has estimated that Jackdaw could produce 35.8 million tonnes of carbon over its lifetime, the equivalent of 90% of Scotland's emissions for 2023. Adura said a more likely estimate was about 23.6 million tonnes - equivalent to 60% of the 2023 figure. Those figures are dwarfed by the projections for Rosebank - almost 250 million tonnes of planet-warming emissions. Yet Adura's updated environmental impact assessment, ordered by the Court of Session, says that emissions from Jackdaw would "not materially influence" global warming. The firm says that displacing imported liquified nature gas from the United States with gas from the Jackdaw field would save the equivalent of four million tonnes of CO2. Campaign groups say that would not lower worldwide emissions as the US gas would still be sold and burned elsewhere. Adura also said the climate effects would be "minor" because the UK has a "well-regulated industry" aligned with the Paris Agreement, a legally binding commitment to limit global warming to between 1.5 and 2C. However, Greenpeace UK chief scientist Doug Parr said opening a new field was "wholly incompatible" with the Paris Agreement. Industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) has said Rosebank and Jackdaw would support a peak of more than 3,500 jobs during the construction phase. It says the fields would support 880 jobs, external throughout during their lifespans, with an average salary of £85,850. OEUK also says they would provide £1.4bn in tax revenues by 2029, rising to £3.8bn by 2034. Such figures are particularly attractive in the north-east of Scotland, which is contending with the decline of an industry which has long been its economic lifeblood. title: Crystal Palace urged to retire bald eagle mascot
description: Animal rights group Peta is urging Crystal Palace to retire their bald eagle mascot, saying a "bright stadium filled with boisterous fans is no place for animals".
body: Crystal Palace were rebranded as the Eagles in the mid-1970s, having previously been known as the Glaziers An animal rights group is urging Crystal Palace to retire their live bald eagle mascot with immediate effect, saying a "bright stadium filled with boisterous fans is no place for animals". In a letter to Palace CEO Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) asked the Premier League club to stop using the eagle, named Phoenix, in pre-match displays at Selhurst Park and to never use live animal mascots again. The London team, known as the Eagles since 1973, introduced a live eagle to matchdays in 2010. Kayla, who died in 2020, performed the role for 10 years and her replacement Phoenix made her debut against West Ham in August 2024. Peta says birds can become "frightened, disoriented and panicked" in stadium environments, putting themselves and fans at risk. Using them for displays and entertainment also denies the animals, who "would naturally avoid humans", the opportunity to engage with their natural instincts, leading to "frustration and stress", the group said. The organisation has "detailed records" of incidents involving live mascots, including birds, being injured or killed in collisions with walls, windows and match balls, as well as a falcon embedding its talons in a spectator's scalp after landing on his head. In 2017, a Charlton Athletic fan was found guilty of trying to punch Kayla the eagle at a League Cup fixture two years earlier. "Many professional sports teams use only willing humans as mascots and the club already has Pete the Eagle to excite the crowd," said Dr Carys Bennett, Peta's senior corporate projects manager. "Bald eagles are widely recognised as symbols of freedom. They deserve better than to be used as an entertainment prop to amuse the Eagles' fans." title: Why Elon Musk is considering a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla
description: Musk says there's "a lot to be gained" by combining the firms in what would be the biggest merger in history.
body: Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together. Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. This video can not be played Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models. Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. This video can not be played Taking Stock: Who owns Space? However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said. The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month. Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn. "I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said. The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars. title: Pakistan arrests man wanted by US over $126m postage fraud case
description: Faheem Akram allegedly sold more than 5 million fake postage labels for a fixed price of $2 a piece.
body: Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service. Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023. He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website. Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest. According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com. US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination. The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service. An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release. Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said. title: Massive wasps' nest in wildlife office dismantled
description: The insects lived in a nature reserve office for four months.
body: The wasps built a huge nest which took over Eilish Rothney's office shelves A nature reserve manager has finally dismantled a large wasps' nest in her office after the insects made it their home for four months. Eilish Rothney, a nature reserve manager for the Trinity Broads at the Norfolk Wildlife Trust, found wasps buzzing around the room in June, when she returned from conducting surveys. The wasps had made their home on the shelves of the Ormesby St Michael office, wrapping around binders and other items. They left the nest a few weeks ago. Rothney said: "It's kind of a fitting tribute that we've welcomed what many, many people see as a pest...and we've helped them survive, which will help this whole ecosystem that we rely on." Eilish Rothney, nature reserve manager for the Trinity Broads at the Norfolk Wildlife Trust, with the wasps' nest in her office before it was dismantled Rothney said that when she first saw the size of the nest in June it was about the size of a paperback book. She added: "There was just like constant [wasps] coming and going, probably 10s, 20s in and out all the time." Rothney started dismantling the nest on Tuesday and said that she knew in the autumn, it would be time for them to leave. When she hadn't seen any wasps for a number of weeks she decided to explore by cutting away at the nest. She said that she was "amazed" to peel back a number of layers before reaching the shelves. She added that it was not until she got closer to the ring binders that she could see "hexagonal cells where the larvae would have been". Rothney said she will miss her office colleagues, but she knows they will be back and added: "I think if they do come back in here next summer they will be welcome." Eilish Rothney made a start at dismantling the nest on Tuesday. Rothney said it was important that we make space for nature. She added: "Although people don't like them, [they] are part of nature. "They have a really, really important role to play, as do all the insects, even mosquitoes, which are not my favourite." She said she thought the wasps struggled because of the warm summer. Due to her office being near a pond and a meadow, the wasps were able to get food and water. title: Woman given cancer diagnosis by hospital employee who accessed her records
description: Pippa Boardman says she lost "dignity and privacy" after she was told by an acquaintance she had cancer.
body: Pippa Boardman was told she had cancer by a hospital worker, days before her scheduled appointment with a consultant A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant. Pippa Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said she had lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. She said she did not receive an apology from the hospital until it was contacted by the BBC. The trust said it was "truly sorry" and "appropriate action had been taken". It added: "While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously." Boardman, who is now recovering well from cancer, said her personal information was accessed by a man she vaguely knew who worked at the hospital. She said: "I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play. "This man said to me 'Pippa, I don't want you to worry, but you've got cancer'. "I just couldn't really believe it". Two days later Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer. Nine months on, she said her strong recovery did not undo the damage done by the experience, adding: "I lost my dignity and I've lost my privacy." Along with Boardman's case there have also been other recent NHS data breaches, described by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper as a disgrace. The Royal Cornwall Hospital Trust said it was "truly sorry that Ms Boardman was contacted in this way" Boardman said part of her trauma had been caused by the Royal Cornwall Hospital's handling of the case. She said: "It really distresses me people can't see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately." She said the trust told her the breacher's rights meant it could not give her information, and it only apologised after being contacted by the BBC. She said: "It took a lot of courage to complain... and I didn't understand why the hospital wasn't really prepared to engage with me. "I understand that it's because his rights have to be protected. But I kept thinking where are my rights in this." Boardman said she wanted to prevent others going through a similar experience. "I'm in a very good place in terms of my cancer. I'm just in an awful place in terms of what happened and how it happened," she said. The Royal Cornwall Hospital Trust said it was "truly sorry" about how Boardman was contacted. It said: "Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her. "This should not have happened and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused. "Appropriate action was taken following our investigation which was carried out immediately after Ms Boardman raised her concern." The trust said it had reminded staff records "must only ever be accessed for a legitimate work-related reason" and it was also reviewing policies "in light of the strengthened NHS England guidance on inappropriate access to patient information". title: Fabregas and Como prepare for historic Man Utd tie
description: Serie A success story Como have gone from Serie A to the Champions League - now they are ready for a historic night against Manchester United.
body: The picturesque setting of Como's Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium, by the banks of Lake Como "It's Manchester United. We are only just getting our heads around the fact we are playing Inter, Milan and Juventus. "This is without doubt the biggest night in the club's history." The words of a Como staff member say it all. United may not be the force they once were and travel to Italy on the brink of a full-blown crisis after six games without a win, their worst run since 2018-19. But, in terms of global stature, they are immense. To put this into context, when United savoured the last of their three Champions League triumphs in 2008, Como were a Serie D club, playing in one of nine semi-professional regional leagues, where attendances tend to be measured in their hundreds. According to chief executive Mirwan Surwaso, it was their status as an amateur club - they returned to Serie D in 2017 after being unable to convince the authorities of their financial wellbeing - which first attracted the London-based media company Sent Entertainment, owned by Indonesian billionaires Robert Budi Hartono and Michael Bambang Hartono. When they concluded a deal in 2019, the Hartono brothers were planning a TV project, with the idea of screening matches involving young Indonesian players back home. A visit from Manchester United was not part of the plan. This video can not be played Fabregas,film stars and Disney: How Como are disrupting Italian football There cannot be many Champions League stadiums you can walk around and in addition to seeing an iconic tourist attraction. Lake Como is 29 miles long and 2.5 miles wide in some parts - you also come across a yacht club and an 'Aero Club' for the sea-planes that take off at regular intervals. The clubs themselves have been there for a long time. But Como also use their natural surroundings to offer one hour Lake Como tours, followed by 'pre-match Lakeside hospitality'. The Aero Club at the back of a stand at the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium In town - Como's population is just over 83,000, which means 90% of them could fit in the San Siro Stadium - there is a plush new club shop, selling all kinds of branded merchandise. There was no need for that in Serie D. "Somehow the team got promoted, we had to go professional, and the plan had to be scrapped," Surwaso told Piers Morgan's Football Uncensored Podcast this month. The alternative plan is still being amended substantially. Initially it was expected this season would be a selling year, when some of the developing talents Como thought they could cash in on would be sold. Instead, manager Cesc Fabregas steered his squad to fourth place in 2025-26, capitalising on AC Milan's shock defeat at Cagliari. It meant in the space of five seasons from Fabregas' arrival as a player, Como had gone from Serie B to the Champions League. Earlier this week, Lionel Messi's son Ciro gave Como his seal of approval by being pictured with his dad wearing a replica Como kit. Tangible evidence of a meteoric rise. Former France internationals Raphael Varane (left) and Thierry Henry (centre) are both investors in Como Como head coach Cesc Fabregas with Argentine forward Nico Paz "Compared to when I finished my career here, it is completely different," said Fabregas. "It is not even night and day. It is another world. "Playing Manchester United is a historic day once again for the club, the city of Como and fanbase. "When I retired as a player, I coached to get experience. I explained what I thought of the club and my vision and put the plan to work. We are a family here. Even when we lose, fans come and celebrate. We need to be humble and remember who we were because the story of Como will be beautiful, and we will remember it forever." This video can not be played Europe's next great coach? How Fabregas led Como to Champions League The captivating nature of the Como story does bring with it some questions. In the short term, some wonder how they can possibly comply with Uefa's financial rules, which European football's governing body does not intend to amend despite Como's rise from Serie B. Surwaso told Morgan: "The scrutiny is on us but we always have our books in order, so we are not too worried." The other point, which will become an issue if the forecast heavy rain at kick-off arrives, is that three quarters of the 12,300-capacity Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia is uncovered. Growing both sides of the club is essential if Como are to maximise their potential. For Fabregas, whose responsibility is clearly on the playing side, there is a balance to be struck between celebrating the spectacular journey Como have been on, and ensuring his players are not resting on their laurels. "We were at minus 10 when we started, but we don't want to spend time thinking about what has passed," said the former Arsenal, Barcelona and Chelsea star. "If you want to do that, retire and go write a book about what Como did. We must look at what is in front of us." Como fans show their support before the club's Champions League debut against RB Leipzig on 10 September While Como now attract thousands to their games, those who followed the club when crowds were in the hundreds remain. "I had an uncle who supported Como," said Marco Melillo, an out-of-town fan. "He showed me the sticker collection, I saw the blue shirt and the blue colours and totally went crazy about it. "I know in England a lot of people support teams in lower leagues, but that is not so true in Italy, where people support bigger teams. I do not like that that much. I was not really interested in supporting a team that was winning something. I liked the colours. I liked the stadium and when I came here and saw the lake, it was 'wow'. "We know the club is in the best situation ever in its history but when I see the faces of the guys and ladies that were also here in Serie D, we just see in our eyes a

title: Estate records 'abundance' of wildlife despite drought
description: Wimpole's "long-term approach to nature recovery" has seen more than 5,000 species recorded.
body: Corn buntings were one of the species recorded at the Wimpole Estate A country house and farming estate in one of England's driest and most nature-depleted areas has an "abundance" of wildlife with more than 5,000 species recorded, the National Trust has said. Rare species, including barbastelle bats, great crested newts and corn buntings, have been spotted at the Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire in the last six years. General manager David Hassall said the number was "remarkable in any landscape, but particularly here in Cambridgeshire, where wildlife is facing the combined pressures of habitat loss and increasingly hot, dry conditions". The government said the East was one of seven UK areas in drought, external, with hosepipe bans in force across parts of the region. The charity said 5,242 species were recorded across the estate's parkland, farmland, woodland and wetlands. Hassall said the number "reflects five decades of careful stewardship and shows that nature can flourish alongside farming, public access and heritage conservation". The National Trust said it had recorded 5,242 species at Wimpole Estate in the last six years Since 2021, the National Trust said it had planted 125,000 trees and created 35 hectares of woodland and 52 hectares of wood pasture, with another 77 hectares of tree planting currently being designed. Species recorded also included a tiny pygmy ant, which the charity said was recorded at only one other UK site. Ben McCarthy, head of nature conservation at the National Trust, said: "Across the UK, wildlife is under immense pressure from habitat loss and fragmentation as well as climate change, making the need to restore nature more urgent than ever. "Places like Wimpole demonstrate the value of taking a long-term approach to nature recovery. "By creating and restoring habitats across whole landscapes, we can provide more space for wildlife and help reverse decades of decline." Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? title: Sex, lies and police spies: The disputed story of the 'creepy' undercover officer
description: Andrew Coles denies claims he deceived a young woman into sex while infiltrating an activist group.
body: Andrew Coles says a campaign against him is "payback" for his undercover work Andrew Coles sings in a church choir, is active in local Conservative politics and was once an undercover Metropolitan Police officer – a so-called "spy cop". Jessica – not her real name – is an animal rights activist who says he deceived her into sleeping with him. This is a story about sex and lies. But who is telling the truth? Coles, 66, lives in a thatched cottage in the Cambridgeshire countryside with his wife and their greyhound. He is the brother of broadcaster the Reverend Richard Coles. But between 1990 and 1995, he served in the Metropolitan Police Service's (MPS) undercover Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), which infiltrated political and protest groups. For the past decade, its activities have been probed by the Undercover Policing Inquiry (UCPI), external. "The MPS has accepted that Andrew Coles had a sexual relationship with Jessica," wrote the force's commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, "and is disappointed he did not tell the truth to the inquiry." Coles is also accused of appearing to advise colleagues to have similar relationships. He vehemently denies the claims against him, insisting he is the victim of a deceit. "It's payback, pure and simple," he says. For decades, undercover police infiltrated protest groups to gather intelligence. Some deceived women activists into sexual relationships. Andrew Coles, pictured with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, is a former councillor and president of Peterborough Conservative Association Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Coles lists resilience, bravery and ruthlessness as the qualities needed in a good undercover police officer. "I suppose so," he says. "Though I didn't behave very differently to my own personality." Coles's current life is a far cry from his covert past when, he says, he sometimes had to break the law to gain trust and maintain his cover. "I took drugs – cannabis. It was necessary – you had to be vouched for," he says. "I was given a lemon squeezy bottle, allegedly full of acid, and squirted it over a butcher's shop window. "I was also involved in a raid on a chicken farm when some chickens were stolen and damage was done to the property." Coles posed as an animal rights activist in the early 1990s in order to infiltrate the Animal Liberation Front The SDS had already existed for more than 20 years when Coles, then a constable in the Met, received a tap on the shoulder. Taking the name Andy Davey from a dead child, he began making connections with the Animal Liberation Front, an extremist direct-action group. "The work was certainly not everyone's cup of tea, but I protected a part of society from some very dangerous people, and I think I did a good job," he says. The only known image of Coles and Jessica (foreground, left) shows them with the Brixton Hunt Saboteurs in 1992 In 1991, Jessica met Davey for the first time. She was a naïve 19-year-old, she recalls, living in a shared east London terrace and looking for adventure. Jessica, now 54, remembers Davey as an awkward older man who drove a van, which endeared him to her close circle of like-minded activists. "Late in the evenings he would come to the house and we struggled to get rid of him," she says. "Then one night, without warning, he went to kiss me. I didn't have the confidence to get out of the situation and he became my first proper boyfriend." But he was not 24 as Jessica had thought. He was 32, married and had children. Nor was he a fellow hunt saboteur. He was secretly gathering intelligence as part of a criminal inquiry into the ALF after several members were convicted of arson and bombing offences. Andrew Coles took this photograph of Jessica (left) during the raid on Hookley Farm in Elstead, Surrey, in June 1992 "He groomed me," she says. "He would sleep in my single bed several times a week, and I didn't know who he really was. "It's difficult to describe it as rape, but he knew that having sex with me would have been against my consent." Coles has admitted sharing Jessica's bed on one occasion but says there was never any sexual contact. "Her story is not true, absolutely not true," he insists. When pressed about the weight of evidence, he concedes: "It is very hard to defeat." Jessica wrote to her best friend from France in 1993 That evidence includes two handwritten letters that Jessica, then staying in France, wrote to her best friend in 1993. In the first, she writes: "It's really weird, but I'm still going out with Andy." And in the second: "[Andy] suggested that we see other people because if I decided to stay here for another year... he wouldn't be getting enough sex." Jessica wrote two letters in different hands, which allude to her relationship with Andrew Coles Coles has a theory about the provenance of these letters. "So, the first could have been written at the time. The second, what it talks about is absolute nonsense. I think it was written much later and added to the evidence bundle," he says. "The handwriting is nothing like her handwriting in the original letter, which is almost a childlike scrawl. The second one is an elegant, joined-up cursive." Jessica has shown the BBC more letters from the same period, written in noticeably different hands. "If I write slowly, I can make it neat, but if I'm writing in a hurry or I'm angry, it's completely different," she says. "The letters themselves are really embarrassing, and if I was to make something up it wouldn't have all that excruciatingly awful stuff in it." Forensic graphologist Kate Barr told the BBC Jessica's handwriting "appeared to vary" and it was possible she had written both letters at around the same time. title: Missing German WW2 U-boat found 82 years on
description: The U-672 sub was identified 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe after divers discovered it in August.
body: The U-boat was scuttled by its own crew after it was attacked by the Royal Navy in July 1944 A German submarine that went missing during World War Two after being damaged by the Royal Navy has been discovered 82 years on. Plymouth dive team Gasperados identified the U-672 about 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe, Devon, after it was discovered by a deep sea diving team from Portland in August at a depth of about 230ft (70m). The vessel was attacked by HMS Balfour in July 1944 but was scuttled by its 52 crew - all of whom survived. A navy log showing the sinking had incorrect coordinates, resulting in it not being found until recently. Members of Gasperados said they were "really pleased" they could help identify the vessel. More news stories for Devon Listen to the latest news for Devon Gasperados diver Dominic Robinson said: "Once we started moving around it and I started seeing the individual features - I saw the snorkel, I saw the conning tower, all those kind of things - I knew that we were going to get the video needed to identify it, so I was really pleased about that." After its attack, the U-boat was left leaking underwater. Its commander waited for as long as possible before making the decision to blow the tanks and bring the sub up to give its crew a last chance of survival. Robinson said they "managed to get it to the surface" before getting into their life rafts for survival. "They were bobbing around in the sea and then the very next day they were found by British aircraft, British vessels and then taken away to the prisoner of war camp," he explained. Divers discovered the boat in August before it was officially identified German World War Two historian Dr Axel Niestle, who specialises in U-boats, said the wreck "was in the correct position" but, "due to a clerical error in the documents", had a position recorded which differed "some 46 miles (74km) from the actual position". The surviving crewmembers returned to Germany after the war, including the U-boat's skipper. Robinson said he had spoken to his family, who said he lived a "long and happy life". He added: "They just said how proud he would have been and how pleased he would have been to know that it had been found at last." title: Undercover filming shows lawyer advising how to avoid £45,000 illegal-worker fine
description: Mohammad Alias Yousaf made his claim to an undercover reporter posing as a mini-mart owner.
body: This video can not be played A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal working fine go away. Mohammad Alias Yousaf, also known as Alias, made the claim to an undercover reporter posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker. The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could get out of the fine - if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart. Alias has denied ever providing such advice, or giving false information to the Home Office. In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way illegal working fines are issued and collected. Our UK editor, Ed Thomas, reports. title: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
description: Because of our investigation, the home secretary has ordered a review of how fines are issued and collected.
body: This video can not be played Lawyer Mohammad Alias Yousaf advised how to avoid paying a £45,000 illegal-worker fine A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal-working fine go away. Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker. The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart. Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office. At least £150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC. In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected. In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules". Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously. She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth £40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter. When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'" A number of social media videos, like this one, advertised Alias's details (phone details blurred out) Alias came to our attention during a wider BBC probe into illegal working and criminality linked to some High Street businesses, including mini-marts and barbershops. His name was mentioned in social media videos, including on Kurdish Facebook pages, where business owners in the UK praised his ability to resolve problems linked to immigration fines. For months we monitored these videos, which carried Alias's name, that of his law firm, Liberty Solicitors, and a mobile phone number. Some had more than 20,000 views. In one, a Kurdish-speaking shop owner explained that, after having been issued with a penalty for employing an illegal worker, he had "tried two or three different places to get it sorted but nobody could resolve it". He went on to say that "Mr Alias" had got the fine cancelled - showing a letter as evidence. Alias told the BBC he had not commissioned, paid for, approved or circulated videos on social media. Watch the full film of Ed Thomas's investigation here, external Our reporter contacted Alias on the phone, claiming to be a business owner who faced a fine after immigration officers had found somebody working at his mini-mart illegally. There was no actual shop, worker, or fine. During the call, which we recorded, Alias told our reporter his services would cost 10% of the fine - in this case, £4,500 - and he would want money up front. Alias explained how liability for the fine could be shifted to somebody outside the UK, if that person could be named as owner of the business. "Do you have anybody's name who we can use? Anybody who's gone back to Iraq, gone back to Iran?" he asked. He then offered a fictitious example: "Say we put forward Karwan, yeah? Then fine come on Karwan's name. Karwan not here, Karwan in Iraq." What Alias appeared to be proposing was the use of a "ghost director" - in other words, someone who is paid to put their name on official documents, thereby masking the real owner of a business. Using ghost directors is a widespread illegal practice, the law enforcement official told us. This video can not be played Watch: Business owners facing fines "just laugh in my face", says anonymous law enforcement official Bryony Rest, a senior immigration lawyer who listened to the recorded conversation, said it was "quite appalling" that a solicitor would appear to suggest a false name for the business owner. Our reporter told Alias that to mask the real owners of the mini-mart, other people had been paid to put their names on its lease and utility bills. The solicitor sounded encouraged by this news. "OK, fine," he said. "Then I think we should be able to find a way out of this." An employer in the UK, who hires a worker with no legal right to work, faces being fined. In 2024, the maximum penalty for knowingly employing illegal workers rose from £15,000 to £60,000. A total of 5,755 fines were issued for illegal working between 2021-2025, the Home Office has told us. These would have been worth a total of £215m, but only £60.5m has been collected. The Home Office points out that not all fines issued in the past five years would have been paid during the same time period, and the amount collected would always be lower than the value of the fines, because of appeals or discounts for fast payment. Fitted with a secret camera, our reporter went to Alias's office in Bradford with £250 as an upfront payment. Alias seemed annoyed, having originally asked for £500, and made a show of counting out the notes, but did not provide a receipt. Our reporter had by this time told Alias he had found someone in the Kurdish Region of Iraq ready to declare they were the owner of the mini-mart business. From Alias's office, the reporter rang this supposed contact, a man who gave his name as Saman. In reality, Saman was another BBC undercover journalist based in the UK. As a solicitor, Alias could only ethically argue the case for transferring the fine if Saman were to declare to him, either verbally or in writing, that he was the real owner of the business. In our secret recording of their conversation, Alias repeatedly asks Saman to confirm this, despite knowing there is a question mark over the mini-mart's true ownership. Alias's frustration appears to mount with each attempt. Alias: "Am I right in thinking that you are the owner of the shop and I'm going to write to them explaining that you're the owner of the

title: Giant tunnel proposed to clean up Windermere's sewage problem
description: The plan would eliminate sewage spills into Windermere, blamed for turning the water green.
body: Windermere sits at the heart of the iconic Lake District A £3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled. The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake. At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming. It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the £3.6bn price-tag is acceptable. The Lake District is a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts close to 18m visitors each year. Windermere is at its heart, with the lake holding around 300bn litres of water. That is so big that it can take 9 months for water entering one end to reach the other. Louise Beardmore, chief executive of United Utilities, says its time to think about the long term Louise Beardmore, chief executive of United Utilities, told the BBC the proposals were a "100 year solution for this lake". "In the UK we invest in five year periods and so we come along all the time and we do a bit, then we go away and we come back and do a bit more. This is saying we need to do something differently," she said. Beardmore said she was excited that a broad coalition including her company, regulators, the local authorities and environmental campaigners had come together to draft this proposal which is called "Only Rainwater into Windermere" (ORiW). Founder of the Save Windermere group Matt Staniek has campaigned outside United Utilities local offices on a toilet Perhaps the unlikeliest member of the group is activist Matt Staniek. He called today's proposal a "milestone". "For me this is a plan on a piece of paper. It is not definitive action and that's what I want to see." he said. "This is the beginning, and the end of this is the moment that sewage stops entering Windermere." It will now be up to the government to decide whether the plans are developed further, and if so how. At present the sewage network around Windermere is fragmented, with homes served by a mix of public wastewater treatment works and privately owned treatment facilities and septic tanks. When treatment works are overwhelmed, such as during heavy rain, they spill raw sewage. The rest of the time they emit a continuous stream of treated effluent which, while cleaner than raw sewage, can contain high nutrient levels. On several occasions in the last five years the high nutrient levels and warm temperatures have combined to cause algal blooming turning parts of the lake a lurid green. The ORiW proposal would see 12,800 people connected to the sewage network for the first time with up to 86 miles (138km) of new sewage infrastructure and a single wastewater treatment works built to serve them at the end of a 4m-wide sewage tunnel. Two slightly different plans are being put forward. Both have the tunnel at their heart but one would see the treated effluent discharged into the River Leven, the other into the Irish Sea at Ulverston. The report highlights two options for paying for the project. One would see the cost passed on to United Utilities' customers and would -depending on the route chosen - add up to £3.17 to their monthly bills. People like Nigel Wilkinson from Love Windermere group, which is linked to many local businesses, would like the cost to be spread nationally, increasing all bills in England by up to 35p a month. "We believe Windermere is of such national significance and international significance that it is justifiable to treat this as a national asset and fund it accordingly," he says. Much now depends on the government's enthusiasm for following through on promise made then Environment secretary Steve Reed in March 2025 to stop all sewage going into Windermere. "We share the public's determination to protect this iconic lake." a Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs spokesperson said, stressing that further work needed to be done to test alternative options. title: 'Trash Island' or DC landmark? How a golf course got Trump in a messy legal dispute
description: Trump said he has plans to turn a 106-year-old public golf course in Washington DC into a tournament-capable golf course for pros, but local golfers are not happy.
body: This video can not be played Watch: "Old, broken and dilapidated"? - Trump's plan to renovate historic golf course For Jourdain Yardan, golfing at the East Potomac Golf Links on Washington DC's waterfront is a twice-weekly ritual. "Anyone from any walk of life, whether they're starting to play golf or whether they're a ... seasoned golfer, they can come out here and play golf at a pretty reasonable rate," the 35-year-old told the BBC while putting on the course on Monday. But President Donald Trump does not seem convinced of its charms, calling the 106-year-old course "Trash Island" Monday evening on Truth Social. Now, he intends to shut it down for renovations to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments". The renovation is part of the president's sprawling and controversial efforts to shape the US capital, which include a new White House ballroom, a 250-foot-tall arch and other changes to longstanding landmarks. The golf course is a smaller project, but deeply personal to many who live in the city. Jourdain Yardan worries regular people will not be able to golf at the course if it is renovated as Trump suggested Yardan described a potential shuttering, even if temporary, as a "huge dent" in DC culture that could change the heart of the space. Trump, an avid golfer and owner of more than a dozen courses, says his vision for the course will make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". But courts will need to mediate the dispute between the White House and the community before Trump can realize his plans. The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital. A lawsuit from the DC Preservation League and two golfers from the course asks the court to stop Trump's planned renovation. "Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves," Democracy Forward, the group representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement on social media. The legal fight intensified this month after the government began large-scale tree removal on the course without giving the court or plaintiffs notice. A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to stop its redevelopment plans until at least 26 October. Despite the work stoppage, Trump took to social media on Sunday to announce that the course will be closed for 15-months beginning in November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign. "The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," Trump wrote in his post on Sunday. While golfer Thomas Snow, who is not part of the suit, conceded the course could use a "facelift", he thinks the president's description of the course is a "gross overstatement". Thomas Snow has been golfing at East Potomac for 15 years Currently, East Potomac does not offer the manicured experience one might find at the luxury, private golf courses the president is known for building. The public course is open to all and does not require a membership to access. The facilities at the DC course are more modest, offering food court-style dining rather than amenities such as white tablecloth restaurants and upscale locker rooms. Golfers like Snow and Yardan who regularly play the courses at East Potomac, told the BBC it offers a rare combination of affordability and proximity to the city. "You start to clear everything out and it just starts to become an empty plot of land that you just hit golf balls on; I think it gets rid of the culture of the golf course," Yardan said. As a 70-year-old golfer, Snow pays $29 (£21.65) for 18 holes when he visits East Potomac. "There's no place in the whole DMV (the metropolitan region including DC and its Maryland and Virginia suburbs) that you can play a nice 18 holes for that price point," he said. Snow worries that if Trump's proposal moves forward, people will be priced out. Yardan, the twice-weekly golfer, echoed those concerns. "Anytime you hear about big league, big golfers, that also includes big prices," he said. "The biggest thing that I like about this golf course .. is that it's affordable," he said.
