title: Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again
description: The president thrust Springfield, Ohio, into the spotlight with a false pet-eating claim - years later, it remains at the heart of the immigration debate.
body: Springfield, in south-west Ohio, was thrust into the spotlight in 2024 when Trump repeated a false claim about Haitian immigrants eating pets In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it. To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back". But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country. This story contains some distressing details Pierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024. He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico. Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States. TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country. Bel aspired to build a life in America, the friend said. He was an honours student, talented athlete and cadet in a high school programme training students to become officers in the US Armed Forces. But in June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US. Pierre Damas Bel's family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear an ankle monitor Bel was told to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office where he was fitted with an ankle monitor which is used to track migrants facing deportation. He wrote on Instagram that he felt "shame and humiliation" at having to wear the tag. And on 31 August, he parked his car on the side of a highway near Springfield, walked into oncoming traffic and was killed. His family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear the ankle monitor. The Department for Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions from the BBC about Bel's case. ICE has previously rejected "any attempt to blame ICE for the death". "Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," a spokesperson told US media earlier this year when asked about the case. In the weeks before his death, Bel attended a Springfield support centre for Haitians facing deportation. Its co-founder, Viles Dorsainvil, told the BBC that Bel had been in the process of filing a motion asking ICE to remove the tag. "He went twice to the ICE facilities… begging them to remove the ankle monitor," he said. "He did everything right to be here until they put the tag on him." In total, more than a million immigrants from 13 countries have had TPS terminated by the Trump administration. The changes meant many went from being legal to unauthorised migrants overnight. In 2024, Trump made securing the border and the mass deportation of undocumented migrants core pledges in his election campaign. Polls suggest the border policy continues to have strong support among Republicans, but the nature of his immigration enforcement campaign has seen a drop in backing this year. This video can not be played Watch: How Trump's mass deportation drive is playing out in Ohio Ohio has become a swing state in the coming midterm Congressional elections, and one of two Republican-held Senate seats is up for grabs. Trump has visited the state twice already in an attempt to rally turnout and counter a slide in his approval ratings. At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, Trump returned to the topic of Springfield. "You have a little town, beautiful little town in Ohio where they dropped about 35,000 Haitians. Well, they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone and we're giving their town back," he said to cheers. The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in its favour in the summer. "The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said after the court's ruling. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense." In a social media post in August, the Department of Homeland Security posted a video of Haitians in chains wearing white uniforms being led onto a deportation flight. The video, accompanied by jaunty music, told Haitians whose TPS had expired to "LEAVE IMMEDIATELY". The Trump administration has said it is conducting law enforcement operations in the town to keep Americans safe. It has also argued that Haiti is safe enough to return to. The country is subject to the US State Department's highest Level 4 "Do Not Travel" danger warning. GUIDE: What are the US midterms? EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midterms IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope The signs of decades of economic decline are still visible in Springfield, through shuttered factories and boarded up homes. This part of the American Midwest was hit badly by last century's de-industrialisation, when those laid off from its once prolific factories sought work on the coasts or migrated to warmer, southern states. Within the last five years, a Haitian population estimated to be around 20,000 strong arrived

title: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots
description: In France and beyond there is widespread disagreement over what led to some of the worst unrest seen in French cities in modern history.
body: The French prime minister has blamed far-left groups for planning some of the violence "This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!" Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October. I'd stopped her and her friend to ask what they thought of what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears. "My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely." But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure. Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play. The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised. French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend. French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes. A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. This video can not be played 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight The mass looting of what's said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity? Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. President Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice. Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts has lead former French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence. Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's Interior minister Bernard Quintin, warned of the 'TikTokisation' of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liege on "known far left groups". In France, Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu and his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire," said Nunez. On Tuesday Mr Lecornu spoke of "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups". Previously he'd accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos. It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied. Mélonchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all. The conservative mayor of Limoges Guillaume Guérin blamed the radical left LFI for the chaos in his city, which the party denied In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians. "Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa. But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned." France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday. The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics. Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist Prime Minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy." Mélonchon went on to apparently imply Mr Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure

title: The Papers: 'Burnham faces climate revolt' and 'Harry wants to fix feud'
description: Several papers lead on remarks from the Duke of Sussex yesterday, where he said he hoped to reconcile with his family.
body: The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead today, according to the Guardian. The paper says the move signals Prime Minister Andy Burnham's commitment to the North Sea oil and gas industry, but "threatens to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs". It reports that the shift will be a "major boost" for Britain's oil and gas industry, and once fully operational, will account for 6% of North Sea gas production. The Prince of Wales is pictured back-to-back with his brother, the Duke of Sussex, on the front page of the Sun. The paper focuses on a "bombshell" interview Prince Harry gave GQ magazine, where he said he hoped for reconciliation with his family. In a comment that the paper says could be seen as "a dig at Wills", the duke said: "Some people don't want it to work out. I want to work it out". The Daily Express says the Duke of Sussex has been "forced to deny taking a swipe at William", in regards to his remarks in GQ. "It was absolutely not intended as a swipe at his brother or any other members of this family," a spokesperson for the prince told the paper. The interview is described as a "new Sussex psychodrama" by the Daily Mail, which reads: "Oh, do put a sock in it Harry!" "Mahmood's fight to save her migrant crackdown" reads the Times, which reports the home secretary is "under pressure" to water down plans that would make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence. The paper says Burnham is considering exempting care workers from a proposal to extend the qualifying period for claiming indefinite leave to remain from five years to 15 years. It adds that Mahmood is expected to formally announce the plans next month, despite opposition from more than a hundred Labour MPs. The Telegraph says teachers face being banned from wearing pro-Palestine badges following a review of anti-Semitism in schools. It says that Sir David Bell, former Ofsted chief inspector, will detail the scale of abuse suffered by Jewish pupils across England in a report set to be released on Wednesday. He is expected to make 27 recommendations to deal with anti-Semitism in schools and colleges, the paper reports, including strengthening guidance on political impartiality - particularly regarding geopolitical issues. The front paper of the i Paper is dedicated to its exclusive report that the owners of Manchester City struck a rights payment deal with the council months before they were sold to Etihad Airways in agreement worth an estimated £10m a year. The airline reached a 10-year sponsorship deal for the council-owned stadium - as well as the club shirt and campus - which it says is worth a reported £400m. The Independent considers an inquiry which found that government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to "spread like wildfire" among the most vulnerable. The paper says the inquiry found ministers treated the sector "like an afterthought" during the pandemic, and then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock's claim that the government had placed a protective ring around care homes was unfounded. The Mirror has similarly focused on the "protective ring" claim, which is says has been slammed as a "cruel lie". The paper says some 43,000 residents died after hospital patients were discharged to care homes in the first weeks of the outbreak. "More shame for Hancock", it writes. The former health secretary is also pictured front and centre of the Metro, paired with the headline "Hancock and bull". The headline of the Financial Times reads: "AI debt nerves trigger race for default insurance in case boom turns to bust". The paper reports $9bn of credit default swaps are being traded a week, triggered by the wave of borrowing to finance trillions of dollars of AI infrastructure spending. It is a sign of investor unease, the paper says. A photograph of singer Gary Barlow leads the Daily Star, which says it was snapped as the Take That frontman was on his way to lunch with a wine expert. title: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
description: A "Super El Niño" has fuelled months-long fires in Indonesia, making hundreds of thousands of people sick.
body: Firefighters have been battling the stubborn blaze for weeks now When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks. But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful. "Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow? "Those thoughts haunt me every night." Nastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze. Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas – an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire landmass of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone. But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines. As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five. "The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week. "I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them." Dianyra Eka Nastiti is worried about how her children will recover Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body. Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death. Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air. "Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body – specifically the brain – doesn't get enough oxygen." Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate. In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Nastiti says this is unrealistic. "I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here." Nastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside. "With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house." Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks – from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange – she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors. Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air. People have been turning up at hospitals after complaining of feeling sick from the toxic smog Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm. "If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option." The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities. Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke – from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires. "At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN). "It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can." But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground. For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. title: Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
description: The US has advised its citizens to reconsider travelling to Kenya but the government tries to reassure people.
body: Nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with. Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago. Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him. But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens. The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert. Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely. More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease. With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread. The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way. Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya. As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern. The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport. Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed. However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment. When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings. Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic. Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival. Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases. Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital. It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people. The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease. Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated. Kenya has increased screening at border points In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population. That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee. The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement. A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms. Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent". The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus. The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases. The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams." In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment. Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU). With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers. Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids. title: The Interview
description: Julie Etchingham speaks to Archbishop Paul Gallagher about diplomacy in the Vatican
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·21 Oct 2026,·23 mins Available for over a year “Diplomacy is about talking to lots of people with whom you don't agree. And that's what diplomats do. And I think we would do that... The Vatican has always had very little difficulty, perhaps too little difficulty, in dealing with all sorts of political actors, all sorts regimes, all sorts of political systems.” Julie Etchingham speaks to Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Holy See’s Secretary for Relations with States and International Organisations and one of the Catholic Church’s more senior diplomats. The 72 year old, who was born and brought up in Liverpool, was appointed to the post in 2014 by Pope Francis and is frequently referred to as the Vatican's foreign minister. Although a tiny city state, the Vatican has significant reach and influence on the world stage, being a permanent observer at the United Nations and having diplomatic relations with 184 countries. Its diplomats pursue a policy of ‘positive neutrality’ - supposedly an impartial moral authority which allows it to dialogue with all sides. With no signs of various geopolitical tensions subsiding, the Archbishop’s role in navigating these instabilities on behalf of the more than 1.4 billion Catholics around the world has arguably never been more important. Thank you to the Sunday team for their help in making this programme. The Interview brings you conversations with people shaping our world, from all over the world. The best interviews from the BBC, including episodes with the Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally, former California Governor Jerry Brown, and Princess Diana’s brother Earl Spencer. You can listen on the BBC World Service on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at 0800 GMT. Or you can listen to The Interview as a podcast, out three times a week on BBC Sounds or wherever you get your podcasts. Presenter: Julie Etchingham Producers: Catherine Murray and Ben Cooper Editor: Farhana Haider Get in touch with us on email TheInterview@bbc.co.uk and use the hashtag #TheInterviewBBC on social media. title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
description: Musk says special committees within both companies have been formed to look at a possible mega-merger.
body: Elon Musk is the top executive of both Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday. While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move. "The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained." With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history. Shares of SpaceX rose 8% in after hours trading. The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google. That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn. SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year. Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks. Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned. The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together. Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more. Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger. He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX. Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield". He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve". Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion. While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics. SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut. title: Is Donald Trump ready to do business with Myanmar?
description: There are signs the United States is shifting its policy towards Myanmar, formerly a global pariah.
body: A top US official recently met with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing for the first time in years Has Washington's long-standing policy of isolating the military regime in Myanmar now changed? The revelation that a top official in the Trump administration met its leader Min Aung Hlaing last month, and the removal of some business figures from the US sanctions list, suggests that it has. Until now, the US had had very little official contact with the regime following the 2021 coup, when Myanmar's military ousted democratically-elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. More recently, it had applied a series of targeted sanctions against those judged to be supporting the junta. The meeting on 15 and 16 September was with US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, and it took place in Myanmar's capital Nay Pyi Taw. Its ostensible focus was to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen who had been detained in June over a dispute with the local American Chamber of Commerce. But Vance was the most senior US official to meet Min Aung Hlaing since he seized power, and they almost certainly discussed other matters of mutual interest. Vance is also known to have met Burmese officials in Tokyo in June, again in Tokyo this month, and to have met representatives of the groups opposing military rule. Signs of a shift in US policy towards Myanmar, though, go back to July last year, at the height of President Donald Trump's tariff war. That was when Min Aung Hlaing, along with other leaders in the region, received a personal letter from the US president informing him that his country's shattered economy was about to be hit by, in Myanmar's case, 40% tariffs. Other countries reeled in shock at the punitive levies imposed on their vital trade with a country they had once seen as a friend and ally. Much of Myanmar has been devastated by a civil war that has been raging since 2021 But Min Aung Hlaing was delighted. He replied immediately to express his "sincere appreciation for this encouraging invitation to continue participating in the extraordinary Economy of the United States, the Number One Market in the World", mimicking Trump's hyperbolic phrasing and eccentric capitalisation. "It is with great esteem that I wish to acknowledge Your Excellency's strong leadership in guiding your country toward national prosperity with the spirit of a true patriot." This was not just a dictator's hunch that flattery might be the best way to win favours from Trump. Min Aung Hlaing's coup, and the civil war it ignited, had turned him into an international pariah. His regime was largely unrecognised. He was accused of being a war criminal, with cases lodged against him at the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice. Aside from Russia and, more recently, China, he was shunned by other governments. Yet here was the US president addressing him just like any other president or prime minister, as "Your Excellency. There was no mention in Trump's letter of the appalling human cost of Min Aung Hlaing's power seizure; of a democracy crushed and leader Aung San Suu Kyi jailed. That same month the regime signed a $3m (£2.3m) contract with DCI, a long-standing Washington lobbying firm which had been used by a previous Burmese military regime in 2002 to try to improve its image. Since then the military government has also hired Roger Stone, a controversial lobbyist and confidant of President Trump, at a fee of $50,000 a month. Also around the same time Adam Castillo, a former US marine and Trump supporter who had just stepped down as president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Yangon, was in Washington trying to persuade Vice President JD Vance's team that it was time to re-engage. Castillo believed that the US reliance on sanctions to isolate the junta had failed. "Myanmar mattered to America not only as a morality play but as a strategic interest," he wrote in his book Finding Our Voice: A Story of Leadership in Crisis and the American Spirit Abroad. He discussed with the vice-president's team how the US "could engage Myanmar without war or isolation, loosen China's grip on critical minerals, and align peace with American interests". This video can not be played Watch: The rebels at the front line of Myanmar's civil war Castillo was pushing at an open door. The US dependence on rare earths from China had been exposed when China blocked them in retaliation against Trump's tariffs in April. The administration began prioritising finding alternative sources. Myanmar happens to have large reserves of rare earths which are currently being exploited solely for China's use. At almost exactly the same time, the state department issued new guidance to US embassies around the world on what to say about elections. From now on, it said, "messages should avoid opining on the fairness or integrity of an electoral process, its legitimacy, or the democratic values of the country in question". So, when Myanmar held its much-criticised general election in December and January, allowing Min Aung Hlaing to turn himself from coup leader into a notionally civilian president, the US did not, like most Western governments, condemn it as neither free nor fair. For decades the US has consistently pronounced judgement on other countries' elections. Now the US had nothing to say. Washington's decision to lift sanctions on some of those targeted by the Biden administration seemed only to confirm the new direction of US-Myanmar policy. "For years, the US approach to Myanmar has been defined by isolation, sanctions, and distance," wrote the lobbyists DCI in a recent newsletter. "That era is over… thankfully, President Trump has the courage to try something different." The tone is certainly different, but not so much the substance of US-Myanmar relations. title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
description: Investigative genetic genealogy can help hunt down criminals but raises worries over privacy.
body: Crime scene evidence is often not enough to identify suspects Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois. The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma. The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found. For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator. The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US. Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases. The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer. They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms. Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual. Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member. "That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime. It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year. Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this." Albert Zigler was charged with murder in May The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved. It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations. Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map." Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect. However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed. An Othram scientist prepares a bone for DNA extraction DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases. One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up. Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993. They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case. The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot. This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence. But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them." Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique." "But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds. While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data. "There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent. A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it." Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund. While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment. The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says. title: Tighter rules planned to protect people from cosmetic surgery that goes badly wrong
description: There will be restrictions on who can carry out procedures and fines for those who flout the law, in England in 2027.
body: Alice Webb died after becoming unwell following a liquid Brazilian Butt Lift procedure Only properly trained professionals will be allowed to offer high-risk cosmetic procedures like liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), vampire facials and chemical peels, under long-awaited government plans for England in 2027. The government said it wanted to "drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market" and shield people from treatments "that can go badly wrong". Currently, there are no restrictions over who can carry out these 'no scalpel' procedures, which can harm or kill if not performed safely. Under the new rules, high-risk procedures for under-18s will also be banned, and rogue providers will face new criminal offences and fixed fines of up to £4,000. Sasha Dean from Bedfordshire was left in a coma after receiving a liquid BBL The government began consulting on changes to the cosmetic surgery industry in 2023, but there have been calls for stricter regulations for many years. It comes following horror stories of procedures reportedly carried out in Airbnbs, hotel rooms, garden sheds and even public toilets, by "cosmetic cowboys", external. Women have told the BBC of dangerous complications, pain and permanent scarring after treatment by rogue operators. Alice Webb, a mother-of-five from Gloucestershire, died within hours of getting a liquid Brazilian butt lift in 2024. That same year, Sasha Dean, from Bedfordshire, was left in a coma after receiving a liquid BBL. A BBL is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which dermal fillers are injected into the buttocks to alter their size or shape. Some of Sasha's treatment took place in a private house and she ended up developing sepsis. She told BBC News: "Very quickly it turned into a complete nightmare. "I had a heart attack, one of my lungs had collapsed, my kidneys were failing. My body was just completely shutting down." Under the government's new rules: Fillers injected into parts of the body other than the face, like liquid BBLs, will be legally defined as cosmetic surgical procedures, meaning only doctors could perform the surgery High-risk non-surgical or wellbeing treatments, including deep chemical peels, vampire facials, dermal micro-coring and some laser procedures would be restricted to doctors, dentists and some nurses, midwives and pharmacists who have been trained Cosmetic surgery and risky treatments will be banned for under 18s - lip fillers and face Botox on children has already been stopped The dark side of the Brazilian butt lift boom Vampire facials involve drawing a patient's blood and then separating out platelet-rich plasma from it using a centrifuge. The plasma is then injected back into the face through tiny needle punctures Dermal micro-coring involves removing tiny sections of skin using thin hollow needles, small enough to allow scarless healing Chemical peels are skin resurfacing procedures that use a chemical solution to remove the top layers of skin Health Minister Karin Smyth said: "We want to drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market and raise standards across the board, giving reputable businesses a fair chance to thrive by helping people identify safe, qualified providers they can trust." The British Beauty Council said the government should be congratulated for tackling the issue head-on. But Mr Keith Allison, from the Royal College of Surgeons of England, said the consultation was "long overdue" and, while welcome, the proposals did not go far enough. "Ministers must ensure they do not create a new loophole in patient protection by regulating non-surgical cosmetic procedures more robustly than cosmetic surgery itself. "A doctor should not be able to carry out cosmetic surgery simply because they hold a medical license." The government will now ask doctors, businesses, regulators, the public and other experts for their say on the draft rules, before plans go through parliament in spring 2027. A licensing scheme for Botox clinics in England to improve safety standards has already been announced. In Scotland, laws passed in March mean cosmetic procedures must be performed by, or alongside, certain healthcare professionals in a registered setting. Non-surgical procedures are banned for under 18s. There are no dedicated regulations around cosmetic procedures in Wales or Northern Ireland. title: Universities face 'substantial' funding cuts amid budget delay
description: Both Queen's University Belfast and Ulster University are expected to have financial deficits in 2025/26.
body: Both Queen's University Belfast and Ulster University are expected to have financial deficits in 2025/26 Northern Ireland's universities are facing a "substantial" cut of £21m in the Stormont funding they receive to teach students. The top official at the Department for the Economy (DfE), Ian Snowden, said the universities were facing a reduction of 6% on the opening funding they received in 2024/25. The potential cuts come as the Northern Ireland Executive remains seven months into the financial year without a budget. Snowden said both Queen's University Belfast (QUB) and Ulster University (UU) are expected to have financial deficits in 2025/26. With no agreed budget for 2025/26, Stormont departments have been operating under contingency arrangements allowing them to spend up to 95% of last year's funding. The DfE is the Stormont department with responsibility for higher and further education in Northern Ireland. Universities are mainly funded through student fees and a "teaching grant" provided by DfE. Further education colleges have already announced big cuts to student places and courses. Ulster University, meanwhile, is making 450 staff redundant across its campuses to save about £25m. The chair of Stormont's economy committee, Democratic Unionist Party assembly member Phillip Brett, said a further cut in university funding could mean that the universities would not receive money for three months for students they have already enrolled. "The universities have taken students on in the anticipation that they will receive funding from the department," he said. "We're now six months into the financial year and they still haven't received a formal letter of offer from the department. "And despite students enrolling in September, one of the contingencies from the department is now that come January, February, March you might say 'actually we're not going to pay you for these three months of the students that you've taken on'?" "It's a possibility," Snowden told the committee. He also said the universities could only get confirmation of how much funding they would get when the executive agreed a budget. "At this point we still don't know how much money we have to spend," he said. Amy Smith is the president of the National Union of Students-Union of Students in Ireland Amy Smith, the National Union of Students-Union of Students in Ireland (NUS-USI) president, said it was "disappointing to hear that our universities will be facing cuts to their teaching grants". "Any cuts directly impact students, their access to their education and the quality of the experience they receive while at university costs to them remain the same," she added. "Students and staff must not be left to shoulder the cost of underfunding. "We stand together in calling for the investment needed to protect jobs, access to education, and the quality of teaching." Universities are mainly funded through student fees and a "teaching grant" provided by Department for the Economy A spokesperson for Queen's said the university was "operating in a challenging financial environment and has consistently highlighted that the current higher education funding model, and continued budget uncertainty, are unsustainable". "We continue to work constructively with the Department for the Economy and government partners to secure a long-term solution that will benefit students and the wider economy," they said. "Queen's continues to monitor the financial and funding environment closely and remains focused on managing resources responsibly to protect the university's long-term financial sustainability while continuing to deliver for our students, staff and wider society." A spokesperson for Ulster University said it was "already enacting a substantial savings plan". "Given the deteriorating funding situation from the department, which we regard as very serious, we will continue to enact appropriate caution in relation to our finances," the spokesperson said. They also said 735 university staff had applied for voluntary redundancy. title: I left state secrets on the train - I'm proof you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life
description: Top civil servant Richard Jackson recounts that fateful day and how he recovered in the aftermath.
body: Former civil servant Richard Jackson made headlines in 2008 when he left top secret files on a train Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late. He had left highly classified documents on the train. The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation. Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath to BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life. Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university. "We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career. "My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility. "I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off." He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6. Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official. Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret". I left top-secret files on a train In hindsight, Jackson says he should have phoned the Cabinet Office and asked someone to collect the documents securely. But he puts what he did next down to "maybe a bit of self-preservation". "Maybe if I get them back, no one else will ever know." He put the top secret papers in a bright orange cardboard folder and sat on the train the next morning thinking over and over "do not forget this". He got off the train and walked briskly towards Whitehall. Then he "realised I hadn't got the folder... it just felt for a moment like the world had stopped." Jackson went to every station the train stopped at and asked whether someone had handed a folder in. Nothing. "I was frantic. Everything, every movement felt very jerky... I felt sick." He didn't outwardly break down until he saw Maddie: "I told her I'd ruined our lives. She just held me. She told me it would be all right and we'd get through this." Richard credits wife Maddie for helping him recover from the worst mistake of his life At work the next day, Jackson discovered the documents had been found and handed to the BBC. Jackson says his first sense was "relief in that the papers were back somewhere safe" before the realisation "it was now going to be public". "I was the main story on the 6 o'clock news that night. And they [the Civil Service] suspended me, pending an investigation." Richard says he feels lucky to have magical people like stepdaughters Charlotte and Becky in his life Jackson hid away at home. One lunchtime, Maddie found him sitting cross-legged on the sofa sobbing. "I'd spent the morning trying to find a painless way to die," he says, "I've often thought what would have happened if she hadn't come home that lunchtime… but I guess I'll never know. "We spent that afternoon talking… and I think that was the first time where I thought, 'if I'm going to get through this, I can't do it on my own'." The Cabinet Office found it was an act of gross misconduct and demoted him three grades. He was charged under the Official Secrets Act, avoided jail, and was fined £2,500. On paper it was over. But Jackson could not shake the feelings of shame, regret and humiliation. He credits the many people who cared about him for helping him piece his life back together. "I fixed very little myself. Lots of people fixed me." After returning to the MoD in an HR role, then moving to the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to work on the Olympics, Jackson left the Civil Service and worked for the Samaritans. He then took on a role running a team of analysts looking at global terror risk, and started training as a life coach in his spare time. When he was made redundant, he set up a coaching company, NewDay, which helps people cope with the stress of handling distressing material. "I could tell my story... and there'd be a point to it. There'd be a reason for what I did." Richard keeps an evidence board of things he has achieved and kind things people have said to help him remember his success and worth He wants people to know there is a way back from the biggest mistake of your life. "You can be in a really bad place, and you can still stand up, and you can get through it and there are ways to help yourself do that and get help." Asked if he's forgiven himself he says no - but he is happy again. Maddie is happy too that he no longer works 100 hour weeks. "My life is not defined by my career and I'm more present at home," he says. "I am much more appreciative of how lucky I am to have magical people in my life." Richard Jackson has shared steps that helped him move through his traumatic episode: Get your thoughts out of your head. In a dark place, your mind jumps from "I made a terrible mistake" to "I am a worthless person" at the speed of thought. Writing it down or talking to someone slows things down to give you a chance to notice the illogical leaps. Continue activities you enjoy. When you feel unworthy, you stop doing the things that lift you up. Work out what they are - the gym, a book, a long walk - and make them non-negotiable fixtures in your routine. Remember your worth and your success. I keep an evidence board by my desk with notes of things I have achieved and kind things people have said. It's a tangible reminder that I am not that mistake, I am so much

title: Ali G is back. But is the character past its sell-by date?
description: Borat and Bruno creator Sacha Baron Cohen returns as Ali G, more than two decades after the release of Ali G Indahouse.
body: Ali G's appearance at the Wimbledon men's final on Centre Court went viral in July "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent. Behind him, hundreds of fans cram onto a London Underground escalator, all wearing Ali G's trademark yellow shell suit and skullcap. Baron Cohen shouts the character's catchphrases through a megaphone, with the crowd enthusiastically finishing each one. Earlier this month, more than 300 fans attended an official Ali G lookalike competition, ferried around London on an open-top bus that stopped at landmarks including Big Ben, Leicester Square and Covent Garden. The stunt was promotion for an upcoming sequel to 2002 film Ali G Indahouse - called Ali G: Who iz I? - which hits cinemas on Friday. But not everyone is excited about the return of Baron Cohen's comedy character. Critics have long accused the actor of perpetuating racial stereotypes with Ali G, and criticism of the upcoming sequel has gained traction online, with social media posts from comedians, content creators and film fans attracting thousands of likes and comments. Among them is singer and presenter Jordan Stephens, who has posted multiple TikToks criticising the franchise's return. And last month, discussing the film's trailer on the Jeremy Vine show, Labour MP Paulette Hamilton called the character racist. She said she believed Baron Cohen would not get away with portraying any other racial group "in the way he has done with the black community". Baron Cohen has not directly addressed criticism of the character's return, and did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. However, he acknowledged an inevitable backlash when he first announced the sequel, writing on X: "In an age where a comedian's career can be ended by a single un-PC joke, I thought I'd play it safe and bring this guy back." Recently, he shared a video, external posted to a newly created Instagram account, in which a grey-haired academic urged viewers to boycott the upcoming film. The character appeared to be Baron Cohen in prosthetic makeup. Has Ali G passed his sell-by date? Or are racial stereotypes, and those who believe them, the true butt of the joke? Alternatively, as some critics argue, is the whole thing simply not very funny? David and Victoria Beckham show off their Red Nose Day 2001 noses while filming an interview with Ali G, during which the famous "goldenballs" line originated The character of Ali G rose to fame through a series of deadpan TV interviews with figures including Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed and the Beckhams, from which catchphrases such as "Booyakasha" and "Is it because I is black?" entered popular culture. But some critics say these catchphrases have since been appropriated by others in a real-life context to mock black people and dismiss their concerns. Comedian Dane Baptiste, the first black British comic nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award, remembers hearing Ali G catchphrases everywhere during the character's noughties heyday. "A lot of the time, I would hear people using phrases like 'Is it because I is black?' or 'Booyakasha'," he recalls. "Even taking the phrase 'Is it because I is black?'... that was used to the point of caricature, whereby, whenever black people experienced actual grievances relating to systemic and institutional racism, it was reduced to this catchphrase." Baptiste believes the character, which he calls a "black caricature", is returning at a time when black creatives are being "starved of opportunities". Baptiste hosted shows such as Tonight at the London Palladium and Live at the Apollo The controversy around Ali G is not new. When the Ali G Indahouse movie was released in 2002, protesters gathered at its Leicester Square premiere and organiser Peter Akinti branded the character the "new Al Jolson", a 1920s entertainer who used to perform in blackface. Little is known about the plot of the Ali G sequel beyond the character discovering his girlfriend Julie is pregnant and travelling to America to interview a slew of unsuspecting real-world participants, including American physicist Alan Lightman and retired Army General C Stewart Rodeheaver, who appears in the film's trailer. Ali G: Who Iz I?, which opens in late October, sees Ali G learn his long-term girlfriend, Julie, is eight months pregnant When Ali G first arrived on our screens, characters like him were far more common, says social psychologist Amy Kean. She argues they are no longer "culturally relevant". "Ali G, Little Britain, Catherine Tate, all of those comedians and sketch shows, they made the voice the joke," says Kean, who has written on accentism, drawing from her experiences being teased for her Essex accent. "I remember going to school in the 90s and people would take the piss out of anyone whose voice wasn't exactly the same as everyone else's." Baron Cohen has in the past suggested that his character had a knack for pushing powerful interviewees into uncomfortable territory by playing with biases and expectations. Speaking on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in 2020, Baron Cohen reflected on interviewing Donald Trump for Da Ali G Show, and recalled how the programme's producer was a well-spoken Englishman who Trump had assumed would be conducting the interview. "I remember Donald Trump looking at me, and I'm wearing a sweatsuit," Baron Cohen said. "His face dropped. He was immediately furious that he was going to have to speak to somebody from a lower-class borough rather than this rather astute Etonian producer." Writing for Time magazine in 2020, Baron Cohen said: "By getting people to reveal what they really believe, I have at times exposed the ignorance, bigotry and conspiratorial delusions that often lurk just below the surface of our modern lives." title: Where to spot brilliant colours after 'false autumn' spoils some leaf displays
description: The UK's hottest summer on record has caused some trees to shed their leaves early, but experts say spectacular autumn colours could still be on the way.
body: There was a stunning display of autumnal colours in 2025 after a warm and sunny summer, but how will this year's heat affect the seasonal display? This year's display of autumn leaves could look rather different following the UK's hottest summer on record. Months of heat and drought have put trees under stress, causing some to shed their leaves earlier than usual in a phenomenon known as a "false autumn". Experts say this could mean a more varied display of autumn colours, with some trees losing their leaves prematurely while others are yet to change colour. However, some trees could still produce spectacular shades of red, orange and gold. The UK's record-breaking summer brought prolonged periods of heat and dry weather, with some parts of the country particularly affected by drought. Kevin Martin, Head of Tree Collections at Royal Bontanic Gardens, Kew, said: "Following the UK's hottest summer on record, we may not see the usual blaze of autumn colour arrive all at once this year." Many trees, particularly in southern England, have already shed their leaves prematurely. This happens when trees respond to heat and drought stress by dropping their leaves early to conserve water. "False autumns are a warning sign. Trees can live for hundreds of years, but they are increasingly under pressure from a rapidly changing climate," Martin said. However, some trees could still produce spectacular autumn colours. "Recent rainfall could still bring a strong display from individual trees in October, and some species may put on an even more impressive show than usual," he added. Brown leaves covered the ground along The Mall in London in August 2026, following the summer's prolonged heat and drought Forestry England says autumn colours are developing at different rates across the country's woodlands. Its Autumn Leaf Watch tracker , externalshowed early signs of yellow, orange and red in forests including the New Forest, Delamere Forest, Wyre Forest and the Forest of Dean at the end of September. Silver birch, rowan and horse chestnut were among the species already changing colour, while many oak and beech trees remained predominantly green. Some western and central forests were showing stronger early signs of autumn colour, although this does not necessarily mean they will have the most vibrant displays later in the season. Chris Sorensen, Forest Management Advisor at Forestry England, told BBC Weather: "Rather than a single moment when autumn arrives everywhere, colour tends to develop at different rates depending on local weather, elevation, tree species and site conditions." "That's why visitors to the nation's forests can see very different stages of autumn even between forests that are relatively close together." Trees in Coventry show contrasting autumn colours. A mixture of sunny days and cooler nights generally provides the best conditions for a colourful autumn display. "The ideal autumn conditions are generally a mix of sunny days and cooler nights, without prolonged periods of strong winds or heavy rain," Sorensen said. "Those conditions allow colours to develop gradually and help leaves stay on the trees for longer, extending the display." This year, however, the exceptionally dry summer faced by some parts of the country has left trees parched. UK trees "desperately need more rain following months of drought", Martin said. title: No jeopardy but loads of fun - Champions League sets new goals record
description: It was goals galore again in the Champions League on Tuesday, with the competition setting a new record this season.
body: Phil Foden scored a hat-trick in Manchester City's 5-1 win over AEK Athens More teams, more games - and more goals. Since the current Champions League format was introduced at the start of the 2024-25 season, Europe's elite club competition has delivered all of the above and more. Already trending upwards over the past two campaigns, there has been a genuine goals boom in this year's competition. The 187 goals scored so far have come at an average of 4.16 per game - the highest in Champions League history. "Look how many goals have been scored, it's phenomenal," ex-Manchester United and England winger Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live. "The attackers are being clinical." Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock described the volume of goals as "incredible" - so how unusual is it? Ready for lots of numbers? Not only is the current goals-per-game percentage the highest ever in the Champions League, it is the third highest in European Cup history - behind only 1959-60 (4.19) and 1955-56 (4.38). While 40 goals were scored across nine games on Tuesday, last week was even more spectacular. Last Wednesday saw the third highest-scoring day in Champions League history (46 goals), bettered only by the final league-phase matchdays of 2024-25 and 2025-26, when 18 matches took place. The 78 goals scored across Tuesday and Wednesday last week made matchday two the highest scoring in history. That was nine more than the total scored on matchday one this season (69) - which, at the time, was the second highest-scoring matchday since the new league phase was introduced in 2024-25. Will we see the record fall again this week? It's already halfway there. Doue impresses as PSG beat Barcelona in thriller Ever since Uefa announced its plans to alter the format of the Champions League in 2021, the impact on matches has been a hot topic. Scrutiny has only increased since the changes were implemented in time for the 2024-25 season. After beginning life as a six-team invitational tournament in 1955-56 before growing to a 32-team knockout tournament in 1967, the Champions League as we know it began in 1992. A group stage was added, with the last 16 entering a knockout phase. There was a brief spell with two group stages, but this was reverted back to the single group-stage format for the 2003-04 tournament. The group stage previously featured 32 teams in eight groups of four, with the top two sides from each of those groups qualifying for the last 16. For the start of the 2024-25 season, the group stage was replaced with a 36-team league phase, with each side playing eight one-off fixtures instead of six games against three teams. The top eight finishers qualify directly for the knockout stages, with those placed ninth to 24th entering a two-legged play-off stage. The bottom eight are eliminated, meaning that after eight matches, 24 sides are still in the competition. Some argue that that creates a lack of jeopardy, which encourages teams to play more expansively. But do more goals equal better quality? "I think the entertainment has gone up, although I'm not sure the quality has gone up," The Times football writer Tom Arnott told BBC Radio 5 Live. "If I'm looking at the games it's brilliant to watch and thrilling because the football itself is fantastic - but what do they mean? "The lack of jeopardy, why would PSG and Barcelona play for a draw, why not go for it? If you need five wins from the eight games you know you've got some margin there. If you lose it's OK. I think the format allows all the teams to loosen up. "The entertainment value is there but I think you come away from these matches sometimes and still think 'what does it all mean?'. The lack of jeopardy early on does deliver entertainment." The night 'ruthless' Ngumoha came of age for Liverpool No Haaland, no problem - can Foden be Man City's alternative goalscorer?
