title: The night 'ruthless' Ngumoha came of age for Liverpool
description: Rio Ngumoha produces a coming-of-age performance in Liverpool's comeback win over Villarreal, writes Aadam Patel.
body: Rio Ngumoha, aged 18 years and 52 days, became the youngest Liverpool player to either score or assist for the club in the Champions League In a game of seven goals, none were scored by Rio Ngumoha - but this was his night. The 18-year-old was simply a class apart from the rest in Liverpool's 4-3 win over Villarreal. It is over a year since Ngumoha burst on to the scene for Liverpool with a memorable stoppage-time winner at Newcastle. He has been in and out since then, impressing in flashes and even going on to make his England debut earlier this season. But this performance was different, inspiring his team to a memorable comeback win in the Champions League. By the time the teenager was replaced in the 74th minute, with Bradley Barcola taking over, the chants of "Rio, Rio, Rio" had already repeatedly rung around Anfield. It was quite the sight to see Alisson embrace Ngumoha shortly after he was given Uefa's player of the match award. "It's up there with one of the best [games] I've played. I enjoyed myself out there and the team helped me a lot," Ngumoha told Amazon Prime. "Whenever I get the ball and there's an opportunity to go one versus one, or two versus one, I believe in myself to do it. I'll just keep going and be ruthless." Liverpool were woeful for much of the first half as they trailed Villarreal by two goals, but Ngumoha took responsibility. After Alexis Mac Allister pulled one back, Ngumoha found space to dink in a delightful ball that was met by Ronald Araujo for an equaliser. Ater the break, Ngumoha - as he had done all evening - waltzed past Sergi Cardona to set up Mac Allister to give Liverpool the lead. Ngumoha inspires Liverpool comeback win - report and player ratings The match statistics alone showed what a threat Ngumoha can be. He had 12 touches in the opposition box, completed seven out of eight dribbles, and registered two crucial assists. But watching Ngumoha is more than just a numbers experience. There's a fearless nature to his play that can get the crowd going, and he was the one bright spark in a first half where Liverpool lacked any sort of rhythm. In a game increasingly focused on structures, Ngumoha's raw ability to take a man on is what helps to set him apart. "He was magnificent tonight," said former Liverpool forward Daniel Sturridge on Amazon Prime. "On the ball, this kid has so much potential - and I say 'kid', but he's a young man. He has so much quality and it's stuff that you can't teach to be honest. "What he does with the ball at his feet - that is God-given ability - and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he said in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that." Ngumoha, who has grown up playing down the left, has struggled to get minutes on his preferred side this season, especially with Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola often playing down that flank. But head coach Andoni Iraola wants his wingers to be able to play on both sides and Ngumoha's improvement on the right flank has been impressive in such a short space of time. Ngumoha also spoke about his rapid development on the right on Saturday, after Liverpool beat Brentford. "I feel like I've got a lot better playing there from the Newcastle game [at the start of this season] until now," Ngumoha said. "I'm understanding it more. And going away with England helped a lot as well. I like playing on both sides. It gives me another tool in the toolbox." Iraola praised Ngumoha's attitude and how he is playing more minutes "endurance-wise" but stressed the need to remember the youngster is not done with his development. "I am happy with his attitude because he is eager to improve the things we think he needs to improve, and to add more things to his game," Iraola said. "He has played a lot on the right lately and is feeling so comfortable now, but he is only 18 and still not the full package. "I hope it continues the same way, but it is not always going to be like this. "There will be ups and downs in the process, but I'm happy because attitude-wise I think he's in a great place." Talks continue over a new deal, with Ngumoha currently on the contract that he signed in September 2025, weeks after his 17th birthday, that tied him down until 2028. The expectation is that he will sign with more lucrative terms now that he is 18 and - as Ngumoha said at the weekend - those negotiations are going well and in the hands of his agent. He will focus on letting his football do the talking - as he did on Tuesday night against Villarreal. What is certain is that Liverpool have a truly special talent on their hands and one that they will hope can entertain the Anfield crowd for years to come. title: No Haaland, no problem - can Foden be Man City's alternative goalscorer?
description: Phil Foden's magnificent man-of-the-match display in Manchester City's Champions League win against AEK Athens serves as a reminder of his talent and ability to influence games.
body: Phil Foden is the third Englishman to score a hat-trick and provide an assist in a Champions League match after Wayne Rooney and Raheem Sterling Phil Foden's magnificent man-of-the-match display in the Champions League against AEK Athens served as a reminder of the prodigious talent that the player still possesses. After two disappointing seasons in which, by his own admission, he failed to hit the heights expected, there may be those who had forgotten what he can produce. Being left out of the England squad for the World Cup last summer did not help, but he came into this season telling reporters he was looking forward to a "fresh start" under new manager Enzo Maresca. Up until last weekend, that fresh start had been a slow burner with the low point of being sent off in the derby against Manchester United in September, before he sparked into life by netting against Ipswich on Saturday. That was his first Premier League goal in 10 months and a strike that seems to have opened the floodgates, with the 26-year-old netting a superb hat-trick in the 5-1 hammering of Athens at Etihad Stadium on Tuesday. "I enjoyed that a lot," Foden told TNT Sports. "The lads were great again. We showed determination again. I am a forward so I have to keep scoring and helping the team. It is good for my confidence." Asked if he was returning to his best form, Foden said: "Slowly, but surely. Still got a long way to go, but I am going in the right direction. Scoring along the way definitely helps. "I want to keep working hard and keep being the best I can for the manager and the team." Foden stars with hat-trick as Man City thrash AEK Athens A smiling Foden gliding across the turf in full flow is a joy for City fans to watch and he sent them home happy after a performance in which he had a hand in four of the five goals. Boss Maresca took a risk by making eight changes from the side that beat Ipswich in their last outing, with Gianluigi Donnarumma, Ruben Dias and Foden the players retained. Striker Erling Haaland was named in the squad but ultimately given the night off after sustaining a blow to the foot in the previous game, giving Maresca the chance to explore his suggestion that Foden could offer a "solution" in the false nine role. After starting on the right, he moved into that position later in the game and it paid dividends, with Foden saying he "really enjoyed" the role. Though there was a brief scare for City at the start of the second half when the visitors pulled a goal back to trail 2-1, they found another gear and were out of sight by the final whistle. And by then, Foden had become just the third Englishman to score a hat-trick and provide an assist in a Champions League match after Wayne Rooney for Manchester United in 2004 and former team-mate Raheem Sterling for City in 2019. While the first and third goals were converted from close range, the second was a stunning finish from just inside the area, Foden opening up his body and caressing a first-time effort into the top corner. "Beautiful - that's the word I would use to describe him," former City defender Joleon Lescott said of Foden on TNT Sports. "His finishing was exquisite. "I think he has convinced the manager that if Erling Haaland isn't available for any reason throughout the season, then he is the man to play at number nine." Foden scored 19 goals as City won the Premier League in 2023-24 and was named the Professional Footballers' Association player of the year and the league's player of the season. He ended last season by failing to score in his last 31 games for club and country but despite the struggles, he signed a new four-year deal in July. The red card for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes at Old Trafford could have been damaging but the aim now will be kick on and build on this showing. "I was very happy with Phil, even before the red card to be honest," said Maresca. "I said since day one that I consider him one of the best English players. "We know that Phil is a top player. Again, for different reasons, he had some problems in the last two years but he is going to help us. "That is why we are so keen to have him in the best way." Former England winger Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "When Phil Foden gets his opportunities tonight, he takes them with both hands. By getting a hat-trick, his confidence is going to be sky high. "Enzo Maresca is going to be happy he hasn't had to bring on Erling Haaland or Jeremy Doku. He has been able to use the players that are in his squad. "This is no way a second-string but you have got to go our there and show the manager 'I should be playing'. "Foden is answering his manager's questions." No Haaland, no problem - can Foden be Man City's alternative goalscorer? title: Tory MP questions government advisor's position after wife's Palestine Action post
description: A Downing Street spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."
body: Shadow Home Affairs Minister Alicia Kearns has written to the prime minister Conservative MP Alicia Kearns has raised concerns over whether Jonathan Powell, the National Security Advisor, can remain in his post following his wife's references to Palestine Action on social media. The shadow home affairs minister has written to the prime minister questioning whether Powell's position is still tenable, despite the Metropolitan Police concluding no action was necessary over his wife's, Sarah Helm, comments. A Downing Street spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity." Posting on X last Thursday, Helm wrote: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action," responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney. The Normal People writer announced last week that her books will not be supplied to UK booksellers after she announced she would use her royalties to support Palestine Action. The Met investigation into Helm's post found "it did not meet the criminal threshold" and the matter was dropped on Saturday. But Kearns has written to Andy Burnham about the handling of sensitive national security information, asking whether the government has investigated the posts and whether he retains full confidence in his adviser. She told the BBC: "We cannot have the NSA's wife tweeting about what decisions her husband has or hasn't made." Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation last year, making it a a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years imprisonment to belong to or support the group. An appeal against the proscription of Palestine Action is due to be heard by the Supreme Court next month, external, in a battle that has now gone on for more than year. title: Alberta's decisive decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
description: The overwhelming vote by Alberta to stay in Canada gives Mark Carney political capital to focus on remaking the country's economy, writes the BBC's Lyse Doucet.
body: This video can not be played "Let's move on": Albertans react to separatist movement referendum results "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners. It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada. But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province. Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world. Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders. Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other." Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too. "Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome. Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world". Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state. The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls. "I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding." For Canadians, it's no laughing matter. In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is. And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific. But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast. Mark Carney and Alberta's leader Danielle Smith has worked closely on pushing for an oil pipeline to the west coast from the landlocked province. "Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto. "Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build. An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations. At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night. After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance – pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials. 'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat "Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year. At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes. Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too. The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union. "I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel. For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians woul

title: 60 years on: The Aberfan disaster through the eyes of those who survived
description: It is 60 years since one of Wales' darkest days, when a mining community changed forever.
body: 60 years on: The Aberfan disaster through the eyes of those who survived Few events have left a deeper mark on Wales than the Aberfan disaster. Sixty years on, the tragedy remains woven into the nation's collective memory, a day of unimaginable loss that reshaped a community and changed attitudes to industrial safety across Britain. At 09:15 on 21 October 1966, an ordinary school morning was shattered when a coal tip above Aberfan collapsed. 144 people died following the Aberfan landslide in October 1966 Black slurry thundered down the mountainside, engulfing Pantglas Junior School and nearby homes. Within moments, 144 people were dead, including 116 children, on what was the last day of school before the half-term holiday. On the 60th anniversary, those who were there share their harrowing memories. Mair was a 25-year-old teacher and had worked at Pantglas School for a year "What I remember was the drizzly rain, it was misty. I rang the bell to start school at about ten to nine, before the children went in. There was this terrible noise, and I looked out of the window. I could see a wall had collapsed and realised I had to get my pupils outside. As we escaped, I saw the caretaker rushing to get other children out. They opened Bethania Chapel to take children who had died, but the first bodies were placed in a shelter in the playground. We identified them before they were cleaned up, and before their parents were told. I found that very hard. I remember one little girl, I can see her face now. She had beautiful black curly hair." "There was this really unusual sound, like a rumble. Like if you chuck stones across the floor, but it was getting louder and louder. Next thing, water was seeping through the floor, the walls were cracking and timbers were breaking. The teacher put a desk on a table, and a small chair on top of that. She climbed on top and smashed the window. And then she held us up, probably by the scruffs of our necks, to get us out through it. I am so grateful for her quick thinking, she saved our lives. When I got outside, I could see a mountain of coal and slurry, with dust and water everywhere. I ran home, and remember saying: 'Mam, mam, the mountain came down to the school'." Gaynor Madgwick was eight and went to school that day with her brother Carl, seven, and sister Marylyn, 10 "I heard this tremendous sound, like a hurricane. It was so overwhelming, I knew something was coming, but didn't know what. Then this mass of black came crashing through the window, hurling me from the front of the classroom to the back. I woke up to find the classroom was no longer the classroom. The roof had caved in on us, and we were completely buried. I couldn't see my legs, I thought they had gone. A pupil in front of me was trapped, and he had blood trickling down his head. Another one was trying to get through the roof to get help. My head was cut open, and I couldn't move my hand as it was stuck in the cracked wall. I pinched the hand of a child near me to see if it would move. It didn't. Then I heard someone shout 'I'm going to smash the window' and saw my grandfather. I started to cry and will never forget the look in his eyes knowing I was alive. I'd broken my femur, my leg was just swinging and my shoes had gone. 'I'll buy you all the shoes you need,' my mum said as she greeted me outside. My parents then ran off to find my siblings. I was later told Carl and Marylyn had died, and all my friends had gone as well. This video can not be played Jeff Edwards: 'The rumbling sound got louder and louder' "As the teacher spoke by the blackboard, there was a rumbling sound that got louder and louder. The lights started to sway back and fore, but the teacher reassured us there was nothing to worry about. It was only thunder. The next thing I remember was waking up and seeing light from the sky because the roof had come in. I was stuck but awake and could see a dead girl on my shoulder. There was screaming, shouting and crying, but this got less and less. Jeff Edwards was the last child to be pulled out alive This was because the children were dying of physical trauma, the roof and slurry coming in, or they couldn't breathe, they had no air. I was lucky because I had this balloon of air around me. The fire service broke through the window from the hall, and somebody saw my white hair. They started digging and eventually they got me out, passing me in a chain from one fireman to another. I got out just after 11, and was the last child to come out alive. Tom Harding, the local grocer, threw me in his van with the cabbages and the carrots, and took me to St Tydfil's Hospital." David Davies was presumed dead and placed with other bodies before somebody noticed his foot moving "I was at my desk, quite close to the western side of the school that took the fullest impact. Almost immediately I was engulfed with debris and falling masonry, which knocked me unconscious. I'm told I was brought out and placed with the deceased bodies and covered with a blanket. Then someone thought they saw my foot move. I was evidently still alive and taken to hospital." "After having pneumonia, I almost stayed at home - but was determined to go in for the last day. I looked out of the window towards the tip and told my teacher I could see smoke. He said it was just steam from the canteen, which I thought was odd, because there was no canteen in the infants' school - that was in the senior school. But it was coming closer and closer. I put my head on the desk with my book over it - I don't know why, it was just instinct. The next thing I knew, I woke up and I was under coal, soil and muck. When I tried to breathe, I just sucked water in, and I had coal waste over my face. There was lots of crying and screaming, then it went black again. When I woke up, there was silence, nobody crying, and the little boy next to me

title: Royals to visit Aberfan to mark 60 years since disaster
description: King Charles III, Queen Camilla and Prince William will join survivors and bereaved parents.
body: Wednesday marks 60 years since the disaster that killed 144 people King Charles III, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales will be among the visitors to Aberfan on Wednesday to mark 60 years since the coal waste tip collapse in the former mining village that killed 144 children and adults. A prayer and moment of silence will take place and a male voice choir formed after the disaster is set to perform. The royals will also join survivors, bereaved parents and other members of the community to mark the anniversary, who will share their personal reflections. On 21 October 1966, 116 children and 28 adults were killed when the colliery spoil tip collapsed and engulfed a primary school and surrounding houses. The King, Queen and Prince William will visit the Aberfan Memorial Garden, built on the site of the destroyed Pantglas school, as well as the community centre where they will meet retired emergency service workers who helped in the response. They will also look at an exhibition that shows the huge scale of the rescue effort, and spend time with former pupils at Pantglas school, siblings of those who died and members of the Aberfan Wives, a support group for mothers who lost children in the disaster. The village's Ynysowen Male Voice Choir, formed in the aftermath of the disaster, also became a support group for local men to share their experiences. Among those to speak are Jeff Edwards, who met the prime minister on Monday, and who was one of the last children to be brought out alive from the rubble. Prince William will visit Ynysowen Community Primary School - which was established to carry forward the legacy of Pantglas Junior School - to unveil an Aberfan Memorial Tree. King Charles III, Queen Camilla and Prince William will join survivors, bereaved parents and other members of the community Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Aberfan on Monday and described the disaster as one of the "most horrifying tragedies this country has ever seen", adding it was something he was told about by his parents as he was growing up. He addressed the issue of coal tip safety in Wales during his visit, saying it was of "critical importance" that the remaining tips in Wales are made safe. Burnham met with survivors of the tragedy, including former Pantglas pupil Irene Hollett, who said the anniversary was a difficult time but that it was important for her to speak about what happened. "A lot of stuff comes back to you. You feel grateful that you are still around 60 years on, but then you miss your friends and family that we lost at the time," she said. "You can feel a bit of guilt that you are still here." Queen Elizabeth II visited Aberfan days after the disaster The royal visit comes after Queen Elizabeth II reportedly described her response to the Aberfan disaster as one of the biggest regrets of her 70-year reign. While Prince Philip, Lord Snowdon and the then Prime Minister Harold Wilson visited the scene the following day, the Queen waited eight days before going to the village, arriving to comfort the community shortly after a mass funeral had taken place. Years later the Queen's former private secretary, the late Lord Charteris, said he felt he had given her poor advice and that it was the biggest regret of her reign. But she returned several times, and whenever she was in the area, her thoughts would turn to Aberfan. In a personal message read to the community by the then Prince Charles on the disaster's 50th anniversary, the late queen spoke of a fondness for the people of Aberfan, saying she was "deeply impressed by the remarkable fortitude, dignity and indomitable spirit that characterises the people of this village and the surrounding valleys". title: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
description: Ukraine had accused the US of withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by Washington.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now" Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff. The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed. Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link. A US official later described the talks as "very productive and constructive", saying there was a "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps". The official confirmed that Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin in Russia tomorrow to discuss the proposals and that Kushner will again participate virtually. Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions". Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine". Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran. Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war". Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro. Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC Trump envoy Witkoff (L) joined Finnish President Stubb (C) and Zelensky (R) before their talks in Oslo Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now". "Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said. He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia. Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink. Last week, a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine. And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war. "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said. The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved. Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally. European leaders meanwhile have expressed concern about recent US statements from the US towards Russia. On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly". "It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV. Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy". "We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said. title: Carrick wants more clean sheets to turn season around
description: Manchester United boss Michael Carrick needs more clean sheets as he looks to change his team's fortunes, as they take on Como in the Champions League.
body: Michael Carrick after Manchester United's 1-1 draw at Leeds "You're dead right. I can't argue with that." Michael Carrick's response was to the point. The question that prompted it in his pre-match news conference at a rain-lashed Giuseppe Sinigaglia stadium in Como concerned his side's failure to keep clean sheets. It was put to Carrick that it would help if United could manage some shutouts, and he was asked if he had figured out the problem. United have kept the opposition out just once in 10 games this season, against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK last month. "There's definitely parts of our game we have to improve to make things easier. I am fully aware of that," said Carrick, whose side take on Como in the Champions League on Wednesday. The problem goes further than this season though. They managed six clean sheets in Carrick's 17 matches in charge last term, including two in their final three games. Prior to that they had only managed two all season, part of an overall tally of nine in 63 games under his predecessor Ruben Amorim. It is an extreme comparison given solid defence was the bedrock of Arsenal's Premier League title triumph, but the Gunners, who face Bayern Munich in Germany on Wednesday, have recorded seven clean sheets in 11 matches this season. Fulham's Josh King celebrates Lisandro Martinez's own goal at Craven Cottage on 20 September Continuity of selection would presumably help Carrick achieve defensive stability. It has proved virtually elusive so far. Only once has Carrick been able to name the same back four, when Diogo Dalot, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Luke Shaw started the victory against Ipswich at Old Trafford on 30 August and kept their places for the trip to Everton the following week. Carrick described his fitness update before the Como encounter as "a mixed bag". That was largely based on him saying Netherlands defender Matthijs de Ligt was "fit and ready" after 11 months on the sidelines with the back injury that required surgery in May. Yet De Ligt was on the bench at Leeds on Sunday when Martinez went off with the thigh injury that prevented him travelling to Italy, and instead Carrick turned to Noussair Mazraoui, usually a full-back, for the central slot. United's defensive resources are stretched thinner as Leny Yoro is ruled out through suspension. Shaw is still not fit and is expected to be out for "a little bit longer" than the 10 days Kobbie Mainoo is going to miss, which could mean the left-back won't return until after the November international break. Diogo Dalot became the fifth different player to start for Manchester United at left-back this season at Leeds - and Harry Amass could become the sixth To many observers, the Manchester United left-back situation was one that could have been anticipated and should have been addressed in the summer. The fact United spoke to Manchester City about Algeria international Rayan Ait-Nouri on deadline day suggests they did view it as a potential issue. After starting all 38 Premier League games last term and the first three this, Shaw has played only twice since, and the number of games missed could reach double figures before the 31-year-old returns. When Diogo Dalot lined up at left-back against Leeds, he became the fifth different player to start there for United in six games. Aside from Shaw, none of the quintet could be regarded as a natural left-back. However, after it was suggested Martinez's post-match outburst following the defeat by Atletico Madrid was partly down to 20-year-old Ayden Heaven playing at left-back, sources did point out the youngster played more often in that role than in the centre during his youth days at Arsenal. It was also suggested in the summer that United's coaching team did not believe 19-year-old Harry Amass, who was Shaw's stand-in during pre-season, was yet at the right level. Amass' single appearance so far this season, as a substitute for the final 18 minutes against Sabah, backs up that view, although Carrick has countered it. "He's right in contention," Carrick said. "At some point, young players need an opportunity. It's just finding the right time. "Sometimes it's because there's an unfortunate thing happened to somebody else. Sometimes it's just you're doing so well we have to give you a chance. "All the young players are in a similar boat. There's maybe four, five, or six of them trying to make that next step in terms of getting into the team and trying to start games, and Harry's definitely one of them." Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada (right), next to sporting director Jason Wilcox (second right) The failure to sign competition for Shaw is a stick that has been used to beat Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox. There is sympathy amid the agent fraternity for Wilcox, who was given a budget to work to that many in the game felt was inadequate to address United's needs. There is a theory that the £50m spent to acquire Andrey Santos from Chelsea should have been diverted elsewhere. With Santos sitting next to him as he spoke to the media on Tuesday, it was hardly a topic Carrick was going to engage with. "When we've got injuries at different stages, we can always look at what could have been done and where we could have improved," Carrick said. "I spoke to you about making the best of the transfer window in the situation we had. This man next to us [Santos] was a big part of that. I'm delighted to have him. "We had to make decisions in the summer. We did what we could do and made the best of it." title: Man, 26, charged with woman's murder
description: Lawrence Johnson has been charged with the murder of Alisha Samuels who died on Thursday.
body: Alisha Samuels was found dead after police responded to a "disturbance" in Newton Heath, Manchester A man has been charged with the murder of a woman who was stabbed to death in a street in Manchester. Lawrence Johnson, 26, of Dorking Avenue, has been charged with the murder of Alisha Samuels, also 26, and the attempted murder of a man following the incident on Thursday. He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Manchester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. Det Ch Insp Justin Bryant said officers were continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ms Samuels' death and to provide answers for her family. Police are still appealing for information. Det Ch Insp Bryant said: "I'd like to thank those that have called and supported our investigation thus far. Your reports are always taken seriously and prove vital to our work. "I urge others who may have information, no matter how small, to please come forward." title: Second Labour MP suspended over Covid loan repayments
description: Perran Moon, MP for Camborne and Redruth, voluntarily referred himself for investigation.
body: Perran Moon has referred himself to be investigated A second Labour MP, Perran Moon, has been suspended over Covid loan repayments, after voluntarily referring himself for investigation. Moon, the MP for Camborne and Redruth, is listed on Companies House as the co-director of a training company called Autoswot, external, which last filed accounts in June 2021. Government Bounce Back Loans of up to £50,000 were made available to support small businesses during the pandemic, but a government report found the scheme was vulnerable to fraud and error. In August, Labour MP Bayo Alaba was suspended after queries about a Covid-era loan, and a third MP, James McMurdock, quit Reform in 2025 after questions about eligibility for loans he received. Bounce back loans worth a total of £46bn were issued when the scheme was launched in May 2020, making it the biggest of the government's pandemic-era loan schemes. Each one had a 100% government guarantee, meaning taxpayers' cash was used to pay back banks if the companies failed, but the Covid counter-fraud commissioner later found total fraud and error estimated at up to £2.8bn to the public purse. Autoswot had been set up in June 2019, a year before the loans became available, and at that time had forecast revenues of more than £200,000. Moon stressed he had applied for the maximum loan of £50,000 within the rules, regularly seeking professional advice about its obligations, and would provide documents to the Labour Party investigation into the matter. He said the loan was used to pay for "staffing and other essential business costs" during the pandemic and partial repayments were made until the company ceased trading in late 2022. The BBC understands that Moon was repeatedly assured in writing by Companies House that no accounts needed to be filed after the company applied to be struck off, but that guidance was incorrect. Moon, who was first elected in the 2024 Labour landslide following a career in communications and marketing, said the business folded due to unforeseen external market pressures and "despite the best efforts of staff". He said: "In order for these matters to be looked into, I have voluntarily referred myself to the Labour Party's investigations process and will cooperate fully with this process. "The loan application was made in good faith, and the information provided, including the company's turnover forecast, was accurate and properly based. "I will continue to work hard every day representing my constituents while this party process is ongoing." A Labour Party spokesperson confirmed Moon had referred himself for investigation. "The Labour Party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and we have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld," they said. "We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing." This is the second investigation the Labour Party has launched into the loans, with Alaba, the MP for Southend East and Rochford, also referring himself for investigation over loans made to a real estate company, Alaba Properties. At the time, Alaba said: "There has been no attempt to avoid my financial obligations, and I am wholeheartedly committed to ensuring that the liability is met in full." McMurdock, who now sits as an independent, was the first MP to be questioned over bounce back loans given to two fitness companies worth £70,000. In 2025 McMurdock said all his business dealings had been compliant with the rules, adding that after taking "specialist legal advice" he had decided "to continue my parliamentary career as an independent MP". title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
description: No formal investigation has started, but the regulator is making inquiries into the case.
body: The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City. The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September. No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case. It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than £900m. City are appealing the verdict. The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations. It routinely oversees accounting standards at bigger institutions such as listed public companies, but not football clubs. The FRC can look into the conduct of BDO, Manchester City's auditors, to ask whether the audit was in line with the rules. It can also apply sanctions to individuals such as directors or employees of the Etihad club, if they are members of professional accountancy bodies. BDO is the UK's fifth-biggest accounting firm, but claims to be a market leader in football, advising more Premier League and Championship clubs than any other firm. The independent commission which looked into Manchester City found that the club gave a "misleading impression" of the scheme used to disguise the origin of shareholder funds injected into the club to its auditors, who were "unaware" of the scheme. Manchester City have said they will appeal against the commission's decision, arguing that it contains "material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe". Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, called for greater powers for the FRC to look into similar cases. He wrote on X: "The regulator's letter exposes gaps in its ability to compel evidence from the club and pursue directors who fall outside its disciplinary rules. "This raises serious questions about the powers available to hold companies and directors to account. "The government has a responsibility to explain why reforms to close these gaps were abandoned - and what will now be done to strengthen accountability." title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
description: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.
body: Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country. Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!" But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner? The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all? Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship. Just listen to the way they talk about each other. "Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week. The verbal assault has continued this week. "Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history. Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously. In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister". "Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad." This video can not be played Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now" For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart. But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us." Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever. "We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday. But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship? In some ways, we've been here before. After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing. The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead. One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles. Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles. The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks. Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv. Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel. Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv. This video can not be played Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin. "What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks applied to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC. Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment". For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025. Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service. Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking. "We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News. title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
description: A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination.
body: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago. A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out. Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations. The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds. District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case". "Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order. The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri. In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12. However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing. The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help. The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue". Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022. If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line. title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
description: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
body: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies. The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August. The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers. The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses". The White House has been contacted for comment. Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border. Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry. "These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday. The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks. That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises". The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338. Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol. It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began. Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said. The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada. "The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said. The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection. It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year. Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear". title: Cornell Jane Doe says embattled university head doubted her gang-rape allegation
description: As a no-confidence vote looms, Cornell says the characterisation of the head's reaction is "incorrect".
body: Cornell's faculty debated the university's handling of sexual assault cases during a faculty senate meeting on Wednesday A former Cornell student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity house has said she felt "unsupported and disbelieved" by the university president. Known anonymously as Jane Doe, she has written a letter accusing President Michael Kotlikoff of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident. The Ivy League institution in upstate New York says her account of the Cornell head's reaction is "incorrect". She addressed her letter to campus faculty who will hold a rare vote this month on Kotlikoff's leadership. Doe filed her lawsuit last month alleging she was raped by several men in October 2024 at a Chi Phi fraternity party. All seven former fraternity members accused by Doe have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime. Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police, and the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but the case has since reopened. Responding to Doe's initial allegation, Cornell said it had opened an internal investigation, as well as a civil rights inquiry. What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation In a two-page letter dated 14 October and obtained by the BBC, Doe told the faculty senate that after she reported the alleged rape, she received "a second-hand account" of Kotlikoff's reaction and that his "initial response" was "along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'" Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on 8 November, about three weeks after the fraternity party. She noted that Kotlikoff had a conversation with the then-president of her sorority and that other staff members were present, at least one of whom "appeared distressed" by the college president's question. Doe said in her letter: "It diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school." She said she wrote the letter so that faculty "can make an informed choice" ahead of their 28 October vote on whether to express no confidence in Kotlikoff's leadership. The university confirmed receipt of the letter from Doe's lawyer. But in a statement to the BBC, a Cornell spokesperson said: "The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account." The spokesperson said Kotlikoff's question about the delay in reporting the alleged rape "was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024". "He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting," the spokesperson said. This video can not be played Watch: "I am Jane Doe" protests across US call for end to sexual violence Kotlikoff, who has led the Ithaca-based institution for 26 years, was grilled by the faculty senate last Wednesday. Staff said they were "deeply disturbed" by his handling of the case and accused him of lacking an "emotional response", according to recordings obtained by the BBC. Kotlikoff highlighted changes the university had introduced as a result of Doe's allegations, including banning fraternity parties. "We are all extraordinarily upset by the events at Cornell in October of 2024," he said. The faculty senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff at Cornell, scheduled their no-confidence vote for 28 October. In recordings of the meeting, faculty said sexual misconduct on campus was a systemic problem that demanded "systemic attention". Paul Ortiz, a labour history professor who sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said students had told faculty they "feel unsafe walking to the library after dark". He accused Cornell of treating rape "as more of a 'PR problem' than a heinous crime". title: Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says
description: The government is expected to accept all 27 recommendations made in the review by ex-Ofsted boss, Sir David Bell.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'It's a bit scary' - Jewish students explain classroom security measures Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it following a major review, the BBC understands. It means anti-Jewish hatred would be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying. The government-commissioned review into antisemitism in education is also expected to recommend dedicated training for teachers, more consistent recording and reporting of incidents, and better education about antisemitism and modern-day Jewish life. The BBC understands it will also call for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers. The review, led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell, is due to be presented to Parliament on Wednesday. The government is expected to accept all 27 recommendations. It was launched amid growing concern about antisemitism in the UK, following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed. Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBC Antisemitic incident reports rise by a fifth in first half of 2026 Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBC Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws. The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse. It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters. Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools. It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year. It jumped by 59%, from 112 reported incidents in the first half of 2025 to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026. The review is also expected to recommend that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism. Bell told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries." Students at Yavneh College in Hertfordshire speak to Judith Moritz about their security concerns Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism. Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role. "When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said. "We think about it a lot." Staff and pupils told the BBC they have become so used to these measures that they barely notice them anymore. Lock-in - or "in-vacuation" - drills for dealing with intruders have become second nature, even to the youngest pupils. "It's a bit scary sometimes, but you know you're safe," said Livi, a Year 6 pupil. "It's sad that we can't be equal to everyone else, but people don't like us just because of the way we are," added her classmate, Sadie. A group of a dozen older pupils who spoke to the BBC said that while they feel safe inside school, hearing about antisemitic attacks in the UK, including reports of pupils at other Jewish schools being harassed on their commute and at sports fixtures, has left them feeling targeted. Some said that they were reluctant to wear skullcaps or necklaces featuring the Star of David – a Jewish symbol – outside school. "Other religions get to be out and wear their necklaces and be proud - I don't get why Jewish people can't do it as much," said Year 9 pupil Ilan. In response to the recommendations, the government is also expected to encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory. The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities. However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial. The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism". In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability." He added: "We have advocated these measures be accompanied by other steps including improving education about Jewish life and ensuring schools maintain their duties in relation to political impartiality." Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations. The Department for Education has declined to comment before the review is published. title: Jane Dodds standing down as Welsh Liberal Democrats leader
description: Dodds said it was time to hand over the leadership to a "new generation" after nearly nine years in the role.
body: Jane Dodds has been a Senedd member since 2021 and became Welsh Lib Dem leader in 2017 Jane Dodds has announced she will stand down as leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats. Dodds said she would remain the party's only Member of the Senedd (MS), but that work to increase its presence in Wales' parliament "should be led by a new generation". "Leading the Welsh Liberal Democrats has been the honour of my life," she said in a statement on Tuesday, adding "now is the right time" to hand over the role. Only Welsh Lib Dem MP David Chadwick is eligible to seek nomination to replace Dodds at this stage, the party said. Relations between Dodds and the UK Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey were strained after he previously called her leadership into question. The Liberal Democrats have been represented by just one member in Cardiff Bay since 2016, initially by former Welsh Lib Dem leader Kirsty Williams and later by Dodds since 2021. Dodds, who represents Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd in the Senedd, is a former social worker who was made her party's Welsh leader in November 2017. She made headlines last year by getting the previous Welsh Labour government to agree to a greyhound racing ban and £1 bus fares for under-21s in return for helping it pass its budget. In 2024 Lib Dem leader Sir Ed asked Dodds to reflect on her position over her handling of a sexual abuse case when she worked for the Church in England. A 2021 report found Dodds made a "grave error of judgement" by not organising a meeting to discuss a particular case of abuse by a late former bishop who sexually abused at least 18 victims over a 15-year period. Dodds accepted there were "shortcomings", but said she would continue as leader. After nearly two years of cool relations over the matter, Davey backed Dodds before May's Welsh Parliament election, describing her as an "excellent member of the Senedd" who deserved to be re-elected. Nominations to replace Dodds will open on 23 October and close on 16 November. "After May's election, I've thought hard about what our party needs," she said. "Wales needs more than one liberal voice in the Senedd. "Building that team will take years of hard work in communities across the country, and I believe that work should be led by a new generation. "Now is the right time to hand it over." Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe MP Chadwick said Dodds had "given an enormous amount to the Welsh Liberal Democrats and to public life in Wales, and she deserves our sincere thanks for her service as leader". "There will understandably be questions about what comes next. "Today should be about Jane and her contribution to our party. "I will make a statement about my own political future in the coming days." Welsh Liberal Democrat president Tim Sly said Dodds had "led our party with warmth, determination and integrity through some of the most turbulent years in Welsh and UK politics". "She leaves the Welsh Liberal Democrats stronger in our communities and ready to build," he said. Chadwick requires the support of 50 party members to be the only candidate to replace Dodds and take over as leader. Should that not happen, or he were to decide not to run, all members on the party's approved parliamentary candidates list could then throw their hats into the ring. body: This video can not be played The Duke of Sussex has said he wants to "to work it out" and repair his relationship with his father and brother. Speaking to GQ Magazine in New York, external, Prince Harry also said: "With everything else that's going in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile". BBC culture and royal correspondent Noor Nanji breaks down what he said in the magazine interview and what it means for the royal family going forward. Read more about what the prince said here. title: Two re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident
description: The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing said they consider Iranian state involvement "highly likely".
body: Police officers were deployed to the area of the airbase in the days after the incident Two men have been re-arrested after an incident near RAF Fairford last month, counter-terrorism police have said. A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, are being held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, with police saying the investigation relates to Iran. Police had been alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the US airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September - a major incident was subsequently declared and dozens of homes evacuated. Seven men in total have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation. Gloucestershire Police said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on 27 September. A bomb disposal team was deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles. Petrol was found in three vans near the airbase and five men were arrested. They had been initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. Police later said they did not find "improvised explosive devices". The re-arrests announced on Tuesday relate to a 24-year-old man who was initially arrested on 27 September near the base and a 25-year-old who was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts days later on 1 October in the borough of Westminster. The other five men - who also include a 22-year-old British national arrested in Westminster on 6 October - remain on police bail. The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement. "Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it." The officer added that national security investigations can take time to progress due to their sensitive nature. "Our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation," he said. Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications" Iran had played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details at the time. Iran has previously denied any involvement. RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran. In the week after the incident, it emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America. US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details. Vice-President JD Vance said it was done out of an "abundance of caution". title: Farage vows to scrap tax on armed forces reserves
description: A large group of protesters turned up outside the Reform UK rally in Plymouth with Nigel Farage.
body: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage spoke at a rally in Plymouth The leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, has told a rally in Plymouth he would get rid of tax on pay for armed forces reservists. Farage said he wanted to get more people in the reserves at the event for party supporters as part of Reform's 100 Days to Save Britain tour. When questioned by the BBC over a Reform councillor in Plymouth who was investigated and cleared over social media posts, Farage said he was "still part of the party was because everyone believes he's a solid bloke". About 100 protesters against Reform gathered outside the Plymouth Arena near the city centre, chanting before, during and after the event. Reform leader Nigel Farage greeting supporters at the rally in Plymouth Farage spoke to about 300 Reform members and councillors and opened his speech by paying tribute to Ann Widdecombe, who was killed at her home in Devon. On cutting tax for reservists, he said: "Anyone that signs up as a reservist and does their bit will face no tax on the pay they receive. "Let's get more men and women signing up for the reserves." When asked by the BBC about the UK deploying fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, Farage said the UK was "not even a player any more". He said: "Should we help with peacekeeping missions? As much as we can. "But what we've got to face up to is the reality that we've lost our ability to be an effective player". More news stories for Devon Listen to the latest news for Devon Plymouth Reform councillor Ben Rowe was investigated in May after being accused of sharing Islamophobic posts on social media but was then cleared. The BBC asked Farage if Rowe's behaviour had been acceptable. He said: "These are working class people, going into politics, venting their spleen on certain issues and maybe there's a little bit of political growing up to do. "But let's not condemn everybody for everything they say, and the reason he's still part of the party is because everyone believes he's a solid bloke." Pretesters against the rally gathered outside Plymouth Arena Outside the event, amid a significant police presence, protesters gathered with placards and joined in chants saying Farage was not welcome in the city. Liam Condron-Farnos, from the campaign group Stand Up To Racism, said: "The way he's built his politics over the years, and still is, is on anti-immigrant hysteria. "We need to show him that's not an uncontested view in this country." Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external.
