title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
description: The long-awaited decision about the controversial North Sea field is expected on Wednesday morning.
body: The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North Sea The UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made. The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months. Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea. Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to issue any new oil and gas licences in the North Sea but to honour existing ones such as Jackdaw. Jackdaw, about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months. Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas. The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government. Licences for the fields were granted by the Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups. The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites. Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe. They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs. Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply. title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
description: A truck carrying people to a funeral and a market alleged to be supplying fuel to the RSF were targeted.
body: Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town has been treating people wounded in Monday's attack on the market Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral. The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said. A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF. The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011. South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border. A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan Drones hammer Sudan's gold and oil zone - the pivotal new front line Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict. The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes. "We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday, external. The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said. Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands. The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state. A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said. Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said. Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known. Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them. The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border. On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people. "It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying. BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks. It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market. "The market was completely destroyed. The bombing spread terror and fear among the local population," market trader Fadlallah Adam Hamouda told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily. Another trader told the BBC the attack had come as shock as UN peacekeepers have been in Abyei since 2011 - with more than 2,800 uniformed personnel currently deployed. "Our area is a weapons-free zone under United Nations protection, yet it was targeted by drones," he said. "The attack caused extensive material damage after the fuel market was struck, sparking a massive fire that spread to nearby homes." This screengrab is from a video taken 600m from Amiet Market Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes. On Monday, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town. "So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement. Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source. It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport. Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF. title: The Trip's Rob Brydon originally against playing fictional version of himself
description: Rob Brydon and Steve Coogan initially thought playing fictionalised versions of themselves was "passé".
body: The 61-year-old, renowned for his role as Uncle Bryn in Gavin and Stacey, stars alongside Steve Coogan in The Trip Actor and comedian Rob Brydon has said he was initially against the idea of playing a fictionalised version of himself in The Trip, but ended up enjoying it and thought it made viewers "more curious". The 61-year-old, known for his role as Uncle Bryn in Gavin and Stacey, stars alongside Steve Coogan in the comedy series as exaggerated versions of themselves. Directed by Michael Winterbottom, it follows the pair as they travel around the world and dine at different restaurants. Brydon said he and Coogan originally thought the idea was "a bit passé" but eventually concluded that Winterbottom was right to suggest it. Speaking ahead of the series' season five premiere in London, Brydon said despite his initial hesitation, he enjoyed playing a heightened version of himself. "When [director Michael Winterbottom] first suggested it, we were both against the idea of playing versions of ourselves," he said. "But in fact, as ever, Michael was right because it just gives the show... you're more curious about it. Is that how they really are?" Rob Brydon stars alongside Steve Coogan in The Trip, directed by Michael Winterbottom (centre) Brydon, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, is often seen engaging in competitive mimicry of famous actors, such as Michael Caine, Al Pacino and Hugh Grant, in the programme. "When we have a meal, it's not combative," Brydon said. "We don't do impressions to each other, or if we did, we would never argue over that. It's all just for comic effect. "But then there are other times when I suppose [our characters] are pretty close to us. "But you just do little tweaks and you do little extracts, so there'll be grains of truth. "We just exaggerate it until it becomes funny." The Trip has covered different locations since its first season in 2010, with the fifth series set in Scandinavia The Trip has covered different locations through the years, with its first season in 2010 set across north England, while other instalments have included Italy, Spain and Greece. The latest season, titled The Trip to the Northern Lights, is set in Scandinavia, as the duo move from Swedish hotels to remote Norwegian fishing huts while searching for the aurora borealis. Speaking of the weather conditions while filming, Brydon said "it wasn't that cold, apart from when we went into the Arctic Circle", adding that the scenes were "so breathtaking that you didn't mind the cold". Brydon previously said he and Coogan found themselves "stripped down" to their underwear "quite a lot" during filming, as the pair immersed themselves not only in dramatic scenery but also in Scandinavian traditions. "We also stripped down to our pants quite a lot," Brydon told The Times. "There were plenty of saunas and cold plunges in crystal Nordic waters," he said, describing it as "wonderful". A release date for The Trip to the Northern Lights is yet to be announced. title: 'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism
description: The Canadian province has voted overwhelmingly to remain part of Canada, though deep political divisions endure.
body: This video can not be played 'Conversation far from over': BBC reports from pro-separatist watch party Prime Minister Mark Carney says an overwhelming vote by people in Alberta to remain part of Canada is a "great result" for the country. Speaking to reporters as he walked into a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney said he was "thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity" by rejecting a proposal to pursue separation through a binding referendum. Preliminary results indicate more than two-thirds chose Canada over a push for independence for the province, according to Elections Alberta, external. Monday's referendum was the result of a months-long campaign by separatists in the western Canadian province to get a public vote on the issue. Provincial leader Danielle Smith welcomed the initial results, commenting: "Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada." Premier Smith herself opposed the separatist push but said the public will for a vote was undeniable, and many supporters of her own political party - United Conservative Party - were in the separatist camp. Smith said she would address Albertans later on Tuesday on the path forward for the province. In making the case for independence from Canada, many of the separatists said the oil-rich province's economic growth had been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa. But those who opposed a breakup - including Carney - called for Canada to present a united front in the face of external pressures, including an ongoing trade war with the United States. "They've chosen to build together," Carney said. "They've chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward, to move forward together, with purpose, high ambition." Carney added that he had spoken to Smith that morning and discussed "moving forward in the spirit of cooperative federalism, including on issues of immigration, other common priorities". Over the past year, the prime minister has worked with Smith on a number of shared goals, including pushing for an oil pipeline to the Pacific coast. Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat At a pro-separatist watch party in Edmonton, the hum of upbeat chatter quickly quieted as those present saw the projected results. After overnight vote projections were published by Canadian broadcaster CBC and others, the mood soured. The watch party attended by the BBC packed up quickly, and people went home. One of the separatist leaders, Jeffrey Rath, struck a defiant tone, however, vowing that "our movement isn't stopping and we're continuing to move forward". Speaking to the BBC World Service's Newsday programme, Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary, said he saw Monday's vote as a "first step" which had taught the movement some "valuable lessons". Asked whether his movement would push to keep holding votes on independence until it got the result it wanted, he responded "why not?", and insisted that "the math and the economics" all added up on his side of the argument. Separatist leader Jeffrey Rath was defiant even as results went against him Premier Scott Moe, from the province of Saskatchewan, said he was glad Albertans chose unity, but added that "there is still work to be done on improving how Western Canada is treated by Ottawa". Pierre Poilievre, the leader of Canada's Conservative party and a member of parliament from Alberta, said on social media that "the promise of Canada is worth fighting for". "Now our focus must be on results in people's lives: affordable food and homes, safe streets, strong borders, and less immigration," he said. Smith called the vote after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition seeking a binding referendum on separation. The petition was blocked by a judge, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations people - however, Smith opted to go ahead with the ballot. Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The key question on Monday's voting paper asked: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?" It's the first time a Canadian province has weighed the issue of separation since Quebec's two referendums, in 1980 in 1995. Both of those were unsuccessful, but Alberta separatists believe Quebec used the threat of independence to gain significant political leverage over Canada's central government. Smith said before the vote that if Albertans chose the remain option, a binding referendum on separation would not be held - at least, not while she was in power. Those who favoured remaining part of the Canada cheered the result at an event in Edmonton Despite the projected results, the conversation around Albertan sovereignty is not over. Separatists leaders have indicated that they plan to try and push Smith out of power within her United Conservative Party, in the hope of installing a leader who is more sympathetic to their cause. Another separatist leader, Mitch Sylvestre, told the BBC on polling day that "a lot of work will have to be done" to curb the appetite for independence if his side did lose. Although responses to the referendum question were tallied first, there were nine other non-binding questions on Monday's ballot paper. Five of these dealt with immigration, while the other four focused on the Canadian constitution. Early results suggest that most will pass, including proposals for the province to take increased control over immigration levels. title: Webb backs VAR over Botman challenge on Jackson
description: Premier League referees' chief Howard Webb says Sven Botman's challenge on Nicolas Jackson was a "high-end reckless challenge" but backed the video assistant referee's decision not to intervene for a red card.
body: Sven Botman picked up his second yellow card of the season for the foul on Nicolas Jackson Premier League referees' chief Howard Webb says Sven Botman's foul on Nicolas Jackson was a "high-end reckless challenge" but backed the video assistant referee's decision not to intervene for a red card. Botman was shown a yellow card - the correct sanction for a reckless tackle - by referee Jarred Gillett for the Newcastle centre-back's 18th minute challenge on Villa striker Nicolas Jackson on Saturday. The Dutch defender went in strongly and over the top of the ball, though contact on the opponent was with his trailing leg. "I think it's reckless," Gillett said of the challenge. "Even though you get a touch on the ball, it's still reckless." The VAR, Stuart Attwell, decided to support the on-field call of a caution because there was "no secondary scissor action" and contact was "not with the studs". "I know the referee said yellow card but it was so high and hopefully maybe next time a red card, but it was a yellow," Jackson said after the game. "I nearly broke my leg, but anyway, it's part of football." Webb says the on-field decision would have remained whether Gillett showed a yellow or a red card. Villa won the game 1-0 through a 36th-minute Johan Manzambi goal. This video can not be played Manzambi goal gifts Aston Villa win against Newcastle On Match Officials Mic'd Up, Webb said that "robust tackling" is "part of the English game" but that referee still had "a responsibility to ensure players' safety". "The referee in the moment, on the ground, sees it as a reckless challenge - no doubt a high-end reckless challenge - as Botman comes in and gets a touch on the ball," Webb said. "There's obviously some speed he comes in with. The VAR looks at that decision and tries to identify whether that was clearly wrong. "We don't want the referee's decision to be re-refereed by the VAR. We want the referee to have ownership of the decision and the VAR to only step in when there's an element that's clearly wrong. "So if the VAR had seen strong stud contact from Botman's extended leg into the ankle or shin of Jackson, or there had been a closing of the scissor, I think we'd have probably come out with a different outcome after the VAR had looked at it. "But he doesn't see that. He realises it's subjective, and he allows it to stay on the field with the referee's call standing. "Equally, if that had been a red card, for sure it would've been check complete by the VAR as well. "So, it's a good example really of how the referee's call is working in the Premier League this season. "A lighter-touch approach: let the referees referee the decision and the VAR step in when there's something clearly really wrong." After seven rounds of Premier League games there have been 21 VAR interventions, with nine of those subjective. At the same point last season, there had been only three, with zero subjective. However, mistakes are markedly down relative to the number of interventions. This season, the Premier League Key Match Incidents Panel has judged one VAR intervention was wrong - Man City's offside winning goal at Man United - with one missed to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa. Last season, there had been four errors for missed interventions after seven rounds. title: Teenagers tell BBC of their hopes and fears as they prepare to start work
description: Follow four students from Newcastle as they try out roles for the first time as part of their work experience placements.
body: This video can not be played More than four in 10 UK teenagers want more work experience opportunities at school, with a similar proportion calling for more guidance on how to apply for jobs, a survey for the BBC suggests. The online survey, by Survation, external, asked 2,000 young people aged 13 to 18 about the world of work and the help they need to secure employment once they leave full-time education. As part of the Teen Summit project by Radio 5 Live and BBC Bitesize, we followed four students from Newcastle - Param, McKenzie, Jasmine and Javaris - as they tried out roles for the first time as part of their work experience placements. title: Bavuma epic drags SA back into Test - do they have time to beat Australia?
description: Captain Temba Bavuma drags South Africa back into their Test series against Australia but did his side bat on too long on day three?
body: Bavuma bettered his previous high score of 172 Second Test, Gqeberha (day three of five) South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81 Australia 3-1: Boland 2*; Rabada 1-0 Australia trail by 422 runs Captain Temba Bavuma dragged South Africa back into their Test series against Australia with a masterful 179 on day three in Gqeberha. Bavuma, who emerged in the gloom at 12-2 on day one, batted for 552 minutes across three days in making his highest Test score, allowing the Proteas to declare on 425-9 with half an hour to play having been 110-6 earlier on day three. Kagiso Rabada nicked off Australia opener Nic Maddinson in the first over of Australia's reply to further boost the hosts' cause. Bavuma's knock was every bit as impressive as Matthew Renshaw's 190 for Australia in their first Test win - arguably more so given the momentum that had built behind Australia since South Africa's batting struggles and the quality of the tourists' attack. He remained composed in sharing partnerships of 132 with Marco Jansen and 183 with number nine Simon Harmer - the best eighth-wicket partnership in South Africa's Test history. The century was Bavuma's fifth in Tests - 10 years after his first made him the first Black African to score a Test hundred for the Proteas. He said it was "definitely" one of his best innings. "That bowling attack, at least three are in the top 10 of the bowling rankings," he added. "There is a reason why." More relevant for this series and England's tour to come over Christmas, it was Bavuma's fourth century in 14 Tests as South Africa captain. He now averages 54.36 as Test skipper, compared with 34.53 across 93 innings before taking the reins. Few can match that improvement. It was Bavuma's dismissal - caught behind off Mitchell Starc - which triggered South Africa's decision to declare with half an hour to go in the day. They had resisted doing so earlier in the session and when Harmer was bowled by Marnus Labuschagne a ball before the Bavuma wicket. With the floodlights on and skies dark, conditions were perfect for seam bowling when Australia's reply began. Maddinson was only able to resist four deliveries before nicking to third slip. The umpires then deemed the light too poor for seam bowling to continue, however, and after three overs of spin with the new ball the players left the field. Had South Africa declared earlier, Jansen could have bowled in tandem with Rabada in the gloom. "There was thought of that," Bavuma said. "I was a little hesitant because of the weather. "If we [had declared] a bit early we would have got one or two more overs. Saying that we got the one we wanted. "Right now I hope things go our way and we set ourselves to be on the field for the majority of those two days." After only 42 overs were possible across the first two days, South Africa now have an outside shot at victory over days four and five, ideally by dismissing Australia cheaply and enforcing the follow-on. "We have given ourselves a chance," Bavuma said. "There is the other side of the draw but going into [the third Test in] Cape Town whatever the confidence we can get here, being able to put their bowlers on their feet for a considerable amount of time, hopefully that can pay off in the long run." title: Who is Chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
description: The softly-spoken former defence secretary is gearing up for the biggest moment of his long political career.
body: Andy Burnham's decision to appoint John Healey to the crucial role of chancellor of the exchequer was the rarest of things at Westminster - a genuine surprise. It's not that the 66-year-old lacked experience or credibility - just that he had not been seen as a likely contender, with all the speculation about who would replace Rachel Reeves centring on more high-profile figures. Healey had flown under the radar since his explosive resignation as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June this year. His assessment of the government's defence investment plan - that it fell "well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time" - was devastating and undoubtedly hastened Sir Keir's departure from Downing Street. But his resignation letter also included pointed criticism of Reeves's Treasury, which he said had been "unwilling" to "commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats". Now he is in the Treasury hot seat and under pressure to spell out how he will get defence spending up to 3% of national income, at the same time as cutting government borrowing costs and tackling the cost of living. Like his predecessor, he faces the difficult balancing act of keeping Labour MPs happy without spooking the financial markets, while delivering on the government's key priorities. Never the flashiest of politicians, his early speeches as chancellor have been focused on stressing his commitment to fiscal discipline and cutting the welfare bill, as well as banging the drum for Burnham's plan to "reindustrialise" Britain. But he did show his lighter side in a social media video with the prime minister, which saw "Andy and John" bantering about twiglets and scampi fries in the pub., external "I will always stand by my political choices as chancellor, including pork scratchings as the best pub snack," he revealed on X. What is the Budget and what could be in it? Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor The softly-spoken Yorkshireman has a remarkable record as someone who has been on the Labour frontbench almost continuously since 2001. Born in Wakefield in 1960 and educated at Lady Lumley's Comprehensive School, Pickering, and Peter's School in York, he studied social and political science at Christ's College, Cambridge. Before entering politics, he worked as a journalist, briefly editing Parliament's in-house magazine The House, before becoming a disability rights campaigner and trade union official. He is married and has one son. He first came into Parliament in Tony Blair's landslide general election in 1997 as MP for Wentworth, a former mining area north of Sheffield, which following boundary changes is now Rawmarsh and Conisbrough. He retained the seat with a majority of 6,908 in the 2024 general election, with a Reform UK candidate in second place. In the early 2000s, he held a string of ministerial posts, including housing, local government in the Blair and Gordon Brown governments. He spent five years at Brown's Treasury where he oversaw policies such as the child trust funds and attempts to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government. Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson earlier this month, Healey said: "The Treasury's a paradox. You have some of the very best and brightest officials in the Treasury, but you have too often a Treasury orthodox that's a dead hand on dynamic government." He added that maintaining financial stability was a key function of the Treasury but "also it can and it has to drive economic growth, raise levels of productivity, support business competition, investment for the for the future". And he claimed the department "was in denial about the commitment that the UK has rightly made to NATO and to our people" to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, which would not come until 2034/35 under current plans. "The Treasury still often sees defence as a drain on public spending and not the driver of economic growth that we've demonstrated in two years," he told Nick Robinson. Healey's other area of expertise is housing. He served as shadow housing secretary when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader, despite supporting a failed attempt to oust Corbyn in 2016. Pundits had not touted Healey (right, dressed in a suit) as a frontrunner for the chancellor job When Sir Keir was elected Labour leader in 2020, he made Healey shadow defence secretary, becoming defence secretary when Labour came to power four years later. Healey was a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and made several trips to the country to meet President Zelensky. At his first meeting with Nato allies, in September 2024, he said he was "confident" Labour could honour a commitment to increase defence spending and "make the decisions that allow us to set out a long-term plan to make our forces better equipped to fight and to deter the threats we face". Healey also drove investment in housing for armed forces families, with a £9bn spending plan. Despite his low key style, he proved capable of delivering stern warnings to the UK's enemies. In April this year, he delivered a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, in a briefing on "covert" operations by Russian sumbmarines, saying: "We see you. "We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences." Following the announcement of the defence investment plan, he condemned what he called "Treasury trickery" and the lack of clarity on what new money the Ministry of Defence would get. title: Sloppy England start winter with Pakistan defeat
description: England begin their wandering winter with a sloppy loss to Pakistan in the one-day tri-series in Rawalpindi.
body: Pakistan have won their first two matches in the tri-series, while England next play Sri Lanka on Thursday Pakistan 302-9 (50 overs): Baker 3-65; Nawaz 79 (74), Arafat 59 (58) England 215 (38.4 overs): Banton 57 (53), Arafat 6-40 Pakistan won by 87 runs England began their wandering winter with a sloppy loss to Pakistan in the one-day tri-series in Rawalpindi. In the opening match of five separate tours to four different countries on three continents, England's mistakes opened the door for Pakistan's Arafat Minhas to take advantage. The all-rounder made a crucial 59 with the bat, then bamboozled England by taking 6-40 with his left-arm spin. Asked to bat, Pakistan were 190-5 in the 37th over when diving wicketkeeper Jordan Cox put down Arafat on 12, one of three catches England dropped. Arafat, alongside a powerful 79 from Hasan Nawaz, lifted Pakistan to 302-9. Faced with making the second-highest score to win an ODI at the Rawalpindi Stadium, England made a rapid start to the chase, only for further errors to let Pakistan back in. At 91-0, Ben Duckett top-edged a pull to depart for 45 and, crucially, Tom Banton was caught for 57 when he shovelled Arafat's long hop to mid-wicket. Arafat's fine all-round performance continued with a beautiful delivery to bowl England captain Harry Brook for five and Naseem Shah got one to keep low to bowl Joe Root for 33. When Cox was lbw and Jamie Overton holed out, both off Arafat, England were floored. They spluttered to 215 all out, losing their last seven wickets for 50 runs, capped by a calamitous run out of Gus Atkinson. Pakistan have two wins from two in the tri-series and are already on the brink of the final, while England next meet Sri Lanka at the same ground on Thursday, with both sides looking for their first victory. Not only is this the beginning of England's winter – two trips to Australia and Test tours of South Africa and Bangladesh follow – but also the start of a long run-in to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year. This was the first of a potential 21 ODIs in preparation for the World Cup, the tri-series format designed to replicate the pressure and permutations of tournament cricket. In fairness to England, they have improved in ODI cricket - winning their three previous series this year - and they were without three first-choice players in Jos Buttler, Jofra Archer and Jacob Bethell. Nevertheless, this was a game they could have won had they not wasted their opportunities, while squad players missed chances to press their case. Cox dropped two catches behind the stumps, Sonny Baker was expensive with the new ball and Banton squandered the platform to make a huge score at the top of the order. The outcome was a defeat in their first ODI in Pakistan since 2005 and a loss in their first taste of tri-series ODI cricket since 2015. To focus on England's shortcomings would be a disservice to Pakistan, who are a vastly different proposition in this format on home soil to the team soundly beaten in the Test series in the UK last month. From 133-5 in the 28th over, the hosts could have wilted, yet Nawaz's slog-sweep for six from the first ball he faced from Adil Rashid was the beginning of Pakistan's fightback. Along with Arafat and Faheem Ashraf, Nawaz carried Pakistan to what seemed no more than a competitive total on a flat pitch. When night fell, Arafat produced his magical spell to the delight of a noisy full house. He produced the best figures by a Pakistan spinner in an ODI against England, then Arafat also ran out Atkinson to complete the hosts' win. Bavuma epic drags SA back into Test - have they time to beat Australia? England coach should be English, suggests Fleming How one rule change is altering the face of one-day cricket Arafat Minhas returned the best figures by a Pakistan spinner in an ODI against England This was a good test for England's batting, not unlike the kind of chase they can expect to face at the World Cup, albeit in different conditions. Much like when they were tasked with overhauling 325 to beat Sri Lanka at Headingley in an ODI less than a month ago, they fell short. Banton made a century in that series but knows the injured Bethell will be back for the tour of Australia next month. Another hundred would have made the selection decision difficult, explaining Banton's obvious disappointment when he somehow belted Arafat to Shaheen Afridi. Cox will have a run in the ODI side because Buttler is out until at least the new year and the Essex man will also have an eye on securing a place in the Test team in South Africa. At number six, Cox had the opportunity to make amends for his two drops, yet he was deceived by the wily Arafat to be lbw for 18. In between, England lost their biggest wickets. Brook was all at sea in missing a beautiful turning delivery from Arafat, Root was arguably unlucky to be bowled by Naseem and Sam Curran, playing for the first time since The Hundred, shovelled to deep square leg. When Curran departed for 27, England were 177-5 midway through the 32nd over and the game was beginning to slip away. What followed was Arafat singled-handedly ripping through the lower order. Cox was done in the flight to be leg before, Overton was caught at long-on and Will Jacks, so often England's saviour in white-ball cricket, found the hands of mid-wicket. Rashid was palpably leg before and the mix-up between Baker and Atkinson that resulted in the latter face down on the turf epitomised England's collapse. It was another chapter in England's long history of capitulating to spin on the sub-continent. England captain Harry Brook: "We were quite happy with 300. We thought they were slightly under par. It got dewy as we thought it would do. We were pretty happy at halfway." On not pushing on after a strong opening partnership: "That was the story of the innings. title: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
description: Janine Lochrenberg, 65, was out on her daily morning swim with her club when she was attacked, her family tell the BBC.
body: Janine Lochrenberg had "a deep affinity with the water" her sister told the BBC A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year. Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked. Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore. Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File. Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water. She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time. Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water. She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London". "She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said. Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave. "She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life." Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together. Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed. title: Allen considers retirement after NI Open exit
description: Mark Allen says that retiring from snooker is "something I have been contemplating for a while" following his 4-2 loss to Jordan Brown in the Northern Ireland Open.
body: This video can not be played Emotional Allen contemplates retirement following NI Open exit An emotional Mark Allen said retiring from snooker is "something I have been contemplating for a while" following his first-round loss to Jordan Brown in the Northern Ireland Open. Allen was beaten 4-2 by fellow Antrim man Brown in his first event since losing to Wu Yize in heartbreaking fashion during the semi-finals of the World Championship in Sheffield in May. The former world number one said showing up to play his match against Brown was an "achievement" after a "really difficult" period in his life while he took a break from competitive action. "I think if I hadn't have been playing Jordan, I probably would not have played," Allen told BBC Sport NI after his defeat at the Waterfront Hall in Belfast. "I felt like I did not want my last match to be remembered for that semi-final in Sheffield. "I thought it would be a bit of nostalgia to go out playing Jordan in the Waterfront where it all started in 2005 and that would be a more fitting end if I do call it a day." Asked if he is considering drawing the curtain on his career, he replied: "Yeah." Speaking earlier to TNT Sports, Allen said he was in a "bad place at the minute", adding he does not "see a future with snooker in it". Allen exits NI Open with Brown loss on return The 40-year-old has had a decorated career, winning 12 ranking tournaments including the 2022 UK Championship since he turned professional in 2005. This year has been a challenging one for Allen, after he missed a match-winning black in the semi-final against Wu in May during the penultimate frame that would have taken him into his first World Championship final. Allen went on to lose the final frame against eventual champion Wu and has since been a notable absentee from the World Snooker Tour circuit. "The last three months have been really, really difficult and I think even just being here today is an achievement," added Allen. "For me, today was not about the result or the performance, it was trying to enjoy the experience of playing one of my best mates in one of my favourite arenas, in one of my favourite tournaments. "I am not going to announce [retirement] right now after a defeat, but it is something I have been contemplating for a while and something needs to change within the next six weeks before the UK Championship for me to show up. "And I need to work hard on myself in the next few weeks and see what is around the corner." Jordan Brown said he hopes to see Mark Allen remain in snooker Allen received a warm response from his home crowd as he returned to the venue where he became back-to-back champion in 2021 and 2022. It was clear the respect that both players had for each other following the match with Allen adding he "wished Jordan well, I always do". The world number 65 said the win was "the least satisfying" he has ever had as he progressed to the last 32 to face Michael Holt. "It is overwhelming for Mark here with his family, friends and all the fans who have paid good money to see him play," said Brown. "It is very difficult. I have my own battles to go through. I am in a precarious place in the rankings, and I lost my mum recently. It just puts everything into perspective. "The general public seem to think we are just robots who just turn up to pot a few balls - it is not like that at all." Matches between Brown and Allen have always been close contests, with Tuesday's win the 39-year-old's first victory over his close friend. "I really hope so," Brown replied when asked if he thought Allen would reconsider retiring. "The first words I said to him today was it was great to see him back and we had a big cuddle. It is tough to see him going through that. "I have no doubt he will come back. Snooker is his love, he is absolutely brilliant and he is a top bloke. I wish him all the best." title: Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family
description: Prince Harry says he wants reconciliation with his family, in an interview with a magazine in New York last month.
body: Prince Harry carried out visits in Nottingham last week The Duke of Sussex has said he wants to repair his complicated relationships with his father and brother, in a magazine interview. "Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point," Prince Harry told GQ in New York. "Scars stick around forever. But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, letting go of the past, that's something that I would encourage everybody to do," said Prince Harry. Last week Prince Harry and Meghan carried out their first public engagement together since their return to the UK in the summer. The GQ interview with Prince Harry was conducted last month and released as the Royal Family were on duty in Windsor welcoming the Sultan of Oman at the start of a state visit. But a spokesman for the Sussexes said the interview was recorded in late September and it was the entirely the publishers' decision when to run it - and that nothing should be read into the timing. The spokesman also said that the reference to "some people don't want it to work out" was not a swipe at his brother Prince William or any other member of his family. Prince Harry and Meghan moved from the UK to the United States in 2020, stepping down as working royals in what was an acrimonious departure. Harry's memoir, Spare, showed the depth of the family fall out and the damaged relationship with his brother William. Despite Prince Harry now being physically nearer to his family in the UK, there hasn't seemed to be any more emotional closeness with his brother Prince William, and in this interview Harry seems to be open to reconciliation. It was a message of wanting to build bridges that he had previously sent in a BBC interview in May 2025, when he had been living in the US. Prince Harry recognised that this royal story of family disagreements fascinated the public, saying it was "massively relatable". "Sibling disagreements, broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent - that continues to come up with me the whole time with people that I speak to," he said. Asked by GQ about the reason for his move back to the UK, Prince Harry said: "Opportunities for the family. Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn't know how important it was to me." "They [Archie and Lilibet] are loving it, and it's just giving them a whole different experience." He told the magazine: "To be back, closer to my family, and to be back on UK soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there". The Duke and Duchess of Sussex - seen here on their recent public appearance in Nottingham - returned to the UK in August Prince Harry also reflects on the King's health, following his treatment for cancer, saying: "He's getting better". There were also comments about growing up with a sense of loss after the death of his mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1997. "I love the fact that I'm able to now sort of carry the memory of my mother with me, with my work, rather than it hold me down, pull me back, or wallowing in that grief," he said. He rejected any sense of wanting public sympathy. "I certainly don't want any sympathy. That's where we're way past that. Why? Because I'm a prince. I've got a support network around me, I've done different forms of therapy, and I put in the work. I wonder where I would be if I didn't - it could be a very different situation," he said. title: Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
description: The sixth report from Covid inquiry criticises the lack of PPE and the way patients were discharged from hospital.
body: Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said. The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time. There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022. The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes. It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves. Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit. Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said. Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire". "At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said. "The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals." Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says Covid inquiry PPE report - key findings At the start of the pandemic, the then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock said the government had placed a protective ring around care homes. But the report said that this claim was unfounded. a lack of PPE meant staff had to resort to make-shift workarounds, including bins bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls the decision to discharge hospitals patients into care homes at the start of the pandemic was understandable, but guidance should have made clear they needed to be isolated. This did not happen in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which was a significant oversight a lack of financial support for care workers at the start of the pandemic made it difficult to allow them to stay away from their job if they were infected long-standing weakness in the care sector, including financial struggles and staff shortages, exacerbated problems by September 2020, evidence suggested care home visitors posed only a marginal infection risk, yet many care homes failed to ease restrictions in line with updated UK guidance, contributing to a significant decline in residents' health and wellbeing. there was evidence of blanket do-not-resuscitate orders being put in place in some care homes, which is considered unlawful millions of unpaid carers were left to take on evermore complex care and struggled because of a lack of support Jean Adamson, of the Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK, said: "Today's report is a devastating account of one of the darkest episodes in our country's history. "It shows that the government knew the care sector was extremely vulnerable to a pandemic and yet did nothing. Failing to act until it was too late." Caroline, Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said the report was "devastating". "When Covid took off, people using social care and the staff and unpaid carers providing it were left totally exposed." She added it also demonstrated how important the overhaul of social care promised by Andy Burnham when he became prime minister was. "If a national care service had already been in place... the various disasters that befell social care during the pandemic would have been lessened and some might have been avoided altogether." Meanwhile, Natalie Grayson, from the GMB union, said care workers were "left vulnerable and terribly exposed" during the pandemic which saw "care homes turned into morgues". "That cannot be allowed to happen again," she added. Nadra Ahmed, co-chair of the National Care Association, which represents care providers in England described the findings as "really upsetting", adding that the social care workforce has "never fully recovered" from the pandemic. She said we need to "start thinking about social care in a more constructive way" and the mantra that "we all had to protect the NHS" appears to have come at the cost of "some care home residents' lives". Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government would provide a "full response" to the report's recommendations "in due course". Speaking in the Commons, Cooper said she agreed that social care had been "undervalued and under-recognised" for too long. "My thoughts are with all those who lost loved ones in the pandemic, and especially those who endured the immense distress and harm of visiting restrictions in care homes, which meant they could not be with loved ones even as they died," she added. title: Inside Health
description: Experts warn poor at-home injecting techniques and new drugs mean new health risks.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·20 Oct 2026,·28 mins Available for over a year We investigate how self-injecting is leading to people being hospitalised and is creating new challenges for support services. Laura Foster meets NHS endocrinologist Dr Bonnie Grant, criminologist at the University of Lincoln Dr Luke Turnock and Jon Findlay, Harm Reduction Lead at Waythrough. They discuss the problems they are seeing from self-injecting on hospital wards, at needle exchanges and talked about in online discussions. Also this week, scientists have identified a protein that provides one of the strongest clues yet as to why two conditions that are major causes of stillbirth and severe health risks for pregnant mothers occur. It could be a breakthrough for predicting pre-eclampsia and foetal growth restriction and Laura talks to Dr Gordon Smith, head of the department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Cambridge University, about how they identified a little known protein and how the discovery could help millions of women every year. And there has been a lot of headlines around the idea that making medicines in space could improve cancer treatment. British company BioOrbit has just had a mini drugs factory return back from manufacturing crystrals for cancer antibody treatments on the International Space Station. We'll be asking whether this could be something that becomes part of day to day medicine in the not-too-distant future. Presenter: Laura Foster Producer: Tom Bonnett Editor: Martin Smith Sound engineer: Tim Heffer Production coordinator: Stu Laws The show was made by the BBC’s Audio Science Unit in collaboration with The Open University.

title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
description: She said in a Tuesday release of her Messy podcast that she was not happy about the new information and her symptoms have only "gotten worse".
body: Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis. The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out. "You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse." The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what is causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week. "I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said. In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted. During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS. Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she in fact did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking. "She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment. "I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy." Applegate with her Dead to Me costar Linda Cardellini, carrying a cane as she receives a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2022 Dr Marwa Kaisey, a guest on Tuesday's episode, said MS misdiagnoses are not uncommon because symptoms are inconsistent and there is no universal testing. One in five people people who were told they had MS "didn't actually have it". "It's not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says 'yes, you have it. No, you don't,'" Kaisey said. "It's a list of criteria." Applegate was first diagnosed with MS in August 2021, after experiencing symptoms for a while, saying at the time: "It's been a tough road. But as we all know, the road keeps on going." Years later, she described being in a "real depression" and said in a 2024 episode of her podcast that "I don't enjoy living. I don't enjoy it. I don't enjoy things anymore". She had said in a New York Times interview that she could not walk without a cane and used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix series Dead To Me. title: Katie Razzall: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed
description: The BBC announced it will close its BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels.
body: The BBC's announcement that it will close three of its linear broadcast channels - BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra - makes sense financially. BBC Three's most popular show on Monday night was a repeat of an old episode of Top Gear. Around 77,000 people tuned in. BBC Scotland's TV channel was watched, according to this year's annual report, by a weekly average of 12% of the Scottish population. Scots simply aren't tuning in in the numbers to make it cost-effective. (Interestingly, BBC Alba, which is aimed at Gaelic speakers and learners, reached 43% of Gaelic viewers in Scotland weekly - was it boosted by its rights to broadcast Italian football's Serie A?) It's hard to argue - although no doubt some will - that there is a business case for keeping BBC Scotland's TV channel open. The same goes for BBC Three, although the hokey cokey that has gone on with that channel - launched to fanfare in 2003, later made digital-only, then brought back to linear in 2022, now back online only again - has looked indecisive. Bizarre even. But the bigger picture is that viewers and listeners are already migrating online - increasingly finding the BBC's programmes not via those linear TV and radio channels but on iPlayer, BBC Sounds, and, more recently, YouTube. So that's the business case - and the BBC needs to save £500m over the next three years. That figure is concentrating minds. But axing the three linear channels is a drop in the ocean financially. I understand it will save less than £10m in total per year. BBC Three launched hits including Normal People, starring Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones Last year the BBC spent £42m creating content for BBC Scotland. It still plans to create many of those shows for iPlayer - and BBC Two in Scotland will be reconfigured to deliver Scotland-only programming. The part of BBC Three that commissions programmes will actually get more money to spend on creating content aimed specifically at 16-34s (with a core focus on the 16-25s). This was the network that commissioned Normal People, Fleabag, Killing Eve - programmes of quality and wide appeal. There's also been a recent announcement of commissions dreamt up specifically for YouTube - to reach those 16-24s who the BBC (and other public service broadcasters) find so difficult to lure to their own platforms. Many of Radio 4 Extra's programmes will also still be on BBC Sounds. If you listen to the Daily Service, first broadcast in 1928 and the longest-running programme of its kind anywhere in the world, you will still be able to find it. So these aren't major cost savings. The BBC would likely argue, when it comes to audiences, who are at the heart of everything, it is pivoting to find them where they already are. What's been announced today is more about the direction of travel. It's about the continuing evolution of the BBC, a streamlining as audience habits change. That doesn't mean it isn't painful to all of us inside the BBC. Job cuts are always difficult. In News, 100 more roles are being axed. That's on top of the 200 already announced. And the news division is still nowhere near its target of £51m of cuts. And with only two fifths of the £500m of total savings now announced, there is still a very long way to go. As a BBC user, you are going to hear much more about cuts in the coming months. Some will think that is a good thing as the BBC reflects the belt-tightening going on in most homes and companies across the UK. Others fear that the BBC's important role in public life is being chipped away. There is a bigger fight going on here. The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future - and how it will be paid for. It won't harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient. As long as it can also demonstrate that audiences aren't being left behind. title: Immersive Beatles museum described as 'like Graceland or Dollywood' to open in 2028
description: The surviving Beatles have welcomed plans for an immersive visitor experience in Liverpool.
body: Artist's impression of plans for a Yellow Submarine experience at St John's Beacon Sir Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr have backed plans for a major new Beatles visitor attraction in Liverpool. The development will see The Beatles Story move from Albert Dock to the former St John's Market site, alongside a new Yellow Submarine experience at St John's Beacon. McCartney said he "can't wait" for people to be able to "step into our story", while Starr said: "Liverpool was, and still is, Music City". The attraction will feature immersive technology, original artefacts and recreated sets charting the band's rise from post-war Liverpool to international fame. Apple Corps Ltd, which manages The Beatles' creative and business interests, will take over operation of The Beatles Story in 2027 ahead of its relocation the following year. The attraction has been based at Albert Dock since 1990. Under the plans, it would move to the former St John's Market Hall, vacant since the market closed in 2024. At 100,000 sq ft, the new site would be more than four times the size of the current attraction, while the former Radio City tower, St John's Beacon, would house a new Yellow Submarine experience. It follows plans unveiled earlier this year for an official Beatles attraction at 3 Savile Row in London, where the band staged their final public performance during a famous rooftop concert in 1969. Fans will be able to explore seven floors of memorabilia and archive material connected to the band when it opens in 2027. Announcing the Liverpool plans, Apple Corps chief executive Tom Greene said Liverpool was getting a Beatles destination worthy of the city's musical heritage. "Just like Graceland or Dollywood, it's fitting that The Beatles will have a world-class destination for fans to visit in the city where the story started," he said. Apple Corps said visitors would be taken on a journey from the band's post-war Liverpool roots through Hamburg, The Cavern, Beatlemania, Abbey Road, Shea Stadium, Savile Row and beyond. The attraction will tell The Beatles story using immersive technology, Apple Corps Ltd said Commenting on the announcement Sir Paul McCartney said: "I love Liverpool. It's part of who I am, it's part of who The Beatles are. "I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it's very exciting to me that The Beatles Story and The Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city. "It couldn't have happened without Liverpool and I can't wait for people to be able to step into our story and share the experience." Tickets sold for The Beatles Story will contribute to the The Apple Corps Liverpool Trust, a charitable initiative to provide support and opportunities for emerging local artists. Ringo Starr said: "Liverpool was, and still is, Music City. "And now we are expanding The Beatles Story Experience in Liverpool - how far out. The beat goes on. "I also love that proceeds from every ticket will go back to support new Liverpool artists. It is great to be part of this. Deep down I am still a scouser. I love what Apple Corps and Liverpool are doing." The plans will transform the former site of St Johns Market in the city centre The project is a partnership between Apple Corps, Liverpool City Council and Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, with support from central government. Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram said it felt right that the "definitive Beatles experience" should be located in the city where the band's story began. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "The Beatles are one of the greatest examples of what Britain can give to the world. "Four young men from Liverpool changed music and popular culture forever and, more than 60 years later, their story is still a source of enormous pride for this city and for our whole country." Reflecting on what his bandmates would have made of the plans, Sir Paul McCartney said: "If you'd told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started, we'd never have believed it." title: Union attacks NatWest plans to get workers back to the office
description: The bank says workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week from February.
body: The Unite union has hit out at a plan by NatWest to reduce the rights of 30,000 of its employees to work from home. NatWest says it is moving to a hybrid approach where workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week, from February. The bank says this is still very competitive with the rest of the finance industry, and exceptions will be made for colleagues who require additional flexibility. But Unite said NatWest's decision was "out of touch with the realities facing its workforce", with many facing higher travel and childcare costs. Firms have been gradually drawing people back into the office since working from home became the norm for some office workers during the Covid pandemic. In January last year, Amazon required staff to return to the office five days a week after they had been working two days at home. Other firms such as Boots and JP Morgan have brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day. But Barclays faced a backlash from staff last month over plans to require workers to go to the office three days a week. It brought in a longer transition period in response to staff and union complaints. Unite said NatWest was abolishing its "remote first" employment category, which allows 13,497 workers to attend the office around twice a month, and requiring 17,272 hybrid workers to increase their office attendance. The union says that many of the affected workers are lower-paid grades, and the new requirements will increase cost-of-living pressures, while disrupting the arrangements of disabled workers and carers. In a statement, Unite general secretary Sharon Graham called NatWest's move a "kick in the teeth" for its workers. "Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities," she said "For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce." Graham called on NatWest to "ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers". A NatWest spokesman said: "Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we've also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers - helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another. "That's why we're introducing a more consistent approach across the bank, with colleagues expected to spend at least two days a week in the office, depending on the needs of their role and business area. "We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we're giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition." title: Robinson shared photos of reporter's family, court told
description: The political activist is on trial after pleading not guilty to harassing two Daily Mail reporters.
body: Tommy Robinson is accused of harassing reporters after they posted photographs of him on holiday Political activist Tommy Robinson shared pictures of a journalist's family online and threatened to visit his home, a court has heard. In July last year, the 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, pleaded not guilty to two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. After three young girls were murdered in Southport in July 2024, Robinson posted on social media, which alerted the Daily Mail to the fact he was on holiday in Cyprus. The paper published articles of him "on a sunbed". Southwark Crown Court heard that photos of Young's wife and child were later shared to Robinson's social media followers. Prosecutor Ben Holt said the trial was about Robinson's reaction to the articles, and accused him of using "bully-boy tactics" to "intimidate" the journalists. In his statement read to the court, Young said someone who appeared to be a Robinson supporter leaked his home address on X. Later, a man who introduced himself as Robinson called him and became "increasingly menacing, swearing and shouting". Young added: "I believe he said the words 'I'm coming to get you'." The court heard that Young's family told him on 6 August about a grey Audi that had been parked outside earlier that day, with a man sitting inside. Young said: "It was clear to me that Tommy Robinson was following through on his threats." In the days following the publication of the article, the court heard that two men in a car shouted at Young's daughter, and she believed they photographed her. He said Robinson's actions caused his family an "undue amount of stress". Holt told the court that Dirnhuber, the other alleged victim, was scared to be in public after Robinson's alleged harassment. The journalist's witness statement told of the unrest in the days following the Southport attack in 2024. He claimed there was public interest in covering the "far-right agitation" online from figures such as Robinson that had led to riots across the country. Holt said that in August that year, Dirnhuber received a number of messages from Robinson and that eventually the journalist had to move house. In a statement read to the court on Tuesday, Dirnhuber said: "It made me scared to go out in public, it made me scared to go to my own house, it made me feel guilty about how it had affected my loved ones. "Even now, when I step out my front door, I'm aware I'm at risk of a vigilante attack. "I feel vulnerable. I feel I will be looking over my shoulder for a long time." title: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
description: The UK announces it will provide additional defensive military support to Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate in the region.
body: This video can not be played Watch: UK has 'responsibility to back allies and protect civilians', says defence secretary The UK will deploy RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi Arabia in response to escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, the government has said. The defensive mission will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure - a move authorised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham - against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group. It follows Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as on energy sites on the country's coast. "These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a written statement on Tuesday. An RAF Typhoon in flight (file image) The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and were ousted by the group from capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Since September, Saudi Arabia has been struggling to defend its skies from Houthi attacks after a ceasefire of sorts in Yemen broke down. The Houthis launched a fresh offensive against Yemen's officially recognised government and seized effective control of the crucial Bab al Mandab strait. Government forces - backed by Saudi aircover - mounted a counter offensive and the Houthis in turn struck targets deep in Saudi territory. The Houthis successfully hit Saudi infrastructure including the King Khalid airport, energy facilities and key ports. Saudi authorities said last week that 19 people had been killed in Houthi attacks on the kingdom's airports. One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. This video can not be played Footage from inside Riyadh airport on 10 October shows the moment the strike hit Houthis have been retaliating for strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa. More than 70 security personnel were killed earlier this week in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa. A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city. The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations". According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, Saudi air and artillery strikes have killed at least 141 people and injured 395 since 3 September. The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August. Saudi Arabia has struggled to bring down incoming missiles and drones because so much of its air defence capability was used up against Iranian attacks earlier this year. The sheer size of the country also makes it hard to provide comprehensive air defence. The UK warplanes will not only help Saudi Arabia defend its skies, but they will also free up the country's own aircraft to carry out offensives strikes against the Houthis. The UK will also deploy military advisers and an RAF A400M transport aircraft to support the movement of defence equipment within Saudi Arabia. It is already providing Saudi Arabia with defence support equipment to protect against aerial attacks and air-to-air refuelling for defensive Saudi operations. The refuelling has now been extended by 90 days. In a separate statement, Streeting said the targeting of Riyadh airport "shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region". "That's why today I have approved further UK military support," the defence secretary added. Streeting also pointed to violence in the Gulf disrupting energy supplies and increasing costs for families and businesses. Earlier this month, Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia". Who are the Houthis and what do they want?
