title: Zelensky and US envoys to hold Oslo talks as Rubio denies withholding intelligence
description: The US secretary of state rejects accusations Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence.
body: Zelensky met Finland's Alexander Stubb and Norway's Jonas Gahr Støre ahead of talks with Witkoff US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky are due to meet in Oslo, with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the meeting with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine". Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" and "outrageous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv. He was speaking after Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, told the BBC that the lack of reliable US warnings meant lives were being lost. "This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not." Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine". Zelensky first met the Norwegian prime minister and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, ahead of his planned talks in person with Witkoff, with Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner taking part via video link. Støre said the aim of the Oslo talks was to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace. The Ukrainian leader said earlier he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network. Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to the Starlink network in Ukraine, and unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors had not yet been approved. The US secretary of state is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally. Steve Witkoff was due to hold talks in Oslo in person while Jared Kushner was taking part remotely Zelensky was set to join his Norwegian and Finnish counterparts for a press conference after the talks, but Witkoff was not expected to join them, according to the government in Oslo, external. It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after his visit to Oslo, however the Kremlin spokesman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's special envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators". Earlier this month Russia's Vladimir Putin discussed the war with Trump over the phone, and afterwards the US president announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Trump's deal with the Russian leader coincided with Witkoff and Kushner's last meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami, and Zelensky reacted by calling it "a happy birthday present for Putin". Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have reached record highs at the pump since the start of the US-led war on Iran. European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly". He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden. "It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV. Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy". "We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too." title: Woman describes alleged assault by Russell Brand as 'frenzied' and 'violent'
description: The entertainer denies three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
body: Warning - this report contains graphic content A woman who claims Russell Brand sexually assaulted her has described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent". Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. On Tuesday, the jury heard from the fourth complainant in the trial, who alleges Brand sexually assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s. She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside. "He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury, "he grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me." The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on. "He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point." From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack. "His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me." The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him. She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault. The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth. She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck. "His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping." She said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken." You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts When questioned by Brand's barrister on why none of the people who may have seen what happened raised concerns, the woman said: "It was not the present-day environment." "On the day it happened - and I ask myself this question - why I didn't share it," she said. "It wasn't the culture where something happened to you and you tell people." Asked by the defence barrister why she did not go to the police, the woman said: "I would have thought about a few things. Who would have believed me? "I could lose my job and I had a mortgage to pay," she said, adding that she "buried it for so long". The woman said she came forward with the allegation after watching a documentary on television about the TV star and his alleged behaviour. Another complainant also gave evidence to the jury - again from behind a blue screen to the right side of the court. The woman who worked with Brand on a Channel 4 project in 2009, said members of the defendant's team asked her for a massage on his behalf while they were in the same space. She said after replying no, Brand "came into the room and lay his head into my lap, into my groin area". When asked by the prosecution counsel where exactly his mouth and nose were, the woman replied "in my vaginal area". The woman who worked for channel 4 at the time - said she was "so repulsed at the situation". She described him as "bony". She said she reported the alleged incident to her line manager at the time who then reported it further up the chain. Brand stared straight ahead as the witnesses gave evidence - barely changing his posture. His hands sometimes resting on his lap. His wife Laura Brand remained sitting to his right side outside the dock - seeming to listen attentively to what the women were saying from the witness box. Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual. title: Why O'Sullivan faces battle to stay in world's top 16
description: Snooker's World Championship without Ronnie O'Sullivan is hard to conceive, after years of him being so often the central figure at the Crucible. But it may not be far away.
body: Ronnie O'Sullivan last won the World Snooker Championship in 2022 A snooker World Championship without Ronnie O'Sullivan? The prospect seems almost unthinkable, with the 50-year-old a near ever present in the top 16 of the world rankings since he became a professional in 1992. However, the seven-time winner at the Crucible now faces a battle to maintain his place within the 16-man group guaranteed automatic entry to the World Championship. Already down at number 13 in the world rankings, O'Sullivan fell in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open on Monday and is in need of prize money that would solidify his place among the current world elite. Still seeking the eighth world title that would mean he surpasses former rival Stephen Hendry, O'Sullivan has said he would prefer to retire rather than ever enter qualifying events. With a challenging decision potentially looming, BBC Sport takes a look at how close one of the sport's greats is to leaving the game forever. O'Sullivan has had a quiet start to the 2026-27 season, with a run to the semi-finals of the Wuhan Open the only significant result in his five tournaments to date. Two last-16 finishes preceded his final-four finish at that event, but he has been defeated in the first round in his two subsequent appearances, in Shenzhen and Belfast. Having earned £513,750 at ranking events over two years, O'Sullivan is £99,350 ahead of Ali Carter, who holds 16th spot in the world rankings, and £154,650 clear of Zhou Yuelong, who sits in 17th, with winnings of £359,100. On first glance, that appears to be a comfortable cushion, with only a set of significant runs from his rivals putting him at risk of having to qualify for the World Championships in May next year. However, there are issues over the horizon, because over a third of O'Sullivan's winnings come from reaching the final of the Saudi Arabia Masters in August 2025. The £200,000 he won in Jeddah will continue to count towards his ranking past the 2027 World Championship, but that money will slip out of the eligibility period soon after the start of the 2027-28 season. O'Sullivan will also not be able to replace his earnings with another run at the event, after the tournament, which offered the highest prize money outside of UK-based competitions, was abolished in April. That means he is likely to need strong performances over the next 18 months to remain in contention for an automatic spot at the 2028 World Championship. O'Sullivan might improve his chances of earning ranking prize money by competing in more tournaments, having operated on a reduced schedule in recent years. It should be noted he has cited medical reasons or the need to prioritise his mental health for his withdrawals from several tournaments in recent years. He played predominantly in Asia in 2025-26, only competing in two tournaments in Britain - the UK Championship and World Championship. His appearance in Belfast this week was his first in a ranking event in the United Kingdom outside the Triple Crown events (Masters, World Championship, UK Championship) since the English Open in September 2024. His last ranking title came at the World Grand Prix in January of the same year. After his defeat in the semi-finals of the Wuhan Open in August, O'Sullivan said he did not "want to throw in the towel just yet". But he has also acknowledged he has limited time left in the sport, giving himself until 2028, external to beat Hendry's world title total by landing an eighth. Should he slip out of the top 16, O'Sullivan has said he has no interest in competing in World Championship qualifying - held this year at the English Institute of Sport in Sheffield - stating he would retire from snooker instead. There are 16 places available for the World Championship through the qualifying rounds, with Hendry, Mark Williams, Ding Junhui and Steve Davis among players past and present who have taken that route after slipping out of the elite 16 amid declining results. It seemingly holds no appeal to O'Sullivan, though. "I'd love to win another World Championship. I've got two attempts at it," O'Sullivan told World Snooker Tour in July. "If I don't do it this season or the next season, then it'll definitely never happen. "I'm not going to play qualifiers. You won't be seeing me go down to Barnsley trying to win qualifying matches and all that sort of stuff. "I have to be realistic. If that happens, then obviously that's the end of my career. But hopefully, I can keep going for at least another two seasons." Playing in more tournaments may be the most obvious way to avoid a difficult retirement decision, but O'Sullivan has spoken candidly about his battles with depression and anxiety and may feel he cannot compete more regularly. O'Sullivan has threatened to retire on multiple occasions during his career before deciding to stick with the sport, going back as far as his teenage years. Those have usually quickly been forgotten and the reality is that he has displayed remarkable longevity, with his first World Championship win coming in 2001 and his latest in 2022. However, faced with fading powers and a resulting lack of prize money, we may be entering the end stage of the all-time great's career. title: Student who stabbed housemate 30 times admits murder
description: Zack Coughlan changes his plea and admits murdering Jamie Collins near their Bristol home.
body: Jamie Collins, 21, was ambushed and killed after returning home from university A student who stabbed his housemate more than 30 times in a masked ambush has changed his murder plea to guilty. Zack Coughlan, 23, attacked Jamie Collins, 21, in an alleyway near the garden of their home on 8 April and then left his body outside for eight hours before calling police. A murder trial had been under way at Bristol Crown Court because Coughlan initially denied the charge, although he did admit killing Collins. He told jurors he stabbed Collins because he feared his housemate would kill him. However, Coughlan, of Cleve Road, Filton, has now changed his plea to guilty and will be sentenced for murder on Wednesday. Describing him as "gentle" and "kind", Collins' family said he had been "looking forward to finishing his journey" at the University of the West of England (UWE) and returning home to Swansea "in just a few weeks' time". Coughlan initially tried to blame masked attackers for his housemate's murder The men were both final-year robotics students at the UWE and lived together in a house in Filton, owned by Coughlan. During the trial, Coughlan said he stabbed his former friend because he felt he "had no choice", describing himself as "broken". His defence relied on his fear, telling jurors he was "barely able to think" when he lay in wait for Collins to return home from university before stabbing him repeatedly. Coughlan then left his housemate to die in the alleyway behind their home before cycling away on the victim's bike to dispose of bloodstained evidence. He dumped the bike at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing in a pond, in carrier bags weighed down with bricks. This video can not be played Killer's 999 call claiming housemate's body found cold On returning home he ate pizza and played video games, claiming he "had to disconnect" from what happened. He did not call 999 for another eight hours. The entire attack was captured on a CCTV Coughlan had installed himself, which also shows the moment he staged the discovery of Collins' body. Jurors were told he later rewatched this footage five times as he claimed he wanted to "make sense of what was happening and disconnect". Det Ch Insp Lucy Edgeworth, of the major crime investigation team, said "all the evidence suggests" the killing was a "pre-planned, cold-blooded execution". She said despite Coughlan claiming his housemate's political views had become more extreme and that he had talked about killing Coughlan, the motive for the murder was "not clear". "We know there was a dispute about rent. We know that they held different political views. But none of those things make any sense to why somebody would carry out such a horrific crime," she said. This video can not be played Police bodyworn camera footage shows student shortly after attack Edgeworth pointed out inconsistencies in Coughlan's story, including claims he had injured his hands climbing a tree after the incident, which she called "slightly odd". She said that CCTV evidence showed Coughlan proved he had changed his shoes, "yet in his account he'd given us no indication that he'd changed his trainers, and that's just one of many things that then began to unravel with his account". Judge Justice Linden ruled Coughlan's partial defence of manslaughter by reason of loss of control could not be left to the jury to consider as part of their deliberations on the murder charge. He told the jury: "You will have just heard that the defendant has changed his plea to the indictment to guilty. "That means that he now admits the charge of murder." He added: "I would like, on behalf of us all, to thank you for the service that you have given in this case." Follow BBC Bristol on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat
description: Leaders of the movement for independence vow to push on but the margin of defeat could make that difficult.
body: It was a decisive result in a referendum that could have strained the bonds of national unity. But preliminary results show that more than two-thirds of Alberta voters sent a clear message that they want to remain in Canada. It's possible that once the final tally is counted, the rejection by a comfortable majority of voters to pursue separation through a binding referendum could halt Alberta's separatist sentiment in its tracks. This would push the idea that had been discussed quietly for decades back into the political fringes. For leaders of the Alberta separatist movement, while the result was expected given the polling, it was still disappointing after more than a year of campaigning and pushing for a vote on separation. Asked by the BBC how he felt in one sentence after the results, separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre simply said: "Not happy". This video can not be played 'Conversation far from over': BBC reports from pro-separatist watch party The outcome was celebrated almost immediately by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said in a statement that "Albertans made a clear choice". But the movement's leaders say their battle is long from over and that the issue could dominate Alberta politics for years to come. Jeffrey Rath, a Calgary-lawyer and one of the main spokespeople for Alberta separation, said he and others "plan to roll up our sleeves and work harder". Keith Wilson, another separatist, told supporters in Calgary that while the vote is over, "the conversation about Alberta's future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue". Smith, who openly supported and campaigned for the unity vote, thanked voters for the result. The Alberta premier has been criticised for taking a "dangerous" gamble that the independence push would likely face defeat while still giving her restive base what they wanted. She lowered the petition threshold needed to get the citizen-led campaign the ballot in the first place. How oil-rich Alberta's economy might fare if it broke away from Canada Carney pitches oil pipeline as a response to US-Canada trade war At Canada's biggest rodeo, the starting gun is fired in the fight over Alberta separation By making Monday's result non-binding, she got around a court decision blocking the pro-separation petition because it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated. That gamble could test her leadership of the United Conservative Party, which she has led since 2022. "She's lost the confidence of the (party) base," said Rath. Albertans who voted against an independence referendum told the BBC throughout the campaign that they were motivated by a desire to keep the country united, especially as Canada grapples with tariff threats from the US, its longtime ally. They also feared that an independent Alberta could be vulnerable to outside influence - or even annexation. Thomas Lukaszuk, a prominent pro-unity campaigner, told a crowd of supporters on Monday night that the early results made him proud to be Albertan. At a pro-unity results watch party in Edmonton, Lukaszuk appealled directly to separatists, saying that "some of the issues they have raised are legitimate", and that the province must do the hard work of healing the divisions laid bare by this debate. "I don't want to see us doing another referendum like this ever again," Lukaszuk said. Premier Smith told CBC earlier in the week that she would not hold an independence referendum if Albertans vote against it as long as she is premier. Some of the rifts can't easily be smoothed over. The separatist sentiment has its roots in "western alienation" which is a term that has been used for decades by some in Canada's western provinces to describe a feeling of being ignored or overlooked by the federal government in central Canada. This video can not be played WATCH: The father and son on opposite sides of Alberta’s separation referendum Alberta independence supporters - and many on the unity side - believe that Ottawa has long undermined the province's oil and gas industry, most recently through environmental policies. That anger later deepened as some Albertans grew frustrated with the response by former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to the Covid-19 pandemic and vaccine mandates, viewing them as yet another example of government overreach. Carney, who was raised in Alberta, has worked with Smith to address some of these issues, signing an agreement that would see a new pipeline from Alberta built to Canada's pacific coast. He nodded to that in his statement on Monday night, saying that his plan is to unlock Canada's "full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core". But there are signs that there could be tension in the future between Carney and Smith, an able politician and a survivor - so far - of Alberta's rough and tumble politics. She also put nine other questions to Albertans on Monday, most that seek to give the province more autonomy from Ottawa, including on matters like immigration. The (very) preliminary results suggest that many might pass. Some who voted in favour of a second binding separation referendum have said they didn't want outright independence, but some leverage over Ottawa. Smith has said these other nine questions help give her just that. Quebec, another province with similar sovereigntist sentiments, could offer clues on where Alberta's separation movement might end up. They held two separation referendums, in 1980 and 1995, both of which were defeated by a close margin. Alberta independence supporters don't hide the fact that they gain inspiration from the majority French-speaking province. They view Quebec as having successfully used the threat of separation to gain significantly more autonomy over provincial affairs. title: Royals roll out red carpet for visiting Sultan
description: The Sultan of Oman, leader of a Middle Eastern strategic partner, is welcomed to Windsor for a state visit.
body: Catherine was part of the royal welcoming party for the Oman state visit The King and Queen, along with the Prince and Princess of Wales, were part of a colourful ceremonial welcome for the Sultan of Oman as his state visit to the UK begins. The red carpet was rolled out in Windsor for the ruler of Oman, which is an important strategic partner in the Middle East against the backdrop of the conflict with Iran. It has been seen as a diplomatic bridge between the West and Iran and Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said will be given the full soft power treatment from his royal hosts. Prime Minister Andy Burnham will join the Omani visitors at a spectacular state banquet on Tuesday evening, ahead of political discussions at Downing Street on Wednesday. The Sultan of Oman inspected the guard of honour with King Charles The Prince and Princess of Wales are in Windsor to meet the Omani delegation Prince William greeted the Sultan on Tuesday morning, the pair sheltering under umbrellas. Waiting to formally welcome the Omani delegation were the King and Queen and the Princess of Wales, before they all travelled in a carriage ride to Windsor Castle. State visits are a mix of pageantry and politics, with the carefully choreographed hospitality providing an opportunity for talks about important strategic alliances and to promote military and business links. This visit is taking place against the sensitive background of tensions in the Middle East, with Oman facing Iran, on the other side of the strategically important Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman. Oman is a strategically important Middle East partner for the UK Windsor Castle provides the backdrop for the state visit Tuesday evening will see Burnham's first state banquet since becoming prime minister. He will take one of the places of honour in St George's Hall, on a lavishly decorated table that can seat about 160 guests. Burnham previously spoke to the Sultan in July, when they discussed efforts to open the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, and the prime minister said he was grateful for Oman's attempts at mediation. The guest list does not include non-working royals, like the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. An interview with Prince Harry with GQ was released as the state visit was getting under way. He talked about his complicated relationship with his father and brother - recognising that it was something that was "massively relatable" for the public. "Some people don't want it to work out," he said. "I want it to work out. "With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point... scars stick around forever." In the interview, which took place in New York, he said he would "encourage everybody" to let go of the past. "If there's certain things from the past that are still affecting you every day, that's harder to let go of," he told GQ. "But, for me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives to continue with issues with family." title: What in the World
description: Should we be worried about its effect on our health - and the environment?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·20 Oct 2026,·10 mins Available for over a year Have a look at the label in the clothes you’re wearing today. Chances are, you’re wearing some polyester. It’s the most- produced synthetic fibre on the planet and it’s having a bit of a moment on socials. In a bad way…people are giving it up and swapping for more natural fibres. You might’ve seen claims that polyester is linked to diseases like cancer and can cause fertility issues. But how worried should we be? Professor Mohamed Abdallah from the University of Birmingham breaks it down for us and Chelsea Coates from the What in the World team explains how we can make better clothing choices. title: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
description: Dan Mackenzie initially defended his father but now says he felt he had to report his own grandmother.
body: Paul Mackenzie said education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil" The eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago. Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre. "They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday. His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast. He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus". Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder. Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings. "When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child. Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother." The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil". "I left school when I was seven," says Dan. Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings. He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life". "I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday. More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest On Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict. "I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie. Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece". One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows". Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said. Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education. The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November. title: Labour will not have the courage to cut spending, says Badenoch
description: Speaking ahead of next week's Budget, the Conservative leader says her party would make £70bn of cuts.
body: Kemi Badenoch has said Labour will not have the "courage" to make the public spending cuts she argued were necessary to bring down debt and fund defence. Speaking in central London, the Conservative leader said the chancellor was hoping to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" next week but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible." Highlighting her own plans to reduce spending by £70bn, Badenoch said: "Cuts are never easy but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair." Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson described Badenoch's solution as "reverse Robin Hood politics – giving tax breaks to the wealthiest while offering nothing to ordinary people". Chancellor John Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans on 28 October - the first Budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister. Healey has come under pressure to set out how he will boost defence funding to 3% of national income by 2030. However, this announcement is not expected until the government's spending review next year. The Budget is also unlikely to include details about any changes to the welfare system, with those expected once former cabinet minister Alan Milburn produces his review into young people and work. Badenoch said: "If Labour's plan is to kick tough decisions into the long grass, come out with tiny bits of micro-policy, put up a few taxes, spend a bit more on welfare, and hope nobody notices before the next election, they are kidding themselves." The Tory leader noted that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had recently praised the UK for its plans to reduce its borrowing. "The IMF clearly don't know this Labour Party like I do," she said. She said Labour's plans required "huge cuts to the public sector" in 2029 and that the party would call an election before then. "They are not suddenly going to find the courage to cut spending in the final year of a Parliament right before an election... Investors aren't buying these fictional cuts either." Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget What is the Budget and what could be in it? The most recent figures show that in August government borrowing stood at £18.3bn. The government is paying £8.8bn on its debt - the highest level since records began in 1997. Badenoch said her party would reduce borrowing by finding £70bn of savings, including through cuts to the welfare bill. Under her party's "golden economic rule", half of the savings would go towards reducing the deficit. "Cuts are never easy, but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair," she said. "Fair to taxpayers, fair to future generations, and fair to those who really do need support." The Conservatives have recently announced they would scrap inheritance tax on family homes and allow couples to leave £1m tax-free. The party has also pledged to scrap a rule that sees parents in England earning more than £100,000 a year lose out on childcare support. Asked if the Conservatives were the party for the rich, Badenoch told the BBC her policies would "help everyone". "Quite frankly, getting people off welfare is doing something for them... the best welfare is a well-paying job," she said. Pressed on whether she would make changes to the triple lock to reduce the amount spent on pensions, Badenoch said she did not want to see "pensioner poverty" and that there were other things the party could do to grow the economy. The trade unions and the Liberal Democrats have urged the government to raise money by putting a windfall tax on banks, who have reported large profits in recent years. Badenoch dismissed this suggestion, arguing it would hit bank shareholders, including people's pension funds. Setting out her party's policy Liberal Democrat leader Daisy Cooper said: "It's outrageous that while households have been grappling with the cost-of-living crisis, the big banks have benefited from a taxpayer-funded windfall worth billions." She said the money raised from putting higher taxes on the bank could go towards reducing the cost of petrol and diesel and transport fares. Responding to Badenoch's speech, Phillipson said: "Under the Tories debt rocketed, interest rates went up, while family finances and businesses were hammered. "Labour has taken the fair decisions to reverse the Conservatives' decline. The economy is growing, interest rates have fallen, and private investment has returned. "We're giving people breathing space on the cost of living and delivering everyday fixes to make life that little bit easier." title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close
description: The closurse are announced as the corporation continues to try to save £500m over two years.
body: The BBC is to close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation continues to make £500m of savings over two years. Both services will become online-only, meaning they will continue to produce and host some content on iPlayer, without the need to fill a terrestrial TV schedule. The BBC has also announced the closure of Radio 4 Extra, which largely airs speech programmes from the BBC's archive, including comedy, drama and documentaries. BBC director-general Matt Brittin said: "We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices." Discussing the closure of linear broadcast services, Brittin said: "Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy them on iPlayer and Sounds. "While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues." Outlining the plans, the corporation confirmed: BBC Scotland will remain a channel on iPlayer, with some content also broadcast on BBC One and BBC Two in Scotland BBC Three commissions, supported by increased investment in content for younger audiences, will be available on BBC iPlayer and on other platforms including YouTube Programmes from Radio 4 Extra will be available on BBC Sounds - while its religious programme The Daily Service will be on BBC Sounds and local radio BBC Three launched hits including Gavin & Stacey, which returned for a Christmas finale in 2024 BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022. BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment. However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels. Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day. The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes. Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotscast, the corporation said. While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds. Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks. The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save £500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures". Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport. Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks. RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus and Ski Sunday are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far, while other formats such as DIY SOS have been temporarily rested. title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
description: The government increased taxes on online casino and sports betting in last year's Budget.
body: Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry. Staff based in the UK and Ireland, as well as British and Irish workers at Flutter's sites in Portugal and Romania will be affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed. The government announced increased taxes on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last November. Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market". "We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter said on Tuesday. Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland. Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future." The company delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York. In its most recent results, Flutter reported a $299m (£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June. compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn. Revenue in the UK and Ireland rose by 4%, due to strong growth in online gambling games. Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%. General betting duty, paid on other forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year. Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering". Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets. Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m. The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact. title: BBC Scotland TV channel to close amid cuts to services
description: The station, which started in February 2019, will move to BBC iPlayer in spring next year.
body: The BBC Scotland channel has been broadcasting from Pacific Quay since 2019 The BBC has announced plans to close its Scotland linear TV station as it seeks to make £500m savings. The channel, which started in February 2019, will move to BBC iPlayer in spring next year, although its nightly News at Seven programme will close. The change is expected to see about 10 posts cut in addition to the 60 BBC Scotland announced earlier this year. Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine, said: "Against the backdrop of significant financial challenges, we must focus our resources where they will have the greatest impact for audiences." The BBC said a wide range of its programming currently shown on the linear TV channel would be available online or on BBC One or BBC Two in Scotland. Shows include Scotland's Home of the Year, Murder Case, Inside Barlinnie, the Scottish Cup Final and Hogmanay. The broadcaster's SPFL Championship matches on Friday evenings will move to BBC Two in Scotland. In other changes, the corporation said BBC Three and Radio Four Extra would be moving online. BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra channels to close Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine, said: "We must focus our resources where they will have the greatest impact for audiences." Last month, new BBC Director General Matt Brittin said given current finances and changing audience habits it "may well mean" some channels and radio stations close so resources can be invested in on-demand services. Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever". The BBC previously announced it would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 - almost one in 10 jobs - as part of measures to make £500m savings in the next two years. In June, 550 job cuts were announced in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage of cuts. In recent months, the BBC announced a series of closures of programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus. Cuts to radio programmes have also been announced. The broadcaster, which has about 21,500 full time employees, gets most of its income from the licence fee, but the number of TV licences sold has been declining in recent years. The Nine was the BBC Scotland channel's flagship programme Plans for a dedicated BBC Scotland TV channel were announced in 2017 by then BBC Director General Tony Hall. He said the "bold, creative and ambitious" channel would replace BBC Two Scotland as the main home for Scottish-produced programmes. It gained Ofcom approval and was launched in February 2019 with the investment of 80 journalism jobs. It was fronted by flagship news programme The Nine which covered Scottish, UK and international stories from a Scottish perspective. The channel also became home to Scottish drama, comedy, documentaries, current affairs and sport including Debate Night and Scottish national team football games. In 2024, five years after it went on air, the BBC announced plans to scrap The Nine alongside entertainment news show The Edit and weekly news review Seven Days. It was replaced by a shorter 30-minute news programme News at Seven, as well as extended versions of Reporting Scotland. Valentine, who was launch editor of the The Nine, said it was "always sad" to see programmes come to an end. She praised staff by saying: "I am extremely proud of the News at Seven team and everything they have delivered since launching. "Our teams are highly skilled, and we will continue to evolve our news and current affairs offer to reflect the changing way people consume journalism today." Valentine added that by "continuing the channel on BBC iPlayer, we can ensure Scottish content thrives in a digital environment". "BBC Two in Scotland, alongside BBC One Scotland, will maintain a strong and distinctive Scottish presence on linear television," she said. BBC Scotland's Head of News Howard Simpson said: "Losing one of our programme brands is hard. "Reporting Scotland: News at Seven succeeds in bringing our audience closer to the day's news and has been incredibly effective at adding context from experts and from a first-person experience. "The team who work on the show bring energy and creativity and a fresh look at our TV offer. I am extremely proud of what they continue to accomplish." BBC Director General Matt Brittin told staff: "We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices." title: My son has disappeared off the face of the earth fighting for Russia
description: Nathan Stobbart’s family say he faced deportation from Russia if he did not join the country's army.
body: Valerie Stobbart, from Newcastle, says her son Nathan was given no choice but to join the Russian army to avoid deportation from the country British man Nathan Stobbart has been declared missing in action while fighting for Russia in Ukraine. He kept his military service a secret from his family in the UK, who are now desperately trying to find him. In December 2025, Nathan's mother Valerie Stobbart received a text message that plunged her life into turmoil. It was from her panic-stricken daughter-in-law, Ksenia, who lives in Russia with Valerie's 30-year-old son and the couple's newborn baby. Nathan had been fighting for the country against Ukraine and had vanished. "I can't even describe it," Valerie says. "I remember walking in and telling Sean [Valerie's partner], and we were just both in total shock." Her son had told her he was working as an electrical contractor and she had no idea he had joined the Russian army in April last year. "You think that somebody is living this lovely little life with a new family and then suddenly you find out that they've gone, they're missing," she says. "They've completely disappeared off the face of the earth." Nathan Stobbart was declared missing in action by his military unit in December Nathan's voice was last heard on his military radio a week before Ksenia's message. A Russian army document, seen by the BBC, shows he was officially declared missing in action by his unit on 12 December but no body has been found. Valerie says Ksenia revealed the Russian authorities had warned Nathan he would not be granted a visa to remain in the country and faced deportation if he did not sign up for a year's military service. Russian media has previously reported , externalforeign men in the country have been forced to join the invasion in Ukraine in return for citizenship. Valerie does not agree with her son's decision to fight but accepts he faced a difficult choice - he could either return home to Newcastle in north-east England without his wife and newborn son or join the Russian army. "He was so desperate to stay with his family he would do anything," she says. This video can not be played Newcastle man missing fighting for Russia It is illegal for Britons to fight for foreign nations involved in conflicts with countries with which the UK is at peace, unless they hold dual nationality, according to the Foreign Enlistment Act 1870. But Nathan is not the only British national without dual nationality to fight for Russian president Vladimir Putin against Ukraine. Ben Stimson and Aiden Minnis are believed to be the first and were given Russian citizenship for fighting in the occupied Donbas region. Bradley Townsend was killed in Ukraine in June and is believed to be the first British citizen fighting for Russia to die in the conflict. Their situation is different, Valerie says, as Nathan did not travel to Russia with the intention of fighting in the war. "He never wanted to join the army," she says. "He was there to live with his family." She understands people may have strong opinions about Nathan fighting for Russia and stresses she condemns the country's "awful" invasion in Ukraine. "I really don't care about changing people's opinions," she says. "What I care about is trying to find him." Nathan Stobbart filmed a diary while serving on the front line in Ukraine Nathan moved to Russia on Christmas Day 2024 to start a new life with Ksenia. They had met online and she had visited him and his family in the UK. The couple got married in Russia and were bringing up their son like a "normal, little family". They were also raising Ksenia's three children from a previous relationship, which meant relocating the whole family to the UK was deemed unaffordable, Valerie says. She questioned Nathan's initial decision to move to Russia but warmed to the idea because the couple lived "miles from any fighting". They did talk about the conflict "but it was happening in Ukraine, it wasn't happening in Russia", she says. "It had no effect on them at all." Prior to Ksenia's text message, Valerie had no reason to believe something was not right. Receiving photos and videos of her newborn grandchild made everything feel "normal". Nathan's family say he reluctantly joined the Russian army to be close to his newborn son As the days and weeks passed since Nathan went missing, the enormity of the situation became increasingly clear. The family discovered he had recorded a goodbye video at the start of his military service, which he sent to his wife to be passed on to his mother in the event of his death. "I could only watch it once," Valerie says. "I had to turn it off." Despite the video and his prolonged silence, she believes her son is still alive. The fight for answers has been long and torturous for Valerie, who has approached the government and several charities, both in the UK and Russia. "I contacted the Foreign Office and got a caseworker there, but they admitted themselves that they can't do anything," she says. "Nobody tells you what to do." The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) said it was aware of reports a British national was missing after fighting for Russia in Ukraine and was "in contact with his family". It said it advised against all travel to Russia and "our ability to provide consular support in these circumstances is severely limited". Questions to Russia about Nathan's last known whereabouts failed to provide any leads. "They just kept saying everything was classified," Valerie says. "They wouldn't even tell us where he was." All of Valerie's spare time is spent trawling the internet for clues. "The days just roll on, the weeks roll on," she says, wiping away tears. "We're nine months down the line with no more answers than we had in the beginning." But she still has hope he may be captured, but alive. and watches offi

title: Pair sentenced for human trafficking crimes
description: The pair were arrested in November 2022 in what was described at the time as the PSNI's largest operation against human trafficking.
body: Corrigan (left) and Mariano (right) were sentenced on Tuesday A man and woman have been sentenced for a series of offences including human trafficking. Gerald Corrigan, 66, of Keeragh Park, Pomeroy, previously pleaded guilty to human trafficking, possessing criminal property and transferring criminal property. He was sentenced to 16 months; this was broken down as eight months in custody and eight months on license. Mavie Martins Mariano 51, of Ard Aveen Park, Bessbrook, previously pleaded guilty to human trafficking, acquiring criminal property, possessing criminal property, transferring criminal property, brothel keeping and controlling prostitution. Mariano, who is originally from Brazil, was given a three year sentence. This is broken down as three months in custody and 33 months on license. The court heard that both defendants had already spent time in custody on remand and therefore it was likely that time in custody had been served. Speaking at Dungannon Crown Court on Tuesday, Judge Brian Sherrard said he took into account the fact that both defendants had pleaded guilty and had expressed remorse. He said he also considered the impact of imprisonment on Mariano's family and Corrigan's health issues when delivering his sentence. Judge Sherrard said: "You were both concerned in the trafficking of women for the purpose of sexual exploitation and you both acquired a considerable amount of money during this offending period." He added: "I acknowledge this is not a case involving threats or violence and it is accepted by the prosecution in this case there is no evidence of coercion and the defence contend these women were acting voluntarily." The pair were arrested in November 2022 in what was described at the time as the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI) largest operation against human trafficking. During the operation police said that 27 brothels were raided across Northern Ireland, with some 150 officers involved. The offences took place between 23 March 2020 and 21 November 2022. The court had previously heard that a large amount of money in the region of £174,000 was transferred between the two defendants. At a previous sentencing hearing in Dungannon Crown Court on 22 September the prosecution summarised their case against Corrigan and Mariano. The prosecution said the case boiled down to "the organisation of sex work and controlling of prostitution" in an operation that spread throughout Northern Ireland over a period of two years and eight months. In relation to Mariano, a prosecuting barrister said she had a lead role in the offending and there was evidence that £174,000 passed between the accounts of the two defendants. The barrister said that Mariano had admitted at police interview to being involved in the booking of property for women described as "escorts" and that an apartment had been booked by her on 22 occasions for "sex workers". The prosecuting barrister added that "once you get into arranging the properties and organising them, it is controlling prostitution". The prosecution said Mariano had also admitted during police interview to helping to organise escort adverts and organising the moving of around "five to six girls a week". The judge asked if there had been any "evidence of lifestyle change or any large amounts of money benefiting her". The prosecuting barrister outlined that Mariano had funded a trip to Turkey for gastric implant surgery for a "not insignificant amount". A prosecution barrister also said that the case revolved around "the exploitation of sex workers" and there was "always harm in this type of offending" adding that "it is built into it". In relation to Corrigan, the prosecution outlined how he was primarily a driver of sex workers and he had a role of getting and collecting money. A prosecution barrister said that Corrigan had accepted he had "lodged money into his bank account knowing the money came from prostitution". A prosecution barrister also said Corrigan's role was "the moving of sex workers with the knowledge and acceptance that were being exploited". One of the central arguments from the defence barristers in the case was there was no sign of coercion of the women in these cases. A defence barrister also addressed the prosecution's point about Mariano's trip to Turkey. A defence barrister said: "In respect of when the prosecution can only muster that this lady went to Turkey to get a gastric band fitted, this speaks for itself. "Citizens have been advised not to go Turkey because [these procedures are] alarmingly cheap and inquests have identified that people have died. "This lady does not have money, she has no trappings of wealth, zero, had she had money she would have went privately to somewhere like Dublin." On Mariano's role a defence barrister added that she was "not a principal, she was not an organiser and she played no leading role". The defence barrister also raised concerns about the impact that a custodial sentence for Mariano could have on her family. A defence barrister added: "There was no coercion in this case, these were adult women engaging in sex work voluntarily". Commenting on Corrigan's role, a defence barrister said that he "wasn't involved in the overall scheme, he knew he was driving prostitutes, but any planning was limited" and that he gained "a very modest amount of financial gain". A defence barrister also outlined that Corrigan had already spent 10 months in jail and that he suffered from ill health, including prostate cancer. title: Three children injured after school bus roof ripped off in crash
description: Three children receive hospital treatment after a bus on its way to Ysgol Gyfun Gwent Is Coed crashes.
body: This video can not be played Recovery workers at the scene of the crashed double decker bus in Newport Three children have been injured when a school bus crashed into a railway bridge, police have said. Gwent Police said it received a report of a crash in Tregare Street, Newport, at about 07:45 BST on Tuesday. The bus was travelling with pupils from St Julian's School, Heather Road, and Ysgol Gyfun Gwent Is Coed, a Welsh‑medium secondary school on Duffryn Way. Worried mum Jo Townsend's 13-year-old son, Gruff, was one of the pupils taken to hospital. She said: "I was worried, frantic. I went under the tape, I was getting to my son." Newport Transport said it takes matters of safety "extremely seriously" and that it was establishing the full circumstances of the incident. The pupils' injuries are not thought to be life-threatening, Gwent Police said The pupils' injuries are not thought to be life-threatening, the force said, but the children have been taken to hospital for treatment. Crews from South Wales Fire and Rescue Service and the Welsh Ambulance Service attended the scene, and the road was closed with diversions in place, but has since reopened. Jo Townsend said: "You send them off to school and you think everything will be OK... you don't expect anything like this to happen." Transport for Wales said the bus hit a bridge at Maindee West between Newport and Cwmbran. Townsend said: "The whole top of the bus came off. My son was sat at the top back of the bus which was probably the worst place." She said Gruff was "incredulous" when he called her. "He said, 'I can't believe it mum'. He was tripping over his words. He was shocked. He's got scratches and bumps on his back," she said. "He said it all went dark and then lights were flickering, there was the sounds of screaming and metal scraping metal." The roof of the double decker bus was ripped off during the crash Townsend, from Maindy, Newport, said Gruff was "hit in the head with a pole" during the crash, but was OK and being treated for bumps and scratches. "Luckily there isn't a lot of blood. He was very, very lucky," she said. She said a nearby nursery, Lullabyz, had moved its children elsewhere to allow paramedics to use the site to treat the injured. There did not appear to be any visible damage to the bridge, and the bus had been removed from the scene by midday on Tuesday, with the ripped-off roof recovered first. However, visible damage to the bus showed the extent of the crash as the rear of the upper floor had bent back on itself. The bus was removed from the scene on Tuesday morning During First Minister's Questions, Rhun ap Iorwerth said his thoughts were with the children involved. "We're grateful to the emergency services for their swift response and to everybody involved in supporting the children affected," he said. "This is an ongoing police investigation so it would be an appropriate think for me to comment further, but our thoughts are very much with those injured and those, for whom this has caused anxiety today." Newport council thanked the nursery for its response, which will continue to "offer support through the schools to those affected." "There will naturally be a formal investigation into the incident, and the council will fully support that process," it added. A Newport Transport spokesperson said they "wish those who have been affected a swift recovery" as they carry out a full investigation. "We are continuing to establish the full circumstances of the incident and are fully cooperating with the relevant authorities," they said. The council also apologised for the disruption to rail passengers. During rush hour, commuters at Newport station faced significant travel disruption, with Transport for Wales reporting delays and cancellations throughout most of Tuesday morning, in both directions between Newport and Hereford. Newport council said it was working closely with the emergency services and its priority was "ensuring the well-being" of those involved. title: Burnham risks wrath of Commons Speaker for talking too much at PMQs
description: The prime minister takes longer than his predecessors to respond to questions from MPs, writes Matt Chorley.
body: Andy Burnham has only been prime minister for three months, but he is already in trouble with the Commons Speaker for talking too much. During the first three sessions of Prime Minister's Questions with Burnham at the despatch box, Sir Lindsay Hoyle has made repeated appeals for brevity. But is he really any more verbose than his predecessors like Sir Keir Starmer, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss and Boris Johnson? Armed with a stopwatch for a dive into the archive, I've found that the new prime minister does seem to give fuller, longer answers – by some margin. The weekly session of PMQs is scheduled to start at midday on Wednesdays when the Commons is sitting, and last for 30 minutes. However it routinely runs for 10, 15, even 20 minutes longer. And that has caused problems. Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics " Can I just say I admire the prime minister?" Sir Lindsay said during Burnham's first PMQs. "At least he's answering detailed questions. My problem is I'm not going to get through the list, and both of us will be in trouble with the backbenches when we don't make it." Just last week he complained again: "We really are going to have to try and speed up some of the answers." Based on an average of his first three times taking PMQs, Burnham has spoken for a total of 22 minutes per session. That's between three and six minutes more than the average for the other PMs I looked at each over three similar autumn sessions. The number of questions asked each week can differ though, in part because time is running out. So I looked at the average time spent on each answer, Of those I looked at, Truss was the fastest - averaging just 33 seconds per answer, followed by Johnson on 35 seconds, Sir Keir on 38 seconds and Sunak on 39 seconds. By contrast Burnham was an outlier, taking on average 51 seconds per answer. That means he talks for a third more per question than Sir Keir and Sunak, and up to 50% more than Truss. Obviously the quantity of words is easier to assess than the quality. Number 10 thinks there is a simple reason why the current PM takes longer than his predecessors. A senior source tells me: "It's because he actually answers the questions." A spokesman for the speaker said: "The speaker is always keen to get in as many backbenchers as possible for any question session." Listen to Matt Chorley weekdays from 14:00 on BBC Radio 5 Live and on the Urgent Questions podcast. title: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech
description: Proposed changes could lead to new digital wallets and keys as well as ticketing apps, the regulator says.
body: UK smartphone users could benefit from new payment, ticket and travel apps if Apple widens access to its contactless payment tech, the competition watchdog says. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) also wants the fees Apple charges firms to use its contactless tech to be "substantially lower". It believes the iPhone maker's current fees and charges are "blocking" financial technology firms and others from innovating and growing - and is consulting on proposals it believes would cause these fees to fall. Apple maintains that widening access could undermine security, and that its current arrangements do not stop innovation. Nearly 2 in 5 payments are now contactless, the watchdog said, with nearly 60% of people using digital wallets - with Apple's the most popular in the UK. In a statement Apple told the BBC that the current arrangements had permitted developers in the UK and around the world to securely offer contactless transactions directly within their apps, for everything from in-store payments and transit passes to car keys and event tickets. "This solution enables developers and banks to create innovative products and services for their customers and facilitates competition between wallets, while ensuring users' sensitive data remains protected by the highest security standards". "We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users." Last year Apple warned UK regulators against following the same path as the EU which forced it to open up a range of its technologies to rivals. However, the CMA argued that, unlike the EU, it is focused on ensuring the interoperability of particular aspects of Apple's tech, such as digital wallets and watches. The proposed measures would force Apple to grant access to apps that make payments via a widely used alternative contactless technology standard, called Host Card Emulation (HCE), which the firm does not currently permit in the UK. The UK is one of the world's leading fintech hubs, the CMA said, generating more than £214 billion in turnover and supporting more than 360,000 jobs. But Apple's fees and rules contactless payments are restricting growth and innovation, it argued. Changes could enable the development of a wide range of new products, such as account-to-account payments, digital IDs, travel passes and digital keys, it claimed. The regulator said moves to open up the tech in the EU had resulted in the creation of new businesses. In the six months since the EU forced Apple to widen access to its tech, an alternative payment app Vipps launched, followed by PayPal, Klarna, Curve, and BBVA. Apple argues however that the these new apps could easily have been launched prior to the changes. But in the UK not a single firm has launched a wallet-type product to compete with Apple's the watchdog argued. The CMA said it was not proposing to set the price and terms Apple could demand for use of its devices contactless tech, but the effect of its plans would be that prices would fall. Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA said it had been told that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology made it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete. "By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services," she said. title: Key takeaways from Covid report on care homes
description: From the shocking lack of PPE to restrictions on visitors - the key points from the sixth Covid inquiry report.
body: The sixth report of the Covid inquiry is highly critical of the way the government tried to protect people in care settings in the UK. Around 500,000 people were living in care homes at the start of the pandemic – with another million receiving care in their own homes. The inquiry said action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences. There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022. Here are the key findings of the 287-page report. At the start of the pandemic, the then-health secretary in England, Matt Hancock, said the UK government had placed "a protective ring" around care homes. But the inquiry says this was not the case, listing a catalogue of failings. It says the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought". A lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) meant staff had to resort to makeshift workarounds, including bin bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls. The report is also critical of the way hospital patients who may be infected with Covid were moved to care homes to make space for others. The decision was understandable given the need to free up beds for Covid patients. But, without sufficient testing, it was important to keep these people separate and isolate them from others in case they were infected. Official guidance in March 2020 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland did not request this. That, the report says, was a significant oversight. When the pandemic started, high levels of staff vacancies and turnover in the social care sector meant that the workforce was "fragile and lacking resilience". This undermined the ability of the sector to respond to the pandemic, the inquiry says. For example, care homes tend to rely heavily on agency staff who work in a variety of different homes. But a desire not to have staff going into multiple homes, to reduce the risk of infection transmission, meant staff shortages got even worse. Financially, care providers struggled too, as the number of people using services dropped. And for a sector that uses zero-hours contracts, there was a lack of financial support to help care staff stay off work if there was concern they might be infected. The response also suffered because of the fragmented nature of the system, with thousands of different providers and services overseen by councils. It meant the sector was more distant from government than the NHS. The pandemic, the inquiry said, exposed and exacerbated these existing weaknesses. The report is clear that precautionary steps taken to restrict visiting, as part of infection control, went too far. It acknowledges there was little choice to introduce bans on visitors at the start of the pandemic, saying that was rational. But as the pandemic progressed, so did the balance between the benefits and harms of restrictions. Visits are extremely important, allowing loved ones to help residents with everything from personal care to maintaining their mental health. By September 2020, evidence suggested visitors posed a "marginal risk" – staff were judged to be the key entry point for infections. The four UK nations then started to relax their guidance, but many care homes failed to implement this and visiting remained heavily restricted. This, says the inquiry, resulted in a significant decline in the health and wellbeing of residents. CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation), including chest compressions, can be life-saving if a person's heart has stopped beating. But doctors can sometimes opt not to resuscitate people - as can individuals themselves in advance - for example, if the individual is extremely frail or has a life-limiting illness. This should be done on an individual basis and the use of blanket do not resuscitate orders (DNACPR) is considered unlawful. The inquiry says it heard evidence of GPs imposing blanket DNACPRs on care home residents. And it pointed to records showing a sharp increase in orders being put in place – they jumped from 16,800 to 26,500 in the first nine months of the pandemic. This concern mirrors an earlier Care Quality Commission investigation which found evidence of unacceptable and inappropriate DNACPRs being put in place. The impact on staff working in care homes was huge, affecting their mental health and wellbeing, the inquiry said. Some moved into the care homes where they worked, in an attempt to protect residents from infection. One care home owner in Wales described how 39 staff moved in for a fortnight at the start of the pandemic. Seeing so many residents die placed an enormous strain on workers, who often had to provide end-of-life care to multiple people at the same time. One care home, for example, lost half of its residents over the course of three weeks. Staff told the inquiry of the deep distress they suffered. "Staff were sitting on video calls with families, saying their last goodbye to loved ones. That was horrendous… staff were crying with the residents, because it was just so emotional for them," one said. title: Ronaldo let Manchester United down - Ten Hag
description: Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag says Cristiano Ronaldo "let the team and let me down" during the Dutchman's spell at Old Trafford.
body: Ronaldo gave an interview in which he said he did not "respect" Ten Hag Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag said Cristiano Ronaldo "let the team and let me down" during the Dutchman's spell at Old Trafford. Portugal forward Ronaldo was in his second spell at United when Ten Hag took charge in the summer of 2022 but left in controversial circumstances a few months later. "He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," Ten Hag told The Athletic, external. "I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United. "Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in." Ten Hag had dropped Ronaldo for a Premier League game at Chelsea in October 2022 after he had refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham three days earlier. Ronaldo gave an interview in the November in which he said he felt "betrayed" by United, did not respect Ten Hag and was being forced out of the club prior to his departure being "mutually agreed". Ronaldo was 36 when he returned to Manchester United from Juventus in 2021, when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was manager. Under Ten Hag, he scored just three goals in 16 outings before his exit during the 2022-23 campaign. "It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted," added Ten Hag. "But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself. "Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team. "He was telling the players, 'save your legs at the training'. I understand it when you are top fit - you have sessions you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels." The publication of Ten Hag's interview comes as Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and fined 255 euros (£215) by the Portuguese Football Federation for leaving his country's international camp last month. Ten Hag was sacked by Manchester United in October 2024, having won the Carabao Cup in 2023 and FA Cup in 2024. On his time at Old Trafford, Ten Hag added he wanted to sign Frenkie de Jong, Harry Kane and Declan Rice, and was against the sale of Scott McTominay to Napoli in August 2024. "I said for the first season, 'centre-half, there's a problem, centre-midfield, there is a problem, and especially I need a strategist, then we need goals'. And that was the biggest issue in all my three years: goals," said Ten Hag.
