title: Google Cloud says 'power event' behind outage hitting UK banks and websites
description: It has since been linked to a number of services, most notably British neobank Revolut, going down for customers or suffering problems on Tuesday morning.
body: Revolut was among UK banking services seemingly affected by the Google Cloud outage on Tuesday Google Cloud has said a "power event" is behind an outage affecting a range of online services in the UK, including banks and the courts. The company, which is one of a handful of large cloud computing providers whose infrastructure and services are used to power millions of online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its UK data centre complex "europe-west2". Banks Revolut, Lloyds and Halifax are among those to report disruption to their apps, thought the link to the Google Cloud outage has not been officially confirmed. Google Cloud has not given a clear timeline for when the issues will be resolved but it has apologised "to all who are affected by the disruption". In a statement on Tuesday morning, a Google Cloud spokesperson said "we are investigating this further" and referred journalists to its service health dashboard for details. A range of online platforms reported issues with some services on Tuesday morning, after users and customers flagged problems on social media and to platform outage monitor Downdetector. But few have explicitly tied problems they are experiencing to the Google Cloud incident. After Downdetector saw more than 1,500 reports of issues affecting Revolut services shortyl after 08:00 BST on Tuesday, a spokesperson for the company confirmed its problems had been caused by a third-party issue. "We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services," a Revolut spokesperson told the BBC in an earlier statement - adding "we can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe." "We've been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused," they added. Other popular services, including Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland - all owned by Lloyds Banking Group - were also experiencing some problems on Tuesday. A Lloyds spokesperson told the BBC its app was functioning normally, but said "we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning". "We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely," they added. The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings, and delivery firm DPD flagged that it was "aware of connection issues." The incident at Google's UK cloud site, europe-west2 was first indicated on its service health dashboard, external on Monday evening UK time. It was updated in the early hours of Tuesday morning to flag that the region was experiencing "elevated errors and intermittent network failures" across some of its services. title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
description: France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Clean up begins after some of the worst disorder in France's modern history, but police remain Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder. France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted. A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure. So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children. But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder. Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media It seemed to work; the largest central gathering we witnessed was a posse of weather-beaten tourists trudging around the quayside. Nonetheless, an overnight curfew for minors will come into force in parts of the city from Tuesday evening. Marseille is one of France's most ethnically diverse cities – a place where generations of new arrivals have landed. 18-year-old student Maryame only arrived in the southern city a few weeks ago, albeit from the countryside not too far away. "It was very scary because it's my first time in a big city, and also my first time demonstrating," she said. Maryam (R) joined the protests on Saturday, which began in September over poor school conditions before escalating to cover broader issues such as the cost of living Maryame said violence engulfed the student demonstration her friends had joined as looters began attacking shops. She said the solidarity of the earlier march was "beautiful" and the subsequent disorder "terrifying", but went on to say that she was conflicted as to whether even more violence would make the government sit up and listen. "It is a very complicated question if violence is legitimate," she began. "But the thing is, France, our history is really based on revolution, and sometimes we really have to make a really big impact. "Sometimes it goes too far." For the police, the extent to which order disintegrated was a shock, according to one organisation representing rank and file officers. "It was a war," said Arnaud Blaise from the UN1TE police union. "An unheard-of level of violence. Unprecedented." Looting was reported across the city centre, including along La Canebière - Marseille's equivalent of Paris's Champs-Élysées - Rue Paradis, and at the Centre Bourse shopping centre. Businesses were also hit further afield, such as in the Grand Littoral and Le Merlan shopping malls to the north. Hundreds of businesses were looted in several locations across the city Blaise said he was concerned that future protests could follow the same destructive pattern as Saturday, with young people from the deprived northern suburbs seizing the opportunity to steal amid chaos that, in his view, was stirred up by far-left agitators - referred to in France as the Black Bloc. "The Black Blocs provoked, and the youngsters took advantage to start looting," Blaise said. "That created chaos, with police officers running right, running left, and in effect, we got overwhelmed." I put it to Blaise that the police had been accused of heavy-handedness with peaceful students but sitting back as the most violent protesters pillaged local businesses. "That is not the case at all," he replied, arguing that more police than students had been injured. "Four thousand tear gas grenades were fired and then we ran out of ammunition. So at a certain point, you have no choice but to retreat." 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Watch: Shops looted and restaurants gutted in Paris riots France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez - whose resignation in the wake of the riots was rejected by President Macron - travelled to Marseille on Monday evening. He came to the City Hall, which was briefly occupied by protestors on Saturday, and met Marseille's Socialist Mayor Benoît Payan. Payan said he wanted answers from the government as to how the chaos was allowed to happen. "Order was lost, and an attempt was made to restore order. I believe that from start to finish, it was a fiasco," he said on Monday. He said under-staffed and poorly deployed police needed to change their tactics. "If there isn't a radical change of approach on this issue - if, by chance, the only target remains high school students - then we will see looting scenes again." He continued: "I don't know what's left to loot in Marseille, but for the little that remains, it will be looted." Chantal Bellanger said she was worried for young people rioting out of anger and despair While the ban on public gatherings in Marseille and partial overnight curfews in other French cities have brought some temporary calm, more demonstrations are planned for the weekend. At a smashed out tram stop, 79-year-old grandmother Chantal Bellanger said she had been "worried - but then, I've been worried for a long time". "We can clearly see that France has lost its grip on many things. Public services, hospitals, education is in a horrible state, the peripheral neighbourhoods are dilapidated, they are abandoned." She said she used to work in these deprived northern suburbs, where poverty and crime rates are very high, and feared a whole lost generation was criminalising itself through anger and despair. title: Moment giant fin whale's huge mouth engulfs thousands of gallons of water
description: Videographer Rhys Morgan captured footage of the worlds second largest whale lunge feeding on his drone.
body: This video can not be played Videographer Rhys Morgan captured footage of the world's second largest whale lunge feeding This is the moment the planet's second largest living creature opens its giant jaws and swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding. The fin whale was filmed by videographer Rhys Morgan off the Pembrokeshire coast in Wales, and it shows the mammal's expandable pleats take in up to 18,000 gallons of water and krill. Morgan said "it was complete luck" that he captured the whale feeding and swimming with dolphins on his drone while fishing with a friend. Second only to the blue whale, the fin whale is one of the largest animals ever to have lived, reaching up to 24m in length and weighing up to 70 tonnes. Despite its enormous size, the fast-swimming creature is elusive and spends much of its life in the open ocean and often surfacing only briefly before disappearing beneath the waves. The mammal can be found all over the world's oceans but is most at home in cooler waters. The fin whale is about 24m (79ft) in length and weighs up to 70 tonnes Morgan, from Houghton, Pembrokeshire, works at an oil refinery by day, and said he was "brought up on the water", but became interested in marine videography after using his friends drone to capture footage of sea creatures across the surface of the ocean. "It's pretty incredible really," Morgan said. "It makes you feel very small out there." Rhys Morgan said he was "brought up on the water" and has been going out on boats since he was a young To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes. "There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us. "The wildlife will approach you sometimes." Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter". Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular. "In theory, they should have migrated." Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks. Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary. Fin whales have a pretty simple diet which is usually made up of krill, small schooling fish and squid. Due to the small size of its prey, fin whales have to eat a lot to survive and can spend several hours each day feeding, consuming up to 2,000 kilograms of food. title: Immigration protests 'could get worse', says Badenoch
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch warned of immigration protests getting worse as France deals with riots across the country.
body: This video can not be played Kemi Badenoch tells the BBC that protests in the UK over immigration "could get worse". Asked if she thinks the UK could be on the brink of rioting because of people's concerns about immigration, the Conservative leader said that the country "could see those sorts of scenes" if concerns were ignored. Badenoch's comments come after more than 2,500 were taken into police custody in France following a weekend of widespread demonstrations and violence. title: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
description: North Korean state media has published photos of the dictator with his daughter after the unsubstantiated rumour spread.
body: North Korean state media released photos of Kim Jong Un shortly after rumours of his death started spreading online Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage. Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter. The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died. For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine. In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation. This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him. He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death. Yet the photographs tell a different story. Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials. While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim. This video can not be played Watch: What do a teenager's clothes tell us about North Korea's future? There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health. China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened. South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports. The rumour also echoes previous false alarms. In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled. So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession. North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors. Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth. Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader. Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats. Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays. But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle. All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention. South Korean intelligence believes Kim may be preparing his daughter as a successor The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible. Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family. If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability. Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea. Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news. Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact. The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country. So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it. He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see. Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership. Could Kim's teen daughter become North Korea's next leader? What do we know about Kim Jong Un's daughter - and expected successor? title: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend
description: Brendan Nugent's family say they have known Helen Haines, who remains in a critical condition, for more than 20 years.
body: The community in Wangaratta remains in shock after the alleged attack A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday. The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime". Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs. "Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement. "All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends." They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can". Police say they will allege the incident was targeted. Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital. Helen Haines sits as an independent MP for the electoral division of Indi in Australia's state of Victoria She was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help. A local barber who was there says he pulled the suspect out of his car. "I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way," said Ricky Jefferies. Others who helped "didn't even check for danger", he added. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration." In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through. As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta. "At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta. Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum. The community, and country, remain in shock. At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the aisle of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects. Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement. One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world." title: £30 rise in payments for crisis-hit households
description: More money is made available through a resilience fund for hard-pressed households in Sheffield.
body: Sheffield City Council's crisis resilience fund can be used to pay for essentials such as utilities Crisis payments for people in Sheffield who are facing severe financial difficulties have been raised by £30. Single person households which qualify for help from Sheffield City Council's crisis and resilience fund will now be entitled to a one-off payment of £95, up from £65 previously. Meanwhile, two-person households can apply for a payment of £110, while homes with three or four people are entitled to £120 if they qualify and households with five or more people can get £130, the authority confirmed. Announcing the change, councillor Elle Dodd, chair of the authority's finance and performance policy committee, said life was "difficult and expensive" for "too many people" in Sheffield. The fund can be used to help people buy essentials such as food, toiletries and utilities, the council's website stated. The increase was put in place after a cost-of-living review conducted by the committee, which is made up of a group of Sheffield councillors. The review found almost 50,000 households in Sheffield were struggling to make ends meet and could not pay their bills. At least 7,000 crisis grants, totalling nearly £600,000, have already been awarded by the council since April. Dodd said: "Behind every statistic is someone making impossible decisions, feeling stressed and looking for a little breathing room. "We are determined to tackle the root causes of poverty, and to provide immediate support to those who need it. "We are keeping tackling poverty and the cost of living firmly on the agenda." title: Residents warned not to drink tap water after hundreds fall sick near South Africa capital
description: More than 400 people, mostly children, become ill after drinking contaminated water, east of Pretoria.
body: Tests found traces of E. coli in water supplied to residents living near Pretoria Residents living near South Africa's capital, Pretoria, have been warned not to drink or cook with tap water after more than 400 people, mostly children under four, fell ill after drinking contaminated water. The cases were detected in Tshwane, the area which includes Pretoria, after people reported to their local hospital with "stomach cramps and diarrhoea" over a two-week period, officials said. No deaths have been reported but high levels of E. coli were found in the water. Tshwane has faced numerous outbreaks from waterborne diseases in recent years. In 2023, 29 people were killed by a cholera outbreak in a township just outside Pretoria. That outbreak, in Hammanskraal, was linked to substandard water purification practices. In 2025, officials confirmed 48 cases of typhoid in the same area east of Pretoria. The source of the outbreak remains unclear. No cholera bacteria has been found in the latest cases. The departments of water and health, in a joint statement on Monday, said 408 cases had been detected between 7 and 18 October in about five townships. They said that lab tests "indicate that the illness has been caused by residents being exposed to contaminated water" from a local water treatment facility supplying water to several communities east of Pretoria. Samples tested found norovirus, campylobacter, shigella and "other pathogens that cause stomach cramps and diarrhoea", officials said. The team's early investigations found that local authorities had failed to warn residents about the contaminated water. The water supplied to the area has been declared unfit for human consumption and authorities urged residents to only use it to flush toilets. Tankers have been dispatched to supply clean drinking water. "Previously stored water should be discarded, and water containers must be disinfected using household bleach," officials said. title: Armed police swoop as man, 61, arrested for murder and woman in car crash dies
description: South Wales Police said a 47-year-old woman had suffered injuries "unrelated" to the crash.
body: This video can not be played A 61-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 47-year-old woman died on Monday A 61-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman who crashed her car died. South Wales Police said the woman, 47, from North Cornelly, Bridgend, crashed into a wall on Coity Road at about 12:43 BST on Monday. But the force said she had suffered injuries "unrelated" to the crash. It followed armed police swooping on a nearby sheltered housing retirement complex, Ger-y-Nant, where the man was arrested. There remains a heavy police presence in the area, including six officers, police cars and vans. A cordon is in place around Ger-y-Nant, which is accommodation for over-60s and consists of 13 flats. Armed police on the roof of a sheltered housing complex in Bridgend Ch Supt Jason Rees said this was a "deeply distressing incident" and thanked the local community for its support which resulted in an arrest and no further injuries sustained. "We thank those displaced from their homes overnight for their co-operation at a worrying time as we support them in returning home." Ger-y-Nant, a sheltered housing retirement complex, where a man was arrested Eyewitness Darren Owen, 33, has lived on Brook Street opposite the retirement home for 18 years. He said: "I was concerned to see all the police. It was very strange to see it outside your front window, armed police, drones and there were vans, police vehicles all the way to the hospital. "I've never seen anything like it before, you see police but the amount of armed police and swat teams climbing on to the roof of the building. "We do get some trouble at the top end of street, but when I heard it was at the retirement home it caught me by surprise that was last place I expected to see armed police." Owen said he "heard a bit of commotion outside at about 1am and saw the police bringing a man out of the building". Local residents say they have never "seen anything like it before" Another resident, Muhammed Bobalazi, 19, said he could not go home because of the police cordon. "I turned up after college to try and get home and the road was closed, but I wasn't allowed (in) and came back at midnight and finally got in just before one in the morning. "There were fire service and police and I couldn't get close to my flat." Roz Thomas had concerns about the area. "The flats have all complained about problems at the nearby houses," she said. "It used to be lovely place but I won't even walk with my granddaughter now because of all the problems with drink and drugs." title: Watch: Pigs on the loose bring A-road to a standstill
description: The decision to shoot five of the 20 animals over safety concerns was not taken lightly, police say.
body: This video can not be played Motorists filmed the moment 20 pigs brought cars to a halt on an A-road. The animals caused mayhem on the A127 at Dunton, near Basildon, as they darted in between cars on Sunday afternoon, leading to the road's closure. Firearms officers from Essex Police decided to fatally shoot five of the pigs due to the perceived danger to road users, while the rest were safely captured. A spokesman for the force said the decision "was not taken lightly" and that it was unknown where the animals came from. title: Storm Austen to bring severe gales to UK as weather warning issued
description: The first named storm of the season - Austen - will bring damaging winds and heavy rain to parts of the UK on Friday.
body: Storm Amy in October 2025 brought some damage and disruption as severe gales and heavy rain hit parts of the UK The first named storm of the autumn - Storm Austen - is set to batter parts of the UK with severe gales and heavy rain beginning from Thursday night. Ahead of the storm, the Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for wind, which will come into force at midnight Friday. Damage to buildings and transport disruption is likely, with the possibility for power cuts. While Storm Austen will move away later on Friday, another deep area of low pressure will bring more wet and windy weather on Saturday. Storm Austen will move across southern England through Friday Over the next few days there willl be heavy rain across the UK, along with strengthening winds on Wednesday around west Wales and southern England. But, it is from late on Thursday where a rapidly deepening area of low pressure - named Storm Austen by the Met Office - starts to approach from the Atlantic. Heavy rain will move in across England and Wales through Thursday night accompanied by strengthening winds. A Met Office yellow wind warning will be in force from midnight on Friday to 12:00 BST and covers south Wales, south-west England and along southern coastal counties of England. Wind gusts of up to 70mph are expected which will likely bring damage to buildings, travel disruption and the risk of power cuts. The wettest and windiest weather of the autumn will hit much of the UK over the coming days More widely gusts of 50-60mph will be felt around west Wales and through southern England. While the strongest winds will ease from the south-west later on Friday morning, the rest of England and Wales will stay blustery with heavy rain at times through the day. Scotland and Northern Ireland will largely miss any of the impacts caused by Storm Austen. Storm Austen will clear away into the North Sea later on Friday and while there will be a quiet spell with clear skies overnight into Saturday, another area of low pressure will move in for the start of the weekend. This deep area of low pressure - not expected to be as severe as Austen and therefore unlikely to be named - will head towards Scotland. Gusts of 70-80mph will affect western Scotland with delays or cancellations to ferries and restrictions on bridges. It will turn windy elsewhere across the UK throughout Saturday with heavy rain spreading east for most of us. Sunday will turn drier but it will remain very windy, particularly towards the north east of Scotland. title: Reform leader accuses MSP of 'squatting' in seat after resignation
description: Malcolm Offord says he is 'disappointed' at Amanda Bland's decision to leave the party and sit as an independent.
body: Malcolm Offord called called on Amanda Bland to resign her seat after leaving the party The leader of Reform UK in Scotland has accused an MSP of "squatting" in a Holyrood seat won by the party. Malcolm Offord said Amanda Bland did not have a "personal mandate" to stay in the Scottish Parliament after she resigned from Reform to sit as an independent. Bland, who was elected as a list MSP for Central Scotland and Lothians West in May's, denied claims she had stood down after being called to a meeting about high turnover among her office staff. Offord said he was "disappointed" by her decision but Reform "wanted people who could work as a team". Bland's departure relegates the party to third-largest in the Holyrood chamber, behind the SNP and Labour. Offord told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast he had not spoken to Bland since she announced her departure from the party. Reform MSP quits party to sit as independent Conservative MSP Graham Simpson defects to Reform Reform MSP Graham Simpson did not resign when he defected from the Scottish Conservatives in August 2025. Offord said that situation was different as Simpson only had eight months of his term left before May's election, while Bland is just a few months into her five-year tenure. "Amanda's got her own reasons and, clearly, I'm disappointed. But she feels she can make more impact standing as an independent," he said. "She is now proposing to squat in a list place won by Reform for four-and-a-half years." He added: "It just looks to the voting public like there is a distinction between a constituency, where I would say you have won a personal mandate. If you are a list MSP, you are there just on the vote for the party." Amanda Bland resigned from Reform to sit as an independent at Holyrood A Reform source told BBC Scotland Bland's departure came amid claims she was "difficult to work with". She had allegedly been called to a meeting last week to discuss high staff turnover within her parliamentary office, but Bland denied her resignation came as a consequence of that. In a statement, Bland said her "principles and priorities remain unchanged" and that she believed she could best pursue her goals of "holding the Scottish government to account" as an independent MSP. Under Holyrood's rules, any list MSP who resigns their seat is replaced by their party's next candidate at the last election. As Bland is remaining as the Scottish Parliament's sole independent, Reform now have 16 MSPs, one behind Labour's 17. That means they will not receive joint billing as the main opposition during first minister's questions. Offord described Reform's slip into third place as "irritating" but said it would not "derail" their objectives. He said: "We want people who are talented and bright and Amanda is talented and bright, but we also want people who are prepared to work as a team. "One of the great things we're doing at Reform is building a team." Offord said some in his party had been "surprised" by what he called the "poisonous atmosphere" at the Scottish Parliament. Prior to their election only former Conservative MSP Simpson had previous Holyrood experience. Offord claimed other parties were "resentful" of Reform's presence in the chamber. The party attracted widespread condemnation for tabling a debate about banning face-coverings, including burkas, from public places. "We've been taken by surprise frankly, in Holyrood, by the amount of vitriol," he told the programme. "It's a pretty poisonous atmosphere, quite a difficult atmosphere to be in. The other parties are very resentful of Reform being there. "For the Reform folk coming in, some of them have been taken by surprise by the amount of unpleasantness around and some of have found it more difficult than others." title: Why Israeli Gen Z voters are drawn to the far right
description: More than half a million young people will cast their ballots in Israel next week - and they could make all the difference.
body: Far-right minister Ben Gvir (left) has significant support among Israeli youth When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme. His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers. On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards. At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote. "We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said. Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country" More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity. Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result. More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth. And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network. "Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle. "Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing." "Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav. "I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology." Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice. "Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7." Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next week Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis. Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition. As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks. "I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people." The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks. But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that. "For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me. "They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time." Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matter A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis. The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website. Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions. In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference. Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates. Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc "In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett. title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
description: Influential Labour figures had been pushing for equalising CGT and income tax, but critics have said this could drive wealthy people out of Britain.
body: Chancellor John Healey says he wants to avoid an investor exodus from the UK Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July. Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times, external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences. The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets. If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%. Last year, HMRC estimated that lifting the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by £3.6bn in 2028-9. The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits. "I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said. Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business". But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate. Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government. He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work". Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to the Financial Times, external. Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget. Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living. It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes. Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices. The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year. The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers. The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt. In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to urge the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing. She will tell the prime minister and the chancellor to "live within our means" and signpost her party's plan to save £70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid. The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise £14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks. The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses. title: Job vacancies fall as small firms cut back on recruitment
description: Small firms cite labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring, the Office for National Statistics says.
body: Job vacancies in the UK have seen their largest fall since the start of the year as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate. Vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), which said small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring. Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff. The ONS figures also showed the unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the lowest for more than a year. The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before Chancellor John Healey presents his first Budget next week. ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment". "The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said. "The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor." The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs. Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms. Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty". However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment". The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added. The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year. Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment. Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover". But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said. Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened". But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising". The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body. The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates. In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? title: Can a simple photo of your face reveal how ill you are?
description: AI may help doctors judge how ill a patient is using a single photograph of their face, say US researchers.
body: An AI tool may be able to help doctors judge how ill a patient is using a single photograph of their face, say US researchers. Trained on millions of healthy faces, and 35,000 photos of cancer patients, the tool can make estimates on survival by looking closely at features near the eyes, the scientists say. While it's a long way from being suitable for use in hospitals, the researchers say their goal is to help doctors recommend the right treatments for their patients. The preliminary findings are published in the Lancet Digital Health, external journal. The researchers developed two AI tools to estimate biological age and predict cancer survival from a single face photo. The face on the left shows features most important to cancer survival outcomes, while the right face shows those key to age. Areas shown in yellow had the greatest impact on predictions. The 'FaceSurvival' AI tool suggests the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose are the most vital parts of the face to assess when estimating how long they might have left to live. These metrics applied across many different types of cancers, varying in severity, including ones that had spread to the patient's bones or brain. Most of the cancer patients, who were from the US and the Netherlands, were in their 50s or 60s, but some were children, while others were in their 90s. Doctors already examine patients and run comprehensive checks and tests to judge how unwell they are, and what their prognosis might be. The AI tool, which has a patent application pending, is designed to help doctors doing this work, not replace them. Lead researcher Dr Raymond Mak, from Mass General Brigham in Boston, explained: "As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy. "Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment." Collagen: Do you drink it? Inject it? Rub it on your skin? And does it work? Why doing a mix of exercise could be the key to longer life Can two hours of strength training a week reduce the risk of dying early? Mak and colleagues are also evaluating an AI tool for predicting biological age, or how old someone looks, as opposed to their birthday age. The 'FaceAge' tool suggests the skin below the nose and near the mouth - the so-called nasolabial folds and marionette lines - plus the forehead (frown lines), temples (crows' feet) and cheeks are a good indicator of how fast we age. Some lifestyle habits can speed that process up, like heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking. Mak says the tool was "surprisingly consistent" across common real-world photos despite variations in pose, lighting, facial expression and make-up. "It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty [a nose job]," he says. But the researchers stress they need much more data and photos of faces, particularly from lots of different ethnic groups, to determine how well the tools work. They are still very much under development. The research team is inviting the public to take part, external and receive a personalised biological age estimate by uploading their own facial photo the research team. Prof Miroslaw Bober, an expert in video processing and machine learning at the University of Surrey in the UK, says any claims that the tool could track ageing or lifestyle changes over time would be "premature". "This is a promising proof of concept, but it is not ready for clinical use," he said. "The tool still needs testing against doctors' own judgement and across different hospitals and patient groups." And he warned: "Predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it." title: Will Lindblad and Lawson be retained by Racing Bulls? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the United States Grand Prix.
body: Liam Lawson (right) is ninth in the drivers' championship with 75 points, while Racing Bulls team-mate Arvid Lindblad is 11th with 38 points Kimi Antonelli has his first opportunity to secure the 2026 drivers' championship at this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin. Antonelli must win the race with Mercedes team-mate George Russell finishing ninth or lower and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fifth or lower. Austin is the first of six races scheduled to take place between now and the end of the season in December. BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the race in Texas. Will Liam Lawson get the Racing Bulls seat for next year? - Chris Racing Bulls are one of only two teams where the 2027 driver line-up is not finalised. The other is Haas, where Oliver Bearman has not yet been confirmed alongside new signing Rafael Camara, although that is only a matter of time. At Racing Bulls, it's a three-don't-fit-into-two situation, with current race drivers Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad in the frame along with Red Bull junior driver Nikola Tsolov, the Bulgarian who is second in the Formula 2 championship at the moment. This is the first time in Red Bull history that Helmut Marko is not in charge of driver choice at the junior team and it's unclear what approach they will take under the new management. In the past, one might have expected them to drop Lawson, on the basis that he has had his chance and is not likely to be considered a long-term candidate for a full-time seat at Red Bull, and put Tsolov in alongside Lindblad. But there is an argument that the Red Bull young driver programme has been mismanaged for 20 years by Marko and former team boss Christian Horner and they should take a more considered, patient, methodological approach. In the past, Marko and Horner took a very ruthless approach. A driver would get a shot, and if they did not deliver pretty much immediately, they were dropped. On one level, it made sense - they were looking for world-class drivers who could lead Red Bull. And if a driver was not that level, they felt they had no use for them. But at the same time, it sometimes meant putting two unknown quantities together, which made it harder to judge the quality of either. An alternative approach might be to keep a known-quality benchmark on board against which it is easier to judge the ability of a newcomer. On that basis, it would make sense to keep Lawson and Lindblad together for 2027 and make Tsolov the reserve, put him in the simulator and give him some tests in older cars to provide him with F1 experience. The reasoning is that while Lindblad's debut season has been impressive in patches, Lawson is consistently quicker at the moment, both in qualifying and in races. So if Lindblad is to be considered a future candidate for Red Bull, this argument would go, he should be given an extra season to prove whether he can consistently beat Lawson. Because if he can't, the obvious conclusion is that he is not a candidate for the senior team. If they put Tsolov in with Lindblad, they have two unknown quantities, which helps no-one in the bigger picture. A decision has not yet been taken, and ultimately it rests with the shareholders, Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz, with under them Red Bull CEO Oliver Mintzlaff, who is in overall charge of the F1 programme. Why is F1 going to another country, Rwanda, with what can only be described as very poor human rights? Is this another case of if you have the cash we'll come to your country irrespective of significant international concern regarding the suppression of political dissent, press freedom and the country's military involvement in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo? - Paul Formula 1's owner Liberty Media has been looking to establish a race in Africa since it took over the sport in 2017. It was the one glaring omission from the calendar, and the race in Rwanda will give F1 a presence on every single inhabited continent, as well as access to a largely untapped market. But finding a country that is suitable to be a host has not been easy. Various possibilities were investigated. There was a project in Morocco near Tangier, but that didn't have the necessary finance. At one point, F1 looked quite close to a deal to return to Kyalami in South Africa for the first time since 1993, but there were issues with the promoter. There are currently as many as four separate projects in South Africa, including Kyalami and two in Cape Town. But they are all too far away from being realistic possibilities. Many - if not most - grands prix are funded by governments in one way or another, so it's hardly a surprise that the one African bid to come to fruition has government backing. It's a sensitive situation because Rwanda receives international aid, and the government and F1 have been keen to emphasise that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment. Then there are the accusations of 'sportswashing' - a term given to the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic. Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture. DRC's Minister of Foreign Affairs Therese Kayikwamba Wagner issued a statement last week to say that while DR Congo supported the idea of a grand prix in Africa, they were opposed to Rwanda being its host. She accused Rwanda President Paul Kagame of "fuelling a devastating war in our country", adding that wars in the DRC have claimed millions of lives, that people continue to be driven from their homes and Congolese natura

title: French cities calm overnight after curfews imposed to quell violence, PM says
description: Sébastien Lecornu said new curfews for Tuesday night would be decided where necessary.
body: This video can not be played Clean up begins after French riots but police remain Targeted curfews across France contributed to a quiet night following a weekend of riots and looting across the country, the Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said. Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area. Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they are necessary. Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors. The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities. He had been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron. More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured. Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups. title: Orionid meteor shower to peak in UK skies this week
description: Clear skies permitting, skygazers could be able to spot as many as 10-20 meteors per hour as the shower peaks this week.
body: The Orionid meteor shower, which is capable of producing bright fireball meteors, is set to peak in UK skies this week. While it has been active for most of October, the celestial spectacle will be at its best in the early hours of October 22. Clear skies permitting, skygazers could be able to spot as many as 10-20 meteors per hour. Where the weather is less cooperative, there will still be chances to catch a glimpse of the shower until 7 November. The Orionids are an annual meteor shower caused by debris left by Halley's comet in its journey around the Sun. Every year, Earth passes through the comet dust and the debris burns with the friction caused by the atmosphere, creating a bright streak of light through the sky. The Orionids are fast and bright, entering our atmosphere with speeds of around 41 miles per second. They can often produce long glowing trails and fireballs. To spot them, find a dark spot with wide open skies, away from city light pollution and let your eyes adjust to the night sky for 20 minutes. The meteors are visible to the naked eye so you won't need any specialist equipment like binoculars or a telescope. The meteors will appear to originate from the constellation of Orion, near the red supergiant star Betelgeuse. This is known as the radiant. Between midnight and dawn the constellation will climb higher in the sky to the south and then the south-west. It is best to view the meteors slightly away from the radiant as they will be more visible. Unfortunately, the Moon will be in the waxing gibbous phase on the night of the 21 October, throwing extra light into the night sky and reducing visibility. However, conditions will improve once the Moon sets around 03:00 BST on Thursday morning. Meteor showers are best seen in cloudless skies. Unfortunately for skywatchers, this week looks to be the wettest and windiest week so far this autumn with a strengthening jet stream propelling low pressure systems across the UK. All is not lost, however. While Wednesday is looking wet and windy for many parts of the UK, a brief ridge of high pressure could mean that there is a chance of clear spells for many parts of England, Wales and Northern Ireland for the second half of the night into Thursday morning. There may also be some clear skies for a time for western Scotland. Eastern Scotland looks cloudy and wet with a lingering front and the far south coast of England could also see outbreaks of rain. title: England unchanged to face France after Tonga defeat
description: Brian McDermott keeps faith with the England team beaten by Tonga as they bid to revive their Rugby League World Cup campaign against France in Perth this Saturday.
body: AJ Brimson, who keeps his place at full-back, scored one of England's two tries against Tonga England coach Brian McDermott has named an unchanged 19-man squad for Saturday's Rugby League World Cup match against France. This is despite a 30-12 defeat by Tonga in their opening game which has put England's chances of progression to the semi-finals in danger. AJ Brimson retains his place at full-back in the XIII with Jack Welsby among the interchanges. McDermott has kept faith in his players as they prepare for Saturday's Group B-C match in Perth (kick-off 07.35 BST). England men: AJ Brimson, Dom Young, Hugo Savala, Herbie Farnworth, Zach Eckersley, George Williams, Harry Smith, Max King, Brad O'Neill, Luke Thompson, Junior Nsemba, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley. Interchange: Jez Litten, Ben Currie, Ethan Havard, Sam Walters, Jack Welsby, Matty Ashton. Reserves: Kallum Watkins, Mikey Lewis, Ben Talty. 15 October - 15 November Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app Luke Thompson will continue at prop with Morgan Knowles still not fit to play after picking up an injury before the Tonga game. And Mikey Lewis, who was a much-debated pick for the squad as one of the half-backs ahead of 2025 Super League Man Of Steel Jake Connor, remains out of the team. Harry Smith will continue alongside England captain George Williams in the half-back roles, despite both being overpowered by Tonga last weekend. This video can not be played Tonga stun England in World Cup opener That defeat, England's first ever against Tonga, has left McDermott's side with a tough task to reach the semi-finals. England must win their next two games, against France next Saturday and Papua New Guinea on 30 October, to stand a realistic chance of progression - and because of the World Cup's format, probably need to win them both by a big score. Even then, there is the strong possibility that England will not know their fate for certain until two days later, when Tonga face 2022 finalists Samoa in their last group game. Jenna Foubister had a superb campaign with Wigan Warriors last season In contrast to McDermott, England women's coach Stuart Barrow has made a big selection change before their blockbuster meeting with co-hosts Australia on Saturday. Jenna Foubister will start at half-back, replacing Georgia Roche, after a superb year in the Super League where she was named Woman of Steel. The 19-year-old, who scored on her debut in a 62-0 win against Wales in August 2025, will partner Izzy Rowe in the halves. Rowe scored two tries and kicked nine conversions for 26 points as England opened their World Cup campaign with a 70-6 win against Wales last Saturday. She equalled the record for the most points by an individual England player in a Women's World Cup match. There are two other changes to the XIII, as Molly Jones replaces Georgia Wilson in the centres while Liv Wood plays at prop ahead of Mary Coleman. Lucie Sams is named among the interchanges as England take on reigning champions Australia in Perth with kick-off at 10.05 BST - immediately after the men's match. It will be the first time England have played Australia since they suffered their record defeat - 90-4 - in Las Vegas in March 2025. England women: Fran Goldthorpe, Anna Davies, Molly Jones, Connie Boyd, Amelia Brown, Izzy Rowe, Jenna Foubister, Liv Wood, Keara Bennett, Hollie-Mae Dodd, Jasmin Strange, Eva Hunter, Megan Williams. Interchange: Jodie Cunningham, Vicky Whitfield, Georgia Roche, Lucie Sams. Reserves: Mary Coleman, Georgia Wilson, Lucy Murray. This video can not be played Brown scores stunner as England thrash debutants Wales Wales face Samoa in their second ever World Cup match on Friday at 07:45 BST, and coach Thomas Brindle has made several changes. Amberley Ruck replaces Ffion Lewis, with Zoe Heeley moving from centre to the wing. Jade Mullen comes into the centres, while wing Sian Williams also gets a start. Wales women: Leanne Burnell, Zoe Heeley, Jade Mullen, Hannah Bluck, Sian Williams, Amberley Ruck, Tayla Preston, Agnes Wood, Jasmine Gibbons, Emily Hughes, Georgia Cussons, Paige Travis, Bethan Dainton. Interchange: Carys Marsh, Kathryn Salter, Erin Williams, Gracie Hobbs. Reserves: Ffion Lewis, Lucia Davies, Frances Layton, Katie Carr. This video can not be played Australia clinch thrilling World Cup opener against New Zealand Australia coach Kevin Walters has dropped Reece Walsh to the bench for their second group game against Fiji on Sunday (09:05 GMT). James Tedesco replaces Walsh, and will captain the co-hosts and men's World Cup favourites. Walsh, who had not played since 15 August amid injury troubles, was rusty as Australia were pushed by New Zealand in a thrilling World Cup opening match last Thursday. He scored a try but kicked just two of five conversions as the Aussies squeezed to a 24-22 win at Sydney Football Stadium. Tedesco won the Clive Churchill medal for best player in the NRL Grand Final as Sydney Roosters beat Newcastle Knights 19-18 on 4 October. And he earns his place in the XIII here as one of five changes made by Walters. Bradman Best, Sam Walker and Blayke Brailey all come in for their Test debuts. Tedesco takes the captain's armband from Isaah Yeo, who is rested. Yeo has delayed surgery on a torn pectoral muscle to play at the World Cup. title: Race, illness, injury, repeat - REDs and why men are suffering in silence
description: British long-distance runner Jake Smith was enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat - he had no idea he had REDs and was under-fuelling.
body: Race, illness, injury, repeat - REDs and why men are suffering in silence Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders "If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30." That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago. From the outside looking in, his career was flying. By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage. But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat. Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over. After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport. It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems. The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027. But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence. BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science. REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues. Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake. "Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says. "In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely." Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check". Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off". For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue. The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad". But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes. "We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says. "It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented." Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men. Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability. Jake Smith was regularly getting injured So why is REDs so common? One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'. For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics. And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started. "I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says. "I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went." Initially, the strategy can work. When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement. It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results. But eventually, the luck runs out. Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries. This video can not be played The athletes affected by relative energy deficiency in sport Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries. "I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport. "You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well." Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue". "In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
