title: The British island where red squirrels are thriving
description: Conservationists say that, with red squirrels dwindling in the UK, Jersey is an "important refuge".
body: Conservationists say Jersey is an "important refuge" for red squirrels With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England, one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold. Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins. Red squirrels are endangered in the UK, with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers. There have some strongholds in England, external, particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland, external. However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey". He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK. "That is actually really special for them." Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885. However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years. The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey, external tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle. National Trust ecologist Henry Glynn says red squirrel sightings can be a highlight for visitors The National Trust of Jersey said the island was an "important refuge" for the red squirrel, where they were "fairly widespread, external". It said the inland valleys and woodlands were the best places to spot them. The species is legally protected, which means it would be a criminal offence to harm them. Nina Powell, senior animal carer at the JSPCA [Jersey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals], said Jersey has a "good population" of squirrels and that "you can see them almost anywhere". While the primary reason for their success is the lack of grey squirrels, Powell said they also thrived "because people look out for them". She said: "A lot of people do support them, put out feeders and stuff like that. "Their habitats are decreasing everywhere... but we do have quite a lot of nature reserves. "In some places, we've got rope bridges which really help them cross the roads, and our speed limits are quite low, so that helps them as well". Nina Powell from the JSPCA said the red squirrels it comes into contact with can have quite different personalities More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey She said the JSPCA had handled 50 red squirrels so far this year, including hand-raising eight babies, called kits (kittens). She said: "We want to keep all animals as wild as possible, so we try and be as hands-off as possible. "Some of them don't like us... some of them are quite sweet. They really do vary in personality." Glynn agreed that their success had come in part because of the efforts of islanders. He said: "They're really beloved amongst the local community as well. A lot of people put out squirrel feeders or love to see them in the garden. "We get lots of reports from people who just want to tell us they've seen them because they're so happy to have them around." title: NHS trust prosecuted over children's sepsis deaths
description: Charges relate to the deaths of a two-year-old and a three-year-old at Broomfield Hospital in Essex.
body: Zadie Ajetunmobi was described as a "beautiful little girl" by her parents An NHS trust is being prosecuted over the deaths of two children who had sepsis, the BBC has learned. Two charges relate to Zadie Ajetunmobi, three, who died within hours of being taken to Broomfield Hospital, Essex, with a temperature of 40C (104F) in November 2022. A third regards two-year-old Selina Samarina, who was sent home by a doctor at Broomfield in April 2024, only to die two days later. Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust (MSE), which runs the hospital, said it was "working closely" with investigators. It is due before Chelmsford Magistrates' Court in December. Care and treatment was allegedly "not provided in a safe way" to the girls, court documents revealed. The prosecution is being brought by the Care Quality Commission under the Health and Social Care Act. Zadie died within 10 hours of being taken to Broomfield on 10 November 2022, having suffered a cardiac arrest. A post-mortem examination showed her death arose from complications associated with sepsis, external. She was not given a potentially life-saving dose of intravenous antibiotics for more than seven hours. Zadie Ajetunmobi died at Broomfield Hospital in Chelmsford in November 2022 Zadie's family were previously told by MSE that staff had not updated local sepsis guidance since 2017. Her parents, Theo and Rhiannon, described her as a "beautiful little girl" and added: "This is a tragedy from which we will never recover." Selina Samarina was taken to Broomfield with symptoms of fever, a rash and irritability on 7 April 2024. She was discharged by a doctor but died there two days later, after her parents readmitted her. The sepsis protocol was triggered on Selina's initial arrival at hospital, however a coroner previously said a doctor of appropriate seniority was not available until two-and-a-half hours later. Selina, who had Down's syndrome, was sent home by a "very junior doctor" in the meantime, assistant coroner Stephen Simblet KC said during an inquest into her death. Adam Sewell-Jones, group chief executive of MSE, said: "We are working closely with the CQC on its investigation. "As there is an ongoing legal process, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage." MSE is expected to enter pleas to the three charges on 3 December. title: Northern Ireland needs 'courage and leadership' to tackle climate change
description: The new chair of the Climate Change Committee is spending two days in Northern Ireland on a fact-finding mission.
body: "Courage and leadership" are needed to ensure Northern Ireland catches up on tackling climate change. The new chair of the Climate Change Committee, Nigel Topping, is spending two days on a fact-finding mission to hear the thoughts of people across different sectors. He said Northern Ireland was a small nation that could be "agile and innovative" in tackling challenges like increasing renewable energy, improving waste management and reducing emissions. But he warned that a failure to act would mean missing out on innovation opportunities, paying more for energy and damaging the health of children. The Climate Change Committee is an independent body advising the UK and devolved governments on emissions targets. Over the course of a two-day visit, Topping is meeting farmers, people from the business sector and politicians. It is being described as a fact-finding mission, looking at "challenges and opportunities". He acknowledged that politics in Northern Ireland was "complex" and that "when things flip-flop, it doesn't help", due to the impact on investment decisions and people's choices. But he said there was "a real sense of collectively wanting to catch up" and avoid anyone being left behind on the road to net zero. "You've had these lags where there's been no ministers sitting and so there hasn't been policy - there's been civil servants working but no policies," he said. "It's going to take some real courage and leadership from all sectors of society to make sure that the just transition process is a conversation, that it doesn't just disappear into polarised views in different corners of different rooms." A really simple guide to climate change Updated plan aims to boost NI's resilience to climate change Northern Ireland was the last part of these islands to adopt climate change legislation, which brought in legally-binding targets for reducing emissions. Topping said people were experiencing climate change firsthand, with the effects of extreme weather being felt around the UK. And he added that that would continue, until emissions reached net zero. "But I see this as a race between our kind of obstinate, greedy selves and our brilliant, innovative selves," he said. "And all of us have a bit of both of those extremes and we have those as societies, and I think if we can really tap into backing ourselves as innovators, then we can take this as an opportunity. "The most important thing for me is that we're going to do this and we're going to have to do this because this is a collective chance for humanity. "So we can either see it as a burden and complain all of our way and be laggards, or we can see it as an opportunity and say, we're resilient, we're adaptive, we're innovative. Nigel Topping is the new chair of the Climate Change Committee When asked what will be the consequences of not taking that "opportunity", he is blunt. "There's two ways of answering that question. One would be, oh, if Northern Ireland doesn't do anything, it doesn't make much difference to the world," he said. "The other would be, if Northern Ireland doesn't do anything, it misses out on all the innovation opportunities, because other people take those. "It continues to poison its children's lungs because it doesn't fix the air quality, and it continues to pay more for energy than it needs to. "So that's like, dumb, dumb, dumb - why would you do that? "So don't get stuck in the we're only small, what difference do we make? "But see it as an opportunity as a small nation to be agile and innovative and derive benefit in all those different areas." title: Changes to GCSE Maths 'pulling the rug out from under pupils'
description: From 2027, students will only be able to take a GCSE Maths exam in November if they are re-sitting the subject.
body: Cara is hoping to raise her grade by sitting more Maths GCSE exams in Year 12 There have been calls to pause changes to GCSE Maths which will lead to many exams taken in November each year being scrapped. From 2027, students will only be able to take their exam in November if they are re-sitting the subject. One head of maths in a County Tyrone school said that was "pulling the rug out from under pupils who need those structured manageable steps to succeed". But the Department of Education (DE) said that schools had been given "sufficient notice to plan for the revised arrangements". In some schools, pupils take their Maths GCSE exams in stages throughout the course, using a staggered approach. For example, at Dean Maguirc College in County Tyrone pupils sit some exams in November and summer of year 11. That gives them a GCSE grade which they can increase by sitting more maths exams in year 12. But from 2027, they will not be able to do that anymore as the November exams will only be for students who have finished their GCSE Maths course and want to re-sit the subject. The decision has been taken by the Council for the Curriculum, Examinations and Assessment (CCEA) exam board and DE. Spacing out exams allows for extra revision, Maeve says At Dean Maguirc College, an all-ability school, 15-year-old Maeve said maths was a vital subject to learn. "It's to do with everyday life and you need it for loads of stuff like money and most jobs," she said. She said that being able to sit some of her maths exams in November gave her more time to revise for her other GCSEs in the summer. "They're not all crammed together," she said. "For maths, like, there's a lot of stuff to learn so when you have the one exam to do in November you can learn all of that for November, you don't have to keep looking over it until summertime." Maeve said that, in her opinion, the decision was "not fair". The changes are set to come into effect next year Fifteen-year-old Cara is also currently studying maths for GCSE at Dean Maguirc College and she also has concerns. "Getting half of your exam done with in November I found it really eased the pressure," she said. "And it allowed me to focus half of my subject into June." As she had achieved a C-star grade by the end of year 11, she is hoping to make her grade higher by sitting more maths GCSE exams in year 12. She said that being able to divide the maths exams up and take them in stages benefitted everyone and is worried about the impact of the changes. "I think it's unfair and gives less of an opportunity for the people upcoming," she said. "Nearly for every single career you need maths and you need GCSE Maths." Liam, 17, says it feels like the exam board are "pulling down a ladder that helped students" Seventeen-year-old Liam is now studying A-levels at Dean Maguirc College but said that being able to take GCSE Maths on a "staggered" basis had helped him get a B grade. "I did struggle at maths when I was younger," he said. "It feels like CCEA are pulling down a ladder that helped students like me climb higher, because not all students are able to do it in one go and instead have to do it step by step. "So they can gradually reach their full potential." Máire McGinn is head of maths at Dean Maguirc College and had previously served on Northern Ireland's literacy and numeracy task force. "Maths is everywhere and it underpins everything that a pupil is going to need to get through their future life," she said. "For about the last seven years we have had a carefully structured, staggered approach to the study of maths." Máire McGinn says a staggered approach to maths exams has worked for students The "staggered" approach has worked for students at college, as the proportion of their students achieving grades A* to C at maths is well above the Northern Ireland average for non-grammar schools. "It provides manageable milestones for pupils, structuring it like that," McGinn said. She said CCEA was "pulling the rug out from under pupils who need those structured manageable steps to succeed". Many other maths teachers across Northern Ireland also felt that "this policy change is not in our pupils best interests", she added. "I would ask CCEA to pause what they have suggested is going to happen and consult with teachers." A DE spokesperson said: "The decision to change the November CCEA GCSE Mathematics examination series to a resit-only series from 2027 was an operational decision taken by CCEA. "CCEA has advised the department that the decision followed consideration of a range of educational factors, including the impact of assessment arrangements on pupils' learning and on teaching time in schools. "CCEA's Maths GCSE will continue to be a modular qualification with pupils able to sit modules at the end of Year 11 as well as the end of Year 12. "The November series will remain available for pupils who have completed the qualification and wish to improve their grade." The changes will apply from 2027, "providing schools with sufficient notice to plan for the revised arrangements". title: Food aid charity under pressure from fuel costs
description: FareShare South West says fuel costs are putting immense pressure on work helping thousands in need.
body: FareShare South West has its distribution hub in Plymouth Soaring fuel prices are putting extra pressure on efforts to get food to thousands of people in need across Devon and Cornwall, the South West's largest food redistribution charity has warned. FareShare South West said demand for food support had risen by 45% since the Covid-19 pandemic, while the cost of collecting and delivering surplus food had increased sharply. The charity, which redistributes surplus food to about 70 organisations across the region, said it was facing the challenge of meeting growing demand while absorbing higher operating costs. Bosses added they were also concerned about the impact on volunteers and staff, many of whom were paying more to travel to their shifts. FareShare South West is an independent charity that obtains surplus food from food producers, farmers, supermarkets and other businesses before it goes to waste. It relies on a mix of government, corporate and independent funding. Recent increases in wholesale oil prices have contributed to higher fuel costs, making travelling and transporting goods more expensive for charities, businesses and households. Ryan Jackson said costs had "increased significantly" It operates from a distribution hub in Plymouth, where about 80 volunteers and four paid staff help sort, organise and load tonnes of surplus food each week. Much of the food, including fresh fruit, vegetables and dairy products, is distributed to charities and community groups. Hub manager Ryan Jackson said: "With petrol rising by 31% and diesel by 41% in the last six months, our costs have increased significantly and those are costs the charity has had to absorb. "At the same time, the number of charities requesting support from FareShare South West has grown across the region." Jamie Henshaw said there "may come a point" when some volunteer cannot afford to come and help The charity said the rising cost of fuel could also affect the people it relied on to keep the service running. Volunteer Jamie Henshaw said: "Everybody's feeling the pinch, but we love what we do. "Volunteers aren't paid, so this comes out of their own pockets. They're giving their time and goodwill. "There may come a point when some simply can't afford to come to work." A crate of apples is ready to be delivered from FareShare's Distribution hub Jackson said prolonged high fuel prices could create further challenges for the charity. "If fuel prices stay high for a long period, it could affect our ability to recruit and retain volunteers," he said. Despite the additional costs, FareShare South West said it remained committed to meeting growing demand. The charity said it planned to move to a larger hub in Plymouth later this year and create more food collection points across the region. title: Locals honoured in Notting Hill Frieze exhibition
description: London street artist Endless's new installation, Endless Frieze, includes buildings and street scenes.
body: Some of the local Notting Hill legends featured in an installation in west London as part of the annual Frieze art fair. (Clockwise from top left - Karl Amata, Allyson Williams, Jama Emli and Karen Millen) A fourth-generation Portobello market trader, a Notting Hill Carnival stalwart and fashion icon known locally as "Notting Hill's best dressed man" are among the people featured in a new artwork by street artist Endless, about Notting Hill's identity. The installation, Endless Frieze, displays local buildings and street scenes celebrating the west London neighbourhood as part of the annual art fair Frieze London. Guests and celebrities specifically chosen for their contribution to the area's identity were photographed during a live event on Friday and now feature as part of the exhibition. The work is "about the community and bringing them into the art world and into my world," Endless said. Cheryl Devlin has worked on a fruit and vegetable stall in Notting Hill since she was five years old This world includes Cheryl Devlin, a greengrocer whose family have had a fruit and vegetable stall in the market for more than a hundred years. She has worked on the stall since she was five years old. "I used to stand beside my mum and dad and sell lemons, five for a shilling," she says. "And if you didn't, you didn't get your dinner; it was really that tough in the '50s." The area has changed since then, she says. There used to be around 350 people selling fruit and veg, but that's been replaced with stalls selling cooked food or bric-a-brac. "A lot of people downsize who can't afford the housing. "It's just tough to live around this area now where it was quite cheap and reasonable." Street artist Endless says the installation recognises the contributions locals have made to the area Like the area, the exhibition is ever-changing. It's being created in real time - as soon as the portraits are taken they appear on the wall, in a collage - something Endless says can be a creative risk. "It becomes a frieze, a moment in time of the architecture, the buildings and the people. So it's really about the energy of the place. "Whenever I make any artwork, I plan it and I have a vision, but then it can go either way," he says. "There's like elements of risk even when you're making a painting. So with this the risk is life, anything could happen. So the camera could go wrong or I could stick it up wrong but that's part of it. "In art we say it's like a happy accident and that's when something good happens as well." "I'm in the art, in the fashion, I'm a walking art," says local legend Jama Emli Also part of the artwork, and perhaps a gift to photograph is Jama Elmi, a recognisable individual who admits he is a "local icon". "Notting Hill, it's vibrant, the energy, the love, it's absolutely, I wouldn't live anywhere else but here," he says. Allyson William's company Genesis Mask Band is always visible at Notting Hill Carnival For Allyson Williams MBE, Notting Hill simply is the carnival. She is a board member of Notting Hill Carnival Limited and has been involved with its organisation since 1975. In 1980, she launched her own costume brand with her husband, called Genesis Mask Band. "I have been a seamstress, I've been a designer. I've been bringing the costumes - the designs of my husband and my daughter - bringing the costumes to life." Part of the reason she loves the carnival is because it is part of her history. "I'm a Trinidadian and so it all started there and it was the Trinidadians who came, who were part of the Windrush generation who came and brought all the art and culture here," she says. Karl Amata says Notting Hill needs more community events to bring people together Karl Amata works at Sound Records on All Saints Road. He says the exhibition is a good thing. "I hope it continues. We need more things like this to bring the community together. "Because there's the lack of it. Everything's been shut down, the shops, every cultural centre, anywhere people can gather together." Karen Millen, founder of the Karen Millen clothing brand said she was "very honoured" to be part of the installation. She added Notting Hill is the "epicentre of where people come for creation really, so I don't think that will ever go away." The exhibition at the Cris Contini Contemporary Gallery runs till the end of October. title: 'Alice Cooper is a character, like Jekyll and Hyde'
description: Alice Cooper reflects on faith, fame and addiction ahead of his Wolverhampton book tour appearance.
body: Alice Cooper opens up about his stage persona in his new book Rock legend Alice Cooper has opened up about his redemption arc from the stage to the church ahead of a book tour pit stop in Wolverhampton. "It's such a strange life that I had because I was the prodigal son. I grew up in a Christian church, went as far away as you can, then came back," he told BBC Radio WM. It comes after the singer-songwriter published his autobiography, Devil on My Shoulder, earlier this month, detailing the highs and lows of his nearly six-decade career that earned him the title of the Godfather of Shock Rock. He is set to appear at the University of Wolverhampton at The Halls on Tuesday. Known for hits such as School's Out, Poison and I'm Eighteen, Cooper, whose real name is Vincent Damon Furnier, spoke about the stark difference between himself and his on-stage alter ego. "Alice, the character I play on stage, couldn't be more opposite to me. Fans pay tribute to Liam Payne two years on Call for artists to bring dragon trail to life Fire stations face reduced cover under new plans "All through the book, I'll say something and the character will come in and go, 'Wait a minute, that didn't happen like that', so I'm arguing with my character - the Jekyll and Hyde thing all the way through the book, which is kind of unique," the 78-year-old said. He added: "I love playing him because that's who he is and he should be that on stage, but off stage we don't think alike at all. "I'm in church on Sunday. I even teach Bible study sometimes and you would look at the character on stage and go 'how can that be?'" The rock star also spoke openly about the dangers of drugs and alcohol and warned that today's young people face a far more dangerous environment than previous generations. "When I was on cocaine, I was an entirely different person. All of my senses went away and I was living for the drug, so it's a form of possession," he said. "And same with alcohol. I know people who are the nicest people in the world but, as soon as they drink, they become just the opposite. It's almost a poison or an allergy or something." The singer spoke about Solid Rock, an organisation he launched to support young people by offering free after-school training in music, dance and art. "I think kids are living in a really dangerous world right now. What's going on on the street is a much more dangerous world than what we had. Fans will have the chance to meet the legend during his book tour stop in Wolverhampton "The drugs that are on the street right now will kill you very quickly, whereas in our day, if you got caught with a joint or got caught with a beer you were in trouble if you were underage. Now it's heroin, that's a big jump. "In the 70s, when we were going, it was normal. In fact, it was unusual if you weren't doing it. Now, we've all learned from all the people who died at 27 that it doesn't work." During his trip to Wolverhampton, there will also be a Q&A session for fans to engage with the star. The event will be the last of eight dates on the UK book tour, which has also included Cardiff, Cambridge, Brighton, Manchester, Stockton-on-Tees and Glasgow, as well as the London Palladium. title: Unseen Only Fools clips add depth, filmmaker says
description: New clips from The Jolly Boys' Outing, shot in Margate, feature in a new show about the sitcom.
body: David Jason, Buster Merryfield and Nicholas Lyndhurst as Del Boy, Uncle Albert and Rodney in The Jolly Boys' Outing Previously unseen footage from a much-loved episode of Only Fools and Horses will reveal more depth and texture to the characters of the classic British sitcom, the maker of a new documentary has said. Only Fools and Horses: The Lost Archive will show previously cut clips from a number of episodes including The Jolly Boys' Outing, filmed and based in Margate. Richard Latto, a comedy archive specialist who unearthed some of the material, said it showed how well written the characters were and he hoped the scenes could be used in extended episodes. He told the BBC the Jolly Boys' Outing footage "was absolutely amazing to find" and he remembered watching it with his family on Christmas Day. Latto added: "The episodes are so well known, so to now have scenes that aren't so well known that are still incredibly funny made it special. "I think people will see much more depth and texture to the characters, and learn a bit more about them." Latto said much of the newly-found content was scenes which had been removed to meet time restrictions, but were still of good quality. The episode saw the characters embark on a chaotic, ill-fated coach trip to the seaside New scenes from The Jolly Boys' Outing include an extended look at the coach trip to Margate as well as the entire footage of the group's rollercoaster ride at Dreamland from the 1989 Christmas episode. The episode saw Del Boy, Rodney and Uncle Albert, played by actors Sir David Jason, Nicholas Lyndhurst and Buster Merryfield, embark on a chaotic, ill-fated coach trip, along with the Nag's Head pub regulars, down to the coast from their home in Peckham, south-east London. It has become one of the shows most beloved episodes, reaching a viewership of more than 20m people and inspiring tours of Margate based on the show. Latto said that new shots for the documentary had been fully digitized, and he hoped this could help episodes of the show be restored in high definition. "I think a full restoration would be excellent. We could do it in high definition, with extended, full versions," he said. title: Rantzen felt 'deprived of choice' over her own death
description: A note written by Dame Esther Rantzen is released by her family following a private funeral.
body: Dame Esther Rantzen died at her home in Bramshaw, in the New Forest, on 30 September A posthumous note written by Dame Esther Rantzen said she was "deprived of any choice over my own death". The farewell message was released as the 86-year-old broadcaster and campaigner's family confirmed she had been laid to rest in an "incredibly beautiful" private funeral last week. The Childline founder, who was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023, died at her Bramshaw home in the New Forest, Hampshire, on 30 September. A larger memorial service is expected to take place at a later date. Rantzen's daughter Rebecca Wilcox said the family had been inundated with messages since her death. "It's been hugely comforting to know that people around the world felt the same way about her as we did," she said. Dame Esther became a prominent campaigner for assisted dying in her later years, something MPs voted against legalising in September. In her note, she wrote: "It would have transformed the way I died if the law had allowed me to ask for assistance to die when my life had become unbearable. "I was extremely lucky because I had the talent, skill and support of my local Oakhaven Hospice. "But I was still deprived of any choice over my own death by the current messy criminal law." She said she had become "too physically frail to take the flight" to an assisted dying clinic in Switzerland. More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight Addressing those who opposed the change in the law, she wrote: "Rest assured I will not come back to haunt you, I have better things to do." She also wrote: "Nobody wants to shorten life, just to shorten death." Arthur Stickland, who has been on the committee at Bramshaw Cricket Club for 60 years, said the That's Life! team played annual matches against the village side for about seven or eight years. He said Dame Esther always came along with the show's presenters and backroom staff, and remembered her as "an ordinary person". "You wouldn't know she was actually here. She just mingled amongst the crowd," he said. He said she was a vice president of the club, and that in the village "everybody knew who she was and nobody tried to bother her". Dame Esther presented That's Life! for 21 years and set up Childline in 1986, and later The Silver Line helpline for older people. Her family has asked for donations in lieu of flowers to Oakhaven Hospice, Childline, The Silver Line and Cats Protection. title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
description: Ahead of the midterms Trump has boasted about the performance of the US economy. BBC Verify looks at inflation, jobs and economic growth in the country.
body: President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs. Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world." While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households. The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up. So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims. The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards. The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%. And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term. That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period. The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025. It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending. Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy. The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country. Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office. Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic. The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%. That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025. Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office. While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation. The price of a gallon of diesel in the US, external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September. The price of some grocery staples , externallike beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen. And some US retailers have warned, external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till. Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump. The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external. However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households: - The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans - Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off. The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts. ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external. Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border. Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month. ​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external. And the number of Americans employed in manufacturing, external - 12.6 million in September 2026 - is slightly lower than it was when Trump's second term began. However, the US unemployment rate remains relatively low, external at 4.2%, which is broadly where it was when Trump returned to the White House. Part of the reason for this is Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation programme, which has reduced the size of the available US workforce, external and means a lower number of jobs need to be created each month to stop unemployment rising. US government borrowing has increased in Trump's second term, partly driven up by his significant tax cuts. The federal government deficit - the gap between its revenues from taxes and its spending - was $2 trillion in the year to September 2026, external. That's equivalent to around 6%, external of US GDP. And the US deficit is projected to rise to above 8% of GDP by 2030, external. title: We asked teens what schools should teach them about work. This is what they said
description: Teenagers say they want more work experience at school and opportunities to improve their communication skills.
body: More than four in 10 UK teenagers want more work experience opportunities at school, with a similar proportion calling for more guidance on how to apply for jobs, a survey for the BBC suggests. The online survey, by Survation,, external asked 2,000 young people aged 13 to 18 about the world of work and the help they need to secure employment once they leave full-time education. Some called for more support with their communications skills and raised concerns about stress management and personal finances. Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was the government's "mission" to ensure teenagers leave school "confident about their next step and equipped with the skills and experience they need to succeed". In England, the government wants to guarantee two weeks' of work experience for every young person, external during secondary school. It's an opportunity not all teenagers are currently given, the survey for the BBC suggests, with more than half of respondents saying they had not done any. When teenagers were asked in the survey what skills or guidance they would like more of at school, the most common responses were more work experience opportunities (44%) and help managing finances (43%). Respondents said they also wanted guidance on how to apply for jobs (42%) as well as how to manage stress and mental health (39%) and develop their communication skills (38%). As part of the Teen Summit project by Radio 5 Live and Bitesize, the BBC followed four students from Newcastle - Param, McKenzie, Jasmine and Javaris - as they tried out roles for the first time as part of their work experience placements. "I'm terrified about the future. I feel very uncertain about it," 15-year-old Jasmine said. Jasmine said she was determined to make the right choices with what she does after school Jasmine said she enjoyed her placement working on logo designs at web design and development agency Readysalted. But she said the placement made her realise she was probably unsuited to an office job. "Hats off to all the workers that have to do this every single day," she said. She said it gave her a real taste of working life, but that she was still worried about making "the wrong decision" around what to do next. "I think about exams and not getting the right grades, which leads to not getting into the right course and then not getting into university, and it's very stressful," she said. "That's always on my mind." A 15-minute walk up the road from Jasmine's placement, near the centre of Newcastle, her classmate Param had his work experience at social housing group Re:Gen. Param said it showed him there was more to work than simply having the right knowledge and understanding. "Social skills are just as important as academic skills," he said, after a day of meeting clients and working with people he had never met before. He also spent time with staff carrying out quality checks on social houses, looking for loose fittings or uneven surfaces. "It's given us a taste of the real world," he said. "It's bringing us out of our comfort zones." As an aspiring pilot, he said schools should not just provide work experience opportunities, but additional teaching on other aspects of adult life outside of work. "We need to know about houses, mortgages, selling and tax," he said. Param said he enjoyed working with new people, which brought him out of his comfort zone Javaris, who spent a week's placement at Siemens Energy alongside friend and classmate McKenzie, also said the work experience challenged his social skills in a new setting. "I've really never been in a workplace with people I don't know, having to socialise and having to teach me about things I've never learned before," he said. Javaris ultimately wants to become a doctor, but said the week had given him an insight into how different parts of a company are run. McKenzie, who wants to study chemistry or become a firefighter, said he enjoyed speaking with people in different jobs and seeing the differences between "hands-on" roles and office work. Javaris and McKenzie were able to learn about how a business is run at Siemens Energy In light of AI and new technologies in the workplace, nearly a third of teenagers responding to the survey (32%) said they thought school was preparing them badly for the future of work - although more than half of teenagers said it was preparing them well. One of the areas young people said they wanted more help with was developing communication skills. The BBC set Javaris and McKenzie a challenge to help develop their own communication skills, and put some of their thoughts directly to one of their work experience company's bosses - Aaron Smith, head of business for Group Technology Service at Siemens Energy. So, beyond academic results, what skills are employers really looking for? "You know, you can be extremely academically strong, but if you can't do a presentation, if you can't speak in public, if you are in a group exercise and you step back, these are the kind of softer skills that will be picked out in an apprenticeship assessment centre," Smith said. This video can not be played Teens ask bosses what they're really looking for The pair were also keen to know if they should be studying AI as part of their education. McKenzie said he thinks AI should be added to the national curriculum, adding that "it's getting harder and harder to see what's AI and what's not". He said he was also concerned about the impact AI may have on the availability of jobs, but added that he was "positive" about his future prospects. "Certainly AI is huge within the industry," Smith said. "We're actively encouraging AI training, AI learning, AI applications in our business to make us better." title: Canadian tourist found guilty of animal cruelty after stealing Las Vegas flamingo from enclosure
description: The man testified that he snatched Peachy from its enclosure at the Flamingo hotel and casino after drinking 30 to 40 beers, but did not mean any harm.
body: Fairbarn was seen on CCTV in an elevator on the way to his hotel room with the flamingo A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender. Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March. Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison. Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions. A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions". "He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external. "The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions." His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest. Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird. He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird. The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles. During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges. Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December. A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans. title: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
description: Almost 300 people have been injured, more than half of them police, as violent anti-government demonstrations show no sign of easing.
body: Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes. The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence. "The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen". A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation. The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack." In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait. People in Rinia park loosen cobblestones to use as ammunition against riot police A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters. Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas. Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range. "The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested. "In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said. "Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said. Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem. Protesters were ready with saline spray to help to relieve the effects of tear gas Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her. "In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK." The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said. She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it. "When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said. "They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up." At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down. "We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups. Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said. "I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said. Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it. title: US church on frontline of battle against drug known as 'tranq'
description: Synthetic opioids like fentanyl are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.
body: This video can not be played America has been fighting the War on Drugs for decades, but the drug cartels, the suppliers and the dealers appear to be always one step ahead of the authorities. President Trump has declared the cartels, "terrorists" and labelled fentanyl, the powerful synthetic opioid, a "weapon of mass destruction". But the drug supply is changing, with other deadly synthetics being added to the mix, including strong animal tranquillisers, known on the streets as "tranq". While overdose deaths are falling, the potency of the new drugs has recovery workers worried. For some the answer might lie in reducing demand, giving users support and helping them end their addiction. BBC international correspondent Quentin Sommerville and camera journalist Darren Conway travelled to Columbus, Ohio to find out more. title: 'The French correction' and 'Labour cuts £2bn from Army'
description: Violent unrest in France continues and Defence drops funding for frontline military vehicles lead Tuesday's papers.
body: Many of Tuesday's front pages depict the unrest sweeping through France, where violence sparked by student protests continues to cause major disruptions. "The French correction" is the Metro's headline, embedding a picture showing a row of Paris riot cops next to the caption "Formez vos batallions". President Emmanuel Macron is quoted saying "extreme-left thugs and thieves will not win", as the paper goes on to explain: "French towns and cities have been told to declare curfews in a bid to end days of rioting and looting". The Independent continues with "Curfew imposed to stop France riots as unrest grips Europe", below a photo showing a masked demonstrator in Marseille holding a French flag as a fire burns in the backdrop. "Italy prepares crackdown" it says as cost of living and housing anger spreads to "Lisbon, Albania and Serbia". "Challenges facing Macron deepen" says the Financial Times, taking a markets perspective of the riots to report "10-year bond yield sharply up" in France following a "self-off in French government debt". It cites experts who say "the protest had made investors 'more reluctant' to hold the debt" ahead of the "high-stakes election" when Macron gives up the presidency in 2027. Returning to the UK, the Daily Telegraph writes: "Labour cuts £2bn from Army", reporting that the Ministry of Defence has "dropped plans to three new frontline vehicles". It comes as Chancellor John Healey "attempts to fill a hole in defence spending in his first Budget", due on 28 October. Continuing with pre-Budget speculation, the Times says "no increase to capital gains tax" is expected to be handed down as "chancellor resists pressure" from allies of Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Healey is quoted saying he wants a "steady as she goes" budget rather than, as the paper describes as a "huge package of tax rises and public spending that dominated the fiscal events of Rachel Reeves, his predecessor". The i Paper leads with its scoop that the government will lift the "two-child cap on childcare benefits" by April, meaning parents on benefits will get "£736 extra per additional child to assist with nursery costs". The paper quotes experts who believe "lifting the cap on nursery fee support offers a route back to work for parents on universal credit with more than two children 'at a critical time of rising costs'." Tory leader Kemi Badenoch's criticism of John Healey's expected budget tops the Daily Mail, where it summarises her perspective: "Budget could be even worse than Reeves bloodbath". Badenoch suggests Burnham's new government could impose "more damage to the economy than his predecessor, despite Labour already hiking the tax burden to a post-war high", according to the paper. The Guardian tops with Burnham ordering his policy advisers "to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company". It explains that the proposal is a "test" of the prime minister's promise "to bring the 'essentials of life' under public control". The Sun leads with a "£20m crash probe" after "two pilots steered away from buildings and ejected before the Hawk T2 nosedived and exploded near RAF Valley, North Wales, last month". According to an early investigation, the "RAF fireball jet was flying with its fuel cap off". The Daily Star picks up on the latest Manchester City alleged financial misconduct saga, reporting that they are set to get a "huge" points deduction risking "relegation", attributing the details to "shock reports". It could be "Man City's tipping point", the paper says. The Daily Express carries the warning from NHS doctors that the health service is "simply not ready" for another winter crisis, writing that "patients are dying every week in struggling A&E departments" amid rising flu admissions. Finally, the Daily Mirror caps off with a lighter touch headline about the paper's Pride of Britain awards. "Trophies and tears for nation's everyday heroes" it writes, as "Stars humbled by tales of courage and sacrifice", including young fundraiser of the year Kirsty Waugh and Dr Eli Prior "who helped train crash victims". title: Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists
description: Will Fatima El Mansouri advance women’s rights amid religious and political barriers?
body: El Mansouri (left) was named by King Mohammed VI (right) as the country's first female prime minister The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister. Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office. He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men. Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch. El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament. El Mansouri, 50, presented her appointment as a milestone for Moroccan women El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power. The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government. Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice. One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me." Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy. Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire. A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like. However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment. While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight. Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce. Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances. The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence. It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones. In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women. Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife. But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality. These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody. A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law. As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls. Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%. "Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC. She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products. "Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says. El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament. For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch. After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women. "Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said. Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code. In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated. The king of Morocco, Mohammed VI, holds the title of Commander of the Faithful, a traditional Islamic title embedded in the Moroccan constitution Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests. "Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minis

title: England coach should be English, suggests Fleming
description: New Zealander Stephen Fleming, England’s new Test coach, suggests the national team should be led by someone from England.
body: Stephen Fleming was appointed England Test head coach in July New Zealander Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, has suggested the national team should be led by someone from England. Fleming, who will take charge of his first series in South Africa in December, is the latest overseas coach to lead the England men's team. Since 1999, only two Englishmen - Peter Moores (twice) and Chris Silverwood - have been in charge of the Test side, while Ashley Giles had a spell as white-ball coach. In the same time period England have been led by two Zimbabweans, in Duncan Fletcher and Andy Flower, and Australian Trevor Bayliss - while Fleming has succeeded his fellow Kiwi Brendon McCullum, who remains white-ball coach. Another Australian, Matthew Mott, also had time in charge of the white-ball team. Fleming's backroom team, announced last week, is heavily weighted towards homegrown coaches. Former England opener Marcus Trescothick, who was in interim charge of the Test team earlier this year, is joined by ex-England wicketkeeper James Foster and former spinner Richard Dawson. Jonathan Trott, an Ashes winner with England, is about to begin a spell in charge of England Lions. Both Trott and Dawson were in the running for the Test job before Fleming was appointed. Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former New Zealand captain Fleming said it will be a "priority" of his tenure to help develop English coaches. "I do believe that primarily the national team should be coached by a national representative," said Fleming. "I'm grateful for the opportunity, but there will be some development in terms of the coaching, and you can see by our staff." As well as Fleming and McCullum filling the head coach roles for the men's national teams, England's selector, Marcus North, is Australian. In September it was announced that another Australian, Leah Poulton, will become the managing director of England women. Between 2020 and 2023 England women's head coach was Lisa Keightley, the former Australia international. In addition to developing the coaches on his own staff, Fleming said he will also occasionally invite county coaches and former England players into the set-up. "There are some really key people who have come back into the system and I'm really pleased about that," he said. "I look forward to working with them, but it is a real focus and it's an ambition as well that you will also get county coaches who will be introduced at certain times and you will get past players that will be asked to come back as well. "It's really inclusive and a comfortable nature of using what's around, but also driving what should be driven within the county game and the English game." Listen to the full interview with Stephen Fleming on the TMS podcast One of the criticisms of McCullum's four-year spell in charge of the Test team was his lack of time spent around the county game. In September, Fleming visited some counties and also spoke of his affection for the domestic game in England. The former batter had spells as a player with Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Middlesex. He confirmed he will spend part of next summer watching county cricket in the build-up to the home Ashes series. "Yep, I'll be around and I really enjoyed this year getting to catch up," said Fleming. "A lot of the guys I played with are now in positions either coaching or the head positions at counties. "It was good to catch up with those guys and get a feel for where the county game is at. I really enjoyed it and it will be a key part to continuing developing players." Fleming was appointed in July, though did not take charge for the series against Pakistan in August and September, meaning his first series at the helm will be the three matches in South Africa in December and January. The squad for that series is due to be named in the first week of November. England did not pick a specialist spinner in any of the three Tests against Pakistan, instead fielding four frontline seamers. In South Africa's ongoing Test against Australia in Gqeberha, the tourists have omitted Nathan Lyon despite the off-spinner sitting sixth on the all-time list of Test wicket-takers with 573. Last week, Shoaib Bashir was named as the only specialist red-ball spinner on England's list of fully centrally contracted players, while Mason Crane and Liam Patterson-White were given development deals. Following the tour of South Africa, spin will play a big role on the two-Test tour of Bangladesh in February. Asked if Bashir's contract means he is England's number-one spinner, Fleming said the Derbyshire man represents "continuity". "I acknowledge there's a raft of spinners just below that, that at times are putting their hand up," said Fleming. "There is a raft of spinners there and are probably looking for an opportunity, and finding those conditions, it could be Bangladesh, where there could be two or three that will come along. "The team could look quite different and that's the horses for courses example. "But Bashir has got some experience and is still very young. There's an aspect of still looking and developing, and trying to find that right combination in the spin department." title: Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?
description: After every round of Premier League matches this season, Troy Deeney gives us his team of the week. Do you agree with his choices?
body: After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week. Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page. Bart Verbruggen (Brighton): I was looking at other teams, but there were so many games this week with very poor quality. Even David Raya against Forest had two shots to deal with, terrible from a goalkeeping point of view, so Verbruggen goes in for his clean sheet. Levi Colwill (Chelsea): He goes in only because Chelsea got a clean sheet in the league for the first time since January. He stepped up with the young goalkeeper Mike Penders in there. Gabriel (Arsenal): Arsenal win 1-0 and get the job done. He was right at the heart of it. A lot of people talking about Ezri Konsa, I like him but Gabriel offered that bit more in terms of experience and quality that you need to get the job done, so he goes in. Luka Vuskovic (Brighton): It is the same reason Verbruggen was in. Everyone else can't defend. He was good. They had a clean sheet against their nearest rivals. Diogo Dalot (Manchester United): Played at left-back and I thought he was amazing. Could he offer a little more in terms of quality? Absolutely. But high energy, dealt with the physical threat, defended well and offered an outlet going forward in a game that was very scrappy. Manchester United just needed to show resilience and he was right at the front for that. Sander Berge (Fulham): It was a massive game against Hull, a six-pointer and if Fulham lose that they are going down in my opinion. But they got the job done and he was at the heart of everything good for them. Diego Gomez (Brighton): He scored from the halfway line, nothing more needs to be said. Pedro Neto (Chelsea): Two goals, wins the game for Chelsea. He is one of those players when you look at him you think 'he is good, but I don't know why he is good', but in this game he put it all together. With all the talk of Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer, he could have a sneaky good season because these guys will take the attention of defenders and Neto can get in with his pace at the back post. Johan Manzambi (Aston Villa): By far the player of the month so far. An unbelievable young talent from Switzerland, 21 years of age, carrying this Aston Villa team with an aura and humbleness of 'I want to learn and do more', but also 'I'm the man of this team, give me the ball, let me show you what I can do'. James Maddison (Tottenham): Welcome back James Maddison. Spurs needed a bit of quality in the final third and we were unsure who would score for them, and Maddison puts it in the top corner. Great to see him back, great to see him healthy and great to see him smiling. Erling Haaland (Manchester City): For already the third time and with probably another 10 times to go, Mr Erling Haaland. Started up top, job done, two goals against a really poor Ipswich team and he could've had a hat-trick. Unreal from him. Fabian Hurzeler (Brighton): He is doing an unbelievable job. A lot of people, including myself, were wondering whether he doing a 'pat myself on the back lap of appreciation tour' after beating Arsenal - but actually what he was showing is that he is a very good manager who can continue to deliver week in and week out. He was fantastic, got the tactics spot on and also introduced some players who had been out injured. Do you agree with Troy's selections? Who would be in your Team of the Week? title: Criminals detained in hospital set to lose benefits
description: The families of the victims of Nottingham killer Valdo Calocane had been campaigning for the change.
body: The families of the victims of killer Valdo Calocane had been calling for his benefits to be stopped Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families. Regulations due to be laid in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to £800 a month in universal credit over several years while already having their bed and board funded through the NHS while receiving psychiatric treatment. The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds annually. The parents of Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023, welcomed the announcement. The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to Parliamentary approval. Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were killed in the Nottingham attacks Students Barnaby and Grace, and caretaker Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020. Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, and detained at a high-security hospital. Barnaby's mother, Emma Webber, said: "This is long overdue, and simply the right thing to do. "It was a disgrace that Calocane and offenders like him have ever received taxpayers' money. "A hospital bed does not erase the egregious crimes committed, nor the destruction they have caused. "Closing this loophole finally delivers some basic accountability that victims deserve." Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness. "Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount. "On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits. "On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated." Gogoa Lois Tape, 28, was also detained by hospital order after strangling his partner The mother of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche who was killed by her partner Gogoa Lois Tape in Hackney, east London, in April 2024, also lobbied for benefits paid to offenders in psychiatric hospitals to stop. Tape was given a hospital order detaining him indefinitely after he pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility. Kennedi's mother Linda Westcarr said: "For many victims' families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society. "In my view, this is not simply a question of policy, it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised." Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche was killed in April 2024 The government said the move followed engagement with victims' families and experts as part of its plan to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system". Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "We said we'd act to tackle this gross unfairness and we're delivering on that promise. "For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price. "That ends today because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it." Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately said: "Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed. "Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control. "The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers' money goes only to those who genuinely need it." The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983 and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995. The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13. Murder is not included because a hospital order is not an available sentence for the offence. The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the government said, with the full financial impacts of the move due to be published as part of the 2026 Budget on 28 October.
