title: I have a condition people are too embarrassed to talk about
description: Women share their experience of lichen sclerosus.
body: Monica is the founder of charity Women's Health Hope This report contains detailed descriptions of medical symptoms. Monica Thomas was in her teens when she started experiencing intimate itching and soreness, but despite numerous trips to the doctors it was dismissed as thrush. Her symptoms got worse, with sores and blisters leaving her in constant pain. "I was bed bound for quite a long time because I couldn't walk," she says. Monica says she was examined 28 times in six months before being offered a biopsy. She says "we don't really talk about" gynaecological health as a society so there is a taboo around speaking about symptoms. "Even when we go to the doctors, for me, the embarrassment of having to get undressed...with these doctors looking it is embarrassing," she says. "But equally when you're in pain or it's itching and you've got discomfort, living with it is just as bad." The 34-year-old from Suffolk was eventually diagnosed with a condition called lichen sclerosus. Dr Nighat Arif is author of The Knowledge: Your guide to female health – from menstruation to the menopause The lifelong inflammatory condition affects genitals and can cause white patches to form with itching, soreness, splitting and tears, says Dr Nighat Arif, a GP specialising in women's health. It affects men and women but is more common in women over 50, external. There is also a small risk of vulval cancer., external "It's very sore to have sexual intercourse, to pass urine and it gets mixed up with sexually transmitted diseases but it's not contagious," she tells BBC Radio 5 Live podcast That Time of the Month. Research into the prevalence of vulval lichen sclerosus is limited but analysis by the University of Bristol of people in the West Midlands and Warwickshire estimated it affects about 1% of women. Dr Sophie Rees, who helped conduct the research, tells the BBC: "This is almost certainly an underestimate, as we know that there is often a very long delay to diagnosis, and some people probably go their entire lives undiagnosed. "There is unfortunately a lot of shame and embarrassment around seeking help for vulval symptoms, as well as a lack of awareness, even amongst healthcare professionals." She adds: "More research is badly needed into true prevalence." Monica says multiple misdiagnoses had a "significant" impact on her mental health. "I didn't know how to go on... with having no answer, it was just a horrific, lonely time." She was given medication for herpes. "I was very upset in an appointment with a dermatologist who got quite angry with me because I was like, 'it's not that'. "Then she said that she wanted me to have blood tests for HIV." Doctors told her she was "too young" to have lichen sclerosus. "But sadly, women do have it at all ages, you can have it as a child. So I found that really quite difficult, but I always knew that it wasn't right." That Time of the Month What is lichen sclerosus? Listen now. Monica believes there should be more support for those with lichen sclerosus. "Once you have a diagnosis, you're still necessarily not treated in the manner that you should, I don't even get a checkup," she says. "I manage it on my own with my steroid cream and hope that I'm doing everything right." According to the NHS website,, external the cause of lichen sclerosus is unknown. It might be caused by the immune system mistakenly attacking and damaging your skin. It is not contagious, caused by an infection or by poor personal hygiene. Rubbing or damage to the skin can trigger the condition or make it worse. Clare urged anyone with any symptoms to make sure they were examined by a doctor Clare Baumhaeur, 53, from Kent first experienced symptoms aged five. "I was itchy and I was sore, and I was always told off, I wasn't obviously aware what was going on." Her symptoms worsened into adulthood with tears, blisters and sores. "But you don't see other vulvas, so I had no idea mine wasn't normal. I'd had in that time eight smear tests as well and nothing was ever said." In 2016 Clare experienced a tear which did not heal. "I was 43 that year, having it for 38 years at that point, I just couldn't take it any more." A GP told Clare she had herpes and to go to a sexual health clinic, she says she was "shocked" as she had been married for 25 years. She was eventually referred for a biopsy and was diagnosed with lichen sclerosus and vulval cancer. "I'd never heard of lichen sclerosus and also I had a cancer that I'd ever heard of in a place I'd never heard of. "That was the first time I heard the word vulva, no health professional had mentioned it, so it was a lot to take in at that time." Clare had been in remission from vulval cancer for seven years, when a regular check-up revealed a cancer recurrence and she underwent surgery three years ago. In June another check up found pre-cancerous cells and she had a sixth surgery. Clare believes if she had been diagnosed with lichen sclerosis earlier, her cancer may have been diagnosed before it got to stage three. "I had to have radiotherapy twice and that's left me with instant early menopause, lymphoedema and nerve damage." Monica encourages women experiencing any changes to their body to keep a diary. "It's really important that we get to know our bodies better, to know what's normal for you in your private parts as well, because actually our vulvas do change. "If you are being dismissed, get multiple opinions, just keep going back because you don't have to live without answers." She recommended the Lichen Sclerosus Guide, external which has a diagram and template to help you talk to doctors. title: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world
description: As the strongest El Niño on record continues to intensify, what impacts on weather patterns are already being felt across the globe? Sarah Keith-Lucas looks at the evidence.
body: El Niño has been strengthening for several months now and is already having a significant impact on global weather patterns. Countries including Indonesia, India and the United States have been experiencing droughts, floods and heatwaves in line with projections about how extreme weather events will be supercharged by the phenomenon. The World Meteorological Agency says the record-breaking El Niño will strengthen further and persist until at least 2027. Here are five ways its impact is already being felt around the world. Several regions around the world are already experiencing anticipated El Niño impacts Indonesia, which typically trends drier and hotter in El Niño years, is battling its worst wildfire season since 2015. This year, since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned. This is more than twice the area burned last year without the influence of El Niño. The wildfires have led to school closures and an increase in hospital admissions across Indonesia. Millions of people in Sumatra and Kalimantan have been exposed to toxic haze from the fires and around 175,000 people have suffered from respiratory illness. More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers. In the eastern Pacific, where El Niño tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season so far. There have been 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes. This is already above the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season, with two months left to go until its end. Here, El Niño provides the ingredients of higher ocean temperatures and weaker winds high in the atmosphere, making it easier for storms to gain strength. Hurricane Polo is one such example of this. The hurricane experienced rapid intensification, producing wind gusts of 180 mph (285 kmh), fueled by the very warm waters produced by El Niño. Polo was also one of three hurricanes churning away in the same basin at the same time, along with Odalys and Nolo. Moreover, it has happened twice now in the space of a month. Earlier in September, the energy produced by exceptional ocean heat resulted in three simultaneous hurricanes in the central and eastern Pacific: Lowell, Karina and Marie. Until this year, the last time there had been three Pacific hurricanes at the same time was 2015. In contrast, the Atlantic Ocean has remained eerily quiet. El Nino has a tendency to increase wind shear in the north Atlantic, a factor which tears apart storms and limits formation. There has only been one hurricane - Isaias - which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama. This was the latest forming hurricane on record in the satellite era (1960s onward). Before this year, the record was 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013. In an average season, there would have been 10 named storms, five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by this point. This year, however, there have only been eight tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna. The drier and warmer theme has also taken hold in India, where the essential monsoon rainfall has been 13% below average. While the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) would consider this still to be in the 'normal' range, the overall average doesn't reflect the variation in rainfall across India. While Central India had around its normal expected rainfall, the east and north-east were around 26% drier than average and put into 'exceptional' drought. Southern states of India were 24% drier than average. Even where rainfall was nearer to average, the rain did not fall continuously as is typical during the monsoon, instead flipping between long dry spells and extreme rainfall. This adds more stress and vulnerability to agriculture yields. India is influenced by a number of different weather patterns that can affect the monsoon season and so scientists suggest that El Niño may not have been the only factor. Further west in the Pacific, it's also been an active season in eastern China and Japan as storms including Maysak and Dujuan have brought recent widespread floods and landslides. According to the Japanese Meteorological Agency, there have been 10 tropical cyclones forming in the western Pacific Ocean - the highest number in a season since 1966. During El Niño the warmer Pacific brings changes to wind patterns, meaning cyclones tend to form further east, away from Japan and east China. However, this means there is a bigger distance and more time where storms can feed off the warmer waters, gaining energy to become more intense typhoons before they hit land. Scientists believe that additional typhoons are likely to develop this year with the potential for further impacts to Japan or east China. title: Human trafficking 'hidden in plain sight' online
description: A Stormont inquiry looked at four main websites that advertise women for sexual services across Northern Ireland.
body: A Stormont inquiry said 95% of women and girls trafficked to the island of Ireland were brought for the purpose of sexual exploitation Human trafficking is a "catastrophic" problem that is being "hidden in plain sight online", a Stormont inquiry has found. The investigation into "pimping websites" in Northern Ireland was prompted by growing concerns about the exploitation of trafficked and vulnerable women on online platforms. The All-Party Group (APG) on Human Trafficking and Commercial Sexual Exploitation is due to release its inquiry report on Tuesday. The report said such sites allowed criminal gangs to manage multiple profiles and conceal abuse behind the pretence of the women being independent. It said 95% of women and girls trafficked were "brought for the purpose of sexual exploitation". The APG inquiry looked at four main websites that advertise women for sexual services across Northern Ireland - Locanto, Adult Works, Viva Street and Escort Ireland. The websites are publicly available and people will select women and make contact usually through the website, WhatsApp or Telegram. The women are listed as "independent escorts" offering an extensive list of services. However, the reality is much different, the report found. Victim A was forced into prostitution at 19 and advertised online. She said the sites were not neutral platforms. "They provide the infrastructure through which sexual exploitation can be organised, marketed and monetised," she said. "You have the websites but they bring the people from online actively looking for girls, our customer base knew that we were either being drugged before the appointment so that we were completely incoherent, you could not say yes or no, your body is paralysed, that's not said online." Another survivor was managed by a man who controlled the profiles of multiple women trafficked from Brazil. "None of us had access to the emails from buyers. They came directly through him, he answered as if he was us." The report also states the National Crime Agency has identified websites advertising prostitution as "significant enablers of trafficking and sexual exploitation". Ruth Breslin is the director of the Sexual Exploitation Research and Policy Institute BBC NI has spent months looking through these websites and, on average, there are more than 500 women advertising sexual services daily in Northern Ireland. Many of the women are moved around, from city to city. For example, "Chloe" was advertised as being in Belfast for 24 hours. The following day she was being advertised in Dublin with the same line "in the city for 24 hours". Over the next week, she was advertised across the island of Ireland in six different cities, always for 24 hours only. Ruth Breslin, from the Sexual Exploitation Research and Policy Institute, said there were many cases before courts, "both in the Republic and in the north of Ireland where these sites have played a key role in the sexual exploitation and in the human trafficking of women in the sex trade". "We know that women who have been exploited and trafficked are being advertised on these sites," she said. "Banning these sites is the right way to go. Regulation just won't be strong enough in this space. Even if we regulate this space tightly, the exploitation would still continue." The BBC contacted Escort Ireland for comment, but it did not respond. It is the biggest site on the island of Ireland and has been in operation for 30 years. It carries a disclaimer that "the charges are for time and companionship only", adding that "anything that occurs is a matter of coincidence and choice between consenting adults". The report rejected the idea that the platforms can be safely regulated. It stressed that criminal networks would "continue to exploit regulated environments unless the digital infrastructure itself is dismantled". It outlines some recommendations, including criminalising website operators, improving cross-border operational cooperation with the Republic of Ireland and targeted interventions for men. Connie Egan said this report should not be "read,noted and shelved" Connie Egan is the deputy chair of Stormont's all party group on human trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation. "We now owe it to every woman who is advertised in Belfast today and every girl trafficked across this island against her will to ensure this report is not just read, noted and shelved," she said. "Hidden in plain sight across our country is the reality of sexual exploitation and all its associated harms and websites advertising prostitution are undeniably driving this. "I hope survivors and those still trapped in prostitution will hear and read of our recommendations and recognise that they do have a voice." The exchange of sexual services for money is legal in England, Scotland and Wales. But legislation introduced in 2015 makes it a criminal offence in Northern Ireland to pay for sex, either directly or indirectly. However, selling sexual services is not illegal, nor is loitering or soliciting to do so, but running a brothel or controlling prostitution for profit remains a criminal offence. Det Ch Supt Emma Neill is said sexual exploitation was often an unseen crime Since the legislation was introduced on 1 June 2015 to 28 February, there were 134 arrests for the offence for sexual services; of those arrests, 105 were referred to the PPS; five led to conviction. Det Ch Supt Emma Neill, who heads the Police Service of Northern Ireland's organised crime branch, said: "Our clear focus is on identifying and safeguarding victims who have been exploited, while identifying and gathering evidence against members of organised crime groups involved in that exploitation. "Our huge challenge is that sexual exploitation is often an unseen crime. It can happen in plain sight. It's a challenging issue, which cannot be solved by policing along and which requires collective efforts." Stormont to investigate rise

title: In pictures: Dussehra celebrated across India as triumph of good over evil
description: The festival, which commemorates the triumph of good over evil, is celebrated with different rituals across India.
body: The festival includes a variety of celebrations involving actors playing deities - pictured here an actor portraying Lord Ram prepares ahead of a procession in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh Millions of people across India are marking Dussehra, one of the country's most widely celebrated Hindu festivals, with processions, prayers and the ceremonial burning of giant effigies to symbolise the triumph of good over evil. The festival is observed with different rituals and traditions across different parts of the country but with grand celebrations everywhere. It commonly marks the deity Lord Ram's victory over the mythological 10-headed king Ravan. The festival coincides with Vijayadashami, celebrated in eastern, southern and other parts of India, to honour goddess Durga slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Giant effigies of the 10-headed king Ravan are brought out and burnt as part of festivities in Ahmedabad Ramlila, a theatrical performance based on the Hindu epic Ramayan, is performed as part of Dussehra celebrations, seen here in Noida The vanquishing of the 10-headed king Ravan is celebrated as the victory of righteousness over evil, with Sita placing a victory garland around the neck of her husband Lord Ram Smaller Ravan effigies are a common sight at markets ahead of the Dussehra festivities, such as at this one in Delhi The festival is celebrated in different ways across the country - here, people buy flowers at a market in Bengaluru ahead of Dussehra Marigolds are associated with the celebrations as a symbol of the victory of good over evil, harvested ahead of Dussehra around the country Hindus follow a lunar calendar, and Dussehra falls on the 10th day after Navratri, a nine-night festival of worship and celebrations. In the days leading up to Dussehra in northern India, performers wear elaborate costumes and make-up to stage Ramlila, the dramatic retelling of the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana. They recount Lord Ram's exile and his wife Sita's abduction by Ravan, culminating in the battle that symbolises the victory of good over evil. The final act is followed by the ritualistic burning of the effigies of Ravan, his brother, Kumbhkaran, and son Meghnath. The vibrant stage is usually accompanied by a carnival-like atmosphere with food stalls, rides and smaller performances. Ramlila performances often coincide with wider family-friendly events including stalls and rides, as pictured here in Noida In the east and some other parts, as well as among Hindus in Bangladesh, the festival sees devotees worshipping the divine feminine power with Durga Puja celebrations. Temporary tents housing idols of Goddess Durga and other deities are set up across cities and towns. People visit these structures, known as pandals, where Durga is often depicted slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Current affairs often make their way into the traditional celebrations, like theme-based decoration of tents in Kolkata city, which is famous for its Durga Puja celebrations. Goddess Durga is depicted in celebrations as part of Durga Puja, who is said to have slayed the buffalo demon Mahishasura - artisans work on idols for weeks ahead of the event, as seen here in Kolkata Devotees light oils lamps during Sandhi Puja, an auspicious moment of Durga Puja Elaborate and artistic temporary tents are set up to house idols for Durga Puja Traditional dances such as Gujarat's Garba form a key part of community celebrations Dussehra also marks the beginning of preparations for Diwali - the festival of lights - which is held 20 days later. title: The singles choosing in-person dating events over apps
description: The BBC hears from people who think dating events are better value for money than dating apps.
body: Olivia says she chose to attend this dating event because she has "app fatigue" Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive. Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night. "It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs. This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue". She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on. According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year. Edward believes apps are designed so you don't actually find "the one" Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold. "I'm fed up with apps," he says. "I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app." The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker. Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute. "The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes. This video can not be played As you may expect at a dating event many of the singles told us they were keen for that in-real-life or IRL experience. There are a lot of #SingleTok and #Singlelife accounts on TikTok and Instagram reviewing dating events. Candice Gallagher runs an account called @Candilicious and recently went to 10 different dating events in 10 weeks. She describes herself as an entrepreneur and thinks in business terms dating events deliver "much greater return on investment". The 40-year-old says all too often dating online can lead to "chat graveyards" with very limited conversation. "At a dating event, everyone is single, everyone's ready to mingle, and your chances of having a good conversation are much greater." Dating events provide a better "return on investment" than apps, says Candice Gallagher Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money because "you get to meet a range of people" in person for a similar cost to one date from an app. These events typically cost around £15 to £30 and often include a drink and activity or icebreaking gimmick, in this case an app that is used throughout the night. Olivia believes money plays a big factor in dating. "I wasn't working for a bit because I changed careers and because of that I put dating on hold." Olivia remembers thinking it "couldn't be a priority" and feeling she needed to wait until she was "earning enough" before dating again. She is not alone in finding dating expensive. More than a quarter of daters surveyed by Barclays suggested rising costs had changed how they date. And a couple of recent studies suggest the monthly cost of dating - from apps to entertainment and clothes - can add up to around £130. Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet. New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club. Among Gen Z, it was just 4%. The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends. Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, said Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters. As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together. And she said Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app. "What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps." In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with. When pushed by the BBC on whether she thought she had met "the one", she laughs and becomes understandably guarded. "No, I'm not going to name anyone specific. But you'll be invited to the wedding if there is one!" I've been with my boyfriend for two years and don't know his salary 'I'd be put off if he asked to split it': Who should pay on a first date? My friends always want to split the bill equally, how do I say no? title: Maddison's magic moment for Spurs - 18 months in the making
description: On his first start since May 2025, James Maddison provided the moment of magic Tottenham were waiting for in their 3-1 victory against Coventry, writes Phil McNulty.
body: This video can not be played Spurs beat Coventry to earn first league win of the season Roberto de Zerbi has used all the tools at his disposal to discover the missing spark in struggling Tottenham Hotspur, from acting as an amateur psychologist to team bonding dinners, then a sunshine break in Marbella. The answer, at least when Spurs finally moved off the bottom of the table with their first Premier League win this season against Coventry City, came in the shape of James Maddison as he made his first start in 18 months. He missed most of last season after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in pre-season, before fracturing his shoulder in the opening-weekend defeat at Brentford in this campaign. The 29-year-old finally made it back into the Spurs starting line-up to face Coventry - and delivered in spectacular style to set them on the way to a 3-1 victory that De Zerbi hopes will finally give their season lift-off. Maddison could barely keep the smile from his face as he warmed up, then made his mark in the 14th minute by showing what Spurs have been missing with a brilliant right-foot finish from 20 yards, taking Mohammed Kudus' pass first time to arc a sweeping strike high beyond Coventry City keeper Carl Rushworth. It was a moment of sweet relief for Maddison, the goal getting loud gasps of admiration from Spurs supporters as it was shown several times on the stadium's big screens. Maddison shines on return - Tottenham v Coventry ratings Tottenham overcome Coventry to end winless start Even though the goal came against his former club, Maddison celebrated with his trademark imaginary dart throwing motion before kissing the badge on his Spurs shirt. Maddison's significance to Spurs is illustrated by the fact they had won just 12 out of 57 Premier League games since his last top-flight goal, in a 1-0 victory against Manchester United in February 2025. They had averaged less than a point a game since then. And since his last start, at Liverpool on 27 April 2025, Spurs had won only 11 of 49 league games in between, losing 23. Spurs cannot kid themselves that this was a glorious victory. It was actually only their sixth win in the past 37 home league games - drawing 10 and losing 21 - and just their fourth league victory overall in 2026, having played 27, drawn 10 and lost 13. And it was the first time they scored three goals or more at home in the league since the opening day of last season, when they beat Burnley 3-0 in Thomas Frank's first game in charge. There are still too many nerves around Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and in De Zerbi's team for calm and relaxation. The victory margin flattered them somewhat, with Jack Rudoni equalising for Coventry City before Omar Marmoush's strike for his first goal for the club, then another from Ben Davies in stoppage time after a dreadful Rushworth error finally allowed Spurs to enjoy the relief of victory. And there were other things to celebrate. As well as Maddison's successful return to the starting line-up, there was the sight of Dejan Kulusevski finally back as an 87th-minute replacement for Kudus after 526 days out with a knee injury. This video can not be played Spurs 'lack confidence' but we are a good team - De Zerbi Maddison got a deserved standing ovation when he was substituted for Conor Gallagher after 69 minutes, but the reception for Kulusevski was arguably even more rapturous as he finally took to the pitch again after such a long battle to regain fitness. It was Maddison, however, who claimed the major plaudits after he was the driving force behind the win that has proved so elusive - his positive approach playing with a smile on his face provides refreshment of its own after such a depressing sequence of results. He was eager to get on the ball, was constantly probing and prompting, all before he inevitably tired after the break. "I spoke to the gaffer this weekend about it, feeling like it was the right moment for me to go back into the starting XI after a bit of a stop-start start to the season," Maddison told Sky Sports. "I just wanted to play well and show my abilities, show what the team has missed the last 18 months. The gaffer asked me to play and wanted to enjoy watching from the side. Hopefully I did that, and a goal is always nice." If his aim was to show what Spurs have been missing, this was very much mission accomplished. And as well as Maddison and Kulusevski, Marmoush will gain confidence from his strike, another superb curling effort that gave Rushworth no chance. De Zerbi will know this is only a start, with a tough trip to face Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday evening (17:30 BST). He welcomed the return of Maddison and Kulusevski, saying: "They are different players, different talents, different personalities. With them in the dressing room there is a different atmosphere." What changes the atmosphere in the dressing room and beyond most are victories. Now De Zerbi and Spurs can actually build on three points at last, and the sights of Maddison and Kulusevski back in action will have the Italian hoping they can accelerate an improvement after the misery of recent times. title: 'I started ketamine at 14 and needed nappies at 22' - the rise of young people going to rehab
description: For the last two years Megan has been in agony and unable to stand straight because of her ketamine use.
body: Megan said four weeks in rehab for ketamine use is already helping her feel physically better, though it's unclear yet if her bladder damage can be reversed Megan Harmes was 14 when she first tried ketamine. A decade later, rehab is helping her rebuild her life after bladder issues caused by the drug have left her needing to wear incontinence pads. The drugs charity Kaleidoscope says it has seen a huge rise in referrals to its detox and rehabilitation facility over the last five years, with two people referred in 2021 compared to 112 so far this year. The majority of clients are aged 18 to 24. Research is now underway by the University of South Wales into the specific needs of this group, as the harm caused by "chronic, escalating use" of ketamine is far more rapid, over a shorter space of time, than from alcohol or Class A drugs. Services traditionally designed for older adults are having to adapt to support much younger people, it said, with very different needs, with habits often formed while they were in school. For 24-year-old Megan, from Flint in north Wales, drug use became more common among her peers during lockdown. As an aeronautical engineering apprentice, she was suddenly working from home, on full pay, with access to a drug whose price had plummeted. She said at its worst, she was on it "all day, every day", as according to Megan it helped to suppress symptoms or feelings associated with ADHD and borderline personality disorder. "I'm very hyperactive now that I'm sober. I haven't been like that since I was 14, it suppressed pretty much everything," she said. Eventually her ketamine use meant she lost her apprenticeship, causing her to "spiral". Megan later found work elsewhere, but four years of night shifts further entrenched her use, as she would use ketamine to stay awake through the night even on days off. For the last two years she has been in agony, unable to stand straight and needing to wear incontinence pads. "For a 22-year-old wearing pads or nappies, it takes away all dignity," she said. "Back then I really didn't care whether I lived or died - now I don't want to die. "I've been in rehab just over four weeks and I'm getting back to my old self." Megan said she wouldn't know the extent of the damage to her bladder for some time, but she has put on weight and is physically feeling better than when she arrived. Jo Moore said support sessions are also provided for the families of young people who have become dependent on ketamine Jo Moore runs the Birchwood rehabilitation facility for Kaleidoscope and said five years ago they had just one referral for inpatient detox from ketamine. "Since January this year we've seen 112 people come through the door," she said, adding that half their clients are currently being supported for ketamine use. "It's very, very cheap and very accessible - that's what allows people to use it more frequently and at large amounts at the same time." The drug is prescribed in healthcare settings as a dissociative anaesthetic, and also used with animals, but was reclassified as a Class B drug in 2014. This means it is illegal to take, carry, make or sell. Illicit ketamine use among those aged between 16 and 59 in the UK was estimated, external to be about 264,000 people in 2024-25, with those seeking treatment for ketamine use disorders increasing twelvefold over the course of a decade. While younger people have driven the rise in its use, Moore said the last year had seen a rise in referrals for adults aged 25 to 34, particularly in Cardiff and south-east Wales. Dr Darren Quelch says rehabilitation for ketamine dependence differs from traditional drug and alcohol services Dr Darren Quelch, from the University of South Wales, said interviews with service users at Birchwood suggested use started from as young as 13. He said the physical harm caused by persistent use ranged from memory problems and chronic pain to bladder damage and kidney failure, but that support services were having to rapidly adapt as the needs of users are more complex. "Their bread and butter isn't dealing with really complex medical presentations," he said. "Even if they were, we actually don't know what the right answer is yet." He is now conducting research alongside Kaleidoscope to establish what types of support work for this specific patient group. "The population is inherently different to lots of other groups that might engage with drug and alcohol treatment services," he said. The Birchwood detox and rehabilitation centre has three therapy dogs which have proved popular among service users like Megan Mark said his health had deteriorated to such an extent that "at the age of 25 I probably had the body of an 80-year-old". "I was no longer functioning like a proper human being," he said. As a keen footballer growing up in Liverpool, he now looks on jealously at others his age, walking without pain. "It stopped me being a father to the little girl that I've got - I stopped being the big brother, the responsible son," he said. Mark would regularly pass clots and experience pain during urination, but said the collapse of his nose from snorting drugs has had a huge impact. "It completely destroys self-confidence - which leads to more drugs, because that just blanked out what I think of myself." It's one of the reasons he has asked to remain anonymous. "I started getting looks of disgust from my own family, which destroyed me. It was a very lonely time through my addiction," he said. Mark's drug use started at 18, but by 21 he said he was using "copious amounts of cocaine and ketamine". He initially sought help from his GP in Liverpool, but was too ashamed to admit he was using ketamine for fear of being dismissed or judged. "It's a hard lesson learned," he said. title: Hundreds of holiday lets operating without planning permission
description: Hundreds of holiday-let properties are operating in Edinburgh despite being refused planning permission, new figures show.
body: Clusters of key boxes can be a sign that there are short-term let properties in a building Hundreds of holiday let properties are operating in Edinburgh despite being refused planning permission, new figures show. Analysis from housing campaigners suggests that 800 of the 1,754 entire homes in the city which are licensed short-term lets (STLs) have had planning applications refused. But because they have a licence they can continue advertising the properties through websites such as Airbnb. Campaigners are calling for Edinburgh City Council to make more use of its enforcement powers, which include fining owners who do not have planning permission, while operators say STL laws introduced in 2023 are not working properly. City of Edinburgh Council said its licensing policy was helping make sure holiday lets were safe and properly regulated. The new laws were introduced to help tackle problems with housing demand and anti-social behaviour, especially in hot spots such as Edinburgh. Edinburgh has been identified as a hot spot for short-term lets Anyone providing STL accommodation must have a licence or face a ban and fine of up to £2,500. There are different licensing requirements depending on whether you are letting out a spare room or an entire property on a permanent basis. Any STLs which started operating after the city introduced a control zone in September 2022 must also have planning permission if the owner does not live in the property on a regular basis. The rules say that planning permission will also be needed for some residential properties which had already changed to a short-term let before that date. Insiders from the industry claim the reality is that every full house is now expected to have planning consent - and that the majority of applications are rejected. Living Rent and Leith Harbour & Newhaven Community Council carried out an analysis of the publicly available planning and licensing documentation. This showed that on 6 September this year a total of 1,754 entire flats or houses had the relevant licenses. The vast majority - 1,225 properties - did not have planning permission. This was either because they had not applied (in some cases it was not required) or it had been refused. Of those properties with valid STL licences, 800 had been refused planning consent and not subsequently been granted it on appeal. Despite this, these holiday lets can continue to operate until their licence is due for renewal, typically between one and three years after being issued. Properties in residential tenements or located in areas of high concentration of short-term lets are among those being rejected for planning consent. As with all breaches of planning laws, the council has the power to take action against STL owners operating without permission - but enforcement is not automatic and is carried out on a "reasonable and proportionate" discretionary basis. Those applying for a licence in Edinburgh must either be in the process of applying for the correct planning permission or have it in place. Campaigners claim some owners are "gaming the system" by submitting planning applications while applying for their licence but then withdrawing the planning application after the licence is secured. Living Rent's analysis shows 465 of the licensed full property STLs have withdrawn a planning application once, with 110 having withdrawn more than one application. Chas Booth is a Scottish Green Party councillor in Leith who sits on both the licensing and planning committees. He said the council was not doing enough to enforce the planning and licensing system, and that the Scottish government's legislation was not fit for purpose. "There is a massive loophole in the law, which hundreds of STL owners are exploiting, and which is causing misery for residents," he said. "Scottish ministers need to wake up and smell the coffee. This legislation has a loophole as big as a barn door, and they need to take urgent action to close it." Niall Robb, of campaign group Living Rent, said the council needed to step up its enforcement. "For the majority of STLs to have insufficient planning permission demonstrates how landlords are taking advantage of weak legislation and a lack of enforcement to profit at the expense of tenants and neighbourhoods," he said. "Increasingly, communities are being undermined at the hands of holiday-let landlords who only care about profit. "As a result of their actions, residents who keep the city ticking over every day are being forced out by sky high rents and a lack of homes." Katie Beale says there is constant noise from neighbouring properties Leith resident, Katie Beale, has had multiple incidents with guests staying in the STL in her stair. "It's the constant noise, the constant turnovers, strangers in the hallway," she said. "When you live here and you know your neighbours, you've all got your little routines and everyone's very considerate of each other. "But your stomach just drops when you hear the wheelie suitcases coming up the street." Beale said there had been instances of guests running up and down the hallways, pressing all the buzzers in the stair and throwing things out the window onto the street. She added: "We have had to call the police with noise complaints. I suppose I'm quite resilient but it does wear you down because it's a constant turnover of new people. Who are you going to get is just a bit of pot luck." "We definitely welcome visitors to Edinburgh," she added. "It's just they need to be in the right places." Holiday-let owner Paul Phillips says the law needs to be amended Paul Phillips owns a holiday-let flat in Edinburgh city centre and is a non-executive director of trade body the Association of Scotland's Self-Caterers (ASSC). title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
description: Penalties are seen as too harsh on motorists who are penalised for parking on private land.
body: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham. The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised. In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped. Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies". Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat. "These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them." The new rules will give drivers: a guaranteed 5 minute period to decide whether to park A 10 minute window to leave without facing a penalty Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, like vehicle breakdowns in car parks Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines Maximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking A freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge. Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier. With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day. The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car. The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action. The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024. But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament. The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice". The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry. Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up". But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one. The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority. title: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
description: It comes after the country's interior minister admits that police "lost control" in some cities.
body: This video can not be played Are the riots in France a warning of an intense election to come? French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of central Paris and other cities after a weekend of riots and looting across the country. Police in Paris said a curfew would be in force between 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) and 06:00 in Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area. A ban on unauthorised gatherings has also been imposed in several other parts of the city centre. Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were announced for cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder but whose resignation was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron, admitted police had "lost control" in some cities. The protests began last month with students demanding better school conditions, but they have have since escalated to take in a broader range of concerns, with numbers at demonstrations this weekend bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups. More than 2,500 people have been arrested, officials said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured. Following a crisis meeting on Monday, the prime minister said local mayors were being given the power to implement curfews "where they need", without specifying which cities where they would be enforced. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who did not rule out imposing a state of emergency in the country, said the government would also set aside money to help affected areas recover from the damage, and the funding would be recovered from those behind the violence. "There will be a law that will be put in place to find ways of making sure that those who have damaged properties will have to pay," Lecornu said. He also announced a partial unemployment fund for those who could not work as a result of the riots and looting. French police officers check a person during a partial curfew in Lyon Meanwhile, Nuñez said 200 investigators were analysing CCTV footage to try to identify possible ringleaders. He attempted to resign on Sunday, but Macron refused "given the need for continued command of law enforcement", the Élysée Palace said. The statement said Nuñez should be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings". More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) says. Its head Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that damage from the riots was estimated at "hundreds of millions of euros". Jean-Luc Chauvin, the president of the CCI's Marseille branch, told the BBC that many of the city's shop owners were in "deep distress" and fear for their survival. Looted goods have been listed on certain selling platforms, two French government ministers said. A Vinted spokesperson said the sale or solicitation of stolen goods was "strictly prohibited". "Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," it said. Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale This video can not be played 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets over the weekend for protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns. In the central city of Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing as the flames took hold. The US Embassy in France has issued an alert advising its citizens to avoid areas affected by the recent demonstrations. The warning says to "exercise caution" if they find themselves close to large gatherings. China and Germany have issued similar warnings. Some politicians have accused the left-wing La France Insoumise party of playing a role in the violence, with Lecornu alleging in an earlier news conference that some groups "want to create chaos in our country up until the presidential elections". The party's leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who will stand in next year's presidential election, responded by calling for the French PM to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder". description: How Spurs and Coventry City's players rated following their Premier League match.
body: This video can not be played Spurs beat Coventry to earn first league win of the season Tottenham finally got their first Premier League win of the season against Coventry City. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. Premier League: Tottenham squeeze past Coventry to end winless start - reaction What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? James Maddison toned down his goal celebration as he is from Coventry and started his career at the club Antonin Kinsky: Fumbled first-half corner and not great with his feet. 5 Tosin Adarabioyo: Powerful in the air and did well in the physical challenges until he went off injured. 6 Jan Paul van Hecke: Disappointing night. Uncertain moments and lost possession for Coventry City's goal, but did make one brave clearance. 5 Micky van de Ven: Superb tackle to stop Brandon Thomas-Asante in the first half and solid all-round display. 7 Archie Gray: Busy and did his best to give Spurs some creative edge. 6 Sandro Tonali: Occasional flashes but still struggles to justify his £100m price tag. Needs to produce more. 6 James Maddison: Brilliant strike on his first start for 18 months. Always prompting and probing. Revelled in his return to the starting line-up until understandably tiring. 8 Andrew Robertson: Some trademark surging runs and always willing to join the attack but picked up an injury. 6 Mohammed Kudus: Mixed night. Some good things but too often short of end product. 5 Omar Marmoush: Had struggled but then scored a superb goal. 6 Dominic Solanke: Tireless but little luck. Booked and had a shot on the turn over in first half. 5 Conor Gallagher (on 69, Maddison): Not able to get into the game. 5 Mateus Fernandes (on 69, Tosin): Little impact. 5 Ben Davies (on 69, Robertson): Experienced head to close out the win and got himself a goal. 6 Mathys Tel (on 87 Marmoush). Dejan Kulusevski (on 87 Kudus). Subs not used: Dubravka, Senesi, Olusesi, Williams-Barnett. Carl Rushworth: No chance with first two goals but a horror show for the third from Ben Davies. 5 Milan van Ewijk: Long throws a threat, especially in the first half. Caught an elbow when trying to challenge Marmoush for his goal. 6 Bobby Thomas: Vital headed clearance and tower of strength in defence. 7 Ethan Pinnock: Another dependable performance as Coventry looked solid and well-organised at the back. 6 Jay Dasilva: Quiet night. Booked for challenge on Kudus. 5 Caleb Yirenkyi: Not able to exert much influence and was substituted. Booked for a poor challenge on Gray. 5 Matt Grimes: Always busy but not able to have a significant impact. 5 Brandon Thomas-Asante: Industrious and was only denied a goal by Van de Ven's superb first-half tackle. 6 Jack Rudoni: Showed great determination to bustle his way through for his goal. 7 Tatsuhiro Sakamoto: Some dangerous deliveries and had a good chance in the first half. 6 Sidiki Cherif: Some nice lay-offs and full of effort. Hurt his shoulder in an awkward fall. 6 Frank Onyeka (on, 60 Yirenkyi): No effect. 5 Taiwo Awoniyi (on 60, Cherif): Bustling but unable to provide threat. 5 Ephron Mason-Clark (on 78, Thomas-Asante). Gustavo Hamer (on 78, Sakamoto). Kaine Kesler-Hayden (on 87, Rudoni). Subs not used: Bentley, Simms, Mfuni, Torp. title: First minister promises to look at Welsh council powers
description: Plaid Cymru's leader makes pledge ahead of talks with Andy Burnham, who wants more devolution to councils.
body: Rhun ap Iorwerth delivered a speech about devolution to Cardiff University on Monday evening The Welsh government is to examine the powers councils have and how authorities work together regionally, the first minister has announced. At a speech at Cardiff University, Rhun ap Iorwerth announced that this could lead to new legislation after the next election in 2030. He is due to meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who says ministers in Cardiff should hand more powers to local authorities, later this month. Ap Iorwerth denied offering a quid pro quo to the prime minister, who the Plaid Cymru leader is hoping will give the Cardiff government more powers and funding. In the same speech, he also called on the UK government to stop duplicating the Welsh government's economic development work. "Where power can sit as closely to the people it affects, it should," the first minister said at the event at Cardiff University's Glamorgan building. "Whilst I am clear that we should never assume that what works for England will work for Wales, and vice versa - and I hope the prime minister acknowledges this – I know that our current arrangements aren't perfect either. "I am convinced that, over time, Wales should move towards a more coherent and more streamlined system of local and regional governance. "But that vision cannot be imposed." Ap Iorwerth promised a green paper by the end of the term, followed by the "option" of new legislation from the next Welsh government. He said he wanted to be in a "good position to reflect on what is working and where change is needed" by the end of the term, but said the "conversation" had to start before then. The first minister said it would be a "detailed, meaningful exercise reflecting on where powers and specific competences should lie, how regional working works best and what effective cooperation looks like". Rhun ap Iorwerth has previously written to the prime minister calling for Wales to have the same powers as Scotland - including on railways, policing and justice. Rhun ap Iorwerth is set to meet Andy Burnham at the end of the month Asked by BBC Wales if he was trying to offer the prime minister a "quid pro quo", ap Iorwerth said: "I don't quite see it in that way. "As somebody who wants power close to the people in Wales, I like the fact that the UK's new prime minister is talking that kind of language, but it means different things in Wales and England. "The devolution programme that we're hearing from Andy Burnham is largely an England programme. What I want to do is find common ground with him." The first minister questioned whether Downing Street's "devolution agenda" was "really an England-only agenda", and whether it came to a "shuddering halt at Offa's Dyke". Economic development in Wales is devolved to the Welsh government. But ap Iorwerth said Wales was living with a "confused" and "increasingly fragmented system". "A succession of UK government programmes has been layered on top of devolved responsibilities and in some cases undermining them," he said. "Some have funded worthwhile projects. Some have brought genuine benefits. But, taken together, they have made the landscape more complicated, more fragmented and more difficult to navigate." He listed city and growth deals, and the former Conservative UK government's levelling up and shared prosperity fund projects, as examples. "If powers have been devolved, central government should not continue to duplicate them," he said. He called for a "practical agreement about how our two governments work together to unlock Wales' economic potential". Asked later to clarify, he said he was not saying he wanted to get rid of city and growth deals - agreements between the UK government, Welsh government and local councils to help fund local projects - of which there are four in Wales. "Whatever we have, lets look at what works well and how we can improve it," the first minister said. title: Man held after three Jewish women report assaults
description: Three women, one pushing a baby in a pram, reported being assaulted in Clapton Common, Hackney.
body: Police were called to the Clapton Common area on Monday afternoon A man has been arrested after three Jewish women, one of whom was pushing a baby in a pram, reported being assaulted in north-east London. Police were called to the Clapton Common area of Hackney at about 13:40 BST on Monday after a man had been detained by members of Shomrim, a Jewish neighbourhood watch group. Officers arrested a 33-year-old man on suspicion of racially aggravated common assault. The women are believed to have suffered minor injuries. The Metropolitan Police said it was treating the incident as a suspected antisemitic hate crime and had increased patrols in the area. The man has since been further arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in connection with a separate incident in Islington on Friday, the force said. He remains in custody. Ch Insp Erica Crawshaw said it had been "an alarming and distressing incident" and thanked Shomrim volunteers for detaining a suspect before officers arrived. "We recognise the concern that this incident will have caused the Jewish community here in Hackney," she said. "We have increased patrols in the area and we are speaking to community leaders to provide further reassurance." The Met has appealed for anyone with information, or anyone else who believes they may have been assaulted, to come forward. title: Building Lionesses 2.0 - Wiegman's new challenge awaits
description: England head coach Sarina Wiegman has changed women's football in the country, so what does she face after signing a contract extension?
body: Sarina Wiegman has won the past three Women's European Championships - with the Netherlands in 2017 and England in 2022 and 2025 When Sarina Wiegman took the reins as England manager in September 2021, she declared she had "come to bring the next level". Winner of the 2017 Women's Euros with her own Netherlands and runner-up at the subsequent World Cup in 2019, she certainly had the pedigree, but could she deliver on her promises? Five years on, Wiegman has pocketed two more European Championships and acquired another silver medal on the global stage. Not only that, but the success of her Lionesses exploded the women's game in this country, taking it not just to a new level, but to previously unthinkable heights. And yet on the day Wiegman extends her deal until after the Euros in 2029, her newest challenge could be her hardest yet. England manager Wiegman signs contract extension Wiegman's successful England teams have been built on a core group of players from an outstanding generation - but a few cracks have appeared this year. Seven of the team that started against world champions Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - and their 4-0 defeat in Mallorca laid bare the gap England must bridge to the world's best. That result also consigned England to two rounds of play-offs to reach next summer's World Cup. Beating Greece this month navigated the first of those, with games against Ukraine, who they have beaten twice already in 2026, to come before Christmas. Nevertheless, finding successors to those who have spearheaded the success will not be straightforward. Defensive stalwarts Lucy Bronze and Alex Greenwood will be 37 and 36 respectively by Euro 2029, while Leah Williamson and Keira Walsh will be 32. Other key players such as Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway will also have turned 30, far from past their best, but still a consideration. "We have to continue the evolution of the Lionesses," record goalscorer Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast. "We can't stay stagnant or keep trying to win in the same ways all the time." Former England goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis thinks one of Wiegman's strengths as a manger is her willingness to give young players a chance. "She's not afraid of bringing in players who have never been capped before," Brown-Finnis told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Wiegman is looking right across the spectrum and asking who's on form, who can add to my squad, who can fill a position or a couple of different positions?" Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club, former Lionesses captain Steph Houghton said: "You can see Wiegman is trying to change a few things. The last camp she brought on Lexi Potter for her debut and she is now starting regularly for Chelsea. As a young player you need that to thrive in this environment. "She is seeing the progress of young players coming through to press those who have been in the squad for a long time." Greek takeaways: What did we learn from Lionesses' win? It is not as though Wiegman has ignored squad regeneration. During her time in charge, she has handed debuts to 24 players, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters. Those games against Greece offered a clue to her next steps. In Crete, Manchester City's Laura Blindkilde Brown, 23, showed glimpses of her ball-playing ability, while in the second leg 20-year-old Chelsea academy graduate Potter impressed in midfield. London City's Freya Godfrey, 21, and talented 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson also got their first caps as Wiegman scrutinised her options. Figures earlier this season showed the number of homegrown starters has been dropping in the Women's Super League (WSL) over the past four campaigns, with the league's growing prestige attracting more foreign stars. The Football Association (FA) chief football officer Dan Ashworth said Wiegman has helped bring "a golden age for women's football in this country". To prolong it, she will need to keep producing fruit from increasingly arid ground. 'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem? Could Potter be England's next breakthrough star? Prior to Wiegman's appointment, England women had performed well at major tournaments - finishing third at the World Cup in 2015 and fourth in 2019 - but winning Euro 2022 was something new. WSL attendances rocketed, media coverage surged and clubs amplified their women's teams. However, four years on, there is evidence to suggest interest has plateaued. Initial crowd figures for the 2026-27 season are down on previous campaigns, while only 18,587 fans watched England beat Greece 5-0 at King Power Stadium, nearly 10,000 fewer than qualifiers at Nottingham Forest's City Ground and Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium this year. With so much competition, Lionesses success is crucial for sustaining momentum in the women's game - but expectations are higher now. A fanbase was born from success and has become accustomed to it. Will they tolerate anything less than finals and trophies? After all, Spain, Japan and hosts Brazil are among the many nations that look poised to have a significant say at the World Cup next summer. Only four of the top 10 nations in Fifa's world rankings have female managers (Spain, USA and Canada), with Wiegman the longest serving. If she sees out her contract, only Hope Powell (1998-2013) and Martin Reagan (1979-90), will have been England head coach for longer. As she signed her new contract, she said she "could not think of a better job in world football". It is hard to think of many who have done a better job than Wiegman has already accomplished. Committing to three more years means her legacy may now be defined by what she achieves next. title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
description: Serhii Beskrestnov says there has not been enough time to warn people about incoming missile attacks. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing.
body: Serhii Beskrestnov said "people have already died" due to lack of warnings about incoming missile attacks Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died." The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows. Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence. On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter." Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause. "We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles." But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue. "This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not." He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack." However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component." Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications. Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h). This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas. Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement. Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine. He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'." Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems. He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step. "We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink." Earlier on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing. "I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday. Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system." The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response. A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine. The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country. Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park café in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity". Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? title: Ukraine says it carried out first drone airlift of wounded soldier from front line
description: The serviceman was surrounded by landmines and enemy drones so a ground rescue was not possible, Ukraine's military says.
body: This video can not be played The Ukrainian military has released footage of what it says is the world's first drone airlift of a wounded soldier from the front line. The 92nd Assault Brigade said a ground rescue mission was not possible as the wounded serviceman was surrounded by landmines and there was high Russian drone activity in the area. It says a "heavy" hexacopter, piloted by a remote operator, was able to maintain stability during the "very difficult" operation. BBC Verify has found confirmed the identity of the army personnel involved in the video, and found no signs of AI generation of manipulation. title: Man in his 20s dies after four-vehicle crash
description: The crash, which involved a lorry, a van and two cars, occurred in Newry on Monday morning.
body: The crash happened at the junction between the Armagh Road and Church Road A man in his 20s has died following a four-vehicle crash in Newry. The crash, involving a lorry, van and two cars, happened on Monday morning at the junction between the Armagh Road and Church Road. Two other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries. The Armagh Road remains closed following the crash. Det Insp Stewart, from the collision investigation unit, said the report came in at 06:30 BST. "The collision involved a white Scania lorry, white van, blue BMW and white Toyota Auris," he said. "The driver of the BMW, a man aged in his 20s, was sadly pronounced deceased at the scene. "Both the passenger and driver of the van were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries believed to be serious, while the drivers of the Toyota and the Scania lorry were uninjured." title: Ronaldo given 30-day suspension and £215 fine by Portuguese FA
description: Cristiano Ronaldo is given a 30-day suspension by the Portuguese Football Federation after leaving his country's international camp last month.
body: Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension by the Portuguese Football Federation after leaving his country's international camp last month. The 41-year-old captain walked out of Portugal's Nations League squad in September after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark. Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement he had left because Portugal coach Jorge Jesus twice "broke his word", accusing him of an "absolute breach of trust". The Al-Nassr forward was provisionally suspended on 9 October. On Monday, the federation's disciplinary council said it had upheld the charge against Ronaldo in full and imposed a fine of 255 euros (£189). It is not clear which matches or activities the suspension would cover, or whether time already served under a provisional suspension would count towards the 30-day sanction. Portugal boss Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return following his side's 2-1 victory. Ronaldo accepted accountability and apologised to his team-mates and fans for his actions, before adding he deserved to be punished. Pedro Proenc, president of the FPF, told Portuguese outlet Record there is a "strong desire" to have Ronaldo back with the national team once the matter was resolved. Ronaldo, who has won the Ballon d'Or five times, has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both men's world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.
