title: Palace manager Sage facing fight to keep his job
description: Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage faces a fight to keep his job, but will be given more time.
body: Pierre Sage joined Crystal Palace on a three-year deal in June While no-one doubted that following in Oliver Glasner's footsteps as Crystal Palace manager would be a difficult task, Pierre Sage now finds his position under close scrutiny. A string of poor results - most recently Sunday's 5-0 drubbing by Brighton - makes this week a crucial one in determining his future. Sage has won just two of his opening seven Premier League games in charge, while the 17 goals they have conceded is the most in the league. But there is a degree of sympathy from some behind the scenes at Selhurst Park that the Frenchman has been dealt a difficult hand. Injuries have not been kind, while the absence of Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr - due to a mixture of fitness and personal issues, related to both players' desire to leave the club - has not helped the start of his reign. Co-owner and chairman Steve Parish is not one to act on impulse. He resisted the temptation to act when Glasner publicly criticised the club's board for "abandoning" the team after the decision to sell Marc Guehi to Manchester City in January. Glasner saw out his contract and added the Europa Conference League title to the FA Cup won the season before. Not that Sage is out of the woods. With crucial games against Besiktas and Newcastle on the horizon, further poor results will leave Parish with a decision to make. Some figures close to Palace believe the writing is already on the wall and, when the right replacement is in place, his short tenure will come to an end. But, having failed to appoint first-choice target Andoni Iraola following Glasner's exit, Palace are well aware of the difficulties of the managerial market. What is for sure is that the 47-year-old is facing a fight to keep his job. Sage feels 'shame' at Palace thrashing with future in doubt Sage may point to the disbanding of the squad that led Palace to their first ever major trophies, with the FA Cup in 2025 before last season's Europa Conference League triumph, as the reason for his tough start to life in south London. Eberechi Eze, Michael Olise, Maxence Lacroix, Daniel Munoz and Guehi have all departed Selhurst Park since the summer of 2024. The departure of highly influential sporting director Dougie Freedman in 2025 has also been keenly felt. In addition to Sage, the position of Freedman's replacement Matt Hobbs is also under the spotlight. But conceding 17 goals in seven Premier League matches points to a problem, at least in part, of Sage's own making. The team's recent DNA is rooted in defensive stability. Predecessors Glasner and Roy Hodgson produced well-organised teams with a solid base for its attacking players. Conceding close to 2.5 goals per game is so far removed from what the team's recent successes has been built upon that it has raised major concern from the club's powerbrokers. Palace are currently on course to concede 92 goals this season. No club has conceded more since Sheffield United shipped 104 goals to finish bottom in 2024. Personnel is contributing to those defensive deficiencies. Losing Guehi, Lacroix and Munoz in the space of six months represent significant losses. From the three centre-backs that started in Sunday's 5-0 loss to Brighton, Jaydee Canvot is 20 years old and Honest Ahanor only 18. Nevertheless, there is a clear sense from inside the club that Sage's system and approach has been a major contributing factor towards their troubles in defence. There is a perception from sections of supporters that the club's summer defensive recruitment has not helped. Takehiro Tomiyasu, Ben Chilwell and Oscar Mingueza arrived on free transfers, while Axel Disasi and Ahanor arrived on loan. As mitigation, it is understood Palace have encountered major difficulty in complying with Uefa's financial rules, leaving them hampered in the transfer market. Trying to stay within Uefa's guidelines was among the reasons why the club sold Munoz to Nottingham Forest for £22m. But those financial difficulties do not make the situation Sage finds himself any less critical. With a Europa League trip to Besiktas and home Premier League game against Newcastle on the horizon, Sage has an opportunity to change the mood music. Two positive results and the Frenchman will hope he can mount a more consistent upward trend. Two defeats, however, and Palace may well feel that enough is enough. title: US bans DeepSeek AI from government use as tech tension with China continues
description: DeepSeek is a powerful, popular and relatively inexpensive artificial intelligence model out of China.
body: The US has ordered all artificial intelligence (AI) technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek to be removed from most government systems. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, and any technology built with the aid of its AI models. As a powerful AI model that is open source - meaning it is free to access and less expensive to use - DeepSeek has been seen as a disruptive force in the ongoing AI technology race. While the DHS notice did not detail the exact security concerns surrounding DeepSeek, the White House has this year criticised AI firms from China. The DHS, DeepSeek, and the Chinese embassy in Washington DC have been contacted for comment. The DHS made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect from the end of July. The order is specific to civilian agencies, including the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State and the Department of Justice. However, agencies within the Department of Defense are excluded. The ban follows criticism of Chinese AI from the Trump administration, and from American firms. White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote earlier this year in an internal memo that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had been occurring, mainly by rival firms in China. Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which are poised to list on the public stock market in the coming months, have also claimed to have had their AI models essentially copied by some Chinese AI firms, including DeepSeek. US president Donald Trump has made clear that he sees China as the key US rival when it comes to development of AI, something he sees as crucial to the future of the country. DeepSeek has grown in popularity since its initial public release in 2025, with models being in such demand that the company's servers have gone down at times. While DeepSeek's free chatbot app is one of the most downloaded apps in the Apple App Store rankings, its AI models are also used by US tech companies. Companies like Snowflake, Vercel and OpenRouter all incorporate DeepSeek in their offerings to customers. Startups have flocked to open source models like DeepSeek. For a technology or AI developer, using DeepSeek in their work costs a fraction of what a closed model like Google's Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's Codex would. Similarly, the expense borne by DeepSeek to develop its models has been astronomically less than what it has cost US AI firms to develop their own. Last year, DeepSeek said it took about $6m (£4.5m) to train the debut version of its model, while the costs associated with OpenAI's GPT-4 were roughly $100m. Such revelations sent tech stocks tumbling. The most recent version of DeepSeek was released last week. Users of the model have praised it online, saying it beats even the most advanced AI tools out of OpenAI on common tasks for AI tools like computer software coding. title: Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents
description: Uefa's letter contained 42 questions, covering Fifa's failed private investment proposals, its Peace Prize and the fallout from Folarin Balogun's World Cup red card.
body: Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time European governing body Uefa has told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by a deadline of 2 November. At the Fifa Council on Thursday, president Gianni Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan - but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised. In the letter seen by BBC Sport, Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis said that world football's governing body had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions". "Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided," it read. The letter included eight pages containing 42 questions covering a number of issues, from the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) private investment, to the Fifa Peace Prize and the controversial suspended ban given to USA striker Folarin Balogun at the World Cup. "The withdrawal of FFE, the acknowledgement of mistakes and the announcement of 'potential governance reforms' do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the Fifa Council was not involved at the appropriate stage," it continued. "Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon. "These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council - nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them." Uefa did not outline what steps it intended to take should Fifa not meet the deadline. The questions were first put to Infantino at the Fifa Council last week, with Infantino then asking that they were submitted in writing. Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that "if he doesn't answer those questions, he's not fit to be Fifa president". Fifa has been approached for comment. Uefa has posed a great number of questions about FFE. "When was the idea of FFE first explored, by whom and with what objective?" Uefa asked. "Who within Fifa authorised the development of the project, and which members of the Fifa administration were involved? "What concrete measures will Fifa put in place to ensure that the shortcomings identified in the FFE process cannot occur again in the future?" Uefa goes on to ask about the circumstances surrounding Infantino's initial presentation of the FFE plan to senior Fifa executives. In particular, it raises a question about a potential investigation into Fifa in the United States. BBC Sport has approached Uefa to ascertain what this is in relation to. "According to information received from several sources, two days before the vote by the bureau of the management board on the FFE proposal, the Fifa president informed members of the management board that the US authorities were investigating Fifa's administration," Uefa claim. "Can he confirm whether such a statement was made and, if so, explain the information on which it was based, the reasons for raising it at that particular moment and whether he considered the potential pressure it might place on members immediately before their decision on FFE?" Uefa requested information on whether Infantino would have held or expected to hold any position, role or function in FFE, either during or following his tenure as Fifa president. The relationship with Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital was covered in detail, asking why an agreement granting exclusivity to the company was signed without prior consultation of the Fifa Council. "Why was Thrive Capital selected as lead investor, without any competitive tendering process and under conditions of strict confidentiality, despite its links to the family of the recipient of the Fifa Peace Prize?" Uefa asked. Kushner is the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, while the US president was awarded the Peace Prize. Uefa also requested answer about the award of the Peace Prize, specifically who decided to establish it, for what purpose, and who decided that Trump should receive it. When the FFE plan was revealed in the days following the World Cup final, Infantino told the 211 member associations (MAs) they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed it. He then set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m). However, once the scheme was abandoned, Uefa and Concacaf called on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the MAs and, last week, Infantino agreed, proposing to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn). The releasing of cash from its reserves will result in double the level of planned distribution funding for MAs from 2027 to 2030, with $25m (£19m) available per member association. "Why was substantially increased funding for MAs presented in connection with FFE and external investment, rather than being financed directly from Fifa's own resources?" Uefa has asked. "Given Fifa's strong financial position, why was it considered necessary to seek investment from private investors? What financial or strategic advantages would such an arrangement have offered compared with funding football development directly from Fifa's own resources, particularly in light of Fifa's subsequent proposal to do precisely that on a substantially increased scale?" While Fifa is yet to respond, sources have indicated its ability to answer certain questions are restricted by the legal action that Uefa has launched. Last month, it filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland. title: Leicester to visit Oxford City in FA Cup first round - see full draw
description: Leicester City will travel to National League North side Oxford City in the 2026-27 FA Cup first round - five years after winning the competition.
body: Leicester City won the FA Cup just five years ago but have since dropped down to League One Leicester City will travel to National League North side Oxford City in the 2026-27 FA Cup first round. It is the first time the Foxes have taken part at this stage of the competition since 2008 and they face sixth-tier opposition for a place in the second round. The 2021 winners were relegated to League One for this season with Russell Martin's side currently 14th having had an inconsistent start to the season. Meanwhile, there will be a family affair as Peterborough United face Reading as Posh boss Robbie Savage will take on his son Charlie's side when the first round kicks off around the weekend of Saturday, 7 November. A whopping 91 teams were named during the draw with four sides reaching the first round proper for the first time. Lowest-ranked team Tadley Calleva came from behind twice to force a replay with Aldershot and will make the trip to League One Barnsley should they progress. Meanwhile highest-ranked team Bradford City will welcome National League North side Marine as the League One leaders enter the competition. Eighth-tier AFC Rushden & Diamonds have won five games in the competition this season to reach the first round, with their reward a trip to League One side Burton Albion. title: Trial hears Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters
description: The activist is accused of "bully-boy tactics" and denies harassment causing fear of violence.
body: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark Crown Court for his five-day trial Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or leave home, a court has heard. The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. Opening the trial, prosecutor Ben Holt said the case was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to what he perceived to be "an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday" in the aftermath of the 2024 Southport attacks. Robinson, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to the charges in July last year. Holt said Dirnhuber had to move house because of the alleged harassment, while Young was given a close protection officer by the Daily Mail after photographs of his wife and children were posted on Robinson's X account. The judge at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Justice Cavanagh, told the jury: "This is not a trial about or an assessment of the defendant's political views." Ben Holt, for the prosecution, described Yaxley-Lennon as a "well-known public figure" with a "large, vocal online following" that now included more than two million followers on social media website X. Robinson posted on X before the trial began to thank the social media platform's owner Elon Musk for funding his case – and said his court fees to date had cost him £400,000. The trial at Southwark Crown Court concerns Yaxley-Lennon's response to articles published by the Daily Mail and MailOnline Holt said that after the murders of three young girls in Southport on 29 July 2024, Yaxley-Lennon made a number of posts on social media. This alerted the Daily Mail and Mail Online to the fact that he was in Cyprus. The Daily Mail published articles that included photographs of the defendant, including one showing him "reclining on a sunbed using his mobile telephone". Southwark Crown Court heard that over the following days, he made a series of posts on his X account in response. On 4 August, these included: "The daily mail have purposely gave the location of where I am with my children knowing full well that people want to kill me." Another post said: "The daily mail have purposely doxed the exact location of my family. How can they be allowed to do this'." There were no identifiable pictures of Yaxley-Lennon's children published by the Daily Mail or in the Mail Online, jurors were told. Holt said the trial was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to the articles, and accused him of using "bully-boy tactics" to "intimidate" the journalists. "He chose to frighten them, arrange for individuals to go to their addresses," said the prosecuting counsel. "On social media — to millions of followers — he circulated images of their homes. "His supporters got involved — threatening the journalists. "Understandably, you might agree, they were scared; in some circumstances, being forced to leave their homes." Stephen Yaxley-Lennon spoke to crowds outside Southwark Crown Court before heading inside The court heard that on 5 August, Dirnhuber received a number of direct messages from Robinson/Yaxley-Lennon. These included "you have endangered my children", "I'll be knocking at your door," and "let your bosses know I'm coming to all of your houses". The jury panel also heard details of an alleged phone conversation between Yaxley-Lennon and Young. "He said that he had Mr Young's telephone number. He recited his home address," Mr Holt told jurors. Yaxley-Lennon then became, according to Mr Young, "increasingly menacing". The prosecutor continued: "He raised his voice, he was swearing and shouting. "He said that he had been researching Mr Young's family and threatened to publish photographs of them and their addresses online. "Mr Lennon told Mr Young that he would be coming to Mr Young's house and he would have to move house. "He was going to shove a camera in his face and ask questions. "Mr Young told him that he did not want to engage with him — all complaints should be directed to the Daily Mail legal department. "Mr Young believes Mr Lennon said 'I'm coming to get you'." The prosecutor said it would have been "inevitable" that Robinson's posts would lead his supporters to "pick up the baton" and target the journalists. He referred to a post from somebody who had displayed a picture of Mr Young's Suffolk address online. The prosecutor said: "This was never going to be a one-man campaign; it was inevitably going to draw others in." Editor-in-chief of the newspaper Ted Verity also provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual identifying himself as "Tommy Robinson", who allegedly told him that he had "already located every... one of you". The jury was told that Yaxley-Lennon's case was that his family "had been put in danger by the actions of the Daily Mail" and he had acted to "protect his family". On X he posted: "What is good for the goose is good for the gander." The trial, in front of a jury of nine men and three women, is expected to last for five days. title: Tom Cullen says he doesn't take playing LGBT roles lightly
description: Welsh actor Tom Cullen says he approaches queer roles "exactly the same" as he would a straight character.
body: Tom Cullen takes on the role of Barry in Black Church Bay, whose life starts to unravel after an intimate encounter with younger man Tom Cullen says he does not take the privilege of playing a gay character lightly. Speaking at the screening of mystery-thriller Black Church Bay at the Iris Prize Festival, the Downton Abbey and House of the Dragon actor said representation mattered. In the film, Cullen, from Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, plays a closeted man who finds he will go to any lengths to keep up appearances in his insular community. It is not the first time Cullen has played a gay character, taking on his first ever role in 2011 British romantic drama Weekend. He said: "What is wonderful is I feel like people can often pigeonhole queer cinema, and those two films show the spectrum and diversity that can be found." The Cardiff-based Iris Prize LGBTQ+ Film Festival celebrates stories from across the world. The annual festival, which works in partnership with BAFTA Cymru, is a seven-day event and this year celebrated its 20th anniversary. Black Church Bay was written and directed by Rhys Marc Jones (second left), and stars Tom Cullen (second right) and Joe Locke (right) Cullen said he approached the role of Barry "exactly the same" as he would a straight character. "They are characters that you have to empathise with and understand. And fundamentally my job is empathy," he said. "I remember doing Weekend and a big part of my research was interviewing and talking to my gay friends, talking about their experiences and trying to fully understand - but that's just research, which you should do for any character." The 41-year-old said the script was "really challenging" and that was why he went for the role. "The script was extraordinary and something that isn't usually made in the UK," he said. "It's so dark." Black Church Bay was filmed in Anglesey and written and directed by Welsh-Irish filmmaker Rhys Marc Jones, who said he was inspired by the "real locations". "The whole film was written with those locations in mind. I always wanted my debut film in Wales," he said. His partner Paix Robinson, who said he was a Welshman by marriage, added that Wales held a special place in their hearts as somewhere they got married and spent holidays, "so it was only right that the first film was in Wales". Describing the film as a "fantasy that becomes a nightmare", Jones said: "I needed a location that could be beautifully idyllic and hopeful and then turn and become brutally unforgiving". He added that Anglesey fitted the brief: "It can be absolutely stunning but has a foreboding quality." Joe Locke (left) says filming in Anglesey reminded him of home Cullen said he had never filmed on Anglesey before but had holidayed a lot in north Wales, adding it was great that Black Church Bay was "showcasing Wales". As he was filming House of the Dragon at the same time, he would have to drive down to London once filming in Wales had wrapped for the week and spend the weekend shooting for that. Cullen said he and his partner, Alison Sudol, were massive fans of Locke, who was "an absolute joy to work with". "Joe and I had each other's backs," he said. Locke, best known for playing Charlie Spring in Netflix series Heartstopper, said filming was not his first time in Wales but his first time in Anglesey. "I'm from the Isle of Man so it kind of felt like sister islands in a way. Very similar apart from the fact everyone speaks Welsh," he said. "The landscape is very similar, the small town aspect is very similar, so it kind of felt like being at home." He added that knowing island life really helped, especially as he said most shops on Anglesey shut at 19:00 and he would end up eating a Pot Noodle in the evenings. Luís Hindman won £40,000 for his film Magid/Zafar at the Cardiff-based Iris Prize LGBTQ+ Film Festival A film about tensions arising in the heat of a busy Pakistani takeaway scooped the top honours at this year's film festival. Luís Hindman received the prize for his film, Magid/Zafar, and was awarded £40,000 to make a new film with an LGBTQ+ theme in the UK. Hindman said it was "very humbling" to win, and wanted to create something in a British Asian setting that was a "chance to display my mosaic of what British Asianness can look like". title: CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour to leave network after 43 years
description: The network's chief international anchor has covered wars including Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran.
body: CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the organisation next year after more than four decades. "After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said in a statement., external The 68-year-old said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral". CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her "before she departs next year". Amanpour began working for CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk, and went on to become one of the network's best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars. She has presented her own nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009. Amanpour pictured covering the US-led peacekeeping operation in Mogadishu in 1992 In a memo to staff on Monday, Thompson wrote: "Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. "Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally. "In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship," he added. In her own statement, Amanpour said she wanted to thank "all the amazingly talented people I've worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews." Amanpour reflected on her "very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between". "It's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she continued, "as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favour." title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
description: The platform said since the weekend it had "taken immediate action to idenitify and remove listings linked to looting".
body: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France. The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting". Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend. "The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said. Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people. More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI). Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage. Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses. Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast. "Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC. "When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans." The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour". eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen. French PM calls for partial curfews as he condemns 'thieves' and 'thugs' behind riots Reuters news agency reported luxury shops and boutiques were shuttered and surrounded by security guards at the Place Vendome in Paris. But it said a host of stores in the French capital, including Dior, Rolex, Louis Vuitton and Ralph Lauren had their shopfronts damaged In Marseille, football club Olympique de Marseille said its official store on the city's historic main avenue had been looted. It has closed the store, along with fellow Ligue 1 club Lille, which said its club shop would remain closed until further notice. title: Jury in Katie Price ex's trial told to ignore egos
description: Kieran Hayler is charged with three counts of rape and one of sexual assault of a 13-year-old girl.
body: Kieran Hayler denies all the charges against him Jurors in the rape trial of Katie Price's ex-husband have been told to cut through the "big egos" and "big personalities" involved in the case before considering their verdicts. Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court charged with three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault of a 13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, which he denies. In a closing speech on Monday, prosecutor Ryan Richter told jurors: "You've seen the whirlwind of what is Katie Price and you're going to make an assessment of her, how it affects this case, how much it helps you decide. "The prosecution accept you're likely to treat her evidence with caution." Katie Price gave evidence during the trial Richter added: "You may well put 90% of her evidence to one side, it's irrelevant, it doesn't help you. "I'm sure you will concentrate on what is relevant and look for support to assess what she says." The prosecutor said jurors had seen enough of "the egos, posing and posturing". "You've seen the big personalities, the big egos in this case, and you'll judge it, you'll cut through it," he said. "You'll decide whether those big voices drown out the voice of [the complainant] or whether that voice has made you sure on the counts of this indictment." Referring to messages between the alleged victim and Price in 2017 where the media personality told the girl "I will make you a little star", Richter asked: "Is that the key to this case, that message?" He added: "Is it the suggestion seriously for nine years Katie Price has been biding her time to make [the complainant] a star?" Defence barrister Arlette Piercy said in her closing speech that Hayler had been consistent and clear throughout his defence in what had been a "rollercoaster ride for everybody in this court". She called for the jury to take care, be calm and rational, warning "emotion is enemy of reason". Piercy pointed to inconsistencies in the complainant's evidence that on more than 30 occasions she said she did not know or could not remember. "We submit lack of coherent account is an important factor which supports what we are saying and undermines the credibility of the witness as a whole," Piercy said. Hayler denies all the charges against him and says the allegations are a "smear campaign to ruin me" by Price. Additional reporting by Press Association. title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
description: The apparent attack on MP Helen Haines suggests the worst fears of politicians and public figures appear to have been realised.
body: Police have been guarding the hospital in Melbourne where independent MP Helen Haines is being treated As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did. Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory. But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter. And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised. Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta. Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack. He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear." Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets. Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country. In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised. Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy. According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year. "We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC. Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic. But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds. "We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life. "This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum." And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too. Helen Haines at Parliament House in Canberra Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia. "Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026. And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people. "They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month. There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk. It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas. Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night. "Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said. "I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy." title: Reform UK mayor investigated over naked photo claims
description: Reform UK's Luke Campbell denies claims that he showed nude photos of himself to a female colleague.
body: Reform UK's Luke Campbell was elected mayor in May 2025 Reform UK's Hull and East Yorkshire elected mayor Luke Campbell is under police investigation for allegedly sharing naked images of himself. A spokesperson for Hull and East Yorkshire Combined Authority (HEYCA) said: "The mayor firmly denies the allegations. "We recognise the seriousness of the matters reported and understand the concern they have caused among our staff, partners and the wider public. "With a police investigation ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment further on individual allegations or speculate about the outcome." The spokesperson added: "The combined authority has established procedures for handling complaints about members and officers, which must be conducted fairly and independently." According to The Observer newspaper, external, the Reform UK mayor and former Olympic gold medallist boxer is accused of allegedly showing naked pictures of himself to a female member of staff. Liberal Democrat leader of Hull City Council Mike Ross, who came second in the mayoral election last year, said that Campbell should "stand aside" during the investigation. "I'm saying if there's an investigation taking place at the moment in any other circumstances a person in that position would be asked to stand aside while that was taking place," he said. "And certainly if that is something that should be happening now then I believe that would be the right course of action." Conservative leader of East Riding of Yorkshire Council Anne Handley said: "I think to look after the mayor, to look after himself, I think the best thing he could do was to just stand aside for now just until the investigation comes to a conclusion." In a statement, Reform UK said: "Luke firmly denies the allegations." "They come from a disgruntled employee attempting to leverage a settlement in a meritless workplace dispute." title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support says court filing
description: The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
body: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California. US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest. It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment. Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder. The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September. A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted. He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated. The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed. It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son. Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same. On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official. "Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued. The FBI investigation is ongoing. Alfozan is scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine. title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say
description: Three missiles hit a camp in government-controlled Shabwa province that officials say was being used as a training centre for new recruits.
body: Yemen's government said the missile strike killed recruits to its internal security forces (file photo) More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say. A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police. The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response". The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations". Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months. At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis. With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September. However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces. The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia. Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged 'We are terrified but we want to get an education', say Yemeni schoolgirls Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation. Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added. A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground. Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target. He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes". The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities. In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children. According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks. The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August. In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. title: Obama blasts federal probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
description: Obama says federal agents' search of the Democrat's home was an effort to intimidate a Trump critic.
body: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump. "The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling". The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order". Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child. US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995. Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date. Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship. "Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote. "If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same." According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated. "Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC. "The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe." Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated. The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process. In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism. Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation". But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer". Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago. Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker. The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS. Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law. When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii. Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday. title: Capybara pups at Manx zoo draw record crowds
description: Curraghs Wildlife Park has its busiest October weekend ever after the birth of eight capybara pups.
body: Eight capybaras are the first litter since just one pup at the park four years ago Curraghs Wildlife Park has experienced its busiest October weekend ever after the birth of eight capybara pups, which staff say have "delighted" people and boosted conservation funding. The pups were born to two females within days of each other, on 26 September and 1 October. Their arrival has sparked huge public interest, with the park's manager Kathleen Graham saying the reaction to this "overload of cuteness" had been extraordinary. "The car park was full, it was like a bank holiday. Everybody coming to see the capybara babies," she said. This video can not be played Visitors "oohed and aahed" at the pups, the zoo says The arrival marks a milestone for the park, which last welcomed a single capybara pup four years ago. Graham said the scale of this year's births has been "a super overload of cuteness really." The animals, native to South America, are the world's largest rodent, and thrive in wet marshland environments. The two litters were born within days of each other Graham said the pups' appearance on social media immediately drew far more attention than expected, and the surge translated directly into visitor numbers "They have been delighting people. Even grown men were like cooing," she laughed. Although capybaras are not endangered, Graham said they play a vital role in helping visitors understand threatened wetland habitats The park is part of the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria's Eaza Wetlands for Life campaign and sits on a Ramsar‑designated wetland. Graham said the pups helped highlight how wetlands supported both wildlife and people. "We rely on wetlands to soak up excess rainwater. And they're management systems, really. So they need looking after and protecting," she said. The pups' popularity also directly supported conservation work, she explained, as each visitor contributed £1 to the park's conservation fund unless they opted out. "Although themselves [capybaras] may not be endangered, they've actually created a lot of extra money this weekend for the conservation fund and spread a lot of joy and oohs and aahs," she said. The fund supports projects locally with Manx Wildlife Trust and internationally, including work in the Pantanal, where wild capybaras live. She said the pups arrival had lifted spirits at a time when many people were seeking moments of joy. "I think when there's so many just awful things that happen in the world, sometimes these little things just give us a bit of light relief, don't they?," she added. title: Bikes 'not for jousting,' says Lime after duel video
description: Footage emerged on social media of hundreds of people gathered in east London to watch a bike joust.
body: This video can not be played Hundreds watch e-bike jousting in London Fields in Hackney, east London E-bike rental company Lime has said its bikes are "not for jousting" after footage of two riders dressed as knights charging at each other in an east London park circulated over the weekend. Hundreds of people congregated in London Fields, Hackney, to watch artist Jack Carden and actor Camtholomew the First joust, while riding the bright green rentable e-bikes. The videos on social media showed them dressed as knights in armour, complete with chainmail and lances, attempting to knock each other off the bikes. A spokesperson for the company said: "While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first." The crowd can be heard chanting "joust, joust, joust" before one of the men falls off after being jabbed Ahead of the event, Carden said the "free public joust" was "performance art" in a post on social media. A video on his Instagram account of the event has been watched more than four million times. Despite their popularity, hospitals have reported an increase in injuries to both e-bike riders and pedestrians. A spokesperson for Lime said on Monday: "We always love seeing Londoners come together and build a sense of community in unexpected ways. "While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first. "Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting. "We discourage anyone from attempting similar events, to help keep riders and those around them safe." title: In pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters
description: France is used to protests but the violence and damage seen across the country is shocking many people.
body: Local curfews may come into force in French towns following a weekend of disorder. Most of the protesters were peaceful in expressing their opposition to rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. But others - dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas - set fire to cars, shops and buildings. The scale of the destruction - including to some iconic landmarks - has shocked many in a country used to street protests. The damage in the capital city is extensive. Shop fronts have been broken and stores looted. Kiosks, vehicles and buildings were set alight and destroyed close to some of the city's most recognisable areas, including here at Place De La Republique in Paris Front doors and windows were broken down as looting broken out in several cities Some groups erected barricades on the Champs-Elysees in Paris The iconic Place de la Republique was vandalised, too. A yellow vest - representative of the movement which helped co-ordinate the weekend protests - was draped around the body of the Statue of the Republic, erected in 1883. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, took over parts of the capital and wreaked havoc. Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people but police struggled to contain smaller groups of people roving around the city attack businesses. The full extent of the damage did not become clear until dawn broke on Sunday. This bakery was one of several businesses set on fire in Paris Some groups piled rental bikes in the middle of roads and set them alight Cars were set alight close to the Porte Saint-Denis in the capital Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. A bust of Marianne - symbol of the French Republic - was damaged and knocked to the floor in Marseille as people ransacked the building. City Mayor Benoît Payan was furious with the "almost total lack of control" by the security forces. "The world's sixth largest power does not deserve this. The world is watching us, this morning we are the shame of Europe," he said. In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office, housed in a 19th Century building, was "a tragedy". This video can not be played Chaos around the tourist office in Lyon as flames engulf it Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost". "A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department. In Limoges, the spire at the top of the ornate city hall has been destroyed by the fire French authorities have admitted they lost control of cities to the protesters. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation - which has been rejected. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has given local mayors the power to introduce partial curfews in some parts of the country, which he says is designed to protect people and businesses. But the French are holding their breath - in anticipation of another chapter in this protest next Saturday. Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election? title: Freud confirms Beatles' songs to star in musical
description: The Beatles agree for their songs to feature in a stage version of Yesterday, says the co-producer.
body: Screenwriter Richard Curtis and his wife Emma Freud are looking to bring the movie Yesterday on to the theatre stage Film producer Emma Freud has confirmed The Beatles have agreed for their songs to feature in a stage version of the movie, Yesterday. Freud is working on the show with her husband, Richard Curtis. They were behind the 2019 film and other box office hits, including Love Actually and Bridget Jones's Diary. She called it "a huge deal", saying: "They've [The Beatles] never done that with a West End musical before. So it's the first time that you can kind of legally see The Beatles' music on stage, which is amazing." Freud spoke to BBC Radio Suffolk on Monday, after she received an honorary doctorate for her work in film and broadcasting at the University of Suffolk on Saturday. Emma Freud received an honorary doctorate in Ipswich on Saturday She said a theatre where the stage show will be performed had been chosen - "but I can't tell you what it is because I will get killed". She confirmed the stage version of Yesterday would also be directed by Oscar-winner Danny Boyle, who oversaw the movie. Freud said: "We're at workshop stages, so we've already had two workshops and we've got a third one coming up this month, where you sort of ask actors to come into a room and just interrogate the script and the songs and the staging, and see how it's going to work. "Currently we're on the 11th draft of the script, because it isn't just taking a movie script and putting it on to a stage. "It's the same story, but actually every beat of it becomes different, becomes theatrical rather than filmic. "So it's been an incredible process to be a part of. I don't feel like I've ever done anything as big in my entire life." The Beatles were one of the biggest bands on the planet, with a multitude of hits including Hey Jude, Let it Be and Yesterday Yesterday is about a struggling musician who wakes up one day to find an altered world where no-one has heard of The Beatles. He becomes famous after singing their songs and passing them off as his own. The film stars Himesh Patel and Lily James, along with Suffolk-based singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran. It was shot throughout Suffolk, Essex and Norfolk, including a scene with 6,000 extras in Gorleston-on-Sea. Richard Curtis with the lead actor in the film Yesterday, Himesh Patel On receiving her doctorate from the University of Suffolk, Freud said "the honour" was "so massive", because "Suffolk is my home and it's where I was brought up, and it's where my family has lived for generations". Her family arrived in the county as Jewish refugees from Germany in the 1930s, escaping the tyranny of the Nazis. Freud's work has also involved tackling poverty and inequality, and has included working as a creative director and executive producer at Comic Relief, external. Emma Freud, who lives in Southwold with Richard Curtis, said receiving the accolade from the University of Suffolk was special Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below. title: Prime minister visits Aberfan ahead of 60th anniversary of 'horrifying tragedy'
description: A total of 116 children and 28 adults were killed on 21 October 1966 when a colliery spoil tip collapsed.
body: This video can not be played Andy Burnham (middle) visited the Aberfan memorial garden alongside survivor Jeff Edwards (left) and Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock Prime Minister Andy Burnham has visited Aberfan ahead of the Welsh mining village marking 60 years since a coal waste tip collapsed and engulfed a school, killing 144 children and adults. Burnham laid a wreath at the memorial garden on Monday, alongside survivor Jeff Edwards, who was one of the last children to be brought out alive from the rubble, and Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock. "It's been 60 years since one of the most horrifying tragedies this country has ever seen. All of those children lost," Burnham said. On 21 October 1966, 116 children and 28 adults were killed when a colliery spoil tip collapsed, catastrophically engulfing a primary school and surrounding houses. A scene of devastation caused by the mining waste tip sliding down the mountainside A survivor who spoke to the prime minister said that although she felt some "guilt" and missed those who died, it was important for her to talk about what happened. The prime minister said the tragedy was something his parents had told him about when he was growing up, adding that he was there to "recognise the community" and what they had been through. "The strength of the community today is something to see and something to feel," he said. "To say also to them, I don't think Aberfan was treated properly by the authorities and that also needs to be recognised. "Because at a moment like this, I think all of those things need to be said and it's right that the prime minister is here to say that to them." Burnham met with residents at the Aberfan Community Centre Burnham spent about 15 minutes in the memorial garden, before speaking to people who had gathered outside, and visiting a community centre. Burnham also addressed coal tip safety in former mining communities in south Wales. "It's of critical importance that we make sure that all of the remaining tips around Wales are safe indeed across the country," he said, adding he represented a former mining community in Makerfield near Manchester. He said his government was providing around £140m to the Welsh government, who were "adding some extra funding themselves". "There's an organisation that is being set up to manage all of these ongoing risks," he said. Irene Hollet, who survived the disaster, said it was important to talk about what happened Burnham met with survivors of the tragedy, including Irene Hollett, a former pupil at Pantglas school, who said it was a difficult time but that it was important for her to speak about what happened. "A lot of stuff comes back to you. You feel grateful that you are still around 60 years on, but then you miss your friends and family that we lost at the time," she said. "You can fell a bit of guilt that you are still here. "It's a difficult time, but it's got to happen. All of this has to happen for nothing ever to be forgotten". She said the conversation she and her fellow survivors had with the prime minister was "pleasant". "We were laughing about being naughty in school, how we played truant, and we just chatted about who we were and how we are all together today," she said. Marilyn Brown lost her daughter Janette in the Aberfan disaster Marilyn Brown's children were in Pantglas school and she lost her daughter Janette, but her son was saved by a teacher. She said: "I didn't realise he was saved because he'd run up from the school and I had run up to the school, and we sort of passed one another. "But I didn't think Janette would die. In my mind, she was still alive. "We stood up at the top by the school, and all the women were together, and I ran from the house." Speaking to BBC, she recalled that her daughter didn't want to go to school that day, but Brown and her husband told her "you've got to". She then watched her children walk up the street to school. "I thought, 'oh, I'll sit down now and have a cup of tea,'" she said. "I sat down. It wasn't there hardly any time at all, and my nephew run down the street and said, 'you'd better come up to the school... there's something gone wrong.'" Brown ran up the street in her slippers and remembers being stood waiting for "a long, long time" to find out what was happening. "We didn't realise then the children had died," she said. "It's still there. It'll never go away, and I hope people will remember, and they have today." Burnham has been described by survivors of Aberfan as 'very down-to-earth' and 'respectful' Brown described Burnham as "very nice, very down-to-earth and very, very respectful". While sat around a table with him, Brown said she "didn't say about losing a child" or that she "was a survivor". "We didn't really say an awful lot to him," she said, but he made them "feel very comfortable", which she described as "lovely." Holly told the prime minister her family had a close connection with the tragedy Pupils from Caegarw Primary School in nearby Mountain Ash, Rhondda Cynon Taf, were on a visit to the memorial garden - built on the site of the destroyed Pantglas School, on Monday morning - unaware that the prime minister would also be there. Burnham met pupils including Ellis, 10, whose granddad travelled across the valley to Aberfan to help with the rescue effort. "It means a lot to me and he tells me stories," said Ellis, who described visiting the memorial garden as "emotional". Holly, aged 10 from Caegarw, also told the prime minister she had a personal connection with the tragedy. "I told him about my godmother's daughter being one of the children who passed away in the disaster," she said. "He said 'wow'. It means a lot for us to be here." When a colliery waste tip collapsed, slurry crashed into Pantglas Junior School, killing 116 children and 28 adults

title: Are free-scoring Brighton genuine Premier League contenders?
description: Brighton's start to the season has surprised many outsiders. But how high could they finish?
body: This video can not be played 'Why not?' - 'Breathtaking' Brighton in title race says Dublin When Jack Hinshelwood unapologetically smashed home Brighton and Hove Albion's fifth goal of the game against bitter rivals Crystal Palace on Sunday, it completed a fourth straight Premier League win for the high-flying Seagulls - with an aggregate scoreline of 15-0. Hinshelwood's volley from two yards out to wrap up a 5-0 victory was in stark contrast to his team-mate Diego Gomez's audacious effort from the halfway line that put Brighton two up in just the seventh minute of the A23 derby. Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring side have arguably been the most entertaining top-flight team to watch this season, but they have backed up their attacking flair with a robust defence. No team has scored more and no team has conceded fewer goals. After seven games, they sit third on 16 points behind reigning champions Arsenal and table-toppers Manchester City, who have a 100% record. But can the Seagulls maintain their momentum and mount a serious title challenge? That's the opinion of Match of the Day pundit Dion Dublin, who played in Manchester United's 1992-93 title-winning side. "Because what we've seen of them this season is just togetherness, harmony... the manager's making good decisions. "[Pascal] Gross is leading the line in regards to what goes on on the pitch and what is the right kind of way they want to play. And everybody's chipping in with goals. The look a very, very frightening team at the moment." Shades of Barca and Beckham - Brighton aim to maintain superb start How Brighton attract and develop the best young players ahead of their rivals Timely recognition or long overdue? How Gross is proving all-time bargain Brighton are the Premier League's leading goalscorers this season In the summer of 2025, Brighton lost their top scorer Joao Pedro to Chelsea, and history repeated itself this year when the Blues lured veteran forward Danny Welbeck to Stamford Bridge. Once again, however, the Seagulls' enviable data-led recruitment model, aided by club owner Tony Bloom's close links to Jamestown Analytics, appears to have found a promising replacement. Having been used primarily as a substitute last season, Greece striker Charalampos Kostoulas has been entrusted to spearhead the attack, and the 19-year-old has repaid the faith shown in him by Hurzeler with three league goals and two assists. Only Lamine Yamal has more goal involvements among teenagers in Europe's top five leagues this season. Kostoulas has a strong supporting cast including Hinshelwood, Yasin Ayari, Malick Yalcouye and Maxim de Cuyper, not to mention a rejuvenated Pascal Gross pulling the strings from a deeper position. With 11 league scorers already - while also being the beneficiaries of three own goals - Hurzeler's men are sharing the load impressively. As well as being the division's top scorers, Brighton have had the most shots on target and sit second for xG, shots and big chances. In the top five European leagues, only Barcelona, with 39 goals from nine La Liga matches, have more domestic league goals than Brighton. Equally as encouraging is how well they have coped defensively despite the loss of centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke and midfield anchorman Carlos Baleba. Luka Vuskovic looks to be a tremendous acquisition from Tottenham Hotspur, and he has helped the Seagulls, who remain unbeaten at home, record a league-high five clean sheets. The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager There are only seven previous instances of a team scoring 23 or more goals after seven games of a Premier League season. All bar one have gone on to finish in the top three, with Manchester City winning the title in 2011-12 and 2022-23. The outlier? Kevin Keegan's Newcastle United team of 1994-95, who faded and finished sixth. Comparisons have already been drawn between that side, dubbed 'The Entertainers', and the swagger of the current Brighton squad. With that in mind, Alan Wares co-host of the Albion Roar podcast suggested that perhaps a Champions League place, rather than a full-blown title challenge, might be a more realistic aim. "I think with the Premier League being seven games in and the other matches we've already played, I think the dream for us is sustainability. I wouldn't go for a target, just as high as possible," said Alan. "The club is really wanting to qualify for Champions League at the end of the season but yes, we've made a good start - are we title contenders? It's way too early to consider that. I would say that, at the moment, is fantasy stuff. But every football fan's got to have their dream and our point is, why not? "If we can continue this, and that is the main point we've got to look at, if we can be sustainable in what we're doing and what we achieve, then yes. Why not? Go for the sky, see what happens." With Conference League football to juggle, it seems improbable Brighton's squad can last the pace with the likes of Arsenal for the duration of the season. Leicester City, the last outsiders to lift the title, do provide some hope. They were eighth with 12 points after seven games of their memorable 2015-16 triumph. There is a chance Brighton's final league position could be affected by matters off the pitch. Last month, an independent commission found Manchester City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-season period. City are appealing against the verdict, meaning the severity and timing of any punishment - which could take the form of a points deduction - remain unknown. title: Southport killer faces trial for alleged prison attacks
description: Axel Rudakubana appeared at Monday's hearing via a videolink from Broadmoor Hospital.
body: A court sketch of Axel Rudakubana during his last appearance at Westminster Magistrates' Court in September Southport killer Axel Rudakubana is due to face trial next year over allegations he threw boiling water mixed with sugar at a prison officer. Rudakubana, who is serving a life sentence for the murders of three young girls in 2024, appeared via videolink at the Old Bailey on Monday where he spoke only to confirm his name. He has been charged with attempted grievous bodily harm of a prison officer, two other assaults of officers and possession of a knife or other offensive weapon across separate dates last year at HMP Belmarsh, south London. Rudakubana was not asked to enter any pleas and a preliminary hearing has been set for 5 February, with a provisional trial date of 8 October 2027. Rudakubana, 20, is serving a life sentence for the murders of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024. On 8 May last year, it is alleged he threw hot water through a hatch in his prison cell door. It is further alleged that two days before, on 6 May, Rudakubana threatened to "soak" a female officer outside his cell if she did not pass him a newspaper and then threw liquid at her. Rudakubana also allegedly punched a male officer on 28 October. The offensive weapon charge relates to sharpened stone shards that the prosecution say had seemingly been prised from the floor of the defendant's cell. In July, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh, where the attacks allegedly took place, to Broadmoor high-security psychiatric hospital. title: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation
description: The two top tennis pros married in 2021 and have one child together.
body: Monfils and Svitolina played in the mixed doubles together at this year's US Open and reached the semi-finals Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country. The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside". "This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage. She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget". "Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote. It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said. "Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said. Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. "What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself." The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai. Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".
