title: US airman dies as daredevil descent goes wrong before Texas college football game
description: The game continued after the incident. The American Conference said the decision was made before his death was known.
body: A member of the US Air Force died after he fell while abseiling from the ceiling of a Texas stadium ahead of a college football game. Footage shows the serviceman plummet feet first to the turf midfield at San Antonio's 170ft (52 metre) high Alamodome on Saturday during a ceremony ahead of the game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the Naval Academy. The airman, identified, external by the military as Sgt Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor at Joint Base San Antonio, died in hospital. The incident is being investigated. The game between the UTSA Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen continued as planned following the tragic incident. A collegiate athletic association said the decision to press ahead with the fixture was made before the airman's death had been confirmed. "We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, teammates and members of the 57th Wing," the American Conference, external said in a statement. US Air Force Brig Gen Scott Mills said in a statement issued by Nellis Air Force Base: "This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing. "Tech Sgt Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing." Patterson, from Fort Stewart, Georgia, had served in the US military for 15 years, according to Nellis Air Force Base. He held multiple military decorations and was in 2022 named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level. UTSA president Taylor Eighmy said: "I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member's family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy." title: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
description: The independent politician is in hospital after what the prime minister says may have been a deliberate attack.
body: Helen Haines is well-known and well regarded as an anti-corruption campaigner Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have been a deliberate attack. The independent MP, 65, was struck outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria, on Monday afternoon. A man, 43, from the nearby town of Tarrawingee was detained at the scene by a passerby and police say a knife was found in the car. Police are investigating whether it was an "intentional act" but say they do not believe there is an "ongoing threat to the community". Political leaders have expressed shock and dismay, with Albanese saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy". While Albanese said it was too early to understand the motive behind what had happened, he did say the political temperature had been rising in Australia. His Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke backed up that statement with figures showing that reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 in the past year. Haines was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at 15:35 (04:35 GMT) outside her office on Murphy Street in Wangaratta, police say. The town, which has a population of around 30,000, is a few hours north-east of Melbourne. A witness told Australian broadcaster ABC they had heard a bang and seen a woman pinned between two cars, external. Haines was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta but later moved to Melbourne by helicopter. After being subdued and detained by the passerby, the suspect was arrested by police. Announcing that counter terror police were involved in the investigation, the prime minister said: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear." In a statement, Victoria Police said: "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act. "It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other... The investigation remains ongoing." Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car Although not necessarily a household name across Australia, in the political sphere Helen Haines is both well-known and well regarded as an anti-corruption campaigner. There has been an outpouring of messages from politicians and party leaders across the breadth of the political spectrum. In an age of increasingly divisive politics, she is seen by many as a unifying force. The independent MP has only been a federal parliamentarian for a relatively short time, having been elected in 2019. However, in that time she has become an influential advocate for integrity in politics. Haines proposed legislation for a national anti-corruption watchdog in 2021, and has been credited for driving the creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission under Labor in the previous parliamentary term. She currently sits on the parliamentary committee responsible for its oversight. Haines has often banded together with other key independents on issues that include climate action and gender equality. Allegra Spender, another independent MP who has collaborated with Haines, called her "the best of us". This video can not be played Watch: 'Helen Haines is a thoroughly decent human being,' Australia PM says An Australian parliamentary report warned last year that threats and physical attacks had increased "significantly over the past decade". A threat assessment by the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation - the country's equivalent of MI5 in the UK - warned last year that the risk of politically motivated violence was "already flashing red". Albanese became emotional as he talked about Haines in a live television interview on ABC's 7:30. He appeared close to tears when asked whether he and his colleagues talked among themselves about the threats and risks they face. "Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one, one of my colleagues." He described Haines as having "integrity". In other political reaction: Opposition leader Angus Taylor - head of the Liberal Party - said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the news, and that Australians would be "angry and appalled by the attack on Helen" Senator Matt Canavan, leader of The Nationals, said his heart went out to Haines and her family "upon the news of this shocking attack" Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge said he was "horrified" to hear of the "apparent attack", adding: "Helen is an extraordinary human being and brings people together like few others" Senator Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader, said violence against elected representatives is "never acceptable". She added: "Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety" Police at the scene in Wangaratta Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC Overnight curfews announced in parts of Paris and Nice after riots across France Are the French riots a warning of an intense election to come? title: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
description: The court upholds a decision to lift an arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont linked to the independence bid he led in 2017.
body: Puigdemont pictured during his only known return to Spain since fleeing, in 2024 - an appearance which prompted a police manhunt Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid. The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid. Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt. But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue. Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president. In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded. It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum. The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain. Ex-Catalan leader ‘eludes police manhunt and flees Spain’ Catalonia's bid for independence from Spain explained Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party. He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him. Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained. While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021. Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions. In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad. "My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said. It is still not known when he might return to Spain. Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP. The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco. The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election. But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda. The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election. But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters. And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time. title: Charity offers to meet James McClean over therapy comments
description: Michael Lynch, from Men's Action Network (MAN) offered to meet the Derry City footballer James McClean.
body: Men's Action Network (MAN) has offered to meet James McClean after he was reported as saying he would view seeking therapy as a sign of 'weakness' A men's mental health charity has offered to meet footballer James McClean after he told a newspaper he views speaking to a psychologist as "weak". In an interview with the Sunday Independent, external, the Derry City player said he had never tried therapy because "as a man I would see that as a weakness". Michael Lynch, from Men's Action Network (MAN) based in Londonderry, said the charity would welcome the opportunity to meet with him to discuss the importance of encouraging all men to feel comfortable seeking support when they need it. McClean has been contacted for comment but the club has distanced itself from his views and agreed to meet MAN. McClean has previously spoken out over his lack of playing time at Derry City this season McClean, who is currently not playing for his hometown club amid an ongoing contract dispute, gave the comments during a wide-ranging interview on topics including his new book, which details the social media abuse he has faced for refusing to wear a poppy, as well as death threats he has received. The former Sunderland, West Bromwich Albion and Stoke City player spoke about his wife's view that he had "built-up anger and frustration" that he had blocked out, to which the interviewer asked him if he had ever tried therapy. McClean responded that he had heard his brother, fellow Derry City player Patrick McClean, "on a call to a club psychologist, having a lovely chat". "And a lot of the players speak to him and for me that's just weak. "As a man, I see that as weakness. I don't need to open up. "I see it as a weakness that I'd have to speak to someone about my feelings, my emotions." Michael Lynch says James McClean is an influential figure, particularly for young men Lynch said he would welcome a meeting with McClean to discuss his views, as first reported by Derry Now, external. He told BBC News NI that McClean was entitled to his views and "neither I nor anyone else is entitled to say otherwise, because men's mental health is such a complex issue". "In some ways, I agree with him, in the sense that he mentioned that the only person who can decide whether seeking support is right for them is the person themselves, because nobody can do it for you. "But what I and others involved with MAN would say is that there is certainly still a stigma around men feeling that they cannot reach out at times and say, 'I am not OK and need to seek support', when that is so far from the truth." Lynch added that "asking for help isn't a sign of weakness". "For men to recognise that they need support and act on it is incredibly brave." Lynch said James McClean was an influential figure, particularly for young men from Derry, given his sporting and personal achievements. "We would obviously welcome a meeting with someone of that stature, for him to come and meet with the people we speak with every day, and we would love for him to have a conversation with us. "I think it would be really beneficial for people to hear from someone who has achieved so much in his career and has been a role model for so many people, to show what can be achieved with hard work." In a statement, Derry City Football Club said McClean's views "do not reflect our core values or beliefs". "The club places the highest priority on the mental health and wellbeing of our players, staff and the wider Derry City community," the statement said. "Supported by our in-house psychologist, the club actively encourages anyone facing mental health challenges to speak openly, seek support and know they never have to face such challenges alone." James McClean has had an acclaimed club and international career, having earned 103 caps for the Republic of Ireland. The 37-year-old began his career at Derry City before moving to Sunderland and appearing for a number of clubs in the Premier League and Championship, including Sunderland, West Bromwich Albion, Stoke and Wigan Athletic. He later made more than 100 appearances for Wrexham in all competitions, scoring eight goals, before returning to Derry City in January last year. His return to his hometown club, however, has been derailed by a contract dispute which he has described as "incomprehensible". McClean has described the past few months as "one of the most difficult periods of his life" and also apologised over social media posts in which he aired frustrations over the ongoing issues at Derry. title: Watch: Are the French riots a warning of an intense election to come?
description: Rioting, looting and vandalism has gripped France over the weekend after protests spiralled out of control across the country.
body: This video can not be played Cities and towns across France have seen rioting, looting and vandalism over the weekend as protesters took to the streets. It follows disorder last month when students began protesting over school conditions. The protests became broader and represented other concerns some French people have about issues in the country. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on Monday that local authorities would be able to implement a partial curfew to protect people and businesses. The BBC's Paris correspondent Hugh Schofield looks at how France is "reeling" from the violence and what it says about the upcoming election in the country. title: Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded
description: Former army sergeant major Robert Kabera was a popular YouTuber and singer, who had sought asylum in Uganda.
body: Robert Kabera was a popular YouTuber and singer A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda. Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution. Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad. His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety. "It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said. According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death. Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration. Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice. In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?" His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile. In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa. Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government. Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics. "Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said. In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya. title: Charging battery believed to have caused house fire
description: The fire caused extensive damage to the property, especially in the kitchen, officials say.
body: Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Service said no-one was injured in the fire, but added it caused extensive damage to the property A house fire in Leicestershire is believed to have been caused by a charging lithium-ion battery, firefighters have said. Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Service (LFRS) said crews were called to reports of the blaze in North Street, Ashby-de-la-Zouch, shortly after 15:00 BST on Saturday. The fire, which is thought to have started following an electrical fault involving a battery, caused extensive damage to the property, particularly in the kitchen where it had been left charging. The service said four firefighters wearing breathing apparatus were deployed to extinguish the blaze, but the occupant managed to safely evacuate the house. The service believe the fire was started by a charging lithium-ion battery Joe Warren, community safety station manager for LFRS, said the service was responding to more incidents involving lithium-ion batteries both locally and nationally. "These batteries are used in many electrical products, and if they are damaged, defective or charged incorrectly, they can become unsafe," he said. "We recommend only buying batteries, devices and chargers from reputable suppliers, using the correct charger for the product, avoiding charging batteries unattended, and never charging or storing products where they could block an escape route. "If you notice a battery overheating, swelling, making unusual noises, smoking or giving off a strong smell, stop using it immediately." title: Apu returns to The Simpsons with new voice after race row
description: The much-loved shopkeeper has been seen but not heard around Springfield for eight years, until now.
body: The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes. Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode on US network Fox, titled The Revengening, but now voiced by India-born, US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra. The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret. Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said. The character, who has been part of the long-running American animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent. Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes. The Simpsons' Apu: 'A stereotype hiding in plain sight' The following year, an episode of The Simpsons addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations but some viewers found it insufficient. Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes. Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise." Sunil Malhotra has featured in Star Wars: Tales of the Jedi and The Legend of Vox Machina Speaking to Variety, external ahead of the weekend's latest episode, Azaria's replacement Malhotra explained: "When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink. "But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers' room look different now?" The Grey's Anatomy and The Legend of Korra actor continued: "Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologised for past mistakes? "Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn't disappoint fans?" After years of Apu having become a mere background character, Malhotra said he spoke with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos about how they could make the returning fans' favourite more culturally appropriate for 2026. "It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for long-time fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way." Apu's wife, Manjula, will now be voiced Janina Gavankar - who previously appeared in Apple TV's The Morning Show - taking over from Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille. You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. In Apu's haunting comeback episode, a man in a "Daft Monk" Halloween costume - a play on French electro duo Daft Punk - appears to be accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents. A year on he returns to wreak his revenge. Eventually he summons everyone to the Springfield City Hall, takes off his helmet and reveals himself to be Apu. He then shares his story of having been nearly killed dozens of times, before winding up on The Island of Forgotten Garbage, where he was healed by Dr Nick. "I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed," he declares. Just as he is about to set the city hall ablaze, Marge Simpson - serving as a thinly-veiled mouthpiece for the producers - intervenes, telling him: "Apu, we're so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing." Her famous bratty son Bart adds: "But we were so scared, and just didn't know what to do." Bart's father Homer then offers to sacrifice himself to save the rest of the town, reminding viewers of how important Apu has been to the town. "You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands," said Homer. "We took you for granted. I took you for granted." The episode will be made available for viewers in the UK to watch on Disney+ next week. title: Volunteers help save one of London's rarest plants
description: Tower mustard has suffered steep decline in London but has been successfully grown and replanted.
body: Leaders from the tower mustard project said the plant has been saved in London More than 1,000 tower mustard plants have been successfully grown and planted out by volunteers in London. It marks a successful first year for a major community-led effort to restore one of the capital's rarest native wildflowers, vital for bees, butterflies and rare moths. Led by Citizen Zoo and Habitats & Heritage, the tower mustard project brings together a network of land managers, community groups, conservation partners and volunteers. The plants, grown by volunteers, are being reestablished at sites across London, in regions where tower mustard was previously known to occur. At the core of the project are the Mighty Mustard volunteers. In March, they attended a workshop, learned how to sow the tiny seeds, and were given their own growing equipment, including pots, seed trays and soil. Seeds were sourced from London's last remaining tower mustard populations in Lesnes Abbey Woods in Bexley and Stain Hill Reservoir in Richmond-upon-Thames. Charlotte Harris, nature conservation manager at Habitats & Heritage, said: "[We] are passionate about engaging people in conservation initiatives. Through this tower mustard project, we have enjoyed giving local residents the unique opportunity to get hands-on in conserving one of London's rarest plants. "We've found the volunteers have become really attached to [them]." Seeds have now been planted at Wimbledon Common, Hounslow Heath, Lesnes Abbey Woods and Barnes Common. Harris added: "We are hoping that this model can be used as a blueprint for helping other rare plants with volunteer input in the same way." The final planting day is at Hampton Court Palace's Home Park on Tuesday, where plants raised separately by the Historic Royal Palaces Gardens Team and volunteers will be used. Botanist Dr Mark Spencer has also provided expert support throughout the project. Prior to the project, the once widespread plant was only found in two locations in the capital Tower mustard, or Turritis glabra, is a native UK herb that has suffered steep decline due to habitat destruction and changes in land management. It is thought to survive at around 30 sites across England. The species is assessed as near threatened on the Great Britain Red List and endangered in England. Growing to around one metre tall and producing delicate white flowers, tower mustard is associated with open and disturbed habitats and supports pollinators. This community-led model builds on Citizen Zoo's successful Hop of Hope project which saw volunteers rear large marsh grasshoppers from eggs at home, going on to release the species in wetlands across Norfolk. Elliot Newton, director of rewilding at Citizen Zoo, said the company hopes to roll out more projects to preserve plants in the face of climate change. "In London alone, we've lost 185 species of plant. They have gone extinct in recent history." He said Citizen Zoo have many other plants on their radar, including copse bindweed, a native British climbing plant. Native to the UK, tower mustard – or turritis glabra – features small white flowers and grows to about one metre high Tower mustard is the first plant species Citizen Zoo has worked with in London, joining a growing portfolio of rewilding projects that also includes beavers, water voles, German hairy snails and white storks. The tower mustard project is funded by the Greater London Authority's Green Roots Fund and Thames Water. The project brings together Habitats & Heritage, Barnes Common, Lesnes Abbey Woods, Wimbledon Common, London Borough of Hounslow, London Borough of Richmond upon Thames and Historic Royal Palaces. Newton said: "These projects may sound small, but they're helping safeguard the future of the city." title: Masts from explosives-packed ship taken to museum
description: Removing the poles has reduced the risk of them toppling on to the bombs, a junior minister says.
body: The wreck remains surrounded by an exclusion zone in the Thames Estuary Three masts removed from a bomb-laden shipwreck in the Thames Estuary have been successfully taken to a maritime museum. The poles, delicately removed from the SS Richard Montgomery in September, will be kept at the Historic Dockyard Chatham. The masts had been visible from the Essex and Kent coasts since the doomed vessel sank with 1,400 tonnes of explosives onboard in 1944. Junior transport minister, Kier Mather said removing the masts had reduced the risk of them toppling on to and detonating the bombs. "As the vessel has aged, the masts continued to place significant load on the structure," he said in a written statement to Parliament. "Their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site." A deadly secret in the Thames - what is the SS Richard Montgomery? The salvage team used cranes to support the masts as they were cut free Engineers cut the masts free during a daring project, initially estimated to cost £9.5m. A crane supported the poles as they were sliced off and lifted to safety. Mather said despite the "unique risk and a challenging site", the project was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs. The BBC has asked the Department for Transport for details of the final costs. SS Montgomery was loaded with 7,000 tonnes of munitions in 1944 and directed to anchor off Sheerness, Kent, but grounded on a sandbank. Much of the cargo was removed, but the wreck remains in the sea and is visible about five miles away (8km) in Southend-on-Sea on a clear day. Chatham Historic Dockyard will conserve the masts, following a campaign for them to stay in Kent, as they technically remained property of the US government. The wreck remains subject to continuous monitoring and control via the exclusion zone in place. This video can not be played Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below. title: Kylie Jenner's debut at Victoria's Secret Fashion Show in $50m bra sparks mixed reaction
description: The reality star's surprise appearance on the runway in the diamond encrusted piece has sparked mixed reaction.
body: The Fantasy Bra has historically been worn by supermodels Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra. The make-up mogul surprised the crowd at the lingerie giant's annual show on Sunday while wearing the famed Fantasy Bra, which was made of 18-carat gold and 4,410 diamonds, according to the designer. The Fantasy Bra has been a key feature of the show over the years and wearing it is typically seen as an honour and defining moment for the chosen model. The Kardashians star, 29, being selected to wear the piece delighted some fans, while many others criticised the brand for not giving the opportunity to a veteran supermodel. Social media and marketing expert Joel Marlinarson says the moment was well-engineered and generated "a lot of conversation" on what it means for the "future of modelling and social media". "Of course Kylie represents a new era of celebrity where brands are prioritising who's going to bring the most eyeballs, as opposed to who fits the cookie cutter definition of a model," he tells BBC Newsbeat. Marlinarson says young viewers have a connection with Jenner having grown up watching her on social media and through her reality show with her Kardashian sisters. However, he says there will be a section of the audience who remembers "the iconic Naomi Campbell era of fashion" who might see Jenner being given this moment as a "betrayal of what they know". "Ultimately, this represents this new era of marketing where brands, particularly Victoria's Secret and legacy brands, they don't want to take risks," he says. "They want to bring in somebody who they know is going to generate eyeballs, who's going to generate those headlines and who can consistently raise a crowd and that's exactly what Victoria's Secret has done." Joel Marlinarson, who advises brands on social media strategy, says Kylie Jenner represents a "new age of celebrity" Some fans cheered on Jenner in the comments of a video shared on Victoria's Secret Instagram page unveiling the dramatic look., external While many others branded it as "pure disrespect to real models" and questioned why she was picked out of a "room full of talented models". One said the show has "gone from iconic glamour to an influencer circus" and they felt "social media clout and performative inclusivity have replaced real modeling talent, elegance, and runway presence". Chief creative officer at Victoria's Secret, Adam Selman, told Vogue, external that Jenner was picked for being a "cultural powerhouse". "Kylie really extends beyond fashion, beyond culture, beyond TV, beyond one singular thing," he adds. "That's the exact same thing that we do. "Like, the show is so big, it's true entertainment, and I think that she is a great catalyst for that." Model Summer Nesbeth says she can "understand people's frustration" around Kylie Jenner being used to model the famous bra British model Summer Nesbeth tells Newsbeat that she feels Victoria's Secret choosing Jenner was their attempt to keep up with young fans. "She's an influencer with a lot of power and we are in the social media age," says the 25-year-old, who has walked the runway at New York Fashion Week. The lingerie brand's catwalk show was scrapped after its 2018 edition drew low ratings, as well as criticism that it was sexist, outdated and lacked diversity. It returned in 2024, with a promise to "celebrate all women" and featured more a diverse range of talent, including Ashley Graham's appearance as a plus-sized model. Victoria's Secret created this year's Fantasy Bra in collaboration with jewellery brand Jacob & Co, who said it was the "most valuable" one ever created and took 15 artists more than 1,000 hours to create. Nesbeth believes the focus on the bra shows "how detached we are". "People can't eat, people can't afford to keep their lights on," she says. "I think there's a lot of things to say about where we're focussing our attention and where we're putting our money." BBC Newsbeat has contacted Victoria's Secret. title: Uber wins bid to throw out £200m black cab claims
description: Claims that Uber misled TfL over its licence were thrown out because they were brought too late.
body: The group action focused on Uber's operations in London between May 2012 and March 2018 Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about £340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms. The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012. But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true. Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity. About 13,000 drivers were seeking nearly £200m in damages, Reuters reported, while a claim on behalf of Kabbie and Iride, two private hire firms that have since closed, sought about £140m. The lawsuits were filed in 2024, and Uber argued they fell outside the six-year limit for bringing such claims. In a written ruling, Mr Justice Birt said the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018. RGL Management, which ran the cases for the claimants, said it was very disappointed and was considering its options with the legal team. Since gaining its licence, Uber has taken much of the trade once dominated by black cabs. The company faces a separate case next week, when it challenges HM Revenue and Customs in a tax dispute worth more than £1bn. title: Morgan Gibbs-White fined after his car ran red light
description: The midfielder failed to respond to two police letters asking whether he was driving at the time of the offence.
body: Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White failed to respond to two police letters, according to court documents England and Nottingham Forest attacking midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White has been handed a £1,000 court bill after his Range Rover was caught running a red light. The 26-year-old's vehicle was caught on camera going past a set of lights in West Bridgford, Nottinghamshire, 1.1 seconds after they turned red. Gibbs-White, who earned his first England cap in 2024, failed to respond to two police letters asking him to confirm if he had been driving at the time of the red light offence, according to court documents. Last Tuesday, he was convicted by a court of failing to provide the identity of a driver at the time of an offence. Nottinghamshire Police put out an alert on Gibbs-White's car when the force tried to investigate the traffic light incident, and found the number plate registered with the DVLA was one letter different from what was on the vehicle. Staffordshire Police then pulled over the Range Rover in April and confirmed it belonged to Gibbs-White. At Southern Derbyshire Magistrates' Court, he was fined £660, given six penalty points on his licence and ordered to pay £120 in costs and a £264 victim surcharge. Gibbs-White was called up to Thomas Tuchel's recent England squad for the Nations League A court official said Gibbs-White did not enter a plea or mitigation, and was sentenced behind closed doors under the fast-track Single Justice Procedure. Court papers show a Nottinghamshire Police camera caught Gibbs-White's car going past a red traffic light at 15:17 GMT on 28 January in Radcliffe Road. "At the time of the offence, the vehicle was captured failing to comply with a red light signal, the time into the red light was recorded as 1.1 seconds," a police worker wrote in her statement. Gibbs-White was banned from driving for six months in May last year after he was caught speeding six times in the space of three months. At the time, he was ordered to pay just under £4,000 in fines for the spate of offences, including two speeding tickets acquired on the same day. Gibbs-White, who signed for Forest in 2022 from Wolverhampton Wanderers, has made 10 appearances for England and was called up to Thomas Tuchel's recent squad for the Nations League. title: When to switch your clocks back as British Summer Time comes to an end
description: British Summer Time will soon comes to an end as the clocks go back an hour to Greenwich Mean Time.
body: Smartphones will often change automatically but analogue watches and clocks will need to be manually changed British Summer Time (BST), also known as Daylight Saving Time (DST), will come to an end this week as the clocks go back an hour. The change happens on Sunday 25 October at 02:00 BST meaning you may get an extra hour in bed. Sunset will move forward an hour as well and initially you may notice the sun coming up earlier too. The clocks don't go forward again until on Sunday 28 March 2027. Changes to the clocks have been taking place for more than a century. The first country to make use of DST was Germany in 1916. It was intended to save fuel consumption during World War One. Making the most of the evening daylight in spring and summer meant less heating and lighting was needed. Many other countries followed suit, such as the UK where it became known as British Summer Time. Here the time shift has continued ever since, despite a short period in World War Two where the clocks went forward two hours for British Double Summer Time, and a spell from 1968 to 1971 when the UK experimented with all-year-around BST. Once we go back to GMT sunsets will occur earlier In the United States earlier in 2026 there was a bill to make daylight saving time the new standard time called the Sunshine Protection Act. With a 308-117 vote, members of both parties approved the bill, which would remove the need for Americans to change their clocks twice a year and put the US under time currently observed between March and November - known as permanent standard time. The idea of winding our clocks forward permanently has been a talking point in the past. Arguments for keeping summer time include a potential boost in economic productivity as well as a possible reduction in evening road accidents. However, it would also mean some darker winter mornings, especially in Scotland. In some parts the sun rises around 08:45 GMT in the second half of December, which would equate to 09:45 BST. Currently there are no plans in the UK to get rid of the biannual clock change. This year most of Europe turns their clocks back on the same day as the UK - Sunday 25 October. In Asia, Oceania, South America and Africa there are only a few places that follow DST. In Egypt DST comes to an end on Friday 30 October. In North America, however, the clocks go back on the first weekend of November which this year will be the first of the month. title: 'It's messed with my family too much' - inside the US opioid crisis
description: The BBC's Quentin Sommerville spoke to a former heroin addict who now helps other people overcome addiction.
body: This video can not be played Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis. In 2022, 110,000 people in the United States were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over. Former heroin user Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby. She is now 17 years free from hard drugs. Karen, now a recovery worker, says the drugs being used now are more dangerous. Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply - and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Read more on this story: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external. A list of UK organisations that can help is available via the BBC Action Line. title: Police investigating hoax threat emails sent to Scottish schools
description: The message was received by schools in areas including Glasgow, Edinburgh and East Renfrewshire.
body: The email was received by schools across the country Police are investigating after a number of schools across Scotland were targeted by a bomb threat email which is being treated as a hoax. BBC Scotland has confirmed that messages were received by schools in Glasgow, Edinburgh, East Renfrewshire, Perth an Kinross and East Lothian among other local authorities. They are believed to have been sent to both primary and secondary schools. Schools in Northern Ireland were also sent an email claiming "an explosive device" had been put into 160 schools. Their education minister said it was not being treated as a "viable threat". A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We are aware of threatening messages being sent to a number of schools across Scotland. "These are being treated as a hoax and officers are investigating." BBC Scotland has contacted all 32 local authorities. So far, Scottish Borders, East Lothian, East Renfrewshire, Glasgow, Edinburgh, East Dunbartonshire, Midlothian, North Lanarkshire, Moray and North Ayrshire have confirmed they are aware of schools receiving the threat. Highland and Aberdeenshire councils said they were not aware of any threat, while West Dunbartonshire and East Ayrshire referred to the Police Scotland statement. A spokesperson for East Renfrewshire Council said many of its schools had received a "malicious threat" and staff immediately followed relevant procedures. "After notifying Police Scotland, the communication is being investigated as a hoax, and our schools are operating as normal," the spokesperson said. A message sent to parents and carers by Perth and Kinross council said the email had been received by some of its schools and nurseries. The statement said: "Similar emails have been received by schools across the country and reported to Police Scotland. They are being investigated as a hoax communication and, importantly, there is currently no information to suggest any cause for concern. "We know reports like this can be worrying for families. As children and young people prepare to return next week, please be reassured that their safety and wellbeing, and that of our staff, remains our highest priority." In several parts of Scotland pupils are still on holiday and in others only teachers are in school for an in service day. Schools in England and Wales are also on half-term holidays. Edinburgh city council's education convenor, James Dalgleish, said: "While I'm obviously relieved that this is has been confirmed as a hoax, I'm hugely frustrated that someone would target schools and young people in this way - causing unnecessary disruption right across the UK. He said the impact on pupils was "thankfully more limited" due to the in service day it "doesn't take away from the stupidity of this person's actions". title: Brook says he has 'learned a lot' from off-field issues
description: White-ball captain Harry Brook says he has "learned a lot" as a captain and a person - and wants to be the player England fans rely on.
body: England have climbed to sixth in the ODI rankings and are top of the T20 rankings White-ball captain Harry Brook says he has "learned a lot" as a captain and a person - and wants to be the player England fans rely on. It is almost a year since Brook, 27, was punched by a nightclub bouncer on the eve of a match against New Zealand in Wellington, which led to doubts over his future as skipper. He has not made a Test hundred since, including failing to do so during last winter's Ashes, but has been in excellent white-ball form and has overseen a resurgence in England's 50-over and T20 sides. "I've learnt a lot as a captain, I've learnt a lot as a person," Brook, whose side return to action in a 50-over tri-series on Tuesday, told Press Association. "I know it wasn't an ideal situation to put myself in, but I feel like as a captain and a leader I've learnt a lot. "Responsibilities and leadership aren't just on the field, they're more so off the field as well and actions speak louder than words." How one rule change is altering the face of one-day cricket Brook remains one of England's most fascinating cricketers. Despite being white-ball skipper and serving as Test vice-captain, he was overlooked for the red-ball job when Ben Stokes retired, with Joe Root preferred. He averages a formidable 53.08 in Tests - the highest for England in almost 60 years - with 10 centuries, but often draws criticism for his aggressive, some say reckless, batting. While he has failed to convert any of his seven fifties into centuries since the Ashes, he still averages 41.57 and has scored hundreds as captain in T20s and one-day internationals in that time. "I enjoy the extra responsibility," he said. "I like the extra little bit of added pressure. "I'm not going to go out there and score runs every time I bat but I want to be the man that is in that match-winning situation who can get us over the line. "I know there have been a few innings where I haven't managed to do that but hopefully I've turned that corner and I can really be the man England fans and the team rely on." The debate around Brook was perhaps best summed up by Stokes telling the Yorkshireman he is talented enough to average 65 or 70. "Personally I'm not that bothered about the stats, I've always said I think there should be a match-winning column in your stats – that's not there," Brook said. "I write stuff down and I try and judge myself on whether I've had a match-winning performance or match-winning impact in that specific game and I try and tally it up at the end of the year and see how well I've done." His 50-over side play Pakistan in Rawalpindi on Tuesday (09:00 BST) in their first match of a tri-series that also includes Sri Lanka. The hosts beat Sri Lanka in the series opener on Sunday. After struggling in the format since their dismal World Cup defence in 2023, England have won three ODI series in a row this year as they build towards next year's World Cup. Wicketkeeper Jos Buttler is injured for this series while fast bowler Jofra Archer has been rested. England resisted naming their team 24 hours early and will instead do so at the toss. "In the last six to eight months we're certainly trending in the right direction as a squad," Brook said. "We're really building towards the make-up of the side that we want. "Me and Baz [head coach Brendon McCullum] feel like we've got a squad where if someone does go down five minutes before the toss, we're in a position where someone else can come in and fill that role perfectly well." title: What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car
description: Helen Haines was hit by a car in what the prime minister has called a "deliberate act".
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'Helen Haines is a thoroughly decent human being,' Australia PM says Australian MP Helen Haines has been taken to hospital with critical injuries after she was struck by a car, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has called "a deliberate act". Haines was hit near an office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne on Monday afternoon local time. Albanese said counter-terrorism police are involved in the investigation. Haines was struck by a White Toyota Landcruiser, which was driven by a 43-year-old Tarrawingee man, police said. The suspect was arrested at the scene by a passer-by before being taken into custody by officers, it added. A knife was also seized from inside the Toyota, the force said. Victoria Police said it was unknown whether the suspect and Haines knew each other and its investigation remains ongoing. Haines is a 65-year-old Independent MP for the Indi division in Victoria, south-eastern Australia. She grew up in the south west of Victoria on a dairy farm with four brothers before training as a nurse and a midwife, according to a biography on her website. It goes on to say she became the matron of the Chiltern Bush Nursing Hospital in Victoria when she was 26, before later completing a master's degree in public health and a PhD in Medical Science while raising her three children and working. She lives with her family on a small cattle farm outside Wangaratta. The MP was first elected to the Australian House of Representatives in 2019 and was re-elected in 2022 and 2025. Australian MP has critical injuries after being hit by car in what PM calls 'deliberate act' Haines's family said the incident happened outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, a city of about 30,000 people, a few hours north-east of Melbourne in the state of Victoria. Police said she was hit outside an office on Murphy Street at about 15:35 local time (05:35 BST). Albanese appeared close to tears during a live television interview on ABC's 7.30 programme when he was asked if Australian politicians talk among themselves about the threats and risks they face. "Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one, one of my colleagues." He later described how there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia. Speaking in a news conference, Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said there had been an increase in reports of harassing and threatening behaviour towards lawmakers in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with 951 for the previous year. Paying tribute to Haines during a news conference, Albanese described her as "incredibly hard-working". "She is fiercely intelligent but most importantly she is just a thoroughly decent human being full of integrity and respected right across the Parliament and from everyone who comes into contact with her", he added. He said the attack will come as an "incredible shock" to her community. Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong described the incident as a "shocking and deeply disturbing attack". The Premier of Victoria Ben Carroll said he was "deeply appalled" by the "violent attack". Meanwhile, Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the attack. "This is a shocking day for our nation," he said. "No-one should be targeted in this way." title: Schools 'explosive device' email a hoax, say police
description: Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police consider the risk to the public "as low".
body: Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police consider the risk to the public as "low" An email threatening that "an explosive device" is located within hundreds of schools in Northern Ireland is being treated as a "hoax" by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI). Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police take "incidents of this nature very seriously" however "at this stage we consider risk to the public as low". Some schools have closed after receiving the email, however others have decided to stay open and are taking advice from the PSNI. Police Scotland said they are investigating emails sent to schools and are also treating threats as a hoax. One school in Lambeg emailed parents to say that they should "come immediately" and collect children adding: "Please don't panic the children are all safe." The email originated from outside the UK police say and similar emails have been received by some schools across the UK. The PSNI said up to 300 schools have reported receiving the same emailed message which contained a generalised threat. "Checks have not, at this time, resulted in anything untoward," added the PSNI. "Based on enquiries and information to date, police are treating this email, which originated from outside the UK, as a hoax." Henderson said police "understand the concern in the community, not to mention the disruption it has caused in some school communities and for students and parents". "We will continue to liaise with schools impacted and have been working closely with the Department of Education and the Education Authority this morning to provide reassurance." Police enquires into the email are continuing. Paul Givan said that the email has "caused huge alarm" and condemned the "level of disruption caused to young people's education" The Education Minister Paul Givan said the email has "caused huge alarm" and condemned the "level of disruption caused to young people's education". In a statement he added: "Schools should continue to operate as normal." "I recognise that this has caused huge alarm and distress among pupils, parents and school staff and I understand that schools have had to make decisions in the best interests of their pupils and staff. This has unfortunately led to a number of school closures. "My Department will continue to work with the PSNI and the Education Authority and we will continue to engage with the PSNI as their enquiries continue." Claire Robinson said she feels that principals have been left to make the decisions themselves Claire Robinson, who is the head teacher at Holy Evangelists' Primary School in west Belfast, told BBC Radio Ulster's the Nolan Show that the advice schools have been given is "practically non-existent". "There's been nothing from the Education Authority, there's been nothing from CCMS [Council for Catholic Maintained Schools], bar two letters that are more or less telling us absolutely nothing," she said. Robinson said she feels that principals have been left to make the decisions themselves. "We need guidance in the event these things happen. "It's wholly unacceptable when we're dealing with children". Emma Quinn said that there has been conflicting advice provided to school principals Meanwhile, the principal for Rathcoole Primary School in Newtownabbey, Emma Quinn, said that although her school is having a staff training day, it had gone into a lockdown procedure. However, she said there has been "very little guidance, if no guidance, from the Education Authority". "It's left to principals to make a very vital decision about the safety of their pupils and staff." Quinn added that there has been conflicting advice provided to school principals. Chantal Ailsby collected her child from school At Rosetta PS in south Belfast, Chantal Ailsby told BBC News NI that the school handled the threat well. Parents were given the option to collect their children from the school. Nora Xhemha also collected her children. She said she was "so scared". "We don't know what is going on. I hope that every child here is safe." The Education Authority (EA) has been contacted in regards to the critical comments made by Quinn and Robinson. On the actual email itself, the EA said it was "aware" of it adding: "We recognise the concern this may cause for school leaders, staff, pupils and families. "We are engaging closely with the PSNI and will act on their advice. "Communications have been issued to schools, and we continue to support school leaders and keep them informed." Similar threats were received by schools in the Republic of Ireland last week. An Garda Síochána said it was "aware of a communication" that was sent on the 14 October. "Gardaí are currently assessing the contents and credibility of that communication. "Gardaí are engaging with a number of educational establishments. No further information is available at this time." title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
description: The 51-year-old faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
body: Warning - this report contains graphic content A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place. In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her. Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation". A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her. The woman is the third complainant the jury have heard from in the trial - and the second to allege rape. The pair had been attending a birthday party in Soho in London in 2004 when the alleged incidents happened. She said after the alleged sexual assault, "The visual I remember is just this big grin - it felt like a clown, (with) that sort of weird look in the eye. It was a normal conversation about him being on Big Brother. He just moved towards (me) and grabbed both my boobs". She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock". "The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said. "Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here". "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added. After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now'". Russell Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual. The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks. title: Personal attacks fire up debate before Brazil's run-off vote
description: The race heats up just days before the run-off between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing challenger.
body: Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are competing for the presidency in a run-off election due on Sunday Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election. Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters. But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further. In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula. Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open. Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election. The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round. Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time". Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks. Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments. "The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression." Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin". Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off. Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking. One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk. Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia". Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen." He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt). Bolsonaro had highlighted the initials for the Workers' Party on his hand "Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese. Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power. He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula". Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father". title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
description: The chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee says families should not be taxed through no fault of their own.
body: Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned. Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free. Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own. The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman. However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait. The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK. Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases. Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases. Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills. Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions Retired civil servants left in pension limbo According to the latest figures up to 30 September, external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old. Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days. The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved. If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance. The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate. Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty". His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability. Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim". He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month". He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear." Money Box Live: Capita, What Went Wrong? Money Box Live looks at what is going on with Capita, which administers millions of people's pensions Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death. On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed. Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on. "It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said. "It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult." Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings. However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive. Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up". Rob is hoping the government will waive the tax due for people in his situation Fran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures. "If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said. A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off. "We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays. "If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses." Capita has been contacted for comment. The company has previously apologised for the impact of service issues on pension scheme members and said it is working to resolved outstanding cases. title: Italian PM Meloni to hold emergency meeting after weekend of violent clashes
description: More than 200 people were detained during two days of rioting in the city, Italian media reports.
body: More than 200 people were arrested across the weekend, according to Italian media Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan. More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers. "To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos". Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania. Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself". Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world". Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported. The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI. Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured. Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north. Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder. The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting. "Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification". Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported. The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets. title: Man accused of mass train stabbing admits wounding
description: Anthony Williams is in court after multiple stabbings on a train that was forced to stop in Huntingdon.
body: Emergency crews met the train at Huntingdon railway station, one stop south of Peterborough, after 999 calls were made from people on board A man accused of a mass stabbing on a train in Cambridgeshire last year has pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent. Passengers and staff were injured on the 18:25 Doncaster-London service on Saturday, 1 November after it left Peterborough, causing it to make an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon railway station. Anthony Williams, 33, has denied 14 counts of attempted murder, relating to the train and to incidents in London and Peterborough, and is due to stand trial next week. Appearing at a pre-trial review at Cambridge Crown Court, Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, pleaded guilty to the lesser wounding charges and several other offences. He appeared via video link from Rampton Hospital in Nottinghamshire. At an earlier hearing, Williams pleaded not guilty to attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett, and Samir Zitouni on the train near Huntingdon on 1 November. In front of Mr Justice Calver this Monday, Williams pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent in relation to incidents on the train, and earlier in Peterborough and London. Huntingdon Station was closed for a couple of days while evidence was gathered He also admitted affray at a barber shop in Peterborough on 31 October and the theft of knives from an Asda store in Stevenage on 31 October. He pleaded guilty to possessing a bladed article in a public place in Peterborough on 31 October, at Pontoon Dock DLR station at Silvertown, east London, in the early hours of 1 November, and on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on 1 November. He also admitted assault occasioning actual bodily harm of a male police officer on 2 November, and common assault on a Govia Thames Link train between London St Pancras and Biggleswade in Bedfordshire on 1 November. Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said the "guilty pleas do not resolve the indictment, so there will be a trial". Williams also denies one count of attempted murder at Pontoon Dock DLR station on 1 November and three counts of attempted murder in Peterborough on 31 October. The trial, which is expected to last six weeks, is due to begin next Monday. Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. title: Reform MSP quits party to sit as independent
description: Amanda Bland's decision relegates the party to the third-largest group at Holyrood, with one member fewer than Labour.
body: Amanda Bland represents Central Scotland and Lothians West MSP Amanda Bland has quit Reform UK Scotland to sit as an independent. The resignation relegates the party to the third-largest group at Holyrood, with one member fewer than Labour. A Reform UK source told BBC Scotland News that Bland was "very difficult to work with" and had been called to a meeting on Wednesday to discuss a high turnover of staff in her office. Bland, who represents Central Scotland and Lothians West as a list MSP, is yet to comment. A Reform spokesperson said: "Amanda Bland should reflect on her reasons for choosing to isolate herself from that team of capable individuals. "It is incumbent on her to resign as a regional MSP for Central Scotland and Lothians West and allow her constituents to be represented by the next Reform candidate on that list." Under Holyrood's rules, a list MSP would be replaced by the their party's next candidate at the last election if they resigned. Bland, a former primary school teacher and police officer, was among 17 Reform candidates to be returned to the Scottish Parliament in May as the party made its electoral breakthrough north of the border. The party finished in joint second with Labour, behind the SNP on 58 seats. Reform's cohort, led by former Conservative minister Malcolm Offord, have repeatedly invoked the condemnation of the chamber - most notably after staging a walkout during an independence debate, and by tabling a motion proposing a burka ban. Currently, Offord is first to question John Swinney at First Minister's Questions every other week, alternating with Labour. The party is now likely to lose that privilege. Scottish Labour deputy leader Jackie Baillie said: "No one will be surprised to see chaos at the heart of Reform." She said the party had been "utterly useless at holding the SNP to account or getting results for the Scottish people", adding: "It's been a series of stunts, gimmicks, photo calls and precious little else." Scottish Liberal Democrat David Green MSP said that Reform had been hit by "scandal after scandal". He added: "I'm sure more and more of its MSPs will be taking a long hard look at what they've signed up for." The Scottish Parliament confirmed Bland's resignation and said its website, external had been updated accordingly.
