title: Four arrested after police officer injured in shooting
description: The officer was shot in the foot and remains in hospital in a stable condition, police say.
body: A male police officer remains in hospital after being shot in the foot Four people have been arrested - including a woman on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm and possessing a firearm - after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre. Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday. The male officer remains in hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added. Two women, 27 and 25, and a 24-year-old man were arrested after police stopped a vehicle in the Radford area of Nottingham on Sunday evening, while a 30-year-old man was arrested in Bedfordshire in the early hours of Monday. The 27-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life. The 24-year-old man and 25-year-old woman were also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender. Separately, after stopping a vehicle in Bedfordshire, the 30-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender. Detectives said a gun was found at the scene Assistant Chief Constable Claire Rukas said: "A team of experienced detectives continues to work tirelessly to establish exactly what happened before, during and after this appalling incident. "I am pleased that four arrests have now been made and hope this provides some reassurance to the public as those detained are questioned in connection with the discharge of the firearm." A large police cordon - which was put in place in Angel Row following the shooting - has now been lifted. ACC Rukas thanked local businesses, residents and members of the public for their patience, support and understanding while the force carried out its investigation. "The injured officer continues to recover in hospital and is receiving support from colleagues and loved ones," she said. "We ask that his privacy is respected at this time. "Our thoughts remain with him, and with his family, friends and colleagues, who have all been affected by this deeply shocking incident." The large police cordon in Angel Row has now been lifted On Monday, Nottinghamshire Police and Crime Commissioner Gary Godden said the officer's injuries were "not life-threatening - it's most likely to be life-altering". The PCC added the incident highlighted the dangers of being a police officer. "This officer was going to speak to two individuals who were acting suspiciously, and this happened," he said. Labour MP for Nottingham East Nadia Whittome has told the BBC she understood the officer was "now out of surgery". She added: "This incident will no doubt will be damaging to the reputation of the city, especially because of our past, but I think that we also saw was an extremely rare incident that was the worst of our city. "But we also saw the best of our city. At quarter to five on Sunday morning, people coming together doing everything that they could to assist and I think that we have to take comfort in that as well." title: You Can See Everything documentary stuns with huge box office debut
description: It shows fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invite a sceptical film into her home before she's sent to prison.
body: A three-hour documentary on the tech fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has raked in a whopping $15 million (£11.25m) on its box office debut, despite a limited run at 855 screens across the US and Canada. The eagerly anticipated A24 film, titled You Can See Everything, was co-directed by comedian Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. It finds Holmes at her home in 2023 during the month before she began an 11-year prison sentence. US publication Deadline has described it as "easily the second best opening ever for a documentary at the box office after 2004s Fahrenheit 9/11", Michael Moore's movie about the US's 2003 invasion of Iraq. Ticket sales at the box office were enough for second place behind Paramount's new video game adaptation, Street Fighter, which opened to $31 million in North America and $51.1 million globally. You Can See Everything also secured the largest debut for any film playing on under 1,000 screens since 2006's Borat, which scored $26 million. Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors in her medical testing company Theranos, fuelling a media circus that has been chronicled in books, podcasts and the mini-series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried. In You Can See Everything, comedian Fielder - known for shows including The Rehearsal and The Curse - places himself inside the action, once again blurring the lines between documentary, social experiment and prank show. We see notorious Silicon Valley founder Holmes invite a sceptical film crew to document her every move, thirty-four days before she's sent to prison. The first teaser trailer dropped last month, right after the film's surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado. It went viral and launched many online memes of Holmes unblinkingly asking Fielder: "Why would I deceive you?" The stranger-than-fiction documentary has garnered rave reviews and is already being talked about as an Oscar contender as we head into awards season. Remarkable for a documentary - that isn't based on a live music event - produced in secret over three years which no-one really knew about until recently. The Guardian awarded the film five stars, external, calling it "a modern masterpiece of deceit", stressing how "TV's grand illusionist meets his match when he moves in with Theranos founder and her family". The Financial Times, external also offered five stars describing documentary as "a mind-bending revelation". The New York Times, external noted how it sees Holmes and Fielder "joust in a dizzying movie about truth, reality and the contours of knowledge". The buzz around the film is likely to see it be in the running, at least, for a nomination for best documentary feature at next year's Academy Awards, though no documentary has ever been nominated for the main prize of best picture. title: Israeli police arrest 10 over settler attacks on journalist and diplomats in West Bank
description: It comes after masked settlers attacked Palestinians and European officials visiting the West Bank during olive harvesting season.
body: Photojournalist Heidi Levine was knocked to the ground by a group of settlers and kicked repeatedly Israeli police say they have arrested 10 suspects in the occupied West Bank after attacks by settlers on an American journalist and European diplomats last week. The unnamed suspects were detained at several locations on suspicion of acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction, according to a statement. Potential evidence and vehicles were also seized. On Friday, masked Israeli settlers beat and severely injured Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine as she covered an olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A day later, diplomats from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church were attacked by masked settlers in nearby Taybeh. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, welcomed the arrests. "A very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat Heidi Levine," he wrote on X. Settler violence in the West Bank is at an all-time high, according to UN records. However, it has escalated dramatically during this year's olive harvest, which is essential to Palestinian livelihoods. The Israeli human rights group Yesh Din said on Sunday that it had logged 269 incidents of violence directly related to the olive harvest over the previous 20 days. They included 98 cases of violence and physical assaults against harvesters, as well as crop thefts, and the damaging and burning of olive trees. This video can not be played Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest A BBC team witnessed one of several settler attacks during an olive harvest near Khirbet Abu Falah on Friday, which a local official said injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian-American citizens, as well as Heidi Levine. The veteran photojournalist, who was wearing a flak jacket clearly marked "PRESS" on the front and back, said she was knocked to the ground by a group of settlers, kicked repeatedly, and stripped of her cameras and phone. She suffered four broken vertebrae, a broken rib and lacerations across her body. She required surgery on a finger that was ripped open. In a telephone interview with the BBC's Today programme from her hospital bed in central Israel on Monday, Levine said it "could have been a lot worse". "We [journalists] don't always want to wear flak jackets and helmets - it's heavy, it can be a pain when other people aren't wearing them, you feel kind of silly - but we all did and I'm grateful for that." "I think I would have suffered more serious injuries for sure, especially [to] my head. I tried to keep my face to the ground as much as I possibly could so that protected it... I don't guess, but I know that I'm actually really, really lucky." Huckabee called the attack on Levine a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards" and said they should spend years in prison. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump "does not want to see friction or anything - a crisis in the West Bank". Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he had told Levine that the "despicable behaviour of the perpetrators of this attack does not represent the citizens or the values of the State of Israel". On Saturday, a delegation of Belgian, French, Polish and Catholic Church envoys visited Taybeh, about 6km (4 miles) to the south of Abu Falah, to watch an olive harvest. Belgium's Foreign Minister, Maxime Prevot, said a car from its consulate was damaged and that a French mayor, Bernard Baudoux, was assaulted. Video from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy and a man wearing a French tricolour sash slumped beside a vehicle. Reports suggested that stones were thrown. Prevot condemned the attack in the strongest terms and said that Israel, as the occupying power, had to protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. The European Union also demanded "full accountability". Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy Despite the international condemnation, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office questioned the video evidence and testimony from the incidents in Abu Falah and Taybeh. It described them as "alleged" attacks and said they came amid what it called a "co-ordinated campaign to smear Israel" and West Bank settlers. "I've had the president of Israel call me, and he was very, very sweet. He called the attackers thugs, promised to do everything in his power to have them arrested," Levine told the BBC. "I was just reading another article regarding the prime minister's response, and it's shocking to me. It's a big slap on my face." She said Netanyahu should have sent a "clear message" telling settlers to end their attacks, "instead of the message that I feel was presented, which is... 'Keep at it.'" Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law. At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN's figures. Twenty-five of those deaths have occurred in the context of settler attacks. Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, the UN says. Israel's police commissioner, Daniel Levy, said the law applied to everyone in the West Bank, "regardless of identity or affiliation". However, prosecutions of Israeli settlers accused of attacking Palestinians are rare. Between 2005 and 2025, more than 93% of Israeli police investigations into ideologically-motivated offences

title: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
description: Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie faces 191 murder charges - all but one of them children.
body: Paul Mackenzie operated his church for 16 years, attracting thousands of followers A Kenyan judge has started to deliver a verdict in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie. Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 people, all but one of them children. His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil". Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die. Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution. Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country. Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day. "Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old." "We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets". Salim Karisa was paid about $8 a day to dig up dozens of bodies Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside." Stephen Mwiti, 48, recounted losing all six of his children to the cult and seeing "many bald women and tens of children" surrounding Mackenzie in his house when he went to confront him. Mackenzie forbade make-up and hairstyles, so told women to shave off their hair or keep it unkempt. Mwiti's former wife is one of those accused alongside Mackenzie. "If I met Pastor Mackenzie today, one of us will have to die," told the BBC. Stephen Mwiti says his six children died in the forest "All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel." "This little thing here was the start of all my misery," Mwiti said as he pointed at a dusty TV and cable box in his home in the coastal town of Malindi, 70km (43 miles) from Shakahola. It was from that TV that Mackenzie's doctrine made it to his home. The pastor established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in the church's branches across Kenya. His church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi. His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil". This is the building from where Mackenzie broadcast his sermons Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning." The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons". The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned. "My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said. The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said. By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers. Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover. "My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said. "I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest." Peter Shukrani says he would have died if he had stayed in the forest but still believes Mackenzie is a good man In the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, 190 victims of the 191 Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children. Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition. title: England manager Wiegman signs contract extension
description: Sarina Wiegman says she "cannot think of a better job in football" as she commits to staying on as manager of the Lionesses until after Euro 2029.
body: Sarina Wiegman has been in charge of England for more than five years England manager Sarina Wiegman has signed a two-year contract extension with the Lionesses. The 56-year-old's previous deal was due to expire after next summer's World Cup, but her new contract will run until the end of Euro 2029. Dutchwoman Wiegman guided England to their second straight European Championship title with victory over Spain in the Euro 2025 final. The victory meant the Lionesses became the first England team - women's or men's - to win a major trophy on foreign soil. "I am so happy to be able to carry on with this squad and cannot think of a better job in football," said Wiegman. "Working for a world-class organisation like The FA, and alongside so many people dedicated to winning England teams and the growth of our game, excites me every day." England thrashed Greece 8-1 on aggregate last week to qualify for round two of the World Cup play-offs, where they will face Ukraine. Should the Lionesses win that two-legged tie, they will qualify for next summer's World Cup in Brazil. "My main concern right now is absolutely the World Cup, and helping this squad realise their potential in the years to come," Wiegman added. "We have an important job to do to confirm our place in Brazil, and hopefully we can do that and give the country another special summer to remember next year." Wiegman replaced Phil Neville as England manager in September 2021, guiding the Lionesses to their first piece of major silverware at Euro 2022 when they beat Germany 2-1 in the final at Wembley. England then reached the World Cup final in Australia in 2023, only to lose 1-0 to Spain. By reaching the 2025 Euros final, Wiegman became the first women's or men's manager to reach five consecutive major international finals after leading the Netherlands to the Euro 2017 title and runners-up at the 2019 World Cup. England's Euro 2025 victory meant Wiegman became just the second manager after Germany's Christina Theune to win three successive European Championships. FA chief Mark Bullingham described Wiegman as an "incredible coach with an unparalleled record in major tournaments". "While we will all remember the trophies and thrilling moments she has given us, I know she is only looking forward," Bullingham added. "There is no one better to lead the Lionesses into the next two tournaments. "Sarina's impact on English football has been immense, and she continues to inspire so many throughout the game. We have so much more to do in the women's game and she will be instrumental in helping us to achieve that." Does Scott's Disney+ exit unmask wider issue in coverage of women's game? The FA and England fans alike will be delighted that the 'Wiegman era' is set to continue beyond the 2027 World Cup. Having led the Lionesses to back-to-back European titles and the 2023 World Cup final, many expected Wiegman to leave after next summer's tournament in Brazil in search of a new challenge. Instead, her commitment to stay until 2029 underlines the strength of her relationship with the FA and her team. While today's announcement may have surprised some, the timing now allows Wiegman and the players to focus fully on World Cup qualification, without the distraction of a looming succession plan. Widely regarded as one of the game's greatest-ever coaches, Wiegman has already achieved what few can match. But even after three consecutive Euros, this contract extension proves she still has an appetite for more as she chases an elusive World Cup title. title: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
description: The blaze that killed four men and injured dozens of others spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.
body: This video can not be played Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire The fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest. It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds. "The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds." Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity" being to blame for the fire. The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died. Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright. What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base Tributes are being paid to the servicemen who died. Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father". Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers". The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life." This video can not be played Watch: Incident at Canadian military base 'unheard of', says local mayor In account of Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range. He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time". "I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said. Rutland said it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire. Some witnesses had said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure". The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBS said. According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month. Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day. title: Alberta heads to polls to decide whether to hold vote on separation from Canada
description: Polling suggests most Albertans favour remaining part of the country, although the debate alone has proven divisive.
body: This video can not be played WATCH: The father and son on opposite sides of Alberta’s separation referendum People in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a referendum at a later date on separating from Canada. The vote was called earlier this year by the leader of the province, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation. Many of those who support separation say the oil-rich province's economic growth has been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa. But those who want Alberta to remain part of Canada - who include Prime Minister Mark Carney - have called for the country to show unity in the face of external pressures. Polls have suggested that the majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, though the pre-vote debate alone has proven divisive. Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The province's population is about five million people. If Albertans do vote on Monday to move ahead with a binding referendum, that could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said. Smith's decision to allow Monday's vote came in spite of the fact that a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated from Canada. Following the judge's ruling, First Nations groups have branded Smith's decision to allow the voting process to play out as "undemocratic" and "authoritarian". Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party of Alberta (UCP), has defended her decision to put the issue to voters. She opposes separation herself, but says the process gives the province's residents a chance to have their say on the issue. The key question on the voting paper will ask: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?" Why is Alberta voting to separate from Canada, and how likely is it to happen? The separatist movement is led by Mitch Sylvestre, a gun shop owner from the town of Bonnyville, and Jeffrey Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary. They are both members of a group called the Alberta Prosperity Project, which argues that the province's economic growth has been hindered by years of Liberal party rule in Ottawa. Successive Liberal governments of the last 10 years have put environmental policies above helping Alberta develop its oil and gas sector, they argue. They say Alberta would get to keep more of its wealth if it splits from Canada. Chris Scott, founder of pro-separatist group Let's Talk Alberta, told BBC News on the eve of the poll that the campaign had already achieved some of its goals, regardless of what happened on Monday. "The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue," he said. "What's started can't be stopped now," he added. Those who oppose separation say a newly independent Alberta would be left responsible for billions of dollars in debt. They warn that the uncertainty - which they liken to the UK's Brexit vote to leave the European Union in 2016 - would drive thousands of jobs and investment out of the province. Carney has called on voters to deliver a decisive vote against separation. Speaking at a rally on Thursday, he warned that the stakes were high. "The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," Carney said, echoing warnings he has made in the past about his country's ongoing trade war with the United States. Alongside the separation question, Albertans will vote on nine other issues - a number of which focus on whether the province should have more control over its immigration system. Hundreds of thousands of people had voted early by post ahead of Monday, and early figures suggested a strong voter turnout. The province's election officials will count the ballots by hand, and have 48 hours to complete the task - starting from no earlier than 20:00 local time on Monday (02:00 GMT on Tuesday). The key question, on separation, will be counted in its entirety first. Officials have said results should be available in the early hours of Tuesday. title: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
description: Researchers travelled to a remote Pacific Island to confirm whether an object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the mystery of the pilot's disappearance.
body: A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object, which some had hypothesised could have been Amelia Earhart's plane, in a lagoon on Nikumaroro Researchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees. The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance. But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit". By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said. Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937 Images of the Taraia Object - which Purdue University said was visible in photography dating back to 1938 - led researchers to wonder if it was the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters. "This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years and the mystery continues," said project director Rick Pettigrew, speaking from near the site of the object. "The island has been holding on to its secrets and it continues to do so. I think eventually someone will find conclusive evidence here," he added. Earhart's plane vanished without a trace in 1937 on the third-to-last leg of her attempt to fly around the world. She had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea. Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to then travel towards Hawaii before returning to California. But their plane vanished while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote uninhabited coral island about 400 miles (644km) from Nikumaroro, to refuel. One theory is Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway. The research team had travelled for five days by sea to reach Nikumaroro and was forced to spend several days on their ship following rough seas and strong winds, delaying their search on the island. They spent four days onshore investigating the site. title: Selena Gomez says vaping has affected her voice
description: The 34-year-old says vaping nicotine "a lot" permanently affected her singing and speaking voice.
body: The singer and actress recently completed filming the fifth series of Only Murders In The Building in London Selena Gomez has said vaping nicotine has changed the way her voice sounds. "I'm not gonna be able to change my voice," the singer, 34, said in a candid Instagram post, external on Sunday. "I vaped nicotine a lot." "Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you're going through it, or if you're even trying to vape, it's just not worth it," she continued. "It's so stupid and it changed my voice," she reiterated, then laughed: "So if you guys don't like listening to my voice, that's totally understandable. I don't mind. Just don't listen to it." The singer and actress, who has the chronic autoimmune disease lupus, has previously suggested that the condition was affecting her vocal cords. Asked about her voice in an Instagram Q&A last December,, external she said: "Sometimes things happen. I get weird. My throat kind of swells inside sometimes. That's all."⁠ Lupus flare-ups can cause inflammation around the larynx (voice box), which can cause your voice to become raspy and strained - similar to the symptoms of a cold. Gomez's voice has also deepened with age, which is not uncommon. However, some fans have fixated on the change, posting compilation videos showing the evolution of her speaking style, external on YouTube. In her Instagram video, the Only Murders In The Building star noted she had recently weaned herself off nicotine. "I am really excited because I stopped and I just hope I can keep it up," she said. "It's really hard, but I know if you are going through something you can get through it too. It sucks." The star made her admission in an Instagram story Evidence on some of the side effects of vaping are becoming a little clearer, although the long-term effects are still not known. A recent report from doctors said vaping was linked to breathing problems, wheezing and coughing, dental issues, poor sleep, mental health problems and even eye symptoms. Vaping isn't harmless - the nicotine in vapes is very addictive - which is why the NHS says children and non-smokers shouldn't take it up. But it has been shown to be an effective way to stop smoking. Last month, the pop singer Lola Young said her "breathing feels like a chore" due to the effects of vaping. The singer received a kidney transplant from her friend Francia Raisa (left) in 2017 Gomez first revealed her lupus diagnosis in a 2015 interview with Billboard. The announcement came after she abruptly ended her 2013 tour to check herself into a rehab facility for treatment. "I was diagnosed with lupus, and I've been through chemotherapy," she told the publication. "I locked myself away until I was confident and comfortable again. "That's what my break was really about. I could've had a stroke." Symptoms of lupus include muscle and joint pain, fever, rashes, chest pain, hair loss, kidney problems, fatigue and more. In 2017, Gomez received a kidney transplant from her friend Francia Raisa, which helped move her lupus into remission for a period of time - although in her 2022 documentary Selena Gomez: My Mind And Me, the singer said she had had a flare-up in 2020. However, after revealing her vaping habit, some people questioned her nicotine use, given the potential negative effect on her kidneys. "Francia really gave this girl her kidney and she continued to smoke... oh wow," wrote one user on social media. "To have someone generous enough to donate their kidney but still vape yourself into a nicotine addiction is absolutely wild," added another, external. But most fans supported the star for being open about addiction. "Selena Gomez being honest about nicotine addiction is a reminder that some habits are harder to quit than people realise," wrote MaxB on X, external. "Proud of her for owning up to it and for wanting to do better," agreed Em. title: 'Postcode lottery' driving children's inequality in England, commissioner warns
description: Dame Rachel De Souza's landmark report says children are being failed by a "postcode lottery".
body: Dame Rachel de Souza's landmark report examines the challenges faced by children across England Services for children are in a "state of emergency" and young people across England are facing extreme and unfair inequality, a new report says. Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza has analysed a hundred different metrics including health and social care, education, safety and play, concluding that a "postcode lottery" has resulted in a "litany of failures" affecting children. Her report found that deprivation alone could not explain the differences in their experiences. Some poorer areas had scored highly in her analysis compared to relatively well-off ones. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government will make sure "no child is held back by where they grow up". Dame Rachel called for a minimum standard for children's services, and an emergency fund for improvements where needed. She said she had previously resisted the call to "reduce everything to funding", but the "extent of failure is too great". In her report, called Childhood Lottery, she wrote that she could not see the status quo as "anything less than a national emergency". She urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to give larger local authorities and mayors more of a role in providing better education, health, youth services and policing for children. More than one million children had been referred to mental health services in 2024-25 55% of children do not achieve a good standard in English and maths GCSEs A million people in the UK aged 16-24 are not in employment, education or training 12% of children said they did not feel safe in their local area Dame Rachel told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that one group of children talked to her about seeing knife crime "virtually daily", people urinating on their school and kids not being able to go to the park because it's "so full of crime". "Now that to me is an emergency... it's an emergency for childhood," she said. Burnham says youth employment and training crisis is a 'moral failure' Middlesbrough, Hounslow, Bradford, Nottingham, Halton, Peterborough, Leicester, Liverpool, Sunderland and Medway were ranked the hardest places to grow up in England. Cheshire East, Merton, Surrey, Richmond upon Thames, Hertfordshire, Cheshire West and Chester, Haringey, Leicestershire, Central Bedfordshire and Wokingham were described as the "least challenging places to be a child". In some cases the difference in standard was stark. It took six days for a child to be referred for mental health assessments in Leicester, and 118 days in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. In Richmond upon Thames, 70% of children got good grades in English and maths GCSE compared to 31% in Knowsley. Just 6.7% of children in Bedford felt unsafe in their local area, compared to 24.9% of children in Croydon. In four local council areas, spending on youth services per teenager was zero. 86% of Redcar and Cleveland's children saw a dentist in the last year compared to 39% in Hackney, which was among 25 areas where fewer than half of children saw a dentist. General poverty was not always to blame for poor children's services, the report found, external. Haringey in North London scored highly in an assessment of its services for children, despite having high levels of deprivation. Conversely Cambridge was ranked lower, even though it was one of the least deprived areas in England. "There is a poverty issue, but there are also service issues, and capacity issues," Dame Rachel told the BBC. "What I want to see is rocket-boosted support for these places," she added. Dame Rachel recommended there should be a minimum set of standards for the way children were affected by levels of education, policing, health, and youth services. "Strategic authorities", which include areas with mayors, and larger local councils, should be required to have a deputy mayor for children with responsibility for testing every policy to assess its impact, she said. A children's emergency fund should be set up to pay for improvements in services, she added. In a separate article for the Times, external on Monday, the prime minister promised more investment in "the success of our young people" and said the government could no longer support their "failure through the benefits system." The Department for Education said it's working to improve childcare support and school standards, and is giving more power to "local leaders" to shape the future of their education. "We're investing and reforming at every stage of a child's journey, from more childcare support for their earliest years and higher standards in our schools, broader community support with the rollover of our National Youth strategy and Young Future hubs, to more training and job opportunities as they approach adulthood," it said in a statement. The government said it is opening 1,000 Best Start Family Hubs in England, which offers joined-up support for parents and children, including health, education and advice services. The Local Government Association said the government needs to make sure public services have the right resources and "powers at the right levels" to deliver better outcomes for children across the country. title: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
description: Saudi Arabia said it executed two Bangladeshis last week for committing an "indecent act" in a mosque.
body: Two Bangladeshi nationals were executed over an "indecent act" in a mosque, Saudi authorities say Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports. A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act. Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case. The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties. More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh. According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge. The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque. Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam. The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said. She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad. The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported. This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities. According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences. In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian. Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man. title: Watch: The father and son on opposite sides of Alberta’s separation vote
description: Albertans are voting on whether to stay in Canada or pursue independence via a referendum, splitting even some close-knit families.
body: This video can not be played On Monday, people in Alberta will cast their ballots in a vote that includes a question on whether the western province should remain in Canada or pursue a binding provincial referendum on separation. The other questions on the ballot paper ask Albertans about options to gain more autonomy from Ottawa, including on matters such as immigration control and access to social services for non-permanent residents. In the separation vote, the remain side is expected to win, but the debate has caused tensions in Alberta. The BBC’s Nadine Yousif travelled to Buck Lake to speak with the close-knit Pietsch family, who have a father and son on either side of the debate. title: Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
description: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Police 'lost control' in French cities, interior minister says France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez tried to hand in his resignation, the Élysée Palace (French President Macron's HQ) announced on Monday morning. But instead, Macron has asked him to examine how to make France's streets safer and to bring the perpetrators of the weekend violence to justice. Over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated on Saturday against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared. An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously. Interior Minister Nuñez has been accused by political opponents, some trade unions and on social media forums for being ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests. The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened. "Things are dark in the City of Light" - the nickname for Paris - was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night. There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished. Macron's speech has been roundly criticised in the French media for lacking concrete detail. How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account? How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time? Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated? And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education? That is how these demonstrations started in the first place, last month. Vandals defaced Statue de la Republique in central Paris over the weekend On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France. The president has apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Macron is widely viewed in France as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There is a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines. That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets. Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks. Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets. What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment. People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation. This video can not be played 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility. "While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me. Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order, posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented". For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday. But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests. France is holding its breath. title: Rural lives cannot be an 'afterthought', healthcare campaigners say
description: Campaigners warn that rural communities face being cut off from vital hospital services.
body: Donal O'Cofaigh of Save Our Acute Services (SOAS) says people are "already losing their lives" due to a reduction in rural services Rural lives "cannot be an afterthought" when it comes to health transformation, campaigners have said. In a joint "letter of concern" to the Northern Ireland Executive, four hospital campaign groups have called for a cross-departmental working group on rural health access. The campaigners have warned that rural communities "face the real threat of being cut off from timely access" to acute and other vital hospital services. In a statement the Department of Health said "every decision across the health and social care system is taken on the basis of safety and delivery of the best outcomes for all citizens". It added that the minister is "acutely aware of the issues faced by those living in rural areas and he takes those issues very seriously". Donal O'Cofaigh from Save Our Acute Services (SOAS), based in County Fermanagh, said it is "vital" that executive ministers collectively consider decisions about removing services from local hospitals. SoS Causeway Hospital group, Save Our Services Daisy Hill and the Down Community Health committee were the other three groups that signed the letter. No time for new minister to fix health service warns top doctor Removing emergency surgery will create 'domino effect', campaigners warn 'Lives will be lost' unless services are restored at hospital For several years the groups have been campaigning against the closure of acute services in their areas. In their letter, the campaigners said that past healthcare decisions have been framed as "purely operational or clinical, with too little cross-departmental scrutiny". After being temporarily suspended in February 2022, emergency general surgery (EGS) was permanently removed from Daisy Hill Hospital in Newry in 2024. Maternity services at the hospital could also be suspended from next month after the Southern Health and Social Care Trust said it was preparing for the "possible consolidation" of services to Craigavon Area Hospital from 23 November. In 2023, maternity services were permanently suspended at Causeway Hospital and consolidated at Antrim Area Hospital. EGS was temporarily withdrawn from South West Acute Hospital (Swah) in Enniskillen in 2022. In July 2025, the Western Health and Social Care Trust's board agreed to consult on the permanent removal of the service from the hospital, but the public consultation was later closed after the trust agreed to "pause and consider". The health trust said it is now working with stakeholders "to develop a clear vision" for healthcare in the area, with EGS remaining suspended at Swah while this takes place. Last year, the Northern Health Trust recommended providing EGS at just one of its hospital sites - meaning it's likely to be removed from Causeway Hospital. But the move cannot proceed without approval from Health Minister Robbie Butler, after his predecessor, Mike Nesbitt, resigned amid a party dispute over the proposal. Inpatient maternity services are likely to move from Daisy Hill Hospital in Newry to Craigavon Area Hospital next month O'Cofaigh said: "It's simply not good enough to allow services to temporarily [be removed] or collapse under pressures and then do nothing about it for years and just leave that as the situation." The groups called for a "presumption of restoration" - a pathway to restore services in cases where they were removed from rural hospitals without the appropriate assessments or scrutiny. "We cannot accept the situation where our communities are disadvantaged simply because of where they live," O'Cofaigh continued. "We are second-class citizens at the moment. Stormont is presiding over that system." The campaigners said communities are forced to travel "long, unsafe distances for emergency care when they are at their most vulnerable". O'Cofaigh said this was an "outrageous situation". "It has very significant impacts on people's lives," he added. Members of the campaign group Save Our Acute Services (SOAS) pictured outside Stormont in February 2026 O'Cofaigh hopes Stormont ministers will recognise the "severity" of the situation. "If you have to travel long distances, waiting long times to receive life-saving, treatments...then the health outcomes are different. They're not the same. "The procedures can be much more complicated... People are already losing their lives. We're seeing it." The campaigners have also told the executive that rural-proofing is "non-existent", stating that "decisions have been repeatedly made without meaningful assessment of the differential impact on our communities". They have called for independent rural-needs and equality assessments, as well as a cross-departmental ministerial working group on rural health access. In September, Health Minister Robbie Butler said a new independent expert committee would provide him with advice on major or controversial proposals for permanent changes to health and social care services. He also asked officials to review the existing guidance governing the change or withdrawal of services, including consideration of rural and equality impacts. title: NHS bosses say smaller maternity units may have to close
description: The NHS Alliance said "difficult decisions" lie ahead and some maternity services may have to be consolidated.
body: NHS bosses in England say the way maternity care is organised is "not fit for purpose" with safety at risk, and warn up to 20 smaller units may have to close. The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, says difficult decisions lie ahead and maternity services need to be consolidated to support safer care. It said a government taskforce into neonatal and maternity care must tackle key issues such as a lack of specialist staff and a rise in C-sections. The Department of Health and Social Care said every woman deserves safe maternity care, and the taskforce "will deliver the reforms needed to ensure services meet the needs of women and families now and in the future". The NHS Alliance said there are particular pressures on smaller units in rural and coastal areas and that those delivering 1,500 to 2,000 babies each year might need to close. The organisation said up to 20 out of 155 consultant-led maternity units in England face closure. It says staffing problems and rising numbers of C-sections are making smaller units potentially unsafe. The rise in C-sections was a challenge, according to the NHS Alliance, and there were inadequate operating theatres and beds in outdated and decaying buildings, posing a safety risk. The NHS leaders' organisation also said some smaller units struggled to maintain safe staffing numbers for 24-hour care, including midwives and consultants such as obstetricians. It goes on to say the government's taskforce must "grasp the nettle" by tackling these strategic issues, including significantly worse outcomes in deprived communities and raised maternity mortality rates for Black and Asian women. The director of the NHS Alliance's acute and ambulance network, Matthew Hopkins, said: "Difficult decisions lie ahead, consolidating maternity services to support safer, more sustainable care." He said any local plans had to involve NHS leaders, clinical staff, patients and communities, and that politicians "must have the courage to make the case for patient safety". "It is time now to take a step back and consider how we should best organise maternity services across England, and where those services should be located", he said. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists called for "other solutions" to be explored that would prevent closing maternity units. Dr Alison Wright, president of the college said the government should commit to "expanding the maternity workforce to ensure safe staffing levels, along with investment in training and retention of dedicated staff." "The distinct needs and challenges of smaller units, especially in rural and coastal communities, must be recognised and supported," she added. One in four births in England is now emergency caesarean, BBC analysis shows Racism and 'poor' staff relationships factors in maternity care failings, report finds Maternity services under strain as report finds insufficient staffing levels In August, a Devon trust suspended standard birthing services at a hospital in Barnstaple leaving pregnant mothers having to make a 53 mile journey to Exeter to give birth. The Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust said it was the "only safe course of action" due to staffing issues. The trust added that it had explored every option including locum cover and support from other health organisations but that a temporary suspension was the best solution. The North Devon maternity facility remains suspended with the trust saying there would be a "readiness assessment" later in October with patient safety the "overriding priority". Campaigners say the delay is "disappointing". One couple told the BBC the thought of the longer journey for the birth of their second son had left them anxious and angry. Catherine Mchomvu, chief executive of the Devon Antenatal Family Centre, has been campaigning to secure the future of the Barnstaple facility, and warned that reductions nationally would undermine the quality of care. "If we had closures of smaller units you are going to find that women are not going to receive any level of continuity of care - that's purely because they are not going to see the same healthcare team more than once throughout the whole antenatal and post-natal experience", she said. In June, Baroness Valerie Amos's review found women and babies were not being "listened to, heard or believed", with racism and discrimination "embedded throughout the system". title: Beer & Blackpool beach was how British players bonded - Pulis
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains what Spurs will get from their team-bonding trip to Spain, and how differently managers built team morale in his day.
body: Hearing about Tottenham's team-bonding trip to Marbella last week made me think about the similar methods I used as a manager to build team morale. While some things have changed from my day, the idea behind taking your players away to a new environment where they will benefit from spending a lot of time together has not. I wrote a few weeks ago about how Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi needed time with his players on the training pitch after their poor start to the season, to bed them in and build a proper team. He will have used their warm-weather camp in southern Spain to do more of that, getting to know what is almost a new squad of players. With De Zerbi being cut from Italian cloth, I am sure the players will have been working mornings and afternoons to drill in the manager's principles in respect to team shape and direction. But that's not the only purpose of taking them away. De Zerbi will also have been able to monitor the different personalities within the group away from the grass. If the trip has worked then, as well as getting them ready to face Coventry on Monday night, I am sure he will now, for the first time, understand the strengths and weaknesses of each individual, on and off the field. Tottenham spent more than £250m on new talent over the summer - adding 10 players to De Zerbi's squad A few eyebrows were raised about Spurs going away so early in the season but it makes perfect sense to me when you consider so many new players arrived there this summer, with several signings late in the transfer window. When I was Stoke manager, I often took my teams away to Austria in our pre-season for the same reasons De Zerbi and Spurs have gone to Spain. Those trips were set up not only to test the players' fitness, but also to see how the group worked together. I have always believed in building a family togetherness within the dressing room, with a commitment from every player to the benefit of the team. The extreme tests that we asked our players to do over that 10-day period brought out an inner determination to fulfil the tasks given them and, in my opinion, helped us through some tough times early on in our Premier League campaigns. Watching the lads slowly bond together on the training pitch and at meal times was great to see and I found out a lot about all of them, good and bad. Yes, I have to admit one or two players were short of the character we wanted and needed, but they didn't last long and left with no bad feelings on my side. A bucket and spade were not required when Pulis went to Blackpool for pre-season training with Bristol Rovers Today, whether it's pre-season or a winter break, most Premier League clubs who take their players away go first-class and enjoy great hotels, great facilities and wonderful food. Wherever the team bus goes, it is followed by an even bigger bus with all the non-playing staff on it. It is very different to my experiences in my early years as a player, when we would be taken to Blackpool for three days' pre-season training. Again, the idea was to bring the lads closer together, but that happened in a different way than today's professionals are used to. We stayed in a guest house with three-quarter beds that we all shared - that certainly brought us closer together! - then trained on the beach each morning, doing our running sessions on the sand. Then we played seven-a-side games in the afternoon on a local park pitch, after clearing the dog muck off first. In the evenings, we were allowed out for a few beers, with no time stipulated for our return - apart from having to be downstairs and ready to hit the beach again at 8am the next morning. That is where things have changed most of all, right through football, during the past few years. In the 1970s and 80s, there was a massive drinking culture right through the leagues - just listen to the stories that came out of clubs as big as Liverpool, Manchester United or Arsenal, when they had teams who not only dominated English football but the European game too. In my early years of management, the bonding I've been talking about used to happen right through the season through the lads meeting in pubs after games and after training on week days as well. Winter breaks were rare and, rather than for a training camp, the only time most players I knew went to Spain was at the end of the season when more alcohol would be consumed. That was what British players classed as bonding sessions and, as I've written about before, even the ones at the top level were much more connected to normal society, rather than living in an eternal bubble. Now, while they are certainly more aware of the dangers of drinking to excess, as a manager you have to find other ways for them to connect when there are other distractions to contend with. One item I am very glad my generation was not brought up with is mobile phones. I used to go mad if I walked into a dining room at the training ground or a hotel to see a group of lads looking at their phone and not engaging with each other. I sometimes think that, as a young player, I had nothing compared to the players of today but, really, we had everything. The stories, the friendships and the memories of the togetherness I remember from every dressing room during that time still resonate with me and recreating them was always my aim as a manager. You're in the army now, Harry... Pulis is not the only manager to take his players to a military boot camp - Gareth Southgate did the same in 2017 when he took his England squad to a Commando Training Centre in Devon Some other things have changed too - I am not sure De Zerbi has ever considered taking his team away to an army camp like I did on many occasions early in my managerial career, where we worked on the players in different ways. One year, I took Stoke down to Exmouth, where the lads were put through their paces doing cross-country circuits. That probably doesn&#x2

title: Best images of F1 in the US through the years
description: A selection of images from F1 races in the US, from Indianapolis, Watkins Glen and Long Beach to the streets of Dallas and the Caesars Palace car park.
body: Formula 1 heads to the United States this weekend for the US Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, which has become a firm favourite on the calendar since its inaugural race in 2012. Austin is one of three F1 events to be staged in the US, with Miami hosting a grand prix in May and Las Vegas holding a night race in November. The sport has grown in popularity in the US in recent years, helped by Netflix's Drive to Survive series. However, it's fair to say F1 and the US has had a mixed relationship over the years. Some races were very successful and fondly remembered; others less so. From Indianapolis, Watkins Glen and Long Beach, to the streets of Dallas and the Caesars Palace car park, we take a look back at some of the best images from the 11 US cities and towns to stage an F1 race. The first F1 United States Grand Prix took place in Sebring, Florida, in 1959. Australian Jack Brabham won the first of his three drivers' championships by pushing his Cooper over the line after it ran out of fuel on the last lap. His fourth place was enough to beat Britons Tony Brooks and Stirling Moss to the title. Briton John Surtees drives his Lotus through the streets of California on his way to Riverside race track, which staged the 1960 US Grand Prix. The event didn't go well for Surtees - he was the first driver to retire by spinning off on the third lap. Another fourth place ensured Brabham won his second title, ahead of Bruce McLaren. The Lotus of Innes Ireland is retrieved from bushes after going off the circuit in 1961 at Watkins Glen. Despite his excursion, the Briton recovered to win the race - the first to be held at the circuit in upstate New York which staged the US Grand Prix until 1980. Briton Jim Clark on the grid before the Watkins Glen race in 1965, the year he won the second of his drivers' championships. With fans outside desperately trying to get a glimpse of him, Scotsman Clark celebrates victory in 1967. Six months later he was killed in a Formula 2 race. An early morning Sunday church service conducted in the Watkins Glen pits in 1973 had added poignancy following the death of Tyrrell driver Francois Cevert the day before during qualifying. Alfa Romeo's Bruno Giacomelli leads the final US Grand Prix at Watkins Glen in 1980 as Williams' Alan Jones goes off line and throws up dust behind him. Australian Jones recovered to win the race and with it the world title. The inaugural United States Grand Prix West took place on the streets of Long Beach, California, in 1976. Here, the field heads down Linden Avenue with Ferrari's Niki Lauda at the head of the pack. It appears as if some people are going about their daily business while a F1 race happens around them. Two-time world champion Emerson Fittipaldi shocked F1 by moving from McLaren to his brother's Fittipaldi team in 1976. A crash in Long Beach practice damaged his car but he was able to claim the final point for sixth place in the race. The McLaren of James Hunt is tipped into the air as it collides with the Brabham of John Watson at the start of the 1977 race at Long Beach. It was a popular venue for F1 but the promoter decided to switch to IndyCars from 1984. F1's first venture into Las Vegas was not successful. The 1981 and 1982 Caesars Palace Grands Prix staged the climax of both world championships but did not find favour with the drivers. Races were held around a car park in the heat of the day, and the drivers were pushed to the limit by the conditions and the featureless anti-clockwise circuit which put tremendous strain on their necks. Here, Williams' Alan Jones leads the field into the first corner in 1981. The Dallas Grand Prix had a shorter lifespan than Caesars Palace, happening once in July 1984. Extreme heat was an issue here too, leading to the track breaking up. Eighteen of the 26 drivers retired, 14 of them after hitting the wall. Heading the survivors were winner Keke Rosberg, Ferrari's Rene Arnoux in second and Lotus' Elio de Angelis in third. They were joined on the podium by actress Linda Gray - Sue Ellen in the Dallas TV series. It seems appropriate that F1 has been to the Motor City. The Detroit Grand Prix took place on a street circuit from 1982-88. Ayrton Senna is pictured on the grid speaking to members of his Lotus team before the 1986 race, which he won from pole position. F1 swapped the streets of Detroit for Phoenix from 1989-91. The most memorable of those three races was in 1990 when McLaren's Ayrton Senna had to twice pass the Tyrrell of Jean Alesi to get the win. The race dropped off the calendar because of poor attendances. After an eight-year absence, F1 returned to the US in 2000 and did so in style at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. About 225,000 fans attended the first race, which took place on a 2.6-mile circuit that combined a new road course and the banked oval used for the Indy 500. Ferrari's Michael Schumacher won the first event to take control of that year's drivers' championship. F1's relationship with the United States effectively broke down because of the farcical nature of the 2005 US Grand Prix. Only six cars started because of a row over safety focused on the teams running Michelin tyres. When those 14 drivers pulled into the pit lane before the start, boos broke out and bottles were thrown on to the track as thousands made for the exits. The final Indianapolis US Grand Prix was in 2007. Nick Heidfeld covers his helmet with his arms and braces for impact as his BMW Sauber barrel-rolls in 2006 in Indianapolis, following a collision involving the McLaren of Juan Pablo Montoya and the Honda of Jenson Button. Heidfeld was unhurt. The US Grand Prix finally put down proper roots in Austin, Texas, with the first race staged at the Circuit of the Americas in 2012, the start of which can be seen above.
