title: Cardinals upset Rams as Eagles lose - five things from NFL week six
description: Week six in the NFL produced some unlikely heroes as the Arizona Cardinals pulled off a huge upset while the Philadelphia Eagles suffered another loss.
body: Both the Arizona Cardinals and Philadelphia Eagles now have a 2-4 record Week six in the NFL produced some unlikely heroes as the Arizona Cardinals pulled off the biggest upset of the season so far. Kicker Chad Ryland scored all of Arizona's points at the Los Angeles Rams to leave the former Super Bowl favourites bottom of the NFC West division. The Philadelphia Eagles continued to struggle but their former Super Bowl rivals the Kansas City Chiefs remained unbeaten. The Cleveland Browns maintained their surprise start while the Houston Texans concluded this year's London series by winning a thriller at Wembley. Here are five things you need to know from Sunday's action. The Los Angeles Rams started the season as the clearest Super Bowl favourites in nine years but were replaced by the San Francisco 49ers after last Monday's overtime defeat by the Buffalo Bills. They cut kicker Harrison Mevis on Tuesday and signed Blake Grupe from the New York Jets' practice squad, and although Grupe's field goal opened the scoring against Arizona, he injured a knee while making a tackle from the ensuing kick-off. The Rams edged back in front with 47 seconds remaining as punter Ethan Evans took on the kicking duties to add the extra point after Colby Parkinson's touchdown. But Arizona hit straight back and a career-high sixth field goal by Chad Ryland clinched an 18-16 win as time expired. After just three wins last season, the Cardinals now have two this year and both have come at SoFi Stadium having also beaten the Los Angeles Chargers in week one. Arizona also crept above the Rams in a division which features the unbeaten 49ers and defending champions the Seattle Seahawks. "We've got to be able to figure it out and it starts with me," said the Rams' head coach Sean McVay. Kenneth Walker (centre) is arguably the first elite running back Patrick Mahomes has had at his disposal during his 10-year NFL career Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes reached 100 regular-season wins in his 131st start, tying Tom Brady's record. After missing out on last season's play-offs, the Chiefs boosted their roster by signing the Super Bowl's Most Valuable Player Kenneth Walker and he rushed for another 128 yards and two touchdowns in Sunday's 22-6 win over the Chargers. The running back now leads the NFL with 665 rushing yards, a record from a player's first five games with a new team, and the Chiefs visit his former team Seattle next Sunday. Kansas City and the Minnesota Vikings are now 5-0 while San Francisco - the only other unbeaten team after five wins - are at home to Washington on Monday night. The Buffalo Bills held on for a 33-30 win at the Las Vegas Raiders to improve to 5-1 while Caleb Williams returned from a hamstring injury to help the Chicago Bears to a 31-23 win at the Atlanta Falcons. The Philadelphia Eagles were already struggling with injuries before last Sunday's loss to Jacksonville at Tottenham. They then revealed that quarterback Jalen Hurts played that game with a superficial blood clot in his calf and a follow-up ultrasound showed that it had moved. The 2025 Super Bowl winner was then placed on injured reserve so will miss at least four weeks, with back-up Tanner McKee coming in for his third NFL start at home to the Carolina Panthers. Tight end Tommy Tremble scored his first two touchdowns of the season as the Panthers won 25-14, meaning the Eagles have lost four straight games for the first time since Nick Sirianni became head coach in 2021. Offensive linemen Lane Johnson (retirement) and Cam Jurgens (traded to Baltimore) both left the team two weeks ago and after seeing the Eagles reach two of the past four Super Bowls, many Philly fans fear this could be the end of an era. They face all three of their divisional rivals over the next three weeks. 'Ran through me' & 'good value in pub' - ex-NFL star Kelce tries rugby Travis Hunter (centre) finished with four catches for 59 yards on offence and claimed the Jaguars' only interception on defence After last week's last-gasp win over the Eagles, it was a role reversal for the Jacksonville Jaguars as they remained in London to face the Houston Texans. The divisional match-up produced the highest-scoring London game since 2015, with Ka'imi Fairbairn's field goal securing a 34-31 win for Houston, but it was a landmark day for Jacksonville's Travis Hunter. The second overall draft pick in 2025, Hunter came into the league determined to become its first full-time two-way player in 30 years and in his 13th NFL game, he made a significant impact on both offence and defence for the first time. The 23-year-old, who plays as a wide receiver and cornerback, became the first player to claim a touchdown catch and an interception in the same game since Brian Dawkins (Philadelphia Eagles) in 2002 – and the fourth since the league merger in 1970. Hunter made both plays in the fourth quarter, with his pick leading to a Cam Little field goal which made it 31-31, before Fairbairn clinched Houston's second win of the season while the Jags slipped to 4-2. The Draft 'unicorn' that NFL teams just can't figure out The Baltimore Ravens had a divisional clash at the Cleveland Browns and star running back Derrick Henry had a crucial fumble in the fourth quarter. That allowed Cleveland running back Audric Estime, who started the week on Minnesota's practice squad, to punch in a touchdown before Andre Szmyt's second game-winning field goal in three weeks gave the Browns a 13-10 victory. After being booed by Cleveland fans in pre-season, quarterback Deshaun Watson has now led the Browns to a 4-2 start and they are surprise leaders of the AFC North on a tie-breaker. Baltimore and the Pittsburgh Steelers are also 4-2, with the Steelers having come back from 16-3 down in the fourth quarter to win 26-19 in overtime at the Tampa

title: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza
description: The number of people helped by the UN agency in the Palestinian territory will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
body: Dalal al-Dahdouh said the WFP food handouts her family received were insufficient even before the cuts One of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages. Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves. One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day. Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive. Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster" "It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat." "This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family. The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do." Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-Mawasi Already, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month. The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months. Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, violence has continued, including almost daily Israeli strikes, and humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire. There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid. Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed experts Families currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets. "The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact". The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers." There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food. "It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now." Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cooking Humanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory. In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026". For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children. In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September. The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement. title: Volunteers plant 109,000 trees in new woodlands
description: In the last two seasons, almost 500,000 trees and 27,233 metres of new hedges, have been planted.
body: In the last two tree-planting seasons, the Lancashire Woodland Partnership has planted almost 500,000 trees New woodlands have been created by volunteers planting more than 109,000 trees across Lancashire in the last year. More than 1,200 volunteers from communities, landowners and environmental organisations have created woodland over an equivalent area of 154 football pitches, 61 new orchards and 17 new micro-forests. In the last two tree-planting seasons, the Lancashire Woodland Partnership has planted almost 500,000 trees and more than 27,233 metres of new hedges. Lancashire County Councillor Joshua Roberts said the woodlands were "supporting wildlife, helping tackle climate change, improving people's wellbeing". The partnership brings together environmental organisations, local authorities, landowners, volunteers and communities to combine resources, expertise and local knowledge. The organisations then plant trees where they can deliver the greatest benefits for wildlife, people and the environment. They are encouraging more landowners to get in touch with the partnership to explore how they can create new woodlands and restore habitats. title: The portraits that helped bring the lost Aberfan children home
description: An artist living hundreds of miles away felt compelled to help the village that lost its children.
body: This video can not be played The portraits which helped to bring the children of Aberfan home For almost 60 years, many of Aberfan's lost children have watched over living rooms, hallways and family gatherings across the village. Some were painted from faded school photographs. Others were shaped by the memories of grieving parents, who wrote letters to an artist describing the children they had lost: the colour of their eyes, their favourite clothes, the flashes of personality that made them unique. The portraits arrived in the years after one of Wales' darkest days. And for many families, they became far more than paintings. In a new BBC programme, Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits, some have shared their paintings and spoken about how the art helped them grieve. The portraits helped families grieve after the Aberfan disaster "It brought her back to life," said Denise Morgan, whose younger sister Annette was among those who died in the Aberfan disaster. On 21 October 1966, a coal tip collapsed above the village. The torrent of slurry engulfed Pantglas Junior School and nearby homes, killing 144 people including 116 children. The disaster remains woven into everyday life in Aberfan. It is felt most strongly in the memorial garden on the site of the fallen school, and among the white arched monuments of the cemetery. But it is also felt in the empty places left behind at family tables, in childhood bedrooms which were suddenly occupied by one child instead of two, and in the portraits that came to represent those who never grew up. Jeanette Keane has fond memories of her sister Edwina. "It was just such an idyllic childhood really," she said. "She was very quiet and gentle. She had a mischievous streak as well." The morning of the disaster remains painfully vivid, as Jeanette recalled how Edwina quickly returned home before the school day had begun. "She came running back and she said, 'Mammy, I forgot to give you a kiss'," Jeanette said. "And so my mother gave her a kiss. "My mother always said that, at that time, she wanted to keep her home. "And my mother rued that day for the rest of her life. She just wished she'd listened to herself." Jeanette Keane lost her sister Edwina Jeanette's father found eight-year-old Edwina trapped beneath the wreckage. "She was alive," Jeanette said, but it was a heartbreaking situation. "He couldn't get her out because the roof would have fallen in. "The men all said, 'Teddy, you can't and my father laid by the side of her, held her hand and she suffocated." Jeanette has fond memories of her sister Edwina The trauma echoed through the years that followed the disaster. "It explains to me why we used to hear him walking back and fore in the corridor at night, banging his head on the wall," Jeanette said. "It wasn't a very happy life afterwards. Everything changed." The black coal waste smothered Pantglas Junior School, killing 144 people including 116 children Denise Morgan was attending a different school when word began to spread that something terrible had happened in Aberfan, where her little sister Annette was in class. "They didn't really give us any details," she said. Racing off the train, the devastation was clear. "When we looked across to Aberfan, we could just see this black mass." As rescue efforts began, families across the village waited for news. Some of the memories remain too painful to revisit. Brothers Kelvin and Malcolm Andrew were the sons of school caretaker Stephen Andrew, whose family still treasure their portrait For the surviving siblings, that sense of loss seemed to arrive in the most ordinary moments. "We always slept together," said Jeanette. "And suddenly I was alone." Denise remembered the same absence. "We shared a bed... and then she was gone." Paintings of Lynn Harding, Gareth Davies and Terence Davies still hang on the walls of their family homes The scale of grief was impossible to escape. "In our street, five children were lost in 25 houses," Denise said. "Four children died in my street," Jeanette recalled. In an era when grief was rarely discussed openly, many survivors were left to process the tragedy alone. William Richardson made a living as an artist on Llandudno Pier, where he sketched visitors and celebrities including Margaret Thatcher and the Bay City Rollers Hundreds of miles away in Llandudno, Conwy county, one man was following events in Aberfan on television and in the newspapers. Artist William Richardson had no connection to Aberfan, with his skills being used most often on the pier where he sketched caricatures of visitors and celebrities performing in town. But he was deeply affected by what he saw. According to his children, Jean and Ken, he felt compelled to do something for the bereaved families who had lost their sons and daughters. "He saw it on the news and he was so moved by it, he decided to paint them," Jean said. "He just wanted to give something back, to show he cared," added Ken. Richardson never sought payment or recognition. Instead, he began creating portraits of children killed in the disaster, working from school photographs and detailed descriptions supplied by parents. "It's like looking back at old friends now." Ken and Jean Richardson remember their father's tireless work to complete dozens of paintings for families in Aberfan "The parents would write to him and tell him about the children," Jean said. "What colour their eyes were, their hair, what they wore." "They even sent bits of fabric so he could get it right," Ken added. Jean said her father wanted to capture more than their appearance. "He'd ask about their personalities, so he could build that into the painting." Over the years, Richardson is believed to have produced about 100 portraits. title: How one rule change is altering the face of one-day cricket
description: One rule change has changed the face of ODI cricket. BBC Sport looks at its impact, who is benefiting and what it could mean for the future.
body: England return to action in ODI cricket against Pakistan on Tuesday (09:00 BST) . There will be Test Match Special commentary of every match in the tri-series, which also involves Sri Lanka England had just been beaten by Sri Lanka in the second one-day international at Headingley and coach Brendon McCullum was speaking to his players in the dressing room. "The game is slightly different now," he said. "The ball is playing a massive part." The difference McCullum referenced is reverse swing - the way an older ball moves in the air in the opposite direction to convention. The playing conditions in ODIs were changed in July 2025, allowing captains to choose after 34 overs which of the two white balls used at either end they would like to use to complete the rest of the innings. With the chosen ball now able to get older and scruffier, the result has brought a reverse swing renaissance, something which is already having an impact on the format and poses intriguing possibilities for the future less than 12 months out from the next World Cup. When Sam Curran bowled England to victory with four wickets at the death in the third ODI against India at Lord's in July, he found more than twice as much swing with the old white ball across his final spell than he did at the start of the innings. A year earlier, Saqib Mahmood found less than half as much swing in an ODI at Cardiff against West Indies at the death compared to the start. Those are two random examples. Different days, different players, different situations. But it is reflected worldwide. The change to using one ball for the last 16 overs was made to help bowlers, and it is having the desired effect. Half of full deliveries from pace bowlers in the final 10 overs have swung more than one degree since the rule change - a jump from 35% compared to the 18 months prior. As a result, the economy rates of pace bowlers in the final five overs have dropped from 8.40 runs per over in the period before the change to 7.95 - a small but not insignificant decline. Pacers' bowling averages have dropped from 19.2 runs per wicket to 18.3 too. The verdict? Hitting out at the death is not as easy as it once was. As has always been the case when reverse swing is in play, pacers are bowling fuller and utilising more inswing now the ball is reversing. Sri Lanka were particularly effective with this against England in the Headingley ODI last month, bowling 69% of deliveries six metres from the stumps or fuller. It helped them close out a 16-run win. Despite that, England have, statistically at least, benefited most from the rule change, though it should be noted they have taken a significant step forward with their ODI cricket this year. Their numbers may have improved with or without the change. Their bowling average (from 36.76 to 20.91) and economy rates (from 9.78 to 7.53) at the death have plummeted since July 2025, while their batting run-rate has actually improved (from 8.07 to 9.16). After defeat in Leeds, McCullum asked his players to "think" about what the changes may mean for their own plans, suggesting tactical switches may follow. Three days later at The Oval, England progressed from 104-2 to 214-2 in the 10 overs prior to the Sri Lankans picking their preferred ball. Australia, New Zealand, West Indies, South Africa, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan have all scored slower during the death overs since the rule change. West Indies' death run-rate has dropped by 2.39 runs per over in that time. As for individual bowlers around the world, Windies quick Alzarri Joseph and South Africa's Lungi Ngidi have benefited from massive jumps in the amount of swing they have been able to find at the death. Joseph's average amount of swing has increased by 84%, leading to his bowling average dropping from 24.1 to 17.4. Similarly, Ngidi's bowling average has dropped to 13 and his economy has fallen from 9.34 to six after a 63.3% increase in swing. Others to see their movement jump include New Zealand's Nathan Smith, Pakistan's Naseem Shah and Bangladesh's Mustafizur - each with varying results. Shaheen Afridi, Pakistan's captain in this tri-series, is one of the world's best at finding swing at the death (an average of 1.3 degrees since the rule change), although he was swinging it plenty before the change too (1.2). Shaheen and Naseem in tandem against England on Tuesday could be a fascinating sight. Jofra Archer is the England bowler finding the most movement late on, with an average degree of 0.97 - an increase of 37%. Reverse swing is not impacting ODIs everywhere in the world - not yet, at least. The change has been most significant in England, where the ball is swinging 63% more at the death. There has been a 33% jump in Bangladesh, with matches held in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Pakistan - relevant for the next two weeks - also featuring significantly more late movement than before. The increase has been less significant in Australia, where England travel next, however, and in South Africa where the majority of next year's World Cup will be held. There have only been three ODIs played in South Africa since the rule change, making predictions for next autumn difficult. While the change has not taken effect there, South African ODIs already have some of the higher levels of movement late in an innings but, at the same time, teams have scored at 7.35 runs per over there in recent years - again on the higher side. If a spike in reverse swing does come, teams may have to get their scoring done earlier than previously. Statistics correct prior to ODI tri-series between Pakistan, Sri Lanka and England. title: 'I could die before my family's murder is solved'
description: The deaths of a mother and her five children in a house fire are now being treated as a cold case.
body: Dr Abdul Shakoor fled the fire as he tried to get help to save his family The suspected murder of a mother and her five children in a house fire is now being treated as a cold case, the BBC has learned. Dr Sabah Usmani and her five children – Hira, 12, Sohaib, 11, Muneeb, nine, Rayyan, six, and Maheen, three – were killed by the blaze at their home in Harlow in October 2012. Detectives say there are no longer any viable lines to investigate but will "continue to assess any new information". The children's father Dr Abdul Shakoor, 59, who was the only survivor that night, says he fears he will die before the case is solved. Inquiries become cold cases when police believe a homicide has been fully investigated but remains unsolved. It does not mean the case is closed but detectives will not actively pursue it day-to-day. Shakoor has been told that unless new information surfaces, Essex Police will review the case in a decade's time. "Who knows in 10 years whether I will be here," he told the BBC. "I don't know whether I'll be alive at that time." He said the development from police was "very disappointing" news. "I know that Essex Police have done a really great job and I still feel that they would like to resolve this case as a top priority. It is the matter of the six lives lost, all innocent. In one night, everything was taken away from me." No-one has been taken to court in relation to the family's deaths The family were asleep when the fire broke out in the early hours of 15 October 2012, quickly engulfing their home in Barn Mead. Shakoor tried to raise the alarm to save his wife and children. A neighbour's silver Ford Focus was set alight nearby at the same time. Police launched Operation Shakespeare, but despite arrests, no-one has been charged. This video can not be played Dr Abdul Shakoor has made a direct appeal to a mystery letter writer who could hold information on the case In July 2025, an anonymous handwritten letter was posted to police in Harlow, weeks after a BBC podcast was broadcast examining the case. Det Ch Insp Louise Metcalfe said it was "clearly" written by someone who wanted to progress the inquiry. "They reference the 'nightmare' of having information but not feeling able to share it," she explained. Metcalfe declined to share further details from the letter, but urged the author to come forward. Forensic analysis was unable to identify the writer. The fire took hold at the home in Barn Mead in Harlow Shakoor, who is an endocrinologist, added: "I have a direct appeal to the author of the letter that you have made a very courageous first step. "You came forward, and really, really, I feel it's my belief that you will come forward again. "This is the really only thing which can help us resolve this case." An Essex Police spokesperson said: "We remain determined to establish the truth about what happened and hold the person or people responsible to account. "At this stage, unfortunately we do not have any viable lines of inquiry to actively pursue. "Dr Shakoor knows we will continue to assess any new information which is provided to us." title: 'We didn't know a cold sore could kill a baby'
description: Ben Brookes and Meg Edmonds want to raise awareness of HSV after losing their daughter.
body: Ben Brookes and Meg Edmonds want to raise awareness of HSV and the danger it can pose to new babies A bereaved mother whose newborn daughter died after contracting the herpes simplex virus (HSV) is urging other parents to learn about the little-known dangers cold sores can pose to babies. For most adults, cold sores are usually a painful but common infection. But in newborn babies, whose immune systems are not yet fully developed, HSV can cause a life-threatening illness. Meg Edmonds' daughter Magnolia died aged just 10 days in February and it is suspected the virus may have been passed on by her mother. "The guilt is obviously unbearable, it's horrific, but I just try and remind myself that I didn't know and I did what I could have done with the knowledge that I did have," she said. Warning: This story contains distressing details She has decided to speak publicly as part of an infection prevention campaign run by the Lullaby Trust, a charity which promotes infant health. The 22-year-old, from Rugeley in Staffordshire, said Magnolia was born healthy after what she described as a straightforward birth. "I had a lovely birth with her, a water birth. She was nearly two weeks overdue like her big sister but everything was fine and she was born perfectly healthy," she said. Meg said she later realised a sore visible on her lip might have been her first cold sore Only later did she realise she appeared to have a sore on her lip at around the time Magnolia was born. "Looking back at photos now, I can see that I had a lesion or sore on my lip whilst I was giving birth which I thought nothing of at the time," Meg said. "I had never had a cold sore or anything before. "I'd asked health professionals if they thought it was a cold sore, but I was reassured that it wasn't, it was nothing to worry about. "They just thought that I might need to drink more or that it might just have been hormonal from giving birth only the day prior, so I thought nothing of it." But Magnolia's condition deteriorated and she later died from HSV. Magnolia was born healthy but died aged 10 days after contracting the herpes simplex virus The experience left Meg living with what she described as a constant reminder of her loss. It was the first cold sore she had experienced, but another outbreak since Magnolia's death brought back painful memories. "I'm now going to get them for the rest of my life, however regular that might be," she said. "It's horrible. I was really dreading it because I'm constantly reminded anyway that my daughter isn't here any more and why that is, but to actually have a physical reminder on my face is horrible." She said one of the hardest things to accept was that she had never realised a cold sore could pose a danger to a newborn baby. "I'd heard of herpes before, but I'd only heard of it as the sexually transmitted infection," Meg said. "I'd never heard that a cold sore could be the herpes virus and that the herpes virus could be so dangerous to a newborn baby." The family had already taken precautions to protect Magnolia from infection. "We chose not to have family round who were poorly at the time because I knew that was not safe," Meg said. "But I'd never ever seen anything about cold sores, HSV, neonatal herpes, nothing, and it's only since that I've found so much out that I just wish I'd known before." Meg said she never kissed her daughter and was careful about hygiene because Magnolia had been born during winter. "I washed my hands constantly because I was worried in general about infections. "But I never knew that if that passed to her it could kill her." Research by the Lullaby Trust has highlighted the pressure some parents feel when asking people not to kiss or touch their baby. "We know that parents can feel awkward, embarrassed or even guilty about asking someone not to kiss their baby, wash their hands or keep their distance when they're unwell," chief executive Jenny Ward said. "But protecting your baby from infection is never something you need to justify." She said the charity's THANKS advice - think hands and no kisses - was designed to help families reduce the risk of infection. "Wash your hands before touching your baby and don't kiss them if you are unwell," she said. "Viruses are really common, particularly at this time of year, and while we can't avoid them all we can put some steps in place to reduce the chance of your baby getting unwell." If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line. title: Charities 'busier than ever' with furniture poverty
description: Charities in Hampshire tell the BBC that furniture poverty is becoming an increasing problem.
body: BBC South visited charity Scratch's warehouse ahead of deliveries being made Charities say they are "busier than ever" helping people living in furniture poverty. BBC South spoke to people and organisations affected in Hampshire after national charity End Furniture Poverty said about six million in the UK were living without essentials such as beds, cookers and fridges. And a group of MPs is calling on the government to develop a national strategy to address the problem. They said they believed that a safe, secure and sustainable home should include access to the basic furniture necessary for everyday living. The government said it was already taking action to support households. Among those who have needed help is Yana Osibchuk, who moved to the UK from Ukraine after the war began with her son, her dog and two suitcases - and was placed into social housing. "It was absolutely empty - no furniture, no cooker, no fridge, nothing and no flooring," she said. Yana Osibchuk spoke to the BBC about her experience of furniture poverty Yana was referred to charity Southampton City and Region Action to Combat Hardship (Scratch). "It's really changed my life," she said. But Yana's situation is not unusual. The overwhelming majority of social housing is let unfurnished. Scratch has been running for 27 years and its managing director Mike Taylor said the charity was "busier now than it's ever been". "We are always chock-a-block, our diaries are full every week," he said. "We have two vans going out every day." Mike Taylor, from charity Scratch, said demand for furniture was increasing He said household budget pressure were a factor but that there were lots of reasons people found themselves needing help. "It could be that they've had a crisis in their life, they've had to flee a relationship or flee domestic violence and they've ended up somehow in a property with no furniture," he said. "They may have children with them. They haven't got disposable income. They just don't have the facilities or the money to get going again." Scratch relies on donations and grants from the council. It then makes up packs and sells them on to people at minimal prices. The charity does not deal directly with the public but takes referrals from the council, housing association or other professionals like social workers. National charity End Furniture Poverty defines furniture poverty as the inability to access or afford to buy or maintain any household furniture or appliance item that is essential to achieve a socially acceptable standard of living. Claire Donovan, from End Furniture Poverty, said not having access to household essentials had a significant impact on people's lives Charity director Claire Donovan said: "There are harmful physical, emotional, social, and financial consequences to furniture poverty, and it's not just about material needs as furniture poverty is a consequence of the broader issue of poverty. "Over a quarter of social housing tenants live in furniture poverty and yet only around 3% of those are let as furnished." End Furniture Poverty questioned people living in furniture poverty and 30% said their physical and mental health had been impacted. Claire added: "Not being able to get a good night's sleep because you haven't got a bed. Not being able to store or prepare fresh food because you haven't got a cooker or a fridge - and just the grinding stress of that day in day out - it really affects every area of your life." It is not a problem confined to one area. The Moving on Project Portsmouth charity helps people in the city struggling with furniture poverty. Every day it sees people in desperate need. Sarah Knight, from Moving On Project Portsmouth, said the problem had become "huge" Sarah Knight, from the charity, said: "It's huge. People are digging deep - the only other alternative is to enter loans which have a high interest rate and can lead to problems along the line. "It used to be people on benefits - now it's not, it's people from all walks of life. Reduced hours, higher bills - it affects everybody. "The foodbanks and pantries are on the increase and it's the same with furniture - there are so many families struggling. "Some may not have a bed, they may have a couple of kids sharing a bed. It's horrendous to think that we are in 2026 and to think this amount of poverty is still going on." End Furniture Poverty is calling on the government to ensure 10% of social housing is let as furnished. A government spokesperson said in a statement: "No one should have to live without essential furniture in the place they call home. "We're taking action to support renters by launching a £1bn fund that can be used to help households get furniture." title: Villagers fear losing quiet life to 'monstrosity' meat processing plant
description: Ecclefechan residents say they are concerned about the traffic, smell and visual impact of the factory promising 90 jobs.
body: Pickstock Telford said the site would employ about 90 staff once it was fully operational Residents of a small south Scotland village say they fear losing their "quiet life" after work started on a £24m meat processing plant nearby. The Pickstock Telford development at Ecclefechan promises about 90 jobs in a rural area as well as help to reduce food miles. The company has said that at its factory in England "you wouldn't even know there was a food processing plant on site". But villagers remain concerned about the potential for traffic, odours, noise and pollution from the plant which should be up and running by 2029. Dave Cooper retired to Ecclefechan from America looking for a "quiet life" Dave Cooper, 60, spent the last 10 years in southern California before moving to the cooler climes of Dumfries and Galloway. "I retired to Ecclefechan looking for a quiet life in an uncomplicated village with good facilities for our boxer that we brought across with us," he said. "When buying property towards the north-west end of village I knew nothing of the animal processing facility - or the rest of the phases." He said the village already suffered from "heavy vehicles occasionally speeding down the main road" and he feared that could get worse. "The meat processing plant, I hope, is far enough on the periphery to not be an issue though light, noise and odour pollution are a concern and the potential for much higher rates of heavy livestock vehicles," he said. "We have been told that they will advise all such vehicles not to use the village - but advising doesn't always mean much without proper controls." Villagers have questioned whether Ecclefechan was the best site for the project One local - who asked not to be named - asked why they had picked a site close to the village playing field. She, too, was worried about traffic, smells and possible contamination of nearby waterways. "They should stay at their slaughterhouse in Shropshire," she said. "It's not wanted or needed here, especially located where it's started to be built and the sheer size of it. "It is going to spoil our little village which is quite a historic village and has two holiday sites nearby, it might impact the tourism in a negative way." She added: "I for one would not want to come on holiday to a little Scottish village and have to go past the monstrosity that is being built." Locals have raised concerns about the traffic impact of the plans Another resident who also preferred to remain anonymous told the BBC he did not object to beef production or having a modern abattoir in the region. But he had an issue with the location and scale of the factory and how the community had been treated. "My biggest concern is the continued loss of greenfield land to major developments in Dumfries and Galloway," he said. "The council's own planning policy promotes the reuse of previously developed and brownfield land, yet we continue to see large developments being placed on greenfield sites because the land is available. "For me, the fundamental question is simple - was Ecclefechan genuinely the best place for a development of this scale, or was it simply the most convenient place to put it?" Liam Davies from the Pickstock group, pictured when development started on the site near Ecclefechan last month The company has said the venture - backed by nearly £5m from South of Scotland Enterprise - made sense for its business with the quality of Scottish produce "second to none". It also said the location was in a "very accessible corridor" which could benefit both its operations and local farmers. It said experience at its other site in Telford had shown that neither smells nor visual impact should be an issue. "The Ecclefechan facility has secured planning consent, with local concerns considered and addressed through the application process," said a company statement. "The location supports our ambition to create local jobs, support Scottish farmers and retain more value in Scotland's rural economy." The development is forecast to create about 250 jobs during the construction phase and a further 90 permanent positions once operational. About 40 apprenticeship opportunities are also expected, including 25 during construction and 15 after the site opens. title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15
description: Ethan gives CPR to a 75-year-old man he found collapsed on the street in cardiac arrest.
body: Ethan has wanted to be a paramedic from a young age When aspiring paramedic Ethan ordered three resuscitation manikins so he could teach CPR to others, he had no idea how quickly he would put his training into practice and help save a life. Just two weeks after the dummies arrived at his home in Mansfield Woodhouse, in Nottinghamshire, the 15-year-old found himself performing CPR on a man he found collapsed in the street. Ethan, who had completed a one-off CPR course with East Midlands Ambulance Service (EMAS) last year, said he went through "a million and one emotions" as he realised he was about to apply his knowledge to a real-life emergency. "It was adrenaline like never before, but I knew I had to stay calm, and not think too hard about the immense pressure of putting someone's life in your hands," he added. The teenager was on his way home from a casual gardening job at about 14:30 BST on 18 September when he saw a 75-year-old man slumped over "half in the road and half on the pavement" on Ley Lane. Ethan described the man as being unresponsive with a "raspy-sort of breathing" known as agonal breathing, and he was in cardiac arrest. Having completed his course with EMAS, and watching countless TV programmes about front-line emergency workers, Ethan's training kicked in. Ethan, a Year 10 pupil at The Manor Academy, said a lady who was on the phone to 999 was happy for him to take control as she did not know how to do chest compressions. Together, they moved the man to a safe, flat surface, where Ethan knew the CPR would be more effective. He said: "Even though I've spent ages preparing for this moment, to put it into practice was completely different." Ethan was soon joined at the scene by an off-duty carer from King's Mill Hospital and a teacher from a nearby primary school, who took turns with the compressions. He said it was a "massive sense of relief" when the paramedics arrived and prepared a defibrillator, and he felt a sense of hope once he saw the man had a "shockable rhythm". According to Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK), an expert organisation on resuscitation, survival rates for cardiac arrests outside hospital "remain low", with one in 13 people surviving in the East Midlands. The organisation said the statistic highlighted a need to improve confidence in CPR and using defibrillators in the region. Ethan told the BBC he was thrilled to hear from the man's family that he was making a steady recovery. The man who Ethan helped wishes to remain anonymous while he continues his recovery but his daughter, Erica, said: "As a family, we are so grateful for the bravery that Ethan showed and our gratitude for assisting saving his life. "If it wasn't for Ethan and other passing public, there would have been a very different outcome. "It is incredibly important that people know at least the basics of life saving and we support Ethan totally on his journey [to becoming a paramedic] and will help where we can." Ethan bought three resuscitation manikins so he could share his training with others Ethan became interested in learning basic life-saving skills from the age of 11 while helping to care for his grandparents. He bought the £60 resuscitation manikins with the aim of running free life-saving sessions, particularly for young people, and has already led training at local scout groups. He believes young people are reluctant to learn CPR because they feel awkward about "putting their hands on someone else". He said: "There needs to be awareness that people performing CPR are protected by the Sarah Act." The Sarah Act is also known as the the Social Action, Responsibility and Heroism Act 2015, which is designed to protect people who help others or intervene in emergencies. Robert Gladwin, head teacher of The Manor Academy, said he would now look at investing some money to help more pupils learn life-saving skills. He added: "Quite often young people get a bad reputation but, actually, this shows we generate students who have a real community value. "It is absolutely critical that a Year 10 boy took charge of a situation that most people wouldn't know what to do with, and actually made a difference to the family and the wider community." Jay Astles, clinical improvement manager for out of hospital cardiac arrest at EMAS, praised "Ethan for stepping forward to help in what must have been a very stressful situation". He added: "We would encourage people of all ages to learn CPR and how to use a defibrillator. "As Ethan's experience shows, having the confidence to act in an emergency could help save a life." title: Companies exploiting welfare system by using residents as 'cash cows', BBC finds
description: Agents try to attract people on housing benefit by using social media videos that offer free rooms and holidays.
body: This video can not be played Watch: How private companies are cashing in on social housing Some private companies are making huge profits and exploiting the welfare system by receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but failing to give them the support they are required to, BBC Panorama has found. Property agents are drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos that offer free rooms, PlayStation consoles and even holidays. The system - called supported exempt accommodation (SEA) - is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including former prisoners, people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse. It provides housing along with care, support and supervision. For many residents it works well to help them get back on their feet, but charities, politicians and residents tell us parts of the system are being exploited. There are often complicated, multi-layered financial and management arrangements in place. Rather than going to residents, most welfare payments are made to non-profit registered providers. In many cases these providers then hire profit-making private companies to manage properties and deliver support. Many vulnerable people are being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords", said Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex. Panorama has learned the DWP paid out £410m for SEA in Birmingham alone in the last financial year. The city is the epicentre of the sector, with more than 34,000 people living in SEA. For context, in London about 22,000 live in supported housing despite its population being more than seven times larger. Labour MP Jess Phillips, whose Birmingham constituency contains large numbers of these properties, said companies spending taxpayers' money while providing a poor standard of support was "an absolute catastrophe" and bad landlords "can make loads of money". But she added that there are some housing providers who "get this money who are absolutely providing supported accommodation". The leader of the city council, Liberal Democrat Councillor Roger Harmer, told us that "taxpayers' money is being wasted. It's a scandal." In Birmingham, BBC Panorama's investigation found: Vulnerable people are being left with little to no support in often unsuitable accommodation One big housing provider wrote off £1.8m because of payments to some former directors and companies they ran Evidence that some are willing to make benefit claims for people who do not live in their properties Supported accommodation was set up for people like Alysha. When she escaped a violent relationship, she returned to Birmingham seeking shelter. But her family did not have room so she had to look elsewhere. Alysha became homeless after experiencing domestic abuse in a relationship Alysha lived in three different SEA properties, including a shared house managed by a company called Second City Support Ltd. Things soon started to unravel, she told us. Last December, residents of the house went eight days without any heating or hot water when the boiler broke, she says. "I was at my wits' end. I'd be begging [Second City] and they would just cut the call because they didn't want to deal with it." As a survivor of domestic abuse, she also wanted help to get her life on track, including looking for a job, but said there was no support from Second City. By law, the registered provider of the accommodation only needs to offer "more than minimal" care. "On the [social media] adverts, they will often say that you have weekly support sessions, help with GPs. It's not the case at all, they're not interested. They come, they want you to sign a paper to say, yes, Alysha's gone to support [sessions] this week." A closer examination of Alysha's shared house shows how taxpayers' money is used and how companies in the system can make money in other ways too. The registered provider of the supported exempt accommodation was Dawson Housing, a not-for-profit. Dawson Housing was being paid £443 a week in housing benefit from the DWP - which it received via Birmingham City Council - for Alysha's room and her support costs, equivalent to £23,000 a year. Dawson Housing hired Second City Support Ltd to manage it and deliver her support. Why are vulnerable people, including victims of domestic violence and those facing homelessness, not getting the supported housing they’ve been promised? Separately, a sister company, Second City Housing Properties, had bought and sold the house for a substantial profit. Land Registry records show it bought the property for £191,000 in 2024 and sold it a year later for £410,000. Both Second City companies are owned by Darren Davey. He told Panorama that his company had spent about £150,000 on renovation and other associated costs, prior to the sale. Davey has been very successful in profiting from housing vulnerable people in recent years, operating in both the supported exempt and temporary accommodation sectors. An analysis of his companies' records shows that over the past three financial years, Davey has paid himself £2.9m in dividends from his network of companies, as well as earning more than £900,000 in salary. Davey said his salary and dividends must be considered in the context of his wider group of businesses. Any suggestion his earnings came entirely from supported accommodation "would be misleading", he added. Lawyers for Dawson Housing denied Alysha's support was poor and say that regular in-person support was provided. They said there were unavoidable interruptions in the provision of a dedicated support worker and that Dawson Housing accepted communications with her fell below the standard expected. title: China's growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness
description: Exports have helped offset weak spending at home, but trade tensions and AI doubts cloud its outlook.
body: China's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports. The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from 4.3% in the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data. The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges. Exports have helped offset weak spending at home, but global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook. China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure". With exports climbing, China's trade surplus - the amount of goods and services it sells abroad compared to what it buys from other countries - is on track to overtake the record $1.2tn (£900bn) seen last year. But property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months from the same period last year, official data also showed. Oxford Economics researcher Sheana Yue said manufacturing and high-tech exports have boosted China's growth, despite weak investment and domestic spending. China's economy has struggling to shake off a long-running property slump, after years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers. There are still no signs that this trend will end soon, Yue said. Trade uncertainties and geopolitical issues have also made Chinese consumers more "pessimistic" and unwilling to spend, she added. 'Investing in people': Can China's new push to boost spending revive the economy? Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses The technology industry has been a key driver of China's growth in recent quarters. Global demand for computer chips and other components used to build AI data centres has helped to ease pressure on Beijing and cushion the impact of sluggish domestic consumption. Chinese businesses have leaned heavily on exports as a prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and high youth unemployment have weighed on consumer spending at home. In September, Beijing unveiled a raft of support measures, including lower interest rates for some businesses and subsidies for property buyers, in an effort to boost the economy. But Beijing is facing a backlash from Western economies - including the US and European Union - as manufacturers struggle to compete with large amounts of cheap Chinese goods. There are also concerns over the billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure and whether the companies making those investments can deliver on their promises of generating huge profits. Why is China spending billions to get people to open their wallets? title: Threat forces Israel to Austria flight into emergency landing
description: The Airbus jet landed safely in Bulgaria and all passengers and crew aboard were unharmed, officials said.
body: An Austrian Airlines jet similar to the one diverted to Bulgaria An Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria has been forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat. The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement. The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the transport ministry said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun. It comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight en route to Tel Aviv last month by attacking the captain, before the flight's crew and passengers overpowered him and landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia. Bulgarian and Israeli media reported that a bomb threat had been made. Austrian Airlines has confirmed a threat was made, without giving further details. A spokesperson told the AFP news agency there were 51 passengers and six crew members on board the jet. Authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed in Sofia, about 30 minutes from when the alert was first raised. It was over Romania when it diverted to Sofia. Flight tracking data showed Austrian Airlines 82 left Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening before landing at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia three hours later. Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert. The BBC has sought further comment from Lufthansa, the owner of Austrian Airlines. title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
description: The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a blockbuster stock market listing.
body: Jack Clark, a co-founder and Head of Public Benefit of Anthropic Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good". The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy. Anthropic reportedly said in its initial public offering (IPO) filing that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity". Anthropic said its proposed fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market. None of the shares held by the the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas, it added. Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion, the Claude developer said in a statement released on Sunday. Technology billionaire Elon Musk responded to the announcement on social media with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." "This is what I will be doing," he added. Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September. In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models. Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption. Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? title: BBC visits wildfire front in haze-choked Indonesia
description: The BBC is in central Kalimantan, where a toxic haze fuelled by wildfires is choking millions of residents.
body: This video can not be played As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic haze is choking millions of residents in the region. The BBC's Liza Tambunan is in central Kalimantan, where air pollution levels have plunged to hazardous levels. The haze has been linked to hundreds of thousands of respiratory illnesses in Indonesia, and has drifted to neighbouring countries like Singapore and Malaysia. title: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
description: Video published by several news outlets shows gunmen firing multiple shots at a car while it is moving past a crowd.
body: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff did not sustain gunshot wounds in the shooting, police say Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff has survived a shooting in Mumbai and has not sustained any gunshot wounds, according to Indian police who are investigating the incident. The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening, while he was in a car that was leaving a football club in the suburb of Juhu. Several news outlets have published a video showing at least two gunmen firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of a car while it is slowly moving past a crowd. The incident has heightened concern about the safety of public figures in India, with some killed or injured in targeted attacks in recent years. "These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," said Eknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state, where Mumbai is located. He paid a visit to Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor and his mother had been left "shaken" by the attack. Police said two people were injured in the shooting, including Shroff's driver, local media reported. This is the latest in a string of attacks on some of the country's biggest public figures in recent years. In 2024, police in India arrested two members of a criminal gang for a gun attack targeting the home of Bollywood actor Salman Khan. That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai. The son of two actors, Tiger Shroff made his acting debut in 2014 with the romance film Heropanti and went on to star in several films. He is also a football enthusiast who plays for the professional football club Mumbay FC. title: Burnham says youth employment and training crisis is a 'moral failure'
description: The UK faces "economic catastrophe" with one million young people not in work or training, the prime minister says.
body: Britain needs to "invest in the success of our young people", Andy Burnham says Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training. Writing in the Times newspaper, external, Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system". "Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper. Later this week, the government is expected to announce plans to give young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster". According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training. In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life". "This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote. Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis. "Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job." He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them". The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen." Ministers are this week set to release plans for tens of thousands of new youth apprenticeships and placements in the construction industry, and at accounting, consulting and legal firms. Shadow Business and Trade Secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder." What does Neet stand for and why does the UK have so many? Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously". The review's author, former health secretary Alan Milburn, has argued for the need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support" in an interview with the Guardian, external published on Sunday. "This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job." Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful". Chancellor John Healey, who is due to hand down his first budget on 28 October, told the Labour party conference in September the government had a "moral duty" to address welfare spending. title: Australian Greens senator denies claims of misconduct towards women
description: Jordon Steele-John says the timing of the claims is motivated by "nasty political games" within the Greens.
body: Greens senator Jordon Steele-John denies claims of misconduct against women An Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nasty political games", days after the claims emerged. Last Thursday, Greens leader David Shoebridge said Senator Jordon Steele-John, 32, had taken leave from the party room after a letter from seven current and former members said he had been accused of "multiple allegations" of misconduct between 2017 and 2025. In an online post on Sunday, the senator denied the claims and said he was not on leave. On a sexual assault claim, he said police investigating the matter had closed the case and no charges were laid. An internal party probe has been launched into the allegations. Steele-John, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, was first elected to the senate in Western Australia in November 2017. In his letter responding to the claims, Steele-John said his nickname - "Feels on wheels" - initially referred to him being emotional when advocating for disability rights but had since taken on a "more sinister meaning" about his alleged mistreatment of women. He accused Shoebridge of mishandling the matter and questioned the timing of the letter, saying "it is no coincidence" that the allegations were sent to the leader "the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection" ahead of the next federal election. Days after the letter with the claims was sent to Shoebridge, local media reported that the party had created a 47-page dossier years earlier that listed a number of allegations against Steele-John and how to manage media coverage if they emerged. Steele-John said the dossier was made so that the media would not "bombard" the two women at the centre of those claims and that neither woman had made a complaint. He acknowledged the allegations against him would have "damaged" the public's trust in him and said he was "committed to rebuilding that by acting with as much transparency and accountability as I can". Shoebridge's office confirmed that the allegations had been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission. title: Chance of storms this week as Atlantic jet stream roars into life
description: Gales are possible later this week as a deep low pressure system crosses the UK, but uncertainty remains whether impacts will be enough for it to be a named storm.
body: The UK may see its first named storm of the autumn as forecasts show the potential for a deep area of low pressure to cross the UK later this week. A strengthening jet stream triggered by temperature contrasts across North America will cause turbulent conditions to develop. All areas will experience rain at times, including those currently in drought, but amounts of rain will depend on the exact track of a stormy low pressure system later in the week. After a chilly weekend, temperatures will generally remain slightly below average for mid-October. Autumn has been relatively calm in many areas with little in the way of disruptive weather and rainfall has remained deficient across a huge swathe of England and Wales. Parts of Herefordshire have seen only a tenth of the rainfall typically expected by this stage of October, and the dry conditions persist for much of England. The Environment Agency recently declared severe drought for parts of southern England. This month continues the warming trend we have seen so far this year, with mean temperatures - which is an average of maximum and minimum temperature - between 1 and 3 Celsius above normal for October. Over the weekend, all four nations saw their lowest temperature of autumn so far. Parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland dropped to minus 4 Celsius on Sunday morning with minus 2 Celsius recorded in northern England while Wales registered its first air frost of the season. Frost on the ground in central Scotland as the UK experienced the lowest temperatures of the autumn so far over the weekend After a frosty start in Scotland and Northern Ireland on Monday it will turn more cloudy. Overnight rain in England and Wales will largely die out and skies will brighten. It should be a slightly milder to start the week. Expect cloudy skies on Tuesday with rain developing again in England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland may be dry with some sunshine, before another band of rain arrives from the Atlantic by the end of the day. Bands of rain will move across the UK on Wednesday before the weather takes a turn for the worst in some areas at the end of the week. Current forecasts suggest a deep low pressure system will pass the south of the UK on Friday with the strongest winds limited to southern areas Weather models suggest there is the potential for the jet stream to guide a deep area of low pressure across the UK by Friday. In addition to heavy rain, gales or even severe gales will be wrapped around the deep low. At the moment most computer models take the centre of the low pressure system across the south of the UK. The highest risk of disruptive winds would be over southernmost parts of England and Wales and possibly some eastern coastal counties of England later on Friday. Such a track would leave Scotland and parts of Northern Ireland with quieter weather conditions. However, some computer models show the deep low taking a more northerly track. If this happens, then gales and disruption could be expected more widely with impacts also in Scotland and Northern Ireland. The uncertainty of the track means the forecast could change and it is important to keep across any potential Met Office weather warnings. Amber weather warnings were issued as Storm Ashley hit October 2024 The UK storm season runs from September until August and it is not unusual to reach this stage of autumn without any named storms. If the UK Met Office or Ireland's Met Éireann expect this week's low pressure system to bring significant impacts, that would lead them to issue weather warnings at an amber level or higher . If the storm is then named, it will be called 'Storm Austen'. It is possible that the low pressure system could follow an even more southerly track, meaning greater impacts in France and less across the UK, and the French weather service MeteoFrance could name it 'Storm Bruna'. Developments at the end of the week will also dictate potential weather conditions into the following week, with some computer models showing further stormy weather at times, while others suggest quieter conditions under a developing high pressure system. title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
description: Antisocial behaviour on buses in England could lead to fines while a new campaign is also being launched for trains. A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is being launched.
body: Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour. The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport. Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities. A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is also being launched. The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced. "We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000. The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said small changes in behaviour "can make a massive difference to people's experience on public transport". The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England. These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport Secretary Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100. The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents. Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyone The campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network". The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction". However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers". "Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said. Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with different accessibility needs. He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police." Richard Holden MP, Shadow Transport Secretary, said: "After we led the charge against antisocial behaviour on public transport last summer, Ministers have worked out that nobody wants to endure pounding techno or blaring hip hop on a packed train or bus. "But passengers and railway staff face far more serious problems. Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways." Liberal Democrat Transport spokesperson, Olly Glover MP said: "Tough talk means nothing without enforcement. "Unless the Government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on." Independent watchdog Transport Focus said research it had published in June showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway. "Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell, Transport Focus's director of policy and insight. "Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."
