title: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?
description: Grand Theft Auto VI lets you build and nurture a romantic relationship but some say dates with a fictional character are a step too far.
body: The relationship between the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, is at the centre of Rockstar's latest Grand Theft Auto title Imagine your partner spending hours flirting with someone else, trying to hold their hand and taking them on dates. Most people would have questions. But what if that someone only exists inside a video game? The latest instalment in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto franchise is set to be the biggest entertainment launch of the year when it is released next month. Judging by previews, the connection between its two main characters is a central feature. Rockstar has hinted that the Bonnie and Clyde-type protagonists Jason and Lucia do not have to become a full-on romantic couple. But their relationship can grow by spending time together outside of the main crime and life-on-the-run storyline – through shopping, visiting bars and restaurants and working out together. Smaller interactions like holding hands and quickly responding to each other's texts can help build a bond. The idea has restarted a debate almost as old as gaming itself: if you are that invested in a fictional relationship, is your real-life partner entitled to be upset? In September, polling company YouGov put that question to more than 4,000 British adults. About 6% said they would regard it as cheating, while a further 19% said they would "not be okay with it". Women were considerably more likely than men to take a dim view. Alli Franco, a 30-year-old Texan who posts anime and gaming content to more than a million followers, external on TikTok, says she felt "dismayed" watching the debate unfold online. "If your partner is insecure about a fictional character, then there needs to be some serious reflection," she told the BBC. "It's similar to having a crush on a TV star, but even further removed from cheating since there is no other actual person involved.” After Franco posted a video on the subject, hundreds of commenters appeared to agree with her, although some did have reservations. "To be honest, it depends," wrote one. "If you're cancelling plans with your significant other or directing your intimacy towards a fictional character, then that is a little odd." Rockstar has said players do not have to build a romantic connection in the game For decades, video games have allowed players to build relationships with non-player characters, or NPCs. Gamers could marry villagers in Harvest Moon in 1996, shape emotional storylines in Final Fantasy VII and pursue more complex romances in role-playing games like Baldur's Gate II. In life simulator The Sims, they could flirt, date, marry and have children with computer-controlled characters. But all those interactions were tightly scripted, based on rules and storylines written in advance by game developers. GTA 6 appears to offer something more dynamic, allowing players to shape the relationship between Jason and Lucia through a wider range of open-world interactions and choices. "The more sophisticated games get, the less likely it is that players get pulled out of the experience," says Arienne Ferchaud, an associate professor at Florida State University who studies how people form connections with fictional characters. "Games are doing a better job of mimicking reality and mimicking social relationships." This video can not be played Can you cheat on your partner in a video game character? Grand Theft Auto 6 may represent the current cutting edge of game design, but the next leap forward could come from artificial intelligence. Nvidia, Ubisoft and other huge tech companies are already experimenting with generative AI systems that allow players to hold more natural conversations with NPCs. Future characters could remember past encounters, react to a player's actions and build relationships that change over time rather than following a pre-written script. Ferchaud believes that could make games feel even more immersive. "You could have relationships that feel more solid or more special," she says, although she argues AI as it exists today would still be creating "a stronger illusion" rather than a genuinely meaningful connection. Whether that is exciting or unsettling may depend on the player, and there has been some resistance to the wider use of the technology in gaming. Franco says she is already seeing adverts for AI chatbots that let fans talk to their favourite anime characters. "I can definitely see AI integrating into games and making it a more realistic experience," she says. "But should that happen I would still see it as just a game. At the end of the day you can't cheat with lines of code." title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
description: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia. One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil. He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs. The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves. He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him. Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities. The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself." And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out. The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this. There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify. Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Two men tell of secret operations inside Russia. If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome. "At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says. His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets. "When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said. He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield. If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades. Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance. Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers "You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers. Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information. He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets. "This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live. "In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points." He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints. Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals. "As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not." But he argued that his team's actions were justified. "I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared." Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves. title: The Papers: 'Neets crisis is moral failure' and 'Credit crunch'
description: PM brands Neets "crisis" a "moral failure" and cereal prices could rise in healthy food crackdown lead Monday's papers.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham writes in the Times that Britain faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" if "a generation of young people is being written off to a life on benefits". He writes that one million young people are not in education, employment or training, known as "Neets", partly blaming a welfare system that does not provide "support, skills, or help getting a job". The Metro leads with a new report highlighting "inequalities for children depending on where they are brought up". Citing what it describes as "damning findings" within the report, the paper says "youngsters in Blackpool, for example, are 27 times more likely to miss school than those in Lambeth". Children's commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza is quoted by the paper as saying: "the postcode lottery is real". Elsewhere, pop stars Taylor Swift and Sabrina Carpenter are pictured hugging at the Academy Museum Gala under the caption "Taylor (heart emoji) Sab". The Daily Telegraph says Chancellor John Healey has drawn up plans for what it calls a "tax raid on family businesses" ahead of his first budget on 28 October. The paper says he is considering charging income tax when "business owners hand their company down to the next generation, potentially almost doubling the bill". The Treasury told the Telegraph "decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour." A separate headline reads: "BBC suspends use of embedded Civil Service fact-checkers" who it claims worked on "sensitive topics" such as "small boat crossings and the Covid pandemic". The corporation has released a statement saying "all BBC journalism and editorial decisions are made by BBC journalists and editors, in line with the BBC's editorial guidelines, so the statisticians never make editorial decisions." Warnings from Lord David Blunkett against the prime minister's "pledge to change UK voting system" tops the i Paper. The former Labour cabinet minister suggests "adopting proportional representation" and ditching first-past-the-post could lead to "Israeli-style politics", the paper writes, with one Labour MP telling the paper that it could mean Andy Burnham could end up being "the last ever Labour prime minister of a majority Labour government". "Credit crunch" is the Sun's headline, writing the government's plans to ban "supermarket deals on items like bran flakes, porridge and fruit juice" could see the cost of grocery staples "soar". A government spokesperson told the paper: "We will ensure any changes help families make healthier choices while keeping food affordable". "UK has to rejoin the EU," is the verdict of a new report published by the Institute for Public Policy Research splashed on the front page of the Independent. The paper summarises the think tank's warnings that: "being part of the European Union has now become imperative in the light of Russian aggression and US President Donald Trump's unpredictability". The paper also embeds photos of burnt-out vehicles in the centre of Paris following national protests, writing: "France cleans up after weekend of violence and destruction". French President Emmanuel Macron condemns "unbridled violence", says the Guardian in its top story. The paper reports there were "2,000 arrests as public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted", embedding a photo of a burning car at Place de la République in central Paris. Elsewhere, former British Health Secretary Alan Milburn, who has led a review into Neets, is quoting urging the government to "cut welfare spending 'to fund support for young people'," according to the paper. The Daily Mail says "at least 200,000" people have been given the "right to remain" since the government promised a crackdown, citing official figures. The paper says that 5,000 people per week who have lived in the UK for at least five years "having legally arrived on visas" have earned settlement, known as "indefinite leave to remain". The Daily Express leads with pleas from numerous farmers for the prime minister to "axe the family farm tax" ahead of next week's budget, urging Burnham to U-turn on the inheritance levy introduced by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Reports of threats to the US "AI boom" lead the Financial Times, reporting that $10tn (£7.5tn) worth of infrastructure plans, which mostly involves building data centres, faces the combined headwinds of "project delays, a public backlash and shaky investor confidence". It writes that the "ambitious data centre plans are running into reality", reporting that "some 47 big projects have been delayed, blocked or withdrawn this year – at a 'conservative estimate'." Singer Ellie Goulding features on the front page of the Daily Mirror, which reports that she posed "in pink diamonds from a mine embroiled in a pollution scandal". After spending years campaigning for climate action, the paper describes Goulding's move as "eco hypocrisy", although it quotes the singer who says "I am mortified to have made this error in judgement". Finally, the Daily Star says Libertines frontman Pete Doherty "did scoff a mega meal", an eating feat that "brought him a new found respect from the British public". The paper's verdict on the 2018 Margate cafe meal: "What a Brekkie Shambles". Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: The Interview
description: Author and activist Arundhati Roy on her mother’s influence, writing and politics
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·19 Oct 2026,·23 mins Available for over a year “When I was writing it I didn’t think it would touch such a universal chord, you know, because it seemed to me so weird, my childhood and my mother and my life, it was, but of course, everybody has something. And a lot of people I meet have said this to me and that it helped them see their parents as human beings and not just parents.” Ishadrita Lahiri speaks to acclaimed author and activist, Arundhati Roy. One of India’s most celebrated writers and outspoken political voices Roy rose to international fame in 1997 with her Booker Prize-winning debut novel The God of Small Things. Since then she has become as well known for political activism as for her fiction, challenging those in power and using her writing to engage with questions of inequality, nationalism and human rights. In her latest book, Mother Mary Comes to Me, Roy reflects on her complex relationship with her mother and the ways it shaped her life and work. We explore her literary journey, political convictions and what’s shaped her writing. The Interview brings you conversations with people shaping our world, from all over the world. The best interviews from the BBC, including episodes with Indian youth campaigner Abhijeet Dipke, UNICEF chief Catherine Russell and author Maggie O’Farrell. You can listen on the BBC World Service on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at 0800 GMT. Or you can listen to The Interview as a podcast, out three times a week on BBC Sounds or wherever you get your podcasts. Presenter: Ishadrita Lahiri Producer: Asmita Nandy Editor: Farhana Haider Get in touch with us on email TheInterview@bbc.co.uk and use the hashtag #TheInterviewBBC on social media. title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
description: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.
body: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in". He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market. A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy. The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations. It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels. There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey. Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures. "Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia. "Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help. "I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union." The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%. The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years". "Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer. But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment. All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently". At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added. Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began. Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids. "The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks." "Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged." Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history". "We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive." title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
description: Trading standards officers say AI is "super-charging" existing scams through clones and fake websites.
body: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams. Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot. If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say. AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards. For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist, external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using. Cloned or new websites that look polished and professional in rapid time and at a low cost Romance scams in which AI is used to remember victims' personal details and keep conversations going over weeks or months AI-generated deepfake videos and voice-cloned audio is used to impersonate family members or close friends asking for money in an "emergency" Error-free, personalised phishing emails, text messages and social media posts can be generated by AI on a huge scale Some of the old scam-avoidance techniques may now be less successful due to the benefits of AI. Typos or grammatical errors can no longer be relied on to spot scams, says consumer group Which?. Some of the ways to protect yourself, according to trading standards, include: Never sending money, gift cards or personal or financial information to someone you have not met in person Doing your research - such as checking whether a shop's address is real, using the Financial Conduct Authority's Firm Checker, external, to ensure a company is authorised to give financial advice, and contacting a business directly to check whether a job advert is real Not assuming someone is genuine just because you've heard their voice or seen them on a video call In general, they say stop and think before paying, sharing personal information or taking action. You should be especially wary of pressure or urgency because criminals want you to act before you have time to think. Fraud and scams can be reported to Report Fraud, external or by calling on 0300 1232040, or you can call the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline on 0808 223 1133 for advice. title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
description: Prime Minister Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".
body: Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta. Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity". "The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died. Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening. Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC. Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing. "There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition. A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range. "What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area." Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there. News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation. Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable". The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said. In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference". What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright. The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down. Wainwright is about 200km (125 miles) from Edmonton, the provincial capital The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units. "It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province. STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed. Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance. Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said. "I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie". title: Mission set to blast off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
description: A spacecraft is set to launch on an ambitious mission to bring 10g of Martian moon dust back to Earth.
body: The spacecraft will head to Mars's larger moon, Phobos A space mission is set to launch on Monday that will attempt to grab a piece of Mars' moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth. If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. The spacecraft will blast off from Japan and arrive at Phobos in August 2027. It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed. Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. "I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said. There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos. Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes. The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos. It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat. Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon. "The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained. "But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface." Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formed The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos. Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust. This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia. The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g. "It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission. "However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said. The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of Phobos Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from. There are two competing ideas. Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris. Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity. "When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell. "It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly." The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs. "One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell. "And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars." Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists. The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters. But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress. China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031. We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites. These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth. Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water. Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine. The MMX mission is scheduled to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Center at 0441 local time on 20 October (2041BST 19 October). title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
description: More property asking prices are being cut than at any time in 15 years, data shared with the BBC shows.
body: Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC. The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations. The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since. Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs. "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove. "In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter." Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly £21,000 cut from a typically valued home. Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price. The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023. Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed. With mortgage rates at a three-year high, Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable. So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed. September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year. Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price. The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell. Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Rightmove. 'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak? You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England. One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier." Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home". But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget. Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial. "That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said. Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price. "The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said. But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it. In Scotland, the Home Report system, external requires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market. Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain. His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London. He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England. title: Northern Ireland Troubles Bill to be debated in House of Commons
description: The government has published hundreds of amendments, including that the attorney general must provide consent for any serious prosecutions related to the conflict.
body: The Troubles was a period of conflict which lasted for 30 years and cost the lives of more than 3,500 people Labour's Northern Ireland Troubles Bill will return to the House of Commons later on Monday for hours of debate before MPs vote on proposed changes to the legislation. Last week, the government published hundreds of amendments, including that the attorney general must provide consent for any serious prosecutions related to the Troubles under the new plan. The legislation seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict which cost the lives of more than 3,500 people. It has been more than a year since it was first introduced to Parliament, following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government. A debate known as the "committee of the whole house" will take place on Monday, with its remaining Commons' stages on Tuesday. If it is passed by MPs, it will then move to the House of Lords for further consideration. NI Secretary defends planned changes to Troubles bill Attorney general approval required for serious Troubles prosecutions New legislation on Troubles legacy deal introduced in Westminster The government has defended the changes it is hoping to get support for, with Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant saying the bill will help provide answers for many families. However, it has received a mixed response from political parties in Northern Ireland, as well as from victims and veterans' groups. Sinn Féin said the plans amounted to a "veterans' charter", while the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) accused the government of seeking to rush through the bill without a proper chance for MPs to scrutinise it. Mark Thompson from the victims' group Relatives For Justice said he feared the bill could lead to unlawful killings being covered up by the state. "Essentially, this impacts the victims of collusion and state violence," he told the BBC's Sunday Politics programme. He accused the government of trying to take "control" away from local courts because it did not like some of the recent rulings in Troubles-era cases. He pointed out that judges had ruled against the Army in "dozens" of inquests into killings carried out by soldiers, including those at Ballymurphy and Springhill. Thompson argued that local courts had provided a "level playing field" but instead the government caved under pressure from the Army veterans' lobby in London. "What they [the government] want to do is lift it out of a rule of law process and bring it to London and have a political decision." However, lawyer Philip Barden, who has represented several ex-soldiers, claimed Army veterans were "put through the mill" in cases where there was "no evidence". "What we want is an independent process so its not the PPS and the DPP deciding in Northern Ireland who it is who should be prosecuted," Barden told the programme. "We, frankly, wanted a Supreme Court judge as being the most independent person that we could conceive of - not being a political appointment. "The government have come up with the attorney general of the UK, who of course makes many decisions to prosecute people." Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan Smith (centre left) supported a veterans' protest in London last month Barden defended the government's choice, saying if people disagreed with the UK attorney general's decisions they could always seek a judicial review. "So there is complete independence," he argued. He added that veterans' "primary cause of concern" was the number of repeat investigations into Troubles cases, despite a lack of any new or compelling evidence. Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant said the bill will help Troubles victims' families It seeks to replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act, which introduced a ban on inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents. The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful. Labour's bill involves a legacy commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police). The government said its amendments "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations. While some MPs have previously argued that planned protections for veterans do not go far enough, Stormont's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has accused the government of giving former soldiers "preferential treatment". The legislation will make clear the commission and coroners "must not regard the lawful conduct of members of the armed forces as equivalent to the actions of paramilitaries responsible for acts of terrorism" The attorney general, currently Ellie Reeves, will be required to consent to all "serious" Troubles-related prosecutions There would be measures to prevent "cold-calling" of veterans and extending provisions for remote attendance as part of the commission's work Before any witness can be approached, the commission should consider if "compelling new evidence exists, or the likelihood of a witness being able to provide new information" The commission must consider the "context and command orders" in which military veterans were operating Former paramilitaries are barred from being appointed to the Victims and Survivors Advisory Group, and there is a requirement for at least one veteran or veterans' representative to be on the panel There is a statutory review of the measures for veterans to ensure they "deliver as intended" Opposition parties and backbench MPs have also tabled separate amendments aimed at changing the bill, but it is up to the Commons Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle to decide whether any of them will be accepted for debate. title: 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight
description: A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests
body: This video can not be played A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests on Saturday. Dramatic footage shared online shows the 19th-century building engulfed in flames, with the spire of its clock tower later collapsing. On Sunday, stunned residents watched as firefighters, who had battled the blaze through the night, assessed the building's structural integrity. Officials have not yet confirmed whether the town hall is at risk of collapse. "Damaging heritage buildings because you're angry with the government is selfish", one resident told the BBC. BBC correspondent Chris Bockman reports from Limoges. Read more about the protests across France. 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight. title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
description: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
body: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table". Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened. Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake". Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment", and saying the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market. Trump also claimed in his Truth Social post that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now". Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support. Since then, Zelensky declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing a European Union summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin. title: Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US
description: The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from Chicago, where communities are battling a new wave of synthetic drugs.
body: This video can not be played Warning: This video contains descriptions of drug-taking and distressing images A new wave of synthetic drugs is sweeping across the United States, raising fear of a worsening drug crisis. Earlier this year, President Donald Trump pledged a crackdown on drug cartels, proscribing many as terrorist organisations. Drug overdose deaths have fallen from a peak of around 110,000 in 2022, down to roughly 70,000 last year. However, America's decades-long drug crisis may be accelerating and authorities are increasingly concerned about cheaper, more powerful synthetic drugs, including an animal tranquilliser called tranq. The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from the frontlines in South Side, Chicago, where communities are battling the crisis. Read more about the synthetic drug crisis sweeping the US. title: House prices on the rise - how does your area compare?
description: Affordability continues to be a "real challenge" for buyers, as prices rise by an average of 4%.
body: Affordability continues to be a "real challenge" for some house buyers, after prices in Wales rose by 4% in the year to June. The market has shown "real resilience" with prices more than 7.5 times the average income in some areas, according to new figures from the Principality Building Society (PBS). Anglesey topped the chart with a 22% annual rise, but 17 of Wales' 22 local authority areas saw price increases, the Wales House Price Index said. Ceredigion was one of four regions to see a price drop and Aberystwyth estate agent Layla Mangan, said she has noticed "a lack of confidence" amongst buyers and sellers who were feeling "uncertain" about cost of living pressures. The overall average house price was £258,129, but Andy Mottram of PBS said, while the market had shown "real resilience" with "strong price growth" in many places, "affordability was a real challenge for people". Flintshire, saw no annual change and, of the four local authority areas to see a decline, Ceredigion had the the biggest drop of 9% - although Mangan said that did not reflect her experience in Aberystwyth. First-time buyers were facing average house prices equivalent to four-and-a-half times household income in Cardiff, compared with just over three-and-a-half times in Blaenau Gwent where houses were cheapest, according to the data. For people who were already home owners and wishing to move, purchase prices were equivalent to 7.6 times income in Cardiff and 5.2 times in Blaenau Gwent. Blaenau Gwent saw a 47% increase in the number of mortgages issued between April and June compared to the first three months of 2026, the biggest increase in Wales. First time buyer properties in the area cost an average of £155,000 with an overall house price of £167,239. But Blaenau Gwent also had the lowest average household pre-tax income at £42,000 according to the report. This contrasts with Monmouthshire which had the highest household income at £61,700 as well as the most expensive average house prices at £285,000 for a first-time buyer and £387,606 overall. Layla Mangan from Alexanders estate agent in Aberystwyth said she was "surprised" at the 9.3% drop in prices recorded for Ceredigion. "That's not been our experience" she said, "it's a hard market, yes, but it doesn't feel that we've dropped nearly 10%". Estate agent Layla Mangan says the Ceredigion housing market is reflecting uncertainty But Mangan said she has noticed "a lack of confidence" among buyers and sellers. "We don't have to look hard to work out why that would be. What an uncertain time we're in," she said. "I can understand people feel reluctant to wanting to essentially get into more debt. I understand that and it's hard at the moment." "Everybody is really into house prices, whether you're a homeowner or not, because we can use it as this kind of thermometer, this gauge for what the economy and our finances are doing in general," she said. "If you aren't looking at selling again in 12 months' time I'd hold your nerve, I'd go for it. "We can't expect to be buying houses and making money on them straight away and where we go wrong is if that's what we're expecting." The number of houses sold in a region can impact how much prices rise or fall compared to other places. On Anglesey, which saw the biggest annual rise in house prices of 22.2%, the market can be a mixed picture. Richard Tuke has lived on the island for 20 years but now wants to sell up and live in Spain. "Anglesey has always been a desirable area for people to live," he said, adding he thinks the market is "not as bad as it was". After several months of little interest he has twice reduced his asking price, from the initial £475,000 to £425,000, and that has made a difference. "We've had a wave of viewings in the last two weeks and a lot of strong interest, so I think we're at the right price level now," he said. The turbulence in the Middle East and the knock-on effects on oil and gas prices have already led to higher rates for fixed rate mortgage deals, and the Bank of England is widely expected to increase interest rates, making borrowing more expensive in the months ahead. "If you look back over the year to date, the market's shown remarkable resilience in spite of those pressures," said Mottram. "I think that's broadly likely to continue as we look forward." Mottram said that despite building cost of living pressures, there were a variety of options for would-be home buyers. "There's still going to be pressures," he said, but "if people are worried, the best thing they can do is talk to their lender or talk to a mortgage broker to understand their options". title: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
description: French President Emmanuel Macron made a national television address after rioting caused widespread damage.
body: French President Macron (centre) chaired an inter-ministerial crisis meeting at the Élysée Presidential Palace, in Paris, on Sunday French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday. In a national address from the Élysée Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame." Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted". Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry. The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings. On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon. Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police. Local officials said the Limoges town hall was "largely lost" after fire caused part of the building to collapse Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history. In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold. Speaking near the ruined building, Annèyse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody." "It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before." Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets. This video can not be played Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owvers on the streets of Paris Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas. Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protections in place for shops and civic buildings. The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations. Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously. title: Madueke's 'anger and conviction' shows he's more than a 'finisher'
description: Noni Madueke may not have the role he wants at Arsenal but his winning goal against Nottingham Forest showed why he is one of Mikel Arteta's valued players.
body: Noni Madueke has scored two goals this season in all competitions for Arsenal. Noni Madueke may not have the starting role he wants at Arsenal but his winning goal against Nottingham Forest showed why he is one of Mikel Arteta's valued "finishers". The England international scored a second-half winner to earn Arsenal a vital three points in their defence of the Premier League title. Madueke has started just one top-flight game this season, a 2-1 win over Leeds in the Gunners' last Premier League outing before they beat Oliver Glasner's side on Sunday. Arsenal's summer was dominated by talk of their search for an elite forward, with the left wing one of the positions identified. But after unsuccessful pursuits of world class players such as Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez, the only new addition in that position was Christos Tzolis, the winger brought in to replace the outgoing Leandro Trossard. Tzolis has started the season well and has been the first-choice winger for Arteta, meaning that Madueke and Eberechi Eze have had to be content with the majority of their minutes coming from the bench or in the Carabao Cup. However, Tzolis is now out with a hamstring injury picked up while playing for Greece, and that has presented a chance for Madueke to show Arteta why he should be considering the former Chelsea man as much more than a finisher - that's a term Arteta uses for his substitutes. Madueke did well when starting against Leeds, praised by Arteta for being the best player at the club during the international break. The Arsenal boss said the winger "grabbed it (the start) with both hands". The England international also started on the right wing, his more natural position, against Lille in a Champions League win on Tuesday, assisting the opening goal. Against Forest on Sunday, Madueke was introduced at half time by Arteta and said he took the manager's instructions with him onto the pitch. "Hang in there, stick to the game plan, go out there and try to attack the opposition, be dangerous, be yourself and be good defensively as well," Madueke said. He scored with a deflected shot in the 80th minute when he cut in on his weaker right foot. "I'd beaten him on the outside a couple of times so I thought I'll come inside and just let rip," Madueke said. It's fair to say that the Arsenal fans have not always taken to Madueke since his move from London rivals Chelsea. There was a 'No to Madueke' petition started when he joined the club and his performances have been criticised for being inconsistent. But since his £48.5m arrival, Madueke has helped the club lift their first title in 22 years and played a big part as Arsenal reached the Champions League final. Madueke scored eight goals and provided four assists in 43 appearances in all competitions last season, but questions over his end product remain. He is one of Arsenal's most direct players and England manager Thomas Tuchel and his staff also rate the winger as one of the best players in one-versus-one situations. "Noni, look at me, a smile on my face because he is a special character," Arteta said when he was asked about Madueke's character. "It's someone that's very much loved in and around the dressing room. The way he connects, talks with people. He is just a special guy. "I think I saw an interview where they were asking a few of our players 'who would you call if you had a problem?' And some of them said Noni, which I was surprised. "But I think it is a massive credit and describes the type of person he is." The 24-year-old has now put in three good performances in a row. "He is in a good moment," Arteta said. "After the break, he is showing something else, another level of anger, another level of conviction as well as in his actions and he is becoming decisive in matches, which is what we expect from a player like him. "He is a player that doesn't really mind left or right, but he has played many more minutes on the right side. The team needs him there at the moment and he is doing well." Madueke scores as Arsenal win tight game at Forest Arteta has made a big point of referring to his substitutes as "finishers" as he points to the importance of the squad. That mentality is seeming to have the desired effect. Since the start of last season, Arsenal substitutes have contributed to 26 Premier League goals, which is more than any other side in the league. Bruno Guimaraes scored the winner against Leeds from the bench last time out in the league while substitutes Bukayo Saka, Kai Havertz and captain Martin Odegaard played a major role in the last two goals in the win over Lille. But Arteta is not concerned the Gunners are overly reliant on players from the bench. "There have been other games as well that we have had to score in the first half," Arteta said. "We have played 11 competitive matches and we won 10. We are getting a variety of ways to win in many different contexts." Arteta said he expected few chances against a well organised Forest at the City Ground but added: "I had the belief that the moment the physical level was going to drop, the spaces would be a little bit bigger, the timing more and we would be more efficient there. "And the finishers delivered because the context of the game changed a little bit." Latest Arsenal news, analysis and fan views Ask about Arsenal - what do you want to know? title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' after death of son Presley at 27
description: Presley Gerber's death in September is being investigated as a suspected overdose.
body: Presley Gerber, Kaia Gerber, Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber in May Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber. "He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," she posted on Instagram, next to a black-and-white photo of him. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability." The 27-year-old died on 20 September at a rehab facility in California. Police said officials are investigating his death as a suspected overdose. Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16. Crawford wrote in the post on Sunday: "We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years." "We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain," she also posted. "Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia," she wrote in closing, with an emoji of angel wings. The tribute also listed the dates of his birth and death. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner lists Gerber's case as pending additional investigation. The Santa Monica Police Department has said there is no indication foul play was involved in his death. Gerber's sister Kaia also dedicated a post to him on Sunday which included a video of the two siblings as children dancing together, a photo of them standing near the ocean, and a four-page letter to "prez" typed out on a blue background. In the letter, she said she had been scared of getting her ears pierced, so "you went first". "But when I held the earring they took from your body, all I could think was: That belongs to you," she wrote. "I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you," she also wrote. "How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in," she wrote. In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use and frequently posted videos on Instagram himself for what he called "Mental Health Mondays". His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney. If you're affected by any of the issues in this article you can find details of organisations who can help via the BBC Action Line. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external, external. title: Sage feels 'shame' at Palace thrashing with future in doubt
description: Crystal Palace manage Pierre Sage says he feels "shame" at the Eagles' performance during their 5-0 thrashing by Brighton and does not know if he will be given time to save his job.
body: This video can not be played Pierre Sage post match interview - Brighton v Crystal Palace Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage said he felt "shame" at the Eagles' performance during their 5-0 thrashing by Brighton and did not know whether he would be given time to save his job. Sage's side conceded three times in the opening 10 minutes as they suffered their worst loss to their rivals since January 1956. "It's my fault because I am the coach, I gave the motivation. I prepare the situations. We played so bad it's my fault," said Frenchman Sage, who was only appointed Palace manager in the summer. "It's difficult to summarise because there are a lot of negative points. "We started really bad. It's completely not normal to concede three goals in this kind of game after nine minutes. "I prepare the team, that is why I am responsible of what's happened on the pitch. I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing." Asked if he will get time to turn Palace's poor form around, he said: "I don't know." Under his predecessor Oliver Glasner, Palace enjoyed the most successful phase in the club's history, lifting the FA Cup for the first time in 2025 and then winning the Conference League in May. But Sage has had a tough start at Selhurst Park since he arrived after guiding Lens to the French Cup and second in Ligue 1 last season. Palace are 14th in the Premier League with two wins from seven games but their 17 goals conceded are the most in the top flight. "I just want to apologise to the fans," added Sage. "We were not at the level we expected, and I'm really sorry for that because I know how important it is for them, but we didn't show today that it's really important for us too." Asked on his emotions after the game, he replied: "Only one feeling - shame. When you play this kind of game you have to show another face. It was our worst face." Palace, with one win and one loss from their two Europa League matches, play on Thursday with a trip to Turkey to take on Besiktas before returning to Premier League action on Sunday at home to Newcastle. title: What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base
description: At least four people are confirmed to have died after a huge fire swept through the base.
body: The busy training base is located behind fences on remote land in Alberta A huge fire swept through a Canadian military base on Saturday, killing at least four people and seriously injuring dozens more. Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as one of the worst peace time tragedies on Canadian soil in the history of the military. Here is what we know about the deadly incident so far. Few details about what triggered the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, which broke out at around 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT), have been confirmed by authorities so far. Local media reported it may have been started when a gas main was struck during a live firing exercise taking place on the grounds. Carney said a "violent, fast-moving fire swept through the base" without confirming what started it. The Municipal District of Wainwright posted on social media that the fire had "spread rapidly due to high winds". The prime minister said military and civilian fire crews "fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians". The Canadian defence ministry has said the cause remains under investigation, and "at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". It has not been confirmed if those injured were on the base's sprawling ranges where exercises are carried out, or whether the fire spread to living quarters. This video can not be played Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire Four service members are confirmed to have died, Carney said on Sunday. He also said "dozens" had been "seriously wounded", without providing further information on their conditions. Prior to Carney addressing the nation, Canadian media reported the death toll as seven citing unnamed military sources. The prime minister did not indicate whether or not the government expects the death toll to rise. The names of those who lost their lives have not been identified but their families have been informed. On Saturday evening, Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton declared a code orange - a disaster response protocol for a high-casualty incident. It was stood down on Sunday afternoon. Alberta's health service said the emergency response lasted for 10 hours, and involved 22 ambulances and eight aircraft. Ongoing care for the injured is expected to be "intensive", a statement continued. A stream of ambulances were seen arriving at the hospital and one doctor told Canadian public broadcaster CBC that the facility had been "completely overwhelmed" by the number of patients. Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is located in a rural area of the western province of Alberta - around 120 miles (193km) from Edmonton and 180 miles (290km) from Calgary, the province's two largest cities. It is one of Canadian Army's busiest military training bases and its airfield is also used by the Royal Canadian Air Force. It population fluctuates but more than 1,000 people can be based there at any given time. title: Fears for protected bats if glamping pod plans are approved
description: Without a mitigation strategy the effect on the creatures would be "major", a survey says.
body: The common pipistrelle was among the multiple species of bat found on the land Fears have been raised over plans for a glamping site in a woodland with multiple species of bat. Gwynedd council was considering the application for 11 pods at Bluebell Woods, Caerhun, which would also include pathways, a parking area, soft landscaping and drainage. A bat survey commissioned before the proposed work concluded that without a mitigation strategy the impact on the creatures would be "major" and restrict many of "the most light-sensitive species" from continuing to use the location. In Britain, all bat species and their roosts are protected by law, external. Applicant Michael Williams hopes to create 11 glamping pods on a proposed site in Bluebell woods It is an offence to kill, injure, take or disturb a bat, or to destroy, damage, obstruct or otherwise interfere with a bat roost, breeding site or resting place. Several species of bat were identified on the proposed site, including the common and soprano pipistrelle, as well as the myotis bat. They were observed entering the woodland from the north of the site and along the road corridors in the area, as well as "congregating" in the open parkland in the south-west corner. The mitigation strategy recommendations included "maintaining the woodland as a suitable flight corridor and foraging area", to preserve part of the woodland as a "dark area for bats". Without mitigation, the impact would be assessed "as major" at a national level, primarily due to the effect of lighting on bat access through the woodland, the survey said. Further ecological mitigation proposed included use of bat boxes, a lighting plan with "properly positioned and shielded lighting minimising light spill", standard trees and 20 smaller trees and hedging. title: Man and woman in their late teens die in collision
description: Police say the driver dies in hospital as a result of her injuries.
body: Police, paramedics and fire crews were at the scene in Debenham Road near Little Stonham Two people in their late teens died in a collision involving two cars, Suffolk Police said. Officers were first called by the ambulance service to Debenham Road near Little Stonham at 10:15 BST. Fire crews and the air ambulance were also called to the incident that involved a red Peugeot 107 and a silver Volkswagen Passat. Police said a male passenger in the Peugeot died at the scene. The female driver was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge by land ambulance, but has since died as a result of her injuries. The occupants of the Passat suffered minor injuries, the police spokesperson added. The road was expected to reopen later in the evening. Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below.
