title: Shades of Barca and Beckham - Brighton aim to maintain superb start
description: With 23 goals in seven Premier League matches, including some stunning strikes, Brighton continue to delight their fans and get them dreaming of what might be.
body: This video can not be played Brilliant Brighton put five past struggling Crystal Palace Not only are Brighton scoring more than everyone else in the Premier League, they are netting better goals too. Centre-half Lewis Dunk won the Premier League goal of the month for September with a 35-yard stunner against Coventry. Now, five weeks later, that has already been eclipsed. Step forward Seagulls team-mate Diego Gomez, who shot from the halfway line having seen Crystal Palace goalkeeper Walter Benitez off his line during Brighton's emphatic 5-0 win over their rivals on Sunday. Benitez made a rapid dash back to his goal and produced a desperate dive but could not stop the ball going in just under the crossbar. "As soon as he struck it, I knew it was in. He's taken the club goal of the season off me," joked Brighton skipper Dunk. "That's the goal of the season so far, what a hit," added former Premier League striker Efan Ekoku, part of the commentary team for BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra. "[It was] superbly struck and right over the head of the keeper from the centre-circle." Gomez's seventh-minute goal at the Amex put Brighton 2-0 up and was from 51 metres, the furthest long-range Premier League goal since Wayne Rooney scored from 58m for Everton in their 4-0 win over West Ham in November 2017. "When I scored, I didn't know where to run, or what to do," admitted 23-year-old Paraguay midfielder Gomez. "When I got the ball, I knew the goalkeeper was a little bit ahead. I was very happy with the goal." Former Newcastle goalkeeper and Match of the Day pundit Shay Given said the goal was "reminiscent of David Beckham [for Manchester United versus Wimbledon in 1996]" and added: "I don't even blame Benitez the goalkeeper. "We're always talking about sweeper goalkeepers and you've got to be high up for the through ball and the defence playing a high line. I think his position was fine. "You've just got to take your hat off to Gomez. That is just a brilliant, brilliant goal." Diego Gomez (right) played alongside Luis Suarez and Lionel Messi at Inter Miami before joining Brighton in January 2025 Brighton have never finished higher than sixth in English football's top flight, but now have 16 points from seven matches, with fan hopes rising that they could make a real push for Champions League qualification, or even a title challenge. Their tally of 23 top-flight goals is four more than league leaders Manchester City, and more than double the 11 of reigning champions Arsenal. Since the top flight was rebranded as the Premier League in 1992, only three sides have scored more goals across their first seven games of a season - Arsenal in 2009-10 (24), Manchester United in 2011-12 (24), and Manchester City in 2019-20 (27). In the top five European leagues, only Barcelona, with 39 goals from nine La Liga matches, have more domestic league goals than Brighton. With 10 different goalscorers, Brighton, third in the table, have also been the great entertainers of the season so far. They won their opening league game 4-0 against an Aston Villa side that came fourth in 2025-26 and Fabian Hurzeler's team have shown that was not a one-off. Results since have included winning 5-0 at Coventry, 3-0 against Arsenal, 2-0 at Sunderland despite having a man sent off, and now 5-0 against rivals Palace. In the Carabao Cup, they fought back from 2-0 down to win 3-2 at Old Trafford and eliminate Manchester United. In Europe, they have justified their position as Conference League favourites, putting four past both Norwegian side Tromso and Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris. This video can not be played Fabian Hurzeler post match interview - Brighton v Crystal Palace For Hurzeler, the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in June 2024 at the age of 31, the atmosphere at the Amex could not have been any more different to their previous match with Palace. When the Eagles won 1-0 in February, Brighton were 14th, had only won one of 12 league games with the home fans chanting "you're getting sacked in the morning" at their own boss. Therefore, it is no surprise that Hurzeler is not getting carried away at his side's good form. He was quick to shut down any talk that Brighton could be involved in the Premier League title race and said: "We have to stay very humble. The season will be long. "We have to keep going. We can't be satisfied. We have to keep pushing, stay humble and understand why we are successful at the moment to keep pushing at that level." The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager Hurzeler was also keen to ensure Gomez remained grounded. "It's not simple to score a goal like this," added Hurzeler. "Everyone speaks about his goal, but to me the most important thing is the things we can improve, small easy passes we missed. "It's good to celebrate the win but understand there is still space for improvement especially for individual players. "We don't train shots from 50 metres. Overall, we know he has a really good finish. In these moments it's about being very precise with his long kick. The perception to recognise the keeper and be quick to go to the action was impressive." Brighton fans will have to savour the memories of this win and Gomez's goal as all of their next five matches are away from home. That run includes league games at Liverpool and Manchester City, another trip to Etihad Stadium in the last 16 of the Carabao Cup, as well as Conference League matches in Czech Republic and Spain, against Jablonec and Getafe respectively. By the time Brighton return to the Amex on 8 November to face Brentford, we will have a better indication of just how optimistic the Seagulls fans can be about their season. title: Northampton beat Cardiff for only English win of Champions Cup openers
description: Northampton edge to a nervy Champions Cup pool win against tenacious Cardiff at Franklin's Gardens.
body: George Hendy made his Northampton debut in 2021 Tries: Pater, Thame, Hendy, Dingwall Cons: Belleau 3, Pater Tries: Millard, Grady Con: Evans Northampton became the only English side to win in the opening round of the Champions Cup by battling past Cardiff. Saints, quarter-finalists last season, scored four tries at Franklin's Gardens in a nervy Pool Four encounter. The English champions led 14-0 at half-time thanks to efforts in tricky conditions by James Pater and Toby Thame. Tenacious Cardiff struck back through Harri Millard and Mason Grady to make it a two-point game in the final quarter. But George Hendy and Fraser Dingwall responded as Northampton got off to a winning start, albeit without a bonus point. Northampton's success came at the end of a chastening opening weekend of the top-tier tournament for Prem clubs, with Gloucester drawing against champions Bordeaux-Begles but six other sides losing. Champions Cup recap: Relive wins for Northampton, Toulouse and Pau Toulouse deny Exeter famous Champions Cup victory Late tries give Pau bonus-point win over Leicester Cardiff's return to the top tier of Europe after two seasons in the Challenge Cup was a considerable one. Saints had scored 24 tries in their three opening fixtures of their Prem title defence, including 11 against Bath last time out at Franklin's Gardens. The Welsh side also had to contend with a five-day turnaround to a United Rugby Championship (URC) fixture against Sharks at Cardiff Arms Park. That led to several influential players being held back, although they did give first appearances of the season to Wales and Lions internationals Taulupe Faletau and Josh Adams after injury. Northampton also made changes because of a big fixture on the horizon - the short trip to Leicester on Saturday - but got the job done. Full-back Pater opened the scoring for Saints with a supporting run and centre Thame crashed over after 20 minutes. Both Northampton number eight Callum Chick and Cardiff lock Tom Manz knocked on going for the line as slippery conditions led to it being 14-0 at half-time. The Blue and Blacks struck back early in the second half when centre Millard hit a nice line in the 22 and then defended stoutly to frustrate their hosts, forcing them into a raft of handling errors. It was 14-12 on the hour when, after Saints fly-half Anthony Belleau was sin-binned for a breakdown offence, the ball was floated to the right by Jarrod Evans for Grady to cross. Cardiff scented an upset only for Hendy to respond swiftly, juggling the ball for a try that Pater converted. The Northampton wing went from scoring five points to saving them by chasing down Adams when a try seemed certain. Dingwall dashed over in the 78th minute but the hosts could not find the fifth try that was needed for a five-point haul. Tributes to Andrews before Champions Cup matches Wales' Thomas to miss Nations Championship restart Saints travel to Stade Francais in December and return to France in January to face Montpellier before a home finish to the group stage against Bulls. Cardiff host Bath in December and then face a pair of French teams in January, travelling to Stade Francais and entertaining Montpellier. Replacements: Langdon, Els, Neculai, Prowse, Ulcoq, McParland, Smith, Dingwall. title: Hearts roll out red carpet ... and Celtic walk all over it
description: Hearts thought attack was the best form of defence at Celtic Park. They were badly wrong, writes Tom English.
body: Stephen Kingsley and Jamie McCart cannot stop Celtic scoring a fifth Jimmy Thunder was having none of Crawford Grimsley's chutzpah, none of his mouthing off before their heavyweight contest back in the late 1990s, none of his pre-bout arrogance. Thunder took precisely 1.5 seconds to put Grimsley down - one punch, an overhand right to his opponent's temple. Lights out. Fight over. Statement sent. As Celtic unloaded on Hearts at Celtic Park it was football's equivalent of Thunder's devastation; speed and accuracy and ruthlessness in the face of a challenger akin to a rabbit caught in the headlights. Hearts didn't give it the big one in the preamble to this evisceration, but they set up in the manner of a team who truly believed they were a whole lot better than they actually are. Poor concentration and lack of physicality cost them two set-piece goals inside 10 minutes. The game was effectively over, but the visitors' suffering had only just begun. Celtic score seven in humiliation of title rivals Hearts All the latest Celtic news, views and analysis Everything you need to know about Hearts The pretenders came to Glasgow with a weak away record in the league - two wins in 11 between this season and the end of last, both against Hibs - and tried to go toe-to-toe. Thinking attack is the best form of defence is all very well as long as you can back it up, as long as you can defend competently, as long as you can pass from A to B without losing your mind, as long as you don't concede acreage of space to exploit. Time and again, Hearts rolled out the red carpet to Celtic. A clinical Celtic made them pay for their naivety and maybe their arrogance, too. The footballing version of poor Crawford Grimsley. On their backside before they knew it. Hearts played the highest line with slow defenders, they pushed up the park and left themselves exposed to Celtic's speedsters. That gameplan was not high-risk, it was reckless. This video can not be played Martin O'Neill needed a win after his recent travails and this was a stroll in the park that he could not have imagined. Football management can be a horribly stressful business that can put years on you. After this, O'Neill looked younger not older. The ageing process worked in reverse thanks to his team feasting on Hearts' scarcely believable weaknesses. The stats are, frankly, hilarious. If it was a horrific day for Wouter Vrancken and his players then it was every bit as grim an experience for those who try to see sense in numbers. Hearts had more shots than Celtic (20-18). They had more shots inside the box (16-13). They had more possession (52%-48%). They had more crosses (16-10). They won more duels (51%-49%). They had more passes in their opponents' half (244-202). They had more accurate passes (458-423). That last one was laugh-out-loud funny, for Hearts' use of the ball was comically bad. So often, when under a little bit of pressure, or no pressure at all, they passed into space only for Celtic to gobble up the loose ball and launch an attack which usually ended in a big chance or a goal. The home team was slick. Benjamin Nygren, Callum Osmand, Camilo Duran and Haissem Hassan were devastating. Seven did not flatter them in the slightest. It began with those two early goals - Liam Scales showing the desire to win a near-post header from a corner and Kieran Tierney left alone a few yards out to force in, then Dane Murray outfighting Claudio Braga to help it back to Nygren to score. Hassan hit a post when he turned and darted away from Stephen Kingsley. People wondered what was Vrancken going to do to change this. Answer: nothing. This video can not be played 'Elated, delighted, relieved' - O'Neill on Celtic's thrashing of Hearts When Celtic score seven it seems odd to talk about pieces of defending they did that were significant, but Colby Donovan's cameos warrant mention. Around the midpoint of the first half, Hearts stirred a little. You wouldn't say that they had momentum, but they had a bit of a possession and their hair-on-fire panic of the early minutes seemed under control. Twice in the space of three minutes, Josh McPake - one of the form players in the country - took on Donovan and twice Donovan routed him. Those little duels might disappear from relevance after the deluge, but at the time they were important. The Hearts dangerman had been snuffed out. His morale had taken a hiding. And the stadium loved it. Hearts fell apart at the seams from there. Sabri Guendouz gave the ball away and Duran combined with the impressive Osmand to score number three. Jamie McCart then became detached from his trolley and Celtic scored from that error, too. Osmand, again, but with lovely work from Duran. And easy, oh so easy. Celtic's pace in attack was terrific. Their alertness was outstanding. Their disbelief was there, too. How could a team with a seemingly good coach and a strong squad of players be performing like a pub team? Hearts fans started heading home at that point. They missed the goal that made it 4-1. They won't have shed any tears. Had they gone back they'd only have suffered on. Best get out of dodge as quickly as possible. Soon, it was 5-1, Mika Baur slaloming his way past the comatose figures of McPake and Malachi Fagan-Walcott to dink a shot on goal, helped on its way by Kingsley and McCart, sitting on the floor, all flailing legs, like an octopus who had fallen out of a tree. This video can not be played Hearts performance 'not acceptable' but Vrancken 'won't kill players' Hearts' heads had long since gone. They were a broken team, psychologically. The doubt and fear coursed through their veins. The easiest things became difficult. The difficult things became impossible. They had no discipline, no direction. Vrancken spoke later about individual errors and that was obvious, but what else? He was

title: Mbeumo offers Carrick solace as Man Utd winless run goes on
description: Michael Carrick said he had his headphones on this week so didn't hear the noise around Manchester United, but a 1-1 draw at Leeds means it is six games without a win.
body: This video can not be played Manchester United's winless run extends to six games after draw with Leeds In a season that is forcing Manchester United fans to dig deep for reasons to be positive, Bryan Mbeumo scored again at Elland Road. That is four goals in seven Premier League games for the Cameroon forward. Apart from Bruno Fernandes, who scored a hat-trick against Ipswich in August, no-one else in Michael Carrick's squad has scored more than one. But it's meagre fare. It is true to say Manchester United did reasonably well in their 1-1 draw at Leeds United, just as they did at Atletico Madrid on Tuesday after conceding inside the first minute. Carrick told BBC Radio 5 Live afterwards he "had the headphones on" this week so he hasn't heard the external noise created by Lisandro Martinez's rant. However, he knows his side have to win matches at some point. That is six without a victory now, the worst run since 2018-19, when form nosedived after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was confirmed as permanent manager. "Because they haven't lost at Leeds, we're thinking United have done all right," said former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher on Sky Sports. "But in some ways that is a negative. We are dropping the standards. We shouldn't really be talking about Manchester United like that." This video can not be played Man Utd showed 'unity' in draw with Leeds - Carrick After the corresponding fixture last season, Ruben Amorim gave the explosive press conference that triggered his dismissal within 24 hours. This time, it was Lisandro Martinez who lit the touchpaper before the game, criticising sporting director Jason Wilcox and the United hierarchy for failing, in his view, to recruit effectively during the summer. Wilcox was in the stands at Elland Road, while Martinez started the game following his apology for the timing and forum of his attack rather than the words themselves. To highlight the general view that United failed Carrick by not bringing in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back, Diogo Dalot became the fifth different player to start in that position this season. It remains to be seen if Shaw will be fit enough for Wednesday's Champions League trip to Serie A outfit Como, but the repeated changes cannot be helping Carrick. Martinez went off at half-time with a thigh injury, and such is the delicate nature of Matthijs de Ligt's fitness after almost 11 months out with a back complaint, Carrick preferred to bring on full-back Noussair Mazraoui rather than the Netherlands international. Carrick's side ended the game 13th in the Premier League table, with the possibility they might drop further before the match round is complete. Unlike Amorim, Carrick found it easy to come up with a positive spin on the present situation. "It felt like a bit of a fresh start today, to be honest, with where we're at - accepting it and doing something about it," Carrick said. "I'm not accepting it as everything's great by any stretch. I'm realistic with that. "But sometimes you do struggle. Sometimes there's a bit where you have to find a way through. "There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We've got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things. We're more than capable of winning football matches. "I understand the situation doesn't look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I've got no doubts that we can go on a good run." Manchester United sporting director Jason Wilcox (bottom centre), sat next to chief executive Omar Berrada (bottom right) at Elland Road Calvert-Lewin scores as Leeds deny Man Utd Everything a struggle for Fernandes - Leeds v Man Utd ratings Manchester United striker Bryan Mbeumo (second left in huddle) celebrates scoring the opening goal against Leeds at Elland Road Mbeumo's performance wasn't flawless by any means. He should have done much better when he missed the target with a free header before he scored, and the former Brentford man then failed to prevent Dominic Calvert-Lewin powering in an equaliser just after half-time. But in a campaign when so many of Carrick's attacking players are struggling – skipper Fernandes has been a shadow of the player who broke the Premier League assists record last season even though the United boss said the Portuguese was 'absolutely fine' – Mbeumo's performances have been vital. Their importance has been heightened by the continued absence of striker Benjamin Sesko with a shin injury. Mbeumo spent the first few games on the right of United's attack when Amad Diallo was ruled out by injury. When Amad returned, Mbeumo moved into the number nine role. At Elland Road he was shifted again, to the left as Fernandes played more through the middle. Bryan Mbeumo's touchmap in his past three Premier League games "When you are the kind of player who can be very good in a lot of positions, managers will always say: 'Can you do this? Can you do that?'" former Red Devils striker Dion Dublin told BBC Sport. "When you're in this Manchester United team at the moment, you just have to go where is best for the team." Carrick was even more effusive in his praise. "Bryan gives so much to the team," he said. "He sacrifices so much. "He's willing to do pretty much anything that needs to be done to benefit the team - whether that's defending in certain areas, whether that's attacking. He'll give everything he's got. "He's getting in really good positions to be really dangerous for us, and it's great to have him." This video can not be played 'Man Utd just can't seem to hold on to a lead.' title: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
description: Tech firm Nscale says it is still committed to building the site in Essex.
body: Nscale said it remained committed to building a £2bn AI data centre in Loughton A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project. Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton, Essex. However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement. A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment. "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said. "Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term." What is the new AI supercomputer planned for Essex? The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year. But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday, external, Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s. "This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC. Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States. The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens. Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer. Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? title: West Midlands Police officer who accessed police records 2,000 times sacked
description: A misconduct hearing said many of the records accessed were sensitive and held "intimate information".
body: Many of the records accessed were sensitive and held "intimate information" the panel said An officer who inappropriately accessed police records more than 2,000 times has been sacked for gross misconduct. A West Midlands Police misconduct hearing acknowledged PC Shannon Parsons felt "isolated and disconnected" due to working part-time and returning from maternity leave, but had breached standards of professional behaviour. Parsons had claimed there was a policing purpose to her searches, the panel said, and was seeking to "keep herself up to date, informed and was often in a position to support and assist other colleagues in operational matters". However, chair of the panel Debra Tedds concluded the searches were carried out for the officer's "own personal benefit". As a result, Parsons was dismissed without notice and barred from future work in policing. The searches took part over a period of about five years, the panel heard, and many included incidents near her home address. Parsons had an otherwise unblemished career in policing in the West Midlands, lasting 13 years, but was said to show no insight or remorse "as to the potential harm that has been caused by accessing the amount of information over a significant time period," according to the panel's report. The panel said accessing confidential police information without a legitimate policing purpose was an abuse of an officer's position "I do not believe the officer's conduct was targeted, however I do believe that it was deliberate and intentional and by her own admission had become a habit in between shifts," Tedds said. "Policing holds a significant amount of information about members of the public of which most of it is sensitive." She added that some of the incidents accessed by Parsons were are "of the most sensitive and hold intimate information involving some of the most serious crimes". Tedds said: "I have determined that the access was for personal use. Under no circumstances should anyone access or use police information for personal reasons. "Accessing confidential police information without a legitimate policing purpose is an abuse of an officer's position." She concluded that amounted to a significant breach of trust, likely to cause a loss of public trust and confidence in the profession. However, she added there was no evidence to suggest any of the information accessed by Parsons had been passed to a third party. "I accept that PC Parsons felt isolated and disconnected from policing and her team working part time, returning from maternity leave, and working from home as she described," she said. "I accept the officer's submission in relation to her difficult personal and medical circumstances at the time and seeking to reintegrate herself back into policing after her maternity leave and absence." Nevertheless, she found the allegations were proven and that Parsons had failed to treat sensitive policing information with respect. title: Fuel leak spreads more than two miles along River Taff
description: Public Health Wales advise people living nearby to shut their doors and windows due to the smell.
body: Residents said the area began to smell "like a petrol station" on Friday People have been advised to keep their windows and doors shut due to a widespread fuel leak in the River Taff. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it had received multiple reports about pollution affecting the Taff in places such as Nantgarw, Treforest and Taffs Well. GE Aerospace confirmed fuel got into the river while repair work took place at its site nearby. NRW said the source was identified at 19:30 BST on Friday, and its officers are working to identify how it entered the drainage system, after kerosene spread down almost 2.5 miles (4km) of the river. "The safety of our employees, neighbours, and environment is our top priority," GE Aerospace said in a statement. "We are working closely with Natural Resources Wales and South Wales Fire and Rescue Service to clean up a fuel spill that occurred on site while repair work was under way." The environmental body also received reports of pollution affecting the Taff in Glan Y Llyn, Gwaelod-y-garth and Tongwynlais. It said South Wales Fire and Rescue Service workers helped with specialist equipment to reduce the amount of kerosene entering the river. "Our officers are again on site where action has been taken to significantly reduce the amount of pollution entering the tributary, whilst investigate work is ongoing to try and stop the pollution entirely," NRW said in a statement. It is also taking samples to understand "the actual environmental impact of the spill". Reports of a leak affecting one mile (1.6km) of the river were first received on Saturday morning from residents. NRW later said it had spread as it continued "to investigate the source of the incident to understand how it is happening, stop the pollution completely and collect evidence". Eurig Thomas, a resident in Taff's Well, Rhondda Cyon Taff, said: "It smelt like a petrol station, it hit you as soon as you came out." Absorbent materials have been deployed to try and contain the leak. Thomas added: "The river had a shiny sheen on it, the stream flows behind my house, it comes down from the GE factory and into the Taff. "The smell has dissipated – but you can still smell it this morning." Another resident, Sarah Llewelyn, added: "I haven't slept in three days. Friday afternoon lunchtime I opened the door and could smell fumes, it was burning my eyes." She dubbed it "a national disaster". NRW said it had found the source of the pollution on Friday night "NRW have told us that up to 25,000 litres of kerosene has entered the river." Gareth Llewelyn, a former hazardous materials environmental protection officer with South Wales Fire and Rescue service, said there was "no quick fix" and it needed "years not months" to restore. He added: "I have visited the culvert across the road from the GE site yesterday and it was full of kerosene. It doesn't mix with water and will continue to pollute." Llewellyn said the spill has "torn the heart out of our community", adding: "The village is Taff's Well – it's named after the river." He said "now there's no animals, no birds" and all the fish have died. NRW said the pollution was discharging from an underground surface water drainage system, but the amount of fuel had reduced significantly. It added that its staff had been working with the fire service to install equipment to collect the fuel and that the smell had died down. Water samples have been collected to check the damage the pollution has had. Public Health Wales advised people living nearby to keep windows and doors closed, avoid any contact with the water and to call NHS 111 if they felt unwell. GE has been asked to comment. title: Three officers injured after lorry crashes into police vehicle
description: A 36-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of driving while unfit through drink or drugs, driving while disqualified and dangerous driving.
body: The suspect remains in custody Three police officers have been injured in County Down after a lorry they were pursuing drove on the wrong side of the road and collided with their vehicle at speed. A 36-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of driving while unfit through drink or drugs, driving while disqualified and dangerous driving. A police vehicle was extensively damaged but the officers injuries are thought not to be serious at this time. The incident began following a report of a blue articulated lorry swerving on Moygannon Road in the Warrenpoint area shortly before 23:30 BST. "Officers responded and located a lorry matching the description on the Derryleckagh Road, Newry," said Ch Insp Will Brown. When signalled to stop, the lorry then made off "at speed and on the wrong side of the road", before smashing into a police vehicle and continuing towards Rostrevor. Brown continued: "The lorry later came to a stop in the Water Street area of Rostrevor where the driver, aged 36, made off on foot but was detained by officers following a short foot chase." Brown said: "Our officers put themselves on the front line to help keep people safe. Thankfully, no one sustained more serious injuries during this incident, including officers and other road users." title: Everything a struggle for Fernandes - Leeds v Man Utd ratings
description: Dominic Calvert-Lewin's second-half equaliser means Manchester United have now gone six games without a win for the first time since 2019 - find out who rated highest at Elland Road.
body: Bruno Fernandes had another tough afternoon in what has been a difficult season for him so far Manchester United have gone six games without a win for the first time since 2019. Who rated highest in their Premier League draw with Leeds? James Trafford: Brave enough to race 30 yards out of his box to clear when failure to execute would have been disastrous. Leeds defenders know they can give him the ball under pressure. 7 James Justin: Swung over a couple of early crosses to test the visitors' defence but caught on his heels by Mbeumo for Man Utd goal. 6 Nico Elvedi: Near-post header almost put Leeds in front. 7 Tarik Muharemovic: Calm in possession but visitors' set-up left him with no-one to mark at times. Major threat at the other end though, with header setting up Calvert-Lewin equaliser. 7 Jayden Bogle: An attacking threat from wing-back as Leeds pushed forward and had shot saved by Lammens. 7 Ethan Ampadu: Lucky to get away with no card for a late tackle on Mbeumo at start. Usual assured display. 6 Ao Tanaka (off 79, Longstaff): Maybe a little too cautious at times. Got into the game as Leeds pressed after leveller. Long-range effort over. 6 Gabriel Gudmundsson: Caught Andrey Santos from behind and was booked. Did really well to force Amad back when the Ivorian wanted to run free on goal. 7 Anton Stach: Wasn't able to control midfield duels in opening period but second half was better. 6 Noah Okofor (off 72, Nmecha): No chance to repeat Old Trafford heroics. Lashed a second-half shot over and poor pass when he might have released Calvert-Lewin. 6 Dominic Calvert-Lewin: Grew into the game after subdued start. One first-half header wide, another straight at Lammens in second. Strong enough to control and apply finish to level. 8 Lukas Nmecha (on 72, Okafor): Worked hard to try and create. 5 Sean Longstaff (on 79, Tanaka): 6 Subs not used: Zetterer, Wilson, Aaronson, Bijol, Bahoya, Bard, Gruev. Man Utd's winless run extended against Leeds Senne Lammens: Good save to deny Elvedi and solid performance. 7 Leny Yoro: Given a stern physical test despite starting at right-back. Thrown in at the deep end this season. 6 Harry Maguire: Another largely solid display. Came out on top in one-to-one duel with Calvert-Lewin in first half but found it much harder in the second. 7 Lisandro Martinez (off 46, Mazraoui): Kept his place despite inflammatory comments and was cheered by Man Utd fans, booed by Leeds'. Did well enough. Replaced at the break. 6 Diogo Dalot: Yet another different left-back option. Held his own but he shouldn't really be in that position. 6 Andrey Santos: Another industrious performance which questioned why he had been used so sparingly previously. 7 Carlos Baleba: Keen to get on the ball and carry it forward. Partnership with Santos brings energy. He even tried a 25-yard shot but it was off target. 7 Amad Diallo: Pace was a threat, even if visitors didn't make most of it. Second-half shot blocked. 6 Youri Tielemans: Excellent cross for Mbeumo opener. More effective with two midfielders behind him. 7 Bruno Fernandes: Overhit a free-kick in a dangerous position and sent it out for a throw, then booked for late tackle on Muharemovic. Everything seems forced and a struggle at the moment. 6 Bryan Mbeumo: Started in an inside left position and tried to link play but not a natural role. Should have scored with first-half header, didn't threaten with another opportunity but persevered and eventually got his goal. Not strong enough to hold Calvert-Lewin off for equaliser. 7 Noussair Mazraoui (on 46, Martinez): Leeds more of a threat when he came on. Vital injury-time block. 6 Mason Mount (on 72, Baleba): Can be effective and tried to create but limited impact. 6 Matheus Cunha (on 84, Tielemans): 6 Subs not used: Darlow, De Ligt, Rashford, Zirkzee, Lacey, Amass. After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: BBC pauses civil service secondment scheme
description: The BBC said all journalism and editorial decisions are made by BBC journalists and editors.
body: The BBC says it will pause secondments of government statisticians to its fact checking service, BBC Verify, and review their roles. Since 2018 the BBC has offered six-month secondment opportunities for up to two civil servant statisticians to work for BBC News's head of statistics. A BBC spokesperson said: "All BBC journalism and editorial decisions are made by BBC journalists and editors, in line with the BBC's editorial guidelines, so the statisticians never make editorial decisions." Those currently on secondment would not be involved in the publication of news or content during the review and the current round of recruitment will be paused while the role is reviewed, the corporation added. The decision follows a report in The Telegraph which said embedded civil servants had been engaging in editorial tasks and raised questions about a breach of impartiality rules. The spokesperson added that the BBC "takes independence and transparency incredibly seriously, and we must ensure we are meeting the highest standards". They said although statisticians' work had sometimes been recognised with their names on the BBC website, "they never made editorial decisions". According to The Telegraph, external, a job advert for the 2027 secondment said a successful candidate would have "the ability to influence decision making, working with credibility and proactively with customers to share knowledge and information". A now-removed blog post written by one civil servant about their placements showed a secondee describing how they had drafted copy for the news website. Under the scheme, it is understood that statisticians explain data in writing that can be incorporated into stories, but they do not write the copy itself. Secondees' contributions can be incorporated into journalism that scrutinises the current government, as well as all political parties. The seconded statisticians also have to adhere to the Civil Service Code of Practice for Statistics. It requires them to present and use data and statistics objectively and not to withhold or misrepresent data due to political or commercial influence. title: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather
description: An expedition to a remote Pacific island hoping to uncover the American aviator's wreckage was on hold for three days.
body: Sirisha Bandla (right), pictured with expedition lead Steve Schultz, said the crew was "really excited" A search for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote island in the Pacific Ocean has resumed after severe weather caused researchers to stop for several days. A team has travelled to Nikumaroro Island, part of Kiribati, hoping to solve the mystery of the famed aviator's disappearance by investigating the so-called Taraia Object, spotted in the atoll's lagoon in aerial imagery. The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation about her fate. Rough seas and strong winds forced the team to remain on their research vessel for three days, until the weather cleared on Sunday. "We are finally getting off the ship and able to land on Nikumaroro," Sirisha Bandla, a technology specialist who is part of the expedition, said in a video update from the deck of the Marin Mainiku. The researchers arrived at the uninhabited atoll last week and began an underwater survey of the area of interest. But the weather - powered by strong El Niño conditions in the Pacific - has so far prevented them from beginning a second of three phases, in which underwater objects will be probed to determine their depth and sediment will be dredged. Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937 "We're working to get everything done today if we can," Bandla said. "The crew's really excited." Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937. From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California. But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel. One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway. Images of the so-called Taraia Object - which Purdue University says is visible in photography dating back to 1938 - show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters, though other explorers remain sceptical. A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro Interest in the expedition prompted New Zealand's Air Force Museum to publish, external previously unseen reconnaissance images of Nikumaroro on Friday. While the Taraia Object is not obviously visible in any of the black-and-white slides, taken in 1938 from a seaplane, they do show the beached wreck of the SS Norwich City, a British merchant vessel that ran aground on the island during a storm in 1929, killing 11. Purdue, which with the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is spearheading the expedition, said the incident demonstrated the risks surrounding the island. To get into the atoll's lagoon, a boat has to navigate through a narrow gap created in the reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited. But the university said wind gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph) present around the island until Sunday meant the transport boat could be knocked into the reef by crashing waves. Images from 1938 released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand this week show Nikumaroro - then Gardner Island - with the SS Norwich City wreck in the bottom right corner However, it said the Norwich City wreck may lend credence to the researchers' theory. Purdue said a 15-year-old in Florida reported hearing Earhart's voice repeating "New York City" over her father's shortwave radio shortly after the aviator vanished. Proponents of the castaway theory argue this may have been a misunderstanding of Earhart giving her location as near the Norwich City. As a result of the three-day hold, the research team has extended the expedition time to complete its fieldwork and has yet to indicate whether they had found any promising evidence of Earhart's plane. ALI director Rick Pettigrew said the team was aware of the global interest in the expedition and would share its results "as soon as we are able". Purdue suggested before the poor weather hit that it could identify the Taraia Object in a matter of days. While researchers have previously found evidence of a human presence on the island around the time of Earhart's disappearance, some skeptics believe the Taraia Object was just a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the lagoon. Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short. In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation. Similarly, an expedition in 2019 to investigate a photograph of what might have been landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything. title: Britain's Kartal misses out on biggest title of her career
description: Britain's Sonay Kartal fades from a strong position in a gripping Wuhan Open final against Grand Slam runner-up Maja Chwalinska.
body: Sonay Kartal will become the British number one when the WTA rankings are released on Monday Britain's Sonay Kartal missed out on what would have been the biggest title of her career as she faded in a gripping Wuhan Open final against French Open runner-up Maja Chwalinska. Kartal, 24, was bidding to lift the trophy in only her third event since returning from a six-month absence caused by a back injury. But an extraordinary week in China seemed to catch up with Kartal as she ran out of steam - physically and mentally - in a 2-6 6-4 6-2 defeat. Kartal was playing in just the 10th match of her impressive comeback and was attempting to become the first Briton to win a WTA 1,000 title since Johanna Konta in 2017. Ranked 170th in the world at the start of the event, Kartal reached Sunday's final by seeing off a host of notable opponents, including current top-10 players and former major champions. However, Poland's Chwalinska, who made a shock run to this year's Roland Garros final, dragged Kartal into a brutal battle and ultimately got the better of it. Kartal dominated the first set and led by a break in the second before Chwalinska turned momentum in her favour. Chwalinska, 25, felt a few nerves as she closed in on her first WTA 1,000 title, but took her third championship point when Kartal hammered a forehand long. Despite losing the final, Kartal has enjoyed a transformational week which even she did not see coming. On Monday, she will climb to 50th in the world rankings - just below her career high - and become the British number one for the first time. She also earned prize money of about £290,000. Addressing her team before receiving the runners-up trophy, Kartal said: "It's not the result we wanted today, but those three people in my box are why I'm here, healthy and back to fitness. "We've had an unbelievable week - not many people expected me to be here and bring the level I did." Throwing herself into the "deep end" - as Kartal described going straight into WTA 1,000 tournaments after her long lay-off - has proved to be a sound decision. The British number five was able to enter the Wuhan Open, one of the tournaments in the tier below the Grand Slams in terms of field strength and prestige, through a protected injury ranking. Those are given to players who have been out for six months or more. Kartal acknowledged even she has been taken by surprise by how well she has played so early in her comeback. Her scalps included former Olympic champion Belinda Bencic, the 2024 Wimbledon runner-up Jasmine Paolini, and world number six Elina Svitolina. She added 2017 French Open champion Jelena Ostapenko to the list in Saturday's semi-finals. Ostapenko often took the racquet out of Kartal's hands with her explosive - and often erratic - brand of first-strike tennis, but Chwalinska was a different proposition. Chwalinska is largely a counter-puncher who looks to draw mistakes from opponents, meaning Kartal quickly found herself in longer rallies than she did against Ostapenko. Chwalinska has joined Karolina Muchova, Jessica Pegula, Aryna Sabalenka (2), Marta Kostyuk, Elina Svitolina, Iga Swiatek, Coco Gauff and Zheng Qinwen in winning WTA 1,000 titles in 2026 The Briton played confidently and consistently from the baseline in the first set, waiting for opportunities to inject pace into shots and land winners. After the pair exchanged breaks inside the opening three games, Kartal took Chwalinska's serve again for a 3-1 lead and underlined her dominance by taking a third set point on her seventh break opportunity of the match. Kartal asked for medical advice when Chwalinska went off court for a short break and her physical level came under severe scrutiny at the start of the second set. Three break points were saved by Kartal in the opening game of set two, but she moved ahead at 2-0 before the Pole hit straight back. Chwalinska grew in confidence and introduced more variety as she asked more questions of Kartal's body and mind. Kartal had to face 13 break points in a gruelling set, losing serve three times as Chwalinska forced a decider. Like Kartal, Chwalinska is a player who relishes a scrap and she carried the momentum going into the third set. The left-hander used the combination of a drop shot followed by a lob to break Kartal's serve for a 3-2 lead and held her nerve from there. It meant she clinched the most prestigious title of a career that has only really taken off this year, and her first at WTA Tour level. Rebels, rockstars, revolutionaries. On court, they were legends. Off court, they challenged the world. Ashe, McEnroe, Borg, King, Navratilova, Evert - the golden age of tennis. title: Man arrested after boy, 16, dies in crash
description: The 19-year-old man is held on suspicion of causing death and serious injury by dangerous driving.
body: The crash involving a Seat Ibiza happened on Shaftmoor Lane in Birmingham on Saturday evening A man has been arrested after a 16-year-old boy was killed in a crash in Birmingham. Police said the teenager was in a white Seat Ibiza which was understood to have hit railings on Shaftmoor Lane at about 20:30 BST on Saturday. A second passenger, a boy in his teens, was taken to hospital with a serious arm injury. A 19-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of causing death and serious injury by dangerous driving and failing to provide a breath specimen, West Midlands Police said. The force stated the 16-year-old boy who lost his life was pronounced dead at the scene, in the Acocks Green area, despite the best efforts of paramedics. It appealed for information, adding specialist officers from the serious collision investigation unit were asking anyone who had dashcam footage from around the time of the crash to get in touch. title: McGill's accuse Swinney of behaving like dictator over bus plans
description: The first minister outlined plans to bring buses under public control during his speech at the SNP conference.
body: Sandy Easdale, Ralph Roberts and James Easdale pictured with one of their buses A major bus firm has accused First Minister John Swinney of behaving like a dictator over his government's plans to bring buses under public control. Sandy Easdale, who owns McGill's alongside his brother James, said Swinney "appears to have transformed into the next Idi Amin or Robert Mugabe". "Both men, incidentally, who bankrupted their countries through catastrophic financial policies," he added. Jenny Gilruth, Swinney's deputy, said her government was "protecting" the public, who had faced a series of route closures in recent years. Speaking at the SNP conference in Aberdeen on Saturday, the first minister said buses would be brought under public control by 2031 through franchising and regulation, with a Bill tabled in Holyrood next year. The changes, it is understood, will allow regional transport partnerships to have more control over routes and fares on the bus network, without the government having to actively own it. This video can not be played Jenny Gilruth and McGill's bus firm disagree over bringing buses under public control Ralph Roberts, chairman of McGill's, told BBC Scotland's Sunday Show that the Easdales had invested in local services. He accused Swinney of trying to confiscate their business - a move he said had "incensed" owners. "One of the problems that we have with this is the complete lack of dialogue," he said. "You can understand why the owners want to refer to African dictators because that's how it feels from their perspective." Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham As it happened: John Swinney speaks at SNP conference Roberts claimed the SNP's plans could cost the taxpayers hundreds of millions of pounds each year. "I've put forward a number of different alternative ways for the authorities or government to take control of bus services if that's what they want to do," he added. "But these always fall on deaf ears. There's a bit of tunnel vision going on." Under the proposals, he claims the firm would be competing for contracts from local authorities, meaning they could go "out of business" if they failed. Roberts warned that McGill's was prepared to pursue legal routes to protect the company - and would go to "every court in the land" if required. Mid Fife and Glenrothes MSP Jenny Gilruth is John Swinney's deputy and finance secretary Despite the attacks, Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth promised to work with bus companies on the plans. She told The Sunday Show: "Fundamentally, we're trying to protect our people, and across the country just now we see a number of routes having been removed." Gilruth said the current private bus model was "a legacy of Thatcher's time when she took away that opportunity for there to be direct intervention from the state" on bus routes. "So we're going back to an approach that better protects people," she said. "We only need to look at the approach that's used, for example, in the city of Edinburgh to see how public ownership on this issue of McGill's benefit the public in terms of the number of routes that are available." The Easdale brothers were "significant donors to the Labour Party", she noted. Gilruth said the Scottish government was already providing significant investment in buses, including free travel for under 22s and over 60s. "Of course we work with bus operators like McGill's and others to hear their views," she added. "We've always done that in terms of how we've rolled out our approach to the under 22s, and of course to the £2 bus cap." At the SNP conference, Swinney announced the extension of the £2 bus fare cap, with Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire to be covered from April. The current cap covers Glasgow and West Scotland as well as the Highlands and Islands, with the government planning to expand it to the whole country by the end of the parliamentary term in 2031. title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
description: At least one person was killed in the strikes, which also hit a data centre used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook.
body: The St Petersburg Oil Terminal was among targets hit in the city overnight At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities. The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five. A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit. Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week. Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing. It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel. Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July. Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday. St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed. He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible. Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning. Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes". As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans. Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year. Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years. Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter. Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said. title: Watch: Pope thanks well-wishers in first event after cancer surgery
description: The Pope's first event since his lung cancer diagnosis and surgery saw him recite the traditional Angelus prayer from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.
body: This video can not be played Pope Leo XIV held his first public engagement since his lung cancer surgery on Sunday, as he recited the Angelus prayer from the window of Vatican's Apostolic Palace. The surgery had taken place just a few days before, after Pope Leo had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. After the prayer, he thanked the people who have prayed for him in recent days and said he appreciated the support. He added he will now gradually return to his commitments as he recovers. title: Gleaning group gives £1m of produce to food banks
description: Gleaning Cornwall warns that more funding is needed as costs rise sharply.
body: Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to reduce food waste on farms A gleaning group has saved £1m worth of fruit and vegetables that would have been left in field and donated them to food banks. Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to collect unwanted produce from harvested fields, delivering it to 160 food banks, community larders and kitchens across the South West. Despite reaching the seven-figure milestone, the group has warned more funding is needed in order to keep up with demand. Reliance on food banks is increasing and since 2015 the number of known settings providing food aid in Cornwall has risen from 20 to 180, according to Cornwall Council. The gleaning group has saved 460 tonnes of produce since the start of 2020 Gleaning Cornwall started in 2020 and said it had repurposed more than 460 tonnes of produce since then. But the charity's founder, Holly Whitelaw, warned it was now threatened by economic constraints. "There is less money around and we need to do more with it," she said. "Our infrastructure urgently needs funding if we are to keep going." The charity said it fed 11,000 people every week with the stipulation that all its produce must be completely free to recipients. However, the organisation said the cost of transport, storage and coordination was rising sharply. More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall It comes at a time when food bank usage is higher than ever with statistics from Cornwall's Trussell Trust showing its food banks distributed more than 35,500 emergency food parcels between April 2024 and March 2025. A study by Cornwall Council found that 30% of children in the county are living in food poverty. Whitelaw encouraged people to play their part by reducing the amount of food they wasted at home. She said: "If we waste food, we waste the substantial energy that went into producing it. "Utilising what we already have saves money and helps the environment." title: Free clear-up has big engagement on social media
description: One man's battle against weeds and overgrown pathways makes a big difference to the town
body: Jeremy Vernon said: "I'm not getting paid for it and all the materials and fuel is coming out of my own pocket" A resident of Launceston, Cornwall, goes above and beyond battling weeds and overgrown pathways free of charge to keep fit and help the community. Jeremy Vernon, 51, said despite having his kidney removed due to cancer he could not resist clearing neglected paths in his free time and it had made him a hit on social media. In one area he cut back the brambles and scraped off all the weeds before spending several hours pressure washing the steps. He said he did it due to "the satisfaction after walking down the path after it has been cleaned and the reaction you get from members of the public and people on social media that seem to appreciate what's being done". Jeremy Vernon scraped away the weeds along Roydon Road in Launceston Vernon is a self-employed steel erector who has worked on rollercoasters and movie sets, such as Death on the Nile and Ready Player One. He had been living in Wiltshire until he discovered he had kidney cancer, had a kidney removed and moved back to Cornwall for what he called a "better, nicer pace of life". "But work is still up London way, but when I get back down here I go for a walk see a mess get my shovel and wheelbarrow and start clearing places up. "It keeps you fit and I think it is better than going to the gym. "I rang Launceston Town Council, they explained the pathways are not theirs and gave me a number for Cornwall Council. "I have rang them two or three times explaining that I have the public liability insurance but I don't have permission to be where I am so it kind of invalidates my insurance." In a statement Cornwall Council said: "We support residents volunteering and our contractor Cormac oversees a range of community-led projects on council land, from working on woodland to re-wilding parks to weeding open spaces. "Last year 60,000 hours of volunteering were undertaken on council land. "To ensure volunteers can carry out their work safely on council land and indemnity insurance is provided we request that volunteers register with Cormac at volunteers@cormacltd.co.uk so we can give ongoing advice and support." Jeremy Vernon demonstrates how close the lorries are to the pavement, which is impassable due to overgrown vegetation More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall Resident Elz Ravenscroft asked Vernon if he would cut back the overgrown bushes on the pavement which her daughter used to walk to and from school. "Jeremy has worked so hard for all of town and gone above and beyond for us all out of his own free time," she said. "We're all so massively grateful for all his hard work and dedication to the town and town's people. "From making the zigzag a safe space to walk through, to tidying up graffitied benches down the Ridgegrove to cut through a path." She said: "The man honestly deserves so much recognition by the town council and beyond for all he's done." Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops
description: Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living.
body: This video can not be played Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence", as shopfronts were smashed and stores looted. For shop owners, this morning marks the start of clean-up efforts, with some reporting damages and stolen goods amount to €100,000 (£85,000). The BBC's James Waterhouse reports from the streets of Paris outside damaged buildings. Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops. title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, says health secretary
description: A total of 15 NHS staff are sacked for accessing records of the Nottingham attacks victims.
body: Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were killed in the Nottingham attacks NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said. Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who have breached NHS data and privacy standards. Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately. Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason". Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff. "Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS. Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020. NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation. At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation". In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff" and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed. NUH added a new system, currently under testing, is being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches. Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said he it was "time to get a handle on these failures" Reacting to the dismissals on Saturday, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said the families of the victims of the attacks would like to meet with Cooper. He also called for action to be taken over the data breaches. Kumar added: "I'd like to ask Yvette Cooper the question, when is this going to stop and what is she doing exactly to make this stop and decrease the suffering of people who are victims of crime and of major incidents, when is this going to stop? "I am appalled. It's time to get a handle on these failures. "Clearly, the way that the highest confidential data, which is medical data, is being looked at by voyeuristic people in the NHS is disgraceful." William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on 10 October On Friday, Yorkshire Ambulance Service said staff members may have accessed the records of William Chapman, 24, who was mauled to death by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on 10 October. It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches". On Thursday, an inquest into Chapman's death heard that he died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, near Doncaster. In a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said there had to be a "proper respect for patients" in the NHS Cooper said: "Every member of NHS staff knows that, and every member of NHS staff needs to abide by it, and the overwhelming majority of NHS staff not only do that, they also hugely value those privacy and dignity standards. "It is a disgrace that we've had cases where people don't, and we do expect action to be taken, including people being sacked, and I've spoken to the NHS England chief executive about this. "We also expect where there are these breaches taking place, we expect people to be swiftly suspended while investigations take place. "There's got to be proper respect for patients, and I think that is a core value in the NHS." title: Pony herd gathering raises money for air ambulance
description: Kristina Auckland said the herd was made up of around 100 ponies.
body: The ponies will be gathered towards Lancombe Crossing before being brought to Brendon Barton Farm A herd of ponies on Exmoor is being gathered as part of an annual inspection. Tippbarlake Exmoor Pony Herd has about 100 ponies, which are being gathered in Brendon Barton on Sunday. Kristina Auckland, who looks after the herd with her family, said gathering ponies on Exmoor was a tradition that had been going on for generations. She said members of the public were able to watch at Scobhill Gate from 10:00 for free but would be asked to donate to the Devon Air Ambulance. More news stories for Devon Listen to the latest news for Devon Auckland said the ponies lived freely on Brendan Common and "we try and manage them from afar all year round". "Once a year we will gather them in to have a bit of a closer inspection and make sure that they're all healthy and their welfare needs are met," she added. The numbers of people watching the gathering had "steadily increased" over the last few years, which Auckland attributed to the rise of social media. She added there were also many local families who came to watch yearly. Auckland said they had chosen to collect donations for Devon Air Ambulance this year because it was "absolutely crucial" for people in rural communities. "We're completely reliant on the air ambulance being able to help us, whether you're a farmer, a local resident, or someone visiting," she said. She added: "Whatever anyone's able to donate, as as little or as much as possible is amazing." Auckland said the ponies were a "really important part of Exmoor's heritage" Auckland said she wanted to "raise awareness of the breed and the role the ponies play in managing the common itself and what they can contribute to conservation projects around the country," she said. "They are born to eat ... and they're really good at eating certain types of grasses and sort of managing habitats." She added: "They're a really important part of Exmoor's heritage and we're so lucky to have many herds still living freely on the moor. "We want people to understand their value and the role they play, and we want them to be here for generations to come." Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
description: The Green Party leader said, while he wanted to amend it, the motion would stand until 2028.
body: Zack Polanski was interviewed by Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday morning Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism to be racist. The party leader told the Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday programme that, while he would like to amend it, the motion would be party policy until 2028 and denied it was controversial. The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population". It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement. The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership. He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813, a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members. Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it. "At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves." He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years". Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members." Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without amendments. Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote. title: Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting
description: Around 1,800 people were arrested after nationwide protests saw outbreaks of violence and vandalism.
body: A vandalised shopfront in Paris in the aftermath of protests France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris. Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful. They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings. The destroyed interior of a restaurant in the capital on Sunday morning Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas. In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups. Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons. Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the damage, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace. Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris. Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich." The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la République which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor. The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process. The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations. CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves. This video can not be played Watch: How day of protests unfolded on Saturday as disorder broke out across France Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building". Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze. Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost." "A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department. Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media. "Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said. A woman jogs past burnt out vehicles in Paris, near the Place de la République France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also in Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse, and the western city of Angers. Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.
