title: After Dubois' dominant win, what's next for heavyweight boxing?
description: After world champion Daniel Dubois' emphatic win over Fabio Wardley, what's next for the heavyweight division?
body: This video can not be played 'Devastating & dramatic' - Dubois stops Wardley to retain title Daniel Dubois' demolition of Fabio Wardley has strengthened his position among the heavyweight elite. The 29-year-old needed only two rounds to stop his British rival at London's O2 Arena, retaining his title with a performance far more emphatic than their thrilling first encounter in May. Dubois can now turn his attention towards unification and some of boxing's biggest names. Meanwhile, Oleksandr Usyk is approaching retirement, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to meet and a new group of world champions are looking to establish themselves. So what is next for the heavyweight division? Daniel Dubois has picked up 13 of his 24 victories inside two rounds IBF champion Filip Hrgovic made his intentions clear, entering the ring after Dubois' victory, with both keen on a rematch. Dubois stopped the Croatian in June 2024, but Hrgovic has since rebuilt his reputation, claiming the vacant IBF title with victory over British prospect Moses Itauma in August. But Hrgovic, 34, has Cuba's Frank Sanchez waiting as a mandatory challenger. Promoter Frank Warren is working towards staging Hrgovic's first defence in Croatia early next year, potentially delaying a reunion with Dubois. The biggest financial prize for Dubois could be a meeting with the winner of Fury and Joshua's December showdown. "All those names are there to do a unification fight next year and that's what we'll be working on," Warren said. Wardley, meanwhile, has shown he can compete at world level, but the manner of Saturday's defeat exposed a gulf in technical ability. A return against a lower-ranked opponent could help restore confidence, but questions remain over whether Wardley can make the adjustments needed to challenge the division's elite again. Dubois v Wardley II - The Debrief After years of negotiations and false starts, Fury and Joshua are finally scheduled to meet at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on a card that begins on 11 December, with the main event expected in the early hours of 12 December. The Netflix-streamed contest has demonstrated its extraordinary commercial appeal, with about 80,000 tickets selling out within an hour. Warren says the vacant WBA 'super' title will be at stake, potentially opening the door to unification fights in 2027. However, WBA 'regular' champion Murat Gassiev has questioned the decision and called for the winner to face him. That appears unlikely to be a priority for either Briton, with both reportedly set to earn close to $100m (£75m) in December. A rematch would offer another enormous payday, particularly if the first encounter is close or controversial, but a one-sided defeat could push the loser towards retirement. This video can not be played AJ reassures fans that Fury fight will happen... Germany's Agit Kabayel has built one of the strongest records in the division. The unbeaten 34-year-old has stopped Arslanbek Makhmudov, Sanchez and Zhilei Zhang, but remains a relatively unfamiliar name to casual boxing fans. Kabayel, elevated to WBC champion when Usyk vacated, makes his first defence against Albania's Nelson Hysa on 28 November. A unification fight against Dubois in 2027 could provide the opportunity to become a much bigger name in the sport. Oleksandr Usyk beat boxing novice Rico Verhoeven when the referee stopped the fight with one second left in the 11th round Usyk's decision to vacate the WBA, WBC and IBF titles in June means the unbeaten Ukrainian can call the shots over the final chapter of his career. The pound-for-pound star, who defeated former kickboxing world champion Rico Verhoeven in May, has indicated he wants one final contest before retirement. Dutchman Verhoeven exceeded expectations before suffering a controversial 11th-round stoppage defeat, and wants a rematch. Verhoeven says he has accepted an offer to face Deontay Wilder on the Fury-Joshua undercard, although the American has yet to agree and has also been linked with cruiserweight Jai Opetaia. Wilder previously emerged as a contender for Usyk's farewell, but negotiations appear to have stalled. A third meeting between Usyk and Fury has also been mooted. But having already beaten Fury, Joshua and Dubois twice apiece, how much more does Usyk have to prove? Itauma's charge towards a world title was halted when he suffered his first professional defeat against Hrgovic. Itauma, 21, is expected to return in January, with Warren promising credible opposition rather than a straightforward confidence-building contest. The priority will be developing the stamina, pacing and tactical patience required over 12 rounds before pursuing another world title opportunity. A rematch with Hrgovic remains a longer-term possibility, but there is little need to rush with time firmly on Itauma's side. Moses Itauma (left) had stopped 12 of his previous 14 opponents before losing to Filip Hrgovic American Jarrell Miller remains highly ranked, while compatriots Jared Anderson and Richard Torrez Jr, an Olympic silver medallist, are rebuilding. New Zealand's former world champion Joseph Parker is seeking a return after his provisional doping suspension was lifted in August. Australia's Teremoana Teremoana has stopped all 12 professional opponents within two rounds, while Uzbekistan's two-time Olympic champion Bakhodir Jalolov extended his unbeaten record by beating Solomon Dacres on Saturday. In Britain, Derek Chisora, 42, is considering another comeback and says he expects to face WBA 'regular' champion Gassiev in December. British champion Richard Riakporhe is pursuing world honours after moving up from cruiserweight, while former cruiserweight world champion Lawrence Okolie is targeting a return after reaching an agreement with the WBC over an adverse drugs test finding. David Adel

title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
description: The flying instructor has been described as "a gentleman and an experienced aviator" by former students.
body: Ian Haggis died when the light aircraft crashed near Loch Lomond An 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis. He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released. The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling. Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash at about 16:45 on Friday. Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene. Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries. Tributes posted on social media by former students describe the flying instructor as "a gentleman and an experienced aviator", and a "good friend". The plane - a Piper Tomahawk II aircraft - is registered to Leading Edge Flight Training in Renfrew, according to the Civil Aviation Authority's aircraft register., external Previous social media posts on Leading Edge's Facebook page report the instructor's nickname as the 'Flying Haggis', and show that he had been working with the flying school. BBC Scotland has approached Leading Edge Flight Training for comment. Police cordoned off the scene of the crash in marshland near Drymen Gavin Birch-Williams, managing director of Glasgow Airport, said: "We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow Airport. "This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow Airport are with the friends and families affected." The plane had earlier taken off from Cumbernauld Airport at 11:46, before flying 15 minutes to Glasgow Airport. It stayed there until about 13:00, before doing a two-hour flight north east to Newport-on-Tay then turning round and heading back to Glasgow. It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and started its final flight. title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children will be a priority, says health secretary
description: Yvette Cooper also announces £140m investment in England's urgent care system, ahead of winter.
body: This video can not be played No patient should be treated in a corridor, Yvette Cooper says The NHS must take urgent action to stop children receiving treatment in hospital corridors, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has told the BBC. Cooper told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she has asked NHS England to draw up urgent plans to eliminate what is known as "corridor care" for children as a priority, and to introduce new standards for how children should be treated at A&E. It comes after more than a dozen health groups urged the health secretary to take action to end corridor care. The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August. Cooper said the way this data is collected will be changed to have the number of children included in the figures. "I'm clear that child health needs to be a much greater priority for the NHS," says Cooper. The government has an aim of ending corridor care more broadly by the end of this parliament, she added. Kuenssberg highlighted the case of Finlay Roberts, a two-year-old boy who died in 2024 after spending the final hours of his life in a crowded A&E corridor. Finlay's father David Roberts told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family briefly moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor. "He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said. Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to Finlay in the corridor because there was no other option. After hearing their story, Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS. "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor," she said. The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened said they extended their condolences to Finlay's family. They said they continue to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors. They said: "Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions." On Friday, 16 health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) - sent a letter to Cooper, urging her to take action on ending corridor care. It said the practice is fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it. Before speaking to Kuenssberg, Cooper had warned the NHS was facing a more challenging winter than normal, after multiple heatwaves led to its busiest summer on record in England. She announced £140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus. The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments. Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from, while the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) England said the funding was "just another sticking plaster". In a statement, Cooper said: "Winter will be more challenging for our NHS this year, after such a heavy summer. "That's why we have been preparing early and investing in extra urgent care capacity to help get patients the care they need." It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period. Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover. NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals. Swords said earlier this month there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year. "And unfortunately, people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she added. RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome in the short term but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point". "The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said. The waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row, according to the latest data. An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients. These were the highest numbers since October 2025, and have raised questions as to whether the NHS will meet the government's target to treat 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029. title: Martinez breaks jaw in Chelsea win at Everton
description: Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez says he will be back "in a few weeks" after breaking his jaw in a collision with Jarrad Branthwaite.
body: Emiliano Martinez joined Chelsea this summer after six seasons at Aston Villa Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez says he will be back "in a few weeks" after breaking his jaw in the 2-0 Premier League win at Everton on Saturday. The 34-year-old Argentina international and Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite clashed heads in the second half at Hill Dickinson Stadium. Martinez needed treatment for eight minutes before leaving the pitch on a stretcher. He was taken to hospital, where Chelsea said he had "successful" surgery. Martinez posted a photo of himself wearing a hospital gown on social media, external on ‌Sunday. "Thanks to everyone for the messages. The operation ‌went well," he wrote. "The most important thing is that we won, and kept a clean sheet. In a few weeks we'll be back." Mike Penders, who replaced Martinez to make his Premier League debut, looks set to play in Chelsea's next three matches at least. They face Tottenham and Manchester United in the Premier League, with a Carabao Cup tie at Liverpool in between. Penders, 21, signed from Belgium club Genk for £17m in 2024. Alonso said: "Mike has personality. He's brave and we have full trust ‌with him. He did well when he came on. "He played in the cup games and whenever he's ⁠needed. Like the other players, whenever they are needed they can perform. "It's all about the squad - ‌that all the ​players feel important and can have ‌their moment whenever they are needed, ​and that's very positive." title: Police officer in hospital after being shot in Nottingham
description: A firearm has been recovered by officers after a man and a woman fled the scene, detectives say.
body: The officer was shot after approaching two people in Angel Row, Nottingham A police officer is being treated in hospital after being shot in Nottingham city centre. Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday. The officer is now being treated for a wound to his foot, the force added. Detectives said a firearm was recovered and that two suspects, a man and a woman, fled the scene. Angel Row is currently closed and a large police scene remains in place. Forensic officers have attended the scene in Nottingham city centre Assistant Chief Constable Claire Rukas said: "This is a shocking incident and a sobering reminder of the potential dangers faced by officers as they work to protect and serve the public. "As we investigate what happened and work to apprehend the individuals involved, my thoughts today are with the injured officer, his family and colleagues. "I also ask that anyone with additional information shares this with us without delay. Even the smallest bit of information could make all the difference to this investigation." Detectives have asked anyone with information to come forward Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting. "My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family, and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire Police," she added. ​"Nottingham City Council is working tirelessly alongside the police to support the investigation and ensure those responsible are swiftly caught and brought to justice. ​"While incidents of this nature are extremely rare, our commitment to keeping Nottingham safe is absolute. "Thanks to the daily bravery of our police and community protection officers, Nottingham remains a safe city, and residents can be assured that every available resource is being deployed." A large police scene has been put in place in Angel Row Police cars are parked along the road, which is lined by fast food stores and shops, and orange traffic cones have been laid out alongside items left on the road. The cordon has also been extended to St James's Street, where an officer is standing guard. In a post on social media East Midlands Ambulance Service sent its best wishes to the injured officer. "Sending our heartfelt thoughts and support to the injured officer, his family, and all our colleagues at Nottinghamshire Police today," the post said. "We're wishing him a full and speedy recovery." title: Finucane will 'come back fighting' after missing gold
description: Emma Finucane says she will "come back fighting" for gold medals after narrowly missing out on the top step in the Keirin.
body: This video can not be played 'It's so close' - Finucane has to settle for keirin bronze Emma Finucane said she will "come back fighting" for gold medals after narrowly missing out on the top step of the podium for the third time at the Track Cycling World Championships, external in Shanghai. Finucane, 23, was forced to settle for bronze in Sunday's keirin after being pipped to the finish line by neutral athlete Alina Lysenko and Lea Friedrich of Germany after leading into the home straight. She finished just 14 thousandths of a second off top spot, with her bronze adding to silver medals won in the team sprint and individual sprint - both won by Chinese cyclists. Finucane was part of Great Britain's team sprint gold medal-winning trio at the Paris Olympics in 2024 and Finucane says retaining that title in Los Angleles is the big aim. She told BBC Sport: "To medal in all three races at the world champs, I'd never done that before. "The confidence I have gained this week and the way I've been riding my bike, I can take that into the years to come. "I'm actually really proud. I am frustrated not to be on the top step but I'll come back fighting. You can beat yourself up about races but I am learning all the time. "Ultimately we are learning for the Olympics, that's a huge goal. I put myself in winning positions in every race and that's something I am proud of." Finucane, who took bronze in both the individual sprint and keirin in Paris, won Britain's first Olympic gold in the women's team sprint alongside Katy Marchant and Sophie Capewell. In Shanghai, Rhianna Parris-Smith replaced the newly-retired Marchant in the team which was beaten by Chinese trio Jiang Yulu, Tong Mengqi and Yuan Liying. Finucane says the strength in depth inside the British team will drive them to success at the LA Games in 2028. She said: "We won the team sprint in Paris which is one of the best moments of my life and there are 10 girls back at home fighting to be in the team. That's how we progress, and we will build on the momentum of this silver medal. "Internal competition is how we win bike races. World records keep falling, we are pushing each other and it's really exciting." Great Britain topped the medal table overall at the championships with 12 medals, including a hat-trick of gold medals for Anna Morris. After Dubois' dominant win, what's next for heavyweight boxing? title: Several dead or injured in major fire at Canada military base
description: Officials have not given a cause or death toll, citing the "very active and delicate" situation at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.
body: Ambulances lined up outside Wainwright Health Centre after the deadly blast at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright Several people have been killed or injured as a result of a large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta, the nation's defence minister has said. David McGuinty did not confirm the cause or the number of casualties, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate". The Canadian military and local authorities were managing the fire, he said. Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out, is one of the country's busiest military training bases. Canadian TV network Global News reported that at least seven were killed and dozens more injured when a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise, citing unnamed military sources. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding that his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected". The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) said Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton had declared a code orange, a disaster response protocol for responding to a high-casualty incident. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor there, told the broadcaster that the number of patients would otherwise "overwhelm" Edmonton's healthcare facilities. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster." After the fire erupted on Saturday, it "spread rapidly due to high winds" and tore through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said. The region experienced gusts of up to 100km/h (62mph), though local officials indicated fire crews had contained the blaze. The defence minister told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory". It is unclear when the fire broke out, but the district first posted about the incident at about 17:30 local time (23:30 GMT). Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way. The mayor of the nearby town of Wainwright, Bruce Pugh, said it was a "heavy day" for his community. "We have neighbours who are either serving or former members of the Canadian Armed Forces. We're integrated, our kids play in the same hockey teams, attend the same schools," he told CBC. While details on the impact of the fire remain unclear, Pugh said he believed this would come to be the area's largest-ever mass casualty event. Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is a busy military training base used for live-fire exercises Alberta's Premier Danielle Smith said the "significant and tragic fire" was "affecting many of [the province's] brave military personnel". Neighbouring provinces have mobilised in support. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said he had deployed resources to Alberta and was "ready to provide more if required", while British Columbia Premier David Eby said his government had offered "all possible assistance". Wainwright is the main base used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, according to CBC, with about 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers on-site on a typical day. title: House that looks like boulders to be built on moor
description: Town council had objected to the plans but the folklore-inspired house will now be built.
body: The house is designed to look like rocks on the edge of Ilkley's famous moor Plans for a house designed to look like rocks on a famous Yorkshire moor have been approved. The contemporary structure, which has large irregular-shaped windows and a natural outdoor pool, looks similar to the landmark Cow and Calf Rocks in Ilkley, West Yorkshire. The house will be built on green belt land which is the garden of a home off Heber's Ghyll Drive, and will be eco-friendly, to an ultra-low energy standard called Passivhaus. Harrogate-based architects Shaw & Jagger said the scheme was eventually passed by HM Planning Inspectorate through the country house clause, which allows development on green belt for buildings of "exceptional quality". The architect Matt Masserella-Gill was commissioned to design the home by the landowner David Rasche. He said the design was "arguably the most complex country house application ever made in this country". The house has been named Fomorian - meaning a supernatural race of giants in Irish mythology - taking inspiration from the mythical giant Rombald who is told to have lived on Ilkley Moor. Masserella-Gill said: "The design approach was to propose a scheme that is intrinsically linked to the spirit of its place. Fomorian is of its place, part of the moors, its geology and its spirit. "We took cues from local folklore, the surrounding rocks; ancient carvings, standing stones and escarpments that are synonymous with the landscape." Designs for the house - named Fomorian - include an outdoor pool and courtyard The application was originally submitted to Bradford Council planners, but was not passed on the grounds of non-determination - meaning a decision was not made within the required timeframe. The plans had received an objection from Ilkley Town Council, who recommended it be refused as it would be a "visual anomaly to the moorland". The land "forms part of the South Pennine Moors Site of Special Scientific Interest, the South Pennine Moors Special Protection Area and Special Area of Conservation, and more recently, which has been designated as a new National Nature Reserve," it said. The council also noted the proposed development was close to the Swastika Stone, a prehistoric rock carving which is one of hundreds of Scheduled Ancient Monuments on Ilkley Moor. Bradford Council's decision was appealed however, and was passed by the Planning Inspectorate in August. The Cow and Calf Rocks are a local landmark in the West Yorkshire town Masserella-Gill added: "The site is subject to restrictive planning policies which made the principle of development very challenging. The country house clause requires an isolated design of "exceptional quality" in that it "is truly outstanding", would "significantly enhance its immediate setting and be sensitive to the defining characteristics of the local area". He said the planning inspector noted that Fomorian was "an innovative design" that "would help raise the standards of design in the rural area more generally". The design was passed on appeal by the Planning Inspectorate in August Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. title: Turning the tides: Could hidden sea power energise our coastal towns?
description: Engineer David Mummery has developed a tidal energy generator that he says can change lives for people living in coastal communities.
body: Engineer David Mummery says tidal power could change lives in coastal communities In a secret location in the Highlands of Scotland, there's a fast-flowing river that's the key to understanding the massive power of water. It's where engineer David Mummery found himself more than a decade ago. With a length of cord tied tightly across the river, he swam out, gripped firmly, and let the unstoppable current rush over as he sunk his head below the surface. "As an engineer we do the maths and stuff," he says, "but sometimes you can get a lot more from actually touching the water and feeling it". As he lay down in the powerful rapids, he visualised a new type of small-scale tidal energy generator. It's an innovation he says could change lives for people in coastal communities. "I'd be under the river, feeling the turbulence of the water rushing over me. "Trying to envisage how this turbine needed to interact with that environment - to understand the way the water was working." The Swimmer Turbine prototype at Strangford Narrows in Northern Ireland Mummery's idea became the Swimmer Turbine - a 50kw tidal generator named after his experience in the river. Anchored to the sea floor, the fiberglass and steel device lies invisible below the water's surface. It can generate enough electricity to power about 30 homes. He began tests in the river in early 2010s. On a patent lawyer's advice he found a secret location, far from curious Highland tourists and their cameras. "You're trying to be quite discreet because you're working with new technology," he says. It was in the first years of his company, Flex Marine Power, long before Britain was gripped by the soaring costs of an energy crisis. Fishermen on Islay learn how to assemble the Swimmer Turbine The size of the Swimmer Turbine is what sets it apart from large tidal projects dotted around Scottish waters. Scotland is a world leader in the sector at sites including: Nova Innovation - The world's first tidal stream array, deployed in 2016 in Bluemull Sound in Shetland MeyGen - The world's largest tidal array, with four large 1.5MW turbines on the seabed of the Pentland Firth Orbital O2 - The world's most powerful floating turbine, generating 2MW, anchored at Fall of Warness in the Orkney Islands Mummery's turbine is ultra compact and low cost compared to these giant machines. Fishermen and local workers can build and install it themselves from their own village harbour. "Can you imagine like an Ikea furniture kit? You get a shipping container and you'll open it up and it will be about 20 components. "You'll bolt them all together and then you've got your turbine ready. "There'll be a launch plan, you follow these instructions, then you'll be in the water." Mummery's work did not always focus on small-scale power. Originally from Guildford, he studied mechanical engineering at Surrey University. Before founding Flex Marine Power, he was a sought-after consultant in the UK energy sector. For a time he specialised in nuclear work and decommissioning, designing robots for pulling material out of contaminated tanks. He moved north after falling in love with a girl studying at Glasgow University. Jo became his wife and they now live in the city suburbs with three young children. Conveniently, Mummery's relocation came at a time when Scotland was establishing its reputation as a centre for marine power expertise. The 180m-long Pelamis wave power project, nicknamed the sea snake In 2010 he took a secondment at Scottish Power Renewables on the ground-breaking Pelamis project in Orkney. The 180m-long (591ft) Pelamis P2 - nicknamed the sea snake - was the first deep-water, floating wave energy machine to generate power for the national grid. Ultimately, Pelamis went into administration in 2014, but the ill-fated device remains celebrated as a milestone in marine power innovation. "The industry is littered with these examples of fantastic technologies and teams that do brave things that take decades," Mummery says. "But at some point the market doesn't step up and they falter. Some really good ones have lasted the course, but others have not and it's sad." David Mummery at home in Glasgow, where he established Flex Marine Power Mummery says the UK has "phenomenal waters for tidal power" and he loved being a part of major projects - but couldn't shake a discomfort. His work felt incongruous to the many small coastal communities he found himself in. "I'd be going out on boats around Scotland doing sonar surveys with all these really expensive pieces of kit. "But the equipment was all really big, utility-scale stuff that would weigh hundreds of tonnes, shipped by people from the mainland. "All the people I was meeting in harbours or in the pub were fishermen. And they were knowledgeable and they were interested. "I thought 'we've got to do this in a way that they can take the lead'." That, he says, is what motivated his Swimmer Turbine idea. The Swimmer Turbine is assembled on land and can be launched from a slipway In 2011 he left big projects behind to found Flex Marine Power and focus on his turbine concept. He spent hours at his desk sketching, working out how to make the technology smaller and lighter. He hired a student employee and found a sleek, glass office space outside Glasgow - which he quickly discovered wasn't entirely suited to an engineer and his tools. "It was a lovely place, but I wasn't allowed to take a hammer drill into the office. "We were trying to make prototype turbines under the desk so the landlord wouldn't see them when he came in." Learning the ropes, the local team in training off the coast of Islay Mummery turned to Clydeside's shipbuilding past in search of a more suitable workspace. title: 'I took a chance on the whisky industry and I haven't looked back'
description: Zoey Darnbrough had no idea there was a distillery near her home - now she has a top tourism role there.
body: Zoey Darnbrough took a job at Annandale Distillery after finishing her studies Zoey Darnbrough is the first to admit that just a few years ago she did not even know there was a whisky distillery near her hometown in southern Scotland. But it hasn't stopped her rising rapidly from tour guide, to group tourism and events co-ordinator at the site near Annan. She went away to study heritage and tourism in Stirling after school, but unlike many of her peers, she returned to Dumfries and Galloway for work. Now she hopes to play her part in changing people's opinions of the world of whisky "one woman at a time". Annandale distillery shut in 1919 before reopening 90 years later The 26-year-old, who attended St Joseph's College in Dumfries, was recently nominated for "rising star" recognition at the South of Scotland Thistle Awards. Zoey said her journey had not been straightforward as she did not get the exam results she had hoped for at school, so she spent time working in the kitchens at Dumfries Infirmary. But when a job came up at Annandale Distillery, she jumped at the chance. She said: "My first thought was - there's a distillery in Annan? And my second thought was - whisky? "I thought I'd give it a chance and see what it was like because there's a lot of heritage when it comes to whisky. "And I've now been here three-and-a-half years and I've not looked back." Revived distillery toasts first 10-year-old malt Whisky wait is over after 99 years What does she think the area has to offer that others her age might ignore? One thing she highlighted was the relative costs of property compared with city prices. Zoey also believes the area has a lot to shout about and is happy to have returned after university. "The south of Scotland has so much heritage and it is a passion of mine," she said. "So I would naturally like to be somewhere where there's a lot of heritage and where I can kind of grow as an individual." Zoey is passionate about what the south of Scotland has to offer But she agrees that a lot more could be done to stop young people from leaving. "I would like to think we could go back to the local schools across the region and try and explain that there are other careers out there including in heritage and tourism," she said. Zoey would also like to see the area market itself better. "We've got so much to offer in terms of castles, in terms of scenery, in terms of attractions, accommodation, it's so vast," she said. "I always like to say that we've got everything that the Highlands have, but just in a much quieter area. "But we're going to use that quietness to our strength." What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland? She has certainly achieved that in her own career in the whisky industry - despite some people assuming she might lack the knowledge of older, male counterparts. "It has been tricky, I'm not going to lie," she said. "But I always think that if you prepare yourself well, those types of questions cannot faze you. "I've been so fortunate that all my experiences have been mostly pleasant and so I have not really felt it, but I do understand the struggles that other people face. "We just need to start changing people's opinions one woman at a time." Zoey is happy to do that from Dumfries and Galloway for the foreseeable future. "I'm only beginning to stick my teeth into the south of Scotland," she said. "So to leave, it would have to be a fairly big jump." title: New Zealand avoid World Cup shock against Fiji
description: New Zealand women are given a World Cup "wake-up call" after they are forced to come from behind to beat debutants Fiji in their opening game.
body: New Zealand are the joint most successful team in Women's World Cups, with three titles New Zealand women were given a World Cup "wake-up call" after they were forced to come from behind to beat debutants Fiji in their opening game. The Ferns are one of the most successful teams in women's rugby league history – they have reached the final of all six World Cups, winning the first three before finishing runners up to Australia in the previous three years. They are generally considered second favourites this time around and were expected to win easily against the Fijians in Newcastle on Sunday. Instead, New Zealand were made to battle to an 18-12 win, having trailed 12-4 in the first half. They were 12-10 down at the break – the first time they have ever been behind at half-time in a World Cup match. "I've not really got any nails left. Or teeth," New Zealand coach Ricky Henry told his post-match news conference. McDermott seeks fix as England fight to save their World Cup England crush Women's World Cup debutants Wales Brown scores stunner as England thrash World Cup debutants Wales "The good thing is we found a way, but the way we played is not what we should. "We went away from what we were meant to do, so we are a little disappointed there. Rustiness is not an excuse. "I reckon it's a wake-up call, and the girls will think so too. We fought our way back, so we will take that away with things to work on." New Zealand looked to be on course for a comfortable day when Stacey Waaka scored after two minutes, but Fiji grew into the match before scoring after 21 minutes. Skipper Sereana Naitokatoka made a clever run from dummy half to find Losana Lutu who scored Fiji's first women's World Cup try And when Sienna Laing extended the lead five minutes later, suddenly the upset looked on. Waaka scored her second try to close the gap before the break, but after the interval Fiji's staunch defence still refused to give way. But the pressure eventually told as New Zealand levelled then took the lead from Zehara Temara penalty kicks. The win was not secured until the final minutes when Raecene McGregor's cross-field kick found Leianne Tufuga to score. "We didn't put any expectations on ourselves, but they played like they had nothing to lose," New Zealand player Georgia Hale said. "They tested our waters for sure. "Everything was in our control, then we lost it. It was uncharacteristically ill-disciplined, untidy play. "What we wanted to do today was basic. We wanted to set the tone for the tournament by being physical and by going forwards, but we went far away from that which is not us. "We then had to work extremely hard to make up for it. It was definitely luck in the end." New Zealand face France at home in Christchurch next in Group B, while Fiji play Papua New Guinea. Solomone Saukuru scored two tries for Fiji in their win against Cook Islands In the men's World Cup, Fiji made a strong start to their competition with a 40-12 win over Cook Islands in Newcastle. The two sides are in Group A, alongside co-hosts Australia and New Zealand, so face a tough ask to finish in the top two and reach the semi-finals. Fiji have endured a turbulent build-up, with Mick Potter replacing Wise Kativerata as head coach, a power struggle within the national governing body, and captain Tui Kamikamica having to retire after suffering a stroke in March. But they gave themselves a boost with a comfortable win - running in seven tries and scoring 34 unanswered points until two late consolation scores for Cook Islands. Fiji will face reigning champions Australia next, aiming to go one better than their women's team and cause a seismic upset. "Preparation will be standard," Potter said of getting ready to face Australia. "It is a two-horse race [for the championships] as far as I am concerned, so it is a chance to upset them." title: Boy, 14, stabbed in shopping centre attack
description: Greater Manchester Police say the boy's injuries were not thought to be life threatening or life changing.
body: The Arndale was closed for several hours after the stabbing A 14-year-old boy has been stabbed in a car park at Manchester's Arndale Centre shopping mall. Greater Manchester Police said the boy was injured on the 9th floor of Manchester's Arndale Centre just after 15:00 BST on Saturday. The force said his injuries were not believed to be life threatening or life changing. The Arndale was closed for several hours after the stabbing. Det Insp Sam Jones said: "This is believed to be an isolated incident with no risk to the wider public." The BBC understands a row with other males had taken place beforehand. No arrests have been made in connection with the stabbing so far and inquiries were continuing. title: 'Learning to read in my 80s has changed my life'
description: Alan, from Southampton, learned to read through the charity Read Easy.
body: Alan, 86, at a certificate ceremony on 6 October An 86-year-old man said learning to read has enabled him to read his and his wife's anniversary cards for the first time in 65 years. Alan Hannay, from Dibden Purlieu, learned to read through the charity Read Easy, which helps adults across the country who struggle with the skill many of us take for granted. Hannay told BBC Radio Solent: "It's changed my whole life, my confidence, changed my family life and everything around me. "It's one of the best experiences I've ever had in my life." Hannay said he now reads every morning for about an hour and a half and goes to the class twice a week. "I enjoy it so much now," he said. The charity said Hannay is an "inspiring example of determination and courage". It said he asked his local library in Hythe, Southampton, about learning to read, which led him to the charity and his reading coach, Angie. During his working life as a professional chauffeur, he relied on his memory to drive his clients around London, and at the age of 70 he attended evening classes to improve his reading. However, he found the group situation difficult. Alan said Read Easy has been "absolutely outstanding" He decided to seek help when one of his great grandchildren asked him to read a story. Read Easy, external says 2.4 million adults in England alone cannot read at all or struggle to read. Hannay said for those who cannot read, the "first and most important thing is to admit to people around you that you're not able to do this". "And once you've admitted that, then you can go and get some help, and the help is there," he added. title: How wedding content creators take you from aisle to Insta
description: A growing industry is helping newly weds post video content on social media 24 hours after their big day.
body: Jade Burton is part of a growing number of wedding content creators offering next-day social media ready videos for newlyweds From the nerves before the ceremony to the tears of laughter during the best man's speech, Jade Burton is documenting every moment on her smartphone. The 22-year-old, from Poole in Dorset, is one of a growing number of wedding content creators - a job that did not exist just a few years ago. She films and edits social media-ready videos, giving newlyweds a record of their day just 24 hours after they say "I do". For couples eager to share their big day on Instagram and TikTok, it's a service bridging the gap between the wedding itself and the professional photos that arrive weeks later. Using a smartphone rather than a traditional camera, Jade Burton records candid moments from the wedding day As guests mingle in the autumn sunshine and staff put the finishing touches to the reception room, Burton hovers with her phone. She started her wedding content creator business, Wed In Focus, in July. "With the way technology's evolved and the rise of social media, naturally the way we document memories has changed a lot over time," she said. Unlike a traditional videographer who might take a few months to produce a polished wedding film, Burton edits short-form, vertical videos called highlight reels that can be shared the next day. "It'll kind of tell the wedding story, right from getting ready, through to first looks and ceremony, walking down the aisle - all the key moments." Nikita Thorne says more couples are prioritising social media content on their wedding day Industry experts say the number of content creators has grown rapidly since first appearing in the UK wedding market in 2022. Wedding website, Hitched, reported a rise in searches for wedding content creators, external in 2025. Nikita Thorne, the UK Wedding Association's digital wedding expert and head of strategy at Oxfordshire-based Guides for Brides, said it was down to a combination of social media's growing influence on weddings and the relatively low cost of launching a content creation business. "We've seen more content creators coming in the last couple of years where more people have been able to start a business," she said. Thorne said the average price for a wedding content creator can range between £200 and £1,000 and usually covers the day of filming and the time spent editing. Emily and Michael Errington only learnt about the concept of wedding content creators within the last year The promise of receiving the memories within one day is proving attractive to some couples. Between greeting guests and posing for photographs, bride Emily Errington knew there would be moments she would miss. She hired Burton alongside a photographer and videographer to capture her wedding in Symondsbury, near Bridport in Dorset. "I want to be looking at stuff straight away," she said. "Right now it's all a bit of a whirlwind. I don't really know what's going on." The couple banned guests from taking their own photos during the ceremony, knowing they would have the social media content to post themselves the following day. "I don't want people to share videos or pictures without me having a say-so or seeing what it is that they're putting out there," she said. "It's more for us to let the world know than anyone else." Burton has produced content for nine weddings and says she is booked into 2027 But experts caution the growing popularity of the role has also attracted newcomers to the industry. Thorne said the "relatively low barriers to entry" meant some people could try and do the job, despite having little experience of working at weddings. Urging couples to check experience and credentials, she said: "A lot of people, while they might have relevant experience, such as working in social media, they're not experienced in wedding delivery." Back at the wedding, Burton is weaving between tables and scanning the room for reactions she might otherwise miss. She is keen to challenge the idea that the role simply involves pressing record on a smartphone. "I think there's more to it than meets the eye. You have to have a good eye for composition, lighting, storytelling. Anticipating moments is really important. "There's one take of the ceremony - you can't miss it." title: Seal pups spotted at nature reserve for 12th year
description: Two pups have been recorded at South Walney, home to Cumbria's only breeding grey seal colony.
body: Two seal pups have been spotted at South Walney Nature Reserve near Barrow Seal pups have been recorded at a nature reserve for the 12th year running. Cumbria Wildlife Trust confirmed two pups had been spotted at South Walney Nature Reserve near Barrow, Cumbria. The reserve is home to the county's only breeding grey seal colony and major haul-out site, a spot where seals come to shore for rest. A record number of 14 seal pups were counted at the nature reserve last year, with the trust saying it hoped there would be "many more to come". The pups were the first two healthy ones spotted at the nature reserve this season during a routine seal count. Two were seen earlier in the summer but did not survive, the trust said. Marine conservation officer Beth Churn said: "This is always an exciting time of year for us, and we hope that there'll be many more to come. "We regularly reach double figures of pups, a trend that's been improving each year, so let's hope this season is a successful one for the colony." Cumbria Wildlife Trust is asking people to take care not to disturb the seal colony The highest number of grey seals recorded to date at South Walney Nature Reserve was 563 in December 2024. The previous highest seal counts were 518 in 2021, 483 in 2019 and 360 in 2018, showing an upward trend year on year. Grey seals started breeding at South Walney in 2015 and pups have been recorded every year since. "It's the result of concerted and ongoing efforts to keep disturbance of the seal colony to a minimum," Churn said. "We work hard to make the beach safe and secure for the seals, so that they feel able to return here to breed." There is no public access to the haul-out site at South Walney but three hides around the site let people see the seals from a safe distance. A new hide at Groyne is currently being built and will include a telescope. The trust is asking people to take care not to disturb the seal colony and maintain at least 100m (328ft) distance at all times. "You can get good views of the seals with binoculars from a safe distance, so there's no need to get too close," Churn said. "You'll know if you're too close because the seals will start to look at you and move nervously. "If this happens, you should immediately start backing away quietly to avoid further disturbance." title: Heating oil customers face tough winter
description: The government plans to regulate heating oil prices after increases.
body: Nicola Sharpe said she would normally have stocked up by now but was holding off in the hope the price would fall Some people say they are finding it hard to heat their homes after increases in heating oil costs fuelled by the US-Israeli war with Iran. Residents in the South West told the BBC they have held off buying fuel for the winter in the hope prices could come down and feared some people might go without. It comes as the government announced new measures aimed at regulating the market and reviewing the minimum amounts some people have to buy. Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the conflict, according to the Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington. Billington told the BBC: "We need to make sure the market is working as fairly as possible." She said it was "striking" how rural communities with "so many people off grid" were "some of the most exposed" to the price increases. Nicola Sharpe, from Dunsford, Devon, said this time last year she was paying about £340 for 500 litres, but the price was currently just over £600 for the same amount. "I'm looking at ways to spread the cost when I have to bite the bullet and get it," she said. Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector. Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, would also be reviewed. Pauline Trubody said she usually had the heat on during the day in the winter Sharpe said she was not hopeful the government measures would help. "I can't see how regulating it is going to bring costs down." Pauline Trubody, from Porkellis, Cornwall, said she had already spent more on two deliveries of 500 litres this year compared to previous years. The 76-year-old said: "I probably won't put it [the heating] on as much as I would have. "There is going to be a lot of people who can't afford it and folk who are going to go cold." Lee Fossey, from St Agnes, Cornwall, pays £30 a month into a savings scheme to spread the cost of heating oil throughout the year. She said: "I have done everything I reasonably can to budget and prepare for winter, yet despite this, the dramatic increase in prices means I can no longer afford to fill my tank." She said she faced the prospect of having no heating this winter or using the money for an alternative heating source. Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: How parents of murdered stalking victim are campaigning for change
description: Alice Ruggles's parents continue to raise awareness of stalking through the trust set up in their daughter's name.
body: Alice Ruggles grew up in Leicestershire, but lived in Gateshead after university A decade after the brutal murder of her daughter, Dr Sue Hills still believes there needs to be change. Alice Ruggles was 24 when she was killed by obsessive ex-boyfriend Trimaan "Harry" Dhillon in 2016. Originally from Leicestershire, Ruggles had been subject to a lengthy campaign of stalking from the soldier, who drove from his barracks near Edinburgh, broke into her flat in Gateshead and killed her. He was later found guilty of her murder and given a life sentence, with a minimum term of 22 years. "Losing a child is a life-changing thing," Hills said. "My life before, my life after are completely different and I'm not on the path that I would have been on." Of Ruggles, Hills said: "She was absolutely brilliant - lively, hilariously funny, full of energy. "She was really caring and empathetic. She was everything that you want out of a young person." Sue Hills said the Alice Ruggles Trust helped to educate young people about stalking through school assemblies Following her death, Hills, 65, and her husband Clive Ruggles, 74, started to campaign for better education surrounding stalking and changes to legislation. It is now compulsory for secondary schools to include teaching about stalking, but the couple said they believed there should not be a distinction between stalking, and stalking involving fear of violence. An independent review looking into the effectiveness of the current stalking legislation, led by Richard Wright KC, was submitted to the government in April. Hills said she wanted to make sure the review was not "submerged" by changes of prime minister and cabinet. "I think the review has a potential to have a really big impact," Hills said. "It's one of those horrific things, every time the government changes or some big political thing happens, you just have a real worry that it's going to be submerged and never see the light of day. "We want it published as soon as possible." The review will look at whether existing laws sufficiently protect victims and hold perpetrators to account, as well as if legislation adequately addresses emerging forms of stalking, including online abuse and technology-enabled behaviours. Ruggles was 24 when she was killed in her home by an obsessive ex-boyfriend Hills said stalking victims should not need to be scared for more serious charges or punishments to be imposed. "It's a weird thing, if something is trying to scare you, and you say you're scared then they've sort of won," she said. "If you admit you're afraid, you're handing your stalker a bit of help. Why is it all on the victim, and how the victim feels? "You would never say that about a burglary to a house, would you? "It's a weird judgement to make." Ten years on from Alice's death, the Alice Ruggles Trust is continuing to focus on educating young people about stalking, through school assemblies and PSHE (personal, social, health and economic) lessons. In the past year, the trust has taught more than 4,000 young people to spot the signs of stalking, understand what healthy relationships are, and how to get help. It said it had also trained 600 professionals to recognise stalking and respond appropriately. Hills said the trust aimed "to put an end to stalking". "I think that it's true that the work that the trust is doing is changing people's lives," she said. "It's for both stalkers and potential perpetrators. "It's important that people who are potential perpetrators get that education as well. Do they actually know that it's wrong to keep messaging someone? "I know it's happened quite a lot that people have said they've realised that a friend was actually stalking his partner. "So they were able to say to him, do you realise what you're doing is wrong, and you've got to stop?" Alice's school friend Lucy Parkinson ran 250 miles over nine days to raise more than £16,000 for the trust To support the trust's school assembly programme, Ruggles' friend Lucy Parkinson ran 250 miles over nine days from Newcastle to Leicestershire. The 35-year-old, from King's Norton in Leicestershire, raised more than £16,000 for the trust. She also wanted to raise awareness about stalking. "It's happened to me," she said. "It's happened to other people and what we want to do is prevent what happened to Alice happening to other people." During her challenge, Parkinson said "lots of people" had come forward to share their stories showing "how common stalking is". Ruggles' parents said Parkinson's fundraising would help to educate more young people about stalking Latest figures from the Office for National Statistics, external (ONS) showed an estimated 1.4 million people aged 16 years and over had experienced stalking, in the year ending March 2025, with women and younger people most commonly affected. The ONS data also showed one in five women, and about one in 13 men aged 16 years and over, had been a victim of stalking. A government spokesperson said: "We must use every lever available to tackle violence against women and girls, moving further and faster to stop harm before it happens. "We are strengthening the use of Stalking Protection Orders, investing over £13m to establish specialist protection order teams, and last year we appointed Richard Wright KC, who prosecuted Alice's case, to conduct an independent review to ensure the law is fit for purpose." title: Corby metal pollution may harm people, says study
description: However, the Environment Agency says it has not found evidence that could cause significant harm.
body: Earthwatch Europe said volunteers found the chemical element cadmium in six freshwater samples in July Campaigners trying to examine the effects of the toxic waste scandal in Corby say they have found a presence of metals which could post a risk to human health. Children in the Northamptonshire town have been born with birth defects, believed to have been caused when steelworks were demolished in the 1980s. Charity Earthwatch Europe says trained citizen scientists have found potentially harmful levels of metal or metalloid at 52 freshwater sites across Corby. The Environment Agency (EA) welcomed their work but said some metals occurred naturally and that its own evidence did not indicate "widespread or significant harm". Earlier this year, Earthwatch Europe said its volunteers collected evidence that the presence of metals could harm aquatic life - findings that were disputed by the EA. But this time, the group believes the samples show a potential effect on people. Dr Sasha Woods, a scientific advisor for the group, said the results highlighted "where further investigation and remedial action may be needed". "The findings indicate that some metals are present in freshwater at levels that could pose a risk to aquatic life, and in soil at levels that could impact human health, particularly in areas close to known historic waste sites," she added. What is the story behind Netflix's Toxic Town? Earthwatch Europe said its trained citizen scientists were out collecting in July, which as well as the freshwater samples, included taking 28 soil samples. It said at every freshwater site, at least one metal or metalloid was present, at concentrations exceeding the level where "no adverse ecological effects are expected". Nickel was found in 28 freshwater samples and cadmium was detected in six, the charity said. A spokesperson said the comparison between its summer and winter sampling indicated a "relatively constant source of pollution; likely groundwater and landfill leachate rather than urban run-off". "Elevated concentrations of cadmium and nickel in freshwater, and cadmium and arsenic in soil, were largely confined to Deene Quarry and a former slag heap in Weldon," the group added. Tracey Taylor's story was portrayed in the Netflix drama Toxic Town Tracey Taylor, whose baby daughter Shelby-Anne died at four days old, has spent years campaigning for justice over the scandal. In 2009, Justice Akenhead ruled in favour of 18 Corby families and that Corby Borough Council was negligent in managing the waste. She hoped the new Earthwatch Europe report would mean "people are going to start to listen to us". "It's got to stop," she said. "I'm 30 years down the line, I don't need that apology, I don't need justice, but I will fight on for the children and the community of Corby, because the Corby community always come together and they support each other. "They should not have to deal with this or be living with this on their land. It needs sorting." Lee Barron, the Labour MP for Corby and East Northamptonshire, said "local authorities have a duty to inspect and identify sites where contamination is causing unacceptable risks". He urged North Northamptonshire Council - which replaced Corby council in 2021 - to publish a plan "to make these sites safe". The steelworks in Corby, pictured, closed in 1981 An EA spokesperson said it was reviewing the Earthwatch Europe report alongside its own evidence. "Our monitoring to date does not indicate widespread or significant harm to the freshwater environment across the Corby area," they said. "We will continue to assess the evidence and take any further action needed." A spokesperson for the council also welcomed the report and said it would "fully assess the data and supporting information". "Residents can be assured that any credible evidence of a risk to human health or the environment will be thoroughly considered and investigated through the appropriate regulatory processes." title: Watch: Police hunt for synthetic drugs in Chicago jail
description: BBC News hears from users, dealers, prison and recovery workers as America battles with a deadly new drug epidemic.
body: This video can not be played Chicago's largest jail, and the largest single use jail in America, is Cook County. In 2023 it saw a spike in overdose deaths. The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures. Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening. However, a new way of drugs entering the prison was uncovered. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the paper of the pages of books and in letters. The BBC's Quentin Sommerville joined corrections officers at Cook County as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. To understand the challenge that authorities face in tackling the problem the BBC interviewed a former inmate and dealer, who explained how synthetic drugs can be made in the US using household ingredients and how this could change the demand for drugs from outside of the country. title: The town swapping lie-ins for early morning raves
description: A seaside town is hosting an early morning alternative for clubbing fans.
body: Ravers in Felixstowe have been enjoying some early morning dancing It's an idea that has already taken off in cities like Berlin, Sydney and New York, and now a seaside town in Suffolk has become the latest place for people to go partying in the morning. A Coffee and Clubbing event has started in Felixstowe for those who want to have fun dancing at 09:00 without the late nights and hangovers. Event founder Vanessa Fullerton-Batten said she wanted to let people enjoy "music that transports you back to those heady days of the '90s club dancefloors - but in the morning". She added: "If you have kids too, you don't want to have a late night and be hungover the next day, so to avoid all of that you can go out early." Organiser Vanessa Fullerton-Batten said people don't have to be "seasoned ravers" to take part Fullerton-Batten and her husband, Ben Kay, who DJs at the events, moved to the town earlier this year from Hertfordshire and wanted to help bring the community together. High street coffee shop Cuppa has hosted two of the events so far where people of all ages can enjoy a mid-morning dance and a brew. "I think there's just this sense of wanting to be connected again," said Fullerton-Batten. "You can go to the gym, but I think going to something like that you can just come along, you can chat, you can listen to the music - and, of course, you can just dance. "It only lasts for an hour, so it's a really good atmosphere and just great vibes." Fullerton-Batten said those who turned out were mainly Gen X-ers, in their 40s and 50s. "You don't have to be a seasoned clubber or a raver to enjoy this sort of thing," she stressed. Ben Kay plays at the events and said he enjoyed being able to see people smiling and dancing Kay, who has DJ'd across the country and produced music over the past 30 years, said there were advantages to being on the decks during the day. "You can see people, so you can see them smiling and dancing," he said. "It doesn't feel that different to playing in a club, it's just lighter. Coffee raves have been taking place at venues across the world, with some people seeing it as a fun alternative to the gym Susannah Hinchey, who owns a local fitness company, said dancing at whatever time of day or night is also good exercise. She puts on silent disco walks along Felixstowe's promenade and "clubbercise" evening classes where people work out to music with glowsticks. "Music speaks to people in lots of different ways - and to move your body to the music just feels really, really good," she said. "My [indoor] class is done in the dark, which obviously mimics the nightclub vibe, so you get all the happy hormones... without the hangover or sore feet." Susannah Hinchey runs "clubbercise" classes in Felixstowe and thinks people like the fun of dancing without the hangover The Coffee and Clubbing events in Felixstowe start at 09:00 BST and Fullerton-Batten hopes there will be many more. "It's a pop-up, so the idea is that we go to different venues. It could be a bakery, restaurant or a bar," she said. "We want this to become more regular, ideally once a month, and we've got another one coming up soon, which is going to be an afternoon session." She added that they want to create a welcoming space for people of all ages. "Us Gen X-ers, we're in our 40s and 50s, and you might feel a little bit out of place in a club, but there are plenty of people that age and older who go to really big outdoor raves and festivals," she said. "So, age shouldn't really matter at all. It's just how people around you make you feel." Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below. title: Chin-up champion secures Guinness World Record title
description: Former mixed marital artist Damien Rooney has broken the Guinness World Record for most chin-ups in an hour whilst wearing a 20lb weight.
body: Damien Rooney has earned his Guinness World Record title for most chin-ups A former professional mixed martial artist has broken the Guinness World Record for most chin-ups in an hour whilst wearing a 20lb weight. Damien Rooney from Burren, outside Newry, clocked up 499 reps to beat the previous record of 495. He now intends to build upon the record and push towards a fresh challenge for the 24-hour record which could require as many as 10,000 reps. Damien, who runs his own gym, hopes to take on his next record attempt in April 2027. In a nutshell Damien says a chin-up is performed with your palms facing towards you and the brunt of effort being felt in the bicep. This compares with a pull-up, where your palms are facing outwards and your lats take the bulk of the strain. During his fighting career Damien fought under the moniker "The Rage". He says it was this period of his life which fuelled a desire to compete for a Guinness World Record. "I've always been in and around the fitness game and during my fight career I took a full liking to the strength and conditioning element of it," he said. He says his training was more suited to chin-ups, rather than pull-ups. This video can not be played From MMA professional to chin-up world champion "In 2018 I first attempted the most chin-ups in 24 hours and had a few unsuccessful attempts at that through injury." These unsuccessful attempts included torn muscles and heat exhaustion. But Damien says these are inconsequential when compared with the realities of the fight game. "It is pretty extreme. The constant overload on the body. But as painful as this is, its very localised and very much in your control – but a really rough fight? It doesn't compare. It's night and day." After his last unsuccessful attempt he recalibrated his training, focusing on the shorter, weighted, one hour target. Despite being much shorter, he says it is far from a sprint race. "I think people think you'd just go out and start pumping them out but if you do that the body will fatigue and it will fatigue quickly making recovery hard. So the better way to do it is to go on a cycle where you are maximising your work but maximising your recovery in between." Damien clocked up 499 reps to beat the previous record of 495. To this end he broke the hour down into two minute blocks with 30 seconds of rest in between. Ahead of a fresh assault on the 24-hour record, Damien will next take on the one- hour, unweighted challenge. "Without the weighted jacket the record is something like 1,010 so it is night and day without it." Those future challenges are for a different day. After beginning this journey in 2018, having his record confirmed by Guinness is an achievement worth waiting for. "I did this on June 1 and they told me in September. It can be up to 20 weeks because they have to go through the tapes and watch it from different angles. They are very stringent to make sure it is authentic." title: Two damselfly species return to restored woodland
description: A three-year project to restore woodland at seven nature reserves is completed.
body: The Beautiful Demoiselle damselfly was recorded for the first time at Astonbury Wood Two species of damselfly have been recorded for the first time in a woodland after the completion of a three-year project to restore habitat across seven nature reserves, a wildlife trust has revealed. Work on the Ancient Astonbury and Wilder Woodlands project, in Hertfordshire, was made possible with a £162,698 grant from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. An increase in flowers attracted more butterflies, with Silver-washed Fritillaries also recorded in much higher numbers during summer 2026 than in previous years, the Herts & Middlesex Wildlife Trust said. The Beautiful Demoiselle and Willow Emerald damselflies were spotted at Astonbury Wood, close to Stevenage. The seven sites that made up the project were Astonbury Wood, Balls Wood near Hertford, Fir & Pond Woods near Potters Bar, Gobions Wood near Brookmans Park, Old Park Wood in Harefield, Long Deans in Hemel Hempstead, and Hawkins Wood between Buntingford and Royston. An ancient woodland, the size of a football pitch, was turned back into coppice management, to allow more light to reach the woodland floor and encourage flowers, insects and birds to thrive. A coppiced area at Astonbury Wood An area of hornbeam trees at Astonbury Wood was also coppiced in December 2025 and showed "strong regrowth following its first growing season, despite the dry summer," the trust added. Further coppicing is planned to take place in the future. The practice is an ancient method of tree management, external which involves felling trees at their base to create a "stool" where new shoots will grow. At Astonbury Wood, woodland glades were reverted to woodland after about 20 years without management. "Clearing trees and dense bramble, followed by annual cutting and raking, is helping to restore these open habitats and the flowers and insects that depend on them", the trust added. Bluebells at Old Park Wood, Harefield Iain Ward, wilder woodlands officer at the trust, said: "It has been fantastic to see these habitats responding so positively to careful management, and to see more wildlife making use of the restored glades and coppice areas." He hopes more work can be carried out at Astonbury Wood to restore the ponds and prevent them drying out completely, as summers "become increasingly hot and dry". title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
description: BBC News hears from users, dealers, prison and recovery workers as the country battles with a deadly new drug epidemic.
body: This video can not be played The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raid Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says. The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars. "You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says. He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune. We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction. Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs. America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic Wave Extraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanyl Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States. At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over. It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl. The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added. When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce." Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me. They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat. At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma. They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty. One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life. As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid. "It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement. Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood Church One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose". "In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers. Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so. "The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it." Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope Dealers Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds. His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme.
