title: Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protests
description: An historic town hall in the southern French city of Limoges was set ablaze during national protests.
body: This video can not be played A clock tower spire has collapsed in a ball of flames in the French city of Limoges amid nationwide protests. The local prefecture said the town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze started deliberately. Fire crews were still battling the blaze late into the night, while eyewitnesses captured the dramatic moment the tower's turret fell. title: Three takeaways from Elon Musk's latest political donations
description: New filings show the world's richest person spent this summer again trying to help Republicans win office, with most of his focus on one candidate.
body: Billionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk is once again pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into a US election - this time with the aim of helping Republicans maintain their control of Congress. Musk donated upwards of $200m (£150m) in the quarter that ended on 30 September, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings reviewed by the BBC. The fillings were released with just over two weeks until the 2026 midterm election, where many races for the House of Representatives and Senate are close and Republicans risk losing their majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate. Musk also put significant money, $290m, and effort into helping elect President Donald Trump and other Republicans in 2024. Here is where the richest person in the world has been donating this time around, and what it might mean for his businesses. The bulk of the money donated last quarter by the world's only trillionaire, $158m, went to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) Pac, the filings showed. It is one of the largest publicly known single political donations in US history, and some have suggested it is the biggest ever. SLF is a super Pac backing Republican Senate candidates in tough races. It quickly sent the money on to a group supporting Texas Republican Ken Paxton. The state attorney general, Paxton is at risk of losing to Democrat James Talarico in a race for a seat his party has held for decades. They have been polling neck and neck and the election's outcome is considered a bellwether for the future of Republican power. Super Pacs are independent "political action committees" that can raise unlimited amounts of money and play a major role in funding US political campaigns. Musk also donated more than $80m to the America Pac that he founded during the 2024 election. GUIDE: What are the US midterms? IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lost NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox America Pac last quarter spent millions on digital communications, mailings and phone calls opposing Talarico, as well as thousands on political marketing to support Paxton. At the same time, Musk donated another $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, a group primarily backing Paxton, records show. The flow of money highlights a major theme for Musk: Texas. In recent years, the tech CEO has been moving his business empire - including SpaceX, Tesla and X - to the southern US state after expressing frustration with operating in California. Texas has offered Musk fewer government regulations and no state personal income tax and no corporate income tax. Keeping politicians who favour looser government restrictions in charge, as Republicans typically have, could help maintain that environment for Musk. And his big spending in Texas and in the Texas Senate race seems to point to Musk's understanding of that, political analyst Cayce Myers told the BBC. "Republicans have a fundraising advantage this time, but fundraising by itself does not actually guarantee success," he said. For many voters this year, technology has become a top issue. People across the country are pushing for increased government oversight of artificial intelligence, data centres and social media. That's something that has tech leaders like Musk developing closer ties to the Republican party, which historically has promoted lighter government regulation, Myers said. "What [tech leaders] are looking at is a future where there is growing demand and call for regulation and I think they want to be in an advantageous position," he said. "We're seeing them shift, and fall behind Republicans." Other tech leaders, such as OpenAI president and his wife Greg and Anna Brockman are also putting big money behind Republicans. The couple donated $25m to the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc Pac last year. Myer noted it's not just the tech sector, but industries like cryptocurrency and gambling where large sums of money are being donated in an attempt to exert influence. "This is the idea of shaping the regulatory environment through contributions," he said. Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here. title: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions
description: It's not just treachery and villainy - the soundtrack for Traitors helps set the show's campy tone.
body: This video can not be played Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions? Suspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all. But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music. Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab. As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest. Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning. "I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later). Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach. "They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun." Sam Watts' Traitors theme helped to establish the show's identity For the title sequence, the 44-year-old wanted something memorable. As a kid, his favourite song was Bernard Hoffer's gloriously over-the-top Thundercats theme, external, so that's the level he aspired to. "I was trying to write something that signified the show was starting, so that people would run in from making their cup of tea in the kitchen to watch it. "And I wanted a memorable melody that people could hum, because it helps with the identity of the show." The Traitors theme is "one of the biggest pieces of music I've ever written", he says, recorded with a full orchestra and overdubbed with dozens of electronic elements to create a heightened, hyperreal atmosphere. That bled into the 20 or so other pieces Watts wrote, which also appear in dozens of international spin-offs. The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you What role would you play in the Traitors castle? Take our quiz to find out The idea, he says, is that the whole hour feels like a film trailer, with viewers permanently waiting for the psychological pressure chamber to explode. To achieve that, he employed several techniques of trailer music - most notably the "Braam", a klaxon-like punctuation mark invented for Christopher Nolan's Inception (see video for a fuller exploration). Show producer Sarah Fay took that concept and amplified it. "We wanted to just supersize it and make it feel like a drama, not like your usual reality [show]," she said in a rare interview with Metro, external when the first civilian series aired in 2022. "We wanted to make it feel like that edge-of-your-seat cinematic drama with, you know, elements of Succession, and we wanted it to feel like Knives Out when you get into the castle!" To achieve that, she commissioned additional music from film trailer composers, including Hans Zimmer's company Bleeding Fingers. But she also sprinkled in a handful of creepy cover versions. Some became instant classics - such as a sinister spin on Britney Spears' Toxic, external, or a version of Tears For Fears' Mad World, external seemingly broadcast on a tannoy from Hades. They're so integral to The Traitors' aesthetic that it might surprise you to learn they weren't recorded specifically for the show. The Traitors score has proved so popular that an entire BBC Proms concert was devoted to the show's music last year Both examples were created by German writer-producers 2wei. Based in Hamburg, they had no idea their music had appeared in The Traitors until friends in the UK messaged them in excitement. "We were just flipping out," says 2wei's Simon Heeger. "It's completely different to how we ever thought it would be used." Heeger founded 2wei, pronounced "zwei", in 2016 with his old college friend Christian Vorländer. They had both spent time in LA working on advertisements and (stop me if you're sensing a theme here) film trailers, before moving home to build a music production empire. "Christian worked on the Mad Max soundtrack, which is really known for the big drums and the orchestral scale – and that was really the starting point of our sound," says Heeger. "Whenever you hear big epic drums with an orchestral sound and maybe a female vocal on top of it, it's usually something we had our fingers in." Simon Heeger is the co-founder of 2wei, which is responsible for some of Traitors' most memorable cover songs Their big break came with a stormy reworking of Destiny's Child's Survivor, which featured in the trailer to Alicia Vikander's Tomb Raider, external. Since then, their music has appeared in films like Wonder Woman and video games such as League of Legends. In The Traitors, original 2wei songs like Blindside, external now feature alongside their covers (other producers, including SYML and Damned Anthem also contribute songs to the show). Heeger says their background in commercials makes the music perfectly suited to the show's slippery skullduggery. "In adverts, you only have a few seconds to convey a certain emotion and, especially in Traitors, where there are cliffhangers and moments that you don't expect, you need music that comes to the point right away but still has a boldness to it. "It's a sweet spot, and it's not easy to convey, but every now and then it works quite well." On Spotify, there are hundreds of playlists dedicated to the program

title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?
description: The sports industry's lucrative business model is being undermined by dodgy TV sticks and illegal streaming links, writes Theo Leggett.
body: There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control? "Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than £20m on new players. The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of £8.5m. That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when £100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business. All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than £300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time. It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate. But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis. This year's Champions League final - won by Paris Saint-Germain - sparked an argument about TV viewing rights And this summer saw signs of a clampdown. In August, a man in Lancashire was jailed for six and a half years for running an illegal streaming service that police said had generated almost £1m in illicit profits. In June, a postman from Pembrokeshire was jailed for over three years for selling illegal subscriptions and supplying pirate software to nearly 2,000 people. A third man, from Merseyside, received a suspended 32-month sentence in August for similar offences. Several pubs have been fined thousands of pounds for screening matches illegally. TV companies that have paid huge sums for exclusive rights to high-profile sports are having to work harder than ever to protect their investments. To some extent, broadcasters used to see copyright theft as a cost of doing business: irritating and expensive, but not an existential threat. But now, as advertising revenues fall, and viewers move away from long-term subscription services like Sky or TNT Sports, the industry is getting seriously worried. There is a great deal at stake. The Premier League alone is a sporting monster. In its most recent deal, it sold its viewing rights to domestic audiences for £6.7bn over four years, with almost as much coming from foreign rights. Armed with bundles of TV cash, clubs have been able to attract the finest players in the world. That in turn has given the league a major international profile. Although football has been the main beneficiary of paid-for TV in the UK, other competitions such as Formula One, Six Nations rugby and the Wimbledon tennis championships have also commanded very high fees for selling exclusive rights. Live sport on free-to-air television has become increasingly rare. Yet that wealth could be threatened by a surge in piracy and illegal viewing. The practice is most common among younger, digital-native audiences, who each year become a larger and larger share of sports fans. But many older viewers also seem comfortable with it. Rupert Murdoch (left) launched Sky TV with the broadcaster Andrew Neil in 1989. It went on to transform Britain's sports-watching landscape "For 18 to 34-year-olds, it's over 70% who admit to doing this regularly," says Daniel Monaghan, a researcher at Ampere Analysis. "Over half of 35 to 44s admit to doing it, and about a third of those aged 45 to 64." This year's Champions League final went behind a paywall in the UK for the first time in more than 30 years. Viewers were asked to pay at least £4.99 to watch it, prompting a backlash, including from the then-prime minister, Arsenal fan Sir Keir Starmer. "Hardworking people shouldn't have to fork out for a subscription to watch this match," he wrote on X. Many simply refused to pay: 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match in the UK, according to research carried out by the Gaming Compliance International consultancy, on behalf of the Guardian newspaper. That compared to around seven million people who watched it legally in the UK. One prolific user of pirate streams is "Kiran", a tech sector worker in his 30s, who prefers not to give his real name. A keen Arsenal fan, he likes to watch Premier League and Champions League games, as well as big matches in Spain's La Liga. He has a paid subscription to TNT Sports, but uses streaming websites to see games that are not available there. Many fans watched this year's Champions League final legally at pubs - but at home, 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match, according to one analysis "What it comes down to is the financial side - that's the big one - and ease of access as well," he says. "Getting every single game will cost you hundreds of pounds a year." Meanwhile the streams he uses are free, with links readily obtainable on social media. But there's another issue, he says: the famous blackout. Games taking place between 14:45 and 17:15 on a Saturday are not usually screened live in the UK, a decades-old policy designed to protect crowds at lower league matches. But broadcasters outside the UK can and do show those matches, fuelling pirated streams. "I pretty much got into streaming stuff due to [the blackout]," Kiran says, "and I'd say I sort of did it a bit more as subscriptions got more expensive." Those searching for pirated material have plenty of options. Streaming links, along with advice on how to avoid their pitfalls, are freely available in online discussion groups. These links, used by Kiran and his friends, have practical downsides – such as frequent buffering or poor

title: Comedian Paul Whitehouse mugged at London cash machine
description: His wife wrote on Instagram that the actor had been "mugged at a cash machine behind a Sainsbury's in Islington".
body: Actor and comedian Paul Whitehouse has fought back against someone who tried to steal his card at an London cash machine, according to his wife. Dr Mine Conkbayir posted on Instagram that her husband had gone out to get some medication on Friday, when he was mugged at a cash machine behind a Sainsbury's in Islington. "He did fight back and retrieved his card, with the perp scuttling away empty-handed," she wrote, warning people to be "super vigilant" out there. The Welsh comedian, 68, is known for his work on The Fast Show and BBC's Gone Fishing. In her post, Conkbayir said Whitehouse was picking up medication for her after she had a bad reaction to some treatment. "Well, a horrid start to the weekend, would be an understatement," she wrote, adding that she had been encouraged by her husband to make the post "in the hope that it might help folk to be more aware when out and about". Friends and fans alike have flooded to the comments of Conkbayir's post, condemning the attack and wishing Whitehouse a speedy recovery. Among them were fellow comedian Dawn French, who wrote that the incident in Islington was "utterly not okay", and Angela Barnes, who said it was a "horrible thing to happen" and she was "sending love to you both". Whitehouse is best known for his work on Gone Fishing, which he presents alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer. The BBC Two series began in 2018 and sees Whitehouse and Mortimer discuss life while fishing. It has been nominated six times for a Bafta TV award. The comedian has also been cast as Hogwarts caretaker Argus Filch in HBO's upcoming Harry Potter television series. title: The Papers: 'French protests become violent' and SAS men 'arrested for murder'
description: The Times reports soldiers accused of murder were sent into war zones while still under police investigation.
body: The Independent focuses on the hundreds of people who have been arrested across France, following what it says were "some of the country's most violent protests in recent times". The paper says a tourist office has been torched in Lyon, and a town hall vandalised in Marseille, as people protest "rising costs and declining services". The Times leads with an investigation, reporting that Special Air Service (SAS) soldiers accused of murder were sent into war zones while still under police investigation. It says that five men were arrested on secret bases in Syria and Iraq in 2022, kicking off an "unprecedented three-year criminal investigation" that the paper says "plunged the regiment into crisis". It writes that the five men were sent back into the war zone just 48 hours after being questioned by police, and "left in limbo for three years" before they were told no charges would be brought. The former suspects have all since left the military, the Times says, in addition to writing a letter to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to complain about their "potentially unlawful arrests". A Ministry Of Defence spokesperson said personnel are "entitled to expect that any investigation is conducted fairly and professionally and rightly there are procedures in place for people to report concerns ... If allegations of wrongdoing arise, it is right that they are properly assessed and, where appropriate, investigated". Protesters in Paris have also been pictured on the front page of the Sunday Telegraph, captioned: "Rioters on the rampage across France." The paper carries a story about the use of Civil Service fact-checkers at the BBC, a revelation which it says has lead to questions about the broadcaster's impartiality. A spokesperson for the BBC has denied that civil servants had editorial influence on stories, and stated that all editorial decision-making was made by BBC journalists and editors. The Mail on Sunday has accused the BBC of "brainwashing children" in its main story, alleging the broadcaster's education website, BBC Bitesize, is pushing "'extreme' Left-Wing views" on millions of pupils. It reports that the website included an online game called "Increasing Immigration", which rewarded students for choosing to open borders and grant amnesty to "illegal migrants". A BBC spokesman said: "BBC Bitesize works with educational consultants to develop resources that help young people explore and understand a wide range of topics, aligned to the respective curriculums across the UK ... While we don't accept the characterisation of Bitesize in this story, we regularly review content to ensure it remains relevant and to ensure it meets the BBC's editorial standards and will review these examples in that context." Reform UK Nigel Farage has spoken to the Sunday Express, declaring that Britain will never "vote to rejoin" the European Union. Farage accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of having an "outdated view of the world", and warned that pressure from "Labour's traditional heartlands in the North" will prevent him from leading the UK straight back into the bloc. A photograph of television presenters Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates walking together leads the Sun on Sunday, which says the "Match of the Day lovebirds" were stepping out together as a couple for the first time. An off-duty doctor who helped wounded passengers in the Bedford plane crash earlier this year is set to receive a Pride of Britain Award, according to the Daily Mirror. The paper reports Dr Eli Prior had multiple injuries herself, but stayed on the train to help others who had been hurt in the crash. Air ambulance doctor Rob Wilmore said he was "humbled" by Prior's bravery. "Rich pickings", reads the headline of the Sunday People, homing in on campaigners who argue that a wealth tax "could help so many". It comes ahead of the Budget, which is set to be delivered on 28 October. "Comedy legend fights off mugger", reads the Daily Star, alongside a photograph of comedian Paul Whitehouse. The paper reports the 68-year-old was accosted at a cash machine, but fought back against the thief, who it says "scuttled away empty handed". The Observer explores what it is calling the "childhood lottery", writing that a child in Blackpool is 27 times more likely to miss school than one in Lambeth. The piece hinges on a new study, which it says has exposed the vast inequalities of childhood in England and prompted the children's commissioner to declare a national emergency". title: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley Arena in one turbulent year
description: Turkish girl group manifest on taking their music to a global audience, as they prepare for their first UK concert.
body: manifest performed their first UK concert at Wembley Arena When I first meet Turkish girl group manifest, we're on a boat cruising down the River Thames. The six band members are clutching Union jack umbrellas as they pose for press photographs and mingle with British pop acts, including K-pop-trained boyband dearALICE. Netflix cameras are filming the evening for a six-part documentary. The group are in London hoping to build on their success in Turkey and reach an international audience. Their ambitions come after a turbulent year at home, during which the band were prosecuted for public indecency over their outfits and dance moves during a concert in Istanbul. A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the following night. As the staging - complete with giant LED screens and the group's logo - is set up around them, the six members rehearse synchronised choreography alongside their back-up dancers. The group consists of main vocalist Sueda Uluca, lead vocalist Lidya Pınar, sub-vocalist Mina Solak, sub-vocalist and main rapper Zeynep Sude Oktay, lead dancer Hilal Yelekçi and main dancer Esin Bahat. But Wembley is just the beginning of their ambitions. "After Wembley, we'll manifest Coachella and other big stages," says Hilal Yelekçi, playing on the group's name. manifest were formed in February last year through the Turkish reality TV talent competition Big5 Türkiye, which saw contestants compete over several months for a place in the group. They were mentored by established Turkish pop stars, including Gülçin Ergül, a former member of girl group Hepsi, who was also a judge on the show. The band's rise has been rapid, and they now have more than six million monthly listeners on Spotify. The group hopes to keep their Turkish identity while reaching global audiences While in London, they released their first English-language single, TRALALA, which topped YouTube's daily music video chart on its release, ahead of videos from Shakira and Taylor Swift. The music video was also their first to be filmed outside Turkey, with the group working with a largely British production crew in east London. "Getting out from that safe zone was a bit stressful for us," says Pınar. Despite their hopes to perform on British and American stages, they're keen to retain their Turkish identity. "We want to reach a global audience with our Turkish songs actually, not with English ones," says Sude Oktay. "We want to teach people to sing in Turkish." Alongside Turkish girl group Hepsi, manifest cite the Spice Girls among their musical inspirations. Pınar says her favourite Spice Girl is Baby Spice. "Because of the pink. I'm pink and blonde, so it's obvious," she laughs. They have also had the chance to meet one of the world's biggest pop stars, Dua Lipa. The British-Albanian singer met manifest backstage before watching them perform at her Sunny Hill Festival in Kosovo in July this year. "She came to our backstage and said a lot of great things," one member recalls. "We really love her, her songs, her stage presence." manifest performed at Dua Lipa's Sunny Hill festival this summer However, the band's road to success was threatened last year. The trip to London comes just over a year after Turkish prosecutors launched an investigation into the group over allegations of violating public decency, following criticism of their outfits and choreography at an over-18s concert in Istanbul. A Turkish court later ruled that their choreography and physical contact on stage amounted to exhibitionism. In a post on X, Turkish politician Oktay Saral called for action so the group "can never repeat such acts". The case also prompted criticism over artistic freedom in Turkey, where authorities have previously cancelled concerts and festivals over concerns about public morality. Turkish singer Ceylan Ertem described the investigation as "an open attack on women's freedom and the performing arts". The six members were handed suspended prison sentences of three months and 22 days. A ban preventing them from leaving Turkey was also lifted by the court. Speaking to me in London, the group would not talk about the sentencing. Instead they spoke about wanting to inspire a new generation of Turkish girls. "We are six different women, we have different hobbies... " says lead vocalist Pınar. "We really, really want to see that little girls look at us and maybe they want to sing too, they want to dance too. "Maybe they can get the power from us." About 300 fans attended a signing event at a Turkish restaurant in London, giving the group their first chance to meet some of their UK-based supporters in person. "Our concerts and events have been in Turkey before and we never met them face-to-face," says Pınar. "It was a really cute moment for us." Alara, 26, Elif, 31, Begum, 31, and Zeynep, 25, called the concert "a once-in-a-lifetime experience" On the day of the concert, there was a sense of excitement outside Wembley Arena as fans wearing manifest-branded headbands and carrying banners gathered. The crowd was predominantly Turkish women in their 20s and 30s, many dressed in colours associated with the group. Among them were friends Elif, 31, and Zeynep, 25, both Turkish women living in London, who reflected on the band's past year. "I don't think I've ever heard of a girl band performing there," says Zeynep. "I think I was seven when Hepsi were last together. It's maybe a once-in-a-lifetime experience." Turkish pop star Tarkan previously performed at Wembley Arena in 2008. For Elif, the concert has a wider significance. "We are going through difficult times back home. It means girl power and empowerment, and just having fun and being together," she says. "I feel like back home people came together to support them and criticise the treatment that they were receivi

title: The playground murder: Trauma, loss and a love that endured
description: Diane Watson's best friend Pauline recalls a shocking school murder and its lasting legacy.
body: Best friends Diane (left) and Pauline (right) did everything together When Diane Watson was stabbed to death in the playground of a Glasgow school in 1991, her best friend Pauline was standing by her side. Pauline watched as 16-year-old Diane collapsed after the knife attack by another pupil and then helped to carry her across the road to the arms of her parents who lived in an upstairs flat within view of the school. Diane's murder would not only devastate her family, her friends and the local community, its shockwaves would go on to be felt for decades. Diane Watson was 16 when she died Warning - this story contains descriptions of violence, death and suicide. Thirty-five years later, Pauline Love Thomson has spoken for the first time about the trauma of that April morning when she was just 16. In a new BBC Scotland podcast, Crime Next Door: The Playground Murder, she relives the day 15-year-old Barbara Glover came to Whitehill secondary school in Glasgow's east end armed with a large kitchen knife. Pauline describes how a large crowd of schoolkids gathered round as Glover shouted at Diane while waving the knife - and the chilling moment she dealt the deadly blow. "She actually let out a growl when she stepped forward," Pauline says. "She stabbed her and people started just moving away. Everybody just vanished. "I went over, I just put my arm around her [Diane's] shoulder because I hadn't actually appreciated the damage that the knife would have done. It was a big knife." Diane lived with parents across the road from the school Pauline tried to help her bleeding friend get home to the flat across the road she shared with her mum, dad and brother Alan. She recalls Diane saying: "I don't believe it. She stabbed me." It was only a short distance to the flat but Pauline felt her friend slumping even before they reached the school gate. With the help of two other girls she got Diane across the road but by the time she reached the entrance to the flat, she collapsed. Her father Jim, who had been alerted by another girl battering on his door, ran down and took his daughter in his arms. He carried her upstairs and desperately tried to revive her as her mother Margaret and 15-year-old brother looked on in horror. Jim tried to give her mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, Pauline said. "I'm shouting, 'you're not doing it right'," she said. "I could hear her gurgling. There was blood coming out her mouth." Pauline helped her friend across the road to her parents' house Diane Watson was later declared dead at Glasgow Royal Infirmary and Barbara Glover handed herself into the police. Three months later, Pauline was the first to give evidence at Glover's trial. She told the court that in the days leading up to the stabbing Glover had been hassling Diane. It was only later, she said, that she found out it was because Glover thought Diane had been going out with her ex-boyfriend. This had culminated in a fight outside a shop which ended with Glover's hoodie being pulled up and her bra exposed, making her feel humiliated. The following morning the schoolgirl put a kitchen knife in her bag and took the bus to school where she stabbed Diane to death. Diane and her brother Alan were very close Pauline said Diane was not interested in the boy and that they barely knew Glover, who was in the year below them at school. However, when Glover took the stand she told the court she had been bullied by Diane for over a year. Pauline and others gave evidence saying Diane had never treated Glover badly. The jury unanimously passed a guilty verdict on Glover and because she was under 16 she was detained without limit of time, meaning there was no fixed date for her release. It was a controversial sentence which led to two journalists – Jack McLean in The Herald and Meg Henderson in Marie Claire – writing campaigning pieces about the unfairness of children being detained never knowing when they would see freedom. Crime Next Door: The playground murder Audrey Gillan traces the ripple effects of the murder of a child, by a child - uncovering a decades-long crusade which transforms a Glasgow family. Neither had attended the trial, but they both latched on to Glover's testimony that Diane was a bully. McLean went further, introducing a class element to his claims. He wrote that Diane "came from a background which was rather upper working class" and that she had the "smart white socks of the daughter of the Labour aristocracy". Pauline said nothing could be further from the truth. Margaret Watson was a dinner lady and her husband Jim was doing casual shifts as a postman. The articles compounded the Watson family's pain at their loss and they felt Diane was being victim-blamed and besmirched. Margaret wanted to sue but was advised they had no legal redress as it was not possible to defame the dead. Alan Watson was angry about the treatment of his sister after her death Alan, who was incredibly close to his sister, struggled deeply with her death and how she was portrayed in the media. Less than two years after Diane was killed, he took his own life. Pauline said newspaper and magazine cuttings about Diane were found in his hand, alongside a note saying he was sorry but he just wanted to be with his sister. Margaret gave evidence to the Leveson inquiry in 2011 The catastrophe inside the Watsons' home sparked a decades' long crusade from Margaret. In the chasm left by her children's deaths, she set out to challenge the power of the media and hold them to account. She said she was not able to rest because of the malicious lies printed about her daughter and demanded an apology from The Herald and Marie Claire. The former dinner lady's campaign brought her into contact with prime ministers, lords, and Hollywood actor Hugh Grant's Hacked Off campaign. It also led to her giving powerful testimony at the Leveson Inquiry into press ethics in Nov

title: Health workers run out of patience with Stormont budget delay
description: The practical impact of Northern Ireland's budget delay seemed relatively muted until earlier this week when hospital doctors announced two strikes.
body: The health minister accepted an independent body's recommendation of a 3.5% pay uplift but it cannot be given without a budget The Northern Ireland Executive is now seven months into the financial year without a budget. One of the remarkable things about this situation is the relatively muted practical impacts. Public sector managers have adapted to emergency budget procedures; the money still flows, services are delivered, wages are paid. But this week real consequences began to emerge as hospital doctors ran out of patience and announced two strikes next month. The lack of a Stormont budget means the doctors cannot be given the 3.5% pay uplift which was recommended by an independent body and accepted by the health minister. Elsewhere in the UK doctors have had that extra 3.5% in their pay packets since April. Hospital doctors to strike as pay dispute continues Resident doctors in England accept pay deal and end strikes Divided executive 'speaking as one' on budget, says finance minister "I don't know long you'd like us to wait?" said Clodagh Corrigan from the doctors' union, the British Medical Association (BMA). The BMA met the health minister two weeks ago, and Corrigan said they were told that there will be no pay rise before Christmas "if at all". In response resident doctors will hold a 24-hour walk out on Friday 20 November while consultants and specialists will operate a much-reduced service on the following Monday. A nurses strike may not be far behind. Rita Devlin says "people have to start making decisions" to address the pressures on the health system The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) has opened a ballot, external for industrial action for the same reasons as the doctors. "It is despicable that, year after year, nursing staff in Northern Ireland are forced to fight for a pay award that colleagues elsewhere in the UK receive as a matter of course," said Professor Rita Devlin, executive director of the RCN in Northern Ireland. "Would governments in England, Scotland or Wales allow their health service staff to go indefinitely without a pay award? The answer is no. "So why is Northern Ireland expected to accept this?" A 3.5% pay uplift has been recommended by an independent body and accepted by the health minister Health Minister Robbie Butler has attempted to strike a conciliatory note while acknowledging there will be no movement without a budget deal. "I remain committed to implementing this year's pay award but unfortunately, I am currently unable to do so in the absence of a sufficient budget being agreed for my department," he said. There is no budget because of a consensus among the executive parties that the operation of the UK's devolution funding formula now leaves them so short that they cannot produce a workable financial plan. The UK government has conceded that more funding is necessary and has offered an additional £1.5bn over the next three years, with a first tranche of £525m to be paid this year. The Stormont parties say this is nowhere near enough. Discussions are ongoing between the executive and the secretary of state On Tuesday, Finance Minister John O'Dowd laid out his position in the assembly. "Pressures across departments in the current financial year are around £1.6bn. The offer that is currently on the table is around £525m. "Public sector pay alone is £500m or thereabouts, and any settlement or agreement has to include money for pay uplifts for teachers, nurses and other public-sector workers." Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant has reacted with exasperation. "You cannot keep overspending willy-nilly and not expect consequences from that. It's just irresponsible," he told the BBC. He held a virtual meeting with Stormont ministers on Friday. There was no sign of agreement. More discussions will be held next week. Bryant has suggested the absolute deadline for reaching a deal is January because at that point the money available to spend under the emergency arrangements will run out. A deal will need to be reached much sooner than that if strikes are to be avoided. title: Dubois destroys Wardley in two rounds to retain title
description: WBO world champion Daniel Dubois underlines his status as Britain's leading heavyweight with a devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley.
body: Daniel Dubois (left) has picked up 13 of his 24 wins inside two rounds Daniel Dubois underlined his status as Britain's leading heavyweight with a devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain his WBO title in London. The 29-year-old floored Wardley with a straight right inside the opening 20 seconds of their eagerly anticipated rematch at the O2 Arena and continued his relentless assault. Wardley survived the opening round but was overwhelmed by another sustained attack in the second, prompting his corner to throw in the towel. Dubois registers a second successive stoppage victory over Wardley, just five months after climbing off the canvas twice to dethrone his British rival in a thrilling 11-round contest in Manchester. This time, there was no such drama for the champion, who was dominant from the opening bell as he extended his professional record to 24 wins - 23 by knockout - and three defeats. "Fabio is a great boy, coming in for the second time, but it was my time and my era. I had my intentions, bad intentions from the beginning," Dubois said. "My back was against the wall the first time, this time we just had to go out there and show that we mean business, which is what we did tonight." Wardley, 31, suffered the second defeat of his 23-fight professional career. "I have always thrown myself in with the best competitors out there, the best in the business, the biggest, hardest, meanest guys around so, there is no shame in a loss when you're testing yourself against the best," he said. 'My time, my era' - Dubois beats Wardley to retain WBO heavyweight title - reaction Daniel Dubois turned professional in 2017 A sell-out crowd of 19,000 packed the O2 Arena and made their allegiances clear. Wardley's charismatic yet measured personality has made him a popular figure. He looked full of purpose as he took his time on stage, fireworks exploding in front of him, his usual smile replaced by a look of determination. Dubois, meanwhile, was greeted by jeers as he marched straight past the fireworks and towards the ring, wasting little time soaking up the occasion. Actor Paddy Considine, comedian Rob Beckett, Oasis star Noel Gallagher and darts world champion Luke Littler were among the famous faces in attendance. With 41 knockouts between the fighters, few expected the judges to be called upon. The feeling beforehand was that Wardley's best chance lay in making another fast start, having dropped Dubois inside the opening moments of their first meeting. But in a stunning reversal, it took just 17 seconds for Wardley to hit the canvas as Dubois backed him into a corner and landed a straight right. Chants of 'oh Fabio Wardley' were quickly silenced as Dubois continued to unload punishing combinations. Another furious attack towards the end of the round left Wardley in deep trouble. Trainer Ben Davison, criticised for not withdrawing Wardley sooner in their first contest, stood poised with a towel in his hand as his fighter survived to the bell. There had already been concerns over whether Wardley had returned too quickly after the punishment he absorbed in May, when he was left bloodied and badly swollen. And those fears appeared justified as the challenger struggled to cope with Dubois' relentless pressure. Wardley's hands were low and his punches wild and telegraphed, lacking the menace he had shown in Manchester. Backed into the corner again in the second round, he was subjected to another barrage before Davison leapt up and threw in the towel. Daniel Dubois is a two-time heavyweight world champion Dubois continues to fly the flag for British heavyweight boxing. After losing to Oleksandr Usyk in 2023, he responded with impressive victories over Jarrell Miller, Filip Hrgovic and Anthony Joshua, only to suffer another defeat by Usyk last year. But back-to-back stoppage victories over Wardley have reinforced his standing among the world's leading active heavyweights. IBF champion Hrgovic, whom Dubois stopped in June 2024, entered the ring afterwards, with both men keen on a rematch. However, promoter Frank Warren wants Hrgovic to make his first title defence in Croatia before pursuing a unification fight. The biggest payday for Dubois could come against the winner of Joshua and Tyson Fury's December showdown, which is expected to have the WBA 'super' title at stake. Asked who he wants to face next, Dubois said: "Whoever is next in line, really. I'm the champion now, and I want to get some big fights in. At this stage in my career, big money, big fights." For Wardley, successive defeats represent a significant setback, but his remarkable journey should not be forgotten. The former recruitment consultant had just four white-collar fights before turning professional in 2017. Less than a decade later, he was a world heavyweight champion. Rather than rebuild against lesser opposition following May's punishing defeat, Wardley gambled on an immediate rematch with one of the division's most destructive punchers. It was a gamble that backfired and, after two bruising defeats, he may benefit from some time away. title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
description: Satellite images give clues about how Kim spends his holidays - something far out of reach for most North Koreans.
body: An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year. What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end. After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula. This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family. It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC. The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size. "In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho. Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership. The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures. The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme. Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished. But the regime has long been known to live in luxury. We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m. While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view. Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule. A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer. North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it. North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors. State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists. North Korean tourists on a beach in Kalma A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227. For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure. Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed. Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays". Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself. Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year. The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July. Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan. Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel. The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026. Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view". The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week. Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea. title: Can Hearts prove credentials at scene of title heartbreak?
description: Hearts' last trip to Parkhead ended with their title dream being crushed in the space of 11 minutes. They return to face Celtic on Sunday refreshed and reshaped.
body: Hearts suffered a crushing title-deciding defeat at Celtic Park in May Hearts' last trip to Parkhead ended with their crestfallen players being bundled out of a chaotic Celtic Park and back on to the team bus in their strips and boots after watching their title dream die in the space of 11 crushing minutes. Meanwhile, the 800 Jambos in attendance - and the thousands back in Gorgie - were going through their own football trauma. The mere thought of ever returning to the home of the Scottish Premiership champions would have been harrowing. However, refreshed and reshaped, Wouter Vrancken's men are embracing the trip to face a Celtic side still failing to convince a support that are becoming increasingly disgruntled after another chastening European defeat at Benfica. Earlier this week, influential Hearts investor Tony Bloom repeated his faith in his title ambition for the Tynecastle club. Sunday's fixture (15:00 BST) will give an indication as to whether or not that is likely to come this season. O'Neill defiant in defeat, but Celtic's 'flat-track bullies' fail another big test Celtic suffer fourth defeat in five against classy Benfica Late Nordsjaelland leveller denies Hearts winning start Josh McPake has scored or assisted six of Hearts' last seven goals scored from open play in the Scottish Premiership Despite the back story to this weekend's encounter, Vrancken has demanded his side do not "live in the past". Meanwhile, Oisin McEntee, who was part of last season's squad, has insisted the trip to Glasgow is not a revenge mission. Versatile McEntee scored Hearts' opener against Nordsjaelland as they raised the curtain on their Conference League campaign, but they were served a late punch in the gut in the 1-1 draw. The Gorgie side have only won two of their past 11 away league outings, failing to keep a clean sheet in that period. However, last weekend's 5-0 win over St Mirren forms part of a run of five victories and a draw in seven matches under Vrancken after a challenging introduction to his tenure. Now with the opportunity to make a real statement early in his reign, the Belgian coach is urging his players not to dwell on May's heartbreak. "I'm convinced the players will be [focused] on the game on Sunday and not in the past," he said. "You can't live in the past. You have to move forward and look forward, and you have to take on the next one. "I hope the fire is there every game we play, and not only because something happened in the past. You also don't look in the past too much because it is negative energy, and we need positive energy. "This fire has to burn when you play every game, especially the top games." This video can not be played Celtic 'just have to focus on next game' - Nygren Post-match in Lisbon on Thursday, Martin O'Neill expressed the emotions of a man who had just watched his team cruise to a 4-1 triumph. But the 74-year-old had just witnessed his side suffer a reverse of that, a fourth defeat in five games. The reason for the veteran manager's upbeat vibe was because of his players' response after crumbling in the first half of their Europa League loss to Benfica. The performance level from the Scottish champions improved and they could have scored more than the one goal they managed in the second period, though they were also fortunate not to have shipped more. Like last term, unrest between the fans and board is in the backdrop, but those same supporters are also growing restless at what they are watching on the pitch. Despite that, Celtic have still won 14 of their past 15 league games, scoring two or more goals in 11 of those. And they can go four points clear with a win on Sunday after Rangers drew at Dundee. They have also won 26 of their past 29 home league games against Hearts, although have lost two of their last six. Last term, Hearts picked up seven points in four league games against Celtic - the most by any non-Old Firm side in a single campaign since the 1999-00 season. O'Neill believes Hearts are genuine contenders again and is anticipating a match that will be as challenging as May's dramatic title decider. "I think it will be every bit as tough as it was on the last day of last season," the Celtic boss said. "I genuinely do [think they are title challengers]. I know they've lost two [league] games, but overall, I do, I think they can challenge." After Dubois' dominant win, what's next for heavyweight boxing? title: How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France
description: Demonstrations across the country turned violent, with cars and buildings set alight and shops ransacked.
body: This video can not be played An estimated 550,000 people took part in protests across France, demanding greater investment in education and action on the rising cost of living. The demonstrations quickly descended into violence, with cars and buildings set alight and shops ransacked. At least 1,200 people were arrested on Saturday as riot police deployed tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds. The unrest follows weeks of student-led protests, with demonstrators joining forces to express growing anger over economic conditions and French President Emmanuel Macron handling of the crisis. In a social media post, Macron denounced the violence and said that vandals and looters will be "prosecuted and punished". BBC correspondent Adina Campbell reports from Paris. title: Villa's Manzambi shows Newcastle what they missed out on
description: Aston Villa are a side back in form, with Johan Manzambi scoring the winner against a Newcastle team he turned down to move to Villa Park.
body: This video can not be played Manzambi goal gifts Aston Villa win against Newcastle Johan Manzambi saw first hand how good Aston Villa were last season and is now playing a crucial part in Unai Emery's rebuild in this campaign. Switzerland midfielder Manzambi, who turned 21 on Wednesday, scored his third goal in Villa colours with the winner in a 1-0 victory over Newcastle - the club he turned down before moving to Villa Park in the summer. Manzambi played a crucial role in helping Freiburg reach the Europa League final, before the Germans were comprehensively beaten by a Villa side that scored three times in the opening hour on their way to a 3-0 success. Asked why he had joined Villa, Manzambi said: "The team was very good and I played against them in the final. It's a very good team with a big coach and that was perfect for me." For Newcastle fans it was one that had got away, as Manzambi had looked set for a move to St James' Park before opting to join Villa in a club record deal of just over £50m. Manzambi headed in the winner in the north east on Saturday, unmarked eight yards out when found by Joao Gomes' excellent cross. It comes after he also found the back of the net in the 3-2 win at Tottenham and in the 6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce in the Champions League. "He has made a very good impact with his qualities," said a delighted Emery. "Skills and intelligence, both he has, and his physicality is very important as well to help us defensively and to help us try to keep the duels offensively. "So happy he has scored another goal, fantastic for him." Among players in the Bundesliga in his position last season, Manzambi ranked first for progressive carries of 10 metres or more (116), shot-ending carries (13) and fouls won (78). He then impressed in the World Cup, scoring twice in the 4-1 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina, getting a goal and an assist in the 2-1 victory over co-hosts Canada and also registering an assist in the 2-0 success over Algeria. Unfortunately for Manzambi and Switzerland, a knee injury ruled him out of the last-16 penalty shootout win over Colombia and their quarter-final loss to Argentina. So impressive were his performances last season, that Manzambi finds himself on a 10-man list for the Kopa Trophy, awarded to the world's best player aged under 21. Also on the shortlist are Spain World Cup winners Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsi, along with Yan Diomande - whose performances earned him a move to Real Madrid, with the winner named on 26 October. Since his first start for Aston Villa on 19 September against Spurs, only Manchester City's Erling Haaland - with six - has been involved in more goals among Premier League players in all competitions than Manzambi's five (three goals, two assists). Team-mate Nicolas Jackson, another to join Villa in the transfer window in a deal worth up to £65m from Chelsea, was quick to praise the youngster. "He's an amazing player," said Jackson. "He's still growing. Hopefully he can be better and better every game, score goals and assist me as well. Hopefully we work together and achieve many things together. "He will go a long way and hopefully gets no injuries." This video can not be played Aston Villa manager Emery reacts to victory over Newcastle While playing a crucial role in Villa's present and future, the team he has joined is a lot different to the one he played against in the Europa League final. From the Villa side that won in Istanbul, six of them - goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, defenders Lucas Digne and Ezri Konsa, midfielders Youri Tielemans and Morgan Rogers and striker Ollie Watkins - all left in high-profile moves, while substitutes Harvey Elliott, Jadon Sancho and Leon Bailey are also no longer at the club. It proved a challenging start to the season for Villa as they only picked up one point from their opening four league games, but this win over Newcastle has extended their unbeaten run in all competitions to five matches. As well as moving up to 12th in the Premier League, Villa have six points from two ties in the Champions League after thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 on Wednesday and are in the last 16 of the Carabao Cup, where they play at Bournemouth. How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents Sven Botman was one of six Newcastle players to be cautioned against Aston Villa Jackson has scored five times for Villa since his move and said he was lucky to avoid a serious injury when he was caught in the first half by Newcastle's Sven Botman, who was only shown a yellow card despite an over-the-ball challenge. "I know the referee said yellow card but it was so high and hopefully maybe next time a red card, but it was a yellow," said Jackson. "I nearly broke my leg but anyway it's part of football. The most important thing is we win and we won, so I'm OK." Villa entertain Norwegian side Viking in their third Champions League match of the season on Wednesday before hosting a Manchester City side that have won all seven of their Premier League matches this season. "It was very important after our poor start [to the season] that we needed to try to come back feeling confident, feeling comfortable in how we are building our structure," added Emery. "The players themselves tried to be demanding to change the situation where we are. "Through the [Premier] league we are going to achieve our priority this year, so the league is the competition where we must try to be very consistent." With seven points from their past three league matches, Villa are a side on the rise again. title: Reform politician says smart glasses helping him make speeches in Wales' parliament
description: Jason O'Connell sparked debate when he started wearing the glasses, which have an autocue feature.
body: Jason O'Connell last wore the glasses with a built-in autocue in the Senedd chamber on Tuesday A Reform politician says he is using smart glasses with an in-built autocue feature to help him make speeches in the Welsh Parliament. Jason O'Connell said the technology had helped boost his confidence when speaking in the Senedd, and denied it risked misleading people into thinking he was speaking without notes. "I'm delivering my words in the manner that I see fit," he told the BBC's Politics Wales programme. But the Welsh Liberal Democrat leader called for the glasses to be banned from use in the Senedd, while a parliament spokesperson said a review was under way. They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image? The Meta glasses revolution - is it okay to film people in public? The smart glasses have allowed O'Connell to make speeches by reading a digital script that appears on the lenses of his glasses. The text scrolls as he speaks, and it can also be controlled via a ring on his finger. The Senedd member for the Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr constituency said he had been looking at ways to improve his oratory skills since being elected to the parliament in May. He said: "One of the things I identified as a weakness of mine was that my head was down looking at my notes a lot, and I wanted to get away from that and these glasses enable me to do that." O'Connell says the glasses allowed him to deliver speeches "in the manner that I see fit" Asked if he risked misleading people by giving the impression he was speaking without notes, O'Connell said: "I'm delivering my words in the manner that I see fit. "Other people might use an iPad, they might use a phone, they might use printed paper. "This is the method that I find works best for me during those long debates. "This is authentically my voice, and it's just me relaying that in the way that I feel most comfortable." O'Connell said the glasses had boosted his confidence "massively". "As a new member we do have to get over that hurdle and the more of these you do the more confident you get," he said. "It enables me to communicate effectively with the constituents, the people of Wales. "When I'm scrutinising government, I want to be able to look the government in the face." Unlike other types of smart glasses at the centre that have caused controversy, like the ones above, O'Connell's do not have a camera built into them However, concerns have been raised about the use of the technology, particularly ones that have a camera and can record video - although O'Connell's glasses do not have a camera. Welsh Lib Dem leader Jane Dodds said not enough was known yet about what the glasses could do, and said Members of the Senedd (MSs) needed to have equal access to their use. "What I've called for is that there is a ban on the use of smart glasses in the Welsh Parliament until we have rules and regulations in place which standardise them, and make sure that everybody can have access to them, if that's what they want as well," she said. A spokesperson for the Senedd's presiding officer said: "Rapidly advancing technologies such as smart glasses offer opportunities to improve accessibility and support Members of the Senedd in their work, but we recognise that they also prompt concerns. "A review of the use of this technology on the Senedd estate is under way, and we will bring forward its conclusions shortly." title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
description: There were violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police throughout Saturday in the capital Tirana.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on Saturday Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time. Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration. Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street. The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday. During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard. Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days. Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic. Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks. Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyes Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon. As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police. Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation. The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris. George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes. He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June. In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police. Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too. "We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution. "Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence." Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana. She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights." She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations. Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades. The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative? Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections". The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join. In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things". He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030. He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind. Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity. Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule. Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni. She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest. Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services. Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups. Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions. "Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC. "He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances." Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029. title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as over 1,000 arrested after protests
description: Disorder broke out in cities across the country on a day in which more than half a million joined cost of living protests.
body: This video can not be played How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets. In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse. Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported. La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fire Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving". However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République. Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups. Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons. A car was set alight at the Place de la République in Paris In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building". Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze. Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse. Limoges town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze, the prefecture said A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened." The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers. Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence. Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied. Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers. Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups. These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history. While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty. French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party. The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson. Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on Saturday This video can not be played Watch: 'The mood has really shifted' at the Paris student protests Prime Minister Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical". He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence." Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence. Police fired water cannon at protesters in the Place de la République, Paris French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished." The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October. However, the protests have continued and intensified.
