title: England crush Women's World Cup debutants Wales
description: England scored seven tries before the break, and 13 in total on their way to a comprehensive victory over Wales in their Group A opener.
body: Hat-trick hero Connie Boyd was one of three England debutants against Wales Tries: Boyd 3, Davies 3, Brown 2, Rowe 2, Wilson, Dodd, Strange Goals: Rowe 9 For a moment, when Paige Travis bundled over the line to spark wild celebrations, Wales were in dreamland. On their Women's World Cup debut, they had scored against England, taking advantage of multiple English errors to deservedly pull level inside the opening 10 minutes. Wales could dream of causing a major upset. By half-time, though, England had thoroughly disabused Wales of that notion. The shock of conceding against a team they had scored 114 points against without reply in two previous meetings brought renewed focus to Stu Barrow's England team, who are aiming to reach a World Cup final for the first time. They scored seven tries before the break and 13 in total on their way to a comprehensive 70-6 victory in Perth in their Group A opener. Wing Anna Davies and debutant Connie Boyd scored hat-tricks in Perth, while Izzy Rowe scored two tries and kicked nine conversions for 26 points - equalling the record for the most points by an individual England player in a Women's World Cup match. Women's Rugby League World Cup: England score 70 in emphatic win over Wales While Wales provided threat going forwards, in defence they provided little resistance as England's powerful attack pierced through with frightening ease. A slick move after three minutes resulted in Amelia Brown scoring the England opener, before Wales got their time in the sun. A series of England errors allowed Wales to apply pressure, and they deservedly scored through Travis - who represented England at the World Cup four years ago. The shock concession brought England focus, and a well-constructed move ended in Georgia Wilson scoring in the corner. From then, England were motoring. Hollie-Mae Dodd's drive and offload ended in Boyd scoring her first, before Dodd deservedly got on the scoresheet herself, following up after Fran Goldthorp was held up on the line. On 27 minutes, a quick move of the ball through hands to the left allowed Boyd to power through, before Davies ran more than half the length of the field to score under the posts. Rowe got a try of her own before the interval, making it 40-6 at half-time. The heavy scoring continued after the break. Another debutant, Jasmin Strange - one of two heritage players not born in England - also bagged her first try, before Rowe rolled over her second. The match was summed up by England's 10th try, when a promising Wales attack involved a chipped kick to the corner, but the bounce went kindly for Brown behind her own try line. Brown raced 109 metres up to the other end to score one of the longest-range tries in women's rugby league history, and thoroughly demoralise Wales. Boyd and Davies wrapped it up with three tries in the final five minutes. When England and Wales met for the first time, at Headingley in 2024, England won 82-0 in a match which could be best described as women against girls. Two years down the line, they took to the field as teams who had each earned their spot on the World Cup stage - but England showed why they remain by far the more dominant force. Paige Travis scored Wales' first Rugby League World Cup try It was always going to be a difficult Rugby League World Cup debut for Wales, who had lost their previous two games against England by a combined score of 144-0. Captain Bethan Dainton had said in the build-up to the tournament they wanted to remain competitive despite only having played 13 international games as a nation. And for the opening quarter of an hour in Perth they were exactly that, and will have been delighted when Paige Travis crossed for Wales' first ever Rugby League World Cup try. But the intensity soon caught up with Wales, who by the half-hour mark looked exhausted compared to their opponents, who never showed signs of stopping. And as the game wore on, the gulf between the two sides became more evident, with England running in three tries in the final minutes to put an exclamation point on their win. But head coach Tom Brindle will take positives from the game, and in the long run Wales will benefit for the experience of competing at a World Cup despite the heavy defeats they will encounter along the way. Next up for Wales is Samoa on Friday, a game which on paper serves as their best chance at picking up a result, having also been drawn in Pool A alongside reigning world champions Australia. Izzy Rowe scored two tries and kicked a further 18 points It's sometimes easy to pick halves for player of the match because they have so many touches of the ball, but Rowe has put women's rugby league on notice with a display that shows her immense talent. She combined brilliantly with her back-rower Jasmin Strange on numerous occasions and scored two tries of her own - linking up well with Georgia Roche and then Jenna Foubister when she came on. Georgia Wilson, Hollie-Mae Dodd, Amelia Brown and Connie Boyd also put their hands up, but Rowe's control was such that she just nudges it. Underdogs? title: Eight-try Australia send Scotland to eighth straight defeat
description: Scotland suffer a chastening eight-try defeat by Australia in their WXV Global Series match in Sydney.
body: Brittany Merlo scored the first of Australia's tries against Scotland Tries: Merlo, Stewart, Miller (2), Whitaker (2), Ellis, Karpani Cons: Wood (6), Moleka (2) Tries: Buchanan, Malcolm Con: Nelson Scotland suffered a chastening eight-try defeat by Australia in their WXV Global Series match in Sydney. It was the visitors' eighth straight defeat, four of them in the new competition, having lost to Canada, New Zealand and the Aussies in their home ties. Australia have two victories, both against the Scots, after losing to England and France, their 30-10 win in Edinburgh having lifted them above their hosts in the world rankings. As they sought revenge, the Scots, under caretaker head coach Dave Butcher, lost Sarah Bonar to illness shortly before kick-off and the Harlequins lock was replaced with Bristol Bears' Hollie Cunningham. And they started brightly, with Katie Buchanan collecting the ball on the wing, beating a defender and sprinting over the line to give them a fifth-minute lead in her first international start. Australia, though, responded with five tries by half-time. England's 41-match unbeaten run ended by Canada New Zealand thump France in WXV The Scots held on to the lead until the 17th-minute, when hooker Brittany Merlo went over to draw the hosts level and wing Maya Stewart added another six minutes later, with Samantha Wood converting both. Australia took complete control after centre Meryl Smith was sent to the sin-bin and Desiree Miller, Amelia Whitaker and Ellis all scored to give the hosts a commanding 35-5 lead at the break. Miller crossed for her second two minutes after the restart, but the Scots did manage a reply soon after as captain Rachel Malcolm would not be denied close to the line and Helen Nelson added the conversion. Scotland managed to hold out for close to another 20 minutes before Whitaker broke clear to score her second try with 15 minutes remaining. The hosts completed the scoring in the closing seconds through Eva Karpani after Scotland lost second row Eva Donaldson to a yellow card. title: Man jailed for Starmer-linked arson attacks is deported
description: Romanian national Stanislav Carpiuc was sentenced in June over arson attacks targeting the former prime minister's car and property.
body: Stanislav Carpiuc was convicted over attacks against the former prime minister A man who plotted to carry out arson attacks on property connected to Sir Keir Starmer has been deported, the Home Office says. Stanislav Carpiuc, 28, was one of two men convicted over the attacks, which took place in May last year and targeted a car and two houses. The Ukrainian-born Romanian national was sentenced to two years in prison in June. The Home Office said he had been removed from the UK, without specifying where he had been sent. The BBC revealed the attacks were ordered on behalf of Russia, with an anonymous handler known as EL promising payment to Carpiuc's accomplice, Roman Lavrynovych. Lavrynovych, a 22-year-old Ukrainian national, was sentenced to seven years imprisonment in June. A Home Office spokesperson said: "This was an abhorrent attack and the conviction and imprisonment of these men should send a clear message to anyone blinded by the promise of money from strangers. You will be caught and face severe consequences. "This individual has now been deported from the UK," it added, referring to Carpiuc. Sir Keir Starmer's former Toyota car was set alight in May 2025 The attacks, which took place while Sir Keir was prime minister, began on 8 May 2025, when a car he had previously owned was found on fire on a street where he used to live in Kentish Town. Three days later, on 11 May, a fire was discovered at flats linked to Sir Keir in nearby Islington. He had lived there years before. The next day another fire was discovered at the entrance to Sir Keir's Kentish Town home, which he was renting out to his sister-in-law, Judith Alexander. She told the trial of billowing black smoke rising up the stairs while she was in the house with her partner and her daughter. Lavrynovych and Carpiuc were found guilty of conspiring together and "with others" to damage property by fire between 1 April and 13 May 2025. A BBC investigation revealed the arson attacks were part of an extensive campaign of sabotage, provocation and lies leading all the way to the Russian state. The handler EL, who directed Lavrynovych, offered Russian citizenship in return for other attacks and glorified President Vladimir Putin. Evidence identified by the BBC suggested EL was a young Russian diplomat. Panorama - The Starmer Fires: The Russian Connection In May last year, three arson attacks targeted the prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer. Two properties and a car were set alight. But who lit the fires and why? Daniel De Simone investigates. title: England's 41-match unbeaten run ended by Canada
description: England's 41-match unbeaten streak ends in dramatic fashion as Shoshanah Seumanutafa's late try hands Canada a thrilling 24-21 victory in Toronto.
body: This video can not be played Late Canada fightback ends Red Roses' unbeaten streak Tries: Bauder, Corrigan, Menin, Seumanutafa Cons: De Goede (2) Tries: Feaunati, Harrison, Bern Cons: Harrison (3) England head coach John Mitchell challenged his Red Roses to "find something more" after their 41-match unbeaten streak - dating back almost four years - ended in dramatic fashion as Shoshanah Seumanutafa's late try handed Canada a thrilling 24-21 victory in Toronto. Canada, who previously snapped England's 39-match winning run with a 26-26 draw in Exeter in September, are the first team to defeat them since November 2022, when they lost to New Zealand in the World Cup final. Playing in front of 18,621 fans, a record for a standalone women's fixture in North America, the result also marks England's first defeat by Canada since 2016 and their first against their hosts on Canadian soil, having won their previous 11 away matches. Canada's Savannah Bauder took advantage of Zoe Harrison's yellow card to open the scoring in the 15th minute, but it was England who took a 14-5 half-time lead, hitting back late in the first half through Maddie Feaunati and Harrison, with Laetitia Royer in the sin-bin for the hosts. Sarah Bern cancelled out a stylish solo try from the hosts' Alysha Corrigan early in the second half to preserve England's nine-point lead before Canada's DaLeaka Menin crashed over for a converted score just after the hour mark to set up a tense finale. Three minutes from time, Canada mounted an attack from halfway after a fumble put Harrison's clearing kick under pressure, and replacement Seumanutafa charged down the left wing to complete the comeback. "We're disappointed by the result but there was some very good things in our performance. So we'll stick to our processes," said Mitchell, following his first defeat since being appointed in late 2023. "I guess [the loss] frees us up and allows us to find more. I know this group has got more in them. Sometimes it requires the context that we've just received to dig deeper and find something more." The two sides will renew their rivalry in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October (in the early hours of Saturday on UK time) before England conclude their 2026 WXV Global Series against the USA in New Jersey on Friday, 30 October (21:15 GMT). This result has been coming for England, who showcased vulnerability in their three WXV Global Series home matches in September. Against Australia, the world champions trailed at half-time for the first time since 2020 before roaring back with seven second-half tries for a 48-15 win. The following week, Canada held them to a draw in Exeter while a nail-biting 26-19 win over New Zealand at Twickenham was secured with the clock in the red. This time, Canada's defensive resilience in the face of repeated attacks kept the world champions off the scoreboard until the 32nd minute, but England also lacked a clinical touch in their opponents' 22, with multiple opportunities going begging. Notably, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald had an early try chalked off for a knock-on in the grounding. In defence, multiple penalties afforded Canada the freedom to form free-flowing attacks while it was an individual handling error when delivering the ball to fly-half Harrison which gave the hosts field position to score their match-winning try. The result places England in uncharted territory, with several players in the squad never having tasted defeat on the international stage - winger Jess Breach was unbeaten in her previous 59 caps. But for captain Meg Jones, it is no time to panic. England are "still world champions" and her message is simple: "Stick together, look out for each other, and we go again." She added: "We've got to remember, there's a target on our back continuously. Everyone's got that underdog mentality, that underdog fight. "We've got to be in a position now where we've got to be the quickest to respond. That's the nature of the game. "What an amazing achievement for us as a group. I think they will go down in history as one of the best sporting teams. "We're still world champions, we're still number one, and we'll still keep pushing to be the best we possibly can." In September, Canada captain Sophie de Goede confessed she still has sleepless nights about her side's World Cup final defeat by England in 2025. Even after ending the Red Roses' winning run in Exeter, she was frustrated at being denied the opportunity to go for the win, although reluctantly conceding that head coach Kevin Rouet's call to kick the ball dead was the sensible one. After a historic performance in Toronto, where De Goede's side showcased "the DNA of our team" and "found a way to win", sleep might once again be hard to come by – albeit for far happier reasons. While several Canadian players play their club rugby in England's Premiership Women's Rugby, the national side – ranked third in the world – does not benefit from the same facilities or depth of talent as the Red Roses, even launching a crowdfunding campaign before the last World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps. In the aftermath of their run to the final, the country's government announced a new 775m Canadian dollars (£401m) fund for sport in Canada. Achieving both an attendance record and victory over England in their first home match since August 2025 demonstrates the growing momentum behind women's rugby in the country. "It's a little bit more than just the score at the end because we won on so many levels," added scrum-half Justine Pelletier. "Off the field, the crowd, being home. That win at the end on the pitch was just the cherry on [top]. "It was good to beat England but I think for a few years now, we knew that we could beat them. It was just a matter of time and a matter of putting every detail together." En

title: Dubois v Wardley 2 - heavyweight title fight predictions
description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's heavyweight world title rematch between Fabio Wardley and Daniel Dubois.
body: This video can not be played 'Life on the line' for Dubois & Wardley in rematch Five months after producing one of the most dramatic heavyweight fights of the year, Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley will renew their rivalry in London on Saturday. Dubois, 29, makes the first defence of his WBO world title after climbing off the canvas twice to stop Wardley in the 11th round of their thrilling encounter in Manchester in May. Ipswich's Wardley, 31, suffered the first defeat of his professional career that night but immediately activated his rematch clause in a bid to reclaim his world title. With 41 knockouts between them in 43 combined victories, another explosive contest could be in store at the O2 Arena. Can Dubois repeat his victory or will Wardley gain revenge and become a two-time world champion? BBC Sport spoke to figures from across the boxing world to get their predictions. "It's very hard to pick against the winner of the first fight when there's a rematch. Dubois was so composed, even after being knocked down twice. Wardley can knock out any person at any time, that's what took him from no experience on the white-collar scene to a world champion. You know what you will get with him. "Dubois' issue has never been power, strength or bravery. It's when he has to think and can't find an answer and the panic occurs. If you whack him with big shots, he knows he can whack you back and hurt you. "When he was knocked down, his corner played a great role to keep him calm and he knew what he had to do - hit Wardley clean and often. "I think it will be the same result but Dubois might win a lot earlier this time. Wardley might knock him down and it will still be a thrilling fight while it lasts, but I think it will be Dubois inside five rounds." "Repeat or revenge? I guess you have to go for repeat. Wardley had his moments in the first fight but Dubois was so dominant. Aside from the two knockdowns, Dubois was bullish, strong and aggressive. Getting up from those two knockdowns showed a lot as well. "So I favour Dubois. We know Wardley has the knockout power but I think Dubois is the best heavyweight in the world - with Oleksandr Usyk on an island by himself and we'll wait to see what he will do next. "Dubois is number one - with Wardley top five in the world - and I think he will take a lot of confidence knowing a) he is world champion and b) it's a very quick turnaround for Wardley who took a beating in the first fight five months ago. "If I had to put money on someone, I'm putting all my chips on Dubois getting the stoppage again." "It's a great fight. Credit to Wardley for going back in there after taking some serious, serious damage and still standing - unbelievable tenacity from the man. And he can hurt Dubois - we saw that in the first minute or so of the fight. "For me, though, the smart money would be on another Dubois victory." "It's a fascinating fight. Dubois has tremendous power and is dangerous at any moment, but I slightly favour Wardley. I think his resilience, work rate and ability to find a way through tough moments could make the difference. "I'd give Wardley a 60-40 edge, but I wouldn't be surprised either way." This video can not be played Dubois v Wardley: Relive the First Fight "I think Daniel Dubois will come into this fight with enormous confidence, particularly after the way he came through two early knockdowns and went on to dominate thereafter. I struggle to see what Fabio Wardley can do differently this time to change the outcome. "I expect Dubois to be even more aggressive and menacing from the opening bell. His jab will be sharp, but what makes him so dangerous is that he has more than just a big right hand in his arsenal. "Wardley is a huge puncher himself, but I believe Dubois has more dimensions to his game, with a Plan B and Plan C if things don't go exactly as planned. I don't think we're going to see a long feeling-out process here. "Dubois will look to impose himself immediately, put Wardley under pressure and take control of the fight early. This could be explosive from the very first exchange, so don't blink - because I don't think this one is going to last very long." "I think it's going to be a repeat scenario, and it may even end earlier. I'm not trying to be disrespectful to Wardley but when you're involved in those types of fights and are on the end of a beating like he was, sometimes you're not the same when you come back. "His nose doesn't look like it's recovered. The only way for Wardley to win is to throw the kitchen sink at Dubois for the first three or four rounds. That gives him a chance. But the longer it goes on, Dubois' jab will do damage and Wardley's nose will be damaged again. "Wardley is extremely tough but that can sometimes be your downfall. We've seen it in the last fight and in his previous fights. He's been in some wars and that takes something away from you. "I see Dubois winning between rounds seven and 10." "I'd love Fabio to level the score so we get a trilogy, and he certainly can, but it'll be a tough night's work. My head says Daniel will be too confident and too calculated this time around for Fabio to pose much of a threat, and he'll get taken out again. I think Daniel will pick up where he left off, making it an easier and quicker win than the first fight. But let's see!" "The first fight was called 'don't blink' and I think it should be a legal requirement that you do not blink for this rematch either. It has every single component required to be an absolute barnstormer. "Wardley was second best last time. He had his moments but he is going to have to up his game. title: Online event offers support for menopause and pain
description: Menopause Matters is holding a county-wide online forum on Sunday for World Menopause Day.
body: South Cumbria support group Menopause Matters is inviting people from across the county to share their experiences A support group is holding a county-wide event for women coping with pain associated with menopause and perimenopause. South Cumbria support group Menopause Matters is holding an online forum for World Menopause Day, inviting people to share their experiences and ask questions. World Menopause Day is an annual event started by the International Menopause Society (IMS), with this year's theme Chronic Pain At Midlife. Facilitator Leigh Williams said she hoped Sunday's free online event, being held between 19:00 and 20:00 BST, would "open up the conversation" around pain and menopause. Menopause Matters also holds a monthly cafe-style drop-in in Barrow-in-Furness, offering women the opportunity to meet up in an informal environment. Williams was inspired to become a facilitator because of her own experience with perimenopause and chronic pain. "I know what it feels like when pain starts to shrink your world," she said. "Some of the women that come to the support groups are really desperate for an outlet, they haven't been able to talk about these topics or get the support that they wanted." The online session will bring together a number of professionals and personal perspectives on menopause, and will be an open conversation format rather than a traditional webinar or expert panel. Participants will include a GP, pelvic health physiotherapist, local authority health professional, support group facilitators and people with lived experience of persistent pain. "What we've seen through the menopause cafe is that women's experiences don't fit neatly into boxes," Williams said. "We might start with menopause and very quickly find ourselves talking about pain, sleep, mental health, stress or neurodiversity. "No one person on this call has all the answers. That is exactly why we're bringing different perspectives together." Menopause Matters holds a monthly cafe-style drop-in in Barrow-in-Furness, facilitated by Leigh Williams According to the International Menopause Society, almost three in four women experience joint or muscle pain during perimenopause, while women are up to 70% more likely than men to experience chronic pain generally. Some of the common symptoms of perimenopause and menopause, external are painful, similar to musculoskeletal pain or symptoms of ﬁbromyalgia. They can include muscle and joint aches, stiffness and swelling, reduced strength and pins and needles. "Menopause is something that effects 50% of the population, so we absolutely should be expecting a level of health," Williams added. "Some women can be experiencing these symptoms for a decade - that's a long time to be uncomfortable. "Health and wellbeing isn't just the absence of ill-health, it's about being able to thrive and that's what I'm striving for." Anyone wishing to take part in the free online conversation can do so by reserving a space on the event's booking website, external. title: Call for more food funding due to high living cost
description: Deputy Louise Doublet does not think the cost of living was considered in the ending of a trial.
body: Deputy Louise Doublet said she thought the cost of living was not taken into consideration in the decision A Jersey politician said she thought cost-of-living pressures were not considered by the government when it chose to end a trial of free fruit in primary schools. Since 2024 children in four primary schools have been able to get apples, bananas and other fruit as part of the pilot scheme. Deputy Louise Doublet said: "To have that taken away at a time when the cost of living is still increasing I think has been quite hard for some families". The education minister ended the trial because not enough children were eating the fruit and it was leading to a lot of wastage. The Government of Jersey has been approached for a comment. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey The government announced in September fresh fruit would be included in a school food programme that provides hot school meals for government primary schools. Minister for Education and Lifelong Learning Catherine Curtis previously said the free fruit scheme was leading to "a lot of wastage" and parents "actually asked" for fruit to be incorporated into the school food programme instead. The topic was debated 29 September, external in the States Assembly. Doublet said the minister had responded to her questions in the assembly "centred around the evidence and she informed the assembly that it hadn't resulted in much of an increase in children actually consuming fruit and vegetables and I do accept that". But she added she did not think benefits in terms of cost of living were measured by the scheme. "Personally I would like to see more investment in healthy food especially if it's locally grown food to help families with the cost of living," she said. When asked about the contract with UK company Apetito Limited to provide hot school meals for government primary schools across Jersey she said it was the "best available option". She added she understood people's concerns around the freshness of the food but her "understanding is that the meals are actually frozen rather than artificially preserved". "I would like to see these funded meals extended further because it hits the cost of living for parents and... provides healthy meals for children," she said. title: 'Law change will be my sons' legacy - I hope they're proud of me'
description: Jack and Paul were 12 and 9 when their father killed them during a contact visit despite concerns.
body: Paul and Jack were due to tell family court officers about their father's behaviour before he killed them Claire Throssell missed seeing her sons by five minutes. She was on her way back from work when they set off for a visit to see their father. When police knocked on her door later that night, her first thought was: "What has he done?" Her estranged husband, Darren Sykes, had started a fire in his home while Jack, 12, and Paul, nine, were inside the attic looking at a train set, then locked them in. The unsupervised access visit had been sanctioned by the family court despite evidence that Sykes had abused both his sons and Claire, and was capable of harming them. Paul died on that same night, 22 October 2014, and Jack passed away a few days later, believing he had saved his younger brother's life. Claire made Jack a promise while he lay in her arms in hospital - and this week she feels like, more than a decade on, she kept that promise. Claire, from Penistone near Barnsley, has spent 12 years campaigning to change the law around presumption of parental involvement, which assumes children benefit from contact with both parents after separation, and on Tuesday she saw the Courts and Tribunals Bill go through its final stages in the Commons. That means it will become the law she has spent so long fighting for. I remember sitting in her front room more than a decade ago, nearly a year to the day after the boys were killed. Some people's nightmares stay with you for a long time. But Claire has gone through what happened to her, Jack and Paul, thousands of times, in incredibly intricate detail, with hundreds of different journalists. All because she wanted to keep doing her best to keep her promise. "There are many days when they are dark. I can sit and think 'how do I get through the next minute?' Never mind the next hour or the next day. "But then I remind myself that that are dozens of children that don't have that day tomorrow and I've kind of made it my mission to try and educate other people. "For anyone at risk of harm there is only today, there is no tomorrow and if we can do something better, do it today." Twelve years on, 2026 marks the year that Jack has been dead for as long as he was alive. "The right thing to do is love. The right thing to do is take the boys' love and move it forward and share it with the world. Make difference in their names and make a legacy that will last," Claire explains. "This year, Jack will have been sleeping as long as he was alive. It never feels like a victory, how can it because the boys are not here anymore. "But it does fell like this is a step to the future, to give generations of children to come, a safe, happy life, free from fear." Looking back, Claire now realises that Sykes, who also died in the fire, had been manipulative and controlling throughout their relationship. After they met through work, there were too many flowers, too many phone calls, too much interest in where she was. That turned into insults, shouting and physical abuse. His behaviour got worse after they married and had Jack and Paul. By 2014, she had left and moved in with her mother. Custody of the boys was shared. The boys told social workers that they were scared of their father. Paul told them he was "pure nasty". Claire also had tried to tell authorities that she was scared of what Sykes was capable of. She submitted statements to the courts that he'd told her "he had nothing to live for" and that he could "understand fathers killing their children". His access to his children was limited - but, crucially, unsupervised visits were still allowed. One of those visits was after school on the day of the fire. Claire had dropped Jack and Paul off at school that morning, with a call of "I love you" to the pair as they walked away. Jack, a Toy Story fan, responded with his usual "to infinity and beyond," mimicking the catchphrase of the Buzz Lightyear character from the movie. She noticed that Jack, who normally looked back at her while he was going into school, turned and looked a second time and issued the same line as his brother. Their father had texted that morning saying the boys could play with the train set in the attic. He said he had "two new trains. all he needed was two drivers". Later he set up the track and then lit 14 separate fires, making sure they could not escape. Jack tried to drag Paul towards the attic door, and was found on the landing. He was able to tell a firefighter who rescued him: "My dad did this and he did it on purpose." Jack and Paul were killed in a house fire started by their father Jack's determination to make sure people knew the truth while he was still able to tell them has driven Claire on. "What I've done in the many dark times in the last 12 years is I've taken Jack's courage. The fact he made a conscious decision to think about other people even though he was dying. "He thought he'd saved his brother's life." Paul was alive until Claire arrived at Sheffield Children's Hospital. She says he smiled at her then the light went out of his eyes. "He just fell asleep in my arms." Jack was taken to hospital in Manchester, but died as Claire held him five days later. It was the same day he had been due to have an interview with family court representatives about his father. Claire believes that changing the family court presumption, that children should have contact with both parents, will save lives. "This is not aimed at good parents. This will not affect good parents. This will not affect their access to their children. It will not affect their rights. "What it will do is look at an abuser that's known to the courts and will say 'you don't have automatic access to your children'. "It will not presume you're safe." Not everyone agrees with Claire, The Conservatives tabled an amendment which attempted to keep presumption of contact. In

title: Charity reflects on changing needs over 25 years
description: Help a Guernsey Child says it has provided in excess of £1.2m worth of essential support.
body: Help a Guernsey Child says it works through professional referrers who know the children A charity that raises funds to provide children with "essential items" has said families are facing "changing pressures" as celebrates its 25th anniversary. Help a Guernsey Child said since it was created in 2001 it has provided more than £1.2m worth of essential items, equipment, services and support to local children and young people. The charity said in its early years it gave financial support to a number of larger community projects benefiting children but there was now an increasing focus on helping individual children and families. Alex Jenner, from Help a Guernsey Child, said: "Over the past 25 years, we have seen significant changes in the types of support families require." More news stories for Guernsey Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Jenner said despite changes in needs the charity's "purpose has remained the same, to ensure that children in the Bailiwick are not disadvantaged because they lack the essentials that every child deserves". The charity said it works through professional referrers who know the children and families involved. Applications for grants come in from social workers, health visitors, teachers, doctors, nurses and other frontline professionals and are considered individually by the charity's Directors. The charity said the increasing focus on helping in individual cases meant providing something as "fundamental as a bed, flooring, white goods, clothing, safety equipment or a heating appliance, as well as specialist disability equipment and educational opportunities". It added the nature of their work reflected the "changing pressures" faced by local families. These included the rising cost of living and increased demand for essential household items and practical support, it said. Jenner said: "A relatively small grant at exactly the right time can make a profound difference to a child's safety, wellbeing, education or independence." title: Nightclubs are disappearing - and it's affecting young people
description: One young person said with no nightlife in their town they cannot "let loose and mess around".
body: One under 30 told the BBC they preferred to live somewhere relaxed Under-30s have described missing out on being able to "let loose and mess around" because of a "bleak" lack of nightlife where they live. Henry Gannon said that growing up in Woking he had seen places for young people to gather and socialise "die away". "Communal areas just seem to have vanished," he added. Woking once had multiple late-night venues - now it does not have any traditional dedicated nightclubs left in the town centre. Gannon blamed the situation on the cost of living crisis, which he said was "pricing out" those in their 20s from enjoying themselves. "There isn't really anything to do for younger people who often don't have much expendable income," he said. Alternative options, the 23-year-old added, were "Wetherspoons, sitting in the park or getting a prohibitively expensive taxi back from another town or city". "I feel like I am missing out on a crucial part of being my age, which is being able to let loose, mess around and enjoy life. A quarter of UK towns have lost all their nightclubs, the Night Time Industries Association (NTIA) said in 2025. It added that one in six towns have no late-night venues left. "These figures are a stark warning of the systematic erosion of Britain's nightlife infrastructure," said NTIA CEO Michael Kill. "We are facing a national cultural crisis. "The damage, as we see it, is increasingly irreversible. Once these venues disappear, they rarely return." Adam said the nightlife situation in Tonbridge - where the last club closed several years ago - was "pretty minimal". "There are some nice pubs and small bars, though most things close around midnight," he said. But the 29-year-old, originally from the US, said he was drawn to Kent town as it was "quieter and more relaxed". Still, Adam said, the lack of nightlife forced younger people to go elsewhere for a night out, which impacted the local economy. "It is definitely a missed opportunity," he added. While he recognised nightclubs were spaces for meeting others, Adam said there was also a trend of younger people going out and drinking less - which was good for their health. The twenty-somethings going out - in the gym The BBC previously heard from under-30s that were opting out of drinking culture and getting their "social fix" from the gym. They said that alcohol-free socialising was empowering, avoided hangovers and let them meet like-minded people. Others have also pointed to a cultural shift with more people skipping clubs for sober social events. Finn Ashcroft, from Chichester in West Sussex, said after Covid "people were finding it harder to get out and socialise". However, he said it was important to emphasise that many under-30s were "making do" without clubs and instead creating their own events. Ashcroft urged people to speak up if they wanted more nightlife where they live While its traditional nightclubs had closed, Ashcroft said Chichester had plenty of spaces that could be used for music and dancing. He told the BBC he had set up the event companies C-Side Sounds and Strictly Grooves to "push music locally" in these spaces. "Students were champing at the bit for somewhere to go," he said. "We've definitely helped nurture nightlife within the city." The 22-year-old said the "most important thing" people looking for more nightlife where they live could do was "be vocal about it". "They have the power to [get] local councils and governing bodies to make sure there are spaces for people... to make memories together." title: Avian flu and costs among reasons for loss of captive birds at Castle Espie
description: Difficulties in transporting animals since Brexit has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds.
body: Bird migration is a visible annual event at Castle Espie Avian flu, cost-cutting and Brexit are among the reasons behind the transfer of captive birds from one of Northern Ireland's best-known wildlife sites, according to the charity that runs it. Director of Operations at Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) Alex Lane said avian influenza, as well as difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit, has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds at Castle Espie. The closure of both the site's captive bird programme and guided school tour programme is part of wider WWT cost-cutting measures. An Assembly member has described the changes to the education offering as "disappointing". Alex Lane said the site used to have around 500 birds in its captive collection - but, a combination of Brexit and avian influenza means today, there are fewer than 100. Both the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs and the UK's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs have been contacted for comment. From November onwards, all captive birds at Castle Espie will be transferred to other WWT sites across the UK. The centre, which is located in County Down, will also no longer offer guided school tours. However, the centre have said they will "continue to welcome self-guided school visits". The centre has different types of wetlands Castle Espie, which is managed by the WWT, is located on the shores of Strangford Lough, just outside Comber. The reserve is a safe haven for native and exotic birds, ducks and geese, and some of its collection including globally at-risk species. It has different types of wetlands, including freshwater and sailing lagoons as well as seasonally flooded areas. Cara Hunter said the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing" SDLP MLA Cara Hunter, who sits on the Stormont education committee, told BBC News NI that the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing". "Castle Espie has played an important role in introducing generations of young people to nature, conservation and the unique environment on their doorstep. "I would be concerned that these changes could reduce opportunities for schools, particularly those with limited resources, to access high-quality environmental education." The MLA added that "opportunities that educate, inspire and broaden horizons are quietly lost while Stormont remains distracted from the issues that matter most to families". Captive mallards at the Castle Espie site Castle Espie will cease to offer its formal education offer Alex Lane, Director of Operations at WWT, said rising costs and the challenge around income means charities like the WWT are facing "increasing pressure". "We've got a sizeable deficit and obviously that's unsustainable in the long term," she told BBC News NI. Lane said it is important the WWT have surplus income so that they can "do the conservation work that is part of their mission". She said the site used to have over 500 birds in its captive collection - but, in part due to avian influenza, today there are less than 100. The reserve is a safe haven for native and exotic birds Lane added that another factor in the decline in the number of captive birds is the increased difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit. "There is no aligned system for bringing birds into Ireland from mainland UK. "We've got a vastly reduced collection, and that's not by choice. That is the impact of avian influenza and the restrictions placed on bird movement as a result of Brexit." It is thought that diverging post-Brexit bio-security checks has increased red tape for moving birds between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Under the strict mandates of the Windsor Framework, these regulatory shifts also mean heavy administrative and logistical costs. According to the UK Government's official website, external, the movement of captive birds from Britain to Northern Ireland requires an export health certificate. There is also a requirement for captive birds to be checked at the point of entry when transported to Northern Ireland, to protect animal health and welfare and public health. However, Lane said there will be benefits to the decommissioning of the captive bird collection. "The intent with the site is to reset it as this hub for wetland nature conservation. "We're effectively opening up more space for wild birds." A curlew at the Castle Espie site Lane said the site "needs to stop" its formal education offering in part due to financial pressures WWT faces. She added that there is also an insufficient number of schools booking guided tours at the site to cover costs. Lane said the low number of school visits may be partly be caused by the cost of transport. title: Pope's health should not be taken 'for granted', says top Vatican diplomat
description: Archbishop Paul Gallagher tells the BBC there was no sign of the Pope's ill health prior to his operation this week.
body: Pope Leo pictured arriving at the Gemelli Hospital in Rome for his surgery on Tuesday Pope Leo XIV's health should not be taken "for granted", a British senior Vatican official told the BBC. Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican's foreign minister since 2014, said the news of the Pope's ill health was "a bit of a game changer", adding "it's going to make things a bit different". The Pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung. Speaking on Tuesday after the Pope's operation was announced, but before his cancer diagnosis, Archbishop Gallagher said: "I think we were maybe taking him a little bit for granted." The 71-year-old had surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications. Speaking to Radio 4's the Sunday Programme, due to air this weekend, the Archbishop said: "It's in some ways I think going to be a bit of a game changer after having the latter years of Pope Francis when he was in the wheelchair. "And Pope Leo comes along and he's sporty and he seems to be in excellent health, and now we're told that he's not in excellent health and things have got to be sorted out." Asked how it will make things different going forward, the Archbishop said church figures might have assumed "that he was not quite like the rest of us who are very aware of our vulnerabilities and the ageing process". He went on: "But lots of us have been through similar experiences at different times in our lives, and we've got through them, and so we hope it's going to be the same case with Pope Leo. "I am concerned. I think we've got to ask the question: how was it discovered? What happened?" The first photo of Pope Leo after surgery has been released, showing him celebrating Mass at hospital The Vatican has said the Pope is showing steady improvement in hospital, and he was expected to lead Sunday prayers. They had stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure. The Angelus prayer is traditionally recited at the Vatican, overlooking crowds in St Peter's Square but has sometimes been given from a hospital window by previous popes when necessary. No date has been given for Pope Leo's hospital discharge, but recovery was expected to take around a week. Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis Leo himself announced the news of his operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. Archbishop Gallagher, who is from Liverpool, also said he expected the Pope to visit the UK at some point. "We have exchanged a little bit," he said. "He's just beginning to think about what he might do in 2027, but it's still very much at the examining the possibilities (stage)". He would "bring a spirit of renewed hope", said the Archbishop, after the Pope received a rapturous welcome in France and Spain earlier this year. "But these things do take quite a lot of planning, and so you don't just do it overnight." title: Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says
description: It comes after the prime minister refused to say whether he backed expansion.
body: British Airways planes lined up at Terminal 5 at Heathrow Airport Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion. Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok. His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners". Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business. Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity". Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth." He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department. "We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow." The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners. Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer". Asked about the project in September, Burnham suggested it was an argument for London to decide. "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added. The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow. The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbye said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project. He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said. Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built. The project, which has an estimated price tag of £33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15. The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues. title: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian and US surfers in Mexico
description: Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were killed on a surfing trip in an apparent botched robbery.
body: This video can not be played How a harrowing trial of two murdered Australian surfers ended in a guilty verdict A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each. The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial. The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico. The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them". The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery. The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads. At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings. Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico. The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them. Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California. title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as new US law takes effect
description: Trump says parts of a new law that aims to punish Moscow for its war against Ukraine are against US national interests.
body: US President Donald Trump has used his presidential authority to block numerous sanctions on Russia that were recently passed by the US Congress in an effort to punish the country for its war on Ukraine. In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US "national interests" to withhold some of the sanctions. Trump signed the sanctions bill into law in September, and it was due to take effect on Sunday. It comes days after Trump said the US would import Russian diesel in an effort to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress. The plan shocked lawmakers, and has triggered a bipartisan backlash. The US sanctions law is named for the late Republican South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July. The law took aim at Russian's economy, and gave Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India. Additionally, the law includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions. On Thursday, a bipartisan group of 20 US lawmakers issued a letter calling on Trump to respect the new law, which is due to take effect on 18 October. The lawmakers thanked Trump for signing the sanctions bill, and urged his "full and faithful implementation" of the law. The lawmakers said it would be "decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously" and called on the Trump administration "to apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay". Last week, Trump announced that he had held a phone call with Putin, and had agreed to purchase diesel from Moscow. US allies criticised the move, anxious that it could help Russia in its war effort. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
description: The Amazon rainforest is a crucial buffer against climate change - but deforestation had expanded under former president Jair Bolsonaro.
body: Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off where the rainforest's future is a key issue. Left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro. On 25 October, Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon. Satellite data shows that in the year up to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%. The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil. Why the Amazon rainforest is so important | What in the World podcast Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were cut. During Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2022, the Amazon lost nearly 60% more in forest lands compared to the previous four years, AFP news agency reported, citing official data. Lula reversed Jair Bolsonaro's policies and saw deforestation rates drop to a six-year low during his first year in office. Lula tightened up environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging. "Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," he said in a post on X on Friday. Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species. In a healthy state they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool. But they have come under increasing pressure from decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create conditions for wildfires. Brazil's Environment Minister, Joao Paulo Capobianco, described the decline in Amazon deforestation as "absolutely stratospheric". It is a "historic achievement" for Brazil, said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima. It shows that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions", Astrini said. title: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
description: At the IMF meeting in Bangkok this week finance and business leaders grappled with uncertainty.
body: When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on. There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies. Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity. At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go. In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France. However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions. In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US. Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing. And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis. Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget 'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering. Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs. It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing. This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade. The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own. Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn". It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump. But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far. title: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation
description: A publicist for the actress said the incident stemmed from a "medical emergency" and said she has a neurological disorder that can cause out-of-control responses.
body: US actress Selma Blair has spoken out after being accused of assaulting multiple people on a flight to New York. A publicist for the Legally Blonde star said she "did not intend to harm anyone" and that there was "much more to this story". Blair "experienced a medical emergency on the flight" and is still fighting ​multiple sclerosis (MS), a statement read. Blair's publicist said that the 54-year-old had a neurological disorder that "bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her". The star pleaded not guilty to charges that she assaulted an officer and a nurse after being removed from the flight. She was also accused of assulting two flight attendants on board. Blair's team said the public account of what happened to her aboard a Delta Airlines flight to New York had been "built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline". They also denied media reports that she had attempted to open the door of the aircraft. The publicist noted Blair's fight against multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic illness the actress revealed publicly in 2018. She announced in 2021 that she was in remission for the disease, but the statement noted that the Hellboy and Cruel Intentions star "still has bad days". It added that she also has pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - a disorder that develops in the context of a brain injury or underlying neurological dysfunction, according to the US National Institutes of Health. The disorder affects emotional expression that can result in sudden involuntary and out-of-control episodes of laughing, crying or anger that do not match how a person actually feels. This video can not be played Watch: Selma Blair is seen leaving court after plane incident Blair's publicist described the actress's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and said she still lives with pain daily. "Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night," she said. "There is much more to this story than has been reported and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgement, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion." The incident happened on a flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday evening. New York airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said. A pilot asked for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to audio recorded on air traffic control obtained by CBS News, the BBC's US partner. Blair was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons by the FBI for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US that relates to the on-board altercation. The two additional charges of assault were filed in state court after she was taken off the plane. She has pleaded not guilty to those charges and was released on bail. title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
description: So far this autumn wet and windy weather patterns have been steered away from the UK. When could we see that change?
body: With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season. Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure. This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales. However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El Niño strengthens in the Pacific. As autumn sets in and the nights get longer temperatures around polar regions start to fall. This causes a greater contrast with the warmer tropics which can fire up a more potent jet stream - the fast moving, narrow band of fast winds high in the atmosphere. The jet stream is largely responsible for developing and delivering our stormier pressure systems. Typically in autumn the jet stream would be a regular visitor to the skies above the UK, steering wet and windy weather towards us. However, so far this season it has often been sitting to the north or north-west of the UK. This has meant south or south-westerly winds bringing warmer than normal conditions and high pressure having more of an influence leading to reduced rainfall for many. So far this autumn the jet stream has been largely to the north-west of the UK, steering stormy low pressure systems away These weather patterns have therefore meant only occasional bouts of stronger winds across the north-west of the UK, with little disruption. The heaviest of the rain has also been focused across Scotland and Northern Ireland while parts of England and Wales have continued to be much drier than normal. Parts of Herefordshire for instance have only received a tenth of the rainfall they would normally have seen by mid-October so far this month. Some of the biggest impacts of the dry weather have been across the southern England where exceptionally low reservoir levels have prompted the Environment Agency to declare "severe drought" in some areas. Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know A change in the position of that jet stream and its strength is expected through the coming week. This will allow deeper low pressure systems to affect more parts of the UK marking a shift to a more widespread wetter and windier weather. Forecasts will need to be monitored closely as there is potential later in the week that we could see our first spell of widely disruptive weather this season. There are also longer term signals for increased rainfall and storminess later in autumn and early winter in the UK. The Met Office's current three month outlook covering October, November and December forecasts a double the normal chance of wetter weather and 1.3 times the normal chance of windier weather which is consistent with the type of patterns seen with previous El Niño events. Storms are most often named when potentially damaging winds are forecast, but can also be named for flooding rain or disruptive snow. They were first named to help bring public attention to episodes of severe weather, to help people prepare to avoid the worst impacts by planning ahead. In Europe, there are five storm naming groups created from the meteorological agencies based in a similar geographic location. The UK, Ireland, and the Netherlands form the western storm-naming group which started naming storms in 2015. Weather systems are named by the the UK's Met Office, Ireland's Met Éireann and Netherland's KNMI based on expected weather impacts as well as how likely those are. The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer. The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May. The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months. This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year. It is not unusual to still be awaiting the arrival of the first storm at this time of year. In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November. title: Evacuation orders as fast-moving California wildfire burns homes
description: Fanned by the fierce Santa Ana winds, the Norte Fire is one of 13 burning across the state.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Aircraft deployed to fight burning Bryson fire in Malibu Evacuation orders in California are in effect due to a rapidly growing wildfire that has already burned six homes in the southern Los Angeles area. The Norte Fire erupted on Friday in Orange County and quickly grew to 465 acres by the evening. One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion while battling the blaze. Officials say the fierce Santa Ana winds will blow until Saturday, bringing further risk of more conflagrations. The US National Weather Service (NWS) has issued a red flag warning for several California counties due to strong, gusty winds combined with low humidity and dry vegetation that create critical wildfire spread conditions. The Norte Fire is one of 13 burning across the state, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. In an update on Friday evening, Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff said that six homes had either been damaged or destroyed by the Norte Fire, and one firefighter had been injured from heat exhaustion. "We continue to engage in the firefight, and have additional resources coming," he said. Footage posted online showed blazes tearing through homes in the communities of San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano. The Bryson Fire, burning in the affluent coastal city of Malibu in Los Angeles county, has also sparked evacuation orders throughout the Santa Monica mountains and has grown to 147 acres. More than 400 firefighters have been fighting the blaze. This video can not be played Watch: Smoke towers over California neighbourhood as wildfire burns homes Further south, the Henderson Fire in San Diego country erupted on Thursday, and has grown to over 2,000 acres, including around Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton. The size of the blaze has twice forced officials to close the I-5 highway, an important route that runs the length of the US West Coast. The fires are being fanned by the Santa Ana winds, which normally begin during cooler months from late September to May. Officials say the winds peaked on Friday, but will remain dangerous into early Saturday morning. Six homes have been damaged or destroyed in Orange County Winds topped 40mph (64km/h) in the Los Angeles area, the NWS said, adding that motorists should watch for debris blown into roadways. Temperatures were far above average for this time of year in southern California, further driving up the fire danger. The NWS has issued a heat advisory, saying that the danger of heat-related illness remained high. Forecasts expect temperatures to reach 95F (35C) in southern California on Saturday.
