title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
description: Miranda Hart became emotional and spoke about her health problems as more action unfolded on Friday.
body: Leigh-Anne offered to make Miranda's "dreams come true" by teaching her a Little Mix dance move Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom. The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn. Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight. The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious. This video can not be played Sleepy time at The Celebrity Traitors castle If one of the faithful succumbs to the traitors' soporific tactics and yawns as well, they will be put to sleep for good. We must wait until next Thursday to find out who, if anyone, is murdered in plain sight. That was what passed as a nail-biting cliffhanger this week. There was, thankfully, some more animated action elsewhere in Friday's episode. After Thursday saw King Kenny recruited by the traitors - that episode ending with his deliciously evil laugh - the YouTuber and former aspiring boxer brought fresh and fiendish energy to the turret. "This threesome's going to be different," mama traitor Maya Jama predicted. "There's a new vibrance." James Acaster, her reluctant fellow traitor, was also happy with their choice of ally. "As predicted, Kenny's taken to this like a duck to water," the comedian said, visibly relieved. "He's the opposite of me. So relaxed. He's a natural born traitor." Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked Kenny is relishing the role, barely able to disguise his pleasure as Miranda Hart confided to him over breakfast that "you're my main faithful". The self-declared modern-day Miss Marple warned Kenny to be on the lookout for anyone acting differently, reasoning that "if you're suddenly a traitor, you're going to be a bit on high alert". "I agree," was his straight-faced reply. In the show's diary room, he said: "The first taste of being on the other side - it does feel good, because you have the power. "I'm good at staying calm because as a boxer you have to have a poker face. You can't let the other people know that you're intimidated." However, he later admitted: "On the outside I look calm, cool, collected, but on the inside I'm incredibly nervous." Joe Lycett "just looks so like Cruella de Vil", James Blunt remarked Meanwhile, all eyes were on a different player as the traitors' possible new recruit. The previous day, Joe Lycett had loudly declared that he longed for a ticket to the turret - and even though it would have been, as he later protested, too obvious for the traitors to grant him his wish, it was enough to arouse suspicion. Acaster observed: "I feel like today is one of those days where maybe we [traitors] don't even have to do anything. You have no idea of the gift that I've been given." And in a game where the group often latches on to any conspicuous sign of questionable behaviour, Acaster's prediction was confirmed. "I sort of laid my own trap, and now I'm in it," Lycett conceded ruefully before he headed to the round table. He received 11 of the 14 votes. Standing in front of his fellow celebrities before being whisked out of the castle, he informed them: "I always wanted to start as a faithful and end as a traitor. "I started as a faithful. I did not get my wish. I am a faithful." Joe Lycett, Sharon Rooney, Maya Jama and Bash pictured during Friday's mission One of the few who did not vote for Joe was Miranda. In fact, she was laughed at around the table for not being able to bring herself to write her friend's name. So when his faithful status was revealed, she exclaimed: "Oh my God, my love was real!" The pair had formed a bond, and her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment. "Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said. "I've had times in my life when I haven't had that, through illness, and it's brought up that silly, sensitive soul." The comedian revealed two years ago that she had been bed-bound and housebound with chronic fatigue after being diagnosed with Lyme disease. “Suddenly the floodgates were kind of opening. It was suddenly not about a silly faithful or traitor, you know?” Miranda said it was "very exciting" to be able to take full part in the mission after suffering from a debilitating illness several years ago Miranda also referenced that difficult period during Friday's mission, when the players had to collect and assemble parts of Easter Island-like statues on a rainy hillside. "Three or four years ago, due to illness, I thought that I may not ever have a gentle walk around a park again," she said. "And I find myself up a Scottish Highland, wheelbarrowing along a very large head. It's really exciting." Miranda has been one of the most astute faithfuls (despite not sniffing out Kenny's switched allegiances, yet), but has also proved to be one of the most likeable celebrities. And she provided the clear highlight of the show on Friday - not during a mission or a round table or a scheming chat, but when pop star Leigh-Anne Pinnock offered to console her by making her "dreams come true" and teaching her a Little Mix dance move. title: The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas
description: An international rescue operation for the last 30 captive whales in Canada made headlines. Then five of them died.
body: Marineland was once an iconic Canadian attraction, known for its Everyone loves Marineland jingle Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides. Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls. Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised. That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group. Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio, and even Valencia, Spain. Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes. Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago, and Osorio felt the weight of the moment. "This is the last one to happen, and it's never going to happen again," he says. This video can not be played Watch: First beluga whales rescued from closed Marineland park arrive at new homes in the US Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin. Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has seen the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer. Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain. Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appear to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago. Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease. Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died. Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. According to a tally by the Canadian Press, about 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025. Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes, and following the death of its longtime owner. Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico. Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals which includes whales, dolphins and porpoises. But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild. The Georgia aquarium took in two belugas: Balor and Zephyr Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands". Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales. "If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement. In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs". Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care". They said the remaining rescued belugas show positive signs, including eating well. World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project. As they can't be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales. "I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds. The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m). But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales. One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed, and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer. "They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state, who adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks. "It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild. title: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
description: Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century site almost synonymous with demonstrations in Delhi, has been denotified as a protest site.
body: The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement What is the point of a protest? To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen? For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi. But that may now be coming to an end. This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site. The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned. Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown. Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day. Delhi Police says, external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford. Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed. This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory. Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to it Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand. In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions. Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined. Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament. Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament. "Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper, external. Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years. Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes. Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause. It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance. "It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra. In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar. "It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says. Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise". But sustaining a protest for months was not easy. Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up. In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests. A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution. When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time. "That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she

title: Judge throws out child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
description: The judge in the case said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner".
body: A judge in the US state of New Mexico has thrown out charges against Emmy-winning actor Timothy Busfield on Friday, saying there were issues with how prosecutors presented the case. The West Wing and Field of Dreams actor was indicted in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. Busfield has denied all allegations. The charges stemmed from accusations brought by child actors he worked with on the Fox series The Cleaning Lady, which he directed and produced. The judge said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". The district attorney's office said it is evaluating options on how to move forward. Actor Timothy Busfield indicted on child sexual contact charges State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process. "Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday. The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield. The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial. Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse. The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13. The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him. In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady. Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated. Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother. The BBC's Nardine Saad contributed to this report. title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
description: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto tells the BBC the US risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to end it.
body: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto has warned against showing any weakness to Russia's Vladimir Putin Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks. In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace. US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine. Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US. Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine. Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices. Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table. "Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome. Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war. "If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned. "I think that is completely wrong." Italy's prime minister has become a close ally of Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid. The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified. In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached. The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners. Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace' Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground. At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian". Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with". But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia. "When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said. But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy. During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education. Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs." In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices. Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%. There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too. But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia". "In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued. "It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining." Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe. The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity". A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us. But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response. "You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said. With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione. title: The Papers: 'Mystery drones over UK' and 'Troops heading to Poland for war games'
description: The Daily Telegraph leads with reports that RAF jets had two close encounters with unidentified drones earlier this year.
body: The Daily Telegraph leads with reports that RAF jets had two close encounters with unidentified drones earlier this year while they were completing training exercises over the North Sea. The paper says the "near-misses" took place just days apart, and the mystery objects were spotted at 17,000ft - which it notes is more than 40 times the legal height limit for commercial drones. Incident logs, which have been seen by the newspaper, suggest that the RAF reported the sightings to police and "multiple different external investigations" are ongoing. Hundreds of British troops will head to Poland next month, the Times reports, in order to simulate deploying to Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire. The paper says the exercise, which it calls "the first of its kind", will also include military personnel from France and Germany. The front page also features a photograph of Pope Leo leading mass, just days after surgery to remove part of his lung. The caption reads: "Leo's miraculous speed of recovery". The Independent focuses on what it says is a "pivotal week" in the war in Ukraine, as the White House looks to cut diesel prices further by easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet. The paper highlights "Zelensky's despair", writing that the shift comes just as Ukraine runs low on vital American Patriot weapons. "Police force apologises to women 'abused by officers'," reads the Guardian's front page. The paper reports that nine women have said they were subjected to abuse while in relationships with officers from Devon and Cornwall police, alleging that some of those officers were serving in positions that protect women from male violence. The police force has denied claims that it "covered up" the crimes, but vowed to improve the way it protects women from police-perpetrated domestic abuse. The Guardian adds that the women have alleged at least four of the officers who abused them are still serving. The European Union is working on a plan to ensure that Britons under 30 can take paid jobs in Europe, according to the iWeekend. The paper says that Brussels "could back down" on demands for tuition fees and young people's work visas, which it understands is due to a desire to get an updated Brexit deal over the line quickly. The Sun says television programme DIY SOS, hosted by Nick Knowles, is set to be axed by the BBC as a cost-saving measure. The "telly favourite" has been airing for 27 years, the paper says, adding that the show has helped hundred of families, including building a £1m children's cancer unit. Sources have told the paper the cancellation is a "disgusting outrage". The headline on the front page of the Star says: "Star's suicide threat to gag TV chiefs". It reports that a person described as "well-known" has asked London's High Court to prevent two media organisations from publishing "serious allegations", including of a sexual nature, against him. The individual, who has been granted anonymity in the court proceedings, denies the allegations. Army chief Gen Sir Roly Walker has warned that political leaders will call on "ordinary Britons" to prepare for war, the Daily Express reports. The paper quotes part of his "extraordinary address" in its headline: "You will need to fight for us". Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has spoken to the Daily Mirror, telling the paper that she has never for a moment considered walking away from politics. Rayner said that the "hell" she went through after the 2008 premature birth of her son, Charlie, has given her the strength to deal with anything that comes her way in Westminster. The Daily Mail says a "Tory renaissance" has seen the Conservative Party become the main opposition in British politics again. A pollster told the paper that "tectonic plates are shifting on the Right of British politics", after the Ipsos poll found that leader Kemi Badenoch has "toppled" the 28-point lead held by Reform UK in May. The weekend edition of the Financial Times reports that Apple is "gearing up for a fight" with the Competition and Markets Authority, which wants the tech leader to open up its digital wallet technology to rival payments providers. title: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked on vaping
description: More than one million people now vape who have never been smokers, according to the ONS.
body: When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking. "I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says. But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling. "The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time." Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school. Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data – and that number has risen year-on-year. When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes. Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS. Gracey says the thought of quitting her vape scares her So why are people like Gracey, who have never smoked a cigarette, taking it up? The Londoner believes vaping helps when she's feeling socially anxious. "It's the hand action," she says, "just having something in your hand, just having something in your mouth." Like cigarettes Gracey's vape contains nicotine, a highly addictive substance that triggers withdrawal symptoms like irritability and anxiety when it leaves your system. Vaping has become a "mindless action," she says. When she answers the call to talk to BBC News for this article, Gracey says that without thinking about it, she had been lying in bed, with her vape in one hand, and her other hand scrolling Instagram. The habitual aspect of regular vaping is something GP Dr Helen Wall hears a lot from her patients. "It's that kind of psychological dependence on something else to almost regulate their emotions," she says. Like Gracey, Malin Andersson, who vaped until recently, says her habit went hand in hand with doomscrolling. She had also tried cigarettes but never considered herself a smoker. At 33, she falls in the age range most likely to vape. The ONS report suggests nearly one in six people aged 25-34 in the UK may use e-cigarettes daily or occasionally. The domestic abuse campaigner and former Love Island contestant started vaping when she was going through a stressful break-up and looking for comfort. She believes it was the physical action that got her hooked. "It's a dopamine hit," Malin says. "It's literally an adult's version of a dummy." She says it was dulling her senses and leaving her demotivated. Malin became so frustrated with how reliant she had become on her banana ice-flavoured vape that she quit in May this year. "It was annoying me so much that it was always in my hand that I'd end up throwing it across the room," she says. Malin said she believed her mental and physical health had improved since quitting vaping in May Alex, from Manchester, also gradually formed a vaping habit, which started after she occasionally vaped on nights out and then began to take the vapes home. The 26-year-old, who didn't want to give her last name, says the habit would become such a constant part of her life that she would work while "lying in my bed with my laptop in front of me and then my vape on my chest". Prof Sarah Jackson, from the University College London Alcohol and Tobacco Research Group, points out that while "alarm bells" may ring at the recent ONS figures, it could be the case that some of the people in this group would have started smoking if they hadn't started vaping. "In which case, vaping has diverted them away from a more harmful behaviour, which is good news," she says. "On the other hand, there will be people that are being exposed to more risk than they would have otherwise." She points to a 2024 study from UCL researchers that found nicotine use had risen among young adults in England, although cigarette smoking had declined. "We can infer from that that some of the people who are vaping wouldn't have smoked otherwise," Jackson says. The ONS report says about 5.4 million people aged 16 and over vape in Britain, while the number of smokers of all ages continues to steadily fall. Some 4.9 million adults in the UK smoke. The UK is aiming to cut smoking rates and reduce the appeal of vaping among children and young people. The marketing of vapes - which has featured bright colours and sweet flavours - is being looked at, with a recent government consultation on new measures expected to give a response in due course. Within the 1.1 million vapers who never smoked, "there probably is a group who would not be vaping [without] the marketing of vaping which is very prominent", says Hazel Cheeseman from charity Action on Smoking and Health. The NHS warns non-smokers and those aged 17 and under to never vape, while it's illegal for anyone under 18 to buy vapes. Disposable vapes - seen as a key driver in the rise of youth vaping – were banned last year. Gracey says she buys a refillable vape at a cost of £5 every day Wall says the heavy marketing of vapes in recent years has helped to fuel a "misconception" that they are "safe and not addictive". Gracey thinks vapes should be sold in the same standardised plain packaging as cigarettes because it "looks scary". "With vapes, they have all these flavours, all these pretty colours - it's just making us more attracted to it". While she says vaping is seen as far more socially acceptable among her generation than smoking, she finds her habit problematic and has considered quitting to save the £35 a week it costs her. But just like smoking, giving up vaping can be a struggle. And for Alex, vaping led her in the opposite direction. S

title: Not sure what to wear for Halloween? These outfits are set to be the most popular this year
description: Freaky Nikki, Dolly Parton and whimsical costumes like gargoyles are popular among adults dressing up this year.
body: If you're still on the hunt for the perfect Halloween costume, then you might want to look to gargoyles, Freaky Nikki and Dolly Parton for inspiration - they are all predicted to be popular outfit choices for 2026. "People don't necessarily want to look frightening - they want to look extraordinary," says costume designer Tamar Zaig, who runs a fancy dress hire shop in London and says she's seeing a "real appetite for escapism, glamour and a bit of dark humour" right now. And as usual, the year's major film and TV releases, as well as news and pop culture trends, are also driving outfit choices. So, here are some spooky ideas to try. By order of the Traitors, channel your inner Claudia The Traitors is a timely choice, with host Claudia Winkleman's look easy to pull together. Think fringe, tartan, chunky knitwear and some heavy eyeliner. Winkleman is "a classic that we see every year", says the creator behind the popular Love of Huns Instagram account (who did not want to be named). But she "will definitely be making a return this Halloween off the back of all the Traitors love and the icon that she is". Released at the beginning of the summer, ice hockey romance drama Off Campus sees characters Allie and Dean attend a Halloween party dressed as J-Lo and Top Gun's Maverick Ice hockey romance series Off Campus also features in many of the outfit inspiration videos trending online. The show's main characters, Dean and Allie attend a Halloween party in the series, with Allie dressed as J-Lo and Dean as Top Gun's Maverick, which could provide a rather meta costume opportunity for fans or couples. Another of this year's most popular TV shows, Widow's Bay - which scooped up at this year's Emmy Awards - is also inspiring outfits. Maria Nichol, 35, a horror aficionado from Ely in Cambridgeshire, plans to dress as Kate O'Flynn's character Patricia - and is trying to replicate her gothic headdress, which includes antlers and a taxidermy fox, by crafting her own from foam clay, foil and fur. Inde Navarrette's character, Nikki, in Obsession is providing huge costume inspiration One of the most replicated outfits looks set to be Nikki from indie horror film phenomenon Obsession, say fancy dress shops, influencers and make-up artists. The character's red and black zebra print top went viral earlier this year, selling out online and reportedly leading to a 27,000-person waitlist, external before returning to stores. "We've had customers asking for Nikki," says Muhammad Rai from shop Fancy Dress Town in London, with people trying to recreate her with a red corset and wig, "although unfortunately, we currently have none in stock". "I've had a few people ask me to do that make-up for them," adds special effects make-up artist and prosthetics designer Meg, from Liverpool. Meg (left), from Liverpool, took inspiration from Buffy the Vampire Slayer during a previous spooky season We might also see a surge in 1990s and 2000s nostalgia, believes Nichol, with party-goers dressed as Buffy, Hilary Duff and characters from Practical Magic, after the film's sequel was released last month. Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman cast a spell in Practical Magic 2 Gothic horror: Jessie Buckley in The Bride! and Margot Robbie in Wuthering Heights As well as Obsession, some of this year's other top grossing films – such as the Michael Jackson biopic, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey – are also on the cards. Look to ancient Greek epic The Odyssey for costume opportunities "I'm seeing a lot of Gothic romance and historical influences not only in films such as Wuthering Heights, The Odyssey and The Bride!, but in fashion too, with corsets, lace, dramatic silhouettes appearing on the catwalks, particularly at London Fashion Week," says designer Zaig. "Along with Peaky Blinders, I think these kind of productions have brought some great theatrical costume styles back into the spotlight, from elaborate period gowns and Greek mythology to 1930s glamour." Ready to scream? Horror franchises Scream 7 and Scary Movie 6 will likely provide inspiration Classic horror franchises such as Scream and Scary Movie (Scream 7 and Scary Movie 6 were both released this year), should also not be overlooked, say fancy dress shops. Ghost face masks from Scream have made up 30% of sales at Hollywood Fancy Dress in Bournemouth, says the shop's head manager Ben Cook. Meanwhile, characters from hit series Wednesday and Bridgerton are likely to make a return. And outfits from KPop Demon Hunters – which won best animated film at this year's Oscars - are the current biggest seller for children, according to Cook. Demand for Dolly Parton-style stage outfits are in demand from those wanting to pay tribute to the music icon It's not just fictional characters who might be joining your Halloween night out. "I also expect to see plenty of instantly recognisable personalities, from the iconic Dolly Parton with her extravagant wigs and rhinestones to political figures such as Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin," says Zaig. Rai from Fancy Dress Town also says blonde wigs, cowboy-style waistcoats and microphones are in high demand, following the death of Parton aged 80 in August. Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin could prove to be popular outfit choices Meanwhile, pop icons Charli XCX and Madonna could make a good duo costume, suggests Love of Huns, following the pair's collaboration on remix Danceteria Afterhours. "Both have had enough iconic looks between them, so there's plenty to work with." Other fresh pop culture references could include Mariah Carey and The Last Supper, after the star became a meme for sharing a selfie with the Leonardo da Vinci painting in Milan,, external they add. title: Two-week half terms: The school holiday no one can agree on
description: Parents are divided, with some struggling to arrange childcare while others eye cheaper holidays.
body: Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school that has just introduced a two-week half term. Buckland, 45, has two jobs: teaching medical students at a hospital in Brighton and working at a vintage shop in her home town. The 45-year-old receives universal credit and is worried about the cost of looking after her son while school is closed. "What I'm trying to do is find out who I can get childcare from and work around that," she says. "I'd like to work, I need money. It's not cheap to live these days." But money isn't Buckland's only concern. She's also trying to piece together the patchwork of childcare needed to cover the break. There's a local holiday club, but it's only running for one of the two weeks, which Buckland says "parents are up in arms about". She'll also have to work at the hospital some days. As a result, she's considering asking family to help, or even going to stay with a fellow mum so they can take turns with the kids. Samantha Buckland, pictured here with her son, says she's trying to piece together the patchwork of childcare needed to cover the break Most councils in England still favour the traditional one-week half term, according to the website School Term Dates, but several local authorities have opted for a fortnight in 2026/27 - including Nottinghamshire, Bromley and the Isle of Wight. The BBC spoke to many parents for this article and while some cited the advantages of a longer mid-term break - cheaper holidays and their children's educational wellbeing - others said they would struggle with childcare and that it placed too much strain on the family, especially coming so soon after long summer holidays. Local authorities don't determine term dates for all schools in their area. For example, academies and faith schools can often set their own. But those schools with the freedom to choose may still decide to follow suit. Education is a devolved power in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland - with differing academic calendars in each nation. Wales shelved plans to adopt a two-week autumn half term in 2024, while there are some schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland that have introduced the longer break. Surrey County Council switched to two weeks this year, but then decided to return to one week next year after head teachers expressed worries about the impact. Most schools that bring in a longer half term will shorten the summer holidays in turn. The number of pupils in England attending academies has grown rapidly in the past decade, according to Department for Education data, external published in June 2026. Indeed, 60.4% of all pupils now attend an academy. As academies spread, the school calendar is becoming increasingly fragmented - creating fresh challenges for parents. Alistair Pringle, 42, lives in Washington in Tyne and Wear with his wife, a teacher, and two children aged 11 and six. His eldest has just started at a secondary academy with a two-week half term, while his youngest goes to a primary academy with a one-week half term. "This is the first time we've had to deal with different half terms," Pringle says. His children and wife will be off together for the first week. His eldest then has a second week off, but by then the others will have returned to class. Pringle works full-time in marketing - often in the office - but is fortunate his employer "can accommodate it if I need to work from home". "The thing that concerns me is not so much the childcare, it's the fact that I have to work," he says. "Yes, my eldest would be at home and she'd be looked after, but what's she getting out of that second week?" Parents paid by the hour and those in less flexible jobs, such as those working unsociable or set hours, or in specific locations like hospitals or shops, told BBC News two-week half terms could be particularly challenging. Annual leave is also a big issue. Full-time workers should get at least 28 days' paid annual leave per year, but this is well below the average amount of school holiday. Workers are entitled to take up to 18 weeks' unpaid parental leave for each child up to their 18th birthday. They can't take more than four weeks in a single year, however, and the cost of taking time off makes it an unrealistic option for many. But a two-week break can work well for parents, depending on their circumstances, often allowing families to take a cheaper holiday rather than paying over the odds in peak season. Fay Harding is a fan. The 43-year-old lives in Nottingham with her husband, a teacher at a local authority-run school, and three children at academies. Because her husband and children all go to schools with two-week half terms and are all off at the same time, she says "we don't have to worry about additional childcare costs". Harding's family is planning to spend the first week visiting family in Wales, then she'll work the second week while her husband looks after the children. "It also gives us the opportunity to have two weeks away," she says. "We don't have to pay premium prices in the summer." Lucy Walker-Etchells, 40, is a teacher at Dixons Brooklands Academy in south Manchester. Her school has a two-week half term, but for the majority of her teaching career she's had one week. "I definitely much prefer two weeks," Walker-Etchells says. "Most teachers would agree because autumn is an intense term. It's really nice to have two weeks to recharge and come back feeling refreshed." Moving a week's holiday from the summer to the autumn half term could benefit pupils too, she believes. "Sometimes, vulnerable students really struggle being off for so long over the six-week holiday if they're in difficult circumstances," she says. title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
description: The 16-year-old suspect previously attended the primary school and had targeted a special educational needs classroom, police say.
body: This video can not be played Oregon school shooting: Police name victims and say suspect was former student An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class. As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander ran inside. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, he opened fire and killed the teen. The bystander, a dad of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend when he saw the suspect firing in the car park then shooting through a window to enter. The details of the Thursday attack were confirmed by police, who said the 16-year-old suspect was a prior student at the school. Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class. "To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday. Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert. The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said. Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition. Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives. He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed". He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there. A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said. Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear. Police identified two of the victims as five-year-old Rhoam Summer (left) and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert (right) Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect. But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action. The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside. Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him. In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition". The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy". US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero". Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention. "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said. Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well". Kayla Epstein contributed to this report. title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
description: For 15 months, a high-security courtroom in Hamburg has been hearing the case of Christina Block, accused of ordering the abduction of her children.
body: Christina Block, 53, denies knowing about the planned abduction of her children It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history. Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband. There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel. In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage. Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children. There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year. Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire. Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark. They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others. The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment. Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car. On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands. The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg. After Stephan Hensel and Christina Block separated, the children lived with their mother Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention. Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting. All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation. The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children. Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him. In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed. A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back. In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending. He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her. She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative. She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that. The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation. Former foreign intelligence chief August Hanning was arrested after police investigating the Christina Block case searched his home Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them." The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022. Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case. However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers. Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation. Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded". Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months. The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court. title: £800,000 spent on scrapped sports dome project
description: Ulster University has also revealed the multi-million pound dome would have cost a further £1m to run each year.
body: Announced back in 2024, the proposed dome was billed as a first for Northern Ireland A Northern Ireland university spent £800,000 on a planned indoor sports dome in Londonderry before the project was scrapped. Plans for Ulster University's (UU) multimillion pound dome, which was to house multiple sports, including rugby, football and Gaelic games, were first announced in 2024. But in August UU axed the project saying it was no longer financially viable. The university, which earlier this year announced it needed to make savings of about £25m and would be making up to 450 staff redundant, has revealed it spent hundreds of thousands of pounds on the dome project before it was axed. UU said, in response to a Freedom of Information request from BBC Radio Foyle's Mark Patterson Show, that approximately £700,000 had been spent "on project-related activities". Project management and governance arrangements cost the university a further £100,000, UU said. Sinéad McLaughlin says it is 'regrettable' it too so long to determine the dome was not viable financially SDLP assembly member Sinéad McLaughlin told BBC Radio Foyle the dome had been announced to "much fanfare" but it had become clear the dome was an "unaffordable project". "But my problem is that there is legitimate questions about how we reach the position after spending £800,000," she said. McLaughlin added: "It does seem a lot of money to be spent before they came to the conclusion that it was unviable and financially unsustainable." The Foyle MLA said it was unfortunate "it took so long to get to that point." According to the UU figures given to BBC Radio Foyle, the overall costs to build the dome had spiralled from an initial £16.8m to £20.1m at the time the project was scrapped It further said that as a commercial entity the dome would have cost in excess of £1m in running costs annually. McLaughlin said with the higher education sector in Northern Ireland in financial crisis there was "is no way that Ulster University could have sustained the upkeep of that dome." When plans for the indoor sports arena were first announced, the 15,000 square metres (3.7 acres) dome, was described as "game-changing" for Derry. UU said as well as hosting sport, the dome would also host community and musical events, adding it was "a first-of-its-scale facility for Northern Ireland". It was being part funded by the international PeacePlus programme - jointly supported by the European Union, the UK government, the Irish government and Stormont - which was to provide €10.86m (£9.16m). In their Freedom of Information response, UU said its proposed contribution to the dome was to be £8.3m. At the time the university announced the dome would not go ahead, UU said the decision not to proceed with the project was "an inevitable consequence" of the "lack of a sustainable funding model for higher education" in Northern Ireland. The Special EU Programmes Body (SEUPB) told BBC News NI that no PeacePlus funding had been paid. It said it was working on options on how the funding will be reallocated "and remain committed to delivering impactful projects for communities across the area and throughout Northern Ireland and the border counties of Ireland". It added it could not give a commitment that any reallocation will be in the north-west. title: Swinney insists 'stars are aligning' for Scottish independence
description: The first minister will tell delegates at the SNP conference in Aberdeen that 2026 has been a turning point in Scotland's "journey to nationhood".
body: John Swinney will deliver his keynote speech to the SNP conference in Aberdeen John Swinney will insist that "the stars are aligning" for Scottish independence during his keynote speech to the SNP conference later. The first minister will tell party members in Aberdeen that 2026 has been a turning point in the country's "journey towards statehood". Swinney will stress that "in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast, every first minister now supports our nations' right to self-determination". He will seek to press the case for another independence referendum in the wake of elections in May which saw the SNP win a record fifth term in government at Holyrood. Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution' Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say 'Bring it on': Flynn challenges Burnham on independence referendum The nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland held a summit in Cardiff last month where they signed an agreement, which is not legally binding, that said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy". Swinney will tell his party's supporters that "one by one, the stars are aligning in our favour". He will say that if the SNP lost May's Scottish Parliament election, the case for independence "would have been set back decades". While the SNP won the Holyrood ballot, the party failed to win the overall majority Swinney had set as a target for trying to force a second referendum in the face of Westminster opposition. Despite that, Swinney will declare that "there is no turning back". He is expected to say: "The SNP is making the weather. "And make no mistake – the wind is now firmly in the sails of Scotland's independence movement." The first minister will go on to claim that the unionist parties at Westminster are "weaker than they have ever been". Swinney introduced Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth to the conference on Friday Swinney's address to the SNP conference comes the day after Andy Burnham made his first major speech in Scotland since moving into Downing Street. The prime minister used that visit to extend an olive branch to Swinney, saying he wanted to work together on giving more power to local communities. Speaking in Motherwell, the Labour leader said he wanted to "move beyond the old politics of conflict" as he offered to work with the SNP to deepen devolution in Scotland. Burnham previously told Swinney during a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits". The meeting came after Burnham told MPs that a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed. Since 2014, successive UK governments have opposed any further referendums. Scotland previously voted against becoming an independent country by 55% to 45%. In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that any further vote would require the agreement of the UK government. title: Data centre developers may build 'climate-wrecking' gas power plant next door
description: Plans for a data centre at Cardiff East Park and Ride site faces growing opposition from politicians.
body: The proposed site for the development is surrounded by greenery on one side, and flanked by the A48 on the other The developer of a proposed data centre in Cardiff has said it is also seeking permission to build a gas power plant to get it up and running. Developer Curtis Hall said the plant, which could operate for up to five years, may be needed if the site cannot get on the national grid quick enough. It also said the gas turbine plan was a "worst-case scenario", and the project - planned for the site of an existing park and ride near Llanrumney - would bring significant benefits. Friends of the Earth called it "climate-wrecking" infrastructure, and almost all the area's Members of the Senedd (MSs), and a Welsh government minister, have now formally objected to the plans to build the data centre. A senior Labour councillor from Cardiff council - which has an agreement to sell the site to the developer - had also objected. The proposed data centre at the Cardiff East Park and Ride near Llanrumney has prompted significant local concerns The Welsh government is considering whether it will take over the planning process for the facility - meaning Cardiff Council is unable to grant planning permission in the meantime. The government is also planning to publish its own policy on the wider issue by the end of the year. Interest in building data centres has increased with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies - but they have been controversial worldwide, in part for the amount of electricity they require. Cardiff East Park and Ride currently serves staff and patients using Cardiff's University Hospital of Wales. James George is among those worried about the development near Llanrumney Some of those living in a new-build housing estate nearby are concerned about the project, including James George, 32, who said he was worried about the impact on the environment and his home. "The main concern is the noise and the pollution, like they have to run a diesel generator in case of any power disruption," he said. Alexander Grant, 51, said: "My main worry is the situation with the Heath hospital with regards to the staff and the patients." "There's also other reasons as well, from the environmental side of things. I think it's an absolute travesty." Dale Harvey said he was concerned it would add the noise from the A48 dual carriageway, saying the proposal was "not great". "You buy a new build, and we're being told all of a sudden there's going to be generators run - all the fumes and all the noises," he said. The developer said the site would not be audible locally, and air quality would not have a significant impact. Alexander Grant says he is worried about the impact of patients at the University Hospital of Wales Planning documents for an outline planning application detail a "temporary ancillary energy centre" with gas turbines that have a maximum generating capacity of 49.9MW. They say that the energy centre is "proposed to start in operation in July 2028 and last approximately for five years until the site has a full electricity connection [until July 2033]". The centre, according to the documents, would include five gas turbines, a steam generator, and another two gas turbines on standby. In the long-term the data centre would require a connection of 150MW from the national grid. This may not be delivered, however, until between 2030 and 2034. Energy generation facilities of 50MW need planning permission from the Welsh government. Curtis Hall denied it was trying to avoid having to make such an application by limiting the plant to 49.9MW. Another 40 diesel backup generators would also be needed after a connection is made to the grid to ensure "continuous power". In Case You Missed It Why a hospital park and ride could be replaced by an AI data centre The use of fossil fuels to power the centre prompted criticism from environmental campaign group Friends of the Earth Cymru. Its interim director Jenny Lloyd said: ​"After a summer of heat waves and drought and worries about flooding over the autumn and winter, it's completely irresponsible to give the green light to this climate-wrecking piece of infrastructure." Plaid Cymru MS Nick Carter, who represents Cardiff's Caerdydd Fynnon Taf constituency, said: "There is no reason why a data centre needs to be sited in an urban area close to schools and care homes, when in fact underneath the headlines is a small gas-fired power station." Senior Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman added his voice to those objecting this week. The member of the Cardiff Council cabinet and Llanrumney ward councillor said in a letter it was "hard to reconcile" the centre's emissions "with Cardiff's climate emergency declaration and Planning Policy Wales". As well as the data centre, the plans included a new bridge and link road for pedestrians and cyclists. Curtis Hall previously had planning permission for a logistics centre. According to Cardiff Council the company had switched to a data centre because of "changing market demand". The company said the gas generation was "not the data centre's permanent power supply, and once the grid connection is live it would no longer be needed". "If the connection arrives in time, the energy centre will not be needed at all," it said. "Gas turbines appear in the planning documents because they represent the worst case for emissions and noise, so assessing them tests the upper limit of any impact." The company said the technology was "not confirmed" for the energy centre - suggesting fuel cells that convert gas or hydrogen to electricity could be used. It said the air quality effects of gas and diesel generators were also "not significant". In response to climate change concerns, Curtis Hall said south Wales' electricity grid was "decarbonising fast" with plans for floating offshore wind.
