title: Ranking the Premier League's all-time greatest super subs
description: Some players are destined to make their biggest impact off the bench, but who are the top 10 Premier League super subs of all time?
body: Mikel Arteta may be attempting to rebrand them "finishers" but there's only one phrase in the footballing lexicon to sum up today's focus: super subs. Yes, we're looking for those players renowned for making a devastating impact off the bench, those guaranteed game-changers a manager turns to when in desperate need of a goal. First, an honorary mention for some who missed out, such as one-season wonder Adam le Fondre, who holds the record for the most goals off the bench in a single Premier League campaign - five of his eight came in a three-game spell in January 2013. Hernan Crespo boasts the best goals-per-game ratio but his six in 16 substitute appearances for Chelsea represents a small sample size, likewise ex-Norwich and Leicester forward Mark Robins with five in 14 outings as a replacement. To make the all-time top 10 Premier League super subs, players need to have consistently delivered throughout their careers, providing goals and assists. So here we go, I've ranked mine below - you can have your say in the comments, too. Theo Walcott, replaced on 168 occasions, holds the record as the most subbed off player in Premier League history. Yet it's his impact coming on to the pitch we're interested in here. Bursting on to the top-flight scene as an explosive teenager, the flying forward was often used by Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger to stretch defences with his pace and movement - a lactic acid-inducing sight for flailing full-backs. The England international pieced together an impressive substitute CV throughout his Premier League career. No-one has more than Walcott's 14 assists as a sub - Ryan Giggs and Marc Albrighton are level - while he also scored 10 goals as a replacement across his time with the Gunners, Everton and Southampton. It puts him fourth on the list for overall goal contributions off the bench. This was a toss up between Victor Anichebe and Divock Origi, with both forwards contributing exactly half of all their Premier League goals as a substitute. Ex-Everton, West Brom and Sunderland striker Anichebe edges it having notched a couple more - a tally of 13 placing the former Nigeria international in joint-eighth on the all-time list - while he also chipped in with five assists off the bench. Roman Pavlyuchenko was also unlucky to miss out - 45% of his 20 Premier League goals came as a substitute for Tottenham. Anichebe scored 50% of his 26 Premier League goals as a sub - the joint-highest percentage for any player to have scored at least 20 times in the competition There's a good case for Danny Welbeck, who as the only current player in the top three, with 19 goals, still has time to catch those above him. Welbeck was a goalscoring sub at Manchester United and Arsenal but perfected the art on the south coast, with 12 of his tally coming during six years with Brighton. The 35-year-old is now at Chelsea but - with apologies to Danny - there is another former Blue whose stats demand a place on this list. Daniel Sturridge has two fewer substitute goals then Welbeck but has scored a slightly higher percentage of his overall Premier League tally as a sub - 22%. The former England man, who played for Manchester City, Chelsea, Bolton, Liverpool and West Brom in the top flight, was good for an assist, too. In fact, when you take his total goal contributions of 24, he provided at a more prolific rate than every substitute in Premier League history - bar Edin Dzeko and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. Richarlison matches Sturridge for minutes per goal contribution, but with eight fewer the Brazilian, perhaps harshly, misses out. Sturridge scored 17 of his 76 Premier League goals as a substitute and also made seven assists off the bench A World Cup and Champions League winner, one of the few trophies Olivier Giroud hasn't got his hands on is the Premier League title despite a knack for scoring important goals off the bench. The Frenchman is second on the all-time substitute scoring list, accounting for 21 of his 90 top-flight goals - that's almost a quarter - with only Dzeko, Solskjaer and Javier Hernandez boasting a better minutes-per-goal record as a sub. Giroud honed his ability to make a late impact at Arsenal and Chelsea, making 103 substitute appearances in total across 10 seasons in the Premier League. Good feet for a big man. Tore Andre Flo was a menace for Premier League defenders not merely because of his tall, gangly frame but for the silky touches the Norwegian often showed with his giant boots. Flo scored 34% of his 38 Premier League goals as a substitute - the eighth-highest ratio for those with 20 top-flight goals or more, while he is also joint-eighth overall for goals from a substitute. The first of those came just three minutes into his Chelsea debut in 1997, and it was with the Blues he enjoyed his best Premier League output before a later stint at Sunderland. Having also provided three assists as a sub, he ranks fifth for minutes-per-goal involvements, contributing to his side scoring once every 78 minutes on average when used off the bench. Twelve of Flo's 34 Premier League goals for Chelsea came as a substitute The Little Pea. Small in stature but a giant headache for tiring defenders. Of all players in Premier League history to have scored at least 10 goals as a substitute, only one - Sergio Aguero, and it feels a stretch to call the competition's sixth-highest scorer a super sub - has netted at a more prolific rate than Javier 'Chicharito' Hernandez. He has 19 in 78 sub appearances, a rate of 0.24 per game, with 36% of all his Premier League goals coming after he started on the bench - predominantly for Manchester United but also later in his career at West Ham. He netted on average every 88 minutes when used as a replacement. Indeed, only Jermain Defoe and Giroud have scored more goals as a substitute than the Mexican, while he sits among a leading group of seven - including Defoe - who have scored

title: Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
description: Her public debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.
body: This video can not be played Trump: New White House press secretary should 'reconsider' job Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax. Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider". Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters. She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job. Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One. "I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said. "You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media. The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later. As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House. "The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X. Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president. During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam. She replied: "When I was in China." After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam. She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials". Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday. When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'" Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?" When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning. She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one. Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?" She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me." Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team. In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days. "Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain." title: Analysis: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
description: The White House is facing growing adversity, writes the BBC's Anthony Zurcher, weeks before crucial midterm elections.
body: The political strategist was a frequent fixture on conservative Newsmax and Fox News before her appointment The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances. These were not the best of circumstances. Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. In just five days, she was out – the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career. The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered – in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day. "Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this." He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her". In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job. This video can not be played Watch: The BBC's Sarah Smith on what went wrong for Katie Zacharia Trump may be wondering whether Zacharia "needs" the press secretary job, but presidents – including this one - benefit most from a competent press secretary in times of crisis. And while there may not be an immediate crisis, this White House is certainly facing growing adversity. Across the US, Republican candidates are scrambling to hold on to their seats in the upcoming elections. Some are doing so by distancing themselves from the president and his policies, creating new stresses and faultlines within a party that has for so long been broadly unified behind Trump. Meanwhile, the White House has been beset by a series of controversies – including allegations of corruption that forced the resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and an abrupt reversal of plans to publicly air a military execution in December after widespread bipartisan backlash. A skilled press secretary may have been able to navigate these political landmines while continuing to push out the White House's preferred message in the face of a building media frenzy. Karoline Leavitt, who worked as Trump's press secretary from the start of his second term until she resigned in August a few months after welcoming her second child, proved highly adept at defending the administration from the press room lectern while avoiding stumbles and maintaining a collegial relationship with journalists. Her performance set a high bar for Zacharia, who was a relative novice. It was a mark she failed to reach or even approach, although she never really had much of a chance. The speed at which she failed was astounding, setting a modern record for the shortest-tenured White House press secretary. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia leaving role days after taking job How did Katie Zacharia do at her first - very brief - White House briefing? White House defends new press secretary over her legal credentials Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary Zacharia's halting Tuesday press conference performance, combined with those questions about her legal background, essentially sealed her fate. And subsequent press appearances, including a less-than-welcoming interview with conservative pundit Sean Hannity on Thursday – which Trump said he watched – did nothing to change that. As president, Trump has essentially acted as his own press secretary, making major announcements and changing policies from the Oval Office, the White House lawn, airfield tarmacs – wherever he happens to be. Zacharia herself noted this phenomenon prior to being tabbed for the White House job. "President Trump does not need a spokesperson," she posted on X. "He is his own best press secretary." Now, he will have to be. Trump's penchant for speaking off the cuff, however, has made the job a difficult one over the course of his two terms in office. His press secretaries have sometimes had their public statements undermined by presidential pronouncements. At other times, they've been left out of the loop of key decisions. When they have been effective, they have managed to ride the choppier waves while also smoothing relations with the media - providing context for inquisitive journalists and helping tamp down any simmering issues. In comments to Fox News on Friday, Trump said that he is in "no rush" to find a new press secretary. But at such a critical time in his second term, Trump will be without the help that someone like Leavitt offered so consistently. He may come to regret not having it. title: Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland
description: UK political debate has a distinctly Scottish feel after SNP's annual conference, says the BBC's political editor Chris Mason.
body: UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days. As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at the Event Complex on the outskirts of Aberdeen, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has been in Paisley and Edinburgh and the prime minister has been in Motherwell. The SNP is buoyant, its activists gathering for the first time since it won, in May, a fifth consecutive Scottish Parliament election, albeit with fewer seats than they won in 2021. Next year will mark the moment the party has been in devolved power at Holyrood for 20 years. It is quite the contrast with where the SNP found itself just two years ago, pulverised by the landslide at the general election in 2024 where Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP. As I wrote a year ago, the SNP's critics point to what they see as a dismal domestic record, on the NHS and the number of deaths among drug addicts, for instance. The SNP counter Scotland has more police officers per person than England and Wales and the highest spend per school pupil in the UK. No matter the arguments, the result in May was clear - the SNP leader and First Minister John Swinney has his own mandate. Little wonder, given the state of the party when he took the job, that the conference brochure has a front page photo of a smiling Swinney cradling a glass of whisky. And remember it wasn't just an electoral pummelling the SNP was dealing with, but the jaw dropping details which culminated in the jailing of Peter Murrell, the party's former chief executive - and estranged husband of the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon - for embezzling more than £400,000 from the party. Swinney now looks ahead to a parliamentary term with all that behind them and a new prime minister to deal with in Downing Street. Burnham and Swinney share a diagnosis that Westminster has failed to deliver and political power is better administered closer to people than it ever has been. But, crucially, the prime minister sees the "drama" of the constant questions around Scottish independence as a distraction. For Swinney, independence has been and remains his lifelong political goal. We have had a glimpse this week as to how that dynamic between the two men may play out. Burnham's critics, including the SNP, have seen this former Mancunian mayor's devolutionary instincts as having a distinctly English flavour. The prime minister, on his trip to New College Lanarkshire, sought to counter that. "I do want a good growth in every postcode here, and in the rest of the UK, and I want to work with the first minister to deliver it. We won't agree on everything, but we can agree on something," he said. "I want us to design a new model together of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, one that puts control in the hands of local people." Burnham has offered to devolve powers on localised employment support, currently held by the Department of Work and Pensions. Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland, Douglas Alexander, said Scotland was "one of the most centralised nations in Europe", an assertion flatly rejected by Swinney. Scottish First Minister and SNP party leader John Swinney with Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth. Scotland's first minister has said he wants "much more opportunity for a regional dimension to take forward skills, economic opportunity and planning" and his team acknowledge this vision includes overlaps with the regional combined authorities seen in parts of England, albeit without mayors. It will be intriguing to observe, given the rivalry and grit that exists between Labour and the SNP, how things develop beyond the prime minister's speech. Here in Aberdeen, activists have seized upon the prime minister's reflections on Brexit to argue that if he can revisit the outcome of the referendum in 2016 on the European Union, Scots should be able to revisit the one in 2014 on independence. There have been plenty of mentions too of an exchange in the Commons last month between SNP MP Chris Law and Andy Burnham, when Burnham suggested another Scottish independence referendum could be held, if public opinion showed demand for one. SNP folk think - perhaps hope - this represents the prime minister's authentic view. He and Downing Street have seen sought to squash this idea and he said he wanted to "move on" from a debate about Scottish independence. Privately, senior SNP figures accept the authority to sanction another referendum lies with Westminster and the UK government says no. So, their focus is seeking to steadily build the case for independence in how they choose to govern. Within the party, a new group called, you guessed it, "Independence" has been set up. Speaking at its launch event, the SNP's former Policy Convener Toni Giugliano argued that "countries don't become independent by waiting for permission. They do so when support becomes unstoppable and when a national consensus for change is built". Furthermore, he argued, fundamental questions about what an independent Scotland would look and feel like must be answered now - such as the currency that would be used and how the state pension would work. These are the long term questions. For now, the tussle is more short term, as the SNP ponders when the prime minister might call a general election. Buoyed by its recent victory at Holyrood, the party senses Labour vulnerability in the swathe of seats Labour took from them two years ago. title: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
description: Speed curbs limited Ukraine's defences against deadly Russian attacks on Tuesday night.
body: US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks. "It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House. Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown. Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon. The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries. Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US. Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks. "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday. Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin". But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart. Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down". Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible. In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict. On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network. Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks. A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network. "Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read. On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine. Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine. Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda. The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons. Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid. title: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
description: As the 3 November election approaches and both parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged.
body: Susan Collins shakes Troy Jackson's hand Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks. As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races. Here's what you need to know. Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump? Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters. The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices. While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated, external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle. Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president. "I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week. "The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said. Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead. Josh Turek (L) and Ashley Hinson Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself. In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race. She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead. Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points. During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments. The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it." GUIDE: What are the US midterms? IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lost NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents. The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share. Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist". El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly. He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop". Abdul El-Sayed (L) and Mike Rogers On Thursday, as a protester interrupted a Maine debate between Jackson and Collins, who suggested that the person interrupting the debate was associated with her opponent. Jackson then said to Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid." Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Representative Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican. What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich". Mike Collins (L) and Jon Ossoff Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race. In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America". Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness". "I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said. There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found. One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general. Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority. Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton, meanwhile, has not accepted any of those invitations. In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets that he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign, and Paxton, have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has even urged the candidates to debate. title: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
description: Downing Street says Sarah Helm, the wife of Jonathan Powell, "does not represent the government in any capacity".
body: Jonathan Powell is the government's national security adviser Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office. Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action." She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action. A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment. On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action. "It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required." Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post. The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking". "Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said. However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery." He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian". Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent. Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics". Earlier this year, four of the group's activists were jailed after causing £1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm. In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk. The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison. The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group. Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month. Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland. In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister. title: 'Well-known' man asks court to stop publication of sexual offence allegation
description: The unnamed individual asks London's High Court to prevent the publication of "serious allegations".
body: The hearing was held at the High Court in London An individual described as "well-known" has asked London's High Court to prevent two media organisations from publishing "serious allegations", including of a sexual nature, against him. The court heard he had submitted medical evidence saying that if the allegations were made public this would "almost certainly" lead to him "attempting to take his own life", and that the prospect of publication had already led to two suicide attempts. The court was told that Independent Television News and Guardian News & Media had carried out an investigation into the individual's "conduct over a period of years". The individual, who has been granted anonymity in the court proceedings, denies the allegations. The court was told that following an investigation that ITN, which produces news for ITV and Channel 4, and Guardian News & Media, which publishes the Guardian, sent two letters to the the well-known individual in the spring of 2026. As well as denying the allegations, the individual responded with medical reports stating that there was a risk to his life if the information was published. At an injunction hearing at London's High Court, lawyers representing ITN and Guardian News & Media said that "it would be wrong" for the court to "restrain publication" when the "law provides for a detailed and well-established scheme by which the interests of those at risk of suicide is specially protected by NHS mental health professionals". The court has also granted anonymity to other individuals in the case. Two individuals who have agreed to be identified in any ITN and Guardian News & Media report concerning the allegations were given anonymity in the current proceedings by High Court judge Mr Justice Nicklin. The nature of the allegations or how these two journalistic sources relate to them is not known. A third journalistic source for the ITN and Guardian News & Media investigation has also been granted anonymity in the current proceedings. She has alleged that she was the victim of a sexual offence by the well-known individual. The court will decide whether the ITN and Guardian News & Media will be permanently prevented from naming the well-known individual and publishing the allegations against him at a trial due to be held later this month. If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line. title: Dubois and Wardley at career-heaviest for rematch
description: Britons Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley both weigh in at their career-heaviest for Saturday's heavyweight world-title rematch in London.
body: This video can not be played 'Life on the line' for Dubois & Wardley in rematch Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley both weighed in at their career-heaviest and promised another explosive encounter in Saturday's heavyweight world-title rematch in London. WBO champion Dubois tipped the scales at 18st 2lb (115kg) while Wardley came in at 17st 10lb (112kg) before their meeting at the O2 Arena. The British rivals produced a fight-of-the-year contender in Manchester in May, with Wardley flooring Dubois twice before the Londoner rallied to stop his bloodied and battered opponent in the 11th round. "I draw confidence from the successes I had in the first fight - getting knockdowns in the first and third," Wardley, 31, said. "I need to capitalise on those moments better. I'm ready to put on a cleaner performance." Dubois, 29, is more than 2lb heavier for the rematch, while Wardley has added more than 6lb. Asked for his prediction, Wardley added: "Revenge, Fabio Wardley, knockout win." This video can not be played Dubois v Wardley 2 - blood, bravery & a heavyweight gamble Dubois v Wardley 2 - all you need to know Daniel Dubois (left) has won 23 of his 26 professional fights, with 22 knockouts, while Fabio Wardley has 20 wins, 19 by knockout, one defeat and one draw. The final pre-fight formalities took place at Old Spitalfields Market in east London, with the two heavyweights taking to the scales amid the bustle of street-food stalls and shoppers. A couple of hundred fans gathered beneath the market's Victorian roof, some having made the trip specifically for the event while others stopped to see what the fuss was about. It was a rather subdued affair, with a smaller turnout than when Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic weighed in at the same venue in August. Wardley arrived more than an hour before the event, appearing as relaxed as he has throughout fight week and even stopping for selfies with supporters afterwards. Dubois arrived much later and has appeared in little mood for conversation this week. Once again, he was typically economical with his words. "I know him now and know what to expect. I'm ready to go and do my job," the Londoner said. "I'm ready for a tear up. Let's go." There was no drama at the obligatory face-off, despite the fierce rivalry that has developed between them, and two-time world champion Dubois was quick to leave the stage afterwards. With 41 knockouts between them from 43 victories, few expect the contest to go the distance. Wardley, sporting Ipswich Town's newly-launched third kit with his name printed on the sleeve, was still bearing the scars of his punishing defeat in Manchester five months ago. A cut across the bridge of his nose, first sustained during his 2024 draw with Frazer Clarke, reopened against Dubois and left his face badly swollen and bloodied. The punishment he absorbed has raised questions over whether his decision to take an immediate rematch has come too soon but Wardley remains confident he can reverse the result. "It's simply seek and destroy now," he said. Promoter Frank Warren is predicting a "blockbuster" 2027 for the heavyweight division, with lucrative fights awaiting Saturday's winner. Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in Cardiff on 11 December, while British prospect Itauma is set to return in January following his world-title defeat by Hrgovic. Warren confirmed there is no clause for a third fight between Dubois and Wardley but the Queensberry Promotions boss refused to rule out a trilogy if the Ipswich fighter avenges the only defeat on his record. "If that happens it's a natural fight," Warren said. "That's what's so intriguing about this. Who will they fight next year? We want to find out who is the best." title: Police feared Andrew would delay search by saying King owned his home, documents show
description: Legal records have emerged which show why police wanted to search the royal's home and what they were looking for.
body: Mountbatten-Windsor remains under police investigation despite a ruling that the way search warrants were issued was unlawful Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might have tried to stop officers entering his home in Sandringham by saying it belonged to the King, according to legal documents. Senior officers were concerned the King's brother could argue it was not his property, and that separate legal permission would have to be sought before officers could enter it. Delaying access would have risked the loss of evidence, the force said. The background to Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February has emerged in legal documents, when police asked a judge for warrants to raid the former prince's homes. Lawyers for Mountbatten-Windsor successfully argued those warrants were unlawful in court last week. Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest came after the US Department of Justice published material which showed his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The BBC has approached Mountbatten-Windsor's representatives for comment and he has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein. The arrest of the former prince, on 19 February, was on suspicion of misconduct in public office. Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says Why was Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor arrested and what happens next? How Andrew's 11-hour detention on his birthday played out On 18 February, Thames Valley Police asked for permission from the Central Criminal Court for warrants to search Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor. The request included the police outlining the scenarios in which they believed they would need search warrants to ensure access to the properties. They feared that Mountbatten-Windsor or his legal team would want to see "judicial authority" before allowing the police to enter, the documents show. The police were concerned that Mountbatten-Windsor or his representatives could argue that the Sandringham Estate was the property of King Charles - and that it would be a slow process getting a separate right of access. Such a delay would "frustrate the nature and purpose of the search," said the police, in their application for search warrants. There was also a concern that no one would be present at the property and that media attention could be drawn to the police presence outside while not being able to enter. Any of those delays could have meant the police would have been unable to gather the evidence they wanted, they argued - and "given the gravity of this investigation", the police asked for search warrants. In separate documents filed as part of Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge against the warrants, he said: "These assertions were no more than speculation." The documents also detail the type of information the police were seeking inside the properties. They say: "Paper-work, diaries, business records or other documentary evidence of AMW's [Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's] time as Special Representative for Trade and Investment. "Further evidence as to any action, communication, comment or in relation to matters following the release of material by the FBI concerning the late Jeffrey Epstein as AMW will be aware that Thames Valley Police is conducting an assessment. "Specifically mobile phone(s) and computer(s) [to include electronic notebooks, surfaces, iPads and any older electronic devices," which could have held information about links to Epstein at the time when Mountbatten-Windsor had been the UK's trade envoy." The documents show the search of Royal Lodge, Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor, continued until 24 February. They also reveal his police interview at Aylesham Police Station began at 15:00 GMT and he was released under investigation at 18:36. The legal documents give details of why the police wanted to talk to Mountbatten-Windsor, including the claim that when he was a UK trade envoy he had forwarded Jeffrey Epstein official reports from official visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong. There was also a claim, arising from emails in the Epstein files released in the US, that Mountbatten-Windsor had briefed Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan. Also mentioned is the suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor held meetings with a private investment firm and then suggesting to Epstein that he might invest in the company. The legal documents have emerged after a High Court hearing earlier this month in which Thames Valley Police accepted the warrants it used to search Mountbatten-Windsor's homes were unlawful. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers used a judicial review to successfully challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest. Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search. That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine. But items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence. Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing. Thames Valley Police force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties. At the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful. title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
description: Australia has proposed a switch to force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they work Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old. Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition. Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day. "I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC. "I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't." Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words. Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week. The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow. It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality. Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier. But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech. Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral. Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago. It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric. He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order. "You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC. "I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character." The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay. Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man." Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor. Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users. Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools. But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture. Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline. Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line. "The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC. Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021 While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change. "Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them. Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite. More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts. The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off. title: Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV Golf
description: Jon Rahm sacrifices a reported $100m (£75m) still owed to him by LIV Golf to secure his exit from the league.
body: Jon Rahm joined LIV Golf after leaving the PGA Tour in December 2023 Jon Rahm will give up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV Golf after reaching a separation agreement that will secure his exit from the league. The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its multibillion-dollar backing. Spaniard Rahm was listed as the organisation's top unsecured creditor when LIV filed for bankruptcy, with $7.4m (£5.5m) owed to him for the rest of the 2026 season alone. ESPN reported he is owed about $100m (£75m), external from the remainder of the $300m, (£222m) contract he signed when he left the PGA Tour for LIV Golf in December 2023. Despite LIV securing a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit to try and move forward with 'LIV 2.0', Rahm has deemed the proposed terms are "unacceptable". Instead, he has waived his entire claim in order to have a "complete economic walk-away". However, he will take the rights to 'Legion XIII' - the name of the LIV team Rahm captained - although he will not be allowed to use it to make a team in TGL - the indoor high-tech golf league launched by Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy. Rahm was the most high-profile name to join LIV when he left the PGA Tour. Some players, including Brooks Koepka, have since returned to the PGA Tour, which rewrote its rules in December to allow the five-time major winner to come back, subject to certain sanctions. Rahm did not follow suit and remained under long-term contract with LIV, but in May reached a deal with the DP World Tour - formerly the European Tour - to retain his membership and remain eligible for next year's Ryder Cup. LIV golfers are automatically banned for a year by the PGA Tour. The DP World Tour offers a pathway because the leading 10 players on the European circuit currently gain access to PGA Tour membership. In August, former world number one Rahm won his third straight LIV season title. He previously said he had no regrets over joining LIV and backed organisers to make it sustainable. title: Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline
description: Kyiv says it has recaptured 277 sq km (106 square miles) of territory in the eastern Donbas region in recent months
body: This video can not be played Deep inside an underground bunker in eastern Ukraine, commanders monitor the battlefield through a live video feed as a Ukrainian drone intercepts a Russian surveillance drone. The footage shows the Ukrainian drone hovering above its target, before dropping a net and dragging it from the sky. The interception is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive that Kyiv says has recaptured 277 sq km (106 square miles) of territory in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. But Ukraine says new restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite network, are threatening its drone operations. The technology has played a key role in helping Ukrainian forces detect and strike Russian targets. Dan Johnson reports from the bunker. Read more about Ukraine's counter-offensive. title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moved to low-security facility in Pennsylvania
description: The decision to move the rap mogul while he is serving out his 50-month sentence was made with 'safety and security in mind'.
body: Former rap mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs is now being housed in a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders in the US state of Pennsylvania Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says. The rap mogul was moved to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, a prison official said, but declined to discuss why he was moved, citing privacy, safety, and security reasons. "His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction," Combs' spokesman told the BBC, adding that the move "is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind". Combs, 56, who was sentenced to 50 months behind bars, has asked an appeals court to release him from prison and overturn his conviction on two prostitution-related crimes. Combs' spokesman, Juda S Engelmayer, did not comment on an Associated Press report, external that Combs had been living a "luxury lifestyle" behind bars in New Jersey or on reports swirling about his health and treatment in lockup. The move comes about two weeks after NBC News, external reported that the Bad Boy Records co-founder had access to mobile phones, liquor and other contraband at Fort Dix, as well as allegations that he had paid inmates to cook, clean and make his bed for him, and give him massages. He was also involved in two fights, according to NBC. "It's because of the disruptive behaviour," Jose Rojas, union secretary for local federal prison employees, told NBC News of the move. "He's been causing too much trouble over there." NBC reported Combs was stripped of 41 days for good conduct, pushing back his scheduled release date, which is now listed in the prison's online records as 2 March 2028. He was originally expected to be released in January 2028. Engelmayer said he appreciates that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is "taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously" and "we are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption". The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the reports. "For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or disciplinary sanctions," spokesman Donald Murphy said. FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders that is about 155 miles (250 km) west of New York City. The facility houses about 1,044 inmates, according to its website, a significantly smaller population than the one at Combs' previous facility, Fort Dix, of more than 4,200 inmates across two campuses. Allenwood also has medium and maximum security facilities nearby. What has Sean 'Diddy' Combs been convicted of? Sean 'Diddy' Combs files appeal asking for immediate prison release Federal prosecutors in New York have accused Combs of using his money, power, and the threat of violence to coerce women into unwanted sexual encounters. After a high-profile jury trial in New York last year, two of Combs' ex-girlfriends testified that he abused them and forced them to participate in so-called "freak-offs" with male escorts. Fame Under Fire Podcast: Diddy on Trial In July 2025, Combs was convicted on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. They jury acquitted him of two more serious charges, sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy, and he was sentenced to more than four years in prison that October. Later that month, Combs was transferred to the federal correctional institution at Fort Dix in New Jersey, where he had been serving out his sentence until his transfer on Friday. In April, a US appeals court heard arguments to overturn his prison sentence but has not yet issued a decision. title: Dame Judi Dench joins Archers Birmingham campaign
description: The cast have described plans to leave Birmingham as similar "to Corrie leaving the north-west."
body: Dame Judi Dench is among more than 100 current and former cast and crew members calling on the BBC to keep The Archers in Birmingham More than 100 current and former cast and crew members of The Archers, including Dame Judi Dench, have called on the BBC to keep the programme in Birmingham. The appeal follows a decision to shelve plans for a dedicated studio at the broadcaster's new Digbeth headquarters. Supporters say recording the drama elsewhere could affect its quality and future. The BBC says the move is part of wider cost-saving measures and alternative options are being explored. In a letter to director general Matt Brittin, actors, writers, directors and sound engineers argued that moving recordings away from the Midlands would have a "tangible impact" on the programme. The letter compares the prospect to "Coronation Street leaving the north-west, or EastEnders leaving the south-east", adding that it risks "ripping out the heart of Ambridge". Supporters say recording The Archers outside the Midlands could affect the programme's future Signatories said Birmingham had been central to the show's identity since it began and warned that separating cast and production teams could affect the way the programme is made. "A flagship show deserves flagship facilities, from which both the BBC and the city of Birmingham would benefit for decades," the letter said. It was signed by more than 100 current and former cast and crew members, including Dench, Felicity Jones and Kellie Bright, as well as representatives from Equity and the Writers' Guild. The Archers, set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge, celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year and has always been recorded in Birmingham. The intervention follows the BBC's announcement that plans for a bespoke studio at its new Tea Factory headquarters in Digbeth would not go ahead. The Worcestershire village of Inkberrow is believed to have inspired the show's fictional village of Ambridge, while The Old Bull Inn is closely associated with the show's pub, The Bull. BBC director general Matt Brittin said alternative options for recording the programme were being explored Speaking earlier this week, Brittin defended the decision, saying the BBC needed to make savings but remained committed to the programme. "We're going to explore how we can best house The Archers where they need to be," he said. He added there was "other studio space around the country" which could accommodate the programme, while alternatives in the West Midlands would also be considered. West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker also called for the show to remain in Birmingham, describing it as a key part of the region's broadcasting heritage. Equity general secretary Paul Fleming said cast members were "angry" at the proposals. "It's beyond offensive, I think, for any Midlander, the idea that you would record something that is so iconic and so ironically about the Midlands, anywhere other than in the region where it's set," he told BBC Radio 4. title: Reform councillor calls TV report 'vote interference'
description: ITV News filmed undercover with Reform councillors and candidates around the country.
body: George Madgwick was featured in the ITV Exposure report on Reform candidates A Reform councillor has accused ITV of "electoral interference" after undercover reporters joined its Portsmouth council election campaign as part of an undercover investigation into the party. The ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform raised questions about Reform's vetting procedures for candidates following undercover filming. The party's Hampshire leader George Madgwick was featured voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group. He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections. ITV News has denied accusations of electoral interference. A spokesperson said the programme was produced in accordance with broadcasting regulations and was "in the public interest". Reform has been under pressure following the two ITV News reports, which showed undercover footage, gathered over the past year, showing some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language. It comes two years after party leader Nigel Farage promised to root out "bad apples" from his party. ITV News said it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last. The ITV Exposure documentary was produced by Hardcash Productions. The full 90-minute documentary - Undercover: A Year in Reform - is due to be broadcast on Sunday on ITV1 and ITVX. A second ITV News report, external broadcast on Thursday showed footage of Madgwick admitting that the Portsmouth Patriots - members of whom were shown expressing far right views - were actively helping Reform to campaign in the run up to the council elections. In a statement, he denied being a member of the group but said he had "supported their movement over the years from the sidelines". Madgwick said the two undercover reporters campaigned with the party in Portsmouth in March and April. "It leads me to wonder whether their interference in an election is a potential criminal offence." "We have no way to know whether they posted flyers they were meant to. Or whether they gave us correct door knocking information," he said. He said they had campaigned in four seats, three of which the party narrowly lost "Their involvement would have had an impact on the result," he said. He also said he was a "shocked and disgusted" the party had been "infiltrated" by the reporters. "On a personal level I allowed these men in my home. I made them drinks. They met my dogs. It's an entirely disgusting invasion of personal privacy." The Liberal Democrats took control of the council following the elections earlier this year, holding 22 seats, with Reform as the second-biggest party on 12 seats. An ITV spokesperson said: "ITV's programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest. "All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme's producers." The Electoral Commission said it sets out details of electoral offences which relate to campaigning for agents and candidates. "Our Code of Conduct for campaigners provides a guide to what is, and is not, acceptable behaviour." "The consideration of any potential offences would be a matter for the police." title: Collaboration with Off Campus star 'gave me chills', says Babydoll singer Jamie Miller
description: Jamie Miller hopes he's "doing Wales proud" as his viral hit narrowly misses out on UK number one.
body: Jamie Miller (right) says he's found a "best friend" in Off Campus star Antonio Cipriano The singer behind the TikTok viral hit Babydoll says collaborating with an Off Campus star was "mind-boggling". Jamie Miller, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, was close to calling it quits on his music career at the start of 2026, deciding it was his "last chance", financially and emotionally. But over the summer everything changed when Babydoll caught the attention of people on social media, leading to a viral dance, his first UK top 10 single, and reaching number one in the US iTunes pop chart. When Miller saw a comment from actor Antonio Cipriano, saying he "needed this song", he sent him a message suggesting he feature on a recording – then "panicked" and added "haha, joking". "I'm a fan of Antonio's voice, and I have been a fan for a long time," he said. "He messaged back and was like, 'If you're actually not joking, I'd be honoured'." Cipriano headed to Los Angeles, where Miller now lives, and they recorded Babydoll on the day they first met, external. "It was the best time ever," said Miller. "We're coming up at the same time, he has an amazing career in acting and I feel like the stars aligned even for us to do this and the world is rallying around us as a duo too. The opportunities that we're having right now are incredible." Amazon Prime Video's ice hockey romance series Off Campus – based on a book series by Elle Kennedy - has similarly taken the world by storm this year, ranking as the third most-watched series launch in the platform's history, external. It has raised the profile of numerous artists, with a soundtrack merging old favourites with new music. Asked if he would like to be involved with the series in future, Miller said: "I'm such a fan of the show. I think it's absolutely incredible what they're doing, what Antonio is doing. In any capacity, I would love to. We'll see." This video can not be played Babydoll singer Jamie Miller on 'the craziest journey' On Friday, the original version of Babydoll moved from number three to number two in the official UK charts - beaten only by Taylor Swift's Patient Zero. Miller also recently supported The Jonas Brothers on the US leg of their tour, and said bringing Cipriano out as a guest star at some of the shows was "mind-boggling". "I think the easiest thing about it was we're doing it together, for the first time. It was his first arena, it was my first arena, and I think that's the most amazing situation to be in, because we can lean on each other. "Backstage we would say to each other, 'we're so lucky, our lives are not normal, we're going out to play for 20,000 people, what are we doing bro?'. "Introducing him gave me chills because, as well as my dreams coming true right now, his dreams are too. "It's so nice and needed, to have a friend who can guide you through." Antonio Cipriano (left) plays John Logan, best friend of series lead Garrett Graham, played by Belmont Cameli At 19, Miller competed in The Voice UK, coming third place with coach Jennifer Hudson. But his love for music first began accidentally, when he took part in a primary school show. "If you auditioned for the play, then you got to skip out math class," he recalled. "Just to see the reaction from the teachers after they asked me to sing a song, was just absolutely like 'I want to do this, this is actually incredible.' "All my mates were rugby players and football players, whereas I just wanted to do music. After that one audition, I was hooked." Now 29, Miller admits the past couple of years have been "really tough", adding changes in the music industry and in his personal life had left him feeling quite lost. "Going into this year was my last chance to try and cut through. This industry is really hard, it's really expensive as well," he said. "I think the thing with success, people think you have a lot of money... I didn't really see that side of that. So financially, this year, I couldn't really make it work anymore. I was on my last legs." Miller, pictured outside The Travellers Rest pub in Caerphilly, says he loves the support he gets from people back home in Wales He continued: "Going into this year, I'd built my career off sad music, and I'm not sad anymore, I'm happy. "I think Babydoll maybe brought a bit of light to a world that needed it. I know that sounds really cliché to say, but I do feel that is true, we needed some joy." Miller said the whirlwind nature of Babydoll's success had led to accusations he was an "industry plant" - someone who appears to be self-made, while actually having backing from significant investors or supporters. "I wish I was an industry plant, I've done this for nine years," he said with a laugh. "At first, I was getting told this was coming across as a gimmick. But that's the thing, I'm not trying to be cool, I'm trying to just have fun. "Literally, my mentality was 'if I'm going out, and this is my last chance at music, I'm going out my way.'" Jamie Miller, from Cardiff, says he hopes he's "doing Wales proud" Miller said he "never had any social media campaign" planned and it "happened the most organic way possible". As the Babydoll dance took hold of social media, Miller collaborated with an array of stars including actors Jennifer Love Hewitt, Lucy Hale and Julianne Hough, as well as popstar Meghan Trainor. "All these incredible people I've been able to do it with, they've said it themselves, they've said 'we needed this song'. "From all sides of the world, it's kind of unified people in a way, and it's just a beautiful thing to be a part of something that made someone smile." Miller said he was "proud" of his new music and was excited to share his latest album with the

title: Ex-top official Robbins reaches settlement with government over sacking
description: Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson.
body: Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top official in the Foreign Office in April Sir Olly Robbins has reached an out-of-court settlement with the government, after he was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson to be US ambassador. Sir Olly was fired by then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer earlier this year, after it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials. The FDA union, which represented him in the legal action, said Sir Olly had been made a "scapegoat" to "mask the misjudgement" of Sir Keir. How much Sir Olly received in the settlement has not been made public. It came after he requested a judicial review over the decision to dismiss him. A government spokesperson said Sir Olly "had a distinguished public service career over three decades". A statement added: "The government has reached a settlement with Sir Oliver following his dismissal. We will not be commenting further on HR matters." Lord Mandelson was announced as the UK's ambassador to the US in December 2024, before in-depth vetting had been carried out, and formally took up the role in February 2025 after being granted security clearance. Just seven months later, he was sacked after further information emerged about his previous friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Sir Olly was sacked in April, in the wake of a Guardian story that revealed the peer's security clearance had been granted despite vetting officials raising concerns, with the prime minister later saying he was "furious" he had not been informed at the time. Sir Keir has previously said he sacked Sir Olly after not accepting his explanation for why clearance was granted, telling MPs in April: "I did ask him, and I did not accept his explanation. That is why I sacked him." Sir Olly has since defended his role in the process, saying that the government's vetting processes must "remain absolutely confidential". He previously told MPs that he had not seen the documentation from UK Security Vetting, the government's in-house vetting unit, containing their vetting assessment of Lord Mandelson. He said that instead, he was given an oral briefing, during which he was told the vetting agency considered Mandelson to be a "borderline case", but that the Foreign Office may wish to grant clearance with "appropriate risk management". Starmer sacks top Foreign Office official after Mandelson vetting revelations Key evidence from sacked official at heart of Mandelson vetting row Dave Penman, head of the FDA union, said: "This settlement may bring an end to the Judicial Review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government. "The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgement of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations - which is quite the feat. "We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process." Sir Olly said: "I am grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time. "I want to thank the FDA for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life". Sir Olly, who was appointed to the Foreign Office job in early 2025, has held a number of senior civil service roles and was previously the government's lead official during Brexit negotiations with the EU.
