title: Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?
description: Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" to overcome if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, a leading lawyer has told BBC Sport.
body: This video can not be played BBC Sport's Dale Johnson, Dan Roan, Laura Scott and Sami Mokbel assess Manchester City's position Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, a leading lawyer has told BBC Sport. City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating "sham contracts" to inflate sponsorship deals by £830m. The club have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and they have "irrefutable evidence" the ruling "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe". In their appeal, City will argue the payments were made by the United Arab Emirates government as a shareholder of the sponsors, while there are inconsistencies in the Commission's judgement. Therefore, City say the sponsorship amounts were legitimate and not topped up by the owners. James Severn, Member of the London Solicitor Litigation Association (LSLA) and Partner at Penningtons Manches Cooper, told BBC Sport the appeal is "not simply an opportunity to invite a new panel" to get the verdict overturned. "City will need to identify a material error of law, principle or fact, or serious procedural unfairness, which materially affected the Commission's decision," Severn said. "The Appeal Board nevertheless has broad powers to allow or dismiss the appeal, vary the decision or make any other order it considers appropriate." Manchester City have been sponsored by Etihad since May 2009 Etihad Airways, one of City's principle sponsors at the centre of the case, had previously stated that the Abu Dhabi government had not paid for its sponsorship of Manchester City. That came in court documents as part of a US investigation in New York in 2015. City will argue this does not have the full context of the situation and is not proof they have been inconsistent with evidence. The club are adamant government documents fully support their case - but, Severn said, if these were already available to the Commission they may not be much use in an appeal. "The bank statements, government records and contemporaneous payment documents could be powerful evidence if they establish a clear audit trail showing the disputed funds came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the owners," Severn added. "However, if that evidence was already before the Commission, which nevertheless concluded that the arrangements were a sham, City will face an uphill struggle to demonstrate the finding was materially wrong." Shortly before City's appeal was confirmed, Etihad Airways issued a statement saying it had never been "given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon". Severn said Etihad Airways' complaint "does not, of itself, establish procedural unfairness". "Etihad was not the respondent and is unlikely to have had an independent right to participate in the proceedings," Severn said. "It is likely to have been open to either party to obtain and present such evidence to the Commission. "If the Appeal Board is prepared to consider new evidence from Etihad, it is likely to carry greater weight if supported by contemporaneous documents." How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team? Were any current Man City players signed during charges period? Manchester City’s inflatable banana craze A key part of City's defence will be that the Independent Commission relied too heavily on the emails obtained through the Football Leaks files. "If City can demonstrate the Commission fundamentally misunderstood the emails, failed to consider their proper context or reached conclusions inconsistent with other contemporaneous documents, that could amount to a material factual error," Severn added. "City's difficulty is that the Commission heard extensive witness and documentary evidence but nevertheless made serious findings of sham arrangements and disguised owner funding." Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport the commission found "the documents were retrofitted to fit the crime". "The Commission must have concluded that the evidence and the credibility of the witnesses put up by Manchester City were poor," Maguire said. "However, from a legal point of view, this is an area they could attack if Manchester City's team can prove that the commission itself was a flawed construct in the sense that the members were Premier League picks rather than Manchester City's, and therefore the deck was stacked against the club to begin with. Severn added that the retired senior judges and leading barristers, who sat on the Commission, have "spent their careers interpreting complicated facts, dealing with witnesses and applying relevant weight to evidence". While adding that it would be "impossible to assess reliably" the chances of City winning their appeal, Severn added that "doing so will not be easy". But Maguire believes that while it will be difficult for City to be successful, "there is a route". City have brought in Mark Howard KC to advise the club in their appeal, while Etihad Airways has enlisted the services of respected law firm Quinn Emanuel. Maguire said: "Given the lawyers that have been recruited by Manchester City, they may go down what's been described to me as a mess and noise approach. "That means trying to discredit everything to do with the process of the Commission rather than necessarily the evidence that was presented. "I've seen the documents that Abu Dhabi presented to the New York case. I'm not a lawyer, but from an accounting point of view, they can be seen in more than one way." title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
description: Rebecca Louise Burwood saw the vulnerable victim "as her nanna" but stole to fund her lifestyle.
body: Rebecca Louise Burwood saw the victim "as her nana" but stole for her own personal and financial gain A nurse who stole £750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off. Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain. She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home. A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register. The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018. The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact. It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care. Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles. Evidence presented showed more than £370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with £160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs. She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her £400,000 house. The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery". She convinced the resident to pay £20,000 for a car and £9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days outs. Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK. Burwood told the tribunal the woman asked her to withdraw cash from her bank account and make donations to charities each week. She claimed the donations, which were between £250 and £500 each time, would usually go towards charities that supported the blind or those with heart issues. Burwood said she would either put the cash in charity pots while she was out and about, or hand donations directly to staff in local charity shops. Her legal representative Victoria Rees said the resident had told her "she didn't want anything to be left by the time she died, as she didn't want the government to have her money", adding Burwood "didn't keep any records of the amount of money she withdrew or the amount of money she donated". The pensioner's bank referred the matter to North Wales Police and the force launched an investigation. The resident's bank account was frozen following concerns about spending, but Burwood attempted to have restrictions lifted and took the resident to a bank branch. Bank staff claimed Burwood was "almost blackmailing" the woman, and told her to ask for the accounts to be unlocked. The panel found Burwood told the woman she would not be able to take her on outings if she could not access her money. The hearing was told the resident later told safeguarding staff she was shocked by the amount of money that had been spent from her account. Another nurse also said they overheard Burwood tell the woman, "I will give you the money back" and "sign here". She reported the conversation as evidence of financial abuse and it was decided Burwood would only make supervised visits to the woman. Burwood claimed she had only been asking the pensioner to "sign a condolence card" and it was "not in relation to signing a document". She claimed the resident's eyesight was "very poor" so she had held the card for her, showed her where she should sign and stopped her from signing over the printed words in the card. Police investigated, but the woman did not want to take further action as she described Burwood as a friend, and believed she had "learned from her mistakes". The panel concluded there had been a significant imbalance of power in the relationship. Burwood convinced the vulnerable 99-year-old to hand over £750,000 over five years In its ruling, the panel said Burwood had engaged in a "sustained, calculated course of conduct" and had manipulated the resident for personal gain. It added Burwood had taken advantage of the trust the woman had placed in her and "weaponised" it against her. The panel also found Burwood acted dishonestly by failing to tell her employer she held financial lasting power of attorney for a resident at the care home where she worked. It said her actions amounted to serious misconduct, breached fundamental nursing standards and caused both financial and emotional harm. In its decision, the committee said Burwood's actions were "deplorable" and she was "morally culpable", adding that public confidence in the profession would be undermined if a finding of impairment was not made. The panel determined Burwood's conduct was "morally reprehensible, showed premeditated behaviour and indicated a deep-seated attitudinal problem". It determined her behaviour fell far below the standards expected of a registered nurse. Burwood said she "deeply regretted her actions" adding she "saw the resident as her nanna" as an explanation for why she crossed professional boundaries. The victim has since died, but had only been left with enough money to pay for 23 months of care before the council would have had to step in. title: Ukraine pushes Russia back on front line where Starlink has played key role
description: Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi has regained crucial territory in the Donbas but optimism has been dampened by souring relations with President Trump.
body: This video can not be played Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker. Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back. This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control. While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return. The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warning The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front". Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day. Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas region He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed. This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower. Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield. Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability. Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine. Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy. Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground. The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion. Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front line An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times." He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target. Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous". "The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive." Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation. "As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed." "I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy". That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present. title: Does Scott's Disney+ exit unmask wider issue in coverage of women's game?
description: Alex Scott's sudden departure from her Disney+ presenter role reveals a pressing challenge for broadcasters of women's football.
body: Alex Scott regularly presents the BBC's live coverage of the Women's Super League On Thursday, former England footballer Alex Scott stepped away from Disney+'s coverage of the Women's Champions League after two rounds of matches. The streaming giant is in the second season of a five-year deal to cover European football's flagship competition and this year introduced new formats, including a watchalong show with Scott alternating presenting duties with Shebahn Aherne. However, it has had some technical issues and been criticised for a difficult opening night that included an unscheduled advert break during Arsenal's game against HB Koge. Scott has not said why she left this role but told BBC Sport she was "grateful" for the opportunities she had at Disney+ and hoped to "continue working together" in the future. But does her sudden departure highlight the challenges broadcasters face covering the women's game in an ever-changing media landscape? Ad break in Women's Champions League was unscheduled The explosion in interest in women's football during the past five years has been spearheaded by two of the biggest broadcasters in the UK – Sky Sports and the BBC. In snapping up the Champions League before the 2025-26 season, Disney added its heft into the game, recognising its potential for capturing new audiences. Indeed, Scott herself has launched her own YouTube show this season, One More Word WSL, which she presents on a Sunday night alongside ex-England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams. Broadcasters have ramped up experiments with format, style and tone - Disney+ even had a dog on set during their coverage - but perhaps unsurprisingly, not every idea proves to be successful. Journalist Carrie Dunn, who has covered women's sport for more than two decades, says opinions about coverage reflect a tension at the heart of the game. "The challenge broadcasters are finding is that they are not sure who the audience is," she says. "A lot of it is targeted at a new generation and it's clearly not for people who have watched women's football for longer. "Often it's a resourcing issue. Budgets are being cut and you're finding the same presenters and the same pundits trying to be all things to all people. It just doesn't work." Alex Scott, Fara Williams, Ellen White and Steph Houghton are among the former England internationals that front coverage of women's football in the UK In the summer, the BBC announced its Women's Super League highlights show would not return for the 2026-27 season, but insisted it remained "fully committed to women's football". To illustrate, it cited a bespoke new YouTube channel, the introduction of a debate show entitled The Women's Football Fallout, exclusively on BBC iPlayer, and the availability of clips and analysis on the BBC Sport website as evidence. The decisions are part of a move away from linear television that the BBC says reflects changing audience habits. It is a shift in emphasis that comes with difficulties. "It's a tough balance where you've got to explain some context to the new fans without patronising your older fans," Dunn adds. "That's something the major broadcasters have not found a solution to yet. "If people are willing to take risks on different kinds of women's sports coverage, that's fantastic. "But start by choosing one thing and doing it really well – and that's got to be decent match coverage." Watch The Women's Football Fallout on BBC iPlayer Follow BBC Sport's Women's Football channel on YouTube Bigger and more ambitious than ever - women's football on the BBC Aston Villa interim boss Brian Sorensen started as a coach in Denmark in 2009 and believes the innovations in women's football coverage are a good thing, even if some do not always work. "A lot of positive things are happening, but there are a lot of new areas that we haven't tried before," he said. "Sometimes it's trial and error and finding the right way for us. "From when I started - with the worst live stream you've ever seen - to where we are now, is a very big improvement." Andree Jeglertz, manager of champions Manchester City, agrees, acknowledging that the fact women's football has a much bigger audience now is a huge positive. "I think the most important thing is that it is available and that people can see the best players on TV or live," he said. "The more, the better, no matter what." Tottenham counterpart Martin Ho says the onus is on clubs and players to ensure the product on the field is worth watching. "Whatever a broadcast partner decides to do, they have their reasons for it," he said. "All we can control is that we put on a good advert for women's football." Finally, Chelsea's Sonia Bompastor suggested she was open to new expressions in covering the game provided they were properly analysed. "Anytime you try to do something new, you will please some people and upset others," she told BBC Sport. "Sometimes you need to be patient and analyse as it is too soon to say if something is right or not." title: Housing loans granted while Burnham was mayor investigated by councillors
description: A senior councillor says concerns have been raised about the transparency of the process to approve the loans.
body: Loans made to property companies - including three controlled by Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owner - while Andy Burnham was Greater Manchester mayor are being investigated by councillors. About 50 developers have been lent more than £1bn between them from a fund managed by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) since 2015. John Leech, the chairman of the GMCA's Overview and Scrutiny Committee, told the BBC concerns had been raised about the transparency of the process to approve the loans. "We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process," said Leech, who is the Liberal Democrat opposition leader on Manchester City Council. He said the approval process had been criticised as "very opaque in the past and that it's not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn't". A GMCA spokesperson said it was supporting the committee with its enquiries. Downing Street did not comment. The money came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund (GMHILF). The fund was set up in 2015 with an initial £300m of government investment to help developers build new homes across Greater Manchester. Three property companies ultimately controlled by Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan were granted loans worth about £55m in total. The decisions to approve these loans were taken in 2017, in two meetings which were both chaired by Andy Burnham when he was mayor of Greater Manchester. The decisions to grant loans from the fund were taken publicly by all members of the GMCA, not the mayor alone. One of Manchester's leading property developers, Renaker, has received the majority of the £1bn lent out from the fund. Renaker has been involved in a long-running legal battle over £140m worth of loans made to the developer through the GMCA's fund. A rival developer, Aubrey Weis, claims the the loans were unfair subsidies. In June, the Court of Appeal found there had been "no error of law" in the GMCA's decision to provide the loans but Weis is appealing the decision. The Overview & Scrutiny Committee, which reviews the activities of the mayor and the GMCA, agreed to launch an inquiry into the loans earlier this year and Leech is now taking that work forward, after being elected chairman recently. Leech, a former Lib Dem MP in Manchester, said he felt the fund was intended to be for property companies struggling to access financing. In 2015, when the loan scheme was launched, Bill Enevoldson, the GMCA's chief investment officer, said, external: "It is not designed to finance unviable projects but can unlock currently unfundable ones." An evaluation of the fund, external from 2025 said it was designed to provide loans for "projects which might otherwise struggle to secure financing". Leech said it was "not unreasonable" to ask why seemingly successful businesses needed to borrow public money through this loan scheme. "In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn't have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well," Leech said. "And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015." Leech said the committee had asked GMCA officers to produce a report about the use of these funds. He said the committee will ask officers questions about the fund at a private meeting, before potentially making recommendations to the Greater Manchester mayor. The committee does not have the power to sanction the mayor but it can investigate, require answers, expose problems and challenge decisions. The committee could call forward witnesses, such as current Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig, to give evidence as part of the inquiry. Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said Burnham had "serious questions to answer" about the loans. French said "taxpayers deserve transparency over how this money was awarded". Manchester's relatively strong economic record has been driven in part by a property boom In a statement, the GMCA said the funding for the loans had been lent "at commercial rates" and had delivered "11,000 new homes and regenerating brownfield land across the city region". The GMCA said "not a single viable scheme was ever turned down". A GMCA spokesperson added: "The fund is open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector. "Every penny loaned from the fund is being fully repaid, delivering billions of pounds worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer." In 2014, Manchester City Council and Abu Dhabi United Group, which owns Manchester City FC, formed a joint venture called Manchester Life. Abu Dhabi United Group and Manchester Life were involved in three property developments that were partially financed through the GMCA's loan fund. A Manchester Life spokesperson said: "It is standard for property development to be funded through a combination of investor equity and borrowing. "All three sites had previously been derelict. The loans were provided on commercial terms and have been repaid in full, including interest." The BBC asked Renaker for comment but it did not respond before publication. Julia Hatmaker, the editor of the Place North West property news website, said viability was "always a struggle" in the development world. She said the GMCA's loan scheme had been successful in building more homes in the city and generating a return on that investment. But she said it's a "good time for the combined authority to re-evaluate what kind of project it wants to support with similar loan programmes and whether it wants to put stricter rules in place as to what developments can benefit from them". body: This video can not be played President Zelensky has thanked the European Union for the support it has given to Ukraine, describing heads of state and government gathered in Brussels as "real leaders". Meanwhile, President Trump has said Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries was a disgrace. Zelensky made the comment flanked by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. The BBC's Nick Beake reports from Brussels. title: Real demand Tebas resign over Goebbels comparison
description: Real Madrid have called for the "immediate resignation" of La Liga president Javier Tebas after he compared the club's management to Joseph Goebbels.
body: Javier Tebas has had several past disputes with Real Madrid Real Madrid have called for the "immediate resignation" of La Liga president Javier Tebas after he drew comparisons between the club's management and Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels. Tebas said Real Madrid's communication and the use of its in-house TV channel "recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels". Real Madrid have called the statement "deeply offensive" and "morally repugnant". The club have also demanded Tebas steps down as both the head of the Spanish top flight and vice-president of the Spanish Football Association (RFEF). "Real Madrid considers it absolutely intolerable and extraordinarily serious that someone holding two positions of utmost responsibility in Spanish football resorts to a comparison with the propaganda methods of the Nazi regime to discredit our club, its management and its television," the club said. In a lengthy post published on X on Friday, Tebas said: "Real Madrid's management directs an orchestra of mouthpieces and Real Madrid TV leads the singing. "Their score is always the same: select the plays that suit them, repeat the grievance, feed the suspicion, and point fingers at the enemies. "That method recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels, Nazi Germany's minister of propaganda: systematic repetition, construction of an enemy, and subordination of facts to the narrative." Tebas later said he was drawing comparison with "those propaganda techniques" and "not with an ideology". Real Madrid rejected this clarification, saying it did not mitigate the "institutionally unworthy nature of his statements". The club added: "These statements constitute yet another episode in the repeated attacks by Javier Tebas against Real Madrid, its president and its media outlets." Last month, Tebas criticised Real Madrid for claiming there was a refereeing conspiracy against the club. He also has been critical of Real and its president Florentino Perez in previous years after disagreeing with their plans to join a European Super League in 2021. In 2025 he said Real had "lost their head" after the club sent a formal letter of complaint to the Spanish FA about officiating in the league. title: Man killed by tiger may have had medical records breached by NHS staff
description: William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Saturday.
body: William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Saturday. Medical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Trust, a spokesperson has said. William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday. In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case. It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches". Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday. In a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives. They said: "We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so. "We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits. "The trust has commenced an investigation to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches and the actions of these individuals. "We have also reported this matter to the Information Commissioner's Office and we will continue to keep William's family informed as our investigation progresses." title: Arteta told Arsenal job cuts will help create success
description: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta says he was told the club's decision to cut 60 jobs had been made to "achieve the success we want to create".
body: Mikel Arteta was appointed Arsenal boss in December 2019 Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta says he was told the club's decision to cut 60 jobs had been made to "achieve the success we want to create". Gunners chief executive Richard Garlick informed staff this week that Arsenal's workforce would be reduced across a number of departments. The cuts are set to affect up to seven per cent of Arsenal's 871 permanent staff, but will affect neither coaching nor performance staff in the men's or women's setups and will come from off-the-field roles. Jobs in the Arsenal Foundation, Arsenal in the Community and within the security staff will also be unaffected. A review carried out by an external company into the workforce was ongoing before the club won the Premier League. The decision to make the redundancies comes a week after Arteta was handed a new four-year contract, having guided Arsenal to their first Premier League title since 2004 last season. The 44-year-old's new deal included an increase on his previous salary of £10m a year, plus an additional £5m in bonuses. Asked about the cuts at a news conference before Sunday's trip to Nottingham Forest, Arteta initially said "this question is not for me" before offering a brief response. "It was explained to me about the exercise, and the analysis that has been done across the club, and with the intention always to evolve, to improve," said the Spaniard. "Some decisions have to be taken to put people in the right roles, and keep investing, to achieve what we want to achieve, the success that we want to create. That has been explained. "Obviously, I am not the right person to answer that question. That's for sure. And hopefully everybody will respect that." Arsenal announced in February that they had recorded record revenues of £691m for the 2024-25 financial year, although they still made an overall loss of £1.4m. The accounts also showed that operating costs rose to £200.8m, compared with £147.9m in the previous financial year. title: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
description: The 28-year-old detained by German police is accused of being part of the cyber-crime gang that hacked blood-test firm Synnovis in 2024.
body: The alleged Qilin hacker Vladimir K. was detained upon arrival in Frankfurt German police have detained a Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang which caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death. The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death. The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates. Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime. The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K. He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday. According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country. He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims. Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency. While his extradition was first reported in early October, external, the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations. Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab. A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere. King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly". A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result". "The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time. In total the hack disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption. The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom. The hackers refused to answer any more questions once challenged by the BBC The criminals eventually published the highly private data online after no ransom was paid. At the time, they told the BBC the hack was not just for the money but to protest the UK's lack of help in the Russian war on Ukraine. But the hackers did not say if they were from Russia or Ukraine, and their claims were dismissed as an attempt to distance themselves from the cyber-crime extortion tactics Qilin were known for. The group, which has been tracked since 2022, is behind a string of criminal hacks targeting schools, hospitals, companies, councils and health organisations. It was also behind the high profile and disruptive hack on Japanese beer maker Asahi in October 2025. It is very rare for hackers to be arrested in Russia as its government refuses to co-operate with Western law enforcement requests. title: Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks
description: Alan Feeney was captured on undercover filming calling Asian homeowners "parasites".
body: Alan Feeney has stepped down as deputy mayor of Solihull, and given up his role as a councillor in both Solihull and Birmingham Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language. A Reform UK councillor filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites" has resigned from two councils and apologised for his comments. Alan Feeney, who has since stepped down from the party, was heard making the remarks during undercover filming for an ITV News investigation, external in the run up to council elections in May. Feeney said he had resigned every post he held on Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council, adding that his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable". He has also been suspended from his job with the prison service, with the Ministry of Justice [MoJ] describing the comments captured during the documentary as "despicable". In July, his register of interests with Solihull council recorded he was employed as a custodial manager, a position described on the HM Prison and Probation Service website as "the most senior uniformed officers in a prison". Feeney was one of several Reform members featured in the ITV investigation, which was gathered over the course of a year. In it, while campaigning in the run-up to May's elections, Feeney described an area as "infested" with Asian families and called them "absolute parasites". He was also recorded saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white. Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Friday, Reform MP Robert Jenrick said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film. He added that all parties had "bad apples" and denied it was any more of a problem in Reform than other parties. On Thursday, the party told the BBC that Feeney had "mutually agreed" to resign from the party. Writing on Facebook on Friday, Feeney said he wanted "to offer my sincere and unreserved apologies for the comments I made in the recording that has recently come to light". He added the comments did "not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report". These were communities he had "supported countless times" over many years, he added. He stated his true self was reflected in more than a decade of public service, but achievements "cannot reduce the impact of what has been said". Feeney, who defected from the Conservative Party to Reform last year, was elected to the Shard End ward on Birmingham City Council in May. A spokesperson for Reform Solihull said Feeney was briefly with the party, but spent the majority of his time as a Conservative councillor, and did not reflect "the views of the group". The MoJ has stated the comments featured in the documentary would be investigated and action taken in line with its policy. title: Covid vaccine compensation scheme set for overhaul after Inquiry criticism
description: Ministers promise to reform the scheme that provides financial support for those injured or bereaved by vaccines in the UK.
body: More than 24,000 Covid vaccine-harm claims have been made - most relating to the AstraZeneca jab The government has committed to reform of the scheme that provides financial support for those injured or bereaved by vaccines. It was a key recommendation of the UK Covid Inquiry, and has been a focus for campaigners. One campaign group has welcomed the recognition that vaccine injury and bereavement is real and that the current scheme is not fit for purpose. But it says it wants a clear commitment to action by ministers, rather than simply saying they will look further at what needs to be done. The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But some people have experienced harm. In her fourth report, the chair of the Covid Inquiry, Baroness Hallett, called for better support for those affected. She said while this was a minority, the way they are supported needed urgent reform. More than 24,000 people have made Covid-related claims to the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS), a form of financial support paid by the government, but just over 1% have resulted in one-off tax-free awards of £120,000. The report called for "urgent" reform of the scheme, saying that it is "not sufficiently supportive". It said the current system, in which those affected must show they have been at least "60% disabled", does not work effectively for Covid vaccines. In its response to the report, the government says, external it is committed to reviewing the scheme to ensure it is "fit for purpose and delivered effectively." Ministers in England have promised to work closely with the other nations of the UK as well as those injured by the Covid vaccine and their families. One of the main campaign groups for those who were injured by the Covid vaccine is Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK. The group welcomed the government's acknowledgement that vaccine injury and bereavement were real and that the VDPS is not fit for purpose. But in a statement it said that was not the same as committing to action. "After more than five years of campaigning, and with the Covid-19 Inquiry explicitly calling for reform as soon as possible, we had hoped the Government would finally come forward with a clear commitment to action, not simply say it would look further at what needs to be done. "We understand that work may be needed to develop the reforms, but there is a real difference between saying you will look at something and committing to deliver it. "Today, we have no clear timetable, no certainty about what will change and no assurance about when families will finally see meaningful progress." The Government response also said it recognised there were concerns about the running costs of the scheme. Last month it was revealed that the VDPS has cost £83m to run since April 2022. The amount spent on administration costs and medical assessments was more than double the £32m paid out in financial support to victims so far. Ministers say they will ensure the scheme is working properly. title: Patients in chains rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa
description: Some of the 200 patients were found with "sores all over their bodies" and in overcrowded rooms.
body: Officials uncovered "gross inhuman conditions" when they raided the centre A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country. The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday. Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other". Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented. Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country. Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg. A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre. Two minors were among the 200 people found living in crowded rooms at the facility The couple running it told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women. The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water. "Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said. The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; £137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church. Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said. Officials said 132 have been reunited with their families. The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday. title: Labour calls for M4 relief road, seven years after axing the plan
description: Seven years after the party axed the project, Labour says the Welsh government should build the road.
body: The former Welsh Labour government axed the plans in 2019 Labour's Welsh leader has called for the Plaid Cymru administration to start work on an M4 relief road - seven years after his party had axed it. Ken Skates told BBC Wales that there was "no other option on the table" to solve congestion in Newport, and has backed a version of the original plan with changes. The move will be seen by some as an attempt to distance Welsh Labour from part of the legacy of former First Minister Mark Drakeford. Labour will table a vote in the Senedd on Wednesday calling for an "appropriate relief road" to be built. A report said the road could now cost £3bn to build. The Welsh government has declined to comment. Skates' announcement comes weeks after the Welsh government set out some options for tackling congestion, including proposals to close junctions in Newport. It also means that all opposition groups - Reform, Labour and the Tories - are in favour of a relief road. Drakeford axed previous proposals for an M4 Relief Road in 2019 - on the grounds of cost and the impact on the environment. The Welsh government could close junction 27 at High Cross, and eastbound slip roads at junctions 25 and 26 The Welsh government has also commissioned an 18-month project to assess possible "roads-based" solutions - although it has ruled out the black route. A report published earlier in October set out a number of alternatives to a new motorway, and said the relief road could cost around £3bn. It also warned that the route was no longer safeguarded through the planning system. "Over time, new development or other land use changes may occur within parts of the former corridor, making it progressively more difficult or expensive to deliver the same highway alignment in the future," it said. But Ken Skates said the report "shows that no single or combined solution will adequately alleviate congestion on the M4 around Newport. "That means that there is no other option on the table other than a relief road if we wish to solve the problem of congestion on that route." He said he believed that an amended version of the original black route - the proposed motorway south of Newport that had been examined and backed by a public inquiry in 2019 - should be the road that got built. Skates had served as transport minister under four Labour first ministers The Welsh Labour leader said the proposed blue route alternative - using existing roads in part - was not appropriate. "In reality, the black route remains the only appropriate route," Skates said. "Further work would have to be undertaken to make sure that all environmental concerns today are met and adequately responded to, but something has to be done about congestion." Asked what he would say to accusations of a U-turn, Skates added: "Well, it's a world away from where we were in 2019. "Back then, we had come out of the EU, Brexit was causing enormous concern, we were planning for a no deal. "We were... almost a decade into austerity. There was simply not the sort of money that was required to build the black route available to the Welsh government. "It was right not to go ahead with it at the time because of the financial cost. I do believe firmly that had we gone ahead with it, it would have been paused or cancelled during Covid." Skates said he wanted to know from the Welsh government what the status was now of the protected route for the relief road - which was ditched after the scheme was axed. In a debate on 29 September, Deputy Transport Minister Mark Hooper said the black route was not achievable. "The protected route status went when it was cancelled," he said. "So, we're talking about decades of work to even get that off the ground." Skates spoke ahead of the Co-operative Movement conference on Saturday, where he will say that people in the region "should be trusted, empowered and respected in deciding what affects them". "Their need for congestion to be dealt with can only realistically be met through getting to work on a relief road. "The debate over an appropriate solution and the balancing of environmental, human and economic concerns should be led by the people of the region, who know best what is needed in and for their communities." Local Plaid Cymru MS, Peredur Owen Griffiths, who represents Casnewydd Islwyn, said Labour's "hypocrisy is astounding". "It's as if they've forgotten they were in government for 27 years and scrapped plans to address the issue of congestion in and around Newport - only to now U-turn in opposition," he said. "Plaid Cymru is clear that doing nothing isn't an option... the action we're considering could reduce traffic by 10% in just four years," he said. title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
description: The pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after having surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday.
body: Pope Leo thanked medical staff as he was pictured for the first time since his lung surgery Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery. The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications. The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital. Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said. Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure. His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung". The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital. The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure. Who is Robert Prevost, the new Pope Leo XIV? title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
description: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
body: Tirana has seen four days of clashes and the protests are spreading Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades. Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too. Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale. And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east. The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living. Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers. Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons. Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony. Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation. A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too. There have been violent scenes involving protesters and police in central Tirana Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign. The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead. The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder. One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue. For almost five months over the summer, Albanians carrying images of flamingoes called on the prime minister to resign Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania 'Flamingo Revolution' takes off as thousands demand Albanian PM's resignation Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president. They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night. But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands. The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership. Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement. Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard." Another called Brunela said she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth." An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward. After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system. Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos. "All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday. The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward". Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama. But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance. So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it. On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved. Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU. Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday. "These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence." Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being. The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local autho

title: Former Sale Sharks player Hyron Andrews dies ahead of new club's Champions Cup match
description: Hyron Andrews dies at his Johannesburg Lions' team hotel before their Champions Cup match at La Rochelle on Saturday.
body: Andrews joined Sale in February 2024 and made 45 appearances for the club before heading back to his native South Africa at the end of last season Former Sale second row Hyron Andrews has died at his Johannesburg Lions' team hotel before their Champions Cup match at La Rochelle on Saturday. A statement from SA Rugby stated that his death had been an "accident" and that the 31-year-old had "died after a fall". "We are heartbroken by the passing of Hyron," said Lions chief executive Rudolf Straeuli. "He was not only a gifted rugby player, but also a cherished member of our Lions family having recently joined us this season. "On behalf of our chairman, Mr Altmann Allers, the board and everyone at the Lions, I extend our deepest sympathies to [Andrews' wife] Maighlin, their young sons Hendrix and Emerson and the entire Andrews family. "We stand with them in their sorrow and will remember Hyron with great affection and respect." The Lions will fulfil their fixture against La Rochelle, which kicks off at 17:30 BST, in Andrews' honour, while a moment's silence will be observed at all the opening round's fixtures. "This is terrible and distressing news; our hearts go out to Hyron's family and the whole Lions rugby community," said Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union. "There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maighlin, and for his extended family, friends, team-mates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow. "His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him." Andrews left Sale in the summer to return to his native South Africa. He made 45 appearances for the club after arriving in February 2024 from the Durban-based Sharks as injury cover for England international lock Jonny Hill. "Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant team-mate," said Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson. "He was so skilled on the field but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with. "He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him. "It was a big move for Hyron and his wife Maighlin to come to England, but he truly made a second home in Manchester. It was incredible to see how he and his family embraced the club and area. "Most importantly, he was a loving husband to Maighlin and a doting father to his two gorgeous boys. It was an absolute privilege to get to know him and it's just absolutely devastating for everyone." While he was yet to earn senior international honours, Andrews had represented the Junior Springboks in 2015. Andrews' death comes 10 years on from the sudden death of Munster coach Anthony Foley in Paris before a Champions Cup fixture. Foley, 42, died in his sleep on the eve of a match against Racing 92 after a heart condition caused fluid to build up in his lungs. Munster's present-day players will wear commemorative tops, featuring the Munster club crest and Foley's shirt number eight as part of their pre-match routine at their match against Racing on Saturday. The Lions, who play their home matches at Ellis Park, are making their first appearance in Europe's premier club competition, with South African sides introduced into the continental competition in the 2022-23 season. They have won two of their first three matches in the United Rugby Championship so far this season, including beating defending champions Leinster in their first game of their campaign. title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
description: The BBC sees masked settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest olives, amid a surge in similar incidents.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt. Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby. The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car. "We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!" Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured. Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own. "As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him. Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said. Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me. The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack. In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below. Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts. Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support. "This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today." But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees. There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave. But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return. As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back. The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene. "I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes." In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist. "We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined. As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing. Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts. The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank. title: US senators call for investigation into Ukraine's Starlink restrictions
description: Ukraine says temporary speed limits to the Starlink internet network disrupted its battlefield missions.
body: Democratic Party Senator Jeanne Shaheen has spearheaded the cross-party statement from several US senators A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an urgent investigation into disruptions to SpaceX's Starlink internet network in Ukraine. Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said it had unexpectedly restricted how fast drones could fly while maintaining internet connection. In the letter, sent to the US defence department inspector general, the senators express "grave concern" about reports of speed curbs between 12 and 14 October. Asked whether the US might have had a role in the slowdown, a US official told the BBC "no such request was ever made by the president [Donald Trump]". The letter, led by Jeanne Shaheen - a Democrat on the Senate's Foreign Relations Committee - calls for the inspector general to find out whether the restrictions were caused by the US defence department or its contractors. It says "restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure". Starlink, which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network. On Friday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told a news conference in Brussels that Starlink services were still being restored in his country. "Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," he said. The senators also say they are "deeply concerned" by reports of disruptions or "glitches" affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine. "We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids," the statement says. "Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation," the senators add. The letter's signatories include Republican Senators Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John Cornyn, alongside Senators Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, Richard Blumenthal and Christopher Coons from the Democrats. Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? SpaceX owner Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind restrictions. On Wednesday Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]". Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas. Starshield, which relies on the Starlink network, is designed for government and military use. Both are owned by Musk's SpaceX. Zelensky has accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks against Russian energy sites. On Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine's attacks would continue after Russia had continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure during an "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday. Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days and would agree to the "energy ceasefire" if Moscow also abided by it. However, he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal and Russia said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied. Zelensky has also criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort. That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.
