title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
description: The 51-year-old faces three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault, all of which he denies.
body: Russell Brand was pictured outside court on Friday as he arrived for the third day of his trial Warning - this report contains graphic content A woman who alleges she was indecently assaulted by Russell Brand has told his trial she was left feeling "bewildered and confused". The woman, who worked at MTV at the time, said the entertainer went from "jovial" to a "wild-eyed maniac" as he attempted, she alleged, to pull her into a toilet. Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. The woman gave evidence on Friday from behind a screen at Southwark Crown Court in London, on the third day of Brand's trial. She told the jury the alleged incident at MTV lasted for about 20 seconds, adding: "It was a very short exchange." Asked how she felt after the alleged attack by Brand, the woman said: "Bewildered, confused, 'what the hell happened there?'" She said Brand went from someone who was "affable" to a "wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet". "I was confused that that actually just happened - anyone would be," she said. The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV. She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially. After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it. "He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first." Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom. The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next. She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door. "He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware". Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in." She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm. The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away. "I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said. The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength. She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be". Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his." But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said. Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand. "I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court. Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary. "You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said. "It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation." The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet." The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them." Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..." The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual." Fame Under Fire: Russell Brand on Trial You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Fame Under Fire: Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts The woman was speaking after a former flatmate of Brand's, Andrew Dobson, earlier told the jury that "sex was a huge preoccupation" for the entertainer. Dobson gave evidence after another woman told the court on Thursday that Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room in Bournemouth in 1999. She said she had met Brand, before he was famous, while she was attending the Labour Party conference. Dobson told the court on Friday he attended the Bournemouth conference and had written music for a fringe event that Brand was part of. Karmy-Jones asked Dobson how he would describe Brand's character as he got to know him before he was famous. Dobson told the court Brand was a "very vibrant character, very egotistical". "I would say lively," he continued. "Sort of quite demanding and persuasive. I think erratic would be maybe a slightly better term." Dobson also told the court that "sex was a huge preoccupation for him", referring to Brand. He said he recalled a couple of nights when "clearly the pursuit of getting somebody in bed would be a preoccupation" for Brand. The jury heard that Dobson was staying in the same guesthouse with Brand and other cast members. The morning after Brand is alleged to have raped a woman, he returned to the place where some of the cast had been staying, the jury heard. Asked by the prosecutor to describe the "circumstances of how he came home", Dobson replied: "My primary recollection is very hurried and rushed... I recall Russell coming in and suddenly an urgency we had to leave, things being really hurried". The prosecutor asked the witness: "Where did urgency come from?" Dobso

title: 'I am telling you the truth' - Carrick on Martinez fallout
description: Manchester United boss Michael Carrick says he is telling the truth about the club moving on from Lisandro Martinez's explosive post-match interview.
body: Michael Carrick's Manchester United have won just one of their opening six Premier League games Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says he is "telling the truth" when he says the club have moved on from Lisandro Martinez's explosive post-match comments this week. Carrick's close friend and team-mate Wayne Rooney led the condemnation of Martinez, saying the Argentine defender could "rip the dressing room apart" with his attack on United's hierarchy after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid. Former United skippers Roy Keane and Gary Neville have also had their say, among a huge amount of analysis. Martinez has apologised for the timing of comments, which turned the spotlight on director of football Jason Wilcox, but not for the words themselves. "There's a lot of people who say a lot of things - ex-pros or not ex-pros - it doesn't necessarily mean they understand what is going on here," said Carrick in his pre-match media conference at United's Carrington training ground. "Just because people talk on the outside doesn't mean that is the truth. I am telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I have seen it for a while. That is it, plain and simple. We are living it every day and know what it feels like. "We are emotional and care a lot. Sometimes someone says something that maybe you shouldn't say at that certain time, but it doesn't distract us from what we are creating here and the environment and spirit within the group. "It [the squad] is not affected, I am telling you." Carrick confirmed Martinez would be "part of the squad" for Sunday's Premier League trip to Leeds at Elland Road (14:00 BST). Martinez apologises for outburst and fined by Man Utd Man Utd a circus after Martinez comments - Keane Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout Martinez singled out the 'technical director' for criticism in Madrid. There was no mention of Wilcox in his statement, although the former Leeds and Blackburn player, who was made United's director of football in the aftermath of Dan Ashworth's sacking in December 2024, was part of the discussions with Martinez that led to his latest statement on his conduct. Wilcox is back in the spotlight, after also being targeted by Ruben Amorim in his final press conference before his dismissal in January. The 55-year-old has only spoken publicly once since, to United's own media channel, 12 months ago. "I don't think it's for me to say whether he should or not," said Carrick, when asked if Wilcox should be the one explaining his actions to the media. "I've got no problem sitting here, talking to you guys and leading the group, leading the team, leading the football club from this position. We're all in it together. Carrick does not feel Martinez's failure to mention Wilcox by name is an issue. "He's released his statement, he's realised he's made a mistake, and I think that's enough for all of us to move on with," he said. "We ask for passion, we ask for emotion, we ask for fire and we ask for players to care. There's a way of doing that, and that's already been acknowledged. "But we need to carry that intensity, that willingness, togetherness and spirit and everything else you can bring with that. As a group, we need to use it, and we've got to use it in the right way." The negative headlines are the last thing Carrick needed at the present time. His side go to Leeds on the back of a five-match winless run. United have not gone six games without a victory since the end of the 2018-19 campaign, just after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer had been confirmed as permanent manager. Carrick knows the importance of ending that sequence in terms of easing the pressure on his own future. However, he refuses to accept that as being crucial. "I don't need results," he said. "We all need results. "It's not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual. It is bigger than me, bigger than any player, or anyone else who works at this football club. It always has been. "I don't go into every day at work in this situation, [ahead of] this game, thinking it's about me. It's really not. It's about the football club; what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to. That's what drives us." Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko Martinez's outburst was triggered by United's lengthy injury list that led to Ayden Heaven playing at left-back in Madrid. Cover for Luke Shaw, who missed the game through injury, and Benjamin Sesko were viewed by some as being crucial in the summer. In addition to Shaw's absence, Sesko is yet to start a Premier League game this season. The Slovenia forward, a £74m signing from RB Leipzig in August 2025, suffered a recurrence of the shin injury that curtailed his 2025-26 season in last month's EFL Cup defeat by Brighton. For the third pre-match press conference running, Carrick said he was unable to give a timescale on Sesko's return. "Ben's kind of still undergoing a couple of checks before we update on timelines," he said. "We're just trying to be clear with what that looks like but he's still a little bit further away." title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' detained for UK murder plot
description: Johannes Natland, 19, travelled to West Yorkshire to carry out a "hit" in March last year.
body: This video can not be played Moment 'hitman' mimed shooting police during arrest A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention. Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard. During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime. Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday. The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear. Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was." The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS). At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes. "You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target." Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about £21,000, to carry out the killing. He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday. Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden. He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone. There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England. Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country. "You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money." Johannes Natland was found guilty of conspiracy to murder He was told: "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to." Natland was at the Briar Court Hotel with two handguns hidden under his bed when he was arrested by police. When he saw officers at the door, he mimed shooting one of them with his hands before he was pushed against the wall and handcuffed. "There was pressure because he'd come into the country, and we knew his intention was to carry out a murder on UK soil," said Flanagan. "We had to move at pace and we intervened really quickly, and just before he sort of moved towards committing that murder." Natland grew up in the oil city of Stavanger in south-west Norway. Despite being a promising young footballer, he started taking drugs aged 13 and later dropped out of school. He previously told the Old Bailey that by last year he was taking drugs "pretty much every day". He became paranoid his parents were trying to kill him and he ended up in a psychiatric unit with drug-induced psychosis. Johannes Natland at Manchester Airport after being allowed to enter despite Border Force officers' suspicions Natland's barrister, Paul Hynes KC, said the "mental illness was exacerbated, if not created, by the self-induced consumption of drugs", which had "affected his ability to make rational, good decisions". The defendant said he spent a short period in a "home for problem children" where he met one of those who later recruited him to the Foxtrot Network, a teenager with the username UnknownHustler. Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself." Within two days of being recruited, Natland flew from Stavanger to Manchester, using the emergency passport as his normal one had expired. He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester and was told to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home. Instead, he took a taxi to the hotel in Huddersfield before taking another taxi to a wooded area. He picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, and was directed to a stolen Nissan with false plates to be used in the killing. The judge added at sentencing: "You returned to the hotel with two guns and 19 bullets. "You were sent directions to where a stolen car bearing false number plates was parked with its key, after which you bought rubber gloves, took photos and made videos of what you had acquired, including with the money spread out on the hotel bed." From his hotel room, Natland bragged to his girlfriend he had the "bangs in the bag" and took selfies in his room. Johannes Natland, pictured with cash on his bed at the Briar Court Hotel in Huddersfield At his trial, one of Natland's footballer friends recalled him talking about the "Swedish Foxes" and telling him: "I'm going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die." Natland also confided in his girlfriend before leaving for the UK, saying in a message: "I'm going on crazy mission." According to her, he said: "Now I can finally kill someone and it's perfect as I get money to do it. "I can kill someone and life will be wonderful." Giving evidence, Natland said he wanted to look "cool" to his peers but it was just "bravado" and inside he was "terrified". He told jurors: "I wasn't an international assassin. I thoug

title: Underdogs? We like that tag, says England captain Williams
description: Captain George Williams says England will relish their "underdog" tag when they take on a powerful Tonga side in their World Cup opener in Perth on Saturday.
body: George Williams has been a member of England's previous two World Cup squads England will relish their underdog tag when they take on a powerful Tonga side in their World Cup opener in Perth on Saturday, captain George Williams says. They defeated the Pacific Islanders 3-0 in a hard-fought Test series at home three years ago - having previously edged to victory in a dramatic World Cup semi-final in Auckland in 2017. But England - who have already suffered a blow with the withdrawal of Morgan Smithies through injury - have been forced into a late change to their starting line-up, with Luke Thompson replacing the absent Morgan Knowles. And with humidity expected to be above 60% inside HBF Park, Williams expects the toughest of starts against a Tonga side who have evolved since 2023 and are packed with NRL talent. "Tonga are a stacked team. They have been for a few years now," Williams said. "We'll be underdogs but we'll quite like that kind of brush on our head and we'll bring our game tomorrow night against a great team. "I think it's always different over here as well, with the heat and different conditions. It helps when you drag them to Leeds and it's minus two or whatever it normally is in November. "We're looking forward to the challenge. They are stacked full of world-class players who play across the NRL, so we know what we are in for, but we are fully prepared and ready." 15 October - 15 November Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app This video can not be played England captain George Williams looks ahead to his third Rugby League World Cup England's recent World Cup history is one of heartache and near misses. In 2022, they fell to a golden-point loss to Samoa in the last four and in 2017 they were beaten 6-0 by Australia in the final. Williams, 31, who was part of those squads and captain when England lost 3-0 in the Ashes in 2025, dismissed any idea that baggage could inhibit the group now at head coach Brian McDermott's disposal. "I don't think it hinders us. Some of the lads were talking about the last World Cup and it was probably one of the most difficult losses of my career to date," Williams added. "It does sit there. You can't hide away from what happened but what it can do is give you drive and motivation and there's still numerous players within the group that felt that but the good thing is we've got a mixed bag. "Some youth, some heritage and some old lads like myself can all mingle together and get the job done." NRL gap a factor in France defeat by Samoa, says boss New Zealand's Ponga has surgery on broken forearm Brian McDermott was named England head coach in April, on a deal through to the end of the World Cup England's toils in the Ashes 12 months ago led to McDermott replacing Shaun Wane at the helm. And it has also brought the promise of a "point of difference" in attack as they prepare for a potentially pivotal first match. With Australia and New Zealand expected to advance from Pool A, it leaves England likely to fight it out with Tonga, Samoa and Papua New Guinea from Pools B and C - which will be combined into one six-team table - for the other two semi-final spots. "It's definitely been different. I'm not going to tell you all the tricks and what we're up to and what we're talking about, but it has been different and it's been enjoyable," added the Dolphins-bound Williams, who is keen to impress as he goes up against his his new club head coach Kristian Woolf and future halves partner in Isaiya Katoa. "I think the group have all bought into what he wants us to do. "Most Test matches start the same way, very physical, and that won't be changing at all this week for any game. "Don't be expecting this mad expansive style of free-for-all but we're going to put some stuff in there that we've not done previously." This video can not be played Explaining the unusual group format of the Men's Rugby League World Cup Jodie Cunningham will start on the bench against Wales England get their Women's World Cup campaign under way directly prior to the men's match, as they take on Wales in a must-win opening game in Perth (07:35 BST). Stuart Barrow's side thrashed the World Cup debutants 62-0 in August 2025 and claimed a record 82-0 win at Headingley over the same opponents in 2024. However, Wales have strengthened since then, with second rower Paige Travis - who has switched allegiances from England - and Canterbury Bulldogs half-back Tayla Preston lining up for them on Saturday. "I've seen Paige Travis and Dani McGifford and my team-mates at St Helens. I know all their strengths and how fantastic they are," said captain Jodie Cunningham, who has been named on the bench for Saturday's match and is set to appear at a fourth World Cup. "Hopefully we come out on top. The combinations are really starting to come together now, so we're just excited and we're all ready to go." England, ranked third in the world, will then take on reigning champions Australia and Samoa as they attempt to reach the last four for a fifth time. title: Mum of four says pipe bomb attack was case of 'mistaken identity'
description: Nicola Nugent and her children escaped injury after their house in north Belfast was targeted.
body: Nicola Nugent says she is still in shock A mother of four whose north Belfast home was pipe-bombed has said the attack was a case of mistaken identity. Nicola Nugent said the device was put through the letterbox of her home on Stanhope Street at about 03:00 BST on Friday. Police said it "exploded fully", setting off the fire alarm and causing damage to the front door and the hallway. Nugent and her four children escaped from their home and no-one was injured. Det Sgt Stevenson, from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), said: "We are thankful that they escaped injury, though they are obviously very shaken by their ordeal." Cordons have now been lifted and residents are able to return to their homes. Damage was caused to the front door and the hallway Homes in Stanhope Street have been evacuated, with police cordons in place as Army bomb experts carry out an investigation. Nugent said: "I was just woke up with an explosion at just after three o'clock. [I] jumped up, trying to get the kids out. "There was so much smoke so we couldn't really see what they were doing." Army bomb experts have been deployed to the scene Nugent said she "definitely, 100%" believed it was a case of mistaken identity. She said she was still in shock and did not want to think about what could have happened. Carál Ní Chuilín appealed for anyone with information to contact police Sinn Féin assembly member Carál Ní Chuilín condemned the attack and said the family were "very, very lucky". "She has four children, the youngest of which is a baby of a year old," said Ní Chuilín. "As far as I'm concerned, this was attempt of murder." Police have appealed for anyone with information to get in touch. title: Damages for Greens deputy over false disorder claims
description: Mothin Ali is handed damages over claims made by a TV presenter and a social media commentator.
body: Mothin Ali will receive 'substantial damages' over the defamatory posts A TV presenter and a social media commentator have apologised and will pay damages to the deputy leader of the Green Party after wrongly suggesting he participated in disorder. Mothin Ali, a councillor on Leeds City Council, attended the 2024 Harehills unrest to assist police and appeal for calm, but posts on social media accused him of taking part in the trouble, the High Court heard. Ali sued GB News presenter Alex Armstrong and social media commentator Bernadette Spofforth for defamation over posts on X. Both have apologised and agreed to pay "substantial damages". Speaking outside court, Ali said: "The harm is already done. The smears leave their stench, even when proven to be false." Trouble erupted in Harehills on the evening of 18 July 2024 after police helped social workers who were taking four children into emergency foster care. Hundreds of people took to the streets, with a police car flipped over and a double-decker bus torched. "I tried my absolute best to calm tensions, to protect police officers," said Ali, who has been deputy leader of the Green Party of England and Wales since 2025. "I stayed on the scene to calm rioters and to reassure residents while buses burned. I stayed there to limit the damage, to limit the harm to my community. "For my service to my community, I was not only accused of rioting, but something I take even more seriously - my honesty was brought into question." A torched double-decker bus has become an enduring image of the Harehills unrest As a result of the negative coverage, Ali said he was "harassed for days and weeks" and his family "lived in fear". His car was also damaged. "The context of this is how black and brown people are treated when they enter public life," he told reporters gathered outside the court. Samantha Thompson, who represented Armstrong and Spofforth, a businesswoman from the Chester area, said the pair "apologise to the claimant for the serious harm to his reputation and his distress". Green Party leader Zack Polanski said Ali was a "hero" for his actions on the night, adding: "He did exactly what an excellent councillor would do, working to calm down and heal division, and was praised across party lines at the time for doing so." title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
description: Tesla CEO Elon Musk showcased the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
body: This video can not be played A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas. "You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model. Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets. But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains. Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? title: NRL gap a factor in France's heavy defeat by Samoa, says boss
description: France boss Laurent Frayssinous suggests the gap between the NRL and Super League was a huge factor in their 78-4 defeat by Samoa at the Men's Rugby League World Cup.
body: Sua Fa'alogo scored four tries and later had a fifth ruled out France head coach Laurent Frayssinous suggested the growing gap between the NRL and Super League was a huge factor in Friday's 78-4 defeat by Samoa at the Men's Rugby League World Cup. Melbourne storm winger Sua Fa'alogo came off the bench as a replacement for the injured Deine Mariner to score four of Samoa's 14 tries in an emphatic Pool B-C victory in Parramatta. Mariner had opened the scoring, with two tries for Benaiah Ioelu and one each for Jermaine McEwen, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Stephen Crichton, Shawn Blore, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Izack Tago and Francis Molo. France's sole try came in the first half from Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet. Frayssinous admitted his team were "all over the shop" in an opening 20 minutes where Samoa scored five times - with France not helped by head injuries to winger Leo Darrelatour and stand-off Cesar Rouge, although the latter was able to return after an assessment. But, asked why France had fallen to an even heavier defeat than the 62-4 loss they suffered against Samoa in Warrington at the last World Cup four years ago, Frayssinous pointed to the level of NRL talent in the opposing ranks. "I have a question for you," Frayssinous said. "Do you think the NRL is far better now than four years ago? Then you have the answer." All but one of the Samoa squad are with clubs in the NRL, while France's team is largely made up of Super League players, although they do have South Sydney Rabbitohs centre Latrell Siegwalt in their line-up. "The NRL keeps growing and keeps getting better every year," Frayssinous added. "Watching NRL every year, it's at the top, at the top, at the top. A step up, step up, step up. "Does that mean Super League isn't? No. Super League is [getting] better every year, but not as fast as the NRL. The smartness, the skill the guys have under pressure, the touches, week in, week out, that's something we need to improve in Super League, simple as that." Frayssinous made clear he would welcome the NRL's proposed investment in Super League. "Definitely," he said. "What the NRL has done here is so good, what they bring to the game is great, so we want the NRL to do it the same in Europe." Fa'alogo's performance as a replacement for Mariner - who will have a scan on a hamstring strain - demonstrated Samoa's strength in depth, as their head coach Ben Gardiner acknowledged. "We were planning for him [Fa'alogo] to play at some stage, and he just got on a bit earlier than he probably would have thought," Gardiner said. "And to his credit, he went out and had a blinder." 15 October - 15 November Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app Keeley Nizza was one of Australia's seven try-scorers Australia are widely expected to win a fourth successive Women's Rugby League World Cup, but a 40-0 victory over Samoa in their Pool A opener still had head coach Jess Skinner seeking improvement - in the stands as well as on the pitch. Samoa, playing at the women's World Cup for the first time since 2008, were much better than the scoreline suggested, defending their try-line superbly and causing the co-hosts problems without being able to convert pressure into points. Stand-off Jocelyn Kelleher was the standout Australia player on her debut - her kicking game was superb - and the defending champions scored seven tries without reply, through Jaime Chapman, Julia Robinson, Shaylee Bent, Keeley Nizza, Olivia Kernick, Keilee Joseph and Jessica Sergis. Skinner, though, wants to see Australia cut out errors before they face England in Perth a week on Saturday. "There are lots of work-ons for us moving forward," Skinner said. "It was a little bit scrappy at times. "We need to work on our starts, and we need some high finishes to end our sets and probably some strong defence in the first three tackles. But overall, there were lots of little wins to be proud of." Skinner also called on the crowds to be more supportive of the women's game at this World Cup. Australia's opener at Western Sydney Stadium in Parramatta was staged as the second part of a double-header with the men's match between France and Samoa - with a number of fans not staying to watch the defending champions. "Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that. "Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt." title: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth
description: The Princess of Wales launches a project encouraging a greater emphasis on children learning from nature.
body: A new photo of the Princess of Wales was released with the early years project The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development. "Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post. This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing. She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing". In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary". She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons. This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood. She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall. A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project. "This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess. "We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing. "My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK." Dr Nicola Kemp of the Froebel Trust, which supports early years education research, said: "A growing body of evidence shows that regular contact with nature can support children's development in many ways, helping to foster curiosity, creativity, emotional wellbeing and social connection." The Princess of Wales has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play. There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work". The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life. title: Street Fighter movie is 'made by fans for fans' - but can it KO the critics?
description: Cast members Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji and Callina Liang discuss the latest video game adaptation.
body: Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji play Ken Masters and Ryu in Street Fighter Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently. First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie version of the long-running horror game series. The next contender is Street Fighter, the arcade classic fighting game that's been separating fans from their loose change since 1987. Both have been turned into disappointing live-action films before. But Cregger's attempt at Resident Evil, which impressed both critics and fans, seemed to break the curse. BBC Newsbeat spoke to Street Fighter cast members Noah Centineo, Callina Liang and Andrew Koji to find out why they think the action movie can do the same. The film, directed by Kitao Sakurai, follows Ken Masters, played by Centineo, and Ryu, played by Koji. The two characters - long-standing icons of the games - are martial artists who trained under the same teacher before their relationship went sour. Chun-Li, played by Liang, recruits the pair to compete with other elite fighters in the World Warrior tournament, organised by crime boss M. Bison. The large ensemble cast includes about 15 characters from different instalments of the video game series, and is packed with references and Easter eggs. "It's absurd, it's wild, it doesn't take itself too seriously," Centineo tells Newsbeat. "And everyone who made it loves the world of Street Fighter. Grew up playing the game, loves the game." He says it was "extremely important" for the film to stay faithful to the series, describing it as "a movie made by fans for fans", who can expect "meticulous" attention to detail. The film recreates details including Street Fighter's famous car-smashing minigame Centineo says the film's stunt team closely studied each character's video game movements to ensure their signature moves were accurately depicted on film. His co-star Liang says her intense training regime was designed to help her replicate character Chun-Li's famous moves and distinctive, muscular look. "I was eating 12 eggs a day, like, 4,000 calories, training a lot," she says. "My motto the whole time was just 'give it your best and some more'". Liang says she wanted to put work in "for the fans" but does stress she was careful not to take things too far. Her fellow actor Koji thinks it's a winning formula. "I think we've got the right approach, got the right cast, right energy," he says. "I think we could feel it when we first read the script." Critics, though, haven't been convinced. Callina Liang's performance as Chun-Li has been well-received The Guardian called it a "garish and incoherent mess",, external but praised Liang as "formidable" and complimented her "genuinely impressive" fight scenes. Gaming website IGN described the film as getting off to a "stylish start",, external but said it "increasingly feels disconnected from any sense of reality, even its own" along the way. There was almost universal criticism of the "confusing" and "chaotic" plot, but some reviewers did praise the fight choreography and visuals of the film. It's a contrast to Resident Evil, released last month, which was almost universally praised by critics and hit $300m at the global box office four weeks after release. But will fans show up for Street Fighter? Tayyib Mahmood, who uploads film and video game reviews to his tsreeltalk accounts, says he enjoyed Street Fighter. "I think that it was true to what the games are," he says. "It's taking these characters and putting them into these costumes which are unrealistic, it embraces how ridiculous these games are. "You've got the different fighting styles, you've got these larger-than-life characters and I think the movie commits to all of that and I think there is a lot of personality to this film." Film reviewer and Street Fighter fan Tayyib Mahmood says he enjoyed the film Mahmood says he has criticisms of the film, such as a weak story, but thinks the attention to the "visual identity" of Street Fighter is impressive. He also points out that fandoms of specific video games don't always agree on what would make a good adaptation. "I don't think that every movie needs to be loved universally," he says. "I think that sometimes a film knows exactly who it's for and I think it does need to commit to audiences and accept that other people might hate it." title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
description: Israeli settlers were seen attacking Palestinian farmers and setting fire to olive trees in the West Bank.
body: This video can not be played The BBC has witnessed Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and set fire to olive trees in the occupied West Bank. About a dozen settlers dressed in black charged down a hill near an outpost – illegal under international law - to a field where Palestinians and activists were harvesting olives. They torched about a dozen trees and hurled stones from slingshots. Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was at the scene, was taken to hospital where she told reporters she "got jumped" and described being kicked on the ground. The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. It says this year levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high. The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson reports. title: Action needed to save water, minister urges
description: Severe drought was declared across parts of southern England after months of low rainfall.
body: The government is urging people to save water as it warns action is needed to prevent severe drought conditions becoming "the new normal". Water and flooding minister Emma Hardy told MPs current drought conditions "is something we have not experienced for decades" and urged people to "think about ways to use water wisely over the coming weeks". Severe drought was declared across parts of southern England on Thursday after months of low rainfall. Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex are all affected by the move announced by the Environment Agency. The government said supplies would not be interrupted but declaring severe drought would ensure "proactive steps are taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs". Speaking in the House of Commons, Hardy said the measures were down to "exceptional low rainfall" and depleted reservoir levels. "This has been the lowest rainfall in over a century," she said. The latest figures for Wimbleball Reservoir on Exmoor show it is at 14.9% capacity, while Ardingly is 19.4% full. Other major reservoirs are also low, including Roadford in Devon at 36.8%, Burrator at 33.6%, Colliford in Cornwall at 35% and Stithians at 21.9%. title: Zelensky rallies EU support as Trump says Ukraine leader 'more difficult to deal with than Putin'
description: The US president launches a new wave of blistering criticism at Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels.
body: Zelensky arrived at a summit in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen US President Donald Trump has renewed his sharp criticism of Volodymyr Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader is "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin". Trump, who recently made a controversial deal with Moscow to import its diesel to the American market, called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries a "disgrace". Zelensky had paused the attacks for three days at Trump's request for a ceasefire on energy targets, but said on Thursday they would resume because Moscow had never stopped. Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have escalated recently over the US-Russia diesel deal and restrictions on Ukraine's satellite communications on the battlefield. Zelensky has not commented on Trump's latest criticism. He arrived at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday flanked by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. "Of course we supported President Trump's energy ceasefire but we've seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute," Von der Leyen told reporters, adding that sanctions on Russia "have to increase". Moscow said it had never agreed to the energy ceasefire that Trump suddenly announced last week. Costa did not mention the US, but said that "this is no time to withdraw support" to the country and "no time to relieve Russian sanctions", as the US has done in agreeing to the deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel. The summit's agenda focuses on funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another cold winter - the fifth since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. "Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure," Von der Leyen told Zelensky before the summit began, "but we stand by your side, we support you as we did in the other winters." Zelensky said his country wants the war to end "as quick as possible", but added that Russia is not showing signs that it wants the same thing. "That's why we have to prepare for the winter. A winter package is not only energy, it's also defence and funding," he said. Deadly attacks on Ukraine continued overnight, with several people killed in a Russian drone strike in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, while some 270,000 households were without power after strikes in the western Volyn region, the local governors said. A member of Ukraine's emergency service sifts through rubble at the scene of a Russian drone strike in the north-western Rivne region Trump's comments about Zelensky, during an interview with US outlet Newsmax on Thursday evening, reflect the deteriorating relationship between the US and Ukraine. The US president said he is "not a big fan of Zelensky" and that he is "not a good guy for us to deal with. "He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't," Trump said. "As you know, Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin," he added. "And when you have that kind of hatred, it's very hard to get something settled." When asked about Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries, Trump said it was "a disgrace". "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher... There are a lot of targets that you can hit." Trump is frustrated at Ukraine's continued targeting of Russian oil refineries because it affects Moscow's ability to export its diesel to America, as per the deal the US recently made with Russia, in an effort to bring down fuel prices. Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, souring Trump standing with the American public - something he wants to fix before next month's mid-term elections. The diesel deal infuriated Zelensky, who called it a gift to Putin and an "investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged." His anger was further heightened earlier this week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself. On Tuesday night, when the communications network was limited, there were several deadly Russian strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning of the incoming attack. The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence sharing - which is crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries. Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire Zelensky has been holding back-to-back talks with EU leaders while in Brussels. On Thursday he met Nato chief Marke Rutte, as well as the leaders of Poland, France, Denmark and Belgium. A day earlier, he met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at No 10 in London. At the summit on Friday, Zelensky said he would hold talks with the chiefs of the European Council and European Commission, and the prime ministers of Hungary, Finland, and Sweden. Supporting Ukraine through another freezing winter is high on the agenda at the summit in Brussels Ukraine also continued its strikes against Russia overnight. The airspace above Moscow was closed for several house, causing flight delays, as 644 drones were intercepted above 26 Russian regions, the defence ministry said. Ninety-four Ukrainian drones were shot down as they approached Moscow, the mayor said. In the Vladimir region, east of Moscow, the governor said that Ukrainian drones were intercepted to prevent an attack on heating infrastructure in the area. And the governor of the southern Rostov region said that Ukrainian drones hit industrial and warehouse facilities, causing a fire and injuring one person. Watch our pick of standout clip

title: Rew, 18, to captain England Lions in West Indies
description: The elevation of teenager Thomas Rew to Lions captain is a further sign of the high regard he is held in by the England hierarchy and follows him being given his first senior call-up and central contract.
body: Thomas Rew led England Under-19s to the final of the World Cup earlier this year Teenager Thomas Rew has been named England Lions captain in the same week he earned his first senior call-up and central contract. It is thought the 18-year-old will become the youngest captain in Lions history when he leads the side in three T20s against West Indies A in St Kitts and Nevis in November. Rew skippers a squad that includes his older brother, James. Earlier this week, Thomas was given an England developmental deal and named in a full squad for the first time for the T20 series in Australia. Thomas, Hampshire seamer Eddie Jack and Sussex all-rounder James Coles are the three players who will be involved on the Lions tour and then travel to Australia. The Lions' T20s in the Caribbean are followed by five one-day matches, with the squad for that series captained by Test batter Dan Lawrence. Lawrence is joined in the one-day squad by seamer Sam Cook, as both men use the Lions tour as part of their preparation for the senior team's three Tests in South Africa in December. The elevation of Thomas Rew to Lions captain is a further sign of the high regard he is held in by the England hierarchy. The wicketkeeper-batter skippered England Under-19s to the final of the World Cup earlier this year, then made his first two first-class hundreds for Somerset during the summer. Rew does not turn 19 until 29 November. If he plays on the senior tour of Australia, he would become the third-youngest man to make his England debut in any format after Rehan Ahmed and Brian Close, and the youngest man to play for England against Australia. Hampshire seamer Scott Currie is also part of the T20 squad. Born in Poole, Currie played three one-day internationals for Scotland in 2014 and his brother Brad has 39 caps for the Scots. Scott was called into England's squad for a T20 series in Ireland last year. Although he did not play, he was subsequently barred from reverting to Scotland at this year's T20 World Cup because he was named as an England substitute fielder in Dublin. Former England batter Jonathan Trott is taking charge of the Lions' winter tours following the departure of former head coach Andrew Flintoff. title: British father fined for causing his two-year-old son's death in Cyprus hotel fall
description: Joshua Foster "lost control" of his son while showing him the view of a water park from a window.
body: A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death. Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard. The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas. Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning. He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter." The auditor, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident. They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening. The incident happened on the first day of the family's holiday at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards an elevator and was playing with his son, said his lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou. The court was told that as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside. It was said that Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react. Alexandrou told an earlier hearing, which took place on October 6, that Foster's life "changed forever" from that moment. Police were called to reports of a child falling "under unknown circumstances" at about 18:40. The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead. In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him". While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk. Alexandrou said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened. The court heard the window was 2.85m (9.3ft) wide and 1.2m (3.9ft) high. Alexandros Alexandrou said his client's remorse was "clear" In a statement outside court, Alexandrou described his client as an "incredible father". "[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side." He added Foster was "very emotional" after the sentencing and the family needed time to grieve properly. "They have been in a defence mode during this procedure," Alexandrou said. title: Wildlife park reopens after man killed by tiger
description: Yorkshire Wildlife Park says the decision was made after 'engagement with the relevant authorities'.
body: Yorkshire Wildlife Park has reopened to visitors Yorkshire Wildlife Park has reopened for the first time since a man was killed by a tiger in an enclosure. William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday. The public were evacuated after the incident with the attraction closed since then. An inquest that opened into Chapman's death on Thursday heard of his history of mental illness and a diagnosis of schizophrenia. His family expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services leading up to his death. City of Doncaster Council, which is responsible for licensing the park, is carrying out a health and safety investigation and said it would share the outcome with the coroner, the inquest was told. On Thursday, Yorkshire Wildlife Park confirmed it would reopen on Friday following "engagement with the relevant authorities". In a previous statement on social media, the park said "many, many people" had contacted it about Altai, the Amur tiger involved in the incident, and it confirmed he was "safe and well" and would not be euthanised. A spokesperson said its "Land of the Tiger" area, where Saturday's incident took place in front of staff and members of the public, would also reopen. Several hundred cars could be seen at the popular attraction on Friday morning, with many young families and wildlife enthusiasts carrying cameras heading in. Among them was Taylor, who was visiting with her partner and their two children, aged one and three, for the youngest child's birthday. She said: "We just want to support the centre, it's just very sad and we feel for staff who must have been through a lot. "We will go to the tiger enclosure and feel safe." Glyn, an animal enthusiast, was "glad to be coming" and also remarked on the "sad incident". He said he never "felt unsafe" at the park, adding that the animals were "secure". An eyewitness took this photograph of the tiger minutes before the incident A statement said Altai's "ongoing welfare at YWP remains a priority of our experienced animal care team". The statement went on to say: "We continue to assist South Yorkshire Police and other relevant agencies with their ongoing inquiries into the circumstances of this tragic incident. "As we welcome visitors back, we would ask everyone to be understanding and respectful towards our staff team, who have shown tremendous professionalism and dedication during an exceptionally difficult time. "We are providing specialist trauma support and ongoing care for those affected. "As inquiries remain ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further on circumstances at this time. "We would like to thank everyone for their patience, understanding and support during this difficult period, and we look forward to welcoming visitors back to the park." William Chapman's family described him as "bright, warm and engaging" Chapman's inquest at Doncaster Coroner's Court was told he had suffered previous bouts of psychosis. The self-employed online trader was born in Chichester, West Sussex, and living in Doncaster at the time of his death. He had been under the care of the Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS Trust but was "highly functioning and independent with no care requirements", the inquest heard. A trust spokesperson said it had launched an investigation after Chapman's death but would not comment further due to patient confidentiality. The inquest was adjourned until 18 March 2027. title: Burnham to urge Swinney to work with him on devolution during Scottish visit
description: The prime minister will speak on his first substantive trip to Scotland since moving into Downing Street.
body: Burnham has said he wants Swinney's government to help him deliver economic benefits to Scotland Andy Burnham will invite John Swinney to work with him on devolution and unlock jobs and opportunities for every area of the country during a visit to Scotland later. The prime minister will say "there is no limit to what we can achieve for the people of Scotland" at an event in North Lanarkshire. Burnham, the former Mayor of Manchester, has said he wants to devolve more power to local areas around the UK, while the first minister has called for a second Scottish independence referendum by 2031. The PM's visit coincides with the SNP's annual party conference in Aberdeen and Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's latest visit for an engagement in Glasgow. What does Andy Burnham have up his sleeve as he crashes SNP conference? Burnham is expected to say: "During my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland's regions and cities. "Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this. "This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people." The prime minister will use his speech to claim the Scottish government is one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe. He is expected to say Holyrood does not give enough of a say to people who know their areas best, despite significant devolution from Westminster over the last 27 years. The PM will call on the Scottish government to work with No10 North and the Scotland Office to develop "a new model of regional empowerment for Scotland, ensuring communities with their own strengths, identity and ambitions can seize new economic opportunities and unlock their potential". Without knowing the details of Burnham's proposals for regional devolution in Scotland, there should be scope for him to co-operate with Swinney. The first minister is already considering a major overhaul of local government in Scotland with greater emphasis on developing a regional level of decision-making. My sense is that if the UK government is willing to transfer powers to Scottish regions, it will want the Scottish government to do the same. The Scottish government tends to want any new powers to come to Holyrood, but may in turn be prepared to hand those on to regional authorities. I think it is also open to considering giving more transport and economic powers that it currently holds to Scottish regions. This discussion worries some in existing councils who fear powers being sucked up from local to regional level. While the Scottish and UK governments have a major disagreement over independence, they do work together in other areas. Two defence technical colleges are to be established in the central belt with funding from each government matched by the other. Kemi Badenoch says the Tories have no plans to take away powers from the Scottish Parliament Swinney is expected to promote his renewed push for independence in his keynote speech at the SNP conference on Saturday. He previously welcomed Burnham telling MPs that a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed. But Burnham later pushed back on that by telling Swinney at a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits". Meanwhile, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said the Tories currently have "no plans" to take away powers from the Scottish Parliament - but that "maybe we need a review" into how devolution is working. Speaking during a visit to Edinburgh on Thursday, she said: "Devolution is a process. It's not a religion which we should worship. "This is a process. If a process isn't working, how can you improve the process rather than just say the process is there, there's nothing we can do? We are about solutions." Badenoch added: "We don't have any plans to take powers away. What we do have plans for are how to make people's lives richer." title: What is behind the success of dark skies festival?
description: Stargazers are preparing to enjoy an annual festival that celebrates the beauty of the night sky.
body: The Exmoor Dark Skies festival celebrates its 10th anniversary in 2026 Stargazers and astronomers are preparing to enjoy a festival that celebrates the beauty of the night sky. The annual Exmoor Dark Skies Festival is being held from 16 October to 1 November and this year is its 10th anniversary. Taking in villages and towns surrounding Exmoor National Park, the event offers walks, talks and shows - putting the dark, clear, night sky into full focus. But what is the event all about - and what is behind its success over the past decade? 'Strong and brave' heritage railway chairman dies Police warn online grooming of children is 'getting easier' Top autumn walks as leaves expected to be more vibrant The event celebrates the national park's status as a Dark Sky Reserve. Granted by the International Astronomical Union in 2011, the status aims to safeguard the right of any citizen to enjoy the night sky by helping to limit light pollution. Festival organiser Julie Colman said: "We bring together lots and lots of events across the two-week period, celebrating the skies, the wildlife, the wellbeing elements of it." There are about 80 events taking place across the park, from moonlit swimming and astronomy sessions, to bioluminescence walks and planetarium shows. Photographers and astronomers can enjoy clear views of the stars during the festival Colman said there is "very little light pollution on Exmoor", adding it "enables the dark to be really dark with none of the pollution impacting". "In the core of the reserve, there's an area where there is no light at all in a huge area - and that just makes the sky so much clearer and you're able to see some incredible constellations. "You can see the Milky Way - it really is fantastic." Photographs taken during previous dark skies events show incredibly clear views of the stars against a clear, dark backdrop. Locations such as Wimbleball Lake are big draws The National Park said it designed the event in 2017 to, in part, help local businesses towards the end of the traditional tourism season. In Dunster, on the edge of Exmoor, the Yarn Market Hotel manager Antony Brunt said in recent years, "it has become much more widely known - and now we literally have people ringing us up to book". The hotel hosts special trips during the festival, led by a local astronomer, and runs visits to various sites and events across the park. Brunt said the festival brings in people from all over the UK, adding: "It's getting to a quieter time of year and these people, they really enjoy coming down. "We have a group that come each year, in fact, twice a year. For people to come regularly twice a year to the same hotel, they must be enjoying the stargazing part of the weekend." The growing popularity of the festival meant that many events sold out before the opening day. Follow BBC Somerset on Facebook, external and X, external. title: Police officer who raped two women jailed for 12 years
description: Campbell Petrie was found guilty of physical and sexual abuse towards the women between 2006 and 2023.
body: Campbell Petrie was found guilty of offences against two women A former police sergeant who was found guilty of a catalogue of sex crimes, including raping two women, has been jailed for 12 years. Campbell Petrie had been convicted of eight charges involving physical and sexual abuse towards the women in Glasgow over a 17-year period between 2006 and 2023. Petrie, who had denied the allegations, will be supervised and monitored in the community for a further three years after his release. He is one of four serving or former Police Scotland officers who have been exposed as rapists in the space of five months. In May, Alan Greer took his own life just days after a police raid on his home as part of an investigation into offences dating back to 2012. An investigation has since established that the officer was a violent serial sex offender with at least 15 victims. In July, former constable Cameron Ross was jailed for 10 years for raping two women and abusing a third. And on Thursday, serving officer John Williamson was found guilty of raping a teenage girl and a woman in Shetland. He will be sentenced in December. Petrie was first arrested in 2009 after one of his victims accused him of threatening behaviour. He was held in a police station for five hours, but no further action was taken at the time because of a lack of evidence. In 2023, a second woman accused him of rape, prompting an investigation by specialist sexual crime officers. Petrie was arrested, charged and suspended in December 2023. He retired from the force a year later. In September this year he was found guilty at the High Court in Glasgow of eight charges involving sexual and physical assaults against the two women, including four counts of rape. Judge Alistair Watson said Petrie posed a risk of significant harm to the public Judge Alistair Watson said he was imposing a sentence which reflected the seriousness and persistence of Petrie's crimes. "I have read the eloquent and moving descriptions provided by both of the women and they describe the trauma at your hands, and the nature of the psychological harm that affects them today," he said. The judge said the women had shown "remarkable courage" during the court proceedings. "It was obvious that they suffer enduring pain for what you did to them," he told Petrie. "I hope the resolution of these proceedings may close a chapter on their lives and allows them to move on with the process of recovery." He placed Petrie on the sex offenders register and said he posed a risk of "significant harm to the public, particularly women you come into contact with in future". Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women Rapist police officer was first arrested and released 17 years ago Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years Assistant Chief Constable Tim Mairs said Petrie had committed "a series of severely abusive, exploitative and violent crimes towards women. "His offending is in stark contrast to the professionalism and commitment of the officers who investigated him and ultimately helped bring him to justice." Mairs said Petrie's victims had shown great courage in reporting his crimes and that he hoped the sentence would bring them some "closure and comfort". He added: "This investigation shows the public that when matters of this nature are reported to us, regardless of who the perpetrator is, victims will be listened to and supported as we take immediate action to identify, investigate and bring to justice those responsible." Petrie's conviction raised fresh questions over background checks on police in Scotland. In 2023, all UK forces carried out a "historic data wash" following the crimes of Met officers Wayne Couzens, who abducted and murdered Sarah Everard, and serial rapist David Carrick. Officers and staff were checked against the national police data base to identify whether they had a criminal past which had been missed. Police Scotland has said that the 2023 data wash had not identified any unknown information on Petrie. Earlier this month the force's commanding officer, Chief Constable Jo Farrell, told BBC Scotland News that 45 serving officers were currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls. Under new regulations brought into force this year, about 8,000 police officers and staff will undergo renewed vetting. title: Community 'heartbroken and horrified' after Oregon school shooting
description: A 16-year-old killed three children and a teacher at a primary school in Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, police say.
body: This video can not be played Three children and a teacher were shot dead by a 16-year-old at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, police have said. The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors. "We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement. title: School's plan to use toilet chaperones puts pupils at risk, says campaigner
description: Some pupils will have to be escorted to the toilet over vandalism and attendance problems.
body: Molly Fenton says many pupils do not use the toilets in school because "they're embarrassed" A school where some secondary-age pupils are escorted to the toilet could be discouraging them from seeking help for periods and other health issues, a campaigner has warned. Molly Fenton, founder of the Love Your Period campaign, said she would have been unlikely to use school toilets if she had needed to be accompanied as a pupil, and said it put students "at risk". Ebbw Fawr Learning Community in Blaenau Gwent introduced the chaperones in response to costly vandalism and excessive time spent out of lessons. Councils set a school's toilet policies, the Welsh government said, adding they must be "accessible to all learners throughout the school day, taking into account pupils' basic needs". Parents were initially told that all secondary-age pupils asking to use the toilet during a lesson would be escorted by a member of the pastoral team to the entrance of the toilet block. The school then said, after meeting with 50 "pupil representatives", that the policy would only apply to pupils on stage three of the school's behaviour policy or persistent late attenders. "I think that this is a very broad, problematic thing... putting many people at risk," said Fenton. The 24-year-old from Cardiff said she was "quite shocked that was even thought of". "I started the period of campaigning when I was in school, if I had to have a chaperone come to the toilet with me, I probably would not have gone to the toilet at all as someone that was not comfortable enough to talk about periods," she said. Fenton warned the policy could bring stigmas about using the toilet in school to "a whole new level". She said: "We know there's already an issue with young people not going for the toilet in school. "They're embarrassed. They're holding in their poo when they should be going. "When I was in school, I had really, really harrowing periods. "I was often in the school toilets, blood all over me, thinking, 'I don't actually know what to do in this moment and I'm stuck and I don't know who to go to, where to go. Can I go back to class like this?'" She said she would not have trusted a chaperone enough to confide in them, a problem exacerbated by the pandemic, and that "young people are even less likely to trust authority". "There's a bigger conversation with that," she said, adding "culture change" was needed to make toilets "shame and stigma free". Ebbw Fawr Learning Community said: "To address costly vandalism and prolonged periods of absence from the classroom, the school wrote to parents several weeks ago to introduce [the] new toilets arrangement for secondary aged pupils. "Sadly the vandalism to toilets by a small minority of pupils has resulted in thousands of pounds worth of damages over recent months. "To address this the new arrangements involved learners being escorted to the toilet during the lessons either side of the lunch break, when incidents were most prevalent." title: Chelsea's James out for three months after knee surgery
description: Chelsea captain Reece James is set to miss three months of action after undergoing knee surgery.
body: James is Chelsea's longest serving player Chelsea captain Reece James is set to miss three months of action after undergoing knee surgery. The defender, 26, was injured in training before Chelsea's 5-1 win over Bournemouth last weekend, and the decision was taken for him to have surgery. James is now undergoing rehabilitation with Chelsea's medical staff, with no time-frame given for his return. Chelsea next travel to Everton in the Premier League before hosting London rivals Tottenham and Manchester United in a difficult run of fixtures. A trip to Liverpool in the Carabao Cup is sandwiched between those two home matches. James has suffered multiple injuries over the past few seasons, causing him to miss several international tournaments with England since the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. His injury record improved significantly last season, allowing him to play a prominent role in England's World Cup campaign, during which they reached the semi-finals before winning the bronze medal match. James was among the players to withdraw from England duty during the most recent international break. The next international break begins at the start of November, when England are scheduled to face Croatia at Wembley Stadium. Did Chelsea benefit most from extended international break?
