title: Councils warned of risks of high street pedestrianisation
description: The government says the process "needs to be well considered", warning that banning traffic could damage local economies.
body: The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street in London has been subject to much discussion The UK government has warned councils against ill-considered plans to pedestrianise high streets in England. In evidence submitted to an inquiry by MPs, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said pedestrianisation can make high streets "more attractive, safe and welcoming". But the department added that "the process needs to be well considered", warning that removing traffic could make high streets less accessible and damage local economies. "Local leaders pursuing pedestrianisation must be aware of the risks and work to mitigate them, within a broader spatial strategy," the evidence says. The evidence was submitted, external to the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee, which is investigating the action needed to revitalise England's high streets. An MHCLG spokesperson said the government had not issued formal guidance to local authorities on pedestrianisation. The government is due to publish a new strategy on high streets later this year. "We support local leaders to make their own choices about pedestrianisation based on the needs of their communities," the spokesperson said. "Our upcoming high streets strategy will also set out more detail on how we are bringing high streets back to life and making sure they are accessible for everyone." Studies suggest banning cars from high streets has become increasingly common in city and town centres across the UK. Some councils attempted pedestrianisation experiments during the Covid pandemic, which spurred debates about the use of outdoor public spaces. But the pedestrianisation of some high streets has proved contentious, particularly in London, London Mayor Sadiq Khan has clashed with the local council over plans to make Oxford Street traffic-free. Parts of Oxford Street will be pedestrianised from 26 October. The London mayor's spokesperson said he was focused on making high streets "cleaner, greener and more pleasant places to spend time, and helping to drive economic growth and prosperity". "Pedestrianisation can help reduce conflict between vehicles and pedestrians, making high streets more attractive for visitors and shoppers," the mayor's spokesperson said. They added the Greater London Authority would use data and feedback from the Oxford Street scheme to "understand how a range of people will use the newly pedestrianised space, and help refine the design of permanent improvements". Most pedestrianisation schemes are immediately countered by some level of local opposition, said Professor Lee Ivett, who heads the School of Architecture at the University of the Built Environment. He told the BBC that while opposition usually focuses on short-term disruption to local businesses, evidence does suggest that pedestrianisation increases the economic viability of high streets in the long run. But he said pedestrianisation had to be paired with improvements in public transport to realise those economic benefits. "If you want to defeat the argument that a reduction in the amount of traffic will reduce the amount of trade, then you need to also be able to make an argument that an investment in public transport infrastructure is actually going to be the vehicle that still keeps providing accessibility to the centre," Professor Ivett said. In urban design guidance and previous high street strategies, the UK government has supported making high streets more attractive and people-friendly. The last high street strategy - which was published in 2021 when the Conservatives were in power - said the government wanted to see more town and city centres "designed with a sense of place and to be attractive to people walking, cycling and using public transport". But the government's approach to date has focused on giving local authorities the tools and flexibility to make their own decisions on pedestrianisation. Pedestrianising roads can be a long and complicated legal process, involving consultations with residents and impact assessments. It has taken a decade for London Mayor Sadiq Khan's proposal to pedestrianise parts of Oxford Street to come to fruition, after he first suggested it in 2016. Elsewhere some pedestrianisation trials have failed. Last month, West Berkshire Council ended Newbury's evening pedestrianisation trial, after it was opposed by 75% of respondents to a public consultation. In contrast, the majority of Stevenson Square in Manchester's Northern Quarter has transitioned into a permanent pedestrian-friendly space, following a successful trial. title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
description: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of a conference.
body: China has been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said. The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday. Beijing has been a longstanding supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction". It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East. In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran. Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity. In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented. Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe". China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", Wang said. In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East". "I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote. China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme. One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges. Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025. The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement. title: Kartal upsets Svitolina to reach Wuhan semi-finals
description: Sonay Kartal's winning streak following a long injury lay-off continues as she seals a hard-fought victory over fifth seed Elina Svitolina in the quarter-finals of the Wuhan Open.
body: Sonay Kartal has dropped to 170 in the world after her long-term injury, but reached a career-high ranking of 44 last summer Sonay Kartal's winning streak following a long injury lay-off continued as she sealed a hard-fought victory over fifth seed Elina Svitolina in the quarter-finals of the Wuhan Open. The 24-year-old Briton, who missed more than six months with a stress fracture in her back, beat Ukrainian Svitolina 6-2 2-6 6-4 to mark her sixth win in eight matches since returning from injury. It was another eye-catching performance by Kartal, who defeated Italian 15th seed Jasmine Paolini and Swiss ninth seed Belinda Bencic in the previous rounds. She will face 2017 French Open champion Jeļena Ostapenko, who came through a tense opening set to beat 11th seed Diana Shnaider 7-6 (8-6) 6-1, in her first WTA 1000 semi-final on Saturday. Kartal is only the second British player, after Johanna Konta, to reach a WTA 1000 semi-final since the format's introduction in 2009. Kartal wins again as impressive comeback continues Speaking on court after her victory, Kartal said she knew "what a great fighter" world number six Svitolina is, so she "was never safe" in the match. "It was solid composure from me throughout," she added. "It's breaking new ground for me this week. "I love playing here and on this court. The atmosphere was amazing, so big thank you to the crowd." Kartal had not dropped a set during her run to the quarter-finals at Wuhan, and she broke Svitolina early in the first to start on a positive note. Svitolina then called for a medical timeout for treatment on her right arm, but she came back strong to take the second set 6-2 and send the last-eight tie to a decider. The two players were evenly matched in the third set but it was Kartal, using a protected injury ranking to play, who managed to break Svitolina's serve at 5-4 and book her place in the last four. In the other quarter-finals, Polish 16th seed Maja Chwalinska faces Greek Maria Sakkari, while American Ann Li takes on six-time Grand Slam winner and seventh seed Iga Swiatek. title: Doctor regrets not going to police earlier about Lucy Letby
description: Dr Stephen Brearey was the lead neonatal consultant at the hospital where the nurse worked.
body: Dr Stephen Brearey said he began to associate Letby with unexplained deaths in 2015 A senior doctor who raised suspicions about Lucy Letby has said he should have gone to police sooner. Dr Stephen Brearey was the lead neonatal consultant at the Countess of Chester Hospital when the nurse murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others. In his first interview since the publication of the Thirlwall Inquiry report into what happened, Brearey reflected on the effect on staff and said he had "naively" assumed senior managers would respond to suspicions about the nurse's involvement in a series of baby deaths. The inquiry found a "toxic negativity" within the NHS that continued to discourage staff from speaking out, despite stronger whistleblowing guidance, and said regulation was lacking. Brearey claimed his warnings about Letby were repeatedly ignored by bosses at the hospital, which is now under new management - and also fears cultural change at the NHS will take time to implement. "I was naively thinking that raising concerns with senior managers, they had the same values that I did and, once they got it, they would be thinking the same way," he said. The doctor led a group of seven consultants who shared the same concerns about Letby. Hospital bosses carried out a series of internal reviews into increased infant mortality in 2015 and 2016, but Cheshire Police was not asked to investigate until May 2017. Letby remained employed at the hospital until her arrest more than a year later. "I think one of the reasons we got through this and ended up picking up a police investigation is that the seven of us stuck together," he said. "But obviously in retrospect, clearly, if we'd known what was ahead of us, we would have gone to the police earlier." Lucy Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others Letby was eventually arrested in July 2018 but, in the aftermath, Brearey said there "wasn't any psychological support" for staff. "It really was the team looking after the team, and colleagues looking after colleagues," he said. "It's a bit akin to a soldier in a battle with PTSD being taken out of the battle zone to recover, and yet the staff on the neonatal unit were still coming back to work and being re-traumatised. "If they had to stabilise a sick baby, you can understand the triggers that might elicit, and the personal costs to staff who are parents dropping the kids off to school, and not wanting to talk to other parents." Chairing the inquiry, Lady Thirlwall made 17 recommendations, including CCTV for all cots and incubators in neonatal units, restricted access to insulin, mandatory safeguarding training for staff, a harmonised NHS IT system and improved data handling. Asked whether the measures would have prevented Letby from carrying out her crimes, Brearey said: "It certainly would have either prevented or hastened an alarm to say things need to be looked at in more detail. "I think all the suggestions are very sensible and if they are all enacted then they'll go a long way towards preventing further incidents on neonatal units and elsewhere in hospitals." The Thirlwall Inquiry was critical of the actions of former hospital leaders Tony Chambers, Alison Kelly, and Ian Harvey Brearey also gave his thoughts about his hopes for wider cultural change in the NHS in the wake of the inquiry, but indicated he remained sceptical about the speed of change in some areas. He said Lady Thirwall had recommended "the uncontroversial duty of every manager to put patients first". "It feels a bit of a sad indictment on the organisation when that has to be written down into the contracts of senior managers," he said. "It's one thing writing into a contract is another thing actually enacting it into the entire organisation and that takes a cultural change and cultural changes take time, and I very much hope that the NHS and the Department of Health can make that turnaround effectively. "But it doesn't feel like something that's going to happen overnight to me, certainly, no." In a joint statement issued after the publication of the inquiry report, former Countess of Chester Hospital executives Tony Chambers, Ian Harvey and Alison Kelly, along with former HR director Sue Hodkinson, said: "We are carefully reviewing the Thirlwall report and its recommendations. "Given that there are a number of investigations under way, and that the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission has not yet completed, it would be inappropriate for us to offer any further comment at this time. "Our thoughts remain with the families affected by the tragic events that took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital." In a statement given after the conclusion of the inquiry, the hospital trust said: "We know that no apology or action can undo what happened at our hospital. "We are however truly sorry for the events that occurred in 2015 and 2016. We acknowledge the findings of the Thirlwall report and will approach its recommendations with openness and a firm commitment to build on the progress we have already made in improving our hospital's governance, safety and culture since that time. "We are a different organisation today with new leadership, stronger governance and safety processes, and a more open culture where speaking up is encouraged and acted upon." Letby, from Hereford, who maintains her innocence, has twice been denied permission in 2024 to appeal against her convictions. The Criminal Cases Review Commission, which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is considering her case. title: Temperatures to drop for weekend as stormy weather could return next week
description: A sunnier but chillier weekend is on the way, ahead of some potentially stormy weather next week.
body: A brighter but chillier weekend is forecast as high pressure takes hold across the UK, following a week of fluctuating temperatures. Northerly winds on Friday will bring in colder air, with daytime temperatures falling back to around the October average of 10 to 16C (50-61F). Some areas will see their coldest spell of the autumn so far. Clear skies and light winds overnight could lead to patchy fog and some frost away from coastal areas. The cooler conditions follow unseasonably warm weather earlier this week when it felt more like late summer in some areas, with exceptionally mild nights. A northerly airflow will bring an observable drop in temperatures to the UK as high pressure extends eastwards. This will set the scene for a mainly bright end to the week. Most areas can expect sunny spells, although scattered showers may linger in northern and western parts on Friday before reaching south-east England over the weekend. High pressure will usher colder air (shown in blue) across the UK, bringing a more autumnal feel this weekend. Despite the chillier feel, temperatures will be closer to the average for the time of year. This comes after some unseasonable warmth this week. Thursday saw Holbeach in Lincolnshire record a temperature of 22.8C, closely followed by Heathrow and Northolt at 22.7C. A fresh breeze will also make it feel colder, particularly along eastern coasts of both Scotland and England. Nighttime temperatures could fall into single figures across most of the UK. Patchy mist and fog may develop, along with a risk of frost. Parts of rural Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England could even see temperatures dip below freezing. While it could be the coldest spell of this autumn so far in some areas, these temperatures are not that unusual for the time of year. Huge wave crashing over Roker lighthouse in Sunderland during a storm The latest forecast data increasingly points towards a change in the weather pattern as we head into the new week. High pressure is expected to retreat, allowing Atlantic low-pressure systems bearing rain, wind and milder air to move in as the jet stream strengthens. Some of the developing low-pressure systems could become particularly deep, raising the prospect of some very wet and windy conditions, with the potential for stormy weather towards the end of the week and into the weekend. This shift could bring much-needed rain to drought-hit parts of England and Wales, particularly southern and south-west England, where severe drought has been declared. However, the exact track and strength of the incoming weather systems remain uncertain, and the forecast could change over the coming days. Keep up to date with the forecast via the BBC Weather website and app. You can read our latest thoughts on the forecast even further ahead in our monthly outlook. title: The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager
description: How Brighton's Fabian Hurzeler has gone from Germany's fifth tier to being reportedly of interest to Manchester United.
body: Fabian Hurzeler has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to being one of Europe's most feted young managers When Brighton lost at home to Crystal Palace in February, Fabian Hurzeler was booed by his own supporters and subjected to chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning". "There are only two options," said the German after the 1-0 defeat by their fierce rivals left his team floundering 14th in the table with one win in 12 Premier League matches. "Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life." Eight months on, Brighton are reaping the benefits of keeping faith with the man who became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in June 2024 at the age of 31. Palace return to Amex Stadium on Sunday (14:00 BST kick-off) to face opponents who are third in the table after statement wins over defending champions Arsenal and Europa League winners Aston Villa. Hurzeler's stock has rocketed after 11 wins in 18 top-flight games, a run that has propelled the Seagulls back into Europe and left fans - who shouted "you don't know what you're doing" at him just a few months ago - worried that he could be lured away. Following last Saturday's win at Sunderland, there was chat on the post-match phone-ins that Hurzeler, rewarded with a new long-term contract before the end of last season and given £150m to spend on signings in the summer, could be a prime target for a big club looking for a manager. "You learn more about yourself and the people around you when you are losing games," former Brighton striker Glenn Murray told BBC Sport in reference to last season's poor run. "Hurzeler has come out the other side and the way he has got this group of players performing is exceptional." Scott McCarthy, from the We Are Brighton fan site, said Hurzeler appeared to have lost the crowd to such a degree at one stage last season than even a few wins would not be enough to turn it around. "He looked like a manager who was out of ideas," McCarthy told BBC Sport. "Leaving the stadium after losing at home to Palace, the only conversation fans were having was: 'he has got to go'. "It's totally different now. It's worked out phenomenally." Will Brighton manage to keep hold of Hurzeler, who has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to reported interest, external from Manchester United? Hurzeler signs to 2029 as Brighton rival elite clubs Hurzeler's Brighton choice and Barber's favourite moment - fans' forum Hurzeler (left) has been linked with Manchester United should they decide to replace Michael Carrick (right) The determination Hurzeler demonstrated in the face of anger from fans following last season's defeat by Palace has been evident throughout his 10-year coaching career. In 2016, after one injury too many following spells in the reserves at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich, the former midfielder gave up playing professionally to accept a player-manager role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23. It was the start of a coaching journey that has led to the Premier League. To make ends meet at village club Pipinsried, which is about 30 miles from Munich, football-obsessed Hurzeler worked for an art dealer selling paintings to wealthy Bavarians. In an interview with the Guardian, external in 2024, he revealed he was fired from that job because he was spending too much time watching games. "If you want to sell something to a person, you have to try to convince them by doing something," he said when comparing selling pictures to managing Premier League players. "And you can't go there and say: 'Look at this picture, it's an amazing picture'. You have to understand the needs and the wishes from the clients. "That's a little bit similar to being a coach. "The most important thing is to understand the person behind the player. What are his needs? What are his values? How is he educated? How was his past? Where does he get education?" Hurzeler's obsession to succeed runs deep. While managing St Pauli - who he left in 2024 to join Brighton after guiding the Hamburg club back to the Bundesliga following a 13-year absence, external - he was invited to Tottenham's training ground to watch Ange Postecoglou's side train. Hurzeler - who was born in Houston, Texas, before moving to Germany at the age of two - asked so many questions that Postecoglou had to ask another member of his coaching staff to step in and take over. Hurzeler is covered in beer by his players after St Pauli's promotion to the Bundesliga in 2024 He also picked up tips from Roberto de Zerbi at Brighton, a few months before replacing him after Kieran McKenna,, external who had been heavily linked with the job, opted to stay at newly promoted Ipswich. Despite respectable back-to-back eighth-placed finishes, Hurzeler's time at Brighton has not been without its difficult moments. In addition to fans calling for his dismissal last season, the Seagulls were thrashed 7-0 at Nottingham Forest in his first season in charge, while former Arsenal and England defender Martin Keown labelled Hurzeler "wet behind the ears", external on the BBC's Final Score following Brighton's 4-2 defeat at Chelsea in September 2024. So what is the reason for the shift in fortunes since his own fans called for his dismissal? "It's partly because Hurzeler went back to basics," adds McCarthy. "He relied on an experienced core in the side to get out of the hole, which is testament to him because it shows his pragmatic side. You get managers who are wedded to their philosophy and won't change. "Hurzeler realised what he was doing was not working and that it could cost him his job, so tried something else. You can now see this is a team more in his image, because they press insanely." Will Hurzeler leave Brighton if another club

title: Does the Premier League 'Big Six' still exist?
description: For years the Premier League has had a defined 'Big Six', comprised of Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur., but could this era be coming to an end?
body: Tottenham have not finished in the top six in each of the past two seasons For years the Premier League has had a defined 'Big Six', comprised of Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur. They were not just the sides who often dominated the top positions in the table, but also had the biggest fanbase, most financial clout and were usually the league's most successful sides. But that has not been in the case in more recent seasons. In the last couple of years Tottenham and Manchester United have found themselves fighting at the wrong end of the table, while teams like Aston Villa, Brentford and Brighton have been battling at the top. Meanwhile, Manchester City - the top-flight's dominant side over the past decade - are facing a period of uncertainty after the club was recently found guilty of breaching financial rules over nine years. The 'Big Six' remains in financial terms, with City, Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Spurs and Chelsea all inside the top 10 of highest revenue generating clubs in world football. , external But is the era of the traditional 'Big Six' on the field at an end? One of the most memorable stories of the Premier League era was Leicester City upsetting the odds to win the title in the 2015-16 season. It captured the imagination of football fans everywhere, because it seemed so difficult for anyone outside the 'Big Six' to get even close to being champions. But it seemed as though it was destined to be a one-off as, for the following three seasons, the 'Big Six' locked down the top positions once more. Indeed, the gap between them and the rest was bigger than ever, with the smallest deficit between seventh and sixth place during those three seasons being eight points. Between 2010-11 and 2018-19, the so-called 'Big Six' finished in those leading positions five times. They also finished in the top seven twice and top eight once. But things changed after that. In only one of the six seasons since have they all finished in the top six, with Aston Villa, Newcastle and Brighton in those places at some point. Tottenham, in particular, have struggled and ended one place above the relegation zone in each of the past two campaigns and are currently second bottom on three points after failing to win any of their first six games. This season, albeit early days, Manchester United are in 13th spot and Liverpool ninth. Since 2021-22, Chelsea and United have finished out of the top six twice, while Spurs have missed out three times - twice finishing 17th. Five of the top six places have gone to clubs not in the traditional six in the past three years - the same as the previous eight years combined. This video can not be played Brighton sporting director Mike Cave explains the club's approach to recruitment One reason for the end of their dominance as a collective is because other clubs have closed the financial gap. Newcastle are an example following a £305m takeover led by the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund in 2021. They went from finishing 11th in 2021-22 to fourth in the following campaign and then fifth two seasons later. Meanwhile, others, like Brighton, have leaned into data and smart recruitment to help them close the gap. The Seagulls have an impressive record of buying promising talent for low prices before selling them on for significant fees. In 2021 they signed 19-year-old Ecuador midfielder Moises Caicedo from Independiente del Valle for £4m and sold him two years later to Chelsea in a deal a worth £115m - a British record at the time. They also signed Marc Cucurella for £15m and sold him to Chelsea for £62m and brought in Alexis Mac Allister for £7m before selling him to Liverpool for a deal worth £55m. "Our recruitment strategy and philosophy has been something that we've built on over a long period of time now," sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast. "The data element of it gets a lot of attention because going back a few years it was quite novel in comparison to some other clubs. "Really it's just a component of a bigger process that goes on. It's an important component, it helps us to identify talent from around the world in quite an efficient way which allows us to move quickly in what is a really competitive transfer market." How Brighton attract and develop the best young players ahead of their rivals Has your team made the list of the world's richest football clubs? Since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013, Manchester United have struggled to get close to the success they enjoyed under the 26-year reign of the legendary Scot. The 20-time top-flight champions have had a high turnover of head coaches in recent years in an effort to find the winning formula and since the start of the 2020-21 season they have had four different permanent managers. But they are not alone in this high amount of chopping and changing - and not even the worst. In the same period, Chelsea have had seven different people in charge on a permanent basis, while Tottenham have had six as they too have tried to find a way to challenge for trophies. Meanwhile, Arsenal have shown patience can pay dividends by giving Mikel Arteta - appointed in 2019 - time to build a squad that resulted in the Gunners ending their 22-year wait for a Premier League title last season. The 'Big Six' hasn't always been a thing in the Premier League, so an evolution of what it is and who they are was always likely to happen. Indeed, when the league was first formed back in 1992 there was a 'Big Five' of Arsenal, Everton, Liverpool, Manchester United and Tottenham - clubs who were seen at the time as the ones with the biggest fanbase and financial power. That evolved into a 'Big Two' during the late 1990s and early 2000s as Manchester United and Arsenal dominated, before expanding to a '

title: The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day
description: Beth Dobbin ran for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. Five years on, she is largely bedbound after being diagnosed with ME, a devastating illness for which there is no cure.
body: This video can not be played 'It feels like you're days away from death' - Beth Dobbin Beth Dobbin is so determined to raise awareness of the illness that has decimated her life that she is speaking out, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health. Five years ago, she ran for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics. Now, at 32, she spends more than 22 hours a day in bed. "I've done little things like attend a blood test at the doctors and been in bed for months after. So doing this interview, chatting away for 30 minutes, that could have an impact on me in 2027," she says. "But I felt like it was really important to do that to get the message out." She now only gets out of bed to eat and use the bathroom. Dobbin has been diagnosed with ME, or myalgic encephalomyelitis - a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more. A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end. This year, Dobbin has left the house on just five occasions. "It's life-decimating like I can't even put into words," she says. "I feel like I've lost everything. "I have still got my family, but I've lost my independence, my health, the ability to work, the ability to exercise." For Dobbin it all started with back-to-back Covid and glandular fever infections in the winter of 2021-22. She had not been unwell with either, only discovering she had contracted both through retrospective tests. She had been sleeping a bit more and her running times were slightly down, but nothing that raised alarm. As time went on, she noticed soreness in the glands of her neck and armpits and a general sense of not quite feeling herself. British Athletics doctors ran tests that gave no answers, so she carried on, assuming it was lingering glandular fever that would eventually pass. She qualified for that year's World Championships, Commonwealth Games and European Championships in what was an unusually condensed season owing to the backlog from the pandemic. Her health progressively deteriorated. At the Worlds, she struggled with a painful throat and was waking at unusual times in the night. At the Commonwealths, she was dizzy while running and her body was more sore than normal. At the Europeans, she false-started after losing all feeling in her legs while in the blocks. She spoke of her "year of hell" in an emotional interview with BBC Sport after that race. This video can not be played 'It's been a year from hell' - Dobbin emotional after false start "When the Europeans had finished, I had this huge rest and the symptoms were just piling on. Things were getting worse and worse," Dobbin says. "I was struggling to stand up, I was sleeping loads, in bed all the time. "After six weeks, I went back to training. I managed three weeks. "[Doctors] were just really shocked that I still wasn't doing well and I'd had these viruses months ago. "I think I saw four or five different specialists because the symptoms that I was having, they were across multiple [body] systems. All the specialists said 'this is ME' and we don't want it to be that because there's nothing out there for it." ME has no known cure or specific treatment, with patients often relying on off-label medication to manage a condition that can cause more than 200 symptoms, including nausea, headaches, poor cognitive function and brain fog. The condition is also known as chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), a label Dobbin strongly rejects. As a former athlete who balanced working eight-hour shifts with training before turning professional, she says she has "known fatigue my whole life" and believes the term fails to capture the severity of the illness. "I wish it was just fatigue, that would be a walk in the park," she says. "It's so much more than that. If I thought of fatigue in my top 20 symptoms it might just make the cut." Instead, she says, it feels like her entire body "is shutting down; it feels like you are a few days from death". More than 400,000 people in the UK are thought to have ME, although the true figure could exceed one million, with severity ranging from people able to work or study to those requiring round-the-clock care and tube feeding. Despite the length of time she spends in bed, Dobbin often feels too unwell to sleep and requires medication to help her do so. "Even things like sitting up for a prolonged period of time can take it out of me so I prefer to be just propped up in bed, and that doesn't mean I feel fine. It doesn't get rid of my symptoms, but it makes them less hellish." This video can not be played The Olympic sprinter who can't leave her bed For Dobbin's parents and sister Faye, who sit close by to her in support during the interview at the family home in Doncaster, the impact is clear. "I'm just so desperate to help her but I can't because there is nothing. I'd take her anywhere, I'd take her to America if I had to, but there's nothing," says her father Jim, a former footballer who played for Barnsley, Grimsby and Doncaster Rovers. Mum Jean adds: "You wake up every day and just feel sad. She should be building her life, living her best life. "Every day you worry about how she's going to be that day. It's a worry about what our future life's going to be like, who's going look after her if we can't look after her. "There is nothing out there. There is nowhere to go. You go to the GP and there's nowhere for them to send you to. It's really at the back of the queue as far as research, knowledge, expertise, funding." There is no specialist service for ME within the NHS and Dobbin says she has found herself educating

title: Fuel costs squeezing margins for some businesses
description: Diesel recently topped £2 per litre and there is concern that a duty freeze will not go far enough.
body: Diesel prices in Jersey have reached more than £2 per litre in recent weeks Some businesses in Jersey have expressed concern about the impact of rising global fuel prices. Locally, and in the UK, diesel prices recently topped £2 a litre, and global leaders have since made efforts to ease the strain on supply. The Government of Jersey has proposed to freeze fuel duty in 2027 in a bid to "help ease cost-of-living pressures". A&A Scaffolding Solutions said it welcomed that move, but said it would provide "limited relief if global prices continue to rise". More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Fuel duty was frozen in Jersey from 2023-2025, before rising in line with inflation in 2026. In the proposed budget for 2027, external, the government has suggested freezing it once again. It said "maintaining fuel duty at its current rate will help avoid additional costs for households and businesses that rely on transport, providing continued support at a time when many islanders remain under financial pressure". However, some businesses on the island worry that it will not be enough to offset global prices. Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine? Kelly Keating, from A&A Scaffolding Solutions, said "rising diesel prices are a real concern for us, particularly when they come on top of so many other costs that seem to be increasing across Jersey". "Construction is taking a hard hit. We rely on diesel for machinery, vehicles and deliveries, so increases put direct pressure on the cost of carrying out work. "Alongside rising material, freight and operating costs, this is squeezing margins and making it harder to price projects with confidence". "A freeze in fuel duty would be welcome, but our concern is that it would offer limited relief if global fuel prices continue to rise. "The wider issue is the cumulative impact. Businesses can only absorb so many increases before they affect investment, project viability and ultimately the prices customers pay". Businesses said it was becoming more difficult to absorb price rises Fuel costs are also having a "noticeable impact" for tree surgeons, Jonathan Le Maistre Ltd. Darren Hopkins, from the firm, said "we depend on our vans, trucks, chippers, stump grinders, and other machinery that consume significant amounts of fuel". "Increased diesel prices will raise our operating costs, reducing margins on jobs and making it more difficult to absorb costs without passing some of them on to our customers". Hopkins said continued increases would be a "concern for their business, and the wider industry". However, some businesses are managing through the disruption. Jeremy Phillips, from Barette Plant Hire, said it "hasn't been too much of an issue so far, but that fuel surcharges are being added to hourly rates". However, he said that "if the prices keep going up, customers aren't going to be carrying on with their projects". Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said support was being targeted directly at consumers rather than expecting businesses to absorb costs In the run-up to the unveiling of the 2027 budget, Deputy Lucy Stephenson called for a reduction in fuel duty, but those plans were withdrawn following assurances from ministers that support was coming. Speaking at the time, Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said the government "didn't like the idea of reducing fuel duty because it wasn't targeted". Instead, ministers opted for a freeze on duty for 2027, prioritising targeted support for families and those "struggling the most". Responding to the fresh concerns from businesses, Maclean said: "Rather than expecting businesses to absorb increased costs such as higher fuel prices, the budget provides support directly to consumers to help them manage those pressures and spend in the local economy". "Fuel prices are largely driven by global markets and geopolitical events outside Jersey's control. "What the government can do is avoid adding further pressure where it can. "The proposed freeze in fuel duty will help mitigate the impact of prices rises by reducing the level of duty in real terms". title: 'People call them pervert glasses': Blind users fear backlash over smart tech
description: Concerns about the use of smart glasses are having an affect on visually-impaired users.
body: Fraser Fleming says his glasses help him navigate public transport and read street signs Fraser Fleming approaches the corner of a busy Glasgow city centre street and asks his smart glasses to describe the road ahead. A voice coming from tiny speakers in the arms of the specs tells him there are several parked cars and a person walking in his direction. For 44-year-old Fraser, who is registered blind, this is "game changing" information. "I know how to approach the street and what sort of care to take," he says. "If I need to maybe take my time or if I can just walk at normal pace." Fraser, who began losing his sight in his early twenties, says his AI-powered Meta smart glasses have become part of his everyday life during the past two years. They help him to navigate public transport, read street signs and order from menus – but he's started to think twice about wearing them in public. "People are calling them pervert glasses," he says, referring to multiple reports of them being used to secretly film and harass people, particularly women and girls, with the footage being shared online. Fraser says this is having a negative effect on anyone wearing them, including visually-impaired people. "We are definitely not using them to record people in dodgy situations," he says. "We're using them to lead an independent life." They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image? The Meta glasses revolution - is it okay to film people in public? TikToker faces police probe over secret filming using 'smart glasses' Fraser, from Motherwell, told the BBC's Your Voice he would often take his glasses off if he thought there was a chance of a confrontation. "I've got enough to worry about getting from A to B," he says. "I'll just put the glasses away and have to rely on my other senses in order to navigate around, which is going to make life a lot more difficult for me." Tracey Rogerson says the technology is a big part of her independence Tracey Rogerson, who uses the technology to help with her sight loss, shares Fraser's concerns. "I was shocked to hear that they were being called pervert glasses because for me, they're such a big part of my life to help me maintain my independence," she says. Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, started selling smart glasses in 2021, and has sold about two million pairs since February last year. It says there is a light on the frames which makes it clear the smart glasses are recording, but it also warns users not to engage in harmful activities. As a result of the backlash against the glasses, some venues and events have banned or at least restricted their use over fears about covert filming, including ComicCon Scotland, which takes place in Edinburgh later this month. Gordon Brown is severely sight-impaired This means Gordon Brown, who is severely sight-impaired and has attended the event with his family for the past three years, won't be going this year. He says the impact of the ban on people with disabilities has been overlooked. "Even if I was to put my glasses on quickly, just to read a sign or something, I wouldn't feel comfortable," says Gordon, from Inverkip. "I think it's a matter of principle now, the fact that they're not willing to engage, and they're not willing to listen to a minority group. "You know, we're not talking about thousands of people all of a sudden turning up wearing smart glasses." Monopoly Events, which runs some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK, announced in July that it had banned Meta glasses to "stop secret filming" of guests and attendees. The ban applies to Meta glasses and other "wearable recording devices." The company was contacted by the BBC about Gordon's comments. Cosplay artist Teah Pearn says she was secretly filmed by someone wearing the glasses Cosplay artist and performer Teah Pearn was at a comic convention in Birmingham earlier this year when she was secretly filmed. She later discovered the footage was posted online. Teah, who performs as Spill The Tea and has 1.9 million followers on TikTok, says she felt "violated". "He was purposefully trying to provoke me or purposefully trying to make strange comments to get a reaction out of me so that he could get that perfect clip that he could post on social media and capitalise off it," says the London-based artist. Teah says her experience demonstrates why restrictions are needed, but she thinks there should be exceptions for people with disabilities. "For people who need the glasses and who really have to use them, I think they should be able to use them," she says. "They shouldn't have to deal with the fact there's been a certain group of people who have spoiled it for them." In a statement, Meta said: "We are proud that our AI glasses give blind, low-vision and hearing-impaired people greater independence in daily life. "They were built to be noticed, which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. "It cannot be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it." title: Charity 'terrified' closure could leave mums suicidal
description: The Happy Mums Foundation supports women experiencing postpartum mental health challenges.
body: The Happy Mums Foundation was set up in Carlisle in 2015 by a mum who experienced isolation after being treated in a Psychiatric Mother and Baby Unit A charity has said it is "terrified" new mums suffering from suicidal thoughts will be left with nowhere to turn if its group sessions end due to funding pressures. The Happy Mums Foundation, which supports women experiencing postpartum mental health challenges, was set up in 2015 and has helped more than 1,000 families across Cumbria. Charity director Lucinda Bray fears the loss of the in-person "safe place" could worsen the mental health of vulnerable women in the county. Women who have attended the sessions say the charity, which would move online only, offers "no judgement" peer support and helps mums feel less isolated when experiencing trauma. Bray said: "I'm terrified, if we don't have in-person groups for mums, where will they go? What will they do? "Being able to talk about suicidal thinking, is actually quite a good preventative factor, if that doesn't have an outlet and you don't have a safe space to talk about those things, where might they go?" The charity says young mums are 40% more likely to experience perinatal mental health challenges First-time mum Amy described motherhood as "absolutely wonderful" but admitted it could be stressful and overwhelming at times. "The long nights, the crying and not knowing what it is they want, you've just been handed a tiny human being and you're meant to just know what to do and having the expectations of mum knows best. "I didn't have a clue and I think a lot of mums are in the same boat." At first Amy found it difficult to leave the house with her daughter who was born prematurely. Now, she attends the charity's teen to 25 group, which has helped her build confidence. "Obviously everyone absolutely adores the babies here but it's called Happy Mums for a reason," she said. "There's plenty of support out there for babies, but it's nice to have something that is more about the mums." Amy said without the support of the group she would struggle more to get out and about. "When I'm feeling low with my depression or anxiety and more anxious about going out I know that I can come to Happy Mums, I look forward to it," she said. "Without it I'd struggle more with speaking to people and asking for the help." Director Lucinda Bray says moving some help groups online would help save money but in-person groups are really important for isolated mums If you have been affected by the issues in this report, support is available at BBC Action Line The Happy Mums Foundation had previously received funding from Comic Relief, The National Lottery, The Cumbria Foundation and the NHS. The group says over the last year funding for preventative mental health services has become increasingly difficult to secure. Bray said the 13 weekly support groups have already been reduced to five, and without investment the charity will be forced to move groups online or close completely. Growing financial pressures across the charities sector has been evident in recent months, including the closure of suicide prevention charity Papyrus in September. Cumbria has a limited number of groups offering the type of support available through Happy Mums National Council for Voluntary Organisations' chief influencing officer Leigh Brimicombe said the current financial climate was "tough" for charity organisations. He said the cost of living crisis meant there was a "growing need for support in communities but also less money available for donors or funders to give, compounded by increased running costs for charities themselves". Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, Markus Campbell-Savours, sent a letter of concern about the future of foundation to the Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Trust. In reply, chief executive James Duncan said "peer-led and community-based support can form a valuable part of the wider network for support available to women and families". He added although formal joint working with the NHS was not possible due to the distinction between peer-led and clinical services, the potential closure was "particularly concerning given the relatively limited number of voluntary and community sector organisations providing this type of support across Cumbria". The Department of Health and Social Care has been approached for comment. title: Teen's death inspires mum's drive for earlier rare cancer diagnosis
description: Hannah York hopes new guidance will help doctors spot signs of soft tissue sarcomas sooner.
body: Liberty York died aged 19, a year after she first experienced symptoms of an angiosarcoma Liberty York was 19 when she died from a rare form of cancer, two days after her birthday. A year after her death, her mother Hannah York has talked about her strength and the parts of her daughter that existed outside of her illness. "The first thing that comes to mind when I think about Liberty is how kind she was and thoughtful," she said. To Hannah, she was still the same determined teenager throughout the final year of her life, before she died from an angiosarcoma, a rare form of soft tissue sarcoma, a type of cancer which starts in areas of the body such as muscle and fat. The first signs appeared in May 2024 when Liberty, from Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire, began feeling unusually tired and nauseous. A year earlier she had been diagnosed with Addison's disease, a rare autoimmune condition, so at first the family thought it was possible the two could be linked. Liberty was referred to see a specialist but while the family waited for answers, she developed swelling and pain in her left breast. "We went to see the GP about the swelling and she thought it was mastitis because it was red as well and painful.," Hannah said. "The [cancer's] main symptom is the swelling or change in skin. Liberty's swelling kept getting bigger and bigger." Antibiotics were prescribed but they failed to work and doctors initially thought she had an abscess. Liberty was remembered as being strong and kind by her mother Hannah Later, Hannah said, attention turned towards the possibility that hormones could be responsible. "Liberty was on a teenage cancer ward and they said it was very common," she said. "So many teenagers, it's put down to hormones and unfortunately they said they see it every day." The swelling that had begun as a small area of concern just weeks earlier had become a tumour weighing 10lb (4.5kg) by the time surgery took place. For Hannah, that moment brought relief that they finally had an answer, but also the harsh reality of what her daughter was facing. "Liberty's type of sarcoma was a particularly aggressive sarcoma and, after she was operated on, it had spread to her lungs in just six weeks," she remembered. "The difference between days and weeks to diagnosis is so important with sarcoma. She didn't get a fighting chance." Liberty died in the early hours of 1 June 2025, two days after celebrating her 19th birthday. Hannah hoped more early diagnoses will help other teenagers beat the disease In the months since, Hannah said she had tried to channel her grief into raising awareness of the disease that took her daughter. She is supporting the Child Cancer Smart campaign, led by CCLG: The Children & Young People's Cancer Association, as it launches new guidelines for healthcare professionals, aimed at improving recognition of soft tissue sarcomas in children and young people. These cancers account for about 7% of childhood cancers, according to the charity, but experts say diagnosis can often be delayed because symptoms resemble more common conditions. "Liberty was an incredibly strong person with a very strong sense of right and wrong. She was very opinionated, which I loved about her," Hannah said. "I don't know if any earlier diagnosis could have saved her, but she'd have had more of a chance. "Her cancer was rare, underfunded and under-researched, so the best chance of helping other people is by making sure they are diagnosed early." title: Snapchat and Instagram grooming becoming 'easier'
description: Online grooming is rising, with children as young as five targeted, prompting calls for reform.
body: Experts warn children as young as five years old are now being groomed on social media and gaming sites Experts are urging parents to talk to their children amid warnings social media grooming is becoming "quicker" and "easier" than ever before. Childline said Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram were the top platforms children named in counselling about online sexual abuse last year. The companies have been approached for comment. Avon and Somerset Police's child exploitation prevention officer Andri Nicolau said children as young as five can be targeted through social media, gaming and messaging platforms. She urged parents to encourage kids to ask for help without fear of blame or punishment. The warning comes after three men were jailed for grooming a 17-year-old girl on Snapchat before raping her. Research by the NSPCC found sexual communication offences involving children in the South West have more than doubled since the offence was introduced seven years ago, to 756 in 2024/25. Of those, 300 were recorded by Avon and Somerset Police, 96 by Gloucestershire Constabulary and 61 by Wiltshire Police. The charity also said Snapchat was mentioned in 324 counselling sessions about online sexual abuse between April 2025 and March 2026, a 19% increase on the previous year. TikTok (234) and Instagram (197) were the next most frequently mentioned platforms. Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, said: "It's deeply disturbing that hundreds of children have come to us in the past year alone, disclosing experiences of online sexual abuse linked to these popular apps and platforms. "These crimes are highly distressing for victims, often leaving children and their families to deal with devastating lifelong impacts." Suleman Aqeel, 23, was charged with 29 sexual and violent offences, including raping and sexually abusing a woman and a child in Bristol Another recent example involved Suleman Aqeel, from Speedwell in Bristol, who was jailed for 17 years at Bristol Crown Court on 30 September. Aqeel used social media, including Snapchat, to arrange to meet young girls. He also filmed some of his offences and threatened to share intimate videos and images. New data suggests that this particular form of exploitation of children, known as 'sextortion', has also reached record levels. The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) said there has been a sharp rise in the number of young people contacting its confidential Report Remove helpline, external because they fear sexual images of themselves have been shared, or could be shared, online. Criminals try to extort or blackmail their victims by threatening to publish the images, which have often been taken by the child themselves. Nicolau said children spending more time online meant they were increasingly vulnerable to grooming, which is "easier" and "quicker" than ever before. "With online gaming and social media, you have kids from five years old online, some of them have their own phones, so it can be any age," she said. She works with schools to inform children how to be safe online, but said they are often unaware of the risks, including not viewing people they meet online as strangers and expecting them to be "nasty" from the start. Nicolau encouraged any child or young person who believes they are being groomed to "find someone they are comfortable with and speak to them". She said the police might not be the first choice, but speaking to somebody they trust is what mattered. Nicolau urged parents to talk to their children and not take away devices or ban them from platforms, warning this could make them feel they were to blame. "Sit down with your child, tell them it's not their fault, even if they've sent indecent images of themselves," she said. "Believe them and give them the authorisation to say whatever they need to say." Andri Nicolau, Avon and Somerset Police's child exploitation prevention officer, works with schools to inform children about the risks of online grooming Ella Bradshaw, the NSPCC's policy and public affairs officer, advised parents to start conversations about online safety as early as possible so that children know that they have a "safe adult" to go to. "Often, particularly if it's to do with grooming or any kind of sexual or romantic relationship, children can be really scared of being judged and embarrassed to talk," said Bradshaw. "Making sure that your child knows that you will stand by them, that you will respond with warmth and care rather than judging them or blaming them for what's going on is really important." James Simmons-Read, who leads the Children's Society national exploitation prevention programme, said there are "huge concerns" about the growing scale of child sexual abuse and exploitation online. "Perpetrators are always adapting ways they can better reach young people, whether that's through gaming or social media," he said. He said another worrying trend was young people turning to AI rather than adults for advice and support about online harms. Simmons-Read urged parents to normalise conversations with young people about their online lives. Ella Bradshaw from the NSPCC said children don't speak out because of fear of judgment Ellen Roome, from Cheltenham, who has been campaigning for improvements to online safety since the death of her son Jools in 2022, said not enough is being done to protect young people on social media. "Children are regularly being fed content that is either violent or grooming material and I think as it stands, there isn't any platform that is fully safe for them," she said. "I do think that the social media ban for children will help, but they need to make sure that it is enforced and social media companies are held to account." title: The hero dinner lady who died saving five children in the Aberfan disaster
description: As coal slurry engulfed the school, the dinner lady threw her body on five children, protecting them.
body: Five children were found alive under the body of Nansi Williams following the disaster On 21 October 1966, as a primary school and surrounding homes in Aberfan were engulfed by slurry from a collapsed coal tip, a dinner lady was collecting money from pupils. Within moments, 144 people were dead, including 116 children, on what was the last day of class at Pantglas Junior School before the half-term holiday. But five children were saved that day by the heroic actions of Nansi Williams, who died shielding the group. "Apparently she was holding as much of us as she could, and trying to get us under a table," said Aberfan survivor Paul Harries, who has spoken to the media for the first time. Harries, who was aged six at the time, was one of the five who was found alive under Williams' body. "She gave everything to give us a future, and she lost everything," he said. "Nansi Williams was a hero. A true hero. My hero." He continued: "If it hadn't been for Nansi Williams, then instead of 116 children dying that morning it would have been 121. "It would have been us, 100%." As the 60th anniversary of the disaster approaches, Williams will be honoured with a purple plaque, external to commemorate her courage. Paul Harries was giving his dinner money to Nansi Williams when the school was engulfed The King, Queen and Prince of Wales will visit Aberfan, in Merthyr Tydfil county, next week to mark the anniversary, following on from the late Queen Elizabeth who visited Aberfan eight times. "The only reason I'm speaking about it now is because Nansi's story needs to be told and recognised for what she has done," Paul, now 66, said. He recalled how an avalanche of slurry swept through the school just minutes after lessons began. He had walked from the infant school to the junior school hall to pay a shilling for his school dinner. It was there Williams was collecting the money from him and four other children. When a colliery waste tip collapsed, slurry crashed into Pantglas Junior School, killing 116 children and 28 adults "The infant school was totally missed by the tips," he added. "So it was only by chance that we were not in the infant school, which was safe. We were in the junior school which caught the brunt of it." Harries cannot remember the moment the building collapsed, but said: "I can remember being dug out. "I was rushed straight to hospital with the other four children that were buried with me." It was only later that he learnt of Nansi's heroics. "My mother and father told me the story," he said. "They said 'your dinner lady died protecting you five children'." When rescuers found them, Williams was still shielding the group. Nansi Williams grew up in Aberfan and worked as a dinner lady and playground supervisor at Pantglas Junior School Williams, who was 44, was a familiar figure to that generation of Aberfan children. Another pupil, Janett Bickley, remembers her as a kind and popular presence. "Oh, Nansi was lovely," she said. "My mother and Nansi were friends. "If you were lucky you could hold her hand in the yard at break time." She recalled proudly walking around the playground thinking "I'm holding Nansi's hand today". Like many pupils, Bickley remembered Williams collecting dinner money and leading children to lunch. Janett Bickley recalled how all the children were very fond of Nansi Williams "She was trying to protect children," she said. "She died, and they lived." Bickley believes there are many people who should be recognised for their courage on that day, but agreed Williams was a hero. "I think Nansi went way, way beyond what she needed to do," she said. "She could have saved her own life. She cared more for the children." Nansi's godson, Dai Powell, campaigned for greater recognition and said stories of what happened were passed down through his family for decades. "My ultimate hero. No-one will ever touch her," he said. "We'd all like to think we'd do the same thing, but until it happens we don't really know. "Her heroism is just unbelievable." Dai Powell has led the campaign for Nansi's courage to be honoured with a purple plaque The purple plaque scheme, external celebrates women who have made important contributions to their communities in Wales or shown exceptional courage. "She didn't think of herself at all, she just thought of the children," said Rhian Connick, secretary of the Purple Plaque Committee. The plaque will be placed near the cemetery in Aberfan For Harries, the plaque will ensure her story survives long after those who remember her are gone. "Every year I go straight to Nansi's grave and put flowers there," he said. "My family know the story of Nansi because if it hadn't been for her, they wouldn't be here today. "There would be no son, no grandchildren. "People can look at it and read it, and find out about her story." title: 'TV and cheap booze' blamed for landlord quitting
description: Lincolnshire has lost 27% of its pubs and bars since 2009 and some are calling on the government to act against cheap supermarket booze.
body: Landlord Patrick Hughes says fewer people are going to the pub Former pub landlord Patrick Hughes is blunt when explaining why he has called time on his tenure behind the bar. "I thought there was a gap in the market but there was no market for the gap", he said. The 66-year-old took over The Royal Mail Cart pub in Spalding, in August 2025, hoping to attract customers with live music nights and "a sense of community". Just over a year on he is packing boxes and looking around the empty rooms after he quit his tenancy with the pub's owner, Stonegate Group. The government said it was supporting pubs with business rates discounts. Patrick has given up his tenancy of The Royal Mail Cart in Spalding Patrick told BBC Politics North that he blames a perfect storm of rising utility and wage prices, people's changing habits and major roadworks directly outside the pub, which began in the summer. "These days people are used to staying at home, watching TV, having cheap drink from the supermarket or off licence and getting food deliveries," he said. "To make a pub like this work you need to turn over £12,000 a week, some weeks we were doing quite well, around £8,000, but once the road works began outside that went down quite dramatically." Figures from the Office for National Statistics, external show that 27% of pubs and bars in Lincolnshire closed between 2009 and 2025. That is a drop from 710 to 515. In South Holland, of which Spalding is a part, the rate is almost double that, at 53%, a drop from 75 to 35. That is also way above the England average of 19%. "The government needs to look at the low cost of alcohol in supermarkets primarily," said Patrick. "Certainly the taxation in supermarkets needs to be looked at to bring about some kind of equilibrium." Duty paid on draught alcohol in pubs and bars is up to 11 pence cheaper than that sold in supermarkets. But other costs associated with running a business still makes supermarket alcohol cheaper overall. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced a 20% cut in business rates for qualifying pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, effective from April 2027. Emma McClarkin OBE, chief executive of the British Beer and Pub Association, says they want that to be made permanent at the Budget this month, "alongside a freeze in beer duty and a widening of the draft discount". "We're set to lose one pub a day by the end of the year and 295 have closed already," she said. "When a pub does close, it's not just the front door that's closing, it's the heritage, the culture, the economic contribution to society and the social value." Mark Newlands believes that people still want to visit their local pub Just outside Spalding, The Ship Inn pub stands by the River Welland in the small hamlet of Surfleet Seas End. "There used to be tables and chairs with people eating food and drinking by the river," said Mark Newlands, who lives a few doors down. The pub closed last year but now some locals, led by Mark, have formed The Shipmates group to try to raise £600,000 to buy and run it. So far they have managed to get the pub listed as An Asset of Community Value under the Localism Act 2011. That gives them the right to bid for the property, if it goes up for sale. "People have become fed up of the Covid way of living and they want to see their pub open," said Mark. "The indications from smaller and larger investors is that it's worth doing and we've proven to our own satisfaction that it is a viable business." An HM Treasury spokesperson said: "The Chancellor prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues - saving thousands of locals over £1,000 a year." Stonegate has been approached by the BBC for comment. Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North. title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
description: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.
body: The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows. Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks. Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks. As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests. BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported. Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes. Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts. The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners". The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby. The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard. Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said. Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route". Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen. About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day. The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August. Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman. These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore. So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships. Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day". "The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added. The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media. Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman. A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard. Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said. Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
