title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
description: Over the past year there has been a stark rise in anti-government activists deported to Russia from the EU and US where they were seeking refuge.
body: Criticising the government, whether on the street or on social media, can result in a prison sentence in Russia (file pic) Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum. "It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia. Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face. US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement. In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account. Russian security services frequently televise special operations against perceived "spies" and "traitors" The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours. "At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere." Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home. "I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?" Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees. Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia. One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison. Andrei Pivovarov was imprisoned in a penal colony for four years for "carrying out activities of an undesirable organisation" "We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee. And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere. Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025. "Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC. Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data. Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns. Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds. Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries. Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face. "I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me." Artyom deserted the Russian army in 2022 but was deported back to Russia via Egypt He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt. "I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'". Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad. "Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instea

title: Three children and teacher killed by 16-year-old at Oregon primary school
description: The suspect was shot dead by a local community member who followed him into the school, said police.
body: This video can not be played Police: Three children and one teacher killed in Oregon school shooting A 16-year-old shot dead three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, according to police. The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, police said. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the teenager was shot dead by a community member who "pursued him into the school and engaged him". The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition, police said. It is unclear if the attacker had any links to the school. The suspect was shot dead moments after local law enforcement arrived at the scene "We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement. "No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing." Emergency services responded to reports of an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, at 12:59 local time (04:59 BST), Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters. The first call came from a person who said that an unknown suspect was shooting into their car with a long gun, police say. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes. Minutes later, the local county dispatch received multiple 911 calls reporting that the attacker had entered the school. Police say he shot at locks on the doors in order to force his way inside. A bystander saw the shooting begin to unfold, pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead, police said. Three minutes later, officers arrived at the scene. They confirmed that the attacker had been killed, and then searched the school. The victims include three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher, Krantz said. A seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a local hospital with "critical injuries", he added. While police said the shooter was a local 16-year-old boy, they declined to add further details pending the ongoing investigation. Police have not released the identities of any victims, the attacker, nor the bystander who shot him. Schools throughout the city of Bend have been closed on Friday, with officials saying the community needs time to heal. Around 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary School, which has more than 40 adult staff members, police say. Local media reports suggest the school received new doors in 2022 which can lock classrooms with a flip of a switch. According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, there were 235 shooting incidents at American schools last year and at least 140 so far this year, including this one. title: 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded
description: Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed after a 16-year-old suspect opened fire in the city of Bend, local police say.
body: This video can not be played Four victims, including a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11, were killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon, local police say. A 16-year-old suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors. He was also killed in the shooting by an armed member of the community who followed the suspect inside the school, police said at a press conference. Two additional victims, a 7-year-old and another teacher, were hurt and transported to hospital in critical condition. 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded. title: 'We got penalised for saying 'pregnancy' on Instagram'
description: Creators say women's health content is getting them shadowbanned on social media. So what's really happening?
body: Irene Breen told the BBC her business suffered a significant financial hit from the restrictions When Irene Breen got a notification in January 2025 that Instagram was removing adverts for her company's pregnancy pillows, she was confused. What was so offensive about a pillow? She was later told on a call with Meta that the problem was the word "pregnancy". "We had to scrub the word from our entire website… from the product name," Breen said. "We had to remove all our URLs which had pregnancy in them and rename them all." The restrictions were eventually lifted but, she said, it took 10 months of conversations with Instagram's parent company Meta - by which time her business had suffered a significant financial hit. Meta, which also owns Facebook, declined to comment on specific cases, but told the BBC that while businesses can run adverts that promote wellness, sexual health and reproductive products and services, there are restrictions to avoid users across countries and cultures having a negative experience. It's not just businesses taking out paid adverts who claim their content has been unfairly restricted. Women's health creators and charities have told us their content has been removed, had sensitivity filters added, or had its reach suppressed - a practice known as "shadowbanning". The campaign group CensHERship monitors claims that women's health content is being suppressed. In a report last month, it surveyed nearly 200 creators, clinical providers, health brands, charities, and educators - 96% of whom said they had experienced restrictions in some form. The advert was returned to Bella Moon with the word "pregnancy" crossed out Sensitivity filters heavily blur posts requiring users to press a button before they can see it and are usually reserved for graphic imagery - including nudity or violence. Dr Carolina Are, a digital criminologist at the London School of Economics who studies social media moderation of women's content, said research shows AI is often used to flag posts that might breach platform guidelines. But that can mean an "algorithm misdetecting" content, as it is created to do, storing that information to repeat "previous mistaken decisions", she warns. The system often uses automated messages, Are says, which can mean users are then unable to question a decision. Some hashtags just don't appear on Instagram, said Athena Lamnisos, CEO of gynaecological cancer charity Eve Appeal. "One of the hashtags, unbelievably, was #vaginalcancer." "We put a post on Instagram about vulval anatomy - it was very clearly an anatomical diagram with labels around it, talking about vulval cancer and the need to check for changes, lumps and bumps. It was pulled." The diagram was put behind a sensitivity filter The charity appealed, which was initially denied - but after several weeks the post "suddenly reappeared" behind a sensitivity filter. Lamnisos added it wasn't exaggerating to say that "life-saving health information isn't getting to the people who need it most". Despite her raising this with Meta, the problem has continued, she said. Deirdre O'Neill, from fertility test company Hertility, said it had a similar issue with a Facebook and Instagram video featuring a woman with endometriosis. "She doesn't sell our services, she doesn't talk about Hertility, she simply describes her pain," O'Neill said. But the video was removed by Meta, she said, and classified as political content. Asked about Eve Appeal and Hertility's cases, Meta did not comment specifically, but said it allows women's health content on its platforms, and is consulting with women's health organisations to improve systems. The post featuring a woman talking about endometriosis was flagged and classified as "social issues, elections or politics" Trying to advertise on TikTok has also become "like an obstacle course", O'Neill added. "It's so much resource to try and put something forward that it ends up not being worth our time, because everything gets appealed, flagged, removed," she said. O'Neill says Hertility has given up advertising on TikTok TikTok said while certain content can't be promoted on the For You feed, it's transparent about posts that fall into this category and lets creators know so they can appeal. It added that millions of women share health stories on the platform, including with hashtags like #Period and #Endometriosis. CensHERship found the number of respondents self-censoring as a result of shadowbanning had gone up, from 53% in 2025 to 65% this year. This includes using euphemistic terms such as "seggs" instead of "sex", using asterisks or emojis, and avoiding certain topics altogether. CensHERship co-founder Clio Wood said this was "really damaging", because "women's health historically has been surrounded by shame and guilt… and we are just reinforcing [that]". Are told the BBC that platforms' policies "tend to be incredibly broad, whereby more often than not, nudity is conflated with sexual activity". And this ultimately hurts audiences, Wood said. "We talk to so many people who say, 'The only reason I found out about my vulval cancer was because Eve Appeal posted about those symptoms, and then I researched it and could ask my doctor the right questions'," she said. But Wood said that, since starting CensHERship in 2024, she has noticed that social media companies "can see this is something that they need to engage on now.". "It's all very well the policy saying XYZ content is allowed, but if the algorithm is still flagging all of that content and suppressing it, that's where the problem comes in," she said. "I think within the platforms those departments are very siloed - so what we would love is for those conversations to be much more holistic." title: Your child wasn't invited to the party - here's how to handle the disappointment
description: This very common scenario can be sad for little ones but there are ways you can help them.
body: Being left off the party list is a sad time for little ones but there are ways to help It's around this time of year when children start coming home with party invitations in their school bag. It's exciting and a sign they're making friends as they embark on school life. But what do you do when your child doesn't get an invitation? If your little one has been left off the list, here are some ways to help them cope. Dr Sasha Hall says not being invited to a birthday party is going to happen to our children at some point Educational and child psychologist Dr Sasha Hall, who's mum to a three-year-old boy and five-year-old girl, says the first thing to understand is that this scenario is "completely normal". "Unfortunately it's going to happen to all our children at some point in our parenting journey," she tells CBeebies Parenting Download. Dr Hall says while it may be tempting to get involved, it is not helpful in the long term. "We can't remove all the obstacles, but we can give them the skills to manage," she says. "It's about building their resilience... what skills can we teach rather than change their outcomes?" Comedian, author and mum-of-two Cariad Lloyd says it is a "rough" position for a child to find themselves in. "When they're little, it feels like first love... everything feels so heightened, especially with the party thing. Everyone gets not invited to somebody's party." Cariad Lloyd and Dr Sasha Hall joined CBeebies Parenting Download Dr Hall suggests planning an alternative activity for your child to focus on instead of the party. "Yes, that child said you can't come, but let's find another friend you can do something else with," she says. Lloyd adds that the more the party situation crops up throughout their primary school years, the more you can explain the different outcomes to them. "They will be invited to lots of parties and not invited to loads and you'll stop counting them," she says. "They will come back and be like 'so-and-so was upset because they're not invited'. And you'll be like, 'oh, do you remember when you were not invited to that one's party?' They all kind of take it in turns so it becomes less dramatic." Dr Hall says it's important to explain to your child that the decision to leave them off the list is not about them. "There are so many factors at play, especially with five to seven-year-olds, they're too little to have built up any kind of idea that they're naughty, it most likely has nothing to do with your child," she says. Lloyd agrees it's worth explaining possible reasons: "They can't afford to have 20 kids at a party so they're doing six instead and you didn't make the cut." Dr Hall says there could be a myriad of reasons why your child hasn't been invited. "It's about the parents' own childhood experience - if they only had a couple of friends at that age they may be happy and comfortable with a smaller party - or they might want a big party in the hope of bringing their child out of their shyness." Dr Hall says parents should remember it is not until children are slightly older that friendships take on a deeper meaning, so what may seem like a big deal now is likely to blow over. "Around the age of two is when we start seeing them show an interest in others, but it's still kind of parallel play," she says. "And then it's around three to five where they're actually socially motivated to choose preferences. So they might say 'I played with this child today', but it's around about five to seven where those friendships become more stable and that they're really meaningful to the child." She says parents should give children plenty of time and opportunities to form friendships. "There's a piece of research that looked at how do adults go from acquaintances to friends and it says it takes 40 to 60 hours - acquaintance to good friend is 200. "We then can't assume that because you've gone to soft play and your child has seen that kid twice that therefore you can say that's your friend." title: Same-day test helps doctors detect hidden infections in critically ill children
description: Metagenomics offers a new way of detecting infections in intensive care patients.
body: This video can not be played Same-day test helps detect hidden infections in critically ill children A pioneering same-day test has been used to detect hidden and drug-resistant infections among children in intensive care. Respiratory samples from more than 100 critically ill young patients at London's Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) were sent for what is known as metagenomic testing., external It can identify bacteria, viruses and fungi from a single sample, which in many cases influences what doctors prescribe. Metagenomics can detect infections that standard tests miss, meaning better outcomes for some critically ill patients. In March, 10-year-old Willow Crowther became dangerously ill with pneumonia, which triggered a seizure and multiple cardiac arrests. Willow, from Kent, was admitted to intensive care at GOSH. Her mum, Stacey Moore, was told she had a 50% chance of survival. "The consultant said... we should bring our family up to say goodbye to her. This is how critical and in how much danger she was of passing away." The team at GOSH used metagenomics - a diagnostic test that works by sequencing all genetic material present, in contrast to conventional methods where clinicians need to decide in advance what they're looking for. The test identified that Willow had a drug-resistant bacterial infection which needed a different antibiotic to the one she had been prescribed. The test helped doctors identify which antibiotic would be effective in treating Willow "The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount. It saved her life," said Stacey. "It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ. With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital. She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing. During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH. The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe. Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens. By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times. Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect. Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples. Willow celebrated her 10th birthday in August In a quarter of cases, the results influenced prescribing decisions, including starting, stopping or changing an antibiotic. Dr Sam Ray, consultant in paediatric intensive care medicine at GOSH and co-author of the study said traditional testing required clinicians to make an educated guess about which infection they were looking for. "The study has helped us to spot infections we would have missed, get children on the right treatment and stop antibiotics when we know they aren't going to work. "Removing unnecessary treatment is incredibly important for the fight against growing antimicrobial resistance." Metagenomic testing at GOSH also detected 50 organisms not identified by routine diagnostics, meaning it could play an early warning role against new infections. Dr Julianne Brown, head of the GOSH Metagenomics Service and co-senior author of the study said the new testing was being gradually rolled out to around 30 intensive care units across the UK treating both adults and children. "It could be a powerful tool for identifying new infections that pose a pandemic threat," she added. "In the future, if there was to be a new mystery pathogen that could be a cause of the next pandemic, we would detect that very quickly and put the right measures in place." The project at GOSH builds on trials at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust which first used metagenomics to test for respiratory infections in adult patients. title: The Papers: Healey's 'tax raid on banks' and Brand 'topless monster'
description: The chancellor's possible plan to tax banks and new evidence in Russell Brand's rape trial dominate Friday's papers.
body: A number of Friday's papers focus on reports that Chancellor John Healey plans to tax Britain's banks in his upcoming budget. Healey is "poised to launch a tax raid on banks" despite describing them as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, according to the Daily Telegraph. Ahead of the Budget on 28 October, the chancellor is said to be "considering raising a surcharge on bank profits", the paper says. Similarly, the Guardian reports Healey could "tap the financial sector for additional revenue" to "help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East". One option is to tax banks more heavily, which think tanks and trade unions have been calling for, the paper says. It has been reported the biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year. The i Paper focuses on household impacts from the chancellor's proposed Budget under the headline "energy bills set for double rise in new year". The paper says "Healey refuses to commit to extending PM's cost of living measure". An alleged victim told court the comedian and actor Russel Brand became "monster-like" and asked her to take a picture of him before he allegedly raped her, the Daily Mirror reports. Brand faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. He denies the charges. "Topless Monster", the Daily Star says in its coverage of the Russell Brand's rape trial. Similarly, the Sun headlines on the photo shown at the Brand rape trial where he is seen blowing a kiss to the woman he allegedly raped. The Metro splashes on Harry and Meghan's "(not) royal walkabout" with a picture of Meghan "beaming in burgundy" as the couple walked through Nottingham. It was Meghan's first public outing since returning to the UK, the paper says. Elsewhere, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused Donald Trump of "betrayal" after the US leader agreed to a diesel deal with Russia. "I will not" step down, Germany's Chancellor Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Financial Times amid growing pressure for him to resign. Merz has "vowed to fight on" as he pushes through unpopular welfare reform, the paper reports, as well as confront an age of upheaval. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage's "fury" about the case of a failed asylum seeker who was jailed after an attempted rape is the headline of the Daily Express. The UK government is planning to extend the public broadcaster's licence fee to online platforms such as Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon to help the "struggling BBC", the Independent reports. Any new revenue will be "used to boost journalism and tackle misinformation", the paper says. Under a new NHS England (NHSE) guideline, transgender people should be treated on single-sex hospital wards that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, the Times reports. The move is a reversal of its previous policy that trans patients "be placed on wards in line with their gender identity", the paper says. And the Labour government has been criticised for its plans to improve students' "speaking skills", the Daily Mail reports. When Education Secretary Lucy Powell announced measures to improve speaking to be as important as reading and writing, she was told "children will be losers" by Conservative shadow minister for work and pensions Baroness Spielman, the paper says. title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
description: Reform UK says the party has "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".
body: Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News, external. In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party. It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place. Reform said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures". In a statement, Reform said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations." It follows undercover filming broadcast on Wednesday night, which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language. The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases." Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters. Two years ago, Reform leader Nigel Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments. However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes. Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments". Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments Reform councillor suspended from prison job after 'despicable' comments ITV News says one of its undercover reporters was asked if he would consider standing to be a councillor, after spending time leafleting with Reform activists. He meets with the chairman of a local Reform branch in Chester, Ian Frost, who describes the meeting as "the first stage" of the vetting process. After the reporter says he has previously posted in support of Robinson on social media, Frost advises him to delete the posts. "Anything where you've got, things, Tommy Robinson or anything like that, okay, I would delete the account and I'd start again," Frost adds. Farage has said Robinson would not be allowed to join Reform. Frost later suggests the undercover reporter could apply to stand for the party, saying: "You might become a councillor. You might then want to go to the MP route. So, social media, yeah. And apply." Frost told ITV News he thought the reporter was a genuine candidate and gave him the benefit of the doubt. He added that it was not fair to judge people on a single conversation and he had since left Reform for unrelated reasons. In another part of the film, a former Reform candidate - Alex Lomas - claims he failed the party's vetting process twice, including for sharing social media posts from Robinson. However, Lomas says a few days after he failed for the second time he was asked to stand for the party. "On my second application, I got declined on the Friday, I got an email from them on the Tuesday saying you've passed vetting," he is recorded as saying. "I said, well, I think you better check with your paperwork, mate, because I've just failed on Friday. Now, you're saying I've passed it, I've not changed anything. "And then I got a phone call a few days later. Hi, will you stand for Reform UK? I'm like, yeah okay." He stood for Reform in local elections in Oldham in May but did not win a seat on the council. The BBC has not been able to contact Lomas and he did not respond to requests for comment from ITV News. Reform denies Lomas failed vetting in the first place. ITV's undercover report also shows Farage ruling a controversial mayoral candidate Dr Chris Parry – who said the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy should go home to the Caribbean – should be made to apologise, but not stand down. In a conversation at Reform's headquarters, the party's director of communications Ed Sumner suggests Farage is "protecting" Parry. In response Farage says: "It's showing a bit of sorrow." In a separate conversation several weeks earlier, where Farage was not present, Sumner is recorded saying Parry is "clearly a racist" and "needs to go". After apologising to Lammy in January, Parry was allowed to remain Reform's mayoral candidate in Hampshire and the Solent until he was later suspended in March "pending investigation", following comments about a Jewish voluntary patrol service. Parry told the BBC there was never an investigation and he has since left the party. He said: "I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. "They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people." Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK. "Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party. "Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform's house in order and every single time he has failed." title: India's 'cockroach' protesters set to return despite police crackdown
description: The youth-led movement plans a fresh Delhi protest after mass detentions last week and the jailing of two leaders.
body: Several protesters were detained during last week's protests Thousands of 'cockroach' protesters are set to return to the streets of Delhi on Friday, days after police prevented their last mass demonstration and two of their leaders were jailed. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement seeking electoral reforms, has called on supporters to gather at Central Park in Connaught Place, a busy commercial district. The call follows the jailing of two CJP leaders for five days after they entered Jantar Mantar, a protest site recently declared off-limits by police. What began as a campaign against alleged electoral fraud has since become a wider fight over the right to protest. Central Park is not an approved protest venue either. The Delhi High Court on Thursday declined to pass an order restraining the CJP after a local trader filed a petition citing disruptions to traffic and business as reasons why Friday's protest should not be allowed. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, meanwhile, has named the protest Lehra Do Tiranga, or Wave the Tricolour, as many Indians informally refer to the country's orange-white-green flag as Tiranga. Dipke has said he is prepared to risk arrest himself. Getting to Central Park, however, may prove difficult. Police barricades and mass detentions prevented many protesters from joining their demonstration last Saturday. Dipke has urged those unable to make it to Delhi to raise the Indian flag and protest wherever they are. The CJP has come a long way from May, when the movement began with an insult. After India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches, Dipke embraced the label and turned it into an online protest movement. By July, he and his supporters were filling the streets over examination paper leaks, in protests that forced India's education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Within months, the "cockroaches" had become one of the most visible expressions of youth anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government. Now they are taking on something bigger - India's elections. The CJP leadership has said their protests will continue no matter what At issue is a sweeping revision of electoral rolls, known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR), that critics say has removed more than 130 million names, putting legitimate voters at risk of losing their right to vote. The CJP wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign, accusing the poll panel of favouring Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the commission and the government deny the allegations. Friday's march comes less than a week after police prevented the movement's last mass demonstration from taking place, detaining its leaders and deploying officers across the capital before protesters could assemble. Dipke and two senior organisers, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained from within the aircraft upon landing in Delhi. The capital was put under a sweeping security lockdown. Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel had fanned out across Delhi, sealing roads, shutting metro stations and intercepting protesters long before they could reach Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned its mass demonstration. The BBC witnessed dozens of people being detained, including journalists and students. In footage from across Delhi, protesters could be seen shouting as police seized them by the arms, dragged them across the pavement and pushed them into waiting buses. Some struggled against the officers; others, already detained, pressed towards the bus windows, waving Indian flags. Those who managed to gather elsewhere were swiftly dispersed. There were also reports of protesters being assaulted by police. The BBC captured footage, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters. The scale of the crackdown drew accusations that the authorities were determined to prevent the protest rather than police it. The CJP likened the police action to India's Emergency, when civil liberties were suspended between 1975 and 1977. Delhi police defended the measures as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings. Many journalists were detained in the police crackdown Dipke, Das and Ranka were released on Sunday after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour. Police then took Jantar Mantar off Delhi's list of approved protest sites, telling demonstrators to go instead to Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground. But Jantar Mantar is no ordinary patch of ground. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory sits near parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accuses the authorities of pushing protesters away from the seat of power to make their demonstrations less visible and easier to ignore. On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned anyway, bringing a handful of supporters. They unfurled the Indian flag and shouted slogans against Kumar. Police said they had entered the restricted site without permission, some by climbing over a locked gate, and violated the conditions of their earlier release. The following day, Das and Ranka were sent to Tihar Jail for five days in judicial custody. Another organiser, Ajinkya Shinde, was released on a bond to maintain peace and good behaviour. With two of its key organisers behind bars, the CJP heads into Friday's protest with its leadership depleted, though Dipke insists the march will go ahead and he does not intend to back down. "I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said in a video message. Police, meanwhile, are preparing for another large gathering in the heart of Delhi. Senior officers met on Thursday to discuss security arrangements and possible traffic restrictions aro

title: The Interview
description: Nigerian opposition leader Peter Obi on his presidential bid and his claim he won in 2023
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·16 Oct 2026,·23 mins Available for over a year “Nigeria can fight insecurity, head on. It only requires it for the commander-in-chief to be determined that this will end. Those criminals live with us. In our communities, people know them. I will go to the communities and find them. I will take control. And I will not do it from Abuja.” Madina Maishanu speaks to Peter Obi, one of Nigeria’s leading opposition politicians, now with the Nigeria Democratic Congress, and a former governor of Anambra State. He came third in the 2023 presidential election, attracting significant support from young Nigerians fed up with unemployment and police brutality who demanded political change. But Obi has never accepted the outcome, insisting he won and that the official results were manipulated, although Nigeria's courts rejected his challenge. Now he's hoping to become president in 2027, promising to address some of Nigeria's biggest problems, including widespread insecurity and government corruption. The Interview brings you the best interviews coming from the BBC, including episodes with the head of the World Meteorological Organisation, Celeste Saulo and the former Australian prime minister Julia Gillard. You can listen on the BBC World Service on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at 0800 GMT. Or you can listen to The Interview as a podcast, out three times a week on BBC Sounds or wherever you get your podcasts. Presenter: Madina Maishanu Producer: Osman Iqbal Editor: Farhana Haider and Damon Rose (Image: Peter Obi. Credit: Reuters)

title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
description: The move follows a review into pornography regulation in 2025 by Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin
body: Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced. From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16. The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people. Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon". She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable". Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex. It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences". Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent - but its depiction online is currently not illegal. Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales. Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences". But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said. "If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added. "It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal." 'He strangled me without asking' - experts say choking during sex now normal for many The new offences each carry a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, for publication. According to the government, this could include uploading, posting or otherwise making the content available to someone online. Possession, meanwhile, could include keeping an image stored on a phone, computer or in cloud storage, the government says. Someone found to be in possession of images depicting sexual activity involving a person pretending to be under 16 could face up to three years' imprisonment, after 6 November. Those found to be in possession of images depicting strangulation, suffocation or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives could face up to two years' imprisonment. Porn that shows or depicts sex between step or foster-relations where one person is pretending to be under 18 will also be captured by the new offences. Durham University law professor Clare McGlynn - who has previously warned widely available extreme content normalises sexual violence - welcomed the laws taking full effect. "This is a potential turning point, the commencement of these laws marking a line in the sand when we decided that we were no longer going to accept the normalisation of sexually violent content in pornography," she told the BBC. But she said questions remained over how swiftly tech platforms and regulators would act to remove and mitigate the spread of violating material. "While these are criminal offences, this is not about prosecuting individuals, but transforming the online pornographic landscape and that requires the platforms and regulator to act," Prof McGlynn added. title: Tip-off foiled US teen suspect's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say
description: The alleged plot only failed because the 19-year-old suspect's gun jammed outside the place of worship, say police.
body: A Taco Bell cashier's alleged plot for a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago was thwarted by a tip-off from one of his colleagues, investigators say. Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon. Paporakis allegedly sent a message about the planned attack on Sunday to the co-worker, who alerted authorities, officials said. Police said they found writings in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people. Palatine police chief William Nord said on Thursday they were notified about a mass shooting plot on Sunday by someone who had received "concerning electronic communications" from Paporakis. "These communications played a vital role in bringing this matter to the attention of law enforcement," said the police chief. According to CBS, the BBC's US partner, prosecutors said the tipster had worked with Paporakis. Nord said a red Honda RDX registered to Paporakis entered the car park of a "known Hindu temple" in the suburb of Aurora at Sunday lunchtime. The suspect allegedly tried to open fire, but the gun jammed, so he drove home, where he lived with his mother. According to NBC Chicago, Paporakis told his colleague over phone messages that his gun had jammed and he got out of there "super-fast". Once home, he "searched internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun & called a colleague informing them of [his] intent to carry out a mass shooting", reports NBC Chicago. He is thought to have acted alone. The police chief said officers had searched Paporakis' home, where they found a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and body armour. Nord said they also discovered an eight-page document by the suspect containing "extremist ideologies" and revealing his plans for an attack. In the writings, he described himself as a "sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi", according to CBS. Police have questioned Paporakis' mother, who was said to be unco-operative. The Hindu temple identified by local media as the intended target said it had implemented new security measures. India's Ministry of External Affairs said the incident "adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US". US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois said he was "horrified" by the incident. In a Facebook statement, he said he and his family worship at the temple and were there last Sunday. The Chicago metropolitan area is home to one of the biggest Indian-American populations in the US. title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
description: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.
body: The French prime minister has accused the radical left of weaponising the high school movement for electoral advantage The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe. Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs. For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets. This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France. Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement. France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election. The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history. Jérôme Rodrigues (R) played a leading role in the gilets jaunes movement several years ago Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations. The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video. "Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added. So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy? Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt. Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of? This video can not be played Watch: 'If we don't scream, they won't listen to us', student protester tells BBC in Paris "You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me. She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt. "The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary." "Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates. "The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself." "Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes. Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected. But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further. France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts. Radical-left LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon (C) has been accused of exploiting the student protests ahead of next year's elections I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest. They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs. "France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit." None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway. The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities. 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation France's school protests: What lies behind the anger France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests They are part of a defiant French tradition. Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas." ("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.") Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity." Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response. Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in

title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
description: Smells from rubbish dumps and industrial facilities are being more carefully monitored.
body: The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered to take action over odours Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem. For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill. "When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump. While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day". Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology. The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells. Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts." The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality. Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory. When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells. In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue. Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance. This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks. "You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world. Bad smells from waste sites are among the most difficult to resolve The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away. Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells. But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers. Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner. Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says. In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city. A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits. "Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume." The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus. The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns. This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?" In Des Moines, authorities have set up "electronic noses" to pinpoint bad smells Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems. Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints. Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air. Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic." The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it ea

title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
description: After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores.
body: Jess says returning online purchases is less hassle than shopping in person Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online. As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says. "The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough. Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on". And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection". Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22. But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain. Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases. The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes. Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein. Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic. Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019. Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town." Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online. "I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says. "I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important." Julia does most of her shopping online, but likes going into book stores Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted. The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces." Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically. "I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed." The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule. Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale". However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete. "Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks. "When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time." But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns. This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor". "Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again." title: O'Neill defiant in defeat but Celtic's 'flat-track bullies' fail another big test
description: Celtic have now lost two Europa League group games, as well as two derbies - but Martin O'Neill is adamant he can see positive signs.
body: Celtic manager Martin O'Neill chose to focus on the second-half positives from his side's 4-1 Europa League defeat by Benfica and insisted they can still reach the knockout stages despite their slow start. In stark contrast, Chris Sutton branded his former side as "flat-track bullies". Celtic have lost four of their past five games. Every high-stakes match this term - both meetings with Rangers and both European outings - has ended in a defeat. By the time their performance improved in Lisbon on Thursday, they were three goals down and effectively already out of the contest, hamstrung by their own sloppy mistakes. Dane Murray upended Jhon Duran to concede a penalty inside four minutes, an error which characterised the first 45 minutes. Sebastian Tounekti then allowed Alexander Bah to run past him for Benfica's second and goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo was beaten too easily as Duran scored the hosts' third. Celtic suffer fourth defeat in five against classy Benfica Visit our Celtic page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views Camilo Duran pulled one back after the break and struck a post as the Scottish champions improved, but Vangelis Pavlidis struck Benfica's fourth late on to kill any faint Celtic hopes. "Last thing you want to do is concede so early on," O'Neill said. "We could've capitulated, but I thought the second-half performance was terrific. We created chance after chance. "The second-half performance gives me the determination... I think we can still qualify. We can still do it. "We came roaring back. We could've scored a number of goals. I accept on the break they could have scored themselves, as they did with their fourth goal." Even the most ardent Celtic supporters would struggle to share their manager's optimism given they sit 34th of 36 teams in the competition after two games. Captain Callum McGregor admitted Celtic were masters of their own downfall in the first half. "First half we didn't help ourselves," he told TNT Sports. "Unforced errors lead to the second and third goals and you have a mountain to climb. "We know at this level if you don't look after the ball you're going to get punished." This video can not be played Although Celtic conceded four, the scoreline did not flatter Benfica. The Portuguese side created chances aplenty in both halves and hit the woodwork twice in addition to their four goals. Celtic's lack of depth in defence was exposed once again in the absence of the injured Cameron Carter-Vickers as Gianluca Prestianni and Duran tormented the visitors' back four. However, it is in forward areas where O'Neill perhaps has his biggest headache. Club record signing Kasper Hogh was hooked at half-time and has now failed to score in 10 of his first 11 outings since joining from Bodo/Glimt in the summer. Duran shifted inside for the second half and posed far more of a threat than his Danish team-mate. "If I'm a creative midfield player and I've got Duran and Hogh to pick from, I'm taking Duran every day of the week," former Celtic midfielder Scott Allan said. "He looks to get off the side of defenders, if you put a ball in the area, he's more likely to be alive to it. "Hogh just isn't firing on all cylinders. I can take that if he's doing the other side of the game a lot better than he is. "You can see why Martin O'Neill made the substitution at half-time and there's no doubt Celtic looked much better going forward." O'Neill admitted he sees Duran as being better through the middle, when asked about his Colombian talisman post-match, but given Hogh's price tag he might not be inclined to pull him out of the firing line just yet. "[Duran] has played wide at his previous clubs," O'Neill said. "But I personally feel his best position is through the middle. "It's now a matter of us trying to fit him in and I think we can do that. It's a real battle for places now." title: Donaldson jail term poses 'complex challenge' for prison staff'
description: Jeffrey Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years for committing sex abuse, including one of rape, against two women when they were children.
body: Jeffrey Donaldson pictured in June arriving at Newry Crown Court Protecting convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson from harm inside jail will be a "massive risk-management headache" for prison bosses, according to a former governor. The ex-Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader was given a 15-year sentence on Thursday after being convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including rape, against two women when they were children. Ian Acheson, who spent about a decade working for HM Prison Service, said Donaldson, the former Lagan Valley MP, faced risks from fellow inmates. Acheson said Donaldson represented a "very complex challenge to the Northern Ireland Prison Service". Donaldson leaving Newry court in a prison van after being sentenced on Thursday "There are always hierarchies within prisons - and there are even hierarchies within sex offenders - and the lowest of the low and the most vulnerable in terms of hostility from others are those who've been convicted of sexual violence against a minor." But he said it would also be necessary to "examine potential political or sectarian targeting" relating to Donaldson's leadership of the DUP and his service in the Ulster Defence Regiment, a former Army unit. "The prison has a duty of care to protect him and he is uniquely vulnerable," Acheson told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme. "Maghaberry, in previous inspections, has indicated that it operates an integrated regime, where sex offenders can be safely managed in the wider prison community. "I don't think that is remotely viable for Jeffrey Donaldson, given those offence characteristics and his background. "So either he is kept, in effect, in conditions of solitary confinement for years and years or another solution has to be found. "I don't think it's acceptable to keep him in conditions of solitary confinement - it may not even be legal." Donaldson spends up to18 hours a day in his cell at Maghaberry, which holds about 1,600 inmates. It is thought he has been put in the Moyola Unit, which primarily houses prisoners with health issues, for his own safety, as it isolates him from risk of attack or verbal abuse from other prisoners. He is believed to spend much of his day reading books from the prison library. Acheson said there was a "precedent within the UK" to transfer prisoners within different jurisdictions, therefore Donaldson "could be potentially compulsorily transferred" to another jail. Former DUP leader Donaldson sentenced to 15 years in prison for child sex abuse Dawn arrest to 'descent into disgrace': How victims exposed Jeffrey Donaldson's lies Jeffrey Donaldson's life in politics: From DUP leader to convicted child sex abuser Donaldson was convicted in June of sex offences against two females referred to in his trial as Victim A and Victim B. He was sentenced to 11 years for his crimes against Victim B and four years for offences against Victim A. During sentencing, Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson's crimes had led to a "catastrophic descent into disgrace". Donaldson, who denied the charges, is seeking to appeal his convictions. He will also be required to sign the Sex Offenders Register for life. Jeffrey Donaldson's time in politics began in 1985 when he was elected for the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) as an MLA in South Down. In 1997, Donaldson became the MP for Lagan Valley, representing the UUP. He would remain an MP until 2024. However, in 2003, he quit the UUP and defected to the DUP. Donaldson was awarded a knighthood in the 2016 Queen's Birthday Honours list, and, in 2021, became leader of the DUP. He remained leader until March 2024, when he was charged with sexual offences of a historical nature. He was found guilty of all 18 child sex abuse charges, including one count of rape, in June 2026. Donaldson subsequently asked for his knighthood to be forfeited and tendered his resignation from the Privy Council with immediate effect. In July, Donaldson was stripped of his knighthood by the King. title: Sparks fly at the Celebrity Traitors round table and a 'terrifying' death march
description: The celebrities turn on each other at the round table, and have to beat the death marchers for their mission.
body: The death marchers terrified Leigh-Anne Pinnock, who felt like she was in a horror film Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fifth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. Things are hotting up a bit in the castle, not least for Ross Kemp, who doesn't seem to be enjoying it very much. "I'm quite angry," he said, his brow furrowing even more than usual. "I've suffered at the hands of the traitors and now they've put heat on me, so I'm quite angry about that," he said. "They're using me like a donkey." Clearly they aren't hitching rides on him at the seaside - that would be another show entirely - he's referring to them pointing the finger of suspicion at him by making him stand out when he doesn't want to. Firstly they kept the former EastEnders star and documentary maker above ground at the grave-digging task, sparing him from being buried. In this episode, he was one of four celebrities who had to sit alone in a tomb, before one of them was murdered. This was intended to get tongues wagging about him, deflecting suspicion away from the actual traitors. Joanne McNally was convinced enough by this to say: "The vibe with Ross is off. His eyes do not close. "He has not blinked since we've been here. He is giving cyborgs." Ross Kemp was not amused Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses? Meanwhile poor Rob Beckett was murdered face-to-face by the traitors, while Romesh Ranganathan was spared, along with Little Mix's Leigh-Anne Pinnock, who received a key granting her immunity. Beckett, who has wisecracked his way through the series, found being murdered hilarious. "I'm a dead man," he grinned, when he finally saw the traitors in person. "And in a way, this is good news for the faithful because I was nowhere near getting Maya Jama and James Acaster. No chance." He did manage to leave with a veiled threat though. "I know one thing - my boy Ramesh Ranganathan will avenge my death and he will get them." Ranganathan was genuinely saddened and regretful the next morning at losing his comedy comrade. "He's so unthreatening that he's never going to get banished, so he's the guy we should have given the key to," he said. "He also happens to be one of my best friends. I'm sad. It's not going to be the same without him." Whether all this will sharpen his sleuthing skills, as Beckett hopes, is another matter. Rob Beckett laughed when he saw James Acaster was about to murder him Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked Comic James Acaster, possibly the most reluctant traitor in recent memory, accurately called killing off Beckett a "chaos murder". "This is a bunch of faithful who read into everything," he said. "They go, why did this happen? And with this murder, there's no answer, and they won't suspect it's us." More accurately, he should perhaps have said: "They won't suspect me or Maya," given only two-thirds of this tactic worked. Meanwhile, the task for this episode made some of the celebrities quite jumpy. This was despite it not involving being buried alive, drinking stinky water or diving down an old toilet, all of which wouldn't have been out of place on I'm A Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here. This episode's death parade saw them having to solve puzzles to avoid being seized and held captive by guards looking like Skeletor, from He-Man and the Masters of the Universe. "That is genuinely terrifying," said Pinnock as the marchers approached them on the edge of a forest. "We are literally in a horror film." Michael Sheen took each puzzle as an opportunity to flex his acting muscles, using his finest Shakespearean actor's voice to bellow out the instructions to everyone else. He should have grabbed one of the death marchers to do a quick burst of Hamlet. The celebrities were victorious though, winning all the prize money for charity, and the task ended with Kemp and James Blunt using flints to spark a flame, igniting some gunpowder to hold the death marchers at bay. At the end of the task, players captured by the death marchers were held in a cage until the round table. This included all three traitors - Hannah Fry, Maya Jama and James Acaster - as well as Ranganathan, Jerry Hall and McNally Oops, bad move. This left a traitor-free zone at the castle, where theories could fly without the traitors trying to derail them. This mission was a race time for the celebrities By they time everyone was reunited at the round table, traitor shade was being thown at several celebrities. Kemp firstly had to defend himself, which he did by saying: "In my defence, I would say if I was picked to be a traitor, I wouldn't have been so paralysed on the first day about the hat [where he thought he was killed in plain sight]. "And the grave thing, I don't think it would be traitorous behaviour to get everybody out before you start looking for the money, so I would say that in my defence." This seemed to work, before James Blunt was briefly questioned. But Fry - an actual traitor - came in for the most flak. YouTuber King Kenny swooped, saying: "There's no surprise that I'm going to be talking to you, Hannah. I just don't understand, how are you still here? "Because when I think about it, as a traitor, you'd be one of the first people that I would get out. But also, as the traitor, you'd be extremely good because you're very smart." He wasn't wrong, and this ignited the growing chorus of celebrities who also suspected Fry.
