title: Minus 17 to European dreams as Bournemouth fairytale continues
description: It was a night 127 years in the making as Bournemouth added another chapter to their fairytale with victory in their first-ever European home game.
body: Bournemouth started their 2008 League Two season on -17 points It was a night soundtracked by the Impossible Dream. And it was no coincidence that was the song chosen at the Vitality Stadium before Bournemouth's first European home game in the club's 127-year history. As supporters lucky enough to bag a ticket for the historic occasion waved flags to the Andy Williams classic, a giant tifo rose from behind one of the stands, bearing the words 'Minus 17 to European dreams. AFC Bournemouth, established 1899'. As recently as 2008, a night like this would have been unthinkable for Cherries supporters. Just 18 years ago, Bournemouth were facing the prospect of no longer existing. After entering administration, the club were relegated from League One after being handed a 10-point deduction. But that was not the end of their troubles. To be allowed to compete in the 2008-09 season, Bournemouth, then managed by Eddie Howe, had to accept a further 17-point deduction in League Two. It left them at the bottom of the Football League and seemingly destined for life as a non-league side. By the end of the season, the Cherries had not only completed one of the greatest escapes in English football history to secure a 21st-place finish and survival, but had also laid the foundations for a decade of success, which culminated in a first promotion to the Premier League in 2015. Fast-forward to the present day and Bournemouth are making history for all the right reasons in the Europa League. Thursday's 3-0 win over Sturm Graz meant they became only the second English side to win their first two matches in a major European competition since Bolton achieved the feat in the Uefa Cup 21 years ago. "It's a moment that will live long in their memories," former defender Joel Ward told TNT Sports. "The club should relish this night. "The owner [Bill Foley] manifested this moment when he first came into the club. He set the standards for this club, he has invested a lot into it and he wanted to see this club in Europe. "He got his wish, and they have certainly started incredibly well so far." Bournemouth earn historic win over Sturm Graz It was a night that always seemed destined to produce a fairytale storyline, such has been the nature of Bournemouth's rise since 2008. At Wednesday's pre-match press conference, defender Adam Smith - the club's longest-serving player after initially joining on loan from Tottenham in 2011 - admitted he would never have imagined captaining the Cherries in Europe. But there was more to come for Smith. The right-back earned his own piece of history by providing the assist for Bournemouth's first European goal on home soil, with Evanilson heading his cross home late in the first half. "It's been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it, so we are very happy," Smith told TNT Sports. "We had a chat with each other and we got a reaction today. That's an AFC [Bournemouth] performance right there." Since making his move from Tottenham permanent in 2014, Smith has made more than 430 appearances for the Cherries. In that time, the 35-year-old has helped Bournemouth secure three promotions, two of which have taken them to the Premier League. When he was replaced by James Hill midway through the second half, the home supporters rose to their feet and chanted Smith's name as he departed the field. "He's an example to everyone of what hard work looks like and the rewards that you get, even towards the latter stages of your career," added Ward. "He's extremely professional, and he fully deserves the success he's getting now. Nights like this are what you live for. To walk out captaining that side is emotional and makes the hair stand up on the back of your neck." Bournemouth put on a show on Thursday at the Vitality Stadium It was no surprise to see Bournemouth supporters remain in their seats long after the final whistle as they attempted to soak up as much as they could of a landmark night on the south coast. For Marco Rose and his players, though, the focus will quickly shift to Sunday's Premier League clash with Sunderland. Despite soaring to new heights in the Europa League during the opening weeks of the season, their Premier League campaign is yet to get going. The Cherries sit 18th in the table and are one of only three teams, alongside Fulham and Tottenham, yet to win a match this season. "If we stick together and play like this and we have our fans, then we are hard to play against and it's hard to beat us," said Rose, who succeeded Andoni Iraola in June. "That's what we should take into the next game." Bournemouth's remarkable story will enter arguably its most glamorous chapter yet when AC Milan visit the Vitality Stadium next week. title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
description: Two people were airlifted to hospital but no-one's life appeared to be in danger, officials said.
body: This video can not be played Watch: BBC at scene as emergency crews head towards Channel Tunnel crash A bus has hit a stationary freight train near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, French authorities say. The bus, which was carrying lorry drivers due to take a shuttle rail service, struck the train at the loading platform of the tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais, at 19:27 (18:27 BST) on Thursday. The bus driver and one passenger were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter. None of the injuries were life threatening, a local official said. Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said freight and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel had not been disrupted after a brief stoppage to evacuate injured people. An investigation has begun. Trains near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel (file image) "Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said. "For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train. "The bus did not overturn, it is still upright – but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved." The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added. It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured. Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform. The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France. "There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene. Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord, external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers. Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel. "This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected." The Eurotunnel runs under the sea between England and France, from Folkestone in Kent to Coquelles on the French side. Three different rail services operate through the tunnel - the Eurostar, a passenger train that begins in London and goes to several European destinations, freight trains which transport goods and Le Shuttle, which transports vehicles. title: Farmer says hosting 4G mast is a 'nightmare' as fees cost him thousands
description: Alan Watson says farmers are being "bullied" into terms between telecoms operators and landowners.
body: Alan Watson has had a mast on his land for more than 20 years but says negotiations with telecoms has become a "nightmare" A farmer says hosting 4G masts on his land has become a "nightmare" after the rent he receives was halved, and it costs him £5,000 in fees. Alan Watson, 68, from Llanbadarn Fynydd in Powys, has had a mast on his land for more than 20 years, but claims farmers are being "bullied" into accepting worse terms due to legal changes between telecoms operators and landowners. The Farmers' Union of Wales (FUW) said it was concerned a cut in rent would put people off putting up masts, affecting connectivity in rural Wales. The UK government's Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (DEFRA) said its reforms ensured landowners were "treated fairly when negotiating with mobile operators". Nearly a quarter of Wales lacks 4G coverage from every mobile network operator, according to Ofcom, external - leaving some communities reliant on masts hosted by farmers and landowners. Watson said he had been left with "no negotiation" about how much rent was paid to him for his land, and warned landowners tempted to host masts not to "touch it with a barge pole". "It feels like landowners trying to do their bit are being bullied into accepting worse terms, putting people off hosting the infrastructure the country needs," he said. "When I tried to get my agreement finalised, the process ended up costing me more than £5,000." At the centre of the dispute are changes made to the Electronic Communications Code in 2017, external, which governs agreements between telecoms operators and landowners hosting their infrastructure. The reforms changed how rents are calculated in an effort to reduce the cost of deploying mobile infrastructure. But landowners argue the changes have driven down payments by as much as 90% in some cases and made negotiations more adversarial, according to former Tory MP for South Derbyshire, Heather Wheeler, external. "It was very much like David and Goliath, I was the little one fighting the big company," said Watson, adding that under the code, he felt there was "nothing he can do". "I've always been happy to do my bit to support better mobile connectivity in the local area. "But changes to the system have seen my rent cut in half, from £5,000 to £2,500, while dealing with the telecoms companies has become a nightmare." Watson estimates he has received about £55,000 in revenue before tax over the 20 years he has hosted masts, with tax then taking 40% off. He claims he has now paid £10,00 in fees and legal costs "dealing with telecoms companies". Nearly a quarter of Wales still lacks 4G coverage from every mobile network operator Watson said: "The boot is on the telecommunication companies' foot. I could take it to court but it wouldn't be financially viable... and there is no guarantee of me winning if we took it to court." He added: "Within the act it says negotiations are supposed to take place, and if negotiations aren't fruitful, then the company can take you to court. "There is no negotiations, it's going straight to court." Watson said he was worried that connectivity across the UK could be "severely reduced" as a result of the changes. "Why would a land owner want to rent space on their land when they're going to be paid next to nothing for it?" "It's only the company versus you... you're fighting your own corner," he said. The farmer compared his situation to renting out a home, adding: "I set the rent... it's like my tenants coming back to me and saying 'no, it's too much I can only pay half of it'. "It isn't being used in the matter which it is meant to be used." In a statement, Mobile UK, the trade association for the UK's mobile network operators, said mobile connectivity is "an essential service, not a luxury". It said the government reformed the Electronic Communications Code because the cost of accessing land was becoming a "significant barrier" to building and upgrading the mobile networks across the UK. It added that the total demand and network traffic continues to rise, and the mobile operators are investing around £2bn each year to "meet the challenge". Watson says the reforms cut his rent in half from £5,000 to £2,500 Watson has called upon the government to intervene, which he claimed was "blind to what is happening to landowners across the country". "If we genuinely want to improve mobile connectivity, we need a system that encourages co-operation between landowners and operators, rather than driving them further apart," he said. The National Infrastructure Commission for Wales, external has warned that falling rents are reducing incentives to host mobile masts and putting existing sites at risk, with Cardiff and Swansea facing growing pressure from landowners submitting notices to quit. Tim Faire, FUW's land use and climate change committee chair, said: "Farmers across Wales have hosted mobile masts in good faith for decades, helping to keep rural communities connected." "But they cannot be expected to continue doing so while rents are slashed and reaching agreements becomes increasingly costly and difficult. "At a time when too many rural communities still struggle with poor mobile coverage, we need a policy framework that treats farmers fairly and encourages landowners and operators to work together, rather than driving them further apart." In response, DEFRA said it recognised the "vital role" landowners played in providing digital connectivity. It added it wanted to "strike the right balance" between their needs and the connectivity needs of communities. "Our reforms support the ambition for high-quality 5G coverage across all populated areas by 2030 and ensures landowners are treated fairly when negotiating with mobile operators." title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US election offices
description: A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana.
body: Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US. The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received. Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters. Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail. "This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday. Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail. The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder. The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it. Senator Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was also sent a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted before reaching the office, his spokesman said. The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC. The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress. Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages. A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states. title: London housing project wins top architecture award
description: Lion Green Road in Coulsdon was recognised for the way it responds to its surroundings.
body: Lion Green Road in Coulsdon was praised by judges for blending high-density housing into an area of natural beauty A suburban housing development in south London has won the UK's most prestigious architecture award, with judges praising its sensitive design and integration into the surrounding landscape. Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, comprising 157 homes across five distinctive 13-sided blocks, was named winner of the 2026 Stirling Prize by the Royal Institute of British Architects (Riba). Designed by Mary Duggan Architects and built with RUFF Architects, it combines affordable and private housing for Croydon Council. Replacing a former car park on a challenging, sloping site that varies in height by eight metres, Riba president Chris Williamson praised the design as a "new approach to higher density development" creating "a new connection between the bustling Lion Green Road and a distinctive area of green parkland beyond". Mary Duggan said Lion Green Road was a project "about the culture of dwelling" Duggan said the win was "extraordinary, unexpected and humbling". "Lion Green Road began in 2016 with a very clear vision, to create genuinely non-institutional housing and to think differently about what affordable housing could offer commnities. "We think of Lion Green Road as a project about the culture of dwelling... architectural ambition, social value and social realities can co-exist." Riba president Chris Williamson said the judging process was "inspirational and emotional" Williamson told the BBC that until he went to study architecture he lived in a council estate in the East Midlands, "and every time I go back there all the council houses have been sold off, they're in private hands. "Which in a way can be a good thing - we're in a homeowning democracy - but the sad thing is they haven't been replaced. "Every time I go back - without getting too emotional - I think 'where would we have lived?' "So to me that's why this particular project was important. I think a lot of people from that sort of background live in terrible accommodaiton - temporary accommodation which isn't safe or secure. "These houses are fantastic and they're part of a mixed scheme so it's got a fantastic feel to it. "For me it was a very inspirational, emotional, part of the process." Duggan, who was brought up in south-west London, said the scheme "challenged conventional suburban housing layouts centred on roads, private gardens and clearly defined front and back spaces". Winding paths and planting weave between the blocks, connecting them and linking shared outdoor spaces. She said she wanted it to be a public space people felt they could belong to. "Housing needs to be progressive. People who live in the building have access to green space, allotments." The site fronts onto Lion Green Road, with low-rise green belt housing set on higher ground to the south and traditional suburban streets to the north. Lion Green Road comprises 157 homes across five distinctive 13-sided blocks. Nestled amongst trees on the edge of green-belt land, the development's soft purple and pink brickwork blends high-density housing into an area of natural beauty. At a time when housing developments are often judged by their cost and number of homes they can deliver, the project was recognised for the way it responds to its surroundings. Williamson said "the housing blocks blend into the parkland beyond, while small variations in pattern add texture and give each building its own identity." He added: "The way it fits into the hillside - it doesn't look like a large housing scheme. "It has community gardens, it's the sort of place i would have liked to have grown up in." Winding paths and planting weave between the blocks The project was funded by Croydon Council as a public asset, and a change in building regulations meant it "fought against five or six circumstantial elements beyond the normal challenges". The building was praised by the jury for its "inventive and site-specific response to a highly constrained plot". Buildings are assessed across a range of criteria, including design vision, innovation, sustainability, functionality, and the ability to delight users and visitors. title: Lockerbie accused's alleged confession can be used in trial, US judge rules
description: Defence lawyers claim Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi was forced by three masked men to make the confession while in custody in Libya.
body: Pan Am flight 103 was destroyed over Lockerbie on 21 December 1988 A copy of an alleged confession by the Libyan accused of building the bomb that brought down an American airliner over Lockerbie 38 years ago can be used at his trial, a US judge has ruled. Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi, 74, has claimed he was forced by three masked men into making a false confession while in custody in Libya. Masud's lawyers asked a federal court in Washington to rule the alleged confession inadmissible in advance of his trial in April next year as it was not the original document. But Judge Dabney Friedrich denied the motion, meaning it can be used in evidence. This video can not be played Media outlet Libyan Review previously broadcast footage of Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi in a US prison The accused, dressed in a green prison jumpsuit, was in court where he listened to proceedings through an interpreter. Mas'ud has denied building and priming the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people. He has insisted that the masked men men ordered him to memorise information about the destruction of Pan Am 103 and another terror attack. Mas'ud said he repeated what he had learned to a Libyan official, under duress, after the men threatened his family. He has also claimed he was illegally removed from Libya to stand trial in the United States after "a cloak and dagger operation conducted in the dead of night". Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has been in custody since December 2022 Details of the alleged confession were first made public five years ago, after the US department of justice announced it was charging Mas'ud over the Lockerbie bombing. A criminal complaint summary compiled by the FBI claimed he had admitted playing a key role in the attack when he was in detention in 2012, following the collapse of Colonel Gaddafi's regime the previous year. The FBI has said the Libyan official who noted Mas'ud's confession in 2012 is prepared to give evidence at his trial. Of the 259 passengers and crew who died on board the airliner, 190 were from the United States, where the Mas'ud case will be tried. The only Lockerbie trial so far took place between May 2000 and January 2001, when three Scottish judges convicted Libyan intelligence agent Abdulbasset al-Megrahi of playing a key role in the plot. Megrahi was jailed for life but released on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government in 2009 after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer. He died three years later at home in Tripoli. title: At the scene of a school roof collapse in Pakistan
description: At least 33 pupils and a teacher were killed according to hospital officials, and more than a dozen were injured.
body: This video can not be played A school roof has collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar. At least 33 pupils and a teacher were killed according to hospital officials, and more than a dozen were injured. Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes". title: Why Harry and Meghan's UK relaunch felt so much like a royal engagement
description: The Duchess of Sussex has not done anything like the day of events in Nottingham for several years on British soil.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Harry and Meghan at first joint engagement since UK return There was something so very familiar about today. The first time the Duke and Duchess of Sussex visited Nottingham together in 2017 they were plain old Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. They'd just announced they were getting married and it was in the East Midlands that an American actress would be hard launched as a working member of the Royal Family. You could view today as the UK-relaunch of Meghan. She'd not done anything like the day of events in Nottingham for several years on British soil. Those close to her told me she wasn't nervous about how people would react to her and she wanted to get out there. This was definitely not a royal engagement. But the thing is, it felt like one in so many ways. There was planned choreography for each event. Harry and Meghan visited charities and met volunteers. There was a shared media pool working together to distribute the best video and images. There were crowds and walkabouts. Buckingham Palace has made it very clear that they view the Duke and Duchess of Sussex as private citizens. Whatever they do is their own business - but it certainly won't have royal status attached. There was no pomp and ceremony today. No line up of dignitaries. No obvious police presence. It was still a reminder of what Harry and Meghan have to offer. Meghan makes first official public appearance since moving back to UK Meghan shares glimpse of family life after Sussexes return to UK Much of the crowd that came out to see them was young and diverse - the vast majority of people I saw were under 30. The mood at each event was informal with a strong emphasis on getting stuck in. They baked cupcakes, made West African food, played pool and had a go at basketball. Watching both Harry and Meghan up close is a reminder of their ease at these kind of charity events. It plays to their strengths and Meghan brings that air of American self confidence. Their return has unsettled the Royal Family with King Charles III just getting a few days notice ahead of the news breaking in August that the Sussexes were coming back to the UK with their children Archie and Lilibet. While his son and daughter-in-law were in Nottingham, the King was at the ceremonial opening of the Senedd in Cardiff, firmly on royal duty, delivering a speech rich in references to community, to character and identity with an overriding message of the power of endurance. And the complexity of the Harry and Meghan story is requiring endurance on all sides. I get lots of messages and emails asking me why the BBC covers Harry and Meghan if they are not working members of the royal family. The answer is because they have contributed to one of the most turbulent periods in the Royal Family in recent times and our audiences are interested whether they love or loathe the Sussexes. And on a personal level, they remind us all how painful family breakdown can be and the deep damage it can cause to family life with the blame and bitterness hard to resolve - even more so when much of it is being played out in public. We will continue to report on the work of all senior royals. Later this month, the King goes on an important trip to the Caribbean and the Prince of Wales will be in India next month with his Earthshot environmental prize. Both trips will provide insights into the priorities of father and son The joint Harry and Meghan event we saw in Nottingham won't be a regular occurrence but will happen occasionally. The Sussex's representatives have stressed that they both have their own separate interests to focus on with plans for Meghan to launch a UK version of her lifestyle brand As Ever - possibly before Christmas. And talking of Christmas - don't expect to see Harry and Meghan in Sandringham with the rest of the Royal Family. They will instead spend that time with Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, possibly here in the UK. Families are complicated. The return of Harry and Meghan is a clear reminder of that. title: Watch: What the data centre boom means for Arizona ahead of midterm elections
description: The BBC's Shaimaa Khalil travelled to the US state to hear from residents who live alongside these giant facilities.
body: This video can not be played As America’s midterm elections approach, the data centres powering America's AI expansion are becoming a political flashpoint. A new proposal in Washington would require them to cover the additional electricity infrastructure costs they create. President Donald Trump champions their expansion, and supporters point to investment and America’s technological future. But Arizona’s attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals amid concerns about water and electricity demand. The heat produced by a single data centre can surpass the amount emitted by 40,000 households. The BBC's North America correspondent Shaimaa Khalil travelled to Arizona to hear from residents who live alongside these giant facilities. title: Bullets hit microwave and wall in shooting targeting young child, court hears
description: A woman and her son were asleep when two bullets were fired into their home in Pyle.
body: Callum Pearson, Kian Darkes, Daniel Clarke and Kyle Long are all on trial at Cardiff Crown Court Bullets were found lodged inside a wall and microwave after a gang targeting a young child fired shots at the wrong home, a court has heard. A woman and her son were asleep inside the house in Pyle, Bridgend, during the shooting in the early hours of 22 September 2025, but neither were injured. A jury at Cardiff Crown Court were shown footage of two men firing a 9mm pistol at the property before fleeing on an electric motorbike. The court heard the incident was carried out in retaliation against alleged drug dealer Daniel O'Callaghan, after the gang believed he had taken drugs worth thousands of pounds from a hiding place in Guernsey. On Thursday the jury were told the gang dealt drugs, including cocaine and ecstasy, on the Channel Islands and across south Wales. The court previously heard police discovered a photograph of a child on a mobile phone belonging to one of the men standing trial, along with text messages between them both discussing targeting the youngster. Kian Darkes and Daniel Clarke, both 21, and from the Bridgend area, admit having a firearm and ammunition in a public place but deny possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life. This video can not be played The jury were shown footage of two men firing a pistol at the property in Bridgend The video shown in court, filmed by the two men, show the 9mm pistol being pointed at the house before two shots are fired. It then shows the two men running away from the house. Doorbell and security cameras in the area capture the two men making their getaway. A carrier bag containing a hoodie, two sets of gloves and two face masks were later found in a shed at the Bridgend home of alleged gang member Kyle Long. Gunshot residue was found and DNA tests later confirmed a match to both Darkes and Clarke. Cardiff Crown Court was told O'Callaghan messaged Darkes after the shooting, telling him he had not taken the drugs. "WTF is going on. Someone shot a gun. Is that for me? You need to tell me what is going on. I haven't done anything wrong. I've paid whatever I needed to pay. You need to know this wasn't me." Long, 40, and Callum Pearson, 24, from Cardiff, both deny conspiracy to commit grievous bodily harm with intent. Jade Evans, 40, from Bridgend denies three counts of conspiracy to supply a Class A drug. My contraceptive coil saved my life after it revealed I had cancer Wales has an education crisis. title: Mother of Henry Nowak killer could be deported
description: Kiran Kaur was found guilty of assisting an offender and was jailed for three years in July.
body: Vickrum Digwa's mother Kiran Kaur was jailed for three years in July for assisting an offender The mother of murderer Vickrum Digwa could be in line for deportation from the UK, the Home Office has signalled. Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three years in July for removing the knife used by her son, Vickrum Digwa, to kill student Henry Nowak from the crime scene. However Kaur, who spent several months on remand, could serve less than half of her sentence and be freed around the anniversary of Mr Nowak's death under the Government's early release scheme, ITV News reported., external The Home Office and Ministry of Justice declined to comment on individual cases, but said: "We will always seek to deport foreign criminals at the first opportunity." Kaur, who is an Indian national, could be eligible for the government's deportation scheme. She is also appealing against her sentence, with a hearing scheduled at the Court of Appeal on 5 November. Kaur's son Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years on 1 June for the murder of the 18-year-old student, after falsely claiming Mr Nowak had racially abused him in Southampton on 3 December. Some 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to be released in stages over the next year, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to exempt rapists and the most serious child sex offenders. Ministers say the expanded early release scheme is needed to prevent the justice system from collapsing, after a summer when the issue dominated news headlines. Some 650 criminals were this week released from prisons around the country under the scheme, less than two weeks after 700 were set free early. The Home Office said: "Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Henry Nowak, whose life was cruelly cut short in a horrific act of violence." The arrest and handcuffing of Henry Nowak as he lay dying prompted intense scrutiny of police actions Sentencing Kaur in July, Judge William Mousley KC told her "a responsible parent would have challenged their son" and asked their child to "do the right thing". He continued: "You took the knife and put it at home with other weapons in your son's bedroom." By putting it among "a larger collection of ceremonial and other weapons" it would have "helped to conceal what it had been used for" because she wanted him "to avoid being caught", the judge said. He acknowledged that Kaur was unlikely to reoffend and said her motive was "mistakenly, to protect your son rather than for any personal gain". He added: "However, the seriousness of your offending, requires you to be punished and others who might find themselves in a similar situation to be deterred from doing as you did." Digwa gave the knife to his mother and it was later found by police at their family home along with more than 20 other weapons. Prosecutor Nicholas Lobbenberg described Kaur's actions as "criminality of the highest order" and her role as "crucial" when it came to removing the knife. title: An Australian band’s ‘unreal’ journey to break a gig world record
description: The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.
body: This video can not be played Dream rock band Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia to play nine shows, setting a new Guinness World Record for most concerts performed in 12 hours across multiple cities. In order to beat the record, venues needed to be at least 50km apart in cities populated by more than 15,000 people, with half of the cities needing to have populations of at least 100,000. Fathom partnered with a mental health service, Beyond Blue, donating half of the revenue from ticket sales and merchandise. The BBC sat down with the duo to recount the day full of excitement and hurdles. An Australian band’s ‘unreal’ journey to break a gig world record. title: Suspected fly tippers shamed with online photos
description: Hillingdon Council has shared social media posts showing people allegedly dumping rubbish illegally.
body: The council said it had received thousands of comments on the social media posts from residents who had also "had enough" of fly tipping A west London council that says it has "had enough" of fly tipping has begun sharing CCTV images on social media, showing people allegedly being caught in the act of dumping rubbish in public places. Hillingdon Council described the crime as a "blight" on the borough, and as a local authority, it had "allowed the problem to get bigger". Cabinet member for community environment and enforcement, Adam Bennett, said the action was a "really good first step" adding: "We really need to up our game on all forms of of enforcement." He said since its CCTV images were shared earlier this week they had over 850,000 views, received 2,500 comments including information on who the perpetrators might be. Hillingdon Council's enforcement teams have identified a hotspot outside the car park for St Anselm's Church in Hayes Bennett said the reaction to the posts showed fly tipping was "a really important issue to residents". Hillingdon Council says it issues a £1,000 fixed penalty fine to culprits, and last month it seized and crushed a vehicle that was linked to fly tipping. "We've had enough as have residents, of the very small minority of individuals who choose to blight our neighbourhoods and communities by thinking it's acceptable to just dump their waste here on the pavement, on a verge, or on a lay-by." He said by sharing images of suspects' faces the council was "taking action to try and bring the perpetrators to account". Bennett added: "If you see your face on social media or perhaps on one of our screens in our libraries, our leisure centres, you're going to think twice about wanting to fly tip again." Bennett explained that "a certain evidential threshold" had to be reached before identifying individuals online, but said as a council they did not want to "shy away" from the problem. "If you're going to do it in Hillingdon, we're going to call you out for it, and we're going to take every opportunity we can to penalise you for what is unlawful environmental crime that blights the lives of our communities and all of the hard-working taxpayers in this country." The council said images like this would be shared on their social media platforms as well as on screens in libraries and leisure centres, to identify individuals Liberal Democrat London Assembly committee member Gareth Roberts said he was "interested" to see if Hillingdon's tactics of "naming and shaming" individuals worked to prevent fly tipping. "We need to use everything at our disposal to make sure that we clamp down on these people who think that they can simply trash London because they're too lazy to take things to the appropriate recycling or dumping sites," he said. This week, City Hall's Environment Committee looked at how London boroughs are responding to the problem of fly tipping, as well as the overall coordination of the response to it. Roberts said fly tipping is a "major problem" for London and explained there were nearly half a million incidents, across the capital, last year alone. "Unfortunately clearing up this mess costs councils money and it costs Londoners money," he said. "What we need is governments to recognise that there is a particular problem in London. We have more fly tipping than anywhere else and it would be great if they could find a way to give councils the money and the resources and the powers to tackle this scourge which is blighting parts of London." title: Martinez apologises for outburst and fined by Man Utd
description: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez issues an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy.
body: Martinez's contract at Manchester United runs out next summer Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has issued an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy. After United's Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday Martinez said that the club had left head coach Michael Carrick with an under-equipped squad. Following talks with United on Thursday, the Argentina international released a statement. "Today I met with the club's leadership and the manager," Martinez said in a social media post. "It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday's game. "Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity. "The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise." It is understood Martinez has been formally punished for his outburst with a fine. Carrick will hold a news conference on Friday, prior to the game against Leeds United on Sunday. He takes his side to Elland Road on the back of just two wins from nine games this season, placed 13th in the Premier League with six points from as many games. This video can not be played 'Players have a different responsibility' - pundits react to Martinez comments Following the loss to Atletico, Martinez said he expected more investment in the Manchester United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]". The 28-year-old later said he "spoke out of anger and frustration" in making those comments and that he had "belief in my team-mates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward". Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane, speaking on The Overlap podcast,, external described the situation at his former club as "a bit of a circus". Martinez's statement on Thursday added: "Our club is at its best when we are all united, and I recognise that my words in that moment did not help with that. "I know that every single person at Manchester United is doing everything possible to achieve our shared ambition: bringing the success that this club and its supporters deserve. "With this situation now behind us, we are fully focused on winning together." It remains to be seen whether Carrick selects Martinez for the trip to Leeds. Nevertheless, there is understood to be significant doubt over the centre-back's long-term future at Old Trafford. His current deal expires at the end of the season but the club have the option of extending it by 12 months. While the issue over his recent comments is now considered closed, the club are still to decide whether they want to trigger the contract option. title: Katie Price 'coached' alleged victim, court told
description: Kieran Hayler says claims were fabricated amid the breakdown of his marriage.
body: Kieran Hayler denies all the charges against him Kieran Hayler has told jurors he thought his ex-wife Katie Price was "coaching" a 13-year-old girl he is accused of raping after discovering messages she sent to the alleged victim. Hayler, 39, said he took photographs of messages on Price's phone in which she discussed claims that he fancied the girl and wrote: "I will make you a little star." Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault involving the teenager in West Sussex in 2016. Giving evidence on Thursday, the former stripper denied the allegations and said: "I believe they've been fabricated." He told the trial that "trust had gone on both sides" of his marriage to Price by mid-2013, and he admitted affairs with three other women during their relationship. He told jurors "I am attracted to older women" and that all his significant relationships had been with older women. Kieran Hayler told the court Katie Price was also unfaithful during their relationship Hayler said Price was also unfaithful during their relationship. Asked by his defence barrister Arlette Piercy why he took pictures of the messages between Price and the complainant, he replied: "Because she made out that I fancied [the complainant]. "I thought, 'this is a bit weird'." He said he accessed her phone the same way she had accessed his, by using his fingerprint. Asked about what this showed, he said: "The relationship is breaking down." The court previously heard that Price messaged the teenager saying she had heard that Hayler and the girl had kissed and he had "tried it on" with her, adding later: "I will make you a little star." Asked during her evidence about the phrase, Price said it was "a figure of speech". On Thursday, Hayler said: "Everyone can interpret it how they want, it's very pushy. It's a very strange comment to make. "I thought she was coaching her into [saying] something she shouldn't. "I didn't send them anywhere, I took a picture on my phone." He told the court he found the picture of the messages "recently" after taking his phones out of storage when moving home. He then sent them to his solicitor. On Thursday, he also pleaded not guilty to four alternative counts of sexual activity with a child following the close of the prosecution case. The charges were added to the indictment for the jury to consider as alternatives to the three rape counts and one count of sexual assault. Judge Mark van der Zwart told jurors the prosecution alleged the complainant was raped, while Hayler's case was that nothing sexual had happened between them. Hayler denies all the charges. The court previously heard Hayler had claimed Price had "launched a campaign" against him after their marriage broke down and that the allegations formed part of it. The couple were married at the time of the alleged offences before separating in 2018 and divorcing in 2021. The complainant first contacted the NSPCC in 2021 and the charity referred her to police. title: Watch: What does Starlink have to do with the Ukraine-Russia war?
description: Ukraine's president has told Elon Musk that any restriction on the Starlink's system cost lives.
body: This video can not be played Ukraine says there has been a restriction to the speed of SpaceX's Starlink internet network in the country. Starlink - owned by Elon Musk - plays a vital part in the war between Ukraine and Russia, allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect itself. Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind the restriction on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connect to the network. The BBC's Dan Johnson explores who has said what in the row and how the situation affects the war. Watch: What does Starlink have to do with the Ukraine-Russia war? title: Marvel fans to meet Welsh superhero - complete with Cardiff accent
description: Lauren Morais will play villain Lisa Molinari in the new Disney+ superhero series VisionQuest.
body: Lauren Morais will play Lisa Molinari in the new superhero series VisionQuest Marvel fans around the world are set to meet a Welsh villain - complete with a Cardiff accent. Lauren Morais, from the Welsh capital, will play Lisa Molinari in the new superhero series VisionQuest - a spin-off from the miniseries WandaVision. The Disney+ show, exploring whether AI and humanity can co-exist, also stars Paul Bettany, returning as Vision, and James Spader as Ultron. Morais said getting the role was a "pinch me" moment and that she was "very proud" to introduce her accent to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU). Speaking to Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales, Morais said she initially auditioned with an Essex accent for the part. In the fourth round of auditions, she also did a northern accent and American. But during a reading, not knowing if the Marvel team wanted a Welsh accent, Morais decided just to "go for it". "I said, 'can she be from Cardiff?' and they were like, 'of course'. So she's from Cardiff now," she said. Cardiff-born actor Lauren Morais is "very proud" to bring her accent to the MCU Morais will follow in the footsteps of Catherine Zeta-Jones who used her Swansea accent in Kill Jackie, a Prime series which follows a former cocaine dealer who is being targeted by hitmen. The actress said it was important to hear different accents on screen. "There's a myriad of accents in the UK and sometimes people forget there's so many sick accents around... I think it's so nice that we've got that representation," Morais added. She said it was a "pinch me" moment when her agent called and told her she got the part. "I just exploded! I said 'are you sure? Are you joking?' Then an hour later I had to go to a cast dinner," she said. The cast of VisionQuest at the series' UK premiere in October Morais recalled being like "a rabbit in the headlights" surrounded by all the stars of the show, but was also worrying about who was going to cover her shift at a cinema in London. During the audition process she was given time off for the VisionQuest auditions, even though she could not tell her manager what the auditions were for. She said: "I went to my final Pinewood audition and then went back to the cinema to the west end to finish my shift. "It's such a dichotomy of worlds and that's what it is as an actor, you're always grafting and then it happens and you're like, what is life." The character of Lisa Molinari has undergone a transformation from the original Marvel comic book character - known as Coat of Arms - who gains extra arms and weapons from a mystical coat. In VisionQuest, she is instead given a high-tech backpack equipped with robotic arms. Morais said co-ordinating the choreography for the fight scenes was "funny". "I'd be with the fight director who was like 'you just need to imagine that a huge arm is coming out of your right side and just absolutely go for it and imagine where it's hitting.' So I used a lot of imagination on that job," she said. But Bettany, whose character Vision is an android attempting to piece together his wiped memories and fragile humanity, had some sage advice. "He said 'you're going to feel very silly while you're doing these scenes, but if you commit to it, it's going to look really sick'. And I can confirm, he was right," she said. I got to use my Welsh accent as a lead in the new Marvel series Lauren Morais from Cardiff talks about her role in the new Marvel series, VisionQuest. She speaks to Lucy Owen about the evolution of how her villain character became Welsh. The MCU has seen a Welsh character before - the role of Welshpool appeared in Deadpool and Wolverine in 2024. Wrexham AFC striker Paul Mullin played the surprise role as a Welsh version of Ryan Reynolds' character Deadpool. It is not the first time Marvel fans will have heard a Cardiff accent, as Kingsley Ben-Adir, who played Gravik in Secret Invasion, previously told Buzzfeed he looked to Butetown, in Cardiff, when developing the character. Morais said she was very proud her character had a Cardiff accent. "I'm just so proud to be from Wales, I love it, that's why I wanted my accent in it," she said. "I love Welsh people, I love Wales, let's go for it." My contraceptive coil saved my life after it revealed I had cancer Wales has an education crisis. Can it be fixed? title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
description: Yemen's information minister says the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.
body: Verified video footage showed smoke above the presidential palace in Aden Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden". A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis. Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour". He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines. Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines. The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa. On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom. "Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency. "We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added. There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically. Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran. Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes. At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry. The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases. title: Burnham asks for his Widdecombe remarks to be corrected
description: The prime minister had faced calls to apologise for his comments about the alleged murder of the former minister.
body: Andy Burnham has asked for Parliament's official record to be corrected after telling MPs an "individual" was "responsible for the murder" of Ann Widdecombe. The prime minister had faced calls to apologise for the remarks, made during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, with a senior Tory saying they breached the "presumption of innocence" in criminal cases. A man was charged with Widdecombe's murder in July, but is yet to enter a plea for the charge and is not due to stand trial until next year. A No 10 spokeswoman said a correction had been issued to Hansard, the official report of parliamentary debates, and would be "published in due course". Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform spokeswoman. A trial before a High Court judge is scheduled for 8 June next year, and a plea and case management hearing on 29 January. Earlier this month, Kerry was also charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. Speaking on Thursday, Conservative shadow Commons leader Jesse Norman accused Burnham of breaching Parliament's sub judice rule, which says MPs should not refer to pending court cases in order to avoid influencing the outcome. He added that the prime minister's comments at PMQs had "breached the legal presumption of innocence". He asked Commons leader Sir Alan Campbell, a government minister, to "correct the record, withdraw the remark and apologise on behalf of the prime minister". In response, Sir Alan said the prime minister had "said that he misspoke, he has apologised and he has corrected the record". "There is no excuse for misspeaking in the House and I am not trying to explain that away, but this prime minister is characterised by an authenticity and a passion in the way that he responds," he added. "It is not unusual for prime ministers or anybody else to misspeak in the House. "As long as they correct the record, which he has done, that should be put into perspective." title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
description: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
body: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time. John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector. The biggest four banks collectively made around £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes. However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode". What is the Budget and what could be in it? The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets. The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in. The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn. There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector. The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year. The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation. In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth. In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers. There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since. Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive. It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness. However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business. Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie. Do you have comments or questions about this story? Get in touch. title: Watch: Moment drone hits supermarket in Odesa
description: CCTV video verified by the BBC shows the drone strike in the town of Mayaky in Ukraine's Odesa region.
body: This video can not be played CCTV video verified by the BBC shows the moment of a drone strike on a supermarket in the town of Mayaky in Ukraine's Odesa region. The drone can be seen flying into the roof of the Tavria supermarket and exploding on impact. Three people were injured in the attack, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky, who blamed Russia for the attack. Russia's war in Ukraine is in its fifth year, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Moment drone hits supermarket in Odesa. title: Australia clinch thrilling World Cup opener against New Zealand

title: What we know about the criminal investigation into US congresswoman Ilhan Omar
description: The nature of the investigation is unclear but comes after officials cast doubt on her US citizenship.
body: Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has has represented Minnesota since 2018 US government officials raided the home of Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar this week as part of what's being called a "federal criminal investigation". The search warrant was approved by a court, the justice department said. The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear. The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya. Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has said the raid is "the latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "campaign of political intimidation". He has denied being involved. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched Omar's home in Washington DC on 12 October, while she was there with her husband. The Wall Street Journal reported that her mobile phone, notebooks, personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized. "This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the justice department said in a statement at the time. Since then, investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas to Omar's family members, Fox News reports. Multiple US media outlets have reported that the investigation is tied to Omar's US citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995. Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date. Her marriages have also come under suspicion. Trump is among those who have accused her of marrying her brother to get US citizenship. Omar's finances have been scrutinised in relation to her current marriage to former Democratic political consultant Timothy Mynett. She has denied any allegations of wrongdoing and has called the investigations into her "complete shams". US Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures. Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and, earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records. Mynett told Fox News that Omar came to the US when she was 12 as a war refugee. He said he had "no concerns" about her citizenship. Omar was born in Somalia before fleeing with her family to a refugee camp in Kenya. She arrived in the US with her father and others in 1995 before becoming a naturalised US citizen in 2000. According to US media, the crux of the investigation is whether her father lied about her age on the application, writing she was 17 rather than 18. If Omar was 18 at the time her father applied for citizenship, she would have needed to pursue her own immigration process separately. After arriving from Kenya, Nur Omar Mohamed initially settled with his family in Washington before later moving to Minnesota. He worked as a cabdriver and postal worker. Omar described him as an educator and said he died in 2020 from Covid-19 complications. According to the New York Post, which cited an Oxford University doctoral researcher, Mohamed "misrepresented himself as a refugee". The Post said he had a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under former Somali President Siad Barre's military dictatorship. Barre seized power in Somalia in a bloodless coup in 1969. While his supporters saw him as a pan-Africanist who supported causes such as the campaign against South Africa's racist system of apartheid, his critics viewed him as a dictator who oversaw numerous human rights abuses until he was driven from power in 1991. "[Nur Omar Mohamed] was a full colonel in Siad Barre's military regime," historian and researcher Mohamed Haji Ingiriis told The Post. "Ilhan's father was never an educator." The BBC has contacted Omar for comment. Homeland Security Investigations agents were seen outside Omar's home on 12 October The Trump administration has made a concerted effort to detain and deport immigrants suspected of being in the US illegally. Permanent residents and green card holders have also been affected. According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonpartisan data research company, there has also been a surge in denaturalisation lawsuits filed by the Trump administration. Denaturalisation is where the US citizenship of a person who was not granted it by birth is revoked. The justice department must file a lawsuit proving the person lied in a material way during their application process. This appears to be where the groundwork is being laid in the current investigation into Omar. Trump has repeatedly suggested Omar should be deported, calling for her to "go back" to Somalia. At a rally in Ohio on Monday, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster." Trump went on to denigrate Somalis in the US more generally, which was greeted with chants of "deport" in the crowd. After her home was searched, Omar wrote on X: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "I will not be silenced." Trump has said the investigation into her has "nothing to do with me". The timing of the federal probe has defied justice department precedent of not taking action against officials running for office this close to an election. The raid happened with the November midterm elections only weeks away, drawing condemnation from some of Omar's Democratic colleagues, who said she had been subject to relentless "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations". title: Maduro pleads not guilty to new torture-related charges in New York
description: "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in court, responding to newly added torture-related charges.
body: Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are seen in a federal court in New York in July. Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture. The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week. Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail. The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027. In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured. Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me." "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator. Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro. "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator. Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn. The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states. The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system. Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups. Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves. He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn. title: Equality watchdog writes to Greens over 'Zionism is racism' motion
description: The party was reported to the Equality and Human Rights Commission by MPs and antisemitism campaigners.
body: Green leader Zack Polanski said the motion was 'imperfect' but supported the substance of it The equality watchdog has written to the Green Party asking for more information about a controversial "Zionism is racism" motion passed by members. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it recognised that "many Jewish people will be feeling vulnerable" following the motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month. The motion described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population". In a response to the ECHR letter, the party said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and was committed to tackling antisemitism. Dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners wrote to the regulator raising concerns about antisemitism after the Green motion was passed. Alongside Jewish groups, the motion was criticised by four of the five Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive". It piled some pressure on Green leader Zack Polanski in the wake of a by-election defeat. He said the motion was "imperfect" and he wanted to see it amended. Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion. On Thursday, the EHRC confirmed it had written to the Greens following the complaints received. A spokesperson for the watchdog said: "We have written to the Green Party of England and Wales about its recently adopted 'Zionism is racism' motion to ask for more information and assess its practical implications and potential impact. "We have received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns that Jewish people could face discrimination because of their beliefs following the adoption of the motion." The watchdog said it would "take action where appropriate" after assessing the extra information. "In the case of the Green Party motion, compliance with the Equality Act is likely to hinge on the practical effects of the motion," the spokesperson added. In a letter earlier this month, some MPs raised concerns not only about the motion itself but also amendments to protect Jewish Green members at Zionist synagogues being voted down. "Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter said. Separately, the Campaign Against Antisemitism wrote to the EHRC alleging the party had breached the Equality Act through discrimination against Jews. The campaign group said the motion "effectively states that the state of Israel should not exist" and "defines support for a Jewish homeland in any form as racist". Having been backed by members, the motion has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election. In response to the EHRC letter, the Green Party of England and Wales said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and the motion sets out a political position with "no impact on membership conditions or internal disciplinary processes". "The party's comprehensive antisemitism guidance, which forms part of our framework of ethics, remains unchanged," a spokesperson added. "We remain committed to tackling antisemitism and ensuring Jewish members feel welcome and respected." title: Taxi driver given fake cash drove customer to police
description: Nottinghamshire Police called the move a "fantastic piece of work" by the driver.
body: The taxi driver was handed counterfeit notes for a ride, Nottinghamshire Police said A man was arrested after a taxi driver who was given fake cash drove the suspect straight to a police station. Nottinghamshire Police said the driver picked up the suspect from Nottingham Road at 23:30 BST on Tuesday. When the customer continued to change his route, the taxi driver asked how he would be paying, which is when he was handed a counterfeit £20 note, the force added. After questioning the customer and being given further fake notes, the driver took him straight to Radford Road police station. The force said officers also carried out a search of a man's address, where they discovered a "Rambo knife" under his mattress. It added no further counterfeit cash was recovered, but a cannabis cultivation kit was seized from the address. A 23-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of using counterfeit currency and possessing an offensive weapon in a private place. The driver promptly took the suspect to Radford Road police station in Nottingham, instead of his final location Neighbourhood inspector Liz Gaskin, who covers the Radford area, said: "This was a fantastic piece of work by a Nottingham taxi driver. "As soon as they noticed the man's suspicious behaviour in the back of the vehicle and saw that the money was fake, they decided the end of his journey would be a night in our custody. "We were of course happy to help, and following a search of the individual's property uncovered further concerning behaviour, which included taking a dangerous weapon out of circulation."
