title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
description: Protests have taken place over the rules which have seen pupils wearing hijabs turned away from schools.
body: These schoolgirls were not allowed to enter classes because of their headscarves "You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school. The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?" Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad. Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people. Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that. President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail. Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally. But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni. The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order". Videos have circulated of protests taking place in and around the capital Baku The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October. In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education." Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday. In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison." An example shared by the Azerbaijani government of an acceptable school uniform under the new rules Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class. According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since. The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed. Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN). Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran. The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself. On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites. A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility. Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families. "A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said. Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh. The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states". President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation". His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake". "A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X. Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in. Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der. President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs. Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life". Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil. Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries. That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall. title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
description: New guidance says trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex.
body: Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance. It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made and the dignity and safety of all patients should be maintained. The guidance also says staff facilities should be used by people based on their biological sex, while trusts should ensure enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, such as single-occupancy toilets, are offered. Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity. That meant that a trans woman – a biological male who identifies as a woman – could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man – a biological female who identifies as a man – could have opted for a men's ward. That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman. The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it. Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces. But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met. It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings. In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff. Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity. The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets. Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex. NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward. The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025. Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentus shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied. "NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said. Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients. "This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said. The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations. In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected. The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them. The nurses are currently seeking £400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs. One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it. "The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said. "Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses." In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces. Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms. She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation. An appeal is under way and expected to reach the courts next year. title: BBC Inside Science
description: How can we to compete against a natural force with the power of 25 atomic bombs?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·15 Oct 2026,·28 mins Back in May, we checked in on the developments in the eastern Pacific’s ocean currents, that we call El Niño. We said that stirrings in the surface suggested there might just be quite a big one. Now, it seems, everyone is talking about it, and it’s definitely big. What is the El Niño? And what is it really up to? Mark Maslin, Professor of Physical Geography at University College London, tells us. This week the film Whalefall opens in cinemas - think Jonah, but with a lot more about the intricacies of whale digestion. But, is it an excellent bit of Hollywood nonsense? Or is it even remotely possible for this to happen? And even if it isn’t, can we still learn useful things about sperm whale biology? Only one man can answer that question...Deadly Steve Backshall. For the next few weeks we talk to scientists from around the world, nominated for this year's John Maddox Prize, and whose evidence-based contributions to public discourse has not been universally well received. Dr Cyriac Abby Philips is a clinical hepatologist, based in Kerala, India, who is famous in his country for speaking out against traditional Indian medicine. Presenter: Tom Whipple Producers: Ben Mitchell, Alex Mansfield, Katie Tomsett, Keiran Manetta-Jones Editor: Martin Smith Production Co-ordinator: Jana Bennett-Holesworth

title: Former DUP leader Donaldson sentenced to 15 years in prison for child sex abuse
description: Jeffrey Donaldson was convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including one of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.
body: Jeffrey Donaldson, pictured here during the trial, was convicted in June Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences, including one count of rape. The former DUP leader stood with his hands clasped in front of him in the dock of Newry Crown Court as his sentence was handed down. Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson's crimes, which took place between 1985 and 2008, had led to a "catastrophic descent into disgrace". He was sentenced to 11 years for his crimes against Victim B and four years for offences against Victim A. The 63-year-old, who was convicted in June, is seeking to appeal his convictions. Both sentences will run consecutively. But Donaldson will spend only half his 15-year sentence behind bars. Because the offences were committed before the Criminal Justice (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 came into effect, he qualifies for 50% remission. Should his attempt to appeal his convictions fail, it means he will be released from prison at the end of 2033. The remainder of his sentence will be under supervision in the community on licence. Donaldson was taken back to Maghaberry Prison to serve his sentence Donaldson will also be required to sign the Sex Offenders Register for life. The former Lagan Valley MP has been in Maghaberry Prison since then and returned to it on Thursday afternoon after being sentenced. Donaldson spends up to 18 hours a day in his cell at the prison, which holds around 1,600 inmates. Since being convicted, he has been held in its Moyola Unit, a part of the jail used for prisoners with health care needs, and does not share a cell. It is thought he is in this unit for his own safety from risk of attack or verbal abuse from other prisoners. Judge Ramsey said aggravating features include the length and protracted nature of the offending spanning many years. He also took into account the youth of the victims and the age difference between them and Donaldson, adding that he could not accept Donaldson's lack of other convictions as a mitigating factor. The judge said by contesting a case, a defendant avoids the reduction in sentence they would have got if they had pleaded guilty. "It is highly significant that the defendant denied the offences to the police, he denied them in evidence and to the probation officer he continues to maintain his denials," the judge said. "He has doubled-down in his denials. "There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort." The former DUP leader stood with his hands clasped in front of him in the dock of Newry Crown Court as his sentence was handed down Jeffrey Donaldson's wife, Eleanor Donaldson, had faced a trial of the facts on mental health grounds, meaning the jury was asked to find out if she did the acts or did not do the acts of which she was accused. The jury found that she had done the acts in relation to five charges – including four counts of aiding and abetting her husband's offending. She has applied to appeal the verdict. She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge. The judge is due to decide on this at a later date. Dawn arrest to 'descent into disgrace': How victims exposed Jeffrey Donaldson's lies Jeffrey Donaldson's life in politics: From DUP leader to convicted child sex abuser Statements from both victims were released after the sentencing and read out by Det Ch Insp Leah Crothers. Victim A said the impact of the crimes committed against her did not end when the abuse ended. "For years I carried shame, anger and guilt, and questioned whether I was worth protecting or worthy of being loved. "The last few years have been nothing short of a battle. "The conviction does not erase the abuse or undo the impact of what happened to me, and I will always carry the consequences of it. "But those responsible do not control me now. They forever changed me, but they will not take my future. The cycle is being broken and it ends with me." Victim B said what happened to her as a child had "affected everything since then". "What would it be like not to be afraid at night, not to wake up shaking, not to have nightmares and not to lock away every feeling I have? "What happened took away my ability to trust people and, in all honesty, I don't think I really know what trust or love truly is. Nothing can ever change what was done to me. I wish it could. "I stood up, many years later, because for me this is about drawing a line in the sand and knowing that the Donaldsons can no longer hurt anyone else. "Many people get to look ahead and plan their lives with hope, I've never known what that feels like. My hope was taken away from me a long time ago." Det Ch Insp Crothers from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), said Donaldson's victims have "suffered immeasurably as they come to terms with what has happened to them as children". "He robbed them both of their childhood and innocence." She added that police "worked tirelessly" to build a "robust case against this man and his wife" whose offending "has shocked our local communities". "The police service and our criminal justice system have sent a clear message: No-one is above the law." Det Ch Insp Leah Crothers The head of the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) Serious Crime Unit, Catherine Kierans, said the case "shows that sexual abuse can be hidden behind a facade of respectability". "It also shows that no individual, irrespective of their position, status or public reputation, is beyond the reach of the law." Kierans added that the "courage shown by the two victims in reporting the sexual abuse was the catalyst for a thorough PSNI investigation". "I want to pay tribute to the victims in this case. We recognise that it took great courage to speak out," she said. "Victims of sexual abuse should never feel shame for what w

title: Severe drought declared in parts of southern England
description: Reservoir levels continue to drop after a hot summer and less September rain than normal.
body: Ardingly Reservoir's level of about 20% helped spark the severe drought Severe drought has been declared across parts of southern England after months of low rainfall. Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex are affected by the announcement from the Environment Agency, which followed a review of water resources and drought conditions across England by the National Drought Group. Water supplies have been significantly impacted by high demand following the hottest summer on record. The government said customer supplies would be uninterrupted and declaring severe drought "ensures proactive steps are taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs". Ministers instructing water companies to conduct daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels and tougher water quality monitoring The Environment Agency to increase compliance checks on businesses that withdraw water from natural sources to ensure they are only taking permitted quantities of water The government said the change to severe drought status had been prompted by specific concerns for two major reservoirs, Ardingly in West Sussex and Wimbleball in Somerset. The latest figures, external for Wimbleball Reservoir on Exmoor show it is at 14.9% capacity, while Ardingly is 19.4% full, external. Other major reservoirs are also low, including Roadford in Devon at 36.8%, Burrator at 33.6%, Colliford in Cornwall at 35% and Stithians at 21.9%. The Environment Agency has classed Colliford and Wimbleball as having exceptionally low levels, external. Wimbleball serves about 300,000 properties across east Devon, north Devon, Somerset, west Dorset and West Somerset. Ardingly Reservoir serves 280,000 customers across East and West Sussex. The Environment Agency said it expected reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of the year. In its latest drought report, external it said reservoir storage had continued to fall at most reservoirs in England. The agency has granted South East Water and South West Water drought orders giving them permission to cut the amount of water sent from reservoirs to rivers by millions of litres per day. Southern Water also applied for an order to restrict usage in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The agency also has concerns about several smaller reservoirs in Devon and Cornwall, including Stithians near Falmouth. Water levels have fallen to about 15% at Wimbleball reservoir on Exmoor MP raises concern over 'reservoirs running dry' Your hosepipe ban questions answered Drought permit issued in bid to secure supply Environment Agency chief executive Philip Duffy said: "Record-breaking summer heat and severe drought have put our water resources under immense pressure. "Recovery depends on both rainfall and how much water we use. We cannot change the weather, but water companies can act now. "We expect them to follow their drought plans and take the steps needed to secure public water supplies. "We are also asking everyone to use less water. That will leave more in our rivers and the environment, helping farmers and protecting wildlife and nature." Will we see standpipes on the streets this winter? The government said the South East and South West had experienced their driest April to September in more than a century, impacting reservoir levels in that area. Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: "This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades, so this government is stepping up our support and planning. "We are working closely with water companies to protect public supplies in the areas affected, and I'd continue to urge everyone to think about how they can use water wisely over the coming weeks." A hosepipe ban has been in force across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset since 8 August and there is no definite end date. South West Water said a "prolonged period of hot and dry weather" along with "continuous high demand for water" was behind the ban. Stithian's Lake in Cornwall is just over 21% full South East Water's operations director Douglas Whitfield said standpipes remained part of the company's drought plan but were unlikely to be needed. Whitfield said a wet winter had been forecast but timings were not clear and the firm was making any adjustments it could to protect supplies. Whitfield said South East Water, which supplies more than two million customers, said 92 repair crews were out across Sussex and Kent tackling leaks to minimise loss from the network. In an email sent to customers South East Water said it was optimising water pressure across the county and had more than doubled the number of teams tackling leaks in the region, increasing from seven to 16. It said the number of leaks in the affected area had fallen from 181 to 97 and that more than 1,300 leaks had been repaired since 1 April. Wessex Water, which supplies customers from Wimbleball, introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years in August and said the restrictions would remain in place for the foreseeable future. The water company said it had increased leak repairs, moved water into the area from more resilient sources and adjusted water pressure in some communities to conserve supplies and urged customers to continue using water carefully. Will Willoughby, director of water supply at Wessex Water, said: "We saw record levels of demand through the network - and it sustained above the 400 million litres a day for 48 days, which is far and away the toughest year that we've seen in terms of that height in demand." He said customer impact "should be none" but encouraged customers to continue to be mindful about water usage. Paul Tompkins, deputy president of The National Farmers' Union (NFU) said it had been a "torrid year for farmers", where the conditions proved "very difficult" to harvest crops, provide water for livestock, and a "potential dry winter could have implications for next year's cro

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
description: Trump said some would "rather not watch" the killing of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years.
body: Thirteen US soldiers were killed in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood in Texas US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad. Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it. Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die". "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years. Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said. After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others. The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent". While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things". This video can not be played 'We'll make sure people can watch Hasan execution' - Hegseth But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. The president also called Hasan "totally nuts". "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said. Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward. title: Fifty arrests in crime probe after fatal A66 crash
description: The arrests are made as part of a wider operation against organised crime after the A66 fatal crash.
body: Seven people including two police officers were killed in the crash on the A66 in the early hours of 22 August A total of 50 people have now been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following a fatal crash. The arrests have been made after the head-on smash on the A66 on Teesside which killed seven people, including two police officers. Ten of the 50 arrested are alleged to be linked to the Volvo reportedly involved in driving into two properties in the early hours of 22 August, police said. Det Ch Sup Helen Barker of Cleveland Police, said: "Over the last two months, we have identified 50 people who we believe are associated within criminal networks that seek to cause serious violence and harm within the community through the supply of drugs." The force said shotguns, hand guns, machetes and ammunition had also been seized, as well as £60,000 worth of class A and B drugs and more than £30,000 in cash. Barker said: "Our pursuit of this criminality will continue, and I want to take this opportunity to thank the community for their support and patience but also for the information that we keep receiving. "I want to encourage you to keep on reporting behaviour that is related to drugs or organised crime - no matter how small - and be assured we will act." Safeguarding interventions have also been made in relation to three children, the force said. On 22 August a Volkswagen Passat with five young men hit an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the dual carriageway near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST. Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene. The occupants of the VW Passat, which was travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy - also died. A number of those arrested have now been charged with various offences including possession of a firearm and possession with intent to supply drugs including cocaine and crack cocaine. Fifteen people have been charged - 13 men and two women ranging in age from 19-45. title: Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?
description: Parts of southern England have entered "severe drought", while about 30 million people are under hosepipe ban.
body: Severe drought has been declared in parts of southern England after months of dry weather drove some reservoirs to exceptionally low levels. Most of England and all of Wales were already under drought conditions after both nations' hottest summers on record, which has taken its toll on rivers, crops and nature. Roughly 30 million people across parts of England and Wales are covered by hosepipe bans, as part of water companies' efforts to manage supplies. So how is your area doing and are you in a drought? "Severe drought" - the highest category - has now been declared for parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. It means environmental authorities will ramp up monitoring of reservoir levels, river flows and water quality, as well as carry out extra checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources. The "severe drought" classification was introduced following the 2012 drought and this is the first time it has been implemented. The UK government says two previous events would have met the "severe drought" classification, had it been in place. They are: August 1976, for Devon and Yorkshire in England, and Gwent, Monmouthshire and Glamorgan in Wales November 1995, for Yorkshire only Most of England and all of Wales were already in drought, following earlier announcements by the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales. Parts of north-east and north-west England are in the category below drought, called "prolonged dry weather". There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland. There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle. If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies. The EA says that south-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century. Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity" - when there is not enough water of sufficient quality to meet demands of people and the environment. While conditions have improved in parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some south-eastern areas remain in the most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency. Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans - officially called "temporary use bans" - if they are not already in place. So far, 11 UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans in 2026. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools. Ten companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales. Our three main sources of water are reservoirs, rivers and from deep underground. A key reason why parts of southern England have entered "severe drought" is low reservoir levels. At this time of year, the Environment Agency says it would expect England's reservoirs to be about three-quarters full, but they are just over half full on average. Ardingly Reservoir in West Sussex and Wimbleball Reservoir in Somerset are among those at "exceptionally low" levels, at 23% and 21% respectively. Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water says most reservoir levels in Wales are normal for the time of year. And reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data. Many of the UK's rivers have also been affected by the low rainfall. Most monitored river flows in England were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH). South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs. Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks. Groundwater levels are generally declining following the prolonged dry weather. In September, about half of monitored sites across the UK recorded levels considered "below normal" or lower, with southern England and Wales typically faring worst. Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions. These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey. It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur. Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes. The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far. But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation. "A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading. But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water. In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure. And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed. As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire. But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control wat

title: Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments
description: The Reform leader says "you can't vet for future comments", after undercover filming of party activists.
body: Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language. Nigel Farage has insisted Reform UK does not have an issue with vetting, after ITV News broadcast undercover filming of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language. The Reform leader told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments". In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform, external, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites". ITV's filming, gathered over a year, involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total. Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended. Two years ago, Farage vowed to root out "bad apples" among Reform's candidates, saying "bigots" and "extremists" were not welcome. Defending the party's vetting processes, Farage told BBC Look East: "You can't vet for future comments. You can look at someone's CV. You can look at someone's social media... "I can't predict what they're going to say after a drink, when they're being provoked by somebody or egged on to say something." Pressed over whether the party had an issue with vetting, he said: "No, not at all. We actually vet to a much higher standard than the other parties." He insisted "appropriate action" would be taken following the broadcast, but added: "I'm promising you, however heavily you vet, you cannot stop what people say in the future." This video can not be played Watch: Reform UK councillor filmed making racist comments, ITV investigation shows ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last. These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, after defecting from the Conservative Party in 2025. Feeney, Solihull's deputy mayor, told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites". Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than 1% of British population can be non-white." Farage said "the most egregious case" in ITV's filming was "somebody who is a long-term Conservative councillor", in an apparent reference to Feeney. He said "anyone who says stuff like that" was "not welcome". The Reform UK leader added: "But I promise you, if an undercover investigation spoke to hundreds of Labour councillors or Conservative councillors or however many hundreds they spoke to, and you provoke people, you'll find unsavoury things said by all parties." Councillor suspended from prison job after 'despicable' comments Bigots not welcome in Reform UK, says Nigel Farage Reform candidate defects to Tories over racism row On a different day in the ITV broadcast, Feeney is joined by two other Reform candidates, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, who discuss speculation of a mosque being built in the local area. "There's got to be a way of stopping them - like, go and buy some pork chops; we'll bury it in the ground," Campbell is heard saying in the film. Whelan says "we'll take pictures of it", prompting Feeney to add: "I was gonna say, 'Unfortunately, this is a pig cemetery, mate'." Discussing a female Reform candidate from Birmingham, Feeney is heard saying, "I didn't know where to look", before Whelan adds: "I'd have been sniffing that seat as soon as she got up." The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons" and would be continuing as an independent councillor. The BBC has contacted Campbell and Whelan, who has resigned as a councillor, for a response. A Reform UK Solihull spokesman condemned Feeney and Whelan's "misogynistic and offensive comments" and confirmed they were no longer Reform councillors. The spokesman said Campbell's comment "was a joke in poor taste but with no malicious intent", adding: "It's something that he deeply regrets, and the party will not be taking any further action." Elsewhere in the film, Dean Miller, a councillor in the south London borough of Bromley, is shown campaigning for Reform in the Makerfield by-election. "We've been ethnically cleansed out of London because you never used to get any blacks over in Bromley," he tells an ITV undercover reporter. "And now, you know, Bromley's like massive Nigerian communities there." Miller says he is "not racist", before later adding: "The Muslim thing, that is going to be that thing that takes over everything and then everyone just has one religion. Because, apparently, King Charles is a [expletive] Muslim... I think that's [expletive] traitorous." ITV reported that Miller would now sit as an independent councillor having resigned from Reform and had told them in a statement that he was heavily medicated due to a chronic pain condition when he made the comments. The BBC has contacted him for comment. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Reform should take "immediate and firm action against those who've been revealed to be making these abhorrent comments". He added: "There is no place for any form of racism, antisemitism, discrimination in British politics, and we all should be relentless in repeating that and taking the firmest possible action." The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed." Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
description: Children were buried under the debris after the roof crashed through three classrooms, police say.
body: This video can not be played On the ground in Pakistan as school roof collapse kills more than 30 children At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials. More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC. The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris. Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes". Warning: This article contains distressing details An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances. Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said. "I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away." "There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water." Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels". A rescue worker said an upper-floor roof collapsed, crashing through three classrooms The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak. Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down. There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said. It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too. Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear. The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals. Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead. The police chief said the building was still "extremely dangerous" and urged people to move away. The Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Faisal Karim Kundi, has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary". "We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," he said. Furious family members of deceased pupils accused the school of ignoring safety concerns. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all," Mohammad Zaman, a man who lost two nephews in the disaster, told Reuters news agency. The roof crashed through three classrooms and buried schoolchildren in debris, police say In June, fourteen children died after the roof of a private tuition centre near Lahore collapsed. And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, which an inquiry found lacked fire alarms and sprinklers. title: Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport
description: The man, a Mexican firefighter, looked "nervous" as he tried to leave Cologne Airport, officials say.
body: Not all the the snakes and lizards were alive, officials said A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes. Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport. They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase. They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks. "My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office. Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul. The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance. He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul. As for the surviving animals, they are being looked after at a snake farm in Germany. "Last year, we had over 1,300 seizures nationwide involving more than 56,600 protected animals and plants or products made from them," the Customs spokesman said. Six years ago, 26 rare reptiles - 10 of them dead - smuggled inside parcels of toys and sweets from Mexico, were found by customs officials at Cologne Bonn Airport. They were destined for private buyers in Germany. title: Labour to break from Green council groups that back Zionism policy
description: Labour says it will end power-sharing deals with councillors that do not disown the party's new stance.
body: Sheffield is one of the areas where Labour currently shares power with the Greens Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Green Party on local councils, unless its councillors disown the party's newly-adopted policy that Zionism is a form of racism. Labour says it will give local Green groups seven days to confirm they reject the policy, which was recently approved by Green members at its party conference. The ultimatum applies to 18 councils where it shares power with the Greens, either directly or alongside other parties. The Greens hit back at the move, accusing Labour of meddling and arguing it would be undemocratic for the party to "tell local parties what to do". The policy motion adopted by members of the Green Party of England and Wales said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians. It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs. Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future. He has however said that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology", arguing this was the "substantial part" of the motion. Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza. The party's two deputy leaders have been at odds over the policy, with Mothin Ali backing the move and Rachel Millward voting against it. Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on local councils in Sheffield, Lewes and Warwick. In other areas, it runs the council as part of a broader coalition alongside other parties. Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote On Wednesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy, although Downing Street did not confirm what this meant for local government. The party has now said it wants all local Labour groups to write to their Green counterparts, demanding "clear and unambiguous" statements rejecting the policy. Green groups will also be asked to call on their party's "national leadership" to reconsider the policy. "Where they are unable to provide that assurance, Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end," the party's chair Bridget Phillipson said. In response to Burnham's comments, Polanski said: "I'm the only Jewish leader of a political party. I'm a victim of antisemitism every day and I've made it clear Jewish people are welcome in my party." A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong. "Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic." The Board of Deputies of British Jews, the UK's largest cross-community Jewish organisation, welcomed Labour's announcement. Its vice president Karen Newman said the Greens had adopted an "antisemitic platform", adding of Labour's position: "This is a commitment we have been pressing for, and we are urging other mainstream parties to take the same clear and principled stand." National parties exercise various levels of control over groups of local councillors who wish to do deals to govern locally. Labour councillors require the approval of its ruling National Executive Committee before entering into local tie-ups. According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office. By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally. title: Walsh vomit & Ponga pain - the physical toll of World Cup opener
description: Australia's Reece Walsh exerted himself to the point of throwing up, while New Zealand's Kalyn Ponga tried to play on with a suspected broken arm in a dramatic Men's Rugby League World Cup opener.
body: Reece Walsh & Kalyn Ponga have both played for Queensland in State of Origin If anyone doubted the physical commitment of rugby league's greatest stars, they only needed to watch an exhausted Reece Walsh doubled up and vomiting during Thursday's epic World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand. And during the Kangaroos' dramatic 24-22 victory in Sydney, there were plenty of other examples of that commitment - aside from the normal rough and tumble this punishing sport regularly delivers. New Zealand full-back Kalyn Ponga bravely battled on for 20 minutes with a suspected broken arm before almost having to be scraped off the pitch minutes before hat-trick hero Jack Bostock's winning try for the Kangaroos. Mitchell Moses initially tried to run off a calf issue before being forced from the field just after the break, while Australia captain Isaah Yeo demonstrated his durability against a powerhouse Kiwis pack, having elected to delay surgery on his injured pectoral muscle just in order play in the tournament. But understandably, much of the focus was on the star full-backs - Ponga and Walsh. The Kangaroos number one was playing for the first time for eight weeks after recovering from an ankle injury. Australia edge New Zealand in epic World Cup opener Reece Walsh was Australia's star player in the 2025 Ashes series And he delivered a superb try-saving tackle on Ponga during the first-half before scoring a with a sensational 60-metre burst to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp victory. "Walshy was very good tonight having not played for eight weeks," said Australia head coach Kevin Walters. "I thought he was really good. That try-saving tackle he did is equal to anything that he can do an attack, and then he comes up with a couple of big plays in attack as well. "He's cramping and vomiting and all sorts of things. He didn't have the energy to kick the goal. He's a chucker [he throws up]. People get nicknames and his nickname is 'Chucker'. "He's not an endurance athlete. He's a power athlete and he had some big efforts there a couple of times, back-to-back and we've seen him do that before." Yeo added: "For Reece to come back in a contest like that with some of those plays is a massive effort after not playing for eight weeks. It won't get spoken about enough but it is really hard to do at this level. "He has just got the ability to just make people miss. I think he made two people miss on the one move but he's just one of those players that can just break a game open, and we probably needed that." Kalyn Ponga (left) switched his international allegiance to New Zealand before the tournament Having finally fulfilled a long-held desire to represent New Zealand, Ponga's night was going sweetly - he scored two tries that included one trademark run from deep and elusive step that left Walsh clutching at air - but it ended on a bitter note. For one thing, Australia swiped victory from the grasp of Stacey Jones' team. For another, Ponga's futre participation in the World Cup is now in serious doubt. Speaking after the game, Jones admitted that the Newcastle Knights man would now have medical checks after playing on for a quarter of the contest with an injury sustained in a tackle with Cameron Munster. "It's a possible fracture of the arm but he's going to go for scans and we're not going to make a call on him right now where he's at," said Jones. "He had a pretty good game. "I think he played on for 20 minutes, he toughed it out. It's a tough one. They scored a try and that's when we were told what it possibly was and that he would have to come off. "He couldn't catch the ball or anything like that, he was in a lot of discomfort." Should Ponga be ruled out it would be a huge blow to New Zealand's hopes of winning a second World Cup, 18 years on from their first. title: Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common
description: A 75,000-year-old Neanderthal spear wound may be evidence violence shaped human life far earlier than thought.
body: A wooden spear caused the hole in this Neanderthal shoulder blade, scientists say A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say. They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon. From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole. The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought. Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens. The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found. A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology. "The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News. Scientists have used Neanderthal remains to imagine what they could have looked like Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s. The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy. "It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone." But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident. But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation. "The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said. This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear. We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest. "I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News. A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago. Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object. The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago. For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores. But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way. The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups. The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports. title: Another man admits raping woman drugged by husband over 20 years
description: The husband is accused of inviting 13 other men to abuse her at their family home in Stockport.
body: The victim looked on from the public gallery as Graham Brougham, 74, changed his plea to guilty Another man has pleaded guilty to raping a woman who was drugged and abused by her husband without her knowledge for over 20 years. Graham Brougham, 74, is the oldest of 13 men who were charged with sexual offences against the victim after being allegedly invited into her home, in the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, to abuse her by her husband. The husband, in his sixties, has already admitted 62 offences against his wife - including rape - and has given a witness statement detailing "what he says happened". Brougham, from Northwich, was told by a judge at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court that he "should be under no illusion his sentence will be custody and a long time in custody." The victim, who held hands with a family member, watched on from the public gallery as Brougham answered "guilty" in the dock to a charge of raping her in September 2024. Graham Brougham leaving court after admitting his guilt The husband, who remains in custody, cannot be identified to protect the anonymity of his wife. Two other men, 59-year-old Keith Fotheringham from Dundee, Scotland; and Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport, had already admitted sexually abusing her at previous hearings. The trial of 10 other defendants accused of sexual offences against the victim has been delayed until 2 November for legal and practical reasons. Sean Peers, 38, changed his plea to guilty and admitted sexually assaulting the woman earlier this month They are all alleged to have committed offences against the same victim between 2015 and November 2025. Brougham was released on conditional bail and will be sentenced at the conclusion of the trial of his co-defendants. Earlier this month, the nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, were told that the husband had provided a witness statement detailing "what it is he says happened" after his guilty pleas. Judge Maurice Greene said: "That statement is a long statement and that has been disclosed to all defence counsel and it contains a lot of detail." Alan Keelan, Jonathan Kirk and Jordan Wallace deny the charges against them and, along with seven others, will go on trial next month The judge said the statement contained "lots of pages and lots of documents" and that lawyers in the case were "going through it carefully", which was ongoing work. title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
description: The culture secretary says the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
body: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division. Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape. Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal. "We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said. ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries". The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service. The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here. It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix. What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite shows But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up. In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including: The need for free expression of opinion in news media The need for a range of views in news media across the UK The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV. Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added. But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV. The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued. This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added. Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns. A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices." An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process. "This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries." Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration. This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes. She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes." title: £15m for zero-emission testing at Belfast Harbour
description: It comes after a £15m investment from UK Research and Innovation's Local Innovation Partnerships Fund.
body: Testing technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption Belfast Harbour is to become a live environment for testing zero-emission transport and energy systems. It comes after a £15m investment from UK Research and Innovation's Local Innovation Partnerships Fund. The cluster led by Artemis Technologies, will connect electric vessels, high-power marine charging, autonomous transport and energy systems through secure digital twin technology. Testing these technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption. Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use. "What does that mean for most people? It means your bus turns up at the right time in terms of transport. "But in terms of energy it means, more significantly that when the wind is blowing too hard, the network tells our boat 'take the power' and ultimately as we build up, it tells Belfast Harbour which uses a huge amount of energy 'take that energy'. "Equally when the wind doesn't blow, it says 'don't use that energy' and what does that mean? "It means we don't have to shut down windfarms and ultimately lower energy prices," he added. Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said it will be "developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the Harbour" This is the second project announced from the £30m allocation to the Belfast-Derry Innovation Corridor. Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said: "It will be developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the harbour, which is a really big user. "We are really world leading in terms of this so it is a really good investment," she added. It's hoped what is learned in this project could have wider applications across Northern Ireland. Dr Percy said: "Where the real accelerator value add comes in here, what can be done on that network can be rinse and repeat anywhere else." title: Seven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
description: A search and rescue operation is under way in the Black Sea after the latest attack in the area.
body: A search and rescue operation involving boats and helicopters is now continuing in rough seas, Romania's authorities say Seven of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania's coast on Thursday morning, naval authorities say. The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire. Romanian President Nicușor Dan confirmed that the Wine Trader and another chemical tanker in the area, the Yara J, had both been struck by drones - the Yara J on Wednesday. The Wine Trader was empty of cargo at the time. Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port had been hit. It did not name the vessels. Overnight, a swarm of Russian drones was detected not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island. The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing. Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy. A search and rescue operation for the missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed. The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel. The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area. The Wine Trader tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 (05:00 GMT). Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader had been hit by two drones. The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked. This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened. The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state." Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region. The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area. Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable". Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine. A fire broke out on the Comoros-flagged Yara J late on Wednesday after being struck by a drone, but its crew - who are all reportedly safe - were able to douse the flames themselves. Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi. Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports. Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked. Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea. Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. title: Cult Leicester Square cinema saved from potential closure
description: The cinema had faced an uncertain future, but has now signed a 25-year lease with its landlord.
body: The Prince Charles Cinema opened as a theatre in 1962 before becoming a cinema The Prince Charles cinema in Leicester Square has been saved from potential closure after signing a 25-year lease. It has faced a lengthy period of uncertainty following difficulties with its landlord, Zedwell LSQ Ltd, whose parent company is Criterion Capital. Now the Leicester Square cult cinema has secured the new lease with no break clause, offering it security so the "projectors will keep rolling for years to come". Vaq Farooq, CEO of Criterion Capital, said he was pleased to reach an equitable solution for all, and said: "A 25-year commitment provides real security for the cinema and its fans, and we are delighted to be continuing our partnership for many years to come." The venue faced closure at the start of 2025 due to the potential addition of a six-month break clause in its contract. Prince Charles launched a petition to withdraw the break clause from its contract. In May 2025, the cinema was declared an Asset of Community Value by Westminster City Council, which grants it additional protections from redevelopment. Despite this, the cinema's boss, Ben Freedman, told the media in August that a resolution had still not been found. However it seems that both parties have now reached an agreement, with the Prince Charles announcing the signing of the new lease on its Instagram earlier. A spokesperson for the cinema thanked the 168,645 people who had signed the petition to save it and said: "The Prince Charles Cinema is thrilled to announce that we have signed a new 25-year lease with no break clause, ensuring our projectors will keep rolling for years to come. "After 21 months of uncertainty, we're delighted to have secured the future of the cinema, and we couldn't have done it without the support, commitment and belief of many, many people. "We are so incredibly thankful to each and every one of you. You have all placed your trust in us, and as we continue on for at least another 25 years, we promise to never forget that. We'll be right here…" Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external.
