title: Infantino apologises to Fifa Council - but told he is still not fit to lead
description: President Gianni Infantino apologises to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but is asked to go further.
body: Gianni Infantino celebrated 10 years as Fifa president in February 2026 President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all the documents and answers key questions. The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged. Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm. In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations. Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered despite the "most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting" she had experienced. "One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers from FFE," Hewitt said. "I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing. "I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting." Hewitt added: "I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them. "It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize. "The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate. "That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change." Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology. "Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added. "What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the Council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us." Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down. It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released. Hewitt hopes Infantino now freely releases the documents so the Council can understand what happened. "Those papers coming to Council are a crucial next part of us feeling comfortable as to what, if any, criminal proceedings need to take place," Hewitt said. Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, she added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic." This video can not be played 'Nothing has changed' - FA chair on Infantino Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency? Infantino says he is open to talks over Fifa reform Infantino will stand for re-election as Fifa president for a third time in March, and as yet no credible candidate has emerged to challenge the Swiss-Italian. Former Tottenham and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has said he intends to run, but it appears unlikely he will get the five letters of support from member associations let alone be a serious contender. Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run. But it is unclear whether Wenger would be prepared to give up his position as Fifa's global head of football development for a fight against his boss that he may not win. Hewitt accepted Uefa - and Infantino's other opponents around the world - must find someone to put their name on the ballot before the deadline of 18 November. She also indicated it would be important for the president to have a rival after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023. "I think it's important to Gianni to have somebody who stands with a different manifesto, and good for Fifa to have that choice," Hewitt added. "We're in a democracy here. We must remember there are 211 associations and it's really important that all 211 associations have the opportunity to vote according to how they feel. "This is somebody first and foremost who puts football first right at the heart of everything that they do. Secondly, it has to be somebody who unites the world. Thirdly, somebody who needs to have the courage to bring about reforms." Hewitt said Balogun avoiding a suspension after being sent off at the World Cup was one of the "biggest issues". Balogun's ban was suspended after US President Donald Trump asked for the decision to be reviewed. BBC Sport understands a proposal was put to the Council to amend the Fifa disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat. Under that, regulations would be amended to state the disciplinary committee could not suspend an automatic one-match ban for a red card. "What happened in July did not serve football... whether it's the Balogun case, the FFE case... the reputation of football was put under serious threat," said Hewitt. "Once behaviour starts to influence what happens on the pitch, then I think it's a dark day for football and a number of people said that in the room." The Fifa Peace Prize - awarded to President Trump - was also raised, but Hewitt said Infantino's behaviour with "other maybe celebrities and dignitaries" was also discussed. title: Arrests made after couple and two children killed in arson attack in Waterford
description: Gardaí (Irish police) have arrested a man and a woman in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members.
body: Four family members died in the suspected arson attack in Waterford Gardaí (Irish police) have arrested a man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in Waterford. They are currently being held in a station in the east of the Republic of Ireland. Kim English, Philip English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire on Tuesday. Two other children who were also in the house at the time remain in a critical condition in hospital in Crumlin in Dublin. Post mortems on the four deceased family members have been carried out but their results are not being released for "operational reasons". Officers have also appealed for anybody with information on the "murderous attack" to come forward and have also appealed for dash cam footage. title: GTA 6 - all you need to know about Rockstar's blockbuster game
description: A new launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto VI reveals more details about what's set to be the biggest game of the year.
body: GTA 6 will feature Jason and Lucia as playable characters Rockstar has released a new launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto VI, revealing more details about what is set to be the biggest game of the year. GTA 6 became available to pre-order at midnight on 25 June in the UK and elsewhere around the world, after Rockstar revealed the game's pre-sales launch date and cover art in mid-June. Analysts believe Rockstar's action adventure could become the most expensive game ever made, with estimates, external putting development costs at more than $1bn (£866m). Here's what we do and don't know about GTA 6 so far. The new launch trailer, external again confirmed GTA 6 will be released on 19 November. Suggesting no further delays to its release, the video gave fans a glimpse into the missions that protagonists Jason and Lucia will take part in. It also featured a new song from French electronic music artists Justice, who were revealed to be the game's original score composers. The game has been previously delayed twice, from autumn 2025 and May 2026. In a statement when the second delay was announced, Rockstar said it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve". Rockstar said players who pre-order will be able to begin pre-loading it on their consoles on 12 November to ensure they are able to play at launch. The sixth game in the main series will be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S. There's no news on when a PC version will be released - it's also currently unknown whether it will come to Nintendo Switch 2. The game will cost £69.99 in the UK and $79.99 in the US - with an ultimate edition, featuring extra vehicles and weapons, priced at £89.99 and $99.99, respectively. Physical copies of the game will contain a code for a digital download for the game inside a box, rather than a disc. Rockstar has not yet confirmed whether an updated online mode will be released as soon as GTA 6 launches. The game's PlayStation Store listing currently states "Grand Theft Auto VI is a single-player experience" - implying there will be no online mode at launch. But given GTA Online's success, external, it will likely exist at some point. How any future age verification legislation in the UK around social media and particularly messaging in gaming could therefore affect it, if at all, is still unknown. GTA 6 will cost $80 - and physical edition will not contain a disc What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview GTA 6 will feature its first ever playable female protagonist in a 3D setting - Lucia - alongside her partner in life and crime, Jason, as a second playable character. From what we've seen in two gameplay trailers and Netflix's extended look, the story will follow the pair in a Bonnie and Clyde-esque adventure through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong, external". Like other GTA games before it, the sixth chapter is set in a fictional US state - this time in Leonida, which is Rockstar's version of Florida. Fans of previous games will be excited to hear that Vice City, which is inspired by Miami, will return, featuring as the main city within the state. GTA 6's cover art revealed by Rockstar on 18 June made several nods to the setting with alligators and flamingos. GTA 6's cover art features the game's protagonists Lucia and Jason Rockstar Games breaks silence on Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks It's no secret that GTA 6 has been a few years in the making. The franchise's last instalment, GTA 5, was released in September 2013 - and quickly became one of the best-selling games of all time. It's unclear whether Rockstar has been working on the sixth instalment for all of that time, however, as in 2018 it also released another huge sequel - Red Dead Redemption 2. Rockstar confirmed for the first time that it was working on a sixth game in the series in February 2022. The rising cost of development and immense pressure to live up to the series' hype are all contributing factors as to why gamers have had to wait so long for the game's release. Several months later, footage and images leaked after teenage hackers targeted the company. It has also seen some issues since, including accusations of "union-busting" by sacked workers at Rockstar North, its Edinburgh HQ, where developers have been racing to get GTA 6 ready for release in November. Grand Theft Auto boss denies trying to keep tabs on union membership To put it simply, the GTA franchise is one of the biggest and most profitable entertainment properties in history. GTA 5 has sold nearly 230 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of all time - which has generated billions of dollars in revenue for Rockstar. The game's sandbox gameplay, where players can explore vast open worlds with considerable freedom - sometimes controversially - has seen it be continuously lauded as the ultimate expression for what the interactive medium can do. Freelance video games journalist Vic Hood said each entry in the series "continued to push technical and gameplay boundaries", with GTA Online helping to "pioneer the live service model as we know it". She added that the games were also "extremely culturally relevant" too. "Rockstar has always had its finger on the pulse of music, entertainment, societal, political, celebrity, and online culture trends, and they've never shied away from satirising these things in GTA games," she said. British gaming entrepreneur Sir Ian Livingstone told the BBC's Today programme that the series, originally developed in Scotland, was "bigger than any film or song" and an "incredible achievement in interactive software". Speculation as to how a sixth game can top even the gigantic heights of its predecessor has meant that any latest news, no matter how small, has been met with a flurry of hype and excitement. title: Sheep are disappearing from our hills - and our dinner plates
description: Have we have passed "peak sheep" in the UK?
body: Sheep are disappearing from our hills - and our dinner plates Listen to NJ read this article For four generations, Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm, perched on the hillside of Malhamdale amid the dramatic landscape of the Yorkshire Dales. And for most of that time, sheep were the mainstay of the business. But, Neil says, over the past 20 years there has been "a complete turnaround" and he has shifted away from sheep farming to stay afloat. In that time the 1,500-acre farm has gone from a peak of over 800 lambing sheep to just 45 this spring. "I dread to think where the farm would have been financially had we not started to make those changes," he tells me. "I either continued along the sheep-farming route because of sentimentality or made bold decisions." While most upland farmers still keep sheep on their land, the changes here have been mirrored across not just the Dales but the entire British farming industry. The shepherd's life has never been an easy one, but for many it's getting tougher and more difficult than ever to make a profit. Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm for four generations The average British farmer is 60 years old, according to the National Farmers' Union (NFU), and prices for everything from fuel to fodder have risen hugely for them in recent years. Meanwhile, many farmers are facing significantly reduced income from subsidies and there are worries that recent trade deals will mean increased competition from overseas. The UK's recent trade deals with New Zealand and Australia, struck since Brexit, eliminate tariffs and give producers in both countries large quotas on the amount of lamb they can export into the UK. There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK - the lowest figure in living memory according to Phil Stocker, chief executive of the National Sheep Association. Overall the national flock is also falling, down to 30.4 million sheep in 2025 - numbers last seen in the mid-20th Century, when the UK population was smaller and thus the potential market for lamb and mutton reared here was much lower. And over the last 50 years there has been a significant fall in lamb and mutton consumption according to Becky Smith, a senior analyst at the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), which represents farmers. In 1980 the average UK household purchased 128g of sheep meat (lamb and mutton) per person, per week. In 2024 that same measure was down to 23g per person, per week. Sheep farming has shaped the image many of us have when we picture somewhere like the Dales with drystone walls to keep livestock enclosed and green, rolling hills kept short by seasonal grazing. But any desire to protect the heritage of one of the UK's oldest agricultural industries is rubbing up against not just a diminishing appetite for sheep meat but also the question of whether some of our uplands might be better used to promote nature recovery and biodiversity. All this raises the question of whether we have passed "peak sheep" in the UK - and, in turn, what that might mean for consumers. Will my children still be eating our lamb for their Sunday roast or in their baltis and bhunas in 25 years time? And, what will happen to some of our most revered and beloved landscapes like the Lake District, Yorkshire Dales, Scottish Highlands and Welsh mountains, and the people who live and work there? At Craven Cattle Mart on the outskirts of Skipton, North Yorkshire, the auction ring is buzzing as farmers from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors come to buy and sell livestock. To an outsider, business might look brisk - but general manager Jeremy Eaton says it's nowhere near as busy as when he started in the industry 47 years ago. "We'd have some sales at this market where we'd regularly be selling 19,000 store lambs," he says. "Now we're fortunate if we get to 8,000 or 9,000." At Craven Cattle Marts, farmers come from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors to buy and sell livestock People who work sheep know that it's some of the hardest farming there is. A former shepherd once told me that sheep are only ever trying to do one of three things: "Escape, or die, or escape and then immediately die." Globally, lamb consumption is expected to grow by 15% between now and 2032, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the Food and Agriculture Organization. But changing tastes in the UK mean mutton, made from mature sheep, is no longer eaten in the same volume it was by previous generations and lamb has seemingly gone from a weekly staple to a meat more often eaten on special occasions, with "white meat" like chicken being increasingly chosen over lamb and beef. The drop in the national flock has actually led to robust growth in the price paid for lamb according to Becky Smith from the AHDB, with the sheep price hitting record highs in 2024. But despite the higher price for their sheep, upland farmers with tight margins feel the pinch more than many when diesel and oil costs go up. And on top of that, the cost of feeding sheep has also rocketed - the average cost of a bale of hay is £155 a tonne this spring compared to £75 a tonne this time last year. There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK, according to the National Sheep Association Farmers and groups such as Compassion in World Farming have also raised concerns that new trade deals could undermine UK agriculture because farms here must meet high welfare standards that may not be not required in several partner countries. Extremely tight margins mean growing numbers of younger people can't see a future in farming. This is immediately apparent as you wander around Craven Cattle Marts. title: 'Bring it on': Flynn challenges Burnham on independence referendum
description: The SNP's Stephen Flynn tells his party's conference independence supporters are "winning the argument".
body: Stephen Flynn insists independence supporters are "winning the argument" SNP minister Stephen Flynn has called on the prime minister to "bring it on" and let the people of Scotland decide the country's future in an independence referendum. Flynn, the party's former Westminster leader and now transport secretary at Holyrood, said the independence movement was facing its greatest-ever challenge. But he insisted "we are winning the argument" and told delegates at the SNP conference in Aberdeen that "all of us should feel pride in how far our movement has come". It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed. The PM later moved to clarify his position by telling First Minister John Swinney a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits". Flynn told SNP members on the opening day of the conference that the party's focus was firmly on independence, with a major new campaign being announced. He said: "Look at where we stand now – three nations of the UK whose leaders are committed to constitutional change, a British prime minister telling us we can have our independence when the people of Scotland want it. "All of us should feel pride in how far our movement has come." He added: "We are winning the argument, we can see that by reading the newspapers or listening to the panic of unionist politicians." Burnham previously told Swinney that an independence referendum remains "off limits" But Flynn warned there was "no shortcut" to achieving independence. "One by one, we must persuade our families, our friends, our neighbours, of our cause. One by one, step by step," he said. "It takes effort, it takes patient persuasion, it takes hard graft, but we can see that it is working and it is precisely because it is working that the period ahead will be the greatest challenge our movement has ever faced. "With the weight of Scottish public opinion moving to our cause, we will see that final lap through together – for Scotland." Swinney will bring the SNP's three-day conference to a close with a keynote speech to delegates on Saturday. He is expected to promote his renewed push for independence, having said he wants to hold a second independence referendum by 2031. The Supreme Court has ruled that the Scottish government is unable to do so without the consent of Westminster. What does Andy Burnham have up his sleeve as he crashes SNP conference? title: Burnham asks for 'manual trawl' of records for former Man City links
description: The PM has faced fresh questions about hospitality dinners since the club was found guilty of Premier League rule breaches.
body: Andy Burnham has faced calls for transparency since his comments about Man City's owners shocked many in the world of football Andy Burnham has said he has asked for a "manual trawl" of records relating to his previous contact with Manchester City football club. The prime minister said on Thursday he had asked the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to search "everything" to ensure "full transparency". He continues to face questions over any relations he had with Man City while mayor of Greater Manchester for almost a decade until June. The club has been found guilty of "systematically" breaking Premier League rules. Declarations of Burnham's contact with the club were released on Monday, but confusion grew later when it emerged records of two dinners Burnham had with Man City's chairman had been deleted. Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday, Burnham said of the GMCA: "I've asked them to do a more manual trawl of everything, as I want everything possible to be out there." He insisted that the occasions he dined with Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches at the Etihad in 2017 and 2018 were "included" in a statement issued by the local authority on Monday. It comes after he was accused by his political opponents of seeking to cover up the meetings. The GMCA statement, external mentioned a meeting Burnham had "informally" with Al Mubarak in the stands at a 2019 match, and a formal meeting the pair held at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit in October 2021, but did not specify the two dinners. It went on: "In his capacity as Mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City FC at home matches on a small number of occasions [...]." As mayor, Burnham previously declared the dinners from Man City, valued at a combined total of £1,000 for hospitality. Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) chats to Andy Burnham in 2019 at the Etihad Stadium, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester But records of them have since been deleted from the GMCA website. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term - but the authority has not clarified why the register dates back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024. It also remains unclear what, if anything of significance, was discussed at the two dinners. The BBC has asked the GMCA if it has received a request for a "manual trawl" and what this will entail. Burnham has faced pressure since comments in a BBC interview in September, saying he would be "really concerned" if Man City's owners now sold the club, following an independent commission finding the club guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch told him at Prime Minister's Questions this week that the issue was not "going away". The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period to 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into football operations. The findings have outraged many and left the top flight of English football in limbo with its top team facing potential sanctions. Man City continues to deny any wrongdoing and has lodged an appeal. title: GB win two golds at Track World Championships
description: Great Britain claim gold in the women's team pursuit and the men's scratch race at the World Track Cycling Championships.
body: This video can not be played Gold for GB women in team pursuit Great Britain secured gold medals in the women's team pursuit final and the men's scratch race on day two of the World Track Cycling Championships. Erin Boothman, Anna Morris, Josie Knight and Millie Couzens overturned an early deficit in the team pursuit final to beat world champions Italy by more than five seconds. In the scratch race, Matthew Bostock made his move for glory at the halfway point and held on to the lead to take his first world title in Shanghai, China. Henry Hobbs, Noah Hobbs, Ethan Vernon and Ollie Wood also won bronze for GB in the men's team pursuit, defeating France in the bronze medal ride-off. Bostock, 29, also earned a bronze for riding in the earlier rounds of the team pursuit. Denmark beat Italy in the gold medal race - their fourth consecutive title in the event. GB men 'on back foot' as women take silver Meanwhile, Sophie Capewell - who won silver in the women's team sprint with GB team-mates Rhianna Parris-Smith and Emma Finucane on day one - advanced to the semi-finals of the women's sprint. Capewell, 28, took two victories against China's Jiang Yulu in the best-of-three quarter-final, and will be joined Finucane, who won the sprint title in 2023 and 2024, in the last four. GB's preparations for the championships have been overshadowed by Matt Richardson's withdrawal from the squad amid reports he is under investigation for misconduct. British Cycling confirmed the 27-year-old Olympic medallist's removal in a statement but did not give a reason. Richardson, who had been expected to contend for medals in the individual sprint and keirin, said he would co-operate with a British Cycling investigation into the allegations. title: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant
description: The 51-year-old faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
body: Warning - this report contains graphic content A woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel has said she was left feeling "dirty" and afraid she may be pregnant in the aftermath of the alleged attack. The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. Video evidence played to the jury at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday showed one of his complainants tell the police: "He raped me basically and I know that happened." The jury heard one of Brand's accusers say she had met him in 1999, before he was famous. The woman was heard speaking in a police interview recorded in 2023, when reporting the alleged crime. She said she had attended the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth and went to a fringe event where she said she spoke to Brand. She alleges he later raped her. The complainant said they had both gone back to a hotel room. She told the officer she thought Brand "was gay" when they met earlier and she didn't feel like he was "trying it on with her". During the video evidence, Russell Brand watched the tv screen attached to the dock - rarely taking his eyes away She said she had been in the bathroom, but when she came out "he had like briefs on - and I was like taken aback and shocked. He was prancing around". The complainant alleged Brand told her: "Don't worry, that's how I am". She recalled thinking "what on earth have I got into" when, she claims, a shirtless Brand made her take photos of him before the alleged attack. She told the officer: "I'm reporting that Russell Brand did rape me. "What I'm going to say now - then, I second guessed myself if it was rape because it was so normal. "Sorry... he raped me basically - I know that happened. I remember him touching my breasts a lot - while kissing my neck." The woman recounted how Brand acted "like Basil Fawlty when he does his goose steps" before the alleged rape. She told the officer: "I remember him being like an ostrich - like a bird because he was very leggy. "I wasn't laughing, I just remember him jumping up and down being silly." The woman said after Brand left the room she was "just sitting there crying and I felt stupid," adding: "In that moment in time I was just shocked." At one point in the police interview, she cried while saying "this was something dirty that had happened". She said she "thought it was my fault", adding that she was "having nightmares" about the possibility of being pregnant. Fame Under Fire: Russell Brand on Trial You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Fame Under Fire: Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts During the video evidence, Brand watched the TV screen attached to the dock - rarely taking his eyes away. He appeared to be listening attentively and hardly moved his position throughout. The complainant said she delayed coming forward because she was worried it would impact her professional life. "I was told if you come out with this, your career is done," she told the court. Russell Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual. The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks. Brand rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music. He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States. title: King Charles praises Welsh 'sense of belonging' as he opens Senedd
description: The monarch and Queen Camilla officially open the Senedd's seventh term on their visit to Cardiff.
body: The King said he was proud of his "special connection with Wales" King Charles III has praised Welsh people's "sense of belonging", as he and Queen Camilla officially opened the Senedd's seventh term. The visit marked the King's first official meeting with First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth following the election victory of Plaid Cymru - a party rooted in a strong republican tradition. In his speech to the Senedd, with most of its 96 members in attendance including opposition parties Reform, Labour and the Tories, the King also expressed concern for the impact of climate change on the Welsh countryside. About 30 protesters by the steps of the Senedd were vocal throughout the royal visit, and one was arrested on suspicion of breaching the Public Order Act. Chants of "not my King" and "down, down, down with the crown" could be heard from protesters during the visit. Wales' national poet did not take part in the ceremony as had been planned, after Senedd officials rejected the poem she had written for the event and cancelled her performance. The King used his visit to the Senedd to say he would return to Wales next week to visit Aberfan, scene of the 1966 coal tip disaster, and met a survivor who had been pulled from the rubble aged six. A 21-gun salute in Cardiff Bay marked the King's arrival in the city, and Plaid leader ap Iorwerth greeted the King on the Senedd steps, together with the Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies and the Labour Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock, who represented the UK government. The King praised the "connection between place, people, culture and belonging" found in Wales Addressing the Senedd chamber, the King said he had "always felt immensely privileged and proud to have had such a special connection with Wales, with its language, its culture and its landscape for so much of my life". "The character and identity of Wales have always been built from the strength of its places, and the relationships of trust, service and neighbourliness found within them - that distinctively Welsh idea of connection, the profound connection between place, people, culture and belonging," he said. "As you take forward your task of government, we know you will bear always in mind, and draw inspiration from, those shared strengths, as you work on behalf of the people of this most special corner of the Earth." The King then expressed concern about the impact of climate change, following a number of wildfires this summer that blighted parts of Wales. He said: "No-one can have failed to have been struck by the way the very colours of our countryside changed during this summer's heatwaves. "Nor could they have failed to be deeply concerned at what this means for our rapidly changing planet. "I am sure we all share that most profound concern for the environment of this country entrusted to our care." It was the King's first official meeting with Rhun ap Iorwerth since he became Wales' first minister Ap Iorwerth said the ceremony marked a "new chapter" for national democracy and that it was a Senedd opening "unlike any that has gone before it". The Senedd expanded to 96 members for May's elections, which represented a "significant moment in the continued evolution of Welsh democracy," said the first minister. He said the parliament was "strengthened in its capacity to scrutinise" as a result of the change. Buckingham Palace said the King also held an audience with the first minister at the nearby Millennium Centre. Irranca-Davies said his message for new Senedd members, elected in May, was that the "institution is at its best when we recognise that disagreement need not mean division". "We will disagree, we should disagree, vigorous debate is part of a healthy democracy," he said. "But we should never lose sight of what brings every one of us here: a shared responsibility to serve the people of Wales," he added. Elizabeth II had opened every previous session of the Senedd before her death four years ago, her last one being 2021 when she had been joined by the current King and Queen. "I'm disappointed more than anything," Hanan Issa, the National Poet of Wales, told BBC Wales Briefings to the media before the event had said a poetry reading would be made by the National Poet of Wales, Hanan Issa, at the ceremony. On Wednesday, Issa posted to Instagram saying To Grow, the poem they submitted, was rejected on the grounds that the ceremony was "apolitical". Among other issues, the poem referred to Gaza and trans healthcare, and Issa said a second version that used "more abstract language" was also rejected. Issa said she had received a brief to "celebrate" Members of the Senedd (MSs) and their "achievements in being elected, while serving as a reminder of their commitment to the people of Wales". "I'm disappointed more than anything. This is the chamber where political discussion is had, and this very much says that political discussion framed as a poem is not welcome," Issa added. The Senedd commission said: "After a development process, we concluded that the poem was not the right fit for this occasion." It added: "We respect the National Poet of Wales' artistic independence and continue to admire and value their work." Aberfan disaster survivor Gareth Jones showed the King a photograph of his father meeting him and his sister on the day after the tragedy The King and Queen, along with the Prince of Wales, will return to south Wales next week to pay their respects at the Aberfan memorial garden exactly 60 years since the disaster. The incident saw a junior school and surrounding houses in the village engulfed in coal slurry after a colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966. Gareth Jones, now 67, said he had joined Thursday's ceremony in the Senedd to show the King a photograph of his father meeting him and his sister on the day after the tragedy. title: Charlotte Church to 'pause' wellness retreat and consider its future
description: The singer-songwriter bought the former home of Laura Ashley in 2021 and opened the retreat in 2023.
body: The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021 Charlotte Church will "pause" her wellness retreat from December to "germinate new dreams for the future", the star has shared. The Dreaming, based in Rhydoldog House near Rhayader, Powys, offered retreats aimed at helping people reconnect with nature and spirituality. The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021, with its renovation later featuring in a Discovery Channel documentary series. In a statement on social media, the team said the retreat had hosted more than 3,000 guests over the last five years, and wanted to "reassess" what it should offer in a changing world. They said: "Through the harvest season, it is important to discern what requires attention from that which is falling away, what needs to be put to compost. "We need the chance to compost, mulch, go fallow, listen deeply to the earth, so that we can germinate new dreams for the future." The statement said the world was "different" today from when the project began and that The Dreaming needed to consider what services it should offer. "As we stare clear-eyed at the exponentially complexifying crises that have been spreading out ahead of us all like cracking ice, we at The Dreaming need to reassess, with candour and courage, what it is we should be offering to be in service," it said. The team said it could not give a date for when the retreat might return, but added: "We cannot say when exactly we will be returning from the dream realm, but return we shall." Rhydoldog House was the former proerty of fashion designer Laura Ashley Church bought the £1.5m, seven-bedroom property in 2021. The house, with origins in the 15th Century, belonged to textile, fashion and retail entrepreneur Laura Ashley and her husband Bernard and owned by the family until his death in 2009. A planning application for the retreat in 2021 said Church wanted to transform Rhydoldog House into a carbon neutral wellbeing and healing retreat with four log cabins in the grounds as tourist accommodation. title: Kartal wins again as impressive comeback continues
description: Britain's Sonay Kartal beats former Wimbledon finalist Jasmine Paolini in straight sets to reach the Wuhan Open quarter-finals.
body: Sonay Kartal is playing in only her third tournament since a six-month injury absence Britain's Sonay Kartal continued her impressive comeback from long-term injury with a comfortable win over former Wimbledon finalist Jasmine Paolini to reach the Wuhan Open quarter-finals. Kartal, 24, missed more than six months with a stress fracture in her back, but has won five of her seven matches since returning to action. The former world number 44 ruthlessly brushed aside Italian 15th seed Paolini 6-2 6-0 with a performance that further validated Kartal's patient approach to recovering from the first serious injury of her career. It was another statement performance from Karta following her straight-set win over ninth seed Belinda Bencic in the previous round. "Against someone as good as Jasmine is, I knew I had to be solid from the start and not let up," Kartal said. "From my side, it was a pretty flawless performance." This video can not be played Sonny Kartal reflects on Wuhan Open round of 16 win Kartal was riding the crest of a wave in the early part of the season, having broken into the world's top 50, reached two WTA quarter-finals and recorded wins over top-class opponents. Victories over 2025 Australian Open champion Madison Keys and former world number eight Emma Navarro in Indian Wells led to a meeting with now world number one Elena Rybakina in the fourth round. However, Kartal was forced to retire with a back injury that proved more serious than first thought. After initially hoping she would make a quick recovery, Kartal was left unable to brush her teeth without "being in agony", leading to some difficult decisions. Missing Wimbledon was a particularly tough choice, especially given she reached the fourth round of her home Grand Slam in 2025, but resigning herself to not rushing a comeback has proved wise. Her first match back a little over three weeks ago - representing Great Britain at the BJK Cup - ended in a narrow defeat, before she won two matches to reach the Beijing third round in her WTA Tour return. "At the BJK Cup, the level I produced was much higher than I thought and I left super happy," Kartal said. "Now I'm growing in confidence with every match I'm playing." Paolini, who reached the French Open and Wimbledon finals in 2024, became the second former top-five player to lose a set 6-0 to Kartal this week Using a protected injury ranking to play, Kartal carried that momentum into Wuhan. She has not dropped a set in victories over Ukrainian world number 48 Anhelina Kalinina, 2020 Olympic champion Bencic and two-time major singles finalist Paolini. Kartal maintained a high level from the baseline as Paolini unravelled with a series of unforced errors, securing a meeting with Ukraine's Elina Svitolina in the quarter-finals on Friday. Meanwhile, Alexander Zverev continued to show why he is the best men's player in the world this season with a dominant 6-4 6-4 win over Australia's world number nine Alex de Minaur in the Shanghai Masters quarter-finals. Zverev, now assured of finishing the season as the year-end ATP number one, will face Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina in the semi-finals. title: Everton's Thierno Barry on the emotional video he was scared to post
description: The Everton striker explains why he chose to post an emotional video from a training session.
body: Everton player Thierno Barry says it took him three weeks to post a video that showed him breaking down in tears Head in hands, tears flowing. It's not a sight you often, if ever, see from a top-flight footballer. Keeping calm under pressure comes with the job description, but there's a sense it's what's expected from fans and team-mates. So when Everton striker Thierno Barry posted a video last month, external of him breaking down during a private training session, it sparked conversation around showing emotion in an industry where revealing any sort of vulnerability can be a risk. BBC Newsbeat met the French footballer at the club's training ground to find out why he chose to show the raw moment - and how he's using it to drive forward. "I was really scared about posting that. "And I said: 'No, I just need to show myself'," says Barry of the video released on his YouTube channel last month. "Last season I showed a version of me [that wasn't] me and [people] need to learn about me." In the video, the 23-year-old is seen getting frustrated and upset about his performance. He then leaves the private training session, where he begins to cry, as his team works to reassure him. The next day, Barry is seen reflecting on how it felt positive to let go. "Sometimes it feels good to just lose it," he says to the camera. Barry reveals he sat on the video for three weeks before choosing to release it. This video can not be played 'I was scared to post' - Barry on viral crying clip "It's the first time I cried in front of my friends, they always see me as a strong [person]," he says. "I'm happy that I can show that moment. They know I care about the club and I care about playing good on the pitch." A Premier League move from Villarreal for £27m at the age of 22 was always going to be a jump for the Lyon-born player - and fans expect a lot from new signings. Everton ended up re-posting the clip from his vlog on their own feed, external, with the caption "emotional resilience". Comments streamed in underneath urging the player to keep his head up. He acknowledges the support he has received from fans and his club. "The people around me helped a lot because, like I said, I'm really hard with myself and the people with me try to help me to be more positive." And for Barry, any disapproval wouldn't reach the levels of his own inner-critic. "I'm always harder with myself, and I just need to be sometimes more calm," he says. "Like, you're a crying guy, and I just want to show that I'm strong to show that, because I'm not scared to show that. "That's why I posted this video." He also spoke about the early days of adjusting to a new club and home, something he describes as "really difficult". "It's hard because it's the hardest league in the world. New league, a new language." This video can not be played 'It's difficult for my family' - Barry talks about impact of online criticism Last season he made 41 appearances and scored just eight goals. This season he's already scored six. "People can say I miss a lot of chances, but I also create a lot of chances," he says in his defence. But he also knows the cost of not capitalising on chances. "Every fan counts on you to score goals, so imagine you didn't score, you know, for three months like me [last season] it's difficult." And he won't fully relax. After Barry scored against Hull last weekend, he posted on his Instagram that he was "still learning". "This season is more easy to switch because I know I have time on the pitch," he says. "And I think when I miss that chance, seven minutes later, I have another opportunity to score. That's a real pressure. "When I come to the ball, in my head, it's like time stops." Barry is also finding time to celebrate on the pitch, even rolling back the years by bringing back the dab and hip-swinging celebrations. As for his second year with the club, the 6ft 5in player says he wants to keep focus. Does he see a call up to the French team any time soon? "I didn't think a lot about that because for me it's like really far, you know? "I just do my job, if something happens, something happens." title: BBC News channel launches on YouTube for viewers in UK and US
description: The move forms part of the BBC's wider strategy to reach digitally-native new and younger audiences.
body: The channel went live on YouTube on Thursday (BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri pictured) The BBC News channel has been made available to stream live on YouTube for viewers in the UK and USA. The trial, which began on Thursday, external, has been described by BBC bosses as "a significant step" in expanding access to "trusted, impartial journalism in more places people use every day". The move is an expansion of what the BBC has already done in other countries, with the news channel also available to YouTube viewers in Australia, Kenya, Nigeria, and Poland. Broadening access to the service forms part of the BBC's wider strategy to reach digitally-native new and younger audiences. The channel offers rolling coverage of international and domestic news, as well as breaking news and the latest developments in the worlds of politics, business, technology, culture and sport. The BBC's YouTube strategy is widely seen a response to the increasing fragmentation of audiences. The guarantees that viewers sit down and turn on their favourite channel - whatever is on it - are long gone. Now, their TV sets take them into a world of infinite choice and the BBC (along with the UK's other public service broadcasters) knows it needs to go to where audiences are - as well as trying to entice them to its own platforms. Streaming giant YouTube is owned by Google Thursday's development is part of the specific drive by the BBC to take its trusted news to audiences who aren't tuning in to the news channel directly or via the iPlayer. BBC News's director of AI, innovation and growth, Anjali Kapoor, said in a statement that audiences "increasingly expect news to be available wherever they are, on the platforms they use throughout their day. "Launching the BBC News channel on YouTube in the UK and US is an important step in bringing our trusted journalism to even more people." She added: "It will make it easier for audiences to access live coverage of the stories shaping our world, while helping us reach new audiences in the places and at the times that work best for them." The move is all part of the fight to combat the disinformation taking hold across social media and beyond. But it also won't hurt in the continuing negotiations over the BBC's charter and its future funding after 2027. This is another signal to the government that the BBC takes its mission seriously; that it is the place for trusted, impartial news and that it understands it must make that news available as widely as possible. However, viewers in the UK, watching the channel live on YouTube, may not realise they still need a TV licence to do that. But with no guardrails around who's watching, no ability - for now anyway - for the BBC to insist you prove you've paid the fee before you can access its YouTube channels (or its own streaming channels), it's going to be hard to enforce. Director of BBC News and Current Affairs Rachel Jupp began her new role this week First launched on UK TV in 1997 under the name BBC News 24, the service became the BBC News Channel in 2008. In 2023, it merged with BBC World News into one channel called BBC News, which is also available via the broadcaster's iPlayer, website and app. Last year, broadcast regulator Ofcom revealed in its annual report that YouTube had become the UK's second most-watched media service, behind only the BBC. One in five young viewers were going to the video sharing platform first when they turn on their smart TVs, the country's media watchdog found, while older people were also watching more of its content. Earlier this year, the BBC announced a landmark deal with YouTube, which will see the corporation make content that is tailor-made for the video streaming service. The new programmes will feature adverts when viewed from outside the UK, generating extra funds for the corporation at a time when its future funding model is being debated. BBC director general Matt Brittin joined the BBC this year after nearly two decades working for leading tech company Google In July, the corporation's new director general described the traditional TV licence model as "a busted flush" and "no longer fit for purpose". Former Google executive Matt Brittin told MPs that the licence fee is "yesterday's model". He did not specify what he wants to replace it, but he and BBC chair Samir Shah suggested the government should reconsider a compulsory household levy, which it previously ruled out. The BBC receives most of its funding from the £180-a-year TV licence, but the number of households paying has declined in recent years, and the broadcaster is discussing reform of the system with the government. title: Watch: Harry and Meghan at first joint engagement since UK return
description: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are making several public appearances in Nottingham.
body: This video can not be played The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived in Nottingham to cheers from crowds in their first joint engagement since returning to the UK. Harry and Meghan were pictured arriving at the Community Recording Studio charity on Thursday. They are expected to visit two more locations in the East Midlands city during the visit. The decision to visit Nottingham bears some significance as it is the city where the couple - who are no longer working royals - made their first joint appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017. The BBC's Royal correspondent Noor Nanji reports from Nottingham. Watch: Harry and Meghan at first joint engagement since UK return. title: Hospital doctors to strike as pay dispute continues
description: The British Medical Association says hospital doctors in Northern Ireland plan to strike in November.
body: Doctors also took strike action in June Hospital doctors in Northern Ireland are to strike in November over pay. It comes after the Royal College of Nursing announced that it is also balloting its members on potential strike action. The doctors will stage two separate 24-hour strikes on 20 and 23 November. The British Medical Association (BMA) has warned doctors are prepared to escalate the strike action if progress is not made in addressing the pay issue, which they say has seen doctors' pay drop from upwards of 26% over the past 18 years due to below inflation pay awards. The Department of Health (DoH) has been approached for comment. Resident doctors will hold a full 24-hour strike starting at 07:00 BST on 20 November until 07:00 the following morning. Consultants and specialist, associate specialist and speciality grade (SAS) doctors will also take 24-hour action from 07:00 on 23 November until 07:00 the following morning. They will provide what is known as Christmas Day cover, which means that most routine and elective services will be cancelled but full emergency cover will remain in place. Resident doctors are fully qualified medical practitioners who are completing postgraduate clinical training in a hospital or general practice under the supervision of a senior doctor. SAS doctors are specialist doctors employed by health trusts. The three branches of hospital doctors also took strike action in June. Dr Clodagh Corrigan said "we need a credible offer from government" to avoid further industrial action The BMA said if Health Minister Robbie Butler was serious about transforming the health service and addressing the waiting list crisis he needed to value doctors by paying them fairly. Dr Clodagh Corrigan, chair of BMA's Northern Ireland SAS committee, said: "We have been clear to avoid further industrial action we need a credible offer from government that makes meaningful progress towards full pay restoration. "We met with the new health minister recently, hopeful that we could begin fresh discussions on agreeing a credible pay offer. Regrettably, this did not happen." She said the minister was unable to confirm if the minimum annual pay uplift for 2026/27, which has been paid to doctors elsewhere in the UK, would be paid "this side of Christmas, or indeed at all". "We were informed that the decision ultimately lay with the executive," she said. "Therefore, we have been left with no alternative but to announce more dates for industrial action and we are fully prepared to escalate action if no progress is made." Dr David Farren said "pay is central to recruitment and retention of doctors" Dr David Farren, chair of BMA's NI consultants committee, said pay was central to recruitment and retention of doctors and hindered the delivery of a sustainable and safe health service. "There is palpable anger among our members at continuing sub-inflationary, late pay awards while we work beyond capacity in under-supported services," he said. "This annual uncertainty over when we will receive our pay award reinforces the widespread feeling that we are not valued, and leads to doctors seeking better paid roles elsewhere." He said this impacted service delivery and it was "unacceptable that our government continues to let this happen". It comes after the Royal College of Nursing announced on Wednesday that it will ballot its members on industrial action and strike action over pay. The union said the move came after many months of inaction on the pay award. Earlier this year, the NHS pay review body recommended a 3.3% pay increase for staff across all pay bands. While nurses and healthcare workers in England and Wales have received their award, nursing staff in Northern Ireland have not. In a statement the DoH said the health minister was clear that the 2026/27 award should be implemented and pay parity with colleagues in NHS England restored as soon as possible. title: Man Utd a circus after Martinez comments - Keane
description: Lisandro Martinez's outburst shows Manchester United are in "chaos", says former captain Roy Keane.
body: Lisandro Martinez joined Manchester United from Ajax in 2022 Former captain Roy Keane says Manchester United are "like a circus" after defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy. Speaking after Tuesday's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, Martinez said he had expected more investment in the squad in the summer and "more from our technical director". In a social media post on Wednesday he said he had spoken out of "anger and frustration". The loss in Madrid stretched United's winless run to five games, and they have won just one of their opening six matches of the Premier League season. Keane, speaking on The Overlap, external podcast, said Martinez's statement reflected the overall state of the club. "There will be some fans saying it's great and some saying you're letting the team down, especially from a player who hasn't been at his best, when the team is struggling," he said. "I think as a reflection of the club, it's obviously chaos there, like a bit of a circus. "When you're going through a difficult spell like United are, the issue I have with certain players saying things is you always have to start with the man in the mirror before you start coming out with all these comments." Outburst came out of 'anger and frustration' - Martinez Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout Man Utd defender Martinez issues scathing attack on board Martinez, 28, is out of contract at the end of the season, though United have the option to extend his deal by another year. "I don't think it will be a big falling-out - because I think we have question marks over this dressing room anyway," Keane said. "I don't think there's enough characters - enough men in there - but I don't see him as a senior player at Manchester United. I see him as a centre-half who's making lots of mistakes." Former United defender Gary Neville compared the incident to comments made by Wayne Rooney when they were team-mates in 2010. Rooney pulled out of contract talks, saying he had not received "any of the assurances I was seeking about the future squad". Two days later he signed a five-year deal and later said staying was the best decision of his career. "I've got a problem with this from a player's perspective," said Neville. "That is a direct attack on the players you are playing with. "So if I were Harry Maguire or Bruno Fernandes, or any other senior player, I would be absolutely fuming with him because you're basically saying we shouldn't be here and we should be bringing more players in." United travel to Leeds United in the Premier League on Sunday. title: Watch: Swimmer's emotional TV plea for cancer research leads to meeting with PM
description: Scottish athlete, Archie Goodburn, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Andy Burnham after an appeal for more investment into brain cancer research.
body: This video can not be played Swimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures. The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making an emotional plea on BBC Breakfast for more investment to be put into brain cancer research. After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner. Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details. The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street. Emotional TV plea for cancer research leads to meeting with PM. title: Obama says drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
description: More than 12,000 people filled a major venue in the city to hear the former US president's take on the challenges the world is facing. .
body: Barack Obama warned that online platforms were stoking anger and fear in people Barack Obama has told an audience in Glasgow that hope is worth fighting for despite big challenges facing the modern world. The 44th president of the United States said online platforms had shifted in recent years to focus on content that stoked anger and fear, but he believes a drift to extremism is "not inevitable". The comments came as he addressed an OVO Hydro crowd of 12,150 people while in conversation with British journalist and author Sathnam Sanghera, part of three speaking dates in the UK. He reflected on his time in the White House and examined the political and social challenges facing the US and the wider world. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope But he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups. He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill". "It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said. "So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that." But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable". He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler. "We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'." "We have not chosen to do that." The former President was speaking at the OVO Hydro Obama, who was president until 2016, said there was a "critical balance" that must be struck between free speech and regulation. But the 65-year-old said that the world and its leaders are going to need to find mechanisms and new institutions to allow rigorous debate and disagreement while helping people sort out basic facts. He said: "If I had a blame pie for why politics is so polarised and why we're seeing a rise of populism in many places, it's because of that information that is going into our brains every day." Obama said this resulted in young people feeling discouraged, and that "it's not a healthy diet that our brains are on at the moment". He added that he feared this could become even worse with AI making it hard to distinguish between what is true and what is not, something he believes will make democracy hard to function. Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice. The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make. He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet." He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible. "I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said. Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted. "We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'." He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant. Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for. title: Police officer guilty of raping teenage girl and woman in Shetland
description: Carmichael John Williamson was found guilty following a trial at the High Court in Edinburgh.
body: A police officer has been found guilty of raping a teenage girl and a woman in Shetland. Carmichael John Williamson - known as John Williamson – was found to have engaged in sexual activity with a girl when she was under-age in 2014 and raped her between 2014 and 2015. Williamson, of Burra, also raped a second woman in 2020 and again in 2022 when she was intoxicated and unable to consent. The 32-year-old was remanded in custody after the jury delivered their verdict at the High Court in Edinburgh, with sentencing deferred until 8 December. Williamson, who had denied the offences, cried in the dock when the guilty verdict was read out. He was handcuffed and said "I love you" to his partner as he was led away. Judge John Morris KC described it as an "anxious and distressing" trial. Williamson was initially charged with nine offences, but five were dropped by the Crown before the closing speeches were delivered. title: Man killed by tiger climbed two fences before suffering multiple injuries, inquest hears
description: William Chapman climbed two fences to enter a tiger's pen at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, an inquest hears.
body: William Chapman was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at the weekend A man who was attacked by a tiger after climbing two fences to enter its enclosure at a wildlife park died of "multiple traumatic injuries", an inquest has heard. William Chapman visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and entered the animal's pen. The 24-year-old was pronounced dead at the scene and died of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction", the opening of his inquest at Doncaster Coroner's Court heard. Senior coroner Nicola Mundy said he had a history of mental illness, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had suffered previous bouts of psychosis. His family had raised concerns about his contact with Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS Trust, the hearing was told. Chapman was under adult mental health services in Doncaster but was "highly functioning and independent with no care requirements," the inquest heard. The self-employed online trader was born in Chichester, West Sussex, and living in Doncaster at the time of his death. Coroner's officer Caitlin Brookes said his family had expressed "a number of concerns" in relation to his contact with mental health services, with the trust launching an investigation following his death. On Wednesday, a trust spokesperson said it would "never comment on whether someone uses our services or does not use our services". The BBC approached the trust for further comment. An eyewitness took a photograph of the tiger at the wildlife park shortly before the incident Brookes told the hearing: "He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death." Park staff secured the tiger and paramedics attended but confirmed his death at the scene. The senior coroner said her office was awaiting a more substantial report as to the extent of his injuries. Mundy opened the inquest, which his family chose not to attend, on Thursday morning and adjourned proceedings until 18 March 2027. The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation of the wildlife park. An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in. Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass. The park remains closed and a reopening date is yet to be confirmed. A park spokesperson previously said the rare Amur tiger involved, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. A health and safety investigation has also been launched by City of Doncaster Council. South Yorkshire Police had provided a number of witness statements from the public and staff who were at the wildlife park at the time, the hearing was told. Mundy instructed staff to contact Yorkshire Wildlife Park to ask them to keep any relevant CCTV and inform the coroner of any previous visits by Chapman to the park. title: Poet says being dropped from Senedd royal visit over poem is 'concerning'
description: Hanan Issa's poem To Grow, referring to Gaza and trans healthcare, was rejected from the ceremony.
body: The National Poet of Wales, Hanan Issa, says she is "concerned" by the decision Wales' national poet has said it is "quite concerning" that a poem raising political issues was rejected from the Senedd's opening ceremony. Briefings to the media about the event said a poetry reading would be made by Hanan Issa at the ceremony on Thursday, which will be attended by King Charles III and Queen Camilla. But on Wednesday, Issa posted on social media that the poem she submitted, To Grow, which referred to Gaza and trans healthcare, was rejected on the grounds that the ceremony was "apolitical". The Senedd Commission said the poem, that Issa had reworked and had already been translated into Welsh, was "not the right fit for this occasion". Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, Issa said she would not be attending the ceremony where King Charles and the Queen will officially open the Senedd's seventh term. The poet added: "I am not welcome anymore. I won't be part of the ceremony." The first minister will be among those greeting the King on the Senedd steps with the presiding officer Huw Irranca-Davies and the Labour Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock, who will represent the UK government. The King, pictured on a previous visit, will give a speech in the Senedd debating chamber, known as the Siambr Issa said the feedback received was that the poem had an "edge" and could "perhaps be softened." "That's what I thought I'd done and obviously, it wasn't enough," she said. Issa added it was "telling" that in the chamber where political issues are discussed "a poem that raises political issues is not welcome, that feels quite concerning". The Welsh-Iraqi poet, filmmaker, and artist said she was inspired by Welsh poet Saunders Lewis' imagery of Wales as a vineyard, and developed that around the brief's request. "The brief asked for something that celebrated members and their achievements, and something that served as a reminder of their commitment to the people of Wales. "I don't know about you, but celebrating the achievements of members when they are just about to be sworn in feels a bit premature." Instead, Issa decided to write something to remind the politicians of "their commitment". "I wrote something that described Wales as a garden, and our Assembly Members as its gardeners." Issa said that after submitting the first version she could have refused to make changes, but instead chose to compromise and try to find a halfway point. A second version used "more abstract language", Issa said, but it was also rejected. Based on the brief, Issa said it didn't sound like "they want a poem just about daffodils, and so it felt like a disservice to write something that was quite surface level". "We've just faced a summer of wildfires. We're going into a season, no doubt, of floods. The proposed data centres, people have lots of concerns about that. "There's so many things, and so it felt important for me to speak to those things." Quoting John Lennon, Issa said: "'A poet's role is to try to express how people are feeling' and it felt like an important moment to do that." Elizabeth II attended the last official opening in 2021, while Wales was still subject to Covid-19 restrictions The Senedd Commission said: "After a development process, we concluded that the poem was not the right fit for this occasion." It added: "We respect the National Poet of Wales' artistic independence and continue to admire and value their work." Also speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, Irranca-Davies described Issa as a "fantastic poet" and said it was "disappointing" for her not to have her poem there, but added it had been "deemed not appropriate for this occasion". He said: "I think the reason that's been made clear by the Senedd Commission is there's plenty of debate and political debate, not just in Wales, but within the Senedd day in, day out, week in, week out, and that's a really good thing, that robust debate on difficult issues." He said the ceremonial opening was not a day for political debate, but a chance to mark the start of the Senedd term. "It's the one day of the term when this official opening, when we come together to pause, mark the start of the Senedd, celebrate the communities of Wales, remind members of their service to the people of Wales that they serve, and there will be many fantastic performances here today as well," he added. Reform sources said they felt the commission made the correct call. My contraceptive coil saved my life after it revealed I had cancer Wales has an education crisis. Can it be fixed? title: Meghan makes first official public appearance since moving back to UK
description: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are taking part in a series of events linked to their charitable work in Nottingham.
body: The Duchess of Sussex has made her first official public appearance since moving back to the UK, telling well-wishers "it's great to be back". Meghan arrived at a youth charity in Nottingham alongside her husband, the Duke of Sussex, on Thursday morning. The pair, who are also expected to visit a food bank later, hugged and posed for selfies with the public. The duchess spoke to a number of people in the crowd, telling one "we got lucky" as they chatted about the weather. She has shared glimpses of her life back in the UK on social media, but this is the first time she has attended any public events since the family returned from California. Meghan clutches some flowers and some friendship bracelets she was handed A spokesperson for Harry and Meghan said Nottingham is "a special place" for them both, as it is where they made their first joint appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017. The pair are attending these events not as working royals, but as public figures and supporters of the projects they're visiting. The Royal Household has made it clear they view them as private citizens. Despite that, Thursday’s schedule has a distinctly royal feel to it. The first stop on their visit to Nottingham is the Community Recording Studio, a charity which Prince Harry has been supporting since 2013. Its CEO Trevor Rose told the BBC they only found out about the trip a few weeks ago, and could not believe it. "It's exciting times. Completely random, phoned, mentioned a idea, said they'd like to come down," he said. The duchess joins in with a friendship bracelet making session in the centre "I thought it was going to be something in the future, next thing I know it's two weeks later and we are here, so yeah it's a complete shock." A group of fans had built up steadily throughout the morning, some carrying flowers whilst one child has a unicorn balloon. Later in the day, the pair are expected to visit Himmah Hub, a local charity tackling food poverty, where they will observe cooking classes taking place and help to prepare food parcels. Their third engagement is at Epic Partners, a group working to support young people through youth work, sport and mentoring. The couple have a private security team with them in Nottingham and local police teams are understood to be aware of their visit. Harry and Meghan's spokesperson told BBC News they were "really excited" to be back together in Nottingham, nine years since their last joint visit. The Duke and Duchess beam as they greet fans in Nottingham on Thursday "They are back here primarily because they support and believe in the organisations they are visiting. "They enjoy coming back to revisit projects they are personally invested in, to meet the same people and understand what is happening and how things are changing." In 2017, Harry and Meghan visited Nottingham's Lace Market before a visit to a World Aids Day charity fair. Pictures from that trip showed the couple smiling as they met enthusiastic crowds. The pair and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, returned to the UK in August after living in the US for six years. The royal couple shared a laugh as they take their seats inside the centre They have reportedly settled in the Cotswolds, and their children have moved schools after issues were raised by their security team about the school run. It also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK. It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is reconsidering Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors. The Sussexes will not be spending Christmas with the King at the traditional royal family gathering at Sandringham, Norfolk. BBC News understands that they are likely to spend it privately with Meghan's mother Doria Ragland.
