title: Crew in Lewis fishing boat tragedy named by police
description: The alarm was raised after the men's fishing boat failed to return as planned to Lewis on Tuesday.
body: Murdo Morrison, 23, along with his crew-mate Norman Murray remain missing A fisherman whose body was found after a boat went missing off the Western Isles on Tuesday has been named as Douglas Craigie. The 49-year-old's crew-mates, Norman Murray, who is 40 and known as Tam, and 23-year-old Murdo Morrison are still missing. The three men, who are all from Lewis, had been fishing in a boat called Kilda. The vessel went missing off Port of Ness in north Lewis. The search for the missing crew and boat was suspended on Wednesday night, before being resumed on Thursday. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said aircraft and coastguard teams were involved. Police Scotland said it was believed the fishermen had sailed from Brevaig in Lewis at about 07:30 on Tuesday before travelling to the Port of Ness area to fish. The Kilda was reported overdue at about 21:20 on Tuesday. Extensive searches were conducted on Wednesday despite bad weather, with gale-force winds. The body of Douglas Craigie was recovered in the Port of Ness area at about 02:45 on Wednesday. Ch Insp Ross McCartney, local area commander for the Western Isles, said: "Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragic incident. "The families of all three men involved are being provided with specialist support as our searches continue. We would ask that the privacy of the families of all three men are respected at this difficult time." He added: "We are working closely with the HM Coastguard and RNLI to search for the vessel and the two missing men "We know that the local community will be keen to help in any way they can. "However, conditions are very challenging and I would urge people not to put themselves at any risk. Please do not attempt to carry out searches in areas which put you at risk of harm. "Instead, if you believe you may have any information which could assist emergency services then please call 101 quoting reference 3575 of 13 October." McCartney said a police presence would remain in the Port of Ness area. This video can not be played Minute's silence was observed at the Royal National Mòd in Glasgow A spokesperson for the MCA said: "A range of search and rescue assets have been sent in response, including HM Coastguard helicopters and aeroplanes, coastguard rescue teams, lifeboats, and a nearby vessel. "The incident is currently ongoing." The search is taking place off Ness, a sparsely populated area on the northern tip of Lewis. It is an area of rugged coastline, with many of its roughly 1,300 people living in crofting townships - small holdings where families can raise livestock and grow crops while working other jobs. The parish has one of the highest concentrations of Gaelic speakers in the Western Isles. A minute's silence was held earlier at the Royal National Mòd, Scotland's annual celebration of Gaelic culture and language, which is taking place in Glasgow. Searches have been taking place off Port Of Ness, pictured on Wednesday On Wednesday, Kenneth Macleod, convener of local authority Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, told BBC Radio Scotland's Lunchtime Live programme: "It is a very dark day for the community of Ness and the community of Lewis in general. "Our thoughts and condolences are with the families affected. "We cannot comprehend what the families of the three fishermen are going through at the moment." In a message on X, First Minister John Swinney said: "This is deeply distressing news. "My heart goes out to the families of the three fishermen in Ness, and the communities on the Isle of Lewis." title: Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says
description: Russia reports a Ukrainian strike on an oil refinery on Thursday, after Ukraine's president says a pause is over following fresh Russian attacks.
body: Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support. The Ukrainian president said he had restricted such attacks for three days at Washington's behest, while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times. Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending the attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and said a slowdown of Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military was deliberate. The Kremlin said Ukraine had "attempted a large-scale attack" on an oil refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday. According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris had caused a fire at the site in Ryazan. Zelensky meanwhile said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day. He previously said he would agree to the so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it. But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it agreed to the deal. Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support. The Ukrainian leader told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence". Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet uplinks are used throughout its war effort. There were suggestions that the slowdown to Starlink services was due to a technical fault - something owner Elon Musk appeared to deny was the case, suggesting it was the Trump administration. Trump denied halting intelligence-sharing. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defence told the BBC early on Thursday that Starshield services - the military-focused version of Starlink - had been restored. They said officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances behind yesterday's restrictions". Zelensky has questioned Trump's relationship with Russia President, Vladimir Putin Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv. European leaders have also rallied around Zelensky, with the matter expected to dominate their summit in Brussels later on Thursday The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles. Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles. Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Russia's Vladimir Putin. He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week. "We didn't destroy any relationship." Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal. Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just. But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort. That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public. Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas." With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support were no coincidence. High-speed internet via Starlink satellites is used by the Ukrainian military to guide drones and communicate with the front line. Ukrainian officials have said they were not warned before a speed limit was imposed on the uplink. Its sister service Starshield is provided under a US Department of Defense (DoD) contract. Musk denied that his company SpaceX was responsible for restrictions on the system, suggesting the US government could be responsible for the slowdown. He wrote on Wednesday that the systems were owned and controlled by the US government and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [Trump]." The Trump administration has not commented on the issue. The BBC has approached the White House and the DoD for comment. title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
description: Residents have been told to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
body: Flooding in the Kucukcekmece district of Istanbul Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported. A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement. Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts. Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut Gül to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary. The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted. Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue. Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding. "I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X. He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time. The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said. A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks. More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces. In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave. title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
description: Lula's supporters hope the measure will boost his popularity ahead of a presidential run-off in 10 days.
body: The measure had broad support and trade unions held rallies in its favour in recent weeks Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary. The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988. Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election. Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off. The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round. Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it. The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one. Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote. Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers ‌want to ⁠see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it." The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters. Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment. Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers. "It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media. Parent groups were among those to back the change Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices. But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work. The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage. The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating. Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life. The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores. "My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil. "I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home." title: Historic cannons airlifted for restoration
description: Cannons are lifted from St Michael's Mount by helicopter so they can be taken away for restoration.
body: This video can not be played When 300-year-old cannons at St Michael's Mount in Cornwall needed to be restored, the Royal Navy stepped in. The cannons could only be taken off the island by helicopter, and a Merlin Mk2 helicopter from Atlantic Flight 814 Naval Air Squadron lifted each cannon individually off the island. The operation was planned by the crew based at the Royal Naval Air Station at RNAS Culdrose, near Helston, in Cornwall. Years of exposure to salt spray contributed to corrosion of the cannons - which will be treated at Dorothea Restorations in Bristol. Historic cannons airlifted for restoration. title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
description: The economy grew by 0.1% in August, defying analysts' expectations of a slight contraction.
body: This video can not be played Challenge now is to safeguard UK economy's resilience, says chancellor The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey. Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction. It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week. Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time. Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will". But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending". The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August. "It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said. The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain". Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply. The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted. Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period. But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period. August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%. Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought". He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs". PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance. "The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added. What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you? What is the Budget and what could be in it? Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register". He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents. The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations. Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks." The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget". Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing." He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate". "The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet." What would you like to see in the Budget? title: No money for new emergency department, says minister
description: Robbie Butler says a new ED at Altnagelvin hospital in Derry is a priority but he does not have the money to pay for it.
body: Robbie Butler visited Altnagelvin hospital in Derry on Wednesday A new emergency department (ED) at Altnagelvin hospital remains a priority project but there is currently no funding for it, Northern Ireland's health minister has said. Robbie Butler, who visited the Londonderry hospital on Wednesday, said a new ED would be "incredibly high on the project list if the money becomes available". A new ED is one of two Western Health and Social Care Trust priority capital projects and has an estimated cost of around £73m. Altnagelvin's emergency department - the oldest one operating around-the-clock in Northern Ireland - was designed to treat about 40,000 patients a year but is now dealing with up to twice that amount. The minister said the ongoing work by the trust had helped mitigate the waiting times at the ED but that these were still "much too long". "People living in this area will know that acutely," he said. "They're messaging me, they're emailing me, and I hear those messages. "But the senior leadership team of the Western Trust, like me, have an ambition to see that reset and transformed. "If the money became available, I would say the case has been well made." Altnagelvin has the oldest around-the-clock emergency department in Northern Ireland In July 2025, the trust submitted revised proposals for the new emergency department at Altnagelvin to the Department of Health. At that time, Butler's predecessor Mike Nesbitt told the Stormont Assembly that any progress would depend on the availability of both capital funding and the running costs. Meanwhile, Butler also told BBC News NI the Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant had fallen short in relation to what is being offered on the budget. The executive has not agreed a budget for this year, blaming the UK's devolution funding formula for leaving it short. Extra funding of about £1.5bn would be released in three tranches, with £525m available this year. Bryant has accused executive ministers of being financially "irresponsible". Butler said: "I don't agree with the Secretary of State on this because we are not funded at the agreed level of need." title: White House defends new press secretary after questions about her legal credentials
description: Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived.
body: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials. President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week. She has referred to herself as a lawyer. But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China." She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people". Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials." On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association. It is seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime". The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed. A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US. The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself. She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney. The new press secretary also told the paper that when she answered China to a question about her bar exam, it was a misunderstanding. She had mistakenly thought, above the din of Marine One, the reporter had asked: "Where were you after law school?" Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass. A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be. This video can not be played Watch: How did Katie Zacharia do at her first - very brief - White House briefing? She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there. Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13. In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles. In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China. The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment, as well as Zhong Lun Law Firm. It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work. Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile. title: What's going on between Kelly Clarkson and a Brooklyn store bird?
description: The Since U Been Gone singer claims she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" an item in the store.
body: This video can not be played A boutique store called Art of Play in Brooklyn has found itself at the centre of a social media storm, after Grammy winner Kelly Clarkson complained that they would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was on the wall. The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000). Art of Play has defended how it treated the star, saying the wooden bird is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000. title: Actor Imran Khan ordered to leave India after participating in protest
description: The Bollywood actor had been detained and released while participating in a protest in Mumbai on 10 October.
body: Imran Khan had been briefly detained by the police on 10 October while participating in a protest in Mumbai Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms. An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections. "Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday. Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court. Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting. But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest. The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic". Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na. He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992. Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly. The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade. Khan also shared a photo from inside the detention van on his Instagram page On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges. "Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement. The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India". Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest. "I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said. He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation. Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters. He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform. Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call. On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi. On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi. The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital. title: Indian woman and boyfriend get death sentence in 'blue drum' murder case
description: The body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum.
body: Sahil Shukla and Muskan Rastogi were found guilty of the murder on 30 September Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find distressing. A woman and her boyfriend have been sentenced to death for the murder of her husband in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. Muskan Rastogi, 26, and Sahil Shukla, 28, were convicted on 30 September by a court in Meerut city for the 2025 murder of her husband Saurabh Rajput. Rajput's body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum - leading to the case being dubbed as "the blue drum murder". Wednesday's death sentences have to be confirmed by the high court. Rastogi and Shukla have the option to challenge the verdict. The prosecution said in court that Rastogi and Shukla had been classmates in school and had grown close in the absence of Rajput who worked in London. When Rajput first came to know of their affair in 2021, he had wanted to get a divorce but was persuaded against this by his family since the couple had a young daughter. Rajput was murdered on 3 March 2025 when he was visiting Meerut. Police said he was given food laced with sedatives by Rastogi before he was killed. Rastogi and Shukla fled to Himachal Pradesh state but used Rajput's mobile phone to send text messages to his family to make it seem like he was alive and travelling for business, they added. A few days later, however, Rajput's family lodged a complaint with the police saying that he was missing. On 17 March, when Rastogi visited her parents after returning from Himachal Pradesh, her six-year-old daughter asked about her father. Rastogi initially blamed her in-laws for her husband's murder. Unconvinced, her parental family took her to the police station. Rastogi confessed to the crime during interrogation and she and Shukla were arrested and charged with the murder. "My brother was killed by cruel people," Rajput's brother told BBC Hindi. Rastogi's parents also demanded strict action against her. "My daughter, along with a friend, murdered her husband in her own home. She is not fit for this society and is a danger to others," her father told ANI news agency. Rastogi gave birth to a second child while in jail. title: Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency?
description: Senior figures in European football tell BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run as a surprise candidate against Gianni Infantino.
body: Arsene Wenger joined Fifa as chief of global football development in 2019 Despite the backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors, Fifa president Gianni Infantino looks increasingly likely to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next year. But could there be a sensational twist? Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run as a surprise candidate. But would the man who has been the governing body's head of global development since 2019 really challenge his own boss? And what lies behind the support he has? On Thursday the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since the emergence of Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme plunged the organisation into crisis, leading to calls from the game's leaders in Europe, North America and Asia for him to step down. A defiant Infantino will come face to face with some of his fiercest critics at what could be a spicy gathering in Zurich. Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development. But Infantino will also face scrutiny over governance reforms, FFE, the awarding of the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize last year to US President Donald Trump, and disciplinary procedures in the wake of the Folarin Balogun affair. But the meeting will also bring into sharp focus the failure so far to identify a unifying figure with the worldwide appeal to challenge Infantino. While potential rivals like Victor Montagliani, the president of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (Concacaf), and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders, Infantino has been busy touring the world, shoring up his position. The growing expectation is that such is the support he retains in his power base of Africa, South America and Oceania, he will be returned, despite only carrying the backing of roughly half of Fifa's 211 members. To date, the only person to declare their intention to run is the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although few rate his chances. So could Wenger be the answer? Here in Zurich, there is no indication that he is plotting a bid. On Wednesday evening Wenger joined Infantino and other Fifa Council members for dinner in a Zurich restaurant. As a senior member of Fifa's management team, he will also be present at Thursday's meeting. When BBC Sport asked about his intentions via Fifa, no comment was provided. Meanwhile, those close to the 76 year-old, who left Arsenal in 2018 after 22 years in which he became the most successful manager in the club's history, will not be drawn on whether he is interested. One told BBC Sport he would be "an ideal candidate, but he is his own man". A high-ranking Fifa official insisted he had no idea if Wenger was tempted. But what is clear is that he does have supporters, who believe he commands the level of respect beyond Europe that would be essential if the Uefa-led rebellion against Infantino is to have any chance of success. "He's a brilliant football man who truly understands football development because he's been running it," claimed one senior official at a European national association. "People don't see him as just a European. He's very respected in Asia, for instance, from his time working in Japan. A lot of people are saying he'd be the ideal candidate. With him, it's not about money, status or ego. He genuinely loves the game. "He's made a difficult role work and understands Fifa, and that's why he'd be a really good candidate. "That said, he's in a really difficult position." That was highlighted amid the fallout over FFE, when Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot. "I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said in a statement at the time. "The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity." Some may have expected Wenger to resign over the controversy, given his thinly veiled criticism of Infantino, the way he had been kept in the dark, and the condemnation of the plot from stakeholders across the game. But he has carried on in a role in which he oversees youth development at academies in 60 countries, as well as youth competitions around the world. He is also a technical adviser to rule-making body International Football Association Board (Ifab). Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups, and the idea of a 'daylight' offside law. But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding. Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent. Indeed, at the weekend Wenger was in Cape Verde at a Confederation of African Football conference, telling the delegates: "We want to see an African team win the World Cup, and the numbers show that it is feasible." Such sentiments would do him no harm if he was to stand for president. BBC Sport has been told that a large number of Fifa's staff also want Wenger to run, and believe he could change the organisation's image. Others, however, are more sceptical. One well-connected figure in Fifa circles told BBC Sport that he would be "amazed if Wenger would rise up against the man who appointed him in the first place. Arsene

title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
description: China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces.
body: The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours. China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme. The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them. Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty. Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties. The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region. The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges". Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea. A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC. "Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds. "China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually." Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong. This video can not be played Watch: Why did Xi Jinping visit North Korea? But the alliance is not without tension. Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan. China's attitude has shifted more recently. "Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC. Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war. At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops. Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day. So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties. Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month. Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. "The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. "But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing." title: The F1 pit stop that helped save lives
description: How an F1 pit stop inspired changes to hospital care that have helped save lives ever since.
body: A seven-second McLaren pit stop inspired a new approach to patient care that saved lives When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs. But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child. The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track. At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the GOSH medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers. Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit. Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process. As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time. How hospitals used inspiration from F1 for surgery-to-ICU handovers Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step. "And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up. "It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right." The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams. Fifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation. Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting. Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment. Gemma Fisher (left) and doctors from the University Hospital of Wales Standardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response. Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies. The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame. The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital. F1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine. At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half. This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team. David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured." Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further. Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response. title: Southgate does not see return to Premier League management
description: Former England manager Gareth Southgate says he does not see himself returning to club management in the Premier League.
body: Gareth Southgate's last game in charge of England was the final of Euro 2024, which they lost to Spain Former England manager Gareth Southgate says he does not see himself returning to club management in the Premier League. The 56-year-old has been out of management since resigning as Three Lions boss after guiding them to the final of Euro 2024, where they lost to Spain. Southgate, who also took England to the Euro 2020 final, has not managed at club level since a three-year spell with Middlesbrough from 2006. When asked if he would consider a return to managing in the Premier League, he told The Amol Rajan Connection podcast: "I don't see a scenario where I do that." He added: "Towards the end of my time with England, I stopped enjoying, at the very least for a period, the wins keep you going. "By the end, I didn't even enjoy the wins for any longer than a couple of minutes. So, I've hardly watched football. "I went to the FA Cup final to see my team, Crystal Palace, win their first trophy. I've not been to a football ground since. So my sort of desire to be involved in football has changed." Since leaving the England role, Southgate has also spent time working in the media and earlier this year he fronted a BBC documentary where he travelled across the UK to understand challenges facing young men and boys. He has also spent time as a visiting lecturer at Harvard Business School in Boston. "I've loved the last 18 months of my life," he added. "I've had 37 years where my sense of self depended on did I win or lose on Saturday. And actually I've loved having different experiences. I've met politicians, I've met people in the media industry, I have learned about leadership in all sorts of areas, I've travelled around the world learning things. "I've just enjoyed playing a different film in my life." Last month, Manchester City were found guilty of the majority of charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs". The club have denied any wrongdoing and submitted an appeal on 2 October. "There'll be the tribal fans' response to punish Manchester City as much as we can, relegate them, fine them, do whatever you can," added Southgate. "I've been in football boardrooms, I've been in meetings with Uefa, I've been in meetings with Fifa, I have been in all these spaces and I know how complicated all of this is. "My underlying thought is none of this is good for football and there are no winners because if you're at the Premier League, for a very brief moment you might feel justified that all the flak you've had for this case taking so long, this is why it's taken so long and there's the verdict, and I'm sure there's an element of justification in that. "Then there's this realisation of how do we deal with all of this because you know the possibility of all the different legal cases that emerge from this, how long this could still take, what's the right sort of punishment, how do you keep the whole game on track? title: 'Some think endometriosis is just a bad period, but it's so much worse'
description: Women with endometriosis are suffering financially as well as physically, a new report by MPs warns.
body: Megan Gomersall has been out of work for about two and a half years because of her symptoms Women with endometriosis are being forced out of work, losing income and facing significant financial hardship because of the condition, according to a new report by MPs. The inquiry by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Endometriosis, supported by Endometriosis UK, found 47% of women with the condition had lost income because of their symptoms, while 28% had left a job altogether. Among them was Chloe Ward, from Bolton, who said her endometriosis - which can cause severe pain, fatigue, heavy bleeding and fertility problems - had cost her thousands of pounds and affected her ability to run her own business. She said: "A lot of people think it's just a bad period, but it's so much worse." Chloe Ward says years of treatment, surgery and time off work have left her paying a heavy financial price for endometriosis About one in 10 women suffer from the condition, but diagnosis can be a lengthy process. Chloe said it took seven years for her to be diagnosed. She said being self-employed in the beauty industry meant she had flexibility, but no financial safety net. "If I'm not there to do the treatments, nobody pays me," she said. She told BBC Radio Manchester she had lost clients over the years because flare-ups could leave her unable to work at short notice. Chloe is now waiting for a hysterectomy, which will mean more time away from work. "There's so much to it that people don't understand," she said. The financial impact has extended beyond lost earnings. After receiving a stage-four endometriosis diagnosis in 2023, she paid about £6,000 for private surgery because NHS waiting times were too long. She and her partner also spent about £8,000 on a third round of IVF after two NHS-funded attempts failed. The report found 39% of women with endometriosis had experienced financial hardship because of the condition, while 40% said they had turned down career opportunities due to a lack of workplace support. Endo the Night encourages people to host fundraising events while raising awareness of endometriosis Megan Gomersall, 30, from Rochdale, said the condition ended a career she loved. The former paediatric nurse has been out of work for about two and a half years because of her symptoms. She said endometriosis, which affects her bladder and bowel, left her in severe pain during shifts and frequently off sick before she received a diagnosis. It took 13 years for her condition to be identified. "It has been really, really difficult," she said. "It's been like a grieving process in a way. I feel like I've completely lost my identity and purpose." Megan said she believed more could be done to help women remain in work through reasonable adjustments and greater awareness of the condition. The inquiry found fewer than half of employees with endometriosis had received workplace adjustments, while 94% believed employers lacked a good understanding of the condition. A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said endometriosis can have a "devastating impact" on women's lives and said the government's renewed Women's Health Strategy identifies it as a priority condition. The spokesperson said the findings highlighted the need for better support, both in healthcare and in the workplace. title: Little tern colony has worst breeding season
description: Planning is under way to improve the colony for the 2027 breeding season.
body: Little terns first came to Seaton Carew in 2019 A little tern colony has experienced its toughest breeding season since establishing themselves at a site. Since 2019 the seabirds have travelled about 3,000 miles (4,828km) from West Africa to Seaton Carew, near Hartlepool. But this year the colony's 83 nesting pairs produced just 17 fledglings, compared to 67 in 2025. Tees Valley Wildlife Trust said flooding and damage to the colony's perimeter fence contributed to difficult conditions for the birds. The protective fencing around the nesting ground was washed away in high tides earlier this year. Lead warden Derek Wood said a late arrival of their inshore food supply as well as predation also contributed to the birds' tough season. In June, it was reported numbers were down 50%, which the team attributed to dogs being inside the exclusion zone. Tees Valley Wildlife Trust is looking at how to make the 2027 breeding season more successful "The season has been a difficult one for the dedicated wardens and volunteers who work tirelessly to protect the colony," Wood said. But the team is hopeful the colony can bounce back when they return from Africa in spring, with plans to improve the site and further protect the birds under way. Little Terns are currently classed as amber on the UK list of conservation concern. title: Professor shares 'most important thing to do' when someone is grieving
description: Dr Lesel Dawson, co-director of Good Grief Weston, says avoiding grief is not a good way to cope.
body: Dr Lesel Dawson encourages bereaved people to talk about their feelings in order to cope with grief Knowing what to say or how to support someone after a bereavement can be difficult. Fear of saying the wrong thing or intruding at a sensitive time can leave people worried about getting it wrong and avoiding reaching out altogether. But Dr Lesel Dawson, from the University of Bristol, said this is the worst thing people can do. Speaking ahead of an annual Good Grief Festival that Dawson is co-director of, she said: "The most important thing when helping someone dealing with grief isn't what you say, but that you don't turn away. "A simply acknowledgement like, 'I'm so sorry and I'm here' can mean a great deal and it's vital to let the grieving person lead- to follow their pace, their language and their need to talk about the person who died." The associate professor in Literature and Culture also said people avoiding dealing with their own grief can create lifelong challenges. Woman 'taken too soon' as husband charged with murder Improv community 'devastated' by theatre closure Mum faces heart transplant wait far from home Dawson's own understanding of grief was shaped by the stillbirth of her younger sister when she was eight years old and learning that for many years her mother blamed herself for the child's death. "The way we avoid grief can be really harmful to us," Dawson said. "Being able to turn toward the pain of the experience is the only way we process what's happened." She said the lack of conversation about grief meant it took "a while" to fully grasp what had happened. Research commissioned by Marie Curie found , externalthat while 70% of people feel comfortable talking about death, far fewer have actually had those conversations with family, friends or healthcare professionals. While her mother struggled to cope with the bereavement, Dawson found an interest in psychology and emotions. But after Dawson's first son was born at 29 weeks and suffered complications linked to the premature birth, the loss of her sister and the memory of her mother's "great pain" came to the forefront of her mind. When Dawson revisited the difficult topic of conversation with her mother after her own pregnancy experience, she realised that her mother "felt [the stillbirth] was her fault". "I said to her, 'was it my fault that my son was born early?' and she said, 'no of course not'. "I said, 'okay, why can you not show the same compassion to yourself and your own loss?'" Dawson told BBC Radio Bristol. She added that feelings of blame and guilt were "very common" during bereavement and could lead to "destructive" coping mechanisms. "The biggest myth about grief is that it happens in neat, orderly stages and that you eventually get over it," said Dawson. "In reality, grief is messy, unpredictable and deeply individual. People move back and forth between feelings, and the idea of a tidy, linear process simply doesn't reflect how grief actually works." Good Grief Weston offers workshops, talks and musical performances aimed to start and normalise conversations about loss Following her own experiences with grief, Dawson took up the role of co-director of Good Grief, a festival in Weston-super-Mare that aims to start and normalise conversations about death, dying and bereavement. The festival, which begins later, offers a number of workshops, music events, talks and light installations until Sunday. "Grief involves lots of emotions, it involves sadness, but also anger, numbness, jealousy, rage… they're not sequential. "Everybody's individual. We have our own ways of grieving and coping and we have our own timelines," Dawson said. If you or someone you know has been affected by the details raised in this story, advice on where to find help and support can be found at BBC Action Line. title: Tiny critically endangered puddle frogs hatch at London Zoo
description: The Afia Birago’s puddle frogs are a recently identified species from a single Ghanaian forest.
body: At about 5mm long, the froglets are about the size of the tip of a pencil Fifteen critically endangered frogs have hatched at London Zoo, which says it marks the first time the species has been bred in captivity. The Afia Birago's puddle frog lives in Ghana's Atewa Hills Forest Reserve, where the Zoological Society of London (ZSL) says it survives in just two pools that are both under threat from mining. Twenty adults were brought to London in September 2025 so experts could learn how to care for and breed them, and pass that knowledge on to conservationists in Ghana. The froglets are about 5mm long, roughly the size of a pencil tip. Ben Tapley, curator of reptiles and amphibians at ZSL, which runs the central London zoo, said: "They may be tiny enough to sit on your fingertip, but their arrival represents a huge step forward for an amphibian facing an uncertain future." ZSL said no other zoo or institution was known to keep the species. It was only described by scientists in 2018. Fully grown, the frogs weigh less than 1.75g. ZSL said almost nothing was known about them when they arrived, and keepers have since developed breeding techniques that are being shared with the CSIR-Forestry Research Institute of Ghana's breeding centre in Kumasi. The aim is to build up a population in Ghana that could be released into the wild. Ghanaian conservationist Caleb Ofori-Boateng, who helped identify the species, named it after his mother, Afia Birago. "I named this frog after my mother so that her legacy would live on," he said. "Thanks to this breeding programme, it will. Her name will be linked to a species we saved, not one we lost." The births follow the zoo's success last November in breeding the Atewa slippery frog, another critically endangered species from the same forest, which had also never been bred in captivity before. title: 'I paid thousands to a company for jobs that never came'
description: Apurv Patel is one of several people who say they were promised job opportunities that did not appear.
body: Apurv Patel said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 and claimed he was verbally promised a guaranteed sponsored job A company has been accused of promising jobs in the healthcare sector which never materialised, leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket. Registered in 2025, Synetal Solutions Ltd says it offers career-focused training programmes in the healthcare and IT sectors. But the BBC has spoken to a number of people who claim they were promised training and support to secure sponsored healthcare jobs that never became available to apply for. London Citizens Advice says it has seen an increase in recruitment-related scams since the government stopped overseas recruitment for care workers, external. The charity described the firm's practices as "unethical". Synetal Solutions says it "takes these concerns seriously and disputes the broad allegation that its services or candidate outcomes are fictitious". Apurv Patel, who has been in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa since 2023, said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 across February and March for healthcare training after he and a friend were verbally promised guaranteed sponsored jobs. Eight months later he has received no job offers, interviews or meaningful employment support, he said. "I'm frustrated. I paid money, I wasted my time. I did whatever they wanted without any result," he said. "It's had a miserable effect on my family and finances." Patel said he did receive some training but described it as poor quality and ultimately "worthless". Having previously worked for two years as a healthcare assistant, he said he became concerned when a trainer was unable to answer routine questions about care work. "She didn't give us any answers and we realised she didn't have any experience of healthcare," he said. The company disputes claims that training was ineffective. He also alleged communication with the company deteriorated after he made his second payment, with responses sometimes taking several days. Patel has since complained to his bank and sought help from Citizens Advice. The BBC has seen emails from the company advertising a "three-month recruitment programme" offering "training and placement with sponsorship" for £5,500. Home Office guidance, external states agencies may charge for services such as training or CV-writing assistance, but cannot charge fees solely for finding, or attempting to find, employment. Responding to questions about its marketing, Synetal Solutions said: "We acknowledge the 'guarantee' wording in the emails supplied and recognise that contractual terms alone do not resolve concerns about those assurances." As part of its programme, Synetal Solutions created accounts for trainees on iHasco, a health and social care training platform. The BBC contacted iHasco, which confirmed the company was a customer. However, it said its terms did not permit customers to resell its training content to individuals who were not employees. The company said it was reviewing Synetal Solutions' account and would take appropriate action if necessary. Synetal Solutions said it had acted in accordance with its agreement with iHasco. The Care Quality Commission said there was no single qualification that automatically qualified someone to work as a care worker. Instead, providers are responsible for ensuring employees are appropriately trained and competent for their roles. The BBC also contacted a number of healthcare organisations whose logos appeared on Synetal Solutions' website as examples of employers where graduates had worked. Those organisations that responded said they had no links to the company. Some also said they had not authorised the use of their branding, and some said they would not accept certificates provided through the company's training. Daniel Blake says the way Synetal Solutions has operated is unethical Daniel Blake, director of London Citizens Advice, described the company's approach as "exploitative". "The promises that were made are impossible promises," he said. "They are targeting people with vulnerable immigration status. "This company is asking for large sums of money upfront without any reputable standards, without any reputable evidence of success, and yet when it goes wrong they are refusing to take any responsibility. "For us, it seems a very unethical way of conducting business." He added that no reputable recruitment agency would guarantee a successful outcome without first assessing a candidate and matching them to a suitable role, and urged anybody asked to pay large sums upfront to seek independent advice. "If it seems too good to be true, it probably is," he said. The company's website states: "Synetal Solutions provides the right support, guidance, and guaranteed job placement to help you succeed." Its social media channels also promoted healthcare as "one of the most reliable paths" for people seeking visa-sponsored work in the UK. Sarah and Rahul, whose names we have changed, said they paid £3,000 to Synetal Solutions while seeking sponsored employment before the expiry of their student visas. Rahul, a former dentist in India, could remain in the UK on a graduate visa for longer, but Sarah's immigration status was close to expiring. To pay the fee, the couple said they borrowed money from a family friend and took out a loan. Rahul said he was shocked by the quality of the training. "The mentor didn't know anything about healthcare," he said. The couple said they were also shown the names of established healthcare providers, including Bupa, as examples of potential employers. Bupa told the BBC it had no connection with the company. Synetal Solutions says some of their candidates "told us they had secured employment with Bupa" and the reference was "not intended to suggest a formal partnership with Bupa". It says it had not verified those outcomes and "cannot attribute the recruitment decisions to our training".

title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings still have no public outcome, BBC Verify finds
description: BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents from the past three years the Israeli military said it is reviewing after being accused of harm.
body: BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome. Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded. BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible. Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them. Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children. For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case. A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range. The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers. A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations. In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations. In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation. The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents", external, had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war. These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked. Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify. In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security". It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures". Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations. Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said. Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute it

title: UK temperatures to rise to 23C before autumn chill sets in
description: Warm air will bring unseasonable warmth to the south and east of the UK on Thursday but chillier conditions are set to spread to all areas by the weekend.
body: Leaves littered the ground in Liverpool's Clarkes Gardens on Tuesday as autumnal colours set in across the UK Thursday will bring unusually high temperatures as warm air wafts across the south of the UK, while colder conditions dig into northern areas. Afternoon highs in parts of eastern England are likely to be about 5-8C (9-14F) above typical mid-October values, probably peaking at 23C (73F). It will be a different story further north and west with temperatures in much of Scotland and Northern Ireland sitting around the seasonal norm. The two air masses are divided by a weather front which will bring outbreaks of rain. As that sinks southwards, chillier air will spread to all parts of the country bringing a colder feel to the weekend, though there will still be plenty of sunshine. Frost and patchy fog are likely to develop in some locations. A weather front that has already brought rain to Scotland and Northern Ireland will edge slowly southwards on Thursday, meaning a soggy afternoon for northern England, Wales and parts of south-west England. To the south-east of the rain band, brisk southerly winds caused by a very deep area of low pressure passing close to Iceland will continue to feed warm air across many central, eastern and southern parts of England. Sunny spells in these areas will lift temperatures to 19-23C (66-73F) making it feel unseasonably warm for late October. Thursday's top temperatures will be well above the October norm in southern parts - but chilly weather will be arriving further north. As the rain band clears from northern parts of the UK, Scotland and Northern Ireland will turn mostly sunny with blustery winds and scattered heavy showers. Afternoon highs here will be around 12-15C (54-59F) and these chillier conditions will be a sign of things to come for the whole of the UK, with colder air set to spread southwards by Friday and linger into the weekend. High pressure will take charge of the weather for the end of the week providing sunny spells in many areas. A few showers are also possible - especially in the north and west of the UK on Friday, then in the south-east of England over the weekend. As the high builds from the west, widespread northerly winds will develop delivering colder air and a chilly feel. Cold air will spread southwards across all areas to bring an autumnal feel to the weekend Daytime temperatures will end up near the October average, ranging from 10 to 16C (50-61F) across the UK, although it will feel colder than that where winds turn blustery - particularly along the coasts of eastern Scotland and eastern England. The nights will also turn cold with single-digit lows in almost all areas and the chance of a touch of frost as well as some patchy mist and fog. Thermometers are likely to dip below freezing in some locations in Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England. For some places it could be the coldest weather of the autumn so far but it is worth noting that these temperatures are not unusual for this time of year. There is a lot of uncertainty about the forecast for next week with conflicting signals from computer weather models. High pressure is likely to remain close to the UK initially but there are signs that Atlantic weather systems will eventually break through, powered by the jet stream, bringing a return to wetter, windier and somewhat milder conditions. However, there is uncertainty about how quickly that change will take place so it is worth keeping an eye on the BBC Weather website and app. You can read our latest thoughts on the forecast even further ahead in our monthly outlook.
