title: Australian woman charged with lacing colleague's curry with snail poison
description: The alleged victim, who was in a relationship with the woman, had spotted bright green pellets in the meal.
body: A stock photo of curry An Australian woman has been charged after allegedly lacing a colleague's curry with snail poison. Police in the state of Western Australia say the alleged victim made a meal for her co-workers in February, which they shared at morning tea. But when the 58-year-old returned to eat leftovers at lunch, she noticed bright green granules in the food and that her tongue felt numb after tasting it. The accused - who was in a relationship with the alleged victim - has been charged with endangering the life, health or safety of another person after a months-long investigation, and will face court on 5 November. Police allege the 43-year-old woman - who hasn't been named - visited a chemical storage shed before returning to the staffroom where the curry was kept. After tasting it, the alleged victim handed the meal over to detectives, who identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance. Commissioner Col Blanch told reporters the poison can cause serious injury or death. "We're just very thankful that the person who tasted the curry was aware of something that wasn't quite right," he said, according to the Seven Network. title: 'Nowhere to escape' - Indonesians share footage of orange haze blanketing towns
description: Thick orange smog descended on the Indonesian city of Palangka Raya as wildfires continue raging nearby.
body: This video can not be played A thick orange smog has descended on the Indonesian city of Palangka Raya. Witnesses captured videos of the haze washing over the Kalimantan region not far from where wildfires continue to burn. The ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200, according to data from the national environment ministry, four times higher than the "hazardous" level of 300 on Wednesday. Toxic smog is choking millions across Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia, with authorities partly blaming the agricultural clearing method known as "slash and burn" for compounding the intense haze. Read more on this story here. 'Nowhere to escape' - Indonesians share footage of orange haze blanketing towns. title: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel 'barbaric' execution livestream
description: Livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," 72 former officers said in a letter.
body: A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. "We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," they wrote in a letter where they also argued the livestream would turn the mass killer into a "martyr". Last week, the Pentagon announced it would publicly show the 3 December execution of Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base. Lawmakers from both parties, as well as religious leaders, have criticised the plan. Last week President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but some administration officials are now leaning against it, according to CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. CBS reported that Trump had not yet made a final decision on the livestream as of Tuesday. In the open letter released on Wednesday, the former military leaders - which included 45 generals, 12 admirals and several former judge advocates general - said they did not oppose the death penalty being carried out. But they argued a public execution would violate the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment and turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into "a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators". "This type of exploitative broadcasting - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," they also wrote. "It will be used by our nation's enemies to stoke hatred, harm American soldiers and citizens in the future, and will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers." The letter's signatories came from throughout the military and included a handful of officers who retired during Trump's first term. Some also had served during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. Hasan said in court that he carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American base, believing he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair. Retired Maj Gen Tony Taguba, who led the Army's investigation into reported prisoner abuses at Abu Ghraib in Iraq, and retired Air Force Coll Moe Davis, a prosecutor at the Guatanamo Bay detention centre who called waterboarding torture, signed the letter. So did Charles Bolden, a US Marine Corps Major General who became the head of Nasa, and retired Lt Gen Claudia Kennedy, the first woman to become a three-star general in the Army. This video can not be played Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made. It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts. Who is Nidal Hasan? title: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
description: It comes as some investors have become concerned about the amount of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
body: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands. The figures were reportedly revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year. It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have come under pressure over concerns about the large amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure. An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment. Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period. The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row. Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology. Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI. Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply. In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 8.4% and SK Hynix dropping by more than 6%. South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi index was 7.6% lower in morning trading. The falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending. How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire Tan said at an conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino". There also been concerns over the safety of AI models. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety. The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn. Anthropic has also been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down. The company has continued expanding globally, opening an office in Singapore on Wednesday. title: The Papers: 'Zelenskyy blames Trump' and Brand a 'sex predator'
description: Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to London and the first day of Russell Brand's rape trial dominate Thursday's front pages.
body: Many of Thursday's front pages are dominated by Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to London, during which he agreed that he had felt betrayed by the US. The Ukrainian president made the comments during an interview in which he was asked about a plan by President Donald Trump to import Russian diesel into the US and also what appeared to be restrictions placed on the speed at which some of its weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network. The Elon Musk-owned Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies. The Times also leads with Zelensky's comments, with the leader saying "people will die" because of the decision to restrict access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system. Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]". The other story leading many of the newspapers is the start of Russell Brand's trial for rape and sexual assault. The 51-year-old actor and comedian, who faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault, was described as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator" by the prosecution. He denies the charges. Brand is described as "the 'predator' in sunglasses' on the front page of the Daily Mail. Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, read out a litany of sex charges at Southwark Crown Court in London, the paper reports, as Brand "sat impassively in the dock". The Sun leads with the prosecution's description of Brand as a "ruthless, calculated sexual predator". The paper reports that the comedian allegedly attacked women over 10 years and was "demanding and manipulative". The prosecution's description of Brand is repeated on the front page of the i Paper, which also detailed the first day of the trial. It says the jury heard details of all alleged offences, which Brand says were consensual. "Predator," declares the Mirror alongside a picture of Brand. It also highlights a moment in court when a witness recalled Brand saying "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far". The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks. The Financial Times leads with the latest economic figures in the US, where inflation rose to 3.7% in September. The increase, driven by a rebound in fuel prices, piles pressure on households ahead of the midterm elections, the paper reports. Official figures show there are more seven-year-olds on disability benefits than 50-year-olds, according to the Daily Telegraph. A total of 69,799 children aged seven now receive Disability Living Allowance (DLA) while 66,670 50-year-olds are on similar welfare support, the paper reports. The figures come as ADHD and learning difficulty claims soar. The Daily Express leads on the plea of nine women from Piddington, who visited Parliament on Wednesday to demand Labour shelves plans to house 1,256 asylum seekers next to the Oxfordshire village. It came as MPs rejected a Conservative call for the government to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights "in order to deport illegal migrants". They voted by 309 to 113, majority 196, against the motion, which would have also condemned plans to house the asylum seekers at a disused Ministry of Defence (MoD) site near Piddington. Donald Trump's sharing of an AI-generated video of him grappling with a tiger leads the Daily Star. Branded a "video nasty", the US president posted the video on social media after also sharing footage of William Chapman being fatally attacked by a tiger at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Tuesday evening. And finally, the Independent is celebrating its 40th anniversary, with Andy Burnham paying a glowing tribute to the "bravery, spirit and values" of the news outlet. The prime minister said the digital news provider should be lauded for consistently championing "democracy, human rights" and the UK's role on the world stage since it was launched in 1986. title: How West Midlands shed its gun crime capital label
description: Firearms discharges drop by more than half in the past six years in the force area.
body: This video can not be played Crowds flee as shots fired outside club More than 10 years ago, the West Midlands was dubbed the gun crime capital of England and Wales. It was an area suffering from high-profile shootings. Gun fights between rival gangs were happening regularly. Figures at the time reflected that notoriety - there were more firearms offences per head in the West Midlands Police force area than anywhere else. "Back then, there were shootings every day, reported shootings every day and unreported shootings every day," says Simeon Moore, also known as Zimbo, an ex-Johnson crew member - one of the Birmingham's most notorious gangs in the noughties. New figures seen by BBC News show shootings in the West Midlands force area - covering Birmingham, Wolverhampton, the Black Country and Coventry - have dropped significantly over the past six years. "Things have calmed down dramatically since the early 2000s," Zimbo, who now mentors youngsters, said. While the numbers are not directly comparable, due to the criteria in the way they were gathered and published, in 2002-03 the force recorded about 1,300 gun crimes, external, compared with 504 in the 2024 calendar year, external. A more direct snapshot of the past six years also shows things are improving. In 2020-21, there were a total of 157 firearms discharges, while a year later in 2021-2022 there were 148. By last year, the number of discharges had dropped to 69 and in the first seven months of 2026, there had only been 30, according to figures from West Midlands Police. Zimbo says there are more influential voices now that young people listen to The force said the fall was down to way it now dealt with firearms incidents. A major crime unit deals with all firearms events. Every time gun fire is reported, it is treated as if it was a murder. But it is not all down to policing, Zimbo said. He thinks there has been a change in culture, with more people speaking out about that kind of lifestyle, keeping the next generation out of trouble. He was jailed for six years for possessing a semi-automatic weapon as a teenager and was in and out of prison for two decades. "We lived it," Zimbo said. "There's more people that have been involved in that life talking about it, turning away from it and speaking bad about it in the sense that this isn't the right way to go. "Now you've got man that have lived that life, done crazy sentences and they're telling the young people now, 'if you're going to start living like this, expect jail, expect to lose your friends or possibly lose your own life.'" A 3D printed semi-automatic gun, sawn-off shotgun and converted blank firearms are among the weapons that have been seized and are in the police armoury Zimbo also credits various organisations across Birmingham which are working with young people and delivering projects, and the impact that is having. "Most young people within the city are engaged with organisations that are supporting them to stay away from the streets," he adds. It is this kind of work, he suggests, that is leading Birmingham to "become more of a village." "The village is starting to work together." But gun crime has not gone away and rivalries still exist. The most recent statistics from the Office of National Statistics for England and Wales showed the West Midlands force area remained second only to the Met for the total number of discharges. However, it is also second only to the Met in terms of the population it serves. A shooting outside a nightclub in Aston earlier this year was captured on CCTV. People could be seen fleeing in fear as shots rang out when two men fired at each other outside FJ Lounge. One of them was injured, as well as an innocent bystander working on a food stall outside the club. Two men were convicted and are due to be sentenced next week.. And in 2025, a man was left in a critical condition following a shooting at Mango nightclub in the city centre. "I don't believe there's fewer weapons out there. I just think a few less people are using them," says Zimbo. Armed police gather outside a flat in Dudley ahead of a raid in the early hours At Revere Records in the city, where Zimbo heads up its urban division, a young artist, Solitary, is recording a track. His lyrics reference life in parts of the city, avoiding jail and being a product of your environment. This is just one of the projects Zimbo is involved with that gives youngsters opportunities. Zimbo added: "It's very hard for these young people to stay away from the lifestyle." West Midlands Police believes the reorganisation and creation of its major crime unit has led to the fall in gun crime, and a rise in seizures of weapons. Det Supt Ryan Chambers said the unit specialised in the most serious elements of criminality, targeting offenders and those in possession of firearms. He said 50% of the discharges the force dealt with were from shotguns which had been owned lawfully, but stolen in burglaries and ended up in criminal hands. Chambers said: "We've had a good level of success over the last 12-months. We've had the most recoveries and biggest reduction in discharges we've seen in recent years." The arrested man had a bandage on his hand from a shooting the previous week We joined officers on a raid in Dudley and while they did not find a gun, they found a machete and crossbow, and arrested a man who had a wound to his hand from a shooting a week earlier. He was also suspected to have been involved in a machete attack, and will stand trial in 2029. Despite successes like these, gun crime has not gone away. Weapons are still getting into the country despite tough gun laws, but what is clear is that work being done by both police and the community is having an impact. title: Wales has a school standards crisis. Will plans to fix it actually work?
description: Wales scores poorly on international test results but it is not clear a new curriculum will help.
body: Wales has a school standards crisis. Will plans to fix it actually work? As you dip into the valley on the way into Merthyr Tydfil, a new earthy-toned building dominates the view. It's the new site of Saint Carlo Acutis Catholic School. With its rooftop science garden, solar panels and floor-to-ceiling windows, it's an impressive sight. Excited staff and 940 pupils moved into the £50m complex at the start of September. But they did so just as the Welsh education system was being painted in a less positive light, with Wales once again ranking the worst of UK nations in global tests. "It casts doubt over a system we're proud of and children that we're proud of," says Sarah Hopkins, who's been a headteacher here for eight years. She says it doesn't tell the full story but admits "it is disappointing". Welsh parents are currently thinking about the next steps for their children, with application deadlines for secondary school places at the end of this month. That comes at a time when the test results pose difficult questions about why Wales has so clearly underperformed relative to its closest neighbours. And with Wales's devolved government now run by a party other than Labour for the first time ever, can the new Plaid Cymru administration do what it's promised and improve standards? Sarah Hopkins started teaching in 1998 - a year before the Welsh Assembly, now the Senedd, took over responsibility for education in Wales from Westminster. In that time she's had to navigate many system-wide and school changes. The latest challenge has been managing the big move from the old mishmash of 1960s-built classrooms to the vast new building. But buildings alone do not drive excellence, and the gap between Wales and the other UK countries is getting wider. Sarah Hopkins describes the Wales Pisa results as "disappointing" Pisa (Programme for International Student Assessment) measures teenagers' skills in reading, maths and science. Sat by a sample of 15-year-olds – 3,406 in Wales in 2025, including some in Sarah Hopkins' school - it provides a snapshot of how education systems are performing. On the day results were published, Wales' education Minister, Anna Brychan, euphemistically said they were "not where we want them to be". Others called them catastrophic. Wales first took part in the tests in 2006. There have been upticks along the way. But when the pandemic affected scores across the board in 2022, Wales fell back furthest. And the gulf grew in the latest results. The OECD, the global economic development body which runs Pisa, says that 20 points equates to roughly a year of learning. That would mean Welsh 15-year-olds are about two years behind England's in reading, science and maths. In reading, they also trail teenagers in Scotland and Northern Ireland by a year. The tests alone don't capture everything schools do to support pupils, "whether that's a clean jumper, whether that's having a pen and a pencil" says Hopkins. And there are long-standing debates about the methodology of the tests. But nobody in Wales is pretending there's nothing to worry about. Soon after the devolved administration was established, the Welsh Labour government of the early 2000s used its powers over education and other public services to go off on a different course to Tony Blair's Labour government at Westminster - creating what the then Welsh First Minister Rhodri Morgan called "clear, red water". Secondary school league tables and standardised tests at seven, 11 and 14 (SATs) were scrapped. A new learning-through-play approach for the youngest pupils was an early flagship policy. Poor Pisa results in 2010 brought about a drastic reappraisal. Plain speaking Education Minister Leighton Andrews called the results a "wake-up call" for a "complacent" system and introduced a new raft of reforms. Alongside a literacy and numeracy drive, Andrews re-introduced accountability measures with annual reading and maths tests for seven-to-14 year olds, and a new school performance regime, called banding. Pupils at Saint Carlo Acutis Catholic School are studying in a brand-new building There were some parallels between the political styles of Andrews and the man in charge of England's schools system at the time, Conservative Michael Gove, who was on his own controversial education mission with an emphasis on high-stakes accountability. The two seemed to relish their occasional public spats over policy. But policies introduced by Andrews lost their bite over time. The school banding system was changed and eventually dropped altogether during the pandemic. Tests later evolved into personalised assessments. And the focus moved to developing a new curriculum in Wales, something which Andrews recently said was a "distraction" from efforts to drive up standards. Sir Nick Gibb, a former schools minister at Westminster who worked under Michael Gove, believes the main reason for Wales' Pisa woes is weak accountability. He says "schools are spending billions of pounds of public money and they're not being held to account for the results that they produce". He argues that focusing on the "science of learning" paid dividends with England's move up international education rankings. Primary schools in England were told they had to use a structured form of phonics to teach young children to read. This was reinforced with a phonics screening check for six-year-olds. Sir Nick claims education standards in Wales and Scotland suffered because they didn't do the same. In general, education ministers in England have been more likely to set direction for teachers, highlighted by the approach to phonics. In Wales, for the most part, the mantra has been to trust the profession. And though that freedom sounds good in theory, it has pitfalls. It's the thinking at the heart of the new curriculum for Wales - dubbed the biggest reform to We

title: I'm 12 and I want to try protein powder - should I?
description: We asked experts how safe it is for children and teenagers to take protein supplements.
body: Louis, Otis and Ben all have differing opinions on whether teens should use protein powder Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it. In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders. Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder. As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet. So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good? In recent years, there has been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein"... ... however, protein is found in lots of everyday foods, including meat, fish, eggs, dairy, bread, grains and pulses My sport-obsessed son, who already eats a healthy balanced diet, asks me about protein powder on a regular basis. His friend Louis, 12, has been using protein powder once or twice a week for nearly a year, after a workout and on top of whole foods. His parents are aware of this. "I think it's helped, it gives me more energy and it's helped me grow, probably," he says. But Ben's other friend Otis, who is 13, is not keen on the idea and feels there is pressure on young people to take protein supplements. "They might just start using them without thinking about the consequences or what effects it may have on them." Proteins break down into amino acids that help the body grow and repair. But your body can't make all the amino acids it needs on its own, so you need to get more - known as essential amino acids - through your diet. For an adult with a healthy weight, the recommended daily amount of protein you should be eating is 0.75 grams per kg of body weight, according to the NHS. A good rule of thumb is that the amount of protein you have for each meal should fit into the palm of your hand. If you exercise a lot, and when you get older, you need more protein so you could have up to 2 grams per kg of body weight. But do teens really need it if they're eating well? This video can not be played Do you really need protein powder to build muscle? For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine. It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients. Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet. There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea. Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor. Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines. "Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says. "And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow." Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants. Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust. He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods. So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost. Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes. During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass. But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein. "If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much." He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded. Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away." The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein." Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly. If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first. Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same. £170 a bag? title: Dog that hunts invasive 'sea vomit' honoured as animal of the year
description: A working is named animal of the year for hunting out an invasive marine creature, the carpet sea squirt.
body: Marine ecology dog Sgiath at work A working dog from the Scottish Highlands has been named animal of the year by a charity for hunting down an invasive marine creature called the carpet sea squirt. This organism, also nicknamed "sea vomit", is particularly harmful to coastal wildlife and economies. Working at low tide with her owner, Dr Texa Sim, black labrador Sgiath has found hundreds of colonies of the sea squirt, which - if left uncontrolled - can smother and kill native species. Sgiath is thought to be the UK's first sea squirt-hunting dog. Carpet sea squirt can be tricky to spot among seaweed "She's a natural" says Dr Sim proudly. The marine ecologist, who is based near Glencoe, has had her dog since she was a puppy and the bond btween the two is strong. "Sgiath is incredibly clever. Her problem solving and her ability to take on new challenges and learn so quickly are just phenomenal, and it's so amazing to watch." As a pup, Sgiath (pronounced Skee-ah) was trained as a mountain rescue dog. The labrador proved to be so good that Dr Sim wondered if she could use her skills to help with marine conservation work. Sgiath has been trained to recognise the scent of the carpet sea squirt. And now, the six year old lab joins her owner on the beaches to sniff it out. Dr Sim says the dog is always right when pointing out a sea squirt, which can be difficult to spot, looking like slime among seaweed and on structures like pontoons and oyster cages. Carpet sea squirt, or sea vomit, has spread to several places around the UK "When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Dr Sim. "No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had." Dogs' scent detection skills are often used in conservation work on land, including tracking endangered species and helping investigate environmental crime. At low tide, Sgiath can, as Dr Sim puts it "dive down under the seaweed". "She just does a survey with her nose, essentially, she can pinpoint exactly where it is, so it's much easier," she said. Marine experts believe that carpet sea squirt, formally named Didemnum vexillum, came from Japan. It arrived on the shores of the south of England and Wales in 2008. It can appear in various shades - from orange to cream - and has now spread to several seaside locations across the UK. It reproduces quickly during the warmer summer months and, with warming seas, there are fears it could spread further. Dr Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist from Bangor University told BBC News that non-native or "biofouling" species, like the carpet sea squirt, can outcompete native wildlife for valuable nutrients. "These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellors," he explained. Efforts to control and clean up these problematic marine invaders costs millions of pounds every year across Europe. Sgiath is also a trained mountain rescue dog To get Sgiarth proficient in both mountain rescue and marine conservatuion has needed hard work and long hours from both dog and owner. To locate and draw attention to a lost hiker on mountainous terrain, Sgiath is trained to bark and bounce around to attract attention. Conservation work requires a quieter approach. Dr Sim explained that she trains Sgiath to give what's known as a "passive indication" when she finds the sea squirt. "It's a kind of a stillness, or a stare - a sit stare, or just a freeze stare." Sgiath has been trained to stare when she finds carpet sea squirt When we speak to Dr Sim over Zoom from her home, her two dogs are curled up in their beds at her feet. Apparently, when Sgiath is not out finding lost people or marine creatures, she likes to be wrapped up in her dog blanket. Sgiath, and Dr Sim's younger labrador Uisage, are both working dogs that are driven to do their jobs with treats and play. Dr Kurr, from Bangor University, said that scientists were just starting to realise that "these wonderful animals can smell changes in water that signal a marine invasion which otherwise might have gone unnoticed". He added: "It's fantastic to see Sgiath get this much deserved award, and I'm very excited to see what other wonderful work we can do with sniffer dogs." The International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) , external is awarding Sgiath animal of the years at its 26th annual animal Action Awards ceremony on Thursday 15 October. title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
description: Can Nepal bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in the Himalayas?
body: The recent floods in Nepal have highlighted the need for cross-border co-operation in the Himalayan region Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August. But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention. Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions. "Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said. A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage. "The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said. Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment. But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes? India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control. But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat. Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods. Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important. Balendra Shah has urged neighbours India and China to collaborate on climate risks in the Himalayan region A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period. Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online. Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau. The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily. And the dangers extend beyond flooding. A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau. The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress. The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations. Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas. In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet. Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project. Hundreds of people were killed in the deadly flood that tore through the China-Nepal border in August But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort. "One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute. "What happened after that no one knows," he added. Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet. But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said. title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
description: Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The BBC's Shaimaa Khalil is in Arizona to hear from residents about the expansion of data centres. A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​ Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country. "This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press. The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity. Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it. "I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC. A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators. Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US. There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center. Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process. Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand. "This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit." Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation. "There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them." That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology. Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor". His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents. The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities. During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs. Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago. "People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry." New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy. Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs. Yet, recent research, external from Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages. LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, has made stopping data centre development one of their key issues Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project. Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash. Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate. In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees. Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should

title: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
description: With Christmas on the horizon, we trace children's toys from factories in China to US shelves.
body: China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the US On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China". Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far. As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes. Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry. In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting. The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business. Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed. Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it." Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months. The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 people So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang. On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes. Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it. Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour. He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive." And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises. Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail price Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report, external at the start of this year. Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so. The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories. Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries. From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong. Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance. Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September. Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents. Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more. This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents. This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China. "We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg. Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the country The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total. That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys. title: How much is the minimum wage?
description: What are the National Minimum Wage and the National Living Wage, and how much are they worth?
body: The official minimum rates of pay rose for 2.7 million workers on 1 April. The rate for workers aged 21 and over is called the National Living Wage, while those aged 18 to 20 are paid the National Minimum Wage. The rates apply across the UK. From 1 April 2026, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage are paid £12.71 an hour, 50p more than in 2025. For someone working full time (37.5 hours a week), that amounts to £24,784.50 a year - an increase of £900. The rate for 18 to 20-year-olds has gone up to £10.85 an hour. That's an increase of 85p per hour. It amounts to an increase of £1,500 a year for a full-time worker. The government said its goal is to eventually scrap this separate rate for 18 to 20-year-olds, and have one rate for all adults. The minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds has also risen to £8 an hour. There are different rates of pay for apprentices, external depending on their age and what stage of apprenticeship they are in. Apprentices aged 16 to 18 are entitled to the National Minimum Wage rate for that age group which is currently £8. Those aged 19, or in the first year of their apprenticeship, are paid the same amount. But those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage rate for their age. What is an apprenticeship and how much is the pay? Some workers do not qualify for either the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage. This includes the self-employed, company directors, volunteers, members of the armed forces and prisoners. People with disabilities or in long-term unemployment who take part in government work programmes are paid fixed amounts at different stages of the scheme. These are less than the equivalent National Minimum or Living rate. Yes. It is a criminal offence for employers not to pay the correct National Minimum and Living Wages to eligible employees. The rates apply even if workers are not paid by the hour. Calculator: Am I getting the right wage?, external If you think you are being paid the wrong amount, you can complain via the HMRC website, external. You can also get advice from workplace experts Acas, external. Any employer not paying the correct amount can be penalised by HMRC. In March 2026, the government said that 389 employers had been fined around £12.6m for failing to pay staff properly, external. They must also repay the missing £7.3m to the around 60,000 workers who were underpaid. Firm named included the Nursery chain Busy Bees, Norwich City Football Club, Hays Travel and Costa Coffee. The Real Living Wage, external is an unofficial hourly rate of pay which is overseen by the Living Wage Foundation charity, who say it is set at a rate to meet the cost of living. Some firms choose to pay the Real Living Wage, but it is not mandatory. According to the charity almost 500,000 employees working for nearly 17,000 firms receive the voluntary rate of pay. In October 2026, the foundation said the UK rate would increase by 4.8% to £14.10 an hour, while the London Living Wage for workers in the capital would go up by 4.4% to £15.45. The Living Wage Foundation says the rate is worth over £2,700 more per year than the legal minimum wage in the UK, and over £5,300 more in London. title: Warning to women amid shortages of some HRT products
description: Two brands of HRT patches, including Estradot transdermal and FemSeven Conti patches, have been affected, the Department of Health has said.
body: Women have been urged to seek advice from their GP or pharmacy if they find their usual HRT has been affected by supply shortages Women have been warned against self-medicating to manage menopause symptoms amid a shortage of some Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) medications. Pharmacist Paul Irvine said he understood that women "are concerned" but urged them to speak to their GP or local chemist who could advise them about alternatives. The warning follows official confirmation from the Department of Health that supplies of two major HRT patch brands have been disrupted. The affected products include Estradot transdermal and FemSeven Conti, both of which are currently facing manufacturing or distribution delays. Paul Irvine said it is important that women contact their GP or pharmacist for advice on alternatives Irvine, a pharmacy manager in Belfast, said much of the time with HRT medications, women often become comfortable with a particular brand. "When they are short and they like to try alternatives, they may suffer side effects or it might just not work as well," he said. "So it is important for us as pharmacists that we are there to guide people and offer them alternative and the correct advice." Dr Ursula Mason said that finding a suitable substitute "can cause real anxiety for patients". Dr Ursula Mason, chair of the Royal College of General Practitioners Northern Ireland, said finding a substitute "can cause real anxiety for patients". "This can be particularly so for HRT medication when a woman has found a preparation that works well for them," she said. "Patients can be assured that the protocol in place only allows a substitution for exactly the same active ingredient at the same dose. "If a woman finds that for whatever reason the new formulation is not managing their symptoms or they are having side effects, it would be important that they contact their GP to discuss both their symptoms and the options available around suitable alternatives." The Department of Health said it was aware of "supply disruptions" affecting some HRT medications across the UK, including ongoing issues with Estradot transdermal patches and a more recent disruption affecting FemSeven Conti patches. "Communications have been issued to healthcare professionals regarding the products affected, including advice on suitable alternatives that remain available," it said. It added: "Serious Shortage Protocol (SSPs) for Estradot transdermal patches are currently in place until 8 January 2027, permitting pharmacists to supply alternative products to patients without the need for a new prescription, where the patient has agreed to this. "If patients cannot access their prescribed medication or have concerns about an alternative, they should speak to a healthcare professional for advice about their treatment options." Roisin Hillman said ongoing HRT patch shortages are deeply frustrating for women Roisin Hillman, co-founder of Menopause Together, Northern Ireland's first menopause support charity, noted some women forced to switch brands due to medication shortages have reported side effects like itchy skin or patches falling off. She said that ongoing HRT patch shortages are deeply frustrating for women. Once they find a medication that works, it often falls in short supply. "This is an issue going on for years," she said advising women to request longer-term prescriptions from their GPs to stay ahead of supply gaps. She also warned against sharing HRT with others. "It is also really important that if you do have a shortage, and you can't get your normal HRT, to make sure you go back to your doctor. "Please do not share HRT with other women because what is prescribed to you may not suit someone else so it is very important that you go back to your GP," she said. "I know that when women have that fear and anxiety that the HRT they are on is helping so many aspects of their life and in particular a woman's mental health. "If she on HRT that works for her and then if she is not getting that HRT it can be really hard." Women 'borrow menopause drugs due to shortage' What is the menopause and what are the main signs? title: Guardiola's return, Man City's defiance - and a game of glorious chaos
description: On their return to Etihad Stadium Manchester City put on a show of defiance - even in the face of a PSG masterclass, writes Phil McNulty.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: Impressive PSG beat Manchester City 4-2 at the Etihad Manchester City returned to the welcoming surroundings of home for the first time since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations awash with defiance and presenting an 'us against the world' united front. Pep Guardiola was back at the place he decorated with success for a decade in a public show of support to embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and chief executive Ferran Soriano, the Catalan a low-key presence clad in a flat cap sitting a row behind the pair. If his appearance was relatively under the radar, the fact that he chose a game certain to attract a global audience to make his return was heavy with significance. Guardiola is ignoring the outside noise to back his former bosses to clear their name on appeal after the guilty verdict passed down by an independent commission. The stand bearing his name was emblazoned with a 'CTID' - City 'Til I Die - mosaic, while the build-up to kick-off saw a display of fireworks and pyrotechnics worthy of several rock concerts. The strategy to show an unabashed City ready to face down any enemy was going well, until the game kicked off and Champions League holders Paris St-Germain produced a ruthless first-half reality check cloaked within the brutal beauty of their football. With City providing a dramatic backdrop off the pitch, the game more than matched the setting. A second-half revival ensured embarrassment was avoided - and instead gave us a classic. Man City suffer as PSG masterclass sets up Champions League win How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team? This video can not be played PSG run riot against Man City City's first step back into the limelight on the hostile territory of Anfield on Sunday ended with a 3-0 win at Liverpool and wild celebrations. Here, with Guardiola watching on from the directors' box with an agonised expression mirroring that of successor Enzo Maresca in his technical area, City ran headlong into a whirlwind of magnificent football from Luis Enrique's PSG, the half-time scoreline of 3-0 actually doing them a kindness. To City's great credit, and also Maresca's after he made three half-time changes, they responded superbly after the break, creating a host of chances before eventually losing 4-2. It did not retrieve what was lost in the first half, but it did at least allow City's fans to ramp up a frenzied atmosphere and give their team a rousing send-off at the final whistle. In these surroundings, there was no question of any backlash against City's Abu Dhabi-based owners, despite the fact they were found guilty of such serious financial charges to leave the club in crisis and attracting pariah status. The damage was done in PSG's staggering opening 45 minutes, with Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha the scorers as City were ripped apart. A game that began in a wall of sound, with Guardiola's name resounding around the stadium at kick-off, was reduced to stunned silence in the first 15 minutes. City, so composed and ordered amid the toxicity of Anfield on Sunday, were shell-shocked on home territory as even born streetfighters such as Enzo Fernandez were reduced to chasing shadows. The players who rose in the face of the storm raging around Manchester City at Liverpool suddenly looked like they were carrying the weight of the world on their shoulders, which made their outstanding display after the break even more praiseworthy. Pep Guardiola appeared to go through every motion during Manchester City's 4-2 defeat Erling Haaland gave City hope, which looked to be snuffed out when goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, who had a very poor night against his former club, saved from Maghnes Akliouche, only to see the ball drop behind him into the net. Guardiola sometimes looked just as engaged as he did when he prowled the touchline here at Etihad Stadium, collecting the trophies now being called into question. When Josko Gvardiol had a header cleared off the line Guardiola clutched his face in anguish. When Haaland scored a goal that threatened to offer City an unlikely lifeline, he remained seated but pumped his fists into the air. If the Catalan was a neutral observer, he would have relished a game of glorious chaos, the first half embellished by PSG before City mounted superb momentum after the break. As a lover of pure football with the emphasis placed firmly on attack, he may have enjoyed it anyway. The post-match discussion with Maresca would certainly have had a busy agenda. Maresca felt he saw enough to give City hope should they meet PSG again later in the Champions League, despite the manner in which they were dismantled in the first half. "I really like playing against PSG because they are brave," said Maresca. "We know the way they want to press. They go man-to-man and they are very dynamic on the ball. They are the best team in Europe. They play fantastic football. "But I think we are there. The reason why we struggled was because we conceded two early goals so quickly. When you are on the pitch you might think this is difficult, but in the second half we created enough to maybe deserve something. "We feel sorry for the first half but I think we're quite happy now." Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha, watching for Match of the Day, described it as "great entertainment", but "not a normal game of football". "I don't feel like both teams were going at it at the same time," he said. "In the first half, PSG were excellent and City looked really off the pace. As a consequence they were heavily punished and the game basically left them. "But then in the second half they have made some changes, they have rallied, knowing they are playing in front of their own crowd and their performance had to be better. title: Jackson steps up again as Aston Villa revival continues
description: Nicolas Jackson continues his fine goalscoring form as Aston Villa record an impressive Champions League win.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: Aston Villa hit six past Fenerbahce to enjoy record European win Nicolas Jackson celebrated his first-half double by making a cutting motion which proved fitting on a night Aston Villa found their clinical edge. A first win at Villa Park this season, three first-half goals with six in total and a commanding Champions League victory - all in the biggest European win in their history. Unai Emery said his side had been impacted by the rebuild of the North Stand after three winless games at home this season but they showed no signs of struggle against Fenerbahce. A dominant victory against the Turkish visitors leaves Villa already well placed to reach the Champions League knockout phase and will add to their slowly growing momentum. Questions had been building as Villa picked up just one point from their opening three Premier League home games this season even if Saturday's 2-2 draw with Brentford ensured they avoided a third-straight home league defeat under Emery for the first time since February 2024. Against Fenerbahce, they found a willing opponent. Scattered with former Premier League players, including Ederson, Nathan Ake, Romelu Lukaku and Nelson Semedo, the visitors would have been a formidable foe five years ago. Instead, they folded quickly in the first half - despite Zion Suzuki's two important saves - as Johan Manzambi and Jackson's double put Villa in complete control. The goals came in front of the skeleton of the North Stand, which will not have gone unnoticed as they had previously scored only once when attacking that end this season. Ross Barkley's double and Tammy Abraham's late tap in added to the visitors' woes and underlined Villa's dominance. They last scored so many in a 6-1 win over Brighton three years ago and had previously put five past Hibernian in the Europa Conference League in 2023. The result provides another springboard and extends Villa's recent form to just one defeat in their last seven games. However, Emery's rebuild will still take time. Before the international break, he described the opening five weeks of the campaign as similar to still being in pre-season with 10 new players to adapt following a chaotic summer of change. Reflecting post match on how things are now progressing, he said: "They (Fenerbahce) didn't deserve 6-0 but for us it was very important how we achieved the first win at home and how we managed with different players, our progression and step forward. "There is still a lot of work to do and we need time, we are progressively getting better and it was a good step forward. In the Champions League the three points are important. We want to be a protagonist in the Champions League. "Now the clear objective is against Newcastle because of the lack of points in the Premier League." The shoots of progress are already evident. Manzambi glided past powerless Fenerbahce tackles, Ibraham Mbaye found space to exploit - even if he needs to improve - and Jackson was clinical. Leon Goretzka made his debut as a late substitute and Suzuki remained commanding, continuing to slip into his role with ease. "I think that's what Emery has been talking about with the potential of this team and what they can do," former Villa captain Stiliyan Petrov told TNT. "There's been a lot of questions from the start of the season, even for this game as well. People asking how far they can go in this competition but it seems as though they're clicking together and there's a flow to their game. "The players that Emery has brought in are starting to perform really well and it's a well-deserved win." Record £65m signing Jackson came to replace the departing Ollie Watkins after his £50m switch to Al-Hilal. He joined having helped Bayern Munich win the Bundesliga last season on loan from Chelsea, and on moving to Villa Park was reunited with Emery. The pair worked together at Villarreal, with Emery giving him his debut with the Yellow Submarine. The 25-year-old scored the final goal for Emery at Villarreal before the manager left for Villa in October 2022, a last-minute winner against Almeria, and has repaid the faith quickly on their reunion. The only thing missing for Jackson was a potential hat-trick, with Barkley - the pre-arranged penalty taker - scoring from the spot. "I wanted to take it but the most important thing is we win. Hopefully next time I'll get the hat-trick," Jackson told TNT Sports. "It's very important. We haven't won at home. Our keeper is amazing." Jackson's four goals in three games and five for the season in total allow Villa and their fans to move on quickly from Watkins, their record Premier League scorer, following a summer exit that threatened to turn acrimonious. Emery added: "Jackson is doing a fantastic job. "He's scoring, he's working defensively [and] helping the team. This is very important and maybe in the future he can shoot (from the spot) as well." Villa, and their new-look forward line, will now be eager for Saturday's trip to Newcastle, especially as Matthias Jaissle's side shipped four against Coventry on Monday to leave them with the joint-worst defensive record in the Premier League. And Jackson hopes he can prosper alongside his attacking colleagues. "He [Johan Manzambi] is a top player. I'm really happy we're playing together. I hope we score many more goals together," Jackson said. "[Ibrahim Mbaye] is [also] an amazing player. We're in the [Senegal] national team together and hopefully he'll get more time to play [for Villa]. He's very fast and it's good to have him." title: Martinez outburst came out of 'anger and frustration'
description: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez says he "spoke out of anger and frustration" when launching a scathing attack on the club's hierarchy.
body: Lisandro Martinez joined Manchester United from Ajax in 2022 Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez says he "spoke out of anger and frustration" when launching a scathing attack on the club's hierarchy. The Argentina international criticised United for not strengthening the squad in the summer following qualification for the Champions League in comments made after the 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid in the Champions League group phase on Tuesday. Martinez said he expected more investment in the United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]". However, while he stopped short of an apology, he said he has "belief in my team-mates, our manager [Michael Carrick] and everyone working to help this club move forward". "After the match, I spoke out of anger and frustration at not getting the result we all wanted," he wrote in a social media post. "Those who know me know how I live football, with passion, commitment and a huge desire to win. And when things don't go our way, it hurts, especially when representing a club with the history and stature of Manchester United. "My words reflect how I feel and how much I want to see this club competing for the biggest honours. "Those high standards are part of how I see football and the responsibility that comes with wearing this shirt. "When I talk about wanting more, I'm talking about the ambition we must all have as part of this club. "To keep growing, to become stronger and to have everything we need to compete at the highest level. "These are standards we must all hold ourselves to, starting with me." This video can not be played 'Players have a different responsibility' - Pundits react to Martinez comments Man Utd defender Martinez issues scathing attack on board Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout Manchester United have not won in five games since beating Sabah in the Champions League on 10 September. They have won just two of their nine games this season and are 13th in the Premier League with six points from as many games. Martinez's contract expires at the end of the season and United have the option to extend it by another year. He added: "I know that, first and foremost, it's us, the players, who have to deliver, and I put myself at the front of that responsibility. "We need to demand even more of ourselves and work together to take Manchester United back to the top. "I believe in my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward. "I'm convinced that the way forward is to keep working together, with ambition and commitment. "My goal has been the same since day one, to win, compete at the highest level and to give everything I have for this badge." Manchester United's next game will be at Leeds United in the Premier League on Sunday, 18 October. title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
description: Reform says all of those people filmed by ITV are under investigation having resigned or been suspended.
body: Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language. Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language. In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites". Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples." A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions. The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting. ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total. Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended. ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last. These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025. He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites". Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white." The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor. Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples." Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all". "I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said. In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting". The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed." Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community." A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."
