title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
description: Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What's going on between Kelly Clarkson and a Brooklyn store bird? On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual. Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?" Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall. The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000). "Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items. In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable". Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000. They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day. "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity." Molly the mechanical bird now has a price tag of $15m Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception." When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers. A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual. Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m. The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!" The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them. This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson. Customer Emily Trantanella likes Art of Play The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit. The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird. She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier. But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise. Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here. "I really like it here." title: Fewer than 800 Scots have received weight loss jabs on NHS, BBC finds
description: Only five of Scotland's 14 health boards currently offer the treatment specifically for weight loss, it has emerged.
body: Kathleen McLaughlin says she is grateful to be one of the patients accessing the jabs on the NHS Fewer than 800 Scots have received jabs for weight loss on the NHS despite them being approved for use three years ago, BBC News has found. While private prescriptions for Wegovey and Mounjaro have soared, fewer than half of Scotland's health boards currently offer the treatment specifically for weight loss - and then only as part of small pilot schemes. Leading doctors have described the situation as "discriminatory" and argued that the lack of access on the NHS is widening health inequalities. The Scottish government said the medicines were part of a range of treatments for obesity, and that individual health boards were responsible for decisions on the availability of medicines. A third of Scots are classified as obese, which can lead to serious health complications including cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes. Medications like Mounjaro and Wegovy have been prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes for many years, and are thought to have been used by thousands of patients. These GLP-1 injections suppress people's appetites, causing them to feel fuller sooner - but are not suitable for everyone and can have side effects. Mounjaro is one of the weight management drugs Mounjaro has been approved for use specifically for weight loss on the NHS in Scotland since 2023, and Wegovy was approved in 2024. We sent a freedom of information request to every health board in Scotland, asking them if they prescribe the jabs to patients specifically for weight loss. Five told us that they do prescribe the drugs as part of pilot projects which allow a small number of patients to access the jabs on the NHS. They are: NHS Forth Valley, NHS Borders, NHS Lothian, NHS Lanarkshire, NHS Western Isles and the NHS State Hospital. The figures showed that a total of 705 patients had received injections for weight loss by September 2026. It has been estimated that at least 300,000 people are accessing the drugs privately, according to the company Simple Online Pharmacy. Scotland's nine other health boards say they do not currently routinely prescribe for weight loss specifically, although some are looking to introduce access. There may be some exceptional circumstances where patients in those areas are able to access the drugs. Kathleen has been losing weight to prepare for surgery Kathleen McClaughlin, from Laurieston, is one of the patients who can access the injections on the NHS. The 54-year-old was referred to NHS Forth Valley's programme by her gynaecologist because she needs surgery, but her weight was too high for it to go ahead safely. Having "tried and failed many times" to lose weight, she now has arthritis and other mobility issues. "It stops your life progressing. You're just vegetating your life away," she said. Kathleen did not want to pay privately for the jabs, concerned about not having the right support. "I didn't want to go down that route without having somebody by my side to guide me through it," she said. Strict criteria were used to select patients for the Forth Valley pilot The pilot in Forth Valley involves regular check-ups with a pharmacist and dietician. Studies have found that people who come off weight loss injections can regain their lost pounds four times faster than those who stop conventional diet and exercise. To keep the weight off, experts say a package of measures is key, from healthier eating habits to exercise regimes and health monitoring. Kathleen has lost four stone since April - equivalent to 13% of her body weight - and says both her physical and mental health have improved. "I can't believe that I'm having the opportunity when so many other people are having to pay for it or not having even the chance for it," she added. Who can get weight loss drugs on the NHS in Scotland? Weight-loss drug approved for use by NHS Scotland Strict criteria were used to select patients for the programme, which is based at Falkirk Community Hospital. They needed to have a BMI of 40 or above and be living with at least four serious medical conditions, or in need of life-altering surgery. It currently involves 48 patients, while a further 18 receive the drugs directly through their GP practices. However, the weight loss service is not accepting new referrals while the pilot is under way. Claire Colligan, NHS Forth Valley's associate director of pharmacy for primary and community care, says the board wants to expand the programme but needs to ensure it is manageable. "It's very frustrating for people to know that these medicines are available and that they're not able to access them through the NHS - but these drugs are not going away," she said. "We'll have more understanding of how they work, which groups to target." Access to weight loss drugs on the NHS is governed by strict criteria across the UK. Last year, BBC Scotland News established that very few people were accessing them on the NHS in Scotland. Dr Mark Strachan, a diabetes specialist and president of the Royal College of Physicians, said it was "unacceptable" that there had been "no meaningful progress" since then. "The NHS is spending colossal amounts of money every year to treat the complications of obesity," he said. "And the NHS pays for these rather than paying for interventions that would treat the underlying obesity and reduce the health consequences." Doctors have previously warned that if everyone eligible for the jabs could get them on the NHS then it would bankrupt the health service overnight. Dr Strachan said they were "safe" and "cost-effective", and could be rolled out in a targeted way to those at most risk. Dr Mark Strachan is a diabetes specialist "The problem that we're seeing at the moment is that many health boards aren't rolling out these medicines at all, even to those who are in the highest possible risk categories and individuals

title: My contraceptive coil saved my life after it revealed I had cancer
description: Caroline Bailey was diagnosed after suffering with "a stabbing pain in the middle of my abdomen".
body: Caroline Bailey says she has completed several goals on her "tick list" since being diagnosed, including travelling to Italy and moving to a cottage in Wales When Caroline Bailey was suffering with sharp, stabbing pains in her stomach, she thought it was being caused by her contraceptive coil. In severe pain, the 54-year-old went to her GP, desperate to have it removed, only for scans to reveal it was in fact a 13cm (5in) tumour pressing against her coil, external. She was diagnosed with stage three ovarian cancer, external in June 2023 and feared she might not live for another two years. Now, with no evidence of disease after chemotherapy and surgery, she said: "I absolutely think that the coil saved my life, which is mad." She had been experiencing severe abdominal pain since March and thought the coil was to blame. "I started to have the worst stomach pains – like a stabbing pain in the middle of my abdomen," she said. "So, I kept going back into the doctors and said, 'I think the coil needs to come out'." Caroline, from Trelogan, Flintshire, said she was referred to a sexual health clinic as there were no appointments available, but staff there could not remove it. With her pain getting worse, she "crawled into the doctors on my hands and knees" in May, asking for the coil to be removed. "I wanted to rip it out myself, but you can't. I thought it was killing me." "I was going to the doctor, saying, 'This coil is stabbing me', and I just hate how long it took for me to be taken seriously. "I wish it was easier for women to get diagnosed." Caroline was diagnosed with endometriosis – where cells similar to those in the lining of the womb grow in other parts of the body – in her mid 20s. But, with "no history of ovarian cancer in the family whatsoever" so thought her pain was being caused by her coil. Caroline had a total hysterectomy - where the womb and cervix are removed - along with the removal of her omentum and appendix Caroline said she was given a CA125 blood test form, which is used to check the level of the CA125 protein in the blood and can support a diagnosis of ovarian cancer, as her doctor wanted to see if that was causing the problems. She was given this form as, although she believed it was the coil causing her pain, a doctor wanted to check for ovarian cancer due to her symptoms. She took a blood test that can support a diagnosis of ovarian cancer that returned a reading of proteins of 72 units per ml (U/ml). According to charity Ovarian Cancer Action, women over 40 should be referred for further investigations if it is over 35 U/ml. Caroline was put on a two-week pathway, which she described as being "in this crazy world of, oh my God". Subsequent scans revealed the tumour and a biopsy confirmed the cancer was stage three and it had spread to the omentum – a large piece of fatty tissue that lies near to the womb and ovaries. The NHS lists the main symptoms of ovarian cancer, external as frequently - approximately 12 or more times a month - having: A swollen tummy or feeling bloated Pain or tenderness in the tummy or the area between your hips No appetite or feeling full quickly after eating An urgent need to wee or needing to wee more often "I couldn't believe the size of it. I actually thought, 'I won't live for another two years'," Caroline said. She started chemotherapy soon after and had four rounds of treatment at The Christie in Manchester, which shrank her tumour to 8cm (3in). On October 26, she had a total hysterectomy - where the womb and cervix are removed - along with the removal of her omentum and appendix during a six-hour operation. The surgery means Caroline now has no evidence of disease, but she was told ovarian cancer can be "unpredictable" with a high re-occurrence rate. One month after her surgery, Caroline's grandson Roman was born, and she underwent two further rounds of chemotherapy in January 2024, along with follow-up CT scans. As part of the testing, it was revealed that she had gene mutations that increased her risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Caroline now wants to encourage other women to get any unusual symptoms checked and to advocate for themselves Caroline is now having consultations about a double mastectomy to remove both breasts, along with reconstruction surgery and implants, as part of a trial, and her family members are being genetically tested. "But the best thing about this, about having ovarian cancer, is my girls know what they're dealing with and they can have preventative surgery," she said. "My diagnosis makes me live for now... and what I know now is, tomorrow is definitely not guaranteed." Caroline moved house several times during her treatment, got divorced and lost her job - even living out of her car - and said money was her "biggest worry". She now wants to encourage other women to get any unusual symptoms checked and to advocate for themselves. "I've definitely had to change my life because I had cancer," she said. "My motto is: Be healthy, be happy, be kind." Cancer Research UK, external said ovarian cancer was the 16th most common cancer, with about 7,700 new cases every year. In July 2026, 51.3% of women started their first definitive treatment within 62 days, external of first being suspected of having gynaecological cancer - well below the target of 75% - according to Welsh government data. title: PSG on 'different level' - are they building greatest European dynasty?
description: Paris St-Germain are eyeing a third successive Champions League crown after dismantling Manchester City, but where do they rank against Europe's most dominant clubs?
body: PSG are looking to win five pieces of silverware this season Some find success sweet but fleeting, others spend years building to the pinnacle, and then there are those whose lasting glory evolves into a dynasty. After tearing Manchester City apart in large spells of their 4-2 Champions League victory on Wednesday, Paris St-Germain look well on track to join the latter bracket. The back-to-back European champions sliced through City with astonishing ease to take a 3-0 lead into half-time, and were still able to score another despite a spirited second-half fightback from the Premier League leaders. After obliterating Inter Milan 5-0 in the 2025 final before squeezing past Arsenal on penalties in last season's showpiece game, Luis Enrique's side are aiming to win a third consecutive European crown. They would be the fifth team to do so going back to 1956, and just the second in the Champions League era. "This PSG team are on a different level," Chris Sutton told BBC Radio 5 Live at half-time. "They have just run all over Manchester City, who haven't been able to string passes together. It's been an absolute pummelling for Man City." To mark PSG's latest display of attacking excellence, we're looking at how the Parisians compare to those clubs who have enjoyed the most dominant eras in European competition. Some will point out that football existed before the European Champion Clubs' Cup began in 1955 - so apologies to Stan Cullis' 'world-champion' Wolves outfit and the Mitropa Cup's early Vienna heavyweights. However, this top 10 debate is centred around winning European football's grandest prize. OK, straight in with the current champions, because this is a dynasty in the making. Paris St-Germain are hoping to enter that bracket and the 4-2 win against Manchester City on Wednesday reminded the rest of Europe why you shouldn't bet against them becoming continental champions for a third successive season. PSG had a lacklustre start to the domestic season - they always do, don't they? - but boast an uncanny ability to click into gear when it matters. In Manchester, Luis Enrique's side were at their unstoppable best. A ruthless blend of silky flicks and slick off-the-ball movement that saw a dazed City caught several frames behind. "Unbelievable. PSG, what a team," Sutton said. "PSG's press, I don't think there's another team that press with their intensity and ferocity. "This [City] is one of the best teams in the Premier League getting an absolutely roasting. This is them [PSG] having a slow start to the season. Heaven help everyone." The Parisians have been France's most dominant force since the arrival of Qatar Sports Investments 15 years ago, but it took a change of approach for the holy grail of continental success to arrive. "It's the end of the glitter," professed president Nasser Al-Khelaifi after years of lavish spending, ushering out the "flashy, bling-bling" era. Instead, Enrique arrived in 2023 intent on building a coherent team. There was still significant investment, but on younger players who could be moulded by his philosophy and discipline while given room to flourish. The result was two scintillating Champions League triumphs. PSG thrashed Inter 5-0 to win their first Champions League in 2025 Guardiola's return, Man City's defiance - and a game of glorious chaos Talking of discipline. Helenio Herrera, the Argentine-born defender reared in Casablanca and Paris, had already traversed the dugouts of Atletico Madrid, Malaga, Deportivo and Barcelona before landing in Milan in 1960. Herrera set about implementing his tactical brand of catenaccio at San Siro - one he insisted is misremembered as being more defensive than it actually was - and developing a ruthless counter-attacking team known as 'Grande Inter'. Winning the Scudetto in 1962-63, Herrera's outfit became the first to lift the European Cup without losing a game the following season as Sandro Mazzola netted twice against Real Madrid in the final. The Italians defended their crown the following year, despite losing their semi-final first leg at Anfield, edging Benfica in the final. It was the Portuguese giants' second final defeat in three seasons. Some may say they were cursed... Helenio Herrera won league titles with Inter, Barcelona and Atletico Madrid The story goes that Bela Guttmann, fresh from winning the title with Porto, rocked up at Benfica, sacked all the senior players and promoted a talented bunch of youth team players instead. Those promising youngsters won the title and then went all the way in the European Cup, beating Barcelona in the 1961 final. That summer, a teenage Eusebio also joined Guttmann's squad and steered them to European glory once more, seeing off Tottenham Hotspur in the semi-final before beating the great Real Madrid in the competition's showpiece. The legendary Ferenc Puskas scored a first-half hat-trick for the Spaniards, but Eusebio netted twice after the interval to seal Benfica a second successive crown. Guttmann, buoyed by his remarkable success, left the club after not being offered the pay rise he felt he deserved and the curse the Hungarian boss supposedly put on the club - that they would not win another European trophy for 100 years - has become fable. Whether the often-disputed story is true or not, the Lisbon giants have not landed another since - losing eight European finals, including three in the 1960s. Eusebio scored 47 goals in the European Cup, including two in the 1962 final This was Bayern's coming of age. Emerging from what was a fiercely competitive West German football scene, the Bavarians - promoted to the Bundesliga less than a decade earlier - were able to establish themselves as heavyweights in Europe. title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
description: The home secretary said she would not hesitate to impose measures on other countries "refusing to co-operate".
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders. From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs. Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans. Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals, external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library. The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment. "Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood. She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate". The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year. The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission. The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara. Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved. Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced. When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies. Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally. According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year. There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year. Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence. title: Musk says any limits on Ukraine's Starlink access down to US, not his firm
description: Ukraine says Starlink access has improved but it is still facing speed limits which are disrupting its battlefield "missions".
body: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network. Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions. An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington. Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]". Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on." Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network. It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support". About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company". The US government has not commented. While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use. The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits". At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning. This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities. Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this. Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel. "Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed. During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles. Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones. "We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky. title: On night of mayhem for Liverpool, Barcola arrives in style
description: Bradley Barcola's form was the subject of pre-match questions before Liverpool faced LASK - but the France forward's Champions League hat-trick was the perfect answer.
body: This video can not be played Hat-trick hero: Barcola scores three as Liverpool hit six against LASK On the eve of Liverpool's meeting with LASK, manager Andoni Iraola was repeatedly asked about the fortunes of Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. Given their price tags, the pressure was on both to start delivering after stuttering starts to their individual campaigns. Iraola, as most managers would, stood by his players, insisting he trusted them "100%". Iraola insisted the focus was on the collective rather than individual stats but there is no denying that when you spend such eye-watering sums - £116m on Wirtz and £123m on Barcola - you want those players to be match-winners. Wirtz delivered a fine display in the Austrian city of Linz as Liverpool won 6-3, with an assist to show for his efforts. However, this was a night where the headlines belonged to Barcola, who on the 238th appearance of his career across clubs and country combined, scored his first hat-trick. And it was those three goals which proved to be the difference as Liverpool returned to winning ways after their 3-0 loss to Manchester City on Sunday. In truth, the 24-year-old could have scored more such was his quality, but he did enough to take the match ball home after two fine finishes with his right foot and left foot, followed by a tap in after the break. And a little over 24 hours after defending his players against those pre-match questions, Iraola was speaking with a smile on his face. "I'm really happy for Bradley," Iraola said. "You were asking me yesterday about him not making the numbers and [the same with] Florian and I think both of them today played really, really well. I think they made a difference. "Bradley was a threat, always when one-on-one [and] certainly in behind. He helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am and happy for both of them. "I think for their confidence it's very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. I think it's going to be very good, very good for them." On what it could mean for Barcola, Iraola added: "I think he has to enjoy this [as] to score a hat-trick in the Champions League is always very difficult. "Even yesterday in training, I could feel he was very lively. Sometimes you feel these things [are going to happen]. We were feeling he was in a good place going into the game." Barcola will now hope to show that level in the Premier League, starting with a visit to Brentford on Saturday. This video can not be played Highlights: Nine goals, six for Liverpool, three for Barcola as LASK lose at home Iraola's side were relentless in the first-half against the Austrian Bundesliga champions, racing into a three-goal lead. Such was their dominance, they could have easily scored more. The 19 shots Liverpool had by half time against LASK was the most on record since 2003-04 by any team in the first half of a Champions League away match. If there was any criticism, it would be that they were guilty of becoming a little complacent in the second half, conceding three goals after the hour mark but in fairness, the job was all but done. There were more positives to take on the night, with both full-backs coming into the side and performing well. Jeremie Frimpong scored and registered two assists while Kostas Tsimikas added two assists of his own. Ronald Araujo also scored his first goal for the club since joining in the summer and Lewis Koumas got no less than he deserved when he got on the scoresheet in the second half. The 21-year-old even had two goals ruled out for offside but his first-half assist for Barcola meant that he became the youngster player to score and assist in a Champions League match for Liverpool (21y 25d), with the previous youngest being Steven Gerrard (21y 139d v Dynamo Kyiv in 2001). Fine company, indeed. But Liverpool will know that they won’t get many easier games than this over the course of the season. LASK came into this game, winless in their last four matches. “What do you take from that? It's very difficult because the game was very passive for large periods,” said Stephen Warnock on 5 Live. ”There were parts where I am watching Trey Nyoni in midfield and he has literally got no pressure on him at all, he is picking passes off. “Barcola has got the run of his full-back who was taken off at half-time, which tells you everything. “I don't read too much into it, because I expected Liverpool to go there and win, and win comfortably." Warnock added that a bigger test for Liverpool will come at Brentford on Saturday, the Bees fourth in the table and unbeaten in the league. “Can Barcola do that again, away at Brentford, because that is what they have essentially bought him for, to play in big games away from home," Warnock said. “He hasn't played that much football this season so [this game] was about getting minutes in his legs and getting him fit and getting him sharper. The acid test will be Brentford away.” Latest Liverpool news, analysis and fan views Ask about Liverpool - what do you want to know? title: Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as Ukraine's leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine.
body: This video can not be played Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine. Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine. Burnham previously told MPs that he would try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States and that Ukraine won't leave "empty-handed". The two leaders met at No 10 Downing Street where Zelensky was welcomed with a military ceremonial guard - thought to be a first for a foreign leader. BBC World News correspondent Joe Inwood explains what we know about the meeting. Read more about the meeting in London. Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters. title: Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania
description: Buildings were set alight on the second day of demonstrations from thousands of students who want better university conditions and job prospects.
body: The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on Wednesday Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests. The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects. Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked. Albania's Deputy Prime Minister ​Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change". Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gates Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them. One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania". "The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said. Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen". Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things". Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system" Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters. "Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building. Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said. Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters. "The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported. This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government. title: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
description: It is the "backbone of military communications in Ukraine" that provides vital high-speed internet to forces across the country.
body: Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on. Kyiv has adopted it as a vital battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare. Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones are able to maintain stronger connections with operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming. But a sudden speed restriction for drones connected to Starlink means some battlefield "missions" have been disrupted, according to a top Ukrainian official. Serhiy Beskrestnov also said officials had not been told about the 100mph (160km/h) speed limits set overnight on Tuesday by Elon Musk's SpaceX company. Throttling drones connected to the network at this relatively low speed makes Ukrainian efforts to intercept jet-powered Russian drones all but useless, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW). Musk's network of satellites makes Ukrainian drone operators more effective Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces. Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized." Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network. Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said. Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible. Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need. The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine. Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington. President Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk. Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX. Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology. And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders. title: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
description: The Ukrainian president visited London in an effort to bolster support among European allies following a row with Donald Trump.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Burnham welcomes Zelensky to No 10 with military ceremonial guard "We are behind you and that will not change," Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelensky, as he hosted the Ukrainian leader in Downing Street. Zelensky was in London as part of efforts to reinforce backing from allies after Donald Trump called for him to go and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel. The prime minister said Ukraine was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire proposed by the US president but said Russia's response had been "further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine". Zelensky said: "Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I'm very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it's your people, Andy." The Ukrainian president was greeted with a hug from Burnham, cheers from civil servants and a rare honour guard as he arrived in Downing Street. Ahead of Zelensky's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones. Burnham careful as he meets Zelensky but promises Ukraine won't leave 'empty handed' Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC Ukrainian officials have said that overnight strikes by Russian missiles and drones had left at least 600,000 people without electricity. For the second consecutive night, Ukraine said it had not received advanced warning from its allies of a wave of missile strikes coming from Russia. Zelensky has suggested the US had threatened to restrict intelligence-sharing unless he agreed to sign up to an energy ceasefire. Trump has denied the US is holding back information. An adviser to the president has also said Ukraine's ability to defend itself from incoming missiles has been hindered by disruptions to its connection with the Starlink internet network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company. Serhiy Beskrestnov said the move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented. Speaking in Downing Street, Burnham said the recent days had been "dark and difficult" for Ukraine, with the country suffering "heavy bombardment". He told the Ukrainian leader: "You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. "We are behind you and that will not change." Earlier in the day, Burnham had been invited to criticise the US decision to lift sanctions on Russia, when, at Prime Minister's Questions, Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey asked if the PM agreed there had been a "shameful Trump betrayal". Burnham acknowledged that Zelensky was "carrying the heaviest of weights" but avoided attacking Trump, instead telling MPs that his role was to "repair bridges so that the support comes back". "Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together." He added that Zelensky would not come away from his trip "empty-handed". In a statement following the meeting, a Downing Street spokeswoman said the leaders had discussed "Russia's blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure". She said the prime minister promised that the UK would continue to develop "innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners". On Friday, Trump shocked European allies when he announced that he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel, with more to follow. Concerns about the cost of living are playing a key part in the US's November elections and the US president hopes his deal with Russia will reduce the cost of diesel. The agreement runs counter to sanctions imposed on Russia by the US and its allies in a bid to choke off funds for Putin's war in Ukraine. The deal came days after Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" and that it was time for Ukraine to "get a new president". The criticism marks a renewal of Trump's previous hostility towards Zelensky which resulted in an infamous public row between the two men in the Oval Office. title: The Media Show
description: An extended interview with acclaimed screenwriter and producer Russell T Davies.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·14 Oct 2026,·42 mins Available for over a year This week, an extended interview with the screenwriter and producer Russell T Davies. He talks to Katie and Ros about his long career in television, from early days in children's TV, to bringing back Doctor Who, to his more recent successes like the critically acclaimed Tip Toe. He also gives his thoughts on the media landscape today, including the role of AI and the lack of commissioning opportunities. Also, former barrister and legal correspondent Clive Coleman, now a specialist in crisis PR and reputation management, and former BBC news exec Katy Searle discuss the BBC's defamation settlement with the founder of LGBTQ+ news site Pink News and his husband over a 2024 investigation. How should the BBC respond when it gets things wrong? And after Reform UK's Deputy Leader Richard Tice issued a statement criticising ITV for an upcoming investigation, we explore the editorial and legal implications of going undercover. Presenters: Katie Razzall and Ros Atkins Producers: Lisa Jenkinson and Tim Bano

title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
description: Confirming the review, the government said it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".
body: Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years. Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10. Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City. The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly". The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives". The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers". "We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC. "Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do." The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year. None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC. It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports. Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport. "Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports. She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution". The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports. Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households. Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? title: Cokayne back as England face Canada threat in Toronto
description: England welcome back the experience of Amy Cokayne at hooker as their 41-match unbeaten run comes under serious threat away to Canada.
body: Cokayne celebrates scoring a try in England's win over France in May England welcome back the experienced Amy Cokayne at hooker as their 41-match unbeaten run goes on the line against Rugby World Cup runners-up Canada in Toronto on Friday. Cokayne has not played Test rugby since scoring the Red Roses' final try in a Grand Slam-sealing win over France in Bordeaux in May. Saracens' Bryony Field, who has three caps to Cokayne's 94, drops to the bench after deputising impressively in the first half of the WXV Global Series last month. During that part of the campaign, Canada ended England's near four-year winning streak with a nail-biting 26-26 draw at Sandy Park in Exeter. Saturday 17 October, 00:00 BST Live on the BBC iPlayer, BBC Sport website and app Coach Kevin Rouet has targeted victory over the Red Roses as the main aim for Canada in 2026, with his team playing on home soil for the first time in more than 14 months. Canada also play England in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October, with the two matches branded as the hosts' Rugby Rematch Tour. The attendance for the Toronto match is expected to exceed 14,000, comfortably beating the previous record for a standalone women's rugby match in North America which was set when 11,453 watched Canada beat the United States in the most recent home match. This video can not be played Watch highlights: England 26-26 Canada Elsewhere in England's line-up, prop Hannah Botterman features after coming on as a replacement in the dramatic win over New Zealand last time out. With Marlie Packer staying in England as her partner and Red Roses team-mate Rosie Galligan is due to give birth, Abi Burton takes a spot in the back row, while Tatyana Heard's direct running is preferred to Helena Rowland's playmaking ability at inside centre. Sadia Kabeya, who missed the win over the Black Ferns with a leg injury, is on the bench, alongside Bristol Bears' 20-year-old Demelza Short, who covers second row. "The first Test in Exeter gave us a valuable opportunity to test our game under pressure and identify where we can improve," England head coach John Mitchell said. "Playing in Toronto presents a different environment and challenge, and we're excited by the opportunity to express our game, improve our performance and continue to grow as the Red Roses." England's last loss came in the Rugby World Cup final against New Zealand in November 2022. England: Kildunne; Breach, Jones, Heard, Moloney-MacDonald; Harrison, L Packer; Botterman, Cokayne, Bern, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Matthews, Feaunati. Replacements: Field, Carson, Muir, Short, Kabeya, Hunt, Rowland, Sing. title: Watch: Dolphin in river freed by fire crews and divers
description: Marine medics work to remove netting from its beak and release the dolphin back towards the sea.
body: This video can not be played Marine experts and firefighters have together helped to free a tangled dolphin spotted out of its depth in a Suffolk river. The marine mammal, which had become trapped in netting, was filmed swimming in the River Orwell in Ipswich as crowds gathered to catch a glimpse. Andy Hollis filmed the dolphin swimming, describing it as "quite a spectacle", but said he was worried about it "getting injured". The British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR), which attended, warned people to keep their distance, adding: "This is a critical period of recovery for the animal and it needs time and space to do so without any additional stress or distraction." The BDMLR said it was "distressingly spotted" with green netting "wrapped around its beak and pectoral fins". "Despite the entanglement," the service added, "the dolphin was able to breathe and swim strongly, moving up and down the river and actively avoiding vessels nearby." Initially, the animal was spotted swimming in circles and travelling some distance upriver. The BDMLR said it was "a behaviour occasionally seen in some species of dolphin and harbour porpoises following food sources, so is not always a cause for concern". Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service deployed a crew on a boat, which marine mammal medics used to cut the dolphin free, before assessing its condition. It had sustained minor wounds, the BDLMR said. Volunteers would continue to monitor the dolphin, the spokesperson added, and "we remain hopeful that it will find its way back to sea". title: Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim
description: It follows the death last week of a man who had arrived in Kenya after travelling from DR Congo.
body: The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant". "Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said. "Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added. Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi. A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected. Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said. Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. "Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said. The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way. Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death. It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities. He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings. Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations. title: Millwall's Neil criticised over racial abuse stoppage comments
description: Anti-racism campaign group Kick It Out calls on managers to "set the tone" after Millwall boss Alex Neil criticises halting a game following an accusation of abuse.
body: The game was stopped for seven minutes while referee Edward Duckworth sought to speak to Millwall's safety officer Anti-racism campaign group Kick It Out has called on football managers to "set the tone" after Millwall boss Alex Neil criticised the decision to halt their game against Swansea City following an accusation of racist abuse. Tuesday's Championship match was brought to a standstill for seven minutes, midway through the second half, after reports of discriminatory chants directed at Swansea substitute Ji-sung Eom, which the Metropolitan Police is investigating. After the game, Neil told BBC Radio London: "It needs to get dealt with. [But] stopping the game doesn't deal with anything. All it does is kill the momentum." A statement from Kick It Out said: "Player welfare should always take precedence over the momentum or flow of a match, and it's essential that managers and all leaders recognise this and set the tone with their language so that everyone can stand up to discrimination." Police investigate alleged racial abuse of Swans' Eom When he was alerted to the accusations, referee Edward Duckworth had lengthy discussions with both sets of coaches and paused the match while he waited to pass a message on to Millwall's safety officer. Following the stoppage, an announcement was made over the speakers at The Den confirming there had been alleged chants of racism and that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV. "I understand, obviously, there's been an incident," Neil said. "That's not something I'm going to get involved in - that'll be for the authorities to deal with. "But the fact that it stops the game, I just don't see the point. "The referee was wanting to speak to whoever the safety officer is, and then when he spoke to him, it [the game] restarted. "That's partly my frustration. I want to get the game restarted, I want to get the game played. "I understand there's other things that are going on, but you're not dealing with it down there, are you? It's going to get dealt with after the event anyway." After the match restarted, Millwall went on to concede a 90th-minute goal to lose 1-0. "If we score, I probably don't feel this way, let's be honest," Neil added. Kick It Out, which has campaigned for more than 30 years to eradicate racism from football, said it was disappointed to hear reports of racist abuse towards Eom. "Both clubs have condemned the incident, and it's positive that Millwall and match officials followed the right protocols so that action can be taken to identify any individual responsible," the organisation said. "In that moment, protocols are in place to help match and security officials respond appropriately. "That ensures that players are protected and key details are captured so that accountability can follow, regardless of how long it takes." This video can not be played Listen to Alex Neil's post-match comments Millwall stated they were "aware of an alleged, individual incident of discriminatory abuse towards a Swansea City player during the second half" of the game. "The club operates a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of discriminatory abuse," a club statement said after the game. "Any individual found to have engaged in such behaviour will face the strongest possible action." Swansea City head coach Vitor Matos praised the referee and Millwall's club staff for their responses to the incident. "The referee followed the protocol for these sort of situations, they did the right thing," he said. "Millwall did the right thing by announcing there is no place for this sort of thing. I'm happy with how it was handled, but really sad that it happened." title: I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats, says Swinney
description: The first minister speaks to BBC Scotland News ahead of the SNP's annual conference in Aberdeen.
body: This video can not be played John Swinney: There is an obligation on the UK Government to ensure the country is safe First Minister John Swinney says he does not have confidence the UK is safe from potential Russian threats. The SNP leader said the UK government, which is in charge of Britain's defences, did not have a sufficient "presence" in vulnerable areas off Scotland's coast. He said he was "very worried" by security fears highlighted this week by the head of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, who named Russia as "aggressor number one". Speaking to BBC Scotland News ahead of the SNP's annual conference, Swinney also denied that independence would weaken Scotland's security. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government is committed to investing in defence, including nuclear deterrence, while not seeking to escalate tensions with Russia. MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI Burnham to visit Scotland during SNP conference No probe into claims Swinney misled Holyrood Asked about the MI5 chief's comments, the first minister said he was "very worried" about a "lack of coastal and offshore protection". He identified waters north of Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity. "I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News. "There's an obligation on the United Kingdom government to make sure that the country is safe. And I don't think the defence posture of the United Kingdom enables me to have that confidence." Scotland is home to the UK's nuclear submarine fleet at Faslane, west of Glasgow. The SNP wants those weapons to be removed, but is in favour of an independent Scotland joining Nato. Swinney insisted that independence would not hamper Scotland's security, but rather give the country "more choices". The SNP leader said he had "always been a believer in defence co-operation between Scotland and other countries", citing Canada joining the EU's SAFE defence programme, external. Responding to the first minister's comments, a Ministry of Defence Spokesperson said: "The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe, and this government is investing £298bn over the next four years to ensure we can tackle rising threats. "The Navy is helping to patrol Nato's northern flank, with this year's carrier strike group deploying to the Arctic and the high north. "To tackle these threats, we're also investing in new frigates for the Navy and high-tech uncrewed vessels as part of our Hybrid Navy, backed by £1.5bn in funding." Delivering a speech at the UN General Assembly, external last month, Burnham said his government would invest in defence and build up the UK's "hard power and deterrence". He added: "But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation." SNP members are gathering in Aberdeen for the party's annual conference, which starts on Thursday and ends with Swinney's keynote speech on Saturday afternoon. Burnham has also selected this weekend to visit Scotland. He is expected to travel to the central belt to discuss plans to devolve power to local communities. Swinney, who has invited the Labour leader to the SNP conference, said he had "not yet" accepted the offer. The first minister welcomed Burnham's recent announcement that he wanted to secure better trade terms with the EU for producers of salmon, shellfish, and seed potatoes. The prime minister also wants to discuss even closer ties with the bloc and has not ruled out a future referendum on rejoining. Swinney told the BBC: "I think it's an interesting precedent that if we can reopen an issue that's been decided by a referendum, then we can also reopen Scottish independence." John Swinney and Andy Burnham have clashed over Scotland's constitutional future Ahead of the conference, the SNP announced it would launch a new independence campaign - including a national day of action, digital and broadcast adverts, and an independence survey delivered to almost 1.5m people. The Scottish government is aiming to hold a second referendum by 2031. The Supreme Court has ruled that could only happen with Westminster's consent. Arguing the case for a second vote, Swinney points to the record number of pro-independence MSPs elected to Holyrood in May - though the proportion of pro-independence votes decreased from about 50% to about 41% since 2021. Burnham said in the Commons last month that a second referendum could be held once there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed. However, he later insisted that there was no consensus, adding that such a vote remained "off limits". Burnham later made a special mention of Swinney In his speech to the Labour Party conference, insisting he was "utterly determined" to prove wrong the SNP leader's prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK. Swinney was also challenged on the preparedness of the NHS for winter pressures after an emergency doctor warned of "unsafe levels of care" and a "toxic normalisation" of corridor care. Dr Fiona Hunter, vice-chair of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine in Scotland, told BBC Scotland News that she was "completely terrified" of the situation. The first minister said he could "hear, understand and appreciate" these concerns and accepted that there were "significant challenges" in the system. However, he said hospital flow plans were designed to reduce pressures and the Scottish government intended to end corridor care "at the earliest possible opportunity". title: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
description: The Irish writer is best known for novels such as Normal People, Intermezzo and Conversations With Friends.
body: Sally Rooney has sold more than six million copies of her novels globally Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action. The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK. In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK. "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said. Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies. Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves. Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData. Normal People was released in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones. Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You. Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. "To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher. "As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format." Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories." Rooney's four novels, including her most recent, Intermezzo, will be removed from sale in the UK The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage. The group's activities have included targeting arms companies linked to Israel's war in Gaza. In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: "In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. "The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland." In her article last August in the Irish Times, Rooney said she would continue using proceeds from her work to support the group despite that being an offence in the UK, and cancelled a UK trip to pick up an award over fears she would be arrested. On Wednesday, Rooney continued: "As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. "After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK." Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said Rooney had taken "a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced". Ammori said the author's work being withdrawn marked "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action". More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of Palestine Action. About 2,500 have been charged, although none have gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription continues and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month. title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
description: The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide.
body: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals. The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce. Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to". The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers. In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation". Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount. Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". TV series Below, starring Josh Hartnett, is one of Netflix's most popular shows The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October. Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series. It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films. However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer. He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau. "Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said. The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade. title: Danny Dyer in floating poo water protest on Thames
description: Along with the Sittingbourne and Sheppey MP, Dyer is calling for water companies to be nationalised.
body: Danny Dyer led calls for nationalisation of the water industry on the River Thames on a float with a large poo sculpture on it Actor Danny Dyer has delivered a petition to Downing Street calling for water companies to be nationalised after floating a giant poo sculpture down the River Thames on a boat. Dyer and Sittingbourne and Sheppey MP Kevin McKenna sailed along the Thames with the sculpture as part of a protest calling for the water industry to be brought into public ownership. The actor, who runs a caravan park on the Isle of Sheppey with daughter Dani Dyer, delivered the petition having previously joined a local sewage protest in Leysdown in September. A government spokesperson said it would "give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible". Nearly 350,000 people have signed the petition, started by campaigners SOS Whitstable. Rivals actor Dyer and his daughter, who is currently competing on Strictly Come Dancing, joined the protest in September alongside singer Becky Hill, and Surfers Against Sewage. He previously called the quality of bathing water "a disgrace", adding that issues with sewage discharges were "a very dangerous thing". Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he wants to see "greater public control" of the water and energy sectors, but suggestions that water companies could be nationalised have received pushback, including from lenders to Thames Water. A government spokesperson said the prime minister had been "clear that the failures of the past must be corrected". It added: "We are bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment." Dyer and Sittingbourne and Sheppey MP Kevin McKenna (left) delivered the petition to Downing Street According to Defra's Bathing Water Quality site, the most recent classification for Leysdown is rated good, based on samples taken from 2022 to 2025. There have been no pollution incidents reported there, the website states. Speaking outside Downing Street, McKenna told the BBC: "What you see is what you get with Danny, he is a man of passion and he is determined to do this. "He has been meeting with a lot of local people who have shown him the scale of the problem. "The vast majority of the public is really sick of it [sewage discharges] - they want it ended, I want it ended, and Danny wants it ended." A spokesperson for trade body Water UK said it was working to end sewage discharges "as fast as we possibly can". Southern Water, which supplies water to the Isle of Sheppey, said it was "tackling the root causes of pollution through our record £8.9bn investment programme" and cut pollution incidents by almost a third between 2023 and 2025. "No pollution is acceptable and we're working as fast as possible to bring about the improvements our customers expect", it added.
