title: Man, 70, died of eye cancer after scan concerns weren't followed up
description: A coroner warns there's a risk of future deaths due to "substantial delays" in ophthalmology follow-ups.
body: Figures indicate there are about 140,000 ophthalmology follow-up appointments awaiting review in Wales, but just 65 consultant ophthalmologists available A 70-year-old man died of eye cancer after a recommended appointment was not followed up by health professionals, an inquest found. Alexandar McDonald died at the Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen, on 30 November 2025, from the effects of metastatic choroidal melanoma, external. But a coroner found he could have begun treatment six months earlier, and warned more patients in Wales were at "significant risk", as figures showed 140,000 ophthalmology follow-up appointments awaiting review, but just 65 consultant ophthalmologists available. The Welsh government said it was "vital that lessons are learned from this tragic case, caused by unacceptable failings in the management of referrals". The inquest into McDonald's death heard he had attended an urgent ophthalmology appointment in June 2022 following a routine eye test, where concerns were raised following a scan. Although a consultant determined he needed to be reviewed again in six months, he received no follow-up appointment. At a routine check-up in June 2023, however, concerns were raised and a further scan led to an eye cancer diagnosis. Gwent area coroner Rose Farmer heard that, had McDonald been given a previous follow-up appointment as recommended, the melanoma would have been diagnosed six months earlier, with treatment beginning almost immediately. Following the "delayed diagnosis", the inquest heard McDonald underwent several treatments, but the cancer had later metastasised to his liver, leading to his death. Outlining her concerns, the coroner said there was a "risk that future deaths could occur unless action is taken". In a prevention of future deaths report sent to the Welsh government's department for health and social care, Farmer said there were "substantial delays in ophthalmology follow-up appointments across Wales". She also said the ophthalmology "capacity appears insufficient to meet the demand", adding that the absence of a national mechanism means those "requiring surveillance for ophthalmic conditions may experience prolonged delays". Alexander McDonald died at the Grange Hospital in Cwmbran in November 2025 "This case demonstrates the impact of not having timely follow up appointments," the coroner added. "Similar delays may place other patients at risk of delayed diagnosis of malignancy and death." Responding to the report, the Welsh government said: "It is vital that lessons are learned from this tragic case, caused by unacceptable failings in the management of referrals, and our thoughts are with the family of Alexander McDonald. "All health boards should have standard operating procedures in place to manage specific operational matters raised in the report, including capacity to meet the demand for follow-up surveillance and ensure patients who require ongoing monitoring are reviewed within clinically intended timescales. "As a government we will robustly hold health boards to account for performance." Mohamed Elalfy, president of the Royal College of Opthalmologists, said services in Wales face a "number of long-standing challenges, including dilapidated estates, workforce shortages and poor IT infrastructure". "These are key reasons why many patients often unfortunately face unacceptable delay," he said, calling on the implementation of reforms "as an urgent priority". title: Fifa to offer extra £2.6bn for football development
description: Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development across the world.
body: Fifa president Gianni Infantino will be standing for re-election in March Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development across the world. World football's governing body wants to release the money from its reserves in a move which would more than double the level of planned distribution funding for 2027-2030. It says it has been able to release the extra cash because of the commercial success of this summer's World Cup. The proposal will be made at a meeting of Fifa's council on Thursday and comes at a time when the organisation is under pressure following president Gianni Infantino's aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan. Infantino wanted to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors but faced huge criticism for the proposal, with Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation questioning his position. Uefa and Concacaf wrote to Infantino in September calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations. In a letter then sent to Fifa's six continental confederations, Infantino - who will be standing for re-election for a fourth time in March 2027 - said he would support "the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered". Fifa will now offer extra money from its reserves in addition to the current $2.7bn (£2.05bn) budgeted to be paid to all 211 member associations, the confederations, regional associations and certain non-Fifa affiliated associations. In total, Fifa will now be spending $6.35bn (£4.83bn) on football development for the 2027-2030 cycle, with a focus on investment and development of women's and youth football. The breakdown is as follows: • $25m (£19m) per member association • $99m (£75m) for each of the six confederations • $8.25m (£6.3m) for each of the 13 zonal/regional associations • $1.1m (£836,000) for 100 member associations for travel and equipment solidarity The terms of the distribution would be as follows: • One third would be allocated to women's and youth football development • One third would be allocated to infrastructure (of which there shall be equal access to women's and youth football) • One third would be allocated to projects The plan, including the eligibility, application, approval, disbursement, control and audit requirements, will be finalised by the Fifa council at its next meeting in December 2026. It will all be subject to approval by the 77th Fifa congress in March 2027. BBC Sport understands there is a proposal on the table at the council to change the disciplinary code and prevent a repeat of the Folarin Balogun situation, an unprecedented scenario which meant the US striker did not miss a game after being sent off in the World Cup. If approved, it will be expressly noted in the regulations that an automatic one-match ban for a red card cannot be suspended. Questions have been raised over the process which led to Balogun having his ban suspended. US President Donald Trump said he called Infantino to get the ban rescinded, which raised serious concerns over political interference. A proposal has been put forward to add to Article 27 of the regulations a list of instances whereby a ban cannot be suspended. This would include an automatic one-game ban for a red card. title: 'It's rough out here': Americans struggle with rising inflation
description: US inflation continues to rise, and this month the jump was above forecasts. Here's how some are surviving.
body: Kathryn Vaughn works many odd jobs to supplement her teacher's salary Kathryn Vaughn returned to work at a rural West Tennessee elementary school this autumn with a lot more stress on her plate than in previous years. The 46-year-old, like many Americans, is juggling how to provide for her family with rising costs of, as she described it, "everything". She spends her days working three different jobs to support her family of four, including as a primary school art teacher, as US inflation continues to rise. Inflation in September was above forecasts. Over the past 12 months, prices rose by 3.7% - up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to officials numbers released on Wednesday. High energy prices have driven up the cost of living in America as diesel prices have hit record highs and the price of gasoline has risen too, and all of this has landed on the shoulders of everyday Americans. Once school finishes, Vaughn heads to her second job as a facilitator at an after-school programme for at-risk youth. Her five-year-old son can join too, reducing the need and cost of after-school care for Vaughn's family. "I have done some incredibly unhinged things to survive," she said. "I hand-modeled for a local jewelry store, I sell everything that sits longer than ten minutes at my house on Facebook swap sites, I resell clothes on ThredUp and Poshmark." Vaughn even writes obituaries for people who have died to make extra money. And it is still not enough to support her family. Vaughn said she had to cancel a trip to see her parents because she couldn't afford gas Punal Bhavsar thought 2026 was going to be the year he saved enough money to purchase a home. "I was thinking the interest rates would decrease and then I'd be able to purchase a house, but I don't think that's likely now," he said. The 39-year-old said the rise in the cost of goods has made saving money difficult. And the biggest burden for Bhavsar has become the price of gasoline. "I drive a car that takes premium gas, and unfortunately, in California and the area that I live in, it's almost $6 (£4.5)," he said. Come November, when midterm elections happen and the economic tumult is bound to be on voters' minds, Bhavsar said he may become a single-issue voter: "For me, it's just like gas prices have got to be under control." Punal Bhavsar says he can't afford a home with interest rates as high as they are He described the current economic outlook as bleak, and the numbers back him up. The Gallup Economic Confidence Index summarizes Americans' assessments of current economic conditions and economic outlook and puts them on a scale of -100 to +100. In September, Americans put that number at -40. A summer survey from the Guardian showed a staggering 95% of respondents think the US is in an affordability crisis. This fall, across the US, people are finding ways to cope with that. When Caitlin Green first moved to Utah seven years ago, her mom moved her into her new home and left her with some wisdom: "If you ever need a cheap, easy meal, always get ground beef." As prices have increased, Green has struggled to follow that guidance. She remembers paying $2 a pound for ground beef; now she is paying $8, she said. Caitlin Green says she's had to get creative with recipes because of the high cost of beef Instead, Green and her husband sometimes choose alternatives, opting for ground turkey or ground chicken. "[Ground beef] is almost ...not a luxury like steak... but it's just to the point where it's become a luxury; we have to think about it if we're going to purchase it," she said. Green and her husband have gone from spending some $200 a month on groceries to $400 a month. "I understand inflation is a thing, but I just feel like in my lifetime, I've never seen inflation hit so quickly and so drastically." For Vaughn, the Tennessee school teacher, the difficult choices keep coming. She was gobsmacked as her children returned to school, at the $130 bill she faced for her five-year-old son's school supplies. Vaughn made the call to have her son purchase lunch at school each day, rather than take homemade lunches, as the cost of groceries continues to rise and she calculated it would be a cheaper choice. The family has even made the call to forgo a trip to Florida this autumn to see Vaughn's parents because the price of gasoline is too much. "It's rough out here," she says. "The cost of everything is insane. Gas to get to work, my insurance costs have gone up, feeding two children and a husband. It's a lot." title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
description: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.
body: A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L) A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications". As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings. But, here's we do know so far. The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court). Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability. Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room". The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely. Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder. The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated. Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states. But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September. On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper. A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted. The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room. When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID. In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from". It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data." Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020. He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated. Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream. "These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why." Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt." On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue. The FBI investigation is ongoing. If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine. Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. title: Container ship hit by projectile sinks in Strait of Hormuz, Singapore says
description: All 21 sailors on the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride were evacuated safely after it was hit by an projectile on Tuesday, maritime authorities say.
body: The China-flagged container shipping vessel Hui Fa off Khor Fakkan, in the Gulf of Oman, on Tuesday A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities. All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said. Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz. The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water. The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday. Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added. Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February. At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time. However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency. One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping. title: Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout
description: Lisandro Martinez's explosive comments after Manchester United's Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid turn the spotlight back on director of football Jason Wilcox.
body: Jason Wilcox's role at Manchester United is under scrutiny after Lisandro Martinez's comments It is almost 10 months since Jason Wilcox was in the line of fire when Ruben Amorim gave the explosive post-match news conference at Leeds that triggered his dismissal. Amorim was furious Manchester United's director of football had subtly advised him to change tactics for the previous game against Wolves. "I will do my job and every department, the scouting department, the sporting director, needs to do theirs," said Amorim. Less than 24 hours after that chiding, Amorim was sacked, and the focus was on the part Wilcox played in that. Now Wilcox is in the crosshairs again. This time Lisandro Martinez was doing the firing and had a target in mind. He might have got the job title slightly wrong, but there was no doubting who Martinez meant after the 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid when he said: "I expect more from our technical director." There is no doubting either that Martinez knew what he was saying. Working as a post-match interviewer for US broadcaster CBS, legendary former United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel tried to steer Martinez away from discussion about his old club's summer transfer window on four occasions. Each time, the Argentina defender refused to be deflected. "We don't have the best squad at the moment compared to other top teams," said Martinez. "I'm not going to close my mouth. We need more ambition. If we don't say the truth, nothing will change." During the summer, BBC Sport was told by dressing room sources the club needed to sign more players than the three - Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba - who eventually arrived, and it was "fairly obvious" where they needed to be - left-back and striker. Another source with extensive knowledge of the inner workings at Old Trafford describes the current situation as "a mess". This video can not be played 'We expect more from the top' - Martinez hits out at Man Utd board Man Utd defender Martinez issues scathing attack on board Quiz: Do you remember the big names who took aim at football club chiefs? Lisandro Martinez (left) and Cristian Romero were team-mates for Argentina during the summer's World Cup Martinez said he felt it was important to speak out the way he did. Many United fans are delighted he went down that path, and the defender was highlighting inadequacies in the club's leadership structure. However, there are a couple of other basic realities. The first is that Martinez's contract expires at the end of the season. United have the option to extend it by another year. By being so outspoken against senior figures at the club, was he trying to ensure that option is not triggered, which would allow him to leave for nothing in the summer, or, potentially, for a lower fee in January? Martinez is good friends with Atletico Madrid defender Cristian Romero and the international colleagues spoke after last night's game. Romero was similarly forceful against the Tottenham hierarchy last season. Also, while the vast majority of United fans may agree with Martinez, internally his comments create a problem. Most obviously, head coach Michael Carrick, having deflected questions about the defender's outburst in the immediate aftermath of the game, will face more probing on the matter when he speaks to the media before Sunday's trip to Leeds. Any players lined up to talk around the Elland Road trip will be similarly quizzed. When Tielemans was asked about it by Amazon Prime on Tuesday night, he replied with a "no comment". Given the comments about recruitment, he would clearly be within his rights to ask Martinez outright "did you mean me?" Carrick has to manage the delicate dressing room dynamic at a point when he needs a collective focus on trying to win enough matches to keep him in a job. Sources who know the United boss well are adamant there is no better person to handle the turmoil, and it is at times of crisis like this that his innate calmness is a major strength. However, after five games without a win, it is a problem Carrick could do without. This video can not be played Martinez 'expects more' from those off the pitch Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), with chief executive Omar Berrada (centre) and director of football Jason Wilcox Firstly, it must be pointed out Wilcox is going nowhere. United sources say the 55-year-old is not in any danger of losing his job. The club's recruitment department is working on potential targets for January given it is accepted the strategy of not signing left-back competition for Luke Shaw and striking support for Benjamin Sesko was flawed. Both players have missed matches already this term, with Sesko sidelined for an indefinite period after suffering a recurrence of the shin issue that flared up in May and prevented him from playing any part in United's pre-season matches. Unlike other major footballing countries on the continent, there is no expectation for sporting or technical directors to speak to the media. Former United sporting director Dan Ashworth did it once during his five months at the club and was sitting alongside chief executive Omar Berrada. Wilcox's only extensive interview since he was appointed in April 2024 has been with United's in-house media, when a couple of answers stood out. "I am a coach at heart," said the former Blackburn Rovers and Leeds United winger, who spent several years working in coaching at Manchester City's academy. "I am a coach inside, even though I know I have a different job now. That is a strength in my role, but it also causes me a bit of a problem because I always want to interfere in what the managers are doing." title: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
description: The 71-year-old Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the 90-minute procedure on Tuesday.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said. The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican. The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications. Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy. The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital. The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers. What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread. The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness. The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits. Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life. This video can not be played Pope Leo announced on Sunday that he would undergo surgery to remove a growth on his lung Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer. The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades. Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss. title: Teen shot friend by mistake, inquest told
description: Connor Bell, 17, died two days after being shot with an air rifle at a party in Chineham.
body: Connor Bell, 17, died two days after he was shot with an air rifle at a gathering in Chineham A teenager told an inquest he fatally shot his friend with an air rifle at a house party after mistaking the trigger for the safety catch. Connor Bell, 17, from Tadley, had been drinking with friends at a house in Chineham, near Basingstoke, on 8 November 2025 when he was hit by a pellet fired by Jack Beechy, the Winchester inquest heard. The pellet entered through his right eye socket, causing an "unsurvivable" brain injury and cardiac arrest. He died at Southampton General Hospital two days later. Coroner Jason Pegg recorded a conclusion of accidental death, exacerbated by a lack of weapons-handling skills. The inquest heard Joshua Brown, now 18, had agreed with his parents that only a couple of friends would come round and the air rifle would stay locked in a cupboard. But he said more friends came than he had told his parents about, and the group drank vodka, cider and beer. He took out the .177 calibre rifle and it was used to shoot at bottles in the garden from the conservatory. Beechy, now 18, said he was "a little bit drunk" when Brown asked him to put the rifle away. He fired off the remaining pellets from the conservatory because he "thought it would be safer", believing the gun was then empty. Beechy said that as he walked into the kitchen, with Bell standing nearby, he fired the rifle by mistake. More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight "I tried to put the safety on but it was the wrong trigger," he said. "The safety is directly in front of the trigger." Brown said Beechy then ran into the lounge and said: "I shot Bell." Pegg said what was planned as a small gathering had turned into "more of a house party", with friends bringing "copious amounts of alcohol". He said he was satisfied Brown, who had been shown how to use the rifle by his father, had told his friends how to load and fire it, and how to use the safety catch. Pegg said there had been a "real risk and a degree of inevitability" of an accident among young people who had been drinking, calling it "a deeply tragic case". Hampshire police said a 17-year-old boy from Tadley, now 18, had been arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm with intent. He will face no further action following discussions with the Crown Prosecution Service and Bell's family. In a statement, Bell's family described him as "a much-loved boy, who was very sporty and had a large circle of friends". They said CPR carried out by his friends at the scene had allowed him to become an organ donor, and he had since been awarded an Order of St John in recognition. His father, Robert Bell, said his son "never took himself too seriously and had a wicked sense of humour". The family urged people to remember the dangers of air rifles, saying they should be safely stored and only used by people with the necessary skills and training. title: Semenyo 'froze' after alleged racist abuse, court told
description: A Liverpool fan denies racially aggravated behaviour during a match against Bournemouth in 2025.
body: Antoine Semenyo was playing for Bournemouth when the alleged incident happened during a match against Liverpool in August 2025 Footballer Antoine Semenyo "froze" after he was allegedly racially abused by a Liverpool fan during a Premier League match at Anfield, a court has heard. The Manchester City winger, who was playing for Bournemouth at the time, was preparing to take a throw-in when Mark Mogan, 47, allegedly shouted a racist insult at him on 15 August 2025. Prosecutors said Semenyo was "clearly hurt and upset" and reported the incident to referee Anthony Taylor when the ball next went out of play. Mogan, of Dovecot, Liverpool, denies racially aggravated behaviour. Liverpool Magistrates' Court heard Mogan, who uses a wheelchair, shouted an offensive slur about 30 minutes into the opening match of the Premier League season. Prosecutor Simon Jones said: "Mr Semenyo briefly froze as he couldn't believe what the male had said." Mogan, 47, denies racially aggravated behaviour during the Premier League match at Anfield The court heard Mogan then shouted further abuse at Semenyo, who did not respond and went on to take the throw-in. Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time, the court was told. Two short video clips were shown to the court, with Jones describing Mogan as being in an "agitated and angry state". Semenyo now plays for Manchester City but was at Bournemouth when the alleged racist abuse took place He said witnesses saw Mogan throw chewing gum at Semenyo, hitting the right side of his shorts. In a statement read to the court, Liverpool supporter Neil Sherratt, who sits next to Mogan at matches, said he saw him approach the pitch from the disabled section of the Main Stand. Sherratt said he heard Mogan shout something along the lines of "hurry up" and saw Semenyo turn towards him. He said the footballer had a shocked expression and he believed he replied: "you what". Another Liverpool fan, Nicholas Collins, said Mogan became "very cocky and brazen" after the incident and threatened to assault police if they approached him. Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police during an interview the following day that he had shouted at Semenyo to hurry up. He claimed the footballer had called him "a cripple", which had upset him, and said he had thrown chewing gum on to the floor rather than at Semenyo. Jones told the court the prosecution's case was that Mogan had lied during his police interview. Semenyo, who was born in London to Ghanaian parents and has represented Ghana in the World Cup, is expected to give evidence over a videolink. Mogan, of Templehill Close, Dovecot, denies racially aggravated behaviour. title: Burnham - Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas decisions coming 'shortly'
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to stop "faffing about" with the North Sea oil and gas fields.
body: Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said he will set out decisions "shortly" Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said a decision on whether to give the go-ahead to two oil and gas fields will be made "shortly". Burnham has been deliberating over plans for Rosebank, an oil field off Shetland, and gas field Jackdaw, east of Aberdeen - with a decision on the latter "imminent", according to the energy secretary. The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government. Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged Burnham "to stop faffing about" when it comes to the North Sea drilling. She said: "In July, he said he would approve the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields in the North Sea. What's he waiting for? "If he'd approved them back then, we would have British gas warming British homes this winter. "All of the gas from Jackdaw goes onto the British grid, so will we now stop faffing about and approve Rosebank and Jackdaw?" Jackdaw, which is about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months. Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas. The prime minister responded: "She asked me what I'm waiting for – I've had to wait for the government process, which was struck down by the courts under the Conservative government, to be fixed because they messed it up, and we inherited that situation. "So I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas, we will set out our decisions shortly." Speaking at the Energy UK Annual Conference, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "We have got all the information on Jackdaw and the department has gone through that so there is a decision that will be imminent". She added a decision on the development of the Rosebank oil and gas field will take a little longer. The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North Sea Licences for the fields were granted by the Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups. The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites. Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe. They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs. Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply. Burnham has previously left open the possibility of granting approval to Jackdaw and Rosebank. However he has said he will stick to Labour's promise not to issue new oil and gas licences while honouring existing ones. It is not yet known when the government will announce its decision. What is happening with the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields? Is Burnham promising a new dawn for North Sea oil and gas? title: Bryant attacks 'irresponsible' Stormont ministers over budget
description: The Northern Ireland secretary says there is "very little financial accountability or responsibility" across the executive.
body: Sir Chris Bryant said ministers "cannot keep overspending willy-nilly and not expect consequences" Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has accused the Stormont executive of having little "financial accountability" while also ruling out "front-loading" extra money the UK government is proposing to give over the next three years. The executive has not agreed a budget for this year, blaming the UK's devolution funding formula for leaving it short. Additional funding of about £1.5bn would be released in three tranches, with £525m available this year. One idea being suggested is that a larger chunk of the money could be spent in the first year but Sir Chris told the BBC that was not on offer. "There is no front-loading to be done," he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme. "I've made it absolutely clear about 17 times now, both to members of the executive and to others, that there is no additional money beyond the £525m we have set aside for this year." Bryant also criticised the performance of Stormont ministers. "There is very little financial accountability or responsibility across the whole of the executive," he said. "That's abnormal. There's no local council anywhere in the UK that doesn't have to bring in a balanced budget. That's what the executive is going to have to do." He added: "You cannot keep overspending willy-nilly and not expect consequences from that. It's just irresponsible." Bryant can ultimately impose a budget on the executive by legislating through Westminster. He suggested the absolute deadline for that is the end of January 2027 when executive departments would run out of money under the emergency budget rules on which they are currently operating. Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member Trevor Clarke hit back at Sir Chris's comments. He argued that all ministers in the Stormont executive agreed that Northern Ireland was "underfunded" compared with Scotland and Wales. "He can't look at two different devolved regions where they are funded at a higher level than we are in Northern Ireland, with all of the problems we have," he told the BBC's Nolan Show. "We've actually got a united executive which are all saying there's insufficient funding to deliver the services that we require in Northern Ireland." Trevor Clarke said Northern Ireland had not been allocated enough money from the Treasury People Before Profit (PBP) does not have representation on the executive but its assembly member Gerry Carroll also agreed that Stormont was underfunded. "It's time the secretary of state and the British government coughed up the money to make sure that we're funded properly," he told the Nolan Show. "We've a situation where corporate wealth is through the roof in Britain and Ireland, and the fact that he's telling people here that there's no more money I think is a bit obscene." Carroll added that if Sir Chris's argument was taken to its conclusion it "will mean services being cut, it will mean water charges, it will higher fees - which is the only plan that any British government have ever had for this place". "The executive are right in standing against those regressive measures." One of the consequences of failing to agree budget is that healthcare staff have yet to receive a pay rise this year, unlike their counterparts in the rest of the UK. On Wednesday, the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) opened a ballot for industrial action, external, which may lead to nurses going out on strike over their delayed pay rise. "It is despicable that, year after year, nursing staff in Northern Ireland are forced to fight for a pay award that colleagues elsewhere in the UK receive as a matter of course," said Prof Rita Devlin of the RCN. Health Minister Robbie Butler told the Nolan Show that it would be "unconscionable, unethical and immoral" if funding was not released for the pay rise. Robbie Butler said the lack of a budget was the "primary obstacle" holding up a pay rise for health workers Butler took over the job from Mike Nesbitt less than two months ago and has previously warned the pay issue could jeopardise recent progress on health reforms. "We have huge problems that we're trying to fix and sort out and unfortunately industrial action will set us back further," Butler said. "I impressed this upon my executive colleagues in the very first meeting that I had with them that any good work that has been made and any of the transformation that we have embarked on could be undone if industrial action isn't avoided. "And the only way we can avoid industrial action is to make the pay award." Asked what was holding up the release of funding, Butler said the failure to agree a Stormont budget "seems to be the primary obstacle". "Unfortunately with the political instability at the moment it's hard to see that happening," he added. SDLP assembly member Matthew O'Toole said public sector workers needed to know if they would receive their pay awards in time for Christmas Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) assembly member Matthew O'Toole, leader of the official opposition at Stormont, said public sector workers needed to know if they would receive their pay awards in time for Christmas. He said the situation was reaching a "critical" point because it would eventually become "logistically impossible for payroll to be updated in time for Christmas wage packets". Speaking at the assembly's finance committee, which he chairs, O'Toole called for an "urgent update" from the Department of Finance. "Public sector workers out there rightly want to know whether they're going to have their pay increase that they're all expecting and deserve in time for Christmas. "Both to meet the costs of Christmas, which is not getting any cheaper, but also the cost of increases at the pump and indeed increases in home heating oil and gas." O'Too

title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
description: Learner drivers in September had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test.
body: Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures. But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test. The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020. Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about." The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn. The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing. Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects. Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them. But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test. Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, previously showed the BBC hundreds of driving tests being offered for sale by resellers on messaging groups Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, told the BBC: "Whilst the re-selling of tests does seem to have stopped, which is a massive positive, they've still failed to recruit enough examiners to cope with demand." She didn't believe that the slight fall in numbers for waiting times "is anything to boast about", adding that in many areas the wait for a driving test when booking is 21 weeks. "On many occasions, my drivers wake up at 5.45am on a Monday, only to not end up with a test as when they click on something, by the time they put their details in, they are told the test has already been taken." Sophie added that the waiting time to get a test meant that many learner drivers "who haven't even started driving lessons will book a test knowing it's 5 months away", putting themselves and the instructor under a lot of pressure. Justin Madders, the minister for roads, said the government "inherited record waiting times and a significant backlog". "While driving test waiting times are still not where we want them to be, these figures show real progress is being made," he added. A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was "committed to reducing waiting times" and that "examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017". "But we know there's more to do and we won't stop until every learner can get a test slot when they need one, wherever they're learning to drive," the spokesperson added. title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', says prosecution as rape trial begins
description: The actor and comedian has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Russell Brand arrives at court for rape and sexual assault trial Russell Brand was described as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator" by the prosecution at the start of his trial for rape and sexual assault on Wednesday. The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told Southwark Crown Court in London the women "did not know each other", "have never met each other" and "came forward independently of each other". Warning - this report contains graphic content Russell Brand pictured in the dock on Wednesday in a court sketch The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career." She said that "regardless of who the women were and what they said or did, Brand was not deterred". "His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious," she told the court. The prosecutor told jurors that Brand would be "nice when he wanted to be, funny - undoubtedly - charming, likeable even, when he wanted something in return". But she said he would also be "demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite - childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met". The prosecutor said Brand would "appear indifferent, normal and untroubled by what had just occurred" after the encounters. She added that "sometimes he would leave promptly after the incident, sometimes making an excuse to get away, or sometimes simply continuing as though nothing wrong had happened". Brand's wife Laura joined him at court on Wednesday On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences. The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told. She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her. The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, "he said if it happened, he didn't remember the incident". He added that he did not remember the first complainant's name and that he "had never engaged in non-consensual activity". The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her. She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him. When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to "come in" before grabbing her forearm. She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: "Please please come in – oh go on." The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004. Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told. The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a "big, weird grin" on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets. The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard. "He said, 'Come on, come on, suck it' – to which she just said, 'No no'," the prosecution added. "He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal." Fame Under Fire: Russell Brand on Trial You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Fame Under Fire: Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively". She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said. The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009. The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion. The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell. They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further." She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry." The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009. He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said. After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting". The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks. Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday. He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music. He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States. title: US inflation rises more than expected ahead of midterm elections
description: The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs.
body: US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month. The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August. Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have spiked following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran. The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US. Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%. Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI). It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy. The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change. There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise. If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example. Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices. Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel. Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100. Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices. Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months. In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics. Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year. Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%. Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world. While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. US President Donald Trump raised tariffs Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost. In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax. Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas. Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year. What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years. During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up. Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel. Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%. It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace. A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates. Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions. Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect prices to fall further. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand. title: Deja Vu: Dancing with The Pussycat Dolls was surreal
description: The band says: "Nicole did tell us that she was proud of us."
body: Elle Botterill, Carolina Diaz and Tyrece Lewis make up girl group Deja Vu A girl group that toured Europe with The Pussycat Dolls said it was 'surreal' to join their childhood heroes on stage. Deja Vu, formed of Elle Botterill and Tyrece Lewis from Buckinghamshire alongside Venezuelan-born Carolina Diaz, performed their first-ever live shows during the 20-date arena tour across the UK and Europe. The group were left stunned when Kimberly Wyatt personally invited them to join the headliners during the dance break of their hit song, Buttons. Botterill said: "Even afterwards, we were just like, 'I can't believe that's actually just happened, we've been on stage dancing with The Pussycat Dolls in front of thousands of people'." The PCD Forever Tour, celebrating the 20th anniversary of The Pussycat Dolls, saw the trio visit cities including Prague and Paris, before finishing at London's O2 on Tuesday. The group had formed during the Covid-19 pandemic and reached the semi-finals of The Voice UK in 2023, but the tour was the first time they had performed full shows for an audience. Deja Vu said they watched the Pussycat Dolls perform during the tour to learn from them Lewis said: "We were genuinely thrown in at the deep end, we went from dancing for social media videos on street corners to swimming with great whites. Diaz added: "I'm not going to lie, we did have a bit of imposter syndrome at the first shows. "But it taught us that we are capable and deserving of these things after working so hard for all them years." The trio announced their first London headline show would take place in December Now, the group will focus on their own original music ahead of their debut headline show on 1 December at The Grace in London. For the trio, who grew up as massive fans of the American pop group, the entire tour served as a masterclass. Lewis beamed: "Nicole did tell us that she was proud of us... That is everything to us." Botterill laughed: "I almost cried big girl tears... I'm going to get it tattooed across my chest!" Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion
description: Andy Burnham condemns the motion approved by Green Party members and says his party would "have nothing to do with it".
body: This video can not be played Burnham condemns Green Party's 'antisemitic' Zionism declaration Andy Burnham has said he will not support his party forming a partnership with the Green Party as long as it maintains a policy of defining Zionism as a form of racism. Speaking in the House of Commons, the prime minister said the motion, backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month, was "wrong" and "antisemitic" and Labour would have "nothing to do with it". The motion said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population". It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive". Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" and that he had wanted to see it amended. However, he has defended the substantial part of the motion arguing that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide. The motion, having been backed by members, has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election. The subject was raised during Prime Minister's Questions, when Conservative MP Dame Harriett Baldwin urged Burnham to "rule out co-operating" with the Green Party. Burnham replied: "Can I condemn the motion that was passed unequivocally. "It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it. "We will always take the right response when it comes to any partnerships we have with other parties. "We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds the position that has recently been adopted." Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on some local councils including Sheffield. A Downing Street spokesman would not confirm if the prime minister's position extended to local areas or just applied to national government level. The adoption of the motion has prompted some Green Party figures to call for changes to the party's rules. Last week, MP Ellie Chowns told the BBC: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process." Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the 230,000 members in the party. Key backer of the motion Lubna Speitan has defended the motion arguing that it aimed to oppose "racist systems of oppression" adding: "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions." title: Australia's first-ever Michelin stars go to 11 restaurants in one state
description: All of the spots are in South Australia, reportedly because the state government paid for incognito inspectors to visit.
body: Magill Estate Restaurant, pictured here, was the only eatery to get two stars Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction. Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each. South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country. The announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia. Michelin has approached the national tourism board about bringing the guide to the country more than once, with no luck. South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News. "It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said. The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion. Created by brothers André and Édouard Michelin in 1900, the guide was originally designed to encourage motorists to travel - ultimately boosting their core business of selling tyres. It offered drivers maps and recommendations for places to eat and stay, before evolving into one of the best-known names in restaurant recognition. Michelin stars were introduced in 1926 and have since become a major distinction for chefs and restaurants around the world. One star recognises high-quality cooking, two stars indicate excellent cooking worth a detour, while three stars are reserved for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey. Among the one-star recipients is Arkhé in Norwood, which specialises in open-fire cooking, while Aptos in Adelaide serves a tasting menu focused on native Australian ingredients. Here is the full list: Magill Estate Restaurant, Rosslyn Park LVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand, Woodside The wider guide includes more than 70 other South Australian restaurants, with some recognised through the Bib Gourmand category, which highlights restaurants offering good food at more moderate prices. title: Big scorelines, one-sided games - are Women's World Cup play-offs working?
description: The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
body: England have lost just once this year but have still not qualified for the 2027 Women's World Cup The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is. The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world. Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat. England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically. It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years. It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa. One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification. The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate. Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0. Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively. So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off. "Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday. "For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on. "Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that." The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December. Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1. It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process. England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain. They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley. England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary. Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations. In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group. There were several heavy aggregate results in European qualifying When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 . That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story. England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament. The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group. A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025. There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign. Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high. "What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify. "I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is." What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams. Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting. Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision. But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority. title: Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says
description: Elon Musk's system allows Kyiv to protect Ukrainian skies and effectively guide drones to Russian targets.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine New restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and still connect to the Starlink internet network have disrupted Ukraine's battlefield "missions", President Volodymyr Zelensky's adviser has warned. Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukraine had not been told about speed limits set overnight at 100mph (160km/h) by Elon Musk's SpaceX company. Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to effectively guide drones to Russian targets and also protect Ukrainian skies. Beskrestnov said SpaceX's move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented. In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Beskrestnov said SpaceX had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals" and this had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions". This comes as at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, Zelensky said. He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv – despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine. Three people were killed in Kyiv, local officials said. Russia said its "massive" strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Later on Wednesday, at least six people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a warehouse in the north-western city of Lutsk, local officials said. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. In the follow-up post, Zelensky's adviser stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones. The Starlink system has become a vital tool to give troops in Ukraine internet access A source in the Ukrainian defence ministry later told the BBC: "Last night, we detected restrictions affecting Starlink connectivity at speeds above 160 km/h." The source added that the "root cause" of the issue was being investigated. Defence ministry sources later explained that "once a vehicle or asset exceeds this [160km/h] threshold speed, the terminal loses its connection". They told the BBC that this made it more difficult to carry out drone operations, "specifically interceptors and middle-strike drones", and also degraded "capabilities for front line logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relaying". In February, Musk's decision to deny Russian forces access to Starlink blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders. Musk's SpaceX has not commented on the reported speed restrictions. Zelensky has said the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire. Trump on Tuesday denied that Washington was withholding intelligence. Overnight, Russia had launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones, and that four of those missiles and 115 drones had been shot down, according to Ukraine's air force. It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and came as Zelensky prepared to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv. During the past two nights, ballistic missiles have struck targets in the Ukrainian capital without any warning, before air raid sirens could be sounded. Ukraine relies on US satellite systems to track Russian missiles in order to issue alerts and to try to shoot them down. People watched the emergency services at work at the scene of the strikes in Ukraine Meanwhile, the Russian defence ministry said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea – Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014. On Sunday, Trump wrote in a post on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Zelensky has since repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same. But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons", enabling it to continue the war.
