title: Amputee told he needs more proof for blue badge
description: Nigel Ward, 71, says he believes fraudulent claims have led to more scrutiny of genuine applicants.
body: Nigel Ward said he was asked for more evidence for his Blue Badge application, despite having been granted one three years ago For amputee Nigel Ward, the evidence is undeniable. The 71-year-old from King's Lynn assumed that providing photos showing his missing leg would be enough proof to get his blue badge renewed by Norfolk County Council. But Ward has been asked to verify his disability further, with one council worker suggesting amputees can run marathons - a level of physical endurance he insists he does not have. Norfolk County Council has insisted it is following correct procedures. But Ward, who lost his leg following a medical incident on a cruise three years ago, has been left "very disheartened" and says he worries it will affect his independence. He added: "I am a genuine applicant, not a benefits cheat and I need a blue badge." Nigel Ward submitted photos as evidence to Norfolk County Council, including this one, but was told more medical evidence was needed to reapply for his blue badge The Department for Transport (DfT) blue badge scheme, external allows people who have severe mobility problems to park closer to their destination, even in restricted areas. The scheme is open to eligible people irrespective of whether they are travelling as a driver or as a passenger. Norfolk County Council said there was no renewal process and that applicants had to provide evidence with each application to prove ongoing eligibility. The process still applies to those who have a permanent disability. A spokesperson said: "We know how important blue badges are for helping people to remain independent. "We have to work within the guidance set for us by the Department for Transport, which includes detailed guidance how eligibility should be assessed through evidence and assessments. "Applicants must adequately evidence the difficulties they experience whilst walking; this applies to those reapplying for an expiring blue badge as well as first-time applications." They said evidence could include letters, reports or details of treatment from a medical professional. A spokesperson for the DfT said: "The blue badge scheme is a vital lifeline for many disabled people, and we are committed to ensuring it reaches those who genuinely need it. "Decisions on individual cases are a matter for local authorities and we expect councils to assess applications fairly." Nigel Ward, pictured with his wife Gill, first got a blue badge three years ago Ward said he could not provide medical evidence of limited mobility, as he no longer needed to attend consultations or meetings with doctors after receiving his prosthetic limb. "I am regarded as independent now," he said, "and would only need their assistance if something went wrong, either with the prosthetic limb or the stump". Charity highlights abuse of disabled parking bays Blue Badge fraud: 'More fakes than ever before' Ward, who lives with his wife Gill, first applied successfully for a blue badge three years ago and said the process had been relatively simple before. Now he is facing uncertainty. Without the permit, journeys will become "troublesome to say the least", he says, and he has not been told what specific evidence to provide to complete his application. Blue badges are sometimes used fraudulently by drivers who do not need them After his plight was raised on social media by his daughter, Ward said several people had been in touch to say they faced similar issues getting blue badges renewed. He said he believed fraudulent claims had led to more scrutiny of genuine applicants. Norfolk County Council has taken dozens of people to court for misusing blue badges. , external Disabled Motoring UK and Equal Lives, two Norfolk-based disability charities, previously warned blue badge users frequently face abuse and suspicion from other drivers when parking in disabled bays. title: Woman died after suffering 55% burns when paint can exploded in fire
description: Katie Louise Marshall suffered sever burns to her body as a result of the fire.
body: A woman died three months after suffering severe burns when a paint canister exploded in a garden fire. Katie Louise Marshall, 32, of Vaughan Williams Drive, Newport, died at Bristol Royal Infirmary on 24 September. In June, she put a black bin bag containing rubbish and a paint canister on the fire she had lit in her garden, Gwent Coroner's Court heard. The canister exploded, and a neighbour raised the alarm. Marshall was initially taken to the Grange Hospital in Cwmbran but then moved to Morriston Hospital, Swansea, after suffering 45-55% burns. Marshall was transferred to Bristol where she died from bacterial pneumonia caused by inhalation and burns. Senior coroner for Gwent Caroline Saunders said Marshall's death was "unnatural" and adjourned the hearing. Saunders said her investigation would look into "the circumstance of the fire and how she obtained her injuries and a narrative of the treatment thereafter". A full inquest will be held on 9 June 2027. title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
description: The prime minister has been under growing pressure since the club was found guilty of Premier League rule breaches.
body: Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) chats to Andy Burnham in 2019 at the Etihad Stadium, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged. The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club. Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal. The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up. On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade. The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany. It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions". But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches. A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality. Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699. Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018. But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term. Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024. Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman. But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount. Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City. "This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football." And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners". Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club. Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester". "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021." Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me." With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club". When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement. The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned. In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations. The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict. Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG). Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report. title: BBC director general defends plan to shelve new Archers studio
description: Plans to build a bespoke studio for the long-running Radio 4 soap were shelved this week.
body: This video can not be played DG defends decision not to record The Archers at new Birmingham site. The BBC's director general has defended the decision not to record The Archers at its flagship new Birmingham headquarters - and said options were still being explored to keep it in the West Midlands. Plans to build a bespoke studio for the long-running Radio 4 soap at the corporation's new Tea Factory building, in Digbeth, were shelved this week as part of a wider drive to cut costs. Matt Brittin, who met with West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker on Wednesday, said the broadcaster needed to save money but they were working together to look at future recording locations. "We're going to explore how we can best house The Archers where they need to be and at the moment, we have other studio space around the country which could accommodate them," he said. The Equity entertainment union said cast members were "angry at the proposals and will fight them". The drama, set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge, celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year. Brittin said The Archers was "going strong and... going nowhere" but acknowledged the BBC was "living in financial constraints" and had to make £500m worth of savings. "So what we've said is, we're not going to build a £1.5m bespoke studio for that production, which is something we might have afforded previously. "But what we are going to do is make sure The Archers continues to exist here." Brittin added there was "other studio space around the country" which could accommodate the soap The region's mayor Richard Parker has said he is disappointed by the news and he wants the recording to remain in the city. "The Archers was born in Birmingham and is a key part of our broadcasting heritage," he wrote in a statement on Tuesday. "We have the talent and the facilities here. There is no good reason why we should lose a programme that has called Birmingham home for decades." Equity said the proposal was short-sighted and would leave the West Midlands, and the BBC, poorer. Actor Tony Turner, who plays Vince Casey in the soap, said the proposals were troubling. He said the show's history meant it had "a commitment to Birmingham, and we're proud of that, and we'd like to stay here". Speaking during a visit to the BBC's current Birmingham base at the Mailbox, Brittin described the programme as "magic" and said there was still time to explore other options before the broadcaster moved to the new Tea Factory site in 2028. "We shouldn't really go behind the curtain, but we need a drama studio and that's different from a radio studio normally, and we've got others that we could use," he said. "We've also got the opportunity to explore here in the West Midlands alternatives and that's what we'll do now." The Archers, the world's longest-running soap opera, has been recording in Birmingham for 75 years The BBC has increased its production spend from £24m to £40m in the West Midlands and recently signed a "strategic partnership" with Birmingham City University to help train new talent, he said. He added the mayor and other organisations in the region were "brilliant partners for us". "We are at a time of big change. And if we want original drama that's rooted in the places and the people and the stories that matter to us, then we need to protect public service broadcasting and the BBC's at the heart of it." title: What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis
description: The Pope is recovering in hospital after a successful surgery to remove part of his right lung.
body: This video can not be played Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had a successful surgery to remove part of his right lung, the Vatican has confirmed. The Pope, 71, underwent a 90-minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is expected to stay for about a week. BBC Southern and Eastern Europe Correspondent Sarah Rainsford is in St. Peter's Square in the Vatican as people sent their well wishes to the pontiff. title: 'Dark day for Lewis' as one fisherman dead and two missing
description: The alarm was raised after the men's fishing boat failed to return as planned to Lewis.
body: Searches have been taking place off Port Of Ness, pictured earlier on Wednesday Police say a body has been found in the search for three men who were onboard a fishing boat that has gone missing off the Western Isles. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said the alarm was raised at about 21:20 on Tuesday when it emerged the boat was overdue from Lewis. A plane, two helicopters, two lifeboats and volunteers were making searches off the Port of Ness in north Lewis. Local councillor Kenneth Macleod said it was a "very dark day" for islanders, and their thoughts were with the families of the three men. Police Scotland said: "The body of one of the men has been recovered, however formal identification is yet to take place. "The next of kin of the men are aware and are being supported by officers. "Extensive searches, assisted by HM Coastguard and RNLI, are ongoing." The RNLI said Stornoway's all-weather lifeboat was launched at 21:42 on Tuesday to search for the overdue fishing boat. A spokesperson said: "The search, involving coastguard air and ground assets, was joined by Lochinver RNLI's all-weather lifeboat a short time later and continued into Wednesday morning." Kenneth Macleod, convener of local authority Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, told BBC Radio Scotland's Lunchtime Live programme: "It is a very dark day for the community of Ness and the community of Lewis in general. "Our thoughts and condolences are with the families affected. "We cannot comprehend what the families of the three fishermen are going through at the moment." Macleod said the search involved coastguard helicopters from Stornoway in Lewis and Shetland, as well as coastguard teams and local boats. The search has come during warnings of bad weather in the area. A weather system containing the remnants of Hurricane Isaias is forecast to send gales, heavy rain and a surge of warm air to parts of the UK. A Met Office yellow warning has been issued for parts of the Highlands and Western Isles with the risk of gusts touching 70mph (113km/h) in places. title: Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next
description: With few details so far, it is unclear what might need to change for a Pope who has been focused on stability.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis Vatican transparency about papal health has come a long way from the secrecy of the past. But that does not mean Catholics were prepared for such seismic news about cancer and removal of a large section of Pope Leo XIV's lung - even after he announced on Sunday that doctors had discovered a nodule. On Tuesday, the 71-year-old was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following 90-minute surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung. Part of the shock has, of course, been because there had been few signs until now that concern was needed about any imminent risks to the Pope's health. A member of the Order of St Augustine, a saint who placed great importance on developing good habits, the Pope is known to place great importance in good habits, including when it comes to health and fitness, such as weekly games of tennis. Now, with so many unknowns about the pontiff's prognosis and what treatment he might need, questions swirl around what may have to change in his routine, and for how long. Pope Leo is expected to remain at Rome's Gemelli Hospital for a week as he recovers from surgery Certainly, given the dangers surrounding air travel soon after lung surgery, and the high altitude of some of the stops involved, a November trip to South America – including to Peru, the country Pope Leo called home for more than 20 years – may be in doubt. His predecessor, Francis, once wrote that he had started his papacy thinking he might only have a few years in the role, having already suffered health complications throughout his life. As such, it was clear that he was intent on making waves quickly and implementing what some saw as fairly radical change in the Church at a swift pace. While Pope Leo's papacy has undoubtedly started in what appears to be a comparatively measured way, he has still grown quickly into being a powerful, uncompromising and compassionate moral voice on the world stage. His messaging in opposition to war, in support of the dignity of migrants and on the dangers of AI in particular has stood out in its clarity. To some extent, he has already done what many Catholics had feared was barely possible, in starting to bring closer together different factions of a Church that had seemed somewhat divided. Noticeably, both progressive and traditionalist followers often talking of him as a voice that reflects their own. But even after successful surgery, and with no details yet about what happens now, speculation has already begun as to whether a cancer diagnosis will mean an evident shift in Pope Leo's pace in implementing changes he sees as necessary. On the other hand any dramatic moves, such as on doctrine, would certainly feel out of character for a Pope who for nearly a year and a half has shown himself to be measured, thoughtful and discerning, as well as having a focus on stability. Who is Robert Prevost, the new Pope Leo XIV? title: Hidden video recording device found in cabin of Australian navy ship
description: Australia's military confirms the device had been discovered, after a senator reports being contacted with allegations of concealed cameras on the ship.
body: A video recording device was located on Sunday in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin in Cairns, Queensland A hidden video recording device has been found in an Australian navy ship's cabin, the Australian Defence Force (ADF) has confirmed. The device was located on Sunday in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin in Cairns, Queensland. The confirmation came after independent Australian senator Jacqui Lambie, a former veteran and defence advocate, told parliament she was contacted by personnel with allegations that "concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors' showers facilities". Australia's defence department has not said whether the device was found in a female-only space and said the incident was referred to the Joint Military Police United. Lambie told the Australian Senate on Wednesday: "I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered. "How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy." Later on Wednesday, the defence department confirmed it became aware of a video recording device being found in a HMAS Leeuwin cabin but did not give specific details on where it was discovered. "Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form," the department said in its statement. "The ship remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship's crew. The welfare of individuals remains Defence's priority, and support is ongoing. "As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time." title: Quiz: Do you remember the big names who took aim at football club chiefs?
description: As Lisandro Martinez launches a blistering attack on the Manchester United hierarchy, do you remember these famous past examples of well-known football figure calling out leadership figures?
body: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez launched a blistering attack on the club's hierarchy on Tuesday night. The Argentine was speaking after United's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid - but he is not the first player, or even manager, who has publicly called out a football club's leadership. title: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
description: The Competition and Markets Authority has fined Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym £6m in total.
body: Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds. The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said. Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £48,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships. It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate. Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment. Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA. The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds. Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March. The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added. The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%. The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing. Eight firms under investigation over online pricing AA and BSM ordered to refund learner drivers for hidden fees A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers". Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead. Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics. "When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added. Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics. "Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines." Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, praised the CMA's response. "The refunds secured by the CMA are a much-needed win for consumers at a time when household budgets are under strain," she said. The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways. Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers. However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false. Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines. Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said. title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
description: Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently juggling multiple government jobs while working from home.
body: Kashim Chowdhury allegedly juggled five government jobs A civil servant is accused of earning almost £350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload. Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning £350,000 overall. The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin. Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care. The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave. Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs. Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell. "This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit." Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother. But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered. The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers. Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them. title: Mauritius reels from worst riots in decades after woman shot by police
description: Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam imposed a curfew after days of unrest that first began over water shortages.
body: Mauritius is a well known as a tourism and financial services hub Police in Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew overnight to quell the worst riots to break out on the Indian Ocean island in decades. Peaceful protests over water shortages and the high cost of living that started a week ago erupted into violence on Friday when a woman was shot and wounded by police at a roadblock. The circumstances of the shooting are not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody. Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam ordered the curfew on Tuesday, warning against those "acting against the interests of the country", which is a tourism and financial services hub. "Those who have carried out these actions will have to face the very heavy consequences warranted by their anti-patriotic acts," he said in an address to the nation. Protesters burned tyres and blocked ‌roads as the unrest escalated over the weekend, with police stations and other public infrastructure properties being vandalised. The mayhem prompted the closure of schools and public transport, with foreign embassies issuing alerts warning its nationals to be cautious. Despite the curfew, police said there had been several incidents overnight and some arrests. But the police assured people that by Wednesday morning traffic was again moving throughout the island and said people should resume their normal activities. When protests over the shortage of water initially started, the government had responded proactively by providing more water to households, according to Zoë McCathie, an analyst at South Africa-based Signal Risk. The escalation had presented a more "unusual situation for the country's security situation", with the government resorting to closing schools and imposing a curfew, she told the BBC's Newsday programme. "Protests to this scale and to this extent haven't been seen… since around 1999. So the government's response to this in that case is logical and is necessary," she said. While the government had managed to "curtail the worst of the unrest" there was still a possibility that protests could return in some areas, with water shortages expected to persist until the rainy season in December, she said. The cabinet is due to meet on Wednesday afternoon to reassess the situation and decide on the next steps. title: Racial bias in London music licensing, report says
description: Genres including Afrobeats, hip-hop and R&B are routinely flagged as "high risk", a report finds.
body: Charisse Beaumont, chief executive of Black Lives in Music, said the disparities in licensing affected entrepreneurs and artists at the beginning of their careers Black-led music events in London face disproportionate restrictions and cancellations because of "racial bias" in licensing and policing, a report has concluded. The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report, external, commissioned by the Greater London Authority, said that black-led events were blocked at higher rates than white-led events in the capital, and South Asian-led events also faced restrictions. The report said genres including Afrobeats, hip-hop, drill, R&B and dancehall were routinely flagged as "high risk", while indie, pop and rock nights faced less scrutiny. Cameron Leslie, chairman of the mayor's London Nightlife Taskforce, welcomed the report and its recommendations. The Metropolitan Police said it understood the "concerns and differing views" on the matter, and would "carefully consider the report's findings". London Councils, which represents local authorities across London, has been asked for comment. The report, carried out by Black Lives in Music, was informed by interviews, focus groups, workshops, a survey and internet research. Freedom of Information (FOI) requests were also submitted but were largely rejected or only partially answered. Researchers said that a lack of race-disaggregated licensing data (data broken down into racial and ethnic categories), limited official datasets and rejected FOIs made some patterns difficult to measure. Alongside black-led events, the report also looked at South Asian-led events, but found that South Asian music was "largely invisible within licensing records". The report suggested that South Asian music and cultural events were often allowed to proceed through "negotiation, modified hours and conditions", but said the evidence did not demonstrate that South Asian music was "disproportionately cancelled" in the capital, and incomplete licensing records made firm conclusions difficult. The report was welcomed by the Musicians' Union, UK Music, the Music Venue Trust, the Night Time Industries Association and LIVE trust, among other organisations. Dr Hakeem Stevens said the report highlighted "long-term issues" Dr Hakeem Stevens, report co-author and lead researcher, said they looked back to the beginning of recorded sound in the late 1800s as part of the research. "We've got incidents of licensing decision issues based around race going back that far - to the 1910s, 1900s and so forth," he said. "People assume that the problems came about in the last 10 to 15 years," he said, adding that the issue dated back to approximately 100 years. Issues dating back more than a century were not cited within the report, but the legacy of Form 696 was discussed. The Metropolitan Police form, which was scrapped in 2017, had been dubbed a "racist" risk assessment. It was introduced in 2005 after a spate of shootings at London club nights, and influenced similar forms used by other police forces in England. The report said that licensing decisions for live music events were influenced by risk and "racialised assumptions about culture and safety". The report said this meant that "institutional racism" was "reproduced" through routine processes rather than explicit bans or policies. Event organisers and venue owners told researchers that "police intelligence" was "routinely used to justify heightened scrutiny of black and South Asian events", and gave examples of being asked to fund a police presence or private security for an event. One licensing officer interviewed for the report said that sometimes this intelligence was credible, and other times it was "hearsay". "These practices act as a hidden form of economic exclusion," the report said. "Events are not directly banned but are made logistically or financially impossible to run. "Police intelligence, which is often unverified, becomes a tool for discouraging organisers and forcing them to pay additional costs." The report added: "Each [event] cancellation represents not only a financial loss but also a denial of economic and cultural participation in one of the UK's most successful creative industries." Kwame Otiende, who runs a live music venue in Dalston, said the report evidenced what was "always known" Charisse Beaumont, chief executive of Black Lives in Music, said entrepreneurs and artists in the capital at the beginning of their careers were "oppressed and suppressed due to the licensing system" and its "disparities". Kwame Otiende, owner of The Jago, a live music venue in Dalston, and chairman of Hackney Council's Licensing Committee, said: "The report evidences what we have always known. Inequality has always existed, especially within the night-time economy." The report set out 19 recommendations, including a review of the licensing system, transparent evidence standards and a requirement for cultural impact assessments for major licensing decisions. It also called for "a licensing system rooted in fairness, transparency and equality", adding: "Safety must never be used as a cover for racial bias, cultural misunderstanding or disproportionate restriction." Michael Kill, chief executive of the Night Time Industries Association, said the report highlighted an "uncomfortable reality" in parts of the licensing, policing and local authority decision-making system, and provided "evidence, recommendations and a platform for change". Metropolitan Police commander Neerav Patel said the force understood the "concerns and differing views" on the matter. "Our focus will remain on making fair, evidence-based contributions to the licensing process which balance the interests of venues, promoters, artists and local communities, while never compromising on our ultimate priority which is to keep Londoners safe," he said. "We will carefully consider the report's findings in that context." List

title: Job cuts could fund diesel price drop says deputy
description: With the ongoing war in the Middle East increasing prices, one deputy is ask for duty to be frozen.
body: Prices at the petrol pump in Guernsey have reached record highs A Guernsey deputy has said leaders could fund a fuel price drop for drivers by cutting civil servant posts. Deputy Neil Inder said he plans to submit two amendments around the cost of fuel in relation to the upcoming States budget amid "exceptional circumstances due to global events". The proposed amendments are to freeze fuel duty and to also cut the cost at the pumps of white diesel - used by cars, trucks and buses - by 5p. Asked how the States would fund this, he added: "What the States needs to start looking at properly is reducing the size of the civil service." Deputy Neil Inder said rising fuel price rises were set to get worse amid global unrest In the 2027 budget, fuel duty is due to increase by inflation (4.3%) from 1 January 2027, increasing duty rates to 94.4p per litre. With the war continuing in the Middle East, fuel prices have increased across Europe, with diesel prices hitting an all-time high, according to the RAC motoring organisation. It comes as fuel prices recently hit record highs across Guernsey, and the price of diesel hit £2.00 per litre in the UK. White diesel, used for regular road vehicles, is subject to the standard fuel duty rate, while red diesel, used in industries including farming and fishing, is a rebated fuel that is duty-free or has a heavily reduced tax rate. "I think we've got to realise what's happened to the world diesel prices," said Inder. More news stories for Guernsey Listen to the latest news for Guernsey "There's been an unreasonable spike in diesel prices over the last three or four months and it really is set to get worse." He said this would inevitably impact the cost of living and added: "Whether we like it or not diesel really does make the world go round and the wheels turn in Guernsey." Inder said under "normal circumstances" he would probably go along with the P&R proposal to "up duty on the diesel", but said the global climate called for greater consideration. "In reality the biggest cost to the States is the amount of people we employ," he said. "Given the cost of the revenue they would gain, all that really is, is four or five civil servants - stop employing them, those that retire, don't replace them." "There's only one budget a year and this is the time to address it," added Inder. The BBC has asked the States for comment. title: Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
description: On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised UK plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing.
body: The managing director of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva, has praised the UK's approach to debt reduction. "Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand. The IMF is worried about the debts of the world's biggest economies. It is doing its job as a watchdog, looking for and warning about financial vulnerabilities. In the meantime, the finance ministers of former crisis countries are boasting about how little their borrowing costs have gone up, compared to the world's biggest economies, such as the US. On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised the UK's plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing, bucking the trend of the rest of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. The IMF clearly seeing the UK in a different light to these major economies is very interesting. "The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively and we see the UK in that sense enjoying a bit of a better growth prospect," managing director Kristalina Georgieva said earlier. Her comments followed those of the IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro who told me that UK borrowing reductions "stand out". Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year The IMF's twice-yearly assessment of global countries' economic prospects showed only the UK among the G7 having a serious plan for consolidation of its annual borrowing over the next few years, worth nearly 4% of the size of the economy. The US, Germany and Japan are increasing borrowing. Canada and Italy are keeping borrowing at the same level. It appears the UK is now the IMF's model pupil - at the top of the G7 table for reducing deficits. This matters because for the past half decade the UK has been on the bond market naughty step, often having the highest borrowing rates among the G7 since the Liz Truss mini budget, as political and economic crises afflicted different governments. While this is good news for the chancellor and the Treasury, it also points to the sort of Budget we will get in a fortnight's time. To keep its plans to reduce debt on track, John Healey is likely to have limited room for extra spending. He will want to marry this with limited tax rises. There could be a modest decrease in the margin for error around meeting debt rules - so-called headroom. If so that will be tied to providing a cushion against an expected rise in energy prices due to the ongoing Middle East conflict and the impact on the cost of living overall - the so called global inflation shock. This is likely to mean disappointment for many public services expecting cash injections to account for rising inflation, as suggested this week by think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It will mean tough public sector pay discussions. It won't be "austerity" but the chancellor is likely to lean into the IMF framing of a government with austere plans, relative to other advanced countries. The initial prize is to avoid the direct gaze of the bond markets, whose full glare is on others, such as France now. The bigger prize could be lower relative borrowing costs for government and households. Ultimately forecasts mean nothing without the underpinning of solid plans. Those plans will be here for everyone to judge soon enough. title: Pastor died when festival arch fell, inquest told
description: Horsham District Council is continuing a health and safety investigation into what happened.
body: Robert Guanco, pictured with wife Isaeli, was described as a "big brother" to all who knew him A pastor died from "multiple severe injuries" when a large wooden arch fell on him at a Christian event in West Sussex, an inquest opening heard. Robert Guanco, 41, was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex, and attended the Big Church Festival, near Steyning, on 28 August. An inquest opening at Woodvale Coroner's Court in Brighton on Wednesday heard that Guanco suffered multiple severe injuries and blunt force trauma. Speaking afterwards, his widow Isaeli said she hoped learning the truth about what happened to her husband would "help us grieve" and "prevent other families going through the same thing". Six others were injured, four of whom were taken to hospital for treatment. After a post-mortem examination, a provisional cause of Guanco's death was given as "1a multiple severe injuries and 1b blunt force trauma", the inquest was told. Area Coroner Joseph Turner offered his "sincere condolences" to the family and adjourned the inquest until a pre-inquest review on 9 March. Guanco's widow added: "Suddenly losing Robert has been a huge challenge - I've gone from planning our daughter's birthday party a few weeks ago to organising his funeral. "It brings a deep pain to my heart." A fundraising page for Guanco's widow Isaeli (pictured) and daughter has so far raised more than £243,000 In August, witnesses at the festival described people rushing to lift the heavy arch, which read "Everything's Unmissable", after it was blown over in the wind. Organisers at the Christian festival, which was founded in 2009, were said to have been "heartbroken" by events. A funeral service for Guanco, who was also described in court as a healthcare assistant, was held at his church on Friday. One mourner paid tribute saying he was "a beautiful soul who touched our lives profoundly", adding: "We all looked up to him because of his faith and dedication." A fundraising page for Guanco's widow and daughter has so far raised more than £243,000. Horsham District Council is continuing a health and safety investigation into what happened. A spokesperson said: "A number of lines of inquiry are still being pursued." Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. title: Mechanic who falsified MOT before crash that killed three given community order
description: Eve Smith, Darcy Ross and Rafel Jeanne died when the car crashed into woodland in Cardiff in 2023.
body: Neil Lewis pleaded guilty to one count of fraud by false representation A mechanic who gave a car a fraudulent MOT just weeks before it was involved in a fatal crash that killed three people has been given a 12-month community order. Neil John Lewis, 47, from Cardiff, had previously pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation. Eve Smith, 21, Darcy Ross, 21, and Rafel Jeanne, 24, died when the car crashed into woodland in St Mellons, Cardiff, in March 2023. They lay undiscovered for two days. Two other people survived. Cardiff Magistrates' Court heard Lewis had owned G and J Motors for 21 years and had voluntarily surrendered his testing certificate following the incident. Eve Smith, 21, Rafel Jeanne, 24, and Darcy Ross, 21, died in the crash in March 2023 The car had been sold at auction to a friend of victim Rafel Jeanne, who was driving on the night of the fatal crash. The car had previously been involved in a crash in Scotland. It failed an MOT carried out on 9 February 2023 with the warning system light on, indicating a fault with the seatbelt, air bag, or both, and with the mileage recorded at about 98,000. Lewis retested the car two weeks later, telling police in interview when he did so "the seatbelt and warning light were now off and the rear seatbelt was now working", so he "passed it with some advisories" and it was collected by Jeanne. He sent a text starting with a grin emoji which read: "Car is done. It's 560 you have to sort the seatbelt and the airbag light. I've passed the car though." The seatbelts on the car had not ever been replaced and were defective. Abigail Jackson, prosecuting, said she was not asking for the fatal crash to be treated as an "aggravating" factor to the offence. Jon Lewis, defending, said Lewis had been in the motor industry for 30 years "with no prior criticism or complaint". He said Lewis's decision to pass the MOT was "baffling" and it was unclear why he chose to ignore the standards "that had become the very foundation of his professional business". Judge Charlotte Murphy said choosing the "harm" levels in the case was "not straightforward", saying she was able to consider the "wider impact" of the defendant's actions. She said his actions represented a "dereliction of his duty" as an MOT tester but she accepted it was a "one-off offence" and "not motivated by financial gain". Lewis was ordered to do 100 hours of unpaid work, and pay a £185 court surcharge and £114 costs. The crash involved five people - Sophie Russon, Smith, Ross, Jeanne and Shane Loughlin, 32. They were last seen at about 02:00 GMT on 4 March 2023 following a night out. The families of the three young women had all reported them missing on the evening of 4 March, with Gwent Police receiving the first missing persons report in relation to the group at about 19:30. Family and friends of the five made repeated appeals to find the missing group over the course of the weekend, with the mother of one of the girls saying she had been told to stop contacting police for updates. They were eventually found just after midnight on 6 March. The car had crashed deep in undergrowth near a roundabout, and they were not found for 46 hours. Smith, Jeanne and Ross died while Russon and Loughlin were critically injured and taken to hospital. In November 2025, the IOPC said four Gwent Police officers would face gross misconduct hearings. Family members of those involved have previously expressed their upset and frustration over delays in getting answers about what happened that night. In July, there were angry scenes outside the court when Lewis was confronted by the family of Darcy Ross. They showed his a picture of Darcy, telling him to "remember her name". On Wednesday, none of the victims' families attended the hearing. title: Turkish police raid opposition TV station, halting live broadcasts
description: It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on media critical of the Turkish president and his government.
body: Police in riot gear were seen outside the office in Istanbul early on Wednesday Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channels, halting its live broadcasts. Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and that 11 people had been taken into custody in a raid linked to the channel's owner. The government also appointed a new administrator to run the channel. It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his government. Halk journalists were initially unable to get into the building, although they later were allowed in, several reporters said on X. There was a heavy police presence in the building, they said. Halk's news channel and live broadcasts on its YouTube page were both offline early on Wednesday. The channel has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of Erdoğan's ruling AK party. Prosecutors said arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people as part of the investigation into Halk chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on allegations of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering, Turkish media reported. Mahiroğlu, who was reportedly not in the country during the raid, wrote on social media that seven members of his family were among those detained. "Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons." The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, which it noted came hours before Ekrem Imamoğlu, widely seen as Erdoğan's biggest political rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court, for which he has been in prison for over a year. A Halk TV staff member shared images of police stood beside a TV studio during the raid Özgür Özel, leader of the opposition New Party, called the raid "weak and cowardly". "Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do," he wrote on social media. Özel set up the party after being removed as the CHP's leader by a court in May and replaced by a party veteran who had previously been voted out, in a move which further cemented Erdoğan's grip on power. Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) 2026 World Press Freedom Index, external. The organisation stated that 90% of national media outlets were under government control and criticised the "abusive prosecution" of critical publications in the country, which Erdoğan has led since 2003. The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship. In September, a court ordered the blocking of access to the website and social media accounts of T24, on the grounds that it had published "LGBT propaganda". In October 2025, the authorities seized control of Tele1, another pro-opposition TV channel, appointing a trustee to oversee broadcasts, which were stripped of all hard-news content. The channel still exists but its pro-opposition stance has been completely neutralised. title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
description: The TV presenter says she suffered memory loss following her operation to remove a benign tumour.
body: TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery. Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024. "After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith. "When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'." The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after a colloid cyst was found in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work. In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer. She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner. Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there. "I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before." A year ago, for the first time since the surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day. This video can not be played Watch: Davina McCall tears up on Comic Relief as she discusses brain surgery According to the NHS, external, later stage symptoms of Alzheimer's disease include "significant problems with short and long-term memory". Alzheimer's is a progressive disease and so symptoms gradually worsen over years. After brain surgery, though, problems tend to be worst early on, then stabilise and improve over weeks to months. Some people are left with milder lasting changes. Music therapy can help people to recover from brain injuries and McCall said she believes it was ultimately singing lessons that had "healed" her. In April 2025, McCall revealed she had been told - following MRI scans - that her tumour was "not coming back". A benign tumour is not cancerous, but such cysts tend to grow slowly, according to the Brainstrust charity. Non-cancerous brain tumours are more common in people over the age of 50, and symptoms can include headaches, vision problems and drowsiness, the NHS says. McCall's surgery, known as a craniotomy, involved part of her skull being removed to take out the tumour. She has spoken about the procedure and her recovery, including on her own podcast called Begin Again. title: Struijk red card shown after VAR intervention is overturned
description: The red card controversially shown to Brighton defender Pascal Struijk against Sunderland is overturned.
body: Pascal Struijk was shown a red card by referee Thomas Bramall after 57 minutes of Brighton's victory at Sunderland The red card controversially shown to Brighton defender Pascal Struijk at Sunderland after an intervention by the video assistant referee (VAR) has been overturned. Struijk was sent off after 57 minutes of Saturday's match at the Stadium of Light when he was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland forward Wilson Isidor as he tried to run on to a through-ball. Neither referee Thomas Bramall nor his assistant gave a foul initially, but VAR Neil Davies intervened and called the on-field official to the screen. After watching the replay multiple times, Bramall showed Struijk a straight red card for denial of an obvious goalscoring opportunity. The decision, which was greeted with disbelief from the Brighton players, has now been reversed following a successful claim of wrongful dismissal. This video can not be played Highlights: Brighton beat Sunderland despite controversial Struijk red card The outcome of the appeal means Struijk will not have to serve a one-match ban and will now be available to face Crystal Palace in the Premier League this weekend. Struijk joined Brighton from Leeds in a £20m move in the summer, and was making his second Premier League start for his new club. Despite the red card, Brighton went on to win the match 2-0 and continue their strong start to the season. The Seagulls are third, five points behind leaders Manchester City. Follow Brighton & Hove Albion on BBC Sounds Pre-match, post-match and topical Albion content Subscribe and listen for everything you love about the Seagulls If Struijk had been sent off by referee Bramall it would have been a poor decision. That it came via a VAR intervention is much worse. Red cards for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity via video review are rare, simply because there are so many subjective considerations. Last season, for instance, there were three - for Liverpool's Dominik Szoboszlai, Crystal Palace's Maxence Lacroix and Bournemouth's Marcos Senesi (though this was wrongly rejected at the monitor). There was far too much doubt that Isidor would get to the ball before Bart Verbruggen. That means it was a possible goalscoring opportunity rather than obvious. With such a high bar on VAR in the Premier League, Bramall should not have been sent to the monitor. Perhaps when sent to the screen, his judgement was clouded because he did not give a foul. But it was the kind of situation where the referee should be rejecting the advice of the VAR. title: 'It's definitely tight trying to budget on maternity leave'
description: An estimated 47,500 people in Sheffield are unable to make ends meet and pay their bills.
body: Sara Ody was among the first customers at a new community food pantry in Sheffield Almost 50,000 households in Sheffield are struggling to make ends meet and cannot pay their bills, according to a new cost of living report by the council. Described as having a "negative budget", these people are unable to afford the necessary costs even after all benefit entitlements have been claimed and their outgoings have been reduced to the bare essentials. In the same week the report was published, a new food pantry opened in the Woodseats area of the city, offering low priced food for anyone struggling with the cost of living. Within the first hour 14 people called in, with 37-year-old Sara Ody among those through the door. "There's always a thought process, 'can we afford this? do we have to sacrifice this to be able to afford food, childcare and clothes?' It's definitely tough," she said. The Community Grocery pantry, run in partnership by The Message Trust and Ikon Church at Woodseats, offers membership for £1 per year, with food and household staples from just 50p. Sara said her finances were especially tight now she is on maternity leave from work. "There's four of us now, and I've got to the point in my maternity leave where there is not really any money coming in, so it's definitely tight trying to budget, especially in the run up to Christmas," she said. "It's frustrating because I saved up so much money while I was working to be able to still have opportunities and do things while on maternity leave, but you have to budget all the time. "We're finding food is so expensive and every week it seems the prices are going up and up so things like this are amazing. We can get definitely some staple bits to see us through winter." According to the report to Sheffield City Council, external, Citizens Advice estimates 47,500 people in Sheffield have negative budgets. It says that poverty in the city predates the cost-of-living crisis and reflects longer-term inequalities in income, employment, health, housing and opportunity. However, it says years of financial pressure have also left some households with depleted savings, debt and arrears, reducing their ability to absorb further shocks It adds that children are particularly affected, with approximately one in three children in Sheffield living in poverty, "substantially above" the national rate. John Lawson is from The Message Trust John Lawson is the regional lead for The Message Trust, which has 35 stores nationwide, and is based in Sheffield. He says community grocery stores can bridge the gap between food banks and supermarkets, as they offer a variety of food but at a fraction of the cost. "We opened here after seeing the need on the doorstep and the challenges that people are facing with the cost of living," he said. "Even a lot of the community who wouldn't necessarily have been struggling five years ago are now finding themselves living paycheck to paycheck." The store is open to everyone and there is no means testing. Lawson added: "We want to make it accessible for everyone, so if someone is passionate about saving food from landfill, they should shop here. If someone's in crisis and needs free food, they can come here. "Or if someone just wants to be in the community, in an amazing space like we've got here, they can come and hang out. "We want to create an opportunity and a resource where anyone can come and access healthy food and wraparound care so we can holistically look after the whole person with mental health support, debt advice, cookery courses or just simply offering a social space for people to come together." Another customer Debbie Schofield, 44, said she thought the pantry would help people realise they are not alone. "I think Woodseats needs this community hub where people can get some cheaper resources and have a chat somewhere warm," she said. "I like the concept of the community pantry. I think everybody's struggling with the cost of living, everything has gone up quite considerably, but I also feel like social media isolates us in our own homes. "I don't feel there's a sense of community like when I was growing up, like in the 1980s and 90s. It's really important for these pantries to exist because they bring neighbours together and then people in the wider community start to recognise each other." title: Block of flats in ruins after Russian strikes on Ukraine
description: BBC Ukraine Correspondent Dan Johnson is in Kyiv, where at least three people were killed in overnight strikes.
body: This video can not be played A key energy facility and a residential building in the outskirts of Kyiv have been hit by overnight Russian missile and drone strikes. In the capital, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said. At least 600,000 people across the country are without electricity after strikes hit critical infrastructure in the Kyiv region and the north-eastern city of Kharkiv. The strikes come after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine. Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes had targeted communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. BBC Ukraine Correspondent Dan Johnson explains. title: The Gentlemen star Ray Winstone charms locals in Welsh market town
description: Winstone plays Alan "Razor" Sharp, an ex-SAS operative, in the action comedy Danger Money.
body: Ray Winstone, who has starred most recently in Guy Ritchie's The Gentlemen series, has been filming a new six-part action comedy for Amazon Prime in Cowbridge An actor renowned for his "hard man" image and London gangster roles looked at home filming on the more genteel streets of a south Wales market town. Ray Winstone, recently seen in Guy Ritchie's The Gentlemen, as well as star of The Departed and Sexy Beast, was spotted in Cowbridge in the Vale of Glamorgan, filming the six-part action-comedy Danger Money. Winstone leads the cast as Alan "Razor" Sharp, an ex-SAS operative, with Cowbridge portraying a town in England. "It created a real buzz," said Nadine Price, supervisor at Ground coffee shop on High Street, one of the filming locations. The cast and crew spent an hour and a half filming at Ground coffee shop on the high street Price said there was "real excitement" in the town, with Winstone spending time joking with residents. The Welsh flag was taken down from the town hall for the filming, with Price saying Cowbridge would be depicted as a town in Herefordshire. Winstone, 69, who was born in east London and is famous for his Cockney accent, walked the high street of Cowbridge wearing military medals and a flat cap in character as Sharp. Winstone previously said his character was "a bit of a scrapper, surly and getting on a bit". "I told them it doesn't ring any bells, but I like a challenge," he joked. Ray Winstone wowed fans on the streets of Cowbridge including Molly Ridge who was filming an Instagram reel for the shop she works in Molly Ridge, a stylist at Minnie May Closet, was about to film a promotional Instagram reel for the shop when she noticed the filming outside. "I had one of our dresses on so I ran up to him and asked him for a selfie and he said 'yes of course babes, that's fine babes'. He was just really sweet. "He said the dress looked gorgeous and I thought he could have been a bit off as he was just about to start filming but he wasn't." She described Winstone as a "lovely man" who was "exactly the same in character as in real life with his proper gruff East End accent". Anna Groom also works at the shop and asked for an autograph. "He signed it to the 'Lovely Anna' which I thought was sweet and he came across like a really nice guy," she said. The film star also enjoyed a drink with locals the night before filming Gary Simms, a Cowbridge local, also had a picture with the actor when he saw him in the Bear Hotel on Sunday evening, the night before filming. "What a nice guy. We were watching [the] Liverpool-Man City game and we had a great chat about football, and he was wearing his West Ham joggers. "It was surreal to see him in the pub as I'd just finished watching season two of The Gentlemen." Winstone also recently appeared on Strictly Come Dancing, where his daughter, Jaime, is a contestant, sending a video message of support after she was in the dance off. title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn to meet prime minister over cancer funding
description: The Scottish athlete, who has inoperable brain tumours, previously made a tearful plea for more investment in brain cancer research on BBC Breakfast.
body: This video can not be played Watch Archie Goodburn's emotional plea for more brain cancer funding on BBC Breakfast Swimmer Archie Goodburn is to meet the prime minister later after making a tearful plea for more investment to be put into brain cancer research. The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, said the Downing Street meeting offered a "unique opportunity for change". He previously called for Andy Burnham to introduce a brain cancer lead to give patients a chance to "fight for their lives" during an appearance on BBC Breakfast. Goodburn, 25, cried while looking down the camera, saying he was "on my knees begging" for help to ease the "unbearable suffering" of patients and their families. Burnham later contacted Goodburn on social media to set up the meeting at Downing Street. Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials. He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord. The Edinburgh-born swimmer underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible. Burnham invites swimmer Goodburn to meeting after cancer funding plea Swimmer Goodburn diagnosed with inoperable brain tumours During his appearance on BBC Breakfast, Goodburn called for more resource to be put into research and care, and for clinical trials happening elsewhere to be brought to the UK. "Please establish a national brain cancer lead and give us a chance to fight for our lives because the things that patients are going through out there are unbelievable and so unjust," he said. "There are clinical trials around the world, in the US, in Australia, in China, that could change lives. We are not seeing them in the UK and it is unfair and unjust. "Please invest and make the difference. I'm on my knees begging for - not just my own life - but for those of my best friends and those that are affected and the families around the country." Goodburn added: "This has to change. It's been going for too long and the suffering is unbearable." Before the meeting, Goodburn said he hoped it would be a "unique opportunity for change". "We cannot accept the status quo in the system, we cannot be risk-averse. People are dying," he said. "My advocacy has opened doors to have conversations at the highest level of government about the injustices faced by the brain tumour community and campaign for change for myself and for them. "But I hope I can also inspire people on an individual level." Archie Goodburn was diagnosed with three oligodendroglioma tumours in 2024 Charity Brain Tumour Research said the disease was the cancer most likely to kill patients under 40 in the UK. They said charities made up more than 75% of the total national investment in brain tumour research, with the government funding sitting at 25%. The Rare Cancers Bill, led by Edinburgh South West MP Scott Arthur, became law earlier this year. The legislation aims to incentivise research and investment into the treatment of rare types of cancer, defined as those affecting fewer than 1 in every 2,000 people. Goodburn said that did not go far enough and a dedicated brain cancer lead would allow for greater focus on specific research and trials. Arthur said the act was "vital" to driving research needed into the condition, but that Goodburn's meeting with Burnham could lead to further work in the field. "There is real opportunity in the sector to dismantle the barriers to research that charities, clinicians, and researchers have known about for decades," he said. "Having met Archie a number of times I know he is a fantastic advocate for the brain tumour community. "I hope his meeting with the prime minister is a moment for concrete progress to be made." title: 'No excuses' - but is Villa's stadium rebuild affecting team?
description: With Villa Park's North Stand currently closed for building work, is the reduced capacity affecting Aston Villa's performances?
body: Aston Villa's rebuild of the North Stand is due to be completed next year "No excuses," said Unai Emery. The Aston Villa head coach was talking about his team's form amid Villa Park's rebuild. He had already turned the air blue when describing their defeat to Nottingham Forest last month. It was a rare moment of candour from the Spaniard with Villa yet to win at home this season after Saturday's 2-2 draw with Brentford. The North Stand is a shell and currently closed for building work as the club increases the stadium's capacity to over 50,000. It is part of the club's plan to help Villa bridge the financial gap in the Premier League, but they may have to endure some short-term pain for long-term gain. This video can not be played Highlights: Ajer scores late to earn Brentford draw at Aston Villa Fenerbahce visit on Wednesday as Champions League football returns to Villa Park. With them is Marcos Asensio, who scored eight goals for Emery's men during a successful loan from Paris St-Germain in 2025 - and a reminder of the swagger Villa used to have at home. He scored in Saturday's 3-0 win over Rizespor, with Fenerbahce netting 11 goals in their last two games, including an 8-0 victory against Turkish Super Lig strugglers Eyupspor. That could present a problem for a Villa defence that has kept just one clean sheet this season and been increasingly fallible at home, something Emery knows must improve regardless of the rebuild. "Our handicap is less supporters for the situation, but the club decided it. It is something to improve us for the future," said the Spaniard. "We must try to be together and without 7,000 supporters we must push everyone. We must play better football, compete better, be more focused. Those are more important than the stand. "We are realistic with how we are working, improving. The things are not [good] enough yet, a lot of conversations with the team, meetings, video, practising and each match trying to show and improve." Villa, though, have lost just once at home in Europe under Emery - against Olympiacos in the Europa Conference League semi final in 2024 - and he ended their wait for silverware by lifting the Europa League in May. "Over the last few years our home form has been amazing, especially in Europe," said defender Matty Cash. "We need to get back to that. "I don't want to sound like I am making excuses, because obviously we have to deal with the circumstances and it is really good to make the stand bigger and the stadium bigger, but it is obviously different. "I am not going to sit here and lie and say it isn't but you have to deal with the circumstances. You can't make excuses. You have to play what is in front of you. When it is done it will be amazing but yeah, at the moment it is a bit different." Champions Arsenal and Forest have already claimed three points at Villa Park this season, with unbeaten Brentford taking a point. Nicolas Jackson's equalising goal against the Bees was the first Villa had scored in front of the skeleton that was their North Stand this season. Yet Villa's home struggles are not new. Since the turn of the year they have lost the aura of invincibility which Emery has brought since his arrival almost four years ago. Between November 2022 and January 2026, they lost just eight of 61 home Premier League games, winning 44 of them. That included 15 straight wins between March 2023 and December 2023. They also went 12 months unbeaten in the top flight between August 2024 and August 2025, but since the turn of the year Villa have been fragile at home in comparison. Defeats by Everton, Brentford, Chelsea and Tottenham threatened their top-four place last season, with Villa needing late goals to earn a draw against Leeds and claim victories against Brighton and Sunderland. That has continued this season with Villa Park's capacity down to around 37,000 in the void left by the North Stand, something Brentford boss Keith Andrews picked up on, saying he hated playing when one stand was missing. Villa could still make light of it in Europe, though, with Viking also travelling to Birmingham in the league phase on 21 October. After an opening win at Club Brugge, successive victories would put them on course for qualification before November, despite their home issues. "It is a massive test against a good team but we need to be winning these games," added Cash. "That is the bar we have set for ourselves. Hopefully we can make it loud - three-stand loud."
