title: Why 'cool kids' won't let Swindon in Thames Valley
description: Why the "popular kids" in Oxfordshire are not letting Swindon in on the Thames Valley devolution deal.
body: Swindon leaders want the town included in the Thames Valley region If you have ever been picked last for a sports team, or not invited to a party, you might know how the Borough of Swindon feels right now. The government wants district and borough councils to be scrapped to make way for larger combined authorities, many of which will be run by mayors. The issue for Swindon, however, is that some of the council leaders in Berkshire and Oxfordshire do not want Swindon to join them in a Thames Valley authority, arguing the geography does not work. Swindon Borough Council leader Gary Sumner said: "It's like not being invited to the party with the popular kids." The leader of Oxfordshire County Council Tim Bearder said: "With no offence to my friends in Wiltshire, you are not in the Thames Valley." The government wants most areas of England to be under a mayoral authority, promising each area a greater say on how money should be spent as well as more power to unlock growth. It means council areas being combined. Under current plans Swindon would be included in the Thames Valley, which Sumner said would be good for the region. "Swindon is a vast economic powerhouse in a potential Thames Valley devolution deal," he said. "This is about coming together for growth we can pitch for infrastructure funds that can unlock investment in our town centre." Plan for £303m bypass dropped by government Work to turn derelict site into museum set to begin Plan for 2,000 EV charging points gets green light Conservative Sumner also said Swindon could help rural Oxfordshire councils reach a housing target under spatial development strategy , externalby agreeing to allocate more land for housing in the town centre. "Oxfordshire don't want their green fields covered in houses," he said. "We've got brownfield sites that could deliver thousands and thousands of homes, at pace". However, Bearder said: "It is not something you can use as a bargaining chip to get into a Mayoral authority." Plans are stalling, with some council leaders arguing against Swindon being involved. Swindon's high street would benefit from investment, said the council leader "Perhaps they don't like the cut of Swindon's jib," said Sumner. "Perhaps they think they're too good for us. "I'm really proud of our town and I'm upset when people think less of us and that's how it feels with two ends of the Thames Valley." Windsor and Maidenhead council leaders also objected to the most recent plans, partly on the basis that a Foundation Strategic Authority was being proposed, instead of one run by a Mayor. But on Swindon, Liberal Democrat Bearder said: "I don't think its a good fit. You would have to rearrange all the boundaries." It is hoped under combined authorities, mayor and deputy mayors would also oversee things like the police and fire services - but currently Swindon's services operate in Wiltshire. "It makes sense to have the set-up with Swindon staying in Wiltshire," Bearder said. Meanwhile, Wiltshire Council leaders are looking to form a Wessex Mayoral Authority with nearby Somerset, Dorset and Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole. Some leaders across Oxfordshire and Berkshire are keen on Swindon being involved. Labour leader of Oxford City Council Susan Brown said it was "vital" Swindon was part of the Thames Valley. "We're incredibly closely connected in terms of our economies," she said. For a plan to be submitted to government, it needs approval from all parties across affected councils. "It has to be unanimous and I will only do that when it is right," said Bearder. Councils are waiting to hear what the next steps will be but elsewhere in the country local government reorganisation has been paused. Sumner said he would continue to make the case for Swindon, hoping other leaders will have a change of heart. "We need the Prime Minister to say, "If you want to see it happen, welcome Swindon," he said. "This is the only thing that is going to get it across the line." There are also discussions about whether or not Buckinghamshire and Milton Keynes would be part of the same group. Follow BBC Wiltshire on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: Hundreds of thousands of workers on strike across Republic of Ireland
description: It comes amidst an an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government.
body: The strike action will last 24 hours More than 300,000 workers, including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, are on strike across the Republic of Ireland. It comes amid an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government, with a further strike planned on 21 October. It is expected schools could be closed with hospital appointments cancelled and picket lines formed across the country during the 24-hour strike. At the end of September, more than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures. At the start of October, primary and secondary school teachers in the Republic began work-to-rule action. Previously almost 97% of Fórsa members, who voted in an industrial ballot, did so in favour of action. It is the Republic's biggest public service union. Brendan O'Brien divisional organiser of SIPTU, which represents public sector health and administration workers, previously said the "goodwill" of workers was a large part of what kept public services going. However, he said the Irish government's failure to establish a basis for formal talks "left our members with no alternative but to act collectively". On Tuesday Jack Chambers, the Republic's minister for expenditure, described the strike action as "deeply disappointing" saying it would cause significant disruption to the economy, with thousands of hospital appointments set to be cancelled and schools closed. title: New team to save Antarctic port from climate change
description: The mission aims to protect the base which is home to the world’s southernmost Post Office.
body: The team will live on Goudier Island, working in sub-zero temperatures, 24-hour daylight and without running water A new team of UK specialists is embarking on a 9,000-mile journey to Antarctica to protect a British science base threatened by climate change. The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT), a Cambridge-based charity, is in its second year of a three-year mission to save Port Lockroy. Its goal is to restore the site, which has the world's southernmost Post Office, museum, and more than 1,000 gentoo penguins. This year's team will install beams and props to help the buildings withstand increased precipitation and snow loading, as well as monitor the penguins. The site is more than 80 years old and faces structural deterioration due to rising temperatures and extreme weather on the rapidly warming Antarctic Peninsula. After initial assessments revealed serious structural weaknesses, last year's team prepared the site ready for this season's interventions, which UKAHT said was the charity's "biggest ever conservation season" at Port Lockroy. The team will be counting penguin nests, eggs and chicks as part of a study to monitor and protect the colony Port Lockroy faces escalating deterioration from age, climate change and environmental factors, said UKAHT. A team of eight will spend five months at remote Base A, Port Lockroy on Goudier Island, while a field team of six specialists will travel further south to carry out the first comprehensive survey of another British heritage site, Wordie House, external, where one of the longest continuous climate records on the continent began. Thousands of cruise ship passengers stop off at the remote Post Office to send messages home The Port Lockroy team will be led by Carole McCullough, who previously worked in the RAF, and said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure. "The teamwork, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience." She will be joined by others with various life experiences including conservation carpenters and museum and mountain rescue specialists. Postmaster George Clarke, spending his third season at Port Lockroy, said: "I've really fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness" Camilla Nichol, UKAHT's chief executive officer, said: "With the demanding conservation season ahead at Port Lockroy and beyond to Wordie House, we have selected a team who bring specialist knowledge and understanding of the Antarctic environment, as well as some much needed enthusiasm and resilience. "This is a huge year for us as we meet the growing challenges of climate change. "Since Wordie House's records began in 1947, the Antarctic Peninsula has become one of the fastest-warming places on the planet and we see the impact every year on the wildlife and special places in our care." title: Heating oil users face fuel or food winter choice'
description: It comes as ministers say they will tighten up rules on heating oil and promote competition
body: Liz Humphris said although she can afford it, she does not like to look at the price heating oil has reached With the summer gone and the central heating going on, people who use heating oil in their homes are facing the prospect of filling their tanks, at much higher prices than they have been used to. Many will pay nearly double what they had to last year because of a rise in prices since the start of the Iran war. It has led people like Liz Humphris, from Bishop's Castle in Shropshire, to limit how much they buy at once to help ends meet. "Now, I just order 500 litres at a time because it costs too much," she said. Ministers said on Tuesday they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. As prices remain volatile, but significantly higher than in recent winters, campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from a similar cap to that on mains gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. There is no promise this will happen, but ministers said they would work to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition." Humphris said she had noticed the jump in prices: "It is costing over £500 for 500 litres, so it has gone up hugely." Humphris added that she felt for people she knew who had to use food banks, like the one she volunteers for. "I am reasonably OK because I've got a teacher's pension, so I am not destitute or anything," she said. "For people who are on a very fixed income, it literally is coming down to the point where it is fuel or food, which is awful because you've got to heat your home." According to Shropshire Council, about 15 per cent of households in its area rely on oil-fuelled central heating, which is between 16,000 and 21,000 properties. But within the county there are large variations, with the South Shropshire constituency having one of the highest percentages of homes without mains gas across the UK, at 53%. It has led to co-operatives forming to bulk buy heating oil at cheaper prices, including one set up by the charity Community Resource., external Hanna Clarke, who is the fundraising lead at the charity, said people coming to them were struggling with rising prices. "It is different to your electricty and your gas. You can't necessarily put it on a direct debit and spread that cost out across the 12 months - you have to fill up your tank," she said. "To be able to do it, lots of the suppliers have minimum orders, so that is the one sort of key issue that we are having, that they just literally cannot afford that big increase in the cost per unit now." Campaign group Action with Communities in Rural England (ACRE) said the government's move to regulate the heating oil market did not go far enough. Chief executive Corrine Pluchino called for an immediate cut to VAT on heating oil and LPG. "While we welcome the government's announcement that they intend to accept the recommendations of the Competition and Markets Authority's study of the heating oil market, we do not believe the action will address the fundamental problem facing the 1.7 million UK households who are off the gas grid, mostly in rural areas," Pluchino added. "For those households, especially those nearing the end of their current supply, the real issue is the high and volatile price of heating oil, which is adding hundreds of pounds to their bills because the fuel has to be bought in bulk." title: 'Unprecedented' murder cases see police force consider 'zero-hours' detectives
description: The chief constable said the force had seen "unprecedented" demand in the past year.
body: Gwent Police say the number of murder cases the force was investigating had risen sharply in the last year An "unprecedented" number of murder investigations this year could see Gwent Police hire detectives on "zero-hour" style contracts to cope with demand. Chief Constable Mark Hobrough said the force would normally see two or three murder probes a year, but has launched 11 in the past 10 months. As a result it has had to fund record amounts of overtime payments and take neighbourhood officers away from community policing duties to cope with the demand. Hobrough said the 1,535 officer-strong force would use the additional detectives if the same trend continues next year, but did not specify where they would come from or how the scheme would work. Hobrough told Monmouthshire councillors that if demand continued he would consider cheaper alternatives to support investigations such as an "almost zero hours-type situation" to conduct interviews or special investigations outside the force's boundary. "But that has to be of the same quality," he said, adding that he did not want to risk burnout among his staff. He said: "They are the same people going to these incidents... They are young officers doing an outstanding job and I want to make sure we are looking after them and they stay with us long term." The chief constable described one particular dog attack involving a baby as an "absolute tragedy", adding: "Our neighbourhood officers were the first on the scene, it's left trauma, it is bound to. "They've been to the two murder scenes [in Monmouthshire] which were particularly harrowing incidents. It's about making sure we look after the teams, to support them and keep them in service and healthy and leave healthy." Mark Hobrough was appointed chief constable of Gwent Police in December 2024 Hobrough said in the last 10 months the force had dealt with the number of murders that would typically take place in two to three years. "That is a huge extraction for officers," he said. Hobrough stressed there was no link between the incidents, which involved factors ranging from alleged organised crime to mental health issues, substance misuse and domestic violence. "There is no correlation between them at all," he said. The force had also responded to public order protests outside its areas as part of an agreement to support deployments nationally, as well as helping the fire service as it tackled wildfires, Hobrough said. He said that while neighbourhood officers had been "extradited" in response to the major demands during the first half of this year, their numbers were still at an "incredibly low" level. "It's absolutely what we don't want," he said. "Historically it used to be the go-to for community officers to staff response cars in a shortage, that isn't the case now," he said. title: Home of oldest restaurant given to National Trust
description: Rules, in Covent Garden, which opened in 1798, will be looked after and conserved by the charity.
body: Rules is an "outstanding example of living history", the National Trust said The home of London's oldest restaurant, which has hosted famous faces from Charles Dickens to Madonna over the past two centuries, has been given to the National Trust. Rules originally opened in 1798 at 34-35 Maiden Lane in Covent Garden and has outlasted empires, survived the Blitz and fought off development plans. The £11m freehold gift of the restaurant building along with its historic collection such as visitor books, menus, and photographs will now be protected for future generations, the National Trust said. Rules restaurant will continue to trade, while becoming a commercial tenant of the charity. Under the deal, the rent payments will go towards conserving the building. Owner J-P Mayhew said the National Trust would protect the restaurant's future Rules, which has a well-preserved interior, has welcomed generations of high profile figures including Charles Dickens, Charlie Chaplin, Edward VII, who would meet with his mistresses there, and stars David Bowie, Liza Minnelli and Harrison Ford. It was favourite spot for poet John Betjeman, who once gave an impassioned speech in defence of the restaurant when it was under threat of redevelopment. Writer Graham Greene was known to enjoy birthday meals there and featured it in his novel The End Of The Affair. Rules is located in Covent Garden Hilary McGrady, director-general of the National Trust, said: "This place is an outstanding piece of living history, with its corners where kings dined and writers and politicians plotted, and the traditions it kept alive through wars and upheaval. "It has defied the odds to be standing here today, doors still open and treacle sponge still on the menu. "Mr Mayhew's extraordinary generosity, and the care he has poured into Rules over many decades, mean this beloved place has a future measured not in years but generations." The restaurant was a favourite spot for poet John Betjeman The building's owner, J-P Mayhew, said: "There are few restaurants in the world that have endured the test of time like Rules. "The trust will protect this place in a way that no-one else could, safeguarding its bricks and mortar, its famous interior and its invisible atmosphere, too. "I am grateful to them for believing in this idea and for protecting this building and two centuries' worth of stories for people to enjoy forever." The restaurant's proprietor Ricky McMenemy, who has worked there for 35 years, will become a commercial tenant of the conservation charity. He welcomed the donation, saying: "As an independent business, it gives us both the security and peace of mind that our home will be in very good hands and be protected and secure going forward." title: Dreams on hold: The 'frustrating' education limbo facing teenage asylum seekers
description: Young refugees describe their frustration at the lack of access to education for older teenagers who come to Northern Ireland to live
body: Mona came to Northern Ireland with her family in the hope of continuing her education In war-torn Gaza, 16-year-old Mona was able to receive more education than she says she's currently able to get in Northern Ireland. That is because, as a refugee or asylum seeker aged 16, she is not automatically able to enter school or college in Northern Ireland. At present, the legal age until which education is compulsory is 16. But that can leave young people like Mona who have fled conflict to come to Northern Ireland, with no automatic right to education. BBC News NI has asked the Department of Education and the Department for the Economy for comment. Mona came to Northern Ireland from Gaza with her family, including her younger siblings. "I came here to continue the education and be safe here," she said. "In Gaza I studied online, because of the war." When Mona arrived she was 15 and did not speak English, though she has learned English since. She initially attended school in Coleraine, but since her family moved to Belfast she has not been able to get a place in school or college. "I feel stressed because I cannot find anything for me," she said. "I would like to study nursing... Because I want to go back to Gaza and help the people in Gaza. "We are still children and we need education and support." Sara, 19, who came to Northern Ireland from Sudan in 2024 faced similar frustration. She received qualifications in Sudan, but although she wants to be a doctor she has been unable to get a university place to study medicine. "When I came and I tried to get into university they said that as I am a refugee my qualifications would not suffice," she said. "I had to get the same qualifications as students in Northern Ireland which can be quite frustrating." Sara speaks very good English but had to wait a year to be admitted to Further Education (FE) College to study A-Levels. Like Mona, Sara has received some help and support from Anaka Women's Collective, a community organisation which provides support for asylum seekers. Anaka has previously called for a specialist education programme for those aged 16-24 who come to Northern Ireland as asylum seekers and refugees. Hani wants to set up her own business but is frustrated that little has changed since the Stranded Dreams report Hani, 20, from Kurdistan and 22-year-old Hossam from Sudan both previously contributed to a report called Stranded Dreams, which outlined the problems older teenagers who were asylum seekers could face when trying to access education. Both want to set up their own businesses but both are frustrated that little has changed since the Stranded Dreams report was released over a year ago. Hani has been living in Northern Ireland for four years, and as she was 16 at the time she came her younger siblings could start school but she could not. Although she registered for English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) classes she had to wait two years before a place was available. That has delayed her being able to enter classes to take GCSE courses. "Personally I would love to study a course in business and marketing," she said. "Young people that have arrived in this country need to have a fair opportunity as other young people in this country. "Whenever me, my friends and young people come to this country we are starting from zero and we need a pathway to walk in." Hossam wants to combine a career in business with fashion design Hossam, who has been living in Northern Ireland for three years, feels the same. "It's surprising, it's really hard to continue in education," he said. "I really want to be a businessman and fashion designer also." "So that's my dream and it's really hard to do it here." The Northern Ireland Executive published a Refugee Integration Strategy in 2025, external to help refugees and asylum seekers integrate into Northern Ireland. While it aimed to help asylum seekers and refugees "to achieve their full potential" it did not include any specific commitments to provide better access to education for older teenagers. Where do lone asylum seeking children end up? title: Chris Mason: Lib Dems rally behind Davey as he pledges change
description: The BBC's political editor Chris Mason looks at the fallout from the Lib Dem frontbench resignations.
body: The Liberal Democrats don't tend to go for rhetorical fireworks or verbal kneecappings when grumbling about their leader. But that doesn't mean there hasn't been grumbling going on. In the last week, two members of Sir Ed Davey's frontbench have resigned because they were unhappy with him, the party's direction and how policy is decided. It meant the prospect of a lengthy and potentially testy meeting for Sir Ed with his MPs on Tuesday evening. The Liberal Democrat leader arrived smiling, flanked by several loyal MPs, but made no comment as he entered the room. Nearly four hours later, when the meeting broke up, his deputy Daisy Cooper said: "There is overwhelming support for Ed in the parliamentary party and a real sense that we need to come together as a group." Earlier, behind closed doors, we understand Sir Ed told his MPs: "We have made changes. I am happy to embrace more changes. I want us to work as a united front." Another tacit nod to things being less than united recently. In recent months he has appointed a new chief of staff, Ruth Younger, and James Holt, a veteran of the party's years in coalition government, as political director. Last week's resignations were described to the BBC by one party figure as a rather Lib Dem insurrection – dissent expressed modestly. Neither Charlie Maynard, a former Treasury spokesman and Alison Bennett, a former care and carers spokeswoman, have been publicly explicit about the reasons for their departures and both sought to express their concerns to Sir Ed privately and discreetly. And, it is understood, there was no coordination between them in the timing of their resignations. They were departures that led to fury among some of their colleagues, irritated that it made the party look divided. The resignations were the most clear indicators yet of an anxiety that has been bubbling away for over a year among some Liberal Democrat MPs. The essence of that anxiety is a fear they are not making enough of an impression and impact for the 72 MPs they have in parliament. "The big frustration is the lack of cut through, being noticed. We are the biggest third party in the Commons in a century. But parliament doesn't shape things as much as it used to. It's about algorithms now," is how one figure put it. They added: "In the world of social media there is an incentive, even a financial incentive, to be divisive and extreme. That's a sandpit we refuse to play in." Nonetheless, the party is planning to up its social media game, but do so in line with what it sees as its authentic temperament and values. Those around Sir Ed Davey privately acknowledge there is what they claim to be a "small group" of Lib Dem MPs who are not happy with his leadership. It is suggested that number isn't greater than "half a dozen" - a phrase used by several people we have spoken to. But the anxiety about a perceived lack of impact involves far more MPs than that. Some previous private critics have been won over by the recent changes to Sir Ed's team and are pleased to see the government talk about issues they care about: the European Union, changing the voting system for Westminster elections and social care in England, for instance. They also hope the scale of their local campaigning, rather than poor national opinion poll ratings, will be more significant come the next general election. Al Pinkerton, the party's Europe spokesman, told the BBC there had been a frank exchange of views during the meeting, but Sir Ed's willingness to make changes had been "very well received." "It is a slog in the middle of a parliament, it's hard being the third party and it's such an enormous leap going from 15 MPs to 72," another party figure present told us. "But we're getting there putting in place the structures to better deal with that and keep MPs happy." "Why would we get rid of our leader when no one else is pitching to be our leader? We need to let Ed get on with it," said another MP. But they all know the underlying concern about impact – the challenge of being noticed – is real and not going away. title: Look North sofa to be pushed 80 miles for Children in Need
description: Lindsey Burrow and Amy Garcia will travel 80 miles across Yorkshire.
body: Amy Garcia and Lindsey Burrow are planning to push the Look North red sofa across Yorkshire for their Children in Need challenge The wife of rugby league legend Rob Burrow will join BBC Look North presenter Amy Garcia for this year's Children in Need charity challenge. Lindsey Burrow and Amy plan to push the programme's red sofa 80 miles (129km) across Yorkshire over five days, covering 12-20 miles each day. The pair will start at Ripon on Monday 9 November and pass through South Yorkshire before crossing the finish line in Wakefield on Friday 13 November. Their efforts will be broadcast live along the route. Last year, they raised tens of thousands of pounds on a three-legged walk for BBC Children in Need. "We'll take the sofa out of the Look North studio and try to push it 80 miles across Yorkshire with a specially-designed trolley," Amy said. "We're going to visit dozens of towns and villages and we'll attempt to scale some of the region's highest peaks, including the famous Holme Moss climb." They will also make stops at Children in Need-funded projects along the way to see how they are supporting children and young people in the region. Lindsey has run several marathons in memory of her late husband, rugby league legend Rob Burrow, who died in 2024 Lindsey has also run several marathons in memory of her late husband, who died in 2024, four and half years after his diagnosis of motor neurone disease. She said she was expecting the sofa push to be one of her toughest challenges yet. "We did a test push for about 500 yards and it's a lot harder than I expected. "I think it's going to be a real challenge, to say the least. "I like to take part in fundraising, and to be able to support Children in Need with the incredible work that they do and support the charities, is just really special." In 2018 the Big 50 Sofa Challenge raised almost £200,000 for Sport Relief It is not the first time the studio's red sofa has been out on the road. In 2018, Amy took part in the Big 50 Sofa Challenge with the late Harry Gration and weather presenter Paul Hudson, in aid of Sport Relief. "It's going to be a slog, the sofa is heavier than in 2018, but it's such an incredible opportunity to meet our viewers." She said she was also looking forward to taking on a challenge again with Lindsey after the pair walked 30 miles across Yorkshire with their legs tied together in 2025 for the Children in Need Three-Legged Challenge. "Lindsey and I are both mums and we are passionate about trying to help other children who don't get the same opportunities." title: Isle of Wight fossil identified as new dinosaur species
description: Invictibellatrix would have been up to four metres long with feathers and had 20cm claws.
body: Invictibellatrix amberina is thought to have lived in the Early Cretaceous period about 120 million years ago A new species of dinosaur - a long-clawed predator the size of a large tiger - has been identified from a fossil found on the Isle of Wight more than 100 years ago. The dinosaur, named Invictibellatrix amberina, is described in a new paper in the journal Royal Society Open Science and belongs to a group of agile, two-legged carnivores called megaraptorans. Megaraptorans were closely related to tyrannosaurs including Tyrannosaurus rex but had slender heads and attacked prey with their large arms and giant curved claws instead of their jaws. Dr Cassius Morrison of University College London (UCL) said it was a "real mystery" why the fossil - a chunk of the back of a skull - had been overlooked in the Natural History Museum. The fossil was originally found at the foot of a cliff on the south-west coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur palaeontologist Reginald Walter Tooley and was acquired by the Natural History Museum in 1924. Invictibellatrix, meaning "unconquered female warrior", is one of the smallest and earliest of the group to be found, living in the Early Cretaceous period about 120 million years ago. The researchers undertook a CT scan of the fossil Researchers believe Invictibellatrix would have been three to four metres long and just over a metre and a half in height - about as tall as a human. It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long. It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals – occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today. Megaraptors are regarded as the most mysterious of the large, meat-eating dinosaurs, as few megaraptor fossils have been found. Until now no megaraptorans had been found in Europe. Lead author Dr Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) said: "It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. "Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight – who knows what else is waiting to be discovered." The researchers undertook a CT scan of the fossil, creating a 3D model of this part of the skull. They compared the fossil with skulls and brain cases from tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors and other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs. Cliffs on the Isle of Wight are hotspots for fossil discoveries The research team also used mathematical modelling to investigate how the spread of megaraptors around the world might have changed over time, based on fossils discovered so far, dinosaurs' evolutionary trees, geography and climate. It was one of more than 1,000 specimens discovered by Tooley that were acquired by the Natural History Museum after his death. Professor Paul Barrett, the study's senior author from the Natural History Museum, said: "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species. "Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made." The study did not explain why megaraptors likely died out in the north, but this may have been a result of shifts in climate or environment, or the presence of competing predators such as other tyrannosaurs. title: Ian McKellen set to perform as a hologram in new play
description: The Lord of the Rings actor stars in An Ark which will have its European premier in Manchester.
body: The 87-year-old Lord of the Rings star features in the play An Ark Sir Ian McKellen is set to star in the European premier of a play in which he appears as a hologram. The 87-year-old Lord of the Rings star, who was born in Burnley, will perform in An Ark when it comes to Manchester's Factory International Aviva Studios. The play, which debuted in New York, will feature McKellen and Bridgerton star Golda Rosheuvel in 3D holographic form, which was achieved using 52 cameras filming them from multiple angles. McKellen said: "A new Simon Stephens play is always an excitement but when it is written to be performed in this unique way, it feels more like an explosion." McKellen said the actors involved had "relished the chance to explore a new way of acting". "New York has already been impressed with the result. Now it's Manchester's turn," he added. West End star Arinze Kene, and Rosie Sheehy, best known for her starring role in Guess How Much I Love You, complete the cast. Sheehy described the making of the production as "a true adventure", adding: "Experimenting with what theatre can be is always a thrill – when the boundaries are being stretched this far it can feel terrifying at times. "However, being surrounded by such an extraordinary group of people took away that fear and replaced it with excitement and reward. "It felt very good to be part of it all." McKellen moved to Wigan as a child, but remained faithful to his Burnley roots, and performed at Burnley Youth Theatre in 2019 as part of his 80th birthday tour. The production will run from 27 March to 10 April. title: One stolen every four minutes - inside the police battle against vehicle thieves
description: Officers tell the BBC they are overstretched and struggling to keep up with sophisticated criminals.
body: This video can not be played Watch: BBC joins police on front line against car theft It is 01:00 on a Thursday and we are in the back of an unmarked police car on the hunt for vehicle thieves in east London. A call comes in over the radio about a stolen Ford Transit van. Within 25 minutes officers have found it, chased it down and arrested a suspect. Officers tell us the night has been successful, with further arrests made, yet across the UK a car is stolen every four minutes. Despite a recent drop, vehicle thefts are up almost 50% in England and Wales compared with a decade ago, according to Home Office data. Last year, just 3% of vehicle theft offences resulted in a charge or summons. As well as spending time on the front line in London and Sussex, we have privately spoken to 20 police officers from six forces. They told us while they have the skills and experience to tackle vehicle crime, they are overstretched, under-resourced and struggling to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated criminal networks. Thieves are becoming more confident. A man who claims he receives stolen vehicles and breaks them into parts at a so-called "chop shop" told the BBC he does not fear the authorities, because they "couldn't catch a cold". Once the preserve of joyriders and opportunists, vehicle theft is now a lucrative global criminal business. Cars are stolen to order, and moved across the country or dismantled within hours, say police, making them difficult to recover and suspects hard to track. Many vehicles are sent overseas to places like the United Arab Emirates, The Democratic Republic of Congo and Jamaica. Victims of car theft have told us they feel frustrated and helpless. One woman said it took car thieves just 35 seconds to steal her BMW, yet police only began investigating a day later. Another man said he feared for his life when masked thieves broke into his home demanding his car keys. The success criminals are having is also hitting motorists more widely, with insurance quotes having risen by 82% since 2021, according to security think tank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi). Police arrested three suspects in the targeted Sussex operation the BBC attended Our night-time ride in the unmarked police car takes place during an eight-hour Metropolitan Police operation targeting vehicle crime. "Havering has been affected quite badly," PC Yoosef Outaleb tells us - partly because thieves use the back roads as a cut-through to neighbouring Essex. Police say the county has particularly high numbers of illegal "chop shops", which dismantle vehicles for parts so they can be sold and exported. "They [the criminals] don't have borders, whereas we do," he says. When criminal activity straddles police force boundaries, investigations can often slow down - which gangs look to exploit. Two stolen vehicles are recovered, yet Met officers also uncover other crimes. They pursue armed robbers on e-bikes, apprehend a drunk driver and arrest three men in a car full of Class A drugs, cash and phones. It is all important work, but police admit that responding to these crimes diverts them away from targeting known vehicle thieves. The thieves, known as "grafters" within criminal networks, are out every night stealing cars, the man claiming to work at a chop shop told us. Many vehicles are then broken into parts. Such is the demand, he says, that deals to re-sell the parts are often done before he has even finished dismantling a vehicle. Some stolen vehicles are left intact, given new number plates and sold in the UK or abroad, while others are used to facilitate drug dealing and human trafficking, or as getaway vehicles for robberies and break-ins. Stolen: Chasing Britain's Car Thieves Join police on the hunt for high-tech thieves behind a wave of UK car crime. See the latest weapons gangs are using in action, including electronic skeleton keys and military grade signal-jammers. While the long-term trend presents difficult reading for police, reported vehicle thefts fell 5% in England and Wales last year, to 119,000. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, vehicle thefts remained largely flat, at about 5,000 and 1,200 a year respectively. Fifteen of the 32 police forces in England and Wales that responded to a BBC Freedom of Information request said they do not employ any full-time, specially-trained stolen vehicle examiners, who can carry out detailed examinations of cars and bolster investigations. But Assistant Chief Constable Sarah Grahame, the national police lead on tackling vehicle crime, tells us officers' efforts - like the night-time operation in east London - are having an impact. UK forces are also collaborating with Interpol, shipping companies and vehicle manufacturers to address an issue "that spans globally", she says. She admits current theft levels are unacceptable, but says there is no funding to routinely carry out large-scale operations within current police budgets, set by the Home Office. Instead, forces organise "intensification weeks" aimed at disrupting criminal networks. One involving 32 forces last month, called Operation Alliances, led to at least 286 arrests and 319 vehicles seized. Three keyless Toyota RAV4s were stolen in Sussex, but all were recovered In East Sussex in September, where we witnessed a smaller, targeted operation, we were told that 17 cars had been stolen in the Hastings and Rother areas in the previous two months. Many of the vehicles were keyless Toyota RAV4s - taken by thieves using technology that bypasses vehicle security systems. Three of the vehicles had been taken the previous night. Within hours, officers recovered all three vehicles and arrested three suspects, including one they believe had been in charge of the other two. Two suspects have now been charged, including one arrested after a stolen Toyota was found near his home. title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
description: Archaeologists say the wreck is up to 4,700 years old, dating to the Early Bronze Age.
body: This video can not be played Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova Island The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say. They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built. The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside. The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. "The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition. The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves. Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae. The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age. Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, differerent styles are linked to particular periods. The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base. Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old. "Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%." The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research ship After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conserved Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater. Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue. "I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said. The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae. "It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said. "It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years." The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world. The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. They believe is it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete. The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefacts Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships. There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaelogy Association specialises in finding and studying them. Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel. "We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years. "We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back." The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring it The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks. Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago. The oldest known shipwreck where some of the wood is still preserved was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago. title: Not building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', warns Heathrow boss
description: Thomas Woldbye tells the Today progamme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after comments made by the prime minister.
body: Not building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned. Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion. The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year. The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps". A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment". They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around £40 billion in economic benefits across the country". Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners. Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer". Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation. "If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said. "It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country." A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost £33bn to build. Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built. This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs. The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues. Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners". "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said, speaking to the BBC last month. Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions. Thomas Woldbye, seen here speaking to the BBC last year, has stressed the importance of Heathrow's third runway He added that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK." Downing Street declined to comment on Woldbye's remarks. Questioned about the noise impact on nearby communities of more planes taking off and landing, Woldbye claimed Heathrow had seen a "stark" reduction in noise over the past 40 years and said the "trend will continue". "My biggest concern is actually the years of uncertainty. And I think it's time that we give them certainty on what we want with this project so that we can move on and they can move on in their lives," he said. Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow Woldbye told the Today programme he had not yet met the current Chancellor John Healey, but if he did, he would outline that the airport "contributes dramatically to the economy" but that "we are now full". "That means we will stop contributing or stop growing that contribution. If we want to avoid that, we need to now take this decision, move forward and continue the work of the previous government to move at speed and deliver this," he said. The Department for Transport said it was still finalising its Airports National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow. It was last updated in 2018. Woldbye said Heathrow was working on a planning application which has planned to submit in the next couple of years, but said any decision would be guided by government's the national policy statement. title: Russell T Davies criticises BBC boss's 'clumsy' AI Doctor Who comments
description: BBC director general Matt Brittin said he had seen a "pretty good" AI-generated episode of the show.
body: Longtime Doctor Who writer and showrunner Russell T Davies has criticised the new BBC director general over comments he made about an AI-generated episode of the show. Matt Brittin told a Royal Television Society conference in September that he had been sent a "pretty good" 50-minute unofficial Doctor Who episode. "That's a clumsy thing to say in an industry where he's got writers and artists and it specifically affects people, they're the first to take the blow," Davies told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show. Addressing criticism he has received, Brittin told a staff meeting last week he was attempting to make a point around the "pace of change" while stressing he believed in "human creativity". The director general joked he had "got into trouble" over what he had said, but added: "I was just trying to make the point: Look at the pace of change and what this stuff can do." He said: "I want to be really clear: Humans are leading, and I believe in human creativity, enhanced by whatever tools." He emphasised human-led creativity would always be at the heart of the BBC's mission. But speaking to BBC Radio 4, Davies said that the new director general, who joined the BBC after a career at Google, "hasn't worked in television for that long and might not be so fruity with an opinion in future". "My inbox went ping ping ping ping ping, so God knows what his was like," he added. Matt Brittin became the BBC's director general in May 2026 Davies was also asked more broadly about AI, including how, or if, writers should use the technology. "I have heard stories of some writers using AI prompts to do a first draft which I find shocking because I think... What are you paid for otherwise? What are you there to do?" He said he did not use it to write his scripts but he "very much" worried it would start to replace writers, and in some circumstances that may already be the case. Davies is one of the UK's most influential television writers - from the ground-breaking Queer as Folk to acclaimed dramas including It's a Sin, Years and Years and, more recently, Tip Toe, he has had a major impact on British TV. But perhaps his most significant achievement is his work on Doctor Who. In 2005, he brought the Timelord back after a 16-year absence after pitching it to the BBC's then-head of drama at a party in Manchester. He revived the show again in 2023, although he confirmed earlier this year he would be stepping away. He told The Media Show there were times he "used to dread going on a Doctor Who set" because of the expensive special effects and "explosions going on, people pulling themselves in to prosthetics". "It's more difficult than any other set." The show is now at a crossroads. The BBC cancelled the planned Christmas special and Disney+ no longer co-finances the series. But Davies had good news for Doctor Who fans. Another series is on the cards, he promised, even though he will not be involved. "You'll start to see production with a brand-new Doctor, a brand-new companion, summer next year." Davies - who recently released his memoir 'The Queerest of Folk: A Life in Television' - got his first break aged 22 working in BBC children's TV "for £50 a day". "It was the best training you could possibly have," he said. The Swansea-born writer later honed his skills in the heyday of Granada Television "when Coronation Street was getting 18 million, 20 million [views]". Also in the interview, he revealed inspiration can come from the most unlikely sources - he "records the phone-ins on This Morning" and listens to them in the evening. "All human life is there… just a couple of times a year, you'll get an extraordinary human story or something very funny. One of my favourite ones about a year ago was a woman whose mother-in-law was insisting on wearing white to her wedding". He believes he will get a script out of that "one day": "What a great little problem that is - two women just at war." title: Watch: Hong Kong crowds queue to see Van Gogh painting unveiled for first time in 60 years
description: Châtaigniers en fleurs, also known as Chestnut Trees in Blossom, is expected to receive record bids at auction this weekend.
body: This video can not be played One of Vincent van Gogh's paintings not seen publicly for more than 60 years has drawn crowds in Hong Kong, where it has been displayed ahead of auction this weekend in New York. Van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom) in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise, about two months before he died in 1890. Sotheby's estimates the painting will fetch $180m (£136m), which would mark the highest auction price for a Van Gogh artwork. title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on alleged espionage
description: The Hokkaido Shimbun journalist is accused of collecting information on Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.
body: The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in the far eastern region of Sakhalin Russian authorities have charged a Japanese journalist for espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo. The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in Russia's far eastern region of Sakhalin, a day before he was due to leave the country. The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands, claimed by both countries, in August. Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities are "verifying the facts" and will "respond appropriately" thereafter. Russian authorities allege that Imai had "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported. The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. Imai has been taken to Moscow and will be remanded until 12 December, before the trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency. Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be jailed up to 20 years in prison. "Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday. "We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity. Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin. Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter, but did not comment further on the incident. Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two. Takaichi slammed Putin's visit in August – his first-ever to the islands – saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories". Moscow dismissed her criticism as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded". Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo for requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese. The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine. In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison. Gershkovich, a US citizen, was in 2024 released in a prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War took place. In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours. title: Lena Dunham's Girls to return for limited HBO run
description: Ten years after the series finale, the "Girls" are getting back together to explore the "milestone of turning forty", HBO says.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Lena Dunham invites the cast of Girls to reboot the TV series next year HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired. Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars – shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells. All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer. "We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement. Girls' stars Lena Dunham, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Allison Williams "I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said. "Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said. Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting. It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s. The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century. "We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said. "To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when." The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as". Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show. In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations. In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival. Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude. "I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote. Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick. title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
description: The bank inadequately flagged transactions linked to potential Chinese money laundering networks, the Treasury said.
body: Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday. The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said. Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury. "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC. The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning. "Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added. In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks." The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said. The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied. OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said. title: The Papers: 'Spy chief's grim warning' and 'tiger victim was child actor'
description: Wednesday's papers are dominated by coverage of a speech given by the MI5 chief and the death of a man in a tiger enclosure.
body: Many of Wednesday's papers lead on a speech from MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum. Under the headline "red alert", The Daily Mirror reports on his warning that Russia is the "number one threat" to UK security. Danger exists in the form of "sabotage, arson, AI, bio-weapons, coercion and violence", with the MI5 chief comparing the situation to that the which existed after 9/11. The Daily Express also leads with the warning, headlining that the "UK must not 'play into hands' of Putin". It notes that the MI5 chief said "Russia trolls" who are alleged to have attempted to sway the Brexit referendum will be "delighted" to be "front page news once again" after being mentioned in the prime minister in a recent interview. The Telegraph pulls out a different line from the MI5 chief's speech, headlining "Russia did not sway Brexit vote". Sir Ken said it was "a matter of public record" that there was interference in the referendum by online trolls and bots. The Times also includes coverage of the MI5 chief's speech, noting that AI is being used by terrorists in attack plans. Its main story is the "online tax crackdown to boost the high street", reporting that "Healey's budget plan will stop foreign sellers avoiding VAT on Amazon, eBay and Temu". The Guardian's take on the spy chief's speech is "MI5 warns of rightwing shift from anti-migrant opinion to terrorism". The Guardian also reports that the UK has resisted "EU pressure to hit China with tariffs". The i Paper also leads with the spy chief's speech, quoting him as saying threats from foreign adversaries have quadrupled in a decade. Also on its front page, television chef Dipna Anand shares that she had 13 miscarriages. The Independent goes with Sir Ken's warning that "AI is 'supercharging" threat to Britain" for its lead story. It also carries a picture of the man killed in a tiger enclosure, who has been named as William Chapman. The Daily Star says that 23-year-old Chapman was once a "child actor" in its headline. He had appeared on both the BBC and ITV, it says. Tax fears have been "eased in Burnham's 'pro-business' pitch to bosses", according to the Financial Times. The paper also reports a warning from Anthropic, developers of chatbot Claude, which has warned that "AI worms" will soon able to "hijack smart home devices such as ovens and televisions". "Toxic water spills surge", writes the Metro, saying a toxic spill "pollutes our waterways every 90 mins." This is an exclusive for the paper. According to the Daily Mail, "four out of five new jobs went to foreigners in the past decade". It also announces the arrival of Trump's "very glamorous" new press secretary Katie Zacharia, saying "move over Eyelashes Andy" - a reference to Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The Sun headlines with "Man shifty" as it says the prime minister has been "accused of covering up his links to scandal-hit Manchester City". It says he had two "freebie dinners" with City and that a Sun probe has found "deleted records". Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
description: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died on Monday after police say he was ejected from a ride at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'Super bizarre, traumatic' - Witnesses recount fatal Six Flags incident Warning: This story includes distressing content A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of Georgia. The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was found dead under the ride after being ejected and hitting other people on it, according to police. An investigation is under way and few details have yet to be released about what happened. Six Flags, the largest amusement park operator in North America, has temporarily closed nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution. Here's what we know so far about the incident. This video can not be played Watch: Aerial footage shows riders stuck on Six Flags roller coaster The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday. "Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday. "Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction." The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident. The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review. Officials have not held a news conference on the incident. The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five. The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones". Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground. "It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that." He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him. One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement. Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed". "Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen." He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched. Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood. Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off". Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears. "I broke because we were just on there," she said. Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer. His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death. He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach. "Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account. "His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did." Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website. The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims. According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool. Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico. In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet. In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.
