title: Our memorial garden helps us grieve - a cemetery felt too far away
description: Emma Moore shares how creating a special place at home has helped her family.
body: Emma Moore says the garden has given her family, including elder daughter Penelope, a focus following the death of baby Mabel When Emma Moore's daughter Mabel died, the idea of visiting her in a cemetery felt too far away. "I don't like going to them and I feel like [visits] fizzle out," she says. "At first, you'll go regularly and then it'll start being once a year." Mabel was born prematurely at 27 weeks in April, her lungs had not fully developed and she lived for just two days. Emma keeps Mabel's ashes next to a photograph of her tiny feet but she wanted a special place to feel close to her. "So we created something in the garden... [to] always be reminded of her every day," she tells Morning Live. The stillness of green spaces "can help us connect with memories" of loved ones, says Andy Langford, clinical director at Cruse Bereavement Support. And there are ways to create a special place of calm to remember anyone you've lost - even if you don't have a garden or know much about plants. Emma, with her partner Louis and daughter Penelope, says the garden reminds them of Mabel each day "I'd never done anything like this before, so I had no clue about where to start," says Emma, 35, who lives near Bolton with her partner Louis and elder daughter Penelope. She chose to dedicate a part of the garden with a willow tree to Mabel. "I've enjoyed doing the gardening and planting. It was nice to focus on something." Of all the flowers the family have planted in Mabel's garden, Emma's favourite are the lilies. Morning Live - Memorial Gardens Families speak about the healing power of nature and how some have created dedicated green spaces at home. The story about memorial gardens starts at 1:02:20 White lilies are said to represent peace and are a traditional choice for acts of remembrance in the UK, says botanist James Wong of BBC Gardeners' Question Time. The flowers are low maintenance and can last for decades in your garden, he says, and there are a number of varieties to suit your soil. The colour of your flowers is a personal choice, adds Wong, so there is no need to "follow the rules" of British tradition with white lilies. You may find soft pink, mauve and lilac relaxing, or you may find yellows and reds more vibrant and lift your mood. Emma hadn't done much gardening before but has enjoyed creating one for Mabel Wong says smell helps people connect to nature and works in harmony with the sight of beautiful flowers to create a peaceful atmosphere. Many rose varieties have a fragrance but Wong also suggests choosing plants with scented leaves for when flowers are not in bloom. "If you were to plant something like a mint, a eucalyptus or a rose geranium - they have very strongly scented leaves and they're around for a long period of time." He also suggests evergreen Italian cypresses, tall and thin plants more commonly used for commemoration in warmer climates, as they are capable of growing "perfectly well outdoors in the UK". They have a woody aroma likened to pine or juniper. Wong also says chrysanthemums - "a classic funeral flower" in East Asian cultures - will also readily grow here. They have a herbal almost medicinal fragrance. The family dedicated a part of their garden under a willow tree to Mabel Emma has placed a bench with a plaque featuring Mabel's name near the willow tree. She often sits on the bench in the morning with a cup of tea. "It's her little garden," says Emma. "It's a really personal space." Langford says benches are common in public memorial gardens because they offer "a sense of permanence" and, on a practical level, help you take a break from the stresses and rigours of everyday life. If you want to use plants to create a memorial space indoors on a balcony or window box, think about nearby seating for two which opens up the opportunity for conversation about your loved one. Emma keeps Mabel's ashes next to a photograph of her tiny feet in her home If you don't have a garden, Wong suggests choosing commemorative house plants suited to warmer conditions. The peace lily, native to the rainforests of Colombia, will "grow perfectly well indoors all year round" but should be kept in warm conditions with low levels of light. Frangipanis are "incredibly popular [in] Southeast Asia" and grow well indoors provided they have a reasonable amount of space and are placed in bright, warm spaces all year. In Mabel's memorial garden there is also a swing surrounded by planters full of flowers. It's a place that has given Emma comfort. "I feel like I'm still very much grieving but I can just go and sit there and think about her and reflect on things." If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line. title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
description: William Chapman was attacked by the tiger after he entered its pen at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.
body: The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging". William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene. In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication". It said it was for the coroner to decide whether his mental illness played a part in his death, asking that the public respect that process. City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death and the park remains closed. "William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said. The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time". "The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued. "The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did." A spokesperson for the South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family are being supported by specialist officers. The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation and ongoing closure of the park. An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in. Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass. Chapman was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe. "We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe said in a tribute on Tuesday. "It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him." "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time," the statement continued. As a child, Chapman appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd. He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories. Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park have separately said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" are with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to Chapman's family and those who were at the scene. title: Gales and heavy rain to impact UK as yellow wind warning issued
description: The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind in north-west Scotland on Wednesday with 70mph gusts possible, as Ben Rich explains.
body: A weather system containing the remnants of Hurricane Isaias is forecast to send gales, heavy rain and a surge of warm air to parts of the UK this week. The centre of the low, and its most significant impacts, will stay hundreds of miles from UK shores but north-west Scotland will see a spell of gales. A Met Office yellow warning has been issued for parts of the Highlands and Western Isles with the risk of gusts touching 70mph (113km/h) in places. Heavy rain will also affect parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland but much of England and Wales will remain largely dry with spells of sunshine. The area of low pressure will also send a renewed surge of warm air across the country bringing above-average temperatures for many. The track of the storm means the UK will avoid the most significant impacts Hurricane Isaias was the first Atlantic hurricane of the season and made landfall in the southern United States last Friday. It weakened rapidly and ceased to be a hurricane but its remnants threw heavy rain across the eastern side of North America. Since then, the leftovers have emerged over the Atlantic and been scooped up by a powerful jet stream. This has developed a new area of low pressure that has been undergoing what meteorologists describe as explosive cyclogenesis, also referred to as a weather bomb. The jet stream is steering the centre of the storm hundreds of miles away from our shores, passing close to Iceland where it will bring the threat of blizzards. Wind gusts over the sea between Iceland and the Faroe Islands could exceed 110mph but nothing this severe is expected in the vicinity of the UK. The far north-west of Scotland will bear the brunt of the winds. A Met Office yellow weather warning is valid on Wednesday from 10:00 until 19:00 BST, and warns of a high risk of moderate impacts including disruption to rail, air and ferry transport, delays on roads and bridges - especially for high-sided vehicles - and possible short-term power cuts. A Met Office yellow weather warning for wind comes into force on Wednesday morning Widespread gusts of 50-60mph are likely with 70mph possible for exposed coasts and hills around the middle of the day. Outside the warning area, Shetland is also anticipated to see 50mph gusts - although the risk of disruption here is less - and 40mph gusts are possible in other parts of Scotland, Northern Ireland, northern England and north-west Wales. After a mainly dry start, outbreaks of rain are expected to arrive in many parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the end of the day, with heaviest rain in the north and west. Some patchy rain may also spread into north-west England and north Wales, but most of both countries will stay fine with sunny spells after any early mist has cleared. The deep area of low pressure is set to send warm south-westerly winds across the UK. Temperatures will widely climb into the mid to high-teens Celsius, possibly peaking at 20C in a few locations in southern England. This will leave most places 2-4C above the mid-October average. This warmth will linger in many parts of England and Wales on Thursday with temperatures expected to peak at 22C in East Anglia. Afternoon highs of 11-16C would be typical in the middle of October However, a weather front will move slowly southwards taking rain across Scotland, Northern Ireland, northern England and north Wales and behind it things will start to turn cooler. Those chillier - and eventually drier - conditions will then spread southwards across the UK through Friday and over the weekend. Temperatures will fall much closer to the seasonal norm with brisk winds accentuating the colder feel around some eastern coasts and the chance of overnight frost in places. Computer models suggest that high pressure will then settle close to the UK which should keep Atlantic low pressure systems at bay for the time being, bringing long spells of dry weather for many. title: Robot seized by German police after allegedly groping teenage girl
description: Police have launched an investigation on suspicion of sexual harassment after the robot's owner, 16, and his companion are said to have streamed the incident.
body: German police have launched an investigation into two teenagers accused of controlling a robot that allegedly groped a 16-year-old girl. Police in Cologne have confiscated the red and gold robot that allegedly grabbed the girl's buttocks and made thrusting motions against her before she screamed and moved away. North Rhine Westphalia Police said the robot's 16-year-old owner and his companion, 19, are believed to have streamed the incident live on social media and commented on it. According to a police statement on Facebook, the 120cm (3.9ft) tall device approached the girl from behind while she was with her friends close to midnight local time (23:00 BST) on Saturday. The girl was in front of a fast-food outlet near the city centre when the incident took place, police said. Emergency services were alerted, and the teenage boy and the man now under investigation with him were found a block away a short time later. The robot was discovered in the back of a car, where the boy had placed it, police said. A photo released by police showed the robot wearing a black moustache, a gold-coloured chain and white vest. Along with the robot, police seized two mobile phones belonging to the suspects. They are trying to determine whether someone was deliberately controlling the robot's movements at the time of the incident. In a follow-up post on Facebook, police warned some social media comments on the case "can be a crossing of the line and in the worst case, a criminal offense". title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
description: Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.
body: Serhii K was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany. Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue. The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place. Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts. He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia. In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame. Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts. As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied. Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock. They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat". Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022 Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction, external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies". They say the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime" as an attack by military means against civilian objects". Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin. Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war". He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions." However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case. "They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained. In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany. After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year. German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert. While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court. In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just". Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage. Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial. Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us". title: Watch: 'Traumatic' - Witnesses recount moment man fell out of Six Flags roller coaster
description: One person has died and others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia.
body: This video can not be played One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia. Six Flags Over Georgia park officials said staff found the man, identified as 42-year-old Atlanta resident Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, beneath the ride. He was unresponsive and not breathing. Witnesses have described the incident and its aftermath, with one man who was also on the ride describing it as "super bizarre, traumatic". title: Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story
description: Simbarashe Kundizeza was responding to an accusation that has caused an uproar on social media.
body: Simbarashe Kundizeza says he was inspired by a poem about fish tanks to write a story about his family struggles in Zimbabwe Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing. His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated. "For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X, external. The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing. "I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme. The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI, external - had been published on Sunday. It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies. Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong. The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers. Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being "crazy, racist and wildly unethical", external. Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk", external. Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised. "There's something incredibly sinister about this," the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X, external. "Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added. Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025, external. In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development. Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original. She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was "against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case". Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested". "I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready." Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate". In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels, external, which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to English-language writing by non-native English speakers. The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation". Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human". "I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both." In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing." For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts. "Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother. "The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI. The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks. He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zi

title: Pictured: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
description: Striking images including an urban coyote and an elephant carrying a dead calf are among this year's winners.
body: An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed. Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain. Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females. For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals." He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said. The competition's annual exhibition, external opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images. Category: Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years Location: Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required. While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task. "I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world," says Whitfield. Category: 10 Years and Under You do not need a camera or a plane ticket to take an award-winning photo. Davis captured this shot in the garden using her dad's smartphone. The image freezes in time a single wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it prepares to land on a flower. Category: Animals in their Environment Location: Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya Lewin captured this dreamy, black-and-white photo of a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole. He softened the usually harsh light by using a camera converted to infrared. Common octopuses are usually found in the warmer Mediterranean Sea. But with global warming pushing up springtime sea temperatures, sightings across south-west England have massively increased. Sanders described the moment he spotted a single eye peeking from behind the kelp: "We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity." Photographer: Isak Pretorius, South Africa Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebill storks are estimated to remain in the wild. Yet Pretorius, while canoeing with a guide, was able to capture these two – likely a breeding pair collecting material for their nest. Despite their name, shoebill storks are actually more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Spring sees male blackbirds search for high vantage points to sing and try to attract a mate. This photo was taken in a vineyard at dawn, when the birds sing their most complex compositions. Location: Lumphini Park, Bangkok, Thailand Forestson lowered himself onto the mud to capture this common water lizard against the city skyline. These adaptable lizards live in cities across South and South East Asia and will take whatever food is available, such as catfish and koi. Location: Kagoshima Prefecture, Kyūshū, Japan This is probably the first time the courtship ritual of Abbott's moray eels has been photographed, the NHM said. Wu worked with biologists and used dim red light and a customised fisheye lens to minimise disturbance. San Francisco is estimated to be home to around 100 coyotes, living alongside a large human population. While they can prey on domestic animals, they also help control disease-carrying rodents, and residents' attitudes towards them are mixed. Category: Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles Location: Contra Costa County, California, USA Sorokin dipped his camera and lights in a murky pond to catch this glimpse of a California newt laying her eggs. Location: Thar Desert, Rajasthan, India A scorpion is photographed burrowing into the shifting dunes of India's Thar Desert. Exploring the dunes at night, Raul saw many scorpions searching for prey but as temperatures rose after sunrise, the scorpion dug into the sand to escape the intense heat. Category: Oceans: The Bigger Picture Location: Off Cenderawasih Bay, Papua, Indonesia A whale shark investigates the catch of a mobile net-fishing platform, known as a bagan. Lindbloom searched for sharks around dawn, using the bagan's bright lights to illuminate them when there was too little natural light for his drone. Papatsanis used ultrviolet light to illuminate mushrooms known as "beautiful bonnets" growing from a decaying log on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus in Greece. Location: Germany and Northern Ireland, UK Tinker-Tsavalas uses macro photography to reveal the intricate details of tiny animals that are easily overlooked, particularly in urban habitats. His interest in macro photography developed during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when he was restricted to habitats close to his home in Berlin. title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
description: AI dominates the translation business, but for high-stakes work, humans are still needed.
body: Google's translation service handles one trillion words per month "Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard. "It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator. "You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS. He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs". "But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon. A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather. In April, Google said people are now translating, external one trillion words a month with Google Translate. That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems. Direct sales of machine translation, external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year. AI translation is the "right call" in many cases says John Zimmerman "For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages. "For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says. With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia. Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI. "Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains. But that human input is required less and less. "The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft. "Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman. Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French. She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them. "There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said. The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié. When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y". In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase. The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees. Ariella Baltié specialises in legal translation work Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field. "The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations. She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth). "That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter. She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult. "Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot." Carol Bereuter is a specialist in medical translations "If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon. Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says. "When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon. Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner". Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work. "27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman. Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging. "As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% rel

title: Is it OK for jobseekers or employers to use AI?
description: Graduates are increasingly using AI to misrepresent themselves in job applications, research suggests. But some say their peer group has no choice.
body: This video can not be played Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired? Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job? We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates, external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason. But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating? Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager. He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI. "Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that." Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicants While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on. He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates. "That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening." This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process". According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions. However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments. On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market. EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employees Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem. EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year. Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process. "What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't." Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible. It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills. But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews. "A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script." AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff' AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews. While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would. "I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?" According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says. And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving. EDF does not currently use AI screening but Hollie Moody says they may have to in future. She says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" that employers and employees will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits. "It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business." title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
description: The CWU says more posties are leaving since a new delivery system was brought in, that it claims is not working in hundreds of offices.
body: About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year. The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance. The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases. Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service. Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26. It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds. But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class. "I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out." A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time. Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobs Only three-quarters of first class mail delivered on time Royal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff say Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload. We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day. Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare". "We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands. Bryn Dymott says he is speaking out now because he wants people to know what's really happening Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas. "People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered." Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening. He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise." So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices. Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems. The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others. "Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU. The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing. Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas. It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses." The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period. The BBC saw returned post that couldn't be delivered so ended up back on the frames in a Royal Mail office Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027. The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out. The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets. But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday. "We need to think outside the box," Dave Robertson, Labour MP for Lichfield, Burntwood and the Villages in Staffordshire. "We need to bring as many people to the table on this to make sure we come up with a long-term solution because what's been tried up to now clearly isn't working." An Ofcom spokesperson said not only has it issued fines to Royal Mail in recent years but it has also demanded an improvement plan and reformed the obligations imposed on the company, adding: "We will continue to hold it to account using the full extent of the powers available to us." Postal Services Minister Kate Dearden said Royal Mail's improvement plan was "a step in the right direction, but it must deliver tangible improvements for customers. We will continue to hold them to account on their performance." title: Saka responds to Arteta's challenge with 'huge impact'
description: Bukayo Saka responds to the challenge set by Mikel Arteta as he comes off the bench to change the game against Lille in the Champions League.
body: Bukayo Saka scored a goal and registered an assist in the win over Lille. Bukayo Saka responded to the challenge set by Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta as he proved a game-changer in the 3-0 Champions League win over Lille. The England forward has been told he should aim to score "two or three" goals per game - such was his quality and the expectation from his boss. Saka did not achieve that tally against the French visitors, but shook off illness to come off the bench and assist Eberechi Eze's strike that made it 2-0, before rolling in his side's third goal. The 25-year-old has now scored four goals in nine games this season and looks to be taking the next step in his evolution as Arsenal's key man. With the majority of his side's attacking play involving him, he has always been an influential figure. But with opposition defenders doubling up on him and injury issues over the last two seasons, there were doubts over whether Saka could still do what was asked of him in attack or if he had lost a yard of pace. Arteta has tweaked Saka's positioning this season and, prior to Lille's visit, said it has been done deliberately to get him closer to the goal. This video can not be played 'It was a joy to watch' - Arteta's praise for subs' impact "That is where we need to get him," said the Gunners boss before the game. "And if he misses the chance, so be it. At the end, the more volume we generate, the bigger the probability of him scoring more goals." Saka's strike against Lille was a confident one-touch finish and came after he missed a late one-on-one opportunity in Saturday's Premier League victory over Leeds. "He has been getting in great positions, getting shots, getting one-touch finishes and tap-ins," added Arteta. "That is the kind of unpredictability we have with that player, otherwise we know how the opponent is going to defend him. He is doing well, he could have had another four or five goals by now, easily. But if he continues like that, we know. "When he talks about scoring a certain amount of goals, he needs to be thinking about scoring a certain amount of goals per game. If that shifts, that mentality, he will get into those positions and score more goals." Saka has scored 20 goals in a season just once in his career, which came in the 2023-24 campaign and 16 in the Premier League. But the winger has also been in good goalscoring form for England with five in his last four matches and scored a double in the 7-0 Nations League demolition of Croatia in the recent international break. Saka is now on 19 goals in major European competitions for Arsenal, only behind Thierry Henry (42), while he has nine assists in the Champions League which puts him behind Henry (16) and Cesc Fabregas (14). He has refused to disclose the targets he has set himself, but Arteta welcomed Saka's response following his message to do more in front of goal. The Spaniard said: "I don't know if that's the case, but I am very happy. "He wasn't feeling that good yesterday and today, as he had some sort of illness. He wasn't ready to start but he was really wanting to contribute to the team if it was needed and he came on and made a huge impact and delivered with real quality." Arteta revealed he also spoke to Saka after telling the media about his desire for the player to have a greater impact. "After the press conference... I said 'Bukayo, I just killed you in the press conference, good luck tomorrow'. "He was laughing. He knows that we have discussed these kind of things and he takes it because he wants to be the best version of himself. "In order to do that, you have to put big objectives and challenges and try to reason by working and being consistent - and when it doesn't work, keep going because he has the ability to do it." Arteta made five changes to the team that started the win over Leeds as the Gunners looked to navigate six matches in all competitions during this month. Noni Madueke moved to the right wing after putting in a good performance on the left at the weekend, with Mikel Merino, Eze and Viktor Gyokeres all coming into the starting XI. Eze had started just two games in all competitions before the match with Lille and Arteta had said his attitude had been "phenomenal" despite a lack of game time. The 28-year-old showed flashes of his undoubted quality and his finish for Arsenal's second goal - and his first of the season - will give him confidence going forward. Madueke had a mixed night as he showed his ability to beat a defender, but questions remain over his end product - even if he provided the assist for Jurrien Timber's classy opening goal. However, it was not a good night for Gyokeres. The Sweden striker scored 21 goals in all competitions last season as Arsenal won the title for the first time in 22 years and displayed his willingness to run and work hard. But Gyokeres had just 12 touches before being replaced and Kai Havertz, as he so often does, looked a much better and more natural fit for the Arsenal frontline, teeing up Saka's goal too. Arteta brought on Saka, Havertz and Martin Odegaard after going 1-0 up and all three contributed to show why they are still the first names on the teamsheet and why the Arsenal boss will be so reliant on them if they are to achieve more honours. title: 'I could never hear on my left side - until I got a prosthetic ear'
description: Stephen Gilbert, 74, was born with unilateral microtia, a rare condition in which the external ear is underdeveloped or missing on one side.
body: Stephen Gilbert was born with unilateral microtia, a rare condition in which the external ear is underdeveloped or missing on one side Imagine being born without an ear and spending your entire life without being able to hear on one side. Stephen Gilbert, 74, from Aghalee, was born with unilateral microtia, a rare condition in which the external ear is underdeveloped or missing on one side. But he was recently fitted with a newly-designed prosthesis that accommodates a hearing aid, allowing him to hear on his left side for the first time. That's thanks to oral and maxillofacial surgery at the Ulster Hospital; the only service of its kind in Northern Ireland, providing bespoke prostheses for people affected by birth defects, traumatic injuries and cancer surgery. "To be able to hear someone on my left that I could never do before is just very special," Gilbert said. "It's a huge thing to be able to have a prosthetic part of your face." Artificial tongue helps doctor speak clearly Boy, 8, gets bespoke Lego prosthetic arm Model wants to inspire others to be 'proud of their prosthetics' "In my case with an ear, it's not just as visual as someone maybe needing a prosthetic for the front part of their face, maybe through injury or through cancer," he added. "I'm very conscious of that, but I'm very grateful for what has happened to me." Growing up during the 1960s, when boys commonly wore their hair long, Gilbert could cover the area where his ear should have been. But he became increasingly conscious of his condition as he grew older, particularly as hairstyles changed and his hair became thinner. The back of Stephen Gilbert's prosthetic ear (on the left) and how the ear will look from the front ( on the right) Gilbert first attended the Ulster Hospital in October 1997 for a prosthetic ear and over the past 29 years has had artificial ears made, repaired and adapted. Previously, plastic surgery had attempted to reconstruct "some semblance of an ear" using skin and tissue taken from other parts of his body, but the results could not replicate the shape of a natural ear. But after his wife read a magazine article about advances in prosthetics, describing how they had progressed from basic skin grafts to realistic artificial ears, Gilbert went to his GP. "I'd managed for so long, but I suppose I knew that the hair wasn't always going to be there and something needed to be done," he said. The photo on the left shows the left side of Stephen Gilbert's head pictured without the prosthetic ear; you can see small implants which will enable the ear to attach to his head. The picture on the right shows Gilbert wearing his prosthetic ear The previous grafted tissue was then removed and small implants were inserted to support the artificial ear. A mould of his right ear was then used to create a matching left ear, before getting the colour and fit right. "Amazing, that I had something that I didn't have there before. "That was just remarkable," he said. His new prosthetic ear holds a hearing aid which transmits sounds from his left side to his functioning ear. The prosthesis has helped Gilbert feel less self-conscious when his ear is exposed, while advances in hearing aids have also made a "huge difference" to his life. Consultant maxillofacial prosthetist Brian Bigmore says the impact of a facial defect often goes far beyond appearance Consultant maxillofacial prosthetist Brian Bigmore has made about 4,000 prostheses and devices for more than 250 patients at the Ulster Hospital. These include artificial ears, eyes and noses, as well as fingers, thumbs and nipples. Each prosthesis is individually made, from the initial impression of the defect through to the final fitting of a life-like silicone device. Bigmore said the impact of a facial defect often goes far beyond appearance and can affect confidence, social interaction and quality of life. The aim is to help restore appearance and function, but also to help patients regain confidence following what can be a life-changing diagnosis, injury or surgery. He said he has seen patients in a "really dark place" and even patients who have not wanted to see family members because they are afraid of their reaction and they are afraid they will look differently at them. But he described seeing a patient's reaction when they first look in the mirror wearing their new prosthesis as one of the most emotional, but rewarding, parts of his work. "Some of my patients say they never want to leave the house again and then after I'm finished with my prosthetic, they phone me up maybe three or four months later to say they've booked their holiday and they're going. "They're confident to go through an airport and they're confident to lie by a swimming pool, they're confident to go for a drink with their family and not have to worry about someone staring at them because of the way they would have looked without their prosthetic," he said. "All I can do literally is try to make them want to continue on - not to give up - because life doesn't have to finish." Brian Bigmore says prosthetics hopefully "build the confidence" of patients While many prostheses are designed to restore appearance, some also serve a practical purpose. Artificial fingers and thumbs, for example, can help patients feel more confident in social settings while addressing some of the challenges associated with missing digits. Bigmore said he has seen an increase in patients coming to him with head and neck cancer, with patients having their whole nose removed or their eye taken out. He said these patients "are literally afraid to look in the mirror anymore". "They just see something different than was there before," he said. "Not only are they dealing with that cancer and the prognosis of the cancer, the long-term outlook, but they're also dealing with the fact that they're now different and relati

title: Actress Selma Blair faces charges for kicking nurse and officer after plane incident
description: The Legally Blonde actress faces two counts of assault for allegedly kicking a police officer and a nurse after allegedly attacking attendants on a flight.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Selma Blair is seen leaving court after plane incident US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a flight. Blair was arrested late Sunday in New York after she allegedly attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane travelling from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI issued her a federal summons accusing her of assault on board. While appearing in court over the additional charges, the Legally Blonde star's attorney asked the judge to consider the actress's "body of work", and called Blair the "gold standard." The judge said she should not "get special treatment". Blair has pleaded not guilty. She has since been released on bail. She was taken to hospital after the incident on the flight. Her representatives have told the BBC that she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct". As the flight landed in New York on Sunday evening, airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said. Audio recorded on air traffic control details a pilot asking for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner. Blair, 54, who also starred in Cruel Intentions and Hellboy, was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US. The two additional charges of assault, filed in state court, came after she was taken off the plane. One of the alleged assaults happened when she was being transported in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at hospital, prosecutors allege that she also assaulted a nurse. Selma Blair's lawyer Shawn Barnes asked the judge to consider her "body of work" At her arraignment in Queens, Blair's attorney Shawn Barnes asked the judge for leniency. He said that "violence" is "not who she is" and asked for the judge to consider her body of work. The actress is somebody that people she look up to, he said, referring to her as "the gold standard". The judge denied his request and said she "should not get special treatment...because she is a celebrity". The judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond with the next hearing scheduled for 19 January. It is unclear when a date will be set for the federal case against her, which concerns the allegations of assault aboard the aircraft. title: 'Unplayable' Stanway a free-scoring warrior for Lionesses
description: Whatever the game, whatever the result, Georgia Stanway always seems to score for England.
body: Georgia Stanway is England's top scorer this season Whatever the game, whatever the result, Georgia Stanway always seems to score for England. Manager Sarina Wiegman called the midfielder a "warrior" after her performance against Greece helped seal an impressive 5-0 victory to complete an 8-1 aggregate triumph. Stanway scored in both matches as the Lionesses progressed to round two of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs with ease. She opened the scoring in Crete as they won 3-1 and when Wiegman called for more ruthlessness in Leicester, Stanway delivered again. The 27-year-old is quickly becoming one of England's most important players. So what makes her so effective in front of goal? Lionesses advance after comfortable win against Greece Stanway's strikes in the last five days capped off a season in which she finished as England's top scorer and netted 11 times in her last 11 matches. She also ranks inside the top three for most goals scored by European players in international football since Euro 2025. While Wiegman was frustrated by her side's lack of ruthlessness in Greece, Stanway always looked dangerous and made sure she got on the scoresheet. It felt inevitable she would join in the fun in Leicester when Alessia Russo and Lauren James grabbed a double each. Stanway came close to matching them when the Arsenal midfielder coolly took control of a long ball inside the box with one deft touch and, with the second, fired it powerfully into the bottom corner. It would have been the perfect strike to mark an impressive few days but it was ruled out for offside, much to Wiegman's dismay. "She is always so eager to go towards goal. She has that tenacity in her," said the England boss when asked about Stanway's goalscoring form. "She is always aggressive out of possession but also in possession. She scored a great header and controlled that really good ball from Alex Greenwood. "That was really good athleticism and composure. Unfortunately that was disallowed but it was really good! "Football is about scoring goals, but also playing in the pockets, keeping the ball and connecting with other players - and I was happy with her [doing those]." Former England goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis told BBC Radio 5 Live that Stanway was "unplayable at times" against Greece on Tuesday night. She won all her tackles, had a 90% passing accuracy rate, took four shots, scored once and had another disallowed. It was also a slightly different role for Stanway for most of the match as she played more as a right winger after changes in the midfield. "She has something different to others," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live. "She is goal-orientated, has a great shot and the disallowed goal showed her great mobility and athleticism. "When you really need a fight, or a duel, or a counter-attack breaking up, she is there. She is a warrior who you can play a possession game with too." Stanway was even more effective in large part to a new-look midfield which included 20-year-old debutant Lexi Potter. The Chelsea midfielder provided cover for the experienced Stanway and Keira Walsh to push higher up, while Lauren James played in the number 10 role. It proved to be an inspired change from Wiegman as Stanway caused problems throughout for the visitors and was able to adapt to the tweaks impressively. "Stanway has shown how flexible she is, how exceptional she is both at the bottom end of the pitch, breaking up play, as well as at the top end," added Brown-Finnis. "She was playing as a second striker, playing out on the right, dropping deep as a number 10. She's been absolutely brilliant." England still have a job to do to qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil with a two-legged play-off tie against Ukraine to navigate at the end of the year. They have already beaten their opponents 9-1 on aggregate in two games of the league phase of the qualifiers. After Wiegman's formation experiment worked so well this week, could it be an option for the future that brings out the best in Stanway, as well as others? "I liked the balance of the midfield. There is a lot of competition going on in that area," admitted Wiegman. "There were a few reasons. First of all, I wanted to see Lexi Potter deeper on the pitch and what that might bring. "There was also the option to put Georgia Stanway higher up the pitch. We wanted to score more goals and we know that she can do that. "She can play in the pocket and also deeper on the pitch so we wanted to see all of that." Head here to get involved Martinez issues scathing attack on Man Utd board - has he made things worse? title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
description: The Ukrainian president says the ballistic missile strikes came with "no early warning from our partners".
body: Firefighters work at the site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian missile strike A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners". Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said one person was killed and 13 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. Four people were in a serious condition, he said. It comes two days after US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine, although Kyiv reported multiple Russian strikes following the announcement. "Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people," Zelensky said on social media following Tuesday's strikes. "This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added. "It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing." It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles. Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case. "We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said. "We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end." Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before." But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there". It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow ⁠his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president". Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war. CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war. It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down. That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters.
