title: Pakistan has locked down Imran Khan's stronghold - but it could backfire
description: Some fear the government's standoff with the former PM's supporters could bring more instability, not less.
body: Thousands of Khan's supporters have been rallying for days throughout the province demanding his release Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town. Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less. According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror. "The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon. Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored. While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding. On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area. The imposition of emergency rule in Imran Khan's stronghold has escalated tensions with his supporters To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental. For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release. "The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House. "I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party." The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody. Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September, accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since. Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years. In the provincial capital Peshawar, police used shipping containers to block roads The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated. With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities? "The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council. "There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government." The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics. Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion. But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party. "The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says. Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision. "The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says. Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks. "The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally." Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan Imran Khan not the only one silenced as Pakistan military stifles dissent The cricket star and former PM dividing Pakistan But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most. The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India. Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous. Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame. "I

title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
description: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children' "The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV." Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia. "I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer." Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner. Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact". There are many causes of isolation in China. Most of it happens when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country. Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own. But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives. Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that. "We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs. "For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine." "The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added. Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver. Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents. The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible. His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows. There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles. Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile. "After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC. She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult. Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit. But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood. "I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him. Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits. Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic. "Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards." She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves. "So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious." Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals. At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection. Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee. "If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect." Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province. title: Who's to blame for the toxic smog choking South East Asia?
description: Anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning land in Indonesia and the authorities who have failed to stop them.
body: Wildfires have been raging in Kalimantan, Indonesia for weeks As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region. The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra have turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels. The smog - also known as the haze - has also drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia. Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland - as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them. The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño - a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world. According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land. Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn". This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops. But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land. While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky. But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism". Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed. But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy amid the haze problem. This video can not be played Watch: What makes fires in Indonesia so hard to extinguish? A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning. This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace. First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implement robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations". Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded. Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished. "We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said. It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies. In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze. The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law. But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies. Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-Vice-President Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset". Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads Indonesia's government communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests". "When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans. This video can not be played Watch: Toxic smog makes thousands sick as Indonesia wildfires rage But Indonesia has in the past also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze. This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires - though it has not officially requested international support. In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society to force the government to take action. In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze. They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the coverage of healthcare costs. A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra, but it was dismissed. Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have remained at dangerous levels for weeks. title: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
description: A new industry being dubbed the “loneliness economy” has emerged in China, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly.
body: This video can not be played In China's cities, despite the huge crowds, or maybe because of them, residents can feel very isolated. Now, a new industry being dubbed the "loneliness economy" has emerged, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly. The BBC's China correspondent Stephen McDonell visits a company that does just that, to see how their business works. Read more about the paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely. title: More tea? How Scotland's crops of the future could be set to change
description: Experts are examining the ways Scotland's farmers might diversify and adapt to a changing climate.
body: Susie Walker-Murno has been growing tea on her family farm in Angus since 2007 Susie Walker-Munro is one of a handful of tea growers in Scotland. She says the acidic soil creates ideal conditions for the perfect artisan brew. Costing about £40 per packet for her most expensive product, it's not going to replace the supermarket brands any time soon. Droughts, intensive downpours and diseases have created challenges for tea growers across the world as they deal with the impact of a warming planet. But some experts believe Scotland's relatively settled climate could give the tea industry here a helping hand. Only the top few leaves are picked from each bush to make the perfect tea As the picking season draws to a close, Susie plucks the last few leaves before proudly pouring me a small glass of her Kinnettles Gold, which is grown in a walled garden on the family farm near Forfar. She believes Scotland's latitude – sitting 57 degrees north - will always be a bar to having a year-round crop like those countries close to the equator. But she says wetter weather could help boost production. "Our yields are never, never going to be high," she says. "Maybe with climate change they might come up a bit, it depends if we get enough rain. Scotland could be absolutely ideal." Workers transplanting sprouts into the ground on a farm at Haddington in 1950 Susie isn't convinced tea will ever be a major crop for Scotland. But others say it could be one of a numbers of options in the future, as farmers are forced to diversify and adapt to a changing climate. Rethinking the way we farm the land might be one way to extend the range of crops produced. Countries like the Netherlands are already embracing glass houses, which could become more commonplace in Scotland. Susie says they would be a good way of growing more tea. They would also allow Scotland to produce more Mediterranean vegetables like tomatoes, cucumbers, aubergines, and even melons, according to Pete Ritchie from campaign organisation Nourish Scotland. He says an abundance of renewable energy from wind farms later in the century will make heating them relatively cheap and will cut down on air miles. "We're going to be able to produce those plants with a lower carbon footprint and provide secure all-round jobs for people on brownfield sites in the cities and also on the islands and remote parts of Scotland," he says. Scientists at the James Hutton Institute in Dundee are stress-testing plants like fava The James Hutton Institute already has a large number of glass houses – but it is going even further by artificially creating the sort of conditions that may exist in 75 years. Climate modelling shows that Scotland can expect hotter, dryer summers and milder, wetter winters by the end of this century. The institute's new advanced plant growth centre is effectively a climate simulator. It's able to control plants' light, water and nutrient intake to test how they cope with stresses - and then select species which are likely to fare best against all that climate change can throw at them. For the past three months they have been experimenting with fava beans, which are photographed daily so scientists can monitor their progress. Dr Robert Hancock says they need to switch from breeding crops for specific environments, such as hot or dry climates, towards ones which are more generally resilient. "We need to start breeding those crops now and start understanding what Scottish farming's going to look like," he says. "Farmers need time to plan, we need to get those crops out to the farmers and registered. "Ultimately it's about what those guys do in the fields that matters, not what we do inside a climate simulator." Farmer David Murdoch says technology will play an even bigger role in the future The farmers of the 22nd Century are probably only a generation away from those starting out in the industry today. That means the current crop of young farmers will have to give the closest consideration to the businesses they hand on to their own children. And that means more precision farming, more artificial intelligence, and automation. Modern tractors and combine harvesters are so high in technology such as GPS steering that it's no longer such a leap to consider autonomous harvesting. But the chair of the Scottish Association of Young Farmers, David Murdoch, believes traditional skills will always be important. "There's no point in doing it if you don't know your cattle, but embracing the technology is what keeps us competitive. "Working with larger herd numbers and larger machinery to keep us producing more with less people - that's the way the world's going," says David, who farms dairy with his father at Beith in North Ayrshire. The use of glass houses to grow food is becoming more common But it's not just food production that will drive future changes in farming. Protecting and enhancing nature, offsetting carbon emissions, and renewable energy production are already shaping the farms of tomorrow. Health innovations may also play a growing role, with obesity drugs already showing a demand for proteins and nutrient-dense foods. Soya, flax and legumes could become a more common sight as conditions for growing them become more favourable and that desire to grow them locally continues. Prof Wayne Powell - the principal of Scotland's rural college, the SRUC - predicts that Scotland will become "the bread basket of Europe". That title is currently used to describe Ukraine, because of its abundance of fertile agricultural land and exports of crops including wheat, maize and barley. "Climate change is redrawing the farming map of Europe and Scotland could become one of Europe's most important climate resilient food regions," he says. "The possibility of access to cheap renewable energy could also transform the economics of Scottish farming from irrigation, refrigeration, food

title: Rams player suspended for punch & kicker cut by club
description: The fallout from the Los Angeles Rams' defeat by the Buffalo Bills continues as offensive lineman Alaric Jackson is suspended for punching an opponent while kicker Harrison Mevis is released.
body: Harrison Mevis (left) and Alaric Jackson (right) joined the LA Rams in 2025 and 2021 respectively The fallout from the Los Angeles Rams' defeat by the Buffalo Bills rumbled on as offensive lineman Alaric Jackson was suspended for punching an opponent while kicker Harrison Mevis has been released. Jackson was handed a two-game ban by the NFL after he struck Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb following Monday's 37-34 overtime loss. Chubb was talking to players from both teams near midfield when Jackson approached him and punched him in the jaw. "It's just emotions, you know what I mean? Emotional game, it was a close game," Chubb said. Jackson is now set to miss the Rams' next two games against the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders. Meanwhile, the Rams have decided to cut Mevis and sign fellow kicker Blake Grupe from the New York Jets' practice squad. Mevis missed a field goal in regulation and had another attempt blocked in overtime against the Bills, which Rams head coach Sean McVay said "cost us the game". "The kicking game, especially with our PAT, field goal, not even close to good enough," McVay said. Mevis, 24, has made five of his past nine field goal attempts, including only one of his last four across the past two games. Grupe, 27, has converted 81.9% of his field goals and 98% of his extra-point attempts in 50 NFL games with the New Orleans Saints and Indianapolis Colts. title: Martinez issues scathing attack on Man Utd board - has he made things worse?
description: Lisandro Martinez launches a blistering attack on Manchester United's hierarchy for not strengthening the squad following qualification for the Champions League.
body: Lisandro Martinez joined Manchester United from Ajax in 2022 Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has launched a blistering attack on the club's hierarchy for not strengthening the squad following qualification for the Champions League. Tuesday's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid means United have now gone five games without a win. Their most recent victory was against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September. United's only other win in nine matches this season came against newly promoted Ipswich at Old Trafford, when they had to come from behind. The Red Devils finished third in the Premier League last term to seal a Champions League return for the first time in three years. They won 12 of Michael Carrick's 17 games in interim charge following the dismissal of Ruben Amorim in January, which was enough to earn the former United midfielder a permanent two-year contract as head coach. "We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well," Martinez told Amazon Prime. "Atletico have an amazing team and they deserved to win today. "I expect more [investment]. 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. "I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night. "Tonight it is easy to [blame] the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas." Martinez's view has been echoed by many external observers and has also been mentioned by some inside Old Trafford. The failure to bring in striking support for Benjamin Sesko and competition at left-back for Luke Shaw have both been highlighted in a summer when United spent £155m on three midfielders to the exclusion of any other position. Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was sitting next to United chief executive Omar Berrada in the Metropolitano Stadium on Tuesday. They have sacked managers in the past two seasons after backing them the previous summer, with Erik ten Hag dismissed in October 2024, before Amorim was shown the exit door in January 2026. "You can't keep changing, changing, changing the manager," said Martinez. "What about other areas? I can't say more. "Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team." Martinez's comments echo similar ones made by his Argentina defensive partner Cristian Romero against the Tottenham board last season. Ironically, Romero was in Atletico's side against United after his summer move to Spain. Martinez, meanwhile, has one year left on his United contract and has yet to agree an extension. This video can not be played Martinez is part of the problem - Robinson Former United players Wayne Rooney and Ashley Young were in Madrid for the game. Discussing Martinez's comments on Amazon Prime, both said the defender had gone too far and the damage inside the dressing room could be significant. "Something like that will rip that dressing room apart," said Rooney. The former England and United captain recalled his own public criticism of the club in 2010 which drew a fierce response from boss Sir Alex Ferguson. Rooney said it had been a mistake which he had apologised for. "It is disrespectful to his team-mates," he said. "He is saying his team-mates aren't good enough. "Bruno [Fernandes] is the only one with any right to say that. Behind closed doors, it happens - but that interview isn't going to help... "[Martinez] has tried to speak on behalf of the players but done it the wrong way. "It looks like a player trying to look after himself. It was very premeditated. It is sad because you need everyone to stick together, you need to be as one." Tielemans - who United bought from Aston Villa for £35m in July - also spoke to the host broadcaster but opted not to respond to the question. Commentating on the game, and speaking before Martinez, former England striker Alan Shearer said he felt Carrick had been let down. Young feels Martinez should have kept his counsel. "We know recruitment has to work and be better but players have to be better," he said. "They are the ones who have to produce. "There's going to be no change now. That could create [issues] all week after what was a good performance." Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former England keeper Paul Robinson said he could understand Martinez's point. "I question his timing because with the noise around Manchester United at the moment, positivity needs to come out of the dressing room," he said. "But on the flip side, I actually quite like it - a player being honest. "Manchester United fans don't need their players coming out saying 'we're doing OK, the squad's strong enough'. "Everyone can see they didn't recruit well enough and they need more players and the squad's not strong enough." Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), with chief executive Omar Berrada (centre) and director of football Jason Wilcox Although United were much improved on their tepid display against Tottenham at the weekend, conceding inside the first minute did not reflect well on Carrick. And they have now gone five games without a win for the first time since 2024-25, when it happened under both Ten Hag and Amorim. Carrick remains under intense pressure, although Martinez's words will bring renewed focus on Wilcox. The former Southampton executive's appointment as football director is starting to be questioned, as are decisions taken by Ratcliffe and Berrada since the Glazer family stepped back despite remaining as majority shareholders. In addition to sacking Ten Hag and Amorim, they also dismissed highly respected Dan Ashworth in December 2024 just five months after his appointment as sporting director. Ratcliffe has also been blamed for increasing ticket prices and launching what the club said was a ticket tou

title: Saudi man charged with planting 'sophisticated' recording device in OpenAI office
description: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
body: Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee. Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired. According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement. Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product. Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say. On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said. OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier". According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment. Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege. He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'". The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene. That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said. Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation. If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000). title: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street
description: The prime minister is calling for partners to step up support for Ukraine following Trump's criticism of Zelensky.
body: Burnham met Zelensky at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month Prime Minister Andy Burnham will host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street on Wednesday, as the UK announces it will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv. Burnham is also expected to set out how his government will draw up further sanctions against Russia. Speaking ahead of the meeting, Burnham said the UK was with Ukraine "for as long as it takes", adding: "Russian aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent." The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). This will be Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. His first was in late July, days after Burnham entered No 10, when the pair met troops and led a news conference at a naval base in Portsmouth. Burnham said: "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia. "My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe. "It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do." Among the measures being announced is the quicker delivery of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), with the UK having already committed to send more than 5,000 worth £1.6bn over the next four years. The UK will also reaffirm its plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG exports. The meeting between Zelensky and Burnham follows what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described as a "very difficult few days" for UK-US relations due to President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. Zelensky criticised the US deal with Russia, calling it a "gift" to President Vladimir Putin. Trump, in response, called for new leadership in Ukraine and criticised Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries. Meanwhile, Healey will ask partners at the IMF to step up support for Kyiv and ensure Russia heeds the US' call for a full energy ceasefire. Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire - but hours later, Zelensky said Russian attacks on energy facilities had continued. On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine did not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. title: Obama receives honorary degree from Queen's University Belfast
description: Receiving his doctorate, the 44th US president praised Northern Ireland's progress and challenged the next generation to continue building a peaceful and inclusive future.
body: Obama gave an acceptance speech in which he discussed the peace process, the fragility of democracy and the role of young people in shaping Northern Ireland's future Former US President Barack Obama has been awarded an honorary degree from Queen's University Belfast (QUB). Receiving his doctorate, the 44th US president praised Northern Ireland's progress and challenged the next generation to continue building a peaceful and inclusive future. The Good Friday Agreement peace agreement "is still a shining example of what can happen when people put aside old wounds and choose peace," he told university staff and students. During his visit to Northern Ireland, Obama was due to address an audience of paying fans in Belfast's O2 Arena on Tuesday night. Obama spoke and shook hands with students during his time in Belfast Accepting the honorary doctorate during a special ceremony at QUB, Obama made a speech that touched on a number of subjects including the peace process and the role young people can play in shaping Northern Ireland's future. Obama said that, while peace had transformed opportunities across Northern Ireland, its benefits must continue to be shared by all. Comparing Northern Ireland now to the place he encountered on a visit back in 2013, he said young people today faced significant challenges but also had reasons to remain hopeful. "But," he added, "as we have seen in many countries, including in my home country the United States, peace and democracy are not inevitable. "They have to be chosen, again and again." During the ceremony, Obama heard from Emma McAllister, a first-year Law with Politics student from north Belfast. McAllister first engaged with Queen's through a cross-community programme that helped young people from the Ardoyne and Shankill areas to access leadership and educational opportunities. After listening to McAllister, Obama said: "That's what peace makes possible. And it's what Queen's and the supporters in this room are helping to make real." In his closing remarks, Obama set out a challenge for students. "And that is to keep showing the way," he said. Queen's President and Vice-Chancellor Professor Sir Ian Greer congratulated Obama. "We are privileged to welcome President Obama to Queen's. "His commitment to peace, dialogue and public service has left a lasting impact around the world, and particularly here in Northern Ireland." According to the university, honorary degrees are awarded to those who have achieved distinction or given significant service in one or more of a number of broad constituencies. This includes business and commerce, the arts, education, medicine, and more. In 2025, former Manchester United footballer Gary Neville received a QUB honorary degree for his contribution to sport, business, education and philanthropy. Other notable recipients include boxer Carl Frampton, poet Seamus Heaney, former Irish President Mary McAleese and playwright Brian Friel. title: Our baby died on Christmas Eve and we're still waiting for answers
description: Gwilym died on Christmas Eve at just 11 days old, with his parents still waiting for answers.
body: This video can not be played Brooke and Wil say they have spent months waiting for answers about what happened to their son When Brooke and Wil Rees-Webb took their newborn baby home in December last year, they were expecting to enjoy their first Christmas together as a family. But Gwilym died on Christmas Eve at just 11 days old. And, as the couple from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, prepare to mark his first birthday without him, they are still waiting for answers about his unexplained death. Baby loss charities Sands and Tommy's are calling on the Welsh government to ensure bereaved parents are supported to contribute to the review of deaths. The government said it had "committed to ensuring every bereaved parent and family has access to high-quality, consistent and compassionate care". Gwilym's medical notes suggest he had a "serious neonatal infection" according to his mother, Brooke Brooke and Wil welcomed Gwilym Ioan after a caesarean section last December. "Ultimately we trusted the health professionals and wanted to make sure that Gwilym was here safe," said Brooke, 28, who works for the Welsh Parliament for a Plaid Cymru Member of the Senedd alongside her husband. "During that first week he was very sleepy, didn't wake very often and was very difficult to feed." Brooke said they raised those concerns with multiple health professionals but were reassured that everything was normal and that "he would get better if you just feed him more". But his medical records showed he had a "serious neonatal infection", she said. Now, 10 months on, the couple are still waiting for answers about why their baby passed away and shared their story via BBC Your Voice. "We've had no information from the health boards," said Brooke, adding that a report promised in June still has not been presented to them. Brooke and Wil are also waiting for a post-mortem examination and an inquest into Gwilym's death. Last year the Ministry of Justice said there were significant challenges affecting post-mortem pathology services and that it was working urgently to find a long-term solution to improve the service. Brooke said grieving her son and missing out on milestones was particularly difficult and exhausting when you're seeking answers. "The information doesn't come freely, you have to fight for it," she said. "We were told that we'd have a key contact and that someone would come out and take our questions or our concerns, but that didn't happen for at least three months, so we had to kind of fight for that to be included. "It's really hard every day to live a normal life, having to wait for emails, phone calls, just any kind of information about why your baby died, while also grieving." Brooke and Gwilym were cared for by Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board who said their "thoughts and condolences" remained with the family. They added: "As there is an open inquest into this case, it would not be appropriate for the health board to comment while proceedings are ongoing." Georgia Stevenson, head of the Sands and Tommy's joint policy unit, says current reviews don't include parents enough Wales had the highest rate of neonatal deaths in the UK in 2023 - 1.79 per 1000 births - according to Mothers and Babies: Reducing Risk through Audits and Confidential Enquiries across the UK (MBRACC-UK)., external "We would like the Welsh government to set a target to reduce stillbirth, neonatal deaths, preterm births", said Georgia Stevenson, head of the Sands and Tommy's joint policy unit. To "really understand what's going on", Sands is calling for the data around neonatal and stillborn deaths to be considered alongside "patient and staff experience". Stevenson added that reviews were "heavily influenced by clinical notes which is one account of what happened", but believes parents' "voices should be placed on an equal footing". "We don't feel the current reviews really embed parents at the centre of that process," she said. "Too often they are not able, or don't feel able, to participate in that process or they just don't feel like their views are being properly represented and that can be retraumatising for the parents who have already lost their baby." A report into maternity services in Wales this year found families who had experienced loss or serious injury were further traumatised by "defensive responses" and inconsistent processes, which limit the capacity to learn and improve. After losing her own boys eight years ago, Ruth has trained to support other bereaved parents For the last three years, Ruth Mason has helped bereaved parents in south Wales to navigate their loss through a support group in Merthyr Tydfil. She knows all too well how crucial a support network is after her twin boys, George and Henry, were stillborn in 2018. In her groups she said she encountered "desperate" parents navigating a "lack of appropriate and compassionate bereavement care" and a "huge lack of consistency" across health boards. "We are also seeing families accessing us, our group as volunteers, because there is nothing else for them," she said. "We're also hearing so much about people not receiving timely results of investigations and inquiries into their care and that just adds to people's trauma." She said it was "worrying and it's upsetting" that bereaved parents are still going through what she went through eight years ago. Mason recognised the work being done by healthcare staff, such as bereavement midwives, in Wales but said that "where it is good, there's not enough of it". She said the qualified bereavement councillor she was supported by during her loss "saved her life". "If there's one thing I've learned it's that compassionate care makes such a difference to families." title: Horse-drawn carriages in New York City expected to be outlawed
description: Both the speaker of the city council and the mayor have expressed support for ending the practice.
body: Horse-drawn carriages have a long history as a tourist attraction - but people have raised concerns for years New York City Council is expected to outlaw horse-drawn carriages starting in June 2028, a ban that also has the support of the mayor. The legislation follows the death of a teenager who fell off a horse-drawn carriage in Central Park this year, and ongoing concerns about inhumane treatment of the horses. The teenager's death led to Speaker of New York City Council Julie Menin's support of the bill, which she said will come before the council for a vote on 22 October. "Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City's history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability," Menin said in a statement to the BBC. "Next week, the Council will take decisive action by voting on [this bill] to protect New Yorkers, visitors, and the horses themselves." The bill - called Romanch's law for the teenager who died - has support from a council majority, a spokesperson for the speaker said. A Mamdani official said the mayor, who also supports banning the industry, is constructing a plan to transition those in the horse-drawn carriage business. "We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," a spokesperson said. The latest version of the legislation includes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counseling, and financial compensation for those involved in the business. The bill does not allow the horses to be sold for slaughter or for the same purpose. It is not the first time officials have pushed to end the industry, which is a longtime New York tourist attraction. Former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio announced soon after his inauguration in 2014 that he wanted to ban the carriages in Central Park, citing poor treatment of the horses, and proposed a fleet of vintage electric cars to replace them. In the end, he implemented new rules restricting where carriages can pick up tourists. In June, Romanch Mahajan, who was visiting New York from India, was riding in a carriage when the horse pulling it bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall and die. His father, Deepak, later told the city council he could not "properly describe to you the real, true fear inside that carriage". Also this year, a carriage horse named Dennis died in Central Park from eating a toxic plant. Some workers' groups, including the Transport Workers Union - which says it represents 300 horse-carriage drivers and owners - have pushed back against legislation banning the industry. The Transport Workers Union argues the horses are treated well and that the industry employs hundreds of people. Last year, the Central Park Conservancy, the nonprofit group that manages the park, said it was supporting legislation to ban the practice. "We do not take this position lightly," the conservancy's president, wrote in a letter, "but with visitation to the park growing to record levels, we feel strongly that banning horse carriages has become a matter of public health and safety for park visitors". title: Missiles intercepted near Riyadh after Saudi coalition hits Yemen fuel depot
description: The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa.
body: The Houthi-run Yemen Petroleum Company assured residents of Sanaa that it had sufficient fuel supplies Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says. Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said several projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted after the coalition carried out a strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night. The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam. Al-Maliki later said missiles targeting cities including Dammam had been intercepted, while shrapnel had fallen in a residential area in Dhahran. It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom. Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day. On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh. The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa. The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines. A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages. The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products". The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner". After al-Maliki confirmed the strike, first reported by Houthi media, explosions were heard over Riyadh and other Saudi cities, with al-Maliki reporting four missiles and two drones had been intercepted near the capital. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices". Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he'd made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene. Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes. Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children. More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN. title: Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder
description: Davis was found guilty last month over his role in the late rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in 1996.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Moment Duane Davis is sentenced to 40 years for Tupac Shakur's murder Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur. A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict. Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime. Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years. Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world". Ex-gang boss guilty of orchestrating 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur Tupac murder trial: 'All hell broke loose' night of rapper's shooting, witness says Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, told the court: "The loss of Tupac, for a long time, crippled my family." "He had so much promise, intentions for a better world," said adding that her brother had hoped to help his local community. Sekyiwa Shakur asked the judge to give Davis the maximum sentence, telling Davis he will sit in prison and "contemplate what you've done to the world, not just to me". Shakur's brother, Maurice Shakur, also addressed the court, asking the judge for "the longest possible sentence". Davis was asked by Judge Carli Kierny if he had anything to say, to which he replied: "I'm good. I'm gonna appeal this case for sure." Before handing down the sentence, Kierny told him: "You don't get to take a man from his family. "You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur. The world never forgot about him and his death." A 1996 photo of rapper Tupac Shakur (L) and Marion "Suge" Knight displayed during the murder trial The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired. In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview relating to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur. Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews. But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him. Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide. For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month. Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money. Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire. Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur. title: Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations
description: Guilfoyle the allegations of improper conduct are "false" and being ambassador was the "honour of a lifetime".
body: President Trump told reporters earlier this week he was "not happy" with the allegations against Guilfoyle. President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has announced. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, had been facing mounting scrutiny after reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration and behaving inappropriately while in Athens. Trump said she had done a good job, but she will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said. Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself against the "false" claims and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime". Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said. Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president. In a lengthy post on X, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing. "I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding that she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service". Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week. A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally. "It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message. In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today." This video can not be played Watch: Inside Katie Zacharia's very brief White House briefing Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on his behalf before she became ambassador. Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets. According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations. Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy". Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her. Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with his son Donald Jr, to whom she got engaged in 2018. This video can not be played 'I didn't like what I read,' Trump says in response to Guilfoyle controversy That relationship ended in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece. Trump noted on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member. The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign. "She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said. The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing. Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing. For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration sees as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets. She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda". title: 'If we don't scream, they won't listen to us': Student protesters speak to BBC in Paris
description: Student protesters in France have told the BBC's James Waterhouse that they will continue to take action until change has been made. The protests have now entered their fourth week.
body: This video can not be played Students protests in France have entered their fourth week and with a renewed impetus, according to the BBC's James Waterhouse. The nationwide demonstrations against poor classroom conditions, including old buildings, teacher shortages and overcrowded classrooms, have caused disruption to education across France as hundreds of lycées (15-18 year-olds colleges) had to be closed. Students on the streets of Paris told the BBC that they had not achieved anything yet and that stopping now would be a "defeat". 'If we don't scream, they won't listen to us': Student protesters speak to BBC in Paris. title: Cornell bans all fraternity parties over gang sex assault allegations
description: The school has faced an uproar over how it handled assault allegations brought by a woman known as Jane Doe.
body: State officials and others have criticised how Cornell and local prosecutors handled the case Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago. Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house. In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year. "I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said. This video can not be played Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added. Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals. Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended. The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well. Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault. Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus. These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said. Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations. Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe. State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case. Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship". He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus. title: Argentina lodges legal claim against UK's Falklands oil exploration
description: The action filed with an international maritime tribunal is the latest development in an escalating row over the Falkland Islands.
body: The Argentinian government has begun legal action seeking to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields north of the Falkland Islands in an escalating row with the UK. Buenos Aires said in a statement the request lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea aimed to block activity authorised "illegally" by the UK. The claim comes a fortnight after Argentinian President Javier Milei demanded the scrapping of the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies. UK Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran criticised the "escalating campaign" from Argentina against companies operating in the Falklands, while announcing new protections for them. The developments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the self-governing British territory, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentinian forces which had invaded the territory. Earlier last month Milei also threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands. Uma Kumaran accused the Argentinian government of "economic coercion" against the people of the Falkland Islands. "We will do whatever it takes to support them," she told the House of Commons on Tuesday. The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil. The Falkland Islands government extended exploration licences last month and the field is expected to start pumping in 2028, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands. Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – have insisted they have valid licences issued by Britain. The Argentinian government claims the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law. Its application "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorised unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom". In a post on X, Argentinian Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno said the government was requesting the tribunal make a number of orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits. But the UK government insists Sea Lion is lawful, located on the Falkland Islands shelf and regulated by the islands' government. While the Falkland Islands government grants exploration licences, they must be signed off by the UK Foreign Secretary. Kumaran said the tribunal application "does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease". The tribunal that will consider the dispute is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea. FCDO officials have made clear the UK will engage with the tribunal but resist Argentina's claim firmly. They said the aim was not to escalate the dispute but respond firmly to Argentina's latest move, and defend what the UK sees as legitimate economic activity. They also hope to provide reassurance to businesses fearful of Argentine retribution. That is why they are introducing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests Act that would protect firms from any extra-territorial impact of Argentine laws following Milei's sanctions threats. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Argentina's attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion." The latest move comes after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly late last month for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats". On Tuesday Kumaran described Milei's remarks at New York as "inflammatory". Despite its defeat in 1982, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falkland Islands. But over the years successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy. UK officials believes the current Argentine leadership is deliberately picking a fight ahead of elections next year. title: Maserati driver given suspended sentence after killing woman in crash
description: Ronald Dowling overtook a vehicle in heavy rain before aquaplaning, skidding and hitting another car.
body: Ronald Dowling was driving his Maserati Ghibli carelessy in poor weather conditions when the crash happened in October 2023 A Maserati driver who killed a woman and seriously injured two others has been given a suspended prison sentence. Ronald Dowling, 66, overtook a vehicle in heavy rain before aquaplaning, skidding across the carriageway and hitting Sharon Berry's car in the fatal crash at New Inn, Pontypool, on 26 October 2023. His wife, Kim Dowling, was left paralysed, and passenger Jane Beedell also suffered extensive injuries. Dowling, who previously pleaded guilty to causing death and serious injury by careless driving, was sentenced to 27 months in prison, suspended for two years. On Tuesday, at Merthyr Crown Court, Judge Celia Hughes told him: "Your consequences should live with you for life." A Maserati is an Italian luxury car manufacturer The court heard Dowling, from Caerphilly, was driving with his wife and their lifelong friend, who they were taking to a hospital appointment, when the collision happened. Despite wet and windy conditions, heavy rain and high levels of surface water, he was travelling at 76mph (122 km/h) just three seconds before the crash. After aquaplaning, the defendant crashed into a stationary black Audi A3 driven by Sharon, who had pulled over because of the weather conditions. She suffered catastrophic injuries and spent three months in hospital before her death in January 2024. In a victim impact statement, her son Luke Berry, who is expecting a child, described the family's loss as immeasurable, saying his mother would never get the chance to meet her grandchild. He said: "She was loving, caring and would do anything to make sure I was OK. "My family will never be the same without her." The court was also told Jane Beedell suffered multiple injuries in the crash, including chest and elbow injuries, bruising, wounds to her fingers, bleeding on the brain and multiple fractures to her ribs. She was placed in an induced coma for weeks, and told the court the crash had left her struggling with "fear, anxiety and depression". "I used to be confident, strong and an outgoing individual," she said, explaining how she now relies on family and friends for daily support and struggles with everyday tasks, finding it difficult to go out alone. After 48 years working in the civil service, Jane said she had lost her job and now relied on benefits. She said she was devastated by the changes to her life, adding: "I sometimes feel guilty I survived". The court heard how Kim Dowling was left paralysed with a broken back and neck and unable to speak after her voice box was removed following the crash. Mitigating, Dowling's barrister said the defendant felt "deep regret and remorse for the loss of life", along with "strong feelings of guilt and emotional distress". The court heard that every time Dowling looked at his wife, he was reminded of what he had done. The case was initially brought as dangerous driving, but the charges were later changed to careless driving, to which he pleaded guilty. Dowling had previously been disqualified from driving for six months about 15 years ago after reaching 12 penalty points, the court heard. However, he had no previous convictions despite years of long-distance driving for work and was described as a man of "good character" who was a full-time carer for his wife. During the sentencing, Judge Hughes said Sharon Berry had suffered a "senseless death", adding that "no amount of sentence given to Dowling would bring her back". Dowling was sentenced to 27 months in prison for causing death by careless driving and two counts of causing serious injury by careless driving, suspended for two years. He was also disqualified from driving for four years, ordered to complete 250 hours of unpaid community work and pay £1,630 in prosecution costs.
