title: Russia did try to interfere with Brexit vote but had little impact, MI5 chief says
description: It comes after Andy Burnham said Moscow had tried to interfere in the 2016 referendum.
body: MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum has said there was Russian interference in the the Brexit referendum, but warned against overstating its impact on the result. It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham provoked a backlash from some Brexit campaigners by saying it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow in the 2016 vote. Sir Ken said it was "a matter of public record" that there was interference in the referendum by online trolls and bots. However, he suggested Russian trolls would be "delighted" to be front page news again, "despite the comparative unimpressiveness" of their efforts. He added: "There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed. "I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall." Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart branded Sir Ken's comments "an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister". In an interview released on Monday, Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was." He did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities during the interview, and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive. The PM denied claims from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch that he was implying the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference. He said it was a "matter of record" that Russia sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, adding: "We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time". A No 10 spokesperson also clarified that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful. The Conservatives accused Burnham of making an "embarrassing retreat" after "being caught out trying question the legitimacy of the referendum result". It is inconceivable to think Russia did not try to interfere in Brexit vote, says PM MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation? Answering questions after his annual speech at MI5's London headquarters earlier, Sir Ken said: "It is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum. "And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth." He added that he agreed "strongly" with the PM that there was a hack and leak during the 2019 general election campaign. However, he raised concerns about the impact of the debate on Russian interference. "It is kind of up to us how far we allow our various adversaries to divide us," Sir Ken said. "And I'm a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, that Russian trolls who didn't appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they'll be delighted because they are front page news again despite the comparative unimpressiveness of what they do at all points along the journey." Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has accused Burnham of lying, saying there was "no Russian interference" in the referendum. Meanwhile, former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary, the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power". He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told." In 2020, a parliamentary report did not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian "troll" accounts on social media. title: Watch: Inside Katie Zacharia's very brief White House briefing
description: The BBC's Sarah Smith reports on the the briefest briefing she has ever seen at the White House. Katie Zacharia took questions from three journalists on her first day on the job.
body: This video can not be played The briefest White House briefing the BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith has ever seen happened when new US press secretary Katie Zacharia took questions from only three journalists. She gave reporters some big news on Kimberly Guilfoyle being asked to resign as the US ambassador to Greece. But couldn’t answer the question on whether the US will stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine. And otherwise spent more time telling reporters how she planned to balance her family life with her new job. Watch: Inside Katie Zacharia's very brief White House briefing. title: Katie Price denies 'any venom' against ex at his rape trial
description: Kieran Hayler, who denies offences against a girl when she was 13, was married to Price at the time.
body: Katie Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court Katie Price has denied having "any venom" against her ex-husband at his rape trial. Kieran Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one of sexual assault against a then-13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies. When challenged by defence lawyer Arlette Piercy on her view of her ex-husband, Price said: "I don't have any venom against Kieran, it was amicable when we split." Reality star Price also denied being "angry and vengeful" towards Hayler. During her evidence to Lewes Crown Court, Price was asked by Piercy if she "loved revenge or is it just TV?". "It's TV, it's what I say. It's what drives me in my work," Price said. Piercy told Price: "You are angry and vengeful towards the defendant Kieran Hayler, you have evidenced a vendetta against him over a number of years." Price responded: "That is not true." Price also said she was using "a figure of speech" when she messaged the teenage girl allegedly raped by her then-husband. Jurors had previously seen messages sent between Price and the girl, then aged 14, in which the media personality said she had heard Hayler and the girl kissed and he had "tried it on" with her, adding: "I'm only asking as this is a serious allegation." The teenager replied that it was "just a flirt thing" and "nothing happened". Katie Price and Kieran Hayler divorced in 2021 Price then asked: "Did he kiss you? I won't bring up anymore just want truth. I will make you a little star." Asked in cross-examination about use of the phrase "little star", Price said: "That's a figure of speech." Piercy then asked: "When you use that figure of speech, what did you mean?" Price replied: "I don't know, when she was 13 there's no agenda or nothing behind it. "It's just a figure of speech." Hayler, 39, has suggested his ex-wife "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended and the allegations form part of this, the court previously heard. Hayler was married to media personality Price at the time of the allegations, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021. The trial previously heard that the alleged victim first contacted the NSPCC in 2021 over the allegations, who then referred her to the police, prompting the investigation. The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families. Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. title: Police officer tells rape trial he did not commit sex crimes
description: Carmichael John Williamson, 32, from Shetland, has given evidence in his trial at the High Court in Edinburgh.
body: John Williamson is on trial at the High Court in Edinburgh A police officer accused of rape in Shetland has told a court he did not commit the crimes he is accused of. Carmichael John Williamson - known as John Williamson - is on trial at the High Court in Edinburgh. He is accused of assaulting and raping a teenage girl in 2014 and 2015, and of having sexual activity with the girl when she was under age. It is also alleged he raped a woman in 2022 while she was intoxicated and unable to consent. Giving evidence, Williamson, 32, told the second day of the trial it was untrue that he had penetrative sex with the girl when she was an under-age teenager. More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds After the Crown case closed, Williamson took the stand. He said it was not true that he took part in sexual activity with an adult woman outside a community hall during a function in 2022. Defence counsel David Nicolson KC asked Williamson if there was any sexual contact between him and the female at the venue. He replied: "None at all." He also denied that there was any further sexual contact with the woman later on at a house. Asked about the teenager, he said that she made contact through Snapchat when he himself was a teenage student. He said the earliest point he could remember engaging in sexual intercourse was the day after her 16th birthday. Asked if the relationship was sexual when she was 15, he replied: "That's not true." He said he had no recollection of ever recording any of their sexual encounters. Under cross examination by the Crown, he disputed that the women were telling the truth. He told the court he has been a police constable for more than 10 years and was previously a special constable, but was currently suspended. Williamson, of Burra, denies the series of charges alleged to have been committed at locations in Shetland between 2014 and 2022. The trial, before judge John Morris KC, continues. title: Pope admitted to hospital for surgery to remove lump on his lung
description: Pope Leo has said the growth is "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage".
body: Pope Leo arrived at Rome's Gemelli Hospital ahead of his surgery on Tuesday Pope Leo XIV has been admitted to Rome's Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove a lump on his lung, detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks". It said the operation would take place on Tuesday afternoon. The 71-year-old pontiff was met at the hospital by a large crowd, some of whom had been waiting outside for several hours to catch a glimpse of him. They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, waving and smiling back through the lowered back window of his car. He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured. It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing. He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed. The Vatican said the Pope would be operated on by the Gemelli's thoracic surgery team and promised an update on his condition on Tuesday evening. His schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous. But doctors say when a lump is removed it will usually be tested to check for any sign of the disease. The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness. Pope Leo XIV announced the news of his operation during his weekly Sunday prayers in Rome Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically. He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan. The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years. Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world. "Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday. He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery. Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted. Carla had come specially, wanting to be close. "He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray." "I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff. "It turns out he's vulnerable too. I really hope it's something superficial, that can be contained, like he told us." title: Football regulator says he would quit over any political interference in Man City case
description: The head of English football's independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over Manchester City's future.
body: This video can not be played 'We have to go on the evidence' - Kogan The head of English football's independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over the future of Manchester City. As chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives. If an independent commission's findings that the club broke Premier League financial rules are upheld, the watchdog would have to decide whether to force a sale. Last month, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners decided to sell up. When asked about Burnham's comments, Kogan told BBC Sport: "The Prime Minister is entirely entitled to make his own observations on anything. "We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we're doing. "And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that." When asked what he would do if he did come under political pressure over the case, Kogan replied: "I would resign." An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. City insist they are innocent and have appealed. How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team? 'Criticised for what?' - Maresca defends celebrations Kogan, a former sports media rights executive, was appointed to the regulator role one year ago The prime minister initially told the BBC of his concerns, before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings". However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process. Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanded all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club are released. The government released these details on Monday. "As far as we, as the regulator, are concerned, we have a very, very clear course of action that is governed by statute and we are going to follow that course of action and no comment by any politician or indeed any individual is going to affect what we do", said Kogan. "Process is going to drive what we do. Process will lead us to a conclusion. "We cannot reach any conclusion at this stage because we don't know the outcome of any appeal and once we do then we will act accordingly." The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing - which could take months to convene - to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving the club and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty. City's punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or being ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they won in the affected period. Asked how crucial it is that it was resolved as soon as possible, Kogan said: "I think it's very important." Kogan added that the case was "raising very serious issues if Manchester City on appeal is found to be guilty of the allegations within those findings". "We are waiting like everybody else to see what the independent panel will do… and then we will bring in a view in terms of our own investigation and statutory powers if we need to do so. "Our powers relate to individual owners, directors and senior executives. They refer to whether people are in a position to run a club in a way that is safe, coherent and done with probity, and we will be examining those things." An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 that led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation. The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence". title: Majority of English football clubs on the edge of financial disaster, report says
description: English football's finances are "dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster", a new report says.
body: Bury were expelled from the EFL amid financial difficulties in 2019 - the first team to drop out since Maidstone's liquidation in 1992 English football's finances are "dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster", according to a landmark report by the independent football regulator. Research by the watchdog found 94% of clubs are loss-making, and more than 60% of EFL and National League clubs are technically insolvent. The regulator (IFR) warns of "a dangerous cocktail of rising debt and an over-reliance on owner funding, leaving clubs and their fans at risk". The 'State of the Game' report also suggests that despite the economic success of the Premier League, the financial 'cliff-edges' between and within leagues have grown significantly. 94% of clubs in the top five English leagues made losses in 2025-26 17 clubs across the EFL and National League would be loss-making even if their players played for free 66% of clubs could not survive for more than 90 days without new owner funding 29% of clubs reported they could not survive more than 30 days without such funding 68% of clubs have no contingency plan if their owner walks away The IFR claims "the underlying foundations of the pyramid are under intense strain and require urgent reform", and its report "should serve as a wake-up call" for English football. "Seventeen clubs are now trading in such a way that if their players played for free, their non-playing costs would mean they would go bust," IFR chair David Kogan told BBC Sport. "Thirty-two clubs are operating on only 30 days' cash. If the owner chooses not to pay cash at the end of the month, those clubs go bust. "That is a very, very risky scenario. This is the moment of addressing these problems before money starts to dry up. "We can actually fix the house while the sun is still shining and that's essentially what our role is going to be in this." Regulator would quit over Man City interference This video can not be played Majority of clubs on edge of 'financial disaster' - regulator Tasked with improving teams' financial sustainability, the IFR outlined six areas of concern around financial risk, and urged clubs to put robust contingency plans in place in case owner funding is withdrawn. Despite years of talks, the Premier League and EFL are yet to agree a new funding settlement that would see the top flight share more money with the rest of the pyramid. The IFR has the power to impose a deal and warns that "if football can't find a solution we will consider our next steps and will not hesitate to use all the powers at our disposal to bring about lasting change". It also urges action on rising losses and calls on clubs to show how they take fans' views into account, and the steps they are taking to improve boardroom diversity and governance. The average Premier League club now earns more than eight times the average Championship side The existing system of parachute payments paid by the Premier League to Championship clubs who have been relegated "contributes to the incentives for Championship clubs to overspend which drives up player wage inflation" Net transfer debt is going up and deferred transfer payments and transfer financing create links between clubs, owners and lenders which increases "the potential for financial stress to spread across the game". "Nobody in football for 100 years has believed that football was trading in a solvent and effective state," Kogan said. "It's not how football has ever really operated. "But I think now where there's so much more money involved, the extremes get more extreme. "We knew the problems were there, I don't think anybody realised that the data was going to show quite how dramatic they are." The Premier League, the EFL, the Football Association and the Football Supporters' Association have all issued statements welcoming the findings. BBC Sport outlines some of the key points in the report. Over the past five years there has been a growing trend to effectively mortgage off instalments a club is due to receive in transfer payments in return for an immediate injection of cash. Called 'transfer financing', it has become "an increasingly important source of liquidity". In 2020-21, transfer financing stood at £55m. By 2024-25 it had reached £779m - a more than 14-fold increase. Now about £1.2bn of future transfer income has already been monetised through financing arrangements - an almost 22-fold rise on 2020-21. Across English football, payments for transfer outgoings are about 3.3 times transfer incomings. In 2025-26, English clubs reported approximately £4.8bn in transfer payables but only £1.5bn in transfer receivables - a net transfer debt of about £3.3bn. The report says the financial situation is worsening for clubs across the EFL and National League. Most Championship, League One and League Two clubs hold less than 30 days of cash. More than 60% of EFL and National League clubs have liabilities exceeding the book value of their assets. It is a bleak picture for wages, too. Twenty clubs - primarily in the Championship, League One and National League -spent more than 80% of revenue on player wages. The majority of League One clubs spend more than 40% of revenue on player wages, including two spending more than 100%. Wage costs have increased across all leagues between 2021-22 and 2025-26: 33% in the Premier League Seventeen of 18 (94%) EFL club owners surveyed were in favour of more robust cost controls - as one investor told the report: "the single biggest issue is player wages". Average League One losses increased from 6% of revenue in 1992-93 to almost 50% in 2024-25. In League Two, it stands at 40%. title: A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
description: How Rwanda has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed by agreeing a deal to stage the African Grand Prix.
body: The launch of the African Grand Prix took place on Tuesday in Kigali Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement. Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time. But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017. Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed. That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work. Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town. For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with. The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub. At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030. The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing. But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership. "It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem. He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision". "Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past. "It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity." Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed. He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped. And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal. Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka. The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change. President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa. Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return. "We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events." The new track near Kigali has been designed to exploit Rwanda's natural landscape Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment. Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion. The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation. But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic. The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia. Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture. F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda. title: Ex-Met Police officer trained to support rape victims accused of rape
description: Mark Tyrrell raped and sexually assaulted a woman over about two years, his trial is told.
body: The police watchdog began an investigation in April 2023 after the Met Police made a referral A former Metropolitan Police officer accused of raping a woman was specially trained to deal with victims of sexual offences, a court has heard. Mark Tyrrell, 57, denies two counts of rape, 11 of sexual assault and four of assault by penetration against the woman over about two years while he was serving with the force. Opening his trial at Southwark Crown Court, prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said Tyrrell had been trained in Sexual Offences Investigation Techniques. Jurors heard concerns were first raised when officers visited the woman's home on an unrelated matter and found Tyrrell hiding beside her bed. He later phoned her and said nothing sexual had happened, the court was told. Tyrrell is also accused of perverting the course of justice by trying to delete messages between them. In one, he apologised for "being a sex offender" and for ruining her life, jurors heard. When she told him not to say such things, he replied that they were true. The prosecution alleges Tyrrell raped the woman by having sex with her after she had repeatedly said no. Afterwards, he allegedly asked whether she realised that what he had done "was rape", and said he would report himself and would undoubtedly go to prison, Farrelly said. The woman alleges that on several occasions she woke to find Tyrrell penetrating her, despite having refused sex the night before. On one occasion, when she asked him what had happened, he shouted at her and asked whether she realised what she was saying and what could happen to him, the prosecutor told the court. Jurors heard the woman kept a list of incidents involving Tyrrell, including the alleged sexual assaults. In a police interview, she said she had felt pressured by him and feared no-one would believe her because she could not prove what had happened. She was also worried police would protect him because he was an officer, the court heard. After his arrest, Tyrrell denied ever having sex with her. Tyrrell, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, has admitted misconduct in public office. He has also pleaded guilty to a separate count of perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to police about why he was in her bedroom. title: Almost 5,000 evacuated in City of London gas leak
description: A cordon between Threadneedle Street and London Wall has been lifted and people are being allowed back into affected properties.
body: About 4,700 people were evacuated in the City of London after a gas leak. The London Fire Brigade (LFB) said it was called to Old Broad Street at 10:55 BST, where crews found a ruptured six-inch gas main at a six-storey office building. A 200m cordon was put in place between Threadneedle Street and London Wall, with nearby buildings evacuated as a precaution. The brigade has now removed its cordon, and people are being allowed back into affected properties. A Cadent spokesperson said the pipe was "severely damaged by a private construction team" and stressed the work that caused the damage "had nothing to do with Cadent or its pipework". Cadent is keeping a road closure in place on Great Winchester Street while engineers complete repairs to the damaged gas pipeline. Cadent gas and London Fire Brigade have been working to make the area safe Two fire engines from Dowgate and Shadwell fire stations, along with a fire rescue unit from Bethnal Green, attended the incident. title: Theme park worker sexually assaulted 19 girls under the age of 13
description: Police have urged any parents who are concerned their child may have been a victim to contact them.
body: Josef Luke Hammond admitted 19 counts of sexual assault at Stafford Crown Court on Monday A theme park ride operator has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting 19 girls, all under the age of 13. Concerns were first raised about Josef Luke Hammond, 24, from Birmingham, after a girl told her parent he had touched her inappropriately while at Drayton Manor Theme Park in Staffordshire. Hammond, who worked as a ride operator at the park from March 2024 to August 2024, was arrested after CCTV was reviewed. He admitted the offences at Stafford Crown Court on Monday, and was bailed ahead of his sentencing date at the same court on 11 December. An incident in August 2024 was raised with staff at the theme park, who reviewed CCTV footage and Hammond was immediately sent home, according to police. The force was then called in and the 24-year-old was arrested and questioned the same day before being charged. Any parents or guardians who think their child may have been a victim have been urged to contact police. Det Insp Vanessa Furnival, from the Staffordshire Police child protection team, said: "I'd like to recognise the bravery of the victims in this case who have all shown immense courage in coming forward and supporting us with our efforts to secure this outcome." "I'd also like to recognise the rapid response from staff at Drayton Manor, who immediately removed Hammond from his duties," she added. A spokesperson for Drayton Manor said they were "appalled" by the incidents, adding that visitor safety - particularly that of children - was of "highest priority". "As soon as concerns were brought to our attention, the individual was immediately suspended and then dismissed from their employment," they added. "We recognise the impact that such incidents can have on victims and their families, and we commend those who came forward and supported the investigation," they continued, explaining staff reference checks, CCTV and in-person supervisor checks were all carried out as part of safeguarding processes. title: How Breaking Bad's RJ Mitte changed the way we see cerebral palsy
description: The star, who has died at the age of 34, fought for better representation of disabilities on screen.
body: This video can not be played 'Disabled or not, everyone deserves an opportunity,' RJ Mitte says in 2015 BBC interview "I have cerebral palsy but I've never let it hold me back." Those are the words of a 22-year-old Breaking Bad star RJ Mitte in an essay for Huffpost, external back in 2014. Explaining his experiences of learning to stand up to bullies while growing up, he added: "It shouldn't define you. I just happen to have CP." That was also true of Mitte's character Walter 'Flynn' White Jr, the son of Bryan Cranston's character in the drama, which was recently named the best TV show of the 21st Century by the New York Times. "What I really like is that he was on TV playing a character that had cerebral palsy, but it wasn't about the fact that he had cerebral palsy," says Emma Livingstone, founder and CEO of Up - the Adult Cerebral Palsy Movement. "When we see RJ Mitte on TV just playing a role, but who also happens to have CP, I think that's really powerful." Mitte, who died by suicide on Monday at the age of 34, wasn't just an actor - he was also an advocate and supporter, working as an ambassador for charities including United Cerebral Palsy and Can Do Canines, as well as creating The Mitte Foundation, which offered community grants in his home town in Texas. Susan Sellers, president and CEO of United Cerebral Palsy, says: "His advocacy was rooted in a commitment to ensuring that people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities are seen, heard, and afforded the opportunity to reach their full potential." Mitte's legacy, particularly for performers with disabilities, is significant. Ruth Madeley, who stars as disability rights advocate Judy Heumann in new film Being Heumann, tells the BBC: "If you don't see it, you don't think it's possible. When I was younger, acting wasn't even on my radar. I didn't even think it was an option." The actress, who has spina bifida, adds: "To have people like him [Mitte] on screen for so many young people looking at the arts as an industry that they want to get into... He was just a beautiful example of that. "But he wasn't just a disabled person breaking down barriers in the industry. He was a phenomenal talent, and I think that's what's going to be missed so much." Mitte was mobbed by fans on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2013 Another actor, Keron Day, who appeared in Netflix hit Sex Education, tells the BBC: "My biggest tribute I can pay to RJ and his work is that I am emailing you today from a set of a TV show. "That is his legacy: disabled people having careers within the creative industries. If I could have half the impact that RJ has had, I would be enormously proud. It's a sad day for both our industry and our community." Comedian and screenwriter Laurence Clarke concurs. "The more portrayals that we see on TV, that's going to inspire more disabled people to think it's a career for them," he says. "Things have moved on a long way since Breaking Bad came out in 2008. But there's always further to go." Speaking of Mitte's role in Breaking Bad, Clarke tells the BBC: "What's beautiful about it is that the disability is visibly there, always." He also notes the impact on people watching inclusive dramas and shows. "The more you're exposed to those portrayals, as members of the public, it becomes just part of life, and how you see the world." Bryan Cranston (left) played RJ Mitte's dad in the hugely successful Breaking Bad Mitte was aged three when he was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, which the NHS describes as the name for a group of lifelong conditions that affect movement and co-ordination caused by a problem with the brain that develops around birth. He was cast in Breaking Bad at 14, and told Channel 4 News in 2016 that the show "pioneered a lot of TV and writers to be more brave". But he added a note of caution, saying: "We still have a long way to go... it's still a business and we have to do that slowly." Earlier this month, he hinted that he may be interested in continuing the Breaking Bad story, external, but said any revival would have a lot to live up to. "I just want to top Breaking Bad, that's the hardest," he said. "I set a bar for myself as a young man that is kinda unattainable. I tell people, 'Look, it's a long way down from the top of the mountain'." After Breaking Bad, Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year. But his biggest achievement - and his greatest pride - was his philanthropic work. "Where I felt most top of the world was being able to help others through Breaking Bad, with the work I've done with people with disabilities... trying to remind people they have a voice and [to] lend my voice. "The greatest thing that Breaking Bad has given me is to be able to lend my voice to causes that make a meaningful impact, that change people's lives." title: Champion boxer Joe Cordina was 'retaliating' when he punched man to ground, court hears
description: Joe Cordina is on trial charged with two counts of assault by beating after a fight on 27 February.
body: Cardiff Magistrates' Court hears that Joe Cordina was "set up" during a fight at a petrol station in February Former boxing world champion Joe Cordina was "retaliating" during a fight where he punched a man at a petrol station, a court has heard. Cordina is standing trial charged with assault by beating relating to an incident on 27 February involving Jamie O'Brien, who previously admitted a charge of assault by beating. A second assault by beating charge against Cordina was dropped on Tuesday. Cardiff Magistrates' Court heard the altercation came to light days later, after a video was published on Wales Online, filmed by a witness at a Texaco garage in the Pentwyn area of Cardiff. O'Brien's sister told police her brother "hated" Cordina, the court was told, and she feared he had "sought out" Cordina. CCTV footage of the incident "which took place over several minutes" was played to the court, showing Cordina filling up his car and walking over to O'Brien who stood on the pavement nearby. Prosecutor Alex Orndal said O'Brien "pushed Mr Cordina with his shoulder" and Cordina then "punched him with sufficient force to push him to the ground", where he then pushed him "repeatedly". "Mr Cordina has initiated the confrontation," Orndal said, adding "Cordina was not protecting himself but retaliating". There was then "aggression" from O'Brien, the court heard, as Cordina raised a golf club and O'Brien lunged at him, before a number of blows were exchanged. O'Brien was eventually restrained and "posed no further threat", the court heard, but Cordina then threw a further punch at him. In a police interview, Cordina denied the alleged offence, saying that "having been shoved" he "felt threatened" and then punched him later "out of instinct" due to O'Brien's actions. Cordina's defence barrister, Tom Crowther, told the court O'Brien had been identified by family members from the video circulating online, who had raised concerns about his behaviour. Tom Crowther KC, defending, asked investigating officer PC Samuel Penman to watch the video that had circulated online. He said it was plain to see that they were "watching and waiting" for Cordina, suggesting it was a set up. Penman said it was not obvious but he did agree that the person filming "seemingly started recording prior to any physical altercation going on". The court heard that, when O'Brien was arrested, he "argued with officers" and "challenged" them. Penman admitted it was a "mistake" not to question O'Brien's sister about her concerns that her brother held a "vendetta" against Cordina. title: Rusty or something more? South Africa's concern after Australia loss
description: Australia complete 214-run victory over South Africa in Durban. What does heavy defeat mean for the world champions?
body: Hazlewood dismissed Wiaan Mulder, Marco Jansen, Simon Harmer and Anrich Nortje on the final day to beat his previous best figures of 6-67 against India in 2017 First Test, Durban (day five of five) Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56 South Africa 284 & 206: Markram 75; Hazlewood 6-49 Australia won by 214 runs South Africa's 12-match unbeaten run came to a shuddering stop with defeat against Australia in Durban, but were they simply rusty or is there more to read into a Test match in which they were outclassed across the five days? The world champions held on until an hour into the afternoon session on the final day – Aiden Markram fought admirably for 237 deliveries – but Australia, led by Josh Hazlewood with career-best figures of 6-49, eventually broke any lingering resistance to go 1-0 up in the three-match series. "I would like to see more fight," said Proteas coach Shukri Conrad. "I don't know if it is alarming [but] it is concerning." So should South Africa be worried at the start of an eye-catching few months which includes the visit of England over Christmas? Much was made of South Africa's run to the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's. They played only 12 Tests – no team played fewer – and qualified after drawing at home against India and losing in New Zealand, before beating West Indies, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan. Mitigation for this latest Test also comes from the fact this is their first in almost a year and the majority of their batters played one domestic red-ball match to prepare. Australia recently came off an eight-month break of their own and lost to Bangladesh in home conditions, as Conrad was keen to point out. And last summer's famous win over Australia and a 2-0 success in India proves they can beat the world's top teams. However, this Test only reinforced a worrying trend among South Africa's batters. Tristan Stubbs and Ryan Rickelton are fine white-ball players, but Stubbs' two Test centuries have come against Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and Rickelton's against Sri Lanka and Pakistan. This was an obvious step up. In the first innings, Stubbs, two overs after Wiaan Mulder had been bounced out, top-edged a pull to fine leg, and in the second he played a loose drive on one. Opener Rickelton drove and edged at a wide ball late on day two and nicked through a pull in the fourth over on day four. Similarly, Mulder scored 367 not out against Zimbabwe last year, but Bangladesh are the only other side he averages more than 30 against. His 110-ball stay for 29 on the final day before being strangled down the leg side was at least encouraging. Wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, in contrast, lasted only three balls before nudging Matt Renshaw's part-time spin to slip. His Test average of 30.14 drops to 28 against Australia and 15 against both England and India. Conrad said that "a few of the guys need to step up". "The real disappointment was the batting in the first dig on a really good wicket," Conrad said. "Yes, a world-class attack, but quite a few guys getting starts and not kicking on." Aiden Markram's defiant knock in the fourth innings, in which he batted for almost six hours for 75 runs before edging Mitchell Starc through to Alex Carey in the afternoon session, was one positive for the Proteas. David Bedingham also looked comfortable in his new position of number three, albeit he was one of those guilty of failing to make the most of starts after reaching 49 and 46. This defeat was not solely on the batters, either. Bavuma, who tasted defeat as captain for the first time in this match, allowed the game to drift on day two as Australia extended their score from 124-6 to 390 not out. Australia's Matt Renshaw played brilliantly for his 190 but was not challenged as he casually farmed the strike and protected Nathan Lyon in their ninth-wicket stand of 134. And while judging them against Australia's fearsome attack, the most successful quartet Test cricket has seen, is hardly fair, South Africa's bowlers lacked the relentless pressure of their counterparts. Anrich Nortje was impressive in taking four wickets in his first Test since March 2023. His last spell was quicker than his first as he brought pace and hostility, hitting Steve Smith on the helmet with a bouncer on day four. But Mulder offered little after his new-ball spells and Marco Jansen was quiet after dismissing Nic Maddinson and Steve Smith on day one. The return from injury of their premier quick Kagiso Rabada, who was seen bowling at lunch on day five, cannot come soon enough. Spinners Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj did not escape Conrad's gaze either. "Anrich's return was phenomenal and really pleasing," Conrad said. "If we were brutally honest, our spinners were not as sharp as they normally are." With the second Test starting in only five days' time in Gqeberha, South Africa must hope this Test has removed the rust. The alternate takeaway would be far more concerning. title: Have Russian bots been stopped by Ukraine's strikes on 'Russia's Google'?
description: Experts say there is no evidence that Russian trolls have been affected by Ukraine’s Yandex attacks.
body: Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them. Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots". Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade. These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests. Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs. The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services. But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare. Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined. While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines. Cloudflare clarified its data includes all automated internet requests to websites hosted on its network, including bots crawling websites for information. The company also said the drop off was "not necessarily bot behaviour on social media platforms". Tomáš Zdechovský, a Czech member of the European Parliament, shared a post on X which has been viewed more than four million times, that said: "If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets." He has since said he "did not present it as a clear fact", but the post remains pinned at the top of his X profile. Researchers from dTeam, a US-based group that tracks Moscow-linked influence operations, told BBC Verify there has not been "any traffic change from known Russian accounts and bot clusters on any platform". They added that if the offices of known groups involved in these operations "were in flames then we would see a change". Bots linked to pro-Kremlin influence operations like Storm-1516 and Matryoshka - both of which BBC Verify has previously reported on - were still active on social media on Tuesday, evidence shared with BBC Verify by dTeam shows. Zelensky's office told BBC Verify the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity. It added it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users. Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation? Mikhail Klimarev, an independent internet analyst, told BBC Russian that while Cloudflare can establish whether bots or real people have visited a website it does not reflect what these bots are doing. He added that Yandex uses bots to "essentially crawl the entire internet once a day" and index websites for search engine purposes, so it is most likely the company switched these off in response to its computing resources being severely degraded. Yandex has said the use of its cloud services for "large-scale manipulation on social media, spam and other improper activities" are against its rules and that accounts which violate this are blocked. While there is no evidence to conclude the strikes on Yandex's data centres have had an impact on Russia's influence operations, they have disrupted internet services for many. Isik Mater, director of research at the internet monitoring group Netblocks, told BBC Verify disruptions related to Ukrainian strikes "affect all users" globally and "websites which rely on Yandex may be partially or entirely unusable". She said that following Ukraine's attacks there has been a clear impact on the company's cloud services and platforms relying on them, adding that an entire area remaining "out of service indicates a significant infrastructure-level incident rather than a brief service interruption". title: Hungarian MPs scrap Orbán's anti-LGBTQ measures
description: LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but call for changes to other Orbán-era laws.
body: This year's Budapest Pride march went ahead without restrictions, a year after the Orbán government tried to ban it The Hungarian parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but called for changes to other Orbán-era laws. The 2021 Child Protection Law, passed by the large Fidesz majority of then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, banned the "portrayal or promotion of homosexuality or transgenderism". Since Orbán's April election defeat, the Tisza government of Péter Magyar has been working to dismantle the previous government's legacy. Minutes after Tuesday's vote, Budapest said the EU had agreed to release €4.2bn (£3.5bn) of funds frozen in the last years of the Fidesz government. The European Commission said last month that the Magyar government had addressed a number of "rule of law breaches affecting the EU budget", and urged EU leaders to unlock the funds , externaland readmit Hungary to two key EU programmes - Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe. Hungary's 2021 law had affected a wide range of other laws, including education and the right of assembly. Magyar's Tisza party commands the same two-thirds majority that Orbán's party used to have, and the measures passed on Tuesday were bundled together by the new government in a package of laws designed to unravel the Fidesz legislation. "We are very happy that this got adopted," Tamás Dombos of civil rights group the Háttér Society told the BBC. "We've been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years. There have been problems with the bill submitted to parliament, but most of those problems have been fixed." Both the Fidesz and Tisza governments made child protection central to their image. But while Fidesz under Viktor Orbán appealed to the conservative electorate by identifying gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, Tisza under Prime Minister Péter Magyar is trying to remove or soften legislation, without actually identifying as a liberal-minded government in favour of full equality. In June 2025, the Gay Pride march through Budapest drew an estimated quarter of a million people, despite a promise by then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to his supporters that he would prevent it happening. Police stood aside despite an official ban, and proceedings against the city mayor and others for organising the festival were later dropped. This year's event went ahead without restrictions. The child protection issue turned from being a strong card in Orbán's hand to become his Achilles heel, when the public found out that his government had supported the pardon of the deputy head of a children's home who had been found guilty of covering up the paedophile crimes of his boss. In his own election campaign, Péter Magyar presented his party as a champion of the rights of children in state care, while painstakingly avoiding the issues of gay and transgender rights, for fear of alienating right-wing voters. "We are still knocking on a closed door," Dombos told the BBC, "but at least they are listening on the other side." This marked a major improvement on the Orbán years, he said, where his community felt constantly targeted. Other issues he wanted addressed include the full recognition of same-sex marriage, same-sex couples' rights to adopt children, and the restoration of the right of transgender people to change their names in official documents. "I'm very cautious," Magyar said in an interview published in Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat on Saturday. "As prime minister, it's my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities." Fidesz and its sister party, the Christian Democrats, voted against the new amendments to the law on Tuesday. "There is no place for the promotion of LGBTQ content in schools or the media," the Christian Democrats said in a statement on their website. title: Man killed in tiger attack identified as William Chapman
description: A health and safety investigation is under way at Yorkshire Wildlife Park following the incident.
body: William Chapman, pictured, has been identified as the man killed in a tiger attack The man who was killed by a tiger after entering its enclosure at a wildlife park has been identified as William Chapman, the BBC understands. Chapman entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to South Yorkshire Police. An eyewitness described seeing him wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own. A force spokesperson said his family was aware and was being supported by specialist officers. The park was evacuated after the incident and remains closed as investigations continue. City of Doncaster Council has also launched a health and safety investigation into the death, which a spokesperson said was "in line with our statutory duties". Yorkshire Wildlife Park said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" were with the man's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. Chapman, described by eyewitnesses as in his 20s, was reported to have entered the enclosure after climbing down from a walkway. Those who saw the attack said some witnesses had tried unsuccessfully to distract the tiger. A video posted on a social media account believed to be Chapman's appears to show the moments before the attack. In the footage, shot on a mobile phone, the inside of the enclosure can be seen as he approaches the tiger - perched on a wooden platform - across a patch of grass. Shouts of concern, urging him to get out, can be heard. The video ends, and the account has now been removed. An eyewitness took this photograph of the tiger minutes before the incident A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an "urgent review" into "how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next". Dr Campbell Murn, a previous member of the government's zoo expert committee and lecturer at the University of Reading, said while it was a tragic incident, determined people could get inside zoo enclosures. "I view it in the same way a determined thief will get into somebody's house or somebody's car and despite the best security systems and enclosures sometimes these things happen," he said. Floral tributes have been left at the entrance to the park, near Doncaster Ella Ford, 24, from Moreton, Wirral, had visited the park with her boyfriend and filmed the tiger moments before the attack. She described seeing Chapman by the tiger enclosure "pacing around with his headphones in". A few minutes later, she saw he had "climbed up onto the barriers". A woman was close by talking to him, she said, before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there". Ford said she then witnessed the tiger grab hold of him, and he was "shouting for help". She estimates around 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park. She described members of the public as being "confused, like what on earth's going on?" "I just know some man was obviously trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything," she said. This video can not be played Watch: What we know about the tiger attack at Yorkshire Wildlife Park Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated. She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above. Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure." She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised". title: Supreme Court hears church warden murder appeal
description: The Supreme Court is considering arguments over who legally caused Peter Farquhar’s death.
body: Benjamin Field (right) was jailed for the murder of Peter Farquhar (left) A former deputy church warden could not have have legally caused a university lecturer's death by giving him potentially sedated whisky, the Supreme Court has been told. Benjamin Field, 35, was jailed for at least 36 years in 2019 after being found guilty of murdering 69-year-old Peter Farquhar in Maids Moreton, Buckinghamshire. In April, appeal judges quashed Field's conviction and ordered a retrial, but said the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) could take the case to the Supreme Court first. And on Tuesday, five justices at the UK's highest court were asked to consider whether Field could have made Mr Farquhar cause his own death without Field legally being responsible. During his murder trial prosecutors said Field drove Farquhar to believe he was losing his mind, secretly drugging him and spiking his whisky so his death would appear to be suicide or an accident, allowing Field to inherit his home and money. The case has previously been adapted into Bafta winning BBC drama The Sixth Commandment, starring Timothy Spall and Anne Reid. Before his murder trial, Field admitted burglary and fraud offences connected with relationships he had formed with Farquhar and his neighbour, fellow pensioner Ann Moore-Martin, to persuade them to change their wills. He received a concurrent 16-year sentence for those offences. He was cleared of conspiring or attempting to murder Moore-Martin and of possessing an article for use in fraud. The hearing was due to conclude on Tuesday, with a decision expected at a later date. Benjamin Field was jailed in 2019 after being convicted of murdering Peter Farquhar David Perry KC, for the CPS, said Field would not be legally responsible only if Farquhar had agreed to Field's plan knowing it was intended to kill him. Perry told the Supreme Court Field had "set out cynically to seduce Mr Farquhar" even though Field was heterosexual and "covertly" put medication - including the sedative Dalmane and hallucinogenic drugs - into his food or drink. The barrister said that if any substance was covertly administered, or if Farquhar was misled about what he was drinking prior to his death, there would be "no dispute" that Field is guilty of murder. Field admitted to faking relationships with Peter Farquhar (left) and Ann Moore-Martin (right) David Jeremy KC, for Field who is opposing the appeal, said in written submissions that "the act of giving whisky and/or Dalmane was not capable of being a legally effective cause of death". "It must follow that if Ben Field, possessed of a continuous intent to kill over many years, had handed Peter Farquhar his car keys at his request, and Peter Farquhar had driven off and died in a traffic accident, then Ben Field would have caused Peter Farquhar's death and been guilty of murder," he said. Jeremy added: "Peter Farquhar had a choice whether or not to drink whisky given to him by Ben Field. "He chose to do so freely and voluntarily, knowing what it was and knowing what he was doing." The Court of Appeal previously heard there was no direct evidence of how the Dalmane was administered and that a post-mortem examination found a therapeutic dose. Jeremy told the Supreme Court: "There was no reason why, if Ben Field had smuggled Dalmane into Peter Farquhar's food or drink that night, he would have restricted himself to a therapeutic dose." title: 'Criticised for what?' - Maresca defends Anfield celebrations
description: Manager Enzo Maresca reacts to criticism of Manchester City's celebrations after their win at Liverpool by saying: "What do you want us to do?"
body: This video can not be played Could Manchester City be expelled from the Premier League? Head coach Enzo Maresca has reacted to criticism of Manchester City's celebrations after their victory at Liverpool by saying: "What do you want us to do?" Sunday's match at Anfield was City's first game after an independent commission found the club guilty of charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial rules. After the 3-0 win, Erling Haaland looked close to tears in front of City's fans - which included his father Alf-Inge - while Maresca pumped his fists in jubilation. "Criticised for what?" replied Maresca when asked for his response to City's celebrations being questioned by pundits and the media. "We work every day to win games. It's the only thing that we can think about and be focused on. "The rest? It's just things from outside that we need to deal with - but we were so, so, so happy on the pitch, and you cannot imagine inside the changing room." The Italian added: "If I am an Arsenal fan or United fan and you are a City fan I say: 'hey, my friend you cheat'. So it is probably more tough for them [the fans], but we were happy inside the changing room. "We were very happy celebrating the three points because it is very difficult at Anfield." Maresca was speaking on Tuesday at a news conference before Wednesday's Champions League game with European champions Paris St-Germain. It will be City's first match at home since the guilty verdict, which City have appealed against. Captain Ruben Dias also defended the post-match celebrations at Anfield. "I stand by the manager's words," said the centre-back. "It was a win at Anfield. It was a show of how much it means to us." Asked for his reaction to the guilty verdict, the Portugal defender added: "We are very calm and we trust the club." Pep Guardiola, who delivered 20 trophies during 10 years in charge before stepping aside at the end of last season, is expected to return to Etihad Stadium for the match. "This has been his house for 10 years with what he has done here," added Maresca. "It's exciting for everyone, for the fans." It is not known whether Guardiola will address the fans or his former players before the game. The Spaniard posted a message on social media after his former club were found guilty of financial breaches. "I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever," he wrote. "Let me be clear: we will get through this together." title: Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year
description: Millions could be entitled to compensation as a result of commission arrangements between lenders and dealers.
body: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, regulators have announced. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - just over 40% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for at least 35% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. For some customers - especially if their contact details have changed - it could take many months before compensation is paid. Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation. The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain, external. lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027 those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed". The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 to 26 February. It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes. The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme. Without a scheme in place, the FCA has estimated that up to 19 million complaints would need to be handled individually, taking three years and costing lenders £6bn more. It said it would "defend the scheme robustly as lawful and the best way to resolve such a widespread, long running and complex issue". Ultimately, the industry is expected to cover the full costs of any compensation scheme, including any administrative costs. Lenders - including some of the UK's biggest banks and specialist motor finance firms - have already set aside billions of pounds for potential payouts. The body that represents the lending industry, the Finance and Leasing Association, said it had "concerns" about the programme but that it was choosing not to raise a legal challenge. Santander, Barclays and Lloyds also accepted the scheme, despite raising concerns that the level of redress is disproportionate to those who suffered harm. Even if drivers are entitled to compensation from these lenders they will need to wait. There were some concessions made to lenders in a scaled-down final compensation plan from the FCA. title: BBC FM radio transmissions suspended in Afghanistan
description: BBC programming is still reaching audiences on shortwave, medium wave, via satellite and online.
body: Afghanistan's Taliban government has suspended the transmission of BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites across the country. A Taliban government spokesman said the BBC had been suspended because of "repeated violations" but did not elaborate. The BBC has been the only international news organisation to broadcast inside Afghanistan since two US outlets were banned from operating in the country in 2022. "Millions of people across Afghanistan rely on the BBC for accurate news and information and we are working with the authorities to address the situation," the broadcaster said in a statement. The BBC said it was "continuing to report fairly and independently in Pashto, Dari and English to our audiences in Afghanistan, on shortwave and medium wave radio, online and via satellite". It reaches more than 20% of the adult population in Afghanistan each week with news and other output, including educational programming aimed at girls who have been banned from secondary schools. Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture spokesman Khubaib Ghufran told local media: "Due to some repeated violations by the BBC media outlet, it is decided that for time being its activity is suspended across the country." The Taliban government has a tight grip on media operating in the country. Music is not broadcast and women are less visible on screen than before the Taliban retook power in 2021. Women no longer appear on air together with men. People can still use some social media platforms, but a lack of electricity in large parts of the country, high costs and low literacy rates remain major barriers. The BBC's Afghan service has been operating since 1981.
