title: MI5 tackling more state threats than during Cold War, warns intelligence chief
description: Sir Ken McCallum says Russia, Iran and emerging threats from AI were increasing the risks to Britain.
body: Sir Ken McCallum gave his annual address at MI5's headquarters in central London MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said, as he labelled Russia "aggressor number one". Sir Ken McCallum warned MI5 was now facing a situation in which "our terrorism and state threats operational missions are pretty much of equal scale" because threats from foreign adversaries have quadrupled. He used an annual speech at the domestic intelligence service's headquarters in London to also warn of rising threats from Iran and "extreme right-wing terrorism". Sir Ken also said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI", including by integrating the technology with drones - and warned the UK must stay ahead of the risk of new bioweapons being developed by violent groups. The MI5 head said Russia was waging hybrid warfare while carefully avoiding triggering a joint response from Nato, a line which he said the Kremlin would be "foolish to cross". Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against the military alliance, and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly". He said MI5's successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks. He continued: "With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak. So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding." He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand." Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK. The intelligence chief said MI5 had made over 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities. Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites". Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia. On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with AI-enabled drones adding a new twist." The threat he was most worried about, Sir Ken told Thames House, was extremist groups harnessing AI to make bioweapons. He said that threat was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons". Sir Ken continued: "These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MIS, GCHQ, M16 -is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on." In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely. Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism. He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent." Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK". He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil." title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
description: The influential economics body has upgraded its UK growth forecast for this year, but risks remain.
body: Countries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF). What the IMF says matters - it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world. Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel. Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report. The global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran. The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise. To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months. Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI). And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true. There is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this. The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both. By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments. "So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said. Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany. Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context. "We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are." While the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year. While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest. In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%. "There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises," says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot. He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year. title: Mum told to prepare for 'worst' urges others to get respiratory illness vaccine
description: Jo Goldsmith said the RSV vaccine was not available when she was pregnant, but that she would have had it.
body: Jo Goldsmith is advising pregnant women to take up the vaccine A woman whose newborn daughter became ill after catching a potentially serious respiratory illness is urging other pregnant women to make sure they are vaccinated against it. Jo Goldsmith said she was told to prepare for the "worst" after her daughter Phoebe contracted respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) a few days after being born. The vaccine was not available at the time of her pregnancy, but she said she "definitely would have had it". "I wouldn't want any family to go through what we went through," she said. Nerys Evans, Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health, is also urging people to make sure they are vaccinated against Covid-19, flu and RSV ahead of the winter months. RSV is a common cause of coughs and colds,, external and although infections usually get better by themselves, they can sometimes be serious for babies and older adults, according to the NHS. RHS vaccinations were introduced in Wales in September 2024. Phoebe was five days old when she was diagnosed with RSV positive bronchiolitis on Christmas Eve Goldsmith, a children's nurse and health visitor from Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, said that when Phoebe was born four years ago, she realised within days that something was wrong. "She was five days old, she had quite a lot of congestion… and we noticed quite quickly that she seemed to be breathing very fast and was struggling," she said. She said she took Phoebe to hospital and "it escalated from there", with the family told on Christmas Eve that she had RSV positive bronchiolitis. "So, we knew that we were going to be in [hospital] for the Christmas period. But we didn't quite realise how unwell she was going to be." Phoebe soon deteriorated and was admitted to the hospital's high dependency unit, and Goldsmith said her experience as a nurse told her "we were going to be in for a bit of a rough ride". But she said Phoebe took "her own unique path with it", and "really kept the doctors on their toes". She said that after being taken to a room and shown an X-ray doctors "weren't quite sure which way we were going to go with things". "They sort of prepared us for… the worse," she added. Jo and her family were unsure whether Phoebe would make it past Christmas Phoebe pulled through the virus but did face some longer-term problems, including being admitted to hospital several times with chest problems. Her hearing was also affected. Goldsmith is now calling on others to be vaccinated against the illness, describing the experience as "the most traumatic thing we've had to go through". "Watching your baby struggle to breathe and not knowing whether they were going to get through the next couple of hours, of what was going to happen overnight with them," she said. RSV is a common virus that circulates every winter. It usually causes mild symptoms, but for babies, older people and those with weakened immune systems, it can lead to serious illness, including bronchiolitis and pneumonia. During a normal RSV season, infection in children under two years old is responsible for approximately 7,000 to 9,500 GP appointments and 2,300 to 2,600 hospital admissions in Wales. It is estimated that RSV infection in over 75-year-olds is responsible for 7,000 to 9,000 GP appointments, 700 to 1,000 hospital admissions and 400 to 600 deaths in Wales each year. The RSV vaccine is offered routinely year-round to all adults aged 75 and over, and pregnant women from 28 weeks – to help protect newborn babies from the virus. Older people only need the vaccine once and pregnant women should have the vaccine with every pregnancy. The Welsh government is reminding people that the RSV vaccine is separate from the flu vaccine and should not be forgotten. This autumn the offer of a RSV vaccine has also been extended to higher-risk adults aged 65 to 74, including those who are immunosuppressed or have chronic respiratory disease. Evans, from the Welsh government, said Joanne's story was a "powerful reminder of how serious RSV can be", for older people and for babies. "I urge all who are eligible to come forward for their flu jab, their COVID-19 booster and their RSV vaccine. "They protect against different viruses, and it really can make the difference between a mild illness and a serious hospital stay," she said. title: BA flight forced to turn back over cracked window
description: British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick and passengers were due to resume their journey.
body: File photo of a British Airways plane A British Airways flight en route to Portugal was forced to return to Gatwick Airport on Tuesday due to a minor technical issue, reported to be a cracked window. Flight BA2660 was heading to Faro in the Algarve but diverted over north-western France in order to return to London Gatwick. AirNav Radar, a flight data provider, posted on X that "a passenger window is cracked. Flight deck going through checks before deciding were to divert". A spokesperson for British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick due to a "minor technical issue" and passengers were due to resume their journey. "We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey, and our teams are working hard to get their travel plans back on track," they said. Airnav Radar reported that the BA Airbus A321 squawked the 7700 emergency code, which is used when there are mechanical or technical problems on board aircraft. Last week, a BA flight bound for Chicago spent five hours circling over Ireland, before turning back and landing at London Heathrow, where it had taken off. The flight issued an emergency alert and passengers reported oxygen masks dropped in the cabin, as well as turbulence. Tracking data showed it rapidly descended from 37,000 feet to 9,000 feet. And in August Serbian national Ljubisa Karović's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the window on a Ryanair flight, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock". Ryanair subsequently said the window may have been damaged by a foreign object. title: Fortnite-maker Epic Games confirms 'huge pivot' towards using AI
description: The US firm's boss responds to critics, saying "much of the room wants it to be 2016, but it's not".
body: The move comes six months after Epic Games confirmed it was laying off more than 1,000 employees Fortnite-maker Epic Games is making a "huge pivot" towards using artificial intelligence (AI) in its video game development, according to boss Tim Sweeney. The US firm's CEO made the announcement on social media, external, saying developers are being moved to "retool for maximum AI acceleration". It comes after Epic delayed the release of a collaboration with Disney featuring characters from Star Wars and Marvel, according to a report from Bloomberg, external. BBC Newsbeat has approached Epic Games on its use of increased AI and the reported delay to its Disney project. Details on that game are yet to be announced, but Bloomberg reported that developers were asked to use AI tools to finish it. It said directors told staff "no more hand-written code" and are switching to having all the game's art "generated with full AI workflows". Epic's founder and CEO Sweeney didn't publicly comment on the Disney collab, but did confirm further details around the company's use of AI in a series of posts on X. He said the purpose wasn't "to do the same stuff with fewer people" but to give developers the tools to build "more" and "better stuff", something he called "empowering" for creators. Critics of the decision reacted angrily to Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney's social media posts One response on Sweeney's X thread, which received 14,000 likes, accused him of not being able to read the room. Sweeney responded by saying "much of the room wants it to be 2016, but it's not". "Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be," he said. Sweeney said ramping up the use of AI was a "modest aim to survive the AI revolution" and end up "making better code and content faster". The news comes six months after Epic confirmed it was laying off more than 1,000 employees. At the time, Sweeney attributed job cuts to a "downturn" in Fortnite engagement rather than AI. Lisha Howen is in favour of AI being used to "help make things better", but says it shouldn't be used as a replacement The announcement brings a fresh focus to the long-running debate around the role of AI in the creative and arts sector. Lisha Howen is a full-time game designer and says she "isn't completely against AI", but disagrees with it being used to fully generate artwork and graphics. "I have friends who are game developers that use AI to aid them with writing code," says the 23-year-old, who doesn't work for Epic. "And I have artists who don't use AI at all because artists, especially in the game industry, hate it because it's taking away their jobs. "You can tell when something's been generated by AI, it looks terrible, it's cheap, and it's making people lose their jobs and lose their income." In 2025, actor union Sag-Aftra filed a complaint over the use of AI to recreate the voice of Star Wars villain Darth Vader in Fortnite. But Howen, who is also a Fortnite live-streamer, doesn't think that people will be turned off from playing Epic's flagship game. She explains that while there is a "vocal minority" who play Fortnite, the core player base "don't really care about the external politics of it all". "They'll just keep playing like nothing's changed." Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: Murder investigation launched into deaths of four people in house fire
description: A man, a woman and two children died after a house fire and two other children are critically ill.
body: A man, a woman and two children are dead following the fire on Birch Avenue A murder investigation has been launched following the deaths of four people after a house fire in County Waterford, Gardaí (Irish police) have said. Two children and two adults - a man and a woman - died following the blaze on Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford city, shortly after 05:00 local time on Tuesday. Two other children have been critically injured and they are being treated in hospital. Gardaí said they were investigating the fire as arson and appealed to anyone who was in the vicinity in the early hours of Tuesday to contact them. Waterford Fire Service said it was alerted to the fire at 05:13 local time and its crews arrived to a well-developed fire at a two-storey house. It said a number of casualties were removed from the house before the blaze was extinguished and the scene was handed over to gardaí. Gardaí have set up an incident room at Waterford Garda Station and a senior investigating officer had been deployed to the incident. Family liaison officers had also been appointed. Sinn Féin's David Cullinane, who knew the family, visited the scene on Tuesday The housing estate is just off the Killure Road, about 3km (1.8 miles) outside Waterford city centre. Sinn Féin's David Cullinane, who represents Waterford in the Dáil (Irish Parliament), said he knew the family and said his heart went out to their relatives. "I'm just utterly heartbroken," Cullinane said. "There is such devastation in the housing estate itself but also in the wider community in Waterford city." His party colleague, Sinn Féin councillor John Hearne, also knows the family and described it as a "terrible tragedy". Hearne told BBC News NI that residents living in the estate noticed the blaze at about 05:00 and they went out to wake up their neighbours to try to help. But he said it "all happened so fast" and was "hugely distressing for everyone involved". The councillor said the estate had been blocked off by gardaí but he planned to go to the community centre later where the council had set up a support hub. Waterford City and County Council said facilities and refreshments were available at Butler Community Centre in St John's Park for anyone affected by the fire. Birch Avenue, in the Birchwood housing estate, has been cordoned off The Bishop of Waterford and Lismore, Alphonsus Cullinan, described it as an "unspeakable tragedy" which had shocked the entire city. In a statement, he said: "Our hearts go out to the families who have suffered such unimaginable loss. "We stand in solidarity with all those whose lives have been devastated", he added. He said the Catholic Church would "reach out as best we can" to help those affected and the parish priest would minister to the bereaved family and support the local community. "We also wish to express our sincere gratitude to the emergency services, gardaí, firefighters and medical personnel who responded to the scene and who have faced such distressing circumstances," the bishop added. The mayor of the Waterford Metropolitan District, Lola O'Sullivan, urged people not to speculate about the cause of the fire. "It upsets me no end to see people commenting on social media about something that they don't have firm facts on," she said. title: Raye hits back at ticket touts who 'overwhelmed' sign-up for Albert Hall show
description: The award-winning singer said there were 1.8 million sign-ups for her 5,000-seat Royal Albert Hall show.
body: Raye made history when she won six Brit Awards in 2024 Raye has hit back at ticket touts who she says "overwhelmed" the sign-up process for an upcoming live show by using artificial intelligence (AI) bots to create "hundreds of thousands of fake registrations". The Where Is My Husband! singer revealed there were 1.8 million sign-ups for her one-off 5,000-seat performance at the Royal Albert Hall on 23 October. To avoid a pre-sale which she felt scalpers could exploit, Raye said the sign-up list had been manually reviewed to identify a shortlist of people believed to be "real fans". A spokesperson for the Royal Albert Hall said they "invest heavily" in protecting their ticketing systems from "automated attacks" but the "law needs to catch up". The award-winning artist said she had "never witnessed bots on this scale" and was changing the process as it is "so important" to her that fans can buy tickets at the face value price. "I'm not sure what the future holds for ticketing, I do know this experience has really opened my eyes," she said in a statement shared on her social media accounts, external. "Me and my team are going to think really hard about what we can do in the future." Raye said the fans manually selected would receive a pre-sale link and code by email at 11:45 BST on Tuesday, and pre-sale opened shortly afterwards. She added that the remaining tickets would be available to all on general sale. This Symphony May Contain Hope show will showcase songs from her recent chart-topping second album, This Music May Contain Hope, that fuses old-school jazz with orchestral sound, blues, big band and soul. The 17-track record is a concept album which explores overcoming heartbreak, self-doubt and internet trolling. Raye's second album This Music May Contain Hope topped the UK charts Raye has enjoyed an impressive past few years since leaving her label after expressing frustration that they were holding out on releasing her debut album. She was later released from her contract and struck out as an independent artist. By the end of 2022, her dance track Escapism featuring US rapper 070 Shake had gone viral on TikTok and shot up the charts to number one. She finally released her emotionally-charged debut album, My 21st Century Blues, in 2023, which was applauded by critics and peaked at number two in the charts. It went to on to win a record-breaking six Brit Awards, including album of the year, and was nominated for the acclaimed Mercury Prize. This summer, Raye was among the six British and Irish artists who headlined Reading and Leeds Festival. In November, dozens of musicians including Dua Lipa, Coldplay and Sam Fender called on the government to protect fans from online ticket touts in an open letter. The government then announced plans to ban the resale of tickets for live events above face value. A draft Ticket Tout Bill was put forward in May, but music industry and consumer groups voiced their frustration, external that more progress wasn't being made. It will now go through further consultation and scrutiny, before it can become a new law. Following Raye's statement, a spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said it remained "fully committed to stamping out ticket touting for good". The Royal Albert Hall spokesperson said they "strongly support" the government's plan to improve ticketing laws. "Artists and venues are doing everything they can to protect fans, but we cannot solve this problem alone," they added. "The law needs to catch up with the scale and sophistication of the ticket touting industry." Did you sign up to get tickets for RAYE's Albert Hall show? title: Ex-president named leader of new DR Congo rebel coalition
description: Joseph Kabila had previously denied having links to the M23 rebels, which control much of eastern DR Congo.
body: Joseph Kabila was DR Congo president from 2001 until January 2019 Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named the leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government. The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it aimed to coordinate "resistance forces" to end "tyranny" in Democratic Republic of Congo and would pursue the goal "by all means, including force". Its unveiling on Monday is the clearest indication so far of Kabila's direct involvement in an armed movement a year after he was sentenced to death in absentia for treason. He had previously denied having links to the M23 rebel group. The Congolese government has not commented. Claude Ibalanky, the coalition's adviser, announced the group's leadership at a press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the largest city in eastern DR Congo, which has been under the control of the M23 since last year. Video released by the group showed Kabila signing documents at the group's declaration along with other leaders. M23 leader Sultani Makenga will serve as one of Kabila's four deputies in the new movement. The other three also come from the AFC-M23 alliance which last year seized much of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo. What's the fighting in DR Congo all about? The announcement of the new group comes days after Kabila delivered an address in which he said he would set out how Congolese people should act to "rescue" their country. On Friday, Kabila accused President Félix Tshisekedi's government of disregarding proposals he had put forward last year, including some aimed at ending the conflict in eastern DR Congo. Kabila also accused the government of undermining constitutional rule, mismanaging the economy and failing to improve security. He further alleged arbitrary arrests of political opponents and military officers. The government has not publicly responded to those claims. Kabila, 55, ruled DR Congo from 2001 until January 2019, when Tshisekedi took office following a disputed election. The two were once political allies, forming an informal power-sharing arrangement after the transfer of power. They later fell out and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in 2023 before returning to Goma last year. The former president had remained largely out of public view for several years but has become increasingly critical of his successor's administration. The formation of the new coalition comes at an uncertain time in a country that has been wracked by violence for decades. More than 100 militia groups are active in eastern DR Congo amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources. The UN and Western governments accuse Rwanda of backing the M23 and controlling the rebels. Rwanda denies supporting the M23 despite overwhelming evidence, and says its military presence in eastern DR Congo is a defensive measure against threats posed by Congolese armed groups. Tshisekedi's second term ends in 2028 but in May he said that elections, which are due then, may not be held because of the conflict. He also hinted that he may seek re-election for a third term "if the people want". The parliament has since passed a bill that could pave the way for a referendum that could remove the constitution's two-term limit. Last month, authorities clashed with protesters holding demonstrations in the capital against the proposed changes. title: Owls ringed to measure benefits of wildlife farming
description: A barn owl and 15 chicks are ringed to see if conservation-focused farming is working.
body: The ringed owls will be tracked to see how well nature-friendly farming is helping their numbers Barn owl chicks have been ringed in Purbeck for the first time to help track their movements and if the area's conservation-focused farming is working. The 15 chicks and one adult were ringed at nest sites across three farmland sites in a partnership between Birds of Poole Harbour, Carey Ringing Station and the National Trust. Mark Singleton, Purbeck's National Trust countryside manager, said: "This is an exciting project and a first for us in Purbeck. Although barn owl numbers have fallen significantly over the past century, there are encouraging signs they may be recovering locally." Set to run every year, the project hopes to expand with more nest boxes put up next year. The project hopes to expand next year Singleton said National Trust tenant farmers were managing the land to support wildlife with areas of longer grass, maintaining hedgerows and patches of scrub. He said: "These habitats support the voles and other small mammals that barn owls rely on. "By monitoring ringed birds over many years, we'll be able to assess how effective these measures are and continually improve what we're doing." Kate Fox, licenced bird ringer and ornithologist from Carey Ringing Station, said: "Ringing provides invaluable scientific data about these birds, which can't be gained from observations alone. "Barn owls are striking birds, but it's very difficult to tell individuals apart. If birds move to a different nest box, we won't know whether it's a new pair or birds we've recorded elsewhere unless they have been ringed." The ringing was carried out under a special licence and follows strict guidance from the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO). Barn owls are a Schedule 1 breeding species, meaning it is illegal to disturb them during the breeding season without a licence. title: Super El Niño sets another record as it strengthens to 'unprecedented levels'
description: El Niño has continued to strengthen, with several key measures now in record territory. Simon King explores how it compares to previous events.
body: Flooded streets following the arrival of Hurricane Polo in the town of Puerto San Carlos, Baja California Sur, Mexico, on 29 September. The Category 3 storm added to an already busy hurricane season turbo-charged by El Niño. El Niño has continued to strengthen to what some scientists are calling "unprecedented levels", weeks before its expected peak in December. Several key measures are now in record territory. In its latest update, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) said average weekly sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific have reached their highest level on record, external. It comes after scientists declared a new record for daily sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific in September, exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. El Niño this year is creating new ocean temperature records in a background of overall ocean warming due to human-induced climate change, seen especially when comparing previous record El Niño events Temperatures above 30C have also been recorded for the first time in parts of the tropical Pacific, while record sea-surface temperature anomalies and exceptional subsurface warmth have been observed. These measurements come from the region of the equatorial Pacific used to monitor El Niño. El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year. However, the Pacific is also warming due to human-induced climate change and this is starting to mask the strength of the natural warming during El Niño. To remove this additional warming signal, Australian and US official forecasters are now using a Relative Ocean El Niño Index (RONI), to enable better comparison to historical events. Using that measure, the BOM's average weekly data - while only going back to 2008 - is significant as it now exceeds levels during the record-breaking December of 2015. "We are currently witnessing an El Niño event that is unprecedented in the historical record," Dr Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, told the BBC. The warmth across the Pacific now extends well beyond the tropical region normally used to monitor El Niño. Comparisons with previous major events in 1972-73, 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 show much more widespread ocean warmth across the Pacific and into the Gulf of Mexico. Part of this reflects the long-term warming of the oceans but scientists say it is not the whole story. "The strength of El Niño this year is spilling out of the traditional El Niño region," Dr Hausfather said. Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says there is currently no evidence that climate change is making El Niño events stronger or more frequent, external. However, it remains an active area of scientific research. What is clearer is that El Niño releases additional heat from the oceans into the atmosphere. Historically, global temperatures during El Niño years are typically higher than during neutral years. Combined with human-driven climate change, that extra heat is expected to help make 2026 one of the warmest years on record, with unusually high global temperatures likely to continue into 2027. The 1997-98 super El Niño brought devastating floods throughout Ecuador Although the most widespread impacts are expected later this year and into 2027, El Niño's influence is already being felt across parts of the world. The strength of an El Niño does not automatically determine the scale of impacts in any one location. Regional effects can vary considerably from one event to another. However, some common patterns are emerging when compared with previous super El Niños. During the 1997-98 event, severe drought across south-east Asia contributed to extensive peat and forest fires, while parts of East Africa experienced devastating floods. The event also helped make 1998 the warmest year on record at the time. A similar pattern developed during the 2015-16 El Niño. Severe drought and wildfire activity returned to parts of south-east Asia, while southern Africa experienced one of its worst droughts in decades, triggering a major humanitarian crisis. Another recurring signal is tropical cyclone activity. Strong El Niño events typically suppress Atlantic hurricanes while boosting activity across parts of the Pacific, a pattern that has also been observed during 2026. The World Meteorological Organisation says drought and flood-related disruption is already being reported in several regions, with growing concerns over food security in parts of East Africa and the Asia-Pacific. Forecasts from both the European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration indicate El Niño is likely to peak in December. Dr Hausfather said the latest projections were "astonishing" and are likely to set new records "by a remarkable amount". Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter? title: Carragher settles tax debt to avoid bankruptcy
description: Jamie Carragher has settled an unpaid tax bill with His Majesty's Revenue and Customs.
body: Jamie Carragher regularly appears on Sky Sports and CBS Sports. Former Premier League footballer Jamie Carragher, 48, will not be made bankrupt after he settled an unpaid tax bill with HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC). Judge Nicholas Briggs dismissed a bankruptcy petition issued in August against the ex-Liverpool defender at the Insolvency and Companies Court earlier. Kevin Hassan, for HMRC, told the hearing in London that the debt has been paid, with no figure given in court. It was previously said to be in the region of £700,000 to £800,000. Carragher, from Merseyside, spent his entire professional career with Liverpool and was part of the squad which won the Champions League in 2005. He retired in 2013 after making 737 appearances for the club and has since become a pundit, appearing on Sky Sports and CBS Sports. title: Gavin and Stacey stars to feature in festive Julia Donaldson TV adaptation
description: An adaptation of a picture book to be aired over Christmas on the BBC will be voiced by Rob Brydon.
body: Julia Donaldson's characters The Baddies love boasting about being bad A new animated adaptation of a popular picture book to be aired over the Christmas period will be voiced by Welsh actor Rob Brydon and some of his Gavin and Stacey co-stars. The Baddies, by children's author Dame Julia Donaldson and illustrator Axel Scheffler, tells the story of a troll, a ghost and a witch. Brydon, as Ghost, will be joined by Sheridan Smith and Alison Steadman, who also starred alongside him in the popular sitcom, as well as Hammed Animashaun as Troll, Robyn Cara as Girl, and Francesca Mills as the narrator. Previous adaptations of Dame Donaldson's books include The Gruffalo, Zog and The Scarecrows' Wedding, which also featured Brydon as scarecrow Reginald Rake. The half-hour special celebrates courage, kindness and the power of standing up to bullies, according to the BBC and production company Magic Light Pictures. It follows a girl with a blue spotty hanky who moves to a cottage near The Baddies. (L-R) Gavin & Stacey stars Sheridan Smith, Rob Brydon and Alison Steadman will all feature in The Baddies this Christmas A mouse then challenges the Baddies to see who can steal the hanky, but they soon learn that they may have met their match in the little girl. "The Baddies was enormous fun to write because I loved inventing these gloriously wicked characters and then thinking about what might happen when they finally meet someone brave enough to outwit them," Donaldson said. Sheridan Smith said it was "such a joy to be part of bringing The Baddies to life". "The film is funny, spooky and full of heart, and the animation is absolutely beautiful. I think families are going to have enormous fun watching these wonderful characters causing chaos this Christmas," she said. title: Children asked to name Ealing's new beavers
description: Londoners aged four to 18 can suggest names for the kits, born at Paradise Fields, until 7 December.
body: A young kit settles beside an adult at the Ealing site Children in London are being asked to help name two baby beavers born this year in Ealing, west London. Anyone living in the capital aged between four and 18 can suggest names for the kits until 7 December. The winners will be chosen by representatives of the Ealing Beaver Project and the mayor of London's office. A family of Eurasian beavers was released at Paradise Fields in 2023, returning the animals to urban London for the first time in more than 400 years. A beaver feeds at the water's edge at Paradise Fields Elliot Newton, director of rewilding at conservation group Citizen Zoo, said the new kits showed beavers could "coexist with people in the heart of urban London". The project's lead, Dr Sean McCormack, said: "Personally, I'm very excited to see what names the children come up with." The scheme is run by Citizen Zoo, Ealing Wildlife Group, Friends of Horsenden Hill and Ealing Council, with funding from the mayor's office. Its backers say the beavers have created new wetland habitats on the site, improved water quality and made the area more resilient to flooding and drought. Paradise Fields is free to visit and open 24 hours a day. Entries can be submitted through Citizen Zoo's website. title: Bethell returns as England call up youngsters Jack and Rew
description: Jacob Bethell will return for England's white-ball tour of Australia, while there are also first international call-ups for exciting prospects Thomas Rew and Eddie Jack.
body: Jacob Bethell has been sidelined with injury since July Jacob Bethell will return for England's white-ball tour of Australia, while there are also first international call-ups for exciting prospects Thomas Rew and Eddie Jack. Warwickshire's Bethell has not played since suffering a knee injury in July but is back as part of a near-full-strength squad for three one-day internationals. England have made changes for the five T20s, resting players ahead of the Test tour of South Africa, meaning 18-year-old Somerset wicketkeeper-batter Rew and Hampshire's 21-year-old pace bowler Jack are included. The tour begins with the first ODI in Perth on 13 November and ends with the final T20 in Canberra on 2 December – a week before England's warm-up match in South Africa leading into a three-Test series. There will be live ball-by-ball commentary from every match of England's tour of Australia on Test Match Special. England white-ball coach Brendon McCullum had previously confirmed he wanted a strong team for the ODI leg of the trip to Australia in the build-up to the World Cup in southern Africa next year. The New Zealander also conceded he would have to rotate his squad for the T20 leg, given England's schedule in a busy winter of five separate overseas tours. One-day squad: Harry Brook (Yorkshire – captain), Jofra Archer (Sussex), Gus Atkinson (Surrey), Sonny Baker (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), Jacob Bethell (Warwickshire), Jordan Cox (Essex), Henry Crocombe (Surrey), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Joe Root (Yorkshire), Josh Tongue (Nottinghamshire). T20 squad: Harry Brook (Yorkshire – captain), Tom Banton (Somerset), Jacob Bethell (Warwickshire), James Coles (Sussex), Jordan Cox (Essex), Henry Crocombe (Surrey), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Aneurin Donald (Derbyshire), Eddie Jack (Hampshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Thomas Rew (Somerset), Phil Salt (Lancashire), Luke Wood (Lancashire). Rew averages 68 in four first-class matches for Somerset and 44 in List A cricket. In T20s, he has a strike-rate of 153 For the ODIs, Jofra Archer is back in the pace attack after being rested for the tri-series in Pakistan in October. Archer's return means the 50-over squad is close to full strength, bar the absence of wicketkeeper Jos Buttler who is set for a lengthy spell on the sidelines following hamstring surgery. After the ODIs, all of seamers Archer, Gus Atkinson, Josh Tongue and Sonny Baker, along with batter Ben Duckett, miss out on the T20s in order to prepare for South Africa. The re-shuffle means eye-catching call-ups for Rew and Jack, while opener Aneurin Donald keeps his place after making his debut in the series against Sri Lanka last month. The addition of Rew and Jack, who were awarded development central contracts on Monday, offers the tantalising prospect of a first international cap against England's fiercest rivals in one of the most iconic venues in cricket. The first T20 is at the colossal Melbourne Cricket Ground on 21 November. Rew does not turn 19 until 29 November. If he plays on the tour, he would become the third-youngest man to make his England debut in any format after Rehan Ahmed and Brian Close, and the youngest man to play for England against Australia. Rew is the younger brother of James, who made his Test debut for England against New Zealand at The Oval in June. Thomas captained England Under-19s to the final of the World Cup earlier this year and made two centuries for Somerset in the County Championship during the summer. Jack, who has the middle name Vaughan after former England captain Michael, has been on England's radar since last year. He looks likely to earn a debut in Australia because he is one of only three specialist fast bowlers in the squad. Uncapped Henry Crocombe is down under for both series after earning a two-year central contract on Monday, while Luke Wood is part of the T20 squad despite losing his central deal. Bethell's return to both squads is an indication of the selection decision England will face for the Test series in South Africa. In the left-hander's absence for the home Test series against Pakistan this summer, Emilio Gay, Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence came into the England XI. Bethell's comeback could displace any one of that trio. Harry Brook captains England on both legs of the tour and is once again set to play across formats in every game of the winter. He has not missed an international since a raft of players were rested for the T20 series in Ireland last September. The trip will be Brook's first return to Australia since a nightclub incident in Wellington, New Zealand, last October was revealed on the final day of the Ashes series in January. During the Ashes, England's players came under intense scrutiny from the local media, not helped by a series of off-field misdemeanours. Though a white-ball tour will not have the same profile as the Ashes, the tourists can still expect a degree of hostility from the home fans. There will also be the spectre of former Test captain Ben Stokes, whose stint with Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash League begins shortly after England's tour ends. title: Martin Freeman to give Gromit a voice for first time in new audiobook
description: Martin Freeman will be the voice of Aardman's Gromit in new audiobook.
body: Gromit is breaking his 37-year silence for an autobiography He's graced our screens for almost 40 years, but has never said a word - until now. Since 1989 Gromit, the animated dog from Bristol's Aardman Animations, has shared adventures with his cheese-loving owner Wallace, from spaceflight to being pursued by robotic garden gnomes. And now Gromit, created by Nick Park, will speak for the first time in an audiobook voiced by actor Martin Freeman. Park said the actor, who rose to fame in The Office and went on to star in the BBC Drama Sherlock and films such as Love Actually and The Hobbit, was "the obvious choice really." We were scammed by car cloning criminals - it's happening all the time M5 driver four times over limit with dog in car Modern masculinity explored in wrestling show Park said he was "genuinely thrilled and honoured when he [Freeman] said yes." The hardback and audiobook, published by Ebury, is called Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit - as told to Nick Park. "He is not doing a Gromit 'voice' as such," Park explained. "He's reading Gromit's story as Gromit put it; his inner thoughts, his candid insights and endless witticisms bringing to them his usual colour, thoughtfulness and wry humour." title: Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer
description: The leadership team is attempting a buyout, but a union has warned the retailer could fall into administration instead.
body: Retail chain Poundland is in talks with potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, it has confirmed. Executives are working with an Irish property development group on a management buyout, as first reported by Sky News, external. But a union representing shopworkers warned that the retailer could fall into administration if that deal falls through, putting thousands of jobs at risk. This outcome would be "a disaster for our members", the Usdaw union said. Poundland has about 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and 12,000 employees. The chain has been struggling for a number of years due to pressures including rising costs and competition. However, it expects sales to have grown more than 3% in 2026 compared with the previous year, which managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month was evidence that its recovery plan "is working". The retailer was sold for £1 last summer by previous owner Pepco to US investment firm Gordon Brothers. The current owners are in the process of seeking buyers, with the Poundland management attempting a buyout, a spokesman said. Mr Williams, along with the firm's leadership team and Andy Bond, a former chairman of Pepco, have been working with Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group on a management buyout. Martin Property Group is the management team's "preferred partner", the spokesman said, but the team will "work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues and suppliers and build on the successful recovery that's already taking shape," he added. However, Bally Auluk, a national officer at Usdaw, said there are "deep concerns that the business could go into administration" should this buyout fail. "We are aware that a management buy-out has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down," he added. A Poundland source disputed this, however, saying the Martin Property Group is part of the sale process and remains the management team's preferred partner. title: Boulter beaten by Shnaider in Wuhan
description: British number one Katie Boulter loses to Diana Shnaider in the Wuhan Open first round.
body: Katie Boulter is the 23rd woman to hold the British number one ranking British number one Katie Boulter is out of the Wuhan Open after a first-round defeat by Russian Diana Shnaider. After a competitive first set, Boulter lost her serve four times in the second as world number 13 Shnaider convincingly won 6-3 6-1 in one hour and 30 minutes. This has been a largely disappointing season for Boulter, who is ranked 54th in the world and has posted just two wins across the four Grand Slam tournaments. Since suffering a first-round exit at Wimbledon in June, Boulter has won just three of the nine singles matches she has played on the WTA Tour. This one came at a difficult time for Boulter, whose grandfather, Brian, died last week. He was described by Boulter's brother James as "Katie's biggest supporter" and Boulter said in a social media tribute before competing in Wuhan that she had experienced "a tough week". title: Phase Eight and Hobbs owner hit by cyber-attack, as H&M probes separate hack claim
description: TFG London has apologised to customers for disruption after it identified a "cybersecurity incident" on Sunday.
body: The owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident. According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands". "We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement. Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group. TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate". The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident. "As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said. The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly. "We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added. Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers". Fashion giants ranging from Adidas to Alexander McQueen have been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom. "No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages. Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once". She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become". On Monday, it was also reported that fashion giant H&M was investigating a claim of a hack by a cyber-criminal group called ShinyHunters. The hackers have been previously linked to high-profile attacks including targeting the FBI, Rockstar Games and Ticketmaster. "We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims," H&M told BBC News in a statement. "At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised." It also comes only a week after Asos customers were informed the online fashion and beauty retailer had been hacked by another group, via a push notification appearing on their phone screens. Cyber-security experts told the BBC it was an unprecedented move for hackers to effectively transform an app notification system into a "ransom note". It later emerged that hackers had obtained more detailed personal information belonging to Asos customers than the retailer initially suggested. An update was issued to customers after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said the breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed. title: Ronaldo scores after match delayed by missile alert
description: Cristiano Ronaldo scores as Al-Nassr win an AFC Champions League match which is delayed by an hour because of a missile alert in Riyadh.
body: Cristiano Ronaldo is closing on a milestone 1,000 career goals after scoring for the 981st time on Monday Cristiano Ronaldo scored as Al-Nassr won an AFC Champions League match which was delayed by an hour because of a missile alert. Ronaldo scored Al-Nassr's second goal as the Saudi Pro League champions beat Uzbekistan's Neftchi Fergana 3-1 on Monday. Kick-off was delayed after Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence issued a safety warning just 15 minutes before the scheduled start time in Riyadh, the capital city which has been the target of missiles fired from Yemen-based Houthis. Following attacks on Riyadh's airport, explosions were heard in the capital on Monday night. The Saudi-led military coalition said a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed. Future sporting events could be affected by the regional conflict, including Formula 1 races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Once Al-Nassr were able to get under way, Ange Postecoglou's team went ahead through Angelo in the 33rd minute and Ronaldo doubled their lead before half-time. Uzbekistan champions Neftchi pulled a goal back, but they were reduced to 10 men after 65 minutes and an own goal 13 minutes later sealed a first Group B victory for the hosts. Ronaldo also scored on Friday when making his return to club football, having left the Portugal national team camp halfway through the Nations League break out of frustration at limited playing opportunities. Ronaldo scores on Al-Nassr return after Portugal fallout Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports F1 is pressing ahead with plans to run the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. It's fair to say this is causing some disquiet in the paddock, even if few - if any - are voicing it publicly. The argument to press on as planned is that the Qatar and Abu Dhabi governments are saying there is no reason for F1 not to go, there have been no attacks on civilian infrastructure since the spring, and the countries are operating on a business-as-usual basis. On top of that, the UK Foreign Office is not advising against travel, instead warning that there is "a risk of more attacks and unforeseen escalation in the region", and that "British nationals currently in the Middle East should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruption". As Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff put it on Sunday: "Whether Qatar and Abu Dhabi happens at the moment, everybody says so, and so we need to go the direction of this is six more races to go." If there is an escalation in the Middle East, for example after the US mid-term elections on 3 November, and the races have to be cancelled at late notice, then Imola in Italy is being prepared as a back-up option for the weekend of Abu Dhabi. title: Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
description: Rwanda signs a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
body: The new track near Kigali has been designed to exploit Rwanda's natural landscape Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s". The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993. A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come". The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added. F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas. It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year. The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing. Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November. F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races. Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement. "Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers. "The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people." F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent". Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact." The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa. Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture. A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good." The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit. It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape. The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958. South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85. Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end. The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible. title: US emergency call records reveal confusion after failed execution of Christa Pike
description: The killer of Colleen Slemmer was ultimately taken to hospital after two doses of lethal injection did not kill her.
body: This video can not be played Listen: Emergency calls from botched Christa Pike execution released to US media Emergency call records have revealed the confusion that developed among prison staff and emergency call handlers after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong last month in Tennessee. Pike, 50, who killed Colleen Slemmer alongside her then-boyfriend in 1995, was given two doses of lethal injection on 30 September. Once it became clear that she was not going to die from the dosage, she was taken to hospital. The confusion resulted in part from an apparent disconnect between prison staff, according to the AP news agency, which first obtained audio of the emergency calls. This allegedly delayed Pike's treatment. The BBC has asked the state corrections department for comment. The department has not yet stated what it thinks went wrong in the attempted execution of Pike. Pike's legal team has offered the explanation that the pentobarbital chemical, with which she was injected, probably spread under skin rather than reaching her bloodstream in a sufficient quantity to kill her. Pike has now been discharged from hospital, though in their most recent update on her health, her team cautioned that she faced a "long road to recovery". It is not clear what treatment, if any, she is receiving now that she is back in prison. Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection. Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess". Pike's boyfriend at the time of the murder, Tadaryl Shipp, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty because he was not yet an adult when the crime was committed. Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers say Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method? The sequence of events on the evening of 30 September was pieced together by US media using a combination of emergency call recordings and transcripts. The records were published in full by the Nashville Banner, external news outlet. The initial call made from Riverbend Prison - which was reportedly made at 20:40 local time - was considered to have been false by first responders, after the caller was unable to verify themselves using a code. That person seems to have been in a part of the prison where the injections were taking place. They said: "We've been carrying out an execution tonight. We've administered 10 grams of pentobarbital. The person is not yet deceased. That started approximately one hour ago. And we're calling for an ambulance." The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications released records of its conversations with other local agencies as it tried to confirm whether the call was genuine. The confusion appears to have been compounded by other prison staff, from the institution's central command, who said at 21:07 that they "would have been the ones to call in" and that they "did not make that call". It was not until about 21:11 that prison officials verified that the initial call, made about half an hour previously, had in fact been genuine. At that point, the emergency responders were allowed through the prison gates. A later call acknowledged that the situation had been chaotic. At 21:34, as Pike was being taken to hospital, one medic asked a colleague to ensure the prison knew where Pike was being taken, "just 'cause there's been so much other confusion". Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and Shipp Pike's lawyers are yet to comment on the recordings. Over the course of last week, her team provided frequent updates on Pike's condition - detailing how she had regained her ability to walk and talk before ultimately being discharged from hospital care. It is unclear whether or when the state will try again to execute Pike. Some state Republicans have called for a new method to be attempted. Pike's legal team, meanwhile, are calling on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole. For now, Lee has paused the state's executions for the remainder of the year. An investigation is taking place into what went wrong with Pike's execution. The head of the state's corrections department is resigning from his post in the wake of the botched execution. What happened in Christa Pike's failed US execution, and how did she survive? title: Welsh government and Labour strike deal on mini-budget
description: The Plaid Cymru-led administration had failed to pass its spending plans during the summer.
body: The Welsh government has reached a deal with Labour on its mini-budget, which had failed to pass in the summer. Ministers said the Plaid Cymru-led administration had now agreed an extra £60m for children with additional learning needs (ALN). Labour, who sit in opposition after losing May's Senedd election, had rejected a £40m a year deal across three years, in acrimonious scenes at the Welsh Parliament in the last week of term in July. Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates had demanded £100m this year when the supplementary budget was last discussed. On Tuesday, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "This agreement reflects what can be achieved when parties across the Senedd work together." The budget will be debated in the Senedd on 3 November. title: Inside Health
description: Full body scans, nutritious stockpiles and why strokes are rising in black communities.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·13 Oct 2026,·28 mins Available for over a year We investigate the growing business of full-body MRI scans. The clinics argue they can spot diseases and problems early before people feel unwell - but critics say it’s a waste of thousands of pounds and creates unnecessary anxiety about things that may never become a problem. Laura visits a clinic to learn more and also hears about the risks. Also this week, new research shows strokes are increasing among black African and black Caribbean people in the UK at a faster rate in than in white people - and it’s mainly being driven by high blood pressure. Laura meets Dr Iain Marshall, a GP who researches stroke risk factors, and Sheila Chingono, who had a stroke aged 32, to talk about why this is happening and what can be done to prevent it. And most of us hear the phrase ‘emergency food stockpile’ and think of a sad-looking kitchen cupboard full of tins we’d rather not eat. Laura speaks to a nutritional scientist about how you can still have a healthy and tasty meal with non-perishable goods, even if you’ve got no running water or way of cooking food. And crucially she learns that it doesn’t involve giving up biscuits... Presenter: Laura Foster Producer: Gerry Holt Editor: Ilan Goodman Sound engineer: Mary Stone Production coordinator: Stu Laws The show was made by the BBC’s Audio Science Unit in collaboration with The Open University.

title: Ship sinks in new drone attack off Bulgaria, PM summons Russian ambassador
description: Bulgaria's prime minister says two merchant ships were hit by drones and he suspects Russia was behind the attacks.
body: Five crew members on the Ukrainian-registered merchant ship suffered minor injuries in Tuesday's attacks A merchant ship has sunk after drones hit two vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said. He indicated Russia was suspected of the attacks and that he had called in its ambassador. One of the ships went down 17 nautical miles (31km) east of Krapets and one crew member was saved, he said. The other, Ukrainian-owned vessel was hit by three drones 18 nautical miles from the town of Byala and all 15 crew were rescued, he added. The drone attacks come a week after two other commercial ships were hit by sea and aerial drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. One of the ships, the Alfa Watan, sank and all 10 crew, including nine Syrians, are presumed dead. Radev convened an emergency meeting on Tuesday and said he had summoned Russian envoy Eleonora Mitrofanova. Although there was no conclusive evidence of blame on "either side... the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation", he said. Bulgaria is a Nato member and the prime minister said he would speak shortly to secretary general Mark Rutte. Radev had earlier asked Nato and the EU for technical assistance in investigating the 6 October attacks, indicating it was unclear whether Russia and Ukraine were behind them. Radev came to office during the summer and has since rejected suggestions that he is "pro-Russian". Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for the latest attacks and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke on Tuesday of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable". Russia's military has not publicly commented on the issue. It has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the Black Sea, particularly the western side, as part of its war against Ukraine. The same day that two ships were targeted off Bulgaria last week, Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi. Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports - and cited attacks in the ports of Mykolaiv and Chornomorsk last week, along with one in the Black Sea. However, Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked. Rumen Radev described the attack as "absolutely unacceptable" Meeting with his security chiefs on Tuesday, Bulgaria's prime minister said: "Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable". Radev identified one of the hit vessels as the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, which is registered in Ukraine's Odesa, saying that five its crew members were being treated for minor injuries. He gave no further details about the vessel that had sunk. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said "Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters... once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea. "The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength," he added. Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea. Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. body: This video can not be played US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as Walter 'Flynn' White Jr in Breaking Bad, has died aged 34. In 2015, he spoke to BBC Newsnight about how he got into the film industry and about being an actor with a disability. title: Troubles bill to be discussed in Parliament
description: The government has tabled a number of amendments for its bill, which seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the Troubles.
body: The government's Northern Ireland Troubles Bill is expected to be discussed in the House of Commons on Tuesday. The bill seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict. The bill was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government. On Monday it was announced that the Attorney General must provide consent for any serious prosecutions related to the Troubles under changes to the planned legislation. It is among a series of amendments, external the government has tabled for the legislation. A carry-over extension of the bill is happening on Tuesday and will be followed by a small debate. It will then be voted on by MPs next week and if passed, it will move to the House of Lords for further consideration by peers. The Labour government has faced criticism over delays in passing the bill as well as questions over some of its contents. It seeks to replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act, which introduced a ban on inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents. The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful. Labour's bill involves a Legacy Commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police). David Johnstone said the role the Attorney General will play has had a "mixed reaction" as it is a political appointment and will not have veterans "excited" The Northern Ireland Veterans' Commissioner David Johnstone said it is "too early to say in detail" about whether he is pleased about the amendments. "We are going to take our time, we need to take some legal input, we need to consult with veterans. We are not going to have a knee jerk reaction, I don't think anyone's going to be dancing in the streets over the amendments," he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme. "It does appear that the secretary of state and the Ministry of Defence have listened to some of the concerns and there does seem to be some amendments that are welcomed." He added that the bill needs to be amendment so it is "fair and balanced" but he added that that is "unlikely". On Monday Sinn Féin MP John Finucane denounced the amendments as a "veterans' charter". He said they "risk preferential treatment, providing additional protections for former members of the British military while placing further obstacles in the path of effective investigations". Johnstone said he was "not worried about the criticism of Sinn Féin" when it comes to the bill. "While on the surface there does seem to be some improvements to protections, things like the Attorney General being involved to make a final decision on prosecutions, on the surface seems welcome but let's see the actual wording in terms of legal opinion because it is a minefield." Johnstone said the role the Attorney General will play has had a "mixed reaction" as it is a political appointment and will not have veterans "excited". However he said some veterans will see it as "positive" as decisions on prosecutions will involve officials in Westminster, rather than in Northern Ireland. Deirdre Hargey said that the amendments insert political interference into the process Speaking on Good Morning Ulster, Sinn Féin MLA Deirdre Hargey said that legacy needs to be addressed. "We do have families where that trauma, that pain is being passed onto the next generation because they don't have the answers, they haven't been able to seek justice." But, she said the amendments will further knock the confidence of victims and survivors. "Instead of bringing forward measures that would enhance confidence of victims, they have actually risked undermining investigations and importantly the equal application of the law," she said. Hargey said the amendments insert political interference into the process, adding that the British government controlling this would be "extremely concerning considering their key role in the conflict". Gavin Robinson has expressed concerns that the government had published these amendments before the parliamentary process concludes on Tuesday DUP leader Gavin Robinson expressed his concerns that the government had published these amendments before the parliamentary process concludes on Tuesday. "140 amendments have been published this morning and they have be considered, understood, some coherency brought to them. And then an assessment made as to whether they actually do protect innocent victims and assist veterans," he said. "I think it's unfair for veterans and for innocent victims across NI to even comprehend how each amendment interacts with the legislation." He said he thinks the government would have been better to publish "a comprehensive and a concise and a coherent piece of legislation so people could understand the interaction between the changes they're proposing and the bill before us today". Robinson did say he believes it is good that Labour "will legislate to recognise that the actions of soldiers are not equivalent to the actions of terrorists who went out to destroy our country". However, he said that "there are still issues to be ironed out" including being "deeply concerned" that "this government has no intention of extending the dates of the Legacy Commission to include Omagh". He said "this legislation suggests that it wasn't a Troubles event and therefore we won't get the answers that the families in Omagh so desperately need." Emmett McConomy, whose 11-year-old brother Stephen was shot dead by a soldier in Londonderry in 1982, said the planned changes feel like a "backwards step".
