title: Cut screen time in classrooms to avoid long-term health issues, government urged
description: A group of clinicians warns technology use in English schools is driving a rise in health problems like short-sightedness.
body: The amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health", a group of more than 150 clinicians has warned. GPs, paediatricians and other specialists said in an open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper that tablets and laptops are being used without a full understanding of their long-term health impacts, including on eye health. The clinicians said they are prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools". The government said it was consulting on screen time guidance for children aged five to 18 but that technology could be a powerful learning tool if used properly. The group of clinicians said nearly one million children are using screens in most lessons, despite studies suggesting a rise in short-sightedness. They pointed to an analysis of 276 studies covering 5.4 million participants around the world. That analysis, they claimed, found a rise in short-sightedness among children and adolescents from around 24% in 1990 to almost 36% by 2023, warning the condition is associated with an increased risk of a range of eye health problems. Many children now spend longer on screens in the classroom than is recommended in a 24-hour period, the letter said, adding: "As a country, we need to wake up to this now, and start rolling back screen use in schools before the damage compounds further." One of its signatories was, Dr Becky Foljambe NHS GP and founder of Health Professionals for Safer Screens. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme parents had not been given the chance to "opt out" of the "excessive" use of screens in schools, which risks children "just not thriving" in education. She said an "explosion" in short-sightedness "cannot be put down to genetics alone". Foljambe said it was a "lazy argument" to advocate for screen use to prepare children for a digital work, adding: "They also need their sleep, their eyesight, they need rest, they need ability to critically think and appraise." "We are conscious that some of this evidence is still surfacing but the direction of travel is consistent across multiple, independent, and in some cases very large, bodies of research," the letter continued. It also warned that children with special educational needs are "disproportionately" directed to screen-based learning. A Department for Education spokesperson said the government was developing new screen-time guidance for children aged five to 18, and will consult on the safety of artificial intelligence and educational technology in schools. They said: "Used well, technology can be a powerful tool to support learners who need it and free up teachers to deliver the excellent education every child deserves." It comes after a ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day. title: Emergency calls from botched Christa Pike execution released to US media
description: A series of calls, obtained by the Associated Press, reveal emergency services were delayed in reaching Pike.
body: This video can not be played A series of newly-released calls made after the failed execution of US death row inmate Christa Pike reveal emergency services were delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials. The recordings, first obtained by the Associated Press, show that minutes passed as officials and responders attempted to confirm whether the request for emergency help in the execution chamber at Riverbend Prison was legitimate. The first call was released only in a written transcript by the Nashville Department of Emergency Communications (DEC). "We've been carrying out an execution tonight. We've administered 10 grams of pentobarbital. The person is not yet deceased. That started approximately 1 hour ago. And we're calling for an ambulance," the caller told the dispatcher. The dispatcher asked the caller for a verification code, which the caller did not have. The DEC also released other calls between the agency and other departments, including the police and highway patrol. "We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening and we need to send an ambulance and, or if you need police assistance or if this is someone that is just basically prank calling or, like, swatting us," one dispatcher can be heard saying during a call. Another recording shows Kelly Gleason, Christa Pike's defence attorney saying: "She is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care." Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition. title: How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?
description: The potential impact of Manchester City's rule breaking runs deep, including missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money.
body: This video can not be played BBC Sport's Dale Johnson, Dan Roan, Laura Scott and Sami Mokbel assess Manchester City's position Imagine a world where Manchester City had not used "sham contracts" to build a team capable of winning three Premier League titles, one FA Cup and three EFL Cups. If City were the winners, then there had to be losers. Not just those teams who finished runners-up or lost cup finals. The potential impact runs much deeper and includes missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money. Thirty-five other teams played in the English top flight between 2009 and 2018. And every one could in some way claim to have been left financially out of pocket. City, of course, continue to deny any wrongdoing and they have appealed. But as it stands they are guilty of all charges related to inflating their sponsorship income to the tune of £830m, plus another £90m in expenses. Strip that money out and it changes the whole complexion of the competition. BBC Sport has crunched the numbers to assess the potential financial impact on the top flight. When Sheikh Mansour bought Manchester City in 2008 they were far removed from the club you see today. Since finishing fifth in 1991-92, the last season before the formation of the Premier League, City's highest placing had been eighth in 2004-05. The Abu Dhabi money poured in via what the Premier League's independent commission described as a "disguised funding scheme". It took the club's sponsorship revenues from being on a par with Stoke City in 2008-09 to eventually overtaking those of Manchester United. City finished fifth in 2009-10. Since then, not once have they finished outside the top four in the Premier League. Did this money deny other clubs a place in the competition, and other kinds of success? This article is not trying to set out how much compensation a team might be able to claim. Nor is it saying any one team would definitely have avoided relegation or reached the Champions League. It is about chance, the possibility that a very different City team would have taken to the field without the hundreds of millions pumped in by the club's Abu Dhabi owners. It has not considered potential future earnings from success, including sponsors' bonuses and further prize money. Nor has it factored in players who may feel they have missed out on salary increases, or triggered payments, for how their club might have performed. This is purely about domestic impact: Lost prize money by league placing Missed potential Champions League earnings Loss of Premier League status Impact of cup final defeats What Manchester's 'super-profit' deal with City owners has paid out so far The full impact of City's behaviour on other clubs could be calculated at £844m. £188.2m in Premier League placing money £217.8m in missed Champions League prize money £88.3m related to domestic cup competitions and the Europa League We calculated these figures by taking published prize money from the relevant seasons. For Premier League place money, each team that finished below City is considered to have potentially missed a payment for one place. For relegation, this is the minimum value of being in the Premier League for the next season, minus the received parachute payment. For the Champions League, we took City's earnings from the following seasons and deducted the impacted teams' Europa League prize money. But City also earned prize money themselves during this period. Across the competitions, City were paid £1.17bn: £812.3m from the Premier League - total income from prize money and broadcast revenues £363.4m via the Champions League £900,000 from the FA Cup victory £300,000 from the three EFL Cup victories This video can not be played 'Period of deception' - Pochettino on Man City verdict "We have lived through a period of deception," former Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino said last month. "No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done." You can see his point. Spurs finished one place outside the Champions League positions in four (although one only was under Pochettino) of the eight seasons in which City qualified for Europe's elite competition. BBC Sport took City's earnings from the Champions League in the following season, and deducted Tottenham's Europa League prize money. Over the four seasons Spurs missed out, Manchester City earned £148.2m from the Champions League, with Tottenham taking £29.9m from the Europa League. The 2014-15 campaign led to the biggest deficit, as City finished second in the Premier League and Tottenham came fifth. City received £71.2m for reaching the Champions League semi-finals in the following season, but Spurs were only paid £17.7m from the Europa League - a difference of £53.5m. Spurs also finished behind City in the Premier League table six times, with the cumulative prize money difference worth £6.6m. The north Londoners did benefit in the 2013-14 season, as they only qualified for Europe because City beat Sunderland in the final of the EFL Cup. Spurs gained £5.1m from their 2014-15 Europa League campaign which would not have been possible without City's success. Taking into account all competitions, that produced a net financial loss for Spurs of £119.9m. The 2015-16 EFL Cup final proved to be decisive for Liverpool's hopes of European football. Jurgen Klopp's men lost to City on penalties following a 1-1 draw. The Europa League place transferred to the league, and went to West Ham United. Liverpool only finished eighth, which was not enough to qualify for Europe. Had Liverpool won the final, they would have entered the Europa League, and this provides a key financial comparison. title: India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site
description: Protesters climbed over barricades in central Delhi to demand the election chief resign over revised voter lists.
body: CJP members were detained after they managed to "sneak" into Jantar Mantar on Tuesday morning Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls. Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory popular for protests. Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject. There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held. Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar. "You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X. Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained. It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders. Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down. There is heavy security deployment in Delhi since last weekend The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission. Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response. "30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X. Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day. The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed. Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. Tens and thousands of people gathered in Delhi on Monday Separately, opposition parties held a march in Delhi on Monday from Connaught Place - a major shopping district in the heart of the capital - to the Supreme Court. The Congress, India's main opposition party, also petitioned the Supreme Court on Monday, challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise, which has resulted in tens of millions of names being removed from electoral rolls. Critics say the exercise risks excluding eligible voters and making it harder for them to prove their eligibility. Anger over the revision exercise intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration. The Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous. The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms. The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The group began as online satire after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people seeking change. After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability. title: Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Singapore Grand Prix.
body: McLaren's Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri collided on the last lap of the Singapore sprint race Red Bull's Max Verstappen dominated the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, winning the main race and the sprint. His maximum total of 33 points from the event moved him up to fourth in the drivers' standings. Ferrari's Charles Leclerc finished the race in second and championship leader Kimi Antonelli completed the podium. BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race at Marina Bay. After the last-lap incident in the sprint race in Singapore, are 'papaya rules' finally failing at McLaren, and with them the premise of running two number one drivers? - Alexandros The crash between Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri in the sprint race in Singapore left, in Norris' words, "no-one very happy" at McLaren. Norris went for a gap at Turn Five on the final lap. It was a legitimate move, in terms of the racing guidelines, but he tried to back out of it as he saw he was not being left sufficient space, and the two cars collided. Both spun, Piastri into the barriers and retirement and Norris down from fifth place to eighth. What would have been nine points for the team from the sprint therefore became one. There are two ways of looking at the move. On a pure competitive level, between two rivals, Norris had the right to go for the move, and he complied with the driving-standards guidelines as to how far alongside he needed to be up to the point he started to back out. But from a team perspective, it was all risk and no reward. If Norris had pulled off the move, it would have meant one more point for him and one fewer for Piastri, but for the team collectively it would have made no difference. What was interesting was that, despite having had initial talks with the team about it after the sprint, Norris was still pushing his point of view after qualifying. "Really, it's still my fault," he said, "but I deserved to go for the space and I still believe I had the right for it." That raised a few eyebrows, but the truth is both drivers could have handled themselves better. While there is an argument Norris should not have tried the move, there is an equally powerful one that, once he had, Piastri should have given him more space, and carried the fight down the following straight. Team boss Andrea Stella was asked later that evening whether he was concerned about the message about team play not getting through to his drivers, and he dealt with it with his usual diplomacy. Stella maintained his usual calm, even demeanour, but words like "unacceptable", "disappointed" and "serious" made it abundantly clear how angry he was. The following day, Norris had changed his tune. Not only did he offer to help out Piastri late in the race as the Australian was trying to pass Lewis Hamilton's fading Ferrari, but he also finally took full responsibility for the incident. "I can't attempt what I did," he said. "I should never have attempted it in the first place, even if the move was on. I've simply got to think more of the team that I represent rather than myself. It was a mistake on my part and I let down the team." Stella made it clear McLaren would not deviate from their policy of fairness and equal status between the drivers, even though he is well aware it will lead to issues such as this that test its limits from time to time. "I classified it as unacceptable," he said, "which is a statement that comes from the team principal, but I was very encouraged by the fact that it's a statement that very rapidly came from our drivers as well. "So we are aligned as to how we want to lead this team forward in a joint effort between the team and the drivers. The conversations that we are having, they are not finished, but it's not because we need to go back discussing if Lando was alongside Oscar. That's not the interesting bit. "For me, the interesting bit is a reflection that all the stakeholders - the team, the drivers - will have to make around leading together the team, embracing constantly from inside the cockpit the interest of the team as something that is superior to any particular, singular, individual interest. "And while the conversations from this point of view are not concluded, and there's more we can do to become a more united and even stronger team, I'm pleased that Lando at some stage in the race adopted this way of thinking. "This is what I expect as a team principal, this is what the 1,000 people that work at McLaren expect from our drivers." Verstappen dominates for first Singapore Grand Prix win Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Antonelli moves to brink of title I am regularly baffled by teams' tyre strategies, but Ferrari's in Singapore was the worst in recent years. We know Lewis Hamilton is taking responsibility, fair enough, but it wasn't his decision to stay behind Charles Leclerc. Where does this sort of thinking come from? - Julie Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur was especially sensitive about this topic after the race in Singapore, and it led to a particularly awkward news conference as reporters tried to get to the bottom of what had happened, and Vasseur kept cutting them off before they could finish questions. You could see how hard Vasseur was trying to keep himself calm, and it's easy to understand his feelings. The past few weeks, after all, have been a trying period for the team with lots of speculation about the future, which led to an unusual intervention from Ferrari after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix to make it clear Vasseur had the full support of chairman John Elkann. In this case, though, while the strategy certainly looked bizarre from the outside during the race, the explanation was pretty straightforward. title: Lewis left out for England's Rugby League World Cup opener
description: Harry Smith is named alongside captain George Williams in the England half-back roles for their 2026 Rugby League World Cup opening match against Tonga - with Mikey Lewis left out.
body: Mikey Lewis is one of three half-back options in the England World Cup squad Harry Smith has been named alongside captain George Williams in England's half-back roles for their Rugby League World Cup opening match against Tonga - with Mikey Lewis left out. Lewis, who pipped 2025 Super League Man Of Steel Jake Connor to a place in England's squad, has not even made the bench for Saturday's fixture. Hull KR's Lewis, who endured an inconsistent year, did enough to convince England head coach Brian McDermott that he should join captain Williams, the Warrington stand-off, and Wigan's Smith as half-back options. But he will be one of three players, along with Ben Currie and Ben Talty, listed as non-playing reserves. England face Tonga in Perth on Saturday (10:05 BST), before taking on France in the same city on 24 October and then Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on 30 October. England men: AJ Brimson, Dom Young, Hugo Savala, Herbie Farnworth, Zach Eckersley, George Williams, Harry Smith, Max King, Brad O'Neill, Morgan Knowles, Junior Nsemba, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley. Interchange: Jez Litten, Luke Thompson, Ethan Havard, Sam Walters, Jack Welsby, Matty Ashton. Connor out, Lewis in as England name World Cup squad Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad McDermott, who succeeded Shaun Wane in April, has also made a major selection call at full-back. AJ Brimson has been chosen ahead of Jack Welsby in the key role for England's first game in Group B-C - a combined pool of six teams, from which the top two will go through to the semi-finals early next month. McDermott indicated that he was keen to use heritage players - those who qualify for England through family background - to ensure the strongest possible squad. And Brisbane-born Brimson - who made his England debut in last year's Ashes series against Australia - is one of four such players in the squad, alongside England debutant Max King. Bulldogs prop King, born in Huddersfield while his Australian father David was a player there, features alongside fellow debutant Hugo Savala, part of Sydney Roosters' NRL Grand Final-winning squad. Victor Radley is also in the XIII. All of the men's and women's teams for the first round of matches between Thursday and Sunday were announced on Tuesday at 06:00 BST. England women's coach Stu Barrow named his squad for their opener against Wales on Saturday in Perth (07:35 BST). Jasmin Strange and Connie Boyd will make their international debuts, while uncapped Hope Millard is among the interchanges. Opponents Wales will give a debut to second-row forward Paige Travis - who played for England at the last World Cup four years ago. Tayla Preston - who captains Canterbury Bulldogs in the NRL Women's Premiership - will start at scrum-half, with former rugby union international Ffion Lewis alongside her at stand-off, while Hannah Bluck will represent Wales at a fourth different sport. Bluck has won senior Wales honours in rugby union as well as gaining junior rank recognition in football and basketball. England women: Fran Goldthorp, Anna Davies, Georgia Wilson, Connie Boyd, Amelia Brown, Isabel Rowe, Georgia Roche, Mary Coleman, Keara Bennett, Hollie-Mae Dodd, Jasmin Strange, Eva Hunter, Megan Williams. title: Is Man Utd's Fernandes issue a symptom or reason for their form?
description: Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes is yet to reach the highs of last season - is it because of his side's poor start or the reason for it?
body: Bruno Fernandes has scored 111 goals in 335 appearances for Manchester United It is only seven weeks since Bruno Fernandes stood in the Manchester Opera House and spoke of his pride at being named PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26. The Manchester United captain had already won the Premier League and Football Writers' versions, in recognition of the phenomenal contribution to his side's unexpected third-place finish. Fernandes scored nine goals and claimed 21 assists, breaking a Premier League record jointly held by Thierry Henry and Kevin de Bruyne that had stood for 23 years. Over the final 11 games of the season, of the 21 goals United scored, Fernandes either found the net himself or created 12 of them. In the seven-game run that swept United back into Europe's elite club competition after a two-year absence, the 31-year-old was a central figure in nine out of 12 goals. Statistically, it was remarkable, reminiscent of Eric Cantona in the 1995-96 title-winning campaign when he scored in six successive games, five of them when United only scored once. "It was a special season for me," Fernandes told an appreciative audience. "I am very proud. "But we don't play tennis. We don't play just for ourselves. We play for a team, we play for a club, we play for the fans. There is nothing more special than that." Fernandes after collecting the 2025-26 PFA Player of the Year trophy in August Those words have particular resonance now because, compared with those exceptional statistics, there are some far less impressive ones this season. Fernandes has played for every minute of Manchester United's six Premier League games. He has three goals and one assist, all of which came against Ipswich, the second game of the campaign and, so far, his side's only win. The numbers are actually better than last term, when he scored twice in the opening six games and failed to create any. However, at that point, Fernandes was playing in the deeper midfield role Ruben Amorim preferred. Look a bit deeper, and issues emerge. While this season is Fernandes' second highest for actual shots, at an average of 3.3 per game - his best was 3.5 in 2020-21 - it is his joint-second lowest for shots on target, at an average of 0.8. His chance creation (2.5 per game on average) is also the second lowest of his time at Old Trafford and down significantly on the 4.0 he returned last season. Even more startlingly, he has created just one 'big chance' so far this season, the lofted pass that sent Bryan Mbeumo running clear of the Ipswich defence on 30 August. Fernandes' average last season was one per game. A combination of Fernandes' numbers and his general involvement perhaps goes some way to explaining why United have collected just six points from their opening six games, their worst start to a league campaign in 40 years, when Ron Atkinson was eventually sacked to make way for Sir Alex Ferguson. But is Fernandes a reason for, or a symptom of, United's malaise? There is uncertainty over the Portugal playmaker's fitness. Fernandes rarely misses a game but was left out of the recent Nations League encounter with Norway as national team boss Jorge Jesus said the former Sporting man was "playing through pain". However, Fernandes was fit enough to return for the final two internationals of the extended break. Prior to that, he completed the full 90 minutes in the 4-0 win against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. United manager Michael Carrick does not view it as an issue. "He was carrying something but that happens a lot," he said. "Players play with issues. "It's not ideal but it is manageable. Bruno is able to play. That is the commitment he has got. "He is pretty much over it, was really bright in training this morning and is looking forward to the game." Bruno Fernandes scored a hat-trick and claimed his only assist of the season so far against Ipswich on 30 August Towards the end of last season, when Fernandes' contribution was at its most prolific, Benjamin Sesko was a regular in the number nine role, while veteran Brazilian Casemiro was the anchor in United's midfield. Of the nine league goals Sesko has scored in 2026, Fernandes created four. Fernandes was responsible for four of the final five goals Casemiro scored as a Manchester United player from 1 February onwards. Quite aside from goals, it is also clear the presence of Sesko and Casemiro is being missed. Even Casemiro's biggest admirers could not claim United's current low running stats are because the 34-year-old left for Inter Miami in the summer. However, his positioning and game knowledge remain of a high standard. Fernandes could take risks in the belief United would not be overrun on transition if he lost the ball. As for Sesko, his fresh shin injury merely extends a lack of involvement which is being keenly felt and for which, as yet, there is no end date. The club's power brokers ignored a clamour to bring in more striking support in the summer and instead reinforced Carrick's midfield. But a plan to cover the Slovenian's initial absence by using Mbeumo as a number nine had to be scrapped when Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury just before the opening game at Hull. Matheus Cunha was given the job instead, but he repeatedly dropped deep, right into the space Fernandes was occupying, and the pair never really found an effective way of dealing with it. For Fernandes, it feels restrictive, and while he is not a player who lacks confidence, it does seem his decision-making is being affected. Against Tottenham at the weekend, it took Fernandes an incredible 23 minutes just to complete a pass. Carrick said on Monday, as he looked ahead to a meeting with Atletico Madrid, that no-one was "guaranteed" a place in his team - but put enough caveats around it to indicate leaving out his captain is not in his thinking. title: Chronic UTIs made MP 'feel like a drug user'
description: Dr Allison Gardner MP has been living with the "searing pain" of recurring infections for a decade.
body: Dr Allison Gardner, the Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, is leading a group of MPs to improve recognition of chronic UTIs Warning: This story contains reference to suicide An MP says she was left "feeling like a drug user" while trying desperately to find pain relief for chronic urinary tract infections (UTIs). Labour MP Dr Allison Gardner has been living with the "searing pain" of recurrent infections for about 10 years, after first experiencing symptoms with perimenopause. According to the Chronic Urinary Tract Campaign (CUTIC), more than 1.6 million women in the UK suffer from chronic lower urinary tract symptoms, but there is no official medical definition of the condition. That is something Gardner is trying to change, with the support of a cross party group of MPs in Parliament. Gardner told the BBC how a lack of consensus on what constituted a chronic UTI left her feeling sidelined by doctors, who did not always understand the condition and were limited in the length of antibiotic courses they could prescribe. "You end up hunting for a decent length of antibiotic courses that will give you some relief," she said. UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urethra, external. As women have a shorter urethra than men, bacteria are more likely to reach the bladder or kidneys and cause an infection. Chronic UTIs are infections where symptoms do not go away, and do not clear with a short course of antibiotics. They can also be difficult to diagnose, due to a lower level of bacteria shown in urine samples. Gardner told the BBC she had considered selling her home to pay for bladder removal surgery after years of pain "It's a searing pain every time you go to the loo" said Gardner, 60. "It's just like hot needles being inserted inside you and just burning, burning, burning." She told the BBC she had felt "gaslighted" by medics and had been told to "wipe yourself better" after describing intense pain. She was even told by one consultant to give up sex because it can cause a flare up. "You've got to fight all the time just to get treated sensibly and [not told] you've got anxiety, depression or are attention seeking," Gardner said. The pain and lack of answers about her condition eventually led her to a very dark place. "It got to the point where [I thought] 'if this is how my life is going to be, I can't carry on'," she said. She was so desperate she even considered selling her house to pay for private surgery to have her bladder removed. It was around that time three years ago that she discovered Dr Cat Anderson, a Staffordshire-based GP who works in private practice and for the NHS. She was the first to identify that Gardner's symptoms were related to the menopause and prescribed her Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT). "I had two years free of UTI - I just had my life back," said Gardner. Asked whether going private went against her Labour principles that healthcare should be free, Gardner said: "You're stuck with a choice aren't you? "You either suffer or you go private... so I don't judge." She added that she believed everyone should have access to the healthcare they needed. Anderson specialises in challenging UTI cases, and is leading a group of medical experts to develop a medical definition of chronic UTIs to differentiate it from other conditions. The panel hope that an official definition will pave the way for better diagnosis and treatment. Persistent infections, Anderson said, could "ruin a patient's quality of life" - limiting their ability to work or do something as simple as pick their children up from school. She has also seen people "who are quite literally driven to suicide" due to "awful" symptoms. Anderson specialises in recurrent UTIs and is working with other doctors to develop a medical definition for the condition The expert medical panel that Anderson heads up with Sachin Malde, a London-based consultant urological surgeon, is planning to deliver its official definition of chronic UTI in 2027. This will then be presented to the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE). As to why there is no current definition of chronic UTI, NICE said it had recommended further research into chronic UTIs to develop a "clear evidence base" for any recommendations. A spokesperson for NHS England also confirmed that currently there was no single national dataset that specifically captured all cases of chronic UTI as a distinct clinical diagnosis. "This is not just a 'nice to do', this would be transformational - not just within the UK, but globally," said Gardner, of the work she is doing with other MPs in the All Party Parliamentary Group (APPG). In 2023-24, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) found that UTIs accounted for 1.2 million hospital bed days, costing hospitals and the NHS more than £604m. Dr Ron Daniels, founder and chief medical officer of the UK Sepsis Trust, said as many as 20% of all sepsis cases - which can prove fatal - are thought to originate from the urinary tract. Gardner and Anderson hope a formal definition of chronic UTIs will pave the way for better treatment Beyond the definition and improving diagnosis and treatment, the APPG wants to see all GPs trained on chronic UTIs and introduce a "passport" for patients so they do not have to repeatedly explain their medical history. In April, then-health secretary Wes Streeting said the NHS had an "appalling culture of medical misogyny", external where being "ignored, gaslit, humiliated and disrespected, were common experiences for far too many women". Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor, who co-chairs the APPG with Gardner, said the group was "disappointed" that Streeting's announcement of the women's health strategy "didn't even mention UTIs, let alone chronic UTIs". The group, he said, has now set its sights on lobbying the government to invest in research and improve care. When we asked the Department of Health and So

title: Cost-of-living struggles inspire Community Cupboard
description: New social supermarket offers cheaper groceries with dignity and choice.
body: Thomas Cliffe and Laura Steele welcomed customers into the store for the first time on Monday "Instead of going to a food bank, being handed a bag and getting back home then finding out that they won't use all those items, at least here they can buy the tokens and shop around for the items they would choose to buy." Founder Thomas Cliffe hopes the first "social supermarket" in Newcastle-under-Lyme, designed to help people struggling with the cost of living, will offer the "freedom to shop with dignity". Set up by Community Cupboard NUL CIC, the store allows members to buy groceries at cost price or below, with more choice than other outlets. Customers can sign up for a membership costing £1 for 12 months. They are then able to purchase tokens to spend on items throughout the store. Cliffe said the idea was inspired by his own experience after leaving work because of anxiety. Although his wife was still employed, he said the couple struggled financially and found they were unable to access some forms of support. "It was horrible because you start to panic and think: 'What am I supposed to do? Where am I going to get the next food from?'" "We either had to choose a meal or choose the bills." Cheryl Peeper found that the store was helpful to keep her ticking over to the next big shop without spending to much. The supermarket opened for the first time on Monday. Such stores aim to cut food waste while helping people facing food insecurity by selling surplus goods at lower prices. "It was exciting to have everyone come through the doors for the first time and give them that freedom to shop with dignity," Cliffe said. Voluntary co-director Laura Steele said the level of need in the area often went unnoticed. "One in four children experience poverty from what we have found, and the average income is £29,000." "There was nothing really for the people of Newcastle and it was crying out for it really," she said. Cheryl Pepper, a carer who visited after finishing a night shift, described the supermarket as "absolutely brilliant". "The food's cheap. If you go to Tesco you spend £100, but you come in here, I've put £20 on and I still have some tokens left," she said. Fiona Morris was one of the first to purchase items from the store. Recent research on the growth of social supermarkets, external backed the idea that they were less off-putting than food banks and large commercial stores for those facing food insecurity. But lead researcher, Dr Claire O'Malley from Teesside University, said: "While social supermarkets can improve access to affordable food and reduce waste in the short term, they should not be viewed as a complete solution to food insecurity." The report called for them to supplement, rather than replace, government support for those struggling to put good food on the table. Fiona Morris, who has ADHD, said she had often found large supermarkets overwhelming. After visiting the new store, she said she immediately felt understood by staff. "It feels like Supermarket Sweep - I feel like I'm robbing the place," she said. title: Fly-tippers face £5k fine in new crackdown
description: Cornwall Council introduces new penalties after recording 17,500 incidents in five years.
body: Cornwall Council said it recorded 17,500 fly-tipping incidents in the five years Fly-tippers in Cornwall could face fines of up to £5,000 if they are caught illegally disposing waste. The threat is a part of Cornwall Council's new push to quash the crime after it recorded 17,500 fly-tipping incidents in the past five years. It has introduced the use of covert cameras to catch unlicensed waste carriers in the act, and is also encouraging residents to submit evidence if they catch anything on camera. Households who are found to have employed fly-tippers also face fines. Cornwall Council said there was "no excuse" for the offence, and that it would hold fly-tippers to account. More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall "We work hard to identify those responsible for illegal dumping and will hold offenders to account wherever possible," said Sarah-Jane Brown, group leader for community protection at Cornwall Council. "We're asking people to play their part and work with us to prevent fly-tipping, and to share any information that may help us trace those responsible for dumping rubbish." Councillor Thalia Marrington, council cabinet member with responsibility for community safety and public protection, said: "Fly-tipping can cause serious harm to our communities, the environment and wildlife. "It also costs councils and landowners huge amounts of money to clear up." Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: An insurance policy with no guarantee - the complex issue of egg-freezing in sport
description: BBC Sport examines the potential benefits, risks and unanswered questions facing female athletes about egg-freezing.
body: This video can not be played Should female athletes consider egg freezing? "I remember waking up in the morning and I couldn't stand. I was bent over in two. I could barely walk." For Geva Mentor - England netball's most decorated player - this was the reality of going through the process of having her eggs frozen in 2019. "I had just played in my fourth World Cup and I was at a bit of a loss in terms of where my life was going personally, as I always wanted a family," Mentor tells BBC Sport. Egg-freezing is a process in which a woman's eggs are collected, frozen and stored for potential use later in life. While Mentor's decision was a deeply personal one, the issue is becoming increasingly visible in elite sport, with both Chelsea and the Spanish Football Federation recently announcing support for players wanting to freeze their eggs. It is often presented as a way for women to help preserve their fertility and, in some cases, delay motherhood. For female athletes, whose careers often peak in the years they are most fertile, the appeal can be particularly powerful. "I wanted to go through a check-up and make sure things weren't drying up down there, so to speak, because I didn't know what impact elite sport might have had on my fertility," says Mentor. "Freezing my eggs seemed like the right thing to do at the time because [I thought] whatever happens with my journey, I'd rather use my early 30-year-old eggs than my late-30s or 40s." Mentor is one of a growing number of athletes to consider fertility preservation during their careers, but the practice remains the subject of debate and experts stress it offers no guarantee of a future pregnancy. England captain Jones calls for fertility support Mentor is widely regarded as netball's greatest ever goal keeper, winning 175 international caps. She represented England at six World Cups, winning a silver and three bronze medals, and was part of the Roses side that won Commonwealth gold in 2018. For 20 years, being an elite athlete was her every focus. However, she always knew she wanted to be a mother and worried about when that would come. At the age of 35 she decided to freeze her eggs in the hope it may help her conceive in the future. Mentor was not in a relationship at the time, and living in Melbourne. "I decided that I wanted to do it in off-season, going into pre-season, and not during the season," she says. "I thought that if anything untoward happened, I'd have that time and space to let my body recover before I'd have to sort of throw it into elite training." Mentor had regular monitoring appointments throughout the treatment. "I still trained, did pre-season," she adds. "It didn't affect me at all until I took the last reactive injection, which basically releases the eggs into position for extraction the next day." Geva Mentor retired in 2025 following a 24-year elite career Egg retrieval is performed under sedation or general anaesthetic and typically takes 15-30 minutes. Mentor says it felt like she had "43 golf balls shoved in my lower region" as the fertility drugs she had taken had stimulated a large number of eggs, which were then retrieved. "They pierced my vaginal wall 43 times, which meant that I was probably on a bit of a risk for bleeding and blood clots," she said. "One of the things that really stood out for me was when I came around and I immediately just started crying... like bawling. It was quite emotional. What you're going through, that whole process, there's a lot of a hormone change and imbalance. I guess it really just shook me. "But then I knew at the end of the day, it was an insurance policy for me." Mentor was released from hospital the same day but was unable to return to full training for two weeks as she recovered from experiencing heavy bleeding. She has since had a daughter after conceiving naturally but says she has no regrets about freezing her eggs, which remain available for her to use in the future. While many have hailed fertility support for female athletes as a major step forward, one world-leading expert in women's health says important questions still remain. Professor Kirsty Elliott-Sale, who heads the Centre for Excellence for Women in Sport at Manchester Metropolitan University, says she is "delighted for any player who will benefit" from fertility support. But she believes egg-freezing should be seen as one option among a wider package of support for female athletes, and urges those considering it to look beyond the headlines - and ask plenty of questions. "Egg-freezing is an opportunity which allows them to invest in their fertility journey - at this moment - for the future," she tells BBC Sport. "But we need to make sure that if they want to have children during their careers, that is an opportunity for them." Elliott-Sale says fertility, pregnancy and maternity provision must be as well funded as egg-freezing, so there is never a conversation that starts with: "Oh, but you froze your eggs..." She also warns that egg-freezing should not be seen as a guarantee of future motherhood. The number and quality of eggs collected can vary, some may not survive thawing, and those that do may fail to fertilise. Even when embryos develop, implantation and pregnancy are not assured. There are also unanswered questions about how treatment fits around the demands of elite sport. "One of the things that none of us know right now is how long you should take away from sport, if indeed you need to take any time away from sport to do this procedure," she says. Elliott-Sale also wants clarity about what happens after eggs have been stored. "It's one thing to fund the freezing," she says, questioning whether clubs will also pay for their storage then the treatment needed to use them. And there's an anti-doping consideration, too. title: 'I was dead for 10 minutes, but lived to tell the tale'
description: Medics in Spain raced against time to save Sandra McCartney's life after her heart stopped beating.
body: Sandra McCartney says she is lucky to be alive after going into cardiac arrest on holiday On New Year's Eve of 2019 Sandra McCartney was clinically dead for 10 minutes. She was 59 when she collapsed during a Christmas holiday in Spain, lost consciousness, stopped breathing and had no pulse or heartbeat after suffering a cardiac arrest. Sandra's life was saved when medics managed to restore a normal heart rhythm during a frantic race against time when paramedics gave her "six defibrillator shocks and five shots of adrenaline". Her life may have been turned upside down in that moment but she believes she had been living with a ticking time bomb long before that. Sandra found out that the heart attack and cardiac arrest were triggered by a life-threatening genetic condition called "familial hypercholesterolaemia" (FH). It causes high cholesterol and, if untreated, can lead to early heart attacks and heart disease. A decade after a critical health service review, has there been any change? Trust 'committed to improving facilities' with £2.5m investment in Altnagelvin ED Dáithí Mac Gabhann returns home after heart transplant The mother-of-four, from Londonderry, did not even know she had it. And she is not alone. The British Heart Foundation estimates that more than quarter of a million people in the UK have the condition, but more than two-thirds of people who have FH are never diagnosed. However, Northern Ireland has the highest detection rate in the UK. The experience is something that has left its mark on Sandra. "I had three cracked ribs from the CPR (cardio-pulmonary resuscitation) and I was gone for 10 minutes before they got me back, which is terrifying to think about." On the night she took ill, Sandra thought she had indigestion because of her "hiatus hernia" - a condition common in the over-50s, where part of the stomach moves up towards the stomach. She alerted her husband when she began to feel an acute pain followed by a tingling sensation in her right arm. As he tried to check if the local health centre was open in the middle of the night Sandra's pain left her and she started "drifting off". "I was just falling into a deep sleep and he woke me, roaring at me, and shook me," she said. She was told by a doctor she was having a major heart attack. Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) is quite a common genetic condition, affecting about 1 in every 250-500 people in the population, but many people do not know they have it. If one parent has FH, there is a 50% chance their child could have it, too. FH can be very dangerous if left untreated, as it can lead to very high cholesterol, raising the risk of heart attacks or strokes. Fifty per cent of men and 30% of women with untreated FH will develop coronary heart disease by the age of 55. The good news is FH can be diagnosed quite easily and there are treatments available. A screening service operates in Northern Ireland to provide testing for family members of people who have FH to detect as many carriers of the genes as possible. Source: Northern Ireland Chest Heart and Stroke She was ventilated for 11 days in hospital and her four children flew out to Spain as it was feared the worst might happen. "I remember nothing until day four when I was brought round but a few hours later, I was ventilated again because both my lungs collapsed," she said. "I was woken four days later but I then developed laryngeal stridor, which makes your breathing noisy and harder to do, and which is potentially life-threatening, due to being ventilated too quickly, too many times. I then had to be ventilated again. " It was not until February that she was allowed to fly home. Even then she had to use a wheelchair, as she had experienced so much muscle wastage over her time in hospital. She said it was a "horrendous," not just for her but for her husband and children. "Never in a million years did I think something like this could happen to me. "I was fit, healthy, ate really well, I had no worries about my health." When she returned home she had more problems. "I wasn't home long when I passed out one day and had to be admitted to Altnagelvin Hospital for a week. "The pandemic started soon after I was discharged so unfortunately, I didn't get any cardiac rehab which would have been so beneficial to my recovery." She has also suffered from PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and has an ICD (implantable cardioverter defibrillator) fitted which is a small electrical device because I'm at high risk of having another cardiac arrest." Sandra's heart attack and cardiac arrest continue to affect her life to this day and there are still days when she can "do very little". Even "something as simple as throwing a duvet on the bed", can leave her breathless. She has never been able to return to work, though she volunteers with NI Chest Heart and Stroke and enjoys sewing. But she is upbeat and grateful to be alive. "Not many people survive what my body put me through." All four of her children have tested clear for high blood pressure. The Belfast Health Trust operates a screening service for what it calls a "silent condition". "When someone is diagnosed with FH, their relatives are contacted and offered testing by a team of specialist nurses who cover all of Northern Ireland," a spokesperson said. "Thanks to this programme, Northern Ireland has the highest rate of identification of FH in the UK and one of the highest rates of diagnosed cases in the world." The trust said that once people are diagnosed and established on long-term treatment with standard cholesterol-lowering medications, they do not generally need further intervention beyond "periodic cholesterol checks". A cardiac arrest happens when an electrical malfunction stops the heart from beating and circulating blood to the brain and vital organs - often causing permanent brain damage within minutes and sudden death. A heart attack is not the same as a cardiac arre

title: Red squirrel project opens £250k community grant
description: Groups from around northern England and southern Scotland can bid for funding to help the creatures.
body: Red squirrel populations across Britain have dramatically declined Groups trying to protect red squirrels are being invited to bid for funding from a £250,000 pot. The Red Squirrel Recovery Network (RSRN) said it hoped to "engage people from all backgrounds" with grants of up to £500 available for smaller activities to £5,000 to support ideas with a wider reach. The project, which started in 2025, works with conservation partners and volunteer groups across Northumberland, Cumbria, Manchester, Lancashire, Merseyside and southern Scotland to raise awareness of the endangered species. In May, animal welfare group Save Our Reds said the species "still clings on" across Cumbria, Northumberland and the North Pennines but could disappear within 25 years. Red squirrel populations across Britain have dramatically declined and have been estimated at about 287,000, the RSRN said. According to Natural England, external, causes for the decline include the introduction of grey squirrels from the USA and Canada from 1876 spreading the squirrelpox virus, which is fatal to the red squirrels only. Save Our Reds said habitat loss and weak enforcement of existing protections were adding to the problem. Heather Harris, from the RSRN, said the project - which is funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund - aimed to "remind everyone of why red squirrels are so important to our heritage". "There are many older generations who remember red squirrels, but we'd also would love to hear from younger people where nature isn't as accessible for them or who haven't had the experience of seeing red squirrels," she said. The network said it wanted to support plans which helped local communities celebrate red squirrels and reconnect with nature, such as themed walks or improving spaces linked to conservation. RSRN programme manager Mike Denbury said: "From introducing children to red squirrels for the very first time to delivering larger habitat protection projects, we're keen to hear your ideas on inspiring action for nature." title: Death threats and isolation - the cost of fighting sexual violence in Iraq
description: Women say they share stories of abuse to highlight the issue, despite social pressure and safety fears.
body: "Your camera is your weapon," says Sarah Jassim, who says the videos she posts help document evidence of harassment This story contains details of sexual violence which some readers may find upsetting "Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him. The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys. "Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him." One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says. A video posted by Jassim shows a woman shouting at a man she accuses of exposing himself, then trying to open his car door Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim. "I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent." She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog. There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code. "Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred." Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to. Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation. Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing". Amal - not her real name - has been battling in court for about five years. She accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter - who was under 18 at the time - at gunpoint. She recalls her daughter's harrowing account of the incident, when she says the father walked into the girl's room and laid his weapon on her bed. She says he told her: "No-one will hear you if I kill you." Amal accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter, who was under 18 at the time Sexual abuse has long been seen as a taboo subject in Iraq. I have been in touch with many survivors who say that they prefer to hush it up, because of a potential family backlash. Others told us they were afraid to go to the police, for fear of social stigma and possible harassment. But Amal was determined to seek justice and rushed to police to report the incident. "She had lots of bruises around her wrists, as he held her hands tight. Whenever she tried to scream, he would cover her mouth with his hands," Amal says. Amal showed me medical documents, including DNA evidence, which support her account. A further demonstration of her ex-husband's cruelty came, Amal says, when she heard him tell a family member to "wash off our disgrace" if he was arrested. The expression is used in Iraq to refer to so-called honour killings - carried out in the belief that a woman has compromised a family's reputation. Amal says she believes the father threatened to put an end to his daughter's life "so the medical report would not be released and the assault would not be proven". She says her ex-husband is on the run and the court case remains open. "I fought all alone," says Amal, bursting into tears as she says her ex-husband hired several lawyers but she could not afford legal representation, and her family turned a blind eye to the situation. She no longer has any faith that a court ruling will come in her favour. "I just want him to stay out of my way forever," she says, with a sigh of despair. Amal's daughter is more fortunate than some women who have experienced domestic sexual abuse in Iraq, as she has a safe place to live. Many survivors have no independent income and nowhere to go. Iraq has very few shelters for abused women. Those we know of were established by an organisation co-founded by Yanar Mohammed, an internationally recognised women's rights advocate. Last March she was murdered outside her house in Baghdad by armed men. The perpetrators are still unknown. Experts working for the UN Human Rights Council wrote in April that Mohammed had been receiving death threats and online abuse for years, which were "believed to come from extremist religious militia". Hanaa Edwar (left) shared a photo of her with Yanar Mohammed, taken, she recalls, just two days before the activist was killed Activists repeatedly told us that targeted attacks on their colleagues have been on the rise in recent years. Hanaa Edwar, another prominent women's rights activist, says she saw Mohammed just two days before she was killed. She says she has also been threatened. "There are no laws, no protection, and no justice for women in Iraq," she tells me. "The problem in Iraq is not that women stay silent. It is that when they speak, very little in the system is built to listen

title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
description: An in-depth look at the key polling, races and issues ahead of an election that will define Trump’s final two years as president.
body: Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out. Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress. Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome. Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent. One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s. It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%. Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate. But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years. The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them. Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November. But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner. The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party. Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House. Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three. The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them. Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years. Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way. Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate. But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats. They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent. And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally. What would Democratic control of Congress mean for Trump? Anthony Zurcher: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters. The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US. The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation. Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration. Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years. Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system. Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected. One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage. At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (£303m). On top of that, the Republicans also had more th

title: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
description: In his first interview since being forced from his post, Gen Syrskyi speaks about Ukraine's future in the war.
body: Gen Syrskyi lost his job over the summer after a public disagreement with the defence minister Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has said in an interview with the BBC. Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer. He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces. He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses. Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added. Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified. UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes, external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026. He says this difference in death toll – as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts – accounts for the current stalemate at the front. In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised." The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports, external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took. Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year. But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives. Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43. Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies. Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed. Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia. But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses. Syrskyi pictured after his appointment as Ukraine's commander-in-chief in early 2024 Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk. Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops. Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army. In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued. One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity". "In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained. The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said. He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come". He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said. Such technologies can give a new life

title: Barbells and beats: This is the new student night out
description: Students hit the gym with a DJ on the decks and no alcohol in sight.
body: DJ Esco-bar said it was the first event of its kind he had played at From pecs to decks, students in Nottingham are trying a new workout that turns a gym into a club night. There's no alcohol involved... just high-energy drinks and pure adrenaline. Friends Phoebe Constanta and Ella Birkwood, second-year students at Nottingham Trent University, are among those trying the new night that combines pumping iron with pumping tunes. They said they were looking for "a new gym to try out" and decided to go along to Castle After Dark, a new alcohol-free student event at a city centre gym. Phoebe, 20, said: "We found it really interesting that it's a night event, but it's not based around alcohol and the club. It's about wellbeing and interacting with people your age." Ella added: "I'm loving it." Second-year students Phoebe Constanta and Ella Birkwood say they enjoyed the night At its launch event, which kicked off at 22:00 BST on a Thursday night, popular club bangers could be heard blasting from outdoor speakers as students from across the area, dressed for a workout, queued to get into Castle Gym in Maid Marian Way. As the doors opened, they were met with a live DJ, pre-workout nutritional shots and free reign of the equipment - with not a drop of alcohol in sight. Most recent data suggests young people drink less than other generations. About 39% of men and 31% of women aged 16 to 24, who responded to the NHS Health Survey for England for 2024, said they had not drunk alcohol in the past year, compared to about 24% of adults overall. Gym owner Luke Willmott said no alcohol was allowed on site Gym owner Luke Willmott said he believed the event was the first of its kind. "This is the night out where you feel better in the morning," he said. "You don't even have to be a student to know you feel absolutely terrible the next day after indulging in alcohol and partying. "This is definitely something that's going to catch on because you get all of the partying and all of the happiness and energy, but none of the hangover. "Health and wellbeing is at the forefront. Even if you've consumed alcohol before, you will not be coming into the premises. We've got a really strict policy on that." Fortune Madu believes there could be a market for more student gym nights Among those in attendance was 21-year-old Fortune Madu, an economics student at the University of Derby. "They're bringing the vibes. They've got the competition. I like competition in gyms, so that's really good," he said. "They've obviously got the music, as you can hear in the background. The aesthetic's really nice, so yeah, I'm having fun so far." Talia Miller and Chah Madina are both studying creative writing Roommates Talia Miller, 24 and Chah Madina are both students at Nottingham Trent University. "I think it's definitely a cool concept," said Talia. "We were talking about how this is showing people what their gym has to offer while making it something fun, getting to know people and just seeing the area." Chah said: "It's been really good. I've been trying like every single equipment. I'm role-playing being a member." Luke acknowledges his gym "wasn't built for students" and "not cheap", with typical membership options starting from £65 a month. He said the nights were a way to "include them... and not alienate our current members". "An event like this is really cool to be able to ringfence a time for them [students] to be able to come in and enjoy the facility," he said. Nottingham-based DJ Esco-bar typically plays club events and festivals. He told the BBC in his 15-year DJ career, he had never played at a student night in a gym. "It's lit," he said. "Vibes on vibes. It's crazy inside there. "I feel like it's good to get to know everyone, all the students as well as a DJ. "All the students are happy with the music, so it's a win-win for me." Luke said with 250 students in attendance, the response to the launch event had exceeded his "wildest expectations". "This is definitely going to be a staple," he added.
