title: Watch: BBC's Orla Guerin travels with Yemen's southern national security forces
description: Orla Guerin travelled through Yemen, with forces loyal to its internationally recognised government, to a remote desert battlefield where Houthi rebels were dislodged just days ago.
body: This video can not be played On Yemen's desert battlefield a war with global consequences is being waged. The BBC's Orla Guerin saw the impact firsthand when she travelled with southern national security forces to frontline positions where they've been battling Houthi fighters. Yemen's civil war over expanses of desert land has had devastating consequences for civilians and fighters. One military hospital in Aden reported more than 50 casualties arriving in a single day – many with gunshot wounds, and several needing amputations. title: Watch: US man eyes pumpkin world record after fifth contest win
description: Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin from Minnesota to Half Moon Bay, California where he won the annual event.
body: This video can not be played A five-time US giant pumpkin contest winner tells the BBC he'd "love" to break the world record for a second time. Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin from Minnesota to Half Moon Bay, California, for the annual pumpkin weighing event. His whopping gourd took home the prize, tipping the scales at 2,389 pounds (1,083kg). But Gienger says he's eyeing off a different prize – the world record title – which was set in England's south coast last week with a squash weighing in at 2,857 pounds (1,300kg). As a previous holder of the world-record mantle, Gienger says he's focused on the challenge ahead. Watch: US man eyes pumpkin world record after fifth contest win. title: BBC shelves plans for new Archers studio as part of cost-cutting
description: The drama has been recording in Birmingham for 75 years, making it the world's longest running soap opera.
body: The BBC has shelved plans to build a new bespoke studio for The Archers in Birmingham as part of its wider drive to cut costs, opening up the possibility it could be recorded outside of the city for the first time. The world's longest-running soap opera, The Archers has been recording in the West Midlands city for 75 years. The BBC had initially pledged to build the show a new studio in the Tea Factory, the corporation's new hub in Digbeth, central Birmingham. The broadcaster said it was "currently assessing the BBC's existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands". "We recognise and value The Archers' long-standing relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme's future," the statement added. The BBC Radio 4 drama, set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge, first aired nationally on 1 January 1951. It celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year. Mayor of the West Midlands Richard Parker said he was "very disappointed by news that the BBC plans to move its production out of the city". "The Archers was born in Birmingham and is a key part of our broadcasting heritage," he wrote in a statement shared to Facebook. "We have the talent and the facilities here. There is no good reason why we should lose a programme that has called Birmingham home for decades." Parker said he would meet Director General Matt Brittin later this week to "discuss every available option" to keep The Archers in Birmingham. "The BBC promised to invest and support our regions, this is entirely the opposite of that," he said. A spokesperson for the BBC said they were looking to find a solution that would "deliver significant savings whilst also maintaining The Archers' high production standards." They confirmed that the series' production team is still set to move "as planned" to Digbeth in early 2028, but, "after careful consideration", they would no longer be building a new recording studio in the Tea Factory. The statement also noted that The Archer's recording schedule meant cast members are in the studio approximately eight days a month, with many actors travelling to the recordings as they live in locations across the UK. "The impact on the cast will be fully considered as part of our assessment process," the spokesperson said, emphasising that "no final decision has been made". title: Military police prevented from following evidence in SAS murder probe, inquiry hears
description: Military police investigator tells an inquiry that the probe into suspected murders was "dictated" from above.
body: The inquiry is chaired by Lord Justice Sir Charles Haddon-Cave A military police investigator has criticised a murder probe into alleged SAS executions, claiming senior officers prevented his team from following the evidence. Delme Williams, who investigated allegations against one SAS unit, told a public inquiry: "It was not a standard investigation where investigators were making decisions based on where the evidence led them." He added that he remained convinced members of British special forces should have been criminally charged. It is the first time the inquiry, which is examining allegations the SAS committed murders in Afghanistan that were covered up, has heard from those involved in military police investigations into special forces operations. Williams, who served as deputy senior investigative officer for Operation Northmoor which looked at 11 SAS operations, told the inquiry on Monday that the course of the investigation was being "dictated" to his team from above. He added that he questioned whether the senior Royal Military Police officer in charge, known as the Gold commander, was being "influenced to close the investigation". Williams recalled an occasion during Operation Northmoor when investigators were discussing photographs of one of the 11 SAS operations they were investigating for suspected murder. The operation involved the fatal shooting of nine people at a home in Nad Ali district, Helmand Province, in February 2011. The youngest person killed was aged 14. Williams told the inquiry that, based on his experience as a seasoned crime-scene investigator, he wanted to show the images to a forensics expert. Operation Northmoor investigators suspected those shot had been killed unlawfully, and the photographs showed bullet marks low to the ground, which appeared to undermine the SAS account that those killed had been standing and fired at British forces first, before the SAS returned fire. Williams told the public inquiry: "A picture paints a thousand words - photos are ideal evidence." The military police officer said he was "quickly shut down in an abrupt matter" by the Gold commander and when he tried to push back, his senior officer pulled rank and it would have been "insubordinate" to go any further. He said he believed, to this day, the photographs should have examined by an expert. BBC Panorama investigated the same incident and travelled to Helmand to visit the site of the shooting. An RMP investigator confirmed to the BBC that they had seen photographs from the scene and that the bullet mark patterns had raised alarm among the Operation Northmoor team. "You can see why we were concerned," the investigator said. "Bullet marks on the walls so low to the ground appeared to undermine the special forces' version of events." Panorama's team examined what appeared to be bullet holes from the raid, still visible, which were clustered together on the walls low to the ground. The BBC showed photographs from the scene to forensics and ballistics experts, who said that the clusters suggested multiple rounds had been fired downward from above, and did not appear indicative of a firefight. This supported the version of events put forward by bereaved family members of some who those were killed. Those relatives have told the BBC those killed were all unarmed civilians who were shot in their beds, and that appears to corroborate the RMP investigators' suspicions. The BBC reported in 2022 evidence from another Operation Northmoor investigator, who told Panorama: "I believe there was pressure from above to shut down the investigation. It became increasingly clear to me that it didn't matter what evidence we were able to gather, these cases were never going to be allowed to go to court." At the time, the Ministry of Defence said the incidents had been subjected to "extensive and independent investigation" by the RMP, and no prosecutions had resulted. Operation Northmoor, set up by the RMP's serious crime team, was investigating 45 killings by an SAS squadron in 2011 during a single tour of Afghanistan. The military police officer told the inquiry the investigation team thought the operational photographs could be important evidence and were looked at "in quite some detail", and the dismissal of this evidence was an example of the way in which the investigation was being run. Williams told the inquiry there were "outside forces" that seemed to him to be directing the course of the investigation. "I do recall a general feeling that inquiries were being stopped too soon and that there was no appetite... to pursue all lines of inquiry or for anyone to be referred for prosecution." During the course of his sworn testimony, Williams was shown a number of internal military documents by the inquiry's lawyers. These records showed it was "confirmed Op NORTHMOOR must end" during an RMP meeting of senior staff in September 2017, while his team were still in the process of gathering evidence. Williams said he was "not surprised" but that criminal investigations "should never be guided by an end date" imposed on them. The military police are supposed to be independent from the wider armed forces, but Williams claimed he was shown a briefing note for a meeting between senior military police officers and the deputy chief of the Army at the end of 2017, which set out the intention to close Northmoor. He remarked he was "surprised to see it written down" but it made sense of the "pressure" he felt the investigation was under. Williams said he still believed individuals should have been referred for prosecution based on the evidence they had found. The inquiry also heard that the former head of the British Army, Sir Nick Carter, asked the RMP to cut the staff working on the murder probe to 25, less than a quarter of the team working on Operation Northmoor in 2016. title: One dead and several hurt after rollercoaster incident at Six Flags
description: Aerial footage at the park after the incident shows a stuck rollercoaster with riders being helped off.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Aerial footage shows riders stuck on Six Flags roller coaster One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, an amusement park in the US state of Georgia. The Cobb County Police Department said it was investigating the fatality at the park, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta, according to the BBC's news partner CBS. Police did not specify what ride was involved, but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers. Six Flags Over Georgia said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones." Officials have not said how the person was killed. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials. Witnesses told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride, accounts that the BBC has not verified. Local outlet 11Alive quoted, external a witness saying the man fell from the rollercoaster on to the roof of a haunted house attraction. A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately, and they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident. Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation. The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five. Monday's death is the latest of several at the Georgia amusement park, according to personal injury attorneys. The fatalities include a 45-year-old man dying from an apparent heart attack after riding the Goliath in 2006, said the Doan Law Firm. Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico. The incident comes just weeks after one of its parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride. Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do". title: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027
description: The IMF report comes as final preparations are being made to the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burham.
body: The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said. The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain". Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget. Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October. Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money. But in its economic forecast, the IMF projected that the UK would have a sharp fall in borrowing and the lowest annual rate of borrowing of all G7 countries - the group of the world's most advanced economies - over the next five years. The UK is estimated to have the lowest annual deficit - the difference between what the government spends and brings in through taxes in a year - by 2031, suggesting it thinks public spending will be cut in coming years. The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels. The reversal of downgrades to economic forecasts made at the start of the US-Iran war, mean the UK is expected to have the second-fasted growing economy in the G7 along with Germany. But growth is estimated to slow in 2027 to 1.2% due to higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weighing on household spending and business investment. Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience". When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks. Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget. On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to make "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes". "The challenge of continuing to bring down borrowing must be paired with the pressing need for fresh cost of living support to help families facing a difficult winter ahead," the think tank said. Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it". Burnham has pledged to create "good growth in every postcode" as part of his plans to giving nations and regions more control, but his strategy has faced criticism inside his own party. The IMF said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices, with inflation expected to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England's 2% target in 2027 at 2.8%. The Bank itself has predicted inflation could rise above 4% at the beginning of next year - making it more likely that interest rates will rise. Healey is expected to meet with other finance ministers at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday to discuss how the economic impact of the Middle East and European conflicts could be limited. The IMF said the global economy had shown a "remarkable capacity to absorb shocks" not just from the current Middle East conflict, but also from the Covid pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. title: Bumble shares soar after report dating firm in $1bn takeover talks
description: The jump pushed Bumble's stock market valuation to more than $580m but that is still far below their peak of more than $14bn.
body: Bumble founder Whitney Wolfe Herd Shares in dating app company Bumble soared by almost 50% on Monday after a report that it is in advanced talks to be bought for around $1bn (£757m). Technology holding company Ithaca could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based firm as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after listing on the Nasdaq in 2021. Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder. Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers, book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner. I've seen her name and photo - but we can't talk before the date. Will it work out? title: Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again
description: For the first time since the UK left the EU, we have a prime minister who will "unflinchingly" debate Brexit, says the BBC's political editor Chris Mason.
body: The Brexit debate is back. For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about. I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative election victory in 2015, with the party's promise in its manifesto that year to offer "a straight in-out referendum on our membership of the European Union by the end of 2017." Then there was the then Prime Minister David Cameron's negotiation with the European Union to try to secure what he saw as a better deal and then the referendum itself on Thursday, 23 June 2016. And that, you will remember, was merely the start, as years of wrangling began. Two general elections came and went in 2017 and 2019 and it took the two prime ministers after David Cameron, first Theresa May and then Boris Johnson, before the UK left the European Union at 23:00 on Friday, 31 January 2020. Little wonder perhaps that by that point, almost irrespective of someone's views on the topic, there was an appetite to talk about something else. Anything else. Political parties picked up that vibe and while their long standing instincts on the EU were there to see if you scratched the surface, there was minimal desire to extemporise about them any time soon. With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street. He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons. Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case. First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement. Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum. In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit. "This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said. Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago. "They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost, external, a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph. The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy. Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth. He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success. And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum. "I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was. In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere. A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference. His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt – calling the prime minister "a liar." The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary, external "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power". This video can not be played Watch: PM says there is 'clear' evidence of Russian interference in 2016 Brexit campaign And so a debate resumes about the difference between attempted interference, interference and successful interference. But the key point is this: for the first time since the UK left the European Union, we now have a prime minister who is willing to unflinchingly debate Brexit: whether it is working, how it is working, how to improve it, and if it's proved to be a failure. In so doing he hopes he can tap into public sentiment which opinion polls suggest a perception among a majority that leaving the European Union hasn't turned out how many might have hoped., external On top of this, he hopes to lure pro Europeans broadly on the Left who may recently have supported the Liberal Democrats, the Green parties of both England and Wales and Scotland, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru towards Labour. That is the political logic from the government's point of view, for now at least. And as for where all of this leads – well, good question. In the coming weeks, months and perhaps years, there may be a Back to the Future vibe to our political debate. A splash of familiarity, as a conversation about the relationship we have with our nearest neighbours resumes. title: Hundreds more prisoners to be freed in second phase of early release scheme
description: Second tranche of prisoners will include those serving up to two and a half years for crimes.
body: An inmate walks free from HMP Brixton earlier this month, in the first wave of the government's early release scheme About 650 more offenders will leave jails in England and Wales early on Tuesday in the second phase of the government's plan to tackle the prison population crisis. The group will include offenders serving up to two and a half years for crimes. Under the new rules, they are leaving jail after serving a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than half. The second wave of releases comes as the government takes its plan to radically overhaul criminal courts back to Parliament - but also as probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to a strike over pay and workload. Some 700 offenders left jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months. Monday's second stage begins the process of releasing batches of offenders serving increasingly long sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years. Napo, the probation service union, said the releases have put enormous strain on its members, who are charged with monitoring the offenders in the community. Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence. On Tuesday, the union's members will meet to discuss next week's vote, which could lead to strike action. Probation officers have been offered a 5% pay rise by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), while it had demanded 12% as part of a plan to make up for loss of earnings caused by cuts from 2010. The MoJ says the offer is fair and has been accepted by two other unions and is twinned with a £700m investment in probation to recruit 1,300 extra officers and the roll-out of AI tools to cut the workload of monitoring offenders. While the second phase of prison releases gets under way, the government is bringing its criminal court reform plan back before MPs, after announcing a week ago that it had abandoned the most controversial element of it. The revised plan drops proposals for a new form of Crown Court where a judge alone, sitting without a jury of ordinary people, would reach a verdict against suspects facing up to three years in prison. However, jury trials will still be scrapped for the most complex and long fraud cases - and another 5,500 trials will be kept in the lower magistrates court by ending a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial. The government says it will expand the use of so-called "blitz" or "short trial" courts after pilots have shown that grouping similar cases together can speed up their progression through the courts - cutting backlogs. One of the pilots at the Old Bailey led to the London backlog of 500 cases concerning assaults on emergency workers being cut in half over the summer. A major review of criminal courts by former appeal judge Sir Brian Leveson recommended more virtual hearings for defendants to slash wasted time bringing them to and from cells. The government has now ordered pilots for defendants to appear direct from police cells. On Monday, the government announced it had accepted more than 150 of his 180 recommendations to modernise the criminal courts. It has rejected his advice to retain a restriction on volunteer magistrates that means they can only jail an offender for 12 months. Under the government's plan magistrates will have the power to jail for up to two years - the aim being to keep more cases out of Crown Court, to help clear backlogs. title: The Papers: 'Burnham ready to sign new EU deal' and 'Hand of Gord'
description: Many of today's papers cover the PM's comments on Brexit and the Daily Star writes of an alleged exorcism.
body: According to The i Paper, Andy Burnham is "ready to sign new EU deal next month - as he attacks Brexit 'damage'". Speaking ahead of a long-awaiting EU-UK summit on 20 November, the prime minister told MPs on Monday that a "deal is on the table", which would cover things like food and drink, carbon emissions trading, and under-30s migration. The paper says the under-30s migration is likely to be the most contentious part of any agreement, and negotiations on this "are still taking place". The Independent paraphrases Burnham as saying "I'll let voters decide to rejoin Europe". It also carries a picture of actor Russell Brand, who has appeared in court for the start of his rape and sexual assault trial. Burnham's statement that Britain's relationship with the EU is "not good enough" also leads the Guardian, as it says he promises "serious dialogue" over the UK's relationship with the bloc. Elsewhere, it reports that there will be a security review for high-profile public figures, including politicians and members of the royal family, after Ann Widdecombe's death. The Daily Express says Burnham is making a "bid to betray Brexit vote". It also bids a "sad farewell to D-Day hero Henry Rice at 100". The Daily Mail writes that Burnham is "in retreat over Russia Brexit 'lies'." The prime minister had said that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum but, it writes, "in an embarrassing U-turn", now the PM has "admitted he has no evidence". The "Hand of Gord" leads the Daily Star. It says that former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown "attended an exorcism to help Raith Rovers sign player". Brown has denied the accusations, with a spokesperson telling the paper: "Gordon is always happy to do what he can to support Raith Rovers, but he's never attended an exorcism." "Horrifying" declares the Daily Mirror as Reform "bigwig" Robert Jenrick has said he would order the Royal Marines to use "lethal force" against migrants. The Mirror calls it a "new low in British politics". "Homes under the shammers" is the headline of the Sun, as it says Manchester City footballers are "being used to flog a £3bn Abu Dhabi luxury housing development". This is happening, it writes, "despite the furore over the cheating scandal". The Financial Times covers comments from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in its top story, who says Russia has been breaking a ceasefire declared by US President Donald Trump on energy targets. Meanwhile, it reports that hedge funds and banks have "hit out" at "Burnham's bid to ban non-compete clauses in work contracts". "We'd be ready to fight tonight" Nato's Supreme Allied Commander Europe has said, in what the Metro calls a "stark warning to Putin". General Grynkewich has said Nato would destroy "anything and everything" used to assault a member nation. The Times highlights a call to "cut screen time in class 'for sake of pupil health'" which comes from leading clinicians. The paper says experts "blame devices for stunting development". It also reports that disability benefits for 120,000 teens "cost taxpayers £1bn a year". Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: NHS staff get 'landmark' payout over gas exposure
description: The settlement follows the largest group legal action brought by midwives in the UK, says union.
body: Maternity unit staff were not told for more than a year that testing had revealed their workplace was breaching safety limits for nitrous oxide NHS maternity staff who were exposed to excessive levels of nitrous oxide have received "landmark" payouts totalling £735,000, a union said. Basildon Hospital in Essex settled claims from 121 staff, including 85 midwives, who took legal action after reporting fatigue, anxiety, headaches and "brain fog" after the gas levels breached safety limits. The Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust said it had apologised to staff. The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said it was the largest group legal action ever brought by midwives in the UK. The gas, also known as Entonox, is used to provide temporary pain relief for women giving birth. The staff members behind the claims were found to have breathed it in over long shifts for months and years. According to an internal report from Basildon Hospital, some members of staff were exposed to levels up to 30 times higher than the legal workplace exposure limit between 2021 and 2023. They were also not told for 16 months about test results commissioned by the trust that showed their exposure had breached safety thresholds. The legal action was first revealed by the BBC in May. The trust settled the claims after admitting its staff had been exposed to dangerously high levels of the gas. Gill Walton, from the RCM, said the settlement should "make every NHS employer sit up and take notice" NHS Resolution, which manages legal claims and compensation cases on behalf of the NHS in England, confirmed the payouts. A spokesman said: "We can confirm that 121 claims have been settled for a total of £735,000. Some other claims remain outstanding. We are unaware of any larger group of claims brought by midwives." One claim has yet to be settled according to the RCM. Daniel Poet, from Thompsons Solicitors, who represented the workers, said: "We are proud to have secured compensation for our clients, but they should never have been put at risk in the first place." "The trust knew about the dangers in 2021, but staff weren't told until the following year and it took another year for safety measures to be introduced. That delay is unacceptable," he added. The Mid and South Essex NHS Trust said it acknowledged that it should have acted faster Gill Walton, the RCM chief executive and general secretary, said: "For years, midwives at Basildon were breathing in nitrous oxide at dangerous levels while they cared for women and babies. "Even once the problem had been discovered, it was more than a year before staff were told. That is simply not acceptable and no midwife should ever be treated that way," she said. She continued: "This is a landmark settlement for our members and it should make every NHS employer sit up and take notice. If you don't protect your staff - the RCM will hold you to account". The RCM has also written to every NHS trust in England to make them aware of the risks of the gas and said it had also "raised concerns about the trust's lack of action" with the Health and Safety Executive (HSE). The RCM has since worked directly with the HSE to update and improve guidance on the use of Entonox. Louise Crosby, the chief nursing and quality officer for the Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said: "We have acknowledged that we should have acted faster to address the issues and have apologised to staff. "Since the incident we have learnt lessons, and as part of this, we have improved our oversight of the monitoring of medical gases across the maternity unit at Basildon Hospital." The trust added that it had installed scavenger equipment at the maternity unit and that women could have confidence that it is safe to use Entonox. Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? title: I lost my hair to MS treatment - now my wigs are worn by Naomi Campbell and Serena Williams
description: Antonia Okonma Shittu's wig business was launched after a shock diagnosis, and she now wants to help other women feel their best.
body: Antonia with model Naomi Campbell, who is one of her clients When Antonia Okonma Shittu was told she had multiple sclerosis (MS) and would be using a wheelchair within the year, she was in denial. The 26-year-old, who was in between acting jobs and working in a call centre, said the diagnosis was a "massive turning point" in her life. "It does really make you think about what you want to do in life," she said. She looked back to what she enjoyed doing as a child - styling hair - and decided to use the shock of the diagnosis to spur her on to turn her passion into a business. Antonia, who grew up on a council estate in west London, bought two wigs and went door to door selling them from the boot of her car. Antonia with American actress Niecey Nash Almost two decades later, she is now a multi-million-pound brand owner, with high-profile clients including tennis icon Serena Williams, model Naomi Campbell and actress Niecey Nash. She even won a Black British Business Award last week. Antonia, now 44, still struggles with her health, having also received diagnoses of Graves' disease - an autoimmune condition - and heart failure, but hopes her experience running a hair empire while fitting in hospital appointments can inspire other women. Antonia says she saw a gap in the market when she was surrounded by "terrible" wigs while working in TV and film, including in the ITV series Bad Girls two decades ago. "Women wanted natural-looking wigs and they just weren't available. They looked like helmets!" Antonia set up a Facebook page and began advertising on Gumtree. "I had very limited resources. I didn't have any investors behind me. I come from very humble beginnings." Her experience dealing with MS has helped her success, she says. Antonia lost her hair when she underwent chemotherapy following a bone marrow transplant, so she knows what it is like to be "completely bald". This made her relate more deeply to her customers, she explains, as she understands the loss of control some women feel when they lose their hair. "I didn't feel like myself," she says, "but being able to put on a wig that looks something close to how your hair was, or the look you used to have, it's as though you can feel like yourself again." When she sees a woman put a wig on and her "whole face lights up", it can be "very, very rewarding". "When we feel good about ourselves...we're more confident, we can achieve more. I felt like I was changing the world, one person at a time." Antonia experienced hair loss after undergoing chemotherapy While Antonia's business, A-List Lace Hair, has grown from strength to strength, with salons in London and New York, she has been dealing with the impact of her health conditions. She struggles with fatigue due to her MS and uses a wheelchair, but says this has not stopped her success. Instead, it has simply changed the way she has run her business. "I used to feel that being a good entrepreneur was being able to do as much as I can myself," Antonia said. "Due to my health challenges, there are days where I literally can't feel my legs, they feel like jelly, there's days where I'm completely exhausted after sleeping, I wake up completely shattered." This has forced her to "trust other people and gain strength in building a team". Antonia says she wants to remain open about her health to inspire other women in business As a woman in business, being in a wheelchair can sometimes make Antonia feel "smaller" as people often have to look down at her at industry events. "People are often surprised when I start speaking about my business, as though they're thinking 'how have you accomplished all of this in a wheelchair?'" Antonia, who has three young children, says that being underestimated can be a good thing, and she wants to remain open about her health to inspire other women. She says she used to feel "weak" because of her disability, but now feels she has gained "so much strength" from sharing her experience online. Asked what she would say to another woman who may fear her age, disability or health could get in the way of success, she says: "I would encourage them to just start." "You might not have control over your health, you might not know what tomorrow is going to bring, and you might not have all the resources. But start with what you do have, and let's see what could happen next." title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
description: Meeting travellers' expectations could be challenging, experts warn.
body: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time? The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt. Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night. This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers. Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after. Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working. Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership. August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be. So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement? South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far. At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable." SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands. But how much of this was due to nationalisation? The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems. But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents. Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages. TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations. A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do. So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August. It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over. Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff. But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England. "The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers." Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats. But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working? "I think it's completely hopeless to try and do that assessment over such a short period," Stephen Glaister, a former chair of regulator the Office of Rail and Road who is now emeritus professor of transport and infrastructure at Imperial College London. He thinks a decade is needed to assess the impact of nationalisation. The government argues that official data suggests publicly owned train operators are performing better on punctuality and cancellations overall than those still under DfT contracts to private operators. Experts point out that whoever is running the passenger trains, some limitations remain. Many delays happen because infrastructure, like signals, fails. There's only so much capacity on the existing network. And getting better trains or more staff can take years. title: Boardroom feud tests trusted Indian business empire
description: The dispute raises questions about the Indian conglomerate's governance, succession plans and future.
body: Noel Tata, the chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran, the Tata Sons chairman Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt. When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata." She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software. But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control? A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate. At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran. Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions. But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting. "When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC. While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges. Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public. The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website. Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together". Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy. For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust. Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain. "Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant. Ratan Tata's death in 2024 drew tributes from across the country While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said. "This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says. The group has been traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution. The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions. Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions. Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies. The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance. Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint. Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour. Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades. In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people. At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
description: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills are promised better regulation of the sector by the government.
body: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government. Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect. Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition". In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres. The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need. Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility. A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350. But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation. The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector. Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year. "We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector." Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government. "Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said. He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre. "Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said. He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action. Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically." Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers. However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland. Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate. It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel". title: I earn £120,000 a year making social media videos go viral
description: Social media "clippers" make short, vertical videos that appear on the likes of Instagram and TikTok.
body: Eknoor Singh's successful social media video clips include one of popstar Dua Lipa Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year. The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral. "The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says. The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first. He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms. The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible. With clippers able to earn up to $3 (£2.30) per 1,000 views across platforms, it can be very lucrative if a particular clip does take off. Singh says he got hooked on clipping last year when he made $300 from posting a short video of popstar Dua Lipa on Instagram. "I was like, 'OK, this is a lot of money for simply posting a video.' I instantly knew how lucrative it could be." Now he says he is earning "at least £10,000 a month". He adds that he looks for clips that are funny, quick to watch and engaging, such as a short video he made in May of Sabrina Carpenter's reaction to having the tails of her dress stepped on at the Met Gala in New York. Singh did not reveal who the client was. Singh's clip of Sabrina Carpenter went viral For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping. He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests. Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says. Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says. Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world". Ethan Weems says the income helps him continue to work from home Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick. The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max. For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs. That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos. In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips. "The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions". Eknoor Singh says he can make clips anywhere with just his mobile and a good internet connection Evan Stanfield, the founder and boss of Clipping Culture, is himself just 21. He set up the business last year after dropping out of the University of Kansas. Stanfield says that the website connects brands to more than 340,000 clippers from all over the world. He has a simple theory for the popularity of short videos: "People's attention spans are getting shorter and shorter." He adds that making the clips is a young person's game because "they're most of the consumers of short-form videos". Back in London, Eknoor Singh says he is "kind of clipping non-stop", wherever he is. "I could be anywhere. I could go on holiday and make money." I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree. title: Coventry announce themselves back in the big time
description: Coventry climb out of the relegation zone after ending their 25-year wait for a top-flight goal and victory in front of their own fans.
body: Coventry scorer Jack Rudoni paid tribute to his grandma, in hospital after a heart attack last week The last time Coventry won at home in the Premier League former Spice Girl Emma Bunton was top of the charts with 'What Took You So Long?' The title could not be more fitting as the Sky Blues ended their 25-year wait for a top-flight goal and victory in front of their own fans. Baby Spice's song may not live long in the memory but Coventry's thumping win over Newcastle will stick with the home supporters. Jack Rudoni's penalty, Sidiki Cherif's first Sky Blues goal and late strikes from Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni lifted them out of the relegation zone in style. Level on points with Manchester United after six games and out of the drop zone following successive wins, Frank Lampard's men have announced themselves in the top flight again. This video can not be played Coventry get a statement win against Newcastle United Coventry backed up their victory at Nottingham Forest before the international break, scoring four goals in the top flight for the first time since a 4-1 win over Sheffield Wednesday in May 2000. Those around the Sky Blues' training ground at Ryton feel that, if they are competitive over the next seven games, they will have a platform for survival. A trip to Tottenham and the visit of Fulham - both winless - come next, with games against Sunderland, Everton, Crystal Palace, Leeds and Ipswich to take them into December. "It's big and we have to tap into that in a good way, in a humble way," said Lampard, whose side are now 14th. "We have to be excited and I'm seeing players in my eyes that are developing quite quickly. "A lot of players had low Premier League minutes, or zero Premier League minutes - Jack Rudoni, [Brandon] Thomas Asante, [Ephron] Mason-Clark, a lot of them. "So is it human nature in the first few games we've had two top teams in the league (Arsenal and Manchester City) and we've had Brighton and we've gone: 'hmm, it's not easy here'. "This [win] gives good confidence, so it's the balance of confidence against overconfidence. But it's great when you have a template of feeling when you get a result of that level." It can be a defining six weeks for Lampard's men after a resounding, if not perfect, win against Newcastle. Coventry's previous home games had seen them fall to a 1-0 defeat by fellow promoted side Hull before a 5-0 thumping by Brighton. Sandwiched in the middle was a 3-1 loss to Aston Villa in the Carabao Cup, meaning it was imperative they found form at the CBS Arena. "We're going to be a relative underdog in pretty much every game," added Lampard. "So we have to maximise everything and be on the limit and I thought we were on the limit in loads of ways. "They need to keep their feet on the ground because the next one's tough and the one after that will be tough. "But we look like a team that [will make it] hard for teams to come here. That's the feeling we haven't quite had in our first CBS games this season." Striker Sidiki Cherif scored on his first Premier League start for Coventry Lampard handed a first Premier League start to Cherif after his summer move from Fenerbahce and the teenager repaid the faith. "We've got a lot of belief in Sidi, a big signing for the club," said Lampard, after inflicting a second successive 4-1 away defeat for the Magpies. "He's very respectful but there's a hunger that flicks on when he goes on to the training pitch and in game. I felt it from our first meeting and I've seen it in training, he wants to train and do well. "Sometimes you don't realise he's 19. He'll be disappointed with the one he missed and I've said to him it's no problem because that's good. You get there, you get hungry, you go again. He's got that little edge to him in a good way." At 19 years and 301 days old, Cherif is Coventry's youngest Premier League goalscorer since Robbie Keane against Middlesbrough in April 2000 (19y 282d). He is also the first player to score a Premier League goal from outside the box for the Sky Blues since David Thompson struck against Newcastle in January 2001. His crisp finish, though a forest of defenders, was a first in his fourth appearance for Coventry, having already won the early penalty. Coventry scored 97 goals as they won the Championship last season and the ruthless nature of their finishing was a reminder of their striking power. With Hadji Wright still out with a serious thigh injury, much of the goalscoring burden will fall on £20m Cherif, who was not even born the last time Coventry were in the Premier League. Lampard said: "Sidi has played in European competition with Fenerbahce, so there is something about him that hopefully feels like he belongs on the level. "There's something about him I think is a bit special." title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
description: "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months," a local tells the BBC.
body: Batam's reservoirs are under pressure as the island aims to be a digital hub "Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans. There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating. "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC. People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said. Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres. But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres. This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub. Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater. But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water. "Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. "We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds. Amgry Batam residents protesting over water shortage A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure. People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources. While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying - engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water. Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank. It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming. But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño. Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs. Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest. "The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning." Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements. A view of the data centres inside Batam's Nongsa Digital Park Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC. Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry. Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere. Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions. Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume. Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors - from the US, China, Australia, Singapore - because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes. A data centre under construction in Nongsa Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres - around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households. In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory". By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates. title: Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?
description: After every round of Premier League matches this season, Troy Deeney gives us his team of the week. Do you agree with his choices?
body: After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week. Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page. Walter Benitez (Crystal Palace): His save from Liam Delap's effort, when Delap smashed the ball into his face, is the turning point of why Palace ended up winning that game. If that goes in, it is simply game over. Ferdi Kadioglu (Brighton): He makes a massive block in the second half, which would have made it 1-1, and if the floodgates open it would be a problem. He is not known for his defensive skills, but he was great. Jefferson Lerma (Crystal Palace): A centre-midfielder playing at centre-back. He scored a goal, made some big tackles, and was also was able to play out from the back, being the catalyst for Palace, so he goes in as well. James Justin (Leeds): I know he loves playing against Arsenal, but the transformation he has had from when he was at Leicester to Leeds - the ability to play right wing-back, right centre-back. Everything that he gives you in that situation, he's just a joke of a centre-back. I don't believe he gets anywhere near enough credit. An unbelievable goal and he could have had more on the day. Ethan Pinnock (Coventry): When he moved to Coventry from Brentford, I thought, that's a dodgy one for Coventry. He is decent, but he doesn't move the needle. How wrong was I? He has been excellent. A big physical presence, but also has that calming influence to talk others through games, and you can see since he's been in the team, Coventry have got better week-on-week. Riccardo Calafiori (Arsenal): He's probably Arsenal's best forward at the moment. Getting in really good positions, defensively solid, but also offers you a lot from assists and goals. Jordan Henderson (Chelsea): Two goals from the old boy. Thankfully he didn't climb over any of the hoardings and hurt himself. The confidence to say to Cole Palmer 'I know you just had an eight-year contract extension, but let me just put this in the top corner', and then he scores that free-kick. Matt Grimes (Coventry): One of the unsung heroes. He moves the ball around really well, which he has been doing in the Championship for years. Me and a few others questioned whether he could make the step up, but I think against Newcastle he proved that he can. Rayan Cherki (Manchester City): He's just the best football player to watch in world football, isn't he? He is the perfect player for City in this situation. Everybody hates them, everyone thinks that they cheated and he just walks on the pitch and says, 'give me the ball lads, let me have some fun'. He makes you smile while watching him. Joao Pedro (Chelsea): He's going to have the season of his life with Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer playing just behind him. He's just going to score. Jeremy Doku (Manchester City): He changed the game with a goal and assist, all after he got Ryan Gravenberch sent off. If he can play like that between now and the end of the season, then City will probably win the league and go deep in the Champions League. Enzo Maresca (Manchester City): Got the job done at Anfield, but also galvanised the team and made it all about 'us versus the rest of the world'. The one thing he hasn't got credit for is his tactical change of bringing on Doku, who changed the game. It all comes down to Maresca. Top of the league and just rolling away at the moment.
