title: Crew searching for Amelia Earhart arrives at crab-infested island
description: Researchers will sleep on their ship to avoid giant crabs that can lift heavy weights, split open coconuts, and may have played a role in Earhart's demise.
body: Coconut crabs, pictured here in the Marshall Islands, could have played a role in Earhart's disappearance A team of researchers have arrived at a remote island to inspect possible plane wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart, who vanished in 1937 while flying around the world. The group from the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University arrived at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean on Monday. The search team's work, expected to take five days, could be hampered by giant land-dwelling crabs, as well as the El Niño climate phenomenon which is now the strongest ever recorded. Coconut crabs, also known as Robber crabs, emerge at night to hunt for small mammals and seabirds, and will force the search crew to spend nights on their ship for their own safety. The disappearance of Earhart, an American aviation pioneer who was attempting to circumnavigate the globe with navigator Fred Noonan, has spawned decades of speculation. Researchers will work to locate what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020. Some believe it to be the wreckage of her plane, but others have expressed scepticism that it is an aircraft at all, with one theory suggesting it is a collapsed tree. This is the first authorised trip to Nikumaroro Island in seven years, and the first visit to the Taraia Peninsula in more than 15, according to Purdue. The ship, the Marin Mainiku, on Monday arrived at the western side of the island, part of the nation of Kiribati, after a five-day voyage crossing 830-nautical-miles through the South Pacific. "It is incredibly rewarding to be this close to completing our inspection of the Taraia Object and potentially solving, at long last, the outstanding mystery of the disappearance of Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan more than 89 years ago," expedition leader Rick Pettigrew said in a blog post on Monday. On Tuesday, the crew plans to navigate through a narrow gap "blasted" in the atoll's reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited - to prepare for landing. The first day on the island will focus on "transporting equipment, clearing vegetation, and establishing staging operations", according to the post. One group of researchers will cut a trail through the jungle. Work will then shift to searching for evidence, including magnetic metals, on the Taraia Peninsula on Wednesday. Lastly, the researchers will use dredging equipment to move sediment for a visual inspection of the mystery object, which is believed to be located only 10 feet from the shore in as little as five feet of water (depending on the tides). A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro Weather and ocean conditions "will continue to be a factor", researchers say, and El Niño could limit daily access to shore. Michael Krivor, a marine archaeologist on the trip, said he is currently concerned about a weather pattern traveling from east to west that could interfere with "safe transit in and out of the blasted channels". Another concern is the crabs, the largest land-dwelling invertebrates on the planet. "The crew will sleep nightly aboard the Marin Mainiku for a number of reasons, one of which is the presence of coconut crabs, whose size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical," the blog post says. Several theories suggest Earhart survived a crash on the island before being overcome by giant meat-eating crabs, external that carried away her bones. The crabs, which occupy atolls and desert islands throughout the South Pacific, can lift up to 28kg (62lbs), and are one of the only species that can crack open a coconut, although they also hunt for live prey like rats and birds. With a leg span of up to one metre and a body weight of more than 4kg, they are also the world's largest land-dwelling crustacean and are able to climb trees. In 2018, the International Group of Historical Aircraft Recovery used pig carcasses to demonstrate how the crabs were able to drag bodies to their burrows and strip the bones of flesh in less than two weeks. Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937 Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea, on 2 July 1937. From there, she and Noonan planned to travel towards Hawaii, but the plane vanished without a trace as they tried to reach uninhabited Howland Island, near Nikumaroro, to refuel. While there have been numerous theories about the disappearance, the official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems and, as she and Noonan struggled to find the island, the plane ran out of fuel and crashed into the ocean. title: Student who spells by blinking is denied chance to sit exam
description: Romi Loffler is battling to take her history exam with reasonable adjustments allowing for her condition.
body: Romi says the exam system should adapt so that disabled students have a fair chance It takes Romi Loffler about half an hour to write a sentence, spelling it out one letter at a time by blinking. The 21-year-old, from Netherlee in East Renfrewshire, has Rett Syndrome, a genetic neurological disorder which leaves her unable to speak or move and comes with a range of health problems including epilepsy. For years, people with the condition were assumed to have profound learning disabilities but Romi, who uses special eye-gaze technology to communicate, is hoping to challenge that belief. After months of work, she completed the coursework for National 4 (Nat 4) history and achieved a qualification last year. This year her aim was to go a step further and pass at Nat 5, which would require her sitting an exam. But her hopes have been dashed by Scotland's exams body Qualifications Scotland (QS) which has rejected her family's requests for the adjustments Romi would need. Romi told the BBC she deserved the same chance as everyone else About 18 months before exam time, her college and parents began discussions with QS, asking if she could sit it one question at a time over a number of weeks or potentially months. This would mean her sitting a different exam paper to other Nat 5 students but it would still be at the same level. Her parents also asked if she could use a "bank" of pre-agreed relevant words that would mean she would not have to spell out every letter. Qualifications Scotland (QS) said no despite two children using eye gaze technology to sit GCSE exams in England earlier this year. One, who has cerebral palsy, took five months to complete the exam. "If it can be done for GCSEs, I simply don't understand why it can't be done for Nat 5," says Romi's mum, Gael Gordon. Romi's mum Gael said her daughter was starting with an incredible disadvantage Qualifications Scotland suggested Romi sit the exam all in one go, but her mum said that would be impossible because communicating using her eyes is so exhausting. Her mum said that QS had expressed concern that Romi would get an unfair advantage over other candidates. "I think she is starting from a position of such incredible disadvantage that just getting her to the starting line is incredibly difficult," her mum said. "She is not wanting to be given it and given a pat on the head. "She wants to sit the exam in a way she can demonstrate everything she knows. "It is about proving her capacity and proving her worth and showing what she can do because if she gets that certificate no-one can take that away from her." Romi took time to spell out for BBC Scotland News how she feels about not being able to sit the exam. "Other students got the chance to get their National 5 and I didn't. That was unfair. I deserved the same chance as everyone else. "They shouldn't expect us to fit around their exam system. The exam system should adapt so that disabled students have a fair chance to show what they know. "People sometimes underestimate what I can do because I am disabled. A recognised qualification gives me evidence of what I can do." Teen completes GCSEs in five months using his eyes Tracey Campbell, of Rett UK, said Romi had been dismissed in many areas of her life and she wanted to prove she was capable. "To have these extra barriers put in place is completely unfair and unjust," she said. "What has been fabulous about exam boards in England is that people have been allowed to sit their exams over a long period of time, one question at a time." Glasgow Clyde College, where Romi studies, said she is "highly capable and committed". Claire Donaghey, assistant principal arts and continuing education, said: "Despite considerable discussion with Qualifications Scotland, the mitigating arrangements we have proposed have not been deemed compatible with these requirements. "We remain fully committed to supporting Romi and will continue to work constructively with her, her family and Qualifications Scotland to explore every available option and achieve the best possible outcome for her." Qualifications Scotland said it was committed to making reasonable adjustments so that disabled learners have an equal opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge, skills and understanding. A spokesperson said: "This year over 39,000 learners benefited from assessment arrangements. "We also have a duty to maintain the integrity of qualifications, so must always ensure that any reasonable adjustments put in place for learners do not impact standards." title: Lockerbie bombing suspect seized from Libya in 'cloak and dagger' operation
description: Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi claims he was unlawfully taken from Libya to stand trial over the bombing.
body: Hundreds of people died when Pan Am Flight 103 exploded over Lockerbie in December 1988 A Lockerbie bombing suspect has claimed he was illegally removed from Libya to stand trial in the United States after "a cloak and dagger operation conducted in the dead of night". Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has alleged he was abducted by armed men and handed over "hooded and bound" to FBI agents, who had a plane waiting to fly him out of the country. Al-Marimi, also known as Mas'ud, has denied building and priming the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people. The Libyan argues he was the victim of an unlawful rendition and has asked a judge in Washington DC to throw the case out of court. In response, the US Department of Justice said, under American law, the manner of his removal should not stop his thrice-postponed trial from finally getting underway in January. Al-Marimi's version of what happened is detailed for the first time in papers lodged with the court by his legal team. Lockerbie bombing trial date set as judge warns against further delay I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questions The US government charged him with destroying the airliner in December 2020, and formally requested his "extradition, expulsion or otherwise lawful removal" from Libya to stand trial. At the time, Al-Marimi was in custody in Libya, serving a jail sentence for attacking rebel forces during the uprising against Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. According to Al-Marimi, he was released from prison on "compassionate grounds" on 30 September 2021 and returned to his family in Tripoli. About two weeks later, a group of armed men, many wearing masks, came to his house and rearrested him, without telling him why or who they were. Defence lawyers claim his "abduction" was reportedly carried out by a militia with "a reputation for brutality and disdain for human rights". They allege Al-Marimi was dragged across the floor "with no care for his health and mobility issues", that his son was beaten with a rifle, and that his wife and daughter were attacked. They said the grandfather was taken to a prison in the city of Misrata, about 116 miles (187km) east of Tripoli, where he was placed in solitary confinement for several days. On the morning of 11 December 2022, Al-Marimi said his captors gave him a sandwich and some tea and told him to pack his belongings. He expected to be released, but instead he was handed over to the FBI. Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has been in custody since December 2022 A US government aircraft was waiting at Misrata airport when Al-Marimi arrived with a "loosely fitted cloth hood" over his head. His escorts asked the FBI to hurry up because onlookers were watching and he was placed on board the plane. The Libyan authorities handed over a plastic "trash bag" containing some of his belongings, including a Quran, a prayer rug, clothing, toiletries, and medicine. On the flight to the US, the FBI questioned Al-Marimi, performed a "head to toe medical examination" and provided him with clean clothes and blankets, his lawyers said. They claim the prime minister of the Tripoli-based Libyan government, Abdulhamid Dbeibah, later secured financial investment from the United States, including $16m (£12m) to secure Libya's transition to a democratic state and a contract with US oil giant Honeywell International. Al-Marimi argues that the process amounted to an unlawful rendition and forcible abduction, removing the Washington court's jurisdiction over the case. The defence says the militia group staged an illegal kidnapping when diplomatic negotiations stalled, in a process which showed "an utter disregard for Libyan law and sovereignty." His lawyers said: "This is not the rule of law. "This is the rule of the strong. Mr Al-Marimi's rendition sends a chilling message to the people of the world: 'If we want you, we will take you'." They added: "Mr Al-Marimi must be returned to Libya." The US Government said that, under longstanding legal doctrine, the court's jurisdiction was not contingent on the manner by which the defendant had been brought before it, even if that included forcible abduction. The prosecutors said limited exceptions to that rule did not apply in Al-Marimi's case. In their submission to the court, the government said: "Libya was permitted to transfer the defendant to the United States under any method it chose." They added: "Any actions of the Libyan militias are not attributable to the United States, as would be required for this claim to succeed." The defence has asked for a hearing so it can argue its case before Judge Dabney Friedrich. Al-Marimi's removal from Libya in 2022 provoked a fierce backlash in his home country. Prime Minister Debeibah said his government had been co-operating with an "international judicial framework to extradite accused citizens." An Interpol red notice was in force at the time, requesting law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest Al-Marimi, pending his extradition or surrender. The head of Scotland's prosecution service, the-then Lord Advocate Dorothy Bain KC, told the Scottish Parliament she had received confirmation that Al-Marimi was transferred to US custody "on a lawful basis". title: I've woken from operations to find the surgery hasn't been done - women's health is broken
description: Kelly O'Shea felt there was no alternative but to pay £20,000 for the treatment she needed out of desperation.
body: Kelly O'Shea has lived in chronic daily pain for the last three and a half years Kelly O'Shea says she has woken from more than one operation to be told adequate resources were not available to do the procedure she needed. The 32-year-old, who lives with chronic pain, felt there was no alternative but to pay £20,000 for the endometriosis treatment she needed, out of frustration and desperation. It comes as gynaecologists warn specialist centres in Wales dealing with complex cases of endometriosis are in jeopardy and a national service must be commissioned. The deputy minister for women's health in Wales said the current set up was "not sustainable" and is discussing options for a regional or national service to be established. Changes are being introduced by national accreditation body British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy (BSGE) highlighting the resource challenges faced by hospitals in Wales. Clinical staff say it has been made worse because of the funding differences between England and Wales. They say unless more resources are found to increase capacity and dedicate teams to endometriosis care, BSGE-accreditation requirements will not be met, which would lead to a downgrading of services, a potential skills exodus and large numbers of patients being sent to England for care. At a recent cross-party Senedd group on women's health, gynaecologists said Wales either needed a nationally commissioned service or an overhaul of the funding model to better reflect the true cost of the specialist care. The call is mirrored by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, who said the Welsh government must "commit to sustainable resourcing of gynaecology services - including adequate workforce numbers, staff training and appropriate facilities across the country". Kelly O'Shea has had nine operations linked to her endometriosis Kelly said she had been in daily pain for about three and a half years, though her symptoms started when she was a teenager. As mother to a young son, she said it affected everything. As her endometriosis is also in her bowel, she has been told she needs bowel and bladder specialists alongside endometriosis specialists during surgery. After her last operation she said she was woken 45 minutes later to discover a bowel surgeon had been unavailable, so her endometriosis was left untouched. BBC Wales has spoken to another woman whose surgery was stopped in a different part of Wales, for the same reason. On another occasion Kelly's surgery was cut short because the theatre was needed for an urgent case. "I was promised we'd have the whole team there and they'd get me out of pain," she said. "But it's always the same excuse - they weren't available, or they ran out of surgery time. You just think 'why are you putting me through an operation if you haven't got the surgery time?' "Every time they go in I'm getting more and more scar tissue from these surgeries. As you can imagine, I've lost faith." She said discussions were had about transferring her care to Bristol, but she was then told one of the other specialist centres in Wales would treat her. The wait could be up to two years, she said, depending on clinical need. "I've put so much on hold, I just want my life back," she said. As a healthcare professional, Kelly said she had seen really good care in other parts of the NHS, yet felt "women's health is just completely broken". Earlier this year Cardiff and Vale health board added their specialist endometriosis centre to their risk register, citing that changes by the BSGE could cause its closure unless changes were made to meet accreditation criteria. Lutfi Shamsuddin, one of the team of endometriosis surgeons at the centre, told the cross-party meeting the issues centred around allocating dedicated time for a multi-disciplinary team to be involved in complex cases, and ensuring surgeons performed a minimum number of operations per year. He said limited access to sufficient theatre time meant individual surgeons may be unable to carry out the volume of work required to meet the threshold for BSGE accreditation. In addition, all accredited centres must have named gynaecologists, specialist nurses, colorectal surgeons, urologists and radiologists with time dedicated in their rota for endometriosis care at least six times a year. However, he said his own centre relied on "the goodwill" of a radiologist or urologist when required, rather than having those roles planned into the endometriosis service. It is estimated about one in 10 women have endometriosis. Shamsuddin said about 60% of patients can have their care managed by GPs in the community, however 40% are referred to hospital gynaecology teams. For cases deemed to be "deep infiltrating endometriosis" which affects other organs such as the bladder and bowel, women in south Wales will be referred to one of two BSGE accredited centres. Cases in north Wales are sent to hospitals in Liverpool or Chester. Cardiff and Vale also considers referrals from Cwm Taf Morgannwg, while Swansea Bay will receive referrals from Hywel Dda. Aneurin Bevan is understood to be seeking accreditation, and will consider referrals from Powys. Gynaecologists told the meeting that the acute challenges in Cardiff "could easily be replicated by other centres in Wales". Shamsuddin warned that losing accreditation would mean patients would be sent for care in England, at a higher cost to NHS Wales. Abigail Holmes, clinical board director for women and children at the health board, told the meeting they were "working incredibly hard to make sure our service does not collapse". She said "the only way the service can survive" was for it to be a nationally commissioned service by NHS Wales' joint commissioning committee (JCC). The meeting heard representations have been made to the JCC by the gynaecology clinical improvement network, which is part of NH

title: Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections
description: As election day looms, the president turns his eyes overseas for help with a pressing domestic problem.
body: Trump announced a new deal for diesel with Russian President Putin on Friday With elections that will decide control of Congress just weeks away and American voters already casting ballots in some battlegrounds, President Donald Trump has turned his eyes overseas – and to Russia, in particular - for help tackling one of his most pressing problems. World affairs seldom provide easy answers, however, and developments elsewhere have threatened to undermine his efforts to bring down fuel prices before they provide any political benefit. A whirlwind weekend started on Friday afternoon, as Trump announced a new deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide the US with hundreds of millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel in the coming months. High energy prices, particularly for midwestern agricultural states that rely on diesel to power farm machinery and carry their goods to market, have been a growing source of frustration for American voters. Polls suggest they view the Iran War as the leading cause for their woes, and overall support for Trump, and approval of his handling of the war and the US economy in particular, has dropped precipitously. Trump heralded his Russian deal in a Truth Social post as bringing "lower prices for Americans," while he ordered his Treasury Department to suspend US restrictions that prevented Russian diesel from being sold on global markets. Two days later, Trump was back on his social media website, touting a new energy ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine. The truth, however, was more complicated. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had no advanced notice of the agreement, although he said his nation would abide by it. Russia, for its part, was silent. And on Sunday night, it launched a new wave of attacks on Ukrainian power plants. "It's clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelensky noted wryly on Monday. He added: "This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond." This video can not be played Watch: What could Trump's "energy ceasefire" claim mean for Ukraine? Trump and Zelensky have had a tumultuous relationship throughout his second term. The American president alternates between blaming Russia and Ukraine for the continuing conflict he previously said would be easy to end once he returned to the White House. In recent days, Zelensky has been the primary target of Trump's ire, as Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil infrastructure have contributed to worldwide energy shortages. On Saturday, Trump told reporters at the White House that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. And both the Financial Times, external and CNN, external have reported that the US has threatened to cut off arms sales and intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Zelensky does not halt attacks on Russian refineries. Zelensky "better damn well stop," Trump said. "I think that the president has a decade long public record of lashing out of people who aren't doing what he wants, when and how he wants to do it," Terry Haines, founder of independent think-tank Pangaea Policy, told the BBC. Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky said he had no advanced notice of Trump's energy ceasefire announcement It now appears Trump's celebration of the "energy truce" may have been a familiar move for this president, touting an agreement before it had been sealed and delivered. In the past, for instance, he has prematurely announced Middle East ceasefires and sweeping peace agreements. Whether it is impatience on the president's part with the slow pace of diplomacy or a savvy negotiating tactic to push a deal across the finish line, the result has been to set off a scramble as the world decides what it means – and how to react. Those reactions didn't take long to arrive. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has become a vocal critic of the president's on the international stage, offered "strong support" for the energy ceasefire, but condemned the diesel deal as undermining peace and stability in Europe and helping Russia to finance its "illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine". In the US, Trump's diesel announcement prompted similar concern, even among members of his own party. Four Republican senators joined with Democrats in a letter calling on the president to "immediately reverse course". "Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the senators wrote in a statement released on Sunday. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law." Meanwhile, as the latest twists in the Russia-Ukraine conflict unfolded, new violence in the Middle East threaten to further strain global energy markets, regardless of what happens with Russian oil. A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on airports and energy infrastructure that killed at least 13 over the weekend, have threatened to escalate a decade-long conflict that had been simmering throughout the US-Iran war. "This is the Houthis sending a message that it's not just military targets, it's not just energy infrastructure, they're going to strike at civilian airports that could kill a lot of people," Michael Ratney, former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told the BBC. title: Jordan 'Last Dance' jersey sells for record £10.6m
description: A Michael Jordan jersey from his 'Last Dance' season sells for $14m (£10.6m), a record for a piece of basketball memorabilia.
body: Michael Jordan came out of retirement after three years to play two seasons with the Washington Wizards, from 2001-2003 A Michael Jordan jersey from his 'Last Dance' season has sold for $14m (£10.6m), a record for a piece of basketball memorabilia. Jordan wore the Chicago Bulls jersey during game two of the 1998 NBA Finals and has autographed it too. He scored a game-high 37 points that evening before ending his last season with the Bulls with a 4-2 series win for his sixth and final NBA Championship. He was named the Finals' Most Valuable Player in all six. The only item of sports memorabilia that has cost more is the jersey worn by baseball legend Babe Ruth when he "called the shot" during the 1932 World Series, which was sold for $24.1m (£18.2m) in 2024. The previous high for a basketball item was a card featuring Jordan and Kobe Bryant from 2007-08 which sold for $12.9m (£9.8m) last year. The previous record for a piece of game-worn Jordan memorabilia was set just two weeks ago when his jersey from game three of the 1998 Finals, which is not autographed, sold via auction for $12.3m (£9.3m). The latest purchase was made by Miami real estate investor Ron Firman in a private sale through Hunt Auctions. David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions, said in a statement: "While Michael Jordan's importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established, it has now escalated to an elite asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art." title: Qantas flight grounded after bedbug outbreak
description: The flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled after passengers on the plane's previous journey complained of bug bites.
body: A Qantas Boeing 787 Dreamliner (file photo) A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane. During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald. They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out. The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC. "We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said. All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said. Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says, external. But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days. Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs. In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight. And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported, external of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it. title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
description: Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role in the Emmy-winning drama series.
body: RJ Mitte was best known for playing Walter White's defiant son on the Emmy-winning drama Breaking Bad US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34. "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative tells the BBC No immediate cause of death was provided. Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award for his work in the series. title: US actress Selma Blair accused of assault after incident with flight attendants
description: The Legally Blonde star is investigated by the FBI following an alleged altercation on a flight from LA to New York.
body: US actress Selma Blair was arrested on Sunday and taken to hospital after an incident on a Delta Airlines flight bound for New York US actress Selma Blair has been issued with a summons accusing her of assault after she allegedly attacked attendants on a plane, officials say. The Legally Blonde star was investigated by the FBI following an alleged altercation on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York. Airport officials said they had responded to a call on Sunday about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said. Blair, 54, who also starred in Hellboy and Cruel Intentions, was arrested and taken to hospital. Her publicist told the BBC she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct". "Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition," her publicist said. On Monday, a federal law enforcement source told the BBC that Blair had been issued a summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US. The source said she will be required to appear at the petty violation court in Brooklyn, New York City, but no date has been set. The incident occurred around 23:00 local time aboard Delta Airlines Flight 938. According to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the flight crew allegedly restrained Blair on the flight. Air traffic control audio obtained by CBS includes the pilot calling for medical personnel to come to the plane, citing a "bloody nose as well as some bite marks". A spokesperson for Delta Air Lines said that law enforcement responded as the flight arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York, and that there was no operational impact to the flight because of the incident. "Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," Delta Air Lines said in a statement to the BBC. Blair largely retreated from film work amid her 2018 multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis, telling the BBC years later that she blamed the disease for taking "my career down" because "I had to stop working". In 2021, she announced she was in remission for the disease. In 2016, she had another incident on a flight after a drunken outburst caused two nurses to have to subdue her on board. Blair issued a public apology after the incident. She said she accidentally mixed her medication with alcohol and "made a big mistake" that caused her to "black out" and "say and do things that I deeply regret". "I am a flawed human being who makes mistakes and am filled with shame over this incident. I am truly very sorry," she said at the time. US media reported at the time that the actress was screaming uncontrollably and that nurses had to prop her up with a pillow and give her oxygen to calm down. She was taken off the plane on a stretcher when the flight landed in Los Angeles from Mexico, and was taken to hospital. title: Attorney General approval required for serious Troubles prosecutions
description: It is among a series of amendments the government has tabled for its bill, which seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict.
body: The bill was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government The Attorney General must provide consent for any serious prosecutions related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland, under changes to the government's planned legislation. It is among a series of amendments the government has tabled for its bill, which seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict. The bill was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government. Northern Ireland secretary Sir Chris Bryant said the amendments give "robust, permanent safeguards" to ensure former soldiers and police officers are treated with "fairness, dignity and respect". The Labour government has faced criticism over delays in passing the bill as well as questions over some of its contents. It seeks to replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act, which introduced a ban on inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents. The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful. Labour's bill involves a Legacy Commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police). The government said its amendments "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations. While some MPs have previously argued that planned protections for veterans do not go far enough, Stormont's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has accused the government of giving former soldiers "preferential treatment". The government said the amendments include: The legislation will make clear the Commission and coroners "must not regard the lawful conduct of members of the Armed Forces as equivalent to the actions of paramilitaries responsible for acts of terrorism" The Attorney General will be required to consent to all "serious" Troubles-related prosecutions Measures to prevent "cold-calling" of veterans and extending provisions for remote attendance as part of the Commission's work Before any witness can be approached, the Commission should consider if "compelling new evidence exists, or the likelihood of a witness being able to provide new information" The Commission must consider the "context and command orders" in which military veterans were operating Former paramilitaries barred from being appointed to the Victims and Survivors Advisory Group, and a requirement for at least one veteran or veterans' representative to be on the panel A statutory review of the measures for veterans to ensure they "deliver as intended" Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he is "confident that this legislation will be a significant step towards a more reconciled society" Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said the bill was about completing the "unfinished business" of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement peace deal. "I am confident that this legislation will be a significant step towards a more reconciled society," he said in a statement. Bryant said the "significant package of amendments" would provide "robust, permanent safeguards that ensure former Armed Forces personnel and police officers are treated with the fairness, dignity, and respect they deserve". He added: "These amendments have been developed through extensive engagement with veterans' groups, whilst ensuring that this bill will also enable victims and bereaved families, including the families of soldiers, who have waited long years for answers, to seek information and, potentially, closure, on what happened to their loved ones." Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said "the amendments will help ensure that decisions on historic cases properly take account of the operational realities faced by our Armed Forces" Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that "for too long, veterans have faced uncertainty over historic investigations, despite serving honourably during the Troubles". "The amendments will help ensure that decisions on historic cases properly take account of the operational realities faced by our Armed Forces, who often make split-second decisions in exceptionally difficult circumstances," he added. The Sinn Féin MP John Finucane denounced the amendments as a "veterans' charter". He said they "risk preferential treatment, providing additional protections for former members of the British military while placing further obstacles in the path of effective investigations". "The requirement for the British Attorney General, who is a political appointee, to approve prosecutions raises serious questions about whether families will be able to get truth or justice," he added in a statement. The bill is expected to be discussed in the House of Commons on Tuesday and voted on by MPs next week. If passed it will move to the House of Lords for further consideration by peers. title: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
description: While Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggests he would sign up to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, Russia has said little.
body: Employees of DTEK energy company in Ukraine work to restore power supply following a missile strike in July On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly. So who is saying what? Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed. Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up – if Russia does. Russia is saying: Very little. Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists. "Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied. "As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you." Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has. It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow. "Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded. "It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery. "That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway. "But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have. "In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it." In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's. In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country. Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests – as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November. Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel. Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices. Vladimir Putin has shown little desire to stop the fighting Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv. Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv. It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine. "The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said. "Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that. On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections. That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer. It comes as no surprise though. Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting. Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine. On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting. On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning. "This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written. The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation. Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal. title: Saracens sack academy player Auvaa after latest incident
description: Saracens sack Totoa Auvaa, the academy player who was involved in a nightclub incident with England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson, after another incident.
body: Totoa Auvaa is a Samoan back row Saracens have sacked Totoa Auvaa, the academy player who was involved in a nightclub incident with England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson in June. The English Prem club have confirmed that the 21-year-old Samoan forward has left with immediate effect following another incident in St Albans on Saturday. Auvaa had originally been stood down from all club duties while Saracens investigated the matter. "The club has determined that his conduct falls short of the standards expected of everyone who represents Saracens, both on and off the pitch," read a club statement., external "We take our responsibilities to our supporters, young people and partners seriously and we remain committed to upholding the standards of our conduct expected across the club." A disciplinary hearing by the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) found that then England captain Stokes and pace bowler Atkinson breached "contractual obligations" but were blameless for "violent conduct" in an incident in June. Both were present in a London nightclub when a member of England's security staff was left bloodied and in need of medical attention after being struck by Auvaa. Stokes and Atkinson were made unavailable for England's second Test defeat by New Zealand while Auvaa was not sanctioned. All-rounder Stokes was restored to the team for the deciding third Test, during which he made a stunning announcement to retire from international cricket at the conclusion of the match. title: Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest
description: Former Chelsea FC director, Eugene Tenenbaum, helped to manage the oligarch’s wealth.
body: Eugene Tenenbaum (left) with Roman Abramovich (right) at Chelsea FC, in 2014 One of Roman Abramovich's closest associates misled a UK court to help secure ownership of Siberian oil fields, leaked documents seen by the BBC suggest. Eugene Tenenbaum, a former director of Chelsea Football Club, helped to manage the billionaire's wealth at the time of the case in 2008, which Abramovich won. Tenenbaum was giving evidence during proceedings taken against Abramovich by a company owned by another Russian billionaire, who was claiming the oil fields had been stolen from him and other investors. The leaked documents now suggest there was a premeditated attempt by Abramovich to reduce the value of the other investors' stake in the Siberian venture. Roman Abramovich's lawyers say their "client denies all the allegations made against him". Lawyers for Eugene Tenenbaum say he "denies in the strongest terms any suggestion that he committed perjury or contempt of court". The 2008 court case centred on the ownership of Siberian oil fields being developed jointly between Abramovich's company, Sibneft, and the Russian subsidiary of the British company, Sibir Energy PLC, owned by Russian billionaire Chalva Tchigirinsky. Sibneft contributed money, while the subsidiary Yugraneft provided the licences for the oil fields. Their partnership - which became known as Sibneft-Yugra - ended acrimoniously. Sibir's 50% interest in the joint venture had been diluted, or reduced, to less than 1%. It said this had been done without its knowledge. Unsuccessful attempts to sue Sibneft in both Russia and the British Virgin Islands led to the court proceedings in London. At court in 2008, Yugraneft claimed "to have been the victim of a massive fraud directed by Mr Abramovich", as a result of which it had suffered a loss of "not less that $2 billion", which in 2008 was worth about £1bn. But Abramovich's team claimed that Yugraneft had been unable to repay loans of more than $30m, so lost its right over the shares. Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax. Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October. Abramovich won the case on a number of fronts, including that Yugraneft's case had been an abuse of process. However, Panorama has uncovered new evidence suggesting the court was misled, in a joint investigation with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, external. The evidence is contained in a leak of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022. It raises serious questions about the integrity of some of the oligarch's professional advisers. We have already found that the world's biggest accountancy firm, Deloitte, helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well the Bureau of Investigative Journalism - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation, external. In the High Court, lawyers for Yugraneft argued the case should be heard in London, and that Tenenbaum, who was based there at the time, must have been aware of the dilution of Yugraneft's interest. But Tenenbaum denied this and told the court "he only became aware of Sibneft-Yugra in Spring 2004". He also testified he had "searched" his "files, emails and documents from 2002 to 2004" and had in his "possession no records or documents or other communications that relate to Sibneft-Yugra". But the leaked documents suggest he misled the court. They show that in October 2003, months before Tenenbaum said he first became aware of Sibneft-Yugra, he had authorised Abramovich's purchase of shares in the joint venture. Two months later, Tenenbaum authorised another financial deal related to Sibneft-Yugra. Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, told Panorama that it would be "very serious" if Tenenbaum's 2008 evidence was false and that it could "range from being perjury, to an attempt to pervert the course of justice, to being a contempt of the court". Tenenbaum's lawyers told us "he gave his evidence honestly and in good faith" and that he "cannot recall the context or detail of documents" more than 20 years old. Tenenebaum (left) had final sign-off on most of Abramovich's (right) business projects The judge made clear in his 2008 judgement that Tenenbaum's knowledge of the Sibneft-Yugra deal would not have made a difference to his decision, however the leak also suggests some of the documents presented by Abramovich's legal team to the High Court had been falsified. One of the agreements was dated August 2003, but appears not to have been created or actually signed until 2007. Abramovich's team had argued in court that Yugraneft's interest had been diluted because of the need for finance for the joint venture. They claimed Tchigirinsky had approached them "in the spring of 2002" with a view to new financing arrangements. Tchigirinsky denied this was the case. The leaked documents show that before then, in January 2002, Abramovich's Russian associates had already prepared a bundle of documents. They included agreements under which two Abramovich companies would acquire shares in Sibneft-Yugra, increasing his stake and diluting Yugraneft's. This evidence suggests they were already planning to dilute Yugraneft's interest and that the argument they used in court about financing was a smokescreen. Lawyers for Abramov

title: Public inquiry over Manchester synagogue attack deaths
description: The Home Secretary confirms a public inquiry will examine Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby's deaths.
body: Adrian Daulby, left, and Melvin Cravitz, right, were killed in the attack on the synagogue in Manchester A public inquiry will examine the deaths of two men killed during an attack at a synagogue in Manchester. Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from multiple stab wounds and fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, tried to get in the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October 2025. Announcing the inquiry, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "What happened that day must be fully understood." Syrian-born UK citizen Al-Shamie was shot dead by police while he carried out his attack. Police had already seized Al-Shamie's mobile phone containing details of his extremist mindset but did not analyse the contents until after he had attacked the synagogue. It took place on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for Jews. Mahmood said: "In recent days, we marked the first anniversary of the terror attack at the Heaton Park synagogue. "On that awful day in October of last year, as our Jewish community celebrated Yom Kippur, two brave men – Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby – lost their lives, and three others were seriously injured. "What happened that day must be fully understood. So, as requested by the coroner, I can today announce a public inquiry into the deaths of Mr Cravitz and Mr Daulby. "This will ensure that all evidence can be heard, including any sensitive national security material that could not otherwise be fully heard in the coroner's court." Three other people were seriously injured in the attack Earlier this year a police chief said he was "deeply sorry" over missed opportunities to potentially uncover the plot to attack the synagogue. The apology came after details emerged following the jailing of Al-Shamie's friend and accomplice, Mohammad Bashir, 31, who was sentenced to life imprisonment in July at Manchester Crown Court for planning a separate attack with Al-Shamie on the UK Defence Academy at Shrivenham. After the hearing, Sir Stephen Watson, Chief Constable of Greater Manchester Police (GMP), said: "It is factually the case that Al-Shamie had come to the notice of GMP in respect of two linked criminal allegations which did not relate to terrorist offences. "These allegations resulted in his being arrested on the 13 February 2025 on suspicion of breaching a non-molestation order; and on the 21 September 2025 on suspicion of rape. "At the time of his committing the attack at the Heaton Park Synagogue, Al-Shamie was on police bail." Watson added: "In conducting an internal review, it became apparent that GMP had seized Al-Shamie's mobile devices, at the point of each arrest. "The significance of the data contents of these devices was substantial in respect of evidencing an extremist mindset. "Regrettably, I can confirm that the significance of the information stored on Al-Shamie's devices was not realised, as they had not been examined before the attack took place on the 2 October 2025. "There can, however, be little doubt that the information contained within these devices would have inspired further investigative action. "It is clear that our not having reviewed the data available to us prior to the attack constitutes a missed opportunity." He added: "I am disappointed at the prospect of adding to the distress of all of those affected by the terrible events last October. "For this, I am deeply sorry. "It is my fervent hope and expectation that the continuing independent reviews and processes will be able to draw together all the available evidence such as to leave no question unanswered." The attack at the synagogue in Manchester happened on Yom Kippur - the holiest day in the Jewish calendar Last month, Judge Alexia Durran, Chief Coroner of England and Wales, said she would write to the Home Secretary to recommend the inquests be converted into a public inquiry. At an earlier hearing the same month, Home Office lawyers applied to withhold some information from MI5 being made public at a future inquest due to national security concerns. title: GB's Richardson withdrawn from World Championships
description: Matt Richardson is withdrawn from the Great Britain squad for next week's World Track Cycling Championships amid reports he is under investigation for misconduct.
body: Matt Richardson switched to represent Great Britain after winning three Olympic medals for Australia at the Paris 2024 Games Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain squad for next week's World Track Cycling Championships in Shanghai amid reports he is under investigation for misconduct. British Cycling confirmed the 27-year-old Olympic medallist's removal in a statement but did not give a reason. When approached by BBC Sport, British Cycling declined to comment on allegations first reported by The Times, external it was due to a misconduct investigation. Last Wednesday, Richardson was named in the British squad for the championships, which run from 14-18 October. He had been expected to contend for three medals in the team sprint, individual sprint and keirin. Richardson switched allegiance from Australia to Britain after the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, where he won two silver medals and a bronze. He was also forced to miss his anticipated England debut at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in July after crashing during a keirin event in Japan. title: Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs that he will push for new post-Brexit deals with the EU at a summit next month. He said "deeper cooperation" on some key issues - including youth mobility, food and drink, and energy - would help drive economic growth in the UK. In a statement to MPs, Burnham also warned the EU's Made In Europe plans posed "a risk to UK manufacturing" and said he was in talks to get "an arrangement" that worked for the UK. The EU proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors but could impact British industry and supply chains. But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU. Although he said he was keen to negotiate a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham also made clear Labour's manifesto commitments not to return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement, would stay in place until the next election. Burnham said that the "immediate priority" was securing a successful outcome at the November summit, adding: "I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term. "At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting." While the prime minister has committed to the current Labour manifesto's red lines about Brexit, in interviews after Labour conference, he did not rule out a new manifesto, which could include re-joining the EU. It is increasingly clear that economic growth, and cooperation on illegal immigration, are going to be at the centre of No 10's arguments when it comes to selling a closer relationship both at - and beyond - next month's summit. There will be a series of deals with the EU on the table at the next summit, Burnham told MPs, including food and drink, energy trading, and coordinating on immigration. Burnham claimed these agreements could add the equivalent of £10bn per year to the economy by 2040, arguing that it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn away from the chance to cut bureaucracy. "At present entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay," he said. "Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports. "British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU, seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned - this is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage." The Conservative leader criticised the prime minister for "unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum". Badenoch added Burnham would not get a better deal than the one secured by the Conservatives, accusing him of giving the game away ahead of the summit. "His exact words earlier this year were, 'the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments' and yet here he is unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum," she said. "He is not going to get a better deal. The EU are tough negotiators, and it's not just that the EU are tough negotiators, he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand. "He has just blurted out everything he wants in this statement and I will tell him now, as a former trade secretary, this is not how you conduct negotiations." Mocking the previous negotiations, Burnham said: "She says that, oh, I've revealed what I want to do and this isn't any way to negotiate it - because the Tories were so good, weren't they, at negotiating deals with our partners?" However, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed Burnham's recognition of the "damage" of Brexit and called on him to go further, dropping Labour's red lines and opening negotiations on joining the EU single market and customs union. title: Boy, 6, died after being hit by van while playing on bike
description: Harrison Jones suffered fatal head injuries after falling into the road, an inquest heard.
body: Harrison Glynne Jones has been described as a "cheeky chappy, full of character" A six-year-old boy died after falling into the road and being hit by a van while playing on his bike, an inquest has heard. Harrison Jones had been playing with a friend when he fell into the road outside his home in Llanfairfechan at about 17:30 BST on 1 October. Denbighshire Coroner's Court heard he was struck by a passing Ford Transit tipper van. A post-mortem examination found Harrison died from severe head injuries. John Gittins, senior coroner for north Wales east and central, said the death required further investigation and adjourned the inquest. In a tribute on a fundraising page launched to support his family, Harrison was described as a "cheeky chappy, full of character with a personality that could light up a room", and who had been "loved more deeply than words could ever express". The GoFundMe fundraiser was launched by Kate Jones to help cover Harrison's funeral and memorial costs, as well as household bills and essential expenses while his parents take time away from work to grieve. "There are no words that can truly describe the heartbreak and devastation his parents, sisters and our whole family are experiencing," Jones said on the fundraiser page. title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
description: Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says.
body: Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on Monday Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities". There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight. On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country. He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities." "I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added. Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday. On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks. Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said. Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire". On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district. Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured. This video can not be played Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine? When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire". For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides. Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war". Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter. In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025. Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year. Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market. The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin. This video can not be played What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support. However, there has been a mixed response among European officials. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it." Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working". title: Shetland MSP defends hiring artist with public money
description: Hannah Mary Goodlad says she is using language and culture to reach the public across her islands constituency.
body: Goodlad defended the job roles Shetland MSP Hannah Mary Goodlad has defended her decision to hire an "artist in residence" for her constituency, at a cost of £11,000 of public money. The SNP public finance minister is recruiting a Shetland-based creative, of any discipline, to engage with the community and deliver projects reflecting policy priorities. The 35 hour-a-week job - a four-month-long contract paid from Goodlad's parliamentary staff budget, has been criticised by Reform MSP Max Bannerman as "state-funded propaganda." Goodlad is also hiring a communications assistant to translate content into the Shetland language. She said the roles are essential to make politics "feel more accessible" across the islands. The jobs were the subject of the Scottish Daily Mail, external front page voicing concerns over the creative roles. Speaking to BBC Scotland, Goodlad said: "I don't take much guidance from the tabloids and I'm pretty sure Shetland listeners don't either. "I have also been in politics to do things in a really different way and I'm in this to make sure politics feels different and more accessible. "So I am very excited to advertise these roles here in Shetland to see what kind of passion we can bring into the team and help communicate our message across Shetland and help us connect with folk across Shetland in a very unique way." Goodlad also recently hired a communications assistant. She said she would not be advertising the roles if they were not necessary. "I wouldn't be hiring for the role if there wasn't a need, this is a very specific role that I want to explore different ways of reaching out across Shetland and connecting with different parts of the population. "There is a job that needs done in terms of reaching out right across the community and making folk feel like politics is for them. "This is why I am bringing in this more artistic role, but also the Shetland language role as well," she said. More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland Listen to news from Orkney on BBC Sounds Reform MSP for the Highlands and Islands, Max Bannerman, criticised the move as "state-funded propaganda." He wrote on X: "Contributions in the chamber have been full of sanctimony and faux indignation. "So no surprise at today's Daily Mail splash on her "personal artist". Does she think she's Mary Queen of Scots?" Goodlad responded: "I'll be taking no lectures from Max Bannerman, a man who failed to win his constituency seat, and I'll be taking no lectures from the Reform Party, a party that is creating a lot of division. "Just now we are united in backing the bid to become the culture town of 2028, so I think this is a fantastic opportunity for more creative folk to join the local MSP team." Max Bannerman (right) is a Reform MSP Bannerman later said: "I think Shetlanders will be looking at this and thinking what on earth is going on. The job of an MSP is to focus on the bread and butter constituency issues and escalating that where necessary. "There is also the aspect of spending public money. I do not think this is a wise use of public money and I think most people looking at the £11,000 figure would agree. "I was in Shetland ten days ago speaking to lots of local organisations and people, and my instinct was they have some big issues to do with fishing, energy, infrastructure, ferries and other things and they would prefer an MSP who just cracks on with that job." Scottish Conservative culture and public service reform spokesman, Murdo Fraser MSP said: "Shetland families are being hammered by rising fuel bills and the cost of living, yet an SNP MSP thinks an £11,000 artist-in-residence is a good use of public money. "Residents will rightly question why their hard-earned cash is being spent on this when so many are struggling to make ends meet. "The SNP are completely out of touch if they think taxpayers should be footing the bill for this while ordinary Scots are counting every penny." title: Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, Miliband says as he summons Iran ambassador
description: The prime minister says Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard "almost certainly" directed the RAF Fairford incident.
body: A large cordon was put in place around the base and dozens of homes were evacuated The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford. Ed Miliband said Iran's "continued attempts" to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable". Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs on Monday that the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard". Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities. The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes. Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role. It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran. The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford. A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September. Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site. So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to provide an update on the incident in the Commons later. Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers – about a dozen B-1s from the base – back to their home stations on American soil. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. title: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs
description: Shabana Mahmood says there is "insufficient protection" for those who play a role in public life.
body: Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced. Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insufficient protection" for those serving in public life and that the new announcement will cover peers, former MPs and party spokespeople. She also announced an urgent, independent review of security arrangements for high-profile figures including politicians and royals. It comes three months after Reform UK spokeswoman and former Conservative MP Ann Widecombe was found dead at her home in Devon, having sustained serious injuries. Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder, and he was also charged with preparing acts of terror against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. "For those who serve, politics is a calling. Robust debate and criticism are part of this job - threats, abuse and violence are not," Mahmood said on Monday. She did not elaborate on what the support would involve, but told MPs it would include access to a named police officer and help with wider security measures. The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years, following the murders of Conservative MP Sir David Amess in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016. "We owe it to them and to everyone who believes in a fair and open country to ensure that those who serve at all levels receive the protection they deserve," Mahmood added. The "root and branch" independent review into security arrangements will be led by former national security advisor Stephen Lovegrove, and will look into "physical threats, online risks and the dangers posed within our more polarised society". Mahmood confirmed that the review will report within six months, and complement the existing work of Sir Robert Buckland, who is leading a separate review into the murder of Sir David. In response, shadow home secretary Chris Philp welcomed the extension of protective measures, saying threats to elected representatives are threats to democracy. Reform's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf welcomed the review, but added: "It is disappointing that it took the murder of one of our colleagues, countless threats towards our party spokespeople and months of campaigning from Reform UK to make this government take action". title: Katie Price 'really shocked' by ex-husband rape claims
description: Price tells court she was "really shocked" to learn of allegations against ex-husband Kieran Hayler.
body: Katie Price has given evidence to the trial of her ex-husband Kieran Hayler, who is accused of raping a 13-year-old girl in West Sussex Katie Price says she believed a teenage girl who was allegedly raped by her ex-husband was "afraid" after exchanging text messages with her, and that she was "really shocked" to learn of the allegations. Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler is on trial accused of three counts of rape and one of sexual assault against the then 13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies. Giving evidence behind a screen in the courtroom on Monday, Price said that she was told in texts between her and the alleged victim that Hayler "had tried to kiss her" and "had done stuff to her". She added that when she confronted Hayler about the alleged rape, his "response all the time was 'no I hadn't'". Asked further about what the girl had told her had happened, Price told jurors: "Definitely a kiss and that he said he loved her." "I wanted to get information out of [the complainant] because it's serious," she added. "I could tell that she was, like, afraid." Price also told the jury that she had used Hayler's fingerprints while he was reportedly intoxicated to access his phone. Kieran Hayler, 39, denies raping and sexually assaulting the girl in 2016 The trial previously heard that the alleged victim first contacted the NSPCC in 2021 over the allegations, who then referred her to the police, prompting the investigation. Hayler was married to media personality Price at the time of the allegations, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021. Hayler has suggested his ex-wife "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended and the allegations form part of this, the court has heard. The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.
