title: Plans to tackle violence after Southport attack shelved due to costs, inquiry told
description: Responses set out by the Home Office in the wake of the Southport attack would need more money, the inquiry hears.
body: The public inquiry into the knife attacks is hearing evidence on how the risk from "violent-fixated individuals" can be managed Ambitious responses to tackling extreme violence in the wake of the Southport attack were not taken forward by the Home Office because of cost, a public inquiry has heard. The Southport Inquiry, set up after three girls were murdered at a dance class in July 2024, is hearing evidence on how the risk from "violent-fixated individuals" can be managed. The hearing was told a Home Office unit had identified key issues with the challenge of non-ideological extreme violence (NIEV) ahead of a meeting with the cabinet secretary in June last year. Four "high ambition responses" to the issues were set out by the Home Office but the inquiry heard all of these would require more money to be delivered. Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, were killed by then 17-year-old Axel Rudakubana at the Taylor Swift-themed dance class, while 23 other children suffered physical or psychological injuries. The issues, set out in a report, included that there was limited evidence on the scale and scope of the problem of NIEV; that multi-agency frameworks were not adequate for managing cases; there was uncertainty about effective interventions and there was no clear ownership across law enforcement. The unit also reported that the online environment was "increasingly acting as an accelerant and enabler of NIEV". Jonathan Emmett, from the Home Office, told the inquiry: "The intent behind putting any note of that type together, and that note specifically, is absolutely to get at the strategic issues and not to shy away from them in any sense." The Home Office's four "high ambition responses" to the issues included proposing a "serious and sustained effort" to reduce the risk in the online environment. Prevention partnerships to reduce the pool of extreme violence risk were also listed, along with a national prevention gateway backed by effective multi-agency systems, and strengthening the anti-terror programme Prevent to handle the "sustained surge and broader range of referrals". Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe and Alice da Silva Aguiar died in the attack Details of what the responses would involve were redacted in the copy of the report shown to the inquiry. The inquiry was told the Home Office, in anticipation of a multi-year spending review in June 2025, recognised that work would instead need to focus on "cost-neutral improvements" in the short term. Counsel to the inquiry Nicholas Moss KC said: "It does seem on the face of the record that what were described as 'high ambition responses' were deliberately not taken forward at this time because of the limitations of funding in the then cycle of the spending review? Emmett replied: "Yes, that's correct." Moss KC quoted former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's statement following the conviction of Axel Rudakubana for carrying out the attack, in which Sir Keir said there were questions about the accountability of the Whitehall and Westminster system and that: "Southport must be a line in the sand." Moss KC said: "It might be said by some outside observers that sentiment doesn't sit entirely comfortably with an acceptance that the spending review meant that high ambition responses would need to be, at least for the moment, put on hold?" Emmett said part of the context for the decision-making was that it was understood the inquiry would be making its own strategic recommendations in due course. The inquiry is chaired by Sir Adrian Fulford The inquiry also heard a separate Home Office review in May last year, which looked at how violence-fixated individuals were managed, found a "confused picture", with inconsistencies in implementation and a lack of understanding of the behaviours and profile of the cohort. The report found the system ran the risk of "allowing cases to fall between the cracks". Moss KC said it was a "somewhat bleak but candid assessment of the scale of the problem", which Emmett agreed with. The Southport Inquiry began formally on 7 April 2025 to examine the overall timeline of the killer's history and interactions with various public bodies. The first phase of the inquiry found the attack "could and should have been prevented". Rudakubana was handed a 52-year minimum prison sentence at Liverpool Crown Court in January 2025. title: Do Lionesses lack ruthlessness in front of goal?
description: England take a two-goal lead into the second leg of their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off against Greece - but should it be more?
body: Alessia Russo (left) started, while Beth Mead (right) came on as a substitute in the first-leg victory over Greece last week England take a two-goal lead into the second leg of their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off against Greece on Tuesday - but should it have been more? Sarina Wiegman's side claimed a 3-1 victory in Crete on Friday but left the door open for their opponents - and the manager has demanded more ruthlessness from her team in Leicester (19:30 BST). The Lionesses had 74% possession in the first leg but only netted three goals from their 26 shots and conceded in the second half, while Greece also hit the bar with a powerful strike. It is not the first time the Lionesses have struggled to make the most of their chances, so is it an area they need to address? How do Women's World Cup hopes look for home nations? Russo named England player of the year Alessia Russo is England's second-highest goalscorer since Euro 2025 England's lack of ruthlessness in front of goal has been an occurring theme since 2023 when they finished runners-up to Spain in the World Cup. In that tournament, they came through the group stage unconvincingly, beating lower-ranked opposition Haiti and Denmark, both 1-0. In the knockout stage, they got past Nigeria via a penalty shootout and had to come from behind to beat Colombia 2-1 in the quarter-finals. In World Cup qualifying this year, England have performed well but have not won with ease, edging past Iceland and Spain and under-firing against Greece. They are creating chances though, and had 58 touches in the opposition box against Greece and 210 passes in the final third. "We played differently back then [in 2023]. There's a lot more pressure when you're at the World Cup," said midfielder Keira Walsh. "In these [qualifying] games, the worrying thing would be if we were not arriving in the final third. That would be a bigger problem. "It's the final pass, final cross and final shot. That was what was missing [on Friday]. I see the girls do that in training every day. They are fantastic at it. "It's just putting that in the game tomorrow and hopefully we will." Walsh said their hesitancy in front of goal was "frustrating" and they know there is work to do in the second leg. One player who has stepped up to the challenge is Arsenal midfielder Georgia Stanway, who is England's top scorer since Euro 2025 with 10 goals. She ranks inside the top three for most goals scored by European players in internationals and has a minutes-per-goal ratio of 81. Wiegman hopes others will follow suit and was clear on where she thinks the team can improve when asked about it on Monday. "We got in good positions but then it's staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time and deciding what cross, what cutback and whether to go for the far post," added the Dutchwoman. "That is also about the connections between the players in those situations and taking out the counter-attack [threat]." England's problem is not a lack of talent but perhaps where best to utilise them. Chelsea's Lauren James has switched positions from being a winger, to a number 10 and even a centre-forward on occasion. Injuries to strikers Aggie Beever-Jones and Michelle Agyemang has meant there is little competition for Alessia Russo in the number nine role. Lauren Hemp has been in fantastic form but is not known for her goalscoring prowess, while Beth Mead is used in midfield as well as attack. Former England striker Ellen White, who remains the Lionesses all-time top scorer, believes building connections and setting the right tempo is crucial. "You need to build your own rhythm. You can't just whizz the ball around quickly all the time so you need players in midfield who can dictate it," White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast. "You then have to have connections with players who are close to you, for example between a number 10 and a number nine. "Fran Kirby was like a dream for me because she could always put the ball near me and I felt like we had a good connection. You have to build those." The goals are at least being spread around the team with England having had 11 different goalscorers since Euro 2025. Defenders Lucy Bronze, Jess Carter and Maya le Tissier have all netted in the past 18 months, while England's number nine has added six to the tally. But England are still not clinical and have not won any games in which they have trailed since the end of Euro 2025, losing to Brazil and Spain on those occasions. Regular starter Hemp, who has played 687 minutes, has scored just twice, while the talented James has not found the back of the net in her past 425 minutes. Part of the problem has been that England have often come up against weaker opposition that sit in a low block and they have found it hard to break them down. "The movement you have around the box is so important. You need to be unselfish in your movement," ex-England midfielder Kirby told Women's Football Weekly. "You need runs in behind, even if they won't get the ball. You have to entice teams to come out. You need one person to make a mistake and leave space. "You also need to pass to someone who has a higher percentage shot position than you. It seemed rushed [against Greece] instead of controlled. "You have to be intricate in and around the box." title: On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
description: Yemen's entrenched civil war is now impossible to ignore. But in operating rooms in its port city of Aden, geopolitics feels remote.
body: Southern National Security Forces commander Tawfiq Al Haboun says the Houthis are heavily armed It was a journey at high speed through the desert - in a pick-up truck with armed fighters in the back. We were travelling with Yemen's pro-government forces, catching glimpses of the Arabian Sea, and forbidding mountain peaks in the distance. Houthi rebels were dislodged from here just days ago, we were told. When you are battling over expanses of empty desert, progress can be hard to see. But these soldiers, in Shaab-al-Jinn in Lahj governorate, showed us new sandbagged defences - new lines in the sand. "There was heavy fighting," said Tawfiq Al Haboun, a bearded commander in camouflage uniform. "They have snipers, artillery and ballistic missile launchers." Here in the far corners of the Middle East, a war is being waged with global implications. Yemen's entrenched civil war is now impossible to ignore. It's part of wider conflict, stretching from Tehran to Riyadh, where missiles slammed into the international airport this weekend. Yemen's Houthi fighters – already a threat to global shipping – are an increasing threat to Saudi Arabia. And they provide leverage for their backers in Iran, Saudi's regional rival. Tawfiq Al Haboun pointed to shards of fibre glass and bits of metal at his feet – part of a downed Houthi drone that he said was carrying C4 explosives. Commander Al Haboun is from the Southern Forces, part of the loose – very loose – alliance of groups fighting for Yemen's government, which is internationally recognised, and backed by Saudi Arabia and its air strikes. The Houthis swept into the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, ousting the government. A year later a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened, trying to dislodge the Houthis. Despite years of devastating air strikes, that hasn't worked. The commander tells us about 500 Houthi fighters remain on high ground overlooking a strategic maritime corridor – Bab al-Mandab – connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The narrow waterway, which is crucial for oil exports, was just out of sight on our trip. The Houthis seized the area after a lighting advance in September. The commander claims pro-government forces have wrested back about 85% (the Houthis have denied losing territory in other areas but not here, as far as our local sources know). Until they regain complete control, there will be pressure on global oil supplies and on prices. We heard later that there were heavy clashes the day of our visit. Five military vehicles apparently hit improvised explosive devices planted by the Houthis. It's unclear how many fighters were killed or injured. Why is it so hard to fight the Houthis? As jitters run through international energy markets, hunger menaces weary Yemenis forced to flee this latest spasm of violence. Around 200,000 have been driven from their homes since the start of this escalation at the beginning of September, according to the International Organization for Migration - all this in the Arab world's poorest country. As we left the area, we saw a tableau of suffering with families dotted around seeking shelter under scrawny trees. Among one group of women and children we met Aisha, gaunt and elderly and sitting on the ground. "We have been here for 30 days," she told me. "I have no animals, no money, no water, no food, not even a blanket. And I am scared of the [Saudi] air strikes. We had to run, with just the clothes on our backs." At the weekend it was Saudi civilians at the international airport in Riyadh who were doing the running. The Houthi attack - the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade - sent shockwaves around the region and punctured the kingdom's sense of security. But in operating rooms in Yemen's port city of Aden, geopolitics feels remote. Hospitals are overstretched and doctors are working night and day to treat wounded government fighters coming from the front lines. The southern city of Aden has been the seat of the internationally backed government since 2015 We visited one military hospital where 51 casualties arrived in a single day – many with gunshot wounds, and several needing amputations. In a crowded ward, a Houthi fighter lay alongside fighters from the other side. Doctors tell us they make no distinctions. "I don't care where he comes from, his background or his religion. He is a human being so I should treat him as a human being, "said Dr Bassam Hazar. Dozens of casualties were brought into a military hospital in Aden in a single day Even if the war ends, some will never leave it behind. One man was sitting silently on his bed, a white bandage wrapped around the stump of his left arm, and staples running along his crown. Others have not lost their fighting spirit, like Ahmed Ali Mahmoud who is smiling and animated, despite multiple fractures. "I am not waiting to be fully recovered," he tells us. "I just want to be able to stand. I think it is a religious duty and a national duty [to go back to fight]. The Houthis have destroyed the country. With victory I won't even feel these fractures." Wounded pro-government fighter Ahmed Ali Mahmoud says he wants to go back to the war against the Houthis In the next ward lies 12-year-old Ali, a brown-haired boy, who is just one year older than Yemen's civil war. Ali was injured by a drone as he walked down the street and is facing a complicated surgery. "There is shrapnel near his spine," says Dr Amr Reyadh Assaqaf, standing by his bedside. "The operation won't be easy, but God willing our staff will be able to handle it." He tells me Ali is quiet and gentle. "At first he was depressed," he says, "but we gave him toys to play with and his mood is gradually lifting." Twelve-year-old Ali was injured by a drone as he walked down the street But will war follow him into adulthood? A truce in 2022 brought a few years of relative calm. But now the Houthis are a stronger enemy,

title: PC thought murderer was making 'empty threats' before arson attack
description: PC Gemma Quinn did not think it necessary to arrest Zak Bolland after Michelle Pearson's 999 call.
body: The four Pearson children died during the petrol bomb attack, and their mother died 20 months later. A police officer called to the home of a mother and four children hours before they were murdered in an arson attack has told an inquest she thought the killer was making "empty threats". PC Gemma Quinn told Bolton Coroner's Court she did not think it necessary to arrest Zak Bolland "there and then" after Michelle Pearson made a 999 call saying the 26-year-old had threatened her son and her home on Jackson Street in Walkden, Salford. Four of Michelle's children were murdered in the arson attack on 11 December 2017. Michelle, 37, died in August 2019, after being badly burned. Quinn, a Greater Manchester Police (GMP) officer of 14 years, told the court she planned to arrest Bolland when she was next on shift two days later. "I carry the guilt every day," she said. "Never in my wildest dreams did I think this would happen." A tearful Quinn said: "I have not done front-line policing since." Bolland returned less than three hours later to set fire to the property, causing the deaths of Michelle and four of her children. Demi Pearson, 15, her brother Brandon, eight, and sisters Lacie, seven, Lia, three, died at their Walkden home in December 2017. Bolland and David Worrall were jailed for life in 2018 for the murder of the four children, and in 2021 were also convicted of Michelle's murder. Bolland was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum of 40 years and Worrall was sentenced to life with a minimum of 37 years in jail. An inquest began on 5 October to examine the contact Michelle had with police and social services in the weeks leading up to the fire. It was scheduled to last eight weeks. The court heard Quinn and PC Mike Grundy went to the scene in Walkden around 01:25 GMT after Michelle Pearson called 999 because Bolland and three others were outside her house. Bolland had been heard shouting "I'm going to break Kyle's jaw" and threatened to "boot the door down". Quinn, as the senior officer, told the court she knew Bolland, two weeks earlier, had threatened to set fire to Michelle Pearson's house and smashed windows with a hammer. There were also markers on databases about his drug use, firearms and violence. Yet she chose not to arrest Bolland as she believed it was an "empty threat". "As a police officer, you get to see the worst side of a community and unfortunately, Salford and what I saw in 14 years….individuals make threats like that, quite often." She left Jackson Street around 02:30. Her shift was not due to end until 05:00, the inquest heard. Bolland's last known address was close by, but Quinn chose to go back to the police station. When asked whether she should have tried to arrest him immediately, Quinn said "In hindsight, yes". She told the court: "It's not that we had stopped dealing with the job, we had write-ups to do. The family's barrister, Anna Morris KC asked if that work was more important than questioning Bolland - to which Quinn replied: "No". Quinn said: "As a police officer, you get to see the worst side of a community and unfortunately in Salford and what I saw in 14 years, individuals make threats like that quite often. "We didn't believe we needed to make an arrest, there and then, that night." In his statement, Grundy had told Michelle he expected Bolland to be arrested. It was suggested in the inquest that this was likely to have made Michelle feel she was not in any danger. The inquest also heard that despite asking Michelle if she felt safe in the house, she sought not to try and move the family immediately to a secure location. Quinn said she did not see the point in calling Michelle's housing provider, City West, because it was out of hours. title: Irish army received warning day before Omagh bomb, inquiry told
description: A journalist has told the inquiry that a warning call was received on 14 August 1998 at Finner Camp near Ballyshannon, County Donegal.
body: Twenty-nine people, including a woman pregnant with twins, died when the bomb tore through Omagh town centre in the summer of 1998 The Omagh Bombing Inquiry has heard that an Irish army camp received a warning that the town was to be the target of a bomb the day before the fatal explosion. It was revealed during evidence from the journalist John Ware who has reported extensively on the bombing. He told the hearing that a warning call was received on 14 August 1998 at Finner Camp near Ballyshannon, County Donegal. "The caller wasn't drunk, sounded sensible and said, get onto the guards, tell them to check the back routes or back roads and then repeats three times: Omagh, Omagh, Omagh." This warning call has not previously been reported. "It would appear that a warning that something was going to happen imminently to the town of Omagh was received on the 14th August by An Garda Síochána (Irish police force). "Now what the guards did with that I don't know". Omagh bomb: Timeline of families' bid for justice Omagh bomb: The 29 victims Ware said the information about the call was given to him by the counsel for the bombing Inquiry in preparation for giving evidence. He said the existence of such a call made sense of a situation that had "puzzled" him. That the information from his source saying there was a warning, did not fit in with an "emphatic" denial that one existed in a report carried out by Sir Peter Gibson. "I've always puzzled about this; Sir Peter is emphatic 'no evidence whatever'," he said. "There's no evidence whatever that a warning on the 14th was passed to the police but that is different from saying that there is no evidence whatever of a warning on the 14th. "This is a possible explanation to the conflict that there was a warning on the 14th and it wasn't reported to the RUC (Royal Ulster Constabulary) until the 17th". The bomb devastated Omagh town centre in August 1998 During his evidence, Ware also named the people he believes carried out the attack including the man who he said made the bomb. He told the inquiry his information came from a pool of confidential sources who he would not be naming, and including senior figures within the RUC and in the Republic of Ireland. He would not confirm if he had sources within the UK intelligence community. During his evidence, he said that the RUC and An Garda Síochána did not routinely share information relating to the attack. "It seemed to be much more an inquiry that was operating in parallel rather than in collaboration." He also recounted a disagreement between the forces over the sharing of pictures of 60 suspects which the gardaí (Irish police) had gathered. "The guards had penetrated the dissidents quite well and they didn't want to compromise that in anyway, shape or form and therefore, they weren't going to hand over pen portraits," he told the inquiry. "And there was a bit of a row about that." Ware said the gardaí was "very strict" about intelligence sharing and there was "a culture of control permeating" the force. In a quote from his notes, he outlined how a senior figure in the RUC told him they had extra resources on standby in case of a bombing. "After Banbridge they feared that the worst would happen, in other words that there would be a mass casualty bombing," he said. "The assessment was that it would target the same Newry corridor as previous attacks, Lisburn, Newry and Banbridge. "They thought as a result there was heightened security along the border the following day in the south Armagh, north Louth area but not as far west as Aughnacloy where the Omagh bomb convey made the crossing into Northern Ireland." Ware said that his source told him that on 14 August 1998, the day before the Omagh bomb, the RUC received an alert from the gardaí that some sort of terrorist device was to be moved across the border imminently. "Special Branch assessed this as another car bomb," he said. He was told that special branch held a briefing and had plans for checkpoints and "sealing off the border". But those plans never materialised and the bomb went off. Ware was asked by the counsel for the inquiry who he thinks was responsible for the Omagh bombing. He said while he is "not certain" who did what, he named Colm Murphy, Seamus Daly and Seamus McKenna as being involved. The inquiry heard that following the broadcast of a Panorama documentary in 2000 Ware received threats believed to be from the Real IRA. "I remember I got a call from someone saying 'your washing machine has been repaired', and you know, I hadn't got a broken washing machine and I think the next day, or a day or two later, a washing machine appeared outside where I lived." "I reported that to the police and the police did an assessment of it and that was it really. "I had some security lights and stuff, but it was very odd thing to have happened and I took it to mean, we know where you live." A car bomb also exploded outside BBC Broadcasting house in London on 4 March 2001, which was linked by some to the broadcast. "I guess there was speculation to that effect, but I don't know if there were any links," said Ware. title: Renshaw delivers again as Australia close on win
description: Australia close on statement victory over South Africa in Durban after Matt Renshaw's dream Test continues.
body: Renshaw had South Africa captain Temba Bavuma caught at short leg in the final hour First Test, Durban (day four of five) Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56 South Africa 284 & 102-4: Bedingham 46, Markram 45*; Hazlewood 2-20 South Africa need 319 runs to win Australia are primed to earn a statement victory and end South Africa's unbeaten run under captain Temba Bavuma after Matt Renshaw's remarkable Test continued on day four of their series opener in Durban. Renshaw, in his second game back after a three-year absence, followed his 190 in the first innings with 89 to allow Australia to declare on 314-6. The 30-year-old then dismissed Bavuma with his part-time off-spin late in the day for his first Test wicket. Captain Pat Cummins followed with a perfect set-up of Tristan Stubbs - pushing him back with shorter balls before nicking him off with a full delivery - to leave South Africa 102-4 at the close. Set a world record 421 to win, they need to bat out the final day for a draw with six wickets remaining. South Africa have won 11 and drawn one of their Tests under Bavuma's captaincy, including their run to the 2025 World Test Championship final where they beat Australia at Lord's. This is the first Test in a South African summer that includes two more against the Australians, two against Bangladesh and three against England over Christmas. Even bad light, which cut short the first three days, did not come to South Africa's aid on the fourth evening. The Proteas' hopes rest largely on the shoulders of opener Aiden Markram who battled to 45 not out from 115 balls. The right-hander scored a sensational 136 against Australia in the fourth innings of their Test Championship final win and only one active player - Sri Lanka's Kusal Mendis - can better his average of 45.56 in the fourth innings of Tests. Dragging South Africa out of this position will require immense skill, however. Only twice has a team survived 140 overs to save a Test in the past 13 years. While Markram shared a stand of 66 in 19.4 overs with David Bedingham the pitch appeared becalmed, but by the close even Renshaw was finding extravagant turn. One thing in Markram's favour is he has now faced 313 balls from Australia's premier spinner Nathan Lyon in Tests and is yet to be dismissed. Australia may also be without the fielding excellence of Steve Smith. The former captain spent time off the field on day four having been hit on the helmet by a Anrich Nortje bouncer in making 27. After Ryan Rickelton top-edged a loose pull shot to Josh Hazlewood in the fourth over, Markram showed similar to restraint to that shown by Renshaw in his first-innings hundred. Renshaw again held Australia's innings together, but was more adventurous in his strokeplay to set up his side's declaration. Whether bad light returns on the final day may determine if the tourists were right to bat on until tea. title: Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire mean for Ukraine?
description: The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians face another winter with electricity outages.
body: This video can not be played US President Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that an energy ceasefire had been reached between Ukraine and Russia that was "effective immediately". Ukraine's President Zelensky responded by saying his country is willing to back an energy ceasefire if Russia does the same, adding it could "become a major step toward ending the war". However, Moscow hasn't confirmed its agreement and Zelensky said Russia hit a Ukrainian power plant in Kharkiv "immediately after" Trump's post over the weekend. The BBC's Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians are facing another winter with electricity outages that leave people without heat, light or even water. title: King, Queen and Prince William to visit Aberfan on 60th anniversary of disaster
description: The tragedy saw 116 children and 28 adults killed when a colliery spoil tip collapsed in 1966.
body: Coal slurry crashed into Pantglas Junior School in Aberfan, killing 116 children and 28 adults, when a colliery waste tip collapsed in 1966 The King, Queen and Prince of Wales are set to visit Aberfan later this month to mark the 60th anniversary of the disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults. Pantglas Junior School and surrounding houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966. King Charles III, Queen Camilla and Prince William will join survivors, bereaved parents and members of the community on the anniversary to pay tribute to those who died. The royals will visit the Aberfan Memorial Garden which stands on the site of the primary school, and go to the Aberfan and Merthyr Vale Community Centre. Late Queen Elizabeth II's reaction to the disaster in Aberfan was said to be one of the biggest regrets of her 70-year reign. A short prayer and a moment of silence will be held in the memorial garden, and King Charles and Prince William will lay wreaths. Queen Camilla will place a posy in memory of those who were lost. During the visit to the community centre they will meet retired emergency service workers who helped respond to the coal tip collapse, including a 96-year-old woman who was a police officer at the time. They will also look at an exhibition that shows the huge scale of the rescue effort. King Charles, Queen Camilla and Prince William will mark the anniversary of the disaster with a visit later this month As part of their visit, the royals will spend time with former Pantglas Junior School pupils, siblings of those who died and members of the Aberfan Wives, a support group established for mothers who lost children in the disaster. The village's Ynysowen Male Voice Choir, which formed in the aftermath of the disaster and became a support group for local men to share their experiences, will also perform. Personal reflections will be shared from survivors and family members in the community hall, including from Jeff Edwards, who survived the disaster as an eight-year-old pupil. Jeff Edwards was one of the last children to be pulled alive from Pantglas Junior School Prince William will visit Ynysowen Community Primary School - which was established to carry forward the legacy of Pantglas Junior School - to unveil an Aberfan Memorial Tree. It aims to provide a permanent place for children, families and visitors to remember the victims and reflect on the lasting impact of the tragedy. The tree was designed and created by ArtMetal, a family-run metalwork company based in Rhayader, Powys. The concept was developed by Ynysowen Community Primary School headteacher Simone Roden, along with Edwards who is vice chair of governors at the school. During the early planning stages, pupils helped shape the vision of the memorial by sharing drawings and ideas. The late Queen Elizabeth returned to Aberfan four times following her first visit eight days after the tragedy While Prince Philip, Lord Snowdon and the then prime minister Harold Wilson visited the scene of the disaster the following day, the Queen waited eight days before going to the village, arriving to comfort the community shortly after a mass funeral had taken place. Her former private secretary, the late Lord Charteris, previously said he felt he had given her poor advice to "stay away until the preliminary shock had worn off". He added at the time it was the biggest regret of her reign. But for those left mourning, there was nothing but love and respect for the Queen, who they felt helped them during their darkest hour. In total she returned four times after her first visit during her reign, including to open Ynysowen Community Primary School in 2012. title: Pope pulls out of controversial Afghanistan T20 league
description: England batter Ollie Pope pulls out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League.
body: Ollie Pope has played 64 Tests for England England batter Ollie Pope has pulled out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League. Pope had been due to be the only centrally contracted England player in the running for the inaugural edition of the APL, which is set to take place in the United Arab Emirates later this year. On Monday, when England's latest batch of contracts were confirmed, director of cricket Rob Key said he would not play in the APL but it is "legally hard" to prevent England players from taking part. In order for any English player to take part in the league they would require a No Objection Certificate from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB). With batter Pope being a contracted player, Key would have been involved in deciding the Surrey man's availability for the APL. However, it is understood Pope has taken the decision to withdraw from the draft taking place later this month independently of Key's view on the competition. "Legally it is hard to stop players going over and playing in these competitions," Key told the Test Match Special podcast. "It becomes a moral judgement and players have to be prepared to take the right moral stance. "Personally, and it is easy for me to say, I would not go and play. But it is down to the player to make that decision." How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal The ECB has refused to schedule bilateral cricket with Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in the country in 2021. Last year, ECB chair Richard Thompson described the Taliban's oppression of women and girls as "gender apartheid". England have, however, continued to play against Afghanistan at global events, including World Cups in both limited-overs formats and the Champions Trophy. "I don't agree with the way women have been treated in Afghanistan," said Key. "The way things happen out there is not something I agree with so it is not something I would go and do." Pope has been handed a new 12-month England contract despite not playing international cricket since the third Ashes Test in Australia last December. He was recalled to the Test squad for the series against Pakistan in the home summer and has stood in as captain on six occasions, including against India at The Oval in 2025. When asked if he had made his feelings clear to Pope, Key replied: "I had that conversation and Ollie will have to make his decision." Before England's last meeting with Afghanistan, at the 2025 Champions Trophy, Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi led calls for the fixture to be boycotted. In September, she told BBC Sport: "Why are we here again? Women and girls in Afghanistan are denied the same rights as those in our country, and the women's team lives in exile," she said. "Does that not concern the players, especially those with daughters, sisters or mothers? "I hope the International Cricket Council (ICC) refuses to sanction this event. Continuing to allow Afghanistan full member status makes a mockery of its own membership criteria." Former England batter Dawid Malan is entered into the APL draft, alongside the likes of Moeen Ali, James Vince and James Rew – Somerset's Rew made his Test debut in June. "As players we take our guidance from the ICC and the boards," Malan told the TMS podcast. "As a player it is tough because you have what is morally right and what is by the law. I have a daughter and I want her to play sport and get into sport and enjoy it. I fully understand the argument, but at the end of the day I am a cricketer and need to be able to pay my rent and be able to earn a living while I can. "England don't play bilateral series against Afghanistan, but they do play them in World Cups – what's the difference? As players, you sometimes want a board decision to be made that says 'we don't think this is right, we are making a stance against it', then the players will buy into it. "I don't think anyone agrees with what is happening in Afghanistan, but once something gets approved you sit there as players and say: 'It's a job, and I have to play and do what I need to do', then you're stuck in a position of what is morally right and what is morally not." On Friday, Dean Ahmad, an agent who represents ex-England all-rounder Moeen, wrote on X: "Morality in sport matters, but so does consistency. "The Taliban's treatment of women is indefensible. Yet why are cricketers singled out while governments and corporations maintain ties with states accused of serious human rights abuses. Selective outrage isn't morality." title: Immigration agents search Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
description: Omar was first elected to Congress in 2018, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.
body: US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation". Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC, area, a US justice department spokesperson told the BBC. The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the spokesperson said but no further details were given. Omar was born in Somalia and came to the US aged eight fleeing war. First elected to Congress in 2018, she is running for reelection next month, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump. The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home. The BBC has contacted Omar for comment. While the nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear, it is not the first time her immigration records have been scrutinised by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records. Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", alleging that Omar had previously married her brother "to try to bring him to the United States." Her brother now lives in London, he said. Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations. Omar, a Democrat, denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email. She has been the target of Trump's insults and the president previously suggested that she "should go back" to Somalia and at times said she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative. Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as "unhealthy and creepy obsession." The president has also spoken unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back." Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress. She won the 2024 election with 74% of the vote. The timing of Monday's raid — 22 days to the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power for the next two years — is likely to raise concerns from Democrats. The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" that it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate. title: Wildlife park fatal tiger attack - what we know so far
description: A recap on what we know about the attack which left a man dead at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.
body: Altai the tiger was photographed minutes before the man entered the enclosure Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster remains closed after a man died in the tiger enclosure on Saturday. Here's what we know so far about the attack. The park's Land of the Tigers has a raised walkway where visitors can look down on the animals Yorkshire Wildlife Park was busy with visitors when the alarm was raised on Saturday afternoon. Emergency services were called to the park at about 13:30 BST to reports a man had climbed into the tiger enclosure from a high walkway. Visitors were moved away from the area as the tiger attacked the man, who died a short time later. The park confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. The park was closed on Saturday and has not yet reopened. The park near Doncaster remained closed for a third day on Monday Yorkshire Wildlife Park spans 150 acres with 15 unique habitats featuring wide paths and raised viewing areas. It focuses on large animal conservation, and counts species including lions, meerkats, lemurs, African penguins and sea lions among its residents. The tigers are housed in the park's Land of the Tigers, which has a 300m-long raised walkway so visitors can watch the animals from above. The park's website says people can witness the "majestic cats freely roaming their woodlands and grasslands or playing in their very own waterfall pool". The man has not been named, but eyewitnesses described seeing a man in his 20s on the walkway at the tiger enclosure, wearing headphones and "pacing around" minutes before the incident took place. Speaking to the BBC, Ella Ford, 24, from Wirral, said she saw the same man had climbed up onto the barriers and was spoken to by a woman before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there". Ford said she then saw the man shouting for help and the tiger grabbed hold of him. She estimates about 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park. People nearby were confused, she said, and one man was "trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything". Altai is a rare Amur tiger, also known as a Siberian tiger, the largest big cat in the world. According to the park, the average weight for males is 160-190kg (25-30 stone), while females are smaller, at 110-130kg (17-20 stone). Altai, now five years old, moved to Yorkshire Wildlife Park from Dyreparken in Norway in February 2025. The tiger was moved to Doncaster as part of the international EAZA European Endangered Species Programme for Amur tigers, to join the park's resident tigress Tschuna. Dyreparken biologist Helene Axelsen said: "We were deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park over the weekend. "Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family, loved ones, and the entire team at Yorkshire Wildlife Park during this extremely difficult time." Floral tributes have been left at the entrance to the park A spokesperson for the park thanked everyone who showed concern after the incident. In a statement on Sunday, they said: "Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies remain with the family and loved ones of the man who tragically lost his life. "The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support. "Many, many people have contacted us about Altai, the tiger. "We can reassure everyone that he is safe and well and will not be euthanised as a result of this incident." Tigers are predators which have evolved to attack, said expert Dr David Sands Dr David Sands, a human-companion animal practitioner at the Animal Behavioural Clinic in Chorley, Lancashire, said tigers were predators that would naturally attack. "The animal is just being the animal that a million years of evolution has produced," he said. "It is the top apex predator of its group of animals. "I don't think any blame could be put on the animal itself." He added: "Tigers are territorial. This is a male tiger and the incredible weight and power, there's only one outcome because the tiger is in captivity - the enclosure is its territory and a male who can be scented becomes either competition or prey. "We're so used to seeing them on the small screen in wildlife documentaries. "This is a very big animal that's got the power to bite and break through bones." City of Doncaster Council confirmed a health and safety investigation had been launched into the death of the man in the enclosure. Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene. "As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," he said. "We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident." title: Garvaghy Road residents fail in bid to challenge Drumcree decision
description: Judges said their decision was confined to the lawfulness of the decision, not in deciding whether or not the march should occur.
body: Breandán Mac Cionnaith spoke to reporters outside of court on Monday The Garvaghy Road residents have failed in a bid to challenge the Parades Commission's decision to allow the Drumcree parade to walk down the predominantly nationalist road, the Court of Appeal has ruled. Judges said their decision was confined to the lawfulness of the decision - it was not deciding whether or not the march should occur. Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan said the ruling was decided before the secretary of state banned the parade on Friday. Residents had argued the commission's decision was flawed over how it weighed up the potential for disorder when it approved the parade for the first time since 1998. In September, the Parades Commission announced that a planned Orange Order parade would be allowed in Portadown. The commission said the parade should start earlier than the Orange Order wanted and with fewer people, but could go ahead for the first time in 28 years. On Monday, the Lady Chief Justice found the Parades Commission properly dealt with a police assessment on the potential risk of disorder and gave adequate reasons for its decision. "This application for leave to appeal has no reasonable prospect of success," she held. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Four key takeaways from the Drumcree dispute so far Earlier at the High Court, an Orange Order challenge to a decision to ban the Drumcree parade was delayed after Northern Ireland's police chief Jon Boutcher was added to the case. The Portadown Orangemen want to overturn the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant's intervention on Friday night, which came after he received advice from the chief constable. Spokesperson for the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition Breandán Mac Cionnaith said the decision was "very academic", considering Sir Chris has "banned the march in question". He said that discussions on whether to take further legal action will take place with solicitors "later on". "The ban is in place, that's what we sought, we have prevented the march and we will be back again to prevent further marches," he told reporters outside court. He added that there are "questions there about the parades commission" and said they will have to "provide a full explanation" on their decision to allow the march. Mac Cionnaith also acknowledged there was "continued uncertainty" as the Orange Order would "more than likely" plan other marches along the Garvaghy Road. He said he was hopeful changes to the commission in the new year would "bring a fresh focus and a fresh view" to procedures. Loyalist activist Jamie Bryson spoke to reporters outside court alongside TUV MLA Timothy Gaston Also speaking outside court, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson said the "lawlessness and the lawbreakers have been defeated", adding that "the law is clear". "The Portadown District had a legal right to walk the Garvaghy Road. "The objections to it were unarguable as a matter of law. "They have lost twice in the high court, twice in the court of appeal - how many times do we need to beat them before they will abide by the law?". "For those 11 residents' groups dug up from the 1990s to threaten parades, go ahead, go ahead, open them all up," Bryson added. "Because see after the court of appeal decision today, we're going to be walking all of those traditional routes again." Bryson said the ruling was "humiliating" for the chief constable and the NI Secretary, who he said the Orangemen would be challenging next week over the decision to ban the parade. The Orange Order in Portadown were given permission to walk along the Garvaghy Road The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and it almost derailed the peace process at the time. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches. Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades. Last month the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead on 27 September with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court. That morning, up to 1,000 people - including nationalist politicians - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west. Since then there have been repeated attempts by the Orange Order to walk the route, but they have been stopped by police. Residents maintained a constant presence on the Garvaghy Road, but that ended on Friday when the NI Secretary Sir Chris Bryant banned the parade following advice from the PSNI chief constable. title: Why the US is bringing back firing squads
description: Medical experts and those who study the death penalty say each method can go wrong and cause severe pain.
body: A protester before the firing squad execution of Mikal Mahdi in 2025 Warning: this story contains upsetting descriptions of executions America's use of the death penalty is under the spotlight once again after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the military would livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan. The former military psychiatrist fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009. His execution would be the first time the US Army had used a firing squad since 1945, a method that several states already authorise to put people to death. And it comes on the heels of the botched death by lethal injection of Christa Pike - a woman convicted of murdering her classmate. Pike was taken to hospital and then discharged to prison 10 days later, after making a recovery from the failed attempt, her lawyers said. Amid rising concerns over botched executions - and renewed federal support for the death penalty - the US has introduced both new and old forms of execution like firing squads, the electric chair and the gas chamber. The vast majority of executions in the US have been lethal injections since they were first introduced in Texas in 1982. The Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit think tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, says that there have been 64 botched executions, external over the past 50 years - including 51 botched lethal injections - out of a total of 1,683 executions. The difficulty of carrying out these executions, and the uproar over what some perceive as inhumane treatment, has led officials to consider alternative methods of putting people to death. But medical experts and those who study executions say every method the US uses to put people to death can result in severe pain, especially when botched. "We always have the possibility that there's going to be a mistake made when human beings are involved in executions," said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now? Several medical groups - including the national associations for doctors and nurses - also ban their members from participating in executions. The American Medical Association, which represents doctors in the US, states they are "a profession dedicated to preserving life when there is hope of doing so" and that participating in any way in executions is antithetical to their oath. Lethal injection, which was first used in Texas in 1982, is now the most common way people are executed across the US, with many states making it their default method. Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta, Georgia, said states turned to lethal injection because it appeared from the outside to be a more peaceful means of execution. "That was a myth," he said. Dr Zivot said that sometimes the injection of the drugs can cause pulmonary edema, when a person's lungs fill with fluid, which can give people the painful sensation of drowning. "It's a terrifying way to die - to drown," he said. Other times, people have medical conditions, like Pike - who suffered from thrombocytosis and other medical problems her lawyers warned about - that can complicate the execution and make it more painful. During Pike's failed execution, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said. There are a host of reasons why so many lethal injections have been botched, but some of the same factors persist, said Maher. "Oftentimes, the executions go wrong because training of staff is inadequate, because drugs are degraded or expired or improperly stored, or because states are experimenting with different combinations of drugs that have never been used before," she said. This video can not be played Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? Most of the time, little information is available to the public about the people administering the lethal injection, as the states do not usually share what training they have had. "We have discovered that in many instances, and unfortunately subsequent to a botched execution, that the cause was the inadequate experience and training of the execution staff," Maher said. Drugs for lethal injections are also hard to obtain because many pharmaceutical companies do not want to sell the medications to prisons for that use, since they were developed for life-saving purposes. In light of many of these challenges, some states have turned to executing people with a new and controversial method: nitrogen gas. Alabama and Louisiana are the first states to have carried out executions with nitrogen gas, though three other states - Arkansas, Mississippi and Oklahoma - also allow for it. Two years ago, Alabama used nitrogen gas to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith, after a botched attempt to put him to death via lethal injection in 2022. During the execution, which took 25 minutes, Smith thrashed violently on the gurney as he was given the gas, a witness told the BBC at the time. The method involves forcing a prisoner to breathe pure nitrogen gas until they suffocate. Dr Zivot said people who breathe in the gas sometimes get seizures. Alabama has executed seven people using nitrogen gas since introducing the method in January 2024. "Each time it was a horror show of struggling, of moving, of seizing," Dr Zivot said. At San Quentin prison in California, officials used a gas chamber to execute some people until 1993 While some states have explored new methods, others have reauthorised some of the earliest ways US officials used to put people to death. As of this year, nine states have approved execution by electric chair, with South Carolina using it as their default method. title: PM believes Brexit vote was legitimate despite Russia interference claims, No 10 says
description: It is "inconceivable" that Russia did not try to use the referendum to its advantage, No 10 said, but the PM believed it did not succeed in influencing the result.
body: Andy Burnham believes the 2016 Brexit referendum result was "legitimate", Downing Street has said, after the prime minister claimed there was Russian interference in the vote. It is "inconceivable" that Russia did not try to use the referendum to its advantage, a No 10 spokesman said, but the PM believed it did not succeed in influencing the result. Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast,, external that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was." Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called the prime minister a "liar" while the Conservatives said he had been "at best... carelessly vague". Former prime minister Boris Johnson wrote on X that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power". He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told." Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey backed Burnham, posting on social media: "This statement needed to be said by a prime minister. After the Conservatives suppressed the truth for years, this took courage." In his podcast interview, Burnham said there was "certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics". He added: "I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas." The prime minister did not go into further detail about the nature or extent of Russian activities during the 2016 referendum. Speaking to broadcasters on Monday morning, Foreign Minister Stephen Doughty would not provide specific details about interference in the vote but said Russia had been "attempting to interfere in a series of democratic events". Later on Monday, after being pressed several times on whether the PM believes the Brexit result was legitimate, the No 10 spokesman said: "Yes we believe the referendum result was legitimate." He added: "The PM absolutely accepts the referendum result." The prime minister's initial comments on Russia prompted an angry reaction from some Brexit supporters. Farage, who was a prominent Brexit campaigner, said: "The prime minister is a liar, yes, a liar." "There was no Russian interference - the Russian hoax has run all the way through this," he added. "This is out-of-touch, out-of-date Andy Burnham with all sorts of bizarre ideas." Conservative shadow minister Katie Lam said the prime minister "risks sowing doubt about the result of a professionally-run, independently-monitored democratic vote". In a letter to Communities Secretary Angela Rayner, Lam also suggested Burnham could purposely be seeking to cast doubt on the legitimacy in order to justify his efforts to build a closer relationship with the EU. Burnham says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit vote Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation? In 2020, a parliamentary report did not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian 'troll' accounts on social media. Report chair Stewart Hosie accused the government of having "actively avoided" looking for evidence of interference. Asked in 2017, if he had seen evidence of Russia successfully meddling in UK elections, then-Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson said: "Nyet [Russian for no], not a sausage." Earlier this year, the government published an independent review, external on foreign influence in UK politics which said there were attempts to "sow distrust and exacerbate divisions in UK society with the ultimate aim of undermining confidence in our democracy". Report author Philip Rycroft said it was difficult to establish the impact of these efforts and that the public "can be credited with sufficient common sense to see of the more egregious attempts to suborn their opinions". However, he added that while there was no "immediate crisis" in British democracy "there is no guarantee that this will persist". title: Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine?
description: Both conflicts have led to less diesel being exported - but the data shows more has been lost from the Middle East.
body: US President Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for the global reduction in diesel exports and the spike in prices around the world, saying President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world". "He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal". But others have pointed the finger of blame at the US-Israel war with Iran for cutting exports of the refined fuel from the Gulf region. After Trump announced a controversial deal to import diesel from Russia - promising "lower prices for Americans" - BBC Verify has looked at what has been affecting supplies of the fuel in recent months and years. The figures suggest that while both the Ukraine and Iran conflicts have significantly reduced global diesel exports - the fall in supplies from the Gulf states due to the war with Iran has been greater. While the rising cost of diesel directly hits drivers, there's a wider concern because of its use in the lorries, vans and ships that form the backbone of global supply chains. Any increase in transport costs could be fed through to consumers in the form of higher prices. Average US retail diesel prices on 5 October were $6.20 (£4.69) per gallon, just shy of the record of $6.50 per gallon seen on 21 September, according to the latest figures from the US Energy Information Administration. Before the war with Iran a gallon of diesel in the US cost around $3.50. Similarly, average UK diesel prices are currently touching record highs, with data from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero showing that on 5 October a litre cost 199p. In 2025, around 6.8 million barrels of diesel per day were being exported to the global market, according to figures from the shipping data company Kpler. Exports account for around a quarter of total global diesel consumption. The rest comes from countries' domestic production. In September 2026, global exports had fallen to 5.8 million barrels per day - a decline of around one million barrels per day. Some countries, notably the US, have increased their diesel exports over the past year, but overall net global exports have declined. And analysts say it's that drop which has been responsible for pushing up the retail price of diesel. In 2025 Russia was exporting around 810,000 barrels of diesel per day but by September 2026 that had fallen to around 140,000 barrels per day - a decline of around 670,000 barrels per day. One of the reasons for the decline in Russian exports is Ukraine's sustained campaign of strikes on the country's refineries which take crude oil and turn it into diesel. As well as being a major exporter of crude oil, the Middle East is also a significant global hub for the production of diesel. In 2025 the Gulf states - Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman - were exporting around 1.4 million barrels of diesel per day. In September 2026 that had fallen to around 670,000 barrels per day. This sharp decline has been driven by the impact of the US-Iran war on the flow of exports of refined diesel from the Gulf states through the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic flows in the waterway have been badly disrupted by Iranian strikes on tankers and the US blockade of Iran's ports. While estimates from ship-tracking firms suggest the flow of crude oil through the waterway returned close to pre-war levels last month - due, in part, to the US navy helping to protect shipping - the flow of refined diesel from the Middle East has remained far below pre-war levels. The figures suggest the conflict with Iran has had a greater impact on the global drop in diesel export volumes than the Ukraine war. Exports from Russia are down around 670,000 barrels a day compared with a fall of around 810,000 from the Middle East Though analysts stress both are significant. "The US-Iran conflict delivered a major shock to global energy markets in 2026, but the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict is now amplifying this pressure by taking Russian refineries offline," Paul de Leeuw, director of the Energy Transition Institute at Robert Gordon University, told BBC Verify. His comments were echoed by Rory Johnson, an oil analyst at Commodity Context, who said Ukraine's attacks are "bringing the pain of the war to the Russian homeland and largely knocking the world's second-largest diesel exporter out of the market". title: Zverev secures year-end number one ranking
description: Alexander Zverev is guaranteed to finish his 2026 season as the world number one after Carlos Alcaraz suffers a surprise defeat in Shanghai.
body: Alexander Zverev will be the 30th man to be ranked number one on the ATP Tour Alexander Zverev is guaranteed to finish the 2026 season as world number one after Carlos Alcaraz's surprise defeat in the Shanghai Masters. German Zverev was on course to climb above current world number one Jannik Sinner, who has been ruled out for the rest of the year with a knee injury. Alcaraz still had a mathematical chance of stopping Zverev until he was beaten 7-5 7-6 (7-4) by Belgium's Zizou Bergs in the third round on Monday. "It's been a fantastic season for me. Knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true," said Zverev. After losing three major finals, Zverev landed the first Grand Slam title of his career by winning the French Open in June, and followed that with victory at the US Open last month. The 29-year-old has taken advantage of the injury problems suffered by Spaniard Alcaraz and Italian Sinner - the dominant pair on the ATP Tour in the previous two seasons - to become the world's leading player. Zverev cannot overtake Sinner until Monday, 2 November at the earliest. He will become the first German to end the year as number one, and the oldest player to achieve the feat for the first time. After suffering a serious ankle injury in the 2022 French Open semi-finals which kept him out for seven months, Zverev regained his place in the upper echelons of the sport and been ranked inside the top four continuously since March 2024. "So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury. I look forward to finishing the season in style," he added. Fit-again Kartal beats top-50 opponent in Wuhan At the start of the year it seemed unthinkable that anybody other than Sinner or Alcaraz would finish it as world number one. Going into 2026, Alcaraz led the rankings with 12,050 points, closely followed by Sinner on 11,500. The dominance of the pair - who split all of the eight Grand Slam titles in 2024 and 2025 between them - was illustrated by the huge gap to the rest of the field. Third-ranked Zverev had 5,110 points - closer numerically to the 2,221st player in the rankings than the top two. But as the season enters its final stretch, Zverev has completed what many thought was impossible. There is no escaping the fact that Zverev has benefitted from Sinner and Alcaraz missing large chunks of the season through injury, meaning he won the French Open and US Open titles with at least one of the pair absent. Both his major wins came without having to face Sinner or Alcaraz, and he did not face a top-10 player until the final in Paris and New York. Zverev has said he would "maybe not" be the world's best player if both his rivals were "healthy and at the top of their game". But, as the old adage goes, you can only beat what is in front of you. Zverev has done exactly that to record the greatest season of a career which had threatened to fall short of the lofty expectations placed on him since he emerged as a teenage prodigy. title: South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
description: Shadrack Sibiya had denied grooming a 16-year-old and raping an 18-year-old.
body: Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya has denied all the charges against him South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences. A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said. The charges relate to allegations that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking. Sibiya has denied all the charges. He says he did have sex with the 18 year-old but says it was consensual. He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago after his bail application was denied. Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external. The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals. The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began in September 2025 and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract. title: French supermarket fridges heated to 50C in 'unprecedented' cyber attack
description: Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
body: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Hackers reportedly gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight. The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack. More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while at least 300 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, according to the AFP news agency. Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported. Some supermarket staff reportedly said they were hit by waves of hot air when they opened freezer units on Monday morning. French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C. Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions. The Paris prosecutor's office told AFP it had opened an investigation into the incident, which it called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France". Eoropean Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality." The full scale of the attack is so far unclear. Reports in specialist retail and local media said stores from other food giants, including Carrefour, E.Leclerc and Monoprix, were also attacked. BBC News has approached the supermarket chains for comment. In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible". He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable". title: Man accused of murder had 'beef' with teen before fatal stabbing, court hears
description: Tristan Kerr, 17, bled to death minutes after being stabbed in the heart and lung, a court heard.
body: Tristan Kerr was stabbed through the heart and lung A man accused of murdering a teenager along with three others had been involved in a disagreement with him in the weeks before he was stabbed to death, a court has heard. Tristan Kerr, 17, from Abertridwr, in Caerphilly, bled to death in the street minutes after being stabbed in the heart and lung with a so-called Zombie knife on 5 February. Connor Palfrey, 25 from Abertridwr, Georgie Mears, 19, from Thornhill, Cardiff, Elexi Manny, 25 from Senghenydd, Caerphilly, and Ricardo Elliot, 27 of no fixed address, all deny murder through joint enterprise. Joint enterprise means people who assist or encourage another person to commit a murder can be convicted for the same crime. Kerr was attacked in the living room of the flat in Lower Francis Street in Abertridwr which was home to Ieuan Crane, 31. Giving evidence from a video-linked room at Newport Crown Court, Crane said Palfrey had what he described as "beef" with Kerr following an incident in which the teenager was said to have chased Palfrey with his dog. "He [Kerr] was just chasing him," Crane said. "At that time there was a beef. A week or two after he went to see Connor Palfrey and they squashed their beef," he said, meaning they resolved the issue. On the day the teenager died, Crane said he, Kerr and two other men were sitting in the living room of his flat "just chilling" and playing computer games and watching YouTube when Palfrey and Mears burst in through the unlocked front door. In a police video interview played to the jury Crane said Palfrey had been armed with a block of wood that "might" have had a nail in it. He said Mears ran ahead of Palfrey and began attacking Kerr, who had been sitting on a two-seater sofa close to the stairs. He told officers that at first, he did not realise Mears was armed with what he later described as a "big" knife with a "Zombie, Rambo blade". "I thought he was punching him. "I didn't see the knife until after the fourth time," he said. Crane said he tried to grab Mears' arm and wrist, but Palfrey threatened him with the block of wood. He said he was trying to stop the attack on his friend. Connor Palfrey, Elexi Manny, Georgie Mears and Ricardo Elliot previously arriving at Merthyr Crown Court. They all deny the murder of Tristan Kerr Kerr and another friend known as "Custard" escaped through the back door of the flat. Crane said he threw Palfrey and Mears out of his home, and that Manny and Elliot had been in the hallway. "I pushed them out of the house and locked the door, they went in the car, the car was on the drive," he said. Crane said he only realised Kerr had been badly hurt when he went out into the street and his friend Custard told him: "It's bad." "I didn't even know if he was hurt or nothing. I didn't see no blood as he ran out. I thought he was sound, then I saw him collapsed in the street. "I could see blood dripping down to his socks, he had white socks. I didn't know what to do. I couldn't move him. "A lady came out, a nurse, looking for a stab wound trying to clean it." Crane said he had known Kerr for two years, and that the teenager came to his flat every day to see his lurcher greyhound cross dog which Crane was looking after. He said Kerr would come to visit in the morning or afternoon but had to leave by 20:00 because he was on an electronic tag. A large quantity of cannabis was later found in the freezer at the Lower Francis Street flat along with a shotgun cartridge and weighing scales. In cross examination, Crane admitted smoking cannabis, but said he had forgotten about the drugs in the freezer and did not know anything about the weighing scales or the shotgun cartridge. He said he did not "knowingly" allow any of his friends to deal drugs from his home. Asked by Chris Rees KC, defending Mears, if Kerr dealt drugs, Crane said he was "not sure". "Tristan Kerr was dealing drugs from your address?" Mr Rees KC asked. "Not to my knowledge," Crane replied. He said he knew the teenager was taking ketamine. The four defendants were later arrested in Hereford.
