title: Hincapie and Zubimendi injured in post-match training session
description: Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta says it is "far from ideal" that Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi were injured in a post-match training session.
body: Piero Hincapie (right) and Martin Zubimendi joined Arsenal last summer Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta says it is "far from ideal" that Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi were injured in a post-match training session after the Gunners' 2-1 Premier League win against Leeds. A training session was held after Saturday's match at Emirates Stadium for players who either did not feature in or did not play the full 90 minutes against Leeds. Ecuador defender Hincapie was carried off by goalkeeper Illan Meslier during the session, and Arteta later confirmed Spain midfielder Zubimendi was also hurt. Hincapie, 24, came on after 82 minutes as Arsenal saw out victory against Leeds, while Zubimendi, 27, was an unused substitute. "We had a training session planned after the match for everyone that didn't get enough minutes, and in two unfortunate actions we lost two players," Arteta said in a news conference before Tuesday's Champions League match against Lille. "They'll have further scans to see where they are and we'll have that time frame for how long they are going to be out for." When asked by the media what could have been done to prevent the injuries, Arteta joked the pair should not have trained. "Never train and they don't get injured. The consequence of that is when you ask them to play they have no rhythm and no impact in the game," the Spaniard added. "It's never happened in seven years I've been here. It could happen in the training session the next day. "It's happened now and hopefully it doesn't happen again, but what can you do? "If I had a crystal ball I would just say 'guys, get in the jacuzzi and I will see you tomorrow'." Hincapie has made three Premier League appearances off the bench this season but started Arsenal's Champions League win over Napoli last month. Zubimendi has also largely featured as a substitute, making five Premier League appearances from the bench. Arsenal had planned for the players who did not play a full game or had not had minutes in the 2-1 win to train at the Emirates Stadium so that all of the squad could have a recovery day on Sunday and then train on Monday. Arteta regularly arranges for the players who have not played a full match to take part in a small-sided game on the pitch, and this is how Hincapie and Zubimendi picked up the injuries. The manager does this so that all of the players have a similar output when they are navigating their busy fixture schedule. Arteta, who says it was done to get "everybody in the best rhythm", said Hincapie's ankle injury was more serious than Zubimendi's. Substitute goalkeeper Meslier was seen carrying Hincapie off the pitch on his back, even though there were staff members present. And this is something that Arteta does not seem to be happy about, saying: "that's something else, not to discuss here". title: US detains man accused in multi-billion Venezuelan money laundering scheme
description: US officials had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to Álvaro Pulido's arrest.
body: Álvaro Pulido was wanted by US authorities over indictments accusing him of money laundering A Colombian man wanted for allegedly laundering money that had been illegally syphoned off a Venezuelan government welfare plan has been detained in the United States. The US Department of Justice said Álvaro Pulido, 62, had been arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation on Sunday, but did not provide further details as to how he ended up in US custody. Pulido had been in jail in Venezuela since March 2023 accused of diverting profits from the state-run oil company PDVSA. The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and State Department had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to his arrest. He is due to appear in court on Tuesday, according to a statement released by the US Attorney's Office. Pulido's arrest comes just two months after Alex Saab, another Colombian businessman with close ties to the Venezuelan government, pleaded guilty to money laundering charges in a US court. The US State Attorney's Office said that Pulido had been charged in two separate federal indictments "involving the alleged laundering of more than $2bn (£1.5bn) in connection with Venezuelan government bribery schemes". US prosecutors say Pulido, along with four other co-defendants, bribed Venezuelan government officials to secure contracts to provide poor Venezuelans with food and medicine. They accuse Pulido of wildly overcharging the Venezuelan government and laundering the profits through bank accounts abroad, including in the US. They also allege that Pulido worked with Alex Saab to launder $350m from a separate bribery scheme involving Venezuela's currency exchange system using bank accounts in Florida. Until recently, Saab was a powerful figure in the Venezuelan government with close ties to the then-leader, Nicolás Maduro, who named him minister of industry in 2024. However, after Maduro was seized by US forces in a raid on Caracas in January and taken to New York to stand trial on drug-trafficking charges, Saab's fate quickly changed. Less than two weeks after Maduro was seized, the new US-backed interim government of Venezuela sacked Saab from his post as minister, and in May it extradited him to the US. Last month, Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering charges. title: Normandy veteran Henry Rice dies aged 100
description: Henry Rice, from Cranleigh, Surrey, was a signalman who served off Normandy in the days after D-Day.
body: Henry Rice was a signalman who arrived off Juno Beach five days after D-Day World War Two veteran Henry Rice, who survived a near-miss when a torpedo was fired at the boat he was on, has died at the age of 100. Rice, from Cranleigh in Surrey, was a signalman aboard HMS Eastway as part of the Normandy landings, arriving at Juno Beach five days after D-Day. He received the Legion d'honneur from the French government and had called for schools to teach children more about the Normandy landings because the "world is dangerous at the moment". A spokesperson from the Spirit of Normandy Trust, a charity for veterans, said: "Henry was a great character, with a cheeky smile that endeared him to everyone he met." Rice previously told the BBC that revisiting Normandy for a remembrance service in June this year meant "everything" to him. "I've had a super lifetime," he said. When thinking about veterans who had died, he added: "I find it too easy to wipe a tear away, so I don't let myself think too deeply. But when I'm on my own, then I do." Rice (pictured left) joined fellow Normandy veteran Ken Hay, who died two weeks ago, for a dance on Sword Beach back in June Troops from the UK, the US, Canada, and France attacked German forces on the coast of northern France on 6 June 1944, known as D-Day. Rice delivered vehicles, men and equipment to reinforce the effort. It was the largest military naval, air and land operation ever attempted and marked the start of the campaign to liberate Nazi-occupied north-west Europe. Rice died just two weeks after Normandy veteran Kenneth Hay died at the age of 101. Hay had survived being captured just weeks after D-Day and spent years educating children about World War Two. The Royal Navy said Rice went on to Malta where he was land-based for 12 weeks before travelling through the Suez Canal into the Red Sea. He spent some time based in the Gulf before going on to Sri Lanka, Burma and Singapore. The Royal Navy said one of Rice's close encounters was a torpedo being fired towards the boat he was on, only for the missile to go beneath the hull. Rice attended many remembrance events across the UK In March this year, his family hosted a special celebration for his 100th birthday. He told the BBC that, generally, veterans like himself only shared wartime experiences quietly amongst themselves. "At home or with friends, you just say 'yeah, I was a matelot mate'," he chuckled. The Spirit of Normandy Trust said he was committed to remembering those who were sent to war and never returned. He attended remembrance events in the UK, including the Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey and the Cenotaph Parade. At the planting of ceramic poppies at the Tower of London, he handed Queen Camilla the last poppy to be placed to mark VE Day 80, according to the Spirit of Normandy. Earlier this year, Rice met fellow D-Day veteran Ronald Hendrey, from Clacton-on-Sea in Essex for the first time to share memories of the Normandy invasion - one of his last acts of remembrance. "He will be greatly missed by all and we offer his family our most sincere condolences," a Spirit of Normandy spokesperson said. title: Stinky 'skunk' plant cleared from river
description: The plant is said to smell like "rotting meat" and is is native to swamps and other wetlands in the Pacific Northwest.
body: Affinity Water provides grants of up to £10,000 to support community-led projects that manage invasive species An invasive plant said to smell like "rotting meat" has been cleared from a Buckinghamshire river. More than 2.5km (1.6 miles) of the River Alderbourne has been treated for American skunk cabbage, which is native to swamps and other wetlands in the Pacific Northwest. BBC Gardeners' World Magazine has described the plant, external as having a smell that resembles "rotting meat". Environmental charity Groundwork South received £9,900 from Affinity Water's INNS Out Scheme to carry out the work. The team surveyed and treated several locations, including a site at Harding's Row Nature Reserve near Iver Heath. There were concerns American skunk cabbage could spread rapidly and crowd out native species Surveys conducted after the work showed "promising early results", according to the charity. Matt Mountain, senior project manager at Groundwork, said: "The support from Affinity has been crucial in allowing us to tackle this relatively new invasive species before it reaches a stage where eradication becomes impractical. "It's a real win for local and regional wildlife and the wider ecosystem. This is especially true here in the Colne catchment as the rivers under threat are globally significant chalk streams." title: Schoolboy knife attacker texted 'sorry' to mum
description: The mother of a boy accused of attempted murder at a high school gives evidence at his trial.
body: The trial at King's Lynn Crown Court is expected to last three weeks The mother of a teenage boy who stabbed a girl in a masked attack at a school said she received a message from her son saying "sorry" shortly after the attack, a trial has heard. Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March following reports a 15-year-old had been stabbed in the back. The defendant, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, denies attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent. After learning about the unfolding events on social media, his mother told the jury at King's Lynn Crown Court she "was in complete shock" when she realised her son was involved. The mother told the trial that her son was "very quiet, very funny, very smart" and had a "dry sense of humour". The court has previously heard how the defendant had written notes saying he hated women while the schoolgirl victim described to police how she told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed". During Monday's proceedings, the mother described the night before the attack as "completely normal", and said her son left for school at his usual time the following morning. She said she first became aware something was happening when she was "doom-scrolling". She messaged her son asking if he was OK, but said she did not "get an immediate response". "When you realise there has been an incident at the school and you don't hear from children, it's worrying," she said. She had the ability to see her son's location using a phone app, and messages on social media had said there had been a knife attack and that someone had left the school grounds. "When I saw he wasn't at school and someone had run away I was concerned [my son] was involved," she told the court. She said she received a message on her phone saying "I'm sorry", and when she called her son and asked what had happened, he replied "nothing good" and that he had "hurt someone". She told the court her son did not sound like himself, spoke in "very short sentences" and "sounded very upset". A photo taken from within a classroom showed an armed police officer at the scene Alongside her husband, she went to try to find her son and was passed by two police cars "with blues and twos on". She called 999, gave the police her son's location, and was advised to head home. "I was in complete shock," she told the court. Prosecuting counsel Christopher Paxton, KC, asked the mother if there were any concerns about how her son was using his phone and if she was checking his phone. She answered "no" to both questions. A teacher who chased the boy following the attack described how the then 15-year-old had "legged it". He told the court that a person who witnessed the stabbing came to him and said "she's been stabbed". When he went to the corridor, the teacher said "the only person I saw was dressed completely in black". He said he was "very shocked" and shouted to the boy to stop. He told jurors he ran after the boy for about 25 seconds and continued to shout "stop" and saw that a black glove had been dropped. title: US Homeland Security chief defends plan to livestream execution by firing squad
description: Markwayne Mullin rejects concerns that livestreaming the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan could fuel radicalisation or make him a martyr.
body: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his department had weighed up the national security risks of livestreaming an execution The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) chief has defended a plan to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan, rejecting claims that it could fuel radicalisation or make him a martyr. "I don't see an elevated risk," Markwayne Mullin said on Sunday. "I think people need to understand that if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime." Hasan, a former US Army Major, is due to be executed by firing squad in December for shooting dead 13 soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas. The Trump administration has said it plans to livestream his death, prompting shock and concern from both Republicans and Democrats. President Donald Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made. It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts. Alaskan Republican Senator, Lisa Murkowski, called the decision "gruesome" and said livestreaming an execution was something she would expect "from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America". "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks," she wrote on X, external, adding that "how we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself." Virginia Democrat Mark Warner said that allowing the public to tune into the execution could heighten the national security risk. "Beyond the profound moral concerns, a public execution could hand terrorist organizations a propaganda victory, fuel radicalization, and put American service members, diplomats, and citizens overseas at greater risk," he wrote, external. But speaking to CBS news programme Face the Nation on Sunday, the DHS secretary rejected these concerns, and insisted the risks had been considered. "[Hasan] killed 13 individuals on Fort Hood. I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies," Mullin told presenter Margaret Brennan. Who is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now? Nidal Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted to fatally shooting 13 unarmed troops at a crowded medical building at the Fort Hood military base. A further 32 others were injured in the attack. In court, Hasan apologised for "any mistakes" and said he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair. His execution would be the first by the US military since 1961, and the military's first execution by firing squad since World War Two. title: Hepworth piece could fetch up to £8m at auction
description: A post-war sculpture inspired by the Cornish landscape is set to go under the hammer.
body: Dame Barbara Hepworth's Sculpture with Colour (Eos) was expected to fetch between £5m and £8m at auction A "pivotal masterwork" by Dame Barbara Hepworth inspired by the Cornish landscape is expected to sell for up to £8m at auction. Hepworth carved Sculpture with Colour (Eos) in 1946 and named it after the Greek goddess of dawn. Auction house Christie said it would be the highlight of a modern British and Irish art sale on 21 October and was estimated to sell between £5m and £8m. The auction house holds the world auction record for a Hepworth piece, The Family of Man: Ancestor II, which sold for £10.7 million in 2023. More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall Auctioneers said the Cornish landscape "strongly influenced" Hepworth who moved to the county in 1939. She moved to St Ives with her artist husband Ben Nicholson and their family at the outbreak of World War Two. She lived and worked in Trewyn Studio, which is now the Tate Barbara Hepworth Museum, from 1949 until her death in a fire in 1975. Auctioneers said the Cornish light, sea, cliffs and ancient stones "became central to her artistic practice" and influenced her technique of adding colour to her sculptures. Alice Murray, Christie's head of modern British and Irish Art, said the sculpture was carved "the year the world began again" after the war. "Three hollows, painted blue, grey and white, catch the light like the first minutes of morning," she said. Dame Barabra Hepworth, seen sketching near her home in St Ives, was inspired by the Cornish landscape The auction house said the sculpture was a "pivotal" piece by Hepworth, who became a leading light in the Cornish artistic community. It said the post-war work "suggests emergence, awakening and renewal: a new world coming into being". It is one of several pieces by Hepworth in the auction. title: Pupil arrested after two teachers shot at French school
description: A 14-year-old was detained after the middle-school principal and teacher were injured.
body: A police presence could be seen at the school in Aubagne, near Marseille on Monday A student has been arrested after a principal and teacher were shot at a school in southern France on Monday morning. The 14-year-old entered Lakanal middle school "with a shotgun inside a guitar case" and opened fire before being restrained by a member of staff, regional officials told French media. No children were harmed and the teachers have been treated for injuries which are not life-threatening, according to Aubagne Mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari, who said the suspect had been in the ninth grade. Local media reported that the incident was not thought to be related to ongoing protests over school conditions, citing sources familiar with the investigation. The pupil entered school grounds with a gun before several shots were heard, Bouches-du-Rhône departmental council president Martine Vassal told reporters. The headteacher, 53, was reportedly shot in the leg and lower back, while the 37-year-old teacher's thigh was hit. A third person is said to have sustained minor injuries. The boy was restrained by a member of staff in a school corridor, according to the city hall, and taken into police custody. "All students were immediately confined and made safe within seconds," Mayor Squillari said in an update on social media. A psychological support unit was set up on site to provide emergency support. "The kids saw practically nothing since it happened in the hallway," Mayor Squillari told reporters, but "psychologically, quite a few were affected, and those in a distressed state are being examined by the psychologist". He said the suspect was a child "just like any other". "The father had requested a meeting with the school's educational advisor, but we don't know any more than that," he told broadcaster BFMTV. Education Minister Édouard Geffray is due to visit the scene in southern France with Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Monday afternoon. "Two staff members from the National Education system, a principal and a teacher, were victims this morning of gunshot wounds at Lakanal middle school in Aubagne," he wrote on social media. "A student is said to be the perpetrator." He added: "This unacceptable act is yet further evidence of the rise of unchecked violence in our society, against which we must all take a stand." title: Who are the Houthis, and why are they so hard to fight?
description: Security correspondent Frank Gardner explains how the Iran-backed Houthis' precision strikes and guerrilla tactics have made it difficult for Saudi forces to gain the upper hand.
body: This video can not be played Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed to respond to the attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement. It comes after the Houthis fired missiles in strikes across Riyadh, killing at least 14 and injured more than 300 in two strikes on the city's airport. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen. The BBC's security correspondent Frank Gardner explains how Houthis' precision strikes and guerrilla tactics have made it difficult for Saudi forces to gain the upper hand. title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
description: Kanishka Narayan said the government will use advanced AI to strengthen the UK against cyber attacks.
body: The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached. Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June. He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us". Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents. The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems. He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system." In his speech, Narayan also confirmed that scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), are now conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe". "Over the last few weeks, we have been working closely with the US government... to retain access for Britain's AI Security Institute to the most powerful AI models before they are released," he said. He said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported. The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems. On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown. However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. Meanwhile, President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals. title: Appeal for major energy storage system rejected
description: Plans for the battery system site near the Devon-Dorset border have again been dismissed.
body: A key risk highlighted was what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed. Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year. The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire. In her decision, inspector RC Kirby said such mitigation "would not be effective" in ensuring an acceptable balance between harm and benefit", stating the proposal was "not suitable for its location". A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, external. Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway. A rejected BESS on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster has seen a planning appeal by its developers dismissed The appellant said it believed it would be about eight years before water used to fight a notional fire at the BESS would reach the drinking water source, but the inspector said there had been "insufficient evidence" to substantiate this. The appeal decision notice stated the appellant had put forward revised plans that East Devon had not had put before it. These included an increase in the size of the water tanks, relocation of some of the tanks, the separation distance between pairs of containers being 6m (20ft) apart, and other alterations. Campaigners from Devon branch of the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) and the Hawkchurch and Monkton Wyld Action Group said they were "massively relieved" plans for the site had been blocked. Devon CPRE energy spokesperson Dr Phil Bratby added: "For years, Devon CPRE has been highlighting the risks from the hazardous materials that could be released and contaminate the groundwater." Kirby said that, while the benefits of the scheme would "outweigh the moderate harm that would be caused to the Dorset National Landscape", they were "insufficient" to outweigh the "very substantial, overriding, unacceptable risks in respect of pollution of the water environment". Proponents of BESS systems highlighted their benefits in helping the nation reach net zero aspirations, notably because they could store energy. The UK government noted BESS systems used batteries, for example lithium-ion batteries, to store electricity at times when supply was higher than demand. "They can then later release electricity when it is needed. BESSs are therefore important for "the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable energy", it stated. title: Points pile-ups, old-school Saracens and a royal pint - Prem talking points
description: After a try-filled round of action, how high can scoreboard inflation climb and what is behind it?
body: There were an average of 10 tries a match in the third round of the Prem It is worth taking a step back to fully appreciate the scale of scoring in the Prem currently. Ten seasons ago Northampton hosted Bath in round three. As on Saturday, Saints won to end Bath's unbeaten start to the season. The score then was 24-6. Northampton scored four tries - from Courtney Lawes, George North and David Ribbans (twice). Bath had only two penalties from Rhys Priestland to show for their visit. This weekend it wasn't just a different game. It was like a different sport. Between them the teams scored 18 tries en route to a ludicrous 71-48 scoreline. The 119-point aggregate score was the second highest in English top-flight rugby history, beaten only by Northampton's 94-33 win over Bristol in May. Those two games are part of a recent trend. Five of the 10 top-flight games to have breached the 100-point barrier have come since the start of the 2023-24 season. Looking back at that round of games from 2017-28, there were 26 tries in total across six matches, an average of 4.33 per game. This weekend there were 50 in five games, an average of 10 per match. That is an increase on even the first two rounds of this season, which delivered an average of 9.3 tries per game - the highest-scoring start to an English top-flight campaign since data specialists Opta began gathering the statistic in 2007-08. "The game can be too slanted to attack," Northampton head coach Sam Vesty, whose speciality is attack, told BBC Sport after his side's win. "I don't want to watch basketball, but we saw some fantastic rugby on both sides." Vesty believes the current scoring spike is a product of laws of the game and the philosophy of the teams playing it. "I think officiating [is one factor]," he said. "The offside line is being reffed hotter; tackle height is lower so therefore people can keep the ball alive more quickly. Then there is the speed of the game - the ball is on a little longer so people are more fatigued. "I also think there is more intent from teams, going out to score points, when that has not always been the case." Former England head coach Eddie Jones was always sceptical about how well the Prem prepared players for the grind of Test rugby, where scores are invariably harder earned. The flip into international action may take some acclimatisation for England's stars this autumn. It isn't just the throwback kits and spiky presence of Brendan Venter that is giving a retro feeling to Saracens this season. Defence coach Adam Powell's aim at the start of the season was not just plug some holes, but change the way the game is played in the Prem. He told his players he wanted Saracens to challenge the dominance of attack and make defence a hallmark of the team, just as it was in their heyday last decade - the Wolfpack reformed. They have started the season well on that front. Only Gloucester have conceded fewer points, and keeping previously unbeaten Bristol to just seven points in a 30-7 victory was Saracens' most impressive defensive display of the season. There was a heft to Sarries' pack with new signing George Martin paired with 6ft 9in prospect Olamide Sodeke in the second row and Maro Itoje, looking revitalised after his summer break, impressing at blind-side flanker. Owen Farrell piloted the hosts well from fly-half, bringing his accuracy as well as his usual intensity. Saracens' most destructive defensive force at home, though, might go unseen. Bristol rested three players - Pedro Rubiolo, AJ MacGinty and Steven Luatua – because of concerns about their bodies, external holding up to playing on the artificial surface at the Stonex Stadium. The Bears are not the only club who will avoid selecting players, external with particular injury histories on artificial surfaces. With Newcastle's pitch having been relaid over the summer, and Gloucester's first put down in 2021, Saracens' surface is now the oldest of its type in the Prem. It may be the one area where Saracens will look to the future soon. Charlie and Jack Bracken are the sons of former Saracens and England scrum-half Kyran After starting Northampton's first two games of the season, scrum-half Archie McParland had a bench role in the win over Bath. The 21-year-old, who would have toured with England this summer but for lacerated leg suffered in the Prem final win over Exeter, got on for the final 20 minutes against Bath. Meanwhile, 22-year-old Charlie Bracken got 40 minutes on his first start of the season for Saracens in their win over Bristol, providing speedy service and aiming some well-judged bombs for brother Jack to chase. However, both McParland and Bracken face formidable roadblocks in the way of more regular game time in the Prem. British and Irish Lions Alex Mitchell and Tomos Williams are their respective team-mates at Saints and Sarries. How will their clubs manage their resources at nine? Is it possible to keep everyone happy? Does 20-year-old Lucas Friday, who signed a new contract at Harlequins last month and may see a clearer route into the first team, have an advantage? It will be intriguing to see how the next generation of England nines plays out. After a round in which three of the five games finished within a winning margin of seven or fewer points, there is not one unbeaten side in the league. It is still early days. The form lines are still murky. Sale, who saw off Harlequins 28-24 on Sunday, are particularly difficult to pick as their new combinations and more expansive gameplan coalesce. If they come good, you could see any of the top eight sides contending for the play-offs. In the first season with a salary floor as well as a salary cap, it feels like a tighter, more competitive tournament after some chasms in the table last time round. title: Key suggests Carse can return as England reveal contract list
description: Director of cricket Rob Key believes Brydon Carse can play for England again, despite an ongoing investigation into an incident outside a Derby nightclub in August.
body: Brydon Carse has played 14 Tests and 44 white-ball matches for England Director of cricket Rob Key believes Brydon Carse can play for England again, despite an ongoing investigation into an incident outside a Derby nightclub in August. Carse was arrested then de-arrested, with Derbyshire Police subsequently taking no action over allegations of an assault. The pace bowler has since been charged by the Cricket Regulator with breaching England and Wales Cricket Board professional conduct rules. The 31-year-old is among 39 players named in England's updated list of contracted players, announced on Monday. The two-year deal he was given last year runs until the autumn of 2027. Carse is available for England selection but has not been part of a squad since the Derby incident as he takes time away from international cricket. Asked if he can see a situation where the Durham man plays for England again, Key told the Test Match Special podcast: "Yeah, I can do, depending what happens with the outcome of that [the Regulator charge]. "Myself, like a lot of people who work for the ECB, you get in these jobs to make some decisions that help English cricket and you also want players to be able to maximise their potential and have great careers. You don't get in them to sit on calls about all the things that have happened off the field over the last bit. "As far as Brydon Carse is concerned, we'll find out what happens in the near future, and there's a chance he can come back and play for England." Mahmud takes Test hat-trick - can you name the others in past 40 years? As well as announcing player deals, England also confirmed new-look backroom teams underneath Test head coach Stephen Fleming and white-ball counterpart Brendon McCullum. Fleming has brought in Richard Dawson, who leaves his position as Glamorgan head coach, alongside former England wicketkeeper James Foster and South African Eric Simons. Fleming worked with both Foster and Simons at Indian Premier League side Chennai Super Kings. Marcus Trescothick, who took interim charge of the Test team for the home series against Pakistan, remains with the red-ball team. McCullum keeps the bulk of the staff who worked with him across formats: Sarah Taylor, Jeetan Patel and Tim Southee. Kevin Pietersen will also work with the white-ball teams in the run-up to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year. Of the 39 players handed England deals, 30 have full central contracts and nine are on development contracts. The large number of players on England deals is a result of high-earners like Ben Stokes and Mark Wood retiring from international cricket and freeing up space in the budget. Eleven players, including Test captain Joe Root and white-ball captain Harry Brook, are given two-year contracts. In an unprecedented move for an uncapped player, pace bowler Henry Crocombe is also given a two-year contract. England's centrally contracted players: Joe Root* (Yorkshire), Harry Brook* (Yorkshire), Rehan Ahmed (Leicestershire), Jofra Archer* (Sussex), Gus Atkinson* (Surrey), Sonny Baker* (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), Shoaib Bashir (Derbyshire), Jacob Bethell* (Warwickshire), Jos Buttler (Lancashire), Brydon Carse (Durham), Sam Cook (Essex), Jordan Cox* (Essex), Henry Crocombe* (Sussex/Surrey), Sam Curran* (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Emilio Gay (Durham), Matthew Fisher (Surrey), Will Jacks* (Surrey), Dan Lawrence (Surrey), Saqib Mahmood (Lancashire), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Ollie Pope (Surrey), Matthew Potts (Durham), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Ollie Robinson (Sussex), Phil Salt (Lancashire), Jamie Smith (Surrey), Josh Tongue* (Nottinghamshire) *Denotes two-year deal through until 30 September 2028. England development contracted players: James Coles (Sussex), Mason Crane (Glamorgan), Josh Hull (Leicestershire), Eddie Jack (Hampshire), Ben McKinney (Durham), Liam Patterson-White (Nottinghamshire), Thomas Rew (Somerset). Matthew Revis (Yorkshire), Mitch Stanley (Lancashire). Crocombe is one of five specialist fast bowlers to be given a multi-year deal, joining Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Sonny Baker and Josh Tongue. Before the Derby incident, Carse had not played for England since the Ashes in January because of a wrist injury. Prior to the injury, the Durham man was an international regular across formats and was the only England seamer to play in all five Tests in Australia. With inexperienced bowlers like Baker and Crocombe receiving longer contracts, Key was asked if a lack of extension for Carse revealed England's feelings on his international future. "No," replied the former Kent batter. "I think it means if he gets a chance to come back and play for England he's got to try to maximise his career and be the best bowler he possibly can be. "That investigation is going on with the Regulator. I don't know a lot about what happens in that investigation, because that is with them and we deal with that afterwards. There's nothing really I can say about that. We haven't had those conversations. We'll find out more in due course. We'll find out more when that investigation comes to a head." Along with Crocombe, Emilio Gay, Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence, Tom Banton, Sam Cook and Matt Fisher are given full central contracts for the first time. Ollie Robinson returns to the contract list after missing out for the past two years, rewarded following his superb return to the Test team in the home summer. Off-spinner Shoaib Bashir keeps his deal and is the only specialist red-ball spinner on the list. However, Mason Crane and Liam Patterson-White are given developmental deals as an indication of how England could grow their Test spin-bowling options. title: Daniel Kinahan's lawyers to apply for bail in due course, court hears
description: He is charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.
body: Daniel Kinahan, shown here in a court artist's sketch, during a previous hearing An application for bail is to be made on the behalf of Daniel Kinahan in due course, the Special Criminal Court has heard. The application will be made through the High Court in Dublin. Darragh Mackin of Phoenix Law, who is Kinahan's solicitor, appeared in court on Monday where he confirmed an application will be made for bail. Kinahan is charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017. Mackin also told the court Kinahan's defence legal team is looking for an expert to examine the digital evidence and that they are seeking information on other international investigations that Kinahan was acquitted of. The prosecuting barrister from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) said there is "complex factual matrix" behind Kinahan's single charge. He told the court that behind Kinahan's extradition from Dubai earlier this year, a statement of facts which is 189 pages long was behind it. Kinahan was remanded and scheduled to appear in person at court again on 21 December. The DPP barrister said the book of evidence should be ready by that time. This is Kinahan's third time before the special criminal court and second time he appeared in person. He was dressed in a grey suit with a black shirt and black glasses. Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April and extradited on 9 August when he was flown back to Ireland on board the Irish government's jet. title: Julie Hesmondhalgh left Celebrity Traitors 'with head held high'
description: The former Corrie star says she had some apologetic texts after being banished on Friday's episode.
body: Hesmondhalgh said she received apology texts from her fellow contestants Actress Julie Hesmondhalgh - the most recently banished contestant from The Celebrity Traitors - says she left the show with her "head held high". The former Coronation Street star, from Accrington in Lancashire, starred as a faithful contestant in the second series of the BBC One show - before being voted out by other players on Friday's episode. She said she "had no idea" she was going to be banished, but it "became clear it was going to be me and I was a bit worried". "I did feel it was my time," she told BBC Radio Manchester, adding: "I left with my head held high... but I had some very gratifying apologetic texts on Friday night." The actress said being on the game show had been an "amazing experience". "I absolutely loved it," she said. "I'm a huge fan of the show anyway. "I've watched every episode of them all - even the New Zealand one." Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players Traitors claim their first victim as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses? Hesmondhalgh also revealed she was personally recruited to be a contestant on the show while the first series was in full swing in 2025. "I got asked to do it at the height of last year's celebrity series," she said. "I was doing a play in London. "They came to see me in my dressing room and asked me. "I couldn't believe it. I like fell on the floor. "Keeping it a secret was so, so hard." Hesmondhalgh said she would have been "a terrible traitor" The actress, who was the third celebrity to be banished from the Traitors' Castle, said it had been a "total relief" to now be able to watch the series as a fan. "I can't tell you how stressful it is to watch yourself - especially when you're playing badly," she said. "I was doing good but I knew what was to come. "I knew I'd turn into this crazy lady Traitor hunter." You know their names, but you don't know their game. An all-star cast take on the ultimate test of deceit and betrayal. She said her "overriding feeling" was now one of "total relief that I can watch it as a fan again, because my nervous system will never recover". "It was a total thrill to be in there... and amazing to be representing, not just the North West, but the whole of the North," she added. "I'm very much looking forward to just watching it and I am backing Sharon [Rooney], Leigh-Anne [Pinnock] and Bash [Sebastian Croft]." title: Tom Cruise film Digger could lose $245m at box office
description: The film dropped by around 60% in its second weekend, and could become one of Hollywood's biggest flops.
body: Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance in cinemas. Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend. It brings Digger's total box office takings to around $35m (£26m) globally so far. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market. But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve". The film's takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history. Digger's performance is in sharp contrast to the success of IP-driven hits starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of the Top Gun and Mission: Impossible franchises. Digger is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant. Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide. The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign. However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m). Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount. Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning, starring Mikey Madison and Jeremy Allen White, also preformed poorly Meanwhile, the new sequel to the Oscar-winning hit The Social Network also struggled at the box office on its opening weekend. The Social Reckoning took $5.5m (£4.1m) in the US, significantly lower than the $22m (£16m) its predecessor took on its opening weekend in 2010, not adjusted for inflation. Globally, Aaron Sorkin's latest film, starring Mikey Madison, Jeremy Strong and Jeremy Allen White, took around $9m (£6.8m). The film tells the true story of a Facebook engineer, Frances Haugan, who leaked internal documents to a reporter after becoming concerned about some of the company's practices. The Social Reckoning was beaten in the US box office chart by horror movie Other Mommy, psychological thriller Verity, video game adaptation Resident Evil and Brad Pitt's wilderness thriller Heart of the Beast. title: Amy Dowden praised for 'iconic' clapback at ex-Strictly professional dancer
description: Former Strictly professional Brendan Cole claims Amy Dowden is "not up to" the challenge of the show.
body: Strictly professional dancer Amy Dowden has been praised for her response to critcism from her former colleague Brendan Cole Strictly star Amy Dowden has been praised for her "iconic" clapback after ex-Strictly dancer Brendan Cole claimed she was "not up to" the challenge of the show. Dowden, who has previously spoken openly about being treated for breast cancer, was the first professional to be eliminated in the 2026 series, with her celebrity partner Chris Appleton. "To be a pro on Strictly is a big job and one has to be up to the challenge," Cole reportedly told Sky Vegas, adding: "Amy has not been up to the challenge, in my opinion." Rather than a direct response, Dowden posted a video on her social media which has been praised as a "perfect" reaction by viewers and some of her fellow Strictly professionals. Miming the opening line from Mariah Carey's track Obsessed, Dowden can be seen blowing a kiss at the camera, adding: "Why are you so obsessed with me?" "If you know, you know", a cryptic caption read, along with hashtags reading "be kind" and "in a world where you can be anything, be kind". Cole's criticism of Dowden's performance continued: "I don't think Amy's been doing a very good job for the last few years and she's been out first for the last few years. One can do the maths on that." He also claimed he could see Dowden "counting in" her partners, a sign to him that the "job has not been done". Dowden's post prompted followers to jump to her defence, as fans applauded the Caerphilly-born dancer's response, with many leaving words of encouragement, telling Dowden to "keep being you". Current and former Strictly stars also showed their support, including Aljaž Škorjanec, Dianne Buswell, Kevin Clifton and Carlos Gu, who replied "iconic as always". Presenter and journalist Stacey Dooley left gold medal emojis under her post, while previous Strictly cast member and actress, Sarah Hadland, commented "beautiful inside and out". Ex-Strictly pro Brendan Cole, who was on the show from its launch in 2004 until 2017, has critiqued Dowden's performance Dowden made history as Strictly's first Welsh professional dancer in 2017. Then, aged 32, she was diagnosed with grade three breast cancer in 2023, after finding a lump the day before her honeymoon. She has been candid about her experiences of the disease, including having two mastectomies, chemotherapy, and fertility treatment. The star has also been open about how dancing got her through "the toughest of times". "Even when I couldn't dance, even being able to watch it made me feel so much better as well," she previously said. Dowden first returned to the show in 2024, but an injury to her foot meant she had to leave the competition early. She was also eliminated first in 2025 after being paired with The Apprentice's Thomas Skinner. Speaking on Strictly's It Takes Two programme, Dowden and Appleton, who lost the dance-off against actor Jaime Winstone and professional dancer Carlos Gu, became emotional as Dowden admitted she was "gutted" their journey was cut short. Dowden said celebrity hairstylist Appleton's confidence had "grew and grew", adding: "I honestly think there was so much more to come." Appleton, who has worked with a host of A-list stars as a celebrity hairstylist, including Kim Kardashian and Ariana Grande, added: "I'd literally go out there shaking and there's times I didn't know if I could do it, but I did it. "I would just look at Amy and see her smiling and knew she was with me." Strictly Come Dancing returns to iPlayer and BBC One from 18:15 BST on Saturday 17 October. title: HMV to close Oxford Street store after three years
description: HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End, but its current site is "unviable".
body: HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End HMV has said it will shut its flagship Oxford Street store three years after it reopened the site, blaming a proposed doubling of the rent for the closure. The entertainment chain said it would leave the shop in March 2027, in a move affecting more than 50 staff. It said it was looking for a new site in London's West End district for its flagship shop and said it planned to maintain a "significant presence" in the capital. Phil Halliday, managing director of HMV, said it was "frustrating" that the Oxford Street shop was "commercially unviable". He said: "This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history. "We are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027." HMV shut its Oxford Street store in 2019 after it went into administration The group said its landlords had proposed doubling the rent on the site at 363 Oxford Street, and it was also facing a bill for "substantial" renovation works at the store, which together would make the shop "commercially unsustainable". HMV said it would look to transfer affected workers to its two other London stores and head office while it looked for a new site. The chain reopened its historic Oxford Street store in November 2023 after a four-year absence following a deal secured with landlords. It first opened the Oxford Street site in 1921. HMV has 113 stores across the UK, including six sites under the Fopp brand, as well as another eight in Europe. The group said it remained committed to high street stores. title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
description: It comes after the armed group hit Riyadh's international airport and another facility, killing 13 people, in a significant escalation.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Footage from inside Riyadh's airport shows the moment the strike hit on Saturday Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement. "The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh. On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure. The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen. The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday. A Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas. One killed, 11 injured in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport in two days Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict Who are the Houthis and what do they want? Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing. Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea. They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis. Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory. title: New mental health directory launches
description: It provides information about a range of services to support mental health, officials say.
body: Support for mental health care is available via the directory A new online directory bringing together mental health services across Jersey has been launched. The Mental Health Directory, external provides information about a range of services designed to support islanders' mental health and wellbeing. It aims to help people understand what support is available, find services that meet their needs and access help for themselves or others, health officials said. Andy Weir, managing director of the Health and Care Service, said: "Many of us need support at times. Islanders have told us that finding the right support can be difficult." More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Weir added: "The new Mental Health Directory brings together information on mental health services in Jersey in one place, helping people find the support they need. "Seeking support can be an important first step, and the directory is designed to make that step easier by helping Islanders understand what help is available and how to access it." title: Women's billion-dollar boom leaves players behind, union says
description: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress, a Fifpro survey indicates.
body: Players from Real Madrid and Barcelona joined strike action in Spain's Liga F in 2023, as unions sought improved pay and conditions Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress. That is according to the findings of a new global survey of more than 800 footballers by the players' union Fifpro., external Players were asked why they might leave football early. The report stated 59% cited financial reasons, while psychological stress was another factor identified by 46%. Alex Culvin, head of women's football at Fifpro, said there was no single explanation for the increase. She pointed to growing public exposure, financial insecurity and inadequate support systems as possible contributing factors. "Players are now very visible," she said. "Players are not only expected to be visible, but are obligated to be visible because of the low income to subsidise the lack of solid income they receive." While awareness of mental health issues has improved, Culvin explained many players felt they were being left to cope alone. "Players also reported, whilst having a higher psychological stress, that they didn't have the support they needed in a mental health sense, either at the club or internationally," she said. In total, the report shows 57% of women who responded to the survey struggled with their mental health and half of them were not provided with support by their clubs. Most women players earn less than £15,000 - Fifpro Legal action against Fifa to include women's schedule Women's football could become 'billion pound' industry The report states that global revenue in the women's game is expected to rise from about $581m (£439m) in 2024 to over $1bn (£756m) in 2027. It also highlights emerging psychological pressures facing professional women's footballers. In an increasingly digital world, players are more accessible than ever through social media, bringing them closer to fans but also exposing them to online harassment and abuse. The Fifpro survey suggested that although salaries, visibility and investment have risen significantly since 2017, much of the professional game still operates in precarious conditions. For Culvin, the sport's commercial growth is not yet being matched by safeguards for the players driving it. "The economic case for women's football has been made," she said. "I think the institutional regulatory and policy case needs to catch up quickly to protect and enhance our women's players and enable them to perform maximally." One of the report's most striking findings is how players view their own professional status. Under Fifa's definition, a professional player has a written contract and is paid more than the expenses incurred playing. In the survey, 62% of players described themselves as professional, 27% selected semi-professional and 12% chose amateur. All players in the survey were playing for clubs in the top tier of their country, yet only 78% reported having a written contract and 82% said they were paid by their club. However, just 57% said that payment was enough to cover the costs of playing football. "Players who are professional but don't see or feel themselves as professional are not receiving the full benefits of being an employee," Culvin said. The report also highlights the limits of salary growth. Although mean average monthly earnings have tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (£1,970), the median salary is just $1,669 (£1,250). Average monthly pay varies considerably by region, from $6,450 (£4,886) in North America and $3,982 (£3,016) in central/Western Europe, to $878 (£664) in Eastern Europe and just $480 (£363) in Africa. While salaries have risen sharply in leagues such as those in the USA and Mexico, average pay in 10 Eastern European countries remains below the national minimum wage. Even in regions such as Western Europe and Asia/Oceania that span some bigger football markets, average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wage levels. Fifpro was unable to provide average salaries per league as the report focused on regions rather than individual countries. Average contract lengths have also increased from about one year in 2017 to 19 months, but many players still face periods without guaranteed income. "Only two-thirds of players are paid for the whole 12 months," said Culvin. "There's a lot of players who are on seven-month contracts, nine-month contracts, which means that they've got to work to make up the rest of the calendar year." She believes the rapid commercial growth of women's football has helped to obscure some of these realities. Despite the rapid growth of England's Women's Super League, Fifpro says conditions at the top of the game could obscure the reality for many players elsewhere. Culvin warned the economic boom in women's football could "mask some of the realities that players face and actually endure on a day-to-day basis". The report also found that 24% of players had experienced late payments over the past two seasons, while 42% were not provided with a pension. Culvin argues there is a growing disconnect between expectations and reality. "I think there's a wake-up call needed for the ecosystem, that our players are suffering and that there is not the kind of wraparound support and accountability that's needed for players," she said. However, not all trends were negative. One significant improvement being felt in the game concerns parenthood. In 2017, nearly half of respondents considering leaving the game early said wanting a family could drive them out of football. That figure has now fallen to 19%, which Fifpro attributes in part to maternity regulations that were introduced by Fifa in 2021 and updated two years ago. "What we've conclude

title: Man denies racist murder of scientist in Dundee
description: Kyler Rattray, 21, is alleged to have repeatedly struck Dr Fortune Gomo with a knife last year.
body: Dr Fortune Gomo completed her PhD at the University of Dundee in 2022 A man has denied the racially-aggravated murder of a scientist on a Dundee street. Kyler Rattray, 21, is accused of attacking Dr Fortune Gomo in South Street in July last year. Prosecutors allege the 39-year-old academic was repeatedly struck on the body with a knife and that the attack was aggravated by prejudice relating to race, colour nationality or ethnicity. The trial is due to begin on 5 January 2028 at the High Court in Dundee and is expected to last eight days. Rattray also faces a separate charge of illegally having a knife in a public place. The case called at a virtual hearing at the High Court in Glasgow earlier. Dr Gomo was found fatally injured on the street and was treated by paramedics at the scene, but never recovered. At the time, Police Scotland acknowledged that her death had caused great shock throughout Dundee. She was originally from Mutare in eastern Zimbabwe, had graduated with a PhD from Dundee University, and had recently started working for Scottish Water. title: Watch: CCTV shows people take cover as missile hits Riyadh airport
description: Footage from inside the airport shows the moment the strike hit on Saturday.
body: This video can not be played Two strikes on the international airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh have left 14 dead and more than 300 injured. There have been a series of other attacks earlier in the week. CCTV footage from inside King Khalid International Airport shows people taking cover as one of the missiles hit the building on Saturday. The Houthis in Yemen say they were behind the strikes and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace. The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. title: Sinn Féin ministers facing no-confidence vote after Drumcree dispute
description: The motion against Michelle O'Neill and three other Sinn Féin ministers will be debated after receiving the backing of unionist parties last week.
body: The motions against Michelle O'Neill (centre), Liz Kimmins (left), John O'Dowd and Caoimhe Archibald (right) will be debated after it received the backing of unionist parties last week The first minister will face a no-confidence vote at Stormont on Monday over her handling of the Drumcree parading dispute. The motion against Michelle O'Neill and three other Sinn Féin ministers will be debated after it received the backing of unionist parties last week. However the attempt to oust them will fail as it requires cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the assembly. It comes amid a major political row over a planned Orange Order march in Portadown, County Armagh. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Michelle O'Neill has defended her actions, saying she was "proud" to stand with the residents O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians have been heavily criticised by unionists for joining protests which have blocked the parade from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry. O'Neill has defended her actions, saying she was "proud" to stand with the residents and adding that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it". The exclusion motions have also been submitted against John O'Dowd, Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmins. O'Dowd, who is also the finance minister, told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme on Monday that it was not Sinn Féin who brought the Drumcree dispute "back to the table". "Those who seek to drag us backwards need to be stood up against." He added that he will go to Stormont to work with other parties. "I am seeking engagements around the budget, I want to work with parties to make a better society for everyone." TUV assembly member Timothy Gaston (left) alongside party leader Jim Allister The no-confidence motions were tabled by Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) assembly member Timothy Gaston, who has branded O'Neill the "first minister of lawlessness". The motions gained the required 30 signatures with the backing of assembly members from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP). Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme, the TUV leader, Jim Allister, said: "Let me be absolutely clear, of course this debate today is not going to succeed because the absurd system whereby it needs cross community support, but that accentuates the pressure on the DUP to be seen to do something because as things stand lawbreakers are sitting in our executive." Motions of no-confidence in the assembly are not binding even if a majority of MLAs vote in favour of them, and cannot automatically force a minister from office. Gavin Robinson said that removing Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister would "punish everybody else" The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party. Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister. The DUP leader Gavin Robinson told Good Morning Ulster: "When somebody breaks the law they should be punished for breaking the law." He said that removing Little-Pengelly would "punish everybody else". "Colleagues and I have discussed continually about options that are available to us. "It is absurd that there will be a motion of no confidence, which we know before it starts, whether it concludes successfully, we know it can't because of the system that we have." Robinson added that he is "not in the territory" to "destabilise". However his party colleague, Carla Lockhart, who represents the Upper Bann constituency in Westminster, said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont and the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill from her position. Robinson said that when the party comes to a "consensus, that is our position". He added that Lockhart has "the right to stand up for her constituents". DUP MP Carla Lockhart said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont Ahead of the debate at Stormont, the leader of the opposition, the SDLP's Matthew O'Toole said politicians were entitled to express their views but needed to move forward once proceedings had concluded. O'Toole said attention should then return to issues affecting people across Northern Ireland, adding: "If they work in the public sector, they might be waiting on a pay rise. They might have a family member stuck on a waiting list." UUP leader Jon Burrows said removing ministers would not resolve the situation UUP leader Jon Burrows has said withdrawing ministers from the executive is not the answer. Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's Nolan Show, he said: "I will not remove Robbie Butler at this late stage, because to do so would affect the people of Northern Ireland in all the work he is doing." Burrows said he was instead calling for changes to Stormont's rules. He said there should be "proper accountability mechanisms" to hold ministers who breach the pledge of office to account. title: DP World Tour to refuse LIV players in 2027 season
description: The DP World Tour will not allow LIV Golf players to compete at its events in the 2027 season.
body: Tyrrell Hatton is one player who has been able to play on the DP World Tour and LIV Golf circuit The DP World Tour will not allow any player who signs up to LIV Golf next season to be a member of its circuit in 2027. The European tour says players must "make a choice" regarding where they play and has taken a significantly tougher stance than it has done in recent seasons. Players must be members of the DP World Tour to be able to play for Europe in the Ryder Cup. Deadlines for both tours are in the next five weeks, although there remains uncertainty surrounding LIV Golf's future, despite it securing a possible $300m in funding as it attempts to restructure. "Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, CEO of the DP World Tour, told BBC Sport. "We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by. "Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour." In previous years, conditional releases were struck with some top players - including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton - enabling them to play on both the DP World Tour and LIV. Next year, however, players will be asked to disclose which tours they intend to play on, and their answer will be taken into account when deciding on their membership. Rahm to leave LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0 Around 15 LIV players, including Rahm, Hatton, Victor Perez and Tom McKibbin, have "status" with the DP World Tour, meaning they have eligibility under one of the membership categories. Other LIV players, like Joaquin Niemann and Thomas Pieters, do not have such status so would either need to go through qualifying school or sign agreements with the DP World Tour whereby they would receive invitations to a set number of tournaments. However, those agreements would only be available to players who were not part of LIV in the future. BBC Sport has been told that the DP World Tour will not accept membership from anyone intending to play on what is being called LIV 2.0. If players do not disclose their intentions to play LIV and go on to do so, that will be considered grounds on which to have their membership terminated. LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September as it attempted to restructure, following the withdrawal of its multi-billion dollar funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. Last week, it announced it had secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season. John Rahm is the first high profile LIV player to say he won't continue in the league While the DP World Tour agreed to grant conditional releases with nine players this season, it is understood the change for 2027 is predominantly down to LIV offering players equity in future and a feeling this is incompatible with the European tour being a members organisation. However, it also comes at a time when the DP World Tour's strategic alliance with the PGA Tour is being negotiated, so the move likely reflects a desire to put itself in the best position possible in those discussions. Players will have until 16 November to sign up to the DP World Tour for next year. Under the terms of its court-supervised restructuring process, LIV Golf needs to sign players up by 25 October. Ted Goldthorpe, head of BC Partners Credit, told BBC Sport last week he was "confident" LIV would have a "critical mass" of players. But since then two-time major winner Rahm has said he will not continue playing on the LIV tour. Lawyers representing a number of other players, including fellow major winners Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith, sought clarification from the court that rejection of contracts would equate to "termination", enabling players to hold discussions with third parties about their futures. Richard Bland is currently the only player to have stated publicly a desire to play on LIV 2.0. However, Perez indicated last month he hoped there would be a future for the league. title: Russell Brand arrives at court for start of rape trial
description: The 51-year-old actor and comedian denies charges of rape and sexual assault against six women.
body: Russell Brand arrived at court on Monday for the start of his trial wearing a navy suit and sunglasses Russell Brand has arrived at court for the start of his rape and sexual assault trial. The 51-year-old comedian and actor is facing several charges of rape and sexual assault against six women, which are alleged to have occurred between 1999 and 2009. The trial at Southwark Crown Court, which could last up to 10 weeks, is expected to begin with the process of jury selection on Monday morning. Brand pleaded not guilty to the charges during pre-trial hearings. The comedian and actor arrived at court wearing a navy suit and sunglasses, accompanied by his wife Laura. There was a large media presence at the court for the start of the trial, which is expected to last up to 10 weeks. He has been charged with three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault. Brand arrived at Southward Crown Court with his wife Laura He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music. Brand went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting. title: Wildlife park closed for third day after tiger attack
description: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains shut after a man was fatally attacked by a tiger on Saturday.
body: The park was evacuated after the attack on Saturday afternoon Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed for a third day as investigations continue into the death of a man who was attacked by a tiger when he entered its enclosure. The park near Doncaster was closed over the weekend after reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway on Saturday afternoon. An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. A park spokesperson said: "Due to the events over the weekend, the park will remain closed today. Thank you for your understanding." South Yorkshire Police said the man died at the scene and his family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said. Yorkshire Wildlife Park said the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. Cars could be seen coming and going from the park earlier, but there were no visitors. In a message to ticket holders on Monday morning, Yorkshire Wildlife Park said anyone with a booking would be contacted within the next five days to reschedule. The park remains closed to visitors Dr Campbell Murn, a previous member of the government's zoo expert committee and lecturer at the University of Reading, said while it was a tragic incident, determined people could get inside zoo enclosures. "I view it in the same way a determined thief will get into somebody's house or somebody's car and despite the best security systems and enclosures sometimes these things happen," he said. "One of the fundamental approaches of a modern zoo is to give people a wildlife experience and keep them safe so they can learn and they can enjoy being near the animals, but keeping a safety distance that is relevant but not making it too heavy handed." Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Murn said public safety was an "enormous consideration" for zoo standards in the UK. An eyewitness took this photograph of the tiger minutes before the incident A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an "urgent review" into "how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next". Born Free's co-founder Will Travers said: "Putting dangerous wild animals on public display in zoos and safari parks creates a false relationship with humans. "Visitors are encouraged to get up close and personal - that is a deeply unnatural situation and not without risk."
