title: AI spots nearly 19,000 'shocking' road offences
description: Captured images include a front-seat passenger holding a small child on her lap without a seatbelt.
body: One image showed a front-seat passenger holding a small child with no seatbelt on An artificial intelligence trial identified almost 19,000 potential driving offences in Birmingham and Wolverhampton in just two weeks. West Midlands mayor Richard Parker called the findings "shocking" saying the number of drivers putting themselves and others at risk was "far higher than we expected". The trial used AI-powered cameras outside Ladywood and Fallings Park fire stations in March to identify potential seatbelt and mobile phone offences. The images they captured included a front-seat passenger holding a small child on their lap without a seatbelt and a driver holding a mobile phone with both hands. Dozens of images showed children travelling without age-appropriate restraints. At Ladywood, the technology identified 11,045 potential seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone offences. At Fallings Park, it recorded 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences. Parker said: "The number of people risking their own lives and the lives of others, including some very young children, is frankly shocking and far higher than we expected. "I've met families who have lost loved ones to reckless driving," he added. "They never recover from those tragedies." He said he would use "every resource available" to make roads safer as the findings were reviewed. The trial was funded by the West Midlands Combined Authority working with the police and fire service. No enforcement is planned as a result of the trial, which was intended to establish the potential scale of mobile phone use and failures to use child restraints. Simon Foster, West Midlands police and crime commissioner and chairman of the region's road safety partnership board, said the findings were "deeply concerning". "We are closely evaluating these trial results to consider how this advanced AI technology can be deployed for future police enforcement," he added. "We will use every effective tool at our disposal to ensure our roads are safer." Mat MacDonald, the West Midlands road safety commissioner, said mobile phone use at the wheel and failing to wear a seatbelt were two of the leading causes of death and serious injury on the region's roads. The WMCA said road safety data for last year showed mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths on UK roads while unfastened seatbelts were linked to 133 deaths. About 2,000 drivers a year in the West Midlands are fined and given penalty points for using a phone while driving. title: Ray Quinn says baby boy was 'born sleeping'
description: The former Brookside actor says it is "heartbreaking" that his son Rio was stillborn on 20 August.
body: The actor and singer said he hopes sharing the news will help other couples Singer and actor Ray Quinn has spoken of the "heartbreaking" loss of his baby son, Rio, who was stillborn. The former Brookside actor said his son Rio was "born sleeping" on 20 August at Liverpool Women's University Hospital. Quinn said his son was a "beautiful boy" as he paid tribute on his Instagram page. He said: "No words will ever be enough, just a lot of indescribable feelings." Ray Quinn shared the picture of his wife and baby boy, Rio, on social media Quinn married dance teacher Emily Fletcher in October 2023. His statement on social media continued: "The last few weeks have been a lot but our saving grace has been each other." The X-Factor star thanked staff at Liverpool Women's Hospital for their care. He said it had been "the most heartbreaking week of our lives" but that medical staff had helped make "special memories with our boy to keep forever". The couple have also talked about the loss on their YouTube channel The Quinns. In the episode Emily said: "Pregnancy and having children is a very special thing, but it does have risks and things can happen that you least expect. That's happened to us." The 34-year-old described how, when a nurse broke the news that there was no heartbeat during a scan at six months, their "whole world stopped". "All our hopes and taking our little baby back to our renovated house just crashed before us", she added. The couple said they were sharing their story in the hope "it helps those out there who find themselves in a similar situation to us." Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place from 9 to 15 October. title: Teen who discovered her painting talent in garden shed competes for TV art prize
description: Makenzy Beard discovered her talent after she decided to try out her mother's old paint brushes.
body: Makenzy Beard paints at her studio on Gower after discovering her talent while deciding to use her mother's old brushes in the garden shed A 19-year-old painter from Swansea who has sold artwork for tens of thousands of pounds is due to appear on the TV art competition, Portrait Artist of the Year. Makenzy Beard discovered her talent for painting during the Covid lockdown after she decided to try out her mother's old paint brushes in the garden shed. She said she felt "up for the challenge" of painting celebrity sitters in front of TV cameras and a highly respected panel of judges. Beard is currently putting together her second collection of work, which will include about 20 paintings that reflect her "view of the world" and interest in philosophy. Makenzy says her latest collection contains pieces which have a "deeper meaning" as she tries to draw attention to issues which matter to her After completing several portraits against the clock, the winner of the competition on SkyArts gets a £10,000 commission to paint British actor and musician Damian Lewis for the National Portrait Gallery. "I suppose I wanted to give it a go. I've watched the show and it seemed like a challenge, so I thought why not," Beard said. Since displaying one of her first portraits at the Royal Academy Summer Show in 2021, she has sold paintings for thousands of pounds and raised more than £45,000 for charitable causes. "I don't think I had time to reflect much on what I thought of the work because I was having a lot of opinions from other people. Makenzy Beard paints a celebrity sitter during her time on the Portrait Artist of the Year show "As I've got older, people still, I suppose, have some nice things [to say] about my work, because it's not about my age but the work itself." Beard said her latest works have more depth, especially since developing a keen interest in philosophy. She said: "I think having not been taught, everything I do is quite intuitive. I just do what I feel like and that's always changing. "This collection tries to capture things I see in the world and [they] have little messages." Art enthusiasts from across the world have expressed interest in the teen's work with pieces in her first collection selling for tens of thousands of pounds Entering the art world at a young age has been a "crazy" experience, which she said she had found "difficult to understand", especially with some of her pieces selling for tens of thousands of pounds. "It's difficult to navigate because unlike lots of things where you work hard and kind of get results and do well, with art it's so subjective," she said. "You can work hard and absolutely love something and if someone else doesn't, it doesn't mean it doesn't have value." Beard's latest collection covers a variety of topics including animal cruelty, child poverty and mental health. There are also some "light hearted" takes on some of life's challenges. Beard says her latest works have more depth "I do see the potential for my work to become more political as I get older but I have no desire to force my work into a direction. "If things come to me and I want it to come through in my art then it will, but I don't have a headstrong vision in terms of political stuff. "I still feel a little bit young, too naive to project any of my opinions on these things." Beard said she's looking to partner with a gallery in order to display her latest collection. title: Niners go 5-0 and a rare tie - five things from NFL week five
description: The San Francisco 49ers and the Minnesota Vikings maintain their perfect starts to the season on another gripping Sunday in the NFL.
body: The San Francisco 49ers went to 5-0 but the New York Giants' game against the Washington Commanders ended in a farcical tie Week five in the NFL was a wild one from the very first play in London to overtime in Atlanta 14 hours later. Sunday started with a disallowed touchdown and two players being ejected on the first play at Tottenham, before two field goals in the final eight seconds helped the Jacksonville Jaguars beat the Philadelphia Eagles. That was a sign of things to come as frantic finishes became a theme, including a farcial overtime climax in Washington as the Commanders tied with the New York Giants. Big wins for the Green Bay Packers, New England Patriots and Detroit Lions moved that trio to 3-2 for the season, while the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings became the first teams to go 5-0. Here's the pick of Sunday's week five action. San Francisco beat Super Bowl champions Seattle 32-29 in a typically brutal contest between divisional rivals, with the Niners having defensive star Dre Greenlaw ejected early on for a headbutt on Ernest Jones, who was not wearing a helmet, on the sidelines. Both defences are elite and forced a season-high seven turnovers in the game, with the 49ers in particular taking advantage by scoring three touchdowns from theirs. The 21 points off turnovers was the most Seattle have allowed in a decade. Brock Purdy eventually got San Francisco over the line thanks to new wide receiver Mike Evans, who had 113 yards receiving and a touchdown, taking some great catches late on. The only team to have a top-five scoring offence and defence, the 49ers again have injury problems this season, but if Evans stays fit he could be the missing piece in the puzzle. San Francisco are now 5-0 for the third time under head coach Kyle Shanahan. They made the Super Bowl on both previous occasions and, if they keep finding ways to win, they have every chance again. The Minnesota Vikings are also 5-0 after another defensive masterclass from Brian Flores' unit in their 23-13 win at the slumping New Orleans Saints. With wins over the Saints (1-4), Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) and Miami Dolphins (0-5), we will know more about the Vikings after their bye, but allowing only 13 points a game will always give you a chance. There was a comedy of errors at the end of the Washington Commanders' 27-27 tie with the New York Giants as both teams fluffed their lines with victory within their grasp. The Giants scored two late touchdowns to force overtime but, when within range of a winning field goal, they ran the ball with Cam Skattebo, who fumbled to lose possession. Washington then had the game at their mercy in the dying seconds but, instead of taking the kick, ran a play - and ran out of time. With play-calling like that, neither team deserved to win. The Baltimore Ravens showed them both how it is done as quarterback Lamar Jackson's back-up Tyler Huntley earned a 30-23 overtime victory at the Atlanta Falcons, throwing a touchdown with 40 seconds left of regulation time before running in the game-winner in the extra period. The Ravens are 4-1 and lurking. More poor finishing came in the rain in New York as the Cleveland Browns missed an extra point and then Corey Bojorquez fumbled a late punt which the Jets turned into the winning touchdown. Although it was messy at times, the Jets seem to have a fine defence, with eight sacks on Deshaun Watson in their 17-12 success. Jameis Winston and Jayden Daniels traded touchdowns but neither could force the win The 201st meeting of the NFL's oldest current rivalry went emphatically Green Bay's way with Jordan Love showing the importance of a franchise quarterback as the Packers pounded the Chicago Bears 31-7. Love let it fly with 367 yards passing, including touchdowns of 42 and 53 yards to Christian Watson, while the Bears - without starter Caleb Williams - struggled with Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum under centre. Williams stunned the Packers twice last season with fourth-quarter comebacks, including one in the play-offs, but Chicago are not the same threat without him. They need their top man back from his hamstring injury as soon as possible. After a tough start, last week's win over the Buffalo Bills was a huge confidence boost for the New England Patriots, as they showed with a 45-17 hammering of the Las Vegas Raiders. Drake Maye has his critics after last season's Super Bowl loss, but 374 yards, four touchdown passes and one rushing score against a Las Vegas defence allowing 21 points a game previously was a huge effort. It was a similar story with the Detroit Lions, who also hung 45 points on the Arizona Cardinals thanks to a monster game from running back Jahmyr Gibbs, who had 207 yards and two touchdowns. Joining that pair on 3-2 is Aaron Rodgers and his Pittsburgh Steelers after a 34-22 win over the Indianpolis Colts. Rodgers threw three touchdown passes to make it 582 in his career and move above the great Peyton Manning into third on the all-time list. Only Tom Brady (737) and Drew Brees (608) have more. With 166 regular-season wins, Rodgers sits fifth on that list but, more importantly, his team look in decent shape in his final season. Only Tom Brady and Drew Brees have thrown more touchdowns than Aaron Rodgers (centre) in NFL history We are already at the stage when struggling teams may be looking at top spot in next year's NFL Draft. Three teams are now 0-5, with the Los Angeles Chargers, Tennessee Titans and Miami Dolphins all losing again. Jim Harbaugh's Chargers are the big disappointment of the season. They suffered another self-inflicted defeat as poor play-calling and execution cost them the lead at the Denver Broncos. They are 0-5 for the first time in 23 years. title: Indian opposition leaders to march to top court to demand election chief resign
description: The march follows a chaotic weekend in Delhi which saw thousands of protesters being detained by police.
body: Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi holds up a copy of India's Constitution at a press conference on Monday India's opposition parties are set to march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud. This will be the latest in a series of demonstrations in Delhi, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital. Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained. Opposition parties allege that under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, India's voter rolls are being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the charge. The opposition lawmakers want to submit a memorandum to Chief Justice Surya Kant, but he has told reporters he declined the meeting citing "certain reasons". He did not provide the reasons, but media reports citing the letter have said that he pointed out that some of the issues the opposition wanted to raise with him were also pending before the court. The BBC has not seen the letter. "Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law," he told reporters. Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, has called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march. In a press conference on Monday, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to the Chief Justice, laying out their concerns with Kumar's alleged conduct and with the contentious electoral roll revision. He said that Kant had asked them to file a petition, which they would do at the end of their march. Authorities in Delhi have announced heavy restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some key metro stations. There is also heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march. Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi. On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down. The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened. But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut down and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters. Protesters holding on to a woman as security personnel try to take her away The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke has returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders, however, did not join the protests on Sunday but have said they will seek a new protest date from the police. Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. The BBC also captured visuals, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi Police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters. In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists. "Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said. Congress leader Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up. BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were. title: Kartal takes top-50 scalp with Wuhan win
description: Britain's Sonay Kartal continues her impressive form since returning from injury by beating Anhelina Kalinina in straight sets to reach the second round of the Wuhan Open.
body: Sonay Kartal has slipped to 170th in the world rankings after her back injury Sonay Kartal continued her impressive form since returning from injury by beating Anhelina Kalinina to reach the Wuhan Open second round. The British number five reached the third round at the Beijing Open earlier this month in her first WTA tournament for six months, having been sidelined with a stress fracture in her back. The 24-year-old followed that up by defeating Ukraine's Kalinina 7-5 6-3 in an hour and 31 minutes. World number 170 Kartal will face Swiss ninth seed Belinda Bencic next. Kartal returned to action last month for Great Britain at the Billie Jean King Cup team event, where she narrowly lost to Czech Marie Bouzkova, who sat 26th in the world rankings. Wins over Spain's Andrea Lazaro Garcia and Wang Xinyu followed for Kartal in Beijing, before she lost to Armenia's Alina Charaeva. Against world number 48 Kalinina, Kartal served four aces and won 23 of 30 points when landing her first serve. She sealed her spot in the last-32 stage at the third time of asking after Kalanina saved two match points. Zheng Qinwen withdrew from her home tournament in Wuhan after becoming the first Chinese player to win the China Open. In a statement, Zheng said she would not be competing because her "body is feeling very fatigued" after "an intense run of matches". Zheng underwent elbow surgery last year and had struggled with form and fitness over the past 12 months, before a recent upturn led to her triumph in Beijing. title: The 'Kane-esque' striker Spurs may regret letting go
description: Will Lankshear's positioning, finishing and poacher's instinct have made him an instant hit at Riverside Stadium – and a cause of lament at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.
body: Will Lankshear has scored in all but one of Middlesbrough's home matches this season Leaping high, six yards out, to nod in Tommy Conway's cross from the left wing, Will Lankshear notched his ninth goal in 12 games for Middlesbrough. It is that positioning, finishing and poacher's instinct, earning Boro a 1-0 win against Wolves on Saturday, that has made Lankshear an instant hit at Riverside Stadium – and a cause of lament at Tottenham Hotspur. Lankshear joined Boro from Spurs in the summer on a five-year contract in a deal that could rise to a club record buy of £20m. Since then, he has scored as many goals in all competitions as Spurs' combined team. His old side, despite snatching a draw at Manchester United a few hours after Lankshear's latest winner, remain in the Premier League relegation zone while Boro sit in the Championship's automatic promotion places. Dominic Solanke's last-minute goal at Old Trafford was the first league goal scored by a Tottenham forward in five months. It is enough to make Spurs fans despair. "A lot of fans are wondering why he was sold," Ali Speechly, co-chair of the Women of the Lane supporters' group, told BBC Sport. "It was likely to do with money - his sell-on price is relatively high, so let's cash in on him. "I was definitely disappointed. Given how badly we have started this season, as a fan it feels like the wrong decision." Amid a multi-million pound summer splurge, Spurs allowed Lankshear to leave for an initial fee worth about £10m, with an additional £10m due in add-ons based on various clauses. Follow Middlesbrough on BBC Sounds Pre-match, post-match and topical Boro content Subscribe and listen for everything you love about Boro Boro saw off competition around the Championship, and in Europe, to sign the 21-year-old who impressed at Oxford United in the second tier last season, scoring 12 league goals on loan for a relegated side. Good form for a young player, but not so compelling he had to go straight into the Spurs first team. "If you are a young kid at a club where you are not getting any first-team football and you get the opportunity to go and play men's football, you should go," former Spurs goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Sport. "The academies are great and Premier League 2 is a great feeder for the first team, but if you are 21, 22 or 23 and still mostly playing in the under-23s then you have missed the boat. "Getting first-team football is the best grounding you can get for a young footballer, getting the opportunity to play in the first team, regardless of what league it is. Will has been given this opportunity, and he is taking it." Lankshear scored 23 goals for Tottenham's U23 team in the 2023–24 Premier League 2 season and played for the senior side in the 2024-25 Europa League campaign – most notably scoring then getting sent off against Galatasaray. But amid a churn of players and managers at Spurs, he has moved on – and Boro fans couldn't be happier. Middlesbrough have built a reputation in recent years of providing a springboard for promising youngsters. Most notably, Morgan Rogers spent six months at Riverside Stadium before joining Aston Villa, and the rest is history. Not only that, but Boro - who missed out on promotion last season after scoring only once in three play-off games - badly needed a skilful, physical presence who could finish the multitude of chances made by Kim Hellberg's creative but blunt side. Lankshear scored on his England under-21 debut, against Kazakhstan in September "Boro was a team that made a boatload of chances, and he knew he would be able to get on the end of them," BBC Tees commentator Mark Drury told BBC Sport. "But what people have been impressed with is his instinctive finishing - one touch, just being in the right place. It's simple but not a lot of people know how to be there at the right time, to give yourself the highest percentage chance. "He's taller and stockier than he might look from the sidelines, and he is only 21. He seems to have the all-round package - good with both feet and in the air." A 6ft 2in English striker with a deadly finishing touch, who came through at Spurs before learning his trade in the Football League. Remind you of anyone? "I can understand the comparisons with Harry Kane," said Robinson. "He has headed down a similar career path to Harry and, physically, he has a similar stature as well. "Like Kane, he looks like a player who is developing a little later, compared to others who are Premier League regulars before the end of their teens. "You look at him and the career path he is on; it is a very similar one to the one Harry Kane has been on, and that is a big positive. There is no substitute for playing in the first team somewhere, regardless of what level you are playing at." Like Kane, Lankshear also had early career setbacks. Initially at Arsenal's academy, he was released and signed with Sheffield United before being picked up by Spurs for £2m when he was 17. He also had hit-and-miss loan spells. An unremarkable stint at West Brom was followed by a more fruitful spell with Oxford. "Harry Kane didn't always have brilliantly successful loan spells, they are not always a marker of a player," says Speechly. "He didn't do anything remarkable, but it is unfortunate as we are not scoring goals. It is painful to see. "I don't think we will ever get another Kane, but there are definitely similarities. He is a real poacher and has a strong work ethic. It is very Kane-esque." Lankshear helped Spurs to win the Europa League in 2024-25 Tottenham do not have the right to immediately bring Lankshear back next summer. Clauses in the deal give them the right to be notified of and match any future accepted bid that Middlesbrough receive, and Spurs will get 20% of any profit on any future sale. title: Stormont 'failing to plan' for ageing population
description: Politicians are urged to prepare as over-65s are projected to outnumber children in NI by next year.
body: Projections suggest the number of people aged over 65 in Northern Ireland will overtake the number of children by 2027 Northern Ireland's leaders have not absorbed the implications of a rapidly ageing society and are continuing to "plan for a population from a previous era" the Commissioner for Older People Siobhan Casey has warned. In a new report, Casey said: "The ageing population is here, whether we are ready for it or not." The report draws on official population projections which suggest that next year the number of people aged over 65 will overtake the number of children. Northern Ireland's population as a whole is projected to fall slightly over the next 25 years but the population aged over 65 is projected to increase by almost 45%. Casey said that is a positive reflection of improvements in life expectancy but brings challenges which need "long-term planning and coordinated action". She said the healthcare system is already experiencing the impacts of an ageing society but there will also be implications for housing, public transport and workplaces. "An ageing population is not simply a health and social care issue. It will affect almost every aspect of life," the report said. "The reality is that Northern Ireland has yet to develop the coordinated and long-term approach needed to prepare for the scale of demographic change that lies ahead." Siobhan Casey was appointed as Northern Ireland's commissioner for older people in March 2025 Ageing populations are an issue for governments across the world. A key consideration is the economic impact of what is known as the "dependency ratio". It is a way of assessing how many children and retired people are dependent on the economic output of the working age population. In 2024, for every 1,000 people of working age in Northern Ireland there were 586 dependants. That is projected to rise to 614 per 1,000 in mid-2049. That is an increase of about 5% but more significant is the shift in the composition of that dependency. For children, the ratio declines from 316 to 248, while for pensioners it rises from 269 to 366 per 1,000 - a near 36% jump in the ratio of pensioners to workers. If the ratio of workers to pensioners continues to compress, the tax base required to fund rising healthcare and pension costs becomes increasingly strained. That is a challenge beyond Stormont's competence and will have to be tackled at a national government level. Casey suggests that the areas under Stormont control have so far been approached in a piecemeal way. "At some level, government officials and elected representatives acknowledge that our society is changing," she said. "However, despite their well-intentioned support and the fact that the demographic trends and issues outlined in this report have long been foreseen, the finalised Pro-gramme for Government document contains one reference to an 'ageing population', which was hugely disappointing." title: Why some have no choice but to pay costly oil prices
description: The rural communities vulnerable to heating oil prices rises as the weather gets colder.
body: Many heating oil customers are having to buy early in preparation for the colder months As the temperature drops, some of us will start putting the heating on but for the one-and-a-half million people across the UK that are not on the mains gas network - and who are relying instead on heating oil - that decision may give them pause. The vast majority of those people live in rural locations. The heating oil market is unregulated, unlike gas and electricity, so any changes in the global price quickly gets passed on to customers. Tensions in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine are two issues currently both affecting supply which is causing prices to rise. Author shares how books have 'magical way' of reaching you when struggling Accessible playground to 'allow all children to play' 'What terminal cancer has taught me about life' Until March this year, the price was quite stable at about 60p per litre (ppl) but when the war in Iran started in March, it jumped to a high of 134ppl. After a dip in the past few months, it is rising once again and it currently stands at 111ppl, according to price comparison site Boiler Juice. The BBC has spoken to a number of business and homeowners across the West about how that rise is affecting them. Peter Mason lives in Minety, in north Wiltshire, where most homes rely on heating oil. "I'm getting toward the end of the tank and need to top up for winter... it will be over £550," he said. Mason said that last year "it was about £300 to fill up - it is horrendous". He said: "The price goes up and down. It can vary plus or minus £50 but it has never been as high as it is today. "It means I'll have to eek out what I spent my money on. I'm retired, its not like I can change jobs. "I have to be really careful and pull money out of savings." Most tanks hold 500 litres of oil and would cost about £550 to fill currently Dylan Williams owns van-driving business Van & I of Monmouth, Wales and regularly operates in the Forest of Dean, Stroud and South Gloucestershire. The 51-year-old said he was currently paying more for fuel than he ever had in the three years of running his business. He said he had had to put the prices of his services up to offset the rise. At the start of the year he would pay between £120 and £130 for a full tank, he said, but that had now gone up to £160. "It's ever increasing, ever worrying - keeping an eye on the news, keeping an eye on the diesel prices," he said. "I mean I've got fuel cards... you don't pay the pump prices, you pay the fuel card prices but it doesn't make much a difference these days. "It's a few pence really." Tristan Holland (pictured with Mel Holland) runs a small team of community care workers Yvette Farrell, volunteer director for Dean Forest Kitchen, which cook fresh meals every day and delivers them to clients within the Forest of Dean, said they might have to increase prices as there's "not going to be much choice in the future". She said: "It's impacted us a lot because we work on a not-for-profit scenario so there is not a lot of wiggle room when it comes to increase in any expenses. "So the cost of fuel is really, really hitting the business hard and we're having to do our best to still keep going to our clients who are spread across a very rural area with no public transport. "But we have to take these meals to them because... they will not have somebody coming to see them during the day because they're so isolated." Tristan Holland, company director at TLC Support Service, manages a small team of community care workers who travel around Wotton-under-Edge and Dursley. Staff use their own vehicles and the company pays mileage at 55p per business mile. He said: "We had an increase in our fees back at the start of the year, just kind of taking into account all the extras that were coming in this year but even that does make it tight. "Everything has risen - the cost of the fuel, the training, even the uniforms that we purchased. "Everything has gone up and so we try to keep our services as affordable as we possibly can but there has to be a profit or else we just can't carry on going." The Iran war has disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and prices can rise or fall based on the words and actions of key political figures. It is thought prices could come down if there is a peace deal between the US and Iran. For people who rely on heating oil, it means feeling helpless. Richard Willan, who runs the Nadder Oil Buying Club in Wiltshire where more than 1,000 residents buy in bulk together to get a better price, said rural residents were increasingly vulnerable as the colder months set in. "We are watching to see what happens with (Donald) Trump in the mid-term elections in America, that might change things again," he said. The Competitions and Markets Authority (CMA) said heating oil customers in remote areas were too vulnerable to price shocks. CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell said: "Stronger safeguards are needed - including regulatory oversight and better support for vulnerable consumers as well as communities living in areas of the UK that are particularly exposed to higher and more volatile prices." As prices sit above 100ppl with the temperature falling, there are calls for more support for rural communities. Chief Executive of Action in Rural Communities England Corinne Pluchino said: "Without specific targeted support for heating oil and LPG users, thousands of rural people risk becoming the forgotten victims of the energy crisis." The organisation is asking the government to remove VAT on heating oil and LPG for six months in this month's budget. There are also locally-run support schemes like the Surviving Winter campaign run by a group of charities in Wiltshire which supported more than 3,000 people last year with the cost of heating. title: Teen 'detached from reality' to cope with return of aggressive cancer
description: Ethan found out his cancer had returned two weeks after successful treatment.
body: Ethan Griffiths, 14, was diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma in January A teenage boy with lymphoma says he coped with the return of his cancer by detaching himself from his illness, following advice from his father who also faced the disease. Ethan Griffiths, 14, was diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma, external - a type of fast-growing non-Hodgkin lymphoma (nHL) - in January, undergoing chemotherapy and being declared cancer-free in May, before having an "aggressive" relapse. The sport and gaming-mad teen, who underwent a new treatment being trialled in Bristol, came home to Maesteg cancer-free again in September. "Through it all I tried to stay as positive as I could," said Ethan, adding it was his dad Lloyd, also a cancer survivor, who was often "losing his head". News of the young rugby player's relapse came just two weeks after getting home from the hospital. "It was much more heartbreaking because I was getting back into everything," he said. "I went to school for half a day, and I was going to the gym quite regularly and getting back into fitness. "Then obviously to hear that news was really horrendous." His family faced "immeasurable stress" as Ethan joined a clinical trial at Bristol Royal Hospital Children for patients with B-cell nHL who had not responded to treatment or had relapsed. The UK-wide trial involving two new drugs, external offered just a 50% chance of success. Ethan got his first cap for West Wales Rugby League U14s "I would just switch off and he'd be losing his head next to me," Ethan said, nodding to his dad. His strategy for staying calm was simple: "Stick my earphones in, listen to music and try to fall asleep." Lloyd admitted his son probably got his "stoic side" from mum Rusanne. But the 56-year-old project manager said his own experience with a different type of lymphoma may have also helped. Ethan and his dad both had similar types of cancer He said: "One thing I said to Ethan from the start, probably when we first found out he'd relapsed, was: 'You're a passenger on this journey. You're not in control, you can't affect the outcome. So you have to kind of keep trying to detach yourself'." Lloyd said Ethan "seemed to detach himself entirely from this whole nine months in a way". "It's been quite inspiring really, how well he's managed to do that." Ethan said knowing what to expect from the treatment made it easier in some ways Ethan said in some ways undergoing treatment a second time was easier because he knew what to expect. But mentally he said it was harder. "Obviously you are thinking to yourself 'When is this all going to end?'" His latest treatment involved intensive chemotherapy followed by a transplant using stem cells collected earlier in the process. It meant spending several weeks in hospital in protective isolation. "I found it alright to be honest," Ethan said. Ethan Griffiths celebrated his first cancer-free diagnosis with his rugby teammates in May "It was just very boring because we were in isolation." Now home, Ethan is trying to get back to normal life. He said he still becomes "really tired just walking" and knows it will take time to get back to rugby. His immediate priority is to "build things up slowly with fitness" and catch up on schoolwork, initially through online lessons before gradually returning to the classroom. "When my health is back up, start going in for half days maybe and slowly build everything back up," Ethan said. title: Fire that killed two sisters was started by candles in flat below
description: Shikshya and Aanchal Subedi, who were 24 and 28, died in the fire at a block of flats in Aberdeen two years ago.
body: Sisters Aanchal, left, and Shikshya Subedi died in the fire A fire which killed two sisters in Aberdeen was started by candles in the flat below and spread rapidly, an investigation has found. Shikshya and Aanchal Subedi, who were 24 and 28, died at the block in the city's Back Hilton Road in January 2024. A joint police and fire investigation was launched into the blaze, but there were no suspicious circumstances found. It was already known the fire had spread from a neighbouring flat. A Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) incident report - which has now been obtained by BBC Scotland News through a Freedom of Information (FoI) request - reveals that the fire was started by candles. The report said a mattress in a lower flat bedroom ignited, and a lithium battery then caused the fire to spread rapidly. Family asks law firm to investigate blaze that killed two sisters The report said the victims were already thought to be dead when firefighters got to them, after being trapped by smoke. The fatal fire on the evening of 29 January 2024 led to a large emergency response. SFRS sent seven fire engines to the scene as well as specialist resources. The two sisters originally came from Nepal, but settled in Aberdeen with their family when they were children. An online fundraiser after their deaths later raised thousands of pounds. The fatal fire happened in early 2024 Last month, the family asked a law firm to help a search for answers about the blaze. Speaking for the first time since losing her younger sisters, Susan Subedi, 35, had said the family still did not know the full facts of what happened two years on. Susan said: "To say we are devastated doesn't come close to describing how we feel. "It's very hard to describe how losing Shikshya and Aanchal has affected our family. As sisters we were incredibly close. "They were only in their 20s, they had everything in life to look forward to but that's been taken away from them and from us." More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds "We won't laugh or talk or share another family celebration together and sometimes that's too much to bear. I miss them. I will always miss them." Legal firm Digby Brown said it would seek "all available evidence to help the Subedi family in their pursuit for answers". The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS) said it received reports of the deaths of the sisters at the time. A spokesperson said: "Following a thorough investigation the procurator fiscal concluded that no further action was required." title: Campaigners claim minister attempting to undermine 'Holiday Hunger Bill'
description: The education minister has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget.
body: Paul Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect Campaigners have accused the education minister of attempting to undermine a proposed Stormont law which would help poorer families with the cost of food. The Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation which is being brought forward by Sinn Féin assembly member Danny Baker. Givan has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget. The Holiday Meals Payment Bill, external would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals which would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food. The matter is due to be discussed in the assembly on Monday. Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him the power to delay implementation. He will need support from other parties for the amendments to be accepted. It is not clear if he will get that support, although the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has expressed reservations about the proposal. The payment would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food As it is based on school meals, the cost of the scheme would be on the Department of Education. It is modelled on the School Holiday Food Grant scheme introduced during the pandemic, which paid qualifying families £27 per child every fortnight. In April, Givan warned MLAs that his department did not have funding for the scheme, so they would be voting to cut education spending if they supported it. He has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect. A coalition of campaign groups, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) and Save the Children, say the amendments would mean "no guarantees about when, if ever, payments might begin". They added: "We are calling on all political parties and all MLAs to reject the amendments tabled by the education minister and support the bill as it currently stands." title: New rule, no change - has cricket missed a trick again with bad light?
description: More than 60 overs have been lost from the first Test between South Africa and Australia despite a change by the ICC. Has cricket missed a trick?
body: Australia are still in command of the first Test against South Africa, leading by 139 runs despite the early finishes It is one of cricket's oldest and most frustrating problems: bad light. A fascinating passage of play halted when things get too gloomy. The issue has reared its head again this week in the fascinating first Test between South Africa and Australia in Durban, wiping out more than 60 overs across the first three days. The fact a solution was added to cricket's rules just last week, an option so far unused around the world, only adds to the frustration. Australia veterans shine against South Africa Play is already starting at 09:30 local time in Durban. This is the first October Test at Kingsmead, where the sun sets shortly after 18:00 at this time of year on South Africa's eastern coast. Still, on day one, play was halted at 15:23 local time after clouds built. Only 65.2 of the scheduled 90 overs had been bowled and the players were unable to return. Day two was slightly better with play continuing until 16:25, but that finish was still 35 minutes earlier than it could have been. Day three's end came at 16:31. On each occasion, the first two sessions have been played in hot, sunny conditions, only for clouds to build in the afternoon - a familiar weather pattern in Durban. "Very quickly in the morning, as temperatures have risen inland as the sun heats the ground, a sea breeze has formed with winds coming from the sea into Durban," said BBC weather presenter Chris Fawkes. "This has increased humidity levels through the morning and brought some cloud in. As temperatures have started to fall again towards the evening, this has increased the relative humidity with the air getting increasingly saturated. "That has caused the cloud to get thicker and lower." Play is suspended Test cricket if the umpires decide light conditions are "dangerous or unreasonable" for the players Following a trial earlier in the year, the International Cricket Council amended its playing conditions to allow the pink ball to be used in Tests. It was supposed to help in these exact scenarios. Crucially, it does not allow a red ball to be switched for pink when the light becomes poor - something previously suggested by former England captain Michael Vaughan. Instead, if problems with the light are expected, it allows teams to agree before a Test starts to use the pink ball throughout. No such discussions were held between the Proteas and Australia before the Durban Test, however. The pink ball has been a fixture of day-night Tests because it is easier to see than the darker red in night-time conditions. Former South Africa bowler Shaun Pollock was part of the ICC committee which recommended the change and he believes there is a "stigma" around the pink ball in the game. "They say it moves too much," Pollock said. "If Australia were 124-6 [as they were on day one] and we were using the pink ball, everyone would have said it was the pink ball's fault. "If Australia were 124-6 and got to 390 [as they did in their first innings] everyone in South Africa would have said it was the pink ball's fault, that it got soft. "The pink ball would have meant we played 45 more overs of Test cricket and that is why I am keen to introduce it, and not just for day-night games." One narrative exists that the pink ball moves more under floodlights, though that is not backed up by ball tracking data. Instead, various batters have spoken about the pink ball being more difficult to see. Batting averages are lowest in the evening of day-night matches. Australia have also played in 15 of Test cricket's day-nighters - 10 more than anyone else. Unsurprisingly, the four leading wicket-takers in day-night matches are all Australians. Left-armer Mitchell Starc's haul of 89 wickets in 15 Tests has positioned him as the undisputed pink-ball king. You would not blame teams if they would rather face Australia with the red ball. Former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander said he prefers the idea of switching balls during the match if conditions require it, but that would raise questions over the Test's integrity. Is the potential injustice of one team having to face a pink ball outweighed by the need to get more action of the field? "They have to take it out of the hands of the players completed and enforce it from the umpires' point of view that the pink ball will become in play when the light has faded enough," Philander said. "You are always going to have the argument of who is ahead of the game. "I would like to see the ICC enforce it on to the officials to make that call." title: Orangemen and residents both back in court over Drumcree dispute
description: It follows a decision on Friday by the Secretary of State, Sir Chris Bryant, to ban the march, after receiving police advice.
body: Both sides have sought court intervention from differing perspectives The Drumcree parading dispute is back in front of judges on Monday, with Portadown Orangemen and Garvaghy Road residents involved in separate court cases. It follows a decision on Friday by the Secretary of State, Sir Chris Bryant, to ban the march, after receiving police advice. While the move has eased the immediate security situation, the issue remains unresolved. Both sides have sought court interventions from differing perspectives. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Although Sir Chris Bryant subsequently banned the parade, he did not "strike down" the commission's ruling, which still stands Portadown Orangemen are seeking permission to challenge the secretary of state's decision to ban the parade on a number of grounds. They include the police assessment of the situation. An emergency hearing took place at Belfast High Court on Saturday, but it was adjourned until Monday. The Court of Appeal is also set to rule on Monday whether the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition can contest the original Parades Commission determination allowing the parade. Although Sir Chris subsequently banned it, he did not "strike down" the commission's ruling, which still stands. The court heard arguments in the case last week. A lawyer for the residents' group claimed the commission's decision was flawed over how it weighed up the potential for disorder if the parade was permitted. The parade, by 35 members of Portadown District Orange Lodge, was meant to have gone ahead on 27 September. However, an unlawful protest blocked the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and a two-week stand-off developed. Chief Constable Jon Boutcher urged the secretary of state to intervene On Friday, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher urged the Secretary of State to intervene. Boutcher said "proportionate options" to police the parade had been "exhausted" and any operation to clear the route would have "catastrophic" consequences. Policing the stand-off has cost around £5m, largely due to officer overtime. title: What happens to sports kit that never gets worn?
description: A look at kit wastage in elite sport and what is being done to reduce it.
body: This video can not be played How Team GB is cutting down on kit wastage For an elite athlete, pulling on Olympic kit can be the reward for years of sacrifice. But some of that clothing never makes it out of the packaging. Inside a warehouse on England's south coast, boxes are stacked with pristine Team GB clothing from Paris 2024 and Milan Cortina 2026. Tracksuit bottoms, jackets, hoodies and T-shirts sit untouched. Among them are garments created for Olympic opening ceremonies. All of it is unworn. Commercial constraints can make excess stock difficult to shift at scale. Now a new partnership means hundreds of items of surplus Team GB clothing and unsold merchandise will be resold through a specialist platform, with proceeds supporting the British Olympic Association's (BOA) charity arm, the Team GB Foundation. The initial launch will include 700 items from Paris 2024. It is one way of giving sportswear a second life. But why does that surplus exist, and why can perfectly usable clothing be so difficult to pass on? The BOA is far from the only organisation dealing with excess kit – elite sport in general struggles with kit wastage. 5thread, a consultancy specialising in sustainability, estimates that up to 100,000 items of sports kit end up in UK landfill every year. "It is a huge issue and it's also a complex issue," says Joanna Czutkowna, director of 5thread and a doctoral researcher in sports apparel and the circular economy. "A lot of this kit is bought before they know which athletes are going to complete in the sport or the event. So there's a lot of excess stock generated at the point of order. "Also, the types of contracts that you get for this have something called value in kind, so it's not a transactional contract. There's almost an incentive to get free product." Czutkowna is describing practices across elite sport, rather than Team GB's arrangements. Performance requirements also complicate efforts to reduce waste. Athletes need clothing designed to help them compete, so reducing quantities or changing materials is not always straightforward. The total surplus is difficult to measure. Kit can remain in warehouses or athletes' garages without entering a waste stream where it can be counted. The issue extends across sport, from clubs to countries. European football governing body Uefa estimates that up to 60% of professional team apparel, external is disposed of at the end of the season, although this figure has not been independently verified. The obstacles are not to do with the condition of the clothing. "Contracts can prohibit reuse because they don't want it on the market or there might be a particular innovation that they want to hold back," Czutkowna says. Adam Stevens, co-founder of Kitround, the specialist resale platform working with Team GB among others, says sponsorship and supply agreements remain financially important to sport, but there are ways to respect them while allowing clothing to be used again. "There are an awful lot of people, whatever sport they do, whatever teams they support, who simply can't afford to buy new," he says. British kitesurfer Lily Young training off the coast of Weymouth For British kitesurfer Lily Young, who is targeting a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, the pressure to find a competitive edge can itself create surplus. Athletes preparing for major championships want to leave nothing to chance. "That does mean that we also end up with a lot of waste, a lot of things where you're like, 'this is basically brand new, but it's not quite good enough to maybe win'." Changes in sponsors can also leave athletes with clothing they can no longer wear. Young and fellow athletes have passed T-shirts to younger squad members and youth teams. Wetsuits and other equipment can also be passed on where they remain suitable. But equipment that no longer meets an elite athlete's needs could help someone else start, and more organisations such as Sail GP and the Royal Yachting Association are using specialist platforms to sell second-hand elite kit to the public at much lower prices. "We know that one of the main barriers to entry is cost," Young says. For Czutkowna, organisations need to think harder about how long their products can remain useful - and who could benefit from them. "A lot of this comes back to common sense," she says. "It's kind of a waste not, want not." Jen Rouse, managing director of the Team GB Foundation, says ordering is becoming more precise and the amount left over is reducing. Team GB is also considering producing some clothing without dates or event-specific names, so it could be used across more than one Olympic cycle. It is also exploring opportunities for athletes to return clothing they no longer need. She rejects the suggestion that excess clothing has previously simply accumulated unused. "It's not necessarily been sitting gathering dust in storage. It's always found a way out," she says. The partnership with Kitround creates another route, with sales supporting the Team GB Foundation. The aim is a circular economy for kit: keeping clothing and equipment in use through reuse, repair and resale. For Stevens, the principle behind finding kit another home is simple. "A kit was made to be worn. It was made to be out there on the field, on the water, in the pool, and it should be back out there. "That's really what underpins everything - making sure this kit doesn't go to landfill and that it can have a second life." title: Halloween 'bigger than Christmas', say businesses
description: From scare parks to pumpkin patches, Halloween is driving huge crowds and spending.
body: Catarina Vieira spends £150 to £200 on Halloween decorations and events Halloween has become so popular that some attractions now make more money from the spooky season than Christmas, operators say. From pumpkin festivals and haunted mazes to zombie experiences, businesses say demand for Halloween events has soared as the celebration grows from a single night into a month-long attraction. At Avon Valley Adventure Park near Bath, Halloween activities now generate around a third of the site's annual income. Founder Doug Douglas said: "Halloween is really important for us, it has surpassed Christmas." "We make half of our turnover in October, and one third comes from the week of Halloween alone," said David Gaze, owner at Chaplins fancy dress shop in Bristol. Retailers, farm attractions and scare parks say people are spending more on costumes, decorations and immersive experiences, helping to make October one of their busiest times of the year. Chaplins has been a staple in the city centre for 35 years, back when people wore fancy dress on New Year's Eve. "People don't do that so much anymore, now it's mostly for Halloween," Gaze said. Last year, it saw its busiest October to date, with customers individually spending an average of £40 on fancy costumes and accessories. "People are spending more and the week of Halloween is our busiest every year, we get queues outside the front door." "It's usually what people are seeing on TV that sells well. Some years ago it was boiler suits from Squid Game, everyone wanted that," he added. Guard suits from the Netflix show Squid Game have been a popular Halloween costume since the series came out in 2021 Halloween's growing popularity is also benefiting supermarkets and retailers selling sweets, decorations and party supplies. In a survey carried out in March by market researcher IGD, external, 36% of shoppers said they planned to celebrate Halloween this year, up from 27% in 2025. Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the British Retail Consortium, said at this time of year "retailers will be competing hard" as they see "greater demand for sweets and chocolate, as well as decorations and costumes". "Halloween has become an increasingly popular occasion for people to enjoy," he said. Scare attractions like FEAR, near Bath, now run throughout October And some like to start celebrations as early as possible, like Catarina Vieira, who lives in Swindon and started decorating her house last week. "I spend between £150 to £200 every year on Halloween," she said, adding that is mostly on decorations and thrill events. Vieira said feeling scared about monsters is a "fun escape" from the stresses of her everyday life as an A&E doctor. "I think having a holiday where you are scared about something that is 'real', instead of the usual daily mental pressures, touches me in a way." "It helps me escape reality for a bit, being scared about something that is tangibly scary, like monsters or bats," she added. Pumpkin patches are "a real festival", says operator Avon Valley Adventure Park But it is not just retail. Many farmers have found ways to diversify their land, by turning it into lucrative family attractions on Halloween. In October, pumpkin patches where you can pick your own pumpkin are high in demand, with popularity being largely driven by social media. Farms often charge an entry fee which can vary significantly, from around £2 to £15 per person, for children and adults alike. With the biggest whoppers selling for upwards of £15 a piece, a fun family day out pushing wheelbarrows full of pumpkins can become costly, yet some attractions sell out quickly. Heather Parry, managing agent at National Farm Attractions Network (NFAN), said Halloween has become one of the biggest seasons of the year for some farmers. "Ten years ago, a pumpkin patch was a field and a wheelbarrow. Now it's a wonderful experience for the whole family," she said. The network has around 200 members and "almost all" embrace the spooky season with a mix of "maize mazes, after-dark trails, scare attractions and pumpkin festivals". "Diversification is key for many farms to thrive," she added, saying it has helped them mitigate existing challenges. Parry said: "Farmers are coping with climate change, change in government support and requirements, high input costs, the changes to inheritance tax relief on farms along with many other things." "Halloween gives farms a short, high-footfall season," she added. Doug Douglas, founder of Avon Valley Adventure Park, said their Halloween events grow every year and now generate a third of their yearly income. "We turn over £2m from our activities in October," said Douglas. He added: "Halloween is really important for us, it has surpassed Christmas." The park sits on a 90-acre farm in Keynsham, near Bath, and was once a fruit farm after his dad bought the land more than 30 years ago. Now Douglas runs family activities during school holidays and seasonal events, including for Halloween and Christmas. FEAR Scream Park is their award-winning attraction offering "immersive scare experiences" over 13 nights in October, with scare mazes and live actors. This month, they are expecting around 30,000 visitors but Douglas said the event is not "massively profitable" due to costs. "It costs us about £750,000 to put on the event," he said. "On staff wages alone, we employ about 200 staff, including around 120 actors." In addition, they run a popular pumpkin event which attracts around 120,000 people each year. Douglas said: "Everyone thinks they're easy [to put on], but we've got fire shows, stilt walkers, actors, we put in a big bar and we turn it into a real festival field." title: Rejecting closer EU ties would be dereliction of duty, PM to say
description: Addressing the Commons, Burnham is expected to say that a new deal with the EU could help tackle illegal immigration and boost economic growth.
body: The prime minister is expected to tell the Commons later it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn down a closer relationship with the European Union - if one can be negotiated with Brussels. In a statement to MPs on Monday, Andy Burnham will argue it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." He first pledged to explore closer ties with the bloc at a UK-EU summit later this year at the Labour Party conference last month. Addressing the Commons, Burnham is expected to say that a new deal with the EU could help tackle illegal immigration and boost economic growth. He will claim that if he could secure that then "the vast majority of the public would expect us to take it". Last month, Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the EU. A summit between the UK and the EU was due to take place in the summer but was postponed after Sir Keir Starmer announced his resignation. It has been rescheduled for next month. The prime minister hopes to secure tweaks to the current arrangements between London and Brussels and also begin a wider conversation about the long term relationship between the UK and its nearest neighbours. A No 10 source said: "Andy understands why some politicians don't want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised. "But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be. Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty." In his speech at Labour's conference, he said "immigration control" had been "weakened by Brexit" because the UK "lost collaboration with our European partners. And we are still having to work hard to bring it back". Speaking at her party conference last week, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said it was "a terrible idea" to "reopen the Brexit debate." "Can you imagine having to go through that again? So much time lost, arguing with ourselves with the EU. Going round in circles, businesses not knowing whether they should invest. He wants to do it all again." The Commons sits on Monday for the first time since 15 September, having been in recess during some of the party conferences. title: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth
description: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, BBC finds.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax. Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003. Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts. When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained. Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading. Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts. title: 'Tax rises needed to plug £35bn gap' and 'Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire"
description: A warning over the upcoming Budget and coverage of the Russia-Ukraine war lead Monday's papers.
body: Several of today's papers cover a warning form the Institute of Fiscal Studies (IFS) of a funding gap in UK finances ahead of the chancellor's Budget. The i Paper leads with the £35bn "gap", saying tax rises will be "needed to plug" it. It attributes this to "high inflation and the UK's defence spending pledge". The Treasury declined to comment on speculation surrounding the Budget. The paper also covers the deadly attacks on Riyadh airport, saying they have alarmed "Saudi elite - and Washington". According to The i, the BBC will fill its "license fee hole" by selling Blue Planet III and launching a "new dating show for right-wing men". Atop the Daily Telegraph is the headline "Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire'." Russia attacked a power plant in Ukraine "just hours" after the US President "claimed" he had brokered a ceasefire on energy sites, it reports. Like The i, the Telegraph also writes that "Healey faces £35bn hole in Budget", saying the warning comes from "Britains top economic think tank". The paper also covers a pledge from Reform UK to ban asylum applications for five years. The Guardian also covers the UK's finances in its top story, writing that the heat pump subsidy will be "cut to fund defence plan". On US President Donald Trump's reported ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on energy sites, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is quoted as saying the deal was "news to me". The Times notes that the IFS has said the tax rises needed to fill the funding gap would be equivalent to raising every tax bracket by three percentage points. It leads on its own investigation, which it says reveals that the government is "paying out sickness benefits to almost 2 million people without knowing whether they still qualify". It echoes the Guardian's coverage that Zelensky was unaware of the "energy truce". "Lettuce Liz iceberg ahead!" warns the Daily Star, saying a "Truss-style crash can happen again". The chancellor has been "urged to steady the ship", it writes. Leading the Metro are comments from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's that Russia played a role in Brexit. He is the "first PM to confirm Kremlin meddling", it says. The Financial Times reports that the US has threatened a "block on Kyiv's arms in push to halt Russian refinery attacks". American officials have been lobbying European capitals and Kyiv, according to European officials quoted by the paper. It also reports that oil executives have pulled out of an energy conference in Riyadh after the attacks on its airport. The Daily Mirror covers the fatal tiger attack in Yorkshire, saying a "hero tried to save" the man who died. The woman "fought desperately to hold the man back as he climbed into enclosure". But another person who was at the zoo tells the paper that she "was not strong enough". The Independent uses its cover to celebrate its 40th anniversary. "Independent then. Independent now" reads its headline. The Daily Express leads on an investigation into rickshaws in Westminster, saying "honest pedicab riders" have been "bullied out of the market by an organised group from Romania". It quotes Reform UK mayoral candidate Laila Cunningham in its headline as saying this is a "sign of broken Britain". The Sun headlines with "BBC in Strictly trans ban row". It says the organisation is "embroiled in a censorship row" after editing out a slogan supporting transgender women from a t-shirt worn by star Bethany Antonia. A BBC spokesperson said: "As is standard practice on any entertainment show on the BBC and in line with our editorial guidelines, appropriate steps are taken to reduce the inclusion of any overt branding or slogans that may be present, regardless of the wording or statement in question." title: Watch: Endangered orangutans released back into the wild after Borneo fires
description: The critically endangered apes were rescued from intense wildfires that destroyed their habitat in August and September.
body: This video can not be played Eight orangutans have been released into the wild in Borneo after being rescued from intense wildfires. Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday. Indonesian wildlife authorities rescued 46 of the apes, which are critically endangered, before fires tore through their habitat in August and September. Read more on this story.
