title: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV
description: The actor portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator, in his latest film.
body: This video can not be played Pattinson says 'Primetime' plot is 'most terrifying' thing that can happen to a parent Robert Pattinson is having quite the year. The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey. But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator. The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers. For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning. "It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival. "It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added. Robert Pattinson: Being a dad makes life 'more fun' The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators. The show was a ratings hit. But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television. Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy. "The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said. "And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory." Robert Pattinson, who welcomed his first child with Suki Waterhouse in March 2024, says that as a parent, the events depicted in his new film are "terrifying" When asked whether he thinks attitudes towards entertainment have now changed, Pattinson paused. "I think on mainstream TV, but then it's just been replaced," he replied, pointing out that similar content has since appeared on social media. "That's why I was interested in the show, because I could see the beginning of a new wave of 'predator catching' in pretty much the same format that it was in the early 2000s," he said. "And I was just interested as to why that was happening." "And it got bigger and bigger and bigger, and now it's one of the most massive things on social media." Lance Oppenheim and Robert Pattinson at London Film Festival's Primetime screening on Sunday night Hansen himself has been critical of the film, calling it "bizarre" and "detached from reality" in a video posted on X, external. Addressing his criticisms, director Lance Oppenheim said: "I agree, that was by design. "I always thought of this movie as more of a fever dream than something that was representational portrait." Oppenheim added there was something "ancient" about the desire to watch people getting publicly punished. "It's happened for thousands of years," he added. "I wanted to make something that interrogated that." Oppenheim, who is also currently co-directing with Nathan Fielder a highly anticipated documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, said separately of that project: "I want everyone to see it. It's a really special movie." Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart. Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films. This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come. He’s also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused, external. When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didn’t give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.") Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder? "I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds. "But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life." title: Iconic Australian band Powderfinger announce first tour in 17 years
description: The band, who announced their reunion last week, say they are "absolutely ecstatic" to be playing together again.
body: Powderfinger, pictured in 2010, are reuniting for an 18-date comeback tour next year Powderfinger, one of Australia's best loved rock bands, has unveiled details of a comeback tour – to take place 17 years after they broke up. The Brisbane-based group, who confirmed their reunion last week, will kick off with four nights in their home city next September. They will then play another 14 shows across Cairns, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Melbourne, with all gigs to be staged in a "stadium sized big-top" tent. In a statement on Monday the band said they were "absolutely ecstatic" to be getting together and playing again. "Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us," they said. "We have always been so grateful for the continued support from our long-term fans and over the years we've picked up a lot of new ones who have never seen us play." "People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories," they added. "We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia's best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all." The tour schedule of only playing on Friday and Saturday nights is similar to that adopted by Oasis in their world tour last year. No gigs outside of Australia have yet been announced. Powderfinger released seven studio albums during their career including 2000's Odyssey Number Five which was voted best Australian album of all time by listeners of Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) music station Triple J in 2011. That included the single My Happiness, which was voted sixth best Australian song of all time by the same station in 2025. The group's other hits include On My Mind and These Days and Sunsets. Since the band split, frontman Bernard Fanning has maintained a solo career while bassist John Collins has gone on to open two of Brisbane's largest live music venues. title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
description: One in 10 scams reported to Citizens Advice relate to fraudsters charging for work not done, or done badly.
body: Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice. The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them. It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket. The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters. She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of £5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete. "We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said. Her neighbour's house was also damaged. "They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC. The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly". In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing. Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before. Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them. "Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said. Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics. Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England. Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for £250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost £2,500. "An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said. It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500," she said. But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said. To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests: Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callers Gather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receipts Know your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refund Lord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes". He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes. "Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said. title: Debt advice that may leave you owing even more money
description: People are increasingly falling behind on credit card repayments, so here's the best way to get debt advice.
body: An increasing number of people are missing credit card repayments as finances are stretched by rising bills. Lenders have told the Bank of England they expect the number of unpaid credit card debts to keep going up this autumn. This could lead to more demand for advice on how to deal with debts – but, if you are struggling and need help, there are some traps to avoid. And it is worth remembering that impartial advice is available free of charge from debt charities. So here's what to think about. If you find yourself with money troubles, it can be tempting to seize any opportunity to get things back on track. Social media and internet search pages are full of supposed quick-fix debt solutions. Cold calls and WhatsApp messages also promise debt help. But they may well come with upfront fees, unrealistic claims about writing off debt, and pressure to make a quick decision. Suggestions on the best way to find help include: Impartial, authorised debt advice comes free. You can find a provider on the government-backed Moneyhelper website, external Check whether a firm offering debt help is authorised by the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You should cross-check the authorisation details they give with the FCA's register, external Anyone unhappy with the service from an authorised firm can complain and, if you are still not happy, go to the independent Financial Ombudsman Service. Alison Walters, director of consumer finance at the FCA, said: "Anyone struggling with debt deserves advice that puts their interests first. "Free, impartial debt advice is available to everyone, and no one should be pressured or misled into paying for a debt solution that may not be right for them." The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice charities or debt collectors, and pass this information on to firms offering debt solutions that you pay for. A quick search online will throw up lots of businesses offering ways to clear your debt, not all of which are trustworthy, according to charities. Warning signs of unscrupulous firms include pressure tactics, such as repeated contact, often in messages and on the phone, pushing people to agree to a debt solution, the FCA says. Some people have been encouraged to change financial details on lenders' paperwork, or are "coached" in ways to respond. Sometimes people are steered towards a fee-charging debt solution, such as Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs) or some debt management plans, without alternative options being properly explained or offered first. And, do you know who you are talking to? Ask them who they work for, and check if their details match the firm's official details. "Before making any decisions around how to deal with your debts, it's always worth getting full, free and impartial debt advice first, exploring all options to clear your debt in the safest and most sustainable way," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive at debt charity StepChange. title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
description: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.
body: Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices. Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments. That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago. The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws. As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that. This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course". "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said. They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine". The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden. Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products. Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong. Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel. The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress. Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, which amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war. Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow. title: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
description: Many farmers in states that backed the president say they are being hit from all sides, with the crucial midterm elections just weeks away.
body: Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef imports Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year. In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines. Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed. With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000. On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year. Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold. The cattle market tanked immediately. "So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry." "It just felt like a betrayal," she said. Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain. That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances. Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race. Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months. Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices. And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive. Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle. "All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas. Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing. Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own. Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market - but believes the President The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry. But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning. "Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head. Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day. "It really makes a guy think," he said. A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left. But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market. "People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said. Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall. "The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said. "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit." Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago. But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said. He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House. "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms. But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate. That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate,

title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
description: After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles.
body: This video can not be played 'There were so many people, why him?' Yvonne Akinyi remembers the day her husband was shot dead Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found. During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force. BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles. Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones. In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones. The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives. Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots. Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures. A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account. The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute. "The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said. Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment." Evans Kiche (l) and Jidah Burka (r) were shot in the head, while Vincent Ogutu (c) was shot in the chest Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said. Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home. The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked. After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful. In total, three people were killed. One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head. The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion. Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head. Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered. Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons. The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection. The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium. Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment. The shooting caused panic among the thousands of people inside the stadium Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join. Within hours, he was dead. His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans. As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government. "I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said. "It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him." title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
description: Brad Smith calls for global rules on AI, and says the UK is in the "best position" to lead the charge.
body: Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said. Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released. His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals. But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection." Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology its a threat to humanity. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this. Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated. "Let's get started today," he said. He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way. He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology. "We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI." Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute, external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute. "In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best." Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI. Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins". However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU. "In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said. "When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived. "Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country." This video can not be played Microsoft President: Britain Should Write World's AI Rules At the end of last month, Trump hosted the leaders of US tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, and Google at the White House where the executives signed a "morally binding" document. The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and make sure they do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways". Smith said he applauds the statement and Microsoft is "happy to sign it". "It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer." He added that the challenge for any "self-regulatory regime" is that "the good companies will do what you want". "It's the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about." title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns
description: The impact of the Iran war poses significant risks for the government’s spending plans, the Institute for Fiscal Studies says.
body: The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned. Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said. It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up. The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation". However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home. "But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together." He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space". However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises. The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring. "A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said. "Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course. "Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added. The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world. These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps. The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey. Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said. Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30. However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues. But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale. However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion. The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra £25bn in 2029-30. That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises. The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different. But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time. It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans. However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line. What is the Budget and what could be in it? title: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino's West End play
description: The Borat star said he was "beyond delighted" to be working on the show, The Popinjay Cavalier, with the Pulp Fiction director.
body: Cohen became famous Ali G Borat actor Sacha Baron Cohen will star in a new play in London's West End from Hollywood director Quentin Tarantino. The Popinjay Cavalier, set in 1830s Europe, was announced earlier this year and is the first play to be written for stage by the US filmmaker, who is also set to direct. Baron Cohen said he was "beyond delighted" to be working with Tarantino, saying: "When the best director in the world calls, you don't ask questions." The director, best known for violent film classics Pulp Fiction and Reservoir Dogs, has said he is "keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out". The play is set to premiere in March next year, with tickets available from Monday. The production was announced in March this year as a "rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen". Baron Cohen, 54, is known for his self-created comic characters including infamous spoof wannabe gangster Ali G, Kazakh reporter Borat Sagdiyev, and Austrian fashionista Brüno Gehard. He has won two Baftas and three Golden Globes, as well as being nominated for three Oscars and six Emmys. The full cast for The Popinjay Cavalier is planned to be announced at a later date. The play will be co-produced by Sony Pictures Entertainment, which distributed Tarantino's most recent film Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood, and Sonia Friedman Productions, which has overseen hits like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Paddington the Musical. Tarantino said last summer that the play was already written The director has repeatedly spoken about planning to retire from movies after making 10 films. He has made nine so far - he counts Kill Bill Volumes One and Two together - and has won two Oscars, for writing Pulp Fiction and Django Unchained. Tarantino revealed his plan to stage a play last summer, telling the Church of Tarantino podcast it was "all written". "It is absolutely the next thing I'm going to do. We'll start the ball rolling on it in January. It's probably going to take up a year and a half to two years of my life, if it's a success and I've got to do the tour version of it and all that," he said. "I'm preparing for it to be a success. If it's a flop, I'll be done very quickly." The Popinjay Cavalier will premiere at the Phoenix Theatre on 18 March 2027, with tickets starting from £25. The 63-year-old director lives in Tel Aviv with his Israeli wife, Daniella Pick, and their two children. He told the podcast last year that he would "more than likely move to England and bring my family with me" while working on the play. Tarantino is also known for his forthright personality and made headlines at the end of last year for launching a stinging criticism of actor Paul Dano, as well as in March this year for a spat with Pulp Fiction actress Rosanna Arquette after she criticised the use of the N-word in the 1994 film. title: Could you spot cancer symptoms in children?
description: Although rare, cancer is the leading cause of death from disease among children under 15 in the UK.
body: Amelia Carroll was 13 when she got her cancer diagnosis last year Although rare, cancer is the leading cause of death from disease among children under 15 in the UK - yet just under a third of parents say they feel confident recognising the symptoms. About 1,900 children aged 0-14 are diagnosed with cancer each year, according to Cancer Research UK. Thirteen-year-old Amelia Carroll, who is now in remission, was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) last year. Her mum Gemma recalls the initial symptoms being easy to overlook. There was the tiredness, she says, and being out of breath after mild exercise but both were put down to being unfit and just post-school fatigue. It was only when Amelia started presenting with bruises Gemma knew something wasn't right - within 10 days Amelia got her leukaemia diagnosis. Prof Bob Phillips, a paediatric oncologist, says it's key for parents to look out for clusters of symptoms that may be persisting, getting worse or bigger. Consider contacting a doctor over the following: Bruises that you can't explain Lumps and bumps that are getting bigger or not going away and growing over time Cancer in children develops much more quickly than in adults - effectively due to them growing. Experts like Phillips at CCLG, the Children and Young People's Cancer Association, are urging people to follow a national campaign aiming to raise awareness and improve diagnosis times. It includes a rule-of-three for professionals: If a child has had three persistent symptoms, or has visited their doctor three times, or has had three weeks of unexplained symptoms consider making a referral. Although, it's important to note survival rates have risen significantly since the 1970s, with eight out of 10 children surviving beyond five to 10 years or more after diagnosis. This video can not be played Could you spot the signs of childhood cancer? For Amelia, her cancer journey began with a single red bruise that came out of nowhere, says Gemma. Three days later, she had bruises down both of her shins on both legs, which were sore and raised. "We'd gone to the opticians for a routine appointment and they noticed that she'd got some burst blood vessels but they weren't sure why," she adds. Within 10 days, doctors had confirmed what type of leukaemia Amelia had and she was admitted to hospital to begin treatment. Her mum became particularly concerned when raised red bruises appeared on her legs "On the day that they confirmed what she had, I sat her down and she said to me 'have I got cancer?' and I said yes you have. She asked me if she was going to die." "I said no, they're doing everything they can, they've got a plan in place and the treatment is going to do everything it can to beat the cancer." Amelia is currently in remission, undergoing regular bone marrow and blood tests every three months, and has returned to school. Phillips says survival rates for childhood cancer in the UK are over 80% but that even quicker diagnosis would lead to less intensive treatments. Around the UK, about half the children diagnosed with cancer get their diagnosis within two weeks, he says. "It's pretty quick but we want the other half to not have the wait of 16, 18, 20, 25 weeks from those first symptoms to get a diagnosis." Cancer Research UK data shows that there are more than 400,000 new cases of cancer diagnosed every year in the UK, with only 54% being told within the 28-day NHS target window, according to the British Medical Journal (BMJ). An additional 2,300 teenagers and young adults (aged 15–24) are diagnosed each year. Jake Swinscoe died of soft tissue cancer at the age of 13 after opting out of treatment Lynsey Swinscoe is mum to Jake, who died of soft tissue cancer aged 13. Jake was diagnosed with stage three, fusion positive alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma in July 2023. Before his diagnosis, Jake's initial symptoms of a stuffy nose and watery eyes were put down to hayfever, and falling asleep after school was thought to be just end-of-term tiredness. "It was only when he started to get a swelling across the bridge of his nose that we thought right, we need to take him to the GP," Lynsey says. "But at that point we didn't really think the fatigue and hayfever symptoms were related." A mass was found in Jake's nose and nasal cavity and he was diagnosed with soft tissue sarcoma. He completed nine rounds of chemotherapy and proton beam radiation. After suffering seizures and feeling very unwell from the chemotherapy, Jake opted out of continuing treatment. Jake completed nine rounds of chemotherapy and proton beam radiation He passed away peacefully at home on 26 April 2024, just two weeks before his 14th birthday. "I think the main thing with Jake is he was not scared to die. We had lots of conversations about dying and what it might feel like to die and the only thing that he was sort of scared about was, 'are all the people going to remember me? Is everyone just going to forget who I am?' "That's why I'm doing this, to make sure that people know who Jake is, to make sure people know how incredible he was. And so with that comes the raising awareness, which I think, that's his legacy." title: Ex-hurricane to bring warm weather to the UK this week
description: Close to record-breaking warm nights are possible this week as warmer air heads for the UK.
body: The remnants of Hurricane Isaias, which hit the southern US on Saturday, is set to bring a warm spell to the UK this week. Close to record-breaking warm nights are possible, with Monday night temperatures for some parts of England possibly staying as high as 18C, not far off the country's October record of 18.6C (65.4F). Daytime temperatures will be above average for the time of year for many parts of the UK. Rain is likely at times across much of the UK, but will still fall below the amount required to help ease drought hit-parts of England. Drought declared in Yorkshire after dry weather North-westerly winds over the weekend meant it felt rather cool in many areas, but with southerly winds on Monday comes milder conditions to most parts. Temperatures will peak at 14 to 19 Celsius, slightly above the mid-October average of 12-16C. However, weather fronts tied in with the southerly winds mean that most areas will be cloudy with occasional spells of rain or drizzle. Sunshine will be fairly limited with areas around north-east Scotland, east Wales, the West Midlands and the north coast of Northern Ireland most favoured for some sunny breaks. A warm night will follow with temperatures only dropping a few degrees, but heavier bursts of rain are expected to develop through the night. Overnight rain will then sweep across the UK through Tuesday morning. In the sunnier weather that follows, temperatures are likely to hit the low 20s in southern and eastern counties of England, with 23C possible in parts of East Anglia. Night and early morning temperatures will rival average October daytime highs on some days this week Clearer skies into Wednesday morning mean all should experience a cooler start to the day, but a sunnier one too. Cloud and strengthening winds will move into north-western parts during the afternoon, all linked to an area of low pressure passing between the UK and Iceland. which contains some of the remnants of ex-Hurricane Isaias. Isaias hit the Florida coast on Saturday as a Category 2 storm, before weakening rapidly over land. As the resulting area of low pressure moves out into the Atlantic this week it will merge with another area of low pressure coming out of Canada before sweeping towards Iceland by the end of Wednesday. Gales are expected for a time in the north-west of Scotland, and a narrow corridor of humid ex-tropical air will proceed an active cold front that will sweep a band of rain south-eastwards during Thursday and Thursday night. Before the rain arrives in south-east England we could once again see temperatures exceed 20C in many locations on Thursday. As ex-Hurricane Isaias heads towards Iceland midweek a plume of tropical air and stronger winds will arrive Following the passage of the wetter and windier weather, an area of high pressure will move in during Friday and this could hang around into the following week. This will bring in cooler air again, dropping temperatures back to where they should be for the time of year and introducing chillier nights again. High pressure also means rain amounts will be sparse which will be little comfort to those monitoring the ongoing drought. After a summer of extreme heat and little rain for most, some parts of the country have continued to experience below-average rainfall so far this autumn. While we are almost halfway through the season some parts of Yorkshire have seen less than 20% their normal autumn rainfall. However, the Met Office continues to highlight the potential for late autumn and early winter being wetter than normal due to the record El Niño conditions this year. Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather? title: Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent
description: Zelensky says Kyiv would support such a truce. Moscow has yet to comment.
body: Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment. The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post. Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market. The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it. The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel. That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation. This video can not be played Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia". "Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said. The BBC has asked the White House for further details. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support. Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. "All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said. For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure. Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war". The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides. Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located on 6 August Earlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday. The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties. Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports. "Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course". Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk. On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal. The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president". Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire. The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation. Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power. Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war. Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said. One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said. title: Reform would suspend asylum system for parliamentary term if in government
description: All asylum applications would be rejected and existing ones voided, with all claimants marked for deportation.
body: One of Reform UK's pledges for its first 100 days in power would be stopping small boat crossings, Nigel Farage has said Reform UK has announced plans to close down the UK's asylum system for a full parliamentary term if it were to enter government. The party said all new asylum applications would be rejected and existing applications voided, with all claimants marked for deportation, which Reform said would effectively suspend the asylum system. Reform would scrap the asylum tribunal system, which hears asylum appeal cases, and claimants in more than 90,000 outstanding appeals would be deported. It said no grants of humanitarian protection or refugee status would be made. Labour chairperson Bridget Phillipson called the proposals a "clear sign of desperation and weakness". "Running away from basic decency by entirely abandoning those escaping war and persecution might look to Reform like a way of winning a bidding war with other parties on the right, but the vast majority of British people will reject it as an assault on our common values," she said. Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the proposals "largely copy" his party's policies, arguing: "Only the Conservatives have a serious and credible plan to fix our borders." Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesperson Max Wilkinson said: "Reform and the Conservatives were the architects of the failed asylum system and now they will exploit it at every opportunity - including Farage's latest announcement." Reform said it would pull the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 and disapply the 1951 Refugee Convention to prevent legal challenges to its plans. Party leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "facing a national security emergency" and "we cannot accept more asylum seekers while we still have no idea how many people are in the country illegally and the threat they pose." Home Office staff who currently oversee asylum claims would be "reprioritised to reviewing and overturning previous refugee grants", Reform added. The party said it would attempt to pressure other countries into accepting those marked for deportation from the UK by using visa bans and tariffs on goods and services. Pakistan, Somalia, Eritrea, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan could be hit with visa bans under these measures. If these policies are unsuccessful, Reform would "apply further sanctions, including banning a country's airlines from British airspace and their citizens from transit", the announcement added. In "extreme cases" where no country is willing to take custody of a deportee or it is inappropriate to return someone to their home country, Reform said it would negotiate deals with third countries. In April, Reform pledged an immediate review of all asylum claims from the last five years should the party win the next general election. Around 400,000 people would be liable for deportation under the plans, which would target anybody granted asylum, overstaying a visa, or from a country deemed safe by a Reform-led government. The party previously announced it would bar anyone arriving on a small boat, and suggested this could mean 600,000 deportations over five years. Both Labour and the Conservatives have also pledged to make changes to the asylum system. Phillipson said Farage is "casting around for more and more extreme policies" as he deals with questions about finances and rival party Restore Britain. Phillipson said Labour is showing "we can control immigration and get numbers down with serious action, not by abandoning the asylum system altogether", adding the "right approach" is "not giving up or caving to the most extreme voices, but ensuring that the rules we have are properly enforced". Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, a total of 20,478 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 40% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 6 October 2025 to 5 October 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. In March, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said any asylum seeker given refugee status will now only be offered temporary protection, reviewed every 30 months. In September, she also reopened a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK, saying she hoped that offering "safe and legal" routes would deter small boat crossi

title: Dozens of gold prospectors killed in strikes on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
description: Neither Egypt nor Sudan has commented on the alleged strikes on an artisanal mining camp on Saturday.
body: File photo of gold prospectors in northern Sudan At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says. Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining sites in Sudan's River Nile state on Saturday. Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented. Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border. Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region. "The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes." It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise. The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured. Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote. The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers. Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining. At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens. Gold lies at the core of the border tensions. Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders. Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels. Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment. Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups. This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market. title: Gavin and Stacey's Melanie Walters voted off Strictly
description: Walters, best known for playing Gwen West in the BBC comedy, was partnered with professional Aljaz Skorjanec.
body: Melanie Walters and Aljaz Skorjanec performed together for the final time at the weekend Gavin and Stacey's Melanie Walters has become the second celebrity eliminated from this season of Strictly Come Dancing. The actress, 64, had been paired with professional dancer Aljaz Skorjanec, 36. On Saturday night's episode, Walters and Skorjanec had performed a Charleston to Ooh Ahh… Just A Little Bit by Gina G, receiving a score of 17 from the judges. Judge Craig Revel Horwood said he "didn't love" their dance while Motsi Mabuse encouraged her to "keep going". After finishing in the bottom two on the first two weeks of the competition, the judges sent the pair home. Melanie Walters said her Gavin and Stacey co-stars had been very supportive On Sunday night's results episode, they were sent into the dance-off against former footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and his partner Alexis Warr, who had received a score of 15 for their quickstep to I'm A Believer by The Monkees. After both couples performed their routines again, the judges delivered their verdicts on who they wanted to save. While Mabuse wanted to save Walters, fellow judges Shirley Ballas, Anton Du Beke and Revel Horwood all chose to save Wright-Phillips and Warr. The eliminated couple will appear on It Takes Two on Monday. Sunday night's episode also saw Ballas and Du Beke take to the floor as part of a special group performance, with two teams of professional dancers going head-to-head for glory in a ballroom vs Latin showdown. There was also a performance from musician Jalen Ngonda of his song Burning Temptation, accompanied by professional dancers Neil Jones and Lethabo Monametsi. Walters is best known for playing Gwen West in the BBC comedy, which she appeared in from its launch in 2007 and then reprised her role for the 2024 Christmas special. During the first week of the contest, the Welsh actress received a score of 15 for her cha cha cha, also being given the same score the following week while performing a waltz to Edelweiss from The Sound of Music during Movie Week. The remaining 13 couples will take to the dancefloor next week for icons week. title: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
description: The US president made the announcement in a social media post, which was an apparent surprise to Ukraine and Russia is yet to comment.
body: This video can not be played US President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire". Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me". Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections. The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election. Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? title: 'Prepare for the unthinkable' warning over autumn flooding
description: Those living in flood-hit areas say they are worried, and have started preparing.
body: Communities can often be at risk from both rivers and the sea People are being told to prepare for "the unthinkable" as flood response teams warn of a heightened risk over the autumn. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it was concerned by long-range forecasts, external which indicated an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual over the coming months. Those living in flood-hit areas told BBC Wales they were worried, and had started preparing. One in seven properties in Wales is classed as being at risk of flooding, but NRW said just 27% of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up. NRW's Jeremy Parr says understanding your flood risk, signing up for warnings and having a plan can make a difference After a summer marked by drought and wildfires, the organisation has urged people "not to become complacent" and said conditions could change quickly. Wales has seen a series of major floods in recent years, often in the wake of powerful storms such as Dennis in 2020, Bert and Darragh in 2024 and Claudia in 2025. The threat comes from both rivers and the sea, while surface water flooding - where local drainage systems become overwhelmed during heavy downpours - is seen as an increasing danger. NRW argues that the country's geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and several so-called "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys. More than 274,500 homes and businesses are currently classed at risk of flooding, with this figure set to increase significantly by the end of the century. Monmouth is still recovering from the impact of Storm Claudia in November 2025 On the high street in Monmouth, people told BBC Wales of "harrowing" and "dreadful" scenes when major flooding hit in November 2025. Friends Malcolm Butcher, 82, Jim Tyler, 81, Brian Churches, 82 and Dave Blake, 82, said they had lived in the town all their lives "and never seen anything like it". "At 2:30 in the morning when it hit it was unbelievable... absolutely raging," Malcolm said. If it had happened in the daytime "people would have died", he added. Eighteen cars on his road were lost to the flood waters - including his own, while the houses in the street behind were all flooded out. "It is a worry, we have three rivers running into Monmouth... and the winters are changing," he said. People could help prepare for floods by moving "the good stuff upstairs" and making sure they had sandbags to hand ahead of bad weather, he said. "It's not back to normal yet but we're getting there," added Imogen Elliot, 82. "Waitrose was four feet in water and it went right up the street - we've had flooding before but not like that." Friends Brian Churches, Jim Taylor, Dave Blake and Malcolm Butcher [left to right] said they had lived in Monmouth all their lives and never seen flooding like it Jane Roche, who runs a café and fishmongers on the banks of the River Teifi in Cardigan, Ceredigion, has helped coordinate a community flood plan for the area. "Flooding is something we've learned to live alongside for many years - we've seen first-hand the disruption it can cause for businesses, residents and visitors," she said. "Developing a community flood plan has brought local people together, helped us understand what actions we need to taken when warnings are issued and given us confidence to support one another when severe weather is forecast." The River Monnow burst its banks and flooded Monmouth back in November 2025 during storm Claudia More frequent and intense weather extremes are expected as a result of climate change, with Wales facing the prospect of wetter, wilder winters more often. Meanwhile, this year scientists are monitoring the El Niño event over the Pacific Ocean - which set to be "strongest in living memory". The powerful natural climate phenomenon pushes up global temperatures and can increase the risks of extreme weather. While this does not automatically translate into bad weather in the UK it is "part of the picture" that is leading to concerns for the coming months, according to Jeremy Parr of NRW. "We do invest in flood defences... but you can't stop all of the flooding all of the time," he said. "So that means that people need to think the unthinkable really - or the unpleasant - and [consider] if it were to flood around where I live, what would I do?" "Time and time again" the organisation was told by people who had experienced devastating flooding that "they'd never flooded before, and didn't think it would happen to them", he added. NRW advises people to check their flood risk by postcode online, external, sign up for flood warnings and access advice about what to do, external if flooding is forecast in their area. The organisation's flood warning service is available to 181,158 properties in Wales, but new figures show just 48,844 were currently signed up to receive the alerts via phone or email. "It is low - 27%," Parr admitted, suggesting that people may be being put off by myths that signing up could affect their insurance premiums. A new flood gate prevents flood water from the River Ebbw reaching properties near this park in Risca, Newport Cardigan's mayor Olwen Davies has bought a flood door for her own house, and also uses a flood gate for extra protection. She said: "The river comes up once or twice a year... if there's a high tide, with a strong south-westerly wind that's what creates the most havoc. "We work together and we know who to call on," she said. Cardigan has been repeatedly hit by tidal flooding from the Teifi Sarah Davies from the Met Office said long-range forecasts for October, November and December suggested "a greater chance of weather-related disruption".
