title: Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
description: Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit less than two months ago, leaving thousands dead and missing.
body: This video can not be played Flash flood washes building complex in central Nepal A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said. Around 50 people have been rescued from along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing. A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex. Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing. Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar. Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies. The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said. Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said. Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location." However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August. What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche. Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood. "Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said. "We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet." The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster. title: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
description: The 71-year-old pontiff said the nodule was identified "at a very early stage".
body: This video can not be played Pope Leo announces he will undergo surgery for early-stage lung nodule Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check up. "The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome. The 71-year-old pontiff said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation. Pope Leo reassured pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage". He concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers. Holy See Press Office spokesperson Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week". Bruni added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover. Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome. The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" to the Pope in a post on X as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days". Pope Leo, born Robert Francis Provost, succeeded Pope Francis in 2025. He is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – and is the first American. He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities. During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead. title: Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
description: The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, and while the physical damage can be quickly repaired, its reputation for stability is taking a battering.
body: Houthi soldiers stand guard during a protest against Saudi Arabia, in Sana'a, Yemen, on Friday Saturday's attack on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh is another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict. Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this. In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease. The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering. As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait. The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel. Who are the Houthis and what do they want? Houthi attacks raise fears of wider Middle East conflict and more global economic damage Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat. The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen. It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March. But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the war-torn country, particularly in the north and west. But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy. As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy. The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war. Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran. In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia. However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen. Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said. But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month. When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters. This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement. title: Emergency doctor 'completely terrified' of looming winter pressures on NHS
description: Dr Fiona Hunter says A&E departments are providing "unsafe" levels of care, with some patients spending 72 hours on trolleys in hospital corridors.
body: Dr Fiona Hunter called for an end to overcrowding in A&E departments A leading emergency doctor has said she is "completely terrified" about upcoming winter pressures on Scotland's already-stretched NHS. Dr Fiona Hunter, vice chair of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine Scotland, said A&E departments were providing "unsafe" levels of care, with some patients spending 72 hours on trolleys in hospital corridors. Although Health Secretary Angela Constance vowed in August to "eradicate" corridor care, Hunter told BBC Scotland's The Sunday Show there had been a "toxic normalisation" of this practice which can lead to patients dying. Constance told the programme that the winter would be "difficult" but reiterated that corridor care was unacceptable. She said her priorities were to reduce avoidable hospital admissions, including with "robust" public messaging, to ensure people were accessing the right sort of medical care. She said she wanted to remedy a lack of statistics kept around corridor care and to move towards a system where preparing for winter was a "year round" activity. The Health and Care Improving Flow Plan asks health boards to reduce corridor care Last month First Minister John Swinney confirmed plans to cut the number of mainland health boards from 11 to two in a bid to free up more time and capacity for treatment. But with major reform some way off, fears are growing about the months ahead. Asked how concerned she was, Hunter said: "Completely terrified, to be clear about the situation currently, before we get into proper winter where the viruses really hit. "We are providing unsafe levels of care in emergency departments. "There has been a real toxic normalisation of corridor care. We accept it on a daily basis. "You come into a department that is completely stacked with ambulances outside and we have got trolleys up and down corridors." She added trolley mattresses were designed to keep patients for up to four hours but some are being kept for "up to three days". Hunter said: "We know that excess mortality happens when you languish on a hospital trolley." The Royal College of Emergency Medicine has repeatedly voiced concerns about the pressures facing the NHS The doctor said she did not want to "scare patients away" from coming to an emergency department. However, she warned: "We are not able to provide safe levels of care because what emergency staff are being asked to do across the country is to look after essentially a ward's worth of extra patients and keep seeing every patient that comes through the front door. "Some departments across the UK are working at 500% capacity but they don't have 500% extra staff to deal with that. "So we have really high rates of sickness and burnout among staff - and this is before the viruses really hit." She told the programme staff naturally want to isolate sick patients but were unable to do so due to "completely stowed out" waiting rooms. Hunter added: "It is just impossible." The medic said that, month-on-month, almost 2,000 patients were experiencing delayed discharge across the country. She said: "If we could free up a quarter of those patients then we would have flow to bring our patients through the system." Has Scotland's NHS recovered from the Covid pandemic? Will walk-in GP clinics deliver one million extra appointments? Councillor Paul Kelly, Cosla spokesman for health and social care, agreed the problems facing the NHS now amount to a "year-round crisis". He told the programme: "Like everybody we are very worried about what the winter will bring." Asked about the additional time some people are spending in hospital, Kelly said: "Delayed discharged is a significant problem, as is people waiting for a care package in the community. "We are very, very clear to the government that we need to see investment in social care." The health secretary earlier told the programme that there should not be a focus on outcomes, not just money. But Kelly responded: "I think we have to focus on the money. "If we are saying the government are focusing on delayed discharge then part of that is about the role of councils and supporting people to get out of hospital." He told the The Sunday Show that health and social care partnerships currently had "almost half a billion pounds of a budget gap" but added it was vital to invest in the workforce. Kelly said "urgent" investment was required and added: "We don't want to see anybody in hospital longer than they should be." Angela Constance stressed the importance of the public choosing the right service for advice and treatment this winter Earlier, the health secretary was asked about the outlook for the coming months. Constance said: "We do know that the winter will be difficult. "There are always increased pressures as we enter the winter season but what we have seen in Scotland, over the past few years, is an increase in demand on our NHS services." The minister said a range of factors were responsible but added the government was aiming to reduced "avoidable hospital admissions". She also stressed the importance of the public choosing the right service for advice and treatment. Challenged on lack of capacity, Constance said: "We are supportive, both financially and in terms of a policy perspective, of being able to get, what they call, a better flow through the hospital when people have to be admitted." The health secretary was also asked if treating patients in corridors was "becoming the norm". She said: "We cannot accept corridor care." The minister said the problem was particularity acute in certain hospitals and parts of the country. Asked about concerns delays were costing lives, Constance said: "Our NHS is safe but we need to be sure that people get the right care at the right time." BBC Scotland has asked the Scottish government for a response to Hunter's comments, which were broadcast after the health secretary's interview. Watch our pick of stan

title: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
description: The defence secretary says the US and its allies need to increase pressure on Vladimir Putin to end the war with Ukraine.
body: This video can not be played UK 'does not support' Trump-Putin diesel deal, says defence secretary Streeting The UK does not support Donald Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin, which would see the US purchase millions of tonnes of diesel from Russia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House, he said the agreement had been done in the context of the US president facing elections in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living. He argued that the US and other allies should focus on increasing pressure on Russia to shorten the war "and to secure Ukraine's freedom". Trump's diesel deal is aimed at lowering fuel prices in America, which have risen following the US and Israel's conflict with Iran. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement would allow Moscow to raise funds to source new military equipment to continue the war. In response, Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader" who could reach a deal with Russia to end the long-running conflict between the two countries. Streeting said it was a matter for Ukrainians to choose their leader but added that the country was "fortunate to have someone of his calibre, his courage and his integrity leading their war effort". He added that responsibility for the war "lies squarely and solely with President Putin and his imperialist ambitions". The defence secretary said it was not the first time there had been public disagreements between Washington and Kyiv, adding: "In these situations we see it as our role and our responsibility to try and bring our friends back together again." He also sought to emphasise the US's support for Ukraine, saying there was "often an understatement" of how much help they had provided. "We're seeing US support for Ukraine in a number of ways from the provision of weapons - and we do a lot of procurement through the Americans - through to intelligence support and through the diplomatic initiative that Washington is leading." This video can not be played Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Trump was "wrong" to call for Zelensky to go, adding: "The US is our closest ally but even close allies can disagree." Speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he also criticised the diesel deal saying it "sends out all the wrong messages". "If you want a peaceful world, you don't do that sort of deal - you properly fund defence and prepare for war." Also appearing on the programme, Streeting said the UK had to plan its defence spending on the basis that there could be a Russian attack on Nato - the military alliance made up of 32 countries - by 2030. He said the UK didn't "seek conflict with Russia" but added: "Strength is the best form of deterrence." Earlier this year, John Healey - now the chancellor - resigned as defence secretary accusing Sir Keir Starmer's government of not providing enough money for defence and said the UK had to be spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030, up from an estimated 2.6% this year. Streeting said Healey would use the coming Budget to "plug" a £4.7bn funding gap to pay for the Defence Investment Plan. He also said the government would set out a path to increase spending to 3.5% of national income by 2035 at next year's Spending Review. Pressed on whether the government could commit to spending 3% of GDP by 2030, Streeting said he would "always push for more defence spending" but added: "We're not going to set out a spending commitment without showing how we will pay for it." "If I were the chancellor to sit on your programme now and say '3% in 2030' without saying how we would pay for it, the markets would price in that risk and the cost of borrowing would go up." title: Firefighters spend second night at scene of Glasgow scrapyard blaze
description: The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said the alarm was raised at the business in the Scotstoun area of the city on Friday night.
body: The site, pictured from across the river, was damaged in the blaze which started on Friday night Firefighters have spent a second night at the scene of a major blaze at a scrapyard in Glasgow. The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said the alarm was raised at the business on South Street, in the Scotstoun area of the city, at about 23:23 on Friday. One local resident captured dramatic footage of the fire at its peak, with explosive bangs emitting from an area engulfed in flames. Nine fire engines, two high-reach vehicles and specialist resources responded to the incident. No casualties were reported. This video can not be played Firefighters spend night tackling Glasgow scrapyard blaze The SFRS said crews were in attendance overnight into Sunday with four fire engines and two high-reach appliances. A high volume water pump is also being used to draw water from the nearby River Clyde. The public were advised to keep windows and door closed if they could see smoke. title: Russo named England player of the year
description: Arsenal forward Alessia Russo is named England women's player of the year after scoring five goals in 10 games.
body: Alessia Russo has scored 31 goals in 68 games for England Forward Alessia Russo has been named England women's player of the year. The 27-year-old, who also won the award two seasons ago, has been a key player in the 2025-26 campaign, featuring in all 10 games and scoring five goals. Last week she scored the third goal as England beat Greece 3-1 in their 2027 World Cup play-off semi-final first leg. Arsenal's Russo pipped Chelsea pair Lucy Bronze and Hannah Hampton to the award, which is voted for by fans. "To receive the award is really special, particularly as it comes directly from the fans. I am so grateful for their support," said Russo. "A big thank you also to my team-mates - it is always about the collective." England host Greece in the second leg at Leicester's King Power Stadium on Tuesday. title: Could Alberta's vote on independence be Canada's Brexit moment?
description: WATCH: The BBC's Nadine Yousif meets the separatists who want to quit the country - and the Canadians calling for unity in the face of threats from US President Trump.
body: This video can not be played People in the province of Alberta will vote on 19 October on whether they want to start the process of separating from the rest of Canada. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the upcoming referendum a "dangerous bluff", comparing it to the Brexit vote that saw the UK leave the European Union. But supporters of Albertan independence believe that the oil-rich province has long been overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa, the national capital, and that federal environmental policies have hindered its ability to develop its natural resources. So, could Alberta really become its own country? The BBC's Nadine Yousif takes us on a journey through Alberta to talk to both supporters and opponents of separation about their hopes for the country's future. title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
description: A flash flood at the Budhi Gandaki River has swept away several buildings and bridges, two months after catastrophic floods hit the country.
body: This video can not be played A flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal. The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed. It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river. Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing. title: Man, 36, arrested six years on from double murder
description: Junior Ajose, 36, and Cheriff Tall, 21, were gunned down at a lockdown party six years ago.
body: Junior Ajose and Cheriff Tall were both killed in the shooting A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fatal shooting of two men more than six years ago. Junior Ajose, 36, and Cheriff Tall, 21, were shot dead at a lockdown party in the Moss Side area of Manchester in the early hours of 21 June 2020. A Greater Manchester Police (GMP) spokesperson said a 36-year-old man was detained in Turkey and transported back to England on Saturday, where he was met at Stansted Airport by GMP officers. He remains in custody. Det Ch Insp Neil Higginson from the force's major incident team said: "This arrest demonstrates our unwavering commitment to securing justice for Junior and Cheriff and their loved ones." "Over the last six years, myself and my officers have been carrying out multiple warrants, analysing evidence, examining devices that have been seized during the investigation and pursuing every opportunity to identify those responsible," he added. Ajose and Tall, who did not know each other, were both shot in the head in a car park off Caythorne Street shortly before 01:00 BST and died in hospital. GMP said it was estimated that between 300 and 400 people were present in the car park that night. The force issued a further appeal for information on the fifth anniversary of their deaths last year. Higginson said they were continuing to appeal for information that could help them to establish the full circumstances of what happened that night and to identify any outstanding suspects. A £50,000 reward remains available for key information that leads to the conviction of the killer. title: Delhi sees more protests as 'cockroach' group's leaders released
description: Police say they will keep restricting access to the city centre after thousands of people were detained and released on Saturday.
body: Reports said 7,000 people were detained on Saturday and released late that night A court in Indian capital Delhi has released the top leaders of the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) as the city sees more protests for a second day with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded. Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders were arrested on arrival in Delhi on Saturday to lead protests seeking electoral reforms. In his first comments after his release, Dipke said "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated". On Saturday, media reports said, 7,000 demonstrators were detained and released late at night. The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections. It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied. On Sunday morning, the CJP lawyer Ratna Singh said she had been informed by the police that Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - would be produced before the magistrate by the police seeking their remand "to maintain public peace". She subsequently posted on X that the three had been set free by the court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year" - she later deleted the post about the condition and it's not clear what that means and whether the CJP leaders can take part in protests. After his release, Dipke posted on X, external, saying: "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India." In another post, external, he said he was going to his village to attend his grandmother's funeral who died around the time of his arrest yesterday. "Heading back to my village to be with my family during this moment of grief," he posted, adding that Das and Ranka would address a press conference in Delhi. "The CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated," he added. Saturday saw dramatic scenes as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed. This video can not be played 'Cockroach' leaders say they have been detained ahead of march Police had refused permission for Saturday's protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital, and the city was in a virtual lockdown with unprecedented curbs in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue. At least 45 metro stations were closed and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route. Internet was also curtailed in central Delhi for the entire day. For a second day in a row on Sunday, much of central Delhi has roads barricaded and offices, shops and restaurants shut and internet services curtailed. In Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest shopping and entertainment hubs, there are rows upon rows of bright yellow police barricades, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel. While some shops were open, people working here said they were worried about how the day would unfold. Protesters have returned to the area for a second consecutive day, but, for now, they are vastly outnumbered by security personnel and the BBC has witnessed many detentions. Some were put into buses before being driven away. Some could be seen peering through the windows, others trying to push their way out while shouting "Gyanesh must go!" At one point, an entire bus reverberated with similar chants. Security forces have been deployed across Delhi The CJP had called for a protest on Saturday at Jantar Mantar - the road that the demonstrators had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms. But it remained barricaded at both ends, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel. After the police detained the CJP leaders and other activists, lawyers and students leaders, the CJP called for more protests on Sunday. On Sunday, the Indian Supreme Court held a special hearing to deal with complaints of shutdowns and detentions. The court ordered the government to restore internet and ensure that metro and rail services functioned normally, unless there was disturbance to public order. The court also said that free movement of people should be permitted and there should be no illegal detention. This video can not be played Watch: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi The row centres over a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - the commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters. At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed. The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated. The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this. The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted. Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?" The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment,

title: Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon
description: Double Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.
body: Eliud Kipchoge's victory was his 12th at a World Marathon Major Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41. The Kenyan crossed the line in two hours nine minutes 10 seconds for his 17th career win over the distance and first since the Berlin Marathon in 2023. "I believe that my body is still peaking - still able to compete with the next generation," Kipchoge said. "The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs." The course was partly raced along the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG). "On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," added Kipchoge, who slowed down inside the MCG to wave to the fans. "It was actually different - running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground. "It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne." Australian Thomas do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35, with compatriot Reece Edwards third. New Zealand's Camille French won the women's race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver and Nichola Sheridan of Ireland. The Melbourne Marathon was the third leg on Kipchoge's world tour, on which he hopes to complete a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years. Each marathon will raise funds for the Eliud Kipchoge Foundation, which focuses on education, environmental sustainability and health. Kipchoge is considered one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time, winning two Olympic marathon golds, plus a silver and bronze over 5000m. His honours also include a world title, 12 World Marathon Major victories and two official world records. In 2019 he became the first person to break the two-hour marathon barrier under special conditions in Vienna, clocking an unofficial time of one hour 59 minutes 40 seconds. title: Lost monastery masonry may have been reused for hospital's drain
description: Archaeologists hope to uncover more fragments of the medieval site in Perth.
body: Archaeologists believes they have found fragments of masonry from a medieval monastery in Perth Surviving parts of a monastery set up by King James I of Scotland almost 470 years ago may have been found in an old drain. The Charterhouse was established in Perth for monks of the Carthusian Order, external, and at the heart of the complex was a lavishly decorated church. The monastery was later demolished and over the centuries the medieval site disappeared under a hospital and houses. During an excavation last month, archaeologists and volunteers uncovered an 18th Century culvert that appeared to have been partly made using stone from the torn down monastery. More stories from Tayside and Central Listen to news from Tayside and Central on BBC Sounds The culvert once drained waste water from King James VI Hospital, which was built around 1749-1750 and was converted into flats in the 1970s. The drain was discovered during the dig in a grassy open space at the former hospital. Covering the top of the drain were flat stones, which are believed to be medieval masonry. Archaeologist Dr Gavin Lindsay told BBC Scotland News: "You can see clear chisel marks from when they had been worked very carefully to create these beautiful smooth sides. "They are clearly far more elaborate, and far more effort had gone into their production, than you would do for a drain in the 1700s." The selection of masonry also include stone floor slabs. Dr Lindsay said a stone mason who visited the dig suggested the slabs' smooth surfaces were the result of people walking on them over many years. "Possibly by many monks' feet, and to push it a bit further, maybe King James's feet had been across it," said the archaeologist. Specialists will examine the masonry to determine how old they are Dr Lucy Dean, of the University of Highlands and Islands Centre for History, is also involved in the Perth Charterhouse Project. She said: "The volunteers that we had did a lot of sifting through the soil that we were taking out. "They were finding, alongside quite a lot of 19th and 20th Century pieces of pottery and glass, a number of pieces that are probably medieval." The stones from the drain along with fragments of pottery will be examined further by specialists. The drain, which is lined with handmade 18th Century bricks, after the top slabs had been removed The archaeologists said the next stages of the project included studies of archives to find out more about the monastery, and going back to the local community to let them know what has been found so far. Further digs could take place in the future. Residents of Perth have also been asked to look out for more masonry that had survived and been reused. Dr Lindsay said: "We have identified a number of different fragments that have been incorporated into the retaining wall of Perth Station, for example, and into boundary walls of gardens." The University of Stirling and Perthshire Society of Natural Science have been involved in the project, while funding for the dig was provided by the trustees of the King James VI Hospital and The Guildry Incorporation of Perth. title: Service increases access to mental health support
description: The programme covers a range of topics, including managing anxiety and boosting self-esteem.
body: Workshops are currently being delivered across the East Riding, the council says People struggling with their mental health and wellbeing are being encouraged to access free support ahead of World Mental Health Day. East Riding of Yorkshire Council said its Wellbeing for Us programme, aimed at residents aged 18 and over, was designed to help people build confidence and make meaningful social connections, while reducing isolation. The programme includes face-to-face workshops and informal peer support social groups and covers a range of topics, including managing anxiety and stress and boosting self-esteem. The council said the programme also aimed to help residents access wider support, including community organisations, NHS referrals and other health services. Workshops are currently being delivered, external on a rolling basis in Withernsea, Hornsea, Bridlington, Beverley, Driffield, Pocklington, Goole and Hessle, with drop-in sessions taking place in Goole and at Lelley Fields Crematorium. Informal peer support social groups are being held in Goole and at Lelley Fields Crematorium, with more planned, the council said. World Mental Health Day takes place on 10 October. title: Globe opens Shakespeare library and archive
description: London's only public Shakespeare library featuring more than 6,000 books, is set to open at the Globe.
body: The Globe's 1632 second folio lists the plays as comedies, histories and tragedies, with The Tempest first Shakespeare's Globe has opened a new research centre on its Bankside site, which it says is London's only dedicated Shakespeare library and archive open to the public. The Research and Collections Centre holds more than 6,000 books on Shakespeare as well as early modern literature and drama, alongside the theatre's own archive of past productions. The rare book collection includes nearly 500 plays, poems and other works from the 16th and 17th centuries, among them a second folio edition of Shakespeare's complete works, published in 1632. Entry is free, but anyone wanting to consult the collections has to register and book an appointment in advance because of the nature of the material. Those who are not there to research can still visit a foyer space which hosts free temporary exhibitions. Dr Will Tosh, who leads higher education and research at the Globe, said: "We want anyone with an interest to come and enjoy this space. "In a time when libraries tend not to open, they tend to close, and we're in a real crisis of library provision and also a crisis of reading, I'm extremely proud at the Globe that we are putting our name and our energy into the importance of books and libraries." The theatre has had a library for years, but Dr Tosh said it "wasn't housed in facilities that were appropriate" and was "harder to access". It now sits at the heart of the building, where he said it would "be quite hard to miss". The centre opened to researchers on 22 September and to the public two days later. At its heart is the Audre D. Carlin Reading Room, where visitors can request items from the library and archive, including recordings of every production staged at the Globe since the mid-1990s. The rare books are kept behind glass, but researchers can book an appointment to see them up close The building also houses the John Wolfson Rare Book Room, a lecture theatre, the Weston Foyer exhibition space and a climate-controlled store for the archive. Books that belonged to the Globe's founder, the American actor and director Sam Wanamaker, will be on display, some containing his handwritten notes. "Institutions have histories," Dr Tosh said. "Shakespeare has the most extraordinary history globally and in London. "This is somewhere that can bring those stories together." The archive also keeps costumes made using the Globe's "original practices" approach, which aims to recreate how plays were staged in Shakespeare's time. The Weston Foyer's displays are tied to the Globe's events programme, which this month includes a Shakespeare and race festival. title: Action on knife crime needed more than ever, says Damilola Taylor's brother
description: A new BBC documentary retells the story of Damilola Taylor's killing in Peckham, 26 years on.
body: Damilola Taylor was 10 years old when he was fatally stabbed in Peckham in November 2000 The brother of schoolboy Damilola Taylor, killed in an attack in Peckham 26 years ago, has said work to tackle knife crime is "needed now more than ever". The 10-year-old was fatally stabbed while on his way home from Peckham Library in south London on 27 November 2000. Babatunde (Tunde) Taylor now chairs the Damilola Taylor Trust, set up by their parents in his brother's memory. It works to provide support for disadvantaged children vulnerable to falling into crime. He said issues they were currently facing were "more diverse" than they were when his brother died. Damilola's killing is now the subject of a BBC documentary called Damilola: The Untold Story. Tunde said the problems faced today by young people were different to his experience growing up. "We've got the emergence of social media... we have to find a way to keep evolving and adapting," he said. Tunde says knife crime prevention services are still much needed, 26 years after his brother's death Tunde said the charity trust was facing an uncertain future, despite its many successful programmes. "One of the challenges we're facing is sustainability, just like every small charity there are issues regarding funding," he said. "We're trying to keep the trust sustainable for the next generation. We're open to partnerships with people who share what we are looking to achieve. "We need all hands on deck and we need that support to help us to continue to provide." Damilola was born in Nigeria and moved to the North Peckham Estate with his mother and siblings in August 2000. On 27 November, he was at Peckham Library with friends, including future actor John Boyega and Boyega's sister Grace. While walking home, Damilola was attacked and stabbed in the leg with a broken bottle. It severed an artery. Damilola was found in a stairwell on the estate by a caretaker and later died. His death sent shockwaves around the country. But convictions for his death were not secured until 2006 when two teenagers, who lived on the estate and were believed to be part of a local gang, were found guilty of manslaughter. Two previous trials had failed. John Boyega and his sister Grace were childhood friends with Damilola Speaking in the documentary, Boyega said the killing of his friend had a profound effect on him. He said it had spurred him on to pursue the opportunities that were available to him, which ultimately led to him achieving his dream of becoming an actor. "Damilola's legacy to me means being able to be unrealistic with your dreams," he said. "He wrote a poem and he used to recite it all the time: I will travel far and wide to choose my destiny and remould the world, I know it is my destiny to defend the world, which I hope to achieve in my lifetime. "From that poem [you can tell] he had plans and he didn't care about the environment he was in, he was more fixated on where he was going. So what's my excuse?" Tunde said it was "very important" his brother's story was told again, more than a quarter of a century on. "There's a whole generation of young people who were not around at the time and they get the chance to see him as a person, a young boy, his ambitions and how the tragedy cut that," he said. "If they can think of that and think about the choices they're making then we will have actually achieved something positive." title: Council exceeds Surrey tree planting target
description: A report finds some 885,000 trees have been planted, but there are concerns over survival rates.
body: More than 116,000 trees were planted in Surrey in the last financial year, according to a report More than 800,000 new trees have been planted across Surrey over the past five years, exceeding the council's own target, according to a report. Surrey County Council's report found 116,359 trees had been planted in the 2025/26 financial year alone. It said the total planted between 2021 and 2026 was around 885,000, surpassing its initial target of 600,000. However, Elmbridge Borough Council recently passed a motion calling for the future East Surrey council to update its tree strategy to consider survival rates. It said many trees planted in the borough were dying within a year as a result of not receiving the right aftercare. "There is little point celebrating the number of trees we plant if a significant number of them are dead a year later," said councillor Katerina Lusk. Surrey County Council has committed to 1.2 million trees being planted by 2030, representing one for every resident. The authority's report looked at the progress of its climate change delivery programme over the past five years. It said the council was "broadly on track" to meet its 2030 net zero targets, stating that its carbon emissions have been reduced by around 60%. The report said: "A major success of the programme has been supporting residents to reduce energy bills and improve their homes. "More than 1,438 low-income households received energy efficiency improvements, including insulation, solar and low-carbon heating measures." It also acknowledged challenges ahead in continuing to pursue decarbonisation policies. The programme was "significantly affected by external market conditions, supply chain constraints and wider economic pressures", it added. title: 'I watched Apollo 17 launch with Neil Armstrong'
description: Dermot Gethings was 16 when Nasa picked him to watch the Apollo 17 launch alongside Neil Armstrong.
body: Dermot Gethings is vice chair of the Preston & District Astronomical Society Nearly 54 years ago, Apollo 17 blasted off from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, bound for the moon. Standing alongside legendary astronauts like Neil Armstrong and Dick Gordon, a schoolboy from Lancashire was there to see the final manned lunar landing mission. Ahead of the screening of a documentary about his experience, Preston astronomer Dermot Gethings recalled how, at 16 years old, he was hand picked by the United States embassy and Nasa to witness the launch. "As it launched there was this incredible adrenaline and a shockwave that rattled every bone in your body," said the now 70-year-old of the events of 7 December 1972. "It is the stuff that you dream about." Dermot Gethings with Neil Armstrong at the Miami motel the pair stayed at ahead of the Apollo 17 launch While Gethings grew up in Frenchwood in Preston, he was shaped by the ongoing Cold War Space Race and the quest to put a man on the moon. A childhood of sci-fi, The Thunderbirds and televised Nasa missions meant space was always a keen interest of his. He said the "trigger moment" for his lifelong interest in astronomy was seeing the Milky Way in the night sky when he was 10. "It hit me straight away - that was where I wanted to be," he said. "And I took a deep interest in space." From then on Gethings started an astronomy club at the former St John Fisher's School in Preston - putting on talks both at his school and others and running public exhibitions. Gethings got an O-Level in Astronomy, at age 16, after teaching himself the curriculum at home After Gethings' exhibitions were photographed by the Lancashire Evening Post, his life changed forever. "A few months after the photographs were published I received a letter out of the blue from the United States Embassy in London," he recalled. "It said 'We have a very special project to discuss with you regarding the forthcoming Apollo 17 mission'." Gethings was then told he was one of 16 UK students being invited for an interview at the embassy. One of the students was to be selected by Nasa for an all-expenses paid,19-day trip to watch Apollo 17's launch. "I didn't hear anything for a couple of weeks," he said. "When I got the letter of congratulations inviting me on the trip I couldn't believe it - it was amazing!" Gethings was one of 80 students from around the world to be invited on Nasa's first and only International Youth Science Tour And after boarding his first aeroplane flight at Manchester Airport, he began a tour which would see him chatting to the first man on the moon Neil Armstrong, dining with senators in The White House, and getting behind-the-scenes looks at Nasa bases across a dozen states. Gethings pictured in front of the White House on 5 December 1972 A memorable moment for Gethings came when he accidentally met Armstrong - the first man to have ever walked on the moon. "On the day of the launch I stepped out of my motel room and clumsily walked into a tall gentleman," Gethings recalled. "I stood on his foot by accident and I was really embarrassed. "I looked up and the man smiling down at me was Neil Armstrong!" The pair walked downstairs together chatting about the upcoming launch, before Armstrong offered for his wife to take a photograph of them. "I handed her my camera and Neil and I shook hands beside his car as she took the photograph - it was fantastic." Gethings also received a signed photograph of the student representatives from Neil Armstrong In the early hours of the following morning Gethings sat just inches away from Armstrong in the VIP viewing box at the Kennedy Space Center when Apollo 17 lift-off occurred at 00:33 local time. They were only three miles (5km) away from the launchpad. "My heart was pumping in my chest," he remembered. "And when the vehicle cleared the tower suddenly you got punched in the chest by a shockwave. "The ground beneath your feet was like an earthquake and the stands were rattling. "And then you got hit by this incredibly painful crackling staccato snapping sound against the skin on your face. "Minutes later Apollo 17 became a bright star moving across the sky and away from us. "The experience was something one never forgets or can be equalled." Gethings met and later received a postcard from Apollo 17 mission commander Eugene Cernan During the 14-day mission the Apollo 17 astronauts, led by mission commander Eugene Cernan, performed three space walks on the lunar surface. The third moonwalk, on 13 December, was the last time anybody walked on the moon. Gethings was at the Space Center in Houston, Texas, when the astronauts on the moon's surface spoke directly to the group of students before collecting a moon rock from the surface. Once back on earth, that moonrock was split into 80 pieces - distributed to each student - and Gethings became the custodian of the UK's Apollo 17 Goodwill Moon Rock. The UK's Apollo 17 Goodwill Moon Rock is on display at the Natural History Museum in London When Gethings returned home he presented the moonrock to Prime Minister Edward Heath at 10 Downing Street in July 1973. Brigadier Jim McDivitt, Walter Annenberg, PM Edward Heath and Dermot Gethings at Downing Street Gethings has continued his love of astronomy ever since. A fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society and vice chair of Preston & District Astronomical Society, he also works with the Jeremiah Horrocks Institute of the University of Central Lancashire delivering talks. The story of his journey to becoming custodian of the UK's Apollo 17 Goodwill Moon Rock is set to be told in a 30-minute documentary by University of Lancashire graduate Sarah Bullough. Ahead of his big screen debut, Gethings said: "Space had been a passion all my life. "To be brought over there to see places and meet people that you have only ever read about or seen on TV - it was the stuff of dreams. "I knew what

title: Woman racially abused at work by boys awarded £15k
description: The woman was a council intervention worker when two boys inflicted the abuse in April 2024.
body: The council spokesperson said the authority "respects the findings of the tribunal" A black council worker who was subjected to "serious racial abuse" and faced with "dismissive" managers after she complained has been awarded £15,000. The woman was an intervention worker in West Berkshire Council's Youth Justice Support Team when two boys inflicted the abuse in April 2024. An employment tribunal in the summer was told authority managers inferred to the woman that "absorbing that kind of abuse simply 'went with the territory'". A West Berkshire Council spokesperson said it "respects the findings of the tribunal and will reflect carefully on the points raised". The worker joined the council in July 2023 before she resigned in June 2024. When she complained to managers about the racial abuse, they were found to have focused on her response after she referred to them as "little boys". The tribunal found she had suffered "severe provocation" and that the council "failed to recognise the seriousness and unpleasantness of the [boys'] racial abuse". David McMullen, who helped the woman in her case as a senior organiser for the GMB union, said she was "treated horrendously in the first instance and this was further compounded by management at West Berkshire Council". He added: "Racism has no place in society at all and certainly workers should not have to face this treatment when at work – in fact it is the job of employers to protect against such abuse." The West Berkshire Council spokesperson added: "The safety and wellbeing of our staff is extremely important to us. "We do not accept abuse, discrimination or harassment directed towards our employees and we are committed to supporting colleagues when incidents occur." title: Carys lived with endometriosis pain for decades, then everything changed
description: Carys Thurlby says "intense pain had become my normal" but surgery changed her life.
body: Carys Thurlby says surgery transformed her life, helping her lose 10 stone and regain her energy A woman who lived with "intense" pain from endometriosis for decades has lost more than half her body weight after surgery transformed her life. Carys Thurlby lost 10 stone (140lbs) in 18 months after having a hysterectomy, which she said finally brought lasting relief from years of pain and exhaustion. The 43-year-old said the change had been "night and day". "Having intense pain had become my normal," she said. Thurlby believes she had been living with endometriosis since she started her periods as a teenager. She remembers sitting her GCSE exams "chewing on paracetamol" as pain spread through her pelvis and legs. "I didn't really know that being in so much pain each month was not normal," she said. "I didn't really know that what I was experiencing wasn't what women were meant to experience." Man missing in flooding discarded by police, family say Do not speculate about girl's death, public asked City redevelopment could include major NHS facility She was diagnosed at 19 after undergoing a laparoscopy when she was in "excruciating" pain. "That was the first time I had ever heard of it," she admitted. Like many women with endometriosis, Thurlby spent years living with symptoms. The condition, external, which can affect multiple parts of the body, can have a major impact on work, education, relationships and day-to-day life, and there is currently no cure. Over the years, she had several operations, but the effects were only temporary. Her ovaries were eventually removed after being damaged by endometriosis, before she later had a hysterectomy. Symptoms of endometriosis can include heavy periods or severe period pain, and pain in your stomach, lower back or pelvic area, among others Thurlby, from Worcester, said chronic pain and fatigue affected every aspect of her life as she balanced raising her children with her career. "I've been so fortunate," she said. "I can't describe how different it felt and it was a real shock to me to understand this is how normal people function, and not to accommodate pain and fatigue into everyday life." She said she often relied on sugar for a quick burst of energy just to get through the day. "The idea that I would then go out and exercise or move, even a gentle walk to the shops, was just not on the cards," she said. "There was no room in my life for me to look after my wellness." As her health improved, the weight began to come off. She gained confidence, started exercising and discovered a passion for running. Eighteen months ago, she could not run for longer than a minute. Since then, Thurlby said she had completed the Worcester Half Marathon and is now training for next year's London Marathon. Her experience is shared by Vicki Shattock, from Belbroughton, who has written a book about her own struggle to have health concerns taken seriously. Shattock urged women experiencing persistent pain to trust their instincts. "You know your body better than anyone," she said. "If someone is telling you pain is normal and you know it isn't, don't let it go." title: Charities and businesses wrestle with diesel cost
description: Cancer charity Daft as a Brush and Teesside Minibus Hire say they are struggling with pump prices.
body: Cancer charity Daft as a Brush's Scott Jobson said funds raised by donations were being lost at the pump Charities and businesses across the North East have said they are struggling with the rising cost of diesel. The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group. Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide. The North East cancer charity Daft as a Brush said it could no longer afford to upgrade its diesel vehicles to electric as they grappled with filling them up, whilst Teesside Minibus Hire said soaring prices were "not sustainable". Daft as a Brush, which provides cancer patients with transport to their hospital appointments, said it was shelling out £15,000 a month on diesel - £5,000 more than last year. The Newcastle-based charity - which drives 600,000 miles every year in its 30 vans - said it had planned on replacing them with electric vehicles, but now could not afford to because the money was being swallowed up at the pump. Volunteer driver Davey Hall said: "Before the big hikes, we used to maybe fill up and it would take £40-45. "Last week, it was £94 to fill the tank from half full." Head of income generation Scott Jobson said the money was being taken from funds raised by donations, and they were not eligible for any kind of discount. "At the pump, what you see is what we pay," he said. "It stunts our growth and development." In Middlesbrough, Teesside Minibus Hire director Billy Johnson said they often signed contracts with schools and businesses which could span multiple years - and were based on the cost of fuel when they were written. "We're not running at a loss yet, but we're running close it to it not being worthwhile or sustainable," he said. Johnson said they were having to pass the cost on to customers using services such as day hires, but because those customers were struggling with inflation themselves, they were not always prepared to pay the increased price. Instead, people were turning towards cheaper, unlicensed hire services which did not pay the same overheads, he said. Asked whether the business could survive if fuel prices did not drop, he said: "Long term, probably not." In May, the government announced it would extend a fuel duty (tax) freeze until the end of the year. It caps the tax at 5p per litre for petrol and diesel, and was introduced by the previous Conservative government after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine pushed prices up in 2022. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages over the Iran War and has said the country has a "diverse and resilient supply". title: It's within DUP's gift to remove O'Neill as first minister, says Lockhart
description: Carla Lockhart says unionist voters are angry at Michelle O'Neill over her role in the Garvaghy Road protests.
body: O'Neill previously dismissed a call from the DUP to resign over her role in protests against the Drumcree parade A DUP MP says unionist voters are angry at Michelle O'Neill over her role in the Garvaghy Road protests and says it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont. Carla Lockhart said the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill as Northern Ireland's first minister. On Friday, the secretary of state banned the Portadown District Lodge from marching down the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. His decision was welcomed by nationalist politicians but unionists have criticised the move. O'Neill is one of a number of Sinn Féin politicians who have confirmed they received letters from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Four key takeaways from the Drumcree dispute so far Speaking to BBC NI's Sunday Politics programme outside Drumcree Church on Saturday, Lockhart said her constituents are angry. "They're angry at the chief constable for allowing lawlessness to win, for allowing the mob to dictate," she said. "They're angry at the secretary of state for his intervention, but the most palpable anger is at Michelle O'Neill, this self-proclaimed 'first minister for all' for breaking the law flagrantly on the Garvaghy Road, and thumbing her nose at unionism and at the Orange Order and at this community." Police had repeatedly warned those taking part in the unnotified protest that they could be liable for arrest. O'Neill has defended her involvement, saying she was standing with the local community in opposition to an Orange Order parade through the area. She previously dismissed a call from the DUP to resign over her role in protests telling the assembly she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them". Lockhart says her party must take action against O'Neill The DUP (Democratic Unionist Party) share power with Sinn Féin in the Northern Ireland Executive, but Lockhart says it can no longer be business as usual. "You can not continue to engage with someone who is so blatant in her disregard and disdain for a large section of this community," she said. "Very clearly it cannot be business as usual at Stormont." Lockhart says her party must take action against O'Neill. "People want to see consequences, and we have said very clearly, profound consequence, and therefore we should use whatever is in our armoury to ensure that Michelle O'Neill, the person who really is supposed to be that first minister for all, as she claims, is dealt with in the appropriate way," she added. The DUP could remove O'Neill from the first minister's position if the deputy first minister quits. That role is held by Emma Little-Pengelly, but that seems unlikely. Over the weekend the DUP leader Gavin Robinson and Little-Pengelly said they would not collapse the power-sharing institutions. But Lockhart wants that option to be considered. "There is lots of options on the table with regards to Michelle O'Neill and her continued position, and we have it within our gift to ensure that she is actually removed from that position," she said. "So it is time for the anger to be seen in the politics and for profound consequences to follow. "We've been told that all options are still on the table. So that is a very clear option. "What I am saying is, within the community, within the unionist community, within the Orange community, and within grassroots loyalism there's a real anger towards a first minister, who claims she is the first minister for all, for thumbing her nose, laughing on the Garvaghy Road last night at this community, who have stood lawfully." Sir Chris Bryant said his decision to ban the Drumcree parade 'was in the best interests of peace' The Parades Commission ruled that the march on Sunday 27 September could go ahead with restrictions in place. That parade did not happen and, after a series of legal challenges and talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state banned the procession on Friday. Sir Chris Bryant said his decision to ban the Drumcree parade "was in the best interests of peace". The secretary of state said he received advice from the PSNI chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest. On Saturday, a High Court judge said a legal appeal by Orangemen following the secretary of state's decision was not an emergency case and adjourned the hearing until Monday. Lockhart said the 35 Orangemen from Portadown District Lodge had "stood lawfully" for the last two weeks on Drumcree hill. "I've been on this hill from I was 10 years of age, it means something to me. It means a lot to my constituents here in Upper Bann," she said. So does the Upper Bann MP still have confidence in her own party? "I have confidence that I will ensure that my constituents' voices are heard within the party, and I will ensure that I continue to represent the views here in Portadown," she said. title: 'It shows you there is hope': Football coach on anorexia recovery journey
description: Jordan Caldwell, who once struggled to see a future beyond anorexia, says bodybuilding gave him a new purpose in life.
body: Jordan Caldwell recently did a photoshoot to mark his 30th birthday For Jordan Caldwell, turning 30 meant more than celebrating another birthday. It was the chance to stand in front of a camera, strike a bodybuilder post and reflect on how far he had come after almost two decades of battling anorexia. It was also an age his parents feared he would never reach. Jordan, who has lived with an eating disorder since he was 12, said the photoshoot was the culmination of a dream he had held onto since a relapse in his teens. He said reaching out to online fitness coach Aamir Ishtiaque four years ago helped change his life, giving him something to work towards. It was the day, he said, that "everything changed for the better". Years later, he said he hopes that by sharing his journey it will show others in the same position that it is possible to find strength "in something that you love and have a passion for". A youth coach with Glentoran FC in Belfast, Jordan said he has always had a love for sport, particularly football and bodybuilding. "I've always looked up to bodybuilders as like superheroes and something I aspired to be," he said. This video can not be played Jordan said he hit his lowest point at 18 years old, when a relapse led to a stay at a London treatment centre specialising in eating disorders. The trauma of his intense struggle with anorexia resulted in a diagnosis of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). But with Aamir's support and a goal in mind, he said he began to find a way forward. "The first year or so, it was just getting myself back on the straight and narrow and actually seeing there is a point in living again," he told BBC News NI. Having someone to speak to and trust on his journey back to health and well-being was, he said, the "most important" thing. A photo from Jordan's photoshoot Now actively navigating recovery, Jordan said he is taking steps every day to manage his disorder. "I believe it is something I will battle with every day, but I can be on top of the negative side more than the negative side being on top of me." As his renewed sense of purpose shifted into ambition, Jordan began looking beyond the day-to-day and decided to set himself a long-term goal to mark his 30th birthday with a professional gym photoshoot. "I said for my 30th I want to be in a state again where I can say 'I had anorexia, it's not stopping me anymore' and I've actually built back muscle and built towards something that I've said I've dreamt of since I relapsed again." Aamir Ishtiaque is Jordan's fitness coach For Aamir, working with Jordan has changed him as a coach. "The journey with Jordan has been quite interesting. First and foremost it's made me a much better coach, it's made me understand that everyone comes from different positions." Aamir said establishing trust was particularly important because Jordan had found it difficult to take advice from other people. "If I can gain his trust, do small things initially, then that leads onto bigger things," he said. With the photoshoot goal achieved, Aamir is already thinking about what comes next. "Once you hit a goal there is always a period of where you're kind of in limbo and I didn't want that. I couldn't afford to have that with Jordan." Aamir acknowledges that Jordan's battle with his eating disorder is not a linear journey, but their close working relationship has reached the stage where he now considers him family. "I have transformed thousands of people in my career but this is probably the best, simply because the relationship I have developed with Jordan has been a lot more than just a coach and a client." Reflecting on the moments leading up to the camera rolling, Jordan said it felt "pretty cool" to get a spray tan and try out bodybuilder poses for the shoot. "I would probably say, if not the best day of my life, then it was the second best day," he said. The only other moment in his life that could compare, he said, was playing high-level sport as a young boy, before his eating disorder took hold. "Bearing in mind my whole life basically has been living with anorexia - yes, it was the best day of my life. "For me to now look back and think 'that was me', it shows you there is hope." The Department of Health has specialist eating disorder services in place since 2006 supported by an annual investment of £2 million since 2008 Every Health and Social Care Trust has a specialist Adult Eating Disorder Service and a specialist Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service Eating Disorder Team The Mental Health Strategy 2021-2031 includes a commitment to further strengthening community-based care and treatment The department-led Eating Disorder Managed Care Network brings together, health trusts, people with lived experience, community and voluntary sector and academia to drive regional improvement If you have been affected by the issues raised in this article, you can access help and support at BBC Action Line. title: Toxicity and uncertainty await Man City - will their season even matter?
description: Manchester City visit Liverpool on Sunday with a lot of uncertainty hanging over them. Phil McNulty looks at what lies ahead.
body: Manchester City will be guaranteed a hostile reception when they face Liverpool at Anfield after being found guilty of breaching financial rules Manchester City will face an atmosphere of toxicity and hostility they have never experienced before when they walk out to face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. If City made a list of clubs they would prefer not to visit immediately after being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, Liverpool would be at the top ringed in red. The relationship between the clubs has often been fractious for more than a decade, tensions fuelled by a sense of injustice felt by Liverpool fans who believe more Premier League titles should have been theirs instead of City's. In 2013/14, 2018/19 and 2021/22, Liverpool finished second behind City – on the last two occasions by a single point - in what became, especially with Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp in charge, the defining domestic rivalry in recent years. Liverpool supporters have long been convinced they would have won those titles had City not wielded the vast financial firepower that brought them under investigation, while those of a sky blue persuasion counter by simply highlighting the enduring brilliance and beauty of the teams Guardiola produced. City, under new head coach Enzo Maresca, arrive at Anfield continuing to maintain their innocence after launching an appeal against the decision of an independent commission to deliver a guilty verdict. And they arrive top of the table – but with a shadow cast over the entire season and its potential outcomes as the Premier League weighs up City's punishment, with their appeal running alongside. As the cloud of City's guilty verdict hangs over the Premier League, each victory will carry a qualification, each league table will contain an unseen asterisk, each achievement viewed through the prism of potential future penalties and the fallout at each end of the top tier. It has even led to the unheard of suggestion that the entire Premier League season could be rendered meaningless, given the potential scale of the consequences facing City, with talk of expulsion and relegation as well as record points deductions. This must wait for what is likely to be a lengthy legal process, but it is against this backdrop of bitterness that City play their first league match since the verdict, in an Anfield arena that barely disguised its contempt for their fierce rivals even before that guilty verdict was handed down. The Kop will be in no mood to await legal finalities or the outcome of an appeal. There will be sound. There will be fury. There will be resentment. This video can not be played Top five Liverpool-Man City moments Maresca, who has not only inherited Guardiola's legacy but also the fallout from City's punishment, was calm itself in the face of a barrage of questions at his media briefing before Sunday's game. While being at pains to point out he was present to preview a game against Liverpool, he said: "The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don't have doubt about that. "It will be a tough game, for sure. We need to be ready, the focus needs to be about the game, but we know the environment at Anfield. "It probably will be worse because of the situation but, again, it will be our duty to do our best and try to win the game. The reason I decide to become manager is for this type of game." Maresca placed the emphasis on "when" City win their appeal, as they vehemently insist the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe". The commission, in contrast, used the word "sham" eight times when describing City's dealings, including artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" deals. The danger now is, with sanctions and appeals to come, that this could be known in future as the "sham" Premier League season. City have assumed their familiar position at the top of the table – but is this a title they cannot "win" with a guilty verdict hanging over them? Former England striker Alan Shearer told BBC Radio 5 Live Sport: "I just think it's such a bad look that we're still having to wait for the consequences. "We've never seen anything like this. This is the biggest thing to happen to the Premier League since it started in 1992, that's how big it is. Credibility matters and you won't get anything different from any coach or player at Manchester City other than we're going to stick together and we believe in the club. "They're about to find out the anger from every club, starting at Anfield. Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca spoke about "when" the club wins their appeal "It needs sorting out now because they've spent a fortune in the summer. They've won every game and that could still be the case in two months, three months, four months. They could end up winning the league. That's why it needs sorting out now because it's such a bad look if it's allowed to fester. "The level of hostility will rise wherever they go. The ramifications are endless to this case. Where it goes after is something we don't know. It's huge. It really is massive." Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola, preparing for his first experience of this meeting of Premier League superpowers, admitted: "The worst thing probably is the uncertainty. No-one knows what's going to happen. We have to focus on Liverpool and being the best club we can be, the best team we can be. That's my challenge." City's insistence that they will clear their name will not prevent a torrid, to put it mildly, Anfield reception.
