title: Adventurer who lost leg says 'don't send me money'
description: Luke Tarrant says he is "disgusted" that fraudsters are pretending to be him on social media.
body: Luke Tarrant said there were too many people out there pretending to be him An adventurer who lost a leg in a motorbike crash has warned people not to send money in response to social media messages from someone pretending to be him. Luke Tarrant, 30, from Bedford, who has more than 770,000 followers on TikTok and Instagram, said he was "disgusted" and extremely angry after discovering someone had being scammed into transferring their life savings to a fake Facebook page. He said the page had been created in his name with private messages asking if people had "anything you can spare" as "things have been a bit difficult lately". Tarrant said he reported it to Meta, which owns the site. The company confirmed the page had been removed "for violating our policies". Tarrant posted his annoyance on his Instagram page to warn people that others had been stealing his videos and posting them on fake accounts. He said: "If you're speaking to me on Facebook, stop right now, do not send any money." Luke Tarrant was left fighting for his life in Colombia, in May 2024 He said he is bad at responding to direct messages and had been alerted to the issue by his girlfriend and his gym. They told him a woman had transferred her life savings to someone she thought was him and was left totally embarrassed. He said money was raised for him by his gym in 2024 when he lost his leg while travelling through South America, but the fundraiser was quickly taken down when he didn't need any more money. The only other time he has asked for money was when he fundraised for care, support and specialist equipment for gold medal Paralympian, David Smith who has terminal cancer. Luke Tarrant said he asked people to donate to provide support for David Smith MBE who has terminal cancer He said as his following has grown on social media, so have the fake accounts pretending to be him. "I keep reporting them, they get taken down but it seems to take forever, it should be easier to get them taken down." Tarrant said he was also aware of AI being used to impersonate his voice in messages and videos and it was "scary". He said: "If you are ever asked for money online or are chatting to someone with a public profile, have a second thought. "This is the new way that's smarter at impersonating people, we all need a new level of awareness we didn't need before. Please be careful." Luke Tarrant said people need to double check who they think they are communicating with A spokesperson for Meta said: "Scammers are relentless and continuously evolve their tactics to try to evade detection, which is why we're constantly developing new ways to make it harder for scammers to deceive others. "Last year alone we took down more than 159 million scam ads with over 92% detected proactively before anyone reported them. "We also removed 10.9 million accounts associated with criminal scam centres. "We've built additional detection models, specifically for celeb-bait, that automatically incorporate what we have learned about the changing tactics used in ads to help us improve." A spokesperson for Bedfordshire Police advised people to be vigilant when approached by online accounts alleging to be public figures or friends. They said: "Scammers can easily create convincing false profiles, which are built to use trusted relationships to manipulate people into sending money, bank details or vouchers." The spokesperson advised people to read the force's online safety guides, external. Report Fraud said if anyone is asked for money by someone they have recently started speaking with online, it should be warning sign. The organisation said anyone who believes they have been a victim should report it online , externalor call 0300 123 2040. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Why are so many four-year-olds not potty-trained before school?
description: A third of school starters in the West Midlands last year were not toilet-trained, a survey suggests.
body: Ruth Lu-Quee is a mother and early years specialist who says parents should not be blamed for delays in their children's development For some parents the countdown to starting school means buying uniforms, labelling water bottles and trying to squeeze in one last summer holiday. For others there is a more basic question to tackle: can their child use the toilet on their own? According to a survey by the charity Kindred Squared, almost a third of children starting school in the West Midlands last year were not fully toilet-trained and 42% of those arriving in reception were deemed not school-ready by primary school staff. This week the charity announced its potty-training scheme, which provides resources and support including increased training for nurseries, schools and professionals, will be rolled out in Solihull. In a pilot in York, which began in April, parents were sent potty-training and school readiness guides with their offers of a school place. Workshops were held, resources distributed and support offered through GPs, pharmacies, libraries and community hubs. As a result, the number of non-toilet-trained children starting reception fell by almost half. An early years specialist based in Wolverhampton has said the conversation about school readiness needs to extend well beyond the toilet. Ruth Lu-Quee, a former deputy head teacher and founder of My Mummy Teacher, works with parents and schools to support children's development through play-based learning. She said: "We want to be setting the foundations. Can they talk and have conversations? Are you reading stories to them? Are they moving their bodies? Because all of those things are what then underpin the skills to be able to learn, practising everyday independence. Can they hang their coat or can they take their socks off?" But she warned that school readiness could become a source of anxiety for families and said it was important to recognise that children reached milestones at different speeds. "We need to be careful that school readiness doesn't become a checklist that four-year-olds are expected to pass or something that leaves parents feeling they have failed if their child develops differently," she said. "Childhood isn't a race." Lu-Quee believes there is more to school readiness than just toileting Rachel, a mother-of-two from Nottinghamshire, is one of Lu-Quee's clients. She tried to toilet-train her son when he was three but he had problems with withholding stools. She works as a teacher but said being on the other side of the problem as a parent was very different. "I'd say as a teacher, I feel I'm quite an informed parent in this area," she said. "So I was thinking, 'I know what's going on but I don't know what to do'. "It's not the parent, it's not being lazy; it's hard and it's a lot of effort," she added. She was told she would not be able to access funded support for her child until he was five, and it was not until the end of his reception year that the family received help. Now aged eight, her son is awaiting an assessment for ADHD, which Rachel believes could have affected aspects of his development despite going unnoticed in his early years. "Withholding can be trauma-informed and it can be because of passing something that has hurt at some point or someone has reacted badly to them having an accident," she said, adding she believed embarrassment and shame had contributed to her son's difficulties after he had an accident at nursery. Helen Davies, a health visitor and children's nurse based in Stafford, said children who repeatedly had accidents may be frightened of the toilet, leading to constipation. "A child who is struggling may be frightened of the toilet, withholding poo or experiencing constipation. Repeated accidents should prompt curiosity about what is getting in the way rather than an assumption that parents have not tried hard enough," she said. Helen Davies says problems with toileting could have underlying causes Annamaria Bailey, 37, a mother-of-two from Wolverhampton, said toilet-training her two-year-old involved taking four days off from her job as an independent travel agent. "I'm a stay-at-home mum," she said. "I don't know how I would block out four consecutive days of work." She said helping children with skills such as toileting and communication could be a particular challenge for families where both parents worked full time. "There's no longer that time to sit and play with your children now as much as you would like," she said. "I just genuinely don't think it's the parents' fault." Annamaria Bailey took time off work to potty-train her child Lu-Quee highlighted that older generations are working later too, meaning some families "don't have the village like they used to have". Kindred Squared said the West Midlands had seen one of the biggest declines in school readiness in the country, with the number of children lacking skills such as toileting increasing year on year. Solihull Council said it had "had reports locally of a higher proportion of children arriving at school in nappies or pull-ups in comparison to a few years ago", adding that its new potty-training scheme would form part of its wider Best Start in Life programme. Bailey, a former reception teacher and early years lead, said she had worked in "deprived and affluent areas" and had seen inequalities in school readiness. "It comes down to income," she said. While some parents were able to buy parenting books, she said those on lower incomes had less access to information. "Books are quite expensive," she added, suggesting families could be given free toilet-training resources when their children turned two. title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
description: The White House had blocked access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, leading them to restrict pool coverage.
body: The row over the White House pool affected live TV coverage of Trump events last month The US justice department (DoJ) says it is investigating several television networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump. The agency has asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the White House TV pool, a system where networks switch off covering the president and providing the footage to other publications. The networks temporarily suspended this system last month for several days after the president blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media. "Group boycotts among commercial competitors ​can violate the Sherman Act," a DoJ spokesperson said, referring to the federal law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices. "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ​news organisations have violated the antitrust laws." Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team. The White House later reinstated their access after a ruling from a judge. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights. The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage. The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president. In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. title: UK launch flood taskforce to prepare for extreme winter weather
description: The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.
body: The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter. After a summer of record breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office has described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months. "We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting. The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding. Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, bringing together the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries. Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next." The government has committed at least £10.5 billion up to 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding. The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El Niño weather event. It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year. The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter. It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies. The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record. Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average. title: 'Tiger attack horror' and Trump tells Zelensky 'time to go'
description: The majority of the papers on Sunday are dominated by a man who was attacked by a tiger at a wildlife park near Doncaster.
body: The majority of the papers on Sunday are dominated by the death of a man in Yorkshire after he was attacked by a tiger. The Daily Star declares "Tiger attack horror", and says the unnamed man was killed on Saturday after he climbed into a big cat enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park. Similarly, the headline on the front page of the Sunday People reads: "Killed in tiger horror". The Sunday edition of the Mirror has spoken to several witnesses to the attack, one told the paper that "the keepers did everything they could". It reports that both staff and visitors to the zoo "desperately tried to distract the big cat", but police said the man died at the scene. The front page of the Sunday Times has focused on remarks from US President Donald Trump, after he told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that it was "time to go". It comes one day after the US announced plans to buy more that one million tonnes of diesel from Russia, to what the paper describes as an "outpouring of anger and disbelief" among European leaders and security officials. The president told reporters that Ukraine's continued airstrikes on Russia were driving up American fuel prizes and creating "problems for the world". The Sunday Telegraph says the US anger at Ukrainian strikes "threatens to deepen the rift" between Trump and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The paper reports that Burnham has offered Zelensky his "full support" in addition to stronger sanctions on Moscow and says the Ukrainian leader was blindsided by the announcement, issuing a "rare public rebuke of the Trump administration". Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the Mail on Sunday that she is ready for an election "at any point", amid growing speculation that Burnham will call a "snap poll". According to the paper, Badenoch said she does not believe Burnham's assurances last month that there will be "no election any time soon", and believes he might strike while "both the Green Party and the Liberal Democrats are in disarray". "EU would 'plunder' Britain if Brexit reversed" reads the Sunday Express, amid fears Burnham will sign up to "catastrophic" deals in Brussels. The paper says Badenoch has accused the prime minister of wanting to plunge the country into an era of "tedious and divisive Brexit debates", ahead of a landmark UK-EU summit next month. title: I was told I had depression for 14 years until I got sectioned - it was bipolar
description: Kimberley Atkinson assumed her symptoms were depression until her behaviour started to change dramatically.
body: Kimberley Atkinson was told she had depression but she was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder When Kimberley Atkinson was told she had depression, the diagnosis made sense to her. She had struggled with her mental health since she was a teenager and hoped being prescribed antidepressants would improve things. "My mood had always been up and down, and my emotional regulation was never very good," Kimberley said. She said the impact it had on her life was awful, with depressions that felt like "sinking into a dark hole", leaving her stuck in bed and not able to face the day. For 14 years, she assumed these were all the symptoms of her depression until her behaviour started to change dramatically. This video can not be played My bipolar disorder was misdiagnosed as depression for years "I started becoming really erratic in my thinking style, having delusional ideas, speaking really fast, becoming very irritable," Kimberley said. One night, while she was studying for a PHD at the University of Edinburgh, she drove to London after seeing a news report that someone was in trouble and becoming convinced she was the only person who could save them. She also became convinced her moods were causing bad weather. Friends and family became concerned and she was eventually admitted to a psychiatric ward against her will. It was here that doctors finally realised she had bipolar disorder. Studies have suggested that a significant number of people with severe/recurrent depression could actually have bipolar, with some research putting it as many as one in five, external. 'I'm not sure who I am' - Bake Off winner in shock after bipolar diagnosis 'It was a relief to be diagnosed with bipolar' Prof Danny Smith, chair of psychiatry at the University of Edinburgh, told the BBC that better "screening" was needed by health professionals, such as asking about symptoms like mania and if patients had a family history of the condition. His call for screening guidance to be urgently updated is backed by the Royal College of Psychiatrists and charity Bipolar UK. They say better screening could be "life-saving" as medication for depression can often make people with bipolar more unwell. During Kimberley's three-month stay in hospital, psychiatrists looked beyond her depression for the first time. At first she didn't want to accept her bipolar diagnosis but she said years of symptoms eventually made sense. "When I think about how my life was before my diagnosis, it was so chaotic," Kimberley said. "Whereas now I'm stable, which is in large part due to the medication." Formerly known as manic depression, bipolar is a mental health condition that causes extreme changes in mood. During 'high' periods, known as mania or hypomania, people with bipolar often feel very excited and creative or have unusual amounts of energy. They often experience racing thoughts, a reduced need for sleep, and being very irritable. In severe cases, mania can cause a break from reality. It's not known exactly what causes bipolar, but people with it appear to have physical changes in their brains and it often runs in families. Treatments can involve mood-stabilising medication like lithium and talking therapies, helping people go long periods without symptoms. Jacqui Armstrong took more than 30 years to be diagnosed with bipolar Jacqui Armstrong also spent years being treated for depression before receiving the correct diagnosis. The 64-year-old began treatment on various antidepressants from her teenage years and over the next three decades her depressions led to several hospital admissions and a suicide attempt, all while she worked as a teacher in a primary school then a nursery. "I couldn't even get up the stairs, I was just broken," she said. "I just felt like a huge failure the whole time, thinking 'why can't I get well?'." Jacqui said that during one episode, she was even given electroconvulsive therapy – a treatment that uses an electric current to induce a controlled seizure. But she said the signs of bipolar were always there. As well as frequent depressive periods, she experienced 'hypomania' episodes, spurts of unusually high energy, activity, or mood that were less severe than full mania. "I would suddenly feel like a confident person, and I had all these ideas, and I was very sociable, thinking how many things can I fit into my diary," she said. "And then I would energise myself into a breakdown." It was only during her final hospital admission for depression that a psychiatrist asked Jacqui if she'd ever experienced symptoms of hypomania. She was then assessed further and diagnosed her with bipolar II – more than 30 years after first seeking help for her mental health. Meanwhile Kimberley, who had experienced a "full" manic episode that resulted in a break from reality, was diagnosed with bipolar I. Experts say bipolar II is even harder to diagnose because it involves more frequent depressions and the manic episodes are not as severe, which is why they are dubbed hypomania. Prof Danny Smith said bipolar is a "highly manageable" condition when diagnosed Experts such as Smith believe bipolar disorder is significantly underdiagnosed. He said about one in 100 people receive a diagnosis during their lifetime but research suggests the true figure could be closer to one in 50. Studies also suggest patients in the UK typically wait almost a decade between first reporting symptoms and receiving a diagnosis. Smith said the long delays suggest that people are not being routinely screened properly for symptoms of hypomania or mania which should result in a referral to a psychiatrist to rule out the possibility of bipolar. While existing UK-wide guidelines, external say doctors should already do this, Smith said updated and better-publicised screening tools are "really important" because research suggests this is routinely not happening. title: Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
description: Film-maker Sue Kim talks about having unprecedented access to K-Pop idol Lisa Manobal at her most candid.
body: Lisa, who was born Pranpriya Manobal in Thailand, became one of the world's most-recognisable K-pop idols as a member of Blackpink What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal? That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus. The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system. The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored. The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025. Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement. With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room. "I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC. The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no". Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart. "It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves. Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English". Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history. "Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better. It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external). Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October. "There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds. "I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness. "And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her." Sue Kim (right) followed Lisa for a year, as she launched her solo career during a break in Blackpink's activities The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego. In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head". "To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much". In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort. That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product. Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece. "You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says. "And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional." Lisa put aside scandal and online death threats to put on one of the standout performances of 2025's Coachella Music Festival The documentary captures Lisa's joy - and relief - after she pulled off the hour-long show The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market. When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari. But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships. "I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life." As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US. "Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim. "In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat. "Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years." Blackpink are one of K-pop's biggest bands, with hits like Whistle, How You Like That and Kill This Love The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks. In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice. At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact. Kim says that began to change as they filmed. "I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse." Kim

title: AI is creating a 'human premium' for art made by people. But will it hold?
description: Amid a surge in AI content, many are placing extra value on art that's obviously made by a human. But can that last, asks Ros Atkins
body: AI is creating a 'human premium' for art made by people. But will it hold? A few weeks back, in a former bank building that's now a music venue in Falmouth, Cornwall, I was DJ-ing at a night I run called Rave Machine. It was a noisy, high-energy, sweaty affair, just as a night's dancing should be. All of the elements - the crowd, performers, staff, music, the journey home - connected to create something special, a one-off. It was also completely human. Something, in theory, well out of reach of what technology could possibly offer. In the DJ world, though, technology has already changed the equation. In the 1990s, a DJ had to not only pick the tracks, but also thread them together armed only with vinyl records, a pair of turntables and a mixer. Now, much more assistance is on offer, including software that will sync beats on different tracks should you ask it to (I don't). Apple Music and Spotify have an AI tune-mixing option too. Ros Atkins at his DJ night in Cornwall - a fundamentally human experience, he writes If you were out dancing, would it matter to you if a DJ was, well, not really DJing? If you loved the music being played, would you care if technology was doing the work? It's a question that generative AI - the type of AI that creates content - is asking of us all. One of the thrills of that night in Falmouth was seeing our special guest, Andy Cato from Groove Armada, artfully weaving an array of tracks. How would I feel if a DJ was just pressing play? (And that does happen). I mention all of this because that experience in Falmouth connects to a far broader question: whether we actually care if a piece of art has been created by a human, be that a painting, song, book, poem, or any other type of art. The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated. Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't. But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI. They want humans to be involved. Daniel Susskind, an economics professor at King's College London, says many of us place huge value on the human role in making art. It's what makes the creative process different from more functional, practical tasks, he thinks. "I was once in a room of accountants, and one of them stood up and said, 'My clients come to me for the personal touch, the human process'," he remembers. "And I said, 'That isn't why they come to you, they come because they want their taxes done properly'." But it's different with art, he says. "If I walk into the Sistine Chapel and look at the ceiling, I think not only is that extraordinarily beautiful, but isn't it amazing that a human hand, flesh and blood like my own, came up with that. A mind like mine dreamt that up," he says. As Susskind describes it, what we value isn't just the destination, it's the knowledge that a human - one of us - got us there. We can wonder at that achievement. Many people feel awe when they look inside the Vatican's Sistine Chapel, says Daniel Susskind Of course, it could be argued that computers and AI software were themselves created by humans. If Susskind feels awe walking into the Sistine Chapel, others might experience awe of a different type using a chatbot like ChatGPT. Susskind points to another example, this time a chess match in 1997, when a world champion, Garry Kasparov, lost for the first time to a computer, Deep Blue. At the time, there were fears the computer's success would mean our interest in chess would wane. In fact, chess is more popular than ever, played by millions. "It wasn't simply the moves on the board that people care about. It's the fact that it's a human being sitting behind them, moving those pieces along that matters," Susskind argues. And some think that the advent of AI has actually placed extra value on things created by people. You might call that a human premium. Kyle Chayka, a journalist at The New Yorker focused on technology, says AI writing is now widely considered to be "generic, obsequious and banal". As a result, he says, "I think readers are coming to value very obviously personal writing, and maybe even writing that's messier, less structurally sound or composed or perfected, than they maybe once would've desired." Chayka goes on: "I think illustration and graphic design is going in the same direction, where the average is too easily accessible, and so designers are leaning into being weirder and more eye-catching and more unusual, trying to find things that AI can't generate so easily." In response to the surge in AI-created content, academics are racing to develop a universally recognised symbol to denote something that is "human made" (similar to the "Fairtrade" label that emerged in the 1980s). Labels like "AI-free" are already appearing on covers of some books, films, and albums. For C Thi Nguyen, a philosophy professor at the University of Utah, it's a question of our underlying values. Russian chess grandmaster Garry Kasparov was beaten by IBM's Deep Blue machine in 1997 - the first time a world champion lost to a computer in tournament conditions He says you can often work out your values by following what he calls a "why chain". If you like something or want to do something, ask "why?". If the answer is to make money or be successful, keep asking 'why?' When the process ends, that will be what you really value, he explains. The question, he says, is whether human involvement and shared human experience will keep its place at the end of the "why chain". Author John Lanchester is optimistic. He thinks the value of what only humans can do will prevail. In fact, he sympathises with the idea of a 'human premium'. title: Three friends on their student debt: one paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up
description: Lizzy, Charlotte and Libby studied at the same time, but their student debt now looks very different.
body: Lizzy, Charlotte and Libby studied at the University of Newcastle between 2012 and 2015 When Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte met as freshers in 2012, their main responsibility was making it to lectures on time after early morning sports practice. Their student debt, growing with interest from the day they took out their loans, was the last thing on their minds. "The conversation was just so much less relevant at that time," says Charlotte. "As our careers have gone on and our paths have diverged more and more... those conversations start to come more to the forefront." The friends, now in their early 30s, went to the University of Newcastle in the same year tuition fees tripled to £9,000 a year in England and Wales, and new loans called Plan 2 were introduced. Each borrowed about £37,500 to cover three years of tuition and living costs. This year marks a decade since the first students in their year started repaying. They may have started out in the same position, but over that time their career trajectories, life choices and earnings have shaped how much they've repaid, how much interest they've racked up, and how much they owe - with very different outcomes. Student loans have come under scrutiny this year and there's been a particular backlash over Plan 2 loans. The government has said it wants to make the whole system fairer and campaigners are waiting to see what, if anything, changes in this month's Budget. The anger about Plan 2 grew after the government announced updated terms in November. The income at which graduates start repaying is set to be frozen for three years, meaning graduates would start making payments sooner and pay more each month. But it has also been brewing because the interest rate is higher than most other student loan plans, and many have seen their debts rise despite making monthly repayments. "Since April this year, I've paid off in the region of £450 and I've accrued over £500 in interest," says Charlotte, a physiotherapist in Bristol. She did a master's degree after uni and worked in the NHS before moving to the private sector. She earns about £50,000, but her loan is still going up. "It makes me angry... it's just disheartening." All three friends earn above the national average of £39,039. But research from the Institute for Fiscal Studies, external in February suggests Plan 2 graduates need to earn about £63,000 or more for a loan balance of £50,000 to start going down. "I just had no concept that the debt was going to go up," says Libby, who remembers being in tears when her first student loan letter came through after graduating. Now a project manager in a housing association and living in Worcester, she earns £72,000 and says her student loan balance has hovered at about £47,000 for a number of years. But she is currently on maternity leave and knows the interest will continue to accrue while her earnings - and therefore monthly repayments - drop. "It feels like I will never pay it off, so it's something that I'm kind of just sucking up until the loan is written off," she says. Her partner did the same course, starting a year before her and before tuition fees near tripled with the introduction of Plan 2 loans. She says it is "so frustrating" that she has to pay out thousands of pounds a year more on her student debt. Current and former students have different student loan plans depending on where they live in the UK and when they went to university. Plan 2 loans were given out in England for a little more than a decade from 2012 and are still issued in Wales. The debt is written off after 30 years. Lizzy, who studied economics and now works in financial services and lives in Bristol, is the highest paid of the friends, who bonded over rowing at university. She earns £85,000 a year and decided last year to clear her student debt by borrowing money from her family instead. She had estimated that, based on her current earnings trajectory, she would repay her loan in 11 years. By paying off her debt in full early she has accrued less interest and hopes to repay her family in four years - saving about £20,000. The amount graduates are voluntarily repaying towards their student loans has been growing. MoneySavingExpert.com founder Martin Lewis has warned that only higher earners could benefit from making voluntary repayments and most should not be "panicked into overpaying". Finance journalist Holly Mead told the BBC it could make sense for those who are confident they will clear the debt and can make "a really significant overpayment" of tens of thousands of pounds, like Lizzy. But smaller voluntary repayments could mean "you're just voluntarily paying more interest that you don't need to pay", she added. Lizzy, Charlotte and Libby say they are grateful they met at university and would go back if they had their time again The three friends pictured on Charlotte's wedding day Lizzy says she knows there are many "scenarios in which it doesn't pay off" for people to repay it early. "I made a gamble on my future self to actually repay it," she says. "I'm in a very privileged position to be able to do that... Buying your way out of the system or not being in at all is in itself a luxury. It buys you freedom." She and Libby finished their A-levels in 2011 but took a year out before going to university - Libby on a gap year, and Lizzy to resit economics after missing the grade she'd hoped for by a single mark. Lizzy says she knew the delay would mean her fees would be higher, but "it was never explained" that the repayment terms would "look and feel very different". "I think that's something that took me probably the best part of 10 years to understand," she adds, noting that her twin sister did start university in 2011 and had less debt as a result. title: Bid to overturn ruling which stops police being sued for failings
description: MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying when police fabricate evidence or are dishonest or negligent.
body: Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings. The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations. Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling. Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month. The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims. The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality. A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again. The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security. She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again. The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there. The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct. Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes. Ali Kololo is suing the Metropolitan Police after he was wrongly convicted in Kenya The amendment by Mitchell and Phillips, which will be debated on Tuesday, states that, except while acting as witnesses, no immunity applies to actions by police officers in preparation for criminal proceedings, including in cases where there are specified grave failings. Mitchell told BBC News the "police misconduct immunity created by the Court of Appeal's ruling" was extremely concerning and that if "we fail to close this legal loophole there will be devastating consequences for victims". He cited the case of Ali Kololo, saying his life was "ruined by a wrongful conviction secured, in large part, by the Metropolitan Police". Mr Kololo, a Kenyan woodcutter, spent 11 years in jail after being wrongfully convicted of assisting a gang that attacked two British tourists in Kenya in 2011 - one of whom was murdered. He was sentenced to death following a trial in Kenya, at which a senior Met officer who was called to appear as a prosecution witness omitted key evidence. Mr Kololo - who is represented by human rights group, Reprieve - is suing the Met, but the force has said it will rely on the legal principle of core immunity in defending the claim, a position likely to be bolstered by the Court of Appeal ruling. A Met spokesperson said the force would not comment on the ongoing civil claim, but said its thoughts were with Mr Kololo, the victims of the crime and their families. Kate Ellis, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told the BBC forces may now argue they cannot be "held legally responsible at all for serious mistakes made in a criminal investigation" and it could lead to an "accountability gap" where police forces who fail to investigate rapists, stalkers or domestic abusers "face no consequences for their failings". A government spokesperson said: "The home secretary and lord chancellor commissioned a review into police accountability following long-standing concerns from policing leaders, officers, victims and their families that the current system is not fit for purpose. Any changes to how the police are treated should be considered alongside the wider findings of this review." Sussex Police and the National Police Chiefs Council both declined to comment at this time. title: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
description: A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and and civilian resistance.
body: Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductions You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom. But Zaw Min has no choice. "I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time. "People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken." Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service. According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements. Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk. Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison. The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement. An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscriptedby the junta since early 2024 Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions. "Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says. The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months. They said they had no comment on the matter. With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot. The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme. International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service. In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025. Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law. "In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded. Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons. This video can not be played Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels "They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband." Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time. "We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened." Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city. The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin. In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release. U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities. title: 'I kissed Rodrigo and said thanks' - De Zerbi 'liked' Spurs red card
description: Roberto de Zerbi praises Rodrigo Bentancur after he was sent off in a 1-1 draw against Manchester United.
body: This video can not be played Solanke scores in added time as 10-man Spurs draw with Man Utd Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi praised Rodrigo Bentancur after he was sent off in the 1-1 draw against Manchester United. The Uruguay midfielder was shown a red card for headbutting Luke Shaw during a feisty 78th-minute melee when Spurs were trailing 1-0 at Old Trafford. Despite being reduced to 10 men, Tottenham managed to salvage a point as Dominic Solanke headed home in the second minute of added time. Spurs remain winless in the Premier League this season after six games, but De Zerbi was thankful to Bentancur for providing a "spark" against United. "I kiss Rodrigo and say thanks," De Zerbi said in his post-match press conference. "In that moment maybe with 10 players we played with more courage, more energy. "For a long time Tottenham played without this blood, this character." The incident happened when Shaw, on the receiving end of a reckless challenge by Bentancur, raced towards the Spurs player and shoved him off the pitch. Bentancur reacted by planting his head towards Shaw's face. The pair were separated by their team-mates before referee Stuart Attwell sent the substitute off. De Zerbi said it was a "mistake" by Bentancur, but added it was the type of reaction Tottenham needed to finish the game. "I kissed Bentancur in the dressing room because we need this type of reaction, this character. Football is character," he told Sky Sports. "I liked the situation with the red card. We need at this moment the situation, not to bring a red card but we need to not accept the defeat." Spurs remain winless in the Premier League after six games Despite the late elation sparked by Solanke's 92nd-minute equaliser, Tottenham remain in the relegation zone with just three points from their opening six matches. It is just the fourth time the club have failed to win each of their opening six games of a league season, after 2008-09, 1955-56 and 1912-13. Spurs have often looked lively in attack this season, but they have lacked conviction in front of goal and only 19th-placed Coventry have scored fewer goals than Tottenham's three. However, Tottenham fans can take belief from their overall performance at Old Trafford as they ran United ragged in the opening half with fluid, high-tempo football. "Today has been the game where for the first time this season we showed we are a team," De Zerbi said. "We played for the team-mates, we played together, we stayed inside of the game in every situation and we attacked as a team and defended as a team." The Italian manager added on Sky Sports: "I'm very happy because I've seen the right spirit, the right character and I want to start from this character, this reaction, this behaviour." Tottenham spent more than £250m on new talent over the summer - adding 10 players to their squad. But their poor start has prompted the club to organise a warm-weather training camp in Spain, with the team expected to travel to Marbella on Sunday in the hope it will provide a chance for their new-look squad to bond. "Now the target is to build the team," De Zerbi said. "We are a great group of players but we are not a team yet and to be a team is to play for the team-mates, suffer together, attack together." Spurs face newly-promoted Coventry on Monday, 19 October before making the short trip to Chelsea the following Saturday. title: Northern Lights stun UK down to England's south coast
description: The natural phenomenon, known as the Aurora Borealis, is the result of increased solar activity.
body: Kendal in Cumbria paid host to the breathtaking scenes on Saturday Residents across the UK were left stunned as the sky was illuminated by the spectacular colours of the Northern Lights on Friday and Saturday evenings. The natural phenomenon, known as the Aurora Borealis, is the result of increased solar activity. Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland, but particularly strong activity levels meant they could be seen as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent on Saturday night. The Met Office has said sightings could continue to be possible during clear skies until Tuesday. The phenomenon was visible as a pink haze in Winterton-on-Sea, Norfolk, on Friday Owston Ferry in North Lincolnshire was graced by a stunning purple haze Sightings stretched to Herne Bay in Kent Northern Lights are caused by powerful solar eruptions from the Sun, called coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Towards the end of last week, the Sun was observed to unleash CMEs directed towards the Earth. This stream of charged particles can get captured by the Earth's magnetic field and directed into our atmosphere, especially towards polar regions. When these charged particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen, photons of coloured light are emitted - this is the aurora. Revellers were able to take in a mix of green and purple in Saltburn-by-the-Sea, Redcar and Cleveland Stenness on Scotland's Orkney Islands served as a strong location for the phenomenon The sky was illuminated in Holmwood, Surrey The chances of seeing the aurora vary across the UK depending upon its strength. When activity levels reach 200nT (nanotesla) the aurora would be visible in the north of the UK, but not the south. On Saturday evening, those levels reached 600nT, meaning it would be visible across the whole of the UK, even in the south, which is a much rarer phenomenon. Experts have previously said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting as the Sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle. A purple glow could be seen across the sky in Salisbury, Wiltshire on Saturday North Yorkshire did not miss out on the action, as shown here in Scarborough An array of pink, blue and green could be seen in Gourock, Inverclyde If you missed out this time, the aurora may return on Sunday. The Met Office has said sightings remain possible across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies until Tuesday. To see them, you need to look northwards, away from bright streetlights, and look through a mobile phone camera. The reason you need to use a camera is because in low-light conditions at night our eyes use rod cells to see - these cells do not perceive colour and so we actually see in black and white. Cameras do not have the same limitations. title: Boos, anguish & fading belief -'worrying day' for under-pressure Carrick
description: It couldn't happen again could it? Another failure to beat 10 men increases pressure on Man Utd boss Michael Carrick after a 1-1 draw against Tottenham Hotspur.
body: This video can not be played Solanke scores in added time as 10-man Spurs draw with Man Utd For the second time in successive home Premier League games, Manchester United failed to beat opponents reduced to 10 men. For the third time in as many seasons, a United manager finds himself under severe pressure before the clocks have gone back. Four weeks ago, Manchester City needed an incorrect video assistant referee (VAR) decision to take advantage of an ineffective United performance after Phil Foden had been shown a red card in the 23rd minute for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes. On Saturday, the damage was self-inflicted as a Spurs side, who had given every indication of being unable to score before Rodrigo Bentancur's headfirst charge at Luke Shaw just five minutes after Bryan Mbeumo's opener, came up with an injury-time equaliser. Centre-back Lisandro Martinez was outmuscled embarrassingly easily by Dominic Solanke, with goalkeeper Senne Lammens failing to read the striker's deft touch that crept in at the far corner. The anguish on United faces told its own story. "A worrying day for Michael Carrick," observed former United skipper Gary Neville on Sky Sports. Late Solanke strike salvages 10-man Spurs draw at Man Utd Tottenham grab a draw but who got 1/10 - Ratings for Man Utd v Spurs Michael Carrick after Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Tottenham at Old Trafford First, a couple of sorry statistics. Manchester United have just six points from their opening six games of the Premier League season, their fewest at this stage of a league campaign since 1986-87, when they amassed four under Sir Alex Ferguson. They have failed to win five of their six Premier League games this season (D3 L2), already as many as in 17 league games under Michael Carrick last season (W12 D3 L2). United have collected two points from their last two games, both of which were against teams who began the match at the bottom of the Premier League. In points terms they are closer to the relegation zone than the Champions League spots. Carrick's side are now winless in four league games and face an always tricky trip across the Pennines to face old rivals Leeds at Elland Road on Sunday, 18 October. Either side of that are daunting Champions League trips to Atletico Madrid and Como. United officials have repeatedly offered their backing to Carrick in recent weeks. However, no fan needs reminding that two seasons ago a run of two wins in nine games in all competitions put Erik ten Hag under severe pressure before the axe fell after a defeat at West Ham on 27 October. Last season, a combination of a shocking EFL Cup exit at the hands of League Two Grimsby and an insipid 3-1 loss at Brentford on 27 September did so much to undermine confidence in Ruben Amorim before he was sacked on 5 January. The start to this campaign is starting to look increasingly familiar. This video can not be played 'We've got to do better' - Carrick calls for improvement after Man Utd draw with Tottenham "I'm not happy with he amount of points we've got so far, for sure, you know," said Carrick. "I'm not hiding, there's no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we've got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that's pretty plain." The 'little things' Carrick talks about are the defending for Solanke's goal, the lack of pressure put on Everton's Ainsley Maitland-Niles when he smashed another injury-time equaliser at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on 6 September, and the preventable Martinez own goal that nearly gave Fulham victory at Craven Cottage just before the international break. "We've got to be a little bit more streetwise in moments, a little bit more stubborn and a little bit stronger in seeing out certain things," he added. "It doesn't change my belief or the confidence in the players, you know. We're a really good team and capable of being a really good team, but we've obviously got to start getting more points on the board, that's for sure." The problem is with each disappointment, the belief of United being 'a really good team' starts to ebb away. Yet again, a post-match focus centred on how much Carrick's team ran, even though running for the sake of it has proved to be of little benefit. "The stats don't lie when every time the other team runs more than you," said Sky Sports pundit and former Spurs captain Jamie Redknapp. "Tottenham ran 5km more than Man United. OK, they had 10 men but that is every game. If you outrun your opposing number, you will win games. I'm not saying they are not trying. It is that physical battle they are losing though." It feels as though some fans are losing faith already, judging by the way they reacted at moments during the game, aside from the boos that accompanied the end of each half. Forward Matheus Cunha - one of a number of Carrick's squad who have failed to reproduce the form he showed in the second half of last season - gestured to the crowd during the opening period. It wasn't clear whether he was responding to a negative comment or urging more noise, but the Brazilian clearly wasn't happy. Carrick's family are season ticket holders. He knows what it is like to watch United struggle at Old Trafford. "Obviously, it hurts," he said. "It hurts a lot. It's not nice to go through. I care as much as anybody about this place. Sometimes you could say too much because then it overspills. But it's coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it." It is in moments like this that Carrick, who presents such a calm front in public, must be churning inside. He knows how the pressure can mount around Old Trafford and how fierce the debate around the club in the search for answers can b

title: Worker paralysed in 30ft fall from pylon gets £10m payout
description: The HSE found Gavin Pugh's injuries could have been prevented if correct safety steps were followed.
body: Gavin Pugh was 33 when he fell 30ft and was left paralysed A maintenance worker whose life was "turned upside down" when he fell 30ft from a power line and was left paralysed has won at least £10m in compensation. Gavin Pugh was dismantling a pylon in April 2022 when he unknowingly clipped his safety line to a section that was only secure at one end. His safety rope slipped loose, causing him to plunge to the ground and suffer life-changing injuries to his brain, neck, shoulder, ribs and internal organs which mean he needs a wheelchair for the rest of his life. Pugh, who was 33 at the time, sued his employer, Wood Transmission and Distribution Ltd, after the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found "adequate safety arrangements" had not been in place. Before the fall, Gavin Pugh was an "active and sociable person" who enjoyed fishing The Cheshire-based firm was fined £240,000 at a magistrates' court hearing in 2024 over the HSE's findings, before facing High Court proceedings brought by Pugh, from Bangor, Gwynedd. HSE inspector Robert Gidman told the court the "tragic incident" could have been prevented if the company had "adequate arrangements to protect its workers from harm". The pylon in Staffordshire had already been worked on by others, with a nut left loose, but this was not something Pugh knew about. "Proper assessment of the risks and consideration of work methods, adequate staffing and clear procedures for transferring towers between teams could have enabled this work to go ahead without incident," Gidman added. "Instead, because of the company's shortcomings, a worker has sadly and unnecessarily been left paralysed." After out-of-court negotiations, a care and compensation package was agreed, described by Pugh's lawyers as worth "eight figures". The money was compensation for his injuries and lost future earnings, as well as to help fund 24-hour live-in carers and more than £1m in rehabilitation costs. The incident happened while carrying out maintenance work on a pylon in Staffordshire Pugh's lawyers said that, before the fall, he had been an "active and sociable person" who enjoyed his job and had his own fishing boat. But his injuries left him unable to walk and suffering "life-changing physical limitations" and "significant psychological consequences". The firm, Stewarts, secured interim payments to fund his vital private rehab and care while negotiations were taking place. Pugh said the incident "turned my life upside down". "I wasn't able to work or go out with my friends. My life fell apart," he said. He added that he was "very grateful" for the settlement, which would allow him to regain some quality of life, adding he had already been able to "get back into some of my past hobbies". "I'm fishing and I'm able to get out and about. I'm able to go out with my friends again and enjoy myself, albeit not to the same extent, but I'm still happy." Wood Transmission and Distribution Ltd, now known as United Infrastructure Power T&D Ltd, has been asked to comment. title: Ceremony marks return home of kiwi feather cloak
description: The kahu kiwi, given to a British doctor in 1900, was "crying to come home", Māori campaigners say.
body: A kahu kiwi, or feather cloak, worn by a Māori chief in 1903 A ceremony has been held to mark the return of a Māori kiwi feather cloak to New Zealand by a British museum. The kahu kiwi was one of the farewell gifts presented by Māori leaders in 1900 to Dr George Cleghorn, a medical doctor who had been working in New Zealand. It was loaned to the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford by Cleghorn's widow in 1913. The Homebound Project, a charity which funded the return, said the cloak was "crying to come home". Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire Dr Lorraine Eade, chair of Ngāti Rārua o Te Wairau Society, which now owns the item, said its significance was "beyond measure". She said its return was an opportunity to acknowledge Cleghorn's work for Māori people. The doctor advocated for their right to attend a local hospital instead of being required to travel further afield for medical treatment, Pitt Rivers Museum said. He also spent time educating families at their homes on the importance of taking public health measures, it added. Shane Graham, chief executive of Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Rārua, a Māori authority, said the return was a momentous occasion. "It restores mana [prestige] and honours the deep emotional and cultural significance of our living connection to this taonga [treasure]," he said. Prof Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum, said: "We are very pleased that the day has come for the Kahu Kiwi to return home." A ceremony was held in Oxford earlier to mark the cloak's departure. "It's time for Ukraine to get a new president" he told reporters. On Friday Trump announced a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, a deal Zelensky described as "a gift" to President Putin. title: Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US
description: Roofs were ripped off buildings after Isaias barrelled into the US on Friday evening, before it weakened to a post-tropical cyclone.
body: A shop also had its roof torn off in Milton, Florida Four people have died and hundreds of thousands are without power after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern US with powerful winds and heavy rain. Officials reported two deaths each in the states of Alabama and Florida, which included people who were killed when trees fell on their houses. At least 600,000 people were without power in several states as of Saturday afternoon, according to tracker PowerOutage. Isaias made landfall in Florida late on Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105mph (168km/h) before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone. The storm felled trees and ripped the roofs off buildings. Alabama, Florida and Georgia all declared states of emergency ahead of its arrival, while both Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders to thousands of people. The roof was blown off an apartment complex in Milton, Florida Two deaths were reported in Florida's Escambia County. A woman was killed when a tree fell on her house, local Sheriff Chip Simmons said. Joey Williams told NewsNation his wife had died in the storm. He said they went outside to snap pictures of the damage but, when they went back into their home, a tree fell through the roof and trapped them. "I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told the outlet. Simmons later reported that a man had died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage that was not properly ventilated. Four other people who were in the same house were taken to hospital. Officials had to rescue people in vehicles that became submerged by floodwaters. The Florida National Guard shared pictures of a truck stuck in a flood ditch, saying soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety". Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation". In Florida, the storm tore through houses The canopy of a petrol station collapsed in Gulf Breeze, Florida In neighbouring Alabama, a sheriff was injured when a tree fell on him as he was responding to a car crash. "Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Governor Kay Ivey said in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths. She also said officials were concerned about "spinoff tornadoes" in the state from the strong winds and heavy rain. "As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop," she said. In Charleston, South Carolina, officials asked people to stay home on Saturday night as high tide is expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m). "After dark, floodwater is much harder to see and it's impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city said. The storm is expected to continue to weaken as it travels to the north-east, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) warned that the Carolinas and Georgia could see floods from up to 10 inches (25cm) of rainfall. In addition to Isaias, Tropical Storm Rachel is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday, and Hurricane Simon will hit the Pacific coast of Mexico on Sunday. Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific. title: Expedition hopes to find aviator Amelia Earhart's plane on remote island
description: The team en route to the suspected crash site aim finally to solve the mystery of her 1937 disappearance.
body: The research team departed Kiribati's capital on Wednesday and hope to arrive at the suspected wreck site by Monday A team of researchers are on their way to a remote island to inspect what they think could be the wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart's plane. The group, from the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean by Monday in the hopes of solving the mystery of her disappearance. The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation on her fate. The team are aiming to find what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020. Purdue University said the object had since been confirmed to have been visible in aerial photography of the area dating back to 1938. The researchers are currently roughly halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard the Marin Mainiku, a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel. They departed the capital of Kiribati on Wednesday to begin the 830-mile journey to Nikumaroro, which is also part of the multi-island country. When they eventually arrive, they will have to navigate through a narrow gap created in the atoll's reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited. "Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the ALI and the expedition lead, said. A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937. From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California. But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel. Earhart's disappearance spawned numerous theories - from a simple crash due to fuel exhaustion to more elaborate claims of interference. The official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems while the two struggled to find the island, and Earhart eventually crashed into the ocean when she ran out of fuel. While this version of events is largely accepted, no physical evidence has ever been recovered. Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937 One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway. Images of the so-called Taraia Object show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters. But some - including rival explorers - have expressed scepticism that this could be a plane, let alone Earhart's. Ric Gillespie, who specialises in recovering historic aircraft wrecks, told news agency Reuters that the object looked like a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the nearby water. "I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," he said. The researchers en route to the island credit Gillespie with previously finding evidence of a human presence on the atoll in the 1930s and forensic analysis of skeletal remains found there in the 1940s they say lend credence to their theory. But Gillespie suspects Earhart's plane had likely broken apart and its fragments carried into the depths of the Pacific long ago. Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short. In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation. Similarly, an expedition in 2019, conducted by the marine archaeologist who discovered the Titanic wreck, to investigate a photograph of what might have been a landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.
