title: Eight men arrested by Greater Manchester Police days after early release from jail
description: Some are held for breaching criminal orders, others for robbery or domestic violence, police say.
body: About 50 people from Greater Manchester were released early under the scheme Eight men have been arrested by Greater Manchester Police days after leaving prison under the government's early release scheme. About 700 prisoners from across the country were released early on 1 October in a bid to tackle overcrowding, with about 50 of them being from Greater Manchester. GMP confirmed that five men had been arrested for breaches of criminal orders, including a domestic abuse prevention order, and others were held on suspicion of robbery, drug offences and domestic violence. In response, the Ministry of justice (MOJ) said: "We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests." Under the first phase of the early release scheme, offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months were eligible to be released after serving one third of their sentence. The move, which will see a further 2,500 prisoners released across the country by the end of the year, is due to the prison system running on 98.2% capacity. The MOJ said: "We will never jeopardise public safety. That is why we are putting thousands more Neighbourhood Police officers on to our streets, upping police funding to £18.5bn and taking investment in the probation service to record levels. "To manage offenders out on licence, we are rolling out the toughest-ever controls, including world-first restriction zones, the largest expansion of electronic tagging, and giving victims a say in licence conditions." GMP Deputy Chief Constable Terry Wood said the force had been working "closely" with partners so that "robust plans are in place to ensure offenders are adhering to their conditions" adding that any breaches "will be, and are being - enforced by GMP". "As with any offending in Greater Manchester, where there is a report of a crime we will respond promptly to take positive action to protect victims and pursue criminals," he added. title: 'Cockroach' group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest
description: The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - want electoral reforms ahead of crucial state elections.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) calling for electoral reforms. The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi. Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead. Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital. The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections. It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied. Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters. But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed. The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated. The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this. Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken." He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday. The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented. This video can not be played 'Cockroach' leaders say they have been detained ahead of march Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's new designated leader while the others are in detention, released a video telling protesters that "if Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar". Student activist Neha Bora, who had also been detained by Delhi Police, urged demonstrators to "hold the line". The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks. Announcements could be heard across the city, asking people to co-operate with the police. One protester, Sabika Muzaffar, told the BBC she and her mother expected to be detained. "On the way to the protest site, instead of reciting hymns and verses as we usually do, my mother and I were rote learning our lawyer's number," she said. She said that showing up to protest was "her way of defending the country and its democracy". A few minutes after Muzaffar spoke to the BBC she was taken away by police. Several trains to and from major Delhi stations had been cancelled and dozens of metro stations were closed from Friday night. Buses packed with detained protesters were seen being driven away from the protest site. Detained protesters were driven away from the site in police buses The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted. Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?" The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability. In July, Dipke watched from the stage as the five-week-long protest ended in celebration after the resignation of India's education minister. title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
description: Former students launched their own investigation, spending years collecting evidence and testimonies from others who say they were abused by the headteacher.
body: Ex-headmaster Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, has been accused of sexual abuse A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report. Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok. Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities. The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police. Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external. Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar. They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school. By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta. Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school. Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school. Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations. In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation. "Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said. Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC. In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent. Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions. Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name". The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases. This video can not be played Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands. One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter. "I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school." Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students. "It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'." Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse. "They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said. Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously. "It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC. Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process. The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time. NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals. In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward. title: Dad thankful charity scan revealed 'silent' heart attack
description: A charity heart scan led to Simon Morris having surgery for a blocked artery he didn't know he had.
body: Simon Morris said it felt appropriate to take on something as big as Yr Wyddfa A man has described how a routine cardiac screening led to potentially life-saving treatment and showed he had unknowingly suffered a heart attack. Simon Morris, from Cardiff, said he had no reason to believe anything was wrong when he agreed to pay £300 for a heart scan after his daughter had been offered free screening by a Welsh charity. "I was 55, I'd never had such a scan before, so I thought, why not... just get it done and out of the way. "It turns out it was the best £300 I've ever spent." Morris was advised to go to hospital and tests revealed he needed an angioplasty, external - a procedure to reopen narrowed or blocked arteries supplying blood to the heart. Investigations also showed he had suffered what is known as a "silent" heart attack as he had not experienced any symptoms. But, looking back, he said there had been warning signs. "When I was going for big walks with my daughter and my son there were pains in the chest area which I just attributed to stomach issues," he told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast. "But now... I look back and go, 'what an idiot. You should have done something about that then. That was your chance, you missed it'." Following cardiac rehabilitation, he has since returned to an active lifestyle, climbing Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, aiming to raise £10,000 for charity Calon Hearts UK which provided his scan. He said he was grateful one of its cardiologists who identified his heart problem during the scan. And he has since been helping raise awareness of its work providing CPR training and free screening for those aged between 15 and a half and 26 and part-funded tests for those older. "I wanted to give something back to the charity that had potentially saved my life, and if I was going to do something, it felt appropriate to take on something as big as Yr Wyddfa," said Morris. A heart attack happens when blood flow to your heart is blocked. It can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital. chest pain which may feel like crushing or squeezing on your chest - the pain may also spread to your arm, neck and jaw feeling like you have indigestion - you may have a burning feeling in your chest and feel full or bloated pale, blue or grey skin - on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands The NHS said you should call 999 if you have any symptoms. A "silent heart attack" is a heart attack that has no symptoms, external. They're often only diagnosed weeks, months or years afterwards, during a routine check-up, or because of ongoing symptoms, like chest pain or breathlessness. Silent heart attacks are common. They are estimated to make up around a third of all heart attacks. title: 'We lost the life of a brother' - rider protest delays Giro di Lombardia
description: Riders at the Giro di Lombardia stage a protest over safety concerns which delays the start of the race for five minutes.
body: Remco Evenepoel addressed the crowd in Bergamo after the peloton did not set off on time Riders at the Giro di Lombardia staged a protest which delayed the start of the race for five minutes as they sought to draw attention to safety concerns following a series of incidents. Organisers completed the countdown and a starting flag was waved but the peloton remained stationary, creating confusion among spectators in Bergamo, Italy. Belgium's Remco Evenepoel then addressed the crowd, saying "there's too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race" and highlighting the death of British cyclist Fin Tarling, who died in a collision with a vehicle at the Volta a Portugal in August. "Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do," added double Olympic champion Evenepoel. After five minutes had elapsed, a second starting flag was waved and the riders set off for Como. "This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses," said the CPA union, which represents professional cyclists, in a statement which was re-posted on Instagram by riders including Evenepoel and Great Britain's Tom Pidcock, external. "This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer." The CPA has called for cycling's governing body, the UCI, to help ensure race organisers "take responsibility" and "act" to improve safety standards. Earlier this week, Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubi were struck by a police motorcycle travelling in the opposite direction during the Tre Valli Varesine race. "Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the UCI and race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met," the CPA statement added. "We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one. "We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones." The Giro di Lombardia is the last of the season's five Monuments, a set of long-standing, prestigious one-day races. It has been won by Tadej Pogacar for the past five years but the Slovenian is not present at the race, which is also the penultimate event on this year's UCI World Tour calendar, after sustaining a season-ending injury at the Vuelta a Espana. title: Man arrested after boy, 11, injured in 'dog attack'
description: Three dogs were allegedly "out of control" in the Newton Heath area of Manchester, police say.
body: A man was arrested on suspicion of possessing an aggressive animal, police say A man has been arrested after an 11-year-old boy was injured in an alleged dog attack. Three dogs were reported to be "out of control" in the Scotland Hall Road area of Newton Heath in north Manchester at about 16:00 BST on Thursday, Greater Manchester Police said. The force said one dog was seized and the other two were placed in kennels. The boy suffered minor injuries. A 31-year-old man has been held on suspicion of possessing an aggressive animal. The force has not confirmed the breed of dog. title: Drumcree parade ban was in interests of peace, says Bryant
description: The decision followed a warning from the chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest across Northern Ireland.
body: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant believed an agreement had been close The Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant has said his decision to ban the Orange Order's Drumcree march was in the best interests of peace. He announced the decision on Friday after an agreement couldn't be reached between the Portadown District Lodge and the Garvaghy Road residents. The dispute led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks. Sir Chris said he received advice from the the PSNI chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest across Northern Ireland. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Speaking to BBC News NI, Sir Chris defended his decision after it was put to him that unionists believed it had undermined the rule of law. "It's my job to try and make sure that we have a peaceful set of outcomes in Northern Ireland," he said. "I didn't come to this decision lightly." He appealed for a lowering of political tensions. "I really would urge everybody to stand down any rallies or gatherings that there may be. Nobody wants to wind this up any further. "There's been, I would argue, too much winding up already over the last couple of weeks. "It's easy to stir up a sectarian grievance, much more difficult to calm it down. "But we will need to look at the long term establishment of trust ." Sir Chris told BBC News NI that the original Parades Commission determination would remain in place, despite his decision to stop the parade. "I've decided not to strike down the original determination that still stands in law. "The Orange Order won that right," he continued. "But I have decided nonetheless that the march should not go ahead, partly because of the significant disruption to community relations that it would represent, partly because of the way in which the police have advised me that it would have to proceed and could lead to significant unrest." The Court of Appeal has reserved judgment on a legal challenge brought by Garvaghy Road residents against the decision to allow the march. This video can not be played 'I thought we were very close to an agreement,' says Northern Ireland secretary Sir Chris also outlined two possible compromises that had been discussed in an attempt to resolve the dispute. One proposed compromise, he said, would have allowed the Orangemen to complete one final march along the Garvaghy Road, on the condition it would not apply to march the route again. The other would have seen the group accept that it had won the right to march, but agree not to exercise that right. Sir Chris said he believed an agreement had been close, but talks between the lodge and residents ultimately failed. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he defended his decision to stop the parade, saying he could not see how the procession could safely take place. He also said Stormont's power-sharing institutions had proved more resilient than expected, despite concerns the dispute could lead to the collapse of the Northern Ireland Executive. The stalemate has reopened what was once one of the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. For decades, the situation at Drumcree has settled into a relatively minor stand-off that no longer made headlines, however that changed when the Parades Commission ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place. That parade did not happen and, after a series of talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state has banned the procession. Sir Chris said he had spent the last fortnight trying to reach a resolution between Garvaghy Road residents and the Portadown District Lodge, holding a series of negotiations at Hillsborough Castle. "I thought we were very close to an agreement, but unfortunately that was tantalisingly difficult to achieve." He explained that two possible compromises had been considered. "One was what people called one done and dusted. In other words, they would do one march and never apply again." "And another version was that they would accept that they had won the right, but they wouldn't exercise that right." Sir Chris said neither proposal had secured agreement from both sides. He said the Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had written to him requesting intervention under the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998. "But it seemed to me that the real threat was, precisely as the chief constable had outlined, I couldn't see how the procession could take place." Sir Chris also said he believed the original determination by the Parades Commission to allow the march had been "legitimate". There have been 13 days of deadlock in Portadown since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on 27 September Asked what he had learned from the dispute during his time as Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Chris said: "It's not the easiest gig in the world." He said he had encountered people willing to compromise, but others who found it more difficult. "And I've learned that there are a lot of people of good will who want to make compromise. And there are some people who find compromise much more difficult." Sir Chris said there had been concerns that the dispute could lead to the collapse of Northern Ireland's power-sharing executive. However, he said the institutions had remained in place despite the tensions. "The institutions of the Good Friday Agreement are probably more resilient than people think." Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. title: Rail disruption after overhead line fault
description: A fault with overhead wires near Penkridge is causing disruption between Stafford and Wolverhampton.
body: There are problems on the West Coast Main Line in Staffordshire Rail passengers are being urged to check before they travel due to overhead line problems on the West Coast Main Line in Staffordshire. Work was ongoing to fix a fault with the 25,000-volt wires which power trains near Penkridge, causing disruption between Stafford and Wolverhampton. At 12:00 BST, National Rail confirmed that lines have reopened between Stafford and Birmingham New Street, but residual disruption can still be expected until 16:00 BST on Saturday. Adam Checkley from Network Rail, said: "Our teams have now cleared the issue allowing the route to reopen, but with trains and their crew out of position, delays and cancellations will continue throughout the day." Rail replacement buses are in place at Birmingham, Stafford and Wolverhampton. Checkley added: "We're sorry to passengers impacted by the overhead line problems at Four Ashes near Penkridge. "With disruption to train services likely throughout the day, I'd urge people to check National Rail Enquiries before they set off on their journey." Ticket acceptance is in place on alternative routes including the East Coast Main Line, and Midland Main Line via Sheffield. title: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people including three children
description: Children are among the victims, authorities say, and more victims could still be buried in the rubble of a large apartment block that was destroyed.
body: Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said. The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning. Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: "Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come". The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US. Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed. "The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene. She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day. The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble. Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city." Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged". More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said "Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war. "Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses," he wrote on X, external. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on. Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles. The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties. On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region. The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv. According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55%, external in the first eight months of this year. Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia's infrastructure - with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex. title: Green Party wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
description: The party's Westminster leader Ellie Chowns made the comments after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said some members had joined to vote in the Zionism motion.
body: Green MP Ellie Chowns leads the party in the Commons, where it has five MPs The Green Party has said it wants to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism. The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups. Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the party. It comes after former leader Caroline Lucas said she felt the Green's structures were not protecting if from "entryism" - where people sign up to a party to try to change it. The controversial policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists." The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country". Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights. She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process." Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813. There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference. The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants". It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state". The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it." Caroline Lucas led the Green Party of England and Wales from 2008 -2012 Appearing on BBC Radio 4 programme Any Questions on Friday, Lucas said she was not putting any blame on the party's current leader, Zack Polanski, who she said had done "great things" for the party. "Our constitution was written decades ago, well before we had MPs, before we had mayors, before we had anything like the number of that we have today," the ex-leader said. Lucas, who was for years the face of the Greens as its first and sole MP until 2024, added the party needed to be made "a welcoming place for Jewish people." A Green Party spokesperson said: "Green Party membership has increased since Zack Polanksi announced his leadership bid in May 2025. Unlike other political parties, our members can bring and set policy. "This is one motion alongside dozens of others that was discussed at our biggest-ever party conference. Every motion submitted to conference undergoes debate and no single interest group drives policy. " Polanski, who is Jewish, previously told the BBC he would not have voted for the motion and instead would have voted for an amended version. However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide. Ashok Kumar, a Green Party member and part of the Greens for Palestine group, voted for the motion and told the BBC last week it was about "Palestinian liberation." He said he didn't feel the vote was harming the image of the Green Party, and that a growing number of people see this as a core issue. "They see the violence that's (been) occurring over the last three years," he told BBC Politics Live., external "So, I think the Zionist position is actually the marginal position. The Greens have had a surge in support after Polanski took over as leader in September last year but in recent months polls suggest this has waned Following Polanksi's by-election defeat in Holborn and St Pancras this week, the leader of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said he should resign. She added it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism. Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on the motion or amendments. He left early to campaign for the north London by-election, which Labour won on Thursday with Greens coming second. Following his defeat, Polanski told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that. He lost out to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election. title: Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out
description: Red Bull's Max Verstappen wins an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after George Russell crashes out of the lead.
body: The Mercedes of George Russell spins on the start-finish straight at the end of the first lap of the sprint race Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after Mercedes driver George Russell crashed out of the lead. Russell was leading in tricky conditions, with half the track dry and half wet, when he got a little too wide at the final corner at the end of the first lap. He lost control of his Mercedes, which spun across the track into the inside wall, before bouncing back again to the outside, the rest of the field somehow avoiding him. Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton took second having made a superb start from sixth on the grid with team-mate Charles Leclerc third. A final-lap collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri at Turn Five promoted Russell's team-mate Kimi Antonelli to fourth place. In combination with Russell's retirement, that extends the Italian's championship lead to 89 points. A chaotic race saw the start delayed by 30 minutes by a tropical downpour, and then Verstappen navigating a safety car period following Russell's accident, a restart, and initial pressure from Hamilton to eventually ease away into a comfortable lead. It was the Dutchman's second Formula 1 win in seven days, after his maiden victory this season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and the first time he has won in Singapore. The rain before the start hit only parts of the track. The second sector stayed dry while the first sector, particularly Turns Two and Three, were soaking wet with standing water. Once the rain abated, the field did two laps behind a safety car to check conditions before racing began with a standing start. Russell gave himself a golden opportunity to breathe some life into his almost-extinguished title hopes when he beat Verstappen off the line and took the lead into the first corner. But after leading the first lap, he made a mistake at the final corner. Russell said: "I just misjudged it, got more power than I was expecting from the battery, got a little wider than I expected and touched the white line. Rule number one in the wet is don't touch the white line. Very silly mistake." Russell climbs out of his damaged Mercedes That left Verstappen in front, with Hamilton behind. But after the seven-time champion pursued his erstwhile 2021 title rival for a few laps, the Red Bull began to ease away and was clearly in control, leading Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris and Antonelli. With overtaking difficult around Marina Bay, the field was static until the closing stages. Leclerc was struggling, and he began to be caught by the McLarens and Antonelli. Norris had been pressuring Piastri for some laps before the Australian also began to close in on Leclerc, and Antonelli, struggling with oversteer in the early laps, picked up the pace. On the final lap, Norris made a better exit out of Turn Three and saw an opportunity to try to pass Piastri at Turn Five. He got the car well enough alongside to make a legitimate passing attempt, but Piastri defended his position robustly, the cars touched, and spun in unison. Piastri, who hit the barriers, was out on the spot, but Norris was able to keep going, although he fell down to eighth, behind Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, Haas driver Oliver Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg. The stewards will investigate the Norris-Piastri incident after the race. The delayed start to the sprint means grand prix qualifying will begin 30 minutes later than originally scheduled, at 14:30 BST. title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
description: Philadelphia police said the tip was "flagged as spam", but criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.
body: AI tech company Anthropic was running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent a fake homicide tip to police An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed. The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach. In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description". It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms. Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip. Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said. But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October. "The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external. "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable." The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder. But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said. Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken. Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said. The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports. President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups. Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare. In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face. title: Palmer signs new Chelsea contract until 2034
description: Cole Palmer signs a new Chelsea contract on improved terms until 2034, one of the longest active deals in the Premier League.
body: Cole Palmer has been involved in six goals in seven matches for Chelsea in the early part of the season Cole Palmer has signed a new Chelsea contract on improved terms until 2034. The England international, 24, was already under contract until 2033 but is being rewarded for his performances following his emergence as one of Chelsea's key attacking players. He is also increasingly viewed as a dressing-room leader behind the scenes. The deal leaves Palmer on one of the longest contracts in the Premier League, with only Manchester City's Erling Haaland and Chelsea team-mates Joao Pedro and Geovany Quenda also contracted to 2034. "Chelsea means a lot to me and I think the club is going in the right direction, so I'm delighted to sign and I'm obviously very happy," said Palmer. "Speaking to the owners, to the sporting directors and obviously the manager, they gave me a lot of confidence so it was only right to sign. "Speaking to players as well, everyone has the same ambitions. I feel like we win major trophies here consistently and I want to be a part of that and play a big role in it too." Palmer signed his previous contract only two years ago having joined in a £42.5m move from Manchester City in 2023. The renewal is the latest in a series of contract extensions at Chelsea designed to reward established and emerging players while maintaining the club's wage structure. Joao Pedro also signed a new contract until 2034 in August, followed by Pedro Neto signing a new six-year contract last month. Palmer has developed a strong understanding with the Brazil forward, while also rekindling his on-pitch partnership with his "best friend in football", Morgan Rogers, during the early stages of Xabi Alonso's reign as manager. He was one of the few people privy to Chelsea's negotiations to sign Rogers from Aston Villa for a club-record £117m fee this summer. Palmer has scored four goals and provided two assists in seven matches this season. It represents a return to form for Palmer after suffering a niggling groin issue throughout last season, when he admitted he had played through the problem even though he "probably shouldn't have done". Ultimately, his lack of availability led to his omission from England's World Cup squad over the summer, having previously sought specialist advice on whether surgery was required. Palmer has played more minutes than any Chelsea player this season but missed England's recent international break, prompting Thomas Tuchel to say he "misses too many opportunities". Alonso confirmed Palmer is expected to be available for Saturday's game against Bournemouth and insisted he remains committed to playing for England. "Absolutely. He's committed, but he needs to be fully fit to play," Alonso said. "And when he's fully fit, he will enjoy his minutes. We need him in that moment. The club and the national team. "He trained over the past week and has been feeling better, but we didn't want to rush him." Alonso's side are 10th in the table after five matches, having conceded 12 goals. title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
description: Dramatic flames from the huge Cairngorms wildfire in July have disappeared - but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.
body: Drone pilot Pete Short hunts for hotspots in the Cairngorms National Park which was devastated by a huge wildfire over the summer It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park. It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July. The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all. But that is exactly what we have come to find. After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky. I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen. "Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight." "We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree. Three months after the fire first ignited, heat is still being detected beneath the ground. We make our way towards the coordinates identified by the drone, and at first, there is almost nothing to see. The soil is warm. A rock Pete picks up from the ground is, too. Nearby, after scraping away a thin layer of earth, smoke begins to rise. "It's really now cooking away," Pete says. "Without the thermal technology we would be totally blind to this." The wildfire began in the middle of July and burned across about 3,300 hectares – 33 sq km – of land, according to the Cairngorms National Park Authority. At the height of the emergency, five experienced drone pilots were brought together to provide aerial information to the agencies fighting the fire. Pete describes it as one of the most challenging environments he has ever flown in, with "multiple walls of flame", personnel and vehicles moving around the site and helicopters operating overhead. Now the challenge is different. The dramatic flames have disappeared, but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth. This video can not be played On the scene at the Cairngorms wildfire Each one found by the drones is reported to the land manager. They send teams who can dig into the ground and douse it with water. For Ben Jones, senior site manager for the RSPB at Abernethy, knowing exactly where to send those teams has been crucial. "We've been fighting this fire for over two months now and obviously we've got limited resources in terms of the number of people we have and we can't send everybody out everywhere all the time," he says. "So we really need to know where these specific hot spots are - where we should be sending people - so that they can be as efficient as possible." And despite the arrival of colder, wetter weather, the remaining fires cannot simply be ignored. "Each of these hot spots has got the potential to reignite a larger fire," Ben says. Walking through the forest, the scale of what happened is almost haunting. Tree trunks are blackened and charred. The acrid smell of fire still hangs around. Large areas of the forest floor have been scorched. But look closely and there are splashes of colour. Green shoots are emerging. Fungi is growing. I even spot a small yellow flower shooting up from the blackened ground. Dr Sarah Henshall, head of conservation at the Cairngorms National Park Authority, says it is too early to know the full ecological impact of the fire. Dr Sarah Henshall says drone information will show how the park is recovering "Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says. "It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet." And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job. Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape. Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes. "This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says. There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread. Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical. "It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says. Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot. Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot. Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil. Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish. Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning. title: Head of Met's volunteer force fired after AI tool found deleted intimate images on work phone
description: Special chief officer James Deller copied intimate images on to his work phone, AI monitoring finds.
body: Special chief officer James Deller's actions were "an abuse of trust", the Met Police said The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman. Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday. The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller. Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing." Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone. The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened. He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone. The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met. Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again. Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust. "That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe. "They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives." The Met's dealings with Palantir have come under fire from the mayor's office In April, the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, urged officers to be "extremely cautious" about carrying Met-issued devices while off duty after the force upgraded its Lawful Business Monitoring software. The federation's general secretary, Matt Cane, said staff had not been told the upgrade included the introduction of Palantir's artificial intelligence technology, appearing to mark its first deployment to monitor Met systems. In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force began using AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour. He said the Met had considered the reputational risks of using the "divisive" technology, but added that it helped identify "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" among officers. The London Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac) blocked the Met from signing a two-year contract with Palantir to provide artificial intelligence technology for criminal investigations. Mopac said the force had failed to set out its procurement strategy, describing this as a "clear and serious breach" of procedure. Palantir is now suing Mopac, alleging it unlawfully blocked the deal after taking the company's "values and ethics" into account, which it said was an "irrelevant consideration. Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with a number of UK public bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is currently facing growing pressure from Labour MPs and trade unions to end government contracts with Palantir. Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, who recently joined the company, warned against "mob rule" in government procurement. Lord Watson told BBC Radio 4's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is, 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule lead procurement practices?' "Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one." title: Delight for Scotland's Cuthbert after long summer of recovery
description: Erin Cuthbert expresses joy and relief at making her first appearance of the season in Scotland's impressive 2-0 win over Czech Republic.
body: This video can not be played 'A moment of magic!' - A superb strike from Caroline Weir Erin Cuthbert expressed joy and relief at making her first appearance of the season in Scotland's impressive 2-0 win over the Czech Republic. By winning the Women's World Cup round-one play-off away leg, the Scots are well set up for the return in Paisley on Tuesday, with Sweden the likely opponent for the team that progresses. Chelsea captain Cuthbert, 28, is yet to feature at club level this season following a knee injury and came on as a substitute in Pardubice. Fellow sub Claire Emslie finished superbly for the Scots' second after captain Caroline Weir's stunning opener. "It's so good," Cuthbert told BBC Scotland. "It's been such a long summer. It's always great to come on and play for my country again - I'll never take it for granted when I get a serious injury. "I'm just glad to get back on a football pitch. The relief, the amount of self-doubt that you have, the amount of stress - am I going to be back to the same level, how am I going to perform, is my knee going to be alright? All those things run through your head. "It was a bad one. I was in crutches and a brace for the best part of a month. I lost a fair amount of muscle and over the summer I was trying to rebuild all of that again. "It's been a really, really hard journey." This video can not be played Emslie scores first goal since becoming a mum Emslie scored her first goal since becoming a mum, with her son and mother attending the game in Pardubice. "I'm incredibly proud of her," Cuthbert said of Emslie. "I have an enormous amount of respect for her. Everything's just so impressive - to be a mum, to play at the highest level." The Czech Republic were given a late reprieve when the award of a penalty was overturned but, soon after, Cuthbert was "flabbergasted" a late challenge on her in the box did not result in a spot-kick. And while Cuthbert was "delighted" with the win, she cautioned that 2-0 can be a "dangerous" lead. "We're a good team and when we play on the front foot, we can hurt teams," she added. "The best form of attack is defence." title: Four murder arrests after teenagers attacked
description: A murder investigation is launched in Stoke-on-Trent after a man dies and another is seriously hurt.
body: Police were called to Brookhouse Road in Meir on Friday night Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a man died and another suffered life-threatening injuries in Stoke-on-Trent. A cordon remains in place on Brookhouse Road, in Meir, after police were called to reports of violence at 23:45 BST on Friday. A man in his late teens was confirmed dead at the scene, Staffordshire Police said, and another man, also in his late teens, was taken to hospital, where he remains in a critical but stable condition. Two 18-year-old men, a 20-year-old man and a 17-year-old boy, all from Stoke-on-Trent, were arrested on suspicion of murder, while the boy was also arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. All remain in police custody. "This is a devastating time for all those affected by what has happened overnight," said Det Insp Katie Gregory. She added: "I'd like to reassure the community that there is no wider risk to them, and we are doing all we can to understand the circumstances that led to this tragic incident." The force has urged anyone with information about the attack to contact police. title: We sold everything and bought a one-way ticket to take our three children travelling
description: The Woolridge family sold their south Wales home and are travelling the world with no plans to return.
body: Tom, Morgan, George, Dani and Olivia Wooldridge in Indonesia on the first stage of a round-the-world travelling experience with no fixed end date Dani and Tom Wooldridge worked hard to transform a 1970s house into a beloved family home after they bought it about seven years ago. Dani, 39, a nurse, also ran an aesthetics business while Tom, 38, had a construction business. Three children, a close extended family and lots of friends. A happy life. Yet in May this year, the five of them sold their possessions and home, and bought a one-way ticket heading for Indonesia, with the only things they owned in the world now stowed in backpacks in the luggage compartment. With Olivia, 12, Morgan, seven, and four-year-old George, the Woolridges are planning to travel the world, with no endpoint in sight, hoping to see every continent. The "amazing" food and the sunshine was an instant upside to their new way of life Five months in, over a video call from the Indonesian island of Lombok, Dani and Tom explain the decisions which have brought them to the shores of south-east Asia. Both of them had gone travelling for a period of time in their early 20s, a classic gap-year style experience, and had enjoyed taking holidays, particularly to sunny destinations. Dani said: "It was always a conversation we had but once you start having kids and you've got the mortgage and everything like that it's kind of, 'oh it's not the right time'." But nearly two years ago, the family took a holiday to Thailand over Christmas. "We were fortunate enough to have a month over there, travelled round with the kids and obviously they were almost two years younger than they are now, and managed really well. Tom added: "It all went really smoothly and it was great seeing the kids experience a completely different world to what we'd all grown up. It just felt so great exploring with them. Dani said that sparked their interest to start researching and meeting other families who had decided to jet off. "We made lots of lists - lots of positives, lots of negatives," she said. "Can we do this? How are we still going to educate our children? We had a home, we had our businesses, we had careers. What do we do about all that?" Their travels across the Indonesian archipelago took them to visit this Komodo dragon - one of the largest reptiles on earth Once they made the decision, they knew they had to be "100% committed". Dani thought at first they should rent their house out "so we've got something to come back to" but Tom wanted to sell, and the couple realised they didn't want to leave the responsibility of managing it to people back home. The boys were excited about the idea from the start but the couple admit it was harder for their daughter. Tom said: "Olivia was a bit nervous. She'd just started high school in the September and we left in May. She was very apprehensive about leaving all her friends. "Morgan and George do mention their friends now and again, but they're a bit younger so they didn't have that emotional attachment as much as Olivia." When they told their parents about their plans, their initial reaction was "why are you selling everything you've worked so hard to get?" "Most people have got bets on when we're coming back," Dani said, laughing. Tom added: "They've all got a year each." The family are taking opportunities to interact with local people and give the children lots of different experiences, such as a go at Muay Thai boxing After selling their house at the start of the year, they lived in rented accommodation for a number of months, before heading to the airport in May for the big farewell. Leaving was "very emotional", Dani said. "We were very fortunate that we had a lot of family coming to the airport with us," added Tom. "We'd checked our luggage in and we got to the security gates - that was hard. "We were so fortunate to have a close family and friendship group as well. They're the people we miss and that's what we miss from back home, the people that were in our lives. Not so much the material things we had." However once the plane had taken off and the goodbyes were behind them, the excitement started to kick in. "We remembered where we were going," joked Tom. Even though they had both been to their first destination, Bali in Indonesia, before, the culture shock still hit them. "It's just everything. Your senses are just heightened. It's the smells, seeing everything around, it's so different to home. "We went to Bali 15 years ago when it was a lot quieter," added Dani. "People have said how busy it is now, and it was. "The first day or two was very overwhelming. Our daughter was still a bit emotional. She was up and down with things and we were all a bit jet lagged. "We went to Uluwatu first and it has got so busy. Even us walking down a road, I was nervous. Scooters everywhere." But there were also upsides, Tom said. "The food instantly was amazing. And the people are just beautiful, and so kind. And just to feel the heat on our skin." The sunshine and the sea is a big pull for the family, who do not miss the "grey and dark and wet" They moved to different parts of the island, swapping the beaches in the south to climb the volcanic Mount Batur in the north, and spending time in the cultural village of Ubud inland. They then went island hopping eastwards across the Indonesian archipelago before doubling back to Lombok for a second stay. "We were moving around quite a bit," Dani said. "So each time it was almost like that feeling of going home because we were packing up, but we weren't going home. I think it took us months to really think, 'wow, we're not actually going home'." Leaving the UK behind has not meant abandoning education, Dani stressed. title: 'What terminal cancer has taught me about life'
description: A Gloucestershire man with terminal cancer shares the life lessons he wishes he'd learned sooner.
body: Rex used to love mountain climbing but now says he tries to enjoy every small thing like the taste of food or even the rain A man living with terminal cancer says his biggest regret is spending decades carrying childhood trauma without realising it was shaping his life. Rex Mackrill, 65, from Tetbury, Gloucestershire, says being diagnosed with incurable prostate cancer forced him to reflect on what matters most, and one lesson he wished he learned earlier: to relish the joy of every moment. "I knew there was something wrong. I knew there was a blackness that I was carrying and I didn't know what it was, and I wish I'd known earlier," he said. With a limited time left ahead of him, Rex has been looking back on his life and considering what advice he would pass on. Football club makes history with £1m lottery win Headlines: A royal visit and 'shin-kicking' Traitors star coming to Cheltenham Literature Fest Because prostate cancer runs in his family, Rex regularly monitored his PSA levels. After a raised test result, further investigations confirmed he had incurable stage four prostate cancer. Rex underwent chemotherapy but said the treatment took a significant physical toll and he now lives with the side effects of hormone treatment, including intense fatigue. "I stopped doing a job I love as a GP practice manager," he said. "By the time I went through chemotherapy, I couldn't do the job that was needed." Leaving work was one of the biggest practical changes brought about by his diagnosis, although he says his priorities remain firmly focused on his family. "Sarah and I have always had a strong focus on our boys. We structured our lives to give them the best upbringing we could." But while cancer changed his perspective and future plans, he says one of the most important discoveries of his life came years before. For much of his adult life, Rex lived with anxiety but could not explain why. "I knew that I was frightened, but I didn't know why," he said. He assumed he simply had to cope. The turning point came at 60 when a life coach noticed he appeared to "shut down" while discussing certain topics. "He said, 'You've got trauma, dude'," Rex recalled. He later sought help and was diagnosed with PTSD. Rex believes the trauma stemmed from abuse suffered in his childhood and says he is still exploring its impact today. "I wish I'd known I had a trauma earlier," he said. This video can not be played “I knew that I was frightened, but I didn’t know why.” Research suggests delayed PTSD diagnoses are not uncommon, with symptoms sometimes emerging years after traumatic events. Around one in 10 people in the UK , externalare expected to experience PTSD at some point in their lives. At first, Rex said he struggled to accept help. But Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy gradually transformed the way he experienced life. "I used to live at 10 out of 10 anxiety and I don't now," he said. "It influenced all aspects of my life. "People would say I was calm and collected, but they weren't aware of the stress and anxiety I carried." Looking back, he says his advice to anyone struggling is straightforward. "Go get help. Go and see your GP. "You don't have to live like that or carry it on your own. "Go to a trusted friend and say there's something blocking you. They can help you find the support you need." As he comes to terms with terminal cancer, Rex says his priorities have not changed but what has changed is how present he feels. "I used to have to go to the Lake District to be present," he said. "Now I can be much more present wherever I am." Recently, he found himself captivated by a simple moment outside. "I was watching rooks floating on the wind," he said. "One rook wanted to move a little bit along a tree branch, but the wind took it somewhere else. "It had to circle around and land exactly where it wanted to be." He now spends time writing poetry, donating possessions like his car to charity and trying to make life easier for those he will leave behind. "I don't want to burden people with my stuff," he said. Rex has been looking back on his life and considering what advice he would pass on to others Rex has also taken part in sessions at Longfield Hospice in Minchinhampton that help people discuss end-of-life plans and their wishes for care. Sarah Mimmack, director of care at the hospice, said many families avoid conversations about death because they find them uncomfortable, but planning ahead can remove uncertainty and pressure. "If you've done this work before you die, it really helps your family and friends," she said. She added that while around half of people in the UK die in hospital, only a small proportion say that is where they would choose to spend their final days. The team at Longfield Hospice help terminally ill patients prepare for the end of thier lives For Rex, however, preparing for death has become another way of making the most of the present. And if there is one lesson he hopes others take from his experience, it is not to wait. "Enjoy the joy of life and see that this is a beautiful world we live in," he said. "We're so lucky. We can love every moment of it." title: Asbestos mystery leaves beloved beach closed
description: With Mount Batten Beach fenced off since July, residents and campaigners are demanding answers.
body: Grace Stickland said losing the beach had broken up a community For more than six years, asbestos has been washing up with the tide, turning one of Plymouth's handful of swimming spots into the centre of a growing environmental mystery. Mount Batten Beach has been fenced off since the summer, and access restricted to two other areas on the peninsula. It comes after tests in April and July found asbestos fibres in sand samples at levels that could pose a risk to health if inhaled, Plymouth City Council said. Inhaling the fibres can increase the risk of serious diseases - including lung cancer - decades after exposure. The first discovery came in 2019 when 500kg (1,100lb) of material containing the toxic substance was removed from the shoreline, which sits on Plymouth Sound in one of the South West's most popular holiday destinations. In total, more than 1.5 tonnes of material containing asbestos, external, including both white and the more dangerous blue varieties, has been cleared from the beach and nearby sites. Residents and experts believe the material may be coming from roofing and construction waste linked to the former RAF Mount Batten base, where coastal erosion is thought to be exposing the buried material. The closure has left swimmers, business owners and residents wondering when, or even if, the beach will reopen, and how it looks against the backdrop of Plymouth Sound being named the UK's first National Marine Park., external City councillor Grace Stickland, who has been bathing at Mount Batten for several years, said dozens of people regularly gathered for swims throughout the year, with festive dips attracting as many as 80 participants. "It was a really popular little beach and everybody loved it," she said. "All the swimmers feel as though they've been evicted from their homes." Stickland said older swimmers and people with mobility issues particularly valued Mount Batten because of its accessibility, adding that the closure was "breaking up" a community that had grown around the beach. The National Marine Park in Plymouth Sound has faced a number of challenges in the past, including hundreds of old tyres being discovered on the seabed and sewage spills. Yet the asbestos contamination problem has proved difficult to solve. When asbestos was first discovered in 2019, the council temporarily closed the beach and expected the amount of material washing ashore to decrease over time but that has not been the case. "Our beach collections have shown that the amount of material washing up on the beach hasn't shown any real decline," a council spokesperson said. Earlier testing suggested the risk was low. Warning signs were installed and visitors were advised to avoid parts of the beach where asbestos fragments had been found. But council officials described the latest results as a "new and worrying development". Swimmers at Mount Batten before the beach was closed Although two rounds of testing have found no evidence of airborne asbestos on the beach, the discovery of fibres in the sand was enough to trigger the closure. Professor Steve Maddern, Plymouth's director of public health, said shutting the beach had been a last resort. "We understand the disappointment this will cause but the latest sand samples are concerning and we must prioritise the safety of the public," he said in July. While the beach remains closed, attention has turned to the question: Where is the asbestos coming from? Residents have long suspected the source could be the former RAF Mount Batten site, which occupied the peninsula for much of the 20th Century before closing in 1992. During its heyday it was one of Britain's most important flying boat bases, with Sunderland aircraft carrying out anti-submarine patrols and sea rescue missions during World War Two. Today little remains beyond memorials and historic seaplane hangars. Mallory Haas believes buried asbestos from the former RAF base is the cause of the contamination Maritime archaeologist Mallory Haas, director of the Ships Project CIC in Plymouth, said she believed asbestos-containing roofing materials from the RAF base had been buried and were now being exposed through coastal erosion. "If you look at what's on the beach, and if you also look at the deposits behind the staircases when you walk down to the beach, you can see it eroding out of the land there," she said. She added: "It's Britain's Ocean City, the UK's first National Marine Park and it's an MPA [Marine Protected Area]. "It should be some of the most protected waters around." The properties of asbestos made it an ideal material for use in a number of products, including insulation material for buildings, boilers and pipes; car brakes and floor tiles, insulating board to protect buildings and ships against fire; asbestos cement for roofing sheets and pipes. Due to the risks to health following inhalation exposure to asbestos the importation of blue and brown asbestos has been banned in the UK since 1985. This ban was extended to include white asbestos in 1999. Asbestosis is a rare but serious lung condition that affects people exposed to asbestos. It cannot be cured but treatment may improve the symptoms. pain in your chest or shoulder in more advanced cases, swollen fingertips It can take 20 to 30 years after being exposed to asbestos before symptoms appear. There are sometimes no symptoms. The advice is to visit a GP if you have symptoms of asbestosis and think you have been exposed to asbestos. title: Chemicals at former fuel depot 'have been removed'
description: Barrels of forever chemicals left at a development site have been removed, a developer has said.
body: The barrels of fire fighting foam liquid were manufactured in 1988 and stored at RAF Islip Barrels of chemicals left at an approved development site have been removed and testing carried out, a developer has said. The Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire is a former RAF and Esso fuel storage and transfer facility and has had outline planning permission approved to build residential and affordable homes. Concerns were raised after campaigners discovered about 40 barrels of firefighting foam liquid, which contains PFAS - a group of chemicals often dubbed forever chemicals, had been left at the site for decades. Developer, Newcore, said it had already identified the potential contamination and that "this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately." The depot previously supplied fuel to the former RAF Upper Heyford, around five miles north, which is suspected to be the source of forever chemical, or PFAS, contamination from firefighting foam. Images show the barrels to be manufactured by Angus Fire Armour, that settled a legal battle out of court with residents in Yorkshire, after claims they had been exposed to PFAS near the company's foam manufacturing plant. CEO of Newcore, Hugo Llewelyn, who took over the site in 2012, said it plans to regenerate the site with 50% affordable housing and that it was made aware of the barrels "in recent weeks" and had them removed in a "responsible and professional manner". "Whilst firefighting foam containers were present on site from the MOD's operation back in the 20th Century, we do not believe it was ever deployed; the containers were sealed; and successive surveys have confirmed that there is no "pathway" for it to cause pollution," he added. Mr Llewelyn disputes the quality of the testing carried out by campaigners. "A 'pressure group' has trespassed unlawfully to obtain a questionable sample from this site to demonstrate that in the secured area of the site that was purposefully designed to accommodate foam for firefighting purposes, which is likely to contain PFAS, does, according to their findings, contain PFAS. "I'm not sure there is anything to be surprised about here," he said. He added that a Phase 1 assessment of the site last year had already identified the potential for contamination and that, "the specification for the Phase 2 investigation has therefore been designed to specifically address this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately". The Environment Agency's Chemical Compliance team had contacted the site owners to ensure that the drums are properly managed. A development with 50% affording homes is planned for the Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire Campaigners from Gallos Brook community group, who have been regularly testing for PFAS in the area, took a sample of soil near the storage area which they claimed is "likely the highest level of soil contamination measured anywhere in the UK." The group said the sample, which was analysed by a UKAS certified laboratory, came back as having 3.74325 micrograms of PFAS per kilo. PFOS - a particular forever chemical - was found in their testing to be 205 times higher than the safe limit for residential land use. Llewelyn disputed the testing carried out by campaigners and produced his own results which he claimed were taken from the same area, as part of the Phase 2 investigations. He said these produced a total level of 0.0641micrograms per kilo of PFAS, roughly 98% lower than results by the campaigners, and were "the accurate results of our professional testing." The BBC has not been presented with the official lab results to verify these independently.
