title: 'Taking in my great-grandkids at 74 saved me'
description: A Somerset great-grandmother talks about becoming a kinship carer after her daughter died.
body: Valerie says kinship caring has brought her joy, purpose, and adventures A pensioner who became a kinship carer to prevent her two great-granddaughters from going into care says she knew she had to do it despite criticism from some friends. Valerie, 74, took responsibility for the girls when her daughter, who had been looking after them after their own parents were unable to, died suddenly. She has been supported by Somerset Council's kinship team and said she chose to speak out during Kinship Care Week, running until Sunday, to highlight the important but often invisible role kinship carers play in our communities. "My girls needed me. They've saved me as well as me helping them," she said. Headlines: A royal visit and 'shin-kicking' Banned teacher punched wall near pupils' heads Tourism bosses say EDF 'failing' them over Pontins Valerie said overnight she found herself not only mourning the loss of her daughter but also becoming the girls' primary carer. Alongside supporting the children through their loss, she was faced with practical worries about finances and managing a household she had not previously been responsible for running. Valerie admits that returning to parenting in her seventies has been a "challenge". "I was scared because I didn't know what the future would hold," she said. "I'm not young by any means, and I was there signing to keep the girls safe until they're 18. It's very, very scary." She told BBC Somerset she had also lost two good friends since becoming a kinship carer. "They said I was selfish taking them on, that I should let them be adopted to younger parents," she said. "I can understand that for some children that might be better going to a younger family maybe. In my case, I knew my girls extremely well. I knew my health was reasonably good. I've got a lot of energy, and I love my girls tremendously." She said her case worker in the kinship team, Charlotte Stiles, has been "amazingly supportive". The council supports kinship families across the county and works with carers to help children remain safely connected to their family network wherever possible. "Charlotte is there at the end of a phone, she's come to school meetings with me, she's offered me advice, she points me in the right direction," Valerie said. "Charlotte has made the last few years much, much easier." Stiles said she was "blown away" by Valerie's commitment to the girls. "I thought how incredible - she sacrificed her dream of retirement to make sure these girls have the best life they possibly could," she said. title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades
description: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but has now been honoured by Bletchley Park.
body: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but his work as a codebreaker has finally been recognised "My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything." From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two. Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort. But research into the life story of Venke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers. About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945. After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow. The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile. Fred fled Poland after a happy childhood in Krakow Believed to be the last surviving member of these Polish codebreakers, Ferdynand Stanislaw Vanke grew up in Krakow, but fled at the age of 16 when war arrived on his doorstep in 1939. He said: "I did wake up in the morning hearing the planes. I ran to the window and I could see Germans coming over but I thought it was Polish Air Force training. "People were screaming and falling to the ground and we could hear machine gun fire. My father burst in and said 'in to the cellar, the Germans are coming'. That's how my war started." Fred, his sister and a friend travelled east in a Polish Army Hospital van, to his grandparents' home, avoiding Nazi gunfire on the roads. "I could see people coming from all over the place, masses of people," he said. "When Germans would come, my sister said to me 'under the van, under the van'. That's the first time I've seen people being injured to that extent." Fred and his father served together in the Middle East After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. "Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing. "One day my commanding officer, Colonel Mayer, called me and explained 'you're young, I've got a son like you, you volunteer to be dropped in Poland you will last four or five months on average and that's the end of you. I've got something better'. Fred served in the Middle East before his service took an unexpected turn Instead, a captain visited from Bletchley Park, the then-secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School, the forerunner of GCHQ, and the base for Allied codebreaking. "He gave us all a lecture and a little puzzle," said Fred. After cracking the first, he was given a second which he also deciphered. "He said, 'you've got a gift which very few people have'," Fred recalled. So despite being in his early 20s, several years younger than anyone else on the unit, Fred was recruited to work at The Arches in Boxmore, a Polish sigint station near Hemel Hempstead which supported Bletchley Park. The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators. One of dozens of Polish codebreakers based there, Fred would work in a team listening to German signals and attempting to decode them. Poles like Fred worked in secret under the guidance of Bletchley Park Fred said: "You start with the simple things. You've got to learn the language, how it is built, and what is the quirk in that language, and you base your guessing on that. "When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday." However outside of The Arches, life was tougher for Fred. He said: "The people in Hemel Hempstead, because we had uniforms with Poland, they spat on you and called 'why don't you eff off to fight Germans instead'. "You couldn't say what you're doing, so that was a little bit upsetting." But what Fred and his Polish compatriots were doing, both before the war and during it, was pivotal in the Allied war effort. Bletchley Park was the secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School Among those identified during the research were Marian Rejewski and Henryk Zygalski, two of the three Polish mathematicians who alongside Jerzy Różycki first broke the German military Enigma cipher before the war, and who continued codebreaking work in Britain after escaping occupied Europe. At the Pyry Conference near Warsaw in 1939, Polish cryptologists invited French and British counterparts, including Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox, to share their pioneering success in breaking the German Enigma machine cipher. Dr David Kenyon, the research historian at Bletchley Park Trust who investigated Fred's story, said: "This meeting was important because it laid the groundwork for partnership between the B

title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
description: The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong.
body: An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey Bethea, who'd been convicted of the rape and killing of an elderly woman They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow. It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators. By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000. That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70. The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream. Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death. That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later. By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now. Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the US A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas. The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad would be live-streamed. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked. "I never imagined [another] public execution," he told BBC. He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%. "It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said. It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's nearly certain that millions or more will tune in. With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends". This video can not be played How widely used is the death penalty in the US? Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream. "What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific." Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap. The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution. "I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific." But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have, in some way, perhaps set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University. "Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'" This video can not be played Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong. Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said survey data points to a declining appetite for violence in the US. "This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labeled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people." "I think it's this: A public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country." Vice-President JD Vance, a Catholic, has said he would not be watching the execution. President Donald Trump dodged the question of whether he'd tune in himself - but confirmed he approved the decision to livestream Hasan's death. "I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going f

title: Plans to turn Van Morrison's former primary into a special school delayed
description: It was originally hoped that the former Elmgrove Primary School could re-open as a special school in September 2026.
body: The EA said that because the former Elmgrove Primary School is a listed building, the project was 'significant and complex' A plan to turn Sir Van Morrison's old primary school into a special school campus has faced "unavoidable construction delays". It was originally hoped that the former Elmgrove Primary School could re-open as a special school in September 2026. The east Belfast school is right beside "The Hollow", made famous in Sir Van's song Brown Eyed Girl. The Education Authority (EA) said that "as a listed building," the project was a "significant and complex scheme." The Elmgrove building was due to house pupils from nearby Greenwood House special school in east Belfast and is due to be renamed The Hollow. Greenwood House admits pupils aged between three and six, but expansion would mean the school could to take pupils up to Primary 7. It was originally hoped that Elmgrove Primary School, which Van Morrison attended, could re-open as a special school in September 2026 There has been a huge increase in demand for special school places in recent years and the Education Authority (EA) has said that all schools are operating at full capacity. But the governors of Greenwood House have said they have "serious concerns" that The Hollow will be ready for September 2027. They said there had been a lack of progress on the main school building and "limited urgency" from the EA in getting the school ready. They also criticised a lack of EA communication with parents and said there had been vandalism on the school site. Jonny Collins' six-year-old daughter Nancy is a pupil at Greenwood House, and he says the site must be ready to open for September Jonny Collins' six-year-old daughter Nancy is a pupil at Greenwood House, and he said he had made a complaint to the EA about the state of The Hollow site. At present 32 pupils with Special Educational Needs (SEN), including Nancy, are being taught in four portacabins. "The EA have sat on their hands for the guts of a year," Jonny Collins said. "They haven't touched that building. "Especially children with Special Educational Needs, they need sensory rooms, they need breakout rooms, they need a canteen area, they need an indoor play area." Collins said parents wanted to see results and a timescale for the work from the EA. "They knew with the shortfall of SEN places they needed to get children into that school. "The EA aren't giving the parents the answers they need. "We need this site open for September." The chair of Greenwood's governors Gary Forbes said that he was "deeply concerned about the lack of progress on the new special school at Greenwood, The Hollow". "More than a year after the move was announced, there is still little evidence of redevelopment, while children with severe learning difficulties remain in temporary accommodation that does not fully meet their needs," Forbes said. "Parents, staff and pupils deserve clear timelines, better facilities and urgent action from the Education Authority to deliver this much-needed school." The east Belfast school is right beside "the hollow", made famous in Sir Van's song Brown Eyed Girl In a statement, an EA spokesperson said that it was "committed to delivering high-quality, purpose-built accommodation at the Greenwood House dual campus site". "The phased, multi-million pound project has involved extensive engagement with the school to ensure the design meets pupils' needs," they said. "This includes specialist classrooms, sensory spaces, a soft playroom, and secure outdoor play areas. "As a listed building, this is a significant and complex scheme, requiring careful planning, consultation with relevant stakeholders, and input from the Historic Environment Division before final options could be agreed. "Following unavoidable construction delays, the school agreed with EA to provide temporary modular accommodation allowing for full-time education to be accessed." It said detailed design work was under way for the former Elmgrove school building, with enabling works due to start December 2026, ahead of the main contractor appointment expected early 2027. title: Leah Croucher: 'Not knowing was torture, knowing is as bad'
description: The family of the teenager whose body was found in 2022 say the evidence pointing to her killer is overwhelming.
body: Leah Croucher was missing for three years before her remains were found When Leah Croucher's body was found three years after she went missing her family thought their torture would end. Instead it continued with conspiracy theories, fear and heartbreak haunting their lives. The 19-year-old was walking to work on 15 February 2019 when she disappeared. Her parents say they went through more than three years of "absolute torture" before her dismembered body was discovered in a house in Milton Keynes, less than half a mile (0.8km) from her home in 2022. She had been killed by a repeat sex offender Neil Maxwell, a man who her parents have branded "an animal". He was on the run from police at the time. Despite overwhelming evidence of Maxwell's guilt, her parents Claire and John say they have been subjected to "devastating" speculation online, with some pointing the finger at her brother. Leah's parents are now calling for 'Leah's Law', a mandatory minimum sentence for anyone convicted of a third sexual offence. Haydon Croucher took his own life nine months after his sister went missing. Leah's parents say he struggled to cope with not knowing what had happened to her. The Crouchers believe Leah's Law would have saved Leah and by extension Haydon. Leah Croucher's family were subjected to online conspiracy theorists and people contacting them pretending to be Leah after she went missing Leah was the "perfect daughter" say her parents. "She was a very shy, home-loving girl," says her dad but had a "brilliant sense of humour" once she opened up, adds her mum. Leah Croucher's parents last saw her at the family home on Quantock Crescent at 22:00 GMT on 14 February. For three years and nine months they went through "absolute torture", says John before her body was found less than half-a-mile from the family home. On 10 October 2022, police received a phone call, which led them to the loft of a house on Loxbeare Drive, where they found Leah's dismembered body in plastic bags along with some of her belongings. She was identified through dental records. Claire Croucher says she avoids going out on her own because of what happened to her daughter in broad daylight More than seven years after Leah's disappearance Claire says she still fears that what happened to Leah could happen again to Leah's sister and will not leave the house alone. "What I want to know is when I go out tonight to go to the shop to buy some milk, am I going to get home again? "Because that's my main fear, I don't go out on my own. We don't make Jade go out on her own because we know that some days people don't come back. "We've got to remember Leah could have been anyone's daughter, anyone's mum, sister, child," says Claire. Haydon Croucher struggled to cope with the loss of his sister The Crouchers say the impact of the internet sleuths debating if Haydon had been involved destroyed them at times. "Because at the end of the day Haydon loved his sister so much he gave his own life because he couldn't cope with not knowing what happened to her," says Claire. Claire says the family, who have taken part in a new documentary about the case, have spoken out "to clear his name". Similarly John says they want to make sure people know "what a monster [Maxwell] was". He branded him "an animal". "I won't even mention his name. He's just a disgusting, vile, horrible creature," he says. Before Leah's remains were found, the family's torment was also magnified by internet trolls creating fake social media accounts pretending to be her. Many targeted her sister, Jade. Another woman called pretending to be Leah the morning after Haydon died. "Jade was woken up by a female voice saying that it was Leah and that she couldn't believe Haydon had died, but she didn't know how to come home and face us all... it's just disbelief that somebody could do that. Why? Why do they think that's funny? What were they trying to gain?" Leah's parents say it has been devastating to see conspiracy theories online when the evidence against Neil Maxwell is overwhelming There is no doubt in her parents' minds that Maxwell killed and sexually assaulted their daughter. He was named by police as the prime suspect. His handprints were on the loft hatch and bags where Leah's remains were found. And on the saw which was used. There was also DNA evidence left behind which indicated Leah was likely sexually assaulted. "His DNA was all over everything and people still say it's easy to fit a dead man up. It's not. "His DNA was everywhere. Multiple forms of DNA. Multiple forms. One hundred percent, it was him. "How much more damning do you need? It was horrendous," says John. John says he often wakes up in the middle of the night, haunted by the details of what happened to Leah. "We know what happened to our daughter, and knowing is just as bad as not knowing. The not knowing was torture, but knowing, now you visualise exactly what was happening." He says there is not a day that goes by without it going through his mind. Leah Croucher's body was found in October 2022 and the police investigation concluded in January 2024 Leah's parents believe their daughter was killed because she fought against her attacker. At the inquest into her death in 2024 police said they believed Leah, who was a Taekwondo competitor, "would have defended herself" which "may have escalated the situation". Leah Croucher's family warn system needs to change The quiet teenager who vanished on her way to work Leah's parents are now calling for a mandatory minimum sentence for anyone convicted of a third sexual offence. They also want all repeat sex offenders to be sentenced by a District Judge instead of magistrates. Claire says had that been the case before Leah was targeted she believes her daughter would still be alive.

title: Time to rise? Ranking European football's sleeping giants
description: From Sampdoria to Saint-Etienne and Real Zaragoza, who are the sleeping giants of European football?
body: Deportivo, Parma, Hamburg. Not just a football hipster's holiday hit-list, but a sample of erstwhile headline acts who have returned to their respective top flights in recent years. You can throw Leeds United, Nottingham Forest, Schalke and Malaga into the mix too. But with such footballing royalty back in the big time, where can you find Europe's current sleeping giants? Which one-mighty sides are still snoozing? We first need to establish some criteria - history, heritage, fanbase, stadium. Clubs with huge potential who currently exist outside the top flight. Calling a big city home helps, but it is not a deal-maker - sorry to fans of Bristol City and second-tier Russian outfit FC Ufa, where the local population tops one million. Likewise, some clubs with good-sized stadiums have not made the cut. Bari, whose Stadio San Nicola is the third-largest in Italy and was built for Italia '90, stands out, though some of their calcio colleagues outside Serie A also have grounds of more than 30,000 - Hellas Verona, Messina and Palermo among them. There's a plethora of ex-Premier League teams with top-flight worthy arenas and storied pasts, while Germany is stacked full of historic clubs with huge homes who arguably deserve a spot - Fortuna Dusseldorf, Wolfsburg, Hannover 96 - but we can't include them all. A sleeping giant must have experienced some element of former glory and Pro Vercelli are the obvious candidate there, winning seven Italian titles by 1922. But, despite being under new ownership, the third-tier side boast neither the ground nor local population to awaken that historic status any time soon. The other nuance is, that success cannot have come too recently. West Ham, for example, won a European competition three years ago, Wolves are recent top-flight regulars; likewise Stade de Reims, twice European Cup runners-up, and eight-time French champions Nantes. Leaving out Steaua Bucharest was another big call. European Cup winners 40 years ago and Romania's most dominant club, they now play in Liga II. But, following a deeply divisive split, many of the traditional fanbase follow top-flight FCSB. So who really owns that legacy? And there was a case for Boavista, title winners in 2001 but whose existence now hangs by a thread. Facing financial ruin, despite fans' best efforts, they have been ejected from Portugal's professional leagues. Anyway, let's get on with this. Piped through the matrix above, here are my top 10 European sleeping giants - you can have your say in the comments, too. Bursaspor's Centennial Ataturk Stadium is shaped to look like a crocodile League titles: One (2009-10). Domestic cups: One (1985-86). Division: 1.Lig, second tier. Stadium: Centennial Ataturk Stadium (43,361) Historically dominated by Istanbul's elite teams, Bursaspor snapped that long-running streak by becoming only the second club from outside of the capital - and first since Trabzonspor almost three decades earlier - to clinch the Turkish title in 2010. That meant Champions League nights against Manchester United and Rangers, but in 2024 the Green Crocodiles dropped into the fourth tier for the first time in their history. Based in a city of about 2.5m people - Bursa sits in the north west, south of Istanbul, near Mount Uludag - and with a unique crocodile-shaped stadium that can house 43,361 fans, Bursaspor have soared up the pyramid since and are looking to return to the Super Lig for the first time since 2019. Dynamo Dresden last played in the Bundesliga in 1995 League titles: Eight (most recent East German DDR-Oberliga 1989-90). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 89-90). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Rudolf-Harbig-Stadion (32,085). Without wanting to turn this into a 2.Bundesliga table, this is the first of four German entries. But Dynamo Dresden, bearing a complex history and situated in the underrepresented east, feel a little different. Initially enjoying the support of the security forces before their best players were relocated to Berlin, Dynamo became European regulars and lost to Liverpool in the Uefa Cup in 1976 and European Cup two seasons later. One of East Germany's most dominant clubs, they won eight titles and seven cups and joined the Bundesliga in 1991 following reunification, but they dropped into the third tier four years later amid relegation and mounting debts. Dynamo, with alumni including Matthias Sammer, have bounced around the regional and lower leagues for many years but now sit in 2.Bundesliga. Based in a city of more than half a million people, their potential is underpinned by a large, passionate fanbase who averaged over 30,000 for home games in the second tier last term. A young Michael Ballack was part of Otto Rehhagel's Kaiserslautern squad that won the Bundesliga title in 1998 League titles: Four (most recent 1997-98). Domestic cups: Two (most recent 95-96). Division: 2.Bundesliga. Stadium: Fritz-Walter-Stadion (49,327) With their 1997-98 success, Kaiserslautern remain the only side to win the Bundesliga immediately after promotion, albeit following a surprise relegation having also been champions in 1991 and enjoyed cup triumphs in 1990 and 1996. European regulars in the 1990s and early 2000s, it is now almost 15 years since they competed in the Bundesliga, spending four seasons in the third tier before a promotion in 2022. Despite modest league finishes, the club continue to record average crowds of more than 46,000 and almost pulled off another shock in 2024 when they reached the German Cup final, losing to Xabi Alonso's Leverkusen. Ron Atkinson's Sheffield Wednesday, on their way to earning promotion back to the top flight, beat Manchester United to win the League Cup in 1991 League titles: Four (most recent 1929-30). Domestic cups: Four (most recent 90-91). Division: League One, third tier. Stadium: Hillsborough (39,732) Sheffield United fans may argue that they, not city

title: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
description: People who have been adopted or are in care sometimes struggle to access family medical history which could be crucial to their own health.
body: This video can not be played Aaliyah: "Every time you go to the GP when they ask for family history, you have to say you don't know" When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer. But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history. "Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it." The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health. Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby. She says the whole process took its toll. "I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits. Days before Aaliyah's 25th birthday, a large unmarked envelope landed on the doormat of her home, in Birmingham. "I rip it open, thinking it's an early birthday present," she says. But what was inside was the response to her data request - pages and pages of her family history, including some medical details she had been painstakingly trying to track down for years. The documents contained upsetting information alluding to the reason she was taken into care, alongside court records and a personal letter from her social worker. "They were just given to me in a completely nondescript pile, and they contained completely earth-shattering information, of which I don't think I have ever recovered from," she says. Aaliyah, pictured as a baby, grew up knowing nothing of her biological family's medical history Aaliyah says knowing about her biological family's health could have helped her understand her own medical concerns. "My biological mother struggled with eating disorders all her life," she says. "I had very severe anorexia in my teens and that would have been incredibly useful to know." When a child is adopted in the UK, their NHS number - or equivalent health service identifier - is changed to protect their anonymity. Their existing medical records should be merged with their new record, but this does not necessarily include their wider family medical history. And while some local authorities offer specialist support for adoptees up to 21 or 25, the ease of access can vary across the country. The BBC contacted Bradford Council, which said: "We are genuinely sorry that when Aaliyah received sensitive and personal information through her subject access request, we did not offer the support or signposting she needed. We recognise that we should have done more. "Following Aaliyah's experience, we are strengthening our approach so that adults accessing their records are given clear information about the support available." Bradford Children and Families Trust has now offered Aaliyah a meeting to further discuss her experience. For Dr Chris Tennyson, a delay in getting information about his birth father's health could have put his life at risk. The 40-year-old clinical psychologist, from Belfast, was adopted as a baby in the 1980s to "a really loving mum and dad, [in a] really comfortable family home". But in his 20s, he became increasingly curious about his biological origins. He met his birth mother, but his attempts to find out about his father stalled after social workers warned him off asking questions. Eight years later, Chris tried to trace him again, but it wasn't until he was 33 that a meeting was finally arranged. Then, on the afternoon the father and son were due to meet, a social worker approached Chris. "There's something that I need to share with you," the social worker told him. "Your father wants me to let you know that there's a genetic medical condition within your family." Government pledges 10,000 new foster care places in England Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC A member of Chris's biological family died in 2000, when the condition came to light. At the time, other members of the family were offered testing. But Chris, who was then aged 14, was not contacted. The condition, called malignant hyperthermia, causes a potentially life-threatening reaction to certain drugs used during anaesthesia. While genes linked to it can run in families, not everyone who inherits one of these will necessarily experience a reaction with anaesthesia. After undergoing genetic tests, Chris discovered his potential risk at the age of 37 - some 23 years after the condition had become known in his wider family. He says a lack of understanding of how to support adopted adults resulted in the delay in him getting tested. Chris, who now works with adoption and fostering services in Northern Ireland, says the lack of available information for adoptees is "a huge blind spot". "There needs to be some kind of mechanism where adopted people's care records can be updated with family information that becomes available throughout the lifespan." First-time mum Courtney-Grace says she is relieved her baby daughter, Tine, will have access to the crucial family medical history she lacked when she grew up. Now living in the North of England, the 28-year-old was adopted as a baby and spent time in foster care as a teenager. "The only thing we knew about my medical history is my biological mom was mentally ill, and had depression." Courtney-Grace wants vital family medical history to become available for adoptees In her mid-20s, Courtney-Grace was diagnosed with a genetic mutation, which can be inherited and is associated with an increased risk of tumours. title: Queen reflects on reading 'forbidden' Lady Chatterley's Lover under the pillow
description: In BBC documentary The Book That Changed My Life, the Queen speaks about memorable moments in her own reading.
body: This video can not be played "It's like the best tonic in the world": Queen Camilla on why she loves to read Queen Camilla has recalled secretly reading Lady Chatterley's Lover, the passionate and controversial novel by DH Lawrence, as a teenager in the 1960s. "As teenagers you read a lot of romances. It was the moment of Lady Chatterley, under our pillows, reading that by torchlight. You know the minute something is forbidden, you want to get hold of it," she said about the novel that had been at the centre of an obscenity trial. The Queen spoke about memorable moments in her own reading for BBC documentary The Book That Changed My Life, and about the life-changing power of literacy and books. She gave a glimpse of how regular reading is part of her royal marriage: "It's like the best tonic in the world. My husband and I actually read before dinner, just sitting quietly and reading. "He loves biographies, and PJ Wodehouse. I occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something," said the Queen about the King's affection for the author of the Jeeves and Wooster comic novels. "It's very off-putting, I can't get back into my book, or I'll suddenly start weeping. But it's a lovely, quiet time. I think it would be a complete and utter tragedy if books went forever," she said. The Queen also revealed more of her own youthful reading, saying she was "mesmerised" by Charles Dickens's Tale of Two Cities and its depiction of those watching the guillotine during the French Revolution. "Those ghastly women sitting there knitting while everybody had their heads chopped off," she said. The Queen, who is 79 years old, said she was part of a generation of women who missed out on higher education, which made reading and books even more important. "I left school quite young. In my day, women didn't go to university, so I think reading has been most of my education," she said. The Queen said reading is "the best tonic in the world" The documentary shows the impact of reading on people in stressful circumstances - and that includes Omar, who discovered a love of reading while in prison. Reading was a way of escaping the confines of a cell, at least in his imagination - and the book he remembers most was a tattered copy of Jack Higgins's war thriller, The Eagle Has Landed. Chatting to Omar after the screening of the documentary, he said that what struck him most about meeting the Queen was her "authenticity". He said that off camera she was genuinely interested in his role working in prison education - helping a prison population that's facing chronic levels of illiteracy. The pair also shared unexpected connections. Camilla's father, Bruce Shand, had also been a prisoner, in a different kind of captivity, as a prisoner of war captured in North Africa during the Second World War. He had used books as an emotional escape tunnel, during two and a half years of imprisonment. "He said he educated himself. He read every single book, from the Bible to the encyclopedia, whatever was there, he just sat there all day long and read and read. And I think that's how he survived it," said the Queen. Camilla with her father Bruce Shand in 2003, who she says "read and read" when he was a prisoner of war She remembered how her father didn't want to talk about the war - "you bury it all because you've seen such horrendous things" - and so it was only when she read his memoir that she understood his experiences. "It was written from the heart. I mean, I cried through most of it. I found it so moving. Because if you think, I didn't know anything about it, and reading managed to get him through it." Omar said the Queen had recognised a connection. "She talked about the parallels, her father found reading in a prisoner of war camp. She definitely recognised the resemblance… being in a place you don't want to be and using books to escape it and then books elevating you on many levels," he said. Queen Camilla has been running her Queen's Reading Room project for five years, a kind of mega book club, with festivals and events and outreach projects, such as bringing books to homeless shelters. It's part of her campaign to promote and protect the value of reading and to stop us becoming a culture of screen addicts. Perhaps the most moving parts of the documentary are the stories of how books can become lifelines for people facing bereavement or intense loneliness. The Queen's book club this autumn chose a book by the BBC's Reeta Chakrabarti Ian, from the north-east of England, spoke with heartbreaking candour about finding himself in a state of complete social isolation after the death of his mother. "I used to sit with my head on the kitchen table, crying. It was such a difficult period of loneliness, of nothingness," he said. Reading and becoming part of a book group proved a lifesaver for him, coaxing him back to his own happy ending. There's a powerful testimony from Peter, a Merseyside truck driver, who had to admit that he wasn't able to read and needed help, after the shame of having to keep inventing excuses to his children who wanted a bedtime story. He was taught to read by an adult education project - and he proudly shows the copy of JK Rowling's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone that has become his own stepping stone to literacy. Perhaps the most sobering statistic in this documentary is that there are eight million adults in the UK who struggle with even basic levels of literacy. Speaking after the screening, Big Issue founder John Bird blamed the scourge of adult illiteracy on a long-term political failure in tackling the "inheritance of poverty". "We did not educate the people who found education difficult - and I was one of them," he said, having learned to read as a youngster in prison. "People were written off, now we're paying for that,"

title: Profile
description: Conservative Party Leader and Leader of the Opposition.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·10 Oct 2026,·14 mins Available for over a year This week’s Conservative Party conference saw the Kemi Badenoch further cement her position at the helm of her party. But can her increased personal popularity help a party that is still lagging behind Reform UK in the polls? The daughter of a GP and a professor of physiology, Kemi Badenoch was born in Wimbledon but grew up in Lagos, Nigeria. At the age of 16, she moved to London where she worked various jobs including at McDonalds. She studied at Sussex University and it was an introduction to identity politics there that she credits with confirming her conservatism. After graduating, she worked as a software engineer, a systems analyst before embarking on a career in finance. In 2015 she became digital director at the Spectator magazine. In 2005, aged 25, she joined the Conservative Party and in 2015 she became a member of the London Assembly. At the 2017 snap general election she successfully ran to be Conservative MP for Saffron Waldon in Essex. After landing a number of ministerial roles under Boris Johnson she unexpectedly stood for Party Leader when he stood down as Prime Minister in 2022. She came fourth in that contest but ultimately won the leadership contest after the Labour landslide General Election result of 2024. This week she promised to scrap inheritance tax on family homes, proposed a new ‘Britannia Shield’ missile defence system and ruled out a pact with Nigel Farage’s Reform UK But can she overcome the odds and return the Conservative Party to power? title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
description: After four years, a Ukrainian man is set to stand trial in Hamburg accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines.
body: Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022 Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children. Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks. But German police were already closing in on him. After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany. Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine". Both he and his country have denied any involvement. Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov. Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea. There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas. Both have been inoperable ever since. Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers. They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda. Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat. As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow. Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure. But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise. They went on following the forensic crumbs. Eventually they led to Ukraine. The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services. In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich. That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy. He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks. But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected. Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him. By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert. Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs. None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions. But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them. "Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that." Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe. That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it. Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution. "Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out. The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution. Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence. "At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained. Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned". Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far. Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August. He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation. Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him. Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning. He is also a keen and competent

title: Flydubai attacker began a 'drift towards extremism and terrorism' in Australia, UAE says
description: The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general also alleges the co-pilot was trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport.
body: The Flydubai flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia after passengers managed to take back the aircraft's controls The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say. UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack". He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia. Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification. What began as a routine flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into a fight for survival when one pilot allegedly stabs another inside the cockpit. According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001. "The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday. "During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks." The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach". "He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving. This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment". More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September. In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia. The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia". This video can not be played Watch: Tearful pilot recounts moment of Flydubai attack Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft. Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv. Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views. He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials. Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country. title: 'Stain on the country': Trump criticises Norway over Nobel Peace Prize
description: The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay.
body: This video can not be played Trump says Nobel Peace Prize an 'indelible stain' on Norway US President Donald Trump has once again made complaints that he did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize, calling this year's decision "disgraceful and embarrassing". The prize was awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay on Friday. Hours after the announcement, Donald Trump told a rally he had "never heard" of the "mystery person". "This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway" he said, adding "we will not forget". Trump has been outspoken about his desire to win the prize, and made similar criticisms in 2025 when it was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. Last year, Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre explained to Trump it was an independent committee based in Norway, not the Norwegian government, which decides who will receive the prize. Speaking to his supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York, the US president repeated claims that he had settled eight wars and was "about to settle or win two more", without providing evidence. "The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation," he said. This video can not be played Watch: Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay? Pillay, a former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge, was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said. The South African's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes. Shortly afterwards, the 85-year-old reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her. "If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year, the president openly expressed his displeasure at missing out on the prize, with the White House accusing the committee of placing "politics over peace". In January, Machado gifted her medal to Trump during a meeting at the White House, which she said was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom. Trump said on social media that the move was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect". The Nobel committee later clarified that the prize was not transferable. "Once a Nobel Prize is announced, it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others," it said in a statement. "The decision is final and stands for all time." title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels show due to 'security threat'
description: Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat".
body: Ella Langley apologised to her fans, describing her decision as "incredibly difficult" US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat". The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start. In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team". Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs." He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat". "The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made. "We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans. The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible". BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. "We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend." In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history. Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May. title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
description: The storm took direct aim at Florida and is expected to impact Alabama, Georgia, and Louisiana.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Powerful waves crash ashore as Hurricane Isaias approaches US Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate. The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening. Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas. Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean. Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm. In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!" Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm. Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific. It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October. The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned. After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday. As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km). The Florida Panhandle and the rest of the US Gulf Coast are facing fierce winds and heavy rain as the hurricane barrels down. There is also the potential for accompanying tornadoes, Melissa Watson, a Florida-based meteorologist at the National Weather Service told the BBC. For those who have not evacuated, "the main thing will be having multiple ways to receive warnings" about tornadoes and storm surges, Watson said. "If you are near the coast, being able to move to higher ground," is also essential in the event of storm surges. "We want people to be safe, so don't go out there trying to look for damage ... to post on social media," she added. "We want people to remain inside and safe while the hurricane is moving through." Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding. More than 350,000 were in the dark in Florida and another 170,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us. The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 8,000 customers were without power. People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning". Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders. This video can not be played Weather presenter Stav Danaos explains the expected impacts of Hurricane Isaias John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left. "It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said. "Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said, Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over". A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes". Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home. People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this". Two men in Gulf Breeze, Florida board up the windows of a shop as Hurricane Isaias approaches. One indicator of a storm's severity to communities in the southern US is whether the stalwart restaurant chain The Waffle House would close its doors to customers. On Friday, it did. A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions". US President Donald Trump said he will no longer attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead. People in Newport Beach, California walk near coastal floodwaters amid strong waves and high tides generated by Tropical Storm Rachel Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend. Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters. Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific. While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California. title: 'Airlines sound alarm on costs crisis' and 'King's £1.5m bailout'
description: The weekend edition of the Financial Times highlights what it is calling a "mounting crisis" for airlines.
body: The weekend edition of the Financial Times highlights what it is calling a "mounting crisis" for airlines. It reports that persistently high fuel prices are forcing carriers to cut flights, axe costs and delay payments on leased aircraft. Noting the collapse of both Spirit Airlines and airBaltic earlier in the year, the paper has spoken to industry leaders, analysts and financiers, who said the "spectre of airlines falling over the winter season" was higher than it had been in previous years. The "King's £1.5m bailout for Andrew" is the main story for the Daily Mirror, which says King Charles III has been "forced to settle" a repairs bill at the former residence of his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. Sources told the paper that the Royal Lodge was left in an "absolute state", and the former prince was unable to foot the bill. Similarly, the front page of the Sun reads: "The king & I.O.U". It says the King has "loaned" Andrew the £1.5m sum, and notes that the former prince formerly surrendered his 75-year lease earlier this week. "It is not know how Andy will repay it," the paper writes. The Times is one of several considering the upcoming budget, reporting the Prime Minister Andy Burnham has "rejected a plea" from Health Secretary Yvette Cooper for more money to fund a pay deal for NHS staff. The paper says it is a "sign of tension" between ministers before the budget, and notes the "highly unusual move" from the prime minister and Chancellor John Healey to jointly write to Cooper and reject her request. The chairman of John Lewis has warned that a "tax raid" on department stores and supermarkets would "only harm our high streets", according to the Daily Telegraph. In what the paper describes as an "unusually outspoken attack on the potential Budget", Jason Tarry, who is also the chairman of Waitrose, said that "piling more costs" onto large stores would reveal a "fundamental misunderstanding of how modern high streets work". Burnham has signalled his government could ramp up a tax on warehouses in order to help fund tax cuts for businesses with "social benefit", like pubs and restaurants, the paper says. Marks & Spencer boss Stuart Machin has written a piece for the Daily Mail, where he urged the chancellor to "reverse 'the mistakes of the last two Budgets' to get Britain growing again". He went on to ask Healey to take the "handcuffs off business" and put money "back in people's pockets". The paper says the "damning assessment" from one of the UK's top chief executives will "set alarm bells ringing in Downing Street". The Prince of Wales has spoken to the Daily Express for World Mental Health Day, telling the paper that "we do not always know what someone is carrying beneath the surface". Prince William urged people to "check in, listen and show kindness", emphasising the "extraordinary impact" of simply stopping to ask if someone is okay. The iWeekend considers the future of the Green Party, following the defeat of its leader, Zack Polanski, in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. The paper says Polanski's leadership is "now in doubt", adding that the growth in the party's membership has been overshadowed by accusations that he failed to show leadership on the Zionism row. title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
description: Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill.
body: Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October. That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date. Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus. The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell. The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business. Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati. The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there. His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home. Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September. Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection. Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria. On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care. We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases. What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? Why Uganda is winning the battle against Ebola as virus spreads in DR Congo However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town. Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease. But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day. Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May. The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August. But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police. It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border. The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October. Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations. Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks. Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital. By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding. Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo. He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures. The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues. The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital. Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
