title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
description: Students taking to the streets in France have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics.
body: Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets. "There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school. "We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen." He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down. "They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population." The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis. Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country. Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter. The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system. This video can not be played Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them. On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million. But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them. Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem. It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages. When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils). "It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains. Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget. But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country. "It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest. "It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future." Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries. So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry. More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks. But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers. A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens. Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade. A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth. "For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether." Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests. Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests. "These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers a

title: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
description: Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and dozens of metro stations are shut to stop protesters from gathering.
body: Police have been deployed in big numbers even during demonstrations by opposition parties in the lead up to Saturday's 'cockroach' protest Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday. The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists. The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on the resignation demand. Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades. Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering. But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may". "If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X. The CJP held a rally in Bengaluru city on Thursday against CEC Kumar The CJP's weeks-long protest in the summer seeking education reforms was its first major challenge to Modi's government. The CJP scored a major victory when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July. The CJP protesters returned to streets last week with a rally in Mumbai city to press for CEC Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held a huge rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore). Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days. Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups. CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi. In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests. Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference, external that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP. "Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said. Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them. "In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied." The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather. Gyanesh Kumar is at the centre of the voter-roll revision controversy At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year. The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list. But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations. The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission. For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue. Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media. title: Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song
description: US singer-songwriter Ashe reveals the story behind her international smash hit, Stop The Wedding.
body: Stop The Wedding is one of the top 10 most-played songs on Spotify this week No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day. Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck. As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark. She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive. He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean. In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself. On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true. "I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s. "I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around." As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away. Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out. Its name? Stop the Wedding. It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts. "You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt. "Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says. "If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used." What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"? "I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!" Ashe married her second husband John Clark Canada, drummer for the band The Brook & The Bluff, last year Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify. On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships. "I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity. "It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system." The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether. A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations. It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music. After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter. She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words. The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career. Her then-husband was not impressed. "I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'. "It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time." Stop The Wedding is one of the top 10 most-played songs on Spotify this week It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit. Moral of The Story (key lyric: "you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You. Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming. When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month. "There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now. "It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her." In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness. "I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music." Finneas O'Connell co-produced Ashe's breakout single Moral of the Story For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing. She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records. Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently. "You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom. The same can't be said for her new album, Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top. This article contains content provided by Google YouTube. title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
description: The stalwart of Britain's High Street has been sold to a Canadian billionaire family. What will that mean for you?
body: If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK. The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades. But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience. Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic. The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF). What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed. Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail. Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear. "They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says. A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect." Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner". But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how the easy stores are to navigate. "You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well." Katie Burrows and Yasmin Trimble both shop at Boots regularly Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up. Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular. Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck." The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p. Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off. She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with. Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction". "I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions." Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on". "As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important." The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment. The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies. It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity. Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals. "They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says. While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products. "When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says. Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert. But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results. Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops. There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year. For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says. title: Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr on making history at her NFL half-time show
description: The Nigerian star will become the first African artist to headline the show at an international NFL game.
body: The Nigerian star will headline the half-time show when Philadelphia Eagles take on Jacksonville Jaguars in London Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr has already broken numerous records, and her NFL half-time performance this weekend is set to level up her list again. The Nigerian star will become the first African artist to headline one of the American football league's international games when the Philadelphia Eagles take on the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on Sunday. Ahead of the performance at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Starr told BBC Newsbeat her history-making performance "itself is a message". Earlier this year, Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny used his Super Bowl half-time show to celebrate Latin American culture. The 32-year-old also made history by becoming the first musician to perform entirely in Spanish at the sporting event, normally the most-watched each year on US TV. Starr said it's "very important" for singers to seize opportunities like this. "At the end of the day, as artists, we speak for the culture and we speak for the people that listen to us," she added. "And we have to represent any way that seems fit, that they need." She didn't want to give away too much about her performance, but confirmed it would feature tracks from her new studio album, Starrgirl, which was released in August. "Sunday is gonna be amazing," she said. "I'm still in rehearsals. It's a lot of work we're putting in so I'm really excited." Ayra Starr performed at All Points East in London this summer The 24-year-old has been making waves in recent years, becoming the first African woman to win best international act at the Mobo Awards and the first Nigerian woman to surpass one billion video views on YouTube. But before she became a superstar, the singer studied for a degree in political sciences and international relations - and said this has influenced her work. "When it comes to matters of women and equality and the girl child and even just children - I'm very outspoken on any platform that sees fit. "Even with my music, my music is very much like 'I will do what I want' and freedom." The Afrobeats singer will perform tracks from her new album, Starrgirl, at the NFL show The Afrobeats genre, which originates from West Africa, has massively grown in recent years - dominating playlists and seeing artists, including Starr, featuring at major festivals such as Glastonbury. She said the rest of the world is just "catching up" to a style that's been "popping in Africa for the longest time". The singer added that becoming one of the dominant faces of the music she grew up listening to, alongside artists such as Wizkid and Burna Boy, is "crazy". Starr acknowledged it's a male-dominated field and would like female artists to have more "space in the genre" and be "allowed the same privileges". But she also feels this is just the beginning. "Afrobeats just keeps evolving, it keeps growing and it just keeps getting better... I want it to be one of the top genres in the world." title: Weekend showers and sunshine for UK ahead of warmer temperatures next week
description: With sunshine and showers forecast for the weekend, next week could see a return to some warmer temperatures but there will be gales for some.
body: It will be a weekend of two halves weather-wise for most people with many seeing a cool start on Saturday. A strengthening north-westerly wind will carry showers across the UK. But Sunday looks calmer with sunshine in the north and east and rain creeping into the south and west. Looking further ahead, next week will see a return to above average temperatures. Tuesday looks set to be the warmest day of the period and could reach 21C for some. However a deep area of low pressure is likely to bring some stormy weather across the north. It could turn out to be too windy in some places to keep an umbrella up on Saturday Saturday will be the more unsettled day of the weekend, generally cool with blustery showers. Scotland and Northern England are likely to have the strongest winds, with local coastal gales. Sunshine and showers will be the dominant theme, with northern and eastern regions seeing the greatest concentration of these, and possibly hail and thunder too. Elsewhere there will be some scattered showers but many places in the south should see some lengthy dry spells with sunshine, and temperatures average for October. Mist and fog could accompany Sunday's chily start Sunday could get off to a chilly start with a grass frost in rural eastern areas. Some local fog patches are likely first thing, particularly in sheltered rural locations, before lifting to leave spells of sunshine and variable cloud for many. For Scotland and Northern England it is likely to be the drier day of the weekend with sunshine although cloud and patchy rain could move into the south-west by lunchtime. This will slowly make its way across the rest of southern England and into Wales. It will be accompanied by a strengthening southerly breeze and gradually a return to milder air once again. It could be several degrees above the seasonal average in places by midweek Next week, will see a transition to milder more humid conditions. Monday is likely to be a fairly grey day along with patchy rain and hill fog but brighter spells should develop later in the day for some areas. Temperatures will be about 3 degrees higher than Sunday and the cloudy overnight skies will make things seem very mild. Tuesday looks set to be the warmest day of the period. However across the north of the UK a deep area of low pressure will bring a bout of autumn gales. There will also be heavy rain which will drift southwards, but little promise of where it is needed most across eastern England. Once this clears, many places should see sunshine developing, and across England and Wales temperatures could widely reach 18-21 Celsius. This is several degrees above the mid-October average and it might well briefly feel like late summer before more changeable conditions return later in the week. title: Man City whistleblower to remain in witness protection
description: The computer hacker who released documents which helped trigger the Premier League investigation into Manchester City will remain under witness protection after authorities in Portugal suspend the decision to end it.
body: This video can not be played The Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which helped trigger the Premier League investigation into Manchester City will remain in witness protection after authorities in the country suspended the decision to end it. Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto had been scheduled to leave the protection programme on Saturday, a ruling he previously said had put him in a "life-threatening situation". Pinto, 37, disclosed a tranche of confidential football documents, including emails and financial records relating to the English Premier League side. In 2018, he shared documents with German magazine Der Spiegel, which used them for investigations into City's finances and alleged breaches of financial fair play rules. City were recently found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. They have appealed against the decision. Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide information obtained through the Football Leaks operation. However, in a statement on Friday,, external Portugal's Ministry of Justice said a decision to remove Pinto from witness protection had been reversed for the time being, with the body responsible for it - the special security programmes commission - having not adequately "notified" Pinto of grounds for its termination or given him the opportunity to challenge the decision. Pinto will now be given 10 days to assess a risk assessment conducted by the special security programmes commission that indicates a low threat to his safety. He posted on X, external thanking Portugal's Minister of Justice, Rita Alarcao Judice and saying the commission's initial decision had clearly violated the law and amounted to a "manifest abuse of power". Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, but was convicted in Portugal of offences including illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence. He wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020, which was also subject to heightened security measures. Earlier this year, he was acquitted of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to a number of sports bodies in Portugal, including Benfica. title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
description: Episode four saw another contestant killed off, a ghoulish mission near a graveyard and a spooky twist.
body: Romesh Ranganathan lets out a scream while holding a dead woman's wedding dress in a haunted cabin Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fourth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. Being a Traitor must be a nightmare. While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked. Friday's episode saw the the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh. The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle. And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft). When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight. Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players Celebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it? "That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses." Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out." Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go." On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised. "I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room. "I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la. "So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out." I guess now we'll never know. Bella Ramsey was considered to be the Traitors' "biggest threat" and so had to go Back at breakfast, Hesmondhalgh's apparently earnest but over-the-top reaction to Ramsey's removal immediately raised suspicions. The former Coronation Street star had been voted as the most trustworthy of the group by her peers in episode one and given a shield, but that counted for little by episode four. The cleverest among the group, on paper at least, Fry, found questions being asked of her too as the day rolled on. "I did not choose the traitor life, the traitor life chose me," said the latest recruit to the dark side. "I know there are people who are suspicious of me but I'm going to enjoy every last moment." Comedian and Miss Marple impersonator Miranda Hart is one of them. "Hannah lied to us," she rightly noted, with reference to the professor's confusing shield story that helped to see off Myha'la the night before. Singer and ex-military man James Blunt, however, had other ideas, ramping up his campaign against Hesmondhalgh, whom he believed to be a little too trustworthy to be true. The group conversing with the grateful dead Friday's mission raised more money for charity and also raised spirits, but not in a good way. It involved the group paying a visit to a graveside haunted cabin to converse with the dead about matters unresolved. "It's creepy, it's giving murder," noted Barbie actress Sharon Rooney on arrival. Comedian Romesh Ranganathan joked that his mum was going to "absolutely hate this", as the the group gathered in a graveside chant led by the booming voice of big dog actor Michael Sheen. The spooky task made Ranganathan himself let out a hellish scream and saw Hart come face-to face with a masked hooded creature, before team-player Croft volunteered to go head-first into a stinky old toilet in scenes resembling ITV's I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here. "Guys, it's a little bit of poo," noted hardman Ross Kemp, as all around him gagged. "It's not gonna kill you." Croft received a protective shield for his troubles, at least. "If I'd have put my hands and head down a toilet for nothing, I would've been fuming," he fairly noted. Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked James Blunt led the charge against faithful Julie Hesmondhalgh and has seemingly now put himself in the frame as a result The group, with a little help from the undead, had to find a child's toys and a woman's wedding dress and shoes. This later prompted model Jerry Hall to reminisce about her own wedding to Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger. "Before I got married to Mick - we'd already been together seven years, had two children - I put on a wedding dress every day until he agreed that we get married," she revealed. Some rancid wine that tasted like "salty bin juice", according to comedian Joanne McNally, topped off possibly the most revolting task yet. On the way back to the castle, YouTuber King Kenny raised more suspicions about Fry having allowed him to grab a shield. "She held off to make herself look a bit innocent," he told his fellow faithfuls. Traitor Jama smartly deflected attention away from herself by latching on to the growing suspicions around Hesmondhalgh. Hesmondhalgh bade farewell to her fellow faithfuls, describing the show's reveal as "iconic" Ahead of the roundtable, Fry told producers she knew she would have to fight like her life depended on it - because it did - and try to disguise herself as still being a faithful. title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
description: The US president hopes to ease his party's pain before next month's midterm elections, writes the BBC's North America correspondent.
body: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president. Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas. Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months. The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections. As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress. Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin' What are the US midterms? A simple guide For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking. He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having. His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort. Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear. It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy". "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X. It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box. The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market. Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference. With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post. But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand. Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words. Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? title: 'Thuggish' behaviour could see balaclava ban in more cities
description: The hashtag "no face no case" has been gaining traction glorifying balaclavas as a way to avoid prosecution.
body: A masked electric bike rider pictured in Newport Balaclavas could be banned in more city centres over concerns about "thuggish" behaviour, including robberies, burglaries and drug dealing. The social media hashtag "no face no case" has been gaining traction glorifying balaclavas as a way to avoid prosecution. Police across the UK have said face coverings are hampering their efforts to identify potential offenders. Officials in Newport, as well as, Coventry, Stafford and Wolverhampton, are exploring ways to strengthen existing powers to challenge those wearing balaclavas, while Nottingham has already introduced a ban. Luie and Nath back a ban and believe it will help tackle crime Newport college students Luie and Nath, both 16, are supportive of a ban. "It just looks dodgy", said Luie, "I think they should ban it. I think if you wear one you're up to no good. "If you stop these face coverings, you'll stop crime, people can recognise you, there's CCTV everywhere, if you remove face coverings - it's a simple fix really." "There's a lot of crime going on and they're common around the city centre," Nath added. "I just don't think they need to wear them - bad things come with them." Gabrielle says she is intimidated by balaclava wearers and tries to avoids the city centre "I think it's a good idea - they go around on their motorbikes intimidating people with their balaclavas on - and probably involved in crime and never get caught," said Gabrielle. "It's quite intimidating when you're walking and they just zoom past you. "I don't very often go into town - you feel intimidated wherever you go because there's a lot of antisocial behaviour going on. "I tend to stay out of their way." Attela Kis has concerns about religious freedom, but believes a ban would help bring people to justice Photographer Attela Kis, 32, is concerned about the effect it may have on people choosing to cover their faces for religious reasons. "It depends on what type of face covering you're talking about - like a Burka for example, this is part of their religion," he said. "When people are riding their electric bikes and committing actual crimes, it's really dangerous. "They shouldn't cover their faces, if anyone gets hit - or anything gets stolen people need to be found and prosecuted." Matthew Evans, one of two Newport councillors who proposed the ban, said people were wearing "intimidating" face coverings to "rob, burgle and deal drugs in our city centre" and "avoid detection". He proposed "exemptions for religious reasons" and said this was not an "attack on the human rights of young people". This follows a recent joint police and council crackdown, Operation Krypton, which led to hundreds of arrests. Supt Esyr Jones from Gwent Police said 321 arrests had been made since July to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour across Newport. Newport council said the current PSPO is due for review, "and any potential amendments can be considered as part of that process". It said the current PSPO could potentially include face coverings, "and this too is being explored in relation to its practical implication and legalities". But said there would be "exemptions for legitimate reasons, including religious, cultural, medical, occupational, weather or personal safety reasons". Gwent Police arrested and jailed this masked rider, after he raced at high speed through Newport In Nottingham, a senior police officer said offenders who wore them to hide their identity caused "substantial" problems. Now, police there are allowed to ask people to remove their face covering if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or anti-social behaviour. Anyone who refuses could face a £70 fixed penalty notice or face a maximum fine of £1,000. Videos with the hashtag "no face no case" can be found on social media platforms Social media videos with the hashtag "no face no case" are used on social media, glorifying the use of balaclavas to avoid prosecution. Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said anti-migrant protesters covering their faces with masks and balaclavas was "not the British way." It followed protests in Dover where demonstrators were wearing face coverings. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has called for full face coverings, including those worn for religious reasons, to be banned in public. title: Arteta's conscience clear over Man City charges
description: Mikel Arteta says his conscience is clear over Manchester City's rule breaches during a period when he was assistant manager at the club.
body: Mikel Arteta joined Arsenal from Manchester City in 2019 Mikel Arteta says his conscience is clear over Manchester City's Premier League rule breaches during a period when he was assistant manager at the club. The Arsenal boss worked under Pep Guardiola between 2016 and 2019, which overlapped with the nine seasons during which City have been found to have broken rules and disguised secret funding of more than £830m. In his first news conference since the ruling - which the club has appealed - Arteta attempted to bat away questions, saying he wanted to "respect" the ongoing process. However, towards the end of more than half an hour of questioning, he was asked: "You were at City for three and a half years, is your conscience clear? You had a senior position there, is your conscience clear?" His answer was one word, but it was arguably the most revealing part of the whole interaction. It was the only occasion where the Spaniard did not in some way revert to his messaging about not giving opinions on the case until such a time as there is a resolution. Arteta was at no point combative, but it was clear he arrived at Arsenal's training ground with a response he was determined to stick to. Asked if he had spoken to Guardiola, he added: "I prefer not to answer those questions." Arteta was asked for his reaction to the damning report from the independent commission, which found City had arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners to disguise earnings. He said: "I fully understand the question, but obviously I think it's very important that we respect the process, the timelines, and it's still an ongoing process that is not resolved because it's been appealed. "My position, and I think the club's position, is not to make any further comments until this is fully resolved." When asked if he thought, that to preserve the integrity of the Premier League, the appeal and sanction needed to be resolved this season, he replied: "The people are responsible to manage this process and to come to the right conclusions and I'm sure it will be done and it will be resolved in the right way. We have to trust that." Arteta also added he "100%" believed the Premier League remains the best in the world. Arsenal, who sit three points behind league leaders City, face fifth-placed Leeds on Saturday at Emirates Stadium. title: Greek takeaways: What did we learn from Lionesses' win?
description: England come away from Greece with a valuable first-leg lead in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off - but who impressed in the 3-1 victory?
body: Sarina Wiegman has led England to back-to-back European titles England came away from Greece with a valuable first-leg lead in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off - but what did we learn? Sarina Wiegman's side are looking to secure their place in Brazil next year but have to navigate the play-offs after finishing runners-up in their qualification group. The back-to-back European champions won 3-1 in Crete on Friday night and will need to finish the job against Greece on Tuesday in Leicester (19:30 BST). The winner of the tie faces Ukraine or Slovakia in round two to decide who will head to Brazil. Lucy Bronze withdrew from the squad with a minor injury earlier this week, handing a rare opportunity to Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier. The defender is a key player for her club but struggles to break into the England team with Bronze understandably a tough figure to displace. Wiegman sees Le Tissier as a right-back as opposed to a centre-back - which is her position at United - and that meant she was handed a start against Greece. Making her 15th cap, Le Tissier was a standout performer and was rewarded with her first international goal in the 63rd minute, providing optimism for a future without 34-year-old Bronze. "As soon as we were in possession, she was higher on the pitch and she already came close to a couple of moments with crosses," said Wiegman. "I'm very happy for her and for the whole team because that was an important goal." Maya le Tissier scored her first goal for England in the second half It was just England's third win in their past eight competitive away games. A 3-1 victory is a pleasing result, but given the gulf in class, Wiegman admitted frustrations at not keeping a clean sheet. There were familiar lapses in concentration defensively that gave Greece opportunities to pounce. Ioanna Papatheodorou struck the crossbar in the first half, before teeing up Kallisti Brouksair for their goal later on. Those chances came from England errors and the lack of clean sheet means the door remains open for Greece in the second leg. "That's up to us. We have to show up on Tuesday, play a good game and then we should be better than Greece," said Wiegman. "Of course we want to take some more distance [in the scoreline], that's absolutely true, but at the same time we won and that's the most important thing. "Sometimes we played really well and sometimes we were a bit sloppy. We were a bit frustrated as we wanted to do that better. "We want to show more than winning, we want to play really well too." With victory secure, Wiegman was able to hand a debut to 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson, as well as Liverpool captain Grace Fisk. Fisk, 28, had waited more than six years for her debut, having received her first England call-up in 2020 but Parkinson has broken through at pace this season. The teenager was unexpectedly named in Wiegman's squad in March, having only made the jump up to England's Under-23s a few months earlier. She secured a move to the United States this summer, joining North Carolina Courage from Portuguese side Valadares Gaia, and came on in the 85th minute. This week defender Esme Morgan said: "She's a really intelligent player. She has incredibly good movement and timing, picking up pockets for players to find her. "She's really comfortable receiving [the ball] in tight spaces, she's strong holding off players, very aggressive in her tackling and wins back a lot of balls. "I've been really impressed with Erica since she came into camp and also from playing against her in the National Women's Soccer League." Why England teenager Parkinson has a mindset coach Parkinson's debut added to the debate of who Wiegman's preferred number 10 is. She is one of many options available, including Chelsea forward Lauren James, who was given a creative, free role against Greece. James showed flashes of quality and nonchalantly lobbed goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti from 30 yards in the first half, but her effort was ruled out for offside. Other options include Manchester City's Grace Clinton and Manchester United's Ella Toone, who were both recalled to the squad to cover injuries with Aston Villa's Lucia Kendall among those to drop out. Laura Blindkilde Brown started in that position with James in Crete, while Beth Mead and Jess Park have also played there before. The position was a difficult one for Wiegman to nail down at Euro 2025 and more than a year later, the question of who is England's best number 10 remains. "I see there is a lot of competition in that position, where we have a lot of options with different players, who have different qualities," said Wiegman. "You can call it a question mark but I call it many options. Today we had two 10s and sometimes three. [James] was one of them." Local media had questioned why the game wasn't being played in Greece's capital city Athens. And there was an eerie atmosphere with fewer than 4,000 fans in the 26,000-capacity stadium in Heraklion, Crete. The Lionesses are also not used to being in play-offs, a route they are having to take after finishing runners-up to world champions Spain in their qualifying group. But Georgia Stanway, this year's top scorer for England, once again turned up when they needed her to and she opened the scoring after a neat, incisive passing move, in a frustrating first half. That was the spark England needed as they lacked ruthlessness and failed to capitalise on their dominance - an aspect of their game that needs improving. "I think we made it a bit harder. Greece were well prepared and disciplined. We struggled when they tried to press us," added Wiegman. "We could have scored more than the three goals. There are lots of things to take. title: Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary
description: The conservative commentator currently works as a communications adviser at Trump Media & Technology Group.
body: President Donald Trump has chosen conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary. Zacharia, who currently works for Trump Media & Technology Group, will become the president's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations. She previously had a brief stint as a spokesperson at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). In a social media post on Friday, Trump called Zacharia "loyal" and "a devoted fan and member of MAGA", referring to his Make America Great Again movement, adding she "has an unblemished record of support". Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, who left the White House in August, has reportedly taken a job with Fox News. "She was previously involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States, where we won 7 out of 7," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration." Zacharia thanked him in a post on X, writing, "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime." She said Trump has "shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day". She said she looks forward "to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out". The 42-year-old political strategist is a frequent fixture on conservative Newsmax and Fox News, and has been active in Republican politics for most of her adult life, having worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and for the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006. Since June, she has been a senior communications adviser for Trump's media company and Truth Social platform, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in Homeland Security from February to March this year. While she was only briefly in government at DHS - which she later said she left because of the strain of travel between California and Washington on her family - she has long been a ferocious defender of President Trump and his administration's policies. In a June interview with the BBC, for example, she dismissed criticism of Trump's controversial use of the White House to host a televised UFC fight, saying the principles of the UFC "are the kind of principles that founded our Constitutional Republic". "It's about not giving up the fight until the bitter end," she said. "I think there's no better summation of the American ethos than a good UFC fight." A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally - and current Special Presidential Envoy for Special Missions - Ric Grenell. In 2011, she spent nearly two years clerking at a law firm in Beijing, China. Trump says White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post The complex job of press secretary goes beyond the briefing room podium to include managing contentious relationships with the press, coordinating with other parts of the White House, and providing media advice to the president. The secretary also oversees an office that receives a significant amount of inquiries and requests on a daily basis. Trump called Leavitt one of his "most trusted aides" when she left the role, saying she wanted to spend more time with her family, which set a high bar for her replacement. A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia, 42, has four children. She has also worked as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative advocacy group headed by Trump ally Ric Grenell. title: Three men found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers and US friend
description: The bodies of Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were found at the bottom of a well.
body: Callum (left) and Jake Robinson were on a surfing trip in Mexico with their friend Carter Rhoad when they were killed during a suspected carjacking in 2024 Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers, Jake and Callum Robinson, and their American friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024. During the trial, the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well. The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico. The verdict was handed down on Friday in the Mexican state of Baja California. The parents of the two Australian brothers, Martin and Debra Robinson, have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments heard earlier on Thursday. "It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said their father, Martin. Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link. Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us". During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants. In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús "El Kekas" Gerardo, was sentenced in a separate trial to twenty years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery. At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings. The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico. The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers – all in their early thirties – had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them. At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea. Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California. Amid the demands for action, the governor of Baja California, Marina del Pilar Ávila, tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state. "Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said. "I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time." title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he will not watch it
description: The planned execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
body: This video can not be played "I'm not going to be watching it" - JD Vance on possible livestreamed execution US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter. Talking with reporters, Vance expressed doubt that the December execution would move forward as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it". Vance described the actions by former US Army major Nidal Hasan as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11". Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years. The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad. Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," said Hegseth. The BBC has asked the White House whether Trump supported the plans. Responding to a reporter's question on Friday about how the Pentagon's announcement meshes with his Catholic faith, Vance said: "I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen." The vice-president condemned Hasan's actions. Vance noted that Hasan, who was a US Army psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived". This video can not be played Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? The announcement of the livestream plans has been met with criticism from both political parties. Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched them, warning that public executions erode civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment". Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider. "The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent," he said. Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group. Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that he "absolutely" supports the death sentence, but that live-streaming executions "is what jihadists do. America is better than that". The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement. The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture". Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. Military law requires that military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward. While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream When Hegseth told reporters on Thursday about plans to ensure the pulbic can watch the execution, he did not specify where or how live video of the execution would be shown. A Pentagon spokesperson on Friday reiterated to the BBC that Hasan's execution "will be livestreamed," but said the government had no further details "to provide at this time". The White House did not respond to an inquiry about whether it expected to show Hasan's planned execution on its social media channels. The White House maintains official accounts and channels on the most notable and widely used online platforms that are capable of streaming live video, namely Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. The White House also has an app that can live stream events. President Trump's social media platform Truth Social does not have a live-stream video feature. This video can not be played Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in Tennessee All of the platforms have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence. Meta, owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment. YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers". TikTok has a similar rule that bars "extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress." That includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual". Both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest". Asked if a live-stream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned , a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach." title: NI secretary to ban the Drumcree parade
description: The parade has led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.
body: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant says he will ban the Drumcree parade Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has said he will ban the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree. The dispute has led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks. Sir Chris said the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) chief constable advised him "that it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland". The move comes on the 13th day of deadlock between residents and the local district lodge of the Orange Order. The Parades Commission had ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place. But the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the Garvaghy Road. Under legislation, a secretary of state can overturn a Parades Commission determination, especially following some form of input from the police. Sir Chris had been coming under increasing pressure from Sinn Féin and the SDLP to stop the parade. On Friday night, Sir Chris said: "The Parades Commission have advised me that while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect. "Consequently, and in the interests of wider public interest and safety, I've come to the conclusion that the circumstances under which that decision was made have now changed considerably. "As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined." Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the Drumcree parade. That development came as First Minister Michelle O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from police investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute. On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview. Breandán Mac Cionnaith says "we have to remember the price that was paid for to get this decision over many years" Speaking outside a community centre on the Garvaghy Road on Friday night, Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition spokesman Breandán Mac Cionnaith said that "while this is a win for us tonight, it is one that is still tinged with sadness and with loss". "There's no real cause for celebration that we have to remember the price that was paid to get this decision over many years." He said the announcement should mark a "starting point" to rebuilding strained community relations in Portadown. Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald said the overwhelming sense on the road was "one of relief and one of joy", adding that this "awful threat and this sense of menace has been lifted from the community". "To have had the prospect of a march down the road was just incomprehensible, nobody could believe that this decision had been landed and the community said from the get go that they would stand strong and united and that they would not have it and they have. Right has won out here." Protesters blocked the Garvaghy Road on 27 September - the date the parade had been due to take place Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin said in a post on social media that the announcement by Sir Chris "will come as a significant relief to the community on the Garvaghy Road". "It will also be a relief to people in communities right across Northern Ireland, and the island of Ireland as a whole, who were concerned that the situation at Drumcree, if left unresolved, could have had lasting negative repercussions on community relations and reconciliation," he said. There have been 13 days of deadlock in Portadown since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on 27 September The Portadown District said it "notes the chief constable has abdicated his responsibility for policing Northern Ireland". "We further note that the secretary of state has bowed to the republican mob, and rewarded criminality. Again, the consequences should be self-evident," they said. The Portadown District said that they "understand the immense anger which is tonight engulfing our community", but has urged for calm. "The Portadown District will be having no further engagement with the PSNI." Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said in a statement that "it has been clear in recent days that due to the actions of Sinn Féin and the total disregard for the recent determination in favour of a parade that the PSNI cannot ensure the safe completion of the parade". "The decision of the chief constable to refer the matter to the secretary of state and his conclusion that the parade cannot proceed is a direct result of republican agitation, mobilisation and the looming threats of potential violence." "These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest." There has been stalemate in Portadown since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on 27 September. That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west. Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police. The chief constable said last week that the consequences of police forcing an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road "could be catastrophic". title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'
description: Ukraine's president said allowing Russia to sell petroleum products would prolong a war that must be ended.
body: US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel into the global market. Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that. "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. An envoy to Putin welcomed the deal, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war. Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices. That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation. The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary license allowing Russian diesel into the market. An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world." But Zelensky hit out at the deal, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror". "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media. Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%. Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices. But on Friday Zelensky defended the strikes, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector". "Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said. Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear. But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas. The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine. What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on what reimbursement the US is providing Russia in return for the release of diesel. With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain. Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline, and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax. Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.
