title: Early release scheme prisoner jailed days after leaving
description: Michael Bogle had said outside prison last week that "people like me" should not be jailed "for a long time".
body: Michael Bogle spoke to reporters outside prison when he was released on 1 October A man has been jailed for a number of shoplifting offences days after being freed under the government's early release scheme. Michael Bogle, 38, was released from HMP Wandsworth on 1 October as part of the first wave of prisoners to be let out under the plan. Speaking to reporters outside the prison following his release, Bogle said the conditions inside were "awful" and said "people like me" should not be in prison "for a long time". In the four days after his release, Bogle stole more than £100 worth of detergent from supermarkets in north London. He was arrested on Tuesday and admitted the offences in court on Wednesday, resulting in an eight-month sentence. The previous 32-week sentence he was released from early had been suspended but he was jailed for breaching its terms. He served 78 days. Asked if he had a message for Prime Minister Andy Burnham after his early release, Bogle said: "Keep the early release going. It's good." The scheme was brought in to relieve pressure on prisons across England and Wales which were dangerously close to reaching full capacity. It is understood the force's highest ranking commander in north-west London referred to his case in a letter raising concerns about the early releases. Det Ch Supt Luke Williams outlined the details of the "astonishing" case in correspondence to local politicians, which was later shared by Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp. Without naming Bogle, the letter, sent on Wednesday, said he had been identified as a high-risk offender by the probation service but was released on 1 October. "Just one day after his release" he was recorded on CCTV stealing, Williams said. 'Overcrowded' and 'set up to fail': Freed prisoners react to early release scheme Is there a way of stopping repeat shoplifting? How the new prison release scheme will work - and number of inmates to be freed Following reports from supermarket staff that the offending continued over the following days, neighbourhood officers "spent an entire day" locating the man and bringing him into custody, the letter said. Williams said: "While I am sure it is not surprising that someone with this history went onto reoffend, the speed with which he did so, and the impact on front-line policing, is astonishing." Borough commander Det Ch Supt Luke Williams said early releases put pressure on policing "The concerning nature of the Early Release Scheme in this case was a known prolific offender being put back into the community, only to immediately reoffend," Williams said. "Not only does this place communities at risk but puts demand straight back into policing who must arrest, investigate and put the individual into custody." He said this case required 27 officer hours to investigate at a cost of £1,887. Williams told the MPs and councillors that the Met "fully recognises that the government is dealing with significant pressures" in the prison system but that those pressures are being "transferred on to policing with no recognition". He said the case was "not just a localised issue", but one being seen by Met officers across the capital. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests, putting communities at untold risk. "We will never jeopardise public safety. That is why we are putting thousands more Neighbourhood Police officers on to our streets, upping police funding to £18.5bn and taking investment in the probation service to record levels." They added that offenders released early on licence faced the "toughest-ever controls", including exclusion zones and the expansion of electronic tagging. title: Thai Queen makes first solo flight in fighter jet
description: Thailand’s Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household.
body: This video can not be played Thailand's Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household. The Queen was shown boarding a Gripen on 8 October at an airfield in Surat Thani province, southern Thailand, while King Maha Vajiralongkorn watched from the ground. The Royal Household has said she is an experienced pilot, having logged about 1,188 hours across several types of aircraft since she began flying in 2010. She also co-piloted aircraft carrying the King on official visits to other countries, the Royal Household said. Thai Queen makes first solo flight in fighter jet. title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
description: Tsunami warnings are issued for neighbouring countries as videos of destruction circulate online.
body: A maternity ward in Panama City was among the buildings evacuated during the tremors A massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake has hit Panama, damaging buildings and prompting a wide-ranging tsunami warning for neighbouring countries. About 4.6 million people felt moderate to severe shaking as a result of the quake, according to the US Geological Survey, which has said that the effects of the disaster were "likely to be widespread". The quake, which hit just before 15:00 local time (18:00 GMT), could trigger tsunamis in Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile and Mexico, according to the US Tsunami Warning System. The epicentre of the earthquake was about 6.2 miles (10km) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in south-central Panama, with a series of shallow aftershocks following it. Footage shared online, which has not been verified by the BBC, appears to show collapsed buildings in the towns of Penonomé and Soná. The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface. However, the full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, nor whether there have been any casualties as a result. Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km (124 miles) away, according to new agency AFP. The earthquake comes just three days before Panama was scheduled to hold a national evacuation drill for dealing with a major earthquake. It also follows devastating earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela earlier this year. title: Watch: Can the Fort Hood shooter's execution be livestreamed?
description: Rules on the recording and filming of executions differ between state, federal and military regulations.
body: This video can not be played The US Department of Defense says they plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood military base in 2009. It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. But can the US military actually livestream an execution? Rules on the recording and filming of executions differ between state, federal and military regulations - as Aisha Sembhi explains. Can the Fort Hood shooter's execution be livestreamed? title: Four jailed for death of man tortured and set alight
description: Tomasz Samel was kidnapped and attacked over the loss of illicit cigarettes worth £1m.
body: Tomasz Samel was driven to the Liverpool area and attacked over the loss of illicit cigarettes worth £1m Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing Four men have been jailed for killing a member of an organised crime group who was tortured, doused in petrol and set alight. Father-of-two Tomasz Samel, 45, was kidnapped in March 2019 in Birmingham by three men claiming to be from Interpol, before being driven to the Liverpool area and attacked over the loss of illicit cigarettes worth £1m. Passing sentence at Birmingham Crown Court, Judge Mr Justice Wall said Samel "was vulnerable at the time he was set alight – he was naked and outnumbered". Neil Jones, 49, of no fixed address, and Tobiasz Kozlowski, 38, from Kirkby, Merseyside, were jailed for life after being convicted in August of murder and conspiracy to cause grievous bodily harm. The pair pleaded guilty to conspiracy to kidnap and conspiracy to falsely imprison before the trial began, while Jones had also admitted manslaughter. Kevin Wooden, 46, of Banbury, Oxfordshire, and Kye Arthur, 35, from Lockleaze, Bristol, who were found guilty of manslaughter after being cleared of murder and conspiracy to cause grievous bodily harm, were given 23 years and 22 years respectively. They had previously admitted conspiracy to kidnap and conspiracy to falsely imprison. Kozlowski's wife, Sandra Kozlowska, 38, also from Kirkby, was convicted of assisting an offender by helping him to avoid detection by police, hiding evidence and moving money. She received a three-year prison sentence, suspended for three years. Jones (left) and Kozlowski (right) were both jailed for life Samel's killing was linked to the seizure of illicit and counterfeit cigarettes which had been smuggled into the UK from Poland. HM Revenue and Customs seized the cigarettes from a unit he kept in Elkington Street, in the Aston area of Birmingham, during a raid in February 2019. During the sentencing Wall told the defendants they had all chosen to involve themselves in a "truly horrific series of events". He described Kozlowski and Jones as the "organisers" and said they had a "motive to punish" Samel due to the financial stake they had in the missing cigarettes. Samel, who was the subject of an international arrest warrant, was kidnapped from his home in Raleigh Road, Handsworth, on 27 March 2019. "I am sure that the two of you intended that Mr Samel would die," Wall added, telling the court he had been "stripped naked, and, while seated and defenceless, petrol was thrown over him and he was set alight". Arthur and Wooden were found guilty of manslaughter in August "He suffered extensive burns to most of his body," the judge added. After being set on fire he was dumped in a remote area of Lancashire, where he managed to walk to a house in the village of Bickerstaffe to ask for help. He was taken to Whiston Hospital in Prescot but died on 21 June 2019. Wooden and Arthur were paid to kidnap the man, along with a third person who has not yet been identified, Wall said, adding that it was impossible to say how Samel was treated before being set alight due to his burn injuries. He also stated Samel was in hospital for almost three months before he died and said: "The level of his suffering between the time at which the injuries were inflicted and his death is difficult to imagine." A police investigation saw inquiries carried out in Poland, Greece, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Colombia, France, Scotland and Wales, where the gang had operations or had fled to in the aftermath of the kidnap. The CPS said Wooden was arrested in the Dominican Republic under a false name and had to be extradited before the trial. title: 'People don't think recycling at work is part of their job description'
description: Unclear labelling as well as a lack of recycling facilities at work or in public-facing businesses is an issue.
body: Businesses in Wales are required to sort waste into the same recycling categories that households are expected to do There was still "lots of room for improvement" when it comes to how much we recycle at work compared with our habits at home, according to an expert. Figures suggest only 61% of people in Wales recycle often at their workplace, with one in five saying they do not recall seeing the appropriate facilities to do so. Providing more bins or clearer labelling are some of the ways in which businesses could make a difference, said waste reduction charity Wrap. But one business had already seen a "significant improvement" at their offices after removing staff's personal bins, a move that was initially met with resistance. When recruitment firm Acorn by Synergie first moved into their offices on the outskirts of Newport in 2003, they were producing six large wheelie bins' worth of rubbish a week. It now has just one weekly collection thanks to increased recycling, including food waste, which was their biggest adaptation, following the introduction of the Welsh government's Workplace Recycling Law in 2024. Mark Rudge says increased recycling costs are offset by less rubbish going to landfill collections "The main thing that we changed was removing desk bins and individual bins," said director Mark Rudge. "We had quite a bit of resistance to that. Individuals liked having their own little waster station. "But we put central recycling areas within each zone of the business, and eventually, people get the hang of that. "A lot of home recycling is extremely similar, so people brought those good habits to the workplace." Ann-Marie Derrick says she is now surprised when she goes to other offices who don't have separate recycling bins Office worker Ann-Marie Derrick admitted fellow staff members had found it a pain to begin with, but it had now become "second nature". "Anybody new coming to the office is just straight away onboard and I think we're probably quite proud as a team about how much recycling we do." The company's environmental manager Anthony Lee said it had taken a few months for staff to fully mirror their home recycling habits at the workplace, and that there had been a "significant improvement in compliance". Not all workers and business have adapted to the same degree. WRAP's annual tracker survey indicated that although 94% of people in Wales say they recycle at home, only 61% do so "very often at work" with that figure dropping to below half for students at college or university. Only 30% of respondents said they had seen lots of recycling facilities at their workplace, despite the new requirements, while 20% said they could not recall seeing any. Vale of Glamorgan Council's recycling facility was designed to deal with the anticipated increase in the volume of recycling "It's still a relatively new thing to have recycling bins when we're away from home," said Angela Spiteri, senior marketing manager at WRAP. "It's a very positive step in the right direction for Wales, but it's not perfect and there's a lot of things we can do to improve." She said there was a responsibility on businesses to ensure that was possible, "providing the right bins and facilities for people to make that easier". Angela says unclear signage from businesses can be a factor in making it more difficult for people recycle correctly "I don't recycle as much when I am out and about, I just bin it," admits Gerwyn Pugh, 56, from Barry. "It's routine [at home], but out and about every bin takes a bit more time to work out." James Jenkins, 30, said he often took rubbish home with him given the limited options where he works. "We only recycle cardboard because that's our only waste. "The more industrialised businesses need to do more, because they'll have more of an impact than smaller businesses." Natalie James, 47, said she recycled "probably about the same" at work and at home. "Because I work at a hospital we've got the recycling categories everywhere, so we have to." Although businesses in Wales are now required to sort their waste into six categories, collection arrangements can vary from area to area. In the Vale of Glamorgan, businesses use a mix of council and private services, and the local authority said the change has resulted in a "higher quality of recycling". Carys Stephens, the council's waste project officer, said there had been a "fantastic response from businesses." "There's obviously going to be some that are critical of the idea, and they're worried about extra costs and effort that goes into segregated recycling. "But we've been doing segregated recycling for a couple of years now, and most people just take it in their stride." A recycling centre in Barry deals with recycled household waste, as well as local businesses who pay for the council's collection service Although Wales' workplace recycling rates are "reasonably high", said consultant Rebecca Colley-Jones, "there's lots of room for improvement". "It is a new system, so there's always a period of settling down." She said that she was sure "we would see that 61% rise". "Often they can be tourism or hospitality businesses, so they're having to educate their customers what to do." Colley-Jones said individuals also needed to personally take more care. "Our home is our castle, we're responsible for the waste and people are under a little bit of pressure, perhaps from their neighbours to look like they're recycling. "Whereas you don't have that in the workplace. "When people come to work, they come to work, they don't necessarily thing recycling is part of their job description. She added: "It's trying to get people to understand that they also need to be buying into the culture of an organisation, and also the culture of Wales as a country. title: Swinney backs Flynn in ferry gas leak row and says 'nobody's perfect'
description: The first minister says he has confidence in his transport secretary, who denies being briefed about the ferry incident.
body: Stephen Flynn denied knowing about the leak on board the Glen Sannox at a meeting of the transport committee last month First Minister John Swinney has backed Stephen Flynn in the row over whether the transport secretary had been briefed about a gas leak on a CalMac ferry. Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme in an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Swinney said emails showed Flynn had not been briefed ahead of a Holyrood committee meeting last month. The first minister said he had confidence in his transport secretary, who "recognised that he should have been across an issue to be in front of the transport committee and he remedied that right away". Swinney added: "Nobody's perfect, nobody's infallible". Flynn was appearing before the transport committee on 9 September when he said he was not aware of a BBC Scotland News story published online more than nine hours earlier. It revealed how a faulty valve led to 700kg of flammable methane gas being vented from the side of the ferry MV Glen Sannox while it was carrying passengers from Arran to Troon in June 2025. Valve failure on CalMac ferry saw uncontrolled escape of flammable gas Speaking to the committee, Flynn said he had missed the report because he was facetiming his children before the meeting. But a briefing document released via a freedom of information (FOI) request and published by the Scottish Sun, external and The Times, external newspapers on Thursday evening showed Flynn's office was contacted about the story twice in the half hour before the committee meeting began. Flynn later appeared to be blindsided when committee members quizzed him about the story. As Swinney backed his cabinet secretary on Friday, Flynn responded to a media report that he had been told about gas leak, by insisting he had not been briefed. He wrote on X: "This is not true. I should've seen the BBC news that morning - but the FOI confirms I was not briefed. "Jeez, if I'd known, I'd have given a damn sight better answer than I did at the time! "An answer that wasn't acceptable and nobody was more frustrated than myself about that." Stephen Flynn commented on the story in a post on X Transport Scotland said the documents released this week "made clear" Flynn had "not been briefed on the issue" before his committee appearance, and the emails sent to his office had not been shared with him. This video can not be played Stephen Flynn appeared to have been blindsided by the story when he was questioned at a Holyrood committee The Sun report concentrated on emails, external sent by Flynn's office at 17:04 on 9 September, hours after his committee appearance, claiming they suggested an attempt to "cover-up" the minister's lack of preparedness. One email - now seen by BBC Scotland - says the attached statement had been "cleared by Mr Flynn". Quoting Flynn, it says: "I was not briefed on this incident, however details were shared with the former cabinet secretary for transport on 30 June 2025, in line with agreed processes." Reacting to the publication of that email, transport committee convener Willie Rennie told BBC Scotland Flynn was "only making things worse for himself". "What is alarming is that he seems to have attempted a cover-up, dragging in officials and Transport Scotland," he said. "And if he had bothered to listen to the news in the morning before the committee session he would not have been surprised by my questions about the leaking of flammable gas on the Glen Sannox." Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay demanded Flynn refer himself to the independent advisers on the ministerial code. "Stephen Flynn should have admitted that he had simply failed to do his job properly," he said. "But instead, this bombshell new evidence suggests that he conspired with officials to execute a sleekit, skin-saving cover-up." A Transport Scotland spokesperson said: "As the timestamp notes, a draft media statement was sent to Mr Flynn's office shortly before he arrived at the committee and this was not shared with him. "A high-level media statement does not constitute formal briefing, which the cabinet secretary received later. The previous cabinet secretary for transport [Fiona Hyslop] was briefed on the issue last year, at the time of the incident." A "ministerial engagement briefing" issued ahead of the transport committee's meeting on 9 September showed two emails sent to Flynn at 08:48 and 09:04. The meeting - which marked Flynn's first appearance before the committee since becoming transport secretary in May - was scheduled to get under way at 09:15. The initial email was sent to Flynn and Transport Scotland officials. It acknowledges Transport Scotland was "yet to be contacted for comment". However, it includes a suggested comment from policy officials "if the coverage prompts any questions at committee". A follow-up, sent 16 minutes later, includes a comment from CalMac and was sent to Flynn and Transport Scotland officials "for awareness". The transport secretary was questioned about the incident – which came to light after an FOI by BBC Scotland – by committee convener Rennie later that morning. He told Rennie he had not been given a briefing about the story, which was published that morning, though quickly clarified "unless I've missed it". He added: "I wasn't listening or watching the BBC this morning convener... I didn't see the news because I was facetiming my kids - but that is a different matter." Flynn said "it may have been the case" that the incident "may have been conveyed" to him as part of a wider tranche of documents he was given when he took over the role from predecessor Fiona Hyslop. He later clarified that Hyslop had been told about the leak. title: Hollywood actor Luke Evans on 'joyous' four months filming in rainy Wales
description: His family were on the set, and he even managed to get some relatives a cameo in the final episode.
body: Actor Luke Evans plays journalist Martin Gilmour in a new ITV drama Hollywood actor Luke Evans said filming just 25 minutes from his childhood home was "joyous" - and some family members even made a cameo in the final episode of his new drama. The Pontypool-born star, who is also an executive producer of the five-part series, The Party, came up with the idea to adapt the acclaimed novel by Elizabeth Day into a drama for the screen. For the first time in 30 years, Evans was able to film close to Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, where he grew up, as the drama was shot in Cardiff and Bridgend. The star of Beauty and the Beast, Immortals and The Hobbit had been used to being far from home while working on the stage and films. Evans stars alongside Tom Cullen who plays Ben Fitzmaurice, a wealthy and charismatic politician In The Party, Evans, 47, stars as Martin Gilmour, a journalist shaped by his lifelong friendship with a wealthy and charismatic politician played by Aberystwyth-born Tom Cullen. Speaking on BBC's The One Show, he said that he had "shot in Wales" previously - when filming The Pembrokeshire Murders - but "never that close" to his family. "Pembrokeshire is miles away from where my family are in the valleys," he said. "They were only 25 minutes from me up the road [this time]." He joked: "They were there all the time." His parents Yvonne and David Evans still live in the same "narrow" terrace house he grew up in IN Aberbargoed in the Rhymney Valley. He added: "We were having dinners on the weekend, walking the dog, enjoyed a rainy three, four months in Wales over the winter period. "It was joyous. I loved it." Some family members even managed to get a short cameo in the final episode of the upcoming drama. Evans said: "[My cousins] were like 'can we be in the show?' "They are, they're in it. My cousin and his wife and their kids are in the final episode." Evans wrote to Tim Curry three weeks before the end of his seven-month run in The Rocky Horror Show on Broadway After filming wrapped up, Evans headed back to New York where he starred as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the Broadway revival of The Rocky Horror Show. "I did the show for seven months and I was coming to the end of the run - I had such an incredible experience doing the show," he said. "It was just the most wonderful, inclusive, joyous two hours of my day. It was wonderful. The audience were just loving it." Evans said that actor Tim Curry had been a part of his "whole journey", and that he would have people on the stage door and messages "comparing me" to him, and "how proud he would be of the performance." Curry, who died in August, aged 80, first played the role on stage before the film version, which was released in 1975 and has remained a cult favourite. Evans added: "So I had to send him a letter, even if he'll never read it. "I just felt like I had to say thank you because I really believe that if it wasn't for Tim's performances as Frank-N-Furter, I don't think that film would still be around. "He really kept that show, and the messages throughout the show are so prevalent and strong and important today as they were 53 years ago." He received a response from Curry's team three weeks before his final performance, saying that he was "very appreciative" of that letter and thanked him for sending it. "Sadly he passed the day after I finished," Evans said. Luke Evans and his miniature dachshund Lala switched the lights on for the Empire State Building in celebration of NYC Pride Earlier this summer, Evans also got the honour of switching on the Empire State Building lights for pride in New York, in the US, adding: "It was a really special thing to be asked to do." Evans previously said that he knows "several actors" in Hollywood who have chosen not to be open about their sexuality. He came out as gay early in his career and admitted it "wasn't easy" being one of the few out stars for a long time. Speaking about actors who choose to not reveal their sexuality, Evans said you "never know what a person has gone through". Asked if he thought a gay actor would ever be cast as James Bond, Evans said he was "on the list for Bond for a good decade." He takes this as a sign that it would not be a problem but that he is "too old" for the part now. Evans began his career as a theatre actor and later appeared in films including Clash Of The Titans (2010) and the Fast & Furious franchise. He will play the lead role in the upcoming ITV drama The Party premiering on 11 October. title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
description: Several member states of the international tribunal, including the UK, say they "strongly disagree" with the sanctions.
body: The ICC said it would not be "deterred" by the sanctions The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". Marco Rubio said that "either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC" The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. title: US immigration officials defend ICE agents who shot man in same car as child
description: Oscar Belgal, the 28-year-old man, survived the shooting and is now being held at a detention facility outside of New York, officials said.
body: Footage from a NYPD officer's body cam shows the scene after Oscar Belgal was shot by ICE agents US immigration officials have defended the actions of officers who shot and wounded a man in his car in New York on Thursday while his five-year-old son was in the back seat. Markwayne Mullin, the head of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said officers fired their weapons while trying to arrest a man with a criminal history. "We weren't aware the child was in the car," Mullin added at a news conference on Friday, arguing that it was the man, Oscar Belgal, who had put his child in danger. Belgal is now being held at a detention facility. The legal organisation representing Belgal told the BBC that lawyers had not yet been able to speak to him. The shooting happened in the residential neighbourhood of Marble Hill. Marcos Charles, a top ICE official who was also at Friday's news conference, said agents used their vehicles to try and stop Belgal in his car but that he resisted orders to get out and instead accelerated, smashing into two ICE vehicles. Charles said Belgal then "weaponised his vehicle and proceeded to accelerate going towards other officers", adding: "Our officers, using their training, and believing that their life and the life of their partners in the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons." The number of officers who fired their weapons is being investigated. Charles said Belgal "was struck by one of the bullets or fragments superficially in the neck". New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called what happened "unconscionable and incredibly serious", said ICE agents surrounded Belgal's car before opening fire. "They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There is no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents," Mamdani said. He confirmed that the child was unharmed. Mullin said the officers identified themselves and were wearing body-worn cameras that were turned on during the incident. Video of the shooting, including body camera footage, has not been made public but unverified videos on social media appear to align with Mamdani's comments. Body-worn camera footage released by the New York Police Department (NYPD) on Friday shows its officers arriving on scene and attempting to help Belgal after he has been shot. One ICE officer appears to be wearing a neon construction vest and carrying a large gun. The NYPD officers then call for an ambulance and putting him in a police car to take him to hospital. They are later seen pulling Belgal from the vehicle and carrying him into the hospital. This video can not be played Watch: Outrage after person shot by ICE in New York Mamdani said on Thursday that he had spoken to US President Donald Trump and Mullin for two hours but failed to negotiate Belgal's release. Mamdani said he would ask Trump, who has not yet commented publicly on the shooting, to end ICE enforcement actions in New York. Mullin has said he will not pause enforcement. The DHS said Belgal, 28, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession". Belgal was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS. New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said there was also still a pending case against Belgal for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025. DHS has also alleged Belgal was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group. Mullin said the DHS believed Belgal "has either indirect or direct knowledge" of a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer shooting, "and that's why he became a target". Mamdani is not the only New York official to have criticised the incident. Governor Kathy Hochul said federal officials needed to provide answers quickly about what happened. "New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity," Hochul said, adding that she had spoken to Mullin and Trump as well. There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one that caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January. What is ICE and what powers do its agents have to use force? title: Police chief asks secretary of state to review Drumcree determination
description: It is the 13th day of deadlock between residents of the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and the local district lodge of the Orange Order.
body: Jon Boutcher has asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the Drumcree parade Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the Drumcree parade, BBC News NI understands. Boutcher triggered the move under the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998 earlier on Friday. It comes as First Minister Michelle O'Neill confirmed she has received a letter from police investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute. Portadown deputy District Master Alastair Power said there would be "serious consequences" if the Northern Ireland secretary intervened to stop the march. It is the 13th day of deadlock between residents of the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and the local district lodge of the Orange Order. The Parades Commission ruled that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place. But the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the Garvaghy Road. On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview. Unionist politicians have called for action to be taken against O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians who took part in the protests against the Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road at the end of last month. Under section nine of the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998, Boutcher can make an application asking Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant to reconsider the Parades' Commission determination. Neither the PSNI nor the Northern Ireland Office (NIO) has commented on the development. But BBC NI understands Bryant is now in the process of consulting with Boutcher and the commission. Sources state he has not yet reached any conclusion. Under the legislation, the minister has the power to revoke a determination, amend it, or stick by it. Michelle O'Neill confirmed in a statement on Friday she received the letter Meanwhile, in a statement issued by Sinn Féin on Friday afternoon, O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from the PSNI. "I can confirm I have received a letter inviting me for a police interview in relation to a peaceful protest on the Garvaghy Road. I will co-operate with the investigation," O'Neill said. "For the last two weeks, I have stood in solidarity with the Garvaghy Road residents as attempts were made to force an unwanted Orange march through their community," she said. "I will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation," she added. The police statement did not name anyone they planned to issue a letter to. Earlier, Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said the party would "cooperate" in every way it could but that they remained "comfortable" in standing up for Garvaghy Road residents. Sinn Féin MLA Deirdre Hargey also told the BBC that she had received a letter and would seek legal advice. Politicians, including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church to Garvaghy Road on 27 September When asked by reporters on Friday how he would react if Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant intervenes and stops the Portadown District's parade going ahead, Power said they would "obviously not be very happy". He said it would be the "first time the secretary of state has intervened on a lawful parade in over 30 years in overturning it". "We're law abiding citizens and we will have to abide by the law but there will have to be serious consequences from the unionist community on that," he said. The deputy first minister said it was "abolutely right" for the police to issue letters to those involved in the protests Earlier, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) told reporters she welcomed developments in the PSNI investigation, adding that the letters were "absolutely the right thing". "It doesn't matter whether you are an ordinary citizen or first minister of the country, you have to be subject equally under the law." Little-Pengelly also defended her attendance at the business engagement, after the DUP previously said it could not be "business as usual" at Stormont in response to Sinn Féin's involvement in protests on Garvaghy Road. She said she did not want to punish "the work we need to do in terms of growing our economy and investing in public services... just because of the deeply reckless behaviour of Michelle O'Neill and Sinn Féin". Speaking to The Nolan Show earlier, DUP leader Gavin Robinson said he expected "to see sanctions" for those investigated by the police. Carla Lockhart, Jamie Bryson and Alistair Power spoke to the media on Friday Loyalist activist Jamie Bryson held a press conference on Friday, alongside DUP MP Carla Lockhart. He said he had personal details published online on Thursday. "I have received over 1,500 abusive calls, over 280 voicemails, many with threats to kill, to murder me, my family, people around me, and things have just reached a level now where it's totally unacceptable," he said. Lockhart appealed to people to "step back" from making threats to her and Bryson. She said: "People can fight us on our politics and our policies, and they may not like what we say and I'll take anyone on with regards to my politics. "But when it gets personal and when you see and hear these threats online all it takes is for one person to just seriously think 'I really don't like those people' and I firmly believe it's getting to that point." title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
description: Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the tech firm admits customers may experience disruption to digital services due to the attacks.
body: Smoke billows from Yandex's Sasovo hub following a Ukrainian strike on Thursday Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days. Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres. Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex. Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended". Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service". Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online. It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task". The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure. The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems. Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households. Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack. Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity". Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion". Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages. Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad. Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence. But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022. title: Healthcare workers at 'tipping point' as union ballots for industrial action
description: Nipsa has been holding meetings with members working across the health service and said they had given a clear message over their frustrations.
body: Nipsa has been holding meetings with members working across the health service and said they had given a clear message over their frustrations The public services union, Nipsa, is to ballot healthcare members for industrial action over pay and conditions. Following a meeting between union leaders and Health Minister Robbie Butler, they said it was "clear that the time for talking is over", with Nipsa assistant secretary Kevin Kelly stating health workers had "reached a tipping point". The union has been demanding this year's pay award to be implemented immediately, alongside pay reform parity with other regions in the UK and the extension of the Real Living Wage to those in the care sector. The Department of Health said implementing the 2026-27 pay award and Real Living Wage would cost about £280m. Nipsa has been holding meetings with members working across the health service and said they had given a clear message over their frustrations. In its letter to healthcare members, Nipsa said workers should "not have to face increasing workloads, unsafe staffing levels, threat to jobs and continued cuts to vital services". The union said it was now progressing legal steps to hold the ballot, which will run from 21 October and close next month. "Our members are telling us they have had enough of being asked to do more with less while services are cut, staff go unrecognised and pay issues remain unresolved," Kelly said. He added that workers are still waiting for the 2026-27 pay award, with many low-paid staff waiting for the Real Living Wage. He said there remains ongoing frustration around pay reform parity. Union leaders have been demanding this year's pay award to be implemented immediately "At the same time, the Executive is expecting health and social care organisations to deliver cuts of more than 12% over the next three years. Our members have been crystal clear. Enough is enough," Kelly added. Last year's pay offer was also delayed, with the Department of Health making the offer in November in order to avoid threatened industrial action. At that stage, £200m was signed off for the pay deal. Health pay is a devolved matter in Northern Ireland. The Department of Health has said that it currently faces a deficit of between £800m to £1bn. This week, officials told Stormont's health committee that because the NI Executive had still not agreed a budget, they were continuing to base their financial plans on the multi-year budget paper issued in April. title: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
description: The left-wing candidate won a narrow victory in a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, exit polls show.
body: Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores was the candidate for left-wing Ahora Nación A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show. The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes. Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes. Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country. Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote. He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile. That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported. Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018. He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler". A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon. description: Dramatic footage shows huge tornado moving through Marsala and Petrosino, causing damage to buildings and cars.
body: This video can not be played Dramatic footage shows the moment a tornado ripped through the city of Marsala and nearby town Petrosino, in Sicily. The tornado injured two people and caused damage to buildings with the strong winds flipping cars according to local media. Thunderstorms moved across the island on Friday, and while conditions have eased across Sicily, more are forecast across parts of the central Mediterranean. title: Watch: 'I am Jane Doe' protests across US call for end to sexual violence
description: Protests against sexual violence took place across more than 40 US states on 8 October.
body: This video can not be played Protests were held across the US on 8 October, calling for an end to sexual violence, following allegations of sexual assault involving members of a fraternity at Cornell University. Survivors, students and advocates rallied and protested in communities and on college campuses across more than 40 states. This comes after a lawsuit was filed against by “Jane Doe”, who alleges she was given drugs and alcohol before being sexually assaulted by several members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity while incapacitated in October 2024. She has accused Cornell University of failing to adequately investigate and discipline those involved. Following the filing of the civil lawsuit, prosecutors reopened the case. New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed the state’s attorney general as special prosecutor. Watch: 'I am Jane Doe' protests across US call for end to sexual violence. title: Pair bailed after security breach at RAF base
description: Police say the two Latvian nationals have been bailed with "strict conditions".
body: A breach of a perimeter fence was identified at the base near Huntingdon Two Latvian men arrested after a fence was breached at a Cambridgeshire RAF base have been bailed. Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrols at RAF Molesworth, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations, identified an abandoned vehicle at about 22:00 BST on Wednesday. The pair, aged 36 and 32 and who live in the UK, were subsequently arrested inside the perimeter a few hours after searches found a small breach of the fence at the site. Both were taken to a Cambridgeshire police station and have since been bailed with "strict conditions", the Metropolitan Police said. The force's Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating. Its head Cdr Helen Flanagan said: "We're very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but there is nothing from our investigation so far to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week." Both men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage - after Cambridgeshire Police officers joined the search - and were taken to a local station. They were later arrested on suspicion of namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK under Section 4 of the National Security Act. The base is home to a Nato intelligence hub The Met said officers carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area and that the abandoned vehicle was also recovered by officers. "A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity," Flanagan said. "Meanwhile, I would encourage the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police." RAF Molesworth is located west of Huntingdon, close to the border with Northamptonshire. It is home to the US's intelligence operations centres for Europe and Africa, as well as a Nato intelligence hub. It is not used as a flying station. title: Watch: 'This has never happened before!' Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes
description: Olivia Colman stars alongside Alexander Skarsgård in the upcoming film Wicker which has prompted many memes.
body: This video can not be played New fantasy rom-com Wicker, starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård, has sparked a flood of viral memes and tongue-in-cheek jokes on social media ahead of its cinema release. The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman living in a medieval village who hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker. Speaking to the BBC at the film's BFI London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman admitted she was taken aback by the online frenzy surrounding the film. "No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said. "But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking." 'This has never happened before!' title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
description: The camera-maker says it is now re-evaluating the rules and procedures of its Small World in Motion contest.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The competition's former winner and runners up. Nikon disqualified the winning video (shown left). The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake. Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes. The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions. It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images. Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel". The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD. The BBC has approached him for comment. A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real. Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation. University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated". "I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said. Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients". "This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said. In a statement announcing the award, the Nobel Committee praised Pillay's "efforts to promote peace and international law". BBC correspondent Joe Inwood explains how Pillay's childhood in South Africa led her to become a driving force in international law and human rights, from Rwanda to Gaza. Read more about this story. title: Bank cashier outed by holiday photos after stealing £13k is ordered to pay back money
description: Kelly Kershaw stole from vulnerable customers to fund a safari in Africa and a trip to Paris.
body: Kelly Kershaw used the stolen cash to fund several expensive holidays A building society cashier who stole thousands of pounds from customers to pay for "lavish" holidays has been ordered to repay more than £12,000. Kelly Kershaw, 54, stole £13,333 including from vulnerable and elderly customers at Nationwide in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, even forging the signature of a man with learning disabilities. Kershaw admitted five counts of fraud after colleagues spotted Facebook posts of her on safari in Africa, and on trips to Paris, Tuscany and Dubai. She was jailed for 16 months in May but returned to Caernarfon Crown Court for a Proceeds of Crime Act, external hearing, and told to pay back £12,630. Judge Jones ordered Kershaw to repay the sum within three months or face a further five months in prison. The mother-of-two posted pictures of skiing trips, safaris and romantic European getaways on her Facebook page and boasted she was "living and loving life one adventure at a time." Kershaw's victims included an 85-year-old man who had lost some "cognitive abilities" after suffering a stroke - and she stole £6,300 from him. On one occasion, he came to the branch asking to withdraw £200, but Kershaw logged the withdrawal as £500 and pocketed £300 herself. Another victim was a 49-year-old man with learning difficulties who lost £1,400 to Kershaw - he had his bank card kept in the branch as he was a previous victim of fraud. Kelly Kershaw's offending lasted for more than a year and she was caught after posting lavish holiday photos on Facebook During the May hearing, prosecutor Elen Owen said Kershaw had been transferred to work at the branch in June 2020, which had a "high number of vulnerable customers." "After a while co-workers noticed the defendant appeared to have a lavish lifestyle," she said. "She was regularly going on expensive foreign holidays and there were other indications of extravagant spending." Owen said "due to the suspicions raised" an internal investigation had been launched by Nationwide and had identified five victims. She said Kershaw, who also would drive a personalised BMW convertible, would process cash withdrawals from accounts but would pocket either some or all the money for herself. Kershaw admitted five counts of fraud while working for Nationwide Building Society Owen said Kershaw was interviewed by a financial investigator in November 2024 and admitted what she had done and had been arrested by police. Kershaw admitted five counts of fraud. Defence barrister Amy Edwards said Kershaw was suffering from a "compulsive spending addiction" at the time. "She gave a full and frank admission to the offence and showed remorse to each of her victims. That is genuine remorse and regret for what she did," said Edwards. Judge Petts said Kershaw needed to be jailed as a "deterrent" to other cashiers so as to "prevent others from doing the same". He told her: "Your pattern of offending was repeated. You forged people's signatures or you would take their card to withdraw a large sum from the account and only hand over part of it. "You were asked why you targeted those people in particular, you said they were 'easy targets who wouldn't notice the money going from their accounts. "The reality is you only stopped stealing money because suspicions were raised about your lifestyle, investigations took place and your fraud was discovered." title: Dad and son remain critical after masked men attack
description: Leicestershire Police say the attack at the family home appeared "completely unprovoked".
body: Officers were called to reports of a disturbance in Thurnby on Thursday A father and son are in hospital in a life-threatening condition after an attack in their family home which appeared "completely unprovoked", police have said. Officers were called to reports of a disturbance at a house in Station Road, Thurnby, shortly before 00:30 BST on Thursday. Leicestershire Police said a man in his 50s was stabbed multiple times, while a boy, 15, was also stabbed by two masked men who entered the property. The force gave an update on Friday to say both remained critical in hospital. Officers added that the man's wife - who is in her 40s - suffered minor injuries to her hand and shoulder during the attack. Three other children who were in the address were not injured. In the interest of public and police safety, police said armed officers were deployed but the men had left the house prior to them arriving. The force added an investigation, led by the East Midlands Special Operations Unit (EMSOU), to understand the circumstances and motive would continue over the weekend. Police have urged the public to come forward with any information about the attack Police said it would remain in the area as officers undertook searches for anything that may help them to understand and identify those responsible. Det Insp Lorna Granville said: "This was a violent attack against a family in their own home which appears to have been completely unprovoked. "Our investigation to understand what happened and why - and identify those behind such a horrific criminal act - is going to continue over the weekend. "I'm making a direct appeal to people in Thurnby and the surrounding communities to come forward with any information if they haven't already done so. "We owe it to the victims to locate the perpetrators and bring them to justice." One of the forensic officers at the scene on Thursday Granville added: "I'd like to speak to anyone who may have seen or heard anything suspicious, unusual or untoward in the area of Station Road and Somerby Road between 23:00 on Wednesday and the early hours of yesterday morning. "This includes anyone who was driving in the area and captured anything on a dashcam or anyone with CCTV or doorbell footage. "Anything you're able to provide, no matter how insignificant you think it might be, could help us." The force said it had set up a major incident public portal for the public to submit information. title: Verstappen on sprint pole after another settings issue
description: Red Bull's Max Verstappen beats Mercedes driver George Russell to sprint pole at the Singapore Grand Prix.
body: Max Verstappen is yet to win a race in Singapore Red Bull's Max Verstappen beat Mercedes driver George Russell to sprint pole at the Singapore Grand Prix. Verstappen, fresh from his and Red Bull's first victory of the season in Malaysia last weekend, was 0.12 seconds quicker than the Briton, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc third. McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were fourth and fifth ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who went early in final qualifying and fell down the order from initially being second behind Leclerc. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, using the Mercedes upgrade that underperformed in Malaysia while Russell is on the previous specification, could manage only seventh. And there were further glitches with the engine settings provided by governing body the FIA five days after the formation laps in the wet in Malaysia saw cars reduced to crawling speed as a result of a software bug. Mercedes critics think I'm Satan - Wolff The settings issue in Singapore, which was combined with a glitch in the F1 timing system that delayed the start of second qualifying, affected all cars but had a bigger impact on some drivers than others, depending on the timing of their runs. Williams driver Carlos Sainz, who was knocked out in the first session, said: "We were on the bad end of it, and for whatever reason, the FIA, like in Malaysia, again didn't decide to do sporting equity and were happy to do half of the quali with cars with higher power than the other half of the cars. "A bit confused why the sport keeps doing different things depending on who is out in Q1 or who is out in lap one." Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad was also affected and was knocked out in the first session. The problem involved the settings being different before and after a red flag caused by a crash for Sergio Perez's Cadillac and left drivers complaining of reduced power. It involved overtake mode - which allows an extra 0.5MJ of energy to be harvested - being switched on and off again in the space of 28 seconds. The FIA said in a statement: "During the first period of sprint qualifying there was a human error in race control unrelated to the timing issue also encountered in SQ1. "This issue in question meant overtake mode was not available after the red flag period during SQ1. "When it became apparent that overtake mode was not active after the restart, it was then activated for a period of 27 seconds before being deactivated again. "The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap. "The second and third periods of sprint qualifying were not affected." The FIA system automatically disables overtake mode when there is a red flag. A pop-up then appears on the screen asking whether officials want to re-enable it. This was ignored, then overtake mode was reactivated before being disabled again, on the basis that it was fairer to do so than leave it enabled. Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app Verstappen's pole lap appeared to be further confirmation of Red Bull's resurgence after his dominant win in Malaysia but he faces an investigation for overtaking under yellow flags shown before the first session was stopped for the Perez incident. The four-time champion said he had not believed pole was possible before qualifying. "We have some difficulties with the car in ride, as we know," he said, "but at least when we went to the soft tyres (in the final session), it made the car a bit more stable in places where before you were a bit unsure. "I did not expect this but you take it, I'm happy for sure. Qualifying tomorrow is still the main goal and for us the start is always a critical point but at least a positive end to our day." Russell's performance compared with that of Antonelli raises further doubts about the efficacy of the Mercedes upgrade introduced in Malaysia. It was their biggest car update since the Canadian Grand Prix in May but team boss Toto Wolff said at Sepang that it had appeared to take them backwards rather than forwards. Mercedes split the car spec here in Singapore in an attempt to better understand its performance but Antonelli ended the session 0.573secs behind Russell. The Briton said: "As a team there is still nothing telling us it isn't working but it's all driven by the stopwatch and, yeah, the stopwatch hasn't been great for the upgrade yet. Maybe tomorrow's a different day." Antonelli, who leads the championship by 84 points going into the weekend, said: "Already FP1 I was struggling and there is still a lot to understand about this package. Really the car is very difficult, very unpredictable, very difficult to put a lap together. It's a shame. I was coming with high hopes but so far it has been very difficult. "It's going to be a difficult weekend unless we can pull something out tomorrow. Other than that it is going very tricky. I don't really see where we can find 0.7secs but you never know." Wolff said before sprint qualifying: "The new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive. Not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it. The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point." Leclerc was 0.243secs off pole, and ruing what he said was Ferrari "losing a little bit of our raw performance" in the past three or four races. However, he added: "Still I feel there is potential in the car and maybe tomorrow we can be there or thereabouts in fighting for pole." Hamilton said: "We did a slightly different run plan to the others. It was my choice, but I think we got that wrong. But ultimately, the car was very oversteery on that lap. title: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership
description: Deputy party leader Daisy Cooper says "the vast majority of our MPs support Ed... and are furious at this distraction."
body: Sir Ed Davey and Charlie Maynard on the campaign trail in 2024 Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader. As first reported by the Financial Times, external, the Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday. Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is what they see as a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership, of which Maynard is one. Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader of the party, said: "The vast majority of our MPs support Ed, want him to lead the party into the next election, and are furious at this distraction." The BBC has approached Maynard for comment. Maynard was first elected to his Oxfordshire constituency in 2024, winning the traditionally Conservative seat, formerly held by David Cameron, with a majority of more than 4,000. Before becoming an MP, he ran an international mergers and acquisitions advisory firm. He is the second Lib Dem to leave the frontbench this week, following Alison Bennett's decision to resign her post of spokesperson for care and carers. Bennett would not confirmed why she stepped down but it is understood it was not for personal reasons. Under Liberal Democrat rules, a leadership contest can be triggered if a vote of no confidence in the leader is passed by the majority of all the party's MPs. To enter a leadership contest, a Lib Dem MP must have nominations from at least 10% of the parliamentary party, not including the candidate themselves, and have the backing of 200 members across at least 20 local parties. Sir Ed has been leader for six years and in the 2024 general election led the party to its biggest election success, winning 72 seats. However, the party has found it difficult to build on that success, with polling numbers remaining at relatively low levels. More recently, some Liberal Democrats have publicly attacked the leader for his stance on the triple lock - the mechanism which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% whichever is highest. Last week, Sir Ed criticised Andy Burnham's announcement that he would adjust the triple lock, arguing it would "put more pensioners into poverty". "This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he said. One Lib Dem MP described Sir Ed's argument as "nonsense", while another said: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind." Last month, Julian Brazil, the Liberal Democrat council leader of Devon, said the party was "sleepwalking into irrelevance" and questioned whether Sir Ed was the right leader. Speaking to the BBC, he said the Lib Dems were "lacking ambition" and had "allowed other parties to go steaming past us". title: Ex-Deutsche Bank trader jailed for rigging rates has conviction overturned
description: The Court of Appeal quashes the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader jailed in 2018.
body: Christian Bittar, left, and his wife Caroline Another former banker sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis has had his conviction overturned following a long-running legal battle. The Court of Appeal has quashed the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who went to prison in 2018 for "manipulating" the benchmark interest rate, Euribor. It comes after the same UK court overturned five convictions of ex-Barclays bankers in the rate rigging trials earlier this week. Bittar, who watched proceedings via video link from Switzerland because he was not granted a visa to attend court, told the BBC: "I have waited a very, very long time for this day." The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries. There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts. The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties. Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York. Eighteen of these have now been acquitted. Only one former trader in the world now remains convicted: former Barclays trader Peter Johnson, who was also one of the original whistleblowers in the interest rate rigging scandal. He pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance at winning at trial. The court confirmed that he too has now applied to appeal against his conviction. The news has already prompted lawyers and senior politicians to press for the Bank of England and the Treasury to release all their records about their own roles in interest rate 'rigging' during the financial crisis, amid concerns raised of a cover-up of the role of central banks and governments. Speaking after his conviction was quashed, Bittar said: "Finally the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised. "I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it." His wife, Caroline, who lives in the UK, said their family had lost 15 "valuable years", with their children "growing up with this injustice". She added they were looking forward to "enjoying life with our family and friends without this shadow hanging over us". On Wednesday, Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham and Philippe Mouryoussef saw their convictions for 'manipulating' the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor quashed after a 10-year struggle for justice. They launched fresh appeals against their jail sentences following a Supreme Court ruling last year that acquitted Tom Hayes, the first to be jailed for 'rigging' interest rates in 2015, and Carlo Palombo, jailed in 2019. Tom Hayes, who was initially sentenced to 14 years, reduced on appeal to 11, is now seeking damages from his former employer UBS. The traders were among 37 City traders and brokers prosecuted for "manipulating" the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor, which track the cost of borrowing cash between the banks and have been used to set the interest rates on millions of mortgages and commercial loans. The BBC has uncovered evidence of a much larger, state-led 'rigging' of interest rates, under pressure from central banks and governments across the world. Evidence implicating Downing Street and the Bank of England was suppressed throughout the criminal trials. Former Conservative cabinet minister David Davis told the BBC the innocent traders had been the victims of a series of miscarriages of justice. He said the people exonerated this week and before were "the victims of a scapegoating exercise which arose as a result of the government's own misbehaviour in lowballing [falsely understating] Libor interest rates themselves, in order to try and rescue the economy after their own self-induced crash in the late 2000s". In 2015, during the first trial for interest rate 'rigging', of former UBS trader Hayes, Mr Justice Jeremy Cooke decided as a matter of law that any attempt to influence the rates could not be lawful, and that any rate influenced by commercial interest must automatically be false. Judges in the subsequent eight trials followed suit. However, in July 2025, the Supreme Court decided that all the judges had erred, misdirecting juries that it was wrong as a matter of law. Instead, whether the requests were right or wrong was properly a matter of fact for the jury to decide, not the judge. All convictions in the United States were overturned in 2022 after an appeal court ruled that there was insufficient evidence that the traders' requests had broken any rules or laws. title: Widdecombe suspect had 'particular hostility to Reform', court told
description: Kerry is charged with the murder of the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.
body: The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe had a "particular hostility to Reform", prosecutors alleged on Friday. They said Joshua Kerry, 28, "had an extreme left wing and/or anti-establishment mindset". The prosecution also told the Old Bailey Widdecombe's murder had a "terrorist connection" as it was "politically and ideologically motivated". Last week, Kerry, who had already been charged with Widdecombe's murder in July, was charged with a second offence of preparing terrorist acts. He is accused of "online reconnaissance" of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Nigel Farage's home in South London on 19 April 2025, and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed. Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb agreed to the prosecution request to join the two charges into one case. The prosecution argued they were "inextricably linked". Kerry appeared in court by video link from Belmarsh prison wearing a prison-issue grey sweatshirt. The judge set a date for a five-week trial on 8 June next year. The next hearing will be on 29 January. Nicholas Lumley KC, defending, told the court that Kerry was likely to contest all the charges against him.
