title: I've got my own questions on Man City case - Carrick
description: Manchester United boss Michael Carrick says he was personally affected by the Manchester City case which has seen the club found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules and still has questions about the matter.
body: Michael Carrick was still on the pitch at Sunderland in 2012 as Sergio Aguero scored the injury time goal that won the Premier League title for Manchester City Manchester United boss Michael Carrick still has his "own questions" over the Manchester City case which he says "affected me personally". There is a clamour among some for Manchester City to be stripped of their silverware and also be relegated after they were found guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches. The 45-year-old was on the pitch at Sunderland when he learned City had won their first Premier League title in 2012 thanks to Sergio Aguero's legendary injury time match winner. He was still part of Jose Mourinho's squad when United finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City side in 2018 and was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching staff when it happened again in 2020-21. However, Carrick says getting a title winners' medal years after the event would not make up for missing out at the time. "In football, the strive to win, the emotion and the feeling about winning, a lot of it is in the moment," he said. "You can't take that back. It's the moment you strive for. That's essentially what we're all in it for. That's the feeling we all crave. "The beauty of trying to win trophies is a little bit the journey towards it and then the finale. Does it go for you, does it go against you? Once that's done, there's no getting that back in any direction. "I'm not getting blasé about it, but regardless of anything, in any sport in history, if later on you get the medal, it doesn't bring the feeling of when you initially win or you don't." An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. Manchester City have appealed against the decision. City boss Enzo Maresca has said he "trusts" his own club. If the appeal adheres to strict Premier League guidelines, it should be concluded by Christmas Day, with a verdict to follow in the early part of 2027. Carrick does not know how the situation will play out. However, as a very close bystander to the event, he feels there has to be a speedy resolution. "It's thrown up a lot of questions," he said. "Some had answers, some haven't. "Certainly, I've got my own questions about it. It's affected me personally in different ways over a period of time. "As it's still not finalised, I think I'll hold that one (whether titles should be reassigned) until later on. "What I will say is that the sooner it gets sorted, for everyone's benefit, is essential. "It's unprecedented, a unique situation to be in at this level, with such a huge impact in so many ways. We all need to know what's going to happen." Meanwhile, United's fans have delivered their own verdict by getting a 'ticker' banner showing the years since Manchester City last won a trophy rehung from the Stretford End. The banner was initially displayed in 2000, at which point it was 24 years since City's last silverware - the 1976 League Cup. It was increased by one each year until 2011 when City finally ended their trophy drought by beating Stoke City in the FA Cup final. However, fans have a new version to display for this weekend's visit of Tottenham to Old Trafford, with the number 50 - signalling the years since their 1976 League Cup triumph, their final silverware before Sheikh Mansour bought the club. Is £70m Baleba ready for his Man Utd exam? No change to Gabriel situation Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta, who spent time as assistant to Guardiola at Manchester City prior to taking charge of the Gunners, echoed Maresca's faith in his former club's leadership team. "[The] titles absolutely [are] not tainted. I trust the club now, in the future, always. I completely trust the club," Arteta said. "I will respect the process. It is still an ongoing process that is not resolved because it has been appealed." Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola and Chelsea's Xabi Alonso both stressed the need for patience following City's appeal. "I think uncertainty is not good for anyone and anyone involved, but the process is ongoing and we have to patient like everyone else and see what happens at the end," Iraola said. Alonso added: "We need to wait for the final sanctions from the panel. I think they are independent enough to assess all the situations. "We have to be patient for sure. It is out of our hands, we have to respect the independence of the panel and see what happens." Everton were deducted 10 points in November 2023 - in a punishment later reduced to six on appeal - and then docked two points in April 2024 in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR). "I wasn't here when it was difficult for Everton, when things were bad," said Toffees boss David Moyes. "Looking at it now from where I am sitting, it looks terrible that we have been docked points and pay some fines and not that long ago. "There's other things that have been going on - nearly 10 years ago - that have not been dealt with. I find that really difficult. "I hope it's not just Everton who are getting picked on here." Nottingham Forest were another club punished previously for breaching PSR rules, with the City Ground side docked four points in March 2024. "There is no final verdict right now. That's why I don't see any point to comment on Man City because I can't," said Forest boss Oliver Glasner. "But let's say in general, if somebody cheats he needs to get punished. If not, then not. And of course, we all hope for the integrity of the game, for the integrity of the Premier League, that the final word is spoken soon. "But we also know, I think there are thousands of pages to read. title: Woman found dead in burning van was pregnant, police say
description: A court is told Samantha Phythian, from Rhyl, was alive when the fire started.
body: The body of Samantha Natalie Phythian, 35, was discovered in the vehicle in Prestatyn A woman found dead in a burning van was pregnant, police have confirmed. The body of Samantha Natalie Phythian, 35, was discovered in the vehicle in Prestatyn, Denbighshire, on Sunday evening. On Friday it was revealed in a court hearing that Samantha, from Rhyl, was alive when the fire started. Thomas Bell, 38, from Wellington Road in Rhyl, appeared in Mold Crown Court charged with murder and was remanded in custody. The court was told Samantha was known to Bell but he denies setting the vehicle alight. Thomas Bell is remanded in custody following the hearing at Mold Crown Court Bell appeared via video link and spoke only to confirm his name. Judge Geraint Walters confirmed that Samantha died as a result of the fire. He said: "At the time of ignition the person was alive. Someone set the van alight and the person was alive and was killed as a result of the fire." Emergency services were called to reports of a vehicle fire at 23:30 BST on Sunday close to an industrial estate and retail park in the centre of the town. In a tribute issued on Friday, Samantha's family described her as a "much-loved mum, daughter, sister, auntie and friend". Known to everyone as Sammi, they said she would be "remembered for the special place she held in the hearts of everyone who knew and loved her". They said: "No family should ever have to endure the pain of losing a loved one in such circumstances. "She will forever be cherished by those who loved her, and she will be deeply missed." The van was discovered close to an industrial estate in Prestatyn Adjourning proceedings, Walters said Bell would appear before him again at Caernarfon Crown Court at the end of November for a plea and preparation hearing. A provisional date for a trial was set for the beginning of April 2027. title: Two Renoir paintings stolen from French museum are recovered
description: The two works were seized last month when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera.
body: The works, Jeune fille au puits and Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, were stolen last month Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said. The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years. The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief. Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement. The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe. The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886). The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled "These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally. The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference. The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks. Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters. Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August. France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris. Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours. They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses. The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security. title: Hurricane Isaias strengthens as it heads towards land
description: Isaias will bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge with landfall expected late Friday.
body: This video can not be played Isaias, the first hurricane in the Atlantic this hurricane season has been continuing to strengthen and is now a category three 'major' hurricane. Hurricane hunter aircraft have been flying in and around the storm on Friday morning, now measuring sustained wind speeds of 120mph (193km/h). Isaias is expected to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected late Friday. Hurricane and storm surge watches have been issued. It has been a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season so far with development suppressed by the growing El Niño pattern. Read more about Isaias and the El Niño weather event affecting the Atlantic hurricane season here. Hurricane Isaias strengthens as it heads towards land. title: Man who kept wife's body in freezer jailed for life
description: David Barraclough is jailed for at least 22 years for killing Carolann Barraclough.
body: David Barraclough changed his plea to guilty on the first day of trial A man who murdered his wife with a hammer and hid her body in a chest freezer while telling family and friends she was ill in hospital has been jailed for life. David Barraclough, 46, killed Carolann Barraclough, a mother of three, at the family's house in Horbury, near Wakefield, in February. Leeds Crown Court heard he then spent about two weeks trying to conceal what he had done, telling relatives and friends she was in hospital and sending messages from her phone pretending to be her. Barraclough pleaded guilty to murder on the first day of his trial and refused to attend court for sentencing. He was jailed for life with a minimum term of 22 years and one month. The court heard Carolann Barraclough was killed sometime between 19 and 21 February. After her death, Barraclough tied up her body and placed it in a freezer in the utility room of the home they shared. Carolann Barraclough was found dead at a property in Horbury on 5 March Prosecutors said he repeatedly lied to her children, family, friends and neighbours, claiming she was in hospital recovering from an illness and that only he was able to visit her. He also used her phone to send messages suggesting she would soon return home and prevented the children from entering the room where the freezer was kept. On 5 March, Barraclough walked into Normanton Police Station and told a receptionist: "I've killed my wife." Officers who went to the family home found Carolann Barraclough's body inside the freezer. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said evidence showed Barraclough continued with his daily life after the killing, including visiting pubs, withdrawing large sums of cash from a joint bank account and downloading the dating app Tinder two days after his wife's death. He later claimed he had acted in self-defence after being struck with a hammer and described himself as "heartbroken", "in a haze" and "confused". However, prosecutors said CCTV footage showed no visible injuries and rejected his account. Jill May, senior crown prosecutor for CPS Yorkshire and Humberside, said: "After brutally murdering Carolann, Barraclough hid her body in the home she shared with her children and lied repeatedly to her friends and family as he spun a calculated web of lies, pretending she was alive and recovering from illness in hospital." She praised Carolann Barraclough's eldest daughter for her "incredible bravery" in providing evidence. title: What reception awaits Man City at Anfield?
description: Bus welcomes, banners and flags expected as Man City head to Liverpool on Sunday for their first game since they were found guilty of breaching Premier League rules.
body: Pep Guardiola won six Premier League titles during his time at Manchester City It was December 2024 when Pep Guardiola's Manchester City side were 2-0 down at Liverpool and the Anfield crowd chanted "you're getting sacked in the morning" towards the opposition boss. No-one truly believed he was going to be given his marching orders but his side were on their way to a remarkable fourth consecutive Premier League defeat. Guardiola could not help but lift six fingers up to the Liverpool crowd in response - representing the six Premier League titles he won with City. Now, some may question each of those successes after an independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 financial charges the Premier League brought against them. On Friday, current City boss Enzo Maresca said the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted. But come Sunday, he and his players will face up to their new normal. Such is the script that a trip to what promises to be a ferocious Anfield - a place Guardiola always described as difficult - is next. City have won five out of five in the Premier League this term and it would be huge if Maresca can maintain that 100 % start. But for Andoni Iraola and Liverpool, this will be an opportunity to truly kickstart their own campaign, fuelled by a backstory like no other. "It's an exciting game," said the Reds boss. "We are playing at home at Anfield against City that is top of the league, they have won all of their games. "We will go for the game, they will go for it and it will be quite an open game and we have to be ready. I hope we will be at the level of the game, which will be high." Asked if it was the kind of fixture he relished when taking the Liverpool job, Iraola added: "Yes, we are here to play this game. We know it's going to be challenging. They are very good but we also are very good." It will be the first time since 2015 this clash will have neither Jurgen Klopp or Guardiola on the touchline, but nevertheless, a hostile atmosphere awaits and Tom Werner, the Liverpool chairman, will be in attendance. Liverpool finished second in the Premier League to Man City in 2013-14 under Brendan Rodgers and again in 2018-19 and 2021-22 when Klopp's side put up 97 and 92 points respectively, but were one shy of Guardiola's City as they were pipped to the title. A verdict on City's appeal awaits. City insist they are innocent but there will be sections of the Liverpool fanbase and former players and staff that feel aggrieved. "You think about the memories and the successes that you were wrongly denied," John Achterberg, who was Liverpool's goalkeeping coach under Rodgers and Klopp, told The Athletic., external "We won one Premier League title [in 2019-20], but it could have been four given that we missed out to City three times by such narrow margins." Iraola added: "The worst thing probably is the uncertainty. No-one knows what's going to happen. We have to focus on Liverpool and being the best club we can be, the best team we can be. That's my challenge." Man City titles 'absolutely not' tainted - Maresca Maresca will be demanding a siege mentality from Man City - Pulis Liverpool may have a historic rivalry with the red half of Manchester, but since City were taken over by Abu Dhabi in 2008, matches between the two have consistently delivered on the field and there's been off-field action too. In 2018, the Reds were fined 20,000 euros (£17,500) by Uefa after supporters threw missiles at the City bus before the Champions League quarter-final first-leg at Anfield. Liverpool went on to score three goals in 19 first-half minutes and knocked City out. Earlier that season in January, it was Klopp's men who ended City's unbeaten league start with a thrilling 4-3 win at Anfield. "There's something about it that you will find in no other stadium in the world. They score a goal and over the next five minutes you feel that you'll receive another four. You feel small and the rival players seem to be all over," Guardiola said in 2019. Merseyside Police say an appropriate policing plan will be in place for Sunday but chose not to delve into specifics when asked by BBC Sport. There is a growing expectation the team buses will be welcomed when they arrive and posters on social media have advertised a 'Bus Greeting' on Anfield Road. It remains unclear whether a separate bus route could be taken, but that has happened previously at Anfield. Inside the ground, Liverpool are renowned for their collection of banners and flags and plenty are planned. It will be worth keeping an eye on the pre-match playlist, too. One social media post suggested fans could bring stacks of fake money. In terms of preparations, Liverpool's stance is "business as usual" and any talks with the police and around safety concerns are regular meetings that would happen before every game. The fact of the matter is, however, this is likely to be an occasion and game like no other. Latest Liverpool news, analysis and fan views Ask about Liverpool - what do you want to know? title: Ofsted faces fresh calls to halt graded school inspections in England
description: A second head teachers' union says it is "increasingly concerned" about members' "welfare and morale".
body: A second head teachers' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections in England, saying it is "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale" of its members. The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) also raised the prospect of potential strike action, saying a new grading system had become an "overbearing mess". On Friday, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said an independent survey of education providers showed it was "on the right track" with inspections. The Department for Education (DfE) said ministers were "working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better". ASCL's announcement comes after another union, the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), said changes Ofsted made to inspections just under a year ago had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare. ASCL said it had passed a motion of no confidence in "the ability of Ofsted's leadership to address the damage being done by the new inspection system", adding that it was "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members". Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary, said the union did not take the step "lightly", but added Ofsted's "warm words about recognising wellbeing pressures... have not been matched by the action necessary" and that "negotiation [had] hit a brick wall". "The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed," he said. Why the shake-up of school inspections risks causing new problems What is Ofsted and how does the new school ratings system work? ASCL called on the government to pause inspections and review the system, and said it would survey members on whether to hold an informal ballot on industrial action if there was no change. In response, Ofsted said it had "worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge". "We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do," a spokesperson added. England's schools inspectorate introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate". An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023. That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade. An example of a new Ofsted inspection report Last month, the NAHT said testimonies from its members, seen by the BBC, suggested some school leaders had faced "intolerable" pressure because of the new inspections, leaving them "overwhelmed" and "anxious". It warned the system could pose a "risk to life" if changes were not forthcoming. An independent report, commissioned by Ofsted to evaluate its new framework, concluded this week that leaders were "generally positive" about their inspection experience, and that it was "more collaborative and accounts for context better than previous inspections". But it also said nearly half (48%) of school leaders who responded to its survey said their staff's mental wellbeing had been negatively affected "a fair amount" or "a lot" by a recent inspection. The interim report was based on focus groups and nearly 700 responses from school, college and early years leaders who were invited to complete a survey following inspections this year. A full report is due to be published next year. Sir Martyn said: "The data published today shows that we are on the right track. "I know that workload and wellbeing in education continue to be challenging, and I don't take that lightly. "We will keep listening to feedback from professionals and parents alike as we continue to improve what we do." The DfE said "inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face". title: Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
description: Pillay is recognised for her "efforts to promote peace and international law", the Norwegian Nobel Committee says.
body: Pillay was told of the award in Nuremberg's Palace of Justice Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said. Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza. Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes. "Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said. "At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity." This video can not be played Watch: Moment Navi Pillay named Nobel Peace Prize winner Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'". Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her. "If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom". Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban. She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court. Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president. From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law. The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements. The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies". The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes. Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice". It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes." This video can not be played 'It must be a joke': Moment Navi Pillay learns of Nobel Peace Prize win Frydnes said the Nobel organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide. Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people. Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated". UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity". South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally". Amnesty International Secretary-General Agnès Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award. "At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said. title: Teenager, 15, denies 22 sexual offences
description: The 15-year-old is due to stand trial at Northampton Crown Court in October 2027.
body: The boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, appeared at Northampton Crown Court on Friday A 15-year-old boy has pleaded not guilty to 22 sexual offences, including rape, against eight girls. The teenager, who cannot be named because of his age, was charged with one count of rape, rape of a child under 13 and assault by penetration at Northampton Crown Court on Friday. The offences are alleged to have taken place between 2023 and 2025, with the victims aged between 10 and 15. His trial is due to begin at the same court on 25 October 2027 and is expected to last three to four weeks. He is also charged with 12 counts of sexual assault and three counts of sexually assaulting a child under 13. He also faces two charges of making an indecent image of a child, one count of possession of a prohibited image of a child, and one of possession of an extreme pornographic image. The court heard that some of the sexual assault allegations relate to the defendant touching the girls over and under clothing, including slapping one of them on the bottom. One of the indecent image charges related to the alleged possession of three category C images of children. During the hearing, the defendant sat at the back of the courtroom with his mother and responded to the charges from his seat, rather than in the dock. The boy was granted conditional bail and must not contact the alleged victims or witnesses, must not be alone with girls under 16 without supervision, and must work with the Youth Justice Service. title: 'Good value in pub' - ex-NFL star Kelce tries rugby
description: Former Philadelphia Eagles Super Bowl winner Jason Kelce stuns amateur London rugby players by showing up for a practice game.
body: Former Super Bowl winners Jason Kelce (second left) and Beau Allen played a 30-minute match for London amateurs Old Streetonians against Hackney RFC Amateur rugby union players from Hackney had a shock when they turned up for a training match - to see a former Super Bowl champion among the opposition. Hackney RFC's players rocked up on Wednesday for a 30-minute friendly, only to find former NFL star Jason Kelce playing for local rivals Old Streetonians. Kelce - older brother of Travis, the three-time Super Bowl winning Kansas City Chiefs tight end married to global pop superstar Taylor Swift - played 13 seasons with the Philadelphia Eagles. The 38-year-old is now learning to play different sports for his YouTube channel, and had a rugby lesson from former Harlequins and England prop Joe Marler. "It's a nice little story being able to say we played rugby against Taylor Swift's brother-in-law, which I'm sure he loves as a title," Hackney full-back Peter Scott joked to BBC Sport. "It's amazing that the sporting community, not even just the rugby community, can make these sorts of things happen. It was pretty surreal and it's pretty cool." Kelce was part of Philadelphia's 2018 Super Bowl winning side and earned seven selections to the Pro Bowl - the annual NFL game featuring the league's top players - before retiring in 2024. He was joined by former Philadelphia team-mate Beau Allen, also a member of that Eagles championship side of eight years ago, at Hackney Marshes in London this week. Eagles stun Patriots in Super Bowl LII Get American Football news sent straight to your phone Hackney prop Dave Lewis told BBC Sport it took Kelce - a former center, an offensive lineman, whose main role is to snap the ball to the quarterback and then protect him, each play - a while to get used to rugby's rules. "We got a message from our club captain saying our local rivals were coming down with two ex-NFL players, but we didn't know anything else about it," Lewis said. "With the rules, he got there. At the very start, he sort of went round the back of a ruck and picked the ball up, which he obviously was then penalised for. "I handed him off at one point and put him on his back in front of his team-mates and all of our fans as well. I hope they release that footage because I'll be dining out on it forever if they do. "He just got back up and absolutely smashed me later on when he had the ball, running through me. So, I don't think he has an ego. I think he's just up for the physicality of it all." Lewis' team-mate Scott said he thought Kelce picked the game up pretty quickly. "He's a pretty intimidating figure," Scott added. "Very broad shoulders, powerful legs. They were using him as a number 8, which, I think, is the perfect position for him. "There were a few intricacies, like how he was carrying the ball and where he was in the scrum, but he clearly knew what he was. He didn't look out of place at all. "In rugby you are taught to tackle at an angle, and go at people's shoulders. He was a lot more front on, like 'OK, route one, I'm just gonna go straight at anyone that came out'." Jason Kelce and Beau Allen joined the Old Street team for a post-game social too Kelce is in England this week to commentate on Sunday's NFL overseas game between his former club Philadelphia and the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (14:30 BST). Old Street chairman Will Gilgrass said both Kelce and Allen really embraced the whole opportunity. "They were very good value in the pub afterwards," he said. "We took them to one of our locals, and they put their cards behind the bar, chatting with the lads for a few hours after the game and really getting involved. "They even did our initiation, singing a song and downing a pint." The Hackney players also had their 15 minutes of fame after the match, with Kelce's American film crew interviewing some of them. "They were asking how he got on, and what were the major differences to translate to an NFL audience," said Scott. "The one I picked up on was the amount of power that he was able to generate after he would get tackled. His leg drives were sensational. It felt like three people would hit him and then he would go for another 20 metres. "American football seems to be all about short, sharp, explosive power and he had that in spades - like he was rapid, very powerful, and then would take a backseat for a little while and then come back and do it again." title: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border
description: Truckloads of Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving into Ethiopia, which has reportedly responded with drone strikes.
body: Ethiopian forces took control of Tigray's main city Mekelle from rebel forces last week Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country. In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray. Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour. Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago. Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies. During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week. Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray. Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war. US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight. One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed. Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported. Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity." But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory. On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms". In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition". Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power. This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September. Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control. title: Mercedes critics think I'm Satan - Wolff
description: Mercedes Formula 1 boss Toto Wolff rejects accusations of team of bias against George Russell, calling critics "brainless".
body: Toto Wolff has been Mercedes' boss for more than 13 years Mercedes Formula 1 boss Toto Wolff says critics who accuse the team of bias against George Russell are "brainless". The British driver's championship hopes were all but extinguished by an engine failure while he was running third at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last Sunday. Russell enters this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix 86 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli, and will start from the back because of a grid penalty for using too many engine parts. Wolff described accusations of favouritism towards Antonelli as "completely nonsensical". He added: "We've had it in the past with Lewis (Hamilton) fans. "I mean, literally, I don't know what's going on. Do they think I have a button that says, 'George engine failure now', or disadvantaging one driver against the other when we are fighting for a Constructors' Championship, when we have always had the mindset of providing everybody equal material? "But I guess this is maybe where social media goes today. People hide behind their screens and then they lash out. "There's a lot of polarisation going on, and sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. I'm Satan, I've heard." Wolff emphasised that he had always pursued a policy of equality between drivers since he took over the leadership of Mercedes in 2013. He underlined his close personal relationship with Russell and Antonelli, who are both long-time proteges of the team and Wolff personally. "We have had Kimi since he was 11," Wolff said. "He is an integral part of the team. "It is very nice to see him grow, be in a position now that he is fighting for a championship at such a young age, the talent he has. "And then on the other side, George, who has been with us since he was 17, someone that I feel a lot of, how can I say, emotions for and compassion. We are very close." He said he and his wife Susie socialise with Russell and his fiancee Carmen Montero Mundt. "We are spending time with Carmen and Susie off the track with each other," he said. "If people would see that we're travelling together, we're having coffee in the same coffee shop, we're going to the gym. "That's why it's pretty annoying to have some lunatics that have no understanding really about how relationships work coming up with these kinds of accusations. "So, I don't pay any attention to this. Most important is that George knows how the team is and Kimi knows, and we will always try to give them equal opportunity." He said a "good example" of the equal treatment of both drivers was this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix. The team has decided to split the specification of its cars at Marina Bay after an upgrade in Malaysia last weekend failed to provide the expected step forward in performance. Russell is using the previous spec car and Antonelli the new one. Wolff said: "We don't know which one is going to be quicker." He said initial indications were that the "new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive - not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it. "The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point. That is one free practice session, and it will be needing more time to really come to more conclusive information." He said the success or otherwise of the upgrade, Mercedes' first significant change to the car's design since June, could have significant ramifications on Mercedes' preparations for 2027. "We've put a few months of upgrades into the car, clearly pointing in a direction that we think is advantageous," Wolff said, "and maybe we just need to calibrate it a little bit in order to find the right way forward for 2027." title: Two men deny Iran-backed surveillance of Jewish and Israeli sites in London
description: Targets allegedly included the Israeli embassy and consulate, a woman said to be of interest to Iran, a college, and Britain's oldest synagogue.
body: Prosecutors allege that Nematollah Shahsavani (right) directed Alireza Farasati to gather intelligence on London's Israeli communities Two men have pleaded not guilty to carrying out surveillance on Jewish and Israeli sites across London on behalf of Iran's intelligence service. Nematollah Shahsavani, 41, and Alireza Farasati, 22, are accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service under the National Security Act 2023. Prosecutors allege the pair carried out hostile reconnaissance at several locations between 9 July and 15 August last year. Targets allegedly included the Israeli embassy and consulate, a woman said to be of interest to Iran, a college, and Britain's oldest synagogue. Both defendants entered their not not guilty pleas during an appearance at the Old Bailey on Friday. Farasati appeared in person in the dock, while Shahsavani attended via video link from HMP Pentonville. The court previously heard that police confiscated electronic devices from Farasati, a barber, when he was stopped on 14 August last year. Prosecutors allege that Shahsavani directed Farasati to monitor and gather intelligence on London's Jewish and Israeli communities. Shahsavani, who works as a car salesman and delivery driver, was allegedly acting on instructions from Iranian intelligence. Shahsavani, a dual British-Iranian national and father of two from North Finchley, north London, has lived in the UK since 2009. Farasati, an Iranian national living in Colindale, north-west London, arrived in Britain as a 17-year-old in 2021. Mrs Judge Cheema-Grubb scheduled a further pre-trial hearing for 12 February, with a full trial due to begin at the Old Bailey on 26 April next year. Both men, who were detained in March, remain in custody. title: Burnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts
description: The prime minister says restrictions on what workers can do after leaving roles have "gone too far".
body: Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job. In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back. He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff. Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK. Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last. Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months. Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff. He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation." Referencing a landmark 1995 court ruling that is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector". Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms". It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported by Politico, external and The Financial Times, external, alongside the Budget on 28 October. The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban, external on non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally. The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy. He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment. He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy. He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fund launched in Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region. He also hinted that the government was looking at the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies. He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them." "So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale." title: 'Tropical jungle' of wallabies, porcupines and parrots must move after neighbours complain
description: James Wale moved to the site two years ago and keeps animals including wallabies and rare birds.
body: One neighbour says the site sounded like a tropical jungle at night A man who lives in a log cabin and keeps wallabies, mongooses, porcupines, parrots and other rare birds has been told to move. James Wale relocated to the rural Carmarthenshire site two years ago, having previously run a rare bird business in Pembrokeshire. Neighbours said the site sounded like a "tropical jungle", especially at night. Carmarthenshire Council issued Wale with an enforcement notice alleging he had broken planning rules, but he has been given more time to relocate the animals. Planning agents representing the bird enthusiast said he wanted to create a "major tourism venture", and that his former business in the grounds of Picton Castle ended because the lease was not renewed. Wale moved to the 17-acre woodland near Llannon and had hoped to set up an owl garden centre, but scaled back his plans to create a private bird welfare home along with some forestry and farming activities. As well as the exotic animals, Wale also kept horses, goats, chickens and ducks, according to the enforcement appeal. Documents said the abandoned venture planned to include "reptile, mongoose and several animal enclosures". A planning application was then prepared for a smaller-scale venture including about 30 bird and animal enclosures, with Wale not intending to live onsite. James Wale also had mongooses in his collection which are native to Africa, southern Asia, and southern Europe Two enforcement notices were issued by the council last year, one of which was withdrawn, and another sent this year which told him to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and stop keeping non-agricultural birds and animals. During the subsequent appeal, seven objectors expressed concerns about the changes at the land linked to sanitation, stray animals and unusual noises. One objector said the noises were "not those of native species". Another claimed the noise "often sounds like a tropical jungle" which, along with the sound of generators and dog-barking, was "particularly troublesome late at night". A further comment said the site had become waterlogged, turning a "once beautiful forest" into a "fly-tipping incident". The person submitted a photo of goats and a Labrador to the council and said they had strayed onto their land. The site can be accessed from the wooden stockade on the left near Llannon Llannon councillor Llinos Mai Davies claimed the site adversely affected neighbouring properties and had a negative impact on the character of the area. Photos of the land were submitted showing the boggy conditions and the woodland access track off the A476. A planning inspector appointed by Welsh ministers has now dismissed the appeal after seeing the cabin during a visit to the land. "The appellant keeps a few chickens, ducks and horses on site along with a variety of more unusual animals including eagles, falcons, parrots, hornbills, mongooses, skunks, porcupine and wallaby," they said. The inspector said there was a minor element of forestry and agricultural activity taking place, but that the main operation was of a "fundamentally different character" and unauthorised. Wale should be given 12 rather than six months to stop using the land to keep non-agricultural animals, remove the enclosures and restore the site to its original condition, the inspector concluded. "Given the unusual type and mix of the animals, it may well take more time to find a suitable alternative location," they added. Wale also has 12 months to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and its associated foul drainage. His agents told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that a planning application would be drawn up in a bid to keep the birds on site. title: Fury-Joshua tickets priced up to £13,000 sell out in one hour
description: Tickets for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium sells out in just one hour.
body: Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right) are two of the biggest names in British boxing but have never shared the ring in a professional fight Tickets for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium have sold out in just one hour. Fury and Joshua will meet on a bill that begins on 11 December but they are not expected to fight until the early hours of 12 December. The highest-priced tickets were available at £13,128, including booking fees, with the lowest at £88.50. The all-British heavyweight contest, which will be broadcast globally on Netflix, was announced in September and around 80,000 tickets went on sale at 12:00 BST on Friday. Just minutes after the tickets went on sale more than 500,000 people were waiting in the online queue. Tickets quickly began emerging on resale websites, with ringside VIP seats being advertised for £73,645, while upper tier seats were available for £425. Ringwalks are expected to start around 01:00 GMT on Saturday 12 December, following a short live music performance, and the stadium will remain open until 03:30. The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White. Organisers are yet to confirm any of the undercard fights. Joshua, 36, and Fury, 38 - both former two-time world champions - signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, but the date and venue had yet to be confirmed. London's Wembley Stadium and New York's Madison Square Garden were the frontrunners to stage the fight, but both presented issues before Cardiff emerged as an alternative. The Principality Stadium has hosted late-night boxing before, including Joe Calzaghe's fight with Mikkel Kessler in November 2007, which began at 01:00 GMT. Ricky Hatton's victory over Kostya Tszyu at Manchester's MEN Arena in 2005 began at about 02:00 local time, allowing US broadcaster Showtime to show the fight on Saturday evening. This video can not be played AJ reassures fans that Fury fight will happen... Just 11 days ago, there was uncertainty over whether the fight would even take place due to a dispute over the role of UFC chief White in the promotion of the event. Broadcaster Netflix said Alalshikh's The Ring and White would collaborate to promote the event, but Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn said his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role. The British rivals finally met at a news conference on 30 September to begin the build-up to one of the most anticipated fights in British history. title: Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems
description: The firm said users can no longer engage in "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards the tech.
body: Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI. The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior. It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery. While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools. The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances. But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear. Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare". But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it "deeply wrong, external" and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals. "You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn, external. "This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not." Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human, reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji. What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it? The people who think AI might become conscious The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm. It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom, it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections". Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons. But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots. It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools. Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you. Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses. When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was, external "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know". The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools. Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines. Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others. title: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
description: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was charged £1.5m in repair and restoration costs after surrendering the lease on the 30-room mansion.
body: King Charles has paid Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's £1.5m repair bill that's owed for the poor condition of Mountbatten-Windsor's former home at Royal Lodge in Windsor. It's understood that the money is coming from the King's private income - and will cover what Andrew owes his former landlords, the Crown Estate, on leaving Royal Lodge. There was a total £1.8m penalty for the "dilapidations" to Royal Lodge, but that has been reduced by the £300,000 Mountbatten-Windsor would have received for an early surrender of his lease. The Crown Estate say they have not given any money to Mountbatten-Windsor at the conclusion of his lease and have now received the net £1.5m payment they were owed. Why did Andrew leave Windsor's Royal Lodge in such a hurry? Andrew moves out of Royal Lodge home early after latest Epstein files Mountbatten-Windsor left his Royal Lodge home in February, in the middle of a storm of revelations about his connections to the US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein. The former Prince Andrew was moved to Sandringham, with his brother the King using his own money to provide his upkeep and accommodation. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested later that month on suspicion of misconduct in public office - and a court ruling on Thursday found fault with the search warrants used by the police. But despite moving to Sandringham, Mountbatten-Windsor's lease on Royal Lodge had remained until October - and as that officially ends, the Crown Estate is revealing the terms on which it concluded. When Andrew had taken on the 75 year lease in 2003, he had made considerable up-front payments, including about £7.5m for repairs, which meant that he did not have to pay a monthly rent. It also meant that if he gave up the lease within the first 25 years he would be legally entitled to some compensation - with that amount reducing each year. Leaving in October 2026 would have meant that the Crown Estate would have had to pay him back about £302,000. However that amount has been overshadowed by what he owes to the landlord for the state of the building - and so the Crown Estate says it has now received a net amount of £1.5m. It's understood that the payment of that money by the King is to avoid leaving the Crown Estate out of pocket. Whether Mountbatten-Windsor will repay his brother is said to be a private matter - and there are no further details of what this might say about Andrew's personal finances. There was also no comment on how the King feels about this arrangement - and there is said to be no connection between this payment and the King making clear this week that his financial support should not go to cover Andrew's legal costs in his battle over search warrants. It has so far not been decided how the 30-room mansion in Windsor will be used in future, but it is expected to be used to deliver a commercial return - and at present there are no plans for another royal occupant. "The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return," said a Crown Estate spokesperson. A report by the National Audit Office had revealed earlier this year that Mountbatten-Windsor had been sub-letting buildings at Royal Lodge, although the amount was never revealed. That report from the public spending watchdog also showed that Andrew's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Eugenie, had accommodation inside royal palaces which they did not pay for, with the cost being covered privately by the King. title: Autism, ADHD and mental health review: What you need to know
description: It contains big lessons for the NHS, welfare, education and employment policies. What are the key takeaways?
body: The review looks at NHS waiting times and whether young people are being over-diagnosed. It has been called a "generational opportunity" to rethink support for both mental health conditions and ADHD and autism. The review, commissioned by then-health secretary Wes Streeting 10 months ago after saying young people were being "over-diagnosed" and "written off", could have major implications for NHS services, the benefits system, schools and employment support. Its 600-plus pages, external contain a host of conclusions and recommendations. Here are the key takeaways. The report is clear that there is an increasing risk of over-diagnosis, but only when it comes to ADHD and autism. Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups. They gave the example of children aged six to 17 – more than 4% have been diagnosed with autism. That's well above the 1-2% that studies suggest is the true level. But this comes with a big caveat. There are weaknesses in the data. Evidence about the true level of autism relies on surveys that have not been done for nine years, so the review team have had to estimate what has happened since. And there are some age groups where these conditions are still being under-diagnosed, and that should not be overlooked. It is why the review team said it could not yet conclude over-diagnosis was happening "at scale". But there is certainly evidence to suggest we are moving from an era of under-diagnosis to one of over-diagnosis, the experts said. They warn not every difficulty requires a medical response and there is a risk of blurring the lines between diagnosable ADHD and autism and what should be considered the "normal human variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour". Where the review team very clearly rejects the idea of over-diagnosis is with mental health. In fact, the chair, Prof Peter Fonagy, has said Streeting was "completely wrong" on that. He said the increase in mental distress is real – one in four 16 to 24-year-olds are now thought to experience it, up from one in six 30 years ago. He links this to a variety of factors including economic uncertainty, the impact of social media and loss of youth services. This contrasts with autism and ADHD. While diagnoses have increased, the true level in the whole population (regardless of whether they have come forward or not) has remained broadly stable, according to best estimates. What is not happening with mental health, though, is an increase in severe mental illness. Population rates of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, for example, have remained stable. Instead, what is driving the rise is conditions such as anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders. Where the review experts share, to some extent, Streeting's concerns is on the impact of diagnosis. They said there was a risk it ends up closing doors to opportunities. It can, they said, act as a label that defines them by their "difficulties" rather than "strengths and potential". This then hampers them in education, work and relationships. Around a third of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (NEET) report their mental health or autism as a factor. Those diagnosed with ADHD before the age of 17 are four times more likely to be a NEET than those without. Addressing this, they said, would require better support post-diagnosis. Some of that is down to the NHS, but as important is the approach of schools, workplaces and wider society. Another area where the review team is united in its view is that the support system is "falling short" of what people need for both mental health and neurological conditions such as ADHD and autism. Waiting times for assessment are too long. A third of young people referred to mental health services wait more than a year, while of the 900,000 people waiting for ADHD or autism checks, 90% have waited more than three months. In the lead up to publication of the report, NHS Alliance, which represents health bosses, said the system was in chaos. But this goes further than the NHS. The report said support across care, education, employment and welfare remains fragmented, with people having to "jump through hoops" and face repeated assessment and conflicting requirements to get support. No time should be wasted in tackling these challenges, the review says. On long waits, it says everyone on a waiting list should be reassessed so that those most in need are prioritised for help. There should no longer be a first-come, first-served approach. Some of those waiting may benefit from non-medical support, advice about sleeping better or getting more physical exercise, for example. That may even lead to some being removed from the waiting list. There should also be better assessments before people are placed on waiting lists too. Not every problem needs a medical solution, the experts make clear. Quality and consistency of autism and ADHD assessments must be improved, with the review highlighting concerns about those done by the private sector on behalf of the NHS. Half of ADHD and a third of autism assessments are done by non-NHS providers, such as charities and private firms. But they are not subject to the same regulation as NHS providers – and this must change. The experts also said it wanted to see a ban on direct-to-public advertising of assessments. The review has said it wants to see action over the next 12 to 24 months. The government has promised to act – and is expected to set out more details in its forthcoming mental health strategy which is expected by the end of the year. title: Polanski challenged over whether he thinks Israel has right to exist
description: The Green Party leader defends his decision to miss a debate on a controversial motion about Zionism which was passed by party members.
body: This video can not be played Green Party leader Zack Polanski has defended his decision to miss a debate at his party's conference on a controversial motion declaring Zionism a form of racism. Questioned by presenter Nick Robinson on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he denied deliberately avoiding the debate, saying he had been campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. The motion, which was passed by party members, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a single democratic Palestinian state encompassing present-day Israel. title: Ex-first minister Mark Drakeford suggests Wales Office should go
description: Created 60 years ago, most of the powers it used to hold were transferred to Cardiff Bay in 1999.
body: Mark Drakeford was first minister from December 2018 to March 2024 Former Labour First Minister Mark Drakeford has said it is time to consider scrapping the UK government's Wales Office. Drakeford said "the time has come" to think about abolishing the department, which was largely stripped of its powers when devolution began in 1999. Asked on S4C's Y Byd yn ei Le if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that." But Labour MP Ruth Jones described the suggestion as "foolish", arguing Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock was "fighting the corner for Wales". The future of the Wales Office has been the subject of regular speculation since devolution, with successive UK governments considering whether its functions could be folded into a single department, also covering Scotland and Northern Ireland. Earlier this year, then-First Minister Eluned Morgan said there remained "a role" for the Welsh secretary, but argued the post should be "the voice of Wales at the cabinet table" rather than "the UK government's voice in Wales". Under a previous UK Labour government, Peter Hain combined cabinet responsibility for Wales and Northern Ireland between 2005 and 2007. Asked if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that. "Of course, [former Labour prime minister] Tony Blair thought of this too. "This has been part of discussions in Westminster not only now but for more than a decade." The post of Welsh secretary, or secretary of state for Wales, was created by Harold Wilson's Labour government in October 1964, with the Welsh Office opening the following April. In 1999 the Welsh Office's powers over areas including health, education, environment, agriculture and transport were taken over by the Welsh Assembly, now known as the Senedd, and what remained of the UK government department was given the title of Wales Office. Stephen Kinnock was appointed Welsh secretary by Andy Burnham in July Interviewed on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday, Ruth Jones dismissed the idea of abolishing it. "I've got tremendous respect for Mark Drakeford but, let's be honest, he's now retired and, therefore, let the politicians who are elected to get on with the job get on with the job," she said. "In terms of the Wales Office, the only person from Wales actually at the [UK] cabinet table is the secretary of state for Wales, and he is there fighting the corner for Wales. "So I would say to disband that would be foolish." title: Drought declared in Yorkshire after dry weather
description: Environment Agency says Yorkshire saw its fifth driest period on record between April and September.
body: Scammonden reservoir in West Yorkshire - pictured in September - is one of several where levels are well below where they should be at this time of year Drought has been declared across Yorkshire following months of unusually dry weather. The Environment Agency (EA) said low water levels in reservoirs and rivers had triggered the move despite recent rainfall across parts of the region. Yorkshire officially entered drought status on Friday after a lack of spring and summer rainfall, having previously been classified as in a period of prolonged dry weather. Yorkshire Water said it was not planning to introduce water restrictions for customers at this stage despite the drought declaration. Andy Shaw, head of water production, treatment and energy at Yorkshire Water, said the EA's decision reflected dry conditions across the region but "does not mean water restrictions are currently needed". EA manager Vicki Townend said Yorkshire had seen its fifth driest period on record between April and September. Townend said: "The ongoing lack of rainfall means the flow in rivers and groundwater levels in certain parts of our area are very low and have now reached our trigger for declaring a drought. "Even if we receive a few weeks of rain, we cannot quickly reverse the effects of the lack of rainfall during a very dry spring and summer." She added: "We will continue to closely monitor the situation and implement our Yorkshire Drought Plan. "As we see more impacts from climate change, heavier rainfall and drier summers will become more frequent. "We encourage people to be aware of the impacts of drought and use a little less water to speed up the recovery from drought." Water Minister Emma Hardy said: "The recent rainfall is not yet enough to replenish all the water we've used over the spring and summer, and the Yorkshire drought declaration highlights the situation is still serious. "Long-term resilience against our changing climate is a priority for this government." title: 'It's heartbreaking' - Family of hit-and-run victim speak out as driver jailed
description: Richard Boyle, 42, was walking his dog on the Stewartstown Road in February 2021 when he was hit by a car.
body: The family of a west Belfast man who was killed in a hit-and-run as he walked his dog has branded the driver "a hateful, evil person" who had shown "no remorse". Martin Sean O'Lali has been jailed for causing the death by careless driving of 42-year-old Richard Boyle in 2021. O'Lali, 28 of Breton Court in Lisburn, was sentenced to two years and seven months in relation to what the judge described in court as a "shameful litany of events". Belfast Crown Court heard he would serve half the sentence in custody before being released on licence. He was also disqualified from driving for three years. Richard Boyle, who was 42, was walking his dog when he was killed Richard was walking his dog on the Stewartstown Road in February 2021 when he was hit by O'Lali's car which, the court heard, had been travelling at 90mph in a 30mph zone. His mother, Mary Boyle, said after sentencing that she was "broken". "I've got his ashes, I've got his dog's ashes, pictures on the walls, candles," she said. "I talk to him every night. I look at his photograph and talk to him. It's heartbreaking." Passing sentence, Judge Mark Reel told the court: "There is no sentence that will ever bring Mr Boyle back to his loved ones." title: Doctor accused of 1994 Rwanda genocide offences to face trial in UK
description: Dr Vincent Brown was allegedly a "leader" or "supervisor" of violent acts carried out by others in the early days of the genocide.
body: Dr Vincent Brown attended a previous court hearing in person A doctor accused of a number of offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide is set to face trial in autumn next year. Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He is the first person in the UK to have been charged over the genocide. Brown, of Islington, north London, is charged with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. A judge has now set his provisional trial date to begin in October 2027. He denies wrongdoing and has not yet entered a plea. The defendant appeared via video link from Belmarsh prison on Friday for a pre-trial hearing at the Old Bailey during which Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb set a provisional eight to 12-week trial from October 4 2027. A plea and case management hearing has also been set for 15 January. He has indicated he will plead not guilty to the charges against him. An estimated 800,000 Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were killed during the 1994 Rwanda genocide which lasted for 100 days. Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son. Between April 6 and 13 1994, he was allegedly a party to six murders and was later charged following a seven-year British investigation into the killings. The court heard on Friday that a £100,000 bail condition, imposed earlier in October, had not yet been met. Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC told the court the events in 1994 were "the most devastating wave of mass killing in modern history". Jones said: "One hundred thousand were murdered in Kigali especially in the first days and weeks of the genocide."
