title: Polanski vows to stay on as Green leader as criticism mounts
description: Jewish Greens' leader has said Polanski should resign in the wake of a Zionism row and by-election defeat.
body: Zack Polanski came second to Labour in the by-election in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's London constituency Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced calls from within his own party to resign. The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he "should resign", adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism. Lichtenstein's comments come after former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row. Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and "of course" had not questioned that. The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year. Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election. In her comments calling on Polanski to resign, Lichtenstein told Times Radio: "I don't know which Jewish members of the party he's been working with – it certainly hasn't been with the Jewish Greens committee." Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday. The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom". Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told BBC Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election." She later appeared to mollify her criticism slightly, posting on X that Polanski's leadership had "transformed the party" and she hoped he would now "help resolve huge issues we face and transform our internal structures". Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would not have voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended. However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology". Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations. On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist. "I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting." Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly." This video can not be played Polanski was challenged on Radio 4's Today over whether he thinks Israel has a right to exist In private, plenty of longstanding Green figures remain frustrated and accuse Polanski of being "missing in action" over the motion. They say the result is an untenable situation where he leads a party whose policy on the Middle East he disagrees with. "He is in danger of losing the confidence of both wings," one critic pointed out, referring to how some supporters of the motion have now been left irritated too by Polanski's refusal to publicly back them. Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future. Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit. "I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now from the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One. Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters". The Green leader has faced days of pressure over the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion. Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons between her party's previous antisemitism scandal, telling BBC Breakfast she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism. Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and said nobody will be excluded from the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body. title: Fund launched to back community wellbeing projects
description: The fund aims to attract support from individuals, families, businesses and charitable trusts.
body: Jersey Community Foundation said an independent panel would be set up to oversee funding decisions A charity has launched a new fund aimed at improving health and wellbeing in Jersey. The Island Health Fund, external will create a dedicated way for individuals, families, businesses and charitable trusts to support projects such as medical equipment, research, clinical innovation, community health initiatives and specialist training, the Jersey Community Foundation said. Chief executive Anna Terry said: "This is not about replacing government funding. It is about what additional philanthropic support can make possible." An independent panel would be set up to oversee funding decisions and help shape priorities, the foundation said. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Tom Binet, health minister, welcomed the initiative "and the opportunity it creates to attract new philanthropic support for health and wellbeing in Jersey". "This is a new opportunity for individuals, families, businesses and others who want to contribute to the future of health in our island," he said. Jersey Community Foundation said it would now work with healthcare providers, charities, government and businesses to identify areas where extra funding could make a difference. title: France promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests
description: Education minister Edouard Geffray makes the offer after another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students.
body: Thousands gathered at the Bastille in Paris hours before the French government made its first concession to the students The French government has made its first sign of giving ground to teenage protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days. Education minister Edouard Geffray made the offer in a television interview on Thursday evening, at the end of another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students. The government says 6,877 people have been arrested, 86% of whom are under the age of 18, since protests began centred around demands for more resources in secondary education. In what unions have billed as Act Four of the three-week movement, some 71,000 people staged protests across the country on Thursday, with 24,000 gathering at the Bastille in Paris. Police once again intervened with tear-gas to disperse groups who attacked them with paving stones and homemade fireworks. In Bordeaux, a lycée, or high school, was ransacked by protesters, and in Marseille a deputy-head was beaten up. On Friday, some 140 lycées - out of 3,500 - were totally or partially closed, a big drop on previous days. But another day of action has been called for next Tuesday. France's school protests: What lies behind the anger Geffray's announcement was the first material concession to the protesters' complaints. It has long been recognised by all concerned in French education that too many school hours are being lost because of absent teachers and their non-replacement by available supply staff. The minister said that thanks to new software coming online at the ministry, it would be possible to direct 3,000 supply teachers to the 500 or so lycées identified as being in the greatest need. Many of these schools are likely to be in high-immigration city suburbs, where the lack of teachers is most acute. Geffray also said that more money would be made available under an already existing scheme for those teachers who want to work overtime hours in order to plug gaps. And he promised that students' grievances would be taken into account in forthcoming discussions on the education section of the 2027 state budget. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said the extra 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days But the offer contained no major promise of new investment on a scale likely to appease protesters. The government is wary of appearing to buy social peace because it knows France's precarious debt situation is being followed closely by international money markets. Reaction from student leaders has been guarded to say the least. Nathanaël Combary, who represents the most moderate of the three main lycée unions Renouveau Lycéen (Lycée Renewal), said students were waiting to see how the promise was carried out in practice: "We've had some announcements which correspond to part of our demands. But obviously people want to see the money and more concrete results." "As long as we do not have €10bn on the table, we will continue our action," said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Etudiante (Student Union), which is close to the radical-left France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party of presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Mélenchon praised Thursday's demonstrations, saying on X that the students had "retaken the Bastille". But at the other end of the political spectrum, a spokesman for the hard-right National Rally (RN) condemned the government's concessions. "The message is: if you break things, you get given stuff," said Laurent Jacobelli. "When you burn cars, attack police, you gain something in return. It's the legitimisation of violence." The movement is the most serious student unrest in France in many years, and comes against a backdrop of rising tension in the country - with anger over rising fuel prices and distress in the farming sector also liable to trigger protests. Next Saturday, 17 October, has been earmarked as a day of demonstrations by a revived "yellow vest" movement. In addition, the approach of presidential elections in April and May - in which both hard right and hard left are expected to perform strongly - is exacerbating the mood of confrontation. The government is hoping that the approach of half-term holidays at the end of next week - as well as the arrival of colder and wetter weather - will take some of the sting out of the protests. title: US Office star in the running to be new St Andrews Uni rector
description: Brian Baumgartner is among six people vying for the role, after he visited St Andrews in the summer.
body: Brian Baumgartner is among six people vying for the role, after he visited St Andrews in the summer An actor best known for his role as Kevin Malone in the US version of The Office is among the candidates to become the next rector of St Andrews University. Brian Baumgartner is among six people vying for the role, after he visited St Andrews in the summer. In his address to students, he said he "fell in love with the town's culture and history". Other candidates include Green MSP Q Manivannan and a ministry of defence analyst. Previous St Andrews rectors include authors JM Barrie and Rudyard Kipling, and Monty Python founding member John Cleese. Baumgartner has pledged to "continue the storied tradition of comics and performers serving as rector", and to "engage with students, and bring his humour and love for St Andrews to the role". In pictures on his social media account, where Baumgartner was seen playing a round of golf at the Old Course, he commented: "Scotland - you have captured my heart." This article contains content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. Current rector Stella Maris, who has been embroiled in a long-running dispute with the university, is not on the ballot. Maris was initially removed from the university court in August 2024 over comments she made on the Israel-Gaza war, but won an appeal nine months later. Her second dismissal, in January 2026, came after she objected to a series of planned changes to the make-up of the institution's governing body, but she was reinstated after she changed her stance on governance rules. Manivannan, who was elected to Holyrood earlier this year, is also in the running to replace Maris, who they describe as having been "mistreated". The MSP described themselves as "a proud St Andrews alumnus" and said students deserve "safe and affordable housing, more artistic spaces, and the opportunity to express their anger at the state of the world, without fear of risk of isolation". The other four candidates are Dr Arthur Bernhoff, a St Andrews graduate working as an analyst at the Ministry of Defence, Mark Brunner, a previous guest lecturer at the university's school of international relations, Dr Conor Philip, a doctor and recent graduate of the university, and Dr Edison Yau, a student doctor who graduated from St Andrews this year. The position of rector exists at Scotland's oldest universities and is elected by the student body every three years. At St Andrews, the rector is the President of the University Court and presides over meetings which make crucial decisions about everything from budget allocations to academic policies. Students will cast their votes for on 15 and 16 October. title: Wimbledon boss jokes military would love to 'sort out' influencers
description: Royal Marine Commandos providing security at Wimbledon would like "nothing more than to sort out" disruptive social media influencers at the prestigious tournament, its chief executive jokes.
body: Wimbledon's boss said the SW19 crowd is 'self-policing' when it comes to behaviour Royal Marine commandos providing security at Wimbledon would like "nothing more than to sort out" disruptive social media influencers at the prestigious tournament, its chief executive has joked. US Open organisers accredited 100 influencers and content creators for this year's tournament. But when a match involving two-time champion Naomi Osaka was disrupted by a group of influencers conducting a photo shoot, it prompted a debate about tennis etiquette. Richard Atkinson, interim chief executive at the All England Lawn Tennis Club, said Wimbledon did not offer accreditation to influencers and sources have indicated to BBC Sport that is unlikely to change in the near future. While Atkinson acknowledged that influencers were a "crucial part of the marketing mix" and to ban them from attending the tournament entirely would be "nonsense", he said any that were brought in by brands would be "tightly chaperoned". He also backed the traditional "self-policing" ethos at SW19, whereby fans respect the action. After the disruption at the US Open, world number four Coco Gauff said it was important to welcome a "new demographic" to the sport, but said: "I think it's just, follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all." And Wimbledon's boss made it clear he does not expect to see a repeat at the All England Club. "We don't have a category of accredited people called influencers," Atkinson told a panel at Leaders Week London. "That said, clearly influencers are a crucial part of building your brand around the world in the third decade of the 21st century. "What you have to do is keep them under control. One of our big partners, Polo Ralph Lauren, will have their influencer, but they are all tightly chaperoned." He said the atmosphere at the US Open is "very New York City", adding: "It's dead easy for someone who has just bought a ticket to show up there with their ring lights and literally start broadcasting in the middle of a match. "If you tried to do that at Wimbledon, I think you'd probably have some Royal Marine Commando…" He then joked: "We do have military. And they would like nothing more, I suspect, than to sort out some influencer." Fans will also not be allowed to bring portable ring lights - a piece of equipment used by content creators - to SW19. Atkinson did, however, point out that the media landscape has changed, and suggested there is a place for embracing influencers and content creators to ensure Wimbledon remains relevant. "It's just a crucial bit of the marketing mix, of course it is," he said. "We're not in the world of newspapers and television anymore, right? The world has changed. But it's just really important, it's a bit of a cliched expression, you've got to sort it out in a Wimbledon way. But to say "we're not going to have any influencers at Wimbledon", it's obviously nonsense." "Our marketing team work meticulously to make sure they are working in a way that is consistent with our Wimbledon brand and keeps that magic that I was referring to earlier." title: 'Deeply personal moment': Watch Sagal Abdi-Wali's by-election victory speech
description: Labour beat the Green Party with 45% of the vote in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
body: This video can not be played Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, securing 45% of the vote and beating the Green Party which came in second place. In her victory speech, the Camden Council leader reflected on how the borough had given her family a home and shaped her life. "My commitment to this community runs deep," she said, adding that she hoped people who looked like her would see themselves reflected in Parliament. title: Abusive ex admits murdering woman after she began new relationship
description: Lee Inglis had twice avoided prison for previous knife attacks on Stacey Hogg in Hawick.
body: Stacey Hogg was murdered by her former partner A man with a history of domestic abuse has admitted murdering his former partner a day after learning she had begun another relationship. Lee Inglis pled guilty at the High Court in Edinburgh to stabbing Stacey Hogg to death in her home in Hawick earlier this year. BBC Scotland News has learned that the 39-year-old had twice avoided prison for previous knife attacks on the mother of three. He was still serving a home curfew and an unpaid work order when he killed the 35-year-old in June. He waited until his curfew ended at 07:00 before making the three-minute journey from his parents' home to Stacey's house. Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting The court heard that he slipped in through the back door and attacked Stacey as she came down the stairs. She suffered "catastrophic wounds" to her neck and head. Police found her in a pool of blood on a downstairs bathroom floor. The court heard that when he was arrested by police he told them: "I intended to cut off her head." "If I couldn't have her, nobody would," he added. Inglis will be sentenced at the High Court in Edinburgh on 5 November. Lee Inglis will be sentenced in November. Inglis had a history of domestic abuse against his former partner. He was sentenced to 150 hours of unpaid work in 2022 for assaulting Stacey and threatening to kill her with a kitchen knife. Court records show he admitted injuring her by putting his hands around her neck and causing her to fall to the ground and strike her head. He avoided prison again last year after being convicted of holding a knife to her throat and cutting her face. He was sentenced to 200 hours of unpaid work, two years of supervision and a night-time home curfew. The Border Telegraph, a local newspaper, reported that Sheriff Peter Paterson said at the time that the offence met the threshold for custody. But he took into account the "complex family dynamic" and that the victim was opposed to a non-harassment order being imposed. Inglis murdered Stacey at her home in McLagan Drive Stacey's death led to an outpouring of anger and grief in Hawick. Her funeral service was moved to the town hall to accommodate the number of mourners and an online fundraiser to provide support for her children raised more than £45,000. A family statement at the time described her as "a sister, a daughter, a mother and a friend who was taken from us far too soon. "She was a cherished daughter, an amazing sister and a loyal friend who touched the lives of so many. "Her kindness, strength and love will never be forgotten, and she will be deeply missed by everyone who knew her." More stories from South Scotland Det Insp Ross Duthie, of Police Scotland, said he hoped the outcome of the court proceedings brought some comfort to Stacey's family. "This was a horrific incident which understandably caused a lot of concern in the local area, and I would like to thank the community for their patience and assistance throughout our investigation," he said. "Inglis is a violent and dangerous individual who will now face the consequences of his despicable actions." The case is one of a series of high profile violent crimes against women and girls in Scotland in recent months. Stacy Hunter, 35, was murdered by her estranged husband, Jim Mair, at her home near Houston in Renfrewshire in July. His body was found nearby. Three weeks earlier he had appeared in court accused of strangling her and was released on bail. Her family say they saw clear signs she was being manipulated, controlled and abused by Mair, long before the murder. Stacy Hunter's death has prompted calls for stronger protection for women Vicki Solomon, 44, died after being found seriously injured in a house in the East Craigs area of Edinburgh in July. Her former partner Lee Grennan was charged with her murder and made no plea when he appeared in court. He was found dead at HMP Edinburgh a few days later. The Police Investigations and Review Commissioner confirmed Police Scotland had been contacted before the fatal attack on the mother-of-two. Meanwhile, police officer Alan Greer - who took his own life in May - was revealed to be a violent rapist who attacked and attempted to murder women over 14 years. Police Scotland chief constable Jo Farrell said this week that 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls. First Minister John Swinney has described violence against women and girls as a "national emergency". He says he will introduce misogyny education in schools across Scotland and has confirmed a GPS tracking pilot for people on bail - including those accused of domestic abuse - will begin next year. If you or someone you know have been affected by domestic abuse, you can find more information about organisations that can help at BBC Action Line. title: Crazy Rich Asians to return as TV show with original film's stars
description: The show will pick up after the hit 2018 film, and will also star Michelle Yeoh and Ronny Chieng.
body: Constance Wu and Henry Golding starred in the 2019 film directed by Jon M Chu Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name. The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor. "It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said. The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its £110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance. Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes. It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore. Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu. The film won best comedy movie at the 2019 Critics Choice Awards He said the film had "changed his life", calling the cast and crew the "most creative and hilarious group of people I've ever known". "Since then, this cast has become movie stars, superheroes, arena-filling performers and even an Oscar winner, so bringing everyone back together feels like coming home." Lim added: "Our writers room is humming and we can't wait to share what we've come up with." The series, co-produced by HBO and Warner Bros Television, will start production next year. "Constance, Henry, Ronny, and Michelle are global superstars, and we know the passionate fans of the film and megahit novels can't wait to see more," said said Casey Bloys, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance Direct-To-Consumer. title: Alison Hammond: 'I thought I was having heart attack on air'
description: The host says a health scare on live TV was one of the "scariest things I've ever been through".
body: Hammond returned to This Morning one week after her dramatic early exit Alison Hammond has said she feared she was having a heart attack on air when she had to rush off ITV's This Morning midway through the programme last week. The presenter appeared to clutch her chest as she left the show last Friday, and was taken to hospital to have a heart check-up. She turned out to have suffered a panic attack, and said the experience was "probably one of the most scariest things I've ever been through". Returning for her weekly slot on Friday, she told viewers: "I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack. I'm so glad I'm here. I feel so grateful. I feel so thankful to God, to everything in life." She added: "It felt like a heart attack. It was very real." Hammond was alongside Dermot O'Leary as usual on This Morning on Friday Alongside co-host Dermot O'Leary, Hammond introduced the programme by thanking him for holding the fort after her dramatic early exit, and also thanking everyone who sent good wishes. She added: "It was the first time I've ever experienced anything like that. Secondly it was live on TV so I thought, oh my gosh, my son might be watching. "So I just ran. I ran off TV. I would never do that normally but I just couldn't catch my breath." The panic attack came on very quickly, she explained. "It just was like a wave, something which I've now found out is adrenaline. That came into my body. I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack." The experience has given her a new perspective on life, she continued. "I'm so happy that I'm here, and I'm so happy to see you," she said, putting both hands on Dermot's cheeks before hugging him. "You were absolutely wonderful. And I'm so glad we're alive, and if anything it's made me look at life so much differently. Taking stock, look after my health. I'm drinking a lot of water." The 51-year-old compared the feeling of the panic attack to crossing into a "surreal" place like the otherworldly Upside Down in TV show Stranger Things. "I felt like I went into the other world - what's that show that I loved? Stranger Things. You know when you go into the Upside Down world? I felt like I went into the Upside Down world. "I couldn't grasp my breath, and it was a panic attack." Hammond and O'Leary also spoke further about panic attacks with former BBC Breakfast host and psychologist Dr Sian Williams, who has written a book about anxiety. Hammond said she had been unsure about returning to This Morning - but felt that if she didn't come back this week, she may never do so. "I'll be honest with you, I was anxious about coming back. But I thought, if I don't come back today, I probably wouldn't come back... because then I would have made a thing that it's This Morning that's causing the panic. "But it can happen anywhere. It comes in ebbs and flows." She and Williams also discussed the pressure of presenting live TV. "I do live TV all the time, I didn't realise it was having - I don't know if it was having an impact - the fact that you have to be 'on' in order to do it. I don't know," Hammond said. She concluded the segment by telling viewers: "I'm back, babes. Keep rolling." Following her departure from last Friday's episode, Hammond posted a video from a hospital bed saying she was "getting my old ticker checked out" after what she described as "a little bit of a palpitation", which she hoped "was just a little panic attack". She missed the Attitude Awards on Wednesday, where she won the The Honorary Gay Award. The Birmingham-born presenter also hosts TV shows including This Morning and For the Love of Dogs. Also known as anxiety attacks, panic attacks can affect anyone, regardless of age, background or whether they have a history of anxiety. According to the MIND mental health charity, panic attacks are an extreme anxiety response. They can develop quickly, and come with very intense symptoms. title: Man who stabbed ex in 'rage of anger' as she walked her dog jailed for 24 years
description: James McKenna hid for days after he attacked Joanne Sidaway as she walked her dog in the park.
body: James McKenna from Carmarthen was arrested after a four-day manhunt A man who repeatedly stabbed his ex-partner in the chest and then fled, launching a four-day manhunt, has been jailed for 24 years. Joanne Sidaway, 49, screamed as she was attacked by James McKenna, 58, in the bushes of Carmarthen Park in January. He then hid in a wood near Carmarthen for three days without food and water, before being arrested in hospital while he was being treated for frostbite. Earlier this year, McKenna pleaded guilty to wounding with intent, but in July was found guilty of attempted murder. On Friday, Judge Paul Thomas KC said the attack was "wholly calculated", and McKenna had left Sidaway to die in the bushes. There was a large emergency response near the park after the attack McKenna had waited for Sidaway to enter the park on 29 January with her dog, before crouching down in the bushes, ready to launch his attack. Swansea Crown Court heard McKenna was "angry" after their relationship ended a few months earlier, and it was "luck" that she did not die, with her winter coat helping to save her. McKenna used a new, sharp knife from his kitchen and intended to cause Sidaway "serious harm" but not kill her. "I felt she was reluctant to re-engage with me, and not even say hello," he said. He stabbed her multiple times in what he agreed was "a rage of anger". He told the court he was "shocked" at what he had done. "I was aiming for her shoulder area and the upper body. I didn't want to kill her." McKenna told the jury he had put the newest, sharpest knife from his kitchen in his bag that morning He said the attack was interrupted after Sidaway told him to stop and screamed, and a neighbour shouted. Neighbour Susan Edwards heard "high-pitched screaming" and the "bushes shaking" before McKenna ran away. Sidaway phoned for an ambulance and said: "I've been stabbed by my ex-partner... he's been stalking me." McKenna dumped his rucksack and knife at an allotment near the park after eating yoghurt. He then walked three miles (4km) to Bronwydd village along the River Gwili. "I found some shelter, a quiet woodland away from the road," he said. "I was devastated and kept having flashbacks." He was there for three nights before getting a taxi and bus to Bronglais Hospital in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion. Police bodycam footage showed Sidaway sitting on her doorstep with paramedics, covered in blood. There were 17 areas of damage to her coat and her clothing was extensively blood-stained. She received injuries to her chest, arm and hand. Sentencing McKenna, Thomas said: "You had been in a relationship with a woman of whose vulnerabilities you would have been fully aware. "When she decided, as was entirely her prerogative, that she no longer wanted to be in a relationship with you, you reacted, as you had done in the past, immaturely, and more significantly with violence. "You stalked her in the park in Carmarthen that morning, then you returned in the afternoon with exactly the same intention. It was planned, and it was wholly calculated. "You stabbed her no fewer than 11 times. Three of those being to the chest and therefore heart area. "That lady only survived because it was a cold day and she as wearing five layers under a thick coat. But after you did that, you left her to die in bushes in a park. "You only handed yourself in when you developed frostbite from sleeping rough." He said McKenna was "full of self-pity". McKenna dumped his rucksack, with the knife, at an allotment near the park McKenna has a previous conviction for assaulting an ex-partner in August 2016, after pushing her neck and pulling her hair. James Wilson, prosecuting, said it demonstrated that he was "unwilling to accept the end of that relationship". Caroline Rees KC, defending, said McKenna had shown "remorse" and "regret". Lucy Mansfield, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "McKenna's actions were cold and calculated, deliberately taking a knife to a public place to attack his ex-partner. "He committed a shocking act of violence, which must have been terrifying for the victim. "We will continue to work with our partners in the criminal justice system to tackle these abhorrent offences." Welsh Women's Aid Chief Executive Sara Kirkpatrick said this was a "carefully planned" attack. "Sadly, post-separation abuse, stalking, following a domestically abusive relationship is remarkably common," she said. "While we can ask ourselves how we make our spaces and places safer, this was an intentional act by an individual who made a plan and chose a place, and identified where his victim would be. She added that was why the charity campaigned for social change, "so that we don't find ourselves in a place where individuals think that pursuing vengeance in this manner is an acceptable route". McKenna will spend two thirds of his sentence in prison, before being released on licence. title: Man City titles 'absolutely not' tainted - Maresca
description: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted after they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.
body: Enzo Maresca has won each of his first five Premier League games in charge of Manchester City Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted after they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League. Maresca reiterated his faith in the club's owners and belief that they will win their appeal against the verdict during a news conference on Friday dominated by questions on the matter. The Italian, notably relaxed as he offered his responses, rejected the suggestion City's titles have been tainted by the ruling, as he knows "exactly the effort that the club put in to achieve" them. An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. The club have appealed against the verdict and claimed in a statement the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe". Preparing to play their first match since that verdict was announced, away to rivals Liverpool on Sunday, Maresca said in an in-house interview on Thursday the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and they are not affected by "the noise" surrounding the club. He added on Friday: "The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don't have doubt about that. "I spoke with the club for sure. We all trust, and probably the right moment to speak about that is when we are going to win this appeal." He added: "For me, the players - we can control just the pitch side, the football side. So we are focused on that. This is what we can do and what we can control." This video can not be played Appointed as Pep Guardiola's successor in June, Maresca is in his third spell at the club following time spent with the academy and as Guardiola's assistant coach - including during the Treble-winning 2022-23 campaign. The 46-year-old has won each of his first five Premier League games in charge of City, and could become the fourth manager to win his first six of a spell in charge of a club in the competition at Liverpool on Sunday. The announcement of the verdict reached by an independent panel, which found City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m, means Maresca's side will expect to receive an even more hostile reception than usual at Anfield. Asked if he had any concerns over the atmosphere during the match, Maresca said: "It will be a tough game, for sure. We need to be ready, the focus needs to be about the game, but we know the environment at Anfield. "It probably will be worse because of the situation but, again, it will be our duty to do our best and try to win the game. "The reason I decide to become manager is for this type of game." Maresca thanked one journalist who asked a question not related to the verdict, confirming talisman Erling Haaland is "ready" to play against Liverpool after recovering from his efforts for Norway during the international break in Marbella. Maresca will be demanding a siege mentality from Man City - Pulis From doomscrolling to defiance - how do Man City fans feel? The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City Maresca would not confirm whether he has read the independent commission's findings. The former Leicester City and Chelsea boss said the charges against the club were not discussed during his conversations about taking the job in the summer. And he insisted he would "100%" have still accepted the role had the findings been published before an agreement was reached. "We didn't speak about that because I don't think it was a problem for the club at the time and I think they are are thinking in an honest way," Maresca said. "I think they are convinced that in the end we are going to win the appeal." Earlier on Friday, Bayern Munich manager and former Manchester City captain Vincent Kompany said: "I played 11 years for the club and I've loved all the years I've played for the club. Everything we've achieved and done on the pitch I'm really proud of. "Everything else, as a player you're not a part of that. Right now, as a coach of Bayern Munich, I'm not too occupied with that topic." Latest Manchester City news, analysis and fan views Ask about Man City - what do you want to know? title: Video game Cyberpunk 2077 to get live-action movie adaptation
description: The smash hit from the studio behind The Witcher series is to be turned into a film by Paramount Pictures.
body: The Cyberpunk 2077 video game featured Keanu Reeves in one of the main roles A live-action movie version of smash hit video game Cyberpunk 2077 is being developed by Paramount Pictures. The Hollywood studio is working with producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura, known for his work on the Transformers films, and CD Projekt Red (CDPR), the developer of the sci-fi role-playing game. CDPR's joint-chief executive Michał Nowakowski said in a statement, external the company was "excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise". Details of the film's story, potential release date and casting information are yet to be revealed. Despite a troubled launch in 2020, the Cyberpunk 2077 video game, which stars Keanu Reeves, has sold more than 40 million copies worldwide. The John Wick star plays rockstar Johnny Silverhand, a terrorist whose consciousness is stored on a chip inside the body of main character V. Set in Night City, a fictional metropolis in a dystopian version of California, players work to uncover a conspiracy involving the shady Arasaka megacorporation. An expansion, Phantom Liberty, starring Idris Elba was released in 2023 and has sold more than 15 million copies, according to CDPR. Cyberpunk has already been successfully adapted into a popular animated series - Edgerunners - with a second season due to premiere on Netflix later this month. The streamer also produced The Witcher, an adaptation of CDPR's massively popular fantasy role-playing series. It originally starred former Superman actor Henry Cavill, but he was replaced by Liam Hemsworth in the show's fourth season. Anime adaptation Cyberpunk: Edgerunners was a big hit with fans Multiple video game series have been adapted for TV and film in recent years, with more due to follow. Two Super Mario movies, a big screen version of Minecraft and a series of Sonic the Hedgehog films have each seen global box office takings of about $1bn. PlayStation game The Last of Us was made into a hit series by HBO, and Prime Video says its adaptation of post-apocalyptic role-playing series Fallout is one of its most-watched programmes. Xbox maker Microsoft announced this week , externalit had created a new "XP" division to focus on licensing its games for films, theme parks and other tie-ins. Earlier this week, Paramount Skydance completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. It's promised to release 30 films annually for the next two years, but also prompted fears over job losses and price rises for streaming services such as HBO Max and Paramount+. Additional reporting by Peter Gillibrand. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: Three Saudi nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
description: The missile attacks come amid an escalation in fighting between the Iran-backed group and Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government.
body: Three Saudi nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said after Yemen's Houthis said they targeted the facility. The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X. It said the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second one struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia. One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement. Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said. Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two missiles, reports said. The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks. The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on October 6 and 7. Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport. The latest attacks come amid mark an escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west. The Houthi military spokesperson said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours". The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war. The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive. That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government. A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July. The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating for what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade, and for an air strike on Sanaa airport. title: Watch: Fleeing Kyiv for the countryside ahead of winter
description: A Kyiv resident told the BBC she has moved away from "everything that can be a Russian target" as Ukraine braces for another cold winter under intense attacks.
body: This video can not be played Kyiv resident Olena Konoplia has decided to move to Ukraine's countryside, as Russian attacks on the city have intensified and the prospect of another cold winter looms. Russia has been targeting Ukraine's power grid leaving locals without electricity and heating, and they will soon face prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures. Olena told the BBC she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital. "I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explained. Watch: Fleeing Kyiv for the countryside ahead of winter. title: Russell fastest from Leclerc in Singapore practice
description: Mercedes driver George Russell leads Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in practice at the Singapore Grand Prix.
body: George Russell will be starting from the back of the grid in Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix because of a penalty for taking a new engine Mercedes driver George Russell led Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in practice at the Singapore Grand Prix. A late lap from Leclerc, who was 0.198 seconds off Russell's pace, split up what had been an all-British top three. McLaren's Lando Norris was third fastest, 0.273secs behind Russell, and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fourth, 0.499secs off the pace. The top five, concluded by McLaren's Oscar Piastri, were all on the soft-compound tyres, while Red Bull's Max Verstappen was the fastest driver using medium tyres in sixth place. The four-time champion was 0.732secs off the pace and 0.519secs quicker than Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli behind him in seventh, also on the medium tyres. It was the only practice session of the weekend with sprint qualifying taking place at 13:30 BST. The split between tyre compounds made it hard to form any conclusions about relative pace. Russell will start Sunday's race from the back as a result of a penalty for using too many engine parts, following his engine failure while running third in the closing stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. He and Antonelli are also running different specifications of car, Russell reverting to a previous spec and the Italian the new aerodynamic package introduced in Malaysia. This is so Mercedes can get a better read of whether the upgrade package is working after struggling for pace in Malaysia when they expected to make a step forward. Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first win of the year at Sepang, and looked quick at times in the session before tyre strategies diverged. His team-mate Isack Hadjar, also on the medium, was eighth fastest, with Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson completing the top 10. Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso was in the top 10 for a time, but dropped back in the closing stages of the session to end up 14th. The racing action is taking place amid air-quality warnings in Singapore as a result of haze from wildfires in Indonesia, primarily caused by illegal slash-and-burn practices used by farmers and companies as a cheap method to clear vegetation. This is leading to record levels of air pollution in the city state and citizens are advised to limit outdoor activities. title: Survivor of US Army shooting supports gunman's execution but questions livestream
description: Alonzo Lunsford tells the BBC the punishment befits the crime but he has some doubts whether the public should be able to watch it.
body: This video can not be played Listen: 'I played dead', Fort Hood survivor Alonzo Lunsford who was shot seven times tells BBC's Today A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting on Fort Hood has said that while he supports the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he is concerned about it being livestreamed. Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times, told the BBC that the "method is befitting" for Nidal Hasan because other methods like lethal injection would be "doing him a favour". Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers in a medical building at Fort Hood, in Texas, in 2009. But while Lunsford agreed with the method of execution, he said it was "not something you should view for entertainment purposes". Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, he said: "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief." Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the public will be able to view a livestream of the execution, saying it is important for people to see the consequences of this kind of crime. If it goes ahead, and legal experts told the BBC it might not ever happen, it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. Lunsford explained that while he is concerned about the "effect" and "message" a livestream would send to younger people, when it comes to the survivors, their families and the families of the victims, they "should be able to look at it". "I'm gonna be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude you failed, I'm still here,'" he said. "I don't really have any sympathy for him as far as firing squad vs lethal injection, hanging or gas chamber, because he didn't have that same compassion when he did the deed on 5 November," the former sergeant explained. "I think the method is befitting for him because the lethal injection - that's doing him a favour. Gas chamber? Is doing him a favour." This video can not be played But Lunsford said that as a Christian, he has forgiven Hasan because "I cannot heal if I don't forgive him". "We're taught that with your last breath you can ask for forgiveness and I think that's what he [Hasan] should do," he added. Telling his account of what happened that day, he said Hasan got out of his chair and jumped onto a counter, before pulling out a weapon and discharging rounds. Lunford said he was looking for an exit via the back door, which was "two or three strides" away from him when he was first shot above his left eye and then "hit two more times in my back" as he crawled behind a desk. "At that point I played dead," he said. When Hasan moved on, he grabbed a nearby wounded soldier and went outside, where Lunsford said Hasan came up behind them and shot him again. One memory he said that "bothers" him from the day was of a woman who told Hasan she was pregnant. "We heard a gunshot and the last thing that girl was saying was: 'Oh my god, my baby, my baby.'" Lunsford said personnel don't carry weapons in medical facilities, and that Hasan "took the coward's way out" to attack them there. "And then for him to say he is fighting for his cause? I've read the Quran, and everything that he said he was doing that was in the Quran is not supported by the Quran," he explained. Hasan's execution was announced by the Pentagon earlier this week, in what will be the first military execution in more than 60 years. Legal experts have told the BBC there are a number of hurdles around the livestreaming of this which could mean it is successfully challenged in court. Some politicians have been vocal in their opposition. Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN it was "disgusting" while Republican Senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what "oppressive dictators" did. title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
description: The AI firm instead claims the researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive information.
body: Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm. "I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X, external alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees. On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures". OpenAI repeated these claims, external on Friday morning in a note from research leaders. "We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said. "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment." The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society. The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company. Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI". Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote, external: "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave. "I believe that was why I was fired." OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks. "We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X, external. "Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last." title: Thieves steal 30,000 wine bottles worth €5m in Italy, reports say
description: The heist at the Florence-based winery is believed to be one of the largest thefts of its kind in Italy.
body: File photo of wine from Italian company Marchesi Antinori Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about €5m (£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media reports. Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy's biggest family-owned wineries, said the theft at its storage facility in Tuscany took place on Saturday as the company was preparing to ship a consignment to customers abroad. At least seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso Tuscan reds. Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive, told Corriere della Sera this was the largest theft of its kind in Italy. "A theft of this scale and value has certainly never occurred in Italy," he said. He added that he was hopeful the authorities would be able to trace the stolen wine. "Two trucks full of merchandise can't just disappear into thin air. The Tuscan roads are full of cameras; perhaps with a bit of luck we'll be able to recover at least some of the bottles stolen from us." He told the Financial Times: "These wines have a great value and I don't know how they can sell all this wine around the world without being seen." The company believes the selection of bottles, which usually sell for between €150 and €500 each, suggests the thieves were wine connoisseurs and had inside knowledge. The theft was only discovered on Monday morning as staff arrived on site. No arrests have been made. Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and exports to 170 countries. It had a revenue of €263m (£223m) last year. There has been a spate of wine thefts in Italy this year, including two in the northern Piedmont region where hundreds of thousands of euros worth of bottles were reportedly taken. title: Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover
description: Everton owners the Friedkin Group are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.
body: Everton are currently seventh in the Premier League after seven matches Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control. The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of £400m. In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter". "The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said. "When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters. "With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton." TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window. In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025. Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear. Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong. Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after. The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry. TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward". "Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued. The decision of Everton's owners TFG to explore selling the club comes as no great surprise after the turbulent events of recent times. A fracture opened up between TFG and Everton's fanbase over the controversial attempt to sell highly-rated teenager Armstrong late in the transfer window, before a botched deadline day left manager Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players. The failed sale of Armstrong, as well as the departure of Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m, was bolted on to a cautious approach to the markets that suggested limited ambition on the part of TFG. It was in sharp contrast to the more hands-on approach at AS Roma, the other club owned by TFG, who bring in the additional riches of playing in the Champions League. Moyes revealing he had never spoken to Friedkin, who has not attended an Everton game since the Scot was reappointed as manager 21 months ago, strengthened the belief among supporters that TFG were effectively absentee owners. TFG secured a deal for 99.5% of the club, succeeding former owner Farhad Moshiri in 2024 after Everton had fallen into financial crisis. Since then, TFG have put the club on a stable financial footing and Everton have moved into a new stadium - although this was effectively done before their takeover - and have made the club an attractive proposition to potential buyers. This will be TFG's main achievement in what will, when Everton is sold, be regarded as an unspectacular tenure. Speaking on 5 Live Breakfast, former Everton goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis described TFG's plans to sell the club as a "shock". "It's come as a bit of a shock. They have stabilised the club. There was so much financial uncertainty when they arrived, it's felt like a turbulent time," said Brown-Finnis. "We [Everton] have a stadium to be crazily proud of, it's going to generate revenue from a commercial point of view. "If the Friedkin Group sells up tomorrow, they have left the club in a much better place. I just hope that they do their due diligence. "I hope the new owners want to drive the club forward. Everton fans have spent too much time in a financially turbulent era." title: Meet India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
description: Neha Bora has emerged as one of the most recognisable faces from India's recent Gen Z-led protests.
body: Neha Bora is a PhD student at Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student. Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years. But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses. Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained. Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral. In a recent BBC Bangla interview, Neha played down the attention they've been receiving. "I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening." The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power. There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India. Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation. Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate. Congress lawmaker Priyanka Gandhi Vadra hugs a copy of India's constitution as she lies down on the road during a protest this week Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings. After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms. Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him. "It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview. While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed. After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital, Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg. Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right." After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences. Several photos of Neha smiling as she's carried away by policewomen have gone viral But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP". And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged, external in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats, external. Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink, external at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man. The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter. "The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla. "If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said. Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP to "protect democracy".
