title: 'Careless use of AI is the real threat - not the ghost stories'
description: Meredith Whittaker says the tech has been misunderstood, in an exclusive interview with BBC Global Women.
body: Meredith Whittaker believes science doesn't support the idea that AI will turn against humans Warning: This article contains strong language. Meredith Whittaker has little patience for the AI doom that dominates headlines - she thinks warnings of AI turning on humanity is a fear "not anchored in science". "The risk is very real," says the boss of the Signal Foundation, which runs the encrypted messaging app of the same name, "but it's not the shiny ghost stories the wild-eyed boys are talking about". Instead, she believes the more immediate danger is the technology being used carelessly. She cites an alleged incident, reported by CNN, in which a chatbot used by US intelligence invented information about a Chinese vessel carrying nuclear material, reportedly leading the US to prepare a military response. "We almost went to war with China," she tells BBC Global Women. "A system that produces faulty intelligence and almost gets us into a war with China should not be considered super-intelligent by any standards." Signal has an estimated 40-70 million users - a drop in the ocean next to WhatsApp, which has billions. But it is renowned for its tough stance on protecting users' privacy - it hides who is sending a message from its own servers, limiting the data available to outside observers or hackers. Time magazine named Whittaker one of the most powerful people in AI. She moves through the rooms where its future is discussed, from Silicon Valley boardrooms to Downing Street, Davos and the Vatican. She studied literature at university and joined Google in 2006 as an entry-level temp with no computer science degree. In late 2017, she made her name when a colleague told her about Project Maven, a secret Google contract with the US Department of Defense to build AI for drone targeting. She understood what it meant to "compress the kill chain": to shrink the time between a machine flagging a target and someone deciding to fire, reducing deliberation. With thousands of colleagues, she pushed back. "This is going to launder bad intelligence and bad data," she remembers arguing publicly. The following year Whittaker helped organise a walkout, in which some 20,000 staff protested against the company's handling of several issues, including what they felt was the rushed introduction of new technology. Google dropped the contract and Palantir picked it up. Whittaker criticises venture capitalists' lack of support for startups led by women She draws a direct line from Maven to the US missile attack on a school in Iran this year, which she says relied on the system and on outdated intelligence that identified the school as a military target. "This is exactly what we were warning about in 2017," she says. In response, Palantir told Global Women there was "no evidence that Palantir's software was at fault in this terrible tragedy". It added that "Palantir is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies". And earlier this year it's UK and Europe boss, Louis Mosley told the BBC that "there's always a human in the loop, so there is always a human that makes the ultimate decision". The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets". Governments, including the UK's, argue for more access to conversations on messaging apps. They say this is to protect women and children. At London Tech Week 2026, then Prime Minister Keir Starmer said technology companies would be expected to detect and block nude images on children's devices, or face legislation. Whittaker argues children would be able to circumvent any such measures, calling the government's approach "an unprecedented regime of communication and information controls". The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology told the BBC it is preparing legislation. Would Signal leave any country, the UK included, that forced it to weaken its encryption? "Yes! My God, I have a backbone," she says. "It doesn't change based on mood. It doesn't change based on consultants." Faced with exposing people "who rely on us, sometimes in the context of life or death, to surveillance that could be weaponised against them", she says, "we would leave the market". The app is fully or partially blocked in Russia, China and Iran. Whittaker advises women in tech to stand up to bullies Rani Govender, Head of Child Safety Online at the National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children, told the BBC it hears from children who have been groomed and moved on to end-to-end encrypted platforms, where they are coerced into creating child sexual abuse material. "Tech companies are responsible for the design choices they make, and they cannot ignore the risks those choices can create for children." But Signal does have support from some women's groups, often those from the Global South who use the app themselves. "In a time of state surveillance and cyber-attacks, Signal is a tool for survival," says Hera Hussain, founder of the gender abuse charity Chayn, which is active throughout South Asia. "With any platform, it can be used by bad actors too, and we have to hold that truth too." I put to Whittaker a case from Canada, where police officers shared racist and misogynistic messages in a Signal group which leaked only when one of them passed it on to the media. A lawyer for one officer said the men believed Signal was as private and safe as their own home. "If they had that conversation in the kitchen and their bro snitched, would it be: 'What are we doing about kitchens?'" she asks. "It has to work for everyone or it works for no-one. This is the principle of fundamental rights. They apply even to assholes." She points to a US woman jailed after Meta handed over messages showing she helped her daughter access abortion in a state where it had been cr

title: Why Elon Musk is taking on India's richest man over Starlink
description: Musk has taken pot-shots at Reliance owner Mukesh Ambani as Starlink struggles to launch in India.
body: Elon Musk has accused the Ambanis of blocking Starlink's entry into India Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country. The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator. India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory. Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for comment The row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services. The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel. In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment. Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers. "You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India". On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services. "The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly. Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries. "Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday. Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install. The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services. Mukesh Ambani, who owns Reliance, is the richest man in Asia Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services. Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals. Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers." Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals. SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements. Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur. Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network. Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas. India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build. Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday. The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households. In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location. title: How Arteta's response to Brighton loss may shape Arsenal's next chapter
description: Mikel Arteta has shown an increased appetite for risk this season but, as Arsenal look to stay at the top, failing to reinvent would be a greater gamble.
body: Arsenal did not lose by more than a single goal in the Premier League last season Mikel Arteta has fashioned many versions of Arsenal. Taking over a side in need of new life in 2019, he won the FA Cup in his first season by playing a defensive style of football, unafraid of using a back five. As time passed the Gunners played a free-flowing style of attacking football - best seen in 2022 - before creating a side that reduced the variance of a match, maximised control and became physically difficult to compete with. Having finally won the Premier League title, Arteta is reinventing his side again. Perhaps freed by having lifted the trophy, we have seen the Spaniard take more gambles in personnel and tactics. But, while an increased appetite for risk means the wins can be greater - so can the losses. Arsenal finished seven points above second-placed Manchester City last season "Brighton were really good," Mikel Arteta confessed after Arsenal's 3-0 defeat before the international break. Fabian Hurzeler masterminded the dominant victory against the reigning champions - defiantly opting against a pragmatic approach. It is rare Arsenal are totally outclassed, so the loss to Brighton left a lingering sense of uncertainty going into the extended break. But, given the timing of the defeat, it has been easy to forget that Arteta's men had won every game prior to that this season. Last season, the heart of Arsenal had Martin Zubimendi at its base with Declan Rice in a more box-to-box role to the left of him. Arsenal lost some momentum as the end of the season approached but it was the surprise use of Myles Lewis-Skelly in holding midfield that reinvigorated Arsenal, helping them over the line. Arteta has since continued to trust the 20-year-old in that key role. This season, Arsenal have used a 3-1-6 shape in possession, formed by Declan Rice dropping deep - rather than pushing on as he did in the first part of last season - to create a back three alongside Ezri Konsa and Gabriel Magalhaes. Lewis-Skelly plays as the single pivot, linking the back part and the front part of the team. Here we see Arsenal's 3-1-6 shape in possession. Rice is positioned on the right side of the back three with Lewis-Skelly in holding midfield, seen on the ball. To label the rest of the team a 'front six' is perhaps an oversimplification, given the more specific roles certain players have. Riccardo Calafiori, Ben White and Martin Odegaard take turns to drop deep, becoming a fifth player to Arsenal's base in moments. These dynamic arrivals, that create a '3-2' or a '4-1' base, require an alertness and reaction from the opposition to track them that isn't always possible. These movements to drop deep therefore help Arsenal outnumber opponents, play around them and get up the pitch. Moments later, Odegaard drops deep to turn Arsenal's 3-1 base into a 3-2 shape. By arriving here suddenly, Sunderland fail to track him. This gives Lewis-Skelly an easy passing option and Arsenal are able to bring the ball up the pitch. In William Saliba's absence, Konsa is a capable ball-playing centre-back. Rice, however, possesses both the passing and carrying quality of a world-class midfielder. Facing forward and with more time and space on the ball, using him here maximises many of his strengths and minimises the amount of time he spends in small spaces with back to goal - a relative weakness for a player of his frame. Lewis-Skelly has made that link position his own for reasons including his calmness under pressure, his hold-up strength, his ability to dribble past players one-v-one and his willingness to take risk - when deciding to dribble past a player or play direct passes for his attackers. His effectiveness here has been noticed too by England boss Thomas Tuchel who, during this international break, has emulated Arteta's use of Lewis-Skelly. For England it has been Elliot Anderson taking up the 'Declan Rice role' in the back three. Here we see Arteta's influence on England. During the international break, Lewis-Skelly played in the same lone pivot role as he has for Arsenal. England's other holding midfielder, Elliott Anderson, moved into the first line to form the 3-1 shape. Given the demands of this role, part of the reason Arsenal may have struggled against Brighton was that Bruno Guimaraes took up this holding midfield position instead of Lewis-Skelly. Hurzeler has drilled his Brighton side to play with high intensity, both on and off the ball. To play around their press requires superb technique, good positioning, the right timing of movements and an understanding of where team-mates may be. These are things Guimaraes will get to grips with, given the time Lewis-Skelly has already had in this role, but being used in there against an effective Brighton man-to-man press was always going to be a difficult challenge. Brighton's pressure meant Arsenal hesitated on the ball, forcing them to make decisions they normally wouldn't. "You could see from the first throw-in, it was so clear. We put ourselves in trouble one, two, three times," Arteta said. "We need to get out much quicker than that, and that's one of the biggest lessons we have to take from the game today." After playing looser passes, Arsenal, known for their duelling, were beaten by a Brighton side that swarmed around the ball. Following a throw-in, Arsenal are forced long early against Brighton's forward pressure. Two Brighton players read the flight of the ball and win the first ball. With the ball not yet under control, Brighton's right-back immediately makes a long sprint to win the second ball. Around him, three Brighton players converge on the ball. This set the tone for the match. When Brighton were pushed deeper, Arsenal might've expected that things would play out like most games do for them - with them dominating the ball in the opposition&#x27

title: Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election
description: Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali beats Green Party leader Zack Polanski to hold the north London seat.
body: Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, seeing off a challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski. Camden council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali held the north London seat for Labour but the party's majority was reduced from 11,572 to 3,364. The by-election, which was triggered after former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer stood down as an MP, had been seen as a key test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can win over voters who have switched to the Greens. Polanski insisted he would stay on as leader despite the result. He has also come under pressure over his response to a motion passed by members declaring Zionism a form of racism. Labour wins Holborn and St Pancras by-election, beating Green leader Zack Polanski Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by-election loss Chris Mason: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far Labour's Abdi-Wali secured 45% of the vote, followed by Polanski on 33%. However, the Green Party's vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election. Ewan Cameron of the Conservatives came a distant third with 1,922 votes (7%), followed by Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats. The inner London constituency has been Labour since it was created in 1983, with the party taking at least 40% of the vote at every general election. In her victory speech at the count in Camden, Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a testament to the success of diversity in the borough. "Whether you voted for me or not my commitment to this community runs deep," she said. "I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong, for people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain." She added: "That is what this victory represents. Winning not by making people afraid of each other, but by bringing people together." Asked about the threat to his leadership following the result, Polanski told broadcasters: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party. "Of course, I wanted to win. No-one runs an election to lose." But he added that voters had been "excited about our plans for rent controls, tackling the climate crisis and nationalising Thames Water". He continued: "So many people told me on the doorstep, so they want to give Andy Burnham a chance [as prime minister]. "Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it." This video can not be played Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory speech after by-election win The Greens had hoped they could overturn Labour's substantial majority in the constituency after the party made gains in local elections in the area in May. It saw a surge in support after Polanski took over as leader in September last year but in recent months polls suggest this has waned. The by-election came after Polanski faced criticism for his response to a motion passed by members declaring Zionism a form of racism. Earlier, former party leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC Polanski had failed to show leadership over the motion. Speaking after polls closed but before the result of the by-election was announced, Lucas criticised Polanski for not taking part in the debate or voting on the motion at the Green Party's annual conference in Brighton on Sunday, describing the motion as "dangerous" and "divisive". Asked if Polanski should stand down, she said: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election. "I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday. "I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will." The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. Polanski was not present for the vote on the motion, after leaving the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras. title: Data centre raises noise and wildlife impact fears
description: The data centre, which will have 72 chiller units on its roof, will generate 150 jobs, planners hear.
body: An artist's impression shows what the proposed data centre on the outskirts of Norwich could look like A huge data centre planned in a village near a nature reserve would generate "very high noise levels" without extensive measures to block it, experts have said. Plans have been submitted to South Norfolk Council for a 150 megawatt facility in Keswick on the edge of Norwich, which includes assessments of its potential environmental impact. The scheme is causing concern, with thousands of people signing a petition against it, due to fears it could harm neighbouring wildlife sites. But Norwich Apex Data Centre has defended the scheme, claiming assessments showed it would not harm protected areas like Marston Marshes. The data centre could be built on a strip of land off the A140 Ipswich Road opposite the Tesco superstore The data centre is also causing concern over its potential water usage, noise pollution and the scale of the facility harming the landscape. Assessments of the noise it could create found it has the "potential to generate very high levels of noise to the surrounding area" and would require extensive mitigation measures. The majority of noise would come from the 72 chiller units on the roof. A spokesperson said: "Our environmental assessments conclude the data centre will not harm nearby designated wildlife sites. "The data centre will use air-cooling technology, meaning no water will be required for cooling. Water will only be needed for everyday uses, such as toilets and staff facilities, with none taken from nearby rivers or marshes. "The facility has also been designed so that operational noise levels at surrounding sensitive locations are in line with existing background levels." The firm also said the facility could create up to 150 permanent jobs and that it would create planting and landscaping to screen the development and reduce the visual impact. It would also be located close to an electrical substation for offshore wind farms in the North Sea, from which it could draw power. The land already has planning permission for a business park but the developer wants to build a data centre instead The project has already been met with opposition, with thousands signing a petition against it. Daniel Elmer, the Conservative leader of South Norfolk Council and county councillor for Keswick, said he will formally object to the proposed facility. He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "My personal view, is that it is just too damned big for the site it would be on. "It is right next to the marshes and the southern edge of Norwich, while it is near a listed church. "That's the southern gateway into the city of Norwich. I think you have to think, in terms of the Norwich 'brand', what visitors to the city would see when they travel down that road. "What they see needs to be aesthetically pleasing and I am not sure that is what they will get, given the application which has been submitted at the moment." title: Industry leaders discuss island high value scheme
description: More than 260 industry leaders met to discuss the role wealthy residents play in Jersey's economy.
body: Mary O'Keeffe was one of several business people who said high value residents contribute positively to the island's economy More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy. Jersey's high value residency programme, external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals. One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island. However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling". About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme. O'Keefe who runs Mary O'Keefe relocation, external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes. "They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals. "So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy." High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income, external. They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax, external. O'Keefe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way. "First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income. "And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand. "High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off." Industry leaders from law, finance, business and real estate met at a Chamber of Commerce lunch to discuss the role of high value residents in Jersey Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them. He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy. Former economic advisor to the government of Jersey John Christensen said the amount of tax paid by high value residents was "piffling" "If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said. "So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%. "We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax. "We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions." John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme. He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly". "I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community. "As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all. "I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally. "And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work. "They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses." Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Maresca will be demanding a siege mentality from Man City - Pulis
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains why Manchester City players have a great chance to show unity and togetherness when they travel to Anfield on Sunday.
body: If I was manager of Manchester City now, after they were found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules, my whole psychology with my group of players this week would encompass one major point: "No-one is going to like us, but we won't care." I loved being the underdog and I loved to prove people wrong, and that is what I would demand now - a siege mentality from my squad and supporters alike to prove to people that, irrespective of what is happening off the pitch, on the field and the terraces we respect our club and we are going to fight on. City will be vilified by everyone else but their players have a great opportunity to show unity and togetherness, starting on Sunday away to Liverpool. This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City When the Premier League returns this weekend, the spotlight will be on one game in particular - at Anfield. As well as preparing for such a huge match, City's players will be arriving back from international duty and going straight into an off-field fight that has turned into a media frenzy. The allegations seem relentless with finger-pointing from every Tom, Dick and Harry jumping on the bandwagon in hammering a club that has dominated the Premier League for over a decade. It feels like every positive gained by City over the period in question and beyond has been smashed into oblivion. Yet, despite all of the above, the club have remained firm in denying all charges. So, where does this leave Enzo Maresca and his City players as they prepare to take on Liverpool? Firstly, although they themselves have not been involved in any of the allegations about the club breaking the Premier League's financial rules, they must understand that supporters at all away grounds will be baying for their blood. City have become a team that, whenever they play, will provide an opportunity for all critics to attack them, and from all angles - including the frenzied media outlets. So, as the manager, Maresca must first act to reassure his players that the club is not in any way going to take a step back from defending their own position, and also the position of the players, staff and supporters. Once that is established, I would then expect every player to concentrate on what they are being paid for, which is to win games. There should be no distractions or any questions that do not relate to the games they are involved in. No excuses about what is happening off the field would be tolerated, and that would be my final word on the matter. This video can not be played Watch: Manchester City vs The Premier League If the verdict about City breaking the Premier League's financial rules is upheld, it will come at a heavy cost to the club and its reputation. I feel there needs to be more attention paid to all of these rules, and their fairness, because professional football at the top level is now dominated by massive financial investment. Even if you just consider player transfers, it's not unusual for around a billion pounds to be exchanged between clubs in England and around the world during each transfer window. While individual players at the top level are being bought and sold for more than £100m, smaller academies are being plundered by the bigger clubs. They can hoover up the best young players for much smaller 'compensation' fees, enabling them to polish them up and sell them on later for much more - without any Financial Fair Play rules to regulate how much they profit. That's one way of dealing with FFP, I suppose, but is it for the good of the game, or the players involved? Over many years of Premier League governance, clubs have broken the FFP rules that are in place. Some have not been caught yet, I'm sure, but others have and have been punished. It keeps happening, so are the current rules right? Do we need to try to change them or are we taking a bigger risk by leading clubs to find different ways - or loopholes - to try to break the financial shackles that are currently in place? The money in our game today is extraordinary and today massive corporations, billionaires and even countries are buying our clubs and want to invest more and more into the product but are not able to. Gone are the days of local business owners buying their local clubs. In the Premier League, Tony Bloom at Brighton and Matthew Benham at Brentford are the last men standing and, in the Championship, the Coates family at Stoke City and Steve Gibson at Middlesbrough are among the few to have had a taste of the top flight. I always see the top clubs having the power financially to remain at the top but it's important there is a way for the smart guys - people like those I named above - at clubs without the big bucks or big histories, to play a leading role in the top league in world football. At the moment all the negative media attention is on what Manchester City have done wrong but the likes of Brighton, Bournemouth and Brentford have achieved success by being smart, without the 'big club' tag. It's great to see, but surely the rules need to reward all clubs for being smart. Doing the right thing should give everyone the chance to compete at the highest level. Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan. The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? title: Music group with learning difficulties fulfils late MP's Broadway dream
description: The Music Man Project is a charity in Essex that teaches music to people with learning disabilities.
body: The performance told the story of The Music Man Project's journey since it was founded 27 years ago A music group with learning disabilities received a standing ovation as they fulfilled a dream of the late MP Sir David Amess. The Music Man Project is a charity based in Southend-on-Sea, Essex, that teaches children and adults with learning disabilities to sing, sign and play original music. They have performed for the King, at the Royal Albert Hall and London Palladium, but a trip to perform in New York was the dream of their former president and Southend West MP Amess before he was murdered in 2021. The project's founder David Stanley said: "Following his death, I just made it my mission to fulfil that promise, really, in his memory." "So that we remember Sir David for all of the work he did for championing people with learning disabilities in Southend, and then obviously across the country, through the Music Man Project's expansion." Stanley, who wrote, produced and featured in the show, paid a tribute to Amess during the performance. With a crack in his voice, he spoke into a megaphone - one of Amess' signature accessories on the political campaign trail - the words: "We promised we'd get them to the Broadway and we did it my friend, we did it." Group founder David Stanley (second left) praised the American audience who were "whooping and clapping" from the word go The morning after, Stanley told the BBC he was "exhausted" and "overwhelmed with emotion". "We got a brilliant standing ovation," he said. "It's nothing short of what the students deserved. "To be fair though, they've got a standing ovation from the King at the Royal Albert Hall before, so this was expected really with something like this." Stanley said the group's energy throughout their performance was "incredible" and "infectious" They performed at the Town Hall in New York with a full house of almost 1,500 people, and a venue known for its historic significance. It was founded in 1921 by suffragists and one of the only venues in New York to openly welcome Black artists. Stanley said his group were "perfect" and "incredible" on the night. He said it proved what he has always said about people with learning difficulties. "We give them the opportunities and you believe in them and you have high expectations of what they can achieve, then they will always come through, they surprise you. "Decades ago we would have hidden certain parts of society away, now they're performing on Broadway." Stanley founded The Music Man Project in 1999 Their performance told the story of the group's journey, from its beginnings 27 years ago to where they are now with 200 members. Stanley told BBC Essex presenter Sonia Watson that their visit would also include a performance at the United Nations. "I get to make a speech at the UN. So it's full of pinch me moments this tour." title: 'You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world'
description: Car maker Longbow, which hopes to build thousands of cars, says the region has the talent and know-how.
body: Longbow's co-founders and CEOs Daniel Davey (left) and Mark Tapscott show Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds (left in car) and mayor Richard Parker the Speedster A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire. Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year. West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs. Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said. Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it. "So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight." The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car. At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise. Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars. "Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added. People around the world are waiting to buy the limited edition car for around £85,000 The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund, external, which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry. West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year. Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow. "They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car." Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car. "So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing." title: New evidence gives family hope after death in Spain
description: Tobias White-Sansom, from Nottingham, was on a family holiday in Spain and died on a night out.
body: Tobias White-Sansom died in a Spanish hospital in July 2022 Four years after watching his brother die in his arms, Maximilian White believes new evidence could help him get answers. Tobias White-Sansom, a father-of-two from Nottingham, died in a Spanish hospital in July 2022, five days after a night out in Magaluf, and his family believes the way security and police officers handled him that night led to his death. A blood spatter report and a court order received by the family this month have reignited their hopes that criminal proceedings could commence in the Spanish courts. White told the BBC: "I won't stop until we get justice for Toby." The 46-year-old medical cannabis entrepreneur said he found it difficult to talk about the way he lost his younger sibling, who was on a family holiday at the time. White-Sansom was pinned down at a nightclub following a row over him removing his T-shirt because he was too hot, his family said. They told the BBC the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was called and he was handcuffed, Tasered and injected with tranquilisers before going into cardiac arrest. Tobias White-Sansom's brother said they were both born and raised in Nottingham The family believe the blood spatter evidence - which forms part of an ongoing investigation that will see a court judge decide whether a criminal case is warranted - could suggest external force was used. The report, which analysed White-Sansom's T-shirt, trainers and a sock, said several individual bloodstains were identified, which are compatible both with spatter stains caused through the application of an external force and with drip stains, produced by gravity. An ambulance report, seen by the BBC, states White-Sansom had taken drugs and was agitated. He was administered a number of medications including fentanyl, the report added. The Guardia Civil has not provided any further detail on the death. At the time it issued a statement, saying: "Upon the arrival of the Guardia Civil police, this man was violent and police reduced him to be assisted by medical services. "He was taken to the hospital for treatment. There, once while he was being assisted, he was arrested for a crime of injury." White-Sansom was put in an induced coma Days later, White and the rest of the family were forced to make an agonising decision. "The only thing keeping him alive was the life support machine," he recalled. "And we discussed between our family members and we decided it was inhumane and we should let Toby die naturally. "So then, my decision was to turn the machine off myself, and then my brother died in my arms. "The doctors said he would slip away within five to six minutes, and Toby being the strong-willed person that he was, it took 11 minutes." White (left) says his brother should be here, caring for his family In the four years since, White said he had been trying to reach a resolution. "The whole brutality of the situation caused my brother to pass," he said. "Someone needs to be accountable. "It's accountability. And also, for his children to know that he was a good person, not a drunk tourist in Magaluf." White said on the night in question, his teenage son wanted to go out but he did not want him to go by himself, so White-Sansom accompanied him along with his girlfriend. "What never sat well with me was that my brother was not with a group of lads on a stag do," he said. "It just didn't make sense. That's why I went so heavy in return, because I knew that's not how my brother lived and what he was about." A vigil in White-Sansom's memory gathered crowds in Nottingham city centre back in 2022 White spoke to the BBC days after receiving the evidence and a court order. "The process is extremely gruesome because even when you're getting good news, it's bittersweet - my brother is still not here," he said. "It's just the truth - fighting an uphill battle just to get the truth. At this point, it's a sweet picture but also bitter because Toby is not around." An inquest into White-Sansom's death was also opened in the UK in 2022, and paused while investigations in Spain continued. White believes the new evidence could significantly impact the process but if that fails, he says he will take the matter to the UK. "The truth is out there, the evidence is there, we just need help putting it in front of the right people to get this justice for Toby that's needed," he said. "When you lose a sibling, it's like losing your complete history of who you were and what you stood for," White says The family's lawyer in Spain told the BBC he had never seen a case like this before. "I've never seen a case... with a whole package of circumstances and such a delay," said Jaime Campaner. "I've never seen it and I hope I never see it again." He said he had been filing motion after motion to speed up the process, and said the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was to blame for the delay. The Guardia Civil told the BBC the case was before the court and it had no further comment to make. "The Spanish investigation has been very slow," Campaner added. "And this is not common in a city like Palma, where investigations don't take so long." He said the investigating judge in Spain would now consider the new evidence, and decide whether to proceed as a criminal case or shelve it. "We believe this could be key evidence. We are not aware of the conclusions yet but it might end in results [for] this case," he said. They are yet to be given a date for a court hearing but Campaner estimates the investigating stage would conclude by the end of the year, with a prospective court case starting next year. "We all want to get this case closed and see some justice," said White. "We're hoping that at some point in this chapter, we can close the door on this - and we can close the door on this pain." title: Why did Dolly Parton record a song in Welsh?
description: The cover of smash-hit Jolene, with Welsh and English lyrics, is released on Friday.
body: Dolly's niece Jada Star and Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis say the country star was "proud" to sing in Welsh A Welsh language collaboration between Dolly Parton, her niece Jada Star and singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis might not have been on your bingo card for this year. But their cover of smash-hit Jolene, with Welsh and English lyrics, has been released on Friday. The song, recorded before Parton's death on 25 August, is her second posthumous single. A teaser video released last week shows how Parton spent some time understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation and recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville in early 2025. Lewis, a proud Welsh speaker from Neath, started translating some of her favourite tunes in 2024, landed on the Parton classic and recorded a video of herself singing it. "I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada," Lewis said. Star, also a singer-songwriter, came over to Wales from Nashville and bonded instantly with BBC Radio Wales' Lewis. The teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, as she would get her aunt involved too. Star and Lewis said Parton, who has links to Machynlleth in Powys, was "proud" to sing in Welsh. On the track, Parton recites that "heartbreak sounds the same in every language". You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd. She said she had visited Wales "about three times" and it "felt good because it feels like family", when speaking to WalesOnline. Star revealed one side of the family from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens was initially believed to have come from Conwy. Some of Parton's music may have been inspired by her Welsh roots, according to Star. Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, in Powys, not Conwy as previously thought. Lewis and Star recorded their parts in the UK, while Parton recorded her parts in her studio in Nashville Fans across the world reacted to the news last week. "Really looking forward to hearing this version," one commented "Cannot wait for this," another said while another fan commented "anghygoel", which translates to amazing. This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language. She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011. Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046. title: Teen's life transformed by gene editing
description: Vian, 16, has thalassemia and had to have monthly blood transfusions throughout her childhood.
body: Vian hopes to become a nurse, having spent most of her life surrounded by medical staff A teenager has revealed how her life has been transformed thanks to pioneering gene editing, which reversed symptoms of a crippling blood disorder. Vian, 16, was born with thalassemia, a condition that affects haemoglobin - used by red blood cells to transport oxygen around the body. It left her short of breath and with no appetite. Her own stem cells were edited and she no longer needs the monthly blood transfusions she endured for most of her life. "My whole life's different now. It's changed so much," she said. The treatment, for patients with thalassaemia or sickle cell disease, is offered to young people at three children's hospitals in the country. Vian, from Coventry, was one of the first to have it. Vian previously spent a lot of time in hospital and had to have monthly blood transfusions throughout her childhood Her edited stem cells were returned to her last December, following chemotherapy, and she has now recovered well. "It's much easier for me now. I always have energy to do stuff," Vian explained. "I'm like, ‘mum let's go out’. Before, I would just sleep, always tired." She has started studying health and social care at college, with ambitions of becoming a nurse, having spent most of her life surrounded by medical staff. "I have more options now. Before, I couldn't do most things other kids could," she added. "I usually sat out of PE. I really love PE, but I couldn't do that." Dr Sarah Lawson said the treatment did not cure the disease but allowed patients to be free of transfusions Consultant haematologist Dr Sarah Lawson describes the treatment as a "functional cure" - the disease doesn't go away, but the aspects that caused problems are removed. "We collect the stem cells. They are sent off to a manufacturing laboratory where they are edited...and that changes how those stem cells work and it makes them produce more foetal or baby haemoglobin," she said. "And in a patient with thalassaemia, that allows them to be transfusion free, and [in] a patient with sickle cell disease, it gives them a high baby haemoglobin level, which then negates the problems with the sickle haemoglobin. "When I was at medical school, which was a long time ago, I remember learning a little bit about gene therapy and it being talked about then. And for it now to be a reality 20-odd years later is incredible." JoelSamuel is starting his gene editing journey for the painful effects of sickle cell disease, which have meant many hospital admissions JoelSamuel, 14, from Oldbury, is at the start of his journey. His sickle cell disease leaves him in excruciating pain. Like thalassemia, the disease also involves red blood cells and is usually a lifelong condition, affecting patients' joints and leaving them feeling weak and tired. JoelSamuel's stem cells have recently been collected at Birmingham Children's Hospital. They will be edited and in six months he will have chemotherapy before his edited cells are returned to him. He dreams of being able to enjoy sport. Attempts to do that now make him ill. "I get tired and then the next day I get sick and I won't be able to go to school," he said. He explained that he was initially nervous about having the treatment, but also feels hopeful. "I think it's good to make me better, so I can go and do stuff that takes my energy," he said. Throughout his childhood, JoelSamuel has suffered excruciating pain due to severe effects of sickle cell disease JoelSamuel has suffered a lot. His parents say they are praying the treatment will help him. His father Alfred, who is 47 and runs a logistics company, said: "There are a few patients that have been on it, mainly with thalassemia instead of sickle cell. So we are hoping that we might get the same effects from it. "Hopefully he might be able to play football after all." JoelSamuel's mother Juliet, a 41-year-old seamstress, said: "I just can't wait to see him doing the normal things that everybody does at his age." JoelSamuel's parents Juliet and Alfred thought carefully about the treatment he is having, and feel optimistic Vian has now been discharged from hospital. We asked her if she had a message for JoelSamuel at the start of his treatment journey. "Imagine all the things you can do while being healthy again. "I think you can do it, I did it and so can you. I know it's going to be really hard and the trauma and everything, the nurses, the medicine, everything, but it's worth it." title: 'People use AI to avoid paying for school photos, but they don't realise the consequences'
description: Ian Gilbert says he's heard parents boasting about using AI to take the watermark off his photos.
body: Photographer Ian Gilbert says he's heard parents boasting about how they use AI to take the watermark off to avoid paying for school photos A photographer is warning parents who use artificial intelligence to take the watermark off school pictures about the dangers of how companies can use images of their children. Ian Gilbert, founder of Emotion Picture Photography, said he had heard parents boasting at the school gates about how they use the tool to avoid paying for photos. "The scary thing is when you submit a picture to AI by default it is allowed to do whatever it wants and I don't think a lot of parents realise that," he said. An AI safety expert said he understood why people did it, and that it may seem harmless, but uploading any identifiable information, including photographs, was "not worth the risk". Gilbert, from Pontypool, Torfaen, urged parents to think carefully before uploading their child's photograph to an AI tool. Annual school photographs are a rite of passage but, with technology now able to remove watermarks from preview images in seconds, some parents are bypassing the payment process altogether. "It is theft, it is shoplifting," said 47-year-old Gilbert. "People wouldn't go into a shop and take a tag off something and take it without paying. "It's as though because it's something you can do online at home, it seems to numb it in people's eyes." Ian Gilbert says AI is a "huge issue", especially when taking pictures of groups Gilbert said other photographers were increasingly seeing the same behaviour from parents. He noticed that about 25% of images sent out were being screenshot to be used in AI tools as he is notified when it happens. "That's a quarter of parents not paying. A quarter of profit lost for us. Also the school get a cut from the revenue as well, so it's a loss for the school." The photographer said he had noticed a drop in profits in the past 12 months. He said he heard parents at the school gates talking using AI to avoid paying after he had been inside taking photos. "They were referring to my own photos that I took at the school. "One said 'Are you going to buy the pics?' And the other said 'I'm just going to get AI to remove the watermark off and it only costs me a pound'." He said all people had to do was claim they were the owner of the image in order for the watermark to be removed. Gilbert told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast that he wanted his photos to be affordable so charged from £9. "For the sake of a couple of pounds with AI you're getting such a lower-quality product and ultimately it just makes us have to put prices up again, which is unfair for everyone," he said. "You are constantly fighting and chasing your tail." He added that the company he worked with was working to implement "high-tech methods to beat AI" including putting moving images over photos so they cannot be copied. Dr Simon Thorne, a senior computer science lecturer at Cardiff School of Technologies, urged people, as a general rule, to "never upload any personable identifiable photos". "It's a terrible idea. It's a big risk," he said. "The dataset could get leaked online potentially and your material can be used to train future generations of the model. The image could be sold - you have no idea. "Depending on the service, you may have very little idea how long that image is retained, how it is processed or whether it is reused." Thorne said if the photograph contained other children, it raises an additional issue because their parents may have no idea that an image of their child has been uploaded to an AI system. "We recently had a case where a child was ill and missed a school photograph, so a parent used AI to add them back into the picture afterwards," he said. "I can understand entirely why they did that, but they did not seem to appreciate that uploading and manipulating images of children in this way can carry real privacy and safeguarding risks." Gilbert says when parents screenshot the image and use AI, they get a lower quality picture Gilbert says parents may not know what AI can do with the photo once they "cheat the system" using it to remove the watermark Gilbert says people may not realise that the photographer owns the copyright of that picture, and removing the watermark is theft Theft aside, Gilbert said this method also gave people a low-quality photo. "Our work is not just a quick shot - we have really beautiful set ups and spend a lot of time and money creating images. "Across the board it's getting worse and worse and if it gets to the point where it's not profitable for us, I may have to stop my service." "It's a huge issue, but I don't know how we would attack it. How would you make ChapGPT aware and hold them to account? It feels like a David and Goliath situation." He added that the Guild of Photographers was looking at how they can bring prosecutions to people using such services and not paying. Victoria Welton says parents who used AI to remove watermarks from pictures were stealing photographers' livelihoods Victoria Welton, a photographer based in Crewkerne, works across 15 schools and nurseries in Somerset. She also said many parents were using AI to take the watermark off pictures so they could access them for free. She added they were stealing photographers' livelihoods as well as possibly putting children at risk. "To put your child's photograph through AI makes my blood boil. AI is a system we know nothing about. We don't know where the photo is going," she said. Tessa Chapman says parents using AI is costing her a "huge amount of money" Tessa Chapman, a photographer based in south Somerset, said parents removing watermarks were costing her a "huge amount of money". title: Ban school uniforms in porn, say pupils
description: The pupils from Bicester have launched a petition to end adult content featuring school uniform.
body: The girls' petition has so far received over 26,000 signatures and the pupils have also written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, demanding change. "We're not 'sexy schoolgirls'. We're not objects. We're students, and more importantly, children." A group of teenage girls from Oxfordshire are calling on the government to ban the use of school uniform in pornography. The pupils, from The Cooper School in Bicester, have launched a petition arguing that adult content featuring school uniform is 'a clear example of material that sexualises children and young people'. In April this year, the government agreed new legislation making it a criminal offence to possess or share pornographic content featuring adults pretending to be under 16, as part of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, but it has yet to come into force. "I think the idea of a school uniform is meant to be beautiful, because it's meant to symbolise a community," says 15-year-old Aylin "but I think it's been tarnished… and warped by sexualisation." She is part of the school's Little Feminist Book Club, whose members decided to launch the campaign, arguing that school uniform is used in pornography to "evoke childhood and school-age identities". Willow, 14, doesn't wear her uniform in public if she can avoid it: "I go home and change, because I feel vulnerable." Her peer, 15-year-old Mae agrees, saying she is not comfortable walking down the street in her uniform out of "fear". The girls have written to the prime minister, calling for change Rose, 15, says the issue goes beyond adult content, pointing to "the way the media and society have been portraying school uniform." Mae recalls watching a TV drama aged 12 and seeing a woman in her thirties wearing a 'sexy catholic school girl outfit' to impress a man. "It alluded to sex and I thought to myself, tomorrow I'm going to be wearing a uniform just like that and thinking this is something that makes people sexy, but I'm a child," she said. A 2018 survey of 1,004 girls in the UK found that 35% of 14-21 year-olds said they had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing school uniform in public, according to children's charity Plan International UK. The pupils say that they feel "let down by adults" Since launching the petition, Mae says they have heard from "hundreds upon hundreds" of women sharing their own experiences, with many saying they had "never been more sexualised" than when they were wearing school uniform as children. The petition has so far received over 26,000 signatures and the pupils have also written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, demanding change. "If we can get this banned, over time, all of these small changes will add up to a world where it's less normalised to sexualise children and we'll be safer," says Aylin. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and author of Exposed: The problem of Extreme Porn, welcomes the campaign. "It's raising a national conversation about just how problematic it is that we use school uniforms in mainstream pornography," she says, adding that it is very clearly about "eroticising and sexualising young girls." "The genre of teen pornography is, unfortunately, one of the largest categories in mainstream pornography. But it's not just that - it's also closely associated with more violent and aggressive material." In April this year, the government agreed new legislation making it a criminal offence to possess or share pornographic content featuring adults pretending to be under 16, as part of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, but it has yet to come into force. But McGlynn says school uniform does not necessarily fall into this category. "Where someone says they're pretending to be 17 and in school uniform, that's not covered by the law." She says that does not reflect the reality of how some of this material is presented: "Let's face it, the reality is that school uniforms are trying to portray a young girl." Minister for victims, tackling violence against women and girls and international justice, Alex Davies-Jones, said: "Young women and girls should not have to grow up seeing their school uniforms sexualised, and I commend these pupils for speaking out about something they feel so strongly about. "Pornography must never normalise or glorify the sexual abuse of children. That's why we are changing the law so possessing or sharing pornography which depicts an adult pretending to be a child under 16 will be an imprisonable offence. "This is part of our wider crackdown on harmful pornography and tackling the attitudes that contribute to violence and abuse against women and girls." title: £15m spent cleaning illegal waste supersite in ancient woodland
description: Concerns remain over the ancient Kent woodland's future after 39,500 tonnes of rubbish were cleared.
body: The Hoads Wood site before and after it was cleared of nearly 40,000 tonnes of waste The clearance of a notorious illegal waste "supersite" in Kent has been completed after 15 months at a cost of £15m to the taxpayer. The dump at Hoads Wood, near Ashford, which is on a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) known for rare plants and wildlife, was targeted by criminals who dumped nearly 40,000 tonnes of waste over six months in 2023. It was the first supersite in England to have central government money spent on its clear-up, with work at two other sites bringing the total taxpayer's bill to £26m. The government said the completion of works on Friday showed "just how serious" it was about tackling waste crime and restoring affected countryside. It took 2,500 lorry loads to clear the waste which had been dumped by criminal gangs The Environment Agency-led clean-up operation began in June 2025 and has seen 2,500 lorry loads of waste removed from the woods by specialist contractors to a landfill site in Essex. The countryside charity CPRE Kent, residents and Kent Wildlife Trust joined forces in 2024 to campaign for the clearance of the waste, which was piled up to 15ft (4.6m) in places. They welcomed the work's completion but some are concerned the criminal gangs may return to dump waste. One of the organisers of the 'Rescue Hoads Wood' campaign said the cleared site would now be "catnip" to both organised gangs and opportunist fly-tippers. He told the BBC: "Our biggest fear now is people are going to be able to access this site and start dumping on it again and unless the authorities are quick it will happen again." The Environment Agency (EA) said it was extending the current restriction order in place that prohibits access and had dug ditches to make the site inaccessible to waste trucks. Matthew Higginson, the EA's area environmental manager, said the regulator, police and local authorities had a joint "trigger plan" in place. "That will bring all law enforcement partners to work together closely and much more quickly to stop anything like this happening in the future," he said. The rubbish was illegally dumped in an ancient bluebell woodland Meanwhile, there remain conservation concerns over the future of the countryside site. Ian Rickards, area manager for Kent Wildlife Trust, said it would take decades for ancient woodland species to return. But he added: "It won't recover as it was but there are benefits to this. You've now got open space within the woodland. You've got wet bodies. You've got ponds. You've got these piles of dead wood as well. "All of this will start creating, collecting and attracting wildlife back into here so it'll be fascinating to see how the site recovers." Ian Rickards, from Kent Wildlife Trust, is hopeful new flora and fauna will eventually appear in the woods The Hoads Wood illegal waste site is one of hundreds across England that include a number of so-called "supersites" - those that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish - that were exposed by the BBC earlier this year. As well as the £15m spent on clearing Hoads Wood, another £6m has been spent on the clearance of an illegal supersite in Kidlington, Oxfordshire, and a further £4.8m of taxpayers' money has been allocated to the clear-up of a third site near Wigan. In August, the government launched a national action plan to tackle waste crime, which it estimates costs the country more than £1bn every year. But Hoads Wood campaigners have criticised the authorities for not acting quickly enough when the illegal tipping was first reported at the Kent site. At the height of the activity in the summer of 2023, locals said there were as many as 20 to 30 trucks per day dumping waste at the ancient bluebell woodland. The EA's Matthew Higginson said the agency did respond quickly to reports of the dumping but had to spend time investigating "to make sure we had a robust case to take to court in order to get a restriction order which closed the site". Investigations into who was behind the dumping are ongoing, with three arrests made in February 2025. Environment secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: "This government is taking action on the illegal waste sites that have blighted communities. "Handing this ancient woodland back to local people, alongside our nationwide clean-up of waste sites, shows just how serious we are about restoring the places people love." title: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
description: The price of fuel has soared as the cost of living emerges as a key issue for millions of Americans.
body: Prices for gasoline and diesel have more than doubled since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began in February, affecting transport businesses, farmers and anyone who drives a vehicle in America. Ahead of the critical midterm elections, there have been growing calls for more to be done to reduce the price of fuel, and US President Donald Trump has made several comments and announcements aimed at getting costs down. The question is: what is he able to do with just a few weeks to go before election day - and will it work? Trump's announcement of a waiver on the use of red dye diesel at a campaign stop this week underscored the importance of gas prices in a midterm election dominated by affordability issues. The election comes as there is widespread public concern over the rising costs of fuel, food and other goods. Voters have tied the issue to Trump and his party, weighing down Republicans running in November. Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has contributed to high diesel and gas prices in the US. Global oil supplies have been restricted since the conflict in the Middle East effectively halted the usual flow of oil and refined products through the Strait of Hormuz for months. While the flow of crude oil is nearly back to pre-war levels the price remains above $100 a barrel, and sustained high oil prices have had a knock-on effect for diesel and gasoline. David Ruisard, pricing manager for commodities intelligence firm Argus says the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies, contributing to higher fuel prices. "Our estimates are that your price increase from about $3 a gallon up to $6 a gallon [for diesel] is 60% connected to the Strait of Hormuz, 40% connected to the Russia-Ukraine conflict," he says. Those higher energy prices are responsible for most of the uptick in inflation this year, Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce says, which is pushing up interest rates. "The combined impact of higher rates and higher energy prices is squeezing household budgets and adding to firms' costs," he says. While prices remain high, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracking website GasBuddy said there have been modest declines recently for both gasoline and diesel. "A lot of that is likely due to some of the manoeuvres that we've seen the Trump administration employ over the last couple of weeks," he said. The president announced this week that he would allow so-called red dye diesel - fuel which is used off-road and does not face federal taxes - to be used on US highways without facing federal levies. Ruisard said the only difference in the diesel used by truck drivers and everyday consumers and the tax-free red dye diesel is the dye itself. "The problem with that red dye is, it's extremely hard to clean it out of your tank," he explained. The problem that creates is what happens to trucking companies that use the dyed diesel once the temporary tax relief ends, he said. "The fines are pretty high for having that in your fuel tank because its considered tax evasion." The other issue with expanding the use of red dye diesel, according to Ruisard, is that people and businesses - including rail operators - usually set aside a particular amount of the product. "If suddenly people go out and they start consuming that diesel, that depletes their available supply as well," he said. But another move from Trump has been more successful, according to analysts. Last week, the G7 countries announced they would release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to ease supply concerns, following pressure from Trump to do so. De Haan says the announcement itself – regardless of how much has been released so far – "has worked to push prices down to some degree". Economist Pearce agreed but warned the release is only a temporary solution. "As long as energy exports from the Gulf remain disrupted, stocks will need to be drained further to supply the market," he said. "And the need to refill those stocks will mean energy prices remain elevated for a period, even when disruption in the Middle East clears." Earlier this week, Trump said he was "thinking about" suspending federal tax on gasoline. De Haan said the president has also been imploring states to cut state taxes on gasoline and several have done so, including Ohio and Georgia. State taxes form a "moderate portion" of what consumers pay at the pump, and those reductions have helped reduce prices and national averages, he said. However, suspending or reducing the federal levy on gasoline would require the cooperation of Congress. "That may be difficult to obtain ahead of the midterm elections," said De Haan. It is also a costly measure. De Haan estimated that in Indiana, which cut its tax on gasoline in May, it has cost the state government $1bn (£760m) in lost revenue. Trump has also previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US. While that would provide partial relief in the Gulf and Midwest, according to Pearce, he adds it would be of "little benefit" to the Northeast and West Coast. "The policy risks backfiring because it would result in stockpiling of diesel, and as that storage runs out, refineries would need to cut back on production," he said. "That would raise prices of other energy products, including gasoline." De Haan believes the president has "basically pulled all of the small levers that a president can pull, and we're still seeing prices very elevated". "The only way out of this to reduce gas prices in a meaningful way is solve one or both of the geopolitical tensions that are causing high prices," he said. That means reaching a deal with Iran and helping facilitate an agreement between Ukraine and Russia - which, Pearce said, are issues that cannot be directly controlled by the White House.
