title: Chris Mason: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
description: The Green leader faces pressure over his response to a party motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, as well as his by-election loss.
body: In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time. Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north London, Sagal Abdi-Wali, has quite the story to tell. She arrived in the UK as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s, grew up locally in Camden, became a councillor four years ago, the council leader in May and is now Sir Keir Starmer's successor as the MP. But in the offices of Camden Council at three o'clock this morning, the focus of the press pack, me included, was on Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, as we waited for the result. This constituency has long been a safe Labour seat – the political home of the former prime minister and before that the former cabinet minister Frank Dobson. So a Labour victory here falls in the column marked "relief" for Downing Street rather than "jubilation". Nonetheless, the Greens did very well in local elections in London in May, riding the crest of a political wave which began shortly after Polanski became the party's leader just over a year ago. His failure to win here would have prompted questions from some about stalling momentum, but the party can and does point to the big swing to them since the general election and a result that was by a long way the second best ever result for them at a Westminster by-election. Incidentally, in finishing third the Conservatives have beaten Reform UK for the first time in an English by-election since the general election. It seems likely that Reform's result was hampered by Restore Britain, who managed almost half as many votes as Reform did, in a constituency not very favourable to either party. Follow live updates: Labour wins Holborn and St Pancras by-election, beating Green leader Zack Polanski Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by-election loss But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election – and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend. Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism. The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And – until today at least – he has been repeatedly declining to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up. "He has created a monster he either can't or won't control," was how one Green figure put it to me - this person one among many left furious at what has happened. Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns. Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe. And – significantly – the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas, told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue. She also failed to back him carrying on as leader. Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on". He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people". "I believe that is clearly racist," he added. Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide. And asked if he believed in a two-state solution – an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other – he said "I believe it is not our role to decide". He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together". "No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said. But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party. The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't. Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: As freezing winter approaches, Kyiv residents look for shelter elsewhere
description: A renewed Russian campaign of strikes on power and energy infrastructure has made some contemplate leaving Ukraine's capital.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Olena explains what she cannot live near in order to stay safe As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold. "It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat. With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far. "There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this." Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand. "Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said. "Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads." Wreckage from Russian drones can be found on the streets of the capital After weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation". The attacks, he said, were "tearing Kyiv apart". Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too. "I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says. Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision. A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided. "People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter." Iryna's young daughter Polina is struggling to cope and suffers from anxiety Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding. For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent. Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope. "Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK." The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties. "We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says. Iryna and Polina's home is in this apartment block on the edge of the capital The first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation. Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking. "Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling." Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland. "Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says. For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside. Olena Konoplia says she is already sleeping better since her move to a more remote location Olena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital. "I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains. "Everything that can be a Russian target." On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door. In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home. The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation. At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most. "After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good." Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her. "She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains. title: Cars torched and shops looted as anti-migrant violence erupts in South Africa
description: South Africa has experienced recurrent outbreaks of violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.
body: Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses remained shut At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say. Clashes broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast. The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling requiring the government to remove barriers that had prevented some migrants from applying for asylum. South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries. 'We have to prioritise South Africans': Anti-migrant movement blocks foreigners from healthcare The uniformed group targeting foreigners in South Africa Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban. Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said. In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications. Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors. "There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added. Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers. Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property. In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals. Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported. Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence. The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction. The latest unrest follows a July ruling by South Africa's Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines. The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents. It has prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration. Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status. Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa. Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks. Earlier this year, anti-immigration groups staged weeks of demonstrations demanding that undocumented foreign nationals leave the country by 30 June. The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments. South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals. The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce. Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence. Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities. title: Nvidia-backed AI data centre firm scraps landmark listing over market fears
description: Firmus said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions".
body: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings. The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests. Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn). One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said. Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta. It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region. The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street. Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment. The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear. A humming annoyance or jobs boom? Life next to 199 data centres AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost? UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO. "We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors. He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans. "It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment, thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability. OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to. There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more. That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create. In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public. The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each. AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought. description: Labour Party has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, with Sagal Abdi-Wali receiving 12,292 votes.

title: ICE agent shoots man in New York City
description: The Department of Homeland Security said ICE was arresting a "criminal illegal alien"; New York's mayor said early reports suggested a five-year-old child was in the car at the time.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Protesters gather in New York where person was shot by ICE A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the agency, confirmed an ICE officer "discharged his weapon" during "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien". In a statement, it added the man was alive and at a local hospital. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said it was an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation". "Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. We believe the child was physically unharmed," he said. The BBC has approached DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks. Late on Thursday evening, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken to President Donald Trump about the shooting and had expressed "outrage on behalf of New Yorkers". "I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth." Trump has not yet commented publicly on the shooting. The DHS said the man, who has not been named by officials, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession". It also claimed he was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group. FBI officers could be seen searching a car at the scene on Thursday night Mayor Mamdani, meanwhile, said he would ask Donald Trump to end ICE enforcement actions in the city. "I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities," he wrote on X on Thursday evening. A group of protesters gathered at the scene on Thursday evening, chanting "we want justice" and "ICE off our streets now". What is ICE and what powers do its agents have to use force? title: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers say
description: Pike's lawyers say her recovery is "remarkable" as they give an update on her condition after she survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospital Christa Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition. In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said. "Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said. The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection. "Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team says "Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said. Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover. They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer". Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess". Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison. Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people. Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method? A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state. On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels. The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution. She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong. Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole. Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death. Could the US death penalty ever die out? title: 'Stark warning' over ADHD and 'Andrew wins legal fight'
description: A government review of ADHD and austism diagnoses and the police investigation into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor lead Friday's papers.
body: This paper review contains spoilers from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. Several of today's papers lead with the government's review of ADHD and autism diagnoses. A "stark warning over rising demand for NHS autism and ADHD care" tops the Guardian. Elsewhere, it reports that two Latvians have been arrested after they were "found inside RAF base". And, after it was revealed that the three sisters who died in the Brighton sea had taken their own lives, the paper describes their "final pilgrimage". The Times also leads with the report, highlighting one of its conclusions - that an ADHD label risks causing "harm for life" to young people. In defence news, following the series of arrests at UK air bases, the Times adds that the country's most senior military officer "insists" the bases are secure. The i Paper has picked up that the ADHD and autism review "calls for medication and benefits shake-up as diagnoses surge". It also notes that it has found mental health conditions are not overdiagnosed "at scale". The Daily Mail also headlines on the government report on ADHD and autism, noting the "toll on those wrongly given label". It carries a picture of the Duchess of Sussex with Malala Yousafsai, saying the pair had a "cosy Claridge's tea". The Independent leads with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor after he "wins legal fight over police raid on his homes". The High Court has ruled a "significant error" was made in the application for a warrant to search his residences, it writes. This is "no sweat" for the "Andy cops", according to the Sun. It says Thames Valley Police will continue their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor after the "warrant gaffe". The picture of the former prince looking alarmed while lying back in a car after being released from custody is splashed across its front. The Daily Telegraph has spoken to friends of Mountbatten-Windsor who say his "fightback starts now". A warning from the Governor of the Bank of England not to "risk repeat of Truss chaos" heads up the Daily Telegraph's front page ahead of the Budget. The paper also reports that Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch's name appeared "on list at home of Widdecombe murder suspect". The Daily Mirror says "Andrew cops blunder but.. it's not over". A picture of Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband hugging a child in Ukraine is captioned on his "fury at Putin". The Daily Express leads with coverage of the early prisoner release scheme, saying domestic abuse campaigners "slam" the policy. "Failed by a system that should protect you" reads its headline, writing that survivors of domestic abuse are "living in terror". The Metro headlines with "not 100% faithful", writing that a Royal Navy sailor has appeared in court after "allegedly plotting to pass British secrets to Russia". Teddy Young, a specialist in warfare intelligence, has been "accused of being a spy". Investor optimism in OpenAI has been dampened, writes the FT, citing a "$20bn cut to annualised revenues" as the source of discontent. It also covers the bus bombing in Kramatorsk, Ukraine yesterday, in which a Russian strike killed "dozens". The Daily Star headlines with "You Only Drink Twice" as it says James Bond actor Daniel Craig has bought a pub. The paper also trails some spoilers for the third episode of Celebrity Traitors. title: 'I rage and I don't care': Why women are reclaiming their anger
description: Studies suggest women are getting angrier, but are they just more open about it?
body: Music artist Chess Galea says she no longer hides her anger Music artist Chess Galea used to suppress any feelings of anger, fearing she would be branded as "hysterical" or "difficult to work with". From the "mental load" women carry to sexism in the workplace or - worse - violence against women, Galea says "we don't realise how much we accept and how much we close our mouths". But now she says she simply lets it out: "If someone catcalls me in the street, I rage. I don't care." Galea, 34, is one of an increasing number of women in the UK reporting feeling angrier than ever. In 2024, one in five British women reported being angry during a lot of the previous day, external, up from one in 10 in 2020. For nearly two decades, more women than men worldwide have reported experiencing daily anger, and the gap has been growing, external. So are women actually feeling more anger - and what is driving that shift - or are they just more open about it? It's a bit of both, suggests psychotherapist Jennifer Cox, author and co-host of the Women are Mad podcast. She started researching anger after suspecting her female clients' suppression of it was the root cause of some of their physical conditions. "There was this pattern of women coming in with migraines, stomach issues, musculoskeletal and immune issues. Ultimately it was hard to ignore," she says. "They were trying to keep their kids on track, look after their mental health and somehow do their job [too]." Jennifer Cox started to run anger processing groups for women Cox later ran group sessions where many women let out pent-up feelings of anger. "We've been brought up with this ridiculous 'good girl' stuff… indoctrinated in this idea of being good, polite, kind, thoughtful, caring," she says. "The big change from previous generations is that we are expected to do it all." While almost as many women work as men, they spend nearly an hour longer each day doing unpaid work such as chores or caring responsibilities, the Office for National Statistics says. On top of that is the "mental load", the invisible labour of keeping a household running that often falls to women. There are also more positive representations of angry women in the media. Previously, characters like Alex Forrest (played by Glenn Close) in Fatal Attraction or Carrie (Sissy Spacek) in Stephen King's horror classic would often be portrayed as unstable and dangerous. But today, female rage is increasingly positioned as understandable and even liberating. Characters like Alex Forrest (played by Glenn Close) in Fatal Attraction would often be portrayed as unstable and dangerous Take Lily Allen's 2025 album West End Girl, which graphically documented the end of her marriage to actor David Harbour, as well as artists such as Charli XCX, Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan releasing songs featuring violent imagery and even screams of rage. Lily Allen's 2025 album West End Girl graphically documented the end of her marriage to actor David Harbour Singers such as Chappell Roan are releasing songs featuring violent imagery and even screams of rage On screen, even 2023's smash-hit Barbie showed the iconic doll expressing frustration with her supposedly picture-perfect world. These depictions of women's anger are helpful and healthy, Cox says. But when women act upon their anger in real life, they can face a social penalty. A 2020 study found women expressing anger at work were seen as less deserving of status and influence, while their male counterparts were not. So, can women express anger at work and still get ahead? Yes, says life coach Yann Dang, who specialises in coaching senior women in male-dominated fields. Women who people-please and don't show negative emotion can progress to a certain level on the career ladder, but to make it to the top you need to rock the boat, she argues. "Women are so good at learning the rules when we know what the rules are. But the rules in the corporate world are totally different." The key, she says, is knowing how to harness your anger in a way that comes across as authentic. Life coach Yann Dang advises women to 'build the muscle' of standing up for themselves Dang suggests women use direct language such as "That's a hard no for me"; "I don't like that"; and "I'm frustrated too." She also advises them to "build the muscle" of standing up for themselves, even if they don't have a perfectly polished response ready. Alongside everyday sexism, ongoing threats including stalking, harassment and domestic abuse serve as powerful factors uniting women in anger and defiance. Violence against women and girls accounts for nearly 20% of all recorded crime in England and Wales, but it often goes unreported. For Galea, being able to discuss her experience of misogyny in the music industry as well as the sexual assault she was a victim of more openly with other women has helped to crystallise the frustration she feels. "I think we've been angry for a long time but now we can access others because of social media," she says. Psychologist Dr Tara Brach agrees anger has its place. "The key thing is under anger there's something we care about. Anger is a messenger, it brings us energy to protect, confront injustices, set boundaries, to make a change. "It becomes unhealthy when it possesses us, or when we act in ways that harm." To channel it effectively, Brach advocates mindfulness, in particular the "RAIN" strategy - recognise the emotion, allow yourself to experience it, investigate the cause, and nurture feelings of understanding. title: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
description: "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it," the US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Thursday.
body: The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said. An official from the Defense Department told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed. The Pentagon had announced earlier this week that it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said on Thursday. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012 Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be". Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd." Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said on Monday that the defence secretary had made the recommendation and Trump approved it. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution. The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two. Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted in court that he was the gunman in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. The shooting on 5 November 2009 took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. At court Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan. Fort Hood attacker to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two There is no modern-era precedent for having a public execution, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death. "It looks to me designed to be a grotesque spectacle," he said. "It's an unprecedented decision in the modern era, and so it is on uncertain legal terrain," he added. A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgment on its legality to move forward. The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution. As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened. "Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added. Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses. But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods. A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says. "More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore." Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-redistricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing. It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content. I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows. While Trump has never publicly advocated for a public execution, he has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, for example, he took out large ads in The New York Times calling for the execution of the Central Park Five - who had been convicted of rape and assault charges but were later exonerated. Trump has previously condemned public executions in Iran, and has cited the Iranian government's potential killing of protesters as a possible justification for military intervention before attacking the country earlier this year. The US government had not executed anyone for 17 years until the final year of Trump's first term as president, when the government conducted a flurry of 13 executions. Upon returning to office last January, Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions and signed an executive order aimed at "restoring" the death penalty and "protecting public safety". The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
description: A new film paints the Meta founder as a villain. But the tech firm seems immune to bad publicity, writes our North America tech correspondent.
body: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming? Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful. "Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make." Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists. It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company. For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users. That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case. And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him. This year Meta unveiled Muse, its AI companion app, alongside a Tamagotchi-like wearable device that allows users to talk to it His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned". Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole. But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant. It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it? It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta. Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users. Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed. And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube. Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution. Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to one review of The Social Reckoning In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant. And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes. The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users. Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight. Meta faces lawsuits over its handling of young social media users. Outside one case in California this summer, protesters highlighted the names of young people they say died as a result of social media harms. Meta disputes many of the claims To some, the trust issue feels existential "Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business. "It feels like… the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover." But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025. title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire breaks silence to BBC
description: Vitalii Zhykovych gives his own account of the attempted assassination of Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev.
body: Vitalii Zhykovych appeared in open court during the summer and has spoken to the BBC from prison A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency. In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time. Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle". Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent". A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head. But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her. He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut. Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych. Ukrainian agent accused of murdering Monaco bomb suspect changes story For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent. Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev. He understood it was an official mission. "As Reut informed me, this operation […] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says. Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused – he says she was not fully trained – Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead. Vladyslav Reut initially confessed but then changed his testimony Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives. The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that is it "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies. The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer". Two screengrabs from a surveillance video captured Anastasia Berezovska just before and during the explosion Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep. It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force. Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack. He called for "the truth, protection, and justice". Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol. She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine. Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting. The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling. After the Monaco blast, police released an image of Berezovska caught on CCTV The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories. They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine. Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine. Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case. Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us. He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea. "In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison. Zhykovych (C) spoke publicly for the first time at a recent custody hearing in Kyiv Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia. But might this story be even murkier? At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present. At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised". "Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining. Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court. Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets. When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason. As the investig

title: Why are more roofs not made of solar tiles?
description: Solar tiles were touted as an attractive alternative to solar panels - why have they not taken off?
body: From installer to instructor Kate Collardson (left) has a long history in solar systems Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges. She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor. For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles. This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance. For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs, external. This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes, external. Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry. Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity. Tesla abruptly stopped marketing its solar tiles in August For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US. Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20–30% since it was established in 2019. In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat. Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently". Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels. The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'." Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup. She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where. "With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however. But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road." Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof. Freesuns solar tiles on the Lycée Jean-Piaget in Neuchâtel, Switzerland Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller. Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance. Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour." Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy. Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes. While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save". But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs. "Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany. A solar roof can cost twice as much as installing solar panels While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent. One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology. This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires. This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains. In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible. Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size." Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says. What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique. title: Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'
description: Steamy jokes have flooded social media ahead of the release of the actress's latest film.
body: Olivia Colman stars alongside Alexander Skarsgård in new film Wicker It has already been described as 2026's weirdest rom-com, external. And new film Wicker has sparked a deluge of viral memes and steamy jokes that have flooded social media ahead of its release. Speaking to the BBC at its London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman said she never expected such a big reaction. "No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said. "But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking." The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman (Colman) living in a medieval village. Tired of constantly being mocked for being single, she hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker. Enter Skarsgård - but not as you've ever seen him before. As the "wicker husband", he emerges as a strapping, dashing life-size piece of furniture. And he proves to be a devoted partner, and passionate lover, sparking jealousy among the other village women. The film has an A-list cast, with other stars including Peter Dinklage as the basket weaver, Elizabeth Debicki as the tailor's wife, and Richard E Grant as the village doctor. Since the release of the trailer, there's been a huge buzz online around the film - from BookTok and FilmTok fans swooning over Skarsgård’s character, to questions being asked over splinter risks during the film's erotic scenes. Swedish giant Ikea even got involved, posting photos of its rattan furniture on Instagram in a nod to the film, with the caption “husband material”. When asked why she thinks people are so fascinated and so thirsty for the wicker husband, Colman answered: "We all love a little bit of escapism. That's what film is beautiful for. "And it's magical, and a bit of fantasy, and people love that, especially currently. What's not to love about a little bit of escapism and fantasy?" She also said it was the film's originality that drew her to it. "You get a lot of scripts through the post, and you feel like you've seen a bit before. And this, I really hadn't seen this before, so I was excited," she said. Like Colman, Debicki agrees that Skarsgård is the main reason the film has lit up the internet. "I think it was a lot to do with Alex in a wicker man costume, really," she told the BBC. "I think that's something that apparently everybody would like to see." But Skarsgård himself gives all the credit to the designers of the outfit. "All I had to do was get stuck into it," he says. He also said the sex scenes were "super fun" to shoot. "We wanted those moments when the bed crashes and breaks, and the way they comment on that in the scene is quite comedic," he said. "But [the characters] also have tender moments and sexy moments, it was great." The steamy new rom-com has been causing a stir at film festivals The film is based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones. After its premiere at Sundance film festival earlier this year, The Guardian awarded it, external two stars, praising the "eye-catching premise" but cautioning that there was "too much wood but not enough fire". But The Hollywood Reporter, external was more positive, calling it "a warming, sometimes poignant pleasure". Away from the social media buzz, the film's stars say it also taps into deeper themes, from gender roles to breaking societal rules. "It's very funny and strange and wonderful, but I find it very moving. And it's a good one to discover beyond the Ikea memes," said Debicki. "It touches on a lot of stuff. Hierarchy, social structure," said Skarsgård. "But it's done with such a light touch." "It's about love, and it is funny, but it's also a romance, and it very gently laughs at the sort of traditions we have in marriage and community," said Colman. "I think it's something that you will come out and discuss a lot." Wicker is released in UK cinemas on October 30. title: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players
description: Viewers watched to see whether Richard E Grant could save himself at the first round table of the series.
body: Actress Sharon Rooney was visibly shocked to find which players returned to breakfast during Thursday's episode Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall. Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote. His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table. "Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true." There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!" Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!" But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion. Myha'la winked at Richard E Grant before voting for him - which was picked up by some other players Ross Kemp, meanwhile, was a scary level of delighted to have rumbled Grant Julie Hesmondhalgh noticed Myha'la ostentatiously winking at Grant before she voted for him, which later prompted the former Coronation Street actress to make one of the most impassioned - but mistaken - speeches of the night. "It was traitor-on-traitor," she declared (it wasn't). "I don't know if anybody else saw it," (we did). "I am so excited because I truly believe we can get two in a row," (don't count on it). Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it? Traitors commit first murder as Grant tries to save his skin Celebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses? The remaining traitors, Maya Jama and James Acaster, met in the turret later with the choice of murdering previously shortlisted players Jerry Hall and Hannah Fry, or seducing a third traitor to replace Grant. The pair ultimately decided to recruit mathematician Fry, who had the most wonderful and meme-able reaction when she found out that, not only was she not being murdered, she was being seduced. Accepting the offer, Fry joined Jama and Acaster in the turret, exclaiming as she learned their identities: "I had both of you down as faithful!" The new trio discussed how they would approach breakfast the next morning, before Acaster delivered the line of the episode. "It's changing a lot, this Traitors," he observed of the fluid line-up. "It's like the Sugababes." "I managed to checkmate myself," said Grant, "which as far as I'm aware, has never been done" Mathematician Hannah Fry was shocked to find she was being recruited instead of murdered The next morning, there were shocked faces when the players realised everybody had made it to breakfast unscathed, with the celebrities concluding that one player must have been recruited. "It was fascinating seeing Jerry and Hannah come back," said Miranda Hart. "Hannah seemed different, as if something new has happened to her." Oh yes? "I definitely clocked a nervousness in her, which is very interesting." We could have a first-rate traitor hunter on our hands here. But would any of Hart's fellow players feel the same way? "Poor Hannah," said McNally, "she's been recruited." Uh-oh. As the theories continued to float around across various sub-meetings, with Hesmondhalgh, Bella Ramsey and several others setting their sights on Myha'la, the celebrities headed out to the next mission. Presenter Claudia Winkleman explained the latest task would see them use a battering ram to break down the doors of four crypts, where they could find money to add to the prize pot - and also potentially bag some shields. James Blunt immediately took control, assigning players various roles. "He was full army officer," Hart observed. "I found it mildly erotic." "I don't think I've ever used a battering ram," Joe Lycett reflected. "I would use a battering ram to get into [Wicked star] Jonathan Bailey's house, but that's it." Miranda Hart joked that she found James Blunt's command of the latest task "mildly erotic" Myha'la and Fry entered one crypt, found a shield and debated who should keep it. They agreed on Myha'la, partly because she had grabbed it first, although she sweetly suggested that the pair could keep it secret from the other players to protect both of them. Jama and Sharon Rooney, meanwhile, scored two further shields, but the players then found that some shields would have to be given up anyway in order to unlock the final chest of prize money. Rooney and Myha'la surrendered theirs, but traitor Jama quietly held on to hers. The other players didn't know she had one, and the TV presenter asked Rooney to keep it secret. That decision could come back to bite her in later episodes. In the cars on the way back, the players continued to debate various hunches, with one particularly awkward journey where Myha'la and Hesmondhalgh admitted they were suspicious of each other. "I feel like you've been a little bit vague," said Hesmondhalgh. "That's only because I've thought it's been you from day one," Myha'la replied. title: 'Add me to WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
description: The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" that appear to lead to a recruitment scam.
body: The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam. The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July. But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and told BBC Radio 4's You and Yours it was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise. The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog. The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number. Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work. Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages. "Mostly likely it would be a recruitment scam," he said. You and Yours added one of these numbers on WhatsApp and received this message "They would either put you through to a fake job listing, which might involve some form of money muling. It could look like a completely legitimate job, or something ad hoc, but they might pass criminal funds through your account which can lead to terrible consequences. "It could also be a simple phishing exercise - criminals send out these messages, and what they really want to know is who's picking up, who's active - that information can be resold on the dark web. "The possibilities are endless. At the end of the day this is a criminal that has reached out to you and they're trying to defraud you in some way shape or form." Andy Curry, the ICO's head of criminal investigations, told the BBC he believed the calls were coming from abroad. "We are trying to find who is behind this, why they're doing it and the impact it's having on members of the public," he said. The number of complaints received by the ICO would only be a small proportion of the totals affected, he said. "We think there are probably millions of people who are receiving these messages, which appear to us to be largely indiscriminate. "I've had them, my colleague who's leading the investigation has had them. It's likely to be tip of the iceberg." 'I lost my savings after a job interview scam' Rise in reports of 'shameful' recruitment scams Fell said that mobile companies were "working on a range of fronts" to tackle the influx of automated calls. This includes sending intelligence reports to the regulator Ofcom, working with law enforcement, and liaising with Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because if someone does follow up on the request to add the number to the encrypted platform, "any dialogue that happens between you and the criminal then can't be investigated any further". A WhatsApp spokesman said there were features in place to protect its users from scam calls, including silencing calls from unknown numbers. He also said WhatsApp banned millions of accounts each year for "malicious behaviours", such as bulk account registration or automated messaging. While these calls typically appear to be from a UK mobile number, Fell said these numbers will be imitated, or spoofed, by the criminals behind the scam. Last November, the UK government promised, external that call spoofing would be eliminated within a year. A Home Office spokesman said the government was taking "robust action" to tackle scams. "We remain committed to delivering the Telecommunications Charter, alongside industry, by November," he added. title: Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?
description: The developing El Niño may impact the UK's weather prospects this autumn and winter but cold conditions are far from guaranteed.
body: Widespread snow driven by a polar vortex is rumoured to be heading for the UK this autumn and winter. But is that really the case? Headlines have been suggesting it is down to the effects of El Niño but the truth is much more complicated. For the rest of the autumn, El Niño actually increases the chance of wet, mild and potentially stormy weather for the UK. Later in winter it could shift the odds towards cold and snow, something that can be influenced by changes in the polar vortex but none of this is certain. The polar vortex is a ring of strong westerly winds encircling the North Pole every winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) above the Earth's surface. It forms because the air high above the Pole becomes extremely cold and dense in winter. The contrast with warmer air further south drives the very strong stratospheric winds that make up the polar vortex. This is all going on high up in the stratosphere, far above the troposphere - where our weather actually happens. A strong polar vortex tends to encourage a strong polar jet stream in the troposphere. This drives areas of low pressure from west to east, bringing mild air from the Atlantic across the UK with spells of wind and rain. The coldest air is essentially locked away to the north of us. Disruptions to the polar vortex can cause the jet stream to change shape increasing the chance of cold winter weather affecting the UK Sometimes, however, the polar vortex can wobble, weaken or even reverse direction. Over a period of days and weeks this can work its way down through the atmosphere influencing our jet stream, causing it to weaken, become more bendy or reverse. It can deliver colder northerly or easterly winds which can bring the UK its coldest winter weather However, it does not always translate into changes in weather patterns at the Earth's surface. Equally, periods of a meandering jet stream and cold winter weather often occur without significant changes in the polar vortex. El Niño - the naturally-occurring climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean - is continuing to grow and by some measures is already the strongest on record. The heat released from the warm Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere impacts weather patterns around the globe. In autumn it increases the chance of wet and stormy weather in the UK - something that is reflected in the forecasts for this season. In late winter, the waves of energy released by El Niño can move upwards through the atmosphere making it more likely that the polar vortex becomes disrupted, increasing the chance of ice and snow. However, the links are unclear and the evidence is mixed. The so-called Big Freeze of 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest winter in three decades - and coincided with an El Niño. However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and was unseasonably warm. The so-called Beast from the East in 2018 actually occurred during a La Niña year, effectively the opposite of El Niño. So while El Niño is already having big impacts on global weather, and may influence the polar vortex later in winter, snow and ice in the UK is far from guaranteed. Current forecasts suggest no significant cold or snow is likely in the near future. You can read the latest outlook for the next month here.
