title: Teenager who lost mum says she no longer feels alone in her grief
description: About 100 school children have taken part in an art project to help them deal with bereavement.
body: Niamh is a 17 year old pupil at St Patrick's High School in Keady Until recently 17-year-old Niamh says she would often feel alone while dealing with the loss of her mother who died a few years ago. But now she says creating art and talking to other young people has helped her process that grief. She is one of about 100 teenagers who have taken part in a project to help them deal with bereavement and loss. Through storytelling and art, young people are encouraged to think about signs of grief with fellow pupils and are offered ways to cope with their feelings. Niamh said: "The whole experience just made me more comfortable to talk to others about grief and I built a lot of strong friendships from it. "I think it has just helped make me a more resilient person overall and more comfortable with expressing my feelings." Pupils created a memory tree consisting of leaves representing the loved ones they had lost Niamh, who is a pupil at St Patrick's High School in Keady, County Armagh, says meeting other young people dealing with grief she could "relate to", helped her understand it better. "Now you can see them around school, and they would know if you're not okay and come to talk to you, so that has been really nice." The Seasons of Life workshops are run by the Southern Health and Social Care Trust and have been piloted at several schools in counties Armagh and Tyrone during the last year. This video can not be played Joe is a year 10 pupil at St Patrick's who took part in the project Joe, a year 10 pupil at St Patrick's, also took part in the project after the loss of his aunt. "I liked that you could talk about your feelings without anybody judging you. "I never felt I had to worry about what I was saying, because other people taking part had also lost someone. "I'm also really happy and proud of some of the art we produced together." St Patrick's pupil Ailicia, 17, recently lost her grandfather One of the projects involved students writing their loved ones' names on paper symbolising a leaf and hanging it on a tree they had made together. 17-year-old Ailicia recently lost her grandfather. She says she found the project "healing" as it was close to the anniversary of his death. "Putting my grandad's name up on our tree felt quite comforting, and it gave me a sense of it being a special way to remember him. "One of the big things I've taken away from it is that when you lose someone grief is a completely normal way to feel and I felt better talking about it." Pupils at St Patrick's in Keady final art project which is displayed in their school Glennis Doherty is Vice Principal at St. Patrick's High School and says the project has had an immeasurable impact on the pupils that took part. "It has really helped them understand that just like the seasons of the year, there are times when we all feel happy, confident and there are other times we experience conflict, anxiety and loss. "So the project was a chance for them to explore those feelings in a safe space and develop the emotional skills to deal with them." She says pupils have taken away the skills of "resilience and self-expression" and were using them beyond school. "It has hopefully helped them realise that asking for help is a strength and not a weakness." Glennis Doherty is Vice Principal at St. Patrick's High School in Keady One of those behind the project is Dr Sinead Hannan, Assistant Head of Psychology Services at the Southern Trust. She believes bereavement is a public health issue that isn't talked about enough. "In the UK, the parent of a child who are under 18 dies every 22 minutes, and we know from research that 80% of children don't access psychological intervention whenever they need it. Dr Sinead Hannan is Assistant Head of Psychology Services at the Southern Trust "So this means often that children are grieving silently and sometimes on their own, and we know the early intervention around grief can change the trajectory of a child's life. "We wanted to make a difference to a child's grief journey and that's where the project came from. "The main thing we wanted from the project was peer connection, so if somebody is walking down the corridor, the children know they're not on their own and other people are experiencing grief just like they are." As part of their final artwork project, students in St Patrick's worked with an artist on a large mixed-media collage that included a tree representing growth and a heart representing support. The piece has now been given pride of place in the corridor beside the school's sensory garden. Ailicia (pictured left) and Niamh (pictured right) with their final art project Ailicia says the fact the artwork has been displayed in their school for other pupils to see is important. "People might say it's just a picture, but every time I walk past, it makes me very proud, because it's part of my journey." The Southern Trust said that subject to funding being made available, it would like to extend the Seasons of Life project into primary schools. title: ADHD and autism at risk of over-diagnosis, says government review
description: The review, which focuses on younger people, warned there was a risk society was moving from an era of under-diagnosis to over-diagnosis.
body: There is a risk of people being over-diagnosed with ADHD and autism, an official review in England has found. Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups. The review called for tougher regulation of private firms offering assessments for the NHS, saying they had concerns about quality and consistency, and a ban on advertising. It concluded economic uncertainty combined with social media was driving an increase in mental health problems among young people and said there needed to be better support in place for all conditions. The review - led by leading doctors in the field - was ordered 10 months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off". It looked at people of all ages, but particularly focused on young people and children who have the highest rates of diagnoses. It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training. The experts said too often diagnoses of mental health problems and ADHD and autism were ending up as labels that defined people by their "difficulties rather than their strengths and potential", harming their prospects at school, in work and in relationships. Children diagnosed with autism and ADHD before the age of 17 are around four times more likely to end up not in education, employment or training between 16 and 24. With better support after diagnosis, they could be helped to live more fulfilling lives, the review said. Alongside access to therapies, this should also include support for mental health – significant numbers also struggle with conditions such as depression. But the review found people were also being harmed by long waits for diagnosis for mental health and ADHD and autism. The Watsons are just one family who have experience of this. Ryan and his wife knew there was something different with their son Atlas when he was around 12 to 18 months old and missing development milestones. But it took three years to get an autism assessment. As time passed, his needs became increasingly clear. Now nearly seven, Atlas is non-verbal, still wears nappies and relies on others for all aspects of daily care. Despite this, Ryan said there was no fast-track route for children with the most complex needs. "You basically go on the list and wait however long until you get to the top." The wait left the family racing against time to secure support before Atlas started school. Ryan and his wife feared he would be placed in a mainstream school. "We were terrified," Ryan says. "Anyone who has a child like Atlas will have the same panic that they'll start in a mainstream school where it's not safe." The strain was immense. "It was like I had two jobs," Ryan says. "I was going to work and then coming home and dealing with these things." Atlas was eventually diagnosed only months before starting school. Ryan and his son Atlas, who waited three years for an assessment for autism To ensure families like the Watsons get quicker assessment, the review calls for reassessment of those on waiting lists to ensure people with the highest needs are prioritised first and to look at whether some could be removed and offered other kinds of non-medical support. This could include adjustments being made at school or in workplaces and lifestyle support, such as help to improve sleep or address anxiety, it said. Too often, access to help requires a diagnosis, with experts highlighting changes in 2014 that required parents to get a diagnosis of autism and ADHD to qualify their children for extra support in schools. Review chair Prof Peter Fonagy said it was clear the system was "under immense strain" and it was time to get away from diagnosis being a "very narrow pathway" to finding support. "Diagnosis remains essential and must be protected - what has to change is that it is no longer the only door through which help can be reached." The review said not every difficulty required a medical response and there was a risk of blurring the lines between diagnosable ADHD and autism and what should be considered the normal human variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour. It said there was a risk society was now moving from an era of under-diagnosis to over-diagnosis or mis-diagnosis, pointing to data showing more than 4% of children aged six to 17 were now diagnosed with autism, well above the 1-2% that studies suggest is the true level. But it said because some of these figures date back nearly a decade it was not possible to be absolutely certain or conclude over-diagnosis was currently occurring at scale. Mel Merritt, of the National Autistic Society, said the report shows that successive governments "have failed autistic people". "The harm and distress autistic people are facing is real and widespread and there is a desperate need to build a system that supports the needs of autistic people." Abigail Ampofo, of charity YoungMinds, said: "For years, young people have told us they feel blamed for their mental health or accused of making it up. We hope this review goes some way to show them their distress is not their fault and the systems around them are failing." But she said that would require major reform. The government welcomed the publication of the report and said it would be setting out a new model of providing support in its forthcoming mental health strategy, which is expected before the end of the year, and also promised to introduce tougher regulation of ADHD and autism assessments. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "Professor Fonagy's review has shown the importance of early intervention to address mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions and the huge distress these can cause." title: Business Daily
description: Economic conditions around the world are making young people rise up in protest
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. title: Head of maternity review says 'we will listen to parents'
description: The woman leading a national review into maternity services in Scotland promises her work will consider parents' experiences.
body: A review of maternity services in Scotland started this week and will report back next summer The head of a major review of maternity services has reassured bereaved parents their voices will be heard as part of her work. Families had expressed concern the forward-looking national review of services in Scotland would not take into account how they felt failed by the NHS. But Prof Christine McCourt told BBC Scotland talking to a range of people would be valuable in "drawing the right lessons for improvement". The Scottish government said the review, which got under way this week and is due to report back next summer, would consider the "direct experiences of women, families and staff at every level of care". The review was ordered by ministers a year ago following a BBC Disclosure investigation highlighting failings in maternity care across Scotland. In the film, Lori Quate shared his experience of losing his wife Jacqui Hunter in 2020. Jacqui Hunter died giving birth to her stillborn daughter, Olivia Jacqui died at Ninewells hospital in Dundee while giving birth to their stillborn daughter, Olivia. She had been given an overdose of a drug to bring on labour, and an NHS review found that it could have been a factor in her death. The Scottish government announced an independent national review of maternity care a month after the documentary heard calls from families, NHS staff and experts for urgent action to improve safety. 'My wife died in childbirth but wasn't told she'd been given labour drug overdose' As the review got under way this week, Lori said it was not clear what would feed into its findings. "The biggest concern was that the phrase 'forward-looking' seems to necessitate a limited involvement of families who have been through the mill of this culture of failings," he said. "How are they going to face forwards if they're not willing to hear from the families?" "I understand you can't go looking at every single individual case if it's about changing the system," he added. "But a case like Jacqui and Olivia's is almost exemplary of the systemic rot and failings that prevail throughout the entire system." Professor Christine McCourt is leading the review McCourt, a professor of maternal and child health at City St George's at the University of London, is chairing the review. She said it was important to hear from parents with both negative and positive views. "It's not part of our remit to investigate individual cases," she said. "But there's a great potential to learn from people's experience, especially if you actually talk to a range of people. "You can draw out the patterns in the general lessons. What led to a poor outcome in the first place, and then what happened afterwards? "Are parents getting honest, useful explanations? Are they getting support?" The review will also build on themes that have emerged from safety inspections of maternity units, including the need to listen to families, investigate serious incidents fully and learn from mistakes. McCourt said she wouldn't shy away from identifying pressures in the system such as staffing shortages. "We're completely independent, so we have that capacity to feel totally free to say what we need to say," she said "You can't run an effective health service with staff who are excessively anxious, as well as not having the right mix of staff and the right numbers of staff." While she said she would take into account lessons learned by previous inquiries in England and other parts of the UK, McCourt said Scotland had different challenges. "You've got a much more dispersed population in Scotland. So thinking about how to cater for the more rural areas where you've got long distances, and you've got a smaller population concentration, that's quite different from most of England. "So there are going to be things that are quite distinct about Scotland, as well as the fact that you do have devolution in the health system." Claire Fleming travelled 70 miles to give birth to baby Andrew in Dumfries Announcing the beginning of the review earlier this week, the Scottish government said it would look at inequalities such as the higher rates of maternal death among Black and Asian women. The review will also have a "specific focus" on maternity services in Caithness, Elgin and Wigtownshire, where there are longstanding campaigns to improve local services. Claire Fleming's third child Andrew was born in Dumfries, 70 miles from her home just outside Stranraer, after the local maternity unit closed in 2018. She travelled that distance even for short antenatal appointments. She does not expect the review to lead to the full reinstatement of a 24-hour maternity service in Stranraer. "I understand there are constraints and problems in recruiting midwives and staff, so I'm not asking for that. But what I do think is really important is that the absolute basics are covered here, and they're not getting done just now," she said. "So when they find out what is going on down here in Wigtownshire, they need to act on it. "I have been campaigning for more than five years, and I have met every MP and the first minister. I've spoken to them all and nothing's changing, so I am praying this is the thing that changes something." Health Secretary Angela Constance says most care is good, but there have been cases where families have been let down Health Secretary Angela Constance said the independent review would sit alongside ongoing inspections of every acute maternity unit in Scotland. "While the vast majority of mothers receive good care, I have heard from families who were let down," she said. "Their experiences must shape improvement." McCourt said she wanted to hear from people in different areas across Scotland. "We need to take account of the different mix of services and how best to make sure that people have good access

title: What Americans think about the death penalty
description: The BBC spoke to Americans and international tourists in Washington DC about their views on the death penalty following the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
body: This video can not be played Christa Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. title: University 'banter' account criticised for sex assault social media posts and misogyny
description: Cardiff University has since unfollowed the account after concerns were raised about the "harmful" material.
body: Rebecca Rumsey, co-founder of a sexual misconduct campaign group, says students repeatedly sent them screenshots of the posts Warning: This article contains references to sexual assault that readers may find distressing. A university has been criticised after anonymous accounts of sexual assault and misogynistic posts were made on social media by a student-run "banter" account it followed. Cardiff University has since unfollowed the Cardiff Uni Banter Instagram account after students raised concerns about the material being posted. One post included an anonymous confession describing a man continuing to have sex with a woman while she was having a seizure. Cardiff University said sexual violence and harassment and all forms of gender-based violence would "not be tolerated", adding that fact that it had followed the account was not "in any way an endorsement". Cardiff Uni Banter was asked to comment. Jennifer Taylor, National Union of Students Cymru president, said the comments were "dangerous" and "harmful" It is not known if the claim made in the post is true, but some of the page's content has received hundreds of likes and has been widely reshared. Jennifer Taylor, National Union of Students Cymru president, said the comments were "dangerous, harmful and are reinforcing a toxic culture on our campuses that must be tackled head on". The Instagram account describes itself as a place for "the best confessions, memes and banter in Cardiff" and has more than 14,000 followers. It publishes anonymous submissions from students covering university life, relationships, sex, and nightlife. Megan Elmer contacted the BBC after becoming concerned about the content, saying she believes it "contributes to the perpetuation of rape culture by normalising misogynistic attitudes and discussions of sexual violence". Megan said she did not know whether the anonymous allegations published by the account were true, but believed the posts raised questions about the culture surrounding sexual violence within the university community. She said she was particularly concerned that Cardiff University's official Instagram account had been following Cardiff Uni Banter. "I would therefore be interested in whether the university is aware of the account and its content, whether it has received any reports or concerns relating to the account, and why its official Instagram account follows the page," she said. "Imagine being a woman who has been raped or sexually assaulted at university, maybe even one of those girls whose sexual violence has made the account. "How would you feel if your own university followed that account." Megan Elmer contacted the BBC after becoming concerned about the content posted on the Instagram account Some students are calling for a boycott of the social media page, with other posts seen by BBC Wales describing women as "sluzzers", and "tarts". Rebecca Rumsey, 23, a Cardiff University student and co-founder of the sexual misconduct campaign group Time To Act, said students had repeatedly sent the group screenshots of the posts. "We got sent the posts hundreds of times by students," she said. "We tried to reach out to the page — they still haven't responded." Time To Act called for students to unfollow the account, stop submitting confessions and report content they believed promoted sexual violence or misogyny. Rebecca said the backlash had resulted in the account losing about 2,000 followers. "There's a lot of misogynistic and rape culture posts on that page, and it's not good enough," she said. "It's not banter." Cardiff University said it was aware of the account and the "concerning nature of the posts" but emphasised the account was "not affiliated or associated with Cardiff University, nor are we aware who is responsible for it". A university spokesperson said: "This is not just banter. As a university we're committed to creating a safe, respectful, and inclusive environment where everyone has the right to feel safe and treated with dignity and respect." It added that it had received complaints about the account, had reported posts and the account itself, and would continue to do so. "We followed the account so we could actively monitor and report such posts. We unfollowed the account in response to the concerns expressed by our Students' Union and from staff, students and members of the public." Cardiff Uni Banter has been approached for comment. If you have been affected by the issues raised, help is available via BBC Action Line. title: Burnham calls on Polanski to reverse Green Party's Zionism motion
description: The prime minister has intervened in the row over the motion passed by members at Green Party conference.
body: Andy Burnham has called on Green leader Zack Polanski to reverse a motion passed by members of his party declaring Zionism a form of racism. The prime minister said the motion, approved on Sunday at the party's conference in Brighton, was "completely wrong" and showed "terrible judgement". The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. In the wake of the vote, Polanski has said he would not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of". The Green leader has declined media interviews since the motion was passed and did not answer questions from a BBC reporter about the motion ahead of Burnham's comments. It comes as polls close in Thursday's Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which Polanski is a candidate. The motion has complicated the final days of Polanksi's campaign in the contest, where the Greens have been looking to overturn a substantial Labour majority in the seat vacated by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer. It has sparked days of controversy, with four of the five Green MPs opposing it, its co-deputy leaders split on supporting it, the Green deputy leader in Wales resigning, and condemnation from members and Green counterparts in Europe. Polanski did not vote on the Zionism motion, having left the conference early to return to London for the by-election campaign. An amendment he had backed to specify that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist was voted down by members. Before the vote, he had also said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like." The Green Party has an internal democracy model, under which official party policy is decided by members. However, these positions are not necessarily included in the party's general election manifestos. This video can not be played Watch: Polanski was asked earlier on Thursday about the Zionism conference motion In his first intervention in the row on Thursday, Burnham said he felt the motion effectively ruled out a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine. "For that reason, it shouldn't be supported in any way, shape or form," he told reporters while on a visit to Berlin. "I would call on the leadership of the Green Party to say that it will be reversed and it won't be Green Party policy." When asked if he would rule out entering into coalition with the party, he would not be drawn on "any business about what might or might not happen in the future". In a statement on Monday, Polanski did not specify whether he supported the motion passed by members but said he would not accept anyone being excluded from the party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of". On Thursday, a Green Party spokesperson said: "This has been an emotive issue and is complex. It has rightly caused much discussion, and needs to be taken in the context that Israel's behaviour has had. "Israel has been responsible for a genocide, ethnic cleansing and the killing of children, and we've had a political establishment which has not only turned a blind eye but provided support." The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is currently hearing a case brought by South Africa that accuses Israeli forces of genocide, but it could take years to reach a conclusion. Israel has called the case "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims". title: Katie Price 'angry' when told of ex's rape claim
description: The complainant's mother tells court Price "was quite angry" when told about about the allegations.
body: Kieran Hayler denies all the charges against him The mother of a teenage girl allegedly raped by Katie Price's then-husband said she felt the former glamour model was "angry" about the allegation and "didn't care" about her daughter, a court has heard. Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one of sexual assault against the then 13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies. Giving evidence in court on Thursday, the complainant's mother said when she told Price about the allegations, "she was quite angry and I didn't feel she was particularly upset for [the complainant]". She added: "I didn't feel she cared about my daughter." The court heard the teenager told her mother a year after the alleged rapes that Hayler had "done everything to her" to which she was "shocked". The jury was told she tried to ask her daughter to explain but she said: "I can't tell you any more." Asked if she questioned her further, she replied: "I didn't because she was so distressed." The mother told the court she told Price about the allegations because she felt like she "had to". Asked how Price reacted, she said: "She was shocked and probably swore. "I feel she was just angry and feeling revengeful towards Kieran." But the alleged victim's mother said her daughter did not "want anyone to know" and they had to "respect her wishes". In court she said she and her daughter had fallen out after she told Price. Asked if this was because she felt she betrayed her trust, the mother replied: "Yes, she probably didn't want anyone to ever know and yes it did cause arguments." The mother said she noticed changes in her daughter's behaviour including her becoming more "withdrawn". "My main concern was her washing, she would shower about four times a day and scrub her skin and it really worried me," she said. She told the court she asked her daughter why she was washing so often to which she replied: "I just feel dirty all the time." The complainant contacted the NSPCC in 2021 about the allegations which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation. Her mother told the court about the day her daughter informed her she had reported it to the police, adding: "She still hadn't told me exactly what had happened." The court heard after it was reported the two discussed the matter. The mum said: "She said it made her feel sick and dirty thinking about it whenever she thought about what had happened. "At the time she thought it was normal but looking back on it she realised it wasn't because of her age and then she just felt dirty." Hayler has suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations formed part of this, the court heard. He was married to Price at the time of the allegations, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021. The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families. title: Sutton's predictions v Starsailor frontman James Walsh
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on Starsailor frontman James Walsh, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
body: All eyes will be on Anfield on Sunday to see how Premier League leaders Manchester City react after being found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they have been accused of breaching. "It's a mammoth game," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton. "Everyone is looking at this game to see if City's players appear deflated and how much it will affect them. "We don't know what the implications are for this season, either. They are top of the league at the moment but will they get a massive points deduction that changes that?" Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests. For week six, he takes on Starsailor frontman James Walsh, who supports Liverpool. Starsailor have released a 25th anniversary edition of their debut album, Love is Here, this week and are playing it in full, with a string ensemble, on their UK and European tour this month. Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below. The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page. A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points. Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions. Starsailor's debut album, Love Is Here, has sold more than 1m copies worldwide since it reached number two in the UK album charts in 2001, and has amassed more than 56m streams on Spotify When Love is Here was released, Liverpool had just completed an unprecedented treble of FA Cup, League Cup and Uefa Cup. They are not holders of any trophies at the moment, but James is optimistic about winning some silverware under new manager Andoni Iraola. "You have to be realistic whenever a new manager comes in, especially with the big signings we made last year, Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, not hitting the ground running," he told BBC Sport. "I think just give him a chance to implement his way of playing football and give Isak and Wirtz a chance to prove themselves this season. "I don't see us winning the title but I'd be more than happy with the FA Cup or even the Carabao Cup, and having a good run in Europe. "It's a bit greedy but of course you do like to see your team win something every season. Three more trophies like in 2001 would be pretty good!" Chris Sutton and James Walsh were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan. The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'. Brighton were brilliant when they beat Arsenal before the international break - the Seagulls really harried and hassled the champions and went toe-to-toe with them. I don't think Leeds will go about things the same way, but they will still provide a stern test. Daniel Farke's side are really solid but also carry a big threat too, and they are a very different proposition to the side Arsenal thumped 5-0 at Emirates Stadium at the start of last season. So, this game will tell us a lot about where Arsenal are and how they have recovered from that Brighton defeat. I'd still back the Gunners to find a way to win, especially because they are at home, but it will be a lot closer than last time. Leeds don't concede goals as freely any more. James' prediction: Arsenal have just had a bit of a wobble and you wonder if it was just an anomaly, because Brighton have had quite a few scalps, or if it is going to be a slightly more difficult season for them this year. I guess we will start to find out here but I've been impressed by how resilient Leeds have been, to stay unbeaten, so I have made this my outlier prediction to give them some credit for their start. They will probably get thumped now but someone has to give them a chance. 1-1 Brentford were one of the teams who definitely didn't want the international break, while I feel like it might have done Aston Villa the world of good. They have made very different starts to the new season - Brentford are still unbeaten and, while I kept on predicting Villa would win, the only time I was right was when they beat Tottenham last time out. Despite the difference in their form, I am going to stick with Villa here, even though the Bees have been seriously impressive so far. Johan Manzambi is fit again and seems to have found his best form while playing for Switzerland. He could make the difference here too. James' prediction: Villa have lost some key players but I still expect them to get it together at some stage and maybe this is the game, against a Brentford team in really good form. 2-1 Bournemouth have not won yet under Marco Rose, and they are also without key midfielder Alex Scott for a while as a result of his injury on international duty. I feel like the Cherries have been a bit unlucky with their results under Rose so far, because they have conceded some costly late goals, but Scott's absence is a huge blow for them. Chelsea are already turning into a team that are a nightmare to predict - defensively they have got huge issues, but they have got such a talented attack. Some people thought they would be up there challenging for the title but they look far too inconsistent to do that. Anything could happen in this game and I was tempted to say Bournemouth will get something out of it. But Cole Palmer will be rested and refreshed after his injury so I am going to base my prediction on how I expect Chelsea's frontline to click. James' prediction: I don't see Bournemouth getting anything here. 2-0 Ipswich lost last time out, against Everton, but they gave it a real go even when they went down to 10 men midway through the second half. title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
description: An international visa program has for years allowed US tech companies to hire highly skilled workers from abroad.
body: The White House has often made extreme claims regarding international workers and immigration. Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program. Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents. Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants." Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff. "No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said. He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference. Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers. The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment. The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped, external at 85,000 per year. A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide. Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages. The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires. She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive. According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary, external for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000. "We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said. Satya Nadella, Microsoft's longtime CEO, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump. Nadella was also present at other recent White House events, including a luncheon on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping. Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday. "Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said. He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US. Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating, external that grace period altogether. Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more. None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments. The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades. The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely. During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified, external more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories. title: BBC on Hurricane Isaias and its expected Gulf Coast landfall
description: BBC Weather's Chris Fawkes says the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season could bring dangerous winds, storm surge and heavy rains to the Gulf Coast Friday.
body: This video can not be played Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, is intensifying as it heads toward the northern Gulf Coast. The storm is expected to make landfall Friday night, bringing dangerous winds, storm surge and heavy rain to parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida. Isaias also ties the record for the latest first hurricane of an Atlantic season, set in 1905. BBC Weather's Chris Fawkes explains. BBC on Hurricane Isaias and its expected Gulf Coast landfall. title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
description: Hundreds have pitched their tents in central Madrid, while the Spanish prime minister has called a snap election.
body: Jorge Moreno (left) says "vulture funds" are hiking up rents, while Pierina Nicuray points out that there is "a lack of homes" in Spain Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause. "It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes." She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb." Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees. "There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own. "They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home." His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government. On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate". Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month. Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay. Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday. Protesters at Pueta del Sol have been paying tributes to Maricarmen Abascal Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market. Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years. When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent. "When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security." Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista. In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%. Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern. A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market. Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes. Carmen Pérez says high rental costs have affected her health However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation. He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies. Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain. "When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years." The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes. The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million. There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs. Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them. Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand. Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth. However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period. That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building. "It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us." He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rath

title: Ticket rises and more TV packages - why is price of sport increasing?
description: The price of sports tickets and TV subscriptions are on the rise - so what is behind the increases and how are they justified?
body: The price of attending and watching sport in the UK is coming under significant scrutiny At least £115 to watch a day of the Ashes in Birmingham - unless you are an Edgbaston member. A minimum of £255 for a standard seat at the Wimbledon singles finals. Prices starting from £289 for general admission to the British Grand Prix at Silverstone on raceday. Those are the ticket fees British sports fans have been told a single adult must pay if they want to attend some of the country's most beloved sports events in 2027. The cost of entry to elite sport in the UK has risen sharply in the 2020s, but attendances across the majority of sports are as strong as ever. Even for armchair fans watching at home, the breadth and expense of television subscriptions can be a barrier to accessing sport. So what exactly is behind the rise in prices, can the increases possibly be justified and what does it all mean for fans? In a new BBC Radio 5 Live programme - The Price of Our Sport - BBC Sport has taken a look. The Price of Our Sport Fans reacted with anger when some of the ticket price rises for major events next year were announced earlier this summer. The increase in Ashes ticket prices is stark - the minimum price the last time Edgbaston held a Test in 2023 was £65, a rise of £50 to £115 in just four years. Admission to other venues, including The Oval, is even higher. Last time out in Australia, some seats were sold to fans at all five venues for between £16 and £22. At Wimbledon next year, the most expensive standard seat for both the men's and women's singles finals will be £400, £50 more than 2026, and more than double the cost from 2017. That still makes Wimbledon the cheapest of the four Grand Slams, but even a Centre Court ticket for the middle Saturday of the tournament now costs at least £130. General admission for Grand Prix Sunday at Silverstone is up to £289 from £189 in 2021, while the cheapest allocated seat now costs at least £609, up from £276 five years ago. And general admission to the 2027 Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, in the Republic of Ireland, will cost €499 (£434), compared with up to €260 (£220) in Italy in 2023. This video can not be played "I'm not paying £165 for one day!" - are cricket fans being priced out of the Ashes? And other events which took place this year laid bare just how much more fans are being charged. Fans paid £150 to attend a day of The Open at Royal Birkdale earlier this year, compared to £95 at St Andrews in 2022. Prices for the FA Cup final varied from £50 to £285 in 2026, compared with £50 to £120 in 2016. "It's just ludicrous," says Lee Hanlon, an England cricket fan who lives close to Edgbaston, but has decided not to attend next summer's Ashes because of the price rise. "I'm angry. It seems like a lot of the normal cricket fans have been priced out. It seems like just people with money are going now. "The increase is just too much. I find it upsetting." But for event organisers, the prices chime with wider trends. "We exist in an experience economy - we have definitely seen a subtle shift in the value people are placing on belonging, on the atmosphere you can be part of when you attend a live experience," says Mark Darbon, chief executive of the R&A, which operates golf's Open Championship. "So when we set our prices we start by looking at some of the other major sporting events and benchmark ourselves, on price and value for money, by looking at what others are delivering." In a poll on the BBC Sport website, 95% of respondents voted that tickets for the 2027 Ashes were too expensive. A spokesperson for Edgbaston said: "Our entry-level ticket prices roughly match inflation compared to the last time Australia visited Edgbaston in 2023 - but like the rest of the country, we're battling increased costs and trying to manage these wherever we can." Whether prices are set by governing bodies or the stadiums, the costs of putting on a major sports event include things like utilities, staffing, technology, insurance and marketing. The Open offers half-price tickets for attendees aged 16-24, and free tickets for children. "Ticketing revenue generates less than 20% of our total revenue from The Open," Darbon says. "We have seen really significant cost inflation in recent years. It now costs us 25% more than it did five or six years ago to host The Open - that could be £10-12m in incremental costs. We have to cover those costs." This video can not be played "We try to offer a wide range of prices to suit different needs" - R&A CEO Mark Darbon Many prestige events and newly built venues also include an increased proportion of hospitality ticketing, which can drive up costs for fans wanting standard tickets. "We are seeing more and more regular people willing to pay for a special experience at sport," says Richard Flint, chairman of Seat Unique, an online platform specialising in hospitality and VIP ticketing for events. "Corporate boxes are being broken down more and more into individual seats, so it's less about people taking 10 of their colleagues and more about a couple, or four people, going together. "[Teams and leagues] want to grow their revenue off the back of it, undeniably. Premium is much more open to people or go to one or two games a year, or who have travelled from abroad to come. "Sometimes stadiums need updating and the revenue from premium ticketing can help fund a new stadium or new stand, so there are benefits to the everyday fan." In a world with increasingly volatile economics and changing consumer habits, broadcasting live sport has been one of the more reliable ways for companies to generate revenue. And live sport - and entertainment - is one of the few industries whose financial success is unlikely to be significantly compromised by artificial intelligence in the coming years. title: Harry says he 'slipped into depression' after leaving UK
description: The Duke of Sussex says he had an "adrenaline crash" while visiting Vancouver Island to "get some space".
body: The Duke of Sussex moved to Canada temporarily with his wife, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019 The Duke of Sussex has said he "slipped into depression for about two weeks" after relocating to Canada in 2019 ahead of his move to the US. Prince Harry, who recently returned to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children, said he had originally left the country to "get some space." The duke also discussed feeling "emotionally numb" after the death of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales, because he felt "disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her". He opened up about his mental health with a neuroscientist in a session for a video learning platform. He and his brother, the Prince of Wales, have previously been candid about their mental health struggles, including over their mother's death, and both are involved in mental health charities. Prince Harry, who stepped back from royal duties to move to California with Meghan, made the latest comments as part of a paid-for online masterclass on dealing with grief. "Being in Canada, away from the stressful environment where presumably my body was just pumped full of adrenaline, within two or three days, I experienced this adrenaline crash, something that I'd never experienced before," he recalled. "It was as if I needed stress in order to get the adrenaline to make my brain function because I became useless around the house. "I actually slipped into depression for about two weeks and I felt like I couldn't function without adrenaline." Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in Britain after six years in US Will Harry's return heal deep-rooted rift with William? He and his wife unexpectedly announced last month that they were returning to the UK with their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, after spending six years in the US. They are now thought to be living in the Cotswolds. In the video, Prince Harry also revealed that he had a rule that he would never be away from his family for more than 10 days. He talked about struggling to process his grief in the years after the death of his mother when he was 12. "In my 20s, I went to war twice thinking I could outrun my feelings," the duke said, referring to his stints in Afghanistan as a member of the Army. "But that's not what happened. "I'd spent so long emotionally numb, to a large extent, because I felt disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her. "I felt like I had to be sad and I had to be emotionally numb in order to prove to her that I missed her." Prince Harry said he struggled to process his grief for years after the death of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales Prince Harry said in the discussion that after crying at Diana's funeral, he did not cry for nearly two decades, according to news outlets. He said it was a therapist who suggested he spray her perfume to "unlock everything", adding that this allowed him to discover that "she just wanted me to be happy". Mary-Frances O'Connor, a neuroscientist and University of Arizona professor who also featured in the online class, explained: "Your brain doesn't register your loved one as gone - it registers them as lost. "And it will keep searching until you teach it otherwise. We still expect that they're going to walk through the door." MasterClass approached Harry about appearing in the programme last year and it was filmed in California over the summer, according to People magazine. Details of help and support with mental health are available at BBC Action Line. title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
description: The German sportswear brand wants the Sydney-based label to stop selling the clothes and pay damages.
body: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo. The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused. The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile. The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday. In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957. The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark. White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims. It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items. This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim. The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind". Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs. Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops. In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes. A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image. In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes. White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024. In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review. title: E-bike battery in fatal fire had repairs - inquest
description: Gemma Germeney, 31, and children Lilly, eight, and Oliver, four, lost their lives in the blaze.
body: Gemma Germeney, pictured with partner Scott Peden, died in the blaze along with their children Oliver and Lilly An e-bike battery linked to a fire which killed a mother and two children had issues prior to the blaze, an inquest has heard. Gemma Germeney, 31, and children Lilly, eight, and Oliver, four, lost their lives in the fire on Sackville Close in Cambridge on 30 June 2023. The children's father, Scott Peden, survived. Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said at the time the most probable cause of the fire was an e-bike that was charging. Scott Peden told the inquest he had bought a replacement battery after the previous one had been stolen and the bike later cut out, and had visited a repairman twice for work done. Peden told the inquest he had purchased the bike online for £900 and it was in "perfect working order", apart from an incident where he lost the key on a fairground ride. He said the battery was stolen a few months later and they researched a new one, but it would have been "quite a lot of money and I couldn't afford it at the time". Peden spent four weeks in a coma after jumping from an upstairs window before trying to tackle the fire Peden told the inquest he bought a second-hand one online advertised as in "perfect working order" around 9 June. He said the replacement "seemed to take a while to charge", but "it was getting enough for me to get around", however, it then "cut out" near his home. A colleague had given them the details of repairman Stoil Severinov and he went with Germeney's father to his house, where he was told "the battery was too powerful for the fuse so he changed the fuse" for £30. But he returned, this time alone, after it cut out again when he said Severinov told him the battery needed replacing, but Peden said he "had nothing in the bank, so I asked him desperately if he could do anything before I got paid". He "offered to bypass the cells", and he was told this would be a temporary fix. Asked if Severinov told him there were any risks, Peden replied "no". Peden planned to "use the bike until payday" and said he paid £10 on the understanding he would return and purchase a new battery and charger. He said on the night of the fire he heard a "massive bang" that went through the house, which was "very loud and very hard to miss". Severinov, giving evidence through an interpreter, said he was repairing bikes and e-bikes. He said on the first occasion Peden visited he changed the socket and the fuse, and on the second "it was just the fuse". On the first occasion he had explained "it was a temporary fix". Severinov said he remembered telling Peden he needed a new battery, and said he had "never done anything to the battery cells", adding he "didn't have the expertise in the first place". The court heard Severinov was interviewed under caution by the Office for Product Safety and Standards, which has primacy in bringing any criminal proceedings in this case. It was told it had said no final decision had been made on whether to initiate criminal proceedings against any individuals or organisations. A pen portrait from Germeney's mother, read out at the beginning of the inquest by the coroner, said Germeney and the children were "our complete world" and "were beautiful, funny, extremely kind, loving and caring". title: More than 800,000 hours of sewage spills in Wales last year, report claims
description: It is equivalent to a sewage discharge happening every five minutes, according to campaigners.
body: There were more than 100,000 sewage discharges from Welsh water companies in 2025 New figures show sewage was released into rivers, lakes and the sea around Wales for more than 800,000 hours last year. The charity Surfers Against Sewage, which has analysed data from Wales' water companies, said there were more than 100,000 sewage discharges in 2025 - or one every five minutes. The figures are down on the year before when sewage was discharged for more than 970,000 hours. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it had strengthened its approach as regulators through increased monitoring and tighter guidance, and had overseen "significant programmes of environmental investment" by water companies. Surfers Against Sewage said part of the reason for the drop was the dry weather seen during the summer last year, but underinvestment and a lack of enforcement remained an issue. In its annual assessment, it said since 2019 it had received 992 reports of sickness in Wales caused by sewage, with 215 of those coming in 2025. It said the impact of those sickness reports led to more than 2,200 days off work. According to the charity, sewage was discharged into Wales' designated bathing waters for a total of 35,669 hours over the year. At Llyn Padarn, Gwynedd, despite the lake's designated bathing water being classified as "excellent" for water quality, discharges lasted 1,614 hours. Rules allow a limited discharge of sewage in periods of excess rain, but environmental groups remain concerned the levels pose a threat to wildlife and a health risk to swimmers. Surfers Against Sewage has been campaigning for better water quality across the UK Giles Bristow, chief executive of Surfers Against Sewage, said last year's figures equated to a discharge every five minutes, which he called a "shocking statistic". He pointed to 90 places that authorities have said are good places to swim, but said they'd "been impacted by over 4,000 hours of sewage pollution". "It's a really terrible picture that we're seeing of continued underinvestment and a lack of enforcement to ensure that this isn't happening," he added. "People's lives and their health are being put at risk when they go to enjoy these amazing places." Welsh Water said it will invest a record £2.5bn over the next four years, and understood the concerns about sewage discharge. "We take our responsibility to protect these waters seriously and recognise that we need to improve," it said. "In line with Welsh government policy, we are prioritising the overflows causing the greatest environmental harm." The Welsh government says it is "taking full control of water in Wales" Hafren Dyfrdwy - which operates in mid and north-east Wales - said it was "working tirelessly" to reduce the average number of spills but "we know more needs to be done". "Which is why we're investing £11m at our storm overflows to reduce spills to fewer than 20 a year by 2030," it added. The Welsh government said it was "taking full control of water in Wales" and would "apply the polluter-pays principle, including prosecuting serious and persistent offenders". "Water reform demonstrates how Wales and the UK can work together to strengthen and simplify devolution, while keeping effective cross-border cooperation," a spokesperson added. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said water companies must "take responsibility" for record levels of sewage pollution. It added: "Our strengthened Water Bill will deliver cleaner waters, stronger accountability and will create a powerful new regulator to hold companies to account." title: 'I don't know what my partner earns': How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?
description: Talking about salary, spending habits and debt can be some of dating's trickier conversations.
body: You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns? Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all. We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries. Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all. "It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says. Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return. He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does. "He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'" Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees. "It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills." Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for him For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple. Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone. Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make". Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship." He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy". "If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me". Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates. "I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me." For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily". Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think". "In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility." Emily's been in a relationship for two years and has not discussed salaries yet Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though. Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make". She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask. "Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it. title: Woman told PC 'get off me' 300 times as he raped her
description: Ryan Theaker, 30, was secretly recorded by the victim as he subjected her to an 82 minute attack.
body: Ryan Theaker was secretly being recorded as he subjected his victim to an 82-minute sex attack A woman told a police officer to "get off me" more than 300 times as he subjected her to an 82-minute violent rape in a Liverpool hotel room. Former Merseyside Police constable Ryan Theaker, 30, was secretly recorded by the victim after a night out in 2023. The woman, who cannot be named to protect her anonymity, read an emotional statement at Liverpool Crown Court and faced the dock as she told Theaker "monsters never win". He was designated a "dangerous" offender by a judge and jailed for 11 years with an extended five-year licence period. Warning: This story contains distressing details of sexual violence. Theaker, from Park Lane in Netherton, had been convicted of rape, sexual assault and assault by penetration after a trial last month. Gareth Roberts, prosecuting, said the audio recordings captured Theaker demanding the woman let him take naked pictures of her, despite her saying she did not want him to. He also assaulted her with sex toys he had brought to the hotel, the court heard. The recordings, described as "harrowing" by sentencing judge Brian Cummings KC, captured her "crying throughout" as Theaker went on to rape her. Theaker, who was off duty at the time, was heard to tell her: "It'll stop when I say." Roberts summarised the attack as a "lengthy and prolonged period of sexual degradation". The offences were reported about a year later, after the victim confided in family and friends following a "serious" suicide attempt. The woman was invited to read her victim personal statement aloud and wiped away tears as she said: "I always thought when I was younger that monsters were big horrible nasty creatures who weren't even real. "I remember reading a post that said, 'even Scooby doo taught us the real monsters were always the people'. "That is exactly what he is. A monster. The monster never wins." She also said she could not understand how he could have arrested people after "doing what he did to me" and "still been proud to wear that uniform". "He didn't deserve to be in the police," she added. Theaker was told he was a dangerous offender at Liverpool Crown Court Theaker did not appear to react as she read her statement and the woman was embraced and supported by her family as she returned to the public gallery. Jenny Tallentire, defending, said since the trial Theaker had accepted he was guilty of the sexual offences and was "ashamed" of his behaviour. She said he had been an "excellent" police officer who had been commended and nominated for a bravery award during his career. Outlining Theaker's crimes as he passed sentence, Judge Cummings said: "You repeatedly told her get in the [expletive] bath which she refused to do, pushed her on the bed, removed her clothing and took photographs of her despite her repeatedly telling you she didn't want you to." He said he forced her to wear sexual restraints and assaulted her. Just as she thought the ordeal was over, the judge said Theaker grabbed her by the hair and raped her. Judge Cummings said he took into account Theaker's public service and acknowledged that his status as a police officer would put him at increased risk in custody. However, he said: "I am quite sure that your behaviour towards the victim across the offences made at the very least a substantial contribution to her decision to try and kill herself." After the offences were reported in August 2024, Theaker was suspended and subjected to misconduct proceedings. He resigned the day before a hearing in August 2025, which concluded he would have been sacked had he remained on the force. After the sentencing Merseyside Police Assistant Chief Constable Karen Jaundrill said: "The behaviour for which Theaker has been convicted and sentenced has no place in society, and certainly not within policing. "I want to be clear that his contemptible behaviour is in no way representative of the attitude or behaviour of officers and staff at Merseyside Police. "Theaker's former colleagues, and the force, have all been left shocked and disgusted by his actions and the long-term impact they have had on his victim." title: Welsh actress follows in footsteps of Florence Pugh and Benedict Cumberbatch in line-up
description: Leisa Gwenllian says she forgot she applied for the 2026 Stars of Tomorrow talent programme.
body: Leisa Gwenllian says she forgot she applied for the prestigious recognition, thinking she would never get selected A Welsh actress named in a prestigious line-up that has previously featured the likes of Benedict Cumberbatch and Florence Pugh says the selection was "so unexpected" that she forgot she applied. Leisa Gwenllian portrays Effi in the Welsh language film Effi o Blaenau, which follows a young woman as she grapples with unemployment in a north Wales town before a night out drinking dramatically alters her life. She joins a host of Hollywood stars who have previously been part of Stars of Tomorrow, an annual showcase highlighting rising British and Irish acting and filmmaking talent. Gwenllian said she was proud to receive the honour and that Welsh language cinema was currently "having a moment". Gwenllian starred in Effi o Blaenau, which follows a young woman as she grapples with unemployment in a north Wales town Previous actors named in Screen International's talent programme also include Jodie Comer and Paul Mescal. The film magazine received over 350 applications this year and decided on 10 actors and 10 filmmakers for its 2026 list. Gwenllian, from Llanrug, Gwynedd, joked that "the pressure is on now" and said the recognition was a "great opportunity" which will open doors for her. "I've gained a little bit of following in Wales because of this, but what that also means is that I kind of feel like I don't want to let those people down now who are so supportive of me and expect great things," she said. "I just want to make my country proud and make my family proud." Effi o Blaenau (Effi from Blaenau) is an adaptation of Gary Owen's play, Iphigenia in Splott, but relocated from Cardiff to Gwynedd. Directed by Marc Evans, whose previous work includes BBC's Mr Burton, the film follows Effi as she navigates being out of work, clubbing and hangovers. "I absolutely would not be there had it not been for Effi and I just feel very grateful that I got to play her and that it's reached so many people," Gwenllian said. "I'm so proud to receive that honour because it's not only a recognition of my work but it's a recognition of the film and it's a boost for Welsh language cinema." Gwenllian is among 20 actors and filmmakers selected for the 2026 programme The industry here is having "a bit of a moment", Gwenllian said with a laugh. "A director that I worked with, Helen Jones, she always says, 'It's not a moment, it's a movement', and we have to make sure that this continues. "What Effi has proven is that there's an appetite out there for Welsh language films." She said it was exciting that filmmakers were starting to take Wales seriously, and that the Welsh language should not be viewed as a barrier. "People are so happy to watch other films in other languages with subtitles, so why not do it with Welsh." Time Out said Effi o Blaenau was a cross between Greek tragedy and "British social realism", calling Gwenllian "formidable", while The Guardian described the film as a "sensation". Gwenllian has most recently been filming a dark comedy set in Swansea. ITV and S4C series Santa Maria is about a "class divide" in the city, with both Welsh and English versions. "What's exciting about it is that even in the English language version, there's going to be a lot of Welsh," she said. "I love working in Wales and playing Welsh characters, I think it's where I feel most at home." Charles Gant, from Screen International, said Gwenllian was "a great talent discovery". "It's rare that you see a rising young actor playing a role that is not just the lead in a film, but also in every moment of the film," he said. "Leisa is a phenomenal talent, and casting directors and filmmakers will be sitting up and taking notice. She has warmth and charisma and that magical but unquantifiable essence that confers star status," he added.
