title: Black and African cinema hub opens in London
description: EbonyLife Place London is the brainchild of Nollywood media mogul Mo Abudu.
body: EbonyLife Place aims to platform black and African cinema A new black and African cinema and hub has officially opened in south-west London. EbonyLife Place, based near Nine Elms, was unveiled with a ceremony attended by the Mayor of London Lord Khan, and its founder Mo Abudu. Abudu, a Nigerian media mogul who was born in London, explained that the project was born from a desire to showcase and celebrate stories that she felt previously lacked a home. "I do think there is a younger audience of young people now that just want to see great storytelling," Abudu said. She added: "We make great films, and I think we need to create experiences where people can come and they can see the great work that we do in black cinema, in African cinema. "We don't have enough spaces to serve black cinema in the United Kingdom... representation is so important to us." The 160-seat auditorium will have a full programme of black and African cinema At the heart of the cultural centre is a 160-seat auditorium featuring a year-round film programme. The screenings will primarily focus on Nollywood cinema from Nigeria alongside other movies connecting to the black experience. In addition to film screenings, the venue will host masterclasses, industry panels, and live performances by established and emerging talent. Beyond its cinema space, the multi-storey venue features a bar, a lounge called "Fàhinti" (a Yoruba word meaning to lean back and rest), a Nigerian restaurant, a boutique showcasing African and diaspora designers, and walls lined with African diaspora artwork. Mo Abudu founded a media empire based in Nigeria and which is popular across Africa The project, financed almost entirely by Abudu's media group, mirrors the upscale lifestyle complex she launched in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos, in 2019. Speaking at Thursday's launch, Lord Khan said: "London is the number one place in Europe to film," adding that the capital sits just behind Los Angeles and ahead of New York in the global film production footprint. "As long as I'm mayor, we'll invest in culture," he said. The opening coincides with the London Film Festival. title: Watch: What does the ruling mean for the investigation into the former prince?
description: Special correspondent Lucy Manning explains why the Hight Court has ruled that search warrants used to search Mr Mountbatten-Windsor's home were unlawful.
body: This video can not be played The High Court has heard that search warrants used by Thames Valley Police to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year were unlawful. The force has said it accepted that the 'initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect', before they searched the former prince's properties on 19 February. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested by Thames Valley Police on suspicion of misconduct in public. He denies any wrongdoing. Special correspondent Lucy Manning is outside the High Court has and explains what we know about the ruling. Read more about the High Court's ruling. title: US deportations to African countries unlawful and exploit suffering, rights group says
description: More than 500 migrants have been expelled from the US to African countries, HRW says, citing US data.
body: The US has been sending migrants who cannot be deported to their home nations to other countries instead Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits suffering to deter migration. "Many, if not most" of the deportees have no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there, HRW says in a report. Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, more than 500 people have been sent to African countries where they are not citizens, the group says, citing US data. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said "third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets". Tackling immigration was one of Trump's key pledges during the 2024 election. Eswatini, which welcomed 32 deportees from the US, says three people - from Yemen, Belize and Laos - "voluntarily departed" to their home countries recently. According to HRW, some of the countries accepting the deportees have "arbitrarily detained" or sent them to their home countries, where they face "the risk of persecution or torture". The group said that people sent to Eswatini, Ghana and South Sudan, had been arbitrarily detained and faced ill-treatment while in detention. In Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Ghana, the deportees had been sent to their countries of origin despite the risk of "violating the principle of nonrefoulement [that people should not be sent to a country where they face torture, cruel treatment, or threats to their life and freedom]", it said. The group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that the point for the administration was that it could "threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere". "The point is to scare people," HRW said. "Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration," said Michael Garcia Bochenek, the group's interim US programme director. In a statement from to the BBC, DHS said: "ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe. When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them." White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told the BBC that those being sent to third countries were those whose home nations refused to take them or who had court orders preventing them being sent home. "Any illegal alien who wants to go home, we will arrange a free flight for them and give them a $3,000 check," she said. None of the African countries named has commented on the report. Deported from the US to Ghana then 'dumped' at the border: Nigerian man speaks out However, while announcing the recent departure of three migrants on Wednesday, Eswatini said that it was committed to ensuring that the "rights, dignity and well-being of third-country nationals were respected and protected". HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals in six countries - Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan. Some described to the group "abusive treatment" during their deportation flights, including being chained for about 18 hours and with no knowledge of their destination. They were also "denied access to essential medication, and often did not receive sufficient food or water". "The opaque deals that facilitate these transfers, some of which are still secret, are part of a US policy that violates international human rights law," HRW says. According to the report, at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender (LGBT) were sent to African states that criminalise same-sex relations. Among them were refugees granted protection in the US based on the likelihood they would be persecuted back home because of their orientation or gender identity. In November, a Nigerian man deported from the US initially to Ghana expressed his fears to the BBC after he and five others were secretly transferred to Togo. He spoke of his fears about returning to Nigeria, where his association with a separatist activist group could lead to his arrest and torture. In DR Congo, HRW says it was told by a US lawyer that of the 15 people from Colombia, Peru and Ecuador deported to the country in April, none remained there by late September, with 11 having returned to their home countries. "The uncertainty and other conditions they faced in the Democratic Republic of Congo call into question whether these returns to countries of origin were voluntary," the group said. Equatorial Guinea, which received 65 people, quickly sent at least two people to their home countries, HRW said. Burundi announced late last month that it had agreed to take in migrants deported from the US. title: Residents win Curo service charge legal battle
description: People living in a block of flats take their landlord to tribunal over a 300 per cent increase.
body: Alan Rice has helped residents in Weston concerned about their service charges Residents living in a block of flats have won a legal battle against their housing association - after being faced with a service charge increase of more than 300 per cent. Nine families living in Weston-super-Mare in Somerset had seen their monthly fees go up from about £70 per month to more than £300 a month. Housing provider Curo has now agreed to limit the charge to just over £100 after being taken to tribunal. A spokesperson for Curo said that it had "already agreed these reductions before the tribunal took place". Curo continued: "What we're trying to avoid is large bills that leaseholders aren't expecting. "Keeping people safe is our priority, and we need to balance ensuring the right fire safety measures are in place with trying to minimize the financial impact, which we know has been difficult." Alan Rice from Weston Housing Action said the residents are "ecstatic". "Quite a few people told us that we wouldn't win, but we were persistent and we got the result we wanted", he added. Red route 'could make small businesses go extinct' What to expect from a restored Birnbeck Pier Multi-million pound revamp of Clifton Suspension Bridge complete The dispute related to a property called Coombe Lodge. It contains nine flats, all of which are shared ownership - a scheme designed to help people get onto the housing ladder by buying a portion of their property, and paying rent to a landlord for the remainder. When the service charge went up, one resident said they had to take on an extra job, while others said they were anxious they'd be unable to afford the higher fee. Curo said the extra money was primarily to increase the block's sinking fund, which acts as a long-term savings account for building costs. Rice said that while there is "some need" for a sinking fund, it was "devastating" for residents. He said: "Although they were sold to them as affordable homes, suddenly they weren't affordable any more." The residents will now be reimbursed the excess charges they have paid. In response, Curo said "There are always maintenance costs linked to owning a flat in a block, and we completely understand that these can be a shock when significant work is needed. "That's why there are sinking funds, which are like a 'savings account' for the whole building, to help flat owners spread the cost across several years." The provider said it hoped it can "continue to work constructively with residents at Coombe Lodge to resolve all the remaining issues going forward". There is no limit on how much a service charge can increase, but a law passed in 2024 should eventually force managing agents to provide a full breakdown of costs. The Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act is yet to be fully implemented. It promises leaseholders clearer service charge bills, and the right to look back at service charge information over the past six years Samantha Young lives in a Curo-managed block in Twerton in Bath Samantha Young lives in a Curo-managed block in Twerton in Bath, and said she is going to take her case to the ombudsman after her annual service charge rose from £990 to more than £6,000, which she described as "astronomical." "It is absolutely not affordable. This is higher than what you'd paid in zone one in London for flats with gyms and concierges. "It quite frankly feels like we're receiving nothing." Curo told the BBC it was "having ongoing conversations with Ms Young about how we can work together to resolve this, and we visited her at home this week to agree a way forward". title: Body found in Colombia in search for missing British man Anton Green
description: Anton Green's family are told a body found in Colombia is believed to be the missing 43-year-old.
body: There had been an appeal to help find 43-year-old Anton Green, including by footballer Marcus Rashford The family of a British man missing in Colombia have been told a body has been found in the search for him. Anton Green from Manchester had been living in the South American country for two-and-a-half years, but stopped responding to messages in August. Earlier, his family in Whalley Range were told that a body had been discovered, and that it was believed to be the 43-year-old. They told the BBC that the news - which came just hours after they had renewed their appeal for help finding him - had devastated them and that they were "trying to come to terms with what's happened". A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) spokesman confirmed that the body of a British man had been found in Colombia. Anton Green had been living in South America for two-and-a-half years Anton's family had told the BBC that his failure to contact his family had been out of character. His mother, Nylva McKie-Williams, had said his last words to her in August were "we will speak at the weekend". She told BBC North West Tonight he had kept in frequent touch with his family, and that it had been "so unlike him not to be in contact with us". Last month, footballer Marcus Rashhford got behind the appeal to find him, describing him as a "family friend". Anton's brother Ro-Shaun Williams had been part of the Manchester United youth team alongside Rashford. Anton's mother Nylva had said it was unlike him not to be in contact Anton's sister Sian Tuohey described her brother as a "happy, decent guy" who had been living in Colombia for three years, having settled there while travelling. He spoke fluent Spanish and, not long before contact was lost, had moved to the Fontibon area of the capital, Bogota. The news of the discovery of a body was broken to the family by police in the early hours of Thursday, the BBC understands. His relatives said they were now waiting on more information from the Attorney General's Office in Bogota. An FCDO spokesman said: "We are aware of the death of a British national in Colombia and are providing support to their family." title: Zambia signs US health deal after disputes over data-sharing
description: The US will provide $1.5bn (£1.1bn) under the deal that was negotiated after Trump cut USAID funding.
body: Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi (second right) said the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US, ending months of public dispute over whether the country was trading citizens' medical data and mineral rights for aid. Under the memorandum of understanding, signed in Lusaka on Thursday along with a data-sharing deal, the US will provide about $1.5bn (£1.1bn), with Zambia also contributing. Civil society groups had criticised a leaked draft they said allowed too much data sharing, while activists seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to minerals, which the then-US ambassador denied. The deal comes after the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was cut. US President Donald Trump had accused USAID of wasteful spending. After closing the agency last year, Washington has pursued similar deals with a number of African countries, arguing partner governments should take on more of the cost. Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda are among those that have signed. Ghana and Zimbabwe have rejected agreements over conditions about sharing data and specimens. Officials say the revised text of Zambia's new deal addresses concerns about privacy, intellectual property and benefit-sharing. Health Minister Roma Chilengi said earlier this week that clauses requiring Zambia to send biological specimens to the US had been removed, and that the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records. Data exchange, he said, would be limited to information needed to monitor and evaluate programmes funded under the deal. Why some African nations are turning down Trump aid money A draft leaked earlier this year prompted civil society groups to warn that Zambia was accepting wider data-sharing terms than other African countries, including long-term access to pathogen information and specimens. The Chapter One Foundation, a human rights group, said the government risked "signing away" citizens' health data. HIV advocates, including the Treatment Advocacy and Literacy Campaign, said the flow of information would be one-way and demanded the text be published. Opposition figures and activists also seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to Zambia's large reserves of copper and other critical minerals. In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe called the data terms a violation of privacy and "unconscionable", and accused Washington of tying the package to minerals. Then-US ambassador, Michael Gonzales, rejected that account as false. The row was sharpened by an earlier US suspension of drug funding after the embassy alleged theft of donated medicines, which the government disputed. Zambia's new deal replaces support that for years flowed largely through US programmes. The money is intended to support HIV/Aids, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance and wider health system work, including the recruitment of community health workers. The US has described the arrangement as a shift from a donor-recipient model towards shared responsibility, with US funding expected to decline over the five years as Zambia increases domestic spending. Officials have put the combined package covering 2026 to 2030 at roughly $3.6bn, though figures for the Zambian share have varied. Shortly after taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump ordered the closure of USAID, in the process decimating health programmes in some African countries that relied on American funding. Critics say the move has impacted the speed of detecting the current ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the scale of the response, emphasising that the humanitarian agency was crucial to organising logistics, supplies and local outreach. The US denies its cuts have harmed efforts, arguing that they are more "aligned and effective" under the new arrangement and pointing to the $270m it has donated to tackle the epidemic. title: 'It's changed my life' - Eckert on Spygate scandal
description: Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert says the Spygate scandal is an experience that has changed his life.
body: Tonda Eckert has won 30 of his 50 games in charge of Southampton Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has said that Spygate is an experience that has changed his life. The 33-year-old faced the media for the first time since being given a six-week suspended ban and a £28,000 fine by the Football Association (FA) for his role in the scandal. Saints were expelled from the Championship play-offs in May after admitting spying on training sessions involving Oxford United, Ipswich Town and Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final. But Eckert escaped any individual punishment that threatened his job following an FA investigation into his conduct that lasted for more than four months. The FA had proposed a three-month ban, but the commission gave credit to him for what they called "considerable mitigation in this matter, most particularly around the genuine contrition". The governing body is still yet to confirm if it will appeal the independent commission's ruling. "It's tough. It changes your life. If I would say it's been all easy, it's not," Eckert said. "But you have to find a way. You have to come to a conclusion at one point in the summer of how you want to continue. "That first decision [public backing from the owner] was not for me but for the club. And at that very moment, then it's for me to see if I have the energy to be the right one to bring that project forward. "Once you make that decision, there's no excuses." Eckert was in a relaxed mood during Thursday's media conference at the club's Staplewood training ground, sharing a joke with reporters before sitting down to answer questions. Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss as Spygate ban suspended New Eckert deal should be 'high on agenda' - Beattie Time to draw line through Spygate - Parkinson Saints face bitter rivals Portsmouth on Sunday (12:00 BST), and when he was asked about what kind of an atmosphere he is expecting, a grin broke out on his face before responding. Although Wednesday's ruling was a positive outcome for Southampton and Eckert, there was a lot of negative reaction online from supporters of other sides who felt the punishment was too lenient. Before the verdict, Cambridge United head coach Neil Harris told BBC Radio 5 Live that the Saints head coach "should get a ban and a huge ban". Eckert admitted it was not just a relief for him to be able to finally bring an end to the case after more than four months of intense scrutiny and criticism, but also to those in his inner circle, personally and professionally. "It's not just good for me [that it's over]," he added. "I am not the one who shares too much from my private life but obviously it does make a big difference that we can draw a line, not just for me but also for the ones close to me. "I'm grateful for the club, I'm grateful for the people close to me to help me throughout some moments that haven't been easy. "And you just come to the moment now luckily where it's done and for us to look forward and that we get back to the performance that we need if we want to play for big goals this season." title: Maresca says 'feeling is fantastic' among Man City squad
description: Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca says the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and that they "don't care too much about the noise" surrounding the club after it was found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.
body: Enzo Maresca replaced Pep Guardiola as Manchester City manager Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca says the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and they "don't care too much about the noise" surrounding the club after it was found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against it by the Premier League. The club's international players returned to training on Thursday, nine days after the Premier League published a damning report that stated the club had used "sham" contracts to disguise secret funding of more than £830m. BBC Sport reported this week that Maresca would address the players upon their return to domestic duty after news of the verdict broke while the majority of the squad were away with their respective nations. It is understood the City head coach asked his players not to allow the crisis that has engulfed the club to affect their attitude and focus as the Premier League campaign gets back under way this weekend. "The feeling is fantastic, to be honest," said Maresca when asked about the mood among his squad prior to their trip to face Liverpool on Sunday (16:30 BST). "The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league. The players are just focused on that. "They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things. "They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield." Maresca added he felt "calm" and his squad trusts the club "completely". City have launched an appeal and have publicly maintained their innocence. The private communication to those with links to the playing staff at City has been equally as emphatic, it is understood. Speaking to Sky Sports, striker Erling Haaland echoed his manager's sentiments, saying: "I care a lot about this place. I spent my first four years here, it's a special place for us. I care a lot about City and the fans. I am a fan myself. I feel with them. "The fans will have a good time on Sunday - we have to stick together. We have to stay with each other and stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to smile. Stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and enjoy the situation. "We have to stick together and spread the love to each other. Enjoy the ride and smile." Erling Haaland is the leading scorer in the new Premier League season with five goals Guardiola set to attend Man City v PSG next week What Guardiola said about Man City charges As Premier League football returns following a three-week hiatus, rival clubs are proving reluctant to let their managers speak about the City verdict publicly. Managers and head coaches - including Maresca on Friday - will be asked to comment on the matter during compulsory pre-match news conferences. But it is understood a number of clubs have already taken a clear stance for their managers not to comment. Some Premier League news conferences were held on Thursday, but Coventry boss Frank Lampard, Leeds head coach Daniel Farke and Newcastle head coach Matthias Jaissle all steered clear of commenting at length on the matter. Jaissle said: "I think as a manager of another club I am not able to judge and it is not my job. Especially it is not in my job description. "The authorities are taking care of it, a process will be followed, and speaking on behalf of the whole club it is our job to focus on our job and preparing for [the match against Coventry on] Monday. "On behalf of the club, we should focus on what we can influence. Just focus on what we can do better and what we can influence on the pitch." Lampard, who played for Manchester City in the 2014-15 season, said: "What can you say when an appeal is going on? I'm not inside the story, I'm outside it completely. "I played for Man City a long time ago now for one year, but we'll wait and see what the result of the appeal is and onwards. I don't know the timelines at all. "I'm outside the loop. I'm not dodging the question, I just don't feel it's an answer for me to give." Asked what the punishment should be, Lampard said: "It's not my role to talk about a punishment or how much. I just can't answer that one." This video can not be played Could Manchester City be expelled from the Premier League? title: BBC Inside Science
description: What next for the world of maths after a major intrusion by AI?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·08 Oct 2026,·28 mins Tom Whipple investigates one of the biggest days in the 10,000 year history of maths. This week, overnight, OpenAI dropped hundreds of mathematical papers onto the internet. From the Margulis-Platonov conjecture to the Gaussian Propeller conjecture to Banach’s simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem. Decades of maths progress overnight. PhDs of work done in hours. This week saw the Nobel Prizes awarded for Chemistry, Physics and Physiology or Medicine. From mice with blue lights in their brain to massive ice cubes with blue lights underground, science journalists Kit Chapman and Caroline Steel tell us what we need to know. In 2016, President Obama reflected on the moon landings and on the delicate and dangerous task of putting humans there. He commented, when giving a former MIT programmer the Presidential Medal of Freedom: “Our astronauts didn’t have much time...but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton.” Margaret led the programming team for the Apollo missions and was a pioneer, in every sense of the word, until her death this week. Between Cape Horn and the Cape of Good Hope, there is a volcano inhabited by Chinstrap penguins. People don’t visit Zavodvski island much, but if you had been there in 2011 you would have been outnumbered by chinstraps 600,000 to one. Today, almost half a million have gone missing. Professor Norman Ratcliffe from the British Antarctic Survey tells us what he thinks is going on. Presenter: Tom Whipple Producers: Ben Mitchell, Clare Salisbury, Katie Tomsett Editor: Martin Smith Production Co-ordinator: Jana Bennett-Holesworth

title: Two men arrested on suspicion of trespass at RAF base in Cambridgeshire
description: Police say the suspects are Latvian nationals aged 36 and 32.
body: Two Latvian men have been arrested under the National Security Act after a fence was breached at an RAF base in Cambridgeshire. The alert was raised when a Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrol at RAF Molesworth identified an abandoned vehicle at about 22:00 BST on Wednesday. After searches by the MDP and Cambridgeshire Constabulary, a small breach of a perimeter fence was identified a few hours later. The two men, aged 36 and 32, were arrested inside the base perimeter, a spokesperson said. This breaking news story is being updated and more details will be published shortly. title: Venezuela's ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
description: The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power.
body: Nicolás Maduro has been in US custody since January of this year Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture. The fresh charges against the couple were made public on Thursday and are in addition to the drug-trafficking and weapons charges already brought against them, which they have denied. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been in custody since January in a detention centre in Brooklyn, where they were taken after US forces seized them in a pre-dawn raid on their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas. Human rights groups in Venezuela and former prisoners have long denounced what they have described as "systematic torture" in Venezuelan jails. The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens who were being held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power. The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027. title: Birmingham Airport announces £2bn expansion
description: The first stage of development, upgrading baggage systems and terminals, could start in 2027.
body: Airport chiefs said plans would create more than 50,000 jobs, including 3,800 on site Birmingham Airport has announced a £2bn expansion plan which bosses say could more than double passenger numbers and create thousands of jobs. The draft plan, a spokesperson said, sets out the use of existing runway capacity alongside "significantly enhanced" passenger facilities over the next 15 years. Unveiling an eight-week public consultation, chief executive Nick Barton said the scheme aims to ensure the airport was "ready for the future" but needed a "fair and stable taxation environment". Transport secretary Heidi Alexander said the government was "backing our aviation sector to continue growing, right across the country". In 2025, the airport said it had seen a record year with more than 13 million passengers travelling through it. Bosses want to see this rise by more than double, up to 30 million a year. Airport chiefs said the proposals set out a "clear commitment" to continue serving the region and create more than 50,000 jobs, including 3,800 at the airport site. They added that they wanted to make sure the growth was "delivered responsibly and sustainably" for the people living closes to the site. The first stage of development could start in 2027, with significant investments in areas such as baggage and terminal facilities, additional aircraft stands and improvements in surface access. Hundreds of passengers were affected by issues with the airport's baggage system in August, with many left without their luggage. People can give feedback on the plans online, by post or attend any of the 20 events, which start in Hampton on Arden on 16 October, external. West Midlands mayor Rickard Park said the consultation gave local people and businesses the chance to shape the airport's expansion "The £2bn proposed investment is unprecedented at Birmingham Airport and will take our airport close to 30 million passengers," said Barton. "This level of ambition sends a strong signal of support and confidence in our airport and wider region. However, Barton added that the plan came at a time the airport was faced with increased running costs from wage bills, energy prices and taxation. "Unless tax and regulatory environments are made more favourable and stable for major infrastructure investment, they [the plans] may not materialise," he said. Alexander said the city's plan was a "massive boost" to the West Midlands, unlocking investment and "creating 50,000 well-paid local jobs to get people into employment". Richard Parker, the Labour mayor of the West Midlands, also welcomed the "ambitious masterplan" which he said would improve international links and unlock vital backing for local businesses and supply chains. "This consultation gives local people and business owners a chance to have their say and help shape the airport's expansion so that it brings lasting benefits for our communities," he said. title: Plans to shut Marston's Brewery in Burton revealed
description: Burton-upon-Trent's links with beer and brewing date back centuries.
body: Marston's Brewery, its history and legacy in the town were "iconic", Carlsberg Britvic said Marston's Brewery could close in Burton-upon-Trent, under plans revealed by its owners. Carlsberg Britvic said it was proposing to shut the facility together with its primary logistics operation based at that site next summer. Burton-upon-Trent's connections with the brewing industry date back centuries, with the firm describing its own history and legacy in the town as "iconic". However, it said the "stark reality" was that UK cask ale volumes had more than halved in less than a decade and "this trend looks set to continue across the UK". The company said "priority brands" including Hobgoblin, McEwan's and Brooklyn were expected to remain in its portfolio, but it is unclear where they will be brewed. Others have described the Staffordshire town as the "beer capital of England", and at its height more than 30 breweries once operated from there. Burton's links with beer date back to the 11th Century when monks first started brewing. Carlsberg Britvic said it told colleagues and trade union partners the news earlier on Thursday. CEO Paul Davies stated the proposal was "by no means a reflection on any of our people, and every effort will be made to help them through this period of uncertainty". He added Marston's Brewery and the primary logistics operation were expected to continue to operate "during the transition period, while the company works through the detail of the consultation". "As and when key decisions are taken over the coming months, we will share further information with the industry, but always with our colleagues first." Davies said it was important to ensure the firm's portfolio was focused "where consumers are today, and where customer demand is growing". He added: "That said, smaller ale brands are much loved by select consumers, and we will do everything we can to ensure they thrive under more specialist or local ownership in the future." It is not the first big brewing firm to move operations in the West Midlands. Banks's Brewery pulled production out of Wolverhampton in 2025, after 150 years, moving it to Burton. Carlsberg Marston's Brewing Company, which is headquartered in Wolverhampton, had announced in 2024 that the Burton facility would close as part of a company restructuring. Burton beer is known for its earthy, eggy smell - known in brewing circles as "Burton snatch" - a sure sign of the ale's quality and provenance. This is created by the water trickling through unusually thick bands of gypsum under the town, before resting in underground aquifers. title: Police accept Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor search warrants were unlawful, court hears
description: The former prince is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police after his homes were searched earlier this year.
body: Andrew remains under police investigation despite a ruling that the way search warrants were issued was unlawful Thames Valley Police has accepted that the search warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year were unlawful, the High Court has heard. The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the former prince's properties on 19 February. Andrew was arrested by Thames Valley Police on suspicion of misconduct in public. He denies any wrongdoing. The criminal investigation is ongoing and the items seized in the raids on his homes in Norfolk and Berkshire will remain in police custody while his legal challenge over this material continues. Andrew's lawyers have used a judicial review to challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court. His arrest in February arose after the US Department of Justice published documents which suggested he had forwarded confidential information to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein when Mountbatten-Windsor was a UK trade envoy in 2010. He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein. The court heard on Thursday that Thames Valley Police took possession of documents and electronic devices when they raided Andrew's homes. Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and section nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search. That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge established that the court should have issued them under the section nine. The conditions for the warrants were that there had to be reasonable grounds for believing that any documents used for business or in a paid or unpaid role in which an undertaking of confidence had been given should not be seized. Thames Valley Police now admits the judge who granted the warrants could not have been sure of this. A Thames Valley Police spokesperson said: "The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgement on our ongoing investigation. "We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout. "We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed. "Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation." The force said its "investigation into alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his 60s from Norfolk remains ongoing, and we continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation". title: Cummins not worried about potential Khawaja revelations
description: Pat Cummins confirms he has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate’s upcoming autobiography but the Australia captain says he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations.
body: Usman Khawaja (left) and Pat Cummins played 56 Tests together for Australia Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations. On Friday, Australia will begin their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering scandal erupted in Cape Town in 2018. At the time, captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft were banned for their part in the plot. Since then, the four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including Cummins, have denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan to cheat. The quartet, who released a joint statement about the episode in 2021, are once again set to be united in the first Test against South Africa in Durban. Khawaja played in all four Tests in 2018 and retired from international cricket in January. His autobiography will be released in November. "Uz gave me a buzz a few weeks back that he is releasing a book," said Cummins. "He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries. "Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times. "It was dealt with then and all I can say is that as a group, we have moved on and we are very happy with the last eight to nine years how we have been as a group and evolved and obviously my focus is on captaining the cricket team." At the time of the ball-tampering controversy, Smith explained it was devised by the "leadership group" of the Australian team on the third day of the third Test in Cape Town. Bancroft was caught rubbing sandpaper on the ball the same day. While Smith, Warner and Bancroft – all batters – were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball. In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory." How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal Test cricket's biggest scandals - your results revealed Days after Bancroft's interview was published, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again. "We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands. "And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage. "We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on." Earlier this week, left-arm seamer Starc referenced the scandal when he said: "What's left to come out after eight years?" And, speaking on Thursday, Cummins said the episode was "a long time ago". "It's nothing new," the 33-year-old told ABC. "We've spoken about it a little bit. If the crowd gets rowdy or whatever, if someone needs an extra helping hand, we're around. "To be honest, it's so long ago and we, as a group, move on from things pretty quickly. It hasn't taken up too much of our time." The trip to South Africa is the first in a year of high-profile away series for Australia. After what appears to be a stern challenge against New Zealand in their home summer, Cummins' men then travel to India and defend the Ashes in England next year. With all-rounder Cameron Green ruled out because of injury, the tourists are likely to choose between Cooper Connolly and Nic Maddinson for a place in the middle order. On a Durban pitch expected to turn, South Africa have included two spinners – Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer - in their XI. title: Woman found dead in overflowing bath by man investigating leak, inquest hears
description: Laura Marshall's body was discovered in an overflowing bath at her home in April 2016.
body: Laura Marshall's body was discovered in an overflowing bath at her home in April 2016. The body of a 31-year-old Lurgan woman was found in a bath by a maintenance man who was investigating a leak in the block of flats she had been living in, an inquest has heard. Laura Marshall's bruised body was discovered in an overflowing bath at her home in Victoria Street in April 2016. According to a police officer, who was one of the first on the scene, he believed a violent assault had taken place. Gary O'Dowd, 38, from Brookfield Avenue in Banbridge, was arrested and charged with her murder. He denied any involvement in her death. Two years later the case against him was dropped after the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) decided to withdraw all charges. During the first day of the inquest, a statement from the maintenance man was read out to the court. He told how another resident in the block of flats had complained that there was water pouring through his ceiling. He said he had gone to the flat above where Laura Marshall had lived. He said the resident from the flat below had then gone with him to her flat. The man told the court that the lock on the front door of her flat was loose and that he had been able to force it open. He said he called out Marshall's name but that there was no answer. The flat, he said, was in darkness and that he had entered using a torch. He noted that the floor mat in the hall was sodden and that the door handle of the bathroom was on the floor in the hall. The spindle was not in the lock. Unable to open the door, the maintenance man had gone downstairs to his van to get a screwdriver which enabled him to unlock the door which had a childproof button on it. He said he opened the door a few inches and with the aid of his torch he saw Laura Marshall in the bath face down. She was naked and he noticed bruising on her shoulder. The taps were still running. The sink had been smashed and lay in pieces on the floor and there was blood on the floor. He said he reported it immediately to the police and that during the call he asked the police if he could turn off the running taps to which he was told he could. During an opening statement, a lawyer for the coroner said that Laura Marshall had been living with Gary O'Dowd at the property for a few years and that there had been a number of complaints of domestic violence against him. A detective sergeant, who was among the first members of the PSNI on the scene, also gave evidence. He too described the bathroom scene. He noted that there was a circular bruise on Laura's forehead and also bruising on her arm. He said he saw congealed blood higher than the water level of the bath. In his evidence he said he assessed that the death was suspicious and that it had the "hallmarks of a domestic violence-related murder." He said in his initial assessment of the scene, he believed that Marshall had taken refuge in the bathroom and that a violent assault had taken place there. Adding that the assault had ended with the victim drowned in the bath. He also noted that the sink had been smashed and that the inside door handle and spindle were on the floor of the bathroom. A forensic scientist also gave evidence to the court. During questioning by a lawyer acting on behalf of Laura Marshall's family he said that both the door frame and the bathroom door had been damaged when he examined the scene. He was asked if it was possible to lock the bathroom door from the outside. He replied: 'Yes". The inquest is expected to last until at least the end of next week. title: Ceferin to stand for fourth term as Uefa president
description: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin will stand for a fourth term, reversing a previous decision to stand down.
body: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin will stand for a fourth term as head of European football's governing body. Ceferin informed delegates of his decision at a meeting of all 55 national association chiefs in Berlin. The move had been widely anticipated and reverses his insistence he would not seek re-election, which the Slovenian initially outlined in February 2024. At that point Ceferin, who was initially elected in 2016, was embroiled in a row over Uefa changing its statutes to allow him to serve for a fourth term. However, there had been a growing expectation the 58-year-old would stand. This has only been made more likely since Uefa launched its efforts to oust Fifa president Gianni Infantino, who scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors following widespread opposition. Ceferin has ruled out standing against Infantino himself but is committed to finding a candidate the game can unite around when Fifa holds its presidential election in March. title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
description: Bernadette Greene-Placentia says her memory of the attack is spotty and that she was knocked unconscious.
body: A congressional candidate in Arizona has said she was raped in a car park as she repaired campaign signs late at night in her district. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, told the Phoenix New Times, external she was knocked unconscious during the alleged attack in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City on 14 August, waking up to find a man on top of her. She said she did not initially notify police until filing a report with the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office two weeks later. Her Republican opponent, Abraham Hamadeh, urged authorities in a statement to "investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place". "No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community," said Hamadeh, who is running for a second term in office. Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times she was "embarrassed" and "just wanted to forget", but felt compelled stand up for other victims. The candidate said she often speaks on the campaign trail about fighting for Arizonans. She told the Phoenix New Times: "I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault." The BBC has contacted the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for comment. A sheriff's spokesman told the New York Times the investigation was ongoing. After the attack, Greene-Placentia said she withdrew from the public for two days, staying in an apartment separate from her husband and skipping a campaign event. When she emerged, her husband, campaign staff and others in her circle noticed she was acting differently, according to Phoenix New Times. Greene-Placentia said she did not see a doctor following the alleged attack in congressional district eight and did not receive a sexual assault examination. She said her memory of what happened was spotty and she did not get a good look at either of the two assailants, but described them as white men, according to the New York Times. She told the Phoenix New Times that one assailant may have made a comment about her political affiliation, together with a misogynistic slur, although she could not be certain. The candidate said she was concerned voters might think it was a political stunt to win points in a heavily Republican district. She also expressed concern that the allegations might overshadow her messaging around affordability. title: Hate crimes rise after more offences motivated by religion and race
description: Figures supplied by police forces suggest nearly 150,000 hate crimes were recorded between April 2025 and March 2026
body: Burnt remains of Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green after an arson attack Hate crime numbers in England and Wales have seen "a genuine increase", the Home Office says, sparked by more offences motivated by race and religion. Figures supplied to the government by police forces suggest nearly 150,000 hate crimes were recorded between April 2025 and March 2026. It is a 7% increase from nearly 140,000 the year before. The data also suggests recorded hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation, disability and transgender identity are unchanged or falling. Policing Minister Sarah Jones said the rising figures were "a stark warning that hatred continues to blight our communities". Hate crime in England and Wales rises for first time in three years "We are delivering the biggest reforms to policing in over 200 years, alongside record funding to protect Muslim and Jewish people and places of worship," she added. The Home Office said there were a total of 146,825 hate crimes recorded by police in the two nations in the year to March 2026. Racially-motivated offences accounted for the majority of all police recorded hate crimes, at around 74%, with about 8% of other hate crimes classified as religious. The Home Office said the rise in these offences over the last year was due to an increase in public order offences, often taking the form of intimidation and abuse, but crimes involving violence and vandalism were also included in the statistics. "In the last two years, there has been a rise in hate crime offences that is not seen in the overall violent and public order offences trend," the report said. "This may suggest there has been a genuine increase in hate crime offences over the last two years." Where the ethnicity of the victim was known in the race and religion related hate crimes, around one third of victims were identified as Asian and around a quarter as black. The Home Office said that it was likely that hate crime "offences against white victims will include xenophobic abuse against people not born in the UK". The figures showed a 13% rise in religious hate crimes recorded by police during the year to March 2026, with 11,419 recorded offences in total. Of those there was a 15% rise in hate crimes targeting Muslims and 10% increase in those that targeted Jewish people. The increase in hate crimes targeting Muslims (from 4,479 to 5,132 offences) showed a particular rise in September of last year, which the Home Office said "coincided with a number of protests and incidents of public order". There were hate crimes targeting both Muslims and Jewish people following the start of the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel in the spring of this year. Antisemitic hate crimes have been at elevated levels since the beginning of the conflict between Israel and Hamas in 2023, but saw a spike in October 2025 following the fatal attack at the Heaton Park Synagogue in Manchester. Other attacks followed in the months after, including in March when four Jewish community ambulances were torched in Golders Green, north London. Prosecutors say the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community. title: Ex-councillor guilty of running sham Covid-19 lab
description: Faisal Shoukat is convicted of fraudulent trading and money laundering after a trial.
body: Faisal Shoukat, pictured leaving court, previously sat on Calderdale Council A former councillor has been found guilty of running a bogus coronavirus testing laboratory during the Covid-19 pandemic. Faisal Shoukat, who served on Calderdale Council, was convicted of causing public nuisance, fraudulent trading and money laundering after a trial at Bradford Crown Court. Four other people on trial alongside Shoukat - former justice minister Shahid Malik, Lynn Connell, Paul Moore and Dr Alexander Zarneh - were cleared of any wrongdoing. The verdicts were returned by His Honour Judge Chris Smith after the jury was discharged in April during their deliberations, when one member of the panel was arrested on suspicion of conspiring to pervert the course of justice. Judge Smith criticised a catalogue of "systemic failures" at the business, for which Shoukat was responsible for the day-to-day running, telling the court: "The overriding thought at the time was simply to make money. "Put simply, profit was put before professionalism and public safety." RT Diagnostics was set up in March 2021 with Shoukat and Mr Malik named among the directors, after the government invited private companies to help meet the demand for testing, including so-called 'Fit-to-Fly' tests. Prosecutors said 39-year-old Shoukat - who was a Labour councillor at the time - was the "controlling mind" of the Halifax-based firm. However, the court heard that test kits sent out to customers - sourced from Turkey - did not meet the required standards in the UK. It was also said the lab had returned a "suspiciously low" number of positive tests. Between May and July 2021 it reported 138,738 tests, but only 45 of these were positive, with 123,058 showing as negative and one indeterminate. A video published by The Sun newspaper in July of that year alleged tests were being dumped in a side room. The video also showed the firm's laboratory at Park Works to be in poor condition, with rubbish strewn across the floor, its ceiling exposed and bin bags dumped outside. Medical safety inspectors described the site on Lister Lane as a "building site" and said there was evidence of people living there. Delivering his verdicts, Judge Smith criticised the company's "cavalier" and "careless" approach to the accreditation process, which would allow it to conduct testing. There were also "systemic failures" with the company and the service it provided, he added. Customers experienced a "multitude of problems", the judge said, from test kits being delivered in unsealed boxes to results not being issued. Describing the testing and reporting systems at RT Diagnostics as "profoundly flawed", he said there was also evidence some samples "had simply not been tested". One customer was told he and his wife had tested positive for the virus, only to later receive an email from RT Diagnostics which said they had tested negative. Despite the firm only trading for a two-month period, almost 80% of the 1,218 Trustpilot reviews it received were one star. The former RT Diagnostics base was likened to a "building site" by medical safety inspectors Shoukat, a pharmacist, told the trial he was paid about £1.5m in shares from the firm. Mr Malik, who cried after he was cleared of wrongdoing, was also paid a similar amount as a co-director, the court heard. He was not involved in the day-to-day running of the company, and lived outside of the UK for part of its short-lived tenure. Mr Malik, 58, of Colne Rd, Burnley, was found not guilty of causing a public nuisance, fraudulent trading and money laundering. Ms Connell, 65, of Wagon Farm, Ripponden, Mr Moore, 57, of Plober Street, Burnley, and Dr Zarneh, 71, of Wood Lane, Halifax, were all found not guilty of causing a public nuisance and fraudulent trading. title: Stabbed schoolgirl in 'panic mode', court told
description: The girl told police there was "blood all over my hands" following the attack, a court hears.
body: A photo taken from within a classroom showed an armed police officer at the scene A schoolgirl who was stabbed by a masked fellow pupil at school described how "everything was going numb" and she had "blood all over her hands", a court has been told. Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March, following reports that a 15-year-old girl had been stabbed in the back. The defendant, who is now 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, has denied a charge of attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent. In a police interview played to the court, the girl described how she went into "panic mode" after being stabbed, King's Lynn Crown Court heard. Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School at 10:24 GMT on 11 March She told officers: "He was standing there head to toe in black, no school uniform whatsoever." Describing the attack, which took place in a corridor, she said it felt like she had been punched and then shortly afterwards felt a "sharp pain shoot through my back". When she realised she had been stabbed, she said: "I was in panic mode. Everything was going numb and feeling weak." She said there was "blood all over my hands" and described how police had to cut off her clothes to access the wound. When asked during the interview, which was conducted shortly after the incident, how she was feeling, the girl said: "A bit in shock, think it will hit me eventually, but it hasn't yet." She told officers she did not know the attacker and did not have any issues with people at school. Whilst giving evidence, the girl, who cannot be named because of her age, broke down in tears. The trial at King's Lynn Crown Court is expected to last three weeks The court has already been told that the defendant had written notes saying he hated women. One note, which prosecutors said was found by police pinned to the wall of his bedroom, said: "My barren world.. Hello. To all readers out there in the UK and perhaps even the world. If you're reading this, I am either dead or in custody. "I imagine the police will be the first to read this and seize it as evidence, so I will make something very clear. I made this decision to do so on my own." Another note read: "Am I evil for that? Probably. Am I an incel? A misogynist?. No. I just have good judgement." title: Up to 50 Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women, says chief constable
description: Chief Constable Jo Farrell says more officers are likely to be suspended as officers are re-vetted.
body: Jo Farrell said she expected more accusations of violence towards women by serving police officers would come to light The chief constable of Police Scotland has said up to 50 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls. Jo Farrell said she expected more would face sanctions over their behaviour following a spate of former officers being convicted for sexual offences. Farrell said a review into the handling of the case of police officer Alan Greer – who was exposed as a serial rapist after taking his own life – was under way. She added about 8,000 officers were still to be "re-vetted" for their roles after a change in regulations earlier this year. In an interview with BBC Scotland News, Farrell described the scale of violence against women and girls in Scotland as an "epidemic", and that police forces were not immune to the problem . She said: "We've got in the order of between currently 40 and 50 people currently suspended, so not at work, who are being investigated for offences that relate to violence against women and girls. "Those investigations are at various stages." Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years Police officer was violent rapist who attacked women over 14 years A BBC Disclosure investigation in July revealed that Alan Greer had repeatedly attacked and attempted to murder women over a 14-year period. Further inquiries uncovered that Greer had passed vetting checks to join what was then Strathclyde Police in 2009, despite having two reports of criminal behaviour against women on his record. Greer took his own life in May at the age of 47. Farrell said the scope of the review into Greer, parts of which would be made public, would identify whether gaps in the vetting process contributed to his offending being allowed to continue. "It is an ongoing investigation, but it is also subject to an independent review to find out whether there were any opportunities to identify his offending earlier and whether there is any learning from that," she told BBC Scotland. "What is important is that we get that independent review, that colleagues elsewhere in the United Kingdom are looking at that case to identify whether there were any opportunities that were missed." Greer is one of three former officers in Scotland to be exposed as rapists this year. In July, Cameron Ross was jailed for 10 years after he was found guilty of raping two women and threatening to kill another in Stornoway, on the Isle of Lewis, and in Inverness over a 10-year period. Ross, 39, has since launched an appeal against both his conviction and his sentence. Last month, former police sergeant Campbell Petrie, 50, was found guilty of a series of sex attacks on women between 2006 and 2023. Petrie - who was first arrested following a complaint by one of his victims 17 years ago – was convicted of two counts of rape and a number of other charges including physical and sexual abuse towards two women in Glasgow. He was suspended by Police Scotland after being charged with the offences in December 2023 but retired from the force two years later. Another officer, Jay Skivington, 24, was sentenced in October to 160 hours of unpaid work and given five-year non-harassment order for violent offences against a woman. Farrell said up to 50 officers were suspended over allegations of violence towards women Farrell said that between 300 and 400 officers had now been re-vetted as part of new rules brought in following the murder of Sarah Everard by Met Police officer Wayne Couzens. She said the rules would make it easier to "exit people" found to be unsuitable to serve in the force. "It's only now during this year there has been a change in the vetting regime. So for the first time, if an officer fails their vetting, they can be exited from policing," she said. "So that is a very recent change, and a welcome change from my point of view. Up until that point there were no opportunities to exit people from the organisation." Farrell added: "My focus is on identifying where there is wrongdoing, criminality, particularly in relation to violence against women and girls and if that has been committed by our officers and our staff, that we identify it and we ensure that those people feel the full force of the law." Craig Naylor, HM Chief Inspector of Constabulary, said incidents involving officers were taken "very seriously" when reported to Police Scotland. He said: "We've done work over the last number of years on vetting and police conduct on a number of areas that have highlighted where Police Scotland can improve and they are making improvements in those areas. "However, police officers are members of society and our society has violent offenders within it so they are likely to be further offenders within Scotland within policing." Naylor added: "For me, what we've seen with the recent incidents with Mr Greer, with Constable Petrie recently, have shown that when something is reported to Police Scotland they take it very seriously, they put their best resources onto it, they investigate it and they get convictions." title: Russell to take further grid penalty this season
description: George Russell says he will be taking a further grid penalty this season in addition to the one he has been hit with for the Singapore Grand Prix.
body: George Russell is 84 points behind Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli in the drivers' championship George Russell says he will be taking a further grid penalty this season in addition to the one he has been hit with for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix. The Briton will start Sunday's race from the back of the grid because he needs to fit a new engine which takes him beyond his permitted number for the season. But he says that he will have to take another new engine, as soon as a planned upgrade is ready, to get him to the end of the season. Russell said: "You get (a limit of) four engines a season, so six races on each, and we have seven races to the end. So I will be taking another penalty, so yeah it's pretty relentless at the moment." Russell's engine failure in Malaysia scuppered Mercedes' previous plan for him to last out with his older engine until the upgrade was ready, most likely for the next race, the United States Grand Prix in Austin. F1 heat hazard declared for fourth time this season Russell to start from back of Singapore grid after penalty "I knew I was going to have a penalty," Russell said. "The plan was always to go in Austin, and obviously Singapore is the second hardest track to overtake on on the calendars. So you would never choose to do it (here). "But we have no engines because of all of the various failures, so there was no engine I could have reverted to from earlier in the season. With the failure I had to take it. "We don't have the (upgrade) this weekend, and because there are seven races remaining, you can either choose to roll the dice and hope it lasts for seven races, but also suffer a performance offset (as the engine degrades), or just accept I'll be taking another penalty." Antonelli will also likely have another back-of-the-grid penalty when the upgraded engine is introduced, following his previous one at the Italian Grand Prix, which he won from 19th on the grid. Russell will also be reverting to an older specification car in Singapore this weekend. Mercedes introduced an aerodynamic upgrade in Malaysia last weekend, but it did not give the car the performance uplift expected. So in an attempt to prove whether that was because of idiosyncrasies to do with the Sepang track or a problem with the upgrade itself, Mercedes is splitting the specification of their cars. Russell will drive the specification with which he won in Azerbaijan, the week before Malaysia, while Antonelli will run the new spec. Russell said: "I actually asked a question already on Friday in Sepang. At the end of the day it's the car I'm reverting to is a car that was on pole by 0.8secs and Kimi won the race before, so it's important to remember the context. It's not like reverting back to a launch car. "Given the circumstances of the grid penalty as well, it just seemed like a no-brainer. For me, unfortunately we're not going to be fighting for a podium this weekend, it's exceptionally unlikely, so it's more important for us to try and understand, was Malaysia a one-off or was it the upgrade?" Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app Russell's retirement in Malaysia, along with Antonelli finishing second to Red Bull's Max Verstappen, meant the Italian's lead in the drivers' championship has extended to 84 points. Both Mercedes drivers have suffered reliability problems this year but Russell believes his season has been disproportionately affected by factors outside his control. "I've probably had more failures this year than I've had in the three seasons put together, and of course it's tough to take," he said. "If I'm being 100% fair with myself, as I've said before, the performance this season hasn't been strong enough, and it probably would have affected me more if I'd have still been in the fight. "But obviously the pressure and the momentum, every setback has an impact on that momentum. "Since the start of the year (an engine failure) in Canada was the big one, and then, you know, the drive-through penalty in Monaco. The loss at the weekend has basically compromised two weekends for me. "Two races, Silverstone and Spa, with the PU issues we had (involving a loss of performance from the engine), it's been pretty incredible how things have panned out this year, but I think just focus on what you can control."
