title: How student loans work for tuition fees and living costs
description: Many students getting their results will be looking at how to pay for their time at university.
body: Students and graduates across the UK have different student loan plans depending on when and where they studied. Loan rules vary between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but most students still need to borrow to pay for their studies. The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500. Student loans vary depending on where you live in the UK and when you started your course. They are typically made up of: a loan for tuition fees a maintenance loan for living costs Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course, external. Maximum fees vary across the UK: England and Wales: £9,790 a year. Northern Ireland: £4,985 for Northern Irish students or £9,790 for other UK students. Scotland: Free for the majority of Scottish students and £9,790 for other UK students. The separate maintenance loan is intended to cover accommodation, food, books and equipment. Maintenance loans are means tested, so the amount you get depends on your family's household income. You might get extra money if you are disabled, or have children. If you are under 25 and have no contact with your parents, you might be able to apply as an "estranged student"., external This means your parents' financial situation is not taken into consideration. Research by the Higher Education Policy Institute published in May 2024, external suggested maintenance loans in England typically only covered about half the cost of living, and even less for students in London. In April 2026, over 20,000 students were told they had been "mis-sold" their maintenance loans as their courses were ineligible, and were told to pay back the money they had received. 'Huge relief' as students given loans 'in error' get repayment reprieve Students who took out a loan in England to start university between September 2012 and July 2023 have a Plan 2 loan. These loans are still issued in Wales. Graduates with Plan 2 loans pay back 9% of everything they earn over the repayment threshold. In the November 2025 Budget, Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the threshold would be frozen at £29,385 between 2027 and 2030, rather than rising with inflation. That means students will start repaying their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries will lead to greater repayments. Campaigners want to see that change reversed, and for the government to consider a lower repayment rate and a lower interest rate. Plan 2 loans take on interest at the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3% depending on earnings. It means many graduates with Plan 2 loans have struggled to make a substantial dent in the overall debt they left university with, which is often in the tens of thousands of pounds, despite making repayments for years. The maximum interest rate charged on Plan 2 loans is capped. The cap is reviewed periodically and may change from one academic year to the next. 'Deeply misleading' school talks compared student loans to £30 phone contracts Plan 2 student loan interest rates capped at 6% in England The amount of maintenance support available to new students varies across the UK. The maximum maintenance loan for students from England living away from their parents outside London is £10,830 for the 2026-27 academic year. The government is reintroducing maintenance grants of up to £1,000 per year for students from lower income households in England on courses that support its Industrial Strategy. They will be available from 2028 and the government is still drawing up a list of eligible courses. Students from Wales studying away from home can borrow up to £11,570 in the 2026-27 academic year. Welsh students may also be entitled to maintenance grants, external, which do not have to be paid back. In Scotland, the maximum annual maintenance loan is £9,400, external for under-25s. Students can also apply for a number of bursaries and grants. Students from Northern Ireland studying away from home can borrow up to £8,352, external for the 2026-27 academic year. Students from England can use the loans calculator on the Student Finance England, external website Students from Wales can go to Student Finance Wales, external Students from Scotland can go to Student Awards Agency Scotland, external Students from Northern Ireland can go to Student Finance Northern Ireland, external Tuition fee limits and maintenance loan amounts are reviewed by the government each year and can change. The government has said only those universities which provide strong outcomes for students will be able to charge the maximum amount in England. Universities which fall below the quality threshold set by the regulator in England, the Office for Students, may also face a cap on the number of students they can recruit. What does university cost, and is it worth it? The tuition fees are paid directly to your university or education provider. The maintenance loan is paid directly to your bank account in instalments. Payments are made at the start of each term in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and monthly in Scotland. In order to be paid you'll need to register, external at your university or college. You'll usually do this in the first week of your course, and you may have to take along your student finance entitlement letter. In England you should get a text from the Student Loans Company a few days before to let you know the maintenance loan is on the way. You can apply for funding up to nine months after the first day of the academic year for your course. Depending on where you live, you will need to apply through: The Students Awards Agency Scotland, external, or Student Finance Northern Ireland, external Interest rates on some student loans are reviewed regularly. For the 2026-27 academic year, interest on Plan 2 and Plan 3 loans in England is capped at 6%. You are charged interest on the loan from the day y

title: Death of 12-year-old girl prompts call for allergy management ratings
description: Mia St Hilaire had a tree nut allergy and suffered an anaphylactic shock after drinking a milkshake.
body: Mia St Hilaire died after drinking a milkshake in August 2023 The family of a 12-year-old girl who died after drinking a milkshake made in an unwashed blender at a cafe have called for a dedicated rating that scores food businesses on their allergy management. Mia St Hilaire, who had a tree nut allergy, suffered an anaphylactic shock and died after she drank a Twix milkshake at the Pop Inn Cafe in Bermondsey, south-east London, in August 2023. Her order contained hazelnut residue because the blender had not been washed after a Kinder Bueno milkshake was made in it beforehand, an inquest concluded on Thursday. In a statement, her family said "significant changes" were needed to protect people with food allergies. In January 2025, the cafe was fined £18,000 and its proprietor Baris Yucel was given 100 hours of community service after admitting six criminal charges related to the Food Safety Act. These included not making allergen advice available or visible to consumers, failing to manage allergen contamination during the food production process, and serving food that contained an allergenic ingredient that was not supposed to be present. CCTV evidence showed that Yucel had not cleaned the blender before preparing Mia's milkshake. Mia's parents said their "deeply loved" daughter would never be forgotten Assistant coroner Briony Ballard listened to evidence at London Inner South Coroner's Court before publishing a narrative conclusion on Mia's death. In a statement read after the conclusion of the inquest, Mia's parents Adrian St Hilaire and Chanel Spence said families with food allergies should not be "at risk" when eating out. "We hope that lessons will be learned from Mia's death and that changes will be made to prevent other families enduring the devastation that we now have to live with," they said. "Consumers rely on food hygiene ratings when deciding where it is safe to eat, but they do not tell us anything about the way a food business runs allergy management systems. "There should be a separate, clearly displayed rating dedicated to the allergy management, like the food hygiene rating. "This would mean that people with allergies could make more informed choices about where they eat." Natasha's Foundation founder Tanya Ednan-Laperouse, whose daughter died aged 15 from an allergy to sesame in a Pret A Manger baguette, said allergies were "a serious, unpredictable medical condition". "The inquest into Mia's death illustrates just how far we still have to go to improve awareness, understanding and regulation of food allergies," she said. "Natasha's Foundation is working hard with business, schools, communities and the government to increase awareness and understanding of food allergies to try to prevent other families from having to go through the terrible loss that Mia's family endure." title: Chrysler Building to get its crown restored after being sold
description: The distinctive Manhattan skyscraper will undergo a major renovation and provide a new supply of offices.
body: The skyscraper was briefly the world's tallest building The Chrysler Building, one of the most distinctive high-rises in Manhattan's skyline, will undergo a major renovation as part of a multi-million-dollar sale deal. The skyscraper, opened in New York nearly 100 years ago, will see its Art Deco crown polished and restored during a refurbishment that will also involve the restoration of the building's 77-storey façade. Developer Tishman Speyer has taken over the lease from the Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science and Art, a private college. Tishman Speyer and its partners will invest $235m (£178m) in the project, as part of which it will upgrade the 61st floor, which is home to huge eagle gargoyles and will also feature an "upscale" lounge. The developer is planning to use most of the building, which is close to Grand Central railway station, for office space. It is following what it calls a "prebuild approach" that will allow firms to move into their new premises quickly. Tishman Speyer explained that the area "has one of the lowest office availability rates in Manhattan", adding: "Construction of new office supply in the neighbourhood has been virtually nonexistent for decades." The renovation will include internal work, such as upgrades to the building's mechanical, elevator, electrical and air handling systems. At 1,046ft (319m), the Chrysler Building was once the world's tallest building - before being usurped less than a year later by the nearby Empire State Building. Financed by Walter Chrysler, the motor magnate, the skyscraper's construction began in 1928 and was completed two years later. Architect William Van Alen modelled the eagle gargoyles on hood ornaments found on the 1929 Chrysler car. Popping out for lunch: a worker eats a sandwich during construction of the Chrysler Building The Cooper Union college, whose alumni include inventor Thomas Edison, has owned the land on which the Chrysler Building stands since 1902. The land was bequeathed to it by the children of Peter Cooper, a manufacturer and industrialist who founded the college in 1859. As part of the deal, Tishman Speyer will make ground lease payments to the Cooper Union which the college wants to use to finance "a bold plan to restore full-tuition scholarships for all undergraduates". Cooper Union's president Steven McLaughlin, said: "The significance of this agreement is ultimately about what it makes possible for generations of Cooper Union students." title: 'Ominous signs' of winter pressures as NHS waiting list grows
description: NHS winter pressures appear to be building already, with rises in waiting times for planned surgery.
body: The NHS in England experienced its busiest September on record There are "ominous signs" that winter pressures are already affecting the NHS in England, according to senior health leaders. The warning comes as new data reveals the waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row. An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients. The numbers are the highest since October 2025 and have raised questions over whether the NHS will meet a government target of treating 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029. The rise in waiting lists comes despite the NHS in England delivering what were described as record levels of planned, elective care over the summer, while demand for services also reached its highest level ever. A record 4.7 million planned treatments, procedures and appointments occurred across June, July and August – more than in any previous summer. But both A&Es and ambulance services also saw a record number of patients for the month of September. NHS England's national medical director, Professor Frankie Swords, warned that despite the progress delivered by frontline teams, winter pressure was already building. "Staff are already seeing the ominous early signs of pressure, with more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year, and unfortunately many people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she said. The NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, says the government in England is not going to achieve its manifesto promise of hitting the 18-week hospital waiting time target by the end of the parliament in 2029. That 18-week target hasn't been hit for a decade. A separate analysis by the Health Foundation think-tank said progress on cutting waiting times had stalled over the past year, with referrals on to the waiting list rising at a much quicker rate than the number of patients being treated. Sir Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance which represents NHS trusts, said: "The NHS continues to respond to record demand for care, but the relentless growth in demand for services is putting NHS staff under real pressure." Francesca Cavallaro, of the Health Foundation, said: "Thanks to the hard work of staff, the NHS has made progress in bringing down waiting times, but a rise in referrals mean that the service is having to run faster just to stand still and the prospects of meeting the government's pledge are receding. "Andy Burnham's government have yet to set out whether they will give the 18-week target the same priority as it had under Keir Starmer, but our analysis shows the pledge is becoming increasingly hard to deliver." There will be concern too that the pressures of a long, hot summer have merged almost seamlessly into the pressures associated with the winter months. More patients, including children, have been arriving at A&E departments with flu and other respiratory viruses. The number of patients seen within four hours in A&Es last month fell to 74.4%, down from 75.0% in August. The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted – what is known as "corridor care" – stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August. That has alarmed Dr Vicky Price, president of the Society for Acute Medicine. "A 13% year-on-year rise in 12-hour emergency department waits as winter approaches should set alarm bells ringing. "More than 50,000 patients waited over 12 hours from the decision to admit to admission in September - 1,686 people every day. "These are not just numbers. "They represent vulnerable people who are waiting far too long for a bed and staff trying to deliver safe care in overcrowded emergency departments." The government says the 18-week mark could still be achieved, saying it was investing in NHS buildings and equipment to make services more productive. It also pointed to disruption to care that was caused by the strikes by resident doctors, a dispute which has now been settled. But the strain that services are feeling in September, before winter has even really got going, will be a cause for concern among NHS leaders and their political bosses alike. title: 'My donated Brummie accent gives me confidence'
description: Christian Wilson wanted help not to "sound like a character from Star Wars or a cyborg from Doctor Who".
body: Christian Wilson, pictured alongside presenter Tammy Gooding, said his new Birmingham dialect had given him "the confidence to voice [his] opinion" A man who appealed for help to no longer sound like a "character from Star Wars" says he has found his calling. Christian Wilson, from Bromsgrove, has verbal dyspraxia - a difficulty in placing muscles in the correct position to produce speech. He uses text-to-speech software in order to communicate, but said he wanted to sound "like a man from Birmingham". The 24-year-old's dream was made possible in 2024 when he selected two voice donors that blended a Birmingham accent and a Warwickshire accent, which he hoped would help him sound more like his father. Since May, Wilson has worked at Worcestershire County Council as a SEND Peer Advocate. He said his new dialect had given him "the confidence to voice [his] opinion". Speaking to BBC Hereford & Worcester on Thursday, he told presenter Tammy Gooding: "There was a moment where I thought, this is really what I'm meant to do. "I was really excited about it, because as long as I can remember I've always wanted to be an advocate, plus I have always been passionate about education." Death of girl, 11, not investigated as crime Footage shows Dexter 'kill room' murderer's arrest Woman denies abortion clinic buffer zone charges According to the NHS, external, verbal dyspraxia is a speech disorder where the muscles have not been damaged, but the messages from the brain that tell the muscles what to do have been affected. The condition caused Wilson to start his search to find his voice. Previously, he said: "I'm from Bromsgrove and I was born in Birmingham. "I want to sound like a man from Birmingham, not a character from Star Wars or a cyborg from Doctor Who." And now as a SEND Peer Advocate, Wilson said he now had the confidence to challenge Ofsted representatives to "do more" for children and young people with disabilities. This video can not be played Christian Wilson said his new Birmingham dialect had given him "the confidence to voice [his] opinion" He said: "The representatives said they would definitely feed back what I had said. My hopes for the future are that I continue to use my voice as an instrument to do good. "I hope to continue to advocate for disabled children and young people by sharing my expertise and experience with whoever necessary to improve the lives of others in Worcestershire." In 2024, he described feeling emotional when he listened through to the voice submissions with his family. "As I was listening to them, I knew I was getting closer to my dream, something that I thought never would happen," he said. "I hope to use my new voice to share my experiences with other people - that would be great." Wilson's sister felt an instant connection to the Birmingham accent he selected for his new voice. He said: "I liked the voice originally, but when my sister heard it she said 'that is you.'" Wilson's Birmingham voice donor, Martin Brennan, said: "It's such an emotional journey and even sitting here, I'm welling up now. "I just thought why not - it was a no brainer and it was a joy to get involved." Fellow donor, Stephen Robotham, from Warwickshire, said: "Having a voice is so important and especially having your own voice, it's integral to your identity." title: Derry firm becomes one of UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP
description: The Martin Group has become one of the UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP out of administration.
body: A Londonderry company has become one of the UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP out of administration. The deal means the Martin Group will control more than 100 sites. The NCP business collapsed in March 2026 after a sustained period of declining performance left it unable to pay its debts. At that time some of its sites were closed or transferred to other operators. The administrators, PwC, said the majority of NCP's 145 sites would now transfer to the Martin Group along with the staff who work there. Zelf Hussain, joint administrator and partner at PwC, said the deal protected hundreds of jobs and delivered the best outcome for creditors. "Keeping NCP's car parks open also helps keep Britain's town and city centres moving," he added. "We would like to thank all of NCP's staff and directors for their support and professionalism throughout what has understandably been a period of uncertainty." NCP's major problems included being locked into long-term leases with property owners and building up a large amount of debt. The Martin Group already has a substantial commercial property portfolio across the UK including the Fishergate Shopping Centre in Preston and the Mercury Shopping Centre in Romford. It has recently expanded its hotels business, developing The Bedford Hotel in Belfast and buying The Waterfoot in Derry. Gary Martin, director of Martin Property Group, said the company's goal was to "build on the strength and heritage of the NCP brand so it can once again deliver the lasting impact on the communities it serves". "NCP is an iconic brand with a loyal customer base and talented workforce," he added. Rob England, chief executive of NCP, said it was "a fantastic day for NCP". "We have had to make difficult, necessary decisions to keep the business moving forward," he said. England said NCP was "immensely grateful" to its employees, customers and suppliers and its priority was "to restore full operational momentum and build a sustainable platform for long-term growth". title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
description: Casualties have been reported on the vessel, identified by a maritime intelligence firm as the oil and chemical tanker, Acers.
body: Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the start of the Iran war (file photo) A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency. The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said. Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman. Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February. At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO). The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula. This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group. Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates. The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler. title: Russian strike on buses kills 33, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
description: Ukraine accused Russia of targeting the crowded bus in the frontline city to kill as many civilians as possible.
body: Volodymyr Zelensky posted to Telegram providing his condolences to families and loved ones affect and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action" Thirty-three people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say. Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible. Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road. Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Russia is trying to seize as part of Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas. Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025. In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Thursday, said the attack in Pryluky showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy". He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict". Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 22 in block of flats Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Donetsk regional head Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine. Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said. Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine. For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city. Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day. Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population". "Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said. Intensified Russian strikes are tearing Kyiv apart, warns mayor Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks Russia is also launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing throughout the day. Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko said attacks on Thursday had killed three people, with 14 others injured. Two of the eight injured are in a critical condition. The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport. Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts. Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine". Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of warned of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter. Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have. Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics. Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses. title: Teacher who sexually abused pupil back in Indonesia jail after BBC investigation
description: Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani had been secretly released on parole in 2025, after serving less than half his sentence.
body: Bechi was recorded at an event earlier this year by undercover BBC reporters A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early. Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher. A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know. On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief. "I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC. The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations. But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review. That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison. Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions". "We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said. Ira Puspitasari (right), one of several women who accused Bechi of rape, said she was "amazed" to hear the news For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication. "I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said. Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15. "I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said. She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her. She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened". Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external. Watching BBC undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, when he should still have been in prison, Ira became tearful. "It's like nothing ever happened," she said. Ira was invited to a parliamentary hearing this week into the state's handling of sexual abuse cases in religious and educational institutions, held in response to the BBC's investigation. Lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has represented several victims of abuse in educational institutions, also addressed the hearing and said authorities were often reluctant to investigate allegations of abuse because they involved "influential religious figures who have large followings". He told the hearing that he regularly faced threats and intimidation as a result of taking on such cases. This video can not be played Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early Bechi is the son of prominent Islamic cleric Muhammad Mukhtar Mu'thi, founder of the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in Jombang, East Java. He was arrested in 2022 after a 15-hour police siege at the school, where supporters had gathered to prevent his arrest. Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence after Bechi was accused of rape by a number of students, but he was acquitted of the rape charges and convicted of the lesser sexual assault offence of one student. The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah boarding school as part of its investigation but received no response. title: Three sisters who drowned in sea off Brighton took own lives, inquest finds
description: The bodies of Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters were pulled from the sea in May.
body: The three sisters, pictured here as teenagers with their father, died in the sea. From left to right, Jane Adetoro, Joseph, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters Three sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton took their own lives, a coroner has ruled. Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, had been living "very secluded lives" following the death of their mother, who drowned in 2010, senior coroner Penelope Schofield said. On 11 May, the women - who had all been living together in Greenford, London - visited an area of Birmingham close to where their mother died before travelling the next day to Brighton beach, where they drowned in adverse sea conditions in the early hours of 13 May. The coroner said they could not swim. Their father Joseph Jacobsen said it was heartbreaking to lose "all three of my precious daughters". He was among family members who followed proceedings via video link. In an emotional statement read out on his behalf, he said he watched his daughters grow from little girls to beautiful, intelligent women "with a special place in my heart". He said: "There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. "To lose all three of my precious daughters is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined." He could not understand why his daughters' lives ended so suddenly, and hoped they were reunited with their mother "in God's eternal care", he added. The bodies of the three sisters were recovered off Brighton beach in the early hours of 13 May The coroner told the court: "These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private, we don't know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton. "It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known." The hearing was told the sisters left their home in London and arrived in Brighton together by taxi at 22:21 BST on 12 May. They were last seen alive at 02:42 on 13 May. Police searched Christina's laptop and found 227 references to water and 179 references to suicide. The coroner said Christina had been experiencing anxiety and depression since the death of her mother. Rebecca's medical records showed "nothing of note" and Jane was not registered with a doctor, Det Ch Insp Mark Cullimore told the court. A previous inquest into their mother's death had found her cause of death was drowning. Postmortem tests revealed toxicology results for all three sisters were negative for drugs and alcohol. There was no evidence to suggest they had been subject to violence. If you are experiencing emotional stress, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line here. title: Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
description: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says the move will deliver more stable government, but opposition parties say her aim is to stay in power.
body: Opposition parties say the move is designed to keep Meloni's right-wing coalition in power Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year. Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government. Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy. Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority. Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two. The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation. Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election. A coalition or party winning more than 42% of the vote will be awarded dozens of additional seats in parliament - which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority. In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules. "Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein. Elly Schlein pictured during the debate in parliament on Thursday The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia. Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election. "To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens." She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour." Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring. title: Watch: Why was the sign at the British consulate in East Jerusalem removed?
description: The consulate, first established in 1838, was set to be closed by the Israeli government in retaliation for UK sanctions.
body: This video can not be played Israel said in September it would shut the British consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law. The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the building ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement. Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission". The BBC's Middle East correspondent Yolande Knell says the UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband "sees this as being a good outcome". The consulate is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel. title: Bear kills man in home attack near Mongolian capital
description: Police say the bear entered a traditional nomadic dwelling near Ulaanbaatar, killing a man and seriously injured a woman.
body: The Eurasian brown bear (file photo) is found in the region around Ulaanbaatar. A bear has killed a man and seriously injured a woman after it attacked them in their home near the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar. Police say the incident happened in the Bayanzurkh district overnight on Wednesday in their traditional Mongolian nomadic tent-like structure known as a ger. The man, who was in his 40s, died, but the woman, in her 50s, managed to flee and raise the alarm with neighbours. She is in a serious condition in hospital, city official Munkhbayar M told reporters. Sightings of bears around humans are becoming more common in Mongolia, for reasons that include climate change and food scarcity. A team of rangers is searching for the bear while officials have warned locals to be vigilant and report any sightings. There had been 24 bear sightings near the capital this year alone, compared to just two in 2018, Munkhbayar said, in comments reported by the AFP news agency. Videos showing bears entering or damaging gers, and attacking livestock have reportedly gone viral on Mongolian social media in recent weeks, highlighting the increase in bear and human interaction across the country. Bear-hunting permits across eight provinces have been issued and officials are seeking to obtain tranquiliser dart guns to support rangers in rural areas, AFP reports. A significant amount of Mongolians are nomadic, but settled agricultural communities are becoming more common. An increasing number of the population lives in the capital or other major urban areas. title: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize
description: Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.
body: Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature. Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship. The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature". The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regareded as the most prestigious award in global literature with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m). Anne Carson pictured in 1998 In 2019, her performance piece Norma Jeane Baker of Troy drew a line between famous beauties from different historical periouds - Helen of Troy and Marilyn Monroe. In 2021, she released The Trojan Women: A Comic, a graphic retelling of Euripides' ancient story; and her translation of Elektra by Sophocles was staged starring Brie Larson in London last year. Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement. "She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said. "She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice." Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson lives in Michigan and has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022. Anders Olsson, chairman of the Swedish Academy's Nobel committee for Literature, praised the way Carson has "broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature". "This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms," he said. Carson's notable works include The Glass Essay, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, Nox, Float and The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos. She has been a professor of classics for more than 30 years and her writing is often inspired by Greek literature. Her translations have often given a contemporary twist to ancient works. "Her collaborations with visual artists and choreographers and with opera and theatre directors demonstrate the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems," Olsson said. "It is this that lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene." title: Bid to run new trains on West Coast Mainline refused
description: Plans for more trains would “likely increase delays and cancelled trains", the rail regulator says.
body: The West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, Stephanie Tobyn, from the Office of Rail and Road said Plans for new train services between London and Wrexham, Rochdale and Blackpool have been rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR). The proposal to add more trains on the West Coast Main Line would "likely increase delays and cancelled trains for passengers", the regulator said. It rejected Wrexham, Shropshire and Midlands Railway's application for four daily Wrexham to London Euston return services, as well as Lumo's proposal for up to four return services between Rochdale and Euston on weekdays and Saturdays, and three on Sundays. Avanti West Coast's plans for additional services between Blackpool and Euston were also denied by the ORR. The regulator said: "Gaps in the current timetable need to provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers. "ORR concluded that adding more services into these windows in the timetable for recovery would reduce that resilience, increasing the risk of disruption spreading to other services and affecting more passengers." Stephanie Tobyn, from the ORR, said: "New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. "But the West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. "Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers." The ORR said its assessment and decision came after similar applications were rejected in 2025. title: Residents airlifted to safety after flooding in central Chile
description: The Mapocho river has burst its banks after an unusually large amount of rain fell in recent days.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Houses underwater and families trapped by floodwaters in Chile Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes. Recent torrential rains caused the Mapocho river to burst its banks, flooding large parts of the city of Talagante, 35km (22 miles) south-west of the capital, Santiago. Santiago has seen 74mm of rainfall in the first seven days of this month, making it the rainiest October for the area in 76 years, meteorologists have said. They have warned that this year's unusually strong El Niño climate phenomenon will likely continue to bring unusually wet weather, powerful winds and storms to the region during the southern hemisphere's spring. Officials said one person had been found dead in a flooded underpass in the city of San Bernardo, south of Santiago, although they have yet to confirm the cause of death. In Talagante, police used helicopters to rescue people and pets living on the banks of the Mapocho who had been surprised by the fast-rising waters overnight. Dirt roads turned into rivers in the riverside community which, unlike in July's storms, had not been evacuated ahead of the heavy downpours. The Mapocho river in central Chile burst its banks after heavy rains Climate experts have warned that the 2026-2027 El Niño is likely to cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, intensifying droughts in some areas and floods in others. In central Chile, it is expected to trigger above-average rainfall. title: The Bottom Line
description: What's going wrong with the largest economy in Europe?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·08 Oct 2026,·35 mins Available for over a year What is going wrong with the largest economy in Europe? It accounts for roughly one-third of the continent's total manufacturing output but since 2020 there's been very little growth. Some people suggest the problems facing the country have been brewing for decades. It's argued Germany has been slow to adapt to modern ways of doing business and hasn't kept up with industrial competition from abroad. Evan Davis is joined by a panel of experts to understand how much trouble the German economy is in, why it's struggling and what it can do to revive itself. Guests: Verena Pausder: Chair of the German Start-Up Association Nicola Pinder: Business expansion consultant for the German state of Baden-Wurttemberg Marcel Fratzscher: President of the German Institute for Economic Research Wolfgang Munchau: Journalist and Author of Kaput, The End of the German Miracle Presenter: Evan Davis Producers: Nick Holland & Sally Abrahams Sound: Dave O'Neill & Donald MacDonald Production Coordinator: Katie Morrison Editor: Matt Willis

title: Gazans face near-daily Israeli strikes a year into ceasefire
description: The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for the remaining hostages held in Gaza.
body: This video can not be played More than 1,400 people in Gaza have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for the remaining hostages held in Gaza. It was an agreement to end the war, triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire. The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry. Israel blocks international journalists from going in to Gaza to report freely. With the help of journalists in Gaza, Yogita Limaye reports from Jerusalem. title: Cavern Club sold to new owners after 35 years
description: John Lennon's sister, Julia Baird, one of the previous owners, says it is being left "in good hands".
body: The Beatles played at the original Cavern 292 times on the road to stardom Liverpool's Cavern Club and Magical Mystery Tour have new owners after 35 years. A group called 14 Collective have bought Cavern City Tours, which also includes the Cavern Pub and Restaurant. John Lennon's sister, Julia Baird, who was one of the previous owners, said she felt "sad for me personally, yet positive for the future of this world famous, number one music club", adding that it was being left "in good hands". The Beatles played at the original Cavern 292 times as they were on the road to stardom between 1961-63. But the underground club was filled in after it closed in 1973. A replica was built on the site in 1984 and now attracts a million Beatles fans every year. The Beatles' first Cavern Club gig was in 1961 Managing director Bill Heckle trained to be a Beatles guide in 1982 before forming the Cavern City Tours in 1983. Alongside Dave Jones they organised their first Beatles convention, which evolved into the annual Mathew Street Music Festival. In 1991, they acquired the Magical Mystery Tour - bus tours of Liverpool - and the Cavern Club venue. Heckle said the decision to sell was "not taken lightly" but it was "time for retirement". "It is an emotional day, but a proud day, for the four Scouse owners," he said. "It was never about putting Cavern City Tours up for sale to the highest bidder and it has taken over five years to find a suitable and like-minded custodian. "However, we leave with the confidence that the new owners will continue to follow the path we have forged over the last 43 years." In a statement, the new owners, 14 Collective, said: "We look forward to working alongside the existing management team, with a real appreciation for what makes the Cavern so special and excitement about what comes next." title: Everything you need to know about university costs
description: With rising tuition fees and living costs, do higher graduate earnings cover the cost of a degree?
body: Graduates in England leave university with more than £47,500 in student debt, according to the latest statistics. Figures from the 2025-26 financial year suggest that the amount borrowers owe when they first become eligible to repay has, on average, fallen compared to the year before. But is a university degree worth it? And can graduates still expect to earn sufficiently more than those without a degree to cover the cost of going in the first place? Last August, the annual cost of an undergraduate degree in England and Wales went up to £9,535 a year. It rose again to £9,790 in 2026. The increases came after universities expressed growing concerns about funding pressures in recent years, pointing out that tuition fees had been frozen at £9,250 since 2017. They argued that inflation meant those fees were worth less in real terms and there had been fewer international students to help make up the financial shortfall. In October 2025, the government said university tuition fees in England would go up every year in line with inflation from 2026. They are expected to increase every year by an inflation measure called the Retail Price Index minus mortgage payment interest, or RPIx. UK nations set their own fees. In Northern Ireland, external, the maximum annual cost of an undergraduate degree is £4,855 for Northern Irish students or £9,535 for other UK students. That will rise to £4,985 and £9,790 respectively in 2026-27. In Scotland, external, undergraduate tuition is free for the majority of Scottish students and £9,535 for other UK students - rising to £9,790 in 2026-27. Student loans are made up of two components, external: a loan for tuition fees a maintenance loan for living costs Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course. Maintenance loans are means-tested, so how much you can borrow depends on your family's income, and may not cover your actual bills. The maximum maintenance loan for students in England is also set to increase by inflation every year from 2026. For example, the maximum maintenance loan for students from England who live away from their parents outside London will increase to £10,830 for 2026-27, up from £10,544 the year before. You are charged interest on your total loan from the day you take it out, but do not have to start paying it back until your annual income reaches a certain level. Once you reach that level, you make a regular payment which covers both your tuition fees and maintenance loans. Repayment rules are also different across the UK. They changed in England in 2023, meaning current and future students are likely to pay back more, over a longer period of time, than those who went to university earlier. Money saving expert Martin Lewis said the extended repayment period would increase "costs by thousands" for lower and mid-earners., external Graduates in England who became liable to pay back their loans in April 2026 had an average debt of £47,730, external, according to the Student Loans Company - down from £53,000 the year before. That's partly because this was the first year that any students who took out Plan 5 loans – introduced in England in 2023 – became eligible to repay, and their loans accrue less interest than earlier Plan 2 loans. Plan 5 borrowers accounted for more than 10% of the total number of borrowers in the 2025-26 financial year. Everything you need to know about student loans Former students urged to check for loan refunds Student rents have risen sharply in recent years, alongside other living costs. The Higher Education Policy Institute (Hepi), external says average weekly costs for a first-year student in 2023-24 were £260 without rent, or £418 when rent is included. Average annual rent across 10 university towns and cities, external - excluding London and Edinburgh - rose from £6,520 in 2021-22 to £7,475 in 2023-24. Separate figures for London found that, external the average rent for purpose-built student accommodation in the capital was £13,595 in 2024-25. Hepi said last year that students needed £61,000 over the course of a three-year degree in order to have a "minimum socially acceptable standard of living" - and that's excluding tuition fees. In London, that figure is £77,000. The think tank's 2026 student survey, external found the percentage of full-time undergraduates in paid employment during term time was 65% - a slight fall from the previous year, but much higher than the 45% in 2022. My student loan doesn't cover my bills, so I wear my work uniform to lectures Struggling students skip meals as living costs rise Is university right for me? Eligible students in Wales and Northern Ireland can claim maintenance grants which do not have to be repaid. Full-time undergraduates normally resident in Wales are entitled to at least £1,000, external, rising to £1,020 in 2026-27. Students from the poorest backgrounds who choose to study in London can get up to £10,124, which will rise to £10,325. In Northern Ireland the maximum grant is £3,475, external, rising to £3,569 in 2026-27. The government in England is bringing back maintenance grants of up to £1,000 per year for students from lower income households on courses that support its Industrial Strategy. They will be available from 2028 and the government is still drawing up a list of eligible courses. The Scottish government offers financial support to certain categories of students, external, such as those with dependants. Across the UK, students in financial difficulty can apply for hardship funding and they may also be entitled to financial assistance from charities., external Recent research, external from Hepi and AdvanceHE suggests that 45% of undergraduate students think the value for money of their course is "good" or "very good", up from 37% last year and the highest proportion recorded in more than ten years. Whether or not university can be considered "worth it" will vary from person

title: Gaten Matarazzo on life after Stranger Things as he makes West End debut
description: The actor opens up about finding his way in the West End as he makes his debut in a revival of Rent.
body: Gaten Matarazzo is no stranger to musical theatre Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big difference. You don't get the luxury of "thirty takes" to get it right in front of a live audience. The former Stranger Things star's currently playing Mark in a modern revival of rock musical Rent on London's West End. He tells BBC Newsbeat that having a proper schedule and remembering to stay hydrated makes a "refreshing change" from filming the Netflix smash-hit that made him famous. Matarazzo shot to fame in 2016 as endearing super-geek Dustin Henderson - a role he calls "the greatest honour of his life". The saga finally concluded last December after five seasons, and there's been interest in what the show's cast will do next. "It's something you do inevitably step away from," says Matarazzo "We finished filming in 2024 - there's no more show to film." "I still love what I do very much, I want to keep on doing it." Casting big names from TV and film in theatre shows is a growing trend, and one that sometimes provokes accusations of cashing in. But Matarazzo has plenty of stage experience, having performed on Broadway when he was a child. He says the time commitment involved meant it was impossible to "blend both worlds". "My favourite part of theatre specifically is the schedule," he says. "Going to bed at the same time and waking up at the same time. "I've always thrived under a schedule and when I don't have one I feel insane." It has been 30 years since Rent first premiered on Broadway In Rent, Matarazzo plays struggling film-maker Mark, who chronicles and narrates the lives of his friends. It has been 30 years since the show first opened off-Broadway in New York, but the actor says there are "certain songs that weirdly resonate now". "What You Own, which feels like a reflection on information overload, is incredibly relevant," he says. "That's really fun to sing in context of today." When it was first performed, Rent shone a light on young friends and artists living in late 1980s and early 1990s New York during the HIV/Aids crisis. It was considered groundbreaking at the time for tackling social taboos and centering stories of LGBT people. Writer Jonathan Larson died suddenly the night before its premiere. Matarazzo's co-star, Travis Ross, who plays Roger, says the show's themes still "ring true" today. The 25-year-old says having Rent tends to attract people who "care so deeply" about the show's message, resulting in a connection between actors and the audience. He calls it a "really beautiful community-driven piece of art". Both Ross and Matarazzo are keen to acknowledge their fellow cast members and point out Rent is "an ensemble" piece. "In the same way we get our moments to tell the story there's also ten other people who get their moments to tell the story as well," says Ross. Gaten Matarazzo (right) says he and co-star Travis Ross (left) have been learning from each other Many of those in the audience will be there to watch Matarazzo, and he says he's determined to get the role right. "I'm on stage for the majority of the show and singing the whole time," he says. "It's not anything that's particularly high or out of my range, it's actually a part that I think fits nicely in my pocket. "But it's just so much singing, and making sure I'm doing it correctly is essential," he says. Matarazzo also plans to embrace his return to the stage. "Once we're in the run it will be great," he says. "I just always love the opportunity to start and finish a character arc and story in real time. "You don't get an opportunity to do that when you're filming." Speaking of which - if he ever got the call to go back to Hawkins and step into Dustin's shoes, would he take the chance? "If that happens, that's great, and if not, that's completely fine. "I've loved doing the show so much, it's literally the greatest honour of my life." Rent is at The Tom Stoppard Theatre, London. Gaten Matarazzo is booked to perform until 10 January. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
description: Retailer issues update after BBC contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond "basic contact details".
body: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users. It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed. Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and customer numbers are now in the hands of cyber criminals. So too are the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data. With this information, scammers may be able to craft potent phishing attack emails or phone calls. The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams. In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed. "Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said. "We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call." The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach. The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people. Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed." The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording. On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack. The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first. Customers saw this pop up notification on Tuesday Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required". The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials". With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data. In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance". Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins. The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data. Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached. Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action. But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity. "Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio. "Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours." Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information". "We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said. Have you been affected by this hack? title: Wakefield top as all 14 Super League clubs stay for 2027
description: The 14 Super League clubs will remain in place for 2027 with Grand Final winners Wakefield Trinity topping the IMG ratings.
body: Wakefield have had two consecutive seasons in Super League following promotion in 2024 All 14 Super League clubs will remain in the competition next season after the release of the yearly gradings, with Wakefield Trinity topping the ratings for the first time. Following their Super League Grand Final success, Wakefield have come top of the ratings, based on criteria formulated by media giant IMG, with marks for five factors - fan experience, finance, stadium, community and on-field performance. London Broncos have come 16th on the list, below fellow Championship side Barrow Raiders, despite a season in which they won the second tier's Grand Final, the 1895 Cup and were runaway champions in the regular-season standings. The Broncos were overlooked 12 months ago when Bradford Bulls, York Knights and Toulouse Olympique joined the expanded 14-team competition. But, with the backing of Australian businessman Grant Wechsel, former Brisbane Broncos star Darren Lockyer and a squad full of internationals, they do still harbour hopes of playing in Super League in 2027. Australia's National Rugby League (NRL) is looking to invest in the competition, with talks at an advanced stage. It is understood any completed deal would involve the Australian governing body insisting on Broncos featuring in the top flight next season. London Broncos rout Doncaster to clinch treble What are IMG gradings and how do they work? Wakefield have matched 2025 champions Hull KR's record grading score of 17.85 from 12 months ago, to continue their rise on and off the field under Matt Ellis' ownership. In the same rankings last year they were eighth with a mark of 15.47, only just above the threshold for Category A status. "Wakefield Trinity's rise to the top of the 2026 club grading rankings is a fascinating story for rugby league, and a strong example of how sustained progress on and off the field can be recognised through the grading framework," said RFL chief executive Ian Nolan. "Their achievement sits alongside encouraging movement across the sport, from growing attendances and digital audiences to continued improvements in facilities and community delivery." Leeds Rhinos remain second, although their score of 17.03 is slightly lower than they achieved in the 2025 rankings. Warrington Wolves have jumped from sixth to third on the back of a much stronger season which culminated in reaching the Grand Final at Old Trafford, only to lose to Wakefield. It is fourth place again for Wigan, who won both the Challenge Cup and the League Leaders' shield, just above Hull KR and Leigh Leopards. St Helens drop from third to seventh after a season in which they missed out on the play-offs for the first time in the Super League era. Castleford Tigers complete the Category A clubs as they have risen from 11th in 2025 to eighth and move into the top-tier section despite finishing 13th in Super League. Catalans Dragons and Hull FC are ninth and 10th, but both have fallen from an A to a B grade. Then come Bradford Bulls and Huddersfield Giants, with Toulouse Olympique and York Knights, occupying 13th and 14th, albeit with higher scores than last year. However, only six of the 14 Super League clubs have scored higher than they did 12 months ago. But there was a significant gap to the teams outside. York's score of 13.24 was comfortably higher than the next best, Barrow with 9.85, while London only achieved 9.77, which was down on their mark of 11.65 from last year. Overall, 26 clubs were graded on this system,, external split into three categories, A, B and C. title: Seventh man bailed in connection with RAF Fairford incident
description: A 22 year-old British national was arrested on Tuesday as part of the investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire in September.
body: A 22-year-old British national who was arrested on suspicion of preparing acts of terror in connection with an incident close to RAF Fairford has been released on bail. The man was arrested in Westminster, London, under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006 on Tuesday, as part of the counter-terror police investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire. In total, seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged. A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the airbase in the early hours of 27 September. Five men, aged between 23 and 25, were initially arrested on the day of the incident after vehicles were reported near the base. They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing an act of terror. A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual Iranian-British national, was arrested on 1 October in Westminster. The seventh man, a 22-year-old British national, was arrested in Westminster on Tuesday by counter-terror police. Both were arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terror. RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used by the US Air Force for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran. But on Sunday, it emerged the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America. US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details. "There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy," he told reporters. "But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far." Prior to Trump's intervention, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to the US president's previous comments, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base. title: How a folk band, football club and Fifa 11 came together for an unlikely terrace anthem
description: After playing a bit of Fifa 11, Kingfishr leader singer Eddie Keogh posted a song in tribute to English League One club Wycombe Wanderers.
body: Eddie Keogh was presented with a Wycombe shirt on Tuesday It's a tale as old as time. Take one 16-year-old video game, a rising indie-folk band and a League One football team and what do you get? A new football anthem for Wycombe Wanderers, courtesy of the unlikely figures of Irish chart-toppers Kingfishr, whose singer was the special guest under the Tuesday night lights of the club's Adams Park stadium this week. It's a strange musical connection that came about in a way avid fans of sports video games can understand - via Fifa 11, a game the band said they started playing while recording their second album. The band adopted Wycombe Wanderers as their team in the game and eventually posted a song for the club, which has racked up more than 190,000 views on TikTok, external. The club caught wind of the song, written in an Irish folk style and with a lyrical focus on "the Wycombe wanderer, wandering away" and replied to the original post by saying: "You can wander our way anytime." So it came that lead singer Eddie Keogh took up the offer on Tuesday night, as first reported by Irish sports site Balls.ie, external, and attended the club's 4-1 EFL Trophy victory over Bristol Rovers. The song was even playing over the tannoy as he arrived, to the singer's shock as demonstrated by his "what is going on?" post to TikTok, external. The club invited him onto the pitch where he was presented with his own club shirt with 'Kingfishr 1' on the back. This article contains content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read TikTok’s cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. In statement to BBC News NI, a Wycombe Wanderers spokesperson said discovering the song was "brilliant". "As fate would have it, Eddie from the band was able to join us that evening to visit the stadium, watch a game, meet the players and learn a little more about the club he's adopted as his own. "A lot of our players are massive fans of the band, and the song from the TikTok has gone down extremely well with supporters, so we hope it might become a terrace anthem." The club spokesperson added that Kingfishr "are welcome back to Adams Park at any time". The Limerick indie-folk group have topped the charts with a string of hits like Killeagh, Diamonds & Roses and The Sun Will Never Settle It's not the first sporting connection for the band, who first broke big in Ireland due to their viral track Killeagh, a song that has topped the Irish charts on three separate occasions. The track details a community's attachment to their local Gaelic games club. The band also played in Londonderry earlier this year where they were presented with shirts belonging to local clubs.
