title: Paul McCartney's key sells for double the estimate
description: The star composed some of The Beatles' first songs in the Liverpool council house with John Lennon.
body: Paul McCartney moved to the house in Liverpool with his family when he was at secondary school A key to Sir Paul McCartney's childhood home has sold for thousands of pounds at auction. During the 1950s and 60s, Sir Paul lived with his family at 20 Forthlin Road in Allerton, Liverpool, and composed some of the earliest Beatles' tracks with John Lennon there. Sir Paul moved out in 1963, and his father and brother in the following year. In 1965, American superfan Kathy Salt wrote to then-occupant Ashley Jones, who enclosed a photograph of the house and a key, with a tag attached, in his letter back. The three items were sold to a British private collector at Dominic Winter Auctioneers in the Cotswolds on Wednesday, fetching a hammer price of £5,000 - double the estimate. Mother wants justice after boy's 'evil' knife attack on her daughter 'Rare' item from Trump's penthouse sells at auction The 'little piece of post-war history hiding in plain sight' With fees, the buyer paid £6,100, and a collection of four autographs from the band, each inscribed to "Kathy" - the fan to whom the key belonged - sold for a total of £5,124. Chris Albury, director at Dominic Winter Auctioneers, said the level of competition during the bidding "demonstrates that the Beatles' popularity remains as strong as ever". "What makes these particular pieces so extraordinary is the deeply personal links to the band and to the people and places that formed part of their story," he said. "The 20 Forthlin Road key is an example; it has a remarkable provenance stretching back to 1965 and provides a tangible connection to Paul McCartney's family home and to one of the most important addresses in Beatles history. "To see it sell for £6,100 for three times its low estimate after such strong bidding was a fantastic result." title: How Brighton attract and develop the best young players ahead of their rivals
description: Brighton sporting director Mike Cave discusses Brighton's transfer policy and how the club signs and nurtures the best young talent in the game.
body: This video can not be played Brighton sporting director Mike Cave explains the club's approach to recruitment Brighton & Hove Albion sit third in the Premier League, with one of the highest-scoring teams in Europe. To the uninitiated it might seem logical that the Seagulls must have spent big, investing in players ready for the first team. Yet Brighton are, along with Everton, one of only two clubs to record a profit in transfer spending over the past five years. It is a team full of young players, testament to the club's data-led recruitment and development strategy. But how do they do it? "We have a really clear philosophy around how we can be competitive in arguably the most challenging league in the world," Brighton sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Sport. But Brighton are more than just competitive. They went into the international break with a 3-0 home win over champions Arsenal. From identifying players, to providing pathways, integrating them into the team and then selling at the right time, it is a strategy which has worked, year after year. This is how the the club identify, attract and grow talent - and make them into first-team players. Brighton use analytics and data as their primary method of tracking and identifying players. Through club owner Tony Bloom's Jamestown Analytics, the performance of pretty much any player - or coach - who is in a professional league can be monitored. "It helps us to identify talent from around the world in quite an efficient way," Cave said. "That allows us then to move quite quickly in what is a really competitive transfer market." Just how Brighton's analytics set works is a closely guarded secret. But it does involve assessing a number of characteristics to identify signings who fit the club's model. "There's no single attribute or a single metric that we particularly go after," Cave explained. "It's more trying to assess a player's performance and potential. "It'd be great to break it down into one or two things but we're dealing with human beings playing a really complex game - sometimes in different parts of the world, in different leagues." Over time, there is a constant re-evaluation. Success and failure help to refine how the data is interpreted. The Seagulls, along with Brentford and more recently Bournemouth, are widely considered to be the best operators in this sector. Many clubs have tried to copy it without achieving the same level of success. But it is not about data alone. "What's as important is the information we try to gather around the player's character, their background and their suitability for our environment," added Cave, who has been at Brighton since 2022 and was promoted to sporting director in the summer. "Not every player would be right for Brighton and Brighton won't be right for every player either. "We invest a good amount of time in trying to understand the individual, the person, the human being. Ultimately, this is a people industry. "That's where the subjective and the non-football data really plays a huge part in our decision-making processes." The Brighton Blueprint: How to Compete with Football's Giants The use of the loan market, both domestically and in Europe, is crucial for the planned career development of many of Brighton's signings. Since 2018-19, the Seagulls have agreed well over 20 loan deals in each campaign, with 27 last season. This summer, Brighton loaned out 16 players. More will follow in January. "We've had over a period of time now a really productive and successful loan pathway," Cave explained. "So we might identify players that we think have good potential, but maybe aren't quite ready for the Premier League. "We believe we can offer one of the best developmental pathways, be it through the loans strategy that we have, or through our own under-21s programme." Take Alexis Mac Allister, who was signed by Brighton for £6.8m in January 2019 but immediately loaned back to former club Argentinos Juniors, and then to Boca Juniors for 2019-20. Only in the summer of 2020 did Mac Allister become a first-team player at the Amex. The Argentina international, who won the World Cup in 2022, went on to make 112 appearances for the Seagulls before being sold to Liverpool for £35m. It would likely have been a higher transfer fee if the player's contract did not have a release clause. Most recently, there is Jan Paul van Hecke. The defender was signed from NAC Breda for £6m as a 20-year-old in 2020, and spent two seasons on loan with Heerenveen and Blackburn Rovers. The Netherlands international then became a first-team player and, after 131 matches for the Seagulls, was sold to Tottenham for £52m in the summer. Malick Yalcouye had loan spells with Sturm Graz and Swansea City before being integrated into the first team The fruits of the policy this season can be seen this season, with two players signed in the summer of 2024. Malick Yalcouye, a £6m signing from Gothenburg, spent the past two years out on loan, first with Sturm Graz in Austria and then with Swansea City in the Championship. The 20-year-old has two Premier League goals in his first five appearances. Ibrahim Osman, a £17m capture from Danish side Nordsjaelland, was with Feyenoord in the Netherlands, Auxerre in France and Championship side Birmingham City. The 21-year-old winger has made three substitute appearances so far. "Malik's had a really good start to the season," Cave said. "Osman is another young player who has had three loans now and then has come back into the squad for this season. "They're good examples and role models of a commitment to their own development, having an attitude and a desire to want to get better. "Now we're starting to see them delivering in the Premier League for us which is a fantastic success story but real testament to them and their hard work." title: Snakes and jungle mind games as Bottas cycles to Singapore GP
description: Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas says he was chased by dogs, saw snakes and leapt over a lizard as he cycled from Malaysia to Singapore for this weekend's Grand Prix.
body: Valterri Bottas is closely involved with FNLD GRVL, a cycling race held each summer in his native Finland Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas says he was chased by a dog, saw snakes and leapt over a lizard as he cycled from Malaysia to Singapore for this weekend's Grand Prix. The Finnish driver arrived in Singapore on Wednesday after choosing a 260-mile (419km) bike ride over a flight from last weekend's Formula 1 race in Sepang, outside the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur. The 37-year-old began his journey just hours after spinning out of Sunday's chaotic Grand Prix, taking a trip that involved off-road and gravel trails as well as cycling at night. "I saw some snakes, which I was a little bit worried about, but actually they were pretty chill. They were just doing their thing," said Bottas. "I saw one cobra, one python just crossing the path in front of me. I saw some of those big lizards that you also see here, one was on the path. "I had to jump over it on a bike because I saw it last minute. I got chased by one dog, I got stuck behind a group of cows on one small track." Bottas is an accomplished cyclist and earned a spot at the Gravel World Championships after finishing fifth in his age group at a qualifying event in the Czech Republic during Formula 1's summer hiatus. Unfortunately for Bottas the World Championships take place this weekend as well, so he will be competing on four wheels instead of two. When the Emilia Romagna Grand Prix was cancelled in 2023, Bottas decided to use the time to compete in a gravel race in Scotland. Bottas has endured a difficult return to Formula 1 with new team Cadillac this season. He is 22nd in the drivers' standings, is yet to score a point after 16 Grands Prix and has failed to finish eight races. "The wildest part was the riding at night in the jungle. The noise in there, your mind starts to play games," added Bottas. "'What is out there? Who knows what is out there?' But then you just need to crack on and keep going." title: Husband accused of GP murder appears at Crown Court
description: Mark Cain is accused of murdering his wife Hannah Cain, who was found dead at home on Sunday.
body: Mark Cain is charged with the murder of his wife, Hannah Cain The husband of a GP who was found dead at her home has appeared before a Crown Court, charged with her murder. The body of 45-year-old Hannah Cain, known to her patients as Dr Hannah Terry, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday. Mark Cain, 45, also of Fern Hill, was charged with murder on Tuesday. Appearing via video link from HMP Norwich, he spoke only to confirm his name and that he understood proceedings at King's Lynn Crown Court. He was remanded in custody until a plea hearing on 3 December. Steven Ball, prosecuting, said Mark Cain was accused of the murder of his wife on 3 October into the early hours of 4 October at their family home. He said emergency services attended and Hannah Cain was found "unconscious and unresponsive". A post-mortem examination recorded that she had sustained "blunt force injuries to the head" and "neck injuries consistent with compression to the neck", he said. Hannah Cain has been described by her family as "kind, generous and loving" Mark Cain was not asked to enter a plea and no application for bail was made. A provisional trial date was not set. The Fern Hill address is just over a mile from Sandringham House, one of the royal residences of the King and Queen. Dr Hannah Terry, as she was known professionally, was listed as a member of the practice team at Grimston Medical Centre. She served in a pool of doctors who were regularly on call for members of the royal family nearby. On Wednesday, her family described her as "kind, generous and loving". title: Man pleads not guilty to murder of pensioner
description: Adam Krzan was found dead in his flat in Dungannon in February 2025.
body: Adam Krzan was found with three stab wounds to his chest and two to his neck A man has pleaded not guilty to the murder of a pensioner in County Tyrone. Adam Krzan was found dead in his flat in Dungannon in February 2025. The 71-year-old, who was originally from Poland but had lived in Northern Ireland for more than 20 years, was found by police with multiple stab wounds at his flat in the Lisnahull area of Dungannon. He died as a result of his injuries. Ryan Patrick Kerr, 34, of Derrylattinee Road in Dungannon, appeared at Laganside Crown Court on Thursday, where he denied the charge. A further hearing is scheduled for 23 October, when a trial date is expected to be set. The court heard Kerr had a documented history of significant drug misuse, with his defence barrister seeking expert medical opinion ahead of the trial. At a previous hearing, police described arriving at a "disturbing scene" at Krzan's flat, where they found a large volume of blood. Police said Krzan had suffered three stab wounds to his chest and two to his neck. title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
description: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.
body: South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries. It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place. The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter. And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports. But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga. In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly". Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia Thousands of North Koreans fought for Russia. A memorial hints at the death toll Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive". It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang. title: Actor Simon Pegg reveals ADHD diagnosis: 'It's just who I am'
description: The Shaun of the Dead and Mission: Impossible films star had previously put symptoms down to "character fault".
body: Shaun of the Dead and Mission: Impossible films star Simon Pegg has revealed he has been diagnosed with ADHD, which he said "confirmed a lot of stuff that I'd been wrestling with". Pegg, 56, who also co-created and starred in films Hot Fuzz, The World's End, and TV series Spaced, said "there was a lot of build-up and suspicion, and it just took a while actually to get there." Speaking on the podcast I'm ADHD! No You're Not, external on Thursday, he said he pursued a diagnosis as he "just wanted to know". ADHD symptoms focus on three main areas - inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity plus lack of concentration. Although many people may feel like they have some similar symptoms, genetics play an important role in ADHD and a full diagnosis is given to those who are negatively affected on a daily basis. Pegg said he had previously been putting his symptoms down to "just character fault". The actor and writer also spoke about his mental health, including having clinical depression and struggling to control his drinking, which he said he initially thought had "caused" his diagnosis. "I felt like it was something that had come on in later life because I wasn't a naughty child. "I've had bouts of depression in my adult life since 18 and I thought maybe it had come on with that. "Maybe over the years with therapy and medication - whatever - I've been treating the symptoms and not the cause of why I feel that way." Pegg said: "I did feel different in a way I might not be able to put my finger on. Maybe everybody feels that way. "I just assumed ADHD kids were kind of chaotic and difficult and didn't pay attention in school," he added. "But there were other things that I did do as a kid – fidget or whatever – that made me think, 'Oh no, maybe I've had this longer than I thought'." Pegg said his wife has been supportive and is "dealing with it as if I'd been diagnosed ages ago", adding: "It's just who I am, and it's just things that I do. "She makes allowances for forgetfulness and and lack of concentration." ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers Johnny Vegas opens up about recent ADHD diagnosis Richard Bacon: 'Why I quite like my ADHD' Ant McPartlin gets ADHD support Pegg had previously said he felt his poor driving was down to undiagnosed ADHD., external The star, who has had several speeding convictions, told LBC last year that he felt an ADHD diagnosis would help explain his poor concentration when it comes to driving. He reversed into a post while on holiday in Greece, which prompted him to look up the symptoms of ADHD. "I looked up on the phone 'Do people with ADHD get into more car accidents than people who don't have it' and the answer was yes. "And it's because of a lack of focus and ability to kind of totally focus. "And that was the final straw that broke my ADHD camel's back. I need to speak to a psychiatrist and find out for sure if I have this thing." Other celebrities who have been diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood include comedian and actor Johnny Vegas, comic and presenter Sue Perkins, presenters Ant McPartlin and Richard Bacon, comedian Rory Bremner and model Erin O'Connor. ADHD is described by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) as "a behavioural syndrome characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention". The NHS estimates that about 2.5 million people in England have ADHD, including those without a formal diagnosis. Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand. Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018. Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest ADHD is actually underdiagnosed. In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups. title: Clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal
description: Premier League clubs are "concerned" about political interference in Manchester City's appeal after Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments.
body: Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 until he became prime minister this summer Some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by comments made by Andy Burnham - appearing to downplay the verdict against Manchester City - that they are now "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process, sources have told BBC Sport. Senior club figures say they were shocked when they heard the prime minister tell the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club were found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches. They have questioned what his comments to the BBC were designed to achieve, and said it had put the Independent Football Regulator in a difficult position. Burnham is under increasing pressure surrounding his relationship with the club's Abu Dhabi ownership during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester. Such is the level of scrutiny that Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club. Despite clarification from Downing Street that Burnham's view is that no-one is "above the rules", his comments have sparked unease among some senior Labour figures who fear his initial comments have had major cut-through with voters. This video can not be played The politics of Manchester City's guilty verdict Guardiola set to attend Man City v PSG next week Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League Your Manchester City Questions Answered By The Experts Senior club sources have said they found the comments "absolutely bizarre", and that it was "at best naive and at worst quite manipulative, and that is not a good look". A different source said it was "clumsy", while another said they were surprised that the prime minister had "misspoken". The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League. An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with a sanctions hearing still to come. A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing. However, when asked about potential interference in the process off the back of Burnham's comments, one senior club source said: "Everyone would have a degree of concern. How much would depend on how much you read into that comment. "I think everyone is concerned. Because no-one is stupid around the table. We understand the geopolitics as well. We understand the investment they have made in our country. I don't think anyone could doubt that or criticise that. But this is different, this is sport, this is our national game." Another club source, however, said the degree of scrutiny on Burnham now means they think any interference would be impossible. This video can not be played PM: I’d be ‘really concerned’ if Man City owners sell club This is a sensitive area for the prime minister. Manchester City's dominance of English football has overlapped in large part both with a period of economic growth for the city of Manchester, and with Burnham's nine years as mayor from 2017 until earlier this year. As mayor, Burnham championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester's economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city's leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Regardless of Burnham's past career, there are additional sensitivities which would be true under other prime ministers too. The UK as a whole is eager to trade with the UAE, and the country is an important diplomatic ally in the region at a time of turmoil and war. When the guilty verdicts were announced, Richard Masters, the Premier League's chief executive, said the club had "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade". This video can not be played Could Manchester City be expelled from the Premier League? Burnham's comments came in an interview with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason the next day. When asked about 'Brand Manchester' taking a hit, the Prime Minister drew a parallel with a previous Premier League case with Everton, saying he still held the view "firmly" that they "weren't fairly treated". Everton were deducted 10 points, later reduced to six on appeal, by an independent commission for breaching Premier League financial rules. Asked if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is. "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city," he added. Burnham's comments provoked strong criticism. The following day, a No 10 spokesperson sought to clarify the comments, saying: "As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. "If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences." However, this statement was amended following further criticism over the use of the word "if" - which was changed to "wherever". The Premier League is viewed by governments of different political stripes as one of the country's major cultural exports, so ministers are eager for the row not to cause lasting damage to its brand. Additionally, being a football fan is a core part of Burnham's political persona. He is an Everton

title: Girl, 9, dies in two-vehicle crash in the Highlands
description: Police say the girl was a rear seat passenger of a car involved in the collision south of Inverness.
body: The A831 was closed for seven hours following the crash A nine-year-old girl has died in a two-vehicle crash in the Highlands. The girl was a rear seat passenger in a VW Polo involved in a collision with a Ford Ranger at about 17:30 on Wednesday on the A831 between Drumnadrochit and Cannich, south of Inverness. Police said she was pronounced dead at the scene, and a front seat passenger of the Polo was taken to hospital for treatment. The road was closed for seven hours to allow for an investigation. More stories from the Highlands and Islands News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds Emergency services, including an air ambulance, were sent to the crash. Sgt Kate Finlayson said: "Our thoughts are with the family and friends of the girl who died, and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances. "I am appealing for anyone who witnessed the crash or the vehicles prior to contact us, external. "I would also ask anyone who was in the area and who may have dashcam footage that could assist to please get in touch." The Scottish Ambulance Service said it sent several resources, including four ambulances, a critical care team and an air ambulance, to the scene. A spokesperson said two patients were taken to Raigmore Hospital in Inverness. The crash happened on a 13-mile stretch of A831 between Drumnadrochit, a village on the shores of Loch Ness, and Cannich, which is a village at the end of Strathglass. The road passes through a sparsely populated area of farms, forests and lochs. title: England to host 2031 Netball World Cup
description: England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031, when the sport's pinnacle event is held at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.
body: England were beaten 61-45 by Australia in the 2023 World Cup final England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031. The quadrennial tournament will be held at Manchester's Co-op Live indoor arena, World Netball and England Netball announced on Thursday. Liverpool staged the event when England last hosted in 2019. World Netball president Liz Nicholl said: "After reviewing their strong bid, I am confident England Netball will host another thrilling international event, and I am excited to see what we can achieve together in 2031 and beyond." Eastbourne put on the inaugural tournament in 1963, with Birmingham staging the 1995 edition. England reached a World Cup final for the first time in 2023, but the Roses were denied a first title by 12-time winners Australia in Cape Town. England also finished as runners-up in 1975, when the tournament was contested in a league format. Baroness Sue Campbell, chair of England Netball, said: "To have the best netball players in the world coming to Manchester is a hugely exciting prospect, and I know the city will give them the welcome they deserve. "This is a fantastic opportunity not only to showcase our sport on the biggest stage, but also to inspire the next generation of players and fans." England Netball chief executive Fran Connolly said the tournament would provide "a powerful platform to grow the visibility, profile and impact of women's sport and netball across the UK". The announcement comes in England Netball's centenary year. The Co-op Live arena hosted this year's Netball Super League Grand Final between AO Thunder and London Pulse, which was played in front of more than 8,000 fans. title: Drumcree dispute must be 'contained' - UUP leader
description: It is the twelfth day of deadlock between residents of the Garvaghy Road and the local district lodge of the Orange Order over the parade.
body: Jon Burrows said politicians need to "resolve" the standoff rather than "mutliplying" it Politicians should make a "collective appeal to contain" the parading dispute in Drumcree, according to the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader. Jon Burrows called on other parties to join him in emphasising the need to "resolve the dispute and not multiply it". It is the twelfth day of deadlock between residents of the Garvaghy Road and the local district lodge of the Orange Order over the proposed march in Portadown, County Armagh. On Wednesday, a representative for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition (GRRC) said the disagreement was "no longer just about the Garvaghy Road" after a meeting with 11 other nationalist residents' groups. Breandán Mac Cionnaith and Linda O'Neill of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition spoke to the media after meeting 11 nationalist residents' groups on Wednesday After the meeting, Linda O'Neill of the GRRC said: "The Orange Order needs to take responsibility, and so do the Parades Commission for making this issue bigger than the Garvaghy Road, this is no longer just about the Garvaghy Road, this is about all of us." She said support from all over Ireland was "propping up our community right now; we have never seen support and solidarity like it". The Portadown District Lodge have said they are prepared to take further legal action to try to allow the 35 Orangemen to march from Drumcree along the route approved by the Parades Commission. At a separate press conference on Wednesday, Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said the lodge would "not be bullied or threatened by any residents' group who step outside the law". He said he was "very confident" in the support across Northern Ireland for their march adding "there's no threat to our parades. They're legal". Speaking to Good Morning Ulster, Burrows said it might be "easier" to resolve the situation if the police were to bring "consequences at the door of those who have broken the law, from the first minister down". O'Neill has defended joining the protests, saying she was "proud" to stand with the residents and adding that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it". Burrows also said he thought it would be a "mistake" for the Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant to withdraw permission for the parade. "What we need to hear is political leaders saying we must not open these disputes across the country." Claire Hanna, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), also said there was a need to "get a grip" of the situation "before it engulfs the wider political system". She said her party's view was that the secretary of state "can and should rescind the permission" for the parade. She said that "until he does that, there is a desperate need for sensible voices within unionism and the Orange Order to ask that lodge to reconsider, because there is the potential for this to scale out into other areas". The Northern Ireland Office (NIO) has said the secretary of state is continuing to engage with all parties for a resolution. Orangemen turn away from a police barricade close to Drumcree Church formed to prevent them entering the Garvaghy Road on the eighth day of the stand-off It is more than a week since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on Sunday, 27 September. That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west. Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police. The stand-off has caused considerable political fallout in Northern Ireland, with First Minister O'Neill facing a vote of no confidence over her involvement in the protest. The vote is due to fail due to it requiring cross-community support at the Northern Ireland Assembly. Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry. Politicians, including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church to Garvaghy Road on 27 September Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches. Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades. Earlier this year the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court. Meanwhile, the Court of Appeal is considering its ruling in a legal challenge brought by the residents to block the march going ahead. title: BBC to cut raft of Radio 4 programmes including You and Yours
description: The corporation said it would be investing in a new consumer programme, while announcing more cuts.
body: Winifred Robinson has presented You and Yours since 2000 The BBC has announced it will be cutting a raft of Radio 4 programmes including the long-running consumer and social affairs show You and Yours. The social sciences show Thinking Allowed will also be cut along with arts and ideas programme Free Thinking, as the corporation seeks £500m savings. Other shows such The Artificial Human and Open Country will also go, it was announced on Thursday, while Radio 5 Live will also see a reduction in commissioning on its schedule and podcasts. The BBC has committed to investing in a new consumer programme, though, and two new weekly shows exploring ideas shaping the world, and the impact of technology and AI. Radio 4's flagship history, science and culture show, In Our Time, will expand in length, as will Start the Week and Farming Today. Director of BBC Sounds Jonathan Wall said they were "reshaping BBC speech audio" in order to "build a strong future for trusted journalism, distinctive storytelling and programmes that bring people together". "By commissioning fewer programmes overall, we can focus our investment and make our best shows work across broadcast, on demand and different formats," he said in a statement. "That means accelerating growth on our own digital platforms and reaching more people beyond the BBC, while maintaining the strength of Radio 4 and 5 Live, the country's two biggest speech radio stations." He added that the "difficult decisions" about cuts to shows and staff were "not based on cost alone", saying: "We need to make significant savings while investing for the future." Last month, director general Matt Brittin said the BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services. Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever". In June, the BBC announced 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage in its plan to save £500m across the corporation over the next two years. Staff were told of proposals including ending Radio 4's The World Tonight, and reducing the number of permanent presenters on Today from five to four, with a single anchor on Saturdays. It was revealed that BBC One's Breakfast would no longer be shown on Sunday mornings, and that the production teams making Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg and Newsnight would merge. It followed April's announcement that the BBC would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - or almost one in 10 - in an attempt to tackle "significant financial pressures". Last week, an influential group of MPs said the BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV, and that the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent. In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust. title: Royal Navy service member charged with spying for a foreign power
description: The 24-year-old man is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday after being arrested at his home in Bedfordshire.
body: A Royal Navy service member has been charged with spying for an unnamed foreign country, police have said. Teddy Young, 24, from Bedfordshire, has been charged with offences under the National Security Act (NSA) including an allegation of obtaining protected information which could benefit an unnamed foreign power. He has been remanded into custody and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday. Cdr Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter-Terrorism Policing London, said: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces". Police said the charges were not related to the recent RAF Fairford incident which resulted in a number of arrests after suspicious activity was reported near the base. On Tuesday, a seventh man was arrested in connection to the incident which continues to be investigated by counter-terror police. Young was arrested at his home address in Bedfordshire on Tuesday. The charges cover a period between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025 and allege conduct "in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information" contrary to the act. It is also alleged the service member "obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power, knowing or having regard to other matters known to him ought reasonably to know was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom". Cdr Flanagan added: "We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter." A Royal Navy spokesperson confirmed a service member had been charged and added: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage." title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
description: Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
body: Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission". "We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the consul general would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity". UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people". Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law. The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement. The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions. "The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media. However, the British flag could still be seen outside on Thursday morning, and several staff were seen entering. Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel." But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building. As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel". Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations. This agreement is a compromise of sorts and means - for the moment - the heat has been taken out of a dispute that could have further worsened UK-Israel relations. Israel can claim that the British Consulate is "closing its operations". A score of British diplomats, including the consul general, are leaving. But Miliband says they are going only temporarily and only for their safety and security. He continues to insist Israel has no legal right to close the consulate. "The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory," Miliband wrote in a statement. Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday. However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises". "Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added. The Foreign Office said the seven UK diplomats who remain will be "independent and operational" and continue to deliver vital services. Israel said they will provide "only a limited scope of activity". FCDO sources described the deal as a "good outcome" because the entire operation was not closing, as had been threatened. They said that maintaining a UK presence would help build back the mission in the future. Speaking to the Today programme, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty explained: "The building remains open. We retain our presence, we continue having staff able to do important work engaging with the Palestinian Authority... and we are engaging in ongoing conversations with Israel on this matter." Asked if this was a political fudge, Doughty said "you can see what's changed in terms of a name but crucially our presence remains", adding that the "policies towards this Israeli government, which we fundamentally disagree with" would continue. The foreign secretary made clear the UK reserved the right to take what he called "reciprocal action" but said he would not do so while "discussions are under way and credible". That means any UK retaliation is unlikely before Israel's elections later this month. title: Christa Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBC
description: A lawyer says the murderer of Colleen Slemmer is moving around her hospital room after surviving two lethal injections.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospital Christa Pike is "up and walking" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, a member of her legal team says. Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented. Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room for the first time while still being mentally "foggy". Earlier, a court ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state. The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection. The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death. Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison. Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens. How did Christa Pike survive two lethal injections? What happens next in the Pike case? In their updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had previously said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed. In the latest updates, given to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital, which was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September. Once it became clear that Pike was not going to die, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to be in a critical condition. As of late on Tuesday, though, she was "fairly well", Ferrell told the BBC. "What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much." Of her physical movements, he added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far." Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going." Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet." He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now". Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach. They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole. Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair." Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know. For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution. Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt. The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels. The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt. She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case. title: Moment Nasa scientist Margaret Hamilton receives presidential medal of honour
description: Barack Obama awarded the Apollo 11 software engineer with the America's highest civilian honour in 2016.
body: This video can not be played The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". And in 2016, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Honor - the nation's highest civilian honour - by Barack Obama in a ceremony at the White House. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement announcing Hamilton's passing, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. title: Engine size limits and working with Iraola - the Liverpool academy approach
description: Liverpool academy director Alex Inglethorpe talks to BBC Sport about the value and future of Liverpool's academy.
body: Alex Inglethorpe (left) has been Liverpool's academy director since 2014 One of the first things you notice in Alex Inglethorpe's office at Liverpool's AXA Training Centre is a framed image gifted by Trent Alexander-Arnold. It is a picture from 2019 of the academy director and player watching a game together. Alexander-Arnold left for a new challenge at Real Madrid last year, after 20 years on Merseyside, but his story is one of inspiration for everyone that enters Liverpool's academy. He joined as a six-year-old in 2004 and went on to win the Premier League, Champions League, FA Cup, League Cup, Community Shield, Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Club World Cup with Liverpool. "The ideal for any academy, and certainly for us, is wanting young players - and hopefully they're local players - to improve the first team and in doing so, they come and win trophies," says Inglethorpe. "At Liverpool the bar is high, so to have a player capable of winning everything that you could possibly win is a dream." Inglethorpe and his team oversee the development of younger players and ensure there is alignment between the academy and the first team. One of the phrases used is 'the first team pitch is only 300 metres away from the academy building in Kirkby, but the journey might take 10 years to get there'. Under new boss Andoni Iraola, players like Rio Ngumoha, Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and James McConnell, who have spent time at the academy, have all featured this season. "We were fortunate because of how the calendar worked, with players still at the World Cup and a delayed return. Andoni and his staff spent a lot of his first week here watching the academy," says Inglethorpe. "So we felt ahead, in terms of building a relationship from the outset." At the Kirkby academy, phones are handed in on a morning and there is a clause in contracts with a maximum engine size limit for cars that are driven into academy premises. "It comes back to passing your audition. First impressions matter," says Inglethorpe. "Often before you've kicked a ball, the car you drive or the watch you wear can have an impact on how you're thought of - and that could be first team staff or players looking at you. "We've believed in the idea of 'earning the right' for some time." Last week, Manchester United signed 16-year-old winger Isaac Konde from Liverpool on a one-year scholarship followed by a five-year professional deal. Both clubs are now in talks over a compensation package. In February, a tribunal ruled Liverpool must pay at least £2.8m to Chelsea for Ngumoha. The 18-year-old left Chelsea in September 2024 to join the Reds and signed his first professional contract a year later. Both are recent examples of the current climate around talent. At Liverpool, the belief is they have been sensible and responsible with a view to deferred gratification in most cases, but the wage structure is currently under review. "It's always a compliment when other clubs want your players as it means you're doing something right," says Inglethorpe. "But I think the market of players at 16 is distorted because of Brexit and because you can't recruit like you would do before. There's always been movement of players but it feels a little more extreme now. "When there's a clamour for talent - fees, wages and everything else will shift accordingly, so it's dealing with what we have and adapting to a new situation." Trent Alexander-Arnold (right) spent 20 years at Liverpool before leaving in 2025 When Curtis Jones moved to Inter Milan in the summer, it left Liverpool without a first team player born in the city. "I acknowledge the fact that ideally Liverpool would love to have a team full of Scousers," says Inglethorpe. "But it is testament to the supporters that if you adopt the characteristics of a Scouser - and you only have to see the likes of Bill Shankly, Kenny Dalglish and others over the years - you can be treated as one of their own. "So if you are fearless, passionate, play tough and demonstrate those qualities, then it doesn't matter if you've come from an L1 postcode and got a purple bin or not. That's the beauty of the club and the crowd." One name to keep an eye on is 15-year-old Luca Eden. The midfielder was born in the Wirral and has already represented England at youth level. Last month, he became the youngest player to feature in the Uefa Youth League for Liverpool, beating a record previously held by Joshua Abe, Ngumoha and Alexander-Arnold. "We've got plenty of Scousers in the academy and plenty who I think will play for the club. But if not and a lad comes from Warrington or wherever, that's not a problem," Inglethorpe insists. Liverpool's academy players celebrate their Carabao Cup win in 2024 One of the most challenging aspects of Inglethorpe's role is letting players go. Liverpool released eight players from their academy set-up at the end of last season. Inglethorpe explains how the likes of Harry Kane, who was coming through the academy at Spurs when he was a youth coach there, and Alexander-Arnold weren't necessarily the best in their respective youth cohorts. "At that stage, there's too many unknowns. You can't predict how players will react to adversity and natural bumps in the road," says Inglethorpe. "I've been proven wrong so many times in the past. A good example would be Jarell [Quansah] - someone who was always liked and never in danger of leaving but probably never seen in the top three in the group." Quansah left Liverpool for Bayer Leverkusen in 2025 and has since won eight caps for England. "There are no certainties - the point of the academy is to allow them to fulfil their potential," says Inglethorpe. "Sometimes players need to leave to gain an opportunity. title: How can home nations reach Women's World Cup?
description: England, Wales, Northern Ireland, Scotland and the Republic of Ireland are among those hoping to qualify for next year's Women's World Cup. What awaits them in the play-offs?
body: England's Georgia Stanway, Northern Ireland's Rebecca McKenna, Scotland's Rachel McLauchlan and Wales' Lily Woodham are all hoping to make it to the Women's World Cup England must get through two rounds of home and away ties to qualify for the Women's World Cup in Brazil. Sarina Wiegman's European champions will play Greece in Crete in round one of the play-offs, with the first leg on Friday, 9 October at 17:30 BST. The second leg will be played at home, at King Power Stadium in Leicester, on Tuesday, 13 October at 19:30 BST. Commentary for both England matches will be on BBC Radio 5 Live. Should England beat Greece over two games, they will face the winners of Slovakia v Ukraine, with the away fixture played first. The exact dates of the potential second-leg fixtures are to be confirmed, although they will take place between 26 November and 5 December 2026. England head coach Wiegman named her initial squad last month, with Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly notable absentees. When asked why they were left out, Wiegman said: "They have not been playing to their full potential. "Of course, I still believe in these players. They are really good and have shown so much for us." Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "That is also why I didn't pick them this time, because they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks. "I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and, of course, they want to work on that." All you need to know about 2027 Women's World Cup Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are also involved in the play-offs as they chase World Cup places. As with England, they are in action on Friday. In round one, Wales face Albania at 17:00 BST - with coverage on BBC Two Wales from 16:45 BST. Scotland play the Czech Republic at 18:00 BST, available to watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Alba. Northern Ireland take on Portugal at 19:00 BST, available on BBC iPlayer. The Republic of Ireland will play Kazakhstan at 12:00 BST. Despite England securing five wins from their six qualifying matches, world champions Spain finished top of the Lionesses' group and secured the one automatic spot. Wiegman said: "We knew what the play-offs would look like and, while we're pleased with the draw against Greece, the focus now is on making sure we're really well prepared. "We want to dominate games and have a lot of the ball and that's something we will prepare for carefully." England did not want to go through the play-offs but were given an unkind draw in the qualifying groups when they met world champions Spain. However, Wiegman's side are in a strong position for the play-offs and will fancy their chances against Greece, who sit 55 places beneath them in the Fifa world rankings. England also beat potential round two opponents Ukraine in both matches in the qualifying group stage, with an aggregate 9-1 score. Northern Ireland face a tricky tie against a talented young squad from Portugal in round one. Portugal twice beat Northern Ireland in Euro 2025 qualifying. Their task gets even harder if they make it through to round two, with potential opponents Iceland proving to be difficult to break down in their matches against England this year. Scotland are hoping to reach just their second Women's World Cup finals, after a 2019 appearance. They failed to qualify in 2023 but have performed well this year, including drawing with Belgium, showing that they can compete with Europe's strongest teams. They would need to produce their best in round two if they meet big-hitters Sweden, who have been semi-finalists in the past two Women's World Cups. Wales have never beaten a top-20 ranked nation in a competitive fixture and are likely to need to do so to qualify. There is optimism, though, as Rhian Wilkinson's side thrashed play-off opponents Albania 4-0 in their qualifying group. Elsewhere, having performed superbly in qualifying, the Republic of Ireland have a tough play-off route with Belgium potentially waiting in round two. First, Carla Ward's side will have to navigate a 3,100-mile trip to Kazakhstan, to tackle relatively unknown opposition. title: F1 heat hazard declared for fourth time this season
description: The Singapore Grand Prix is declared a heat-hazard race, the second weekend in a row that the designation has been used in Formula 1.
body: The Singapore Grand Prix made its debut on the F1 calendar in 2008 The Singapore Grand Prix has been declared a heat-hazard race, the second weekend in a row that the designation has been used in Formula 1 and the fourth time this year. The definition allows teams to fit cooling devices to their cars that pump liquid through a vest worn by the driver to manage temperatures in the cockpit. A heat hazard is an official status for an event where it is forecast that temperatures will exceed 31C at some point during the race. It was first introduced in 2025. Singapore is close to the equator and has long been known as one of the most demanding for drivers - in 2024, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton were treated for heat exhaustion after the race. Temperatures in the city are always in the 31-33C region across the race weekend, with high humidity and a chance of rain every day. The race is held at night, but temperatures remain in the region of 30C even after dark. A cooling kit is not mandatory, but any driver who chooses not to use it has to carry 5kg of ballast in their car to ensure he does not have a competitive advantage. The system uses a cooling tank and pump, usually situated in the car's nose, that delivers a cooled liquid, such as glycol, through a system of pipes in a fireproof top worn under their overalls. Some teams and drivers prefer not to use the system because of two key compromises. It is difficult to keep the liquid cool enough for long enough so that it lasts for an entire grand prix - a problem exacerbated in Singapore because it is the longest race of the year. And some drivers find the cooling top uncomfortable in the tight confines of the cockpit. If the liquid cannot be kept cool, it reverts to car temperature, which is considerably higher than ambient. It is not unusual for temperatures in an F1 cockpit to rise above 40C. Mercedes are one of the teams who have decided against running the system because they preferred to devote the resource that would have been involved in making it robust enough to last a race into car performance. Governing body the FIA has granted teams an allowance under the cost cap of $50,000 (£38,000) if they can make a system that keeps the liquid cool for an entire grand prix, and a further $75,000 (£57,000) if they could make the top comfortable. Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord described the allowance as "small", adding: "We didn't believe that allowance was sufficient for us to be able to develop a solution that would be robust enough to last for the entire race." Singapore follows the Austrian, Italian and last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in being declared a heat-hazard race this year. title: Holborn and St Pancras by-election gets under way
description: Voters in north London are going to the polls to choose a new MP after Sir Keir Starmer resigned.
body: Voting is under way in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election as candidates from across the political spectrum vie to become its new MP. About 30 polling stations - at churches and community centres - in the north London constituency opened at 07:00 BST and will close at 22:00, when a count will begin. The seat became vacant after former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down to focus on a role in international affairs. Some 15 candidates are standing in the by-election, one of whom is an independent. Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to vote. title: Suffragette role 'a gift' says Beverley Knight
description: The Wolverhampton-born singer stars as suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst in Sylvia the musical.
body: Beverley Knight stars as Emmeline Pankhurst in the show at Birmingham Hippodrome Singer Beverley Knight said she hoped audiences watching her latest musical would leave feeling "empowered" and with the belief that their voices can make a difference. Sylvia the Musical tells the story of suffragette Sylvia Pankhurst and the family rift caused by the fight for women's voting rights. The Wolverhampton artist, who plays Sylvia's mother and suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst at the Birmingham Hippodrome said she was a "history nerd" and described the part as a "gift of a role". "It's an absolutely killer story, and the best thing is it's true," she said. "I want everyone bouncing out of there because it's a joyful musical, even though there's some absolutely heartbreaking moments in it." The soul singer, known for hits including Shoulda Woulda Coulda and Get Up, told BBC Radio WM the musical was telling a "huge part of British history" from 1903, all the way to 1928. "So most people know who Emmeline Pankhurst was, leader of the suffragettes, she was determined to get women the vote," she explained. "But she came up against her middle daughter Sylvia, who not only wanted to get wealthy property owning women the vote, which was the case with men in the country, [you] had to be rich and male to vote, she wanted everybody to be able to vote. "But Emmeline was focused on just the women and that put her on a collision course with her daughter and both of them were on a collision course with the government." Knight added the show, which also features Naomi Katiyo as Sylvia Pankhurst, was "musically up my street" and was being called a "hip-hop musical" because it included elements of R&B, funk, soul, garage, gospel and house. "The engine of the show is the music," she said. The whole thing is either spoken or rapped or sung. Of course, I'm doing mostly singing because I ain't rapping anything." The former Highfields School pupil explained the story also went beyond the Pankhurst family, with some people who attended the show likely to have relatives who were involved in the suffragette movement. "It's not just the story of the Pankhursts, there are going to be loads of people who will come to this show who will be like... my grandma or my great-grandma, she was involved in the suffragette movement. "I want everybody to leave like, let's go, oh my god, that feeling of I can effect change, I can use my voice and effect change. I feel empowered." title: Inside the £1-an-hour official football shirt factories
description: A BBC Sport investigation traces official football shirt production to factories in Cambodia where workers are paid less than £1 an hour.
body: We traced production of Celtic, Arsenal, Liverpool and other kits to two factories in Cambodia Workers are being paid a basic wage of less than £1 an hour to make official football shirts for some of the world's biggest clubs, BBC Sport can reveal. Our investigation traced authentic replica shirts to two factories in Cambodia, where conditions were described as "grim". We followed the supply chain behind official shirts after fans told us they were frustrated by rising prices, with many turning to cheaper counterfeits instead. Images obtained from inside Bowker Garment Factory and Trax Apparel show kits being made for clubs including Arsenal, Celtic, Liverpool and Real Madrid. Employees there told us they struggled to make ends meet and worked on up to 700 items a day as part of a production line. In rare interviews, supported by documentary evidence and published anonymously, workers also described: Verbal abuse when targets were missed. Safety concerns about electrical equipment. The Clean Clothes Campaign, external - a global workers' rights network - said our findings painted a "very grim picture". "These are issues that many garment workers around the world face every day," added spokesperson Emma Vogt. Similar issues, such as low pay and high temperatures, have been reported across Cambodia's garment industry. This video can not be played Workers paid under £1 an hour to make football shirts Research published last year suggested that, of a typical £85 shirt, £8.50 covers fabric, sewing and shipping, £37.45 goes to the retailer, £16.25 to the manufacturer, £9.50 on marketing and £13.60 in VAT. Shirt prices have increased significantly over the past decade, though industry experts argue advances in technology and expensive kit deals with elite clubs have contributed to the rise. Adidas does not own either factory, but both are primary suppliers subject to its workplace standards., external The sportswear giant supplies eight of the 20 Premier League teams. Adidas said: "We have taken a variety of measures to ensure fair and safe working conditions for workers across our supply chain for more than 25 years. "Through around 1,200 factory audits per year, we review and evaluate supplier conduct, work with suppliers to address issues and make improvements where necessary." Shirt production begins months before designs are revealed to fans Six thousand miles from the club shops where these shirts will be sold, a meeting is taking place inside Bowker Garment Factory. In a photograph obtained by BBC Sport, mannequins display Benfica, Aston Villa and Celtic kits beneath an Adidas logo on the wall. About 3,400 people - most of them women - work here on the outskirts of Phnom Penh. Another 3,200 work 10 miles east at Trax Apparel. Fabric is imported from Thailand and Vietnam before a specialist tailor makes a sample for other employees to follow. Much of the shirt-making process then takes place at these factories, including sewing, ironing and packaging. Staff typically work six eight-hour shifts a week and, according to five payslips seen by the BBC, receive basic monthly salaries of $210-$220 (£158-£166). The salaries comply with local minimum-wage laws, and three of the payslips indicate total monthly earnings of about $300 (£226) once overtime and allowances are included, albeit with significant extra hours worked. "It's hard to live with this amount," said a Bowker worker, who explained she had little left after rent, food and utilities. "I want international customers to hear that one shirt they buy costs more than two weeks' salary for a worker," said another worker at Trax. "Every one of these shirts contains the sweat of Cambodian workers." Trax told us its average monthly employee earnings range from $305-$342 (£230-£258) this year. Adidas said average net wages across a sample of its Cambodian suppliers were 34% above the Anker Research Institute's living-wage benchmark,, external adding staff were "usually paid considerably higher than the local minimum wage". Bowker did not respond to our request for comment. More than 80% of Trax Apparel's workforce are women In another photograph taken inside Bowker, a thermometer shows 35.2C and humidity of 57.6%. "The heat stress is really taking a toll on our health," said an employee on the ironing line. Workers at both factories described pressure to meet group production targets of between 300 and 700 items a day. "Just think about that," they added. "If one shirt sells for $120 (£90) in the store, how much are they pulling in from 600 of them? They make a ton of money but give almost nothing to the workers." Others described verbal abuse when targets were missed. "When we can't complete the quota they scold and yell at us and tell us to resign," said a third worker at Bowker. The same employee said they received two electric shocks from an exposed wire. "I tried to report it multiple times, but they only took action after the second time I got shocked," they said. Adidas told us both factories had "heat-management measures", that its standards "do not permit any form of harassment", and that "no electrical-related accidents" had been found in Bowker's records. Trax acknowledged "periods of elevated temperature" but said cooling systems were in place and insisted its approach "is not based on enforcing output targets". Such concerns are widespread across Cambodia's garment industry, with a 2024 International Labour Organization report, external finding 69% of factories had issues with heat and 84% with worker protection. Bowker Garment Factory is in Kandal Province - a major hub for clothes manufacturing It's August Bank Holiday in England and two of the Premier League's top sides - Aston Villa and Arsenal - are about to meet. title: Why hotter summers are making British potatoes smaller
description: Farmers say yields are down because they have had to harvest smaller potatoes earlier than normal.
body: Tim Rooke, farms near Helmsley in North Yorkshire, says growers may leave the potato industry because of the changing climate As the roller shutter door opens to reveal one of Tim Rooke's potato stores, the harvest looks impressive. Seven hundred tonnes are kept in this building alone, ready to be turned into crisps. Yet North Yorkshire farmer Rooke is far from happy. He plucks a large potato from the pile and in his other hand, places two much smaller ones. "We've probably lost two tonnes on every fifty tonnes in here, potatoes that have just fallen through the graders because they are far too small." The prolonged dry spell this summer meant his crop was beginning to die. He was forced to harvest early, but that meant his potatoes hadn't grown to the size his customers want. Tim Rooke's harvest has many more smaller potatoes than he would like "There will be fewer potatoes grown going forward. They are a very expensive crop to grow," says Tim when the BBC visits his farm near Helmsley. "There's less enthusiasm to have the expense of growing that crop when we have some sort of climate change hitting us year after year after year. We're nearly getting to the stage where enough is enough. "Most potatoes require 200ml of rain or other water and this year they've had about 35ml. It's also been incredibly warm. Potatoes don't bulk up above 28°C. I think we've had 40 days above that." It's a similar story of falling crop yields near Selby, where farmer Richard Bramley would like the government to provide interest-free loans to farmers so they can invest. "We think our potatoes will be 20 to 25% down," he says. "We have to generate the income not just to live, but to produce the following year's crop. That's the dilemma so many farmers find themselves in a the moment. "Off the back of two, maybe three really bad years, the resilience in the farming industry is starting to break down. I think we certainly have a problem, quite when it will really manifest itself I am not entirely sure." Farmer Richard Bramley also reports falling crop yields and even his cover crop, planted to enhance soil biology, is wilting A statement from the Department of the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) confirmed the issue is on Andy Burnham's desk. "Food security is national security and one of the Prime Minister's first visits was meeting farmers hit by drought and dry weather, announcing a £65m package." It added: "We're going further to address the risks of climate change and nature loss - including a new taskforce to strengthen climate security." Scott Walker, chief executive of growers' association GB Potatoes, said shoppers should expect fewer large varieties of potato on the shelves this year. "The prolonged hot and dry weather placed significant pressure on the British crop and has restricted the growth of potatoes. With harvesting still under way, we will not know the full impact until the crop has been lifted, but as well as fewer potatoes there will be fewer large potatoes this year. "Consumers are likely to notice this most with baking potatoes, where the sizes available will be smaller than usual. "The supply chain is extremely good at making the best use of the crop that is available, so consumers will continue to find good quality potatoes and potato products that are good value for money." Back in Helmsley, Tim Rooke wants changes to planning laws to make it easier to build and run water storage lagoons, capturing winter rain and using it in the summer. "We need a more relaxed attitude to allow this to happen. "This is our third bad harvest in five. The weather has certainly altered in this area. We have to adapt and it's time we started or we're going to end with not many potato farmers left in this country."
