title: 'I was blamed for my baby's death now NHS needs to change'
description: Neil and Katie Russell are working with the hospital where their daughter died on the scheme.
body: Neil and Katie Russell are working with the hospital where their daughter died When Poppy Russell died shortly after birth, her parents were left bereft. What followed made matters harder to bear - her mother was blamed for the death. An inquest would later conclude that Poppy's death was preventable. But instead of walking away from the trust that had failed them, Neil and Katie Russell are now working with it to bring compassionate care back into the NHS. "We could have very easily been consumed by hate and anger and rage at what happened – and those feelings are still there," said Katie. "But if no change comes from what happened to Poppy, then what's the point?" Poppy Russell died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford. She was just 12 hours old. During her pregnancy her mother told midwives that she had tokophobia, a fear of natural birth and wanted a caesarean section. Katie said she was repeatedly told however that she "couldn't just ask for a c-section." When she went into labour, Katie was induced and then "we were left in a room for long periods of time where I had no care," she explained. "Finally, when we got into the labour suite, I wasn't monitored appropriately and they missed signs that Poppy was in distress." In a bitter irony, Poppy had to be delivered by emergency caesarean. By then however, she had developed a hypoxic brain injury and died later the same day. An inquest into her death found that had Poppy been born an hour earlier, she would have survived. The Shrewsbury and Telford NHS Trust (SaTH), which ran the hospital, subsequently blamed Katie for her daughter's death. They said she had refused foetal monitoring; the inquest concluded that was untrue. "The trust left us in an appalling position," said Neil Russell. "Not only were they found to have neglected our care, but in the months and years following, we uncovered that members of staff had tried to cover it up. Losing your daughter is one thing, but then to find that there was a cavalcade of lies was almost as bad." Following the inquest in 2023 the trust said: "We recognise there were failings in the care we provided and we are truly sorry." It said the death of any baby was a "tragedy" and promised improvements to maternity services. In March 2024, the couple had a meeting with the trust to discuss all that had happened. From the discussions, Neil and Katie decided they needed to honour Poppy. "The first conversations about Poppy's Promise were about being human," said Neil, 45. "It spun from our treatment, and not being treated like human beings." The parents say they wanted to instigate positive change in Poppy's name Poppy's Promise is based on four care principles: Acknowledgement - recognising a patient's feelings Respect - valuing their opinion Empowerment - involving patients in their care "It's seeing the person, not the diagnosis. It's someone coming into a room holding your hand, someone acknowledging the fact that this is difficult for you," said Katie. Even in the midst of her poor care at the time of her daughter's death, Katie, 41, vividly remembers one midwife who showed some compassion. "She came in and said, 'how are you doing? I just want to hug you.' "She sat with me and she cried with me and she said, 'this should never have happened,' and that will always stay with me because it's exactly what I needed at that point." At the time of Poppy's death, SaTH was in the middle of a large maternity inquiry. The review found that 201 babies and nine mothers might have survived with better care. As part of its improvement programme, the trust is now rolling out Poppy's Promise to all 8,000 staff. As well as reminding its existing employees of the principles of compassionate care, the trust has embedded a question about it into its recruitment processes. The most important part of the training is "to remind me that we are here on a woman's journey, they are not on our journey," says Tasha Simmons, a midwifery ward manager at the trust. "They don't need to know that I've answered three emergency bells this morning, that's not important to them. "What's important is I'm fully present with them to support them in their experience, with kindness and compassion." No-one starts a shift intending to provide care that is lacking in compassion. The problem, say staff, is the pressure they are under - from the sheer number of people in Accident and Emergency to the complexity of many of the patients in hospital. Remembering to treat each person with kindness in those circumstances can be a challenge, said Dr Adrian Walsh, an emergency medicine consultant at the Princess Royal Hospital. There is a "high risk of emotional and compassion fatigue. Day in, day out we have a significant amount of competing demands," he said. "But there's been some research done that actually demonstrates if people are treated with compassion and empathy, they have less complications, [their] outcomes are better." Poppy's parents say that other NHS organisations and some universities have been in touch to explore whether they can incorporate Poppy's Promise into their teaching programme. Their goal is to embed compassionate care throughout the health service. title: Faster than F1: The extreme motorsport where women keep winning
description: Top Fuel drag racing is the only elite motorsport class where women frequently beat men to major titles.
body: Faster than F1: The extreme motorsport where women keep winning Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in. She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet. Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes. The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space. It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles. Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race. Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons. So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend? Top Fuel drivers experience more g-force than an astronaut launching into space More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on. Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through. It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length. Callin says she has never felt underestimated or treated badly for being a woman in drag racing Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off. The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath." Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track. "It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car." And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls". Top Fuel cars surge from zero to 100mph in less than a second Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022. Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports. Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel. Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says. Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture". Shirley Muldowney was the first woman to win the NHRA Top Fuel Championship In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago". The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982. She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance. When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car. "I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says. This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online. More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing. Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitive

title: How a scientist used Britpop to reach Mars
description: Colin Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not landed, and now his work is being celebrated around the UK.
body: Colin Pillinger saw himself as the "front man" of the Beagle 2 mission A series of plaques has been unveiled across the UK to celebrate the country's first spacecraft to reach another planet. Yet the mastermind behind Beagle 2 was never your typical rocket scientist. With his mutton-chop sideburns, West Country accent and infectious enthusiasm, Professor Colin Pillinger persuaded politicians, pop stars and the public to support what had seemed impossible: a British mission to Mars. For years the story of this maverick scientist was synonymous with ambitious British failure. So what changed to make it worthy of nationwide celebration? Pillinger was born in Kingswood near Bristol and completed his degree at Swansea University. He gained international recognition for his lunar research before moving to Cambridge University, where he analysed meteorites found in Antarctica that were believed to have come from Mars. By the 1980s, he had become one of the founders of the Planetary and Space Sciences Research Institute at The Open University in Milton Keynes. It was here he conceived the idea of sending a lander, named Beagle 2 by his wife, to Mars, where it could study the red planet directly for signs of life. Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not safely landed on Mars Space exploration was dominated by international superpowers and agencies such as Nasa, which had the funding for such expensive work. Britain had no dedicated space agency, so Pillinger proposed that Beagle 2 hitch a ride aboard Mars Express, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft already scheduled to travel to the planet. When the ride was approved in 1999, the ESA did not guarantee funding or wider support for the project. The scientist believed that capturing the public's imagination would help attract financial backing. Pallab Ghosh, the BBC's science correspondent, recalled being sceptical when he was sent to meet a "bloke in Milton Keynes who is sending a spaceship to Mars". Those doubts deepened when Pillinger placed a model of Beagle 2 on the lawn. According to Ghosh, it "did not look much like a spaceship". On another occasion, Pillinger loaded a Beagle 2 replica into a supermarket trolley and wheeled it around The Open University's car park, demonstrating its compact size to cameras. The footage was later ridiculed on Have I Got News for You, ensuring it reached an even wider audience. While Pillinger worked as the face of the project, it was supported by a huge team of scientists and engineers from around the country Pillinger persuaded Britpop band Blur to compose a distinctive call-sign that Beagle 2 would transmit to Earth after landing. Artist Damien Hirst created a spot painting to serve as a calibration target for the lander's onboard camera. The project eventually won financial support from the UK government, academic institutions, industrial contractors and private sponsors. Beagle 2 was reportedly built for about £50m; in comparison Nasa spent $25bn on the Apollo programme during the 1960s. Mars Express launched on 2 June 2003 with Beagle 2 aboard; it was due to reach Mars on Christmas Day. On Christmas Eve, excited scientists and celebrities gathered at The Open University's London headquarters. Members of Blur drank mulled wine, singer Myleene Klass handed out jelly babies, and the crowd waited for Beagle 2 to confirm it had landed safely. Pillinger and his team believed it had descended too quickly after being caught out by Martian atmospheric conditions. Official inquiries by the government and ESA criticised the project's finances and management structure. Supporters argued the project had brought industries together behind a single planetary mission. Pillinger, undeterred, proposed a successor, Beagle 3, which ESA rejected in 2004. In his 2010 autobiography, My Life on Mars, he recalled a builder stopping him in The Open University car park to shake his hand. He wrote: "There's nobody in the UK I didn't reach." Analysts identified features of Beagle 2 in photos of Mars Pillinger died in May 2014 after suffering a brain haemorrhage and falling into a coma. Eight months later, high-resolution images captured by Nasa revealed something surprising. Sitting in the red dust, just 5km from its intended landing site, was the largely intact Beagle 2. The images confirmed that much of its landing sequence had worked. Its parachutes and cushioning airbags had deployed as planned. However, its petal-like solar panels had failed to open fully, trapping the antenna and preventing Beagle 2 from communicating. Nic Pillinger welcomed plaque to mark the work done on Beagle 2 For his son Nic Pillinger, the discovery meant an achievement that had been "on ice for many years" could finally take its rightful place in history. Reflecting on the fact that his father died without knowing the mission succeeded, Nick added: "My dad always spoke of himself as being the frontman to the band that was behind this. "It wasn't just a one-man project. It was a huge number of people working across different institutions coming together to make it happen." Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? title: Wonky wych elm in County Down crowned Tree of the Year
description: It is the first time a tree in Northern Ireland has won the national title since it was launched in 2014.
body: The 150-year-old wych elm on the central promenade in Newcastle, County Down, took more than 30% of the national public vote in the UK Tree of the Year 2026 Newcastle's 'Bendy Tree' has been crowned UK Tree of the Year 2026 - the first time a tree in Northern Ireland has won the national title since it was launched in 2014. The 150-year-old wych elm on the central promenade took more than 30% of the national public vote. The theme of the Woodland Trust's annual competition was Against All Odds, with trees across the UK shortlisted for being impressive, beautiful and sometimes baffling examples of how nature can survive adversity. Northern Ireland director John Martin said he was rooting for the "whimsical" tree to win and said tens of thousands across the UK had clearly felt the same. "It's a great testament to the resilience of nature." The Bendy Tree in County Down saw off competition from a small yew that has been growing from the masonry of a Devon church tower for 200 years, a Scottish ash that survived a lightning strike, and a Surrey yew, in which early 19th Century villagers found an embedded English Civil War cannonball. The wych elm is the last remaining tree of a row that was planted along the original promenade in the 19th century, to shelter it from the sea breeze. The rest of the trees were felled in the 1980s during redevelopment. The wind it protected people from has made its trunk grow almost horizontal. But its leafy rainbow over the path means it is still protecting people - just slightly differently. "The council have put a bench underneath it where people can come and sit in the shade and enjoy views of the Mournes and of the sea," Martin said. "I think the whimsical nature of it and the fact that it's showed a lot of resilience over 150 years has proven it the winner this year." Northern Ireland director of the Woodland Trust John Martin was rooting for the tree to win But it has survived more than the weather. As a native elm tree, it also resisted Dutch Elm disease, which destroyed most of the 30 million elms around the UK in the 1960s. Martin said it had shown "remarkable resilience" to live as long as it has and added that it was "great" to see a tree of this age acknowledged. The Ancient Tree inventory lead at the Woodland Trust, May Chemais, said it was an "astonishing and bizarre" tree that had endured a lot. "The Bendy Tree has been blasted by extreme winds, over and over again, for well over a century. "But it has continued to exist and remain rooted, adapting to its surroundings and flourishing into this unusual shape that is providing shade and joy to its community. "We've all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are - I think that's why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people." She added that older trees like the Bendy Tree are part of a community's culture, providing shade and stories. The Ancient Tree inventory lead at the Trust said it was an "astonishing and bizarre" tree Northern Ireland has one of the lowest rates of woodland cover in Europe (8.7%). In UK terms, it lags behind Scotland (19%), Wales (15%), England (10%) and also the Republic of Ireland, which has 11% cover. A tree-planting action plan has been launched, with a target of 12% woodland cover by 2050. But tree-planting rates need to more than triple to get on track for that. What makes a winning tree? Who are you rooting for to win Tree of the Year? title: How boxing inspired a play about men's mental health
description: The play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other.
body: Ferris said he wanted to explore what happens when someone loses the structure that has defined much of their life For many athletes, years of training can provide a routine, a purpose and an identity - but what happens when it all stops? That question is at the heart of a new play which explores men's mental health through the world of boxing. The Corner Man follows a fighter forced to confront life outside the ring after spending years dedicated to the sport. Through his story, the play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other. Writer and producer Cathal J Ferris said the idea grew from his own experience of boxing and conversations with fighters. "What is a boxer after he retires really played on my mind," he said, adding that the same questions around identity and purpose can apply beyond sport. Cathal J Ferris said the play was inspired by his experience of boxing and conversations with fighters The play follows Liam Casey, who has dedicated much of his life to boxing, from the age of about nine into his 30s. For Ferris, the story is not only about leaving the ring, but about losing the routine that comes with it. "The idea of structure and what life is like whenever you lose that structure definitely played on my mind," he said. "There are people who work in jobs for 10, 12, 13-odd years and just decide to change industries. "I think there's a lot of people who may not know what to do with themselves after." Ferris grew up performing in amateur theatre in Belfast and Lisburn before going to drama school in London in 2012. He said returning home had given him the chance to tell new stories about the place where he grew up. "I'm a Belfast boy at heart, and it is great to tell stories from the city," he said. Ferris said "the boxing community in Belfast is phenomenal" and that it played an important part in shaping the story. Alongside boxing, the play also looks at how men talk - or sometimes do not talk - about their mental health. "I think the old phrase is 'say nothing', and we know that all too well," Ferris said. "As a man, it is definitely hard for myself to talk about these things, and I try to be a little bit more open." In the play, Liam struggles with life after boxing, but it is the other men around him who help provide a support network - something Ferris said was an important part of the story. "It is healthy to talk, so definitely if you're a man and you're struggling, at least speak to somebody," he said. Director Emma Copeland took up boxing classes while preparing for the production Director Emma Copeland said she knew relatively little about boxing before becoming involved in the production, but soon immersed herself in the sport. "I got really into boxing and went to a load of boxing classes and still going," she said. Copeland said she also watched films, read books and autobiographies and listened to podcasts to make sure she knew the world she was portraying. For her, one of the most important parts of the play is the support the men offer each other. "The angle that I see is that men supporting men, and helping and talking and encouraging support with each other and encouraging that conversation," she said. "Rather than shutting it down or locking themselves away in their own feelings." Gary Trainor plays several roles in the production For actor Gary Trainor, the experience Liam goes through is not something that only applies to boxers. Trainor, who plays gym owner Marty as well as several other roles, said suddenly losing something which has been central to your life could happen in many different circumstances. "He's been so engrossed in the world of boxing for his entire life, to lose it in one injury and to try and figure out his life after that is, I think, probably universal in a lot of men's lives," he said. "That could be maybe losing a job, anything like that." Trainor described the play as "full of heart and humour" and said he hoped it would "make a few lads think". For him, its message is a straightforward one - that "men should talk to each other a bit more about what they are feeling and how they are processing things". title: I want justice after boy's evil knife attack on my daughter, says mother
description: The 14-year-old girl could have died in the frenzied attack, her mother says.
body: The 14-year-old boy stabbed the girl repeatedly using a 6in knife The mother of a 14-year-old girl who was repeatedly stabbed in an "evil" attack by a boy says it is "disgraceful" that he was not jailed. The boy, 14, from Wiltshire, had stalked the girl after she refused to date him before attacking her with a 6in knife in broad daylight at a shop in Cirencester, Gloucestershire, on 15 March. Last month, he was sentenced to a three-year restraining order and a one-year referral order after he admitted wounding with intent, inflicting grievous bodily harm and possession of a bladed article in a public place. The girl's mother said: "If it hadn't been for the shopkeeper and her [own] quick reactions, she would have been dead." The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it was currently "reviewing how the law can better protect victims in the youth courts" to ensure the "punishment fits the offence". If you have been affected by issues of sexual abuse or violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line The 'little piece of post-war history hiding in plain sight' Paul McCartney's item sells for double the estimate City's only residential tower block to be demolished The boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, waited for the victim to enter the shop as he watched her from a nearby car park. He then followed her inside and stabbed her multiple times in a prolonged attack. Det Supt Ian Fletcher said of CCTV of the attack: "Anyone who sees footage would say she is very lucky to not have very serious, if not fatal injuries." He likened the attack to the award-winning TV drama Adolescence, in which a teenager fatally stabs his female classmate. The mother added: "If you're big enough to commit an adult crime, you should have the punishment, regardless of your age. It was not a petty crime - it wasn't petty theft." She told the BBC that the family remained "scared" after the boy's "evil and sick" attack. She added that his age should not have spared him from a youth detention centre. "I feel angry. We're incredibly let down; we feel like everyone's failed us," she said. "It's disgusting. It's absolutely disgraceful after watching [footage of the attack] that someone can say the guidelines are 'first offence and the injuries weren't life-threatening'. "They weren't life-threatening because she managed to defend herself. "I want some justice for my child - I want some protection." An MoJ spokesperson said they had received "multiple requests" to reconsider the sentence under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme, but sentences passed by youth courts are not part of the scheme. "We share the public's shock at the details of this horrific crime," they added. "Our thoughts are with the victim and her family, and we recognise it will be deeply disappointing that the sentence handed out cannot be referred to the court of appeal. "We are reviewing how the law can better protect victims in the youth courts." They added that sentencing decisions are made by independent judges and magistrates, in line with the sentencing guidelines. Carole Gould (L), whose daughter Ellie (R) was murdered by her ex-boyfriend, described the sentence as "immoral and unjust" Carole Gould, whose teenage daughter Ellie was murdered by her ex-boyfriend in May 2019, described the sentence as "wrong, immoral, and unjust". Ellie was strangled and stabbed in the neck multiple times after she tried to end her three-month relationship with 17-year-old Thomas Griffiths. After initially attempting to stage the scene as a suicide, Griffiths later admitted murder and was jailed for a minimum of 12 and a half years in November 2019. "I'm absolutely appalled at the outcome of this case," she said. "In my mind, there is no doubt about it - this was premeditated attempted murder. "All I could think of was that poor girl and her family, and the terrible trauma that she's going to have to live with for the rest of her life." Gould agreed "the outcome could so easily have been different", as many of the knife wounds were focused around the victim's neck. "I thoroughly believe in rehabilitation, but equally, there has to be repercussions for such behaviour," she said. "It just sends the message that violence against women and girls is not being taken seriously." Jane Harvey, from domestic abuse charity the Hollie Gazzard Trust, advised victims against blocking stalkers In a statement read out in court, the girl described having nightmares since the attack. "I relive the incident, but in these dreams it happens in different places. "I sleep in the dark but when I wake, I constantly feel like there is a presence in the room. I can't stop thinking about it," she said. After the girl ended their brief relationship, she blocked the boy's number on her phone to prevent him from contacting her. But The Hollie Gazzard Trust, a Gloucestershire charity that aims to raise awareness of and help reduce domestic violence, advised against this. Jane Harvey, the charity's chief executive, warned obsessed partners are "more likely to physically come round and find you" when blocked. She added: "If we have to go down the route of reporting to police and getting the criminal justice system involved, what we need is evidence of the unwanted contact in order for the police to be able to prosecute the case. "By blocking someone, we potentially lose evidence that could help secure something like a conviction or a restraining order." title: Shocked NHS colleagues grieve 'exceptional doctor'
description: Hannah Cain, known to patients as Dr Hannah Terry, is described as a cherished colleague.
body: Flowers and tributes were left outside the surgery where Hannah Cain worked The colleagues of a GP found dead at her home have spoken of their profound shock at the loss of an "exceptional doctor". Hannah Cain, 45, known to her patients as Dr Hannah Terry, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday. Her husband, Mark Cain, is due at King's Lynn Crown Court later, charged with her murder. The GP was based at Grimston Medical Centre and had previously been at Heacham Group Practice for several years. "We have lost an outstanding doctor, a cherished colleague and a friend, and her absence will be felt deeply across our health community," said a statement issued on behalf of primary care organisations across west Norfolk. "The profound sense of shock and sadness across our practices and the wider NHS community speaks to the impact Hannah had on so many people." It said its thoughts were with everyone who knew and loved Hannah, and it was grateful for the compassion and understanding shown by patients, communities and partner organisations. St Nicholas Church in Dersingham is open for prayers and reflection The statement continued: "Hannah was an exceptional doctor and a deeply valued member of our NHS and primary care community. "Highly intelligent, kind and generous, she brought warmth and positivity to those around her. "She gave freely of her time and knowledge and, in the words of colleagues who knew her well, was simply a joy to know and work with. "Throughout her career, Hannah earned the trust and respect of colleagues through her professionalism, skill and commitment. "From her time in training through to becoming an accomplished doctor, she approached her work with tremendous care and a genuine determination to make a difference. "That was particularly evident in the way Hannah cared for her patients. "She was a passionate advocate for people, taking time to listen and ensuring everyone felt heard, understood and cared for. "Improving patient care mattered deeply to her and was at the heart of her work." It added: "Colleagues from across our local NHS and primary care community stand together in remembering Hannah and celebrating the difference she made. "Her contribution to healthcare, her dedication to her patients and the positive impact she had on those fortunate enough to work alongside her will be her lasting legacy. "She will be deeply missed and very fondly remembered. " On Wednesday, the GP's family said she was kind, generous and loving; a beloved mother, daughter, sister, auntie, daughter-in-law and friend. "We are incredibly proud of the woman she was and of the great care she took of all her patients who knew her as Dr Terry," they added, in a statement released via Norfolk Police. Reverend Mark Capron said people had come together to support one another In Dersingham, the Reverend Mark Capron, from St Nicholas Church, knew Hannah Cain, as did many people in the village and surrounding area. "She brought joy to all who met her and that's certainly a memory that holds dear to me and many within this community," he said. Several parishioners had come into the church to light a candle and to pray, he said, with Hannah's photo displayed on its door. "People want to support and be there for everybody, which is really encouraging," he added. "It is a loving caring community and that's something that's shining through in this challenging time." title: New vape tax made me swap e-cigs for dartboards
description: The Vaping Product Duty will be imposed at a rate of £2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid from April 2027.
body: This video can not be played A vape shop has been forced to reinvent itself with a new tax on the horizon. Vapers Cave in Bracknell sells vapes, but now also sells darts equipment too. The Vaping Product Duty, AKA Vape Tax, will be imposed at a rate of £2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid. It comes into effect from April 2027, giving sellers a six month window to sell old stock at the pre-duty price. Shop owner Daniel Buckland said: "We are genuinely concerned will stay open with the tax coming on board, because of the concern and impact it would cause, we decided to diversify." title: Why are there so many mushrooms around this year?
description: The RHS says the hot, dry summer followed by autumn rain could lead to record sightings.
body: Colin holds olive amanita mushrooms found while foraging Have you spotted more mushrooms than usual on woodland walks or in your garden this autumn? The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) has predicted mushroom sightings across the UK could reach record levels this autumn, saying drought followed by wetter weather could help some species flourish. Lancashire forager Colin Unsworth said some species had appeared in "bumper" numbers, although others had been harder to find. But Unsworth, who leads foraging trips across Lancashire, warned people not to eat wild mushrooms unless they were certain they had identified them correctly, as some poisonous species can closely resemble edible varieties. Unsworth, who runs Forest Horizons in Adlington, said fly agaric, the distinctive red mushroom with white spots, and blushers had been found in good numbers. Porcini mushrooms, also known as penny buns or ceps, had been "a bit thin on the ground", he said. He added there was an EU-wide shortage of the edible fungi, which are prized by chefs for their "lovely, robust flavour". However, he warned that some poisonous species, including the brown roll-rim, can be mistaken for edible mushrooms. "You get look-alike mushrooms," he said. "They can be really dangerous." Unsworth says fly agaric mushrooms have been particularly plentiful this year The RHS said prolonged hot weather and drought, followed by a wet autumn, could help some fungi flourish. Its advice team recorded a 43% rise in inquiries about garden fungi following the 2025 drought, compared with the previous year. Some species benefit from extra dead plant material left by drought, while others respond to stress in trees by producing more mushrooms. Jassy Drakulic, RHS senior plant pathologist, said gardeners could notice a "remarkable variety of mushrooms and toadstools" appearing in lawns, borders and around trees this autumn. She said fungi were mostly a sign of a healthy ecosystem, helping to break down organic matter and support plant health. For Unsworth, autumn is the highlight of the foraging calendar. He said understanding mushrooms helped "join the dots" between different parts of the landscape and explain why species were found in particular habitats. A typical forage at this time of year could produce 20 or 30 edible types of mushroom, he said. "In the autumn time, mushrooms take centre stage and they're so beautiful and they're so varied," he said. title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
description: Pioneering computer scientist led the development of the software for Nasa's Apollo mission and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
body: Hamilton after she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division. It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. "I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring. The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved. But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT. The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her. Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969 In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel. At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space". Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958. She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree. From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts. "We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media. "Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. title: New electric car 'make or break for Jaguar'
description: Prof David Bailey says there is a lot riding on the Type 01 in terms of jobs and investment.
body: The Type 01's design has had a mixed reception from car enthusiasts Jaguar's new electric car represents "make or break" for the brand, an industry expert has said. Parent company JLR has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and has faced mixed reactions over the design of the Type 01, which was unveiled this week. Last month, it emerged Jaguar Land Rover, which has manufacturing sites in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood on Merseyside, is to cut 4,000 jobs as it struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs and the transition to electric. David Bailey, professor of business economics at the University of Birmingham, said it was a "perfect storm" for the firm, which has struggled since a cyber attack last year. "I think it's make or break for Jaguar as a brand," he said of the Type 01 launch. "Clearly it was failing to compete in the premium market, they've had to completely reinvent it, take it luxury and electric and that is a big gamble." Bailey said the market for luxury electric cars was in its infancy, but that "Jaguar is right at the forefront of that". He added: "It's going to have to create a whole new market where one didn't exist before, so it's a big, big gamble for the company." Professor David Bailey said JLR was facing tariffs from the US and "huge pressure to go electric" Last month, Bentley unveiled its first fully electric car, the Torcal, after investing £350m to upgrade its factory in Crewe. At the time, the government hailed the news, adding that it followed multimillion-pound investments by McLaren and Nissan in the UK car industry. The minimum cost of Jaguar's Type 01 is £130,000 in the UK and $130,500 in the US. The new model's electric motors produce about 1,000 horsepower, allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR, which has its global headquarters at Whitley in Coventry, says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles. The car was designed and built in the West Midlands and transferred to Manhattan for the launch. The vehicles will be assembled at Lode Lane in Solihull, while their battery packs are being made at the Wolverhampton plant. The Type 01 will retail from £130,000 in the UK and $130,500 (£99,000) in USA The cyber-attack caused JLR, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month. Bailey said the firm was facing tariffs from the US and "huge pressure to go electric". "So the company itself is struggling, [has] announced 4,000 redundancies, so there's a lot riding on this car in terms of jobs and investment." Jaguar's pivot to become an all-electric brand is seen by many in the industry as a high-risk decision. Speaking last month, Kevin Moreley, a former managing director of the Rover Group, said the Type 01 would be a pivotal moment for the firm. He said the 4,000 job losses would not be the end of the cuts if the car "doesn't sell the numbers they hope". While JLR does not break down its accounts by brand, Jaguar is widely believed to be the worst performer in the group. There are 11,800 members of the Jaguar Enthusiasts Club around the world, including Tim Brookes, Ian Martin, Geoff Johnston, Graham Kinsey and Peter Bennett (left to right) West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, meanwhile, has suggested the race to electric could be happening too quickly for consumers and that it could lead to production shifting elsewhere. He has has called for the government's electric vehicle targets to be slashed to protect the sector. The Type 01's looks have had a mixed response, but West Midlands members of the Jaguar Enthusiasts Club, which has 11,800 members worldwide, have welcomed the new model. One of them, Tim Brookes, from Kingswinford, said he thought it would be "fantastic". "I like that it's typically Jaguar as it's low, long, wide. It looks beautifully made... Although it looks like it's got the Jaguar heritage, everything about it looks fresh and new." Ian Martin stated: "It's quite a bold statement and I think you have to be bold to compete and take Jaguar into a new market." Tutor Matthew Callaghan (left) was pictured with City of Wolverhampton College students on a level three light vehicle maintenance course, Joshua Hartland, Jacob Peccolo and Muhammad Ali Adnan Peter Bennett, from Walsall, also a member of the group, said the level of technology in the new car and those that follow it "is way in advance of anything that we've seen". "But the Chinese are bringing out cars for a lot less money with similar technology, so it's going to be tough, but I just hope that it works out for them." Trainee car mechanics at City of Wolverhampton College also liked what they saw with the new car. Student Muhammad Ali Adnan said: "I think I could see this in a James Bond movie in the future. "[It] is very different from the old ones they made, so I think this is a risk and I think it has a potential to go positive." title: My magical daughter went to school and never came home - I want everyone to remember her
description: Olivia-Grace's father says his world crumbled when his daughter died after falling in school.
body: This video can not be played 'She went off to school and never came home' "I know I'm biased because she was mine, but she was the best human I've ever met," says Aaron John Huxter of his daughter Olivia-Grace. The 33-year-old says his "entire world crumbled from a phone call" when he was told his eight-year-old daughter had fallen at her school in Rhondda Cynon Taf. He was more than an hour's drive away, and when he was just around the corner, he was told they had restarted her heart. Aaron says he got out of his van and collapsed in shock, before being taken to the ambulance where a paramedic told him: "We've stabilised her but you have a very, very sick little girl." Not long after, they were told Olivia-Grace's brain could not recover. Aaron and Olivia-Grace's mum, Melanie, stayed with her at Cardiff's University Hospital of Wales until she died on 8 October 2025. "It kills me that the worst day of my life was just a normal Wednesday for everyone else," he says. "She went off to school, just as she did every day, and then never came home." Olivia-Grace Huxter, who had Down's syndrome, died aged eight in October 2025 after falling at school The coroner's report is still outstanding, and they are not sure they will find out the exact cause of Olivia-Grace's death, but Aaron says he does not blame anyone. He described his daughter as a miracle who "defied the odds" as she had Atrioventricular septal defect, external (AVSD), underwent heart repair at six months old and overcame pneumonia at five. "I'm sorry you never got to meet her," Aaron says, "that's how I feel when I tell everyone about her. "Nothing can ever prepare you to lose your child. Not just to lose your daughter, but to lose your entire reason. Trying to move forward from losing a child, it's the most difficult thing in the world. "The pain I feel now, I know I will always feel, but I know it's completely necessary. I wouldn't want anything that would stop me from missing her, she was so incredible she deserves to be missed every day. "I'm just grateful it was me, I'm the one she chose." Aaron says Olivia-Grace was a miracle who was at the centre of the whole family Aaron is part of a men's bereavement campaign run by the charity 2wish, external, which supports those affected by sudden death in young people. It aims to encourage more open conversations about grief. "The general standard is that the mum would be the one really struggling, and the dad is there as the strong one," he says. "I wish I could say that's how it happened but we just went around it in a completely different way, we leant on each other when we both needed it." Aaron says men could find it difficult to express their feelings "as it's bred in us that it exposes weakness or vulnerability". "As a man you could just bottle it up... it will fester and grow and it can very quickly turn very, very dark," he says. "I won't sit here and lie and say I haven't had those thoughts, because I have. The day we lost Olivia was the darkest day of my life. "You feel like your main job in life is to protect your child and keep your child safe, and I wasn't able to do that. "As a dad you can feel like you failed, even though it's completely out of your hands, you have still had to bury your child." "I'm sorry you never got to meet her," says Aaron about Olivia-Grace Aaron says he tries to embrace the darker times that come with his grief. "Whether you're wailing or it's a little cry on the way home. I feel it necessary, it's Olivia-Grace coming through." He recalls receiving a 2wish memory box the day after Olivia died, which gave them a "tiny light in a dark time" and included thumbprints and elephant cuddly toys. One elephant was left with Olivia-Grace, and the family kept the other elephant, because "elephants never forget". Her parents say Olivia-Grace "defied all odds" overcoming pneumonia and heart repair The family was also assigned 2wish caseworker Jo who helped them with arranging Olivia-Grace's funeral, and continues to provide support through monthly coffee mornings and regular check-ins. Aaron says the coffee mornings were a time when he could be vulnerable. "I put on a face of Aaron the funny one, who makes everyone laugh. In that room I don't need to put on a front, they know the pain I'm feeling. "Everyone's process with grief is completely different, but with how easy we find it to speak about our grief and Olivia-Grace, we find that it helps others to speak. "I always make sure to see a picture of their child, to ask about their child," he added. "I know there are families out there that feel [grief] needs to be something very personal and very private, but it really doesn't." Olivia-Grace "could change your entire day, with just a look or a smile" Describing what Olivia-Grace was like, Aaron says she had a "sixth sense" for people having a bad day and was a natural at lifting people up, greeting strangers with a smile and hug when they needed it. "She would make the angriest bloke smile, and the saddest lady laugh, that's just who she was... she was who everyone went to when they needed to be fixed." He says she was a huge part of her school, who are marking her death with an "Olivia-Grace day" celebration, which Aaron and Melinda will be attending. But passing one year since her death brings painful emotions. "Because it's the first, we just don't know what to expect or how to react," he says. "Once that day passes, I can no longer say I lost my daughter in October. I will have to say October 2025. "For me, every day that goes by, it's not just another day where I haven't had her... it's an extra day I haven't seen her." title: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls
description: Many Palestinians are still living in cramped tent cities, with the US plan to end the war largely stalled.
body: This video can not be played Fida al-Toutah's family say they witnessed her being killed by Israeli gunfire in their tent two weeks ago In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted. "My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke. He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in. "Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said. Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head. She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Fida was one of the more than 1,400 people killed since the ceasefire began, according to Gaza's health ministry The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory. But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry. Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire. "It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband. In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident. The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry. Ibrahim has lost four siblings, including Fida, since the start of the war in 2023 Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces. "This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians." Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said. The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures. On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza. His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry. The IDF said it had no information about this incident either. Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire. Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west. Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space. The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas. In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters. In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%. Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza a year after a ceasefire came into force Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline. "Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said. Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own. Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began. Amal Alabadla says she's struggling to raise her sons alone inside a tent on Gaza's coast "During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said. "Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed." There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding. The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an i

title: Hygiene poverty at tipping point, charity warns
description: The BBC hears people "you would not expect" can no longer afford items to be clean and healthy.
body: Hygiene poverty is affecting people who previously felt finanically secure, the BBC was told People are increasingly unable to afford items they need to feel clean and healthy, a charity has warned. Rosemary Ashworth, deputy chief executive of The Hygiene Bank, told BBC Radio Surrey the "face" of hygiene poverty had changed and it was affecting people who previously felt financially secure. "We're at a bit of a tipping point so now feels like the time to do something about it," she said. Janice Sedgwick, a volunteer at the charity's Guildford branch, said needed items were things like "toothbrushes, toothpaste, shower gel, shampoo, sanitary pads and laundry detergent". But she said people were also struggling to get products to keep their houses clean. A recent survey of 3,042 UK adults by The Hygiene Bank and In Kind Direct suggested one in five (18%) had experienced hygiene poverty in the last six months, or someone in their household had. The charities said two in five (41%) of those affected said they had experienced it for the first time this year. Ashworth (pictured) said the number of people affected had increased significantly The Hygiene Bank said the phenomenon "can create a vicious cycle, affecting health, confidence, education, work and social participation". Ashworth said "It's not people who [you] might necessarily expect experiencing it," she said. "It's working families. People who previously felt financially secure... "It feels like a problem that is worsening." Tom May, from Guildford-based mental health charity Oakleaf, said a common issue was women needed hygiene products on a "certain basis", though stores were "pretty much empty by the end of the week". The Hygiene Bank is urging people to donate essential products or money for National Hygiene Week, which ends on 11 October. title: 'I won Gladiators - now I'd love to become one'
description: Josh McDonald won the third season of the hit TV programme, which aired earlier this year.
body: Josh McDonald won the third season of Gladiators earlier this year Having been bashed, bumped and bruised on his way to winning Gladiators earlier this year, you might expect Josh McDonald wants to put his feet up. But the Glasgow fitness coach has not only signed up for another go on the famous Eliminator challenge - he fancies becoming one of the Lycra-clad stars. The 29-year-old triumphed in the third season of the popular programme, which was filmed in Sheffield last year. He is now getting the chance to go again on games like Duel, Gauntlet and The Wall as part of a live tour across the country. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Several new Gladiators have joined the show for the new season, including three-time World's Strongest Man champion Tom Stoltman. And Josh admitted he wouldn't mind "turning to the dark side" and joining the likes of Viper, Legend and Scotland's own Sabre. He said: "I'd love to be a Gladiator and I think I'd be fantastic at it, with the message I bring, the personality I've got and the athletic ability I have. "The problem is that while the gladiators are the pinnacle, they can't actually win the show - only the contenders can do that, and I'm really competitive. "So you're better off being a contender than a Gladiator in some ways, as I don't think you would get the emotional rollercoaster that a contender will get from it. "But if the opportunity to be a Gladiator came up, then I'd be there." Josh was actually edged out in the first round of the show, but returned in the next stage after an injury to another contestant. He did not let his second chance slip away, storming through to the final and taking the trophy after beating Tyler Spence, a teacher from Wigan, in a closely-fought contest. Josh took part in Gladiators events like Collision during his time on the show However while Josh was jubilant to win the competition, the victory also brought with it a mixture of emotions. He first watched the show growing up alongside his mother Clare, a single parent who raised him and his two younger brothers. But in 2024, a few months before he got the offer to appear on the programme, his mother died after a long illness. Josh then became the guardian of his younger brother Max, who was 14 at the time. "I used to watch the show growing up with my mum," he recalls. "She loved Wolf [from the 90s version] and it was something you'd sit on the couch going 'oh I could do that, I'd love that' and then the opportunity came up. "Just before the show [was filmed] I wasn't taking care of myself as much, as I had lost my mum and was taking guardianship of Max and having that extra responsibility. "There was a motivation of trying to prove myself that I could still compete and give Max something to cheer about, so I got back in training again." Josh's mum Clare died in 2024 Now he is trying to get ready for the games again, this time for the live tour. It starts in Aberdeen this weekend and includes four shows in front of a home Glasgow crowd later this month. "You can't go into a gym and just practice Duel, so what I am trying to do just now is focus on staying fit and healthy in general," he says. "I've been at the local climbing centre trying to prepare for the Wall as that was the game I struggled with the most. "In training I had been one of the quickest, and I'd thought to myself 'oh I'll get 10 points here' and then I messed it up every single time. "I don't know if it was the pressure that got to me, as it's different when you have a Gladiator behind you, or maybe I just had too high expectations. "I'm determined to do better on the tour." Getting back involved with Gladiators was not something Josh - who proudly displays the trophy from the show on a table in his living room - had to think twice about. "I'd have Gladiators champion tattooed on my forehead if I could so I bit their hand off to do it," he said. "Doing the TV show was one of the highlights of my entire life and something I'll never forget so having the opportunity to relive it in Scotland is so exciting." Josh (right) is the oldest of three brothers, and guardian to his youngest brother Max (centre) But no matter what is thrown at him Josh said being a guardian to Max was the toughest challenge he faced in life. He added: "I've always had big brother responsibilities, and my mum was a single parent so I always tried to support her. "But as soon as I stepped into the guardian role it flipped everything on its head. It's not something you can prepare for." Since winning Gladiators he has become involved in various charities, including raising awareness for kinship charities, external. Josh hopes he can help highlight that there is support available for people in similar situations to himself. He said: "I thought I was one in a million and I had to stumble my way through it. "A lot of the information I obtained was just me sourcing it and I felt very isolated. "But there are thousands of us out there and I want them to feel like they are not alone." title: 'The wood is alive': Ranger retires after 38 years
description: William McLaughlin leaves a "lasting legacy" of care at Bourne Woods in Lincolnshire, bosses say.
body: McLaughlin said working in the woods was his 'dream' job A "passionate" woodsman who spent almost four decades caring for wildlife has retired. William McLaughlin spent 37 years working as Forestry England wildlife ranger at Bourne Woods, in Lincolnshire. The 68-year-old, who was responsible for conservation and deer management, said: "If your job is your hobby, you don't work a day in your life." Scott Martin, Forestry England manager for Bourne Woods, said: "His passion, expertise and dedication have made a lasting difference to these forests and the wildlife that depends on them." McLaughlin said his love of the outdoors stemmed from childhood. "I just always loved being in the woods," he said. "It was my environment." He moved to Lincolnshire in 1990 after spending 15 years as a gamekeeper in Scotland's Western Isles. "I couldn't think of anything else I would have done. "The wood is alive – why would you want to be anywhere else?" William McLaughlin has retired as a wildlife ranger from Bourne Woods Reflecting on his career, McLaughlin said: "I've traveled in the London underground, people do that daily, all their working lives, and I think why would anyone want to do that? "My favourite thing is being out here in the woods." Deer management was an "integral" part of his role. "If you have an unmanaged deer population, they pretty much destroy it, grazing on young vegetation meaning trees can't grow, which has a knock-on effect to wildlife." Martin said McLaughlin's "wealth of knowledge" had been invaluable in "helping us care for these special places". "His work on deer management has played a vital role in supporting the natural regeneration of native tree species, while his collaboration with local conservation groups has helped deliver positive outcomes for wildlife across the area. "His contribution leaves a lasting legacy and we thank him for his remarkable service and wish him a long, happy and well-deserved retirement." Despite retiring, McLaughlin said he would remain a familiar face in the woods. "I won't miss it, because I'm still going to be here. I will miss my colleagues and the friends I have made though." title: Syrian general accused of atrocities paid and protected by US and Lebanon, BBC finds
description: Bassam al-Hassan, linked to reporter Austin Tice's abduction, is being sheltered in return for information.
body: Bassam al-Hassan is wanted for crimes against humanity during Syria's Assad regime A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity, external is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found. Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024. An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told. Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation, with Hassan in the chain of command. Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this. We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return. In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive. "This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial." Josh Baker enters a dangerous world of fear, greed and betrayal as he uncovers what happened in one of the biggest missing-person cases of our time - the abduction of Austin Tice. As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed. In it, Hassan is offered "residency", "protection" and help securing his "living needs" in return for information, primarily about Tice. Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government. Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025. Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan's arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain. Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad. One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice's case. It was "not in his interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC, "in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]". Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice. The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case. US journalist Austin Tice has been missing since 2012 - Bassam al-Hassan is believed to have been involved in his disappearance Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan is believed to have initially escaped to Iran. A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place - involving the US, Lebanon, and Iran - to bring Hassan to Lebanon. The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria's chemical weapons programme and its military relationship with Iran - secrets that US intelligence was allegedly interested in. The aftermath of the 2013 chemical attacks in Ghouta, Syria - Bassam al-Hassan is alleged to have shared responsibility Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found - according to multiple sources familiar with the dig - casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information. There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns. When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission

title: Funding to help more people access healthy food
description: Local authorities in Hull and Lincolnshire have each been given £220,000.
body: Five local authorities in Hull and Lincolnshire will each receive £222,000 to help people overcome challenges accessing healthy food People in Hull are facing a "stark" challenge when it comes to accessing healthy food, the leader of the city's council says. The local authority and four from Lincolnshire are among 45 in England that will each receive £222,000 from the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) to help improve access to healthy and affordable food. The authorities were chosen after being identified as having the greatest levels of deprivation and childhood obesity. Councillor Mike Ross, leader of Hull City Council, said: "It can be incredibly difficult for some people to get the healthy food they need. So, anything that helps tackle those barriers is really important." DEFRA said the Good Food Neighbourhoods funding could support schemes such as community food shops and mobile greengrocers, as well as helping local authorities strengthen their capacity to plan for and meet local food needs. The National Child Measurement Programme, external for the school year 2024/25 shows 10.2% of children in reception year (aged 4-5) in Hull had a BMI status of obese, while in Year 6 (aged 10-11) that figure was 19%. Those figures are above the national average, external. Ross added: "This whole picture demonstrates there is severe need here. "Of course, this funding will help tackle that, building on the work that's already taking place and wanting to work with not just the council but with local communities and groups across the city to make sure everything is done to support local residents." Darren Squires, from the Hull Food Partnership, says there are a number of reasons why some people struggle to access healthy food Darren Squires, from the Hull Food Partnership, which brings together all the community food organisations in the city, said it was not just a case of low income that made it difficult for people to access food. He said: "When we talk about deprivation, some of it is poverty, some of it is access to food if you're so far away from a supermarket and don't drive or if you're running two jobs. "For some people it's not about income. People can be financially secure, but still time poor. "There are areas in the city where it is much easier to get a takeaway meal than it is to get any other kind of food that you would cook at home." Other local authorities from East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire allocated the funding include North East Lincolnshire Council (NELC), North Lincolnshire Council, City of Lincoln Council and South Holland District Council. Councillor Nige Oliver, portfolio holder for health, wellbeing and adult social care at NELC, welcomed the announcement. He said: "Families in areas like ours can face significant challenges in trying to access affordable, healthy food. "We're now looking at how we can use this funding to support people in our area." The BBC understands a government meeting next week will provide further details to local authorities about this funding.
