title: UK bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF
description: The tuna is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF.
body: Bluefin tuna have returned in significant numbers to the waters off Cornwall Bluefin tuna have returned in huge numbers off the British coast after almost disappearing from UK waters. The return of the giant predatory fish is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF, which it says shows conservation can work. However, the Living Planet Report 2026 also found that monitored wildlife populations around the world have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970. The wildlife conservation charity said nature remains in "freefall" but it called the report one of hope. "It's not too late," Mike Barrett, chief scientific adviser at WWF-UK, told the BBC. Restored wetland becomes haven for rare birds Five endangered African birds hatch at Chester Zoo The UK was once home to large tuna fisheries, but overfishing of both the tuna and the smaller fish it preys on meant that by the 1960s it had largely disappeared. The report credits its recent recovery to a concerted international effort that included reducing catch quotas, size limits and protection of spawning grounds, which was backed by campaigns from consumers, chefs and retailers. Hannah Rudd, head of marine at the Angling Trust, said the result of this effort was close to an "explosion" in the population of the species. "I think bluefin tuna is a golden case study that fisheries management works," she said. This video can not be played Climate editor Justin Rowlatt visits the UK Bluefin Tuna Championships The WWF report highlighted other species recoveries around the world, including an increase of more than 70% in the number of wild tigers - from around 3,200 in 2010 to about 5,700 in 2025. Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to have its protection status downgraded from "endangered" to "least concern", after 50 years of conservation work in about 80 countries. Elephant numbers are stable or growing in parts of southern Africa, thanks in part to new laws that give local people a share of the income elephants bring, including tourism. Khata Biological Corridor in Nepal has been restored, helping local tiger numbers to recover Barrett said these successes resulted from a clear goal with a credible plan and people who believed they could make a difference. The report calls it "the science of hope". "Hope is not the same thing as wishful thinking," he said. "Hope is not passive. Hope's about action." Elephant population numbers have also stabilised or are growing in parts of southern Africa But despite the individual successes, the overall picture for nature remains stark. Working with the Zoological Society of London, WWF tracks nearly 36,000 populations of almost 6,000 species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians. It estimates global monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970. The figure measures the average change in the size of those populations, not the number of animals lost. About half of the populations are stable or growing, but their gains are outweighed by losses elsewhere. Dr Katie Collins, a senior curator at the Natural History Museum in London, also said the index misses out vast numbers of important species because it covers only vertebrates, missing plants, insects and other creatures they depend on. "If you lose garden snails, you lose the song thrush," she warned. The green sea turtle has undergone monitoring in Fiji along with dozens of other countries WWF says conservation alone cannot reverse the decline but there must be efforts to tackle the causes. The biggest pressures come from farming, which can destroy the habitats wildlife depends on, and burning fossil fuels for energy, which drives climate change. The organisation says the money is flowing the wrong way. In 2023, about $7.3 trillion (£5.53tn) went into activities that harm nature, compared with $220bn spent protecting or restoring it, the report estimates – a ratio of roughly 33 to one. Barrett has worked on seven Living Planet reports, but he said this was the first where the takeaway message was to focus on hope. "The fact that the science is still telling us that we've got a way out is actually extraordinary," he said. "So it's a closing window of opportunity, but it's still open, just, if we act now." title: 'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK
description: Roland Lescure tells the BBC that being in the bloc enables members to better address the challenges facing the world.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Roland Lescure says Britain leaving the EU was "very sad" French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the EU, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled a second Brexit referendum was "possible" in a future Labour election manifesto. Lescure said being in the bloc comes with some difficulties, but it enables members to better address the challenges facing the world. Last week, Burnham said the UK needed to "consider the options", ranging from staying as is, rejoining the customs union or single market, or going "all the way". Asked about the PM's comments, Lescure told the BBC: "British people decided, and that's obviously their 100% right, and if they're willing to come back, they will have to decide." "But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime." Burnham recently warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK. The prime minister expressed concerns about how British industry and supply chains could be affected by the planned Made In Europe scheme. The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies. The EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its own supply chains. Asked about the possibility of Britain being kept out of the scheme, Lescure said: "Come back, and you'll be at the table, and we discuss all these things together." The finance minister's interview with the BBC also touched on French domestic matters, including the student protests that have swept the country, with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut as of Wednesday. Hundreds of thousands of people have been taking to the streets to call for better conditions in schools. Lescure said it was a "tough world" for young people, saying he understood why they were anxious and that "our duty as leaders is to listen to them". "It's hard to tell young people we're not going to have the money for you because we're spending a lot on health and pensions," he acknowledged. "We're getting people more healthy. People live longer. But we cannot just say 'this is fine' and then we don't have money left for the kids, so we need to rebalance that." In France's upcoming budget he said he will cut back on health spending and ask retired people to accept a below-inflation rise to their pension next year. While he said "not all" French schools were crumbling, he promised further investment in education, adding: "If we need to do more, we'll have to see." Other challenges France is currently facing include its budget deficit, and markets pushing up borrowing costs. Lescure acknowledged that France's annual public borrowing of over 5% of its gross domestic product (GDP) was "alarming", and said "that's why we need to act now" to avoid being forced to act later. Asked about the possibility of an intervention from the eurozone's central bank, Lescure said his job was to make sure France did not have to "go there". With significant rises in French borrowing costs, especially the premium paid over its eurozone partner, Germany, Lescure acknowledged it was "more expensive" to borrow but said there was "no issue" with issuing its debt. He said that his budget "will pass" a fractious French parliament and there were "lots of different ways" to ensure that. title: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar dies at 75
description: Known for his intense performances, Patekar carved out a distinctive place in Indian cinema.
body: Patekar suffered a cardiac arrest at his home in Goa Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense performances and distinct dialogue delivery, has died at the age of 75 in Goa, his son Malhar told BBC Marathi. One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing complex, often volatile characters. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre. He was rushed to hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday. "Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency. On Thursday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi led tributes to the actor, praising Patekar's versatility and outspoken personality. Patekar portrayed characters that would "remain etched in the memory of generations", Modi wrote on X, adding that his death had left "a vast void in the artistic world". Bollywood star Akshay Kumar, who appeared alongside Patekar in the comedy film Welcome, remembered him as a rare performer whose voice, intensity and honesty could command an audience's attention. Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. His portrayal of the volatile, gritty gangster Anna won him his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award. He didn't look back after this and played many memorable characters in several films through the 1990s. The range of the characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery over his craft. His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. Then there was the villainous character of Majid Khan in Angaar, the patriotic firebrand of Tirangaa, and, most notably, Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, for which he won the national award for best actor. Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak. Born in Maharashtra in 1951, Patekar began his career in theatre before moving into films Director Prakash Jha's Rajneeti in 2010 added another dimension to his acting as his portrayal of an astute politician was delivered with perfection. The breadth of Patekar's career showcases the wide range of his work. He has played gangsters, soldiers, policemen, politicians, patriots, villains, comic characters and tragic figures, while moving between Hindi and Marathi cinema and sometimes also working behind the camera as a director and writer. His three national awards for Parinda, Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi are a testament to his career. Patekar was also an influential figure in both Marathi and Hindi theatre. Before cinema made him a familiar face, he spent years working in theatre, where he developed his gritty style of dialogue delivery and also mastered the intensity he brought to his on-screen characters. Purush and Hamidabai Chi Kothi were two of his most famous plays. Despite being successful in films, he remained active in theatre throughout his professional life. Patekar was also an influential figure in both Marathi and Hindi theatre Patekar was also known for his activism and didn't mince his words while criticising the government of the day. He was direct, and almost brazen and unapologetic, when it came to criticising ministers and their policies and that too quite publicly. Issues related to farmers were particularly close to his heart. His work moved beyond just giving statements. In 2015 he and actor Makarand Anaspure established the Naam Foundation, which has worked on farmer welfare and water conservation in Maharashtra. But his career was not without controversies. In 2018, allegations of sexual harassment made by actor Tanushree Dutta against Patekar over an alleged incident on a film set a decade earlier helped spark India's #MeToo movement. Patekar denied the allegations. In 2019, he was cleared of the charges after police said they had not found sufficient evidence against him. title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
description: Students' blockades and marches spring from real grievances – and from France's habit of settling policy on the street.
body: Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools. The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested. The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds. "Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves. There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 7 pm, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2. France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point. The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque. This video can not be played Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas on Tuesday Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries? According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools. Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay. Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries. The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system. In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too. And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks. Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law. To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else. In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées. In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff. On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994. This video can not be played Why has France suspended the use of stun grenades on protesters? Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment. The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence. French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials. The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending. The street does not always win. In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people. On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BMFTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement. Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon. Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election

title: Three people killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia airports, officials say
description: The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which mark an escalation in the conflict.
body: Houthi fighters seen in Yemen after militia group claims attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha, Saudi Arabia Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom. Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday. In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added. The attacks, which the Houthis have claimed responsibility for, mark an escalation in the renewed war between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. The two airports were attacked on 6 and 7 October, according to Gaca, which did not specify when each airport was hit. Two women, of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, were killed during the Abha airport attack, near the Yemen border, according to Gaca. Meanwhile, a male resident of Sudanese nationality was killed at King Khalid airport, it added. The country's civil aviation authority did not name who was responsible for the attacks, but Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said its armed forces had attacked both Saudi Arabia airports with ballistic missiles and drones. The Houthi military spokesperson also said the Houthis attacked Aden's International Airport in Yemen on Wednesday. The airport is a main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control and has been repeatedly targeted when fighting erupts in the country. Saree said the two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours". The civil war in Yemen has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west, seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive. That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. But Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. They also declared an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis. In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports "will not go unpunished". The spokesperson said the Saudi coalition had targeted more than 80 Houthi military sites across "governorates of Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf and Ma'rib". The Saudi-led coalition formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government. A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting". Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides since the latest Houthis' advance. The UN said on Wednesday more than 200,000 people have been displaced by the escalation. Who are the Houthis and what do they want? title: Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections
description: Lawyers for Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution after Christa Pike's botched lethal injections.
body: A death row inmate was executed by lethal injection on Wednesday evening in Texas, the first execution in the US since the failed attempt to put Christa Pike to death last week. Lawyers for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution in light of Pike's botched injections last week, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News. But courts denied their requests, and he received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was pronounced dead at 20:03 local time. Howard was convicted and sentenced to death for the 2000 murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery he committed. His lawyers had argued that because Texas planned to inject Howard with the same drug - pentobarbital - that was used on Pike, he faced the same risks. They also alleged that Texas' supply of the drug had become degraded, as Pike's lawyers have similarly argued. A court twice denied their appeals and the US Supreme Court also turned down the appeal late Wednesday. "Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys had argued, CBS reported. Howard's attorneys also asked Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, to delay the execution by 30 days so they could seek additional information about the drug used in the execution. The governor did not grant the delay. Howard was 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, who was working at a convenience store in Texas. Howard stole a carton of cigarettes and $114 from the register. Asked if he had a final statement before his execution, Howard apologized to Swartout's family, who watched from a witness room, US media report. "I wish that you accept my apology, and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days." title: Trump wants a new Camp David-like retreat at his Florida golf club
description: Trump's estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David and mark another tradition transformed by Trump.
body: President Trump gestures before boarding Marine One after a Cabinet meeting at Camp David on 31 July 2026 in Thurmont, Maryland US President Donald Trump is looking to create a presidential retreat similar to Camp David at his Florida golf club. The club would foot constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and provide free memberships to future presidents - and accommodations to visiting foreign dignitaries. "It's only about two minutes away from the airport … and they could spend the weekend there, like a retreat, like a sort of Camp David retreat," Trump said on Wednesday. If it comes to fruition, Trump's transformed golf estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David, once a Great Depression-era camp in the woods for federal employees. It would also mark another tradition transformed by Trump. A view of the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida The US president has sought to cement his legacy through changes to the White House, including gilded gold leaf accents in the Oval Office, demolition of the East Wing and construction of a ballroom. He is pushing ahead with plans to erect a massive triumphal arch elsewhere in Washington. He has hosted national security meetings and other events at Camp David, known as the president's country residence. The Camp David property - set deep in Catoctin Mountain Park in Frederick County, Maryland - was first taken over as a retreat by President Franklin Roosevelt, who nicknamed it "Shangri-La". The area is rustic, and in some ways resembles the military facility it officially is - Naval Support Facility, Thurmont. The entire facility is staffed by uniformed members of the US Navy and Marine Corps. US President Joe Biden, center, greets Fumio Kishida, Japan's prime minister, right, and Yoon Suk Yeol, South Korea's president, left, during a trilateral summit at Camp David in 2023 The secure facility is largely hidden from public view, with Marines guarding the perimeter and airspace above restricted. It is not marked on maps of the national park, even if its location is known to locals. Press is only very rarely allowed on the grounds - meaning that photography of the wood and stone cabins and lodges that make up most of the facility are tightly controlled. On a recent visit by the BBC, for example, reporters in the White House press pool were under strict instructions to avoid taking images in unauthorized areas or providing details on the camp's layout. Then-US President Barack Obama meets with Eurozone leaders on the Laurel Cabin patio during the G8 Summit in 2012 at Camp David Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, on the other hand, is connected to the rest of the city by ample roadways, some of which are lined with supporters or protesters when the president is there. The 27-hole golf course and club bills itself as having "a lively social scene" and fine dining - and is visited often by Trump's political allies during his many weekends in Florida. It includes a luxurious clubhouse, a gift store and hosts frequent social events for members. The president's argument that the area is "secure" is notable. In recent months, Trump has frequently used national security and safety arguments to justify various projects in Washington DC, including his White House ballroom project the planned Triumphal Arch. Asked by reporters if he would call the new presidential retreat at his golf club "Camp Donald", Trump replied, "Well, it's already called Trump International. It's one of the best golf courses in the world." He said among advantages is the absence of high buildings and homes looming "so you don't have ... people hiding behind windows". "They can get maximum safety," the president said. "It's a great idea and it'll be used a lot." The entrance driveway at Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County, Florida Trump said at the Oval Office on Wednesday that Secret Service officials first suggested the idea of using the golf club as a presidential retreat, and that he thinks it is "a great idea". "It's about as safe as they could possibly get," he said. The BBC has contacted the Secret Service for comment. A letter dated 3 September from the golf course's attorney to the county commission in Florida said Trump offered to deem the club as a "U.S. Presidential Golf Course" for presidents and visiting heads of state, according to USA TODAY's Palm Beach Post. The letter, obtained by the local outlet, states that the golf club would provide access to all its facilities at "no cost to the federal government" and provide free membership to future presidents. The golf club would front constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and local residents, according to the letter. "This wouldn't be for me," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday. "This would be for all future presidents." title: AI chip boom pushes Samsung profits to record $80bn
description: The tech giant is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.
body: Samsung is also one of the world's biggest smartphone makers Samsung Electronics says it expects a nine-fold surge in its quarterly profits compared with a year earlier, driven by surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres. The tech giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months to the end of September will jump to 107.4tn won (£61bn; $80bn), its fourth quarter in a row of record earnings. Samsung is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron in the US, which produce chips crucial for AI firms like Nvidia. Samsung, which makes the Galaxy Fold and S26 smartphones, is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August. The firm's full third-quarter earnings will be released at the end of October. Major South Korean companies tend to release previews of their earnings to advise investors ahead of more detailed reports. There has been huge global demand for computer chips that power AI development, helping to lift the earnings and shares of manufacturers linked to the technology. The surge in demand in recent years has resulted in a shortage of semiconductors globally, pushing up sales for firms like Samsung, with its stock market valuation crossing $1tn (£757bn) earlier this year. Investment in the industry has surged, with US tech giants including Google, Amazon and Meta pledging to pour more than $650bn into AI projects this year. In June, South Korea unveiled plans for at least $880bn in projects led by Samsung and SK Hynix to build out the country's chip manufacturing capabilities in the coming years. Rival Asian firms in Japan, China and Taiwan are also investing heavily in chip plants as demand for AI soars. A chip shortage driven by surging demand has led firms including Samsung to raise prices, making products such as smartphones and computers more expensive. title: The Papers: 'Kemi's family home pledge' and 'Badenoch invokes core Tory values'
description: Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch's speech at the Tory conference dominates Thursday's papers.
body: Most of Thursday's papers lead with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's speech at her party's autumn conference. The Daily Mail focuses on what it calls "Kemi's family home pledge", highlighting her promises of "no stamp duty... no mansion tax ... [and] no inheritance tax". Her speech "electrified" the Conservative Party at the conference, the paper says The Metro similarly headlines on "Kemi's no inheritance tax on homes pledge", which the Tory leader says will allow couples to "leave £1m tax-free to loved ones". It's part of a bid to "woo voters", it adds The Independent carries a photo of Badenoch and her husband arm-in-arm at the conference, saying the Tory leader "bets the family home to win back voters". The paper adds that the inheritance tax pledge comes as she "pitches for [the] middle-close vote" The Daily Express also leads on the Tories' inheritance tax pledge, quoting Badenoch as saying "nobody will ever pay death tax on family homes". It says the tax is "hated" and describes Badenoch's speech as "rousing", saying she has pitched the Tories as a "no nonsense" party The Financial Times says "Badenoch invokes core Tory values" with her inheritance tax pledges, calling it a "new wave" for the Conservatives. The story is accompanied by a large photograph of Badenoch smiling and waving, as she stands behind the podium to deliver her speech. Meanwhile, the paper leads on what it calls a fear of "tax rises and spending cuts" as the Iran war "blows £12bn hole in [Chancellor John] Healey's room for maoeuvre" "We're ready for the fight" is the Telegraph's headline, accompanied by a photo of a grinning Badenoch alongside her husband Hamish. Meanwhile, the paper says Prime Minister Andy Burnham is "ready to raise tariffs on China to get closer to EU", specifically targeting Chinese electric cars The Times also headlines with Badenoch's speech, echoing her promise that the "Tories 'will make you better off'." Elsewhere on the front page, the paper says Israel is set "to close UK consulate as relationship hits a new low". That, it says, is "despite British efforts to reach an agreement to prevent the closure" The Daily Mirror reports on Reform UK's internal investigation that said the party did not breach electoral law when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party. "Reform not dodgy, says Reform" is the headline on the Mirror's front page. The Metropolitan Police is currently carrying out a separate criminal investigation into Reform, over allegations it broke foreign funding laws The i leads with the publication of a report on support for people with ADHD, with the paper saying it will conclude that "young people should get ADHD help even without diagnosis". The full independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism "is expected to be published within days", the paper adds "Labour's flagship plans to reform special education in England are at risk of unravelling", according to the Guardian. The paper says "parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes", citing analysis from the Institute for Government think tank The Daily Star covers the trial of Katie Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler, who is accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault against a 13-year-old girl. Hayler denies all the charges Meanwhile, the Sun says a man who travelled to the UK in a small boat had been given a taxpayer-funded home shortly before committing a sexual offence. He has been remanded into custody and will be sentenced next month, the paper adds Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Cornell rape case accuser has received ‘threats’, attorney tells BBC Newsnight
description: Thomas Giuffra is representing a woman, known in legal documents as Jane Doe, who alleges she was raped at a frat house on campus in 2024.
body: This video can not be played The lawyer for the woman who alleges she was raped at a Cornell University fraternity house says both he and his client have received death threats following the publicity of the case. Thomas Giuffra is representing a woman, known in legal documents as Jane Doe, who alleges she was raped at a frat house on campus in 2024. No criminal charges were initially filed in connection with the allegations. The case has since been reopened following a civil lawsuit filed by Doe. Giuffra spoke to BBC Newsnight about recent developments in the case and Donald Trump's recent comments about it. Cornell rape case accuser has received ‘threats’, attorney tells BBC Newsnight. title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
description: A search for forecourts will now display their pricing, using the government's Fuel Finder scheme.
body: The prices will be displayed when people search for fuel, as well as listed underneath descriptions of forecourts Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar. From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme. It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them. It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time, which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross". There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom. Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96. The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK. Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones. Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable. "At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices. "There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe." She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time. Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date. "Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said. The Retail Motor Industry Federation, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying. Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year. title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
description: The skipper who led India to the historic 2025 World Cup win has stepped down from her role in all three formats.
body: Harmanpreet Kaur is stepping down as the captain of the India women's cricket team When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India. India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan. That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later. Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport. Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats. Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless. Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience. The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana. In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer. Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago. Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world. Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped. Harmanpreet led the India women's team to a famous World Cup win in 2025 Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains. Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on. Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post. "I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote. "Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again. "Captaincy ends, the journey continues." Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future. In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision. The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket. Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones. Harmanpreet (left) has now passed the captaincy baton to Smriti Mandhana (right) Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age. Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai. The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development. She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since. An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills. Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome. That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name. Harmanpreet made her debut in the India women's cricket team in 2009 The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history. Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Aust

title: Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
description: Wicknell Chivayo divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
body: Wicknell Chivayo, who had a fleet of personalised luxury cars, loved white Rolls-Royces Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death. He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes. He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving. Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes. His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality. But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank. "He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people. He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders. Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures. Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell. Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts. "He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said. Wicknell Chivayo's death last week has dominated conversation in Zimbabwe Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10. His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis. In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended. Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts. He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation. In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career. Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid. A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment. Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle. Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day. Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it. As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power. In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo. Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company. His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa. But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF. He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term. title: New York court hears arguments in ongoing 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia
description: The families allege that men with links to the Saudi government helped those who carried out the 2001 attacks, something the country denies.
body: Saudi government employee, Omar al-Bayoumi, seen in February 2000 The Court of Appeals in New York has heard arguments from both lawyers for families of 9/11 victims and the government of Saudi Arabia as it decides whether the families' long-running legal case against the Middle Eastern country can move to trial. Almost 3,000 people were killed on 11 September 2001 after hijackers seized four US passenger jets and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon, and a Pennsylvania field, following resistance from passengers. The families allege that a Saudi government employee, Omar al-Bayoumi, knowingly supported two of the hijackers and that he was working with a network of officials linked to the Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs. Thousands of people were killed on 11 September 2001 after hijackers seized US passenger jets and crashed them into two New York skyscrapers Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Arabia has said that any allegation that it or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false. The Kingdom has argued that, as a foreign sovereign state, it has immunity from prosecution in US courts. The families, who first filed the lawsuit in 2002, spent several years lobbying US Congress to pass an amendment to the foreign sovereign immunity law to allow the case to go ahead. In 2016, Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), which allows civil claims against a foreign state or official for injuries, death, or damages from an act of international terrorism. In August 2025, the Manhattan District Court ruled that the 9/11 families had presented enough evidence to meet the terms of the act and the case was allowed to proceed towards a trial. Saudi Arabia on Wednesday asked the Court of Appeals to reverse that decision. Counsel Gregory Rapawy argued core issues of fact – including the central question of the nature of Bayoumi's employment by the Saudi state – had not been decided and needed to be done so before the country could be stripped of immunity. 9/11 families' lawyer Gavin Simpson argued that the District Court had already found that Bayoumi's actions "were not just acts of a good Samaritan or an innocent participant". "He was, in fact, following Saudi Arabia's instructions when assisting the hijackers," said Simpson, and that these were points that Saudi Arabia had "failed to rebut." One option the judges seemed to wrestle with was whether to send the case back to the district court to make more concrete findings, which could involve taking testimony from live witnesses. Asked by Judge Guido Calabresi which witnesses Saudi Arabia could call in that eventuality, Rapawy suggested that if the issue ultimately came down to Bayoumi's credibility, "we would have to see" if he could be called to testify. As he drew the hearing to a close, Judge William Nardini said "it's a difficult case, and we will take it under advisement", meaning that the panel would issue a ruling at a future date. Speaking outside the courthouse, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the World Trade Center, told the BBC she felt positive about the hearing. "25 years is an extraordinary time to go without accountability and justice for the murder of your loved one. What we hope is that the judges will uphold [District Court] Judge Daniels' decision and move to a trial." title: What independence could mean for oil-rich Alberta's economy
description: Albertans vote this month on staying in Canada or moving ahead to a binding independence referendum.
body: Albertans will vote on 19 October whether to hold an independence referendum in the future For Alberta independence supporter Keith Wilson, the western Canadian province is in a league of its own. With its wealth of rich oil and gas reserves, a significant agricultural sector and a young and skilled workforce, its economy is one to be reckoned with, says Wilson. The province will hold a referendum on 19 October, giving residents two options: vote to stay in Canada, or vote to move ahead with a formal binding referendum on independence at a later date. The vote, despite not being a cut and dry "stay or leave", still stands to be among the most consequential in recent Canadian history, and a significant test of national unity. One key issue has become central to the debate: Would Alberta be richer if it were to become an independent country? The answer for Wilson is yes. "Alberta's economy is unique. is fundamentally different than the rest of Canada's - we have the people, the institutions, the infrastructure to excel," he says. Alberta separatists have long argued that the province has been short-changed by being part of Canada, and that more of the oil and gas wealth would be kept within its borders instead of being shared with Ottawa, delivering it tens of billions in savings. But many disagree with their accounting. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who opposes independence, predicts a more sober outcome. She says the province could risk paying C$400bn ($283bn; £213bn) in transition costs alone, while bleeding billions more in lost investments and trade due to the political upheaval. A report commissioned, external by her government released earlier this month calculated the costs of separation as between C$50bn and C$170bn over five years - and a highly unpredictable outlook over the long term. The report cautions that the to-do list for a newly independent Alberta would be long and costly. It would have to set up agencies to manage taxes and national security, develop its own constitution, legal and court systems, and pension plans, and negotiate the division of federal assets like national parks and military bases. At Canada's biggest rodeo, the starting gun is fired in the fight over Alberta separation Alberta will vote on whether to remain part of Canada. What now? Lennie Kaplan, a former finance official in Alberta, says the province would be expected to take on a share of Canada's national debt, among many other fiscal challenges and responsibilities. A report on Alberta independence by the CanadaWest Foundation, external, a non-profit Alberta-based think tank, estimates that the province could be stuck with additional debt ranging from C$258bn to C$333bn. With a projected hit to Alberta's GDP and the additional costs, the report estimates separation could hit Albertans' bottom line and reduce their disposable income by 5.8% on average. "Why do we have to create all this uncertainty that might impact and impair the province's fiscal position going forward? Why wouldn't we just work within Canada to address these issues?" Kaplan asks. Opinion polling indicates that around 20% to 25% of Albertans plan to vote in favour of moving ahead with a binding separation referendum, with higher support among younger, rural and conservative voters. Behind the separatist push is the belief that Alberta is misunderstood and overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa. For decades, that sentiment fuelled a sense of "western alienation" in the prairie province. Once a fringe movement, a number of factors pushed it to the forefront of Alberta politics. There was anger over environmental and political pushback that killed proposed pipelines from landlocked Alberta to coastal waters. A decade of Liberal government in Ottawa has also caused frustration in reliably conservative Alberta. And, in addition, there is also leftover distrust of the federal government over what some Albertans saw as excessive lockdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic. Over the past year, separatist organisers held townhalls across the province to gauge interest from the public. They then launched a citizen-led petition to separate earlier this year, which got more than 300,000 signatures. Smith, the premier, decided earlier this year she would authorise a vote. Alberta is home to Canada's oil and gas sector, with oil reserves estimated to be the fourth-largest in the world. Crude oil is by far Canada's most profitable commodity, accounting for C$142bn in export value in 2025 alone. Most of it is sold to refineries in the US. The province has the highest GDP per capita in the country, and it contributes billions a year to the federal tax pool because of its strong economy. It has not received any "equalisation" payments - money that so-called "have not", or less wealthy, provinces receive from the federal government - since 1965. Calculations by Tegan Hill and Nathaniel Li, economists at the Fraser Institute think tank, show that Alberta's total net contribution to Ottawa since 2007 has been C$322bn, or an average of around $17bn per year. "That's nearly four times that of British Columbia, more than four times Ontario," Hill tells the BBC. "The other seven provinces were net recipients, meaning Ottawa spent or transferred more money to those provinces than it collected." Hill explains that the amount Alberta contributes to the rest of Canada is one of the main frustrations cited by those in favour of separation. The sentiment, she says, is that: "We're paying to support these other provinces, and if we just went our own way, we could keep all that wealth for ourselves." title: We spent thousands on a Tui river cruise but ended up on coach trips
description: Passengers have described their anger after their itineraries changed to involve hours spent on coach trips instead.
body: Richard Pearson says he barely got to experience any river cruising on his holiday, but spent hours on coaches Passengers who paid thousands of pounds for European river cruises with Tui have described their anger after their itineraries changed to involve hours spent on coach trips instead. Several have told the BBC they believe they should get some money back, but have been offered no refund. Tui apologised and blamed low water levels on the Danube, adding that customers continued their holidays on amended itineraries under its standard booking conditions. It follows previous complaints about conditions on board two of Tui's river vessels. Richard Pearson took this photo of one of the coach journeys he had not expected as part of his river cruise Those who contacted the BBC include Richard Pearson from Lincolnshire, whose week-long holiday began on 21 September. Upon arrival in Budapest, he says passengers were told their vessel, Isla, was in Vienna and could not get to them, so they were being put up in a hotel instead, which he describes as "average". The next day involved a four-hour coach journey to reach the ship. The vessel then sailed overnight - meaning no chance to take in the scenery - to Krems. It then stayed there for a few days, with passengers bussed on day trips to locations between 45 minutes and two hours away. The return sailing to Vienna was also in the dark. The one time there was a "scenic sail" during the day, it was a round trip back to Krems which started early in the morning. Richard says the food and the staff on board Isla were excellent, but overall the experience was not what he expected when he booked the trip - especially the schedule. He worked out that "we spent 14 to 15 hours of that holiday on a coach trip, plus time wasted waiting for coaches". Richard says the reason people were given for the changes of plan was "circumstances beyond [Tui's] control because of the low water levels". "[But] the main thing for us was it wasn't relaxing. It wasn't a river cruise, it was a little bit of sailing, a floating hotel with coach transfers." If they had been offered a refund, Richard and his partner would have not gone. He is now contacting Tui to complain and request some of their £3,300 back. Sue Crosby says she and her husband didn't want to go on a tour on coaches every day Sue Crosby and her husband booked on Isla, with the holiday starting on 14 September - her 70th birthday. She had a similar experience and told the BBC: "We feel as though we've been had." A revised itinerary was sent a few days before departure, making clear there would be multiple coach trips on offer due to low water levels on the Danube. The couple didn't want to do this and so asked for a refund. But after being told no refund was possible, they travelled "reluctantly". Sue Crosby says there was significantly less river cruising time on her holiday than expected when she booked Even during the trip, the schedule changed further. It wasn't the river levels themselves that frustrated Sue. "It's how they handled it, and the fact they're still advertising the holidays now." She also describes the food and the people on the ship as great. However, her complaint is "about the drastic change of itinerary... and the fact we weren't able to get a full refund". Sue says there were only two half days of sailing where people could actually experience a river cruise. "We didn't want to go on a tour on coaches every day." David Mallon and a group of five others were due to travel on 21 September. But they decided the new itinerary presented to them a few days before departure was so different from what they had booked that they didn't want to go. "What they were planning to give us was not a cruise but a glorified coach trip," says David. One reason for not wanting to accept the new plan was that a member of the group was meant to be avoiding long periods of sitting down - such as coach journeys - for health reasons. With no offer of a refund, the group booked a last-minute holiday to Kos instead and decided to try and claim money back on their return. "We don't blame Tui for the water levels, but it's the way they've handled the consequences of that," David says. He has now submitted a complaint to Tui and says he will take his quest for a refund to the small claims court if necessary. The BBC contacted Tui River Cruises about passengers' unhappiness with the extensive itinerary changes and the fact they were not offered any refund. In a statement, a spokesperson said: "Extreme heat across Europe this summer caused low water levels on the Danube, affecting river cruise operators across the region. We review every sailing individually with our nautical partners. "Customers on the Tui Isla departures on 14 and 21 September were sent revised itineraries before travelling. Where the ship couldn't sail sections of the river, we arranged coach transfers, hotel stays and adjusted travel arrangements to minimise transfer times so customers could still visit destinations, including Budapest, Vienna and Bratislava. "We reviewed the revised arrangements carefully and customers continued their holiday on the amended itinerary under our standard booking conditions. While customers were still able to visit the key destinations on their itinerary, we're sorry some did not get the river cruise experience they had anticipated." title: Burnham to hold security talks with German chancellor in Berlin
description: Downing Street said deeper co-operation in the face of rising hybrid threats from Russia would be high on the agenda during Burnham's first official visit to Germany.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet his German counterpart Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Friday Prime Minister Andy Burnham will hold talks on tackling cyber-security threats and sabotage with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday. Downing Street said deeper co-operation in the face of rising hybrid threats from Russia would be high on the agenda during Burnham's first official visit to Germany. Intelligence services in both countries have warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The Berlin talks come days after Burnham told the Labour Party's conference he wanted to set out options for a closer relationship with the EU later this year, including the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc. A German government spokesman has said any future in-out referendum would be primarily a question for Britain, but that Berlin supports stronger ties between the UK and the EU. Burnham is set to be greeted with military honours at the German capital's Chancellery ahead of his first face-to-face meeting with the chancellor. On Thursday, the two leaders will formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity through deeper cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and growth. Speaking ahead of the visit, Burnham said the UK and Germany were "joining forces to find, expose and disrupt" threats. He continued: "Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat. "They reach into people's homes and workplaces, and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided." The talks come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny. Burnham replaced Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in July after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory. Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and following setbacks in regional elections. Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future. The security talks also come in a week when questions have been raised about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a former spy chief on suspicion of espionage. August Hanning has been accused of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says. He ran the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant. title: Hedgehog among four chosen animals to feature on your new banknotes
description: The decision comes after nearly half a million people cast their votes from a shortlist of 18 creatures.
body: Banknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money. The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote. The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said. Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians. "We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier. A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which were put forward to public nominations. Respondents were invited to select up to six. More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes. The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba). The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category. The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal. The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline. The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of the Royal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively. Mock-ups of the new Bank of England banknotes featuring all four winners Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes. Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years. He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch. "We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said. Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring on notes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland, external. This video can not be played Churchill's granddaughter happy with his picture being replaced on the £5 note Yet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history. On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing. The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do". The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time. title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
description: British people need more incentives to invest in big firms listed in the UK, Dame Julia Hoggett, boss of the London Stock Exchange, says.
body: This video can not be played Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the past The UK needs to do more back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC. Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth. Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market, are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors. The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations. "If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss podcast. "We need to take the handbrake off." The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion. Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries. But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange, travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York. Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled. Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised. It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns. "We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said. There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added. But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said. "We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit." Big Boss Interview: LSE's Dame Julia Hoggett The boss of the London Stock Exchange speaks to the BBC about the attraction of the UK as a place for companies to list. However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks. She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax, external Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks. She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016. Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange. It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow. The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month. "As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said. title: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
description: The new charges are expected to accuse Maduro and his wife of playing a role in the torture of Americans in Venezuelan prisons, US media reports.
body: Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported. The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS. US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny. The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan ​which brought the charges. Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports. Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges. Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York. The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027. The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term. Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups. They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States". Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves. He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.
