title: What could happen next in Christa Pike's case?
description: Christa Pike is conscious after surviving a botched lethal injection, leading many to wonder if the state of Tennessee will try again to execute her.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Christa Pike’s "unprecedented" recovery after failed execution The botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory. After state officials administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, Pike survived and was transported to a nearby hospital, where she was intubated. Six days later, her lawyers announced she was "conscious and speaking". Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into what went wrong at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville and suspended all executions for the rest of the year. The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area. Doctor Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defence team, says he suspects the deadly chemical spread under her skin instead of her bloodstream, and, because of the the large dose, it could take days or even weeks for a clear picture of her health to emerge. At a hearing on Wednesday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court. Pike's lawyers are seeking to have Pike's death sentence commuted to a lesser punishment of life in prison without parole. Lee, who has the power to pardon Pike or commute her sentence, has not indicated what the state will do in her case. The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next. The Tennessee Department of Correction could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment. "For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said. Johnson said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of the state’s lethal injection protocol. Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Johnson called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition. Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure. Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Johnson said. But Johnson, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method. This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature. Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair." Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging". Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws. She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said. Given Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there is a scenario where the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method. It is also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained. Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage. Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment. Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection. That means it will likely take a while for any movement in Pike's case. "At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Johnson said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied. Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered. "If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said. There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state. The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed. The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes. How did Christa Pike survive two lethal injections - and what happens now? title: Watchdog and critics raise concerns over reliability of NHS medical records
description: Victims of disgraced brain surgeon Sam Eljamel have complained of "significant gaps" in their records and said they often do not reflect the reality of their care.
body: Patients operated on by brain surgeon Sam Eljamel will raise the issue of inaccurate or missing medical records during the ongoing public inquiry into the disgraced medic Concerns have been raised about the reliability of the NHS medical records systems used in Scotland. Their accuracy has been questioned by the public services watchdog and critics warned there were doubts about their reliability in safety investigations and court cases. Victims of disgraced brain surgeon Sam Eljamel have complained of "significant gaps" in their records and said they often do not reflect the reality of their care. The Scottish government said it took the concerns raised seriously and was engaging with health boards over ways to improve the reliability of patient records. There are millions of patient records in Scotland, which contain information about your health, care and treatment. When things go wrong they are relied upon for investigations and legal challenges. However, there is no central NHS system where these records are kept and a number of concerns about their accuracy have been raised in recent years. The long-running Scottish Hospitals Inquiry's probe into patient safety issues at Glasgow's Queen Elizabeth University Hospital campus has heard concerns about missing medical records and about how information was recorded. The issue of accurate medical records will also feature heavily in the recently started public inquiry into the actions of Eljamel at Dundee's Ninewells Hospital. Alan Ogilvie said many patients operated on by Eljamel have major concerns about the accuracy of their medical records Alan Ogilvie, who was operated on by Eljamel in 1995, is spokesman for the Patients Action Group which campaigned for the inquiry. Ogilvie said many of those affected had found their official medical records "often don't match their lived reality". He added: "We see significant gaps where complications occurred, and narratives that seem massaged to suit the clinician's reputation rather than the patient's history. "When the 'official' computer record says one thing, but our own letters and memories prove another, you have to ask: Is the system there to record the truth, or to protect the institution? "If we cannot trust the records from the past, how can we trust the lessons they claim to be learning for the future?" The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO) has often raised the issue of accurate medical records. Last month, NHS Lothian was criticised by the watchdog for not carrying out a Significant Adverse Event Review into the death of a patient from a blood infection at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh. The SPSO found "concerning" gaps or incomplete nursing records for the patient, external. These included four occasions where it said in the clinical notes that the doctor in charge had asked for a microbiology report - but there was no evidence of such a report in the patient's clinical records. The sharing of information from patient records between NHS boards is the focus of an ongoing fatal accident inquiry (FAI) into the death of two-month-old Michael Wilson at the Royal Aberdeen Children's Hospital. The inquiry has heard from a doctor who said he would have advised against operating on Michael if he had known, from the child's medical records, about an inherited heart condition. It had been the suspected cause of death of Michael's older brother in Glasgow two years previously. At an earlier hearing the Press and Journal reported that Sheriff Christine McCrossan said: "It's almost verging into a public inquiry situation - something as fundamental as the medical records situation in the country. "These boards are inde­pend­ent and they set up com­puter sys­tems that don't seem to talk to each other." Labour MSP Daniel Johnson said important questions need to be answered Labour MSP Daniel Johnson said medical records were an invaluable resource for medics. "But at the point they are being relied upon by other public agencies, including the Crown Office, we need absolute clarity about their reliability," he added. "Important questions need to be answered about how the Crown Office, the Central Legal Office and other publicly funded bodies assess the reliability of patient medical records and the user protocols which support their use." A Scottish government spokesperson said: "We recognise that accurate, complete and accessible patient records are essential to safe care, continuity of treatment and effective investigation of adverse events. "NHS boards are responsible for the electronic patient record systems they operate and for ensuring that clinical information is accurate, secure, accessible and appropriately governed." The added a range of assurance mechanisms to support the reliability of patient record systems were used including national standards and data quality controls. The spokesperson said: "We take the concerns raised from recent inquiries seriously and continue to engage with boards to consider findings and any recommendations for improving the reliability of patient records to support safe and effective care." title: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after failed execution, lawyers say
description: Lawyers say the convicted killer was surprised to have survived and remained "shackled" to her hospital bed.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we know about Christa Pike’s "unprecedented" recovery after failed execution A lawyer for convicted murderer Christa Pike says that she woke up in hospital "angry and confused" after she survived a botched execution attempt last week. Her first words were to ask "Where am I?" and "Who are you?", her lawyer Randy Spivey recalled during a news conference. Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September in Tennessee. Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented, and that no other US inmate has survived a lethal injection from executioners. A court on Wednesday ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care and is being restrained at her hands and feet in her hospital bed, her lawyers said at the news conference after a court hearing on Wednesday. Spivey said that her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead, and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment. However, in a "shock to everyone", she began to talk on Tuesday, while recalling only limited details about the execution attempt. Pike, he said, had helped the execution team find a vein in her arm, and she was kind and polite while she was being injected. Then she woke up in a hospital with a tube down her throat and people she didn't know. Both of her arms, he said, are now "tremendously swollen". "We don't know the toll all of this will take" on her mental health, Spivey said, noting how she was left "angry and confused" by the ordeal. He added that she also has a blood clot in one of her arms, pneumonia, and is not able to swallow. Pike is believed to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection. After it became clear Pike would not die, following two rounds of the drug pentobarbital, she was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical. Earlier on Wednesday, lawyers appeared before a judge for an emergency hearing, where her team requested that all evidence from the botched execution be preserved. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state. Luke Ihnen, one of Pike's lawyers, began by describing the "roadblocks" that have made it challenging to communicate with his client. "Up until yesterday our client was unconscious, and unable to communicate," he told Judge Chancellor I'Ashea Myles. Pike is now "speaking limitedly", he said. Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers called attention to the "unusual procedural position here", prompting agreement from the judge. He argued that an emergency motion was unnecessary because the state is already compelled to preserve evidence. Still, Judge Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels. The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt. The judge agreed when a state lawyer called the situation 'unusual' She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case. Asked by the judge whether the state intended to reschedule execution for Pike, Ayers said he did not know the answer. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief said he is resigning after the failed execution. Ihnen asked the judge to allow Pike access to a phone so she can call her lawyers, and they can have "continuous liberal access to Ms Pike". He said they were kept waiting for over two hours during a recent attempt to visit her in hospital. This video can not be played How widely used is the death penalty in the US? Ihnen added that Tennessee prison officials are keeping her "shackled" to her hospital bed, despite requests from medical staff that the handcuffs be removed. Her lawyer also requested that the Tennessee Department of Corrections be required to notify his team 48 hours before she is transferred from the hospital to any state hospital or other government-run facility. Ayers (left) argued the case for the state, while Ihnen (far right) represented Pike Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens. Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison. title: Cancer survivor with a stoma 'made to feel like a criminal' at airports
description: Paul Scanlon says airport travel can be "degrading and humiliating" for people with stomas.
body: Paul Scanlon says his treatment at airports makes him reluctant to use them, so he has chosen a cruise for his next holiday A cancer survivor said he was screamed at by airport security staff and "made to feel like a criminal" after trying to retrieve his stoma supplies from his luggage. Paul Scanlon, from Cardiff, has had a stoma for nearly four years after being diagnosed with stage three bowel cancer, external and said he had suffered "degrading" and "humiliating" treatment at UK airports. Now, a charity wants better training for airport staff so people with stomas are treated with "dignity" and "respect". The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said airports must ensure staff have disability awareness training and that security officers were expected to treat people in a "sensitive and understanding" way. Travel has always been something 57-year-old Paul has enjoyed - even more so since his diagnosis. "When you've gone through what we've gone through over the last four years, it makes you really appreciate that you can go away," he said. Paul was initially reluctant to have a stoma - an opening in the stomach , externalthat allows waste to leave the body and into a bag - after having his large bowel removed due to the size of his tumours. "It's having your bum on your belly and it's not for the faint-hearted, but it's a lifesaver," he said. "I don't know if you 100% come to terms with it. You end up just living with it." What Paul did not expect to have to come to terms with was hostility at airports. Paul Scanlon had a stoma fitted after an operation for bowel cancer Paul said he was once told by security to remove his stoma bag at a UK airport - something he is unable to do. His most recent experience was at Cardiff Airport while travelling on holiday with his wife Deborah, and their friends. He said he was "screamed" at after trying to remove his bag of stoma supplies from the conveyor belt after security screening. "This very large gentleman started shouting and screaming: 'You can't touch that bag, leave it alone, get away'. "He kept walking towards me, shouting and screaming. He and his colleague escorted me, one flank to either side, into an interview room where I was searched. "Everyone can see going through that airport. Anyone can see. You're just made to feel like a criminal." Paul said he was "mortified" and, while understanding the need to keep everyone safe, felt there was a lack of "dignity, compassion and empathy". Paul Scanlon has always loved travel, but has encountered problems since having a stoma During the incident, Deborah and their friends were also left waiting without any explanation of where he had been taken. "If you're in that job, you should be looking at treating people with respect," he said. Cardiff Airport said, when additional screening was required, passengers can be offered a private search room "to help ensure the process is carried out with dignity and discretion". It also said its teams had done training "to help them better understand the experiences of people living with a stoma and ensure any necessary screening is carried out sensitively, respectfully and appropriately". A spokesperson said that while the company did not comment on individual cases, anyone unhappy with an experience was encouraged to contact the airport so it can review what happened. Lisa Barker says airport security can have a "psychological impact" on people with stomas These experiences have left Paul reluctant to travel through airports. "It's completely changed my thought process of going on holiday. I don't want to fly," he said. His next holiday will be a cruise leaving from Southampton, allowing him to avoid the stress he associates with flying. "I've got next year to get through and I'll be hopefully cancer free. You know, we've got loads of life left in us and we still want to go on holiday." Paul's experience is not unique, according to the Ileostomy and Internal Pouch Association (IA). It has a survey open which has received 70 responses and identified 16 different UK airports where people have reported negative stoma-related incidents. IA chief executive officer Lisa Barker said people were being forced to make a choice between living with a stoma and getting to travel, and that airport security procedures caused "a lot of stress and anxiety". The organisation offers a free service providing travel certificates explaining a person's condition which can be shown to airport staff, but Lisa wants that information translated into better understanding. "What we want is that once that information is shared, the knowledge about that then enables them to have a dignified process," she said. Emma Greenwood is an internal pouch nurse specialist and has a stoma - she said she had faced similar problems at airports. "If you're spoken to abruptly or fairly aggressively in some situations, it can naturally be quite upsetting and it can have a negative impact on your holiday," she said. Emma said people with pouches could be self-conscious and sensitive and may be particularly concerned about being embarrassed during security checks. "It's a quick win to be kind to someone," she said. "It's not a massive adjustment that the majority of people are asking for." The CAA said it placed obligations on airports "to ensure their staff receive disability awareness training" and expected security officers to engage with passengers in "a sensitive and understanding manner". Kat Watkins says people with different types of disabilities face problems while travelling Disability Wales said the issue was not limited to people with stomas. Access to politics policy officer Kat Watkins, who has brittle bone disease, said she had experienced several negative incidents including damage to her wheelchair and being left on the plane for an hour while waiting for assistance. title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
description: Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years in September.
body: Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her flat in Madrid two weeks ago An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union. Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases. The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital. "We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country". Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us". Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction. Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020). The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension. Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week. That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend. Protesters gathered at one of Madrid's main squares, Puerta del Sol, following Absacal's death Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process." It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high". "Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours,'" it said. In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs." "All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own." Protesters gathered at one of Madrid's main squares, Puerta del Sol, following the announcement of Abascal's death. The site has become a protest encampment for protesters over the last two weeks. Photos show demonstrators lighting candles and holding posters of Maricarmen at the housing protest camp on Wednesday evening. Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms. The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain. On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress. The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further. Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms. Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems. Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government. title: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
description: The research found that important guardrails for teens using ChatGPT often failed.
body: Young people's use of internet platforms like ChatGPT has come under increased scrutiny. OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short. The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use. On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity. However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail. When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens, external, it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents". Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive." The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating. OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work. In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder. The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases. But Common Sense Media's new research, external determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable. An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete." "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said. While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide. The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents. It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert. In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found. The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour. "ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said. The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common. This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companies like Meta, TikTok and others responsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms. OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT. The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT. OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facing several lawsuits over the incident. title: Chinese runner dropped by sponsor after riding bike during marathon
description: Sun Yuanyuan was seemingly pictured on the back of another person's bike during part of the Berlin Marathon.
body: The influencer was seen riding a bike during the Berlin Marathon, which took place at the end of September A Chinese fitness influencer has been dropped by her sponsor after she apologised for riding a bicycle during the Berlin marathon. Sun Yuanyuan, known as Abeeeer on Chinese social media, had claimed a personal best during the event which was held in September. But an Instagram page dedicated to monitoring inaccurate or misleading race times posted by influencers published a picture which appeared to show Sun on a bicycle between the 35km and and 40km marks. Sun apologised and admitted to "breaking the rules". Brooks, the running shoe company, has ended its sponsorship deal with her and her finish time has been disqualified by the marathon organisers. An Instagram account calling itself the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) posted a photo of Sun apparently on the back of a bike being ridden by another person during the marathon. The page also posted a grid of Sun's "splits" - which are the times taken to complete different 5km segments of the race. The grid appears to show that she sped up between the 35 and 40km marks, when she was allegedly on the bike. Sun posted an apology on the Chinese social media platform Rednote, which was shared by OMTIU, admitting that she had broken the rules. She wrote: "I won't make any excuses for this behaviour. "I was feeling physically unwell on the course, [but] that is absolutely not an excuse for breaking the rules. "My attempt to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the fairness of the competition and the spirit of the marathon." Sun, who has 520,000 followers on Rednote, also said she "deliberately concealed" her actions, adding: "I feel deeply guilty about this." Brooks confirmed to BBC News that it had dropped Sun. A company statement said: "Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition. "After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual and publicly addressed the matter." OMTIU was set up to highlight "the growing trend of GPS-based fabrication, selective Strava displays and false PR claims" among marathon runners, particularly fitness influencers. Strava is a fitness tracking app. The page's mission statement says: "We exist to protect the integrity of the sport by ensuring that the times athletes share publicly reflect the times they actually ran." Its Instagram bio describes it as "satire". BBC News has contacted the Berlin Marathon for comment. title: Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims three years after deadly Hamas raid
description: Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attack that sparked the devastating Gaza war.
body: A man comforts a woman at the fountain at Dizengoff Square on Wednesday Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza. Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage. "The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day. In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN. Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas-led attacks grapple with how to rebuild Violence has continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed almost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire. On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack. Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid. Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive. Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose 21-year-old daughter Adi was shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the site was "dystopic, unimaginable". At the Nova festival, 378 people were killed, with 44 more taken hostage "Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12. He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival. Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killed in captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here." Residents and relatives pay tribute beside graves in Kfar Aza, Israel Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October. Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened. "This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October." A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid. Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others". In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October. "We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added. At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day. The water of the fountain at Dizengoff Square in Tel Aviv was stained red to symbolise blood In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack. The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall. Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning. They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu. Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure. The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him. Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement. "They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth." This video can not be played Dalit Ram Aharon and her husband Achi say they want to move back to Nir Oz "in the memory" of the friends they lost Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture". "We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve". UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you." "The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said. Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting

title: Guardiola set to attend Man City's first home game since guilty verdict
description: Pep Guardiola is expected to attend Manchester City's Champions League tie against Paris St-Germain next week - the club's first home match since they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.
body: Pep Guardiola won the Premier League six times as Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola is expected to attend Manchester City's Champions League tie against Paris St-Germain next week - the club's first home match since they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League. It will mark the first time the Spaniard has returned to Etihad Stadium since he left the club at the end of last season after a decade as manager. Earlier this month, an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. City continue to deny any wrongdoing and have lodged an appeal against the findings in the Premier League's report that stated the club falsely inflated commercial revenues by £830m through "sham" contracts. In the aftermath of the verdict, 55-year-old Guardiola backed City's owners and leadership and says he will "always" be behind the club. "I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever," he posted on social media. "I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters. "Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all." This video can not be played Could Manchester City be expelled from the Premier League? Your Manchester City Questions Answered By The Experts Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League City return to action after the three-week international break against Liverpool on Sunday (16:30 BST) in what promises to be a searing Premier League atmosphere at Anfield. Enzo Maresca's side then host Champions League holders PSG on Wednesday, 14 October when Guardiola is expected to watch from the Etihad stands. During Guardiola's decade in charge of City, he led the club to six Premier League titles - including a record four in a row from 2020-21 - as well as the Champions League, three FA Cups and five League Cups. Prior to his departure, Guardiola spoke about the charges against City in November 2024 and said he "will be here" even if the club were relegated. title: Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's ‘shock’ recovery in hospital
description: The US death row inmate's legal team said at a press conference that she is now "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution.
body: This video can not be played Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" and expected to make a recovery, nearly a week after her failed execution, her attorneys have said. They added that at this time, Pike's future remains uncertain. In court earlier on Wednesday, Pike's lawyers secured a legal win by convincing a judge to order the state to preserve the broadest amount of evidence possible from the US death row inmate's botched execution. The BBC's Gary O'Donoghue breaks down the recent events in court and what comes next for Christa Pike. Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's ‘shock’ recovery in hospital. title: Masked 15-year-old stabbed schoolgirl, court told
description: Prosecutors say the boy had an "intention to kill" a 15-year-old girl.
body: Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School at 10:24 GMT on 11 March A masked 15-year-old who was captured on CCTV stabbing a schoolgirl had written notes saying he hated women, a court has heard. Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March, following reports that a 15-year-old girl had been stabbed in the back. The defendant, who is now 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, has denied a charge of attempted murder - but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent. The boy brought a knife to school, dressed in black with a face mask and had an "intention to kill", prosecutors told King's Lynn Crown Court. Police were called to reports of the stabbing at 10:24 GMT, not long after parents had gathered at the gates. Opening the prosecution case, Chris Paxton KC said the defendant armed himself with a kitchen knife and "went to school not to learn, but to kill". He was "dressed in black, masked up and tooled up", jurors heard. A photo taken from within a classroom showed an armed police officer at the scene CCTV footage shown to the court captured the moment the girl was stabbed in the back, before her attacker ran off while "pursued by a teacher". The girl was treated in hospital for minor injuries and later discharged. Her alleged attacker was said to have written down his motive as "misanthropy, misogyny, suicide, bullying". His notes continued: "Death = 2+ hopefully, injuries a lot hopefully." The prosecution described it as "sheer good fortune" that the girl was not seriously hurt and said she had been "defenceless and vulnerable". "This was a knife strike delivered, we the prosecution say, as an attempt to kill," Paxton added. The trial at King's Lynn Crown Court is expected to last three weeks A search of the defendant's house revealed evidence of his "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", it was alleged. Jurors heard about notes found by police which said "I really want to do it really bad", adding: "I need a plan." Paxton said further notes - including one called "victims list" - displayed a hatred of women. The trial, which is expected to last three weeks, continues. title: Fraudster jailed over multi-million pound PPE scam
description: Craig Morris was sentenced to three years and nine months in prison at Northampton Crown Court.
body: Craig Morris was sentenced to three years and nine months in prison at Northampton Crown Court A fraudster has been jailed for helping to scam medical companies out of millions of pounds through bogus personal protective equipment (PPE) deals during the Covid-19 pandemic. Craig Morris, 43, and Jogesh Bhandari, 60, bought luxury cars, holidays and a new home after pretending they could supply millions of boxes of nitrile gloves in the US and Germany. They were convicted of two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation as well as concealing and transferring criminal property at Leicester Crown Court in July. On Wednesday, Morris received three years and nine months in prison. Jogesh, of Mitchell Drive, Loughborough, Leicestershire, will be sentenced later. Jogesh told his counsel he was taking a "very extreme painkiller" after having a pacemaker fitted last week and was not able to travel to Northampton, where the sentencing hearing took place. His wife, former pharmacist Meenakashi Bhandari, 58, also of Mitchell Drive, did attend the sentencing hearing. She was found guilty of concealing and transferring criminal property. She was given a two-year prison sentence, suspended for two years, 250 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of rehabilitation activity. Judge William Harbage KC said there was "no medical evidence" to properly explain Jogesh's absence and said a bench warrant would be issued. He is expected to be sentenced on 16 October. Prosecutor Michael Bisgrove told the court Jogesh was the "driving force and the instigator" of the offending, while Morris, of Forest Drive in Lytham St Annes, Lancashire, was "very much working for him". He said: "The offences took place during the Covid-19 pandemic at a time when there was a desperate shortage of personal protective equipment (PPE). "In that shortage, the offenders, particularly Mr Bhandari and Mr Morris, saw the opportunity to make money by fraud." The court heard that Jogesh and Morris made fraudulent deals under a company called Banton. "They pretended to be big players in the PPE market. They pretended to have PPE for sale and to be able to buy vast amounts of it," Bisgrove added. The court heard they defrauded US company Med18 and German firm MedTech by sending contracts for equipment they did not have. Bisgrove said: "In the course of the fraud, they took millions of pounds which they used for their own benefit to buy cars, luxury goods and property." Jogesh Bhandari spent thousands of pounds on luxury cars The court heard the Bhandaris also used the money to pay off family debt, while Morris bought a house, the court heard. The value of money Jogesh obtained and kept in the course of the fraud was £1.75 million, and Meenakshi laundered money to the value of £960,000, the court heard. Morris had been receiving regular £5,000 payments from Jogesh before the two men fell out at the end of 2021, the National Crime Agency (NCA) previously said. Craig Morris (left), Jogesh Bhandari (middle) and Meenakashi Bhandari were convicted at Leicester Crown Court The agency said Jogesh worked with Frank Labruzzo, an attorney in the Louisiana Attorney General's Office, who provided a fraudulent escrow service - a bank account which holds funds until pre-arranged conditions are met. The court heard that Labruzzo and another person involved have been convicted and sentenced in the US. Sentencing Morris and Meenakshi, Judge Harbage said the pandemic was a time when "all of us had to make sacrifices and pull together for the good of society as a whole". He added: "There were a few people though who sought to exploit that to make money for themselves, motivated by greed. "I'm satisfied Jogesh Bhandari and Craig Morris fall into that category." title: Western civilisation at risk of 'atrophy, servitude and decline', Rubio says
description: In a speech overlooking the Acropolis, the US Secretary of State also said the US believes Europe "can awaken from its long slumber".
body: Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline. Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together". "We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said. While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests". Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers. But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads. "The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century." Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation". That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world". "The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit. "In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay." Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships. Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence. Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal. title: Eritrean troops move deep into Ethiopia's Tigray region, residents tell BBC
description: Residents of Adigrat tell the BBC they have seen truck loads of soldiers from Eritrea moving south.
body: Eritrean soldiers were involved in fighting in Tigray during the 2020-2022 conflict Eritrean soldiers have crossed into northern Ethiopia heading towards an area where clashes have been taking place between national army troops and regional forces, residents in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat have told the BBC. Fighting in the region broke out two weeks ago after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Both blame one another for violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war. Ethiopia has also accused Eritrea of backing the TPLF - something Asmara has previously denied. The latest unrest follows the launch in September of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia, which includes the TPLF. How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia The young women who fought in Ethiopia's last civil war and don't want to see another one Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? Over the weekend, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control. Eritrea was a key ally of landlocked Ethiopia during the 2020-2022 war, fighting against the TPLF in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century and which drove the Tigray region to the precipice of famine. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports. Last week the two countries severed diplomatic relations as the renewed fighting raised fears of a wider regional conflict. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas, though mobile phone connections and internet access have been restored to most areas since the military took over Mekelle. According to multiple accounts, Eritrean troops have moved from the border town of Zalambessa towards central Tigray, with convoys reportedly passing through Adigrat and heading toward Edaga Hamus, a town between Adigrat and Mekelle. "I saw about 40 trucks carrying soldiers. The convoy was moving south," one resident of Adigrat, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told BBC Tigrinya. Pro-government forces have control of Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region A second resident reported seeing troop movements, initially at night: "We have been seeing trucks with Eritrean registration plates passing through the city. "Now this morning we witnessed around 20 to 30 large trucks heading toward Edaga Hamus." He added that acquaintances travelling along the route had seen additional vehicles carrying heavy weapons, including anti-aircraft guns, and noted some troops were also moving on foot. A source in Mekelle told the BBC that relatives in Adigrat described even larger troop movements, and estimated they saw up to 60 trucks carrying soldiers who were later deployed in mountainous terrain near Edaga Hamus. Images circulating on social media appear to show heavily loaded military trucks carrying uniformed personnel towards Adigrat, Edaga Hamus and possibly Wukro, another key town along the corridor between Adigrat and Mekelle. The BBC has not independently verified the images. Sources in Wukro told the BBC that national army soldiers and allied fighters had entered the town on Wednesday after an exchange of heavy weapons about 15km south of the town. The BBC has not yet been able to independently verify any of the reported troop movements. The reported return of Eritrean forces has sparked anxiety among many of Tigray's residents, with some recalling the atrocities allegedly committed by soldiers from Eritrea during the recent civil war, when they fought against the TPLF. One Adigrat resident said that seeing Eritrean soldiers again was emotionally distressing: "The memories are still fresh. I was emotional myself. People are saddened to see them back again." A resident of Edaga Hamus also reported Eritrean troops passing through the town and said drone strikes had occurred nearby, with soldiers targeted. In a recent interview with private station Fana Television, senior Ethiopian government official Abraham Belay accused Eritrea of direct participation in the conflict. "The Eritrean army has participated with its full capacity and logistics," he said. "Many Eritrean soldiers have been killed and captured. There is no doubt that the retaliation will be double. They will see what it means to enter the border of another country and fight alongside bandits." Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. title: Man charged with 13 attempted murders including British child after Alps attack
description: Abdalmasih Hanoun, accused of carrying out an attack at a French park in 2023, is set to face trial.
body: People laid tributes to the victims of the park attack in the French Alps in June 2023 A man accused of attacking 13 people, including a British three-year-old and three other children, with a knife at a playground in the French Alps will go on trial charged with attempted murder, prosecutors have said. Abdalmasih Hanoun is also charged with armed resistance after the attack at a park in Le Paquier, southeast France, in June 2023. In addition to the four children, who were aged between 22 months and three years, two adults were wounded in the attack. The three-year-old British child was visiting the area with her parents. She suffered a single stab wound, French prosecutors said, but was later confirmed to be in a stable condition. Hanoun will face trial at Haute-Savoie Assize Court in Annecy within the next year, the French public prosecutor's office said on Wednesday. The prosecutor's statement said: "The defendant will have to answer charges of attempted murder in respect of 13 victims, violence with a weapon without total work incapacity in respect of two victims, and armed resistance." It added that the defendant's mental state had been assessed by a panel of experts, who found he had not been "suffering from a psychological or neuropsychological disorder" at the time of the attack. This means there could be "no grounds justifying the decision not to indict Mr Abdalmasih Hanoun". The statement also said that the decision to order a trial to proceed could be subject to appeal. Shortly after the attack on 8 June 2023, officials confirmed that the four young victims were in stable condition, including the British toddler. One of the children was a Dutch national and the other two were confirmed to be French nationals from the eastern region of Haute-Savoie. Two adults were also hurt in the attack, but were later said to be out of danger. title: Rice close to agreeing new Arsenal deal
description: Declan Rice is close to agreeing a new long-term Arsenal contract, sources have told BBC Sport.
body: Declan Rice joined Arsenal from West Ham in 2023 Declan Rice is close to agreeing a new long-term Arsenal contract, sources have told BBC Sport. The England midfielder has become a crucial player for the Gunners since his arrival from West Ham for £105m in July 2023. His current deal expires at the end of next season but BBC Sport revealed in March that talks over a new contract were underway with the process now at an advanced stage. The 27-year-old has made more than 150 starts for Arsenal, and is also a key player for England, with manager Thomas Tuchel saying this week he is one of the best midfielders in Europe. Rice would receive a significant pay increase to his reported £240,000-per-week salary, putting him on a par with the club's best earner Bukayo Saka, who is believed to earn about £350,000 a week. The news comes after Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta's new four-year deal with the Premier League champions was announced on Wednesday. title: BBC's Nicky Campbell tells court teacher who attacked him 'completely lost it'
description: The presenter is giving evidence to a court examining accusations against two former Edinburgh Academy teachers who are unfit to stand trial.
body: BBC presenter Nicky Campbell has been giving evidence about alleged abuse at Edinburgh Academy Broadcaster Nicky Campbell has told a court a maths teacher "completely lost it" and violently attacked him in the courtyard of Edinburgh Academy when he was a pupil there in the 1970s. The 65-year-old said he was around 15 when he was initially "yanked from behind" by Colin Turner beside a school noticeboard when he was running late for class. Campbell said he was then "rag dolled" by the teacher and described being shaken, slapped and dragged across the playground. He was giving evidence during an examination of facts hearing held at Edinburgh Sheriff Court. Turner and David Bourne, another former teacher, are accused of attacking pupils at the prestigious fee-paying school but have been deemed medically unfit to stand trial. A sheriff will instead hear evidence in the case and determine whether there are grounds for a conviction. More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East Campbell was a pupil at Edinburgh Academy between 1966 and 1978, from when he was aged five until he was 17. The BBC Radio 5 Live presenter told the court he was a "skinny teenage pupil" when he was attacked by Turner - who he said was a "physically imposing" man. Prior to the incident, he said that he and another pupil were looking at a timetable on a noticeboard after the lunchtime break, trying to find out where they should be. He said there were a few stragglers in the playground but most pupils had gone to class. Campbell told the court he was "yanked from behind", adding: "I didn't know what was going on, didn't know who it was until I turned around and he [Turner] started hitting me. "He shook me around and started slapping me. He utterly lost it. It was an absolute frenzy." Campbell said immediately after the incident it was as if "the red mist lifted" and he and Turner went into a nearby common room and sat down at a table. He told the court he was still sobbing. The presenter said he told the teacher "I could call the police on you for that" and that the teacher appeared "chastened." Campbell said he went home with a torn shirt. He told the court his mother saw he was "distraught" and called the school. Following this, he said there was "correspondence" and that he remembered his mother later saying that Turner had been "dealt with". Later in his evidence, Campbell told the court that he saw his Edinburgh Academy pupil file for the first time three or four weeks ago. Asked if there was any record of this incident in it, he replied: "No, it was ridiculously scant." Campbell will continue giving evidence on Thursday. title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
description: People with mental illness alone were to be eligible for assisted dying in Canada in March 2027, but that has now been paused indefinitely.
body: Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the decision to pause the expansion was a difficult one Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible. It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded. On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time". Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to healthcare. A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness. Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future. Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned. The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said. That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so. However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces. Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses. "These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said. Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases. Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent. In Canada, that mechanism is known as "track two" Maid. Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery. Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness. But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility. "When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said. Canada should 'indefinitely exclude' people with mental illness from assisted dying, report says What is a 'safe death'? Mentally ill woman asks for assisted dying in Canada 'I could live 30 years but plan to die': How assisted dying law is dividing Canadians Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that assisted dying would offer her "a safe death". Brosseau's lawyer, Michael Fenrick, told the BBC on Wednesday that the government's decision is "deeply disappointing". "People will continue to suffer intolerably while the case goes through the courts," he said. More broadly, some experts have also raised concerns that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort. In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying. It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services". The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium. Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased". Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support access, external to medically assisted death but that support falls it comes to patients with mental illness alone. title: Is it too early to look at Premier League table?
description: Just five games in, it might seem a bit early to pay much attention to the Premier League table - but it's probably more settled than you think. BBC Sport takes a look at the statistics behind the early season standings.
body: Arsenal are chasing back-to-back Premier League titles Just five games in, it might seem a bit early to pay much attention to the Premier League table - but it's probably more settled than you think. While it would be no surprise if Manchester City and Arsenal finish as the top two -outside of any points deductions or sanctions directed City's way - will Brentford really qualify for Europe, Hull stay up and Tottenham be involved in yet another relegation battle? Recent history certainly suggests it's likely. It has to be mentioned there is a huge asterisk hanging over the Premier League table at the moment after Man City were found guilty of the majority of the Premier League charges levelled at them. The Premier League leaders have appealed but, if the guilty verdict remains, potential sanctions could have a significant impact on the table. Until then, we can only deal with the table as it is now. If we look at the Premier League after five games last season and where teams ultimately ended up, the final table was already starting to take shape as 13 of the 20 sides finished within four places of where they sat even at this early stage (65%). Eventual champions Arsenal were second, Sunderland were already seventh ahead of finishing there eight months later, and two of the three sides that were relegated were already in the bottom three. There were some notable exceptions. Aston Villa and Tottenham effectively swapped places at either end of the table, with Villa rising up from the bottom three to finish in the top four and Spurs dropping to 17th. It's a similar story across the last 10 seasons of the Premier League. Over two-thirds of teams finished within four places of where they were after five games (138 out of 200), with 27 of those sitting in exactly the same position 33 games later. Another 50 teams finished between five and nine places from where they were at this stage, meaning that just 12 teams in the last decade moved up or down the table by double digits after this point, with three of those coming last season. However, one part of the table that doesn't settle quickly is the top spot. The side leading the Premier League after five games has gone on to win the title in just one of the last six seasons – Man City doing so in 2023-24 – and just three times in the last 11 seasons. Even the fact that Man City have five wins out of five so far doesn't mean much. They also won their first five games under Manuel Pellegrini in 2015-16 and in Pep Guardiola's first season in 2016-17 but didn't go on to win the title on either occasion (although they did in 2023-24). Chelsea in 2018-19, Arsenal in 2022-23 and Liverpool last season were also top with a 100% record at this stage but had little to show for it at the end of the season. However, the eventual champions have been in the top two at this point in each of the last four campaigns, suggesting - potential punishments aside - it will be Man City or Arsenal that lifts the trophy. The last team to be outside the top two after five games and win the title were Man City in 2021-22, who were fifth with just 10 points. The top end of the table overall has sometimes settled surprisingly quickly in recent years. The top eight after five games in 2024-25 finished as the top eight at the end of that season (although not in the same order), while the top six in 2019-20 and top seven in 2016-17 were also in place at this early stage. While being top after five games hasn't meant much in recent seasons, being bottom certainly has. After finishing just one place above the drop in the last two campaigns, Tottenham could well be in trouble once again as the side bottom of the Premier League after five games has been relegated in six of the last seven seasons. Being bottom this early didn't used to be such a bad omen. Between 2013-14 and 2018-19, only one of the six sides that were propping up the table after five games ended up going down – Newcastle in 2015-16 – while Crystal Palace finished as high as 11th in 2017-18. In fact, the good news for Tottenham fans is that the last time they were in this situation, they finished eighth. The club were bottom with just two points after five games in 2008-09 but, after replacing manager Juande Ramos with Harry Redknapp three games later, still finished in the top half. Looking at the relegation battle more broadly, at least one of the teams in the bottom three at this stage has been relegated in the last eight seasons - so one of Tottenham, Fulham and Coventry will very likely be heading to the Championship in May. The pool of contestants for this season's relegation battle may already be decided too as the three sides that ultimately went down in the last three seasons were all in the bottom six after five games, which would add Bournemouth, Aston Villa and Crystal Palace to the mix. The last sides to be outside the bottom six at this point but relegated were Leeds and Southampton in 2022-23, who were both in the top half (7th and 9th). With their teams currently sat in 8th and 11th place, Hull and Ipswich fans will hope that's still the case at the end of this campaign. While the season may well have barely begun, the Premier League table is already starting to take shape.
