title: Chris Mason: Tories united behind Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters
description: Kemi Badenoch has the support of her party but the Tories still trail Labour and Reform in opinion polls.
body: It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now. Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham. It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago. The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence. Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland. Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that. The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax – which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people, external but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax, external. Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income. But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it. Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people. Badenoch pledges inheritance tax changes as she pitches Tories as 'no-nonsense' party What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits? I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch Policy announcements aside, what stood out in this speech for me was a broader point. The veteran Conservative elections strategist Sir Lynton Crosby once suggested the party ought to "scrape the barnacles off the boat" as he put it, in reference to unpopular policies that could cause the Tories a headache during an election campaign. This speech felt like Badenoch revelling in pointing at the clean hull of the Conservative ship, what she sees as those barnacles removed, not least the high-profile defections of Jenrick and Suella Braverman. There was a striking glee and anger in her reflections about Reform UK. She sought to portray them as sleazy and pointedly decided to lean into an argument of recent months about Englishness. Braverman has argued that, given her Asian heritage, "I'm not English". "I'm proud to be British. My family and ancestors have a link to Britain which spans centuries. But in no way are we English," she wrote on social media last month, external, adding: "Englishness is an ethnicity." Badenoch expressed her personal fury at this, saying that as the mother of mixed-race children "I don't want to explain to my son, when we're watching our brilliant England team play football, that some people don't think our black players are English". The recurring message, today and over the last few days, is Badenoch cannot stand Reform and won't work with them before or after the next general election. But what she said amounted to an attack on Reform's character and the judgement of their prominent figures, rather than a significant focus on the policies we hear talked about most often by Nigel Farage. Badenoch did talk about immigration, but not at length. She largely left the issue – and the Conservative policy to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights, as Reform also advocates - to her shadow home secretary Chris Philp who spoke before her. Instead, Badenoch grounded this speech in the big picture tussle to be trusted between Labour and the Conservatives – and in particular who was better placed to deliver a growing economy. In tone, language and public enthusiasm for the argument, Badenoch and Andy Burnham are quite the contrast with their immediate predecessors Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer. Badenoch and Burnham both look like they are enjoying themselves on the stage, and are both enthusiastic purveyors of the core of what are their very different worldviews. Badenoch acknowledged this with what she called the "battle for the soul of this nation" in the opening minute or so of her address. It is a trailer for the debate to come this autumn and beyond. This video can not be played Watch: The big test facing Kemi Badenoch after her conference speech The Conservatives feel chipper and are united. But while both of these things are better than the alternative for any party leader, they are not the same as being popular. And, as Kemi Badenoch acknowledged, they are not there on that score yet, by a long chalk, with opinion polls suggesting they are more unpopular than when they were annihilated at the last general election. The numbers, for them, are dire. Just not as bad, relatively speaking, as they were. But they hope things are looking up for them: Reform has had a bruising few months, and Labour, they believe, are leaning to the Left, trying to lure Green and Liberal Democrat supporters towards them. Can the Conservatives also lure recent Lib Dem supporters in the south of England with talk of help with childcare costs whatever your income, not hiking the council tax of very expensive homes and this inheritance tax plan? title: Rahm to leave LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms
description: Jon Rahm will leave LIV Golf after deeming the terms for LIV 2.0 "unacceptable", his lawyer has told a bankruptcy court hearing.
body: Jon Rahm was arguably the most high-profile name to join LIV when he left the PGA Tour in December 2023 for a deal worth a reported £222m ($300m) Jon Rahm will leave LIV Golf after deeming the proposed terms for LIV 2.0 "unacceptable", his lawyer has told a bankruptcy court hearing. The league, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season. Rahm's lawyer, John Beck, told the hearing the 31-year-old Spaniard "independently reviewed the terms of LIV 2.0 and determined those terms are unacceptable as to him". It was later said that LIV and Rahm's representatives are "in advanced discussions for a consensual separation agreement between Mr Rahm and LIV". It is hoped this will be finalised by a court hearing on 5 November. LIV's participants are owed at least $45m (£33m) and have the option to leave. However, the agreement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until 25 October. Documents outlining the money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims show that two-time major winner Rahm tops the list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m). BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf. Spain's Rahm was arguably the most high-profile name to join LIV when he left the PGA Tour in December 2023 for a deal worth a reported £222m ($300m). Some players, including Brooks Koepka, have since returned to the PGA Tour, which rewrote its rules in December to allow the five-time major winner to come back, subject to certain sanctions. Rahm did not follow suit and remained under long-term contract with LIV, but in May reached a deal with the DP World Tour - formerly the European Tour - to retain his membership and remain eligible for next year's Ryder Cup. In August, the former world number one won his third straight LIV season title. He has previously said he had no regrets over joining LIV and backed organisers to make it sustainable. title: What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits?
description: BBC Verify looks into the party's move to overhaul the tax that is levied on inherited wealth.
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has announced she will overhaul inheritance tax if her party wins the next general election. She told the Conservatives' annual conference that "nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home" and couples will be able to leave an additional £1m tax free. Tax experts say the party's £6bn per year estimate of the cost of the plan is reasonable, but warn the policy would primarily benefit wealthier households and could discourage older people from moving to smaller homes. BBC Verify has looked into the details of the policy. Under the current system, inheritance tax of 40% is paid when someone's estate - the total value of their money and property exceeds £325,000. Anything under this amount is not taxed. And, when a person dies, they can currently transfer this tax-free allowance to a surviving spouse or civil partner which increases the combined threshold for a couple to £650k. On top of this individuals can get an additional transferable allowance for a family home of £175k each when it is left to children or other direct descendants. So at present most married couples can potentially leave £1m without paying inheritance tax. The Conservative plan would increase the £325,000 threshold - the point at which you start paying the tax - to £500,000 and fully exempt a family home from inheritance tax. At the moment an estate with a £2m house could be liable for £400,000 in inheritance tax. That would reduce to zero under the Conservatives. Official figures show that in 2024-25 around 30,400 deaths in the UK left estates which were liable for inheritance tax. This was around 5% of all UK deaths in that year. But the number of estates paying inheritance tax is set to rise, due to the increasing value of inherited wealth being passed on and the threshold having been frozen. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has estimated that by 2032-33 around 12% of people will have inheritance tax due either on their own death or that of their spouse or civil partner. Citing analysis by the consultancy Oxford Economics, the Conservatives say the number of estates paying the tax will rise to 52,100 in 2029-30. The Conservatives estimate their reforms would reduce the number of affected estates in 2030 to 22,000. Official data shows higher value estates pay the majority of the inheritance tax collected. The IFS has estimated that if inheritance tax were to be entirely scrapped, which Badenoch has identified as a longer term aspiration, the wealthiest 1% of estates - those worth £2.1m or more - would get half of the benefit of the tax reduction. And one long-standing criticism of inheritance tax is that the wealthy use legal ways to avoid paying it like putting their assets into family trusts to reduce the amount of inheritance tax ultimately due from their estates when they die. In 2023-24, estates with a valuation of £10m only paid an average effective inheritance tax rate of 18%, according to estimates from HM Revenue and Customs. Responding to Wednesday's conference announcement, the IFS said: "The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes – and their descendants. "This is a very well-off group, mainly living in London and the South-East of England." The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the official forecaster, estimates inheritance tax will raise £9.5bn in 2026-27 - equivalent to around 0.3% of GDP. The OBR projects this will rise to £14.5bn in 2030-31 or 0.4% of GDP. The Conservatives estimate their plan would cost £6bn a year in 2029-30, based on Oxford Economics' analysis. The party says it has identified £71bn in annual savings including £36bn a year from welfare cuts. Prof Andy Summers, director of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation, told BBC Verify this was "just about about the worst possible way to deliver an inheritance tax cut". "Exempting the family home however much it's worth will just encourage older people to concentrate their savings in their home, prevent downsizing, and so further gum up the housing market," he said. The Conservatives argue in their press release accompanying the policy announcement that inheritance taxes are "bad for growth". But analysis by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development suggests inheritance taxes in general are less damaging to economic growth than taxes on income from work. title: Katie Price messaged ex's rape accuser, court told
description: Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler is accused of raping and sexually assaulting a 13-year-old in 2016.
body: Kieran Hayler denies all the charges against him Katie Price messaged a teenage girl allegedly raped by her then-husband, telling her: "I will make you a little star," a court has heard. Price's ex-husband, Kieran Hayler, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault against the then 13-year-old girl in 2016 in West Sussex, all of which he denies. Jurors saw messages sent between Price and the girl, then aged 14, in which Price said she had heard Hayler and the girl had kissed and that he had "tried it on" with her. "I'm only asking as this is a serious allegation," Price had then asked, to which the teenager replied that it was "just a flirt thing" and that "nothing happened". In the messages shown in court, Price also asked: "Did he kiss you? I won't bring up anymore just want truth. I will make you a little star." In addition, she asked the girl if Hayler had ever said he liked or fancied her, to which she replied: "Yes, but I took it as a joke." Asked in cross-examination as to why she said nothing happened, the complainant, now an adult, replied that she was "trying to brush it off". Pressed on what she took Price to mean by: "I will make you a little star", she told the court: "I don't think I said anything. I think I just ignored it." Arlette Piercy, defending, suggested to the court that the alleged rapes and sexual assault never happened, but the complainant told the jury: "I would never make it up." The complainant said she deleted "I love you" texts exchanged with Hayler after he allegedly told her to get rid of them. Jurors had heard that after the third alleged rape, he texted her afterwards saying "I love you goodnight", and she replied: "I love you too." Piercy said it was not accepted on behalf of Hayler that such texts had been sent to her at any time, to which the complainant replied that they were "deleted, long gone, years ago". Asked if she was the one to delete them, she replied: "Yes, I did. Kieran Hayler was asking to delete my messages." Hayler was married to Price at the time of the allegations but their relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021. He denies the charges and suggests his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations formed part of that, the court heard. The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families. Additional reporting by PA Media. title: Family tribute to 'kind and loving' GP found dead at home
description: Hannah Cain's family say they have been "devastated" by her death on Sunday.
body: Hannah Cain has been described as "kind, generous and loving" by her family The family of a GP who was found dead at her home say they have been "devastated" by her death. Police discovered the body of Hannah Cain, known to her patients as Dr Hannah Terry, at her home in Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday morning. "She was kind, generous and loving; a beloved mother, daughter, sister, auntie, daughter-in-law and friend," the 45-year-old's family said in a statement. Her husband, Mark Cain, 45, of Fern Hill in Dersingham, appeared before magistrates in Norwich earlier, accused of her murder. He did not enter a plea during the hearing and will return before a judge on Thursday. "We are devastated by the loss of our beautiful Hannah," the family said. They added: "We are incredibly proud of the woman she was and of the great care she took of all her patients who knew her as Dr Terry. "We would ask people to respect our privacy at this difficult time." A police cordon was put in place outside the property in Dersingham on Sunday Hannah Cain was listed as a member of the practice team at Grimston Medical Centre, which reopened on Wednesday after two days of closure. She also served in a pool of doctors who were regularly on call for members of the Royal Family, The Sun newspaper reported. Dersingham is on the edge of the royal Sandringham estate in west Norfolk, while Grimston is to the south. Speaking at Norwich Magistrates' Court earlier, prosecutor Jacqui Hanlon said paramedics were called to Hannah Cain's home, on Fern Hill, at 02:25 BST on Sunday. The GP was "found in an upstairs bedroom not breathing, not conscious", she said. Mark Cain was remanded back into custody after his court appearance in Norwich Hanlon said a post-mortem examination noted a "blunt force injury" to the right side of Hannah Cain's head, as well as an injury "that could be suggestive of compression of the neck". District judge Matthew Bone remanded Mark Cain in custody to appear at King's Lynn Crown Court on Thursday. After reopening on Wednesday, Grimston Medical Centre said it would not be commenting "on the circumstances surrounding the tragic death" of Hannah Cain. title: Blue Planet III ventures into darkest depths of ocean
description: Sir David says the series uncovers marine life that is "even more precious than we ever realised".
body: The third instalment took nearly four years to make and comes around 25 years since the first series premiered Sir David Attenborough has promised to "venture even further" and uncover marine life that is "more precious than we ever realised" in Blue Planet III. The broadcaster, who turned 100 earlier this year, narrates the new six-part series exploring the darkest depths of the world's oceans, produced by the BBC Natural History Unit in Bristol. After almost four years of filming, the latest instalment in the franchise will air on the BBC later this autumn, marking 25 years since the first series premiered. At a launch event on Tuesday, Sir David said: "When I narrated the first Blue Planet series, it didn't occur to me that I would be narrating a third series in my centennial year." Two-year revamp of suspension bridge is complete 'Joy and inclusion' at black trail running event New red route could be introduced in parts of Bristol The production uses advanced equipment including remote underwater cameras, drones, and manned submersibles to capture newly discovered animal behaviours. Viewers are taken into some of the world's least understood marine environments, ranging from coral reefs and tropical islands to the darkest depths of the ocean. In the newly released extended trailer, Attenborough promised to "venture even further" than ever before, describing the ocean as "an endlessly fascinating place". "We will uncover life that is more surprising, more intelligent, and even more precious than we ever realised," he said. "We will discover the extraordinary relationship we have with the ocean. One that has never been more important to understand." Sir David said he was "proud and delighted" to be associated with the project. Sir David said it "has never been more important to understand" the ocean The new series is accompanied by an original score from Hans Zimmer and Bleeding Fingers Music. Zimmer, who also scored Blue Planet II, said the series was the "most important work" he has ever done. "I think everybody who comes to Blue Planet comes to it with the knowledge that it is something that changes the world by making you fall in love," he said. "It's not something where you're being lectured or cajoled about things, but it's something that just shows you how spectacular and beautiful our world truly is. "How we need to preserve it and how we need to love it, and how whatever we love, we need to treat with great kindness and great respect." The series examines the habitats and behaviours of animals including humpback whales, dolphins, and bioluminescent deep-sea creatures It also features an original song, Into The Deep (Seas Cry) co-written by Jade Thirlwall - best known for being a member of the pop group Little Mix. Thirlwall described herself as a "huge fan" of the franchise, praising Attenborough as "a true hero". "Being part of Blue Planet III in this way feels incredibly special and a real privilege," she added. The premiere launch event took place at Piccadilly Circus in London on Tuesday, with footage from the new series taking over the digital displays. title: Do England already have their Kane replacement - or is he yet to emerge?
description: Harry Kane's record-breaking England career can't go on for ever. But do the Three Lions already have a ready-made replacement?
body: Kane celebrates scoring for England against Czechia Where would England be without Harry Kane? With every record he breaks and landmark he passes, the question becomes increasingly difficult to tackle. But, now aged 33, there is a growing need for an answer. The Bayern Munich striker became his nation's joint-highest appearance-maker on Tuesday at Wembley, netting twice in the 3-0 win over Czechia, taking his tally to 91 goals in 125 caps. He is arguably in the form of his life. He won a league and cup double with Bayern last term - scoring 61 goals in 51 games for the German giants in 2025-26 - and he's among the favourites for the Ballon d'Or. However, when the next European Championship kicks off in the summer of 2028, Kane will be 35. Alternatives and eventual replacements will surely be on the mind of whoever is at the helm then. Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel said: "You will not get another Harry Kane, first of all. We look for different options and solutions." So what are England's options in a world without him? Is the answer already in front of us - or could it be someone yet to even emerge? Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender Tuchel believes Bellingham could play as a centre-forward for England Tuchel seems to think England may have an option within their ranks already in the guise of fellow superstar Jude Bellingham. He shrugged off question marks over his place in the team ahead of the World Cup to quickly become a rival to Kane as England's most influential player. "I like him as a nine," Tuchel admitted ahead of England's 7-0 win over Croatia. "He is a natural goalscorer and he has the hunger to be on the scoreboard. "He wants to be there and have the decisive action, so it makes not a huge difference if he plays as a nine or a 10. The German has certainly helped Bellingham add a productive edge to his game. Since the start of the 2026 World Cup, the Real Madrid star has netted 10 times in 12 matches for England, having scored six times in the 48 games beforehand. BBC Radio 5 Live's senior football reporter Ian Dennis said: "The person who is going to replace Kane has already emerged – and that's Jude Bellingham. "We have seen it at times, when they play that false nine, Bellingham can go into that advanced role. He will also eclipse Kane in terms of appearances. This is a player who will continue to go from strength to strength." At Real Madrid, Bellingham played frequently as a false nine in his first season for the club, with Vinicius Jr. and Rodrygo offering penetration from the wide positions. It was Bellingham's most productive season for Real Madrid, with the numbers indicating just how much of an all-round package he's developed into now. In a similar style, so much of Kane's good work for England comes from dropping deep, operating as a playmaker and then surging into the box to finish chances. If England want another player who can straddle the No. 9 and No. 10 positions simultaneously, then Bellingham could be their best fit. And, with the likes of Phil Foden, Cole Palmer, Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze, there are no shortage of options to fill the Bellingham role. However former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said on 5 Live: "He is not a nine, Bellingham plays off others. "I do think if England are going to play this system – and remember Kane has a long time left – I don't see Bellingham as the out and out number nine." Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest' Calvert-Lewin has had a brilliant start to the season for Leeds In terms of natural centre-forward replacements for Kane, England do not have much depth. Dominic Calvert-Lewin has made a case to be Kane's back-up. He has 17 goals in 40 Premier League appearances since moving to Leeds United last summer. However, there is a sense that Calvert-Lewin is not a dependable finisher - he underperformed by 2.13 in terms of xG in the Premier League last season - while at 29 he is not a long-term solution to Kane. Away from the Leeds striker, there are not many centre-forwards making a case. The only other English strikers to score in the Premier League so far this season are Nottingham Forest's Liam Delap, rebuilding his career after a difficult spell at Chelsea, and Ipswich Town's Chuba Akpom, who both have one goal each. Across the 2026-27 season, English left-backs, with six, have more goals than English centre-forwards, with five. Danny Welbeck was pushing for a recall last season with 13 Premier League goals but at the age of 35, his time is likely to have passed and he is certainly no long-term solution. Ivan Toney and Ollie Watkins, previously considered by Tuchel, are both playing their football in the Saudi Pro League and were both left out of the most recent squad. Both are also already into their thirties. If England do have an issue at centre-forward due to a Kane injury or suspension - or his eventual retirement - they could always opt to play without one. Tuchel has used the tactic before, with Kai Havertz often deployed at the point of the attack during his time as Chelsea boss. Havertz scored 10 goals in the 33 league games in which he was used as a centre-forward by Tuchel. A more fluid system has also been used to great effect by world and European champions Spain, who have deployed converted wingers Mikel Oyarzabal and Ferran Torres as strikers. Anthony Gordon, who scored three times during the international break, could fit that particular bill. The winger was used as a striker by Newcastle United late last season and had success in the Champions League, netting 10 times in 12 appearances overall. title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
description: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has refused to take any personal responsibility for what happened or order a state inquiry.
body: Residents of Kfar Aza attended a memorial ceremony on Wednesday for those killed on 7 October 2023 As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz. It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day. The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure. "I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza. The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages. Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen. And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies. "Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said. More than 60 residents of Kfar Aza were killed by Hamas-led gunmen and 19 were taken hostage three years ago Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew. For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack. Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza. "There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened – not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that." "The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again." They were Israel's 'eyes on the border' - their warnings went unheard Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected any personal responsibility for security failures three years ago Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours – which he denies. Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation. Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper. Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people. Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop". Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation. "God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network. "What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks. Netanyahu denied reports that he was warned by the UAE's president days before Hamas attacked Yaacov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault. In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border. He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters. "So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference." But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening. "You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state." Israelis have held protests to demand the establishment of a state commission of inquiry For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of ai

title: Compulsory media duties like something in an autocracy - Venter
description: Saracens' Brendan Venter compares Prem Rugby's media obligations to "something from an autocratic land" after reluctantly speaking at a press conference.
body: Brendan Venter appeared alongside head coach Joe Shaw (left) to preview Saracens' game against Bristol on Saturday Saracens' Brendan Venter compared Prem Rugby's media obligations to "something from an autocratic land" after he made a reluctant appearance at a press conference. The 56-year-old returned to a full-time role at the club in the summer, initially as director of rugby, but has since been given an updated job title of head of culture and technical director. His no-show at a pre-season media event cost Saracens a £5,000 fine and he avoided questions before and after the club's opening-round win over Leicester. However, he appeared alongside head coach Joe Shaw to preview this Saturday's match against Bristol and, after initially offering only short answers to reporters' questions, railed against the expectation that he would be the public face of the club. "I have the desire as a human being not to want to talk," he said. "It is not about me, it is about the team… I expressed that desire before I came." Venter added: "I asked really kindly and eventually I bent over backwards to explain my position. And then I'm expected again to come and do an interview. "If we get obsessed, get into an argument and fine a club, that for me does not make sense. "It sounds like something from an autocratic land, not a democracy where people have the right to say: 'This is what I want to do'. "If you want an interview, you have a brilliant person in Joe. I do not have the desire to do an interview. It stole my joy the previous time and I want to have a low profile. "That was my desire and to help to coach the rugby team. I do not want to be doing interviews. It's not because I think I'm better than anybody else. To be put over as an arrogant person who thinks he's better than doing interviews… it's not at all that." Venter's previous 16-month spell in charge of Saracens was littered with controversy. He was punished for accusing a referee of "being influenced", making provocative gestures at spectators and claiming officials were not being trained well enough to keep up with the latest laws. He also ignored the obligation for club captain Steve Borthwick to attend a Heineken Cup launch event, instead sending the now England coach on a beer-fuelled team-bonding trip to Munich. After one reprimand by European rugby authorities, Venter gave a viral post-match interview, inspired by a scene from the film Mike Bassett: England Manager,, external in which he agreed with the premise of every question asked of him. England boss Borthwick was Venter's Saracens captain during the South African's first stint in charge of the club After leaving Saracens in 2011, Venter, who won the Rugby World Cup as a player with South Africa in 1995, worked in roles with Durban-based club side the Sharks, as well as with Italy and South Africa. The changes to his job title since his return to north London, which reportedly included a stint as the club's wine consultant that lasted a matter of days,, external appeared to be an attempt to escape his media obligations. Prem Rugby rules require the most senior coach in every club to carry out routine media duties. Their job titles can vary. Rob Baxter is Exeter's director of rugby. George Skivington is Gloucester's head coach. But as the principle decision-maker for their team, both answer questions each week. Venter claimed in a weekend interview with TNT Sport, the broadcaster who pays £40m a season for action and access to the Prem, that decisions over team selection are done on the basis of a consensus, rather than any single person having a final say. Regardless, it is expected the Venter will continue to face the media for the rest of the campaign. Venter added that, despite his reservations, he had been tempted back by a love of coaching and the high-intensity dressing room environment. "I love coaching rugby. I love working with players. It is a privilege we get as human beings to be in a position where we can influence things, both good and bad," he added. "People in life rarely get that privilege. "It's a phenomenal game to be a part of and that's why when [Saracens owner] Dominic [Silvester] asked me, I agreed to come back. "You make friends like you never make in your life. When there are good times and difficult times, it builds character. I'm privileged enough to be doing that on a daily basis." Venter did not win any silverware during his first stint in charge of Saracens. His side lost to Leicester in the 2010 Premiership final, a match Venter was banned from as part of a touchline suspension. However, he left behind a formidably talented and closely bonded squad who would win multiple domestic and European honours under McCall in the following decade. In behind-the-scenes footage of Venter's speech to his squad at the start of pre-season, he set out his ambition to contend for the Prem title. "I promise you I don't want to be competitive in this league. I want to dominate," he said. "This is not a team with a ceiling, this is something special, I have not come all this way to be average." title: Greens investigate party member behind Zionism motion
description: It has emerged Lubna Speitan was listed in court documents as a "close friend" of a man later jailed for supporting al-Qaeda.
body: Lubna Speitan gave evidence on behalf of a British national who was accused of plotting to carry out a suicide attack at Heathrow Airport The Green Party has launched an investigation into party member Lubna Speitan, after it emerged she was listed in court documents as a "close friend" of a man later jailed for supporting al-Qaeda. Speitan was behind a controversial Green Party conference motion which described Zionism as a form of racism. A Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate and an investigation is underway." In a post on Instagram, before the Green Party had confirmed its investigation to the BBC, Speitan said: "I reject all defamatory and nonsense claims made about me." She added: "I reject all attempts to decontextualise past statements I have made." "This is a classic distraction. I am not the conversation," she said, adding: "Racism is. Zionism is. The ethnic cleansing and genocide of Palestinians is. Let's talk about that." In June, a UN commission of inquiry said Israel had deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the Gaza Strip. Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence. Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism' Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green Party conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state". The motion - which was approved by party members by 1,022 votes to 813 - also called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine". Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election. The motion attracted criticism from opposition parties and some Jewish groups, who labelled it an "attack on the Jewish community". Four out of five Green Party MPs also opposed the motion. Adrian Ramsay, a former party leader and Green MP for Waveney Valley, said the motion was an "unhelpful distraction" and "wrong in principle" as "the Green Party has always supported the right to self-determination and that has to apply to all peoples". Asked if he would consider leaving the party, Ramsay told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live he was "not ruling anything in or out at this stage". "What I'm doing at this stage, and we're only a few days after the motion, is to talk carefully with colleagues to reflect both with Jewish Greens but also with Green MPs and other people in leading roles in the party to look at how best can we get things back on track," he said. On Tuesday, the Jewish Chronicle reported, external the existence of a 2015 letter from Speitan in which she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham. US prosecutors said Pham had been directed by al-Qaeda leader Anwar al-Awlaki to detonate explosives in Heathrow's arrivals area after spending several months in Yemen being trained by him. He was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack. In US court documents from 2015, Speitan was listed as a "close friend" who could provide "critical testimony regarding Pham's mental state". In a later letter to the US District Judge, Speitan said Pham was one of the "few people I regard with such high respect and esteem". She said if the judge "truly knew the Minh [Pham] that I and others grew to love and respect", they may have "probably had the whole case dismissed". She acknowledged he "may have had and developed some behavioural issues" but added: "He turned out to be one of the kindest, honest, most sincere, trustworthy and respectful people I have ever known." There is no suggestion in the documents Speitan knew of Pham's criminal activities at the time they knew each other. Following the emergence of the letter on Tuesday afternoon, a Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate." On Wednesday, the party released an updated statement adding "an investigation is under way". The spokesperson said: "Lubna Speitan holds no party positions other than being a member." title: Ex-Spurs player Vega set to run for Fifa president
description: Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.
body: Ramon Vega made 23 appearances for Switzerland between 1993 and 2001 Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election. The 55-year-old is the first person to confirm they want to challenge Gianni Infantino, who has defied calls to step down in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, which has sparked a major backlash across football. A former Switzerland centre-back, Vega also played for Celtic and Watford and has worked in finance since retiring from football in 2004. "I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," he said. Last month, Infantino said he was "fully committed to leading Fifa" despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to quit. Vega considered running for Fifa's top job in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter. Four years later he said he would stand against Infantino, but failed to garner enough support to be included in the ballot, having required the backing of five of Fifa's 211 member federations. "I am standing because my life has prepared me to serve the game," Vega said in a statement announcing his candidacy. "Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution. "It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life. "It belongs to every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and the billions of supporters whose passion makes football the world's game. "Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family. "The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged Fifa's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family. We must stop this conflict from escalating. "Ego-driven battles within football administration must never be allowed to damage those who matter most: the players, coaches, referees and supporters around the world. They are not responsible for these conflicts. They deserve better." Vega concluded: "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. Fifa needs a new direction and fundamental reform. "We must reunite the football family, restore trust, bring stability and modernise Fifa's governance. This requires decisive change - not cosmetic adjustments." title: Notorious gangland enforcer Paul Ferris dies aged 62
description: The criminal-turned-author is believed to have died on Tuesday night after a short illness.
body: Ferris turned to writing about his life in Glasgow's underworld A Glasgow gangland enforcer who wrote books about his underworld experiences has died at the age of 62. Paul Ferris is believed to have died on Tuesday night at the city's Queen Elizabeth University Hospital after a short illness. He was cleared of the murder of crime boss Arthur Thompson's son, Arthur Thompson Jnr, in 1992, before being jailed for seven years in 1998 for gun-running. His first book, The Ferris Conspiracy, was published in 2001. It was later made into a 2013 film, The Wee Man, starring Line of Duty star Martin Compston as Ferris. The 'scandal' of Scotland's longest gangland trial Thompson Jnr was shot dead outside the family's Blackhill home in August 1991. Ferris' trial, which began the following year, was described at the time as the longest and most expensive criminal case in Scottish legal history. More than 300 witnesses gave evidence during the 54-day proceedings, which were estimated to have cost £4m. The prosecution case relied heavily on the evidence of Dennis Woodman, who claimed Ferris had confessed to the killing while both men were being held in Barlinnie Prison. Defence lawyers challenged the credibility of the evidence and argued the case against Ferris was deeply flawed. After more than 24 hours of deliberations, the jury acquitted him of murder and all other charges in 1992. No-one has ever been convicted of Thompson Jnr's killing. Ferris went on to publish a number of books with writer Reg McKay, who died in 2011. Photographer Brian Anderson, who first met Ferris for a newspaper assignment in 2002, broke the news of his death on his Naked City Facebook page. Describing Ferris as a best-selling author and a "former notorious criminal", he wrote: "News of his death will come as a shock to many who knew him throughout the different chapters of his life." Anderson later told BBC Scotland News: "We got on really well. I found him polite, funny and kind. "It was a shock to everyone that I remained friends with Paul for 25 years." title: Two icons, a glorious farewell and a potentially bitter ending
description: As Lionel Messi's international career ends in fond farewell, Cristiano Ronaldo's is at risk of petering out. BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international career's of two football greats.
body: Messi and Ronaldo are considered two of the greatest players ever On a night where one football legend received a grand farewell from his country, about 6,000 miles away, another released a lengthy statement discussing all the ways in which he had been wronged by his national team coach. Argentina great Lionel Messi took the adulation of the crowd in Buenos Aires as his glittering international career ended with a goal against Benin on an emotional night. Meanwhile, Portugal star Cristiano Ronaldo released a statement on social media, accusing manager Jorge Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" while admitting he should be held accountable for his own actions. The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark. Portuguese journalist Jose Delgado says "things will never be the same again" for Ronaldo and Portugal - so is this the beginning of the end? Jesus has said the door is open for Ronaldo to return to the national team, but is it? Or will this saga continue, potentially closing the book on the international career of one of the greatest players of all time? BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international careers of two football greats. A rivalry that changed football Watch: Rivals - Messi v Ronaldo Listen: Sporting Giants - Messi v Ronaldo The Ronaldo saga has been rumbling on for some time, with many fans critical of former Portugal boss Roberto Martinez's insistence on starting Ronaldo at this summer's World Cup. At 41 years old, Ronaldo is not the dynamic player he once was and many suggested his presence hindered the team rather than helped. However, things came to a head on Sunday when Ronaldo was an unused substitute in the Nations League win over Norway. The player subsequently left camp after finding out he would not start against Denmark in November. On Tuesday, Ronaldo released an almost-2,000 word statement on Instagram in which he said Jesus had twice "broke his word" and accused him of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media. Ronaldo apologised to fans and team-mates for leaving the camp and said the consequences of that must be "assessed and punished" while also dismissing any suggestion that he had played his last match for Portugal. "We will have one or more farewell matches, there will be time for that," the statement said. Manager Jesus said on Sunday the door remains open for Ronaldo to return if he chooses to, but many are suggesting the damage is already done. Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring Portuguese football journalist Delgado told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I don't think there is a way back. In the statement, Ronaldo says he will return to the national team but at the same time he calls Jesus a liar three times. "In the polls in Portugal made about this issue, only 15% of the Portuguese were on Ronaldo's side and people think we owe him a lot but his time is already done and he must understand it. "The problem is that Ronaldo does not understand it, he wants to keep playing as if he was 24, not 41. "Things will never be the same again. No matter what happens, no matter if he plays again or if you have a game to say goodbye to Ronaldo things will never be the same. "What Ronaldo did for Portuguese football is unique and incredible and we must thank him for all the service he gave to Portugal. But at 41, he has no place in the best XI of Portugal." Manager Jesus has reportedly said that he had not seen Ronaldo's statement as he was watching the Portugal under-21 game. Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice. It seems unlikely that Ronaldo will voluntarily retire from the national team before he hits the elusive 1,000 goal mark he is chasing for club and country - he currently has 979. But have his actions made the situation untenable? This video can not be played Jesus fires back over Ronaldo question When it comes to fans, opinions appear to be split. On several billboards in Lisbon posters have been put up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus. They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain. "Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego." At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch. In stark contrast, Messi brought the curtain down on his illustrious Argentina career, where he has won one World Cup and two Copa Americas, in front of an 85,000-strong sellout crowd inside the Monumental in Buenos Aires. The 39-year-old announced his retirement from international football in August after Argentina finished runners-up at the World Cup and following the death of his father Jorge. Messi marked his final appearance for La Albiceleste with a goal before addressing the adoring fans in a speech lasting nearly 10 minutes. Some of his team-mates were in tears as Messi admitted he did not want to leave the field. "There are so many emotions going through me right now," he said. "I'm surely forgetting many things I would like to say because this is a very difficult moment for me. The first person who comes to my mind is my dad. "I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything." Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends Messi departs as the record appearance-maker and goal-scorer for Argentina but will continue his club career with Major League Soccer team Inter Miami. title: Couple killed after portable heater exploded and engulfed home in flames
description: A fire engulfed the home after an attempt to refuel a portable heater led to a gas leak, an inquest heard.
body: Ex-miner William and former factory worker Marlene Mumford died in the blaze at their home on 12 December An elderly couple died when a fire engulfed their home after an attempt to refuel a portable heater resulted in an "explosion". Marlene Mumford, 84, and William Mumford, 90, died at their property at Hoel Fawr, Caerphilly, last December. An inquest in Newport was told that the most likely cause of the fire was a mechanical or connection failure with the gas heater. Assistant coroner Sarah Le Fevre said it was believed William Mumford had attempted to carry the cylinder out of the home in an effort to remove it, but that this had only caused the flames to spread. She recorded their deaths as an accident, and the result of an "unintended act with unforeseen circumstance". The alarm was raised by a neighbour who was in the nearby Tyler's Arms when he noticed smoke and large flames. He and another man ran to the house where they saw a gas canister explode near the front porch with the flames rising above the height of the house. Emergency services were initially unable to enter the property due to the extent of the damage caused by the blaze. Firefighters reported seeing thick, black smoke "pumping out" of the property, the hearing was told. The couple were pronounced dead at the scene. Flames leapt higher than the house when the gas canister exploded, the inquest was told Bridgend fire station commander Melvyn Robert Laidler said burn patterns and the location of the canister suggested William Mumford had been unable to close the cylinder and so had attempted to remove it by carrying it through the house. A pathologist gave the cause of the couple's deaths as exposure to combustion products of fire. "What is possible is that William realised that the fire had taken, that he realised he was unable to close the cylinder or control the fire, and therefore thought, utterly understandably, that the best course would be to try and remove the fire from the house," said the coroner. "The fire started accidentally resulting from a mechanical or connection-related failure of a portable gas heater and gas bottle resulting in an uncontrolled gas release." title: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers
description: Climate change is blamed for dramatic decline of chinstrap penguins living on a remote volcanic island.
body: Chinstrap penguins get their name from a thin ring of feathers from ear to ear Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest. Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade. According to the study, there were 63% fewer occuplied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011. The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered. Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet. The scientists used drones and trackers to study the penguin colony Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory. In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain. BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork". A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds. This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%. Macaroni penguin populations increased as chinstrap penguins declined The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change. Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable. "With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards. "Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said. The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia. Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater. Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening. Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo). Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame. Two chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically. Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet. Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans. Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica". "Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added. "It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems." As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea. The research is published in the journal Current Biology, external. title: Southampton manager to stay in role after being given suspended ban over Spygate scandal
description: Tonda Eckert is free to continue as Southampton manager after being given a suspended ban for his role in Spygate.
body: This video can not be played Eckert speaking to BBC Sport in September, days before the hearing took place Tonda Eckert is free to continue as Southampton manager after being given a suspended ban for his role in the Spygate scandal. A Football Association (FA) independent regulatory commission handed the German a six-week ban from all football, but suspended it until the end of next season. Eckert has also been given a £28,000 fine and a reprimand but avoided a lengthy ban that could have cost him his job. The FA charged Eckert in July with misconduct, and a hearing took place at the end of last month. Saints were expelled from the Championship play-offs in May after admitting spying on training sessions involving Oxford United, Ipswich Town, and Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final. They were also handed a four-point deduction for this season. An English Football League (EFL) independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down". The 33-year-old apologised in June - claiming he was unaware the practice was banned and that it had no impact on his team's performances - but the FA took action. Eckert has been sanctioned for three breaches of FA Rule E3.1. The six-week ban from all football activity would be triggered if he was found to be involved in any other spying between now and the end of next season. Eckert was appointed permanent Southampton manager in December 2025 after taking interim charge when they were 21st in the Championship. They finished the season in fourth place. Saints, who face local rivals Portsmouth this weekend, are 13th in the Championship this season with four wins from their eight matches so far. They argued they had suffered enough as a result of the scandal. This video can not be played Eckert avoids lengthy ban over Spygate scandal Eckert told BBC Sport last month: "It's been a big, big punishment. Absolutely unheard of in the history of sports. "I've asked for forgiveness for what I've done. I've apologised publicly." According to the EFL commission, the club employed "a particularly deplorable approach" by using junior members of staff to conduct the spying "at the direction of senior personnel". An arbitration panel detailed how a junior analyst intern said he felt under "extreme pressure". The FA did not charge Leeds United's former manager Marcelo Bielsa after the club were found guilty of spying on Derby in 2019, instead issuing a formal warning. The EFL fined Leeds £200,000 - which Bielsa said he paid - and introduced a rule prohibiting any club from observing a rival's training session within 72 hours of a match between them. The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year after opponents New Zealand were spied on. It was the morning of Thursday, 7 May. Middlesbrough were at their Rockliffe Park training base preparing for the game against Southampton 48 hours later. The spy - Southampton intern William Salt - is said to have parked at the golf club, then walked a couple of hundred yards down a road that leads to a raised area of ground. Sources told the BBC that Salt stood pointing his mobile at the training session, while wearing in-ear headphones. Middlesbrough staff believe he may have been live-streaming the session via a video call. A member of Middlesbrough's staff approached, say BBC sources, but the person would not identify himself. He then quickly deleted some content on his phone before running into the golf club. He jogged into the toilets, changed his clothes and hurriedly left the site. Middlesbrough's photographer took photos and matched him to a photo on the Southampton website. One of those pictures was subsequently made public. Boro were furious and quickly reported the incident to the EFL, which charged Southampton with breaking two regulations: EFL regulation 3.4, which requires clubs to act towards each other with the utmost good faith; and EFL regulation 127, which prohibits any club from observing, or attempting to observe, another club's training session within 72 hours of a scheduled match between the two clubs. During the investigation, details emerged about the club watching training sessions involving Oxford and Ipswich, in addition to filming Middlesbrough as they prepared for the first leg of their play-off semi-final. Southampton did not win any of the three games - they lost 2-1 at Oxford, drew 2-2 at home to Ipswich and 0-0 at Boro. Salt has since been appointed to a permanent role at Saints in the club's academy. Southampton told the BBC "he's been through a time time". "When your photo is put out to the public, that is something tough to deal with," chief executive Phil Parsons told the BBC last month. "A lot of people probably underestimated how that could have impacted a young lad so we've got a job to make sure that he's looked after in his early career. But he's a talented boy as well. I get good feedback and he's got a good role at the club." title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
description: The sale of the High Street chain was announced on Wednesday.
body: Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to the holding company of Canada's billionaire Weston family. Wittington Investments confirmed it had agreed to buy Boots on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners. Sycamore had only owned the retailer for 18 months after taking over the retailer's previous owner. The deal covers Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. Galen Weston, chairman of Wittington, said the firm played "a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland". The deal is expected to be completed early next year. Boots has faced challenges in recent years with growing debt and changing shopping habits resulting in more people buying cheaper products online. It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK, leaving it with about 1,800 currently and 51,000 employees. But Weston, who will become chairman of Boots, signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain. "We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said. The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges, which it sold in 2022 for $4bn. The family is also the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark. The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost £19bn. title: Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
description: Tory leader says her party is "coming back", as she aims to convince voters it has changed after 2024 election defeat.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The big test facing Kemi Badenoch after her conference speech Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged to scrap inheritance tax (IHT) on family homes while also allowing couples to leave £1m tax-free, in her keynote speech at the party's conference in Birmingham. Badenoch added her ambition would be for a Conservative government to abolish IHT "as soon as we can afford it", but said she could not currently propose this due to spending commitments on defence, prisons and the economy. Badenoch also used her speech to try to make clear how the Tories differed to Labour and Reform UK. She pitched them as the "no-nonsense party" compared to the Reform UK "circus" and accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to "live in the past". Tories united behind Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters Why Tories are talking about winning the next election What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits? Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country. Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation". She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election. In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform. "This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party." With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that". Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back". Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again." One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform. She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home." Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that. "People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter." She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English". In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away". In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT. As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country". She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home. "On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional £1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half." The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around £6bn a year and believe they have identified £71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts. Under the current rules, estates worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold. Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other. In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around £7bn for the government. Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it". Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed. "Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead." Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%". The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a £500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000. "The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country." Kemi Badenoch with her husband, Hamish Badenoch, leaving the stage after delivering her keynote speech Elsewhere in her speech, Badenoch referred to other policies the party has announced in recent days. These include a £10bn anti-missile defence system, 50,000 new prison places and halving the rate of employer national insurance on earnings for people aged between 21 to 24. They also pledged to scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year. Another policy to be scrapped would be the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), dubbed the "mansion tax". This is due to take effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey responded to the speech by saying Badenoch had been "lecturing the country on fiscal responsibility while making tens of billions in unfunded

title: Five arrested for inciting racial hatred outside Jewish group's headquarters, says Met
description: A "spontaneous protest" was staged outside the office of the Board of Deputies, the Met Police says.
body: Two more people were arrested at a separate pro-Palestinian protest in central London Five people have been arrested on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London, the Metropolitan Police said. The force said they were detained when a "spontaneous protest" was staged outside the Camden headquarters of the UK's largest Jewish community group. Elsewhere, two people were arrested at a larger student pro-Palestinian protest in central London - one for breach of conditions and a second for common assault. The arrests came as a number of student pro-Palestinian protests were taking place in London three years on from the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, in which around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken as hostages by the militant group. Israel responded to the attack by launching a military offensive in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Footage from the demonstration outside the Board of Deputies' Camden office showed a few dozen protesters, several of whom were wearing face coverings. In a statement following the arrests, the Board of Deputies said the group "would not be threatened or intimidated" and thanked police for their "swift" response. Slogans "calling for intifada" were chanted during the protest, according to the Met. The five arrested remain in custody. The term intifada came into popular use during the Palestinian uprising against Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1987. Jewish groups have described the term as a call for violence against Jewish people. Pro-Palestinian groups have said it is a call for peaceful resistance to Israel's occupation. The Board of Deputies is set to hold a vigil in Richmond Terrace, near Whitehall in central London, later on Wednesday. Separately, two people were arrested at a student pro-Palestinian march, which went from Lincoln's Inn Fields to Russell Square and was attended by around 100 people. Around 100 pro-Palestinian demonstrators attended a march despite calls for it to be postponed The Met said it ended ahead of a police-enforced dispersal time, which was imposed when organisers rejected calls to move it from 7 October. Counter-demonstrators carrying Israeli flags also gathered in Russell Square. There were some minor scuffles between the two groups. Pro-Palestinian protesters were heard chanting "Zionists not welcome here" and "free Palestine from the river to the sea". Some use the chant as a call for Palestinian control of all land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, including Israel. Critics say the slogan is a call for the destruction of the state of Israel. That interpretation is disputed by pro-Palestinian activists, who say that most people chanting it are calling for an end to Israel's occupation of the West Bank and blockade of Gaza, not the destruction of Israel itself.
