title: Man jailed for killing former partner days after his release
description: Robert Sabat is given a 17-year-minimum jail term for the fatal stabbing of his former partner.
body: Robert Sabat killed Dickiesha Nurse days after he was released on licence after serving 40% of a sentence for knife possession and harassment A violent offender who was released from jail the day after he was sentenced stabbed his former partner and then begged to be returned to prison because he was going to "go on a murder spree", the Old Bailey has heard. Robert Sabat, 60, pleaded guilty to murdering 42-year-old mother-of-two Dickiesha Nurse, who he stabbed at her flat in Tulse Hill, south London, last October. He had been released on licence from HMP Wandsworth on 17 October 2025 after being sentenced the day before to a 12-month jail term for possession of a bladed article and harassment. He had been in prison on remand since May 2025 when he was freed. Sabat, of Balham, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years. When he was released in October 2025, Sabat had served 40% of his 12-month sentence instead of the previous 50% requirement, in line with the government's change to offenders' automatic release dates, which began the month before, external. Last week, the Sentencing Act 2026, external replaced this policy and some prisoners can now be released after they have served a third of their sentence. When he was arrested on suspicion of Nurse's murder, Sabat claimed he had killed before and was planning a "murder spree". He told officers: "I'm a murderer, I don't want to come back out, I wanna go to jail... I've been let out a week. "Let me back... I'm happy in there, I've done wrong. I killed before and got away with it. "I've murdered three people so far. I'm gonna go on a murder spree." Outlining the facts of the case, prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said Sabat and Nurse had been in a relationship and had known each other for many years as the defendant was brought up by her father. Two days after Sabat was released from prison, Nurse's children visited her and on returning home, told their father her "friend or cousin" had been there. On 22 October, Nurse told a neighbour Sabat was at her address and would not leave. Another neighbour saw her in the street shouting: "Get out of my house." Two days later, a neighbour heard a single scream coming from the victim's home, the court heard. Nurse was last seen on CCTV on 25 October. Her children tried to visit the following day but got no response when they knocked on her door. Her family raised concerns on 27 October and paramedics entered the flat, where the defendant, armed with a knife, charged at a paramedic, the court heard. The London Ambulance Service crew and family members withdrew from the property and police were called, Farrelly said. Soon after, armed officers forced entry to the property and used Tasers as they detained Sabat. Farrelly said officers found Nurse on a bed with a pillow over her face and with multiple stab wounds to the face. She was pronounced dead at the scene. A post-mortem examination found she had sustained about eight stab wounds, including to the left side of her face, neck and hands. Police recovered from the flat a knife with Nurse's blood on it, a bag marked "HMP valuables" and prison records in Sabat's name. In mitigation, Alisdair Williamson KC said Sabat had lived "on the margins" with spells in jail and had struggled with his mental health, depression and anxiety. In a victim impact statement, Nurse's sister Samantha Carvalho described Sabat as a "menace to society", and said the "heartlessness" of the killing was "impossible to comprehend". Her mother Claudette McBean described her daughter as kind, loving and the "life and soul of the party". Farrelly said the defendant had convictions dating back to 1987, including for burglary, assault, wounding with intent, knife possession, and harassment of an ex-partner. In 2013, he was made subject to a non-molestation order of a former partner and in August 2023 he was given a restraining order after being cleared of attempted murder after the complainant – his landlady – failed to attend court. title: How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal
description: How a team of South Africa camera operators discovered Australia's sandpapergate scandal as it happened.
body: The Sandpapergate scandal of 2018 was voted as the third-biggest in Test history in a recent BBC Sport poll According to the man who helped catch them, it was blind luck. Sandpapergate, the scandal that engulfed Australia eight years ago, was blatant cheating played out in real time on live television to a global audience. As the Aussies prepare for their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering controversy in Cape Town, the director of the TV coverage that day admits serendipity took down Steve Smith and co. "The way the Australians were caught was an absolute fluke," Alvin Naicker, in charge of SuperSport's live broadcast from Newlands, tells BBC Sport. Not just one fluke, but a series of them. That the "leadership group" of the Australian team hatched their plan during the lunch break on that Saturday afternoon in March 2018; that an alert camera operator lingered on Cameron Bancroft when others would have turned their attention elsewhere; that the big-screen controller showed in the ground what was also being broadcast to millions around the world. In understanding how Bancroft was rumbled, a little knowledge of how live cricket is shown on TV is helpful. "Coverage of rugby and football is very coordinated. It's camera one and two, then when the ball is dead you tell the story with close-up shots," explains Naicker, a highly respected and popular figure in the TV industry with more than 30 years' experience. "Because cricket has so much dead time, there is a lot more storytelling. There are between 80 and 100 people coming together and putting the story together in a matter of seconds, coordinated by the director." Captain Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Bancroft later explained they cooked up the ball-tampering plot during lunch on the third day of the third Test. Reverse-swing had been a key factor in the first two Tests of a bad-tempered series: Warner clashed with Quinton de Kock in the first Test in Durban, then Smith was involved in an altercation with Kagiso Rabada in the second. Australia were exposed before the afternoon session was done, thanks to Naicker and his team. At the time, SuperSport were not on the lookout for cheating, despite the shenanigans of the first two Tests. "No one mentioned anything to me," says Naicker. "The first Test in Durban spiralled out of control in terms of behaviour, then in Port Elizabeth for the second Test, there were still some fireworks going on. We still didn't understand." Reports written live by ESPNCricinfo suggest the ball began reversing in the first hour after lunch, 35 overs into the South Africa second innings. In the 43rd over, Bancroft was caught in the act. "The ball went to the wicketkeeper, then to Bancroft and he was shining the ball," says Naicker. "First it was on his pants, then the next ball, the cameraman happened to stay on Bancroft because he was not shining the ball on his pants, but he was rubbing the ball on his palm. "When he threw the ball on, he put his hand in his pocket. The cameraman - and these are big, big lens cameras - he zoomed into his pocket. The slow-mo operator looked at it, spooled it back and forth, then zoomed in and could see the yellow spot." Cameron Bancroft is seen hiding a yellow piece of sandpaper down his trousers The umpires inspect the ball as Cameron Bancroft looks on Test cricket's biggest scandals - your results revealed TMS Top 10: Cricket scandals Bancroft's work on the ball was not shown live, but as a replay later in the over. Inside Newlands, the operator of the big screen – working independently from Naicker – showed the same footage. "They take a feed from broadcast but they also have to insert their own graphics and commercialisation," says Naicker. "Between deliveries they tend to stay with live play, then at the end of the over they go to their commercials or whatever in the stadium. It was quite fortunate that when we showed it, it was in between deliveries, not at the end of the over." Bancroft would later admit he "panicked" when he saw himself on the big screen. Comically, he hid the sandpaper inside his trousers. SuperSport caught that, too. "When Bancroft looked up at the screen and saw it, he removed it and put it in his jocks," says Naicker. "The cameraman recorded it. It still wasn't live, we played a replay." Bancroft, with Smith by his side, was challenged by on-field umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong. The opener turned out his pockets, revealing only a black bag for his sunglasses. The ball was not changed and Australia were not given a run penalty. Play continued, yet SuperSport were on to what had happened. "Australia coach Darren Lehmann was on the walkie-talkie to 12th man Peter Handscomb, who went on to the field, then the umpires get involved," says Naicker. "An entire team of cameramen played their part. There was one following the ball, one on Handscomb, one on Lehmann, one on Warner. They all told a story that I happened to put together with this great team of replay operators." As for Naicker, there was no hesitation in airing what his team had captured, even with the realisation of the magnitude of what was unfolding. "A lot of people who watch cricket on SuperSport will know we are quite brave in terms of being quite creative and editorially sound," he says. "It was a natural instinct. It wasn't something I previewed with 10 other people to say 'What do you think, should we show it?' I just went for it." The footage was pored over by Naicker's team of commentators, while his phone was "WhatsApping off the hook" with messages from around the world, asking him to show it again and again. Replays drew the attention of the third umpire, Englishman Ian Gould. "He's got comms with me while I'm directing," says Naicker. "There was a moment when he asked me 'I think that's enough now, do you mind not showing it?' "My response to him was &#x2

title: Footage shows Dexter 'kill room' murderer's arrest
description: Benjamin Day lured his victim to a plastic-lined room at an Airbnb in Tividale, in the West Midlands.
body: This video can not be played Police release video from Dexter killer's arrest Police have released bodycam footage of the moment a university forensics student was arrested for murdering a woman after a court heard he had stabbed her to death in a "kill room" copied from US TV show Dexter. The video shows Benjamin Day, who cut open his hand while attempting to dismember the body of Maria Saceanu, lying to officers after the killing, claiming to have been bitten by a wild dog or a fox. Day, 20, changed his plea at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Tuesday to admit to murdering the 24-year-old Romanian. A trial heard his victim, who had been a sex worker, had been lured to a plastic-lined room at an Airbnb in Tividale, in the West Midlands, where she suffered 78 knife wounds. The court heard Day left the Airbnb at about 12:30 GMT on 21 December, before walking some distance away to call 999 at 12:50 where he asked for medical help. Footage released by police on Wednesday shows the University of Worcester student near the junction of Highview Street and Brewery Street in Dudley where he is bleeding from his wound. Woman denies abortion clinic buffer zone charges Allergies leave blind woman without guide dog Landlord's heartbreak as pub shuts down Asked by an officer if he had been set up and attacked, Day said he had been injured by an animal that "might have been a fox". He also falsely claimed to be unable to remember where he had parked his car, which was outside the house containing his victim's body. During his conversations with police, Day said he had driven over to the Dudley area to look for a "random girl" in a bar. Maria Saceanu was lured to a "kill room" inspired by the US TV show Dexter In a further clip released by West Midlands Police, Day is seen wearing a Dexter-style khaki top while lying on a bed at Dudley's Russells Hall Hospital where he was arrested at 03:42. He is also heard saying: "I have got four fingers thankfully." Day, of Yeadon Close, Redditch, Worcestershire, has been remanded in custody and faces a mandatory life sentence when he is sentenced on 4 December. Det Insp Matt Marston, from West Midlands Police's Major Crime Team, who led the investigation, said: "Day had an obsessive personality and had become obsessed with the character Dexter. "He planned this murder in meticulous detail. It was a pre-planned brutal attack on a defenceless woman lured to the room he had rented. "Day had flagged down officers where he offered them a fabricated story about the reason why he had received an injury to his hand. "Officers were suspicious and he was quickly detained. "The details of this case shocked experienced officers and our thoughts continue to go out to the heartbroken family of Maria at this time." Day told officers the wound to his hand could have been caused by a fox Jonathan Roe from the Crown Prosecution Service added that Day had originally tried to blame Saceanu for her own death by alleging she attacked him first. He said: "The evidence presented by the prosecution exposed those claims for the lies they were, and he has rightly been forced to accept responsibility for her murder. "Forensic evidence and pathology were central to this case, and the entire prosecution team was determined to secure justice for Maria." He added that Day's guilty plea on day two of his trial had spared Maria's family "the trauma of a prolonged trial process". title: Rob Burrow would be proud of my knighthood, says Kevin Sinfield
description: Sir Kevin Sinfield is knighted by the Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle.
body: Sir Kevin Sinfield is made a knight bachelor by the Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle Sir Kevin Sinfield has said his late friend Rob Burrow would be "laughing" but "enormously proud" to see him receive a knighthood. The former England rugby league captain and motor neurone disease (MND) campaigner was one of 60 people to receive honours from the Prince of Wales at an investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle earlier. Sir Kevin, who has raised more than £11m for charity, received a knighthood for his services to the MND community, as well as for services to league and union rugby. He said he was "massively humbled by the whole experience" and "very proud to accept it on behalf of the MND community and their families". The 46-year-old said the prince, who presented Sir Kevin and Burrow with their CBEs at Headingley Stadium in 2024, had been "fantastically supportive" of their campaign. William, alongside the Princess of Wales, surprised Sir Kevin on the third day of his 7 in 7: The Grand Finale challenge last week, during which he completed seven ultra-marathons in seven days. It was inspired by Burrow, his late Leeds Rhinos team-mate and friend, who died in 2024 after living with MND for four years. Sir Kevin said: "I think [Prince William] champions pulling communities together, and I have seen how the MND community have come together on the back of Rob's diagnosis and several other high-profile sportspeople over the last six or seven years. "So his support and, obviously, Princess Catherine's as well, they've been wonderful and bring a real credibility to what we're trying to do." This video can not be played Watch: The moment Kevin Sinfield became Sir Kev Asked how Burrow would have felt to see him receiving a knighthood, Sir Kevin said: "I think he'd be laughing. "I think he'd be enormously proud of the support behind a campaign that he started, and we continue in his name. "I think he'd be really proud of it, the support, and the way people got behind what we tried to do, especially Prince William and Princess Catherine, and several other high-profile figures across the UK, and the world. "On behalf of all the MND families, Rob would just be delighted at how we've pulled together." The honour recognises Sir Kevin's services to rugby league, rugby union and the MND community Sir Kevin said he would now like to plan a run in Australia and New Zealand next year, and "ensure that collaboration is taking place between nations that are working incredibly hard to try and find a cure and to look after families better". He said the reaction from the MND community to his knighthood had been "wonderful". "I felt very fortunate to have connected with a lot of families who are going through some real challenging times, yet still continue to be at the roadside or stopping me in the street for a chat to share their story. "So, I feel incredibly fortunate to be here today accepting this on their behalf." He said he had not got used to the title "Sir Kevin" yet, adding: "I don't think I ever will. "It's really nice, but every time I hear that, I go straight back to why we started, and it was a run for a mate, with some mates, and that will never change, what we've been doing this last six or seven years." Olympic triathlon champion Alistair Brownlee, from Dewsbury, was also among recipients at the investiture. Alistair Brownlee, from Dewsbury, was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire by the Prince of Wales The double Olympic gold medal winner, who announced his retirement from the sport in late 2024, has been recognised for his services to triathlon and to charity. Brownlee last year called the OBE a "great privilege". Speaking at the time about his work with the Brownlee Foundation charity, Brownlee said: "I am really proud of the role, hopefully, I've had in inspiring thousands of children to get into sport and live healthier lifestyles." title: Tropical Storm Isaias forecast to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026
description: El Niño has led to an eerily quiet season so far but the first Atlantic hurricane of the year is now set to impact the southern USA.
body: Satellite imagery shows thunderstorms clumping together to form Tropical Storm Isaias. Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf of Mexico and looks likely to strengthen into the first Atlantic hurricane of this year. It is expected to reach hurricane strength late on Wednesday or early Thursday with forecasts suggesting it could then intensify to a category two storm. It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected on Friday or Saturday. Parts of Mexico could also see gusty winds and heavy rain as the storm moves northwards and eastwards. Isaias will bring an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led so far to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season with development suppressed by the historic El Niño that continues to grow in the Pacific. Hurricanes: Inside the deadly storms In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that Tropical Storm Isaias will strengthen rapidly and is likely to reach hurricane strength during Wednesday night. It will intensify further to a category 2 storm by Friday morning. Parts of Mexico will feel the first impacts as the storm swirls out at sea, with 4in (100mm) of rain possible around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula, accompanied by strong winds. Isaias will then make landfall on the Gulf Coast - probably in Mississippi, Alabama or Florida - late on Friday or early on Saturday. Damaging winds, torrential rain and coastal flooding are the major risks from the developing hurricane Forecasters predict that 3-6in (75-150mm) of rain could fall across the Gulf Coast, from south-east Louisiana to the north-west of Florida. A few places could see up to 10in (250mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding. Dangerous winds are anticipated with the chance of a storm surge which could inundate low-lying coastal areas. The US National Weather Service says it expects to issue Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches later on Wednesday with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis declaring a state of emergency across 25 north Florida counties over concerns about potential impacts. As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken but it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather. Between 1-3in (25-75mm) of rain is forecast for large swathes of the south-east USA - as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas - with isolated totals of 5in (125mm). Hurricane Milton was the last hurricane to make landfall in the USA, in October 2024. No hurricanes made landfall in 2025 Forecasters in the US predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average due to the developing strong El Niño in the Pacific Ocean. Eight to 14 named storms are forecast, three to six of which would become hurricanes, including one to three major hurricanes. So far it seems this quiet forecast has come to pass. Isaias is the ninth tropical storm of the Atlantic season, but will be the first to become a hurricane. On 12 September the season set a new record for the latest date reached without a hurricane forming since the start of the satellite era in the 1960s. Almost another month has passed without one since then. A major reason for this is the very strong El Niño that is continuing to intensify over the Pacific. The heat released into the atmosphere by the very warm seas in the eastern tropical Pacific has weather impacts that ripple across the globe. It can disrupt wind patterns above the Caribbean and the Atlantic leading to increased wind shear, meaning winds that blow at different speeds and directions at different levels in the atmosphere. This can rip storms apart before they have time to strengthen. However this is not the only factor that determines whether hurricanes will form. While it reduces the odds, it does not make it impossible - as Isaias proves. Isaias has formed over the Gulf of Mexico where sea temperatures are currently 30-31C - around 2C higher than normal. It is the warm ocean that gives hurricanes their fuel, providing energy and moisture allowing them to grow. There is currently limited wind shear meaning the storm has chance to strengthen. However, wind shear is expected to increase dramatically in the 24 hours before Isaias makes landfall which may limit how intense it can become. However the range of factors influencing hurricane development is complex and exact forecasts are likely to shift slightly over the coming days. title: Watch: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
description: France has halted the use of stun grenades after a 15-year-old boys hand was blown off during student protests.
body: This video can not be played France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests after a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off earlier this week in Lens. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of the incident had been "clarified". Rights groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers who have been protesting against old buildings, a lack of teachers and overcrowded classrooms all week. Police unions have said they need non-lethal options such as stun grenades to protect officers in these increasingly violent situations. title: Watch: Why family who lived at site of 7 October attack want to return
description: The BBC's Middle East correspondent visits kibbutz Nir Oz - one of the worst hit places during the 7 October 2023 attacks.
body: This video can not be played As Israel marks the third anniversary of the 7 October Hamas attacks, the BBC has visited residents of kibbutz Nir Oz - one of the worst hit places. Sitting just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border, 41 Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby. Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies. Fourteen of those hostages were taken alive and killed in captivity. During the 7 October attack, about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. The ensuing war between Israel and Hamas has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza according to the Hamas-run health ministry – whose overall figures are seen as accurate by the UN. title: King Charles and Elton John in the audience for Apple music workshop
description: Charles and Sir Elton visit an Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs music event offering industry skills to young people.
body: King Charles has visited a hi-tech music workshop for young people, in a collaboration between his King's Trust charity and technology firm Apple. Pop royalty, in the form of Sir Elton John, was a special guest at the event, sitting beside the King, as they listened to a short performance from singer-songwriter Skye Newman. The event was held at a music hall in Apple's headquarters building, in the restored Battersea Power Station in south west London. The project being backed by the King is intended to equip young people with practical skills to work in the creative industries. The King met young people getting technical skills for careers in creative industries The King was introduced to Prophet Guillory, Apple Music's head of artist services, tools and community, who was praised for his work as a mentor for young people. "Wow, you did your homework," Prophet said, when the King seemed familiar with his efforts. The King was introduced to young performers at the event. Another young musician said the problem was getting the money together to launch creative ideas. (Left to right) David Furnish, Sir Elton, the King and Tim Cook heard the performance Young performer Skye Newman faced what must have seemed like a very unusual X-Factor style panel - King Charles, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish and Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook. The music workshop was part of a project between Apple and the King's Trust Creative Labs, and is the latest link-up between the royals and the Californian tech giant. Last year, the King revealed a playlist of 17 of his favourite tracks, which was issued on Apple Music. The King didn't include Sir Elton John in any of those choices - but the pop star has been a long-time supporter of the King's Trust charity, which was previously known as the Prince's Trust. Now in its 50th year, the charity was set up to give opportunities to deprived and marginalised young people - and has so far helped 1.3 million people across the UK. The tie-up with Apple shows the changing demands for work skills, including using the latest technology for young people wanting to build careers in the music and creative industries. There was also a royal link with Battersea Power Station - as that had once provided the electricity for Buckingham Palace. In the power station's control room, the link to the Palace had been discreetly labelled as "Carnaby Street", in case any intruders had ever been tempted to switch off the Palace lights. title: Ten people linked to Kenya's first-ever Ebola case quarantined as screening concerns grow
description: The patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, drove to Uganda and eventually flew to Kenya.
body: Those placed at the Ebola isolation facility are under constant observation Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, health officials in the East African nation say. They are also trying to trace 57 other contacts of the Kenyan patient after he travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, dying in hospital in Nairobi on Monday. This is the East African nation's first-ever Ebola case and there is now growing concern about the country's screening measures. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention chief has told the BBC that despite being sick for a month, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, driving to Uganda and eventually flying to Kenya without his sickness being detected. "We know that he left Buta, a city in [northern] DR Congo, to drive to Kisangani. And from Kisangani, he took a flight to Beni. From Beni, he drove to Uganda. And from Uganda, he took a flight to Nairobi," Jean Kaseya told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme. "What are symptoms he was presenting? Why was he not detected?" he asked. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way. Kaseya said the Africa CDC was investigating the case, alongside the Congolese authorities. A team from the organisation was also due to meet the Kenyan health authorities. What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? Kenya's health ministry official Patrick Amoth said the patient might have passed screening after taking medications that masked his symptoms. After arriving at the airport in Kenya's capital, he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city where he died, and was buried on Tuesday in line with health safety guidelines. Kenyan authorities have urged people not to panic, with the health ministry assuring of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings. But Dr Dennis Miskellah, a representative from Kenya's main doctors' union, said the Ebola case did not come as a surprise to him and most health workers. He told the BBC's Newsday programme that he had witnessed "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenyan's main airport. "How could you have been sick for almost a month plus in DR Congo, come all the way to the country through not just any small border point, but the main entry point, the main gateway into the country and pass unnoticed? "That's the question that most Kenyans are asking." The health ministry says it has intensified measures to contain the spread, with a joint response involving county administrations, humanitarian partners and others. President William Ruto has said that surveillance and rapid response teams are on the ground, building on the systems that the country adopted following the outbreak in DR Congo in May. His spokesman said Kenya had the capacity to detect, isolate and manage suspected cases, adding that so far more than 650,000 travellers had been screened and 267 samples tested. Facilities in four main hospitals have been designated for the management of Ebola patients, including at the Nairobi Hospital, where the first Ebola patient died. Kenya has established isolation facilities in some hospitals In June, a US plan to establish an Ebola treatment facility at a military base in the central Kenyan town of Nanyuki sparked concern, with Kenyans reacting furiously about the risks of cross-border infection. The plan was halted by the courts. On Wednesday, Health Minister Aden Duale told local television station NTV that pending the outcome of the court case, the government was considering turning the facility into the "first" infectious disease hospital in the region, to deal with outbreaks like Ebola. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease. Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August. On Tuesday, Uganda's health ministry emphasised that the country remained free of Ebola and was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health". It said the Kenyan Ebola patient had transited through the country for less than 24 hours and screening teams had "observed he had a normal temperature at the time of departure". According to Africa CDC chief, his organisation was working with all the countries in the region to reinforce response mechanisms. Kasiye said Kenya was "well prepared" and was therefore able to immediately receive the case, "but it is not the case for all other countries". "It means the regional approach is more important today to stop this outbreak." However, Kasiye said there was no quick testing available at border points and the taking of temperatures was unreliable as medication is able to stop a fever. "I have to make it clear - we don't have diagnostics to test for Ebola. It's just about temperature," he said. Dr Miskellah, from the Kenyan doctors' union, said he was concerned that governments were counting on the "honesty and full co-operation of the travellers to self-declare, to say the truth" about their health. This was however undermined by a lack of proper health education to destigmatise the virus, meaning people often wanted to hide their symptoms, he said. title: Neglect case childminder was 'master manipulator', say parents
description: Families say it was traumatic to learn that their children were not being properly cared for by Amanda Mathewson.
body: This video can not be played Amanda Mathewson leaves Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court Parents whose children were cared for by a childminder who has admitted neglect charges have described her as a "master manipulator". Amanda Mathewson had been looking after many more children than she was allowed to - and at one stage left 27 youngsters alone and unsupervised at her home in Dunfermline. Families told BBC Scotland that the 55-year-old had been "loved and trusted" in the community before her crimes came to light. And they said it had been "incredibly traumatic" to learn that their children had not been getting cared for properly. Mathewson pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court on Tuesday to wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health. She will be sentenced next month. Mathewson has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, providing services at her home for children under the age of 16. One parent said she was regarded as "one of the best in the area". "She was loved and trusted throughout the community," they told the BBC. "Building an apparently unshakeable reputation as friendly, caring and trustworthy with the adults she encountered outside her home was part of how she concealed what was happening." Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect Another parent said they considered Mathewson to be "a good friend". "Finding out what happened was incredibly traumatic both for us and the other families," they told BBC Radio Scotland's Mornings programme. "We have had to rewrite eight years of history and have lost happy memories because the belief we had, that our children were being cared for, was not true. "This woman was a master manipulator and she has got away with these things for years." Mathewson was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children. At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12 in her care, as well as 10 children under primary school age and two children under the age of one. The case was heard at at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court The investigation found discrepancies in the number of children in Mathewson's care and the number of children she was seen with on multiple occasions. The court heard parents raised concerns their children had not eaten while in the childminder's care due to their clothes staying in "pristine condition", and that it was a general theme that their children would return home thirsty. Some parents also reported their children came home in dirty nappies or with dry faeces in their underwear. Court documents said Mathewson always had loud music playing and did not let parents enter her home at drop-off time in an attempt to "conceal how oversubscribed she was". Parents said they noticed distress and asked questions but were always reassured by Mathewson, who pre-empted their concerns with "a plausible explanation". "This was sustained, deliberate deception that concealed neglect from families and professionals alike," one parent told the BBC. "If she could build and manipulate the trust of adults across an entire community so effectively, think about how little power babies and young children had behind those closed doors." More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East A Care Inspectorate report published in August 2023 said Mathewson was registered to provide care for a maximum of eight children at any one time. It included conditions that a maximum of six children could be under the age of 12, no more than three could be under school age, and no more than one could be under 12-months-old. An unannounced inspection took place about a year before her arrest. It rated areas including care, learning and the setting as "very good" - the second-highest level in the quality scale. The report said "children were cared for in a comfortable, welcoming and homely environment" and "were cared for with warmth, kindness and a nurturing approach". But after suspicions were raised, parents worked together to provide evidence to the police. One parent said: "I cannot tell you what the first few months were like after all of this came to light. "Every single parent involved has gone over in their head every conversation and any comment their child ever made - anything at the time seemed innocent enough but in hindsight could have been a red flag." A spokesperson for the Care Inspectorate said it was a "distressing case" and they had implemented changes as a result. title: Yorkshire Water admits sewage scheme falls short
description: The firm says the scheme to reduce storm overflow discharges has not performed as expected.
body: Yorkshire Water has admitted the Ripon River Ure sewerage scheme has fallen short of its promise to reduce storm overflow discharge Yorkshire Water has admitted a £1.5m scheme to reduce storm overflow discharges into a North Yorkshire river has not performed as expected. When the investment was announced in 2024 for the River Ure in Ripon, the water company said the scheme would reduce the issue by about 75%. But it said the number of recorded discharges from its Clock Tower combined sewer overflow (CSO), near the Ripon by-pass bridge, fell from 75 in 2021 to 43 in 2025, a reduction of about 43%. The company has described the result as "disappointing", but stressed that comparing individual years was complicated by rainfall levels. "[2025] was a particularly dry year, which will have further contributed to a decrease in discharges," a Yorkshire Water spokesperson said. "As such, whilst there has been a reduction, the scheme did not perform as expected, which is disappointing." Combined sewer overflows are designed as pressure-relief points on sewer networks which carry both wastewater and rainwater. During heavy rainfall, they can discharge into watercourses to prevent overloaded sewers backing up into homes, businesses and streets. Such discharges can be permitted by the Environment Agency under specified circumstances. Recent testing by campaign group Stop Ure Pollution and the Yorkshire Dales Rivers Trust further upstream has raised concerns about bacteria and other pollution in the river, the Local Democracy Service reports. The Skipton and Ripon branch of the North Yorkshire Green Party has now submitted an Environmental Information Regulations request, seeking information held by Yorkshire Water about the performance of the Clock Tower scheme and changes in discharges following work carried out in 2025. Green Party councillor Andy Brown said the levels of sewage going in the rivers "is deeply disgusting" and called the latest testing further upstream "far from reassuring". He said campaigners and organisations, including Ripon City Council, would continue pressing for improvements. "Yorkshire Water must play its part," he said. "It must act, and it must deliver the facts – straight-up and undiluted." Yorkshire Water said it was investigating further projects in Ripon as part of a £1.5bn investment programme aimed at reducing storm overflow use. "We know there is much more to do to protect local watercourses," the spokesperson said. Listen to highlights from North Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. title: Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
description: Asahi, Kirin and Suntory confirmed their premises were searched by Japanese competition authorities.
body: Japanese officials have raided the country's biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages. Asahi, Kirin and Suntory Spirits confirmed to the BBC their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission, adding that they would fully cooperate with the government authority. There are reports Sapporo Breweries was also raided. The firm has been contacted for comment. Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory is not publicly-listed. According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022. All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation. Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched "on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act". It said it takes the matter "very seriously", adding it would "fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission's investigation and any requests for cooperation". Kirin Holdings said: "At present, the impact of this matter on the company's financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise." A spokesperson for Suntory confirmed "an on-site inspection" had taken place "in connection with a potential violation of Japan's Antimonopoly Act relating to domestic alcohol trade practices". The company said: "We sincerely apologise for any concern or inconvenience this situation may cause to our customers, business partners, and other stakeholders. We will cooperate fully with the JFTC's investigation." Asahi Breweries said it was "subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission". It added: "We will fully cooperate with the commission." The Japan Fair Trade Commission has been contacted for comment. title: Reform internal inquiry says party did not break law over donations sting
description: Officials were recorded by undercover journalists discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.
body: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage (right) and Dan Jukes both feature in the undercover filming An internal investigation by Reform UK has said the party did not breach electoral law when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party. Reform leader Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and the party's head of policy James Orr both stood down pending the outcome of the inquiry. The investigation concluded that neither of the men did anything that constitutes a breach of the law. The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a separate criminal investigation into Reform UK, over allegations it broke foreign funding laws. It came after undercover filming, carried out by Verbatim Investigations and broadcast by Channel 4 News, showed the two aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000. It is understood Reform UK will wait until the conclusion of the police investigation before deciding the futures of Jukes and Orr. In the Channel 4 News report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father would not be able to directly donate to the party within the law. Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK. Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father. Elsewhere, Orr suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns. Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them. Reform says it did not commission or pay for the polls. Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son. Farage previously told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation. Reform's investigation concluded no donation was made or accepted by the party and "the party's procedures for checking donors were never reached". The report says Jukes commissioned the three polls personally, describing him as a "contractor" and not an employee of Reform. It added there was "no evidence that any individual knowingly took part in an arrangement to facilitate a donation from an impermissible source". However, it found "people speaking for the party said things that were wrong, careless and in one instance untrue". The investigation also found "the party's arrangements allowed a sustained deception to reach its leader without anyone asking the questions that would have exposed it". It added that the party would implement changes to "prevent that from happening again". Jukes welcomed the findings of the investigation, saying he was "considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me". He added: "For now, I will continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities." Reform UK said the internal investigation "found no evidence that any laws were broken". "Reform UK takes its obligations on governance and conduct extremely seriously," the party said. "We consider that the production company - Verbatim - acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course." A spokesperson for Verbatim, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, previously said its investigation was carried out "to the highest journalistic standards". title: Widdecombe suspect accused of trying to break into Farage's home
description: Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court and was remanded in custody.
body: The man accused of murdering the former MP Ann Widdecombe in July has appeared in court faced with a new allegation of preparing terrorist acts, including trying to break into the home of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. Prosecutor Kashif Malik said Joshua Kerry, 28, is alleged to have carried out online reconnaissance of "prominent people and institutions... including identifying the home address of Nigel Farage". The prosecutor later told Westminster Magistrates' Court that damage was found on the doorframe at Farage's home address, adding: "the inference is that an attempt was made to gain entry to the house". Kerry was accompanied by four custody officers in the dock and was remanded in custody to appear at the Old Bailey on Friday. Kerry appeared in person the court. With a thick beard and wearing a grey sweatshirt and trousers, he spoke only to confirm his address in Rotherham and his date of birth. He was told he faced a new charge of preparing terrorist acts between 31 May 2024 and 8 July 2026 by carrying out research on targets and travelling to, and attempting to gain entry to, the home of Nigel Farage. The court heard that in April 2025 Nigel Farage's partner found that damage had been caused to their main front door at their house and a bottle of lighter fluid was found in the porch. Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman. Widdecombe was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries. She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019. title: Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry
description: The prize was given to the French and Japanese scientists for solving the mystery of life's asymmetry.
body: The winners are awarded the Nobel Prize medal and a share of 12.0 million Swedish Kroner ($1.25m; £900,000) The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry. The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image. For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image. But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other. In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms. You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other. And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules. When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies. So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm. Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life." The chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, Heiner Linke, explains how chiral molecules have mirror forms like our hands By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule. Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular." Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible. Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature, external describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule. In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed. "Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat". At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field. Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society". "Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added. Chirality is the foundation for animal features, like the way snail shells coil to the right Prof Angus Davison, from the University of Nottingham, studies the biology of chirality and said that the Nobel-winning chemistry could help reveal how and why life favours "one-handedness". "In ways that we don't yet quite understand, the chirality of the basic building blocks of life ends up making bodies that are themselves also chiral," he told BBC News. This was the foundation, he explained, of our hearts being on left hand side of our bodies and snail shells that coil to the right. Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said the research awarded this year's prize has become part of "our basic understanding of how chemistry functions". He said showing how a mirror image is created is "probably the most fundamental question in life - because somehow that happened four billion years ago when life was created. And now we have, for the first time, mimicked that in the lab". title: Ex-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed
description: Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham had their convictions overturned by the Court of Appeal.
body: Five former Barclays traders sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis have had their convictions overturned following a long-running legal battle. Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham were convicted following trials for manipulating the interest rates used for loans between banks. But their convictions were quashed on Wednesday by the Court of Appeal. The ruling came after two other former City traders had their convictions overturned last year, which has paved the way for others to appeal. The traders were cast by prosecutors as a symbol of banker greed amid public backlash and anger during the 2008 financial crisis. Merchant, Mathew, Pabon and Bermingham have all served various jail terms. Moryoussef was sentenced in his absence in 2018, never returned to the UK to serve time after France refused to extradite him. The prosecutions were over the manipulation of two key interest rate mechanisms: Libor and Euribor, which at the time were used to set borrowing costs on a range of loans such as mortgages and car finance deals. Mathew said the "strain" of what he had gone through had been a burden on him for the last 10 years. "Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it's about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened," the 45-year-old said. "I now have two children and this means a great deal to have the record corrected for their sake as well." Merchant, 55, added that he looked forward to moving on with life, but said part of that would be "ensuring that those responsible for what happened are held fully accountable". Lord Justice Edis said full reasons behind the overturned convictions would be given later on Wednesday. title: Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League
description: Senior figures within the English game are concerned that Manchester City could play in the Champions League next season even if they are relegated for breaching financial regulations.
body: Manchester City won the Champions League in 2023 with a 1-0 win over Inter Milan Senior figures within the English game are concerned that Manchester City could play in the Champions League next season even if they are relegated for breaching financial regulations. It centres around the possibility that City win the Champions League, which would provide qualification for the competition as titleholders - regardless of their status in the English domestic pyramid. BBC Sport has been told that there is no automatic mechanism to remove City from a European competition they qualify for on sporting merit. An independent commission found City guilty of all charges related to inflating sponsorship revenue by £830m by using sham contracts, as well as hiding other expenses worth an additional £90m. Without this, the independent commission said, City would have failed the profit and sustainability rules in all nine seasons between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. City continue to strenuously deny any wrongdoing, calling the outcome a "Premier League conspiracy". Last week the club lodged an appeal against the verdict. BBC Sport has spoken to a number of senior figures with the game in recent days who are concerned about prospect of City qualifying for the Champions League next season. The feeling is that if City do not win their appeal and are therefore handed a strong sanction, then being allowed to compete alongside Europe's elite, and receiving the financial rewards which come with it, would not be acceptable. The immediate issue surrounds the Uefa licence, which every club needs in order to play in Europe. One source said the issue of City's licence "had been raised" and that a solution "would require the sort of joined up thinking that's been a bit lacking so far". The licences are issued by the Football Association, though the process itself is delegated to the Premier League. The licences are based upon current information which does not take into account sanctions or breaches related to historical offences. If a club fulfils all minimum criteria required for admission, the licence cannot be refused. The key reasons a club may fail relate to overdue payables to other teams, players or outstanding tax liabilities. Match-fixing convictions within the last 10 years, or a integrity conflict related to multi-club ownership, are considered but would not apply to City. A source added that "licences are awarded on the basis of current financial performance, so the grounds to refuse one are unclear". If the verdict is upheld by the appeal board is it likely City will face severe sanctions, which could include heavy points deductions, a large fine and transfer embargos. The sanctioning hearing, which will determine the level of punishment City must face, is yet to be scheduled. While a points deduction could rule City out of qualifying by league position, it might still be achieved through cup competitions. Expelling City from the Premier League immediately is also an option which remains on the table. The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City Which clubs did Man City's 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market? Senior figures both in the English game and in European football are aware of how bad the optics would be if City face strong sanctions yet still play in the Champions League. It is exacerbated by doubts that the whole process - including an appeal against the sanction - is not guaranteed to be completed by the end of the season. The Premier League added new clauses to its regulations to set timeframes around disciplinary processes and appeals in the summer. If applicable, this would mean a judgement on the sanction must come no later than January. But there is no confirmation this applies to the City case. It is not just about City winning the Champions League, however. If they were to win the FA Cup or Carabao Cup - they play Brighton in the fourth round on 28 October - that would provide a place in the Europa League or the Conference League respectively. European football's governing body cannot take any action while the Premier League disciplinary process plays out, but it is understood that potential scenarios are likely to be discussed by the Uefa administration and the Uefa club financial control body (CFCB). The Premier League case found City guilty of five charges of breaching Uefa's profit and sustainability rules. Uefa may open a case in accordance with the disciplinary regulations to find a way to remove City's eligibility. But this does not provide certainly as City's offences are historical. In 2020, City successfully overturned their two-year ban from European club competitions handed down by Uefa. Uefa issued the ban after ruling City had committed "serious breaches" of financial fair play regulations between 2012 and 2016 - with the same period as the Premier League's investigation. But the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned the ban because the offences were "time-barred" under Uefa's rules. If City are not successful in their appeal and win the Champions League, the CFCB will have to find a disciplinary measure to remove the club from next season's competition. Yet with City already having won against Uefa through Cas once before, there is the concern they could do so again. title: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
description: The step comes after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
body: Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets across France on Tuesday, including in the capital Paris France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials. Several groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers. The disruption continued early on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to speak about the school protests in an evening address. Education Minister Édouard Geffray, appearing before France's National Assembly, said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils. Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt. Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions. "There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said, and confirmed the use of stun grenades was being suspended "until the facts surrounding this case have been clarified". The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille. Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks. The stun grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon, but sends out small rubber pellets when it detonates. "When there is suspicion of disproportionate force, there are always judicial investigations," Nuñez said, affirming that the government was "here to protect high school students". The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the decision to halt the use of stun grenades, saying it had been based "on emotion". "We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned. Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged. In a separate development, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg on Wednesday, reportedly while handling a mortar firework. Prosecutors said on Wednesday that an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort. French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer. The prime minister has condemned violence seen at some of the protests which began in mid-September - noting on Tuesday that 215 students, 85 staff, and 715 police officers had since been hurt. More than 6,500 people have been stopped or arrested in that time, according to the interior ministry. President Emmanuel Macron held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycées were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000. Students' unions put the number at 450,000 and have said a fourth round of protests is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities. The head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint." title: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
description: Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague has prompted calls for more transparency from Russia.
body: The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia. "So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday. In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled, and Russia's reporting of the death to the World Health Organization (WHO) was in line with standard practice. He accused the media of reporting "false information". The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request. Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death. They say that those who came into contact with the victim all tested negative and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. Earlier, the head of the WHO called for transparency from Russia. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said. According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early. People can be infected through: contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials the inhalation of respiratory particles Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm. Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death. The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier. Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents. But Russian officials have played down those reports. The country's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology". Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed. The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area. It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death. It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago. What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread? title: Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobs
description: The postal service firm wants to cut head office and other non-frontline jobs by the end of 2027.
body: Royal Mail said posties are protected from the proposed cuts Royal Mail has announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027 as it battles competition and falling demand for letter deliveries. The cuts at the postal service will represent about 2% of the 131,000-strong workforce. However, frontline postal workers - posties and drivers - are not part of the proposed restructuring. Royal Mail said the workforce reduction, designed to improve efficiency, would be achieved through voluntary redundancies and people choosing to leave the company. "These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers," said chief executive Alistair Cochrane. "The proposed changes will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues." It said it was in formal consultation with its unions, the Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Unite CMA, over the plans. The CWU said despite reassurances that there would be no compulsory redundancies, the announcement was "further evidence of a company that is demoralising staff and failing to deliver for customers and the wider community". 'We urge the government to confront the reality of a collapsing Royal Mail and intervene to save this national institution," deputy general secretary Martin Walsh told the BBC. Royal Mail has been struggling to meet its delivery targets for first and second class post, and has been fined by the regulator for missing targets in recent years. Just over 75% of first class letters were delivered on time in the year to the end of March, far off its target of 93%. Fewer people are sending letters, and the company has repeatedly said that its Universal Service Obligation (USO) – a legal requirement to deliver letters six days a week to every address in the UK – is outdated and needs reform. Royal Mail, which is a separate from the Post Office, has faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over the slowness of its letter delivery. This year, more than 100 MPs have written to regulator Ofcom and the business secretary asking for something to be done about the poor service their constituents say they are receiving. The firm has said it is investing £500m over the next five years as part of its improvement plan. Royal Mail is owned by Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky's EP Group, after his takeover was approved by shareholders at the end of April last year. Kretinsky has previously said he will not walk away from the requirement to deliver letters throughout the UK six days a week, as long as he is running the service. Do you work for Royal Mail? title: Greens face conference centre ban over Zionism motion
description: Brighton & Hove City Council says the motion is not compatible with its inclusion commitments.
body: The Green Party conference was held in October at the Brighton Centre The Green Party of England and Wales could be barred from holding future conferences at the Brighton Centre after the party passed a motion declaring Zionism was racism. The leader of Brighton & Hove City Council (BHCC), Labour's Bella Sankey, said she was "deeply concerned at the prospect of the Green Party returning to Brighton for future conferences". She claimed the motion was "divisive, discriminatory and wrong" and was not compatible with Brighton & Hove's commitments to be a welcoming and inclusive city. Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, said he would "not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of". BHCC owns and operates the Brighton Centre, which has hosted party political conferences for decades. Sankey told the BBC she was considering refusing to allow the Greens to hire the venue for future events. In a statement, she claimed the motion had "dangerously" conflated the right of Jewish self-determination with the actions of the Israeli government and risked "the safety of Jewish members and Jewish people more broadly". Sankey said people should never feel excluded due to their religion or beliefs Zionism is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland. Sankey went on to accuse the Green Party's leadership of a "dereliction of duty", adding "the Brighton Centre is owned by all of us in the city and should never be a place where people feel excluded due to their religion or beliefs". Green Party sources have rejected Sankey's characterisation of the motion. Polanski, who is Jewish, said that antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state "are, and must always be, completely distinct - blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe". He added: "It's our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK." The Brighton Centre was used by both the Greens and Liberal Democrats to host their autumn conferences this year. The venue has also hosted Labour's annual gathering in previous years. In 2017, the council's then-leader, Warren Morgan, who also represented Labour, threatened to ban his own party from holding its conference at the venue , externalover concerns that anti-semitic views had been aired.
