title: Rainmakers: The drones used to seed clouds
description: Cloud seeding is gaining attention as countries look to boost rainfall - will drones help?
body: Rainmaker's drones were used over Alaska this year On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall. Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology. The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours. This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below. Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska. Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat. "It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says. Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation." Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished, external", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers, external in more than three decades. Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles. Nevertheless, more than 50 countries, external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain. As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it. Augustus Doricko with a Rainmaker drone Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times. He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable." Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation. Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain. Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region." Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas. While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground. "With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center. What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges. In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive." Olivia Li is developing an alternative to silver iodide for cloud seeding What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li. While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound. "It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states. Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap." X-planes:

title: Jimmy McGovern claims young offender institution staff 'lazy'
description: The acclaimed writer says visiting young offenders institutions for his new drama left him "shocked".
body: McGovern said he was "appalled" after visiting young offender institutions to research his series Bafta-winning screenwriter Jimmy McGovern has said going into young offender institutions to research his new drama left him believing that keeping inmates isolated from each other for long periods allowed staff to "sit on their backsides all day and do nothing". McGovern said he was shocked after visiting "appalling" facilities while researching the latest series of his BBC drama Time. He told BBC North West Tonight those in young offender institutions (YOIs) were "banged up 23 hours a day" as part of a policy to stop offenders mixing, which gave officers an "excuse for being lazy". The Prison Officers' Association (POA) said that criticism was "unfair" to call officers lazy - and the policy was essential due to a daily threat of serious violence. Liverpool-born McGovern focused on adult prison estates in the first two series of BBC hit Time. But his third series, which sees a young cast star alongside David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran, follows young offenders through a system which McGovern said had "got to be better". The new series stars Siobhan Finneran, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and David Tennant In researching the series, which he wrote with Samuel Bailey, McGovern decided to get a behind-the-scenes look inside real-life YOIs. He said what he witnessed left him "truly shocked". "It is absolutely appalling," he said. "There's young boys with enormous energy banged up 23 hours a day [and] not allowed out of the cells. "They call them rooms, but they're cells. "And that's because of the keep-apart system." The keep-aparts policy is a method of separating young offenders in a bid to cut down on violence. The separation of young people in YOIs has been a topic of debate for a number of years - with the most recent review from HM Inspectorate of Prisons finding some held in YOIs were not permitted to leave their cells at all on some days, external. Boy 'left' on cell floor mattress for 22 hours 'Being segregated in prison made me want to hurt people' Prison failing children in custody, says charity 'Young offenders spend most of time in cells' McGovern said he recognised a need for "regimentation" in YOIs, but said he believed keep-aparts had increased following lockdown measures imposed during the Covid-19 pandemic. He said he believed the policy had allowed officers to avoid their duties. "It allows officers to sit on their backsides all day and do nothing," he said. "This happened before Covid, but Covid gave them the excuse to keep them banged up even more. "After Covid, they didn't want to see the kids, so it became worse." This video can not be played Watch the trailer for series 3 of Jimmy McGovern's drama Time He said he did not believe an increased use of the policy was due to staffing and funding challenges. "I'm afraid they're lazy," he said. "I've met wonderful prison officers, but I've seen some lazy ones and the keep-apart system enables them to be lazy with an excuse for being lazy." He said officers should be able to handle fights among the offenders and described conditions as "feral". "They're young boys bursting with energy [being] cooped up," he said. "When they get out, they want to fight, but [the staff] are prison officers. They should be able to handle that." He said he understood how "tough" the job was and that the young offenders in the facilities were "very, very difficult, so there has to be an element of regimentation [and] rules and regulations... but that's your job". While researching for the series, McGovern decided to get a behind-the-scenes look inside YOIs POA chairman Mark Fairhurst said the body shared some of the concerns raised by McGovern. "I have the utmost respect for Jimmy's work [and] he is right to highlight the serious problems within young offender institutions," he said. "YOIs are among the most violent prisons in the country. "Prison officers routinely put themselves in harm's way to prevent serious injury and save lives. "Many of my members have suffered life-changing injuries and been forced to leave the service following vicious assaults." He said the young offenders were "not simply naughty schoolchildren". "Keep-aparts are an essential safety measure in an environment where serious violence is a daily reality." Guilt, violence and impossible choices – what does it take to survive? Tense, gritty and heartbreaking – Jimmy McGovern's award-winning prison drama with an all-star cast He said officers at YOIs were "paying the price" of a lack of investment and staffing and it was "unfair to suggest staff are lazy". "They are stretched to breaking point by chronic under-staffing and unmanageable workloads," he said. "Without serious investment in staffing, facilities and rehabilitation, we will continue to see violent and chaotic YOIs - and prison officers paying the price." The Ministry of Justice said it did not "recognise these claims about our hardworking prison staff". "Their dedication helps ensure young offenders are punished as appropriate while being supported into rehabilitation, and we will deliver on our commitment to give children in prison more time outside their room," a spokesperson said. title: 'Wear more clothes if it's cold,' schools told as energy bills rise
description: The EA suggests cost-saving measures as it warns school gas and electricity bills are set to rise.
body: Staff and pupils at schools across Northern Ireland have been told to "wear more clothes" if it is cold in order to cut heating bills. Schools have been told by the Education Authority (EA) to reduce heating and lighting "wherever possible". The authority has said that school gas and electricity bills are set to rise by about £8m by March 2027. The EA has written to school heads warning that increasing costs will affect school energy bills. Kirsty Logan-Hall says her school is in an older building which presents energy efficiency challenges Rising energy costs are already affecting households across Northern Ireland. The impact of the US-Israel war with Iran is one of the factors behind the increase. The letter from the EA to head teachers said that "recent geopolitical events are expected to have a substantial impact on energy costs across the Education Authority (EA) during the 2026/27 financial year". It said that total school gas bills were expected to go up by 60% from £10.7m to £17m by March 2027. Meanwhile, total school electricity bills are expected to rise by 5% from £23.8m to £25.1m by March 2027. "Given the scale of the anticipated cost increases, we are asking all schools to review their energy usage and identify opportunities to reduce consumption wherever possible," the EA said. Among the measures the authority has suggested to schools are cutting heating use by an hour a day and switching off classroom lights to use natural daylight instead. Staff and pupils have also been advised to "wear more clothes" rather than turn the heating thermostat up if it is cold. But principals have told BBC News NI that it is not straightforward for schools to cut heating costs. The principal of Tullygally Primary School in Craigavon, Kirsty Logan-Hall, said that the school was "committed to promoting responsible energy consumption and regularly reinforce good practice with staff and pupils". "However, our ability to achieve significant reductions in energy usage is constrained by the nature of our estate," she said. "The school operates from an older building which presents inherent energy efficiency challenges. "In addition, our site is particularly spread out due to the accommodation and operational requirements associated with our specialist provision. "This necessitates the heating, lighting and ongoing use of multiple areas across the site throughout the school day to ensure appropriate learning environments, accessibility and pupil welfare. "It is important to recognise that there is limited scope for reducing energy consumption without adversely impacting the quality of provision, staff working conditions or the wellbeing of pupils, including those with additional needs." Claire Robinson says heating can't just be "turned off" in some parts of the school Meanwhile, the principal of Holy Evangelists Primary School in Dunmurry, Claire Robinson, said that energy costs were "ferocious". "We can't play around with the heating," she said. Parts of the school are relatively new and have underfloor heating. "Our classrooms can't drop below a certain temperature so we have to keep the heating on," Robinson said. "We can't just turn the heating off in some areas of the school." Robinson said that although the school was relatively new it had been given an energy efficiency rating of D due to the costs involved in running the heating system. title: 'It's torture and torment without answers' - dad of teen killed in blast
description: Leona Harper was one of 10 victims of an unexplained explosion at a service station four years ago.
body: Hugh Harper's teenage daughter Leona was one of 10 people who died in the Creeslough explosion four years ago Leona Harper's coat still hangs in the hallway of her family home. The soil from the pitch of the last game she played is still on her rugby boots. Four years on from the Creeslough explosion that claimed the 14-year-old schoolgirl's life, along with nine others, her father says their family remains "desperate for answers" about the events of that day. The blast happened at a service station in the County Donegal village on 7 October 2022. No official explanation has been given for the cause of the explosion, and no one has been charged in connection with the blast despite a number of arrests. Gardaí (Irish police) sent a second file to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) in April which is in addition to the primary file it forwarded to prosecutors last September. A commemoration service will be held on Wednesday in Creeslough for the 10 victims of the explosion. Hugh Harper said when Leona was born he was the "first to hold her" Leona had travelled to the village for a sleepover. She had been going to the shop at the service station for ice-cream when the blast occurred. Hugh Harper said that four years on, the family feels no closer to the truth about what happened to his daughter. "You are trying to establish answers yourself - but it takes you down a maze of rabbit holes," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme. "One question leads to another and it just feels like torture and torment. "We go home every evening to a house that's not the same - we are still trying to adjust to that. "You never expect something like this to come to your door as a parent and when it does, and it was so sudden, it is very hard." The Harpers, along with other victims and their families are campaigning for a public inquiry into the Creeslough explosion. In July, a meeting was held between families and the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin in Dublin. Hugh Harper said he believes a public inquiry is the only path to the full facts. "We are steadfast on that - a public inquiry is the only tool to compel people to be questioned under oath and get definitive answers. "Leona went to Creeslough on a Friday afternoon and went into a shop - that's the last we seen or heard of her alive. "Every day, we grieve for our little girl - we are stuck on the 7th October 2022. "When I get up in the morning, the first thought I have is about Leona and the questions around her last moments. "Until we have answers - our grief is frozen in time." Harper said the family will travel to Creeslough on Wednesday to remember their daughter and the other victims. "When Leona was born, I was the first to hold her. "I made her a promise that I would keep her safe and not let anything happen to her and unfortunately, I couldn't keep that promise. "But even though Leona is not physically here, I feel she is still with me. "And I will continue with the promise, even in death. I will do my best to protect her name and get to the bottom of exactly what happened in Creeslough that day. "I will leave no stone unturned." The force of the blast caused extensive damage to the roof of the service station In a statement to BBC News NI, a spokesperson for the Irish Department of Justice said: "As the fourth anniversary of the Creeslough explosion tragedy approaches Minister [Jim] O'Callaghan's thoughts continue to be with the families, loved ones, survivors and the wider community of Creeslough. "The focus of the Creeslough investigation remains on ensuring that the investigative processes are allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice so that the full facts can be established." 'Our grief is frozen in time' Gardaí said "the victims, their families and the community are in our thoughts" on the anniversary. "An Garda Síochána continues to appeal to any person with any information in relation to the fatal explosion – to please come forward and speak to the garda investigation team." A spokesperson for Ireland's Director of Public Prosecutions said it does not comment on individual cases. Those who died were Robert Garwe and his five-year-old daughter Shauna Flanagan-Garwe, 14-year-old Leona Harper, Hugh Kelly, Jessica Gallagher, Martin McGill, James O'Flaherty, Martina Martin, and Catherine O'Donnell and her 13-year-old son James Monaghan The 10 victims of the explosion included four men, three women, two teenagers and a five-year-old girl - all from the village or surrounding areas. Those who died were Robert Garwe and his five-year-old daughter Shauna Flanagan-Garwe; Catherine O'Donnell and her 13-year-old son James Monaghan; Jessica Gallagher; Martin McGill; James O'Flaherty; Martina Martin; Hugh Kelly; and 14-year-old Leona Harper. title: Test cricket's biggest scandals - your result revealed
description: See what BBC Sport readers voted as Test cricket's biggest scandals, together with contributions from the TMS team.
body: Was Hansie Cronje responsible for the biggest scandal in Test cricket's history? On Friday, Australia will play their first Test in South Africa since the sandpapergate scandal rocked the cricketing world eight years ago. To mark one of the biggest controversies the game has ever seen, Test Match Special asked you which is Test cricket's biggest scandal. Ten of the most notorious scandals in Test cricket were picked out by a TMS panel and readers of the BBC Sport website then ranked them. The results have been revealed on the TMS podcast by BBC chief cricket commentator Jonathan Agnew, former England fast bowler Steven Finn and TMS scorer Andy Zaltzman. The full results are below and you can listen to the podcast here. England players pick a new ball during the 2006 Test against Pakistan Pakistan had already lost the series in England in 2006, yet were cruising to victory in the final Test at The Oval. However, Australian umpire Darrel Hair asked for the ball to be changed midway through the afternoon session on the fourth day. Ball-tampering was suggested and Pakistan refused to play after tea. The match was abandoned and years later awarded to England, after some back and forth. Agnew: "Pakistan weren't accused of ball-tampering, they were found guilty of ball-tampering, on the field, without any opportunity to defend themselves. The rule at the time was if the umpire on the field suspected ball-tampering, the ball was changed and penalty runs were awarded. It didn't feel fair." Zaltzman: "It ended up with England awarded the Test so therefore they won the series 3-0. It means that whenever we look at the biggest first-innings deficit overturned to win a Test, this game comes out on top - 331 runs. It irritates me slightly." Mike Gatting, centre, later said he regretted the Shakoor Rana incident England's Test match against Pakistan in 1987 was stopped mid-game for more than 24 hours when the tourists' skipper Mike Gatting became embroiled in a row with home umpire Shakoor Rana. Agnew: "I'm a bit surprised this is so low. The knock-on was England didn't tour Pakistan for many years. England felt they were being stitched up by Pakistani umpires. There was a total lack of trust, going both ways, between England and Pakistan for a very long time." Zaltzman: "This was before neutral umpires and there was a sense umpiring wasn't quite as fair as it could have been, which all exploded in that moment." Finn: "It blows my mind that there weren't neutral umpires. My first summer of Test cricket had DRS and neutral umpires." Australia's Ian Chappell (left) and England captain Tony Greig examine the damaged Headingley wicket in 1975 The third Test in the 1975 Ashes was abandoned when the pitch was vandalised overnight by supporters of George Davis, who had been jailed for armed robbery the previous year. "George Davis is innocent" was written on the wall around Headingley. Finn: "I can't fathom turning up to a Test match and the pitch - the most sacred, untouchable of places - it's staggering that people managed to do that." Zaltzman: "It highlights how vulnerable cricket is to this sort of thing. A small bit of the field is damaged and the whole game has to be abandoned." Agnew: "There was no security. These days, the grounds are locked down. It was set up for an England win, but could have been a really good game of cricket. It's a bizarre story." West Indies players sit on a balcony during World Series Cricket When Australia's richest man, Kerry Packer, failed to boost the ratings of his Channel Nine TV network with live cricket, he created his own product: World Series Cricket. The plan was simple - Packer recruited the best players in the world to stage his own matches. Agnew: "Virtually everything you see about modern cricket can be traced back to World Series. It was incredible, innovative and exciting. I was 18 years old, playing club cricket in Melbourne and captivated by the coverage." Finn: "There's a similar revolution going on at the moment with T20 leagues allowing players to drift away from Test cricket. The temptation to be involved in something new and exciting would have been very interesting." Zaltzman: "It was extremely high-calibre cricket, but not even counted in first-class statistics, let alone Test stats. I don't really see it as a scandal at all, it was more cricket growing up. This really modernised the sport." Atherton, right, considered resigning but escaped with a fine and remained captain for another four years In the 1994 Lord's Test against South Africa, Michael Atherton was caught by TV cameras rubbing dirt on the ball. Atherton's explanation was that he was trying to maintain the condition of the ball, rather than alter it. Trouble was, he told the match referee he was using the dirt to keep his hands dry. Agnew: "This was a really tough time. I've thought about this a lot over the years and I'm not sure Michael knew the rules at the time - cricketers often don't. It's OK to rub your hand in the dirt, but you can't put soil on to the ball. It was a huge story. It was everywhere." Salman Butt leaves court during the Pakistan spot-fixing trial Our top five kicks off with the Pakistan spot-fixing scandal of 2010, when no-balls deliberately bowled in the Lord's Test ultimately resulted in three of the tourists' players - team captain Salman Butt and fast bowlers Mohammad Asif and Mohammad Amir - spending time in jail. Finn: "This was my first summer of Test cricket. It was such a weird atmosphere. We were warming up, looked up to the Pakistan dressing room and there were two officials in suits and blazers reading the News of the World. That was the day we went on to win the game. We didn't celebrate any of the wickets because of what transpired." Zaltzman: "Amir had burst on to the scene as a teenager - he'd only bowled three no

title: Half the harvest, twice the bills: how drought hit farms
description: Farmers gathered much less wheat in 2026 and dairy farmers' costs rose.
body: Charles Day's family farm in Gloucestershire lost half its wheat harvest to the drought The hottest summer on record, the longest drought, the worst harvest. West Country farmers are counting the cost of a "terrible summer", as one put it. The wheat harvest on Charles Day's family farm in Gloucestershire was cut in half. "It's just soul-destroying," he says. Dairy farmers had to rip open silage clamps stored up for the winter to feed the cattle as the grass failed. Sarah Godwin calculates it cost her family's Wiltshire farm "over £100,000". She says "it's shocking". I spent the summer watching farmers install showers for cows, watch their cauliflowers burn to a crisp in the heat, and search for apples in cider orchards reduced to a tenth of their normal crop. So now the harvest is home, just how bad was it? Buy a loaf of bread and there's a good chance it started in the fields of Charles Day's family farm in north Gloucestershire. "I love harvest," the fourth generation farmer tells me. "It's a whole year's work coming to fruition." But 2026 was brutal. The crops were looking "fantastic" in April, he told me. Then in June, the rain stopped and "the sun just stole our yield". Throughout the crucial weeks of June and July, there was no rain at all. Wheat grains shrivelled instead of fattening, and the yield plummeted. Official figures estimate the total UK cereal harvest was the lowest on record, external, wheat down about three million tonnes, or 11% according to the Agricultural and Horticultural Development Board (AHDB). Anthony Hopkins, AHDB director of cereals and oilseeds, says: "At a time of high input costs, arable farmers in the worst-affected areas are really feeling the financial pressure right now." Shrivelled by drought, the UK wheat harvest was the lowest on record But in the South West, it was much hotter and the impact far worse. When the combines went out on Charles Day's family farm, they gathered a harvest "about 50% down, sometimes more". "It's just soul-destroying," he adds. Across the South West, Tom Collins, who speaks for the NFU in Wiltshire, says most cereal farmers had seen harvests down "at least 30%". Spring barley and beans were more than 50% down, he adds, particularly badly hit by the drought. "Most farmers will give this harvest 3 out of 10", he adds. "They're pretty depressed." Put some butter on your bread, or cheese, and that is probably from the West Country's other farmers - dairy producers. But unlike the wheat harvest, the amount of milk produced this summer barely fell. Total production is down just 4.5%, external, according to the ADHB. "That's because we have to feed our cows, and milk them, whatever the weather," explains Sarah Godwin. Her family raise dairy cows west of Chippenham, selling their milk to a major supermarket. Sarah Godwin calculates the drought cost her family's dairy farm more than £100,000 in extra feed for the cows The Cotswolds was badly hit by the drought, leaving grazing pastures brown and without any nutrition for the cows. So like many farmers, the Godwins had to open their sileage planned for the winter and buy in feed to boost their cows diets. "Altogether it cost us around £100,000," Godwin explains. "We also had a drop in production yields, that's around £20,000. "On top of that, cows suffered more lameness, lower fertility, more mastitis. They really did not enjoy the heat." The family spent £15,000 installing new sprinkler systems and huge fans to cool the cattle in their sheds when they sheltered from the heat outside. All vital for animal welfare, but more costs to the business. Tom Kimber said droughts and floods are becoming "far more frequent" on his Somerset farm Even the normally lush fields of Somerset withered in the heat. Tom Kimber's family have farmed near Charlton Musgrove in south Somerset, in the heart of England's most productive grazing land. They run 250 dairy cows on their own grass, cutting sileage for the winter months. By September, they would normally have three large clamps of sileage ready for winter. This year, they have only cut two, and had to raid one throughout July and August, to make up for the lack of grass. But sadly, Tom Kimber is getting used to what was once freak weather. "This is the fourth drought in eight years now, so you barely financially get over the last one and you're hit with another one. It's becoming far more frequent, these events. "It's incredibly difficult this constant lurching between one extreme to the other, that's what keeps you awake at night." Climate scientists are clear that weather like this is the new normal. "What we used to think of as extreme weather, we increasingly consider as normal," says Mike Kendon, a climate scientist at the Met Office. So what can farmers do about it? In Gloucestershire, Charles Day's family have a rare asset: a lake. Fed by a local river, it fills through the winter and then can be used in the summer. They grow salad onions, broccoli and other vegetables on fields nearby, all irrigated by the lake water. The family wants to expand the lake, hold more water, do their bit to turn winter floods into summer irrigation. Charles Day wants to expand this lake on his farm, but says there is too much red tape and expense at the moment "But it's so complicated," Day explains. "The red tape, the planning, the licences, the digging - it will be very expensive. And we just get no help from government." New Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced in the summer a package of support , externalmeasures including grant funding to construct reservoirs and irrigation infrastructure. "I hope it helps," Day adds. Huge cracks opened in cider orchards during the hottest summer on record Others are trying to farm in a more nature friendly way. title: Puffin island on cusp of closure as it runs out of water
description: Lundy is in "real jeopardy" and could be evacuated if supplies run out, bosses say.
body: Lundy Island, in the Bristol Channel off the north Devon coast, is facing closure unless it receives meaningful rainfall Famed for its puffins, the picture-perfect island of Lundy attracts birdwatchers from all over. But the island is on the cusp of being evacuated as water levels drop to the lowest levels ever, forcing residents to take drastic measures to ensure supplies do not run out. Located in the Bristol Channel off the north Devon coast, the 5km (3.1 mile) long island is not the first place you expect to be running out of water. It is rich with wildlife including puffins and seals and its rugged landscape makes for breathtaking views. But speak to the handful of residents here and they will tell you of the battle waged since summer to ensure the taps do not run dry. Entirely self-sufficient, the National Trust-owned island relies on a combination of rainwater and boreholes drilled into the granite for supplies. Severe water shortages in Lundy are not new, with islanders and visitors previously resorting to bottled water. Island managing director Derek Green said closing the island would be devastating But the hottest and driest summer on record has been a "steep learning curve" for islanders, said Lundy managing director Derek Green. He said there had been no significant rainfall since April and it had barely seen 20% of the typical 1.5m (4.92ft) rain it expected by this time of year. Reservoir levels dropped to 13% at their lowest, forcing emergency shipments of water from the mainland to the 28 people who live on the island. Water restrictions are also in place for residents and visitors. Among the more extreme measures is the removal of plugs so tourists are not tempted to take a bath. The island, which is managed by the Landmark Trust, is now pumping water from ponds used by wildlife to a treatment works as a "last resort". "Bringing in pond water is something we've never had to do before," Green explained. "It's really our last chance saloon here. "If we didn't do this, we would be facing the reality of closing Lundy... it would be devastating for us." Visitors are drawn to Lundy for its wildlife, including puffins, but the island may have to close for business Green stressed pond levels had started to drop and a seasonal passenger ferry that has been shipping water to the island is due to end later this month. "Hopefully the reserve in the pond will last until it rains but because it hasn't rained in so long, this is desperate measures," he said. "We've got a working farm here and the animals need water every day... so to evacuate those animals, those people and to cancel all those holiday is something that has never happened in the history of Lundy before. "It would be hugely significant... we're on the cusp of having to make that decision." The island has received emergency shipments of water from the mainland since August The use of pond water led to some recovery in reservoir levels, now at 23.7% full, but Green said islanders were simply "praying for rain". BBC meteorologist David Braine said there was some rain in the forecast for Lundy but it would take weeks to top up the groundwater and reservoirs the island relied on. The very dry spring and summer followed record rainfall in the later part of the winter and it was only in March when most of our reservoirs were full. Shipments of water on passenger ferry the MS Oldenberg from north Devon began in August. The first delivery of about 67,000 litres was the biggest and cost about £7,000, said Green. Since then they have shipped 4,000 litres of water three times a week, with islanders using between 9,000 litres to 11,000 litres of water a day. Getting the water from the port to residents has not been an easy process as the island only has a granite track and a handful of vehicles including three 4x4s, tractors, quadbikes and a fire engine. More news stories for Devon Listen to the latest news for Devon Adding to the logistical pressure, a landslip in June closed off part of the track to the tiny village at the top of the island about 400ft above sea level. Green said: "We have to offload the tanks off the ship and we have to bring them up to a staging post halfway up the hill. "We then have to pump water with a fire hose past the vulnerable part of the road to another tank where it's then staged pumped to the reservoir at the top." Island manager Matt Scantlebury said baths were banned for guests at the island's pub Island manager Matt Scantlebury said the shortages had been a "logistical nightmare". He said the island's pub, The Tavern, closed toilets and removed bath plugs to help conserve supplies. "We can't have baths... all the plugs have been removed to resist temptation," said Scantlebury. "People are showering with buckets to catch the water and then using that to flush the toilets and that's saving water. "We've had to close the pub toilets so the visitors have all been funnelled to the back shed toilets because they aren't on our mains water supply... we now have to fill them from our pond water." Transport issues caused by a landslip means a fire hose is used to bring water to the top of the island Green, who started working on Lundy in 2004, said water shortages had become more frequent and in September last year they also considered shutting the island when reservoir levels hit 33%. He said the changing climate was more "pronounced on Lundy" and islanders needed to adapt. "Forecasters are predicting it will be even warmer next year," he said. "We've got to learn from this and be better prepared next year in terms of increasing the reservoir here. "People need to learn to use a little less water over the winter... it's a sharp learning curve for us and the wider region." title: Landlord's heartbreak as pub shuts down
description: A pub landlord forced to close down says more venues face similar closures without more tax cuts.
body: Jon Dean said "it's a bitter pill to swallow" having to close down The Alma Tavern in Worcester A publican has revealed his anguish at having to close down, saying he has been "crippled" by rising costs and a decline in customer drinking habits. Jon Dean, who ran The Alma Tavern in Worcester for the last seven years before closing its doors this week, has urged the government to consider new tax cuts for hospitality venues or face more pubs going under. He said: "We employed 14 or 15 people here but we've had to let everyone go. It's a bitter pill to swallow." A spokesperson for the Treasury said pubs "were already benefitting from a 20% cut in business rates", with Prime Minister Andy Burnham previously calling it "the first step" to help the industry. Dean, who also lives above the pub, is having to find a new home after opting to hand the business back to the brewery, Star Pubs. "We've been trying to keep it going but there's no light at the end of the tunnel," he said. "Hospitality has taken a battering. We've had the utility crisis, the cost of living crisis [and] now the war in Iran. "All of that has had an impact on prices, but when you add in employer's national insurance contributions, rocketing minimum wage, rocketing VAT, business rates, all of that pressure has crippled us." The Alma Tavern in Worcester, which has now ceased trading Dean told the BBC that customers were not spending as much, something he put down to the cost of living pressures. "People used to come in four or five times a week and they'd have four or five pints, but those days are gone," he said. "Now we'd maybe see them once or twice a week and they might only have a drink or two - people just haven't got the money. "I've tried everything to keep the pub going, but it's like flogging a dead horse." Explaining the financial pressures, he said: "A place like this turns over maybe £800,000 a year, but once you've paid out your taxes, your energy bills, your wages, it's pretty much all gone. "Taxation and the cost of everything is just far too high." In July, the government cut business rates for pubs. But last month, more than 800 businesses, including top UK chefs, wrote an open letter to the PM, saying there would be more pub and restaurant closures unless VAT was reduced. Allen Simpson, chief executive of the trade body UKHospitality, said the tax burden for the sector had "grown disproportionately" in recent years. "We have already seen promising signs from the new government in its approach to hospitality - I hope this [forthcoming] Budget will see further backing for the entire hospitality sector," he added. A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The chancellor has prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues, saving thousands of [pubs] over £1,000 a year. "This is on top of providing a tax break on poured pints and capping corporation tax." A spokesperson for Star Pubs said: "While Star Pubs owns The Alma Tavern, it is leased to an independent operator who runs it as their own business and has taken the decision to close the pub." title: Survivors 'betrayed' after rapist fled to Pakistan while on bail
description: Amar Ilyas left the UK while on bail for sexual offences, and never returned for his trial.
body: Amar Ilyas was released on court bail before his trial, during which time he travelled to Pakistan Three women who were sexually abused by a serial rapist have said they feel "betrayed" and "frustrated" after their attacker fled to Pakistan while on bail. Amar Ilyas, 41, was convicted of 20 sexual offences against five girls in Sheffield and was sentenced, in his absence, to a minimum of 27 years in prison. One of his victims told the BBC she had assumed his passport would automatically be surrendered after he was charged and said she was "so disappointed in the law." The government said "decisions on bail restrictions are a mattter for the independent judiciary", while the National Crime Agency (NCA) said it was "making every effort to ensure Ilyas is brought before the court". A woman who was sexually abused by Amar Ilyas when she was 13 said she had been "cheated" because she felt unable to go out and leave her home, yet her abuser had been able to leave the country. "There is no justice is there really? He didn't take accountability. He's not getting any consequences for his actions," she said. "We were told that he got to keep his passport because of his human rights but he wasn't humane towards other people. "He didn't show any empathy so it was a really big insult when his human rights and feelings were taken into consideration." Amar Ilyas was arrested in 2020 and charged in 2023, as part of the NCA's Operation Stovewood, investigating sexual abuse in South Yorkshire. Sheffield Crown Court heard he had carried out the offences against girls as young as 12 in the Meersbrook and Sharrow areas of Sheffield between 2004 and 2007. The BBC understands he was allowed to keep his passport after appearing in court and had previously travelled abroad while on court bail, but had returned to the UK. He went to Pakistan in July 2025 and did not return for his trial in September of that year, despite being ordered to fly back to the UK by the judge. His younger brothers are both currently in prison for sexual offences against one victim. Kamar Ilyas, 40, was jailed for 10 years and Kamran Ilyas, 39, was sentenced to three years. Kamar Ilyas and Kamran Ilyas were jailed in June Another woman said she had learning difficulties and was in a very vulnerable, dark place when she was abused by Amar Ilyas as a teenager. "Why, when he's committed these offences against us girls, was he allowed to keep his passport? That's my question. Where is the justice?" she asked. "I hope they find him and I hang on to that hope every day, maybe it will be tomorrow, it might be next year but we have to hang on to hope." A third woman, who was raped by Amar Ilyas as a teenager, said she did not have much hope that he would return to the UK to serve his sentence. "I just know he's in Pakistan and they're doing what they can, but I've been told it's very difficult with Pakistan with extradition," she said. "Shame on him but shame on the law too, they allowed that to happen." The women, who have the right to lifelong anonymity, said they had taken the decision to speak to the BBC to call for changes to prevent sex offenders absconding during court proceedings. "Going forwards, I think they need to put into place that they remove the passports," one said. "We live in a world, unfortunately, where these things are carrying on happening. "There are survivors coming forward but survivors might not want to come forward after hearing something like this." Judge Peter Hampton, who did not oversee the bail condition applications at earlier hearings, but sentenced all three brothers in June, described Amar Ilyas as having "taken the coward's route and fled". In his sentencing remarks, he urged law enforcement to locate him and use "all means" to execute the arrest warrant that remains outstanding. It is understood that when Amar Ilyas's defence team applied for bail, which the prosecution had the opportunity to contest, no request for his passport to be forfeited was made. Phillip Marshall, head of Operation Stovewood for the NCA, said officers were carrying out proactive enquiries. He said: "Amar Ilyas tormented and brutally sexually abused vulnerable young girls and women 20 years ago, and he has callously compounded their decades of suffering by not returning to the UK for his trial or sentencing." Marshall added: "Operation Stovewood's meticulous investigation ensured that despite the passage of time, complexity of the case and Ilyas's absence, his crimes against the women were heard, believed and proven in court. "We are just as determined to ensure that Ilyas serves his prison sentence." Lucy Duckworth from the Survivors Trust described the case as "absolutely appalling" and said it demonstrated the need for specialist courts and training in sexual violence response for staff in the criminal justice service. "It doesn't make sense the way we are treating this crime if we're saying, 'you're such a risk to society' and yet we're giving bail and we're allowing them the freedom to potentially commit that crime again or to evade justice by leaving the country," she said. "I think it is widely accepted that the criminal justice system is currently failing victims and survivors and that needs to change. "I hope that cases like this can highlight the massive gaps and make sure that we all work together and work with the government to get the changes in place needed." In response to the story, a government spokesperson said: "These were horrible crimes, and our thoughts remain with the victims. "More broadly we're determined to protect vulnerable girls and bring those responsible to justice. That is why we're cracking down on vile abusers as part of our mission to halve violence against women and girls in a decade." title: How student went from YouTube to Bake Off
description: A Birmingham student in the Channel 4 show taught himself after "stumbling across a YouTube video".
body: On week two of the baking competition viewers watched Mahir bake a biscuit mosaic A student taking part in the new series of the Great British Bake Off says he taught himself to bake after "stumbling across a YouTube video". When Mo Mahir, 22, from West Bromwich, was nine years old, he "found a video of a guy making a mug cake in a microwave", which he said ignited his passion for baking. "I feel like as a Bengali, we don't really have a lot of cakes or baking in our cultural background," he said. "It started with me mixing a bunch of random stuff. My mum used to always be shouting at me saying 'stop, that's making a mess’." As part of the Channel 4 series, Mahir, a student at Birmingham City University, has been competing against 12 other bakers. "Growing up, I've always loved cakes and cookies and stuff and I've always wanted to eat them, but it's just that we never always got the, like, freshly baked stuff. So I kind of had to teach myself," he said. "Nothing turned out right because I wasn't measuring anything, but it slowly just progressed from there." Other contestants competing to win the series include a paediatrician, a competitive sprinter, a hairdresser and a drag artist On week one of the competition, Mahir landed star baker after he stunned TV judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood with his peanut and caramel chocolate stout cake. On week two, viewers watched him bake a biscuit mosaic. His newfound TV fame means he has been spotted while out and about in Birmingham. "It's been really positive, just like all the DMs [direct messages] I'm getting on Instagram is very supportive and kind. "When I'm going to town to do a bit of shopping, I do get recognised and people are like rooting for me, and it's just nice to see and hear that." Mahir's former teacher Sam Hayes, from George Salter Academy, previously said: "When I found out he would be going on, I knew he would do really well. "I'll always remember being brought some of the delicious treats Mo had baked at home, a very welcome perk of having such a talented student. "He always was an absolutely amazing baker while he was at school," he added. Other contestants competing to win the series include a paediatric doctor, a competitive sprinter, a hairdresser and a drag artist. title: Tests carried out on seabirds after nurdle spill
description: Necropsies are being carried out on seabirds to find out the effects of microplastic pollutants.
body: Millions of plastic nurdles washed up on beaches following the ship collision Research is being carried out to find out how a microplastic spillage has affected coastal sea bird populations. On 19 July tonnes of microplastics known as nurdles were spilled into the River Tyne following a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne. A series of necropsies are now taking place at the Dove Marine Laboratory in Cullercoats on dead birds gathered after the spill. Dan Turner, coordinator at North East England Beached Bird Surveys said: "We've already seen samples from contents of stomachs of suspected regurgitation which contain nurdles." Necropsies will be carried out on a variation of seabirds gathered from across the North East including eight guillemots, five herring gulls, a gannet and a pink-footed goose. Necropsies are being carried out on seabirds to find out the impact of the nurdle spill The research was prompted over concerns birds could "starve" if they confuse the nurdles for food and fill their stomachs. "We've seen evidence previously of fulmars eating plastic and they've been found in their stomachs, so it is highly likely we could come across the same in some cases," Turner added. Charities like the RSPB have also warned the pellets could enter the wider food chain, affecting fish, seals and dolphins. Dan Turner from the North East Bird Survey Group is carrying out the research External and internal studies into the seabirds has started with stomach rinsing also taking place to see if the birds have been consuming the nurdles. "It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs. "The nurdles when they float attract pollutants and contaminants, which stick to them, if the birds swallow them it can be the case that they get into the bird's system. "We may need more testing to see if the plastic can make its way into the bird's bloodstream which could cause a drop in the bird's fitness," Turner said. Volunteers across North and South Tyneside continue to clean up the nurdles across the coast Researchers have confirmed 28% of 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles which spilled into the river have been recovered since the spill. Scientists predict that the plastic pellets will continue to wash up on North East beaches as the clean up continues. Colin Porter who has been assisting the clean up in South Tyneside said: "We are very concerned about the wildlife populations, we've seen birds eating them and we know the fish have too." The research on the birds is expected to continue into December. title: 'I made a choice - I didn't naturally lose my baby'
description: Rosanna Brown was advised to end her pregnancy because her baby had a life-threatening medical condition.
body: Rosanna Brown was advised to end her pregnancy because her baby had a life-threatening medical condition A woman whose baby was too ill to be born is calling for better awareness of choosing a termination for medical reasons. Rosanna Brown, who lives near Waterlooville, Hampshire, was advised to end her pregnancy with son William in 2023 because he had a rare and life-threatening medical condition called Chaos syndrome. Continuing the pregnancy would have risked both their lives, but Rosanna said the experience was made even more difficult due to a lack of training around medically-advised abortions. An NHS spokesperson said it offered "comprehensive support for women whose unborn baby is diagnosed with a serious health condition". Rosanna said she understood why so many people who suffered a termination for medical reasons (TFMR) just told others they had had a miscarriage. "Because it's a type of abortion, you have the pro-life pro-choice argument, you are thrown into the middle of that," she said. "You have this feeling that your grief isn't as valid because you've chosen [it]. "It's such a complex and lonely thing to go through and it's so much harder if you can't tell the truth of what happened to you. "Because for so many parents, termination is the most loving thing they could offer." About 5,000 women a year are offered a TFMR, which is more than experience stillbirth and neonatal death. Jane Fisher from the Arc charity said it was important to break the taboo around TFMR Rosanna is campaigning for change, including for the term TFMR to be properly used, which she said it was not on her son's forms. Instead her loss was described as a "late miscarriage", which she said "silences you further". "I made a choice here, I didn't naturally lose my baby," she said. "I didn't come across [TFMR] until a good few months after I'd lost him. And in that time, you're searching for community and for support and for compassion for people to get it. "And if that term is not being used by medical professionals with the patients that they're seeing, I think sometimes it's because they're worried about offending you." Jane Fisher, chief executive of the ARC Charity, said it was a very difficult situation and that using the right term was really important. "It describes the reality of the situation and I think that's important both for parents to accept what happened but also for us to break the stigma and taboo around this particular loss," she said. She added without that, it could be "very difficult to grieve in a healthy way". Ahead of Baby Loss Awareness Month, Rosanna Brown has written a book called The Silence Of TFMR A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "Every woman going through this incredibly difficult situation deserves proper care, compassion and support." They added: "All major abortion providers offer counselling and advice on the options available." A NHS spokesperson also said it provided mental health support for baby loss following a decision to terminate a pregnancy. Earlier this year, Rosanna and her husband became parents again to a daughter. But they said they would always talk about her big brother William and had planted a memorial garden in his honour. Ahead of Baby Loss Awareness Week, she has written and published a compassionate guide to help others, called The Silence Of TFMR. She said: "Some of the most painful advice [was] 'don't let this define you'. I really took offence because your identity changes, your whole life changes. "I am defined [by it] and am quite happy to be. I need to find ways to keep tapping into that identity of parent to him because that's the only way he gets to exist, in this world." Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place from 9 to 15 October. title: Metal detectorist finds second Bronze Age hoard in Scottish Borders
description: Dubbed the Blyth Hoard, the artefacts dating from between 1150BC to 850BC were found seven miles from the Peebles Hoard.
body: The latest discovery, dubbed the Blyth Hoard, features bronze axeheads and a copper ingot A metal detectorist has revealed his "quite extraordinary" discovery of a second Bronze Age hoard in the Scottish Borders. Mariusz Stepien found his latest haul of 3,000-year-old treasure in 2022 at a spot seven miles from where he discovered the Peebles Hoard in 2020. Dubbed the Blyth Hoard, the artefacts date from the Late Bronze Age between 1150BC to 850BC. They feature two bronze axe-heads, and clay moulds potentially used to make some of the unique bronze fittings in the nearby Peebles Hoard - which was saved for the nation in 2024. The Peebles Hoard, found in 2020, includes a complete horse harness The hoard also includes a complete copper ingot, which is said to be the first of its kind found in Scotland. Excavation by archaeologists further revealed an ancient stone cairn. The Blyth Hoard has now been brought to the National Museums Collection Centre in Edinburgh for conservation and analysis. Experts hope that analysis of the ingot might point towards the geographical source of the metals used in the making of the bronze objects in both hoards. Dr Matthew Knight, curator of prehistory, Bronze Age collections at NMS, said: "This is one of those classic archaeological finds that initially doesn't look like much, but is actually really incredible and has many stories to tell. "It's really rare for mould materials to survive at all, so it's a special find in its own right, but the proximity and relationship to the Peebles Hoard makes it all the more extraordinary." Mariusz Stepien made the second discovery at a spot seven miles from the first Mariusz Stepien said he was looking forward to seeing what further research could reveal about both hoards - and about the people behind them. "When I first discovered the Blyth Hoard, I was excited to have found more Bronze Age material in an area that I already knew was archaeologically significant," he said. "At that stage, I had no idea just how important the discovery might turn out to be. "Having previously discovered the Peebles Hoard, it is quite extraordinary to think that two discoveries I made so close to one another could be connected." The Peebles Hoard includes a complete horse harness discovered by Stepien. Archaeologists later excavated a sword still in its scabbard, decorated straps, buckles, rings, ornaments and chariot wheel axle caps. Under Scots law, archaeological finds discovered in Scotland must be reported to the Treasure Trove Unit, external, based at NMS, where they are recorded and assessed. Significant finds may be claimed on behalf of the Crown by the King's and Lord Treasurer's Remembrancer and allocated to museums through the Treasure Trove system, where they can be preserved and enjoyed for public benefit. title: Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas-led attacks grapple with how to rebuild
description: Three years on from the attack on Nir Oz, in which 47 people were killed and 76 taken hostage, some survivors have returned to live there.
body: This video can not be played Dalit Ram Aharon and her husband Achi say they want to move back to Nir Oz "in the memory" of the friends they lost in the 7 October attacks Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023. "We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi. By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents. The postboxes for each household bear stickers put there after the attacks three years ago: red indicates those killed, and black those taken hostage. "That's one out of four of us: murdered or kidnapped," Dalit says. "Including children and babies." As Israel marks the third anniversary of its deadliest-ever day, this is another painful time of reflection for residents of the kibbutz, which sits just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border and was one of the worst-hit places. Time stands still at the nearby burnt-out house of the Siman Tov family, where a wind chime dangles by the door. A picture shows Tamar and Yonatan with their three children, twin girls Shahar and Arbel, five, and their two-year-old son, Omer. The parents were shot through the door of their bomb shelter - designed to protect from rockets launched from Gaza, not gunfire. A red sticker on a postbox indicates those who were killed in the Hamas attacks; black indicates those who were taken hostage Dalit, who survived with Achi and their three children by hiding in their own shelter for nearly 12 hours that day, recalls the last social media messages sent by Tamar to her neighbours. "On that day in the morning, she wrote in the woman's group, at the beginning, 'Is everyone fine?' Then, at another point, she wrote, 'They are shooting us.' And after that she wrote with a lot of mistakes, 'We are very injured,'" Dalit tells me. "From what we understand, they torched the house and the children died from suffocation, so all the family was killed." An estimated 500 Palestinians, led by Hamas's elite Nukhba force fighters, but including civilian looters, some of them children, joined the assault on the unsuspecting Nir Oz. Forty-one Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed, along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby. Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies, with 14 hostages taken alive and killed in captivity. The last living hostages from Nir Oz were returned to Israel on 13 October 2025 and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Amiram Cooper, were brought back two weeks later. As we walk through the greenery, it is eerily quiet bar bird song and the mewing of hungry, stray cats. Dozens of fire-damaged homes, which were simple, one-storey buildings in Nir Oz, have now been torn down, leaving just rows of the reinforced concrete safe rooms, which failed to keep people safe. The Aharons want some damaged houses to be left as evidence of what took place. "We really support that," Achi says. "People should see what happened, should see the destruction, the pure hatred that happened here." The couple point out where a teacher, Maya Goren, was killed while in the kindergarten and the makeshift memorials where three of the seven members of the kibbutz security team were killed after battling Hamas gunmen. The findings of the Israeli Defense Forces investigation into what happened at Nir Oz underscored how the army - left in a state of disarray by the unprecedented simultaneous assault on more than 20 communities and multiple military posts - completely failed to come to the rescue here. On 7 October, the first soldiers arrived in the kibbutz some 40 minutes after the last Palestinian attackers left. Nearly every household experienced killing, violence, including sexual assaults and rape, looting and kidnapping. Dalit pauses to show me a tree planted long ago by her parents, who were co-founders of the kibbutz, known for its farming and peace activists. They survived the 7 October attacks physically unharmed but died just months afterwards. Next door is the small home of Shiri Bibas, the mother of ginger-haired boys Ariel, four, and nine-month-old, Kfir. The three, snatched from their home, became symbols of the Gaza hostage crisis. "This is the hardest house for me because Shiri was a very, very good friend of mine," Dalit confides. "She was like a sister. We even got pregnant together - me with my daughter and her with Ariel. They became best friends also. We used to laugh that they were going to marry." Dalit says Shiri Bibas, who was killed along with her two children after being taken hostage, was "like a sister" "Shiri was very, very funny. She was a happy person - a mother," Dalit says. "She lived a simple life. She never did anything to anyone." While Shiri's husband, Yarden, was released alive by Hamas in a Gaza ceasefire deal in February 2025, she and her sons - held by a different armed group - were killed. Hamas blamed an air strike early in the Gaza war for their deaths, but Israeli forensic experts, who examined the bodies after they were returned later that February, said they were murdered by their captives and their bodies mutilated. Many of the bereaved from Nir Oz, including Yarden Bibas, have moved away for good. However, with 20 houses renovated or rebuilt, a few former hostages have come back to live here. They include Gadi Moses, another kibbutz co-founder, and the oldest living male hostage released during the Gaza war, and Yair Horn, who stops to chat with the Aharons as he passes in a golf buggy. title: Military training sites to be investigated following rape and abuse claims at Army college
description: In August, four young women told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed at the school in Harrogate.
body: The investigation will look at 10 Army establishments, including the Army Foundation College in Harrogate where teenage recruits train An independent investigation is being carried out into 10 military training sites in England, following claims of rape and sexual assault at an Army college for under-18s. In August, four young women told the BBC they had been sexually assaulted and harassed at the Army Foundation College, in Harrogate, North Yorkshire. One said she had been raped by several fellow junior soldiers in an attack that lasted hours. The Armed Forces Commissioner, Polly Miller-Perkins, who is carrying out her first investigation in the role, has called the allegations "absolutely appalling". She will visit the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst (RMAS) - where all officers in the British Army are trained - and Britannia Royal Naval College, in Dartmouth - where the Royal Navy's prestigious officer training base is located. She will also visit the Army Foundation College, where the youngest recruits are trained. The commissioner has the power to visit UK defence sites unannounced and request information from the government. She can compile reports and command the attention of the defence secretary and Parliament regarding issues she feels need exposure. Miller-Perkins said her recommendations will be made public, but critics have questioned whether her findings will lead to change. One survivor of sexual assault, who attended the Army Foundation College, told the BBC she had no confidence in the process. Women tell BBC of rape and abuse at Army teen college Calls for inquiry into Army teen college after reports of rape and abuse Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college Miller-Perkins, a former air commodore, said the BBC's reporting "brought into sharp focus" potential problems in military training establishments, including allegations of predatory behaviour towards women. "I take this hugely seriously," she said. "I already had concerns, but there's absolutely no doubt that your report reinforced these concerns." The Armed Forces Commissioner Polly Miller-Perkins will speak to staff, recruits and their families "Certainly when people go into phase one training, they are coming from a whole swathe of socio-economic backgrounds, and it's up to the MoD (Ministry of Defence) to bring those individuals up to the values and standards that would be expected in a modern armed forces - and that includes respect for women." Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has previously said he wanted to lead cultural change in the UK military. "I expect every woman who serves to be treated with respect, with decency," he said. The Armed Forces Commissioner is a newly-created role to provide independent oversight of the service complaints system. It also acts as a direct point of contact for serving personnel so they can raise problems that are impacting their lives and their ability to serve. Miller-Perkins said she would aim to identify any systemic issues and make recommendations to the government to "ensure the welfare and safety of all personnel". She said she plans to visit each of the 10 establishments in November and will speak to families, staff and recruits. She said the aim was to establish some early findings in the New Year. "I'm interested in following the evidence, so we will go where the evidence leads us," she said. "This is independent - I think that's absolutely crucial. I am an independent voice and advocate of service people and their families." However, one of the women the BBC spoke to as part of our investigation into the Army Foundation College said she had little confidence people would want to be honest about their experience with "another military person". "It's easier for me to talk to you [a reporter] than it is to talk to someone who is an army or RAF person because they already are on the side of them. "It's not easy to trust them because I know they're supposed to be independent but military life is ingrained in you - it's hard to step away from that and see the faults when it's what you've worked in for years." Miller-Perkins said she "understands trust has to be earned" and expects to be judged on what her office delivers. She said she had been planning the review into training establishments since she began the job in the Spring. "I would like to think if I put recommendations in front of the Secretary of State and the MoD, that they will take those very seriously because I certainly do." The BBC investigation into the Army Foundation College also documented women making claims about inappropriate language and behaviour from some of the instructors, including marking young female recruits on their looks. The Ministry of Defence said it welcomed independent scrutiny. A spokesman said: "We are committed to ensuring everyone beginning their military career receives the highest standards of training, welfare and support in a safe and professional environment." In relation to the Army Foundation College allegations, it added: "Unacceptable and criminal behaviour has no place in the military, and it encourages anyone who has experienced such conduct to come forward. It said the college welcomes scrutiny and has received an outstanding report from Ofsted." Details of help and support with sexual abuse or violence is available at BBC Action Line.
