title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
description: Some running in November's elections are deciding whether to distance themselves from an unpopular president who still dominates his party.
body: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will. "We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week. While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy. Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax". The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a gallon and beef prices are at a record high. According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall. Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular. "We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue." Some polls suggest that many of Trump's policies, including the ongoing conflict with Iran, are unpopular That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump? Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free. There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida. But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns. Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement. When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight. "We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive." He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet". In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel. What are the US midterms? A simple guide Byron Donalds is now running for governor of Florida When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces. But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages. Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices. It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction. "Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long." "Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable". "We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America." And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda". "Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said. Many candidates are campaigning hard on economic concerns Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran. For the past two year

title: 'Clear human rights failures' in southern Scotland, report finds
description: A new study concludes basic human rights - including food, health and housing - are being denied.
body: The Food Train charity provides support to older people - including food delivery - across southern Scotland A new report has found "clear human rights failures" across the south of Scotland with basic obligations on food, health and housing not being met. The study was carried out over eight different local authority areas which are home to more than a million people. The Scottish Human Rights Commission (SHRC) concluded that the biggest challenge was accessibility as, even if services did exist, they were often unreachable in practice. Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth said the Scottish government already offered free transport for a range of groups, while public service reform represented an opportunity to "push power out" to communities around the country. In February and March, the SHRC visited communities including Stranraer, Ayr, Dumfries, Kilmarnock, Hamilton, Irvine, Arran, Galashiels, Kelso, Dalkeith, Haddington, Melrose, Ardrossan and Tranent. "Overall, the south of Scotland is a region where many communities and duty bearers are working hard to protect dignity and their human rights, often in difficult circumstances," its report concluded. "But we have also found clear human rights failures. "In many areas, rights are not improving. In several areas, they are getting worse." Prof Angela O'Hagan, who chairs the commission, said the report highlighted the "gaps" between rights everyone was entitled to and the "lived reality" in southern Scotland. She said it was "call to action" for everyone who managed and delivered services with people in the area feeling "distant from decision making". Wheelchair users hit by shortage of accessible taxis I clocked up 7,500 miles getting maternity care The report includes a string of case studies which highlight areas of concern, such as the variation of service provision depending on where people live. Donald worked as landscape gardener before suffering from a stroke and later contracting Lyme disease after being bitten by a tick. He said a locum neurologist referred him to a specialist clinic in another south of Scotland health board, but he was rejected because he didn't live in the right area. "We don't have a national health service, we've got a regional health service," he said. "I'm just left in limbo, unable to work and unable to get better, even though I know there's a solution out there." What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland? Another section of the report highlighted the plight of one woman trying to find the right health care for her husband. But she found navigating services for the former soldier to be "impossible". "He was trapped in the health care system here, and he became suicidal," she added. "He stood on the front line to protect everybody else's rights, and nobody would help him." The report also found many households were cutting back on meals and relying on food banks amid rising costs and low incomes. Meanwhile, one charity service manager told the SHRC: "You have got villages dotted around who don't get the support they should. "There's a big disparity between the town and rural areas which needs to be addressed. "It shouldn't matter where you are." Janice Johnstone recently contacted the BBC to highlight the difficulties facing people in Dumfries and Galloway getting wheelchair accessible taxis The issue of accessibility to services is one which has been regularly raised in southern Scotland. Wheelchair user Janice Johnstone recently highlighted the difficulties faced in finding an accessible taxi with only three available in Dumfries and Galloway. The 70-mile journey facing expectant mothers in Wigtownshire to get to services in Dumfries is also the subject of a long-running campaign and a nationwide review of provision is now under way. Residents of Newcastleton have also spoken of how the extension of the Borders Railway to stop in their village could be "life-changing". A feasibility study is currently looking at ways to take that forward. And Dumfries and Galloway Council had to step in last year after bus operator Stagecoach effectively quit the region. Jenny Gilruth said the issues highlighted were felt in many parts of the country and public service reform could help "push power out" to communities During a visit to Dumfries this week, Gilruth said part of the issue of people feeling distant from government was about geography, which was a "matter of fact". However, she said public service reform was a chance to give more power to communities. "We've got a new prime minister coming into power with a devolution agenda, so we expect further powers to flow back to Scotland and with that commensurate funding," she said. "But we then as a parliament, as a government, have an opportunity to work on how we push that power out of Edinburgh and down into our communities." The deputy first minister said that was an issue across Scotland with people even feeling disconnected from parts of their own region. Gilruth agreed that transport was "challenging" in the area but added that the government already funded bus travel for under 22s, over 60s and those with disabilities. "There are other issues in this part of the world around about some of these bus routes simply not existing anymore," she added. She said there were powers available to allow local government to franchise and take on their own approaches and said those opportunities needed to be looked at. During her visit, she highlighted the number of projects with the potential to boost the economy. She also discussed the unique challenges facing the region in terms of connectivity and how that affected education, health and housing. title: Battle of ideas looming in British politics, Badenoch to say
description: The Tory leader has been seeking to reframe the way the public views her party, which has yet to recover in the polls since the last election.
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch will say there is a "battle of ideas" looming in British politics when she delivers a speech on the final day of her party's annual conference on Wednesday. Badenoch is expected to tell delegates in Birmingham that the differences between her party and the Labour government go "to the very core of what kind of country we want to be". This week the Tory leader has been seeking to re-frame the way the public views her party, which has yet to recover in the polls since the last election. The party has already pledged £10bn for a UK air defence system, and proposed cuts to the rate of employer National Insurance contributions for those aged 21 to 24. There is also speculation that Badenoch could propose changes to inheritance tax. According to the Times, external, Badenoch is also due to announce a cut to the 40% rate of inheritance tax. That rate applies to a person's estate worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren. Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election. During her main conference speech, Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, will pitch the fight against Labour at the next general election as "a battle for the soul of this nation". She will say there is now a clear distinction between the Conservatives and Labour under Prime Minister Andy Burnham. According to extracts released in advance, Badenoch will say Burnham's government wants to "wind back the clock to failed ideas of the past". "They believe economic growth is created by politicians. They think government knows best. "They think that your income, your pension and your savings are theirs to take and then hand out as they see fit." Badenoch will add that Labour will "claim what they are doing is compassionate", but the result will be higher taxes and a poorer country caught in a "doom loop". By contrast, Conservatives believe "what people earn belongs to them, not government", Badenoch will say - adding that growing the economy "will be the central organising principle of the next Conservative government". Earlier this week, Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power. Chancellor John Healey said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space". Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies Kemi Badenoch wants Reform voters to 'come back' Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system The Conservatives have laid out a number of plans during its autumn conference for if it enters government at the next general election. On Tuesday, Badenoch said she was proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) contributions on earnings for those aged 21 to 24 from 15% to 7.5%. Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training, and the government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities. The Conservatives said the policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270. The move would cost £2.3bn, according to party estimates, with a plan on how to fund it to be published on Wednesday. Earlier this week, shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said he hopes to scrap at least one tax every budget if the Conservatives return to power, with the so-called "mansion tax" in his sights. He also said he would scrap the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), which takes effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m. The Tory leader will argue her party is "a renewed Conservative Party fighting again for the belief that what people earn belongs to them, not government". In an interview with BBC political editor Chris Mason on Tuesday, she said "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved". title: Pornhub returns to Australia but only for adults with Apple devices
description: The world's most popular porn site went dark in March in Australia due to age verification laws.
body: Pornhub says Australians with age-verified Apple devices will be able to access its site again Pornhub has returned to Australia, eight months after it went dark due to age verification laws, but only adults with Apple devices will be able to access the site. On Wednesday, parent company Aylo said it was restoring access for "eligible adult users in Australia" who have "confirmed their age through Apple's Australian age-verification process". The world's biggest porn site left the Australian market in March, saying new laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 would not protect children and "instead creates harms relating to data privacy" and exposure to content on non-compliant platforms. Apple recently introduced new age checks in Australia, following a rollout in the UK. In March, Australia introduced stricter laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 in order to access adult content such as porn, R-rated video games and sexually explicit AI chatbots. The country's online safety regulator said the changes would protect children from harmful content and platforms would be fined for breaches. Critics said there would be issues with data privacy and users finding ways to trick age-verification technologies such as facial recognition, digital IDs and credit card details. Aylo said it was returning to Australia as Apple has "set a benchmark" by setting default child safety features on all devices unless owners confirmed they are adults. This, in effect, makes "every phone or tablet kid-safe as a starting point," it said. "For years, Aylo has advocated for device-based age verification as the most effective and privacy-protecting approach to help prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content online," said Aylo's vice-president of brand and community Alex Kekesi. Australians with Apple devices that have been "age-verified" will be "served a standard adult users experience", she said. Apple users can prove they are over 18 using a credit card, their passport, a driver's license or a government-issued ID. Kekesi added that having devices with child safety features as a default meant adults don't have to "surrender unnecessary personal information to multiple apps and websites". It also limits the usefulness of virtual private networks (VPNs) to circumvent age-verification technologies, she said. VPNs are commonly used to trick a site into thinking a user is logging on from another country, giving the user access to the site. title: Former Australian bishop jailed for sexually abusing young men
description: The former Bishop of Broome is one of the most senior Catholic clerics in the world to face sex abuse charges.
body: Christopher Saunders has been jailed for sexual offences against two young men Former Australian bishop Christopher Saunders has been jailed for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men during his time as a Catholic cleric. Saunders - who resigned as Bishop of Broome when first accused of wrongdoing in 2020 - was found guilty of one charge of rape and 12 counts of indecent assault in August. The 76-year-old was on Wednesday sentenced to six and a half years in prison, but will be eligible for release on parole in February 2031. He is one of the most senior Catholic leaders in the world to face sex abuse charges. His trial in the state of Western Australia heard Saunders systematically groomed the two young men, inviting them to "shirts-off" gatherings and plying them with alcohol, often using church funds and church-owned properties to do so. He was convicted of kissing and molesting the men between 2010 and 2019, and in one instance forcing oral sex on one of them. Saunders was acquitted by the jury of alleged offences against a third young man. In a victim impact statement provided to the court, that young man said he struggled to talk about what had happened. "I was a toy that he was using," the victim said. "My head is pounding now, I'm in so much pain." First ordained in 1976, Saunders spent most of his career in the remote Kimberley region in the nation's north-west corner, and was appointed Bishop of Broome in 1996. The diocese stretches about 770,000 sq km (297,000 sq miles) - an area roughly the size of Turkey - and encompasses some of the most remote parts of the country. District Court Judge Martin Flynn said Saunders had "disregarded the dignity" of his victims and caused them lasting harm. In a statement, Archbishop of Perth Timothy Costelloe said the men who had come forward had shown great courage and resilience in pursuing justice. "We are sorry for the pain and suffering that was inflicted on you. We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the church," he said. "No court sentence can undo the suffering that has been caused or restore all that each person has lost." The accusations were first aired in 2020, but the initial police investigation that followed was closed without charge. However after a historic inquiry was ordered by the Pope, police began a new investigation. Costelloe has previously said the church's investigation into Saunders - paused when police resumed theirs - will restart. The church is under pressure to strip Saunders of his remaining title and ministry powers, a decision the Archbishop said would be determined by Rome. Only a handful of "Vos Estis Lux Mundi" - meaning "You Are the Light of the World" in Latin - inquiries have been undertaken around the world. The investigations are commissioned by the pontiff and were introduced in 2019 to combat sexual abuse and hold bishops and other high-ranking Catholic Church officials accountable for their actions. Aside from the late Cardinal George Pell, who was jailed and then acquitted, Saunders is the most senior Catholic official in the country to be charged with sex offences. title: The Papers: 'Badenoch promises tax cuts' and 'Asos hacker havoc'
description: The Tories' financial plans and a hack at online shopping outlet Asos lead Wednesday's papers.
body: The Times leads with a promise of tax cuts from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, previewing her speech to the party's annual conference on Wednesday. The paper says Badenoch "will say the Tories face a 'battle for the soul of our nation'" as she sets out plans to cut inheritance tax and halve employer national insurance contributions for young staff. The Times also carries a photo of police in riot gear at protests over school funding in France, with the paper reporting that the "biggest day of French demos turns violent" The Daily Mail also headlines on the Tory leader's pledge, saying the Conservatives would "slash jobs tax to get young back into work". The Mail refers to this as a "'rescue package' for jobless youngsters" The Daily Mirror headlines on comments from Labour MP Mike Tapp that Reform UK is "too nasty for the nasty party". This comes after Badenoch "rules out [a] coalition" with Reform at the next general election, the paper reports. In an interview with the BBC on Tuesday, Badenoch said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election A picture of Kemi Badenoch behind DJ decks at the Tory conference is splashed across the front page of the Daily Telegraph. Also on its front page, the paper reports on details about former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's legal action against Thames Valley Police following his arrest in February The Duchess of Sussex "wants to apologise" for comments in her and the Duke of Sussex's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, according to the Daily Express. The paper says the couple "realise Meghan's claim a Royal Family member had queried son Archie's skin colour was 'her biggest mistake'" The Sun leads on the "murder of Royal Family GP" Hannah Terry. The mum-of-three was found dead at home her home in Sandringham "while hosting a children's sleepover", the paper reports. It adds that her patients "included Queen Camilla", who along with the King have been "informed of her death". Mark Cain, 45, has been charged with murder "Asos hacker havoc" is the headline on the front page of the Metro. The online retail platform says its customers data may have been accessed after hackers sent what the Metro calls a "threatening notification" Chancellor John Healey has plans for a £1bn support package to "bring down energy bills", according to the Guardian. It says he is considering a "major intervention" to help poorer households at the Budget on 28 October. The paper says it comes after ministers "became alarmed at forecasts that show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January" Oil tanker captains are being paid $100,000 a month to travel through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Financial Times. Owners are paying the bumper rates as a form of "danger money", the paper reports, "to persuade seafarers to stay on vessels" as Gulf countries try to keep oil flowing through the strait The French protests cover the front page of the Independent, as it says "260,000 take to the streets in growing revolt over classroom conditions". At least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff have been injured, the paper quotes French Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu as saying The i says a "blunder over funding teacher pay rises" means school budgets are "set for squeeze". The paper says Education Secretary Lucy Powell has "strained relations" with the Treasury "after suggesting that new money" could pay for the 3.5% pay award The Daily Star says there are "outbreak fears" after the death of a worker at a Siberian plague research laboratory. Russian officials are still investigating the cause of the death, but they say those who came into contact with the researcher all tested negative for pneumonic plague. US officials have said they are watching the situation closely, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no cause for concern Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: From 'woke' ridicule to real car - new electric Jaguar unveiled
description: Two years after JLR relaunched Jaguar into a blizzard of controversy, it has unveiled its new electric car.
body: Two years ago, JLR relaunched Jaguar into a blizzard of controversy. Its bizarre teaser ad was described as "woke" and its "Barbie pink" concept car was ridiculed. Now, the first of its new models has appeared in public for the first time. The all-electric Type 01, unveiled in New York, represents a radical new direction for the classic brand. The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type. But it marks a gamble for JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar, despite the risk of collateral damage from the culture wars. The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles. The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered". However, it comes at a hefty price tag, with a minimum cost of £130,000. Under normal circumstances, the launch of a car like this might generate few headlines. But in this case the attention has been much greater, and for good reason. In 2024 Jaguar unveiled its new identity to the public. The first step was a surreal advert, showing models in a range of bizarre and brightly coloured outfits. There was a new Jaguar logo - but no cars in sight. Two weeks later, Jaguar's denim-clad design chief Gerry McGovern took to a Miami stage to unveil a pair of radical concept cars, resplendent in Miami Pink and London Blue colour schemes. "Jaguar has no desire to be loved by everybody," he quipped. The pink concept car unveiled in 2024 The event was meant to herald Jaguar's future as a luxury all-electric marque, but it triggered a furious backlash in the press and on social media. Critics claimed JLR was betraying its heritage in favour of going "woke". Even the colour chosen for the launch was derided as "Barbie pink", as culture wars erupted around it. The reception appeared to catch JLR by surprise. The reinvention of Jaguar as a luxury electric brand was part of a wide-ranging strategy set out by the company in early 2023, in which it pledged to invest £15bn in new models and technologies. At the time, Jaguar itself was struggling. The badge, which was once an intrinsic part of Swinging Sixties British cool, had lost its lustre. Where in the past it had supplied E-Types to Brigitte Bardot and Steve McQueen, it now struggled to sell upmarket saloons and SUVs to middle-ranking corporate executives, who generally preferred Audis and BMWs. "Jaguar's core demographic, despite the uproar, gave up on the brand years ago, so they effectively had nothing to lose," explains Matthias Schmidt of Schmidt Automotive Research. JLR wound down production of its old Jaguar models in 2024 and 2025. The "woke" row, while it possibly made life briefly uncomfortable for the company's leadership, did at least keep the Jaguar name in the public consciousness at a time when it was selling very few cars. "It brought Jaguar from the back pages to the front pages, given that it was dying in a crowded international market," says Schmidt. "Everyone is now talking about what would have been another boring product." The GT is expected to be the first of three new electric designs from Jaguar. Since that event in Miami two years ago, McGovern has left the company, JLR has parted ways with the agency behind the controversial rebranding campaign, and the company also has a new chief executive. But the future of Jaguar itself still hangs in the balance. "I think it really is a last throw of the dice," says automotive journalist Steve Fowler. "JLR has struggled to make serious money with Jaguar in the past, and that's what it's all about." The question now is whether enough buyers can be found willing to pay £130,000 for a relatively distinctive upmarket electric car, in a market where they can also choose models from the likes of Porsche, Mercedes-AMG or even fast-growing Chinese brands such as Denza. "Forget the controversy, the culture wars and the pink concept car," says Ginny Buckley of the electric car website Electrifying.com. "What ultimately matters is whether Jaguar has built something extraordinary enough to justify blowing up everything it stood for before." She believes the car is good enough to silence critics, but admits "the next challenge will be getting people to buy it". Steve Fowler agrees. "The car is good enough to do it," he says. "Whether the Jaguar brand is good enough remains to be seen." title: What we know about Christa Pike’s ‘unprecedented' recovery after failed execution
description: The BBC's Sarah Smith details the injuries sustained by the US death row inmate after two failed lethal injections, and what comes next.
body: This video can not be played US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after surviving a failed execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee last week. Pike continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, according to a statement from her attorneys on Tuesday. An aneasthesiologist advising Pike's defence team said her survival is highly unusual, and while her prognosis remains unclear, "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery". title: UK set for coldest night of autumn so far
description: The first frost of the season is expected for some places this week as colder, Arctic air moves across the UK bringing a dip in temperatures. But how cold will it get and how long will the chillier spell last? Sarah Keith-Lucas takes a look.
body: After a spell of unusually warm weather, UK temperatures are set to tumble with the coldest night of autumn so far arriving by midweek. Wednesday night will bring the first frost of the season to some places, as colder air arrives from the Arctic. In some areas, minimum temperatures could be just a degree or two above freezing by dawn on Thursday. Along with the plummeting temperatures, some much-needed rainfall is on the way for England and Wales. A southerly shift in the jet stream will allow colder air to flood across the country through the middle of the week So far this autumn, the jet stream - which determines what sort of air mass affects the UK - has been sitting to the north. This has allowed mild south or south-westerly winds to flow, particularly across the southern half of the British Isles. This week, however, the jet stream will start to sink further south, allowing the winds to turn more northerly and introduce a colder air mass. While it will feel significantly colder compared to recent weeks, especially in the south, temperatures will actually be near normal for the time of year or perhaps just a little below. Afternoon highs on Wednesday will be around 12C to 14C in Northern Ireland and Scotland and 14C to 16C in England and Wales. Temperatures by Thursday dawn will be between 3 and 9 Celsius in most towns and cities although rural places could be several degrees lower. Whilst the northern half of the UK has already seen temperatures near the seasonal average this month, it has consistently been several degrees above average in the south, with somewhere reaching above 20C every day since 11 June. By the overnight hours, temperatures will be unseasonably low with a noticeable chill first thing on Thursday. Minimum temperatures at dawn will be around 5 to 7C for most places, but the coolest areas in northern and eastern England as well as eastern Scotland could be just a degree or two above freezing. A touch of frost is likely on grass and car windscreens here. Whilst scattered showers will affect the north-west on Wednesday, a spell of more prolonged rain is expected in eastern England - good news for areas that saw very little rain over the past month. In addition to the autumn chill, much-needed rain will spread across England and Wales from midweek. Wednesday will start cloudy and wet as a frontal system slowly drifts eastwards. Whilst sunshine will return to many places in the afternoon, rain is expected to linger for most of the day in East Anglia and the far south-east. Southern and eastern England, where it has been especially dry lately, could receive around 20 to 30mm. This would equate to up to half a month's rainfall in just 24 hours. Nearly three quarters of England and all of Wales are still in drought. The Environment Agency has previously said that 20% more rainfall than average is needed for at least seven months before all areas will be out of drought status. The chilly feel to the weather will continue into Thursday, with maximum temperatures between around 11 to 16C north to south. With plenty of dry and bright weather though, it may well feel pleasant in the afternoon sunshine for many. By Friday, temperatures will be on the rise once more. Westerly winds will push milder air across England and Wales, where 20C could again be reached in the east. Further north, no frost is expected by Friday dawn and afternoon highs will peak in the mid teens Celsius. Keep up to date with the longer range forecast in BBC Weather's Monthly Outlook. title: 'That nagging feeling of dread': Is 'hang-xiety' a real thing?
description: For some, a hangover can start an anxious spiral. We spoke to experts about the reasons why.
body: Eleanor Tobin (right) says she's no stranger to hang-xiety after a night out You wake up. Your head throbs. Then comes the second wave: a low, gnawing horror at what you might have done. You scroll back through last night's messages, certain you said something wrong. You replay conversations worried you offended someone, embarrassed yourself, or both. "It's that nagging feeling of dread," says 25-year old Eleanor Tobin who works in marketing and events in London. "If the day starts with me doing a checklist of my things - panically checking I have my bag, my phone - I know the anxiety is going to seep into everything I do beyond just reliving the night before." This is hang-xiety, a name coined in social slang a decade ago, for the anxiety that can accompany a hangover. And yes, it is real. "Alcohol affects the body in many ways - the brain, sleep, hormones and nervous system - that all help explain why a night out drinking can be followed by an excessively anxious morning," says Celia Morgan, professor of psychopharmacology at the University of Exeter. This video can not be played Watch: Yes, hang-xiety is a real thing Alcohol affects two chemical messengers in the brain: GABA and glutamate. GABA acts a little like the brain's braking system, reducing nerve-cell activity. Glutamate is involved in excitation and alertness. Alcohol enhances the effects of GABA and suppresses some glutamate activity, helping to produce that familiar feeling of relaxation and lowered inhibitions. But the brain is constantly trying to restore balance. As alcohol wears off, the nervous system can swing towards greater alertness and arousal. This can trigger anxiety. "Everything is always 100% worse in my mind when you have a hangover than in reality," says Tobin. A 2023 study of over 5,000 students from the UK and the Netherlands, concluded that 18.3% reported symptoms of anxiety when hungover. For the 25-year-old, it can lead to an anxious spiral at the end of a weekend Studies also suggest that not everyone gets hang-xiety, and the level of anxiety does not neatly correlate with how much you drink the night before. Existing psychological characteristics – and potentially genetics – appear to play a part. In 2019 researchers at the University of Exeter studied this in 97 social drinkers. Those who drank reported a spike in anxiety the following day compared with a control group who stayed sober. The effect was strongest in people who had scored highly for shyness before drinking. Morgan's research found that shy drinkers often felt less anxious during the evening itself. Alcohol was doing exactly what they hoped, quieting social nerves, but the rebound came the next day. "Shy people were hit even harder the next morning, with hugely elevated anxiety markers, especially when compared with those that weren't naturally shy," says Morgan. There is a psychological layer, too. Innocuous moments get reinterpreted as embarrassing. A perfectly normal joke becomes, in the retelling inside your own head, a terrible mistake. The anxious spiral can outlast the physical symptoms, because it feeds on itself: worry disrupts thinking, and disrupted thinking produces more worry. If Tobin has been out Friday and Saturday night, by Sunday that spiral can become overwhelming. "Suddenly taking the underground can feel like a challenge - normal stuff feels hard when you got a really bad case of the 'Sunday scaries' triggered by two hangovers in a row," she says. Drinking alcohol can affect sleep as well as trigger severe anxiety the next day You may have fallen asleep quickly after drinking, but that doesn't mean you've had a good night's sleep, researchers warn. Alcohol disrupts sleep, including the pattern of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which is important for emotional regulation. Wake up dehydrated and sleep-deprived, and your ability to cope with anxious thoughts is already reduced. "Light and broken sleep means you wake feeling on edge," says Dr Alanna Hare, President of the British Sleep Society. "Even if you have eight hours in bed, you haven't had a proper night's sleep, and a tired brain is more reactive to worry." The advice from researchers is unglamorous but consistent. Moderating alcohol intake matters more than any remedy taken afterwards. Drinking water between alcoholic drinks can help, so can eating during your night out. UK guidelines recommend no more than 14 units a week, the equivalent to six pints of beer or six medium glasses of wine, spread across several days. Alcohol Change UK director Andrew Misell says it's important not to reach for alcohol to manage or mask stress. "Alcohol turns into a depressant and can exacerbate all sorts of problems with our physical and mental health," he says, advising people to see their GP if they are struggling with the spiral. Talking to a close friend can also be a good starting point. And perhaps the most useful trick if you are suffering with hang-xiety is to reframe the thoughts. Recognising hang-xiety as a temporary state, rather than proof that something has gone horribly wrong socially, can blunt its power. The dread is real. The catastrophe it points to usually isn't. So the next time the Sunday morning spiral sets in, remember it may simply be your brain and body trying to regain balance after alcohol. title: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
description: A sharp increase in human activity is affecting the way the Himalayan monal lives and communicates, studies show.
body: The male monal has distinctive green, blue and copper plumage A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found. The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas. But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals. Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird. One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley. "These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas. Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas. "If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan. Found high in the Himalayas, the monal lives in alpine meadows above the forests The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation. While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity. "There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said. The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk' Why the mighty Himalayas are getting harder and harder to see According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios. Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats. The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit. "These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said. The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption. The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says. A male Himalayan monal displays its iridescent plumage during a courtship ritual aimed at attracting a female The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar. They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023. Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said. The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear. "This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said. Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall. title: Froyo's made a comeback. But at £12 a tub will it last?
description: Frozen yoghurt, which was a huge craze in the 2000s and 2010s, has made its return with multiple chains popping up across the wider UK.
body: Froyo has made a return with several stores opening across the UK this year Kiersten Paterno was one of the many people willing to queue up to an hour to treat herself to some frozen yoghurt. "It was a 45-minute wait for my turn but the whole experience of choosing your flavours and customising it with different toppings was a big part of the appeal for me," the 19-year-old student says. Froyo was a huge trend in the UK in the late 2000s and early 2010s and was most popular in London. Chains like Snog had 10 stores in the capital at its peak and other brands like AngelBerry had shops in Bristol and Brighton. And this year it's made a comeback, driven by nostalgia, social media and its perception as a healthier dessert choice. Several brands such as Go Greek, Myka and Yo-Chi launched in London, while Frurt, which operates mainly in the north west of England and Yorkshire, has opened new stores, including one in Leicester. These companies saw hundreds of customers queueing to create their own dessert pot, despite it not being a particularly cheap treat, with tubs costing as much as £12. Kiersten Paterno, 19, values froyo as it's nostalgic and can be healthy Kiersten says she was initially attracted to the dessert as she could manage portion size and sweetness level. "I could control how sweet I wanted it to be through the toppings. It feels healthier overall as it's a dessert I can enjoy without feeling like I've overindulged." She admits it can be pricey but says she doesn't mind spending a little more as an occasional treat. Research suggests the froyo market is steadily growing. Market Data Forecast estimates that the European frozen yoghurt market is worth £434m in 2026, up from £419m last year. Australian brand Yo-Chi opened a Notting Hill branch in August and blew up quickly on social media for its range of toppings and "third space" feel. "Sweet treat culture is huge. People aren't spending a fortune on big things, but a little thing like that, they're happy to," says Bethan Clarke, Yo-Chi campaign manager. There were long queues outside Yo-Chi on its launch day While Yo-Chi would "never call ourselves healthy" - froyo is usually lower in calories and fat than ice cream, but may also contain more added sugar - Clarke says the fact that it is customisable means that people are in control of their own portion sizes and sugar levels. Social media trends like "2026 is the new 2016" are helping froyo's virality. "People are coming back to re-experience childhood a little bit," says Clarke. Ella Light, who also works for Yo-Chi, says she's been surprised by the mix of people coming into the store. "I was kind of expecting to see the Gen Z girlies coming in, [but] this morning there was a group of builders!" Snog was the big name in froyo in the 2010s But how likely is the current froyo craze to survive? After all, it was huge in the 2010s but by the end of that decade was all but dead. Vhari Russell, founder of Food Marketing Experts, says: "Market over-saturation played a role in the initial disappearance of froyo, as well as the natural cycle of dying trends." Market leader Snog faced increasing competition from the likes of Yog, Yoomoo and Pinkberry, while consumers also realised that the dessert may not have been the healthier option they initially thought it was. "But now 2010s throwbacks coupled with a modern twist are seeing huge appetite across the market," says Russell. Will £12 for a tub eventually start to put people off though? Russell doesn't believe so, as she calls it an "affordable luxury". Going out for a froyo can be "an experiential moment" as much as anything, she adds. "For many people, they don't smoke or have expensive lifestyles, so froyo isn't viewed as food, it's viewed as an experience." If the price of froyo seems unreasonable or if you can’t justify queueing for hours, BBC Food have five different froyo variations you can make at home. title: The ‘biggest puzzle game ever’ is being released – its creator explains why it took 10 years
description: Order of the Sinking Star is due out on Thursday and has roughly 1,500 puzzles for players to try
body: For ten years, Jonathan Blow has been working with a small team on what he believes is "the biggest puzzle game ever made". The American developer is renowned as one of the fathers of the modern indie game movement, creating the genre-defining puzzle-platformer Braid in 2008. Now, a decade on from his last project, The Witness, The Order of the Sinking Star is due to be released on Thursday - a game with roughly 1,500 puzzles that he estimates could take around 500 hours to complete. So why make something the majority of players may never get even halfway through, let alone finish? "Some people decide what to make based on what's practical or what makes business sense," Blow says. "It's never been the way that I think." "I sort of make bad business decisions in a sense...because I let the design dominate that process. But then because we did that, we always have something unique," he says. The game's blurb likens itself to a "game design supercollider" - four worlds viewed from overhead, built on the mechanics of four pre-existing free puzzle games from other designers (with their permission to do so). These ideas are then "smashed together" to create brand-new brainteasers. For example, one world's mechanics, based on those from the free 2014 game Mirror Isles by Alan Hazelden, sees players use mirror reflections to swap places across islands. When combined with the system of another free game created by Hazelden, Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes - where players throw stones into water to create paths - brand-new puzzle opportunities suddenly arise. How an AI was tricked into breaking its own rules Taking a risk on making something more experimental is what appears to ultimately drive Blow, who says that as the industry has grown, the culture for developers has also changed. "Somewhere along the way...this idea that the best designers were trying to always make new experiences...just sort of got dropped by the wayside," he says. The outspoken designer is renowned for his frank takes on the industry - previously calling social media games such as Farmville "evil" and World of Warcraft's quest design "unethical". In December 2025, Hazelden publicly distanced himself from Blow - writing in a post on Bluesky, external that he was "dismissive of diversity efforts" and "pro-MAGA". Blow, who has not responded to these critiques publicly, tells me he instead decided to "sit down and focus on the games". "What the players want from developers is good games," he says. "They don't want us to be arguing, especially with each other, about political stances." Blow says the industry faces an uncertainty in how it approaches AI Blow says he is sceptical of AI, which was "not part of the pipeline at all" for Order of the Sinking Star, even though he recognises it as an "advancement" and an "interesting technology". Of the benefits often cited by those who use the tech, such as increased productivity, he asks: "If you're saying you're ten times as productive and it's been 3 years, you should have been able to do thirty years of work." "So where's this output of 30 years of work?" Despite rejecting the tech, Blow says the industry faces an "uncertain time" in how it deals with AI, particularly with newer creators who may rely too heavily on it to code rather than learning the "weird glyphs" themselves. "A danger is that not many people know how to program in the future," he says. "And if AI can't really do everything, then the supply of programmers might not be enough to make good stuff." In 2008 Jonathan Blow released the genre-defining puzzle platformer Braid, the post-release of which is documented in the film Indie Game: The Movie Blow's refusal to compromise on any aspect of the Order of the Sinking Star transcends its core design. The developer decided to make his own programming language, Jai, from scratch. He then used this, alongside a custom engine, to make the game. A game's engine is a piece of software that packs everything needed to craft a playable experience - including graphics rendering, physics simulation and scripting - into one place for creators. Some developers turn to pre-built game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, rather than taking on the considerable challenge of building an engine from scratch. For Blow, creating his own engine in this language meant he could build something "tuned and authored very specifically" to what he wanted to make. It is yet another reason he gives for why this project, which started as a simple "design experiment", has taken ten years to finish. "I do want the next project after this to be less on hard mode, or really it was nightmare mode, because we did so many things on hard mode at the same time," he reflects. "But it's also been rewarding in a certain way. Because otherwise, what else are you in the industry for?" Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. title: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor
description: Equinor warns it may shun further investments in the UK if new oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw are not approved.
body: Anders Opedal said Equinor would have to take "a hard view" about future investments in the UK if it were to reject new drilling Oil giant Equinor has warned it may shun further investments in the UK if new oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw are not approved. "The question will be: is the UK investable in the future? I hope it will not come to that," said Anders Opedal, boss of the Norwegian state oil company which is part owner of the sites. He told the BBC the company would "have to take a hard view about it" if a decision was made to reject new drilling. The warning comes as the UK government is set to decide whether or not to grant final approval to extract oil and gas at Rosebank and Jackdaw, despite a ban pledged in Labour's election manifesto. The government said any decision would take into account all relevant evidence. Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035. The UK already relies on Norway for half of its gas needs, and the Norwegian government has continued to issue new licences for oil and gas exploration in its own North Sea waters. Equinor has predicted production will remain at current levels until the middle of the next decade. Opedal said he remained confident that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's talk of a "pragmatic approach to oil and gas" meant both projects would get approved but he said the current limbo was "an uncomfortable position to be in". He said that the UK could produce more of its own oil and gas. "It's a political choice," he said. "The North Sea oil and gas industry started on the UK side. We learned from the UK and it's actually the same geology on both sides of the border - several fields actually cross it." Rosebank is the United Kingdom's largest undeveloped oil and gas field, located in the North Atlantic about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands and is thought to hold up to 500 million barrels of oil and gas. Opedal told the BBC the exploration licence for the site was originally granted 25 years ago. "The licence was awarded in 2001, the discovery was made in 2004 and the final investment decision in 2023," he said. Both Rosebank and Jackdaw were initially given the go-ahead by the former Conservative government but were delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact. Following a public consultation on the sites, which closed in August, the final decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh. Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank. Adura has previously said that if approval comes soon, Jackdaw could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete". Tessa Khan, executive director of Uplift, an organisation that wants the UK to move away from fossil fuel production, said new drilling at Rosebank "won't cut our bills" and was a "bad deal for Britain". "It's overwhelmingly oil for export – but it will make Equinor and its part-owner, the Norwegian government, richer, while Britain is left with high energy bills and a declining workforce." Khan said Labour's "climate credibility is also on the line". A government spokesperson said the North Sea remained a "vital national asset", adding that "oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come - alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis". "Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process," the spokesperson added. title: Midfield options and a fab front four - what we've learned about England
description: From Trent Alexander-Arnold's return to Alex Scott's debut, Phil McNulty assesses what England have learned during this international window.
body: Harry Kane marked his 125th England appearance with two goals against the Czech Republic England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina felt like the most painful wound of all as the so-called years of hurt stretched to six decades - but the process of recovery has started swiftly. The extended international break and four Nations League games have afforded head coach Thomas Tuchel, so heavily criticised for his defensive tactics in that defeat in Atlanta, the opportunity to rebuild and rehabilitate from that disappointment. Tuchel's squad included players recalled after being excluded from his plans and others who were new to the England fold, while mainstays like captain Harry Kane continued as the centrepiece of his plans. So what has Tuchel learned from the start to England's Nations League campaign? Kane inspires England to win over Czech Republic in Nations League Kane scores twice but who else was a 'real threat'? England player ratings There was a sense of inevitability that England captain Kane would be the star turn in Tuesday's 3-0 win over the Czech Republic as he celebrated equalling Peter Shilton's record of 125 England caps. Kane, still irreplaceable at 33, added to his goals tally as England's all-time record scorer, his total of 91 now 38 ahead of Wayne Rooney, who is in second place in the listings with 53 goals in 120 games. And, with Kane still looking in his prime and fully fit, it now seems only a matter of time before he makes history as the first player to score 100 goals for England. This alone will have delighted Tuchel, but even more satisfying for the German is that he now presides over an attacking quartet that can pose a threat to any side in world football. Kane is the peerless spearhead, but Anthony Gordon - on target in the three Nations League games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia before being rested here at Wembley - has moved his game on to another level since joining Barcelona from Newcastle. Gordon is a creator with burning pace, while on the right flank Bukayo Saka has looked rejuvenated after a World Cup during which he was hampered by an Achilles injury, as he proved with two goals in Croatia. And, just behind them all, with everything he does stamped with world class, is Jude Bellingham, England's player of the year and the golden future of his country at only 23. This may be bad news for Chelsea's Cole Palmer, whose withdrawal from England's squad has allowed others to cement their place in front of him, with Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White proving his commitment by cutting short a family holiday to join the squad after being excluded initially. England's front four looks a natural fit, augmented by Chelsea's Morgan Rogers, while Liverpool's 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha will be an international contender for years to come. If Tuchel can keep his fab four fit and firing, England will be a danger to any opponents. Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender In a camp of positives, a major disappointment for England and Tuchel was the injury suffered by Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott after an outstanding debut in the 7-0 win in Croatia. Scott slipped seamlessly into England's midfield with powerful running, a complete range of passing and an energy to his link play that made the 23-year-old look perfectly at home at international level. Scott's emergence showed the array of riches Tuchel has at his disposal in the central midfield area, even with Arsenal's Declan Rice, a fixture in the team, out as his load is managed after injury. Indeed, Scott was so impressive that Tuchel said: "Is Declan still for me a fixed point in my team? Yes, but some other players are coming and impressing and it's an ongoing competition." It was hardly a shot across Rice's bows, but certainly an indication of the options available to England. So the thigh injury that ruled him out against the Czech Republic was a blow to Scott and England - as well as Bournemouth, who fear he will be sidelined for two months. Elliot Anderson, Manchester City's £116m summer purchase from Nottingham Forest, also goes from strength to strength after a good World Cup, while Tuchel was prepared to give Arsenal's 20-year-old Myles Lewis-Skelly his head in central midfield in these Nations League games. Everton's James Garner has also figured and has a big admirer in Tuchel, even referring to him as England's "mini Valverde" - a somewhat tongue-in-cheek reference to Real Madrid midfielder Federico perhaps, but a sign of how highly he is rated. Manchester United's Kobbie Mainoo pulled out injured while Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton, so highly-rated, has been unable to force his way into Tuchel's plans. Tuchel's treatment of Trent Alexander-Arnold had provided a constant backdrop to his time as England head coach, with what appeared to be his mistrust of the Real Madrid right-back's defensive frailties culminating in his exclusion from the World Cup squad. Alexander-Arnold's card looked marked from the moment Tuchel, after leaving him out of World Cup qualifiers against Andorra and Serbia in August 2025, said: "If he wants to have this impact in the English national team then he has to take the defensive part very, very seriously. "Because when we are talking, especially about qualifying football, and then tournament football, the one defensive error, the one moment where you are not 100% awake, can be decisive. It can be the moment where you pack your suitcases and go home." Tuchel, however, appeared to set those reservations to one side when he recalled him for these four Nations League games - and Alexander-Arnold responded with performances that simply demand his continued inclusion. title: Honeymoon over as Pocognoli's Scotland suffer domestic disharmony
description: Sebastien Pocognoli is left with questions to answer after an inert Scotland performance leaves him still searching for his first home win, writes Tom English.
body: This video can not be played On a dismal night at Hampden when Scotland failed to ask enough questions of Slovenia, there are one or two that could be posed to new boss Sebastien Pocognoli and his players. We knew Pocognoli was a disciple of three at the back - the issue being whether he was rigid or flexible in his philosophy, whether he was a bit of an ideologue or a coach capable of changing things on the hoof. Well, he changed it, that's for sure. Maybe not early as he should have, but at 1-1, and then when Slovenia took a deserved 2-1 lead, Pocognoli switched formation and personnel, not out of design but out of desperation, you felt. He hurled players on in a bid to take a point; strikers, wingers, kitchen-sink stuff. Indiscriminate and messy. Scotland never really got out of the blocks. They got what they deserved. So to the questions. Where did this turkey of a performance come from? As early as the 13th minute there were signs of a rough night when Slovenia got in behind and Adam Cerin's shot had to be blocked by Jack Hendry. Concerning. 'Outfought' and 'not good enough' - Robertson on Scotland defeat Slovenia come from behind to beat ramshackle Scotland at Hampden How promotion, relegation and knockouts work in Nations League It got a touch nervy as the visitors knocked it about, trying to work it into all the space that Scotland were affording them. Hampden was deathly quiet. Then Ryan Christie scored and it stirred, only to fall into a slumber again. The trouble at the back was revisited soon after, Andy Roberton having to make a lung-busting effort to throw himself in front of a point-blank shot from Zan Vipotnik after Hendry was caught dozing. The issues were obvious. Can the back three, so badly exposed by Slovenia, be long for this world when the opposition is decent? Why did all that acreage of space open out wide and through the middle? Slovenia were licking their lips for most of the night. They were clever and creative and should have won by more. Why did Scotland's lauded midfield look so overrun? Seconds into the second half, Slovenia went straight through the middle again. This video can not be played 'Scotland didn't deserve to win' - Pocognoli Was anybody taking note of the warning signs? Where was the intent and urgency? Where was the accuracy and the width? Where were the chances? Where were the bodies in the box supporting the frontman and the pressing game? How could Slovenia go from being thoroughly outplayed by Scotland in the second half in Ljubljana to being so superior in Glasgow? Aljosa Matko's equaliser started with a Scotland throw-in. Danijel Sturm's chance that should have made it 2-1 three minutes later came on the back of Ben Gannon-Doak staying miles up the pitch oblivious to Sturm's danger. Angus Gunn didn't exactly cover himself in glory, either. The goal that we thought had made it 2-1 was disallowed - correctly - for offside, but the build-up was more of the same. Before Matko banged it past Gunn, Slovenia won one aerial duel and then another. Weak, weak, weak. That second goal did come, as everybody suspected it would. Matko down the right, squared to Sturm. Easy. Luis Binks was caught this time. Soft, soft, soft. What does it all mean for Scotland's bid for second place in their Nations League group, a position that would give them a favourable pot two seeding for December's Euros draw? That looks in jeopardy now. The ramifications of this defeat could stretch beyond the disappointment of a cold Tuesday night in Glasgow. It was such a damaging evening for Pocognoli, a bolt from the blue, you sensed. He probably thought he was a little further down the road than he really is. The air of dejection from him and his captain at the end was unmissable. It all sounded like some of the darker days under Steve Clarke. There were giant empty spaces in the stands at Hampden but, at the end, there were enough fans left behind to deliver a lusty verdict on what they saw. Going into this, there was positivity around Scotland's energy and the chances they'd been creating, about a burgeoning attacking style far removed from Clarke's supposed stodginess. All of that was badly undermined. It wasn't so much that Scotland lost the game - bad enough in itself - it was how they lost. It was limp and lifeless for far too long. Gannon-Doak played well as a wing-back last Saturday, but that was North Macedonia, not Slovenia. The youngster got targeted and exposed in a position he's not familiar with. Offensively, he was kept pretty quiet. This video can not be played Scotland were 'outfought' by Slovenia - Robertson A back three that has looked impressive was hassled to distraction, calm replaced with confusion. Scotland's go-to leaders did not lead. Robertson said his team was out-fought, which was a telling comment. Fight is the easiest part to get right, the thing that requires no talent. On Saturday in Skopje, everything was easy for Scotland because North Macedonia were no good. They scored two and could have scored five and six. Was there a sense of them believing in their own hype? Hard to imagine given that it was only North Macedonia they'd beaten, but there was a lack of edge about Scotland on Tuesday that begs that question. Or can it all be laid at the door of the system? Slovenia did their work on that. Ripped it to pieces, in truth. Pocognoli needs time, of course he does. He needs his most potent attacking midfielder, Scott McTominay, at the heart of things and needs more training sessions to drill his message into his players. November is his next chance, away to Switzerland and home to North Macedonia. No real margin for error now. They had a big chance to make it a healthy seven points from four games and they blew it. title: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
description: Relatives are finding themselves with no compensation and facing an administrative nightmare.
body: In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month. In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites. With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead. Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati. The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave. "I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says. He has little doubt they are dead. But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years. The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month. Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance. Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death. But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare. "In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari. He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues. For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate. When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us. Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them. Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed. Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data. The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol. The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over. Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality. Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue. "Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC. He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to. For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses. More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households. This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family. The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster. Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied. "We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities." The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution. In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters".
