title: 'Outfought' and 'not good enough' - Robertson on Scotland defeat
description: Scotland were "outfought" and simply "not good enough" in their 2-1 Nations League defeat by Slovenia, according to captain Andy Robertson.
body: This video can not be played Scotland were 'outfought' by Slovenia - Robertson Scotland were "outfought" and simply "not good enough" in their 2-1 Nations League defeat by Slovenia, says captain Andy Robertson. Having won in North Macedonia on Saturday, Sebastien Pocognoli's side were favourites to back that up with another victory at Hampden Park. The Scots led at half-time through Ryan Christie's close-range backheel, but were alarmingly open defensively and second-half goals from Danijel Sturm and Aljosa Matko turned the game on its head. "Not good enough," Robertson told BBC Sport Scotland. "The whole team. "We didn't do the good things we did on Saturday, I don't know what that's down to. They caused us a lot of problems and we have to find the reasons why. Slovenia come from behind to beat ramshackle Scotland Honeymoon over as Pocognoli's Scotland suffer domestic disharmony How promotion, relegation and knockouts work in Nations League "We wanted to kick on from Saturday because we had a really positive feeling about what we're doing and where we're going. We didn't do that. "It's been a long camp, I don't know if it was down to tiredness, but Slovenia have played the same amount of games as us. They looked a lot fresher, more hungry. "As Scotland, we might lack quality or make mistakes, but I don't think people accept being outfought. I think that's what happened tonight." Pocognoli echoed his captain's assessment that Scotland were well below par. "We didn't deserve to get the win, that's the reality," he said. "On the ball we were not clever enough. We were far from strong enough in the duels. "The reality is each game teaches us some information. We will try to go through the process we want and learn from this one and do better in the next one." This video can not be played 'Scotland didn't deserve to win' - Pocognoli When Pocognoli took over as Steve Clarke's successor in August, the Belgian was clear he would try to take Scotland in a new direction. He promised a more aggressive, more attacking style and called up several new faces - Josh McPake made his debut against Slovenia, following Stephen Welsh, Robbie Ure, Luis Binks and Luke Graham in the three previous fixtures. Scotland should have won in Slovenia in Pocognoli's first match in charge, which ended in a goalless draw, before Jack Hendry's early red card hamstrung them in a 3-0 home defeat by Switzerland. The win over North Macedonia was convincing and delivered a dose of optimism, but that has been severely dented and former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday believes Pocognoli's honeymoon period is over already. This video can not be played Should Scotland have had a penalty here? "I thought coming into this camp, Pocognoli would probably need a period of grace," Halliday said on Sportsound. "I think that period of grace is now over. "That was as poor a Scotland performance as I can remember for a while against an opposition you are expecting us to go and beat." Slovenia got in behind Scotland's high defensive line repeatedly and former national team captain Willie Miller is unsure if Pocognoli will stick with his back three. "This is Pocognoli's preferred system and he's had time to work with the system, it was just all over the place," Miller said on Sportsound. "Time and time again there were huge gaps appearing and Slovenia were taking advantage. "Our situation is we've got a new manager in, he's got a preferred system, what does he do? Does he just bin it? Are we back to a back four? "His preferred system is a back three, but it was unbelievably poor." title: Dad pulled me out of bed by my hair to help on the farm - rural abuse victims need more support
description: Tracy Lewis loved growing up on a farm but said the abuse from her father was terrifying.
body: Tracy Lewis says as a child she would sometimes think about calling Childline because she felt so petrified of the abuse inflicted on her by her dad Warning: This story contains content that some readers might find distressing Growing up on a farm, Tracy Lewis loved being around their animals but said the physical and emotional abuse from her farmer father was "torture". When she was eight, she recalled her dad pulling her out of bed by her hair to go lambing as her battered mum told her "you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die". Tracy, now 48 and a farmer herself, and other domestic abuse survivors are calling on governments to better support victims in rural areas. The UK government said it was working to address disparities while the Welsh government said challenges will be considered in its next national strategy. For many people the idea of growing up in the mid Wales countryside surrounded by trees and animals sounds idyllic, but Tracy says her dad was physically and emotionally abusive. Tracy's family have given their permission to the BBC for her to share her story. "I remember my father pulled me out of bed by my hair to go and lamb a ewe," she recalled. "I walked past the bathroom and my mum's face had blood all over it and her nose was squashed, she'd been crying. She said to me, you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die." This video can not be played Tracy said she felt "trapped" on the farm Tracy said the animals would sometimes be used as a form of control or a catalyst for abuse. "I was getting beaten up when something died, my mum was getting hurt when an animal was poorly," she recalled. "It felt like slavery, we loved the animals and farming but we were isolated and stuck." Tracy, who was raised at the farm in Llanbister in Powys, would sometimes think about calling Childline as she said she felt so petrified. "The farming world is the best place to be, neighbours will always help you out but abuse can be hidden very easily," said the mum-of-three. "Everyone knows everybody, but what goes on behind closed doors will stay behind closed doors. "For me it was terror and horror, my mum got the worst of it and she tried her best to protect us. But she was totally isolated, the farm was her life." She said farmers often had generational businesses and relied on markets and trade with others, adding that raising abuse could affect livelihoods. Tracy Lewis now farms on the smallholding where she grew up between Llandrindod Wells and Newtown in mid Wales Tracy also claims her father, who is now dead, financially abused her, stating that the farm would be passed down to her. She said she worked on it for 20 years and paid rent to him under the impression the family farm would one day become hers. After finding out it was not left to her in his will, she said she has had to "fight" to retain ownership of it. Tracy is one of about 11 million people living in rural areas - more than 15% of the UK population. The National Rural Crime Network says the true picture of rural abuse is often hidden, with survivors often having more barriers to reach support. I Was Held Hostage at Gunpoint After leaving an abusive relationship, Rhianon spent eight hours bargaining for her life while her ex-partner held her hostage at gunpoint. Captive in her own home, in a remote part of north Wales, this is the story of one woman's survival. One smallholding owner said her rurality enabled an ex-partner to hold her at gunpoint for eight hours with no-one to hear her screams. Rhianon Bragg said she screamed when Gareth Wyn Jones ambushed her with the gun in north Wales in 2019 but knew that no-one would hear her because she lives rurally. "There were several moments that night when I thought I wouldn't see my children again," she recalled. Rhianon has spoken in-depth about her experience at her smallholding in Gwynedd as part of a new BBC iPlayer series It Happened To Me. She has since worked with agencies like the police to try to address issues about domestic abuse and stalking in rural areas. "Domestic abuse changed our home from a place of peaceful seclusion to a place of vulnerable isolation and what I experienced was the additional barriers that living rurally created," said Rhianon. This video can not be played Wearing camouflage gear and armed with a shotgun, Rhianon Bragg's partner subjected her to an eight-hour overnight ordeal at their home in 2019 She said all UK and Welsh government domestic abuse policies should be "rural proofed" and highlighted issues such as internet connectivity and distance from police stations. "There is so much that should be addressed for people to be treated evenly, and at the moment, if you live rurally you're on the back foot," said Rhianon. Tracy urged anyone affected by abuse to speak out about it. "Tell someone, a friend, a neighbour, once you start telling people, things will move," she said. "A good overhaul of policy would be for the best because out here you can hide a lot of stuff. I think there's a lot more domestic violence that goes on in rural communities than anyone will ever know," added Tracy. Rhianon Bragg was stalked and held at gunpoint by her ex-partner Gareth Wyn Jones, who was jailed for four-and-a half years in 2020 A report by the UK's first working group focused on rural inequality and domestic abuse said rural domestic abuse victims were being failed. As part of a 12-point plan, the report published in May by RiTA - Rural Initiatives Tackling Abuse - recommended the UK government establish a parliamentary commission on rural domestic abuse and "rural-proof" government strategies. The Domestic Abuse Commissioner for England and Wales said she "welcomed" the report and told the BBC the realities of rural life for victims can be "frequently weaponised by their perpetrators". title: Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court
description: Lubna Speitan offered to testify on behalf of Minh Quang Pham, who was jailed for 40 years after a Heathrow bomb plot investigation.
body: Lubna Speitan gave evidence on behalf of a British national who was accused of plotting to carry out a suicide attack at Heathrow Airport The Green Party member behind a motion which declared Zionism to be racism was named in court documents as a "close friend" of a man who was jailed after being accused of plotting a suicide bomb attack at Heathrow Airport. Lubna Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state". Court documents from 2015 show she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham, who was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack. The BBC has contacted Speitan for comment. The Green Party said she holds no official positions and the party "takes all allegations of this nature seriously". The motion proposed by Speitan, which was passed on Sunday to become party policy, called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. In response, Israel banned Green leader Zack Polanski from entering the country. while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Lib Dem MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog. Speitan argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression". On Tuesday, it emerged she wrote a letter in 2016 to the New York judge in the Pham case describing him as "one of the kindest, honest, most sincere" people she had known. The existence of the letter was first reported by the Jewish Chronicle, external and it has been seen by BBC News. Pham, a Vietnamese-born British national who had lived in London, was arrested at Heathrow Airport in July 2011 after spending seven months in Yemen. He was found in possession of a live round of ammunition. In 2015 he was extradited to the US and in 2016 sentenced to 40 years in prison after he admitted three counts based on his support for the group al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), an offshoot of al-Qaeda. Minh Quang Pham was arrested at Heathrow in 2011 and later convicted in the US US prosecutors said Pham was directed by al-Qaeda leader Anwar al-Awlaki to detonate explosives in Heathrow's arrivals area after spending several months in Yemen being trained by him. In US court documents from 2015, Speitan was listed as a "close friend" of Pham who would provide "critical testimony regarding Pham's mental state". The documents said that would be "crucial in establishing a mental health defense", adding that "bears on the issue of guilt". Speitan had a medical condition that prevented her from giving evidence in person, the documents add. In a later letter to the US District Judge, Speitan said Pham was one of the "few people I regard with such high respect and esteem". She said if the judge "truly knew the Minh [Pham] that and others grew to love and respect", they may have "probably had the whole case dismissed". She acknowledged he "may have had and developed some behavioural issues" but added: "He turned out to be one of the kindest, honest, most sincere, trustworthy and respectful people I have ever known." There is no suggestion in the documents that Speitan knew of Pham's criminal activities at the time they knew each other. Speitan has not responded to the BBC's request for comment. The Telegraph reported that when it asked her if she remained friends with Pham, she replied: "Yes, it's still the case." She was reported as saying she believed Pham had been "targeted" by "the system". A Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate." It came as Green leader Polanski grappled with division among the party's members, MPs and deputy leaders over the motion. Some Green councillors have resigned since it was passed. Green deputy leader in Wales, Phil Davies, resigned and cancelled his membership on Tuesday, describing the motion as "the final nail in the coffin". Polanski released a lengthy statement on Monday night to say he would not accept anyone being excluded from the party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of". The party leader, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct". title: Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas in France
description: Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France amid a wave of protests by high-school pupils.
body: This video can not be played Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions. Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police. Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests. The BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Lille. Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas in France. title: US death row inmate Christa Pike conscious after failed execution, lawyers say
description: Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, according to a statement from her lawyers on Tuesday.
body: US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution attempt, her lawyers say. Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, according to a statement from her attorneys on Tuesday. She was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995. But Pike survived two lethal injections last week and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, for treatment. Her lawyers had said in the days afterwards that she was unconscious while medical staff cleared her body of the pentobarbitol injected during the failed execution attempt. Pike's lawyers said on Tuesday that her recovery is "medically unprecedented", and while her prognosis remains unclear, "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery". They said she is the only person known to have survived a completed execution attempt in the US. Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said over the weekend that he plans to resign. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens. title: Ronaldo says he's not retiring but deserves 'punishment' over Portugal walkout
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after head coach Jorge Jesus "broke his word to me".
body: Cristiano Ronaldo has scored 146 goals for Portugal in 234 appearances Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after head coach Jorge Jesus twice "broke his word". The 41-year-old captain left his country's Nations League camp after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark. Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice. In a lengthy statement, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player said he should be held accountable for his actions. "The Portuguese Football Federation must assess the consequences of my actions and punish me for them. I believe the punishment should not be reduced," Ronaldo said. "I have already apologised, but I know that actions have consequences." Ronaldo's statement comes after Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train. Jesus said on Sunday that the door was still open for Ronaldo to play for the country's national team. Ronaldo said that, provided he was "physically fit, playing with my team, and hopefully scoring goals", he would like to continue to play international football. "After my suspension period ends, I will be available, as I always have been, to compete and win with our national team," he added. BBC Sport has approached the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) for comment. This video can not be played Will Ronaldo ever play for Portugal again? Ronaldo's statement, which ran to nearly 2,000 words, struck a conciliatory tone in places. But he was also critical of Portugal coach Jesus as he provided his version of the dispute which prompted him to walk out on the squad last week. He said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the 72-year-old coach told him he would play for 30 minutes. "Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said. "The manager had broken his word to me." A later meeting with Jesus produced an agreement for the coach to clarify matters at his next news conference. Ronaldo said an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus' decisions and that the coach asking "someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona" to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Portugal's record appearance holder said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach's public remarks did not reflect their private discussion. "The conference was what is known: the attitude had nothing to do with our meeting," Ronaldo explained. "I heard expressions and an aggressiveness I believe I did not deserve, a "High and mighty" attitude that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before." Ronaldo said it was the "second time" Jesus had "broken his word to me" and he decided to leave the training camp "without waiting for any further broken promises". Prior to his appointment as head coach, Ronaldo said he had described Jesus - who had previously managed him at Al Nassr - as the "right choice". Ronaldo had considered retiring from international football after this summer's World Cup - at which Portugal exited at the last-16 stage - and said he had written a letter to fans containing the words he wanted to tell them when he announced it, but he was urged to reconsider by the FPF's president on the flight home from the United States. Ronaldo's behaviour drew contrasting opinions in his homeland with Jesus getting some support in the media and among fans at odds with those loyal to legendary player. Ronaldo said that, despite the "absolute breakdown of trust" in Jesus' word, he should not have left and the "responsibility is mine alone", as he said sorry to his fellow players and Portugal's supporters. He added: "I owe an apology to my national team teammates for having left the camp... I apologise to the Portuguese people once again, but a broken word has, for me, a defining impact." title: Kane scores twice but who else was a 'real threat'? England player ratings
description: Senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel rates the England players after Tuesday's 3-0 win against the Czech Republic.
body: Harry Kane scored twice on his 125th appearance for England - but who else impressed? Harry Kane scored twice as England cruised to a comfortable 3-0 win over the Czech Republic in the Nations League at Wembley on Tuesday. Here's how I rated the players - and you can see how you scored them below. What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? Jordan Pickford: Will return to Everton knowing his place is now under threat from James Trafford. Some shaky moments. 6 Trent Alexander-Arnold: Given another opportunity to impress and took it. Ability on the ball perfect for deep-lying opponents like the Czech Republic. 7 Jarell Quansah: Deployed in his favoured centre-back role and looked comfortable. Slowly becoming a fixture in the squad. 6 Marc Guehi: But for a couple of lapses, cruised through the game. Started all four of England's matches during the extended international break. 6 Lewis Hall: Now in a fight with Nico O'Reilly for the role of England's first-choice left-back. A successful international period for the Newcastle defender. 7 Elliot Anderson: Goes from strength to strength at international level. Brilliant pass to unlock the Czech Republic for England's second. 6 Myles Lewis-Skelly: Can be happy with his output on his return to the international scene. Will be unlucky not to be in next squad on this evidence. 7 Eberechi Eze: Improved after an underwhelming first-half but did not do enough to cause Thomas Tuchel a selection headache after being handed a rare start. 6 Jude Bellingham: Did not hit the heights of his captivating display in Croatia but still oozed class whenever in possession. 7 Morgan Rogers: Showed his versatility by starting out on the right and looked comfortable in the role. Provided a real threat. 7 Harry Kane: Historic night for the England captain becoming the country's joint-highest appearance-maker alongside Peter Shilton with 125 caps. Goes without saying he scored... twice. 8 James Garner (on 63, Anderson): More international minutes in his legs. 6 Jarrad Branthwaite (on 63, Guehi): On for his third cap. 6 Morgan Gibbs-White (on 73, Hall) 6 Rio Ngumoha (on 73, Bellingham) 6 Dominic Calvert-Lewin (on 82, Kane) 6 Subs not used: James Trafford, Jason Steele, Bukayo Saka, Anthony Gordon, Trevoh Chalobah, Rico Lewis. title: How drunk is too drunk? Cornell rape allegations expose 'loopholes' in consent laws
description: The BBC speaks to experts about current US state sexual assault laws and why some believe changing them will help alleged victims.
body: This video can not be played A backlash over the handling of a US woman's sexual assault complaint against Cornell University fraternity members has highlighted what experts believe are issues with the current laws in many states regarding sexual assault and drinking. The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, last month filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped by several men in 2024 at the university in the state of New York. Doe said she had been drinking earlier in the evening of the alleged incident and then went to a fraternity house, where several men pressured her to snort the drug ketamine and plied her with alcohol before advertising a "free" sexual encounter with her in a group message. She said she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent. Under current New York law, a person who voluntarily consumes drugs or alcohol - rather than becoming intoxicated without their consent - is not automatically considered unable to consent to sex. US media has been widely reporting it as the "voluntary intoxication loophole". New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week said: "Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape" and that she would work with the state legislature to close the "loophole". But some experts say the law has been misinterpreted and that it does not stop people who choose to consume alcohol or drugs from reporting sexual assault. It does, however, require them to prove they were so incapacitated they could not physically consent - a higher bar than being intoxicated. The distinction reflects an ongoing debate in the US about what counts as consent when someone has been drinking. Dan Schorr, a former sex crimes prosecutor, told the BBC that New York law still protects victims of assaults who have chosen to drink or take drugs. "If a person cannot express consent or lack of consent due to the consumption of alcohol or drugs, any sexual activity with them is always non-consensual, whether the ingestion of alcohol or drugs was voluntary or involuntary," said Schorr, who also helps universities review sexual assault cases. "I prosecuted many people who sexually assaulted someone who was voluntarily intoxicated," he said, adding: "I got convictions. They went to prison." What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation Some believe issue with the current law is that the bar is set too high with regards to what counts as being too intoxicated to give consent. At least 19 states, including New York, have a higher bar for the level of intoxication required to deem someone incapacitated and unable to consent. The New York law includes a provision that someone cannot consent to sex if they are "unconscious or for any other reason physically unable to communicate an unwillingness to an act". This applies to people who are too incapacitated from drinking to consent, Schorr said. But another legal expert the BBC spoke to says that can be difficult to prove. Some prosecutors "may not bring charges or defendants may be acquitted because someone 'gave consent' while intoxicated, but not completely incapacitated", according to Mitchell Epner, a former prosecutor who has handled sex trafficking cases. He said that in other states that have lower legal bars for incapacitation, someone who is "impaired" or "significantly impaired" cannot consent, and that being too drunk to drive a car could be considered as being at this level. College campuses have different standards for consent than criminal law, including Cornell, which uses a standard of affirmative consent, defined as "a knowing, voluntary, and mutual decision among all participants to engage in sexual activity". Cornell says silence or lack of resistance does not constitute consent. 'Ashamed': Cornell students gather to voice anger over alleged gang rape Epner supports a proposed change to New York's law to widen the scope of when someone is too intoxicated to consent. The New York Senate has passed a bill multiple times, but the state Assembly failed to bring it up for a vote. That bill states that people cannot give consent if they are under the influence of substances that have rendered them "temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling" their conduct, and "such conduct was known or reasonably should have been known" to the other person. Pennsylvania has also made efforts to try and change the law to make it easier for victims who were intoxicated to prove they were assaulted. "If somebody's too drunk to drive, they're too drunk to - fill in your verb of choice," Epner said. Representative Lea Webb, whose district includes Cornell University, told the BBC News Channel she and her fellow lawmakers were working to push through legislation on the issue, which has gone through several amendments. New York's current laws, she said, "puts the onus of proof on the victim". Schorr and criminal defence attorneys, meanwhile, criticised the proposed changes to New York's sexual assault laws. New York's State Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers said in a statement to the BBC New York's current laws were sufficient, and that "people have been convicted of rape in cases involving voluntarily intoxicated victims". The group said using language that a victim was "incapable of appraising or controlling their conduct" was "simply too vague to be fairly enforced", adding that the legislation does not give clear details on what constitutes someone being too intoxicated to engage in sexual conduct. Schorr said it was not easy to answer this question of what exact point someone is too intoxicated to consent. He added: "How should the law address that? It is very challenging to find a clear standard that will be evenly applied." "It's a conversation we should have as a society, as a state". title: Ex-US spy who stashed gold bars in his home admits to $200m scam
description: David Rush, who also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, had revealed the existence of a "clandestine human source", prosecutors said.
body: A former CIA officer who was arrested after authorities found hundreds of gold bars stashed in his home has admitted to defrauding the US government in a sprawling $200m (£151m) scam involving fake contracts and real estate. David Rush, 49, is required to pay restitution to the government and forfeit luxury real estate, cars, watches and other assets tied to his crime as part of the plea deal. Rush also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, which could have caused "grave damage" to national security. "The defendant will plead guilty because the defendant is in fact guilty of the charged offense," prosecutors stated in a court filing outlining the plea deal. The BBC has contacted Rush's lawyer, who declined to comment. Rush was initially charged with theft of public funds, but has now pleaded guilty to wire fraud. At the time of his arrest, a raid on his home uncovered 298 gold bars that he had received for "work-related expenses". Court filings around the deal bring new details to light, including that Rush revealed the existence and description of a "clandestine human source" to a foreign official. "The disclosure of such information could endanger the safety and life of the human source and the US government officers working with the source and jeopardize the US government's ability to recruit human sources, who rely on the US government's assurances of absolute secrecy," prosecutors said in the filing. In a news release, CIA Director John Ratcliffe said Rush "abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions". FBI investigators said that between November 2025 to March 2026 Rush made repeated requests for "a significant quantity of foreign currency and tens of millions of dollars in gold bars for work-related expenses". "Rush fabricated a highly classified program to justify the acquisition of luxury real estate in South Florida, which he then intended to resell for personal profit," the court filing laying out the deal states. Rush "effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny", according to the filing. He then used "fraudulently obtained" public funds to acquire luxury real estate properties in southern Florida. According to the court filing, part of the scam included hiring an interior designer and purchasing $40,000 worth of kitchen appliances for one property. The wire transfer charge was related to a $45m transfer that he initiated in January 2026. The plea deal also says that he provided top secret data to "a foreign government official who was not authorised to receive it and had no need to know it". Stacks of cash and gold bars were discovered at Rush's home in May Along with the gold bars, Rush was also found with $2m in cash and 35 luxury watches. Prosecutors said Rush was moving funds into commodities that could be easily traded, citing "strong evidence" he was trying to hide the money. Under the deal, he is also required to turn in the watches and two BMW vehicles, along with the cash and nearly $39m that was seized from his bank account. A federal judge will set his sentence at a later date, and a hearing has been scheduled for 28 January. The charge carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, but prosecutors noted that the time can be added to under federal law. In June, US Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cited Rush's professional career in deciding he was a flight risk, and ordered him held in jail pending trial. "He's in a different position than most people to flee and avoid detection by law enforcement," he said. Court records do not go into detail about Rush's work for the CIA, and describe him as a former senior executive in a US government agency in Virginia who had top secret clearance and access to classified information. US media have confirmed his former employment with the CIA. According to The Washington Post, external, he was senior executive in the agency's Directorate of Science and Technology, which develops high-tech spy tools. He had also previously been accused of fraudulently taking military leave with pay after being honourably discharged from the US Navy, and for lying about his education and military service when applying for his job in 2009. Court records show Rush was accused of falsely telling employers he had been a navy pilot. "These and other representations concerning Rush's military and academic accomplishments were false," the plea deal filing states. It is unclear how he was able to lie on his application form, and according to The Washington Post, several CIA officials have been placed on leave as they investigate why he was able to pass a background check. The government had argued previously that large sums of the funds are still unaccounted for, a claim which his lawyer has denied. title: Man charged with GP's murder
description: A man is charged with the murder of a GP who was found dead at her home.
body: Dr Hannah Terry's body was found on Sunday A man has been charged with the murder of a GP who was found dead at her home. The man was arrested after the body of 45-year-old Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday. Norfolk Police said 45-year old Mark Cain, of Fern Hill, Dersingham, has been charged with her murder. He has been remanded in custody until a court appearance on Wednesday. A notice on the website of Grimston Medical Centre, where Dr Terry is listed as a member of the practice team, said it was "temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team". Tributes have been left outside the centre, including a teddy bear and flowers on a bench. A card from two patients reads: "Dear Dr Hannah Terry. We are so shocked and saddened to hear such tragic news." A police cordon has been in place outside the property in Dersingham since Sunday The Norfolk and Waveney Local Medical Committee, which represents NHS GPs, has also paid its respects. A spokesperson said: "We are deeply saddened by the news of Dr Terry's death. She was a wonderful GP who was dedicated to providing excellent care for her patients." Tributes have been left for Hannah Terry after her body was found in her home on Sunday Michael Devaney, from the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Mark Cain for the murder of Hannah Cain following a police investigation into an incident at her home in Dersingham. "We have worked carefully with Norfolk Police during their investigation. "Our thoughts remain with the family of Hannah Cain at this time." Cain is due to appear at Norwich Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. Dr Pallavi Devulapalli used to work with Dr Terry Dr Pallavi Devulapalli, a GP, said she was devastated when she found out her friend and former colleague had died. She said the pair used to work together at The Hollies Surgery in Downham Market, Norfolk. Devulapalli, who is also an independent councillor, said she "was such an easy person to work with", "She was universally liked, she was a good GP, someone sensible who you could trust," said Devulapalli. "I never worried about the patients she looked after - just the sort of person you want to work with," she added. A teddy bear and flowers were left on a bench outside the surgery where Terry worked Charis-Mai Ellis, 25, paid tribute and said Terry had been her family GP. "She had the time for you and so much empathy and understanding. You could take your time with her and she wouldn't rush," she said. "It is honestly just heartbreaking." title: Three arrested after raid on gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to get asylum
description: Those targeted by Home Office immigration enforcement officers are accused of charging migrants up to £4,500 for fabricated evidence.
body: This video can not be played Watch: BBC sees police raid on fake gay asylum claims gang Immigration enforcement have made arrests in connection with a suspected criminal network believed to be behind dozens of fake asylum claims from people pretending to be gay. It follows a BBC investigation earlier this year, which revealed that law firms and advisers were helping migrants pose as gay in an effort to get asylum. Those targeted by Home Office immigration enforcement officers this morning are accused of charging migrants up to £4,500 for fabricated evidence, including staged photographs and fake documents. They are thought to have aided dozens of asylum claims from Bangladeshi men, claiming they would be in fear for their lives if they returned home. Three were arrested at addresses in London this morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences Two people were arrested at addresses in London this morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, with Home Office officers also seizing phones, jewellery and thousands of pounds in cash. A third person was arrested on suspicion of being in the country illegally. Chris Foster, a regional lead for criminal investigations at the Home Office, said the fake claims were connected to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon, which is based in Whitechapel, east London. He said asylum caseworkers had initially spotted patterns in suspicious claims, which raised concerns about the group, and that immigration officers had been investigating for several months. "We've got some intelligence that they can provide fake letters and documents, and they could charge anywhere between £1,000 and £4,500," Foster said. "It could be letters of support from Apanjon, it could be staged photographs, suggesting that these people are gay, it could be letters from people claiming to be in a friendship or a sexual relationship - [a] same-sex relationship - as the claimants." More than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network are being reviewed by the Home Office. Foster said some of the fake asylum applications would have "undoubtedly" been granted. Immigration judges have previously criticised evidence from Apanjon as unreliable or not credible and found that an applicant who claimed to have attended the group's events had submitted staged photographs. The Home Office said the group would often vouch for men who claimed asylum on the basis they were gay only after having initially been refused on political grounds. In one case, a man didn't raise his sexuality until nine years after his original claim. The group is accused of using the same tactics as those pushed by advisers exposed in the BBC's investigation earlier this year. A Home Office spokesperson said it was continuing to review asylum claims linked to that reporting, which led to two arrests in May. In the BBC report, published in April, an adviser called Tanisa Khan told an undercover reporter she could provide a "comprehensive package", including photographs at gay clubs and other supporting evidence. She was linked to a community group called Worcester LGBT, which she told the reporter they should attend in order to add to evidence for his fake claim. Men attending one of the group's events at a community centre in Beckton, east London, claimed they were not really gay. One said: "Nobody is a gay here. Not even 1% are gay. Not even 0.01% are gay." The investigation also revealed how bogus medical conditions and fake news websites were being used to bolster fraudulent asylum claims. Worcester LGBT has since closed. Its founder previously said the group did not create or support fabricated evidence in asylum claims and it was not up to the organisation to determine whether any individual was actually gay. Khan blamed communication difficulties for a "misunderstanding" and denied advising the reporter to make a false claim or offering to create fabricated evidence. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said "those faking persecution are beneath contempt and mock real victims who need protection". "To the gangs profiting from this disgraceful fraud: you will be prosecuted, stripped of your dirty money and shut down," she said. "And to those cheating the system, your claim will be thrown out, and you will be removed from this country." A conviction for asylum fraud carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison. title: What can I do to protect myself after 'Asos hacked' message?
description: Asos says people should not engage with the unauthorised notification and says it'll provide further information.
body: The message, which Asos says people should not engage with, popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on Tuesday If a strange-looking message from Asos popped up on your phone today, you may be worrying what it could mean and whether you need to do anything. The online retailer has emailed customers apologising for the "unauthorised push notification" containing an external link, adding that they should disregard the message and not click on it. Here's what has happened, and what those who may have been affected are being advised to do. On Tuesday morning, Asos users across the UK were sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company. "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message read. Later that day, Asos said it took immediate action to restrict the apparent hackers' access, was investigating and working with advisers and relevant authorities on "next steps". Data storage company Snowflake told the BBC its investigations had "found no compromise" of its platform. At this stage it isn't clear what information, if any, has been accessed. On Tuesday evening, Asos told customers it may include "basic personal information including name and contact details". "However, we don't believe that any payment-card information or account passwords have been impacted," it added. While those who received the pop-up message will undoubtedly be concerned, it does not mean your phone has been hacked. For now, the advice is: Don't click the link: The hack notification included a link to a Telegram account - Asos and cyber security experts say not to click on it Change passwords: It's worth updating your password, including across other sites that use the same one as your Asos account. The advice for a strong password is to mix numbers, symbols and upper and lower case characters, and avoid using the same password across multiple accounts Turn on two-step verification for important apps like banking and email: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls this "one of the most effective ways to protect your online accounts from cyber criminals". You can usually turn it on by going into the security settings in your account Monitor transactions: Keep an eye on your online transactions for anything unusual According to Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at global cyber-security firm Check Point, "the biggest immediate risk may be what happens next". She says criminals know people will be searching for information online and expects there to be "attempts to exploit that confusion". Her advice to Asos customers is not to be "scared and frightened". But she says they should be "extremely suspicious" of emails, texts or messages claiming their account has been compromised, offering a refund or asking them to click a link to reset their password. People should hang up the phone if they receive any calls from someone they think might be posing as Asos or another organisation, says Which? spokesperson Kat Cereda. The consumer rights expert says they should contact the organisation themselves afterwards through separate means. It's been less than 24 hours since the notification popped up on people's phones, and there are a number of unanswered questions. It isn't yet clear who is behind the message, what their motivation is, how many people received the notification or how many may be impacted Wilson, from the cyber-security firm Check Point, says there's still "an awful lot" we don't know. Asos said its website and app were operating "as normal, and customers can continue to shop with confidence on ASOS as normal" as of Tuesday night. It said protecting customers "is our priority", and it will provide a further update "as soon as we have confirmed more information". People should visit Asos's official website directly for updates. title: First minister to face no-confidence vote over Drumcree row
description: The motion comes amid a major political row over a planned Orange Order march in Portadown.
body: O'Neill and three fellow Sinn Féin ministers are each set to face a no-confidence vote Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill is to face a no-confidence vote at Stormont over her handling of the Drumcree parading dispute. The motions against her and three other Sinn Féin ministers are set to be debated after receiving the backing of unionist parties. But the attempt to oust them will fail as it requires cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the assembly. It comes amid a major political row over a planned Orange Order march in Portadown, County Armagh. O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians have been heavily criticised by unionists for joining protests which have blocked the parade from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry. O'Neill has defended her actions, saying she was "proud" to stand with the residents and adding that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it". In the assembly on Monday, the Sinn Féin vice-president described the planned Orange march as "unwanted, sectarian and triumphalist". The exclusion motions have been submitted against O'Neill and fellow Sinn Féin ministers John O'Dowd, Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmins. They are expected to be debated as early as next Monday. Orangemen have made several attempts to walk along the Garvaghy Road over the past week - but have been prevented from doing so each time The no-confidence motions were tabled by Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) assembly member Timothy Gaston, who has branded O'Neill the "first minister of lawlessness". A TUV spokesperson told BBC News NI the motions gained the required 30 signatures with the backing of assembly members from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP). They welcomed the support "from across the unionist family" but acknowledged the motions would not remove Sinn Féin ministers from office. "The onus still remains on those who sustain them in office," the TUV spokesperson added. Gaston has branded O'Neill the "first minister of lawlessness" The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party. TUV leader Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister. "Sinn Féin needs to be shown there are real consequences for their actions," the North Antrim MP said. But DUP leader Gavin Robinson has dismissed the idea, arguing that their smaller unionist rivals were "falling into the trap" laid by republicans. Sinn Féin was approached for comment about the no-confidence motions. Little-Pengelly, who jointly leads the Northern Ireland Executive alongside O'Neill, described Sinn Féín's actions as "disgraceful". Speaking in the assembly on Monday, Little-Pengelly said the first minister "chose to follow the law of the mob instead of the law of the land". Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes in the mid-1990s. Stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years. The row re-emerged after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission was overturned, and a fresh application to parade was lodged. Last month, the commission decided the march could go ahead with restrictions in place. The decision is being challenged in the courts. title: Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record
description: Harry Kane reaches another significant England milestone by equalling Peter Shilton's record as the most-capped Three Lions player that he has held for 36 years.
body: Harry Kane has played in all four of England's Nations League games during this international break Harry Kane has reached another significant England milestone by equalling Peter Shilton's 36-year-old record as the most-capped Three Lions player. The Bayern Munich striker made his 125th appearance for the national team against the Czech Republic in the Nations League on Tuesday. Kane is already his country's record scorer with 89 goals in 124 appearances in a full international career he started by opening his account 79 seconds into his debut. Goalkeeper Shilton congratulated Kane for equalling his record, writing on social media: "You will go on and beat it in November I am sure of that, and maybe go on and set a record that may never be beaten. "You're still going strong Harry, still playing well and scoring goals. I know how much dedication and hard work you put into achieving this, especially as a striker as I think that is probably the hardest position to play with goalkeeper just behind it. "You've been a great captain and will be in the future." BBC Sport takes a look at the origins story of the England captain. England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender Harry Kane with older brother Charlie and, right, with David Beckham and now wife Katie Goodland When a six-year-old Harry Kane arrived for trials with Ridgeway Rovers in 1999, the youth side - who a generation earlier had produced David Beckham - thought they had found themselves a new goalkeeper. Dave Bricknell, former Ridgeway Rovers coach: "We're doing a little shooting session, and I ask for a lad who can go in goal. "This little boy puts his hand up and says: 'I'll go in goal.' We give him some gloves, and he performs heroics - makes some fantastic saves. He's tipping it round the post, tipping a couple over the bar. "I'm thinking this is great, we've got a goalkeeper. And then this woman came up to me and said he's better on the pitch. "We put him on pitch and he smacked goals in left, right and centre. So he ends up being our centre-forward." Kane and his Ridgeway Rovers team-mates' goalscoring exploits were recorded in a notebook Kane's prolific form for Ridgeway Rovers and his Waltham Forest district side caught the attention of professional scouts. Arsenal initially snapped up the youngster but decided not to keep him, while Watford also passed up the opportunity to sign Kane. Trevor Bailey, Kane's manager at Waltham Forest: "Harry could have done nothing all game, but if that chance came up it was in the onion bag. "He was always on the move up front. When he got a chance, guaranteed four out of five he was going to score or set someone up." Alex Welsh, former academy coach at Arsenal: "I first met Harry in the academy and he was a very competent goalkeeper, but his real desire was to score goals. "I am absolutely convinced that is the reason why he is such a clinical striker - he intuitively knows what the goalkeeper doesn't like. He shoots early when the goalkeeper's not set." Bricknell: "I believe he was second top-scorer at Arsenal behind Benik Afobe, and then for some reason they decided at 11 years of age that they didn't want him any more." PE teacher Mark Leadon said Kane was a "real team player" and "wasn't one to keep the ball if a pass was on" Kane attended Larkswood Primary Academy before moving to Chingford Foundation School, where he was inevitably the star of the football team. But, as a dedicated student, Kane impressed his teachers across the board. Mark Leadon, Kane's PE teacher: "Aged 11, Harry was technically very gifted, with a great first touch, and a very clever player. He always knew where to go, right from an early stage. "He was also a very good cricketer - he opened the bowling from year seven to 10 and batted at four or five. But he loved football. He was never a prima donna, and he would always put a shift in. "What came through more than anything else was his determination to succeed. That work ethic was clear." Luke Robinson, Kane's childhood friend and team-mate: "The only thing on his mind was football. "We used to have a laugh, a couple of games of Fifa, but he was always driven. He'd always keep himself to himself. "He loved David Beckham, he came in with the Mohican, everyone was laughing but he loved it. He loved football, 24/7, he lived and breathed football." This video can not be played Kane's old coach: He always had 'thirst' for goalscoring It was Tottenham Hotspur who offered Kane hope after his earlier disappointments, but the future England captain was by no means the pick of the bunch for his age group. Kane's desire to learn and improve endeared him to the Tottenham academy staff and he signed scholarship terms with the club on his 16th birthday in July 2009. Alex Inglethorpe, former Tottenham youth-team coach: "When I joined Spurs as under-18 coach, Harry was 13. "I'd like to say he was the gold medallist in the group and we'd all spotted he was going to be the fantastic player, but I'd be lying. He probably wasn't even on the podium. "If there was something that endeared him to you it was that he was very, very low maintenance. It became fairly evident when Harry became a scholar he was someone who could finish. "He was wonderfully demanding to coach because he always wanted to stay out and do extra. That obsession to improve is undoubtedly his greatest strength. "It was probably around 16 he started having an impact on the youth team. We trusted him to come off the bench and have an impact - anywhere from right wing, number 10, centre-forward, sometimes in midfield." title: Amazon wins global rights to stream Emmys in six-year deal
description: The gala is leaving traditional US broadcast networks for live worldwide streaming.
body: Theagreement replaces the "Wheel Deal" system, which rotated the gala among major networks like ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. Amazon Prime Video has secured exclusive global rights to stream the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal, ending the ceremony's run on traditional US broadcast television. Starting in 2027, the agreement replaces a rotation of the gala among major networks like ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. The ceremony will instead stream live for free worldwide each September, with no Prime Video subscription needed. Official terms were not disclosed. The BBC has contacted Amazon and the Emmys for comment. The move is another indication of how live events are shifting to digital platforms as viewing habits evolve. The Oscars, for example, are moving to YouTube live globally starting in 2029. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, said the existing setup had become out of sync with modern television. "The shows driving the industry forward largely originate on streaming platforms, yet the awards themselves were tethered to broadcast television," Proulx said. "That's why a leading streaming service like Prime Video makes sense for the Emmy's next act." Cris Abrego, chair of the Television Academy, said the deal gives the ceremony "unprecedented global reach", allowing audiences in more than 200 countries to watch live. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Abrego said in a statement issued by Amazon. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said the platform is honoured to serve as the "global home" for the ceremony, adding that streaming the show for free delivers " the best entertainment to our customers worldwide." The agreement marks a milestone for Amazon, giving Prime Video its first marquee entertainment broadcast after building a live profile centred on sports, including the NFL's Thursday Night Football, NBA, and UEFA Champions League fixtures. Amazon's latest earnings highlighted strong gains in live viewership, external, including record ratings for its inaugural NBA season, which peaked at 6.5 million viewers for Game 7 of the Eastern Conference Semifinals. The Emmys deal positions Amazon directly alongside Google, whose video platform YouTube holds the upcoming Oscar rights. YouTube relies primarily on an ad-supported model, whereas Amazon is leveraging free live access to draw massive global audiences into its wider ecosystem. Like its live sporting events, the free broadcast will allow Amazon to build a substantial global advertising footprint. Moving exclusively to Prime Video is significant for the Emmys, ending a rotation across the major legacy broadcast networks that has been in place since 1955 and marking the first time the gala will leave traditional broadcast television entirely. First held in 1949, the Emmys honor achievements in acting, writing, and production, serving as a primary showcase for the global television industry. title: A separatist party just won power in Quebec - what does that mean?
description: Canada's Parti Québécois has promised it will hold the province's third vote on independence, but said they won’t do so until Donald Trump is out of office.
body: This video can not be played Canada's Parti Québécois (PQ) is projected to have won enough seats in Quebec's provincial election to form a minority government, though the separatists will need other parties' support to achieve their aims - such as a new public vote on independence. It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014, with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon set to become the province's new leader. St-Pierre Plamondon has previously said a referendum vote would occur after President Donald Trump is out of office in the United States, explaining that a vote would require "conditions that allow for an informed and serene debate". The BBC's senior Canada reporter Nadine Yousif explains what comes next. A separatist party just won power in Quebec - what does that mean? title: Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
description: Crowds of mainly teenagers called for more resources for schools and an end to what they called police repression.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Riot police strike protesters and tear gas fills the air in Paris Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions. Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police. Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers. The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycées - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day. Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement. In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction. A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed. "Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart." Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added. In parliament, the prime minister accused the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of seeking to "sow chaos" ahead of presidential elections in seven months' time. President Emmanuel Macron is nearing the end of his second and final term in office and LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently runner-up in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally. Macron was due to chair a meeting with ministers at the Élysée Palace on Tuesday evening to assess the situation. This video can not be played Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting Education Minister Édouard Geffray said that from the start he had appealed for dialogue rather than school blockades and complained that "ultra-violent elements infiltrated the high-school student movements". He is now under pressure to respond to the students' demands. What has been offered, including a website for students to express their grievances and an afternoon of internal discussion in schools on Friday, has made little impression so far. There seems little chance of the protests coming to an end just yet. France's biggest union, the CGT, has said that further protests involving school and university students are being planned for Thursday. The protests began in mid-September but have spread to high schools across France There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases. One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability". Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the Château d'Épluches lycée for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone. On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens. Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired. The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks. Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police School protests send shivers down French government's spine What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too. Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September. Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing. "We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling. Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris. title: Kimmins orders officials to 'get on with job' of A5 upgrade after court ruling
description: Appeal court judges overturn a decision that blocked work starting on one of NI's biggest road projects.
body: Families who have lost loved ones in crashes on the A5 have long campaigned for the road to be upgraded Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins has ordered officials to "get on with the job" of building one of Northern Ireland's biggest road projects after a court ruling blocking the work was overturned. At the Court of Appeal in Belfast, Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan said a ruling by a judge in 2025 preventing the upgrade of the A5 was "problematic" and could not stand. Proposals to build a new dual carriageway between Londonderry and Aughnacloy in County Tyrone go back almost 20 years but have been beset by funding and legal issues. Concerns had also been raised about the environmental impact of building a new road and how much farmland it would affect. However campaigners have for years called on the road to be upgraded, citing its safety record with 57 people having died on the A5 over the past 18 years. Campaign group Enough is Enough said it was not "a time for celebration" but there was a "sense of pride" over the court decision. Kimmins, whose department brought the appeal, said she was "absolutely delighted" with the ruling. She said it was now her priority to "start construction as soon as possible". A lawyer for the Alternative A5 Alliance, an umbrella body of landowners, farmers and supporters who oppose the road upgrade, said his clients would "carefully consider today's judgement". He added that his clients "have always been committed to ensuring the A5 project is the subject of the rigour of the law". Last year, a court ruled the Department for Infrastructure's (DfI) plans for the road did not comply with climate change targets, leading to an appeal from the department. Reading her judgement in the appeal, the Lady Chief Justice described the legal history of the project as "long and torturous". She added that she considered four grounds of appeal, including climate change considerations and human rights. In her ruling, Dame Siobhan said the previous judgement could not stand on climate change grounds and that the project "is a priority investment and should be proceeded with". She added that the A5 project was "larger than any road project ever undertaken in Northern Ireland" and that "inevitably this issue intersects with the Climate Change Act". More than 50 people have died as a result of crashes on the A5 since 2006 The judge said the previous trial judge had "failed to factor in that DfI and the [Northern Ireland] executive were aware" of wider emission issues. Dame Siobhan also found there were "deficits" in how the original judge considered the issue of human rights. She said there was "substantial evidence" from the Department for Infrastructure on the issue of how the road would affect landowners and their human rights. "Overall we find the argument based on human rights to be unconvincing and the judge went too far and made assumptions which he should not have made," she added. Dame Siobhan addressed the issue of road safety, describing it as an "obvious and pressing issue given the number of deaths" on the A5. The judge also questioned why the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) was only been brought into the case to deal with climate issues when the case went to appeal. She added: "The litigation adopted by relevant departments has been unsatisfactory and caused delay. "We're not satisfied full thought was given to this case at the appropriate stages." Kimmins says she has instructed her department to "now get on with the job" Kimmins described the court's decision as a "hugely positive outcome" but said: "This is about the families, today is their day." "The emotions we saw outside the courtroom really encapsulates just how much this means to so, so many people," she told BBC Radio Ulster's Evening Extra programme. Listen to Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins' full interview on the A5 ruling The minister said that while she did not have an idea of a revised figure of how much the project would cost, you "cannot put a price on a life". "We have a commitment, not just from the executive but across Ireland with our counterparts in the south in the Irish government, and this is a high priority for so many people, so I have no doubt that we can push ahead regardless of the cost." The A5 is a 58-mile (93km) stretch of tarmac that traverses the west of Northern Ireland and provides passage to the south. Although mostly single carriageway with few overtaking lanes, it is a vital artery of the Northern Ireland road network and has more than 200 side roads connecting to it. The road has remained largely unchanged since the 1960s, with the exception of some town bypasses, but there has been a huge rise in the number of cars, lorries and agricultural vehicles using it since it was first built. More than 50 people have died on the road since 2006 and there has been a long campaign to upgrade it. Official statistics show there has been about a 10% increase in traffic on the road in the last 10 years alone, with increase of about 30% forecast over the next 25 years. A plan to transform the mostly single lane road into a dual carriageway was first proposed nearly two decades ago, with advocates arguing a new, modernised road was needed to save lives. Those who back the upgrade project, known as the A5 Western Transport Corridor project, have argued it is necessary to save lives. Those who oppose it, frequently represented by the Alternative A5 Alliance campaign group, believe its impact on farmland and the broader environment will be negative. The total cost of the cross-border project is estimated to be in the region of £1.7bn. The Northern Ireland Executive committed about £1.2bn when the final plan was announced by ministers in late 2024. title: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates
description: The system uses facial technology to check travellers against immigration and passport information.
body: The new system will be 25% faster than having to show your passport, officials said Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced. On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said. The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically. Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials. If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer. Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said. East Midlands Airport said they expected a 'smoother, swifter and simpler' passenger experience Phil Douglas, director general of Border Force, said: "This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country. "By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK's robust border security. "Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families." Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, the trade body for the country's airports, said the move was "excellent news for the passenger". She added: "It is vital that we have the fast, efficient borders that arrivals into the UK now expect, and we will work closely with our members and government officials to ensure a smooth rollout." Steve Griffiths, managing director of East Midlands Airport, in Castle Donington, Leicestershire, said: "We're delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force. "As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers' journeys smoother, swifter and simpler. "This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area." Standard e-gates are currently available at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted. title: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres
description: The order affecting two planned data centres follows concerns over forest clearance.
body: One of Google's data centres is being built in Muhos, Finland Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres amid concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest. The sites form part of Google's record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago and described by the company as its largest single investment in Europe. The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said work at one site was carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment and ordered measures that would "significantly alter the environment" to be suspended by 23 October. Google said it had "fallen short of our own high standards in this instance" and would follow the agency's guidance. The orders relate to preparatory work carried out at the planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani. According to LVV's head of environment Tommi Muilu, work at the sites included the removal of trees and topsoil, the construction of site roads and storage areas, and changes to ditches. Tuike Finland, the company behind Google's data centre projects, has been asked to provide an explanation and set out how it intends to proceed by 14 October. The agency said it could begin "enforcement proceedings" if the company failed to comply with its demand. Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, had previously told the AFP news agency that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been felled. The conservation group had previously called for work to be halted while the environmental requirements were examined. In a statement to the BBC, Google said: "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance." It said it had "acted in good faith under the Forestry Act", carried out nature surveys and put measures in place to protect areas of high environmental value. "As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," the company added. Google announced last month that it would invest at least €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) in Finland over 2027 and 2028. Its plans included new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, alongside investment in its existing facility in Hamina. The company said the infrastructure would help it meet growing demand for services including Search, Maps and its AI assistant Gemini. Google said the construction phase in 2027 and 2028 would support more than 37,000 jobs and contribute an average of €3.6bn a year to Finland's economy. As part of its expansion, Google also signed a 22-year power purchasing agreement with Finnish energy company Fortum covering up to half the capacity of the Loviisa nuclear power plant. Fortum said the agreement would help support the plant's continued operation until 2050. Finland has attracted growing interest in data centres, with its cool climate and low-carbon electricity among the factors making it attractive to developers. Lower temperatures can also reduce the energy required to cool facilities filled with computer servers. title: Kemi Badenoch wants Reform voters to 'come back'
description: Kemi Badenoch wants Reform voters to 'come back'
body: This video can not be played Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK if no party wins the next election. In an interview with the BBC's Chris Mason the Tory party leader said she said that Nigel Farage's Reform Party are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another", adding I don't have time for that.
