title: Afghan men jailed for rape of teenager after being caught fleeing UK by French police
description: Three men tried to flee the UK in a lorry after their crimes, but were stopped by French police.
body: Awal Ahmadzai, Salman Habibkheil and Mehrab Safi fled the UK after committing a string of sexual offences against a 17-year-old girl Three Afghan nationals who raped a teenager, before being stopped by French police as they fled the UK in the back of a lorry, have been jailed. Mehrab Safi, 21, Awal Ahmadzai and Salman Habibkheli, both 19, were found guilty on 26 June of multiple offences against the girl at a house in St Werburghs, Bristol, last year. Safi first met the 17-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, while she was Christmas shopping, and groomed her over Snapchat before paying for a taxi to bring her to Bristol. Safi was jailed for 15 years at Bristol Crown Court on Tuesday, while Habibkheli and Ahmadzai were both sentenced to nine years in a youth detention centre. Sentencing the three men, Judge Michael Cullum said being trafficked and raped by the men will have caused "unimaginable" trauma to the teenager. Warning: This story contains distressing details. This video can not be played Footage of rapists fleeing UK in back of lorry A 17-year-old boy - who is an Afghan national but cannot be named for legal reasons - was also convicted of rape, but he did not try to escape the UK. He was sentenced to two years and seven months in a youth detention centre. In a victim impact statement read out to the court, the girl said the attack had left her "traumatised" and fearful of leaving the house. If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line. Safi transported the girl by taxi from Somerset to a house in Bristol where she was raped by the men and boy She added that she is a "different person" to who she was a year ago. "I had a lot more friends, I would go out a lot more, I was happier. Now, I've stopped going out, I don't even leave the house in general. "If I ever leave the house, it is only with my best friend or mum. I would not be able to go out by myself, even the thought of that makes me panic. "Generally my brain keeps blocking out the trauma that happened to me, but when I am feeling low emotionally it all comes back and makes me feel even worse. "Sometimes I would dream about what happened, which I was not expecting – and I do not like those dreams at all," she said. Det Sgt Jo Babbage praised the bravery of the victim for reporting the attacks Avon and Somerset Police said the girl, who was from Somerset, was plied with alcohol when she arrived at Safi's home. She was then sexually assaulted and raped over a number of hours by the three men and teenager in November last year. Officers attended the property and found the girl after her mother reported her missing. Det Sgt Jo Babbage said the victim had begun communicating with Safi five days before the attacks "via mobile, predominantly Snapchat". She said: "It's clear that that's where the grooming and the contact process was started that led up to her being brought into Bristol by taxi which was arranged [by Safi]." Babbage said the girl has been left "very traumatised" by the attacks, but has been "very brave" throughout the investigation. The victim met one of the men while she was Christmas shopping at the Cabot Circus shopping centre in Bristol The victim came to Bristol for the first time on 25 November 2025 with a friend on a Christmas shopping trip. During the trip, the girl met Safi and they exchanged numbers and Snapchat contacts. Safi later used the platform to persuade her to send nude photos. He then arranged for a taxi to take her from her home to his house in St Werburghs in the early hours of 30 November where he and the three others carried out the attacks. Babbage said: "Just hearing that, reading it, this Christmas shopping trip that ended like that, as a parent, makes you feel terrified for your children to go out." The court heard the victim was plied with alcohol when she arrived at the house The 17-year-old boy was arrested at the scene, but the three men fled from officers and travelled to Birmingham and London before they left the country in a lorry. They were discovered by French police in Calais and returned to the UK where they were immediately arrested on suspicion of rape. Babbage said: "They got into the back of a lorry... and they were able to leave the country without documents and it was just fortuitous that our friends in France located them and were able to return them straight away." Mobile phone footage from Safi's phone showed the men laughing and gesticulating in the back of the lorry, which the prosecution said during the trial had suggested they thought they had "got away with it". Sentencing the men and teenager, Judge Cullum said the victim would have looked "vulnerable from the very beginning". "I have no doubt that was her attraction to you, Safi. After an intense exchange of texts you obtained nude photos of her. "Reading of the exchanges is uncomfortable and starts to suggest an imbalance of power between you [Safi] and the victim. "Having been trafficked she was raped five times, and cumulative trauma will undoubtedly live with her forever and is unimaginable," he said. During sentencing, the judge acknowledged the traumatic experiences all four had endured in Afghanistan. The judge also noted that one of them had lost a parent at the hands of the Taliban. However, he said that this was no excuse. All four were also sentenced to be put on the sex offender's register indefinitely, and received a sexual harm prevention order which stops them communication with children. title: Family of woman who died after 'misread' smear test join calls for inquiry
description: Relatives of Louise Corbett Gibbons support the campaign for an inquiry into screening services.
body: Louise died about a month after receiving her cancer diagnosis The family of a 24-year-old woman who died after her smear test was said to have been misread has supported calls for a public inquiry into Northern Ireland's cervical screening service. Louise Corbett Gibbons, from near Katesbridge in County Down, died from cervical cancer in 2008. Her death is not linked to the cervical screening scandal involving the Southern Health Trust but her widower Neville Gibbons and aunt Joy Fairley joined campaigners to mark three years since those issues came to light. The Southern Trust scandal led to 17,500 women being approached to have their smear tests rechecked as part of a major review of screening dating back to 2008. Louise's loved ones are supporting calls for an inquiry into cervical screening services Campaigners calling themselves the Ladies with Letters have since been calling for a statutory public inquiry into what went wrong. They also argue that while the scandal involved the Southern Trust, other health trusts in Northern Ireland could have been affected. 17,500 cervical smear tests to be re-checked Reports provide 'no outcome' for women impacted by misread smear tests Campaign 'far from over' as minister rules out cervical screening inquiry Gibbons told BBC News NI that when Louise received her diagnosis she was told she would "be gone within the month". He said the pair, who had been together for eight years, got married the following week. Louise died three weeks later. He said the wedding was "the saddest day of my life". "Like, watching your wife in a wheelchair and knowing she's going to be dead in a few weeks," he said. "My mind wasn't good for a very long time." Neville Gibbons was widowed three weeks after marrying Louise He said when the Southern Trust screening scandal came to light, it brought back many difficult memories. He said Louise's family had been told that her smear had been misread but that "she would have passed away anyway". That was something he said the family could not accept. "I think she was never given the chance to start off with," he said. Louise was a patient of the Belfast Health Trust. BBC News NI has written to the trust for comment. Enda McGarrity, pictured with campaigners Heather Thompson (left) and Tracey Bell, says there is a need for further investigation Enda McGarrity, a solicitor for the Ladies with Letters, said there were "many women" from outside the Southern Trust who had been affected by cervical screening issues. He said the renewed call by the Ladies with Letters for a public inquiry therefore went beyond the Southern Trust, which he said had "illuminated things much more clearly". "But there was a cervical screening programme throughout Northern Ireland during that period," he said. "So at the very least, there should be an investigation into whether these issues were replicated in other trusts. "At this stage it's an issue where there is a concern that there's a link between those and how the cervical screening programme actually performed throughout those years and at the least it merits further investigation." The Southern Trust scandal led to 17,500 women being approached to have their smear tests rechecked Earlier this year, former Health Minister Mike Nesbitt ruled out a public inquiry into failings in Northern Ireland's cervical screening service. Heather Thompson and Tracey Bell were among the Ladies with Letters who took to the steps of Stormont on Tuesday, alongside a number of cross-party assembly members, to renew their calls for a public inquiry. Thompson said that when the group became aware of Louise's death, it hit members "very hard". She said the group feared there could be "other ladies out there" with similar experiences. Tracey Bell said the group was to meet Health Minister Robbie Butler next month and that it was hopeful he would "listen carefully to the experiences of women and families affected" and "recognise why this matter could not be considered closed". title: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch
description: The Conservative Party leader also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24 year olds.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Kemi Badenoch says she wants Reform voters to "come back" Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election. The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another". Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories. As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions. Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different to the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election. She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles, external. Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them. She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win. "The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority. "My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan." A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election. Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority." Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another". She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong". Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches. Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received, including a £5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong. Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down. Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK. Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support. Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029. Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party". This video can not be played Young Tories asked if their party should do a deal with Reform UK Elsewhere in her BBC interview, Badenoch said she was making changes to a policy for young people and was now proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) on earnings from 15% to 7.5% for those aged 21 to 24. The Tories announced last year that young people would see the first £5,000 of NI they would have paid in their first job redirected into a nominated savings account of their choice. The party said the policy, dubbed the "First Job Bonus", would have cost £2.8bn a year. On Tuesday, Badenoch said youth unemployed has "skyrocketed" and "you can't give people a first jobs bonus if they're not getting a first job". She added: "We're adapting and updating our policy so that it works for the problems they have today." The Conservatives said the new policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270. They added it "smooths the cliff edge" which exists as employer NI goes from 0% to the full rate when a worker turns 21. The government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities. Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training. Asked why the Conservatives were not proposing to cut NI for everyone, Badenoch said: "We have to find the money first. "So we have a golden economic rule. We are being fiscally credible. We find savings and then we spend it. "If I could afford to cut it for everybody, I promise you that I would. But young people have a much worse problem than everybody else." A Labour Party spokesperson said the NI announcement was "more fantasy economics from the Tories", adding the party had "allowed nearly one million of the next generation to be locked out of work or training". title: Why Tories are talking about winning the next election
description: Kemi Badenoch is more popular than her party right now - Tories are hoping it will rub off on them.
body: The Tories are in an upbeat mood at their annual conference Political party conferences can be weird events - where positive thinking and hopeful rhetoric can crowd out reality. If you spend enough time drinking and socialising with like-minded people anything can seem possible. That could be one explanation for the upbeat mood of this year's Conservative gathering in Birmingham. On the face of it, the party has made little progress since it was emphatically ejected from power in 2024. If an election was held tomorrow, it would do even worse than it did back then, according to some polls. Yet senior figures, including leader Kemi Badenoch, are talking about winning the next general election outright and forming a government. One reason for their optimism is that they appear to have seen off, for now, the threat of being destroyed or swallowed up by Reform UK - a prospect which hung over last year's conference amid swirling rumours of defections and speculation about deals with Nigel Farage. Another is Badenoch herself, who appears to have made a positive impression on the public. Kemi Badenoch puts the finishing touches to her conference speech Her approval rating has soared in recent months and she is now one of only two party leaders with a net positive rating (the other being Prime Minister Andy Burnham), according to pollsters More In Common., external In a presentation to a packed fringe meeting, More In Common's Luke Tryl said the Tory leader is seen as a "breath of fresh air" by focus groups, with many voters on the right describing her as someone unafraid to "say it as it is". In particular, her punchy performances at Prime Minister's Questions have made a strong impression, earning plaudits such as "intelligent", "professional" and "principled" from those who have seen her in action, according to Tryl. But like Burnham, Badenoch's personal popularity has yet to transfer to her party, he added, with the Tories being seen as "outdated" and "divided". It was not all gloom – in contrast to his presentation at last year's Tory conference – and there were "signs of recovery", Tryl said, with a large pool of voters out there who might consider voting Tory, under the right circumstances. Conservatives freely admit the problem they have got is that voters don't trust them to deliver on any of their promises, when they had 14 years in government to do something about the problems they now say are so pressing. "Of course, Kemi's ahead of us, we know that," Conservative chairman Kevin Hollinrake told the More in Common meeting. "Because people do trust Kemi and they don't trust us, that's how I would put it in a nutshell. "But we are building on that." Badenoch answers the trust question by saying that the party is under new management now. She has ditched some of the "culture war" rhetoric and is focusing hard on the economy, and setting out her guiding principles, which amount to a return to old-school Conservatism. She is not saying that the party could win an election outright if it was held now, arguing that no one could. But she has ruled out governing with Reform UK in a hung parliament, telling the BBC she would rather hold another election. Hollinrake sounded a cautious note at the More In Common fringe. "We are not where we need to be right now. We don't want an election right now, ideally. Ideally, it would come way down the track." But deputy leader Alex Burghart was quick to stress that the party is making every effort to ensure it is ready for a snap election. "We are preparing for an election now," he told the meeting. "We are convinced we can win the election outright." I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system Shadow chancellor vows to cut at least one tax in every Tory budget He claimed the Tories were more united than at any time in their recent history, with the possible exception of the aftermath of Boris Johnson's 2019 victory. But they still trail Reform by four or five points in the polls and are as much as nine points behind Labour. The next challenge for the party, former Scottish Conservative leader Dame Ruth Davidson said, was to become one of the "top two". At that point, voters who want to see the back of Labour would start moving to the Tories in serious numbers, she argued. Tactical voting could prove crucial at the next election, whenever it comes, with many people voting to keep parties out of power rather than for who they want to win. The Tories think they have a strong hand here too. "For the first time in history, the Conservative Party is now the least hated political party in the country," declared Hollinrake, to laughter and applause. "When it comes to tactical voting, that's really important." Not the most inspiring rallying cry you will hear at a party conference, perhaps, but it is grounded in reality. title: Winnie-the-Pooh books to fill phone box libraries
description: The original publisher says it will donate Milne's classics alongside a new authorised sequel.
body: Actor Sally Phillips launched the initiative from a phone box library in Kent Free books for 150 red phone box libraries are being made available to celebrate 100 years of two British legends - Winnie-the-Pooh and the K2 red phone box. The story's original publisher, Farshore, said it would donate copies of AA Milne's classics - whose setting was inspired by Ashdown Forest in East Sussex - alongside a new authorised sequel A Little Boy and His Bear. Sally Phillips, actor and narrator of the newly reissued Winnie-the-Pooh audiobooks, launched the campaign earlier by reading to schoolchildren at a phone box library in Chartham, Kent. "He has always been the number one bear in our house," she told the BBC. People across the UK have been invited to nominate their local red phone box libraries for the books to help the campaign's organisers "uncover more hidden gems". Nominations have been opened to phone boxes which have already been adapted into community libraries, with libraries in Derbyshire, Hertfordshire, Leicestershire and the West Midlands having already signed up. Phillips said there was a lot to love about the bear's view of life, both for children and adults. She said the books were "great to read as an adult because they're really funny, much funnier than you remember. "When you read them to children, you remember how much kid-friendly drama there is in them." The initiative comes after the launch of the government's National Year of Reading 2026, with reading enjoyment rising this year after four years in decline, according to an annual survey from the National Literary Trust. Dr Nicole Holt, who runs the phone box library in Chartham, told the BBC: "They are really good for accessibility, they're free and are available to absolutely everybody." The principal lecturer in public health at Canterbury Christ Church University said she hoped the initiative promoted and encouraged other people to set up phone box libraries. Jane Riordan (left) and Dr Nicole Holt (right) hope the initiative will encourage more reading and phone box libraries At the launch, children took part in a storytelling workshop with Jane Riordan, the author of the new sequel, and had an illustration session with Andrew Grey, its illustrator, who taught them about the original's unique style. First published in 1926, Milne's story, illustrated by Ernest Howard Shepard, followed the tales of Christopher Robin and his friends, including Piglet, Tigger and Eeyore. It was based on actual stuffed toys of the author's son, Christopher Robin Milne. A century on, Riordan said being asked to write the follow-up to Milne's beloved tale was the privilege of her career. "The wonderful thing about Winnie-the-Pooh is that it's a book for someone to read to you," she explained. "Enjoy them together - that's a real pleasure." title: Man, 21, who died after city centre attack named by police
description: Daniel Colrain died in hospital after being assaulted in Royal Exchange Square in the early hours of Sunday.
body: Daniel Colrain was attacked in Royal Exchange Square in the early hours of Sunday and died in hospital the following day A 21-year-old man who died after being attacked in Glasgow city centre has been named by police. Daniel Colrain was found with serious injuries in Royal Exchange Square at about 03:05 on Sunday. He died in hospital the following day. A 19-year-old man has been arrested in connection with the disturbance and released pending further inquiries. Another man, aged 21, was also assaulted and suffered minor injuries. A 20-year-old man has been charged in connection with this and is due to appear before Glasgow Sheriff Court at a later date. A post-mortem examination took place earlier. Police Scotland have appealed for information about the attack and have set up a dedicated portal, external where information can be submitted anonymously. Daniel's family are being supported by specialist officers. Police were called to Royal Exchange Square at about 03:05 on Sunday Det Insp Jonny MacKinnon, of Greater Glasgow CID, said: "Our thoughts remain with Daniel's family and friends at what is an extremely difficult time for them. "I would like to reiterate that no arrests have been made in connection with the death at this time and extensive inquiries remain ongoing to establish the full circumstances. "It is vital we get answers for Daniel's family." Ch Insp Stephen McManus added: "We understand this incident will be concerning for the community but please be assured specialist officers are carrying out extensive inquiries. "Increased patrols will be carried out in the area and anyone with any concerns, or information, can approach these officers." title: Rival clubs want retrospective and future punishments for Man City
description: A number of Premier League clubs want Manchester City to be hit with both retrospective punishments and sanctions in the future.
body: Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano (left) and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak have continued to insist the club are innocent despite the guilty verdicts A number of Premier League clubs want Manchester City to be hit with both "retrospective punishments" and sanctions for the future for their mass financial rule-breaking, sources have told BBC Sport. An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. City have appealed against the verdict. However, there is said to be a consensus among a group of top-flight club executives that if City's appeal is unsuccessful, the sanctions should make reparations for the period when they broke the rules, while also limiting their powers in future. There is also a feeling from at least four Premier League boardrooms that a "one-hit" points deduction resulting in relegation to the Championship would be an insufficient punishment given the severity of City's wrongdoing. There is understood to be nuance in exactly what clubs consider a fitting penalty for the eight-time Premier League champions, who were found guilty of all serious financial rule breaches in a damning verdict by an independent commission. One senior club source said City should be stripped of their titles, and added there was "no great rush" among clubs to push for the redistribution of trophies, but rather to take honours away and leave them vacant. The source warned the credibility of the Premier League would be lost if City were allowed to keep the eight major trophies they won during the period they have been found guilty. However, in a sign of a range of opinions across the league, BBC Sport was previously told there was little appetite among other clubs for City to be stripped of titles. Regarding the timescale for sanctions in the future, there is a concern among club executives that a sanction applied just to one season would merely provide City with a "bump in the road" given the likelihood of them returning to the Premier League at the first time of asking. A number of Premier League figures therefore believe any points deduction should be split over multiple seasons, while there is also a sense that transfer bans that stretch over a number of windows would also significantly hinder City's ability to regain their top-flight status as quickly as possible. Which clubs did Man City's 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market? Man City whistleblower to lose witness protection One club source also said it would be "bizarre, almost obtuse" if City were able to trade in the upcoming January transfer window, if this process is ongoing and sanctions have not been applied. Some clubs cited feeling "in the dark" regards the Premier League, including around the chronology and timescales of the appeal and the sanctions hearing. However, sources said there was "empathy" and "understanding" about the difficult position the Premier League is in, given the gravity of this situation and the ongoing legal process. Regarding financial reparations, one idea that has been mooted - and which a club source found "merit" in - was to apply a "tariff-based system", whereby City's past league finishing positions would be altered via a points deduction. Rival clubs could then be paid compensation by City based on where they would have finished versus where they did finish. BBC Sport understands Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca will speak to players collectively after they arrive back from international duty on Thursday, before their Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday (16:30 BST). The trip to Anfield is their first game since news of the verdict broke. Merseyside Police says it has received queries in relation to the match, and when asked by BBC Sport if any special measures would be put in place the force said it will have "an appropriate policing operation in place on the day". Sources at Liverpool have told BBC Sport it is a case of "business as usual" and there are no extra measures being put in place. Conversations and meetings between the club, supporters and relevant authorities take place before every home game. One source said while everyone "has the right to express their feelings" they hoped supporters would not overstep the mark. title: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
description: The death of a worker from a Russian lab that researches plague has prompted questions about the disease.
body: Pneumonic plague is often described as the most virulent form of plague The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information on the death of a worker at a Siberian plague research laboratory. It is still not clear exactly what led to the worker falling ill, but media reports have led to a flurry of speculation. Russian officials are still investigating the cause of the death, but they say those who came into contact with the researcher all tested negative for pneumonic plague. So what is pneumonic plague, and how dangerous is it? Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood. Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types. Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood. It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague. The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases. Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States. Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford. He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world. "Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa. "Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact." Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas. You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal. But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact. You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs. It's thought that pneumonic plague was the main type of plague behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century. Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague. "I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said. "Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form. "Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism. "This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks." According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours. If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal. But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early. Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health. "Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease. "Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age. "It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early. "That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine." In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague. The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" – and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened. US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no cause for alarm. The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low". title: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
description: Use our interactive tracker to explore the latest migration statistics for the UK
body: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012. How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted? Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics. Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, a total of 20,478 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 40% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 6 October 2025 to 5 October 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence. The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026. About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites. The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029. More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year. Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026. The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa. It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum. In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year. As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year. Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear. Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026. About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned. The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave. This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily. People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation. There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year. That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026: 5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026. The UK is trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat. For every person the UK sends back to France, the UK will accept an equal number of asylum seekers. This is called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people have been returned through this arrangement. Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers. title: UK special forces could face prosecution as Afghanistan evidence referred to police
description: Evidence relating to a number of detention operations carried out by British personnel between 2010 and 2013 is being examined.
body: The evidence indicates that serious offences may have been committed by British personnel UK special forces (UKSF) personnel could face prosecution after evidence found following enquiries by the SAS Inquiry, suggesting serious offences may have been committed in Afghanistan, was handed to the military police. The evidence came to light in court proceedings on Monday and is the first time the inquiry has publicly acknowledged that its findings could lead to criminal prosecutions. The referral - made by UKSF earlier this year - was required under the Armed Forces Act, which defines Schedule 2 serious offences as including murder and manslaughter. It relates to a number of detention operations carried out by British personnel between 2010 and 2013. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) found the evidence earlier this year, following investigation by the SAS Inquiry, and then UKSF referred it to the military police's Defence Serious Crime Unit (DSCU), a specialist unit set up in 2022 to deal with the most serious crimes. Court documents obtained by the BBC suggest that the DSCU has undertaken a scoping exercise of the evidence, but the unit has paused any criminal investigations until the inquiry has been concluded. Separately, the MoD told the BBC it was deemed inappropriate for criminal investigations to be undertaken while the inquiry was still ongoing. The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan is examining allegations that the British Army's Special Air Service (SAS) unlawfully killed people during detention operations in Afghanistan between 2010 and 2013, and that senior officials sought to cover up the true circumstances of the killings. BBC Panorama has been investigating allegations the SAS executed handcuffed civilians and children, for more than eight years. The public inquiry was established in 2022 in the wake of Panorama's revelations. The DSCU referral came to light during a High Court hearing brought by a witness to the inquiry. The witness, a senior British military officer who served in Afghanistan, has won permission to have the inquiry judicially reviewed after military witnesses' legal teams were excluded from closed-door evidence hearings with whistleblowers. Much of the public inquiry's evidence is being heard in secret. Lawyers for the senior officer argued the process was unfair and the officer should have an opportunity to question the whistleblowers, either in person or through his lawyers, regarding any allegations made against him. The inquiry's lawyers said it "must be able to obtain highly sensitive information" from people who may be concerned about giving evidence. They said protected witnesses had raised fears of "grievous consequences by UKSF" if their identities were revealed. Do you have information about this story that you want to share? Get in touch using SecureDrop, a highly anonymous and secure way of whistleblowing to the BBC which uses the Tor network. Or use the Signal messaging app, an end-to-end encrypted message service designed to protect your data. Signal: 0044 7714 956 936 Note: The SecureDrop link will only work in a Tor browser. For information on keeping secure and anonymous, here's some advice on how to use SecureDrop. title: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident
description: It is the seventh arrest in connection to the incident near RAF Fairford last month.
body: A 22-year-old British national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident close to RAF Fairford, counter-terror police said. He was arrested in Westminster, London, on Tuesday as part of the investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire on 27 September. It is the seventh arrest in connection to the incident but no one has been charged. A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase. Senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said it "remains a live investigation" and police are continuing to "pursue multiple lines of enquiry". Five men were arrested on 27 September near the base in the connection with the incident and were subsequently released on police bail. The men, aged between 23 and 25, were detained in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base. They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy". A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual Iranian-British national, was arrested on 1 October in Westminster and was also later released on bail. RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used by the US Air Force for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran. On Sunday, it emerged the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America. US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details. While speaking to a group of reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase. He replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident. "There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. "But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far." Earlier, US Vice-President JD Vance said the bombers were moved "out of an abundance of caution". The comments came after US media reports suggested the decision was made after intelligence suggested Iran was plotting a drone attack. The BBC has not verified those reports. On Tuesday, a spokesperson for US European Command, which coordinated American military activity in Europe, said it would be "inappropriate to discuss matters of intelligence" but that the US would "continue to assess the threat environment" at bases. The spokesperson added the US remains at the "highest state of readiness" and would take "appropriate actions to protect our people, our platforms, and the bases where our forces operate". Prior to Trump's intervention on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to his previous comments, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base. title: Student admits murdering woman in 'Dexter' kill room
description: Forensics student Benjamin William Day, 20, lured Maria Saceanu to an Airbnb to murder her.
body: Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing A forensic science student obsessed with the US television drama Dexter has admitted murdering a 24-year-old woman after luring her to a plastic-lined "kill room" inside an Airbnb. Benjamin William Day, 20, changed his plea to guilty on the second day of his trial at Wolverhampton Crown Court. Prosecutors said he had carefully planned the killing of Maria Saceanu, preparing a room with plastic sheeting and items intended to help him murder her and dispose of evidence. Day, who was 19 when the murder took place, was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced on 4 December. The University of Worcester undergraduate, of Yeadon Close in Redditch, Worcestershire, had been expected to argue he acted in self-defence and had set up the room to film a Dexter tribute for TikTok. But after an hour-long delay to proceedings earlier, Day returned to the dock and appeared to smirk as he entered a guilty plea. title: 'We are terrified but we want to get an education', say Yemeni schoolgirls
description: The BBC reports from a school in Taiz, Yemen, where children are determined to keep learning despite the vicious civil war.
body: This video can not be played For many children in Yemen, their education is taking place in the shadow of a vicious civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis. The conflict has made attending school a challenge for many, and according to Unicef, around 3.2 million children in Yemen were out of school even before the war escalated last month. Reporting from a school in Taiz, south-western Yemen, the BBC heard from children who are determined to keep learning despite the fighting. title: AfD candidate elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time
description: Although Tobias Rausch's role is largely symbolic, opponents have described the result as a watershed moment.
body: Tobias Rausch easily won the vote with the backing of nine MPs beyond his own party A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been elected as parliament speaker there too. Not since World War Two has a far-right party secured the post of speaker, and protesters outside the building in Magdeburg held up banners saying, "Never again is now". Although the AfD fell three seats short of a majority in last month's election, Rausch, 35, comfortably won Tuesday's vote with the support of 9 MPs from other parties. "The days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past," Rausch said after the vote, rejecting a post-war consensus in German politics not to work with the far right. This was the first time since last month's state vote that Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected representatives had gathered in parliament, and regional Greens party leader Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said "a line has been crossed" with the election of a far-right speaker of parliament, and it was a watershed moment. "We will not let ourselves be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights are curtailed either here or for people in the state," she said. The AfD is considered pro-Russian and anti-immigrant, with plans to segregate child refugees in schools, as well as intolerant towards the LGBT community. Within Saxony-Anhalt it is also classed as "right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence, a description rejected by party leaders. Until now its members have sat on the right fringe of the state parliament, but ahead of Tuesday's inaugural session it successfully argued that it should now sit in the centre. As the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund spoke to reporters, protesters held up a sign saying "2026. Never again is now." Rausch, a trained estate agent, has been a member of the parliament for 10 years and he is seen as a close confidant of local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic figure who is now seeking to become state premier in December. His new role is largely symbolic, but Rausch will now chair debates, have the power to control access to the parliament building and represent parliament at official events. Although his victory was secured by five MPs from the hard-left BSW, there was surprise that four other unidentified MPs also voted for Rausch. Commentators immediately asked if he had secured the backing of members of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has ruled out working with the AfD. Fourteen of the CDU's state MPs took part in the vote, but only five of them abstained as planned, and one unconfirmed report suggested four may have backed Rausch. Ahead of the vote, all 15 had ruled out voting for the AfD. Outside parliament, more than 300 protesters voiced their anger at the AfD's victory, and they crowded around Ulrich Siegmund as he spoke to German media. Siegmund's bid to become state premier is by no means secure. Like Rauch he will need the backing of 42 MPs in the 83-seat legislature. The BSW has refused to enter into a coalition with the AfD and has said it would instead back a non-partisan candidate for state premier and abstain in December's vote. title: M4 junction closures and new Menai crossing in plans to tackle congestion on Welsh roads
description: Welsh government will also re-examine the case for a new motorway in proposals announced today.
body: The Welsh government has announced plans to tackle congestion in north and south Wales Junctions on the M4 in Newport could close, and a new bridge built across the Menai Strait, as part of Welsh government plans for two notorious transport bottlenecks. It will also begin an 18-month project looking at a range of "roads-based" options for the M4, that could include a new motorway or expanding the Brynglas Tunnels. Ministers are considering whether to close or partially close three junctions, potentially by 2028. However, a review has warned that closing them could cause increased congestion and noise on alternatives routes. It is not clear at this stage how anything would be paid for - the new Menai crossing could cost up to £700m and take up to 10 years. It is the latest set of proposals to tackle congestion on the M4, after plans for a relief road were developed in the 2010s and axed by former Labour first minister Mark Drakeford in 2019. In south Wales, the Welsh government is to hold an 18-month study that will look at a range of options for what it says are "road-based solutions" to congestion on the road. Ministers have ruled out the black route previously proposed for the M4 Relief Road, although it is understood that the study could still include a new motorway south of Newport. Other options include widening the Brynglas Tunnels - one of the most significant causes of congestion on the M4 in Wales. The Welsh government also plans a five-year programme of changes to deliver "shorter-term benefits", including "a delivery plan to improve how the motorway is operated and managed". In a statement, the Senedd Deputy Transport Minister Mark Hooper said this could include potential junction closures in and around Newport to improve traffic flow. "The review found that measures such as these offer some of the quickest opportunities to improve traffic flow and resilience on the M4," he said. The government is considering closing junction 27, at High Cross, and east-facing slip roads at junction 26 - Malpas - and junction 25 - Caerleon. However, firm decisions have not been made and ministers want to consider the impact on local roads, and speak to Newport council, before it goes ahead. The announcement follows a review by transport consultants at ARUP on some of the options that could be implemented along the M4 corridor, which warned that public acceptance of the junction closures was "likely to be low" among their users. It said: "There is a risk that economic costs would be redistributed rather than reduced, with poorer access for local businesses and increased congestion, noise and delay on alternative routes." "The capital cost would [be] relatively affordable, but the option would likely provide limited long-term value," the review said, putting the cost at £14m with a 3% estimate of traffic reduction. The government is considering closing junction 27, at High Cross, and east-facing slip roads at junction 26 - Malpas - and junction 25 - Caerleon The ARUP report looked at eight different options, including new railway stations, a bus rapid transit scheme and road projects. Widening the Brynglas tunnels, for example, could cost £1.7bn, but pose an "engineering/geotechnical risk" and major construction disruption. Changes to the A48 and A4810 to increase capacity - known as the Blue Route - are thought to cost £1.8bn, take eight years and reduce traffic on the M4 by 6%. Other measures backed by the Welsh government include improving the A465 for freight, such as providing facilities for HGVs. The Welsh government said it would immediately recommence development work for a third Menai crossing. Plans had been formally scrapped three years ago, although a year later the then Labour Transport Secretary Ken Skates suggested it was back on the agenda. Officials believe a new crossing could cost around £670m, with development work taking up to two years. It would be at least eight to ten years before the crossing was built. The A55 is currently carried over the Menai by the Britannia Bridge, and unlike the rest of the road it is a single carriageway. The Menai Suspension Bridge has been restricted to vehicles under 7.5 tonnes since repair works began in October 2022. The government has ruled out a three-lane tidal-flow operation on the Britannia Bridge after a review found significant safety and operational concerns. Deputy Minister for Transport Mark Hooper said "people want action, not endless discussion". "They want reliable journeys, less disruption and confidence that government is getting on with improving things and making a difference to people's lives. And that's exactly what we're doing. "We will carry out an 18-month study to consider a range of road-based solutions for the M4 around Newport. Alongside that work, we are taking action to reduce peak-hour traffic by up to around one in ten vehicles." title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
description: The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
body: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers. It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory. The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network. Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings and Mission: Impossible. The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover. Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry. "From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said. Films and streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive. Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology. Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News. Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation". "While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said the company has high debts at a time when interest rates are high. "The combined entity, now called Skydance, needs to cut costs and make bigger profits to be able to get the debt down to more manageable levels," he said. "The fact Tom Cruise movie Digger, Warner Bros' last release before the merger, has been a major flop is a reminder of how the film industry is not a guaranteed ticket to riches." While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning. Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away. Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide". US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead. As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS. Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount. Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained. Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons. Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours. The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick. The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement. To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films. As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob. Paramount also must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising to more than 30% through the following three years. title: 'Means more than just a trophy' - Djokovic claims 102nd title of career
description: Novak Djokovic claims the 102nd title of his astonishing career as Alex de Minaur retires injured from the China Open final.
body: Novak Djokovic was playing the China Open for the first time in 11 years Novak Djokovic claimed the 102nd title of his astonishing career as Alex de Minaur retired injured from the China Open final. The 39-year-old led De Minaur - a player 12 years his junior - 7-6 (7-3) 0-1 when the Australian was forced to quit with an apparent left thigh problem. Both players took a medical timeout after a 68-minute first set, but De Minaur managed just one game on their return before shaking hands. It is the 21st year in a row that Djokovic has won at least one singles title. Only Jimmy Connors (109) and Roger Federer (103) have won more singles titles in their careers than the Serb. Djokovic is on a 34-match winning streak at the China Open, having claimed the trophy seven times. "I always have high expectations and want to visualise myself with the trophy, but particularly here in Beijing, the place where I've never lost," Djokovic said. "This trophy means much more than one trophy, one tournament." The 24-time Grand Slam champion was competing in only his second final of the year after losing January's Australian Open showpiece to Carlos Alcaraz. Djokovic beat world number two Alexander Zverev on his way to the Beijing final and was a set and a break up on third seed Daniil Medvedev when the Russian was defaulted from their semi-final. Djokovic's ability to compete at the highest level is rarely in question - he beat world number one Sinner to reach the Australian Open final and took a set off Alcaraz in the showpiece - but his body has let him down in recent years. He was left in tears following a gruelling first-round loss at the US Open and spoke about struggling with a "serious health condition" that particularly bothered him in oppressive conditions. He reached the semi-finals of Wimbledon, losing to eventual champion Jannik Sinner, but suffered a surprise third-round exit at the French Open at the hands of rising star Joao Fonseca. This is Djokovic's first title in just over a year, having limited his schedule to protect his body. He is the oldest man to win an ATP Tour-level title since 43-year-old Ken Rosewall won in Hong Kong in 1877. Victory will also see him return to inside the world's top 10. "This year has been quite challenging for me, lots of ups and downs and physical and health issues, so I was just trying to find a good feeling on the court," Djokovic said. "I know that when I'm feeling well and striking the ball well I can still compete at the highest level. "This week has been an evidence to that. I'm very proud." Earlier, Alcaraz won the Japan Open, claiming a trophy in just his third tournament since injuring his wrist in April. The Spaniard came back from an early break down to beat Czech Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7-4) 6-4 and successfully defend his title in Tokyo. Alcaraz only returned to competitive tennis at August's US Open, where he reached the quarter-finals before losing in five tight sets to Ben Shelton. It is Alcaraz's third title of the season, having won the Australian Open in January to complete the career Grand Slam, and also February's Qatar Open. "It's extra special after my injury," the 25-year-old said. "It was a tough week that I didn't find my best tennis, my best level, but I did find the good solutions. "I think that's what matters in the end." title: PCs who used Taser and baton on amputee, 92, sacked
description: A disciplinary hearing finds both officers used unnecessary force on Donald Burgess at his care home.
body: Donald Burgess, who had dementia, was pepper sprayed and Tasered in his wheelchair Two police officers who pepper-sprayed and Tasered a 92-year-old amputee at a care home have been sacked for gross misconduct. PC Stephen Smith and PC Rachel Comotto, who were both acquitted of assault occasioning actual bodily harm in May 2025, had been called to Park Beck care home in St Leonards-on-Sea after resident Donald Burgess threatened carers with a dinner knife. Burgess, who had dementia, was hit with a baton, pepper sprayed and Tasered as he sat in his wheelchair in his bedroom in June 2022. At Sussex Police headquarters in Lewes on Tuesday, a disciplinary panel decided there had been "unjustified and excessive use of force" and dismissed both officers without notice. Burgess was taken to hospital after the incident, where he contracted Covid and died 22 days later, but the officers were not held responsible for his death. The misconduct panel found Comotto and Smith did not attempt to de-escalate the situation before using force and had breached standards of professional behaviour. Both were also placed on the College of Policing's barred list. PC Rachel Comotto and PC Stephen Smith were dismissed from the force without notice During a week-long hearing, force lawyer Aaron Rathmell told the panel Smith, 52, and Comotto, 37, "acted, hastily, harshly and lost control". He said Smith had drawn the pepper spray within nine seconds of entering Burgess's room. Bodyworn camera footage showed Smith walking into the room and saying: "Do you want to be sprayed or Tasered? It's up to you. Can you put that down for us?" Despite repeated requests, Burgess, who was a single leg amputee, did not drop the dinner knife. The panel found Smith "made no attempt to assess or understand" Burgess's vulnerability, while Comotto "showed no compassion". The following video contains distressing scenes. This video can not be played Body-worn camera footage shows Burgess being asked to put down the knife Smith failed to consider leaving the 92-year-old in his room to calm down, the panel found, plus the use of Pava, a type of pepper spray, was deemed unreasonable in the circumstances. There was "limited mitigation" for this behaviour, it said. The panel also said Smith's tone and language towards Burgess was "dismissive in nature", while Comotto was "antagonistic". Comotto's statements - such as "last chance" or "seriously" - and giving Burgess limited time to respond, were found to be inappropriate. The panel found her use of force to be unreasonable. Assistant Chief Constable Peter Gardner said Burgess was in his own room, isolated from residents and posed no risk. More information should have been ascertained from care home staff, he said. Gardner added that Smith had shown a lack of remorse and insight into the inappropriateness of his actions, and the panel remained concerned by his evidence which stated he would not do anything differently. While noting Comotto's remorse and evidence that she would act differently, Gardner said the reputation of the police service, along with public confidence in it, must be upheld. title: UK to make last-ditch effort to stop Israel closing East Jerusalem consulate
description: Israel has threatened to close the consulate, which handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city, over British sanctions on Israeli settlements.
body: The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week. Israel said in September that it would shut the mission, which is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv, in retaliation for the UK announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. British sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion. The Foreign Office said it would not comment on "speculation and live discussions" that the UK could expel Israeli diplomats in response. The Israeli government said it would close the mission within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement, meaning that the mission - first established in 1838 - will close on Thursday unless a deal is reached. The consulate handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week for talks but seemingly left without reaching an agreement. According to Israeli media, the UK is threatening to expel up to 27 Israeli diplomats if the closure goes ahead. Such a tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats is more common among adversaries than allies. France and Canada joined the UK in the initial sanctions, but Israel has not taken action against them. Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee, said: "Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem - occupied Palestinian territory - is not in Israel's prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution." She added: "It is illegal, and the UK must resist it." Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has previously said that they do not want the consulate to close. "It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said last month. title: Queen pays tribute to 'irrepressible' Jeffrey Archer
description: The bestselling author and former politician died on Monday at the age of 86.
body: Queen Camilla has paid tribute to the bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer, who has died at the age of 86. "Seldom does an author get to live a life as rich, varied and colourful as any of the characters in their books, or with as many surprising plot twists," the Queen said in a statement. She added that Archer was "not without flaw", but that "friends will recall him as an irrepressible life force through all the many differing chapters of his life". The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star. This video can not be played Watch: Jeffrey Archer spoke about his time in prison, today's politics and retirement in a BBC Breakfast interview last week The Queen said he was "an exception to the end" and that it was "with sadness that I learned of his death yesterday, on the eve of publication of his final work and so soon after appearing at my Queen's Reading Room Festival". Archer was a supporter of the Queen's Reading Room charity. "My sympathies go to Mary and the family at this time of sorrow. I hope it may be some consolation for them to know what pleasure Jeffrey brought to me and to so many millions of readers through the pages of his works. "Wherever the next page turns to, I trust there will be champagne and Shepherd's Pie in abundance. Camilla R." Archer's parties were known for serving champagne and shepherd's pie to guests. Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset. In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions. Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset and in 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth. He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman. He moved to the House of Lords in 1992 but was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001. He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages. The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker. The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi and producing fake diary entries to back up his story. He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial. He was released from jail in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024. Jeffrey Archer, pictured here with Margaret Thatcher, served as a Conservative MP and deputy party chairman Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news". "We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday. Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently." Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world." Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed – and long remembered". Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday. Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form. "He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience." Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him." Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer". James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer. Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company." Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86 Jeffrey Archer: bestselling novelist whose political career ended in scandal Archer 'nostalgic' about Somerset before death Last week, Archer returned to his former school to promote his last book. "It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School. Archer had been due to attend the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel. He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said. The couple have two sons and five grandchildren.
