title: Katie Price's ex told teenager to 'take it to the grave', rape trial hears
description: The alleged victim is not part of Kieran Hayler or Katie Price's extended families.
body: Kieran Hayler denies the charges and has suggested his ex-wife, Katie Price, had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended The former husband of Katie Price told a teenager after allegedly raping her that she should "take it to the grave", a court has heard. Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies. The complainant, who was 13 at the time of the alleged offences, wept during a police interview shown to jurors when she admitted lying to her mum about what happened because she "didn't want her to think I was disgusting". She said: "I thought it was my fault for ages," adding that she told her mum Hayler had touched her but not that it was sex as she feared that "maybe I'd led him on". The complainant told police that Hayler had called her two or three years after the alleged incidents had taken place. She said: "He said something like 'you promise you won't tell anyone? What we had was special - you better take it to the grave', and that it might get me into trouble." The complainant recalled him saying it might end badly for her, but that she had not felt frightened of him. Asked by police how she felt following the three alleged rapes she said: "At the time I thought he really cares about me so he's not doing something horrible… because of the way he described it, he said it was a good thing." The complainant remembered having "four showers a day after that" and said her mum recalled her "always washing" and changing her underwear "several times" a day. She said: "I definitely remember thinking he's a lot older than me, is this something he should be doing? "I remember crying and wondering if it should have been happening." After the jury was shown the video of the police interview, the alleged victim gave evidence in person in court from behind a screen. She was asked if she remembered anything else, and, speaking about the third incident, the complainant said Hayler had messaged her saying, "I love you, goodnight". "I replied, 'I love you too'," she added. In 2021, the complainant contacted the NSPCC charity which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation. Hayler was first interviewed by police in January 2022 and denied any of the allegations took place and that anything sexual occurred. He was married to media personality Price at the time of the alleged incidents, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021. Hayler suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations form part of this, the court heard. The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families. Price is expected to be a witness in the trial which is expected to last about a week. title: NHS supply lorry drivers to strike in pay dispute
description: Drivers who deliver medical equipment to hospitals across England reject a 4% pay increase.
body: Lorry drivers are set to host a series of walkouts in October and November NHS supply lorry drivers are set for a series of strikes in a dispute over pay. Drivers employed by GXO in Tyne and Wear, Derbyshire, Yorkshire, Kent, Warwickshire and Suffolk will stage five walkouts from October 13-15, 20-22, 27-29 and November 3-5 and 10-12, Unite said. Union members have rejected a 4% pay offer from GXO, which runs the NHS supply chain contract for Supply Chain Coordination Limited (SCCL), and is wholly owned by NHS England. Unite regional officer Phil Silkstone said: "There is still time for strike action to be avoided but that will require a deal our members can accept." NHS Supply Chain and GXO said they had "robust contingency plans" in place to minimise disruption. Drivers deliver general equipment such as bandages, dressings, gowns, gloves and needles to hospitals across England. Silkstone described them as "dedicated workers" and said GXO had refused to put forward a reasonable offer. NHS Supply Chain and GXO said they were aware Unite members had voted in favour of industrial action. GXO said it believed the 4% pay offer was fair. A spokesperson for GXO said: "Patient care remains of paramount importance, and we remain focused on providing a safe and effective operation throughout this period." Depots where strike action is due to take place are in Alfreton in Derbyshire, Bridgwater in Somerset, Normanton in West Yorkshire, Maidstone in Kent, Rugby in Warwickshire, Bury St Edmonds in Suffolk and Washington in Tyne and Wear. title: Lawyer for one of Cornell 7 calls for special prosecutor to be removed over previous comments
description: New York Attorney General Letitia James is investigating the rape allegations, but the lawyer says comments she made on the case should disqualify her.
body: A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recuse herself over past public comments. The lawyer had said a social media post from New York Attorney General Letitia James throws into question her investigation's "integrity and independence". In the 28 September post, James wrote that "what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable" and told survivors that "we stand with you". The university's administration is under fire over its alleged mishandling of the October 2024 incident and, according to US media, now faces a no-confidence vote by Cornell faculty. The university's Faculty Senate, a governing body comprised of professors and other academic staff, will vote on a resolution of no confidence next week, according to reports. Cornell is an Ivy League university, alongside Harvard and Yale, and its faculty includes Nobel laureates and other distinguished researchers. A majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture, signalling the broader faculty's discontent and applying pressure on university leadership to act. The BBC has reached out to Cornell University for comment. Allegations made in a lawsuit against seven men and the university have rocked the campus in New York state, with hundreds of students and faculty members gathering there on Monday in protest, and sparked anger across the country. New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week appointed James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case and how law enforcement and the university initially responded to the allegations made by a woman identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe. Jane Doe has accused the university of failing to protect her, after she was allegedly drugged and raped by the men for several hours at a fraternity party. Days before she was appointed special prosecutor, James wrote on X: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. "I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers," she continued. "To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you." The lawyer for one of the seven accused said these remarks were disqualifying. In a statement sent to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the lawyer said her comments conflict with the need for "independently evaluating the evidence". "This is not an accusation that Attorney General James is corrupt, acting in bad faith or incapable of performing her duties professionally," the statement said. "Nor am I suggesting that a court has determined that she is legally disqualified. The point is much narrower: an avoidable question now hangs over this investigation, and voluntary recusal would remove it." Governor Hochul and James were questioned about impartiality concerns during a news conference, and Hochul said James would "follow the facts". "She'll examine the evidence and go wherever it leads, and if the evidence supports charges, she will pursue them," Hochul said. title: Watch: How Russia responded to US after plague researcher death
description: The US and Russia have each offered to help each other tackling infectious diseases.
body: This video can not be played Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has urged people not to "listen to various rumours" after a Russian lab technician died at a plague research centre in Siberia. Peskov called for people to follow only information from Russia's public health watchdog, which named the official cause of death of the lab technician as pneumonia of unknown origin. BBC Russia editor Steve Rosenberg also asked Peskov about US President Donald Trump's offer of support to Russia. title: US televangelist Jim Bakker, disgraced from sex scandal and fraud, dies at 86
description: US televangelist Jim Bakker co-founded The PTL Club with his then-wife Tammy Faye before being jailed for fraud and conspiracy.
body: US televangelist Jim Bakker's death was announced on Monday by his second wife Lori Bakker US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar media empire before being jailed for fraud and conspiracy, has died aged 86. Bakker and his then-wife Tammy Faye founded a Christian television programme called The PTL Club in 1974, which at its peak attracted 13 million viewers per day. The 86-year-old's death was announced on Monday by his second wife Lori Bakker, who described him as "a pioneer of Christian television". By the late 80s, Bakker and Tammy Faye's empire began to fall apart after he became embroiled in a sex scandal and later convicted of mail and wire fraud. Tammy Faye, who divorced him in 1992, was never charged. Bakker remarried in 1998, and alongside second wife Lori launched a new TV ministry in 2003. Lori Bakker described her late husband as "my best friend, and the man I was honoured to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry". She did not specify the cause of death. However, Bakker's first program The PTL Club - short for 'Praise the Lord' or 'People That Love' - was what cemented his fame with his first wife Tammy Faye. The couple built their empire with 2,000 employees and a 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA theme park complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina. The Bakkers had a famously opulent lifestyle, owning a private jet, multiple homes, luxury cars, jewellery and even an air-conditioned dog house. In 1987, Bakker resigned from the PTL ministry after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with a former church secretary Jessica Hahn. It later emerged Hanhn received a $265,000 payoff with ministry funds, resulting in Bakker being defrocked of his ministerial credentials and right to perform religious duties. Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker had a famously opulent lifestyle, owning a private jet, multiple homes and luxury cars Hahn also accused Bakker of sexual assault, though the evangelist denied this, claiming the encounter had been consensual. Bakker was then convicted in 1989 of 24 counts of mail and wire fraud and conspiracy in a scheme involving their Christian theme park, and served more than four years in prison. Tammy Faye stayed with her husband throughout the trial but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007. Following Bakker's release from prison in 1994, he wrote a book titled I Was Wrong and married his second wife Lori in 1998. The couple began a TV ministry together in 2003 and in 2008 they began taping The Jim Bakker Show. title: Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies
description: The government and the Conservatives both agree the UK needs better air defences in an increasingly dangerous world.
body: Current air-defence systems include the Royal Navy's Sea Viper America and Israel's war with Iran has shown that even the world's most sophisticated air defences can be overwhelmed by enemy missiles and drones, if fired in significant numbers. Iran's have broken through the layered air defences of US military bases in the Middle-East causing significant damage. Russia's war in Ukraine has also exposed the huge challenge of defending their own skies from large-scale attacks. The government's Strategic Defence Review, published in 2025, explicitly warned of the threats to the UK – including ballistic and cruise missiles and drones – and highlighted the need for the UK to invest more in its air defences. The Labour government is allocating up to £1bn to address it. The Conservatives now say they will spend more - £10 bn - over a decade. Both parties agree that the UK needs layers of air defences. Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system Currently the country has a number of systems to deal with short and medium-range threats – from drones to cruise missiles. But the armed forces still lack a weapons system to deal with long-range ballistic and hypersonic missiles. And those don't come cheap. Each interceptor used by the US Patriot missile system costs about $4m (£3m). Sophisticated air defences that can deal with a range of threats are expensive. The US Army alone wants to increase its budget for both missiles and interceptors by fourfold next year – to $36bn (£27.1bn). Israel also spends a significant proportion of its $45bn (£33.9bn) annual military budget on air defences. For the Conservatives there's also a presentation problem. Their original press release mentioned building a new air defence systems that would be "in essence, a British Iron Dome", referencing Israel's elaborate air defence system. But any comparison of the challenge of defending Britain's skies with Israel's, about 10% the size of the UK, is naive. Nor is the threat the same. Israel has regularly been targeted by drones and missiles over the past decade. The UK has not. The Conservatives now suggest the phrase "Iron Dome" was just a shorthand for better air defences. But even the words "Britannia Shield" may be a misnomer. It would be nigh on impossible for the UK to develop an air-defence system that could defend the whole country with such limited resources. At best it could afford a system to protect some key strategic sites – including military bases. At present the UK doesn't even have that. What are Israel's Iron Dome and other missile shields? title: Husband who drugged and raped wife for 20 years makes witness statement
description: Jurors were told that the man had given a "detailed" statement about "what he says happened".
body: The trial is being held at Minshull Street Crown Court in Manchester A man who has admitted drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge for more than 20 years has provided a witness statement about "what he says happened", a jury was told. The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, had also been accused of inviting 13 other men to abuse her from 2018 until November 2025. The man, in his 60s and from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, had initially denied the charges but pleaded guilty last month to 60 offences, including rape and administering a substance with intent. A jury was sworn in at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court in early September but the case has since been delayed for legal and practical reasons. One of the co-defendants - 59-year-old Keith Fotheringham from Dundee, Scotland – has also pleaded guilty to several offences. Earlier the nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, were invited into court and provided with an update by Judge Maurice Greene. From left: Graham Brougham, Alan Keelan, Sean Peers, Jonathan Kirk and Jordan Wallace, along with seven others, will still be tried They had already been told at a previous hearing that the husband had admitted 60 offences and would no longer be part of the trial as a defendant. However, Judge Greene said: "What's been happening is that the husband has now made a statement about what he says happened. "That statement is a long statement and that has been disclosed to all defence counsel and it contains a lot of detail." The judge told jurors the statement contained "lots of pages and lots of documents" and that lawyers in the case were "going through it carefully", which was ongoing work. The jury were asked to return on Monday 19 October when the prosecution case against the remaining 12 defendants is due to open. title: Iranian men accused of spying targeted journalists for 'serious violence', court hears
description: The prosecution says the targets were journalists working for a satellite channel critical of the Iranian government.
body: The defendants, pictured in a court sketch during an appearance in May 2025, deny all the charges Three Iranian men have gone on trial in London accused of spying for Iran on UK-based journalists, who were being targeted so "serious violence" could be inflicted on them. The prosecution said Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, was to carry out the attack, with Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, doing the surveillance and reconnaissance. All three were born in Iran but were living in London. The jury at Woolwich Crown Court heard that Sepahvand does not deny his involvement but said he did it out of fear of the consequences of refusing. The prosecution said that is "an entirely bogus claim", adding that he did it for money and to have a criminal conviction for theft in Iran "fixed". Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers. According to the prosecution, Manesh and Noori are expected to say they did not know they were carrying out surveillance on behalf of Iran. All three face charges under the National Security Act, including "assisting a foreign intelligence service". Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC said the men's targets were journalists working for Iran International - a Persian-language satellite channel that is critical of the Tehran regime and has its headquarters in London. Jones said at least two journalists linked to Iran International were targeted in the surveillance. He said at least one of them was to be "subjected to serious violence" as retribution and "to try to silence and deter others who might dare to voice their criticism". Iran International, which broadcasts into Iran, has been declared as a "terrorist organisation" by Tehran. "The evidence we will call illustrates that these three defendants carried out surveillance and reconnaissance, visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos, taking videos, doing online research about them," Jones said. "The defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying," he added. The men also allegedly had a "briefing sheet" on a barrister, Jonathan Turner, who was a founding member of a group called UK Lawyers for Israel. One Iran International journalist who was allegedly targeted was Mojtaba Pourmohsen. Images of him, his workplace and a hotel where he had lived were found in a "briefing document" on Sepahvand's mobile phone. The prosecution says Noori took pictures of the block of flats Pourmohsen lived in in Brentford, southwest London, in December 2024. It is also alleged that Sepahvand and Manesh went there to take photos and videos. Jones said Sepahvand's motivation was to try to resolve a criminal conviction he had in Iran for theft. "He was not just in it for money. He quite explicitly wants something very particular in return for his work - he wanted his criminal conviction in Iran to be fixed," Jones told the jury. The three men, who each had an interpreter in the dock, deny all the charges. All three were granted temporary leave to remain in the UK after claiming asylum. They arrived in the UK between 2016 and 2022. Sepahvand arrived in 2016 concealed in a lorry. The other two arrived in small boats. title: NBA star Wembanyama trains with French rugby club
description: NBA superstar Victor Wembanyama says he was inspired by the unity and camaraderie of rugby after spending time with French second tier side Provence.
body: Wembanyama also represented France in qualification for the 2027 Fiba World Cup this summer NBA superstar Victor Wembanyama says he was inspired by the unity and camaraderie of rugby after spending part of his summer off-season training with French second tier side Provence. The 22-year-old Frenchman, who is 7ft 4in and 16st 11lbs, is known for his off-beat search for ways to improve his game. He spent a fortnight focusing on physical and mental strength with Shaolin monks in China in 2025., external Footage shows Wembanyama, external hitting tackle pads, going through passing drills, taking part in a line-out and looming over the rest of the Provence team in a huddle before a pre-season friendly in August. He was also filmed sharing a dressing-room embrace with former England international Teimana Harrison, who won five England caps in 2016 and now plays for Provence. "It was a great experience, seeing the team spirit they have over there," said Wembanyama,, external who was joined on the trip by San Antonio Spurs' team-mate Harrison Barnes. "It was very inspiring to see the relationship between team-mates, coaches and fans. The training was really hard, really good for stability, movement patterns and developing strength, but I am more grateful for the experience of how I was welcomed there. "I have never been welcomed anywhere like this. I wasn't part of the team but they treated me like I was. I want to do it again." Wembanyama combined his work with Provence with hosting his Hoop Gambit event, in which participants play games of chess and basketball, in his hometown of Le Chesnay. Wembanyama's Spurs fell just short of the NBA Championship earlier this year, going down 4-1 to the New York Knicks in June. Provence, who previously have been represented by Wales internationals George North and Tomas Francis, have begun their season and search for promotion to the Top 14 well, winning their first five league games. title: Boys, 12 and 14, arrested over major Nottingham fire
description: The fire at the Grade II listed Escobar building in Nottingham led to major disruption.
body: About 60 firefighters attended the scene in the Nottingham on Monday night Two boys have been arrested on suspicion of arson after a major fire left a listed building in Nottingham city centre at risk of internal collapse. At its height, 12 fire crews and about 60 firefighters were tackling the blaze at the Grade II listed Escobar building in Market Street shortly before 23:00 BST on Monday. No-one was seriously injured, police said. Closures were put in place in Upper Parliament Street, Goldsmith Street, Market Street and the surrounding area, with a joint police and fire investigation under way. Police said the boys - 14 and 12 - remained in custody. The investigation into the cause of the fire is still ongoing, officers said. People have been advised to avoid the area, with tram and bus services being affected by the emergency response. Nottingham Express Transit, which operates the tram network, also said it had turned off the overhead power lines in the area due to the fire. An aerial ladder platform was used so firefighters could take a closer look at the building Richard Booth, station manager for Nottinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service, told the BBC the building, which comprises several businesses and residential flats, was "not safe to go into". "It's not in danger of collapsing externally, but internally there is no roof," he said. "A lot of the roof trusses are quite highly fire-damaged so there's potential for internal collapse within that building above Escobar." Speaking from the scene on Tuesday morning, incident commander Richard Leighton told the BBC about a dozen residents had been affected along with four businesses. "We need to make sure the building is safe for them to return," he said, adding people living there were likely to be face disruption for the rest of the day. Firefighters have been checking the structural integrity of the building The emergency response was scaled down on Tuesday morning, with about four fire engines at the scene and two police vehicles. Firefighters used the aerial ladder platform to take a closer look at the building and check for hotspots. The Escobar building was badly damaged, with debris scattered across Market Street. The building next to it, with a dental practice in its ground floor, had its windows open. Ian Wikberg and India Morrell saw the flames above the building on Monday night Ian Wikberg and India Morrell found themselves caught up in the chaos after leaving a concert at Rock City on Monday. "We came out at about 22:30, when the doors closed, and we walked down the road and it was all quite active with fire, ambulance and police, and building was well alight," Wikberg said. The 43-year-old said there were "pockets of people" standing around in slippers and dressing downs after being evacuated from the building. "[There was] a lot of people, a lot of cordons, all the roads blocked, the air was full of smoke and red," he said. Morell added: "It was scary really I've never seen anything like it before. "The first thing you think is you hope everyone's out and you hope everyone's OK." When the pair first saw the fire, the flames were "probably five metres above the building". "You could see the redness and there was smoke everywhere," Morell said. A joint police and fire investigation remains ongoing Restaurant owner Erlint Tsalai said he was awaiting an update from police after his business, The Souvlaki, was cordoned off. He said he was alerted to the fire, two doors from his property, by his landlord. "When I looked at the news, I saw the pictures and everything. I was really worried and I came here as soon as possible," he added. "I hope everything is fine for anyone who was here last night." Tsalai told the BBC he was worried about losing a day's business The front door of Tsalai's restaurant had to be smashed so firefighters could check the building and ensure nobody was inside. He added he was worried about the cost of losing a day's business and of replacing the door. Chris Pearson, city commander for Nottinghamshire Police, said the the arrests were made "very quickly" after officers were called to the scene. He has urged anyone with information or footage of the blaze to get in touch or contact Crimestoppers. title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
description: The deal is expected to alter the entertainment and news industries but could it mean higher prices for consumers?
body: Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance. Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom. Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch. HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS. Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time. While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability. The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said viewers will undoubtedly get access to a bigger catalog. But he told the BBC: "There's no way that a combined Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming service won't end up costing more for those who subscribe to only one of the services." As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years. For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year. That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas. The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year. If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein. Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date. "Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said. "Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift". Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema. As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas. Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year. Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground. Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods. Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken". "It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts." A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years. The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022. Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities". She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network." Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts. "Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added. CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount. The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN. Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation. Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role. Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS. Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom. Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless". "The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said. Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said. Are you affected by issues covered in this story? title: Seven arrested for using Ghanaian banknotes to make 'money bouquets'
description: The arrests are part of the country's efforts to curb the misuse and abuse of the national currency.
body: It is illegal to misuse Ghana's cedi, including by defacing or unlawfully altering banknotes Ghanaian authorities have arrested seven people for allegedly using banknotes to make so-called "money bouquets" and decorate cakes. The Bank of Ghana says the practice is illegal and amounts to misuse and improper handling of the cedi, the national currency. The arrests, carried out in collaboration with the police, followed a tip-off that led to a swoop on the suspects, all women, accused of selling the bouquets in different parts of the capital, Accra. The arrests are the biggest enforcement of the law against misusing the currency. In July, the bank issued a notice warning this could amount to an offence. It warned against "acts that tend to depreciate or impair the national currency, including any conduct that undermines its lawful value or use". Bouquets of banknotes or cakes decorated with currency are often ordered as gifts for weddings, birthdays, graduations and other celebrations. The police have launched investigations, and the authorities say the suspects will be prosecuted. They could face a fine or jail term, to be determined by the court. Dinah Bonzi, an official in the Bank of Ghana's currency department, said anyone aiding or promoting such activities could also be arrested and prosecuted. ''The Ghana cedi is legal tender… and must be treated with respect. The misuse or abuse of the currency is an offence and may attract sanctions under the law,'' she said. "Today's arrest should serve as a clear warning to the public. Let us all handle the Ghana cedi with dignity." The central bank has repeatedly warned against activities such as "spraying" - or throwing money at events such as weddings - writing on or altering notes and using them in decorations such as floral-like bouquets in weddings, birthdays and other occasions. The use of money decorations has become more common in Ghana in recent years, with the practice also gaining a foothold in other African countries. In recent years authorities in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Botswana have also issued warnings against misusing the national currencies. title: Ship sinks and crew missing after Black Sea drone attack
description: It is not clear who is behind the attacks which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea as part of its war against Ukraine.
body: Two injured crew members from one of the ships have been sent for treatment A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say. A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued. Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable". Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said. The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania. It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board. A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched. Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain. Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan. Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law". He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable." He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning. "Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning." "Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable." Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea. A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media. On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. title: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect
description: Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty to neglect and abandoning children in her care at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court.
body: This video can not be played Amanda Mathewson leaves Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court A Dunfermline childminder has admitted leaving more than 20 children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home. Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court to neglect and abandoning children in her care. Her offending took place at a number of locations in Dunfermline and elsewhere in Fife. The court heard Mathewson had 27 children in her home, 19 more than she was licensed to look after. Mathewson, who has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children. The court heard she had provided childcare services at her home in Dunfermline for children under the age of 16. At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12, 10 children under primary school age, and two children under the age of one in her care. More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East Procurator fiscal Vicki Bell told the court two parents became suspicious of Mathewson after being informed their children were not present while the childminder carried out a school run. They secretly went to the school and found their children were not with Mathewson, despite being in her care. They then went to her home, where they heard a "child screaming" and found five unattended children in the garden. One of the children told the witnesses there were no adults inside, and Mathewson had told them to "wait in the garden". They approached the door of the house to check if there were any adults present, when they hear another child "screaming hysterically" inside. The door was unlocked, and when the witnesses entered they found a child crying under the kitchen table. A further nine children, all under five, were found in an upstairs bedroom. Two of them were strapped into prams. The children were said to be "distressed" but uninjured. Police attended and Mathewson said the children had been left alone for at least 30 minutes. The court heard ring doorbell footage showed this was the second time that day the children were left inside the house. During the police investigation, various children told their parents that being left alone in Mathewson's home was "commonplace". Some parents told officers that their children became "upset" when they were taken to the childminders home and those who could talk would say they did not want to go. The investigation found discrepancies in the number of children in Matthewson's care and the number of children she was seen with on multiple occasions. For example, Mathewson attended a church Christmas party with three children, despite having nine kids in her care that day. The parents of the three children who were in attendance were sent a photo of their child with Santa, while the other were just send a generic photo. There were other occasions such as a sports day and a visit to Dunfermline fire station where Mathewson was seen with fewer children than she was responsible for. Parents also raised concerns that their children had not eaten while in the childminder's care due to their clothes staying in "pristine condition" and it was a general theme that their children would return home thirsty. Some parents also reported their children returned home in dirty nappies or with dry faeces in their underwear. Court documents state that Mathewson always had loud music playing and did not let parents enter her home at drop off time in an attempt to "conceal how oversubscribed she was". When the childminder was asked about the number of children in her care, or the whereabouts of certain children she claimed she was being assisted by a "child-minding friend". The case was heard at at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court Mathewson admitted wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children to a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health. The court heard she offered childcare places for more children than she could reasonably provide care for at the time. A Care Inspectorate report published in August 2023 said Mathewson was registered to provide care for a maximum of eight children at any one time. It included conditions that a maximum of six children could be under the age of 12, no more than three could have started primary school, and no more than one could be under 12-months-old. The unannounced inspection from about a year before her arrest had rated areas including care, learning and the setting as "very good", the second-highest level in the quality scale. The report said "children were cared for in a comfortable, welcoming and homely environment" and "were cared for with warmth, kindness and a nurturing approach". A spokesperson for the Care Inspectorate said this is a "distressing case" and they have "implemented changes as a result of learning from this case." In a statement given to the BBC, one of the parents said: "The criminal case is important for justice. But our ultimate goal is to ensure no other family has to endure what we have been through. Our trust was broken, but our resolve is not. "We have turned our pain into a purpose: to rebuild the system of childcare regulation and family support so that it is truly fit to protect Scotland's children." Sheriff John MacRitchie deferred sentencing until 6 November to allow background reports to be carried out. Mathewson's bail was continued. title: Boats 'set for people smugglers' seized at UK airport for the first time
description: The National Crime Agency says it is the first time the detection of small boat equipment has been made in air freight.
body: The boats were identified in pallets on an air freight shipment being moved from Turkey to the Netherlands Officers have seized 25 inflatable boats reportedly destined to be shipped to cross-Channel people smugglers. The National Crime Agency (NCA) said the boats - about nine metres in length - were spotted in pallets on an air freight shipment being moved from Turkey to the Netherlands. The shipment went through a freight hub at East Midlands Airport on the way, allowing NCA and Border Force to intercept on Friday. NCA officers added this was the second time a large consignment of small boat equipment had been seized in the UK in 2026, but the first time such a detection had been made in air freight. The shipment was intercepted on Friday In July, 25 boats and 25 engines were seized in a maritime consignment at Felixstowe in Suffolk. The boat carrying them had stopped there on the way to Germany. The NCA said, had the latest shipment made its way into the hands of people smugglers, "each could have been used to transport around 70 people across the Channel". The NCA estimated the boats could have been used to move up to 1,700 migrants. NCA deputy director of investigations Craig Turner said: "We continue to target groups or individuals directly involved in the supply of boats and engines used in the Channel for people smuggling. "This work is happening both overseas, with international partners, and here in the UK. So far it has led to the seizure of in excess of 1,600 boats and engines, denying their use to criminal networks. "Our assessment is that this is having an impact, driving up the cost of boats and engines, making it more difficult to get them to the coast and eating into the profits of the criminal gangs involved. "I've no doubt the boats we've seized here would have ended up being used to risk the lives of a huge number of people in the Channel had we not stepped in. Our investigation continues." NCA bosses said each boat "could have been used to transport around 70 people across the Channel" Minister for border security and asylum Anna Turley added: "This seizure of 25 small boats delivers yet another blow to the evil smuggling gangs. "Disruptions to supply lines like these are happening more than ever before as we bear down on the illegal and dangerous crossings." The NCA said about 100 investigations into gangs involved in organisation immigration crime were ongoing. title: Adjoa Andoh, Rosie O'Donnell and Julie Hesmondhalgh to appear in play about Gisele Pelicot case
description: The four-hour one-off performance will also star Adjoa Andoh and Juliet Stevenson and
body: Adjoa Andoh, Rosie O'Donnell, Tamzin Outhwaite and Julie Hesmondhalgh will take part in the one-off performance US comedian Rosie O'Donnell, Celebrity Traitors star Julie Hesmondhalgh, Bridgerton's Adjoa Andoh and EastEnders actress Tamzin Outhwaite will appear in a play based on the trial of the husband of Gisele Pelicot. Thirty actors and public figures will take part in The Pelicot Trial, a one-off "documentary theatre" style performance at London's County Hall next month. The play has been created from documents from the trial and psychiatric reports of dozens of men who were prosecuted in the case, which caused outrage in France and around the world, and turned Gisele Pelicot into a symbol of strength against sexual assault. Dominique Pelicot was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping his then wife, and allowing 50 other men to rape her while she was unconscious. The play pays tribute to "the ordinary woman who opened the way to change", the Young Vic said Other cast members include Truly, Madly, Deeply star Juliet Stevenson, All Creatures Great and Small actor Samuel West, Sixth Sense's Oliva Wiliams and Slow Horses' Kadiff Kirwan. Comedian Rosie Jones, Dune actress Sharon Duncan-Brewster, Bridgerton's Lorraine Ashbourne and Rizzle Kicks rapper Jordan Stephens will also take part. Further casting for the four-hour play, which was developed in collaboration with journalists and feminist organisations in France, will be announced in the coming weeks. The play was first staged in Vienna last year The Pelicot Trial will be staged by the Young Vic theatre at London's County Hall on 30 November, and will also be streamed online. The Young Vic said the performance is a "profoundly affecting piece of documentary theatre, comprised of testimonies and written accounts from the trial, (which) pays tribute to the ordinary woman who opened the way to change". Gisele Pelicot, 73, waived her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse, and said shame should fall on her abusers, not her. The Pelicot Trial received its world premiere in Vienna last year and has since toured to cities including Avignon, New York, Lisbon, Milan and Bergen. Tickets for the London performance will go on general sale on Wednesday. title: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins physics Nobel
description: Belgian physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space.
body: Prof Francis Halzen won for "decisive contribution" to developing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe. Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said "his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory". He first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988. Halzen, who is now a US citizen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, told a news conference that he was surprised his idea worked so well. "I have to emphasise how lucky I was. Because when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself." Scientists in a race to discover why our Universe exists Galaxy's ghost particles captured in Antarctic ice Neutrinos are elusive subatomic particles. The Sun produces vast numbers of them: every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail. But IceCube is searching for much higher-energy neutrinos, those produced by violent processes far beyond our Solar System — in distant galaxies. It is composed of thousands of sensors on long cables that are drilled and frozen into a 1km cubic block of ice. Neutrinos can be thought of as astronomical messengers that point to those fundamental events. At the observatory, most neutrinos pass straight through the ice, but occasionally one interacts with it, producing particles that give off a telltale flash of light. These rare signals carry clues to where the neutrinos came from and the extreme conditions that produced them — allowing scientists to investigate places that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see. "Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," said Prof Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics. "His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy." This blurry image is of the Milky Way, but it is composed of neutrino particles On the rare occasions when a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it produces fast-moving charged particles. It is these racing through the ice, which give off a blue glow, which sensitive light detectors can pick up. The pattern and timing of that light allow scientists to estimate the direction the neutrino came from — helping them trace its origins in the cosmos. But these interactions are so rare that the observatory needed an enormous volume of clear ice. Halzen's idea was to use a vast natural ice sheet in Antarctica. So began an audacious plan to build a neutrino observatory at the geographic South Pole, with thousands of light sensors embedded deep in the ice. The neutrino's ghostly nature, the very thing that makes it so hard to detect, also makes it a powerful messenger from the distant Universe. Neutrinos rarely interact with material in its way, so they can go right through dense regions that light cannot easily penetrate. And because they have no electric charge, magnetic fields do not bend their paths through space. That means their direction of arrival can point scientists back towards their source. Their energies carry further insight into the processes that created them - helping scientists investigate how exploding stars and the environments around giant black holes accelerate particles to extraordinary energies. Louis Barson, director of science at the Institute of Physics in London, said the IceCube Observatory had enabled astronomers to investigate phenomena that conventional telescopes cannot see. "The discoveries that have followed are helping us understand some of the most energetic and mysterious processes in the universe - and that's thanks to Professor Halzen's work," he added. Prof Subir Sarkar, physicist from the University of Oxford, quoted the French novelist Marcel Proust in describing his assessment of Halzen's contribution to science: "'The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is'. "Francis Halzen has led the IceCube collaboration on just such a voyage of discovery and opened a new window on to our Universe". title: Italian PM files to trademark her voice against AI threats
description: Giorgia Meloni submitted a four-second audio to a EU agency in a bid to protect her voice from deepfakes.
body: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has applied to trademark her voice in a move to protect herself against artificial intelligence (AI) deepfakes. The application to the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) was made on Monday and can be found on their website, external. The prime minister's office also confirmed the application. As part of it, Meloni recorded a four-second audio where she says "Io sono Giorgia" - I am Giorgia Meloni" in Italian - twice. Meloni is not alone in filing to protect her identity from unauthorised use by AI platforms. In January, US actor Matthew McConaughey led the way by trademarking his image and voice. Singer Taylor Swift did similar in April, submitting three trademark applications in the US - one using a photo of herself on stage during her Eras Tour, and the other two being audio clips of her introducing herself while promoting her last album. In August, more than 80 performers called on British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce legislation which would give every person in the UK a legal right to own their voice. Actors including Matt Lucas, Hugh Bonneville and Nicola Coughlan were among those calling for greater protection against their voices being used by AI. Voice clones are created by training AI on recordings of real people. Quick versions can be made from a few seconds of audio, but high-quality copycats tend to require hours. Meloni's decision to trademark her voice comes ahead of Italy's general elections next year. The phrase, "Io sono Giorgia", was the title of Meloni's 2021 autobiography and is associated with the prime minister's political campaigns. In 2024, Meloni sought €100,000 (£84,920) in damages after deepfake porn videos of her were uploaded online. A deepfake image is one where the face of one person is digitally added to the body of another. In recent years, deepfake porn has become commonplace on the internet and victims have spoken out about the trauma it has caused them. More recently, in May this year, Meloni warned of the dangers of deepfakes as several AI-generated images of her wearing lingerie were circulating online. In a post on social media, Meloni added: "The point, however, goes beyond me. Deepfakes are a dangerous tool, because they can deceive, manipulate, and strike anyone. I can defend myself. Many others cannot." title: Chart-topping singer and television host Lena Martell dies aged 86
description: The Glasgow-born singer was the first solo Scottish female singer to top the UK singles chart with One Day at a Time.
body: Lena Martell was the first solo Scottish female singer to top the UK singles chart with One Day at a Time Scottish singer and Broadway performer Lena Martell has died at the age of 86. She was the first solo Scottish female singer to top the UK singles chart with her cover of the song One Day at a Time in 1979. Born Helen Thomson in Glasgow, Martell recorded a number of albums over the years and performed in New York and Las Vegas alongside Frank Sinatra, Sammy Davis Jr and Barbara Streisand. She became a familiar entertainment star in the 1970s when she hosted her own BBC prime time television show for about a decade. In posts on social media, fans paid tribute to Martell and shared memories of listening to her chart-topping single. Fellow Scottish singer Barbara Dickson said she was sad to hear of Martell's death. She said: "She had a lovely melodious quality to her voice and I remember my late father admiring her quiet talent". Martell appeared on Top of the Pops in 1979 Martell first started singing as a child with her elder brother's band before she went on to perform with the Jimmie McGregor Band at the Barrowland Ballroom in Glasgow as a singer. As a teenager, Martell appeared on a 1950s ITV show called Find the Singer. She received her first recording contract at 16. Her musical career took her overseas and she eventually left the UK to work on Broadway, where she understudied Streisand in Funny Girl. The singer performed on cruise ships and in cabarets and concert halls, spending extensive periods in the United States. In the 1970s, Martell had her own BBC television series, which saw her singing and chatting to different big-name guests in front of audiences of more than 12 million every week. Her early studio albums were released under the Pye record label Martell's cover of the song One Day at a Time, written by Marijohn Wilkin and Kris Kristofferson, reached the top of the UK singles chart for three weeks in October 1979. The single sold almost three million copies and earned her a place in the Guinness Book of World Records when it stayed in the charts for 36 weeks. She went on to place six albums in the UK albums chart between 1974 and 1980, including four in the top 20. Martell faced a series of health problems throughout her life. She was diagnosed with cancer and later underwent a triple heart bypass - a surgical procedure which uses a blood vessel from somewhere else in the body to create another way for blood to reach the heart muscle. After her recovery, Martell returned to the stage and continued to perform at the Pavilion Theatre in Glasgow. It is understood she died at a care home after a short illness. title: California leaders hit back after Trump says Iran can 'take out' LA and San Diego
description: The US president said rising gas prices were a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe" at an election rally in Nebraska.
body: President Trump, speaking in Nebraska, said the war with Iran was almost over Leaders in California have condemned President Trump following comments he made during a midterms election rally in Nebraska. Speaking about higher gas prices as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, Trump said Tehran "taking out" Los Angeles or San Diego would be a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe". State governor Gavin Newsom described the US president as "deranged and dangerous," while Mayor of Los Angeles Karen Bass said: "The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives." The cities are the largest in southern California and house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases. Trump described the war with Iran as almost over while speaking in Nebraska, and there were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made. San Diego's Mayor Todd Gloria wrote the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk". In a second post on his official governor of California X account, Newsom shared an article on the comments from the Los Angeles Times saying it was "disgusting and disqualifying". Trump is yet to respond to the comments made by California's leaders. San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast. It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at. Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US. It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base. Trump and Newsom met when the president visited California in January after the state was hit by wildfires This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed. Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent. Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests. Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities. What are the US midterms? title: Jade Thirlwall says working on Blue Planet III song was magical
description: The ex-Little Mix star worked with Hans Zimmer on an official track for the BBC nature documentary.
body: The solo artist says she is a "huge" fan of Sir David Attenborough Singer Jade Thirlwall says working on the official song for BBC documentary Blue Planet III is "one of the best things" she's ever done. The former Little Mix star worked with legendary composer Hans Zimmer on Into The Deep (Seas Cry), a piece created for the launch of the series narrated by Sir David Attenborough. Thirlwall, who debuted the track on BBC Radio 1's Breakfast Show, told host Greg James working on it was a "very special" experience. Blue Planet III is due to air this autumn, but an official release date is yet to be announced. During her breakfast show appearance, Thirlwall said Blue Planet, which focuses on the life of our seas and oceans, was her favourite TV show. "When this opportunity came in, I might have shed a little tear," she said. "I was just so buzzing to be a part of something so special. "I'm a huge David Attenborough fan, I love the planet, I love the oceans. It was so magical getting to write a song all about that." Thirlwall said the track, which mixes her striking vocals with Hans Zimmer's signature orchestral builds, was written to be "celebratory". She said footage captured by Blue Planet III crews played in the background as she worked on creating the theatrical piece. "The song is about the oceans and how special they are, hope, fighting the good fight to make the world a better place," she said. Sir David Attenborough is expected to reveal extraordinary stories through his narration of the new series Thirlwall also said she was "busy writing" a second album after a busy summer of festival performances, including slots at Reading and Leeds in August. It's not the first time a big artist has worked with Hans Zimmer to create a track for the BBC's nature programmes. Singer RAYE and Bastille frontman Dan Smith have previously collaborated with the Oscar-winner. George Fenton, another key Blue Planet composer who'd worked on other BBC nature documentaries, as well as classic films such as Gandhi and Groundhog Day, died this week at the age of 76. title: Calm in real life but demons on court - Medvedev runs out of chances
description: Daniil Medvedev once said you would need to knock on his hotel door at 6am for seven days in a row to make him angry - but his China Open disqualification was no surprise.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Medvedev disqualified after striking fan with ball Daniil Medvedev once said you would need to knock on his hotel door at 6am for seven days in a row to make him angry. On court, though, he is a far more combustible character who finally ran out of chances when he was disqualified from Monday's China Open semi-final against Novak Djokovic. Djokovic was serving for a place in the final when the ball ricocheted off the back of the court. Medvedev swiped it into the stands, where it hit a spectator in the face. A few minutes later the Russian was defaulted, as he had to be, under rules that bar a player from "hitting a ball dangerously or recklessly, or with negligent disregard of the consequences." Players have got away with worse. There is sometimes anger in their actions, but it is rarely of the bulging-neck-vein variety. It is more often a sign of irritation and petulance, with frustrations taken out on the ball with little care for the safety of officials, ball kids and the spectators who line the court. "I can only say I'm a really calm person in life - I actually have no idea why the demons go out when I play tennis," Medvedev said at the 2019 US Open, where he was fined for snatching a towel from a ball person and making an offensive gesture to fans inside the Arthur Ashe Stadium. "Especially when I was a junior, I had a lot of problems with my attitude. "I was not getting defaulted, but to have a game penalty was easy." Returning to the theme at that year's end-of-season ATP Finals, Medvedev said any bad blood soon disappears after leaving the court. "All my temper goes away after I leave the tennis court. If I'm not happy with my practice, I step out of the court and five minutes later, I'm OK," he said. Medvedev has made a habit of arguing with umpires and occasionally taunting the crowd It is hard - and probably unwise - to take your eyes off Medvedev's matches, and he is very popular with the media for his engaging, reflective and humorous interviews once the dust has settled. But he has gone too far on court on many occasions, with much of his aggression directed at umpires. At Wimbledon in 2017, a 21-year-old Medvedev was so incensed about some of the decisions made by umpire Mariana Alves in his second-round match that he sprinkled coins at her feet as she climbed down from the chair. He later apologised and denied he was accusing her of bias. Two years ago, again at Wimbledon, it appeared officials were considering defaulting Medvedev for an outburst towards umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore. Medvedev claimed he said something in Russian which was "not pleasant, but not over the line" - and, after a discussion between the umpire, supervisor and tournament referee, he escaped with a code violation for unsportsmanlike conduct. He was fined more than £60,000 for his behaviour at the 2025 Australian Open, which included trying to destroy a net camera, and had an infamous meltdown later that year at the US Open. On a rowdy New York night, Benjamin Bonzi had match point for a straight-set win against Medvedev in the first round when a photographer inexplicably walked on to court between his first and second serves. Umpire Greg Allensworth awarded the Frenchman another first serve because of the delay, sparking fury from Medvedev. Medvedev accused Allensworth of hoping to engineer a quick finish - as he gets paid by the match, rather than the hour - and there was a pause of over five minutes as he whipped up the crowd. He did save the match point, but went on to lose in five sets before obliterating his racquet by smashing it repeatedly against the table next to his chair. Medvedev was heavily fined for his behaviour at the 2025 US Open Medvedev will lose all the prize money and ranking points he earned from his run to the semi-finals in Beijing. He remains in the eighth and final qualifying spot for November's ATP Finals, but the loss of 200 points could yet prove crucial. The 30-year-old has apologised for his actions and said he hopes to say sorry to the spectator in person. In New York a month ago, Medvedev reflected on the role of genetics when explaining how his eldest daughter has "my personality on the court". "She plays a bit. She enjoys it. Maybe it's a bit of a genetic somewhere there," Medvedev added. "I took her to practice once. She's happy, so she throws the racquet through the whole court. "The coach looks at me and says: 'I don't know where she got this from...' "All the people that talk about that I should control myself more - she's three years old. It's not like we taught her to do the things she's doing on the court." title: ASOS app users receive push notifications apparently sent by hackers
description: Dozens of people appear to have received a strange message from the clothing and beauty store's app.
body: Asos users across the UK have been sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company. Dozens of people have told the BBC about receiving a strange message from the clothing and beauty store's app, appearing on their phone screens. "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message reads. Asos did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for comment. "If confirmed, this is a deeply serious attack because the hackers appear to have done something particularly brazen: turned ASOS's own app into their ransom note," says Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point. "Millions of people trust notifications from apps on their phones because they are supposed to come directly from the company." On social media, dozens of people have posted about receiving the message - confused as to what it means. Although the apparent extortion message has been issued directly to customers, it is addressed to Asos' data protection officer (DPO) and IT team. The message claims the unnamed hackers have "fully compromised the Snowflake instance". This refers to the data storage company Snowflake, whose tools are used by dozens of firms for collecting, analysing and storing data. It is not known if ASOS is a customer of Snowflake or what data, if any, is stored with the service. But Snowflake has been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years and has been linked to incidents targeting services including Ticketmaster and Santander. It is, however, very unusual for a data breach to be revealed quite so publicly - and for customers to be informed in this manner. Most extortions and negotiations by cyber criminals are conducted in private, with hackers hoping their discretion will result in a quiet pay-off. The pop up message contains a link to the hackers' Telegram channel. The new group is calling itself Xuanye Group and only created its Telegram channel today. They have posted only three times with the latest being about the ASOS hack. Dan Bird, from cyber security firm Horizon3 says the pop up message the criminals sent implies that their access has gone beyond the Snowflake database. "Sending a push notification to ASOS's app users would require access to the company's notification system, which is separate from the Snowflake data platform the attackers claim to have compromised." "If both claims hold up, it suggests the attackers got hold of credentials that opened more than one door," he said. Have you been affected by this hack? title: Woman found dead in home named as GP
description: Dr Hannah Terry was working as a GP at a nearby practice, which has been closed since the weekend.
body: Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, worked at a local GP practice A woman found dead at her home has been named locally as a GP. The body of Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday. Norfolk Police said it was called to the property by the ambulance service just after 02:20 BST. A man in his 40s was arrested on suspicion of murder and remains in custody. On Monday, at a hearing at Great Yarmouth Magistrates' Court, officers were granted an additional 32 hours to question him. Terry, who was in her 40s, has not been officially identified by police. A notice on the website of Grimston Medical Centre, where she is listed as a member of the practice team, says it is "temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team". A cordon remains in place outside the house in Fern Hill and a Home Office post-mortem examination was due to be carried out on Monday. Police were called to Fern Hill, Dersingham, at 02:20 BST on Sunday Det Insp Alix Wright, of the Norfolk and Suffolk major investigation team, said on Sunday: "We are in the very early stages of this investigation, working to establish the exact circumstances surrounding the woman's death. "I'd ask anyone who believes they may have information that could help our investigation to please share this with us." Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. title: One million UK people who have never smoked are now vaping
description: Latest statistics also show, for the second year in a row, more over-16s vape than smoke.
body: 1.1 million of those who have never smoked say they vape daily or occasionally More than a million people who say they have never tried a cigarette are now vapers, latest UK data for 2025 reveals, external - up from around 940,000 in 2024. People aged 25-34 are vaping more than any others, overtaking 16 to 24-year-olds, with 16.4% using e-cigarettes daily or occasionally. For the second year in a row, more over-16s are using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Meanwhile, the number of smokers in the UK continues to fall to nearly one in 10 adults, or 4.9 million people, down from 5.3 million in 2024, with more over-16s now vaping than smoking at 5.4 million. Experts say the popularity of cigarette smoking has decreased as the harmful effects of tobacco have encouraged many to quit. Vaping is less harmful than smoking, although the long-term effects are not yet clear, says the NHS. It says non-smokers and people aged 17 and under should never vape. The ONS figures show the percentage of people who had never used an e-cigarette continued to decrease in 2025 (83.0%) compared with 2024 (83.4%). Twenty-five to 34-year-olds are now more likely to use vapes than 16 to 24-year-olds. David Mais, from the ONS, said vapers were getting older and that "may reflect existing users getting older, growing popularity among this age group, or a combination of both". New legislation in the UK, external, taking affect in the new year, will permanently ban the legal sale of tobacco to anyone born on or after January 1, 2009 to create a "smoke-free" generation. Hazel Cheeseman, from the charity Action on Smoking and Health, said the latest statics showed encouraging progress in cutting smoking rates. She added: "Smoking has fallen enormously over recent decades, but it remains the biggest driver of preventable death in the UK. Now is the time to finish the job." According to the ONS, men were more likely to smoke than women in 2025, similar to previous years. And people aged 45-54 had the highest proportion of current smokers (12.4%). Young adults aged 18 to 24 years have seen the largest drop in smoking among all age groups. Of the people who currently smoked in 2025, half said they intended to quit. Some 7.2% of people reported having used an e-cigarette, up from 6.6% in 2024. The vaping data includes people aged 16 and over in Great Britain, while the smoking statistics cover adults in the whole of the UK. title: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
description: August Hanning is accused of obtaining classified information for a foreign power.
body: Agents arrested August Hanning (pictured from 2015) at his home on Tuesday Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says. Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant. Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved. Police also arrested former BND employee Mandred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money. Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage. Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday. Prosecutors say Mandred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration". "The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says. "On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient". Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years". Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block. Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies. State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents. It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia. Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly €400,000 ($450,000; £340,000). His trial is ongoing.
