title: Indian opposition MPs detained in protest against election chief
description: Opposition leaders have alleged that CEC Gyanesh Kumar manipulated voter rolls to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party during elections.
body: Many opposition lawmakers, including Congress party's Rahul Gandhi, were stopped midway as they marched towards the Election Commission headquarters Police in Delhi detained several opposition lawmakers as they tried to march demanding the chief election commissioner resign over a controversial voter roll revision. Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka and other MPs were forced into a police bus. Released shortly after, they resumed their march and began a sit-in near Election Commission headquarters. It is the latest escalation in a growing row over a nationwide revision of voter rolls. Opposition parties accuse Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of overseeing a process that could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), an allegation both the BJP and Election Commission have rejected. Security officials blocked the roads from India's parliament to the election commission headquarters "Some of the MPs tried to take some other roads to the Election Commission building. We have officers stationed at multiple points, from where the protesters were picked up in buses and taken to different police stations," Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Manjeet Sheoran told the BBC. The police did not disclose how many lawmakers had been detained. The opposition said 237 MPs from a range of parties participated in the march. Tuesday's protest came just four days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a Gen Z-backed online satirical movement, organised demonstrations in Mumbai and Delhi, also demanding the CEC's resignation. The group has described those demonstrations as the beginning of a nationwide campaign and has called for another round of protests on 10 October. At the centre of the controversy is the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The exercise began in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 before being expanded to other parts of the country. The Election Commission says the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters from electoral rolls. More than 130 million names have so far been removed from draft voter lists nationwide. Opposition parties and activists allege that many eligible voters have been wrongly excluded and accuse the poll body of conducting the process improperly. The campaign against Kumar gathered momentum after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions and orders they said had been issued in the Election Commission's name without their knowledge. According to the report, the objections related to issues including additions and deletions from voter rolls, access to the voter database and the security of electoral data. Some concerns were linked directly to the electoral roll revision programme. The Election Commission, a three-member body comprising the chief election commissioner and two election commissioners, defended its decision-making process, saying differing views were part of institutional functioning and that decisions had ultimately been taken unanimously. The revelations nevertheless triggered a political backlash, with opposition leaders intensifying calls for Kumar's resignation. India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is at the centre of a controversy over allegations of manipulating voter rolls Security was tightened around the Election Commission headquarters on Tuesday, with police barricading roads along the route between parliament and the commission's office. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge described three demands as "non-negotiable": Kumar's resignation, cancellation of the SIR exercise and a return to paper ballot voting. Mocking the election chief, Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India's lower house of parliament, tweeted: "Gyanesh, it's done, bro. Time to resign." The BJP condemned the protests. BJP MP Sambit Patra described them as a "sponsored attempt" to bring about a change of power through "anarchy". He accused opposition parties of seeking to undermine constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission. The controversy has also reached India's Supreme Court, which has asked both the federal government and the Election Commission to respond to a petition alleging that Kumar took key decisions without the approval of the two other election commissioners. The petition argues that Kumar exercised powers that belong to the commission collectively and seeks a ruling that any such actions were unauthorised. The court indicated that Election Commission decisions must be taken either unanimously or by majority vote and suggested that decisions could be set aside if found to have bypassed that process. However, it declined to suspend Kumar at this stage, saying it would first hear the Election Commission's response and examine relevant records. The BBC has contacted the Election Commission for comment on Tuesday's protest. title: Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks
description: Ukrainians travelling by train are increasingly caught in the crosshairs of Russia's attacks.
body: Russian drones started to attack Ukrainian passenger trains at the end of last year Ukraine's railways have kept the country running since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator. Yuliia Ponomarenko, 27, a marketing specialist from Kharkiv, found her journey to Warsaw last month suddenly interrupted just short of the Ukraine-Poland frontier. "The border guards started running around and shouting "Run! Get out of the carriages! There's shelling!" A Russian drone had just hit a locomotive near the same border, and a special train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European dignitaries, had passed through minutes before. Passengers on Yuliia's train were kept waiting for six hours while the fire up ahead was put out and the line cleared, she says: "We were really lucky that we were delayed a little and it wasn't our train." She is among an increasing number of Ukrainian passengers facing disruption and long delays, as air raid alerts trigger emergency evacuations far from the battlegrounds of the east. In September alone, 5,831 trains had to be evacuated due to Russian drone attacks, state owned railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia told AFP news agency on Monday. This meant on average each day, 205 trains were stopped. It appears to be part of a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv in the past few days and passengers of a metro train caught up in one of the strikes. Passengers are routinely evacuated from trains and forced to wait on the trackside until the danger has passed Seventeen-year-old Anastasiia Ryvbalchenko has also experienced a narrow escape. She and her fellow passengers were forced to leave their train at 4am, towards the end of a long of a journey from Odesa to Kirovohrad on 16 September. "On my way to Odesa, there had been a lot of evacuations and now on my way back it was happening again," she says. "I was already thinking that if there was another evacuation, I just couldn't take it any more." An hour and a half later, as passengers waited in the dark, a drone struck nearby. "There was an extremely loud explosion and everyone started running into the woods," she said. It is not clear what the target was, and in this case the train was not damaged, but with further explosions lighting up the night sky, Anastasiia decided not to linger, continuing her journey on foot before being picked up by her parents. "I'm not going to travel by train anymore," she says. Anastassia's journey was more dramatic than most, but delays – some brief, others that last for hours – are now commonplace. Since Russian drones first started attacking moving passenger trains towards the end of 2025, the routine for passengers has become increasingly familiar: leave the train, scroll Telegram channels for updates on drone and missile launches, send messages to warn friends and family that the train is delayed. Anastasiia says she will no longer travel on Ukraine's railways after a drone strike near her train last month For a railway company proud of its record for punctuality, this year's disrupted schedule is posing a major challenge. "We used to say that that during times of war we performed better than some railways in Europe in regular times,"the head of rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told us. "But now the life of our passengers and crew members is the utmost priority." Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment. The dangers are very real. Attacks on Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply. Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been this year, according to statistics released by the company. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year. Confronting Russia's threat of Ukraine's railways is a game of cat and mouse, says Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, CEO of Ukrzaliznytsia "The latest wave of escalation and real war with railways is becoming extremely intense," said Pertsovskyi. "It's a combination of the deadly force of their shahed drones and precision that they achieve with cameras and mesh networks so they can hit moving targets." According to Pertsovskyi, some of Russia's most recent drones are equipped with AI tools and image recognition. Ukraine is understandably cagey about how it goes about confronting this increasingly sophisticated threat, but electronic methods to disrupt the drones' connectivity are high on the list. "Unfortunately, this is always a cat-and-mouse game," he said. Watch: Why a Russian strike on train near Ukraine-Poland border could mark an escalation Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents We were given rare access to an underground bunker in Kyiv, dubbed – appropriately enough – the "Iron Command Centre", where railway staff monitor threats in real time. On one huge video screen, colour-coded passenger and freight trains could be seen making their way along the arteries of Ukraine's vast railway network. We watched as a red icon representing a drone appeared to loiter over Kyiv, practically above our heads at one point. Each drone had a 100km (62-mile) circle around it. Any passenger trains inside the circle would already have been evacuated, with customers not allowed to reboard until the train was outside the circle and the drone was still moving away. "Our mission is not to let our train or our crew members be in that immediate attack area," Pertso

title: Carbon tracking tower put on Scotland's largest saltmarsh
description: It will track how much carbon is being taken out of the atmosphere by the saltmarsh on the Solway Firth.
body: The carbon tracking tower will give valuable data on how much carbon the saltmarsh is taking out of the atmosphere New technology has been installed to track how much carbon is being taken out of the atmosphere by Scotland's largest saltmarsh. The flux tower has been put in place at Caerlaverock on the Solway Firth. About 85% of UK saltmarshes have been lost since the mid-19th Century as land has been reclaimed from the sea for agriculture, development or coastal flood defences, degraded through pollution or eroded by rising sea levels. Corallie Hunt, coastal habitats adviser for NatureScot, said the installation of the first saltmarsh flux tower in Scotland marked an "important milestone". The study will help improve understanding of the importance of saltmarshes The project is a partnership between UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UKCEH), the Scottish government, NatureScot, and WWF-UK. "By measuring carbon exchange in real time, it will strengthen our understanding of the carbon storage potential of saltmarshes and the value of protecting and restoring these habitats," said Hunt. UKCEH wetland scientist Annette Burden said the Solway flux tower was the most northerly addition to a network around the UK coast. "The data collected will aid in understanding the role saltmarsh plays in climate mitigation, provide evidence for saltmarsh inclusion in the UK Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Inventory, which in turn will strengthen calls to safeguard and restore this valuable habitat," she said. What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland? In addition to supporting biodiversity and providing natural flood protection, the plants covering the marshes draw down carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and can also trap carbon-rich sediments in their roots and stems on the incoming tide. Tom Brook, ocean conservation specialist at WWF said: "The Solway is an extraordinary place for nature. "From thousands of migratory birds that depend on these wetlands to the rare natterjack toad, the saltmarsh supports an incredible variety of wildlife. "It's also working hard for people too – helping to absorb wave energy and reduce the impacts of flooding and storm surges. "The data gathered by the tower will help us better understand and champion the value of these remarkable coastal habitats." title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants feature
description: The regulator said Instagram had not fully assessed risks posed by its Instants feature prior to launching it.
body: Ofcom is investigating whether Meta breached its duties under the UK's online safety laws with the launch of its "Instants" feature on Instagram. The tool - allowing users to take and share an instant image with close friends, that disappears once viewed - was launched on Meta's photo-sharing app in May as "a new way to share photos in the moment". But the regulator said the social media giant had not properly assessed risks posed by the feature prior to launching it - something it is required to do under the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA). A Meta spokesperson said in a statement that it "takes its regulatory obligations under the Online Safety Act seriously". "We conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom about this feature on a number of occasions before launching it," they said. "We will of course co-operate with Ofcom during this investigation." Ofcom said its probe would examine whether Meta breached OSA duties by not carrying out "a suitable and sufficient illegal content risk assessment and children's risk assessment before the launch of Instants". Under the UK's sweeping online safety rules, platforms including Meta must carry out and update risk assessments to comply with a range of duties, including to tackle illegal content. They must also show how they prevent children permitted to use their services from encountering content deemed harmful for them. This spans material relating to pornography, or promoting self-harm or suicide - as "priority primary content" - alongside things like abusive, hateful or bullying content. "Our online safety laws are clear – significant changes to platforms must be risk assessed before they're launched," said Ofcom enforcement director George Lusty. "This is a vital step that tech firms must take to protect their users," he added. "You wouldn't launch a new car without testing it properly, and it's the same for online services." What the Online Safety Act is - and how to keep children safe online Instants rolled out to the app's users in May, external as a way for people to share spontaneous images - something that was once what the app was all about. Images shared with Instants can be viewed by those who have been selected as "close friends" by a user, or those who they follow and are followed back by. Meta says the feature has a range of built-in protections, including for younger users with Teen Accounts, including preventing screenshots, reshares or forwarding of Instants. But disappearing messages and images have been singled out previously as posing particular risks for child or teen users of some apps. "Safety by design must be built in, not bolted on, and today's investigation shows we'll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply," Lusty added. The feature is similar to tools used by platforms like Snapchat and WhatsApp, that allow people to send photos that disappear once viewed Ofcom's decision to launch an investigation into the platform comes as Meta, TikTok and X also seek to challenge the regulator's enforcement of the OSA through judicial review, external. All three companies have appeared in court this week, arguing they should not need to provide so much information in response to Ofcom's formal requests. Meta has separately also argued Ofcom should not be able to levy fines for breaches based on its global annual revenue. It also contends that its messaging and image-sharing apps should not have to face additional requirements under the OSA, such as tackling paid-for fraud ads. title: Nigeria mourns 32 killed as military plane crashes into swamp
description: President Bola Tinubu describes the crash as a "painful moment" for the military and the entire nation.
body: Some wreckage was recovered from the water Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 32 people. Authorities say the plane was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it came down in a swamp near a naval base on Monday morning. After reaching the site, the aircraft was found to be submerged under water, officials said. A resident told the BBC that clothes and shoes had been found at the site. Smoke could be seen rising from the area. Tinubu offered his deepest condolences for the 25 passengers and seven crew members on board and has ordered a full investigation. The president also ordered national flags to be flown at half-mast across the country as a mark of respect for those who died. "This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," Tinubu said. "Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten," he added. Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo earlier said he had been informed "of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today". He said "efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive" before subsequent confirmation that it had crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo state. He said search and rescue efforts were ongoing. The crashed plane, described as an ATR-42 aircraft, carries between 30 and 50 passengers, according to its manufacturers. Officials from Ondo state visited the site of the crash in a swamp Tinubu has ordered the Air Force to immediately begin a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to help prevent similar incidents in the future. The Nigerian Air Force plays a key role in the country's military operations, including efforts to tackle armed groups and insecurity in several parts of the country. The accident is one ​of the deadliest air disasters ​in ⁠Nigeria in recent years. In May 2021, Nigeria's army chief, Lt-Gen Ibrahim Attahiru, was killed in a plane crash alongside 10 other officers in the north-western state of Kaduna amid bad weather. In February of the same year, seven people died after a military plane crashed short of a runway in the capital Abuja. title: Zionism is racist, says Scottish Green co-leader Ross Greer
description: The comments have been described as "disgusting and dangerous" by the Scottish Conservatives.
body: Ross Greer's comments have been described as "disgusting and dangerous" by the Scottish Conservatives The co-leader of the Scottish Greens has described Zionism as racist, after the claim was adopted as Green Party policy south of the border. Ross Greer said, while he did not agree with all parts of a motion passed at the England and Wales Green Party conference, he considered the creation of Israel to have been "an act of racism". Some Jewish groups have called the Green Party motion an "attack on the Jewish community", and Israel's foreign ministry said it was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom". Senior Green figures have been divided on the issue, with the European Green Party seeking to "unequivocally distance" itself from the vote. The Scottish Greens are a separate entity from the Green Party of England and Wales, and set their own policies. I won't accept exclusion within Green Party, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism' Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion Zionism refers to the movement to create a Jewish state in the Middle East. The Green motion defined it as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state". It also backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine". In response, Jewish groups described Zionism as "anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it". Asked if he considered Zionism to be racism, Greer answered: "Yes." He told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast: "You cannot give superior rights in law to one ethnic or religious group. Everybody has to be treated equally before the law, and the reality right now is that that's not the case. "One group's superiority has got to the point where a genocide is being committed against another group. "I want Jews, Christians, Muslims, Israelis, Palestinians, everybody to live equally in safety, in peace." He added: "Jewish people deserve to live in safety, but the creation of the state of Israel was an act of ethnic cleansing. "It was an act of racism, and I don't understand how how people can say it wasn't." Zack Polanski, who leads the Green Party of England and Wales, did not participate in the conference vote Greer said his party agreed with some parts of the motion and disagreed with others - noting that he would not take a position on whether there should be a "two-state solution" in the Middle East. He also condemned "horrific war crimes" committed by Hamas against Israelis. Earlier this year, a UN commission of inquiry said Israel had deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the Gaza Strip, as well as war crimes in the occupied West Bank. Israel's foreign ministry denied the claims and described the report as a "libellous sham". Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay described Greer's comments as "disgusting and dangerous". He told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast: "The Scottish Greens are no longer hiding their view that they don't think Israel has a right to exist. "This anti-Israel obsession has been normalised. The Jewish community in Scotland are living in fear and being blamed for the actions of the Israeli government." First Minister John Swinney told BBC Scotland News on Monday that he did not agree with the Green Party motion. He said: "There are very well established definitions in law of what constitutes racism and I think we should stick by those definitions and not come up with definitions at party political conferences." Responding to the Green Party conference vote, the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council said: "Branding most British Jews and Jewish institutions 'racist' stokes anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed." The European Green Party, of which the Green Party for England and Wales is a member, has said it wanted to "unequivocally distance" itself from the motion. The umbrella body said it would "immediately demand clarity" from the party's leadership on how they would protect Jewish people and self-determination. Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, did not participate in the conference debate or vote on the motion. Polanski, who is Jewish, has said that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct". Four of the party's five MPs opposed the motion. Green MP Ellie Chowns told Radio 4's PM programme that she was "deeply saddened" that the motion had become Green Party policy in England and Wales. However, she disagreed it was antisemitic, saying it was underpinned by "principled opposition to the actions of the Israeli government". She noted that "less than 1%" of the party's more than 200,000 members had participated in the vote. title: Kenya confirms its first Ebola death as outbreak spreads
description: The patient has been living in DR Congo for the past seven years.
body: Kenya has confirmed its first case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years. Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in Nairobi. Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city. Tests conducted confirmed positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease. title: Man charged over Gosport migrant protest
description: Protesters held a demonstration after 149 migrants were brought to Gosport on Sunday.
body: Demonstrators staged a protest in Gosport on Sunday evening A man has been charged after a protest over migrant arrivals in a Hampshire town. The Home Office said 149 migrants were picked up on Sunday in a mid-Channel rescue operation by the RNLI, alongside a French vessel, and were brought ashore at Gosport. Flares were set off and there were scuffles with police during a stand-off involving about 150 anti-migrant demonstrators. Jamie Bennett has been charged with failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction. The 38-year-old, of Thyme Avenue in Whiteley, Fareham, has been bailed to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 26 November. Police made 12 arrests following the protest on Haslar Road, 11 men aged between 22 and 59, and a 57-year-old woman. Suspected offences included assaulting police officers, affray and racially aggravated public order. The remaining 10 men and one woman have been bailed pending further inquiries. Police said a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries but none were seriously hurt. Some demonstrators stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot". The Home Office said 149 migrants had been picked up in a mid-Channel rescue operation A 59-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of racially aggravated public order A 39-year-old man from Emsworth on suspicion of offences including criminal damage, attempted criminal damage and possession of a pyrotechnic article at a protest A 29-year-old man of no fixed address on suspicion of obstruction of a highway after ambulances were prevented from travelling along Clayhall Road A 42-year-old man from Fareham on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in a public place A 22-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of affray and racially aggravated public order A 56-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of assaulting a police officer A 57-year-old woman from Emsworth on suspicion of assaulting a police officer A 36-year-old man from Bognor Regis on suspicion of assaulting a police officer, failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction and failing to comply with the conditions of a dispersal order A 35-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of assault by beating of an emergency worker and failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction A 45-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of assaulting a police officer, criminal damage and being drunk and disorderly in a public place A 29-year-old man from Portsmouth on suspicion of assaulting a police officer and failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction The migrants were picked up in a rescue operation by the RNLI Five people were also issued with Section 35 dispersal notices. The migrants were brought into Gosport onboard an RNLI boat. They were then taken by coach to a processing centre in Kent. A Home Office spokesperson refused to explain why Gosport had been chosen on this occasion, saying they do not comment on "operational processes". Last month, more than 100 migrants landed at Eastney in Portsmouth leading to scuffles between police and demonstrators. title: The small African nation ready for Messi's big night
description: Benin are about to have their own moment in the limelight as they visit Argentina for Lionel Messi's final game.
body: Situated next to Nigeria, the small west African country of Benin is generally used to being left in the shadows of its footballing powerhouse neighbour. But the Cheetahs are about to have their own moment in the limelight. On Tuesday (Wednesday 00:00 BST), Benin face Argentina in Buenos Aires for what will be Lionel Messi's final international match. A specially designed Argentina kit has been created to mark the occasion - and the shirt worn by Messi could go on to become one of the most expensive ever. The historic fixture will see the World Cup runners-up take on players who ply their trade in Finland, Switzerland's second tier and the South African Premiership. One of Benin's best-known players is their captain, Steve Mounie. The forward plays for German Bundesliga side FC Augsburg, but will also be known to Huddersfield Town fans having played for the club between 2017-2020. He's been a regular with the national side for more than a decade but says he's never played a game for them outside of Africa. "When the coach called me and told me about this game. We didn't know it was going to be the last game of Leo Messi," Mounie told BBC Sport. "It was like the cherry on top of the cake. It adds some more values to this big event for Benin, and it's going to be a big event for the world of football." However, injury means Mounie will play no part in the game. Instead of staying at home recovering, however, he says this was not a moment he could miss out on. "I cannot play," he said. "I just came to join the team, to support the team. And, I need to be honest with this because football is my passion. I came for myself. "I even paid for my own ticket to come here. "I would prefer to be on the bench, but if they tell me that I need to be in the stand, I will be in the stand. There is no problem, but I want to see the game from a pitch view." The former Premier League striker says, while the result of the friendly is largely inconsequential, those players who are selected will know it's a great chance to enhance their reputations and that of Beninese football. "We are a team that is very disciplined," said Mounie. "We have a lot of young talent in the team right now that have good technical skills. We are always willing to go forward. We play pressing football, but when we cannot, we stick together and we fight. "We are a team like a family, And I think we can relate to this Argentina team because they feel like they are like a family too, which Messi is a father to." This video can not be played Benin forward Steve Mounie on whether his side will be fighting over Lionel Messi's shirt Shops in Buenos Aires are ready for Lionel Messi's last Argentina game Argentina warmed up for the fixture against Benin by defeating fellow west African side Burkina Faso 7-0. Many will be predicting a similar scoreline this game - and it's unlikely Messi will play the full 90 minutes. A more likely scenario is that, with Argentina a few goals to the good, Messi will be substituted in the second half, allowing the sold-out crowd at Estadio Monumental to say farewell to their country's greatest sports star. Once the final whistle does go - don't be surprised if there's a rush towards the World Cup-winning captain. "To get hold of a Messi match-worn shirt is incredibly tough because everybody knows how valuable they are," said Doug Bierton, founder of Classic Football Shirts. "So every player on the pitch is looking to swap with him. It's the first time a legend has bowed out with a special edition shirt." Bierton, whose private collection of iconic football shirts reaches into the thousands, says the last match-worn Messi shirt would be collector's dream. He ranks it in the same category as Diego Maradona's shirt worn when he scored his 'Hand of God' goal against England at the 1986 World Cup. A jersey which sold for £7.1m in an auction in May 2022. Another item considered in that realm is Zinedine Zidane's shirt from the last time he played for France - which ended in a red card after being sent off for headbutting Italy's Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final. The fact Messi's shirt is being worn in a friendly - yet considered in such high regard - is perhaps testament to the belief he is the greatest footballer ever. So Bierton predicts it won't be just Benin players who will be after the jersey. "I'm sure some of his team-mates will be too, he's good friends with [Rodrigo] De Paul," he said. "He'll probably be after it as well. Does he get a gift, a retirement present? "The kit man will be after it. Who knows? I'm literally going to watch the match just to see who he swaps shirts with." title: Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line
description: In rare access to Taiz, the BBC World Service speaks to children, teachers and families affected by the war.
body: Rafeef says the journey to school terrifies her, but she is determined to keep going Every morning at 6am, 10-year-old Rafeef and her younger brother get ready for school, putting on their cream and brown uniforms. She always looks forward to seeing her friends and learning about everything from maths to Arabic and Islamic studies. She can't wait to start studying English next year. But for Rafeef, the journey to school involves far greater risks than crossing roads or missing the bus. Her school in Taiz, south-western Yemen, stands on a mountain at the edge of a valley known as no-man's land - a heavily contested front line in the civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis. On one side of the school is government-held territory, on the other are Houthi sniper positions. Rafeef's home is further down the mountain. Every time she goes to school, she has to walk uphill with her back towards the snipers. "I'm afraid," she says. Rafeef's school is overlooked by Houthi positions on the mountains beyond the valley According to Unicef, roughly 3.2 million children in Yemen were out of school even before the war escalated last month. It says thousands of children have been killed or maimed since the war began in 2014, while thousands more have been recruited by armed groups on both sides. Yet despite the risks, Rafeef says she does not want to stop going because she loves seeing her friends and it is her only chance to be with them. She begins naming the children in her classroom. Going to school is the only time Rafeef's parents let her go outside. They say they are keen for her to get an education and have the chance of a better life. Rafeef hopes to become a doctor. Rafeef's family moved to Taiz from the coastal city of Hudaydah nine years ago, seeking safety when Houthis took control there. But Taiz has also endured fighting. Rafeef says that two years ago there was a mortar attack outside her new home. "Everyone was out except for me and my brother. Then a mortar came out of nowhere… shrapnel blew through the door and into the house." Her arm was broken and there is still a scar where she was hit. And in recent days the conflict has intensified. On Sunday the Houthis cut off a vital supply route linking Taiz to Aden, which meant they were able to effectively encircle Taiz. Control of that route has kept shifting. Residents have told the BBC they are afraid the Houthis could seize the city at any moment. Government forces have made gains in other areas this week, they say, retaking control of strategic points on the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a key shipping chokepoint - and launching an offensive to try to regain control of the capital, Sanaa. Who are the Houthis and what do they want? Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway Homes in Taiz are mostly scattered across the slopes, but many have been abandoned by families fleeing the fighting. Twice, we try to visit the neighbourhood where Rafeef and her family live, but a community leader advises us it is too dangerous. On the first occasion, residents of the neighbourhood tell us that three people have been shot by snipers. On the second, we are told of another shooting. At Rafeef's school, one of the teachers, Abdel Raqeeb al-Obaidi, 45, takes us on to the rooftop to show us what he says are Houthi military camps, barracks and sniper positions in the mountains. Standing on the rooftop, a Yemeni security adviser accompanying us suddenly tells us to go back inside. We are visible from these positions and could be shot, he says. Abdel Raqeeb laughs, acknowledging the danger. He says the school has been fired on before. "The situation may explode at any moment while we are sitting in class or sleeping or we are in school or we are out on the street. We do not know how our future is and how tomorrow is." For Abdel Raqeeb, the risk has become routine. His familiarity with it is unsettling. Taiz has long been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from the capital Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen. Seizing Taiz would give the Houthis full control over the country's north. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons. Sometimes civilians are collateral damage in the fighting. Later that evening, we get a call from a hospital about a five minute drive away from the school. Two children have been badly injured by a mortar strike. When we arrive at Al-Rawdah Hospital, we see a nurse standing outside the intensive care unit, holding a tiny pair of beige, rubber sandals that are splattered with blood. They belonged to Ahmed, a three-year-old boy who we learn was killed when a mortar struck a mechanic's shop in the city. The shoes a three-year-old boy, Ahmed, was wearing when he was hit by a mortar When I ask about the shoes, the nurse, Ikram Shamsan, begins to cry. "What did this child or his family ever do wrong?" she asks. Ahmed was killed when a piece of shrapnel pierced his heart, entering through his back. The boy had been with his father, who was getting his motorcycle tyre pumped up at the mechanic's shop. The father was unharmed. A doctor tells us the father had intended to leave his son at home, but the boy cried because he wanted to come too. As he takes his son's body from the hospital, the father asks how he will face the boy's mother. Completing a simple errand turned into the worst day of their lives. Amjad's mother does not know if he will survive after he was injured by shrapnel Another boy, 11-year-old Amjad, was also at the mechanic's shop. He and his brother worked there with their uncle, sending money to their family in their home village

title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
description: The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, the insurance trade body, the ABI said.
body: A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters. The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said. Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents. The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said. There was £1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the £1.18bn detected the previous year. At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024. Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters are targeting much bigger payouts. "As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them." Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers." He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg". One of the most notable fraudsters identified by the ABI last year was a man found by IFED to have fabricated reports of stolen high-value Lego sets, external. The man's scam claims to Axa Insurance during 2021 and 2022 also included other high-value items such as MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles and fishing equipment, IFED said. In 2023, IFED said it found collectible Lego sets matching the ones claimed to have been stolen displayed in the man's living room during a search. Alongside his prison sentence handed down last year, he was also ordered to repay the £14,000 he had claimed. Other cases highlighted by the ABI included a man jailed for 20 months for manipulating women he met on dating sites into participating in staged car crashes, and a man sentenced to four and a half years for submitting over £300,000 worth of fraudulent travel medical emergency claims. In general, the ABI said motor insurance remained the area where insurers identified the most fraudulent cases, accounting for 55% of all scam claims. Meanwhile, the ABI's figures found that exaggerated loss remains the most common type of insurance fraud, with 26,900 cases identified. This is when someone deliberately attempts to increase the cost of a claim beyond its true value, the ABI said. title: LIV Golf secures potential $300m investment
description: LIV Golf secures a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to emerge from restructuring before the 2027 season.
body: LIV Golf was founded in 2021, with its first season taking place the following year LIV Golf has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season. The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, starting a court-supervised "restructuring process" that they hope to complete in early 2027. It is unclear how much of the $300m LIV requires to start next year's schedule and which players will start the season. The competition's participants are owed at least $45m (£33m) and have the option to leave. However the agreement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until 25 October. BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf. League insiders see the committed investment as a "significant" step forward in the court-supervised restructuring process. "Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf's emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season," said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement. Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0 The credit firm, which provides financing to middle-market companies, said the funding would support the next phase of LIV Golf, under which players would become equity owners of both the league and its teams. The financing remains subject to bankruptcy court approval and customary conditions. "This investment is an important step forward for LIV Golf," said LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil in a statement. "We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers." Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), with major winners including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money. However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early. Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m). DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m). The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m). A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts. Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business. PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process. title: Wet races and why future of F1 engines appears to be V8 turbos - Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
body: The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia began in wet conditions, though not at the original start time because visibility was considered to be too poor Red Bull's Max Verstappen won his first race of the season in a dramatic rain-affected Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Kimi Antonelli finished second in the Mercedes and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who fought his way back to the front after an incorrect tyre choice at the start, completed the podium. Antonelli extended his lead in the championship to 84 points, after team-mate George Russell retired with an engine failure. This weekend, it's the Singapore Grand Prix - Formula 1's original night race. Before the race at Marina Bay, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions. Do we miss out on exciting wet-weather racing because an overly cautious approach is applied when rain occurs prior to the start of the race? We are watching the best drivers in the world, who have wet tyres, but it seems when it rains prior to the start of a race, the action gets under way too late. - Sam This question comes up a lot whenever there is a wet race, but in this specific situation the delay in starting the race was not caused by any conservatism when it comes to wet running. The cars were sent out on formation laps when the track was still pretty wet on Sunday in Malaysia, but then a bug in the wet-weather engine settings provided to the teams by the FIA affected a number of cars, including those of Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton on the front row. That meant the formation laps had to be aborted, and a new code written and given to the teams to upload to ensure that did not happen again. It just so happened that in the intervening 25 minutes, there had been no more rain, so the track was pretty dry by the time the race started. Although it has to be said that it took a safety car on lap nine before the drivers who had started on treaded intermediate tyres came in for slicks. On a generic level, there is no fundamental objection in F1 to racing in the wet - most of the drivers enjoy it. But there is now a collective agreement that they will not race when they can't see where they are going. So races are not started when that is the case - as it was at the original start time in Malaysia. But if you cast your mind back to Brazil in 2024, and Verstappen's brilliant drive from 17th on the grid to victory, that was run in wet conditions. F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz After the Bahrain Grand Prix, Lewis Hamilton said that, had he started on the intermediate tyres, he could have won the race. Given the race data and his pace, do you think that's a realistic claim had Ferrari put him on the inters at the start? - Michael The truth is that Hamilton - and anyone else - will never know, because there was no direct comparison between his pace and Max Verstappen's in similar conditions. In the first few laps, Hamilton was on slicks and Verstappen on intermediates. When Verstappen switched to slicks, Hamilton's tyres were much older. On the very few laps when Hamilton was in clear air before he caught Isack Hadjar, his pace when generally nowhere near Verstappen's but then his tyres were nine laps older, so you would not expect it to be. And then once he finally passed Hadjar, there were only three laps to go. On one of them, Hamilton was within 0.1secs of Verstappen, on the other two he was 0.5secs and 1.2secs off. But how much were either of them pushing? What we can say is that Verstappen looked imperious all weekend, and it was probably going to be difficult for anyone to beat him - even Hamilton, who, it's worth saying, on Saturday was not sounding that confident of challenging him. But it's just a whole load of ifs, buts and maybes, isn't it? This video can not be played Hamilton's 'pretty incredible comeback' at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia Malaysia, true to form, brought a great race, chaos and weather. It was sold out. Fans have loved it, missed it, drivers liked the track. We know why it dropped off the calendar but what would it take to come back permanently? - Nick Malaysia dropped off the calendar because the government there was no longer willing to pay the rights fee, feeling that the expense did not justify the return. It returned only because the Crown Prince of Bahrain was keen to stage his race, F1 was happy to accommodate him, and he managed to strike a deal with the Malaysian government. There's no doubt the race was a success. It had a record crowd of 261,000 this year, more than double the previous largest weekend attendance of 126,690, reflecting F1's growth around the world. If Malaysia was keen on returning to the calendar on a more permanent basis, there is no reason why F1 would not listen to them. But whether that led to a deal would depend on whether one could be struck that satisfied both parties. This video can not be played Mercedes better 'watch out - Verstappen 'imperious' in Bahrain GP win With Red Bull running their own powertrains, what part does Ford play? - John Max Verstappen's victory in Malaysia on Sunday was not only a landmark because it was Red Bull's first of the season - it was also their first as a power-unit manufacturer. Red Bull Powertrains was set up specifically to make an engine for the new 2026 regulations, so the team could be in control of their own destiny following Honda's official withdrawal from F1 at the end of 2021. Ford came on board as a partner early on, and this is much more than simply a badging deal in return for finance/sponsorship money. Team principal Laurent Mekies said on Monday: "Ford has been with us on this project since pretty much the very beginning. "They are a key strategic partner for us on these operations. They are helping us on a number of topics. "Specifically, to give you a few examples, they are manufacturing some of the key elements

title: Captain apologises for gloating over military service exemption
description: Lee Gi-hyuk apologises for gloating about avoiding South Korea's mandatory military service by captaining his country to the football gold medal at the Asian Games.
body: Lee Gi-hyuk plays his club football for Gangwon FC South Korea captain Lee Gi-hyuk has apologised for gloating about avoiding mandatory military service after winning gold at the Asian Games. His side beat hosts Japan 1-0 in the final and, afterwards, Lee held up his gold medal and triumphantly announced he was "not going to the military". In a social media post reported by local media,, external the 26-year-old later said he was "deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us". South Korean males are, in most circumstances, required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of active military service before the age of 28. However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month. Golfer Tom Kim also avoided military service by winning gold at the Asian Games. Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier. "As an adult I should have thought carefully before speaking," added Lee, who was one of the overage players in his country's Under-23 squad and plays for Gangwon FC in South Korea's K League. "I deeply regret having spoken so carelessly, and I will continue to reflect on my actions. "I sincerely apologise to all the fans who have supported us wholeheartedly and who are doing their utmost to fulfil their military duty." title: NFL suspends two officials for player incidents
description: The NFL suspends officials Jeff Seeman and Adrian Hill for instances of unprofessional conduct towards a player.
body: Jeff Seeman was officiating in a fixture between the Arizona Cardinals and the New York Giants The NFL has suspended two officials for instances of unprofessional conduct towards a player. Line judge Jeff Seeman has been suspended for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one fixture following the incidents on Sunday. Seeman was caught on camera seeming to curse at Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride, whose side lost 36-24 away to the New York Giants. McBride felt he had been interfered with by Giants cornerback Dru Phillips from a pass from Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett that fell incomplete. Having been hit, McBride complained to Seeman, who appeared to yell a profanity at McBride. "It's a tough one for me. You hate to see it for obvious reasons. I don't need to go further than that, but I do want to give the man a little bit of grace too," Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur said Monday. "I know Jeff. He's a good man. It's unfortunate it happened. It can't happen obviously and I'll leave it at that." Hill's incident involved linebacker Eric Wilson, who featured for Minnesota Vikings as they defeated the visiting Miami Dolphins 15-10. Wilson was pushed into Hill by Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon II midway through the first quarter after a play was whistled dead because of a Minnesota penalty. This video can not be played When the NFL meets the hurdles... As Wilson tried to help Hill up, the official jumped up while pointing and shouting at Wilson to move away. "That was funny, honestly," Wilson told reporters after the match. "I ended up apologising to him and explained the situation. He was cool about it. He understood what was going on. He just said he didn't want us fighting." In Monday night's fixture, the Atlanta Falcons won 45-24 on the road at the New Orleans Saints. Bijan Robinson scored an early touchdown following a 53-yard run, while fellow running back Brian Robinson Jr. also reached the end zone three times. The Falcons now sit second in NFC South, following two opening defeats with consecutive victories, while the Saints are third with a 1-3 record. title: UK oil refinery broke toxic pollution limits dozens of times, documents reveal
description: Pollution was spilled into local rivers and protected sites, documents shared with the BBC suggest.
body: Stanlow oil refinery in Cheshire is the second largest in the UK One of the UK's biggest oil refineries spilled pollution into local rivers and the Mersey Estuary on dozens of occasions in 2023 and 2024, documents shared exclusively with the BBC suggest. EET Fuels, formerly known as Essar, which runs Stanlow refinery, pleaded guilty this year to 12 charges of breaching environmental law between 2018 and 2020. But documents obtained by investigative journalists from SourceMaterial describe other breaches from the refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, with toxic chemicals and oil regularly spilled into the waterways and even groundwater. EET Fuels said it "takes its environmental responsibilities extremely seriously". The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed that it is investigating the breaches. The Stanlow oil refinery is one of only four remaining refineries in the UK and processes 10 million tonnes of crude oil each year - producing around 18% of the country's fuel for road transport like cars and trucks. EET Fuels, which bought the refinery from Shell in 2011 for £842m, holds a permit to operate the site. This says it can discharge controlled amounts of oil and chemicals into the air and waterways. However, it must make efforts to limit pollution to the environment and harm to humans. But reports from the EA into activities at the refinery, uncovered by environmental journalists SourceMaterial, show that in 2023 and 2024 the permitted levels for chemical releases were exceeded hundreds of times. The regulator has determined this meant EET Fuels broke its permit conditions 58 times over the two-year period - which could amount to an illegal offence. The documents show the spills included toxic chemicals such as cyanide, benzene, and heavy oils - into the air and local waterways like Thornton Brook and the River Gowy which connect onto the River Mersey Estuary. The Estuary is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and home to endangered species including dolphins and a breeding ground for rare birds. "Species like dunlin, blacktail, godwit and red shank will travel all around the world to feed and roost in the land around the River Mersey," explained Charlotte Harris, chief executive of Cheshire Wildlife Trust. Harris said this has only been possible because organisations, including the Wildlife Trusts, have undertaken years of pollution clean up from legacy industry in the area. "We've seen the Atlantic salmon return to the river and also the critically endangered European eel makes its way up the Mersey and into the River Gowy to breed each year as well," she said. The Mersey Estuary hosts the largest group of protected Dunlins in the UK EA documents detail how pollutants like sulphur dioxide were released into the air at seven times permitted levels, cyanide into waterways like the Gowy at more than eight times permitted levels, and oil at more than thirteen times the allowed levels. In one incident in July 2023, the company breached its permit after rainwater containing oil leaked from the site - the EA classed the event as "significant". In its report it said there were a "significant number" of complaints from locals about the smell and further investigations indicated the oil had contaminated groundwater supplies. EET Fuels told the BBC that the oil lost was on a "low scale" and "was strictly localised to two boreholes, all well within the Stanlow site itself". A year later on 12 September 2024, another EA report says that oil was spilled again from the site. Over a 36-hour period more than a tonne of oil was released into Thornton Brook and spread to the Mersey Estuary. EET Fuels reported the incident to the authorities, but it took nearly two weeks for the company to provide an estimate of how much oil was spilled - another breach of the regulations which requires this within 24 hours. An emergency response team was organised including regulators the EA and Natural England, local port authorities and the Fisheries Authority - according to meeting documents. Natural England (NE), which regulates SSSIs, said in one meeting: "What has gone in there is going to have some impact on the vegetation and salt marsh and there is probably still a risk of ingestion by birds." A drone was sent up to survey the scale of the damage which revealed oil had spread for more than a mile down the river and "there was brown discolouration around the reedbed". The footage showed wading birds - including the red-listed Dunlin - in the area. "Where we have chemical pollution the impact isn't just localised. When it enters the river system, that system is highly dynamic and high energy, which means that pollution spreads far and wide really, really quickly," said Harris. Cockle beds were temporarily closed following the 2024 spill A floating barrier was deployed to try and contain the spill. The regulators decided that because the site was not easily reachable, the public health risk was low, but a decision was made to close local cockle beds in the Estuary while the water quality was tested by the Food Standards Agency (FSA). The beds were given the all clear, but were closed for five weeks whilst testing took place. Mark Taylor, CEO of the Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority North West, told the BBC: "The incident led to a delay in the fishers being able to derive an income from the bed". He added that they were able to make up this income later in the season. The incident was later categorised by the EA as a "minor" breach of the company's permit. EET Fuels told the BBC in a statement: "Selectively chosen, historical permit exceedances from prior years in no way represent the current operational status, improving environmental performance, or governance of the refinery today." title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
description: Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.
body: OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June and said it had added more precautions to its training environments. The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox. "We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said. Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation. An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind. Asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake. "In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said, in response to a question by the committee on why it had not dialled the mobile numbers of government ministers. "The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties but it's not good enough." Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents. "Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party." OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators who are looking at AI and its impact on Australia. The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI". Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and an alarm was triggered if they interact with the internet in a way they were not meant to. This meant that it had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours. The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations". "We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well." Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI. "We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee. The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could means artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard. "In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association. title: Ten NHS trusts referred over monitoring consent
description: Infrared technology is used in patients' bedrooms and can monitor their breathing and pulse.
body: Oxevision uses infrared sensors and cameras to monitor patients while they are in their bedrooms Ten mental health trusts have been reported to the health regulator after problems with patient consent procedures when monitoring patients using camera technology. The issue emerged during the latest hearings of the Lampard Inquiry, which is examining the deaths of more than 2,000 people who spent time in mental health units in Essex between 2000 and the end of 2023. The infrared technology is used in patients' bedrooms and can monitor breathing and pulse without staff having to enter the room. NHS England told the inquiry it had passed information to the Care Quality Commission (CQC) after reviewing the use of digital monitoring systems, including Oxevision. Gareth Harry from NHS England told the inquiry their oversight was not 'ineffective' Baroness Lampard has said she would introduce interim recommendations on the introduction of some technology if she believed there was a "risk to patient safety". The inquiry heard NHS England first became aware of safety concerns linked to Oxevision in 2021. Giving evidence, Gareth Harry, NHS England's National Delivery Director for Mental Health, Learning Disability and Autism, said concerns had been raised about consent, patient observations and human rights. The inquiry was shown an internal NHS England email from 2022 in which one staff member said they had been aware of trusts where patients were "not being given the choice to refuse being filmed". In 2023, NHS England wrote to mental health trusts saying monitoring technology should not be introduced as a blanket approach and decisions should be made for each patient individually. It said if possible, patients should be involved in those decisions. Harry said NHS England later reviewed practice after concerns were raised by campaign group Stop Oxevision, external. The inquiry heard that review found 10 mental health trusts were "not operating their consent mechanisms in line with the digital principles". The trusts that have been referred to the regulator have not been named. Harry said NHS England wrote to the CQC on 2 October and shared the findings with inspection teams. Bereaved families - pictured outside a previous evidence session - have been raising concerns about the monitoring technology What is the Lampard Inquiry and what could it change? Lampard Inquiry: Five things we've learned so far Lawyers representing bereaved families questioned why it had taken several years for NHS England to act after concerns were first raised. Harry said day-to-day responsibility for following the guidance sat with individual trusts rather than NHS England. Counsel to the inquiry Teniola Onabanjo asked Harry if NHS England recognised that the enthusiasm for innovation might "outpace" the scrutiny of consent and ethics when it comes to camera technology. "I would expect every provider of mental health services to have their values and behaviours driven by a human rights approach to mental healthcare," Harry said. A CQC spokesperson told the BBC: "Providers have a responsibility to offer safe, high-quality care in line with relevant guidelines. "CQC considers all information of concern that is shared with us, and should a provider fall short we can and do take action." The regulator is due to give evidence to the Lampard Inquiry on 7 October. Giving evidence in July, Laura Cozens, from LIO Health, the company behind Oxevision, said it was important the technology was properly explained to patients. She also said it had helped prevent serious incidents, including falls on a dementia ward. The current hearings are expected to continue until 15 October, with a further hearing for families on 20 October. Baroness Lampard has said she could issue interim recommendations if urgent patient safety concerns are identified before the inquiry's final report, which is due in 2028. title: Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends
description: Lionel Messi's Argentina career will end in a friendly against Benin. BBC Sport looks at what next for the 39-year-old?
body: Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina. On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goal scorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close - announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give. Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed. His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to. In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it. Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game. Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game. Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give' How Messi's decade of dominance almost never happened Lionel Messi captained Argentina to World Cup glory in 2022 Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls. And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner. A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking. An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything. The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April. CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD. Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner. The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention. For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo". The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him. In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season. A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga. There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan. Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed. It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have. Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona. A rivalry that changed football Goals, records, tears ... Messi's most iconic moments Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup. If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof. He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams. Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day. This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others. Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business. His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017. The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025. MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection. In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ángel Di María's property agency handling the sales. He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels. title: Irish budget to tackle childcare and energy costs
description: The threshold at which people start paying the higher income tax rate is also expected to increase.
body: The Irish government is expected to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs when it delivers its budget later. The threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax is also expected to be increased from its current level of €44,000 (£37,000). The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said the budget has to be about "trying to ease the pressure on families and households". The broad shape of the budget was set out in the Summer Economic Statement, external, promising tax measures worth €1.5bn (£1.27bn) and extra spending of €7bn (£5.92bn). Government party leaders, including the taoiseach, are expected to sign off on the budget Much of that additional spending is "standstill" funding to cover the rising costs of current services. Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services. Figures released last week showed the country is expected to run a surplus of €6.9bn (£5.84bn) this year, lower than the €9.2bn (£7.79bn) forecast in April. That smaller forecast surplus reflects the introduction of fuel supports and additional spending to cover budget overspends, particularly in health. Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments. A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has criticised the government for not saving more. Other measures expected to be announced on Tuesday are a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK ISA. A proposal for a "culture card" for teenagers, to spend on events like concerts, is also set to be announced though the value and eligibility are unclear.
