title: Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
description: In the internet age, medium-sized retail hubs are looking for new ways to survive and thrive.
body: Keith Ely remembers the Brunel Centre's heyday but is looking to the future The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide. "It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973. Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw. Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling. Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left. That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year. But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space. "It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me." The Debenhams store in the Grafton Centre in Cambridge closed in 2021 In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema. There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre. This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country. So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls? "There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre. "The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet." Before the Brunel Shopping Centre was built in the 1970s, people in Bletchley would travel to Aylesbury or Bedford to shop The centre initially had little natural light, before the roof was replaced with glass In 2021 Milton Keynes City Council was awarded £22.7m from the government's Town Deal Fund to redevelop the site Boots Opticians, the last remaining store in the centre, is already closed on Wednesdays Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE, external found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres. Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres. Dr Kardi Somerfield says centres that have leisure businesses can "extend the day" and attract customers into the evening "It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton. Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds. Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops. "The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open." The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses. Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing. Characters from TV show The Flintstones were at the opening of the Weston Favell Shopping Centre in 1974 But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down. Market Walk in Northampton is to become a leisure and entertainment space. "Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use. This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton. Footfall – the number of customers entering the building – has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg. "We are still relevant today," he says. "Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got." What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities. Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible. Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store. Silhouette Youth Theatre currently holds sessions in the Emmanuel Church, inside Weston Favell Shopping Centre George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility. "We've had it before where people are like 'Oh, what's this? We don't know what this is.' "That is how we can get other people to join us." Do you have a story suggestion? Contact us below. title: Banks still refusing credit cards, watchdog says
description: Applications are being denied despite a change to make it easier, Jersey Consumer Council says.
body: The Government of Jersey said whether credit cards were offered to islanders "remains a commercial decision" Islanders are still struggling to get credit cards despite personal data changes to make it easier to apply for one, a consumer council has said. The changes which came into force on 30 July meant the government could securely share personal data with UK credit reference agencies, which had been seen as the main barrier to successful applications. However, the Jersey Consumer Council said several providers had still refused applications and called for the government to work closer with businesses and banks. A spokesperson for Jersey's government said it had "engaged with providers throughout this process" and whether products were offered in the island "remains a commercial decision". Carl Walker from the Jersey Consumer Council said credit card companies may need convincing to bring their business back Carl Walker, from Jersey Consumer Council, said credit card companies would need to be reminded of the change which had allowed more information to be shared. "The last time they were involved... Jersey was slamming the door shut, so they have switched off and turned their attention elsewhere," he said. "We're pushing the government to write them an official letter to say this piece of legislation has now changed, Jersey's now open for business... and then leave it up to them whether they decide they to come back or not." More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey A spokesperson said the government had "successfully delivered a project to share islanders' data with credit reference agencies". "This was a key issue identified by the industry as an obstacle to providing credit cards in Jersey," they said. "It remains a commercial decision for providers to decide whether to offer their products or services, including credit cards, in Jersey. "The government has engaged with providers throughout this process... and will continue to do so." Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: 'Life-saving' charity for mums faces closing support
description: The charity recently lost out on a bid for funding and now might have to close its waiting list.
body: Sarah N'Guio said the charity saved her life after her mental health plummeted following a traumatic birth A "life-saving" charity that supports new mothers may have to close its waiting list if urgent funding cannot be raised. Frome Birth Talk provided counselling to more than 155 mothers in 2026, but charity chiefs warn they will have to cut back on support unless they can raise £10,000 by Sunday. Sarah N'Guio received counselling from the charity a year after giving birth and said it saved her life, adding: "Without them, I probably would have lost my children and lost my life." Suzy Cristinacce, charity director, said: "More and more people are suffering from mental health problems and the charity sector is helping fill the gaps but the pot is getting smaller and smaller." Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86 Bridge replacement delayed due to summer heatwaves 'Devious' scout leader jailed over child sex abuse After a traumatic birth where she nearly died, N'Guio's mental health plummeted. "I was spiralling, had imposter syndrome, postpartum depression and constantly felt under attack,"she told BBC Radio Somerset. "I felt people were plotting against me and that was when I decided to ask for help. "The charity held me, allowed me to let go of my worries and fears and gave me space to make sense of things," she said. The Royal College of Midwives reports that about one in four new mums will face a mental health issue after giving birth. Cristinacce said the charity's recent applications for funding have been rejected Cristinacce said about 50% of the charity's money is generated from grant funding. "I don't know what has happened, but I'm applying for grants, the feedback is that our application is very strong but the grants aren't coming in," Cristinacce said. She added that they have set up a crowdfunding site that will be open until Sunday. A spokesperson for the Royal United Hospitals (RUH) Bath said other support is available for women in the area. They also said an NHS pathway includes a referral into the RUH perinatal mental health team. NHS England has been approached for comment. Follow BBC Somerset on Facebook, external and X, external. title: Teen found dead in ditch 'discarded', family say
description: A coroner has warned of a "significant risk of future deaths".
body: Alan Hirst died in February after falling from his bike into floodwater in Herefordshire A grieving father says he felt his son was "discarded" by police after he went missing in floodwater. Alan Hirst, 19, was cycling home to Adforton, Herefordshire, in February when it is believed he fell from his bike on the flooded A4110 and suffered a cardiac arrest when he entered the water. His family have raised concerns about the police search, with his father Steve telling the BBC: "It was like he was just discarded." A coroner's report into Alan's death said a shortage of specialist search officers, external meant key decisions were not reviewed. In response, West Mercia Police said it was training more officers, with an increase expected in the coming months. Alan's mother Hayley described her son as "very charismatic" with energy levels that were "off the Richter scale". "You knew when he was in the room because it just lit up," she said. Death of girl, 11, 'unexplained' after body found Hauliers raise prices amid soaring fuel costs Couple lived next door to dead body for six weeks Alan, originally from Blackpool, would normally come home late in the evening, but his family initially went to bed on 5 February without realising he had not returned. His mother said she knew something was wrong the following day when the family came together after finishing work. Alan's body was eventually found in a ditch along the A4110, the road he had been travelling along when he disappeared, on 8 February. "You can't put it into words how hopeless you feel when you're searching," Hayley said. "And then you find out they were under your nose the whole time in dirty ditch water that whole time. It's heart breaking." Hayley, Alan's mum, said she felt "hopeless" searching for her son The inquest heard police knew Alan's last mobile phone activity, at about 23:15 to 23:30 GMT, had been around the A4110. However, a Police Search Adviser (PolSA) decided not to search the floodwater on safety grounds and there was no PolSA on duty the following day to review that decision. When the road was deemed safe enough for officers to search Alan's body was found within 20 minutes. Police decided not to search the A4110 because it was not safe, according to the PolSA Hayley said: "And that's what makes me so angry because that's the bit that could have been avoided." She said the PolSA told the inquest the location information from Alan's phone "might not be that accurate". "It just felt like one excuse after another," she said. In a prevention of future deaths report James Bennett, a coroner for Herefordshire, said the inability for police forces to provide round-the-clock specialist search officers was being impeded by a lack of training provision. "In my opinion unless action is taken to address the above concerns then there is a significant risk of future deaths," he added. Supt Stuart Bill, from West Mercia Police, said the force's thoughts were with Alan's family and PolSAs played an "important role" in searches for missing people. He said there was no requirement for forces to have a dedicated 24/7 PolSA capability, but West Mercia Police was working with the College of Policing to increase the availability of qualified search advisers. In a response to the coroner's report, the chief executive officer of the College of Policing said the "acknowledge the concerns raised by the coroner and will continue to work with police forces and national policing leads to ensure that capability, resilience and training arrangements remain appropriate to operational demand". Steve said he felt as though his son had been "discarded" by the police Hayley also criticised the decision not to send officers into the floodwater and other aspects of the search, including what they said was a lack of appeals for information - pointing to the fact the bike he had been riding was never found. She has also called for warning signs to be installed on the A4110 - which she described as a "high-risk road" - following her son's death. Herefordshire Council said it would continue to "review and prioritise highway and drainage improvements across the county based on evidence", adding roads could be affected by flooding during prolonged heavy rainfall. title: Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC
description: With better support, many babies may not have needed to go into care, File on 4 Investigates is told.
body: The number of children involved in care proceedings before they reach their first birthdays is at a persistently high level across England, according to experts who have published new figures. Data from the universities of Lancaster and Oxford indicates care proceedings for babies have risen by 64% over the past two decades, with one in 118 infants affected. The figures - up to 2024-25 - peaked during Covid, before dropping slightly and plateauing. While there are cases where it is unsafe for parents to continue contact with their children, experts have told File on 4 Investigates that many babies may not have needed to go into care if support had been in place. And, since very young children who go into care are more likely to be adopted than older children, there are also concerns from experts that some may have been permanently separated from their birth families unnecessarily. The BBC understands that new guidance for Family Court judges, to significantly reduce the number of short-notice care hearings - within hours or days of a baby being born - will be announced before the end of the year. Only up to a quarter of children's care proceedings are "clear-cut", involving serious harm or abuse, says Prof Karen Broadhurst According to latest government figures, 72% of adopted children in England went into care before turning one. Most of the adoptions, more than 90%, went ahead without parents' written consent - according to CoramBAAF, which represents those working in adoption and care. Courts overruled parents' wishes in just under half of those cases. The rest were classed as "unopposed", with many parents advised not to contest the adoptions, because they would be unlikely to succeed. Adoption should be pursued as a last resort, the government and adoption organisations have told us, because, while it offers stability, it also severs the legal relationship between the child and its birth family forever. Forced Adoption... is it happening today? Some babies taken into care before their first birthdays might have stayed at home if families had received the right support, experts tell File on 4 Investigates. Listen now on BBC Sounds or on BBC Radio 4 at 20:00 on Tuesday 6 October When a child is placed in care, birth parents are often allowed contact - but not always. Analysis of care proceedings suggests between a fifth and a quarter were "clear-cut", where a child had suffered serious harm or abuse, says Prof Karen Broadhurst from Lancaster University. But the majority were "grey area" cases of neglect by families with complex needs, she says, including drug and alcohol abuse, and housing issues, which might have improved with support. However, children's charity Coram - which, like CoramBAAF, is part of a wider network of specialist children's organisations - warns that if infants in care are not adopted, they would likely remain in care. And research shows that many children brought up in the care system experience much poorer outcomes in life than those outside it. Social workers are at the heart of the decision-making process as to whether a child should be taken into care. One of them, whom we are calling Tracy, describes the dilemmas she and her colleagues face daily, balancing giving families time to get through a crisis, against the risk of failing to intervene. She says she and her colleagues carry out wide-ranging and detailed assessments of parents - including judging whether there is enough past and present evidence of a future risk of harm to their children. In some cases, she says, they deal with families "riddled with abuse and neglect" where no-one is able to safely bring up a child. The stakes could not be higher. Extreme, high-profile cases, like those of Baby P in north London and Sara Sharif in Woking, Surrey, have served as a reminder of that. The British Association of Social Workers told us their members are doing their best against a backdrop of increasing caseloads and reduction in resources. With only about 10% of adoptions in England made with written consent from birth parents, according to CoramBAAF, this has led campaigners and some experts to describe the situation as modern-day "forced adoption". Jean with her daughter Tye before the adoption Broadhurst acknowledges that term is "politically loaded" and the modern care system is very different from the coercive practices that took place mainly between 1949 and 1976 - and for which the government recently apologised for cases in England. But she says it "is actually what's happening because parents do not agree". "They want to continue to be in contact with a child," she says. "Even parents who feel they couldn't look after a child at that point find it particularly brutal that they're going to have no contact, or very little contact, with that child until they're 18." One birth mother, Jean, tells us she never wanted to give up her daughter, Tye, for adoption - and describes it as "forced". Her local council says it followed a lawful process. Jean was separated from her daughter for 16 years, after Tye was taken into care at 11 weeks' old and then adopted at the age of two. Now, with Tye an adult, they are reunited. When she turned 18, having struggled with adoption and questions about her identity, Tye looked for her mother on social media. "I knew I had a mum somewhere and it wasn't the people I was growing up with," she says - describing her adoption as something that had left her "completely alone" without a "whole chunk of heritage". When Jean became pregnant, she was looking forward to being a mother. But she had concerns too: "The only thing I knew for certain was that I was disabled, I couldn't look after myself properly, so I wasn't sure how I was going to be able to look after a baby, so I needed help." Her local authority at the time, Newham Council in east London, told her such help was not available, she says. Tye was put int

title: Wood Group offshore workers launch 48-hour strike in row over pay
description: The Unite union said workers had faced the threat of fire and rehire notices and of having their pay cut.
body: At its peak in 2013, Wood reached a market valuation of more than £5bn and employed more than 50,000 people in oilfields around the world Offshore workers on a number of North Sea platforms are taking strike action in a dispute over pay and conditions. The Unite and RMT unions said they are in dispute with the Wood Group over its decision to "slash" the pay and conditions of dozens of offshore workers, including through the threat of issuing fire-and-rehire notices. The strikes will affect a number of installations run by Harbour Energy, including the Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms. The Wood Group said it had been notified of the action and added that staff and operational safety remained its "top priority". Production, instrument and mechanical technicians are among those set to walk out for a total of six days in October and November, beginning with a two-day walk-out which started at midnight. Vic Fraser, Unite regional officer in Aberdeen, said his members had been left with no choice but to strike Further walkouts are expected on 20 and 21 October and 3 and 4 November. The RMT has also instructed its members not to work any overtime from 8 October until further notice. The news comes after a warning that separate strike action by offshore workers at energy firm Apache could "severely disrupt" UK fuel supplies. Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: "Unite will not allow the Wood Group to slash and burn our members' pay and conditions. "This is a profitable company and it is despicable that it is threatening to fire and rehire its workers. This is corporate greed in its worst form." Vic Fraser, Unite industrial officer, said: "Industrial action will inevitably impact the operation of Harbour Energy's offshore assets. "The workforce has been left with no option but to strike against the Wood Group's threats and intimidation. "Our members are saying enough is enough." Oil and gas giant Wood plc sold to Dubai engineering firm Financial watchdog launches probe into Wood Group RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said: "Our members are not asking for special treatment or unreasonable improvements. "They are standing up to defend the terms and conditions they already have. "Strike action is always a last resort, but our members have clearly shown that they are prepared to stand together to defend their livelihoods and the terms and conditions they have worked under for many years. "Furthermore, instead of working with the union to resolve these issues, the company has inflamed the situation by threatening the use of fire-and-rehire tactics." A Wood Group spokesperson said: "We have received notification of planned industrial action involving union members employed by Wood on one of our Harbour Energy contracts. "This is in relation to a recent consultation on changes to employment terms and conditions with employees. "Personnel and operational safety remain our top priority." A Harbour Energy spokesperson said: "We are aware of discussions between Wood and its employees and we hope a constructive resolution can be reached. "Our priority remains the safety of our people and assets. title: Watch: Moment Indonesian sneaker shop is torn apart by explosion
description: Police have said it is “strongly suspected” that the incident was caused by a gas leak.
body: This video can not be played CCTV has captured the moment a sneaker shop was torn apart by an explosion in the San Antonio area of Surabaya, Indonesian authorities have confirmed. Police have said five people have been hospitalised following the incident that was “strongly suspected” to be the result of a gas leak, and no suspicious substances or explosives have been found at the site. They added that at least 41 buildings had been damaged by the explosion. Watch: Moment Indonesian sneaker shop is torn apart by explosion. title: Scotland's 'Chernobyl' housing scheme takes starring role in new horror film
description: Sci-fi horror comedy, Behind, features scenes filmed in Port Glasgow's Clune Park shortly before it was demolished.
body: Jade McDonald in a scene in Alessio Avezzano's sci-fi horror comedy Behind A short film has captured some of the last images of a derelict housing estate nicknamed "Scotland's Chernobyl" before demolition crews moved in. The tenements at Clune Park in Port Glasgow were built a century ago as housing for shipyard workers but most of the buildings lay empty for years. Glasgow-based filmmaker Alessio Avezzano shot scenes for his post-apocalyptic sci-fi horror comedy, Behind, on the estate before bulldozers moved in last May. "It's the last film to be made there. It was announced it would be demolished the day we were filming - we managed to get in there not a moment too soon," said the Scottish-Italian writer and director. Scenes for Behind were shot on the day it was announced Clune Park would be demolished Redevelopment of Clune Park had been delayed for years due to a stand-off between private landlords and the local council, leaving the site frozen in time with just a handful of tenants remaining. Large parts of the site became run-down and comparisons were made with the Ukrainian city of Pripyat, abandoned after the 1986 explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear plant led to a huge radiation leak. This video can not be played Watch: BBC Scotland News footage of Clune Park before demolition teams moved in last year The plot for Behind was inspired by "butt dialling", accidentally calling someone from a phone placed in a back pocket. In the film, it has devastating consequences. Avezzano said he come up with the idea while trying to write a script. "That week my cousin, who hadn't done this before or since, just started to butt dial me every day and by the fifth day the light bulb moment came," he said. "It is basically taking the idea of butt dials and what if they were a symptom of something more deadly." Avezzano added: "It's got elements of how we responded to the pandemic and it's got elements of phone addiction and social media addiction." Avezzano said he was fascinated by the estate The short has been taken on a tour of film festivals Avezzano said Clune Park gave him the ideal backdrop for the short, and scenes were shot in areas accessible to the public. Scenes for 2013's sci-fi horror Under the Skin, starring Scarlett Johansson, were also filmed at the estate. "The idea it was described as Scotland's Chernobyl has always been fascinating." said Avezzano, who is working on his first feature - Midgies - a horror film set in Scotland and due to be released next year. This article contains content provided by Google YouTube. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read Google’s cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. The film was entirely self-funded. The lead character is played by Jade McDonald who was in the female run of Singin' I'm No a Billy He's a Tim, a play about a Celtic fan and a Rangers fan locked in a prison cell together on the day of an Old Firm match. Behind has been taken on a tour of international film festivals, including in Italy and Argentina, following its premiere at Glasgow Film Festival's Frightfest. It was nominated for the best editing prize at Basingstoke's Exit 6 Film Festival and won best international short at Roswell Shorts Festival in New Mexico. title: Community supermarket opens in shopping centre
description: Shoppers can access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries at the new social supermarket.
body: Gina English from the SEK Community Food Shop in Chatham says the store is open to everyone A new community supermarket offering access to affordable and healthy food has opened in a Kent shopping centre. The store run by SEK Community Food Shop welcomed the public to its home on the first floor of The Pentagon Centre in Chatham. Gina English from SEK says the shop is open to all as "in addition to supporting people with food insecurity, people will also be able get wraparound support from us, help with employment, looking at CVs and interview skills. We're also going to help people with budgeting and money management and signposting to other local services". Initial funding to set up the supermarket was provided by Medway Council through the Crisis and Resilience Fund. Shoppers can walk straight into the social supermarket, with no prior booking required, to access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries, including a £1 fruit and vegetable bag. Cost are kept low as the store redistributes surplus food to reduce waste, helping to protect the environment at the same time. SEK already operates two similar stores in Kent. English said: "We've had Ramsgate for about three years, Ashford just for just over a year and across the two shops in the last year alone we saw 55,500 transactions and we were able to save 170 tonnes of perfectly good food from going to waste, so they do work." Rod Taffs and Shirley Graves from Chatham were among the first customers into the newly opened community supermarket Some of the first to experienced the store were Shirley Graves and her partner Rod Taffs who have already filled their basket with bargains. "People want to come down and see what they've got, it's amazing," says Graves. "I've got a box of 20 samosas for £1.50 and a big huge bag of chicken for £6. Times are quite tight at the moment, being pensioners, it's cheap and the chicken is amazing." "That's going to do us three or four meals," adds Taffs. Medway Council leader, Vince Maple, said: "I think most people across Kent and Medway would want to see food not going to waste, so the ability to have good quality food at a reasonable price, helping not just our families and individuals on low incomes but helping all families has got to be a good thing." The shop also has a confidential, soundproofed office pod at the back of the store where customers can seek personal advice and guidance. The SEK Community Food Shop in The Pentagon Centre, Chatham, is open Monday to Saturday between 10:00 and 18:00. Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external. title: Australian soldier dies and five injured in training exercise
description: The incident happened on Monday at the Mount Bundey training area, about 130km southeast of Darwin.
body: An Australian army soldier died on Monday during a training exercise in the Northern Territory An Australian soldier has died and five others have been injured during a training exercise in the Northern Territory (NT). On Tuesday, the Department of Defence confirmed the incident happened on Monday at the Mount Bundey training area, about 130km (80 mi) southeast of Darwin but gave no further details. The area - used by the army for live fire training - is the same location where Jason Challis was killed in 2017 after he was shot in the head during an exercise. The department later pleaded guilty for failing to comply with workplace safety. Monday's incident is the second death of an Australian soldier this year after a paratrooper died after a mid-air collision during training in May. The department requested the privacy of the soldiers and family's affected by Monday's incident. NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the five injured soldiers had been airlifted to hospital on Monday evening, according to national broadcaster ABC. "The Northern Territory supported two injured evacuations by helicopter to Royal Darwin Hospital at about 7:30 last night and another three by plane at about 9:30 last night," she said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the family who are obviously devastated by this loss and of course, the support of our entire community is there for all of our service personnel who will be feeling this loss immensely." The ABC also reported that the NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole had sent resources to the Mount Bundey training area to help with the department's investigation into the incident. "We can't comment on the cause of the injury to the defence personnel but we are assisting and were helping to investigate on behalf of the coroner," Dole said, according to the ABC. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his thoughts were with the family and friends of the victims, adding: "There are no safe or easy days for those who serve in our country's name." During a 2019 inquest into the death of Challis, a 25-year-old soldier from Victoria, the coroner described the training exercise as "shambolic" and that his death had been preventable. Challis, who had less than a year's experience with the defence force, was shot in the head and knee while he stood behind a plywood wall during an urban attack exercise. In May this year, Lachlan Muddle - a Special Air Service Regiment soldier - died when he fell to the ground after a mid-air collision with another paratrooper at the Jervis Bay airfield in New South Wales. title: Separatist party projected to win Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity
description: The Parti Québécois, which secured a minority, has vowed to hold an independence referendum in the years to come.
body: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was elected as Quebec's new premier on Monday. Canadian media project the sovereigntist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier. It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014. It could prove to be a test for Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting up confrontations with Quebec over issues like immigration and the monarchy. The party has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence, similar to an upcoming vote in province of Alberta later this month. The majority French-speaking province has held other votes on this, in 1980 and 1995. Polls indicate only 30% of Quebecers back such a move. Plamondon has said that vote would occur after US President Donald Trump is out of office. Carney may find himself managing dual unity crises in different parts of the country, depending on the outcome of the separation vote in Alberta. Trump is due to leave office in roughly two years, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his pledge, a third plebiscite on independence would likely be scheduled for 2029 or 2030. Separate from sovereignty, Plamondon has made it clear he is willing to fight Ottawa if it is seen as overstepping matters of provincial interest. He suggested during the campaign that he was going to pressure Ottawa, external on issues like immigration, vowing to fight any increases mandated by the Carney government. He also pledged to "abolish the monarchy in Quebec" and reroute money spent on its institutions to social services instead. "We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters in late September. For example, Plamondon suggested defunding Quebec's lieutenant-governor's office - responsible for representing King Charles III in the province - saying he would instead spend that money to tackle homelessness. Plamondon was among the Quebec lawmakers who refused to pledge allegiance to the King in 2022, paving the way for a provincial law that now makes the oath of allegiance optional. His plan to withdraw financial support for the lieutenant-governor's office is likely to face significant legal challenges, given the monarchy's central role in Canada's constitution. Such a move would also put future Quebec laws in doubt, as one of the key roles of the lieutenant-governor is to give royal assent to new legislation. Pressed about these hurdles, Plamondon has told reporters that he is ready for a legal battle with the federal government. The success of the Parti Québécois on Monday is in part due to public fatigue with the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government. Coalition Avenir Québec made safeguarding Quebec's identity and language central to its eight years in office, but its longtime leader, François Legault, eventually lost significant support among voters. Efforts to revive the party by replacing Legault with a new leader, outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, were unsuccessful. Fréchette conceded her own re-election race in Trois-Rivières shortly before 22:00 local time. She said in a speech that she would work with St-Pierre Plamondon on the transition. "Governing Quebec is the greatest honour I have ever had," she said. "I have Quebec tattooed on my heart." The Quebec Liberal Party secured the second-most seats, while the Quebec Conservative Party gained seats. Prime Minister Carney, who leads the federal Liberal party, remains popular in Quebec, though support for him had recently dipped, external as US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on Canada in August, following a breakdown in trade talks. Quebec is among the hardest hit by the latest US tariffs, with experts at global forecasting firm Oxford Economics projecting a C$2bn blow for the province. Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory late on Monday and vowed to work together with the party. "Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," he said in a post on social media. "I look forward to working with you to support Québec's businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec." title: Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
description: Schmidt acknowledged that his actions "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt".
body: Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as prime minister in September 2025 Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering. In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding. Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public". "I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday. The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday. It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering. Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii. It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out. Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025. He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel". "If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said. title: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two
description: Nidal Malik Hasan killed 13 unarmed US soldiers and injured another 32 and his execution will be the first by the US military since 1961.
body: The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years. Nidal Malik Hasan, a US Army major and physician, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two. Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder by a jury panel of 13 officers, which unanimously recommended his death sentence. Parnell said the Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X. Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan. The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row. A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward. The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan. Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level. The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option. Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years. Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah. This video can not be played How widely used is the death penalty in the US? Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025. Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty. The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens". title: Trump says he will stop using taxpayer funds for ads after bipartisan pushback
description: The ads, which tout Trump and his policies, could have violated US laws barring public government funds being spent on political advertising.
body: President Donald Trump has said he will stop using US taxpayer funds to pay for television ads he has fronted, following bipartisan pushback. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," he said Monday on social media. Trump said it is "a rather standard thing to do" but that he has decided to pay for the "Patriotic Ads" himself and with money he raised through his MAGA Inc super political action committee. The ads, which praise the president and his policies, drew criticism and questions over their legality due to laws against using government money for political ads. Are Trump's US government funded ads illegal? There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning Trump's tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump also vows to take action against the "deep state" and others he perceives as enemies. In one ad, Trump says, "We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all". The ads come just ahead of the pivotal November midterm elections, when Democrats hope to take control of one or both chambers of the US Congress as polls continue to show Trump's approval rating falling. Midterm elections often serve as a verdict on how a president is doing - and typically the party of a sitting president tends to lose seats in Congress. The White House has pushed back against criticism, calling the ads "educational" and saying they are not propaganda, but rather public service announcements. They've pointed to previous administrations ads, like those under former Presidents Barack Obama on his healthcare plan and one under former President Joe Biden urging people to get Covid-19 vaccines. But legal experts say past US government adverts have typically been about public health or national emergencies. "It's difficult to see what legitimate government purpose is served by spending taxpayer dollars on ads whose only apparent purpose is to promote the president," legal ethics expert Margaret Dylus-Yukins has told the BBC. Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire introduced a measure, which was blocked by a Republican, denouncing the administration for using government funds for for the ads. "It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language 'paid for by the U.S. Government,' should not be paid for by the United States government," the measure reads. The ads have received criticism on both sides of the aisle. Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that while "I like the message ... it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars". Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, said on CBS News on Sunday that politicians should not spend taxpayer funds on promotional ads. "I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," the Louisiana lawmaker said. title: Major fire breaks out at Nottingham city centre property
description: Nottinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service says on Monday night, it had 12 fire engines at the scene.
body: The fire service said the blaze broke out at a residential property in Market Street A major fire in Nottingham city centre has closed multiple roads and stopped tram services. At 22:55 BST on Monday night, Nottinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service said 12 fire engines were at the fire at a "residential property" in Market Street. Roads are closed in Upper Parliament Street, Lower Parliament Street, Market Street, King Street and Queen Street, the service added. Nottingham Express Transit (NET) trams have been stopped in both directions between the Theatre Royal and Market Square. The fire service has urged the public to avoid the area while emergency services tackle the blaze. Affected residents are being told to keep windows and doors closed In an update on Tuesday morning, Nottingham Fire and Rescue Service said: "Fire service crews remain on scene and are likely to be there for several more hours." A spokesperson earlier said: "If local residents are affected by smoke, keep doors and windows closed." title: Temperatures set to fall as rain and cloud sweep across UK
description: Tuesday will see cool air spread across the UK ahead of a noticeable drop in temperatures for all by Wednesday.
body: After weeks of unusually warm weather, autumn is finally set to make its presence felt on Tuesday as cooler air sweeps across the UK from the north-west. Temperatures will plunge from the low 20s to the mid-teens. Wednesday could be the first day since June when temperatures stay below 20C across the whole of the country. A spell of rain and stronger winds will accompany the colder air, adding to the autumnal feel. But the cooler spell is not expected to last, with temperatures set to rise towards average over the weekend. Cloud, rain and strong winds affecting parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland will spread further south on Tuesday. This band of rain and cloud will usher in much cooler air, setting the scene for a distinctly autumnal Wednesday. Temperatures on Tuesday could still reach 19-21C in the south-east, but northern and western areas will be much cooler, with highs mainly in the low to mid-teens. The change will be particularly noticeable after such a warm start to October with Monday offering a final taste of summer-like conditions for southern and central parts of England and Wales There will be a sharp contrast in daytime temperatures from Monday to Wednesday By Wednesday, the autumn chill will be firmly established and it is expected to be the first day since 11 June when temperatures fail to reach 20C anywhere in the UK. Cooler north-westerly winds will bring sunshine and scattered showers to many areas, while rain could be heavy and persistent for a time across south-eastern England and East Anglia. Temperatures will fall into the mid-teens across much of England and Wales. Scotland could see highs of just 10-13C. The wind will also make it feel colder than the thermometer suggests, particularly around eastern coastal areas. While mid-teen temperatures are perfectly normal for early October, the sharp contrast with the warmth of recent weeks is likely to make the change feel much more dramatic. Temperatures will fall sharply overnight on Wednesday, with frost possible in some northern rural areas early on Thursday Thursday will start off chilly with mist and fog patches along with frost in places. However, the day will bring some welcome sunshine as a temporary area of high pressure moves across the UK. Temperatures are expected to reach around 14-16C in southern areas, with Scotland struggling to get much above 10-12C. By Friday, Atlantic weather systems will bring further rain and stronger winds, although temperatures will recover slightly, reaching 16-18C across much of the south. The cooler spell is not expected to last and temperatures should return towards average over the weekend and even slightly above average again next week. But after such an extended period of warmth, this week's change may be the moment autumn finally feels as though it has arrived. title: The Papers: Badenoch's 'Britannia Dome' and 'King tells Andrew 'I won't fund court fight''
description: Several of Tuesday's papers lead on a Tory pledge to devote £10bn to an Iron Dome-style defence system.
body: Several papers lead on a Conservative pledge to build what the party is calling a "Britannia Dome" to protect the UK from any potential missile attack. The i writes that the project "would link new radar, command systems and interceptor missiles" into a single network. The pledge is an attempt by party leader Kemi Badenoch to "build credibility" on defence, the paper says, but critics say the £10bn price tag is well below previous cost estimates of at least £80bn The Daily Express also leads on the Tory plan, quoting party leader Kemi Badenoch in its headline saying: "Britain needs an 'Iron Dome' to keep us safe." The paper says the interceptor system would be funded by "slashing benefits" The so-called "Britannia Shield", as the Tories have named the project, would "guard cities, power plants and Army bases from missiles and drones fired by enemies such as Russia and Iran", the Daily Mail writes. Meanwhile, the paper features a large picture of novelist and former politician Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86 Also leading on the Conservatives' defence pledge is the Daily Star, which dubs Badenoch "the Iron Lady", after her pledge to build the "Israel-style 'Iron Dome'" defence system The Sun has a similar headline on Tuesday, calling Badenoch the "Iron Dome Lady". It notes that Badenoch's announcement comes shortly after the US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire The Tory's "Britannia Shield" pledge comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham considers delaying a decision on whether to increase defence spending "in the hope that Britain's economy improves", according to the Times. A Whitehall source tells the paper the "working assumption" is that the spending review will be moved to autumn next year The Independent also features a large photograph of Jeffrey Archer on its front page. It says "the prolific storyteller, once jailed for perjury, had only just published his final book". Meanwhile, the paper reports that Badenoch will vow to cut inheritance tax at her party conference, in what it calls a "free-market revival". The announcement comes as the party "languishes behind Labour and Reform" in the polls, the paper writes Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been told his brother, the King, "will not foot the bill for his court action against the police", according to the Daily Mirror. The former prince is understood to be challenging the lawfulness of the search warrants related to his arrest in February. But, the paper reports, Charles has said Andrew cannot use the money he gives him for living costs for his legal battle against Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court The King had "no involvement" in Andrew's application for a judicial review of his arrest, the Daily Telegraph reports. The paper adds that the monarch has "appeared keen to distance himself from his brother's decision to sue the police", which could costs hundreds of thousands of pounds. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office in the wake of information that emerged from the so-called Epstein files in the United States. He has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein The Guardian leads on a warning from experts that "cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England". Prostate cancer diagnoses have quadrupled in people under 50 since 2001, while cases of bowel, kidney and uterine cancers have more than doubled, the paper reports. Experts say the data reflects the impact of the "global obesity epidemic, poor diets and insufficient exercise" A report highlighted on the front page of Tuesday's Metro "estimates 27,000 women starting university this autumn could be a victim of a sex attack by the end of their degree". The paper cites data analysis from the Office for Students and victim support charity Enough, which it says suggests around 7.7% of the 215,000 women starting university this year could be the victim of rape or sexual assault Supermarket giants Sainsbury's and Morrisons held talks this year over "forging [a] new industry powerhouse", according to the Financial Times. The paper says the move was an "attempt to challenge Tesco" and would have been a "fresh test of regulators' appetite for consolidation in the fiercely competitive supermarket industry". Sainsbury's walked away from the talks and there are no active negotiations, the paper says, but it adds that sources "did not rule out" talks restarting Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: A simple guide to the US midterms
description: US voters will head to the polls on 3 November in a ballot that could have a major impact on Donald Trump’s presidency.
body: There are four weeks to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. On 3 November, Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate. Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms. A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide. The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans. The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far. All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. They serve fixed terms of two years. The House is where proposed laws are introduced and debated. Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs. Senators serve six-year terms. Among other jobs, they approve or block proposed laws that have been received from the House. On the same day, voters across much of the US will also choose state-level politicians. Governor contests in California, Florida, Georgia and Michigan will be among the most closely watched. The US economy is on the minds of many voters struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare. Inflation remains above the level targeted by the US Federal Reserve, partly down to the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February. Democrats argue Trump's programme of trade tariffs have also pushed up prices for Americans. Immigration is another key issue. Republicans say Trump has delivered on a major campaign pledge in 2024 by tightening the border and launching a widespread - and often controversial - crackdown on illegal immigration. Concerns over AI have grown in urgency in recent weeks. Senior politicians from both parties have agreed on the need to regulate it - setting themselves in opposition to Trump, who has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology. Congress is one of the three branches of government, alongside the presidency and the judiciary. Control of it matters for the shaping of legislation. Both the House and Senate are currently held by the Republican Party. But its majority is a slender one. They have 218 seats in the House, which is the minimum number needed to control it, plus one independent who votes with them. In the Senate, they have 53 seats and the minimum needed for control is 51. If opposition Democrats win back control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor. Voters have tended to "punish" the party of the president in the past and vote against them. Recent polling shows a low approval rating for the president. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but in early October it was sitting at about 37%. Meanwhile 61% disapproved of him. But not all seats in each chamber are competitive. Some are a safe bet for Republicans or Democrats. The BBC's US partner CBS News has identified nine Senate races to watch, external, in states like Iowa and New Hampshire, and 42 House races, in states like Arizona and Ohio. The vote is more unpredictable this year because of a battle between the two parties over the way voting districts in the House of Representatives are drawn. Republicans tried to gain an advantage by creating more favourable electoral maps in certain states and Democrats followed suit. Josh Turek (Democrat) and Ashley Hinson (Republican) are in a tight race for Iowa's Senate seat If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get any laws through Congress. So his domestic plans could be frustrated, although he has found ways to exercise power without his wider party. Democratic control of either chamber would also mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. Corruption allegations, the new White House ballroom and ICE tactics could be subject to scrutiny. There is also a debate within the Democratic Party about whether to impeach Trump, which means to bring charges in Congress that will form the basis for a political, not criminal, trial. If the Republican Party stays in control of Congress, Trump will be able to keep going with his plans for the remainder of his time in office. The president's name is not on the ballot during the midterm elections, though Trump has urged Republicans to pretend that it is by voting for him as an endorsement of his actions so far. Whichever way the results fall, commentators are likely to use them to make arguments about how voters feel about the direction of the country under Trump's leadership. Trump cannot run to be president a third time. After the midterms, we can expect speculation to start building about who might be his successor as the Republican presidential nominee for 2028 - and who might compete against that person for the Democrats. Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult? title: Dread presenting at work? Read these tips before your next meeting
description: Dani Payne would have panic attacks at the thought of presenting - now she does it most days.
body: Dani Payne would have panic attacks at the thought of presenting - now she does it most days Dani Payne was so anxious about public speaking, she had a doctor's note to excuse her from presenting at school and university. Now aged 28 with a job in politics at a cross-party think tank, she's spoken in parliament, sits on discussion panels and presents social media videos. "Most days I do some form of public speaking," she says. "I wouldn't have believed that at 15." Want to get better, or simply get started? Here are five ways to help you nail your presentation or speech. Speaking in Public: Why it feels so hard to do and how to do it anyway. Listen now. Payne, from Exeter, says she stopped any form of public speaking after developing a severe anxiety disorder and experiencing panic attacks. But looking back, she says avoiding it didn't help her build "coping skills or resilience you need later in life". "The more you avoid what you're anxious about, the more you're anxious about it." In her second year of university she was invited to give a talk on a subject she was passionate about and realised: "I was losing out on opportunities that I felt really strongly about." She presented research she had carried out for her dissertation on sexual misconduct in academic fieldwork settings and that was the start of her getting over her fear. "Picking something you genuinely feel passionately about will always make it easier to speak about in front of other people," she says. Her advice is to pick a topic you feel strongly about and look for or create opportunities to speak about it. A virtual reality headset can help you present in front of a pretend audience Daisy Schofield, a 32-year-old documentary producer and journalist, had her first panic attack at university during a presentation, she tells Woman's Hour. She managed to avoid public speaking until she got her first job and had to present company statistics on Teams every Monday. To build her confidence, Schofield practises by using an app on her phone to create a fake audience in a virtual reality headset she bought online for £10. "It makes practising feel much more engaging and like the real thing, compared to practising at home on your own, which feels a bit awkward and boring." Prof Nazanin Derakhshan, a neuroscientist at Birkbeck, University of London, suggests focusing on six breaths per minute before presenting. You can do this by breathing in for five seconds and out for five seconds. "It can improve the brain-heart communication and the more in harmony they are, the better we feel about ourselves." Viv Groskop, a stand-up comedian, writer and public speaking coach advises picking a word that encapsulates what you want your speech to convey. "It could be something like clarity. No one can ever say that you got that wrong if you were clear. "So choose something that you can think to yourself afterwards, 'did I set out to be clear? Was I clear? Yes. It's a win.' And every time you choose a different word." Groskop also advises putting a post-it note on your laptop camera and reminding yourself to look there and not at people on the screen. "You can hide self-view, resist the temptation to look at it, because it will mean you're looking down, not at people." Groskop does things that relax her ahead of stand up gigs. This could be getting a good night sleep, staying hydrated or having time off your phone. "Always wear something that you can forget about. If you love having your hair done, get your hair done. "Wear makeup or don't wear makeup, whatever makes you feel comfortable so that you won't be thinking about your appearance." Derakhshan advises not to focus in on people's faces when presenting, as we can misinterpret their reactions. "Accept that their facial expression may mean anything, and distract yourself internally from interpreting these facial expressions." Payne says it's important to remember being good at public speaking does not come "naturally to someone". "You wouldn't pick up a guitar, and be surprised that you couldn't play a song when you've never picked up a guitar before - public speaking is the exact same thing." She says to become good at public speaking you need to be bad at it first. "Particularly if you're early in your career, the people around you are not going to expect you to immediately be a master public speaker the first time you do it." Groksop says people who are good at public speaking have just been doing it more. "Many people are spending up to eight hours a day on Teams or Zoom, and if you think about a television newsreader, they've been trained for that." Derakhshan says being vulnerable is a "big asset" when public speaking. "We all make mistakes, we all forget things. It's not the end of the world. If you can go back and make a humour of it the audience are quite forgiving and accepting." Additional Reporting by Simon Richardson. title: Northern Ireland make huge strides despite Georgia frustration
description: With eight points from four games, Northern Ireland show real progress through what manager Michael O'Neill calls "one of the most enjoyable windows" he has had in international football.
body: Northern Ireland drew both home games in the Nations League window 0-0 Northern Ireland's first nine points in the Uefa Nations League were accumulated over the grand total of 17 games. Finishing their four-game window with a 0-0 stalemate against Georgia on Monday night ensured Michael O'Neill's side earned eight across a mere 11 days. It says plenty about the growing mood around this young side that, even after what was undoubtedly their best ever Nations League window, fans filed out of Windsor Park frustrated that it was not more. Isaac Price's saved penalty in the 83rd minute was naturally the most glaring missed opportunity to take all three points in a second consecutive goalless draw in Belfast after Hungary also left with a point last week. There had been other good chances, though, with Paddy Kelly and Josh Magennis both unable to capitalise on promising positions, while Ruairi McConville hit the bar in the incident that led to the penalty. Magennis himself summed up the general mood at the final whistle when he told BBC Sport NI he was "bitterly disappointed" to take only a point from the game. Price misses penalty as Northern Ireland held by Georgia This video can not be played Highlights: Northern Ireland frustrated by Georgia When the dust settles, however, the block as a whole can only be considered a success. Two weeks ago, Northern Ireland were yet to win a game in the second tier of the Nations League and had never picked up all three points on their travels at any level of the competition. Away victories in Georgia and against Ukraine in Slovakia both felt like huge steps forward for a side whose average age was as low as 22 in the latter fixture which they won 3-0. On top of that, four successive clean sheets ensured they are the only team in the competition yet to concede a goal, all the more impressive considering that Conor Bradley remains on the sidelines and Daniel Ballard was only fit to feature in the first game. "It was a hard camp, a lot different to what any of us have experienced before, and I thought we dealt with it really well," said Fulham midfielder Shea Charles who, along with Trai Hume, displayed Premier League pedigree throughout the window. "We've won two away games, drew two at home, no goals conceded, there's not many complaints. I think we've been really good." With this new four-game window presenting something different for managers across Europe to tackle, a myriad of approaches emerged. Germany boss Jurgen Klopp named virtually two separate squads for his side's two pairs of games, while Ukraine made 10 changes between their first two games and then nine for their defeat by Northern Ireland. Having spoken before the start of the campaign about how the condensed schedule would be more difficult for smaller nations, O'Neill kept changes to a minimum. He started only 15 different players across the four games with two of his changes enforced by Ballard's injury and Ethan Galbraith's absence against Ukraine to attend the birth of his child. Despite the relatively small pool of starters, this still feels like a window when Northern Ireland's depth was tested and passed with flying colours. O'Neill was without talisman Bradley and the reliable Ali McCann coming into the window, and then lost Ballard to a hamstring injury after the first game in Tbilisi. Young centre-backs McConville, 21, and Tom Atcheson, 20, looked ready to play at this level, while Ciaron Brown started all four games and drew plaudits having often had to bide his time in past squads. Kieran Morrison, Terry Devlin and Brodie Spencer all impressed when given a chance against Ukraine. O'Neill's praise for his squad is across the board. "For me it's been one of the most enjoyable windows I've had as an international manager, and that's been because of the players," said O'Neill. "How they've applied themselves, how desperate they are to do well, that's a real positive. "We've a brilliant group of players and a lot of them I think will play international football for a long time." Despite what will feel like two points dropped against Georgia, the team remains top of Group B2 before next month's concluding fixtures at home to Ukraine and away to Hungary. Having already secured their League B status at the very least, back-to-back Nations League promotions and second seeding in December's Euro 2028 qualifying draw remain on the table. In a broader sense, the past 11 days have served to heighten the growing excitement around the team's direction of travel. "Honestly, the sky's the limit," said Magennis. "I think they've probably got maybe four tournaments to have a crack at. The group's in a fantastic place." If O'Neill was slightly more coy, he echoed the general sentiment. "I know what the potential of this team is, I'm not always going to share that with you guys if I'm honest," concluded the manager. "For me the team is maturing and growing and progressing all the time. It's good that the fans are excited, that's what we want. We want them to look at this team and be proud. "I know these boys over the last two or three years, I've seen them grow. I see them with each other, which is really important and this team shows all the best sides of Northern Ireland." title: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies
description: Simon Andriesz said he felt let down by the UK's Financial Conduct Authority before his death last month.
body: Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners, died last month in Thailand The treatment of whistleblowers by the UK's financial watchdog must be investigated following the death of a British trader who exposed evidence of links between US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, MPs have said. Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners - the international firm of financial brokers founded and run by Lutnick before his appointment by US President Donald Trump - died last month in Thailand. Earlier this year, Andriesz raised concerns with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the FBI and other watchdogs about evidence he had uncovered of business links between Epstein and Lutnick. It cast doubt on Lutnick's public statements about his associations with the late sex offender. A group of UK MPs have now said his death raises "deeply troubling questions" about the way whistleblowers can be treated when they approach the FCA - the financial regulator - with concerns about wrongdoing and subsequent retaliation. Andriesz's family said he had taken his own life on 23 September, and that there was no suggestion of foul play. How US commerce secretary's Epstein links were uncovered by British whistleblower Andriesz uncovered evidence that Lutnick had sought, in Andriesz's words, to "buy a prince", offering to go into business with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2013 and utilise the former prince's contacts to attract investments, in exchange for a loan of £1m. BGC told the BBC the proposed joint venture did not go ahead. Andriesz also submitted evidence to the FCA to support his allegations of misconduct at Lutnick's former firm, including an allegation that cash from the pool of commission money set aside to pay brokers' bonuses was "embezzled" for improper purposes – an allegation the firm has denied. Epstein Files: Lutnick, the Royals and the British Whistleblower A former trader reveals how he unearthed evidence that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had failed to disclose a business relationship with the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein. Listen now on BBC Sounds Weeks before his death, Andriesz told a public event led by MPs, whistleblowers and campaigners calling for fairer regulation that he felt "thoroughly let down" and had been put through "absolute hell" by the FCA, to whom he had sent evidence of what he regarded as whistleblower retaliation by BGC and its lawyers. The FCA had previously told Andriesz there was "insufficient evidence" to conclude there had been retaliation, a conclusion he believed made it harder to win a claim against BGC at tribunal. BGC previously told the BBC it had strong policies protecting whistleblowers and denied retaliating against him. A 2012 snapshot discovered in the Epstein files shows Lutnick (right) and Epstein (centre) on Little St James John McDonnell, the Labour backbench MP and chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Investment Fraud and Fairer Financial Services, described Andriesz's death as a "profound and preventable tragedy". He said whistleblowers were "an essential part of the financial regulatory system" and warned there would be consequences for the integrity of the system if people did not believe they would be "treated properly, protected appropriately and listened to seriously". The group of MPs called for the FCA to pay for an independent party to evaluate its handling of whistleblowers. In July, Andriesz told MPs and campaigners the FCA had been fully informed about other serious allegations he had made as long ago as 2018 and accused it of inaction. The FCA told the BBC in July it had acted on his allegations and pointed to a supervision order it had issued based on his information. But in Andriesz's view that amounted to little more than a regulatory "slap on the wrist" and made it harder to make a claim for whistleblower retaliation against BGC at tribunal. Later that month, he told a meeting of the campaign group the Transparency Task Force the FCA was not fulfilling its obligations to the public and whistleblowers and merely "pays lip service" to the rules and regulations. "It protects the institution and then exposes the whistleblower to extreme retaliation and devastation to their lives and families," he said. The FCA told the BBC it was appointing a new non-executive director on its board, former Bank of England director Lea Paterson, to conduct a review into Andriesz's treatment and the FCA's handling of his whistleblower allegations. An FCA spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz's death. Our thoughts are with his family and friends. "Since expressing our condolences, we'd asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future."
