title: Five reasons India's stock market is sinking even when its economy is growing
description: The world's fastest growing major economy has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026.
body: India has one of the world's worst performing major equity markets in 2026 India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions. But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks. The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters. Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years. On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research. It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall. Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals. This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too. Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market. India imports over 90% of its crude requirements Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return. "This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins." India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz. While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters. With oil prices rising, inflation is going up and, as a result, interest rates are on the rise globally. The effective yield on US government bonds is above 5%, or at near 25-year highs. These are often considered risk-free investments. As a result, foreign money tends to leave riskier emerging market assets such as Indian equities and chase safer investments like US bonds when interest rates rise. For foreign investors, the problem of muted returns has been compounded by a weaker rupee. In currency-adjusted dollar terms, they have suffered because of the fall in the Indian currency. The Nifty has delivered just 6% annualised dollar returns over the past decade - hardly attractive, especially in comparison with several other competing markets. Indian stocks are still expensive relative to their earnings compared to other emerging markets Stock valuations have been another major concern. The market correction over the last two years has reduced the premium that Indian stocks held over their emerging market competitors. "Stocks are cheaper than they have been on average for the last ten years," says Shyamsunder, adding that the premium that Indian shares commanded over other emerging economies has shrunk substantially in the past few years. However, they are still expensive relative to their earnings, especially since companies in countries such as South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from a huge boom in artificial intelligence (AI) which has pushed up their profits. In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story. "Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition." India seeks AI breakthrough - but is it falling behind? And its smaller companies are yet to reach a scale that will attract foreign institutional funds. While Indian companies are investing in data centres and chip fabrication, the country has not produced a global giant like OpenAI, Anthropic or even China's DeepSeek - this is where the largest share of the profits in the AI value chain lie. Foreign investor interest will only return to India meaningfully if it can build globally competitive industries in these emerging areas, according to Bernstein. "We are seeing early signs of this in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors, and deep-tech innovation, but most remain too small to materially influence capital allocation decisions over much of this decade." Domestic savings into mutual funds haven't reduced despite the market correction There are many immediate factors that will influence how Indian markets behave going forward. "Easing geopolitical tensions and relatively attractive valuations could support a revival in FPI [foreign portfolio investor] inflows," according to CareEdge, a brokerage,

title: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up?
description: The city's space boom raises questions about the role of the state in backing important industries.
body: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up? In 2005, a young space engineer called Craig Clark moved back to his home city of Glasgow. He'd graduated from university just over a decade before, but the only jobs he could find were south of the border. Now Craig wanted to start a company of his own. He called it Clyde Space. I went to school not far from the River Clyde, where the city's shipbuilding heritage was forged, and knew Glasgow had once been an industrial powerhouse. When I was a child, "Clyde-built" really meant something: craftsmanship and engineering excellence. There was a saying that I grew up with: "The Clyde made Glasgow and Glasgow made the Clyde." What I hadn't realised until recently was that, in a different guise, that tradition is still alive. Two decades later, Glasgow is a European leader in building small satellites. Many of those built here are known as CubeSats. Their basic building block measures just 10cm by 10cm by 10cm - think of something about the size of a Rubik's Cube. They are much smaller, cheaper and quicker to develop than the huge contraptions that you might picture when you think of satellites. CubeSats - like this one, pictured in the offices of Spire Global in Glasgow - can be used for anything from weather forecasting to global positioning But crucially, they are modular and can be stacked together, then packed with cameras, sensors, communications equipment or other technology depending on their purpose. And their size belies their significance. The data collected by satellites of all kinds is increasingly woven into everyday life. It helps us communicate and navigate, track ships and transport goods, monitor forests and crops, manage energy networks and understand changes to our climate. For governments, that information can help inform decisions and respond to emergencies. As satellites have become more capable, space has become increasingly important. More than two decades after the first satellite company was established there, the Scottish Government says more small satellites are built in Glasgow than anywhere else in Europe. Across Scotland, the wider space industry generated £335m in income in 2022-23 - up 69% in five years. Excluding traditional satellite television broadcasting, it employed 2,811 people, an increase of 81% over the same period. But elsewhere in Europe, governments are committing big money to their own satellite industries. Could this take investment and jobs away from Glasgow? And if so, what - if anything - should the Scottish and UK governments do about it? And what should be the role of the state when it comes to backing important industries? Perhaps the most surprising thing about Glasgow's success in the space industry is that it wasn't planned. One of the catalysts was Craig Clark's Clyde Space. The company specialised in CubeSats at just the right moment, a few years after it launched, as smaller and cheaper spacecraft were taking off, and would go on to build Scotland's first satellite, the UKube-1. Crucially, the tech was built in partnership with the University of Strathclyde - which provided skills and research, as well as a ready supply of engineers. Other companies followed, including Craft Prospect and Alba Orbital. Expertise grew and a new space cluster began to form. American satellite company Spire chose Glasgow for its European base in 2015. Smaller businesses developed, while established engineering and technology firms became part of the supply chain. Glasgow has transformed itself into Europe's largest producer of small satellites - but some of the sector's leading figures say Glasgow's position is no longer secure. Listen now on BBC Sounds. "Companies started moving to Glasgow because they could see that it was possible to do it here, and there was an ecosystem that was starting to grow," says Andrew Strain, chief technology officer at AAC Clyde Space - the company formed after Clyde Space was acquired by Swedish firm AAC Microtec, although Glasgow remains the group's main satellite manufacturing site. Soon Glasgow was host to an "entire small satellite value chain", from components and satellite manufacturing, through to launch, spaceports and ground stations, according to Daniel Smith, founder of space marketing firm AstroAgency and the Scottish Government's trade and investment envoy for space. There are wider benefits too. According to a review commissioned by Space Scotland, space manufacturing alone accounted for more than 1,000 Scottish jobs in 2022-23. The wider industry generated £202m for the Scottish economy. And as the industry grew, so did the pool of knowledge. There are now more than 100 people working across space-related activity at the University of Strathclyde, with the subject now one of the institution's strategic priorities, according to Prof Malcolm Macdonald, its chair of applied space technology. The university works directly with commercial space companies on research and tech development. Macdonald recalls that when he graduated, there was basically no local space industry for him to join. Now, "when our graduates leave the university, they will go and work in the local space sector because it is now here in Glasgow for them", he says. But what's significant, Macdonald says, is that Glasgow's satellite industry wasn't something the government set out to establish. Instead, the process was "largely organic", says Smith. By any measure it's a success story. But there are warnings about competition from overseas. "It's not necessarily that we're going backwards," Macdonald tells me. "But other people are catching up." Bavaria is emerging as a significant European hub for aerospace and defence technology. title: 'My treatment was a miracle,' says stroke patient as new 24-hour service rolled out
description: An expanded service means the time of day or night a stroke occurs is no longer a barrier to treatment.
body: By the time Gemma arrived at hospital, she had numbness, could not walk or talk and felt "locked in my body" When Gemma O'Hara woke up in the night with "intense pain" in her neck, sickness and vertigo she knew something was "not right". The 40-year-old, who had just come back from holiday, had suffered a brain stem stroke. Gemma was able to have a thrombectomy, which removes blood clots and restores blood flow to the brain, a procedure she has said is a "miracle treatment" that has enabled her to recover well. Northern Ireland's regional thrombectomy service, which had only been available between 08:00 and 17:00 is now operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week after a £5m investment through Stormont's Programme for Government (PfG) Elective Care funding. Gemma, from Ballymena in County Antrim, said the expansion is "amazing" because of the difference the treatment made to her recovery. "You have to get treated so fast. You can't let time go past when it's to do with your brain," she said. "If I didn't get it in time I wouldn't be the way I am now." 'I may not be here if my stroke was at different time' New stroke suite brings life-saving treatment to Kent 'I had a stroke at the weekend so didn't get a thrombectomy' The mother-of three had the stroke, external in September 2025 and said that, while her symptoms were not classic stroke symptoms, she knew she needed medical help. By the time she arrived at the Antrim Area Hospital, she had numbness, could not walk or talk and felt "locked in my body". She was scanned and given thrombolysis - clot-busting medication - before being transferred to the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast for a thrombectomy. Gemma said that within minutes of having her procedure she was "sitting up, back to myself again" and waiting for her family to arrive. "It's a miracle treatment because I was so unwell and for something that can happen fairly quickly like that, and to recover so well, it's amazing," she said. She said having a stroke was "so unexpected". "I was always working, going to the gym and trying to look after myself. "So for everybody that was a big shock for me to have a stroke because they always thought I would have been the fittest one." Gemma said one of her "biggest fears" had been the possibly of having another stroke during the night, when thrombectomy was previously unavailable. She said the 24/7 service gives her "peace of mind" that she would be able to receive treatment if it happened again. The expanded service, which began on 14 September, means the time of day or night a stroke occurs is no longer a barrier to accessing treatment. Dr Patricia Gordon says the stroke team has advocated to expand this service for some time Dr Patricia Gordon, stroke consultant at Belfast Health Trust, said about 10% of patients who have a stroke have a large clot that can be removed through a thrombectomy. She said the procedure increases a patient's chances of making a good recovery by more than 50% and reduces the risk of death by almost 20%. "Whenever you have a stroke that requires a thrombectomy - that was one of the major and main arteries being blocked in the brain. "Those are the most severe type of strokes that you have. "Untreated, there's a risk of death from those types of strokes." She said that if patients survive they can be left with "significant disability" depending on where the blockage is - but "it could be weakness down one side, loss of speech or sometimes loss of function altogether then as well". The consultant said the impact of having a thrombectomy is "quite significant". "You're going from a very dependent state to a nearly independent state again by more than 50% if you can get the clot out in good time," she said. The service will build capacity towards 300 thrombectomy procedures annually, about double what it has been doing during reduced hours. The health minister says thrombectomy "dramatically improve a patient's chances of recovery" Gordon said the stroke team has advocated to expand this service for some time and it is "transformational" for people. She said having it 24/7 means that it is available to all patients and there will be staff there to perform it. "You can see that there's a huge amount of staff that are needed to be able to fill rotas and to be there to be able to treat patients," she said. "It will largely transform patients' lives from being potentially significantly dependent to independent." The service is delivered at the Royal Victoria Hospital Belfast through a regional pathway involving stroke teams at the Causeway, Antrim Area, Royal Victoria, Ulster, Craigavon Area, Daisy Hill, Altnagelvin and South West Acute hospitals. Artificial Intelligence-supported imaging is being used to help clinicians rapidly identify patients who may benefit. In June 2022, a commitment to expand the regional thrombectomy service to 24/7 provision was published in the Reshaping Stroke Care Action Plan. According to the Department of Health, about 3,000 people have a stroke each year in Northern Ireland, which is one person every three hours, and more than 43,000 stroke survivors live in the community. In 2024, Nisra recorded 883 stroke deaths. Health Minister Robbie Butler said Northern Ireland was the first of the UK nations to provide a 24/7 thrombectomy service for its entire population, which he described as a "landmark moment". "Thrombectomy is one of the most significant advances in modern stroke medicine and can dramatically improve a patient's chances of recovery," he said. title: We're saving £100 a month into pensions for our toddler and baby - here's why
description: A growing number of parents are opening retirement funds for their children.
body: Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices now Richard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them. The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules., external So the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083. Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing. "Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow." Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council. He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended. In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18. The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life. Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past. "We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain. "And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids." Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600. The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show. One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open, external as in the same period a year earlier. Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023. While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more? Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years. "The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help." Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says. Hugo Thompson is happy to wait until he is at least 57 to access the pension fund For parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity. "Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound." It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children. In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts. Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half. Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three. Wally Luckeydoo says he is giving his children a "financial head start" "My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally. "For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt. "I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially." title: Blue Planet and Gandhi composer George Fenton dies aged 76
description: The musician received five Oscar nominations, and soundtracked dozens of memorable nature films.
body: George Fenton was one of the UK's most prolific and successful composers Composer George Fenton, whose work included music for films such as Gandhi, Groundhog Day and The Fisher King, as well as TV shows like Planet Earth and Bergerac, has died at the age of 76. The prolific musician received five Oscar nominations for his film scores, including those for The Remains of the Day and Cry Freedom. His work on the BBC TV show Blue Planet also earned awards from the Baftas, Emmy Awards and Ivor Novellos; and he also composed theme music for BBC News programmes such as Newsnight and Breakfast Time. In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today." They continued: "He is survived by his loving wife Amanda, ex-wife Jane, children Gemma, Grace and Bridget, and grandchildren Lola, Audrey, Alfred, George, Frank and Beatrice, and a life of music." This video can not be played Watch: Fenton gives a peak into his studio in 2019 as he describes how to write a TV theme tune Fenton was born George Howe in Bromley, Kent in 1949. According to a biography on his official website, his father was a mechanical engineer, and his mother had been a dancer before becoming a nurse during the war. Both parents were musical - his father played drums and his mother played piano - but Fenton chose the electric guitar as his instrument at the age of seven. That was "when music became more important than football," he later told The Express newspaper. "The Beatles had a huge influence on me." He took his first lessons from a musician called Brian Rudd. "He came into our lives as a chimney sweep, which he clearly wasn't," Fenton later recalled. "My mother went mad at him because he filled the house with soot. "As he left he said, 'I'm really sorry – but I tuned the boy's guitar for you.' She suggested that as compensation for the mess he could give me a lesson, which he did and then carried on doing." Later, Fenton began to study the church organ, but rejected the chance to attend university and music college to pursue a career as a performer. In 1968, he appeared in Alan Bennett's first West End play Forty Years On and was forced to adopt his mother's maiden name, as union rules prevented two actors from having the same name. During that production, he also understudied the musical director of the show, Carl Davis - who similarly became a prominent composer for film and television. The composer spent most of his career writing alone, but he never entirely lost his love of performing. "I love live audiences," he told Radio 4's Sue Lawley in 2003 A year later, he signed a record deal, and scored a top 10 hit in Sweden with a cover of The Beatles' Maxwell's Silver Hammer, but his career as a solo artist was short lived. In the mid-1970s, he had a recurring role as soldier Martin Gimbel in the ITV soap opera Emmerdale Farm. But as time went on, he found that directors were always casting him in roles that required him to play an instrument, so he decided to make music his main focus. Fenton got his first job as composer and musical director for a production of Twelfth Night at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1974. Eight years later, he was nominated for an Oscar for his score for Richard Attenborough's Gandhi, on which he worked with Indian composer and instrumentalist Ravi Shankar to develop a score reflecting the country's musical traditions. It was only his fourth attempt at film music, and he was still almost entirely self-taught. Throughout the 1980s, he wrote the soundtrack for a number of TV series, including the Bafta-winning The Jewel in the Crown, The Monocled Mutineer, and Alan Bennett's Talking Heads. He also wrote many well-known theme tunes, including the BBC's One O'Clock News, Six O'Clock News, Nine O'Clock News, Newsnight, The Money Programme, and Radio 4's PM Programme. For 1987's Cry Freedom - the story of South African campaigner Steve Biko, who was brutally killed by police - he worked with South African jazz musician Jonas Gwangwa, earning two Oscar nominations for best original score and song. Almost by accident, the title track featured Fenton singing a list of anti-apartheid activists imprisoned or killed by the South African government. He'd initially recorded the lyrics as a guide for Gwangwa - but the musician decided to keep some of them intact "as a gesture of brotherhood". "Then it got nominated for an Oscar, so I then found myself singing it on live television to about a billion people, which was not what I intended at all," Fenton later told Radio 4's Desert Island Discs. Fenton's scores for David Attenborough's natural history programmes became an international phenomenon After composing the score for the BBC's Trials of Life in 1990, Fenton went on to create the music for what became known as David Attenborough's Earth Trilogy: The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet. Fenton's music perfectly complemented the stunning visuals of the ocean's depths and the polar ice caps, adding an emotional weight to the narrative, using the full might of the orchestra to evoke everything from wonder and awe to tension and suspense. Following the success of the documentaries, Fenton created a show - The Blue Planet in Concert - which has been performed by leading orchestras in venues around the world. Among his other well-known soundtracks were The Long Walk Home, You've Got Mail, Sweet Home Alabama, The Lady In The Van and Mrs Henderson Presents. Fenton also scored more films for British director Ken Loach than any other composer. Their 18 collaborations included Ladybird, Ladybird; I, Daniel Blake and The Wind That Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or at the 2006 Cannes Film Festival. title: I won't accept exclusion, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
description: Labour MPs and the European Greens have demanded clarity from the Green Party over a "Zionism is racism" motion.
body: Green Party leader Zack Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday Zack Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of", after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism. The Green leader said "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship". The motion defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine". It comes after more than a dozen Labour MPs reported the Greens to the equality watchdog on Monday, saying it raised "serious questions". Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote Nine Labour MPs have also referred the Green Party to Sussex Police, asking the force to investigate whether alleged "possible antisemitic offences" at the conference merit a criminal investigation. Sussex Police and the Green Party have been contacted for comment. It is the latest development in a backlash to the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton and endorsed by 1,022 votes to 813. "The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it said. The motion has exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election. Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday and four of the party's five MPs opposed it. Israel's foreign ministry responded by banning Polanski from entering the country, while some Jewish groups have described it as an "attack on the Jewish community". In his first comments since the motion was passed, having declined interviews on Monday, Polanski released a lengthy statement saying he "take[s] seriously my responsibility to make sure everyone feels safe and welcome in our party". He added: "As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of." He said his party and its leadership stood for "deeply held values of compassion, fairness and equality for all". Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct". On Monday, a group of Labour MPs wrote two letters to the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) - organised by former Home Office minister Mike Tapp - raising concerns about the motion, and amendments to protect Jewish members attending Zionist synagogues being voted down. "Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter to the watchdog said. The EHRC, which regulates equality law in Great Britain, previously found failings in how Labour handled antisemitism. In a statement following the letter, the EHRC told the BBC it would "consider each complaint carefully" and had not at this stage launched an investigation. It added: "We have guidance advising political parties on their responsibilities under the Equality Act 2010. Like all duty-bearers, political parties must comply with the Act and take steps to avoid discrimination." The European Green Party, of which the Green Party for England and Wales is a member, released a statement on Monday saying it wanted to "unequivocally distance" itself from the motion. The umbrella body said it would "immediately demand clarity" from the party's leadership on how they would protect Jewish people and self-determination. Meanwhile, Green MP Ellie Chowns told Radio 4's PM programme she was "deeply saddened" the motion had become party policy but disagreed it was antisemitic, saying it was underpinned by "principled opposition to the actions of the Israeli government". She suggested a review of Green policymaking processes was needed since "less than 1%" of the party's more than 200,000 members had participated in the vote. title: Tories pledge £10bn 'Britannia Shield' air defence system
description: The Conservatives said their plan would protect the UK at a time when Nato allies have warned of Russian drone incursions.
body: The UK's existing Sky Sabre air defence system, seen in 2022 at the Royal Artillery's change of colours parade at Baker Barracks, Thorney Island The Conservatives have pledged to invest in a new missile and drone defence system if voted into government at the next election. Branding it "Britannia Shield", the party said it would spend up to £10bn over a decade on an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles. In a speech to the Conservative Party conference on Tuesday, shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge will describe it as "the most significant upgrade to UK air defence for generations". In response, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Tories had an "abysmal record" of defending Britain during their 14 years in power, adding: "They owe Britain an apology, not another lecture." The Tories described their plans as "a British 'Iron Dome'", a reference to Israel's elaborate air defence system. The party said it would be capable of defending the UK's critical national infrastructure, military bases and sovereign territories from sophisticated threats. It added that the proposal would strengthen the UK's air defence systems at a time when Nato allies have warned they are facing repeated Russian drone incursions. The party also cited a report from the defence committee of MPs last November which said the UK was lagging behind its European counterparts in having a plan to defend itself and overseas territories from a military attack. The UK's existing Sky Sabre system has previously been deployed in Poland as part of its support for Ukraine The Conservative Party said its "Britannia Shield" would have three components - new advanced radar systems, upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain's defences and rapidly decide a response, and new interceptor missiles as well as counter-drone capabilities. The three-tiered design of the proposal is similar to the British Army's current Sky Sabre, external air defence system. This system - which can intercept munitions and aircraft as well as integrate with wider air defences - was deployed by the UK to the Middle East earlier this year for defensive action against Iranian attacks. In his speech at the conference in Birmingham, Cartlidge will say: "With a £10bn budget, this would be one of Britain's most significant military programmes since the cold war. "But one that is totally necessary because of the threats we face." Streeting said in response: "They [the Conservatives] cut the Army to its smallest size since Napoleon and left a £17 billion hole in the equipment plan. "Their own defence secretary, Ben Wallace, admitted our Armed Forces had been 'hollowed out and underfunded'." The Conservatives said their plan would be funded within their existing commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, paid for by welfare reform and reprioritisation of existing expenditure. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been under pressure to set out how he will reach Nato's 3.5% of GDP spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year. The current Labour government's Defence Investment Plan includes more than £350m to double the number of Sky Sabre systems operated by the British Army, with ground-based air defence sitting alongside air and maritime capabilities. title: Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
description: Anojan Sivarasa faces execution after he was found guilty of blasphemy over a Facebook comment.
body: Anojan Sivarasa's family have not heard from him for more than a week "I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us." Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook. The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency. However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place. Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out. Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online. During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad. Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July. His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials. "People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, told BBC Sinhala. The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan. Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath. The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan. His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities. The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention. In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers. "There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, President's Counsel, told BBC Sinhala. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake (fourth from right) recently met Anojan's family Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased. "My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response." In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities. Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia. In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations. "The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time. Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia. There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation. Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia. title: What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford?
description: The mass evacuation of American bombers from the UK points to concern in the Pentagon, our security correspondent writes.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What has prompted the US to withdraw its bombers from Fairford? The unexpected mass withdrawal of America's heavy bombers happened so suddenly on Sunday that it has got everyone wondering what prompted it. An "abundance of caution," says US Vice-President JD Vance, adding that Washington felt Iran was doing what it has "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people". An abundance of panic is how others have seen it. For the last seven months, America's B-1 Lancer bombers and other aircraft have been operating out of Fairford to strike the Iranian missile launch sites. In July, Iran threatened any country that provided the US with such a facility would be considered a "legitimate target". Then on 27 September, a major incident was declared when five British men were arrested and later bailed after being seen acting suspiciously with their three white vans in the dead of night close to the airbase perimeter. At the weekend, a UK-Iranian dual national was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. He was also released on bail. Twelve valuable and strategically important B-1 bombers have now departed en masse and seemingly in such a rush that, reportedly, the air-to-air refuelling aircraft needed to get them back across the Atlantic to their home bases in the continental US were still being fuelled up while the B-1 Lancer crews were being ordered to scramble to take off. So something was considered urgent and dangerous enough to prompt this. Speaking after his vice-president's remarks, President Donald Trump himself said the US had removed its bombers because of "some threats" to the base. "Rather than tempting the enemy", he added, the US had moved the planes "around a little bit". There was almost certainly a fresh piece of intelligence, whether true or not. British officials would not reveal what it was, but they did say "there is an ongoing high tempo of threat from Iran to the UK, and it is logical that US airbases would be pretty high on any targeting list". Iran has denied any connection with events at RAF Fairford. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also played down any suggested link between this rushed evacuation and the arrests made on 27 September. The context here is that while the UK is not at war with Iran, the US is - and that is a distinction Tehran has publicly challenged. As far as the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps is concerned, Britain is already a participant in America's war with Iran. There is also a cost factor involved here. The B-1 Lancer bombers which have now left each cost about $330 million. The Americans have already suffered heavy financial losses from Iranian strikes on US bases in the Middle East. In late March the Iranians hit Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, destroying an E-3 Sentry Awacs early warning plane. That aircraft alone cost over half a billion dollars. General Sir Richard Barrons, who served in one of the highest ranks in the British Armed Forces, said: "We now live in a world where a £1,000 drone could wreck one of those aircraft. "So, I don't know what the threat was but the most prudent thing to do would be to remove them to Texas given that they were not doing very much at the minute." Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites? Peace for villagers as US bombers leave UK airbase But how does the US ordering the bombers to leave RAF Fairford reflect on Washington's confidence in the ability of the UK to keep the base secure? Britain remains an incredibly close ally of the US and there are still hundreds of American servicemen and women stationed at RAF Fairford, as well as at other bases at Mildenhall and Lakenheath. Work will likely be ongoing in secret now to review security at the base on both sides of the perimeter fence. But it is hard not to conclude that, despite efforts to play down the drama, this is an embarrassing episode for the UK. Rubio said the US has "confidence in the security of all our bases" and said the administrations was working "very closely" with UK authorities, who "couldn't be more co-operative". UK counter-terrorism police are still investigating what happened at RAF Fairford and are keeping an open mind as to what exactly was behind events there. I have been told a large amount of data, CCTV and other information is still being trawled through while the men remain on bail. Meanwhile, now that the bombers have left British soil, the US insists it can still deploy them from its domestic bases anywhere in the world. That could be seen as putting a brave face on something which, for Iran, sees a major US strike force effectively driven back to its home base in the continental United States. title: Scotland's first AI teacher warns pupils: Don't trust everything it tells you
description: Jamie Laycock says schools must help youngsters understand both the opportunities and dangers of AI.
body: This video can not be played First Scottish school to appoint AI teacher Some teenagers are already using artificial intelligence to tackle homework, revise for exams and sharpen coursework. Others are steering clear of it completely. At one Scottish school, staff have decided that pretending AI doesn't exist is not an option. Mearns Castle High School in East Renfrewshire is believed to be the first school in the UK to appoint a dedicated principal teacher of AI literacy, creating a role focused entirely on helping pupils and staff understand the risks and benefits of the powerful new technology. The job has gone to Jamie Laycock, a former principal teacher of biology, who says schools must help youngsters understand both the opportunities and dangers of AI. The message underpinning the new role is: "We can't just hope AI goes away". But rather than teaching pupils to embrace AI, Laycock's mission is to ensure they can question it, challenge it and use it responsibly. See if you can spot an AI deepfake with our test In one of his first lessons, pupils were shown a mixture of real and AI-generated images and asked to spot the fakes. It was much harder than many expected. Laycock says it's becoming increasingly difficult by the day, highlighting the rapid advances in so-called deepfakes. But identifying fake images is only part of the course. Laycock also teaches pupils about "hallucinations" where AI confidently provides information it has made up. "I think hallucination is actually a really bad word, but it basically makes stuff up," he says. "For a young person, if you don't have what we call 'foundational knowledge' it might be hard for you to figure out whether something is a hallucination or whether it's genuine." He says young people need to be taught to be sceptical of any AI output and then go and check it to determine whether it is a genuine fact. Another danger is "anthropomorphisation", where people treat chatbots like trusted friends or experts simply because they sound human. "It has human-like qualities but actually this is just a machine," Laycock says. "And for a young person, in particular, that is actually a really difficult thing to keep in perspective all the time." Laycock warns that AI often flatters users and agrees with users rather than challenging their ideas Laycock also warns that AI often flatters users and agrees with them rather than challenging their ideas, creating risks for young people who may accept answers without thinking critically. "It's sycophantic," he says. "It always tells you you're amazing, that your idea is great. "We need to be teaching our young learners about that so that they don't get trapped and hooked into the technology and become over-reliant." Another area pupils will be taught is AI's biases towards certain norms because of the information it is trained on. The teacher says the lessons will be tailored to "different ages and stages" with younger pupils needing to be focused on foundational knowledge and critical thinking skills before moving on to practical uses of AI. "We're not saying that we're advocates for AI, and we're not saying that it is good or bad," Laycock says. "Our learners need to know how to use it appropriately so that they can get the best out of it. "They need to be aware that this is a machine that they are interacting with, and for it certainly not to impact on their own ability to think and critically evaluate things." Tomo wonders whether AI could transform his chosen profession before he even graduates Many schools in the UK have AI leads, teachers who take on some responsibility for AI alongside their day jobs, but this is thought to be the first time in the UK that a school has designated a specific role to AI literacy. It follows a report by Edinburgh University, external published earlier this year which concluded that Scottish schools have not had the time nor capacity to prepare properly for the rapid rise in AI. At Mearns Castle, all pupils in S1 and S2 will receive AI literacy lessons, while older year groups will cover the subject through citizenship and personal education (PSE) classes. An elective course will also be available for senior pupils. Laycock will also help to train colleagues on the use of AI and develop teaching materials which can be used by other schools. The role was created after growing interest from both parents and pupils, many of whom are asking how AI will affect future careers. A number of S6 pupils have volunteered to work with Laycock on how best to teach AI to the rest of the school. Anna said the deepfake exercise left her less confident about her ability to distinguish real images from fake ones Among them is 17-year-old Tomo, who had been planning to study finance and economics as he had always wanted to be a trader. He now wonders whether AI could transform the profession before he even graduates. "I think everybody's worried about what's going to be taken away by AI because we've got our university applications in the next few months," he says. Fellow pupil Aydin said the technology should be used as a tool to aid understanding rather than provide easy answers. "It shouldn't be used constantly," he says. "It shouldn't be abused. I think it is always good to be as a little side help. "It's better to use that for how to get to the answer, rather than just letting it do it for you and getting the straight answer there." Another pupil, Anna, said the deepfake exercise left her less confident about her ability to distinguish real images from fake ones. Head teacher Stuart Clark says it is clear that the implications of AI will be profound Head teacher Stuart Clark says it is clear that the implications of AI will be profound for the economy and on society. "We're really clear that acting on AI is not the same thing as advocating for it or promoting it," he says.

title: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
description: The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed the B1 bombers from the base in England back to their home stations in America.
body: This video can not be played Trump: US "had a threat" that led to withdrawal of bombers at RAF Fairford President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers. Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base. What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford? What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites? Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase. While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase. Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident. "There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far." He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who. The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran. One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance. "Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said. Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world. RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police. Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail. Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident. Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire. Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford. He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out." Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident. Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people". Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency. However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added. The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added. title: Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
description: His last book, Adam and Eve, is set to release this month.
body: This video can not be played Jeffrey Archer's interview with BBC Breakfast in September Bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86. Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset. In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions. The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star. Jeffrey Archer obituary: successful novelist, disgraced politician and convicted liar Archer was born in north London on 15 April 1940 but would quickly move to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where his family bought a house from John Cleese's mother. In 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth. He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman. His political career was paused in 2001 when he was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice. He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against The Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages. He was released in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024. His last book, Adam and Eve, is set to be released this week, HarperCollins added, describing him as a "master storyteller" whose readers "meant everything to him". Last week, Archer returned to his former school to promote his last book. "It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School. Archer was due to attend the Cheltenham Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel. He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said. The pair have two sons and five grandchildren. Jeffrey Archer, pictured here with Margaret Thatcher, served as a Conservative MP and party chairman Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as a "huge shock". Writing on X, she said: "I am incredibly saddened to hear this news. He had sent me a lovely message just this morning and was always a great source of encouragement to me personally." Paying tribute to the bestselling author, Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK CEO and Jeffrey's editor, said: "It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer's editor. "He was the master storyteller and an editor's dream - phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the 'team' nature of great publishing." HarperCollins said the author had been at the Leicester Square Theatre in London on Sunday, signing books for fans with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth. Writing on X, Brandreth said: "Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel – he said it was to be his last. "He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last." Former Conservative chancellor Nadhim Zahawi paid tribute to the bestselling author on X, describing him as a "dear friend and extraordinary human being". He wrote: "His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company." title: Gauff condemns racist abuse after China Open win
description: Coco Gauff says she suffered racial abuse on social media after an incident during her win over Sun Xinran at the China Open.
body: Coco Gauff won the US Open in 2023 and the French Open in 2025 Coco Gauff says she suffered racial abuse on social media following an incident in her win over 16-year-old Sun Xinran at the China Open. The American had been serving at 4-5 in the first set her Chinese opponent thought she had hit a winner. However, Gauff raised her hand to halt play because of a flickering light in the side panels surrounding the court. Gauff won the next three points to hold for 5-5 before she closed out the set, and then dropped just one game in the remainder of the contest as she claimed a 7-5 6-1 victory to reach the last 16 in Beijing. The world number four gave a lengthy explanation of why she stopped the point in a post on X and said it was "an unfortunate situation" but "out of my control", adding that Sun had understood and accepted her apology. Gauff then responded to a reply to her original post which included racist language. "You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff wrote. "The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief." Gauff is far from the first player in the women's game to suffer social media abuse. A report in July said female players were subjected to more than 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025. The WTA and World Tennis said "collective action" was required to make "significant progress" in tackling abuse. title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
description: Donald Trump says the US was looking "very strongly" at the case of a lab technician who died at a research centre in Siberia.
body: Donald Trump says the US was looking "very strongly" at the case but had not discussed it with the Kremlin President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was watching closely amid concerns the incident could lead to the spread of pneumonic plague, but there was no cause for alarm. Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples". Unconfirmed reports suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents. Asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague spreading from Russia, Trump said he had not spoken to the Kremlin about it. "I hate to see them having it," he said, but added: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help." No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since the lab technician's death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead. Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution. Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature. "If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that." The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia. The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area. It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago. Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics. "Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said. He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here." "People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said. "It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it." Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible. "Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said. title: France braces for national day of school protests after injuries and mass arrests
description: France prepares for a day of protests in support of students who’ve been demanding more investment in education.
body: More than 500 schools were partially or totally closed by protests on Monday, the French education minister said France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education. It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested. One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week. France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete". The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement". Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest. The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike. The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers. The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students. Some protesters launched fireworks during clashes with police in the streets near Paris on Monday On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced a series of measures to "address the difficulties faced by secondary school students and education staff", promising "visible changes" in schools. However, he also said: "We will make no concessions to violence. We stand by students and staff who have been assaulted, as well as police officers and gendarmes who have been injured." The unrest has not only seen schools blockaded, but also rubbish bins set on fire. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "burned and ransacked" since the start of the protests. Violent clashes between students and the police have led to some serious injuries throughout the course of the protests so far. On Monday, a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation near a school in the northern city of Lens. The student was transferred to a nearby hospital and his injury is not life-threatening, according to officials. Protesters have set road materials on fire as barricades Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered". "It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying. "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study." Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry, external. Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors. The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner". Masked protesters took to the streets near Lycée Berthelot in Aubervilliers While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised. The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand. The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response. "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed. Meanwhile Mélenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations". The left-wing mayor of Marseille, Benoît Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said.
