title: Disabled woman had to 'crawl on hands and knees' to get off train
description: Phoebe's mum said watching the incident was "traumatic" and left her feeling "helpless".
body: Phoebe Tesoriere has spent almost nine months "fighting to get an answer" from Great Western Railway A wheelchair user was left in tears as she crawled on her "hands and knees" through a train after being told a ramp could not be used to help her off. Phoebe Tesoriere, 24, was on a Great Western Railway (GWR) train from London Paddington to Bath Spa with her parents when it happened. Her family spoke to the assistance desk and was taken to the only designated wheelchair space on the train. Phoebe said she was assured a ramp and assistance would be waiting, but on arrival was told she was in a carriage beyond the platform, leaving her unable to get off. GWR said it was "really sorry" and admitted "we let her down, both when we helped her board and at several points during her journey". Phoebe, who has hereditary spastic paraplegia, external which causes weakness and stiffness in the leg muscles, said: "My mum specifically asked if a ramp and assistance would be waiting at Bath Spa. We were assured it would be." While on the train, staff checked which station she would be getting off at numerous times during the incident in December 2025, she added. Despite this, Phoebe was not told the carriage she was directed to would stop beyond the platform, leaving her unable to use a ramp to get off. Phoebe took her parents to London as a Christmas gift, but on the journey home she was unable to get off the train Phoebe and her parents had been returning to Bath, where she now lives, after attending a concert in London the night before, which she bought as a gift for her mum and dad before her diagnosis. When they got to Bath Spa, she said they were told by staff to stay on the train and get off at Bristol Temple Meads - a 15-20 minute journey - before buying another ticket back to Bath Spa so she could get off. The family explained this was not possible as Phoebe's grandparents were waiting at the station to pick them up and take her back to Caerphilly, where she was living at the time. Phoebe said she was told by staff to try and get her wheelchair through the train aisle, but it did not fit so she crawled through three carriages. "I was crying. People were staring," she said. "One passenger reached down to stroke my back and apologised to me, telling me what was happening wasn't acceptable. "She was trying to comfort me, but in that moment I felt like a dog." Phoebe's mum Kirstin Tesoriere said watching the incident was "traumatic" and left her feeling "helpless". "When I close my eyes I can still see it, the pity on other passengers' faces. It was humiliating for her." Phoebe said her parents lifted her back into her wheelchair to get off the train using the ramp, but staff were not waiting to assist her. Phoebe says people believe "everything is accessible these days, but it really isn't" Phoebe wants to see a big improvement in accessible transport in the UK. She said: "It's ridiculous that disabled passengers are still expected to go through this." Due to the nature of Phoebe's diagnosis, her condition is expected to get worse over time. Kirstin said she wanted to "make lovely memories" with her daughter but that the family had not used public transport since the incident. "She's just scared now and she's already lost so much to her diagnosis," she said. "You just want your children to be happy." Phoebe made a formal complaint to GWR on the day it happened, but the investigation was not completed until May. In its response, the train company admitted Phoebe's experience was "extremely poor" and took accountability for what went wrong. It confirmed Phoebe would receive compensation but, despite sending her bank details as requested, she has still not received any money and said GWR had "ignored every email I have sent" since June. "Nearly nine months after I complained, I am still fighting to get an answer. No disabled passenger should ever have to crawl." Kirstin said she understood "mistakes were made" but believes her daughter has been treated "inexcusably" since then. "I can't forgive them for how they've made an awful traumatic experience last for months," she added. Phoebe's mum said the family have not been back on public transport since the experience on the GWR train In emails seen by BBC Wales, GWR said it had made changes to "how we manage passenger assist for customers travelling from London Paddington" as a result of Phoebe's complaint. It said: "There were opportunities for us to recognise that there would be an issue at Bath Spa, and we failed to identify them. "In my view, the situation you were placed in - and your subsequent action to leave the train - was entirely avoidable. "Put simply, this should not have happened. I am truly sorry for the distressing and uncomfortable experience you had when leaving the service." In response to BBC Wales, GWR said: "We are really sorry. Ms Tesoriere should have been able to travel with confidence and dignity and we let her down, both when we helped her board and at several points during her journey where we had opportunities to put it right. "We have apologised to her personally and have made improvements to how we support customers boarding at London Paddington, so no-one else goes through this." Regarding her compensation, a spokesman added that the company was "doing everything we can to complete the final steps as quickly as possible". title: GP 10-minute appointment slots 'making it harder to do cancer checks'
description: Dr Amara Naseem says appointment times are not long enough to get the information she needs.
body: Dr Amara Naseem says GPs are under pressure to offer more appointments, rather than a focus on quality treatment Pressure to provide more GP appointments is making it harder to include checks for gynaecological cancers within the 10-minute slots, doctors have said. Dr Amara Naseem says her clinics always overrun as it takes about 20 minutes to sensitively take a detailed history and carry out internal examinations. A reduced number of practices in her area means she has taken on more patients and fears there is a risk that women will not raise gynaecological symptoms or attend screenings if appointments are rushed, painful or not handled well. The Welsh government said it was increasing investment in primary care and recruiting up to 100 extra GPs. Research by cancer charity Tenovus, in support of Claire's Campaign, external, found about half of the 100 GPs surveyed across Wales felt limited consultation time was a major concern. A third also had concerns about "over-referring" people for further testing to rule out cancers, given hospitals are already overstretched. Currently, 95% of patients put on the suspected cancer pathway are later told they do not have cancer. But doctors said teasing out the cancer cases at an early stage could be challenging when symptoms such as bloating are hard to distinguish from benign conditions including irritable bowel syndrome. Naseem said the pressure from the Welsh government was to "offer more appointments to the patient, rather than about the quality of the treatment". Lowri Griffiths of Tenovus said incidence and mortality rates for gynaecological cancers in Wales were higher than the UK average - something she added the Welsh government needed "to get to grips with". Pledges to increase GP numbers were promising, she said, "but unless we address both the primary care setting and the hospital setting, the system won't work". Lowri Griffiths says Wales needs to be "more aspirational" in gynaecological care Naseem said many women's health issues may require an internal examination, which requires time to be done "in an empathetic and sensitive way". She added: "I'm working in a very diverse community, also in a deprived community, where uptake of screening is already low." She said in communities where myths existed around screening, time is also required to explain what is involved and allay fears and potentially work with interpreters. Dr Kathrin Thomas said her friend Claire O'Shea was "a real feminist" Dr Kathrin Thomas, a former GP and public health specialist, got involved in Claire's Campaign when her friend Claire O'Shea was given a late diagnosis for a gynaecological cancer. Claire, from Cardiff, died last year, aged 42. Thomas said GP numbers in Wales had "almost flat-lined" while the workload had increased, especially in more disadvantaged areas where there were "fewer doctors, fewer nurses and the healthcare needs are much greater". She is also involved with Deep End Cymru - a network of GP practices in the most deprived areas. "We've got a big difference in the cancer experience in more deprived communities - cervical cancer in particular," she said. "There's a wide inequity between women in more affluent areas and women in poorer areas." Of the 1,200 women diagnosed, about 470 patients die from a gynaecological cancer, either of the womb (uterine), ovary, cervix, vulva or vagina, in Wales each year. Screening is only available for cervical cancer and it does not detect other cancers. "Cancer outcomes are improving dramatically over the decades, but we're struggling in Wales to get the outcomes that other richer countries are getting," said Thomas. The waiting times for gynaecological cancer treatment in Wales have improved significantly over the past year, from 34% of patients being treated within 62 days, to 51.3%. However, the most recent Wales average for all cancers was 60.1% against a target of 75%. Maria Bailey has been fundraising to make more "grab and go" bags for other patients treated for cervical cancer. Thomas said continuity of care came up repeatedly among the Tenovus survey of GPs. "You have a 20% less chance of dying if you have the same team that looks after you," she said. Maria Bailey feels being able to see the same GP was a factor in her own cervical cancer diagnosis. "I feel really lucky that she took me seriously from the off. She knows me - she knew I was alarmed and [the symptoms] weren't normal for me. She took it very seriously," she said. The 55-year-old from Pencoed, Bridgend county, experienced increased fatigue and light vaginal bleeding but put it down to working extra hours and the menopause. But in February she spoke to her GP after the bleeding intensified. "It was heavy bleeding and quite large clots, which I've never had before - they looked like baby seals and that was really alarming." An internal examination followed by a raft of further tests uncovered a 4cm (1.5in) tumour and grade 2 cancer, external around her cervix. "I was in shock, but as soon as they said it wasn't life-threatening, that was it. It was just one gear - and that was go." Maria underwent chemotherapy, radiotherapy and brachytherapy, external across centres in Swansea and Cardiff and has since been raising money to provide essential provisions for others going through treatment for cervical cancer. "I'm quite an organised person and don't like walking into anything blind," she said. But an online search for advice about the things needed when starting treatment yielded very little. She has now donated several "Bailey's bags" to two cancer centres containing items such as a water bottle, strong-flavoured sweets to overcome the metallic taste treatment can leave, a foldable fan, neck cushion, battery pack for USB devices and a medication box. The Welsh government said: "We're committed to strengthening primary care as the foundation of the NHS

title: Niamh O'Brien, dancer and wife of Michael Flatley, dies at 52
description: She was a renowned Irish dancer who performed the lead role of Saoirse in the Lord of the Dance.
body: O'Brien was a renowned Irish dancer and married Flatley in 2006 Niamh O'Brien, a former lead performer in Lord of the Dance and the wife of Riverdance star Michael Flatley, has died at the age of 52. Announcing her death on social media on Monday, Flatley said his "heart is broken". "My gorgeous bride of twenty years has gone to the Lord in Heaven." O'Brien was a renowned Irish dancer who performed the lead role of Saoirse in the Lord of the Dance shows. Flatley described her as "the most loving mother, wife and person and our lives will never be the same without her". The couple had a son, Michael St James, who was born in 2007. A representative for Flatley said that O'Brien died peacefully at the Beacon Hospital in Dublin after an illness, Irish national broadcaster RTÉ reports. "The Flatley and O'Brien families are devastated by Niamh's sudden passing and have asked that their privacy be respected as they come to terms with this heartbreaking loss," said the representative. "They express their sincere gratitude to the doctors, nurses and staff at Beacon Hospital who cared for Niamh over the past few weeks, and to everyone who has offered their kindness and support to the family." title: Flávio Bolsonaro rides right-wing wave to win first round of Brazil election
description: Flávio Bolsonaro's success could be the latest example of a resurgence of right-wing support in Latin America.
body: This video can not be played Watch: How Brazil's dramatic election unfolded Flávio Bolsonaro's success in Brazil's presidential election is being hailed as the result of a "blue wave" - the latest example of a resurgence of right-wing support sweeping Latin America. But despite missing an outright majority – meaning there will be a second round later this month – the unexpectedly clear first round victory leaves his left-wing opponent needing an unprecedented result to retain the presidency. Senator Bolsonaro is the eldest son of ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who became known as the "Trump of the Tropics" due to his ideological alignment with the US president. The younger Bolsonaro is 45 years old and is part of the-right wing political dynasty initiated by his father. He had never before run for the presidency and surprised observers by finishing ahead of the 80-year-old president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, of the Workers' Party. All polls had indicated a close race, with Lula and Bolsonaro statistically tied. But that was not what happened on Sunday. Flávio obtained 56.1 million votes, while Lula received 53.8 million. Part of Bolsonaro's success at the ballot box may be related less to his popularity and more to the numbers of people rejecting Lula. Bolsonaro has presented himself as a dynamic young politician connected to the demands of younger voters, including concerns about rising crime rates in a country that records more than 40,000 homicides annually. But polling groups such as Datafolha, one of Brazil's most respected institutes, suggest that this election has been a battle of rejection rates. Its most recent survey suggested that, on the eve of the election, both candidates had the same rejection rate with voters: 45%. The problem for Lula, however, appeared to be worse. One poll showed that 49% disapproved of his government, while the approval rate stood at 48%. Analysts had been saying that never before in Brazilian history had a president managed to seek re-election with such a high disapproval rate. Voter dissatisfaction with Lula's government shows that the left-wing leader is facing a paradox. The official unemployment rate is at its lowest level in history, around 5.3%. Average income is also at its highest level since records began. Despite the economy's apparent solid performance, Brazilians have shown considerable dissatisfaction with their current living conditions. In an attempt to address this issue, Lula increased by 15% the value of Bolsa Família, the government's main social welfare program. He also banned online gambling, which was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction. Flávio Bolsonaro is part of the-right wing political dynasty initiated by his father A second factor behind Flávio Bolsonaro's success is the way he positioned himself in relation to the Brazilian Supreme Court. He spent much of his campaign criticising the court's actions, in way similar way to his father when he was president. Bolsonaro criticised the conviction of his father by the same court for an attempted coup d'état in 2023, when thousands of people invaded the buildings of the three branches of government in Brasília. It was compared to the 6 January Capitol Hill attack in 2021 in Washington DC. Bolsonaro senior's 27-year prison sentence in 2025 was heavily criticised by the right and remained controversial, particularly because of the role played by Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the case and was close to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro was also able to use another controversy involving Moraes to his political advantage: the Banco Master corruption scandal involving the Brazilian banker Daniel Vorcaro, who was arrested in March. Vorcaro is alleged to have orchestrated one of Brazil's largest financial frauds, embroiling senior figures across the political spectrum. Lula was also impacted by the scandal indirectly, after police suggested Vorcaro had reached out to Moraes to ask for help avoiding arrest. Moraes denies any wrongdoing. Moraes was not appointed by Lula but is seen as his ally, given Moraes presided over Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. A second aspect of Flávio Bolsonaro's victory goes beyond the presidential election. In the Senate, the Liberal Party, led by the Bolsonaros, jumped from 15 seats to 28. The strength of the Bolsonaro family can be seen by the fact that the ex-president's wife, Michelle, and another son, Carlos, were both elected for the Senate. Lula faces an extremely difficult task. Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round. Political analyst Dora Kramer, writing for Folha de S Paulo, argues that both Lula and Flávio will have to focus their efforts on independent voters. Brazilians like to say that politics in their country is so unstable that not even the past is predictable. At this point, a comeback by Lula seems more distant, though not impossible. In any case, even if he succeeds in achieving an unprecedented reversal against Flávio Bolsonaro, one thing is certain: the Bolsonarist right has consolidated itself as an unavoidable political force. title: Jeffrey Archer: successful novelist, disgraced politician and convicted liar
description: Politician and best-selling author whose career was mired in scandal and disgrace.
body: As many have observed, Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, led a life as colourful as the plot in one of his novels. He was, at one time or other, a senior Conservative politician, a best-selling author, a peer of the realm, and a convicted perjurer. Possessed of huge drive, vast wealth and immense personal charm, Archer bounced back from disaster and, more than once, rebuilt a shattered life. But for all his talents, he will be remembered as a man affected by a defective moral compass, whose public humiliation was entirely self-inflicted. Lord and Lady Archer photographed in 2015 Jeffrey Howard Archer was born in north London on 15 April 1940. Within two weeks, his parents moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where they bought a house from John Cleese's mother. Archer's mother Lola was the first woman journalist on the weekly paper, the Weston Mercury. In later life, Archer insisted that his father William, who was some 40 years older than his mother, was a decorated hero of the First World War. In fact, he was a convicted fraudster who, according to a US newspaper, spent the war years conning people in New York. Jeffrey Archer (wearing number 3) runs for Oxford University against Cambridge University at the White City stadium in London in 1964 In 1951, the young Archer went to Wellington School on the edge of Exmoor. Some people mistakenly assumed he had gone to the somewhat more prestigious Wellington College in Berkshire, and he did little to correct them. Archer's academic career was undistinguished, and he left school with three O-levels. He did, however, embark on a fitness regime designed to improve his physique after his originally skinny frame led to taunts from fellow pupils. After school, he drifted. There was a brief spell in the army and then a short course in physical education in America. On his return, he spent five months as a probationary constable in the Metropolitan Police, before quitting to become a physical training instructor at a small prep school in Hampshire. Jeffrey Archer photographed in 1966 with a photograph of his new wife, Mary, on his desk It was while holding a similar job at Dover College that his resume moved into the realms of fantasy. He styled himself Jeffrey Archer, FIFPC, BSc, leading people to assume he had obtained a degree during his time in the United States. In fact, as his unofficial biographer Michael Crick later discovered, Archer's alma mater in the States was, in fact, a bodybuilding club. However, Dover College was so impressed, it backed Archer's bid to go to Oxford as a mature student to do a one-year Diploma of Education course. At Oxford, he excelled in athletics, winning a Blue, although it was doubtful whether his course qualified him to be a bona fide member of the University. He was selected to fight Louth despite objections from Conservative leaders More importantly, it brought him into contact with fellow students who would go on to hold senior positions in politics, finance and the media. He also married Mary Weeden, a chemistry student whose beauty had attracted a long list of suitors. "It was love at first sight for me," the future novelist recalled, "but I don't think it was for her." His public profile had been considerably raised when he managed to persuade The Beatles to come and support a £500,000 fundraising effort for Oxfam, a charity which Archer supported. Margaret Thatcher was swayed by his extrovert personality After serving as a Conservative councillor in London, he was put on the selection list for the safe Tory seat of Louth in Lincolnshire. A reporter on the Times, John Clare, discovered that another charity for which Archer worked alleged he had misused expenses with claims for meals at posh London restaurants. Clare buttonholed Archer and, according to his own account, the would-be candidate burst into tears and asked that the story be quashed. It eventually appeared in the paper but with many of the salient details left out. Threatened with bankruptcy after a disastrous investment, Jeffrey Archer was forced to leave parliament in October 1974 Concerns about Archer's suitability were ignored by the party members in Louth who adopted him. In a by-election in December 1969, he won the seat with a handsome majority. He and Mary set themselves up in an expensive Kensington house and he became a member of Lloyds. He also began to build up his profile in parliament where he was seen as a liberal member of his party. But, in 1974, he suffered a blow after being persuaded to invest in a Canadian company which claimed to have developed a process to cut carbon emissions. It turned out to be a scam. Archer had taken out a second mortgage, as well as borrowing large sums from elsewhere, to raise money for the investment. Threatened with bankruptcy, he was forced to quit his parliamentary seat. Jeffrey Archer became one of Britain's best-selling writers However, he managed to secure an agreement with his creditors and wrote his first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less in 1976. Charting an American immigrant's rise from messenger boy to corporate tycoon, it was inspired, in part, by his own financial problems and did much to solve them. Despite being rubbished by many critics, it sold well in the US and then in Britain, earning Archer a considerable sum in royalties. Three years later, Kane and Abel, a ripping page-turner about the roller-coaster financial fortunes of two men who initially shared nothing but a date of birth, flew off the shelves. A third novel, published in 1984, First Among Equals, about a cutthroat competition to become Prime Minister, cemented Archer's position as one of Britain's best-selling and highest earning authors. Sex worker Monica Coghlan photographed at home in 1987 It enabled him to purchase the Old Vicarage at Grantchester near Cambridge, formerly the home of war poet, Rupert Brooke, as well as a penthouse in London. title: Former American Idol contestant sentenced to life in prison for murdering wife
description: Caleb Flynn, a former music pastor from Ohio, fatally shot his wife Ashley in February before trying to cover it up.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'I am so sorry' - Caleb Flynn apologises to wife's family A US man who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for murdering his wife. Caleb Flynn, 40, was found guilty last week after a short deliberation by the jury, which rejected his claim that an intruder broke into his Ohio home and shot his wife, Ashley Flynn, as she slept. He was also found guilty of eight additional charges, including aggravated murder and tampering with evidence. Letters from his two daughters were read in court during the sentencing hearing on Monday, pleading with him to finally admit his guilt and questioning why he killed their mother. Flynn, a former music pastor, fatally shot his wife, a 37-year-old teacher, in February before staging their home in Tipp City to appear as if someone had broken in through the garage. Flynn claims he was asleep when he heard gunshots and found his wife dead in bed after finding the garage door open. Their two children, ages 9 and 11, were also sleeping in the house at the time. His wife's sister, Kayla Keyt, read a victim impact statement saying the murder had caused his daughters to question their Christian faith and had "shattered a family who trusted you". One of his daughter's letters read: "Dear Daddy, I don't even know where to start. How could you do such a thing?" She also said: "Mommy was the perfect person... And then you chose to kill the only mother I ever had." The other daughter's letter began "Dear Caleb", rather than addressing him as her father, and asked him to "tell everyone what you did it and receive your outcome". "You made me feel like an idiot thinking I could trust you," his daughter said. She added that she continues to have faith in God, and that she will never visit her father in prison. Flynn sobbed loudly as the letters from his children were read. The sentencing hearing also included Flynn reading a statement expressing love for his family, apologising for unspecified "decisions" that he made, and again claiming that he did not kill his wife. "I made vows to Ashley on our wedding day. I failed those vows," he said. Judge Jeannine Pratt called Flynn an "extreme" risk to the public as she imposed her sentence. The murder verdict last week followed eight days of testimony, during which several incriminating text messages Flynn sent to his former mistress, Alleigha Botner, were read out and AI-generated songs were played that prosecutors said he made for her. Evidence presented during trial included police body camera footage and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch from around the time of the murder when he claimed to have been sleeping. The prosecution also called dozens of witnesses, including Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church. Botner read aloud in court some of their 100,000 text messages, including one where Flynn wrote: "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail." In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone." This video can not be played Watch: Moment Caleb Flynn is found guilty of murder Flynn did not testify during the trial, and his defence team called no witnesses. His lawyer, Patrick Mulligan, has said he plans to file a notice of appeal, telling reporters last week: "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design." Mulligan argued that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder and questioned why Flynn was being accused of tampering with evidence because his gun could not be found. This gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open. Prosecutor Paul Watkins read a statement from Ashley Flynn's family in court after the verdict in September, saying: "Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart." "She loved people," the statement continued. "Most of all, she loved being a Mum." Flynn briefly appeared on American Idol in 2013, saying that he loved his wife "more than anything". title: Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election
description: Calling of a snap election was not a knee-jerk reaction from Pedro Sánchez but a carefully thought-out manoeuvre, Guy Hedgecoe reports from Madrid.
body: The chair of Sánchez's Socialist Party (PSOE) Cristina Narbona and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during a meeting earlier on Monday Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat. On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them. That parliamentary result confirmed that Sánchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority. But as has so often been the case throughout Sánchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre. His government has been struggling in recent months. His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos Cerdán and José Luis Ábalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing. In addition, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that Gómez and Sánchez vehemently deny. Meanwhile, Sánchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister. Thousands have protested in cities across Spain against the government's handling of the influx of migrants to Ceuta Although Sánchez had insisted until recently that he would see out the legislature and not call elections until next summer, his government had looked increasingly unlikely to make it that far. The wave of outrage which has exploded in recent days over housing has provided him with the ideal reason to call elections early - and a welcome issue away from Ceuta and the allegations of corruption. Appealing to his own party's voters and those further to the left on Monday, he called for voters to "mobilise and ensure that parliament gives us a much bigger, progressive majority with which to defeat the elites, conquer social rights and keep transforming Spain". On the upcoming campaign trail, Sánchez can point to the fact that his adversaries on the right - such as the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox - voted against his government's housing measures, which sought to prevent the eviction of tenants, improving the conditions of their contracts and preventing investors from buying residential property. About 50 marches calling for greater protections for tenants took place in Spain on Saturday, in cities including Madrid - pictured here - Valencia and Barcelona The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the Sánchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists. However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that Sánchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive. Earlier this year, when Sánchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then. However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left. Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides Sánchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career. title: Gabriel in Man Utd team photo but no hint of reconciliation
description: As he prepares to celebrate his 16th birthday, the rift between Manchester United and JJ Gabriel shows no sign of being healed.
body: JJ Gabriel celebrates scoring his hat-trick for Manchester United in their Uefa Youth League game against Sabah FK at Leigh Sports Village on 10 September JJ Gabriel has been included in Manchester United's official team photo for this season but there remains no hint of a reconciliation with the club as new details of his efforts to leave Old Trafford emerge. The teenage forward - who turns 16 on Tuesday - features in the photographs that were released on Monday. It is understood the pictures were taken on 8 September - two days before he played his final game for the club and informed them of his intention to leave. It is virtually certain his next involvement in a United game will be as an opposition player. United still hold his registration and, according to sources close to Old Trafford, the club have made multiple attempts to reconcile the situation as part of their duty of care to the teenager. So far, it has been to no avail. Gabriel is now a target for several of Europe's top clubs, with Real Madrid and Barcelona among those taking a keen interest. He now has a European Union passport, which is thought could smooth his passage to the continent. However, while no clubs have approached United so far, they would consider legal action if any evidence of an illegal inducement by a club or agent - that would contravene regulations in relation to young players - was to emerge. JJ Gabriel (third from left, middle row) in a combined picture of Man Utd men's and women's teams released on Monday While tensions between Gabriel's camp and United had been simmering for a number of months, sources have told BBC Sport the player's decision to seek a move away was ultimately triggered by his non-inclusion in Michael Carrick’s side for the Champions League encounter with Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September. The youngster's camp had expressed a desire for Gabriel to be used as a substitute against Sabah - which, on paper, was the easiest of United's league-phase games. Sources say the prospect of the Londoner coming on against Brighton in the EFL Cup on 16 September was also discussed, with United officials subsequently insistent that was the plan. Had he played in either match, Gabriel would have become United's youngest ever player. However, by the time the encounter with Fabian Hurzeler's side arrived, the striker had already told the club of his intention to quit and had left the country. Gabriel could not play against Sabah because he had not been registered on United's Uefa A list of players when it was announced on 3 September. The precise reasons for this have not been made clear. It did not prevent him scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game against them at Leigh Sports Village earlier on 10 September. While he has not been back to United since, it is not clear whether anything significant happened after that game. For their part, United believe they made it clear they view Gabriel as immensely important to their first-team future, even though sources have indicated the player did not report for the start of the academy's pre-season training schedule at the beginning of July - a week earlier than the senior squad - despite being asked to do so. Sources also say they lobbied the Premier League to allow the forward to use "JJ Gabriel" on the back of his shirt - which they believe underlined their commitment to the academy prospect. Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - but he is reported to have changed his name for commercial purposes. In addition, United say they have provided Gabriel with first-team care and services - included regular meetings with senior coaches and nutritionists. That he was included in the senior team photo is also viewed as further evidence of their commitment to his development and transition into first-team football. JJ Gabriel (right) collects his Manchester United Under-18 player of the year award at Old Trafford in May When Gabriel committed himself to United in the summer of 2025, the lure of breaking through at United, and the targets he could aim for, was strong. He was only 14 at the time but already he was looking towards the first team. Within a couple of months, Gabriel was called into senior training sessions by Ruben Amorim. Expectation grew to such an extent that interim boss Darren Fletcher was asked if it was possible the forward could make his competitive bow in the FA Cup third-round tie with Brighton in January. Fletcher - then Gabriel's coach at under-18 level - said no, believing the youngster wasn't physically ready. However, as he continued to excel at under-18 level, it seemed a case of when, not if, Gabriel would be given his chance. He ended the 2025-26 campaign as the Premier League's Under-18 player of the year and picked up the same award at United. It seemed certain he would be involved at the start of pre-season, when the majority of United's senior players would be absent after their World Cup exertions. What happened instead solidified existing doubts of those close to Gabriel that United were the right club for him. First, he was not part of Carrick's squad for the trip to Helsinki to face Wrexham in a friendly. On 24 July, he was an unused substitute against Rosenborg in Trondheim, a match in which Carrick made 10 outfield changes. Five of those players have since been sold or loaned out. Gabriel finally got his chance against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm on 1 August, when he replaced Bryan Mbeumo for the final eight minutes. That turned out to be it. He was on the bench for the final two games against Leeds and AC Milan, but did not get on. Against Leeds, former FA Youth Cup team-mate Dan Armer and 18-year-old newcomer Tynan Thompson were both introduced. title: England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender
description: With Harry Kane set to equal Peter Shilton's all-time England appearance record, where does he rank among England greats?
body: Harry Kane is England's greatest goalscorer and is will equal Peter Shilton's record of 125 caps if he features against the Czech Republic at Wembley. Harry Kane will write another chapter in his illustrious England history by equalling Peter Shilton's record tally of 125 caps if he plays a part in the Uefa Nations League meeting with the Czech Republic at Wembley. England's captain is already his country's record scorer with 89 goals in 124 appearances in a full international career he started by opening his account 79 seconds into his debut. Since that 4-0 win against Lithuania at Wembley in March 2015, he has been England's mainstay. He is still irreplaceable at 33 and their top scorer in major tournaments with 21 goals in 36 appearances across six of those showpieces, ahead of Gary Lineker's 10 goals in 18 appearances. He is in the process of building a monument to his goalscoring brilliance at elite level as he currently stands 36 goals ahead of England's second-highest scorer Wayne Rooney, who boasts a record of 53 goals in 120 games. Kane is unquestionably England men's most important and influential player of the modern era. The only blemish on his magnificent career is the failure – not his alone it must be stressed – to add to the one men's World Cup won in 1966. Irrespective of that space for silverware on his CV, how highly does Kane rank in the pantheon of greats who have represented the England men's team? Could he even be the greatest? He has made himself a serious contender. The great number nine decline - where have England's strikers gone? Can Kane buck history and win Ballon d'Or? This argument will instantly cut away from Kane to Bobby Moore, the elegant, unflappable defender who remains the only England captain to lift the World Cup, leading his team to triumph at Wembley in July 1966 as West Germany were beaten 4-2. Moore was only 25 at the time, and had enjoyed success at club level with West Ham United, winning the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup before the World Cup. He won 108 caps between May 1962 and November 1973. And then, of course, the conversation must turn to Sir Bobby Charlton, who survived the Munich Air Disaster with Manchester United in 1958 to become arguably England's most famous footballer of his era. Charlton was a global beacon of dignity and world-class ability, winning the World Cup then, two years later, captaining Manchester United when they became the first English team to win the European Cup, scoring twice as Benfica were beaten 4-1 at Wembley. He remains third on England's list of scorers, with 49 goals in 106 games. Sir Geoff Hurst will always claim a special place with his hat-trick in the World Cup final win, while many others will have their supporters from recent times, including the likes of Wayne Rooney and David Beckham. Former England midfielder Danny Murphy, said: "Bobby Moore will always be in people's conversation. Sir Bobby Charlton also, because of what they did and the memories they created. "As you move forward, for me as a kid Gazza [Paul Gascoigne] burst on the scene and became a hero, especially as a creative midfield player myself. "I think Rooney was arguably the most all-round footballer we have ever had, the most talented I've seen – but no-one can argue with Harry Kane's quality, numbers and longevity. It is the record of an England great." He added: "There is one thing there is no debate about. Harry Kane is England's greatest goalscorer. "No-one can take that away from him. The numbers over such a period of longevity are incredible. This, in itself, deserves all the accolades in the world. To stay at that level and not have anybody displace him is testimony to his ability and professionalism. "He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career. "Is he England's greatest player? This is all about opinions and eras, but his record and longevity alone informs you that he is an England great. He is in that elite group." Kane's status as an England great is beyond question. Where he stands in that list of greats will be shaped by eras and opinions, according to former internationals Paul Robinson and Murphy. Robinson told BBC Sport that the scale of Kane's greatness may only be fully appreciated in years to come. He said: "Harry Kane is an England great. There is no argument. He will always be part of that conversation now. "I think we are guilty in the modern era of underestimating what we've got in front of us. We are quite happy to look through rose-tinted spectacles at what we had in the past. "We will talk about Bobby Moore and Sir Bobby Charlton, but football now is a completely different game. The life of a footballer is completely different and it's almost like they are playing a different game. "What Bobby Moore and Sir Bobby Charlton achieved, nobody in an England shirt has done since. You respect what they did in the era, and the status and legacy that comes with winning the World Cup and everything else they did, but we must also say it is a different game now." Harry Kane replaced Wayne Rooney, who is second behind him in England's all-time record scorers' standings, for his England debut in March 2015. Kane's double in Saturday's 7-0 win in Croatia took his tally to 11 goals in 12 games for England in this calendar year. He has also scored in six consecutive England away games, with only Sir Tom Finney having a longer run, seven between September 1946 and May 1948. Last season alone, Ballon d'Or contender Kane scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for England and his club Bayern Munich. He has scored five hat-tricks in an England career which includes 110 starts,

title: Hidden illegal poker den on industrial estate discovered by police
description: The room was fitted out with six poker tables, a large prize wheel and fridges with drinks and snacks.
body: Noor Rassam and Panayiotis Karayiannis ran illegal poker games from an industrial unit in Splott, Cardiff Two men have been sentenced for their involvement in an unlicensed gambling den on an industrial estate in Cardiff. Noor Rassam, 29, and Panayiotis Karayiannis, 30, both from Pontprennau, Cardiff, operated illegal poker games from an upstairs room in an industrial unit in Splott between August 2022 and February 2024. The room had been fitted out with six poker tables, a large prize wheel, seating areas, and fridges stocked with drinks and snacks. On 2 October, the pair appeared at Cardiff Crown Court for possessing and transferring criminal funds obtained by running the den and received a suspended sentence. A Proceeds of Crime Act hearing has been set for April next year. The illegal poker games were available to join both in-person and online and were promoted through WhatsApp messages, according to Tarian, the Regional Organised Crime Unit (ROCU) for southern Wales. The unit said organisers actively promoted the illegal poker games to people involved in serious crime, including drug dealers and organised crime groups, helping to facilitate further criminal activity. The online games were hosted through a subscription-based poker application under the account name Fish Tank Online, while the in-person events were initially advertised as Ding Ding Poker before later being rebranded as Fish Tank Poker Cardiff. The industrial unit was accessed through a fire exit and monitored by CCTV cameras controlled by Rassam and Karayiannis. Inside the building there was an office containing gambling paraphernalia, including poker chips, tokens and records detailing money paid and owed. The room also featured a cashier's window protected by Perspex, with a small opening for financial transactions. Investigators found that Rassam received approximately £260,000 in third-party payments while the venue was operating, while Karayiannis received around £124,000. Both accounts showed numerous transactions referencing "poker." A text message advert for Poker Sunday The crime came to light after intelligence was received by the Gambling Commission and passed on to Tarian ROCU. In February 2024 warrants were executed and both men were arrested following an investigation. Officers seized cash, documentation, digital devices and other high-value items. Officers also established that the pair profited from the games by taking a commission from each poker hand, known within the industry as "the rake", rather than by directly wagering against players. Det Con Charles Lan, of Tarian ROCU, said the pair generated "substantial profits" from the illegal gambling business, which was never "declared for tax purposes". Lan said: "Their criminal enterprise provided them with significant personal benefits, funding a lavish lifestyle that included foreign holidays and other high-value spending." He said individuals had lost "significant sums of money" taking part in the poker games, "with some becoming indebted to the organisers". "Unlike legitimate gambling operators, there were no safeguards in place to identify or support vulnerable people, nor any measures to protect those experiencing gambling addiction." The pair profited from the games by taking a commission from each poker hand, rather than by directly wagering against players Both Rassam and Karayiannis changed their pleas to guilty to offences of possessing and transferring criminal property, contrary to the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, on the first day of their trial at Cardiff Crown Court. They were sentenced to three years in prison, suspended for three years. Lan said the sentence showed that unlicensed gambling was not a "victimless offence" and warned those who profit from it while ignoring safeguards designed to protect people "can expect to be brought before the courts". Sue Young, Gambling Commission executive director of operations, said: "This case emerged after we received information about an illegal gambling den. The message is clear - if you run an illegal casino, there will be a tip-off, you will be caught, and there will be significant consequences. "We will continue to work with partners and take action against those who run illegal gambling operations in Great Britain." title: It's been a terrible year for farming, Jeremy Clarkson tells Tory conference
description: The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle.
body: This video can not be played Jeremy Clarkson: Farming this year was 'an absolute disaster' Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham. The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle by rising costs, but he was optimistic about the future. He was greeted by loud applause from the Tory faithful, but joked that "a lot of people have come dressed as seats, I notice, around the edges there". In a question and answer session alongside land agent Charlie Ireland, he also criticised the economic conditions faced by business owners, asking: "Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?" Clarkson - who also hosts ITV's Who Wants to be a Millionaire - was introduced to the stage by the Conservative shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins. Asked what kind of year he had had on the farm, Clarkson said: "We worked really hard all year and we ended up with, I think I'm right in saying, three ounces of hen food. "It was an absolute disaster on the farming side but, I mean, luckily we've got other projects going on now. "But the farming is very, very difficult – very, very difficult at the moment." He added: "I'm very fortunate that I do have other income streams and newspaper columns, but if you're an ordinary farmer, it's not just the weather. "Remember, it's as Charlie was saying, the attacks come from everywhere – whether it's Iran or Ukraine or taxes or energy costs – whatever it might be, it's just relentless." The TV presenter has long been a Conservative supporter and was involved in the campaign against the Labour government's inheritance tax plans for farmers. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government would levy inheritance tax on family farms in the party's first budget. But the plan was watered down last year following the farmers' campaign and pressure from some of Labour's rural MPs. Responding to Clarkson's comments, a government source said: "We are working with farmers to strengthen domestic food production and make supply chains more resilient as we build a stronger and more profitable farming sector together." Clarkson also joked about comments by Labour MP Jenny Riddell-Carpenter who said the Britain of country pubs and black Labradors was a "nostalgic" false memory. He joked that he was a "socialist" because he drinks lager and has two fox red Labradors, after it was reported Riddell-Carpenter told a Labour conference fringe event she feared the far right deciding what the vision of rural areas is. Riddell-Carpenter had said: "It'll be that warm ale, a black Labrador by your feet in a pub that doesn't exist, and with symbolism of fox hunting all around them. It'll be a very far-right nostalgic vision of Britain that we don't want to have, (that) never really existed." title: Southport Inquiry: Violent material left online for weeks
description: The public inquiry has found violent content and weapons sales remained online after being reported.
body: The public inquiry into the knife attacks is looking into "violence-fixated individuals" Violent material was still available online two weeks after being reported in more than 80% of cases, a review for the Southport Inquiry has found. The hearing was told a report examining the 'real-world accessibility' of violent content and weapons sales online found concerning material on platforms including X, TikTok and Instagram. The public inquiry, which is in its second phase, is examining issues surrounding 'violence-fixated individuals' following the knife attack at a dance class in Southport on 29 July 2024. Three girls were killed and 23 other children suffered physical or psychological injuries. Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, were killed in the attack at the Taylor Swift-themed dance class. Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe and Alice da Silva Aguiar died in the attack This phase of the inquiry is examining how the risks posed by violence-fixated individuals can be managed, and the role the internet and social media play in influencing and enabling them. Nicholas Moss KC, counsel to the inquiry, said: "The report outlines the result of a single eight-hour search across a selection of online platforms including X, TikTok, Reddit, Instagram and Discord. "It is right to recognise that there was a spectrum of material of concern. "It ranges from material with violent overtones, but which might be argued to be newsworthy, to material which can fairly be categorised as very violent or strong gore material." Moss said 98.9% of the material was publicly accessible and 92.3% was not subject to any age restrictions. All of the material was reported to the platforms, but a week later 87.9% of it remained live, the inquiry heard. Moss said 14 days after it had been reported, 83.8% of the content was still available. He said the platform providers would be asked about the report and "what appears to be, in some cases, arguable delay and failures to remove the material even when it had been reported to them". Representatives of platforms, including TikTok, Reddit, X and Alphabet, the parent company of Google, are expected to give evidence to the inquiry in November. The inquiry which is chaired by Sir Adrian Fulford continues on Wednesday The first phase of the inquiry heard how Axel Rudakubana, who carried out the Southport knife attacks, had viewed degrading, violent and misogynistic material online which "fed" his fascination with violence. In his report earlier this year, inquiry chairman Sir Adrian Fulford found the attack "could and should have been prevented". William Chapman, representing the families of Elsie, Alice and Bebe, said Rudakubana was able to build an arsenal of weapons through the internet. He said: "On one tab of his browser he could indulge in his lust for gore and on the other he could make it real by ordering what he wanted from online retailers. "The internet played a pivotal role in what happened to the victims in this case. "Whatever the current state of the evidence about the influence of the internet on young minds generally, action to limit its pernicious influence on those fascinated by violence cannot wait (for) academic studies." The inquiry continues on Wednesday, when evidence is expected from a panel of experts who have reviewed six other cases of violence-fixated individuals to identify themes. title: Katie Price's ex urged girl not to tell, court hears
description: Jurors at the trial of Kieran Hayler hear recorded police evidence from the alleged victim in court.
body: Kieran Hayler denies the charges and has suggested his ex-wife, Katie Price, had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended Katie Price's ex-husband, who is accused of raping a 13-year-old girl, told her to "not tell anyone" and said he might "get in trouble for this", a court has heard. Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault of the teenager in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies. Earlier, jurors were told that on the first alleged occasion, Hayler told the 13-year-old he really liked her and began speaking to her about having sex. He told her it was a "special thing" and they should do it, before he raped her, the court heard. The court was played the complainant's police interview in which she said Hayler told her how special and "important" the first time was. She said: "He started crying and saying, 'Maybe I shouldn't take it away from you, it's so important'." The complainant said she did not have a "conversation" with Hayler afterwards, and recalled thinking "I was probably a bit young". Hayler allegedly raped the girl again on two further occasions. The second occasion, she said, was two or three weeks later. On this occasion she said she remembered waking up to Hayler being there, and after, he acted like "like nothing had happened". On the third alleged occasion, the court heard Hayler told her she should not tell anyone, and then sexually assaulted her. She said he told her: "You can't talk about it, you can't tell anyone, I might get in trouble for this." It is alleged he grabbed her hand and put it down his trousers. Speaking after this alleged incident, the complainant told police: "I think by that point I knew it wasn't quite right, he kept telling me to 'shh', I had to be secretive and not tell anyone." She told police: "I tried to forget it for so many years." In 2021, the complainant contacted the NSPCC charity which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation. Hayler was first interviewed by police in January 2022 and denied any of the allegations took place and that anything sexual occurred. He was married to media personality Price at the time of the alleged incidents, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021. Hayler suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations form part of this, the court heard. The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families. Price is expected to be a witness in the trial which is expected to last about a week. title: Prisoner took his own life after terror order had 'substantial impact' on mental state, inquest finds
description: Akhtar Uddin was jailed for breaching Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures in 2020.
body: A prisoner took his own life after strict terrorism control measures imposed by the government had a "substantial impact" on his mental state, an inquest jury has concluded. Akhtar Uddin, 35, a builder from east London, died in HMP Wandsworth on Christmas Day 2021 after being jailed the previous year for breaching Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures (TPIM). The jury at Inner West London Coroner's Court also found the prison service had failed to provide the support that Uddin needed. Jurors concluded that Uddin died due to an action he took but said that it was "not possible to determine whether he intended the outcome to be his death". First alleged neo-Nazi under special terror powers The powers being used to disrupt a terror group Prior to being jailed in February 2020 for breaching the TPIM order, Uddin had served a sentence for racially or religiously aggravated harassment. TPIMs allow the authorities to control people whom the government believes are involved in terrorism, but who are not facing criminal charges. The home secretary acts on advice from MI5 when imposing TPIMs. Subjects of TPIMs face measures such as wearing an electronic tag, curfews, relocation to a different part of the country, bans on internet use, controls on finances, and limits on who they can meet and where they can go. Breaches can result in a terrorism conviction and prison sentence. TPIMs can currently last up to five years, up from a maximum of two years when Uddin was under one. Uddin breached the measures 12 times by withdrawing more money than he was permitted. The inquest heard he largely spent it on drugs. He had over 20 previous criminal convictions - none of which were for terrorism offences. The inquest, which was the first ever to consider the impact of TPIMs, heard that Uddin believed the order was originally imposed because he had made reckless statements while under the influence of drugs, but that he insisted he was not a terrorist. It is understood he was alleged to have made verbal threats and associated with people regarded by MI5 as being involved in terrorist activity. Coroner Bernard Richmond KC said Uddin was "loved and loving" but was "not someone without his troubles" and these revolved around his drug use. The coroner said he will be issuing a report to the government out of concern about a risk to other people under the terrorism control measures. When the TPIM was first imposed on Uddin in January 2020, he was forcibly relocated to the West Midlands after being arrested at the prison gates in front of his sister who had come to meet him on release. The full reasons for a person being on a TPIM are typically kept secret, even from the person subject to the TPIM, because they are based on MI5 intelligence. The inquest heard that Uddin feared the TPIM would be re-imposed when he left prison early in 2022, and that he would again breach it due to drugs. Today the inquest jury concluded the following: "We are satisfied that the imposition of the original TPIM and its unusually restrictive nature had a substantial impact on the mental state of Akhtar Uddin." "We are satisfied that the fear of a likely reimposition of such a restrictive TPIM, and its possibly never-ending nature, had a significant impact on the mental state of Akhtar in prison." "We are satisfied, as a result of the consistent evidence that prison services were unaware of TPIM restrictions and their likely impact on Akhtar, there was a failure to provide support most suitably targeted to Akhtar's specific needs and situations." A governor at HMP Wandsworth accepted in evidence that lack of knowledge of TPIMs by prison staff had resulted in "unintentionally cruel" treatment of Uddin. Giving evidence, Uddin's sister Jasmine said that, in the weeks before his death, he had described "counter terrorism officers" questioning him in prison and saying he would never get off the TPIM. A statement from Uddin's family, issued by their solicitors Birnberg Peirce, said they welcomed the inquest's findings. "Although nothing can bring back their loving son, brother and uncle, they hope that this will make a real difference to those who are currently at the mercy of this inhumane regime." His former solicitor, Amer Ahmad, had told Uddin in autumn 2021 there were "highly limited prospects" that he would succeed in having the TPIM legally overturned, the inquest heard. Dr Richard Latham, an NHS consultant forensic psychiatrist, appeared as an expert witness for the coroner and concluded that Uddin had an undiagnosed "personality disorder", associated "psychological problems and vulnerabilities", and this resulted in impulsiveness, grievance and paranoia. He said Uddin probably assumed the worst about the TPIM in future, and that this prospect would have created "distress and a sense of hopelessness". Dr Latham added TPIMs are intended to create a "degree of isolation," but that plays on psychological vulnerability and can create "emotional isolation". Uddin also "felt a sense of injustice" about being branded a terrorist, Dr Latham said. The inquest heard there was little or no awareness by staff in HMP Wandsworth of TPIMs. The coroner said "very few people, if any" knew about Uddin's TPIM, the revocation, or potential re-imposition. In the absence of jurors, the coroner said there was much assessment by the state of Uddin's potential risk to others, but he had seen "nothing" showing any assessment of risks to him. He said there is a "paucity of support for people subject to TPIMs" and there is a potential risk to other people subjected to them. For this reason, he added, he would be writing a preventing future deaths report. There has been a trend towards TPIM subjects having mental health issues. The independent reviewer of terrorism legislation, Jonathan Hall KC, has noted in previous reports that the "Home Office recognises poor mental health as a dominant feature amongst recent TPIM s

title: King's funding for Andrew not to be used for legal action against police
description: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action over search warrants issued ahead of his arrest in February.
body: King Charles provides a private allowance for Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been told that the allowance given to him by King Charles should not be used to fund his legal action against Thames Valley Police. The King uses his own private money to support his brother and to accommodate him on his estate in Sandringham. But a royal source said that this funding should not be used for a legal challenge being launched by Mountbatten-Windsor against the search warrants issued ahead of his arrest in February. The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the United States. Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor photographed leaving a police station in February Mountbatten-Windsor is not a working royal - so Buckingham Palace no longer speaks on his behalf and is not involved in his legal battle. But a royal source said the King's financial support for his brother should not be directed towards paying for the judicial review that Mountbatten-Windsor is seeking. It's not been disclosed how much the King gives to Mountbatten-Windsor, but the funding for his brother was part of the arrangement when the former Prince Andrew was moved from his previous home at Royal Lodge in Windsor. At the time of Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, the King said the "law must take its course", and the Palace has made clear it is not part of the former Prince Andrew's legal pushback. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are understood to be challenging the lawfulness of search warrants used for Sandringham and at Royal Lodge relating to his arrest. Thames Valley Police has confirmed it is "engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court". It added: "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further." Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants. A court hearing will be held on Thursday afternoon as part of this bid to quash the warrants, with the hearing set to begin in private. The judge will initially hear a request by the police to keep some documents private. Sign up here to get the latest royal stories and analysis every week with our Royal Watch newsletter. Those outside the UK can sign up here. title: British Museum boss 'sorry' for Bayeux Tapestry visitor issues
description: Changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition were made after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.
body: The head of the British Museum has apologised for the experience some visitors have had at its blockbuster Bayeux Tapestry exhibition. The London institution has announced changes to how visitors see the historic work over concerns of overcrowding. "Anyone that doesn't have a good experience, we're really sorry about that and we want to put it right," Nicholas Cullinan told the BBC's culture and media editor Katie Razzall. The new plans include longer opening hours, an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage. Some people reported waits of up to two hours. Last week, hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early for a private event. "You don't want anyone that comes to see it to have a bad experience, so our focus is very much on getting it right and learning lessons," Cullinan said. "Obviously we want everyone that comes to have a fantastic experience. To put it into context, we're three weeks into the exhibition run. Next week, we'll hit our 100,000th visitor, which is a pretty extraordinary statistic. The vast number of visitors report having a very good experience." Asked if the museum team had asked the embroidery's home museum in Bayeux for advice on queue management and timings, Cullinan said they had. He also denied the museum had let too many people book tickets and said that the issues arose because visitors want to spend more time with the work than expected. The problem "isn't just the interest, it's that people want to spend more time than anticipated. And that's a good thing. We want people to come and enjoy it, but it means we have to adjust accordingly and that's what we're doing," Cullinan said. Some visitors have been spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry, meaning others have to move through more quickly, he said. British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues Bayeux Tapestry arrives in UK for first time in 900 years under police guard Bayeux Tapestry unveiled to UK public for first time at British Museum While the museum is reimbursing those who have been turned away, when asked if they might also compensate people for travel costs, Cullinan said it was "a possibility", but added that "obviously this is an incredibly expensive exhibition to mount." The exhibition has also faced some criticism over accessibility, but Cullinan said they had done "everything they could", given the stipulation that the tapestry had to be laid flat, making it more difficult for wheelchair users to see. Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day. Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when additional tickets go on sale in October and January. Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared to the €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free. The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain. Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses. The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027. The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago. title: It's A Sin star 'keeps you guessing' in Wales-set thriller
description: Callum Scott Howells stars opposite fellow Welsh actor Gabrielle Creevy in The Night They Vanished.
body: Callum Scott Howells stars in The Night They Vanished, adapted from the novel by Vanessa Savage It's A Sin actor Callum Scott Howells says his role in a new thriller, set and filmed in Wales, offers "exactly the kind of challenge I love". The Night They Vanished, an adaptation of the novel by Vanessa Savage, also stars Welsh actress Gabrielle Creevy. The six-part mystery follows Anna (Creevy) as she discovers her childhood house is listed on a true‑crime website as the scene of her family's future deaths. While police say it's a hoax, Anna's family have vanished. Scott Howells plays the role of Cai, who runs the website but denies posting the listing, describing the character as "charming, complicated and never quite what he seems". Howells, from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, won the Bafta Cymru for best actor in 2021 for his portrayal of Colin in Russell T Davies' 1980s-set drama It's A Sin. "He could be the love of Anna's life, or the centre of a terrifying conspiracy," he said of the role of Cai. "Playing someone who keeps you guessing is exactly the kind of challenge I love." Gabrielle Creevy plays Anna in the new six-part thriller Port Talbot-born Creevy appeared in Netflix series Black Doves and The Guest as well as award-winning drama In My Skin, for which she won Bafta Cymru best actress for her portrayal of teenage protagonist Bethany. Creevy described the part of Anna as "a gift of a role". "Anna is a firecracker - sharp, loyal, and carrying more hurt than she lets on," she said. "The moment her past comes roaring back, she's forced into a nightmare she thought she had escaped. "I can't wait for audiences to unravel the truth with her." The show also stars Tamzin Outhwaite as Anna's stepmother and Steffan Rhodri, best known for playing Dave Coaches in Gavin & Stacey, as Anna's father. Fellow Welsh creative Angharad Elen - who adapted the original novel with Hannah Daniel - said she was "particularly proud to see the series set and filmed on my home turf". The series is produced by CliffEdge Entertainment, part of BBC Studios, in association with Channel 4, and was backed by the Welsh government via Creative Wales. It will air on Channel 4 later this year. title: ECB will 'look at' funding women's Windies Test if needed
description: The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) will “look at” the unusual step of funding a women’s Test in the West Indies next year in order to aid England’s Ashes preparations.
body: England have played only one Test since the last women's Ashes - a defeat by India The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) would "look at" the unusual step of funding a women's Test in the West Indies next year in order to aid England's Ashes preparations. The Test in the Caribbean, part of a multi-format series in the spring of 2027, was announced in 2024 and is scheduled before England's bid to regain the Ashes from Australia. Last week, Cricket West Indies (CWI) announced a wide range of money-saving measures, including cuts to player contracts. In March, a women's Test that West Indies were due to host against Australia was cancelled, though the white-ball element of that tour went ahead. There have been no discussions between the ECB and CWI about cancelling the Test. The tour as a whole – including three T20s and three one-day internationals in April and May of next year – is not under threat, though exact dates and venues are still to be confirmed. Asked by BBC Sport if the Test was in doubt, ECB chair Richard Thompson said: "I hope not. That's not expected to be cancelled. I hope it will take place." However, when it was put to Thompson that the ECB may need to provide some funding for the Test to take place, he said his organisation would "look at" the situation should it arise. Governing bodies usually have reciprocal arrangements for the home board to pick up the logistical expenses of the visiting team, including things like travel and accommodation. In the West Indies, these can be inflated by the cost of flying West Indies and visiting players between islands. Last week, CWI said it has spent more than $80m on domestic air travel in the past 15 years. Thompson pointed to a similarly unusual situation when the Zimbabwe men's team played a Test in England last year, with the ECB paying the visitors a touring fee. "We want that Test match to play out," said Thompson. "It's very important for us because our first women's match in the Ashes is the Headingley Test, so we need a good red-ball warm-up. "We've got to be playing somewhere and we'd much prefer that to be the West Indies. "We all have a huge sympathy for the West Indies, we all want to see a successful West Indian nation. They have very unique challenges and I hope through the International Cricket Council and others we can find a way through this." The first match of the multi-format women's Ashes series is the sole Test at Headingley in June – the only Test, men's or women's, staged north of Nottingham next summer. England have played one Test since they lost every game on the Ashes tour of Australia in early 2025 – a defeat by India at Lord's earlier this year. They have not played West Indies in a women's Test since 1979, while West Indies have not played a Test against anyone since a trip to Pakistan in 2004. The Test in West Indies is one part of England's Ashes Test preparations. In January, the squad will take part in a 10-day red-ball training camp in India. In 2023, England played Australia A and Australia played England A as Test warm-up matches and that arrangement could be replicated in 2027. Plans for domestic players to potentially be involved in some red-ball cricket in the early part of next season are also being finalised. Thompson was speaking at Lord's as the ECB launched initiatives to take cricket to more than 1,700 state secondary schools and more than 3,500 teachers. 'Cricket for Teachers' and 'Secondary Countdown Cricket' are part of the ECB's aim to reach half of all state secondary schools in England and Wales by the end of 2028. Earlier this year, a report by the Sutton Trust found cricket to be one of the most elitist jobs in the country, with 59% of male professionals and 50% of women privately educated. "We really want teachers to upskill and be able to coach," said Thompson. "The second part is to be able to do something no other team sport can do, which is bring boys and girls together until the age of 16. "This adds to the pathway. It's another stepping stone for a late developer, or an opportunity for someone to think they want to play the game properly, with a hardball. "It's meaningful in that we want to reach one and a half million children who have never played the game before. That's a significant programme and the ambition that sits behind this."
