title: Murdered children had been 'petrified', inquest told
description: Michelle Pearson and her four children were murdered in an arson attack at their home in Walkden.
body: The four Pearson children died during the petrol bomb attack, and their mother died 20 months later. Four children had been "petrified" by a series of attacks on their home before a petrol bomb attack killed them all, an inquest has heard. Demi Pearson, 15, her brother Brandon, eight, and sisters Lacie, seven, Lia, three, died at their home in Jackson Street in Walkden in Greater Manchester in December 2017. Their mother Michelle, 37, was badly burned and died in August 2019. The inquest at Bolton Coroner's Court - scheduled to last eight weeks - heard that Michelle had told police she did not feel safe in the house, which had been covered in graffiti and had its windows smashed. Zak Bolland and David Worrall were jailed for life in 2018 for the murder of the four children, and in 2021 also convicted of Michelle's murder. Bolland was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum of 40 years and Worrall was sentenced to life with a minimum of 37 years in jail. Two weeks before the fatal attack, Bolland smashed windows at the house with a hammer, leaving glass everywhere. In a statement read out to the inquest, relatives said Michelle was traumatised and the called police on five separate occasions. Her son Kyle – who escaped the blaze – said in a statement to the inquest that "the police didn't do anything". Michelle Pearson and her four children were murdered after an arson attack at their home in Walkden Michelle suffered 68% burns to her body and "clung on to life" until she died on August 25, 2019, around 20 months after the attack. Her mother, Sandra Lever, said in a statement to the inquest that her daughter had been desperate to move house. "Michelle was beyond distressed," she said. "The children were petrified of living in Jackson Street." Relatives of the family said they believed their deaths were "wholly preventable" and raised "missed opportunities" to protect them. Lever said her daughter had visited her social landlord to say she was in danger but had been told she did not meet the criteria for emergency housing. Her children were having nightmares and Brandon had told her he no longer wanted to live in the house. But Michelle felt "fobbed off", the hearing was told. Elaine Williams, a neighbour, said in the weeks before the arson attack she saw Bolland smashing the windows of Pearson's house with a hammer. Williams said: "She wanted to move from there. "She was fed up of all the trouble. "She was at her wits' end. She was worried." Timothy Brennand, senior coroner for Greater Manchester West, told the hearing: "This is not a trial. This is not an exercise in blame and shame." He said the inquest would seek to examine whether there was "any predictable threat to life" and "what could or should have been done that might have prevented these deaths". The coroner said the inquest aimed to give the Pearson family a voice, but added that their concerns "coalesce into two words of rhetoric – 'What if?'" Brennand read the remarks of Justice Davis, who jailed the family's killers. Brennand said the judge had determined a series of tit-for-tat attacks had taken place as part of a feud in the lead-up to the fatal firebombing, but what lay behind the dispute had never been made public. Anna Morris KC, representing the Pearson family, described Michelle as a devoted mother who read her children bedtime stories each night. She suffered massive injuries in the blaze and remained in hospital for a long time. For some of that time, she did not know her children were dead. Her mental health deteriorated after she was told. When she died in hospital, her family placed a crucifix in her hand, and a photo of her children. "We know she's back with her children and out of pain," the family statement said. Demi was described as a "happy, smiley child" who was "best friends" with her mother. Brandon had an infectious smile and was a "mummy's boy" while his sister Lacie was a little "diva". Lia was described as a little chatterbox with a cheeky laugh. "All of the children had such bright futures ahead of them," the family statement said, adding: "We cherish the short time we shared with them." Bolland's girlfriend, Courtney Brierley, 20, was jailed for 21 years for four counts of manslaughter. title: First minister rejects call to resign over Drumcree row
description: Facing questions in the Stormont assembly, O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them".
body: O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them" First Minister Michelle O'Neill has dismissed a call from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to resign over her role in protests against the Drumcree parade. The Sinn Féin vice-president was branded the "first minister of lawlessness" as unionists criticised the demonstrations on Garvaghy Road. Police are investigating the unlawful protests which blocked an Orange Order march from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh. Facing questions in the Stormont assembly, O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them". She described the planned Orange march on 27 September as "unwanted, sectarian and triumphalist". O'Neill was speaking on Monday in response to an urgent question on the Drumcree dispute tabled by DUP assembly member Phillip Brett. O'Neill returns to Garvaghy Road as police investigate Sunday's 'unlawful protest' Court of Appeal reserves judgement over Drumcree parade dispute An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded Michelle O'Neill was speaking in response to an urgent questionDUP MLA Phillip Brett He called on O'Neill to "drop the bravado" and claimed she had shown "utter contempt" for the ministerial pledge of office. Brett continued: "If you have been found to breach the ministerial code or the law, will you do the decent thing for once and resign as first minister?" The first minister responded: "Catch yourself on, would be where I would start with that one. "I'm going to continue to turn up for the people of the Garvaghy Road. "I'm proud to stand with them and I will continue to stand with them." Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) assembly member Timothy Gaston accused O'Neill of being the "first minister of lawlessness" over her role in the street protests. O'Neill replied: "I am the first minister of what is right." She added that "we won't need to AI it" - a reference to a TUV councillor who posted online an AI image which exaggerated the size of a loyalist rally in Portadown. DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley questioned whether O'Neill would "accept and abide by the lawful decision of the courts" when appeal court judges make a ruling on the parade dispute. Protesters along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of points on 27 September The first minister said that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it" and described the planned march as "morally wrong". O'Neill later said "shame on you" to DUP assembly members over the party's handling of the Drumcree dispute. "Your party has championed this," she said to DUP members on the opposite benches. O'Neill flatly rejected a claim from Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows that many people now regarded the first minister as "completely morally bankrupt". Earlier, Stormont Speaker Edwin Poots raised concerns over the first minister not attending the chamber last week to answer the tabled urgent question. The DUP assembly member said O'Neill's absence last Monday was "discourteous" to the assembly and the public. "Members know my views on ministers being accountable to this house on behalf of the people who put us all here," he said. title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
description: It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools.
body: Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds. The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday. Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay. Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran. It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI. A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement. The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported. The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work. But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products. When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation. Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules Anthropic sues US government for calling it a risk Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI. OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used. It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said. Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data. Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system. "The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said. "Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official. Trump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White House The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said. Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said. Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel. This video can not be played 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage. The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets. Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year. Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration. Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week. After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI. "How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely". Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic." Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the worl

title: Ex-Manchester leader defends deals with Man City owners
description: Veteran former council leader Sir Richard Leese says the relationship has been beneficial to the city.
body: Sir Richard Leese was leader of Manchester City Council for 25 years before he stepped down in 2021 The former leader of Manchester City Council has defended the council's relationship with the owners of Manchester City amid questions over land deals. Sir Richard Leese, who was head of the council for 25 years until 2021 and is also honorary president of the club, said a decade-old deal with Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) was "good for the city". The partnership between the authority and the company owned by Sheik Mansour bin zayed Al Nahyan has come under renewed scrutiny since City was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations with "sham" commercial contracts. The club has denied any wrongdoing is appealing against the charges. The council entered into a partnership with ADUG in 2014 when they formed a joint venture called Manchester Life. It planned to invest more than £1bn over the next decade and develop thousands of homes in the Ancoats and New Islington areas, on the edge of the city centre close to the club's Etihad stadium. But in 2022, a report by the University of Sheffield, called Manchester Offshored, raised questions about the wider public value of the schemes, and a lack of transparency around their finances. It highlighted the absence of any affordable housing in the projects, and that the joint venture companies were ultimately owned by ADUG through firms registered offshore. Abu Dhabi United Group are majority shareholders in City Football Group - which owns Manchester City FC A deal struck in 2015 saw ADUG effectively given the first pick of land in Ancoats and New Islington. The University of Sheffield report argued that land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates". Sir Richard said the 2015 deal was "brokered by the UK government with the UAE government". "It was a time when development in Manchester had stopped," he said. "We were still suffering from the 2008 crash, from the recession that followed that. "There was criticism at the time though - and there still is now - that the land was given away too cheaply by the city council. "The point is, the investment from Abu Dhabi is what created the value. "That deal allowed development to be kick-started - particularly in the Ancoats area. "All of this was documented and went through reports that went through the council's due processes. "I think it has been demonstrated that the deal was a good deal and a good deal for Manchester." Abu Dhabi's investment in Manchester City started in 2008, when City Football Group – majority-owned by ADUG - bought the club in a £200m deal. With significant investment from its new owners, the club went on to win its first trophy in 36 years with an FA Cup win in 2011 and a dramatic Premier League title followed the next year. The club went on to win the league seven more times between 2013 and 2024. But the Premier League began investigating the club's financial dealings in 2018, and City was charged in 2023. Last week, it was announced the club had been found guilty of 115 charges, including some around a so-called disguised funding scheme, which was said to have seen the club's owners topping up sponsorship and commercial deals with their own funding running to more than £800m. Andy Burnham has said Manchester City's owners had been a "huge partner" in Manchester When asked last week about potential fallout from the City charges, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was metropolitan mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to 2026, said he would be "really concerned" if the owners were to pull out of the club. He added: "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is." Since then, it has been reported that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) may halt UK-wide investment schemes worth billions of pounds as a result of the Premier League ruling. Sir Richard said he hoped that Manchester did not lose UEA investment, adding: "I think certainly Abu Dhabi will be thinking that they have been very badly treated given the contribution that they have made - not just to Manchester but to English football as well." He added: "I would be concerned if they did stop investing. I don't think they'd give us up." Sir Richard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier that "the investment in Manchester from Abu Dhabi has been very significant". Stressing he was not speaking on behalf of the club, he pointed to the investment in City, its training complex and the City Football Group headquarters. He added: "I think for the city, one thing about working with Abu Dhabi is everything that they promised they have delivered. "So they have real credibility in the city. That's something we'd want to maintain. "I don't think any other football club has got anywhere near the sort of contribution that they have made to their local community. "What has been created in Manchester City is a phenomenon really and that has to be maintained in some way whatever the final outcome of the allegations against them." Manchester City Council also defended the benefits of the partnership with Manchester Life as a "platform for future development". "The claim that working in partnership with Manchester City's owners has not been a good deal for the council or the city has been debunked repeatedly," the authority said. "Claims that some land was sold too cheaply to Manchester Life ignore the fact that there was zero market interest at the time of the sale, that the land is worth more now precisely because of Manchester Life's investment and the significant financial return the council is receiving through profit-sharing arrangements. "Manchester Life was always envisaged as a platform for further investment. Its success should be measured in what it has delivered directly and what it has unlocked. title: Would the Conservatives' plan make new houses £50,000 cheaper?
description: BBC Verify looks into the shadow chancellor's plan to cut some building regulations to reduce construction costs.
body: Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has said his party, if it was returned to power, would take £50,000 off the cost of building a new home in England and Wales by cutting back on regulations. The £50,000 figure claimed by Griffith reflects estimates by the housebuilding industry of the costs of new regulations and taxes. However, construction and housing experts warn that some of the savings could ultimately lead to higher government spending on schools, roads, and affordable housing. And some analysts also warn the Conservative plans to scrap environmental regulations could potentially push up household energy bills in future. The Conservatives argue a number of regulations are adding to the cost of constructing and delivering new private homes. The Community Infrastructure Levy - a charge on certain new developments in England and Wales which councils can use to fund local infrastructure such as roads, schools and play areas The Future Homes Standard which requires new-build homes in England to meet higher energy-efficiency standards and use low-carbon heating such as heat pumps rather than gas boilers Section 106 which can require developers to provide a proportion of social or affordable housing in England as part of a new development. The Tories say they will scrap or reform these and other regulations, saying: "All in all, we will cut the cost of delivering and therefore buying a new home by up to £50,000." BBC Verify has asked the Conservatives for a full breakdown of their figure. The Home Builders Federation (HBF) has estimated that new regulations, taxes and inflation - since 2020 - have increased the cost of building an individual new home in England and Wales by £76,000. It says this represents around 20% of the value of an average new home. Of this total, it estimates: £985 comes from Section 106 £10,200 comes from the Future Homes Standard £12,700 in environmental protection measures such as "nutrient neutrality" and "biodiversity net gain" Excluding a £37,000 increase in the costs of material and labour, the HBF estimates that regulations and taxes have added around £42,000 to the cost of building a new home. The Conservatives' estimate is slightly higher than the HBF's figure. The HBF also includes nearly £8,000 to reflect changes in building regulations. The Conservatives have not said they would find savings by scrapping all of those. The party's plan also assumes the savings they have highlighted would be passed on to buyers rather than raising house builders' profits. Noble Francis of trade body the Construction Products Association (CPA) told BBC Verify that new costs imposed on builders through regulations and taxes in recent years - including the time firms spend navigating the regulatory system - are a serious constraint on residential construction rates. The Labour government is well off track in terms of meeting its target of building 1.5 million net additional dwellings in England over the course of this parliament - which requires an annual building rate of around 300,000 homes per year. In the year to June only around 203,000 were built, according to official estimates. However, Francis also said: "It's easy for any party not in government to just claim they will get rid of red tape and cut costs but both the Conservatives and Labour have been in power in the last five years and have added extra costs to house building." The Future Homes Standard, for instance, was first proposed in 2019 when Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson was in power. Other analysts point out that the upfront construction cost savings from the plan could potentially lead to higher government spending in the future. Housing expert Anna Clarke said: "Cutting the costs of house building by £50,000 would be really helpful in getting much-needed new homes built. "But if you don't get developers to pay for new schools and infrastructure you need to pay for them some other way." And some analysts argue that updated environmental building standards, such as requiring heat pumps rather than gas boilers in new homes, are forecast to save households money in the long-term by reducing their domestic energy bills. Dr Richard Lowes of clean energy advocates the Regulatory Assistance Project told BBC Verify: "If the energy bill implications are not carefully considered, households may be lumbered with very high bills for decades. "The lowest running costs can typically be achieved with heat pumps paired with solar and batteries." title: Zelensky condemns 'horrific' Russian strike on boat carrying corn in Black Sea
description: The vessel's captain was killed and 11 crew members were rescued after the attack on the Turkish-owned ship, Ukraine's leader says.
body: Romainian authorities launched a rescue mission after reports of a vessel on fire outside its territorial waters Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned a "horrific" Russian attack on a vessel carrying corn in the Black Sea. The ship's captain was killed in the strike involving two drones, Zelensky said, and another sailor was unaccounted for. Eleven crew members - nationals of Azerbaijan and India - have been rescued. Romania said it had mounted a rescue mission after "a fire on the ship Royad Mammadov" outside the country's territorial waters. It said two people had died. Russia has not commented, but its defence ministry earlier said it had struck two cargo vessels. Russia has been pounding Ukrainian infrastructure in what it says is retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and ships in the Black Sea. Monday's attack by Russia targeted "a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkey", Volodymyr Zelensky said. He did not give the location of the ship, but Romania's interior ministry said it had sunk about 30 nautical miles south of its port of Sfantu Gheorghe. "At around 11:00 (09:00 GMT), Coast Guard border police officers were informed that a fire had broken out on board a commercial vessel located within Romania's exclusive economic zone," the ministry said in a statement. "Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased persons have also been identified," it added. Ukraine's president said he had "repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate the situation and ensure security in the Black Sea" - and other countries had made "relevant proposals" too. "But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelensky said. "Pressure is needed to restore global food security," he added. "And everyone who is genuinely interested in this must help." On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. President Vladimir Putin admitted last week Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. The Russian leader has also intensified his rhetoric against Western allies of Ukraine - repeating a threat of even using nuclear weapons. Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes. The head of Germany's foreign intelligence Martin Jaeger said on Monday that "Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia", which was "waging a shadow war" with the threat of attacks against targets in Germany remaining "real and imminent". title: Twelve arrested for allegedly running cat trafficking ring in Vietnam
description: The men are accused of stealing around 2,700 cats in Ho Chi Minh City, allegedly to be slaughtered for food.
body: Police released photos of the cats that were rescued - 13 have been returned to their owners Twelve men have been arrested in Vietnam after allegedly confessing to stealing and selling around 2,700 cats, Ho Chi Minh City police have said. Cat traps, fur removal machines and measuring scales were among the items seized during the investigation. The men are suspected of taking the pets to be slaughtered for food. Police allege the suspects roamed through residential areas in small groups on motorbikes at night to steal the cats. The men reportedly used pieces of fish as bait, placing traps outside houses where they knew cats were kept, state media reported. Thirteen of the rescued felines have since been returned to their owners. According to the animal protection organisation Humane World for Animals, an estimated five million dogs and one million cats are captured, stolen, trafficked and slaughtered for meat in Vietnam every year. The consumption of dog and cat meat is legal in the country, where many restaurants openly advertise it on their menu. But vendors require permits that show the origin of the animals. Each group allegedly stole an average of four to 10 cats per night, according to a police statement in Ho Chi Minh City police department's official newspaper. On 8 July, police said they seized 50 cats, two weighing scales, 55 cat traps, 14 bags, 13 mobile phones, seven motorbikes, two fur-removing machines and 6.7 million Vietnamese dong ($257; £195). The 12 suspects were then brought in for questioning, and police say they confessed to stealing around 2,700 cats. Of the 50 cats that were seized, 13 have been returned to their owners, while the remaining are being kept at the animal welfare centre HavePaws. More than 400 cats were seized by police in Ho Chi Minh City in June While the consumption of dog and cat meat remains more common in Vietnam than other Asian countries, campaigners say attitudes are changing. A 2023 survey commissioned by Humane World for Animals found growing public opposition, particularly among younger people and pet owners, with 71% backing a ban on the consumption and trade of cat meat. In June, more than 400 cats destined for slaughter were rescued after authorities dismantled another alleged feline theft ring, the animal welfare group said. title: Man detained for stabbing dog walker to death
description: Dawood Safi killed Wayne Broadhurst and injured two others in a knife attack in west London.
body: Dawood Safi was given an indefinite hospital order A man who killed a dog walker and attacked two other people in a "frenzy of violence" in west London has been given an indefinite hospital order for manslaughter. Dawood Safi, 28, fatally stabbed Wayne Broadhurst, 49, in the street during a series of knife attacks which began at Safi's home in Uxbridge on 27 October 2025. Safi, who was having paranoid delusions and hearing voices, attacked his landlord Shahzad Farrukh minutes before killing Broadhurst, and also stabbed a 14-year-old boy. At Southwark Crown Court, Mrs Justice Cutts said Safi, an Afghan refugee, had been "in a psychotic state" and recommended that he be deported, but said the final decision rested with the Home Secretary. Ealing Council street cleaner Wayne Broadhurst was described as "a gentle and quiet man" In her sentencing remarks, the judge acknowledged the "devastating" impact of the crime on Broadhurst's family, and added that he was "a hard-working and decent man who was deeply loved". Cutts told Safi: "Wayne Broadhurst, a gentle and quiet man, had the misfortune to be walking his dog at the time. "As he emerged from the alleyway on to the street, you set upon and killed him in a frenzied, random, and completely unprovoked assault involving stabbing him at least 14 times." Broadhurst's partner, Ann Newman, told the court she had had a "future stolen from me" and described facing up to a daily battle with grief and loss. Mrs Justice Cutts recommended Safi be deported, but said the final decision rested with the Home Secretary Safi, who appeared for his sentencing hearing on a video link from the high-security Broadmoor hospital, was born in the Kapisa province of northern Afghanistan. He was smuggled in to the UK on the back of a lorry in November 2020 and lied about his age - saying he was 17 instead of 22 - to stand a better chance of asylum. He worked as an Uber driver, studied for a mechanics qualification at Uxbridge College and had no convictions since entering the country. He had sought help from doctors for his deteriorating mental health prior to the stabbings, which began at his home in Midhurst Gardens. The court was told that in the three days before the stabbings, Safi had attended an appointment at his GP, had a mental health assessment at Hillingdon Hospital and had sought help at Hayes police station. After the stabbings, doctors concluded Safi was suffering from psychotic depression which had led to the violent offences. Dr Elliott Carthy, who assessed Safi at Broadmoor, said he had "paranoid and persecutory beliefs", and voices in his head contributed to his actions that day. He said a hospital order with restrictions was the best way to protect the public "going forward now and in anticipation of his release into the community". He said Safi was likely to spend at least five years at Broadmoor before being considered for transfer to a medium security facility where he would stay for several more years, and if he is released into the community he would be under strict conditions and subject to lifelong monitoring. Safi admitted manslaughter by diminished responsibility, was found guilty by a jury of attempting to murder Farrukh and pleaded guilty to causing actual bodily harm against the teenage boy as well as possession of the knife. Prosecutors dropped a charge of murder after the guilty plea to manslaughter was entered, and after receiving expert reports on Safi's mental health. The judge told the court she would have sentenced Safi to life in prison with a minimum term of eight years if he had not been mentally unwell. title: Player welfare, injury worries & boredom - has extended break worked?
description: The extended international break was brought in with player welfare in mind, but has it been a success?
body: Erling Haaland is an injury doubt after he limped off in Norway's match against Portugal The first international break of the 2026-27 season is almost over - and it has been a longer one than fans are used to. For the first time, the Premier League and Championship paused for three weeks rather than the usual two with players returning to domestic action from Friday. The idea was brought in by Fifa with player welfare in mind, but, with a growing list of injuries, has it really been a success? Who benefits from an extended international schedule? And do people really want a three-week break from domestic action when the season has only just got going? In recent years, Fifa has used five primary international breaks during the season, all consisting of two-week gaps in March, June, September, October and November. The switch to a three-week gap across late September and early October, alongside reducing the number of breaks down to four, was made for a number of reasons. One was that the scheduling of the 2026 World Cup final on 19 July was the latest date for a summer World Cup since 1966. Player welfare also featured in the discussions, this including travel considerations. The reduction in the number of breaks will reduce the number of journeys some players face in having to travel from one continent to another for their international fixtures . One such example is African and South American players who play their domestic football in Europe and have to travel cross-continent to fulfil international fixtures. But with the domestic season just starting to get interesting, fans tend to bemoan the interruption - no matter the length - and long for the return of club football. The extended international break might have been brought in with player welfare in mind, but the reality is that a number of players will return to their clubs with injuries. It is hard to quantify whether more injuries have been picked up during the past fortnight than during other international breaks and it must be factored in that this is a lengthier break with more fixtures. A full and fair comparison might have to wait until the end of the season, after all the international breaks. However, there have been numerous injuries to players since players joined up with international team-mates. On Monday, it was announced that Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott had withdrawn from the England squad with a thigh injury and the Cherries are unhappy with the way they believe England handled the injury. Manchester City striker Erling Haaland asked to be substituted on 67 minutes, subsequently limping off in Norway's match against Portugal on Sunday before leaving camp on Monday while club team-mate Nico O'Reilly returned to City for further assessment. Following the injury to Haaland, the Norwegian players' union (NISO) expressed concern over the increased demands. "Over time, we have seen a worrying trend where the burden on top players has become far too high," NISO chief Kristoffer Vatshaug said. "We want clearer guidelines for workload and recovery. It is about the time between matches, consecutive rest periods, travel strain and how much time players get to recover after a long season." Liverpool duo Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak have both picked up injuries with Gakpo withdrawing from the Netherlands squad with an ankle injury and Isak pulling out of Sweden duty with a minor thigh injury. Portugal boss Jorge Jesus revealed Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes had been playing through pain while Sunderland's Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey both sustained hamstring problems. Club managers will have their fingers crossed that no more names are added to that list with three days of fixtures still to be played. England's Tino Livramento, Kobbie Mainoo, Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford and Declan Rice all pulled out of Thomas Tuchel's squad before the start of the break. Away from the Premier League, there have also been injuries to some of the biggest stars in the game with Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe sustaining an injury while on duty with France and Barcelona's Raphinha also returned from Brazil with a thigh injury. England boss Thomas Tuchel has previously been critical of the three-week break, saying it is "more challenging" than previous years, citing travel and having only two days of rest between games as problems. In a news conference on Monday before England take on the Czech Republic on Tuesday he said: "I can assure everyone that player welfare is priority number one. "But new training styles and training times, different positions to play maybe, increase the chance of injury." On whether the extended break has had an impact on injuries, he said "we need to get the numbers right" before deciding. "Is it really more or is it the same amount [of games] as in two shorter little windows? I don't have the answer to that," he said. "The two-week window is not guilty for everything. If it is a thing, we will adapt and make the most of it as always. "I didn't like the start of it after a long tournament to have a long window. There are also positives to it like we saw against Croatia after having three matches together. "The team is together for longer, more training sessions, more meetings, more of the same language. You see improvements and automatisms clicking in. We made it a very good camp." Shay, Swindon: I don't think any Premier League or Championship fan backs this idea. It's just boring without your club in action for so long. James McCreadie: Fans are getting sick and tired of losing players to what is a glorified friendly. Teams in Europe and Carabao Cup have nine games in 28 days or so before the next international break. Hope clubs pull players out, citing that player welfare comes first. title: Artist 'taking legal advice' over Tories' use of Andy Burnham portrait
description: Manchester illustrator Stan Chow says he was not asked permission for use of his cartoon.
body: Bottles of water and sweets poking fun at Andy Burnham were handed out at the Conservative Party conference An artist has said he is taking legal advice after accusing the Conservative Party of copying his portrait of Andy Burnham at their party conference. People attending the party's conference in Birmingham have been handed water bottles featuring the image and labelled "Bottler Burnham" and "0% strength" and sweets labelled "Andy Panders' People Pleaser Pick N Mix". Labour supporter Stanley Chow, who created the image for Burnham's 2021 mayoral campaign in Greater Manchester, has claimed the party did not ask for permission to use the image. A Conservative Party spokeswoman said the bottles were not on sale and merely handed out to attending media in "goody bags". Manchester illustrator Chow said: "I was stunned and angry when I saw what they had done. It is childish from them. I am taking legal advice. "I'm very disappointed. It's frustrating that an institution like the Conservative Party has no idea that they are infringing copyright." The original image of Andy Burnham was created by Chow in 2021 The artist claimed Reform UK had also infringed his copyright by using the image a few months ago in AI-generated social media campaign posts. A Reform UK spokesman said at the time that it had "removed the posts in good faith and without any admission of liability on our part". Brit Awards art trail turns streets into a gallery 'Simple shapes and sweeping curves' Meet Stanley Chow - the football illustrator. Video, 00:02:35Meet Stanley Chow - the football illustrator Chow said: "I can't quite believe the Tories are resorting to this too. "Regardless of your political allegiance, what the Tories have done is still copyright infringement. "Ultimately, I want to raise awareness that you can't just take someone else's artwork and do what you want with it. "I want to show other artists that when this does happen, you can make a stand, especially in this day and age where artists are struggling, because of AI and the cost of living." Chow's image of Burnham has been used extensively by the politician across a series of campaigns and was recently used by the now-PM when he stood for election in Makerfield in June. Chow's image of Burnham was widely-used in the Makerfield by-election in June Manchester United fan Chow is well-known for his portraits of famous faces and he has previously created images of footballers, including Wayne Rooney, Edgar Davids and Ronaldinho. He has also exhibited a series of portraits of "Great Northerners", which featured the likes of actress Maxine Peake, suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay, and recently curated an art trail for the Brit Awards' arrival in his home city. He has also drawn Eric Cantona and presented a picture of Sir Alex Ferguson to the former Red Devils manager. title: Medvedev defaulted for hitting spectator with ball
description: Daniil Medvedev is defaulted from the China Open after hitting a spectator in the face with a ball during his semi-final against Novak Djokovic.
body: Daniil Medvedev has become infamous for his on-court behaviour Daniil Medvedev was defaulted from the China Open after hitting a spectator in the face with a ball during his semi-final against Novak Djokovic. Third seed Medvedev trailed Djokovic 7-5 5-3 when the Serb hit a winner beyond him for 15-15. The ball ricocheted off the back of the court and Medvedev swiped at a backhand in annoyance, sending the ball into the air and hitting a spectator who was sitting in the front row of the stand behind him. The fan doubled over holding his face and was still holding his eye as he was helped out of the arena. After speaking with umpire Mohamed Lahyani and an ATP official, Russia's Medvedev approached the net to shake hands with Djokovic. "Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all," Medvedev said. "I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels. "I just hope he's OK. That's the most important. I just really care about him right now." Medvedev said afterwards he was "terribly sorry" for the incident Djokovic - who was defaulted from the 2020 US Open for a similar incident - expressed sympathy for the fan and Medvedev afterwards. "It's a bit of a shock to be honest. I hope that person is not badly injured," he said. "I also feel sorry for Daniil. I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match. "I am sure that Daniil did not want to do this intentionally." Defaults in tennis are rare and only occur when players violate the sport's code of conduct. Violations include ball abuse, physical or verbal abuse, or racquet abuse. Players can receive three code violations and then be disqualified if they receive another - but Medvedev's offence was serious enough to instantly default him. He will now lose the points and prize money he had earned during his run to the last four in Beijing. The 30-year-old is a combustible character who has struggled to control his emotions throughout his career. He had a meltdown at last year's US Open when a photographer walked on court, and was fined almost £31,500 ($42,500) for his behaviour. In April, he obliterated a racquet after losing 6-0 6-0 at the Monte Carlo Masters and was again fined for unsportsmanlike conduct. Medvedev told BBC Sport in 2025 that he was attempting to work on his on-court behaviour. "When I'm on the court I hate to lose; I love to win. My first goal is to win the match, so it brings a lot of adrenaline out and it brings all the energy out," he said. "Sometimes it is a good energy. Sometimes it is a bad one." Djokovic beats Zverev to reach China Open semis Sabalenka stunned by Bartunkova at China Open 'I kept fighting right to the end' - emotional Nishikori retires The default brought an early end to an excellent contest, with 39-year-old Djokovic having played superbly to outlast an opponent nine years his junior. Djokovic saved 16 of the 18 break points he faced and will go on to play Alex de Minaur in Tuesday's final. Djokovic has a 33-0 record at the China Open, having won the title six times. He has won at least one title a year since 2006 - but Tuesday will be his first final since the Australian Open, where he lost to then world number one Carlos Alcaraz in four sets. He reached the semi-finals at Wimbledon, losing to eventual champion Jannik Sinner, but lost in the third round of the French Open before suffering a shock first-round exit at the US Open. Elsewhere, defending champion Alcaraz overcame fluctuations in form to beat Jaume Munar and reach the Japan Open final. The seven-time Grand Slam champion struggled on serve throughout but gradually upped his level to win 5-7 6-3 6-1. Spain's Alcaraz led 5-3 in the first set and served for it before losing 16 consecutive points to squander the opener. He will face Jiri Lehecka in the final after the Czech beat Monaco's Valentin Vacherot 6-4 6-2. title: Glasgow City Council and Unison reach agreement in pay and grading row
description: The local authority says this means it will not consider dismissing and rehiring its staff.
body: Glasgow City Council faced a long-running women's campaign for equal pay Glasgow City Council and the largest council union, Unison, have reached an agreement in a pay and grading dispute. The local authority says this means it will not consider firing and rehiring more than 23,000 staff. The dispute was over the new pay and grading structure designed to deal with the underlying issues which led to thousands of equal pay claims from female workers past and present. The original proposal would have resulted in wage cuts for 11% of employees but, under the new deal, their salaries will now be protected for three years. Unison said negotiations were continuing and it would ballot its members later this month. Glasgow City Council pauses plan to fire and rehire 23,000 staff Council leader Ricky Bell said: "I am delighted that we have been able to reach agreement with Unison. "This deal means we are able to remove the unpalatable prospect of fire and rehire, with proposals put to members in a ballot later this month." Bell added that it was a "strong and fair deal" and confirmed that both the GMB and Unite unions had also agreed to take it to their members. He said: "With all three unions now engaging with their memberships, we are moving closer to the outcome we have always wanted to achieve: ending pay discrimination in Glasgow City Council once and for all." The council leader said additional support from the Scottish government had "helped unlock this agreement" and thanked the unions for their engagement. He concluded: "While there is no further money to come as part of this package, I look forward to the outcome of the ballots in the coming weeks. "We have always been clear that our goal is to deliver a fair, sustainable pay and grading system that works for employees and protects vital public services. We are now closer than ever to achieving that." Chris Sermanni, Glasgow City branch secretary, said Unison had secured "significant movement" Unison said it had secured "major improvements on pay and grading". It also confirmed that a proposal for pay protection for workers facing losses had been increased to three years. The council has also agreed to continue discussions with the union on outstanding issues including lower-paid workers, allowances, unevaluated jobs, equality impacts and the operation of the new pay model. Unison said the breakthrough created a route towards a ballot of its membership, without the council dictating the union's recommendation or communications. The union added that important issues remained unresolved but negotiations would continue before members voted. Chris Sermanni, Glasgow City Unison branch secretary, said: "Unison stood firm because Glasgow's workers deserved better than what was originally put on the table. "That position has secured significant movement. "There's now a path for Unison members to give their verdict without the immediate threat of dismissal and re-engagement hanging over them." Sermanni stressed that the union had not accepted the pay and grading package and said the "fight for improvements" was not over. "Thousands of workers are owed substantial and long-overdue increases and we want them to receive every penny," he said. "At the same time, other workers face significant losses and some still don't even know their final outcome. "The period ahead will be used to keep fighting to give the whole workforce the information they need to make their decision." Mandy McDowall, Unison Scotland regional organiser, said the intervention of the Scottish government had "helped create the space for further progress". The timetable for the ballot, which will last four weeks, will be confirmed soon. David Hume, GMB organiser at the local authority, said: "These proposals come after seven years of hard negotiation and that is long enough. "Every day workers are being underpaid is a day too long and there is no more time to lose. "Our members at the council will now vote on these proposals as swiftly as possible." Hume said the local authority had introduced new financial supports, including £110m to cover additional back pay. He added: "We are satisfied these additional measures, along with the protections already in place, mean this framework will deliver fairer pay for workers across the council. "It is their voice that must be heard now. It is their decision to take." title: Priest pleads guilty to 109 sex offences
description: Edward Gallagher will be sentenced in December after pleading guilty to 109 sex offences.
body: Edward Gallagher, 59, will be sentenced in December A priest has pleaded guilty to 109 sex offences at Londonderry Crown Court. Edward Gallagher, 59, whose address is Maghaberry Prison, will be sentenced in December for offences between 22 June 2023 and 18 April 2025. They include among others attempted sexual communication with a child under 16, having indecent images of a child, possessing an extreme pornographic image and attempting to encourage a child to engage in sexual activity. The Catholic Bishop of Derry Michael Router confirmed that he would ask the Vatican to dismiss Gallagher from the priesthood. Gallagher at a previous court hearing When the charges were put to him Gallagher pleaded guilty to them all. Defence counsel Stephen Mooney said that a pre-sentence report was needed and that "the facts are what they are". The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) welcomed the guilty plea and said they now awaited sentencing, which is due to happen on 9 December. Gallagher remains in custody pending that. Bishop of Derry Michael Router is asking the Vatican to dismiss Gallagher from the priesthood In a statement on Monday, Bishop Router said his thoughts were "first and foremost" with those affected by the case, "particularly the children who have suffered harm and those who continue to live with the consequences of abuse and exploitation". The bishop said he would "move immediately to seek the most serious penalty available under church law" - Gallagher's dismissal from the priesthood. "I can confirm that I am petitioning the Holy See to submit the case directly to the Holy Father with a recommendation that Father Edward Gallagher be immediately dismissed from the clerical state," he said. The bishop said the Catholic Church could not "undo the harm that has been caused" but had "a responsibility to respond truthfully, justly and decisively". He said the Diocese of Derry had cooperated fully with the PSNI and all relevant statutory authorities throughout their investigations in the Gallagher case - and would "continue to do so". title: Pickford 'almost caused crash' with careless driving
description: The goalkeeper was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to brake.
body: Jordan Pickford has played 92 times for England and 336 times for Everton England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford nearly caused a crash with two other cars during a bout of careless driving in his £200,000 Lamborghini supercar, a court has heard. The 32-year-old was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to slam on the brakes, and then speeding off into the distance. The incident happened in the Cheshire town of Knutsford on 14 April, sparking a criminal prosecution for driving without due care or attention. Pickford, who has 336 appearances for Everton and 92 England caps, has pleaded guilty to the charge and will next appear at Chester Magistrates' Court on 7 December. According to court documents, PC Cecil Ricardo, from Cheshire Police, said he had just left the station when he saw Pickford's blue Lamborghini Urus complete with personalised number plates. "I was stationary on Bexton Road, Knutsford, waiting for traffic signals to turn green," he wrote. "I then witnessed a blue Lamborghini Urus driving along Princess Street. "It reached the junction with Toft Road, completely ignored the give way lines and pulled onto Toft Road causing two vehicles to slam on their brakes to avoid a collision. "The Lamborghini then sped down Toft Road, Knutsford." Ricardo said he activated his lights and siren to set off in pursuit of the Lamborghini, noticing he was driving at 50mph (80.4 kmh) while the Lamborghini "was still pulling away". "The speed limit on that stretch of Toft Road, Knutsford, is 30mph," he noted. The officer said Pickford appeared to notice the chasing police car and pulled over. Pickford pleaded guilty in writing and told Warrington Magistrates Court: "I would like to attend court to put forward my mitigation." His case was formally adjourned last week. Pickford, who started his career at Sunderland before loan spells at six clubs including Burton Albion, Bradford City and Preston North End, has featured for England at the 2018, 2022 and 2026 World Cups, and was in goal for the country's Euro 2020 and 2024 final appearances. title: Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote
description: What may be troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.
body: It is not exactly typical for a British party conference, let alone that of one of the smaller parties, to elicit international condemnation. Yet that is the position the Green Party of England and Wales is in today after Israel's foreign ministry said it was banning their leader, Zack Polanski, from entering the country. The cause was the motion proposed by party members and adopted by the conference on Sunday, declaring Zionism, which is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland, to be racism. The Green motion describes Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", and supports instead a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine". It's hardly likely that Polanski or indeed many Greens are going to be much troubled by Israel's condemnation of the motion. One major factor in the Greens' electoral gains over the past year or so, a hugely successful period for the party, has been their clear and vocal condemnation of Israel's war in Gaza and actions in the region more generally. What may be more troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party. Many Greens are proud of the party's internal democracy: this motion was proposed by and voted on by party members. Yet that has resulted in the scenario of leading Green elected politicians facing scrutiny over party policy which the vast majority of them opposed. Polanski, who is not an MP, wanted changes to the motion which were rejected by the conference, and ultimately did not participate in the debate or vote. Of the Greens' five MPs, four opposed the motion. The most vocal of them was Adrian Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, who was a Green co-leader for four years until September last year when he and his running mate were defeated by Polanski by a vast margin. Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism' Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion So an element of this is the changing nature of the Greens' activist base under Polanski's leadership, moving away from an environmental focus to a more general left-populist politics, incorporating a large element of 'anti-imperialist' foreign policy. Yet this may not be the last issue where that results in a public dispute between the membership and their MPs, four of whom were elected at the last general election under different leadership. And it is striking that, though Polanski's election as leader was a clear symbol of that shift in the Greens' approach, he did not back this motion. So this could presage tensions too between Polanski and the party membership, some of whom will have been inspired to join the Greens by his leadership. In practical terms, the Green MPs will be able to continue espousing a different position in parliament to the party's new policy. The Greens do not have a whipping system, meaning that MPs are free to vote as they wish. This is also true of their councillors, including in the almost 40 councils where the Greens are in power after the May local elections. It will be interesting to see whether as a result of these tensions there is a push either to constrain the ability of the party conference to make policy, or in the other direction - to constrain the ability of elected representatives to defy party policy. Separately, this motion may present a political headache down the line for Andy Burnham. In his Labour conference speech last week, the prime minister said he was forming a "national commission" on electoral reform, with a view to changing the system used for general elections in the long-term. While Burnham did not specify what system he wanted, he said that Labour would at the next general election commit to a new system where "everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard". Under a move to any more proportional system, on current trends, there would likely be more Green MPs as a result. In the scenario of a hung parliament, the Greens are a party to which Labour would naturally look for support as part of the progressive bloc. And yet the Greens are also now a party whose actions this weekend have been condemned by the Labour chair, Bridget Phillipson, as "shameful" and "fundamentally wrong". Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, said the Zionism motion "crosses a line and is rightly being condemned across the political spectrum." Labour has long been divided on the question of electoral reform. Their leader now has a clear position in favour but the Green motion this weekend could have the unintended effect of bolstering opposition within Labour to that element of the prime minister's agenda. title: Yemeni government forces say they have 'secured' Bab al-Mandab Strait
description: Houthi-run media deny the government has made advances in the Dhubab area, which overlooks the strategic Red Sea waterway.
body: Yemen's government says it has launched an offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement. A Yemeni military spokesman said Giants Brigades and National Shield forces were besieging Houthi fighters in the Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, which overlooks the strategic waterway, after the forces took control of its airport and cut the road to the port city Mokha. Houthi-run media denied that government forces had made advances in the Dhubab area. The government said operations had also begun on several other fronts, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago. Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets had destroyed more than 300 "high-value" targets in strikes supporting the offensive. On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis, insisting that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted. Rashad al-Alimi called on all armed forces, security forces and military formations "to begin carrying out their assigned missions, in accordance with the approved plans, until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia". It came after the Houthi fighters reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded. The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil sites belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Dhubab, Mokha and Perim (Mayyun) Island. They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry. The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced. title: Plaque unveiled to honour Beagle 2 mission leader
description: The plaque, unveiled at the M Shed in Bristol, recognises Colin Pillinger who led the 2003 probe mission to Mars.
body: Bristol-born Professor Colin Pillinger designed the Beagle 2 probe and was instrumental in it landing on Mars A museum plaque has been unveiled in honour of the scientist who developed the Beagle 2 probe - the first British and European spacecraft to land on another planet. The tribute, at the M Shed in Bristol, recognises the space probe landing on Mars on Christmas Day 2003 and honours the contribution to the mission of the late Bristol-born scientist Professor Colin Pillinger. "He was exceptional," said UK Space Agency former chief scientist Chris Lee who worked on Beagle 2 with Pillinger. "He managed to get everybody excited about space exploration." Another 12 plaques were announced earlier this year to be installed at a number of sites linked to the historic landing. Remembering Bristol's Colin Pillinger & Beagle 2 Lee was one of the Filton space crew who contributed to the Beagle 2 mission before he became a leading scientist for the UK Space Agency. "We were at the time the principal place for space exploration in the UK and Colin came to us because of our experience," Lee said. "He was always very positive, one of those can-do figures. Where we would see problems, he would see solutions." The unveiling of the Beagle 2 plaque, located in the People Gallery at the M Shed, took place on Monday. Remembering Bristol's Colin Pillinger & Beagle 2 UK's first Mars landing honoured with 13 plaques Mars mission boss remembered on launch anniversary Bristol City Council's Head of Culture Philip Walker said they wanted to celebrate the achievements of Pillinger, who grew up in Kingswood, and his team. "It's great to be able to celebrate his contribution to the city," he said. Pillinger, who died in 2014, passed away before pictures of the landing site revealed Beagle 2 did not crash-land on Mars as had previously been thought. But although the landing of Beagle 2 was successful, it was branded as a failed mission as it was unable to connect back to Earth once it landed. The mission landing is still regarded, however, as an historic success for the European Space Agency which has subsequently influenced future exploration. Pillinger's sister, Doreen Lindegaard, and his daughter, Shusanah Pillinger, unveiled the ceremonial plaque at the M Shed in Bristol In the years that followed the Beagle 2 mission, the UK contributed significantly to flagship space projects, including the Rosetta comet chaser and the James Webb Space Telescope. "Beagle 2 started the UK down the line of being able to do planetary missions and knowing it could engineer them," said Professor Mark Sims, who managed the Beagle 2 mission. A more recent example is the ExoMars Rover, Rosalind Franklin, which is due for launch in 2028 with the aim of finding out if life has ever existed on Mars. "It's a European Space Agency mission but the rover was built in Stevenage and it will land on Mars hopefully in 2030 and look for signs of life which is what Beagle 2 was aiming to do," Sims said. In 2016, pictures of the landing site revealed Beagle 2 landed successfully Follow BBC Bristol on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
description: The prefect of Pas-de-Calais says the 15-year-old's life is "not in danger" after the "very serious" incident.
body: French school protests have led to clashes between police and students in recent days. File photo of police at a protest last week A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country. The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch. "The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby. Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days. There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury. AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand. However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl who it said was near the teenager as saying he did not pick up the grenade. "He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying. When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified. "Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media. A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened". The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said. Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school. "At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media. "Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred." The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on. "In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment." This is not the first time students have been seriously injured during the recent wave of protests in France. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation. Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered". "His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying. "It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study." title: Creosote found in beach pollution investigation
description: Restrictions remain in place on Blyth Beach after a pollution incident was reported in August.
body: The Environment Agency identified creosote when investigating a pollution report at Blyth Beach (stock image) People are being urged not to bathe at a beach after creosote was identified in a pollution investigation. In August, members of the public were urged not to swim at Blyth South Beach in Northumberland after reports of "oil like pollution" and a fuel smell. Laboratory tests confirmed the substance as creosote, with investigations suggesting the cause as an ex-timber treatment works operating on land adjacent to the affected area until about 1980, Northumberland County Council said. The council, Environment Agency (EA) and Port of Blyth said they were working to respond to the ongoing pollution, and restrictions remain in place on the land between Blyth West Pier and the Dave Stephens Centre. An EA investigation has found the pollution is contained within an area of the beach near the Hole in the Wall, where it is seeping into the sand through contaminated groundwater. The council said the public health risk was low, but urged people to keep their dogs away from the affected area of beach and water and to avoid contact themselves. It is not yet known how long the clean-up will take, but it has been described as a "significant" piece of work. title: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for BBC News chief, says Katie Razzall
description: The new director of news takes over from Deborah Turness, who resigned as CEO last year.
body: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for the BBC's director of news. She is a well-regarded high flier who has impressed in her roles at Panorama, Newsnight and Channel 4 News. She is currently the BBC's director of news documentaries and long form journalism. But she hasn't been in that role for long and hasn't spent years leading huge teams of people (BBC News' global newsroom has around 4,500 staff). A lack of that kind of experience might have been problematic in the past. But the BBC's new director general comes from Google. Tech companies regularly appoint people who may not have the direct experience for a role but have the strategic vision and drive to make a difference. He is talking about distinctive journalism and reinvention. Jupp's appointment signals a direction of travel both on the change that the new boss thinks is required and also on the use of technology. BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news Before Jupp took up her role in documentaries, she had moved to the US and was a senior member of the BBC's AI team, developing and leading the BBC's approach to artificial intelligence. It feels significant that the former Google boss has chosen someone with that experience to run his news teams, raising questions around how AI could open up the next frontier of a modern newsroom. But the new director of news has a lot on her plate. She leads a news operation that is still reeling from a series of crises that eventually brought down her predecessor, Deborah Turness, as well as director general Tim Davie. She'll have to oversee the £51m in savings that news must make (one tenth of the £500m the entire BBC must find). Job cuts are already in train, journalists are having to reapply for their roles - and there is much more pain to come. Staff have told me they want clear direction and an end to the salami slicing of resources. They ask what are the priorities, what are the things we do that are crucial and which are less important? The teams she now leads will want a plan for how they can make such deep cuts without impacting the quality of what they do. BBC News stands or falls by its on-the-ground, eyewitness journalism. Some are asking how much of that can BBC News still afford to do. But there are also questions about whether the BBC needs to learn from its rivals by slimming down the number of stories it does and prioritizing the big hits. A streamlined BBC News. Her challenges are both editorial and practical. Matt Brittin, who previously worked for Google, took over as the BBC's director general in May After 10 months without a permanent boss, I have picked up a sense of drift. Everybody understands - and the new DG repeats this, just as his predecessor Tim David did - that the BBC must go to where audiences are and where they will be in the future. Staff at BBC News have heard this before. They want to know what it actually means in practice and how news will be reorganised. The biggest challenge is the change in viewing habits. News has a loyal base of viewers still watching on linear channels (and who many argue should not be taken for granted in the rush to attract younger audiences online) but the direction of travel is changing fast. There will be resistance - from viewers, from politicians, from campaign groups - as the BBC decides to move away from old formats and old technology. But it must go where audiences are and the new head of news will need a strategy to move much more deeply into a digital world. The BBC has been doing this in a fairly piecemeal way up to now. But Jupp will need to turbocharge it - with fewer resources and a demoralised workforce, some of whom she will need to shepherd out the door. Brittin has talked about the bigger prize of getting the news division's trusted journalism to much larger numbers of people around the world. She has to deliver that. She will also need to give BBC News greater editorial confidence after years of political attack and the errors of recent years. Staff working in news would argue it was the current affairs side of the operation that previously let the organisation down. A documentary about the children of Gaza narrated by the son of a Hamas official. A documentary about Israel's assault on Gazan medical staff commissioned and then dropped by the BBC and later shown on Channel 4. Then, of course, there are the revelations that a Panorama broadcast ahead of Donald Trump's reelection as President had spliced together two clips of the President's speech on the day of the riots on Capitol Hill - changing the editorial meaning. BBC chair Samir Shah apologised to Trump who is suing the BBC for $10bn. The court proceedings are still playing out. Perhaps promoting Jupp - who took over the BBC News' current affairs department after the scandals - to the top of News is a signal she will grip what some have viewed as a weak spot with rigour. Trust is one of the BBC's core values. It's listed on the back of our work passes as "the foundation of the BBC". The new boss will need to make sure that the BBC remains the place of record. An organisation that is trusted. It's still the most trusted source of news, but there are growing numbers of people on all sides of the political spectrum who don't feel the BBC speaks for them. Many will argue that is because people live in echo chambers online, and don't want to hear other voices. But any loss of trust is corrosive.
