title: Historic cathedral introduces £12 fee for visitors from outside Scotland
description: St Giles' Cathedral now charges an entrance fee for visitors from outside Scotland.
body: St Giles' Cathedral now charges a £12 admission fee for some visitors Visitors from outside Scotland now need to pay to enter one of Edinburgh's most popular attractions for the first time in its 900-year history. General admission to St Giles' Cathedral is set at £12, while free entry is still offered to Scottish residents and under-16s. Scottish visitors can get into the historic cathedral for free by registering online and providing proof of residency, while visitors who live elsewhere in the UK or abroad will need to pay for tickets. Located on the capital's historic Royal Mile, the cathedral welcomes more than 1.5 million visitors each year. St Giles': Playing a part in history for 900 years St Giles was first founded in 1124 as a Catholic church but later became a key site during the spread of Presbyterianism in Scotland when reformer John Knox was elected as its minister in 1560. It remains an important setting for major ceremonial events, including the public viewing of the late Queen's coffin in 2022 and the Kirking of the Scottish Parliament, while also hosting Sunday services. While it is the first time the cathedral has charged for entry, other religious sites in the UK have introduced similar fee mechanisms. York Minster charges £20 for general admission tickets and under-18s can accompany paying adults for free, while St Paul's Cathedral in London charges a £26 fee for tourist visits, while permitting service attendees free entry. More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East According to the St Giles' Cathedral charity trust, the site's annual operational costs are more than £1m. The charity, which manages the cathedral, said it did not receive regular funding from the Scottish government or local council and had decided to introduce the entry charge to ensure the site can continue its long-term operation as a visitor attraction, religious site and cultural centre. Alongside providing funding for the day-to-day operation of the building and its religious services, the entrance charge will allow the charity to expand its cultural offerings, according to Jack Oades the cathedral's organist and head of music, said. Oades said the additional funding "will allow us to significantly level-up our musical offering and our in-house concerts and events". "This will not only allow us to improve the frequency of our choral worship, but to attract world-class performers and engage with the wider creative and cultural activities across Edinburgh and Scotland," he added. The Reverend Dr Scott Rennie, who took over as the minister of St Giles in May, said: "As Scotland's High Kirk we want to offer visitors from home and abroad the best possible experience and the opportunity to understand how faith and history have shaped Scotland's life as a nation. "I am confident that these changes will be transformational in incorporating the life and cares of Scottish people into our cycle of worship through the year." title: Man jailed for life over knife attack attempt at Israeli embassy in London
description: Abdullah Albadri arrived in the UK on a small boat 16 days before trying to break into the embassy with two knives.
body: Abdullah Albadri had arrived in the UK on a small boat 16 days before attempting to carry out the attack A failed asylum seeker who tried to break into the Israeli embassy in London to carry out a knife attack has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 20 years. Abdullah Albadri was carrying two knives when police officers caught him as he tried to climb over a fence into the Kensington embassy on 28 April 2025. The 34-year-old from Kuwait had arrived in the UK on a small boat 16 days earlier, having first entered country illegally four years earlier. He was previously found guilty by majority verdict after a trial at the Old Bailey of preparation of terrorist acts and possession of two bladed articles. The court heard how he was motivated to plot the attack by the death of Palestinians in Gaza and planned the attack after sleeping rough in the capital. Albadri first travelled to the UK on a small boat in August 2021 and applied for asylum but returned to France before a decision was made. He crossed the Channel again in April 2025 and was housed in a hotel in Basingstoke for three days, before being told he was not eligible for accommodation due to his outstanding asylum application. On the day of the attempted attack, he walked to the west London embassy from north London wearing a red and white traditional Arabic scarf wrapped around his head and sunglasses. The embassy is located on a street which is home to several large diplomatic buildings and has a round-the-clock police presence. At around 18:00, he saluted in the direction of two nearby diplomatic protection officers before trying to scale a security fence. The armed officers dragged him down from the railings and detained him. Albadri was detained as he tried to scale a fence outside the Israeli embassy When he was searched, police found two 10cm (4ins)-long blades and a handwritten copy of a verse titled "the benefit of martyrdom". His trial heard how he told police: "I want to make a crime inside there. Why are you stopping me? Why are you stopping me from making crimes?" During a later interview at a police station, he said he had wanted "to do something to stop the war". The Old Bailey also heard evidence he may have acted in a way to force the nearby armed officers to kill him. Prosecutor Catherine Pattison said Albadri "intended to do something that would have resulted in the sacrifice of his life". She told the court people were leaving the embassy when he attempted to scale the fence who "would not have had any chance to defend themselves" if he had been able to carry out the attack. Defence barrister Chris Henley said Albadri's plan "could never ever have succeeded", adding "there was no serious risk of any harm to anybody". He said Albadri had acted in an "absurd, performative fashion" which was "deliberately designed to draw attention to himself". Albadri had spent the morning "trying to get help" to access housing, his defence barrister told the court. His trial previously heard he told officers "I wish you'd use that on me", and replied "I might be yeah" when asked if he was referring to a rifle. On Monday, Mrs Justice Lambert KC sentenced Albadri to life in prison with a minimum term of 20 years. Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London, said: "Albadri's attempt to carry out a terrorist attack at the embassy was thwarted due to the courageous and swift actions of officers on duty, who prevented him from breaching the security perimeter. "The significant prison sentence he has received reflects the danger he posed on the day and the lack of remorse he has shown since he was arrested." She said the Israeli embassy had "face various security alerts in recent times" and security measures were in place to "ensure the site and the wider community is kept as safe as possible". title: Twelve arrests after protest over migrant boat arrival
description: Flares were set off and there were a few scuffles with police during the stand-off in Gosport.
body: Police and demonstrators faced off during the protest in Gosport on Sunday evening Twelve people have been arrested for offences including assaulting a police officer after a protest over migrant arrivals in a south coast town. The Home Office said 149 migrants had been picked up in a mid-Channel rescue operation by the RNLI, alongside a French vessel, and were brought ashore at Gosport. Flares were set off and there were scuffles with police during the stand-off at a marina in the Hampshire town, involving about 150 anti-migrant demonstrators on Sunday. Eleven men and one woman were arrested on suspicion of offences including assaulting police officers, affray and racially aggravated public order. All remain in custody. The migrants were taken by coach to a processing centre in Kent. It is the second known landing of large numbers of migrants this far west along the south coast in recent years. A police cordon was in place on Haslar Road in Gosport, where the atmosphere at the protest mostly remained peaceful. Some protesters stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot". The migrants were brought into Gosport onboard an RNLI boat Hampshire Police said it had deployed officers to "support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea", including the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, RNLI, and Border Security Command. The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act, as well as powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings. A small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured, police said. Assistant Chief Constable Simon Dodds said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest. "Our position on this has been clear that we will investigate thoroughly and take robust action against anyone responsible. "Last night saw a number of incidents that were clearly not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe." He said officers "did not deserve to be assaulted as they worked incredibly diligently" to ensure the "safety of everyone in the area". "Neither do they, or anyone from our partner agencies, deserve to be singled out online or subjected to abuse via social media," he said. "We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made. "We will continue to review body-worn video footage and videos posted online to identify any further offences and may make further arrests in due course in required". A 22-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of affray and racially aggravated public order A 42-year-old man from Fareham on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in a public place and failing to comply with the conditions of a dispersal order A 35-year-old man on suspicion of assault by beating of an emergency worker and failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction A 39-year-old man from Emsworth on suspicion of criminal damage, attempted criminal damage and possession of a pyrotechnic article at a protest A 57-year-old woman from Emsworth on suspicion of assaulting a police officer A 59-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of racially aggravated public order A 29-year-old man of no fixed address on suspicion of obstruction of a highway after ambulances were prevented from travelling along Clayhall Road Five people were also issued with Section 35 dispersal notices. A Home Office spokesperson refused to explain why Gosport had been chosen on this occasion, saying they do not comment on "operational processes". "The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border," they said. They said it was "vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival". It is the third crossing in a month. So far this year 19,451 people are recorded as having crossed the Channel in small boats. That number is 43% lower than this time last year, and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024. Last month, more than 100 migrants landed at Eastney, in Portsmouth, leading to more scuffles between police and demonstrators. The 51 migrants were ultimately taken to Dover by sea. title: What we know about Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's legal action against police
description: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest in February.
body: This video can not be played Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has begun legal proceedings against Thames Valley Police over the lawfulness of the search warrants that led to his arrest in February. The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after information emerged regarding his dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are challenging search warrants used to access the former Prince's residences' at Sandringham and the Royal Lodge in Windsor, as first reported by the Telegraph. title: BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news
description: Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor.
body: Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor Rachel Jupp has been appointed the new director of BBC News, nearly a year after the previous CEO resigned. Deborah Turness announced last November that she would step down from the role following the fallout over how Panorama edited a speech by President Trump. Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor, but left several years before the controversial Trump episode aired. In a statement, Jupp said she was "honoured to be asked to lead BBC News", while the corporation's director-general Matt Brittin described her as "an outstanding editorial leader". The appointment comes as the BBC continues to make sweeping cuts to its news division. Around 550 job closures have been announced so far, with more expected to follow. The BBC as a whole will cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save £500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures". In a statement, Brittin said Jupp was "widely regarded for her news judgement, fairness and high standards". "She brings a clarity of vision for the future, and the determined, collaborative approach needed to strengthen BBC News," he added. Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for BBC News chief, says Katie Razzall Jupp joined Channel 4 News in 2005 and served as the programme's head of home news, before moving to the BBC in 2013 to become Newsnight's deputy editor in 2013. She became the editor of Panorama in 2016, a position she held for the next four years. Jupp also served as editorial executive for BBC Content, and more recently has led the BBC's editorial work on generative AI, based in the US. In her statement, Jupp said: "I want to champion our vital, independent and impartial journalism, deepen the trust people have in the BBC and meet our audiences wherever they are. "I'm grateful to Matt for this opportunity, and I'm looking forward to working with our dedicated, brilliant teams across the UK and around the world." The BBC's cuture and media editor Katie Razzall said it was "significant" that Brittin had chosen someone with experience of using artificial intelligence to run his news teams, "raising questions around how AI could open up the next frontier of a modern newsroom". The BBC said Jupp would be paid a salary of £400,000. Turness started on a similar salary in 2022, but that had increased to between £445,000 and £449,999 in her last year before leaving the role. Jupp will have responsibility for about 4,500 staff, and also serve as a member of the BBC's executive committee. Jonathan Munro, who has been acting as interim head of the news division for the last 11 months, will return to his role as deputy director of BBC News when Jupp takes up her role. Brittin said: "I would like to thank Jonathan Munro for his professionalism and leadership of BBC News in the past 11 months. I have been personally grateful for his deep experience, calm head and steady hand." Matt Brittin took over as the BBC's director general in May after Tim Davie resigned over the Panorama scandal The director general said BBC News remained the most used and most trusted news provider around the world and across the UK, but added that it faced significant challenges. "In a world of infinite choice, audiences are fragmenting, trust is scarce and facts are contested," Brittin said. "It is our duty to recommit to the BBC's distinctive journalistic mission while reinventing how we serve audiences, and to rise to these challenges. In Rachel, we have someone who can do both, with a fresh persepctive to lead BBC News into a new era." Jupp's predecessor Turness left the BBC after an internal memo leaked to the Telegraph highlighted that an episode of Panorama broadcast a year earlier had edited a speech by President Trump in a misleading way. In her letter of resignation, Turness said: "While mistakes have been made, I want to be absolutely clear recent allegations that BBC News is institutionally biased are wrong." The BBC's then-director general Tim Davie also resigned over the scandal, and was replaced by Brittin earlier this year. The episode of Panorama spliced together two sections of a speech he delivered in 2021, shortly before the Capitol riots on 6 January. President Trump launched a $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the BBC after the edit came to light. The BBC apologised and said the edit had given "the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action", but rejected his demand for compensation. The case is currently scheduled to go to trial in the US in 2027. title: Bombs preventing rescue of kidnapped youths, Nigerian police say
description: The father of one of the 19 young abductees tells the BBC he hasn't eaten in three days out of worry.
body: Omotosho Adewale, the father of one of those abducted, says he has had no peace and has not eaten for three days Nigerian police say they have located a camp where 19 national youth service recruits are being held by gunmen but cannot move in as they believe the place is mined with explosives. Police Commissioner Audu Bosso said drones helped locate the camp where the prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members were taken after being abducted last week in the south-eastern Imo state. The exact location of the camp has not been disclosed and police have not identified those responsible for the kidnapping. Omotosho Adewale, whose child is among those abducted, told the BBC that the kidnappers had demanded a ransom of 50m naira ($37,680; £28,440), which he could not afford. "There's no peace of mind. I've not eaten in three days," he said in between tears. Adewale appealed to the government for help. Those kidnapped had been travelling from Ibadan in the south-west to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states on Thursday when gunmen attacked their buses near Umunoha in Imo state. The NYSC is a compulsory one-year programme for most Nigerian university and polytechnic graduates. Participants, known as corps members, are posted to different parts of the country to work and take part in community service, as well as to foster a sense of national unity. 'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis Speaking to journalists, Bosso said they had tracked the kidnappers. "The drone actually showed us exactly their location. But our predicament is that with the intel we have... the camp is mined with IEDs [homemade bombs]," he said. Bulldozers and armoured vehicles are being deployed as police prepare for a rescue operation. Kidnapping for ransom is a major security problem in Nigeria, involving both criminal gangs and armed groups. The abduction in Imo state has caused widespread concern, with mass kidnappings less common in southern Nigeria than in some parts of the north. Paying ransoms is illegal and authorities have repeatedly warned families against doing so, but relatives of kidnapped people are often under pressure to do so to secure their release. The latest abduction highlights the risks faced by young people travelling across Nigeria to do their national youth service and has renewed calls for reforms. The NYSC has previously said it would not deploy members to areas considered high-risk because of violence or the threat of abduction. Most parts of south-eastern Nigeria have not previously been classified as high-risk areas. In the south-east, some previous abductions have been linked to separatist groups, including the Indigenous People of Biafra (Ipob). Authorities have not linked the current abduction to any group. title: Mother killed by falling bricks, court told
description: Higgins Homes and four individuals are on trial over the death of a woman near a building site.
body: A mother on the school run sustained fatal injuries when a large pile of bricks fell on her head as she walked past a building site in east London, a court has heard. Michaela Boor, 29, was on Burdett Road in Bow on the morning of 27 March 2018 when the accident happened. She suffered a fractured skull and died two days later. Higgins Homes is on trial at the Old Bailey charged with corporate manslaughter and a health and safety offence. Four construction workers contracted by Higgins Homes - Thomas Anstis, Stephen Coulson, Dawood Maan and Alexander McInnes - are accused of the same offences. Both the company and the four men deny the charges. Opening the case on Monday, prosecutor Alexandra Healy KC said Boor had been walking towards some shops with a friend, Chelsea Mustafa, when the bricks fell from a crane. She said: "Their route took them past a construction site that was being developed by Higgins Homes plc. "A pallet of bricks that was being transported by a tower crane towards a loading bay immediately adjacent to the pavement along Burdett Way fell on to them." The court heard the pallet caught on scaffolding while it was being hoisted, causing the bricks to fall. The prosecution claimed crane operator McInnes had a restricted view of the load and that the operation became a "blind lift" when it moved completely out of sight. Healy added: "Chelsea Mustafa ran into the road, away from the construction site. Although some bricks hit her on the back and her hand, she was able to avoid the bulk of the falling load. "Michaela Boor did not make it off the pavement. "She was hit by the falling bricks which fractured her skull and she sustained catastrophic brain injuries." Boor received treatment at the scene and was taken to the Royal London Hospital, but her injuries were "unsurvivable" and she died on 29 March, jurors were told. The bricks fell from a crane at a building site in east London in March 2018 Higgins Homes was the principal contractor and designer of the project to build a block of flats. The prosecution alleges there had been no risk assessment for lifting pallets of bricks so close to members of the public, and claimed Higgins Homes had not considered the safety of people outside the site. "Higgins Homes failed to give proper consideration to the protection of the public," Healy told the court. Anstis, 69, of Banstead, Surrey, was the senior site manager and temporary work co-ordinator. He was in charge of the building site and overseeing the work of subcontractors. The prosecutor claimed there was evidence showing that he "cut corners" to "save cost". Coulson, 69, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, was director of Coulson Lifting Services and was in charge of lifting services. He was not at the site on the day of the incident. Maan, 61, of Ashford, Kent, was the crane supervisor responsible for overseeing and supervising lifting operations on the site. McInnes, 34, of Islington, north London, was the crane operator. title: Runner dies after taking part in Cardiff Half Marathon
description: Event organisers confirm a participant has died and thanked medical teams working during the race.
body: More than 30,000 people registered for the half marathon, which is Wales' largest mass particpation and multi-fundraising event A runner has died after taking part in Cardiff Half Marathon. Event organisers Run4Wales said on Monday that the participant had died, adding: "We'd like to acknowledge the event and hospital medical teams who reacted with great speed and professionalism. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the runner's family and friends." It said no further details would be released "in respect of the family's wishes". Sunday's race was the 23rd edition of the the 13.1 mile (21km) route, which saw about 30,000 people take to the streets. In 2024, 37-year-old Stephen Jenkins died in hospital after collapsing at the finish line. In 2019, Ben McDonald, 25, and Dean Fletcher, 32, crossed the finish line within minutes of each other, and both died after going into cardiac arrest. (L-R) Stephen Jenkins, Ben McDonald and Dean Fletcher all died after collapsing at the finish line at the event in previous years Cardiff Half Marathon is Wales' largest mass participant and multi-fundraising event, with more than £4m raised each year for charity. It's the UK's second largest half marathon and a member of the SuperHalfs, a global series of the world's most prestigious half marathons including races in Lisbon, Prague, Berlin, Copenhagen and Valencia. It has also been awarded a Elite Race Label by World Athletics. title: Georgia officials hunt for suspect in shooting that killed two and injured 35
description: A homecoming celebration turned into a scene of deadly violence, as dozens of shots were fired into a crowd.
body: Investigators in the US state of Georgia are on the hunt for a suspect in a mass shooting that erupted in the early hours of Sunday, killing two people and injuring 35 more. A crowd of roughly 1,000 people had gathered for a block party in the southern rural community of Vienna when, according to officials, more than 50 shots were fired. Two of the victims were pronounced dead at the scene, while another 25 were transported to multiple nearby hospitals, some in critical condition. No known arrests have been made and authorities have not given a possible motive for the violence. Victims ranged in age from 14 to 51. The incident occurred on Sunday morning around 01:30 local time (05:30 GMT), during a Dooly High School homecoming celebration, though it was not a school-sponsored event. "Our hearts are with the families grieving the loss of loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone affected by this tragedy," the school said in a statement. Anticipating a large gathering, authorities from the Dooly County Sheriff's Office were already positioned at both ends of the crowd as gunfire rang out. "Some people were reporting fireworks and then someone said somebody been shot," Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told local media. Peavy said officials then worked their way through the crowd, as people ran scrambling in different directions, while authorities made their way towards victims. Ashley Gee, who was there, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution news outlet that the barrage of gunfire sounded "like a machine gun". Authorities arrived and found several people injured. The two deceased victims were found several blocks away from the scene of the shooting on Pine Street. Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls told the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the two killed were both men, ages 20 and 23. The Georgia Bureau of Investigations Medical Examiner's Office said it would conduct an autopsy in each case. The bureau also said it would join the investigation at the request of the Dooly County Sheriff's Office, describing operations as "active and ongoing". title: No10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
description: US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week.
body: The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase. A Number 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base. He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world". RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police. Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail. Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire. The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts. title: London City gelling, Man City flying - takeaways from WSL start
description: After five frantic weeks, the Women's Super League takes a two-week break, offering the perfect chance to take stock of a thrilling start to the season.
body: After five frantic weeks, the Women's Super League takes a two-week break, offering the perfect chance to take stock of a thrilling start to the season. Here are five key takeaways from the opening weeks. Alexia Putellas (right) already has three WSL goals since joining London City from Barcelona For the first time this decade, the established order of the WSL looks under threat. London City Lionesses and Tottenham have been bullish about climbing the table, while Liverpool also sought to kick on this season. After five games, London City look the most convincing, with Sunday's statement 6-1 win at Spurs a dazzling example of the talent and depth manager Eder Maestre has at his disposal. Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas headlined some eye-catching summer signings and she scored twice against Tottenham. But it was the manner in which the whole team dismantled their previously impressive opponents that was so spectacular, with fellow forwards Kadidiatou Diani and Danielle van de Donk also looking a class above. "This kind of win can be a game-changer," Maestre said. No doubt. It is the kind of display that can lead to talk of a title charge. For Spurs, a humiliating home loss is a reality check after promising early results. Liverpool acquitted themselves well in narrow losses away to both Manchester clubs but, with key attacking players such as Vivien Endemann missing against United, they lacked creativity. That points to perhaps the biggest thing both Liverpool and Spurs lack in comparison with London City: squad depth. This video can not be played 'It all clicked today' - Van de Donk and Putellas thrilled with 6-1 win against Spurs This video can not be played Man City fight back to beat struggling Arsenal Five wins from five with 16 goals scored, defending champions Manchester City have picked up where they left off. Sunday's comeback victory over Arsenal made it City's best start to a season since opening the 2017-18 campaign with seven straight victories, cementing their status as the team to beat. In so doing, City also likely ended the Gunners' title aspirations even this early on. It helps when their best players are performing. Khadija Shaw's contract renewal in the summer was key and the striker has five league goals already. England winger Lauren Hemp is also in fine form, contributing four goals and two assists. After some quietly shrewd additions in Beth Mead, Carlotta Wamser and Niamh Charles, City look well set once again. Their closest rivals are Chelsea, who have responded to an opening-day draw against Aston Villa by winning four straight games without conceding a goal. While boss Sonia Bompastor wants them to be more clinical, their defensive strength is something they have over City. As for Arsenal, the gap is 10 points to leaders City, and strong pre-season hopes of a first league title since 2018-19 are vanishing, with manager Renee Slegers conceding on Sunday: "At the moment, we are not in the conversation." This video can not be played Man Utd make it back-to-back wins against Liverpool Manchester United's summer of upheaval bled into the start of the season, with Eva Olid's arrival from Hearts beginning with convincing defeats by London City and Chelsea. The message from the club was that this would be a season of transition but recent performances suggest they are getting to grips with her style of play. Saturday's 1-0 win over Liverpool was United's fourth straight victory in all competitions, with 18 goals scored in the process. "I am so happy for the players - they deserve it," Olid said. "We have started to click in a lot of things and they fight for each other. "But there is still a lot to improve. We created chances, but our last pass and our finishing needs to be better." Summer signing Andrea Medina has been a huge positive on the left wing, with her contribution to the team more pronounced than a single goal suggests. A trip to bottom side Charlton after the break is a presentable chance for more points before a stern test against Manchester City the following weekend. This video can not be played Charlton thrashed by Brighton despite taking lead This season is the WSL's biggest ever, literally, with the league expanding from 12 to 14 teams and three coming up from WSL 2. But does bigger mean stronger? Crystal Palace look the most comfortable of the promoted sides, boasting six points from five games and they moved to eighth in the WSL table by drawing at Aston Villa on Sunday. But things are more difficult for the other promoted sides, Birmingham and Charlton, who prop up the table. Despite some promising patches, WSL 2 champions Birmingham have just two points and one of those came against Crystal Palace. At least France forward Oceane Hurtre looks suited to this level, sitting as joint top scorer in the WSL with five goals from five games. Hurtre scored against Everton in defeat on Sunday but defender Neve Herron summed things up by saying Blues were "second to everything" after the game. Meanwhile, it looks bleak for Charlton, bottom of the table with zero points, 15 goals against and only two goals scored. After their 5-1 loss to Brighton on Sunday, goalkeeper and captain Sophie Whitehouse said: "It just wasn't good enough. "It's a tough league. The jump up is so big. You can't make any mistakes." Finally, it is too soon to draw conclusions but attendances at some of the league's biggest matches have been down on previous seasons. For instance, Chelsea hosted Arsenal on 27 September in a fervent atmosphere, but the game had 36% fewer in Stamford Bridge than in January this year. Similarly, Liverpool against Everton at Anfield was 19% down on last season, albeit the Merseyside derby was the first game of the 2025-26 season. title: F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz
description: F1 "needs to have a hard look at" itself in the wake of unprecedented software glitches that affected the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Carlos Sainz says.
body: Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton were among the drivers who lost power before the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia Formula 1 "needs to have a hard look at" itself in the wake of unprecedented software glitches that affected Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Williams driver Carlos Sainz says. A bug in the software for a wet-weather engine map led to a number of cars struggling to move on formation laps before the start of the race. The start had to be abandoned, a new software code issued, and the race eventually got under way an hour and a half later than scheduled. Sainz, who is a director of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "It is clear the regulations are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the power units and for the manufacturers. Who decided five years ago that this was the direction to go? "We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can. "But clearly what was decided four or five years ago was wrong. We need to learn as a sport not to make those mistakes again." Governing body the FIA has launched a "full review" of the situation. It arose because there had been very little wet-weather running this year, and the specific circumstances that triggered the bug had not previously arisen. Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said on Monday: "It's a good reminder for all of us that we should probably make sure that complexity doesn't get out of hand and that we keep things as under control as possible. "And I'm sure we'll have discussions with the teams, with the FIA and with F1 to see how we can protect ourselves from those situations moving forward and make sure we can keep the complexity of the cars and the systems under control." This video can not be played Mercedes better 'watch out - Verstappen 'imperious' in Bahrain GP win Sainz's remarks are a reference to the wider debate about this year's new engine regulations, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power. The engines are fundamentally energy starved, which has led to drivers feeling the cars behave in a counter-intuitive way, and have reduced the impact of driver skill. The engines have about 1,000bhp on full power, but only 540bhp when the batteries run out. Because of the way the regulations have been arranged, the batteries are fully deploying and recharging several times a lap. And a series of highly complex restrictions have been introduced relating to the operations of the engine to try to alleviate some of the issues that have arisen. One of those is what triggered the problem in Malaysia - the total electrical power is reduced from 350kW (470bhp) to 250kW (335bhp) in the wet. One of the idiosyncrasies of the rules is that the cars slow down at the end of straights to recharge batteries, and many challenging fast corners have been neutered because they are being used as what two-time champion Fernando Alonso has described as "charging stations for the car". The 50-50 split was decided upon five or six years ago, and teams have been warning the FIA that these issues would arise since at least 2023. But at no point was the 50-50 split questioned until just before the start of this year, when it became apparent how significant the impact of the engines would be. Since the cars began to run this year, a series of rule changes have been introduced to address the issues. This year, the total amount of recovery allowed is altered depending on how energy starved a circuit is. The energy split will become 60-40 in favour of internal combustion in two steps by 2028. And teams and F1 bosses are already working on finalising a new engine formula that will introduce power units that are never energy starved. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for naturally aspirated V8s with no hybrid at all. But the current likeliest solution is a V8 turbo with somewhere in the region of 15-25% electrical power, which will mostly be used as a simple push-to-pass system. title: Salty celebrations, questionable signings and Test bolters - Prem talking points
description: Bristol set out their top-four aspirations with a statement win, while Gloucester's renaissance continues in the second round of Prem action.
body: Only three teams - Gloucester, Bristol and Bath - have won both their games after the opening two rounds of the Prem The stats piled up after a car-crash performance by Harlequins in a 48-0 shellacking by Gloucester. The biggest league defeat in 26 years. Seventeen penalties conceded. Only two entries made into the opposition 22m. Not one of their starting forward pack making more than four carries. It was a desperately under-powered display. Boss Jason Gilmore described it as "totally unacceptable" in the aftermath. The Australian has overseen a few eyesores during his time in charge; a 38-0 reverse at Sandy Park and a 40-14 reverse at the club's festive fixture at Allianz Stadium come to mind. Gilmore says turning around the tanker will take time. Contracts have to run down and money reassigned to different areas of the squad. Full-back George Furbank was this summer's big investment. The 29-year-old marked his Prem debut for his new club with a couple of trademark breaks, slicing up from backfield. He is a classy addition, but is he the signing they needed, with little room to manoeuvre under the salary cap and a creaking forward pack limiting the supply of ball to the backline? England loosehead prop Fin Baxter has been out for 10 months with a foot injury, but should be back soon. South African tighthead Sampie Swiegers is in contention for selection after his arrival in London. Chandler Cunningham-South and Guido Petti may be due a run from the start. But, with Alex Dombrandt expected to miss the majority of the season with a knee ligament injury sustained in June, Quins will need them all to hit the ground running. Snarl up front, rather than style out back, is where they are lacking. Gloucester thrash sorry Quins to go top of the Prem Rees-Zammit tops the early-season try-scoring standings, having crossed four times Bristol chief executive Tom Tainton caught some flak earlier this year for saying the Bears needs to think like a marketing agency, rather than a traditional rugby club,, external to grow its fanbase. The image of Louis Rees-Zammit mimicking Northampton star Henry Pollock's 'pulse-check' celebration, and the delight it sparked among fans, were evidence in his favour however. A 20,756-strong crowd at Ashton Gate – up 5,000 on their win in the same fixture last year, partly helped by football's international break – relished a spiky performance all round from Rees-Zammit. The Wales international could easily have had a hat-trick in a 34-26 win over Saints, but was body-checked by Tommy Freeman in pursuit of a final-play chip ahead, earning a penalty try and sending his opposite number on his way with a few blunt observations. Rees-Zammit, restored to the wing after dabbling at full-back on his return from American football, has four tries already this season and Bristol, who were well in last year's play-off hunt before a dip in form after the Six Nations, are looking ominous. The next four rounds of action – Saracens (a), Exeter (h), Leicester (h) and Bath (a) – are a big chance to dent some other top-four hopefuls. Rees-Zammit was not the only wing on a wind-up this weekend either, by the way. Adam Radwan's gleeful celebration of his try for Leicester against former club Newcastle, marking his territory by pointing to the pitch below his studs, drew jeers from the Kingston Park crowd. Rees-Zammit stars as Bristol power past Northampton Bath took some measure of revenge after losing a Prem semi-final at home to Exeter this summer England boss Steve Borthwick was at The Rec on Friday night. He will have taken particular interest in one 28th-minute scrum. Beno Obano and Will Stuart, either side of hooker Tom Dunn, made the Exeter front row look as though they were wearing skis rather than studs, sending the visitors skidding backwards at a rate of knots. Considering Baxter's lack of game time and Bevan Rodd being ruled out of the autumn after wrist surgery, Obano may well be the back-up loosehead option to Ellis Genge for England's Nations Championship campaign. Stuart's welcome return from an Achilles injury is likely to have him installed as the tighthead replacement behind the excellent Joe Heyes. Borthwick may well lean into their Bath connection as he rebuilds a 'bomb squad' bench which was crucial to England's good form in 2025. Gloucester fly-half Charlie Atkinson may well be twisting Borthwick's arm as well. The 25-year-old has been central to the Cherry and Whites' electric start to the season. He set up the opening try of their thrashing of Harlequins with a cute jink past Will Porter and then a pinpoint crossfield bomb for Ben Loader a couple of passages later. A hint of a dummy and a dart took Atkinson himself over for his team's fourth. His substandard goal-kicking may count against him. Of players with a minimum of 10 kicks at goal, only Bath's Santi Carreras had a lower success-rate off the tee in 2025-26. Team-mate George Barton had kicking duties on Saturday. But if Borthwick wants a back-up stand-off that more closely replicates the playing style of first-choice Fin Smith, Atkinson may be due promotion after three appearances for England A last season. Bath gain revenge on Exeter to win 11-try thriller James represented England as an under-20, but switched allegiances to play for Wales at Test level Last year's runners-up Exeter have begun the season with successive defeats, but there was significant improvement on their opening-day defeat by Gloucester as they threatened to climb off the canvas and overturn Bath, just as they did in June's semi-final at The Rec. A fit, firing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso - 133m carried, nine defenders beaten and two tries - was an obvious plus for the Chiefs. But Kane James made a major step forward. The 21-year-old Welsh international, who only made his first Prem start at the beginning of this season, was fearless at the Rec,

title: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
description: The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.
body: A second flydubai plane flew the stranded passengers from Saudi Arabia to Israel The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest. The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports. The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday. He attacked and wounded the captain with the emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew travelling on the plane was able to land it in Saudi Arabia. Israel's prime minister has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination" and the captain, passengers and a second crew prevented "a 9/11 disaster". Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says More details about the co-pilot of the flydubai flight – whom multiple reports have named as Hamam al-Hammami – emerged over the weekend as he continued to be questioned in the UAE, with Israeli representatives being updated. Israeli media cited sources with knowledge of the probe as saying the co-pilot told investigators that, having attacked Capt Smit Machchhar, he intended to continue flying the plane as normal into Israeli airspace and receive landing clearances from Ben Gurion airport. He then planned to crash the Boeing 737 MAX – with more than 180 passengers on board – into the airport or into a tower block in central Tel Aviv, in the style of al-Qaeda's 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, according to the reports. The sources are quoted as saying he was most likely to have acted alone rather than on behalf of a radical organisation or foreign government. The co-pilot also reportedly told investigators that he had intended to hijack and crash a previous flight to Tel Aviv but changed his mind because he knew someone on board. There was no immediate comment from Emirati or Israeli authorities. UAE Attorney-General Hamad al-Shamsi said on Saturday that his country's investigations would establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, and that the results would be announced upon their conclusion. This video can not be played Watch: Tearful pilot recounts moment of Flydubai attack Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv. Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views. He was later hired by UAE-based flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials. Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country. Regional officials told the Associated Press on Sunday that Emirati authorities had shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of flight FZ1073's departure. Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said the transport ministry was responsible for vetting such lists from foreign airlines. But Transport Minister Miri Regev said her ministry was not given passenger and crew lists, and that security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines fell under the remit of the Shin Bet and the Mossad foreign intelligence agency. Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has told the head of the National Security Council to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel". Australian authorities are investigating the co-pilot's links to Australia. Sources have told local media that he studied there between 2015 and 2017. title: What to do if you missed out on Glastonbury tickets
description: Those who missed out on Sunday should not lose hope, as there are other ways to secure a ticket.
body: Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in less than an hour Thousands of people were left disappointed on Sunday after tickets for Glastonbury Festival sold out in 42 minutes. Organisers used a new booking system for the first time which entered people into a virtual waiting room. Despite having capacity for 210,000 people, demand is always much higher than supply. But those who missed out on Sunday should not lose hope, as there are other ways to secure a ticket for the world-famous event when it returns to Worthy Farm in Somerset from 23-27 June. Below is everything you need to know about how you can still secure a pass for the 2027 festival. 'My girl lost her limbs to meningitis - get the jab' 'Ageing without children can be hard and lonely' Jeffrey Archer returns to his former school library Glastonbury tickets sold out in 42 minutes on Sunday Organisers confirmed that general admission tickets sold out in 42 minutes on Sunday. Coach package tickets, which went on sale on Thursday, sold out in less than half an hour. Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from the last event in 2025. In a statement on Instagram after the sale ended, organisers said: "Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply. "There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in spring 2027." Identification checks are carried out when the gates to Worthy Farm open Tickets for the festival were sold exclusively by See Tickets and are strictly non-transferable. Security will carry out thorough identification checks at all entry points on the site when the gates open to ensure validity. Any tickets found to be bought through third parties will be cancelled and admission will be refused. In a statement, organisers said: "If someone's claiming - whether on social media or elsewhere - they can get you Glastonbury tickets and it's not through See Tickets or directly from us, do not risk it." They added that they are made aware of people "losing large sums of money" every year on fake tickets. "Please do not fall victim to these scams," they said. The gates to Worthy Farm will open again on 23 June Anybody who missed out at the general sale can attempt to buy resale tickets at a later date. The sale will include cancelled or returned tickets. An exact date is yet to be confirmed, but organisers said the sale will take place in spring. Volunteers are needed in a variety of roles for the festival The festival and its associated charities and organisations always need volunteers to help keep things running smoothly at Worthy Farm. Normally, volunteers are required to work three eight-hour shifts in return for a pass to the festival, but the expectation does vary. Oxfam has worked with Glastonbury for more than 25 years. Anybody hoping to volunteer with the charity can register their interest to join the 2,000-person team to work in roles on the gates, campaigning with the public or helping in the charity shop at the festival site. Meanwhile, the Festaff stewarding team requires three eight-hour shifts per volunteer in return for a pass. According to the organisation, the shifts involve "light enjoyable customer facing tasks". My Cause UK is looking for volunteers to work four shifts lasting six hours and 15 minutes with their Internal Traffic Management team. There are also volunteer opportunities for the medical teams, tent stewards, campsite wardens and property lockups. Aspiring volunteers have also been warned of fraudulent individuals and/or companies who claim to be recruiting. Anybody unsure about the legitimacy of a company is advised to contact the festival. Olivia Rodrigo headlined the festival in 2025 Although the Glastonbury Festival 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, the rumours are rife already. Emily Eavis, co-organiser of the festival, has already confirmed that Oasis will not be performing at Worthy Farm. Liam Gallagher posted on X that "it's not happening". Eavis also told BBC Radio 4's programme that Madonna is "definitely not" headlining either. She did reveal that three headliners were already lined up which the team was "very excited about" - but for now, we will have to wait and find out. The last festival in 2025 was headlined by The 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo. Shindig Festival returns to Charlton Park Estate in Malmesbury next year Those who were unlucky with Glastonbury tickets should fear not because the West Country offers a variety of other festivals throughout the summer: Love Saves The Day - returns to Ashton Court Estate in Bristol 29-30 May Bristol Sounds - returns to Canons Marsh Amphitheatre from 25 June Forwards Festival - returns to Durdham Downs, dates to be confirmed Cheltenham Jazz Festival - returns 28 April-3 May Minety Music Festival - returns to the Cotswolds 1-4 July Valley Fest - returns to Chew Valley 29 July-1 August Shindig Festival - returns to Charlton Park Estate in Malmesbury 27-30 May WOMAD Festival - returns to Neston Park in Corsham 22-25 July Follow BBC Somerset on Facebook, external and X, external. Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630. title: Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion
description: The motion, which has divided senior party figures, backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
body: Chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said the motion "crosses a line" The chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein has told the BBC it is "quite possible" she will leave the party after Green members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism. The motion, which has divided senior party figures, also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel. It has been criticised by some Jewish groups and Israel's foreign ministry. Asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about her future, Lichtenstein said: "I haven't decided yet...It is quite possible that I will leave the party...I'm giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues." Lichtenstein, who is a former chair of her local party, said she had opposed the motion from the first time she heard about it. "I don't think it's helpful and it doesn't make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered devastation, orphans left behind, it doesn't make any difference to Palestinians in the West Bank who are currently suffering, are currently being attacked and killed." Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813. There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference. The party's leader Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, had called for the motion to be amended to add in protections for Jewish members and remove language referring to a "single democratic Palestinian State". Both of these amendments were defeated. Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on either this or the substantive motion. He left early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here. The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants". It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state". The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it". Lichtenstein said she defines herself as "both Zionist and anti-Zionist" depending on the definition, and said a problem with the motion is that there are many definitions. She said she was not concerned about "people accusing me of supporting Israel's right to exist and therefore I'm a racist, which of course is not the case", but said the "very bad motion...crosses a line". One way in which it did that, she said, was that the proposers said they had consulted some Jews, but did not consult the Jewish Greens, who would have made some amendments to improve the motion. She said there was a "vast range" of opinions among Jewish Greens, some who supported the motion entirely, others who supported aspects, and others who were against it. Some Jewish Greens also support one state, she added. She said that party policy was that "it's up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future - one state or two". The UK and 11 allies support a two-state solution, which would recognise a Palestinian state alongside an Israeli one. Israel rejects a two-state solution. Her concern with the motion was that the Green Party may accuse UK, Israeli, or Jewish organisations, including those that partner with Palestinians, of racism. She said she supports many of these groups working "against the occupation and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians". She said she knows of some non-Jews who are planning on not staying in the party because "they think the motion crosses a line" and also because of their work, if they might not be able to be associated with a party that has "Zionism is racism" as a policy. Asked whether she believed there were antisemites inside the party, including at senior levels, she said "there are certainly some antisemites in the party, I don't know about at senior level, that is not my experience". The motion was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813 In response to the motion, Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski from entering the country. A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist. Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression". "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added. Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, but the leadership was divided. In her interview on the Today programme on Friday, co-deputy leader Rachel Millward had called the motion "problematic", while her counterpart Mothin Ali told the BBC on Saturday he would support the motion in its original form. The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the largest and most liberal strands of Judaism in the UK, released a statement condemning the motion, which it said was "antisemitic in its formulation and intention". "Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews," the statement read. Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis also called the motion "poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain". The Green Party motion said it "rejects attempts" to - among other things - "equate anti-Zionism with antisemitism" and said "we affirm that definitions o

title: Indian singer Anuv Jain on finding success without the Bollywood boost
description: The star reveals why he is "very selective" about releasing music - and shares his future collab hopes.
body: The singer-songwriter has opened up about building a career on India's music scene as an acoustic indie pop performer Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you? Well according to Anuv Jain it's possible - and you can even create something "beautiful". The singer-songwriter's soft vocals have gained hundreds of millions of views on YouTube - not an easy feat as an independent artist in India's music scene. BBC Newsbeat met Jain as he prepared for the final shows on the European leg of his first world tour to find out why he's taking his time and "hoping for the best". "It's not about the numbers," Jain tells us backstage, ahead of his sold-out performance at London's Roundhouse. But they do tell a story. Jain is from Ludhiana in the Punjab region of India and began singing as a teenager. His tracks have since racked up hundreds of millions of views on YouTube with their emotional storylines about relationships and heartbreak. Jain primarily sings in Hindi, with his pieces often exploring deep emotions like love and longing. Fans talk about feeling like his music soundtracks their lives, external and is personal to them. His accessible style has attracted 3.9 million followers on Instagram and more than 20 million monthly listeners on Spotify. According to Jain, the secret to his success is simple. When writing music, he says, he imagines how someone listening in the car, going for a run or sitting alone at night would feel hearing the song. "I just try to make a good song and something that I would like to listen to, something my mum, my sister and my wife would like to listen to," he says. "For some reason, the taste that we have in music is gentle enough that when we put it out there, there are millions of people who are wanting to consume all of this." Jain has attracted a sizeable fanbase without the backing of Bollywood, which has traditionally dominated the Indian music industry with opportunities and significant funding for artists. He's one of a growing number of independent musicians offering something different to the rollicking film scores and dramatic ballads that are synonymous with the country's movie industry. Jain describes artists like him as existing in an "alternate space". "We release music ourselves and hope for the best," he says. Jo Tum Mere Ho and Afsos, Jain's track with AP Dhillon, both reached number one on the Asian Music Charts, but the singer says there's no recipe to his success. At one point, Jain was only releasing one song a year Jain says he's "very selective" about the music he releases, only putting out one song a year until recently. But he plans to change that - and insists he has new songs coming "very soon". "They're done and I think they're beautiful songs so technically you might have more music this year," he says. "It's not like it's gonna be just one release, let's see how it works out." The singer explains that seeing a project through is key - which might be why he limits what he puts out. "There are no projects like right now for me that are half or that I haven't completed them yet. "When I start a project, I always finish it. I mean, I might have ideas, but as soon as I start writing, I finish it." Simplicity seems to do the trick, with certain passages , externalof Jain's songs, like Arz Kiya Hai, becoming hugely popular among his fanbase and going viral on TikTok and Instagram. The singer also plays the guitar and has become known for his songs about deep emotions and themes There have been high-profile collaborations between some of western music and Indian music's biggest names in recent years. Jain says he'd be open to working with bigger stars, but only if his own identity can be preserved and things are done "the right way". "The storytelling cannot get diluted just because there's a bigger name attached," he says. But, he adds: "I'm not there yet". However, Jain does admit he could see himself joining forces with former One Direction star Zayn Malik, who's enjoyed success in both the Official Singles Chart and Official Asian Music Chart. "He would be somebody who would definitely work very well with the kind of music that I make," says Jain. "Maybe the universe will just make it happen." title: Nobel Prize awarded for showing inner workings of the brain
description: US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded for their work.
body: The Nobel Committee made the announcement at the Karolinska Institute, Sweden US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in the field of optogenetics. Their research has helped scientists learn more about the inner workings of the brain, to better understand how the human mind works. The Nobel Committee, external praised the trio for laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience by revealing how to switch on and off neural circuits behind "specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders". In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method to try to restore sight in people with visual impairment. "Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain," the Nobel Assembly said. "Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity's great mysteries: how our incredible brain works." The winners said it was "absolutely wonderful" to get the award, and that it was an honour to share the accolade with friends. The three men will also share the £900,000 (12 million Swedish kronor) prize money. Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, explained: "Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of." Before, the inner workings behind feelings, behaviours and bodily functions were more of a mystery to scientists. Optogentics is a way to illuminate brain pathways, using a special protein borrowed from algae that scientists use to control cell electrical activity using light. In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, the algal protein with unique properties. Deisseroth worked out how to use this light controlled protein to switch on nerve cells in the brains of mice. Researchers have since been able to study nerve cells and pathways in animals to see and discover more about what they do. The Nobel Committee said: "Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in the brain. They can bring memories to life, create feelings, drive behaviours and study the types of neurons that are involved in various psychiatric and neurological disorders." That is providing important insights into how the nervous system interacts with various cells in other areas of the body, such as in the heart and gut, the committee added. Researchers have also taken "the first steps" towards using optogenetics as a medical treatment, the committee explained. In ongoing clinical trials, scientists have been working to restore vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye's rods and cones. By inserting a special protein in the damaged region of the eye, the patient regained some vision when wearing special glasses emitting light. This switched on the therapeutic algae proteins. title: Two men die in Channel crossing attempt off northern France
description: Two women were also rescued and taken to hospital with serious burns from the mixture of gasoline and seawater.
body: The UK Home Office has recorded 19,451 people crossing the Channel in small boats this year (file photo) Two men have died after trying to cross the English Channel off the coast of Berck in northern France. According to local media, police saw migrants leaving the beach on a boat at about 22:00 local time on Sunday, and when rescuers arrived, they were bailing water out of the overloaded vessel with their shoes. "When we arrived, there were at least 80 people on board and a terrible smell of gasoline,"Jean-Marc Lamblin, director of the French national sea rescue service (SNSM) told La Voix du Nord newspaper. Two women were taken to hospital after suffering burns that were caused by the mixture of gasoline in the seawater. Their condition has been described as not life-threatening. Lamblin told the newspaper that there were so many people on the boat, including children, that about 20 people were left stranded in the water because they could not get on board. He explained that when SNSM arrived, the two men, aged in their 30s and 40s, were in cardiac arrest. The men and injured women were brought back to shore where firefighters and paramedics helped them, but the men died at about midnight. Boulogne-sur-Mer public prosecutor's office has opened an investigation to determine the circumstances of their death. The two women were from Somalia and aged 20 and 26, La Voix du Nord reported, adding that they are now recovering in Rang-du-Fliers hospital. Between 1 January and 27 September 2026, a total of 19,135 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 28 September 2025 to 27 September 2026 carried an average of 67 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. Separately, the UK Home Office said 149 migrants were picked up on Sunday in a mid-Channel rescue operation and were brought to Gosport, in Hampshire. About 150 anti-migrant demonstrators had gathered at the south coast town to stop the group being brought ashore, with flares being set off and some scuffles with police. Figures from the UK Home Office have recorded 19,451 people crossing the Channel in small boats this year. The number is 43% lower than at the same time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024. title: Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
description: Sánchez says Spain will head to the polls on 29 November after recent defeats on measures aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
body: Sánchez's announcement comes after a series of measures to tackle the housing crisis was defeated in parliament on Friday Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis. Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market. The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform. In a televised address on Monday, Sánchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites". Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for Sánchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration. "We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," Sánchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing". Sánchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament. Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest. Spanish prime minister calls snap election after housing protests Sánchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023. Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority. Sánchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups. Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government. Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide". The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change". The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid home led to public outcry On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants. Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September. A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It was later lowered to €1,650 - still €300 more than her monthly pension. She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital. Protests over housing took place in Madrid on Saturday Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home, but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing. The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests. The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds". The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas. The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further. Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes". The Spanish prime minister currently doesn't command a congressional majority Sánchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months. In April, his wife Begoña Gómez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation. She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by Sánchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition. In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations. And in June, Sánchez's former transport minister, José Luis Ábalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic. The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.
