title: Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?
description: At least 23 huge data centres are planned in Scotland, causing significant concern for campaigners.
body: A Google Data Centre in Cheshunt in Hertfordshire Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes. Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale. The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new "hyperscale" data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world. Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres. Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs. Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make. So what exactly are data centres, and why have they become one of Scotland's most controversial planning battles? The data centre proposed at Chapelcross would be one of the biggest in the world if it went ahead From the outside, data centres look like a factory or a warehouse. On the inside, thousands of flashing lights blink and fans whirr as rows of computer servers power AI. While some are built by tech giants like Amazon, other developers claim commercial sensitivities when asked what they are actually powering. Scotland's centres are currently quite small, but some of proposals for the hyperscale versions are immense. One of the biggest is at Auchtertool in Fife. The site would span 60 hectares (150 acres) - about the size of 84 football pitches. There have been a number of protests against data centres AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. But Scotland's data centre debate is not really about the technology inside the building - it's about the scale and impact of the centres themselves. At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, which has a capacity for 12MW. The new data centres being proposed are a whole new level. If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world. At Auchtertool, the planned 600MW data centre would be the same size as the neighbouring village. their size and impact on the landscape the amount of electricity they require the water needed to cool equipment noise generated by thousands of servers and cooling systems The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies. The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium. One of Scotland's biggest selling points for data centre developers is its strong renewable energy sector. Scotland generates huge amounts of electricity from wind, and some of that power is currently wasted because the grid does not have enough capacity to move it from where it is produced to where it is needed. However, experts caution that this does not mean data centres would run entirely on renewable energy. During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking. The scene inside a Meta data centre in Temple, Texas. As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating. While the tech industry says it is developing more efficient cooling systems, industry sources told the BBC last year the UK government's plan to make the UK a "world leader" in AI could put already stretched supplies of drinking water under strain. An expert recently claimed that Scotland's current data centres use less water each day than its libraries, but there are significant concerns over what the water consumption could be if any of the hyperscale centres were given the go-ahead. And what about the hum? Data centres have many fans cooling down the servers inside and people in the US who live near them have reported hearing a constant noise, with concerns it has also driven away wildlife. Many of the proposed data centres are in Scotland's central belt - including an expansion of the company DataVita's site in North Lanarkshire As well as having a stake in a key future technology, those behind AI data centres say they will create jobs. Lanarkshire has been designated an AI growth zone by the UK government, with data centres at its heart. When it was announced in January, external, £8bn of investment and 3,400 jobs were promised. The type of jobs a data centre creates has also been debated. About 800 are expected to be in AI, with 50 apprenticeships. The rest are in construction. Apatura - the developer behind 10 of the hyperscale data centre proposals in Scotland - highlights its green credentials with its access to renewable energy and battery storage. With China and the US hoping to win the AI race, the UK government does not want to be left behind. The Scottish government also supports the investment in the AI growth zone. In August, it announced that ministers would have to be notified of proposed centres over 50MW in capacity. A month later, it rejected the Scottish Greens' call for applications to be paused until new national guidelines are in force. However, it said environmental impact assessments would have to be submitted. The government also said it was "highly unlikely" any large data centres would be given the green light before Christmas, and promised that new guidance would be published by the festive season. title: England to play 50-over warm-up in stark Ashes contrast
description: England confirm warm-up fixture at the Waca before this winter's white-ball tour of Australia - a stark contrast to last year's Ashes defeat.
body: England's 50-over side began 2026 by winning in Sri Lanka and beat the same opponents and India at home this summer England will play a 50-over warm-up match against a Western Australia XI at the Waca in Perth before their white-ball tour of Australia later this year. The confirmation comes after coach Brendon McCullum said last month he was hoping to arrange such fixtures to get players "up to speed" before next year's 50-over World Cup. White-ball warm-up matches have faded from tours in recent years - England have not played one for six years - but this fixture is also a stark contrast to England's widely criticised schedule for last winter's Ashes series. Before that contest, England played one in-house warm-up at club ground Lilac Hill. At the time, the England and Wales Cricket Board said it had been told the Waca was unavailable. The arrangement of this fixture, which will take place on 7 November - six days before the first one-day international at Perth's Optus Stadium, therefore hints at a more focused approach, while McCullum pointed to the relative lack of experience in his 50-over side. England are learning - these are the World Cup issues they need to solve England avoid Australia & India in World Cup draw With Jos Buttler and Adil Rashid injured, Joe Root was the only player in England's XI for the third ODI against Sri Lanka with more than 50 caps. England, who have struggled recently in 50-over cricket but have won three series in a row this year, have a minimum of 20 official ODIs before next year's World Cup in southern Africa. "Aside from Jos, Joe and Adil Rashid, there's not a lot of experience in that side," McCullum said after victory over Sri Lanka. "We're going to try and put on a smattering of warm-up games to try and get guys up to speed as quickly as we can." England are also due to play warm-ups before their Test tours of South Africa and Bangladesh this winter, and before the one-off 150th anniversary Test against Australia in Melbourne in March. Those fixtures were in place before McCullum was replaced by Stephen Fleming as Test coach this summer. Since the Ashes, the ECB and Cricket Australia have held discussions about a reciprocal arrangement that would mean touring teams are provided with better preparation before Ashes series. England lost the first Ashes Test in Perth inside two days last year and were well beaten in the next two Tests to concede the series at the earliest opportunity. McCullum accepted afterwards mistakes may have been made with his side's preparation. England play three ODIs and five T20s in Australia this winter from 13 November to 2 December. They also play a 50-over tri-series in Pakistan against the hosts and Sri Lanka later this month. The announcement of England's new batch of central contracts, meanwhile, is expected to come next week, having initially been anticipated at the start of October. title: Town's 215-year-old chapel goes to auction for £1
description: The Grade II listed Ebenezer Chapel was built in 1811, but is now overgrown and derelict.
body: The Grade II listed Ebenezer Chapel in Aberdare once held up to 900 worshippers A 19th Century revivalist chapel is going to auction with a guide price of just a £1. The Grade II listed Ebenezer Chapel once held up to 900 worshippers but the building, with its long curved pews and high arched windows, was last used in 2009 and is now overgrown and derelict. Paul Fosh Auctions said the "substantial detached property" in Aberdare, Rhondda Cynon Taf, had partial renovation work done but its planning permission for conversion to five flats had now lapsed. "This large former chapel which also has a domestic-sized single garage is in the sought-after location of Trecynon," said auctioneer Sean Roper. The 19th Century chapel is going to auction with a guide price of just a £1 Roper said: "The Grade II listed chapel has two storeys of accommodation and sits in a sizeable but now overgrown plot with potential access from the front and rear of the site." The site is about 0.23 acres and sits amid "well-established residential housing" about half a mile away from the town centre. The property goes up for auction starting on 8 October. title: Scott out of England squad and faces injury lay-off
description: Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott withdraws from the England squad with a thigh injury that could keep him out for up to eight weeks.
body: Alex Scott won his second cap for England against Croatia on Saturday Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott has withdrawn from the England squad to face the Czech Republic on Tuesday with a thigh injury. The 23-year-old is set to be out for six to eight weeks with the quadriceps issue. Scott was excellent on his full debut as England defeated Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday. He felt the issue prior to the match, but played 70 minutes in central midfield alongside Elliot Anderson before being substituted. Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa has also been ruled out of the fixture at Wembley, with the 28-year-old to return to the Premier League champions for treatment on an injury. Bournemouth are due to play nine games between 10 October and 8 November. Alongside their weekend Premier League commitments, they will play on Wednesday or Thursday for four consecutive weeks, facing Sturm Graz, AC Milan and Sparta Prague in the Europa League and Aston Villa in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup. England coach Thomas Tuchel was effusive in his praise for Scott after the Croatia match. "First start and what a start, what a performance," said Tuchel. "He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making is at the highest level. "He plays with so much confidence. He is so active, so confident. The work rate off the ball. "He is just the complete package. He gave us a lot of mobility and a lot of variety and work rate in the centre of the pitch." Scott made his England debut in a 2-0 win over the Czech Republic in Prague on Tuesday, before his full debut four days later. He joins French forward Eli Junior Kroupi on Bournemouth's injury list, with the 20-year-old still unavailable after sustaining a foot problem in pre-season. The Cherries are 17th in the Premier League and are winless after five matches, drawing three times and losing twice. Marco Rose's side defeated Lincoln to progress in the EFL Cup, and won 2-1 at La Liga side Real Sociedad on their European debut. They return to Premier League action at Chelsea on Saturday (15:00 BST) and play Sunderland, Manchester United, Leeds and Ipswich prior to the November international break. title: Why has Spain's PM called a snap election?
description: his series of measures to tackle the housing crisis was defeated in parliament on Friday
body: This video can not be played Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez confirmed Spain will be heading to the polls on 29 November, after Sanchez's Socialist party, which is currently heading a minority government, failed to pass housing reforms in the Spanish Congress. Sanchez faces an uphill battle in his bid for re-election with polls showing Sánchez's Socialist party is trailing the conservative People's Party - which many expect to attempt to form a government with the far-right Vox. In his statement announcing the election, Sanchez warned Spaniards about what he called the "extreme-right wave" being seen in other countries and said Spain should continue to be a global example of "peace, feminism and prosperity". BBC correspondent Guy Hedgecoe reports. Follow the BBC's live coverage following Sanchez's announcement. Why has Spain's PM called a snap election? title: Average five-year mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
description: The cost of a new fixed-rate mortgage has been rising in recent weeks as lenders face higher costs.
body: The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, figures show. The cost of home loans has been rising in recent weeks, as lenders face higher costs amid international concern over rising prices, interest rates, and government borrowing costs. It means home buyers and anyone renewing a fixed deal have seen about 1,500 mortgage deals priced below 5% vanish since the start of September, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts. It described the situation as "brutal" for borrowers, with the average rate on five-year deals now at 6%, and at 5.98% on two-year fixed mortgages. For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage. Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals. title: How Keith Alexander blazed a trail for black football managers
description: Ex-players and family members on the legacy of the late Lincoln, Peterborough and Macclesfield boss.
body: This video can not be played Listen to Keith Alexander: the man, the manager, the pioneer, on BBC Sounds When Keith Alexander died in 2010, he was honoured up and down the country, including on one of football's biggest stages as England players donned black armbands for a match at Wembley. It was a fitting tribute to a man who was not only an admired and respected figure in the game, but a trailblazer who helped pave the way for more black managers in English professional football. As part of Black History Month, those who knew him best have been reflecting on his lasting impact. "Keith remains a beacon of hope for us all, and I know his story continues to inspire us," says Leon Mann, a co-founder of the Football Black List, external, which gives out an award in his memory. "When we see a number of black British or black managers in the Premier League, we should pause and remember Keith's contribution, because it would have played its part, one hundred per cent." Matt and Paul Alexander say their father's caring nature meant he got the best out of players Although he was not the first permanent black manager in the Football League – Tony Collins took the reins at Rochdale in 1960 – Alexander helped inspire a new generation to follow in his footsteps after spells in charge of Lincoln City, Peterborough United and Macclesfield, among others. Born in Nottingham in 1956 to St Lucian parents, Alexander was proud of his English upbringing and Caribbean heritage, his sons Matt and Paul say. Alexander spoke openly about the racism he encountered as a player, which included monkey chants and bananas being thrown at him. "He experienced loads of it, especially in his early days," Matt says. "There was loads of racism and throwing bananas, that kind of stuff. "I'd be really surprised if you spoke to any black footballer of that generation who hadn't experienced the same sort of thing." Despite this, Paul says race was rarely discussed at home. "It was never a conversation about how difficult it was for black youths growing up. "It was, you will be successful at what you do and you work hard for what you want." However, he adds: "I think he was conscious he did have to work twice as hard." Former Lincoln striker Franny Green says he owes a lot to Alexander After a long playing career, Alexander took charge of Lincoln City in 1993. After a season in charge, he went on to manage non-league Ilkeston Town and Northwich Victoria. In 2002, he was named Lincoln boss for a second spell and, working with a tight budget, helped guide the club from the depths of administration to the League Two play-off places in four successive seasons. Former striker Franny Green says Alexander will always be remembered for "bringing players from non-league and giving them an opportunity". "If you go through Lincoln's history, Keith's name is going to be one of the biggest when it comes to what he did." Green recalls having a real affinity with Alexander. "I think it helped because of my race and Keith's race," he adds. Recalling the first time he met Alexander during a trial at Ilkeston, Green says: "I was 16, this tall slim kid with a mini afro and he was just really charming towards me. "He said just go and play football – there's no pressure." Keith Alexander (second from right, facing camera) won praise for uniting the dressing room Simon Weaver joined Lincoln City in the summer of 2002 after previously playing under Alexander at Ilkeston. He recalls his former boss's great ability to unite a dressing room. One moment that sticks in his memory is the first time he was invited for a training session at Ilkeston. "I played quite well in training – afterwards I went and knocked on his [office] and he was sat there with his feet up and a bunch of grapes." Weaver was asked to "just come and play" for the team on Saturday. "He was just so relaxed," he recalls. "He just made me feel at ease, saying just come and do you what you did [in training]. "We played away first game and won – I got a black eye and I'm thinking, 'I'm liking this, this is my cup of tea'." England players wearing black armbands at Wembley following Alexander's death in 2010 Alexander was managing Macclesfield when he died in 2010. He was 53. Tributes poured in from across football, with clubs across the country observing a minute's silence. At the time, his son Paul described him as "a very humble man", adding: "He didn't realise the impact he had on others just by walking into a room." In recent years, players who have received the Keith Alexander Award from the Football Black List have included Yaya Toure, Shaka Hislop and Kerry Davis, the first black woman to play for the England women's national team. His legacy also lives on through the Sacred Sports Foundation, which he founded in St Lucia to help young people through sport. Mann says Alexander will be remembered for the opportunities he created for others and his willingness to challenge racism in football – and that should never be forgotten. title: Connor out, Lewis in as England name World Cup squad
description: Leeds Rhinos half-back Jake Connor is left out of England's Rugby League World Cup squad, with Hull KR's Mikey Lewis beating him to a place.
body: Jake Connor missed out on an England squad place for last year's Ashes, for which Mikey Lewis was selected Jake Connor has been left out of England's Rugby League World Cup squad, with Mikey Lewis beating him to a place. Leeds Rhinos half-back Connor, the 2025 Super League Man of Steel, had been expected to make the final cut after being talked up by England head coach Brian McDermott and enjoying a strong domestic season. The 31-year-old provided more assists - 43 - than anyone else during the Super League campaign just completed. But Hull KR's Lewis, who endured an inconsistent season, has done enough to convince McDermott that he should join captain George Williams, the Warrington stand-off, and Wigan's Harry Smith as half-back options. For Connor, it is another England disappointment to follow his controversial omission from the squad for last autumn's home series against Australia. England squad: Matty Ashton (Warrington Wolves), AJ Brimson (Gold Coast Titans), Ben Currie (Warrington Wolves), Zach Eckersley (Wigan Warriors), Herbie Farnworth (Dolphins), Ethan Havard (Wigan Warriors), Max King (Bulldogs), Morgan Knowles (Dolphins), Mikey Lewis (Hull KR), Jez Litten (Hull KR), Junior Nsemba (Wigan Warriors), Brad O'Neill (Wigan Warriors), Kai Pearce-Paul (Wests Tigers), Victor Radley (Sydney Roosters), Hugo Savala (Sydney Roosters), Harry Smith (Wigan Warriors), Morgan Smithies (Canberra Raiders), Luke Thompson (Wigan Warriors), Sam Walters (Wigan Warriors), Ben Talty (Brisbane Broncos), Jack Welsby (St Helens), George Williams (Warrington Wolves), Dom Young (Newcastle Knights) Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad Hawkins among five World Cup winners in England squad There has been much debate about which half-backs would make the England squad after McDermott said last month that he would probably take three to the World Cup, and that captain Williams - who is heading to Australia to join NRL club Dolphins after the tournament - would be one of them. But McDermott said in April, following his appointment as head coach, that the Leeds half-back was part of his World Cup plans. McDermott, at the time, described Connor as a "game-breaker" and played down concerns over his temperament, saying: "I think the rhetoric and the narrative around Jake was tremendously unfair." When he replaced Shaun Wane as head coach, McDermott indicated that he was keen to use heritage players - those who qualify for England through family background - to ensure the strongest possible squad. He has called up two Australia-born players for the first time - versatile back Hugo Savala, part of Sydney Roosters' NRL Grand Final-winning squad - and Brisbane Broncos' front-rower Ben Talty. Bulldogs prop Max King, born in Huddersfield while his Australian father David was a player there, also earns a first call-up. Victor Radley and AJ Brimson complete the Australia-born contingent in the squad. Grand Final winners Wakefield have no players in the squad, with Tom Johnstone - who won the Rob Burrow man-of-the-match award for his performance in the 23-10 victory over Warrington - needing time to recover from a series of injury problems. Forward Caleb Hamlin-Uele has also been omitted, with McDermott indicating he is also injured. Finalists Warrington have three players in the squad - Matty Ashton and Ben Currie joining captain Williams - while Wigan have seven, including Man of Steel winner Brad O'Neill and uncapped centre Zach Eckersley. Reece Walsh impressed during last autumn's Ashes but has had a testing club season with Brisbane Broncos Reece Walsh has secured a place in Australia's men's World Cup squad, which was also named on Monday - although head coach Kevin Walters has refused to confirm whether he will be first-choice full-back. Walsh has struggled to hit the heights of last season, when he inspired Brisbane Broncos to their first NRL Grand Final triumph in 19 years before helping Australia to a 3-0 Test series win over England. He missed the end of this season to have ankle surgery, but with Penrith's Dylan Edwards ruled out of the World Cup with a knee injury, Walsh will vie for the full-back spot with James Tedesco - man of the match as Sydney Roosters beat Newcastle Knights 19-18 in Sunday's NRL Grand Final. Loose forward Isaah Yeo will delay surgery on a torn pectoral muscle to captain Australia. Winger Mark Nawaqanitawase - who scored two tries in Sydney's win on Sunday - is not in the squad because of his impending code switch to union with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights. Second-row forward Angus Crichton is absent for the same reason, as he is joining NSW Waratahs. Star half-back Nathan Cleary is out of the tournament with a broken and dislocated ankle. Australia men's squad: Isaah Yeo (captain), Bradman Best, Jack Bostock, Blake Brailey, Pat Carrigan, Lindsay Collins, Reuben Cotter, Tom Dearden, Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, David Fifita, Harry Grant, Keaon Koloamatangi, Liam Martin, Latrell Mitchell, Mitchell Moses, Cameron Munster, Cameron Murray, Jacob Preston, Kotoni Staggs, James Tedesco, Tom Trbojevic, Sam Walker, Reece Walsh. Ali Brigginshaw was in the Brisbane side beaten by Sydney Roosters in Sunday's NRLW Grand Final Ali Brigginshaw has missed out on the chance to go for a fourth World Cup winners' medal after being omitted from Australia's women's squad. Head coach Jess Skinner said the 36-year-old Brisbane half-back - Australia's captain when they won the tournament in Manchester four years ago - was "upset" to be left out. "That was one of the hardest phone calls I've had to make as a coach to a player and to talk about her and where she was," Skinner said. title: BT agrees rescue deal to buy broadband operator TalkTalk
description: The takeover still needs to be approved by the regulator, but would give certainty to TalkTalk's millions of customers
body: The UK's biggest broadband provider, BT, has agreed to buy rival operator TalkTalk to save the company from collapse. The takeover would end of months of speculation over the future of TalkTalk and mean services for its millions of customers will continue as normal. BT chief executive Alison Kirkby said it provided "a safety net" for those who rely on TalkTalk. The administrator said it also provided certainty for TalkTalk's 900 staff. However, Virgin Media called the deal a "stitch up" which allows BT to "tighten its grip" over the market. The government has given itself the power to have the final say on the takeover, citing its importance to critical public services. TalkTalk has 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale customers across the UK. BT's Kirkby told the BBC's Today programme: "Two and a half million customers, including vulnerable households, and key emergency services might have lost their services if Talk Talk had failed, which it was on track to do. "So BT stepped in as we were the only viable option to take the business forward." TalkTalk began as a challenger to BT in the broadband market. It was listed on the London Stock Exchange, but was taken over by private equity in 2021. Since then, the firm has built up debt while losing customers, leaving it unable to pay some of those it owes money to. The Competition Markets Authority (CMA) will need to approve the takeover, which would give BT greater power over the broadband market. Tom Smith, a competition lawyer and former legal director at the CMA, said the regulator will be balancing that concern with other considerations. "When the CMA looks at it, it will look at what would have happened if the deal wasn't going through," he told the BBC. "If TalkTalk would have exited the market, for example, then really any deal is better than TalkTalk exiting, but then there might be alternative bidders as well that would have been less anticompetitive." However, the Department of Culture, Media, and Sport (DCMS) has given itself the power to make the final decision on the deal in the name of the public interest once the CMA has made its report. DCMS has given the CMA until 19 October to deliver its verdict. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure. "If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services – including to hospitals, schools and emergency care. These are unprecedented circumstances that require action now." BT has said it will cost the firm £400m to buy TalkTalk. This includes the amount needed to buy TalkTalk from administration, fees, TalkTalk's £60m loss for this year, and BT effectively writing off the £100m TalkTalk owes BT's Openreach business. title: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
description: For many locals on this island, the arrest has brought decades of frustration back to the fore.
body: For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there. "Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC. "Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?" Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments. "I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC. Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops. US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties. Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty, external or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges. Some locals gathered to protest against the robbery-murder case on Sunday Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City. The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha. Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough. "I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously." "I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said. Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough." US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard was arrested on suspicion of committing the murder Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island. The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime. The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there. In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government. Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes. In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store. In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman. "Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC. "We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace." title: Andrew takes legal action over search warrants relating to arrest
description: Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office and later released under investigation in February.
body: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor photographed leaving a police station in February Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest in February. The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the United States. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are challenging the search warrants used in Sandringham and at Royal Lodge in Windsor relating to his arrest, as first reported by the Telegraph. Thames Valley Police confirmed: "We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court." "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further," a spokesperson for the force that carried out the arrest said. Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, has lodged a judicial review, challenging the legality of the search warrants. A court hearing will be held on Thursday afternoon to consider this bid to quash the warrants, with the hearing set to begin in private. The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor had been arrested - and the legal challenge is against the chief constable of Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court. For several days after the arrest, police were seen searching Mountbatten-Windsor's property at Marsh Farm in Sandringham and at his former home, Royal Lodge, on the Windsor estate. The arrest was carried out on his 66th birthday and led to him being taken to Aylsham police station. A photograph captured his departure later that day, looking exhausted, after he was released under investigation. Thames Valley Police says that its investigation is continuing. Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing in his associations with Epstein. Sign up here to get the latest royal stories and analysis every week with our Royal Watch newsletter. title: £800m in, £800m out - Why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
description: Manchester City's owners have been found guilty of injecting money into the club. At Manchester United, fans are frustrated at how much has been taken out.
body: The Premier League panel's report laid it out in black and white. "The club's income was hugely overstated by over £830 million." In other words, Manchester City's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations over a number of years by pumping money into the club that should not have been recorded as sponsorship income. The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026. Contained within it was an interest payment of £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year. And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of £852m. Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city resulted in money being ploughed in, it meant a similar significant sum being paid out in interest for the other. Carlos Baleba is yet to make his first team debut for Manchester United United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable." This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence. Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate. Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths. In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn. To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m. Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this. Radek Vitek's move to Middlesbrough could eventually net Manchester United £14m When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined. Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad. Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that. In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season. While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance. Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear. When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less. Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho. It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales. Manchester United fans held their latest protest against the club's ownership before the home defeat by Manchester City on 13 September In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020. Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late. The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford. Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch. In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa Leagu

title: Chiefs and 49ers remain unbeaten - five things from NFL week four
description: Five teams went into week four of the NFL season with a 100% record, but only three teams remain unbeaten after Sunday's action.
body: The Kansas City Chiefs, San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings are the only teams with a 4-0 record Only three teams remain unbeaten in the NFL after two more 100% starts were halted during week four of the season. Sunday's slate got under way with the Indianapolis Colts beating the Washington Commanders in the first of this season's three London games. The New England Patriots and Los Angeles Rams then avoided dropping to a 1-3 record by pulling off some big wins on the road. The Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders were among the five teams who made a 3-0 start to the season and one team's '0' had to go as the divisional rivals met, while the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings marched on. Here are five things you missed from Sunday's action. Kansas City have dominated their rivalry with the Raiders in recent years, but Las Vegas are vastly improved after winning only three games last season and pushed the Chiefs all the way. The Raiders led 13-10 heading into the final quarter in Vegas, which featured three lead changes before Kansas City held on for a 30-27 win. The turning point came as new running back Kenneth Walker maintained his stunning start by scoring two touchdowns in 19 seconds, with the Chiefs regaining possession immediately by forcing a fumble on the kick-off return. The Raiders gave themselves hope with a Brock Bowers score and stayed alive until the final play, when Kirk Cousins was tackled as he threw and his wayward pass was intercepted. Walker finished with 177 yards from 22 carries, while team-mate Tyquan Thornton also had two touchdowns and 111 receiving yards. After missing last season's play-offs, the Chiefs look capable of getting back into Super Bowl contention. They next face the Los Angeles Chargers, who are 0-4 after losing 30-23 to defending champions the Seattle Seahawks. The other two teams who improved to 4-0 were the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings. The 49ers hosted the Denver Broncos, who overcame Super Bowl favourites the Rams last week, and they were tied 3-3 until late in the third quarter. Christian McCaffrey's touchdown in the fourth quarter gave the 49ers some breathing space and, although Jaylen Waddle replied, George Kittle scored on a huge catch-and-run down the middle to seal a 24-14 win. While Cousins and Brock Purdy lead the league with 11 touchdown passes, Purdy has been intercepted only once and has not been sacked in the 49ers' first four games. The Vikings are the biggest surprise to be 4-0, having ground out another win, this time 15-10 over the Miami Dolphins, with Will Reichard kicking five field goals. Drake Maye (right) was narrowly beaten by Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matt Stafford in voting for the 2025 Most Valuable Player award Some said Drake Maye's confidence was shot after he was benched during the New England Patriots' blowout loss at the Jacksonville Jaguars last week. After throwing eight interceptions in the 2025 regular season, the 24-year-old quarterback had six in the Patriots' first three games and only one touchdown pass. Next up was a daunting trip to the unbeaten Buffalo Bills - led by the 2024 Most Valuable Player Josh Allen - but Maye showed why he narrowly missed out on the MVP award last season, when he led the Patriots to an unexpected Super Bowl run. After Allen restored Buffalo's lead with a 34-yard touchdown pass to Keon Coleman with four minutes left, Efton Chism made a superb one-handed catch in the endzone to put the Patriots back in front. They then intercepted a hopeful Allen throw to clinch a 29-26 win, with Maye passing for three touchdowns and 269 yards. The Bills joined the Rams as Super Bowl favourites last week and they go head to head in LA next week. After losing a thriller at Denver last Monday, the LA Rams were 1-2 and faced another stern test on the road this week at the Philadelphia Eagles. The hosts led 20-10 at half-time after two Darius Cooper touchdowns, but the Rams fought back, with Kyren Williams rushing for two touchdowns in the final four minutes to claim a 24-20 victory. The fit-again Puka Nacua finished with 125 receiving yards and a touchdown for the Rams, while the Eagles' injury concerns mounted. Wide receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring) was ruled out before the game, joining tight end Dallas Goedert (knee) on the sidelines, and Philadelphia lost star running back Saquon Barkley to an early hamstring injury. That is a big blow for the Eagles and UK fans as they visit Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday to face the Jacksonville Jaguars, who beat the Cincinnati Bengals 22-17 to make it back-to-back wins. The Baltimore Ravens also have fitness concerns over a key man, with two-time MVP Lamar Jackson (ankle) unable to play during the second half of their 24-18 home win against the Tennessee Titans. When are the 2026 NFL London games taking place? There have been at least 48 points in every Dallas Cowboys game this season, and they played their part in another high-scoring affair at state rivals Houston. The Texans led 23-13 after Nico Collins' second score in the third quarter and then 30-27 with two minutes remaining. But Dak Prescott led the Cowboys to a game-winning drive of 11 plays and 74 yards, throwing a touchdown pass to star receiver CeeDee Lamb to claim a 34-30 win. Lamb had a career-high 17 receptions for 189 yards, while team-mate Javonte Williams rushed for three touchdowns as Dallas improved to 2-2. Sunday's highest scorers were the New York Giants after Jameis Winston, filling in for injured quarterback Jaxson Dart, threw three touchdowns and two interceptions in a 36-24 win at home to the Arizona Cardinals. title: Summerlike warmth to give way to autumn chill this week
description: Temperatures on Monday could reach 23C but chillier air will spread from the north making it feel much more autumnal by midweek.
body: This week is set to bring a change in the feel of the weather with above-average temperatures set to give way to cooler conditions spreading from the north. After an unseasonably warm start to Monday, afternoon highs are expected to peak at 23C in south-east England. However, wet and blustery weather will move across some northern parts of the UK and as that sinks southwards later in the week it will introduce chillier air. Maximum temperatures on Wednesday are expected to be around 11-16C, near or a little below the average for early October. The week begins with south-westerly winds and mild air across the UK. In southern England, the Midlands and East Anglia, any early mist and fog should lift to leave a mostly dry day with sunny spells. However Wales and northern England will see rather cloudy conditions and some outbreaks of mostly light and patchy rain. A weather front will bring outbreaks of rain south-eastwards across Scotland and Northern Ireland with sunnier conditions following into northern Scotland - although here it will be windy, with possible gusts of 50-60mph (80-100km/h) across the Northern Isles. Maximum temperatures will reach 14-19C in much of Northern Ireland and Scotland, a few degrees above the seasonal norm in many locations. Meanwhile, forecast highs of 18-23C in England and Wales are closer to typical August temperatures than the values that would be expected in early October. Typical early October highs would be 12-17C The band of rain in the north of the UK will move erratically south-eastwards during Tuesday and Wednesday in association with a weather front. That will bring pulses of showery rain on Tuesday, perhaps turning heavier in some southern parts on Wednesday. Behind the weather front conditions will turn chillier and by Wednesday temperatures in all areas will be around or below the seasonal norm. If the thermometer fails to reach 20C anywhere in the UK, it will be the first day when that has happened since 11 June. Cool, fresh but sunny conditions will develop in many areas on Wednesday and Thursday albeit with some showers, especially in the east. Brisk northerly winds will make it feel even chillier than the actual temperatures would suggest - especially around eastern coasts of Scotland and England. Another change is expected by the weekend with westerly winds set to bring the return of rain-bearing Atlantic weather systems - and perhaps some slightly higher temperatures. Unsettled weather looks likely to continue beyond that with spells of rain interspersed with drier, brighter interludes. Long-range forecasts for the autumn overall suggest an increased likelihood of wetter and warmer-than-average weather, partly due to the strong El Niño that continues to develop across the Pacific. However, long-range forecasting is fraught with uncertainty and while the season as a whole may be mild, some chilly interludes are also anticipated. You can check your local weather forecast, including the expected feels-like temperatures, on the BBC Weather website and app. Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year? title: Murder investigation after body found in van on fire
description: Police were called to reports of the van ablaze, and officers are working to identify the person.
body: The body was found in a van on a lane in Prestatyn A murder investigation has been launched after a body was found in a van that was on fire. Emergency Services were called to Gas Works Lane in Prestatyn, Flintshire, at about 23:30 BST on Sunday after reports of the van ablaze. The identity of the person is unknown, and Det Supt Chris Bell said: "Officers are working at pace to identify the person." A police cordon is in place, as investigations continue. Det Supt Bell said: "Once the identity is known, specialist trained officers will be assigned to support their family as soon as possible. "We understand this incident may cause concern within the local community, and I would like to reassure the public that there is a visible policing presence in the area. North Wales Police appealed for anyone who was in the Gas Works Lane area of Prestatyn between 22:45 and 23:45 on Sunday, who saw or heard anything unusual, to get in contact. title: £117m Rogers failed at Bournemouth - and feared he may not make it
description: A look at the point in club-record £117m Chelsea signing Morgan Rogers' career when he doubted whether he could make it at the highest level.
body: Rogers scored only once on loan at Bournemouth, against Luton Town in the Championship Three years before becoming Chelsea's £117m club-record signing, Morgan Rogers watched his value fall to just £1m and questioned whether he would make it at all. For Rogers, the transition from academy football to the men's game was not as seamless as he had hoped and, in his own words, it took a series of "difficult loans" for him to break through. Bournemouth, who Chelsea face at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, were the first of two underwhelming Championship loan spells for Rogers, alongside a later stint at Blackpool, while he was a Manchester City player. It was a setback for a player who had been a regular England youth international and one of West Bromwich Albion's brightest academy prospects. In a recent interview with Chelsea's club channel, Rogers said that period taught him how to "take knocks". Asked what his rise through the EFL had taught him, he replied: "Everything." After a long pause, he added: "I needed that next challenge, to be taken out of my comfort zone and find the player I was going to be in professional football. "I think the academy player I was, if you watch me then, is not the same player I am now. I am a completely different player. I had to learn that on loan. "The one thing I learned when going through these difficult loans is that I couldn't care less what people say about me. I just care about what I can control." Rogers lined up in an attack with now-Everton forward Brennan Johnson (pictured right) at Lincoln City "I don't think there's such a thing as a bad loan," Rogers' first loan manager at Lincoln City, Michael Appleton, told BBC Sport. Appleton had worked in West Brom's academy and knew Rogers was one of the most highly rated prospects there. He made it his mission to bring him to Sincil Bank in League One. He remembers Rogers having a big personality and speaking up in team meetings despite arriving as an 18-year-old. The forward went on to score six goals and provide two assists in 28 appearances after joining shortly after lockdown. En route to the play-off final, which Lincoln lost to Blackpool, Appleton recalls one moment in particular. "We played Portsmouth away and they had three or four absolute units in the team," he added. "We were setting up for set-pieces and almost running out of players to pick up these giants. "Without any hesitation whatsoever, Morgan said: 'Make me a marker. I'll head the ball out of our box.' "This was a teenager on his first loan. "He was full of confidence because he was playing well, but he took the defensive side of the game just as seriously as trying to impact the opposition's box. For me, that's a great example of him as a person and as a player." However, after earning an opportunity in the Championship with Bournemouth, Rogers started only three matches and scored once under then-manager Scott Parker, whose side secured promotion back to the Premier League. Rogers had little impact and was described as a "slow burner" by former scout Des Taylor, who brought him in. He added: "You could see his ability having scouted him at Lincoln, but it wasn't clear what he would become. We saw his Lincoln loan spell turn him from a boy into a man. "He showed he could handle the physical side of things after coming from Man City's academy. Unfortunately, we signed him late in the window. We saw him as a number 10, but Parker was not really playing with a number 10. "I don't think it was a great time for him because he wasn't getting game time and, when he did, it wasn't in the position he wanted. He was a victim of the transition. It was no fault of Scott's, but it didn't work out." Former Bournemouth team-mate Steve Cook added: "Bournemouth had the opportunity to sign him permanently (reportedly for £9m) but it didn't work out. "He didn't let it stop him. First and foremost, he was a really good lad. He was energetic away from the football pitch and I think that character has helped take him to where he is now. "He's a great example that not every journey is straightforward. You need setbacks to make you hungry and appreciate what you've got. He worked hard, listened, had a willingness to learn and wanted to prove people wrong." Rogers' loan spell was cut short and he returned to academy football before an injury delayed his next move to Blackpool until the following January. The move reunited Rogers with Appleton in the Championship, but the manager was sacked after only two weeks and replaced by Mick McCarthy. Rogers made 20 appearances, both as a starter and substitute, scoring once as the Tangerines were relegated to League One after appointing a third manager in April. "Unfortunately, he played one game against Watford and then I got sacked. That wasn't great for either of us," Appleton added. "He'd been patient, I'd been patient while he recovered from his summer injury, we'd finally reconnected and then I was out of the building. "I don't think he played as much as he would have liked after that, but he dealt with it professionally and in the right way." Rogers says this period was "difficult" and tried not to compare himself to former team-mates who overtook him and got opportunities before him. He even doubted whether he would make it but said his family and friends kept him grounded. Notably, his "best friend in football", Cole Palmer, joined Chelsea for £42.5m having not needed a loan move to establish himself at Manchester City. At the same time, Rogers joined Middlesbrough for just £1m. A run of five goals and three assists during Middlesbrough's six-game run to the Carabao Cup semi-finals alerted Aston Villa, where several of Rogers' former West Brom coaches were working in senior academy roles, to make an initial £8m move in the winter window. title: Girl's death 'unexplained' after body found
description: The girl's body was discovered after she was reported missing on Sunday, says West Mercia Police.
body: The girl's body was found in a park close to the cricket ground in Elmley Castle, police said An 11-year-old's death is being treated as unexplained by police who say they are investigating after her body was found in a Worcestershire park. The girl was reported missing at about 23:20 BST on Sunday and she was later found in the park near the cricket ground in Elmley Castle, near Evesham, detectives said. Inquiries were ongoing into the circumstances surrounding her death, a West Mercia Police spokesperson said. Nearby residents were warned by the force that there would be an increased police presence in the area. title: Model boats banned from lake over speed fears
description: The council says the aim is to prevent people from using high-powered model boats on the lake.
body: The sign has been put up to prevent people from outside the model boat club from using the lake People with model boats have been banned from using a park's lake, unless they are taking part in a session run by a local boat club. Stevenage Borough Council said the sign was erected at Fairlands Valley Park, external to stop people outside of the club from "using high-powered model boats" on Millennium Lake. Ian Searle, secretary of Stevenage Model Boat Club, said there were model boats you can buy off the shelf that travel at speeds of 60-70mph (up to 112km/h). "Those without experience, who are generally not insured, can try them out on the lake which is likely to cause an accident," he said. Searle said restrictions were put on members a few years ago, with boats with internal combustion engines banned. "The sign by Millennium Lake was aimed at other people, just to take away the free for all for everyone else," he said. Stevenage Model Boat Club says it is no longer allowed to run boats with internal combustion engines on the lake The council said Stevenage Model Boat Club had "specific sessions at the lake and it is aware of the restrictions that are in place". A spokesperson added: "Anyone looking to use an authorised type of model boat is welcome to use the lake by contacting the club directly." Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? title: Court of Appeal to hear residents' parade challenge over Drumcree dispute
description: The deadlock over the Orange Order march in Portadown - opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since last Sunday morning.
body: Protesters have maintained a presence on the Garvaghy Road since Sunday - picture taken on 28 September A challenge to the decision to allow a controversial Orange Order parade to go down a predominantly nationalist road is due to be heard in court later. The deadlock over the proposed march in Portadown - opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since last Sunday morning. The stalemate has reopened what was once the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 90s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. The fresh Court of Appeal application argues that the Parades Commission, the organisation that approved the march, had "materially misdirected itself" on the police assessment of the potential for disorder. (Left to right) DUP MLA Jonathan Buckley, Nigel Dawson, the district master of the Orange Order in Portadown, and deputy district master Alastair Power, talk near Drumcree Church on Friday 2 October The application also said the commission had not given an "accurate representation" of PSNI evidence in its decision. Monday's hearing is due to begin in Belfast at about 10:30 BST. On Friday 25 September, the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place. The residents' appeal will be the latest legal challenge since it was given the go-ahead after three separate legal hearings over the course of 13 hours late on Saturday and into the early hours of Sunday morning. Orangemen gathered at Drumcree Church on Sunday but were blocked from completing their march Last Sunday, the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. Protesters have since remained on the road, although in much smaller numbers, and the Portadown District Orange Lodge has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church, about a mile away. On Tuesday, lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition (GRRC) issued a fresh legal bid to try to prevent the march from going ahead. Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition speaks to the crowd outside the court house on 26 September In the meantime, discussions aimed at resolving the dispute have been ongoing. PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher also discussed the dispute at a public meeting of the Policing Board in Belfast on Thursday, where he said the policing operation has cost about £3m so far. A police investigation into anyone suspected of breaking the law in relation to the dispute is ongoing. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? title: Radical change needed to cut Scottish child poverty, says charity
description: The Joseph Rowntree Foundation says Scotland is on course to miss legally-binding poverty targets "by a wide margin".
body: Scotland is on course to miss legally-binding targets to cut child poverty "by a wide margin", according to a report from a leading social reform charity. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) said one in five children was in poverty and "radical change" was needed to put the Scottish government's pledges back on track. It urged ministers to craft a "much bolder and properly-funded plan to reduce poverty" by rewiring local government, public services and the tax system. The Scottish government said it had made great strides, with its policies keeping 100,000 children out of poverty this year, but accepted there was more to do. In 2017, MSPs passed a law requiring ministers to hit four targets, external, including pushing the share of children in relative poverty below 10% by 2030. But the JRF's Poverty in Scotland report, external found the figure remained stubbornly high, averaging 21% from 2022 to 2025. The UK average is 28%. Relative poverty means a household has disposable income after housing costs below 60% of the UK median, adjusted for family size and composition. Overall, the report concluded, 940,000 people in Scotland were in relative poverty – 17% of the population. Scotland misses targets on reducing child poverty Swinney to make eradicating child poverty greatest priority The charity said that "despite some progress" the Scottish government's existing plans "will not deliver the scale of change needed to shift the dial." Reasons for the failure were "complex", it said, but could include UK government austerity, a cost of living crisis, and "a dysfunctional relationship between local and national government in Scotland." Scotland's Social Justice and Housing Secretary, Shirley-Anne Somerville, is currently overseeing a review of the poverty reduction goals after some interim targets were missed and data collection was adjusted, complicating the ability to assess progress. The targets are based on annual figures which can be volatile but JRF and the Scottish government agree that three-year averages are more useful, external. The JRF urged Somerville not to weaken the goals but to set "stretching, statutory, income-based poverty-reduction targets, with strong accountability measures". John Swinney and Shirley-Anne Somerville attend a uniform bank at a Scottish school From day one in the job, the issue has been at the heart of John Swinney's personal political project. "My overriding priority will be to work to eradicate child poverty in Scotland," he told me in his first interview as first minister, minutes after being sworn in at the Court of Session in Edinburgh in 2024. In his successful campaign to retain power at this year's Holyrood election, the Scottish National Party leader repeated his "determination to eradicate child poverty." But the JRF says there is now an "increasing disconnect" between such rhetoric and "the reality of life for families in poverty across Scotland." Its report said relative poverty rates were highest – at 47% – for children in ethnic minority families. It added that 11% of Scotland's overall population was defined as being in deep poverty and 7% in very deep poverty. In a statement issued in advance of the report's publication, Shirley-Anne Somerville said the Scottish child payment was "providing unparalleled financial support to the families of over 320,000 children." The Scottish government would do more, she said, by expanding breakfast clubs for children and investing more than £40m in improving access to transport and skills for parents. "Overall in 2026-27 we are committing around £3.5bn to policies that tackle poverty and the cost of living," she added. The JRF report suggests the following policies can help to reduce poverty. Create flexible, well-paid jobs, especially in parts of Scotland where people cannot find work within easy reach of their homes Expand access to high-quality, affordable childcare with the flexibility to allow parents in low-income families to work Ensure adequate levels of social security payments, especially for people with disabilities who may have to fund their own care Maintain and improve provision of social and affordable housing, which has helped Scotland keep its poverty rate below the UK average The Scottish government has a legal target to reduce the rate of child poverty below 18% by the end of the financial year The report focused on the "critical role" of Scotland's 32 councils in reducing poverty, noting that local government is in the early stages of a big shake up. "Councils are not doing enough," it concludes, "with people on low incomes and living in more deprived areas reporting worse experiences of services and higher levels of disaffection." The report urges Swinney's government to embrace the opportunity to craft "refitted" councils which can play a fuller role in poverty reduction, in partnership with the third sector. This, it says, requires reform not just of local government's structure but of its funding, including the "regressive" council tax which "takes up a much larger proportion of low-income households' budgets than better-off households'." Funding of councils, says the JRF, is "stretched to breaking point", with the current model "increasingly unfit for purpose" and "hampering local efforts to reduce poverty". "Years of austerity, shifting goalposts from the Scottish government, single-year budgets and an ever-blooming number of strategies and action plans mean councils are often acting with one hand tied behind their back," says the report. In her statement, Somerville said tackling poverty was at the heart of the Scottish government's plans for public service reform including tailoring services for individual needs in an approach known as "whole-family support". title: Environmental groups critical of housing levy idea
description: The government wants developers to fund waterways projects in Norfolk.
body: The new plan aims to raise cash for conservation projects in places like The Broads Environmental groups have criticised a pilot scheme that aims to make housing developers pay a new nature levy. The government wants parts of Norfolk to be the first areas subject to its Environmental Delivery Plan (EDP). In order to unlock space for thousands of homes, developers would pay money that could create new wetlands, fund deer culls and restore rivers. But ecology experts fear that it would fail to tackle the sources of pollution, leaving vulnerable chalk streams still at risk. Sally Haines, chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management, said: "While [actions outlined in the plan] would improve ecological habitats in the area, they won't necessarily address the pollution that will be going into the water. "Unless you do that, you are not going to get good nature recovery." Campaigners worry about the health of the River Wensum, one of Norfolk's chalk rivers The EDP, which would apply to much of central Norfolk and parts of The Broads, would pool cash from housebuilders. It would be spent on measures to help offset pollution from new homes. Norfolk's rare chalk streams, often described as England's rainforests, are particularly vulnerable. Environment Secretary Angela Eagle calls it a "win-win" for development and nature, claiming it would unlock space for 15,780 homes that are currently stalled because of rules protecting rivers. With developers paying £2,675 per house, it is hoped the levy will raise about £42m. How much sewage is spilled near you? The scheme is designed to replace the more complicated nutrient neutrality rules that are in place, which were blamed for blocking the regeneration plan for the former Colman's Mustard Factory at Carrow Works in Norwich. A government spokesperson said the introduction of a single levy would make life easier for developers. Natural England is leading on the project and chief executive Marian Spain said: "Instead of tackling pollution piecemeal, site by site, we can now deliver conservation measures that make a real difference for rivers, wetlands and wildlife across Norfolk." However, Haines said it was a "fallacy" to blame environmental concerns as the main stumbling block when building houses - pointing instead to a myriad of issues such as the availability of materials and labour, and land prices. The Environment Development Plan would cover parts of the Norfolk Broads Under the proposals, restoration projects would be put together for the River Wensum, the Bure broads and marshes, and the River Yare catchment area. One eye-catching policy is to put some of the cash towards deer management, including targeted culling. Booming deer populations in The Broads are becoming a growing issue as the animals can cause damage to the environment through grazing. People can submit their views as part of a consultation, external - which opened on 17 September and runs until 27 October - before Natural England submits its final plans to Eagle and her department. Natural England hopes to roll out EDPs in other parts of England in the future. Eliot Lyne, the Norfolk Wildlife Trust's chief executive, worries planning rules will harm nature The chief executive of Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Eliot Lyne, said his organisation needed more time to review the proposals. But he said it was worried about wider changes to planning rules and how they affected natural habitats. "We are concerned that it weakens existing protections for Norfolk's nationally and globally important wildlife sites such as chalk streams, wetlands and valley fens," he added. Mark Dye, a chalk stream campaigner for the Gaywood River Revival group in west Norfolk, said: "Fundamentally, if you are polluting a chalk stream or a river and you're putting more and more pollution into that river, and not seeking to address the underlying causes of that, then it's only going to get worse." Steve Turner, executive director of the Home Builders Federation, claimed pollution from farmers was a bigger issue than new homes and he criticised water companies for not investing in infrastructure to stop sewage entering rivers. title: Charity tea room may close despite Ludwig filming
description: The series, starring David Mitchell, is filming scenes in Hemel Hempstead.
body: David Mitchell has been filming new episodes of Ludwig in Hemel Hempstead A tea room being used to film the third series of Ludwig starring David Mitchell could close permanently unless it raises £25,000. Trustees of the volunteer-run Liberty Tea Rooms and Community Hub in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, said the charity was in an "extremely low cash position". Mark Kitson, chairman of the trustees, said the series being filmed at the venue had created a real buzz and it had been good to hire it out "at a time that we really need the extra funds". The tea room is temporarily closed until 7 October while filming takes place for Ludwig; its frontage has been transformed to resemble a bank, which it was before becoming a community venue. Liberty Tea Room volunteers provide support for people in the community facing difficulty Film crews have made the team room look like a fictional bank for the latest series of Ludwig The charity has already reduced staffing costs, but trustees said it would close permanently unless it raised £25,000 by the end of October. Kitson said: "Lots of towns and high streets are having tough times at the moment. "When you come into the Tea Rooms, someone will welcome you, talk to you if you want a chat, offer a meal if you need it, and can also provide debt advice or a food bank parcel. "You might just want tea and a scone, but if you need something more, we will do our very best to help you." The tea room has been closed between 15 September and 7 October while filming takes place Filming will take place inside and outside the building over several weeks, with a rain machine due to be used for one scene. Kitson said the production team would restore the tea room once filming was completed, as well as repairing a broken window and updating its signage. He added: "The filming has been brilliant. It's created a real buzz and excitement on Hemel Hempstead High Street, and for our team and volunteers, they have also paid us a fee for being in the building at a time that we really need the extra funds."
