title: How Evans defied history to become Britain's first world rally champion in 25 years
description: Elfyn Evans has been the nearly-man of world rally until he finally emulated the feats of Colin McRae and Richard Burns.
body: Elfyn Evans (centre) joins Colin McRae (left) and Richard Burns (right) as British world rally champions For what must have felt like an eternity, Elfyn Evans feared history was repeating itself yet again. At 3.05pm local time in Sardinia on Sunday, Evans could only stand and watch as another world rally title looked to be slipping from his grasp. Evans was preparing in his head yet another runners-up speech - it would be his sixth - as he waited for Oliver Solberg to cross the finish line and be crowned world champion. How could this be happening again? Of the five previous times he had been championship runner-up, three had been decided on the final day and twice after he had taken a lead into the final event. But at 3.06pm, for once the motor-racing gods were on his side. With just two turns to go on the final stage of the final round and with victory in sight, Solberg somehow careered off the track into the Sardinian sand to hand Evans his first world title. In the most dramatic of finishes, the 37-year-old from north Wales became the first British winner of the World Rally Championship (WRC) in 25 years. Only two British men had taken the title since the WRC's 1977 inception, matching the exploits of legendary pair Colin McRae (1995) and Richard Burns (2001). Louise Aitken-Walker was Britain's first world champion when WRC ran a women's version in 1990. As it happened: Evans wins title as Solberg crashes on final stage The five titles that got away as Evans seeks WRC glory "It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done," said Evans. "It's been a difficult weekend. I felt on Friday things were slipping away. We were a bit powerless with the road position we had and Oliver was flying." His experienced co-driver Scott Martin revealed Evans was already apologising for his stage performance as they waited for Solberg to finish. "I've said all week that until we arrived at the beach after that last stage it was never over. How true that turned out to be," said Martin. Evans was roared on to the title in Italy by travelling supporters Evans and Martin have been consistent performers throughout the 2026 championship, through the streets of Monaco, the ice and snow of Sweden, the flowing roads of Chile, and the punishing, sun-baked gravel tracks of southern Europe. Despite winning only two of the previous 12 events, the pair took a 21-point lead into the final race at Rally Italia Sardegna. Solberg, whose father Petter won the 2003 title, was around one kilometre from glory only to suffer motorsport's version of Devon Loch. "The lead up to this event gave us a bit of a buffer and we just about managed to hold on at the end. It was an incredible finish," said Evans. "I feel for [Solberg] after he came so close and lost at the last moment. I've been in a similar situation and it will be tough for him for a few days, but he's shown he's one to watch for the future." Elfyn Evans celebrated his long-awaited world title with Toyota Gazoo Racing colleagues by jumping into the Mediterranean sea Evans, like Solberg, is also from fine rally-driving stock. His father Gwyndaf was British champion, as well as runner-up four times, but the motor dealer from farming stock never got the break to be a major contender on the world stage. The curse of finishing second passed down to his son who had already turned professional by the time his father claimed the last of those near misses in 2010. Evans clinched his first WRC stage win in Germany in 2014 and a first podium in Argentina a year later, before having to drop down to the WRC2 class in 2016. Evans admitted that blow only fueled his determination to make it in the WRC and a first rally victory followed - in his home event in Wales - in 2017. He has been remarkably consistent, finishing second for the title in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024 and, perhaps most agonisingly, to Sebastien Ogier by just four points in the final race of 2025. He appeared condemned to be one of sport's great runners-up until the late drama of Sardinia threw up one of the championship's most thrilling finishes. There may have been a stroke of fortune about the title win, but few can deny Evans earned it. title: Supporters of jailed ex-PM Imran Khan march to Pakistan capital
description: Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock.
body: Some 5,000 people took to the streets on Sunday carrying red-and-green flags of Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party Thousands of supporters of Pakistan's jailed ex-prime minister Imran Khan are marching to the capital Islamabad as they call for his release. Concerns over the 73-year-old's health have grown louder in recent months. His family claims he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action. The cricket star-turned-politician, who faces charges in more than 100 cases, was jailed for 17 years over corruption last year. Khan said all the cases against him are politically motivated. Even behind bars, he remains a force in Pakistani politics, and demonstrations in support for him have led to deadly violence and crackdowns in the past. Sunday's march, which began in Lakki Marwat, a city 275km away from Islamabad, had paused for the night and is expected to resume around midday local time on Monday. Originally scheduled for last week, it was postponed to allow for talks between the government and Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party but the talks ended in a deadlock. Khan, who faces charges ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, was first imprisoned in August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Sohail Afridi, chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province ruled by PTI, expects that the march will make its way to a town about 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday. "[By then] this movement will have reached every corner of the country and every square will have become a centre of activity," he said on Sunday, urging the people to "play an active role in the political process". Authorities in Islamabad have stacked up shipping containers to block key access routes to the capital city. The PTI said talks with government failed because authorities rejected the party's request for access to Khan so that its leaders could consult him on national and political issues. The party also said it had demanded that Khan be given an immediate medical examination and treatment. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi meanwhile accused Afridi of "sabotaging" negotiations, saying the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had backed out of earlier commitments on counter-terrorism issues, according to Pakistan's local media reports. In August, Khan was briefly transferred from jail to a state-run hospital for medical examination and treatment following complaints about his deteriorating health. The doctors later deemed him "medically fit". The intervention was the most significant relief Khan has received from the courts since he was imprisoned in 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated. Khan's family and the PTI, however, criticised the authorities for defying a court order that he be examined by physicians at a specific private hospital. On 20 September, Khan's sister Aleema Khanum was arrested in the eastern city of Lahore. The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government". Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things. At least eight people died in the protests and the army had to be called in to quell the violence. Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging Khan be accorded proper medical care. title: 'Don't axe Youth Parliament' pleads teen member
description: The government plans to no longer fund the scheme launched to get young people into politics.
body: Aman Fatima has been a Member of Youth Parliament for two years A taxpayer-funded programme aimed at boosting young people's interest in politics should not be axed just because "money is tight", one of its members has said. Last month the BBC learned the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) would not be committing to giving any more grants to the UK Youth Parliament. "If the government is to cut the Youth Parliament there should be reasons and there has to be alternatives, even if the funding is tight," Aman Fatima, MYP for Essex, told BBC Politics East. The government said it was working on a new scheme to increase young people's involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements due this autumn. Established in 1999, the parliament takes place at the House of Commons and boasts more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18, including Aman. She said if the scheme – run by the National Youth Agency – was scrapped, an alternative must be found because "young people are the next generation" of government. "Money is tight but you also want young people's opinions; them to tell you what's wrong and the challenges they are facing," she said. "And the [Youth Parliament] really helps young people get their voice out there, especially in a big place such as the House of Commons." Members of the UK Youth Parliament, formed in 1999, hold an annual debate within in the House of Commons every year As part of the programme, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting, once a year. In recent years, they have campaigned on issues such as votes for 16-year-olds and for free period products to be made available to students. "There are lots of opinions from people saying that they haven't seen any difference made, but I think we do contribute to how the government works today," added Aman. In the last year, the youth parliament received £453,000 in taxpayer funding with about £2.4m public money spent on it between 2017 and 2024. No final decision has been made on funding after March 2027, but a government source said Downing Street would no longer commit to it "in its current form." Labour MP Jess Asato believes there are other ways for young people to make their mark in politics Jess Asato, Labour MP for Lowestoft, said she believed the decision had been made because the Youth Parliament was not producing "a diversity of voices". "I think what the government's trying to say is we need things much more locally that bring a lot more young people into that political or democratic engagement," she said. "In East Suffolk we have a fantastic youth council and that means lots and lots more young people can get involved in things that they care about locally. "But I do wish the government might look at this [decision] again." Conservative MP Patrick Spencer said funding for Labour government's plans had to come from somewhere Patrick Spencer, Conservative MP for Central Suffolk and North Ipswich, said: "The reality is this government needs to make cuts because it needs to fund things that it's planning to do. "It's one of the difficult decisions that has got to be made." The DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy" and said it had given elected young people "a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work". title: Early Lampard findings could come within weeks
description: Early recommendations could be issued if evidence highlights patient safety risks, the chair says.
body: Baroness Lampard said that the inquiry was of "national interest" The chair of a public inquiry into mental health deaths said she would make interim recommendations if she identified issues that "might pose an urgent risk to patient safety". Baroness Kate Lampard is examining the deaths of more than 2,000 people who died while under the care of Essex mental health services between 2000 and the end of 2023. The Lampard Inquiry will hear further evidence during hearings beginning on 5 October before deciding whether recommendations were needed ahead of a final report, Baroness Lampard said. Any recommendations were expected to focus on inpatient safety, including resuscitation procedures and monitoring technology used to detect patients in distress. Oxevision uses infrared sensors and cameras to monitor patients while they are in their bedrooms "Those two matters are not specific to Essex and therefore the evidence the inquiry hears will be of relevance to service providers across the entire country," Baroness Lampard said. "It may carry implications for the care and treatment provided on all mental health units." One system under examination as part of the inquiry is Oxevision, which can take footage, record breathing and pulse rates and is used by a number of NHS mental health trusts in England. Concerns have been raised about privacy, dignity and whether the technology could be used as a substitute for face-to-face care. Tammy Smith, whose daughter Sophie Alderman died in 2022, previously told the inquiry: "It actually takes away human interaction. They are at their most vulnerable. "They need those conversations. They need someone to ask, 'Are you OK? Do you need anything?' We all need that." What is the Lampard Inquiry and what could it change? Lampard Inquiry: Five things we've learned so far Oxevision is a system that has been discussed a number of times at the Lampard Inquiry by relatives seeking answers about the deaths of their loved ones The company behind Oxevision, LIO Health, said the technology helped prevent serious incidents, supports staff in providing care and reduces time spent on paperwork. NHS England said any vision-based monitoring technology must support a human rights-based approach to care and be used in line with legal requirements and appropriate patient consent. The inquiry is due to hear evidence from NHS England, the Care Quality Commission and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency during hearings between 5 and 15 October. The latest sessions will take place at Chelmsford Civic Centre rather than in London, where previous hearings have been held. Families will then be invited to give their views on possible recommendations during a virtual hearing on 20 October, before Baroness Lampard decides whether interim recommendations should be issued. The inquiry's final report, which could have national implications for mental health services across England, is not expected until 2028. Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below. title: Dozens 'ripped off' in £500,000 building 'scam'
description: Sian and Simon Romsey lost thousands after paying a deposit for extensive building work.
body: Sian and Simon Romsey say they lost nearly £16,000 after paying a deposit to secure a start date for work to create their dream family home More than 30 customers claim they were scammed after paying deposits totalling nearly £500,000 for building work that was not delivered, the BBC has learned. The BBC has heard from 13 of those customers who say they paid tens of thousands of pounds to South Coast Construction (Sussex) Ltd (SCC), which operated in Dorset, Hampshire, Sussex and Surrey. Sussex Police said it was investigating "a number of reports of alleged fraud" in connection with the company. SCC's director strongly denied he had deliberately scammed customers, saying he did not take customers' money without intending to carry out the work and he was "deeply sorry" to all those affected. More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight Sian and Simon Romsey from Southampton were planning a double-storey extension with two extra bedrooms, a new kitchen-diner and shower room. They said SCC had appealed to them because the company claimed to offer a full design and build package and appeared to have a number of endorsements on its website. "They had all of their accreditations... even talking to them on the phone very, very reassuring... even down to the contract, I looked through it with a fine-tooth comb and everything was just so slick, so professional," Simon said. The couple said they paid a deposit of nearly £16,000 in March which they were told would cover architectural drawings and secure the last available start date in June. But Simon said "alarm bells started blowing up in our heads" when the architect contacted them to say she had not been paid and would not release the drawings a week before work was due to start. "We tried getting in contact with South Coast - they'd disconnected the phone, couldn't get through... my whole world just crumbled and it's a feeling that I never, ever want to experience again," said Simon. Sian added: "Having no control over that was really scary... the fact it can happen in an instant is really frightening." The couple have since joined an action group made up of 36 other customers who also claim to have paid SCC thousands of pounds for work that was not done. Simon said he had called his bank multiple times over two months before he finally got his money back in August. While 29 customers said they had managed to get their money refunded through their bank, eight have been told it is a civil matter and are having to go to the financial ombudsman service. Jo Amas wanted to extend her step-mother's home so she could move in to help care for her after she was diagnosed with dementia Jo Amas from Burgess Hill in West Sussex said she was still fighting to get nearly £12,000 refunded from her bank that had been paid in March towards the cost of a loft conversion for her step-mother who had dementia. She had intended to move in to be a full-time carer after her step-mum, Fran, suffered a serious fall in February. "I checked out everything... and looked at their reviews. I thought I'd done due diligence in checking them out that they were legit," said Jo. She said the contract she had with SCC stated the deposit would be fully refunded if work was not started, so she had been expecting to get the money back when she cancelled the project in April after Fran's condition deteriorated and she moved into a care home. Jo told the BBC that SCC had stopped all communication with her, which had taken a huge toll on her mental health. "I didn't want to tell the rest of my family what I'd done because I felt very responsible... you just feel like a failure and this was someone else's money, it wasn't my money," she said. "Because she [Fran] was in a home and homes are very expensive, we needed that money back to pay for the home and it was heartbreaking., She added: "These people have managed to rip us all off and just got so much money out of us. It's just unbelievable." South Coast Construction (Sussex) Ltd falsely told customers their deposits were insured with Home Improvement Protection On its website and social media pages, SCC claimed to be a leader in high-end construction, with customers telling the BBC they felt reassured by the number of accreditations it displayed online. But the BBC can reveal SCC was falsely claiming to be insured by Home Improvement Protection (HIP) and certified by Certass. In addition, it had only been a member of TrustATrader for six weeks in 2024. A spokesperson for HIP said members must pay a premium to insure each customer contract. They said it had been brought to their attention that SCC had been advertising its membership certificate as proof of insurance, which was a "serious breach" of its terms of agreement. The company was expelled from the scheme in May. Several other accreditation memberships have been terminated, including Checkatrade in March and Which? Trusted Trader scheme in April. Accreditations from the Federation of Master Builders (FMB) and the government-backed TrustMark were ended in June following customer complaints. A spokesperson for FMB said: "This company joined the FMB in May 2025 after passing our rigorous vetting checks. When complaints started coming in and the company failed to respond to them, they were expelled in June 2026." The accreditation scheme providers all said checks had been carried out and SSC had passed the vetting process before receiving membership. South Coast Construction (Sussex) Ltd used cartoons and accreditation logos on its social media pages to appeal to potential customers A BBC investigation also found five outstanding county court judgments (CCJs) against SCC worth more than £37,000. title: Watch: How Brazil's dramatic election unfolded
description: Millions of Brazilians took to the polls on Sunday for the first round of the country's presidential elections.
body: This video can not be played Millions of Brazilians took to the polls on Sunday for the first round of the country's presidential elections. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, is running for his fourth non-consecutive term in office, while his challenger, right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is competing in his first presidential race. His father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, governed Brazil from 2019 to 2022. With the election now heading to a run-off on 25 October, BBC correspondent Ione Wells unpacks the results. title: All six passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
description: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.
body: Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard the flight, which went missing in the early hours of Saturday Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator. On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island. "We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter. "Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues." The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning. On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft. The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT). Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard. "This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening. "Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day." Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home. Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News. FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft). Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net. "You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?" The pilot's response was inaudible. "You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe. The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency. An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue". The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar". Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations. "Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said. title: The Conversation
description: Two women discuss turning crime scenes back into homes
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·05 Oct 2026,·26 mins Available for over a year Cleaning up after a death or violent incident is often far too traumatic and potentially dangerous for family members or for regular cleaning services to undertake. Instead, it’s a task carried out by a small but specialised group of individuals – often women. Ella Al-Shamahi speaks to two female crime scene and trauma cleaners in South Africa and Northern Ireland who are the last point of contact for families after emergency services and forensic teams have completed their duties. Alana Gillen initially made her name by taking care of the mansions of some of the Northern Ireland's richest people. She then transferred her skills and now runs the only female-led and owned company in Northern Ireland, specialising in biohazard, crime-scene and trauma cleaning. Charleen Archibald was trained by two women, known across South Africa as ‘the blood sisters’ (Bloed Susters in Afrikaans). She’s been cleaning up crime and trauma scenes for the past ten years alongside her wife, Sheridan and says that it’s humbling to be invited into somebody’s home on what is often the worst day of their lives. Listeners are advised that this programme will contain some sensitive content - including descriptions of the aftermath of violent crime, which some may find upsetting. title: Potty training scheme to roll out to 20 more areas
description: The government wants 75% of children to end their first year of school with a good level of development by 2028.
body: Parents like Natalie (right) say it's important children are confident enough to use the loo on their own when they start school The number of children who were toilet-trained before starting school this year has increased significantly in a city where parents were given potty training guides with their first school offers. York was the subject of the city-wide pilot, which also put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff. Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes to tackle the number of pupils starting school without being fully toilet-trained. The government said the pilot's results were "encouraging", and confirmed they were committed to 75% of pupils reaching a good level of development at the end of their first year in school by 2028. Since April this year, parents across York have been targeted via GP surgeries, pharmacies, family hubs, schools and nurseries with information and offers of support on how to potty-train their child ahead of starting school. Potty training guides were sent out to all families across York who had a child starting reception in September - with the aim that all children could use the toilet independently by the time they started school, except those with medical issues or special educational needs. The results from all 55 mainstream primary schools across the city, shared exclusively with BBC News, suggested there had been a 43% drop since last year in the number of children who were not fully toilet-trained when they started school. Across York last September, 148 out of 1,364 reception pupils (11%) were recorded as not being toilet-trained when they started school. This year, that fell to 85 reception pupils out of 1,374 (6%). Parents Natalie and Lucy, who both have daughters starting reception next year, have welcomed the extra support on offer. Mum Natalie says there's a lot of conflicting pressures on parents about the right time to potty-train Lucy said she had noticed the drop-in sessions on potty training in her local children's centre and thought it was a "really good idea". "I think it's really important that children are more prepared for that aspect of starting school," she said. Natalie said getting her daughter Freya potty-trained in time for school has been a priority, but feels there is a lot of pressure on parents to do so. "I think going to school is hard enough for children," she said. "But for me it was really important that she's confident enough to use toilets, to be independent, to be able to go without relying on the help of teachers perhaps in an environment where they've already got lots of children to look after." Natalie said the popularity of disposable nappies might be a reason why parents often wait longer to potty train. "When I was little, we still had the terry towelling nappies and they had to be washed and hung on the line. So I think with disposable nappies it's easier," she said. The ability to listen to and follow instructions is another skill that helps pupils get the most out of learning when they start reception class Around one in four children started school in England and Wales last year not fully toilet-trained, and teachers said they have been spending over an hour a day changing nappies, according to the latest research from the children's charity Kindred Squared, external. Jo Mould, who teaches reception at Robert Wilkinson Primary Academy in York, said she has noticed an improvement in pupils being ready for school this year. "We've spent more time teaching in these last three weeks than we have in previous years," she said. "The children have come in so ready to learn, because they're more settled and regulated socially and emotionally. We've had a really, really positive start to the school year." Jo Mould says not having to deal with toilet training has meant more time spent teaching her pupils York councillor Bob Webb said the impact of the scheme had been "so positive" for both schools and families. But he acknowledged a potential "gap in support" for parents between seeing health visitors with their toddler, and the child later arriving at school. He said the key to the scheme's success was collaboration across health visitors, schools and other community settings, but that there was "always more that could be done at an earlier age". Twenty local authorities across England have now committed to adopt York's model, developed by Kindred Squared, and use it to encourage earlier potty-training in their areas. Just over two-thirds of children in England (68.3%) leave reception class with a good level of development - a key measure of school readiness which includes things like communication skills, as well as physical, social and emotional development - according to the latest government stats, external. That means they were assessed by teachers on being able to complete tasks like going to the toilet and paying attention in class. The government has said it is still committed to increasing that proportion to 75% by 2028. Early Education Minister Paul Waugh said it was "encouraging to see this pilot helping more children develop the confidence and independence they need before starting school", stressing the importance of parents taking early steps towards toilet training. In York, Mould said she hopes next year's parents will take on potty-training even earlier. "Ideally we'd be at the point where [children] don't need that support when they get here, because they've already been trained by the time they get to us." title: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
description: The president named his national intelligence chief as the taskforce's head as worries over AI grow.
body: US President Donald Trump says he has created a new task force focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday. Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael will also be part of the task force. Trump said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact to regulate the technology. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote. He also named Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor as a member of the taskforce, which will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The announcement follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology. In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public. "The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded. Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves. The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google. US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton On the same day, the president also signed an executive order to rename AI as "super intelligence", after previously saying the word artificial made the technology sound "fake". Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems. Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI. "SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote. The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war. Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump. title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
description: India’s toy shops provide an unlikely barometer by which to measure its economic relationship with China.
body: Xi and Modi have vowed to address growing trade imbalances Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a batter economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China. Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%. Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked. Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300mn in 2020 to $100mn this year, while exports rose from around $129mn to $200mn in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market. The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world. Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year. "India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC. More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period. "China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI). If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava. Anti-China sentiment hit a fever pitch post border skirmishes in 2020, but relations have now thawed On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues". But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC. That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods. To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones. "Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava. It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment. Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank. "Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production. Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends. China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output. Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year. A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava. India has reduced smartphone imports but depends heavily on China for components On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies. "Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li. "If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same." The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava. But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short. India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds. "Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India." More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sec

title: The Papers: Badenoch's 'bonfire of green laws' and 'Drop in global dealmaking'
description: Monday's front pages include stories about Kemi Badenoch at the start of the Tory conference, plus reports on global finance , abuse in schools and a BBC romance.
body: Many of Monday's papers are leading with coverage of the Conservative Party conference and the Times angles its front page piece on Kemi Badenoch pledging to scape a range of environmental regulations including "strict net-zero standards". The Daily Mail takes a wider view of Badenoch's "reset" of the party, saying she has moved to get it "battle-ready" for an election with a "direct echo of Margaret Thatcher's approach in the 1970s" by releasing plans for "a return to 'common sense' Tory values". Under a large headline reading "Bad to the future" the Daily Mirror runs a piece that opens "Badenoch is accused of trying to take the country back to the days of austerity under the 'nasty party'". The Metro runs a large image of Badenoch next to a story saying she has vowed to be "like a no-nonsense mum" as she moves to make the Conservatives "the 'common sense' party", and also likens her approach to an echo of Thatcher. Badenoch's promise to "save the pension triple lock" and her attack on Prime Minister Andy Burnham for "going after the elderly" is the top line of the front page of the Daily Express. Atop its front page, the Sun has a short story on Badenoch warning that "Britain must not become a nation of 'little ghettos'" and "migrants should embrace our culture". However it leads on what it bills as an exclusive about two of the hosts of Match of the Day dating. A large image of Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates sits behind a headline reading "Love match of the day". The Financial Times looks at a drop in "global dealmaking" for the first time since US President Donald Trump's "trade war last year", and notes "high interest rates threaten to derail a blockbuster period for mergers and acquisitions". Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's decision to take legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest "eight months ago in relation to the Epstein files" leads Monday's Daily Telegraph. It says he has "asked a judge to determine whether the force's action towards him was lawful". Andrew, who the paper says "was questioned for almost 12 hours on suspicion of misconduct in public office before being released under investigation", has always strongly denied any wrongdoing. The headline "'Horrifying' scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools revealed" runs across the top of the Guardian's front page. Further down, a picture of Rowan Atkinson in full Blackadder garb catches the eye as the paper reveals "A cunning plan" to revive the classic 1980s historical comedy as a live show. The "hit show" Celebrity Traitors has brought a smile back to contestant Maya James after her "split from footballer Ruben Dias", the Daily Star says in its front page splash. The link between Manchester City owners and the property where Andy Burnham is set to build No 10 North dominates the front page of the i Paper, in what it calls a "sweetheart deal". title: The Interview
description: James Copnall speaks to Olara Otunnu, veteran Ugandan diplomat, about his UN vision
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·05 Oct 2026,·23 mins Available for over a year “I do not want the United Nations of New York, Geneva or Vienna to be an ivory tower, a diplomatic ivory tower. I want to see the UN not of power and privilege, but the UN of service and impact. That is the UN I want see.” James Copnall speaks to Olara Otunnu, Ugandan diplomat, lawyer and former Foreign Minister. He has spent decades working at the highest levels of international diplomacy. He has also served as a United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict. Now Uganda has formally nominated him for UN Secretary-General, putting him among seven candidates in the running to succeed Antonio Guterres. It is a position widely regarded as the world’s top diplomatic job. Olara Otunnu talks about how he intends to bridge the gap between international politics and the needs of local people around the world. The Interview brings you conversations with people shaping our world, from all over the world. The best interviews from the BBC, including episodes with the UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, South Africa’s Ambassador to the US Roelf Meyer and the author Maggie O’ Farrell. You can listen on the BBC World Service on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at 0800 GMT. Or you can listen to The Interview as a podcast, out three times a week on BBC Sounds or wherever you get your podcasts. Presenter: James Copnall Producer: Sharon Hemans Editor: Farhana Haider Get in touch with us on email TheInterview@bbc.co.uk and use the hashtag #TheInterviewBBC on social media. title: The job interview question you don't have to answer
description: Experts explain what you should do if you are asked for your current salary during a job interview.
body: This video can not be played Watch: How much is your salary? Prepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable. While employers in the UK are within their rights to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, applicants are not obliged to tell them. Recruiters have been encouraged to stop posing questions about salary history and, in the EU, new rules will prevent them doing so. But in the UK, there is still a chance of it coming up, so how best should you answer? When interviewing or deciding on new staff, employers must not discriminate against an applicant based on so-called protected characteristics, including age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. Sometimes it feels like interviewers, and interviewees, tip-toe around the subject of money. But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations. She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly. A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag - #EndSalaryHistory. The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality. Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation supported the move, urging recruiters not to ask. Employers in the EU will be banned from asking about salary history in new rules being rolled out across the bloc. But that's not featured in Cabinet Office plans in the UK, which instead concentrates on telling employers to publish salary information in job adverts. When you're going for a new job, you can reveal your current salary if you are happy to. Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary - so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward. There are no requirements for you to disclose your salary if you don't want to. Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role. Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid, not their salary history. Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with "realism but also confidence". "Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role," she says. "Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package." What was your worst job interview? title: Israel 'tried to intimidate' Irish amid spitting row - Hallgrimsson
description: Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson says he felt Israel were "trying to intimidate" his team amid allegations of spitting during Sunday's Nations League draw.
body: The Republic of Ireland and Israel clashed at half-time Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said he felt Israel were "trying to intimidate" his team amid allegations of spitting during Sunday's tense Uefa Nations League draw. The teams clashed at half-time in the 1-1 draw, played behind closed doors in Serbia, with the Irish Times, external reporting that Republic of Ireland head of athletic performance Damien Doyle alleged he had been spat at by an Israel player. On television pictures, a voice can be heard saying "he spat on me" as the players made their way down the tunnel at TSC Arena. "I don't want to get involved in that, but it's been like this these two games. It's tense, it's a lot of emotions," Hallgrimsson told Off The Ball, external when asked about the incident. "[It] was an accusation of spitting on someone but I didn't see it. No, we don't want to talk about this. This will be reviewed, probably like everything else that's happened between the two teams. "I felt like they were trying to intimidate us from kick-off but I give a lot of credit to the players to stay calm. It could have been a game of yellow and red cards but we were composed, the players were composed, they did well in controlling emotions." Asked about the half-time incident, Israel head coach Ran Ben-Shimon said he "didn't see anything". "[At] half-time I was in the dressing room, my room, with my staff," he said. "I didn't see anything. When I get the chance to check I will get back to you." This video can not be played Republic of Ireland and Israel managers react to spitting allegations No other team should go through this - Hallgrimsson Republic of Ireland denied by Israel in draw Tensions between the sides deepened on Saturday when the Republic of Ireland's pre-match news conference was ended abruptly after Hallgrimsson fielded what he later called a "verbal attack" from Israeli reporters. Hallgrimsson was asked by an Israeli reporter about alleged racism by Irish players during last week's match in Hungary, which the Republic of Ireland won 3-0. The news conference was brought to a close at that point by Football Association of Ireland (FAI) communications manager Kieran Crowley, who said those allegations were "completely untrue" as the mood soured. It followed news that the FAI is investigating whether Republic of Ireland forward Adam Idah was racially abused by Israel fans during the first match in Debrecen. It is understood that midfielder Jayson Molumby spoke to the match officials during play, asking them to listen out for what he believed to be abusive chanting coming from some of the small number of Israel fans present at the match. Israel boss Ran Ben-Shimon said his team's aggression during the game was "nothing personal" against Jayson Molumby (6) Asked if his players targeted Molumby following the Irish player's complaint last week, Ben-Shimon said "it was nothing personal against" the West Brom midfielder. "Come on, come on. We don't do it. We just don't do it, we are not men like this," he added. "It's very difficult to believe us but I will never say to a player to play aggressive against him (an opposing player). Sometimes I don't like this but I say to my players sometimes this is the best way to play the clearest football as you can, but be aggressive. "I never say to them to injure someone. This is not our way, we are human beings." The fixtures, both played at neutral venues, have been embroiled in controversy since February when the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3. The Republic of Ireland players have faced persistent calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with the "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - staging protests before and during Thursday's game against Austria in Dublin. However, while goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu said it would be "wrong" for him to participate in the games as he made himself unavailable, the FAI decided to fulfil both fixtures. The teams did not engage in pre-match formalities in either match, while the Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's national anthem. title: Bellamy bemoans new schedule after Denmark loss
description: Craig Bellamy suggests the new four-match international window has counted against Wales after Sunday's Nations League defeat against Denmark.
body: Craig Bellamy's Wales have won one of their eight matches in 2026 Craig Bellamy suggested the new four-match international window had counted against Wales after Sunday's Nations League defeat against Denmark. His side failed to build on Thursday's win over Norway as they were deservedly beaten thanks to a second-half Rasmus Hojlund penalty. It was a third loss in four games played inside 10 days as part of the newly elongated international break. Head coach Bellamy said his injury-hit squad paid the price for the heavy workload he feels benefits the bigger nations and "puts a real stress" on countries like Wales. "Physically, I completely agree with the ones who don't like [the new window]. It makes no sense," he added. "Four games at this type of level… for the other nations, we know who they are because I was in the room when they all voted for it. "I was one of the ones who wasn't [voting for it], because we know it's a complete disadvantage to us." This video can not be played Nations League highlights: Wales 0-1 Denmark Traditionally, international sides have played six games across three windows - all of which have featured two fixtures - in September, October and November. But for the first time this year, the September and October breaks were merged. Wales' hopes of coping with the new schedule were not helped by a string of injuries, with stars such as Karl Darlow, Joe Rodon, Dylan Lawlor and Harry Wilson missing the entire camp and David Brooks dropping out of the squad after defeat by Portugal in the opening game. Bellamy said Dan James was not fit enough to play against Denmark after he was left on the bench at the Cardiff City Stadium, and acknowledged Ben Davies probably should have been rested after he was withdrawn late on. "If we have a few injuries, which we had more than one or two, they miss four games," said Bellamy. "We can deal with two, do you understand? And then the squad will get really tested. The intensity of the squad, the athleticism, really I think [the four-game break] is designed for the elites. "[They can] say, we can go, we can go, we can turn over these games really, really quickly and we can change, we can change [the team] like for like because we have the numbers. So, it puts a real stress on a lot of us." Wales have three points from their first four games in this Nations League campaign Wales rarely looked like scoring against Denmark, who came close to breaking the deadlock on a couple of occasions before Hjolund's 75th-minute winner. "On Thursday [against Norway] we were on the front foot so we're able to shorten distance," Bellamy added. "Today, we just couldn't work it well enough, couldn't get the energy up enough to be able to have a bigger say in the game." Danny Ward made fine saves from Hojlund and Gustav Isaksen to keep Wales level but it was the goalkeeper's error, and foul, which led to the penalty. Bellamy, though, suggested the game had not swung on Ward's mistake, adding: "Obviously it's the decisive moment, but he made two incredible saves before that. "I thought Denmark with the physicality were able to just crank it a little bit. You see their runs are really menacing, so I felt they were knocking on the door. He did incredibly well to keep it 0-0 to that time." Despite defeat, Wales climbed to third in Nations League Group A4 courtesy of their head-to-head record against Norway after the Norwegians were beaten 2-1 in Portugal. Wales play Norway in Oslo next month before completing the campaign with a home game against Portugal three days later. title: ⁠⁠Forced to call him 'Dad': The trial over sexual abuse in a disabled care home that has shocked South Korea
description: The BBC spoke to one of three residents at a care home who were sexually assaulted by a staff member.
body: "I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story." These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police. Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear. She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled. Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction. The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care. The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother. We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities. Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016. The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case. According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her. Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation. That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury. She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her. Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up. According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it. As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police. "I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer. When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it." The care home was located in the Korean city of Incheon A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents. They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim. Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible. He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling. For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist". A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive. The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims. In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents. The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim. But during the trial, the court did not address this finding. According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all. Saekdongwon was asked to close down in light of this case Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents. Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences". But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims. "If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities. Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole". Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim. Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector". Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organ

title: Protesters gather as migrants brought ashore on south coast
description: A dinghy was believed to be carrying 120 migrants, according to French media.
body: Police and demonstrators during the protest in Gosport on Sunday evening Protesters have gathered in a south coast town as more than 100 people believed to be migrants were brought ashore after crossing the Channel in a small boat. A number of people were seen arriving at a marina in Gosport, Hampshire, having been transported aboard two RNLI boats late on Sunday. Their dinghy appeared to have set off from near Utah Beach in Normandy during the morning, according to ship tracking data. French media reported there were about 120 migrants on board. Hampshire Police said it deployed officers to "support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea". The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act as well as powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings. The migrants were brought into Gosport onboard an RNLI boat A Home Office spokesperson said: "The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border." They added it was "vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival". A police cordon has been put in place on Haslar Road in Gosport, where the atmosphere at the protest mostly remained peaceful. Ambulances and coaches were also reportedly in the area. Some protesters stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot". Protesters gathered in Gosport on Sunday evening There were similar scenes last month when protesters gathered in the area expecting migrants to arrive on a dinghy, but they were ultimately taken to Dover by sea. Departures so far west along the south coast have been rare in recent years but it is the third such crossing in the space of a month. The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451. This is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024. title: Shadow chancellor to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations
description: Shadow ministers will unveil a series of policies on day two of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.
body: Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building costs. Griffith and his colleagues will use day two of the party's conference in Birmingham to also explain how they would want to reduce food costs, support Heathrow Airport expansion and abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency. Another prospective policy is replacing agreements designed to compel developers to fund community projects and services in areas they want to build. Griffith will describe his approach as the "most ambitious deregulation project in a generation". Reform UK suggested the Tories were "copying our policies". Griffith's speech comes after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch published a 100-page document, external explaining her guiding principles and how her party would act should it return to government by winning the next general election. Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again. The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government, including on the economy, between 2010 and 2024. Griffith is expected to say: "No-one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation." He will accuse Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to pursue a "socialist fever dream of the 1970s", adding the Tories want to deliver "cheaper homes, lower taxes, and less red tape". Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space". During a series of speeches on Monday, Conservative shadow ministers will continue to make their case and provide more details of their proposals. This will include ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, including the future homes standard. The Tories believe their changes could cut the cost of delivering a new home by up to £50,000, which in turn they expect could save money for buyers. A single levy for developers would be implemented in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed. The Conservatives argue this new charge would remove delays and improve how the funds are spent to the benefit of residents. The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra). The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would also be scrapped by the Conservatives. The party believes this would help lift a "burden" from businesses and in turn could cut the cost of the weekly shop. On Heathrow, Griffith is expected to say the next Conservative government would do "whatever it takes to end the delays and boost capacity by backing the third runway". Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010. Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves championed the runway to boost the economy after Labour won power, although Burnham has refused to say whether he backs the project since becoming prime minister. Burnham has described it as "principally... a matter for London and Londoners". Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe. She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges." Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies". He added the Tories were unable to match Reform's pledge to raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000. title: US removes all bombers from RAF Fairford base
description: A statement says all bombers deployed to RAF Fairford have been "re-deployed to their home stations" in the US.
body: A Rockwell B1 Lancer heavy bomber takes off to depart for home at RAF Fairford on Sunday The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the British military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter terror police. A statement from a US department official confirmed on Sunday it had removed all of its bombers from the base back to their home stations in America. The US did not give a reason for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire. Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base and subsequently released on police bail. A sixth man was also later arrested and released on bail. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. title: Polls close in Brazil as Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro remain neck and neck
description: If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.
body: About 160 million people are eligible to vote in Brazil's general election today Polls have closed in Brazil's general election, after voters queued in long lines for a tight first round of the presidential race. After casting his ballot, 80-year-old left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva warned that the choice was between democracy and "barbarism". His challenger, right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people". The result is forecast to be close. BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that the gap between Lula and Bolsonaro is only two points. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October. According to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE), more than 158.7 million Brazilians, including one million people abroad, are eligible to vote in the election. Lula is challenged by 11 candidates, although BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that candidates other than Lula and Bolsonaro will get only about 10% of the vote. The TSE has not set a fixed time for the release of the official results, but they are expected within hours because voting is electronic and experience from previous elections shows that results tend to come quickly. A victory for Bolsonaro would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's re-election would create problems for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security. A woman votes at a polling station during Brazil's general election in Barra de Guaratiba, Rio de Janeiro Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva votes in the general election in Sao Bernardo do Campo Flávio Bolsonaro casts his vote at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro Some countries, from which Brazilians living overseas are able to vote, have already released preliminary vote count data. In China, Lula won 56.63% of the votes, while Bolsonaro came in second with 31.33%. Lula also won in countries including South Korea, New Zealand and Saudi Arabia. In Israel, however, Bolsonaro won 74.40% of the valid votes. He also won 71.59% of the valid votes in Japan. Today's result will also determine the composition of the Senate from February 2027 onwards, as 54 of the Senate's 81 seats are being contested, representing two-thirds of the chamber. Currently, the largest bloc in the Senate is Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), followed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD), which has served in a coalition government under Lula. In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father, Jair. But the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup and is barred from standing for office. Because of recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has been prohibited from posting on social media or making public statements. Despite these restrictions, there is little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has his father's backing. title: Humphries wins Grand Prix to end barren spell
description: World number two Luke Humphries ends a 16-month wait for a PDC major trophy with a stunning 6-4 victory over Gerwyn Price in the World Grand Prix final.
body: Luke Humphries took home £150,000 in prize money World number two Luke Humphries ended a 16-month wait for a PDC major trophy with a stunning 6-4 victory over Gerwyn Price in the World Grand Prix final. Humphries, 31, was at the top of the sport two years ago but has found his dominance superseded by Luke Littler and had failed to taste major success since winning the Premier League in May 2025. A ranking title had eluded him since claiming the Masters in February last year, but he showed his class and an abundance of character to lift the title at the unique 'double-in, double-out' tournament in Leicester. The second seed, who was in a record-breaking fourth successive World Grand Prix final, trailed Price 3-0 but won four sets on the spin to take control. Price levelled but Humphries broke in the deciding leg of set five and then won three straight legs to be crowned champion. It is his second World Grand Prix title, adding to his 2023 success that started his march to becoming world number one. The victory ensures he retains his number two ranking from the Netherlands' Gian van Veen. "It's kind of like I needed this to give me a bit of confidence," Humphries told Sky Sports. "It's been a torrid 15 or 18 months, losing so many major finals. I felt like I had not much to give tonight." Defeat for Price means his four-year wait for a major PDC title continues, while he has now lost five successive major finals, including three this year. Price, who was playing in a fourth Grand Prix final, claimed the first set with a stunning 132 three-dart average. He raced into a 3-0 lead and Humphries admitted afterwards that avoiding a 6-0 clean sweep was on his mind such was the brutality that Price was producing. The fourth set saw the momentum swing however. With Price waiting on tops to move to within two sets of victory, Humphries nicked it by taking out a brilliant 105, with what he said "felt like the biggest shot of my career". From there his levels started to rise and he claimed the following three sets to lead. Price rallied in set eight and won three successive legs to force a best-of-three finale, but, after a short break, Humphries found another gear. Set nine went to a deciding leg, but unlike the previous four sets in the match where that had happened, there was a break of throw, with Humphries finishing in 10 darts. That left Price dejected and Humphries won three unanswered legs to claim a ninth major PDC title. "The sport is in such a special place that when you pick these trophies up they mean a lot more," said Humphries. "When I was winning, I don't think there were so many good players. I'm happy to win a couple a year - one a year is great. "To go on and win like I did is going to be tough. I don't think I can't do it, I'm just trying to pick up as many titles as I can. "I worked incredibly hard, showed a lot of grit and determination. I think these are a lot sweeter than the ones you win with ease."
