title: Matthew Rhys takes Best Actor at Bafta Cymru for performance in Netflix thriller
description: The actor added another award to his cabinet after winning two lead acting Emmys last month.
body: The Welsh actor added the Bafta Cymru award to his growing collection Matthew Rhys has continued his fine form this awards season after being announced as the Best Actor at the Bafta Cymru Awards ceremony. The actor made history last month when he became the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night at the Emmy's. Presenter Carol Vorderman said she was "humbled and excited" to receive an award for outstanding contribution, while Lauren Evans took home an award for her contribution to the film I Swear. Lee Walters, Bafta Cymru chair, congratulated the nominees last month and said "each is a testament to the creativity, skill and dedication of the people working across Wales' screen industries, both in front of and behind the camera". Rhys was presented the award at the ICC Wales, in Newport, where the event has been held since 2024. His performance in The Beast in Me earned him his second Bafta Cymru, 29 years after his first for his role in the Welsh-language film Bydd yn Wro, or Be Brave. Gabrielle Creevy won her second Best Actress award and Y Crwydryn took home the Single Documentary award, with Rhys Edwards winning Director Factual for the same show. Mari Grug won her first Bafta Cymru award for presenter in Mari Grug: Yn dydd Ar Y Tro. Elsewhere, Y Golau: Dwr won two awards and Matthew Barry won Best Writer for The Guest. Amour a Mynydd won the Entertainment Programme award and Stori'r Iaith received the Factual Series award. Burton won the Feature/Television Film award and the Short Film award was won by Gofod Ymennydd – Brain Space and the Children's Programme went to Itopia. In total, 17 awards were presented across the evening as well as two Bafta Outstanding Contribution awards. Carol Vorderman arriving at the Bafta Cymru awards ceremony Evans, from Hendy, Carmarthenshire, was awarded the inaugural Outstanding Contribution to Craft award after working on a range of productions including Game of Thrones, King Lear and The Danish Girl. In recent years, she has worked on Sex Education, Lost Boys and I Swear which was nominated for six Bafta awards earlier this year. Evans ended up winning the award for Best Casting saying she was "incredibly proud" to represent Welsh voices at the 2026 ceremony. She said she was honoured to be recognised at the Bafta Cymru awards and that she wants to "keep elevating our Welsh creatives and our Welsh talent". She added: "It's not as much of a closed industry as it was, but there is still so much more work to be done." Walters said the two women have taken "very different paths", but have both "achieved so much and thoroughly deserve to be celebrated". title: I only found out I had cancer after my four-year-old kicked me in the testicles
description: Dad discovers he has cancer after he was accidentally kicked in the testicles.
body: This video can not be played I only found out I had cancer after my four-year-old kicked me in the testicles Ben Lidgey was "messing around" with his son in the garden when he was accidentally kicked in the testicles - but it may well have saved his life. When he was still in pain after a week, he sought medical help and found out he had testicular cancer. A new report from men's charity Movember says a third of men in Wales die before their 75th birthday, and calls on the Welsh government to develop a dedicated plan for men's health. The government said its existing suicide prevention and self harm, mental health and cancer strategies are already working to tackle some of the challenges facing men. As a Movember ambassador Ben encourages men to check in on their friends and look after each other Warning: This article discusses suicide Lidgey, from Cardiff, says his testicle felt "like a cricket ball" after being kicked by his son, but was reluctant to see his GP, thinking the problem would go away. "It's one of those fairly typical things that happens to men and you shrug it off and think, well, it'll get better," he said. "I was in a busy family environment, you know, two small children, there were lots of other things going on." After being given all-clear for cancer, Ben faced a different challenge. He said: "I felt like I was fine but after five years my wife said 'I don't think you are fine. I think you need to talk to somebody'. "She was picking up on the fact that I was perhaps a bit shorter, a bit more argumentative, less patient with people and just not the same person I was before." After counselling Ben saw an improvement, and is now an advocate for more support for men and boys. A reluctance to seek help for both physical and mental health is often cited as a reason why men, in general, die younger. Movember's report says almost 7,000 men died before their 75th birthday in 2024. The rate of premature death in women is significantly lower at 28%. Often, it says, men die from preventable conditions or those likely to benefit from earlier treatment such as certain cancers, heart, lung and liver diseases, those related to drugs and alcohol as well as suicide. Where a man lives also matters, with the premature mortality rate in Blaenau Gwent about 60% higher than in Powys, while men in the most deprived communities can expect to live 7.5 years less than those in the least deprived. The analysis also suggest the costs to the Welsh economy of the top five causes of male premature death is £1.4bn a year. Jonathan Scourfield says social media has a powerful influence on young people adding to previous pressures Jonathan Scourfield, professor of Social Care at Cardiff University, said: "Young men, in particular, are much more likely to get injured and die from physical risk taking. The expectation of physical strength." He said some men may also ignore the importance of building up a social network, or rely on a female partner to take care of that. "And then, if they're widowed or if they retire, they really struggle with loneliness," he said. "Diet is a really important aspect... a lot of healthy foods such as fruit and vegetables, not seen as a particularly manly thing. However, some less good for you stuff like drinking heavily is seen as something that is kind of a boy growing into a man." Scourfield said despite the decline of heavy industry and manual work, traditional images of "masculinity" persist for younger men through social media and influencers. The report says, if implemented, a men's health care plan would complement the existing women's plan published in 2024, and would not be "starting from scratch" with many organisations already working to improve support. Callum Tipton says MenTribe offers men a safe space away from the pub and spending money One of them is MenTribe, a Bangor and Snowdonia based support group focused on building resilience and mental and physical wellbeing through outdoor challenges. It was co-founded by Callum Tipton who left the army after 13 years, with PTSD and depression. To combat his loneliness, the 34-year-old began taking groups hiking. "Being active, it's obviously releasing the natural endorphins in their bodies as well so they're getting a bit of a feel-good factor from it and then obviously when they're opening up and talking about things they're lot more relaxed," he said. MenTribe organise monthly hikes and a weekly football game for men to let off steam Gavin Roberts from Bangor had twin boys five years ago, but they suffered twin to twin syndrome where one of the boys died. His son, now five, has hyperplastic left heart syndrome, meaning he has half a heart and only one functioning lung. Roberts, 44, said: "I tried to deal with it all myself, but it's hard because friends and family will rarely understand exactly what's involved." "When I found the MenTribe group probably two years ago, I thought it'd be nice just to have a bit of company in the mountains because I was quite often in the mountains and I go on my own. "I've lost a couple of friends to suicide and I hope that guys can just reach out and make that first step so that they can just walk and talk, or not even talk, they can just walk and be active again." Gavin says it's easier for men to open up to strangers rather than those close to them Welsh football legend John Hartson is among those supporting the call for a Welsh men's health plan, as a recovering gambling addict. In July 2009 Hartson underwent emergency brain surgery after it emerged that he had testicular cancer that had spread to his brain and lungs. "When I detected a little lump on my testicle... I was just ignorant of my own health - I just thought I'll get on with it," he said. "That's a regret to have put my family through because they were living the cancer with me." title: 'Money-grab' or celebration? NFL kicks off London series
description: The NFL kicked off this season's series of London games on Sunday but the build-up was overshadowed by anger from long-term fans over ticket prices.
body: Neither the Washington Commanders nor Indianapolis Colts qualified for last season's play-offs Once upon a time, tickets for NFL games in London were like gold dust. All 43 games have been near capacity at Wembley, Twickenham and Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. According to the NFL, its UK fanbase has swelled to 18.6 million, with 4.5 million of those considered 'avid' fans. So in the build-up to this year's London series, why were thousands of tickets still available for two of the three games? Next week's clash between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham sold out in hours. But the crowd for Sunday's game at Tottenham between Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts only reached 60,907 after ticket prices were slashed, and large sections remain unsold for the Wembley game on 18 October. The NFL is playing a record nine regular-season games abroad this season but 19 years after the first London game, has the NFL reached a saturation point in the UK? Most of the fans BBC Sport spoke to at Sunday's game had travelled from the United States Tickets to see Indianapolis beat Washington 30-13 on Sunday went on sale in July at £79-£245. But the NFL then dropped prices twice, in late August and again last week. That meant some fans who paid £185 were sat next to fans who paid £79 a few days ago. Some tickets were also discounted or free via the Blue Light Card and Tickets For Good platforms. Matt Cullen has travelled from Cambridge to most of the London games and said there were two main reasons for the slow sales; a price hike and a season-ticket package being scrapped. "I find the prices now mind-boggling," he added. "It's so far above the rate of inflation that it just feels like a money-grab. It's priced out a lot of long-term fans." In 2019, tickets ranged from £55 to £125. According to Ticket-Compare,, external UK inflation has since risen by about 32.4% and the cheapest NFL London tickets have risen by 43.9%. The most expensive have seen a 96.5% hike. Season-ticket packages had been available, guaranteeing seats for each London game with a discount, but they were scrapped after the 2024 season. "It felt like a kick to the head for a lot of loyal fans who'd supported the games for a long time and spent a lot of money," said Cullen, a former season-ticket holder. "But I do understand the NFL wants to bring new fans in." UK fans have also complained about the quality of recent match-ups in London when compared to those in the new countries where the NFL has expanded. Australia hosted a divisional clash between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams last month, while the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys played out a thriller in Brazil last week. "It was an amazing game and we haven't had many of those unfortunately," added Cullen. The best team coming to London this year is Philadelphia, who have reached two of the past four Super Bowls, and their game next week is a sell-out even though it was the most expensive. The Jaguars face the Houston Texans in two weeks and Dave, another former season-ticket holder, will travel from Chorley. "We were all gutted when they took the season tickets away," he admitted. "The way we saw it, we weren't wanted anymore because we didn't spend the money that new fans do on merchandise and we get to the stadium later. "But it has opened it up for more fans to have the opportunity to attend so it's a double-edged sword." Jonathan Taylor ran in two touchdowns as the Colts beat the Commanders and produced a tea-sipping celebration BBC Sport spoke to dozens of fans at Sunday's game and none of them were aware ticket prices had dropped. None seemed to care either. American fans know the London games don't provide the same tailgating experience they get back home, but they - and the players - are still fascinated by the eclectic crowd at international games. Fans still travel from all over the UK, Europe and the US, wearing jerseys of all the NFL teams. "It's still one of the greatest sporting events that neutrals can go to," said Dave. "I don't think there's any other sport where you'd get tens of thousands watching teams they don't support. "It was always a celebration of the game. People would go for the love of the sport rather than the two teams that were playing and I think that's still the same." It sure felt like a Washington home game when they recovered a Colts fumble on just the game's second play. The crowd produced an even bigger roar when third-choice quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis - replacing the injured Marcus Mariota - made a 47-yard touchdown pass to Treylon Burks in the third quarter. The Commanders thought they had drawn level when Antonio Williams ran in an 87-yard score, but the touchdown was chalked off for a Washington penalty. Indianapolis quarterback Daniel Jones then got in to seal their success, with Jonathan Taylor having run in two touchdowns for the Colts. Simone Biles wore a customised outfit bearing her husband's name and number It is hard to imagine anyone went home disappointed, no matter what price they paid. The stands were bathed in sunshine and fans looked like they were having the time of their life as they sang Sweet Caroline and Wonderwall in unison. Oasis' Noel Gallagher was booed when he appeared on the big screen - no doubt because of his football allegiance to Manchester City - and former Manchester United and England striker Wayne Rooney was also among the crowd, wearing a half-and-half scarf. Olympian Simone Biles travelled to London to support her husband Jonathan Owens, who is a safety for the Colts, and as long as stars such as those show up at NFL games, international fans will want to be there too. title: Arsenal 10 points off WSL leaders - is Slegers' job at risk?
description: It is only five matches into the WSL season but Arsenal are already 10 points behind leaders Manchester City and manager Renee Slegers is coming under increasing scrutiny.
body: Renee Slegers led Arsenal to the Women's Champions League title in 2025 It is only five matches into the Women's Super League season and Arsenal are already 10 points behind leaders Manchester City - so is manager Renee Slegers' position at risk? The Gunners have won just two of their opening seven matches in all competitions and sit 10th in the WSL table. It is dismal reading for Arsenal fans, whose optimism has quickly diminished and their 4-2 defeat at City on Sunday added further salt to their wounds. The Gunners have not won a WSL title since 2019 and it has been a familiar story each year as slow starts have ultimately proven costly. Slegers did lead Arsenal to the Women's Champions League title in 2025. But they failed to win any domestic trophies last season, although they did finish second in the WSL and reached the semi-finals in the defence of their European crown. Asked if she was worried about her position, Slegers said: "All I know so far is that the last couple of days we have been together as a club, and a team. "We have been aligned in the direction. Of course, this result is disappointing but I'm here and I'm full of energy. I care a lot for the club and the players. I see perspective. "It's good to have an international break coming up. It's good for the players to change environment, play their football elsewhere, then come back in with new energy." Why are Arsenal struggling to score in WSL? Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed This video can not be played 'The pressure is mounting on her' - Slegers emotional apology At full-time on Sunday, Slegers gathered her dejected players in a familiar team huddle before walking over to their fans. She stood in front of the 2,500 away supporters at Etihad Stadium applauding as they sang "North London Forever" in a somewhat emotional release. She was greeted warmly and it did not look like a fanbase who were keen to push her out of the door. Arsenal had performed reasonably well against City, took the lead twice and were ultimately undone by small margins. "I mostly went there to thank them, connect with them and show them I care for them and I appreciate them coming out to Manchester," said Slegers. "I also wanted to show that – not that I feel sorry for them as I'm a big part of it too – but they are coming here and not getting the rewards, just like the team. "I just wanted to connect with them instead of walking away and hiding. I don't know how they are going to react to me! I just wanted to thank them for being there for us." Outside of the stadium however, noise among the fanbase has been building and Slegers knows her position is being questioned. Sources at the club insist she retains their full backing and, while there is disappointment and acknowledgement that results have not been good enough, they believe Slegers can guide them in the right direction. There was investment in the transfer window with the likes of England international Georgia Stanway and Spain full-back Ona Batlle arriving, as well as the talented, young Germany forward Lisa Baum. Those signings were made early in an attempt to ensure a full pre-season and avoid a slow start with most players returning to Arsenal from their holidays in mid-July. It has clearly not paid off but rather than worry about her job, Slegers is already planning an inquest into where the problems lie during the international break. "There will be a big review of our season so far," she added, when asked if there was a wider club issue regarding their continuous slow starts to WSL seasons. Some of the issues have been obvious. They had scored just twice in the WSL prior to Sunday's match and Alessia Russo's goal in the 49th minute against City was her first in the league this season. That lack of ruthlessness has meant Arsenal have failed to win in their past four WSL games - their worst winless streak since October 2023. Defeat by City also confirmed this as their second-worst start after five games in the WSL, only picking up fewer points (four) in 2014. Confidence has clearly taken a hit and Wednesday's bizarre error from defender Leah Williamson summed up the chaotic nature of their season so far. Emotions were high after their 2-2 draw with Paris FC in the Women's Champions League, so much so that Slegers did not show up for post-match media duties. She later explained her actions, saying she was angry and felt the team needed her in that moment. But despite the obvious concerns for Arsenal, Slegers was defiant on Sunday, stating she believes she remains the right person to lead the club. "First of all, it's not about me anyway. I have energy, I feel the connection and I think we're going through a really difficult time but we also see perspective," she said. "We look forward and see solutions. We see the closeness [of the squad]. It's not that we're totally away from it or off it, it's been consistently about margins. "We have to work to get them on our side but when we do, I think we'll be really good. Of course, it's been a long run without the results we wanted. "It's not about me, it's about the club and I care about the club." title: France to close up to 500 schools on Monday over student protests
description: Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some high schools after clashes between riot police and student protesters, France's education minister says.
body: French riot police were deployed to the manage the protests on Friday Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday. Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said. He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests. Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille. High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests. The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons". "There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed. "Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before". On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France School protests send shivers down French government's spine Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to the AFP news agency. On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff". He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent. Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions. title: Nine fire engines called to Glasgow city centre bar fire
description: More than 40 firefighters are attending and sections of some streets have been cordoned off.
body: More than 40 firefighters have been called out after reports of fire at a bar in central Glasgow. The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said it was alerted just after 14:40 and nine appliances were in attendance on Sunday evening. Images from the scene showed parts of Renfield Street and West Regent Street were cordoned off, with a number of fire crews gathered outside both the Bistro and Maltman bars. There were no reports of casualties. People have been advised to avoid the area. title: Girl, 12, fatally shot in US during 'dispute over parking space'
description: Police in Baltimore have said the young girl was not a target of the shooting but was caught in the crossfire.
body: This video can not be played Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley spoke on Saturday night A 12-year-old girl was killed in Baltimore over the weekend during an apparent disagreement over a parking space, police in the US city said. The girl was caught in the crossfire of bullets between two men who police said were allegedly fighting over a parking space in a park where children were playing American football. In addition to the young girl, a woman was also found with gunshot wounds when police arrived on the scene. Two men also visited area hospitals for injuries believed to be related to the shooting, police said. Police are now searching for at least two suspects, Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said at a news conference. No arrests have been made. "What we know is there was some type of argument between two cowards," Worley said. "They both opened fire on each other. In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl, who was probably down there watching football, was shot and killed." Worley said the girl, who police have not named, was not a target of the shooting. The girl was pronounced dead in hospital. The other three individuals who were injured have non-life-threatening injuries, Worley said. The incident happened after 18:00 EDT (23:00 BST) on Saturday. Authorities are still investigating the shooting and have asked any witnesses to bring information to police. It remains unclear how many shots were fired, Worley said. "Two grown men got into an argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone," Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said at the news conference. "We never should have to say something like that. What happened out here today is one of the most disgusting things I've ever seen in my life." title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' motion
description: The vote has caused divisions among figures at the top of the party at its conference in Brighton.
body: Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party. The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic". Activists endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of members at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1022 votes to 813. Discussion about the vote has dominated the conference, and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last election. The motion adopted by Green members defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine". "The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says. It has attracted criticism from some Jewish groups, including the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council. In a letter to the party sent ahead of the vote, the organisations said Zionism was an anti-racist movement, adding that "modern Zionism was formed in part as a response to antisemitism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it." It also raised concerns about the safety of Jewish members in the Green Party, as well as the implications for Jewish institutions in areas represented by the Greens. Debate about the motion, as well as the conflict in Gaza, has featured heavily during the conference, which is taking place after a surge in its membership in the wake of Polanski's election as leader in September last year. Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression". "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added. Polanski himself did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here. Greens can move Labour in the right direction, says Polanski UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response Asked about the motion on Friday, Polanski said: "If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party." However, he said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like." He had also said he wanted to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist. However, both amendments favoured by Polanski were rejected by Green members. A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist. Speaking after the motion had been approved, chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein told the BBC she could consider her future in the party. Polanski has not specified whether he supports the motion passed by members, but added his name to a joint statement from the party's five MPs and deputy leaders issued after the vote. The statement pledged to ensure the Green Party was "an anti-racist party in every way" and added that there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people". Over the course of the three-day conference, key figures in the party have expressed differing positions about the Zionism motion. Some pro-Israel activists demonstrated outside the conference venue on Saturday Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, with Denyer arguing it could risk "alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people". Chowns, as well as former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas, both spoke against the motion during the debate. Addressing members, Lucas said: "I urge you not to support the over-simplification at the heart of this motion - a refusal to accept complexities which is leading to so many Jewish members feeling scared and unwelcome in our party." Deputy leader Mothin Ali, who had expressed support for the motion before the vote, said it was calling for "a state that's democratic, that guarantees the rights of every single person living on that land". He added that he was "absolutely not" calling all Jewish people who define themselves as Zionists racist. Following the vote, Israel's Foreign Ministry said the motion went beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate" and was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom". Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election. The Conservatives criticised the motion, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core". Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards". "It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she added. Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK. title: Rugby league fans in Wakefield for bus parade
description: The city has been alive with celebrations after Trinity brought home the Super League trophy.
body: Thousands of Wakefield Trinity fans came out to celebrate their team Thousands of rugby league fans turned out to watch an open-top bus parade, after Wakefield Trinity were crowned Super League champions. Trinity beat Warrington Wolves 23-10 in Saturday's Grand Final at Old Trafford - their first title win since 1968, long before Super League was established. To celebrate the victory, two buses, carrying players and staff, travelled from the club's ground at Belle Vue to Wakefield Town Hall for a civic reception. Fullback Max Jowitt, who has made 188 appearances for Trinity and scored three goals in the final, said the parade had been an "unbelievable" experience. "The fans have been unbelievable, the city is unbelievable and the trophy's unbelievable," he said. This video can not be played Victory parade celebrates Wakefield Super League champions Fans lined city centre streets to see the buses, which arrived at Wakefield Town Hall at about 15:00. Jane Robinson became a Wakefield Trinity fan through her late husband, who supported the side from childhood. She was at the game at Old Trafford, where the team became only the sixth club to win the Super League title. "It was absolutely out of this world - the atmosphere was electric," she said. "You can't help but think how good this has been for Wakefield." Jasper and Sarah were still excited after attending the game at Old Trafford Also revelling in the excitement from being at the game, young fan Jasper was wearing a tri-coloured wig his grandfather bought him. He said "everyone was screaming and shouting" each time Trinity scored a try. "It's amazing - it's an incredible feeling," added his mum Sarah. Melvyn Moyles says he has been supporting Wakefield since he was a child Rob (left) brought his whole family along to the parade Claire Slater, who was watching alongside her son Cohen, said she felt "absolutely ecstatic". "The atmosphere yesterday at the ground was absolutely electric, so we wanted to come for the atmosphere today. It's been years in the making hasn't it?" Melvyn Moyes, who was in the city centre with his brother Ken to cheer on the team, described the atmosphere as "buzzing". "I can remember the good old days – and the bad old days," Melvyn said. "Wakefield is back – look out everybody." Following the reception, a free ticketed fan celebration was held at WX on Union Street with player appearances, speeches and highlights from the Grand Final on big screens. title: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest
description: The allegations were made after police detained dozens of protesters demanding the resignation of the election chief over changes to voter rolls.
body: Young people have been protesting against large-scale changes to voter rolls by the Election Commission Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi. The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner. In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry. Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls. The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list. Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi. The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this". "Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests. She said the police were resorting to "brutality". The Press Club of India has demanded immediate action on the complaints against police officers, saying it was "shocked and dismayed" by the treatment of journalists. "Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues," it said in a statement. Demonstrators scuffle with police during a protest in New Delhi over the alleged assault The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries. It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address. But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour the BJP during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations. The protesters have included supporters of the influential Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that began as an online satirical movement. The pressure group recorded its first major victory in July when it forced the then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms. The CJP called for the latest protest after a report in The Indian Express, external said that Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge. The differences were reported to be mostly over the controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year. The Election Commission has defended its way of working and said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously. But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. title: Hamilton bemused after glitch turns F1 into 'Lego race'
description: Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton liken the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".
body: Lewis Hamilton's car lost all of its speed just before the race began Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton likened the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race". The problem led to several cars, including those of the two multiple world champions who were sharing the front row of the grid, not working in the wet conditions that preceded the race. A tropical downpour delayed attempts to get the grand prix under way for the best part of an hour. And when the cars set off on formation laps behind a safety car to test the conditions, audiences were treated to the bizarre sight of many of them struggling to move. A bug in the software that mandates how the engines' electrical power can be used in wet conditions had been triggered by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and specific aspects of the circuit layout. Verstappen, who went on to take a dominant win that was his first victory of the year, said: "These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented. "I triggered [the problem] first and then I looked in my mirror, I was like, 'Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going [on]...?' It was like the Lego race." Verstappen was referring to a show run in battery-powered Lego F1 cars that was held before the British Grand Prix in July. Hamilton, sitting beside Verstappen in the post-race news conference after finishing third, interjected to say: "Yeah, we had the same speed. I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before." Verstappen added: "It was insane. Like, it's the Lego power. At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on. "Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you (Hamilton) by yourself crawling. That's not what you want, right, for the sport." Mercedes driver George Russell, who retired from the race with an engine failure, said: "It didn't feel very F1." Nikolas Tombazis, the single-seater director for governing body the FIA said there would be a full investigation. The issue arose, he added, because, while the software had been tested, it had not been tested in these specific conditions. Largely because there has been so little running in the wet this year. "Cars are complicated," Tombazis said. "We would all like it to be simpler, but when you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated. "We haven't done a full debrief of the situation and see how we can avoid such an issue. Every race, we have a long debrief afterwards, where we identify criticalities. "Obviously, that was a major criticality, and we need to make sure we avoid it. Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem, no, but we will do our best to avoid it, of course." This is far from the first issue created by the huge complexity of the latest hybrid engines introduced this year, with their near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power. Because the engines are fundamentally energy starved, and so cannot deploy their full combined power output at all times, a series of complexities were added into the management of the engines to try to sticking-plaster solutions. Many of these led to the counter-intuitive driving about which many of the sport's stars have been complaining all season - and more changes have been added since. Off-track conversation has been dominated by this all year, and rules are changing for next year to alter the energy split to try to ameliorate the issue. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "What happened at the start obviously is not ideal in terms of presentation of the sport. "But at the same time it is the first year of new regulations, quite complex from a regulatory point of view, and it was also the first time we started in such conditions. "So we have to concede that F1 has done an excellent job in making some new regulations that came with some question marks from a power-unit behaviour point of view when it came to racing for instance. "We have to acknowledge there has been really good work to make the show and racing work, and if there are some glitches occasionally, we have to accept they are glitches for everyone, be supportive and make sure it doesn't happen again." The problem had a secondary consequence - the field order was jumbled up, and one reading of the rules could have meant the grid order should change for any restart. But while the FIA's software engineers were rewriting the code as fast as possible, it was determined that, as this situation had never occurred before, and as the problem was out of any competitor's control, the most appropriate order was to revert to the original grid. Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and it was behind a safety car on a formation lap. That would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did." An entertaining race started an hour and half late following rain and computation delays A record crowd loved it Several others, including Alex Albon, didn't This video can not be played Mercedes better 'watch out - Verstappen 'imperious' in Bahrain GP win "Amazing" was the word Verstappen chose to describe his and Red Bull's first win of the 2026 season at a chaotic, bizarre and, in some ways, unprecedented race. It would be wrong to say the victory was a complete surprise, as it came after three consecutive podium finishes in which the four-time champion appeared to be edging

title: Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis
description: The Yemeni president's announcement comes amid an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.
body: Soldiers ride in the back of a pick-up truck on a dirt road near Taiz, amid fighting between Yemeni government forces and Houthis The head of Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced it will wage an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis. It follows an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in recent days. The Iran-backed group said it had struck sites belonging to Saudi national oil company Aramco, in response to what it described as 50 Saudi-led coalition strikes in 12 hours. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment. The Yemeni government's fierce statement was expected after the Houthis' offensive last month, which saw them seize control of the country's coastline, including the vital shipping lane of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on 3 October On Sunday, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address: "Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory." Yemen's capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the Houthis for more than a decade, has come under sustained attack as government forces try to weaken the group's military capabilities. Attacks on the Houthis have also spread across Yemen, including to the Saada region, the group's northern heartland. Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi addresses the nation in a televised address in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia But security sources say the Iran-backed Houthis have continued to make gains. The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government. On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports. Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz. "They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP. Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government. Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil. On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east. "Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites." It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories". But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis. In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday. On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west. Smoke rises from the site of an air strike in Sanaa on 4 October Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis. A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital city from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north. Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition. After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East. Last month, a lightning offensive enabled the Houthis to seize the country's entire Red Sea coast, stopping Saudi Arabia from using it as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz. The strategy benefited the Houthis' main sponsor, Iran. But it has also forced Saudi Arabia back into direct military confrontation with the Houthis. title: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says
description: Pike's lawyer says doctors are still trying to clear two lethal doses of pentobarbital from her body.
body: Christa Pike appearing in court in 2007 US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday. Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995. She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee. Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days." He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors. He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said. Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday. "If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be." How did Christa Pike survive? I interviewed Christa Pike 20 years ago - I can't stop thinking about her He called on the governor to commute her death sentence to a life sentence "at the very least". "She has endured a torturous attempt at executing her," he said. "She's spent over 30 years in prison, most of that in solitary confinement." "We don't know right now - and we may never know - what sort of torture she endured during [her failed execution]." Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995. She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee. Slemmer's mother May Martinez travelled to Nashville for the execution, which moved ahead despite last-minute legal challenges. Martinez, who supported Pike's death sentence, told local news outlet WJXX that she "broke down in tears" after finding out it was not successful. "I think that the state owes me a big apology," she said. The state's Department of Correction has defended the use of lethal injections, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out". Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection. title: Triathlete was 'very sick' in hospital after swimming in 'dirty' open water
description: A new project is using small sampling devices on triathletes to help test the water quality in Wales.
body: This video can not be played Andrew Jones is an keen triathlete but chasing those triathlon dreams has also meant running the risk of getting ill. A triathlete who travels the world to take part in races says making his dreams come true comes with serious risk after one event led to him being "very sick" in hospital. Andrew Jones, from Carmarthen, takes part in various events, and has even earned a slot in the Ironman World Championship in Kona, Hawaii this month. But the triathlete said swimming in "dirty" open-water made him very unwell ahead of the event after he contracted Campylobacter, external — an infection caused by bacteria. Triathlon Cymru said its Safer Blue Spaces project, which is the first of its kind, was now using small sampling devices on triathletes to test the water and provide reliable data on water quality in Wales. Jones said contracting Campylobacter from polluted water was "pretty nasty". "It made me very sick unfortunately. In the house on a Sunday evening, I felt really unwell," he said. "My temperature went up, my heart rate went up, I was shaking uncontrollably and unfortunately went straight to A&E." Triathlon Cymru has been working on a project to monitor water quality for athletes during open-water swimming events He added: "I was in just over a week before one of the biggest races of my life. So very bad timing. "I was a little annoyed, to be honest, because I think we go into the water with confidence, knowing everything is great and that's a great place to swim... it made me think about swimming in that particular area again." Andrew Jones says becoming unwell makes him unsure about swimming in the polluted area again Triathlon Cymru hopes its Safer Blue Spaces project, in partnership with Swim Wales, Bangor University and Imperial College London, will be able to help. To collect data for the project, some of the competitors from Barry's SWYD Sprint Triathlon in August were pulled to the side and small devices — about the size of a fifty-pence piece — were attached to the backs of their wetsuits. The national governing body for triathlon in Wales said they are new sampling devices and used as part of a pioneering project funded by the insurance group Admiral. The Safer Blue Spaces project monitors water quality at sports sites across Wales using wearable passive samplers Normally, race organisers test the water to see if it is safe for swimming. However, there are limitations to that type of sampling. Samples are usually collected at just one or two locations shortly before the race, which means it does not provide detailed data. These sampling devices follow the swimmers' exact route while they are in the water, thereby providing accurate information. "For us as an organisation, knowing what's in our water is really important because we're putting athletes in the water," said Amy Jenner, Triathlon Cymru's head of development. "Across Wales, we have roughly around 60 events a year, so we want to know what's in our water. "So having the fund available to us to do all of the research and the testing allows us to then go back to the athletes, back to the event organisers, to National Resource Wales, Public Health Wales and say what the picture is with our waters in Wales." Simon Webb, who organises the Barry SWYD Sprint Triathlon, said it was important that athletes could swim "without the risk of potentially getting ill". Amy Jenner, Triathlon Cymru's head of development, says "knowing what's in our water is really important" Once the competitors have finished the swim, they come to the transition area, take off their wetsuits, and continue with the race. The technical team then come along and cut off the sampling devices, ready to send to Bangor University. Kate Herridge, a PhD student working on the project, said the next step was to "concentrate these water samples" and "find if any pathogens have attached themselves to the samplers". "We're able to take them off, concentrate them and then detect them and see what's present within them." Triathlon Cymru hopes that ,in the future, it'll be able to share this data with environmental agencies and water companies in order to improve knowledge of what's in the water, and take steps to improve the quality of seas, lakes and rivers. title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
description: The Tory leader seeks to echo Margaret Thatcher as she sets out her guiding political principles.
body: Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external "I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg. She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle". The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election. Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes". She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum". Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing. "And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?" In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for. Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction. "The result was that the state grew by stealth." The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth". The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says. And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no. "Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything." An 88 foot long satirical take on the Bayeaux Tapestry poking fun at Labour and Reform UK is a popular attraction at the Tory conference As their conference gets under way in Birmingham the Conservatives have pledged to end a childcare "cliff edge", which currently means parents earning more than £100,000 do not qualify for the entitlement. The party has also promised to deliver 50,000 new prison places by slashing the overseas aid budget to £1bn a year in a bid to end the early release of offenders. Over the 14 years the Conservatives were in power, around 500 net prison places were created, which takes into account 14,142 added in existing and new jails, set against 13,660 lost mainly to dilapidation and closures. Speaking in the main conference hall, Badenoch sought to make the case that the party had moved on from 2024 and outlined her expectation that the next few days in Birmingham would be a chance for members to discuss their ideas. She said: "We're going to be having debates, we're going to have arguments, they are going to be fun. "We're going to challenge each other and afterwards we're still going to be a united party." During a question and answer session, Badenoch focused on different topics covered in her essay – including citizenship and how communities need to operate on trust. She said the UK is "not a dormitory, it is not a hotel" before speaking how "British culture means something". To applause in the well-attended hall, Badenoch said: "I don't want lots of little ghettos of separatist communities where they are recreating the place they come from - that will ruin the United Kingdom." Responding, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the Tory Party "is stuck in the past and remains completely out of touch with what people across Britain want to see". "Last week Andy Burnham set out a plan to bring back hope to Britain. Kemi Badenoch wants to drag our country back to a politics that let so many people down over the past 40 years." title: US Marine arrested over murder of woman in Okinawa, Japan
description: Japan's government lodged a formal protest with the US, demanding that military officials take action.
body: The US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, Japan A US Marine has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman's body was found in a hotel in Okinawa, Japan, local officials say. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the crime as a "brutal and heinous" robbery and murder. She said she had urged the US to "enforce stricter discipline" of its personnel. Japan's public broadcaster NHK identified the victim as Yagi Anna, 39, and the suspect as Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma. "We are actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine," the Marine Corps said on social media, extending condolences to the victim's family. Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the woman's body was discovered early Saturday morning in a hotel in Naha City, the capital of the Okinawa prefecture. "Such an incident is utterly inexcusable and fills me with strong indignation," Koizumi wrote on social media, adding that "incidents and accidents involving U.S. military personnel cause significant anxiety to the local community and must never occur". The US Embassy in Tokyo said that it was fully cooperating with the Japanese government and local police. Japan's foreign ministry said it summoned US ambassador George Glass to discuss the incident on Sunday. Okinawa is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops. Okinawa Governor Genta Koja says the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline. "The fact that this kind of event has happened again leaves us no choice but to conclude that the US military's efforts in maintaining discipline, educating personnel, and other such measures are completely ineffective," he said. title: Watch: What we know about Russian strikes on Kyiv bridges
description: BBC Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson is near Kyiv's Northern Bridge, which has been hit for the second day in a row.
body: This video can not be played Major bridges in Ukraine have been the target of Russian strikes over the past four days, as Moscow ramps up attacks in Ukraine's capital city. The Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge, has been hit for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier this week. The latest attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a visit to Kyiv on Sunday. BBC Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson is near one of the bridges that was targeted and explains what we know so far. title: Family of teenager killed in crash to sue acquitted driver
description: Kyle Marshall and another teenager died when a car driven by Charles Gray span out of control in Stirling two years ago.
body: Kyle Marshall was one of two teenagers who died in the crash in March 2024 The family of a teenager killed in a car crash near Stirling two years ago are launching a civil case against the driver who was cleared of causing death by careless driving. Kyle Marshall, 19, and Jayden McConnell, 17, died when a car driven by Charles Gray spun out of control and into the path of a lorry on the A91 near Bannockburn Interchange in March 2024. Gray, who had passed his test a month earlier, was acquitted of causing the deaths of his two friends after a five-day trial at Stirling Sheriff Court last November. According to the Scottish Sun,, external the Marshall family are now suing Gray for a six-figure sum, alleging negligence. A spokesman for Digby Brown, the law firm representing the Marshall family, confirmed: "A civil action has now been raised in the Court of Session on behalf of the loved ones of Kyle to help them secure answers, support and recognition. "It would be inappropriate to comment further at this time however we will continue to support the Marshall family during this time." Teenage driver cleared of causing deaths of his best friends More stories from Tayside and Central The trial heard that Gray, who was 17 at the time of the crash, had lost control of the Vauxhall Corsa on a wet Sunday afternoon, on a stretch of road known as "greasy corner" because it had a reputation for becoming slippery. Soon after leaving a roundabout, the car spun onto the opposite side of the carriageway and was hit by a heavy tipper lorry coming in the other direction. Kyle Marshall and Jayden McConnell, in the rear of the vehicle, were killed while Gray's then girlfriend, Lauryn Moir, who was in the front passenger seat, survived without serious injury. Charles Gray said he had no memory of the crash or the moments leading up to it Gray himself was initially not breathing but an ambulance crew, who were passing the crash scene by chance, opened his airway, saving his life. He was very badly injured with a ruptured spleen, spine damage and a brain injury. Often choking back tears during his evidence, he said he could remember nothing of the crash itself and only learned what had happened to his friends when he woke up from an induced coma four weeks later. The trial heard that analysis of an insurance company "black box" showed that Gray had been a "perfect driver" in the weeks before the collision. The court was also told that police had not tested how slippery the road was or carried out a number of checks that might have established if there was a fault with the vehicle. title: Wales' Elfyn Evans wins his first World Rally Championship
description: Five-time runner-up Elfyn Evans is world champion for the first time after rival Oliver Solberg crashes in the final moments of Rally Italia Sardegna.
body: Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin won just two of 13 races in the 2026 WRC season Elfyn Evans became Britain's first world rally champion for 25 years after rival Oliver Solberg crashed in a highly dramatic finish to the season in Italy. Sweden's Solberg was on course to snatch the lead on the final stage of the last round of the World Rally Championship, and thereby deny Evans the title. But Solberg lost control of his car with less than 100 metres to go of the Rally Italia Sardegna, which meant the glory went to Welshman Evans, a five-time runner-up in the championship. "It hasn't sunk in," said a shocked Evans. "I was sure it was over. I feel for Oliver - he had an incredible weekend. I don't know what to say." The 37-year-old and co-driver Scott Martin had led for much of the 2026 season and took a 21-point advantage into the final round in Sardinia. But that gap had shrunk to a solitary point by the time the drivers lined up for the last of 17 stages, bringing back painful memories of previous narrow misses for Evans. Solberg, 25, needed only to beat his Toyota team-mate in the final stage to claim enough bonuses to be champion, but he crashed two corners from the finish. Evans becomes only the third British man to win the WRC title after Colin McRae in 1995 and Richard Burns in 2001. Relive dramatic final stage shootout for title as it happened The five titles that got away as Evans seeks WRC glory Solberg, whose father Petter won the WRC title in 2003, won the rally by almost a minute ahead of nine-time world champion Sebastien Ogier. He and English co-driver Elliott Edmondson were also on course to win the final stage and collect a maximum 35 points for the weekend to take the title by two points. However, his crash meant he finished five points behind Evans in the overall standings. A third Toyota driver, Sami Pajari, finished a further one point behind in third - having seen his own title challenge evaporate on the final weekend. An inconsolable Solberg remained in his car for some time at the end of the stage before being encouraged to take to the podium by Gazoo Racing team principal Jari-Matti Latvala and team-mate Ogier. "Two corners, two corners," said an emotional Solberg. "First congratulations to Elfyn, he has been very consistent all season. That I even had a shot after my rollercoaster of a season is incredible. "I tried everything. I knew I was pushing but didn't know if it was enough. I pushed even more and I couldn't save the car. I tried my very best." Evans, from Dolgellau in north Wales, had previously missed out on the title on the final day three times and in two of those seasons he had taken a lead into the concluding rally before losing out to Ogier in 2020 and 2025. "I don't really know what my reaction is. It's surreal with how it happened. It's a relief," he said. "It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done." For Toyota sporting director Kaj Lindstrom there were mixed feelings. "That was the hardest thing. The ending was quite something, I didn't expect it," said the Finn. "It was a good fight and we all saw that Oliver was all or nothing. It held all the way to the end. "Oliver still has time but Elfyn finally got his title so we're really happy for him." Jon Armstrong was competing in his first full season at the top level in the World Rally Championship The WRC season was reduced to 13 rounds when the Saudi Arabia event, originally planned for next month, was cancelled because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East. Rally Italia Sardegna marked the end of Jon Armstrong's rookie season at the top level of WRC, and he produced his best result when finishing seventh. "It's been good to have a clean weekend with a strong result," said the M-Sport Ford driver. "It's not been an easy year and this was a rally to show we can put it together. A big thanks to everyone who has been supporting us, it's been a great year and it's been a privilege to drive this car." Armstrong's team-mate and fellow Irishman Josh McErlean did not fare as well despite running as high as sixth on Saturday before retiring after a collision with a tree. He also had to stop twice on Sunday before finishing well off the pace but claimed ninth spot in the championship. 1. Oliver Solberg (Sweden), Toyota 3 hours 24 minutes 57.0 seconds 2. title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
description: Measures include extended opening hours, as well as an audio guide and additional seating for visitors.
body: The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding. The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage. A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted. Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event. Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption. One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing. The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time. From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition. The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition. Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed. The Bayeux Tapestry famously depicts the scene of King Harold II's death Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day. Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when further tickets go on sale in October and January. Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free. The exhibition opened on 10 September but has experienced a series of problems with queues and congestion, with some visitors spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry. Visitors were later stopped from taking photographs and a recorded message was introduced encouraging people to continue moving through the one-way exhibition. The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain. Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses. The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027. The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago. title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
description: Two residents in Mekelle tell the BBC pro-government forces have taken control of the city.
body: A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Sunday Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians. Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city. Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara. The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries. The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours. How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides. However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power. The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied. Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period. The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.
