title: Medieval leprosy hospital uncovered in Lincoln
description: Walls at the site have been unearthed as part of a three-day dig by Time Team experts.
body: Lincoln Funfair is now held on the South Common twice a year The walls of what is thought to be one of medieval England's earliest and largest leprosy hospitals have been uncovered in Lincoln by Time Team archaeologists. A three-day dig started on Friday on the South Common at the site of the Hospital of the Holy Innocents, which housed up to 20 people with leprosy around the late 11th to early 12th Centuries. Time Team's Prof Carenza Lewis said they had found traces of square features where it is thought people were housed, which "haven't been excavated before, anywhere". The dig marks the beginning of a three-year project backed by the National Lottery Heritage Fund. The remains of the building were found last year during a Local Landscapes and Hidden Histories project. More than 100 volunteers were involved in excavating test pits which uncovered what were thought to be the medieval boundary walls of the hospital. An ancient wall is visible for the first time in hundreds of years Time Team carried out a geophysical survey of the area, like an X-ray of the ground, and volunteers have dug a 30m-long (98ft) trench to join up the two test pits where traces of the walls were found. Lewis said a wall runs all the way down the trench and either side of it, according to the survey. Prof Carenza Lewis said the wall runs all the way down the trench "We know from historical documents that there were up to 20 lepers housed here, and we know that they had little sorts of curtilages… which implies they're separate little buildings, little houses with a little yard, perhaps," she explained. "What we've got all along this wall here are traces of little square features, about 5m (16ft) across, that are big enough to be a little building or a yard area, and we've got lots of them." City of Lincoln Council said it believed the hospital remained in use for about five centuries. The Hidden Histories Unearthed project, supported by £248,139 from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and led by Anglia Ruskin University, aims to uncover more about the people who lived and died at the hospital. "You'd need to have resources to get in here," Lewis said. "If you had enough money and could buy your way into a leper hospital, it's a bit like getting a place in a private care home or something like that." The council said local residents would have opportunities to get involved in further archaeological excavations and activities as the project continues. title: Currently
description: What if you could map the outcome of an election before a single vote was cast?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·04 Oct 2026,·28 mins Available for over a year What if you could map the outcome of an election before a single vote was cast? This is the story of the drawing - and redrawing - of electoral battle lines in an unprecedented gerrymandering war that some observers say is undermining democracy in the United States. BBC North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher explores how a once-a-decade act of political admin has turned into a rolling process of extreme political partisanship, as the Democrats and Republicans compete to redraw voting districts in their favour, trying to lock in guaranteed majorities, and upending electoral norms. Anthony looks at the roots of this political chess game, how it has escalated in the past year, and what it means for the future of democracy in the ‘land of the free’. Will the new maps actually secure a Republican victory in November - and how could endless redistricting shape elections in 2028, 2030, and beyond? Presenter: Anthony Zurcher Producer: Ellie House Editor: Richard Fenton-Smith Production Coordinator: Katie Morrison Sound mix: James Beard

title: Daughter of MP murdered five years ago tells BBC politicians still at risk
description: Katie Amess questions if anything has changed to protect politicians five years after her father's death.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Daughter of Sir David Amess says MPs are no safer today The daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians are still at risk and questioned if anything has changed five years after her father's death. Katie Amess told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg what happened to her father "wasn't an isolated incident, we are seeing increased threats towards members of parliament". Sir David was the Conservative MP for Southend West when he was stabbed multiple times while holding a constituency surgery in Leigh-on-Sea, Essex, in October 2021. The government commissioned a review into his death in August, to identify lessons to be learned and recommend steps to minimise the risk of future tragedies. Katie Amess, pictured earlier this year, has long campaigned for a public inquiry into her father's murder The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months. The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years since the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe in July this year, Sir David's murder in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox's murder in 2016. The five years since her father was killed have been "absolutely devastating and heartbreaking", his daughter told Kuenssberg, adding: "It's a very, very real situation that we're living with." She has previously called for a public inquiry into the safety of politicians so people can have "the full facts to hand, full openness, honesty, and transparency". The nearing anniversary of Sir David's murder comes after the man accused of murdering Widdecombe was also charged with preparing acts of terror, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. Amess, who knew Widdecombe as a family friend and called her Aunt Ann, said: "It's absolutely so tragic and heartbreaking that now she isn't here either." She added: "My dad was murdered five years ago so if so much has changed why are we still seeing other members of parliament or former members of parliament being targeted like this." Widdecombe was not a sitting member of parliament when she died, but was a member of the Conservative Party and the member for Maidstone and the Weald from 1987 to 2010. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019. Sir David Amess was stabbed to death at a constituency surgery on 15 October 2021 Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family. Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29. "I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this," she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it". Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be". "We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'." Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop." She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat. His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016. A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments. title: Housing or data centre? London's land-use dilemma
description: A data centre plan in Greenwich is the latest flashpoint in a debate about London's digital future.
body: A Charlton data centre proposal has become the latest flashpoint in the debate about technological infrastructure and housing A growing debate is playing out across London: As demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure grows, what should happen when data centres compete with housing and regeneration ambitions for the same land? In south-east London, a site designated for redevelopment at Charlton Riverside has become the latest flashpoint in the debate about London's digital future. The proposed 100,000 sq m (1 million sq ft) data development on industrial land at Charlton Riverside has been dubbed "concerning", with Greenwich Council opposing the idea before the centre's planning application has been submitted. Supporters say data centres are critical infrastructure that power technology many people rely on. But critics question whether they belong in areas earmarked for new homes and have raised concerns about their energy use, water consumption and environmental impacts. Data centres are not new. Telehouse's Tower Hamlets site was built in 1989 under different ownership. Managing director Mark Pestridge said demand was accelerating rapidly due to London's position as a global technology and finance hub. Mark Pestridge says data centre operators have not done a good job of educating people about how much electricity and water they use "If you think about everything you do on a daily basis, whether you want to look at your bank account online, you want to look at your medical records or book a GP appointment, or stream a video, that will all run through a place like this," he said. "I think London needs to be at the forefront of this moving forward, I think we have an exciting opportunity that we need to develop to make it quicker for us to stand up buildings like this. "There's a huge opportunity for London." And as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used, there is a rising demand for large-scale computing infrastructure. Data centre developers are particularly attracted to London because of the capital's dense concentration of businesses, financial services and internet connections. Operators often want facilities close to the customers using their services, such as the controversial data centre approved for Brick Lane in Tower Hamlets in July, which is intended to provide faster internet connections for financial traders in the nearby City of London. The Charlton data centre is proposed for Charlton's Stone Foundries and VIP trading estates and the CSB Logistics building In Charlton, Greenwich Council said the proposal for a data centre was at odds with its plans for the area. Tom Creswell, the council's cabinet member for planning and development, said they had plans to build about 8,000 homes, improve public transport, and create 1,000 new jobs in the Charlton Riverside area. "Our priorities as a council will always be focused on serving local people and bringing meaningful opportunities to the beautiful borough we call home," he said. At the moment the draft local plan is being formulated, external and so a particular use has not yet been specified for this land - only that it is for "mixed-use development comprising residential, commercial, and light industrial uses". The local plan that was adopted in 2014 and runs until 2028, external described Charlton Riverside as an "key regeneration area" and had potential to be developed into an "attractive and vibrant mixed use urban quarter". A spokesperson for the data centre project said regeneration in the area had seen "limited" progress and highlighted that data centres had been designated by government as Critical National Infrastructure. They said their proposal would both "help unlock the delivery of new homes" through road infrastructure and green spaces, and support the growth of the industrial economy in the capital. "Together, this would make nearby development more viable and transform a disorganised industrial estate into an area that is hospitable to both current and future residents," they said. The data centre project team says its site could help "unlock housing in the area" Data centres are regularly criticised for using a lot of electricity and water and lots of Charlton residents are opposed to the plans. One resident told Politics London: "From what I've heard, it's going to be very noisy with all of the generators, it's on 24 hours a day," while another said: "They use too much energy and where does the energy come from?" A woman said she would rather see homes built on the site. "There's nowhere for people to live. A lot of places are overcrowded as it is. People have been waiting. I think we've got enough technology going around, I really don't think we need any more." Charlton Gateway has said its proposals were not for AI and its data centres would use a closed loop water cooling system, its generators were for backup use only and would be tested intermittently, rather than round the clock. One Greenwich resident said she would prefer to see housing on the site A spokesperson for the government said claims that British data centres were "draining the country's water" were false. "In England, they account for just 0.2% of non-household water usage, and many newer data centres use advanced cooling systems that require very little fresh water," they said. "This does not mean a blank cheque for Big Tech. Developers must use water responsibly, and new developments must be considered through the planning system." Telehouse's data centre uses noise dampening equipment, Pestridge says Pestridge said Telehouse's data centre had a closed water system and the yearly water usage from the nation's data centres was "less than the water lost to leakage in a single day". title: Purchase of field aims to expand 'green lung'
description: It is hoped the prospective sale provides a haven for wildlife in an urban area.
body: The purchase of fields in St Clements aims to provide space for wildlife in the urban environment Conservationists have said they are planning to buy a field to extend a "green lung" in one of Jersey's most built-up parishes. The National Trust for Jersey said it had secured the rights to acquire the land near Maupertuis Farm in St Clement and hoped to complete the purchase shortly. A green lung is an area of fields, parkland or vegetation within an otherwise urban area, providing space for wildlife and helping to reduce pollution. The trust previously raised £50,000 in 37 days to buy a nearby field on Samares Lane in 2021. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey The trust said the latest acquisition would help preserve the agricultural heritage of Maupertuis Farm and the surrounding area. Chief executive Alan Le Maistre said green spaces were becoming "ever more precious" and protecting them was particularly important in densely developed parts of the island. "It is a privilege to have the opportunity to extend this green lung for both the wildlife and people of the area," he said. The National Trust for Jersey, which celebrated its 90th anniversary in August, manages about 1,800 vergées of land across the island. It invited people who want to support the latest acquisition to contact the charity directly. Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
description: Polls suggest the election will be a closely run contest between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing rival.
body: The two candidates leading in the polls are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro Brazilians have begun voting in a general election in which the two front-runners for the presidency bear very familiar names. The incumbent, veteran left-wing leader Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva, will be challenged by 11 candidates, the most prominent of whom is right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro. In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father Jair, but the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election. Here's what you need to know. At the launch of his campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro screened a video in which an AI-generated image of his father endorsed his candidacy Jair Bolsonaro, the right-wing former army captain who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2023, will not be running for president in this election. Not only is the 71-year-old barred from standing for office, he is also serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Due to recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has had restrictions imposed on him prohibiting him from posting on social media or making public statements. Despite these restrictions, his shadow - and sometimes his moving and talking image - looms large over this election. At the event where Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his presidential campaign, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsed his son's candidacy. When pressed by the Supreme Court about the deepfake, Jair Bolsonaro's lawyers may have denied he had given his permission for its use, but there is nevertheless little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has the backing of his father. While there are 12 candidates running for the presidency, there are only two who have reached double figures in the opinion polls, and they are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro. BBC Brasil's poll tracker shows them both hovering around the 40% mark, with Lula slightly ahead of Bolsonaro. The other 11 candidates are polling at 4% or less. If none of the candidates gains 50% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off election on 25 October. The opinion polls suggest a run-off is highly likely - but with a relatively high number of voters still undecided just days before the election, an outright win cannot be entirely ruled out. BBC Brasil's poll aggregator suggests that at the end of September, 9% of voters were either still undecided, or planning to spoil their ballot, cast a blank ballot or not go to the polls at all. Brazilians who are 16 years of age or older are entitled to vote and it is compulsory for those aged between 18 and 70 who are literate, with a fine imposed on those who do not cast a ballot. Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this election and, with polls typically surveying just thousands of people, the end result can differ considerably from the indications given by surveys. In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Lula stressed his country's sovereignty Lula, the 80-year-old candidate for the left-wing Workers' Party, has been president three times already. He served two consecutive terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - and was widely praised for lifting millions out of poverty during this time with the help of a cash-transfer programme called Bolsa Família. The former metalworker left office with record approval ratings of over 80%, but his party was later rocked by huge corruption scandals. Lula himself spent more than 18 months in prison between 2018 and 2019 after being convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he has always denied. Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points. When he started his third term in office, he vowed it would be his last, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 later this month. There is no doubt he remains a towering figure in the left. But while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions. His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism. Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy. His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working. During Lula's latest term in office, relations with his US counterpart Donald Trump have been rocky. Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard". In another thinly veiled reference to both his rival Flávio Bolsonaro and those in the Trump administration who would like to see the right-wing candidate win, the Brazilian leader has also warned that he would not tolerate "foreign and local enemies of democracy" interfering with the polls. Flávio Bolsonaro has been courting his father's supporters Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is Jair Bolsonaro's eldest son and has been serving as a senator since 2019. title: Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes
description: Thousands of people joined the queue in the hope of securing tickets to Worthy Farm.
body: Glastonbury Festival returns to Worthy Farm in June, following a fallow year Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in 42 minutes, organisers have said. Thousands of people joined the online queue at 09:00 BST in the hope of securing tickets to the festival at Worthy Farm in Somerset, which returns from 23 to 27 June after a fallow year. Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from the last event in 2025. Headliners have yet to be announced but organiser Emily Eavis previously said the team was "very excited" and things were "coming together really well". Glastonbury posted on Instagram shortly after 09:40 to announce that tickets had sold out, and notified those who were in the queue. "Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply," the post said. "There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in Spring 2027." People in the online queue for Glastonbury tickets received a notification when they were sold out The first round of tickets, which were for coach packages, went up for sale on Thursday and sold out in less than half an hour. Despite the increase in cost, Zoe Scott, who has been to the festival twice, said "the price is totally worth it". "You're getting to see thousands of acts, there's over 100 stages," she said. "It's such a vibe at Glastonbury- everyone's so happy and free-spirited. You're just on a constant high from friends, music and the sun is usually shining". A couple who first met at Glastonbury will also be heading to Worthy Farm next year to celebrate their 20th wedding anniversary. Nick and Helen Nugget from Amersham met through mutual friends at the festival in 2007 and will be returning next year with the same group. Nick told BBC Your Voice that they were "absolutely delighted" to be going back. The couple last went to the festival in 2011- although they were successful in securing tickets in 2019, they were unable to attend due to the adoption of their daughter. Nick and Helen Nugget met at a "very muddy" Glastonbury back in 2007 Among those who were not successful were Mat Chapman and his daughter Amy. Mat told the BBC that he used to watch the festival on TV with Amy when she was little, promising to take her when she was five years old as "she always wanted to have her own flag that you could see on the telly". Mat had hoped that after 20 years of trying, he would be able to beat the queue this year, on Amy's 26th birthday. Unfortunately he only ever moved from "two bar hell to three bar purgatory". "There's always next year. We'll fly the flag there one day." Tickets cost more than £400 for the first time This year's Glastonbury tickets have breached the £400 mark for the first time. Tickets have increased over the years, from £185 in 2010 to £408 for the upcoming 2027 line-up. Most price rises have come since the pandemic, with tickets climbing from £318 in 2019 to a peak of £408 in 2027. But unlike recent years, much of the 2010s saw relatively steady price hikes. Any tickets from today's sale that are not paid for in full by the early April 2027 deadline will be put back into an official resale pool, festival organisers said. The exact date for this is yet to be announced, but in previous years it has been in late April. Follow BBC Somerset on Facebook, external and X, external. title: Sinn Féin will co-operate with PSNI over Drumcree protest, says McDonald
description: Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road since last Sunday as the fallout over the proposed Portadown District Orange Lodge march continues.
body: Mary Lou McDonald spoke at the protest on the Garvaghy Road on Saturday Sinn Féin will co-operate with the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) over any potential investigation into the protest on the Garvaghy Road, the party president has said. Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road since Sunday 27 September as the fallout over the proposed Portadown District Orange Lodge march continues, and rallies on both sides of the dispute were held on Saturday. Mary Lou McDonald has said that "there's no question with us co-operating with any process that will unfold". McDonald and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill are among those who have attended the protest, which police have described as unnotified and "therefore illegal". The Portadown District has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement on Thursday. The PSNI said that anyone "found to have broken the law will face criminal justice consequences". However, speaking on the BBC's Sunday Politics programme, McDonald said: "There are moments in politically life where you have to take a stand, and this is one of those moments." When asked about the legality of the protest she said: "Others will determine whether or not that is in fact the case." The Parades Commission's decided that the parade - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - could go ahead on Sunday 27 September with restrictions. A fresh legal bid by the residents to prevent the march was due to be heard on Friday - but has now been postponed until Monday. Crowds gathered at the Garvaghy Road to support local residents on Saturday The actions of McDonald, O'Neill and others have received condemnation including from members of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP). In a post on social media, deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said the "behaviour of Michelle O'Neill and her party has been disgraceful" and a "complete abdication of leadership". McDonald said that this "comes down to right and wrong", and that as people who care passionately about the future, her and O'Neill know that for "that to happen we have to stand four square with the community of the Garvaghy Road". She said there was a "broad crowd politically and otherwise" at the rally on Saturday, adding that it was "resolute but good humoured with a real eye for the future". "I cannot fathom anybody suggesting that 28 years on when progress has been made in such significant ways, not least in Portadown and in the wider Garvaghy community, why it is that anybody would seek to reopen that wound." Meanwhile, in response to DUP leader Gavin Robinson's comments that Sinn Féin is attempting to goad unionists into collapsing Stormont, McDonald said it is "anything but", adding that it is about the ability of communities to live work, and build futures together. DUP MP Carla Lockhart speaking at a rally in support of the Orange Order on Saturday Speaking to BBC News NI at Drumcree on Saturday, DUP MP Carla Lockhart said there could be "repercussions for a very long time if mob rule wins over the rule of law". "No, we need the police service to step up and do their job. I do think if the real residents step forward we can and should discuss further options and resolutions, because we do want to see this resolved," Lockhart said. McDonald said that "the real voices of the Garvaghy Road" have called for support and people to come stand for them and "my god have they had a response, not just in Ireland but right across the world". McDonald said her party has pressed Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant and Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin. She said that "we have found ourselves landed in this situation by an utterly reckless determination by the Parades Commission". McDonald added that Martin and her both agree that the Parade's Commission determination as "incomprehensible and wrong". Speaking at a Fianna Fáil dinner on Saturday, Martin said that "absolutely nobody benefits from the reopening of the dispute over the parade on the Garvaghy Road". Sir Chris said he was "concerned at the prolonged standoff" which he said was "ultimately in nobody's interests". "I have been working with all those involved to find a mutually acceptable solution," he said in a social media post, on Saturday. McDonald said the resolution is that Sir Chris needs to "call this, make it clear that he puts a stop to this march and thereby creates the space for a mediation". Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years. The row re-emerged last month after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission was overturned, and a fresh application to parade was lodged. Last Friday, the commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place. However, that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go-ahead just hours before it was due to take place. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? title: Modric 'ashamed' of Croatia's 'catastrophic night'
description: Croatia captain Luka Modric says he was "ashamed" of his side's performance on a "catastrophic night" against England.
body: Luka Modric won the Golden Ball at the 2018 World Cup in Russia after helping Croatia finish as runners-up Croatia captain Luka Modric said he felt "ashamed" of his side's performance in Saturday's 7-0 defeat at home to England in the Nations League. It was the first time in 20 years as an international that the AC Milan midfielder said he had felt such emotion, describing it as a "catastrophic night". Modric, 41, was making his 205th appearance for his country after recently agreeing to extend his international career under returning manager Slaven Bilic. "You can't play football like that... we looked like we had four or five players less," said the former Real Madrid player, who helped Croatia to second-place and third-place finishes at the 2018 and 2022 World Cups during a storied career. "It is difficult to find an explanation for such a performance without duels, fouls, aggressiveness, togetherness. "I've been here for 20 years, but for the first time I feel ashamed after a game." Croatia kicked off Bilic's second spell in charge with a 2-1 Nations League win away to the Czech Republic that put them above England in Group A3. They followed that up with a chastening 4-1 defeat away to world champions Spain but were still level on points with Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions before Saturday's humiliating loss in Rijeka. With the top two qualifying for the latter stages, Croatia had the chance to put themselves in pole position to beat England to a place in the quarter-finals. Yet by the time Modric was substituted in the 57th minute, the home side were already 5-0 down after conceding two goals from Harry Kane and one apiece from Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka. Modric was forced to watch from the sidelines as further goals from Saka and Morgan Rogers extended England's advantage before the final whistle. Luka Modric watches on as Jude Bellingham congratulates Bukayo Saka for scoring England's fourth goal in a 7-0 win over Croatia "You can lose, or play against an opponent who is better - and they are right now," added the former Spurs favourite, who helped Croatia knock England out in the qualifying stages for the 2008 Euros where they reached the quarter-finals in Bilic's first spell as manager. "But in any case, losing like this and squandering the reputation we've built over the years is unacceptable... [it was a] catastrophic night [for Croatia]." It does not get any easier for Croatia, who next host Spain in Split on Tuesday, and will finish their Nations League campaign with games away to England (12 November) and at home to the Czech Republic (15 November). "We need to pull ourselves together, stay together because a new difficult game awaits us," said Modric, with Croatia third in the table, facing a battle to retain their status in the top tier of the Nations League. "We have to show our true colours, that there is defiance and pride in us, desire, willingness, togetherness, these things cannot be lost overnight." title: Verstappen wins in Malaysia after long delays as Russell retires
description: Max Verstappen takes his and Red Bull's first win of the year with a dominant drive in a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that started amid chaotic and unprecedented scenes.
body: This video can not be played Mercedes better 'watch out - Verstappen 'imperious' in Bahrain GP win Max Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first win of the year with a dominant drive in a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that started amid chaotic and unprecedented scenes. Verstappen led home the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli, who took a giant leap towards his first world title when team-mate George Russell retired from third place with a power unit failure with five laps to go. Antonelli now leads Russell by 84 points with either six or seven races remaining. Lewis Hamilton drove an extraordinary race after dropping towards the back with an incorrect tyre choice for a wet start to fight back to pass Red Bull's Isack Hadjar for third place with three laps to go. All that came after a delay of an hour and a half caused initially by heavy rain and then by a series of bizarre technical problems that left several cars crawling as they completed formation laps on the wet track behind the safety car. After that problem, it took some time for governing body the FIA to decide the order in which the cars should take the start. This video can not be played A lot of people didn't believe in 'another win including myself' The key stories of a madcap afternoon were: Verstappen's dominant win in a revived Red Bull The effective death knell for Russell's already faint title hopes A stunning recovery by Hamilton A series of questions over race organisation, particularly over the start Race day started well enough, with Malaysians treated to their first race since 2017 thanks to Bahrain paying to hold it at Sepang following unrest in the Middle East Then the heavens opened causing a long delay... A delay which was made more problematic when cars started failing on the formation lap, leaving organisers with a headache deciding how to form the grid Verstappen eventually controlled things and took a first win for the team with their 'homemade' power train But not before a devastated Russell retired with his own power unit problem, which almost certainly has ended his fight for a title many expected him to win in 2026 Once the race got under way, with the cars in their original order, Verstappen and Hamilton on the front row immediately lost ground and the Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell swept past them into first and second places. Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers took the start on intermediate tyres on the still-wet track after a torrential tropical downpour had delayed the start. Hamilton chose soft-compound slicks and immediately regretted the decision as it became apparent that the track was still far too wet for that option. He and others who chose slicks soon dropped to the back of the field, and lost nearly a minute to the leaders in the early laps. Meanwhile, Verstappen repassed Russell for second place on lap six, and was on Antonelli's tail when a safety car was deployed to allow marshals to recover the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas, who had spun off at Turn 13 on lap nine. The leaders took the opportunity of the safety car to pit for slick tyres, and when the race resumed four laps later, Verstappen immediately passed Antonelli at Turn Four, the Italian also losing out to Russell on the exit of the corner. From that moment on, Verstappen was in total control and he edged away into a race of his own. Behind him, Antonelli had pace on Russell and passed him on lap 21 at Turn Four, the move seemingly settling the top three positions. A late safety car caused by Alex Albon's stricken Williams led to everyone switching to fresh tyres for a four-lap dash to the flag, but again Verstappen was supreme and remained unchallenged. Even then, there was drama, as Russell pulled off just before Turn One with five laps to go before the safety car had even ended. In the immediate aftermath, Lando Norris was apparently distracted by Russell's car and had to take to the gravel at Turn One to avoid running into the back of team-mate Oscar Piastri, dropping from eighth to 11th. He recovered to ninth by the end, immediately behind Fernando Alonso, who scored points for Aston Martin for only the third time this year after their strongest performance of the year. This video can not be played 'I didn't think I'd get back to third place' Hamilton and the others who chose to use dry tyres at the start immediately lived to regret their decision, as they were passed by all the cars on intermediates. Within a few laps, Hamilton was nearly a minute behind the leaders and down in 17th place, his race apparently over. But he stayed out during the safety car, sticking with the soft tyres he had chosen for the start, and when the race restarted he began to pick off the cars in front of him, driving an excellent race to get back into contention for serious points. Hamilton passed car after car until by lap 24 he was on the tail of Isack Hadjar's fourth-placed Red Bull. They pitted together on lap 31, Hadjar sticking to soft tyres, and Hamilton having no choice but to move to mediums. Hamilton trailed the Frenchman for lap after lap, right on his tail, but was never quite able to get close enough to pass, despite a number of attempts, before the late safety car. That gave Hamilton the chance to switch to the preferred soft tyres, and a lap after the restart he passed Hadjar into Turn One to take the final podium position. Ferrari's Charles Leclerc also passed Hadjar in the closing laps, with Oscar Piastri taking sixth after a dispiriting weekend for McLaren, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alonso. Norris and the second Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10. After the tropical downpour, the race was initially started with formation laps behind the safety car. title: Porridge makers from opposite sides of globe triumph in world championship
description: Dutch champion Gina Saarberg took the coveted Golden Spurtle, while Australian champion maestro Rob Reid won the Speciality Porridge category at the finals in the Scottish Highlands.
body: Dutch champion Gina Saarberg took the coveted Golden Spurtle, while and Australian porridge maestro Rob Reid triumphed in Speciality Porridge category Two national porridge-making champions from almost opposite sides of the planet have triumphed in the annual world championships held in the Scottish Highlands. Gina Saarberg, 28, took the coveted Golden Spurtle using the same recipe that saw her crowned Dutch champion in July, using organic pinhead oats, salt and water that she brought with her from the Netherlands. Australian champion Rob Reid took the speciality award - where competitors can combine oatmeal with any ingredients - with his porridge cannoli, an oaty spin on a tube-shaped dessert that originated in Sicily. Thirty competitors from 14 countries took part in the contest, held each year at Carrbridge, just north of Aviemore. What's a golden spurtle and why do so many people want one? Norwegian oats win world porridge championship Gina, from Zuthphen, started eating a kind of porridge using rolled oats in her student days because it was a cheap meal. But she had never tasted the traditional variety until she learned about the Dutch porridge-making contest and decided to enter as a "bit of a joke". "When I first tasted it, it was a world of difference - I've been missing out all these years," she told BBC Scotland News. Gina brought her own water to the contest and thinks it may have given her the edge over other contenders The contest rules only allow three ingredients - oats, water and salt. She only started adding salt to her porridge ahead of the competition, but quickly realised it "really brings out the nuances and different aromas". She believes her secret weapon may have been the water which she brought with her from her home city. "It's very soft, and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it. I'm not sure - but it worked last time and this time as well, so maybe it's the water". In the Speciality Porridge category, Rob, from Sydney, came up with his recipe just a few weeks before competing in the Australian national porridge championships - the Pearly Spurtle - after realising how seriously everyone was taking it. Tapping into his family heritage - his father is Scottish and his mother is Sicilian - he decided to make a porridge cannoli. "I then had to engineer it," the 36-year-old told BBC Scotland News. The cream uses the traditional mix of ricotta, mascarpone and sugar but he blended in porridge, sieved it and added some ground toasted oats. It provides the filling for shells, made like brandy snaps but using Sicilian Marsala wine instead. Australian Rob gave a Scottish twist to a traditional Sicilian pastry recipe "After I came up with the idea, I spent a whole day in the kitchen with one of my daughters at home making multiple different types of shells and different creams, trying to work out how to put the porridge in the cream," he said. Having won the Pearly Spurtle, he then spent the next six weeks improving the recipe in preparation for the ultimate challenge in Scotland. Rob used to own a café, but he now installs blinds and curtains for a living and uses his free time to channel his culinary creativity. "Not working in a kitchen for something like this meant I was able to be really creative with it because it wasn't my job and I was able to play with it a bit more," he said. Porridge makers from 14 countries descended on Carrbridge for the contest The annual contest was started in 1994 in Carrbridge by a local hotel owner as a way of promoting the health benefits of porridge as well raising the profile of the area. Porridge Chieftain Alan Rankin said: "The World Porridge Making Championship is a wonderfully quirky tradition that thrives on good humour and friendly competition, offering a wonderful escape from the daily grind. "Each year, our local community opens its doors and we hope everyone who joined us leaves with fond memories of their visit." title: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
description: Unverified video shows a drone hitting the Northern Bridge as vehicles move across it, creating a large fireball.
body: The Pivnichnyi Bridge (pictured on Saturday) has been hit for a second day in a row Major bridges in Kyiv have been targeted by Russian strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the capital. The Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was hit on Sunday morning for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit in multiple attacks earlier in the week. The latest bridge attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to the capital on Sunday. Meanwhile, Russia's defence ministry said it would be intensifying strikes on Kyiv and other regions of the country. Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge. No casualties have been reported. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote about the strike on Telegram, saying: "Hitting the roadway on the Pivnichnyi Bridge. Emergency services are on their way to the scene." He said the strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result. President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones also attacked a warehouse in Sumy, killing one person. Meanwhile, in Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said. As emergency services responded to the incidents, Germany's Merz met Zelenksy in Kyiv. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war. Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us. "Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well." Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine. He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us." Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany. The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered, Russian drones. Merz arrived in Kyiv by train He joined Zelensky at a memorial to fallen Ukrainian soldiers The attacks on Kyiv's major bridges appear to be a new strategy from Moscow. The first Russian strike on the Pivnichnyi Bridge took place on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires, Klitschko said. Just days before, the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones. The Pivdennyi and Pivnichnyi bridges, which cross the Dnipro River, link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday. Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges, which it said were used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. It also repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv. Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!" German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying". In Friday's attack, a Russian drone hit cables of Kyiv's Pivdennyi bridge Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday. Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities. Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable. Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. title: Scottish Tory leader Findlay says SNP's indy 'obsession' is dangerously irresponsible
description: Russell Findlay says breaking up the United Kingdom would be "a gift to our enemies".
body: Russell Findlay said breaking up the UK would be "a gift to our enemies" Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay has described the SNP's "obsession" with independence as "dangerously irresponsible". First Minister John Swinney has said he wants to hold a second Scottish independence referendum by 2031, despite successive prime ministers refusing to countenance another poll. Findlay said that while the United Kingdom continues to face "grave threats" from China, Russia and Iran, a divided UK would be "a gift to our enemies". And he called on Swinney to respect the result of the 2014 referendum where a majority of Scots voted no to independence. Badenoch unveils plan to end £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge' ahead of Tory conference Swinney aiming for independence referendum by 2031 PM says second Scottish independence referendum remains 'off limits' Findlay told BBC Scotland's The Sunday Show: "Today's world is more dangerous than it has been for many, many years. "Right now, it's no longer just dangerously divisive of the SNP to continue agitating to break up the United Kingdom, it is actually dangerously irresponsible." Findlay defended the Scottish Tories' decision not to back a vote in the Scottish Parliament which states that the people of Scotland have the right to determine their own future. "We had a vote. In 2014, the people of Scotland - more than two million of them - politely, firmly an respectfully said no to separation," he said. "From day one, John Swinney and the SNP haven't respected the outcome of that vote and they've agitated ever since. "It's been a complete distraction and all the while they've run Scotland's public services into the ground and taxed people to the hilt. "Just look at the real problems that John Swinney could be focused on - the NHS and their waiting lists, or the state of Scotland's schools." The Scottish Tory leader will deliver a speech at the Conservative Party's UK conference in Birmingham later, when he is expected to criticise Swinney for "cosying up to Sinn Fein" at a recent summit in Cardiff. Findlay is expected to say: "Since Mr Swinney was a teenager, all he's cared about is breaking up the United Kingdom. "Sorry Mr Swinney, and your new friends in Sinn Fein, but we won't let that happen. "Let's not forget that Sinn Fein has never denounced the IRA slaughter of innocent men, women and children. "Yet Mr Swinney works with them to destroy the United Kingdom. A disgrace." title: 'Get on with the day job' - Welsh Tory leader attacks first minister's independence push
description: Darren Millar says Rhun ap Iorwerth has failed to improve public services or help Welsh businesses.
body: Darren Millar - seen here addressing last year's Conservative Party conference - will focus this year's speech on preserving the UK The Welsh Conservative leader Darren Millar will tell the first minister to "get on with the day job" instead of focusing on the prospect of independence at a speech on Sunday. Darren Millar is expected to tell the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham that "Britain needs Badenoch" and reaffirm his party's support for the UK. It comes after First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth called for a "new deal" for Wales from the UK government at a Plaid Cymru conference, and said at a rally there was "no turning back" on the independence journey. Millar will say in his speech that his party is committed to keeping the UK together and that Britain's legacy should be used to inspire future generations. Millar returned to the expanded 96-member Welsh Parliament after May's Senedd election with a group of seven members - down nine on the previous parliament. Polls at various points during the election campaign had suggested the party could face a wipe-out, in part because of the rise in popularity of Reform in Wales. Darren Millar has backed his party leader Kemi Badenoch to be the next prime minister In a copy of Millar's speech seen by BBC Wales, he says the Welsh government must focus on fixing public services and defend the relationship between the four countries of the UK - saying his party "will never allow" the break up of the union. "A plan to draw a slate curtain between Wales and the rest of the UK will cause more harm than good for our children and future generations," he says. He points to rising NHS waiting lists, claims Welsh businesses have "continued to struggle" since Plaid came to power, and that ap Iorwerth had instead decided to "cosy up to the SNP and Sinn Fein" referencing the recent meeting in Cardiff between the three countries leaders. "He then signed a pact to promote the break-up of our United Kingdom," he says. "The whole jamboree was seized upon by Vladimir Putin's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, who gleefully spoke up on Russian TV about the prospect of independence referendums across the UK. "So my message to Rhun ap Iorweth today is this - get on with the day job." Referencing ap Iorwerth, Millar says: "He told voters in May that the Senedd election was not about independence. "Well, either he didn't get his own memo or he deliberately chose to deceive people. "Because just like the Pied Piper of Hamelin, the Plaid Piper of Anglesey has tried to hoodwink people." Miller describes the UK as "more than a political arrangement", saying each helped to develop industries, abolish the slave trade, liberate Europe, and shape the modern world. "We are a shared family of nations. For centuries, the people of Wales, England, Scotland and Northern Ireland have lived together, worked together, and traded together. "Of course, there are those on the left who say we should apologise or be embarrassed about our history. "But I say that it is a legacy and a heritage that we should be proud of and use to inspire the next generation." title: The hidden daytime dance revolution - and the man who captured it on camera
description: Tim Smith's shots of the early 'daytimers' bhangra scene in Bradford feature in a Tate exhibition.
body: Rani Kaur, known as DJ Radical Sister, was one of the female pioneers of the daytimers scene For decades, photographer Tim Smith's images of Bradford's British Asian "daytimers" dance scene remained largely unseen. Now, some of those shots are taking their place in a major Tate exhibition examining the creativity and rebellion that transformed 1990s Britain. On a bright afternoon in Bradford, shoppers moved through the city centre carrying bags, going about their day. Behind a nearby doorway, another side of Bradford was pulsing to a very different rhythm. Tim Smith remembers stepping out of a small nightclub beneath the Alhambra theatre after spending hours photographing a "daytimers" disco. "I walked out into this bright sunshine and there's all these people walking about with their shopping bags, completely oblivious to what was going on just the other side of this somewhat anonymous-looking doorway," he recalls. More than three decades later, images Smith took inside that hidden world are making another unlikely journey, from Bradford's underground daytimers scene to the Tate Britain art gallery. His photographs feature in new showcase The 90s: Art and Fashion, which opens on Thursday. Curated by former Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful, it brings together more than 100 works by nearly 70 artists, photographers and designers to examine a decade of creativity and rebellion. For Smith, who lived in Bradford for more than 40 years, the inclusion of his photos is also recognition that some of the cultural shifts reshaping 1990s Britain were happening far beyond London. "I'm pleased because I think there's a big shout-out for Bradford," he says. "These culturally significant moments of that time weren't just happening in London and Manchester, like many media people like to think they were." Smith arrived in Bradford in the mid-1980s after studying photography in Newport. A nomadic childhood and life among migrant communities in Newport's Docklands had drawn him towards documenting lives beyond the mainstream. Through the then-recently established Bradford Heritage Recording Unit, he began photographing the city's South Asian communities at work, at religious gatherings, at weddings and in their social lives. "I was quite appalled at the lack of any kind of documentation of Bradford's Asian communities beyond the stuff that you'd see in the local papers," he says. The daytimers bhangra gigs came later, after a friend told him about afternoon club events for young British Asians. Smith's first response was simple: "What's a daytimer?" Cheap to hire while nightclubs stood empty during the day, the venues became spaces where a generation could gather and celebrate, but also shape a unique new subculture: dancing to music drawing on Punjabi and South Asian traditions but fused with contemporary British sounds. What Smith saw was not simply young people celebrating being Asian, but proudly "being British Asian". Tim Smith says there was a lot of luck in some of the shots he was able to get, but the thing they all had in common was joy Among those he photographed was Rani Kaur, known as DJ Radical Sister, one of the pioneering women of the scene. In one of Smith's best-known images, which will feature in the Tate Britain exhibition, she stands at the DJ decks, surrounded by young clubbers. Another frame, shot from above in the darkness with flash, caught a room full of faces in a moment Smith could not inspect until the film was developed. "Part of it's luck, but you earn your luck," he says. "Every single face that you can see in it… just looks like he's having the best time of his life." To Smith, the expressions seem to say: "We're here, this is us, we're having a wonderful time." Yet he appreciates there is another side to the photographs, and to the rebellion they record. Many of the young people attending daytimers gigs were moving between the expectations of family and community and the desires of a younger generation testing out music, fashion, friendship and independence on its own terms. Smith understood that publishing a photograph could expose somebody who had never intended their presence at a club to become public. "I didn't know everybody in the picture," he says. "I thought, 'I don't want to get them into trouble.'" So, apart from images of people he knew were comfortable being identified, much of the work stayed largely out of public view. Only decades later did those photographs acquire another life. When some were exhibited at Bradford's National Science and Media Museum, there were, Smith recalls, "one or two grumblings". But among those who had lived through the scene there was also a growing sense that this was their history to claim. "Come on, it was our moment," was the response relayed back to him. "This is where who we are now began." Tim Smith was a press photographer for many years, but says he was always drawn to documenting lives and communities outside the mainstream Time has now transformed the pictures from informal snapshots of an underground scene into historical documents. And Smith believes the daytimers helped lay the foundations for the vibrant British Asian culture scene that followed. He was, by his own admission, entering worlds that were not his, a young white photographer trusted with access to communities and spaces whose stories were rarely documented. "I felt quite privileged being a photographer generally because it gives you access to worlds that aren't necessarily part of your world," he says. "I loved being let in." Now those darkened daytime Bradford rooms will take their place alongside other defining names and moments in cultural history inside Tate Britain, home to the biggest collection of British art in the world. title: Bowie seizing Scotland shot after World Cup disappointment
description: BBC Scotland speaks to Kieron Bowie after he scores his first goal for his country against North Macedonia.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: North Macedonia 0-2 Scotland Sometimes, the solution to a problem can be hiding in plain sight. On 19 May, Steve Clarke assembled his collection of players to embark on a World Cup journey. Despite featuring and scoring for a Hellas Verona side heading for relegation from Serie A, and with a perennial problem of strikers not firing regularly for Scotland, Kieron Bowie was overlooked. Given the loyalty Clarke showed to those who had served him so well, it was not a huge surprise. Neither was the impotence of the national team in the USA as they conjured up just one John McGinn goal. "I received a message from him saying that I'm not in the squad but these things happen and it's just about how you bounce back from it to be honest," said Bowie. "I scored goals in a struggling Verona team and that was as much as I could do. I was happy with where I was at and I was happy with how I'd played. "I just spent a lot of time at home with my family and then a little golf holiday to Portugal for a week and that was all I did." Two going on four, five or six on good night for new Scotland era Scotland beat North Macedonia in Nations League for Pocognoli's first win Bowie scored his first Scotland goal early in the win over North Macedonia Bowie may have been cursing his luck again on Tuesday when his first international start was reduced to a mere 13 minutes following Jack Hendry's red card in the Hampden loss to Switzerland. The landscape now looks very different. The former Raith Rovers and Hibernian forward was one of the main Scotland heroes in Skopje after sending a deliciously whipped finish into the net in the 2-0 win over North Macedonia. Playing in a new 3-4-1-2, Bowie started the game up top with Oli McBurnie in an ultra-attacking line up set out by Sebastien Pocognoli. Throughout the game, his stats stacked up. The most shots with seven, the most on target with four, most shots in the box with five and the most touches in the opposition box with 11. "You play all your life to represent a country and to score a goal is just an unbelievable feeling," said the 24-year-old Fifer. "This manager's come in and he's put a lot of trust in me. "I think the style that he wants to play definitely plays into my strengths. I think you've seen today a lot of times running them in behind and just showing strength against occupying defenders is one of the main things. "It's a process but I think everyone's enjoying that process and it's a bit of a change." This video can not be played Bowie smashes in first Scotland goal The word "process" has been used so many times by the Scotland head coach and his players in recent days it's probably the new team motto. But there is truth in it. Pocognoli is trying to implement a radically different system to his predecessor. Not only that, it's a different mindset. All while trying to embed a clutch of new players. It's early days for the Belgian, his group, and, of course, Bowie. But the man on loan at Sassuolo believes things are clicking, and it's an opportunity for him to make his mark. "It's a lot longer international break," he explained. "We spend a lot more time together so it's good for him to get his message across and his ideas. Also, we play more games so we have to train a little bit less of course. "I think for me it's a fresh start with a new coach and different ideas. "He said to me 'you don't need to prove yourself, just go and do what I know you can do' and I feel like I'm just doing that." Bowie, who made his Rovers debut at 16, added: "I think people, obviously Scottish fans, have the same idea of how I was when I was at Hibs and that's all they can remember. "But I feel like since I moved to Serie A, it's a different challenge against more experienced players and at a higher level. "So, yeah, I feel like I've definitely kicked into another gear and I feel like I'm showing that." title: Debris in engine very likely caused Spitfire crash
description: Sqn Ldr Mark Long was killed when the plane he was flying crashed in a field in May 2024.
body: Sqn Ldr Mark Long was killed when the Spitfire he was flying crashed in May 2024 Debris which had been present in the carburettor of a Spitfire for decades was "very likely" the cause of a crash in which a pilot died, according to a report. Sqn Ldr Mark Long was killed when the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight (BBMF) plane he was flying crashed in a field in Lincolnshire on 25 May 2024. A report published by the Ministry of Defence says the debris was responsible for causing fuel starvation, "leading to a loss of thrust required to maintain powered flight". Just 56 seconds after taking off from RAF Coningsby, witnesses saw the plane turn and plunge to the ground. Long was flying a Spitfire Mk IX, built in 1944, operated by the RAF's BBMF for commemorative flypasts and displays. The opening of an inquest heard the provisional cause of his death was head and neck injuries. The Service Inquiry report, external said chemical analysis revealed evidence that indicated the debris in the carburettor "had been present for decades". It said: "The presence of multiple, contradictory publications created ambiguity over the correct procedures for carburettor maintenance. "The panel assessed that this inconsistency likely led to varying interpretations of how extensively the carburettor should have been dismantled, inspected and cleaned, which was very likely to have reduced the reliability of detecting any debris build-up." The design of the cockpit and restraint were identified as aggravating factors, but the report acknowledged any structural design change would likely require "significant moderations". "This would not only affect the historic authenticity of the aircraft but would possibly affect overall airworthiness due to a change in aircraft mass and balance," the report said. Twenty-six safety recommendations were included in the report, including improved maintenance records, reviews of cockpit protection and better training for emergencies. The report described the recommendations as "robust" and said they "should minimise the likelihood of a recurrence or similar tragedy". title: Train station returning to village after more than 100 years
description: Cheadle in Stockport has been without a train station since its original hub closed in 1917.
body: A computer generated image shows how the new station in the village of Cheadle will look Work is beginning on bringing a train station back to the heart of a Greater Manchester village more than a century after its original station closed. Cheadle in Stockport had a station just off the high street up until 1917. Funding for a new hub, which would be built next to Alexandra Hospital, was given the green light in 2022, with planning permission granted in 2023 but concerns about its effect on the timetabling of trains elsewhere on the network led to delays. Stockport Council said the issue had now been resolved and council leader Mark Roberts said it was "a hugely significant moment for Cheadle and for Stockport". "For years we've fought for this station because we know the difference it will make to residents, businesses and the future prosperity of the area," he added. Roberts said he was delighted that the initial highways work could now start on site thanks to the persistence and partnership of all involved. Services are expected to run from Cheadle into Stockport town, Manchester Piccadilly and Chester, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said. The project had been held up by an unresolved timetabling issue over concerns the new station could impact trains elsewhere on the network, with a previous proposal made to remove services at Ashley and Plumley. Stockport Council said the latest assessment by Network Rail and Northern Trains concluded that Cheadle Station could be introduced without removing a significant barrier that had put the project at risk and these plans have now been dropped. A computer generated image shows the aerial view of the new station Brian Bradley, chair of the Cheadle Towns Fund Board, said it was "a fantastic milestone for Cheadle and a moment that many people have worked hard to achieve over a number of years". Cheadle MP Tom Morrison said getting to this point had been a real team effort, adding: "Cheadle has waited more than 100 years for a station, and now it's finally happening." "It will connect our 23,000 residents to jobs, schools and opportunities across Greater Manchester, and take traffic off our busy roads." Cheadle Hulme North councillor David Meller, who helped kickstart the plans for the new station, said: "To see that we're finally there is incredible." title: Craig Charles' tribute to 'city that shaped me'
description: Presenter Craig Charles marks 50 years of poetry with a tribute to Liverpool for National Poetry Day.
body: Craig Charles said his life was transformed after winning a poetry competition at the age of 12 Actor and presenter Craig Charles said his latest work had given him a chance to reflect on the city which shaped him. Charles' new spoken word piece pays tribute to his home city of Liverpool in honour of National Poetry Day. His performance coincides with the 50th anniversary of him winning a poetry competition aged 12, which he said had changed his life. "I was just reacting to what was going on," he said. "Reacting to the riots, reacting to Thatcher, reacting to police harassment, reacting to poverty. "Liverpool was getting kicked to pieces at that time." Charles, pictured in Liverpool in 1985, became known for his performance poetry By the age of 16, Charles was performing at Liverpool's Everyman Bistro basement venue, which was known for its open-mic events. Within a year, he was performing his poetry on BBC 2 show Riverside. "I just got stuck into that and started shouting from the rooftops my opinion on things," he said. "I was quite an angry young man, I suppose, but for some reason it resonated with people." He described how Liverpool's "really vibrant" music and poetry scene was a reflection of the city's reaction to hardship. "Liverpool has always had a different kind of attitude, especially to adversity," he said. "We make something out of it, we make a song, make a poem, make a football chant. "We do something with it, and we've always had the gift of the gab." Charles, 62, filmed a performance of his new work at locations across Liverpool He said poetry was in "Merseyside's DNA". Charles' new work traces through Liverpool's cultural history following the split of The Beatles. It references a number of the city's poets, the punk explosion and bands and clubs of the time. Charles said Liverpool was "a melting pot of ideas, warmth and wit" "There was so much stuff going on in Liverpool when I was a lad," he said. "It was all part of the same argument... it all came from this city of ours that is just such a melting pot, so full of ideas, so full of warmth, and so full of wit." Charles' poem featured as part of BBC Radio 6 Music's Way With Words event, a day of programming marking National Poetry Day on Thursday. title: Bees create a buzz at Liverpool shopping centre
description: Staff at St John's Shopping Centre in Liverpool staff are keeping busy with their rooftop tenants.
body: Suzanne Moses, who is sustainability manager at St Johns Shopping Centre, says people are surprised when they hear about the hidden hives A Liverpool shopping centre's lesser known tenants are creating a buzz. St Johns Shopping Centre has thousands of bees in hidden hives on the roof and some of the staff have even had beekeeper training. Two hives were installed in 2021 and a third was set up last year. During summer peaks the hives become home to about 180,000 of the striped insects. They produced a bumper amount of honey this year - enough for 150 jars of the sweet nectar - and local school children are helping design the labels. The project was developed by St Johns and NG Bailey, who provide maintenance support to the site, after they wanted to do something for the environment. Two hives were initially installed and staff were recruited to train as beekeepers. A third hive was added last year, with five members of staff now trained to look after them. Kieron Jones, maintenance supervisor, told BBC Radio Merseyside: "I never thought it would be part of my maintenance routine to look after beehives. "When it was suggested, it piqued our interest and we thought this is another skill set we can get, and it lets us give something back, so it was really good." The hives are positioned on the roof of the shopping centre, in the shadow of the famous St Johns Beacon. Maintenance supervisor Kieron Jones said he never thought looking after beehives would be part of his job Sustainability manager, Suzanne Moses said it has been exciting for the team to learn new skills and it has brought them together. She said the shopping centre's rooftop was "a great spot". "[The bees] get the sunlight. When we tell shoppers and the public, they're always surprised by what's above them." This year, the bees have produced 150 jars of honey – all of which is done in a workshop on the centre roof. The jars will be given away to staff, shoppers, tenants and charities. "It's been a really good yield this year," said Suzanne. "Children from Whitefield Primary School in Everton will be designing this year's labels, so it's a great way to get them involved. "And another of our beekeepers... goes into schools to run workshops, so it's great to get that education to the next generation." Kieron added: "As we come to the winter months, the number of bees will reduce. "Summer peaks about 60,000 bees per hive, so we have about 180,000 bees across the three hives. "That will reduce down to about 10-15,000 bees over the winter. "We'll go back in January to make sure they're OK but the bees will be asleep from the end of this month so it does get a bit easier – and we have a rest with the bees." title: Father of murdered man describes trial as 'hell'
description: Dale Martin says some of his son's killers would come to his house for evening meals as children.
body: Dale Martin said his son had a "heart of gold" The father of a man who was fatally attacked by an armed gang has described the trial following his son's death as "hell". Dale Martin, also known as DJ, was dragged out of a car in Derby in June 2025 and repeatedly stabbed and slashed. On Friday, one man was was given a life sentence, with a minimum term of 27 years, for his murder. Five other men from the city - who were found guilty of manslaughter following a trial more than four months long - were also jailed. Speaking to the BBC after the sentencing hearing, the victim's father, Dale Martin, said some of the killers went to the same school as his son, and some would come to his house for evening meals as children. "That hurts, it hurts a lot," he said. "Some of these children used to hang about on the street late at night, and if we were about and we were cooking tea, someone would come in and have tea in the garden or in the kitchen with us," Martin added. Dale Martin, 21, was described as a "proper family lad" by his father Martin, said he felt "relief" that court proceedings had now concluded. "It hurts, we're just going to go home as a family and just try and get back to some sort of normality which it never will do. "It'll never come to normality because DJ's not there," he said. "He's always in our thoughts, always in our hearts, he's always here with me, it's just hard and I'm just glad it's all over." The attack - the court in Loughborough heard - followed a history of "animosity" between two rival groups, stretching back years, and two "tit for tat" confrontations earlier that weekend. Martin was attacked near to where he had been attending a gender-reveal party several hours earlier at a pub. The court heard a Renault Megane he was travelling in was ambushed when, "in a show of force", the group put their electric bikes in the road to stop the car, which then swerved and stalled. Adrian Langdale KC, prosecuting, told the trial, attackers had armed themselves with swords, machetes and "Rambo knives". Martin was pulled from the car through a smashed window and initially managed to escape, but then tripped on a piece of wood. His attackers set upon him "like a pack of animals", a witness had told the court. Dale Martin's sister said she "adored" her brother "Nobody deserves to die the way he died over a 'tit for tat'," Martin said. "It's just horrible, it's horrible, but he was a lovely lad and he'll be forever missed by a lot of people." Paying tribute to his son, Martin said the memory he would miss the most was his "smile". "He was just a proper family lad with a heart of gold and he'd do anything for his family." Judge Gregory Dickinson KC handed Jayden Mannion-Roberts, 26, of Tennyson Street in Derby, a life sentence, with a minimum term of 27 years, for Martin's murder. Ki Grant-Finlayson, 23, of Addison Road was sentenced to an 18-year jail term, with a three-year extended licence on release for his "leading role" in the ambush. Keenan Hamblett, 27, of Osmaston Park Road, was sentenced to 17 and a half years, and Shaylon McCalla, 27, of Copes Way, received 18 years, with a three-year extended licence. Grant-Finlayson and Hamblett tried to fly one-way to Tunisia following the attack but were arrested at Gatwick airport, each with about £3,000 in cash, the court heard. The judge gave "enthusiastic participants" in the attack, Kayin Holmes, 25, of Nightingale Road, 15 years, and Kelci Thompson, 19, of Osmaston Road, 10 years, to be served in a young offenders institution. Dale's younger sister said the 21-year-old was a "very big part" of her life and said "towards the end is when we got closer, we went everywhere together". "I spent most of my time with him, and it's just hard not having him here," she said.
