title: Young people are taking up bell-ringing to make connections
description: Katie Anderson says making music with others is an antidote to screens and scrolling.
body: Katie Anderson, 19, says bell-ringing is a great way to connect with other people Many students join sports teams or academic societies to make friends at university. Katie Anderson chose bell-ringing instead. The 19-year-old says the hobby has helped her build friendships, learn new skills and spend less time looking at screens. Katie says bell-ringing is a "very social thing to do" and a good way to connect with people away from her phone. "It's nice not having something where you're sat on a screen all day," she says. "You get to do something a bit different with your time." When she arrived at the University of Lincoln last year, she joined its bell-ringing society after learning the hobby from her partner's family. Now president of the society, she wants to challenge the idea that bell-ringing is only for older generations. Despite being the most digitally connected generation, young people are more likely to experience loneliness than older age groups, according to national data, external. Bell-ringers say their hobby offers an antidote, bringing people together to learn, practice and socialise face-to-face. "I love the socialising," Katie says. "You're working with people to create this wonderful sound, but also there's always something new to learn. "You get to learn stuff in such a social way, which I just really enjoy." Society president Katie (left) works alongside vice president Abi Brown (right) Katie says bell-ringing helps people slow down in a fast-moving world, even if it is not always relaxing. "You're learning quite a lot," she says. "I wouldn't say it's quite relaxing in that way, but you're not in the world of technology when you're doing it." Katie says there is a misconception that only older people take part in the tradition and there is a national push to get more young people involved. The committee (left to right: Abi, Katie and George Milfull, treasurer) looked to attract new members during freshers week One of the places keen to attract more young ringers is St Mary Magdalene Church in Gedney, Lincolnshire. Tower captain, John Bennett, 94, says he would love to see more young people take up the hobby. John, who started ringing when he was 14, says it is "excellent exercise for body and brain" and says learning the rhythms can be "quite complicated". "It is very fascinating, you get hooked by it, as I was when I was young," he says. "You meet all sorts of people from all walks of life... you're sure of companionship." John says he will keep going "as long as my legs and arms hold up" but adds he would be "overjoyed" if a young person took the ropes from him. John Bennett has been involved with bell-ringing for 80 years Tina Stoecklin, president of the Central Council of Church Bell Ringers (CCCBR), says the hobby can be particularly beneficial for young people. "There's a lot of mental health and social benefits," she says. "It just gets you out and talking to people and interacting with people in a really safe space." There are about 40,000 bell-ringers in the UK, according to the CCCBR. The organisation recently launched a Young Bell Ringers Hub, designed to help attract more young people to the activity by providing resources and support. Tina, who has been ringing for 40 years, says one of the biggest attractions is the sense of belonging it creates. "It's a chance where you make friends for a lifetime," she says. "From a social point of view, it's really, really important for young people." Tina Stoecklin says bell ringing helped her make friends for life Tina also says bell-ringing offers a rare opportunity for different generations to come together, connecting people of all ages and from all walks of life. "We are like a second family that you can count on when you need it," she says. "Actually putting your hands on a bell rope and ringing with other people... you get that camaraderie and you get that sense of village. "For some people, when they tried out bell-ringing, they found their people and that's them sorted for the rest of their lives. That was certainly the case when I learned to ring." title: Trust warns of 'tangible' climate threat to heritage sites
description: A National Trust manager says recent summers have "brought home" the impact of climate change.
body: Fountains Abbey is feeling the impact of extreme weather, the National Trust says Protecting all heritage sites from the impact of climate change "just may not be possible," according to a National Trust manager. Justin Scully, manager of Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal, said extreme heat, heavy rainfall and wildfire risk were already affecting gardens, moorland and historic structures. He said heavy rain could overwhelm drainage systems and penetrate walls, causing damp and erosion, while repeated cycles of wetting, drying, freezing and thawing could harm stonework. Flooding could also undermine foundations, while hotter, dry conditions could increase the risk of subsidence and wildfires. Scully said the organisation may have to accept it cannot save everything as it is today. "These last two summers have really brought this home to ourselves and to our visitors," he said. "Climate change isn't a thing that's happening out there to other people, it's actually impacting ourselves and the places we love. The threat is tangible." The National Trust is planning for more extreme weather by looking at what could happen to the properties and landscapes it manages over the next 40 years. "We've got to think about what could be the worst possible outcome and then work backwards from that," Scully said. At Fountains Abbey, this could include increasing drainage capacity and gutters to cope with heavier rainfall. It could also result in changing the appearance of the gardens. Scully said the trust needed to be "more open to how we would adapt," with gardens potentially becoming "less manicured". "People expect things to look perfect and crisp," he said. Coastal areas like Ravenscar are difficult to protect from climate change The trust looks after properties including Beningbrough Hall, Nunnington Hall and Treasurer's House in York, as well as miles of coastline from Loftus to Filey. It said coastal sites were among those facing the greatest climate pressures, including erosion and rising sea levels. A National Trust spokesperson said: "Climate change is affecting many of the places we care for, and our conservation work has to evolve with it." Conservation decisions would consider the significance of a place, the benefit it brings to people and whether an approach is sustainable long term, they added. The water cascade into the Studley Lake ran dry during hot weather in 2025 The National Trust is a charity and receives no guaranteed government money, although it can apply for project grants from public bodies and lottery funds. Scully said some adaptation processes could be "very expensive". The trust did not give a figure for those costs, but said it would continue to invest significantly in conservation. It also called for climate resilience to become a national priority, led by a Cabinet-level minister coordinating preparedness across government and supporting long-term investment. Scully said people should not despair. "There are small things that we can do as communities [such as reducing carbon footprints] that will make a big difference over the longer term." title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
description: State police and the country's security agency are looking into the co-pilot, who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel.
body: The Flydubai plane was diverted to Saudi Arabia after passengers managed to take back control from the co-pilot Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel. The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane. The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami. The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives. In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia". The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time". Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it. Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel. Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said. The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in. Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia. This video can not be played Watch: Flydubai pilot speaks with Indian PM Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition. The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu. The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident. He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency. In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history. While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline. It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK. He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school. title: I clawed my way to the top but need a break - Azpilicueta
description: Cesar Azpilicueta says it is time to move to "a different stage of life" following a glorious 20-year playing career, notably captaining Chelsea to several titles.
body: Azpilicueta is sixth in the all-time appearance list after playing 508 times in 11 years for Chelsea. Cesar Azpilicueta was an all-encompassing leader for Chelsea - and, now retired, he reflects on how his passion for education and attention to detail helped him build a career at the highest level. One story sums it up. Before Chelsea's Champions League final victory in 2021, Azpilicueta could not take his customary pre-match nap and opted to study instead. He says his work towards an MBA in business management from the Berlin School of Business and Innovation took his mind off the pressure and noise on the streets of Porto. Later that day, he lifted the Champions League trophy after captaining Chelsea to victory against Manchester City. Azpilicueta told BBC Sport: "When I was a kid my parents pushed me to get good grades and finish school. "I wasn't a professional footballer until I was 17, in my last year of school. Education was always important. When Covid-19 arrived, we had more time. "I found some courses but I didn't start because I thought it was the end of my career. It was more that I wanted to learn, improve myself and do it in another language. "It wasn't because I thought it was my last year as a footballer, but it did help me navigate the final years of my career, become a better person and a better footballer." Azpilicueta, 37, was speaking at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, where he joked he did not feel "entirely comfortable", while collecting a diploma in global football sport directorship through the PFA Business School, adding to qualifications that also include a diploma from Harvard Business School. Now retired from playing after spending last season at Sevilla, he replied "maybe" when asked whether he could become a sporting director one day, but says football has left him in need of a post-career break. Now at a "different stage of life", he cannot even contemplate playing football with friends for fun because it would trigger his competitive instincts. "It was time to stop playing football because, even though I could probably still play, I didn't have the energy to commit myself fully for an entire season," he reflected. "At the moment I have another commitment, which is my family. I want to play some golf and enjoy life. "For 20 years I was constantly travelling, playing and preparing for seasons. This summer looked completely different." After beginning at boyhood club Osasuna, Azpilicueta joined Marseille, where he learned French. However, it was his move to Chelsea in 2012 that proved transformative. Completing his latest course highlights Azpilicueta's thirst for knowledge and a desire for constant self-improvement. It was something he learned at Chelsea, where he arrived as a relatively low-profile £7m signing in a dressing room full of established leaders such as John Terry, Frank Lampard and Petr Cech, alongside star names including Fernando Torres, Eden Hazard and Ashley Cole. He explained: "I started as a right winger, moved to France, then moved to Chelsea. I wasn't a star signing. I had to find my way. Left-back, wing-back, centre-back in a back three. "It was about consistency. I had to work hard to stay fit, adapt to different managers and different positions. "When you arrive at Chelsea, you feel the ambition straight away. Every three days you have to win. Every game and every trophy matters. "That culture pushed me to the maximum and, especially when I left Chelsea, I felt that I had given everything I had for the club." Azpilicueta explained how his education away from the pitch helped him develop into a leader at Stamford Bridge. It gave him the confidence to represent Premier League players during the Covid-19 pandemic, while also helping to organise initiatives and keep the club moving forward after owner Roman Abramovich was sanctioned following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. His defining moment came in that 2021 Champions League final victory. There is little doubt that, having succeeded Terry and then Gary Cahill as captain, Azpilicueta ranks among Chelsea's greatest leaders. Yet he revealed that, since leaving the club in 2023, he has not returned to Stamford Bridge. He was among dozens of players to leave after Chelsea changed ownership from Abramovich to the current American-led consortium in 2022. "I left Chelsea, but Chelsea will always stay in my heart," he said. "I follow every game and I hope the club comes back to where it belongs. "There are some very strong teams around and football sometimes needs a bit of time. You need connections, people playing together and understanding each other. "At a big club like Chelsea, the demands are high. But I think that's normal. It should be demanding and ambitious because, speaking as a Chelsea fan, you always want to see the club winning trophies. "I have confidence that [manager] Xabi [Alonso], the staff and the players will do good work. Hopefully they can bring a lot of happiness to the fans." He has been following Chelsea's latest captain Reece James, who he believes will grow into a better leader, since over-30 players Jordan Henderson, Danny Welbeck and Emiliano Martinez joined over the summer. When it is suggested that he might return to Stamford Bridge in some capacity to be marked by a warm reception from supporters, Azpilicueta responds modestly: "I don't know about that. "I will come back one day. I won't be putting on my boots, though." Latest Chelsea news, analysis and fan views Ask about Chelsea - what do you want to know? title: The Feeling album recorded in a Sussex shed
description: The Feeling's debut album turns 20 as the band prepare for Eastbourne and Margate shows.
body: The Feeling frontman Dan Gillespie Sells said celebrating the 20th anniversary of their breakthrough album was "extraordinary" The Feeling's triple-platinum debut album was recorded in a shed in Horsham, according to frontman Dan Gillespie Sells. Speaking to BBC Radio Sussex as the record marks its 20th anniversary, Gillespie Sells said it came from "a very different world" when music fans bought CDs and "nobody had an iPhone". The singer said much of Twelve Stops and Home was made at the Sussex home of brothers and bandmates Kevin and Ciaran Jeremiah. The Feeling will perform the album in full when a 20th anniversary tour visits Eastbourne and Margate in November. Gillespie Sells, the only member of the band not originally from Sussex, said he spent many of his teenage years in the county after meeting his future bandmates at the Brit School. He said the group began spending time together in Ashdown Forest before starting to record music in Sussex. Asked whether he had visited the studio again since making the album, he said: "It wasn't a studio, it was a shed." "It was an outhouse. There were brick walls but it was essentially a shed," he added. Gillespie Sells said the recordings took place in the Horsham garden building owned by the Jeremiah brothers' parents. "We borrowed some microphones, Kevin had built a small computer and we recorded the first album like that, basically just hanging out together," he said. Dan Gillespie Sells of The Feeling said the album's success was "very unusual and very lucky" Released in June 2006, Twelve Stops and Home reached number two in the UK charts and eventually achieved triple-platinum status. The album produced hits including Sewn, Fill My Little World, Never Be Lonely and I Love It When You Call. Reflecting on its 20th anniversary, Gillespie Sells said: "It's extraordinary. I think about what a different world it was then. All those albums we sold were physical copies and nobody had an iPhone." He said the industry had changed significantly since the album's release but its songs had continued to attract new listeners. "I see people in their 20s who seem to know every word and I think 'you must have been a toddler when this came out, how on earth are you singing along?' but they do," he said. The band's anniversary tour visits Eastbourne's Winter Garden on 11 November and Margate's Drill Hall on 12 November. title: 'The music transported us to another planet'
description: The people captured in a celebrated photograph are reunited nearly 50 years later.
body: The photo, taken in 1978, has been exhibited around the world When Vivienne Dawes first saw the photograph of herself dancing on a crowded dance floor almost 50 years ago, it felt like being transported back in time. Captured at Wolverhampton's Culture Centre in 1978, the image shows her among a group of young people immersed in a night of music and dancing. At the time, none of them could have known the photograph would become an iconic image that has been viewed across the world and one of photographer Chris Steele-Perkins' most recognised works. Nor could they have imagined that, decades later, they would be reunited through the photo and finally have their stories told. "Oh my goodness - oh my, and I do look like me, don't I?" Vivianne said when she saw the image. She is the central dancer in the photograph and can still remember the atmosphere inside the venue. She said: "Back then, everybody was doing their own thing, was all dancing, and when the music hit us, we felt no pain. "At the end of the day, we're showing that we're black sisters enjoying reggae music." Vivienne Dawes said dancing felt like she and her friends were on another planet Nearly 50 years after it was taken, the image continues to attract attention, appearing most recently in the V&A East exhibition The Music Is Black: A British Story. Now it is going on display in its home city of Wolverhampton, at the Grand theatre. Vivienne said she had no awareness when she was dancing that her photo was being taken. "If you notice the way we all dance, it's like we were on another planet," she said. Her dance, as captured in the photo, would also later go on to be recreated in a painting by artist Claudette Johnson, external, which will also appear in the Wolverhampton exhibition. "I appreciated the fact that someone could put their time into painting a portrait of me. "I can't believe I looked so attractive back then, really and truly. I look very lovely." While the photo has become celebrated over the years, the people captured in it have remained largely anonymous, until now. For Winston Logan, who appears at the back of the photo on the far left, the image is a reminder of a very different Wolverhampton. Having arrived in Britain about five years before the photo was taken, he remembers a lack of opportunities for young Black people. "Life is hard, no entertainment, nowhere to go, no fun," he said. But the Culture Centre on Clarence Street offered something different, becoming a hub for music, dancing and community. Looking back, Winston sees the image as a snapshot of a pivotal period in his life. "This is where it starts, [I] went from unemployment, went from there into training, went from there into industry, construction or whatever, and now I'm passing on my skills. "Mum and dad didn't get to see that photo or find out about that photo." "This time, to the present day, my life has, I would say, blown up. Well, I can't hide now, can I?" Winston Logan said his parents never got to see the photo In an interview with the Guardian in 2014, Steele-Perkins said he had been commissioned to go to Wolverhampton in 1978 by the Sunday Times magazine as part of a feature marking 10 years since local MP Enoch Powell's "Rivers of Blood" speech. He described it as a difficult commission, adding that he had not really liked the photo at the time, although it had grown on him since and had become his best-selling print. An event celebrating the launch of the Wolverhampton exhibition on Sunday is set to reunite several of those pictured in the photo, including Macka B, now an international reggae artist, his brother Owen MacFarlane, Casa Simpson, Lisa Green and Sharon Underwood - all of whom still live in and around the city. The idea for the exhibition came after staff at Wolverhampton Grand Theatre spotted the photograph while visiting The Music Is Black: A British Story at V&A East. "It stood out amongst all of the other images," curator Tonia Daley-Campbell said. "It's a memory. It's captured in time." She said the photograph seemed to bring the dancefloor back to life. "You can hear it, you can smell it, you can feel that image. "We want to put all of the young people that were in that photo dancing, vibing, standing by the sound system, whatever they were doing, front and centre," Daley-Campbell said. "We're bringing it back home and we're going to make sure that is displayed and everybody will know their name." The exhibition opens at Wolverhampton Grand Theatre's Encore Lounge on 4 October and will run until 31 October. Admission to the event is free. title: The Kent village that helped shape Audrey Hepburn
description: Audrey Hepburn spent three years in Elham before the outbreak of World War Two.
body: Hollywood actress Audrey Hepburn (centre, wearing a tall hat) spent part of her childhood in Elham, near Canterbury, before the outbreak of World War Two Long before she became one of Hollywood's most celebrated stars, Audrey Hepburn was learning music and dance at a small village school in the Kent countryside. The future Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady actress spent part of her childhood in Elham, near Canterbury, where local historians say her love of performing was encouraged during three formative years before the outbreak of World War Two. Today, a blue plaque on a cottage near the King's Arms pub marks the place where Hepburn lived between 1936 and 1939. "It really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," said Brian Badham, of Elham Historical Society. Hepburn, then known as Audrey Ruston-Hepburn, arrived in the village after her parents separated. Badham said it was decided she should continue her English education in Kent, where family friends were living. She moved into Orchard Cottage with the Butcher family, among a number of Elham residents who offered accommodation to visitors before the war, according to local accounts. She attended Rigden School in the centre of Elham where, Badham said, she would have had her lessons. "One of the sisters encouraged Audrey to get involved with music and dance. That really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," he said. Explore more fascinating stories from Kent Listen and subscribe for the latest episode of Secret Kent Fellow historian Dilys Webb said Elham offered plenty for a young girl growing up in the late 1930s. "I think it was far busier than it is today," she said. "There were more shops, coffee houses and pubs. In Audrey's day I think it was more contained and everything that was here that she needed. "She had quite a nice social life. She did ballet, she obviously went to the coffee houses and socialised with her friends, so I think there was plenty here for her in the few years she was here." By the time Audrey Hepburn starred in Breakfast At Tiffany's she was already a Hollywood icon The wartime years would take Hepburn far from Kent and shape the rest of her life. As war approached her mother, a Dutch baroness, arranged for her to return to the Netherlands, then still a neutral country, in December 1939. After Germany invaded in May 1940, Hepburn spent much of her teenage years under Nazi occupation. She later helped the Dutch resistance by carrying messages and taking part in secret ballet performances to raise money for anti-Nazi causes. The future actress also endured severe hardship during the war, suffering malnutrition as food shortages swept the occupied country. Her son Luca Dotti once said in an interview: "She believed very much that there is a struggle between good and evil and you have to take sides." Although historians are unaware of her ever returning to Elham, residents remain "incredibly proud" that one of the world's best-known actresses once called their community home. Webb said: "Obviously when she was here the village didn't know she was going to be a superstar. Now everybody knows of Audrey and we are a very, very proud village." Badham added: "She was very special. A wonderful lady and fondly loved by the people that she met while she was here. "A short time but a lasting impact on their lives." title: Man rescued after car crashes into house
description: A man is arrested at the scene on suspicion of being unfit through drink or drugs.
body: The home was left seriously damaged after the car crashed into it late at night A man had to be rescued by firefighters from a house that partially collapsed after a car crashed into it. Police officers, paramedics and firefighters were called to the property on Ninefields, in Waltham Abbey, Essex shortly before 23:00 BST on Friday. Upon arrival, they found a silver Skoda, which had smoke coming out of it, that had smashed into the corner of a house, leaving it badly damaged. Essex Police said a man was arrested on suspicion of being unfit through drink or drugs and taken to hospital for treatment. Another man was safely removed from the rear of the property by fire crew using a ladder, while a woman was also taken to hospital for a "precautionary assessment." Essex Fire and Rescue Service said its firefighters had to rescue a man from the house Photos show the car lodged inside the home with a first-floor room and its contents – including boxes of books and bedding – having collapsed on to its roof. The area is also shown to be covered in bricks which have fallen away from the property, which was cordoned off to the public after the crash. A spokesperson for Essex Fire and Rescue Service said: "A car had driven into a house and smoke was issuing from the vehicle. "No-one was trapped in the vehicle. "Due to the damage to the front of the house, one resident was rescued via a ladder at the rear of the property. "The scene was left with the police and resident." title: University asks staff to review some partnerships with China after MI5 warning
description: The UK's internal security service had warned universities they may have unintentionally assisted China's espionage.
body: Staff at QUB have been "strongly advised to review any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI" Queen's University of Belfast (QUB) has asked staff to review some partnerships with China after a warning from MI5. In a highly unusual move, the UK's internal security service had warned universities they may have unintentionally assisted China's espionage. MI5 said the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) was a front company working for China's intelligence and security service. However, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated". Staff at Queen's have now been "strongly advised to review any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI". "Work is ongoing within Queen's to do this," an email to staff said. "However, this may not be obvious through our existing systems and so researchers are also advised to undertake appropriate due diligence to identify the ultimate source of funding for collaborations with Chinese institutions." MI5 issued the alert for UK universities about CGTRI which it said had "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). Universities in the UK often collaborate and partner with universities elsewhere in the world to share research and expertise. But MI5 said it had identified more than 100 UK-linked academics who had contributed to projects funded by Ministry of State Security via CGTRI. It said that in some cases the researchers would not be aware of the front company's role in their project. UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object. MI5 added that academics who failed to cut ties with CGTRI could ultimately face criminal charges for aiding a foreign state. As a result, UK universities were advised to immediately review the funding of any research collaboration with China. A QUB spokesperson told BBC News NI that the university takes "responsibilities around research and national security extremely seriously". "Queen's University has commenced a review around any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI," they said. "We have also contacted staff requesting they review any existing or proposed collaborations with them and report any concerns to the relevant Faculty Dean of Research. "We will keep this situation under review while continuing to support our collaboration, research and innovation projects locally, nationally and internationally." According to its website, QUB has invested over $10m (£7.56m) in China-related research in areas like sustainable energy, information technology, food security and cancer research over the past decade. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Ulster University said they had no research links with the organisation referenced by MI5. title: Queen's University students blast off to US for Nasa robotics competition
description: The students will head to Florida to compete against university teams from Australia, India and the US.
body: The team is made up of 10 students from Queen's University Belfast Could a robot designed by young engineering students from Northern Ireland end up on the Moon? A team, from Queen's University Belfast (QUB), are heading to Florida later this month to take part in a Nasa 'lunabotics' competition. Lunabotics is a university-level competition for teams to use the Nasa systems engineering process to design, build, and operate a lunar robot. The students created a lab-built robot that they will bring to the competition to find out how it would deal with future moon missions. The robots will be expected to dig up lunar material, drive over obstacles and use the material to form a wall. Jack Fitzpatrick, who's studying for a PhD in mechanical engineering, said "it's a great feeling" to have been invited and they're looking forward to the opportunity to take part. Jack Fitzpatrick is studying for a PhD and is part of the mechanical team The team of 10 QUB students made it to the competition following their win at the competition earlier this year. They'll be competing at the University of Central Florida against university teams from Australia, India and the US. Jamie Smith is the team's software lead Jamie Smith is a third-year electrical and electronic engineering student. He explained that the team was divided into three groups for software, electronics and mechanical. Jamie was the software team lead for this project. He said their main task was to control the rover then provide the autonomous capabilities towards it. And, they had to build rover simulations to test their software before they actually got one. Jack, however, is part of the mechanical side. "We analyse that something is physically strong enough, it's well built enough to survive this environment, it's going to have the traction to drive in this environment," he explained. Jack Fitzpatrick, Sandro O'Hara, Eoin Conway, Jamie Smith and Alex Dunne Jamie explained they designed the 52 kg aluminium frame robot rover and took it compete at a competition in Milton Keynes. "We got on very well. We ended up winning the competition and had great fun," he said. Then a few weeks later, they were invited to compete at Nasa's international Lunabotics competition. Jack said that being asked to go was a "great feeling" and "a real opportunity to demonstrate everything that you've learned". "It's just a great opportunity to represent Northern Ireland, the UK and really Europe abroad as we are the only European team that will be there," Jack explained. Both of the students said their success was a reflection of both themselves and also the university and the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering. Jamie explained that the main objective of the rover is that should be able to drive itself around a lunar-simulated room. "That means it should start at a point, figure out where it is within this room, travel to an excavation point, so in that point, it will pick up then some sand which is meant to be lunar-simulant. "It'll pick up the sand and then deposit it at another location, and it's meant to do this all by itself." Jack explained that the purpose of this is to simulate how real rovers carry out these kind of tasks on the moon. "It's being able to autonomously operate on the moon and build environments for humans to later habitat. And that's the real drive behind why this competition exists," he explained. Jack explained that there have been several precursor competitions in different countries and this competition takes the top tier of those competitions and brings them together "to really showcase the talent" that there is internationally. "We are the winning team from the United Kingdom competition and we will be representing the UK and, by extension, Europe at this competition." "We may not win the competition this year but we're building a base upon which we can improve year on year and maybe come back in a few years and really come through with a winning design," he said. Caolán Boyle, Head of Robotics at QPL, said the team is "exceptionally proud and excited". He said "hundreds of hours have gone into making the rover mission ready for the event". title: I was told my baby boy's skin was as fragile as glass
description: Ciara says she found it hard to imagine her son being happy but has started to believe he could be.
body: Six-month-old Ralph was diagnosed with junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB) at a few days old When Ciara's son Ralph was born, he had skin missing from his hands and feet. Doctors said he was as fragile as glass. Ralph was diagnosed with junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), also known as butterfly skin, at a few days old. Ciara and her partner Lewis had to become experts in the rare genetic disorder, which causes skin to tear or blister at the slightest touch. "We were new parents, we had never heard about this before and we had basically been told my son was like glass," Ciara, from Arlesey in Bedfordshire, says. The 30-year-old mum is now calling on the government to increase funding and research into rare skin conditions, with the hope of one day finding a cure. Doctors from Great Ormond Street Hospital taught Ciara and her partner how to manage the condition Five minutes after Ralph was born, following what Ciara describes as a normal pregnancy, she noticed "big raw patches" on his hands and feet. "My partner Lewis went to the NICU [neonatal intensive care unit] with him and left me with a picture of him," she says. "I spent the whole time looking at that picture questioning what on earth was going on." After being put in a heated incubator, Ralph's body broke out in head-to-toe blisters. Two days later, the couple received a diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa, with the specific subtype of junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), of which there are two main forms. Ralph's form is generally milder, rather than the severe type which can be life-threatening. But there is no cure and limited treatment options. Ralph's parents grease bottle teats to avoid damaging his mouth and turn his baby-grows inside out to avoid friction from the seams. They spend up to three hours each night replacing bandages on his feet. "At the start, when he was a newborn, everything felt so heavy. It was really hard to imagine him being happy. "Doctors from Great Ormond Street were essentially saying 'we need to teach you how to care for him' and we were expected to learn it – the medical professionals around us at the local hospital were learning on the job with us," she says. Ciara says she has not been able to use anything she bought for her son due to the damage some items could cause to his skin Young people with the condition are sometimes called "butterfly children", due to their skin's fragility, like a butterfly's wing. According to DEBRA UK, the charity for people living with the disorder, it leads to blistering across the body, alopecia, malformed fingers and toenails and irregular tooth enamel. It is caused by a gene mutation, external which results in faulty or missing proteins in layers of the skin and internal organs. Ralph's DNA lacks the instructions for sticking his epidermis (the surface layer of our skin) to the dermis (the next one down). Two of the most common symptoms, external are pain and itching from frequent and extensive blistering. Ciara describes her son's condition, which has no cure and limited treatment options, as devastating Ciara recently started a petition calling for more research into the condition and after reaching 10,000 signatures, she received a response from the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC). The DHSC, which has also been contacted by the BBC for comment, said it had already committed £1.075m over five years for projects specifically related to EB. It said research had so far covered advanced treatments, symptom management, supportive care and better care co-ordination. But Ciara worries her son's rare condition could get "left behind" in the world of research. "It feels like families like ours are the ones being left to connect the dots. It just doesn't feel good enough. "If enough people knew how devastating this condition is, something would have to happen because no-one, no human in the world, would stand by and allow children to suffer from birth for the rest of their lives. "If the system in place is working, why are families like ours still having to work so tirelessly to raise awareness, contact researchers and campaign for anything that might improve our children's quality of life?" Tony Byrne, chief executive officer of DEBRA UK, says research is "not an abstract ambition" for people with butterfly skin, but "the route to less pain, better treatments, and the hope of a cure". "This petition matters because dedicated, ring-fenced government investment would give researches greater certainty, help promising discoveries move into UK clinical trials and ensure rare conditions are not overlooked," he adds. Despite how painful the condition is and the need for more research, Ciara says she has finally started to believe that Ralph can live a happy life. "He is just the most stubborn, funny, resilient little boy. He loves simple things. When the trees move in the wind, it makes him so happy," she says. "Ralph can have the most awful wounds on his stomach or his elbows and he's still rolling over trying to get toys. He doesn't let anything stand in his way. He's so fragile, but so desperate to move. "Despite everything he's so happy, he's so smiley. He won't let anything hold him back." Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Rare tornado whips through small Australian town
description: The twister was caught on camera in Ulladulla, New South Wales, damaging property and downing trees.
body: This video can not be played Several people in Ulladulla, New South Wales, filmed the moment a rare tornado came through the town on 3 October. The Australian Bureau of Meteorology said the phenomenon was caused by "severe" thunderstorms and that it was "very uncommon to see one in such a populated place". The weather incident caused damage to properties and knocked over some trees, it added. Rare tornado whips through small Australian town. title: Burnham scraps controversial plans to curb jury trials
description: The key policy idea announced by David Lammy when he was justice secretary will no longer go ahead.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has scrapped controversial plans to curb some jury trials. Sir Keir Starmer's government had introduced proposals to allow judges to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-alone - and it proposes that thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury. Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he had changed course after hearing the "strength of feeling" about the original proposals. Criminal lawyers have welcomed the decision and the Conservatives say it is a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury. Former Justice Secretary David Lammy first announced the plans in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales. The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis. The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases - having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during the national lockdowns. Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035. There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused. Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape. Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing defendants' right to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of beig cleared. The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying that eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs. Norris said that he remained committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice. But he added: "I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision to change course. "This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice. "Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment. I remain committed to structural reform which is crucial if we are to bring down the backlog." Old Bailey: All Crown Courts hear trials by jury Andrew Thomas KC - chairman of the Criminal Bar Association, which represents barristers who work in crown and magistrates courts - said the profession was "delighted". "Justice needs juries," he said. "Nothing inspires more public trust than 12 ordinary citizens from all walks of life deciding the facts of a case together. "We are also pleased that the government is going ahead with important changes in the bill to protect victims and witnesses at trial. These include new powers to prevent unfair questioning about a complainant's behaviour and to support witnesses to give their best evidence." But Thomas warned that plans to keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates by abolishing defendants' rights to ask for a jury trial could backfire - not least because of a shortage of magistrates. "The proposal to strip defendants of their right to elect a crown court trial, combined with doubling magistrates' sentencing powers to two years, would shift 25,000 cases a year - including 5,500 jury trials - out of the crown court," he said. "These are not minor offences. It includes serious and sensitive cases including assaults, sexual assaults, child abuse and grievous bodily harm. Our volunteer magistrates do an excellent job but they are completely unequipped to try complex, multi-day trials. "It would be a car crash if they tried to do it, especially at this time." Barrister Karl Turner, a Labour MP who was suspended from the parliamentary party after he criticised the government's plans to reform jury trials, thanked Burnham "for his support during my campaign". Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "This is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour have been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the Crown Court." How did the courts backlog get so bad? title: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you
description: Lots of the stars have worked together, some are good friends - and that can impact the show's dynamics.
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first two episodes of The Celebrity Traitors "I know Rob very, very well. I mean, I've sat next to him as he's had a colonic." That was Romesh Ranganathan, reminding us - in case we were in any doubt - of his close friendship with Rob Beckett in the opening episode of The Celebrity Traitors. His words sum up the key difference between this series and the regular civilian version. In Celebrity Traitors, the players aren't just on-screen competitors - many actually know each other outside the show. Lots have worked together, and some are even friends. And those previous connections can have a huge impact on the show's dynamics. It's also partly why it is quite so delightful to watch - as friendships unravel, and former co-stars turn on each other. We've been unpicking the six degrees of separation. Here are some of the connections we've found - if you spot any more, we'd love to know. Get in touch with your thoughts in the comments section below. The dynamic between Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan is one of the most enjoyable to watch play out this year. As well as being great friends in real life, they have also worked together repeatedly, including in their travel show, Rob & Romesh Vs. They've also frequently made joint appearances on panel shows such as Mock the Week. But their friendship could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said ahead of the show. "Rob is one of my best friends, and we've worked together for a decade now, but I still won't be able to trust it," he said. "I mean, he's just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity." Cast list for 2026: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses? What role would you play? Take our quiz to find out Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked Joe Lycett has said publicly that he's friends with James Acaster, and the pair have a running joke about how everyone gets them confused (Lycett cleared that up here, external). They’ve also worked together on the TV show Travel Man. Lycett is also friends with Joanne McNally, external - he's described her as "one of my favourite people in the world". But those loyalties could be about to be tested, especially now that Acaster has been recruited as a traitor (anyone remember how things panned out for "good friends" Alan Carr and Paloma Faith...?). There are SO many comedians in this year's series. And they are all likely to know each other. In addition to the alliances above, Joe Lycett was on the TV show Last One Laughing with Rob Beckett. Joanne McNally and Romesh Ranganathan appeared on game show Unacceptable together, and James Acaster went on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast. Speaking ahead of the show, McNally insisted she and her fellow comedians "haven't been in cahoots at all". "We know that we're more than willing to throw each other under the bus," she said. As for Acaster, he's admitted the other comedians are his “biggest threat” when it comes to being detected as a traitor. “Romesh, Joe, Rob know me really well. They all know that I don’t change my mind overnight,” he said, as he pondered whether to turn and help fellow traitor Richard E Grant clear his name. It won’t surprise you that the two broadcasters of the group - Maya Jama and Amol Rajan - have met their fair share of the other stars before. Rajan had previously hosted both Michael Sheen and Joe Lycett on the Radio 2 Breakfast show, and also interviewed Romesh Ranganathan on BBC Asian Network. He's also been joined on the One Show on separate occasions by Ross Kemp, Miranda Hart and James Blunt - and earlier this year, he discussed AI on stage with Hannah Fry. But in the end, Rajan became the first player to be murdered, before we really got to see the impact of those past connections. Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Maya Jama were pictured together on the front row during Milan Fashion Week in 2024 Meanwhile, Maya Jama is best known for hosting Love Island, but she's also popped up in loads of other places - including at this year's Brit Awards, where she presented an award with James Blunt. She's also been on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast, attended Milan Fashion Week with Leigh-Anne Pinnock, and she, Joe Lycett and James Acaster all appeared on The Big Fat Quiz of the Year. But Jama played down her connections on Celebrity Traitors, saying ahead of the show: “I've met a few people in the cast, but nobody really knows me, so we're all starting from scratch.” Usually the younger celebs in the castle tend to know fewer people, but Bella Ramsey is pretty well connected. Notably, Ramsey and another younger cast member, Sebastian Croft, both starred in season six of Game of Thrones. Ramsey also worked with James Blunt on the film Sunny Dancer, was interviewed by James Acaster on his Off Menu podcast - and had a funny chat about their "vegan-ish" diet with Romesh Ranganathan on The Jonathan Ross Show. Ahead of the show, Croft said he didn't know many people aside from Ramsey before joining. "One of the other things I'm excited about is this will be the first time I'm playing with people who, on the whole, don't know me and don't know how I work,” he said. “I just don't believe Richard's a traitor. I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour.” That was American model Jerry Hall, speaking after actor Richard E Grant came under (admittedly self-inflicted) pressure in the opening episode of the series. As well as being neighbours, the pair are linked in lots of other ways. title: When parenting advice becomes too much
description: Many parents feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available
body: When parenting advice becomes too much Before Rosie Whitfield became a mum, she imagined herself parenting very calm children. "Then I had two wild boys," she says with a laugh. Following the birth of her kids, Rosie spent hours online looking for the best advice and was drawn to one particular approach to parenting: Gentle parenting, which focuses on empathy and mutual respect with little emphasis on punishment, albeit with boundaries. But she constantly worried her choices, from sleep schedules to handling toddler tantrums, were "ruining their lives forever". Rosie does not blame the gentle parenting philosophy itself but instead says the overall amount of parenting advice online was "overwhelming" and "made mundane parenting choices feel like the absolute end of the world." "I felt like if I was choosing to put the TV on for 20 minutes while I did the dishes or had a coffee, I was choosing to destroy my children's brains," says Rosie, who is originally from Birmingham and now lives in Dubai. Rosie believes her confidence and intuition were stripped away as she questioned every parenting decision. And she is not alone. Government research suggests that around two-thirds of parents with young children feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available and struggle with conflicting advice, with many turning to social media for support. Rosie Whitfield says she felt overwhelmed by the amount of parenting advice online when looking for guidance on raising her two sons. And it's not just the early years. Research from the charity Action for Children found that many parents of teenagers who initially contacted the charity for help with school avoidance, ADHD or mental health, often went on to describe their own anxiety, exhaustion and uncertainty of how to parent with empathy and patience when close to burnout. Faced with an array of parenting philosophies, or "brands" to choose from, is all of this advice helping parents or making them more anxious? And is there really a best way to parent? Or, as we strive to become the perfect parent, are we losing our intuition? Parents today are confronted by parenting styles including "helicopter parenting", which is focused on closely monitoring and protecting children from harm, and "tiger parenting", which involves strict parenting and high expectations for achievement. There are also "snowplough parents", who try to remove obstacles from their child's path, and "dolphin parents", who aim to be firm but flexible. Author Matilda Gosling, who wrote Evidence‑Based Parenting, says many of the parenting fads or trends complicate what should be a straightforward relationship between a parent and child. "Some parents think 'I need to be a snowplough parent and plough all of these obstacles out of the way'." "But it really complicates what is actually a fairly fundamental part of being human, which is that you are warm and you love your children and you put in place some boundaries around them." Matilda Gosling says parenting trends can complicate the relationship between parents and their children Gosling believes parenting trends often represent a pendulum swing, with one generation trying to correct what it believes the previous one got wrong. "Throughout history, you get these swings from one extreme to the other," she says. Gentle parenting is seen by some as the latest swing away from a strict, detached parenting style popular in the 1990s, which often relied on controlled crying, the naughty step and time out. It is built around understanding, empathy and respect but also emphasises the importance of boundaries. One of the most widely studied models of parenting comes from developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind. Baumrind identified three parenting styles, later expanded to four: authoritative (high warmth and high control), authoritarian (low warmth and high control), permissive (high warmth and low control), and neglectful (low warmth and low control). "Authoritative is the gold standard," says Gosling who has looked at more than 1,000 studies. Research has found that children raised with an authoritative approach, combining warmth with clear boundaries, tend to achieve better academic results, have higher self-esteem and stronger social skills. But where gentle parenting fits within that framework is disputed. Gosling believes that it falls on the permissive side. "It's very much child-led. The child ends up having so much control that there's no sense of safety coming from the outside." However, Sarah Ockwell-Smith, who is widely credited with coining and popularising the term 'gentle parenting', strongly disagrees. "It [gentle parenting] is not remotely permissive," she says, putting it firmly in Baumrind's authoritative category. Clear boundaries are "super important". Social media, however, is flooded with memes of exhausted parents calmly negotiating with a child having a supermarket meltdown, something Ockwell-Smith finds deeply frustrating. "I have to step away from the Instagram reels and the TikToks because I just want to comment, 'This is not gentle parenting'". "You have house rules, family limits, discipline and consequences. But the difference is we look at discipline as learning and teaching rather than punishing." Toddler tantrums and teenage behaviour, she argues, should be viewed through a lens of ongoing brain development, not 'they're being naughty' or 'they hate me'. But despite the term being popular, Ockwell-Smith believes that gentle parenting is still a fringe movement and that authoritarian parenting remains the dominant style. Around 80 years ago, American paediatrician Dr Benjamin Spock published a book called Baby and Child Care, which went on to sell millions of copies and became the main source of advice for mothers for generations. title: Autumn chill to arrive this week as temperatures set to drop
description: After highs of 28C in the final week of September, cooler air will arrive this week with temperatures falling closer to the seasonal norm.
body: Temperatures are set to drop across the UK during the week ahead, bringing an end to a run of warmer-than-average autumn weather. By Wednesday, afternoon highs are expected to range from 11C (52F) in northern Scotland to 17C (63C) in southern England. It will mark a significant change from the summer-like warmth that has brought temperatures of up to 28C over the last week. If the thermometer fails to reach 20C anywhere in the UK, it will be the first time that has happened since 11 June. In south Wales, the Midlands, East Anglia and southern England, early mist and fog could linger for a while in a few locations on Sunday. However, once this clears sunny spells are expected. More cloud will develop in north Wales and northern England with the chance of a few spots of rain. Northern Ireland will be even cloudier, with some outbreaks of mainly light rain and drizzle. The wettest weather will be found across Scotland with heavy rain likely in the west, accompanied by wind gusts of 40mph or more in the far north-west. Temperatures will generally be a few degrees above the seasonal norm and could possibly reach 23C in the sunniest parts of southern England. Temperatures of 12 to 18C are typical for an early October afternoon. A weather front will erratically move southwards during Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. This will bring outbreaks of rain which will generally be heaviest in northern and western parts of the UK and lighter further east. It is possible that heavier downpours with thunder and lightning could affect southern and south-eastern England on Tuesday night and Wednesday. As the rain clears southwards cooler air will be left in its wake with daytime temperatures by midweek expected to be at - or even slightly below - the seasonal average. Some chilly nights are also expected with a touch of frost possible in prone locations. Check your local temperature forecasts on the BBC Weather website and app. With meteorological autumn covering the months of September, October and November, the season is now one-third of the way over. Met Office figures show that it has been a warmer-than-normal autumn so far, with September being the joint-fourth warmest on record for the UK as a whole. With a mean average temperature of 14.6C, it was 1.6C above the long-term average. The longer-range prospects for autumn predict more of the same. It is forecast to be warmer and wetter than average with the chance of stormy weather later in the season - partly due to the developing very strong El Niño in the Pacific. The UK is on track for one of its warmest years on record, according to the Met Office. title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations
description: Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations of a woman who says she was drugged and gang raped as "deeply disturbing".
body: A student has alleged she was drugged and gang-raped inside the Chi Phi frat house at Cornell University Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house. In an eight-minute video statement released on Saturday night, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing". The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said. Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024. She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid. Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better". "We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said. He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity". Kotlikoff said it is a "defining moment" in the university's history. "We must lead the way, we owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe," he said. On the university's campus this week, the BBC saw growing frustration about the situation. This video can not be played Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case At a public hearing for students to speak about the alleged gang rape, many told the BBC they were ashamed of what happened and said the university had failed Jane Doe. "Our administration needs to change and it needs to change drastically and it needs to change fast," one student told the BBC. "Something like this never should have happened, this is a disgrace." As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said in his video statement that there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life". "Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said. The university president also said that at the "appropriate time", the school would speak about how Cornell will "use this moment, this conversation, this anger, to help lead the broader effort to combat sexual assault not only on our campus, but beyond it". New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case. Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to lead a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter. Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent. title: The Papers: 'Another tax bombshell?' and 'Terror plot targets'
description: Several of today's papers feature Andy Burnham's latest plans as PM, including experts warning of a potential tax rise to help cover his social care plan.
body: Andy Burnham's latest plans feature in several of today's papers. The Sunday Express asks readers whether "Another tax bombshell?" will fund Burnham's social care revolution. Experts warn that workers could face another tax rise since the PM's "controversial sacrifice of the pension triple lock" will not fully cover the cost of his social care plan, the paper reports. The Observer splashes on Andy Burnham's "road back from Brexit" alongside an image of the prime minister with the stars from the EU flag apparently reflected in his glasses. The Observer's view is that the potential opening back to Europe "has the potential to be historic" for the leader and for Britain. In a move described as "yet another reversal of one of Sir Keir Starmer's flagship policies", Andy Burnham has scrapped controversial plans to cut thousands of jury trials across England and Wales, according to the Independent. The court appearance of two Iranian men harged with "plotting terror attacks at key Jewish sites" in Manchester makes the front page of the Sunday Mirror. The paper shows a synagogue and museum as two of the alleged targets. The Sunday Telegraph has more revelations about the co-pilot accused of attacking his fellow pilot on a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel earlier this week. Under the headline "Hijacker's hate rants while at UK university", the paper outlines claims about his time on a distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University. It said the pilot "advocated violence against women" and "called for severe religious punishments" in posts on Twitter, during the time he was completing the course as a remote student between 2020 and 2023. Former heavyweight champion Tyson Fury has said he wants US President Donald Trump to lead him to the ring "for his epic showdown with Anthony Joshua", according to the Daily Star. Fury and AJ are set to meet in an all-British bout at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December. Sir Kevin Sinfield is in a "league of his own", the Sunday People reports, after he completed his latest endurance challenge to raise money for motor neurone disease causes in memory of his friend and team-mate Rob Burrow, who died in 2024. Meanwhile, the paper headlines on parents of a murdered teen who want to "silence cruel web 'sleuths'." A Mail on Sunday exclusive reveals small boat migrants have received more than 1,000 free hijabs this year. According to internal government figures the UK has handed out 162 hijabs a month to migrants arriving by boat, the paper says. The Sun on Sunday leads with former England striker Andy Carroll confirming he was sexually assaulted "by a star of BBC show Fame Academy". Carroll first revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021 in an autobiography titled 'Owning it', which came out in September. Dance coach Kevin Adams was convicted in 2023 and jailed, the paper reports. And the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) was given "preferential access" to property developments in Manchester under a "sweetheart deal" with the city council, according to the Sunday Times. ADUG owns Manchester City Football Club, the paper says. Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
description: Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
body: This video can not be played Boateng Bismark James has been preaching on buses leaving Neoplan station since 2023 Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country. Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana. Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread. On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel. Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours. The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours. But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end. Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both. The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers. Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023. "I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language. Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city. We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law. Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves. "Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says. Boateng Bismark James and his group start preaching at the bus station before boarding the vehicles The new rules have divided opinion. Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship. One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace. ''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.'' In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board. "Get down, I say get down," he shouts. But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church. Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent. "The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says. Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption. "We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says. "The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds. For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income. "I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching." Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana 2012, but the law banning it has now been beefed up Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety. Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison. But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban. Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban. The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom. He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message. "There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says. For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.
