title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the military is running scenarios in the unlikely case the US invades Canada.
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion. Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency. "That's just risk management," Carney said. Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans. In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims. "President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week. Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence. But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds. In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely. A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions. "I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC. Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence. They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked. The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence. Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare. This video can not be played After President Trump shared an AI meme with gun-toting geese, the BBC's Jessica Murphy asks how Canada could hit back economically After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally. But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum. "Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said. Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled. Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City. In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation. Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles. Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence. It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence. They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy. A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared. "That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios." Canada-US relations have deteriorated under the second Trump presidency. Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted. He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way. "It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said. Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed. So what would it be like if it happened? The first phase of a war could be quite short. According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy. Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials. The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault. The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said. He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging

title: The murder of a journalist 25 years on - why has no one been caught?
description: Martin O'Hagan was shot dead as he walked home from a pub with his wife in Lurgan, County Armagh in 2001. His killers have never been caught.
body: Martin O'Hagan was shot dead as he walked home from a pub with his wife in Lurgan, County Armagh in 2001 The brother of a journalist, who was shot dead as he walked home with his wife, says if he did not continue to fight for answers around the murder "the guilt would kill me". Earlier this week marked the 25th anniversary of the 2001 murder of investigative reporter Martin O'Hagan. The 51-year-old died in Lurgan, County Armagh, and was shot when walking home from a pub - a killing that was claimed by the Red Hand Defenders, a cover name used by both the Loyalist Volunteer Force and Ulster Defence Association. But while his murder received widespread condemnation, and numerous charges that were subsequently withdrawn, no one has ever been convicted. Those close to Martin have said pledges from police and government officials to find those responsible have gone unfulfilled, and they remain frustrated that his death has not received the same recognition as other high profile killings. Martin was the first person to be murdered for being a journalist in Northern Ireland since the outbreak of the Troubles in 1969. As a reporter for the Sunday World newspaper, he had built a reputation for stories which exposed paramilitaries and drug dealers operating in Northern Ireland. He had infuriated County Armagh paramilitary bosses, particularly murdered LVF leader Billy Wright who he labelled 'King Rat', by exposing crime and drugs rackets. His brother Fintan told BBC News NI there was "talk that he was digging into collusion, digging into the finances of the LVF but there was never any proof". "At the time I believed they did it because Martin made a mistake moving up there on the outskirts of Mourneview, a loyalist estate. "Martin said at the time: 'the war is over'. It's all very well wishful thinking but at the end of the day it was a foolish thing to do. He made it easy for them and that's a very hard thing to live with," Fintan said. "Within a short period of time the police were assuring us they were going to catch them" and "we, like fools, believed them". Hundreds of people lined the streets of Lurgan for Martin's funeral Fintan now says he believes the people who murdered Martin were British agents. In 2022, security sources told a BBC Spotlight investigation that police were given names of people said to have been involved in the killing within 48 hours but did not act on the information. Fintan said, given the extensive surveillance of the Mid Ulster LVF, to believe that the intelligence service did not know Martin's murder was being planned is "just unbelievable". He said the family have flagged a number of details about the case with the Police Ombudsman's office and if they are not included in the upcoming report then it's "not worth the paper it's written on". He said while he is "hopeful", the family have had so many disappointments they do not get their hopes built up and deal with it in a "business-like fashion". "It will come out, whether or not it confirms everything that I have experienced and seen and read – I doubt it." In a statement, the Ombudsman's office said that since her appointment as new Police Ombudsman in June, Jacqui Durkin has been in contact with the O'Hagan family and "assured them that the completion of the public statement is one of her early priorities". "She is actively reviewing the draft public statement and will provide the family with a publication timeline in due course." A UK government spokesperson said Martin's murder was a "horrific attack on freedom of speech" and urged anyone with information to contact police. "The safety of journalists is paramount," they added. "The UK government remains steadfastly committed to ensuring journalists are able to carry out their work free from threat, intimidation, or violence." Martin O'Hagan had infuriated County Armagh paramilitary bosses, particularly murdered LVF leader Billy Wright who he labelled 'King Rat' Martin had a history of involvement in the Official IRA (the group from which the Provisional IRA would emerge) and spent five years in Long Kesh prison in the early 1970s for moving weapons. Fintan said he turned his back on violence when he got out of prison, got his degree and became a journalist. "I think the fact that Martin had been in jail and in the Official IRA, which is no secret, I think that affected things," said Fintan. "The first journalist [to be murdered in Northern Ireland], the flag bearers of free speech and the right to know is journalism, and it didn't really catch fire the way it should have, and I think it was his background of being a working-class republican," Fintan said. "If you can't protect your journalists there's no such thing as news or free speech." Journailst Richard Sullivan worked alongide Martin at the Sunday World Richard Sullivan worked alongside Martin at the Sunday World and said the then Secretary of State John Reid stood in their offices and pledged that they would catch his killers and "no stone would be left un-turned in pursuing them". "He also said that he would ensure that journalists would be able to work in Northern Ireland free from threat. "Yet journalists continue to be threatened, even right up to this current day. And obviously, 25 years, a quarter of a century after Marty was killed, there's no sign of a prosecution," Sullivan said. Martin's case has been contrasted with the murder of journalist Veronica Guerin in Dublin five years previously. She had written several exposés of organised crime in Dublin and had been subjected to threats and beatings. Within a week of her murder, the Irish government enacted the Proceeds of Crime Act 1996 and the Criminal Assets Bureau Act 1996, so that assets purchased with money obtained through crime could be seized by the government, leading to the formation of the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB

title: US father and son arrested after 'gas station heroin' deaths
description: They are accused of selling at least one student derivatives of kratom, often called "gas station heroin" in the US.
body: Kratom is legal in some states, including Mississippi A father and son who worked at a Mississippi smoke shop have been arrested and charged in connection with the death of at least one university student who died from a suspected overdose of kratom, sometimes called "gas station heroin" in the US. The pair worked at a shop that allegedly sold derivatives of the substance to University of Mississippi students. US prosecutors charged Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Yahya Mosleh, 18, for possession with the intent to distribute controlled substances in connection with the death investigation of two Ole Miss students last month. Although their deaths have not officially been attributed to kratom, officials afterward issued warnings about consuming kratom. The criminal complaint alleges that on 21 September, an Ole Miss student was found dead in his dorm room. The apparent cause of death "appeared to be consistent with a drug overdose", the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi said in a press release. Law enforcement found packages - with some tablets missing - of suspected kratom derivatives. About an hour later, a second student was found dead from a suspected overdose in another location, also with packages of suspected kratom derivatives. Officials connected the packages with the local vape, tobacco and beer store, the US Attorney's statement said. Law enforcement executed search warrants and seized suspected kratom derivative controlled substances from the store. The Mosleh's, father and son, were later arrested. The two students' deaths have sparked alarm and warnings from officials about the plant-based drug referred to as "gas station heroin". Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form. For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it is illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi. The Mississippi prosecutors said that kratom derivatives, such as MGPI, MGM-15 and MGM-16, are now schedule I controlled substances in the US and can be significantly more potent than natural kratom leaf products and morphine. title: Two going on four, five or six on good night for new Scotland era
description: Scotland scored twice in North Macedonia but the scoreline does not reflect their dominance in Skopje, writes Tom English.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: North Macedonia 0-2 Scotland When Scott McKenna was sent off late in the night in Skopje, North Macedonia did something they looked entirely incapable of doing for 80-plus minutes spent buried in Scotland's collective pocket. They strung a couple of passes together, had a few shots, raised an odd cheer from their dismally small support. Fair play to them because for much of this Nations League game it looked as if they were comatose; out-played and out-fought. Scotland, with their energy and urgency, had reduced them to the ranks of the lifeless. Skopje is a city of statues, two or three hundred of them apparently, great big things in squares and in fountains commemorating tsars and dames, emperors and warriors, royalty and revolutionaries. You could have taken any 11 of them off their perch and put them in the North Macedonia starting line-up and they'd have posed Scotland more of a challenge than the beleaguered home team managed for most of this encounter. At one point in the first half a dog ran on to the pitch. They'd have been better off putting a shirt on his back. At least he'd have had some bite. Scotland beat North Macedonia in Nations League for Pocognoli's first win 'It means everything' - numbers behind Robertson's 100-cap Scotland career Robertson hits 100 Scotland caps - but who else makes top 10? The scoreline does a terrible job in capturing what happened. Scotland had 25 shots to nine, 10 on target to zero. Before McKenna walked, they had touched the ball 37 times in North Macedonia's penalty area, North Macedonia had touched it twice in Scotland's. On the night that Andy Robertson won his 100th cap, this was one of his most straightforward matches of all. A stroll. A rout, if two goals can be called a rout. Two going on four and five, maybe six on what was a poor pitch in a soulless stadium, save for the visiting fans, who made a racket, as ever. It was a good evening for the new era. Scotland were exciting, entertaining and also frustrating. They had ambition but not enough execution. They created chance upon chance but didn't have the killer touch nearly as often as you'd like. That might come as things progress. Certainly, a burden was lifted off the head coach, Sebastien Pocognoli. No more chat about the search for the elusive goal, no more of that creeping negativity as he waited for a first win. The air is a touch lighter for him now as he prepares for Slovenia at Hampden on Tuesday. It was a big occasion for Robertson the centurion; a major achievement in the career of Kieron Bowie, who rifled in a terrific early goal that settled everyone down; a memorable experience for Luis Binks, Stephen Welsh and the substitute Robbie Ure, who now know what it feels like not just to play for their country but to win for their country. Binks and Welsh look at home in that Scotland defence. There was a strong sense from the start that everything would be OK for Scotland and it came in the shape of the Duracell Bunny that was the captain. Robertson began like a dervish. A shot after five minutes, then another and another and another. Four shots in 13 minutes - he's never had four shots in 90 minutes in any one of his 99 caps before Saturday. There was positivity for Scotland from early on. They had six shots in 15 minutes, the most picture-perfect of them being Bowie's strike. Oli McBurnie did some work beforehand - his wait for a goal goes on, 19 caps and counting - then the wonderful Billy Gilmour got involved. Is Gilmour a six or an eight? The truth is that he's both, a tempo-setter when dropping deep, a dangerous passer when moving forward, a complete footballer at the peak of his powers. Then it was all about Bowie. His footwork did for a defender, his accuracy did for a goalkeeper. It was a rare moment of precision in front of goal, another illustration that despite their issues in scoring goals, Scotland have a promising array of strikers these days. Time, and the confidence of this victory, should make them better. This video can not be played Pocognoli on 'special' moment for Robertson Ben Gannon-Doak turned North Macedonia inside out and upside down. He is woefully short of minutes for his club, Bournemouth, and lacks sharpness and ruthlessness as a consequence. His delivery has always lacked accuracy. His raw materials, though, are exhilarating. His pace, his involvement, his number of touches, his chances. He never left North Macedonia alone. They survived only because he blasted over with one of his chances, shot tamely with another, lost composure with a third one. Having tormented North Macedonia, he allowed them off the hook, but he was a one-man thrill-fest. He's 20, that can't be forgotten. He's going to be around for a lot of years and will play a heap of big games, but with his club he's got some decisions to make. Two minutes against Liverpool, 19 against Sociedad, eight against Brentford, one minute against Newcastle and Man City. The only game he has started this season was a League Cup tie against Lincoln. Bournemouth is a tough team to get into, but he needs more time on the grass, more opportunity to develop. Maybe a loan move in January would make sense for him, if his club allows him to go. A big 'if'. That's a situation Gannon-Doak needs to resolve for himself - and for Scotland. This video can not be played 'It's been a pleasure to stand alongside him' - McGinn on captain Robbo The chances flowed - one thunderbolt from the influential John McGinn, one near-miss from Bowie after excellence from Gannon-Doak, one off a post from McKenna. A second came via the penalty. McGinn lashed it home and drew alongside Lawrie Reilly on the all-time list - 22 and counting. After some indifferent performances, that one would have meant an awful lot to him, a strike to silence some mild ques

title: 'An unbelievable story' - inside unfancied Wakefield's rapid ascent
description: Wakefield's stars of yesteryear are remembered in sepia but now the class of 2026 has added glorious colour to their success after winning a previously unfathomable Super League title.
body: This video can not be played Wakefield are champions for the first time in since 1968 beating Warrington There is a moment in the 1939 film 'The Wizard of Oz' where Dorothy swaps her monochrome world for glorious, eye-opening technicolour the minute she touches down in the Land of Oz. The same could be said for the moment that Wakefield Trinity got their hands on the Super League trophy when they beat Warrington Wolves 23-10 in Saturday's Grand Final. Metaphorically of course, but the achievements of that great club had before only been seen in those black and white hues and so were ripe for a dash of colour. Derek 'Rocky' Turner, Neil Fox MBE, Don Fox, Harold Poynton, Ken Rollin... all legends of the 1960s and an era when all the silverware found its way to WF1. Belle Vue, or the DIY Kitchens Stadium as it is now known, has had its special nights since, such as the win to relegate rivals Castleford and secure safety at their expense in 2006. Amid all the adrenaline and excitement, that was survival. Not success. Yet, this season has followed a different storyline. Wakefield could achieve something. Wakefield could be winners. And that they are, landing their first title since 1968. Daryl Powell tapped into the historical significance of the Grand Final in the build up to the showdown, as winger Tom Johnstone explained before the showpiece event. "Daryl put a Powerpoint presentation on the screen, and said 'You could be legends of this club', and that was it," Johnstone told BBC Radio 5 live just days before scoring a try in the Grand Final and picking up the Rob Burrow Award as man of the match. "He didn't really go any further into it, he just put a seed in the back of your mind and just gave you that little nugget." The team of the 1960s was the last Wakefield team to enjoy sustained achievement at the top level Going back to the movie theme, Wakefield's resurrection over the past three seasons is almost too fanciful for Hollywood's scriptwriters, given the rapid ascent. Owner Matt Ellis is without doubt the lead character, having come in as a fan but also an incredibly wealthy and successful kitchen magnate. It has been more than just investment thrown at it; for example Ellis has been hands-on with the stadium renovation in terms of standards and finish on the back of the work of former custodians Michael Carter and John Minards who set the ball rolling. He also has brought drive and vision, and it was he who was determined to bring Powell to the club as head coach almost immediately after taking control. "Everything has changed from the top to the bottom," Johnstone added. "Rather than going into individual key details, the facilities have changed, the manner of the club, just the belief and the ambition of the club is probably the best one. "We used to say a lot of things and say we wanted to compete but we had no chance of doing it at the time. Whereas now, it's an elite club. It's run so well. "Anything you need, you've got it. Matt will provide absolutely anything. He just wants to see success. And the players we've signed and the team we've built, it just shows. It's just night and day." Ellis and Powell has been a near-perfect partnership; with promotion back to Super League, Wembley success in the 1895 Cup, and back-to-back play-off appearances in Super League all culminating in the glorious win at Old Trafford. Powell had enjoyed success at Featherstone and Castleford before a stint at Warrington ended prematurely, and joining Wakefield has had a revitalising impact on both club and coach. "This is an unbelievable story," Powell said. "From me thinking a bloke's trying to sell me a kitchen to winning the Super League is phenomenal. It's been an unbelievable three years. "I'm amazed really at the boys and how good they've been. Obviously, it's pretty sweet for me tonight as an individual but for the club, the players, the coaching staff, everything that we've built up over the last three years is phenomenal. "What happened tonight is the best thing that could have happened to Super League, 100%. A sell-out crowd and a team like us, you know the story before the game, it's awesome. It shows the [salary] cap is working as a team like us can come from the Championship and win in two years, that's big." Wakefield beat Warrington to win Super League Super League Grand Final as it happened: Wakefield beat Warrington to win first Super League title Caius Faatili, known as 'Captain Chaos' at Wakefield, is an eyecatching figure with his aggressive, all-energy style Powell has turned to familiar faces to fill those key roles; Michael Shenton - once his captain at Castleford, is now his trusted assistant while Ste Mills - another acolyte of yore is the brains behind the recruitment. Aside from that, former Trinity player and modern day favourite Danny Kirmond is also on the staff while the experienced Stu Dickens also adds to the brains trust. On the pitch, Powell has reunited with Jake Trueman, whose form in his time at Castleford put him in the international picture, and Mike McMeeken, who was part of the 2017 team at the Tigers who lost to Leeds in the Grand Final. Front-rower McMeeken's authority and presence were a huge pick up for Trinity when he signed from Catalans as a statement signing on their top flight return, part of a powerful pack which highlights the best of Mills' talentspotting. Bringing that power are Ky Rodwell from NRL side Parramatta, and ex-Cronulla reserve grader Caleb Hamlin-Uele - both signed while Trinity were still in the Championship. Since getting up, Caius Faatili was brought in from Queensland Cup side Sunshine Coast Falcons in 2025 and was an immediate success with his raw-boned and aggressive style; lean, muscular Isaiah Vagana is rangy and athletic in the back-row, while Samoa international Jazz Tevaga has brough

title: Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'
description: Jude Bellingham's international future was being called into question a year ago, but now he is regarded as potentially one of England's "greatest of all time".
body: Jude Bellingham is the first player to record three assists in a game for England since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021 Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of football's "greatest of all time". The Real Madrid man was left out of Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad in October 2025 and his place at the World Cup was called into question, with the German head coach saying Bellingham wouldn't get star treatment. But Bellingham did of course make the squad for the World Cup and was arguably his team's standout performer, finishing as England's top scorer with seven goals as they reached the semi-finals and finished third. He has already shown that he is world class with starring performances for club and country, but the way he helped England to dismantle Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday looked like someone perhaps reaching a new level. The 23-year-old was instrumental in Rijeka, scoring as well as registering a hat-trick of assists. He even ended the match wearing the captain's armband as England inflicted the heaviest defeat in Croatia's history. "Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time," former Manchester United and Republic of Ireland midfielder Roy Keane said on ITV after the game. "At this moment in time, he is an amazing footballer. The package – his running power, his delivery, his goal threat. The way he is progressing as a player, I still think there is a lot more to come from him." Bellingham, recently voted England's player of the year for the second year in a row, is now "nailed on as the 10" for the future, former England defender Matt Upson told BBC Radio 5 Live. Keane added: "He has been fantastic in possession, but what he does out of possession lifts all these other players. "If you have a player that good in your team, who is amazing in possession and he's playing for Real Madrid and doing brilliant things, but his work rate off the ball... that will just inspire other players. He is a huge leader for them." Tuchel has started Bellingham over Morgan Rogers during and after the World Cup England's front four will share praise for the way in which they demolished the Croatian backline. Record goalscorer Harry Kane scored twice, as did Bukayo Saka, with Anthony Gordon scoring and assisting too. And Kane will be back in the spotlight on Tuesday when he can equal Peter Shilton's all-time England men's appearance record against the Czech Republic at Wembley. In moving to 89 goals for his country, the 33-year-old again showed how irreplaceable he is for England, but, when he was rested with 20 minutes to go, it was Bellingham who took the captain's armband. And that highlighted the younger man's importance as a leader within the squad. Bellingham was also directly involved in more than two goals in an England game for the first time, and he became the first player to record three assists in a game for the Three Lions since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021. It was Bellingham's performance in front of goal that impressed former England striker Ian Wright. "When Bellingham is on the pitch, he is always driving forward and going again and again," Wright said. "He was involved in everything. His athleticism, his technical ability, his intensity. He never lets up, the way he gets in the box, he is always in there unmarked. He is always in there." Bellingham showed every aspect of his game against Croatia and Tuchel was asked by BBC Sport if he had gone to another level. "Yes, at the moment it seems like it, and you always need to," Tuchel said. "It's like you can never stand still. You have to develop and you have to push for the next level, otherwise other teams will catch up." Tuchel, who said the performance was a way to "move on" after the disappointment of England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, said that he "adjusted some things" following the tournament, giving players, including Bellingham, "a lot of responsibility". Saka was part of the front four and Bellingham assisted his first goal with a high quality cross. "He was amazing tonight," Saka said of Bellingham. "He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special. "[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team." title: Tories pledge to scrap £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge'
description: Party leader Kemi Badenoch tells the BBC that she wants to see "people who work harder" not getting punished for doing so.
body: This video can not be played Watch: People shouldn't be punished for working harder, Badenoch says The Conservatives have promised to scrap the "absurd cliff edge" that mean parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year. Under the current system, only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for government-funded or tax-free childcare. "What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so," Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme. The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham. The party said the move would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest. This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday. Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare, external for children aged between nine months and four years old. However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year. The same £100,000 threshold applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme, external. For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare. The Tories said they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely so parents no longer lose childcare support when their income exceeds this level. The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds. Badenoch told the BBC the party didn't want "people to stop working because of that". Speaking before the party's conference, she added: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning £10,000 or £100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working". Asked if this could result in someone who earns £1 million a year get free childcare under a Conservative government, Badenoch responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy." What does childcare cost and how do government-funded hours work in England? Education secretary to ask competition watchdog to review hidden childcare costs Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference The Tories argue the threshold may mean some people may delay having children until their incomes change, or decide not to start a family at all, describing scrapping it as "both pro-family and pro-growth". By providing an increased incentive to work, the Tories said the move would also boost economic growth. They added that it would tackle the "unfairness" that the threshold is calculated on an individual earner's income rather then for the whole household. In a statement, Griffith said: "Removing this childcare cliff edge is the first step in our mission to deliver lower, simpler, and fairer taxes across the board." The party said the policy would be funded by cutting the number of public servants working in "executive non-departmental public bodies" - organisations which have a role in the processes of national government but operate at arm's length from ministers, such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency. It said this would save £1.6bn by 2029-30, covering the estimated £700 million cost of removing the childcare "cliff edge". Badenoch arrived in Birmingham on Saturday ahead of the annual conference, and vowed the party was new and different from the one that lost the 2024 general election. The party - which is currently polling behind Labour and Reform UK - is expected to use the event to lay out more of its growing policy agenda ahead of the next general election. title: Leicester hold off Newcastle for first Prem win
description: Leicester Tigers pick up their first win of the season with a tense and hard-fought victory at Newcastle Red Bulls in the Prem.
body: Adam Radwan moved to Leicester Tigers in January 2025 after eight and a half seasons at Newcastle Tries: Ene, McGuigan, Jordan Cons: Connon, Henry Tries: Moli, Radwan, Hurd Cons: Searle 3 Pens: Searle Leicester Tigers picked up their first win of the season with a tense and hard-fought victory at Newcastle Red Bulls. Former Newcastle winger Adam Radwan scored on his return to Kingston Park as the Tigers won for the first time in seven matches in all competitions, following a dismal run which stretches back into last season. After being edged out by two points in a high-scoring thriller by Saracens six days ago, Leicester had to show their grit and determination to cling on to victory against a Newcastle side who threatened a late comeback. Newcastle took the lead through Obi Ene's early score but, despite putting in a positive showing, they ultimately came up just short in their first home match of the season. Gloucester thrash sorry Quins to go top of the Prem Rees-Zammit stars as Bristol power past Northampton Wade closes in on record as tries dominate Prem Ene scored three minutes into his Prem debut after Newcastle moved the ball left. The former Sale winger weaved inside, having collected fly-half Brett Connon's excellent cut-out pass, to dive over for the opener. But Leicester hit back when hooker Samiuela Moli launched himself over at the back of a driving maul and Billy Searle popped over the conversion to give Tigers a slender advantage. Gabriel Hamer-Webb had an opportunity to go over for Leicester soon after but was pushed into touch by an excellent try-saving tackle from Christian Wade, before Hamer-Webb made his own outstanding score-stopping challenge as Newcastle's Harrison Obatoyinbo threatened to break clear. That moment proved to be pivotal as former Newcastle winger Radwan latched on to Freddie Steward's exquisite grubber kick to touch down. After Searle kicked the conversion, the fly-half then added a penalty in front of the sticks. Newcastle missed two presentable opportunities to score a second try before half-time and the match restarted in a scrappy manner after the break - until Ene was prevented from scoring a second try of the match thanks to a textbook challenge from Leicester replacement Will Wand. Radwan spurned a good opportunity to score his second, kicking the ball dead when he had a whole half of the field to run into. Leicester were made to pay for their profligacy when George McGuigan's pick-and-go enabled him to drive over from close range to help pull the deficit back to five points. Leicester got a vital third try of the night when Will Hurd's quick tap let him barrel over, and Searle kicked the conversion to make it a two-score game once more with 12 minutes remaining. Newcastle carved through Leicester with just under seven minutes left when Ollie Leatherbarrow's bold carry saw him break a tackle as Cameron Jordan went over with Zack Henry adding the extras. With the clock ticking down, Wade carried Newcastle forward with a trademark burst down the wing, but the home side were eventually guilty of holding on as Leicester gratefully kicked to touch to claim victory. Newcastle Red Bulls director of rugby Dan McFarland told BBC Radio Newcastle: "I'm really disappointed, to be honest. It was a game we could have won. Really pleased with the way we approached the game. I thought we were full of effort, full of energy. "Most importantly, we were full of the endeavour that we wanted to put in, in terms of the way we wanted to play the game. "Unfortunately, we were not accurate enough in key areas - but that will grow. "We are trying not to play in a boring way. Today, we weren't where we wanted to be. In the first half, we gave away penalties at set-piece and let them into our 22. I thought we improved in that area as the game went on." Leicester Tigers head coach Geoff Parling told BBC Radio Leicester: "Gritty and dogged. Defensively, some good resolve and they're [Newcastle] going to break some teams this year with their quality attack and good speed. "You go all pre-season and you try to build some real cohesion and you lose a lot of guys in the same position, but no excuses, we've just got to be better. I've got to help those guys to be able to execute in those moments. "There's loads to improve on. The general feeling in the changing room is disappointment, which is great for me. "Accuracy in the second half, especially at set-piece, we didn't allow ourselves to build up some pressure." Newcastle Red Bulls: Obatoyinbo; Wade, Hearle, Harris, Ene; Connon, Elliott; Rakete-Stones, McGuigan, Millar Mills; Usher, Jordan, Hicks, Christie (capt), Sotutu. Replacements: Fletcher, Brocklebank, Harper, Molina, Leatherbarrow, Graham, Benitez Cruz, Henry. Leicester Tigers: Steward; Radwan, Kata, Bailey, Hamer-Webb; Searle, Van Poortvliet (capt); Vunipola, Moli, Heyes; Thompson, Henderson, Wainwright, Reffell, Cracknell. Replacements: Thunder, Haffar, Hurd, Manz, Moro, Whiteley, Wand, Hassell-Collins. title: How to spot a psychopath at work - from a man who worried he could be one
description: Geraint Anderson says some modern workplaces reward psychopathic traits.
body: Geraint Anderson said success became an obsession for him during his time as a trader in London Most of us have had colleagues who can be tricky to work with. They may act impulsively, be manipulative, or even outright lie to advance their careers - but how can you tell the difference between an unpleasant co-worker and someone displaying psychopathic traits? Geraint Anderson, a former London banker-turned author, said he was assessed by a clinical psychologist who told him he may have had "situational psychopathy" in order to succeed in the cut-throat corporate world. "I had to really become a kind of worse version of myself in order to thrive in this environment," he said. Anderson, 53, who now lives in Monmouthshire, said some modern workplaces and social influences reward psychopathic traits. He worked for 12 years as an analyst in London's financial district and earned millions of pounds before leaving his job ahead of the financial crash in 2008. "The city rewards this dark triad behaviour... being uber confident, being able to control and manipulate others, not getting emotionally involved in decisions and being decisive," he said. "I adapted myself for the city and started bringing out the kind of worst side of myself." Anderson only intended to work in the corporate world for a few years - but ended up climbing the ranks A psychopath is someone with an antisocial personality disorder, external, rather than a clinical diagnosis itself. People with these disorders think and act differently to others and, among other things: Have difficulty sustaining long-term relationships Are unable to control their anger Lack guilt and blame others for problems in their lives In his early 20s, Anderson was enjoying life in Goa, India, selling trinkets to tourists on the beach. His brother convinced him to apply for a finance job, which he only intended to do for a few years. "I cut off my ponytail, shaved off my beard, took all my earrings out, bought a £60 suit - all that's totally true - the day before I had my interview." Once he had his foot in the door as an intern, success became an obsession, with bonuses becoming "a way of gauging how wonderfully successful a human being I was". This figure allowed him to compare himself to people at other banks and "really appealed to my competitiveness". He believes some of the traits that helped him climb the ranks were those associated with psychopathy. "I had a degree of fearlessness. I had a bit of - dare I say - glib charm. I wasn't hugely emotionally affected by things that happened on the trading floor." Anderson became the anonymous columnist Cityboy before hanging up his corporate coat and becoming an author Anderson said a lot of traits psychopaths possess are ones "that the corporate environment rewards" and are "incredibly useful in high-powered jobs in the city". He added the most important thing when it comes to psychopaths is "you don't promote them, you don't marry them and you don't vote for them." Robert Snowden, a Cardiff University psychologist, has studied psychopathy for about 25 years and has worked with Robert Hare, the creator of the psychopathy checklist (PCL-R). It consists of 20 questions, each scoring between zero and two, with a maximum score of 40. Snowden said most people scored below five, while 25 or over was typically the threshold for psychopathy. Anderson scored himself about an eight or a nine. "Psychopathy is on a dimension that I could place you, I could place myself," Snowden said. Robert Snowden says the fundamental trait of psychopathy is the lack of empathy for other people "They can be very strong and, in some ways, make good leaders... but there are many deficits to their leadership and it's all about them and not about other people," he added; "The fundamental trait of psychopathy is that lack of empathy for other people. "Most psychopaths never kill anybody. But they may take advantage of other people, exploit other people, not care about other people." Snowden said some corporate environments may appeal to people with psychopathic traits as they often need "to be quite unemphatic" and focused on making money. There is no treatment available for psychopathy, as "psychopaths often believe that there's nothing wrong with them". Anderson was recently evaluated by Kerry Daynes, a consultant and forensic psychologist, who concluded he was not a psychopath. Daynes said he may have become a "situational psychopath", adapting his behaviour to thrive in an environment that rewarded ruthless ambition. She added: "You don't need to be a psychopath to thrive - for a while at least - in a psychopathic culture." She said Anderson was able to "crank up" his "darker personality characteristics" to succeed in his environment, something that was in "the sweet spot that most people can't attain". Consultant and forensic psychologist Kerry Daynes said Anderson adapted his behaviour to thrive in an environment that rewarded ruthless ambition Despite rapidly rising through the ranks of London finance, Anderson said he became disillusioned by "greed, reckless risk-taking and rule breaking in the industry". "I just looked around and thought 'I'm on the wrong team'... What on Earth are you doing? You are part of the problem." He left and became the anonymous columnist City Boy, for the London Paper every Friday, revealing a world of excessive wining, dining, drugs and illicit sex. It transformed into a the book Cityboy that sold more than 400,000 copies and was translated into six languages. He's also recently just published his fifth book which explores how adopting psychopathic traits can help people climb the corporate ladder. Anderson said he was a "less pleasant person" while in the corporate world but hopes he is a "warmer person" now "I'm more able to feel like trying to have integrity and not manipulate and be ruthless." title: Are AI models the next big danger for body image?
description: Could the rise of AI models in advertising and on social media harm young people's body confidence?
body: AI models such as Aitana Lopez were generated for advertising agency The Clueless AI models are popping up more and more across social media and advertising, but how might this affect body image? Mia Perumal, who has recovered from an eating disorder, said she's worried the technology could make unrealistic beauty standards even harder for young people to escape. The 19-year-old Cardiff University student said she believes if she'd had access to AI during her eating disorder, it would have had a "terrible impact". AI-generated videos and photos are getting harder to spot too, she said. This story contains material about eating disorders and self-harm. When Mia Perumal was 12 she says she was fed harmful content via social media algorithms. Now she fears the rise of AI models is magnifying the damage on other young people. Mia has noticed an increase in very thin AI beautiful people on social media in the past year, the comments often being from 12-year-old girls saying: "Dream body, drop your workout routine I want to look like this." She said she finds it "really sad" because looking like AI models is completely unobtainable, she believes the only option to prevent harm is for AI to be controlled. Mia Perumal says AI models and content should be controlled Mia said: "It's all very well saying 'oh, it's AI, it's not real,' But eating disorders don't really listen to rationality." She said she wants young people to "be cautious, question everything". In the early 2000s Kelly Watts, like most teenagers, was worried about the way she looked and said she was constantly comparing herself to people around her and models in magazines, she said. Now 41, she is worried her 11-year-old son will compare his body to fake photographs of "perfect people". As a freelancer in marketing, AI in business images are something Kelly is seeing everywhere, but often without tags meaning it is hard to determine whether it is real or fake. "At first, I didn't realise they were AI, but the more you see it, the more you can't unsee it. Now, I see it on quite a regular basis," said Kelly. Her son Oscar loves playing rugby and is becoming more aware that "some friends are taller", she said. While he has not raised concerns about his body, she fears he could look up to AI characters online. Kelly Watts says she often compared herself to others growing up and it affected her confidence The 11-year-old watches YouTube and does not yet have social media. But this does not keep him away from AI, which she fears has infiltrated YouTube's content. Watching footballers who have six-packs is already a body-image influence, she said, let alone being then shown AI generated people who are unrealistic. "Especially with children, it's going to be 'can they ever get to that point? "It's putting a lot of pressure on them, which they don't need," she said. "No one and nothing is perfect. I don't want him growing up thinking he has to be perfect." "I'm his mum, and the last person he's going to listen to over a big influencer," she said, even if that influencer is AI. Kelly said AI-literacy is important, and being able to spot real vs fake is essential. "At what point do we need to be aware that it potentially can be damaging to us and our children, and AI should definitely be labelled more." "Why do we want to compare ourselves to a robot instead of a human?" Kelly is worried her 11-year-old son could develop body image issues from AI "As human beings, we have this tendency to compare ourselves to others," said Phillippa Diedrichs, professor of psychology at the Centre for Appearance Research, UWE Bristol. She said: "If we're comparing ourselves to a very narrow beauty standard, which typically tends to be the case, the beauty ideals that we have are very narrowly defined, and that inevitably means that many of us are not going to meet those beauty ideals. "This is particularly the case with social media and digitally constructed images because they don't even exist in biological reality. "We compare ourselves and when we fall short, this can lead us to doubt ourselves and feel negatively about our own appearance." She said if AI was used to create more diversity and inclusion, then "when we compare ourselves, we feel alike and similar, which can either have a neutral or positive impact on our wellbeing". Diedrichs said unless the designers prompt AI to show realistic or diverse features, "it's going to give you an image that defaults to the average" data set of the "narrow" traditional beauty standards. "So for example, people of colour, gender, queer people, people with kind of interesting and distinguishing facial features, it means that they're going to be left out," she said. "You can try and overcompensate that with the way you prompt and create these images. But if you don't do that, you're going to get very generic images, which tend to reinforce a lot of the biases that we have in society." She said it could create even more unrealistic beauty standards, "if it's not done carefully or with some thought because it will default to the average of whatever it's learnt from. Diedrichs said there are "tell-tale" signs like "the texture of the skin or the eyes" and how "coily hair" looks. She added that the absence of blemishes or pores can be a good way of identifying AI, however it is constantly getting better. Some models have AI twins, as pictured here, that let them be in "two places at once", says London-based model Alexsandrah Gondora Diedrichs said teenagers can be influenced but they are also often "critical and aware, and have more knowledge about technology than older people". "The thing is, though, we can be aware that these things are happening, but it doesn't necessarily stop us from wanting to look like those images," she said. title: Fury wants 'old pal' President Trump for Joshua ringwalk
description: Former heavyweight champion Tyson Fury plans to ask US president Donald Trump to lead his ring walk before fighting Anthony Joshua.
body: US President Donald Trump and British boxer Tyson Fury met earlier this year Former heavyweight champion Tyson Fury plans to ask US president Donald Trump to lead his ringwalk before fighting Anthony Joshua. Fury and Joshua are set to meet in an long-awaiting all-British bout at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December. Trump and Fury met at UFC Freedom 250 at the White House in June. The Manchester-born fighter wore a cap emblazoned with the words "Donald Trump for Prime Minister" after his US travel ban was lifted by the 80-year-old. "I'll definitely make that offer to my old buddy, old pal, and we'll see if he's available," said 38-year-old Fury. "Probably unlikely because of the situation he's in at the moment, being the President of the United States." Fury also said his match with Joshua, 36, is preparation for a third meeting with Oleksandr Usyk. Ukraine's Usyk twice defeated Fury in 2024 and is unbeaten in 25 professional fights. Fury said he had "no intention" of retiring after fighting Joshua and views the contest with his compatriot as a "warm-up for Usyk". He added: "This is a bum to me and I can guarantee that on the night, when I knock him spark out, he won't know what time it is. And then I want the rabbit [Usyk] in New York City. "This year will be the most active year for me since 2018. I've done 12 rounds with a 6ft 8in Arslanbek Makhmudov and I've done seven rounds with another 6ft 7in behemoth in Mariusz Wach. "Let's not pull any punches here. I'm firing on all cylinders at the moment. I feel fantastic. I'm 38 years young." title: Wakefield beat Warrington to win Super League
description: Wakefield Trinity end a 58-year wait to be champions as they claim a deserved Grand Final success over Warrington Wolves at Old Trafford.
body: This video can not be played Wakefield are champions for the first time in since 1968 beating Warrington Betfred Super League Grand Final Tries: Lindop 2 Goal: Irwin Tries: Scott, Vagana, Tevaga, Johnstone Goals: Jowitt 3 Drop goal: Sinfield Wakefield Trinity became only the sixth, and most unlikely, club to win the Super League title after a deserved win over Warrington Wolves. Only two years after being in the Championship and in their first ever Grand Final, Wakefield took to the Old Trafford stage as if they were to the manor born. Daryl Powell's side did the bulk of the damage in a devastating first half as they raced into a 19-0 lead on their way to becoming champions of England for the first time since 1968, long before the Super League era. Trinity carried on from where they had left off in the semi-final against Wigan Warriors with tries from Cameron Scott, Isaiah Vagana and Jazz Tevaga and a drop goal from Jack Sinfield. Arron Lindop's try gave Warrington brief hope early in the second half, but when Tom Johnstone went over at the other end, the game was up despite Lindop's second try late on. This video can not be played Wakefield end 58-year wait to become Super League champions This is a final few would have predicted seven days ago, let alone at any point throughout the season. But Warrington snuck past Leeds Rhinos, and Wakefield Trinity then stunned the whole of rugby league as they demolished Wigan on the Warriors' own patch to make it to Old Trafford. While Warrington have been close in previous years, Wakefield have been spectacular bolters in 2026. Only two years ago, they were winning the Championship play-off final before their place in Super League was confirmed by the IMG grading system, having been relegated in 2023. They were sixth last year and went two places better this season before memorable play-off successes over Leigh Leopards and then the Warriors. In the build-up during the week, Powell had challenged his players to earn legendary status, knowing that was their long-term reward if they could emerge victorious. After scoring 33 unanswered points in a spell at Wigan, Wakefield simply brought that momentum with them to Old Trafford as they absolutely bossed the first half, stretching that streak to 52 points. Johnstone had already had one try denied by a TV review before Lachlan Walmsley's brilliant reverse pass sent Scott over to score. And in a period where everything they did was working, Jake Trueman's high kick on the last tackle was spectacularly caught by Johnstone above opposite wing Albert Hopoate and tapped back for the supporting Vagana to dive over. They were overpowering their opponents, exemplified by Tevaga being unstoppable from close to the posts for their third try. And showing the sort of game smarts his revered father Sir Kevin Sinfield had in his Leeds Rhinos days, son Jack added an extra point to keep the scoreboard ticking as the half closed to leave Warrington needing more than three converted tries. This video can not be played Sir Kevin Sinfield presents Grand Final trophy ahead of kick-off In the Super League era, Warrington have been the eternal bridesmaids, watching on as traditional rivals Wigan and St Helens have swept up the silverware. This was their fifth Grand Final, and felt like the chance to finally get their hands on the big prize and be champions for the first time since 1955. Under head coach Sam Burgess, they had lost Challenge Cup finals at Wembley in the previous two years, but they had arrived at this game on the back of nine wins out of 10. Crucially that sole defeat had been at Wakefield in round 26 of the regular season and in the opening 40 minutes, they had few answers. But a high tackle by Trinity centre Corey Hall resulted in him being sin-binned early in the second period and, with a man extra, Lindop went over to offer a glimmer of a comeback. However, Warrington could not score again with that momentum. Wakefield weathered the storm and, with numbers levelled up, they worked an opening for Johnstone's power and pace to deliver the decisive try. Lindop went over again for his second as the Wolves desperately attacked, but with Ewan Irwin missing the conversion, Trinity players and staff were able to count down until the final whistle before celebrations could begin as Warrington's wait for another title now extends to a 72nd year. title: Huge crowds turn out in support of residents over Drumcree parade dispute
description: The Police Service of Northern Ireland said anyone found to have blocked the Garvaghy Road will be treated as participating in an "illegal protest".
body: Crowds gathered at the Garvaghy Road to support local residents on Saturday Rallies were held in Portadown on both sides of the Drumcree parade dispute on Saturday as the stand-off between Garvaghy Road residents and the Orange Order continues. Addressing thousands of people at an event on the Garvaghy Road, First Minister and Sinn Féin vice president Michelle O'Neill said she heard the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant "talk about being between a rock and a hard place", adding she has "never heard such nonsense, this is between right and wrong". The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said anyone blocking the Garvaghy Road will be "treated as participating in an unnotified and therefore illegal protest and that anyone "found to have broken the law will face criminal justice consequences". Speaking at Drumcree church, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Carla Lockhart repeated calls for PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher and his officers to "do their job" and facilitate the parade, describing the current impasse as "mob rule". For most of the afternoon stewards in high visibility jackets kept people off the Garvaghy Road and those attending were told it was important to allow traffic to flow freely. However, by 15:00 BST the crowd was so large that they were standing on the road as police closed it to traffic. The fallout over the proposed Orange Order march - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning after the Parades Commission's decision that the Orange Order parade could go ahead with restrictions. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded Protesters have remained on Garvaghy Road and the Orange Order has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement on Thursday. A fresh legal bid by the residents to prevent the march was due to be heard on Friday - but has now been postponed until Monday. O'Neill told the crowds on Saturday that "if this British government isn't prepared to end this crisis, then it's up to the thousands here, to collectively stand with the Garvaghy Road residents". She said: "We will stand shoulder to shoulder for as long as it takes." In a post of social media, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said the "behaviour of Michelle O'Neill and her party has been disgraceful" and a "complete abdication of leadership". She added: "The full weight of the law must be applied. Unionism must not lower itself to provocation or hate - all should remain calm." Leader of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), Jon Burrows, said the scenes at the Garvaghy Road on Saturday "represent a serious failure of political leadership". "It was a carnival of law-breaking and triumphalism," he said. Former SDLP MLA Dolores Kelly spoke at the rally and said: "Never again did we think we'd be on the Garvaghy Road again to say no going back and no Orange Order parades in the Garvaghy Road." A smaller event was also held in the Edgarstown area of Portadown in support of the Orange Order. The Edgarstown event in Portadown is in support of the Orange Order Speaking to BBC News NI at Drumcree, Lockhart said there could be "repercussions for a very long time if mob rule wins over the rule of law". Asked if we had stepped back from the "abyss" cited by both Lockhart and a High Court Judge in reference to last week's court proceedings, Lockhart was firm that no progress had yet been made. "No, we need the police service to step up and do their job. I do think if the real residents step forward we can and should discuss further options and resolutions, because we do want to see this resolved," Lockhart said. Liam McDonald said people did not want to see any more "trouble or strife" Liam McDonald travelled from south Armagh and said it was important for him to be at the Garvaghy Road. "The majority of people in Ireland, right across the island, don't want any more of this. They don't want to see any more trouble or strife or anything like that. "How they're going to solve this, I would love to know the answer, but I don't. And I think a lot of people are in the same boat. They don't know what the answer is to it. But it has to be solved." Noah Bell was born after the Good Friday Agreement and described himself as part of the "peace process generation" Noah Bell attended the Edgarstown event in support of the Portadown District and said he believed the situation was "really worrying" and wanted the parade to be allowed to proceed. "I think the determination should be upheld. The law's on our side and that lawful determination must be upheld and the parade allowed to go through." Frances McGowan recalled "really frightening" times during previous disputes Frances McGowan said she wanted to show her support for people on the Garvaghy Road and did not want to see a return to the past. "I remember back, it was awful times. Really frightening things as well, so we do not want to return under any circumstances. "Especially for the younger generation, we don't want to go back through the dark, dark days." Jonathan Jackson said he is proud of his identity Jonathan Jackson, who is a member of the Orange Order, said he attended the Edgarstown rally because he believed in his culture and was proud of his identity. "For me, as a young Protestant unionist, it does begin to feel like a cold house for me in my own country. "So I think obviously you can look back and maybe seems like an older person's issue, but I do think this is a civil liberties issue." Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant said he was "concerned at the prolonged standoff" which he said was "ultimately in nobody's interests". title: Astronomers get permission for mini-observatory
description: The Shropshire Astronomical Society plans to install the dome at Rodington village hall.
body: The Shropshire Astronomical Society said the dome would look similar to this one A group of amateur astronomers have been given permission to set up a mini-observatory at a village hall. Members of the Shropshire Astronomical Society (SAS) now plan to transfer over the out of use dome and telescope once used by the Irish Rangers at the Tern Hill army base near Market Drayton. They have been based at Rodington Village Hall, near Shrewsbury, for 25 years but think the telescope will raise interest in astronomy. In granting permission, Telford and Wrekin planners said the curved gloss white fibreglass dome used to house the telescope would be "somewhat unusual" but would add "some visual interest to the site. In the group's application, the society's Stephen Szwajkun wrote: "It will be a first public astronomical observatory in the area and provide inspiration for the diverse residents of Telford and Wrekin as well as the wider area." Society chairman Philip Osman said a permanent observatory would encourage participation and also give the group the opportunity to organise community outreach activities. "The dome will be the only publicly accessible observatory in the county and we hope that this new facility will allow us to broaden our outreach activities and successfully engage with a new generation," he said. Osman also said an agreement had been reached to purchase the mini observatory in May. The domed structure is set to be a little less than 2.7m (8ft 9inches) tall and council officials were satisfied that the proposal would not result in unacceptable noise, disturbance or any other disruption for nearby residents. They added that it was "not considered likely to result in a significant increase in traffic or parking demand". Planners agreed that it would provide a useful additional community and educational facility. This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations. title: Gloucester thrash sorry Quins to go top of the Prem
description: Gloucester thrash a limp Harlequins at Kingsholm to go to the top of the early Prem standings.
body: Seb Atkinson was one of eight different try scorers for Gloucester Tries: Loader, Morgan, Trenholm, C. Atkinson, S. Atkinson, Englefield, Joseph, Barton Cons: Barton 4 Gloucester thrashed a limp Harlequins at Kingsholm to go to the top of the early Prem standings. The Cherry and Whites ran in eight tries to make it two wins from two in the league and three on the bounce in all competitions. Gloucester, who named three new signings in their starting line-up including Wales internationals Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, completely outplayed their opponents in all facets of the match. Visitors Quins, who handed a debut to England full-back George Furbank, struggled to get a handle on the game from the outset and remain bottom of the table without any points after failing to get on the scoreboard. Rees-Zammit stars as Bristol power past Northampton Gloucester winger Cokanasiga out until January A progressive move down the right gave Gloucester fly-half Charlie Atkinson – three days after he signed a new deal committing his long-term future with the club - the opportunity to find Ben Loader free on the left with a pinpoint kick, and the winger dotted down to open the scoring. Harlequins, in their desperation to keep Gloucester out on their own try line, lost Will Evans to the sin bin and mere seconds later Wales flanker Morgan barged over in the left corner to extend Gloucester's lead. On the stroke of half hour, Morgan's strong carry allowed Will Trenholm to force over Gloucester's third try from close range before George Barton slotted the conversio superbly from touch. A spectacular 50:22 from scrum-half Caolan Englefield then put Gloucester in another great position and Charlie Atkinson broke a tackle to go over next to the sticks, as Barton kicked an easy extra two to give the hosts a 24-point advantage at half-time. The interval did not change the momentum as two short passes saw Seb Atkinson race to the line and power over Gloucester's fifth of the evening and Quins' day was perhaps summed up best when Connor Slevin's poor restart failed to go 10 metres. Gloucester ruthlessly made their visitors pay once more as with their next attack Will Joseph's outstanding run and offload allowed Englefield to dive over. Joseph then grabbed the try his own performance deserved, diving in to the right of the posts to claim Gloucester's seventh try and third inside 12 minutes after half-time. Another kick to the corner from Charlie Atkinson found Barton who juggled successfully and managed to extend over for Gloucester's eighth. Joseph thought he had scored his second with the final act of the match to take Gloucester past 50 points, but his try was chalked off for a knock-on in the build up. title: Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
description: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.
body: The search for the plane is being conducted near Nantucket, an island off the coast of the US state of Massachusetts US authorities are searching for six people after a medical plane bound for Boston, Massachusetts, went missing early Saturday morning. The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC that it lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane and put out a search-and-rescue notice just after 1:00 local time (6:00 GMT). An air and water search is underway off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, according to the US Coast Guard's Northeast District. The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was slated to land at Boston's Logan International at 1:30 EDT (6:30 GMT). According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home. Among those on board were two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News. The crew flew to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, who are not Canadian, Togeretz said. FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft). title: Who was the best player on the pitch? - England player ratings
description: England produce one of their best performances in recent times as they thump Croatia 6-0 in Rijeka. How did our report rate the players' performances?
body: Harry Kane, Anthony Gordon and Jude Bellingham all scored as England beat Croatia England produced one of their best performances in recent times as they thumped Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka. Harry Kane opened the scoring, and Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka also found the net before half-time. England captain Kane then added a fifth early on in the second half before Saka scored his second from close range and substitute Morgan Rogers added a seventh to secure a dominant win. Here's how BBC Sport England reporter Alex Howell rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. Ruthless England cruise past Croatia in Nations League What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? Jordan Pickford: A really good decision and save when he raced out and won the ball at the feet of Ivan Perisic early on. Not tested but was lucky to not concede with Mateo Kovacic's incredible miss. 6 Jarell Quansah: Surprisingly chosen at right-back over Trent Alexander-Arnold but the Bayer Leverkusen defender does exactly what manager Thomas Tuchel wants. A powerful runner, a good defender and his ability on the ball is underrated - he showed it with a quality assist for Gordon. 8 Ezri Konsa: Not loads of defending for Konsa to do as England pinned Croatia back but it was a calm assured performance from the defender. 7 Marc Guehi: The centre-back had to take up some risky positions as England pressed man for man all over the pitch. 7 Lewis Hall: The Newcastle left-back looks a great addition to the England back four. Hall offers pace going forward and also underlapped, going into midfield to recieve the ball. 7 Elliot Anderson: Anderson has been excellent throughout this international break and produced another mature performance. The Manchester City midfielder is a crucial part of the midfield and set up Kane for England's fifth. 8 Alex Scott: The Bournemouth midfielder was given his first England start and put in a really confident performance. Scott always looked to get on the ball and did not just try to keep it safe as England dominated. 7 Jude Bellingham: The best player on the pitch. Bellingham produced a lovely pass to thread Kane through for the first goal, scored England's second and assisted Saka for England's fourth. A truly world-class player and his quality was too much for Croatia throughout the game. 9 Bukayo Saka: The winger scored twice and looks to be building a good partnership with Quansah on England's right-hand side. Saka could have had a hat-trick but missed a big chance in the second half. 8 Anthony Gordon: Playing with a huge amount of confidence and continues to show that he has gone to another level in recent months. Assisted Bellingham and scored for the fourth England game in a row. 9 Harry Kane: Just an elite finisher and his goal put England firmly in control. The captain looked full of energy, pressed from the front and showed his passing range as he enjoyed having Gordon and Bellingham supplying him. Scored England's fifth goal too. 9 Eberechi Eze (on 70, Gordon): Played as a number 10. 6 Morgan Rogers (on 70, Kane): Played on the left as England cruised to a win and produced a composed finish for England's seventh, rounding the keeper when played through on goal. 7 James Garner (on 70, Alex Scott): Some strong challenges and kept it simple. 6 Morgan Gibbs-White (on 79, Anderson): 6 Myles Lewis-Skelly (on, Hall): 6 Subs not used: Steele, Trafford, Alexander-Arnold, Branthwaite, Calvert-Lewin, Chalobah, Ngumoha. After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution
description: Pike's lawyers said the failure "goes far beyond any one person". Pike is in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections.
body: The head of prisons in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike on Wednesday. Governor Bill Lee announced the change on Saturday, sharing the news in a joint statement with Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada. Strada said that his stepping down is "in the best interests" of the state, and called the ongoing investigation into the incident "entirely appropriate and necessary". Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, survived two injections and is now in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital as her lawyers seek to commute her sentence. "Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment," Lee said. Lee has ordered an independent review into Pike's attempted execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year. Attorney's for Pike called the resignation "justified" but said "it does nothing to help Christa now". "What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," Pike's legal team wrote in a statement. "We hope the Governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee's entire death penalty system." Pike is being treated at a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, where doctors are attempting to clear the drugs used during the execution from her body, according to legal filings. She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance. While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said. As of Thursday night, she was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator. The state's Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out". Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her failed execution. Pike's attorneys previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection. The attempted execution went ahead after multiple failed, last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers. The US Supreme Court rejected two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection. Tennessee's governor also denied a clemency request from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995. She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.
