title: Sinfield completes fundraising challenge of seven ultramarathons in a week
description: Sir Kevin Sinfield crosses the finish line at Old Trafford after seven ultramarathons in seven days.
body: Kevin Sinfield carried the Super League Grand Final trophy into Old Trafford after completing the challenge Sir Kevin Sinfield has completed his latest endurance challenge raising money for motor neurone disease (MND) causes in memory of his friend and teammate Rob Burrow, who died in 2024. Sinfield completed seven ultramarathons in seven days, crossing the finish line at Old Trafford Stadium in Manchester ahead of the Super League Grand Final. The fundraiser and his team have raised more than £13m for the MND community since his first annual challenge in 2020. Speaking to the crowd, Sinfield said: "The rugby league community has got right behind the MND community and Rob would be so proud to see how you've supported and cared, and showed your love for a community that really needs us." Sinfield began his final ultramarathon challenge in Hull on September 27 and visited all 12 Super League clubs along the way. The 7 in 7: The Grand Finale week ended at Old Trafford earlier where he brought out the trophy ahead of the game between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity. Prince William and Catherine made an unexpected appearance in Wakefield on Tuesday to meet Sir Kevin Along the way he was surprised by royals, including The Prince and Princess of Wales and the Princess Royal, as well as famous names from the sporting world such as former England football manager Sir Gareth Southgate and Leeds boxer Josh Warrington. Each day was split into 7km, hour-long blocks with an additional extra mile for members of the MND community to join. Funds raised by the challenge will go towards the work of the MND Association, Leeds Hospitals Charity, My Name5 Doddie Foundation, Darby Rimmer Foundation, MND Scotland and the Irish MND Association. Sinfield arrived at Old Trafford at about 17:00 BST Sinfield, 45, who played his entire professional career with Leeds Rhinos, is one of the most successful players in Super League history. He and Burrow met at the Leeds Rhinos academy aged 14 and 12. They went on to win seven titles together with Leeds Rhinos. Burrow's wife, Lindsey Burrow, told BBC Radio 4's PM that her late husband "would have been incredibly proud" of his friend. "It's bittersweet that Rob's not here today to see Kevin finish his final challenge but Rob will be with us in spirit and it's just testimony to Kevin that he's so humbled to do this not just for Rob but for the whole MND community," Lindsey said. "It's just incredible. I am in complete awe of the efforts of Kevin and his team over the last seven days, and not just over the last seven days but over the last seven years," she added. Sinfield's son, Jack Sinfield, lined up in the Wakefield side seeking to clinch their first top-flight title since 1968. title: I'm a wildlife cameraman but 'special' rare sightings can still take me by surprise
description: Wildlife cameraman Dan Abbot is caught off guard by a humpback whale, a rare sight in Welsh waters.
body: Abbot has seen the humpback whale before, but never in this area A wildlife cinematographer and shark guide has spoken about the unexpected surprise and joy of seeing a humpback whale in the Celtic Deep just off the Welsh coast. Dan Abbot, known as Sharkman Dan on his social media, shared a recording of the exciting moment just off the Pembrokeshire coast. He has seen the large marine mammals before, on planned trips where humpback whale sightings are not as unusual, but this experience was "a complete surprise". Lloyd Nelmes from Sea Trust said the sighting was "unusual for someone who works in the field... who probably has their eyes on the water every day", adding, "for a normal person, it's insanely rare". Abbot guides blue shark snorkelling trips off of Pembrokeshire Abbot guides blue shark snorkelling trips off of Pembrokeshire and was on a scheduled snorkelling trip in the Celtic Sea on 25 September when he discovered the rare find. The group had just left the snorkelling site after seeing multiple sharks and were 25-30 miles offshore. Abbot recalled seeing lots of feeding going on among bluefin tuna, dolphins and gannets which he said was not unusual in the waters there at this time of year. When a guest on board "saw a whale blow in the distance", Abbot inititally suspected it was a minke or fin whale, the two most common whales in Welsh waters. "I said if it's a big blow, then it's probably a fin whale," he said. "So we then watched it blowing, quite far out, and slowly moved towards the area where there was lots of feeding going on because sometimes you can see whales lunge feeding." This video can not be played Dan Abbot, a wildlife cinematographer, has seen humpback whales before, but this sighting was a complete surprise "As we got a bit closer and parked the boat a bit to let things develop around us, I noticed that when it came up for a blow, it actually had white pectoral fin, which fin whales don't have," Abbot said. "And then the other thing they don't do is they don't lift their tails out of the water, which humpbacks do. You could see barnacles around the front of the head, which fin whales don't have. "I actually went quiet for a moment. At that point, it was pretty clear it was a humpback whale." He continued: "I don't really get that excited, which sounds strange. I'm usually one of the quietest ones on the boat, but I think it was just because it was such a surprise to see that species. "I'm a wildlife cameraman but when something happens like that unexpectedly and catches you off guard, there's something about it that kind of makes it even more special." Guests on the boat were already in high spirits after the four-hour snorkelling trip, but Abbot said 'then to see a humpback whale was just an incredible way to finish the day". Dan Abbot says despite spending his days out in the water as a wildlife cameraman, "special" sights can still catch him off guard Lloyd Nelmes, an aquarium manger and marine project officer with Sea Trust Wales, spotted a humpback whale in Pembrokeshire in 2024. Nelmes said: "The whale jumped out right in front of us. It was incredible, and it's still probably my top wildlife moment of my life." He explained that humpback whale sightings were rare but not unheard of in Welsh waters, with sightings happening once every two or three years. Nelmes said the way to spot a humpback whale was by the overall shape, white pectoral fins, and knobbly skin also known as barnacles, as well as the whales' behaviour. "We've seen humpbacks here on the rare occasion... but it seems to be becoming more common, which is awesome," he said. "It's quite likely just an indication of how much food is about at the moment." He said he had been on an "incredible" trip out to the Celtic Deep the day before Abbot's discovery and had seen six fin whales, tuna balling up and 1,000-plus dolphins, adding it was not too surprising that a humpack was "out there also making the most of the food". title: Man shot dead as families gather for memorial in London
description: The 40-year-old died at the scene in west London from a gunshot wound, the Met Police said.
body: Police attended the scene alongside paramedics on Friday evening A murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a "senseless act of violence" as up to 50 people – including children – gathered for a memorial service in west London. The Met Police said it was called to the scene at 19:47 GMT on Friday after multiple shots had been heard by members of the public at the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street in East Acton. Officers attended alongside the London Ambulance Service but the man was pronounced dead at the scene, despite the efforts of medics. No arrests have been made and a police cordon remains in place in Braybrook Street. Police are appealing for witnesses to come forward. The victim's family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers. A post-mortem examination is scheduled to establish the cause of death, but the victim is believed to have sustained a gunshot wound, the force said. Det Ch Insp Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said: "Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence. "We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated. "We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward." He has asked anyone who was around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 18:00 and 20:00, to "please think carefully about what you saw". He added: "Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously, or vehicles being driven at speed? "We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media. "However insignificant it may seem, the smallest piece of information could prove crucial in helping us establish what happened and identify those responsible." title: Desmond targeted by Celtic fan protest at Alfred Dunhill
description: Celtic's largest shareholder Dermot Desmond is targeted in a protest at the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament in St Andrews as tennis balls were thrown towards him.
body: Dermot Desmond was escorted off the course by security Celtic's largest shareholder Dermot Desmond was targeted in a protest at the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament in St Andrews as tennis balls were thrown towards him. Tennis balls with pictures of the 76-year-old's face scored out were thrown on to the green of the 15th hole of the pro-am competition, with images showing Desmond having to be escorted off the course by security. The Celtic Fans Collective have since released a statement, along with footage and images of the incident. It read: "Dermot Desmond has essentially been allowed to run Celtic Football Club whilst using his wealth to hide from supporters and accountability. Fans took the chance today to send a message that this arrangement cannot continue." Desmond is the largest individual shareholder of the Scottish Premiership club but has been criticised in recent seasons for the club's lack of progress in Europe and underwhelming transfer business. In the wake of Brendan Rodgers' resignation at the beginning of last season, Desmond blamed the former manager for much of the problems that marred the beginning of the 2025-26 campaign. Then at Celtic's annual general meeting last November, which had to be abandoned due to fan unrest, Desmond's son Ross read out a statement on his behalf. He began by defending his father, a "lifelong and passionate" Celtic supporter, and vowed that the board would not be "bullied by aggressive and irrational" criticism. The Irishman defended then chairman Peter Lawwell and chief executive Michael Nicholson, claiming attempts to "dehumanise and vilify them are shameful". Desmond went on to criticise a section of fans over a recent incident that led to the Green Brigade ultras group being banned and added: "Those people are bullies." title: Watch the moment a landslip leaves Skye drivers facing a 40-mile diversion
description: Highland Council says the A855 in the north of the island will have to remain closed over the weekend.
body: This video can not be played The landslip was captured on CCTV from a nearby house Drivers on Skye are facing a 40-mile diversion after a landslide led to a road closure. The ground fell away from the side of the A855 north of Uig onto a local access road on Friday afternoon and an inspection later confirmed it would have to stay shut over the weekend. The A855 road encircles the Trotternish peninsula in the north of the island and a diversion route is now in place. No-one was injured by the landslip - which was caught on CCTV from a nearby house - but a group of visiting schoolchildren found themselves temporarily separated from their packed lunches until a local woman volunteered to retrieve them by bike. The road could have to remain closed into next week as "detailed surveying" works continue, according to local councillor Chrissie Gillies. Soil and rocks fell from the side A855 towards a smaller access road below The local road was left completely blocked An update from Highland Council on Saturday said: "Following this morning's inspection, the A855 at Idrigill Bend will remain closed over the weekend. title: Police appeal to help find heavily pregnant woman
description: Leicestershire Police say they are "extremely concerned" for Charlie Ryan's welfare.
body: Charlie Ryan was reported missing on Friday morning Police have appealed for help in their search for a missing woman who is heavily pregnant. Leicestershire Police said Charlie Ryan was reported missing on Friday morning, having last been seen in the Groby Road area of Leicester near to New Parks Way roundabout. The force said the 31-year-old is white, 165cm (5ft 5in), with bright blonde hair. She was last seen wearing a black jacket, grey jumper, black leggings and black shoes. Officers said they were "extremely concerned" for her welfare and active inquiries were continuing to find her. Police said inquiries carried out so far indicated she may be in the Northfields area of Leicester. Anyone who may have seen her or knows where she may be is asked to contact police. title: Noel Gallagher guitar sells for £12,000 at auction
description: The instrument was one of a number of items which belonged to a former Oasis sound engineer.
body: The Epiphone guitar is believed to be one of five gifted to Noel Gallagher A guitar which originally belonged to Noel Gallagher has been sold for £12,000 at auction. The limited edition Epiphone instrument in Manchester City blue was one of a number of items put up for sale by the son of Huw Richards, a former front-of-house sound engineer with the band. Another of the items in his collection, a Kangol rain jacket produced for the band's touring personnel, sold for £2,000. But a set of unheard Oasis recordings valued at between £1.2m and £1.6m were pulled from the auction last week, after the band filed an injunction. That collection of recordings, known as The Desk Tapes, includes recordings of 63 live shows, soundchecks and more than 100 hours of rehearsals from the band's rise and rise in the 1990s. Littleton Auctions in Worcestershire, which handled the auction, said it had agreed to postpone the sale until the legal dispute had been resolved. The collection of 11 platinum discs celebrates one of the highest‑selling British albums of all time The Epiphone guitar was made in 1997 and the auctioneer said it is believed to be one of five identical guitars gifted to Noel Gallagher by the manufacturer. It was later given to Richards, Littleton Auctions said. A collection of 11 framed platinum discs, from the Oasis album What's the Story Morning Glory which also belonged to Richards sold for £2,000. They had been presented to him by Creation Records to recognise United Kingdom sales of more than 3.3 million copies. Other items in the Richards collection to sell at the auction included tour itineraries, promotional material and a Be Here Now wrist watch. A number of other sellers also had memorabilia up for sale at the auction, including a rare original concert ticket for The Rain, the Manchester band which later became Oasis. That sold for £2,400 and an early Oasis demo tape sold for £3,600. A collection of early Oasis photos sold for £5,400 and a pair of leather shoes which once belonged to Noel Gallagher sold for £1,200. But a baby grand piano which featured in the artwork for the Supersonic single, which was valued at between £100,000 and £150,000 failed to sell. title: Why has Brazil accused the US of election interference?
description: The Latin American country will vote for its next president, as Lula da Silva and Bolsonaro clash over sovereignty, security and ties with Washington.
body: This video can not be played In Brazil’s upcoming presidential election, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing right-wing challenger and ally of Donald Trump, Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Washington has backed closer ties with Brazil’s right wing, while Lula da Silva has accused Bolsonaro’s camp of encouraging foreign interference. The election has raised questions about US influence, trade tariffs, organised crime and Brazil’s sovereignty. The BBC's Ione Wells explains. Why has Brazil accused the US of election interference? title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
description: More than 50 protests are taking place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.
body: This video can not be played Major protest in Spain as millions struggle to find an affordable home Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to get emergency housing legislation through parliament on Friday. About 50 planned marches are taking place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona . "There is a lot of anger in the streets," said a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union, where a demonstration has already started. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city. The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase. Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property. Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer. His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament. Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87 Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit. Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Tens of thousands took to the streets of Madrid to protest Tensions arose between some protesters and police officers in Valencia One of the biggest demonstration is happening in the capital, Madrid. Estimates of the number of participants varied widely, with the city's Tenants' Union putting it at 500,000, while government officials put the figure at 70,000. Demonstrators have been camping in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days. One protester, David, told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction." On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives". It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis. An encampment has been set up for days by protesters at Puerta del Sol in Madrid Madrid is expected to be the site of the largest protests this weekend The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees. The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds". The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union. MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166. Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country. However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure. Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September. The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued. Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE. The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively. title: Police name two men who died in workplace incident near rural road
description: It happened on the Ballygowan Road in Crossnacreevy at about 10:45 BST on Friday.
body: Emergency services attended the scene on the Ballygowan Road Two men who died after a workplace incident at a road in County Down on Friday have been named by police. Joseph Hobbs, 23, from Comber and Mark Glover, 38, from Ballygowan received medical treatment but were pronounced dead at the scene. The incident happened on the Ballygowan Road in Crossnacreevy at about 10:45 BST on Friday. Police said their sympathies remained "with all those affected by this tragic incident". The police said they will continue to work with Northern Ireland's Health and Safety Executive (HSENI) as enquiries continue. On Friday, Democratic Unionist Party MP Gavin Robinson said on social media that his thoughts were with the men's families and loved ones "at this devastating time". Alliance Party MLA Peter McReynolds said it was "an absolutely heartbreaking incident" and his thoughts were with the families and emergency service personnel. title: Alison Hammond returns home from hospital after rushing off This Morning
description: The This Morning presenter said she believes she experienced a panic attack on Friday's show.
body: Alison Hammond has said she is home and "feeling so much better" after she went to hospital for a heart check-up after leaving ITV's This Morning midway through Friday's show. The presenter, 51, left the programme during its live broadcast, appearing to clutch her chest as she was helped off set by co-host Dermot O'Leary. He later told viewers she was "feeling a little unwell". Soon after Hammond said she had "a little bit of a palpitation" and was undergoing tests. In a video on Instagram on Saturday, she said she was "all OK, all-clear, which would mean I had a massive panic attack on live TV. I mean, the shame of it." Alison Hammond has heart check-up in hospital after rushing off This Morning while on air "It felt very real to me. I'm really new to panic attacks, so I need to learn more about it," she added. The Birmingham-born presenter, who also co-hosts The Great British Bake Off, thanked NHS staff and her colleagues at This Morning, including O'Leary. "It's really warmed my heart actually. I didn't necessarily want to be on the news or anything like that but this is a new world to me," she said. "I'm going to take stock, take some rest and I'll see you soon." Friday's edition of the ITV show began at 10:00 BST with Hammond and her regular co-host O'Leary at the helm, before she left at 11:30 during a segment about pets. O'Leary, 53, addressed her absence when the show returned from a break, saying: "Welcome back to This Morning, Alison is feeling a little unwell, so she's just had to duck out. Hopefully she'll be back." He later updated viewers that she would, in fact, not be returning, "so I'll be here for the rest of the show". Hammond rose to fame as contestant on Channel 4 reality show Big Brother before appearing on I'm A Celebrity and Strictly Come Dancing. She became a co-host in This Morning in 2021, and was part of the team that won a National Television Award for best daytime programme the following year. She joined Bake Off in 2023 and took over from the late Paul O'Grady on For the Love of Dogs in 2024. title: Police searching for mum of baby girl found on shoreline tell her not to be afraid to call
description: Police searching for the mother of a newborn girl whose body was found urge her to contact them.
body: North Wales Police appealed directly to the mother to make contact with them Police searching for the mother of a newborn baby girl whose body was found on a north Wales shoreline have set up a special phone line, urging her to contact them. A member of the public found the body on the Menai Strait shoreline near Siliwen Road in Bangor, Gwynedd, on Sunday shortly before 17:00 BST. In an update on Thursday, North Wales Police said a post-mortem examination revealed the newborn was a girl, adding that she may have been in the water for up to a few weeks. Supt Llinos Davies from North Wales Police said a specialist would take a call from the woman directly and could support her confidentially and told the woman not to be afraid to speak to the police. "We understand that you may be scared to come forward, but we urge you to contact us," Davies said. "I want to reassure you that your welfare and safety continues to be our priority and utmost concern and that you receive any medical attention and support you may need. "Whatever has happened, you do not have to face this on your own," she added. The director of midwifery and women's services for Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board Fiona Giraud last week also appealed directly to the mother to come forward. This video can not be played Midwife appeals to mother of newborn baby found on shoreline Davies said a trained specialist whose role was "simply to listen, understand, and help" would speak to her. "This is not a conversation you need to be afraid of. You will be treated with compassion, dignity and respect. "If making that call feels too difficult, please consider telling somebody you trust. A friend, family member, neighbour, healthcare professional, or anyone who can help you reach out." The phone number is to strictly only be used by the mother to seek specialist help, North Wales Police said. "We are concerned the baby's mother may not be in a position to reach out for support, so we are appealing directly to her, the father and those who may have knowledge, such as friends, family, neighbours or colleagues, to contact us," Davies said. She added that all names provided would be treated "with the utmost discretion" and urges people not to speculate on the circumstances surrounding the baby's death. Officers are appealing to anyone who routinely walked in the Siliwen Road and Ashley Fields areas of Bangor between 30 August and 27 September to come forward. They are also asking for any photos or videos taken in and around the Menai Straits shoreline in Siliwen within the same time frame to be uploaded to the force's major incident public portal. title: Republic of Ireland news conference ends abruptly amid accusations
description: Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match news conference ends abruptly as accusations are levelled at his players.
body: Hallgrimsson's side face Israel in Serbia on Sunday after their 3-0 win over the same opposition last week For more than 11 minutes of Saturday's pre-match news conference, Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions centred on Sunday's Nations League Group B3 'home' game against Israel in Serbia. The Icelander revealed that Dara O'Shea - captain in place of the injured Nathan Collins - was not with the squad, as his wife was due to give birth. He may arrive back in Backa Topola prior to Sunday's 19:45 BST kick-off. Hallgrimsson also gave his thoughts on the strain of this four-game international window and reflected on Thursday's 2-2 draw against Austria. As the first section of the media conference, which is allowed to be broadcast live, was ending, the mood soured. One reporter tried to quiz Hallgrimsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday when a co-pilot attacked a pilot on a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane. The Republic of Ireland manager was also asked by another journalist about alleged racism by Irish players during last Sunday's 3-0 win over Israel in Hungary and refused to give up the microphone. Promptly, the news conference was brought to a close by Football Association of Ireland (FAI) head of communications Kieran Crowley after calling those allegations "completely untrue". The allegations of racism by an Irish player comes after it was confirmed the FAI is investigating reports of racist abuse directed towards Republic of Ireland striker Adam Idah by Israel fans in Debrecen. Minutes before the news conference was brought to an abrupt halt, Hallgrimsson insisted he would not be drawn on either matter and would not "get involved in that as others will process that". "It is a game with a lot of emotions attached," Hallgrimsson said. "I haven't read anything and it's not something I want to get involved with. It goes to a process, both in our department and with Uefa. "Something was reported by both teams so I just hope we can focus on football and football will be the winner after this. "I have not gone into details looking at this as I have enough to think about." Second Israel game won't be a friendly - Hallgrimsson Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious The Republic of Ireland boss revealed the team have taken to a group prayer before leaving the dressing room before recent games "just to cool our heads before we go on to the pitch" and said that has been led by midfielder Conor Coventry whom he joked is now known within the squad as "Brother Coventry". It has been a challenging international window for the Republic of Ireland with the Israel double-header dominating discourse in Irish football. Since the teams were drawn together in February, a 'Stop The Game' campaign was launched by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine to boycott the fixtures in protest of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war. Before last week's 'home' game for Israel in Hungary, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the fixtures, saying "it would be wrong to participate" while a vote by players to play the games passed by a "significant majority", according to FAI chief executive David Courell. There were protests during the game against Austria in Dublin on Thursday, with tennis balls thrown on to the pitch and a protester briefly interrupting the game when he ran on to the turf, waving a Palestine flag. Hallgrimmson said under the circumstances, it will be a "a big win for this group and the association if we go through undamaged". "The most pleasing thing for me is to see the togetherness and how they stand up for each other. Whatever they have done, they have done it with respect to the situation, to each other and after this, this bond of brothers will be stronger than ever. All the obstacles this group will face in the future will be lesser than it is. "When we look back, this camp will be a moment we grew the most and stepped up as leaders, supported each other and stuck together. The power of togetherness is stronger than individuals." title: Teenager taken to hospital after Glasgow shopping centre gang attack
description: The assault in the St Enoch Centre came just days after dispersal zone powers to crack down on anti-social behaviour were extended.
body: The attack took place at the St Enoch Centre on Friday afternoon A teenager who was attacked by a gang of youths inside a Glasgow shopping centre has been treated in hospital for his injuries. Video posted on social media shows the young man, who was using a crutch and wearing a medical boot, being knocked to the ground, then repeatedly punched and kicked inside the St Enoch Centre on Friday afternoon. A second person was also pushed to the ground but security staff intervened. Police Scotland said the 19-year-old was taken to hospital and officers were reviewing CCTV footage to identify his assailants. The attackers had run off by the time officers arrived and the injured man, who was bleeding from a head wound, was initially helped by shoppers and security staff. Drugs, violence and racism: A week in Glasgow city centre Glasgow dispersal zone introduced to combat anti-social behaviour The St Enoch Centre is located inside the Glasgow city centre dispersal zone which was established in March as part of a crackdown on crime and anti-social behaviour. Officers are able to ask groups of two or more to leave the designated area if their behaviour is "impacting on the safety and well-being" of others, and they can be banned from returning for 24 hours. The attack came just a few days after it was confirmed that the dispersal zone powers would be extended into December. A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "An investigation is under way after police received a report of a disturbance involving a number of males in the St Enoch Centre, Glasgow. "A 19-year-old male was taken to hospital. Officers have been reviewing CCTV images and enquiries are ongoing to locate and identify those involved. Police are following a positive line of inquiry." Disclosure investigates claims that parts of Scotland’s biggest city have become a no-go zone because of crime, homelessness and antisocial behaviour. title: Greens would offer two-year jobs to unemployed under-24s
description: Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali tells the party's conference many young people are "bored, desperate and lost".
body: Mothin Ali addressed Green Party members on the second day of their conference in Brighton Young people would be offered a guaranteed two-year job within four months of leaving education or training, under a new proposal unveiled by the Green Party. Announcing the policy at the party's conference in Brighton, co-deputy leader Mothin Ali said there were a million "bored, desperate and lost" young people who were out of work, training or education. Under the proposed scheme, youngsters would be offered posts in the private sector, with the government paying half their salary. The Greens have not specified a budget for the policy, but have argued it would reduce spending on welfare and boost tax receipts from employment. The party says it would initially target the plan in areas with the fewest jobs openings for young people, citing Rotherham, Ceredigion, Newcastle-under-Lyme, Broxtowe and South Staffordshire, with an ambition to roll it out nationwide. Employers would be exempt from paying National Insurance contributions, but would have to provide in-job training, the party says. The party is seeking to pitch the plan as more ambitious than the government's own scheme, which subsidises six-month job placements for benefit claimants who have been looking for work for 18 months. Ali also criticised ministers for previously suggesting youngsters refusing a role under that scheme could lose access to benefits, telling activists: "Threatening young people with cuts to Universal Credit if they don't accept short-term work placements - that's not a youth strategy." He added: "Working class kids should be able to dream. But more than dream, they should have a genuine chance of making those dreams a reality. The number of 16-24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training has been rising since the Covid pandemic, with figures reaching almost one million. A long-awaited report into the problem by former Labour minister Alan Milburn is expected to be published this autumn. What does Neet stand for and why does the UK have so many? Greens can move Labour in the right direction, says Polanski In her own speech to the conference, Ali's fellow co-deputy leader Rachel Millward said the Greens would immediately bring both Thames Water and South East Water back into public ownership. She argued this could be done without paying compensation to shareholders, pointing to water supply problems and a lack of new reservoirs. Andy Burnham has promised to bring water under greater public control, but has stopped short of announcing plans to nationalise any water companies. Millward told the conference the prime minister was "making a mistake" and his "10-year plan of gentle threats and vague notions of control is not enough". "We need public ownership now, and we have all the tools we need to make it happen," she said. South East Water said it was "focused on delivering on our commitments by investing £1.9 billion into local infrastructure and resilience over the next five years. "We support working closely with the communities we serve and are accountable to, so that we can provide the best possible service for customers". Thames Water has been approached for a response. title: Homemade bomb part of alleged plot on Manchester's Jewish community, court told
description: Two men were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, considered the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
body: The suspects were arrested in Manchester on 20 September Two Iranian men have appeared in court charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade bomb. Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool, were accused at Westminster Magistrates' Court of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on or before 20 September. One of the buildings they are alleged to have carried out reconnaissance at is the Heaton Park synagogue which was attacked on 2 October 2025. Both men, who had arrived in the UK by small boat, were arrested in Manchester's Northern Quarter on the eve of Yom Kippur - the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Salehi and Ahmadyan were remanded in custody by District Judge Nina Tempia until 23 October, when they will appear at the Old Bailey in London. As part of the investigation, searches were carried out at addresses in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford. The Metropolitan Police said the men were alleged to have obtained instructions to make a chlorine bomb, acquired liquids and other components to make an improvised explosive device. They are accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps. Prosecutor Mark Luckett told the court: "Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device. "The defendants were observed carrying out, what the prosecution say, is a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester's Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park Synagogue." Two British Jews, Melvin Kravitz, 66, and 53-year-old Adrian Daulby, were killed when Heaton Park Synagogue was attacked during last year's Yom Kippur service. Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, drove into the gates of Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue and began attacking people with a knife while wearing a fake suicide belt. Westminster Magistrates' Court court heard Salehi and Ahmadyan, who had come to the UK via a small boat in 2020 and 2023 respectively, were alleged to have been "directed and co-ordinated" by another Iranian individual "most likely operating within Iran". Salehi had previously claimed asylum in Germany and spent five years there, the court heard. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2023 and currently has leave to remain until July 2028. His co-accused arrived via small boat in 2023 and has an outstanding asylum claim, the court heard. The men, wearing grey tracksuits, stood in the dock of court five. Salehi and Ahmadyan respectively spoke through their Kurdish and Farsi translators only to confirm their name, date of birth and addresses. Prior to their court appearance, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the news that two Iranian men had been charged would be "deeply distressing" to Manchester's Jewish community as the city marked the first anniversary of the Heaton Park Synagogue attack. She said "the fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago" was a reminder of the "importance of work to tackle illegal migration". "We will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security," she added. title: Woodlands project records more trees than expected
description: The Lost Woods of the Low Weald and Downs project aims to restore some of Sussex's ancient woodland.
body: Bob Epsom (l) and a Lost Woods volunteer recording ancient trees for the mapping process A project which aims to restore ancient woodlands in Sussex has hit a significant "milestone" with over 5,500 trees now recorded. Since March 2024, volunteers with the Lost Woods project have been recording ancient, veteran and notable trees across a 121-sq-miles (314-sq-km) area from Lewes to Storrington. According to the latest figures, they have now recorded 5,570 trees, a number which Lost Woods outreach adviser, Bob Epsom, said is more than "we expected" and signifies a "milestone" for the project. "When we look at the map of it, we can see the new clusters of trees being added...that's where the volunteers have been active," he said. The Lost Woods is a partnership with four charities: Woodland Trust, Action in Rural Sussex, Sussex Wildlife Trust and Small Woods Association. The work, funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund, is part of a wider Lost Woods restoration programme which Epsom said comprises "19 individual projects". About 20 volunteers are each given a square kilometre area to cover, and once recorded and verified, trees are added to the Ancient Tree Inventory which has been mapping the oldest and most important trees in the UK for 20 years. The volunteers are working to find and record every ancient and veteran tree in the project area by next year, and Epsom, who leads the team, said they still "have a reasonable amount to cover". A group of about 20 volunteers are currently mapping ancient, veteran and notable trees across a 314 sq km area from Lewes to Storrington Of the 5,570 trees recorded, there were 348 ancient trees, those that are in the third and final stage of their lives, and 2,467 notable trees, mature trees which are large in comparison with other trees around them. The biggest proportion of trees, 2,743, are veteran, survivors which have developed some of the features found on ancient trees. The remainder fall into a different category of tree. According to Epsom, these trees are "very important for the landscape, (and) very important for biodiversity" because of their fungi. Epsom said the mapping process was "only the first step", and that ultimately, there was a wider goal. He said: "We need to make sure that trees are recognised, cared for and protected so that they can continue to support wildlife and communities for generations to come." title: Will Spain's housing crisis lead to a snap election?
description: The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is in Madrid, where a series of marches have been scheduled, after Spain's Congress rejected measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis.
body: This video can not be played Thousands of people are continuing protests across Spain, after Congress rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis. Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by government in response to nationwide protests that followed the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home. Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a rent increase by the company that owns her flat. The case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years. The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is at one of the protests in Madrid and looks at whether the government's defeat will lead to an early general election, which is not due until next summer. title: 'Incredible' Red Bull upgrade enlivens F1 in Malaysia
description: Even Lewis Hamilton fears Max Verstappen will be tough to beat in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
body: Verstappen took his first pole position of 2026 at Sepang Even Lewis Hamilton, starting from his equal best grid position of the year in second place, fears Max Verstappen will be tough to beat in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Verstappen has dominated the weekend so far on Formula 1's return to the Sepang track for the first time since 2017. Hamilton joins him on the front row to revive memories of their no-holds-barred title battle five years ago. But at nearly 0.3 seconds slower in qualifying, and with the pace Verstappen has shown all weekend, Hamilton's mindset on Saturday was to "just try my best to hold on to him tomorrow". This was Verstappen's first pole position of the year - a remarkable statistic for someone who came within two points of winning a fifth world title last year after one of the all-time great fightbacks. Red Bull started the year off the pace - the car was on average more than 0.5secs a lap slower than Mercedes in the first half of the year - and for a time there were questions as to whether Verstappen would stick around for 2027. But after being courted by McLaren, Verstappen signed a two-year contract extension over the summer break, saying he believed in the Red Bull project and didn't mind putting in the work to turn things around. Verstappen arrived in Malaysia after a run of three consecutive podium finishes, and with Red Bull hoping to prove out an upgrade that had seen them finish less than 0.2secs off victory in Baku last Sunday. In the tropical heat of Malaysia, around the demanding long corners of this track with perhaps the roughest surface of the season, the upgrade - centred on a new floor - has more than proved its worth. "It's been an incredible result for us," Verstappen said. "Looking at the season, how it started for us and the progression that we have made. At some tracks we were kind of close, but now I think this weekend it was very positive for us. "We have been adding bits to the car and they have worked. It's simple as that. When they work, you gain lap time, you have a better overall balance in the car. "So with tyres that are very sensitive to balance, that gives you also more lap time. "And then on a track probably where it's all very hot and you want a, let's say, stable balance or connected balance, then that's very important. And that's what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends." This video can not be played Team-mate Isack Hadjar, who missed the first three races after the summer break with a wrist broken while boxing as part of his training programme, says the car felt transformed when he returned in Baku last weekend. "I jumped in a car that's way better than when I left it in Budapest," said the Frenchman, who qualified third, but will start eighth after a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted number of engine parts. "Definitely, when you step out actually for three races and you come back, you actually notice a bigger difference. And the last two weekends have been surprising." A good car balance should put Verstappen in a good place for a race that will be dominated by tyre degradation in the stifling heat, whether the threatened rain holds off or not. This video can not be played 'I'm so, so, so happy' Hamilton, for one, but also Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who under-performed slightly in qualifying because of a combination between an unusual tyre strategy and an error on an early run. The world championship leader's fourth place becomes third on the grid with Hadjar's penalty, and he can usually be relied upon to be a factor in the race. Antonelli's main focus will be his advantage over team-mate George Russell, who trails the Italian by 66 points and starts four places behind, his momentum from his Baku win stalled, and somewhat perplexed as to his and his team's lack of pace. At Mercedes, the bigger question is over the aerodynamic upgrade they brought to the car this weekend. Mercedes are lagging behind their rivals when it comes to developing their car this season, apparently at least in part because they front-loaded their spend early in the season. But this first big update since the Canadian Grand Prix in June has not yet proved the step they had expected. The question is whether that is to do with the parts themselves or the very specific conditions of this weekend, in the heat and on the rough track surface, which is putting the tyres through the mill, and massively limiting the useful laps teams can do in terms of set-up work. Antonelli said: "With this new package, obviously the window of the way the car operates is different. So, we're trying to understand in which window the car performance is best, in the high-speed corner and low-speed corners. "Our high-speed performance has been very strong this weekend. We were very quick in the high-speed, but in the low-speed we lacked. So, we need to understand why and try to move on and improve." As for the race, Antonelli said: "Track position is going to be very important. Strategy is going to be really important. "It's a race where we will attack. Because undercut (stopping first and gaining time on a rival on fresh tyres) is incredibly powerful. "So whenever there's an opportunity, we should go for maybe an undercut and try to maximise our opportunity. "Tomorrow might be two stops, three stops. We don't know. But the only thing we know is that it's going to be roasting hot out there." title: Bluetongue restriction zone extension a 'positive thing' for farmers
description: The whole of Scotland is now a restricted zone but the agriculture minister says it will make it easier to get livestock to market.
body: The extension of the bluetongue restriction zone should make it easier to move cattle without a special licence Restrictions aimed at controlling bluetongue, a virus that affects sheep, cattle and other livestock, are now in force across the whole of Scotland. The Scottish government said they should be seen as a "positive thing" which would make it easier for farmers to get uninfected animals to market without requiring an individual licence. The disease, which can be spread by insects such as midges, does not affect people and poses no risk to food safety. Bluetongue was first detected on farms in south-west Scotland in August and there have now been more than 100 infected animals in 41 locations, including four outside the original restriction zone . While no danger to humans, Bluetongue can cause fever, swelling, lameness, birth defects and difficulty eating for cows and particularly sheep. In some cases, animals die or become so ill they have to be euthanised. 'I feel guilty': The farmer whose lamb had Scotland's first case of bluetongue What is the potentially deadly bluetongue virus? Scientists believe the disease probably spread to Scotland after infected midges were blown across the border from England but the risk of transmission is now falling as the midge season draws to a close. Agriculture Minister Jim Fairlie said extending the restriction zone was a "sensible step" at the current time that would make trading easier for the livestock industry. It means the whole of Scotland, along with England and Wales, is now covered by a restriction zone, removing the movement barriers between high and low-risk areas because they all now have the same disease status. He told BBC Scotland News: "It's a bit counterintuitive but extending restrictions is actually a positive thing because it means we've got the ability to move stock freely anywhere in the country now." October is traditionally a time when many Scottish farmers sell "store" cattle or lambs to other farmers who will fatten them up further. "We don't want people to be restricted given the fact that it's now at this time where the vets think there's unlikely to be transmission of the disease," Fairlie added. Farmers are being urged to have early conversations about vaccinations for next year Farmers must still notify the authorities immediately when an animal displays symptoms. Infected animals are generally required to remain on-farm for a minimum of 60 days, but the majority of healthy, non-infected animals can be traded. Fairlie said vaccination remained the most effective way for farmers to protect their animals from the worst effects of bluetongue. "People need to be thinking about the vaccine programme for next year," he said. "There is no other way to protect their stock properly so they should be speaking to their vet and looking forward, thinking about what the vaccination programme looks like for them." Some farmers reported difficulty getting hold of the vaccine this year as demand rose suddenly as cases were reported in England. Fairlie said having early conversations about next year's vaccination programme would spur on manufacturers to ensure there are adequate supplies. title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail
description: The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday.
body: A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail. The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished. A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend. Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London. The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said. Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident. The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles. They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy". Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident. This video can not be played I saw masked men, farmer who called 999 says RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend. Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor." Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released. "We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this. Watch: Were the RAF Fairford arrests 'pure luck'? title: Derelict 'church in the woods' sold at auction
description: St Mary's In The Wood United Reformed Church on Commercial Street in Morley sells for £100,000.
body: St Mary's In The Wood in Morley has been in a state of disrepair for many years A derelict Grade II listed church located in a wooded area of Leeds has been sold at auction. St Mary's In The Wood United Reformed Church on Commercial Street in Morley sold for £100,000 earlier this week, auctioneers BTG Eddisons confirmed. The 19th Century building has not been used for worship since 2008 and fell into disrepair after sustaining extensive fire damage two years later. A previous planning application lodged with Leeds City Council which has since lapsed proposed the site could be repurposed into a hotel, restaurant and car park. Later plans to transform the fire-damaged church into 18 apartments also did not come to fruition. The fire started about 02:30 BST in June 2010 and caused 20 people living nearby to be evacuated to a nearby supermarket due to fears the church steeple could collapse. In 2023, Leeds City Council purchased the nearby former Sunday School building, which was built in 1900, for use as a "learning and skills centre". However, the older, Gothic revival-style building, built in 1878, has remained vacant for more than 15 years. BTG Eddisons could not disclose whether St Mary's was bought by a commercial or private buyer. Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. title: Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage
description: The Conservative leader is expected to set out a return to core conservative principles at the party’s annual conference.
body: Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage The 2026 Conservative conference is big enough to justify using Birmingham's Symphony Hall as its main stage again. So, Kemi Badenoch will tread the same stage ageing rockers Marillion took last month - and where sequinned soprano Katherine Jenkins will perform next week. She'll also avoid the humiliation of a national party leader being squashed into a side room at a corporate conference centre (with drapes portioning off the empty space). Simply, the party is able to put bums on seats again - and by that measure, things are looking up. Badenoch goes into the conference with her own position secure in the party. One senior Tory says "she has actually defied cynics like me" who initially disapproved of her leadership. Her standing with the public has improved and she is now, again on a very simple but crucial measure, much better known. Her allies are sure she has developed a clear identity among the public, confiding: "People now know who she is and they enjoy her interventions - the thing we hear most is I don't always agree with her but I know where she stands." But Conservative MPs are aware that the party itself still has a much bigger issue - in the words of one shadow cabinet member: "The problem we still have is trust of the party and the brand". The shadow of the years of chaos still looms. And while Badenoch has made good progress since she took the job, most of that was up against an unpopular prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, on whom she landed plenty of political punches. She has to show "what being Conservative is now", says another senior Tory, taking on a different, more popular, rival in Andy Burnham. The Tories' warm-up to conference has been so far, so traditional. A proposed dramatic expansion of prison places kicks off Badenoch's second big party get-together. With it, a message that echoes the well-known mantra of the early 1990s Tories, issued by former leader Michael Howard at party conference: "Prison works". They are not just talking about adding on a few cells here and there, but spelling out a monumental increase in the numbers of people that the country locks up. That follows the announcement of a new "tough love" approach for young people trying to claim benefits. Don't expect the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whateley, to produce a moment as controversial as when the then-welfare secretary, Peter Lilley, proclaimed from the stage that he had "a little list" of benefit claimants he wanted to root out. But the Conservatives are determined to keep concentrating on the size of the welfare bill – believing it's right to do so for financial and moral reasons. You can expect to hear more in the week about fundamental conservative principles: people keeping more of their own money, government only stepping in when really required to, pointed concern about the level of the country's debt and public spending. And again, of course, that means Kemi Badenoch disavowing much of what the Conservatives did in office between 2010 and 2024, when the civil service grew, the tax burden grew, a law was passed to try to combat climate change, the list goes on. She'll set out at some length in the coming days what she sees as classic conservative first principles: the core beliefs the party was founded on and drifted from, she reckons, in the years gone by. If anything, Badenoch told interviewers this week the party was "finally saying what we believe" and "should be more aggressive" in displaying the party's core. The frontbench at last year's Conservative conference She believes the arrival of Andy Burnham makes that easier. There's a clearer contrast between the two. A senior ally of Badenoch says Burnham has "opened the door to it quite well, as he has harked back to the '70s in a way that I'm astonished by". Suggesting the pleasing atmospherics of Burnham's Labour are just that, atmospherics, the ally adds: "It's like a fairy story where he has come to the rescue of Britain and he has a wand in his hand and nothing else". As we talked about a couple of weeks ago, the contrasts between Labour and the Conservatives are sharper now Burnham is in post, and the conference season is only serving to exaggerate that. They are both only too happy to emphasise it with their messages, retro or not, designed to show the true souls of their tribes. But while Badenoch might find it easier to argue clearly with Burnham, rather than tangle with Starmer over process, it is harder to face an opponent who, at least for now, is proving more appealing to the public. And while plenty of Conservatives are hopeful in private that Reform might have peaked, they can't be sure that's true, or that the swathes of voters who abandoned the Tories for Farage's party will return. Badenoch has always seemed allergic to the idea of doing any kind of deal with Reform, who she dismisses as a party of protest. And her allies hope, and some believe, that Reform's appeal will fade, making the Conservatives again the obvious alternative government. But fundamental arithmetic displays that, for as long as millions of voters on the right are tempted by Farage, it's harder for the Tories to triumph. One shadow minister admits "we've still got a whole battle on the right" even though "Kemi's boldness" is beginning to break through. So, in the coming next days, prepare for a "classic showing of Tory wares": an attempt by the party's leader to set out their fundamental beliefs about the country and how it should be governed. There are pockets of nerves that Kemi Badenoch risks rewinding to an previous era. One when another newly confident leader, David Cameron, ushered in the modern Tory party on the conference stage in front of digitally produced green foliage and sunlight. One former cabinet ministe

title: 'Perimenopause cost me my job and family life'
description: Sally Williams says she wants other women to be aware of the "danger zone" of perimenopause.
body: Sally Williams told the BBC how isolated she became during the "run-up" to menopause For three years, Sally Williams struggled to understand what was happening to her as her mental health deteriorated and her life fell apart, spending almost 11 months in hospital across eight admissions. She left her finance job, was separated from her teenage son and found herself fighting for her life, unaware her symptoms could be linked to perimenopause. "No one joined the dots," Williams said. "It was only me... I joined the dots and it was transformational to start hormone replacement therapy and literally come back to life." Williams, who initially self-diagnosed, wants other women to be aware of perimenopause, the years leading up to menopause, which she described as the "danger zone". Perimenopause, external, which commonly begins around the age of 46, is when women experience menopause symptoms while still having periods. Symptoms can include anxiety, mood swings, brain fog, hot flushes and irregular periods, with some women taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) to help alleviate the symptoms. What is the menopause and what are the main signs? How does Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) work? When her symptoms began in her late 40s, Williams, from the Wychavon area, said doctors she saw initially thought she had depression. "I had multiple attempts on my life, two significant ones, one where I was in a wheelchair for three months for polytrauma, and this was in Covid, so there were no visitors. I had no contact with anyone," she explained. "I had to leave my job. This was at perimenopause time. My message to women is that, menopause is not the danger zone, it's the run up, it's the 45 to 54." For Williams, who said she was "unrecognisable" before her eventual diagnosis, it was HRT which eventually helped her, but she said it may not be for everyone. The drug, which isn't suitable for some women, tops up and stabilises oestrogen levels, sometimes in combination with a synthetic or bioidentical version of progesterone. Williams is set to speak about her hard fought menopause diagnosis at Meno Fest at Worcester Rugby Club on 7 October, external, as part of Menopause Awareness Month. The free event is being held with the aim of helping people to gain greater understanding of how perimenopause and menopause can affect every aspect of life from physical and mental health to relationships, work and family life. Williams told the BBC of how isolated she became during the "run-up" to menopause. "I lost my job. I didn't see my friends, my family for three years and I was a recluse. I was self neglecting. And my son, who was in his teens, I probably saw him three times," she explained. "He had leave his school and his friends and he had to go and live with his dad because he couldn't see me. I couldn't care for him." It was also important that men recognised what was happening to women during perimenopause, she added. "I think men need to come into the conversation as well, and I'm not just talking husbands and partners, I'm talking sons," she said. "It was devastating and there's relationships that have been broken that will never be put back together. I'm very sad about that." If you have been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line. title: Trains cancelled after bedbugs found on board
description: Southeastern said the insects were discovered in drivers' cabs, with the trains removed for cleaning.
body: Southeastern said the affected trains were removed from service to be cleaned A number of train services were cancelled after drivers discovered bedbugs in their cabs. Carriages on two affected trains were locked to isolate passenger areas from the cabs, said Southeastern, which operates services in Kent, East Sussex and Greater London. The rail firm said the trains only remained in service while they "returned to a suitable location for inspection and if necessary, treatment". The cancellations took place on mainline routes after the bugs were spotted on 22 September. None of the insects were found on any High Speed 1 trains, it added. In a social media post, Southeastern said the affected trains were based at the West Marina Depot in Hastings, the terminus point for trains from London. Services on the route go via Battle, Tunbridge Wells and Sevenoaks. A spokesperson for the firm said trains and stations are cleaned "thoroughly" so passengers can "travel safely and with confidence". Oly Turner, head of drivers at Southeastern, said: "We have a great relationship with our drivers, who have helped hugely in cooperating with us over these isolated incidents. "When we receive reports such as these we check trains thoroughly before they are put back into service when given the all clear. "Cases have been contained to the drivers' cabs in only two of our trains and no bed bugs have been identified in areas for passengers." title: Boy, 6, who died in van crash was 'loved more deeply than words could ever express'
description: Harrison Jones was killed after being struck by a Ford Transit Tipper outside his home in Llanfairfechan.
body: Harrison Glynne Jones was described as a "cheeky chappy, full of character" A six-year-old boy who died when he was struck by a van outside of his home has been named as Harrison Glynne Jones. In a tribute on a fund-raising page launched to support his family, he was described as a "cheeky chappy, full of character with a personality that could light up a room", and who had been "loved more deeply than words could ever express". Officers were called to reports of an incident involving a white Ford Transit Tipper and a child on Mill Road in Llanfairfechan, Conwy county, after 17:00 BST on Thursday, where Harrison was pronounced dead at the scene. North Wales Police said a 39-year-old man had been arrested and later released under investigation. Teddies and flowers left at scene where six-year-old boy died in crash The GoFundMe fund-raiser was launched by Kate Jones to help cover Harrison's funeral and memorial costs, as well as household bills and essential expenses while his parents take time away from work to grieve. By Saturday morning it was nearing its £20,000 target. "Our family's world was changed forever when Kayleigh and Daryl's beautiful six-year-old son Harrison was tragically hit by a vehicle outside of his own home and sadly passed away at the scene in front of his family," Jones said. "There are no words that can truly describe the heartbreak and devastation his parents, sisters and our whole family are experiencing," Jones said on the fund-raiser page. "A child should never be taken from their family so suddenly, under such tragic circumstances and we are all struggling to come to terms with this unimaginable loss," she said. "Harrison's mum and dad are facing the unimaginable task of saying goodbye to their precious little boy, while trying to somehow navigate life without him so we have set up this fundraiser to help Harrison's parents through the difficult weeks and months ahead." An investigation into the circumstances of the crash is ongoing and police have asked anyone who witnessed the incident or was in the area around Pen y Bryn Road and Mill Road at the time to get in touch with them. title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
description: The flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft two and a half hours into its journey before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker.
body: The Indian government has praised captain Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage" during the attack The co-pilot of the Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe in an attempt to take control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged some 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and take control of the plane. Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in. Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia. A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies. The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident. The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline. He completed a three-year distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, ABC News reported. A source told the news outlet Al-Hammami did not take any pilot training at the school. Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!" The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane." He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination". The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency. Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition. The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday. "I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said. About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply. The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking. In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong. Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down." People then began to rush to the cockpit, he said. Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday that the alarm was raised onboard by an Israeli woman, Tali Manes, who heard a commotion coming from the cockpit. Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men - Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan - entered the cockpit after Capt Machchhar managed to open the door despite his injuries. Hayun said, in a video released by the prime minister's office, that the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane". Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down. He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there," he said. In an interview with CNN on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the stabbed pilot, passengers and second crew had "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster". title: Kim wins Asian Games gold to secure military exemption
description: Golfer Tom Kim wins gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.
body: Tom Kim won his first title in almost three years with victory at the Scottish Open in July Asian Games - final round -18 T Kim (Kor); -15 K Higa (Jpn), W Ding (Chn), S Kaewkanjana (Tha); -11 W-H Wang (Tpe) Tom Kim won gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military. The 24-year-old led going into the final round and produced a brilliant six-under-par 64 to finish 18 under and claim victory by three strokes. There were signs of nerves with a bogey on the 17th but, after five birdies and an eagle prior to that, Kim had the margin for error and tapped in for par on the last before letting out a roar, his relief clear to see. South Korean males are, in most circumstances, required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of military service before the age of 28. However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month. This video can not be played Gold medal for Kim helps avoid military service Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier. Kim rushed from the Presidents Cup in the United States to tee off at the Kasugai Country Club in Japan, having to manage on just six hours of sleep and a 14-hour time difference. His efforts were worth it as the world number 32 can now continue his career, in which he has already won four PGA Tour titles and triumphed at the Scottish Open in July, with minimal disruption. Kim had previously come close to securing an exemption at the Paris Olympics in 2024, finishing day one tied for third before ultimately finishing eighth. However, his compatriot SH Kim, 28, missed out on a military exemption as South Korea could only win silver in the team event, alongside Tom Kim and Mun Do-yeob, who has already completed his service.
