title: Film festival aims to celebrate British-Latino identity
description: The Latino film festival in the capital will screen 60 films from 27 countries over five days.
body: Founder Ketty Rodriguez introducing a screening of Cuban film, Death of a Bureaucrat A film festival billed as London's only competitive Latino film festival is now under way, with 60 films from 27 countries showing over five days at venues including the Barbican, the ICA, Ciné Lumière and BFI Stephen Street. Guests include Cuban dancer Carlos Acosta, a former principal at the Royal Ballet, Argentine actor Óscar Martínez, Cuban actor Jorge Perugorría and Oscar-winning Chilean screenwriter Gonzalo Maza. It is running until Tuesday and will screen 60 films from 27 countries over five days. The event was founded by Cuban actress Ketty Rodriguez who, when she moved to London, was struck by the lack of Latin representation in a city famous for its multiculturalism, film and history. Rodriguez says it is the first competitive Latino film festival of this size in London. "We have received hundreds of entries from all over Latin America, and can't wait to support and showcase features, documentaries, animation, and shorts from these incredible filmmakers," she said. She told BBC London: "Everything here is about community, is about connection, and the idea started because I couldn't find my people, I didn't know where they were, so I decided to do this festival and it's very successful, I'm very happy." Cuban Dancer Javier Torres, who developed the festival idea with Rodriguez, said: "This is just the start of something great. We found a gap in the market, we found a necessity of the Latino community to come together and to give voice and narrative voices to Latin American film makers. "This is a platform for diplomacy, for culture, to get together and this is what we are building here." Alongside entries from Latin America are stories made in London for Londoners. Victor Rios, a British-Bolivian filmmaker said the event was a chance "not just to celebrate people of Latin roots but also to celebrate British-Latino identity". He moved to the UK at 16, and has two short films in the selection. He said: "It's very crucial for people to understand that we are not just here passing by. We are part of society, and this festival is establishing that too. "We're very proud to be Colombians, Bolivians, Ecuadorians, Peruvians, Chileans, but we are also British. "So we have a place, we have a say, and we want to be heard." The festival is backed by the BFI through National Lottery funding and by the City of London Corporation. title: Lewandowski, 38, hits hat-trick in 6-0 Poland win
description: Robert Lewandowski, 38, scores a hat-trick in the Nations League and Edin Dzeko plays his final game for Bosnia-Herzegovina.
body: Robert Lewandowski made his Poland debut in 2008 Robert Lewandowski scored a hat-trick as Poland thrashed 10-man Romania 6-0 in the Nations League. After Tottenham defender Radu Dragusin, who is on loan at Fiorentina, was sent off in the 22nd minute, Romania were dismantled in Warsaw. Lewandowski opened the scoring from the penalty spot and doubled the lead early in the second half. An own goal and strikes from Piotr Zielinski and Jan Bednarek followed before 38-year-old Lewandowski completed his seventh international hat-trick. The former Barcelona striker has scored 92 international goals. Poland are third in Group B4, while Romania stay fourth. Gheorghe Hagi, in his second spell in charge, became the first Romania manager to lose his first three competitive matches. In the same group there were emotional scenes as Edin Dzeko retired from international football following Bosnia-Herzegovina's 1-1 draw at home to Sweden. The ex-Manchester City forward, 40, found the net late in the first half but the goal was disallowed as the ball went out of play in the build-up. Fireworks went off after 11 minutes to celebrate the number 11 on his 152nd international appearance, and he was given a standing ovation when he was substituted after 62 minutes in Zenica. The celebrations continued after the match with an official ceremony, a guard of honour and a drone show displaying messages of thanks to Dzeko, who was showered with soft toys from the crowd during a lap of honour. Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres put Sweden in front before Kerim Alajbegovic equalised for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Kevin de Bruyne scored twice as Belgium beat Turkey 3-0 to move up to second in Group A1. The 35-year-old Napoli midfielder scored a goal in each half before Romelu Lukaku completed the scoring. Liverpool defender Milos Kerkez scored the only goal as Hungary beat Georgia in Budapest to claim their first Nations League win of the campaign. Hungary are third in Group B2, three points behind leaders Northern Ireland. title: Joker persona helps Cong 'feel the fear' in opponents
description: Wang Cong dismisses critics who say she she is not deserving of facing Natalia Silva for the flyweight world title at UFC 332 on Saturday.
body: Wang Cong has won 10 of her 11 professional MMA fights Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek. Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain. The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint. On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title. "It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport. "When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality." Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint, and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China. She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter. Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent. Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury. "She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong. Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title. Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way. "To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong. "I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense." The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025. The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023. Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China. If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili. "MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong. The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira. When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response. "I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said. title: The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top
description: Rodri is already playing a key role at Barcelona after turning down Real Madrid this summer. Guillem Balague looks at his journey so far.
body: Rodri never wanted to be interesting. While a generation of players build personal brands and chase clicks, the Barcelona and Spain midfielder stays away from social media and avoids the spotlight, talking about tactics the way other players talk about cars. He is, by his own admission, an introvert who happens to control football games for a living. And it has been some career so far. The 30-year-old won 12 major trophies with Man City and helped Spain to European Championship and World Cup successes. On Saturday, he insisted his successes with Man City could not be taken away from them after the club were found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching by the Premier League. City are set to appeal against the ruling. He also won the Ballon d'Or in 2024 and is in contention to win it for a second time in October, a rare achievement for a holding midfielder. From a Connecticut summer camp through a Castellon lecture hall to a Champions League final, Rodri has shown the willingness to absorb whatever the environment demands, understand why it is being asked of him - and get on with it. Understanding his temperament and character is also the starting point for understanding why Barcelona, not Real Madrid, is where his career has turned next after leaving Man City in the summer. Rodri believes in Man City's 'innocence' Rodri has helped Barcelona to a perfect start in La Liga Rodri's game was shaped by an education system that treats football intelligence as something to be taught and moulded. Spanish academies function on the idea that a coach is a teacher first, and Rodri absorbed that from a young age. But he also came out of his comfort zone very early. At 14, his father wanted him to spend a year at an American high school, but a season in Villarreal's youth ranks made that impossible, so the family found a compromise: a summer camp deep in the Connecticut woods. That stay left him with the fluent, American-tinged English his Manchester City team-mates would later tease him about, and it is where he watched Spain win the 2010 World Cup, alone by a lake, thousands of miles from home. His learning accelerated after being released by Atletico Madrid as a teenager, as his body had not caught up with his footballing brain. Villarreal picked him up, and there the two strands of his life - football and study - ran in parallel. He moved to Castellon, the biggest city near Villarreal, at 17, and enrolled at university to study business administration. He combined training in the morning with lectures in the afternoon. He cycled to training and lived among students who had no idea their quiet classmate would soon be starting in La Liga. When he appeared on television one evening, his flatmates realised the boy from accounting class wore the number six shirt for Villarreal. He has since called that period the best of his life. The rest of his rise is well known. Atletico brought him back in 2018 under Diego Simeone, who sharpened his intensity and competitiveness. A year later, Manchester City paid his 70m euro release clause, and Guardiola turned him into arguably the finest holding midfielder of his generation. There were setbacks, including a Champions League final defeat by Chelsea in 2021 that left him unable to speak to his own family afterwards. Two years later came the redemption, the goal that won City the Champions League in 2023. That goal changed the story of his career. The Euros with Spain came and the Ballon d'Or followed, along with the World Cup title and MVP award that preceded his move to Barcelona this summer. And you get the feeling his story is far from finished. Rodri has been open about how seriously he took Real Madrid's interest in him this summer. Speaking to Spanish sports radio station COPE, he said the club behaved impeccably and pursued him properly from the first approach. He spoke to many in and around the club, and admitted the warmth of those conversations made his eventual decision harder. New manager Jose Mourinho communicated his footballing idea clearly and what he wanted from Rodri personally, and that approach appealed to him. Inside Real, the sense that Rodri was the player they needed went well beyond the coach. Several figures at the club still regard him as the profile the squad is missing now, a controlling midfielder capable of dictating tempo in a way nobody currently on the books quite replicates. The scale of Mourinho's pursuit reflected a genuine conviction that Rodri was required. Madrid have not gone out and found an alternative version of what he would have given them, so the gap the midfielder would have filled remains a gap. Rodri's reasons for turning that interest down was footballing rather than personal. His decision came down to where he could grow and contribute most, a project built around a squad full of young players, many of whom he knew already, and who fitted the way he understands the game. It was a decision about which team needed what he offers, and where he could make the biggest difference. Rodri is a footballing encyclopaedia and, many would argue, the best defensive midfielder in the world. There are few better when it comes to positional play, and he is one of the very best because of what he does himself and what he brings out in his team-mates. Without the ball, both in the press and when dropping back, he gives that sense of security in front of the defence, especially in those moments when Barcelona lose the ball. But he is also outstanding with the ball because he distributes it quickly and always chooses the right route. You can see all that in every Barcelona game. His arrival has been described inside the club as one of the most significant developments of recent years on and off the pitch - playing in all but one match of Barcelona's perfect start to the campaign. title: Island hosts inter-island environment summit
description: The annual event brings together delegates to share ideas and develop joint projects.
body: The event included a field trip to Lihou Island exploring its ecology and archaeology Environmental experts, conservation groups and businesses from across the British Isles and France have gathered in Guernsey for the 26th Inter-Island Environment Meeting. The annual event, co-ordinated by the Guernsey Nature Commission, brings together delegates to share ideas and develop joint projects aimed at protecting the natural environment. This year's theme, Nature for the Next Generation, includes talks on subjects ranging from seabird restoration and woodland resilience to butterfly monitoring in Sark and citizen science projects. A Sixth Form Environment Meeting gave young people the chance to present environmental issues that matter to them and contribute ideas for the future. Students will take part in workshops linked to Guernsey's upcoming Marine Spatial Plan, helping shape discussions about the future protection and management of the island's seas. Angela Salmon, head of education at the Nature Commission and a member of the meeting group said inviting sixth formers to share the environmental issues that mattered to them "makes perfect sense". Among those attending was Sebastian Dufour, an independent consultant for the Alderney Wildlife Trust, who joined a field trip to Lihou Island exploring its ecology and archaeology. He said he had learned about a Benedictine Priory site "which is very interesting" and discovered there had been "a really remarkably large industry in harvesting seaweed". Dufour said he particularly valued the collaborative nature of the event, adding: "We're all coming from different islands and we're all facing similar challenges." He said the annual meeting provided an opportunity to "learn from each other" and "share our successes and failures and everything". title: Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says
description: The attack on Northern Bridge comes after repeat attacks on another major bridge in recent days.
body: The Northern Bridge is the second major bridge to be targeted by Russia in recent days, Kyiv's mayor said A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko says. The attack damaged the road surface and trolleybus overhead wires on the Northern Bridge, he said. The strike comes after the Southern Bridge has been targeted multiple times by Russian drones since Thursday. The bridges link the eastern and western parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday's strikes, signalling a new stage in Moscow's attacks. In the Thursday attack, a Russian drone hit cables of Kyiv's Pivdennyi bridge Writing on Telegram on Saturday, Klitschko said: "Hitting the North Bridge. Emergency services are on their way." "Traffic on the bridge from the left to the right bank is currently blocked," he added. Earlier attacks on the Southern Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday, in which Klitschko warned that intensified Russian drone and missile strikes were "tearing Kyiv apart". He said the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities. Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks. title: 'I watched 800 films in Covid, now I direct them'
description: Benjamin Williams from Malvern has worked on Apple TV's Slow Horses for its upcoming season.
body: Benjamin Williams has loved films since he was a child During the coronavirus lockdown in 2020, Benjamin Williams, a lifelong film fan, watched 800 films. "I just found the time. Plus, it was Covid - I was bored," said the now 28-year-old, looking back. He started out with dreams of becoming an animator, inspired by films like Avatar: The Last Airbender and Pokemon, before going on to study film at Hereford Sixth Form College, which "opened a whole world" for him. Williams, from Malvern, has now directed his own film and worked with the likes of Marvel and, most recently, was an assistant director on Apple TV's hit series, Slow Horses, starring award-winners Sir Gary Oldman and Dame Kristin Scott Thomas. "I have signed many NDAs [non-disclosure agreements] over the years, and obviously, Slow Horses has been one of them. "I can't say anything about it - obviously the cast and crew are amazing - it's a very wonderful show to work on. "That's probably the one I've learnt the most on, because that's the one I've spent the most amount of time on," he said. Williams says Sir Gary Oldman is a "pretty cool dude" The spy thriller series is based on the best-selling novel Slow Horses by Mick Herron and premiered in 2022, with a seventh season set for release in 2027. Oldman stars as the crude boss of a team of failed or disgraced MI5 agents who have been banished to a building called Slough House. "I worked in the production department, which is logistics, all sorts of paperwork and call sheets, and you manage all of the schedules - that's a very heavy admin-based role," said Williams. "I actually have worked on the floor for a couple of days because I'm also an AD [assistant director] as well... which I love doing." He describes Oldman as the biggest star he has worked with. "That is a pinch-me moment every time you see him," he said. "He is pretty cool. He's a pretty cool dude." His short film, Keys, has been nominated at Birmingham Film Festival He also worked on Marvel's VisionQuest, which releases later this year. "I did a lovely film, only a week on it just for additional photography, called The Christophers, with Sir Ian McKellen, who I was very fortunate just to briefly meet," he said. "There's such an incredible aura around him of just, 'Oh god, it's Ian McKellen'." He has also worked on Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan with John Krasinski, the Squid Games reality show and the Peaky Blinders film, Immortal Man. "I did get to meet Cillian, but again, very similar to Ian, I was just like, 'Hi, cool, move on, great', which was really fun." His own short film, Keys, premiered at the Worcester Film Festival in September and has been nominated for "best local film" at the Birmingham Film Festival. Williams said making a good impression in the industry and working hard had helped his journey. "As long as you do a good job, you show up, and you're likeable enough, people want to continue working with you, which is how I landed Slow Horses while I was working on a Marvel show," he said. "I got an email from a lovely coordinator... I think they just did the new The Thomas Crown Affair film with Michael B Jordan. "He just sort of reached out because I'd been recommended... they were like, 'We heard you did a great job on this; could you come and do this or this?'" He added: "I have been lucky, but also at the same time, I think I'm honest enough to know that I can back myself and that I've worked hard to get to those positions as well." title: Ancient bridge hidden under reservoir is revealed
description: The Bessom Bridge on Exmoor was flooded nearly 50 years ago when Wimbleball Reservoir was created.
body: An ancient bridge underneath Wimbleball Lake has resurfaced due to prolonged dry weather Months of dry weather and prolonged heat have revealed a bridge dating back to the Victorian times that had been submerged during the creation of a reservoir. The ancient stone Bessom Bridge flooded nearly 50 years ago when Wimbleball Reservoir was created at Exmoor National Park in Somerset. It was later replaced by a new bridge. In the summer, the Environment Agency declared that Wimbleball was one of the top three lowest reservoirs in the country after levels were recorded as "exceptionally low". Dr Lucy Shipley, historic environment record officer for Exmoor, said: "We live in an ever-changing world and it's not a kind of fixed point where things stay the same." Teenage boy, 16, killed in motorbike crash Complaints about animal sales at Bridgwater Fair Ted Lasso honours Anthony Head with fresh tribute Shipley said there were other archaeological finds beneath the lake which were not demolished before the reservoir were created, including a barrow dating back to the Bronze Age. It is not known why some structures were demolished and others were not. The bridge dates back to the 1800s The former Bessom Bridge used to cross a stream that fed into the River Haddeo, while the new one crosses the north side of the lake. When water levels drop, the old bridge can be seen from the new one. Shipley said the changing landscape on Exmoor was "extraordinary". "The photographs are incredible, they're just so dramatic of the bridge poking out from the silt and sediment that's covered it. "We live in an ever-changing world and it's not a kind of fixed point where things stay the same, but then by contrast… there's been a consistency of settlement and people living in farming and working in similar ways, so it's that balance of understanding how the world around us is always changing and responding, but also recognising that some things are really consistent over time." She added that the historic bridge could be enjoyed from afar and asked visitors to refrain from walking on the dried-up section of the reservoir. Elsewhere around the county, traces of centuries-old gardens were found in Bishop's Palace in Wells, while relics of old structures were uncovered at Glastonbury Abbey due to the record-breaking summer temperatures. Water levels at the reservoir remain low after prolonged heat and dry weather Wimbeball Reservoir, which supplies water to hundreds of thousands of homes across the South West, has a capacity of 21,320 megalitres - one megalitre is a million litres. The reservoir remains low following record-breaking temperatures over the summer, with a current capacity of only 21.1% as of 27 September, according to South West Water. Hundreds of thousands of people remain under hosepipe bans across the country while water sources recover from the prolonged dry weather. The National Drought Group said the recent rain has not been enough to replenish supplies, with drought only being over when rivers, groundwater and reservoirs return to normal levels. Research from the Environment Agency showed the country will need 120% of typical rainfall over the next seven months for all areas to be considered out of drought. title: New baby bank 'open to everybody'
description: The facility offers essential items for free, including clothes for babies and small children.
body: The baby bank is open every Tuesday morning The lead volunteer of a new baby bank, which gives away free children's products to those in need, says it is "open to everybody". The Newent hub of Forest of Dean Baby Bank at The Ark Cafe in Newent, Gloucestershire, offers everything from baby wipes and breast pumps to hats and swimwear, and can also source larger items like cots from a warehouse in Cinderford. Helen Carter, lead volunteer, says no one will be means tested, with parents often picking up new items while donating what no longer fits their child. Kylie, a Newent mum visiting the baby bank, said: "It's always expensive to buy new baby things and food and nappies and wipes. So to have the support locally is wonderful." A lot of the items available at the faciltity are donated, which Carter said the team was "really, really grateful for". Currently, autumn clothing bundles are in demand, but volunteers have already started putting together a Christmas box of festive clothing, blankets, and shoes. "A lot of people say, 'I don't need it, I'm okay', but then a lot of people are just sort of managing their finances and are unable to have a nice day out with their children," Carter said. "But if they [visit the baby bank], then they would be able to pay for that day out, so they might not think they're struggling, but it helps." Parents visiting the baby bank often donate items they no longer need while picking up new things for their children In its latest Parent Experience Report, The National Childbirth Trust said nearly half of parents said they were struggling more financially after having a baby, a figure which rose to about six in ten among self-employed, unemployed or part-time employed parents. Kylie, who was on her first visit to the bank, said clothing and supplies for children were "always expensive". "I'm quite lucky, I do have an older child as well, so I've got a lot of hand-me-downs," she said. "But for everyone who hasn't got an older child and [do] formula feeding and things like that, it is very expensive to keep them clean and fed." Volunteer Isabel said she wanted to give back to the centre after she was helped with food parcels and clothing. "I know from having three small children that there is a massive need in the area, so I think this is a great thing that we're doing here," she said. "I just wish more people knew about it." The baby bank is open every Tuesday morning from 09.30 to 11.30. title: Man desperate to find teen he saved 30 years ago
description: Lee Heyes says he was 15 when he jumped in Eccleston Delph to rescue a teenager from drowning.
body: Lee Heyes said he would love to know how the man he saved is getting on A man who risked his own life to rescue a stranger from drowning 30 years ago is trying to track him down. Lee Heyes jumped into a quarry when he was 15 after he realised the older teen had got into difficulty. The now 45-year-old, from Chorley, who has written a song about the ordeal, said instinct took over when the stranger, who he thinks was about 18 or 19, jumped in the water at Eccleston Delph and disappeared under the surface after getting tangled in reeds. "It has really bothered me ever since," he said. "I would love to know how he is getting on." Lee Heyes said writing a song about the ordeal has helped him Lee, who is a plasterer and singer songwriter, performing as "soundstruggles", recalls there being all sorts in the water - even cars at the bottom - when the incident happened in the mid 90s. He said it took him three attempts, diving deep under the surface, to find the teenager. After managing to untangle him, Lee said it was a struggle to get him back to the surface as he was "much bigger than me". Lee got his friends to enter the water to help keep the teenager's head above the surface while he swam to get help from a dad who was in a dinghy with his son. By this point, Lee recalls being shattered but said the adrenaline spurred him on to raise the alarm. The dad then used the dinghy to get the teenager ashore. Lee said the stranger walked off afterwards without saying a word. "I presume he was in shock," he added. He said looking back it could have been a very different outcome. "I could easily have died myself that day," he said. Lee's message to anyone thinking of swimming in open water is "don't do it because it is so dangerous". The trauma of that fateful day has never gone away and Lee believes it triggered anxiety. Lee, who is one of the stars at this weekend's Chorley Live which features 280 performances across 36 venues in the town and has more than 10,000 followers on TikTok, has written a song about the ordeal called Aqualung. The moving song has helped him deal with what happened, he said. "It is a long time to carry that burden." He said the teenager had blond hair and was about 5ft 10in (1.78m). He was wearing a Liverpool FC shirt and was with two girls. Lee added: "I would love to know how he is getting on so if he or one of the girls was with him, could contact me that would be amazing." title: How rapist priest exploited charisma to abuse his 'cult-like' congregation
description: Chris Brain, who led nightclub-style services in the 1980s and 90s, is convicted of rape.
body: Chris Brain led the Nine O'Clock Service from 1984 to 1995 In the detailed written instructions given to the young women who worked without pay in the then-Reverend Chris Brain's house, there was a revealing demand. The homebase team, as they were known, were to "do anything" the Church of England priest asked of them. Routine tasks - assigned on a rota 24 hours a day, seven days a week - included cooking, cleaning, ironing, shopping, looking after Brain's young daughter, and walking his dog. This housework was intended to free Brain for his mission of leading the Nine O'Clock Service (NOS), a radical congregation of hundreds of young people drawn weekly to a Sheffield church in the 1980s and 1990s by a fusion of rave culture, live music, environmental activism and liturgy. But the lengthy list of homebase team duties did not spell out other demands Brain made in the attic bedroom of his family's end-terrace house in the suburb of Crookes, heard jurors at his retrial on charges of rape and indecent assault. On Friday at Inner London Crown Court, the 69-year-old was found guilty of raping one woman in his congregation and four indecent assaults against three others. He had already been convicted of 17 indecent assaults in August 2025 but faced a retrial as jurors could not reach verdicts on five further counts. Brain will be sentenced later this year and has been told he is facing a custodial term. His sentencing will conclude a dramatic and protracted downfall for a preacher who at one point had been preparing to take NOS global with expansion to the US. The charismatic and domineering preacher, seen by many followers as a prophet, would routinely summon members of his congregation to "put him to bed" with sensual massages, jurors heard. Often Brain would strip to his underwear and expect kissing and sexual touching with the women, who feared being ostracised - or even damned - if they refused, the court heard. "By displeasing Brain, you were displeasing God," explained one woman, who gave evidence last month during her former vicar's sexual assault trial. NOS outgrew St Thomas's, and in the early 1990s moved to Ponds Forge (pictured above in 1998) The movement took root in the early 1980s when Brain, his wife Lynne and small group of like-minded Christian friends joined St Thomas's church in Crookes. These dozen or so new worshippers - clustered around a band called Present Tense - were devout but disillusioned with traditional Anglican worship. Brain, their bassist and de facto leader, railed against "fancy golf club Christianity" which did not connect with them culturally. In 1984, the church's vicar Robert Warren gave the group an opportunity to run their own experimental service, every Sunday at 21:00. The band - who had played gigs across the north of England and performed before U2 at the Christian festival Greenbelt - ditched their evangelical rock songs in favour of a new sound influenced by Sheffield's burgeoning electronic music scene. NOS was a sensation - attracting a youthful congregation of up to 600 people with an innovative blend of cutting-edge music, video, prayer, and dancing. "It's the most entertaining church I've been to. It's the best dance night in Sheffield," one worshipper told a 1990 BBC Radio 4 programme, which reported how NOS was "bridging the gap between the church and the people". One NOS member put it more bluntly in a TV documentary five years later: "We were sticking two fingers up to normal, middle-class church ways of behaviour." The Diocese of Sheffield, thrilled by the sight of students queueing down the road to worship to the pulsing sound of house music, fast-tracked Brain's route to priesthood despite the reservations of his ordination tutor. The Archbishop of Canterbury told Brain he would be happy to see a NOS in every town and city in Britain. The services, which later moved to a larger space at Ponds Forge leisure centre, were a huge production involving a crew of up to 150 volunteers - among them musicians, sound technicians, designers, security, and a trucking team. A new multimedia service was planned each week, with volunteers working unpaid throughout Sunday into the early hours of Monday morning to pull it off. Warren, who had oversight of NOS in its first years at St Thomas's, told the court he initially believed Brain's"controlling" nature helped to get things done. But as the popularity of NOS grew, the vicar noticed "cult-like elements" emerging. Brain's congregation seemed to look at him "almost as a guru," Warren said in evidence at Brain's first trial. NOS members were expected to live simply and pay at least 10% of their income to the tight-knit and passionate community, though the court heard many gave more. Some handed over their inheritances and even houses. Brain, meanwhile, had a modern car, a mobile phone, designer clothes and went on expensive holidays. In 1994, he moved his family to live in a renovated Peak District farmhouse which had been donated to NOS, jurors heard. "He seemed to be living a luxurious lifestyle when other people are scrimping and scraping along," one NOS member told the court. Another, who estimated she had given £40,000 to NOS over seven years, recalled the "manipulative" Brain persuading her to skip her brother's wedding in South Africa and buy a van for the community instead. Brain's ordination was fast-tracked as a result of the popularity of the NOS NOS members told the court they were expected to cut ties with family and friends outside the community. Jurors were told that one woman was reprimanded by Brain and other NOS leaders for going home to see her family on a weekend: "There were messages to the point of, 'This is your family now. Sacrifice now, for the greater good'." Women gave evidence that Brain would "groom" them by pulling up to them on the street in his car and inviting

title: Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers
description: Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect.
body: Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect. Northern Ireland's largest provider of natural gas, SSE Airtricity, increased its prices by almost 19% on Thursday for its 200,000 domestic and small business customers. That means the annual gas bill of a typical household in the greater Belfast and west gas network areas will increase by almost £172. The company said "unprecedented levels of volatility in global energy markets and higher wholesale gas prices" had led to the price rise. Wholesale gas prices in the UK have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran. Keeping the house warm is particularly important for parents with young children and babies. Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave. She said she expects the winter months to be difficult because "most people are going to have to have the heating on, especially if you've young kids in the house". "There's no escaping it - everything feels more expensive and it is more expensive." She added that, despite "budgeting proactively" and "being as careful as you can with savings and credit cards", rising bills mean people's financial situations are out of their control. "You have to cut somewhere else and I already feel we are doing that," she said. Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave Lucy is one of the parents who attends a weekly baby class at Woodstock Library in east Belfast. Branch manager Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using their free activities to combat the rising cost of living. She said: "As well as families, we have lots of older people coming in now to keep warm." "We have people coming in who will stay all day, use the computer, have a chat and stay until closing time sometimes, so it is quite evident that we are providing an essential service at the minute when people are struggling," she added. Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using her branche's free activities to combat the rising cost of living Ryan McStay is a final year student at St Mary's University College Belfast, where he is studying to become a primary school teacher. He said he and his flatmates were "shocked" when they received a letter explaining their Firmus energy bills would be rising by 12.5%. "It shouldn't be normalised," he told BBC News NI. Ryan said increases like this exacerbate an already serious cost of living crisis for students like him. "The price of everything is rocketing. You're always second guessing and thinking about how much money have I got." The 21-year-old, who is from Newry, said the cost of living in Northern Ireland means he plans to move abroad after university. "I personally believe the best option for me right now would be to leave the country." Ryan McStay said he was "shocked" by the energy price increases Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie. She provides palliative nursing care to patients in their homes. "Many of them are affected by fuel poverty," Naomi said. "I think it is getting worse. People are struggling more, and the problem is that your energy needs increase hugely when you're dying at home. "Somebody is already struggling with the fact that they're dying. To then know that they can't keep their house warm." Naomi explained that a number of factors contribute to the increased energy needs, including the need to stay warm, different sleeping patterns, and essential medical devices. She said some patients have turned down services that could help improve their quality of life because they can't pay their electricity bills. Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie Naomi said terminal illness adds further costs for patients, such as the cost of transport to and from hospital appointments. "There is a huge problem, and you see that struggle often. "I'm really saddened. The support is limited, there is very little out there. There is no reduction in costs of their electricity, even though their needs are so much higher and essential for their care." Naomi added that Marie Curie have called for the implementation of a "social tariff" for people with terminal illnesses, to ease their financial burden. "It would make such a huge difference to have that bit of extra money in your last months of life, so you're comfortable and you can spend it with your family," she said. She said some people spend the end of their life working because they "don't have any other access to money". "You end up dying not being able to keep your house warm. That to me is just devastating." It comes as Share Energy announced electricity prices will also rise by 12.6% from today. This will add an extra £129 per year onto the typical household bill of their 41,000 customers. Head of Energy Policy at the Consumer Council Raymond Gormley said: "This increase has been driven by the continued volatility in wholesale energy costs, caused by geopolitics in the Middle East. "I suspect some of the other unregulated suppliers may follow suit and increase their tariffs." Gas prices outside the greater Belfast also rose on Thursday. Firmus energy has announced an 8.98% rise for 77,000 domestic and small business customers in the Ten Towns network area from 1 October. That means a typical annual gas bill will rise by around £87. It comes after an increase of 15.65% in July 2026. Households across Northern Ireland will get the one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month. It will be applied automatically without the need for an application. The reduction is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market. The schemes are being funded by the UK government. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit whe

title: An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded
description: Sometimes in Northern Ireland, the definition of success is "nobody got hurt," writes BBC News NI's community correspondent.
body: All the ingredients of a typical Northern Ireland crisis have been in place for the past week except for one – violence. A stand-off - over a proposed Orange Order parade in Portadown, opposed by nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning. Verbal clashes between politicians, late-night negotiations, appeals for calm and a major security operation have all been in the mix. However, the Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown has not descended into disorder or trouble on the streets. Sometimes in Northern Ireland, the definition of success is "nobody got hurt". The crisis is not over, and fears of an outbreak of street violence remain, but everything is under control at the moment. The truth is few predicted a relatively peaceful week when the crisis first erupted. It was an extraordinary seven days. Tension started to build after the Parades Commission, which regulates marches, gave the go-ahead for the controversial Orange Order parade in Portadown to pass along the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road. That was on a Friday afternoon. Orange Order members stand outside Drumcree Church on Monday Within 24 hours the issue was being battled out at the High Court in Belfast during an urgent Saturday hearing which ended up lasting more than 13 hours.. Sitting under the same roof were those involved in the dispute – Portadown Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition – headed by Nigel Dawson and Breandán Mac Cionnaith respectively. They sat within a matter of feet from each other but their positions were worlds apart. Court proceedings ended in the early hours of Sunday morning, with the parade given the go-ahead. All involved then made the 30-mile journey through the night from Belfast to Portadown ahead of the scheduled start to the Orange parade at 08:00 BST. By that stage, their route along the Garvaghy Road had been blocked. Up to 1,000 people were standing in the middle of the road, many of them linking arms. Some of them were prominent members of Sinn Féin, which helped turn the parade controversy into a political crisis at Stormont. A mile away, outside Drumcree Church, the 35 Orangemen who were hoping to march went back inside. People began to line to block the Garvaghy Road early on Sunday morning and there has been presence, albeit much smaller, since Torrential rain meant everyone got cold and wet, particularly the protesters but the road remained blocked and the parade was thwarted. Police told the Orangemen not even to try to walk down the road. And so the stand-off began. Protesters along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of points on Sunday Since then there has been frenetic activity behind-the-scenes, mainly at Hillsborough Castle, to try to break the deadlock. Four days of talks took place but by Thursday night it was clear they were going nowhere. At Stormont, the power-sharing executive came close to collapse. In the end, it wobbled but it did not fall down. Unionists accused some members of Sinn Féin of being lawmakers who became lawbreakers. They insisted they were simply supporting a community that needed their help. Expect that argument to continue in the days and weeks ahead. In the meantime, the focus now switches back to Belfast High Court, for an appeal hearing on Monday. The residents' coalition is trying to overturn the decision to give the march the go-ahead. Although the court is important, nobody is taking their eye off the situation on the ground in Portadown, especially the police. The Orangemen still want to walk. The protesters are standing by, just in case. The Drumcree stand-off remains tense. The hope is that the only battles which take place in the coming days are in the Belfast courtroom and the Stormont chamber, and not on the streets of Portadown. Alastair Power and Nigel Dawson from the Portadown District arrive for talks with the secretary of state The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident. However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, mainly Catholic or nationalist areas. The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree parade route but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against it. Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years, until recent events. title: Learning from Arteta and inspiring youngsters - Wilshere on management
description: Luton Town manager Jack Wilshere speaks about being back where he started as an eight-year-old and the lessons he learned from his time at Arsenal.
body: Jack Wilshere won the FA Cup with Arsenal as a player in 2014 and 2015 and guided Luton Town to the EFL Trophy in April The Football Interview will be available on BBC One at 12:45 BST every Saturday during the Premier League season, as well as on BBC iPlayer, BBC Football YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app. In the seventh episode of the new season, Kelly Somers sits down with Luton Town manager Jack Wilshere. Jack Wilshere's footballing career has gone full circle. From starting out at Luton Town aged seven, Wilshere went on to win trophies at Arsenal and represent England at two major tournaments, before having to retire early because of injury problems and moving into coaching. Now, he is back where he began, at Luton, this time as manager. Sitting overlooking the pitches he used to play on as a youngster, the 34-year-old spoke to BBC Sport's Kelly Somers for The Football Interview and discussed his career - and how he hopes he can use his experiences to improve his players. An exciting attacking midfielder with an ability to spot a pass or dribble past his opponent, Wilshere twice won the FA Cup with the Gunners. He played in the Premier League 182 times and represented England on 34 occasions, appearing at both the World Cup in Brazil in 2014 and the European Championship in France two years later. But injuries plagued the latter part of his career, with him announcing his retirement at only 30. However, there were no regrets. "I loved it [my career], I'm really proud," he said in the interview, which can be watched on BBC One at 12:45 BST on Saturday, 3 October. "I got to play for my country and represent them at two major tournaments. OK, they didn't go the way we wanted them to, but I got to do it. "I scored for my country, I played for the club I loved growing up, so pride is the biggest thing." Watch The Football Interview on BBC Sport Jack Wilshere - The Football Interview This video can not be played Arteta helped me understand the game - Wilshere On 13 October it will be one year since Wilshere became Luton boss, his first senior management role - although he had been in interim charge of Norwich City for a two-game spell at the end of the previous season. He has already won silverware in his time with the Hatters, guiding them to the EFL Trophy, beating Stockport County 3-1 at Wembley in April in front of a crowd of nearly 50,000. "I'm 34 now and probably could still be playing," he added. "Don't get me wrong, I loved every minute of playing, but I also really, really love this and I'm fortunate to start my [management] journey early. "I'm really grateful to the club and the board for giving me that opportunity because they didn't need to. I was a young coach wanting to make my first step into the game." Immediately after his playing career ended, he was invited back to Arsenal to coach their youngsters and instantly knew management and coaching was for him. "I hear stories about people struggling in retirement and I retired on a Monday, and I was in with the [under] 18s on a Tuesday," said Wilshere. "When I first went and walked through the door to coaching, I realised this is going to take over my life, and I need to commit myself to this if I want to improve." This video can not be played Wilshere 'proud' of playing career despite injuries By that time Mikel Arteta, who had been Wilshere's Arsenal team-mate for five years, was first-team manager. Arteta guided the Gunners to the Premier League title in 2025-26, their first time as English champions in 22 years, and Wilshere felt the Spaniard had played a vital role in developing him as a coach. "I got to see Mikel and how he coached and the influence he was having," said Wilshere. "I would ask him questions, why he's doing certain things, and I started to fall in love with it and how he started to prepare training sessions. "I'd get an opportunity to practice that with the 18s in the afternoon and it was something I wasn't that good at, and I felt uncomfortable at times. "I was influenced by Mikel, but then I had to learn how to teach. I had to learn how to get that across, how to plan a session and how to get the outcomes that you wanted. "I played under some good coaches and was quite good at understanding what a coach wants, but I never dived into 'why is he asking me to do that?' Mikel really made that clear and I was lucky enough to have a relationship where I could say, 'well, why do you want that?' And he was open enough to share it with me." Not only did his former club Arsenal become English champions, but Wilshere gained extra satisfaction as he had coached defender Myles Lewis-Skelly, winger Ethan Nwaneri and midfielder Max Dowman during his time at the club's academy. Wilshere was only 16 when he made his Arsenal debut, and Dowman was 15 when he first played for the Gunners senior team, with Wilshere spotting his talent early on. "Max played for my 18s team when he was 13," added Wilshere. "I remember calling my dad because I played for the 18s when I was 14. I was like, 'was 13 too young?' "In the first game we could clearly see that he was ready for it. And I remember calling my dad and saying, 'you need to come watch this kid'. My dad did, and my dad's very biased, as you could imagine. But even he said, 'he's better than you'." Early in his career he had been pictured drinking and smoking, leading to criticism from then Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger, but Wilshere said he learned from the experience and passes that knowledge on to his players. title: Woman deceived ex-partner that she had given birth to his babies, judge rules
description: The man paid his ex-partner around £30,000 over two years believing she had given birth to his children.
body: A woman convinced her former partner she had given birth to two children who most likely did not exist in what a High Court judge described as an "extraordinary" and "elaborate campaign of deceit". The man, who has not been named but was referred to as John during the hearing, applied to the Family Court after he was told the woman had sold their two children for a combined £500. The case heard that the man received messages and photos of the children and paid the woman around £30,000 over the course of two years. But in a hearing in February, the woman, who was referred to as Jane, told the judge she had lied about the pregnancies for revenge, claiming the man had abused her. The court heard the man believed he was the children's' father because in late 2022 his partner told him she was pregnant, sent pictures of an ultrasound image and had become "visibly pregnant" as time went on. In May 2023, shortly before the first baby was due, the woman called the police alleging she had been assaulted by the man. He was arrested and subsequently held on remand for several months, Mrs Justice Judd said in her ruling which was published on Friday. Following this, the woman sent a message to his stepfather saying the baby had been born as well as sharing baby photos. At one stage she is said to have sent voice notes to her former partner's mother in the middle of the night with the sound of a baby crying in the background. Later, she told the man she was pregnant again and the baby was due in August 2024. However, before the due date, the couple split up and did not reconcile. The woman would go on to tell the man's mother the baby had been born. The woman admitted to the court she had told him she was pregnant when they were together, and afterwards, but conceded she had told a series of elaborate lies and that there were, in fact, no children. She argued she was menopausal at the time and could not have been pregnant and bank statements show she attended a tanning shop on the day she said she had given birth, Mrs Justice Judd said. In her judgement, the judge concluded that the "factors that weigh against the children genuinely existing were very strong, stronger than the factors pointing the other way". She said the man was the victim of a "sustained and elaborate campaign of deceit" which also impacted his mother and closest friend. "Added to this, the behaviour was cruel, leading a man and his mother to believe they had children and grandchildren respectively.", the Judge said. The judge added she was unable to conclude the woman's motive for her behaviour but said financial fraud was a "possibility" and that the "complex mental health problems" she suffered from may have also played a part. title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
description: Immediate action is needed to help households struggling with bills this winter, says trade body Energy UK.
body: The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said. Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis. Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off. Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October. That is the equivalent of about £60 per year - or £5 per month - taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year. But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to £1,999. Energy UK said it accepted the government had already provided some support. VAT on electricity bills was cut on Thursday, and some levies were cancelled or shifted into taxation earlier this year. But the trade body said these savings had been wiped out by high wholesale prices, paid by suppliers, that were the result in part of international events - namely conflict in the Middle East and the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. It said bills were soaring as they had in 2022 when they were driven up by the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "We cannot afford to wait for the same scale of crisis before acting again. We must heed the lessons from that time," said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK. She said that the urgent intervention needed was highlighted by growing levels of customer debt, the cost of which now added an average of £67 a year to everyone's bills. Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years Energy bills are rising by £60 a year - here's how you can bring that down On Thursday, the boss of supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, warned that the UK was "walking into a second energy crisis" and Vyas said that action was needed before bills jumped again. "Last-minute emergency interventions run the risk of being badly targeted and costing us all more," she said. Energy UK is calling for government measures including: targeted support over and above the £150 Warm Home Discount, given to people on benefits, which would eventually lead to the introduction of a discounted social tariff a debt relief scheme for the most severely affected households as part of a strategy that will also help prevent debt build-up among new tenants and homeowners removing more levies from electricity bills and shifting them to taxation, as part of a wider move to electrification At the Labour Party conference last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed". "We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off," he said. title: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
description: “I’ve heard about it many, many, many times” says one doctor who treats motion sickness.
body: Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car. Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys. It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car. Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern. So what could explain these reports of motion sickness? Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles. It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says. "I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles. Lola Baird noticed that she felt sick in electric vehicle taxis as well as her boyfriend's car. "I started to put two and two together," she says But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive. Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point". "There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says. When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs. Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it. She used to get motion sick only on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute drive to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell. On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before. Mark Quigg says electric cars are a "lovely driving experience for me, personally, because they are a lot quieter" Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars. Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says. But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, external, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds. Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness. Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles. Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says. Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the electric car starts to slow down and uses the energy to feed the battery. However, it is a process that needs to be done smoothly with the accelerator being released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration. "It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac. This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time". "It's actually horrendous," says Carolyn Le, who blames regenerative braking for her motion sickness Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness. Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly. She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself. Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, Hac says. Women and children are more susceptible, experts say. Motion sickness typicall

title: Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises?
description: Big moments from headline acts are shared online long before many fans see their favourite artists.
body: Big moments from Olivia Rodrigo's tour were dissected online shortly after her opening night Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned. You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view. When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings. But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not. Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online. Tours by Harry Styles, Charli XCX and Ariana Grande have also been filmed from every angle and shared over the past few months. While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise. Aurélia Collins always aims to go to gigs not knowing what to expect Aurélia Collins is one of them, spending weeks trying to trick her algorithm into not serving her content about her favourite artists and tapping "not interested" when videos come up, even though she says "it hurts my soul". It can mean her social media feed is a bit bland, but she tells BBC Newsbeat "it's worth it for the surprise". The 20-year-old criminology student is a huge One Direction fan and says she just about managed to avoid spoilers for Styles' Together, Together tour over summer. But when one slipped through the net about Niall Horan before she was able to see his show in London on Saturday - her first time seeing him live after being a fan for 16 years - she was "gutted". "When I was younger, we couldn't afford to go to events like this and hear live music and because it's such a moment, I really want to take it in," she says. "I want the full experience, and that includes the element of surprise that people that go to the opening night of the tour can get." Georgia McAdam says videos online help her plan her gig experience Not all fans think spoilers are a bad thing, though. In fact, Georgia McAdam claims she loves them. "I'm the type of person that loves to be prepared," the 22-year-old says. "I love to know what the stage is looking like, what the set list consists of and where to stand." McAdam's a huge Olivia Rodrigo fan and sees online spoilers more as "teasers". She feels no amount of online videos can ever really take away from the excitement of the real thing. "Sometimes you get different surprise songs to what's online or you never know what an artist might do," she adds. Some artists have reacted by switching up their sets in small ways each night to make sure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected. Taylor Swift had bespoke outfits and surprise songs during her mammoth Eras tour, Sabrina Carpenter performed unique positions during her song Juno and switched up her Nonsense outro, and Jay-Z has been changing up his set list on his current run. But the Guardian's deputy music editor Laura Snapes says it's not just fans who can benefit from these twists. "One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok." Figures shared by TikTok with Newsbeat show posts using #CharliXCX have increased by more than 40% since the singer launched her Music, Fashion, Film tour last month. If you want to avoid spoilers, there's only one thing you can do, according to Snapes: "You have to not look at TikTok. "If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture." Have you ever tried this one? Sabrina Carpenter had a number of special reveals for each show on her Short n' Sweet tour Phoebe Bridgers is taking things one step further to make sure fans are surprised at her shows - she's banning phones altogether. Those attending are required to lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out. McAdam wouldn't support a ban on phones, saying recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for a lot of fans. But Collins says she's "not totally against it". What she'd prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos so fans have the option to be surprised if they want. But even if you know the set list, the staging and the outfits, "you're still probably going to get to see moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned," Snapes adds. "I went to the Edinburgh Eras show where Taylor Swift was really snotty and she had to blow her nose. That's not part of the script. "You're always going to be surprised." title: Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'
description: A quarter of all marriages in Scotland involve couples who don't live here but see it as the ultimate wedding destination.
body: Hayden and Savannah from the US got married in a Scottish castle Hayden and Savannah had never set foot in Scotland before they decided it was the perfect place to get married last May. The couple, from Pennsylvania in the US, wanted a destination wedding that would take their family and friends on an adventure with them. They considered locations across Europe, before deciding on Scotland after Savannah saw photographs of a castle wedding online. "I think it was on Pinterest," she said. "Somebody got married in a castle and I was like 'Oh, I have to do that'." The pair are far from alone in seeing Scotland as the ultimate romantic destination. Nearly a quarter of all marriages registered in Scotland last year involved couples who did not live in the country. Figures from National Records of Scotland show that 6,596 of the 27,191 weddings recorded in 2025 involved neither partner being a Scottish resident. But what is it about the country that persuades these couples to travel hundreds and sometimes thousands of miles to get married here? Gretna Green is the most popular destination for non-Scots to get married in Scotland Nowhere attracts more visiting couples than Gretna Green. Of the 6,596 marriages involving non-Scottish residents last year, 3,492 took place in the Dumfries and Galloway town, meaning it alone accounted for more than half of Scotland's destination weddings. The town's association with romance dates back to 1754, when changes to marriage laws in England prompted young runaway couples to cross the border into Scotland, where they could marry without needing parental consent. More than 250 years later, it remains one of the world's best-known wedding destinations. It was this reputation that appealed to Patryk and Angelika, both 27, who travelled from north-west England to tie the knot there. Angelika and Patryk were married at Gretna Green in June The couple said Scotland had long been woven into their relationship. They first met when they were 15, when Patryk's parents moved to England from Poland, and one of the first things they bonded over was the 1996 movie Loch Ness. Years later, that shared childhood favourite took on new significance when Patryk proposed on its shores. Patryk proposed on the shores of Loch Ness Their connection to Scotland first started on a road trip in 2021, and they have regularly returned to explore the Highlands and celebrate their anniversaries in Edinburgh. This year alone, they have travelled north of the border every two months. So Scotland felt like the natural place to say "I do", they said. The couple said even Scotland's weather was part of the charm Both Angelika and Patryk are history lovers and said they were drawn to the centuries-old tradition of a Gretna wedding. "It meant something to us being part of that heritage." Angelika said. Patryk said that his favourite memory was watching his bride walk down the aisle to the sound of Flower of Scotland played on the bagpipes. "That sort of music just creates such a whimsical and romantic atmosphere that really can't be recreated in many countries outside of Scotland," Angelika said. Those moments left a lasting impression on their families who had travelled from Poland. "They hadn't really experienced anything like that before," she said. Angelika and Patryk love Scotland's dramatic scenery The appeal was not just Gretna's history, Angelika said. Less than an hour after getting marries, the couple found themselves surrounded by dramatic scenery for their wedding photographs. "There's not a lot of places in the world where you can do that," she said. Although neither bride nor groom is Scottish, both say they feel a deep connection to the country. "It's not home, but it feels like a home away from home," Angelika said. Chihon and Ana Maria married in August Chihon, from Chile, and Anna Maria, from Moldova, came to Scotland to study, but the country quickly became the backdrop to their love story. The couple first met in 2018 through a dance society at the University of Edinburgh, when Anna Maria was on an Erasmus exchange and Chihon was completing his postgraduate studies. They they spent years as friends, and it was not until Anna Maria returned to Edinburgh in 2024 that their relationship became something more. And their romance blossomed in the same place their friendship had years earlier. "Everything happened again on the dance floor," Anna Maria said. Just four months after getting engaged, the pair walked down the aisle on the Isle of Arran. The couple said they "fell in love" with the island at first sight, due to it having the "complete scenery of Scotland". "You feel that you're in a magical place", said Chihon. "It's very unique." The couple said Scotland felt like the natural choice. "We're from two different continents," Chihon said. "Scotland is where we met and where we built our life together." Friends from around the globe made the journey to the west coast of Arran for the wedding Their wedding brought together family and friends from across the world, with parts of the ceremony translated live into Spanish and Russian for relatives travelling from Chile and Moldova. Chihon said friends from all over the world joined the couple for their celebrations. The highlights of the night included a traditional ceilidh and a final group karaoke singalong of Sunshine on Leith, led by their Scottish wedding guests. While some of their international guests were unfamiliar with Scottish wedding traditions, that did little to dampen their enthusiasm. "We had people saying, 'We have no idea what's going on, but we're going to join in'," Chihon said. Guests took part in a traditional Scottish ceilidh He said Scotland would always hold a special place in their lives. "Like Robbie Burns said, 'my heart's in the Highlands wherever I go'," he said.
