title: The Papers: 'G7 strikes oil deal' and 'Alison's TV heart scare'
description: G7 countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after an export ban threat by Donald Trump.
body: Spoiler warning: This press review reveals details from series two of The Celebrity Traitors. The G7 striking an oil deal with Donald Trump features in today's papers. The Times reports on the agreement by G7 countries to release 100 million barrels of "emergency stockpiles of fuel and avert a US export ban". "The price of diesel at the pump is expected to fall", the paper says, after countries including France, Germany and Italy agreed to release a "massive amount" of diesel to ease supply pressures. The US president had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not offer up more of their own stocks onto the market. John Healey's first Budget this month will likely create "breathing space" for households and businesses by focusing on the cost of living, the Financial Times reports. According to the paper, Healy is set to ease costs rather than "impose tax increases of the scale seen in recent years". Elsewhere in the paper, the G7 agreement on releasing "more diesel reserves" is headlined along with British pumps passing £2 a litre. The United Arab Emirates has warned the UK Prime Minister it will cut billions of pounds of investment to Britain in retaliation for the Manchester City guilty verdict, according to the Daily Telegraph. The paper describes the "diplomatic row" as a "major test" for Andy Burnham and follows comments the PM made on how he was "really concerned" if the club's owners decided to sell up. Man City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations. The club has continued to deny any wrongdoing. The i Paper reports on No 10 feeling the heat amid the "Man City scandal". According to the paper, Manchester City's chairman met with a senior UK cabinet minister two weeks before the guilty verdicts to discuss UAE's future investments in Britain. The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe is featured in the Sun. Joshua Kerry, 28, has now also been charged with a terror offence against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, the paper reports. The charge relates to activity which is alleged to have taken place between May 2024 and July 2026. The Tories have unveiled plans to "slash foreign aid" to instead "fund 50,000 new jail cells", according to the Daily Mail, which underlines that number in its front page headline. In a move to "reverse Labour's soft-justice approach", Kemi Badenoch has vowed to increase the size of prison estates by 50% by cutting the "foreign aid budget to just £1 billion a year", the paper reports. British TV presenter Alison Hammond's "heart scare" makes the Daily Mirror front page after the 51-year-old was rushed off midway through This Morning's Friday show while clutching her chest. Hammond later said "I'm getting my old ticker checked out," according to the paper. The Daily Star splashes on Oasis's Liam Gallagher saying he'll sing Manchester City's Blue Moon during his 2027 tour as "the club appeals in the FA 'sham' contracts decision". The band recently announced they will start a second leg of their successful reunion tour over next summer. The Guardian headlines on "School inspections to be overhauled yet again" after the new system was labelled "dangerously stressful" and "damaging teachers' mental health". Education Secretary Lucy Powell will direct the schools regulator, Ofsted, to "go back to the drawing board" after changes made by her predecessor only created more problems for headteachers, the paper says. And the Daily Express claims in an exclusive that a new medal for "999 heroes" injured during service is set to be approved by King Charles. Elsewhere on the front page, two contestants from this season of the Celebrity Traitors, Maya Jama and Richard E Grant, are pictured scheming in their iconic green cloaks. title: The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
description: The discovery of 12 women's bodies near Johannesburg has again highlighted South Africa's problem with violence against women.
body: Kgomotso Mathekga says a lack of male role models is fuelling violence against women in his neighbourhood "I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk." "I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her." Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa. The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township. "Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am." At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust. At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve. "We are men!" he shouts. The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer. "Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide." Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women. The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women. The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women. Bra Steve says: "We must restore dignity to the men around here" South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer. The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder. A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners. For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions. "We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here." Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation. Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done. The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late. "When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?" He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again." Craig Wilkinson tells the group to "choose what kind of man you want to be" Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains. "And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity. "We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence." He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men. "You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe." Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges. Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women. Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court. But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever. Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket. "We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says. "We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?" It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko. She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve. This video can not be played Women held a memorial run in Johannesburg after the discovery of Moselakgomo's body "Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?" Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other." Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer. Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up. "As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this. "And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends." Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard. "I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. title: Cornell frat house rape accuser 'under siege' online, says lawyer
description: A lawyer for Jane Doe says she is "not doing well" amid attempts to uncover her identity.
body: The lawyer for the woman who alleges she was raped at a Cornell University fraternity house says she is "not doing well" as she finds herself "under siege" from online sleuths seeking to identity her. Thomas Giuffra said the woman known in legal documents as Jane Doe was "incapable of consent" because she was "completely, grossly intoxicated" when she turned up at the home where she says the assault took place. The woman alleges she was raped by seven men at the campus in Ithaca, New York, in 2024. No charges were initially filed in the case. It has reopened since she filed a civil lawsuit that thrust the claims into the national spotlight, reigniting the possibility of criminal charges. In an interview on Friday with CNN, Giuffra said: "She's under siege on social media where people are trying to identify her." He said that postings have "incorrectly" identified other woman as Doe. This video can not be played Watch: New York governor blasts handling of Cornell rape inquiry In an interview with CBS, the BBC's US partner, Giuffra argued that his client, aged 20 at the time, was unable to provide consent because she was intoxicated when she arrived at the fraternity house. Giuffra said she had been pressured into taking the drug ketamine before she was allegedly raped. His comments came as New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed the state's top prosecutor, Attorney General Letitia James, to take over the investigation. At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she had "lost faith" in the county prosecutor's ability to oversee the case. "This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable, and then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her," Hochul said. She also vowed to close a "loophole" of state law that makes it difficult to press rape charges if an alleged victim voluntarily consumes alcohol or drugs. This video can not be played Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case Social media feeds are filled with women trying to shield the Cornell accuser's identity by posting videos of themselves under the title "I am Jane Doe". As well as seeking to complicate internet searches for her name, the messages of solidarity included clips of women detailing their own experiences of sexual assault. Efforts to rally round Jane Doe gathered pace after a political commentator vowed to unmask her, arguing it was unfair for her to remain anonymous while the men are publicly named despite not being charged with a crime. Online sleuths have also tried to locate the addresses of the so-called Cornell Seven, leading to at least one case of mistaken identity. An active-duty US Marine Corps sergeant who had the same name as one of the men was incorrectly served the woman's lawsuit, leading to a torrent of abuse and threats, according to the Free Press, external. title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
description: For the first time in three decades there has not been a single Atlantic hurricane in September, normally the most active month.
body: For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity. The eerily quiet season continues and with just two months left, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all. This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane. The biggest reason for this is El Niño, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific. The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this. With a very strong El Niño forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes. September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity. But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic. While there have been no hurricanes forming in the North Atlantic so far this season, the Eastern North Pacific has been very active with above-average storms There were, however, four named tropical storms which formed in September: Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna. All but Edouard stayed out in the open waters of the Atlantic. The National Hurricane Center suggests there is no sign of any tropical storm activity or hurricane over the next week at least. Forecasters at Colorado State University, who also monitor activity, suggest the strong El Niño is likely to disrupt wind patterns across the Atlantic and "likely result in below-normal activity" over the next two-weeks. As the typical peak of the season has passed and is now on a downward trend until 30 November, a season without a single hurricane is looking increasingly possible. In the historical Atlantic hurricane database, there has not been a year without a hurricane recorded since 1914. However, this was pre-satellite monitoring so it is impossible to say with certainty that none formed. While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe. As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height. Increased wind shear rips apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes. Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El Niño because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns. The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes. This year, temperature records have already been broken in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific, with daily sea surface temperatures now exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. There have so far been 17 named storms in the basin including nine hurricanes, seven of which were major. In terms of the amount of energy these storms have produced - known as the Accumulated Cyclone Energy - this season is around two and half times more active than normal at this point. El Niño is predicted to continue to strengthen with forecasts suggesting it will reach its peak in November or December. title: Traitors claim their first victim as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin
description: There was a murder and a recruitment in the latest episode, and that was just in the opening minutes.
body: Maya Jama is off to a strong start as a traitor, but Richard E Grant is in damage control mode Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the second episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. A comedian, a journalist, an actor and a TV presenter walk into a church. But sadly, the punchline for one of them was becoming the first victim of this year's Celebrity Traitors. As Friday's episode got under way, a delicious new twist saw traitors Richard E Grant and Maya Jama invite James Acaster to join them in the turret, and simultaneously murder a fellow player. Unfortunately, it fell to Amol Rajan to become the Paloma Faith of this series - being taken away in a coffin in episode two before even having the chance to take part in a banishment. "It's gutting to be the first out," Rajan said afterwards, noting that perhaps it was because he had been "a bit bullish with Richard" earlier in the day. "But you know what, games are games, and just as there are winners, so there have to be losers." The next morning, presenter Claudia Winkleman confirmed the University Challenge host's murder to the other players, joking: "That's what I call a starter for 10." Acaster, meanwhile, reflected: "I'm gutted to not be a faithful anymore, I don't like lying. But if I don't join them, they'll kill me." You can't fault his logic. The decision meant that Grant, an Oscar-nominated actor with a Razzie-worthy traitor strategy, did at least manage to commit one successful murder despite his shambolic first day. It was the end of the road for Amol Rajan, who noted he had perhaps been "a bit bullish" in challening Grant The 69-year-old spent much of Friday's episode trying to repair the damage from his earlier exchange in the bar, where he blurted out that he was a traitor to Joe Lycett, Rob Beckett and several others. Obviously a man who made such an excellent Spice Girls manager in the 1997 masterpiece Spice World: The Movie is hard for anyone to picture as a traitor, so many other players assumed Grant was attempting some elaborate double bluff. Jama is off to a much stronger start. "I am quite shocked at my ability to just lie to everyone," the Love Island host said in the castle's diary room. "I'm an all-or-nothing kind of honey." As the players gathered for breakfast, other theories began to surface. Mathematician Hannah Fry said she had spotted Leigh-Anne Pinnock putting on make-up late in the evening, perhaps heading to the turret. "I think it's James," declared Jerry Hall, suddenly giving viewers hope that the new cast will be better traitor hunters than last year's. Until she clarified that she was talking about James Blunt, not Acaster. As the players prepared to head out for the mission, conversations turned to far more important matters. "Do you have more teeth than a normal person?" Grant asked Rob Beckett. This video can not be played Watch: Richard E. Grant hits back at Rob Beckett in The Celebrity Traitors The players made their way to the mission, which had the usual slightly convoluted rules that took Winkleman quite a while to explain. In a nutshell, the celebrities were to be buried alive in pairs, with only one duo left above ground. Ross Kemp was pre-selected by the traitors to be protected from burial along with his grave partner Romesh Ranganathan, who did a delightful dance when he found out he wouldn't be going underground. Kemp and Ranganathan then had the opportunity to dig up some gold graves which would add to the prize pot, or alternatively dig up and free their fellow players. They opted for the latter, which resulted in some other players struggling, external to get the soil off their faces. In the end, all the celebrities were released, with the exception of Fry and Hall. The pair were freed early after Hall shouted the emergency word "Haggis!" – effectively a Scottish version of "I'm a celebrity get me out of here!" - because she was visibly uncomfortable being buried alive. It might have led to an early release, but it ultimately guaranteed that either she or Fry will be murdered next, unless the traitors recruit again. "Just you and me up for murder," Fry told Hall afterwards. "You'd better not be a traitor or I'm really screwed!" In a flashback shown to viewers, Acaster explained the decision to protect Kemp from burial, telling his fellow traitors: "I think if we give it to Ross, he'll overthink it, and behave in a way that would draw suspicion." Very clever. "You're a wonderful traitor," observed Grant. (Certainly better than him.) Ranganathan began dancing when he found out he would be protected from burial along with Kemp Jerry Hall and Hannah Fry face being murdered after Hall requested to be freed from the grave early Finally, it was time for the first banishment of the series, with Grant still in damage control mode. "I have a slight pinprick of advantage," he told himself in the castle's diary room. "Nobody would possibly believe that anybody would be so stupid as to come forward and say 'I am a traitor'. I'm hoping that I do get away with it." His fellow traitors clearly wanted to be supportive, but things were getting dicey. Acaster described him as a "loose cannon", while Jama said: "I want to save him, even though he's dug himself the biggest hole imaginable." Back in the castle, Ranganathan pointed out: "If somebody else had behaved like Richard, we wouldn't even be having a debate about this, you would just go 'you've got to vote for him'." But others had a slightly different take. "Richard feels a little too easy," reflected actress Myha'la, "and then anybody pushing him feels suspicious to me." Comedian Joanne McNally agreed some players were "using him as a fall guy and a decoy," although she did admit later that he's "made such a shambles of it now". title: Women given shorts at Oktoberfest to prevent upskirting
description: The step at the Munich festival comes after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.
body: The famous Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, from which videos are regularly posted online (file picture) The operator of a popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest has been handing out free cycling shorts to women, after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media. Some videos showing women on the Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, have been viewed millions of times. One is said to have made thousands of euros for a woman who posted it online. The Teufelsrad is one of the oldest attractions at the Oktoberfest, the annual beer festival which comes to an end this weekend after 16 days. Its circular platform rotates faster and faster until its riders fall off, and the motion and speed often make skirts fly up. Filming under skirts is illegal in Germany, and carries a two-year sentence in jail. However, critics believe the law does not go far enough, and the videos of women on the Teufelsrad in their traditional dirndl dresses often show their underwear. Sometimes, the images have been digitally altered to show them naked, according to local broadcaster BR. Elisabeth Polaczy says she has handed out more than 100 pairs of cycle shorts this year One woman made €9,000 (£7,650) from a single clip, according to BR, whose investigations found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and several people from Bavaria were behind the videos. At least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad have been in circulation, according to Munich-based daily Süddeutsche Zeitung. Some have apparently been viewed millions of times. The operator of the Teufelsrad, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC that, for the past three years, she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses, to protect them from people filming in the crowd. This Oktoberfest she has handed out more than 100 pairs, she says: "I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure." Polaczy, who is now 80, said donating cycling shorts wasn't cheap, but it was worth it for her own peace of mind. The Teufelsrad tent is hung with signs and police posters in German and English warning against filming under people's skirts, but Polaczy says it is impossible to control everyone filming with smart phones. Some waitresses at this year's beer festival say they have also started wearing cycling shorts under their dirndls. A spokesman for the Bavarian police told the BBC that since 2025, it has run a poster campaign at the Oktoberfest, warning against upskirting. A police poster in Munich timed for this year's Oktoberfest makes clear that "upskirting is a crime" This year, police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for using his phone to film under a German woman's dirndl. Last year there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024. However, Josephine Ballon, who heads German non-profit organisation Hate Aid, which aims to support victims of digital violence, told the BBC that the current law against upskirting does not provide enough protection. Although she says there are plans for a new law, current legislation "applies only when you film under the skirt", and not when a skirt simply flies up and gets photographed. The new camera glasses are also a threat, she believes. Ballon wants anyone who has uploaded intimate pictures of women on the internet to be punished, along with the platforms that put them up. Meanwhile, the city of Munich has sought to tighten up on influencers and content creators who earn money from their social media postings and who want to film at the Oktoberfest. Munich has banned broadcasting live streams from the festival and requires anyone who wants to film there to hold a permit, which is issued by the city for a fee. Hundreds of licences have been issued this year to influencers, who make money from product placement or sponsoring. title: Humphries into Grand Prix semis as Van Veen exits
description: Luke Humphries breezes into the semi-finals of the World Grand Prix with a comfortable 3-0 victory over Niels Zonneveld.
body: Luke Humphries has won eight PDC major singles titles World number two Luke Humphries breezed into the semi-finals of the World Grand Prix with a 3-0 victory over Niels Zonneveld. The Englishman did not quite hit top gear against the Dutchman - averaging 85.91 and throwing four 180s - but was clinical at the key moments with a checkout success of 33.33%. Humphries has yet to drop a set in this year's tournament having whitewashed Dave Chisnall and Jermaine Wattimena in previous rounds. The 31-year-old will face compatriot James Wade in the last four after he knocked out third seed Gian van Veen with a 3-0 win. "The way I'm practising, I feel really good, it's just not been coming out this week. Against James, I know I need it to come out, it'll be a tough task," said Humphries, who won the tournament in 2023. "To make four World Grand Prix finals on the trot would be super special. There's not many players that will ever do that and James will know he's got a tough game as well." Elsewhere, Nathan Aspinall produced a stellar performance at Leicester's Mattioli Arena to secure his spot in the last four with a 3-0 victory over Ryan Joyce. He will play Gerwyn Price in the semis after the Welshman's superb 3-2 comeback success against his compatriot Jonny Clayton, who spurned a two-set lead and match darts in a thrilling tie. title: US road rage killer's sentence quashed because AI video of victim was shown in court
description: The Arizona appeals court ruled that airing an AI message from the dead victim "crossed that line".
body: This video can not be played Watch Chris Pelkey's AI-rendered impact statement shown in court An Arizona road rage killer will be resentenced after an appeals court ruled that an AI-generated video message from his dead victim was improperly aired in court. Gabriel Paul Horcasitas was found guilty by a jury of shooting and killing Christopher Pelkey, 37, during a confrontation at a red light in 2021. He was sentenced to 10 years behind bars. But his legal team appealed, arguing that the trial judge should not have allowed an AI video, created by Pelkey's family, to be shown in court ahead of last year's sentencing. The Arizona Court of Appeals agreed, ruling that Horcasitas, 55, must be resentenced because the AI clip "crossed that line". "Rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister," the court of appeals wrote on Wednesday. Horcasitas' lawyer, Kristen Reller, who filed the appeal, declined to comment. Jessica Gattuso, an attorney for victims in the case, did not respond to a request for comment. Pelkey's sister, Stacey Wales, told the BBC last year the family had used voice recordings, videos and pictures to recreate him for the AI video. "To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me, it is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances," said the AI version of Pelkey in court in 2025. "In another life, we probably could have been friends." "I believe in forgiveness, and a God who forgives. I always have and I still do," the AI version of Pelkey - wearing a grey baseball cap - continued. At the time of the sentencing, the judge who oversaw the case, Todd Lang, seemed to appreciate the use of AI. "I loved that AI, thank you for that. As angry as you are, as justifiably angry as the family is, I heard the forgiveness," Judge Lang said. "I feel that that was genuine." title: The vanishing world of India's street magicians
description: India's street performers are struggling to survive as audiences shrink and public spaces become harder to access.
body: Ishamuddin Khan is one of India's most famous street magicians Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air. The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame. These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick. "The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator." Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft. Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession. Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces. There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana. Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries. Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers. "For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains. Restricted access to community spaces has made it difficult for street magicians to find an audience Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous. The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it. He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka. His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan. Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded. As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations. One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan. Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day. Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces. An old picture of Khan performing the great rope trick Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink. "Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance." Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline. "With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says. It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces. For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed. Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur. Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land. "This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra. Imam Khan has left street performance behind and now makes a living as a ragpicker For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse. When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back. "We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities." For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased. Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia. Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard. Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees. "Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says. The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts. "There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says. For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it. "A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says. His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind. title: Which clubs did Man City's 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market?
description: BBC Sport follows the trail of transfer money flowing to other clubs during Manchester City's period of financial rule-breaking.
body: The previous clubs of Sergio Aguero, Kevin de Bruyne and Bernardo Silva all received significant transfer fees from Manchester City during their era of financial rule-breaking The money flowed around football. It made a lot of other clubs richer. It helped teams everywhere and especially in the Premier League. These have been some of the arguments used by those backing Manchester City in the media and online since the verdicts declaring the club guilty came in and an appeal was announced. The suggestion is that there was a net benefit to the game as a whole, and in particular the clubs to whom Manchester City paid big transfer fees. The more than £900m by which the independent commission found the club had "inflated" its accounts was not all spent on transfer fees. Clubs have many bills, including wages for players and other staff, utilities, insurance, infrastructure costs, commercial fees and much more. But the roughly £1.2bn Man City spent on players between 2009-2018 (about £900m net spend) was more than anybody else in that period. That outlay was vital in making them England's most successful club, and would surely have been heavily reduced had they not knowingly broken the rules, as the independent commission concluded. So where did City's money flow to in the transfer market, and what impact did it have? Man City confirm appeal against guilty verdict Man City whistleblower to lose witness protection Football transfers include many costs. The amount required to sign the player is the most obvious, but there are also agents fees, legal expenses, administration money and potentially signing-on bonuses. That means the money dished out by Manchester City during the 'asterisk era' will have reached people and bodies who work in the background of football deal-making and is difficult to track. But what can be done is analysis of the fundamental interactions between City and other clubs. Below is a list of every club to whom Manchester City paid transfer fees between summer 2009 and winter 2018, in descending order from the most money to the least. The list is for senior players and does not include free transfers, loans or academy graduates. That is 46 different clubs in 19 national league systems. For some of them, the fees paid by City were the highest the clubs had ever received at the time. Looking at the spread of money among clubs demonstrates just how far and wide Manchester City's money was spent. The split in money spent on transfer fees by City during the timeframe is relatively even across some of the highest-ranked leagues in Europe, though the Premier League is higher than any other. Just over a quarter of their total transfer outlay was paid to clubs in the English top flight. They signed players from eight Premier League clubs, and the same amount in La Liga. A combined £13m was spent on two players in the Championship. Manchester City's spending power unquestionably changed the world football transfer market - their willingness to pay higher fees and wages meant prices rose for everybody else too. And once the world knows that a club has a wedge of cash burning a hole in its pocket courtesy of City, it can be difficult to spend it. Asking prices may rise, and having an influx of money is no guarantee of it being well spent. For many of the teams to whom City paid the most during this time, the money did not work out particularly beneficially. Let's take a look at some of the more interesting cases. First up, Wolfsburg. They immediately signed winger Julian Draxler for about half the fee received for Kevin de Bruyne in 2016, as well as others including veteran defender Dante. Having lost De Bruyne, they dropped from second to eighth in the Bundesliga before narrowly avoiding relegation in the subsequent two seasons. And things did not go particularly well for second highest-ranked club Monaco either. The most direct replacements they signed following the sales of Benjamin Mendy and Bernardo Silva in the same summer to Manchester City - Terence Kongolo and Keita Balde - did not work out in the long run, and the team went from winning Ligue 1 and reaching the Champions League semi-finals to almost being relegated within two years. The club City purchased most players from in the 2009-18 period - Arsenal (four) - did not mount a serious Premier League title challenge during that time. Some clubs who did not receive payments from City could also argue that the spending of money from their "inflated" accounts compromised their chances. For example, Manchester City paid very similar totals to Benfica and Porto during the era, but nothing to Sporting, the club which makes up the big three in Portugal. Sporting did not win a title between 2009 and 2018. There are many reasons for that, but could one of them be the fact that their direct rivals received money from City that would perhaps not have been on offer had they followed football's financial rules? What does Man City guilty verdict mean for their squad? HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks There are also some ancillary fees which reached clubs whom Manchester City did not deal with directly. Some players were subject to sell-on clauses, where the club City where buying the player from owed money to the previous team who owned the player. For example, Queens Park Rangers earned roughly £9m from Raheem Sterling's move to City from Liverpool in 2015. Barnsley took about £7m of the transfer fee paid to Everton for John Stones in 2016, and the Toffees also had to pass on about £2.5m to Wolves when Joleon Lescott moved to Manchester in 2009. The Sterling and Stones clauses were worth more than most players operating in the English Football League at that time, significantly strengthening the financial positions of QPR and Barnsley. title: Pretorius breaks Gayle's T20 record score
description: Lhuan-dre Pretorius breaks Chris Gayle's record for the highest score in a men's T20 match with an unbeaten 188 in a domestic fixture in South Africa.
body: Lhuan-dre Pretorius has made a century in a Test and T20 for South Africa Titans 267-3 (20 overs): Pretorius 188* (79); Boast 1-46 Knights 143 (17.2 overs): Cloete 39 (25); Ferreira 3-16 Titans won by 124 runs Lhuan-dre Pretorius has broken Chris Gayle's record for the highest score in a men's T20 match with an unbeaten 188 in a domestic fixture in South Africa. The 20-year-old South African's knock off 79 deliveries, including 13 sixes and 15 fours, helped Titans post 267-3 against Knights in the CSA T20 Challenge. It eclipsed the 175 made by Gayle for Royal Challengers Bangalore (now Bengaluru) against Pune Warriors in the 2013 Indian Premier League. Pretorius, who has played 17 T20s, three one-dayers and two Tests for South Africa, finished with a strike rate of 237.97. He made his half-century off 24 balls but only required 16 more balls to get to three figures and then got to 150 off just 58 deliveries. Titans then bowled out Knights for 143 to wrap up an emphatic 124-run victory at the Mangaung Oval in Bloemfontein. title: What's a golden spurtle and why do so many people want one?
description: The World Porridge Championships are back with the biggest field yet and a fight for the Golden Spurtle.
body: 2025 winner Sven Seljom gets his hands on the coveted Golden Spurtle, presented by former Scottish MasterChef finalist Sarah Rankin What does a bakery owner from San Francisco have in common with a retired British Army officer, a newly-qualified Scottish lawyer, a US Marine veteran, an Edinburgh artist and a teacher from Fife? All of them - plus a 2026 MasterChef UK finalist - are preparing to fight for the title of World Porridge Making Champion. The annual oat-off has never been more popular, with double the number of entrants than the previous highest turnout. The hopefuls all want to leave the Highland village of Carrbridge carrying the Golden Spurtle, porridge making's most coveted award. The trophy is a giant version of the traditional wooden tool used for stirring porridge, thick soups, and stew. The competition has attracted twice as many entrants as its previous best year The surge in porridge popularity could be fuelled by the success of the highly acclaimed documentary film The Golden Spurtle, which followed competitors at the 2023 championships. Its focus on the competition's eccentric characters, intense porridge-making rivalries, and porridge world legends like Carrbridge local Ian Bishop and the "queen of porridge" Lisa Williams, has inspired record numbers to try their hand at competitive breakfast-making. Thirty competitors representing 14 countries will take part - from Australia, the Czech Republic, South Africa, the USA, Norway, France, Switzerland and the Netherlands, as well as from across the UK and Ireland. Among them will be defending world porridge making champion Sven Seljom from Norway, together with national porridge champions from competitions in the Netherlands, Norway and Australia. Porridge in drawers was a traditional way to store the filling food Sven is taking part in the main competition, where competitors must prepare traditional porridge using only three ingredients - oatmeal, water and salt. He can't wait: "The village and the organisers are doing such a tremendous job and it was the greatest experience of my life winning the title last year," he said. There is also a speciality porridge competition, where competitors can combine oatmeal with any ingredients they choose, resulting in an imaginative mix of sweet and savoury dishes. Last year's Speciality Award winner, Caroline Velik from Australia, created porridge jaffles – yoghurt flatbreads filled with porridge, rum-soaked bananas and toffee rum liqueur, and tossed in plum sugar. The boss of it all - Porridge Chieftain Alan Rankin - said the response to this year's competition was unprecedented. "The documentary has introduced the competition, Carrbridge, and the wonderful world of porridge to a whole new audience, and we're really looking forward to welcoming this year's competitors to the village," he said. Robert Reid is Australia's first porridge national champion Robert Reid, who won Australia's first national competition, the Pearly Spurtle, will be competing in Scotland as part of his prize. He said: "It's been a bit of a whirlwind. To go from my wife telling me she submitted my application to actually winning the Pearly Spurtle four weeks later has been pretty surreal. "My dad is Scottish, so porridge has been part of my life for as long as I can remember. The sense of community at the Pearly Spurtle was incredible, I'm excited to now have the chance to do them proud in Carrbridge." He said salted porridge had shaped his life, thanks to his Scottish granny and his Dad, who was born on the Isle of Jura and raised in Greenock. "Their tradition lives on in my own kitchen, where my twins now enjoy properly salted, never sweet porridge cooked by me or their grandad," he said. "Winning the Pearly Spurtle was a proud moment, especially using my dad's treasured Scottish spurtle. The same one I will bring with me to Carrbridge and the Golden Spurtle to represent Australia." title: Steel Queens forge ice hockey history and inspire new generation
description: Elite women's ice hockey league is returning to Scotland after more than 30 years.
body: Caledonia Steel Queens are the only Scottish team in the UK's top women's ice hockey league When Caledonia Steel Queens play Guildford Lightning at Murrayfield Ice Arena later, Scottish ice hockey history will be made. The season opener marks the return of the UK's elite women's league to the country after 32 years. It's a momentous day for the Steel Queens, who have gone from just seven players in 2017 to becoming the only elite team this side of the border, with more than 120 members. The club has described the occasion as "the biggest story in UK ice hockey this year", and hopes it will make the sport more accessible for players who often have to travel hundreds of miles to England to play at the top level. Ice hockey has been enjoying a moment in recent months, possibly thanks to hit TV shows like Heated Rivalry and Off Campus. But the Steel Queens fell in love with the sport long before it boomed on streaming platforms and TikTok - and they told BBC Scotland News why. Maya Low was introduced to ice hockey by her Canadian cousins before she picked up a stick herself at the age of 15. The sport has enabled the 20-year-old to travel around the country and meet new people. But it became more than that in August 2024 when Maya was diagnosed with leukaemia. "I was undergoing very intensive treatment for the first 10 months and I lost the ability to walk," Maya said. "Ice hockey has been incredible for me during this time, it's given me motivation to get up and get out of bed and learn to walk again and get my strength back. "I've always had a goal to look forward to and work towards, which I think has been incredibly important, mentally and physically, and it's also helped me re-connect with my friends and build confidence again," she added. Maya says hockey has been motivating her during her leukaemia treatment While Maya remains in maintenance treatment, she has been busy training with the Steel Queens for a chance to make it on the team's roster for the big game on Saturday. "It's incredible and we are all really looking forward to it - it will be a great challenge and it's amazing for women's ice hockey in Scotland," she said. 13-year-old Drew Henderson and her twin brother Flynn found out about ice hockey from a poster they spotted during a public skating session seven years ago. They both play for the Edinburgh Capitals academy, which shares the Murrayfield Ice Arena with the Steel Queens. Despite being the only girl on the team, Drew says she enjoys being able to play with her brother. When she isn't playing for the Capitals, Drew captains the Steel Queen's development team the Iron Maidens. "When we see Drew playing ice hockey it's actually like she comes alive," said the twins' mum, Fee. "There is nothing else that makes her as happy as ice hockey does," she added. Fee believes that having Scotland's own elite team will make a huge difference for the next generation, including her children. "It shows women can be at that level and the sport that they enjoy and love is getting some recognition and it will let kids, especially girls, follow their dreams and see that there is something high to dream for that's different and cool." Twins Drew and Flynn started playing ice hockey together when they were just six years old Head coach of the Steel Queens' elite squad, Beth Dias-Scoon, swapped roller blades for ice skates at the age of seven. What followed was a trailblazing career spanning more than two decades, which has seen her play for the elite Kingston Diamonds based in Hull, and the Great Britain women's national team. Playing at the top level hasn't been easy - for 15 years Beth had to make a 480-mile round trip to train and play with Kingston. Thanks to the Steel Queens, players based in Scotland will no longer have to face that ordeal. "Just to give them that platform is so important. It means they can focus on hockey rather than the cost and the time spent travelling ," Beth said. Some players from the GB Team have already returned "home" to play for the Steel Queens. "It's amazing to have role models come into our club and give young girls something to aspire to," Beth added. Head coach Beth Dias-Scoon has been with the Steel Queens since the club was established in 2017 When Caledonia Steel Queens was founded in 2017, it was Scotland's only university team exclusively for women. It has grown quickly since then - from having seven skaters at its first practice to attracting more than 120 playing members across three full teams and a development squad. In 2023, the Steel Queens switched from the university league to the Women's National Ice Hockey League, and swiftly made their way up through its regional divisions. When the league announced it was planning to expand its top tier from six to eight teams for the 2026/27 season, the Murrayfield-based club threw its hat in the ring and got accepted. "If we hadn't competed well, we would never have had the opportunity to join the elite league, so it's a testament to the girls' hard work and commitment over the years," said Richard Gray, who founded the team. Richard Gray founded Caledonia Steel Queens in 2017 as Scotland's only university team specifically for female players The last Scottish women's team to play at the top level were the Dundee Royals in 1994. Richard said it was massive to bring it back: "I may be a little bit biased but I think it's the biggest story in UK ice hockey this year." He hopes it will spark more interest in ice hockey in general. "When you see the talent at all levels, men's or women's, it's definitely worth watching," he said. "If you like quick, fast, action-packed sport that has got everything from physicality, to skill, then it's really a sport for you." Caledonia Steel Queens are opening their elite season on Saturday 3 October

title: 'No jobs on a dead planet' - former commissioner defends helping scrap M4 relief road
description: Sophie Howe says she helped scrap the M4 relief road over climate concerns.
body: Sophie Howe said she was "generally not popular" with drivers caught up in the M4 traffic A former independent commissioner says she helped scrap the M4 relief road over concerns about the environment because "there are no jobs on a dead planet". Sophie Howe made the comment on a BBC podcast after it was suggested the cancelled 14-mile (22km) motorway in Newport could have helped boost the economy. Howe, who was the world's first future generations commissioner, described helping get dozens of other road projects cancelled including a third Menai crossing over concerns about the environment and wellbeing. The Welsh government said it was reviewing options for the M4 around Newport after the previous Labour government under Mark Drakeford scrapped plans for a relief road in 2019. Will the new Welsh first minister complete the journey to delivering M4 relief? The government had already spent £114m planning the road, and an inquiry it commissioned - which featured criticism of Howe - found the economic need for a road outweighed concerns about environmental damage. Howe had been a Labour councillor and police and crime commissioner when she was appointed the first future generations commissioner for Wales in 2016, a role she held until she left in 2023. The job meant she had to ensure the government and public bodies considered the long-term consequences of projects and policies. She told BBC Radio 4's Radical podcast that while she could not veto decisions, she could scrutinise and advise ministers to make sure decisions also benefited people who were not yet born. The Labour Welsh government axed the project to build a relief road south of Newport in 2019 Howe said she was "generally not popular" with drivers still caught up in long queues on the stretch of the M4, but said plans for the six-lane scheme had been at odds with some of the Welsh government's core seven "wellbeing goals"., external "The questions that I pose to the government there are: Can you explain to me how you've considered this decision is in line with the goal of a prosperous Wales, which talks about a productive, innovative, low-carbon society, because we're going to be increasing carbon emissions," Howe said. When put to her that getting people to work at a reasonable time could be in the interests of a prosperous Wales, she replied: "Exactly that, and that is usually exactly what happens. Which is why, in these situations, economy always wins and environment always loses. "But in the long term, there are no jobs on a dead planet. So you know you have to be considering this in the round." Howe said the debate over the M4 had not played out as a simple "economy versus environment argument", and instead included questions over how it would fit in with things like making a healthier Wales, how it would boost social interactions, and how it would be in line with a more equal country. "Because 25% of the lowest income families in this region don't own a car," she said. "So are you saying you're spending the entire of the government's borrowing capacity building something that benefits only the already better off?" She said she "probably" would have taken the government to court had it gone ahead with the relief road and a Section 20 Review, external to make sure it fit in with wellbeing goals, but in the end she "didn't actually have to". "The public arguments that we had, I suppose, were enough," she said, and agreed with the interviewer that she had an ally in Drakeford. The former first minister said in 2019 he would not have gone ahead with the road even if it had been affordable, saying he "took a different view" to a planning inspector who had concluded the project would not have a disproportionately harmful impact. The inspector's report criticised Howe, saying that a suggestion by her that the inquiry had not properly considered future generations legislation "were and are wholly unwarranted". It said the M4 scheme had been "anything but short term", stating it had been a "long-term solution to long-term needs". Ex-Labour leader Drakeford cancelled the relief road, saying it would have damaged the Gwent Levels Howe told the podcast that money that would have been used to complete the £1.6bn stretch of motorway had since helped fund a "range" of other public transport interventions, including the South Wales Metro which was nearing completion. Rail passengers increased by 19.1% for 2024-25, while the latest Transport for Wales figures showed a further 9.9% increase for 2025-26. Howe also said she looked into every "pre-approved" road building scheme and asked the government to apply the same wellbeing tests to them, which had led to most being cancelled. In 2023 the Welsh government scrapped all major road-building projects - including a planned third Menai bridge and a "red route" in Flintshire - after assessing 59 schemes, with only 15 smaller-scale projects given the green light. , external The government said at the time it would not consider new projects unless they reduced carbon emissions, supported a shift to public transport, walking or cycling, and helped it adapt to the effects of climate change. Since then, in 2025 the Flintshire road was revived in a proposed transport plan, and this year the new Plaid government was said to be reviewing options to build the third Menai bridge. Howe said that since the creation of her former role, the United Nations had passed a declaration on future generations, Gibraltar had created a similar commissioner, and legislation and campaigns focusing on intergenerational fairness had been launched in other countries. Bills to ensure governments account for the interests of future generations are in development in UK and Irish parliaments, but a proposal for a future generations commissioner was voted down in the Scottish Parliament in January. title: Who has 'no ceiling' as Northern Ireland shine in Nations League?
description: After an impressive 3-0 victory over Ukraine in the Nations League, Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill was impressed with his young side.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: Northern Ireland top of group with seven points from three games Michael O'Neill had spent the build-up to Northern Ireland's Nations League outing against Ukraine playing down memories of their famous win at Euro 2016. His focus was firmly on what was to come rather than reflect on the past. If a stunning 3-0 victory on Friday night was anything to go by, it's going to be a pretty exciting future indeed. His starting team had an average age of just 22, which was the youngest on record for Northern Ireland since World War Two. Oxford's Ciaron Brown, the only player over the age of 25 to start the game in Trnava, Slovakia, was in the right place to open the scoring in the ninth minute from Ruairi McConville's knockdown. O'Neill handed a first start to 19-year-old Kieran Morrison, and his superb cross led to Isaac Price doubling the lead, before Brown's header evaded goalkeeper Dmytro Riznyk in bizarre circumstances with 30 minutes left. While the victory may not be quite as memorable as the 2-0 'Kings of Lyon' success 10 years ago at the Euros, it was extremely impressive. To put it into context - and never mind the manner of the performance - only Sweden and France have beaten Ukraine in the past 12 months. Northern Ireland can now be added to that list. Brown scores two as superb Northern Ireland stun Ukraine Inside Northern Ireland's football conveyor belt Brown's two goals were just reward for a player who has been quietly impressive for far longer than this campaign, and he was part of a back-five which stood out in what was a third consecutive clean sheet. Brodie Spencer and Terry Devlin were drafted in at the full-back positions and both impressed, but Brown's centre-back partners McConville and Tom Atcheson really shone. Norwich City defender McConville, 21, commanded his area well and, as well as an assist for Brown, he also allowed the ball to trickle over the line when he could have touched home for the third goal instead of his team-mate. Atcheson, himself only 20 and playing for Blackburn Rovers in the Championship, made his Northern Ireland debut in Wales in March, but showed composure beyond his years. O'Neill said both players were "terrific" as he told BBC Sport: "They have no ceiling, to be honest. "They are both playing in the Championship at the minute but they are ready to go to the next level. "They will make mistakes at times and we've put a lot on them in terms of the physicality. The two of them were brilliant." O'Neill was also delighted for Brown, who said he had "really grown" into a senior role in the absence of injured Sunderland defender Dan Ballard. "Three 90 minutes at this level is tough," said O'Neill of the 28-year-old. "He plays his club football in League One and he's a better player than that. "He brings a lot to the team. He was our most senior player tonight and he has really grown into that." When asked what was the most pleasing aspect of a positive night, O'Neill added it was the "overall performance". "We played a really good team tonight and we had to be really well set-up," he said. "The team was really well prepared and the staff done an amazing job, from the analysis to the set-pieces and right through everything. "Everything fell into place a little bit, we scored early from a set-piece and the second goal was brilliant. "Another clean sheet and there were some really good performances right through the squad." With four goals scored and none conceded, O'Neill's side are in great shape at the halfway point of the campaign. They are three points clear of Hungary and Ukraine at the top of League B2, and host a Georgia side - who have one solitary point to date - back at Windsor Park on Monday night. Ciaron Brown scored his first two Northern Ireland goals in a famous win over Ukraine If they can end the quadruple-header unbeaten they will head into November's final two matches on a high, and the wider implications are significant. Topping the group would seal promotion to League A for the first time, and mean Northern Ireland will be in a five-team group for Euro 2028 qualification, with a potential fall-back of a play-off should the campaign go awry. They had not won an away Nations League match before Shea Charles' 99th-minute winner in Georgia, and this was their biggest away success in five years. Former international Stephen Craigan, on co-commentary in Slovakia, described it as potentially "a seismic night" for a young group, which was missing Ballard, the influential Ethan Galbraith and Liverpool defender Conor Bradley, while Justin Devenny started on the bench. The real implications of the victory may only become clear further down the line, but all focus for now will be on the recovery before the final game of the window on Monday. "There is a big togetherness in a young group," said the 23-year-old Price, who scored his first international goal in just over a year. "We're loving it and we love coming away. It's about building momentum and we're doing that." Which clubs did Man City's 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market? title: Tories pledge to build 50,000 new prison places
description: The party says its proposals would stop prisoners being released early and cut crime.
body: The Conservatives have promised to build 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales to stop criminals being released early, if they return to government. The party said it would cost £2bn per year to build and run the new prisons, funded by spending cuts including to the foreign aid budget. On Thursday hundreds of prisoners were released early, under new rules introduced to prevent jails reaching capacity, with around 4,500 due to be freed by next summer. Labour blamed the previous Tory government for leaving "our criminal justice system at breaking point" and said the party's proposals were not "credible". The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday. Prisons in England and Wales have been running close to capacity for years, with the latest government figures showing they are 98% full. Under the latest early release scheme, eligible prisoners can now be released on a community licence after serving one-third of their jail sentence. Those excluded include prisoners convicted of murder, manslaughter, a sexual or grooming-related offence, or a driving offence that led to a death. The government has also effectively scrapped one-year jail terms. The Tories said they would use extra prison capacity to reverse these measures. An early release programme introduced by the previous Conservative government saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "A violent criminal doesn't become less dangerous just because the government has run out of prison cells." She added: "[Labour's] answer is to let dangerous offenders out even earlier instead of building the prison spaces we need." Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories are taking the public for fools. Across 14 years in government, they added just 500 prison places and closed 23 prisons. "Now Kemi Badenoch expects the British people to believe they'll build 50,000." Meanwhile, the Prison Governors' Association said "long-term investment" was needed and warned a "staffing crisis" would pose challenges to delivering new prisons. If the party wins power, the Tories said they would introduce legislation early in the new Parliament to override planning and procurement barriers, allowing the process to be "fast-tracked". It said the use of private finance would help speed up delivery and control costs. There are currently around 89,000 useable prison places in England and Wales, according to the latest government figures. The Tories said their proposals would increase this figure by more than 50%, with the vast majority of new places expected within the party's first Parliament in government - up to five years - and the full increase delivered within seven years. The £2bn a year cost would be funded through savings in other areas, including cutting the aid budget by £1bn and reducing the budget of the Department for Culture Media and Sport by £1bn. The Labour government has promised to add 14,000 extra prison space by 2031. The Tories argued increasing prison places would cut crime and prevent reoffending by keeping serious criminals off the streets. Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "Prison works. It works by punishing and deterring, but most importantly by incapacitating. "Prison should keep violent and repeat offenders away from the law-abiding public." Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference The prison population has risen significantly in recent decades, partly as a result of longer sentences and more people being returned to prison for breaching the conditions of their release. Successive governments have pledged to increase the number of prison places - but delivery has often fallen short of those promises. New prisons take years to build, often facing local opposition and obstacles in the planning process. The Prison Governors' Association said: "Building 50,000 cells is one thing; finding the thousands of experienced officers, governors and specialists needed to run them safely is quite another. "Politicians have spent years announcing prison places while the service struggles with overcrowding, ageing infrastructure and staffing shortages. The real test is not how many places can be promised, but how many prisons can be operated safely, effectively, and sustainably." title: King's Caribbean tour will not shy away from 'darkest days of our past'
description: In recent years, the King has expressed his "personal sorrow" at the UK's role in slavery.
body: King Charles's upcoming Caribbean tour will not shy away from "the darkest days of our past", Buckingham Palace has said. During the visits, the King is expected to face renewed calls to apologise for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade and be questioned on potential reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade. The King and Queen Camilla are set to travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, with visits also to Bahamas and Guyana as part of the eight-day trip starting on October 27. According to PA news agency, it is understood the government has not advised the King to apologise or offer reparations. Jamaica to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles The King has previously expressed his "personal sorrow" at the UK's role in slavery. A palace spokesperson said: "There are important discussions taking place in various fora about colonial legacy and the intergenerational impact of the transatlantic trade in enslaved persons. "While these are primarily matters for Governments to address, His Majesty's previous statements on them have been unequivocal, describing them as an 'atrocity' which 'forever stains our history'." The palace said the tour will "principally be oriented to the vibrant present and promising future of each country". Several African and Caribbean countries have called for a formal apology and reparations from countries that benefited from the transatlantic slave trade. In September, Jamaica's government said it would raise a petition on the subject of slavery reparations with the King, the country's head of state. Olivia Grange, the country's culture minister, said the petition would ask the King to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica. Last month, a Downing Street spokesperson said the transatlantic slave trade was "abhorrent" but the UK position was that it does not pay reparations. title: Hawaii's iconic 550-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch collapses
description: The lava rock formation protruding from the rocky cliffs of Volcanoes National Park crumbled some time last weekend.
body: Hawaii's famous Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean. The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said. "The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement. Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination. The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend. The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch. Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline". In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said. Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch. "This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland." Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it. "Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now." Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather? title: Men charged over alleged plot to target Manchester Jewish community
description: The pair were arrested in the Northern Quarter area of the city on the eve of Yom Kippur.
body: They will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Saturday Two Iranian nationals have been charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester ahead of Yom Kippur, Counter Terrorism Policing has said. Rahman Salehi, 35, of Salford and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool, who are said to have arrived to the UK by small boat, are accused of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on or before 20 September. The duo were arrested in the Northern Quarter area of the city, when thousands of British Jews were in synagogues. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the news two Iranian men have been charged over an alleged plot in the Manchester area would be "deeply distressing" to the Jewish community. As part of the investigation, searches at addresses in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford, were carried out Counter Terrorism Police allege the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot. As part of the investigation, searches were carried out at addresses in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors. "Two suspects have been charged with planning a terrorist attack against Jewish communities in Manchester. "This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. "I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue. "The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do. "It would be inappropriate to comment further on this case. But I can say that we will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security." The men are due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Saturday. title: Bath gain revenge on Exeter to win 11-try thriller
description: After losing to Exeter at home in the Prem semi-final last season, Bath beat the Chiefs 40-34 in another thriller.
body: Bath's Finn Russell did not play in the Prem semi-final loss to Exeter in June Tries: Redpath, van der Linde, du Preez, Russell, Penalty, Hill Cons: Russell 4 Tries: Varney, Yeandle, Iosefa-Scott, Feyi-Waboso 2 Cons: Slade 3 Pen: Skinner Bath made it two wins out of two in the new Prem season as they gained a degree of revenge for losing to Exeter Chiefs in last season's semi-final. The two sides produced another thrilling game, just as they did three months ago, exchanging 11 tries as the all-out attack approach to the new season continued. The hosts scored four tries to have a bonus point in the bag by the break as Cameron Redpath, Bernard van der Linde, Dan du Preez and Finn Russell all scored to put them 26-10 ahead. Stephen Varney and Jack Yeandle had got Exeter's first-half scores, before Josh Iosefa-Scott and two great tries from Immanuel Feyi-Waboso turned the match on its head. But Varney gave up a penalty try for a deliberate knock-on and Ted Hill's effort took the game beyond their opponents, although Harvey Skinner kicked a late penalty to ensure the visitors came away from a second consecutive defeat with two bonus points.
