title: US murderer Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after failed execution, lawyers say
description: As of Thursday night, Pike remained critically ill and is being treated at a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.
body: Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator on Thursday night, after authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers say in court filings. Pike, 50, was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance. Pike remained critically ill and was being treated at a Nashville-area hospital. Lawyers for Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, are seeking to have her sentence commuted after the failed execution attempt. Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution. Hospital staff are working to save her life and clear the drug used, pentobarbital, from her system, the filing states. During the execution attempt, prison officials tried to start intravenous (IV) lines by using at least seven needles on Pike, according to her lawyers. At one point, Pike herself offered guidance of where they could try. "One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed," the filing states. While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee ordered an independent review into Pike's botched execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year. The state's department of correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out". Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not not offered any explanations about what went wrong. What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next? I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's Pike's attorneys previously warned that her conditions, including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection. In the latest filings, her lawyers allege that "at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike's body". They are requesting that all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence is preserved. Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said two doses of pentobarbital was enough that "she would have surely died" had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation. The only possible explanation for her survival, Zivot said, "is that the pentobarbital blood level was never high enough to cause death" and that blisters on her arm after the botched execution indicated a ruptured vein. So, instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, he said, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin. Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis may have also played a role, forming blood clots at the injection site that would potentially block pentobarbital from entering her veins. Regarding the possibility the pentobarbital was degraded, Zivot explained that if this was the case, it could be due to factors including poor manufacturing or improper storage. Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder The attempted execution went ahead after multiple failed, last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers. The US Supreme Court thwarted two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection. Tennessee's governor also denied a clemency request from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995. She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee. Before the killing, Pike had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend. Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant Shipp was 17 at the time so was spared the death penalty under state law. He was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole and remains in prison. title: Man jailed for piloting small boat carrying 26 others
description: Jemal Abdela was sentenced after pleading guilty to endangering 26 others, including six children.
body: Abdela was described as a "reckless criminal" by Anna Turley, Minister for Border Security and Asylum A man has been jailed for 18 months for piloting a small boat carrying 26 other people, including six children, towards the Kent coast. Jemal Abdela, 32, was sentenced after pleading guilty to the offence of endangering others during a sea crossing to the UK without valid entry clearance on July 25. Winchester Crown Court heard Abdela, who is Eritrean, had also attempted to disguise the fact he had been driving the black inflatable across the Channel when it was approached by immigration officers. A Home Office spokesman said Abdela was the 20th small boat pilot to be imprisoned in four months for endangering lives at sea. Matthew Parris, prosecuting, told the court that the defendant was seen piloting the boat, which was being followed by French authorities. He said Abdela had "dived into the centre of the boat and moved to another location wearing a hat" before being identified, adding that the vessel did not have flares, GPS or maps onboard. The court heard that Abdela told police he had paid €800 (£680) for the crossing, which had begun at 17:00 BST the previous day. He also claimed to have been sat by the captain of the boat, but was then made to take over control of the vessel by the other passengers. Abdela is the 20th person to be imprisoned in four months for endangering lives at sea by piloting small boats like this (file photo) Francesca Hallett, defending, said that Abdela had managed to "escape" war-torn Eritrea, where he was born. She said that he first went to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, but was imprisoned because of his Eritrean nationality. He then went on to travel through Sudan and Egypt to Libya where he was captured and tortured by people smugglers for eight months and was later freed. Hallett added that Abdela moved on to Italy and France, both of which he described as "not safe for refugees". "At that stage he felt the UK was the safest option," she said. Sentencing Abdela, Judge James Bromige said that he would "ordinarily" be deported on completion of his time in prison. Anna Turley, Minister for Border Security and Asylum, called Abdela a "reckless criminal" who had been "rightly jailed". title: Widdecombe suspect charged with planning terror act against Farage
description: Counter terror police say the further charge comes after a "hugely intensive and complex investigation".
body: Joshua Kerry has been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. Counter terror police said Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity which is alleged to have taken place between May 2024 and July 2026. Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she knew the fresh charge would be "extremely concerning" and her "profound sympathies" were with Farage and his family. "Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all. "This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve." Counter Terrorism Policing Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said the charge on Friday was the result of a "hugely intensive and complex investigation". "This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge," she added. Kerry, from Rotherham, is due to appear in court over the terror charge on Wednesday, police said. Frank Ferguson of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division said prosecutors "worked closely" with police to bring the charge and would continue to work alongside them as the investigation continued. Widdecombe was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries. She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s. Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing and would later become a Reform UK spokeswoman. title: Royal Navy's new attack submarine arrives at Faslane
description: HMS Agamemnon is the sixth vessel in the Astute class and will undergo sea trials after arriving on the Clyde.
body: HMS Agamemnon arrived on the River Clyde after departing Barrow The Royal Navy's newest Astute-class nuclear-powered submarine has arrived at its home port in Scotland. HMS Agamemnon will undergo sea trials and operational preparation after reaching HM Naval Base Clyde at Faslane. The hunter-killer vessel, the sixth in the Navy's arsenal, is equipped with tomahawk land-attack missiles and torpedoes capable of striking targets up to 30 miles away. The Navy's submarine rear admiral, Andy Perks, described HMS Agamemnon's arrival as a "significant milestone". The 318ft-long (97m) vessel joins other Astute-class subs including HMS Astute, Ambush, Artful, Audacious and Anson, in the Navy's fleet. A seventh sub, HMS Achilles, is currently under construction. Astute-class submarines are the Navy's most advanced and powerful class of attack subs. The Astute-class sub conducted its first dive at sea on the journey to Faslane HMS Agamemnon departed its construction home at BAE systems in Barrow last week and went through its first dive at sea in the Navy's Inner Hebrides exercise areas en-route. Rear admiral Perks said: "HMS Agamemnon's delivery reflects the dedication, skill and collaboration of thousands of people across our Defence Nuclear Enterprise, who have worked together to build one of the world's most capable attack submarines and deliver a formidable warfighting capability for the United Kingdom. "I am delighted to welcome the submarine and her ship's company to their new home on the Clyde, and I look forward to seeing them join the operational fleet in due course." The Astute-class fleet are the Navy's most powerful and technologically advanced attack subs The vessel, which has a crew of about 100 submariners, will have its performance tested during sea trials over the coming months. Its arrival coincided with the 125th anniversary of the launch of Holland 1, the Royal Navy's first submarine.. HMS Agamemnon's commanding officer, commander John Gabb, said: "It is an enormous privilege to be the first person to command this vessel at sea. "We will get to know Agamemnon well over the coming months, but this submarine is incredibly quiet, has a world-class Sonar and will be home to us all as we generate for operations." title: Man City whistleblower to lose witness protection
description: Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City set to lose his witness protection despite fears for his life.
body: This video can not be played The Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City is set to lose his witness protection despite his fears he could be assassinated. Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto released a tranche of confidential football documents, including emails and financial records relating to the English Premier League side. In 2018, he shared documents with German magazine Der Spiegel, which used them for investigations into City's finances and alleged breaches of financial fair play rules. Last week, City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, which they have appealed. Man City confirm appeal against guilty verdict The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City What does Man City guilty verdict mean for their squad? Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide files obtained through the Football Leaks operation. He posted on X on Friday, external that the decision to terminate his participation in the programme on 10 October has put him in a "life-threatening situation". The 37-year-old said it had left him with no alternative but to relocate to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period because of "multiple death threats" and "the serious risk of an assassination attempt". BBC Sport has approached the Commission for the Protection of Victims of Crimes in Portugal for comment. Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, but was convicted in Portugal of offences including illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence. He wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020, which was also subject to heightened security measures. Earlier this year, he was acquitted in a second trial of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to a number of sports bodies in Portugal, including Benfica. On Wednesday, Pinto turned his attention to Fifa president Gianni Infantino, saying he had "become a cancer on football" and should "have no place in the future of the game". Pinto repeated allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid financial fair play sanctions from European football's governing body Uefa. Infantino's position has recently come under increased pressure following controversial plans to sell stakes in the governing body's competitions, such as the World Cup, to private investors. A statement from Pinto's lawyers released on Friday said the decision to end his participation in the witness protection programme left him at heightened risk, noting legal proceedings stemming from the leaks remained ongoing, including the case against Manchester City. Pinto has set up a fundraising page to help him "survive this serious situation", which he claims was "created by the Portuguese State". title: Met Police urge students to move 7 October protest
description: The Met said it had tried to contact the University of London Coalition to postpone its protest.
body: Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman says the march will cause distress if held on the anniversary of the attacks on Israel The Metropolitan Police is calling on the organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march scheduled to take place on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks on Israel to move the event. Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman said the force had been unable to identify the organisers behind the group, which calls itself the University of London Coalition. He said that while the march did not meet the strict legal threshold at which police could request the home secretary to ban a protest, many Londoners would be marking "a day of mourning" on Wednesday, with vigils being held to remember those killed on 7 October 2023. The BBC has also contacted the group for comment. Harman said around 300 students were expected to march through central London, from King's College London in the Strand on Wednesday, finishing at University College London in Holborn. He said they had demanded an end to what they described as a "genocide in Gaza". "Serious concerns have been expressed about the impact of this march on students and staff, particularly those who are Jewish, the route, and the day it is being held," Harman said. He urged anyone intending to join the protest to "reflect on the impact and distress it will cause on this very significant day, and exercise your right to protest on a different date". Harman said the force had written to four London universities to ask them to engage with their students and staff and to take "all reasonable steps" to ensure students did not feel "excluded, targeted or unsafe" due to activity on their premises. He said the letter acknowledged "the importance of freedom of expression, peaceful protest and academic debate" but also pointed to findings from the Community Security Trust over a rise in antisemitic incidents at UK universities since the attacks in 2023. A march can only be banned if police consider it would result in serious public disorder, and that placing restrictions on it would not prevent that disorder from taking place. The decision needs approval from the home secretary. Harman said he did not believe the strict legal threshold required in order to request such a ban had been met. Neither the police or the home secretary can ban static demonstrations, although conditions can be placed on them. Harman said that if the march went ahead, police would use their "full powers" to ensure there were "appropriate conditions" in place, including on the route and timing of the march. Police say anyone who breaches conditions will be arrested and officers will take a zero-tolerance approach to hate crime. Harman said although officers had made "every effort through formal and informal channels" to identify the organisers behind the event, they had been unable to do so. "If it goes ahead, we will have to police it," he added. Around 1,200 people were killed by Hamas fighters in the attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, and 251 people were taken hostage. This triggered a massive Israeli military offensive in Gaza, which has killed over 70,000 Palestinians. In June, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel is committing genocide, and a resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) in September came to the same conclusion. More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health. Another pro-Palestinian protest is planned for Saturday 10 October, with 10,000 people expected to attend, as well as a counter-protest, which police said will be subject to strict conditions. On Sunday 4 October, around 5,000 people are expected to attend a march in Whitechapel to mark the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street. Police said they were not expecting disorder, but officers would be present in case of "disagreement between different groups" attending the event. Harman said each of the events, along with the Holborn and St Pancras by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's seat on 8 October, represented a "challenge for policing". He said officers had arrested three men, following reports of "intimidating and obstructive conduct" during canvassing in recent weekends, and "conflict between those canvassing and protesters". Harman said that where police had intervened, it was for the purpose of preventing crime and disorder and not on any political preference, insisting "it's not a two-tier approach". The Met says it expects more than 600 officers will be involved in policing the various protests and events over the next week, coming at a financial cost but also drawing officers away from day-to-day policing in London. title: Woman at centre of Cornell rape inquiry was 'failed' by officials, says New York governor
description: The woman, known as Jane Doe, alleges she was raped by seven students at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
body: This video can not be played Hochul: ‘What we learned yesterday raised... troubling questions’ New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said the woman at the centre of the Cornell University rape case was "failed" at "every turn". The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, alleges she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024. The case was investigated at the time but no charges were laid. It recently reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight. At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She has now appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead the case. This appointment was made after Hochul said she "lost faith" in the local prosecutor's ability to oversee the investigation. Expressing outrage that local prosecutors did not interview the accuser themselves, Hochul on Friday said: "This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable, and then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her." She has also vowed to close a "loophole" that prevents prosecutors from pursuing rape charges in cases when the victim has voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol. Jane Doe is believed to have voluntarily taken drugs and alcohol on the night of the alleged gang rape. "If someone is too intoxicated to consent it should not matter if they chose to use drugs or alcohol," said Hochul, adding: "Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for gang rape." James, who is the state's chief legal officer, appeared alongside Hochul at Friday's news conference, pledging to "lead a process guided by the facts and the law". She said her office would interview witnesses and pursue prosecutions if warranted. District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who previously led the investigation, has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold. Van Houten said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office. In a statement on Friday, he said he supported James' investigation, adding: "It has become clear that we were not provided the full picture by the university." Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault. This video can not be played Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September. Speaking to CNN on Friday, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said she is "not doing well". "She's under siege on social media, where people are trying to identify her; some false court postings, attempting to identify her," he said. Survivor and victim advocates say current state law on sexual assault makes it difficult for charges to be brought against perpetrators if the victim voluntarily took drugs or drank alcohol before the alleged assault took place. A bill to address what Hochul described as a legal loophole was already before the state legislature prior to this week's public outcry over how police and investigators handled the Cornell rape allegations. People who have voluntarily become intoxicated to the point that they are unable to give consent are currently not protected by New York's rape laws, says state assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz, who first sponsored legislation to close the loophole in 2019. "The real bottom line is that right now if you are voluntarily intoxicated, you will not get justice," he tells BBC News. "Being voluntarily intoxicated, basically, is almost like giving somebody a get out of jail free card." Dinowitz says that around half of US states have already changed their laws to say it makes no difference whether intoxication is voluntarily or involuntarily in rape cases. Hochul said she will support the existing bill and that it could move forward as early as the next legislative session which reconvenes in January. As governor, she could also call lawmakers back for a special session before then. title: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
description: More than 600 schools have faced disruption as protests over standards and lack of teachers continue.
body: High school students face off against riot police during a protest in Montpellier Riot police have clashed with protesters as thousands of students demonstrating over education standards disrupted more than 700 schools in France on Friday. Fires have burned in the streets as high school pupils and others objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. The protests began last week in the capital Paris and have spread across the country, with cities including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille affected. French justice minister Gerald Darmanin said things had "gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance". School protests send shivers down French government's spine On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted. BBC Verify has now authenticated two videos that show the man, who was later identified as an officer by a minister, being beaten up near a school in Belfort. In the graphic footage, a group of young men are seen chasing him. The officer falls to the ground, and is subsequently punched and kicked multiple times in the head. At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said. In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers. Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency. Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris. "As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday. She said police actions had made things worse. "It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added. Police published pictures of some of the items they had seized from demonstrators, including petrol bombs, an axe and so-called mortar fireworks. "Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said, after attacks on school gates, entrances and fences. Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes suffered more than €2m (£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government, after fire destroyed its glass entrance and some areas inside the school. This video can not be played Students and riot police on the streets of Paris French firefighters put out a burning barricades during protests in Aubervilliers The blockades and protests started last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country. Students say school hours are too long, classrooms too hot and too many members of staff are off work. It comes at a crucial time for French President Emmanuel Macron, six months before next year's presidential election. Budget cuts planned, which will impact on education funding, have infuriated the young protesters. French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said on Friday that the movement had been hijacked by non-students. He told French broadcaster BFMTV that teachers had said "the people in front of me were not my students". Parents have also been worried that their children have become caught up in a wave of violence and unrest. At the Claude Monet school in southern Paris, 53-year-old Anya was looking for her son. French riot police apprehend a protester during clashes outside a Toulouse school "We banned him from coming. I hope he isn't here, but he did leave the house," she told AFP. "We're afraid the situation might escalate." Darmanin, the justice minister, said prosecutors had been asked to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children and "pay for repairs". He said since the start of the movement, about 2,000 people - most of whom were children - had been taken into custody. Many French unions have given their support to the protesting students. Education union SNEP-FSU, public services union SNUEP-FSU and Solidaires have all called for members to support them. Solidaires Trade Union Federation said in a statement: "Let's not let them fire on our children. "Secondary school pupils have the freedom of assembly, association and demonstration." title: Daniel Thomas in court accused of entering migrant site
description: Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, is accused of multiple offences in Dover in the spring.
body: Daniel Thomas appeared at Margate Magistrates' Court via videolink (file photo) Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has appeared in court charged with entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover. The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, is accused of committing the offence on 31 March, according to court documents. Thomas is further accused of using threatening words or behaviour in the Kent town on 1 April and obstructing a person engaged in a lawful activity on 6 April. He is also charged with entering or remaining in Dover Docks without having lawful business or permission, the documents say. Thomas faces another charge of racially aggravated harassment by allegedly using threatening or abusive words. He appeared at Margate Magistrates' Court on Friday via videolink wearing a grey T-shirt and rosary beads. District Judge William Nelson sent his case for a further case management hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 4 November. Earlier this week, Thomas was refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel. title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
description: The coordinated release is aimed at heading off further price spikes and avoiding a ban on US diesel exports.
body: Emmanuel Macron chaired a meeting of G7 leaders to agree the release of fuel reserves The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket. The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days. President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere. In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another. The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings. Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately." His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar. Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food. But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the coordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA). The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks". Macron said the coordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China. Why UK diesel prices have breached the £2 per litre mark Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday. The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA). Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market. title: London Fire Brigade named in Met's evidence file on Grenfell fire
description: The brigade is among 20 organisations the police have compiled evidence against since 2017.
body: A file has been passed to the CPS which will consider whether any charges will be brought London Fire Brigade (LFB) and a tenants' association have confirmed they are among those facing possible criminal action over the Grenfell Tower fire. Prosecutors were handed an evidence file on 20 organisations and firms and 54 individuals from the Metropolitan Police earlier this week. LFB and Kensington and Chelsea Tenant Management Organisation (KCTMO) have been criticised for failings relating to the fire and will find out next year if they will be prosecuted. The Met is seeking charges including corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences and fraud offences over the deaths of 72 people in the 2017 disaster. The Met's investigation - Operation Northleigh - began soon after the fire in June 2017 and has involved hundreds of investigating officers. The CPS said any charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster in 2027. In a statement, the LFB said: "The London fire commissioner has been notified by the Metropolitan Police Service that, following its investigation into the events surrounding the Grenfell Tower fire, a file has been submitted to the CPS for its consideration in respect of London Fire Brigade. "The London fire commissioner welcomes the progress in the investigation process and reaffirms his commitment to providing the CPS with full cooperation, as LFB has sought to do throughout Operation Northleigh." The commissioner, Jonathan Smith KFSM, said: "We remember the 72 people who lost their lives, and our thoughts remain with the bereaved, survivors and everyone whose lives were changed forever by that night. "We continue working with our partners across government and the fire and rescue sector to ensure the lessons of the Grenfell tragedy are learnt, and this continues to shape everything we do." KCTMO, facing corporate manslaughter charges, said: "We remain acutely conscious of the terrible impact of the Grenfell Tower fire on the bereaved, survivors, their relatives and the wider Grenfell community, and continue to offer our deepest condolences and sympathies to all those affected." LFB crew regularly join justice campaigners on annual events near the tower Most of the organisations facing potential prosecution have not been named. Among those that have been revealed so far are the local authority Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC), which could be prosecuted for three offences: corporate manslaughter, section 3 of Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, and acting contrary to the Regulatory Reform (fire safety) Order 2005. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, which is responsible for building safety, is also among those referred to the CPS. The fire started in the kitchen of a fourth floor flat and then spread rapidly on the outside of the building via combustible cladding. A public inquiry found the fire was avoidable and set out how a chain of failures across government and the private sector led to the disaster. In a report following the first phase of the inquiry, chair Sir Martin Moore-Bick condemned LFB's "serious shortcomings" and systemic failures in its response to the fire. He concluded that fewer people would have died in the blaze if the LFB had taken certain actions earlier. LFB said it had accepted the findings of the inquiry and had implemented all the recommendations from both phases. Grenfell United, a bereaved families and survivors group, has previously criticised the time frame for prosecutions. Earlier this week, the group said: "It has taken more than nine years to get here. Nine years, and no-one has been held criminally accountable for the deaths of our 72 loved ones. "We want those responsible to face justice." title: Motörhead guitarist Phil Campbell died from multi-organ failure, inquest hears
description: The Welsh rockstar suffered complications from "necessary" surgeries, an inquest into his death heard.
body: Guitarist Phil Campbell was the second longest serving member of Motörhead Motörhead guitarist Phil Campbell died from multi-organ failure after suffering complications following "necessary" surgeries, an inquest has heard. The Welsh rock star, who was the band's guitarist from 1984 until it disbanded in 2015, died aged 64 on 13 March. Campbell's death could not have been prevented, St Pancras Coroner's Court heard on Friday. The guitarist from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, underwent two liver transplants and bowel surgery at the Royal Free Hospital in London earlier this year. The inquest heard he had previously drunk alcohol to excess but had been sober for seven years by the time of his death. Campbell had suffered from Hepatitis C, external, but the inquest heard this had been treated. While the second of the two liver transplants was successful, Campbell suffered further complications. He underwent bowel surgery and was moved to intensive care, where he deteriorated rapidly. He died in hospital on 13 March, with coroner Dr Richard Brittain recording his cause of death as multi-organ failure. Brittain said: "My view is that there is nothing here to suggest his death could have been prevented." He said Campbell died from "recognised complications of necessary surgical procedures". Mick "Wurzel" Burston, Lemmy Kilmister, Phil Campbell and Pete Gill of Motörhead, in 1984 Campbell's family previously described him as a "devoted husband, a wonderful father, and a proud and loving grandfather, known affectionately as Bampi" who had faced a "long and courageous battle in intensive care following a complex major operation". "He was deeply loved by all who knew him and will be missed immensely," they added. Motörhead was founded in 1975 by the bass player and singer Lemmy, whose real name was Ian Kilmister. The group helped pioneer heavy metal music in Britain with a string of top 10 albums including 1980 hit Ace Of Spades, 1981's No Sleep Til Hammersmith, and Iron Fist in 1982. Campbell was the second longest serving Motörhead band member, after Lemmy, and went on to record music and tour with his sons, Todd, Dane and Tyla. title: Watch: Why has UK diesel price hit an all time high?
description: Diesel has now hit an average of £2 a litre in the UK, the RAC motoring group says, with petrol prices also rising.
body: This video can not be played The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group, with petrol also soaring to 174.71p a litre on average. Price rises were "showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery onto motorists," the group said. Separately on Friday, the G7 nations agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil to head off further increases. The BBC's Business Editor Simon Jack explains the rising prices in the UK - and how oil prices around the world affect the cost of petrol and diesel at the pump. title: Alison Hammond has heart check-up in hospital after leaving TV's This Morning
description: The host says she is "fine" but getting checked after leaving midway through Friday's This Morning.
body: Alison Hammond went to hospital for a heart check-up after leaving ITV's This Morning midway through Friday's show, but has assured followers she is "fine". The presenter, 51, left the programme during its live broadcast, appearing to clutch her chest as she was assisted off the set by co-host Dermot O'Leary. He later told viewers she was "feeling a little unwell". In a video posted from a hospital bed, external on Friday afternoon, Hammond said she had "a little bit of a palpitation" during the show but was feeling OK and was undergoing tests. "I know you're all worried about me," she said. "Honestly, I am fine. First of all, I'm getting my old ticker checked out." Hammond and O'Leary were presenting Friday's edition of This Morning She continued: "I had a little bit of a palpitation, and now I'm getting it all checked out. But I think I'm OK. I'm hoping it was just a little panic attack or something like that." The Birmingham-born presenter, who also co-hosts The Great British Bake Off, thanked This Morning's viewers for sending her "lovely messages" while apologising for her dramatic early exit. "I'm so sorry I left you," she added. "I would never normally do that. I would never leave a TV show, so you know I wasn't very well. "But hopefully I'm going to be all right. The doctors are so lovely, and they're checking me out, and hopefully everything's going to be fine. "Everything is fine, look. I'm rocking it. Look how good I look," she joked, noting how she was still wearing her make-up from the show. O'Leary and Hammond are the regular This Morning presenting partnership on Fridays Friday's edition of the ITV show began at 10:00 BST with Hammond and her regular co-host O'Leary at the helm, before she left at 11:30 during a segment about pets. O'Leary, 53, addressed her absence when the show returned from a break, saying: "Welcome back to This Morning, Alison is feeling a little unwell, so she's just had to duck out. Hopefully she'll be back." He later updated viewers that she would, in fact, not be returning, "so I'll be here for the rest of the show". Hammond initially rose to fame as contestant on Channel 4 reality show Big Brother before appearing on I'm A Celebrity and Strictly Come Dancing. She became a co-host in This Morning in 2021, and was part of the team that won a National Television Award for best daytime programme the following year. She joined Bake Off in 2023 and took over from the late Paul O'Grady on For the Love of Dogs in 2024. title: Will Warrington or Wakefield be Super League's sixth winner?
description: Only five clubs have lifted the trophy in a Super League Grand Final - Warrington and Wakefield now have the chance to add their name to that list.
body: Warrington captain George Williams (left) and Wakefield skipper Mike McMeeken (right) are 80 minutes away from leading their respective sides to a first Super League Grand Final win Just five sides have lifted the trophy at Old Trafford in a Super League Grand Final. That exclusive club of Wigan, Leeds, St Helens, Bradford and Hull KR will gain a new member on Saturday as Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity battle under the lights at the Theatre of Dreams for a spot at glory. Whereas the Super League era has traditionally been dominated by the powerhouses of the sport with their heaving trophy cabinets, 2026 is the story of one side that has come close but not got over the line and another that has upset the odds to wedge themselves into the conversation. But what is the mood like in either camp ahead of a box office Grand Final? Wakefield's stunning semi-final win over Wigan set tongues wagging across rugby league and beyond, particularly given the nature of the demolition job delivered by Daryl Powell's side to the treble-chasers. It was a performance which suggested Wakefield had the credentials to complete the job at Old Trafford, built on a marauding, metre-chomping pack and skilful, pacy backs capable of racking up points. Head coach Powell has been around the block and knows just how difficult this one-off final is to get right even with a season's worth of momentum behind a team. "We have to get the same performance level," Powell told BBC Sport. "When it really counts. "I'm not saying it's going to be picture perfect, it's very rare there is but I think we have to be at a very high level to beat Warrington and we all know that." 'You could be legends' - inside unfancied Wakefield's rapid ascent Will 2026 finally be Warrington Wolves' year? Quiz: Name every Super League Grand Finalist This video can not be played Wakefield stun Wigan to reach first Grand Final While this is Wakefield's first final and the same for many of their players, like coach Powell a select few have sampled the unique atmosphere of Old Trafford for Super League's showpiece event. Tom Johnstone begrudgingly left Wakefield for Catalans in 2023 and reached the Grand Final in his first season, before rejoining Trinity in 2025. That night ended in disappointment with defeat by Wigan, so the 2026 final represents a second chance for the England winger to pick up the ring he so covets - although it will not be the most important ring in his life as he admits. "It's going to be different in so many ways for me because as much as I loved Catalans, this is my team," Johnstone told BBC Radio 5 live. "This has been my team for almost all of my career, and the team that gave me an opportunity 15 years ago as a youngster. "So, this is special, this is the big one and it's probably going to be, if we get it done, the best night of my life. Sorry, after my wedding, my wife said. She said it has to be second to my wedding." Wakefield shock Wigan to reach first Grand Final 'Pipe dream' to reality? Wakefield one win from title Like Warrington, Wakefield have waited a long time to return to league glory, with a 58-year gap since their last title. That narrative is one of many utilised by both clubs as inspiration for this Grand Final encounter, with several on both sides. One story for Wakefield to thrive upon is the impending retirement of stalwart back-rower Jay Pitts. Born in Ossett and a graduate of the youth set-up at Wakefield, the 36-year-old has amassed just short of 200 appearances for Trinity across two spells bookending his career which will end once Saturday's final is done. Pitts has battled through this crucial period following a bicep injury, and his determination and leadership are integral to the spirit within the dressing room. "After the Wigan game I just went into the changing rooms and said to him 'you know you get to play your final game at Old Trafford'. It's what dreams are made of," Powell added. "While there's a few players leaving us for different reasons, for Pittsy retiring after his final game in rugby league - what better way for us all to do something special for him as a person? "He's been a phenomenal player, a warrior, and I know all the boys love him. He gets a fair bit of stick for how old he is but that comes to us all so I won't worry about that too much." This video can not be played Warrington reach Grand Final with Leeds win It has been 71 years since Warrington last won a league title and it is their first trip to Old Trafford for eight years. In the Super League era, the Wire have now reached five Grand Finals, but are yet to cross the line and write their name on the trophy. For Ben Currie, he is acutely aware of the gap between trophies, having been with the club during their four other visits - albeit he is yet to actually a appear in a Grand Final. "It's hard not to know about it when you've got the opposite fans singing about it every week," he told BBC Radio Merseyside. "Obviously it's tongue in cheek and it's fun for the fans to do that. "We'd love to give our fans the opportunity to sing back to them but there's no added pressure from anyone from above in the club, from the coaching staff or from the senior players. "Everyone wants it just the same as everyone does at Wakefield." Warrington edge past Leeds to reach Grand Final Wigan's O'Neill wins Man of Steel award One member of the Warrington team who could make an impact is 18-year-old Ewan Irwin. Since making his debut in 2025, Irwin has gone on to make 21 appearances this season, scoring six tries and kicking 82 goals. Matty Ashton, who himself was a bright young prospect for the Wire not so long ago, spoke highly of his team-mate, who has the chance to become the youngest player to ever score in a Grand Final. title: Man jailed for 15 years over Ulez camera blast
description: Kevin Rees, 63, faces a tougher sentence because the offence had a "terrorism connection".
body: Kevin Rees, 63, faces a tougher sentence because the offence had a "terrorism connection" A man who blew up a ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) camera in south-east London has been jailed for 15 years. Kevin Rees, 63, detonated the explosives in the camera in Wellesley Avenue, Sidcup, at about 18:45 GMT on 6 December 2023. The device damaged cars and houses up to 100m away, with shrapnel hitting outside of a child's bedroom. Rees, of Harcourt Avenue, Sidcup, was convicted in January at Woolwich Crown Court of causing an explosion likely to endanger life. During the trial, the retired electrical engineer told the jury he "strongly opposed" the Ulez scheme and the mayor of London, Lord Sadiq Khan. The Metropolitan Police said Judge Anthony Bate, who delivered the sentence at the Old Bailey, ruled that the offence had a "terrorism connection", resulting in a tougher sentence and stricter controls after Rees's release. "It was miraculous that nobody was killed or seriously injured in the large explosion caused by Rees," said Det Ch Supt James Derham, who leads local policing in the Bexley area. "He showed a complete disregard for the welfare and safety of the people who live in, or were travelling through, the area at the time of the explosion – all because he was unhappy with the Ulez scheme." This video can not be played Watch: Ulez camera blown up in south-east London The jury previously heard how Rees travelled in his Smart car from his home in Sidcup to Shuttle Close, where a Ulez camera had been installed earlier that day before being cut down in a separate incident. The retired electrical appliances engineer planted the device on the camera and lit a fuse. Rees was identified and arrested on 18 December 2023. Officers searched his home and found chemicals that could be used to make explosives. Rees was also sentenced to three years, to run concurrently, after admitting three counts of possessing a prohibited weapon in relation to stud guns, which were also discovered at the property. Rees denied any involvement in the explosion and told jurors he believed his arrest was due to his posts in "anti-Ulez" groups on Facebook. Police said they found posts which encouraged the damage of the cameras. When he was arrested by counter-terror police on 18 December, Rees asked officers if his arrest had "something to do with the anti-Ulez sites". He told the trial: "I assumed it was just the so-called Facebook police." The blast damaged a van parked opposite the Ulez camera Siwan Hayward, TfL's director of security, policing and enforcement, described Rees's actions as "a reckless and highly dangerous act that could have caused serious harm and resulted in the loss of life". "Tampering with or damaging TfL's property is unacceptable and seriously risks the safety of the public. Those attempting to interfere with Ulez infrastructure show a complete disregard for the law," Hayward said. "Any such incident on our network is reported to the police and will not stop the Ulez operating." title: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
description: The defeat raises pressure on Sánchez to call a snap election, after a series of scandals affecting his party and allies.
body: Before his bruising defeat, Pedro Sánchez made a last-ditch appeal to allies to back changes to the law Spain's Congress has rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, in a defeat for the government of Pedro Sánchez that increases pressure on him to call a snap election. Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by the government in response to nationwide protests that have followed the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from her home. The decrees, which introduced a series of initiatives aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market, required parliamentary approval in order to remain in place. MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166. Hundreds of demonstrators had gathered outside Congress as the debate took place and there were angry scenes. Protesters chanted "shame on you" and "your profits, our misery", after the results were announced. The government's defeat underlines the fact that Sánchez, a Socialist, does not command a congressional majority and it has heightened speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer. Sources told Spanish media that the government would spend the weekend deciding its next step, and whether to dissolve parliament. Sánchez's beleaguered government had already been mired in a series of scandals and judicial cases affecting his Socialist Party and close allies. Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from her flat but later told she could return Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a sharp rent increase introduced by Urbagestión, the company that owned her flat in central Madrid. Hundreds of protesters gathered to oppose the eviction last week and the case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years. The social backlash has seen Urbagestión negotiate the return of Abascal to her flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued, with people occupying squares in Madrid and other cities, pitching tents in squares and with a series of marches scheduled for this weekend. Maricarmen Abascal's eviction last week triggered protests demanding an end to the housing crisis The Sindicato de Inquilinas (Tenants' Union) activist association which has been co-ordinating protests, announced during the congressional debate that it was abandoning the tent protest in central Madrid. It said it wanted to "take the struggle to all the neighbourhoods, residential blocks and homes of Madrid, wherever there are rental increases, expulsions and abuses each day, and turn the energy of the last few days into a permanent organisation". Protesters are also calling for a general strike over the housing crisis. The left-wing coalition government responded to the social anger by hurriedly drawing up the two decree-laws in an effort to defuse the protests. The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds". The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Sindicato de Inquilinas. The conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country. However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure. Friday's debate was fierce and at times angry, as supporters and opponents of the decrees clashed in Congress. "I don't ask you, I beg you to be brave and consistent," Sánchez said, moments before the two votes took place. "Because they are not just ambitious measures, they are necessary". He appealed to lawmakers "to put order and humanity into [the housing] market, because if we don't, it will bring down our society". Social Affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy, of the Sumar alliance, the junior partner in the governing coalition, presented the debate in dramatic terms. "Today is about defending an international oligarchy which is extracting the rent from salaries earned with the effort of working classes of this country in order to share it out with dividends and they don't even pay taxes in Spain," he said. "Voting against these decrees today means defending the interests of this oligarchy and turning your back on your own people." However, Miriam Nogueras, of JxCat, said the decrees had been hastily drawn up and lacked rigour. She said the decrees "will allow [vulture] funds to keep buying, keep speculating and evictions to keep happening… these two decrees would provoke the opposite effect of what they aim to achieve." The political right has argued that the government's attempts to intervene will frighten homeowners, causing them not to put their properties on the rental market and pushing prices up further. Juan Bravo of the PP said "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes". title: Three reasons Middle East oil supply is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels
description: Experts say US military assistance, using shuttle tankers and pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz mean exports have rebounded.
body: The volume of oil flowing from the Middle East region has almost returned to pre-war levels, data shows, despite the continued restrictions Iran is placing on vessels attempting to travel through the Strait of Hormuz. Seven months after the US-Israel war with Iran led to the effective closure of the critical waterway, the maritime intelligence firm Kpler said that in the final week of September, daily oil flow from the Middle East reached 92% of its pre-war baseline. Analysts attribute the rebounding flow of oil to three key factors: Ships being escorted with US military assistance Using shuttle tankers through the strait for transfer to different vessels Bypassing the strait using pipelines But some experts have questioned the sustainability of these measures, given the risk of escalating Iranian attacks or a change in US policy. About 40% of the total oil exported from the region in September bypassed the strait and exited via overland pipelines to ports on the Red Sea or the Gulf of Oman, up from 17% before the war, according to Kpler. Oil exports from Iran, however, have ground to a halt after the reimposition of a US naval blockade in July. The US military has been supporting ships as they pass through the Strait of Hormuz since at least mid-June and US Navy data shows the number of vessels assisted by US forces is up by a third in September compared with August. Martin Kelly, senior intelligence analyst at security firm EOS Risk Group, told BBC Verify that US support is primarily in the form of "air support to ships", including through issuing warnings and intercepting incoming threats from drones, missiles or boats. But ships moving through the US-recommended southern route of the strait near the coast of Oman, rather than seeking permission to use Iran's northern route, continue to be targeted. September saw the highest number of successful Iranian attacks on commercial shipping since March, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data conflict monitor. Naveen Das, a senior oil analyst from Kpler, said the market oil market "doesn't trust that we're going stay in this status quo" because of the risk of further Iranian escalation and the possible impact of the US midterm elections. Most of the oil passing through the strait now moves via a "shuttle system" of more than 60 large oil tankers moving back and forth, according to Kpler. More than 70% of the crude oil which passed through the strait in August was transferred from these "shuttle tankers" onto other vessels in the Gulf of Oman, Kpler said. BBC Verify has analysed satellite imagery which appears to show these ship-to-ship transfers, seemingly more protected from Iranian attack, taking place off the coast of the Omani port city, Sohar. But there is a "question over how long these ships can last", said Martin Kelly, particularly as attacks on them continue. Imagery taken on 24 September shows six pairs of ships docked or paired together near the port. An average of more than four million barrels of oil per day was transferred from ship to ship in the Gulf of Oman over in the week to 30 September, according to Kpler. Overall, an average of 12 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait over this period, compared with a pre-war baseline of 17 million. Oil exporting countries in the Gulf have also responded to Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz by exporting more crude oil overland via pipelines. Just under 20% of crude is now leaving the region from ports on the Red Sea at the end of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which is recording exports of more than four million barrels per day, according to Kpler. Three weeks after an attack on this pipeline blamed on Iran-backed proxies in Iraq, Saudi Arabia is now exporting through the pipeline at "full stretch", according to Kpler. Almost a quarter of all crude flowing from the region is now being piped past the Strait of Hormuz to terminals along the Gulf of Oman, particularly the city of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kpler's data shows. Naveen Das from Kpler said this increased use of pipelines is likely to become the "new normal" because "it seems very improbable that we live in a world whereby the Gulf countries and Iran go back to being relatively harmonious". Oil exports from Iran have fallen almost to zero following the re-imposition of a US blockade in mid-July, down from 1.7 million barrels a day before the war began, Kpler data shows. There are 20 empty Iran-flagged tankers currently off the coast of Sri Lanka, unable to return to the Gulf due to the US blockade, according to ship-tracking data and analysis from the US-based advocacy and monitoring organisation United Against Nuclear Iran. While crude oil flow from the Middle East has resumed to almost normal levels, exports of liquified natural gas and oil products like jet fuel and have remained well below pre-conflict volumes. Fewer than a million barrels of processed oil products passed through the Strait of Hormuz on average in the last week, down from 3.5 million per day before the war began. title: Intensified Russian strikes are tearing Kyiv apart, warns mayor
description: Vitaliy Klitschko says Ukraine's capital is in a "very dramatic situation" as Russia hits critical infrastructure.
body: In the latest attack, a Russian drone hit cables of Kyiv's Pivdennyi bridge Intensified Russian drone and missile strikes are "tearing Kyiv apart", the mayor of Ukraine's capital has warned. Vitaliy Klitschko said the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities. He was speaking after Kyiv's defence council held a crisis meeting, following new Russian strikes on a key bridge that caused traffic chaos. The city's data centres have also been recently hit, resulting in internet outages. President Vladimir Putin earlier said Russia was acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks. All metro and automobile traffic is now suspended across the bridge Russia's strikes caused huge traffic jams across Kyiv "We're talking about survival," Klitschko said at Friday's defence council meeting with Kyiv's top military, security, emergencies and police officials. Russia's aim was to "sow panic", he said, stressing that the capital would "prevail - but only through the joint efforts of those who love it and care for it". The mayor was speaking just hours after Kyiv's key Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was hit in an overnight Russian drone attack. On Friday evening it was struck again - the fourth time in two days. The bridge is one of the main transport arteries across the Dnipro River dividing western and eastern parts of Kyiv. All metro and automobile traffic is now suspended across the bridge, causing major delays across the city. Restrictions are also in place on Kyiv's two other key bridges. Kyiv's current population is estimated to be about three million, and many residents rely heavily on the city's metro network. One person was killed in the capital when a multi-storey residential building was hit overnight, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided in early September that "there are no rules now" when attacking Ukraine. In a published excerpt from his interview to the Financial Times, Zelensky said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings. "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities." Putin insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea. "Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after his Thursday's wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum. Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war. Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. title: 'Cult' priest guilty of rape and assault of women
description: The leader of the Nine O'Clock Service is facing prison for abusing 13 women.
body: Chris Brain has now been convicted of sexually assaulting 13 women who were part of the Nine O'Clock Service A priest who established a "cult" within the Church of England has been found guilty of raping a woman in his congregation. Chris Brain was also convicted of four counts of indecent assault against three other women who were part of the Nine O'Clock Service in Sheffield in the 1980s and 1990s. The 69-year-old was found guilty of the offences after a retrial at Inner London Crown Court, having already been found guilty of 17 indecent assaults against nine women at a trial last year. Brain, previously of Wilmslow in Greater Manchester, is in custody awaiting sentencing at a later date. Prosecutors told the court Brain had abused his position as a priest to sexually assault "a staggering number of women from his congregation". The Nine O'Clock Service, known as NOS, attracted hundreds of young people to St Thomas's church with its ground-breaking nightclub-style worship. But prosecutor Tim Clark KC said it "became a cult" in which members were encouraged to cut themselves off from family and friends, leaving them "utterly dependent" on Brain, and lived in fear of being ostracised if they crossed him. Following his latest convictions, South Yorkshire Police said Brain was a "devious and arrogant sexual predator who caused lasting harm to these women". title: Tuchel would never rule out players not in top flight
description: England boss Thomas Tuchel says he would "never rule out" selecting someone who is not playing in the top flight, should Manchester City be relegated.
body: Thomas Tuchel said that the Manchester City charges are a big topic in the England camp England boss Thomas Tuchel says he would "never rule out" selecting someone who is playing outside the top flight for their club, should Manchester City be relegated as punishment for breaching financial regulations. On Tuesday, it was confirmed that City had been found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. The club, which denies guilt, has appealed against the verdict, saying the ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe". The sanctions for City have not yet been decided but potential punishments include expulsion from the league, points deductions and fines. The current England squad includes City players Elliot Anderson and Marc Guehi, while Nico O'Reilly was in the group until he left with an injury. How Gordon became one of England's main men England are preparing to play Croatia in the Nations League in Rijeka on Saturday (17:00 BST). Speaking to the media on Friday, Tuchel said the City verdict was a "big subject" in the England camp. Asked if he would select players not playing in the top flight, the manager said: "There is always a possibility. "I would always try to pick the best team for the camp, for the occasion, for the tournament. "I will never rule out that because they don't play in the top flight in their country. We need to look at it case by case." All 24 players in the current England squad play in top leagues for their clubs and it is very unusual for a player to represent the Three Lions if they are not in a top division. However, James Trafford was in Tuchel squads in March and June 2025 while still in the Championship with Burnley, but he was an unused substitute on those occasions and did not win a full cap until he returned to Manchester City. Goalkeeper Sam Johnstone was the last player to represent England while playing in the Championship, for West Brom in 2021, while Kalvin Phillips - then at Leeds - made his debut for England before he had played in the Premier League. Asked about his players discussing the City verdict, Tuchel said: "We had some time off between the matches and it is a big subject. Everyone speaks about it, so there is no other voice needed "I am glad to be not that voice. No-one needs my half knowledge on the topic. "Of course, the players talk about it. City players talk about it. We talk with them but only briefly. "They are ready to go tomorrow, that's what they show on the pitch and in camp. But of course, it's a big topic in the camp." title: Watch: Why students in France are protesting
description: Demonstrations started in the French capital, then spread across the country in the days that followed.
body: This video can not be played Protests are continuing across France as students take to the streets to voice their anger over school conditions. Demonstrations began in the capital Paris nearly two weeks ago and have now escalated and spread to other parts of the country. More than 500 schools are facing disruption. At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the country's education ministry has said. The BBC's James Waterhouse is in Paris and witnessed students throwing projectiles and police firing tear gas during clashes. Follow live updates on this story. title: Grangemouth firm took £1m of public money months before closure announcement
description: Syngenta say it will pay back the Scottish Enterprise funding in full if operations cease at its Grangemouth site.
body: A chemical firm collected £1m of Scottish Enterprise funding to create new jobs - just months before announcing plans to close its Grangemouth site. The cash was part of £2.2m awarded to Syngenta in May last year to expand production at the plant. Union leaders are meeting with the UK and Scottish governments after nearly 400 jobs have been put at risk. Syngenta said it would pay back the Scottish Enterprise funding in full if operations cease at the site. The company said it had been unable to make its business at the plant "competitive" in the face of "increasing international competition". A total of 377 workers are set to be affected by the move. A Syngenta spokesperson said: "Scottish Enterprise's grant was awarded in support of a capital investment of close to £15m that Syngenta itself has made at the site as part of efforts to diversify activity and try and secure the site's future. "To date we have received around half of the grant allocation (about £1m), which we intend to repay in full to Scottish Enterprise if we cease operations at Grangemouth post consultation." Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant New £150m funding package to protect jobs at Grangemouth It is the latest job loss blow to the area following the closure of the nearby oil refinery in April last year, which also resulted in the loss of about 400 jobs. In March, bus manufacturer Alexander Dennis announced plans to close its Falkirk plant with 115 roles lost, and focus its Scottish operations on the nearby Larbert site. The UK government, under then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, previously pledged an additional £200m in funding for Grangemouth from the National Wealth Fund. Local MP Brian Leishman had a meeting with the company earlier, which he said went "poorly". Syngenta says a final decision has yet to be taken and it will "continue to consider options". But Leishman questioned whether the company was having a "genuine consultation" on the future of the site. He said: "Syngenta have offered one final solution and that is the closure of the plant. "The whole purpose of a consultation is to try and figure out how we can get a path of saving jobs. That seems to be off the table here. "They have announced that they plan to close the site by the end of 2027 - that seems very final to me. The workers deserve an awful lot better." Brian Leishman said Syngenta failed to give him in depth answers on the closure The Labour MP said the closure was a "Scotland-wide issue", adding: "We saw, with the closure of the refinery, over £400m disappear out of Scotland's economy. "There's going to be a huge implication for Scotland's economy with Syngenta closing." He urged the prime minister to "do the right thing" and save the site, similar to how the UK government saved British Steel. "We're talking about 377 jobs on site - we will be talking about thousands of jobs in the wider supply chain," said Leishman. "A huge piece of Scotland's manufacturing base. Scotland deserves better." The UK government has been contacted for comment. More stories from Tayside and Central Listen to news from Tayside and Central on BBC Sounds Leishman urged both the Scottish and UK governments to work together and not turn the issue into a "political football". Syngenta said it had undertaken a "detailed review" of its Grangemouth operation prior to the plans being announced. It said the Grangemouth site was "significantly more expensive" to operate than other production facilities. The company added that savings had been identified in some areas of the business, but these fell short in "bridging the site's competitiveness gap". Mike Hollands, president of Syngenta UK, said: "The workforce at Grangemouth is highly skilled and passionate, but despite all efforts, we have not been able to make the Grangemouth site competitive compared to alternative supply options." title: Families remember teens who died in river
description: Luke Etheridge was kind and caring and Zara Shaw "had a zest for life", their families say.
body: Luke Etheridge, Zara Shaw and Jackson Duke (left to right) died when the car they were in entered the River Wear The families of two teenagers who died when the car they were in ended up in a river have paid tribute to their kindness and "zest for life". Sixteen-year-olds Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw died along with Jackson Duke, 17, when the black Audi A3 they were in came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, Sunderland, and plunged into the Wear just before 13:30 BST on Tuesday. Luke's family said the Sunderland fan was caring and loved their dog Wilf, adding their hearts would "ache forever". Zara had a "zest for life" and an "infectious laugh and smile", making her family proud "from day one", they said in a tribute. All three teens were students at Sunderland College, which said the news had "devastated" everyone across its community. Jackson and Luke were from Sunderland and Zara was from Newbottle, a village about six miles (9km) from the city. The car came off off the road at Panns Bank, near Wearmouth Bridge, on Tuesday Luke's family said the teen, who played in Seaham Red Star Football Club Youth Section's U17 team, was kind and funny and loved shopping for clothes, watching and playing football. "He always knew the most up-to-date Sunderland football news and shared it with us immediately. Sunderland will miss its number one fan," they said in a tribute. "Luke loved spending time with all his friends and family. As a family we did everything together from football to holidays, shopping trips and spending time with Wilf our dog. "Luke is our life, we miss him so bad. Our hearts will ache forever." Zara's family said she had "come into this world with a fight, and we know you left it doing the same". She had previously attended The Drama Lab in Sunderland. "You had a zest for life and life loved you," her family said in a tribute. "Created as a companion for your sister, Olivia, who loves you deeply and unconditionally. You made us proud from day one, you studied and learnt new skills and made life time friends. "Having fun along the way with your dance videos, infectious laugh and smile, you have always been our beloved daughter, sister, granddaughter, niece, cousin, girlfriend and best friend. "To everyone who has been in Zara's life we thank you from the bottom of our hearts. You made her what she became." The empty black Audi A3 was recovered from the water on Wednesday Sunderland College also paid tributes to the teens. It said Luke was a "charming, approachable and genuinely lovely lad", whose "kindness, enthusiasm and character" touched all at the sixth form. In a tribute to Zara, it said her "friendliness, warmth, kindness and beautiful smile made an instant impression" and she was always willing to support other students. The college added Jackson, who played for Hebburn Town Juniors and the club's U18s team, was a "polite, kind and funny young man", whose presence lifted others.
