title: Greens can move Labour in the right direction, says Polanski
description: The Green leader tells his autumn conference that a vote for his party can force changes from Andy Burnham.
body: Zack Polanksi has urged voters to back the Greens to force changes from Andy Burnham, arguing his party has the power to move Labour in "the right direction". In his speech to the party's annual conference, the Green leader said that "sustained pressure" from his party had made forced Labour into changing its stance on issues including climate and its stance towards Israel. He told activists in Brighton that Labour had failed to take action on housing, as he called for a three-year cap to limit rent rises in the private sector. And he said that voting for the Greens would force changes from the government, telling members: "Vote Green, and watch Labour move". Polanksi arrived in Brighton facing questions over how he would seek to position the party to respond to Labour's change of leadership under Burnham, amid signs the Greens' rise in national polls last year may have waned. He began his address by celebrating his party's surge in membership since his election as party leader a year ago, and electoral successes including the hundreds of councillors it gained in May's local elections in England. In his half-hour address, he did not mention the Conservatives or Reform UK but launched repeated attacks on Labour's record in office. He criticised Labour for making "slogans without action" on the cost of living and vowed only his party would end "Rip Off Britain". And he was particularly critical of Labour's record on housing, where he accused the party of failing to take on the "powerful vested interests of developers and big landlords". Instead, he urged the government to enact an "emergency brake" on private rents, under which they would be prevented from rising above the lowest of consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years. He argued that pressure from the Greens in the face of government "inaction" had forced Burnham into calling an emergency Cobr meeting this summer amid record-breaking hot and dry temperatures. The Greens, he added would not "hesitate" to tax "extreme wealth", as he repeated the party's call for a so-called windfall tax on back profits - an issue where the government has faced pressure from unions. "Now I get asked – isn't your job done? Isn't the government doing everything you wanted? "Through our sustained pressure – and our historic wins – we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check. "And we have started to move them in the right direction. But we can't wait for them to get there on their own." title: Sabalenka 'trying hard to be easier on myself'
description: Aryna Sabalenka says she is "trying so hard to be easier on myself" as she begins her China Open campaign with victory over Renata Zarazua.
body: Aryna Sabalenka's last title came at the Miami Open in March Aryna Sabalenka said she was "trying so hard to be easier on myself" as she began her China Open campaign with victory over Renata Zarazua. World number two Sabalenka hit 11 aces and did not face a break point in a 6-1 6-3 victory over the Mexican. The Belarusian needed just 63 minutes to win her first match since losing her world number one ranking and her US Open crown to Elena Rybakina in September. The 28-year-old is bidding for her first title since completing the 'Sunshine Double' in March, when she won Indian Wells and the Miami Open back-to-back. It has been a mixed year for Sabalenka by her high standards. She will finish without a Grand Slam trophy for the first time since 2022 and has often struggled to control her frustrations on court. Asked about being so self-critical, Sabalenka said: "I think this is a good and a bad side of my personality, that I always ask and wait for more from myself. "Sometimes it can drive me forward, but sometimes it can really drain my energy. "Maybe this is something I have to finally learn. I'm really trying so hard sometimes to be easier on myself." Sabalenka will face Czech 20-year-old Nikola Bartunkova - who came close to beating her at the Berlin Open in June - in the third round. Top seed Rybakina begins her campaign at the WTA 1000 event on Saturday. Earlier, Britain's Katie Boulter fell 7-6 (7-3) 6-1 to Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova, while French Open champion Mirra Andreeva recovered to beat Chinese wildcard Yuan Yue 3-6 6-0 6-0. In the men's event, sixth seed Daniil Medvedev produced 12 aces to beat Spain's Pablo Carreno Busta 6-4 6-2. British pair Julian Cash and Lloyd Glasspool advanced in the doubles, beating Russia's Andrey Rublev and Karen Khachanov 6-3 6-4. title: Two people dead after workplace incident near rural road
description: Emergency services are in attendance at the scene in Crossnacreevy, County Down.
body: Emergency services are in attendance at the scene on the Ballygowan Road Two people have died following what's been described as a workplace incident at a road in County Down, BBC News NI understands. Emergency services are in attendance at the scene on the Ballygowan Road in Crossnacreevy. It happened at about 10:45 BST on Friday. Three ambulances and two hazard response teams were sent but no one was taken from the scene. Northern Ireland's Health and Safety Executive (HSENI) said they were "aware of an incident at a workplace" in the area and inspectors were on-site making enquiries. "We are currently liaising with the emergency services and other relevant agencies," it added. Police have said that the Ballygowan Road is closed and motorists are advised to take another route. title: US jobs market sees sharp slowdown ahead of midterm elections
description: Unemployment rose slightly as American employers paused hiring with midterm elections just a month away.
body: Workforces remained unchanged across major sectors, from tech to retail. American firms are choosing to hold steady rather than hire or fire staff The US jobs market saw a sharp slowdown in September, with employers adding just 29,000 jobs in the final update before the midterm elections. Headcounts were little changed in major sectors from tech to retail as hiring fell significantly from August, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose slightly from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September. The figures signal a cooling US economy, which experts said reduced the likelihood of a series of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve. The 29,000 jobs created in September was down from a figure of 133,000 in August, according to revised BLS figures for the month. But George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, said while job gains have been a “rollercoaster“ this year, a single soft report is unlikely to point to a lasting collapse. And Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, said the lower figure was “not disastrous“, adding that a drop in government roles and temporary visa policy changes weighed on overall growth. Jeffery Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, added that the data showed tension between “goods producing sectors that support the AI boom” and service industries feeling the effect of changes brought about by the tech. “Given the overall softness of the labour market, the likelihood of two Fed hikes is going lower,” he said. The BLS report stands in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump's insistence that America's economy is booming and it is the "hottest" nation in the world. The disconnect is likely to present significant challenges as the president and his fellow Republicans hit the the campaign trail with just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections. According to an AP/NORC poll released on Thursday, just 17% of Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall. Both are new lows for Trump, surpassing the lowest mark for Democrat Joe Biden during his presidential term. There have been some indications that the president understands that his views of the American economy are out of step with those of most Americans. "I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing," he said at a White House event earlier this week. title: Belfast boxing legend Close dies aged 57
description: Ray Close, the Belfast boxer who almost handed Chris Eubank the first defeat of his career, has died at the age of 57.
body: Ray Close pushed WBO super-middleweight champion Chris Eubank all the way in two bouts Ray Close, the Belfast boxer who almost handed Chris Eubank the first defeat of his career, has died at the age of 57. One of the most gifted boxers Northern Ireland has produced, Close was born in 1969 and turned professional in 1988 after a decorated amateur career. Close won the EBU super-middleweight title on St Patrick's Day in 1993 but it was his bouts against Eubank for which he will be most remembered. Eubank, who had won all 35 of his professional bouts, was the defending WBO super-middleweight champion in May 1993 but Close pushed him all the way in Glasgow and the pair could not be separated on the scorecards. A rematch took place at a raucous King's Hall in Belfast the following year and Close put in another strong performance but lost on a split decision. A third fight was scheduled to take place but Close's boxing licence was revoked by the British Boxing Board of Control before it could take place after a MRI scan revealed two lesions on his brain. Close would later return to the ring after obtaining a licence in the USA and he won all five of his bouts in Illinois, the last of which was a knockout victory over Larry Willis in June 1997. His professional record reads as 25 victories, three defeats and one draw - which came against Eubank. Close's professional record reads as 25 victories, three defeats and one draw - which came against Eubank. Ledley Hall Youth and Boxing Club in east Belfast, where Close started his boxing journey as a 10-year-old, led tributes and said he was a "true gentleman, humble, kind and always willing to give something back". "To our young people, Ray was proof of what could be achieved," the club posted on Facebook. "He was someone who had come through the same doors, trained in the same club and gone on to accomplish incredible things." The club added that Close's story has "inspired generations of young people at Ledley Hall and will continue to do so". "There are some people who become part of the history and heart of a place, and Ray will always be part of ours. "We will remember him with enormous pride, affection and gratitude." Bangor Abbey Boxing Academy, where Close had trained, said he will be a "huge loss to the boxing fraternity of Ireland and across the world". "Ray and his whole family have been a huge part of our club over the years, right from the very start and we are truly devastated." title: Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference
description: The party will focus on the economy and welfare, as Kemi Badenoch tells her team to prepare for a possible early election.
body: Leader Kemi Badenoch will focus on the economy at her party's annual conference When Kemi Badenoch arrived for her first Conservative conference as leader last year, a member of her entourage overheard somebody wonder aloud: "Who's that?" This baffled member of the public was actually working at the Conservative conference. Badenoch had been the party's leader and the leader of the opposition for almost a year. It is an anecdote which underlines the scale of the challenge Badenoch faced at that conference, an event her allies are now with distance willing to acknowledge was make or break for her leadership. And it is an anecdote which also underlines that, far from break her, that conference represented the start of a major turnaround for Badenoch. Twelve months on, Badenoch will arrive in Birmingham this weekend in total command of a party whose leading lights are beginning to permit themselves the occasional flicker of optimism after years of misery preparing for, and then experiencing, a brutal election defeat. Yet for all that Conservatives now believe their leader is an electoral asset, they still face an existential threat from Reform UK and the challenge of how to adjust their strategy to face a new prime minister, Andy Burnham. The answer to both those issues for Badenoch is a focus on the economy. "Stronger economy, stronger country" will be the party's conference slogan, with the two speeches Badenoch gives - one on Sunday, the other on Wednesday - building on announcements she has made in the past two weeks about cutting benefits for the long-term unemployed. Welfare spending is increasingly seen by the Conservatives as a core battleground with Labour. During Labour conference they derided the event as the "Welfare Party Conference". Whereas Sir Keir Starmer sought to cut welfare spending before backing down in the face of a rebellion by his own MPs, Burnham has made clear that he believes the way to reduce the benefits bill in the long-term is more up-front investment in support for those out of work. This is a clear ideological difference which both parties are happy to embrace. Conservative strategists believe there is a broader lesson there. "The differences between the parties have been quite muddled for a while," one says. "Now that Burnham is prime minister we have a more traditional left-right split." Another area where Badenoch will embrace that divide in the coming days is the pensions triple-lock. The policy currently guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is the highest. Badenoch will make clear that the Conservatives continue to support that policy in its current form, breaking with some generally supportive think tanks and policy experts who believe Badenoch should follow Burnham's lead. In his conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham set out plans to end the existing triple lock from 2030, so the state pension increases at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. The Conservatives hope the sharpening left-right split leaves Reform UK in a strategic bind, occupying a less obvious place on that spectrum. A year ago some senior Conservatives feared being usurped by Reform as the leading party of the right was a near-inevitability, but now they are optimistic that Nigel Farage's party is on an inexorable slide. That bullishness is fuelled in large part by the difficulties Reform has faced over Nigel Farage's £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the fallout - including a police inquiry - from the recent Channel 4 News investigation. "I find more and more voters raise concerns about Reform with me - people who weren't previously giving us the time of day," one MP said. "These are successful people with big garages and good jobs who do not necessarily pay that much attention but want a small-c conservative government. "They were switching to Reform because they were fed up with us and thought Farage was now the main option on the right. But they are starting to come back." Others are less positive, pointing out that Reform still often record higher shares than the Conservatives in the polls — and more importantly have now won far more votes than them in successive years of local and national elections. Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes Whether or not there is indeed a long-term trend of the Conservatives regaining ground at Reform's expense, Badenoch may not have long enough to wait. She has told her team to prepare for this conference as if it is the last before the general election. While not all of her aides agree, Badenoch is convinced that Burnham will go to the polls within the next year. Party high command started weekly election planning meetings shortly after Burnham succeeded Starmer. Neil O'Brien, a member of Badenoch's shadow cabinet, has begun work on a manifesto alongside the party's head of policy. It is intended to be a more concise set of pledges than the usual sprawling manifestos. Also with an eye to the election, the Conservatives will present new faces at the conference who have applied to be candidates at the next election. Badenoch's ambivalence in some cases, and opposition in others, to ex-MPs who lost their seats in 2024 standing for the party again has attracted some controversy, especially when it comes to the high-profile former cabinet ministers Grant Shapps and Penny Mordaunt. The leader's supporters are unrepentant, arguing that the party "needs to show we have changed". Things have certainly changed since last year, at least. That may prove the easy part. title: I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
description: Texas reporter Michael Graczyk has seen botched executions in his time, but not one in which an inmate survived.
body: Reporter Michael Graczyk has covered nearly 500 executions carried out in Texas, continuing even after his 2018 retirement from The Associated Press. He remembers two instances where needles popped out before reinsertion for successful execution - but never one in which an inmate survived. That's what happened this week in Tennessee, when 50-year-old inmate Christa Pike remained breathing and audibly snoring after two separate doses of pentobarbital, the barbiturate used in the state's lethal injection protocol. Graczyk, 76, says he wasn't entirely surprised to hear of the anomaly - and had actually thought about the possibility during his decades-long career as a Texas journalist. "It seems to me it was just a matter of time," he told BBC News. Tennessee administered two lethal doses to execute Christa Pike, but she lived Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set, according to AP, but does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set. Governor Bill Lee halted executions in the state after Wednesday night's failure, ordering an independent review into procedures. Botched executions have come under scrutiny over the past decade, since a shortage of the drugs used led some states to change the formula, or procure drugs from more questionable sources. Some states even brought back death by firing squad as an alternative. The secret hunt for lethal drugs used in US executions Pike is now in hospital where she is receiving "life-saving care", according to her lawyer. It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, lists 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set. But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered. "That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State. Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job. "There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said. There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people. Why the death penalty is on the rise in US "I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said. "That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened." The death chamber is seen from the viewing area at the Texas state penitentiary in Huntsville, where reporter Michael Graczyk has covered hundreds of executions He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news. "I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been." "Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim … and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right." Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess". Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said. "So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up." In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites. During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said. A Tennessee journalist stands near images of Pike's victim, Colleen Slemmer, 19 He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley. Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words. "He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore." That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years. title: Dolly Parton sings Jolene in Welsh in recording released after her death
description: Parton's niece Jada Star and Welsh singer Bronwen Lewis say the country artist was proud to sing in Welsh.
body: Dolly's niece Jada Star and Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis say the country singer was "proud" to sing in Welsh A new version of Dolly Parton's Jolene is set to be released, with parts of the song sung in Welsh by the legendary country artist. The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star. In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs. The single will come out on 9 October, and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent. In a teaser video released on social media, Star and Lewis explained how the song came to light. As a proud Welsh speaker, Lewis, from Neath, had started translating some of her favourite tunes, and soon landed on the Parton classic, Jolene. "Two years ago I posted a video of me singing the Dolly Parton classic Jolene in Welsh, external," said Lewis. "I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada." Dolly Parton's niece, Jada, got in touch with Bronwen Lewis after hearing her sing Jolene in Welsh A friendship was born, and Star came over from Nashville in the US to Wales to meet Lewis, joining her at Pride Cymru. "Pride Cymru was such an amazing experience and I learned so much about my family lineage," said Star. "I cherish the time I spent with Bronwen exploring one of the most beautiful places I have ever seen." Jada Star asked her aunt, Dolly Parton, if she would sing with her and Bronwen on a version of Jolene The teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, which Lewis "jumped" at the chance to do, with Star then saying she would get her aunt involved too. "Jada told me that her Aunt Dolly would like to sing with us on our version of Jolene. I think I fell to the ground," said Lewis. "Definitely cried happy tears, and called my mother immediately." BBC Radio Wales presenter Lewis said she had always loved Parton's music. "To hear Dolly sing in another language, and in Welsh for the very first time, was unbelievable." This video can not be played Watch: 'Where's Jolene now? You can have him, Jolene' After understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation, Parton recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville, in early 2025. Lewis had planned to go over to meet her to release the music, but Parton passed away before the meet-up could happen. "It was devastating, not just for myself and our family, but for the entire world," Star said. Lewis said the pair realised what a privilege it was to have recorded and collaborated "with one of the greatest musicians and women to grace this Earth". "We did what she always told us to do. We got ourselves together and decided to finish what we started," Star added. Star and Lewis said Parton was "proud" to sing in Welsh. This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language. She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011. Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046. Bronwen and Jada recorded Jolene in the UK, while Dolly recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd. "Some of my mother's people, the Owens, are from there [Wales]," Parton later told Wales Online. "I've been there about three times and it always feels good because it feels like family." Star had also previously spoken about the family's Welsh connection. She said the Owens side of the family, coming from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens, was believed to have come from Conwy. Speaking to BBC Radio Wales in 2024, Star said discovering that part of the family's history had been "really extraordinary". Star suggested some of Parton's music, and her own, may have been inspired by her Welsh roots. Parton's death brought renewed attention in Wales to the country music legend's Welsh links, with her heritage explored in a 2025 documentary. Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, not Conwy as previously thought. title: Black metal mourns pioneering Venom frontman
description: Newcastle rock giants Venom describe Conrad Cronos Lant as "fearless and unmistakable".
body: Conrad Cronos Lant and his band Venom are widely credited with creating an entire genre of music The co-founder, frontman and bass player of pioneering heavy metal band Venom has died at the age of 63, it has been announced. For almost 50 years Conrad Lant, known by his stage name Cronos, led the Newcastle band credited with inventing the black metal genre and cited as a major influence by thrash metal bands including Metallica, Slayer and Anthrax. In a tribute, the group said Lant's "voice, bass and vision were at the heart of Venom" and described their bandmate as "uncompromising, fearless and unmistakable". His son Nathan thanked the band's fans down the decades "for all of the support you have given my dad over the years, I know he really appreciated you all". Venom began in Newcastle in 1978, formed by musicians from three other bands, but it was their second album - Black Metal released in 1982 - that cemented their status in the rock world. Playing a fast style mixed with Lant's dark imagery and lyrics, the album gave its name to an entire subgenre and influenced bands on both sides of the Atlantic. Speaking to BBC Newcastle, rock journalist Simon Rushworth said: "They were massively influential [and] spawned a whole genre of what I'd call extreme metal. "The likes of Slayer, Metallica, Anthrax, they all cited Venom. "Venom took Metallica out on the road in the mid-80s before anybody knew who they were. Then Metallica returned the favour and took Venom on the road with them. "Cronos was right at the heart of it, not only with the music. "He was the one who brought a lot of the early artwork to the table and kind of created this black metal image." That imagery brought the band to the attention of the US government when the track Possessed was included on the "Filthy Fifteen" list of songs compiled by the Parents Music Resource Center, the committee behind the adoption of "parental advisory" warning stickers. Cronos brought much of the imagery to the band, to the delight of fans and horror of censors The original line-up began to break apart following Possessed and Cronos pursued solo projects until a short-lived and acrimonious reunion in the mid-90s. With changing line-ups, but mainly led by Cronos, Venom continued to the present day, releasing a 14th studio album - Into Oblivion - this year. In a tribute on social media, original guitarist Jeff "Mantas" Dunn said: "Despite the turbulent history of this band, it was at the end of the day the three of us, who started something so special and changed the direction, the movement and the history of metal as we know it. "At times like this the thing I remember is the friendship that we had in those early days, that one for all, all for one mentality, that rebellious quality and the absolute driven urge to be something so different whether it was accepted or not." Rushworth said the band were themselves influenced by the likes of Motorhead, Kiss, Black Sabbath and Alice Cooper, adding: "Cronos wanted Venom to be a more evil and flamboyant hybrid of all of those bands. "Many would say he succeeded." Follow BBC Newcastle on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds. title: New free repair shop to launch in Oxford
description: Organisers hope the initiative will attract enough interest to continue on a monthly basis.
body: Repair of bikes and electrical items, as well as sewing, will be available on Saturday at St Barnabas Primary Free help with repairing bikes, electrical items, computers and clothes is coming to an Oxford neighbourhood. On Saturday, the first Jericho Repair Shop will take place at St Barnabas CE Primary School, in Jericho, between 10 and 12:00 BST. Organiser John Mair said everyone was welcome to come along and donations would go back into rental costs and advertising for the event, which he hoped would continue on a monthly basis. He said an initiative such as the repair shop "stops people throwing things away". Mair said he decided to start a repair shop in Jericho after having used the service himself. "I went to the repair shop in Wolvercote maybe a year or two ago and they repaired my garden blower - I thought this is a good idea," he said. "I've brought over the man who repairs bicycles in Wolvercote, people who repair sewing, people who do computers, who sharpen knives." Co-ordinator of Share Oxford, which also runs repair cafes in Oxford, Ben Tuppen previously said society needed to be more innovative in its approach to sustainability. He also said they "were pleased to share how we run things and promote John's new repair café with our volunteers, some of whom have joined his team too". Mair said: "If it doesn't work, repair it, don't throw it away and certainly don't throw it on the pavement." Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire Mair said he was looking forward to the launch and expected "anywhere between 10 and 100 people". "It costs you nothing, but we'll expect a donation," he said. "If enough people turn up, it'll be the first Saturday of November, and if enough people turn up, first Saturday of December." Mair, who has been organising public events in Jericho such as Lazy Saturday and Lazy Sunday in Mount Place, said he wanted to see "how much demand there is". He added: "All communities need hubs and this might as well be one, so why not?" title: How Gordon became one of England's main men
description: Anthony Gordon has been England's in-form player since the World Cup knockout stage - is the Barcelona forward now undroppable?
body: Anthony Gordon has made 27 appearances for England, scoring six goals Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Declan Rice, Jordan Pickford and now Anthony Gordon. All have become guaranteed starters and reliable stars for England, with the Barcelona winger the latest to look, according to captain Kane, like one of the Three Lions' "main men". Gordon was one of England's standout players at the World Cup and earned a big-money move to European giants Barca in the summer, while his good form has continued into his country's Nations League campaign. He scored the opening goal in England's 2-0 win against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night, after also netting in a 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday. In fact, the 25-year-old's England form has been building since the knockout stage of the World Cup began - his run of averaging a goal contribution every 69 minutes started with assisting both Kane's efforts in a 2-1 last-32 victory over DR Congo. The former Newcastle player has scored three goals and provided three assists in his past six England matches, while he also won the penalty in England's dramatic last-16 victory over Mexico at Azteca Stadium. And after a positive start in Spain, where he has already picked up five assists in La Liga, Gordon looks to be joining boss Thomas Tuchel's "undroppable" bracket. Tuchel likes to give his players clarity on their role and makes clear who they are up against in the squad and for a starting position. When asked whether Gordon is getting to be one of the first names on the team-sheet, he said: "He's getting there. He's defending his shirt, he's defending his position - an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain. "He was very decisive [against the Czech Republic] and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult but the technique and finishing was excellent. "He scored against Spain so he has decisive actions and he's defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he's a very important player." Gordon linked up well with his former Newcastle team-mate Lewis Hall on England's left and combined with right-back Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start for the Three Lions in nearly two years, for the opening goal. Gordon said he had been "dying" to link up with Alexander-Arnold, who is also playing in Spain for Barcelona's rivals Real Madrid. "It's a great compliment and it's great to play with him," Alexander-Arnold said of Gordon. "I tried to get the ball, and try and see what the best play is and try and play forward and create something. And I was able to get the pass." Captain and record goalscorer Kane is a guaranteed starter in England's biggest matches but the position to the left of Kane has been a problem area for the team, with no player able to make it their own. Gordon looks to have secured that role and Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England". "His performances in the last couple of games have been some of his best that he has played in an England shirt," Kane said. "I think he is just relishing putting the shirt on and being one of the main men in the team. He is an important player for us and he showed that during the World Cup." It has not always been a straightforward route into the team for Gordon. Marcus Rashford, Eberechi Eze, Phil Foden and Noni Madueke have all featured for England from the left in the past couple of years. Gordon started to emerge as a clear option during Lee Carsley's time in interim charge, but said himself last October that he had only shown "50%" of what he can do for England. Now that seems to be coming to fruition. Against the Czech Republic he attempted four shots, more than any England player and more than any of his team-mates against Spain too. Gordon is ranked in at least the top four of England players for expected assists (0.9), expected goals (0.9), passes into the box (14), touches in the opposition box (29), chances created (eight), and shots on target (five), since the start of the World Cup knockout stage. His importance is underlined by the fact he has contributed the same amount of goals and assists, six, as Bellingham since England faced DR Congo. There has been an interesting subplot with Gordon and Rashford competing for a left-wing space for England and effectively Barcelona. Rashford was on loan at Barcelona last season but they opted to not make his move permanent, instead he returned to Manchester United while the Catalan club splashed out £69m to sign Gordon from Newcastle. Gordon has the ability to take on his full-back on the inside or beat them for pace on the outside before putting in a cross. "People raised eyebrows when Anthony Gordon went to Barcelona for the money that he did and Marcus Rashford came back to Manchester United," former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Radio 5 Live. "He has become a key part of the England team. There were certain games in the World Cup where he was substituted and he shouldn't have been - I think others should have come off instead of him. "Gordon [when he is] full of confidence running at pace like he does, he can go either way and he's causing full-backs all kind of problems." Gordon says that since his move to Spain he has changed people's perception of him being a player who is only quick and presses well, even if they are two of his best attributes. "I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon told ITV. "Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick. title: Car crashes into viral shop shutters where gran was hoisted into the air
description: The shop went viral when a grandmother got caught on its shutters - and has hit the headlines again.
body: This video can not be played The shop went viral when a grandmother got caught on its shutters - and has hit the headlines again A shop made famous when a grandmother got caught on its shutter and was left dangling in the air has hit the headlines again after a car crashed through the front of it. The Best-One shop in Tonteg, Rhondda Cynon Taf, caught the dramatic moment on CCTV when a Jaguar smashed through its doors after mounting bollards and crashing into the shop's coffee machine. In March 2024, the shop went viral after staff member Anne Hughes got caught on the shutter while waiting for the shop to open to start her shift. Anne, who died in 2025, was left dangling 7ft (2.1 metres) in the air and shouting for the owner to help her, with CCTV footage of the incident viewed tens of millions of times. A Jaguar smashed through the shop's doors after the driver lost control of his car People working in the shop could not believe the latest incident on Friday and were left "scared" when the car ploughed into the shop's entrance. Donna Davies, who has worked in the shop for several years, said: "The car just came straight through, it was a loud noise and we didn't know what was happening but thought it could have been ram-raiders. It was scary." She said she ran out and saw an elderly driver and passenger, who are both regulars to the shop, in the car. "The driver said his foot slipped when he went to get out the car and the car came straight in," Donna said. Donna Davies has worked in the shop for several years and said the car crash was "scary" Anne's viral moment was previously immortalised by local graffiti artist Tee2Sugars on the shutter she was caught on. He has now updated the shutter to include the car smashing through the front of the shop. Donna said she had worked with Anne before her death. "Anne would be laughing at this, I think she'd like the updated shutter," she said. "People are coming in the shop this morning and finding it amusing. It wasn't at the time, but looking back we can smile." Hakim Akram, who works in the shop and is the nephew of the shop owner, says the crash felt "unreal" The shop front was badly damaged in the crash but the owner and family worked late on Friday and Saturday to fix the front and keep the shop open for customers. Hakim Akram, who is the nephew of the shop owner and works in the store, said: "It was a bit of a shock, he just came flying through - I didn't even know what happened until I saw the car. "It was surreal and very loud. People thought it was a prank and AI when they first saw it on social media." One customer, Shaun, said he could not believe it. He said: "It's just crazy after the incident with the lady on the shutter and now this." Anne Hughes' viral moment was immortalised by local graffiti artist Tee2Sugars The family of Anne Hughes told BBC Wales they were very glad no-one was seriously hurt. Her son Ceri joked: "We can't believe the shop's luck, we are starting to wonder if all of this is an inside job. "Tonteg Best-One - the only shop in the UK where you can be lifted 7ft in the air on Monday and driven through on a Friday." They said they were pleased the artwork of Anne was not damaged. Her grandchildren Lilly and Alex said their nan would be happy with the new addition on the shutter and joked: "Nan always preferred a Bentley but would settle with a Jag next to her on the shutter." title: School protests send shivers down French government's spine
description: A movement that started nearly two weeks ago has spread, and in France young people on the streets spells trouble, writes Hugh Schofield.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Why are students staging protests at schools in France? It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble. Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth. Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in. Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away. For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed. Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats". A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country. Live: Fires lit on streets across France after student protests force hundreds of schools to close On Thursday – the high point so far – hundreds of lycées (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycées were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in. Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycée in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros. According to Education Minister Édouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facing… were not their own pupils," he said. Since the infamous protests of 1968, French governments have known the power of young people taking to the streets In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people – mainly minors – taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth. The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension – a political and social one – which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past. The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money – the lack of it – and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings. On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system – because money is so tight. The protests have spread across France, and some university students are now joining in This week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts – and this time we're serious!" Whether or not he manages to remove €54bn (£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question. But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed. But that is the lesser of the worries. The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left – and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming. For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students – notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate." Bally Bagayoko (left) and presidential candidater Jean-Luc Mélenchon (right) have supported the right of the students to protest An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI." It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections". In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook. The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests". But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing. title: K-pop giants Stray Kids join BTS in boycotting the Grammys
description: Stray Kids become the second major act to withdraw from the Grammys over the new best Asian Pop award.
body: Stray Kids are one of K-Pop's biggest live acts, and recently headlined the Rock In Rio Festival, alongside Elton John One of the world's biggest K-pop groups, Stray Kids, are joining BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards. The move comes after the introduction of a controversial new category for Asian pop music, which critics fear will ghettoise genres like K-Pop and J-Pop. BTS announced they would not submit songs for consideration in any category in July, saying they hoped their music "can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language". Stray Kids, who recently scored their ninth US number one album, have now followed suit. In a short statement, their record label JYP simply said: "Stray Kids did not submit for the Grammys." Stray Kids had previously refrained from giving a direct answer to questions about the awards. During a press conference for their latest album, This and That, in August, singer Hwang Hyun-jin said: "We have never once set award results or records as our goal. "Our top priority is for our fans to be happy and satisfied," he added. The news will come as a blow to the Recording Academy, which organises the Grammys. Stray Kids are phenomenally popular in the US, and recently headlined the Governor's Ball festival in New York, sharing the bill with Lorde and A$AP Rocky. In the album chart, only one other band has scored more number one albums: The Beatles. Earlier this year, all eight members of the band were given voting privileges at the awards, which gives additional weight to their decision to withdraw. BTS are also voting members of the Academy. Before their decision to boycott the Grammys, BTS had performed at the ceremony and received five nominations - although they have yet to win a prize Stray Kids' announcement came hours after Grammys boss Harvey Mason Jr confirmed the new Asian pop category would go ahead at the 2027 ceremony. "Over the past several weeks, the Academy has been conducting listening sessions and have been in dialogue with leaders of the Asian music community," he said in a statement. "We heard candid feedback from people in our community who don't support the continuation of this category. We also heard from people who didn't have accurate information about the category, and having space to clear up misperceptions has been especially valuable. "But by far, the loudest feedback we heard was from people who were enthusiastic supporters of the category, fellow music creators expressing their encouragement for keeping it." He acknowledged that the decision "will not satisfy everyone" but said the Academy would continue to have discussions over the development of the award. Harvey Mason Jr said the Grammys would "keep striving to honour" music from Asia The Recording Academy announced the new category in June, saying it would recognise "artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets". The prize had been under discussion for years. It was finally introduced after Golden, from the movie K-pop Demon Hunters, became the first K-Pop song ever to win a Grammy this February. "As Asian pop's influence has continued to grow within our process, our members and trustees felt this was the right moment to create a category that more accurately reflects the genre's scale, artistry and global impact," organisers said at the time. But the award received a decidedly mixed reception. Many felt it would stop Asian artists from receiving recognition in the main categories. Others were upset by a stipulation that nominated songs should make "meaningful use" of an Asian language. That requirement ruled out the two most recognisable Korean acts in America, BTS and Blackpink, whose latest releases are primarily sung in English. The arguments against the Asian pop award are similar to those made by Latin artists about Grammy categories such as best música urbana. While the intent is to recognise music of a certain geographic or linguistic origin, some musicians feel it ends up being exclusionary, with their music segregated from mainstream prizes like album or song of the year. That perception was challenged this year, when Bad Bunny's Debí Tirar Más Fotos became the first Spanish-language album to win album of the year. Rosalía's Lux is also expected to feature heavily in the nominations for next year's awards. BTS and Stray Kids would have been eligible to compete for those prizes, but have decided to send a message to the Recording Academy instead. Other major acts may have followed suit. Earlier this week, Kim Hong-joon, leader of the popular boyband Ateez, said he had been impressed by BTS's stance. "I'd love to think about that too," he said in an interview with Variety Magazine. "I'm not sure because no-one can know about the real reason they tried to make that [category]. No-one can recognise the real reason. "But it seems like, for me... I agree [a little] with what BTS did." We will find out who did decide to enter their music for consideration when the Grammy nominations are revealed on 10 December. title: Oasis acoustic guitar sells for record price
description: Noel Gallagher played the instrument at Oasis's 1996 MTV Unplugged gig.
body: An acoustic guitar played by Noel Gallagher at Oasis's 1996 MTV Unplugged gig, and signed by him, has sold at auction for £226,800 setting a "world record". Hertfordshire-based Propstore said it was the "highest price achieved at auction for an Oasis acoustic guitar". It also sold a Yamaha C3 Grand Piano, for £81,900 which was used by Freddie Mercury to compose Crazy Little Thing Called Love. It was expected to sell for at least £200,000. On the first day of its Music Live Auction on Thursday, the highest-selling lot was a notebook by the Queen frontman which contained handwritten working lyrics and notes from the Mr. Bad Guy recording sessions. It sold for £277,200. Mark Hochman, the company's music specialist, said: "Setting a world record with Noel Gallagher's MTV Unplugged guitar is a fantastic result and a testament to the lasting connection fans have with Oasis. "These results show how much collectors value pieces with a personal connection to the artists and their music." The Yamaha C3 Grand Piano was played by Freddie Mercury at Munich's Musicland Studios In one day all items were sold for a combined total of £2.5m, including rare instruments, handwritten lyrics, stage items, and personal memorabilia. The auction included lots from the collection of German Producer Reinhold Mack, who worked with Queen on several albums in the 1980s. The sale of Mercury's notebook offered "an extraordinary glimpse into his songwriting, and seeing it fetch the day's highest price was another highlight", Hochman added. The notebook featured handwritten notes by Freddie Mercury, who died at the age of 45 Items from the King of Pop, Michael Jackson, were also on offer from The Omer Bhatti Collection, a Norwegian rapper and dancer, who Jackson gifted a number of items of clothing to. It included a black and gold military-style jacket, worn at multiple public appearances during the Dangerous and HIStory eras. The jacket sold for £226,800. title: Man arrested over 1993 unsolved Tooze murders faces no further action
description: Harry and Megan Tooze were found dead with shotgun wounds at their farm in south Wales.
body: Harry and Megan Tooze were killed at their home in Llanharry on 26 July 1993 A man arrested in connection with one of Wales' most notorious unsolved murders is no longer under investigation, police have said. Harry and Megan Tooze were found dead with shotgun wounds in a cow shed at their farm in south Wales on 26 July 1993. South Wales Police said an 87-year-old man who had been arrested in December last year as part of a review of evidence was no longer under investigation and had been released with no further action. Police had made the arrest as part of a forensic review of the cold case in 2023 as they investigated the deaths of Harry, 64, and Megan, 67. The retired fruit wholesaler and his wife had left their farm at Tŷ Ar y Waun, in Llanharry, Rhondda Cynon Taf, and drove their Land Rover to Tesco in nearby Talbot Green to do their weekly food shop, stopping to collect their pensions on the way home. They were seen arriving back home at 11:00. At about 13:30, two gun shots were heard by neighbours, but this was not considered unusual on a farm. The farm as it looks today The couple's daughter Cheryl raised the alarm when her regular daily call to her parents went unanswered that evening. Officers went to the farm and found the couple's bodies in a cow shed. Both had been shot in the back of the head from a distance of about 3ft (0.9 metres), then covered in carpet and hidden under hay bales, detectives said. Investigators believed Harry and Megan had not been killed in the cow shed. It was thought they had been carried there after their deaths. The Toozes' daughter Cheryl and her partner Jonathan Jones at their funeral Their daughter's boyfriend Jonathan Jones was found guilty of their murders and sentenced to life in prison in 1995, but was later freed on appeal. Jones, who was a self-employed recruitment consultant, had told police he had taken the day off work on the day the Toozes were killed and was in Orpington, Greater London. His partial thumbprint was also on a cup and saucer that had been found in the couple's living room. He was arrested that December, five months after the murders. The couple's daughter stood by him, moving in with his family in Caerphilly after his arrest. A year after his conviction, Jones was released on appeal. Three appeal court judges took five minutes to reach their decision. The original trial judge was criticised, and it emerged police had failed to seal the crime scene properly. South Wales police said the forensic review of the case, which is being led by the Major Crime Investigation Team, would continue. Det Supt Mark O'Shea said the force remained "committed to solving these dreadful murders" and he encouraged anyone with information to come forward as it "may help us get justice for the family". title: Woman who killed abusive partner has murder conviction overturned
description: The Court of Appeal ruled that jurors were misdirected on Julie Ann McIlwaine's loss of control defence to the killing of James Joseph Crossley.
body: Julie Ann McIlwaine admitted killing James Joseph Crossley but denied his murder A west Belfast woman who stabbed her abusive partner to death while he slept has had her conviction for murder overturned. The Court of Appeal ruled that jurors were misdirected on Julie Ann McIlwaine's loss of control defence to the killing of James Joseph Crossley in March 2022. Senior judges quashed the guilty verdict and gave the prosecution two weeks to decide if it is to seek any retrial. "We cannot be satisfied that the conviction is safe," said Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan. McIlwaine, 35, who has been serving a minimum 12-year jail term, wept on the videolink from Hydebank Prison as the ruling was delivered. She admitted killing her partner but denied murder, claiming to have suffered a temporary loss of control as a victim of domestic abuse. Crossley, 38, was stabbed up to 10 times in the chest and abdomen as he lay sleeping beside the couple's young child at McIlwaine's former home in Dunmurry. The pair had been in a relationship marred by emotional manipulation and coercive control. At the time of his death, Crossley was on bail for an alleged assault against McIlwaine and subject to a restraining order prohibiting any contact with her. Despite a period of separation, they had re-established their relationship by the night of the killing. The court heard Crossley took medication and went to sleep after arguments in which he issued an ultimatum for McIlwaine to choose between him and her family. James Joseph Crossley was killed in March 2022 During police interviews McIlwaine stated that she had considered taking her own life. She described taking a knife from the kitchen, returning to the bedroom and moving the child before repeatedly stabbing her sleeping partner. Prosecutors argued that she made rational choices which demonstrated being in control of her actions. In October 2024, a jury rejected McIlwaine's case and unanimously found her guilty of murder. Defence lawyers argued on appeal that they had been misdirected and reached a verdict which went against the weight of expert evidence. Central to the appeal was how the trial judge advised jurors on the legal test for the loss-of-control defence. Instead of asking them to decide if someone of similar characteristics to McIlwaine "might" have reacted similarly, the question posed was "would" that person have acted in the same way. Dame Siobhan, sitting with Lord Justice Colton, backed defence submissions that the wording used wrongly imposed a higher threshold for establishing probability. Two consultant forensic psychiatrists had also concluded that a properly directed jury could find McIlwaine met the criteria necessary to establish loss of self-control. Both witnesses highlighted the psychological impact of prolonged abuse and the recognised behaviour responses of victims in coercively controlling relationships. "The misdirection we have identified was highly material, given the uncontradicted expert evidence," said the Lady Chief Justice. "The appeal succeeds… and the conviction for murder will accordingly be quashed." Adjourning the case until 16 October, she told prosecution counsel: "You have to come back to court on what steps you want to take." title: Garvaghy Road investigation to start next week - Robinson
description: It comes after protesters blocked the mainly nationalist road to prevent an Orange Order parade from happening.
body: Gavin Robinson said there has to be "consequences" to "people who are law makers who are acting as law breakers" The leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has said he expects the criminal investigation into the unlawful blocking of Garvaghy Road to begin next week. On Wednesday, the PSNI chief constable said there would be an investigation after protesters blocked the mainly nationalist road to prevent an Orange Order parade from happening. Protesters remain on Garvaghy Road and the Orange Order has maintained a presence at Drumcree church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement. Gavin Robinson said there had to be "consequences" for "people who are law makers who are acting as law breakers". First Minister Michelle O'Neill was among those who attended the protest. She has said she understands the law, but chose to "stand in solidarity" with residents. Robinson said he expected the investigation to begin next week "but it needs the space to see it conclude as well". The fallout over the proposed Orange Order march - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning. A fresh legal bid by the residents to prevent the march was due to be heard on Friday - but has now been postponed until Monday. Orangemen and Garvaghy Road residents met Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle on Thursday night but did not break their deadlock. Speaking after Thursday night's talks, Sir Chris told reporters: "I think this is the end of these conversations. "We haven't come to a settled agreement and it's a shame but my door remains open." Breándan Mac Cionnaith, the chairman of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, said there had been no "meeting of minds". Nigel Dawson, the Orange Order's Portadown district master, said it "remains as it has been". Sir Chris Bryant says he is open to hosting further talks On Friday morning, about 20 protesters were gathered on the Garvaghy Road. About a mile away at Drumcree Church, five members of the Orange Order were present. The rector of Drumcree Church has said that he has received hundreds of "extremely nasty" emails, texts and calls in recent days. In a post on Facebook, the Reverend Gary Galway said: "Social media has given a platform for individuals to express themselves without restraint, or the integrity of a face-to-face civil discussion." Hopes of a resolution to the Drumcree dispute have faded but have not disappeared completely. By engaging in a four-day talks process, the two sides have shown a willingness to try to negotiate an agreement. Further discussions at some stage are still possible. Some might say they are inevitable. However, momentum has been lost and the danger is that the problem now just festers for days, months or even years. That would be bad for community relations and a strain on police resources as they keep a round-the-clock watch on Drumcree hill and the Garvaghy Road. For all concerned, a difficult road lies ahead. The stalemate has reopened what was once the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission, which adjudicates on marching disputes, ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years. But last week the Parades Commission decided that the parade could go ahead on Sunday morning with restrictions in place. That prompted a large protest on the Garvaghy Road, preventing the Orange Order from marching. Thirteen councillors have been reported to the local government standards watchdog over conduct surrounding the parading dispute. Some 25 allegations have been received by the Local Government Commissioner for Standards in Northern Ireland in recent days concerning potential breaches of the councillors' code of conduct. It follows unionist parties accusing nationalist politicians of acting unlawfully over their involvement in the protest at Garvaghy Road on Sunday. On Friday, former US diplomat Dr Richard Haass told BBC News NI that Northern Ireland had "failed" to come to terms with the legacy of its past. Haass chaired all-party talks in Northern Ireland in 2013 aimed at resolving contentious issues, including parades. He said the flare-up of the Drumcree dispute should be "a bit of a warning shot or a wake-up call". "I don't think any of us should take progress for granted. Backsliding is always possible," he added. Orangemen gathered at Drumcree Church on Sunday but were blocked from completing their march More than 200 people from a Protestant background have put their names to a letter to the UK and Irish governments, expressing concern over the dispute. In the letter, they said they were distressed by the "trauma that is being visited on the residents of the Garvaghy Road after 28 years of calm". The signatories said they recognised that parading was a "valued tradition" for many but they appealed to the Orange Order to "look towards the bigger picture and bring this impasse to an end in the interests of the entire community". title: Ted Lasso honours Anthony Head with fresh tribute
description: Head played series villain, Rupert Mannion, in the first three seasons before his death at age 72.
body: Anthony Head joined the Ted Lasso cast as Rupert Mannion in 2020 Anthony Head's lasting legacy continues to be honoured months after his death, with a major TV show issuing a fresh tribute to the acclaimed actor. During an emotional penultimate episode of the current Ted Lasso's season, the show finished with a dedication to the Bath-based actor who formerly played wealthy businessman Rupert Mannion. The tribute comes as the series' latest episode reintroduced Rupert's name in the storyline, despite him not appearing in the season. Head died in June at the age of 72 after developing complications from pneumonia. His long-term partner, Sarah Fisher, died several months earlier, in December 2025, after she was diagnosed with thyroid cancer. The ninth episode of the series concluded with a title card reading: 'In memory of Anthony Head', in recognition of world-renowned actor's contribution to the hit Apple+ show. Teen sentenced for string of 'reckless' arson attacks Man arrested after 'explosive substances' found 'Disappointment' as Turbo Island village green rejected Head's career spanned more than four decades, with roles including Rupert Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, King Uther in Merlin and the Prime Minister in Little Britain. Head and his long-term partner, animal welfare advocate Fisher, also had strong ties to the Bath area. The couple hosted charity events at their home, including Forever Hounds Trust's 20th anniversary celebrations They lived near the city at Tilley Farm, Fisher's 90-acre sanctuary in Farmborough, where she cared for rescued horses, ponies and donkeys. Fisher was a long-standing patron of Holly Hedge Animal Sanctuary in North Somerset and also supported many animal charities, including Battersea Cats and Dogs Home. A spokesperson for the London-based charity previously said: "Sarah, alongside her partner Anthony Head, gave so much to our charity, fostering dogs, using her canine behaviour expertise to train our staff and volunteers, and contributing in so many ways to make a real difference in animal welfare. "She will be dearly missed by all of us at Battersea." Follow BBC Bristol on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: UK diesel price hits £2 a litre as US calls for Europe to release more stocks
description: The RAC says diesel price rises are showing no signs of slowing, "heaping more misery" onto drivers.
body: The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring body, as the fallout from the Iran war continues to push up the cost of fuel. Diesel has now hit an average of 200.01p a litre, the RAC said, and petrol prices are also still rising, reaching 174.71p a litre on average. The motoring group said price rises were "showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery onto motorists". The US has put increasing pressure on European countries to release more diesel stocks, to help lower diesel prices worldwide, with President Trump threatening to ban US exports of the fuel. Banning exports would mean more US diesel for the domestic market, which could ease prices for American motorists ahead of the midterm elections in November. However, it would be likely to push up prices elsewhere, including in the UK and the EU. US President Donald Trump said he was considering a ban, and backed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent who has urged European countries to release diesel supplies "immediately", arguing that US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar. On Friday, the EU said it "fully rejects" the US threat to ban diesel exports if Europe fails to release more of its reserves onto the market. "It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner," an EU spokesperson said. EU countries agreed in March to release some stocks as part of an internationally co-ordinated response to the Iran war. With prospects for the war and fuel supplies still uncertain, not all EU countries have met those commitments. UK government ministers said they were working with both the US and the EU. "We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further. Over half of the diesel bought in the UK is imported. Less than a third of imports are from the US, amounting to around 17% of the total UK supply. Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refiners have further constrained supplies of diesel on the world market. China has also restricted exports of refined fuels. High diesel prices affect some drivers directly, but can have a wider knock-on effect by pushing up transport and delivery costs and making food production more expensive. The cost of filling an average family car with diesel is now £110, almost £32 more than it was at the start of the US-Iran war, the RAC's Simon Williams said. "This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders," he added. The cost of filling a typical petrol car has risen to £96.09, the RAC said, up £23.03 since February. How have you been affected by the rising price of diesel? title: Son of ex-Chelsea player died in 40C desert hike
description: Cassius Newton's wife urged him not to go on the hike, a coroner tells an inquest into his death.
body: Cassius Newton was the son of former Chelsea player Eddie Newton The son of ex-Chelsea midfielder Eddie Newton ignored pleas from his wife to not go on what turned out to be a fatal 40C (104F) desert hike, a coroner said. Rescue teams found the body of Cassius Newton, 34, in the mountainous region of Wadi Naqab, United Arab Emirates (UAE), on 18 July - hours after the couple last spoke, an inquest was told. His friend, Aran Martinson, from Bishop's Stortford in Hertfordshire, also died in the sweltering heat after they set off at about 07:00 local time (04:00 BST). Area coroner Michelle Brown ruled their deaths were the result of misadventure and said: "This was an intentional trip with unintended consequences." Newton met Martinson through their work at a "global company" and they both lived in the luxury resort of Ras Al Khaimah, to the north-east of Dubai. He called his wife at about 02:00 to inform her of their planned hike and "she asked him not to go", Essex Coroner's Court heard. "She knew it would be very hot and it can get to about 40C, and the feeling is higher because it's in the canyons," Brown said. "He was also out the night before and wouldn't have had much sleep, and she didn't think he would have charged his phone enough." Newton and Martinson had both recently moved to the United Arab Emirates city of Ras Al Khaimah before their deaths Rescue efforts were launched after the wives of both men called the authorities, having not heard from them for hours. They were discovered between 3km and 4km (1.8 miles and 2.5 miles) from where they had parked, and their bodies were 350m (1,148ft) apart. Brown described the circular route they were walking as "a recreational hike". It was on a designated trail that did not require any equipment and should have taken about four hours to complete. Newton, originally from Poole, and father-of-three Martinson were both lying on their backs surrounded by large rocks. They were taken to hospital in Ras Al Khaimah but pronounced dead later that day. She said Eddie Newton flew out to the UAE to identify his son's body. Eddie Newton went on to have two spells as Chelsea's assistant manager Text messages between Martinson and his wife were also read to the court, in which she said at 09:26: "You must be cooking." Having not heard from him five hours later, she messaged: "[You are] actually trying to tip me over the edge I swear." Brown said the men both died from severe rising body temperatures which led to organ failure. A previous hearing was told it was 50C (122F) in the desert, but Brown said it was 40C earlier. In an earlier tribute, Chelsea said it was "devastated" to learn of the death of Newton, who once played for the club's academy. Martinson's wife wrote online that her husband was "incredibly driven, hardworking and ambitious". Do you have a story suggestion? Contact us below.
