title: 'Dark cloud' hangs over Cornell campus as anger at frat rape investigation grows
description: Students tell the BBC that the tension on campus has become palpable since allegations from 2024 resurfaced.
body: This video can not be played Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case Students have called for drastic change at Cornell University as a result of an alleged gang rape in 2024, with one using an emotional student assembly on Thursday to say: "We're absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on campus." Students and faculty members say the investigation into the incident has cast a "dark cloud" over the campus - stirring anger, concern over fraternity culture, and a backlash against the university's handling of the situation. At Thursday's assembly, some labelled the perceived lack of justice a "disgrace" and criticised the prestigious university, which has defended its handling of the case. "We deserve to know that our institution values our safety more than its reputation," undergraduate Sophia Riley Sim told those at the gathering. Sim said she had been too upset by the case to attend classes for the past week. Under normal circumstances, the Ivy League university is a beautiful place to study at this time of year. Autumn leaves bring pops of colour to its stately buildings, which are set against the backdrop of the rolling hills of upstate New York. But students and staff who spoke to the BBC - some on condition of anonymity - said the tension on campus had become palpable since the 2024 case resurfaced in recent weeks. Cornell University's campus is located in Ithaca, upstate New York The accuser at the centre of the alleged gang rape, known anonymously as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell on 16 September, saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house during the incident two years ago. She claimed that Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved in the incident. The men have been dubbed the Cornell Seven. Cornell has already agreed to an independent investigation into the rape allegation. The university has also defended its handling of the issue to date, external, saying it conducted an "extensive investigation" that lasted several months following the report of the incident, and that it followed applicable federal civil rights law. Shortly after Thursday's student assembly at Cornell, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced she had appointed the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor in the case. She said she had "lost faith" in the Tompkins County district attorney, who was previously leading the investigation. James therefore takes over the case from Matthew Van Houten. Van Houten's office initially concluded that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges - before reopening a criminal investigation last week in light of the new civil complaint, a move that Cornell supported. Cornell accuser was 'failed' by university health care system, lawyer says What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults An upcoming "Justice for Survivors" protest, planned at the university for 5 October, is being advertised in flyers all over campus. It calls on Cornell to take action against alleged rape culture. Student organisers are calling for Cornell to expel and revoke the degrees of the alleged perpetrators of the rape, rewrite policies around sexual assault punishments, initiate an external investigation of the university and mandate prevention training for campus police. As part of its account of its prior investigation of the case, Cornell says: "At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell." Cornell says it is legally prevented from publicly disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes about disciplinary students, adding that "we recognise that this legal limitation can be frustrating". Across campus, the case has stirred anger. One fourth-year student recalled that it had been hard to live there in 2024, in the aftermath of the incident, as rumours began spreading about Jane Doe. Now, two years on, she told the BBC how she and her friends felt "overwhelmed" and "disappointed", comparing the atmosphere on campus to a "dark cloud". Cornell, she believes, mishandled things. She wants the administration to admit what she sees as its mistakes, calling the lack of transparency disheartening. She also asked why multiple men in a group chat for members of Chi Phi - the fraternity group at the centre of the allegations - did not speak up. A chapter of the fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus. Students and staff have spoken of a "dark cloud" over the campus Students and community members also used Thursday's student assembly meeting to vent their frustrations and disappointment. "I am very disgusted to be here, to be paying this institution to be here," freshman Eliana Dolven-Miller said. "There was a lot of anger in that room, I was very angry." Eeshaan Chaudhuri, the student assembly chair, opened the meeting by saying that the campus stood "with victims of sexual violence". "We don't tolerate it here on campus, and I think I can speak for every single one of us, and I can say we're absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on our campus," Chaudhuri said. The student group has also raised a resolution calling on the university to release a written account of how it handled the alleged sexual assault, including what evidence was gathered and whether and when the university referred the matter to campus police. title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
description: The star's record label is sued over similarities between her song I've Seen It and Withers' classic.
body: The lawsuit seeks damages from Dean's publisher and record label, but not from the star herself British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California. The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving. Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone. The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang. In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs. He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said. The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution. To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition. In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It. The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment. How Grammy winner Olivia Dean became Britain's new global star I've Seen It is the closing track of Dean's breakthrough album, which was released in September 2025. A sweet, acoustic ballad, it discusses the various types of love she's encountered in her life - from high school crushes to the love she has for her family and friends. Speaking to W Magazine last year, she said the song was written after "I'd had a lot of red wine". "When I heard it back for the first time, I burst into tears. It felt like the loveliest note to end on. Whether it's within your friends, your family, or just the love that exists in the strangers around you, it's there, and it's inside of you, too." It is has been streamed on Spotify about 246 million times, while Just The Two of Us has racked up 948 million plays. Withers' track went to number two in the US charts in 1981 and earned him a Grammy for best R&B song. He died in 2020. Dean picked up best new artist at this year's Grammys, while The Art of Loving reached number three in the US and number one in the UK, and was named album of the year at the Brit Awards. title: British paratrooper killed by explosion in Ukraine, coroner rules
description: L/Cpl George Hooley is the first UK service member to die in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
body: A British paratrooper was killed by an explosion while assisting Ukrainian troops in the war with Russia, a coroner has ruled. An inquest, conducted partly in secret this week, into L/Cpl George Hooley's death found he had "sustained multiple injuries from an explosion" on 6 December 2025. Hooley, 28, died from his injuries in a hospital in Kyiv three days later - the first British service member to die in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Darren Salter, senior coroner for Oxfordshire, said he had been provided with "limited evidence" about the circumstances and cause of the explosion but Hooley's death was "not suspicious". The location of the explosion is also unknown, other than that it was away from the front line. The coroner's report said Hooley had been transferred from at least one other hospital in Ukraine before his death in the capital. In a statement in December, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said Hooley was "an exceptional soldier and an impressive junior leader with extensive operational experience". It said his death was a "tragic accident" that happened while he was "observing Ukrainian forces test a new defensive capability". The MoD did not comment when asked further questions about the circumstances of the incident. Hooley's company commander in the Parachute Regiment said the 28-year-old was "a born soldier" who "had a rare gift: a deep kindness and genuine time for everyone". Hooley, from Wallingford in Oxfordshire, joined the regiment in June 2016 after completing his training at the Infantry Training Centre Catterick in North Yorkshire. The UK government has never disclosed the number of service people in Ukraine, but has previously acknowledged a small number is there to support Ukrainian armed forces and provide security to diplomatic personnel. After almost five years of war, the front line in Ukraine remains largely stagnant with both sides failing to make significant gains. Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including a large area of Donetsk. Peace negotiations to bring an end to the war have also stalled. Kyiv and its European allies accuse President Vladimir Putin of repeatedly rejecting plans for trilateral talks involving Russia the US and Ukraine and say he is seeking to seize more Ukrainian territory. title: Backshall makes nature 'cool' to inspire children
description: Steve Backshall says growing up with rescue animals helped inspire his passion for nature.
body: He is encouraging children to be outdoors, be active and be interested in animals Wildlife presenter Steve Backshall has told how he sets out to make nature "adventurous" and "cool" for children rather than preach to them. The presenter, known for programmes including Deadly 60, wants as many youngsters as possible to be exposed to the natural world. He spent his own childhood in a house in Surrey filled with rescue animals and said it helped inspire the passion for wildlife that later shaped his career. Speaking in London ahead of his Deadly Live show in Brighton, external on 29 October, he said what made his work exciting and worthwhile was seeing that there are "thousands and thousands of kids out there who have a passion for natural history". Reflecting on how childhood has changed, Backshall said: "I feel very strongly, and I think the scientific evidence backs it up too, that there are many things in an old-fashioned childhood that were much more healthy for kids than the childhoods they have today." He said: "There are immense amounts of benefit to be gained from being outside, being interested in animals, being connected to nature, being active." But he said he didn't want to preach or sound like an "old fuddy duddy bloke", adding: "I've got to make nature and everything that comes with it as adventurous, as cool as it can possibly be." Backshall has set out to get children interested in the natural world The presenter has previously spoken about how his childhood in Surrey prompted his love of nature. He said his parents took on a smallholding in their 30s, adding: "We filled it with rescue animals, about which we had no idea, we were making everything up as we went along." Backshall recalled it as a "crazy version" of the TV sitcom The Good Life. He said: "That was my childhood and it was absolutely incredible." Backshall studied at Canterbury Christ Church, carrying out research into venoms from amphibians, and later received an honorary doctorate from the university. Explaining his focus on the world's most formidable predators in his TV series Deadly 60, he said: "We deliberately deal with animals like birds of prey and sharks and crocodiles and snakes and spiders and scorpions, big cats, that kind that everyone is fascinated by. "Regardless of whether they think they like wildlife or not, they're going to be vaguely interested in those things." Laughing, he added: "Even if they're not, they might watch anyway in the vague hope that I might get savaged by something." title: Parents say toddler found in middle of main road after wandering off from nursery
description: Two-year-old Noah was found in the middle of a busy road in Swansea, his parents say.
body: Two-year-old Noah was found by a stranger after escaping from nursery on Wednesday Parents who claim their toddler wandered off from nursery and was found by a stranger on a busy road say they have been left traumatised. Sarah Durgan, 22, and Tarik Al Roshoq, 24, from Swansea, said their two-year-old son Noah was found on his own on Gors Avenue, Mayhill. "He could have been hit by a car, a bus, he could have been taken," Al Roshoq said. Seren Fach Day Nursery said it had implemented additional safety measures and "the safety, welfare and protection" of every child in their care remained a priority. South Wales Police said it was investigating the incident after officers responded to reports of "safeguarding concerns" when a child left nursery without the knowledge of staff. Sarah Durgan says she has not been able to eat or sleep since the incident "This stuff shouldn't be happening, especially in a safe place," Al Roshoq said, "how is that even possible?" Durgan added: "When you drop your children off in school or nursery you never think that anything could happen to them because they are in a professional's hands." The couple said they had found out about the incident when they had arrived to pick Noah up from nursery about 40 minutes afterwards. They said the nursery blamed the incident on "no-one watching him" and "a door being left open". But Noah's parents said he would have to pass through two baby gates, four doors including fire doors, and the main gate to reach Gors Avenue. Tarik Al Roshoq says it is "a parent's worst nightmare" The couple have since taken Noah out of nursery, and said several other pupils have also been withdrawn as a result of the incident. Despite them keeping a watchful eye on Noah, they said they were fearful for his safety and cannot rest. "It's the worst possible scenario. We can't sleep, we know he's safe, pray to God he's safe, but we keep checking in on him." Noah's parents say they are now scared to leave Noah or his brother Malik (left) in the care of others The parents said they had spoken to three eyewitnesses who claim Noah had been alone with no adult supervision, and that the nursery had been unaware he was missing. "When we first got in, we spoke to the manager, who said they were very sorry and there was no excuse for the doors to be open," said Al Roshoq. The nursery then made the couple aware of posts on Facebook about the incident, including a post from Nicolle Richards, who said she found Noah in the middle of the road and reported the incident. In the post, Richards said: "Today has been one of the scariest days of my life. I was driving up Gors Avenue and could see a little boy walking in the middle of the road. "I stopped and grabbed him, a man went down to the nursery to grab someone, a woman come out I explained he was in the middle of the road." The parents say they could have been looking at a much different situation "We drop him off to nursery and think he's in a safe place. It's scary, the fact our son was in the middle of the road on his own," said Al Roshoq. "The police aren't taking it lightly, this is a two-year-old. We took Noah out of nursery as soon as it happened. "[Sarah] hasn't been sleeping. We just keep checking." South Wales Police and Care Inspectorate Wales are investigating the incident In a statement on Facebook, Seren Fach Day Nursey said it was aware of the post on social media and "completely understand why members of the public and our families are concerned after reading the post". It said: "The safety and wellbeing of the children entrusted to our care is something we take incredibly seriously, and we would never seek to minimise a concern of this nature. "Seren Fach Day Nursery has been part of the local community for over 30 years and during that time we have cared for generations of children and families. "We have established safeguarding and security procedures in place, alongside staff training and risk assessments, all of which are being carefully investigated as part of our response to this incident. "We would ask that people avoid speculation or sharing information about the child or those involved on social media. "Please raise any concerns directly with the nursery or the relevant authorities so that they can be properly addressed." Care Inspectorate Wales (CIW) said it was unable to comment while inquiries were ongoing, but it would take "any necessary action" to ensure children's safety and wellbeing. "Where concerns are raised, we work to ensure providers meet the national minimum standards for regulated childcare, which include specific requirements on safeguarding, premises security and child protection. "We would encourage anyone with concerns about the care of a child to contact CIW directly." title: 'I was not going to let others die' - pilot of Flydubai flight describes cockpit attack by co-pilot
description: Capt Smit Machchhar tells Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi he opened the cockpit door to let others in during the attack.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Flydubai pilot speaks with Indian PM The Indian pilot of the Flydubai plane who was attacked by his co-pilot and opened the cockpit door to let others in has said he was determined not to let others die. Capt Smit Machchhar said he was on the ground and still being attacked when he realised the plane carrying more than 170 passengers was sinking and he had to do something. "I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside," he said in a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. "Others came in and also played a role [in controlling the situation]. I was of course fighting for my own life but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die," he added. Flydubai's flight FZ1073, which was bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai early on Wednesday morning, plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey. It first sent an emergency signal to air traffic controllers before switching to code squawk 7500, which indicates hijacking. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later told the media that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane. After fellow passengers overpowered the attacker, two reserve pilots, who were in the plane as passengers, safely landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia at 06:58 local time. Machchhar, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Netanyahu, was taken to hospital in Tabuk before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition. He told Modi he had been flying planes for 17 years and "can tell what is happening to the plane even with my eyes closed". Indian social media has been awash with praise for him since his identity emerged. Modi told the pilot that "his courage, patience and quick decision-making saved the lives of so many people" and the whole country was proud of him. The Indian embassy in the UAE on Thursday said Machchhar was "in good health and recovering well". Ambassador Deepak Mittal said he was "proud of Capt Smit for his bravery" and "very reassured" to meet him. "I am not looking at this wound like a wound because that would make my recovery even more difficult," Machchhar said. "I am looking at it as a journey which is slowly going on and will take time but I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again." title: Diesel prices in NI at highest level since Iran war began
description: The average price of a litre of diesel hit 193.3p this week, according to NI Consumer Council data.
body: Diesel prices in Northern Ireland are at their highest level since the Iran conflict began, according to Consumer Council data. It shows that over the past week the average price of a litre of diesel was 193.3p. That is below the record average of 197.2p in the summer of 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, however some filling stations have already being charging £2 a litre. Before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, a litre of diesel cost about 132p. Data from the UK's Department for Transport shows that motorists in Northern Ireland are more reliant on diesel than other parts of the UK. The figures suggest that just over half the private cars on Northern Ireland's roads use diesel, compared with a UK average of a third. Sales of new diesel cars in Northern Ireland have fallen sharply in recent years in line with a trend across the UK. The price of diesel hit a record high in the UK this week as a result of the continuing fallout from the Iran war. The conflict in the Middle East has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region - that has caused the price of fuels made from oil to surge. US President Donald Trump has said he may call on European countries to release some of their diesel reserves. He is also considering a ban on US exports of the fuel as American drivers also face higher fuel costs. Such a move could bring prices down significantly in the US. But experts warn that it would put further pressure on diesel prices in other countries, unless they can access further supplies. The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day. Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of the imports coming from the US. title: What does Man City guilty verdict mean for their squad?
description: BBC Sport looks at how Manchester City's guilty verdict will affect their existing players' futures and the club's dealings in the transfer market.
body: Manchester City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons So much has been said about Manchester City since it was revealed they had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 Premier League charges levelled at them. On Tuesday, it was confirmed that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. The club has repeatedly denied guilt. Their potential punishment has been debated, the future of the owners questioned and the feelings of the rest of the league - and wider football world - have been aired. But so far there has been little focus on what it means for one crucial group. Without definitive clarity on what sanctions the Premier League will impose, pending City's inevitable appeal, which must be lodged by Friday, there is uncertainty over their ability to retain players, renew contracts, and make transfers - and whether any of the team have release clauses. Put simply, will players want to join? Will current players want to stay? BBC Sport has spoken to a number of sources in an attempt to understand how the recent judgement will impact City's dealings in the transfer market and how existing players may approach their futures with the prospect of losing Premier League status hanging over the club. Man City verdict has 'implications on game's integrity' - FA Manchester City vs The Premier League Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions The general train of thought is that any drop down the leagues for City will result in a mass exodus. That players will, at the very least, consider their futures at Etihad Stadium in the event of demotion would be understandable. The squad is brimming with international talent, many of whose profiles and personal sponsorship agreements benefit from plying their trade in the Premier League. The reaction from current members of the City squad varies depending on who you speak to. From the conversations BBC Sport have had with sources close to the first team, there is certainly a significant level of concern as to how they will be affected. Given the scathing tone of the Premier League's statement on Tuesday, there is major scepticism from people close to the players that the forthcoming appeals will earn the club any reprieve. But there are others who absolutely believe in City executives Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano's vows to prove the club's innocence. Manchester City chief executive officer Ferran Soriano (left) and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak hold the Champions League trophy in 2023 For those players who decide they don't want to drop down the divisions, should it come to that, the process of leaving is unlikely to be straightforward. Firstly there is the contract and the player registrations. City, regardless of each individual's view on whether they want to depart, have the right to demand transfer fees. Given how much those players are worth in terms of wages and their general value in the market you'd imagine City are unlikely to accept being undercut. That, as BBC Sport understands, the majority of players do not have relegation clauses in their contracts also plays into the club's hands. But it is also understood that as a general rule the players' contracts are fully guaranteed, meaning they would not be required to take percentage pay cuts if they lose their top-flight status. With one of the highest wage bills in the world, maintaining that level of salary expenditure, even for a club as financially capable as City, will become harder without Premier League-level income. Parachute money could ease those concerns, although there are no guarantees that the club would be entitled to those payments if they are demoted. With that in mind, City deciding to keep the squad completely intact should they move down the leagues appears unlikely. Man City Q&A with Kieran Maguire & Dale Johnson How amenable City are to selling players will be dependent on how bullish they are about it all. Are they a distressed seller? Probably not. They still hold strong control of the situation regardless of how their players may feel. It is unlikely the club will just simply roll over and let disillusioned players depart without suitable offers because, ultimately, they can ride the storm financially. Players will have massive decisions to make too, not just in respect of leaving. City are big payers, and other clubs may not be willing to meet similar wage demands. "Some players want medals, all players want money," one agent said to BBC Sport. In terms of potential contract renewals, the current uncertainty over what sanctions will be meted out provides a major element of risk. Amending a contract retrospectively, say for example to include a relegation clause, generally cannot happen. Any deals that include exit strategies for players if the club fall out of the Premier League would have to be negotiated as new contracts. Players will likely want to wait for clarity on the sanctions before entering into contract discussions, adding a layer of difficulty for the club. One way round persuading a player to renew would be to offer a significant financial incentive to re-sign to negate the risk of relegation. But a number of agents who spoke to BBC Sport believe players will be advised to wait for clarity on the punishments before even considering opening talks. Thankfully for City, only Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes, Marcus Bettinelli and Geronimo Rulli have contracts expiring in the next two summers, so that issue isn't as urgent as it could have been. City's potential challenges with player contracts comes with Fifa preparing to introduce new rules that state every deal signed on 1 January, 2027 or after must include a release clause. Guardiola

title: How to move 1,300 plants for Kew's Palm House mega makeover
description: The world-famous Palm House at the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew in London is about to undergo a massive makeover.
body: This video can not be played The world-famous Palm House at the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew in London is about to undergo a massive makeover. The £66m restoration is taking place because the hot and humid conditions inside the Victorian glasshouse have taken their toll on the ironwork and glass. The work will begin in autumn 2027, and the Palm House will be closed for up to four years. But before it can start, the glasshouse has to be completely emptied of the 1,300 tropical plants and trees it has inside. How to move 1,300 plants for Kew's Palm House mega makeover. title: Wade closes in on record as tries dominate Prem
description: Christian Wade sits four away from Chris Ashton's all-time record of 101 as tries dominate Prem Rugby.
body: Christian Wade's 97 Prem tries are split between three clubs The opening week of the new Prem season was all about tries, tries, tries as the league's 10 teams went on all-out attack. No fewer than 52 tries were scored across the five matches, setting a record for the opening round of a season, with an average of more than 10 per game and four players claiming hat-tricks as spectators were royally entertained. Contributing two of those scores was Christian Wade for Newcastle Red Bulls in their 59-26 loss at Northampton Saints, as the veteran winger moves closer to an all-time record. The 35-year-old is now on 97 career tries in the Prem, only four behind Chris Ashton's record mark of 101. If Wade stays fit and the Red Bulls continue to play a game where they want to get the ball wide, it's surely only a matter of time before the record is in his hands. Newcastle Red Bulls v Leicester Tigers Saturday, 3 October 19:45 BST Listen to commentary from BBC Radio Newcastle and BBC Radio Leicester Wade returned to rugby union last December with Newcastle after a short spell in rugby league with Wigan Warriors and he made no secret of his desire to chase down Ashton's tally. He only added two last season as the Red Bulls struggled at the bottom, but his two tries on the opening night away to the champions suggest new-look Newcastle are going to be nothing if not entertaining. It is more than 15 years since Wade scored his first try in Prem Rugby for Wasps but anyone watching his efforts at Franklin's Gardens would not have seen a player of diminishing powers - rather, they would have admired the enduring speed and slipperiness of the Newcastle winger. "Christian bounces across in front of people where they can't lay a finger on him," Red Bulls head coach Dan McFarland told BBC Sport. "He can accelerate through a hole and defenders find it very difficult to cope with that." 101 - Chris Ashton (Northampton, Saracens, Sale, Harlequins, Worcester, Leicester) 97 - Christian Wade (Wasps, Gloucester, Newcastle) 92 - Tom Varndell (Leicester, Wasps, Bristol) 90 - Mark Cueto (Sale) 85 - Danny Care (Leeds, Harlequins) 78 - Jonny May (Gloucester, Leicester) 75 - Steve Hanley (Sale) 72 - Mike Brown (Harlequins, Newcastle, Leicester) 71 - Matt Banahan (Bath, Gloucester) 69 - Paul Sackey (Bedford, London Irish, Wasps, Harlequins) Chris Ashton's swan dive was a regular sight in the English top flight for more than 15 years Wade's Prem tries have come for Wasps, Gloucester and now Newcastle across a globetrotting 15-year career. His sporting journey has also taken in a spell in France with Racing 92 in the Top 14, the 13-man code with Wigan and more than three years in the NFL with the Buffalo Bills, even though he never made it into their main squad. And that period in America has left an indelible mark, according to his new head coach, as to why Wade remains a feared Prem opponent. "Christian Wade is a proper professional," said McFarland. "He spent a few years in the NFL and he's clearly taken a lot from that experience in terms of how to look after himself and how to prepare himself as a rugby player. "He's a really good team man, he's got a lot of time for the young players. He's always calm, a calming and connecting influence. "Christian's in our leadership group because of his capacity to be able to connect with people. He's a really good person." 2025-26: 18 - Tommy Freeman (Northampton), Noah Caluori 2024-25: 13 - Gabriel Ibitoye (Bristol), Ollie Hassell-Collins (Leicester) 2023-24: 14 - Ollie Sleightholme (Northampton) 2022-23: 15 - Cadan Murley (Harlequins) 2021-22: 16 - Max Malins (Saracens) Tommy Freeman has reached double figures for tries in three of the past five Prem seasons for Northampton With Wade four short of equalling Ashton's 101 tally and five tries away from breaking it, the current record holder can feel him coming. The Slough-born winger is the only player in the top 10 still actively playing, but Ashton believes the mark is eventually going to go a long way past 101 with the type of rugby on offer in the modern Prem. Last year's top try scorers, Northampton and England's Tommy Freeman and Saracens' teenage starlet Noah Caluori both touched down 18 times, the highest season-ending figure for five years, while Caluori's tally included him scoring five tries per match on two separate occasions against Sale Sharks. Freeman started this campaign with a hat-trick in the same game as Wade's double and that took his career mark to 58, all at the age of 25. With the England winger having signed a new contract at Saints and their dynamic games delivering tries by the barrel load, could he be the player to eventually take the record? "It's happening [the record being broken], but it's not going to last long, whoever takes it," Ashton told BBC's Rugby Union Weekly podcast. "I think it's going to be absolutely blown to smithereens. "I sat there on Friday and watched Tommy run in another hat-trick and thought he's going to get 20 this year. "Give him another five or six years at this rate that we're going, oh my goodness. He's 25 and he's on 58! By the age of 30, he'll have 100 plus. "Christian Wade is missing more tries per game than he is scoring tries but that probably shows where Newcastle's mindset is." title: Man City verdict has 'implications on game's integrity' - FA
description: The independent commission's verdict against Manchester City has "significant implications for the integrity of the game", according to the Football Association.
body: The independent commission's verdict against Manchester City has "significant implications for the integrity of the game", according to the Football Association. In a statement, English football's governing body added: "We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate." The FA's statement comes after it was confirmed on Tuesday that City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have until Friday to lodge an appeal. "As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage," the FA added. "We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely." Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal. Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m. The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade". This video can not be played How did Man City's 'disguised funding scheme' work? title: Watch: Emotional pilot recounts moment of Flydubai attack
description: He has been hailed a hero for opening the cockpit door, allowing passengers to overpower his co-pilot.
body: This video can not be played An Indian pilot who was attacked by his co-pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai plane has received a call in his hospital bed from India PM Narendra Modi. Visibly emotional, Capt Smit Machchhar said he fought back because he could not allow everyone on the flight to die. He has been hailed a hero for opening the cockpit door, allowing passengers to overpower the attacker. The flight, which had departed from Dubai, landed safely in Saudi Arabia. All on board survived. title: 'Hitchy is always with us' - the keeper who died after one-punch attack
description: The memory of James Hitchcock lives on at non-league Barton Town, almost two years after he died following being punched on a visit to York.
body: James pictured with his baby boy, Freddie, at Barton Town in 2024 "Even now, more than 18 months on, it has still not fully sunk in. I see little Freddie growing up and it hits me so hard." Chris Hitchcock is talking about the loss of his son James, a goalkeeper for non-league Barton Town, who died after a single punch to the head in an unprovoked attack. James, a popular team-mate known as 'Hitchy' to family and friends, was killed in December 2024, just before he was about to spend his first Christmas as a father following the birth of Freddie six months earlier. His death not only devastated his family, it left a tight-knit football club in mourning. "Until you start speaking about it again... it almost doesn't feel real," says Anthony Bowsley, manager of Lincolnshire part-timers Barton. The day before the attack, James had pulled off a fine save in a 1-1 draw with Bottesford Town in the Northern Counties East League Premier Division. "As he was coming off, I said to him 'great save Nigel Martyn' because Hitchy was a Leeds fan and he had a little chuckle to himself," says Bowsley. It would be his last game. The following day, the former Leeds United academy player, 32, was struck from behind at York Railway Station on his way back from a day out with friends. He died in hospital. On Saturday, his widow, April, and son Freddie, now aged two, will be at Barton Town's FA Cup third qualifying round home tie with Chorley - one of the biggest matches in the ninth-tier club's history. April, who married James in July 2022, says being around the football club where he used to play brings comfort after the unimaginable loss of her husband. The pain, however, runs deep. "It's really sad looking at where James used to stand in goal and saying 'where is he?'" April, 32, tells BBC Sport. "He should be stood there." James on his wedding day with April in July 2022 "It was a numb feeling. You don't believe something like that could happen to one of your mates," Barton Town defender Jack Bulless says. Bulless, who also played with James at Bridlington Town, should have been part of the group on the day trip to York but pulled out due to illness. Andy Norfolk, a long-time friend and team-mate, did join James and their friends. "I remember the Manchester derby being on television in the bars we visited," says Norfolk. "It was an annual Christmas get-together, a day trip, nothing too heavy. We arrived back at the station to go home early. "I ended up getting a taxi back to Hull as the train was not for another hour. I remember Hitchy saying he was going to get some food." It was the last time Norfolk saw his friend. Leeds Crown Court heard James suffered a fracture to his skull and brain damage when he fell to the floor after being punched on the right side of the back of his head. Recalling that day, April says: "I'd just put Freddie to bed when I got a call to say James had been hit, that he was unconscious, and was on his way to hospital. "At that point I thought he had concussion and I needed to pack a bag because he was only going to be in for a day or two. "When I got to the hospital they explained that he needed to be transferred to the intensive care unit at Hull Royal Infirmary. He was on a life support machine until he lost the battle." Mckenzie Dicicco, who was then 22, was jailed for six years and eight months in July 2025 after pleading guilty to manslaughter for what judge Guy Kearl said was a "cowardly, deliberate and vicious attack on a man who had no chance to defend or brace himself". Speaking after the verdict, April described being "lost and alone as the love of my life was so selfishly taken from me". James' father, Chris, who used to take his son to Elland Road to watch David O'Leary's Leeds team in the late 90s, says his life has changed forever because of "one senseless act". "I don't live any more - I exist," he says. "I try and be happy, I try and do things and I put a brave face on. But it'll never be the same again for me." James grew up supporting Leeds United and later played for their academy One of James' heroes growing up was former Leeds United goalkeeper Nigel Martyn Pictured with his wife, April, on a night out With his dad, Chris, on a day out watching cricket In action for Barton Town, who he joined in the summer of 2024 after leaving Bridlington Town James' memory lives on at Barton Town, whose 3,000-capacity ground is within eyeshot of the Humber Bridge. "He is always with us," says Bowsley, referring to 'Hitchy #1' which has been sewn on to the back of the club's shirts. "It's a beautiful thing to have on the shirt," adds Norfolk, who attended his friend's stag do in Benidorm, wedding near York and then his funeral - all in the space of two and a half years. "Before each game I look at the back of the shirt and have my 10 seconds with Hitchy before I put it on." There is also a plaque at the entrance to the players' tunnel in memory of James. In addition, his two former clubs - Bridlington Town and Barton Town - meet annually for the James Hitchcock Memorial Trophy to raise funds for the Victim Support National Homicide Service. Stories about James are frequently told in the club house. "You could hear him before you saw him because of his distinctive laugh," adds Bulless. Norfolk agrees. "His laugh was outrageously infectious. We all used to call it a cackle." Meanwhile, Bowsley says James "always had a smile on his face" and was "a bit of a practical joker." Talking about his ability as a goalkeeper, Bowsley adds: "He was a really good shot stopper and really good with his feet. He was at Leeds academy and then played the local leagues in Hull before going to Bridlington and then Barton." Bulless adds: "He always had a way at making you laugh. title: The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up
description: German football is grappling with a sum that doesn't add up - four promotion spots for five league champions.
body: The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion – but he does not always feel like it. This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football. But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion. While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate. "Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters – "your system is sick". "It's the worst thing – injury aside – that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport. "Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow." But it's not that simple. A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck. Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion. So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up. An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues. One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR). In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock. The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections. Even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west. The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there. It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing. "In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says. Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig. "Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west. "The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football." It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" – champions must go up! Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies. They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany. "I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR." Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent. "It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport. "The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act." The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid. title: Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave lands on TIME100 Next list
description: Shoko Kawata's maternity leave drew mixed reactions in Japan, a country struggling to lift birth rates.
body: This video can not be played Watch: First mayor to take maternity leave causes backlash in Japan Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named one of the 100 most influential rising stars by TIME Magazine. The recognition comes weeks after the 36-year-old gave birth to her first child on 15 September. Earlier this year, Kawata, who is mayor of Yawata City in Kyoto prefecture, was plunged into a national debate about whether elected officials should take time off for childbirth. Her decision to take maternity leave drew a mix of support and backlash across Japan, a country that is struggling to lift birth rates. Some on social media said having a baby is tough and Kawata is doing her best. Japanese society has failed to design systems with pregnancy in mind, one claimed. Another said Kawata is setting a wonderful example by putting her family first and making it easier for other women to enter politics. But critics argued that stepping away from public duties is "irresponsible", and that if Kawata wanted to get pregnant "she should have done so before taking office". One said top officials wanting to take extended leave "should resign". Others insisted salaries should be cut during maternity leave. In a sit-down interview with the BBC before giving birth, Kawata brushed off the criticisms, proudly declaring she enjoys her job and believes now is the time for her to have a child and start a family. "If we were to criticise politicians taking maternity leave, it means we are effectively excluding all women in their 20s through 40s - women who are capable of becoming pregnant - from public office," she said. While Japan provides maternity leave for city workers, there is currently no legal framework for local elected officials. So Kawata worked with her office to create a plan. She transferred her authority to her deputy mayor Shigeto Nose for 16 weeks, while working remotely when she could. On 15 September, Mayor Kawata announced she gave birth to a baby girl. She posted a photo on X, external, thanking those who had supported her, and doubled down on her goal to advocate for social issues nationwide. "As I face the countless challenges that lie ahead and learn what it truly means to be a parent, I want to reflect those experiences in real time into the policies I pursue," she wrote. "I want to confront the many challenges facing parents and children today from that same perspective, as someone living through them myself, and think about how we can find a way forward together." title: From Aberdeen to Argentina: How my stolen Ian Wright football top went round the world
description: Kevin Hill's much-loved Celtic top was lost years ago but that was just the start of an international mystery.
body: This video can not be played Two friends, a missing football strip and the ultimate 25-year prank It was a prank that lasted for a quarter of a century. Simple yet bewildering for its unsuspecting victim. It began in 2001 when Kevin Hill went searching for his favourite football top. As a kid in Aberdeen, he'd grown up as a Celtic fan - something he says that required a thick skin. His father took him to games in Glasgow and every season, from age five, his parents bought him the latest strip. Ian Wright scored 128 goals for Arsenal before his stint at Celtic Now 47 and living in Dunfermline, Fife, Kevin says his prized possession was one that brought together his two sporting loves. "As much as I'm a Celtic fan my first footballing hero was Ian Wright," he says. "I remember him playing for Arsenal and had posters of him all over my wall. "When I started hearing the rumour that he might be coming to Celtic, it was like my dreams were coming true." The Arsenal legend was in the sunset of his career when he signed for Celtic in 1999. It was a fleeting spell at Parkhead that yielded three goals for the former England striker in just eight appearances. Kevin, left, and his childhood best friend Kris played pranks on each other But such was Kevin's affection that long after it was over, the green-and-white hooped jersey remained his go-to match day uniform. It was particularly distinctive as it featured his hero's name, but not the number 17. Kevin explained: "The reason it doesn't have a number on the back was because he hadn't actually signed yet and so we didn't know his number when I got it." So when the strip went missing he was gutted. Having recently moved to Edinburgh, he assumed that someone had helped themselves during a fairly raucous flat-warming party. While he had suspicions, he could never identify the culprit. Over time, however, his anger faded and he'd largely forgotten about it when, years later, an email arrived in his inbox from an account he didn't recognise. It began: "Hi Kevin, remember me? Yes that's right, it's your Ian Wright Celtic strip." The message continued: "I hope you aren't mad with me but I decided to embark on a journey of discovery." The jersey appeared in Venice Easter Island was one of the best destinations the top travelled to "Wrighty" made it to Niagara Falls Kris took the strip to Machu Picchu himself, getting someone to wear it for the photo The top enjoyed a fun trip to Las Vegas Turkey was another destination on the football jersey's travels Christ The Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil was Kevin's favourite location A more laid-back trip was in store for the top at Lake Michigan in the US A mystery blonde woman sports Kevin's shirt outside the Vibe Bar in Barcelona When Kevin opened the attached photograph it featured a woman he didn't know on the London Eye holding up what appeared to be his Celtic top to the camera. "I was just mega confused," he says. "Running through my mind was, who has done this? "I mean bravo, it's a really good prank. "But little did I know there were a lot more emails to follow." A few weeks later another message arrived. Once again it contained a photo of a complete stranger wearing Kev's prized possession – this time in Barcelona. After that the emails kept on coming. "The next one was Turkey, then Italy and then it went all the way to South America," Kevin recalls. "Christ the Redeemer was one of my favourite ones. "It made it all the way [to Brazil] and then down to Venezuela and Puerto Rico and then back up to the USA." The first photo featured an unknown woman with the Wright strip on the London Eye As 2008 gave way to 2009 the messages kept arriving until eventually the email trail went cold. It left Kevin poring over clues for who might be responsible. "What confused me was how did they keep this going?" "It wasn't one of my friends globetrotting, from what I could deduce they were handing [the strip] on to someone else and giving them the email address because it was always a different person in the picture. For another decade the mystery occupied a corner of Kevin's mind. When he met someone new he'd tell them about the adventures of "Wrighty'". That included his fiancé Cheryl. What Kevin didn't know that their marriage would become the key to unlocking the secret. The story behind the prank was revealed at Kevin's wedding to Cheryl, 25 years later At the wedding reception in late August, Kevin was sitting at a table with his childhood friends from Aberdeen who all started laughing as one of them handed him a parcel. "When I opened it, I could see it was a Celtic top but then very quickly I saw the white letters of Wright. "I knew immediately and I just couldn't believe it." Alongside the strip was a photobook entitled "Wrighty on Tour: 25 years of adventures around the globe" "It was the best present I could have ever been given." "And the fact that they kept it going that long just shows how good a friendship group I've got." It was Kevin's friend Kris Robertson who came clean after a quarter of a century of intrigue over the missing jersey What would Ian Wright make of the prank that bore his name? Friends since their schooldays, Kris Robertson vividly remembers Kevin's fondness for his Ian Wright Celtic strip. "He used to wear it all the time. I just remember he was very proud of it. It was his prize possession." That affection made it the ideal source of payback after Kevin hijacked Kris's emails with the aim of embarrassing him at work. "It was revenge," says the 48-year-old, smiling. Revenge that took unlikely inspiration from French cinema. Part of the plot in the 2001 movie Amelie involves the main character stealing her dad's garden gnome and sending it around the world. title: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
description: The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian forces battle rebel fighters across northern region.
body: More than 50 people have been killed since heavy fighting resumed in northern Ethiopia last week Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict. On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security. Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action. The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters. It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Addis Ababa accusing Eritrea of supporting an alliance of armed groups fighting the Ethiopian government – an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied. Ethiopia said it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats who "pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security" and would shut its embassy in Asmara. In response, Eritrea announced late on Thursday that it was severing diplomatic ties with Ethiopia, describing Addis Ababa's decision as "astounding". "Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision. The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people had died during that two-year conflict. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of helping the alliance. A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray also told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines. The BBC has not independently verified the allegation. But in a rare interview with the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected the accusations. He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia. The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea. Asmara accuses Ethiopia of pursuing what it describes as an increasingly hostile policy over the Red Sea. Landlocked Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports. The latest diplomatic confrontation came hours after loud explosions were heard on Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, close to the headquarters of the intelligence service. A source linked to the opposition alliance told Reuters news agency that its forces had carried out drone attacks in the capital. Ethiopian authorities have not confirmed what caused the explosions, and there have been no official reports of casualties or significant damage. Residents in two areas of Addis Ababa separately told the BBC that they heard powerful explosions during the night. One resident near the intelligence headquarters said the blast was loud enough to trigger car alarms. The explosions came hours after Ethiopia's National Intelligence and Security Service imposed an indefinite ban on drone flights over Addis Ababa and surrounding areas, citing the need to protect senior officials, important infrastructure and public events. Meanwhile, fighting continues across northern Ethiopia. Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting. The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there. Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray. Independent verification remains difficult because journalists have limited access to the conflict areas and communications across much of Tigray have been disrupted. The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region. The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements. title: Verstappen tops Bahrain GP in Malaysia first practice
description: Red Bull's Max Verstappen tops the timesheets as Formula 1 returned to the Sepang track for the first time in nine years for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
body: Verstappen is a four-time F1 World Champion Red Bull's Max Verstappen topped the timesheets as Formula 1 returned to the Sepang track for the first time in nine years for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Verstappen was 0.383 seconds quicker than George Russell, winner last week in Azerbaijan, in an upgraded Mercedes. The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was third fastest, 0.783secs off the pace, ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, split from his team-mate Lewis Hamilton by championship leader Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes. Alpine's Pierre Gasly was seventh fastest, ahead of the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad, who will start from the back of the grid as a result of a grid penalty for using too many engine parts. Hadjar also has a grid penalty - expected to be five places - for the same reason. F1 has returned to this track, regarded as one of the best layouts among the new generation of circuits that came on stream at the end of the last century and into this one, because of the circumstances around this year's calendar. The Bahrain and Saudi Arabia races were cancelled at the beginning of the year as a result of the war in the Middle East. But Bahrain were keen to hold their race and Crown Prince Salman bin Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa negotiated to hold the race in Malaysia. A bunch of Bahraini-related activities are being held at the track, while the trophy presented will be the Bahrain Grand Prix trophy and rosewater rather than champagne will be sprayed on the podium. The first session was marked by drivers commenting on the high level of tyre degradation caused by the abrasive surface, and Russell in particular noticed this was high on the Mercedes. Questioning it on his race-simulation run late in the session, he was told his tyre wear did appear to be "an outlier" compared to that of Verstappen. Mercedes have introduced their first major upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix, with a new floor and rear bodywork. They expected McLaren to be the team to beat at this track, but the world champions had a low-key first session, with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris down in 11th and 12th places. title: Funding frenzy adds to pressure on worried farmers
description: A six-hour window to apply for funding is compared to the scramble for Oasis tickets.
body: Lex Brun said he was "very, very nervous" about the future of his business A farmer said it was "very, very worrying" to miss out on funding from a new government scheme to support green projects. Lex Brun from Great Massingham in Norfolk said he hoped to get £100,000 from the Sustainable Farming Initiative (SFI), but applications closed down in less than six hours. The Country Land and Business Association (CLA) said Brun was one of many unsuccessful farmers and may now have to cut back on environmental schemes. While the government said there would be more funding next year, farming minister Stephen Morgan said he had "heard" concerns and that lessons would be learned. The SFI is a post-Brexit scheme that replaced EU subsidies with payments to landowners for environmentally-friendly land management. It gives money to farmers who have turned parts of their land over to schemes such as planting hedges, creating wildflower margins and protecting the soil. This year's fund offered £253m in total, with applications opening at 10:00 BST on Tuesday 22 September, but the money ran out by 15:48 the same day. Brun said damage caused by beetles on his oilseed rape crop had been a setback this year "It was unprecedented for it to be such a scramble, it's been likened to getting tickets for an Oasis concert," said Brun, whose crops include wheat, barley and oilseed rape. His environmental projects include turning over some land to wildflowers to support nature, including birds and insects. Brun had hoped to receive up to £100,000 in payments, but when he completed the online application at 16:00, the window had closed. Facing pressures from "massive increases" in costs for fuel and fertiliser and "very mediocre returns" on his harvests, he is now considering using more of his land for commercial crops. "It's a very, very worrying position," he explained. "It destroyed confidence in the government and what they said they were trying to achieve." The CLA's Cath Crowther warned many farmers were considering cutting back on environmental projects Cath Crowther, the regional director for the CLA, said many other farmers found themselves in a similar position and called for more government funding to be announced in October's budget. "We know that there's not much money out there, that health, defence, etc are all so important, but [so is] food production." Adrian Ramsay, the Green MP for Waveney Valley, said "a lot of farmers" had been frustrated by the SFI application process. "There just isn't the confidence the funding is going to be there in the years to come," he added. Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said he had "heard the concerns" of farmers who are "deeply disappointed." He said he was "determined to work closely with farmers as we learn lessons from this year" including "exploring alternatives to a first-come, first-served application process." The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said it would provide further information about funding applications in 2027 "soon". Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? title: Lorry training firm 'riding out' record diesel price
description: Fuel prices have been steadily rising since the US-Iran war began in February.
body: Steve Dulson, who founded Dulson Training in Shropshire in 2013, said it was costing hundreds of pounds more to fill lorries compared with 2025 prices Record-breaking fuel prices have left a firm teaching people to drive lorries and buses having to "ride out" the rising cost of filling up its vehicles. The average price of diesel in the UK hit an all-time high this week at 199.33p a litre, according to the RAC motoring organisation. Prices have been steadily rising since the US-Iran war began in February. Petrol has also risen to 174.23p a litre. Steve Dulson, managing director of Shropshire-based Dulson Training, said it was costing hundreds of pounds more to fill up each lorry compared with 2025 prices. "Over the last 12 months we've seen a rise of up to 50p a litre, excluding VAT, and it's hard to react to that, because of how we deal with our customers," he said. "Our customers have usually been in our pipeline for some time, taking medicals, applying for provisional [licences] or taking theory tests, so by the time they've got to their practical training, and the fuel prices have increase, they've already been quoted. "That makes it difficult for us to put prices up." Dulson Training has six training centres in Shrewsbury, Telford, Ludlow, Wrexham, Wolverhampton and Nantwich The price of petrol and diesel had been largely falling since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. But the war in the Middle East, which started on 28 February, has added 59p to the average cost of a litre of diesel, or just under 40%, and 41p to the price of petrol. Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict. Dulson said his family-run business could find limited fuel savings by "extending breaks" during training sessions or "take routes that don't use as much fuel". "The customer has paid us to do a job and we're going to do that to the best of our ability," he said. "As next year comes round, we might have to increase prices to reflect what we're going through, unless there's a downturn." title: Zack Polanski to call for three-year cap on private rent rises
description: In his speech to his party's conference, the Green leader will frame housing as a key issue of generational fairness.
body: Zack Polanski will address the Green Party's conference in Brighton on Friday Zack Polanski is set to call for a three-year "emergency brake" on private rent increases when he opens the Green Party's conference later. In his speech to party activists on Friday afternoon, the Green leader will seek to frame housing as a key issue of generational fairness. He will urge the government to prevent private rents rising above whichever is lowest out of the consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years. According to the party, he will also argue pressure from the Greens has forced Labour into a change of political direction on some issues. The Green Party of England and Wales is billing the gathering in Brighton as its biggest ever, after announcing earlier this year that its membership had tripled since Polanski's election as leader just over a year ago. In his speech, Polanski is expected to say generations are having to live with their parents because of rent prices, from 19-year-olds commuting to university, 25-year-olds unable to find a job, to 35-year-olds moving back home with their partners. "For too long, landlords have been able to hike prices way beyond wages, leaving renters forced to meet the cost to keep a roof over their heads, cutting back and back and back on everything else," he is expected to say. A slowdown on private rent increases "would give renters vital breathing space" and give time for ministers to create a national Fair Rents Guarantee that keeps rents affordable for the future, he is expected to say. Earlier this year, the government brought in the Renters' Rights Act under which landlords can only increase rent once a year to the property's open market rate. Average UK monthly private rents increased by 3.5%, to £1,377, in the 12 months to January 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics. The Act also means tenancies are rolling rather than fixed term, and makes it harder for landlords to evict tenants. But Polanski is expected to argue it does not go far enough in ending "fear and uncertainty" for the millions of private renters in the UK. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has previously warned, external that rent controls - an issue the Greens have long campaigned for - would result in "unintended consequences" including demand exceeding supply in the rental market. The Green conference follows the party gaining hundreds of councillors earlier this year at England's local elections and its fifth MP, Hannah Spencer, in the Makerfield by-election. But there are signs its rise in national polls may have stalled in recent months, while the party also faces questions over how to react to Labour's change of leadership under Andy Burnham. Since Burnham became prime minister, Labour has shifted its stance in a number of areas where it had been in danger of being outflanked politically by the Greens. In an interview ahead of the conference, the party's co-deputy leader Rachel Millward said Labour was now "rhetorically, on a much more similar ground" to her party. This includes Burnham's move towards electoral reform, where the Greens have long demanded a shake-up of the Westminster voting system, and opening the door to a much closer future relationship with the European Union. Labour has also announced sanctions on Israeli West Bank settlements deemed illegal under international law, and the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees. Speaking ahead of the conference, Polanski claimed those two policies were a result of the electoral pressure his party has applied to Labour. The timing of the conference could, however, prove awkward for Polanski, who is standing for the Greens in next week's Holborn and St Pancras by-election triggered by Sir Keir Starmer's decision to leave Parliament. Polanski said last week he was intending to come "straight back" to the central London seat after his leader's speech. He has even urged the party's activists to leave the conference over the weekend to help him campaign. Victory in the contest would give the Greens their first seat in the capital, but would require them to overturn a huge Labour majority from the last election in 2024. A full list of candidates can be found here.
