title: What are the new rules in Scotland's supermarkets?
description: Restrictions are being put on products with high sugar, fat and salt content, but the meal deal lives on.
body: Sugary soft drinks, biscuits and some breakfast cereals have disappeared from prominent positions in Scotland's supermarkets. The Scottish government has introduced rules meaning some products that are high in fat, sugar and salt can no longer be put in prime end-of-aisle slots, or feature as part of multi-buy offers in store or online. The regulations will apply to the usual suspects - chocolate, crisps, biscuits and ice cream. But it could also include kombucha, seaweed snacks, muesli and chewing gum, depending on their sugar content. The Scottish government regulations, external apply to businesses with more than 50 employees. This could include supermarkets, high street shops, restaurants, pharmacies, petrol stations and garden centres. They are are no longer allowed to display pre-packaged foods including sugary soft drinks, confectionery, biscuits and breakfast cereals in prominent locations such as entrances, checkouts, aisle ends and designated queueing areas. Price promotions on those items - such as "three for the price of two", "three for £10" or "buy five and save 20%" - are no longer allowed. Multi-buy offers, including extra loyalty points, are also banned. Another type of deal that falls foul of the rules is those offering a free high-sugar, fat or salt product alongside another purchase - for example, a free chocolate bar with a newspaper. There are no restrictions on discounts such as half-price or "save £1". Online retailers also face restrictions - including a ban on advertising some foods on their homepage. Similar restrictions are already in place in England and Wales. The short answer is: a lot, if there’s enough sugar, salt or fat packed into it. The restrictions could apply to: Drinks with added sugar - such as lemonade, soda, squash, chocolate milk, almond milk, ready-made coffee, kombucha, energy drinks, and hot chocolate Savoury snacks such as crisps and tortilla chips, and even lentil-based crisps and seaweed snacks, depending on their content Breakfast cereals, granola, muesli and oat-based cereals Pre-made pizzas, roast potatoes, chips, fish fingers and chicken nuggets Ready meals, as well as pasta, rice or noodles with added ingredients or fillings, such as ravioli and tortellini Confectionary, such as popcorn, chocolate, chewing gum and sweets Ice cream, sorbets, ice lollies, sponge cakes, custard, jelly, crumbles Cereal bars, biscuits, scones, flapjacks, doughnuts and Danish pastries Sweetened Greek-style, probiotic, kids' and drinking yoghurts Meal deals are exempt from the regulations, as are "dine for two" offers. However, any foods identified in the rules, whether part of a meal deal or not, cannot be placed in the restricted locations, such as supermarket entrances. The Scottish government regulations are being introduced to encourage healthier eating choices. Public Health Minister Maree Todd noted that two out of three Scottish adults are overweight or obese, with those living in the poorest areas worst affected. She said: "We know that promotions and prominent product placement can encourage over-consumption and impulse buying of foods with high levels of calories, fat, sugar and salt. "By restricting the promotion of less healthy food and drink we can make it easier for people to make healthier choices, improving health and wellbeing, and create a Scotland where everyone eats well and has a healthy weight." title: Six years, hundreds of plants and one tree casualty - Edinburgh's Palm House returns
description: The Palm House at Edinburgh's Botanic Garden is finally restored and ready for the public.
body: David Knott, director of horticulture, said Edinburgh's Palm Houses are iconic After six years and an unprecedented botanical operation, Edinburgh's famous Palm Houses are back. The historic glasshouses at the Royal Botanic Garden have been closed to the public for vital restoration work. Hundreds of plants had to be temporarily moved while repairs were done on the 19th century buildings - the vast majority of them surviving the experience. But members of the public are once again able to enjoy the redesigned space. Sadie Barber is delighted the palm houses are now being used in the way they were intended The shutdown had to happen because the buildings had become leaky and rusty and needed a complete overhaul. Glass house curator Sadie Barber is delighted that, after years of disruption, the palm houses are once again being used for their intended purpose - to protect rare and and endangered plants, and to allow people to enjoy the space. The plants were decanted to temporary homes, and then carefully moved back into the renovated space. Sadie says this has been a great achievement that wasn't without risk. "I think whenever you move a plant and you take it out of the ground and then you stick it in a pot, it's going to suffer or it's going to get under stress. "So there was a bit of trepidation when we picked up the biggest plants, moved them to another place, and left them there for a number of years. "We've done really well. It feels like a huge achievement getting all these plants back in here and having them actually so well placed. "The glasshouse team have done an enormous job, a really exceptional job of getting the plants looking like they belong. "So it's great to see them actually thriving already." Thousands of panes of glass have been replaced during the restoration The buildings have undergone a huge amount of work. More than five thousand panes of glass have been replaced, and the once corroding ironwork has been repaired and repainted. Stone work has been renovated and a partition wall between the two houses has been knocked down to create a light and airy space which shows off the historic architecture and living plants. Prof Julia Knights is the Regius Keeper of the Botanic Garden. She says they have a wide range of plants and species, many of which are endangered. "We've got palms, conifers, ferns, begonias, all of those families, plants are hugely important in our living collection and many of them are extinct in the wild," she said. "So what the palm houses are doing is helping to protect so many of these species, and many of them of course have medicinal properties for human health. "So if we don't save these we are also potentially not helping to save humanity, so it's super important." Prof Julia Knights says the glass houses have a wide range of plants, including rare species Whilst most of the plants were saved in the process of moving, there was one major casualty - the Sabal palm tree which was over 200 years old. It had grown too tall for the glass house and had to be cut down and couldn't be stored. But some seedlings were kept, and so its legacy has not been forgotten. One of the Sabal palm's descendants is growing in its place. David Knott, the director of horticulture at the Botanic Garden, said: "Hopefully, because we've planted it in this glass house which is a bit taller than where it was previously, hopefully it will last a bit longer than the previous one did." He is happy to see the new one growing in place of the old giant tree. "There was no way that we were actually going to ever be able to transplant the Sabal palm. And that was probably one of the hardest, most poignant parts of the whole process." The Sabal palm tree is thriving under the same roof as its parent, although it is significantly smaller David Knott hopes the people of Scotland will welcome the return of the glass houses. "For many people in Edinburgh and throughout Scotland and throughout the world, the palm houses in Edinburgh really are one of the most iconic features of the Botanic Garden here. And we hope when we reopen, we will be able to welcome people and they'll be able to enjoy the space as it was always intended to be." Sadie Barber says there are signs that the plants are enjoying their new home. "You can see new growth coming out of some of those plants that are now in the ground. One thing people will notice is little new croziers coming in, coming up from the fern crowns. "When you see that unfurling you know a plant is happy. And if you look around there's just so much life. It's been an enormous job, but a really well done job. So we are overjoyed" The restoration keeps the palm houses looking much as they were intended, but using modern techniques and materials which should guarantee the future of these much-loved buildings. title: First minister demands 'new deal' for Wales before Plaid Cymru conference
description: Rhun ap Iorwerth will address members at Plaid's first conference since winning the Senedd election.
body: Rhun ap Iorwerth became first minister after Plaid Cymru won the Senedd election The first minister and leader of Plaid Cymru has written to the prime minister requesting "a new deal for Wales" ahead of his first party conference speech since taking office. In his letter to Andy Burnham, sent on Thursday and seen by BBC Wales, Rhun ap Iorwerth calls for more powers to be transferred to Cardiff. Burnham previously said he would "give a fair hearing" to anything put to him by the Welsh first minister. Ap Iorwerth will address party members in Llandudno on Friday, five months on from Plaid's historic success at May's Senedd election. The result saw the party win power for the first time, ending Labour's 27 years in government since devolution began in 1999. 'Too early' to know if Burnham will back more Welsh powers, says first minister PM rules out giving Wales independence referendum powers However, without a majority of the seats in Cardiff Bay, ap Iorwerth leads a minority administration which has to work with opposition Members of the Senedd to pass new laws and budgets. The government lost a key vote on its spending plans in July. In his speech, ap Iorwerth will say the election "delivered a clear mandate from the people of Wales for positive change that makes a tangible difference to their lives". "This mandate includes extending devolution to enable the Senedd and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools - powers, funding and financial flexibilities - to drive the maximum improvement in outcomes for the people of Wales by integrating and improving public services and growing the economy. "As an underpinning principle to support these reforms, Wales should be able to benefit from the same constitutional and fiscal tools already available in Scotland." The leaders of the SNP, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Fein met in Cardiff last month Ap Iorwerth's comments come after he hosted the nationalist first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland in Cardiff last month and jointly declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end". In his 2,000-word letter to Burnham, ap Iorwerth makes a detailed case for the transfer of powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure, and the Crown Estate, external to Wales. He also calls for "funding arrangements that are fair, needs-based and reflect Wales' demographic and economic realities". He adds that "Wales' constitutional settlement should continue to evolve to improve democratic accountability, boost growth, strengthen public services and deliver better outcomes for our communities". Ap Iorwerth is expected to meet the prime minister, along with the first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland, at the end of the month. Andy Burnham has previously said he is "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing. He has also said: "I have to respect the governments in the nations of the UK, and I will, and give a fair hearing to anything that is put to me." title: 'Potential crime' probe into death of Scots wingsuit flyer dropped
description: British champion Liam Byrne, 24, was fatally injured on the Gitschen mountain in June last year.
body: Liam Byrne featured in the documentary The Boy Who Can Fly An investigation into any potential crime after the death of a Scottish wingsuit flyer during a jump in the Swiss Alps has been dropped. British champion Liam Byrne, 24, was fatally injured on the Gitschen mountain after taking off from 7,874ft (2,400m) in June last year. An investigation was launched, but documents from the Swiss Federal Prosecutor's Office seen by BBC Scotland News show it was decided to discontinue proceedings. Byrne, from Stonehaven, Aberdeenshire, had featured in a 2024 BBC documentary called The Boy Who Can Fly. He was described as a very experienced wingsuit flyer - which is a type of skydiving. It involves wearing a special suit with webbing to allow mid-air lift. Byrne had completed thousands of jumps during his flying career. Scottish wingsuit flyer Liam Byrne dies during Swiss Alps jump He had told the BBC documentary: "I think I was about 13 when I said to my dad that I wanted to learn to fly like a bird." He took to extreme sports from a young age. At 12 he climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak standing at 19,341ft (5,895 metres) high. Liam Byrne completed thousands of jumps during his career That adventure led to dog-sledging through the Arctic, scuba diving, and multiple high summit climbs. By the age of 14 he was a licensed paraglider. He did his first skydive aged 16, and by 18 was pulling on a wingsuit, which he described as a "second skin, letting me move through the air in a controlled way". Liam Byrne's family previously paid tribute to his life The Swiss Federal Prosecutor's Office report on the decision to discontinue the investigation said the first two wingsuit jumpers in the party landed without incident. However, it said Byrne collided with the mountainside and suffered fatal injuries. The report said proceedings would be discontinued if there was insufficient evidence of any criminal suspicion, such as knowingly placing life in danger. "The fatal crash was, with a high degree of probability, attributable to a situation from which there was no escape, resulting from insufficient lift and the low altitude above the ground," it said. "There are no indications in the present case of any criminal acts by third parties that contributed to the crash, or of a pre-existing technical defect in the equipment used that contributed to the crash. "The proceedings are therefore discontinued." A family statement at the time of his death said: "We would like to remember Liam not just for the way he left this world, but for how he lived in it. "Liam was fearless, not necessarily because he wasn't afraid but because he refused to let fear hold him back. "He chased life in a way that most of us only dream of and he soared. "Skydiving and base jumping was more than just a thrill for Liam - it was freedom. "It was where he felt most alive." title: Bill Nighy wins best host at British Podcast Awards
description: The actor has become an agony uncle in what award organisers called an "irresistibly endearing series".
body: Bill Nighy also won podcast of the year at the Broadcasting Press Guild Awards in March Actor Bill Nighy's reinvention as an agony uncle has earned him the award for best host at the British Podcast Awards, beating names such as Louis Theroux, Katherine Ryan and Lily Allen. Nighy, 76, known for films including Love Actually, Living and the Underworld franchise, has now found success with what award organisers called his "irresistibly endearing series" Ill-Advised. Billed as "a podcast for people who don't get out much and can't handle it when they do", the show sees Nighy dole out wry advice to listeners, and muse about life, music and books. Other winners at the 10th annual British Podcast Awards on Thursday included Pete Wicks, Sophie and Jamie Laing, Peter Crouch and Alan Carr. Pete Wicks won two awards for Man Made, in which he tries to "unpack modern masculinity" Pete Wicks' Man Made picked up two awards - best interview podcast and best health & wellbeing podcast. Actor Sean Bean's birdwatching series Get Birding also won two prizes - best lifestyle podcast and best video innovation. The Prison Radio Association's series about problem gambling, Hold or Fold, won the overall top prize for best podcast, and the award for best factual podcast. Fans voted Hard Launch with Dan & Phil, hosted by the YouTube veterans, as the winner of the Listeners' Choice award. Alan Carr and Lee Peart won best food & drink podcast for their comedy and wine series Bottoms Up! title: Man arrested after boy, 6, dies in crash
description: An investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident in Llanfairfechan, Conwy, is ongoing.
body: Police were called to Llanfairfechan shortly after 17:00 BST on Thursday A six-year-old boy has died following a crash, police have said. North Wales Police said officers were called to reports of a collision involving a vehicle and a child in Llanfairfechan, Conwy county, at just after 17:00 BST on Thursday evening. The child was pronounced dead at the scene. A 39-year-old man has been arrested, the force added, while the boy's family is being supported by specially trained family liaison officers. Multiple roads in the area of Pen-Y-Bryn Road and Bryn Road were closed and people were asked to avoid the area. Det Insp Tim Evans said: "Our thoughts are with the young boy's family and friends at this extremely difficult time." An investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash is ongoing and police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident to get in touch. title: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
description: Several self-inflicted mistakes have cost the biggest sportswear brand on the planet in recent years.
body: It's been a difficult few years for Nike. The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing of late. Losing sales, losing customers and losing ground to its rivals. The one-time industry disruptor is now the establishment and in the middle of a tricky turnaround plan aimed at clinging on to market dominance. Nike's latest financial results show signs a turnaround strategy put in place by company veteran Elliott Hill, who was coaxed out of retirement two years ago to lead the firm, is working - but the pace of change is more marathon than sprint. However, its recovery has been dented by the loss of football star Kylian Mbappé, who ended his 20-year association with the brand last week to join fast-growing Swiss rival, On. The Real Madrid striker's departure raises the question of whether Nike can remain the top logo for not just elite athletes, but also the fans that idolise them. To be clear, Nike is still a mega brand and popular the world over. But missteps have seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value as its share price tumbled by 75% over five years. Last month, Nike was ejected from the S&P 100 stock market index of the biggest blue-chip firms in the US. So what's gone wrong? And can Hill turn things around? Matt Powell, a veteran analyst and adviser in the sports retail industry, reckons Nike has made "several strategic errors" which have been difficult to reverse, including cutting ties with retailers to sell only direct to customers online and making limited editions items more available. "The more broadly available those shoes became, the fewer people were interested," Powell says. Other self-inflicted wounds he suggests include spending research and development cash on digital operations rather than new products. "They really shut down their innovation on product. Someone jokingly said they were trying to turn Nike into eBay." That jibe was aimed at John Donahoe, the former eBay boss behind Nike's online direct-to-consumer sales pivot, before he made way for Hill. Donahoe's four years at Nike coincided with the company's share price plunge. His tenure saw sales initially soar, driven by pandemic restrictions that boosted online shopping, but subsequent cost-of-living pressures curbed customer spending. As demand weakened overseas in key markets like China, Nike announced cost cuts and redundancies. Its digital distraction allowed newer footwear firms on top of the trends to snap at its heels. Shop shelf space previously occupied by Nike was replaced by brands such as On and Hoka. This was a stark warning to a company that prided and built itself on innovation. Nike was the firm that signed a deal with a rookie called Michael Jordan in the mid-1980s at a time when the company wasn't a major player in basketball and still mostly known for its running trainers. The gamble - spending its entire basketball budget on Jordan before he had even competed in the NBA - made Nike what it is today. The company built a shoe brand around him - Air Jordan. The red and black colours broke NBA rules, but Nike used it as a marketing stunt and paid the fines. In years that followed Nike partnered with generational talents Tiger Woods, Serena Williams and Cristiano Ronaldo, who all donned the Swoosh on their way to golf, tennis and football greatness. Nike athletes Serena Williams, Michael Jordan and Cristiano Ronaldo While the brand retains partnerships with long-retired Jordan, plus Williams and Ronaldo - Woods ended his association in 2024. "[I'm] not saying that what they did wasn't great, but it was in the past," said Tim Derdenger, an academic in marketing and strategy. "It's not the future and it's not the current and that is what drives apparel sales today." Nike's books still boast top athletes, ranging from Rory McIlory to Vinicius Junior. However, it has now lost its biggest footballing star in Mbappé, who had been with Nike since he was nine years old, along with World Cup winner Lamine Yamal. Yamal suggested his move to Adidas gave him the chance to stand out from Nike's star-studded roster, while Mbappé said On would see him "surrounded by innovators who dream of the same things I do". Was that a parting dig at Nike? Derdenger suggests Mbappé's move had parallels to Jordan's decision decades earlier to choose Nike over Converse and Adidas due to the opportunity for the athlete to become synonymous with one brand. "Athletes have egos and those egos want them to be a part of something big and that they're the ones that are helping drive that change, that growth." For all the "doom and gloom", Nike will stay number one, according to Powell - millions worldwide, including young people, remain loyal - but its mistakes have dented its dominance. "Will Nike be the gorilla they once were? I don't think so. Can the brand come back to growth and profitability? Yes," Powell says. "When you shut down innovation, you don't turn it back on and it goes right back to full speed," he adds. Powell thinks Nike's turnaround plan, called "Sport Offense", will start to show positive signs next year. Hill said Nike had "more work to do" on its sportswear, Jordan brand and in China as the company announced quarterly revenues of $11bn, which undershot analysts' expectations. The company said it expected revenues to decline by "high-single digits" in the financial year ahead, adding that it planned to make savings of $2.5bn by 2031, some of which will result in job losses. Last year the company launched a spin-off campaign to its iconic "Just Do It" slogan aimed at younger generations with the line "Why Do It?" Young people, and future sporting stars, may ask themselves: Why Nike? title: Business Daily
description: Protests about 87-year-old Mariacarmen Abascal's eviction reignited the housing debate
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·02 Oct 2026,·25 mins Available for over a year Protests in Spain about 87-year-old Mariacarmen Abascal's eviction from social housing reignited the housing affordability debate globally, as inflation ticks up and career prospects for the young have been impacted by the rise in AI. We head to Nigeria, India and the UK to take stock on the issue. Elsewhere, what can sliding sales at the world's largest automaker tell us about how drivers feel about big purchases? title: Chaos, coffins and 'Claudiapatra' steal the show in Celebrity Traitors
description: There is paranoia, confusion and a battle to survive among the celebrities as they fight for survival.
body: Claudia Winkleman emerged from her coffin to greet the celebrities in church Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two. One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir. Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities. "That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged. "Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen. Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance", but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour. "It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said. Jerry Hall referenced Cleopatra, seen here played by the late actress and former MP Glenda Jackson in a 1971 BBC Morecambe and Wise sketch But the main talking point of this show was actor Richard E Grant, with his shocking admission. Grant and presenter Maya Jama were selected as two of Winkleman's three traitors. But immediately afterwards, Grant appeared to forget the entire point of the game, by gleefully blurting out to those around him he was actually a traitor. You could have heard a pin drop after he said it. Stunned silence. "It's an interesting angle," laughed singer James Blunt just afterwards, while comic Rob Beckett told him: "I think you've just done something that's never happened in the game - it is a bold strategy." Grant later admitted, in footage for viewers of the show: "That may be the biggest mistake I have ever made in my life. I was so thrilled to have been chosen as a traitor that in my unguarded excitement, I said, 'Of course I'm a traitor'. "I clearly need to defuse all the heat that's coming in my direction." Can Richard E Grant hold his nerve in this episode? Ex-BBC journalist Amol Rajan swooped the following day, asking Grant: "What happened last night?" But instead of sowing clever seeds of doubt, Grant said he'd been so "blatant" about wanting to be a traitor that he simply responded he was one, when he was asked. It was an odd reply, perhaps because he was flustered. Rajan labelled him the "Lord of Chaos", but Hall stayed loyal. "I just don't believe Richard's a traitor, I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour," she said. "He says and does eccentric things, he's an amazing guy, but I think he's like acting out because he's not been chosen." Hall's loyalty could be tested though, given Alan Carr murdered Paloma Faith in series one by touching her face. Comic and writer Miranda Hart also thinks Grant could be a faithful, but admitted she is confused. Winkleman told the press launch she thought Grant blurted out his identity in error, because he was so thrilled to be a traitor. "He was giddy, wasn't he? He's just laughing at what's happening. Fantastic," she said. Ed Gamble, the host of BBC One and BBC Sounds spin-off show Uncloaked, added: "It felt like he'd been given the lead role in a film and he just had to tell everyone. It's such an insane moment." Grant may find that no one tells him a secret ever again. He did eventually decide to let the much more cool, calm and collected Jama take the lead in their subsequent decision making. Ross Kemp took joint charge of the mission along with James Blunt Meanwhile the other celebrities also proved their worth on the show, not least "hard man" Ross Kemp, the former EastEnders actor-turned documentary-maker, whose programmes have focused on gangs and the armed forces. Having admitted how nervous he was in the pews of the church, he came into his own for the task, along with ex-army captain James Blunt. They divided the celebrities into teams, leading them to successfully find the treasure on the pirate ship, bagging £15,000. But Kemp quickly crumbled back in the castle, when paranoia set in. The Last of Us and Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsay, a key player in the task, had grabbed a captain's hat from the boat. She playfully planted it on Kemp's head, marking their victory. Little Mix's Leigh-Anne Pinnock then touched Kemp on the arm as she walked through the bar. Clearly remembering how Carr killed off Faith early on, Kemp got understandably fearful he had been killed by a traitor. This tickled Gamble, who said: "It is one of the funniest things I've ever seen - the moment he gets touched on the arm, having already thought Bella Ramsay putting a captain's hat on him is a murder in plain sight. "What a variety of men live within the Ross Kemp sphere. "He's a big hard man running that mission. And then immediately terrified of a member of Little Mix touching him on the arm. That's incredible." Actress Myha'la added she wants to be perceived as "doughy-eyed, fun, and maybe a little naïve", unlike her character in Industry We also learned that although quite a few celebrities wanted to be traitors, including Rajan and Beckett, comics James Acaster and Hart and mathematician Hannah Fry wanted to be faithfuls - Fry said she was "dripping with prefect energy". Meanwhile YouTuber King Kenny and actress Myha'la had their own strategies. "I have an innocent face; I want to avenge Niko [Omilana, the first to be banished in series one]. He left too early," Kenny said, while Myha'la added she wants to be perceived as "doughy-eyed, fun, and maybe a little naïve", unlike her scheming character in Industry. Fashion is likely to be another talking point in the castle. Beckett observed that when actress Julie Hesmondhalgh wore the shield she'd won, she looked like a "cardinal" in her long, red dress, adding: "I thought we were in the Vatican!" Tru

body: This video can not be played Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in hospital after surviving two lethal injection attempts. According to Pike's attorney, she is alive and "receiving life-saving medical care" in hospital. Tennesseean Governor Bill Lee says a review into what happened has been ordered and executions in the state have been halted for the rest of the year. title: Sexual assault case dismissed against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith
description: Actor Mike Smith had been charged with sexual assault in 2025 for an alleged incident in 2017.
body: Mike Smith plays the character Bubbles in the Canadian sitcom. A judge in Nova Scotia, Canada, has dismissed the sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith. The trial was set to begin in provincial court in Dartmouth on Thursday, but after the Crown provided no evidence against Smith, the actor's attorneys requested the case be dismissed. The 54-year-old actor, who plays the character Bubbles on the Canadian sitcom, was charged last year for an alleged sexual assault in 2017. Prosecutor Bryson McDonald told reporters outside court that the Crown offered no evidence in relation to the charge "based on the Crown's ongoing assessment that the prosecution standard has no longer been met". McDonald would not go into further detail about the standard not being met or why, but said his office has been in regular communication with the complainant throughout the process. There is a publication ban in place protecting the identity of the complainant. The complainant said in a statement to Canadian broadcaster CBC that the trial was dismissed because she is "unwilling to sacrifice my mental health" by testifying. Trailer Park Boys Incorporated, the company behind the show, said in a statement that because the charge against Smith was dropped, the actor will resume his responsibilities with the company. Smith's attorney also said his client is "pleased that this matter is now behind him and is ready to move forward". In February, Smith pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault. Set in a fictional trailer park in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, Trailer Park Boys follows the adventures of three longtime friends and petty criminals. The Canadian mockumentary series first began airing in 2001 before ending in 2007, but was later revived by Netflix. Season 13 is expected to be released in the coming months. title: PM warned Rosebank oil field could breach West Bank sanctions
description: Campaigners and Green Party leader Zack Polanski raise concerns about Rosebank's ties to an Israeli firm.
body: A long-awaited decision on the Rosebank oil field is expected soon The prime minister has been warned that approving a controversial oil field risks contravening his own sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The government will soon have to make a long-awaited decision on whether to go ahead with Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil field, which sits off Shetland. Environmental campaigners and Green Party leader Zack Polanski have both separately written to Andy Burnham and the foreign secretary to raise concerns about Rosebank's links to an Israeli company, Delek Group. Last year Delek Group was included in a UN database of firms which allegedly provide services or utilities to support settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. A spokesman for the company told the Daily Telegraph, external it no longer had any involvement in Israeli settlements and was wrongly included in the database. Delek Group controls Ithaca Energy, which holds a 20% stake in Rosebank. The campaign group Uplift, whose legal challenge against the Rosebank project in 2023 led to the ongoing delay over a decision on exploration, has helped organise a letter to Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. In a letter seen by BBC News, campaigners from Stop Rosebank and Greenpeace, with assistance from Uplift, have asked the government to clarify whether Delek will fall foul of the sanctions announced last month. Separately, Polanski has also written to Miliband, asking what steps the government would take to make sure revenue from UK oil and gas production did not finance illegal settlements. He said: "Rosebank is a test of whether Labour's proposed sanctions regime is fit for purpose. "Companies blacklisted by the UN for operating in the illegal settlements should not be financed by oil and gas revenues from the North Sea." What is happening with the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields? UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response Last month, Miliband signalled a hardening of the UK's position when he announced action against companies and individuals who provide services such as infrastructure to settlement expansion. The UK sanctions will also ban imports of goods from illegal settlements. In its letter to Burnham, Uplift asked him to "confirm, unequivocally, whether Delek will be caught by the new planned measures". They added: "If it is not, please explain how that is consistent with the government's stated intent to sanction those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements?" A spokesperson for Ithaca Energy told the BBC: "Ithaca Energy is a London Stock Exchange listed company which is a member of the FTSE 100, and which is governed by the highest standards of corporate governance. "Ithaca is one of the biggest investors in the North Sea and Scotland, is a responsible employer and is a major contributor to both the UK Treasury through tax payments and to the UK's energy security." A spokesman for Delek Group told the Telegraph: "Delek Group has been wrongly included in the UN database. "Together with our legal advisers, we intend to formally challenge this and request the immediate removal of our name from the UN database." The question of whether to approve Rosebank, as well as the Jackdaw gas field east of Aberdeen, has become hugely politically significant. Rosebank was approved by the previous Conservative government in 2023, but that decision was successfully challenged in the courts by campaigners including Uplift. The decision now lies with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, but will be seen as an important indication of Burnham's wider thinking on oil and gas. Miliband was widely thought to have been opposed to Rosebank when he served as Sir Keir Starmer's energy secretary. Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licenses already exist in the North Sea. The decision could also have implications for the relationship between the UK and the US. President Trump has placed pressure on successive UK prime ministers to drill more in the North Sea. While Downing Street is relieved that Trump has not lashed out at the government's recent West Bank sanctions, his administration has said the US will not take the same course of action. Tessa Khan, executive director at Uplift, said "not one penny of North Sea oil profits" should go to a company which "itself now risks being sanctioned by the UK". The Foreign Office declined to comment. Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months. Israel has criticised the UK sanctions, accusing the government of "anti-Israel policies". Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: Thames Water apologises after £145,000 customer billing mistake
description: The firm has apologised to the family.
body: Thames Water has apologised to a customer after trying to take £145,000 from his bank account due to a meter reading error by the company. Adam Bainbridge, a teacher from north London, discovered while routinely checking his accounts on Thursday morning that Thames had debited £145,562 from his bank account. His wife Julia told the PA news agency that Adam "got the shock of his life" and had trouble paying bills that morning as a result. Thames Water said the money had been returned to his account and that he had been offered "a gesture of goodwill". The company confirmed to BBC News that it had returned the money to Adam's account and had apologised to him personally. Julia told PA that the debit took Adam's account "considerably" into overdraft. She said: "It was pre-8am when we looked ... obviously then you try to do some ring rounds, no one's online, no one's answering any phones. "We're a family rushing around looking after a three-year-old trying to get ready for the nursery run and all the rest of it." Julia said Adam initially could only speak to a Thames chatbot, which said the error would be rectified in the next payment. He then contacted his bank. "As it was this morning, Adam had some bills he wanted to pay off his card and things that were due out of his account and everything was blocked. "It's such a staggering amount of money." The billing error comes at a time when the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the industry watchdog has risen by a record 84% in a year, driven by customer concern and confusion over bills. Water customers in England and Wales have been hit with steep price hikes in recent years. The regulator Ofwat has also allowed firms to put up bills by 36% between 2025 and 2030. Thames Water, the UK's biggest water company, owes roughly £20bn to lenders and has been working with creditors and government officials to prevent collapse. Adam told PA that when he saw the debit he felt "really shocked, because you don't feel in control of what's being taken from your account. "It seemed that the numbers being calculated had absolutely nothing to do with reality at all. We're a residential house in north London. "It just seems that the billing is completely detached from reality." A Thames Water spokesperson said: "We apologise unreservedly to Mr Bainbridge and his family. This was the result of human error originating from an incorrect meter reading. "We can confirm the money has been returned to Mr Bainbridge's bank account and we have spoken to him today to say sorry. "We are introducing additional checks to our processes to prevent this from happening again. "We have also offered Mr Bainbridge a gesture of goodwill and are continuing to work with him to ensure the matter is fully resolved." Earlier on Thursday, Julia wrote in a LinkedIn post: "Working parents have enough to contend with in the morning without a utility company emptying their bank account." "How does a payment of this size get taken without basic checks?" title: Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad
description: Vladimir Putin insists Moscow is "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders.
body: Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers it has come under direct attack in its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. Addressing the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin insisted Russia was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that Moscow was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030. Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia. Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing it is a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats". Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months. Last week alone Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes. Rosenberg: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine In a wide-ranging speech, the Russian leader told his audience he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened. Although Putin himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that it had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms. He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries, and on its ships in the Black Sea. "Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said. Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war. Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war on Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, and a key bridge in Kyiv was attacked by drones on Thursday. Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts. "If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said. He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea which he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear. "We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that." He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful". Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used. He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly fire at the end. He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten, and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence. "The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said. title: Cornell accuser was 'failed' by university healthcare system, lawyer says
description: Jane Doe told the school's doctor that she had contracted an infection "in a traumatic way", but they "didn't really follow up", according to the New York Times.
body: Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September, alleging she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024 A woman who has accused several men of raping her at Cornell University in 2024 was failed by the school's health system, her lawyer has said. Jane Doe, as she is known in court filings, said she told a university doctor two days after the alleged assault that she had contracted a urinary tract infection "in a traumatic way", but that they "didn't really follow up", according to the New York Times, external. Her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement provided to the BBC that the doctor visit marked "yet another failure by Cornell". Cornell said it did not have any additional information to share in response to an inquiry from the BBC about the health visit. After Doe was seen by the university doctor, she said she was then told to go to therapy, documents from the institution's investigation show. "Ms Doe's disclosure warranted further inquiry, including a rape kit and consultation of medical professionals trained to deal with rape cases and a physical exam to document her injuries," Giuffra said in a statement to the BBC. "Inexplicably, all the medical professional did was to advise Ms Doe to 'speak with somebody'." The woman filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September, alleging she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024. She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults The case was referred to Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, the top prosecutor in the county, back in 2024. District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged. This week, Van Houten's office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit. Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault. Giuffra accused the district attorney of changing "his story so many times, I can't keep up with it" in his latest statement. "The pattern I am seeing is that whenever evidence comes out supporting prosecution, he claims he never saw it," Giuffra said. "His defensiveness and attempt to save face has not been impressive." Van Houten told the BBC that he had received a six-page statement from Jane Doe and the Snapchat messages from campus police. But there was also a 120-page transcript from a recording of an interview by a Title IX investigator with Doe, with a victim's advocate, a counsellor and one of Doe's attorneys participating by phone, which Van Houten said he had not seen in full at the time. "The full transcript – which I have now obtained – confirms the contents of Jane Doe's sworn statement," he said. "I have no intention of letting Mr Giuffra's unfair criticism distract my office from getting to the truth." Documents from the school's investigation - obtained by the New York Times - suggest Jane Doe's roommates believed that she was sexually assaulted The documents from the university's Title IX review provide the most detailed account yet into the three weeks after Doe was allegedly assaulted and made the decision to report to the university. Title IX is a federal civil rights law mandating that universities follow certain rules when investigating sexual assaults. The morning after the alleged assault, when Doe returned to her sorority house, she told her two roommates she had done drugs and had sex with multiple men, but did not yet use the word "rape" or "assault", according to the roommates. She appeared to be "in shock" and "not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying", a roommate said, according to the documents the New York Times obtained. The review also included Doe's text exchanges with one of the men accused of assault, who apologised to her after the alleged rape. "I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night," he wrote. He said he and other men accused of assault felt awful for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand". Her roommate told the university that as time went on, Doe "kind of came to realise that it was something bad. And that she didn't really enjoy her time there". On 3 November, Doe texted one of the men accused of assault and told him, "let's be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember," she said, using a shorthand for ketamine. "I know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn't know anyone in the room," the text messages included in the document read. Later, at the Title IX interview, she said she felt "100 percent" confident that she was raped, remarks her attorney confirmed to the BBC. Doe went to get a rape kit on 7 November, three weeks after the alleged assault took place, but no DNA evidence was recovered, her lawyer said. Giuffra said that if she had received a rape kit in October when she went to see the university doctor, it is likely there would have been DNA evidence. The lawyer said the messages and other interviews from the investigation show that "Ms Doe's internal processing went from denial, to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends". title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford incident, police say
description: The 27-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London, marking the sixth arrest in connection with Sunday's incident near the airbase.
body: A heavy police presence could be seen near the base after a major incident was declared on Sunday A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said. The 27-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. A second man, a 26-year-old UK national, has also been questioned under caution, and two properties in the area have been searched. Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London. Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said. "The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said. "I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident. The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles. They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy". Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site. The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades. In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. title: Carney hopes an oil pipeline can help Canada fight a trade war
description: A west coast pipeline project is the first to be fast-tracked and will be a major test of Carney's promise to global investors.
body: Mark Carney is pushing to make Canada a major energy exporter Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced that Canada will fast-track the approval process for a 1,250km (775 mile) oil pipeline project to the Pacific coast. Carney argues the Pacific Link project is key to national interests, allowing Canada to diversify its oil markets away from the US. "A pipeline to the west coast is part of our mission to transform our economy, to double our non-US exports over the next decade," he said on Thursday. It will also be a test of his promise to global investors that Ottawa can move quickly to build major projects as he seeks to turn Canada into a global energy "superpower". British Columbia v Alberta - how oil sparked a feud between neighbours The prime minister said the project is expected to boost Canada's GDP by up to C$30bn ($21bn; £16bn) per year and create 140,000 jobs. Carney argues that Canada's economic ties to the US have become a vulnerability in light of protectionist tariffs implemented by US President Donald Trump. Last year, Canada sent 90% of its crude oil exports south of the border. Pacific Link would be capable of carrying approximately one million barrels per day of crude oil from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deep-water port near Delta, British Columbia. The project includes the construction of marine berths able to accommodate vessels that can carry up to two million barrels-worth of oil. From there, the oil would be shipped by boat to global markets. Ottawa says the project will reduce Canada's overall dependency on the US to approximately 65-70% as it opens up the market to the Asia-Pacific region, including key markets such as South Korea, China, and Japan. Pacific Link will be the first project to have its federal approvals and regulatory reviews fast-tracked under a new law put in place last year by the Liberal government. The goal is to give investors a final yes or no on a proposed project within a year. Fierce opposition and the country's lengthy and complex projects review process has contributed in the past some past pipelines projects being cancelled. "People are watching very closely how Canada is handling this process," a government official said in a media briefing on Thursday. They added that if it goes as planned, they expect more private investment to express interest in the project, which is projected to cost between C$35.2bn and C$43.7bn. The second hope is that the pipeline, which would run from Alberta's landlocked oil patch to the coast, will help appease the western province, which argues it has long been hampered from developing its resources. Albertans will vote later this month in a referendum on independence. Pacific Link is "a demonstration of the power of Canada", said Carney, speaking from Fort McMurray, Alberta, when asked if he had a message for the province. The pipeline project is likely to face pushback from environmental groups, especially over concerns about the impact on coastal marine health, as well as from some indigenous communities along the route. Carney argues that discussions with many indigenous communities have already taken place, with "intensive" consultations to come. The plan is for construction to begin by 2032 if it receives final approval. Currently, the governments of Canada and Alberta are backing the project, along with one private investor, the Pembina Pipeline Corporation, which has a non-binding agreement for a 10% stake during construction and the option for another 10% once the pipeline is up and running. A minimum of a 10% ownership stake will also be offered for purchase to indigenous groups. As part of the agreement, Alberta has agreed to develop the world's largest carbon capture programme in a bid to reduce its overall emissions. Ottawa has also worked to shore up ocean protection funding and rules to protect marine life that could be affected by increased coastal tanker traffic, including the endangered Southern Resident killer whales. title: Prince of Wales tells villagers 'holistic' approach is needed to tackle flooding
description: Prince William visits residents of Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, who have faced four floods in six years.
body: The Prince of Wales meets local residents, Rob and Helen Wyatt, during a visit to the village of Skenfrith in Monmouthshire The Prince of Wales has said a "holistic" approach is needed to tackle severe flooding, as a small Welsh village prepares for the upcoming storm season. Residents in Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, have faced four major floods in the past six years. An extreme flood last winter had a devastating impact on the village, when the River Monnow burst its banks after Storm Claudia brought a month's worth of rain in just 24 hours to parts of England and Wales. Prince William was visiting the area to learn about how communities have been affected by recent flooding and what measures were being taken by local authorities and other agencies to mitigate future incidents. Over the years, families have reported that their homes and possessions had been destroyed by the floods. In 2019, about 25 homes were evacuated in the village following flooding and a power cut after heavy rain. The prince sympathised with residents who might be "anxious" about extreme weather events he said were no longer "one in 50-year" occurrences but instead seemed to be happening every year. Prince William also attended a meeting with representatives from Natural Resources Wales, the Welsh Government and Monmouthshire County Council On Thursday, the prince spoke to villagers Rod and Helen Wyatt at their garden gate and was told how the water almost topped gravestones in a cemetery opposite during a flood. The couple have now tiled the ground floor of their house and live with the threat of further flooding. Rod, who has lived in his home for 10 years, made light of the experience when he told Prince William that, at one point, "we had to give up really, we got two bottles of Prosecco and went to watch Strictly upstairs". The prince replied: "It must be so demoralising for you now, the worry each year you've got to go through that again, potentially, is becoming more frequent. "They keep talking about a one in 50-year event, it doesn't make sense anymore. "It might be in the researching and scientific point of view - it's happening every year now, it's mad. "So, it's trying to understand how we can do a better holistic view of the whole catchment area, so we're dealing with the whole problem." He listed a number of ideas, from "slowing the water down" using farming landscaping remedies, to tree planting and better monitoring "so we know when things might be getting worse". The Prince of Wales was visiting the area to learn about how communities have been affected by recent flooding Prince William discussed the ideas in detail while later meeting representatives from environmental charity Stump Up for Trees at Great Tre-Rhew Farm in Monmouthshire. The charity, founded in 2020, aims to plant one million native trees across south Wales and Bannau Brycheiniog, also known as the Brecon Beacons. The prince joined volunteers harvesting seeds from a field maple tree and planted a sessile oak tree - designated as the national tree of Wales. To access the trees, he had to climb over a barbed wire fence and use a small step, joking that he did not want to rip his trousers. As he harvested seeds from the tree, he noted he was taller than others present, adding: "I'm going to reach up here and get these higher ones." The charity collected 35,000 seeds last year that were used to grow new trees for planting, and hopes to increase this to 60,000 this year. Prince William discussed what measures were being taken by local authorities and other agencies to mitigate future flooding incidents The prince joined volunteers harvesting seeds from a field maple tree He also planted a sessile oak tree The prince spoke to Kate and Jim Beavan, of Great Tre-Rhew Farm, and Jenny Knight, the director of Stump Up for Trees. After the visit, Knight paid tribute to Prince William for "looking at not just the problems but the solutions as well". Representatives from the Duchy of Cornwall also joined the visit to share learning about nature recovery, climate-resilient forestry and to start a long-term partnership. Knight added "knowledge exchange is so valuable" and said working together across different areas would have a greater impact. At the end of the conversation, William discussed his enjoyment of cider, which is made on the farm. "He said 'one pint a day keeps the doctor away'," Knight said. Prince William also visited Herefordshire and met farmer Harry Davies, 25, who is set to lead the Duchy of Cornwall's first regenerative farming project on a 25-year lease at the 900-acre farm. The project aims to improve soil health and make farms more resilient to flooding and drought. Davies said: "By us being able to hold that water in that soil profile so it doesn't go into our rivers and streams quite so quickly, we should be able to hold the water on our land. Which in the long term will then benefit us when it's hot and dry. "There seems to be an opportunity to draw on experience from my Grandad's generation, but also a bit of youth and enthusiasm is also needed. I think it's about generations working together, that's just farming." title: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
description: Lawyers for Good's family say US officials created "an unprecedented environment for state sponsored violence" in Minneapolis.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Renée Good's partner speaks publicly for first time since her death The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis in January has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration. Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest. One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family said. The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The lawsuits were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good. Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed." "We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children. In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death". It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death, or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees. The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border chief Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents, and private actors". "Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci said at the news conference. Renee Nicole Good had recently moved to Minneapolis when she was killed by immigration agents Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully, and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents sometimes are "going to make a mistake". Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents". Witnesses disputed that she was attempting to attack officers. Her death sparked nationwide protests that intensified after another Minneapolis resident, Alex Pretti, was killed by immigration agents on 24 January. Weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the city and the official in charge of the operation, Greg Bovino, was removed from his post. Granger, Good's brother, said at Thursday's news conference that "since her death no meaningful change has occurred". "Our family is waiting and we will wait no longer," he said. At least 10 people have been killed in encounters with immigration officers during Trump's second term, which began in January 2025, according to the Associated Press news agency. This video can not be played Unpicking the second Minneapolis shooting frame by frame On Tuesday, Good's mother testified in a congressional hearing, saying: "I am a registered Republican. I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States." "But far more than being a Republican, I am a Christian," she continued. "Jesus teaches us to forgive and I have, but what we are asking for is accountability." title: Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant
description: Syngenta said its Grangemouth operation was no longer 'competitive' due to increasing competition from overseas.
body: Syngenta said its Grangemouth facility was "no longer competitive" Hundreds of jobs are under threat in Grangemouth after an agricultural chemical firm announced plans to cease operations at the site. Syngenta said it had been unable to make its business at the plant "competitive" in the face of "increasing international competition". A spokesperson for the company - which manufactures chemicals used for the protection of crops - said it would enter a consultation period over the move, but added a final decision has yet to be taken. The Economy Secretary, Stephen Flynn, described the plans as "extremely disappointing". The UK government's Reindustrialisation Minister, Blair McDougall, said they had worked with Scottish counterparts to "explore every possible avenue" for support, but Syngenta had taken the decision on a commercial basis. A total of 377 workers are set to be affected by the move. It comes over a year after Syngenta was awarded £2.2m from Scottish Enterprise to expand production at the site. New £150m funding package to protect jobs at Grangemouth Bus firm Alexander Dennis to close Falkirk site with loss of 115 jobs Syngenta added that it was "committed to genuine consultation" with trade unions over "alternative paths" for the site. The firm said it had undertaken a "detailed review" of its Grangemouth operation prior to the plans being announced. It said the Grangemouth site was "significantly more expensive" to operate than other production facilities. The company added that savings had been identified in some areas of the business, but these fell short in "bridging the site's competitiveness gap". Mike Hollands, president of Syngenta UK, said: "The workforce at Grangemouth is highly skilled and passionate, but despite all efforts, we have not been able to make the Grangemouth site competitive compared to alternative supply options. "It is with a very heavy heart that we make this proposal, but we are committed to a constructive consultation and will continue to consider options as part of that process." It is the latest job loss blow to the area following the closure of the nearby oil refinery in April last year, which also resulted in the loss of about 400 jobs. In March, bus manufacturer Alexander Dennis announced plans to close its Falkirk plant with 115 roles lost. The UK government, under then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, previously pledged an additional £200m in funding for Grangemouth from the National Wealth Fund. Flynn said the Scottish government had "strongly opposed" Syngenta's plans. He said he would continue to press the UK government on the £200m funding pot. "My thoughts are with the workers, their families and the local community who will be affected by this decision," he said. "We made clear to Syngenta's board our strong opposition to any potential scale down or closure of their Grangemouth site." Flynn added: "During this period of consultation, I sincerely hope that the UK government will now provide some of the £200m committed to Grangemouth, since not a single penny has yet been allocated from that fund promised in 2024." McDougall said the UK government would work with the National Wealth Fund in the coming days to "explore all options for the area". "I know this will be a deeply concerning time for workers at Syngenta and their families, and I met with the company earlier today to discuss all options for the site and the workforce," he said. "We will continue to work closely with both of them and look at all options for the site and the workforce." Scottish Conservative Central Scotland MSP Meghan Gallacher said: "This is another hammer blow for Grangemouth and my thoughts are with the workers who are set to lose their jobs. "Grangemouth and the surrounding communities have been devastated by the closure of major sites in recent years and this will have a further deeply damaging impact on the local and national economy. "Both SNP and Labour ministers must pull out all the stops to try and protect these jobs and offer support to those who will be affected." The Scottish Green Party co-leader, Gillian Mackay, who is also a local MSP, said the move was another "devastating blow" for the area. "Our governments should be doing more to protect jobs and ensure that workers can benefit from our transition to a greener future," she said. "Grangemouth is my home, and I am concerned about what this will mean for the local community if it goes ahead." title: UK in talks with EU partners to release strategic fuel reserves if needed, BBC understands
description: President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports in a bid to ease prices in the US.
body: Energy Minister Martin McCluskey held talks with EU counterparts about a diesel export ban Britain is in talks with EU partners to release additional strategic fuel reserves, including diesel, if needed, the BBC understands. The talks come after President Donald Trump threatened to ban diesel exports from the US in a bid to reduce record prices at the pumps for Americans. Diesel prices in the UK also hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC. The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries. "We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend. Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban. A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year. "We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further. What a US diesel export ban could mean for you A European Commission spokesperson said today that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration. A meeting of the governing board of the International Energy Agency (IEA) is taking place tomorrow. Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil. An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices. Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections. But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket. Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38p Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand. The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs. There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before. There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.
