title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
description: The prime minister said he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners sell up after Premier League rule breaches.
body: Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) chats to Andy Burnham in 2019 at the Etihad Stadium, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester Downing Street has said Manchester City are not "above the rules" after Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules. The prime minister said on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners decide to sell up after City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced. His remarks were branded "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary" by the Tories and took many in the football community by surprise. In a statement following the backlash, Downing Street said the PM had made clear "the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules". In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. "Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences." Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal. Sources told BBC Sport that City are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal. Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m. The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade". In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process", saying it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League. He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion". Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is. "I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that." In response, the Tories accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied. Man City to argue sponsorship deals came from Abu Dhabi government Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence". "The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said. "Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester. "Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules." And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester." It comes as the chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it has "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications. This video can not be played PM: I’d be ‘really concerned’ if Man City owners sell club In his BBC interview, Burnham also said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners as Greater Manchester mayor would stand up to scrutiny. He compared City's situation to how the club he supports, Everton, had been charged with a more minor breach of Premier League financial rules in 2023, but said he "hold[s] the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process". Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions. The independent panel that found City guilty of rule breaches will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment, which could include a huge fine or points deduction. City have maintained their innocence of all the accusations made. The chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues". In a statement, David Kogan said the IFR "has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate", while "taking account of the findings made by the Leagues". He added that proceedings remain ongoing and he hoped for a quick resolution. Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case
description: The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing HMRC, has urged the body to scrutinise tax implications of the Manchester City verdict.
body: Manchester City were found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges against them Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority. It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday. The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners. The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities". The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report. Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case". Manchester City, who deny wrongdoing, will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners. Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m. This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules. However, as first reported by the Daily Mail and Times, sources have told BBC Sport that City are expected to tell an appeal board that they have evidence showing the money directed to sponsors came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than from ADUG. The independent commission rejected this argument as "untrue" in its findings, saying: "We concluded that it was an 'explanation' that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme." City have claimed the commission's decision contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe". Mansour is a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, and the brother of UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. ADUG took over City in 2008. Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs. On Saturday, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak referred to "irrefutable evidence" that he claimed supports the club's claims of innocence. City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings". The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements". Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president. The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport. title: 'I took Fairford pic - then all hell broke loose'
description: The man who took the famous arrest image says the military is not doing enough to reassure locals.
body: The local resident took this photo of five handcuffed men close to RAF Fairford The man who took a now-famous photo of the five men arrested at RAF Fairford said he thought nothing of it until he woke up the following morning. "I saw the guys being arrested outside the house on Sunday morning and went back to bed and thought, 'oh, well they've got them now'," said the Whelford resident, who did not want to be named. "Then all hell broke loose at half past six in the morning." At a police information point at Fairford Community Centre earlier, he - along with other locals - said communication from the military base following the major security incident had been "poor". The US Air Force, which operates from RAF Fairford, has been approached for comment. A major investigation was launched after five men were arrested at RAF Fairford on Sunday on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. They have since been bailed. Earlier, Counter Terrorism Policing announced a 25-year-old man, a dual UK-Iranian national, had been arrested in London, on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. It follows the prime minister commenting on Wednesday that he believed Iran was involved in the Fairford incident. The man who took the widely shared image said police did not have enough information at Thursday's drop-in event "to be able to give us anything". "Going forward, whats going to happen?" said the resident of Whelford, which is next to the RAF base. "Recently I think [the base's] communication with the local population has been poor. "I can see why people do feel unsafe," he added. This resident, who did not want to be named, took the photo of the men being arrested Another local, Selina Vesey-Hague, said representatives from the military base should have been at the police event to answer questions. "I think obviously a lot of people think it could happen again. And so we need a proper, proper plan," she said. When asked if she felt reassured, Vesey-Hague said "possibly not". "I wouldn't say I feel particularly safe," she added. Event stopped after 'abuse' over beauty spot plans 'Shameful' delays lead to people collecting own mail Families welcome right to challenge A&E care A Whelford resident told the BBC she was not surprised there were suspicions over Iranian involvement, and there was "a lot of resentment" in the village. "None of us wanted the American bombers here. We don't mind the base, but not this bombing campaign." She added: "As a village we're feeling a bit lost and ignored by the machinations of what's going on with the police and the base. "There are 85 homes here with people of varying ages and frailties. "We'd like a lot of answers about why the MOD phone wasn't answered [as the incident unfolded]. If security was increased on Saturday as it was then why were notices not issued to residents?" Selina Vesey-Hague says villages need to be made aware of a "proper plan" in case of future security incidents PC Tyler Harris from Gloucestershire Police said the public sessions were set up because "it's a major thing that's happened and everyone's got lots of questions, and emotions can be up in the air". He said the community had been "very understanding" that the force can "only talk about certain things". Harris said officers would be doing "high-visibility patrols" in the area and that letters had been sent out to the households closest to the incident. There will be more police drop-in events set up over the next couple of weeks, he added. PC Tyler Harris says locals have been "very understanding" that police cannot answer all questions Michael Vann, district councillor for Fairford, called the meeting "very much a first step", if a "tiny bit belated". He added: "There was an elephant in the room who wasn't there - the United States Air Force." Vann said a regular meeting held on Wednesday evenings at the base had been cancelled. "Theres a big difference between being safe and feeling safe," said Cotswold District councillor Tristan Wilkinson. "I have every reassurance from the authorities about the measures they're taking to keep the community safe - that's very different from people feeling safe. "People don't feel safe," he said, adding one person told the meeting: "We feel like sitting ducks." Councillor Trsitan WIlkinson says local people do not feel safe "They need to be told really clearly what the authorities are doing to protect this community," said Wilkinson. "As long as this conflict with Iran goes on we will be living next door to a significant military base, and we need to be planning for the long term. "We need to figure out how we live side-by-side so that they [the base] have the operational independence they need but also how the community is reassured." title: How the the failed execution of Christa Pike unfolded
description: The BBC's Stephanie Hegarty looks at why two attempts to execute the US convicted murderer by lethal injection failed.
body: This video can not be played Two attempts to execute Tennessee's only woman on death row - convicted murderer Christa Pike - by lethal injection failed on Wednesday. Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, was in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" as of Thursday morning. Tennessee's Governor Bill Lee has now said that executions in the state have been halted for the rest of the year. He has also ordered a third-party review to "determine exactly what occurred". title: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives two lethal injection attempts
description: Pike had been on death row since she was convicted in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt Executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee has said, after two attempts to execute death row inmate Christa Pike by lethal injection failed. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Lee said he was "highly disappointed" about the botched execution, which he called one of the state's "most serious responsibilities". He has ordered an independent review. Tennessee prison officials on Wednesday attempted to administer two lethal doses of pentobarbital to Pike but she survived and was taken to hospital. Her medical condition is unclear. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer. Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee for over 200 years. Lee said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time". "There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for." Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures. His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton. In court filings, Pike's lawyers said she needed "life-saving measures" after her botched execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case. It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office". "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening." Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, as per state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings. "This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said. The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened." Pike's attempted execution proceeded after multiple last-minute legal challenges by her lawyers had failed, overturned in the final hour by the US Supreme Court. Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess". US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic". "While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said. Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment". "As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X. This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner. In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve. title: Educating Cardiff teacher admits sexually assaulting teenage girl
description: Gareth Ritter, who featured in the Channel 4 series, pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl.
body: Gareth Ritter was giving defence in his trial when he changed his plea A teacher who featured in the Channel 4 documentary series Educating Cardiff has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl. Gareth Ritter, 44, of Bryngwyn, in Monmouthshire, was in the middle of giving evidence in his defence when his barrister asked for the charge to be put to him again. Ritter, who was also a prominent member of a number of brass bands, was asked to stand up and, when asked how he pleaded, he said "guilty". He was told all of the charges he had admitted carried a custodial sentence and the court would consider immediate custody. Ritter had previously denied intentionally touching the teenager sexually without consent when he was in his 30s. Earlier in the trial, the jury was told that, following an event in Cardiff, Ritter offered to drive the victim home but stopped at a flat he owned in Cardiff Bay, saying he had to check it before a new tenant arrived and invited her in. Once inside, she said he touched her bottom while they stood on a balcony overlooking the city and later kissed her in the hallway. The woman, now in her 20s, said: "One hand went around my back, it dropped to my bum and he lent in and kissed me. "I remember his tongue going into my mouth. "I remember being against the wall, I couldn't step back, I remember him kissing me. I turned my face away, my hands were on him, I wasn't forceful, I held out my hands on his chest. It was a light push but not forceful." Asked by prosecutor Andrew Davies if she said anything to him, she replied: "It might seem like a strange comment, but I said 'I'm a good girl, I don't do this. I go to a Christian school'." The court was told Ritter then drove her home, repeatedly asking her if she was going to tell anyone about what had happened. "I remember him saying 'Nobody needs to know about this. Are you going to tell anyone about this?' "What do you say in that situation? Gareth was someone I really looked up to. How do you confront that? I'd never been in that situation." She said she just wanted to "brush it under the carpet". The court heard the woman reported the alleged incident several years later after Ritter's phone was examined by detectives following an "unrelated matter" that ended with no charges being brought. Police had found intimate images of a young woman who was under the age of 18. When she was traced, it was the same woman who was sexually assaulted by Ritter. The court was told the images had originally been screen grabbed with her consent during an intimate video conversation between the woman and another man. The images had been stored on his tablet, which had been accessed and shared by the man's housemates, and were later found on Ritter's phone. The jury were told Ritter had since pleaded guilty to the possession and distribution of unlawful images, as the woman was 17 at the time the images were taken. The woman said when she was told her images had been found on Ritter's phone she decided to report the incident in Cardiff Bay. The court was told that when Ritter was interviewed by police in December 2022 he denied knowing about the Cardiff Bay flat, and denied taking the woman there. He also told police he had not given her a lift home. A year later he was interviewed by police again. When asked if he had given a truthful account in his first interview, he said no. Ritter was granted bail until sentencing on 4 November. title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest over funding
description: The French government holds a crisis meeting as demonstrations grow and become violent in places.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Why are students staging protests at schools in France? Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions. Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance to another in the northern city of Rouen. Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest. The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence". Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall. In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers. While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework. The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country. French media report 625 people were arrested on Wednesday alone while 83 police officers were injured. More than 600 arrests had been made by midday on Thursday, excluding Paris, broadcaster ICI reports. At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris. On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around. Aftermath of the fire at the Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks. He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets. "The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said. While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised. The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students. Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests. LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations. Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise." The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed. Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said. Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs. title: SpaceX launches crew to ISS
description: The Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from Cape Canaveral with two Americans, a Russian and a Canadian who will spend up to six months aboard the International Space Station.
body: This video can not be played The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched from Cap Canaveral, Florida to the International Space Station carrying Crew-13. The team is comprised of two Nasa astronauts, a Russian cosmonaut and a Canadian astronaut whose wife is expecting their third child two months into the mission. They'll become the fourth couple in the history of space travel to have a child born while one parent was off the planet, according to CBSNews. The launch was originally planned for mid-September, but was delayed to replace a valve in the Crew Dragon's propulsion system. It will take 7 hours and 50 minutes for the crew to reach the ISS where they will be conducting experiments and research toward future missions to the Moon and Mars, according to Nasa. title: England avoid Australia & India in World Cup draw
description: England avoid defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Cricket World Cup.
body: Holders Australia beat India in the 2023 final England have avoided defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup. India and Pakistan are, once again, placed in the same group, alongside Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier. England, who won the trophy in 2019, are in the same group as co-hosts South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and a qualifier. Harry Brook's side, who have enjoyed a resurgence in the 50-over format, begin their campaign against Bangladesh on 8 October, and Sri Lanka on 13 October in Windhoek, Namibia. They will come up against South Africa in Gqeberha on 16 October before travelling to Harare to face a qualifier on 20 October. They round off the group stage when they face New Zealand, again in Gqeberha, on 23 October. The visit to Zimbabwe is significant, with England having not played there since 2004. Political unrest in Zimbabwe under the regime of former president Robert Mugabe caused problems for England's men's team throughout the 2000s. England boycotted their fixture against Zimbabwe in Harare at the 2003 World Cup - a decision which ultimately derailed their campaign. Relations have improved in recent years, however, and BBC Sport reported in 2025 that the two cricket boards were discussing a potential England tour of the country in the next cycle of international cricket between 2027 and 2031. After three matches to decide the final two qualifiers, the tournament group stage will open with a repeat of the 2023 final when India and Australia face each other in Cape Town on 7 October. Arch-rivals India and Pakistan, who do not play each other outside tournaments, will meet in Johannesburg on 10 October. The top three, plus the best fourth-placed finisher, from the two groups progress to the Super 7 stage. From there, the top four teams will qualify for the semi-finals, which are scheduled for 17 and 18 November, before the final on 21 November in Johannesburg. title: Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires
description: It is estimated more than 200 people have died in blazes in the north-east of the country over the summer.
body: Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country. Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday. Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993. The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher. Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa. Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution. The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation. According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes." The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said. The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president. Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities. Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala, external, puts the death toll at 200. While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country. title: 'We must keep going' says charity hit by fuel prices
description: Both petrol and diesel prices have risen by a third or more in just the past seven months.
body: Alex Wood (R) says Yeovil Freewheelers are having to fundraise more to keep going Businesses and charities are being hit by spiralling fuel prices caused by the Iran war. Last week, diesel prices reached an all-time high and are now about £2 a litre after rising more than 40% since the end of February, with petrol prices climbing nearly 34% in that period. BBC analysis has identified the most expensive fuel stations across the West, as prices vary across more urban and rural areas. Alex Wood, from charity Freewheelers which delivers medical supplies, said it has had to dip into reserves to keep afloat. Somerset-based Berry's Coaches has called on the government to freeze fuel duty next year after their fuel costs increased by half since the Middle East conflict began. Petrol prices have increased by 8% to 174.8p per litre in the past month, while diesel has risen by 9% to 200.1p per litre. But in the seven months since the US-Israel conflict with Iran erupted, the jump is even bigger - a nearly 34% increase for petrol and more than 40% for diesel. Man arrested after 'explosives substances' found Families welcome right to challenge A&E care New chapter begins in Hinkley Point B decommissioning In real terms, this is an extra 42.5p per litre of petrol and 59p per litre of diesel. There is variation between different stations in the West too - sometimes as much as 11p per litre for petrol - even if you discount motorway service stations that typically charge a premium. Alex Wood from the Yeovil branch of Freewheelers, which delivers blood samples and other medical supplies by motorbike, said the impact has been "huge". "This year since January, it's gone up 20% so it's quite a big increase across our operational costs. It's so unpredictable too." Both petrol and diesel prices have risen by a third or more in just the last seven months The charity is now having to dip into its reserves to keep afloat. "We're having to do a lot more fundraising so that we can keep operating," Wood said. "We just have to keep going as best we can, we have to keep plodding on." A taxi company based in Stroud in Gloucestershire previously told the BBC the current situation was a "complete nightmare" as it faced "continual pressure to lowball" its prices to stay afloat. James Berry said the government needs to intervene to soften the blow Berry's Coaches, which runs five services from the South West to London every day, said its costs have risen by £750,000 this year due to climbing fuel prices. James Berry said it has had "a big impact", but he was confident the company could "weather the storm" as it had done before in its 100-year history. "We've absorbed a lot of that cost ourselves but unfortunately we've had to apply fuel surcharges across a number of our services - a £2 surcharge on each leg of the journey to London," he said. "The government have delayed the rise in fuel duty but relatively that's quite a small impact - it will go up by 5p at some point by 2027. "Really what we would like to see if further fuel duty cuts. That would be a huge benefit from the industry." Chancellor John Healey said he was "very conscious" of people being hit by spiralling fuel prices caused by international factors. He said he was "glad" to have frozen fuel duty until the end of the year and brought 'fuel finder' apps to help people find the cheapest petrol stations. "I'm very aware as I prepare the budget - I'll deliver it a month today - that this needs to be a breathing space budget, recognising the cost of living and the cost of business pressures," he said at the Labour Party Conference. The BBC has found the most expensive petrol stations by doing an analysis of local prices using Fuel Finder UK, external, which presents prices from individual stations that are fed into a government dataset. Excluding petrol stations at motorway services or right next to motorway junctions, which are often much more expensive than average, there is still some variation from place to place. title: BBC Inside Science
description: What are the next steps for the world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·01 Oct 2026,·28 mins Tom Whipple travels 100m below Switzerland to the tunnels of CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC) where the beams have been powered down to begin the High-Luminosity LHC upgrade. Paulo Fessia, deputy head of the upgrade project, shows us what they're doing and why. In one of the cavernous halls on the site, Antti Onnela explains what the machinery is used for when it's not smashing particles together; understanding the formation of clouds. With Eva Sommer, Run Coordinator of the project, we learn how clouds are born from aerosol particles in a specialised chamber and how this informs climate models. We also learn about what many hope is the next phase of European particle physics, the future circular collider (FCC). The FCC is due to be 3.4 times larger than the LHC and cost around £14 billion. Guy Wilkinson tells us why he believes the cost is justified. And what will they do with all the substrate that is cleared for the new tunnels? Tom visits plant scientist Christiana Staudinger at the OpenSkyLab project in the fields above CERN's tunnels where they are making soil in hopes of replenishing the world's dwindling sources. Presenter: Tom Whipple Producers: Ella Hubber, Katie Tomsett and Ed Prendeville Editor: Ilan Goodman Production Co-ordinator: Jana Bennett-Holesworth

title: Netanyahu says Flydubai flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination'
description: Israel's prime minister says the pilot who tried to take over the Flydubai plane clearly intended to "down the plane".
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination". The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely. Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu also said it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane". Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose". This video can not be played Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes The co-pilot is currently being questioned in Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing. However UAE officials say they have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag. Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal that's not a question". "And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think ... that'll give us a pretty good clue but again I don't make final conclusions yet but that's the indications we have now." The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say". Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight? The attacker was arrested in Saudi Arabia and is expected to be transferred to the UAE, Netanyahu said. Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero". India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well". The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage" Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic. The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane. Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport. Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code. At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi. Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident. Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive. Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers. The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv. title: Lib Dem MPs criticise Davey over pension triple lock response
description: Sir Ed questioned the PM's plans to change the triple lock, telling the BBC removing it "would put more pensioners into poverty".
body: Liberal Democrat MPs have criticised their party leader over his defence of the pension triple lock. Senior Lib Dems, who are on the party's frontbench, have privately attacked Sir Ed Davey for his response to the prime minister's plans to adjust the policy, which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is highest. They joined unsolicited criticism in public and private from others in the party, with one saying the majority of Lib Dem MPs disagree with their leader. It comes after Sir Ed told the BBC removing the triple lock "would put more pensioners into poverty". "This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he told the Today programme. Under Andy Burnham's plan - which he hopes will raise £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s - the automatic annual link with average earnings would be removed from 2030 so the state pension rises with at least 2.5% or inflation, whichever is higher. "His proposals are to deal with social care in the next decade when it needs to be done now," Sir Ed said. "It's a little bit of a vibe. It's not a solution," he said. But multiple Lib Dems at different levels have now criticised Sir Ed's response. Could changing the pension triple lock pay for Burnham's big social care plan? What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it? A Lib Dem MP contacted the BBC after Sir Ed's interview to say the majority of the parliamentary party would not support opposing Burnham's changes to the triple lock. Another, Tom Gordon, who represents Harrogate & Knaresborough, said Sir Ed's criticism of Burnham's plan to adjust the triple lock was "nonsense" and "gaslights an entire generation into believing it's for our benefit". He wrote on X: "The idea that we're keeping the triple lock to help millennials is at best for the birds, and at worst downright insulting. I say that as a millennial." He added: "Telling millennials we're keeping the triple lock to help us in 30 years' time is nonsense. "We're on course to be the first generation worse off than our parents. We're locked out of the housing market, paying higher taxes, repaying student loans that never seem to shrink, and putting off having children because of the cost of living." Vikki Slade, the party's MP for Mid-Dorset and North Poole, said on Bluesky: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind." She added that she was "proud" of the triple lock when it was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010, "but we must plan for future not venerate the past". A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "The triple lock has always been controversial. "It's done a lot of good but its job isn't done yet, so Labour's plan would push too many of today's workers into poverty when they retire. "We want Andy Burnham to get back around the table so that we can find a lasting consensus on social care with a sustainable funding model - not one pulled out of the pockets of a group of people who can least afford it." The Lib Dems, and other opposition parties, are battling to respond to a new set of priorities from the Labour government under Burnham. One frontbench Lib Dem MP told the BBC after Burnham's Labour conference speech: "Lots of us [are] struggling tonight with [a] Labour leader articulating Lib Dem values better than we do." They pointed to Burnham's promises on electoral reform, social care, the water industry, and relations with Europe - all Lib Dem campaign points in recent years. "I'm honestly utterly despondent with the state of things," another Lib Dem MP said. Some senior Lib Dems believe Sir Ed's position as leader has been vulnerable for some time, even if they stressed no challenge is imminent. "A plausible candidate could take him tomorrow in a bloodless coup," one prominent party figure said. "But that person hasn't yet revealed themselves as far as I'm aware. Nobody is going to blow anything up without a clear plan to put something in its place." Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: Hundreds of criminals start leaving prison under new early release scheme
description: Around 4,500 inmates are expected to be released early by June 2027 under a scheme designed to stop prisons becoming full.
body: Around 4,500 prisoners will be released early in waves between October this year and June 2027 Hundreds of criminals are being released early from prisons in England and Wales under new rules introduced to prevent facilities reaching capacity. The first 700 of an expected 4,500 inmates eligible under the scheme were due to be let out on Thursday. The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full. But the plan has been strongly criticised by victims and questions have been raised over whether the Probation Service has sufficient resources to monitor thousands more criminals in the community. Prisons in England and Wales are a matter of months away from reaching capacity, with Ministry of Justice data showing as of Monday 87,499 people were incarcerated, taking prison population levels up to 98.2%. Thursday's release is the first of 10 scheduled to take place, with the final slated for June 2027. Prisoners released initially were serving sentences of up to 19 months, with the most serious offenders - serving fixed sentences of more than 12 years - leaving in later waves. We fear for our lives after being told our abusive exes will be freed from jail early 'Overcrowded' and 'set up to fail': Freed prisoners react to early release scheme What's behind having to release some prisoners early? Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Treasury minister James Murray said: "I know the level of concern and maybe anger will be intense, and it's worth me making clear that this is not a situation where there is any good solution - there's just a series of very difficult choices we've got to take." He said the government "inherited a prison system on the brink" and without early releases the country would face a situation where "people who are arrested now can't go behind bars". Murray said measures were in place to restrict criminals' movements in the community, adding: "I can't guarantee exactly what will happen, but I can tell people we have done everything we can to reduce the amount of people being released as far possible." An early release programme introduced by the Conservatives saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024. Sir Keir Starmer's government introduced the Sentencing Act to deal with the ongoing capacity crisis, which stipulated that offenders who were due to spend 40% or 50% of their sentences in prison would leave after a third - while prisoners who previously served two thirds would leave after half. The number of people expected to be released under this scheme was cut from around 6,000 after Prime Minister Andy Burnham intervened to review its terms, removing eligibility for crimes including all forms of manslaughter, grooming offences and causing or allowing the death of a child. The scheme does not apply to indeterminate sentences, which are handed out for the most serious offences like murder, and require a parole board to deem a prisoner safe to be released. London Victims' Commissioner Andrea Simon said the exemptions "have not included some offenders whose imminent release is a genuinely terrifying prospect for their victims". She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "[There is] no real reason to believe that an even shorter spell in prison will have dealt with the risk that their offender poses." Simon also questioned whether electronic tagging would be an effective safeguard, saying the equipment "will tell you where someone is but it can't stop them from doing something they shouldn't be doing". Earlier this week, the Chief Inspector of Probation Martin Jones said the electronic monitoring regime had "not kept pace" and could create "a false sense of assurance" unless failing are addressed. Some newly released prisoners spoke to the BBC as they were freed, including former bus driver Michael Bogle - who described the conditions inside London's Wandsworth Prison as "awful". "Tagging is better than prison," he told reporters in support of the early release scheme. But others said they were concerned about a lack of support awaiting them on the outside, while one man told the BBC he did not know he was being released until Thursday morning. This video can not be played Watch: Freed prisoners speak to the BBC as they are released early Kirsty Pellant is among victims whose perpetrator was expected to be released in the coming months. A man was convicted of several offences against her, including stalking, and jailed for five years in January 2025 after she discovered her photograph had been used to create a fake identity online and portray her as a sex worker. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had received assurances he would not be let out in the first wave of releases but was not told when he would be. The uncertainty "leaves us in such a dangerous position as victims because we need to be prepared, we need to know what we're dealing with," she added. Prisoners released early can immediately be returned to prison if they breach the terms of their licence, including by committing another crime, contacting a victim or living at an address not approved by authorities. However, charities have raised concerns that domestic abuse survivors may still be put at risk, despite such provisions. "We know that license conditions are frequently breached by perpetrators", the charity Refuge warned, and cautioned that it was "deeply concerned that newly released perpetrators will be able to continue their campaign of abuse" without proper enforcement. Women's Aid chief executive Farah Nazeer meanwhile said the scheme could further erode "incredibly low" trust in the criminal justice system, meaning "even greater numbers of women and children may be left without protection". title: 'My boss stabbed me then left prison early, but no one told me for months'
description: Hannah Pritchett said she was not told for five months that her attacker had been freed from prison.
body: Hannah Pritchett said an administrative error meant she did not find out her attacker had been released early from prison for five months Hannah Pritchett was 18 when she was stabbed in the lower back and hip by her boss Luisa Santos. She was about an hour into her waitressing shift in May 2022 at the Three Horseshoes pub in Princethorpe, Warwickshire, when the blade went in. It was a fish knife, and with its cuts came Santos's false accusation the teen had had an affair with her husband. That October, Santos was jailed for 10 years after being convicted of attempted murder. She was released in January 2026 under the Early Removal Scheme, which allows foreign national inmates in England and Wales, under certain criteria, to exit prison before they would have previously been allowed for the purpose of deportation. Pritchett did not know of her attacker's departure from prison until five months after the fact. Sharing with the BBC the scheme's effect on her, she said she had been made to feel like an "afterthought", which was "just appalling". A Ministry of Justice (MOJ) spokesperson said: "This was an awful crime, and our thoughts remain with Hannah Pritchett. Keeping victims informed is a vital part of our work and we are committed to always improving our service." When asked by the BBC what the timeline should be for victims being informed of an offender's release under the removal scheme, the MOJ said the intention was for all victims to be contacted as soon as possible once information was available. In the case of Pritchett, who was informed by the Victims Liaison Unit in June, there was an administrative error, the MOJ said, adding the matter had been escalated to management in both that unit and the prison in question. Santos was deported having served three years and eight months in prison. The BBC has also sought clarification on her native country. "Foreign nationals deported under the Early Removal Scheme are banned from ever returning to the UK," the MOJ spokesperson said. According to Pritchett, however, the situation had made her "see that victims aren't at the forefront of these decisions". Now 23, she said she had expected Santos to remain in prison until 2032 and thought she would have that time in which to come to terms with what had happened. "When you get told on a random Tuesday in June that your attacker is now out and [is not serving] their sentence any longer it makes you feel that everything you have fought for was for nothing," said Pritchett, who lives in Coventry. "Receiving that news was incredibly difficult and left me feeling let down by the justice system." "It was a reminder that although a sentence may come to an end, the impact on victims continues long after." "I went through a very difficult time when I was told my attacker was released early, especially as I found out five months after – it made things so much worse," she said. Pritchett underwent surgery in hospital following the attack and said she had been "incredibly lucky to survive". Luisa Santos was jailed for 10 years but was released after three years and eight months under the Early Removal Scheme for foreign nationals On Thursday, hundreds of prisoners will walk free from prison as part of the government's expanded early release scheme to free up capacity in overcrowded prisons across the country. Pritchett questioned whether hundreds of victims were going to be made aware that their attackers would be released. "In my case an administrative error led me to find out five months after," she said. "If someone's attacker is released in the UK, what happens if they go out one day and see them in the street without being made aware?" She said victims should be "at the forefront" of decisions on early release. "My case was horrendous and I wouldn't wish that on anyone." Pritchett (right) and her sister Beth (left) have raised money for knife crime prevention charities following the attack As part of her recovery and healing, Pritchett now raises money for knife crime prevention charities. She plans to walk the Great Glen Way in Scotland next year, external and is hoping to raise £5,000 and finish the challenge on the fifth anniversary of the attack. "Five years ago, I was incredibly fortunate to survive - five years on, I'm choosing to keep moving forward," she said. The MOJ said that offenders leaving prison from 1 October would be monitored under the "toughest supervision" with the "biggest ever expansion of electronic monitoring rolled out". Offenders would be electronically tagged and monitored when they left prison and £700m was being invested in probation and community punishment, the MOJ added. It said victims would be offered "better practical and emotional support" through a newly launched helpline operated by Victim Support. title: 'Overcrowded' and 'set up to fail': Freed prisoners react to early release scheme
description: Offenders speak to the BBC as the first wave of early releases see hundreds of prisoners freed.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Freed prisoners speak to the BBC as they are released early As hundreds of prisoners across England and Wales are released early under a new scheme designed to free up prison space, some of those freed have told the BBC of the "hectic" conditions they are leaving behind - and their concerns about a lack of support waiting for them outside. Around 700 offenders are expected to be freed with the first wave on Thursday, as prisoners serving sentences of up to 19 months become eligible for release after a third of their term. The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full. But some victims have questioned how they will be protected, while a probation worker told the BBC that managing the influx of offenders may be "just too much". Why are hundreds of prisoners being released early? Hundreds of criminals start leaving prison under new early release scheme We fear for our lives after being told our abusive exes will be freed from jail early Outside Wandsworth Prison in London, former bus driver Michael Bogle was adamant he would not return to the Victorian-era facility - describing the conditions as "awful". He served 78 days for shoplifting soap detergent, and had initially been given a suspended 32-week sentence but had breached it. Bogle told reporters offenders were locked up for 23 hours a day. He said he knew of one prisoner who had recently taken his own life. The early release scheme should continue, he said: "It's good. Tagging is better than prison". Another man released from Wandsworth on Thursday - who declined to be named and said he had been sentenced for "taking things without paying for them" - said the prison was "so crowded even the rats are complaining". Matthew Johnson, 35 also spoke of poor conditions as he expressed relief to be leaving Leeds Prison. He said he had been released after six months from an 18 month sentence for actual bodily harm. Asked what he would say to opponents of early release, he said: "You want to see what's inside these rooms, then you'll know. "It's hectic. It's crowded. It's overcrowded – cells for one person with two people in them." He added: "Staff are overwhelmed anyway with what they've got to cope with at the minute". Jake Sykes said he expected to be fitted with an electronic tag on Thursday afternoon Jake Sykes, 33, similarly spoke of "disgusting" conditions as he left Lincoln Prison, after being sentenced to 16 weeks in prison for shoplifting. He will be tagged, banned from going to the pub and have a curfew. Sykes said overcrowding inside was "bad", with prisoners sharing cells. "It's full of cockroaches, rats. It's disgusting in there, filthy." But he said the justice system's biggest problem was the lack of support for offenders after they leave prison. "The support is there whilst you're there, so you're secure, you feel safe there," he said. "And then when you get out, there's nothing." David, 50, said he was convicted for stealing some glasses Back in London, a man who gave his name only as David as he left HMP Brixton said he did not believe the scheme could work, because of a lack of support for inmates on the outside. He feared the justice system was "setting us up to fail". "Stop sending people to prison in the first place. Help them before they get there," he said. "I've been in and out of prison all my life. It's help I need", he added. The number of people expected to be released under this scheme was cut from around 6,000 after the prime minister intervened to review its terms, removing eligibility for crimes including all forms of manslaughter, grooming offences and causing or allowing the death of a child. Early release will not apply to indeterminate sentences, which are handed out for the most serious offences like murder, and require a parole board to deem a prisoner safe to be released. Those released early can immediately be returned to prison if they breach the terms of their licence, including by committing another crime, contacting a victim or living at an address not approved by authorities. However, London Victims' Commissioner Andrea Simon is among those to have raised concerns about the provisions in place - warning the exemptions do not include "some offenders whose imminent release is a genuinely terrifying prospect for their victims". Meanwhile, concerns have been voiced about the probation system's ability to manage those released. Earlier this week, the Chief Inspector of Probation Martin Jones said the electronic monitoring regime had "not kept pace" and could create "a false sense of assurance" unless failing are addressed. title: Scottish Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal freed on bail after nine years in Indian prison
description: The Sikh activist from Dumbarton was arrested in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.
body: This video can not be played Jagtar Singh Johal freed on bail after nine years in prison in India A Scottish Sikh activist has been released from prison in India after being detained for almost nine years without being convicted. Jagtar Singh Johal thanked "the almighty" as he walked free from gate three of the Tihar Prison complex in Delhi. The 39-year-old from Dumbarton was arrested in 2017 over allegations he had a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures - which he denies. Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court on 18 September, but has only now been released from detention. He was embraced by his mother-in-law and father-in law after leaving the jail in Janakpuri, in the south-west of the city. Johal was given flowers and presented with a bright orange saropau, an honorary garment given in Sikh tradition to convey respect. His release was welcomed with shouts of "Jo hole so nihal, sat Sri Akal" or "whoever utters these words shall be fulfilled true is the eternal timeless Lord". Jagtar Singh Johal was released from prison in Delhi on Thursday Johal had to surrender his passport as part of his bail conditions and is barred from speaking to the media about the case. He was arrested in the Punjab region in 2017, just weeks after his wedding in the country. He is accused of travelling to Paris in 2013 and handing about £3,000 to the Khalistan Liberation Force – an armed organisation which has carried out violent attacks in pursuit of a separate Sikh state. It is claimed that this money was used to fund weapons to kill, or attempt to kill, religious and political figures in Punjab in 2016 and 2017. The Indian authorities claim Johal is a member of the KLF and that "he actively participated and had complete knowledge of the conspiracy". However, his supporters say he was targeted for blogging about alleged human rights abuses against the Sikh community in India and was coerced into signing a false confession to participation in the killings. Johal's family say no concrete evidence has been presented against him and that the case was built on the testimony of unreliable witnesses. His imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured. Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed. Johal was embraced by family members after his release Last year Johal was acquitted in a case where he was accused of financially supporting the KLF terror group. He remained in prison because he faces federal charges in eight other cases, for which he potentially faces the death penalty. However, his legal team argues that these cases are almost identical and that the other charges should be dismissed. There have been hundreds of hearings over the past nine years and the bail order concludes that the trial is "certainly not likely to conclude anytime soon". At the family home in Dumbarton, celebratory music could be heard after relatives spoke to Johal. His brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has lobbied successive governments for his release, said there had also been tears on hearing confirmation of the news. He described his release as a "first step" but a "step in the right direction". "There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn't dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes," Gurpreet said. "I'll sleep well tonight, knowing that he's not behind bars. Tomorrow morning, the fight continues. We'll keep on fighting until he's home with us." Jagtar Singh Johal (right) with his brother Gurpreet Dan Dolan of the human rights charity Reprieve UK said Johal "still had the threat of a death sentence hanging over him" despite his release. He said: "Jagtar remains on trial in cases that could last for decades and end in capital punishment, centred on a baseless allegation. "His bail conditions deny him any semblance of a normal life." Redress senior legal advisor Chris Esdaile said Johal release was a "relief" but added he still faced "onerous" bail conditions. "The prolonged uncertainty itself amounts to psychological torture," he said. "The remaining cases against him need to be dropped without further delay." title: Injured O'Reilly withdraws from England squad
description: Nico O'Reilly withdraws from the England squad for their final two Nations League games of the international break because of injury.
body: Nico O'Reilly played for England at the 2026 World Cup Nico O'Reilly has withdrawn from the England squad for their final two Nations League matches of the international break because of injury. The left-back played the full game for manager Thomas Tuchel's side in the 3-2 defeat by Spain but missed Tuesday's 2-0 win against the Czech Republic. O'Reilly has now returned to club side Manchester City for "further assessment" and will miss the trip to Croatia on Saturday and the return game against the Czechs on Tuesday. England do not plan to call-up any replacements. Lewis Hall replaced O'Reilly against the Czech Republic and the Newcastle United full-back combined well with former Magpies team-mate Anthony Gordon on England's left flank. title: Tories committed to pension triple lock, deputy leader says
description: Alex Bughart says pensioners are a 'special case' as there is nothing they can do to increase their income.
body: This video can not be played Alex Burghart says pensioners are a 'special case' as they are unable to increase their income Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart has described pensioners as a "special case" as he reaffirmed the party's commitment to the state pension triple lock. He argued that retirees deserve different treatment because, once they stop working, they can do "absolutely nothing" to increase their income. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has set out plans to end the existing state pension triple lock from 2030 to help fund a new national care service. In a round of interviews with BBC local radio stations, Burghart suggested that any "difficult decisions" on welfare should focus on working-age benefits. He told BBC Radio Berkshire that it was "obvious" there should be two different approaches to welfare – one for pensioners and another for working-age adults. He said pensioners had "reached the end of their working lives" and there was "nothing they can do to improve their circumstances", adding that they had "a right to be looked after properly". "The same is not true for people who are working age," he said. Burghart added: "I just think it's a very practical and decent argument and that most people will understand that." Asked about adults with disabilities who cannot work, he said his argument applied to "people who can work and should be in work". The Conservatives have long campaigned for curbs to spending on sickness and disability benefits, including Personal Independence Payments (PIP). Last year, Sir Keir Starmer faced a major backbench rebellion over proposed cuts to disability benefits, leading to a U-turn which saw the plans substantially watered down. Speaking on Radio Hereford and Worcester, Burghart suggested Burnham had missed an opportunity to press ahead with the cuts after taking office. "He didn't do it, and now we're in this very serious problem where this huge budget at the centre of government isn't going to be touched," he said. The Conservative deputy leader also defended his party's "tough love" approach to unemployment benefits for young people. He said 18 year olds leaving school would no longer be able simply to "sign on" the following day. "You will be able to claim some money but that will require you to turn up to the job centre and under supervision either do a course, or do your job applications or look for work," he said. Burghart said some young people were signing on "very early in life" and forming "very bad habits" which could be difficult to break. He argued this "wasn't good for anybody". Burghart also reaffirmed the Conservatives' "very, very firm" pledge not to enter an electoral pact with Reform UK, either before or after a general election. He criticised Reform over what he described as "scandal around their money" and referred to donations from people involved in cryptocurrency. "We do not want to do a deal with those people," he said. "Kemi [Badenoch] is someone with enormous personal integrity and we are not doing a deal with them." title: Russia targets busy bridge in central Kyiv in broad daylight
description: The Pivdennyi bridge came under fire as a metro train was travelling across - the first such attack on Kyiv's bridges.
body: The base of a central stanchion on the Pivdennyi bridge was hit late on Thursday morning Two Russian drones have hit one of Kyiv's main bridges, bringing public transport in the Ukrainian capital to a halt and signalling a new stage in Moscow's attacks. The Pivdennyi or Southern bridge came under fire as a metro train was travelling across. Passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system. The Pivdennyi bridge is one of the main arteries across the Dnipro river dividing western and eastern Kyiv. Kyiv's bridges had not been hit before Thursday's strikes - and despite a dramatic explosion close to a main support section, city authorities said preliminary checks "did not find any critical damage to the structure". For the people of Kyiv, the drone strikes were another powerful reminder that Russia has their city firmly in its sights and is doing everything it can to disrupt life in the capital. Kyiv had just suffered its first co-ordinated attacks on the city's energy grid since the end of last winter, and commentators believe Russia has stepped up its campaign seeing that Ukraine is suffering from a shortage of air defences. Strikes on Wednesday also heralded a return to power cuts in the capital. Although Kyiv authorities have spent months constructing smaller-scale power plants to counter Russia's anticipated winter campaign, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a combined strike on such a scale had not taken place since the end of spring. Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign The first big attack on the capital on Thursday came when a Russian drone slammed into the third floor of a school at about 09:00 local time (10:00 GMT). Although more than 100 students had been at the school at the time, they had all reached a shelter when the drone hit. One of the school's walls partially collapsed. "[The shelter's] structure is strong, so none of the children were hurt, neither were any staff," said head teacher Valentyna Chorna. "They just kept on with their lessons." Russia denies targeting civilians, but Chorna said that to destroy her nation "they need to destroy children". President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had to be held fully accountable. Part of a wall and a staircase were destroyed in the Russian attack Later in the morning, two drones hit the Pivdenny bridge, one hitting the base of a central stanchion. Ukrainian 5 Kanal TV reporter Mariana Mykytenko described how one of the passengers on her metro train shouted the word "Shahed", referring to Russia's Iranian-designed drones, before the blast sent dust pouring into their carriage. No-one in her compartment was hurt, she said, and "the train took people to Vydubychi station on the right bank, then it didn't go any further". The right bank is on the west side of the Dnipro river. Metro trains were suspended but road traffic was eventually allowed to resume. It is not yet clear what kind of drone was used in the Kyiv bridge attack, but Ukrainian officials say a new design of Russia's jet-powered drones came into operation for the first time on Wednesday. The drone has a 40kg warhead and is especially designed to destroy high-voltage electricity pylons and iron bridge structures, according to Zelensky's technology adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, also known as Flash. In recent weeks, Russia has had considerable success with jet-powered drones and Ukrainian air force officials say that, during September, at least 3,177 were launched. Their high speed has caused problems for Ukraine's beleaguered air defences. Kyiv's Institute of Nuclear Research came under drone attack on Wednesday night and, earlier in the week, one person was killed when a drone targeted the National Academy of Sciences. title: New life for dog rescued from house with 83 others
description: Katy is one of the springer spaniels who has now been rehomed after RSPCA investigation.
body: Katy is one of more than 80 dogs rescued from "squalid conditions" at the house in Tickhill, near Doncaster A springer spaniel who was one of 84 dogs living in "squalid conditions" in a family home has been given a second chance at life. Katy was discovered at a property in Doncaster in April last year, where animals covered in faeces and urine had been left to breed by themselves. RSPCA officers executing a warrant at the rural cottage in Tickhill described the conditions as "the worst they had encountered during their careers". Katy has since been adopted by Wendy and Lindsay Cann, from Cowling in North Yorkshire, who said she had "come along at the right time". "I wasn't going to get another dog because I was too upset when I lost my last one, Alfie," Wendy explained. "He was 15 and it was just too distressing, so we weren't having another one, but life's not the same without a dog. "When you've always had a dog, you just can't live without one." Katy now lives with her new owners Wendy and Lindsay in North Yorkshire The owner recalled Katy's first few days at her new home, where she initially refused to venture onto the grass. "She stayed on the patio because I don't think she knew what the grass was," Wendy added. "She did everything she needed to on there and then the second day, she was romping around the grass chasing the butterflies. "It didn't take her long to figure out that she was safe and she was home." When Katy and the other dogs were found, officers reported the kitchen being covered in dirt and faeces "from floor to ceiling". More than 30 dogs were crowded together on the stairs, while others climbed on the kitchen sides or cowered in corners. Although the family responsible for the animals was inside the property, police had to force entry. Faye Gibbons, from the RSPCA, remembered when Katy had been brought into their care. "We could see that she was traumatised," she said. "The team were very shocked at just how difficult she was finding her new surroundings. "When she first arrived, her coat was stained in urine, with faeces. "It was just a harrowing sight and probably one of the hardest cases our team have worked on." More than 80 animals were found living in "squalid conditions" On Tuesday, children's social worker David Parkes was found guilty of failing to ensure the welfare of the animals, which were kept at the home he shared with his family. He had denied animal welfare offences, claiming his wife, Delphine, and son, Sam, were primarily responsible for the dogs' care due to his heavy workload. However, the 61-year-old was found guilty following a two-day trial at Barnsley Magistrates' Court. Delphine Parkes, 60, and Sam Parkes, 28, pleaded guilty to the same offences at a hearing earlier this year. All three will be sentenced on 9 December. An RSPCA spokesperson said one of the dogs later had to be put to sleep due to ongoing health issues, but all of the others had been rehomed. Faye Gibbons agreed Katy was a very lucky dog. "Just looking at her here, she's landed on a paws, let's say," she added.
