title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
description: "My family and I will not truly be safe as long as Putin is in power," says the former chess world champion.
body: Garry Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to found political opposition movements in Russia An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger. Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done. His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors. Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety. Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities. Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US. Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so. "My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions." Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013. He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects. The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine. He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia. Ilya Ponomarev was the only MP to vote against Russia's illegal annexation of Ukraine's Crimea in 2014 A network of individuals working for the Russian intelligence services has operated since at least 2024, the US Justice Department said. It said the so-called RIS Network had been conspiring and conducting attacks and murders on Russian dissidents and defectors around the world. Five alleged members of the network had been accused of operating "as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin", Assistant Attorney General for national security John A Eisenberg said. The five people alleged to be responsible for organising the plots are Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro. All five remain at large, the Justice Department said. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when the indictment was unsealed that he would not comment on the charges until he had heard or seen "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts". title: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
description: Adam Polovincik tells the BBC he told his young children "everything is going to be all right" as flight plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m).
body: Adam Polovincik on the Flydubai flight A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight. A Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes around two hours into its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered him and retook control to land safely. Adam Polovincik told BBC Newshour that he hugged his six-year-old son and three-year-old daughter "really hard" and tried to stay calm for them as the attack unfolded. He praised the pilot who was stabbed and passengers who fought off and subdued the attacker, saying they were "true heroes". The stabbed pilot is in a stable condition in hospital, while the alleged attacker has been arrested. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to say whether Iran was involved in the attack, but that the alleged attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination". Polovincik, who was sitting in aisle 13, was flying home with his wife and children after an "amazing" holiday in Singapore and Thailand. He said there had been a "huge degree of panic" on the plane as there was a "very, very, very sharp decrease in height". What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute". Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said. "After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said. "At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said. Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children. "You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice." But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight. There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period. After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane. In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down. Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers. Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood." Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in. "Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being". Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did". After the situation onboard was brought under control, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where Polovincik stressed the passengers, who were almost all Israeli, were treated well. "They brought us water and food and coffee and even sweets for the kids - even though we don't have any diplomatic relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said. The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, from where the plane departed, Netanyahu told Fox News. The passengers were taken to Tel Aviv on another flight later on Wednesday and were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags. Polovincik said it had been "such a terrible ending" to an amazing family trip and that it would take some time for his family to come to terms with what had occurred. title: Space for Gannon-Doak? Does McGinn keep place? Key questions for Pocognoli
description: Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli has decisions to make as he searches for his first win in North Macedonia on Saturday.
body: This video can not be played Nations League: North Macedonia v Scotland Nacionalna Arena Toše Proeski, Skopje Saturday, 3 October, 19:45 BST Two games, one point, no goals. And a home debut hampered by an early red card. New Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli might have hoped to know more about his side by now. But little was learned at Hampden on Tuesday as his 10-man team were outclassed by Switzerland. That makes Saturday’s match in North Macedonia - live on the BBC - even more important. A first win under the Belgian is needed. How might Scotland achieve that? And what are the key questions facing the head coach? You are the Scotland boss - what would you do? New coach, new players, but same old failings hamper Scotland Hampden debut to forget but Pocognoli looks at bigger picture Goalkeeper Angus Gunn admitted he'd "probably be disappointed" when he looked back at the goals he conceded against the Swiss. The 30-year-old was Steve Clarke's number one at the World Cup and, since then, has remained in the United States with San Jose Earthquakes. But a far from successful start at his new club - where he has conceded 23 goals in 11 games - has continued into international duty. Ricardo Rodriguez's opener was, in pundit Andy Halliday's view, "shoulder height [with] not a lot of pace". Gunn's failure to keep it out was "so poor", he said. While there was little that could be done for the Swiss' deserved second, the goalkeeper didn't cover himself in glory for the third goal, with Zeki Amdouni's finish going through him. Gunn's far from convincing performance sparked a conversation around whether he should start on Saturday. Will Pocognoli change goalkeeper after Swiss loss? In truth, he probably will due to the lack of better options. Scott Bain is in the Scottish Premiership with Falkirk, while Jon McCracken is with Bradford in England's League One. Liam Kelly is yet to be anywhere other than the bench for Rangers this term. But Pocognoli has not shied away from big calls so far - his initial bold squad and his offering of three debuts in two games stand out. It wouldn't be out of the question for him to shake things up in Skopje. "They were good strikes, but as a goalkeeper, I'm always disappointed when I concede a goal," Gunn acknowledged after facing the Swiss. "I'll look back and see what I could have done better and get better for the next game." Who knows when that next game will be... This video can not be played Should Gunn have saved this? While there is a little uncertainty in goal, Pocognoli may have been given a bit of clarity about the make-up of his defence in his first two games. Substitute Stephen Welsh was a winner on a grim night against the Swiss. The Swansea City defender settled nicely into his debut in Slovenia on Saturday on the left side of the back three, and might have felt aggrieved to drop to the bench on Tuesday as the head coach handed a debut to Luis Binks. But Jack Hendry's red card necessitated a reshuffle and Welsh was restored to the team in a more familiar position on the right and performed admirably again. Not only is the former Celtic and Motherwell defender vocal and versatile, he is also comfortable carrying the ball - a key asset in Pocognoli's style. His unexpected home debut ought to help him back into the starting line-up on Saturday, especially with Hendry suspended. This video can not be played 'Red card killed us' says Robertson While the second half in Slovenia showed Pocognoli's system can be exciting, it remains unclear if it best suits this Scotland squad? Two games in and winger Ben Gannon-Doak has yet to start. His impact as a substitute in both has been notable, leading Halliday to say he'd be "shocked" if the Bournemouth player didn't start against Group B1's bottom side. However, in the Belgian's 3-4-1-2 set-up, there is no obvious place for him. Wing-back would seem the most likely, but the 20-year-old's defensive instincts are not the same as those of Aaron Hickey or Nathan Patterson. Perhaps Pocognoli needs to be more flexible - something he said he is but has yet to show in his shape. But if he wants to stick to his preference, is this the game to try Gannon-Doak at wing-back? This video can not be played 'Time to have conversation about McGinn' Gannon-Doak offers an attacking threat like few others do in a Scotland shirt. He could do with a hand from some pals. John McGinn, anyone? The Aston Villa captain won a bounty of fouls against the Swiss, and though he was much-improved like the rest in the second half at the Stozice Arena, he's still not reaching the levels he does at his Premier League club. Pocognoli needs more from the Tartan Army talisman as he hurtles towards a century of caps - he's on 91. The vice-captain is another whose name has been mentioned in the 'does this system suit Scotland' conversation. It's been a while since McGinn delivered one of those big performances for his country, but his ability to create a moment of magic and drive a team forward makes him difficult to drop. Another big call for Pocognoli to ponder... What should be a little more straightforward is giving Kieron Bowie another start. The Sassuolo striker was sacrificed just over 10 minutes into his first Scotland start to make space for Welsh in defence. His partnership with Oli McBurnie showed promising signs in the 20 minutes or so they were together in Slovenia, but there was little time to build on that cameo against the Swiss. Surely he and the Hull City striker will get another chance? If there were any concerns McBurnie wasn't up for the fight - five years on from his last international involvement - they have been quashed in these past two games. His work-rate as a largely solo striker - hauling his team up and holding the ball in - was commendable. If only Bowie was still on

title: Two men jailed for raping woman in underground car park
description: The rape offence took place in September 2023 when both men were 17 and some of it was recorded on CCTV.
body: Luis Dos Martins Mariano (left) and Alcino Soares have been jailed for rape Two men have been jailed for raping a woman in an underground car park in County Tyrone. Luis Dos Martins Mariano, 20, with an address of Sloan Street, and Alcino Soares, 21, with an address of Braeside, also in Dungannon, both previously pleaded guilty to rape. Both men moved to Northern Ireland from East Timor when they were younger. The rape took place on 10 September 2023 when both men were 17 and some of it was recorded on CCTV. The victim was 19 at the time. At Downpatrick Crown Court on Thursday the judge sentenced both men to six years, three of those will be served in prison and three out on license. Both men appeared in court via video link from Hydebank prison. Judge Richard Green said the CCTV footage of the incident "makes for disturbing viewing". He also commended the "bravery" of the victim coming forward and said she was a "survivor". He said her impact statement was both "eloquent and moving". Judge Green said the victim was subjected to a "prolonged and humiliating ordeal" with Soares and Mariano taking turns to rape her. "It should have been obvious to both of them she was intoxicated and she was less able to recognise the danger she was in, she was not capable of resisting this cowardly attack on her and she was not able to call for help," he said. Judge Green said taking her to a car park at this late time showed a "significant degree of planning and foresight". When sentencing the men Judge Green said he took into account their young age at the time of offending, their learning difficulties, the fact they had both entered guilty pleas, delays to the case and time they had already spent in prison. Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting During an earlier sentencing hearing last month, the court heard details of the rape. During the hearing in Dungannon Crown Court on 3 September, the prosecution outlined the victim's account. A Tetum interpreter was present in court and stood beside Soares and Mariano translating the prosecution's account. The court heard that the victim had been on a night out in Dungannon on 9 September 2023. She said she had been outside a fast food shop and was "quite drunk". She said she was approached by two males who appeared to be East Timorese. Her next memory is then of both men walking either side of her down an alleyway which led into a car park. The victim recalled she had difficulty standing and could not talk properly. Soares (left) and Mariano moved to Northern Ireland from East Timor when they were younger The prosecution outlined that the victim said one of the males "started to rape" her while the other male kept watch and "stood laughing". The prosecution said the victim also recalled being brought to the corner of the carpark were she was raped again. She said the males eventually left her and she eventually got up and left the car park. The prosecution also outlined CCTV in the car park recorded the events and that it was "consistent with the defendants pleas". The prosecution said was it was clear the victim was "incapacitated and in a vulnerable state". Both men were subsequently arrested. In March 2025, the pair appeared together at Dungannon Crown Court where Mariano admitted rape but Soares pleaded not guilty. Numerous adjournments followed and just before Soares was due to stand trial, in October 2025 he pleaded guilty to rape. At Dungannon Crown Court on 3 September 2026, a defence barrister for Mariano said he was "not disputing the harm caused by this case". The barrister outlined how an expert report had found that Mariano had a "moderate learning disability". The barrister said when it came to his client it was a question of "age, vulnerability and cognitive ability". The defence barrister said there was no "challenge to the integrity and strength of the victim" and that she "clearly did not consent in this case". Mariano's barrister outlined that his client had apologised and expressed his "shame and remorse" about what had happened. Soares' defence barrister said his client was neither fluent in either Tetum or English. The barrister said an expert report outlined that this "language deficit" had led to difficulties and impacted his "understanding of societal norms and morals". The barrister said Soares apologised and had "accepted his wrongdoing and his remorse". Both men were ordered to be on the sex offenders register for life. They were also disqualified from working with children and young adults. Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Ch Insp Steph Finlay said the incident was an "appalling and deeply distressing attack on a young woman who should have been able to make her way home safely after meeting with friends". "The actions of these two men were predatory, degrading and showed a complete disregard for their victim," the officer said. I want to pay tribute to the tremendous courage she has shown throughout what has undoubtedly been an extremely difficult and traumatic process." She said the sentences "hold both men accountable for their actions". title: Bluetongue restriction zone to be expanded across all of Scotland
description: The Scottish government said the decision will simplify trading for farmers, hauliers, and auction markets.
body: Cases of bluetongue in Scotland were first detected in August Bluetongue restrictions are to be expanded across the whole of Scotland from Saturday. Parts of south-west Scotland were already in a restricted zone, after cases in the region began appearing in August. The Scottish government said the decision will make trading more straightforward for farmers, hauliers, and auction markets. Bluetongue is an insect-borne viral disease that affects sheep and cattle among other animals. It does not affect people or food safety but causes a high rate of death in infected sheep and fertility problems in infected cattle. The first case in Scotland was reported in early August, in a single sheep on a farm in Dumfries and Galloway. The decision to expand the zone follows talks with industry representatives, including the National Farmers' Union (NFU) Scotland, the National Sheep Association, and the Scottish Beef Association. The movement licences currently required to move susceptible livestock into, within, and out of the south-west zone, will no longer be needed after Saturday, due to the whole of Scotland sharing the same disease status. England and Wales are also in restricted zones, after cases escalated there over the summer. There is a high death rate among infected sheep Jim Fairlie, the Scottish government's minister for agriculture, marine and the islands, said bluetongue is "not going away any time soon" and called the restricted zone covering the whole of Scotland a "practical, sensible step." The disease has been detected on 40 premises since the south-west Scotland restricted zone was established in early September. The Scottish government said four of those cases were detected outside of the zone by tracing animal movements from the affected farms. Dumfries and Newton Stewart have the most affected premises, with six in each area. Referring to the autumn trading period, Fairlie said the decision removes "an administrative burden on farmers at what is a critical time in the trading calendar". "While extending the zone removes the need for movement licences, it does not change our long-term approach to tackling this disease," he said. "Vaccination remains the single most effective way for farmers to protect their animals from the worst effects of bluetongue, and I would strongly encourage anyone with susceptible livestock to speak to their vet now to discuss the right vaccination approach and to secure supplies ahead of next year's higher-risk season," he added. A joint Scottish government and industry communications group is being established to promote vaccination and to share advice on the impact of the disease with farmers and veterinary practitioners. Neil Shand, the chief executive of the Scottish Beef Association, said the decision is "the most logical way forward to prevent trade complications." Michael Priestley, policy manager with the National Sheep Association, said there was now a "trade-off" between the benefit of eased restrictions and the increased risk of the virus spreading. He said: "This trade-off is being made because of the faith in the vaccine technology, which to date has offered excellent coverage to livestock in affected areas of the UK." Symptoms of the disease include nasal discharge, redness and swelling of the lips, nose and muzzle, lameness or reluctance to stand, a decrease in milk production, and diarrhoea in cattle. Cases must be reported to the UK government's Animal and Plant Health agency, which publishes daily updates. title: UK on track for one of the warmest years on record after warm September
description: September was the fourth warmest year on record in the UK according to the Met Office and whilst overall rainfall was average there were large regional variations.
body: September was provisionally the joint fourth warmest on record for the United Kingdom, according to figures from the Met Office. And for the eighth month in a row, the average UK temperature was more than 1C above the norm. With warmer than average weather forecast for the rest of the year, we're on track for 2026 to be one of the warmest years on record. While there was some rainfall throughout September, most of it fell in Scotland, while eastern and south-east England had another drier-than-average month. Overall September was an unsettled and - on the face of it - unremarkable month for weather. But, it has still ended up being the joint fourth warmest on record. With a mean average temperature of 14.6C, it was 1.6C above the long-term average. Both maximum and minimum temperatures were consistently above normal with only very short-lived bursts of heat, falling short of any official heatwave. The highest temperature recorded in the month was 28.6C in Northolt, London on 6 September. And Northern Ireland, saw the latest day on record where a temperature above 25C was recorded with 25.5C on 21 September in Helen's Bay. It also remained relatively warm overnight with Northern Ireland recorded its joint warmest September for minimum temperature. 2026 has been remarkably warm so far with average temperatures much higher than normal Putting this month into the context of the year overall, it "fits with the general pattern that we're seeing of more frequent above average temperatures in the UK as our climate continues to change" according to Mike Kendon, Met Office climate scientist. According to the average Central England Temperature - representative of an area between Lancashire, London and Bristol and the longest temperature dataset in the world, going back to the 17th Century - kept by the Met Office, every month this year has been warmer than average. Using this dataset, the temperature is currently running at 2.6C above average and is on track to be one of the warmest years on record. The rest of this year would need to be significantly cooler than average to not beat 2025 which is currently the UK's warmest on record. With the super El Niño expected to peak over the next few months, the Met Office has already suggested that the rest of autumn and into the start of winter, will be warmer than average. Scientists believe that with El Niño - the warming of the tropical Pacific - higher temperatures are likely globally into next year, so 2027 could end up being even warmer. Despite some rain, Baitings reservoir in Ripponden was still very low in mid-September Across the UK, the average rainfall was as expected at 104%. However, this masks large regional variations. Most of the rainfall in September fell across Scotland which ended up having nearly 40% more than average. Parts of Yorkshire and in eastern England with parts of Yorkshire saw less than 20% of their usual rainfall. Lincolnshire only had around 30% of its average September rainfall. Despite most areas having at least some, it won't be enough to alleviate the drought situation across most of England and Wales. Environment Agency (EA) Chief Executive, Philip Duffy, said: "September's rainfall has been welcome, but a few weeks of unsettled weather is nowhere near enough to reverse the water deficits caused by a dry spring and record hot summer". The EA have previously said that there needs to be 20% more rainfall than normal over the next seven months for all areas to be considered out of drought. At least seven months of relentless rain needed to end drought, research shows Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather? Listen: How hot could the planet get? title: Body of baby girl found in Wales may have been in the water for weeks, police say
description: The body of the baby found along the north Wales shoreline was a girl, a post-mortem has revealed.
body: A member of the public found the body on the Menai Strait shoreline in Bangor The body of a baby girl found along a north Wales shoreline may have been in the water for up to a few weeks, according to initial indications. A member of the public found the body on the Menai Strait shoreline near Siliwen Road in Bangor, Gwynedd, on Sunday shortly before 17:00 BST. In an update on Thursday, North Wales Police said a post-mortem examination revealed the newborn was a girl. The force is continuing the search for the girl's mother and urged her to make contact with police. Further tests to find more about the baby are under way, North Wales Police said. "We understand that the mother may be fearful of coming forward but we urge her to make contact with us," Supt Llinos Davies said, adding that she wanted to reassure her that her welfare and safety was their "utmost concern". "Anyone with concerns about a girl or a woman you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us," Davies said. She said all names received would be treated with the utmost discretion and can be eliminated as the mother without delay. "I understand that this is a terribly sad incident for the community and I am grateful for the overwhelming support and assistance that we have received so far," Davies said. Fiona Giraud, director of midwifery and women's services for Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, said her priority remained with the mother. Addressing her, she said: "Our immediate concern remains to be your health, safety and wellbeing. "You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone," she said. "We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death, but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need. "I am asking you personally, please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you," Giraud said. title: Sisters tell of upskirting 'violation' during night out
description: Georgia and Alex Scholes said the men responsible had "picked the wrong girls" to target.
body: Alex (left) and Georgia Scholes said they confronted the men Two sisters have described the "complete violation" of being upskirted during a night out in Manchester but said the men responsible had "chosen the wrong girls" to target. Georgia, 25 and Alex Scholes, 22, had just left a restaurant in the city's Spinningfields area when two men followed them very closely up some stairs while filming them. Actress Georgia, who stars in ITV crime drama The Bay, said "something felt off" when she noticed one of the men holding his phone awkwardly, before realising he was recording. "The moment I realised what had happened, my heart just sank. It was a complete violation," she said. Greater Manchester Police said two men, aged in their 20s and 30s, had been arrested on suspicion of voyeurism following the alleged incident on Deansgate on 19 September. "Both men have been released on bail pending further enquiries," the force added. Georgia said she had confronted the men and told them: "You've just recorded us, please can you delete it. "And at that point I broke down and started crying because I was in utter shock. "I was in a situation where this bloke got footage up my dress, and he's gone off with it - I don't know what he's going to do with that footage. "He was shouting all sorts and one of them started running off while the other stayed oddly quite close to me." Georgia and Alex (right) repeatedly asked the men to delete the recording She asked for help from passers-by but said "not one person batted an eyelid". Alex also repeatedly asked one of the man to delete the video, and when he started running away, she took off her heels and chased after him. It was only at that point that a bouncer stepped in and stopped the other man, and both were later arrested. "If he hadn't had done that, they would have just got off, and I would have had to live with the fact that all happened," mother-of-two Georgia continued. "I'd gone out to town, we got our hair done and our make-up done and I felt good, but that whole feeling just went away. "When I woke up the next morning, I just felt an overwhelming sense of sadness because I felt like the whole night I had to justify myself. "When I spoke to the police, the first question that the woman asked me was are you sure he was recording you? It embeds a seed of doubt. "The message that I want to put out is that telling women to be hyper vigilant on a night out and, you know, be aware of your surroundings and what you drink isn't a solution, it's barely a plaster over what is a massive issue." Alex said: "They picked the wrong two girls that night. "We are not going to be belittled, and we will defend ourselves, and we received a whole load of abuse. "You're not going to violate me, my sister, or anyone in that manner and think you can get away with it. "You just feel violated. It's the complete disrespect. It taints every good emotion that you were feeling before it happened. "I feel like it is a crime that is so minimalised and normalised, and it is almost like you have to accept what has happened. "The norm should be calling out perversion and harassment." title: Watch: Why are students protesting at schools in France?
description: The BBC's Hugh Schofield is in Paris as a wave of school protests over overcrowded classes and teacher shortages spreads across France.
body: This video can not be played Hundreds of people, mostly minors, have been arrested and dozens injured as a wave of school protests over overcrowded classes and teacher shortages spreads across France, officials say. The demonstrations began in Paris last week but have escalated to cities including Dijon, Lyon, Strasbourg, Lille and Marseille, with teenagers blockading their schools for days. The BBC's Paris correspondent Hugh Schofield is in Paris as the protests stretch into their second week. Watch: Why are students protesting at schools in France? title: Water system a 'disaster', Green deputy leader says
description: Rachel Millward says her party would nationalise water companies to reverse years of “radical underinvestment".
body: The Green Party of England and Wales has long called for public ownership of water companies Green Party co-deputy leader Rachel Millward has said her party would nationalise water companies in England and Wales, criticising Prime Minister Andy Burnham's plans to bring them under public control as "vague". Millward told the BBC the country's water system was an "absolutely unmitigated disaster", arguing there had been "radical underinvestment" over decades. She said Burnham's plan, which involves removing limits on government ownership of shares in water companies and giving mayors more powers to scrutinise them, did not go far enough. The Green Party of England and Wales has long called for public ownership of water companies, describing privatisation as a failed experiment. In its 2024 manifesto, the party estimated that nationalising water companies and the five biggest retail energy firms would cost £30bn over the five years of a parliament. Last year, the government estimated, external that nationalising the water industry would cost approximately £100bn. Millward is expected to make a speech about the party's latest policy on nationalising water companies - and how to pay for it - at the Green Party conference in Brighton this weekend. It comes as the government considers the option of nationalising Thames Water, which is facing a severe financial crisis. Ahead of the conference, Millward did a round of interviews with local BBC radio stations across England. Under the leadership of Zack Polanski, the party's brand of "eco-populism" has posed a challenge to Labour on the left of British politics. Labour's polling numbers have improved markedly in recent months, suggesting Burnham may be winning back some supporters that had drifted towards Polanski's party. In her interviews, Millward said the party had had a "historic successful year" by winning a by-election in Gorton and Denton, and making significant gains in May's local elections. She told BBC Radio Newcastle if it had not been for the rise of the Greens, then Sir Keir Starmer - who was ousted as prime minister by his own MPs - would still be in office. "We can take the credit for that really," she said. Millward said Labour's rhetoric had "shifted in our direction" under Burnham. Going forward she said the Greens would push the Labour government to go further and continue calling for rent controls, nationalisation of water companies and wealth taxes. But Millward faced some tough questions on local issues, some of which she wasn't able to answer. She was asked by BBC Radio WM about the bin strikes in Birmingham, where a minority coalition of Liberal Democrats, Greens and independents run the council. She said she hadn't "been given enough information to answer that question" and apologised several times. "I'm sorry it's not in my briefing, it should have been," she said. "I'm happy to come on another time and chat about it." These BBC local radio rounds can be tricky, with presenters often asking about issues in their patches. Millward seemed most comfortable on national topics, arguing the Greens "have the power to set the agenda for this government" and hold Burnham to account. The Greens have five MPs and hundreds of councillors across the country. Green Party leader Zack Polanski is currently contesting the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, which will take place next week. A full list of candidates is available on the BBC website. title: Drumcree policing operation has cost £3m so far, says Boutcher
description: Chief Constable Jon Boutcher is discussing the Drumcree row at a meeting of the Policing Board.
body: Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has said the policing operation over the Drumcree parading dispute has cost about £3m so far. Speaking at a meeting of the Policing Board, he described the situation as "challenging" - but said that despite "very significant tensions" there had been no violence. The stand-off - over a proposed Orange Orange parade in Portadown, opposed by nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has deployed a significant number of officers, with Boutcher saying he had a responsibility to preserve peace and maintain order. He said the cost of the policing operation has been £3m thus far, but warned of the consequences and cost "if they get it wrong". "The consequences of us not getting this right, and the cost of that, the monetary cost of this organisation in having to police potential disorder, and the cost to the security, the safety, the trust, the confidence, the tranquillity of the society," he added. During the meeting, it also emerged that the Policing Board has launched a code-of-conduct investigation into one of its members, Sinn Féin's Deirdre Hargey. She was pictured taking part in an unlawful protest against the march on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday. Hargey attended the board meeting after a failed attempt by Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member Trevor Clarke to have her barred. "I've made it clear to my senior team that our objective is to facilitate the Parades Commission determination," said Boutcher. "The Parades Commission determination means that the Orange Order can lawfully parade down the Garvaghy Road. Without that determination, such a parade would be unlawful. "What it does not mean, however, is that the police must accommodate that determination at all costs." He said the police were not expected to "nor will they force" members of the Orange Order "through a hostile crowd", saying it could be unsafe or have wider consequences for Northern Ireland which could be "catastrophic". With the PSNI currently being unable to police the Parades Commission ruling to allow the march, Boutcher said he was giving "space" for negotiations. Under legislation, he can apply to the Northern Ireland secretary to have the determination overturned or amended. Boutcher said: "The board needs to be reassured that I am constantly reviewing that position. "But at this stage it is my judgement that that is not necessary. "We are creating the time to resolve this and that is in the interests of everyone." He said the investigation into the unlawful protest, which prevented the parade, was underway and was "fully resourced". Boutcher said potential offences included unnotified protest, obstructing a lawful parade and breaching the Parades Commission determination. "Believe me, the evidence gathering process has been extensive," he said. "I want it to be thorough but I want it to be expeditious to send a clear message. "The rule of law will come through." Last Friday, the Parades Commission said the Orange Order's march could go ahead along Garvaghy Road. Rather than start at 13:00 on Sunday as intended, the commission said it could begin no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. But an initial legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition (GRRC) at the High Court saw a judge issue an injunction banning the parade, with Judge Patricia Smyth saying the "long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland". This was later successfully challenged by an Orange Order member at the Court of Appeal. Late on Saturday evening, the GRRC was given permission to challenge that decision at the High Court - an appeal which was dismissed by Justice Humphreys. The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and almost derailed the peace process at the time. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches. Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order - unsuccessfully - over the past three decades. title: Kanye West's Russia shows officially cancelled after weeks of uncertainty
description: Chaos has surrounded the St Petersburg shows since the stadium said it had not agreed to host the rapper.
body: St Petersburg's Gazprom Arena said in August it would not host Ye Two stadium gigs in Russia by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, have officially been cancelled. West had been due to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October. But there was confusion in the lead-up to the shows, as the venue had said it wouldn't host him for what would have been the biggest show by a western artist since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. In a post on messaging app Telegram, gig organisers Say Agency confirmed the concerts had been cancelled with "sincere regret". "The Ye concerts in St Petersburg will not be able to take place on the scheduled dates," the Moscow-based agency wrote. "We will issue an official statement regarding the status of the project and our plans in the near future." West returned to touring earlier this year and has had a string of US stadium shows Gazprom Arena said in August that it had not signed a rental agreement with the concert promoters and so the gig could not take place on its site. Say Agency had said it was working to resolve the issue with the stadium before confirming they could not go ahead. The stadium also acknowledged it had received complaints about West's performance. He has recently apologised for multiple antisemitic and pro-Nazi comments in the past, saying he had "lost touch with reality" as a result of his bipolar disorder. Kanye West controversies - how did we get here? Kanye West concert in Poland cancelled over antisemitic comments Italy bans Kanye West and Travis Scott concerts over security concerns Russia was invaded by the Nazis in World War Two, and the country's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman was among those who criticised the planned shows. Maria Zakharova said they were unacceptable and pointed out West's "glorification" of Hitler. In 2025 West started selling swastika T-shirts and released a song called Heil Hitler. Pro-war bloggers in Russia also questioned whether the country should be hosting an American artist while the US provided financial and military support for Ukraine. West is yet to comment publicly on the cancellation. His first major concert in the US for more than five years was held in Los Angeles in April, and he has since played in countries including Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands. However, his Russian shows aren't the only gigs to have been cancelled. Last summer West was set to headline London's Wireless Festival but was barred from entering the UK, forcing organisers to cancel the whole event. West shows were also cancelled in Poland, Italy and France. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: Tourette's campaigner Davidson asks to watch Scottish Baftas via video link after racial slur row
description: John Davidson, whose condition includes involuntary tics, shouted a racial slur during the Bafta Film Awards in February.
body: John Davidson's tics could be heard several times during the Bafta Film Awards ceremony in February Tourette's campaigner John Davidson has asked to watch the Scottish Baftas ceremony via a video link at the venue after he shouted a racial slur during the Bafta Film Awards in February. The movie I Swear, which tells the story of Davidson growing up with Tourette syndrome in Scotland in the 1980s, has been nominated for seven Scottish Baftas. It scooped three prizes at the Bafta Film Awards in London in February. But the event was overshadowed by Davidson, whose condition involves involuntary tics, shouting the N-word at presenters Michael B Jordan and Delroy Lindo. The BBC later apologised for not editing out the slur from its BBC One broadcast, which was shown on a two-hour delay, and remained on BBC iPlayer until the following day. Bafta Scotland said it had worked with safeguarding and inclusion experts to allow Davidson to take part in its forthcoming ceremony in Glasgow "in the safest way possible for all". It said Davidson, who was awarded an MBE in 2019 for his work in raising awareness of Tourette's, had suggested watching from a separate room in the venue with his family and friends. The racial slur was shouted while Michael B Jordan (left) and Delroy Lindo were presenting an award Davidson, from Galashiels, shouted loudly several times before and during the Bafta ceremony in February. He later said he was "deeply mortified if anyone considers my involuntary tics to be intentional or to carry any meaning". "I have spent my life trying to support and empower the Tourette's community and to teach empathy, kindness and understanding from others and I will continue to do so," he said in a statement. "I chose to leave the auditorium early into the ceremony as I was aware of the distress my tics were causing." At the time, Bafta thanked Davidson for his "dignity and consideration of others, on what should have been a night of celebration for him". "We take full responsibility for putting our guests in a very difficult situation and we apologise to all," it added. "We will learn from this and keep inclusion at the core of all we do, maintaining our belief in film and storytelling as a critical conduit for compassion and empathy." This year's Scottish Bafta nominees include I Swear stars Peter Mullan, Robert Aramayo, Scott Ellis Watson and Shirley Henderson. In the Actor Television category, Dougray Scott is nominated for Summerwater, Jack Lowden for Slow Horses, Peter Capaldi for Criminal Record and Robert Carlyle for The Hack. There are also three nominations each for the Netflix crime drama Dept Q and BBC comedy Dinosaur while Dept Q's Leah Byrne also received an Audience Award nomination. The winners will be announced on 15 November at a ceremony in Glasgow hosted by broadcaster Edith Bowman. title: Boy arrested after river deaths released on bail
description: Jackson Duke, 17, and Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw, both 16, died when a car entered the water.
body: Luke Etheridge, Zara Shaw and Jackson Duke (left to right) died when the car they were in entered the River Wear A 17-year-old boy who was arrested after three teenagers died when a car entered the River Wear in Sunderland has been released on bail. Sixteen-year-olds Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw and 17-year-old Jackson Duke died after an Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank, near Wearmouth Bridge, and entered the river just before 13:30 BST on Tuesday. The 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. Northumbria Police has now confirmed he has been released on bail pending further inquiries. The teenager had managed to reach safety and suffered non-serious injuries. The investigation into the circumstances leading to the car entering the water continues. Northumbria Police said on Wednesday no other vehicles were believed to have been involved. The empty black Audi A3 was recovered from the water on Wednesday Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said: "The last 24 hours have brought unimaginable agony and heartbreak for the loved ones of Luke, Jackson and Zara. "All three had their whole futures ahead of them and will be hugely missed. "We also recognise the impact that this tragedy has had upon the people of Sunderland and further afield, and know that you will continue to be there for one another." On Wednesday, a spokesperson for Sunderland College said they were "deeply saddened" by the deaths of three of their students. "This is a heartbreaking loss for our college community, and the wider city of Sunderland," a statement published on Facebook said. title: Naomi Campbell wins appeal over charity ban
description: A tribunal rules that the model was unaware of misconduct at her charity Fashion for Relief.
body: Model Naomi Campbell has won her appeal against a ban on being a charity trustee, after a tribunal ruled that she was unaware of misconduct at her charity Fashion for Relief. Campbell was banned from being a charity trustee for five years in 2024 after a watchdog found that Fashion for Relief funds had been spent on luxury hotels and spa treatments. However, a tribunal said on Thursday, external that the most serious instances of misconduct in the charity "were concealed" from Campbell by a fellow trustee. "Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct," the three-person tribunal panel said. The supermodel set up Fashion for Relief to help victims of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and went on to front further campaigns for disasters and causes around the world. However, the charity was shut in 2023 and Campbell and two other trustees were banned the following year after a Charity Commission inquiry found "serious mismanagement and/or misconduct" at Fashion for Relief, which was not passing on as much of the money raised as it was supposed to. Campbell appealed, saying one of her fellow trustees, lawyer Bianka Hellmich, forged her signature and impersonated her using a fake email address to misdirect money that was intended for the charity. Her "only mistake" was trusting Hellmich, Campbell told the tribunal in June. Hellmich has denied the allegations. The Charity Commission opposed Campbell's challenge and said the five-year ban should be upheld. In its ruling, the First-Tier Tribunal panel said Campbell's claim that she was deceived had been corroborated by documentary evidence. "For the avoidance of doubt, we accept that both Ms Campbell's evidence, as well as her conduct during the operation of the Charity, was entirely honest," they said. They said Campbell did not know €4,386 (£3,750) of hotel charges from a trip to the south of France in 2018 - including €1,298 (£1,100) for dinner room service, €1,163 (£990) for spa treatments and €112 (£95) for cigarettes - had come out of the charity's expenses. "The panel is satisfied that Ms Campbell was not responsible for the inappropriate use of the charity's resources or any unjustified expenditure, nor did she contribute or facilitate it," they said. Campbell must take some responsibility for failures to maintain minutes and file accounts on time - but that was not enough to disqualify the model as a charity trustee, the tribunal said. "There was serious misconduct and mismanagement in the administration of the charity she founded, Fashion for Relief," the ruling said. "The Tribunal has found, however, that its most serious features, including unauthorised payments to Ms Campbell's co-trustee, Bianka Hellmich, failures in the management of the Charity's finances and the misuse of its funds, resulted from Ms Hellmich's conduct and were concealed from Ms Campbell." Unauthorised payments of more than £290,000 were made to Hellmich for apparent consultancy fees, the inquiry found. The tribunal ruling continued: "Ms Hellmich deceived Ms Campbell, used forged documents and a false email address purporting to belong to her, and also deceived professional advisers and the Commission. "Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct. "The Tribunal finds that she had no reasonable basis to suspect Ms Hellmich's dishonesty before regulatory concerns emerged and, when they did, Ms Campbell took reasonable steps in response." The ruling said Hellmich's solicitors wrote to the tribunal to deny the allegations against her, but she was not called to give evidence and did not take part in the proceedings. title: Travelodge failed sex assault victim 'at every stage', review finds
description: Room intrusions were still being reported at one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, a review finds.
body: Reception staff at Travelodge Maidenhead gave Kyran Smith the victim's room key after he falsely claimed to be her boyfriend A woman who was sexually assaulted by a man given a key to her hotel room was "fundamentally failed" by Travelodge "at every stage", an independent review has found. Barrister Paul Greaney KC said the chain's security policies at the time of the attack at its Maidenhead hotel in December 2022 were "not fit for the purpose of keeping guests safe". He found guests were still not as safe as they should be, with room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls. Travelodge apologised "unreservedly" to the woman. The review did credit the company with making changes since March. Kyran Smith, who obtained the key by falsely claiming to be the woman's boyfriend, was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in January. The review found he was handed the key less than three minutes after approaching the reception desk, by a receptionist who had received no training in key security. Kyran Smith assaulted the victim at a hotel in Maidenhead Greaney said blame rested with Travelodge as an organisation rather than with individual staff, and a culture had developed in which room intrusions were regarded as "one of those things". The woman emailed a complaint to Travelodge in January 2023, addressed to chief executive Jo Boydell and others. The review concluded the email was handled by her office without her knowledge, and did not come to Boydell's attention until March 2026. The woman's complaint was instead investigated by a manager who was himself criticised in it, and the customer services team offered her a refund for her night's stay, which she understood to be £30. Boydell stepped down as chief executive in August following criticism over the company's handling of safety complaints. The review said she deserved credit for driving improvements from March. The attack became national news in March after the woman contacted the BBC, saying the case raised serious questions about room security at Travelodge hotels. Since then, dozens of people have shared experiences of strangers entering their rooms, including a domestic abuse victim whose abuser was given a key to her room at a Travelodge in London. Then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell in March urging her to "seriously engage" with the government over security. Greaney was appointed to lead the review the following month. The review makes 38 recommendations, including moving towards a system that requires guests to show ID to get a room key, which Travelodge has been trialling at some hotels since May. It also calls for body-worn cameras for reception staff, better checks that staff have understood their training, and for housekeepers to always send guests to reception. Greaney said Travelodge must "urgently" create a policy on violence against women and girls, drawn up with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, and train all staff in it. The review said changes made this year had been done quickly "albeit years too late" and its new key security policy would prevent a repeat of the Maidenhead attack if applied correctly. But it found the policy was "not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground". Mystery shoppers were able to get into rooms through housekeeping staff at all five hotels tested, including Maidenhead, without being sent to reception or asked for proof they were entitled to enter. At three of the hotels, staff confirmed a guest was staying there, and at two, room numbers were said out loud at check-in. The Maidenhead hotel scored worst of the five. Other recommendations included networked CCTV across the chain and key card-controlled access to all residential corridors. This video can not be played In an interview with the BBC in March, the then Travelodge chief executive Jo Boydell said she only became aware of the assault during the court case almost three years later Greaney said room intrusions were a problem across the hotel sector. He praised the woman's courage and determination, saying the problems would have remained "beneath the surface" had she not shared her experience. Freddie van Mierlo, the Liberal Democrat MP for Henley and Thame, where Travelodge is based, said he was worried the company was "still trying to do safety on the cheap". He said the review's recommendations would require "significant capital investment", and Travelodge needed to make clear it was prepared to deliver that. Ray Reidy, Travelodge's interim chief executive, said the review made clear there were failures in its policies and in the way customers had been treated. "I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed," he said. "We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go." Travelodge said a new board committee would oversee the changes, with independent assessments of its progress after six and 12 months. title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
description: The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian domains.
body: President Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry. The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites. Register.si spokesperson Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%. She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months. President Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September. "The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence." Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk. Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to only President Trump's comments. She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded. One possible explanation for the purchases is cyber-squatting - where people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit. For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later. On Tuesday, President Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age". He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and they should no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI. SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said. Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath President Trump's signature. title: Nine scandals that rocked the sporting world
description: Manchester City are far from the first. The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of other sports stars to break the rules.
body: Gianluigi Buffon, Joe Jackson and Lance Armstrong all found their careers derailed, to different degrees, by sporting scandal Manchester City being found guilty of fuelling an era of glittering Premier League success via a network of sponsorship deals, found by an independent commision to be a "sham", has shaken the world of sport. But it isn't the first time. The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of others to cheat. BBC Sport looks back on nine more sporting scandals, stretching back more than a century. Lance Armstong was stripped of the seven back-to-back Tour de France titles he won Cancer survivor. Cycling legend. American hero. Cheat. Lance Armstrong had spent years vehemently and aggressively insisting that he had won all seven of his Tour de France titles between 1999 and 2005 without the help of performance-enhancing drugs. His story was remarkable. Aged 25, Armstrong had been diagnosed with testicular cancer, with doctors warning he was likely to die given the disease had spread to other parts of his body. He not only survived, but returned to dominate top-level cycling. His Livestrong Foundation was wildly successful, selling millions of yellow wristbands to raise money to support fellow cancer sufferers. However, as the evidence and former team-mates allegations against him stacked up, Armstrong was stripped of his Tour de France titles. Armstong eventually confessed to cheating in a blockbuster interview with talk show host Oprah Winfrey. "I made those decisions, they were my mistake and I'm here to say sorry," he said, adding that the culture in professional cycling made using drugs non-negotiable. Armstrong says sorry for doping Hansie Cronje's fall from grace came as a shock to South Africa Hansie Cronje was the golden boy of South African sport. Good looking and charming, he led the nation's cricket team with style and authority. President Nelson Mandela singled out Cronje in 1996 for the "excellent manner" in which he captained the Proteas. However, Cronje's love of money, combined with a fast-growing betting industry and the organised crime it attracted, proved his downfall. Cronje entertained the offers of match-fixers, calling team meetings to discuss the possibility of throwing matches and sharing thousands of dollars in inducements. Most infamously, Cronje contrived to lose a rain-affected Test against England in 2000. With South Africa still in the midst of their first innings on the final day, Cronje convinced England counterpart Nasser Hussein that in the interest of sporting entertainment each side should forfeit an innings, producing a sudden run-chase and giving England a shot at victory. Cronje was praised for his Corinthian spirit. In reality, he had been motivated by a bribe of £5,000 to ensure the match did not end in a draw. Cronje was undone when an Indian police wiretap of a bookmaker caught him in discussions about fixing matches. Cronje confessed in early 2000, was banned from cricket for life and died in a plane crash two years later at the age of 32. Hansie Cronje, match-fixing and plane crash that left a complex legacy Renault initially said that Nelson Piquet Jr's claim he was instructed to crash deliberately was an attempt to blackmail them into retaining hm as a driver There was something particular about turn 17 of the Marina Bay Street Circuit. In 2008, before the inaugural Singapore Grand Prix was held at the circuit, Renault driver Nelson Piquet Jr knew it did not have any overhead cranes to lift a damaged car from the track. There were no side entrances to allow a stranded driver to be pushed out of danger's way by marshalls either. On lap 14 Piquet found himself in exactly in that unfortunate position. And, despite his initial claim that he had made a "simple mistake", the Brazilian had put himself there deliberately. When Renault dropped him in 2009, Piquet Jr revealed that he steered himself into a concrete wall to crash his car. The safety car was deployed as officials cleared debris off the track. Crucially, Piquet Jr's team-mate Fernando Alonso was the only frontrunner to have stopped for fuel and new tyres at the point of the crash. As Alonso's rivals went into the pits, the Spaniard, benefitting from the reduced gaps caused by the safety car, moved up the field and went on to win the race. While Alonso was cleared of any wrongdoing or knowledge of the plot, Renault team principal Flavio Briatore and chief technical officer Pat Symonds were banned from F1 for several years. Still in F1 10 years after 'crashgate' The Upton Park lights went out after Frank Lampard's second-half equaliser against Crystal Palace Frank Lampard wheeled away in celebration after his well-hit shot from the edge of the penalty area beat Kevin Miller in the Crystal Palace goal in the 65th minute of a Monday evening Premier League game in November 1997. As he was mobbed by team-mates, Upton Park was plunged into darkness. The following month similar happened at Selhurst Park. Thirteen seconds into the second half - with Wimbledon and Arsenal goalless - the lights went off. The Christmas lights in nearby Croydon were raised as a possible cause. The actual cause was more sinister. An Asian betting syndicate had pulled the plug, using a remote control circuit breaker, to get each match abandoned at a scoreline which would maximise their profits. The gang were foiled in their attempts to pull the deception for a third time. They had bribed a security guard at Charlton Athletic to allow them to plant a device at The Valley before Liverpool's visit in February. However, a suspicious member of staff at the club tipped off police. Four men were given sentences of between 18 months and four years for their involvement. title: The Bottom Line
description: How does the antiques industry work and is it accurately portrayed on television shows?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·01 Oct 2026,·48 mins Available for over a year If there’s one business that’s ingrained in popular culture, you could argue it's the buying and selling of antiques. You only have to count the number of TV shows where people find and flog something hoping for a profit to recognise the appeal. But how does the business really operate? Is it accurately portrayed on television and how do antiques come up for sale in the first place? Evan Davis is joined by a panel of experts to get some answers and asks whether anything we manufacture today will last long enough to be auctioned off in a hundred years-time. title: Why penalty for Williamson handball was correct call
description: Arsenal defender Leah Williamson was at the heart of a bizarre incident in their Women's Champions League draw with Paris FC.
body: This video can not be played Arsenal let two-goal lead slip to draw with Paris FC A bizarre error from Arsenal defender Leah Williamson proved costly in their 2-2 draw with Paris FC on Wednesday in the Women's Champions League. With the Gunners leading 2-1 late on, England captain Williamson stopped a short goal-kick with her hand - believing it had not been taken and that she was to take it - resulting in a penalty being awarded to the hosts, converted by Maeline Mendy. The unusual incident means the Gunners are fourth in the Champions League table after their opening two games, but would have been second with a victory in the French capital. After the ball had gone out of play for a goal-kick, Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez played a quick, short pass to Williamson. Williamson had her arm stretched out to stop the ball and place it so that she could take the goal-kick herself. With the ball being still and on the field of play when Rodriguez played the ball to Williamson, that was deemed to be the goal-kick instead of Williamson's attempt. Therefore Williamson was penalised for handball and Mendy levelled the match from the penalty spot. This video can not be played Paris earn draw after Arsenal give away bizarre penalty While Arsenal felt aggrieved at the decision, the guidance on such incidents state that the decision to award a penalty was correct. Guidance from Law 16 of the International Football Association Board's (Ifab) laws of the game state: "In goal-kick restarts, if the ball is stationary within the goal area and is kicked by any defending player, the goal-kick is considered to have been taken. "If, after the ball is in play, [a player] commits a handball offence, a penalty kick is awarded if the offence occurred inside the kicker's penalty area. Law 12 from Ifab also states: "It is an offence if a player deliberately touches the ball with their hand/arm." Tyrone Mings committed a similar error in the Champions League in November 2024 In November 2024, Aston Villa defender Tyrone Mings committed an identical error in a Champions League match against Club Brugge. Brugge won a penalty that was scored by Hans Vanaken, with the Belgian side winning the match 1-0. "The biggest mistake I witnessed in my career," said Villa boss Unai Emery at the time. Earlier that year, Gunners centre-back Gabriel also made the mistake in a Champions League match against Bayern Munich. However in that instance, Arsenal were given the chance to retake the goal-kick. "He [Gabriel] touched the ball with the hand because he thought it was not in game, but it was in game and the referee admitted it was in game and was handball," said then Bayern boss Thomas Tuchel. The now England head coach also said that the error in not awarding Bayern a penalty was a "kid's mistake". Arsenal's assistant coach Aaron D'Antino conducted post-match media duties and explained that, while the intention was for Williamson to take the goal-kick, they will use the incident as a learning experience. "If we're looking at what we can control, it's just passing the ball to Leah from what I remember seeing. The ball was still rolling and she [Rodriguez] was moving it to Leah for her to take the goal-kicks as we normally do," said D'Antino. "So maybe the learning in that is how we get the ball to Leah, so we don't put ourselves in that situation." Former Arsenal and Scotland defender Jen Beattie felt the referee Iuliana Demetrescu got the decision wrong, despite the correct applications of the laws. "For me, I just don't even know how that happens. Leah knows it's a goal-kick, she's catching the ball. That's shocking from the referee," Beattie told Paramount+. "I would have been fuming and I would have been embarrassed if they gave that. This is not what they're trying to do. It's just beyond frustrating that that's how they've tied the game. "Leah's obviously going [to do that] because she's going to take the goal-kick, not because she's worried about the press or trying to change it - or panicking in any situation. Leah Williamson doesn't panic in those moments, she knows what she's doing. The goalkeeper knows what she's doing as well. "The referee has miscalled it." title: Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
description: It comes a week after fighting erupted north of the capital between the army and a new alliance of armed groups.
body: There have been concerns for security in the capital following the outbreak of fighting last week Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say. The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region. A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes. "It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic. He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT). Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion. He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters. There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage. The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment. title: Man admits posing as medical student at hospital
description: Stephen Simpson, 22, wore medical scrubs and NHS branded clothing at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.
body: Stephen Simpson admitted fraud when he appeared at Aberdeen Sheriff Court A man has admitted pretending to be a medical student for several weeks and accessing Aberdeen hospital wards and files. Stephen Simpson, 22, wore medical scrubs and NHS branded clothing at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI), as well as having a stethoscope. At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Simpson admitted fraud, between 9 December 2023 and 26 January 2024. Sentence was deferred until later this month for reports. NHS Grampian has been asked for comment. More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds Simpson originally faced a total of six charges - one of fraud and five others of theft. The fraud was alleged to have happened between 22 September 2023 and 26 January 2024. However, solicitor Laura Gracie said Simpson was pleading guilty to two amended charges. These were that Simpson, from Aberdeen, pretended to employees he was a medical student authorised to be in ARI. Aberdeen Royal Infirmary was the location of the crime Wearing medical scrubs and NHS branded clothing, and having a stethoscope and pager, he induced employees to allow him to remain in the hospital and gain access to restricted areas and files, staff-only areas, wards, and had access to medical files. He also admitted stealing items of NHS branded clothing, a pager, and perfume. The amended pleas were accepted by fiscal Dylan Middleton for the Crown. Sheriff Morag McLaughlin deferred sentence for a criminal justice social work report and restriction of liberty order assessment.
