title: Russell says his 'confidence is back and growing'
description: George Russell says he "doesn't feel lost any more" as he seeks to end a difficult season on a high and chase down team-mate Kimi Antonelli's championship lead.
body: George Russell has won races in Australia, Austria and Azerbaijan this season George Russell says he "doesn't feel lost any more" as he seeks to end a difficult season on a high and chase down team-mate Kimi Antonelli's championship lead. Russell won his third race of the season in Azerbaijan last weekend, and his first for three months, and says he has made a breakthrough in terms of understanding how to drive the Mercedes car. The Briton trails Antonelli by 66 points in the championship with either seven or eight races still remaining. "The thing that's changed is I feel my performances are strong enough to fight for victory week in week out," Russell said. "I know what I need from the car and myself and I don't really feel lost any more. "Confidence is back and it's growing again and it's all coming a bit more naturally, which is how it has been for most of my career and not how it's been for most of the season." Mercedes are expecting a strong challenge from McLaren at the flowing Sepang track this weekend as its characteristics should suit the world champions' car. But the team have their first major upgrade for some time and hope that will bring them into contention. Asked whether another strong performance at this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia could change the psychology of the title fight, Russell said: "I've never really felt in a position to fight for the victories because my performances weren't strong enough. "But now finally I feel I'm in a place I can fight for victory week in week out. "Of course there is a big deficit in the championship, but there is a third of a season to go and still so much can happen. I am just going to go race by race. I feel more at one with the car and hopefully this upgrade will play into my favour a bit more. So bring it on." Russell started the season as championship favourite but Antonelli took control early on as Russell struggled to get to grips with the Mercedes designed for this year's all-new car and engine rules. He has had to "consciously adjust" his driving style. "I went through a few races where I was having to think how to make those adjustments, whereas now it's all just a bit more intuitive and a bit more natural," Russell said. "So what I set out to achieve, in terms of getting the car [into] a slightly better window, I'm now achieving without having to think about it as much. So I can just focus on driving fast." Antonelli had a difficult weekend in Baku, with a crash in qualifying leaving him 16th on the grid, from where he recovered to finished fifth. The Italian said: "Last weekend was probably there worst weekend from me of the season. "But still good learning from the weekend and was also a very strange race for me in Baku because it was one of those races where I consciously tried not to take any risks and just drive under the limit which was very weird but it was what I needed on Sunday. I needed a clean result after a very disrupted weekend. "I wasn't happy after the race but I learned the most important learning was I need to be always 100% because if I don't try to do everything right in my power then nothing is going to come my way." Frederic Vasseur has been team principal of Ferrari since 2023 Lewis Hamilton has declared Frederic Vasseur as "the guy to lead us" two days after Ferrari made an unusual public statement backing their team principal after speculation over this position. The seven-time champion, who is third in the drivers' title race while Ferrari are second in the constructors' battle, said removing Vasseur would be a mistake. "He's doing a fantastic job," Hamilton said. If you look at the history, how many people [have been swapped] out [of] that role… and I feel like it's in a better place than it's been before. "But it's not a one-man situation. It's lots and lots of people coming together and if you want to point fingers, point it somewhere else. There's people above who are also part of it. "Fred's in his position, he's not going anywhere and I'm here to stay with him and I still believe fully in where we're going. "Swapping him out won't change how the team is moving forward. If anything it will be detrimental." Hamilton pointed to the progress Ferrari have made since a winless 2025 season, in which they finished fourth in the teams' championship. He and Leclerc have each won a race this year. Ferrari started the season with the best chassis in terms of cornering performance, but their engine has fallen short of those produced by Mercedes and Red Bull. Hamilton said: "We're second in the championship, a huge improvement on last year already. And that's with a deficit on power of average 0.4secs [per lap] every single weekend. Some races it's 0.6sec and we've still be delivering really great performances. "And that just highlights how great a job people at the factory have done. All the negativity takes away from that. "Of course we're not where we want to be but you don't go from last year's experience straight to number one. It's a process and I think we've built a good foundation this year, we need to continue to build on it. We're not perfect yet but I do believe we can get there. I think we've had the best car this year. But it's unfortunate we have been down 0.4secs on power. That is difficult overcome but it's something we're working on for next year." title: Train sped up past red signal before fatal crash
description: Investigators say the train accelerated after passing a red signal that was not normally active.
body: The collision happened after one train stopped and a second train passed a red signal and struck it from behind A train involved in a fatal crash had accelerated past a red signal that was rarely ever on, investigators have found. Train driver Shaun Burton, 60, died and more than 160 people were injured when his London-bound service crashed into the back of another train on 19 June at Elstow, near Bedford. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch, external (RAIB) has found the signal had not displayed a red light to any train before the crash during 2026. The latest interim report said CCTV had shown the signal had displayed red correctly, and Burton had acknowledged it, but he had continued to accelerate and applied brakes only seconds before hitting the other train, which had earlier come to a stop. There had been 92 passengers on the Nottingham train and 155 on the Corby train The collision took place between two East Midlands Railway (EMR) services on Network Rail's Midland Main Line, about 2.5 miles (4km) south of Bedford station. The driver of the first train, travelling from Nottingham to London, was learning how to operate a new type of train under the supervision of an instructor. It stopped after receiving an Automatic Warning System (AWS) alert, despite the signal ahead displaying green. Neither the driver nor the instructor recognised the alarm as an AWS warning, and it was not acknowledged within the required window. This caused the train's emergency brakes to be applied automatically. When Burton's train approached from Corby, the signal was displaying red, although he acknowledged its AWS warning, he continued to accelerate. RAIB said no train had previously been recorded passing the signal while it was red since records began in 1985. Train driver Shaun Burton, from Cambridgeshire, died in the train crash near Bedford On 9 July, after the crash, another train approaching the same signal received an incorrect AWS warning despite it displaying green. The AWS equipment was later found to be positioned 16mm below rail level, outside the permitted tolerance. Investigators are examining whether this contributed to the incorrect warnings. However, investigators found no evidence that the signal itself was faulty when it was tested after the crash. RAIB said it would continue to investigate why Burton's train had passed the red signal, as well as the signal's positioning, visibility and status. title: Woman's Hour
description: We find out more about a rape investigation at a US university that's sparked rage online.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·01 Oct 2026,·57 mins Available for over a year New York state prosecutors say they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman, referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in her lawsuit that seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter assaulted her in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine. The case was investigated by university police but will now go before a grand jury. The case has been discussed widely online, with many including actress Florence Pugh reacting with fury over the reported disciplinary actions taken by the university. Nada Tawfik, BBC North American correspondent, and Tracey Vitchers, Executive Director of It's On Us, a non-profit programme dedicated to college sexual assault prevention, join Anita Rani to discuss. The broadcaster, campaigner and charity founder Dame Esther Rantzen has died at the age of 86. She will be best remembered for presenting the BBC TV Programme That’s Life. She also set up Childline – the telephone helpline for children suffering abuse or neglect – and spent a lot of time campaigning for older people and for assisted dying. Guardian journalist Zoe Williams remembers her and her impact on women's lives. Australia has launched its Endometriosis Management Plan, which gives GPs and patients a much greater role in the management of their endo. Professor Danielle Mazza from Monash University in Melbourne has been instrumental in designing and delivering the plan. She discusses how the UK might benefit from something like this with Dr Sylvia Kama-Kieghe, a GP in Sheffield, and Vice President of Membership and Workforce at the College of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare. A social media-driven resurgence in the popularity of sunbeds is said to be fuelling a rise in cases of skin cancer, particularly among young people, according to some experts. Melanoma, the most serious form of skin cancer, is now one of the most common cancers in people aged 15 to 34, according to Cancer Research UK. Meanwhile research by the Teenage Cancer Trust found around 48% of 18 to 34-year-olds in the UK use sunbeds – the highest proportion of any age group. Observer journalist Marine Saint has been looking into this, along with Rosie Vare from the Teenage Cancer Trust. Producer: Melanie Abbott Presenter: Anita Rani

title: Why are hundreds of prisoners being released early?
description: More people going to prison, and for longer, is why governments including the current one have had to release prisoners early.
body: Around 700 prisoners in England and Wales are due to be released under the first tranche of the government's early release scheme. Under the scheme, eligible prisoners will be released after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of their term. People sentenced for manslaughter, rape, serious child sex and grooming offences will be excluded. This is not the first time a government - Conservative or Labour - has had to release prisoners early to make space in England and Wales' overcrowded prisons. BBC Verify has looked at the reasons why ministers say this latest scheme is necessary. The prison population in England and Wales on 28 September was 87,499 which was 98% of useable capacity, external. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has previously warned the prison population will overtake capacity as soon as this November. In the long-term the MoJ has projected that the capacity of all prisons will rise to around 99,000 by 2032 as a result of more prisons being built by this government. But it also projected that the prisoner population would rise to about 104,000 by 2032 if the Sentencing Act 2026 - which provides for earlier release - did not come into force. That is why Justice Secretary Alex Norris says there is a "prison capacity crisis" which means the government has to implement the latest early release scheme. In total 4,500 prisoners are due to be released early by June 2027, external. The MoJ has projected that the Sentencing Act will mean the prisoner population remains below the capacity of the prison system, rising only to around 96,000 by 2032. The England and Wales prison population has risen significantly in recent decades with a significant uptick starting in the 1990s before reaching a record high in 2024. The Institute for Government (IFG) think tank says this is partly the result of longer sentences. In 2023, the average prison sentence at Crown Courts in England and Wales - which deal with more serious offences - was more than 25% longer than those handed down in 2012. For some crimes, the increase was greater. Sentences for robbery in 2023 were 13 months longer on average than in 2012 - an increase of 36%. Longer sentences mean more people being held in prison at any one time. Former Conservative Justice Secretary David Gauke, who led an independent sentencing review for Sir Keir Starmer's government, argues this is the result of a "bidding war" by political parties since the 1990s over who can imprison people for longer. Gauke also points out that the prison population has been rising at a time when overall crime in England and Wales has been falling, according to the official Crime Survey. So despite the fall in crime more people are being sent to prison - and for longer. Another reason for upward pressure on the prison population is that more people than before are being returned to prison for breaching the conditions of their release. There were 51,419 licence recalls in England and Wales in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase. Cassia Rowland from the IFG said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public. "The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said. Successive governments have pledged to increase the number of prison places - but delivery has often fallen short of those promises. Between 2010 and 2024, when the Conservatives were in power, around 13,000 new prison places were created. But around 12,500 places - notably those built during the Victorian era - were closed after falling into disrepair. That means an estimated net total of only around 500 new prison places were added over 14 years. In a 2024 report, the National Audit Office (NAO) cited the MOJ's "unrealistic timelines", and government bodies not working together to prioritise delivery, as reasons for the slow pace of prison building. Work is under way on a new prison - HMP Welland - being built in Leicestershire The MOJ say around 6,500 net prison places were created between 2022 and 2025, once closures are taken into consideration. These include places created in three new prisons. However, further expansion to existing prisons has been delayed by a major supplier going into administration, according to the Prison Reform Trust. Pia Sinha of the Prison Reform Trust told BBC Verify: "Successive governments have found it difficult to increase prison capacity because new prisons take years to plan and build, often facing planning hurdles and local opposition." The Labour government has pledged to build 14,000 new prison places by 2031. Analysts argue that without a major change in thinking about the appropriateness of prison as punishment, or a significant long-term increase in prison building, the system in England and Wales will remain close to capacity. And that means governments will continue to be under pressure to implement early release schemes to avert a capacity crisis. title: What happened in failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
description: The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions.
body: This video can not be played What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection. The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions. These include what went went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was perpetrated alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp. She was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday evening, local time. The injections were allowed by the US Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle. Pike was given two syringes of the drug pentobarbital, though her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring. US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, and said "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening". The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency. Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own. Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure. The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility. One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital. Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning. In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury." A third-party review has been ordered by the state governor, Bill Lee, who also says the year's last remaining execution will not go ahead as planned. May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess". Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend Opponents of the death penalty have similarly been quick to react. Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain – lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life." Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row. Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death. Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering". His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods. Why the death penalty is on the rise in US In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes. The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased. The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective." The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan. The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee. More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm. In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally. The DPI says lethal injection has the high­est rate of botched exe­cu­tions. An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably. In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then. title: Pension tops £16,000 a year after 4.7% increase
description: The full pension rises by £734 a year, or about £14 a week, the Government of Jersey says.
body: The 4.7% increase will bring the overall pension sum to £16,294 per year Jersey pensioners are to receive an increase of £734 a year to their old age pension as a top-up comes into effect. The Government of Jersey said the 4.7% increase, an additional £14 per week for someone on a full pension, would bring the overall sum to £16,294 per year. The pension is updated every October by at least the recorded increase in the pensioner retail price index for June. Minister for Social Security Senator Elaine Millar said further support, including cold weather payments and free TV licences, would be available for those on low incomes. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Deputy Millar said: "Our pensioners have contributed to Jersey throughout their working lives and it is important that the old age pension continues to provide a strong foundation for old age. "We also recognise that pensioners on lower incomes can face particular pressure from healthcare and heating costs, which is why additional support is available through Pension Plus, the Health Access Scheme and the Cold Weather Bonus." Millar said she encouraged anyone who believed they could be eligible for extra help to "check what support is available to them". The social security minister said last month it was a priority for her to introduce mandatory workplace pensions alongside the government pension. title: England call up Crane and rest Archer for Pakistan series
description: Leg-spinner Mason Crane has the chance to play for England for the first time in eight years after being recalled for the one-day international tri-series in Pakistan.
body: Mason Crane has played one Test and two T20s for England Leg-spinner Mason Crane could play for England for the first time in eight years after being recalled for the one-day international tri-series in Pakistan. The 29-year-old won his only Test cap against Australia in Sydney in 2018 and is now given an opportunity in the series which also involves Sri Lanka next month. Crane, who also played two T20 internationals in 2017, could also push his case in the fight to be England's number one spinner in Test cricket. Sam Curran and Adil Rashid both return after injuries, and uncapped pair James Coles and Henry Crocombe are included. Jos Buttler is out with the hamstring injury he sustained last week, while Jacob Bethell is continuing his recovery from knee surgery. Brydon Carse, who is under an investigation from the Cricket Regulator following an incident outside a nightclub in Derby in August, remains absent. England squad for tri-series in Pakistan: Harry Brook (Yorkshire – captain), Gus Atkinson (Surrey), Sonny Baker (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), James Coles (Sussex), Jordan Cox (Essex), Mason Crane (Glamorgan), Henry Crocombe (Sussex), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Joe Root (Yorkshire), Josh Tongue (Nottinghamshire). TMS podcast: Behind the scenes at the PCA Awards England are on a diet of white-ball cricket until three Tests in South Africa in December as they build up to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year. The tri-series in Pakistan involves the three teams taking part playing each other twice, with the top two advancing to the final. Following the trip to Pakistan, England play three one-day internationals and five T20s in Australia in November. As England continue to shape their backroom staff following the arrival of Stephen Fleming as Test coach, Jeetan Patel, Mike Yardy, David Saker and Carl Hopkinson will assist white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum in Pakistan. That means Marcus Trescothick, who took temporary charge of the Test team for the series against Pakistan in the home summer, misses the trip. It is understood the make-up of the coaching staff is part of a plan to rotate the coaches – fielding coach Sarah Taylor and fast-bowling coach Tim Southee are also not going to Pakistan. All of Trescothick, Taylor and Southee are likely to be part of England's coaching team for other tours this winter. The return of Glamorgan's Crane is eye-catching, given the close proximity of the World Cup and the uncertainty surrounding the spin-bowling in England's Test team. The former Hampshire man is rewarded for consistent performances across formats in domestic cricket. This season Crane took 34 wickets in the County Championship and demonstrated his improvement with the bat by making his first two first-class hundreds. England national selector Marcus North said: "Mason Crane has been performing consistently for Glamorgan across both formats during the summer. He's an experienced, high-class leg-spinner who thoroughly deserves another opportunity at international level." Archer is a first choice in all three formats for England and his absence from the Pakistan trip is a clear indication of how the pace bowlers could be managed across the winter. McCullum has already indicated other seamers could skip the T20 series in Australia in order to prepare for the three Tests in South Africa. England are expected to name their squad for the Australia tour, along with their new list of centrally contracted players, next week. title: Ivan Toney denies Soho nightclub assault
description: England striker Ivan Toney pleads not guilty to assaulting a man at a Soho nightclub last year.
body: Toney arrived at court shortly after 09:30 BST England striker Ivan Toney has pleaded not guilty to assaulting a man at a central London nightclub. The 30-year-old footballer, from Northampton, is accused of headbutting and punching Saber Da Silva at a nightclub in Wardour Street, Soho, on 6 December. At Westminster Magistrates' Court, Toney confirmed his name and age, and pleaded not guilty to a charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm. District Judge Briony Clarke said the case could be tried in the magistrates court, but Toney elected for a Crown Court trial in front of a judge and jury. He was freed on unconditional bail until a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on 29 October. Toney won 10 caps for England and was part of the squad that reached the Euro 2024 final. He started his football career with Northampton Town and played for teams including Wigan Athletic and Peterborough United before signing for Brentford in 2020. He currently plays for Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli. Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: Michael Jordan's 1998 NBA finals jersey sells for more than £9m
description: A Michael Jordan jersey from his 'Last Dance' season sells for $12.3m, a record for a piece of Jordan memorabilia.
body: Michael Jordan came out of retirement for two more seasons with the Washington Wizards from 2001-2003 A Michael Jordan jersey from his 'Last Dance' season has sold for $12.3m (£9.3m), a record for a piece of game-worn Jordan memorabilia. He wore the jersey in game three of the 1998 NBA Finals, his last season with the Chicago Bulls. Jordan helped the Bulls win the series 4-2 for his sixth and final NBA Championship. He was named the Finals' Most Valuable Player in all six. The previous record for a piece of Jordan memorabilia was $10.1m (£7.6m) for his jersey from game one of the 1998 Finals. The game three jersey was put up for sale by entrepreneur Ryan Gough and sold at Joopiter, Pharrell Williams' digital auction house, which gave it an estimated price of $10-15m (£7.5-£11.3m). Jordan's 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello was sold for $2.7m (£2m), four times the auction record for that model. "Few objects in the history of sport embody greatness as completely as Michael Jordan's game three jersey from the 1998 NBA Finals," Joopiter said in the auction posting. "Worn during the Last Dance... it marks the culmination of an era that transformed basketball into a global cultural phenomenon. "Today it stands among the most important game-worn sports artifacts ever to come to market." The record price for a piece of game-worn sports memorabilia is the jersey worn by baseball legend Babe Ruth when he "called the shot" during the 1932 World Series, which was sold for $24.1m (£18.2m) in 2024. title: Orange Order says no proposals on table for resolution to Drumcree dispute
description: The secretary of state has been trying to strike a compromise deal between the two sides of the stand-off.
body: Members of the Portadown district of the Orange Order met the Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant, accompanied by Jamie Bryson, on Wednesday Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree dispute are expected to continue as Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said: "There are currently no proposals on the table." Both sides were given a document during separate meetings with the Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant on Wednesday. After its meeting, the chairman of the resident's coalition said his group would agree to it, if the Orange Order did. On Sunday, an Orange Order parade from Drumcree into Portadown did not happen because of a large protest on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road. Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road, although in much smaller numbers, and the Orange Order have maintained a presence at Drumcree. On Thursday, The Nolan Show revealed details of what was in the document. The BBC understands it said the Orange Order had the legal right to walk the Garvaghy Road, the residents would accept that legal entitlement and publicly accept that it was wrong to block the Orange Order from walking down the Garvaghy Road, but in return the Orange Order would choose not to walk down the road anyway. On Wednesday, the Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Carla Lockhart told the Press Association that: "What's on the table is not acceptable." The Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher will address the dispute at a public meeting of the Policing Board in Belfast on Thursday. The parade dispute is expected to dominate the agenda. Board members will want to hear the chief constable's security assessment of the situation, and will receive an update on the PSNI's criminal investigation into the protest which blocked the Garvaghy Road. One of the board members, Sinn Féin's Deidre Hargey, was photographed taking part in the protest and unionists have said she should be barred from attending the meeting. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? O'Neill returns to Garvaghy Road as police investigate Sunday's 'unlawful protest' Drumcree negotiations are 'nowhere near dead' - NI secretary Talks continued at Hillsborough Castle between the Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant and members of the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition. Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said a "large scale criminal investigation" was under way into the unlawful blocking of Garvaghy Road, which prevented Sunday's parade. He has also offered to meet both sides in the stalemate, the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition. First Minister Michelle O'Neill has been accused by the DUP leader Gavin Robinson of breaking the law in taking part in demonstrations on Sunday. In response, O'Neill said on Wednesday if she is investigated then "so be it, that's the chief constable's job". "I can only focus on what I'm focusing on right now which is - I've made a choice to be here top stand on the Garvaghy Road with these residents and I will continue to do so." Speaking after a meeting with the chief constable, Robinson said the DUP have given him their expectation "that within days, if not a week, we need to see the positive out workings of [the investigation]". Protesters spent more than a day along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of points The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident. However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas. The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. The row sparked some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history and was linked to several murders. The Drumcree dispute was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes during the 1990s, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders across Northern Ireland. In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision upheld for the last 28 years. The row reemerged last month after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission was overturned, and a fresh application was lodged. On Friday, the commission decided the march could go ahead with restrictions in place. However that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go ahead just hours before it was due to take place. title: Moment Esther Rantzen surprises Nicholas Winton with children he saved
description: One of her most memorable career moments came during one particular episode in 1988 - the footage of which has gone viral several times over in recent years.
body: This video can not be played In a 1988 episode of That's Life!, Esther Rantzen surprised Nicholas Winton with an audience of children, now grown up, that he had rescued from Nazi forces during World War II. His incredible work went largely unreported for nearly 50 years - until his wife found a scrapbook in their loft, which contained names of the 669 children, who were mostly Jewish, that he had rescued. Dame Esther said she watched the episode "many times" and "each time found myself deeply moved". She said she kept in contact with Sir Nicholas, meeting regularly until his death in 2015 at the age of 106. Moment Esther Rantzen surprises Nicholas Winton with children he saved. title: From Beckham to Bale - ranking the best British exports this century
description: From David Beckham and Gareth Bale to Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane, who are the best British exports this century?
body: Gazza's baggy Roman shellsuit, John Charles plundering black-and-white goals in Turin, King Kev's floodlit perm dazzling Volksparkstadion terraces, Glenn Hoddle's miniscule Monegasque shorts. They were all trailblazers and trendsetters, their tales relayed through continental dispatches and espresso-fuelled Saturday morning showreels. Yet what was once an exotic European escapade for Britain's star footballers is now a well-trodden pilgrimage, as an increasing number of players eye opportunities further afield. Eight of England's most recent World Cup squad are currently playing abroad - from Munich to Madrid, and Milan to the Middle East - while Scotland have even more overseas, predominantly in Serie A. So while we acknowledge and applaud the groundwork put in by those early jetsetters, this week we're looking at the best British exports since the turn of the century. I've ranked my top 10 below - you can have you say in the comments, too. Kieran Trippier won a La Liga title during a two-and-a-half year stay in Madrid 10. Kieran Trippier - Atletico Madrid Kieran Trippier was seemingly deemed surplus to requirements at Tottenham after the north London outfit's Champions League final defeat by Liverpool in 2019, but the defender managed to renew his career under Diego Simeone in Spain. The right-back became Atletico Madrid's first English player in almost a century, and then helped Los Rojiblancos win only their second La Liga title since the turn of the millennium, breaking the Barcelona and Real Madrid stranglehold. It was the first trophy of his career, and Trippier returned to the Premier League after his Spanish sabbatical renewed, refreshed and ready to enjoy a successful spell at Newcastle. Fikayo Tomori has played more than 200 games for AC Milan 9. Fikayo Tomori - AC Milan John Charles, three-times winner; Jimmy Greaves, with Milan in 1961-62; and Gerry Hitchens, with Inter the following season, were the only British players to clinch a Scudetto before Juventus' Aaron Ramsey ended a wait that stretched back more than half a century in 2020. Ramsey's Turin expedition, though, was inconsistent and expensive, and while Ashley Young then helped Inter win a first title in 11 years, his San Siro stay lasted only 18 months. So the Scudetto winner we're plumping for here is Milan stalwart Fikayo Tomori. The England defender lifted the prize in 2021-22, earning a spot in the Serie A team of the season on the way. And, despite ups and downs under various bosses since, the 28-year-old is now into his seventh season with the European giants. A quietly impressive feat. Jadon Sancho spent four seasons at Dortmund before returning on loan in 2023-24 8. Jadon Sancho - Borussia Dortmund Jadon Sancho's career may not have continued on the trajectory many expected when he departed Germany in a £73m move for Old Trafford, four years after initially leaving Manchester, but his time at Dortmund was an undoubted success. It was brave, as a 17-year-old, to reject Manchester City and move to a new country, but the young winger was vindicated with rapid progress at Dortmund. In his second season, Sancho scored 12 goals and added 18 assists in 34 Bundesliga games, the following term he netted 17 times. In fact, by the time Sancho left Dortmund aged 21 he'd scored 50 goals and made 64 assists across 137 games in all competitions, winning a German Cup and finishing runner-up in both the European Golden Boy prize and the Kopa Trophy for the world's best young player. More than that, he helped establish a pathway for young British prospects to grow and develop abroad that many have followed since. David Beckham won La Liga with Real Madrid in 2007, before joining La Galaxy 7. David Beckham - Real Madrid, LA Galaxy, AC Milan & PSG It was tempting to include Bradley Wright-Philips, a man who followed a half-season stint at League One Brentford with a move to New York Red Bulls, winning a pair of Golden Boots, three Supporters' Shields and netting more than 100 goals during his time in the Big Apple. But if we're talking Major League Soccer impact then there's only one winner. David Beckham swapped the Galactico comforts of Real Madrid, where he spent four seasons and collected a sole La Liga crown, for a Hollywood welcome at LA Galaxy. Beckham's presence was at times questioned, especially when spending loan spells in Milan, but the England captain and global superstar brought a huge amount of eyeballs and allure to the American game. He left with silverware, too, twice winning both the MLS Cup and Supporters' Shield. There was room for a five-month stay in Paris before the midfielder hung up his iconic Preds, winning Ligue 1 and waving an emotional goodbye in 2013. Scott McTominay has become a Napoli legend since joining in 2024 6. Scott McTominay - Napoli Maybe it's the tomatoes. Scott McTominay wouldn't touch one back in Manchester, but since moving to southern Italy he boasts the glow of a man loving both the local Neapolitan cuisine and his football. The Lancaster-born Scot has undergone a slick transformation. Few would have expected him to veer from United squad player to cult hero mentioned in the same breath as Napoli's greatest adopted son, Diego Maradona. But McTominay, with a little help from compatriot Billy Gilmour, has thrived in the football-obsessed maze that is Naples, firing the club to only a fourth Scudetto in history with 12 goals from midfield during his debut Serie A season. It landed him the league's MVP award. Finishing runners-up last term, McTominay has already etched his name in Napoli folklore, with more goals - and tomatoes - likely to follow. Owen Hargreaves was born in Canada to a Welsh mother and English father 5. Owen Hargreaves - Bayern Munich Owen Hargreaves is something of an anomaly. title: Nasa heads to Scottish Highlands in its search for life on Mars
description: The US space agency says ancient rocks at Clachtoll have similarities to those on the Red Planet.
body: The Nasa-led team of scientists took samples of ancient rock from the north-west Highlands Nasa scientists are studying rocks in the Scottish Highlands to help them understand if there was once life on Mars. The US space agency announced last year that its Perseverance rover had found potential biosignatures, markings on rocks possibly made by ancient microbes. This summer, scientists took samples from a geological feature called the Stoer Formation, external around Clachtoll, in Assynt, in the north-west Highlands. Nasa said the area's rocks formed in environments comparable to ancient Martian lakes and rivers, but could also hold evidence of microbial life from 1.2 billion years ago. Scientists surveying rocks at Clachtoll in Assynt earlier this year Perseverance, shown in a concept image, has detected potential biosignatures Clachtoll is a small crofting community on the Sutherland coast about 100 miles north of Inverness, and is a popular destination along the North Coast 500 tourist route. Nasa's Goddard Instrument Field Team, which specialises in studying Earth's extreme environments, led the research expedition. Experts from the universities of Glasgow and Cambridge were among those involved. They took rock samples from cliffs for further analysis. Nasa said: "Though Mars is dry today, the Martian landscape, like our own planet's, is shaped by an ancient history of flowing water. "Both worlds have layered areas of mudstones and siltstones rich in clay minerals. "Learning how signs of ancient life show up in Earth rocks like these Scottish cliffs can help us understand the story of habitability and the potential for biosignatures to be preserved and detected on Mars." The scientists said the rocks at Clachtoll were formed under similar conditions to rocks found on Mars Clachtoll is in Assynt in Sutherland It is not the first time Scotland's ancient geology has been used by scientists to help them understand how life could have existed on Mars. Last year, technology which will be used in the search for evidence of Martian life was tested by a University of St Andrews team at Lower Diabaig, in Torridon. The rocks in the area are billions of years old and similar to those found on the Red Planet. Eight years ago, a Nasa Mars rover, Curiosity, explored a part of the planet named after Torridon. Martian geological areas and features have been named by Nasa after places on Earth. Several of the names were taken from Scotland and, as well as Torridon, there is a Siccar Point, Muck, Wick, Sandwick and Holyrood on Mars. Nasa chose the name Torridon due to the Torridonian Supergroup, a geological formation in the north-west Highlands that contains some of the oldest evidence of life of any rocks in the UK. In 2012, Glenelg held a celebration in honour of a location on Mars being named after the small Highland community. title: Tributes paid to 'inspirational' presenter and campaigner Esther Rantzen
description: Dame Esther Rantzen was "an inspirational individual", the director of her Childline helpline says.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Dame Esther Rantzen, broadcaster, campaigner and charity founder, dies aged 86 Dame Esther Rantzen was "an inspirational individual" who was "quite a force" as a campaigner, according to the director of Childline, the children's helpline founded by the broadcaster in the 1980s. "She inspired people, she energised people, she persuaded people," Shaun Friel told BBC Breakfast. "She had a great mind and she had obviously that natural journalistic ability." Dame Esther, who died on Wednesday at the age of 86, was known for presenting BBC consumer show That's Life! for 21 years, and for campaigning on issues including child welfare and assisted dying. Prime Minister Andy Burnham led the tributes, saying the veteran broadcaster had "changed countless lives". This video can not be played Watch: How TV presenter Dame Esther Rantzen set up Childline BBC director general Matt Brittin also paid tribute to Dame Esther, describing her as a "legend of British broadcasting" whose contribution to public life was "immeasurable". "Her warmth, spirit and fight for justice and action that we saw on our screens continued long after the programme ended, with a lifetime of campaigning where she changed the lives of millions," he said. Fellow broadcaster and money saving expert Martin Lewis called Dame Esther an "inspiration" and a "pioneer" whose "impact and memory will long continue to shine". Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, which runs Childline, said Dame Esther had gone to "exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help". Dame Esther set up the telephone helpline in 1986 after featuring a number of incidents of child abuse and neglect on That's Life! and realising that many children had nowhere to turn. How That's Life! gave Esther Rantzen a career-defining moment Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! presenter, Childline founder and campaigner for assisted dying Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen dies aged 86 Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Friel said: "The legacy that Dame Esther created when she created Childline is something quite incredible. She changed how society looked upon children." He added: "When she decided she had a vision or something had to be done or had to be changed, she was quite a force." TV executive Michael Grade paid tribute to "her courage and her fortitude and what she achieved in her life". Lord Grade told BBC Radio 4's Today: "She used her television fame to help an awful lot of people, particularly the children. And Childline goes on today, getting so many calls from distressed and abused children. "That was an extraordinary effort of will to turn the television programme into a long-lasting charity that's so effective and so needed. That's her legacy for me. I'll always remember her for that." Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006. In 2013, Dame Esther founded The Silver Line to help older people suffering from isolation and loneliness. She also led campaigns on car safety, organ donation and bullying, and later in life became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying. She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic, but last month said she was now "too physically fragile to make the journey". Burnham said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life". Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners. Baroness Jan Royall, former leader of the House of Lords and a friend of Dame Esther, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that she was a "formidable" person. "She was an extraordinary, compassionate woman, a passionate woman, and she brought about such change in our world, change for the better." Baroness Royall added that Dame Esther had "a wicked sense of humour" and a "zest for life", which was the thing that "drove her to try and improve people's lives through Silver Line, Childline etc, but also with the assisted dying bill." Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told Radio 4's Today: "I was lucky enough to know her for more than 50 years, and what I remember is her energy, her intelligence, her resilience. Her vulgar streak, which she enjoyed and she said she got from her mother. She was formidable and she was fun." Dame Esther told him her campaigning was rooted in memories of difficult times in her own life as a child during and after World War Two, Brandreth said. That's Life! attracted more than 20 million viewers at its peak Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning. "She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said. Dame Elaine Paige, known for her roles in West End productions like Cats and Evita, paid tribute to a "great broadcaster, journalist and campaigner". She said: "Her Childline, the confidential counselling service for young people in distress, helped so many children and The Silver Line was aimed at older people suffering loneliness and isolation." Anton Du Beke, Dame Esther's partner on Strictly Come Dancing, shared a photo of the pair dancing together in the 2004 series, writing that the two had "remained firm friends" ever since. He praised her "breadth of knowledge and passion" and called her "the ultimate breaker of the glass ceiling", adding: "She will be greatly missed and my sincere thoughts are with her family." title: Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
description: Capt Smit Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard the Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv.
body: The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage" The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar. Capt Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia. The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tabuk, a city in north-western Saudi Arabia, where he remains in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh. Writing on X, Netanyahu said Capt Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster". Capt Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022, having become an experienced pilot. Speaking to the BBC, Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, said he remembers Capt Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis. "We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker." Capt Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile. His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives". Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter. Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added. Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family. "Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised. He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely. "In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations. At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays. He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want." Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral. What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel Capt Machchhar joined Flydubai in 2022 Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel. The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli. Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21. Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking. At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing. Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700. Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots. But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane. He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing". The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data. The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured. "His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery. Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger". Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack. "Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open." title: Zimbabwe tycoon Wicknell Chivayo and wife killed in helicopter crash
description: Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to African presidents and lucrative government contracts.
body: Wicknell Chivayo was a prominent businessman known for his extravagant lifestyle Prominent Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife have been killed in a helicopter crash that left six people dead, his family have confirmed. The helicopter came down in the Marondera rural area, about 70km (43 miles) east of the capital, Harare, on Wednesday evening. Police said all six people on board died. Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo confirmed the deaths of the businessman and his wife Lucy Muteke to state broadcaster ZBC, saying the family was devastated by the tragedy. Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to some African presidents and lucrative government contracts that had repeatedly attracted scrutiny. He had denied allegations of wrongdoing linked to his business dealings. Police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said the aircraft crashed at about 17:00 local time (15:00 GMT) and had six occupants, but authorities did not immediately identify all those on board. Two of the six were pilots, according to government officials. ZBC reported that the group was travelling from Gandami in Chikomba, where Chivayo and his wife were building a rural home, when the helicopter crashed at Kudenga Farm about 40 minutes after take-off. "We are at a loss for words after the tragic news," the family spokesperson, told the ZBC. The cause of the crash was not immediately known, and police said investigations were under way. Emergency services were sent to the scene on Wednesday evening. How a self-styled knight giving away cars and wads of cash got people talking Earlier, government spokesman Nick Mangwana confirmed the crash, saying the helicopter was carrying "a prominent businessman, three other passengers and two pilots". "Current information indicates that there were no survivors in this crash," Mangwana posted on X. Chivayo was the managing director of Intratrek Zimbabwe and had built a high public profile through government contracts, philanthropy and displays of wealth on social media. Among his best-known business ventures was a $172m (£128m) solar power project in Gwanda awarded to Intratrek by the state-owned Zimbabwe Power Company. The project became the subject of years of legal disputes. He also came under scrutiny over the procurement of materials for Zimbabwe's disputed 2023 elections. Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission investigated allegations surrounding contracts awarded to South African company Ren-Form but closed the inquiry in 2025, saying it had found no evidence linking Chivayo or the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission to wrongdoing. Widely known as "Sir Wicknell", Chivayo frequently used the title publicly and on social media, although he was never given a British knighthood. He was also known for giving away luxury cars and large sums of money to musicians, religious leaders and other public figures, often publicising the gifts on social media. His connections extended beyond Zimbabwe. Kenya's President William Ruto, who had previously appeared in public with Chivayo, paid tribute to him as a "dear friend" and sent condolences to the families of those killed. "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent," Ruto added. Kenyan opposition figures had questioned Chivayo's repeated access to Ruto and State House. He frequently publicised his access to African leaders, posting photographs of meetings with presidents including Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa and Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, as well as Eswatini's King Mswati III. title: Watch: The many questions raised by the failed execution of Christa Pike
description: Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening.
body: This video can not be played Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after her heart was still beating following two lethal injections during her execution, her lawyer says. Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening, saying: "Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring." One of her attorneys told the BBC that Pike, 50, was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital after two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered on Wednesday. Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. More on Christa Pike's story. Watch: The many questions raised by the failed execution of Christa Pike. title: Jaissle learned a lot about life after tumour aged five
description: Newcastle United head coach Matthias Jaissle could not move his neck at one point, but went on to play before embarking on a coaching career that sees him in Tyneside.
body: Newcastle United currently lie in ninth place in the early stages of the Premier League season Matthias Jaissle points to his neck. "I had a tumour when I was five years old," the Newcastle United head coach says. "Here in my neck so I couldn't move it anymore. "That was a period where I already learned a lot about life, how important it is to be healthy, and how grateful you can be to be healthy and to follow your dream. "It was not clear that I could play football as a kid anymore." He did not elaborate further, but such perspective would be needed. Jaissle, like so many, visualised one day becoming a professional footballer, but he was among the rare few to actually go on to do so. The former Hoffenheim defender even felt he was on the verge of a senior call up to the German national team at one stage, only to suffer a serious knee injury. He was just 20 at the time. Jaissle refused to give up, and "kept the dream for a lot longer than the doctors did", but the setback ultimately curtailed his career and he retired a few years later in 2014. It left him in a dark place, as he previously detailed in an interview with BBC Sport, but the "wounds" he experienced in life have shaped him. "That makes you the person you are, whatever aspect it is, with the belief you can overcome every obstacle," he says. "Every setback also has a positive side. If you overcome these challenges then you become stronger, more resilient." This outlook gave Jaissle a head start in his second career, but he did not necessarily plan on being a coach. Not at first. Ralf Rangnick, his former manager at Hoffenheim, invited him on to a training programme at RB Leipzig, where his mentor was working at the time, to sample life behind the scenes at the club. Jaissle was due to be redeployed in a new department every six weeks and started his placement as an assistant youth team coach to ex team-mate Sebastien Hoeness, who now manages Stuttgart. He was pencilled in to spend time with the club's sporting director and figures from their administrative, commercial and marketing departments. But he never ended up doing so. "I didn't move on," Jaissle says. "After two weeks, wow, I felt joy back in life." It set Jaissle on the path to Newcastle. He climbed the coaching ladder and won trophies at Austrian side Red Bull Salzburg and Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli. Players and staff alike were quickly struck by his intensity and work rate. "Since the first meeting, it was clear this was our guy," a senior Newcastle source says. It was still a baptism of fire for the 38-year-old, who had never previously managed in the Premier League, after predecessor Eddie Howe stepped down. Jaissle insists friend Thomas Tuchel "didn't need to warn" him about what was coming in the top flight, but he had just three weeks to prepare for the visit of Liverpool on the opening weekend and the squad was in flux. Captain Bruno Guimaraes was about to follow Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali out of the exit door and complete a £75m move to Arsenal at the time. Although Newcastle would end up making eight signings, they were all aged 24 and under as the club went from having one of the most experienced sides in the Premier League to the youngest almost overnight. It was a huge amount of change in a short space of time. There have also been a spate of injuries to key players, but Jaissle has only lost one of his opening seven matches in all competitions, a chastening 4-1 defeat at Leeds United. "I think there were elements in games where we saw a lot of the things we were looking for," he says. "There were also phases in games where we were not happy and satisfied, so there's still a lot of potential that we can improve." Jaissle accepts it has been "tougher than expected" to "get stuff into the players' heads" given pre-season was "so short and packed with friendly matches we couldn't change", adding "but considering all these things, we're doing good". He remains convinced that his aggressive style of play and so-called vertical football will "work anywhere", even if this team is clearly still a work in progress at such an early stage of his reign. Newcastle have made the most errors leading to shots (12) in the Premier League this season while, at the other end of the field, Jaissle's clinical side have only averaged little more than three efforts on target per match in the top flight. It feels like there will be ups and downs throughout, given the age of the side, but Jaissle has been struck by the backing of supporters and has quickly settled into life on Tyneside. He moved out of a hotel into a new home earlier this week and has ventured into the city to sample a handful of restaurants - but only to celebrate wins. Following the 2-1 victory against Hull City at St James' Park last time out, he even paid for a supporter's birthday meal. "I really love the fans and the people here," he adds. title: Fuel prices leave people asking 'what can we do?'
description: Record fuel prices across the country have left people in the South looking for ways to cope.
body: Fuel costs across the UK are currently at a record high Record fuel prices across the country have left people in the south of England looking for ways to cope with the rising costs. Earlier this week, the RAC said diesel prices in the UK had reached an all time high, with the cost of petrol also rising, due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. One garage manager from Berkshire said he had noticed a change in customer behaviour, with customers more likely to put £20 of fuel in, rather than fill their tanks up. Meanwhile, a small charity helping people with multiple sclerosis (MS) in Dorset said it would have to find ways to cut costs, as it was now costing an extra £2,000 a year to run a key minibus service. The MS Centre Dorset runs a fleet of five minibuses, helping users across the county to get to its base in West Parley. But manager Diana Logan‑Watts said diesel prices had "rocketed so quickly" that the extra costs were "not something that we had budgeted into account". Diesel prices at pumps across the south have risen above £2 in recent weeks On Monday, the RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away". It said diesel prices had hit an all-time high of 199.33p per litre - rising by just under 40% since the US-Israel conflict with Iran erupted at the end of February. Logan-Watts said this the MS Centre Dorset would "keep on keeping on" despite the vast cost increases, and ensure users could still get to the centre. "But these rising costs have a knock-on effect, and we don't want to put additional prices and costs onto our members who are already struggling with the cost of living," she said. "So we have to try and absorb those costs elsewhere, and one of those ways is thinking more closely about the additional services that we're able to offer, like trips. "These make a real positive difference to our members lives, but will have to be looked at in more depth and ask where the money's going to come from." Southampton taxi driver Neil McLean said the price increases "need to stop" It's not just charities in the South feeling the pinch though, with Southampton taxi driver Neil McLean asking "what can we do?" about the soaring costs. "We've got to earn a living, and none of us are happy," he said. "It's not putting money in our pockets, it's taking money out of our pockets - and it needs to stop." David Price owns Southampton-based DCP Haulage, and said if things did not improve he would have to look at "parking up trucks" or "actually downscaling". "We just can't physically afford the fuel prices, we're looking an extra £250 a week per vehicle," Price said. "We have downscaled a lot lately and we have talked about packing it all up. "It's not worth it with these prices - you're just not making any money." Ian Govier manages the Littlewick Green Motor Company garage in Maidenhead Ian Govier manages the Littlewick Green Motor Company garage in Maidenhead, and said his costs had "gone up dramatically over the years". "Ten years ago, we'd look at having [a profit margin of] 6p a litre, now I really need close to 15p a litre to still have the same profit," he said. He said he had also spotted customers habits changing, including more using cash as a way to "control their budgets". "We are definitely seeing instead of putting your normal £50 pounds in to fill up, a lot of people are now sticking in £10, £20," he said. Amid the increase in costs, Govier said he was also having to tackle thefts - with some using illegal "ghost" registrations to prevent cameras from reading their number plates. He said he had been forced to invest in a new camera system to tackle such thefts, which also "eats into profits". "If you don't have a profit you can't invest in the cameras, you can't invest in your staff, you can't invest in people," he added. Speaking at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool on Monday, the Chancellor said the time for the government to deal with questions around rising fuel costs would be the Budget - near the end of October. John Healey told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm acutely concerned and conscious about how hard it is for families. I see that at the pumps myself. "We can't remove the cost of living pressures, we can't remove the prices that people are having to pay, but where we can we will act and we will give people just a bit of breathing space, and the same goes for the cost to business." title: K-pop star convicted of violating military service law
description: The member of K-pop band Winner was given a suspended prison sentence for repeated absences from his national service work.
body: Song Min-ho, also known by his stage name Mino, is a member of K-pop group Winner. A South Korean court has handed a suspended one-year prison sentence to K-pop singer Song Min-ho after he was convicted of violating the country's military service law. The 33-year-old member of the boy band Winner was found to have been absent multiple times at a community centre in Seoul, where he had worked as a social worker from 2023 to 2024. All able-bodied men in South Korea have to serve at least 18 months in the military. But some are alternatively assigned as social service personnel for health reasons. The prison sentence handed on Thursday is suspended for two years. That means he can avoid incarceration if he does not commit any crime during that two-year probationary period. The court heard that Song, who is also known by his stage name Mino, had recorded 102 unauthorised absences during his 21-month stint as a social service agent. Military service is a duty to be performed "faithfully", and social service agents are "no exception", the court said. But the court also noted that Song had admitted to the charges and shown remorse. Authorities launched an investigation into Song shortly after he was discharged in 2024, when local media reported that he was frequently absent from his social service duties and took excessive sick leave. Song's supervisor at the social service centre was also given a suspended jail sentence for helping him dodge his duties, including falsifying records to make it look like Song had reported to work. The conscription of South Korea's entertainers has long been a topic of national public debate. Gangnam Style singer Psy famously had to enlist twice, once in 2003 and another time in 2007, after a Seoul court ruled that he had neglected his duties by continuing his showbiz activities during his first national service stint. Steve Yoo, one of the country's biggest pop stars in the 1990s and early 2000s, was embroiled in a national scandal after he was found to have evaded military service in 2002. South Korean authorities banned him from the country after he renounced his citizenship and became a US national shortly before he was due to serve in the military. Going on hiatus to serve in the military is often a threat for budding careers in South Korea's fast-moving entertainment industry. But the evasion of military service also comes with intense public scrutiny and legal repercussions. Ahead of the ruling on Thursday, Song told reporters that he regretted his actions and was "sorry toward the people who gave me so much love", Seoul Economic Daily reported. But he did not answer a question about whether he would re-enlist to serve the mandatory duty.
