title: Celebrity Traitors: Can I visit the castle, ride the train and see the unusual monument?
description: A brief guide to the Scottish Highlands' "Traitors Territory".
body: Claudia Winkleman reprises her role as host for the latest outing of Celebrity Traitors The Celebrity Traitors is back with a new cast of stars vying to be the winner (or winners) of the TV mega-hit. Hosted by Claudia Winkleman, the show will see a group of famous 'faithfuls' attempt to work out which among them are the 'traitors' secretly "murdering" contestants each night. This year's line-up features award-winning actor and campaigner Michael Sheen, comedian Miranda Hart, EastEnders hardman Ross Kemp and Love Island presenter Maya Jama. But one of the biggest stars of The Traitors franchise is the venue - Ardross Castle. Ardross Castle sits in 100 acres of gardens and parkland The Celebrity Traitors is filmed in Ardross Castle, a 19th Century pile about 30 miles north of Inverness. It is set in about 100 acres of gardens and parkland near the Easter Ross town of Alness. The property was built more than 170 years ago in a Scottish baronial style, a type of elaborate architecture featuring complex rooflines with turrets and fortress-like battlements. Ardross Castle in a photograph taken in 1960 More than 200 years ago - long before the castle was built - the land at Ardross was owned by George Granville Leveson-Gower, the 1st Duke of Sutherland. He had a hunting lodge on the site where the castle stands today. The duke was a controversial figure in the Highland Clearances. In large parts of Sutherland, he had people cleared off land where they had lived for generations to make way for sheep farming and agricultural "improvements". Some families were moved to coastal villages, while others became emigrants and made difficult journeys to Canada to start new lives there. There is a statue of the duke on a hilltop north of Ardross. Known locally as The Mannie, and overlooking Golspie, it has been the target of vandalism and even attempts to topple it. A statue of the Duke of Sutherland - known as The Mannie - overlooks Golspie Years later the estate at Ardross was bought by Sir Alexander Matheson. Matheson made his fortune trading in China. He was an MP and an instrumental figure in the building of railways in the Highlands. He had the castle built and, according to Ross and Cromarty Heritage Society, about 400 workers were involved in the construction from 1847. They built 30 rooms and laid out the castle's extensive grounds. According to Ardross Castle's website, Sir Alexander also improved estate workers' housing. Ardross Castle dates from the 19th Century After Sir Alexander's death, the country house and its estate was sold to businessman and philanthropist Charles William Dyson Perrins. His grandfather William Perrins, in partnership with John Wheeley Lea, created the recipe for Worcestershire Sauce. The Perrins family was also involved in the production of Royal Worcester porcelain. Charles William Dyson Perrins joined the family business after four years serving in the Highland Light Infantry. He and his family were annual visitors to Ardross Castle. The Perrins' ownership came to an end in the 1930s and various parts of the estate was sold off. Contestants of series four in the show's Round Table Room In 1983, the castle was bought by the McTaggart family and they still own it today. While not run as a hotel, the property is available as a wedding venue - its popularity undoubtedly boosted by its appearance in The Celebrity Traitors - and UK and US versions of The Traitors. The castle has accommodation for up to 41 for two nights, and various parts of the property and its grounds can be hired for the wedding ceremony and reception. In 2023, Loukas Tsarmaklis, a director of Ardross Castle Enterprises, told The Press and Journal, external they "try to keep a low profile... but there is no chance now". "This has put us on the map and helped local B&Bs, tradesmen, taxi drivers, cleaners. It was a big operation for this part of the world," he added. The castle's owners have previously politely declined to comment on the impact the show has had to BBC Scotland News, but internet searches for the castle have been on the rise. Ross and Cromarty Heritage Society said views of its page about Ardross increased significantly because of the US show. Contestants taking part in a series of The Traitors board carriages A train has featured in previous episodes of The Traitors, including the finale of the first series of The Celebrity Traitors. Strathspey Railway is a volunteer-run company that operates a 10 mile (16km) route between Aviemore and Broomhill, via Boat of Garten. The heritage railway's line is part of the former Inverness and Perth Junction Railway, later called the Highland, which linked Aviemore with Forres. It is one of only a handful of former lines to be preserved following rail closures in the 1960s. Strathspey Railway has been used for parts of contestants' journeys to the castle, and for tasks Strathspey Railway has a fleet of steam and diesel locomotives which are run and maintained by a mix of volunteers and a small number of paid staff. It has frequently been involved in restoration projects, including helping to return a 75-year-old steam locomotive to working order. The Ivatt Class 2 2-6-0 engine - No. 46464 - was one of five built in Crewe, Cheshire, in 1950. It spent most of its working life based at Dundee Tay Bridge Steam Shed 62B, operating on services in Angus and Fife. Last year, Strathspey Railway received a £1m donation from a mystery American donor which secured the railway's long-term future. The railway runs trips throughout the year and is now operating to a winter timetable, which includes a festive Elf Express. Fyrish Monument appeared in series four of The Traitors An unusual landmark was the backdrop for a task in the penultimate episode of series four of The Traitors. title: 'I love the sheep and the people' - Knitters flock to Shetland's wool week
description: The annual event is marking its 17th year and draws visitors from all over the world.
body: Shetland Wool Week draw visitors from Scotland and further afield Almost 1,000 people have gathered in Shetland for the island's annual celebration of wool, knitting and textiles. The week-long event is marking its 17th year and features classes, workshops, talks, tours and social activities. Shetland Wool Week draws enthusiasts from around the world, including the US and Japan. This year's patron, knitwear designer Helen Robertson, said: "I think wool week is just such a fantastic organisation and festival, and it's really brought Shetland textiles to life." We've travelled 5,000 miles to the 'holy place' of knitting The remote island where jumpers are always in fashion Nancy Woodhouse, a knitter from Arizona in the US, brought some of her creations, including a woolly hat inspired by the crime drama Shetland. "I love the show," she said. Describing the head wear, Woodhouse said: "We start on the hat with detective Jimmy Perez of course and Tosh who's taken over as the lead detective, then we have the ever helpful Sandy and Ruth Calder, and this is the chalk outline of the victim. "The hat has muted colours so the detectives would shine - it's the crime scene I wear on my head." Nancy Woodhouse is a fan of the crime drama Shetland The hat features characters from the show Satoko Nagakubo has flown from Tokyo for the festival. "I come from Japan many times to Shetland for wool week because I love the sheep and the local people. I love Shetland lace knitting and spinning," she said. Mary Randles, visiting from Lancashire, said: "I think the fact that you can chill, you can knit, meet people, buy wool and sit on your suitcase until it forces all the wool in before you take it home." She said the event allowed her to see the sheep the wool she uses for knitting come from. Randles added: "Once you've knitted with it and washed it, it drapes beautifully whereas sometimes when you knitting with synthetic it doesn't drape but this stuff does." More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds From Fair Isle knitting to spinning, fleece preparation, weaving, lace knitting to wool skirting, there is a huge range for visitors to discover. It is an event that stretches far beyond the classroom, with activities taking place from Unst to the south mainland. Local communities are at the heart of the week, with community halls, crofts and businesses, makers and musicians all helping to create the unique experience for the wool enthusiasts. Patron Helen Robertson designed the much-anticipated wool week hat - the Birsie Beanny. "It's such a joyful and happy week," she said. Knitwear designer Helen Robertson said the week brought Shetland's textiles to life Shetland Wool Week's Birsie Beanny hats were designed by Helen Robertson The star attraction are Shetland's native sheep and the earthy shades of cream, brown and black of their wool. Ronnie Eunson runs Uradale Farm on the west side of the islands and breeds native sheep and cattle which graze on the nearby hills and coastline. He said: "Shetland wool is a fairly unique commodity. "It's the history and heritage that makes it really special. You're looking at a type of fibre that has clothed Shetlanders for thousands of years." Eunson said the sheep had a double coat of wool which protected them against the islands' harsh winter weather. The finer wool is below the top layer. The farmer added: "Tourists are fascinated to see the sheep and to hear about the way we look after the sheep and how the sheep look after themselves." The wool is produced by sheep that are native to Shetland As the nights draw in and winter approaches the festival is a big boost too for the island's economy. Donna Smith, who runs Langsoond Yarn in Burra, said: "It's really an amazing event that's the highlight of the year for me at the end of the tourist season. "There are so many people coming to visit and so many people coming to buy yarn. It's such an important week in the whole year for the business. The "sewing of the loose ends" of the festival is on Saturday. Then it will be time for the hundreds of visitors to cast off and head home with their Shetland Oo for another year. title: 'We're still cold paying £300 a month energy bills'
description: Redditch residents say they are worried they will not be able to afford heating.
body: Pat Snell (right) with John says she fears how high their energy bills will be later in the year A pensioner says trying to keep warm and afford heating this winter will be "horrific" amid rising energy costs. Pat Snell, from Redditch, Worcestershire, said she and her husband, John, who had a stroke, relied heavily on heating to keep him comfortable last winter. "Even on a fixed-price tariff, our energy bills were £300 a month, and we were still cold," she said. Snell raised concerns about further rises as millions of households in England, Scotland and Wales face higher energy bills from Thursday, when Ofgem's latest energy price cap increase comes into force. The regulator said typical households on standard variable tariffs will pay about £60 more a year, taking annual bills to £1,723. The extra cost comes at a time when, Snell said, her household was already carefully managing energy use. "We never even put the temperature up over 18C, and most of the rooms were closed. "I don't even want to think about what it's going to cost in December, January and February." Snell added that her fixed-rate tariff comes to an end in late October, meaning they could soon face higher costs. The government said households would see some relief through its removal of VAT on domestic electricity bills, which it said had helped limit the increase, while the Warm Home Discount will provide eligible households with £150 off their bills this winter. Lorraine Stevenson says she is already limiting her energy use Snell is not the only resident in the town that is concerned about struggling to afford heating and other essentials this winter. Another pensioner, Lorraine Stevenson, said she was already limiting energy use where possible. "I live on my own, and I live in a small house, so I struggle because obviously, just on a pension, it's not easy," she said. "Any reduction helps. "I look forward to getting the winter fuel payment. People say it doesn't really help, but it does help through the winter months because obviously you're paying a lot more." She added: "You don't keep the house really warm, but you can't be cold, can you? Especially as the older you get." Among others worried about the rise is Najibullah Rahimi, who came to the UK from Afghanistan with his family about a year ago. He told the BBC he is currently seeking work and is expecting his benefits to be capped, leaving him concerned about how his family will manage as household costs continue to rise. "The gas bill and electricity bill and internet bills and money for the children are difficult now for me," he said. The additional pressure of higher winter energy bills, he said, would make an already difficult situation even more challenging. Kelly Birkett, an accountant from Redditch, works from home. She is a mother of two and her husband is self-employed. While they are both earning, the cost of energy is continuing to place pressure on the household income, and they are reining in family experiences. "It's heartbreaking how much money you don't have to actually live your life - not just survive, but to live it and have those memories with your family and your friends and your children. "As a family we work really hard and we wonder why? I don't think the politicians 'get it' and because they don't get it, they think they're doing enough but they're not." The rise affects around 22 million households on default tariffs regulated by Ofgem, while about 11 million households on fixed-rate deals will not see their prices change immediately. A typical household on a standard variable tariff will see annual bills rise by about £60 to £1,723, although the amount paid will ultimately depend on how much energy is used. Ofgem said the increase had been driven largely by higher wholesale gas prices linked to conflict in the Middle East. The regulator said prices remain around 52% lower than they were at the height of the energy crisis in 2022, although charities and consumer groups have warned many households are still struggling with costs that remain well above pre-crisis levels. The government said its removal of VAT on domestic electricity bills had helped limit the increase, with Ofgem estimating bills would otherwise have been about £45 higher. Eligible households can also receive a £150 Warm Home Discount this winter. For many of those the BBC spoke to in Redditch, the concern was not just about a £5-a-month increase, but what it means when colder weather arrives and household budgets are already stretched. "We'll just have to cut down on something else," said Stevenson. "But you can't be cold." Caroline Fortune encourages people to regularly review their tariff Caroline Fortune, from energy advice charity Act on Energy, said many households had not yet felt the full effect of recent energy price increases because energy use typically falls during the summer months. "The price cap went up in July, and because we haven't all turned our heating on yet, we've not felt it yet," she said. "On 1 October it's due to go up again, and it's predicted to go up again in January, so it's something we need to be aware of." Fortune said consumers should regularly review their tariff and not assume staying with the same supplier would offer the best value. She encouraged households to check whether they were eligible for support schemes, including the Warm Home Discount, and to seek advice early if they feared falling behind on payments. As temperatures fall, she advised people to be mindful of their energy use and focus heating on the rooms they spend most time in. "If you're really struggling, heat the person, not the room," she said. She said demand for help from the charity had risen as households grappled with multiple financial pressures. title: Brit Awards boosted Manchester economy by £5m, study finds
description: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig said the awards' move north for the first time was a "massive moment".
body: Harry Styles was among the artists who performed at the 2026 Brit Awards at Manchester's Co-op Live Arena The Brit Awards' move to Manchester for the 2026 ceremony generated £5 million for the city and its surrounding area, research has found. The annual awards ceremony, widely regarded as the UK's biggest night in music, was hosted in city for the first time this year after being held in the capital for its near 50-year history. The move had a positive economic and social impact and created more than 3,000 temporary jobs, according to an independent study conducted by Amion Consulting. Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig praised the awards' move north as a "massive moment for our city region", with the 2027 event also set to be held in the city. The show took place at Manchester's Co-op Live arena on 28 February in a ceremony hosted by comedian Jack Whitehall, and featuring performances from stars including Harry Styles, Olivia Dean, Raye and Mark Ronson. It generated £5m in net additional expenditure in Manchester, with £3.6m coming from visitors and £1.4m as a result of organiser and partner expenditure. Olivia Dean won the artist of the year award during the Brit Awards 2026 in Manchester Craig said the decision to hold the event in Manchester "was a recognition not only of our unmatched music heritage, but our growing reputation for putting on national and global events and making a success of them". She said such events brought millions of pounds into Manchester's economy, boosting the culture and hospitality industries and created opportunities for people. "We've done it once in style, and we'll do it again next year," she said, adding she was excited to help make 2027 an even bigger year for the Brits. Manchester City Council leader Garry Bridges said this year's award show was "phenomenally successful". "The partnership between the Brits and Manchester went so much further – with a massive social and economic reach right across the city and into our communities, which is still being felt now," he added. The study also found the event generated £3.45m in gross value added and created 3,099 one-week temporary jobs for Manchester-based workers, equivalent to 15,497 days of employment. It also found that 92% of award show attendees rated the experience as excellent or good, with the move to Manchester helping to engage new audiences in the Brits themselves and in wider events surrounding the ceremony. The study found that audience feedback on the event was "overwhelmingly positive", while media and digital coverage helped to amplify Manchester's profile on a global stage. It also spawned a number of events centred around the Brits, with community-focused initiatives, educational engagement, networking events and other programmes held in Manchester in the weeks leading up to the ceremony. The study found that the social impact of the event could be monetised at £11.2m, taking into account factors such as cultural participation, digital engagement and Manchester's strengthened profile as an events destination. title: Holiday lets owner 'devastated' by phishing scam
description: Fake property stays were advertised on the website while company was locked out of her account.
body: Victoria Pollard, who runs Exeter-based Life's 2 Short, said she was inundated with angry calls after her Booking.com account was hacked The owner of a small property management firm said she was "devastated and exhausted" after thousands of fake property reservations were advertised in her company's name on Booking.com. Victoria Pollard, who runs Exeter-based Life's 2 Short, said some of those who made the bookings had travelled from overseas and were left with nowhere to stay. The 46-year-old said the phishing attack had left her with no access to her accounts in August, causing genuine reservations to be missed. Booking.com has apologised, saying it was offering its "full support" to Pollard. It added all impacted listings were removed and customers offered "relocations, refunds or free cancellations". "We are sorry to hear about this accommodation partner's experience," it said. "Our investigation indicates the accommodation was likely the victim of a sophisticated phishing attack by cyber criminals, which affected their own computer systems and led to temporary unauthorised access to the accommodation partner's Booking.com account." Pollard, whose business only employs one other person, said she had received "horrendous" abuse online from disappointed guests who thought she was responsible for the fake reservations for properties that did not exist. She explained they were "calling us all the names under the sun, saying we have ruined their life and their holiday, as they have booked their flights and have nowhere to stay". She said she had been forced to put her phone into airplane mode because she was receiving "20 to 30 calls a minute" at one point and had spent up to 12 hours a day working to resolve the problem. "I cannot continue as a business with 10,000 emails a day that are not concerned with my legitimate business," she added. "We are missing actual calls that are for our actual business." At one point, she said Booking.com had told her she would be liable for the refunds, which totalled just over £1m. She said employees at Booking.com had not communicated with each other, describing the situation as "carnage". "Something that could've been dealt with and shut down within 24 hours has taken weeks, and we are still no further forward," she said. Pollard added she was now at her "wits' end" and "devastated and exhausted by it all". Booking.com did not respond to Pollard's criticisms when approached for further comment. More news stories for Devon Listen to the latest news for Devon Kat Cereda, from consumer expert Which?, said: "You'd like to think that situations like this are incredibly rare, but sadly we hear accounts like this all too often... "We listed 10 Downing Street as a holiday rental but the platform failed to spot that this was clearly a spoof, so it's no wonder that... scam listing and phishing attacks are slipping through the net, when such obvious examples failed to raise red flags. "It's time for the prime minister to call on Ofcom to use the online safety act to crack down." In response to the 10 Downing Street listing, Booking.com said: "This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews published on our platform." They said because the listing by Which? was not "live" on its site across the two months it was present, "some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing". People could only see the listing and request to book the property during a 20-minute window opened by Which? so its researchers could try to book it. A government spokesperson said: "The law is crystal clear. Online platforms that fall under the Online Safety Act, including Booking.com, have a legal duty to ensure their sites are not providing a forum for material intended to scam the public and they must remove it where it is found on their sites. "If platforms fail to protect users from illegal fraudulent content they can face consequences, including fines, and the regulator has all our backing to take action." In response, Booking.com reiterated: "All of the impacted listings were removed and customers with future stays contacted and supported, which, depending on their individual circumstances, could mean relocations, refunds or free cancellations." title: Doctors say radical plan to merge Scotland's health boards should be scrapped
description: BMA Scotland says there is no evidence that reducing the number of health boards from 14 to two will improve patient care.
body: The new chairwoman of BMA Scotland, Dr Nora Murray-Cavanagh, said there was no evidence the plan would benefit patients Leading doctors are calling on the Scottish government to withdraw its plans to drastically reduce the number of health boards. The new chairwoman of BMA Scotland, Dr Nora Murray-Cavanagh, said the proposal to cut the number from 14 to just two would be costly and time consuming - and that there was no clear evidence it would benefit patients. First Minister John Swinney unveiled the plan a month ago, saying it would streamline management and free up resources for frontline care. Health Secretary Angela Constance said she stood by the proposals and promised engagement with a range of groups including unions and NHS boards as the details were developed. Swinney announced the plan as part of his Programme for Government at the start of September, describing it as the "most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era". Fourteen existing health boards would be reduced to just two Strategic Health Boards, covering the west and east of mainland Scotland, with different arrangements considered for the three island health boards. The country would be divided into east and west health boards with different arrangements for the islands Ministers said it would simplify administration and reduce duplication so that more resources could be directed to front line treatment as well as delivering more consistency in care across the country. But members of the British Medical Association's Scottish Council raised serious concerns and voted to oppose the plan during a meeting on Wednesday. After the vote, Murray-Cavanagh said it wanted the government to "withdraw and rethink its whole approach" and come up with a more immediate way of helping patients. Swinney to cut number of health boards from 14 to two Swinney suggests Scots will not travel further for health care under reforms The GP from Wester Hailes in Edinburgh, who took up the role with BMA Scotland just a few weeks ago, stressed that doctors did not deny that the NHS needed to change. She said: "Our position is not one that argues NHS reform isn't necessary – no-one thinks we can simply go on as we are. "As doctors, we know better than most the precarious state of services across Scotland. "But this is the wrong set of reforms, and it will set Scotland on a path of a costly, time consuming, resource-sapping reorganisation, with no serious engagement with those of us holding the service together and no clear evidence put forward on how it will benefit patients." Murray-Cavanagh said members of the BMA's Scottish council had spoken passionately of their concerns about the impact the proposals would have on them and their patients. She added: "At the core of everything is the lack of any evidence on how these reforms will practically make care better." Health Secretary Angela Constance said she stood by the plan In response to the BMA's remarks, Health Secretary Angela Constance said the plans for NHS reform were focused on improving services for people across the country, regardless of where a person lives. "They will simplify how people get the care they need and remove the current geographic and bureaucratic barriers that exist between 14 health boards, which we know are currently causing unwanted variation and duplication," she said. She said the changes would build on work that was already under way, involving every NHS board in Scotland, to improve planning. She added: "The development of detailed proposals will be supported by a full business case and will include engagement with NHS boards, staff representatives, trade unions, local government, integration authorities, social care partners and the public." The BMA is the first medical organisation to publicly call on the government to rethink its plans. The doctors' union is very much in favour of reform and for many years has issued stark warnings that without fundamental change, the NHS cannot survive. But it has now come out strongly against the government's current plans to transform healthcare by reducing the number of regional health boards to two. The first minister argued consolidation would reduce bureaucracy while freeing up more time and capacity to improve patient care. He also claimed it would reduce inequality for some patients. But the BMA don't see it that way. They are also not alone in raising concerns that consolidation could actually widen health inequalities if people are forced to travel further for treatment. The patient safety commissioner, as well as some rural campaign groups, have echoed these fears. The union also question where the evidence is that these reforms are in the interests of patients and NHS staff, saying a reorganisation could be time-consuming and costly. Others have argued that structural reform does not address wider issues the NHS faces around access to social care, which the government is also trying to address. It is also unclear whether this new structure will result in financial savings by cutting senior roles or streamlining departments. At the moment, the NHS has a no compulsory redundancy programme which the government reiterated its commitment to after this announcement was made. The union Unite, which represents thousands of health and social care workers in Scotland, warned ministers at the time that it was considering "all options" if the reorganisation results in cuts to jobs or frontline services. title: Tension and violence rising among young people in south London, police tell BBC
description: Some children in Lambeth and Southwark are highly vulnerable to gangs operating there.
body: PC Zoe Ticehurst tries to engage with children who are at risk of exploitation "There are parents who think next time we come to their door, it will be to tell them their child is dead." I'm told this by PC Zoe Ticehurst and her colleague, Det Con Faisal El Issaoui. They are showing me around the neighbourhoods of Lambeth and Southwark in south London, where some children are highly vulnerable to the gangs who operate there. El Issaoui explained: "It's very hard for a lot of young people who are brought up on these estates. That's the only thing they can see. "Unfortunately, when you get to a certain age, there's a choice that has to be made." The officers, who serve on the Metropolitan Police's proactive offender targeting and management team, said summer, when schools are closed and the long, warmer days bring children on to the streets, was a prime recruiting time for gangs. El Issaoui said gang members easily spotted more vulnerable children, who were often from more deprived backgrounds or excluded from school. "They might get offered money in exchange for holding on to something, or to carry something from one place to another, as a means of sort of making some quick money. That's how it starts." Ticehurst added: "They come home with new stuff and the parents haven't given them money, or they go missing for days. And unfortunately they're caught up in stuff they shouldn't be. "I've been to young people's houses and the parents were so afraid, because they're going into that last year of school and they believe they've got to make a choice: Go into the gang, or they don't." The officers told the BBC they needed help from the local community to tackle gun and gang violence This summer, youth violence became a particular concern. Although homicide in London fell to its lowest level in more than a decade last year, 11 of those killings since April - about a fifth - have been in just two boroughs: Lambeth and Southwark. There was also a series of non-fatal shootings and stabbings. Recorded gun crime rose by 23% in Southwark in the year ending August 2026 compared with the previous year, and by 22% in Lambeth. The Met says there have been 14 lethal barrel discharges, where a gun is actually fired, across both boroughs, compared with seven from the previous financial year. Lambeth has also seen a 9% rise in the number of knife injuries reported to police between April and August this year compared with the same period in 2025. Flowers and candles have been left at the spot where bus driver Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa was shot dead in August As he drove around Lambeth, El Issaoui pointed out various roadside memorials to young people who have lost their lives to violence. Outside a pub in Clapham, a woman quietly laid flowers for 25-year-old Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa, a bus driver, who was shot dead in in August. Police investigating his killing said they needed the community to help them find answers. A 22-year-old-man arrested on suspicion of murder after he went to hospital with a gunshot wound has since been released with no further action. "It was early evening, you know," said Ticehurst. "There were people in the pub behind me, and there were people on the high street. "A lot of people saw what happened here and I think it was a big shock." Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa was shot dead on Willington Road, Clapham, on 10 August Police cannot be certain what has driven the increase in violence, but they have launched several targeted operations over the summer. Plain clothes officers and firearms patrol units searched for those suspected of carrying weapons and dealing drugs. Officers said they had made more than 700 arrests and seized more than 40 weapons, as well as Class A drugs. El Issaoui reeled off the names of multiple gangs which he said were dotted across the borough. "There's a gang called the ABM, which stands for All About Money, so they're the local sort of gang here. "They're currently rivals to a gang that's just at the end of this road, which is the Wandsworth Road, O-Tray gang. "It's just literally two minutes away from each other." He said the number of gangs and their close proximity to one another meant tensions regularly and violently erupt on the streets. "It's tit-for-tat stuff, and unfortunately it does affect a lot of innocent people who aren't linked to gang crime." Although many of the gangs have been around for decades, El Issaoui says they have been "re-branded - with the new generation overtaking the old". He told me social media was fuelling the violence. "We see one gang going into a rival's territory and live streaming it. Just to say, 'we're here, come get us' sort of thing." But he says there is also another disturbing trend - a type of league table where violence is treated like a game. "Any affront into another area will be seen as a point score for that gang. "It's even more points if an actual gang member was targeted, but as far as these groups are concerned, normal passersby are fair game. "It's a really sort of dangerous sort of element for local communities, where innocent people get literally caught in a crossfire." Police have released images of some of the weapons and drugs seized during several operations over the summer The officers, who wear plain clothes instead of uniform, try to engage with families and divert young people toward other agencies who may be able to encourage them into education or apprenticeships, but they face significant challenges. El Issaoui said some parents like the police, but others do not. "I think a lot of parents are in denial about what their young children are up to," added Ticehurst. "They kind of shut it down, even though we're telling them, 'we know this is happening'." Others are desperate to get help but feel powerless against the lure of county lines drugs

title: Meet the robot looking after Vera, 74, in her own home
description: At least a thousand people across England use the droids, health tech company Cera says.
body: Vera is one of 24 residents at Hazelhurst Court with a robot Vera Gadsdon, 74, is one of the residents at a retirement housing complex in Lewisham. She has a carer, Pinar Elmaz, and a helper called Robert. Robert reminds her when to take her medication, to do her washing and even gives her knitting tips. Robert is a robot, just one of those that is now providing company and medical assistance in care homes. Some say the droids are cutting costs and freeing up staff. But, having met Vera and Robert, I can't help wondering: if she could choose, would Vera prefer to speak to a robot or a relative? Vera enjoys the company of both her carer Pinar and her robot Robert Pinar says the droids, made by tech healthcare company Cera, are not a replacement for human carers but "another tool for us as well because we can always check in on them... make sure they've taken their medication and then make sure they've hydrated". Hazelhurst Court has 24 residents with robots and they certainly seem to enjoy their new companions. Each one contains their person's medical needs and individual calendar and is programmed to tell users when it's time to eat or play bingo or watch their favourite television show. Some residents say the robots make them feel less lonely, while others say they use them to connect with their grandchildren. These robots can clean, exercise - and care for you in old age. Would you trust them to? During our visit, Robert - who is programmed to be friendly -repeatedly asked Vera how she was, reassuring her "I'll be here if you need me". "What would you enjoy chatting about today?" it asks. But it does make mistakes when Vera wants to talk about knitting, often mishearing essential words and offering conversations on "biscuits and cakes" and "music, television, the garden or something else". Tech expert James Erskine says when it comes to such robots, what needs to be considered is what they can do well and what they cannot. "If a job can be followed to the letter like an instruction, a robot or computer can probably do it. If it needs problem-solving, judgement or emotional understanding, it needs a human," he says. "AI is already helping surgeons during brain tumour operations, and driverless taxis being trialled on London's roads. "In care, robots could be brilliant at monitoring health - vital signs, medication reminders, spotting falls. But can they really read someone's mental state, their happiness, their overall wellbeing? "That depends on human connection, noticing the small things, knowing the person. So it's support, not substitute. "The best outcome is tech taking on the routine tasks so carers have more time for the human side of care." Ben Maruthappu, a former A&E doctor, is the founder and chief executive of tech healthcare company Cera At least 1,000 people across England are using the robots, according to Cera. Dr Ben Maruthappu, a former A&E doctor in London, is Cera's founder and chief executive. He says his personal experience of social care in the capital inspired him to look for solutions in tech. "My mother had a fall and fractured her back and needed care at home so I needed to try and organise that care," he says. "What I thought would be a really simple process was actually excruciatingly difficult. "I called lots of different home care agencies. We had this revolving door of carers looking after my mum, and I didn't even know their name - let alone how the care was going. "How is it in this day and age, when I can get books and groceries delivered to my door at the click of a button, I have no idea the care my mum is receiving which is so much more important?" He added he was motivated to build a better model of care where "technology addressed some of the issues and frictions in the care sector". The robots are programmed to remind residents when to take medication Now with 13,500 staff and almost £500m in annual revenue, Cera says it is Europe's largest health tech firm. The company claims its AI tools reduce hospital admissions by up to 70% and its robots boost care teams' capacity by 20% and productivity by up to 80%. Whether the needs being met include the human need for connection remains to be seen. title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
description: Andrew Bailey says the central bank is watching the waves of cash being invested in artificial intelligence "very carefully".
body: This video can not be played Watch: Governor of the Bank of England Andrew Bailey says quality of deepfakes 'alarming' Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned. Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins". The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses. Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point." He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy. Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed. "But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those." One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off. AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create. Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology. And two of the largest AI companies in the world – Anthropic and OpenAI – are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry. "There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey. "And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver." "Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner". "Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins. "We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient." Bailey also pointed to other risks from AI, such as from the technology being used for cyber attacks. He said AI has created a "much more powerful way of uncovering vulnerabilities". "It's revealing things that have been in bits of operating software that we've had, and all of us have had." "In the wrong hands... it's a very powerful, potentially very powerful, weapon," he added. Another risk is the rise of deepfakes – AI-made pictures and videos of people that look real – which can be used to fool the public. Bailey has had first-hand experience of this. In June, deepfake images depicting him and Nigel Farage having a physical fight were promoted on social media platform X. He told the BBC that the fake images were being done in such a way that the Bank has struggled to find out where they came from. "We've got to be able to trace these things back. And we need a lot of help from the tech sector to do that," he said. However, Bailey said a big potential benefit from AI is its ability of "speeding up the work that supports the Monetary Policy Committee [MPC]" which sets interest rates. "It's not taking a decision, but it's a tool in the hands of the policy maker and that's good," he said. title: Plummeting Israel flight dropped like a rollercoaster, says passenger
description: An aeroplane flying to Israel fell 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes before it was diverted.
body: This video can not be played A passenger on board Flight FZ1073, which fell 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes when a pilot apparently stabbed his co-pilot, told the BBC about his experience. The aircraft had been flying to Israel when the incident took place, which Almog Itali described as feeling like a "rollercoaster". The plane was diverted to Saudi Arabia after several passengers said they took control of the flight and two other pilots at the rear of the plane reportedly came forward to land the plane. title: Japan raises residency fee for foreign nationals by twenty-fold
description: The hikes are part of immigration policy changes introduced to manage Japan's growing foreign population.
body: The hikes are part of immigration policy changes introduced to manage Japan's growing foreign population Japan has raised fees for foreigners looking to reside in the country, with the cost of permanent residency going up 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; £955). Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements. Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours. The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim ito manage its rapidly growing foreign population. In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners – its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations". Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage. Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change. Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year. In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows. "To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote. Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay. From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought – from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more. Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts. Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024. Micaiah Michaela-Spence, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike. The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents. "My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC. "There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term." From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported. Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short. title: 'Hero' pilot stabbed by other pilot on Israel-bound plane, Israeli PM says
description: Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and safely landed the plane in Saudi Arabia.
body: This video can not be played A pilot has been arrested after he stabbed the other pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control of the Flydubai aircraft, landing it safely at an airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia, with more than 170 people on board. The passengers, who were almost all Israeli, arrived later on Wednesday in Tel Aviv on a repatriation flight. The stabbed pilot, named as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, has been taken to hospital but is reported to be in a stable condition. Netanyahu and India's leader Narendra Modi praised him as a "hero". "Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on X. "He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals." The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in a stable condition in hospital. Modi praised the pilot's actions, writing on X: "In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. "India is proud of Captain Machchhar." Passengers arrived in Tel Aviv after their original flight was forced to land in Saudi Arabia No motive for the incident has been given and the pilot was under investigation in Saudi Arabia, Netanyahu told Fox News on Wednesday night, before he was expected to be taken back to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where the flight took off from. Israel was "likely" to contribute to the investigation, the prime minister added. US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack", without giving any details. Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel. Around two and a half hours into its journey, data from flight tracking website Flightrader24 reported a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia, dropping more than 17,000 feet (over 5,000m) in less than two minutes. Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code reporting a hijacking. Around 20 minutes after these codes were signalled, the plane looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing. Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700. Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations. Initial media reports suggested a fight had broken out between the aircraft's two pilots, causing the rapid descent and landing. However, in the hours after the plane touched down in Tabuk, eyewitness accounts and a statement by Netanyahu confirmed one of the pilots had stabbed the other and, according to the Israeli prime minister, "apparently tried to crash" the aircraft. He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member entered the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing". Two on-duty crew travelling on the flight were then able to land the plane safely, Flydubai said. In an address on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu called the situation "a very serious security incident" and said Israeli security forces were "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers". Unlike Israel's defence minister, Netanyahu did not give a motive for the incident. "I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster." Flydubai said in a statement that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport". An airline spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation." The passengers who had been on board flight FZ1073 arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT). They were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags. A number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane," a paramedic from Israel's ambulance service told the BBC. One passenger, Yaniv Hayun, met Netanyahu and told him how he and others on the flight had restrained the attacker. "The pilot who was stabbed was simply very close to the door, so it was hard for us to open it," Hayun said in a video posted on social media by the prime minister's office, but before the stabbed pilot - now identified as Machchhar - collapsed, he was able to open the door. Yaniv said he put the attacker, who was trying to disable the plane, in a chokehold before other passengers helped pin him down. He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane and after it levelled out, another pilot took over control. This video can not be played Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones". He said: "There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event." What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel Passengers describe st

title: Two dead in Canada after vehicle hits pedestrians taking part in First Nations event
description: Police said the driver "may have been experiencing a medical emergency" before hitting four people in British Columbia.
body: Two people were killed and two others were injured after a vehicle hit pedestrians during a community walk marking Canada's National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in British Columbia. The incident occurred on Tsawwassen First Nation land, south of Vancouver near the US-Canada border. The deceased were identified as elders from the First Nation, local media report. Police said the driver "may have been experiencing a medical emergency" before the collision. They added they do not believe it is related to Truth and Reconciliation day, a national holiday that honours victims and survivors of Canada's residential schools, which sought to forcefully assimilate indigenous children. The collision happened at around 10:25 local time (16:25 BST) at a local parking lot, said the Delta Police Department, which covers the area where the incident occurred. Police said that the two injured were receiving treatment in hospital. "Our thoughts are with the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic incident," Delta Police said. Eyewitness accounts by CBC News reporters on scene said more than a dozen ambulances responded to the incident. In a social media post advertising the event last week, Tsawwassen First Nation said it had planned a community walk followed by the unveiling of a house post in honour of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. The event was due to take place from 09:30 to 13:00 local time. In an X post that now appears to be deleted, Canada's energy minister Tim Hodgson said he attended the walk and posted two images from the event. A spokesperson for the minister, Carolyn Svonkin, said he was not near the incident when it occurred. Tsawwassen First Nation is home to 491 members, according to its website, with half living on Tsawwassen lands and others in nearby areas, including across the border in Bellingham, Washington. Canada began observing its National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021, following news of the discovery of unmarked burial sites at former residential schools. The holiday coincides with Orange Shirt Day - an indigenous grassroots-led day of remembrance to honour children who were missing or died in residential schools. title: How the new prison release scheme will work - and number of inmates to be freed
description: Hundreds of eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on 1 October, under the government's early prison release plan.
body: About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on 1 October while some 2,550 are due to be released by the end of the year, under the government's early prison release plan. So why are so many people being let out of jail earlier than expected and how have they been chosen? Quite simply, prisons are almost full - and not for the first time. As of last Friday, there were 87,499 people in 120 jails across England and Wales - with around 1,500 available beds. At this rate, there would be no spare cells by Christmas. The early release scheme was developed because of a crisis the Labour government inherited when it came to power in July 2024. Back then, prisons were rapidly running out of cells because courts were jailing more criminals than the number being released - part of a 30-year trend. The outgoing government had also failed to build the prisons it had promised. By the summer of 2024 there were virtually no free cells left, so the Ministry of Justice ran an emergency scheme, releasing some offenders after serving 40% of their sentence, rather than 50% - when most fixed-term prisoners are eligible for release. From Thursday a permanent scheme passed by Parliament comes into force. The scheme applies to roughly 70,000 offenders. If they had expected to serve half their term in jail and half in the community on a licence, the eligible prisoners will now leave at the one-third point. The first eligible group are those jailed for up to 19 months. From November, it will be offenders serving up to three years and two months. By next June, serious offenders on fixed terms of more than 12 years will become eligible. Many of them will have expected to serve two-thirds of their sentence behind bars. Instead they will be on a community licence after serving half of their time. The total length of their sentences has not changed - just the date when they become eligible to start serving part of that sentence in the community. Some 18,000 inmates are completely excluded - including those convicted of murder, manslaughter, a sexual or grooming-related offence, or a driving offence that led to a death. Their earliest release dates remain unchanged. Roughly 4,500 prisoners are due to be released by next summer. Some 700 will leave jail on the morning of 1 October - if spread equally across all jails that would be around six per prison. In a typical month, around 4,500 people leave jails - so the first year of the scheme will see an 8% jump in releases. Some 700 prisoners will leave jail on the morning of 1 October When someone leaves prison while still serving a sentence, they are released on licence, which means they could be recalled if they break their conditions - this ranges from failing to make a probation appointment or not living at an approved address, through to more serious breaches such as contacting a victim, abandoning a rehabilitation programme or committing a crime. The new rules, called "Earned Progression", are meant to encourage them to work harder to reform through enhanced monitoring and intensive supervision. This means more released prisoners will have to wear electronic tags and be subject to other conditions. If they step out of line, they can be returned to jail immediately. Probation officers will have to work harder to monitor offenders all around the country. Martin Jones, the independent inspector of the service, has said he is "not fully confident" that the system will be able to cope. The staff union says officers already have too many cases and the rate at which they are leaving the profession has increased. A report, published days before the start of the October early releases, warned that almost half of offenders were not tagged promptly, despite electronic monitoring being key to success. The government says the probation service has recruited 1,300 more staff and has also received new AI tools to help it oversee offenders. An offender can be recalled to prison immediately if their probation officer or the Parole Board believes they have broken their licence conditions, if the risk they pose increases, or if they pose a danger to the public. According to the latest official figures, there were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026 - up 28% on the previous year. Those recalls were slightly lower than the previous three-month period. Of those 51,419, around one in five was recalled for general "non compliance" and about one in 10 for failing to be in touch with their probation officer. Around 2,900 had committed another offence. The government hopes - and this is the big bet - that if there is more community rehabilitation, more offenders can be kept out of jail. The original scheme, which was devised when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, would have allowed about 500 more offenders to be released. Sir Keir's successor Andy Burnham said he would rethink the proposals amid public alarm, lobbying from victims of grooming gangs and anger over the potential early release of two of the men who killed Pc Andrew Harper. Burnham said if the scheme was scrapped, prisons would become full and the courts would have to stop sentencing new criminals. The government projects that the prison population will still rise to around 100,000 by 2030. So the £7bn prison-building programme it has promised is crucial - aiming to deliver 14,000 extra cells by then. Another key element of the plan is the effective scrapping of one-year jail terms. The law now says that judges should normally suspend such terms - meaning the offender won't go to prison unless they commit another crime. That policy is backed by some long-standing evidence that fewer people re-offend if they receive intensive supervision to sort out their lives, rather than locking them up for short sentences. title: California bans child marriage, a practice still legal in 32 US states
description: Gov Gavin Newsom called it a "long overdue measure to protect young Californians".
body: Brittany Bee was wed to a man when she was a teen. California has officially banned child marriage, with Governor Gavin Newsom signing legislation to end the practice that is still legal in 32 US states. The new law, which will come into effect on 1 January, states people must be 18 to get married in the Golden State. Newsom called it a "long overdue measure to protect young Californians and minors". He signed the bill into law with Courtney Stodden whose parents allowed her to marry a 50-year-old Hollywood actor when she was just 16. Stodden, who has been advocating to end the practice, called the change a "victory" and said survivors of child marriage should "never have been expected to carry this burden". Gov Gavin Newsom called the law "overdue" Stodden said she would "keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states". She was married to actor Doug Hutchison - known for roles in The Green Mile, A Time to Kill and I Am Sam - in 2011, spurring headlines internationally over the controversy and appearances on several reality programmes in the US, including the VH1 series Couples Therapy. Other survivors of child marriage also applauded the new law. "California has sent a clear message to the world today," Brittany Bee, a former child bride, told the BBC. "A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path." Bee told the BBC she was wed at the age of 17 to escape an abusive home - only to then be allegedly abused by her adult husband. "I was just going from one prison to another," she explained. "People have the audacity to tell me that I made a choice - kids, they can't consent." Bee and other child marriage survivors have been working for years to have child marriages banned in California and across the United States. About a decade ago, the practice was still allowed across all US state but more and more states have been altering laws. California is the 18th to ban it since 2018. In the state, there had been no legal age to wed, allowing children to get married as long as their parents consent and a judge signs off on the nuptials. There was also no mechanism for people under 18 to get divorced and many girls say they were trapped in abusive and predatory relationships. Unchained At Last, an advocacy group fighting to end child marriage across the US, said about 9,000 girls were wed each year in California and that almost all child marriages involved girls to adult men. Advocates say that many in the US don't even know that child marriage is legal in so many US states, nor that is has led to allegations of abuse. Sara Tasneen, who says she was forced to marry a man nearly twice her age when she was 15 years old, told the BBC that it felt "surreal" to finally have the state recognise that child marriage should be banned. She says she started lobbying for this herself in 2017. She was introduced to her husband the morning of their arranged marriage. "I was forced to be his wife and that day, my entire life changed," she told the BBC. She became a mother the following year, at the age of 16, and dropped out of school. "To have seen the arc of this bill come to fruition has been a marathon," Tasneen said. "I'm just grateful that kids cannot get married after January 1, 2027 in California." title: Son who used AI to help save mum's life hopes case unlocks clues for other Parkinson's patients
description: Doctors say clinical trials are needed to understand more after Ed Patrick identified a potential side effect of a Parkinson's drug.
body: Ed Patrick and his mother, Ann, who has Parkinson's Disease, and father John An NHS doctor who says he saved his mum's life with the help of AI hopes what he learned can help others with Parkinson's Disease complications. Ed Patrick, an anaesthetist from Oxfordshire, was at his mother's bedside in hospital ready to say his goodbyes after she began suffering serious and continuous seizures. Using AI to scour recent medical journal articles, he said he identified a vitamin deficiency linked to her Parkinson's medication as a possible cause, and staff then gave her a vitamin dose that appeared to stop the seizures. Doctors say clinical trials are needed to understand more - and warn against patients making changes to their own medication without medical advice. Charity Parkinson's UK welcomed the prospect of more research trials in light of this case and said it could "transform care" for some others with Parkinson's. In May this year Patrick said hospital staff called to say his mother, Ann, was close to death, after she had been deteriorating over several months. "She was taken to hospital with non-stop fits and convulsions," he told BBC Radio 2's Jeremy Vine Show. "I got a phone call from the hospital's medical registrar who told me they'd tried all the anti-seizure medications and they weren't working. 'Sorry, she's dying', the registrar told me. 'Do I have time to make it?', I said. 'Yes, but you've got to leave now' was her reply." When he got to the hospital in Nottinghamshire, Patrick said his mother was "totally unconscious", suffering continuous fits and going into kidney failure. He said he used Google's Gemini AI tool to summarise recent medical journal articles relevant to his mum's condition and symptoms, and then relayed it to the neurology consultant. "I told him what I'd discovered - that the seizures were almost certainly a rare side effect of a vitamin B6 deficiency, possibly caused by her long-term carbidopa-levodopa dopamine use, which was being used to treat her Parkinson's," he said. Carbidopa-levodopa is a combination drug commonly used to boost dopamine levels in Parkinson's patients. Medical staff agreed to give Ann an intravenous supplement of vitamin B6, which appeared to stop her seizures. "She hasn't had a seizure since," he said. "The next day the family and medics were all ecstatic. The neurologist was high-fiving me." The consultant neurologist in question, Dr Bruno Gran from Nottingham University Hospitals, said: "As an anaesthetist, Ed has a strong understanding of clinical pharmacology and his reasoning was sound. "What we did not anticipate was the speed and magnitude of the response. Within minutes of administering vitamin B6, Ann's seizure activity stopped. "We are now working to raise awareness of this potential issue, beginning with changes to practice within our own team. Although Parkinson's affects millions of people worldwide, only 14 similar cases have ever been reported. But if the insights gained from this case can help clinicians identify and prevent similar situations in the future, that would be a significant and positive outcome." Ann has since made a full recovery from the seizures and Patrick said her day-to-day cognitive Parkinson's symptoms have dramatically improved. "It's like we've got mum back", said Patrick. "It feels like we found a silver bullet. She's sharp as a tack. "She's been given a really good quality of life from a solution we never even knew was there. Cognitively, it's like she's gone back in time five to 10 years." After she recovered, Ann was visited by her newest granddaughter, saying: "She's absolutely glorious." Parkinson's is a progressive disorder that affects the brain, nervous system, and muscle control. About 166,000 people in the UK live with the condition, according to Parkinson's UK. Patrick believes B6 vitamins could help other Parkinson's patients, both in emergency settings, but also in some cases of long-term cognitive deterioration. "I think this has potentially wide-reaching ramifications for others. I know that mum's medical team has presented her case to colleagues and that's led to changes in practice in the region. They're looking at where B6 supplementation might be appropriate." Existing clinical evidence on the link between B6 deficiency in Parkinson's patients and any potential impact it can have is still limited. Experts told the BBC that the link is not known about by the majority of NHS staff in the UK. But earlier this year, the US Food and Drug Administration put out a memo, external saying that particular drugs used to treat Parkinson's should carry a warning about potential links to B6 deficiency. Dr Graham Johnson, a consultant in emergency medicine who co-leads the Research in Emergency Medicine in Derby group and has been discussing the case with Patrick, said: "Sometimes the best research ideas come from patients' stories, and experts in Parkinson's may now be able to use this case to build a wider evidence base through studies and clinical trials." The chief executive of Parkinson's UK, Caroline Rassell, said they "support the move towards more research trials into vitamin B6 deficiency and Parkinson's". "It's needed to help us understand the connections. The findings and recommendations could transform care for people with Parkinson's." Rassell and other medics told the BBC that patients living with Parkinson's should treat this information with caution. "This family's experience will definitely raise awareness of the link between vitamin B6 and Parkinson's medications," said Rassell. "However, never make changes to medications or supplements before taking medical advice," she said, and encouraged anyone concerned to speak w

title: The Papers: 'Israel's 9/11 stopped' and 'That was a great life'
description: Many of the papers are leading on the passengers who helped prevent a possible plane hijacking of a flight bound for Israel.
body: Many of the papers are leading on the passengers who helped prevent a possible plane hijacking of a flight bound for Israel. The Daily Telegraph explains that on Wednesday, a Flydubai jet carrying Israelis from Dubai to Tel Aviv went into a nosedive after the pilot was stabbed by his co-pilot at 34,000 ft. Passengers were able to wrestle the suspected hijacker from the cockpit and subdue him, the paper said. It adds that "hero" passengers could have stopped "Israel's 9/11", with security sources telling the Telegraph that the "terrorist" may have been planning to crash the plane into an Israeli city. Photographs from the Flydubai flight are front and centre of the Times, which names the stabbed pilot as Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national. The paper says Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has hailed the passengers who intervened as "lions", and declared Machchhar a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery". It adds that the prime minister has instructed authorities to "ramp up security" on flights to Israel, regardless of whether they are operated by Israeli or non-Israeli airlines. Similarly, the headline of the i Paper reads: "Hero passengers storm cockpit to save Israel flight from disaster." According to the paper, Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz has described the incident as an "attempted jihadist terror attack". "We got him!" says the Metro, alongside a photograph of the man it says "took down" the alleged attacker. It reports that the plane "plummeted 17,000 ft in two minutes" as passengers and crew attempted to subdue the knifeman. Two off-duty pilots, including one the Metro says was British, were then able to take control and safely land the plane. Israeli officials who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity said that the current assessment of the incident was that it was a terror attack. The alleged knifeman is Omani, they told the paper. There has been no comment on the attack from Oman, or the United Arab Emirates, where the flight was boarded. The Guardian's front page also features a tribute to broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen, who has died at the age of 86. "That was a great life, Esther" says the Sun, in a nod to Dame Esther's most well-known television show. The paper reports that the beloved presenter passed away on Wednesday after a three-year battle with lung cancer. Tributes to Dame Esther also lead the Daily Star, which says the Childline founder will be remembered as "our sunshine". The Daily Express focuses on the statement from Dame Esther's three "heartbroken" children, who have said their mother had an "endless capacity for love and joy". It notes that the "indefatigable campaigner" spent her final years as a "vociferous advocate of assisted dying". Dame Esther's own words feature in the Daily Mirror, after the note she left her grieving family prior to her death was shared with the general public. "Esther: See you on the other side" reads the paper's headline. Andy Burnham's comments on the incident at RAF Fairford are considered by the Financial Times in its main story, after the prime minister said there were "strong indications" that Iran was involved. The paper notes that Tehran has "categorically" rejected and strongly condemned the "malicious speculations", but adds that the exact nature of what happened near Fairford "remains unclear". The Daily Mail reports Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has drawn up proposals that would require school-leavers to undergo intensive work coaching, instead of being able to immediately sign on to Universal Credit. The paper calls it a "bid to stop young lives being wasted". Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox.
