title: BBC should not overspend on shows such as Suits and Schitt's Creek, MPs say
description: The issue is one of several raised by an influential committee as debate about the BBC's future continues.
body: Schitt's Creek was snapped up by the BBC after the comedy series left Netflix The BBC should not pay "over the odds" for the rights to overseas hits such as Suits and Schitt's Creek, an influential group of MPs has said. It is one of several issues raised in a wide-ranging report about the BBC's funding and future, published by the House of Commons' cross-party culture and media committee. Although the BBC produces a lot of its own programmes, the corporation buys some international shows for its TV channels and iPlayer streaming platform. The MPs' report said the BBC could "spend more wisely when competing for programming". Overall, the BBC brings "immeasurable benefits" to society but needs reform of the TV licence fee to avoid a fate of "managed decline", they said. Committee chair Dame Caroline Dinenage said the report , externalcomes at "a pivotal moment for the BBC", which is grappling with changing media habits, declining income and negotiations with the government over how it is paid for. Dame Caroline said the government "must ensure the BBC has a universal and sustainable source of funding". But, she added, the BBC "can play its part by sweating its assets and boxing clever for the licence payer by ending illogical practices such as outbidding commercial rivals for overseas hits such as Suits, Schitt's Creek and Scooby Doo". The rights to air all three programmes were bought by the BBC after contracts with other networks or streaming services expired. "At a time of constrained resources, the BBC should not be paying over the odds for overseas content, particularly when it's a bidding war against commercial UK broadcasters," the committee said. The MPs added that they "did not believe that this provides value for money for the licence fee payer". The BBC said it spends less than 5% of its content budget on acquiring shows, less than other broadcasters, and they are a cost-effective way of delivering high-quality content to audiences who go on to discover homegrown programming. Suits, starring the future Duchess of Sussex (second right, in 2012), has attracted new audiences in recent years The committee's report has been published as the government considers its options for the next BBC Royal Charter, which will set out how the broadcaster will be governed, regulated and funded from 2028 onwards. Dame Caroline said: "For all its faults, the BBC drives our creative economy, supports our democracy through media sovereignty, and delivers world-class entertainment and moments that bring us together. "Like a much-loved family member, we may criticise and grumble about the BBC but we would miss it enormously if it were no longer here for us." The committee said there were "considerable challenges" for the BBC and warned that the current TV licence fee is "outdated and no longer fit for purpose". Currently, about 94% of individuals use the BBC each month but only 80% of households pay for a TV licence, the MPs noted. "The licence fee should be reformed so it is no longer linked to the consumption of live TV or to a particular device, such as a television set," the committee said. "This should be an easier sell to licence fee payers if expanding the base is paired with a drop in the individual cost." The BBC's director-general Matt Brittin has previously described the current licence fee model as "a busted flush" and "yesterday's model", and has said the price could be cut if more people pay under an overhauled system. The committee also suggested the BBC should: Explore the opportunity for introducing an international TV licence so it can increase its revenue and global audience Work with independent production companies who own the rights to many of its programmes to ensure more remain on iPlayer Develop its current premises with facilities that can "harness the potential of new media and support the creator economy" The committee suggested the government should: Support the corporation by legislating to put a BBC button on remote controls for smart TVs Press YouTube to give a certain level of prominence for content made by the BBC and other British public service broadcasters Take back full funding for the BBC World Service, describing it as "the UK's number one soft power asset" The committee supported opening up BBC iPlayer to shows from other public service broadcasters such as Channel 4. Earlier this week, Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra said, external she was open to her network's content being hosted on iPlayer. The report also called for the end of political appointments to the BBC board, to improve governance and remain trusted by the public. And the committee recommended that the BBC is given new public purposes relating to innovation and technology and combating misinformation and disinformation. The BBC welcomed the report, which it said made "some important and interesting recommendations on the future of the BBC". A BBC spokesperson said: "We have consistently argued that the current funding model is outdated and needs reform, so we welcome the Committee's support for maintaining universal funding while overhauling the licence fee. "We are also pleased to see their recognition of the vital work of the World Service, with a clear recommendation that responsibility for funding should return fully to Government. "At a time of huge disruption in the media, the BBC's trust, reach and creative strength remain unparalleled. But we also recognise the need to evolve and move faster towards the future." The government's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said it "agrees entirely with the Committee's conclusion that it is in the country's best interests for the next Charter to support an ambitious and innovative BBC, and that the corporation cannot be left to a future of managed decline". A DCMS spokesperson added: "We will review and consider the committee's recommen

title: Celebrity Traitors is back - here's what you need to know ahead of the first show
description: Maya Jama, Michael Sheen and Bella Ramsey are among this year's celebrities taking part in the show.
body: Maya Jama, Michael Sheen and Bella Ramsey are among this year's celebrity contestants The Celebrity Traitors is back for a second series, and viewers will see the likes of Michael Sheen, Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant and Amol Rajan at the round table along with Bella Ramsey, Leigh-Anne Pinnock, Maya Jama and King Kenny. There are 21 celebrities taking part in total - two more than last year - and there will be an extra episode after the huge popularity of last year's series. The extended 75-minute debut episode starts at 20:00 BST on Thursday, with Claudia Winkleman again hosting the murderous game. Viewers can expect some fresh ideas, and executive producer Sarah Fay said they "always want to push the envelope" with the show's elaborate tasks. "We're always trying to evolve existing ideas to bring them into a new life or coming up with different cultural references," she told the show's press launch. The Celebrity Traitors are finally gathered for episode one of series two The celebrities will be playing for a £100,000 cash prize for charity. The final amount will depend on how well they perform in the tasks, regardless of any possible tensions over who is a faithful and who is a traitor. This year's contestants are a mixture of famous faces from TV, film, radio and YouTube: Amol Rajan – journalist and broadcaster James Acaster – comedian and podcaster Jerry Hall – model and actress King Kenny – content creator Maya Jama – broadcaster and entrepreneur Michael Sheen – actor and presenter Miranda Hart – actor and author Professor Hannah Fry– broadcaster and mathematician Richard E Grant – actor and author Ross Kemp – actor and presenter Sebastian Croft – musician and actor Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses? In the show's trailer, external, they are seen arriving in a church, smiling as they greet each other, but looking nervous. They later travel to the castle in a fleet of black cars, before Winkleman chooses her traitors while everyone wears their blindfolds. They then take part in their first mission in a lake in wetsuits, ending with Winkleman saying ominously: "Fame won't save them." Romesh Ranganathan, Myha'la and Richard E Grant are also taking their places at the round table Speaking at the press launch, Winkleman said she is totally focused on the celebrities while she's in the castle, and is glued to the monitors showing footage of them throughout the day. "All of them were tremendous, and when we do any series I have this room with the monitors. I'm like a weirdo just applying fake tan, watching," she said. The presenter added that even when she's told to go home, she tells the producers "I am not leaving", joking that she got barely any sleep. Ed Gamble, host of BBC Two spin-off show Uncloaked, added that he watched "hours of footage a day" as well. "So when they're eating breakfast, I'm eating breakfast watching them eat breakfast. It's actually quite sad... I'm normally sat there in my pyjamas eating cereal, watching them eat cereal," he told BBC News. Viewers can also look forward to more of Winkleman's eclectic wardrobe choices. "I like the fact that it is 'human crow meets golf caddy meets the Artful Dodger'. We're pretty happy with it," she joked about this year's outfits. Claudia Winkleman said her clothes are as distinctive as ever on the show The celebrities have also been speaking about the show before its launch, with comedian and presenter Romesh Ranganathan saying that despite being best friends with fellow comic Rob Beckett, he would have no problem stabbing him in the back. "I mean, he's just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity," he said. The show's other comics include Joe Lycett, James Acaster and Joanne McNally. "I think we're going to be the first ones under the magnifying glass being looked at," Acaster said over suspicions one will be a traitor. Comedian Alan Carr won the first series of Celebrity Traitors, which was the most watched TV programme of 2025 in the UK, watched by 15 million people. The Last of Us and Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey already has experience of playing similar games at drama clubs and at home, which is why they joined the show. "I've been playing a version of The Traitors since I was 10 years old," they said. Mathematician Hannah Fry, who called herself "toxically competitive", added she has already looked for "statistical patterns" in the data for previous games; while Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock said she took advice from singer Cat Burns, who reached the final as a traitor last year. "She had good advice. She said it might get intense around that round table – but remember, it's just a game," Pinnock said. The show is also something of a love letter to the Scottish Highlands, where it is filmed, with sweeping drone shots of the scenery and Ardross Castle in Inverness, where the celebrities meet, eat and of course sit at the round table. "It's breathtaking," Winkleman told the press, adding that she and her family were returning to the Highlands for a holiday. "My husband was like, 'You're already there quite a lot, what's the matter with you?'" she said. "It's the most beautiful place I've ever been in the world, is the truth." After she recently chose to end her recent BBC One chat show, Winkleman is back on familiar ground with Celebrity Traitors. BBC News asked if she would ever want to try being a contestant on the show, perhaps in the US or Australian versions. "No, I'm too thick," she said in typical self-deprecating style. "I mustn't play it in public. I must not. "I'm just being honest - it's a privilege to play that game and to be at the round table, but I think I would just be too awful at it." The Celebrity Tra

title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
description: Scientists say such rapid melting is no longer surprising given the pace of climate change.
body: The front of Morteratsch Glacier in south-east Switzerland, which has been attacked by warm air and water Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks. More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary". They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead. The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August. There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed. But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks. The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting. Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear. "It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report. Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter. And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below. Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy. That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves. "Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report. "What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added. Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions. Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September. Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply. The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent. "Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss. "It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave." The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer, affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs. One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered. Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer. "At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland. Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice. But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear. "Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion. "But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes." Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive. Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared. But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice. This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides. "There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss. "If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levels… which could affect billions of people living along the coast." title: 'I'm very shocked' - College students react to Cornell University rape investigation
description: The BBC asked students in Washington about the allegations from a woman who says she was raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
body: This video can not be played New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university on 16 September alleging she was drugged and assaulted at a fraternity house at the university. She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Cornell has said it supported presenting the case to a grand jury, while rejecting as "false" claims that it failed to punish those involved. The BBC spoke to college students in Washington DC about their reactions to the latest information about the incident. title: US Supreme Court allows execution of Christa Pike to go ahead
description: The death by lethal injection was scheduled to happen earlier on Wednesday before a lower court paused the execution.
body: The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for Tennessee inmate Christa Pike to be executed, overturning a last-minute reprieve. The killing by lethal injection was scheduled for Wednesday morning before judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court halted the execution. Tennessee's attorney general then immediately requested the Supreme Court to overrule the lower court's stay. Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike will be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. It was not immediately clear when the execution would take place. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh granted the application to vacate the stay of the execution. No explanation for lifting the stay was provided in the order. The top court's three liberal justices - Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson - dissented in Wednesday evening's order. Sotomayor wrote that she dissents because the decision cleared the way for Tennessee to execute Pike before her pending legal challenges to her conviction "can be properly considered". "Tennessee's desire to expedite Pike's execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh her 'fundamental interest in [her] own life," she said. The latest ruling from the Supreme Court came just before 18:00 local time, hours before the state's execution order is set to expire at midnight. If time runs out the Tennessee Supreme Court will need to set a new execution date, the Associated Press reports. In a ruling earlier on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court paused the execution saying they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case. Pike's lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that she had lied about being sexually abused as a child. But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape. Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected. Earlier this week, the Supreme Court refused to hear a different appeal from Pike. Tennessee governor also denied a clemency request this week from the death row inmate. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. title: Cornell case spotlights 'confusing' web of systems for reporting campus assaults
description: Victims often have to navigate both university and local law enforcement processes to find justice.
body: This video can not be played "I'm very shocked" - College students react to Cornell University rape investigation Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of sexual assault. When Mary was a first-year college student, she woke up after a fraternity party with bruises and bite marks all over her body. She says it took her a few days to piece together that she had been sexually assaulted while "blacked out", and to find the strength - and the right avenue - to report the assault. The man she accused was eventually expelled, but police declined to bring charges because they said there was a lack of physical evidence. Mary - whose name has been changed to protect her identity - says the process of finding some measure of justice was oftentimes confusing and disappointing. "Even though it was a positive outcome, it was still so emotionally exhausting and draining, because I had to do all of this in tandem with getting used to being a college student for the first time," said Mary. "In many ways, I had to be my own advocate, gathering all my evidence." The experience with local police, she added, "left me with a deep sense of disappointment in the system". How both universities and the criminal justice system respond to these types of assaults on college campuses is once again under the spotlight, after a former student at Cornell University filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was raped by several members of a fraternity two years ago, with prosecutors declining at the time to pursue a case. Mary did not attend Cornell, and her case is not connected with the university. But advocates for survivors of sexual assault say her case, and the Cornell allegations, are emblematic of the larger challenges in responding to sexual assault claims on college campuses specifically. The confusing web of systems and policies - which varies greatly by college - is one of several reasons why the vast majority of sexual assaults on college campuses, research suggests, go unreported. "These processes are hard to navigate if you aren't in trauma," said Nancy Chi Cantalupo, an associate professor of law at Wayne State University who has represented victims on college campuses. "If you are in trauma, they're virtually impossible to navigate." Earlier this month, the former Cornell student known only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against the Ivy League university, alleging she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024. She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Jane Doe said she had reported the alleged assault to campus police, who interviewed her, and provided information to the district attorney's office. The prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but this week, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten re-opened the case. Both Cornell and Van Houten have defended their handling of the 2024 case. In a statement, external, the university said it had "conducted an extensive investigation and adjudication over several months and imposed different sanctions based on the findings and circumstances involving each student" in addition to creating a new framework for addressing sexual assault on campus. Cornell has said it followed the procedures outlined in a federal civil rights law called Title IX. The law mandates that universities follow certain rules about investigating sexual assaults. Cornell said its investigation resulted in the fraternity involved being barred from campus, and that students involved were suspended or expelled. Typically, after a student reports an assault on campus, the university's Title IX office determines whether the alleged behaviour could constitute a violation of policy. Eventually, both parties attend a hearing with a panel of faculty members or other mediators to present evidence and testimony in the case before a decision by the school is reached. One of the biggest challenges sexual assault survivors face is simultaneously navigating the university and the criminal justice system, which "serve different purposes, operate under different rules and timelines, and lead to different outcomes", said Zoey Scheinblum-Brewer, a policy coordinator at the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit anti-sexual assault organisation. "Unclear guidance about the options available through these parallel processes can create so much confusion and uncertainty that some students ultimately decide not to report," she said. Mary said this process at her college was not clear to her when she made the decision to report the assault. "For me, it would've been nice to know what I was getting into before it all happened. It felt like they were learning the process alongside me," she said of university officials. While some colleges, like Cornell, have information sharing agreements with local police, Mary was told she had to go to police separately to file a report - a process she found physically exhausting. Mary's lawyer says there was surveillance footage from the night showing her alleged rapist carrying her "slumped" over, and she had pictures of her bruises and bite marks. But police told Mary they did not have probable cause for an arrest, and that the district attorney wanted to leave it to university administration. "I was left with this taste that because they knew that the college was 'handling' my investigation, that they could wipe their hands clean of it," she said. The local police department told the BBC it did not have the details of this particular case. The local district attorney's office did not respond to a request for comment. University investigations are done behind closed doors, said Helene Weiss, a lawyer who has represented several victims of sexual assault on college campuses. She believes that part of the reason for the secrecy is to protect institutions' reputations. "The secrecy of th

title: The children dying in India's remote tribal heartland
description: At least 32 children have died in India's Balaghat district since May amid outbreaks of measles and malaria.
body: Koushila Markam holds a photograph of her daughter, Bamita, who died aged three Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Markam began convulsing. The three-year-old had spent days with a high fever and angry red sores on her body. Her mother, Koushila, had first taken her to a doctor, who prescribed an ointment. Bamita seemed to recover, then became ill again. A faith healer, called to the house in Matla village, gave her syrups and tablets. Nothing worked. By dawn, Bamita was dead. "She cried a lot," Koushila recalls. "She convulsed all night." The family tried to make her drink water. At one point she vomited blood. They buried her in a jungle after midday. Bamita's death was one of at least 32 child deaths recorded since May in a cluster of remote villages in Balaghat district in India's Madhya Pradesh state, officials say. The victims ranged from babies just three or four months old to an 18-year-old, and most were Baiga, one of India's 75 "particularly vulnerable tribal groups", external. Atilal Dhurwey holds a framed photograph of his 17-year-old brother Rooplal, who died in June. Rooplal died days after developing a fever and rash. Officials attribute the deaths to mainly measles and malaria, possibly aggravated by malnutrition and delays in treatment. They believe eight to 10 deaths were associated with measles, roughly another 10 with malaria, with several children suffering more than one infection. The precise cause of every death is less certain. "I have never seen an outbreak like this. My father was a two-term lawmaker, and I have served three terms, but neither of us has seen so many children die in such a short time," Sanjay Uikey, who has represented the area since 2013, told me. But disease is only part of the story. In remote, forested parts of Balaghat, where Maoist insurgency once took root, reaching a health centre can be a challenge in itself. In the monsoon, the terrain can make that journey harder. Paddy fields glow against red earth and low, forested hills. Narrow dirt tracks wind between fields and mud homes, often becoming slippery and impassable in heavy rain. The countryside is lush, but the homes are sparse. Most Baiga houses have low mud walls, rough timber and bamboo, and tiled or thatched roofs patched with plastic against the rain. Some homes are accessible only by these tracks. Doctors investigating the deaths have travelled through the mud in tractors. On a recent visit, we walked nearly 2km (1.2 miles) uphill to reach some of the more remote homes. The surrounding jungle was dotted with the graves of children who had died. Behru Markam lives with his wife and four children in a mud hut. His daughter, Preeti, died of a suspected measles attack. The nearest state hospital, a 100-bed facility in Birsa, is about 70km away. For families without vehicles, reaching it can mean muddy tracks, a makeshift bamboo stretcher or a motorcycle - and a day's lost wages. When Bamita became seriously ill, the family did not get her to hospital. It was raining heavily. The tracks were muddy and slippery, and the family had no way of transporting her. "If I was able to take her to hospital she might have lived," Koushila says. Her other daughter, Ankita, keeps asking what happened to her sister. The six-year-old has been told what many children in these villages are told: "Mata aa gayi" - the goddess has arrived. For some Baiga families, some illnesses - like chicken pox - are seen as the arrival of a disease goddess, who must be appeased rather than treated. Families perform a seven to nine-day ritual of bathing and offering cool water and neem leaves to the local disease goddess. Many believe that treating the patient before the ritual is completed could cause death. The Dhurwey family home in Bondari village is nearly 2km uphill from the nearest road For weeks, such beliefs shaped how families responded to sick children. Then the scale of the deaths began to emerge. On 21 July, Parshuram Dhurwey, a local village council chief, heard that two children in the same household in Bondari village had died. The next morning, he heard of another death. He called local officials and went to the area. They found a grim picture. "Every other child was sick," Dhurwey says. "They had fever, they had rashes. Many were undernourished." When government medical officer Nimish Gautam arrived, he found severely dehydrated children. The first case he saw was a teenage girl with several days of fever and rash, whose blood sugar appeared dangerously low. Her family refused to let the health team examine her properly. "Police were brought in to persuade them to take her to a health centre. The family still refused," Gautam told me. "They said if we took her for treatment, she would die. So we kept her under observation, and she recovered." Mahasingh Parte, who lives in Matla village, lost two children within two days of each other In one village, Dhurwey says, officials forcibly entered homes and took five seriously ill children to hospital. All recovered. By the time the outbreak became unmistakable to local authorities, children had already been dying for weeks. By September, Dhurwey says, 10 children aged about 18 months to 14 years had died across the four villages in his council - Adori, Kundekasa, Bondari and Usri. The symptoms were frighteningly similar and frustratingly non-specific: fever, rashes, weakness, dehydration and, in some cases, seizures. Some children had scabies, fungal infections or bacterial skin infections alongside suspected measles and malaria. In a district where malaria is endemic, external, fever could mean several things at once. Sagnibai of Bondari lost two children within 24 hours. Her daughter, Lamnin, 12, died on 26 June. Her one-year-old son, Sahil, died the following day. A local healer told the family it was Mata. They also had no money or vehicle to take the child

title: China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game?
description: Beijing has cracked down on AI chatbots that can replicate human relationships. Experts are asking if this is the right thing to do.
body: China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game? In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world." Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi. After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life. The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone. It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology. On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots. China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human. Xi and Trump met last week US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November. But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships. Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population? Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast. There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million. When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation." China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts. The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this. But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member. The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services". For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship". Police work closely with social media firms in China For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online. Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence". Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them. A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants. Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break. In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight. Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025. "My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down." In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says. She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers. But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model." Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world. For exa

title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
description: Dr Ning Xu denies he broke the rules of Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The competition's winner and runners up. Nikon is investigating whether the winning video (shown left) was altered with AI The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI. Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years. The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease. Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules. In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, external, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest. "AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said. Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself. He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images". But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big. Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere". Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated. Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real. Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents. Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself. "If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said. "There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them." Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI. "There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said. So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon. "At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement. title: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
description: A foreign policy speech by the Russian president will be keenly watched, but all signs point to the full-scale invasion continuing.
body: This video can not be played Watch: "This is a war Europe is waging against us", Sergei Lavrov tells BBC When Vladimir Putin arrived to address Russia's parliament on Wednesday, a warm welcome was guaranteed. "The Special Election Operation", as one Russian newspaper dubbed last month's legislative vote, has produced a State Duma even more pro-Putin than anything before it. The ruling party, United Russia, now has more MPs than ever. It allows the Kremlin to claim it has been handed a huge mandate from the Russian people. But for what? How will Putin use it? Are there any signs he is prepared to halt what he calls the special military operation? Or should we brace for further escalation in Ukraine and in tensions with Europe? On Thursday I'll be watching to see whether Russia's leader sheds light on his plans during an appearance at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow. Traditionally the president's speech at this annual foreign policy forum provides insight into Putin's world view. Right now, everything points to Putin continuing Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine: despite his country's huge battlefield losses to date and the damage being done to Russia's economy. Putin's speeches and statements suggest he remains confident that Russia can secure a military victory. Russia's parliamentary vote in September was tightly controlled by the Kremlin and saw more United Russia MPs elected than ever before Judging by what is being reported in Russian media, Moscow is encouraged by the shortage of air defence missiles in Ukraine, as well as the expectation that Russian strikes this winter will increase pressure on Ukrainians. Kyiv has spoken of its difficulty in shooting down Russia's ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, which have been targeting Ukraine every day. The Kremlin has made no secret of the fact it wants European states to slash their military and financial backing for Ukraine: the kind of support Moscow says is prolonging the war - or, rather, getting in the way of a Russian victory. To achieve this, Western officials believe Russia has been sending not so subtle signals. They accuse Moscow of waging an escalating hybrid war on European countries through cyber-attacks, acts of sabotage, and Russian drones violating European airspace. In Germany, a drone carrying an explosive device was found close to Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport. A covert campaign in the "grey zone", that space between peace and war. This week I asked Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, does he admit that his country is waging a hybrid war against European countries? "Do you mean when we destroy drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe are supplying Ukraine with, and which are used to attack us?" Lavrov replied. "If you admit your weapons are being used to strike us and we destroy them, call it whatever you want. But I have no doubt this is a war Europe is waging against us. We've been saying so for a long time." "This is a war Europe is waging against us": Sergei Lavrov speaks to the BBC That, indeed, has been the official Russian stance for some time: that what is happening in Ukraine amounts to a European war on Russia. It is a narrative that skips over the fact that in 2022 it was the Kremlin that launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and that Russia continues to wage war there. How far would Russia go to sever European support for Kyiv? Is Moscow, for example, actively preparing to initiate military conflict in Europe with a Nato member state? That seems unlikely. After more than four-and-a-half years of war Russia's army has not yet managed to occupy the whole of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, right next door to Russia. Fighting Europe may not be the plan, but freaking it out, to reduce support for Kyiv, could well be the intention. "If they continue this war, a European war with American help, against Russia, on Ukrainian territory, sooner or later we'll feel the need to escalate," warns prominent foreign policy strategist Sergei Karaganov, honorary chairman of Russia's Council for Foreign and Defence Policy. "According to my scenarios, the first series of blows will be conventional," he told me. "But if Europe does not surrender, unfortunately, we will have to go nuclear. There will be little left of some European countries." But if Russia went nuclear there would be a response from Europe, and nothing would be left of Russia, I suggest. "No, there will be no response from Europe," said Karaganov. "What, Britain will attack Russia with nuclear weapons? I hope you're not that crazy. I'm sure the Americans are not that crazy." Sergei Karaganov (R) says Russia will "have to go nuclear" if Europe keeps helping Ukraine I asked him if he agreed the last four-and-a-half years had been disastrous for Russia, in terms of casualties and the worsening security and economic situation. "We've lost a lot of people, yes," he admitted, "and I criticise my government for not being rough enough. But now we are getting rough enough in Ukraine. We're doing away with Ukraine as a viable state." If "doing away with Ukraine as a viable state" is Moscow's goal, it is hard to imagine the war ending soon. Meanwhile, Russia continues to rail against what it sees as the double standards of the West. In his recent address at the UN General Assembly, Sergei Lavrov accused the West of resorting to "brute force" around the world. "What they did in Venezuela, was that soft power or brute force?" Russia's foreign minister asked me this week. He was referring to America's military operation in Caracas to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro back in January. "The fact that [the US] bombed and destroyed Iran's leadership, along with their families, including children, is that not brute force?" But was Russia not resorting to brute force every day in Ukraine,

title: The AI telling farmers when to harvest
description: Will farmers want AI tools to help judge when to pick fruit, or is their own intuition enough?
body: Choosing the right moment to harvest can be a make-or-break decision When the first day of the apple harvest rolled around in Washington State last year, the fruit was ripe and the pickers were ready – but the weather had other ideas. "It was like 38C… it's not safe for people to work in that heat," recalls Joel Carter at Okanagan Specialty Fruits. "We had to stop at 10 o'clock in the morning." He says that artificial intelligence (AI) models that forecast ideal harvest dates, taking into account the weather, would be useful. "You need to know more than just when your fruit is going to be ripe. How long do you have to pick it?" he says. "That's where these models are really helpful." Carter's company has more than 1,250 acres of apple orchards in Washington, and the fruit is grown for sliced apple portions – often sold to hotels and schools, for example. The firm is investing in technology with the hope of maximising productivity. Even the apples are genetically engineered so that they don't brown easily once cut. But planning a harvest is tricky. New tools that count and analyse fruit on the tree or vine, and predict when crops will ripen, are emerging. It matters because prices for fruit, especially high-value berries such as strawberries or blueberries can fluctuate wildly. Getting the harvest date wrong means you book seasonal workers when you don't actually need them, and risk missing out on the biggest profits. Okanagan Specialty Fruits is already experimenting with cameras from a Canadian firm called Vivid Machines. The cameras are mounted atop tractors and they scoop up imagery of the apple trees as the tractor trundles by. AI identifies buds, flowers or fruit in that footage. "Right now, Vivid is telling us crop estimates and harvest dates," says Carter. He notes that the system is good at picking out very tiny flower buds, which are hard to see at a glance with the naked eye. But the accuracy of forecasts is noticeably dependent on the quality of historical information fed in to the system, adds Carter. "This isn't something where an AI can scrape the internet and figure out what's the average [yield] for Granny Smith," he explains. "It's going to be bespoke to your farm." Apples are at least somewhat forgiving – the harvest window for those Granny Smiths is three weeks long, says Carter. For other fruit, such as berries, you might only have a few days. "If a strawberry crop is on, you have to harvest it – otherwise your entire crop gets diseased very, very quickly," says Raymond Martin, co-founder and chief operating officer of FruitCast, a UK company that offers harvest forecasts to fruit growers here. His firm offers growers crop predictions for strawberries and also raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and tomatoes. "We're moving on to grapes next year," adds Martin. Don't experienced farmers know when their fruit will be ripe, I ask? Martin says they generally do – but not necessarily across their entire farm, which might be many acres in size, or have both outdoor and indoor growing areas. "We do exactly what the farmers could do but we just do it on a scale that they can't." The system analyses footage of ripening fruit that can be captured by drones, someone walking up and down a field with a smartphone, or a camera mounted on a farm vehicle. This year has been challenging, notes Martin, with hot weather and severe drought hitting much of the UK. This has stressed many fruit plants, putting them into thermal dormancy and slowing down fruit production. There's only a small window for picking berries says Raymond Martin The FruitCast model accounts for weather and irrigation conditions in its forecasts. The company says, "our forecasts land within 10% of actual picked volume one week out (90% accurate) and within 17% three weeks out (83% accurate). We guarantee less than 20% error…" Angus Soft Fruits is one company that has worked with FruitCast. AI tech for forecasting fruit ripeness is not yet "a finished solution" says operations director Neill Finlayson: "This journey is still ongoing and, whilst significant progress has been made, the industry remains some way from achieving a fully integrated forecasting ecosystem." Driscoll's, a California headquartered fruit seller with a big operation in the UK, also confirmed to BBC News that some of its independent fruit growers in the UK have used FruitCast's technology. Yasaman Ghasempour (left) is developing ripeness detection techniques Researchers are also exploring new ways of analysing fruit in intense detail. Many farmers already use handheld brix meters to gauge the sugar content of their crop. These devices work by measuring how much light has changed direction, or refracted, after passing through a liquid – indicating the volume of solids present. Some such meters use infrared light, meaning there's no need to cut into the fruit to take measurements. But Yasaman Ghasempour at Princeton University says millimetre waves, high frequency radio waves, can penetrate deeper "They basically respond very well to humidity, water [and sugar]," she says. She and her students have come up with a millimetre wave-based ripeness detector, external that could be used by farmers – or even customers searching for perfectly ripe fruit in shops. Her students tried it out at a local market in New Jersey. "[Staff] there got kind of scared that we were doing something shady," laughs Ghasempour. Such fine-grained analysis of fruit, if currently unripe, could also help inform forecasts of when it will be ripe. Jing Zhang says new tech has to prove its worth to farmers But while some growers, such as Carter, are interested in trying out new tech, many will wonder whether investing in it is really worthwhile. "Adoption is very complicated," says Jing Zhang at North Carolina State University. "The grower has to have confidence in the research and whether or not it

title: Vape prices to rise as new tax takes effect
description: Vaping is about to becoming more expensive due to a new tax on products.
body: The government is trying to make vaping more expensive and less appealing to young people The price of vapes is set to rise as a new tax comes into effect, with the aim of making vaping less attractive to children and young people. The Vaping Product Duty will be imposed at a rate of £2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid. However, many customers will not see a jump in prices immediately, as sellers have six months to sell old stock at the pre-duty price. The government wants to reduce the appeal of vapes by making them more expensive, as more evidence of its adverse effect on health comes out, particularly on children and young people. The vaping industry has lobbied against the new tax, saying that affordable vapes help people to quit smoking. The duty will apply to all vaping products regardless of whether they contain nicotine. Tobacco rates were also raised on Thursday, by £2.20 per 100 cigarettes or 50g of tobacco. HMRC said this maintains the financial incentive for smokers to switch to vaping. The BBC spoke to vapers in Reading who had mixed views on whether the new tax would encourage people to quit. Mackenzie Bird, 19, has been a regular vaper for three years. She said she was "fine" with the duty and it wouldn't stop her from vaping. Mackenzie Bird said the tax wouldn't stop her from vaping "I don't know how many people it'll actually deter," she said. "I'll probably just stock up." However, Cara Lewis-Rimes and Dylan Killner said they might reconsider the habit in light of higher prices. Cara said she thinks the changes will force vapers to cut down because of the cost of living. Cara and Dylan think the tax will prompt vapers to cut back Dylan said he might be inclined to quit altogether. "I don't think it's doing me any favours... the health factor around it as well is not great." HMRC is also launching a stamp for vaping products which are traceable throughout the supply chain. All vapes sold in the UK must carry this stamp from April. The new tax is also an effort to combat illicit trade, which is a growing problem on UK high streets. Last month, the prime minister announced new powers for councils that will address the decline of the high street, including the amount of vape shops. Changes to planning law in England mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open. Health Minister Karin Smyth said: "These measures are an important step in our ambition to tackle youth vaping by reducing the affordability of vaping products, which goes hand-in-hand with the work we are already doing to tackle the appeal and availability of vapes on our high streets." James Murray, the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, said the government was "backing all those retailers who play by the rules". Vape shop staff like Jordan have seen customers stocking up ahead of the tax coming in But Jordan Apap, a sales assistant in Berkshire Vapers, said the new tax would "put a lot of strain on legitimate vape shops" that provide more specialist advice and services than convenience stores and phone shops that sell vapes. "There is a real and genuine risk that we will cease to exist within a year or two," he said. Vaping rates for schoolchildren appear to drop - is it falling out of favour? Police raid barbers and vape shops suspected of being fronts for crime gangs John Dunne, the director general of the UK Vaping Industry Association, said: "This is nothing short of a tax on public health." He said vapes had helped "millions of adults cut down on or stop smoking". "Protecting young people is essential. But that means stronger enforcement against illegal and rogue traders, not making legal vaping more expensive for adults trying to stay away from cigarettes." Experts say vaping is much safer than smoking, but it is not risk free and the long-term effects are less clear. A recent review of vaping studies found that it had an association with problems in children and young people including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms. The NHS has said that children and non-smokers should never vape. title: Northern Ireland's young drivers first in UK to get new driving licensing laws
description: Northern Ireland becomes the first part of the UK to introduce new rules for new drivers in a bid to reduce fatal road crashes involving young people.
body: Northern Ireland has become the first part of the UK to introduce new rules for new drivers in a bid to reduce fatal road crashes involving young people. Graduated driver licensing (GDL), for learner and newly qualified drivers, apply to all new drivers but are particularly aimed at 17 to 23-year-olds. Among the new rules is that learners must spend at least six months getting driving experience before they can take a practical test. Newly qualified drivers under 24 will also face restrictions on carrying young passengers at night. The rule changes were announced in January last year and will see the current speed limit of 45mph for restricted drivers removed. Drivers who do not follow the restrictions could receive three penalty points or a fine of up to £1,000. Versions of GDL exist in countries including Australia, the US and Republic of Ireland. Campaigners have called for them to be introduced across the UK. Police say it will "save lives" but there has been a mixed reaction from young drivers, with some in favour while others, from rural backgrounds, feel frustrated. However a driving instructor described it as a "terrific" step. According to official figures, 17 to 23-year-old drivers were responsible for 24% of all collisions, external in Northern Ireland in 2024, despite only accounting for 8% of license holders. In the same year there were 251 people killed or seriously injured in collisions involving a young driver, and in 65% of those, the young driver was deemed to be at fault. In January, the government announced that learner drivers in England and Wales could face a minimum period of up to six months between sitting their theory and practical tests. However, it stopped short of introducing GDLs, which motoring organisation the AA described as "a missed opportunity". Earlier this year Scottish ministers called on the government to grant them powers to put their own restrictions on new young drivers. The UK government said it wanted to keep young people safe but had decided not to introduce "blanket restrictions" on new drivers. Tommy turns 17 in January, so he has a while to wait until he can sit his practical driving test For 16-year-old Tommy from Omagh, driving is a "big factor" in his life. He has been learning the basics, driving with his dad in fields and private yards for three years already. However he thinks the new rules will not suit young people who live in rural areas, who don't have access to public transport and rely heavily on lifts. "There's hardly any transport links out here so you sort of have to rely on people giving me lifts," he said. "We're about five miles out from the nearest transport hub and it's just hard to organise lifts even to get to work or college." Tommy has his own car ready to go and considers himself a confident driver who would pass his test first time, but said the time he has to wait to drive it has now been "extended". "It is a bit gutting, because I was so excited until they announced the new rules coming in, it's hard to believe how big of a change it is going to be," he added. Adam says safety is important but, coming from a rural area, also feels frustrated While he recognises that something needs to be done to address the number of deaths on the roads there is a level of frustration for Adam, who is also from Omagh, about the minimum six-month delay to him getting behind the wheel. "I'm really eager to get out on the road, especially since I've been hassling my parents. I go to the gym quite frequently, maybe four days a week, and it's straight after tech. "If I can get up off my own two feet, get into my own car, and go to my gym by myself, it's nobody's problem but mine. "All I used to talk about in high school was 'oh, what car are you getting', 'where are we going on a road trip', and now there's just more complications, it's just bummed everybody out," he added. Moss thinks it's "not that big of a deal" to have to wait six months Moss is already learning to drive, so the new rules will not affect him, but he thinks it is a positive move because "you'll get a lot more confidence and a lot more experiences in different kinds of situations which will be really useful". "Starting to drive by yourself can be a scary thing", so "if it's to help with safety I think its worth it," he added. He recognises that some people are annoyed about the new rules, particularly the six-month wait, but thinks "in the long run, does it really matter if you get your test six months later? It's not that big of a deal". The Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI's) road safety lead Ch Supt Sam Donaldson said that in Northern Ireland "more people per head of population are involved in collisions, basic collisions, serious injury collisions, and sadly, fatal collisions, than any other part of the UK". He has "no doubt" that it will save lives. "Sadly the reality is that young and inexperienced drivers are disproportionately involved in more collisions. "Some are minor, some are serious, and some sadly are result in fatalities as well." Veronica Weir has 26 years experience as a driving instructor Veronica Weir, who has 26 years' experience as a driving instructor thinks the law change is "terrific" and that young drivers can be irresponsible. "It's been a long time coming, about 15 years in the pipeline. "Kids today just think it's a video game, and if they crash, there's no consequences, there's no ripple effect, they'll just brush themselves off and drive off again," she said. She said that dangerous driving can affect "their family, their insurance and other parts of the community". The first new practical tests will take place on 1 April 2027. title: Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s
description: The party says it would bring in new work requirements for young people claiming Universal Credit.
body: Tory leader Kemi Badenoch (left) with shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately in London last week The Conservatives have said they would introduce new work requirements for under-25s claiming benefits in a "tough love" approach to youth joblessness. Young people claiming Universal Credit who are fit to work but have not worked for six months continuously would face new rules to qualify for payments, including daily attendance at a job centre or courses. The party says the scheme would help tackle the almost one million people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are not in education, employment or training, known as Neets. But anti-poverty charity Trussell warned that people on Universal Credit could not afford basic essentials, which harmed their ability to find and keep work. Under the Tory proposals, those aged 18 to 24 who apply for Universal Credit but have not previously worked for a continuous period of six months or more, for at least 16 hours per week, would instead have to take part in a "Get to Work" scheme. Rather than Universal Credit, they would receive a "Get to Work Allowance" paid at the same rate but requiring daily attendance at a job centre, on work experience or work readiness courses. They would be assigned a manager and have to take part in job search workshops and interview preparation sessions. The programme would last six months, or less if a participant secures a job - but those who are still unemployed after half a year on the scheme would have their benefit cut by 30%. Young people on Universal Credit who have previously worked for six months, have health issues or care responsibilities or are estranged would be exempt. The party has also said it would look closer at whether parents' earnings and savings should be factored into welfare payments for their children. Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the measures were designed to "show some tough love" to reduce the number of Neets. "Too many young people are leaving school and signing straight onto benefits - this is a waste of their potential and a disaster for our economy," the Tory MP said. Under current Universal Credit requirements, external, people have to sign a "claimant commitment" to prepare for and look for work or increase their earnings if they are already working - but the Tories claim their rules would be stricter. The proposals were announced on Thursday ahead of the party's conference starting this weekend. Neets have been high on the agenda for political parties ahead of the imminent publication of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn on how to tackle the one in eight young people in the UK who not in education, employment or training. At Labour's conference earlier this week, Chancellor John Healey told party activists: "The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage." He said cutting welfare spending was a priority and announced that every mayor in England would have access to a Local Apprenticeships Service from March 2027 to generate thousands more youth opportunities. And on Thursday, the Department for Work and Pensions said every small and medium-sized business hiring a young apprentice would get £2,000 from the government under a new scheme backed by the Federation of Small Businesses. title: Catching scabies in hospital meant my husband was labelled an environmental hazard when he died
description: Kate Baxter says the infection "cast a shadow over" her husband Paul's final days.
body: Paul, pictured here with his dog Bonnie, was "bright, funny and had an inquiring mind", his widow Kate said As her husband of more than 40 years lay dying in a hospital bed, Kate Baxter was not even allowed to hold his hand without wearing protective gloves. Paul suffered a stroke in December 2025 and, four months before he died in June aged 90, caught scabies in hospital. In his final days, Kate could only touch him while wearing the rubber gloves after he contracted the highly contagious skin infestation, external at Glangwili Hospital, Carmarthen. Hywel Dda health board said it was taking extra measures to control the spread of scabies and was focused on keeping hospitals and healthcare settings as clean as possible. "He was suffering. He said to me, 'my back itches' and when I rubbed his back, his skin was coming off like sand," she said. "To have him die like that wasn't good." Scabies is caused by microscopic mites burrowing under the skin and it spreads through close skin contact. Kate, from Cwrt Newydd in Ceredigion, said Paul also had pneumonia, but the crusted scabies meant his immune system "had weakened". Paul died on 8 June - scabies is noted as a secondary cause of death on his death certificate. Kate said the undertaker told her Paul had a tag on him saying "environmental hazard" while his body was in the morgue. "It means the scabies were still active on him," she added. "You don't expect your husband to go into hospital with one thing and then come out via the morgue as a health hazard." Kate Baxter says scabies cast a shadow over her husband's final weeks Kate said, before he was admitted to hospital, Paul was "very bright" and "funny". "He had an inquiring mind, even at that age. He was great to be around, he enjoyed life," she said. By February, he told his wife he was feeling itchy but Kate said doctors thought it might be an allergic reaction to medication. She said it was 12 weeks and six days before he was diagnosed in May, by which point it had developed to the more severe crusted scabies. People with this type of scabies can have up to two million mites and eggs on them. Kate also contracted scabies from Paul and described it as "dreadful". She added: "You've got an itch, like something you'd have in the middle of the back, and you just simply cannot get rid of it and your skin is constantly in pain. "They're worse at night because that's when they're most active and you'd get this suddenly sharp stabbing pain in your leg or your back, and then it's sort of multiplied out. It's distressing." Crusted scabies is noted as a secondary cause of death on Paul's death certificate Kate feels the infection cast "a shadow" over her husband's final weeks and days and took away "the quality of time together". She said, if her husband had not caught scabies, then "possibly his immune system wouldn't have been compromised and he possibly would be able to fight off the pneumonia that he caught In the end". Kate was given personal protective equipment - similar to that used by medical professionals during Covid - to wear while visiting him in hospital. "Holding somebody's hand with gloves is not good," she said. After Paul's death, Kate wrote to the health board to complain about how long it took to diagnose him with scabies. Health board chief executive Phil Kloer replied saying they had not identified any evidence that concerns regarding the rash were ignored or "that there was a failure to seek appropriate medical review". He added the health board were "unable to determine with certainty whether the rash could have been prevented". Kate said she was unhappy with the response and felt the health board "skated over" the issues, adding that doctors should have "realised sooner that it wasn't just a skin condition". In July, Glangwili Hospital's Steffan ward was closed to treat a scabies outbreak, followed by the Cadog ward in September - both have since reopened. The Teifi ward has been closed since 21 September. This week Hywel Dda health board also closed two wards at Prince Philip Hospital in Llanelli because of scabies. The latest published data in Wales shows there were more than 27,000 reported consultations in the Common Ailments Service, external for the condition last year, compared to 4,810 two years earlier. Hywel Dda confirmed some treatments had been cancelled due to the ward closures and said any people affected would be "contacted proactively as soon as we know that we may need to change their scheduled appointment". Director of public health Ardiana Gjini said: "We are working in partnership with our other partner agencies, Public Health Wales, our local authority colleagues, so that we ensure that that potential transmission that happens through the community is reduced and is controlled. "Infection prevention is much broader and much higher than just what patients might see as clean or not clean. "However, we are very focused in maintaining our hospitals and our healthcare settings as clean as possible, and we ask everyone to help with that." Gjini added that the infection did put "additional burden on our staff and on our services, but also crucially on our patients, carers, and the whole community". Ardiana Gjini says the health board is working to stop the spread of scabies Prof Tess McPherson of the British Association of Dermatology said she had noticed a rise in the infection, but said it was "impossible to avoid" and had been "unnecessarily stigmatised". She added: "It's not to do with being dirty, it's not to do with poor hygiene. We're seeing it in all age groups - particularly young people, children and babies. "I've certainly seen lots of people that may not even want to tell their sexual partners or people they're living with they've got scabies, which clearly is going to lead to ongoing issues with people having scabie

title: Trekkers helicoptered off mountains as more deadly landslides hit Nepal
description: A month after mass catastrophic flooding, around 30 people have died in landslides and heavy rain.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal during floods Another wave of landslides and heavy rain has killed about 30 people in Nepal, as the Himalayan nation reels from August's catastrophic flooding that left 1,400 dead and thousands more missing. The national disaster management authority says more than 1,900 families have been affected since late last week with more than 240 homes damaged. Roads, buildings and bridges have been swept away. Hundreds of trekkers on the Annapurna Circuit - crucial to Nepal's economy - have had to cut short their hikes to get to safety. Many have been helicoptered out of the districts of Manang and Mustang, from a hiking circuit that usually takes up to three weeks to complete. Communities in several parts of Nepal are mourning loved ones. Speaking from a damp, blue tent in Battar, a town north-west of Kathmandu, Buti Tamang told BBC Nepali: "We used to live in a hut, but now there is nothing. We have lost so many of our relatives." "Now it is raining and the tent leaks, so we've been facing a difficult situation. We have nowhere to go," said Ramesh Ghale, who also had to flee his home. Many Nepalis have been made homeless and are staying in emergency tents, as a new wave of extreme weather strikes Several trekkers and their guides say their journeys back down the mountains have been treacherous, taking up to three or four days and requiring them to pass collapsed roads and swept-away bridges. Jake Stacy, a 21-year-old from Suffolk, found himself stranded with his guide in Yak Kharka, upper Manang, due to heavy snowfall last week and decided not to continue to the Thorang La pass, the highest point of the circuit. "We made our own paths on mountain slopes," he said, after returning to base camp in Pokhara on Tuesday night. "It was quite steep and we were clambering because there was river below… It was very muddy and very wet. "Many trekkers were helicoptered out," he added. Jake Stacy and his guide had to craft their own paths on the mountains to return after heavy snowfall Australian Andrew Graham and his guide Prem KC said they had to cross more than 15 landslides after they decided to return from Manang village. "A few of them were quite dangerous, the residual risks have grown now." The two got stuck when they reached the village of Chame, which had been evacuated due to the risk of landslides, and had to spend a night in the jungle, Graham said. A massive landslide has partially blocked a river which passes through Chame, causing a temporary lake that has inundated houses and a key bridge. Authorities have been trying to release the water for the past three days using excavators but have not been very successful, locals told the BBC. Meanwhile, trekking guide Tse Ring Doma said she and her group had to cross 28 landslides. The mental stress was more difficult than the physical challenge, she said, given the fresh memory of last month's enormous disaster: "Even thunder would make us run and come out to see if anything was coming our way." Her client, Norwegian Ellen Wahlström, said visitors were fortunate - they would only have to leave some of their items behind, while locals risked losing their houses and land. She added that authorities had been clearing many of the landslides "surprisingly fast". Trekkers have faced difficulties trudging across the landslide-ravaged landscape - and around 700 have been prevented from even starting the Annapurna Circuit While road damage in Manang has been serious, with several bridges swept away and communications down in some areas, no one had been killed in the trekking region, chief district officer Mukti Prasad Khanal said. But four bodies have been recovered and 12 people remain missing after an avalanche near the base of Himlung Peak, close to the border with Tibet. A representative of the local trekking authority, the Annapurna Conservation Area Project, said some 700 trekkers were still waiting in Pokhara to embark on the Annapurna Circuit. "We have been holding back all these people who want to go to the Annapurna Circuit trek, although we are under pressure from the trekking industry to announce the route open," he said. Indian visitors who often visit the ancient temple Muktinath on a Hindu pilgrimage had been asked to fly from Jomson to Pokhara instead of drive down, due to a cut-off road, he added. Most of the old trekking trails on the Annapurna Circuit have been unused in recent years after the introduction of roads, except for small pockets of Manang and Mustang districts. But now operators say many trekkers have been using these abandoned paths to return, as the main roads have been washed away in some sections of the circuit.
