title: Three unions to strike at once over Glasgow Caledonian job cuts
description: Lecturers and support staff say the action by the UCU, the EIS and Unison on Thursday will effectively close the university.
body: Management plan to cut about 50 posts and say they have not ruled out compulsory redundancies Staff at Glasgow Caledonian University are staging strike action, with all three campus unions walking out together for the first time over planned job cuts. Lecturers and support staff say the action by members of the UCU, the EIS and Unison on Thursday could effectively stop the university from operating. Management at the university plan to cut about 50 posts and say they have not ruled out compulsory redundancies. They say the cuts are needed to secure Caley's finances and blame a £33m fall in income over two years, partly due to a drop in the number of international students. The dispute dates back to March when management announced plans to cut up to 100 posts, blaming a sharp fall in income from international students. Since then, voluntary redundancies have brought that figure down to about 50 but the sticking point is compulsory redundancies. The unions want a guarantee that nobody will be forced to leave - but the management has refused to rule it out. Talks at the conciliation service Acas broke down earlier this month and lecturers went on strike last week. The unions argue the cuts are a choice rather than a necessity. They point to what they say are £95m in cash reserves as well as the university's purchase of land in the city centre for about £4.5m, which they say is foolish at this time. The university says buying and selling land is part of a long-standing strategy. It has previously highlighted that it is facing a £10m financial deficit in the next financial year and said the cuts are needed to put it back on a "sound financial footing". Law lecturer Nick McKerrell said there was no need to cut jobs A university spokesperson said they were "disappointed" the unions had voted to strike. They said the measures the unions had suggested as alternatives to compulsory redundancies had largely already been taken and that was why the number of job cuts had been reduced. "While voluntary measures remain our preferred approach, we cannot rule out compulsory redundancies if the required savings are not achieved," they said. Unison branch secretary Davena Rankin said compulsory redundancies were not the answer. "Staff want to support students and help the university succeed, but they need confidence that their jobs are secure," Rankin said. UCU branch president Karen Lorimer said staff wanted to be welcoming new and returning students but the refusal to rule out using compulsory redundancies left them with no alternative but to strike. Dr Nick McKerrell, a law lecturer and the branch secretary of the EIS, said there were issues across higher education but Caley was in a strong place financially and there was no need for compulsory redundancies. This is the biggest day so far of what is an ongoing dispute at the university. For the first time, all three unions are on strike on the same day. The unions said it was highly unusual for both the lecturers' unions to be on strike at the same university on the same day. They said that adding the support staff - who run IT, security, catering and cleaning as well as the library and student welfare - would bring the campus and the university to an effective standstill. The university has said throughout that it wants to keep disruption for students to a minimum but with so many services affected, that will be very difficult. Further strike dates are planned stretching to the middle of October. The lecturers' unions are out again next week, and Unison is expected to stagger action among its members. Glasgow Caledonian is far from an isolated case. At the University of Edinburgh, about 3,000 staff have begun five weeks of strikes, running until 30 October, over £140m of cuts. Dundee University staff are also staging a five-week walkout. It's the latest chapter in a bruising year. Back in March, staff in Dundee, Aberdeen, Strathclyde and Heriot-Watt all walked out in separate disputes. The underlying problem is money and funding. Scottish universities get a fixed amount from the government for each Scottish student they teach, and they're not allowed to charge them fees. For years they've made up the gap with fees from international students. But we've seen the number of overseas students falling, while the cost of staff, pensions and energy keep rising. Just a few weeks ago, an expert group working for the Scottish government's review of university funding estimated that the sector is short of around £200m a year. It also found a repairs backlog of about £1bn. title: 'Special surprise' as rare moth found in nature reserve for first time
description: Experts called it a "special surprise" to find an "incredibly sparse moth" in this habitat.
body: The Bog Grass Moth is a rare species in the UK A rare species of moth has been found in north Wales. The Bog Grass Moth was found at Cors Geirch National Nature Reserve on the Llŷn Peninsula in Gwynedd, as conservationists were surveying the area's species. Experts called it a "special surprise" to find the "incredibly sparse moth" in the habitat. An exact population figure in the UK for the Bog Grass Moth is not known, but they have only been recorded in a small number of English counties, such as Dorset. The fen, which is an area of low, flat, wet land, is monitored by Natur am Byth's Llŷn and Ynys Môn project, which aims to protect some of north Wales' most at risk species. As experts from the conservation project gathered at Cors Geirch they set up moth traps and in one night 446 moths made up of 91 different species were collected, with 19 of these being Bog Grass Moths - the first time they had been recorded in this area. Natural Resources Wales said the habitat allowed wet sedges to grow - which is the only food source for the Bog Grass Moth's larvae. Sedges are one of the largest plant families in the world and are most common in wet habitats. Other rare species recorded at the site included the Six Spotted Crane Fly and the Black Nightrunner Ground Beetle. Steve Palin and Charles Aron, who are both lepidopterists and specialise in the study of moths, said the beauty of trapping moths was "you just never know what's going to turn up". "It's a significant addition to our knowledge of the region's winged insects and demonstrates the value of targeted moth recordings in these specialist fen habitats, where there is clearly still much to discover," they said in a statement. Clare Sampson, a project manager for RSPB Cymru, said the work of staff, contractors and volunteers had helped to open up the wetland that is "home to these rare invertebrate species". Six Spotted Crane Flies were also spotted at the reserve She added: "While many fens suffered over the hot, dry summer, not only did we find healthy numbers of the Black Nightrunner Ground Beetle and Six Spotted Crane Fly at Cors Geirch this year, but we also discovered this wonderful and rare species of moth." Sampson said about 80% of UK peatlands had been lost or damaged, meaning rare species that depend on specific habitats can "struggle to survive". Healthy peat is the country's biggest carbon store but when damaged it releases planet-warming greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Peat is formed over thousands of years from partially decayed plants in waterlogged conditions. "These important fen sites can be managed and maintained so that future generations can continue to make new discoveries," she added. title: Employers should teach primary-age children about work, says Milburn
description: The author of a major report into youth activity in the UK says children as young as four should be learning about careers.
body: Children should be introduced to the world of work at the start of primary school, says the author of a major report into youth activity in the UK. Former minister Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be learning about different careers, with work experience placements made mandatory for 14- to 16-year-olds. However, teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools and say practical considerations must ensure all schools have access to the support. The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the UK were not in education, employment or training (known as Neet), between April and June 2026. Milburn told the BBC "in primary school, it's really about opening their eyes and giving them a sense about what is possible". Despite a push towards apprenticeships and work experience in Years 10 and 11, for many the journey towards becoming Neet starts well before their 16th birthday. As a result, Milburn says children should be introduced to the world of work much earlier in their school journey, with dedicated space in the curriculum to "broaden horizons". He told the BBC this could be achieved by employers giving talks in primary schools and offering taster sessions to children. "It'd be good if employers came into schools and said, 'Look, this is what's going on, these are things that are possible.'" Milburn says that for Key Stage 4 pupils - aged between 14 and 16 - experience must be given in a real workplace with employer feedback. The final instalment of Alan Milburn's review into Neets is due to be published this autumn "Work experience needs to be mandatory. It makes a big difference," he told the BBC. Milburn also emphasised the difficulty some young people face when trying to find work experience placements. "There are about four in ten people aged 14-16 who aren't getting any work experience at all," he said. "In other schools, students are told to go off and find their own work experience and that often relies on the network of Mum and Dad." These recommendations are due to be published in the final instalment of his government-commissioned report into the issue, which is expected to be published in the autumn. Education is devolved in the UK, so while Milburn's review looks at the picture in all four nations, his recommendations regarding education are specific to England. Currently in England, careers guidance must be offered to students aged 11-18 and work experience is not statutory. The government has said its vision, external is to "guarantee two weeks' worth of work experience for every young person" in England. In both Scotland and Wales, career-based learning is already a requirement in schools for students as young as three. Emma, who has three grandchildren, says primary school is too young to focus on careers Emma, from Kirklees, has grandchildren in Years 1, 2 and 4 and thinks primary school is too young to be introducing careers talks. "In primary school, there is too much trying to get little kids to grow up too quickly," she says. "Just let them be little kids. I know they have to learn and the world's changing, but still, give them a chance to be kids." But Zoe, another parent, disagrees. "I think it's a good idea," she says. "It's something that everyone has to do, so if you learn early, it's something they don't have to learn later on." Teaching unions have responded positively to the idea of introducing career-based learning into schools at a younger age, but have warned about the burden this could place on primary schools in particular. Paul Whiteman, general secretary of school leaders' union National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), warns of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools. "Whenever new mandatory requirements are proposed, it is important to be clear about what might have to give way to make room for them," he says. Whiteman also highlights the value of existing programmes such as "Primary Futures", which bring in volunteers from different professions into schools to "challenge stereotypes and raise aspirations". "The earlier young people can begin to make connections between what they learn in school and the possibilities that lie ahead, the better," Whiteman says. Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL), says having someone come into the classroom can really "enlighten [children's] motivation... and give them that sense of passion for all the opportunities beyond the classroom". Although he acknowledges that finding opportunities in rural areas could be more challenging. Are you affected by issues covered in this story? title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
description: Other passengers on the Israel-bound flight described the "terrifying" moment the plane dropped.
body: This video can not be played Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die. Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped. The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes. "Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media. He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door. When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane". "I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said. "We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure." This video can not be played 'I pulled the controls': Passenger tells Israeli PM how he helped stop attacker Hayun said he then jumped back into the cockpit and "started pulling the controls". When asked by Netanyahu whether he knew what he was doing, the passenger answered: "I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister." Hayun said the plane then started to level out. By then, two on-duty pilots who had been in the passenger cabin were at the front of the plane, and one told Hayun he was taking control from there. Netanyahu praised Hayun, calling him a "great hero" and a "lion". Another passenger, Zvika Meness, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan he helped overpower the attacker, and the passenger and two others "tied him up with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones". "Another pilot who was sitting in the passenger cabin went in to replace the additional pilot, and they essentially landed the plane," he added. The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft. They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags. "Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control". Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment". "Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added. A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane". The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery". The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given. US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack. title: Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
description: Rantzen, who fronted the BBC's That's Life for two decades, went on to found Childline, and in recent years had been a campaigner for assisted dying.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Dame Esther Rantzen, broadcaster, campaigner and charity founder, dies aged 86 Dame Esther Rantzen, who presented BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the charity Childline, has died at the age of 86. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the veteran broadcaster and campaigner had "changed countless lives". Dame Esther hosted and produced That's Life! during its run from 1973 to 1994. It regularly attracted 20 million viewers for its mixture of serious consumer investigations and light-hearted items. She launched Childline, a British counselling service for children and young people, in 1986, and in 2013 she launched Silver Line to help elderly people suffering from isolation and loneliness. Later in life, she became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying. She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In December 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic. But in a statement given to the Press Association earlier this month, she said that despite having "spent the money and made the plans" to go to Dignitas, she had since reached the point where she was "too physically fragile to make the journey". She added that the law must "change and change quickly", as she renewed her plea ahead of the latest debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, which failed to pass through the Commons. Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! presenter, Childline founder and campaigner for assisted dying The broadcaster revealed her cancer diagnosis in January 2023, saying the news had prompted her to express "profound thanks to everyone who has made my life so joyful". In a statement announcing her death on Wednesday, Dame Esther's family paid tribute to the "most wonderful mother" and "cherished grandmother" whose compassion would live on through her charities. "We hope the humour, ingenuity and audacity she brought to her work may continue to inspire you as it will do us." Dame Esther with fellow That's Life! presenters Howard Leader, Kevin Devine, and Gavin Campbell in 1993 Rantzen joined BBC radio as a sound effects assistant before becoming a TV researcher, and in 1968 she trained as a producer and director. The young broadcaster became a researcher and reporter for Bernard Braden's consumer affairs programme, Braden's Week. When That's Life! launched in 1973, she was its figurehead and became a popular fixture on screens as the show's formidable and fun-loving presenter and producer. The consumer show's notable items, according to her website, external, included "talking dogs, Jobsworth Awards and campaigns on behalf of abused children, organ transplants, safe playgrounds, and to provide justice for consumers". Its most-viewed episode featured Sir Nicholas Winton being introduced for the first time to survivors he had saved from the Holocaust, during a 1988 instalment of the show. Later in her career, she also appeared on Strictly Come Dancing, First Dates and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! Dame Esther was married to documentary film-maker Desmond Wilcox from 1977 until he died in 2000. They had three children. She was made a dame in 2015 for her services to children and older people. Dame Esther met some Childline volunteers when she visited its Belfast office in 2009 Dame Esther went on to become a vocal campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying. In December 2024, she spoke of her "great relief" after MPs backed proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, before they ultimately stalled in the House of Lords. In an interview with the Sunday Times, external in November 2025, before the bill ran out of time, she said that "as long as others in the future will be able to ask for help to die as they choose, I will die happy". She expressed her disappointment after MPs voted against a fresh attempt to introduce the legislation in September. Some disability campaigners described the result as a "victory", while Dame Esther said it was "deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it". "I am sure a change in the law will come," she added. Figures from politics, broadcasting and the charity sector have paid tribute to Dame Esther for her impact on public life. The prime minister said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life". BBC director-general Matt Brittin paid tribute to Dame Esther as a "legend of British broadcasting" whose contribution to public life was "immeasurable". "Her warmth, spirit and fight for justice and action that we saw on our screens continued long after the programme ended, with a lifetime of campaigning where she changed the lives of millions," he said. Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners. Chris Sherwood, the chief executive of the NSPCC, which runs the Childline helpline, said Dame Esther had gone to "exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help". Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning. "She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said. Watch Katie Razzall's half-hour special programme Esther! on iPlayer. It will also be shown this Friday, 2 October, on BBC One at 19:30 BST. title: US film-maker loses 'Downton Shabby' High Court case
description: Hopwood DePree took the council to court in his bid to take over the Grade II-listed mansion for £1.
body: Hopwood DePree published a book called Downton Shabby in 2022 about his efforts to restore Hopwood Hall in Middleton An American man has lost his legal bid to take ownership of a historic mansion for £1. Hopwood DePree, who claims ancestral links to the Grade II-listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton, Rochdale, said he was "incredibly disappointed" after a judge at the High Court in Manchester ruled against him. DePree, an actor and filmmaker, argued a 2017 agreement with Rochdale Council gave him the option to buy the manor house after securing planning permission to restore and redevelop it. However, Judge David Hodge KC found the conditions required for ownership of the property to transfer had not been met. Despite its current state, Hopwood Hall was described as being in the top 10% of most important listed buildings in England, the court heard. DePree's plans included a wedding venue, hotel accommodation and visitor attractions aimed at bringing the hall back to life. However, Rochdale Council decided in 2022 not to transfer ownership of the hall to DePree and later locked him and a group of volunteers out of the site. The court heard the legal costs were about £150,000, with the council expected to seek an order requiring DePree to pay them. DePree got planning permission in 2022 to refurbish the hall as an event and hospitality venue A Rochdale Council spokesperson said the council was pleased with the judgment. "It's a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested in this process could have been better spent on the hall itself," they said. The spokesperson said more than £1.6m had been spent on the hall by the council and Historic England since 2017, and that investment in vital repairs would continue while its long-term future was "considered in due course". They added that, once restored and refurbished, the building would be "used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton's rich and varied heritage". DePree published a book about his campaign to restore the hall in 2022, titled Downton Shabby. Speaking after the ruling, he said he was "incredibly disappointed" and described it as "a sad day". He said he was discussing next steps with his legal team, adding: "We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved." "I am getting messages from around the world from people offering money and support," he added. title: Punish Man City this season, say other club chiefs
description: Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures tell BBC Sport.
body: Manchester City won eight trophies during the period for which they were investigated Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures have told BBC Sport. The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of its financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. They included artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" sponsorship deals. City have repeatedly denied guilt and signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by the end of this week. There have been fears that the process, which has taken three years since City were charged, could be drawn out for much longer. However, senior figures within football have told BBC Sport they see no reason why the case cannot be concluded by the end of this season. Speaking on condition of anonymity, one club official said: "It benefits everyone for this to be resolved as quickly as possible." When asked if they believed it would be, they said: "Instinctively yes, but it has to be done right. "We can all see what the risks are if it's not. But those risks have been there throughout the process, as they've won the league multiple times during it." Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches Another source said the process "should" be resolved by the end of the season, and they hoped any appeal would be "compressed". The final decision rests in the hands of the independent commission, with the Premier League board - and City - able to suggest a suitable punishment before the panel makes its decision. There is increasingly a desire to have the case resolved by the end of the season amid fears that allowing City to get to the end of the campaign without punishment could lead to uncertainty and farce, particularly if they were to win the title. One section of the Premier League regulations says an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end. Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season. However, Ferran Soriano, the club's chief executive, has suggested the case will run for a long time. Manchester City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court. The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible". Meanwhile, City club sponsor Etihad Airways said it is considering legal action against the Premier League. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements". It added: "The Premier League's public communication of the commission's findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings." Etihad, City's main sponsor since 2009, also said it was given no opportunity to engage in a process that now reflects "adversely on the airline". The statement added: "Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly. "The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision. "The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented. "Etihad will seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests." The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport. title: Infantino should have no place in future of football - Pinto
description: The computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City says Gianni Infantino "should have no place in the future of the game".
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 The computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City says Fifa president Gianni Infantino "should have no place in the future of the game". City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, though they continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal. The Premier League investigation was launched following information released into the public domain by the Football Leaks website in 2018, via German publication Der Spiegel, and following a separate investigation by European football's governing body Uefa. In a message on X, external, Rui Pinto, creator of Football Leaks, repeated allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid financial fair play sanctions from European football's governing body Uefa. According to a report by Der Spiegel, external, the clubs overvalued sponsorship deals to help meet FFP rules and, when facing sanctions over the matter, the allegations in the documents state Infantino helped arrange more lenient punishments for them in 2014. A PSG statement at the time said it "has always acted in full compliance with the laws and regulations enacted by sports institutions" and it "denies the allegations". "Since the introduction of Financial Fair Play, Paris St-Germain have been one of the most audited and scrutinised clubs in history," the club added. "Back in 2014, there was a man who was already aware of the irregularities involving Manchester City," 37-year-old Portuguese Pinto wrote on Wednesday. "The infamous Gianni Infantino, then Uefa general secretary, abused his authority, shared confidential documents and, in short, outmanoeuvred the investigatory chamber, doing everything in his power to ensure that both Manchester City and PSG would merely receive a fine, avoiding a deeper investigation that could have led to a Champions League ban. "All of these details were also revealed through Football Leaks. "Given his actions as Uefa general secretary and, more recently, as Fifa president, I can only say, in my humble opinion, that Gianni Infantino has become a cancer on football and should have no place in the future of the game." When the allegations first surfaced, Uefa stressed that it was within the remit of the general secretary to assist in such matters, adding: "This may include discussions, meetings, assistance to help find solutions, and other interactions to assist the [investigating body] in its work." Infantino similarly pointed to how his "job entails having discussions, having conversations, exchanging documents, drafts, ideas, whatever, on many, many, many, many, topics. "So if then this is being portrayed as something bad, I think there's not much I can do more than my job in an honest way, in a professional way and trying to defend the interests of football." BBC Sport has contacted Fifa following Pinto's latest statement. Infantino has come under increasing pressure following his now-shelved plans to sell stakes in the World Cup. European football's governing body Uefa accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, while the Swiss Football Association (SFV) is the latest association to withdraw its support for the Fifa president. "The decision follows a comprehensive reassessment of developments over the past few months," an SFV statement read. "From the SFV's perspective, various incidents raise fundamental questions regarding leadership, governance, transparency and decision-making processes within Fifa." Both Fifa and Uefa are based in Switzerland. Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. title: Respect and laughs as Fury and Joshua face off
description: After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchange pleasantries, trade jokes and even discuss going for a pint at a news conference in London.
body: Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right) are two-time heavyweight world champions After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed going for a pint at a news conference in London. The British heavyweight rivals will fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December. But for all the history between them, the launch felt more like two veterans in the closing stages of long, turbulent careers taking stock of how far they had both come. "He's been a role model and poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury, 38, said of Joshua. "I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans in the street." On Monday, there was still uncertainty over whether the fight would happen because of contractual disagreements surrounding the promotion. There had been plenty of reason to expect fireworks on Wednesday. Instead, Joshua, 36, spoke about the magnitude of the event. "It's breathtaking and I'm not saying that lightly," he said. "I'm really grateful for this opportunity and bringing it to Great Britain because I know people in pubs have had proper fights about who will win and family members have fallen out." The mood was perhaps best summed up at the face-off, when Joshua smiled and pretended to tickle Fury's stomach. Relive Fury & Joshua's jovial news conference Fury & Joshua in London for news conference as doubts ease Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right) have competed in a combined 21 world title fights There was something almost surreal about seeing Fury and Joshua finally sitting side by side after so many years in which their rivalry had existed mostly through interviews, social media and failed negotiations. Both had arrived hours earlier for one-to-one interviews. When the news conference began, master of ceremonies Michael Buffer introduced the pair as fireworks shot up from the front of the stage. They entered from opposite sides at the same time - Joshua relaxed and composed in a grey tracksuit and sunglasses, Fury in more flamboyant fashion in a vivid emerald-green suit covered in crown motifs over a white shirt. Alongside the world's media, a few hundred fans filled the balcony above and quickly made their allegiance known as "Oh Anthony Joshua" rang around the British Airways ARC. Joshua has been credited with pushing to keep the fight in Britain and, if Wednesday was any indication, can expect strong backing in Cardiff - even with the main event potentially starting about 02:00 GMT to suit American audiences. For two men whose names have been linked for so long, Fury and Joshua have spent remarkably little time together. But their famous sparring session in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur, soon became the topic of conversation. Fury suggested he had got the better of it, prompting one fan to shout: "Liar." Joshua smiled and said he could not remember. For those who believe the fight has come years too late, Fury had a simple response. "It's the icing on the cake of two great careers," he said. Moments later, he glanced back at the word "Finally" on the giant screen behind them. There were several moments of common ground. Fury nodded along as Joshua spoke about his Christian faith and, even when the pair traded insults, they rarely felt venomous. "This man here is carved in stone and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over," Fury said. "When I crack him on the jaw with a big right hand, he's going down." Joshua laughed and shouted back Fury's own catchphrase: "Get up." The fight has been reported as being for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight title, although current WBA heavyweight champion Murat Gassiev's team has lodged a formal objection over the proposed title arrangement. For a moment, it appeared the mood could turn when Joshua revealed he had received a call asking whether Fury's name could appear first in the promotion. "You've been crying behind the scenes to get out of this fight. I've checkmated you. You have to fight," Fury replied. "I've actually never won a world title here. Now it's on the line, we can become a three-time." That exchange came after several chaotic days in which the role of UFC and Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White had threatened to overshadow the fight. Netflix had presented White as part of the promotion alongside Turki Alalshikh's The Ring, despite Joshua promoter Eddie Hearn insisting his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role. But White did not attend Wednesday's launch. And when Alalshikh thanked the American from the stage, his name was met with jeers from sections of the crowd. Fury did momentarily take aim at Hearn, calling him a "sausage" - but even that did not last long. Within minutes, Fury was offering to go for a pint with the Matchroom boss - and extended the invitation to Joshua. "I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together," Fury said. "Win, lose or draw, let's bury the hatchet." "I don't know if I can trust you," Joshua replied, drawing laughter. The overriding mood was one of relief between two veterans, who were seemingly happy to let the fight settle what years of talk could not. title: The moment police catch drug dealer posing as food delivery driver
description: Watch the moment a drug dealer tries to evade police while posing as a fast food delivery courier.
body: This video can not be played This is the moment a drug dealer tried to evade police on foot while posing as a fast food delivery courier. Body-worn camera footage shows how Nahro Gharib, 25, ran from the scene as officers spotted him "making an exchange". South Wales Police said his bike was later found to be capable of reaching 59mph (95km/h), although the legal limit is 15.5mph. Gharib, of Cyncoed, Cardiff, was jailed for 20 months and disqualified from driving for 17 months at Newport Crown Court. He admitted supplying cannabis, possession with intent to supply cocaine and cannabis, possessing criminal property, namely cash, and use of a motor vehicle without insurance. title: Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after coach denies rift
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain why "in time", hours after head coach Jorge Jesus denied any rift with the player.
body: Jorge Jesus coached Cristiano Ronaldo at Saudi club Al-Nassr Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain the reasons why "in time". It comes after head coach Jorge Jesus earlier said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-times Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train. Ronaldo has said he considered retiring from international football after the World Cup in the summer but opted to continue as he chases down 1,000 career goals. He was included in Jesus' 25-man squad for the current international break and started the opening Nations League game against Wales. However, the Al-Nassr forward did not feature in Portugal's 2-1 win over Norway in Olso on Sunday and did not join his team-mates in going over to the visiting fans at the final whistle. Instead, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player headed to the changing rooms - prompting reports he was unhappy with the manager. Speaking to media before Portugal's Nations League match against Denmark on Thursday, Jesus said: "There was no incident whatsoever. "Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that." Jesus said he had told Ronaldo before the match he would not be starting, but might be brought on later in the game. "Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about," he added. Former Benfica manager Jesus also dismissed suggestions Ronaldo had refused to train on Tuesday, saying the 41-year-old instead had to do individual exercises for "mobility" and "strengthening" but would train as normal on Wednesday. However, Ronaldo did not join his team-mates on the pitch in Denmark with Portuguese media sharing a video of him leaving Parken stadium alongside two members of the backroom staff. And the player later took to Instagram to announce his departure. "After the press conference of the national team and following a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp," he wrote. "In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave." He added he wished his team-mates good luck in their forthcoming games. Goncalo Ramos scored the winner against Norway and Jesus had said the AC Milan striker would again be preferred to Ronaldo against Denmark. "If I need [Ronaldo], he'll come on. If I don't need him, he won't." How much money do clubs get for Nations League players? title: Impossible for England to find another Kane - Tuchel
description: England boss Thomas Tuchel says it will be impossible to find "another Harry Kane" as his free-scoring captain continues to break new ground.
body: Harry Kane is closing in on Peter Shilton's record of 125 caps for England England boss Thomas Tuchel says it will be impossible to find "another Harry Kane" as his free-scoring captain continues to break new ground. Kane scored a record-extending 87th goal for the Three Lions against the Czech Republic on Tuesday. And he is now just two appearances away from equalling Peter Shilton's mark of 125 international appearances as he hones in on becoming England's most capped player ever. However, while the 33-year-old Bayern Munich forward is in the form of his life, with his 73 goals for club and country last term putting him well into the conversation as a possible Ballon d'Or winner, he cannot go on forever and Tuchel admitted that there is no obvious successor. "You will not get another Harry Kane, first of all," Tuchel said. "He is the first one to push everyone and that is his mindset and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills. He is a complete package. "We look for different options and solutions. We finished the game with Jude [Bellingham] up front as a number nine. "There will be someone else, but it will not be Harry or a copy of Harry. We will find a solution when it comes to it but maybe not me. It might be another 10 years." Kane is one of the leading strikers of his generation, but finding a suitable back-up has been a long-standing problem for England. Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney utilised that role at the past two major tournaments but the Saudi Arabia-based pair are also in their thirties and were overlooked for the current batch of Nations League fixtures. While Dominic Calvert-Lewin is in the squad, he is also approaching his 30th birthday and Liam Delap is currently the only English centre forward under the age of 27 to have scored a Champions League goal. And that means Tuchel supplemented his striking options in Prague by deploying Real Madrid star Bellingham in a more advanced role than his normal midfield position after bringing him on for Kane. "I like him as a nine," Tuchel added. "Then he can contribute to both sides and overload the sides and doesn't affect so much of the balance. "We found a bit of a new role for him in the last match, as a central 10, so he can go to both sides and it is more of a 4-2-3-1 than a 4-3-3 to have Harry and Jude closer together and to give them a chance to overload both sides. We are working on that. "He is a natural goalscorer and he has the hunger to be on the scoreboard. He wants to be there and have the decisive action, so it makes not a huge difference if he plays as a nine or a 10." title: Dame Esther Rantzen: A presenter who campaigned for change
description: The veteran broadcaster's career spanned street interviews, national campaigns and emotional reunions.
body: This video can not be played Dame Esther Rantzen, known for her role presenting the BBC's That's Life! and for later establishing the Childline helpline, has died at the age of 86. Her children confirmed her death in a statement, saying: "We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably." "We hope the humour, ingenuity and audacity she brought to her work may continue to inspire you as it will do us." The veteran broadcaster had been diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in January 2023 and in the years that followed, was a prominent campaigner supporting assisted dying. title: 'I pulled the controls': Passenger tells Israeli PM how he helped stop attacker
description: The man says he "pulled the controls" of the plane after it plummeted during the attack.
body: This video can not be played A passenger on the diverted Flydubai flight has told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu how he and others helped stop the cockpit attack. The man, who was greeted by the prime minister at the Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, explained how he helped pin the alleged attacker to the ground and pull the plane's controls backwards to stop it nosediving. The plane was diverted to Saudi Arabia after plummeting 17,000ft in less than two minutes. Passengers have since safely landed in Tel Aviv after a replacement Flydubai plane transported them to their destination. title: How That's Life! gave Esther Rantzen a career-defining moment
description: Sir Nicholas Winton's story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988.
body: This video can not be played Esther Rantzen surprises Nicholas Winton on That's Life! Dame Esther Rantzen's commitment to charitable causes is something she will forever be remembered for. Along with founding Childline, a helpline for children, and The Silver Line, which supports older people struggling with loneliness, she also created a broadcasting legacy during her time on That's Life! She presented the hugely popular BBC One show from 1973 to 1994, helping transform it from a consumer rights programme to an issues-based series, drawing in huge audiences. One of her most memorable career moments came during one particular episode in 1988 - the footage of which has gone viral several times over in recent years. Dame Esther had been told the story of Nicholas Winton, the man who had organised the rescue of 669 children from Czechoslovakia, which was occupied in 1939 by Nazi forces. Sir Nicholas Winton in 2014 receiving the highest order of the Czech Republic, the White Lion. Sir Nicholas was able to rescue the mainly Jewish cohort of children after briefly visiting Prague. He was knighted in 2003 for his humanitarian work. Sir Nicholas, who was born to German-Jewish parents, made a list of the children that needed sponsorship and found homes for them to go to in Britain. He worked alongside activists and humanitarians , externalin Czechoslovakia to navigate complex political obstacles, such as getting children to Britain through the Netherlands, which had closed its borders to Jewish refugees. Sir Nicholas was ultimately successful due to a House of Commons ruling on allowing young refugees in the country, which had been passed a couple of months before his rescue mission began. With the help of his mother, he put photos of the children in British magazines such as Picture Post to help find them homes and organised for hostels to take in some refugees too. He managed to raise money to cover travel for the children and provide them with essentials when they reached British soil. His incredible work went largely unreported for nearly 50 years - until his wife found a scrapbook in their loft, which contained names of children he had rescued. It was given to Holocaust researchers, who helped track down some of the children he had helped. Sir Nicholas' story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988 and Dame Esther Rantzen told viewers about his story. Dame Esther Rantzen on the set of That's Life! in 1978 Speaking in February 2024, Dame Esther said when she first got in touch with Sir Nicholas, who she called Nicky, she "congratulated him on his extraordinary achievement". She told The Radio Times, external he had expressed some disappointment about his efforts, commenting that "not enough" people had been saved. "I was devastated that he felt he had failed. I wanted to prove to this extraordinary man that every life he had saved was precious," Dame Esther added. She invited him onto That's Life and during his first appearance, his scrapbook was shared with the audience, and two women he had saved as children - Vera Gissing and Lady Milena Grenfell-Baines - revealed their identities to him on TV. They were sitting either side of Sir Nicholas, who had no idea of the surprise - something Dame Esther recalled as "incredibly moving". Lady Milena is one of the most well-recognised Holocaust survivors in the UK. She left Prague with her younger sister Eva at the age of nine, travelling on a special train arranged by Winton. The two sisters were looked after by a Tameside family until their mother arrived the following year, having escaped via Norway. Gissing, who was rescued from Prague in 1939 at the age of 11, lost most of her family during the Holocaust and ended up settling in the UK after the war ended. "That was the only time in my career when I had to stop recording to wipe away my tears," Dame Esther also said. The production team at That's Life were then contacted by several viewers who had watched the show and realised their connection to Sir Nicholas. That gave the show's team an idea which would go on to become one of British television's most famous moments. "In our next episode, I asked all those who owed their lives to him to stand, and Nicky, whom we had seated on the front row, turned to see the whole ground floor of the Television Theatre on their feet," Dame Esther recalled. 1988: Holocaust hero Nicholas Winton on That's Life This is a TV moment many will remember and in subsequent years has been rediscovered by new audiences thanks to social media. Dame Esther said she watched the episode "many times" and "each time found myself deeply moved". She says she kept in contact with Sir Nicholas, meeting regularly until his death in 2015 at the age of 106. They would always have a connection due to the TV show, but Dame Esther said hearing the stories of the children he had saved also made her feel "immensely lucky" to have been a Jew born in England in the 1940s. Sir Nicholas' work has been the subject of a number of different films and documentaries, most recently the biopic One Life. Starring Sir Anthony Hopkins, the film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival and was released in the UK in January 2024. Dame Esther said it had been estimated "that 6, 000 people owe their very existence to Nicholas Winton". She added: "The Jewish children Nicky rescued were almost the only ones in Czechoslovakia to survive the Holocaust". And thanks to Dame Esther relaying his story to viewers on That's Life!, millions of people are now aware of the huge impact Sir Nicholas had. title: Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! presenter, Childline founder and campaigner for assisted dying
description: The star presented That's Life! for two decades and set up two national helplines, including Childline.
body: Dame Esther Rantzen, who has died at the age of 86, was best known for presenting the BBC TV programme That's Life! Over two decades, what started as a consumer programme with quirky asides became renowned for its high-profile campaigns, notably against child abuse. It resulted in Dame Esther setting up Childline, a national telephone helpline for children suffering abuse or neglect. She later became a renowned campaigner for older people and, in the last years of her life, for the legalisation of medically-assisted death. Dame Esther Rantzen, broadcaster, campaigner and charity founder, dies aged 86 How That's Life! gave Esther Rantzen a career-defining moment Esther Louise Rantzen was born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire on 22 June 1940. Her paternal ancestors were Polish Jews. Her father, Henry, who worked as a broadcast engineer for the BBC, had moved the family out of London to escape German bombing during World War Two. The family returned to London when the war ended. She later recalled she hated the grey streets of the capital after the semi-rural idyll in which she had spent her early childhood. After a spell at a private school, run by what she recalled was a sadistic headmistress, she went to the North London Collegiate School in Edgware, and then to Somerville College, Oxford, where she read English. Rantzen [centre] had an idyllic early childhood She became an enthusiastic member of the Oxford University Dramatic Society and of the Experimental Theatre Group. Rantzen then secured a job as a trainee studio manager with BBC Radio, before moving to television as a researcher on the satirical show BBC3, which had been created by Ned Sherrin. She met documentary maker Desmond Wilcox when she approached him in a BBC bar and asked him to give a talk to a local youth club. He asked her to dinner and offered her a job on Man Alive, the BBC's current affairs programme. The pair later began a relationship. The relationship caused huge tensions in her department, not least because Wilcox's wife Patsy, one of Rantzen's best friends, also worked at the BBC. By 1968, she was working on Braden's Week, a consumer programme fronted by Canadian presenter Bernard Braden. A decision to allow the researchers a short spot on air gave Rantzen her first on-screen TV experience, where she made a favourable impression on the producers. In 1972, Braden was sacked by the BBC after he appeared in a commercial for Stork margarine and his show was dropped. A year later, the programme was resurrected, given a new title, That's Life! and Rantzen was selected as the main presenter. Dame Esther made her first TV appearance on Braden's Week Braden was sanguine about Rantzen's promotion but his wife, TV presenter Barbara Kelly, was publicly contemptuous of the decision and accused Wilcox of being instrumental in her appointment. Launched in May 1973, That's Life! became an almost instant hit. Recorded just before transmission on Saturday nights, it was initially a consumer protection programme investigating viewers' complaints about shoddy service and faulty goods. Over the years it grew to include more quirky items. It initiated the Jobsworth award for over-zealous bureaucrats and council officials, and Heap of the Week, in which failing domestic appliances would be destroyed on screen in a variety of ingenious ways. Over the years, Rantzen was joined by a series of co-hosts, including Paul Heiney, Chris Searle and Bob Wellings, while the comedian Cyril Fletcher read his Odd Odes. The show quickly became something of an institution but her relationship with Wilcox was causing problems behind the scenes. Patsy Wilcox had reluctantly agreed to a divorce after Rantzen became pregnant, and Rantzen and Wilcox went on to marry in 1977. But there were accusations from some BBC staff that Wilcox, who was her boss as well as her husband, was furthering her career, pointing out that BBC rules forbade married couples working together. Wilcox resigned in 1980 and set up his own successful production company. That's Life! ran for 21 years Rantzen also found time to devise a new talent series, The Big Time, which launched the career of singer Sheena Easton. She became involved with the team behind the new ITV breakfast programme, TV-am, but dropped out before it went to air in 1983 so that she could remain at the BBC. By the 1980s, That's Life! had expanded its remit away from basic consumer issues to take on the role of campaigner. The appearance of Ben Hardwick, a child desperately in need of a liver transplant, launched a drive to raise the awareness of the need for organ donors. As a result, Ben received a new liver at the age of two, but died a year later. Other campaigns helped introduce the replacement of hard surfaces in children's playgrounds with softer material and a change in the law to enforce the wearing of children's seat belts in the rear of cars. Not everyone was happy with the new format and there were complaints that a serious, and sometimes emotionally draining sequence, was followed by a quirky item on, for example, rude-looking vegetables. The programme continued to maintain its high viewing figures after a move to Sunday nights, but the television landscape was changing. The BBC's show Watchdog and ITV's The Cook Report were bringing a much harder edge to consumer journalism. The death of Desmond Wilcox prompted Rantzen to launch a campaign to support older, lonely people The final That's Life! was broadcast on 19 June 1994 and featured a look back at both the highlights of the programme and Rantzen's own campaigning. Possibly the most important and lasting result of any That's Life! campaign was the setting up of Childline in 1986. It followed a number of incidents, featured on the programme, including one in which a toddler had starved to death, locked in a bedroom. Rantzen persuaded the BBC after the pr

title: Saracens boss Venter skips more media duties
description: Saracens director of rugby Brendan Venter misses a second pre-match media conference, as head coach Joe Shaw attends.
body: This video can not be played From director of rugby to 'wine consultant' Saracens head coach Joe Shaw has refused to say when, or if, director of rugby Brendan Venter will speak to the media again, despite the club facing fines for him not doing so. Venter was not at Wednesday's pre-match press conference for their forthcoming game with Sale after not attending Prem Rugby's pre-season launch day, or doing any media duties before, during or after the opening-weekend victory at Leicester. The Daily Telegraph reported on Tuesday that Venter had "resigned" as director of rugby and taken up a new role as "head of rugby culture and wine consultant", but this has not been confirmed by the club nor Prem Rugby. When asked if Venter would resume media duties, as part of his responsibilities as a director of rugby, Shaw said: "I'm just going to talk about the rugby. "I'll leave the club to talk about where we stand on all those kind of things." BBC Sport has contacted Saracens for comment. It is understood Sarries have already been fined £5,000 after Venter was not present at the Prem's pre-season launch day. It is also thought a change of job title would not preclude Venter from his contractual responsibilities. Saracens announced in January that Venter would be returning as director of rugby and have yet to publicly confirm any change to his day-to-day responsibilities. He succeeded Mark McCall, who stepped down at the end of last season after 15 years in the job. Olly Hartley faces another period on the sidelines Shaw confirmed that centre Olly Hartley broke his arm in Sunday's 40-38 win at Leicester. Hartley, who required full knee reconstruction after a serious injury sustained in a match against Gloucester in April 2024, came off 13 minutes into the match at Welford Road. Sarries were already 14-0 up but the next 13 minutes after Hartley's injury saw the hosts reduce the deficit to 14-12. "When you play and train with somebody, like they have been with Olly for so long, and then it's the first game of the season and someone gets properly hurt, breaks their arm, you're human beings, it affects you," Shaw said. "We managed to to shuffle things around really calmly, with good leadership from the people on the pitch, and it was really pleasing to get through that adversity." title: Teens who died in car that entered River Wear named
description: Jackson Duke, Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw died when the car they were in ended up in the River Wear.
body: Luke Etheridge, Zara Shaw and Jackson Duke (left to right) died when the car entered the River Wear Two teenage boys and a teenage girl who died when the car they were in ended up in the River Wear have been named by police. A black Audi A3 with four people inside came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and went in the water just before 13:30 BST on Tuesday, Northumbria Police said. The three who died have been named as Jackson Duke, 17, Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw, both 16. A 17-year-old boy who managed to reach safety has been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, the force said. Jackson and Luke were from Sunderland, while Zara was from Houghton-le-Spring, a town about seven miles (11km) from the city. All were students at Sunderland College. Ch Supt Scott Cowie said the investigation into the deaths was continuing Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said: "The last 24 hours have brought unimaginable agony and heartbreak for the loved ones of Luke, Jackson and Zara. "All three had their whole futures ahead of them and will be hugely missed. "We also recognise the impact that this tragedy has had upon the people of Sunderland and further afield, and know that you will continue to be there for one another." Police divers remain at the scene as investigations continue Earlier, a spokesperson for Sunderland College said they were "deeply saddened" by the deaths of three of their students. "This is a heartbreaking loss for our college community, and the wider city of Sunderland," a statement published on Facebook said. The empty black Audi A3 was recovered from the water on Wednesday Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service, the North East Ambulance Service and RNLI teams assisted with the rescue efforts on Tuesday. The car was recovered from the water earlier on Wednesday and no other vehicles are believed to have been involved. title: Six smugglers jailed for manslaughter over worst Channel small boats disaster
description: Thirty-one migrants died when their boat went down in November 2021. The trial found that the guilty men were part of two smuggling networks.
body: File photo from 2021 of a beach in northern France used by migrants to attempt the Channel crossing to England Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel. At the end of a four-week trial in Paris, the six were convicted of "involuntary homicide" and given prison terms of between six and 10 years. Seven others were given lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was found not guilty. The boat went down early in the morning on 24 November 2021 after sending distress calls to French and British coastguards. The dead, including a child of seven, were mainly Iraqi Kurds but also included Afghans, Egyptians and Iranian Kurds. Only two men survived. The charge sheet said the migrants had been put to sea from the French coast in a boat "that was of poor quality, uncertified, unsuitable for navigation at sea, overloaded, and without correct life jackets". The trial established that the guilty men were members of two separate networks – one of which was Iraqi Kurd, the other Afghan – that co-operated to organise the cross-channel journey and bring migrants to the meeting point. Unusually the court was attended at the start by several family members, who came to France from Iraqi Kurdistan and gave moving testimony about how the victims came to be on board the boat. Some of the victims (from left): Mohammed Hussein Mohammedie, Mhabad Ahmad Ali, Bilind Shakir Baker, Shakar Ali Pirot, Bryar Hamad Abdulrahman, and Hasti Rizghar Hussein Speaking after the verdict, their lawyer Matthieu Chirez said the decision "comes as a relief for all the civil plaintiffs because it confirms the penal responsibility of the traffickers". He said the trial had "humanised the families of victims". One family member, Zana Marmand Muhammed, told the court how his younger brother Twana had "wanted to go to England to find a job and because the geopolitical situation with us is dangerous. No-one in the family wanted him to leave, but we could not dissuade him." Nabi Mustafa Mina, the father of Zanyar who was 19 when he died, told of how he tried to dissuade his son from leaving. "I said I would help him to get married, I would give him my house, I would divide my salary in two. But no, he said he wanted a better life, that he would get by somehow. I ran out of arguments," he said. The family-members explained how they had paid a deposit at a bank in Iraqi Kurdistan and then followed their loved ones' progress through Turkey, Italy and then France. In one of the last messages from Twana, he posted a picture of himself at the Eiffel Tower. The court also heard a statement from one of the two survivors, Issa Omar, read out by his lawyer. Omar said that he "would have liked to appear before the judge but I do not have the strength. Since the wreck I have the impression that part of me disappeared beneath the waves." His lawyer Matthieu Chirez said that Omar had "clung to floating bodies, to a life-jacket. He survived by keeping his eyes open so as not to go to sleep, and swimming to keep his heart beating". Lawyer Matthieu Chirez (C) said the verdict had come as a relief to victims' families Police investigating the disaster used phone tracking to identify members of the two networks. The lesser figures were accused of sheltering migrants, transporting them across France to the so-called "jungle" camp outside Calais, and helping on the night of the departure. The alleged leader of the Iraqi Kurd network – named as Bashdar – was not a defendant in the trial. He is in custody in Iraq. His close aide – Harem Ahmed Abawaker – was given eight years in prison. The biggest sentence, of 10 years, went to Obaidullah Maroofkhel, who ran the Afghan network. He was tried in his absence along with one other defendant. Most of the 14 were Afghans or Iraqi Kurds. All but one of the defendants appeared in the trial as free men, so following the verdict the court issued six arrest warrants. A separate police investigation is under way into seven members of the French armed forces for allegedly failing to come to the help of the migrants on the night of the disaster. The seven were at the regional sea rescue centre or on board a navy ship, and are alleged to have ignored distress calls from the boat. A decision on whether to recommend them for trial will be taken in the coming months. The trial ended as France and the UK announced it was ending the so-called one-in one-out scheme under which the British government sent back irregular cross-Channel migrants to France, and in return accepted individuals with a likely prospect of being granted asylum. France had already signalled that the year-long programme, which has seen a little more than 1,000 migrants switch country, was not producing expected results in breaking the traffickers' business model. title: UK-France 'one in, one out' migrant scheme scrapped
description: Some 1,500 people have been removed to France since the scheme began just over a year ago.
body: The UK government has announced the "one in, one out" agreement with France to send back some migrants who cross the Channel has been scrapped. The pilot scheme allowed the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who were believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain. Only around 1,500 people have been removed to France since the scheme began just over a year ago. The BBC understands the government would have liked the scheme to continue, but felt it did not reach the desired scale. A Home Office spokesperson said "lessons learned" would be used to "accelerate efforts" to return small boat migrants with no right to remain. "The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the spokesperson said. "However, flights will continue over the coming weeks to swiftly remove small boat migrants from the UK, and we will use lessons learned from the pilot to accelerate efforts to return small boat migrants with no right to remain in the UK." The government would continue working with France to tackle small boat crossings, the spokesperson said, adding that "real progress" had been made with numbers "significantly down on last year". The French Interior Ministry told the BBC: "We are discussing with the British the terms of exit from the agreement." Between 1 January and 27 September 2026, a total of 19,135 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 28 September 2025 to 27 September 2026 carried an average of 67 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. Earlier this month, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood admitted the scheme had "not been without its challenges". "The numbers are still relatively small," she told MPs. "What has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system." However, she also said the UN and other agencies had reported that some migrants were not getting on small boats because they thought there was a chance they could be accepted under the "one in, one out" scheme. So far this year, 19,135 people have made the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 crossed in small boats. title: Lawyer jailed for supplying cocaine after getting 'too close' to drug dealing client
description: Ben Garvey passed messages between his drug dealer client and a drug runner before getting caught.
body: A judge told Ben Garvey that he had "let down the whole profession of solicitors" The criminal defence solicitor of a drug dealer has been jailed for three years and six months after he became involved in supplying cocaine. Ben Garvey, 38, encouraged his friends to purchase the class A drug over WhatsApp, and also passed messages between his client and a drug runner. Garvey, from Port Talbot, was told by a judge at Bristol Crown Court that his actions had been "a clear abuse" of his position, after he was found guilty of supplying cocaine and perverting the course of justice. His ex-client, Daniel Baker, 34, was jailed for three years and four months after pleading guilty to perverting the course of justice and admitting conspiracy to supply Class A drugs. Baker's drug runner, Jake Blackburn, 28, was jailed for four years and 10 months after being found guilty of perverting the course of justice, having previously pleaded guilty to being concerned in the supply of Class A drugs. Garvey was part of a WhatsApp group in which he encouraged and "egged on" friends to purchase cocaine Garvey had been a partner at David W Harris Solicitors & Co based in Swansea, Pontypridd, and Talbot Green, and had met Baker in 2021 after purchasing cocaine from him. The court heard he later represented Baker when he was arrested on suspicion of dealing drugs, and passed on messages between Baker and his drug runner Blackburn during his client's time in custody. Prosecutor Ray Tully KC said: "The police investigation into Mr Baker led them to realise Mr Baker was involved in a drugs operation in south Wales, where he comes from, and there was an Oxford angle. He was sourcing and supplying drugs in the Oxford area." Cocaine dealer Daniel Baker and his runner Jake Blackburn have also been jailed Tully said another message from Blackburn to Garvey asked for Baker's iCloud username and password, which he said was so Blackburn could "delete or wipe information online" and "take care of things after the boss had been nicked". "In the circumstances, the prosecution suggest the communication that took place is evidence they were all involved in relaying information to and from Mr Baker whilst he was in custody," Tully said. "We say that it's an attempt to preserve and protect the drugs operation and carry on business whilst the boss is incarcerated, and the communication would be designed to hamper and impede the investigation that has got under way that day." The judge told Garvey that he "got too close" to his client Daniel Baker As a result of messages discovered on Baker's phone, Garvey and Blackburn were arrested and their electronic devices were seized. Messages on Garvey's phone revealed he had been part of a WhatsApp group in which he encouraged and "egged on" friends to purchase cocaine. Images taken from the group included photos and videos of people using the drug. Garvey was found guilty of perverting the course of justice, being concerned in the supply of Class A and C drugs, and encouraging or assisting in the commission of an offence. Judge Cullum told Garvey while he had previously been "a hardworking and qualified solicitor" he had "found kudos by being around high status criminals". The judge said he had "let down the whole profession of solicitors whose professionalism and diligence the criminal justice system depends on daily". "It is a sad day for you today to be sentenced in a crown court," he said. "You got too close to your client."
