title: Michael Sheen campaign on toxic waste sites wins Senedd backing
description: All parties urge Welsh and UK ministers to ensure polluters pay to clean up contaminated land.
body: Michael Sheen investigated Wales' toxic legacy in a BBC iPlayer documentary Member of the Senedd from all parties have urged Welsh ministers to work with the UK government to make sure polluters pay for cleaning up contaminated land. A motion introduced by Plaid Cymru MS Niamh Salkeld, backed across party lines, also calls for a UK fund to investigate and remediate sites where costs cannot be recovered, and for a framework to test affected land. The calls come after a BBC documentary by Michael Sheen examined claims toxic waste poisoned people at 14 sites in Wales and England. A Welsh government minister promised a plan to "progressively restore post-industrial land" and protect communities from "potential risks". Earlier this month, Sheen went to Westminster to urge MPs to support a testing programme. What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales. In the Senedd on Thursday, one member after another recounted in detail the history of sites in their area that they were worried about. Salkeld, who represents the constituency of Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, said her motion was about "making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly". "It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land," she said. "It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest. "It's about giving local authorities the support that they need, and it's about making sure that where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right. "The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks, all the costs." What he told me made my blood run cold - Michael Sheen investigates Wales' toxic legacy Toxic waste sites exposed in Michael Sheen documentary are 'tip of the iceberg' A number of speakers highlighted the results of a Freedom of Information inquiry by the environmental campaign group Friends of the Earth, external, indicating there were potentially over 45,000 contaminated land sites in Wales, with only 82 sites being designated as contaminated. Reform MS Andrew Griffin said communities across Wales living near sites that are potentially unsafe "deserve answers". "They deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through. "As their representatives, the least we can do is to make sure their questions are heard and keep asking them until they get a proper answer." Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates highlighted a combined pledge of more than £240m from the previous Welsh government, led by his party, and Labour ministers at Westminster for coal tip remediation. He said this demonstrated "that all levels of government need to act fast and need to act together in partnership" to tackle this pollution. "Councils, citizens and communities cannot afford the cost of remediation, nor can they afford to wait any longer for action." He called on Plaid Cymru ministers to "stand up for the people of Wales by taking urgent action where it can now". Niamh Salkeld said a "clearer national picture of contaminated land" is needed Conservative Janet Finch-Saunders said local communities "should be able to understand where these sites are located, what risks have been identified, what action is being taken, and whether that action is satisfactory". "Regular inspections and up-to-date public registers would help," she said. "We must ensure that lessons are learned from previous incidents where contamination occurs, the response should be timely, coordinated, and proportionate, with clear responsibility for investigating the source. "This is not simply about dealing with contamination after it has occurred. It is about prevention, enforcement, and accountability." Rural Resilience and Sustainability Minister Llyr Gruffydd promised the Welsh government was "absolutely committed to developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land and to protect communities from those potential risks that come with that legacy". He said he had heard the "calls for action", pledging he would "ensure that former industrial land is made safe". "I will protect public health and deliver long-overdue environmental justice for the communities that have been most affected by this," he added. The motion was passed with no objections. title: Bayeux Tapestry tour added for blind people after legal threat
description: The British Museum will offer an audio-described Bayeux Tapestry tour after a blind man's legal threat.
body: The tapestry is on loan at the British Museum until July The British Museum says it will provide an audio-described tour of the Bayeux Tapestry after a blind man threatened legal action over a lack of access for visually impaired visitors. Dr Yusuf Ali Osman, from Croydon, says the museum breached the Equality Act by not offering such tours of the exhibition. His lawyers, Leigh Day, sent the museum a pre-action letter on 24 September. On Wednesday, the central London museum said an in-person audio-described tour would be held during the exhibition's run. It said it was also exploring adding an audio-described tour to the exhibition's app. Osman, who has no sight in either eye, contacted the museum in July to ask whether audio-described tours would be available, according to Leigh Day. The law firm said the museum told him self-guided visits would be prioritised over tours and events. The museum said this was because limits on how many hours of light the tapestry can be exposed to each week restricted visitor numbers. Osman is seeking damages and a declaration that he was discriminated against. He also wants an order requiring the museum to change its policies and give relevant staff disability awareness training. "I hope that this legal action will help make sure that blind and partially sighted people are properly considered when major exhibitions are planned, so that we can enjoy and engage with our national cultural institutions on a more equal footing," he said. His solicitor, Kate Egerton, said: "The Equality Act places obligations on service providers to anticipate the needs of disabled people and take reasonable steps to avoid substantial disadvantage. "Our client is asking for the same opportunity as sighted visitors to experience this exhibition." A British Museum spokesperson said the museum was "committed to making the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition as accessible as possible" and had worked with specialist access consultants. "Provisions include a sensory map to help visitors prepare for their visit, as well as dedicated tours during the exhibition run which will include an in-person audio-described tour," the spokesperson said. "We are also exploring including a separate audio-described tour as part of the exhibition's app-based audio guide." The 70m (230ft) embroidery, which depicts the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of 1066, is on loan from France and is on display at the museum until 11 July 2027. title: We fear for our lives after being told our abusive exes will be freed from jail early
description: Three victims of domestic abuse tell the BBC why they feel let down by the early prisoner release scheme.
body: Claire Milne said she was "scared" her ex-husband "will come after me" Three women who have been told their abusive ex-partners will be released early from jail as part of controversial plans to free up prison space have said they fear for their safety. Around 700 offenders will leave prison in England and Wales on Thursday under the government's early prisoner release plan - with a further 3,800 scheduled for release over the next year. Ahead of the releases, victims have been sent letters informing them that their attackers will be let out early. Claire Milne's ex-husband, Robert Dales, was convicted in March this year of coercive control and possessing offensive weapons, including samurai and ninja swords. He was sentenced to three years in prison. "There was physical violence," said Milne. "There were threats to kill, there was punching of doors, punching of walls. I trod on egg shells throughout the entire relationship and it was almost like I had to coach myself into what to say just to ensure there wouldn't be an escalation." The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) recently told her Dales, 36, would be released early. "I am scared that he will come after me. I don't want to die," she said. "I am not a silly woman - I know that I've been in a very high-risk domestic abuse relationship and I know what he's capable of because I lived it." She said she was "incredibly angry" with the government, who were "not listening to victims". Extract from a letter sent by the MoJ It comes as prison staff have told the BBC they are increasingly having to put inmates in cells that are unsuitable because of the lack of space. They argue there is no choice but to release more prisoners as room is urgently needed. Prisons across England and Wales are at 98% capacity, with the latest government figures showing there are just 1,134 spaces remaining in the adult male prison estate. The lowest figure of vacant beds this year. Under the new scheme, inmates serving sentences of up to 19 months will be released after completing a third of their jail term. Most will have expected to spend 40% of their sentence behind bars - with the remainder served in the community. The MoJ said that while domestic abuse had a "profound and lasting" impact on victims, the government was committed to keeping the most dangerous prisoners behind bars. It said offenders jailed for rape, child sex abuse offences and manslaughter would stay in prison, but going further than that would risk the prison system collapsing. An MoJ spokesperson said the government was investing £1bn in support services, including placing domestic abuse specialists in 999 call centres. In April, former primary school teacher Christopher Haynes was sentenced to 21 months in prison after admitting to coercive control against his now ex-wife, who has also been notified of his early release. Christopher Haynes was sentenced to 21 months after admitting to coercive control against his ex-wife. He is due for early release Karen Haynes told the BBC she was distraught and said it was "a punch in the gut". "We have fought so hard and we have had to use every inch of the system to get justice," she continued. "I just find it devastating that somebody [who] can admit all of that can be released after only doing seven months of a custodial sentence." She has been told her ex-husband will now be released in November. "He always made Christmas so hard," said Karen. "We were constantly scared, we wanted one Christmas without him and without us being frightened he will turn up - but it looks like we won't even get that now." Another victim, Alice - not her real name - was subjected to domestic abuse. Her perpetrator is due to be released later this month. She has asked that we do not name her or her ex-partner because she is frightened of what he might do. "I am terrified," she said. "I had only just started to feel safe and to process what I had gone through." She said she felt like "the rug had been pulled out from underneath me". From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months. Inmates will be released in nine tranches until June next year. Those serving longer sentences - including more dangerous criminals - will not become eligible for the scheme until next year. They had previously expected to spend two thirds of their sentence behind bars, but instead will complete half of their term in prison before spending the rest of their punishment in the community on licence. Dame Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, called the scheme "shameful" and said she's had "no assurance that the danger perpetrators pose has been properly considered and assessed with meaningful input from victims". "Ultimately, we cannot ignore the fact that the early release scheme has caused untold damage to victims' confidence in the justice system," Dame Nicole added. She said Prime Minister Andy Burnham "must take urgent steps to address this" and called on the probation service to be given "the resources it needs to safely manage more offenders in the community". She also called for additional funding for domestic abuse services to support victims. A recent report raised serious concerns about electronic tagging, which can be used to monitor offenders' movements in the community. It found almost half of tags were not fitted on time. Alice told the BBC she had been looking to buy a doorbell with a camera fitted to help make her feel safer, but said she cannot afford one. "I don't feel prepared in the slightest and I don't feel safe," she added. "I think the early release scheme is a joke to victims and survivors, who spent years preparing for trial, going through evidence and re-traumatising themselves to go to court, just for the perpetrator of their crimes to be released after just 33% of their sentence

title: Singer Lola Young says vaping has made breathing feel like a 'chore'
description: The Messy singer says her lungs feel "battery powered" due to the effects of vaping.
body: Lola Young returned to the stage earlier this year after taking time off for her health Singer Lola Young has said her breathing feels like a "chore" due to the effects of vaping. In a TikTok video,, external the Grammy winner told her followers her lungs feel "battery powered". The 25-year-old has previously acknowledged in videos she "should quit", but suggested in her latest post that is unlikely to happen any time soon. Vocal coach Lizzii Hills has told BBC Newsbeat vaping is "not advised" for artists and that difficulty breathing can affect a singer's voice and performance. "Somebody once said to me, 'Lola there will be a day when you wake up, you'll be 25 or 26, from a deep sleep, and you'll start to feel the effects of vaping'," the Messy singer said in her post. "You know what I said? I said 'nah' and rolled my eyes. "But let me tell you something, the day has come." Last month, The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) linked vaping to higher rates of breathing problems after reviewing more than 80 studies. The review also found an association with wheezing, coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms. Describing her symptoms, Young said: "My lungs feel like they're battery powered, like they're just one big battery. "Breathing feels like a chore, it feels like hard work, it feels like I should be paid for breathing. It feels like there will be no tomorrow." The NHS says vaping is less harmful than smoking, external, but notes there are still risks - many of which are still not known. The government is introducing measures to make vapes less attractive, including a ban on single-use vapes, introduced last year. And from Thursday a new tax will be applied to e-cigarette liquid, with an additional £2.20 added per 10ml. Lola Young won a Grammy for her hit single Messy earlier this year Hills, who helps artists with their vocals, says vaping can have an impact on an artist's voice and struggling to breathe can risk straining your voice. "Vaping may not affect the voice box just itself, it affects the lungs, the airways, the throat - it's all respiratory, it's all connected. So doing that can affect your vocal technique," she says. "Breathing is really important. Singing requires controlled inhalation and sustained, efficient exhalation. "You end up trying harder, putting in more effort for the same results you were getting beforehand." She adds that when artists struggle with their voice, it can have significant psychological impacts on them too. "They can feel like they've lost themselves," she says. "It can become quite a big deal emotionally." Overall, she wouldn't recommend vaping to her clients. "As a performer, as an artist, you want to stay in the best health you can for your voice to work at its best. "We all know it's not the healthy choice and if you can avoid it - absolutely." Young returned to the spotlight earlier this year following a five-month hiatus after she collapsed on stage. She has been open in the past about her struggles with her health and addiction, previously telling The Guardian, external about dealing with cocaine dependency. She has also struggled with her mental health and was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and ADHD when she was a teenager. BBC Newsbeat has contacted Young's representatives for comment. title: Residents near RAF Fairford left 'like sitting ducks'
description: Villagers living near the base say a lack of communication in the days before and after the incident has left them feeling unsafe.
body: Counter Terrorism Policing have been investigating the incident at RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday Residents living near RAF Fairford say they have been "left feeling like sitting ducks" at the centre of major counter-terrorism probe. Five men were arrested on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act after three vans were spotted near the Gloucestershire base, which the US military operates. As 85 homes were evacuated in the middle of the night, one couple said their child had been left traumatised after witnessing armed police point a gun at their father. The BBC has approached Counter Terrorism Policing for comment. However, an anonymous resident from Whelford said she "could not fault" the quick response of UK authorities, describing officers as "calm, thorough and precise". Police said petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans found near the base Gloucestershire Constabulary said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards the military airbase at 00:45 BST on Sunday. A 400m (1,312ft) cordon was established and a bomb disposal team was deployed. The government believes Iran played a part in the RAF Fairford incident which resulted in five men, all UK nationals in their early 20s from London, being arrested and then bailed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said. Counter Terrorism Policing revealed on Tuesday a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices had been found during searches. An army bomb disposal robot was deployed to inspect the three suspicious white vans near RAF Fairford The Whelford resident said she had noticed an "uneasiness in the air" in the the days leading up to the incident, alongside extra concrete barricades around the airbase. "It seems as if they were absolutely aware of something, but no information was passed on to locals until it was in full swing," she said. "We were left feeling like sitting ducks in whatever operation was unfolding. "Regardless of if this was a dummy run, staged, a real threat or something entirely different - the lack of correspondence and care towards locals from a huge military base right next door is what feels most concerning to me." However, she praised the response of local authorities as "incredible", adding "they have been very warm, caring and efficient in any interaction so far". A couple allege two armed police officers pointed guns at them during the evacuation A couple, who asked not to be named, claims Whelford villagers were warned to stay home on Saturday night - hours before the alarm was first raised by a farmer. The pair were evacuated from their home the following morning, after the vans were found abandoned at the end of their driveway. But when the husband stepped outside, he said he was confronted by armed police. "I was trying to get my wallet out to say, 'look I'm a resident here'," he said. "Then one of them got out of the vehicle and put a gun on me, in my direction. "Then the other officer also got out, put a gun on me, and said 'Who's asked you to leave?'." The couple said they and and their terrified child were briefly trapped inside their home before managing to escape through a neighbour's property. UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says Timeline of RAF Fairford incident and the investigation so far One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself After being allowed to return home, the pair saw the van doors had been "blown off" and their contents emptied, with water butts and oil drums strewn on the ground. "All of a sudden, you see on the news the five suspected terrorists have been released," the husband said. "You're thinking, 'Is this for real?'. "We've all been panicking for the best part of a day and a bit. Are our homes going to get blown up? Could we have been blown up?" The family say they are "angry" over an absence of communication from authorities in the days leading up to the incident, alongside the lack of reassurance afterwards. Five British nationals who were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences have been released on bail Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth, of Gloucestershire Constabulary, explained the force was limited in what information it could share with residents. "Some of that information won't be forthcoming while there is a live investigation, and it is really important for everyone in that area to understand that," she said. Blyth assured multiple information points would be set up in the area over the coming days to offer ongoing reassurance and address concerns. "There is a much stronger visibility around the communities affected by this major incident," she added. Residents say they had noticed increased security measures in the days prior to the incident But in Marston Meysey, a village located immediately south-west of the airbase, across the border in Wiltshire, residents say they would like to see equal treatment from Wiltshire Police. Local resident Gerry, who said he was speaking "on behalf of Marston Meysey parish meeting, we've got a little working group for airbase issues," explained: "We don't really see a lot of activity for security protection from Wiltshire Police, but we see quite a lot from the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and Gloucestershire Police. "We wish there was a bit more information so we could put this to bed, but there's very little. We would welcome regular updates that affect us." Wiltshire Police neighbourhood Insp Lawrence Copeland acknowledged the concerns the recent events had caused to a "small, tight-knit community". "Our neighbourhood teams conduct regular patrols in the village and you may notice an enhanced presence over the coming days," he said. "We welcome being approached and we are available to speak to anyone with questions or concerns." Counter Terrorism Policing confirmed the cordon, which was in place near the airbase, had been

title: Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches
description: The prime minister compares the allegations against Man City to the plight of his own club Everton.
body: Erling Haaland has been Manchester City's star striker in recent seasons Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches. The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester. An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal. The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal. It comes as the Independent Football Regulator – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues". The regulator suggested it would be exploring options – including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club – once the disciplinary process was completed. Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m. The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade". The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty. The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period. Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years. Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is." Manchester City's owners have helped develop a huge area around the Etihad Stadium Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester until June, added: "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city". He said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners when he was mayor would stand up to scrutiny. Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions. Burnham was speaking to the BBC from Hill Dickinson Stadium, the home of Everton, the team he supports. Everton had their own run in with Premier League financial rules when they were charged and deducted 10 points for more minor breaches in November 2023, reduced to six on appeal. Burnham said: "Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation because I still hold the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process." Drawing a comparison between that and City's current predicament, he added: "I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and with hindsight I think more people would say that wasn't fair, the way that was handled. "So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister." It is "frustrating when people rush to judgement", Burnham said. He accepted there was "a lot at stake" for City fans, the club and Manchester itself. But he added it would be wrong for him to intervene. City have said in a statement they are "both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission" and maintained their innocence of all the accusations made. Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? title: UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, PM says
description: The prime minister's comments come days after the suspects were released on the 'strictest possible bail conditions'.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'Strong indications' Iran played a part in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says The government believes that Iran played a part in the RAF Fairford incident which resulted in five men being arrested and then bailed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said. "There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," he told the BBC. He did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. Burnham's comments come after it emerged that one of the five men had dialled 999 himself before the group were arrested. Asked why the suspects had been released on bail - a decision which has been openly questioned by President Donald Trump - the prime minister insisted the men were subject to the "strictest possible bail conditions" and added that UK authorities "have this under the strongest grip and closest control". Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump said: "I will tell you, I would have said, 'don't let them have bail'. I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that." But Burnham said: "I think people need to understand that when it says released - that isn't as people might think. It's obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions. "The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that." Burnham's comments come after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that the incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor". Police said petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans found near the base In an interview with Fox News on Monday, Rubio said "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally". Burnham said that the government had been "talking to our counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done", and that he had "complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this". "We will say more in due course but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part," he told the BBC. "Of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," Burnham added. Timeline of RAF Fairford incident and the investigation so far Watch: RAF Fairford suspects are bailed, what happens now? What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe The five men in question were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base. They are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete. The men were released on bail in what police described as an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy". Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans. The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades. In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". However, the Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the latest incident. title: Passengers describe stabbing on Israel-bound plane
description: Passengers on the Flydubai flight bound for Israel filmed the moments following the stabbing.
body: This video can not be played A pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight stabbed another pilot and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The plane was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes, before being diverted to Saudi Arabia. Eyewitnesses inside the plane described the moment the incident happened, with one man calling for help in a video shared on social media. Passengers describe stabbing on Israel-bound plane. title: Execution of US murderer Christa Pike halted an hour before it was due to happen
description: Pike was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
body: If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike would be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years The execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike has been halted an hour before it was due to happen. Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. In their ruling on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court said they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case. It is unclear how long the pause will last. This latest ruling comes after the Supreme Court denied a reprieve and the Tennessee governor declined to grant Pike's request for clemency earlier this week. Her lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that Pike had lied about being sexually abused as a child. But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the State said it does not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape. Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected. The appeal that led to Wednesday's stay is different from that made to the Supreme Court, which refused to hear Pike's appeal. It came from her challenge to Tennessee's lethal injection method, which Pike's lawyers said could cause suffering beyond what is needed to carry out the death sentence - something the Constitution does not allow. The lawyers argued that Tennessee's procedures had denied Pike a fair chance to prove this. "We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue," Tennessee's Attorney General said in a statement. "It is common in capital cases for the defence to raise last minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the Supreme Court of the United States to lift the stay." Colleen Slemmer was 19 when she was murdered in 1995 She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself. She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull. Her attorneys have argued that "an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain" and that Pike was too young at the time of the murder to be sentenced to death for it. At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections. title: Timeline of RAF Fairford incident and the investigation so far
description: From a late-night call about suspicious vehicles, to five men being arrested and then bailed - here is how the incident has unfolded.
body: A heavy police presence was seen near the base after a major incident was declared The public is slowly getting more information about what happened near the RAF Fairford airbase at the weekend - but many questions remain unanswered. We know that two early-morning calls were made to police about suspicious vehicles, and that five men, all British nationals in their 20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism offences. We also know they were later released on bail, and the BBC understands that one of the men was the first 999 caller. Here is what we know about how the incident unfolded, and what has happened in the days since. We now know that in the days leading up to the incident, security was increased around RAF Fairford, one of the UK's most important military sites, which is used by the US Air Force. There were also reports of heightened police activity around the base on Saturday evening, hours before three suspicious vehicles were reported to police. Gloucestershire police say they received a call just after midnight on Sunday 27 September about "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be travelling towards RAF Fairford. The BBC now understands that one of the five men who was later arrested and then bailed had made the call himself. Nearly an hour later, a farmer living close to the base called 999 after seeing three vans parked in a "weird formation". There was "a large group of hooded and masked men" near the vans who started to "panic" when they saw her, she told Radio 4's Today programme. The woman, who has remained anonymous, said she initially tried to contact the Ministry of Defence police at RAF Fairford, but no one picked up, so she dialled 999. "Within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police," she said. Shortly afterwards - although the exact time is unknown - Gloucestershire Constabulary arrested five men in the Whelford area, a village right next to the base. They were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. A grainy image purporting to show the moment of arrest shows five men sitting on the ground, shirtless and in handcuffs under guard by police officers. The BBC has been unable to verify the original source, but BBC Verify has geolocated the image and confirmed it appeared to be authentic. An image sent to the BBC appears to show the five men under arrest After sunrise, police declared a major incident in Whelford, external and set up a 400m (1,312ft) cordon around the three vehicles. The Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit was brought in to examine them, and aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching some white vans. About 85 households in Whelford were evacuated to a local leisure centre. Some residents said they had been "shaken by the incident" but that "community spirit and local support has been exceptional". This video can not be played Aerial footage shows wheeled robot near white vans By Sunday afternoon, Counter Terrorism Policing had confirmed it was leading the investigation. In a statement, it said the five men had been further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. The investigation was still in its early stages, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said, and the public was asked "to follow official channels for updates" and not to speculate. At about 16:00 BST, US President Donald Trump told reporters the arrest of the five suspects was "fantastic" and "an amazing job". "We had them under investigation. They were looking to ‌do big ⁠damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great... We had them under view for a long time, and we got them." The US is connected to this incident because its air force operates RAF Fairford, and has used the base to carry out strikes against Iran. How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail? At about noon on Monday, counter-terror police released more information on the five men, external who had been arrested - they were all from London and aged between 23-25. In a statement, Counter Terrorism Policing said they were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE) and that a custody extension has been secured. A cordon remained in place in Whelford. Within hours, however, counter-terror police announced that all five men would be released on police bail after "extensive interviews and enquiries". Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor stressed that the men were subject to "stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others." "They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said. Speaking from the White House, Trump questioned the decision, saying he was "surprised that they released them", adding: "I wouldn't have done that." Also on Monday afternoon, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts". Taylor defends the decision, saying it was "grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers". Later on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told told Fox News that the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor", but did not provide evidence or further details. Counter-terror police gave another update on Tuesday evening, saying properties in London had been searched as part of the investigation. No further details were given. The three vehicles had also undergone an "extensive examination" with the support of military and forensic experts, Assistant Commissioner Taylor said. The Counter Terrorism Policing boss said that no improvised explosive devices were found in the vans, but a "quantity of petrol" was recovered. Three days on, the BBC has learned that one of the men who had been arrested had made the first 999 call. It remains unclear why the man called police, or what he told them. title: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians, medic tells the BBC
description: The deadly fighting has also spread to neighbouring regions, stranding tourists in Lalibela.
body: Tanks and armoured vehicles were filmed passing through Alamata after days of clashes At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC. It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets. Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war. Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site. "We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region. He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians. Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday. The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters. Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa. There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it denies. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut. The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting. Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region. TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports. Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray. The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes. Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders. Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said. Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure. A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting. "All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe. "Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated." The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash. He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday. "The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said. When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained. But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road. Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said. Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families. The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV. While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout. The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region. Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted. "I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray. "It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service. "Many Tigrayans are now in trouble." title: BBC commentator thanks Cardiff City legend for saving him after heart attack scare
description: Rob Phillips started experiencing severe chest pains after commentating on the Cardiff City game.
body: Nathan Blake and Rob Phillips commentate on matches and host a football podcast together A football commentator has thanked Nathan Blake for saving him when he had a suspected heart attack after a game. Rob Phillips had just finished covering Cardiff City's last-gasp defeat to Bolton earlier this month, when he started experiencing severe chest pains. He intended to drive home to south Wales from the Greater Manchester town, but club legend Blake stepped in and said he wasn't going anywhere, seeing that he had lost all his colour. Veteran commentator Phillips was still laughing and joking when he was taken to see the Bolton club doctor, who casually told him: "I think you're having a heart attack." Blake, who played 131 times for City as well as winning 29 Wales caps, credited his actions to his mum's nurse training. The 54-year-old, who also played for clubs including Sheffield United, Bolton Wanderers, Blackburn Rovers and Wolves, said: "She always used to say to me 'if someone loses colour like that call an ambulance'." It had been business as usual for Phillips alongside him in the commentary box, as Cardiff lost "having played really well", he told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast. Thierry Gale had scored a 90th-minute header at the Toughsheet Community Stadium in the Championship match, and after completing the post-match interviews, Phillips said he started "having severe chest pains" as he got back to the press box. He added: "I said to Nath 'I'll be fine now', but he told me I'd lost all my colour." Phillips said he was still laughing and joking around when he was taken to see the Bolton club doctor, adding: "He casually said to me 'Rob, I can't be sure, but I think you're having a heart attack'." Within an hour he was on an operating table with a pipe up his arm, as doctors tried to unblock his artery. The pair have worked together since Blake retired from his playing career Phillips praised the Bolton club doctor David Humphreys, saying he "can't thank him enough". "The moral of the tale is if you're going to have a heart problem like I had, have it in a football club, because they've got people on hand who know what to do," he joked. Phillips and his partner were planning to attend the Wales Nations League match against Portugal which would have been his first as a fan in "40-odd years". But he instead had to settle for a seat on the sofa as the country slumped to a defeat in Lisbon. Phillips said he was "really fortunate" to be so well looked after following the incident. "My family have been great. Elin, my partner, has been magnificent as well," he added. The health scare happened at the Toughsheet Community Stadium in Bolton Speaking on the Rob and Blakey's Commentary Box podcast, Phillips thanked his co-commentator for his help that day. "It's alright mate that's what friends are for," Blake replied. Phillips thanked his "bro", saying without him, he "might not even be here". The NHS, external said you should call 999 if you have any symptoms including chest pain, shortness of breath or a feeling of indigestion. They also advised people to look for pale, blue or grey skin which may be easier to see on the palms of the person's hands. title: Djokovic wins first match since Wimbledon in China
description: Novak Djokovic beats Nuno Borges at the China Open to secure his first win since reaching the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.
body: Novak Djokovic has won six titles at the China Open between 2009 and 2015 Novak Djokovic maintained his remarkable unbeaten record at the China Open as he beat Nuno Borges to secure his first win since reaching the Wimbledon semi-finals in July. The 39-year-old former world number one struggled in the second set but came through to win 6-3 7-6 (7-2) for his 30th consecutive victory in Beijing, albeit in his first appearance at the event since 2015. Djokovic revealed in August that he has been dealing with an underlying health condition that causes particular issues in hot, humid conditions for "the past couple of years" and was far from his best against Portuguese Borges. During the second set he used his racquet to help stretch his back between games and needed a medical timeout to receive treatment to his right shoulder. But despite that Djokovic battled to victory in one hour and 50 minutes to set up a second-round match against wildcard Bu Yunchaokete of China. Playing in the tournament for the first time in 11 years, the Serb, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, is bidding to win the China Open for a record-extending seventh time. Meanwhile, Great Britain's Katie Boulter is through to the second round in the women's draw with a straight-set victory over Mai Hontama of Japan. Boulter, 30, claimed a 6-3 6-4 win and will now face Czech seventh seed Karolina Muchova in the next round. title: Grooming gangs inquiry expanded to Birmingham and Wales
description: Targeted investigations will be carried out as part of a national inquiry into child sexual abuse.
body: The national inquiry involves a series of targeted, local investigations child sexual abuse by grooming gangs A national inquiry into child sexual abuse by grooming gangs has announced targeted investigations will take place in Birmingham and Wales. The inquiry said the probes would "examine the sexual abuse and exploitation of children by grooming gangs and the response of organisations responsible for protecting children" in both areas. Oldham in Greater Manchester, Bradford and Keighley in West Yorkshire and London were announced as the first locations for local investigations earlier this year. It is unclear whether further locations will be selected. Some survivors have expressed frustration that their area has not yet been included and said they were concerned about expanding the inquiry's scope. Fiona Goddard said there was clearly evidence from Birmingham and Wales "that need to be properly heard" and welcomed their inclusion, but told the BBC the scale of the inquiry "must not come at the expense of the depth of investigation". She said this was especially concerning given "we are already almost a year into the inquiry with relatively little progress". Carly, not her real name, was 12 years old when she was first groomed in Huddersfield in 2004. She said she could not understand "how an investigation covering an area as enormous and complex as Wales can be described as a deep dive". "How are survivors in Huddersfield supposed to have confidence that our experiences will not simply be absorbed into a much bigger national picture and effectively watered down?" The Statutory Independent Inquiry into Grooming Gangs in England and Wales was announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in June 2025 and started work in April. Chaired by former children's commissioner Baroness Anne Longfield, it has the power to compel individuals and institutions to explain what they "did or did not do to protect children from being sexually abused", and will look at the nature and scale of abuse in each area. It faced turbulence prior to launching when abuse survivors called on former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips to quit. The inquiry has previously said areas are chosen for investigation based on criteria including how victims and survivors were treated when they came forward, and whether opportunities to prevent harm were missed. It said its decision to conduct an investigation in Birmingham reflected a combination of factors "including victim and survivor experience, indications of prevalence, harm and risk, and public concern". Panel member Zoë Billingham said: "We will look carefully at what organisations knew, how decisions were made, how agencies worked together, and why opportunities to protect children were missed". The investigation in Wales will also examine the operation of devolved arrangements and cross-border working between organisations in Wales and England. Baroness Longfield said victims and survivors in Wales had waited "too long for answers". title: Garvaghy Road parade will not be policed 'at any cost' - PSNI chief
description: Jon Boutcher also says a large scale criminal investigation is under way "regarding unlawful protest on the Garvaghy Road".
body: A parade by the Orange Order from Drumcree Church was stopped by police on Sunday Northern Ireland's top police officer has said the force's "principle objective" is to police the decision to allow a parade down the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, but added this would not be done "at any cost". Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said his overriding responsibility was to keep people safe. He has also offered to meet both sides in the stalemate, the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition. There has been more than three days of stalemate over the Orange Order parade, which was due to happen on Sunday morning but has not due to protesters on the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. Protesters remain along the road but the Orangemen who had been at Drumcree church since Sunday morning left overnight into Wednesday. The Orange Order has said it was disappointed and frustrated by a "lack of a proper policing plan" to allow the march to go ahead. Separate talks are continuing between Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant and the respective sides in an effort to break the stand-off. The residents have also launched a fresh legal bid to stop the parade from going ahead, which is due to be heard on Friday. Earlier, Boutcher said that the stalemate meant the police had "once again become the shock absorber of our society". He also said that people needed to focus on "solving this situation once and for all". Boutcher added that a "large scale criminal investigation" was under way into the unlawful blocking of Garvaghy Road, which prevented Sunday's parade. "I have given a clear direction regarding prioritising the evidence gathering and a criminal justice process," he added. Residents lodge fresh legal bid to stop Drumcree march What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Parading, policing and power sharing collide amid Drumcree dispute Thousands of people, including the Sinn Féin First Minister of Northern Ireland Michelle O'Neill, blocked the road on Sunday and police stopped Orangemen leaving Drumcree Church. Subsequent attempts since then have also been prevented by police. On Monday, Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police were not able to allow the parade because of an "unlawful and unnotified protest", adding that removing the protesters from the Garvaghy Road would have significantly jeopardised public safety. Boutcher said his officers would "continue to police Drumcree and our communities independently and impartially". "To be clear the upholding of the Parades Commission determination does not come at any cost," he added. "The outstanding officers of the PSNI and our mutual aid colleagues will not allow society to implode into violent disorder and mob rule must not be allowed to win." Unionist politicians have been highly critical of nationalist politicians from Sinn Féin and the SDLP who attended Sunday's protest. The leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) Gavin Robinson said those in attendance had broken the law. The DUP and Ulster Unionist Party will meet Boutcher later on Wednesday afternoon. Ahead of the meeting, a DUP source said: "If people break the law they must be held accountable." O'Neill has defended her involvement in the protest and said she was "standing up" for the community. It appears, as things stand, that PSNI cannot police the Parades Commission determination. It is hoping that an agreed way forward can somehow be found through talks and it continues to assess whether the determination can be enforced. But any move would see hundreds of protesters back on the Garvaghy Road, in essence re-creating the circumstances that stopped Sunday's parade. The PSNI also does not want to "torpedo" talks being held by the secretary of state. Not for the first time, it finds itself in no-win situation, damned no matter which course of action it takes in the absence of some negotiated plan. There is also unhappiness at how the Parades Commission presented the police advice in its determination. The ruling said the police had "no information" the parade would result in disorder, only to look foolish 48 hours later. However, a court judgement published on Tuesday night, external tells a different story. It states a range of potential scenarios had been mapped out, from a peaceful parade to "violent disorder". In just over a month's time, the PSNI will mark its 25th anniversary. And here it finds itself – in the middle of a dispute which is older than it is. The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in 30 years after a series of legal challenges. Since 1998, the Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes. The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation. Many Catholics see its marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas. The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders across Northern Ireland. title: The volunteers baking birthday cakes for children
description: The Hampshire group says it has seen a rise in demand and it needs more volunteer bakers.
body: Volunteers often tailor cakes to a child's favourite characters or interests Volunteer bakers are paying out of their own pockets so children in need do not go without a cake on their birthdays. Free Cakes for Kids Fareham and Gosport buys the ingredients, bakes and delivers cakes for young people whose families are unable to provide one. Natalie Parker, who joined as a baker while on maternity leave in 2024 and now runs the group, said the thought of a child not having a birthday cake was "heart-breaking". The group, part of a national network, said demand had risen and it was on the hunt for more volunteers. Natalie Parker joined Free Cakes for Kids Fareham and Gosport while on maternity leave and now runs the group Parker said she had seen the group advertised on Facebook and had thought about joining for a while. "I was on maternity leave with my son and just wanted something to occupy my brain a bit, so I took the plunge," she told BBC Radio Solent. She said her own son sometimes struggled to understand why other children would go without. "I can't imagine my own son not having a birthday cake. When I'm baking them, he says to me, 'Why don't they?' He can't, as a child, see why," she said. The group does not deal directly with families. Referrals come through organisations like food banks, churches and schools. More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight Requests are posted in a private Facebook group where volunteers can take them on, often tailoring cakes to a child's favourite characters or interests. The volunteers buy the ingredients, bake the cakes and deliver them, with the group only able to provide toppers, boards and boxes when it has managed to raise money. "It's not cheap, especially with food costs going up," Parker said. "But it's a small price, for me and I know for our volunteers, to pay for that child getting a birthday cake that they otherwise wouldn't be able to have." The group has more than 30 bakers, ranging from home bakers who make one or two cakes a year to professionals with their own baking businesses. "You don't need to be an incredible baker to join us," Parker added. title: Former Man Utd defender Smalling signs for Porto
description: Former Manchester United and England defender Chris Smalling signs for Portuguese league leaders Porto.
body: Chris Smalling has played his club football outside of England since 2020 Former Manchester United and England defender Chris Smalling has signed for Portuguese league leaders Porto. He has been without a club since leaving Saudi Pro League outfit Al-Fayha in the summer. The 36-year-old was linked with a move to Rangers but that did not materialise. Smalling has signed a contract until the end of the season with Porto, with the option for a further year. Porto have won all seven league games this season and already have a five-point advantage over second-placed Benfica. Francesco Farioli's side were beaten at home by Manchester City in their opening Champions League game. Smalling was keen to extend a 19-year professional career that began at non-league Maidstone, with the centre-back going on to play for Fulham, Manchester United - where he won five major trophies, including two Premier League titles - and Roma, where he won the Uefa Conference League under Jose Mourinho in 2022. He also won 31 England caps. Friendship with Mourinho & search for new club - what next for Smalling? title: China funding UK research which is being sent to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
description: British universities are being urged to sever ties with China General Technology Research Institute which is linked to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).
body: A group which has funded research in the UK has been supporting Beijing's spying apparatus, MI5 has announced More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned. In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state. Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security. He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation. In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms. This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions. MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). "MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says. "More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project. UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object. "This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said. The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated". It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions." The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law. It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so. Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies." title: Windies break their ODI batting record in India run-fest
description: West Indies dominate India's bowlers to pile up their highest ever total in one-day internationals.
body: John Campbell also holds the record for the highest opening stand in ODIs, having put on 365 for the first wicket alongside Shai Hope against Ireland in 2019 West Indies 405-7 (50 overs): Jangoo 114, Hope 104, Campbell 101 West Indies dominated India's bowlers to pile up their highest ever total in one-day internationals. John Campbell (101), Shai Hope (104) and Amir Jangoo (114) all struck centuries in the tourists' 405-7 in the second ODI in Guwahati. It is only the sixth time in ODI history that a team has had three centurions in one innings and the Windies' total eclipses their previous best of 389, scored against England at St George's in 2019. Campbell and Hope put on 110 in 79 balls for the second wicket, before a huge third-wicket partnership of 182 between Hope and Jangoo set the platform for a recrod total. Left-handed opener Campbell struck five sixes in his rapid century and took 22 off one Prasidh Krishna over. India bowlers Krishna and Naman Dhir picked up injuries while paceman Auqib Nabi had a debut to forget - conceding 84 runs, the fourth-most by an Indian winning his first ODI cap. West Indies' performance comes less than a week since news that their players must take a 25% pay cut as part of wider cost-saving measures. The two-time World Cup winners are also facing a battle to qualify directing for next year's competition, having been consigned to a qualifier in early 2027. title: Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the key questions following the guilty verdicts handed down to Manchester City.
body: Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano (left) and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak have continued to insist that the club is innocent despite the guilty verdicts The verdict that football fans around the world had been awaiting for years is in - Manchester City are guilty. The club still insists it is innocent of the financial rule-breaking charges first brought against it by the Premier League in 2023, and can appeal, so the legal wrangling is far from over. And the verdict has unleashed some huge questions for both the near and long-term future. The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has said the independent commission's decision raises "serious issues". BBC Sport has taken a look at the key questions in the case and what we know about each of them so far. The deadline for Man City to make their appeal is Friday. In previous instances - including the guilty verdicts and punishments handed out when Everton and Nottingham Forest breached spending rules - the appeal was heard and a decision made before the sanctions against the clubs was announced. So precedent indicates that City's appeal will be considered and decided upon before punishments are declared. Though that is not guaranteed. Exactly how long the process - which will be heard by a new three-person commission - will take is as yet unclear. One section of the Premier League regulations says that an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end. Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season. Man City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court. The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible". The phrasing may not offer any exact insight but the tone - of both the statement, and the strong language used in the independent commission's findings about the length of time the case has taken - is notable. "It has taken us much longer than we would have wished, and much longer than we had anticipated would be the case when the hearing concluded, to produce our decision," the commission wrote. "That is regrettable." It is clear that those in charge want the matter wrapped as quickly as can be done. Erling Haaland's goals have powered Manchester City to the top of the Premier League, but whether they are truly in a title challenge is unclear until sanctions are known And it is arguably to the benefit of both Manchester City and all of the other clubs in the Premier League and English Football League to know where they stand sooner rather than later. City are top of the Premier League, having taken a maximum 15 points from their opening five matches, but whether they are genuinely in a title race will be unclear as long as players, fans, and club owners are in the dark about what their punishment will be. Were the appeal and sanctions process to drag on beyond the end of the season, it would be possible that legal challenges could be brought by teams who finished below City in the table, or are relegated, or were knocked out by them in the domestic cups, which would be far less viable if the club's 'real' position is known before that point. There are two key scenarios here. The first is that one of the sanctions Manchester City are given is so significant a points deduction that they finish this season (or another future campaign, if the process takes longer) in the Premier League's bottom three and are automatically relegated to the Championship. The second scenario is that they are expelled by the Premier League, which would require 15 of their rival clubs to vote in favour of a motion decreeing so. Were that to happen, the club's future would be much less clear and would require them to apply to the Football Association for re-entry. Because the EFL and National League are separate entities from the Premier League, neither would necessarily be obliged to accept an entry request from Manchester City. And, even if a request were accepted by the EFL, its 72 clubs would have to vote whether or not to accept them. That is where the possibility of City beginning a reascent in League Two - or potentially even lower - arises from. There is a huge sporting and financial difference between dropping down to the Championship, with the high possibility of being promoted back to the Premier League after a single season, and starting again far lower down the pyramid. When Juventus were relegated from Serie A to Serie B in Italy, after being found guilty of match-fixing charges in 2006, they were able to retain some of the world's best players, including Gianluigi Buffon, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet. Players like Fabio Cannavaro, Patrick Vieira and Gianluca Zambrotta left Juventus after their enforced relegation, but Gianluigi Buffon stayed and captained the club to the title They were willing to put up with a single season in a lower tier and, when the club returned to Serie A after winning the Serie B title, they immediately finished third and qualified for the Champions League. If City faced only a single season outside the Premier League, players on long, lucrative contracts would likely be far more inclined to stay, and the economic damage of losing access to the top flight's TV rights income would be hugely reduced. title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
description: The social messaging app will let parents decide on privacy settings for their child's account.
body: WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children. The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account. In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption. And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness". He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers. "Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said. "I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it." The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries. According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time. The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls. Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups. Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content. And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option. "All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said. The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms. In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027. It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media. WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service. Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends.
