title: Lady A singer Charles Kelley reveals blood cancer diagnosis
description: The Grammy-winning US country music star, 45, says he currently feels "great" and is "hopeful".
body: Charles Kelley is the co-lead vocalist of Lady A, formerly Lady Antebellum Lady A singer Charles Kelley has revealed he has been diagnosed with blood cancer. The US musician, 45, founded the Grammy-winning country music trio, previously known as Lady Antebellum, in Nashville in 2006. The group are known for hits like Need You Now, American Honey and Just a Kiss, and have won six Grammy Awards. Sharing a health update on Instagram in a video, external alongside his wife Cassie, Kelley announced he had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma - a type of blood cancer that affects the bones and different parts of the body. He said: "I had a couple of random rib fractures that happened, which sparked my doctor into having me do several different blood tests. And one of the last blood tests we did, they found a blood cancer in there called multiple myeloma, and it's rare." He added: "But I'm young, I feel healthy, and the treatments I will say have just come so far, even in the past five years. Even life expectancy just far exceeds what it used to be and, I don't know, I feel really hopeful. I really do." Kelley noted how "freeing" it feels simply "getting this stuff off your chest". "But we're going to get through it," he continued - comparing his "one day at a time" approach to dealing with cancer to that of his journey to sobriety. The singer, who shares two young sons with his wife, ended the video by saying he intended to carry on working, despite the diagnosis. (Left to right) Charles Kelley, Hillary Scott and Dave Haywood of Lady A, performing during the 2024 People's Choice Country Awards at The Grand Ole Opry in Nashville "Right now I feel great and we've got a new record coming out soon with Lady A and then we've got Christmas shows," he said. "This first six months of treatment I believe is not going to be too invasive. I can still work. I think physically I will feel like myself. I will have tough days, but I want to keep working... "I need to be happy and doing what I love to do, and spending and soaking up as much time with my family as I can... "It's just another hurdle and, you know, I feel confident that we're going to get through it." Kelley's bandmates Hillary Scott and Dave Haywood posted messages of support for him and his family in the comments. Fellow lead vocalist Scott wrote: "The strongest duo right there! Love y'all so much! You've got this!" Haywood added: "Covering you in prayer brother. Love y'all. We're all here for you!" The group have had three number one albums in the US and reached number two with their single Need You Now, which won record of the year and song of the year at the Grammys in 2011. title: Ex-officer must repay £1.8m for stolen Bitcoin
description: Paul Chowles from Bristol took cryptocurrency seized in an investigation into a dark website.
body: Police say Paul Chowles took advantage of his position in the National Crime Agency to "line his own pockets" A former National Crime Agency (NCA) officer will have to repay £1.8m after stealing the valuable cryptocurrency Bitcoin he seized during an investigation. Paul Chowles, 44, from Bristol, was jailed for five and a half years at Liverpool Crown Court last year after pleading guilty to theft and money laundering. After his part in an NCA investigation into criminals selling illegal goods on the dark web, Chowles transferred about half of the Bitcoin seized from a drug trafficker into his own accounts. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) secured a confiscation order earlier that is equal to the value of the 30 Bitcoin recovered from Chowles, which has ballooned from £36,000 to more than £1.8m. Restoration work on historic pier 'astonishing' Trial date set for man accused of wife's murder Abnormal loads to cause 'significant' delays on M5 As part of the team working on the case, Chowles took part in the analysis and extraction of cryptocurrency from digital devices seized during the investigation. This ultimately led to Thomas White being jailed in 2019 for 64 months after he was found to have sold illegal goods to criminal networks on the dark website Silk Road 2.0. Following the seizure of 97 Bitcoin from White, it was noticed that 50 Bitcoin had been withdrawn from the digital wallet. The NCA assumed White had somehow accessed the wallet while in custody, but he denied any involvement. In fact it was Chowles who had taken the Bitcoin from the confiscated wallet in 2017, and then attempted to cover his tracks through a series of cryptocurrency transactions. An investigation was launched by Merseyside Police into the stolen Bitcoin and Chowles was arrested in May 2022. A total of 30 Bitcoin was subsequently recovered from him. Luke Clements, of the CPS proceeds of crime division, said the former NCA officer had "exploited a position of trust for personal gain". "Confiscation Orders are a powerful tool in ensuring that crime does not pay," he said. "Today's order sends a clear message that we will pursue offenders' assets relentlessly and seek to recover criminal proceeds wherever they are hidden." title: Shane Richie banned from driving after speeding
description: The EastEnders star blames "baiting" from paparazzi as he is banned for six months.
body: EastEnders star Shane Richie has played pub landlord Alfie Moon since 2002 EastEnders actor Shane Richie blamed "baiting" from paparazzi as he was banned from driving for six months after being caught speeding. Court records revealed the 62-year-old, real name Shane Roche, was hit with the driving ban on 23 September after he admitted the offence in Reigate, Surrey. He was also fined £500 at Guildford Magistrates' Court and ordered to pay £320 in costs and a surcharge. Richie, best known for playing Alfie Moon in the BBC soap, is already awaiting trial over a separate alleged offence of drink-driving in Harlow, Essex. In a note to the court, regarding the speeding offence, Richie said he had been pursued daily by photographers due to his "very public divorce". The actor accused the press of "constantly baiting me" for months in an attempt to get an angry reaction on camera. "This is not an excuse for going five miles over the limit, but just a reason why I may have sped up on that particular road," he said. Richie was caught on camera driving a Ford at 35mph (56km/h) along Reigate Hill - which is a steep climb leading to and from the nearby M25 junction - on 15 March. In his note to the court, Richie apologised for the offence and said: "Over the past several months I've been followed from my place of work in Borehamwood (Hertfordshire) where I film sometimes six days a week by our British tabloid press…. to my home." He described being followed into Reigate and to the supermarket. "It's no secret now that I'm going through a very public divorce and for the last several months the British press have suspected this and have been constantly baiting me and almost always looking for a reaction from me to sell their newspapers," Richie added. Richie entered a guilty plea in writing and his case was dealt with in private via the Single Justice Procedure, external. Richie is due to stand trial for a separate driving offence in November 2027 The TV presenter, who came fourth on I'm A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! in 2020, has hosted a number of game shows, appeared in pantomimes and first appeared on EastEnders in 2002. He faces a trial on 17 November 2027 for the separate drink-driving offence, which allegedly happened at a petrol station in Harlow on 29 July. Richie is accused of providing a breath sample of 65mcg of alcohol in 100ml of breath, which is above the legal limit of 35mcg. The actor, from Tadworth in Surrey, appeared at Colchester Magistrates' Court earlier in September for that offence, which he has denied. Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below. title: Car thieves target Nissan Jukes as 11 stolen in one county in 24 hours
description: Security expert Michael Fraser says the cars have "valuable spare parts" and are "easy to steal".
body: Gwent Police said inquiries are ongoing and patrols have increased in the Caerphilly county area Car thieves stole 11 Nissan Jukes over a 24-hour period in one county, police said. The crime wave hit Caerphilly county last Thursday and Friday, with security expert Michael Fraser saying the vehicles were frequently targeted because they have "valuable spare parts" and were "relatively easy to steal". Figures from the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, external (DVLA) show the Nissan Juke Tekna is the UK's most stolen car so far in 2026. On Wednesday, Gwent Police confirmed all 11 Nissan Jukes had been recovered, along with a Kia Niro and a Nissan Navara that were also reported stolen. No arrests have yet been made. Claire, 49, from the Caerphilly county, said her 2016 keyless Nissan Juke N-Connecta was stolen from outside her home during the early hours of 25 September. At 06:45 BST her husband left for work and noticed her car wasn't at the side of their home. "He came up to me and said 'your car's gone'," the health care assistant said. "I popped my head out of the back window which overlooks where I was parked and yeah, it was gone." Despite being a light sleeper, she did not hear anything during the night and said the thieves appeared to be "very quiet". Her car was found two days later - about two minutes from her home - after a local resident recognised it from her Facebook appeal and contacted her. She said it was a relief now that her car had been recovered, and seemingly fine, but it is currently with a forensics team. Claire added: "It's just inconvenient because obviously you can't just pop in your car and go somewhere now, you've got to rely on people and I hate doing that because I'm quite independent." In future, she plans to keep her keys in a safe place and get them re-coded. A total of 13 vehicles were reported stolen from Caerphilly county borough and have since all been recovered Fraser, an ex-burglar turned security expert, said many of the 2010 to 2019 Nissan Juke models used keyless-entry and thieves can use signal-relay devices to steal them from outside owners' homes. "A lot of us do keep the keys near to the front door. We're creatures of habit," he said. He urged drivers to keep their keys in a Faraday pouch and away from the front door, as the signal is "easy to pick up", including through glass. He said the method involved criminals using electronic equipment to capture the signal from a car key kept inside a house, which allows them to unlock and start the vehicle. Fraser said one way to make a vehicle harder to steal was driving it on to a driveway rather than reversing on to it. "Most people reverse on to the drive. That car is ready to be stolen. If you drive on to the drive they've obviously got to reverse first then go forward and it takes a little bit more time," he said. He also suggested parking with wheels turned into the gutter rather than left straight if parking on the street, as this also makes a vehicle harder for thieves to move. Fraser also recommended using security devices such as steering locks, also known as "crook locks". "If you look at the Nissan Juke, that car is very high value on spare parts. So people tend to pinch them, strip them of parts, and then sell them on," he added. Motoring journalist Claire Evans said newer models of the Nissan Jukes were "less likely" to be stolen via relay units as they have "keyfobs that stop emitting these codes once they've not moved, or been used for two minute". Evans said the older model could be a target as it is a small SUV, which is the most popular car class. "Selling them on would be easy, and they're economical cars that are affordable to run, so they have lots of appeal," she said. She added drivers can also keep their keys in a metal container, such as a biscuit tin, or even the microwave at home. "Just as long as they're somewhere that stops the code from being copied," she said. Gwent Police said officers are trying to identify those responsible for these thefts. Inspector Richard Tovey said: "We will continue with our patrols across the borough following these reports, so if you have any concerns or questions then please take the time to speak to our officers. The force has appealed for anyone with information to get in touch. Nissan has been approached for comment. title: Oasis take legal action to stop sale of unheard tapes
description: The auction house said it was "very disappointed" the lot could no longer be sold.
body: The 63 tapes feature sound checks and live performances recorded by sound engineer Huw Richards A set of unheard Oasis recordings valued at between £1.2m and £1.6m have been pulled from an auction after the band filed an injunction. Earlier this month, it was announced that Littleton Auctions, in Evesham, were selling a set of recordings which included 63 live shows, as well as soundchecks and more than 100 hours of Noel and Liam Gallagher in the 1990s. They were collected by Oasis sound engineer Huw Richards, who worked with the band from the release of their debut album Definitely, Maybe in 1994, until 2001. However, the auction house said the sale of the recordings had been suspended after the band intervened. Managing director Ben Homer said: "Littleton Auctions confirms that the Oasis recordings known as The Desk Tapes have been withdrawn from our October 3 auction in light of legal proceedings. "We are very disappointed that we cannot offer this significant archive as planned." 'Why we flushed away Dragons' Den investment' Police hope for new leads in 2001 attack as woman reveals how life changed Reform takes legal advice over 'crazy' council letter The recordings were brought to sale by the sound engineer's son Owain Richards, who said: "It is true that Oasis have sued me and my father to try to prevent the auction of the tapes made by my father many years ago. "We have agreed to postpone the auction [of the tapes] to enable the legal dispute to be resolved either by litigation or otherwise in an orderly way." The previously unheard Oasis recordings were due to go on sale next month Homer added: "The rest of the sale is unaffected and will take place as normal. We respect the legal process and will make no further comment on the proceedings at this stage." When the sale was first announced, Littleton Auctions called it a "once-in-a-generation opportunity for fans and collectors alike", but confirmed the band did not support the sale. The auction will go ahead with memorabilia, which includes internal tour itineraries, original setlists, a band-played Epiphone guitar and an original Kangol Oasis tour Parka. The BBC has contacted Oasis' representatives for comment. title: NHS admits 'failing families' over stillbirths
description: An independent review ordered by the trust finds systemic issues lay at the heart of the failures.
body: The stillbirths all occurred at the East Kent NHS trust between June 2025 and March 2026 An NHS trust has apologised after an independent review found that eight babies might have survived with better maternity care, admitting it has "failed families". The stillbirths all occurred at the East Kent Hospitals NHS Trust's hospitals between June 2025 and March 2026. An independent review ordered by the trust found systemic issues lay at the heart of the failures. These included failures to manage high risk pregnancies, provide appropriate triage, identify foetal growth concerns, and make appropriate use of interpreter services. Since the report, a further seven stillbirths have occurred, including three last month. A review into those deaths has now been ordered. All the stillbirths occurred after 34 weeks gestation. Three years ago, the Kirkup report found 45 babies might have survived at the trust's hospitals if they had received better care. The East Kent NHS trust runs the William Harvey Hospital in Ashford and the Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital (QEQM) in Margate. Papers for a board meeting on Thursday, external contained a report by the acting CEO of the trust, Dr Des Holden, who apologised to the families involved. Dr Holden wrote: "On behalf of the board, and personally, I am very sorry and apologise to the women and families, and their communities, where failings in our care are at the heart of these devastating outcomes." The board papers contained a further report, headed Response to the Independent Stillbirth Review, which said four cases were assessed as having care deficiencies likely to have affected the outcome for the baby. In a further four cases, care issues were identified that may have contributed to the outcome. The review found "recurrent and systemic weaknesses in the management of high-risk pregnancy, foetal surveillance, maternity triage, escalation and organisational learning", documents said. Documents also said since the review "there have, regrettably, been a further four term stillbirths from April 2026 and July 2026 and a further three in August 2026". Three years ago, the trust was criticised in the damning independent Kirkup review After the board papers were published, Dr Holden said: "This review is clear that sadly, we have failed families. We are truly sorry." He said the trust requested the review after increased safety monitoring introduced following Dr Bill Kirkup's investigation identified a rise in stillbirths. Each stillbirth was investigated and an independent review commissioned into 11 cases. "We are implementing the review's recommendations in full," he said, "including improving continuity of care for women with high-risk pregnancies, maternity triage, enhancing staff training and increasing the amount of translated information and access to interpreters. "We are working with the national Maternity and Neonatal Intensive Support Team to ensure our services meet the standards women and families deserve." title: Only 28% of nurdles 'recovered', researchers say
description: Scientists predict that nurdles will continue to wash up on North East beaches.
body: Millions of plastic nurdles washed up on beaches following the ship collision Only 28% of nurdles which spilled into a river have been recovered and are expected to continue washing up on beaches in the future, scientists have calculated. Almost 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles are estimated to have spilled into the River Tyne after a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne in July. However, only 5.14 tonnes have been recovered despite volunteers spending thousands of hours clearing beaches across the region, work by Newcastle University and the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas) found. South Tyneside Council's director of community operations Gary Kirsop, said the multi-agency group in charge of the nurdle response "remained committed". The university and Cefas said nurdles were "likely to have dispersed beyond the Tyne estuary out into the North Sea". The work, undertaken by the university, also said some nurdles "may remain within the river system" and will continue to wash up on parts of the coastline in future, depending on weather conditions, winds and tides. North East mayor Kim McGuinness said this was upsetting for those caring for the region's coastline. She has commissioned an independent review into the response and recovery, and said she is backing calls for a change in international rules about how plastic nurdles are transported. McGuinness said: "It's vital the agencies involved in the clean up are ready and act quickly to continue their work when this happens." McGuinness said she is backing calls for a change to international rules on how nurdles are carried Scientific and Techincal Advice Cell (STAC) has reviewed Cefas' modelling alongside recovery data and shoreline surveys. It said modelling cannot accurately predict exactly when and where nurdles will wash up and the complete recovery of every nurdle was not considered achievable. Dr Robert Bradburne, STAC chair, said: "As with any environmental incident of this nature, ongoing monitoring remains important and the situation should continue to be reviewed as further evidence becomes available." title: Residents fear new rules could mean dangerous cladding is left on blocks of flats
description: The government says it hopes the changes will speed up the process of removing cladding.
body: Natasha Parcell is living in a hotel following a fire in the tower block where she owns a flat When Natasha Parcell first got her foot on the property ladder little did she expect to be one of the latest victims of the cladding crisis. "I was really excited to have something of my own," she says, "[but] very quickly in the first year I was told it was actually no longer safe or mortgageable." The 33-year-old is currently living in a hotel after being evacuated from her flat, in east London, following a fatal fire in her tower block earlier this month. All she was able to take with her were some plastic bags filled with clothes. The blaze came just a day after residents got approval to have all the flammable cladding on the building removed. However, she is worried new rules - which come into force on Wednesday - may allow the developer Barratt to backtrack on that decision. The rules state cladding can remain in place on blocks if the risk is deemed to be "tolerable". "To find out that they're [the government] trying to change the standards in which they might remediate our buildings is quite terrifying," says Parcell. One person died in the fire at the block of flats in Poplar, east London "Literally two weeks ago, we had a fatal fire in our building and we're still being told that they might change the rules and it might be a tolerable risk. I just don't understand when human life, or my life, became a tolerable risk to anybody." The developer of Parcell's flat, Barratt Redrow, says despite the new rules it still intends to remove all the flammable cladding on her tower block as soon as possible. It is nearly ten years since the Grenfell Tower fire, but almost 3,000 tower blocks in the UK with dangerous cladding still need to be fixed. The new rules, known as PAS9980, grade the fire risk posed by a tower block's cladding system into four categories: high, medium, tolerable, and low. Only those assessed as high or medium risk will require the cladding to be removed, but all categories permit the cladding to be flammable. Cladding campaigners say this relies too much on the judgement of fire safety assessors, who are not independently appointed and often employed by the building's freeholder or developer. The government declined to be interviewed about the changes. But the Ministry of Housing said in a statement it would speed up the process of removing cladding, providing a more proportionate, clear and consistent approach to a complex issue. It said repaired buildings would be audited to make sure the work had been carried out properly. Residents still in hotels a week after tower fire Major fires still a risk under 'spineless' new safety law, construction boss warns More buildings to receive dangerous cladding removal funding But cladding campaigners believe a better approach would be to make sure all fire safety defects in tower blocks were addressed, not just cladding on exterior walls. Ed Daffarn, who was the first person to warn about the dangers posed by cladding being added to Grenfell, watched the tower burn on the night of the fire. He said he cannot believe, nearly ten years after the fire, that government officials, the fire safety industry and developers are still wrestling with the definition of what is safe. "It shows the indifference and incompetence of the two different colours of government we've had in the last ten years," he says. Daffarn said the building industry should also be made to fix fire safety defects in the buildings beyond the cladding if they're found to have not met the building regulation at the time of construction - a consideration removed from the new rules. This approach is also supported by the insurance industry, and the Association of British Insurers says all flammable cladding should be removed. When Natasha and other residents at her block were told a fire risk assessment showed the cladding needed to be removed, she says her buildings insurance went up by 94%. As the flat is leasehold, the premium is included in her maintenance charges, which are now nearly £8,000 a year. She and other residents are concerned that if her building is not fully fixed, and insurance premiums remain high if all the fire and safety risks not are addressed, it could remain unmortgageable and unsellable. "I feel like I've been punished for getting onto the housing ladder so early," she says. "It should be you buy a home, it's a safe place to be, no-one should have to be compromised or deciding whether they might live or not based on the home they buy." title: Botswana condemned for slaughtering elephants for independence celebrations
description: The government authorises the hunting of 23 elephants and dozens of other wild animals for independence day feasts.
body: Botswana is home to the world's largest elephant population, with more than 130,000 elephants (file photo) Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations. The southern African country, home to the world's largest elephant population, is holding nationwide festivities on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of independence from Britain. A licence issued by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, seen by local media, authorises the hunting of 23celephants and other wild animals for "complimentary purposes". The Botswana-based Elephant Protection Society warns the decision could undermine conservation, with its chairman Oaitse Nawa telling the BBC elephants needed greater protection. He warned that slaughtering elephants for celebratory feasting could encourage poaching by creating the impression that killing elephants is acceptable when sanctioned by government. "Elephants have lost their social structures because they are always being pushed from one place to another by gunshots," Nawa said. Several social media users in the country have also expressed concerns about eating the game meat amid an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has prompted authorities to impose measures to contain its spread. Tshenatshe Monwela, an elder in Maun, a tourism town in north-western Botswana told local media that his community should have received buffalo instead. He argued that elephants had particular cultural and ecological significance and that Botswana's historic role in protecting the country's wildlife and livestock should have been recognised in the government's allocation of meat for the anniversary celebrations. Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find Botswana's government has organised a series of events to mark the country's diamond jubilee, including a carnival in the capital, Gaborone, as well as cultural performances, concerts and sporting events. The game meat is expected to be served as part of the traditional feasting associated with the Independence Day celebrations. The 23 elephants were allocated in eight districts across the country. It was not immediately clear how many of the animals had been killed by Wednesday morning. The BBC has asked the government for comment. But local media published images from different parts of Botswana showing residents gathering around elephant carcasses, some with knives in hand and sharing the meat. In Chobe, a wildlife-rich district in northern Botswana near the borders with Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, a local MP raised concerns after residents reportedly collected portions directly from a carcass at a school. He said the system risked creating congestion and disadvantaging elderly people, pregnant women and people with disabilities, and suggested the meat should instead be processed into 5kg or 10kg packages to improve hygiene and ensure fairer distribution. "For the sake of dignity, fairness and public hygiene, we respectfully call on the hunter and the relevant leadership to ensure that future distributions are properly organised," MP Simasiku Mapulanga posted on Facebook, attaching photos of people scrambling for meat around an elephant carcass. People across Botswana are gathering to mark the country's 60th Independence Day Elephant meat is common in some wildlife-rich communities, particularly when meat from legal hunts is distributed locally, but it is not an everyday staple. Botswana also tightly regulates game meat, and its legal possession generally depends on proving it came from a lawful hunt. The decision has reignited a long-running and often heated debate in Botswana over how the country manages its huge elephant population. Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and communities living alongside them have long complained about animals destroying crops, damaging property and sometimes killing people. The government has defended regulated hunting as one way of managing the elephant population and human-wildlife conflict while generating income for communities. The country banned trophy hunting in 2014 under former President Ian Khama but lifted the restrictions five years later under his successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi. Hunting has continued under President Duma Boko, who defeated Masisi in elections in 2024. The government says proceeds from hunting supports conservation and local development. Minister of Environment and Tourism Wynter Mmolotsi told parliament last year that special elephant quotas raised 15.6m pula ($1.1m; £820,000) in 2025 for projects in areas where elephants are found. But conservation organisations have questioned whether the level of hunting is sustainable. Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, argue that international criticism often overlooks the costs borne by rural communities living alongside one of the world's biggest concentrations of elephants. They say elephants destroy crops and infrastructure and pose a danger to people, particularly as their range increasingly overlaps with farms and settlements. title: Republic of Ireland will play second Israel game - Hallgrimsson
description: Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson says the team's second Uefa Nations League game against Israel will go ahead as planned.
body: Hallgrimsson said he is unaware of a players' meeting before Sunday's second game against Israel Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson says the team's second Uefa Nations League game against Israel will go ahead as planned. Hallgrimsson's side beat Israel 3-0 in Hungary on Sunday after the Republic of Ireland players voted to fulfil the fixture. They have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war, with the 'Stop The Game' campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - issuing an open letter this week calling for the Republic of Ireland to pull out of Sunday's behind-closed-doors match in Serbia. However, speaking before Thursday's game against Austria in Dublin, Hallgrimsson said the Republic of Ireland will fulfil the second Israel fixture and that he is not aware of a squad meeting to decide whether to play the game. "The FAI (Football Association of Ireland) has said we are playing both games. That was our intention when we came into the camp and it is still our intention," said Hallgrimsson. "We are trying to focus on the football. It is already decided we will fulfil the games." On Saturday, doubts emerged over whether the first Israel game would take place after the Republic of Ireland's pre-match news conference was postponed because of a squad meeting. When the news conference commenced more than five hours later than planned, FAI chief executive David Courell said a players' vote on whether to play the game passed by a "significant majority". While fulfilling the game, the Republic of Ireland players did not engage in pre-match formalities, wore black armbands and bowed their heads during Israel's national anthem. The Republic of Ireland's most recent home game - a friendly against Qatar in May - was interrupted when fans threw tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag on to the pitch. When asked about potential protests during Thursday's encounter with Austria, Hallgrimsson said: "I must focus on football. I will let others think about security and those things. "We are playing Austria, the highest-ranked team in the group. I'm not going to allow outside noise to affect me focusing on football." FAI unclear over possible sanctions if game not played Republic of Ireland 'raised awareness worldwide' in Israel game - Hallgrimsson Gavin Bazunu has been training with the squad before the Austria game On Saturday, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu made himself unavailable for both Israel games, saying he felt it "would be wrong to participate". With Bazunu having returned to training before the Austria match, Hallgrimsson praised the Bolton player and the rest of his squad while hitting out at "lies" that had been reported regarding the goalkeeper's decision. "Gavin is a great lad. I've always had a good relationship with him and it's probably more tough for him than the other players, but they have really welcomed him," said Hallgrimsson, who confirmed Luton keeper Josh Keeley will take Bazunu's place in the squad for the second Israel game. "There's been a lot of lies said around all of this, but we welcome him back and he's taken part, amazing. "I think it shows his character, as well, to be with us, so I want to give him praise for that. I want to give the players praise for how welcome they have been with him. "Life goes on. He is a part of this group and I think that shows how strong the bond is between these players that even a thing like this is not breaking us." Finn Azaz was an unused substitute in the 3-0 win over Israel Hallgrimsson also praised midfielder Finn Azaz, but would not confirm whether he will be selected for the second Israel game after he was an unused substitute in Sunday's 3-0 win. The Southampton midfielder has family links to Israel on his mother's side, with Hallgrimsson lauding the 26-year-old's "incredible emotional control". "He's been one of the persons I admire the most in how he conducted himself in all of this," said Hallgrimsson. "It is about being a member of a team, so you need to listen to all opinions. To do your thing, to do your work with grace and understanding of all opinions. "Talking about walking the extra mile to being a part of a national team, I don't have words to explain to you and you wouldn't understand because inside camp he has so much respect within this group of players." title: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
description: At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, local authorities reported.
body: Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has said. At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, including a child in the Kyiv region, local authorities reported. The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, DTEK, saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital. The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. This has not been confirmed by Ukrainian officials. In a statement on Telegram, Koretskyi said: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure. "However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season." Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. In total 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there were strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions. On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy, Kyiv and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said. State-owned grid operator Ukrenegro advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual. Acrid smoke obscured views over Kyiv on Wednesday In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere. Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared. Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko said. Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building. It is not clear if the three he mentioned included the child. Two people were also killed in the north-eastern Sumy region, governor Oleh Hryhorov said, while another person was killed in the Mykolaiv region, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. title: First Glastonbury 2027 tickets to go on sale
description: Glastonbury Festival will take place from 23-27 June 2027 at Worthy Farm in Somerset.
body: Glastonbury Festival will be back in 2027 after a fallow year in 2026 Those hoping to go to Glastonbury Festival 2027 could soon find out their fate as the first set of tickets go on sale. The event will take place from 23-27 June 2027 at Worthy Farm in Pilton, Somerset, after a fallow year in 2026. Coach tickets will be available to buy for £408 plus the selected coach fare at 18:00 BST on Thursday, before general admission tickets go on sale at 09:00 on Sunday. Coaches will depart from 28 locations across the country including from London, Bristol, Bath, Glasgow, Edinburgh, Manchester and Cardiff. Some of UK's rarest trees are being saved by cliff-climbing pensioners 'My big breasts lead to lewd comments in the street' Restoration work on historic pier 'astonishing' Olivia Rodrigo was the last act to perform on the Pyramid Stage in 2025, before Glastonbury took a fallow year People who want to snag a ticket must have already pre-registered on the Glastonbury Festival website. In recent years, organisers have introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number. Registration closed on 25 September, and will not reopen until after the October ticket sales. Once on the other side of the queue, people can buy up to six tickets per transaction after paying a deposit. Anyone who missed the registration deadline or is not able to buy a ticket on Thursday can have another chance during the spring resale. While the headliners for next year's festival have not yet been confirmed, Emily Eavis has said Oasis are not due to play despite speculation from fans. The band announced a series of 2027 gigs across the UK, Ireland, Europe and the US last week, leaving a potentially Glastonbury-shaped hole in their calendar. But Eavis put those rumours to bed in a direct response to one Glastonbury-goer on social media. Follow BBC Somerset on Facebook, external and X, external. title: Swinney to introduce misogyny education in every school in Scotland
description: The first minister says he wants to challenge misogynistic behaviour in young boys and strengthen and support young girls.
body: John Swinney wants to roll out education and awareness programmes across the country John Swinney has vowed to introduce programmes to educate pupils about misogyny in every school in Scotland. The first minister said violence against women and girls was of "such seismic significance" that it made the move necessary. He has previously described the situation as a "national emergency" with Police Scotland saying more than 200 crimes of violence against women and girls are recorded on average every day. Swinney said Scotland's education system must be a primary focus to challenge misogynistic behaviour in young boys - and give young girls "the strength and resilience to say, that's not acceptable". The Scottish government previously launched an advertising campaign urging boys not to share misogynistic content online The first minister told BBC Radio Scotland's Mornings programme: "We've been working over the summer on what I would call preventative interventions. "These are education programmes and awareness campaigns which are going to be focused on changing the culture of Scottish society. "Our education system is going to be a primary focus for that, to make sure that boys are educated and supported to understand the implications of what some might think of as casual behaviour, but it has consequences." He added: "I'm going to make sure that every school in the country is educating young boys about the dangers and risks of misogyny." Swinney calls violence against women a 'national emergency' as new advert launched New adverts urge boys not to share sexist content online Earlier this year, the Scottish government launched an advertising campaign urging boys and young men not to share misogynistic content online. The adverts warned boys that sexist content is "never harmless" and has the potential to hurt girls, including people they know. Swinney said the fact that Scotland doesn't have a mandatory education system had meant that some schools had been tackling the issue more vigorously than others. "I'm going to address that," he told told Mornings presenter Connie McLaughlin. "We have got to get alignment between the government and our local authority partners. "We've got to make sure that's present in every single school in the country." The first minister said there continued to be debate over the age at which young pupils were introduced to violence-awareness programmes. "I was criticised heavily when I was education secretary (five years ago) about putting in place materials which were educating young people about concepts such as consent in relationships," he said. "Some people viewed that it was far too early for that to be undertaken. "My view was that it was necessary. I think that is inescapable now." During an hour-long radio phone-in, Swinney said he was "terrified" by the influence of toxic masculinity on young boys and teenagers and was talking to the UK government about tougher online regulations. He also said he was looking at providing emergency funding for organisations which were struggling to help victims of domestic violence because of long waiting lists. The first minister was challenged over bail tests by the family of Stacy Hunter, who was murdered at her home near Houston by her estranged husband while he was on bail. Stacy Hunter's death has prompted calls for stronger protection for women Stacy's brother Sean and their mother Ann have supported calls for a dedicated GPS electronic monitoring scheme for domestic abuse perpetrators who are assessed as posing a significant risk to a partner or former partner. Earlier this month Swinney announced that, before recess in October, regulations would be lodged to enable the piloting of GPS monitoring for individuals on bail, including those suspected of domestic abuse. Sean Hunter welcomed news about the GPS tracking but raised concerns about whether the bail system was tight enough. He said: "We don't want this (GPS tracking) to be used as a tool to release more dangerous people because they'll be tagged." The first minister said he believed Scotland had a "very strong bail test" which took into account the perspective of victims and the issue of public safety. However, he said "tragically, there were cases where the judgment was wrong", as in the case of Stacy. Swinney said the GPS pilot would start in the Tayside and Fife areas. He added that if the Scottish government was confident in the system, he hoped to see the initiative rolled out as widely and as quickly as possible. title: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
description: The withdrawal of coalition forces, under a deal agreed two years ago, was a key demand of the Iraqi government.
body: Iraq's security forces have now assumed full responsibility for the nation's security following confirmation of the US and UK withdrawal The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country. The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday. It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month. British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability". Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal. US plans to cut off military aid to key Middle East ally, BBC told Saudi Arabia joins US in strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq 'Attacked 28 times in a day' - BBC visits heavily targeted US-UK base in Iraq "Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym. "With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership." Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq". He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq." The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence. A recent UN report estimated that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only". The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country. Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit. But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence. This video can not be played (April 2026) BBC's defence correspondent visits US and UK military base in Iraq Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base. Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose. A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran. They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby. At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day. RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission. It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region. It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold. The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners. US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan. US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters. This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq. Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait. They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist. The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel. US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country. title: Police seek charges against 20 firms and 54 people over Grenfell Tower fire
description: The force is seeking charges against 54 individuals and 20 companies over the 2017 tower block fire that killed 72 people.
body: The fire in June 2017 killed 72 people The Metropolitan Police has submitted its final investigation file into the Grenfell Tower fire to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), seeking charges against 54 individuals and 20 companies. These include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office. The Met described the case into the fire which killed 72 people at the tower block in North Kensington, west London, as one of the "most complex investigations ever undertaken by any UK law enforcement agency". The CPS said charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which is on 14 June 2027. A public inquiry report released in 2024 found the fire was avoidable and set out how a chain of failures across government and the private sector led to the disaster. The Met's investigation, Operation Northleigh, has run in parallel with the public inquiry into the disaster, but detectives waited for the inquiry to publish its findings before completing their work. Some bereaved families and survivors have said this delayed justice, but it allowed police to consider the inquiry's often highly technical conclusions. Campaign groups have said the process has taken too long Grenfell United, a bereaved families and survivors group, said "no family should have to fight this hard, for this long, for justice". "It has taken more than nine years to get here. Nine years, and no one has been held criminally accountable for the deaths of our 72 loved ones. "We want those responsible to face justice. If people are found guilty of crimes that cost our loved ones their lives, we want to see them behind bars. "Only then will people see that there are real consequences for what happened at Grenfell." Joe Powell, MP for Kensington and Bayswater, welcomed the news but said bereaved families and survivors "have already waited an agonising nine years for justice". "My position remains clear that we must do everything in our power to ensure that justice is delivered as swiftly as possible. "I will continue working with government ministers to ensure everything is done to avoid any further delays," he added. The charred remains of Grenfell Tower were a crime scene for 14 months, during which forensic teams scoured the building for evidence of why the fire spread so quickly. Detectives commissioned their own laboratory tests and examined thousands of pieces of debris from the fire, including the fridge which malfunctioned in a fourth-floor flat, from where the flames spread rapidly to the rest of the building. The evidence has been kept in a warehouse at a secret location, which the BBC visited last year. Police have investigated the actions of 15,000 people across 700 organisations or companies and taken 14,700 statements. The investigation has also examined 45,000 documents, images and exhibits. The files sent to the CPS include examples of this evidence, as well as reports containing more than two million words. Evidence from the fire is stored at a warehouse in a secret location The CPS will decide whether there is a realistic prospect of conviction, as well as considering whether bringing charges is in the public interest. In anticipation of possible criminal proceedings, the Met has said it is building a replica of a section of the tower, which is being dismantled, to help future jurors understand its layout. title: Detective admits 'upskirting' sex offences against a child
description: He was a lead investigator in the case of two-year-old Ethan Ives-Griffiths who was murdered.
body: Det Con Lee Harshey-Jones pleaded guilty to three charges A former detective has admitted taking pictures beneath the clothing of a child without consent - also known as "upskirting". Lee Harshey-Jones, 45, pleaded guilty to one charge of voyeurism and one of perverting the course of justice by applying a factory reset to his mobile phone to conceal evidence on 11 June 2026, in Colwyn Bay, Conwy county. He was a detective constable and lead investigator in the case of two-year-old Ethan Ives-Griffiths, whose grandparents were jailed for murder last year, and has given evidence in other high-profile murder trials in north Wales. Harshey-Jones was given conditional bail following a hearing at Chester Crown Court, and will be sentenced on 19 November. He was suspended by North Wales Police after his arrest, and has since resigned from the force. Harshey-Jones also pleaded guilty to a charge of corrupt or improper exercise of his police powers and privileges by looking up his own incident on the computer log. Ryan Donoghue, defending, asked for a pre-sentence report for his client, who he said was of previous good character. He was told by Recorder Mark Ford KC he must sign the sex offenders register. The recorder added: "The fact that I have adjourned the case for a pre-sentence report should not be taken by you as any indication to you as to what sentence will be passed on these serious counts." Operating equipment beneath clothing without consent is an offence under the Sexual Offences Act 2003. North Wales Police said the former officer had resigned from the force. The force added that as criminal proceedings and misconduct protocols remained active and it was unable to provide comment at this time. title: Peter Murrell's legal aid withdrawn after embezzlement conviction
description: The former SNP chief executive had been receiving government-funded support since last year.
body: Peter Murrell's lawyer has said he will be able to repay the sum embezzled Former SNP chief executive Peter Murrell, who was jailed in June for embezzling more than £400,000 from the party, has had his legal aid withdrawn. Murrell, the estranged husband of ex-First Minister Nicola Sturgeon, was sentenced to five years after using the funds to buy goods ranging from a luxury motorhome to toiletries. He was granted legal aid - government-funded assistance typically given to people who cannot afford it - last year. But The Scotsman, external reported that Murrell was informed his support would be withdrawn on 28 July. The Scottish Legal Aid Board paid out £4,831 to fund legal counsel for Murrell. That total could rise, as his lawyers could request payment for work carried out before the legal aid was withdrawn. Peter Murrell jailed for more than five years for embezzling SNP funds SNP write-off value of Murrell motorhome in party accounts Legal aid is typically granted to people who would struggle to pay for legal help themselves, though in some cases they still need to make their own contribution. A spokesperson for the Scottish Legal Aid Board confirmed that Murrell was "no longer in receipt of legal aid". They added: "Legal aid and data protection legislation strictly limits what Slab can disclose about individual applications." During Murrell's sentencing, the court was told that he had more than £600,000 across two pension accounts and would be able to pay back the sum embezzled, totalling £400,310.65. The Herald reported last month, external that £4,831 of legal aid had been spent on Murrell's case. It is understood that sum has not changed. A Scottish Legal Aid Board spokesperson told The Herald: "Legal representatives can send us bills during a case, or up to four months after it ends. "We have not received any bills from the solicitors in this case yet, so we expect to make further payments." The Scottish Legal Aid Board has not commented on why Murrell's support has been withdrawn. Its website, external lists various reasons why it could drop legal aid - including a client providing false information, failing to disclose relevant information or conducting themselves "in an unreasonable way". The board can also recover funds from recipients if their legal aid has been terminated. The motorhome was parked at the home of Murrell's mother after being picked up in Rosyth Police Scotland began investigating the SNP's finances in 2021 after questions were asked about what had happened to £667,000 raised for a second independence referendum campaign. Officers initially looking into those concerns ultimately uncovered Murrell's crimes. They found the former chief executive had used charge cards, bank transfers and fake invoices to illicitly purchase items including jewellery, cosmetics, stationery, and games consoles. Most notably, he bought a £124,500 motorhome in 2020. Three years later, it was seized from his mother's driveway in Dunfermline with four miles on the clock. title: Giant data centre plans lodged for old nuclear plant site
description: Developers say it could create more than 500 full-time jobs on the Chapelcross site near Annan.
body: Developers say the project would represent a £15.6bn investment Plans have been submitted for a £16.5bn data centre at the site of the former Chapelcross nuclear plant in the south of Scotland. If approved, developers claim the scheme could deliver more than 500 full-time jobs - and it would be one of the biggest in the world in terms of its power capacity. Applicant CX Tech Ltd hopes work could start on the project next year with it taking about eight years to complete. It said the project was in line with attempts to redevelop the site but opponents have raised concerns over its visual impact, as well as its effect on local energy supplies and costs. No consent for large AI data centres before Christmas, MSPs told Will our peaceful rural life be destroyed by a huge AI data centre? Could a huge data centre revitalise Ayrshire - or ruin it? The nuclear plant began operation in 1959 and produced electricity until 2004. Its landmark cooling towers came down a few years later and defuelling of the nuclear reactors was completed in 2013. Other buildings still on the site are not intended to be demolished until 2040 at the earliest with final site clearance expected by 2095. A planning statement on behalf of the applicant said the scheme would bring a number of benefits by delivering "critical digital infrastructure" and "returning a nationally significant site to productive economic use". It said it could support up to 750 jobs during construction and about 540 once operational, plus hundreds of indirect posts. Chapelcross operated as a nuclear power plant for 45 years Graeme Anderson, chief executive of CX Tech, said: "This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Dumfries and Galloway and for Scotland. "Chapelcross has the potential to bring together our renewable energy strengths, digital infrastructure and high-value jobs in a way that few other sites can. "We have an opportunity to seize that potential now, creating a new economic future for a site that has played an important role in Scotland's energy story for generations." A local campaign has been launched against the plans, with the Scottish government expected to publish national guidance for local authorities on such projects within the next three months. About 1,000 people have signed a petition against the scheme claiming it could put strain on the energy grid and see household bills "rocket". It also raised fears that countryside views could be "obstructed and destroyed by the massive data centre and associated operations". Campaigners have described the "large scale industrialisation" of the area as "unacceptable". They have also raised concerns about the loss of agricultural land and woodland. Campaigners have questioned the job creation claims for the development Action to Protect Rural Scotland (APRS) said the data centre's capacity, at 1000MW, was bigger than any data centre currently operating in the world. It said that the majority of the scheme would be on greenfield and not brownfield land. It has also raised further areas of concern including air pollution, waste and climate impacts and has questioned the employment claims. APRS added that the energy needs of the centre would be equivalent to about 2.2 million households. What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland? Laura Moodie, Scottish Green MSP for South Scotland, said it was one of the most "seriously concerning" data centre applications made to date. She added: "The site at Chapelcross should be the best place to put a data centre by utilising a decommissioned brownfield site. "But the proposal which has been lodged is reckless and endangers our energy supply and natural environment." She said the application should be rejected because of the "risks and consequences it could bring to our energy grid and our rural communities". Earlier this month the Scottish government rejected a call from the Scottish Greens for the application processes for data centres to be paused until new national guidelines are in force. However, ministers said they would publish the guidance by Christmas - and that they did not expect any planning decisions to be made before then. title: Danni becomes first contestant to leave Bake Off
description: Danni from Dorset was the first of 12 contestants to leave 17th series of the Great British Bake Off.
body: Danni said they enjoyed the technical challenges, which were "like a puzzle" An HGV service administrator from Dorset has become the first person to leave this year's Great British Bake Off. Danni was eliminated from the Channel 4 TV series during biscuit week after being told by judge Paul Hollywood their cookies were "powdery". During the episode, which aired on Tuesday, Danni said they had been unable to taste the cookies because the ingredients included cream and butter and they were vegan. They said competing on Bake Off gave them "some of the best advice about how to improve something that I love". Speaking to BBC Radio Solent's Dorset Breakfast show, they said: "It was absolutely fantastic, on and off camera. I was just hyped to be there. "Some of my favourite parts were the technicals which I was consistently not great on doing but I loved doing them so much... It's like a puzzle." The 17th Bake Off series began with 12 contestants Reflecting on their time in the tent, Danni said: "I've never been the best with making friends. "I'm quite an eccentric person and quite a Marmite person. "Going into it, I wasn't expecting to make friends. I wasn't expecting there to be so many lovely, lovely people. "It wasn't a competitive environment at all, it's just a bit of fun you are having with your friends." Hairdresser Tom, from West Yorkshire, was named star baker on Tuesday. During the episode, bakers made American-style cookies, recreated iced gems and created a "visually striking" biscuit mosaic. Danni - fourth from the right - is the first to leave the Bake Off tent Danni explained to Hollywood and fellow judge Nigella Lawson that they were vegan so could not try their own cinnamon "Snickerdoodle" cookies, topped with peanut brittle. Tasting the bakes, Lawson said the cookies had "too much cinnamon and bicarb", adding: "It's impossible to know what you are baking if you don't taste it." Following their elimination, Danni said: "I am really happy that I was the first one out because I know everyone in there has more skills than me. "But I think I've learned something about myself, which is that in the right circumstances I can make quite a few friends. "Finding love in a group of strangers – that's just beautiful." They added: "Of all the bakers there, I was easily the weakest, which isn't bad at all. "It means I have 11 other people to bug about baking questions now whenever I want." title: 'Rock, paper, scissors' decides order of London Marathon races
description: A game of rock, paper, scissors is used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place at next year's two-day London Marathon.
body: This video can not be played 'Absolutely incredible!' - Sawe breaks sub 2-hour marathon world record in London A game of rock, paper, scissors was used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place at next year's unique two-day London Marathon. Men's world record holder Sabastian Sawe was beaten by women's wheelchair world record holder Catherine Debrunner - both 2026 London Marathon champions in their respective races - in the contest. As a result, the elite men and men's wheelchair races are set for Saturday, 24 April, with the women's events taking place the following day on the traditional Sunday. Hugh Brasher, chief executive of London Marathon Events, said: "Sabastian and Catherine's rock, paper, scissors battle was an entertaining way to decide which day would host each elite race. "Splitting the elite races will allow us to shine an even brighter spotlight on the extraordinary athletes taking part." Earlier this year, organisers of the event confirmed the London Marathon will be held across two days in what is said to be a momentous one-off edition of the event. The decision was made to enable more people to take part, after a record 1.33 million people entered the ballot for next year. In 2027 a record-breaking 100,000 participants will take part and it is estimated that more than £150m will be raised for charitable causes. The women's championship categories will line-up behind the women's elite field for the first time in the London race. "Our outstanding elite women's wheelchair field will begin the action just ahead of them, creating a true celebration of women's marathon racing," Brasher added. The main events on both days will be a mixed field of male, female and non-binary participants. title: Couple describes relief at rescue after whale destroys their yacht
description: Jeremy and Gemma Cooper were 500 miles off the coast of New Zealand when their yacht, the Tai Tam, collided with a sperm whale.
body: This video can not be played A couple have spoken of their relief to be rescued after a sperm whale collided with their yacht. Jeremy and Gemma Cooper told the BBC that they were 500 nautical miles off the coast of New Zealand when the boat, the Tai Tam, lurched port side and they knew they'd "been hit by something" - only to see a pod of six sperm whales swimming behind the boat. As their boat took on water and eventually sank, the Coopers and two other sailors aboard the vessel evacuated to a life raft. Seventeen hours later they were rescued by a container ship. The couple told the BBC that, despite their ordeal, they would be out on the water again soon. Video produced by Lana Lam, edited by Alex Foster. title: Sussexes condemn 'reckless intrusion' after men spotted near Archie and Lilibet's school
description: One of the men seen outside the UK school attended by the children is understood to be an international press photographer.
body: Meghan and Harry pictured at the Za'atari refugee camp earlier this year The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have accused an international photographer of "extraordinary recklessness" for looking into the grounds of the school attended by their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. Two men, both wearing backpacks, were spotted circling the perimeter of the school, with police later identifying one of them as an international press photographer. A spokesman for Prince Harry and Meghan called it "an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children". Harry, Meghan, and their children returned to the UK last month after living in California for six years. Harry and Meghan's return to UK reignites questions over security Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like? Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in Britain after six years in US The BBC understands that the two men were observed by both private security and school staff, stopping at various points and looking into the school grounds, before returning to a van which police later established was a rental vehicle. One of the men was later identified to be an international photographer is believed to work for a known European press agency. "The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless," Harry and Meghan's spokesman said. "There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day." The spokesman continued: "Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school." The children began school in the UK at the start of September, but changed after a few days after security concerns were raised about traffic during the school run. Earlier this month, it emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their move back. Meghan previously shared a glimpse of family life back in England to Instagram In August, it was reported that the Sussexes would be moving back to the UK and they are thought to be basing themselves at a private property in the Cotswolds area. Their surprise announcement reignited questions over the level of their publicly funded security in Britain, a topic that has long been a source of anger for Prince Harry. It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors. Ravec will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs. title: Jay Slater's mum says retracing his last steps in Tenerife gave her 'more closure'
description: Debbie Duncan went to Tenerife to trace her son Jay's final steps before his death in 2024.
body: Debbie Duncan says retracing her son Jay Slater''s footsteps has given her "more closure" The mother of Jay Slater, who died after he went missing in Tenerife, has said retracing his footsteps was "very tough and emotional" but had given her "more closure". Jay, 19, and from Oswaldtwistle in Lancashire, went missing on 17 June 2024 after attending a music festival in Playa de las Americas on the Spanish island, and was found dead after a 29-day search. His mother, Debbie Duncan, told BBC Radio Lancashire she hoped after watching a forthcoming documentary on the case, people "may well believe the facts". The first episode of the Channel Five series "Cause of Death", which will explore the manhunt and huge social media interest around the case, will air at 21:00 BST on Wednesday. An inquest into Jay's death ruled it was a "tragic accident," and entirely without third party influence. He had fallen in a "particularly dangerous area", and suffered skull fractures and brain trauma that killed him instantly. Jay Slater went missing in Tenerife in june 2024 Debbie said retracing her son's steps helped her, because "we could look at the terrain in more detail". "It was the timeline for me, from his location... to him saying 'I don't know where I am, I am lost'. So that was important to me, to time it." The episode retraces his steps alongside forensic pathologist Richard Shepherd, who carried out Jay's postmortem when his body was returned to the UK. "Having Dr Shepherd there to talk more about his injuries was just really good," Debbie said, adding he had been able "to explain it in more simple terms". "It was very tough and emotional going back there, but we have got more closure. Obviously I didn't question for one minute it was an accident," she said. She said the family were "all coping in different ways" since Jay's death. "I'm trying to keep busy, and I am in contact with other bereaved families. "I can't say it helps, but talking to other parents who have gone through losing their children, you know you are not on your own." Last year, she called for Jay's Law to prevent the online trolling of grieving families. Following his disappearance, a number of theories about what had happened to him began to circulate on social media. She said the law would be "aimed at tech companies" and obligate them "to take down misinformation". She added that "the conspiracies were wild". "People have said you are taking away our freedom of speech. "It's not about freedom of speech. It's downright bullying. They know the facts but they don't want to believe them, they just go along withe their own narrative." She said "the right people were listening" to her campaign. But she said it had not got easier to live without Jay, adding: "It seems to get harder to be honest." title: Luxury prison in Indonesia demolished after public outcry
description: Indonesian lawmakers on Wednesday ordered the demolition of a controversial luxury compound inside a penitentiary near the capital.
body: This video can not be played A prison compound in Indonesia has been demolished after public outcry following the discovery of luxury apartments within the penitentiary. Investigators reported finding luxury facilities in Cibinong Prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, allegedly used by favoured inmates during a surprise inspection on 23 September. The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex. Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff. The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia's prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery. title: Ocon to leave Haas putting F1 future in doubt
description: Esteban Ocon is fighting to save his Formula 1 career after the Haas team announcement that they are splitting with the Frenchman at the end of the year.
body: Ocon has taken one win and four podiums in his 10-year career in F1 Esteban Ocon is fighting to save his Formula 1 career after the Haas team announced they would split with the Frenchman at the end of the year. Ocon, who won the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix for Alpine, joined Haas in 2025. He has been in F1 since 2016 and has also driven for the Manor and Force India teams. There are no obvious berths for Ocon on the grid in 2027 but he insisted: "This is absolutely not the end of my Formula 1 career." The 30-year-old added in a statement on social media: "I leave this project with my head held high and proud of my performances in what were not always the easiest of circumstances for various reasons and factors outside of my control. "My immediate focus is the next race weekend. I will continue to work hard with the team, maximise every opportunity, and keep extracting every bit of performance from the car. "There are still many races to go this season and, as always, I will give it my everything behind the wheel for myself and for my team. "I am still motivated. I am still hungry." Ocon has been outperformed by team-mate Oliver Bearman since joining forces with Haas last year. This year, the Briton is 13th in the championship, three places and 13 points ahead of Ocon. Bearman has out-qualified Ocon 13-6 at an average advantage of 0.144 seconds. Last year, Bearman finished 13th and Ocon 15th, separated by just three points, and in qualifying it was 18-7 at 0.175secs Haas team principal Ayao Kumatso said: "Esteban's professionalism and commitment have proved valuable as we continue to grow as an organisation. "Together this year we tackled the challenge of a major regulation change, where Esteban's driving experience and inputs were significant as we've worked hard to develop the VF-26 across the season."
