title: Regulating AI 'not the right place to start' says Bank of England governor
description: AI needs "rigorous" testing and safeguards to contain risk, Andrew Bailey says.
body: The Governor of the Bank of England has said regulating artificial intelligence (AI) "is not the right place to start" but instead called first for "rigorous" testing to find vulnerabilities and safeguards to contain risk. Writing his first-ever article for Substack, Andrew Bailey said the risks around AI were "real and increasingly significant". Bailey said the development of AI should not be halted or prohibited - "on the contrary, the benefits are immense" - but added there must be a system for intervention and to establish boundaries in which AI operates. In recent weeks, the debate about the potential risks surrounding the rapid development of AI and what it means for humanity has intensified. The bosses of leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI have called for development of the technology to slow down and for an internationally co-ordinated approach assessing risks and putting safeguards in place. OpenAI recently announced that it would not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns. The idea of a slowdown, however, has been rejected by the likes of President Donald Trump who has said the US is leading the AI race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins." But on Tuesday, after hosting a summit with the leading firms in AI such as OpenAI and Anthropic, Trump said executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns Under the agreement, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. In the UK, Bailey said "important work" was underway in testing AI - the UK has set up the AI Security Institute - which, he said, should help form part of a set of standards. "But the pace of progress must accelerate," the bank governor said, though he added: "We should proceed with a degree of humility." He said, with testing, there will be failures and "models will behave unexpectedly". But, he said: "That is not evidence that testing has failed, rather it is evidence of why testing is necessary." Bailey said that testing should not be seen as an alternative to future regulation - over time a more formal regulatory framework might emerge. "But regulation is not, in my view, the right place to start." title: Richards 'devastated' by Man City guilty verdicts
description: Former Manchester City defender Micah Richards felt "absolutely devastated" after reading the Premier League's "damning" verdict on the club's financial charges.
body: Micah Richards was on the Manchester City bench when Sergio Aguero scored his title-winning goal in 2012 Former Manchester City defender Micah Richards says he felt "absolutely devastated" after reading the Premier League's "damning" guilty verdict on the club's financial charges. An independent commission found that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m. The league confirmed City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and all but one in relation to failure to co-operate with the investigation. The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal. During that nine-year period the Sky Blues won the Premier League three times, with Richards part of their title-winning squad in 2011-12. "The reports were troubling," he said on The Rest is Football podcast. "I saw the words which were used by the Premier League in 'sham contracts' and I felt absolutely devastated. "I was at that club since I was 14 years old, I would die for that club. I achieved my dream at Manchester City, but then to hear these reports, and not only me as an ex-player, but the fans, what they have to go through, absolutely devastating." While Richards was part of the City's youth academy he lived in 'digs' with a local family who are long-term supporters of the club. The 38-year-old added: "My digs man, he rang me and he was literally in tears and asking me about information, which I don't know. I haven't got the answers to tell him. "That's someone who's supported the club for 60-odd years and the uncertainty around it is just heartbreaking. "To have a headline of this nature for a club that I love so much, it's been difficult. If you listen to the reports, they are damning. "I feel saddened, I feel angry, I feel a little bit confused because, on the other side, you have City's side of the story." City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a statement on Saturday that the club is still confident of proving its innocence, while on Tuesday chief executive Ferran Soriano said in a video message, external to staff and players that "irrefutable evidence" had been "ignored" by the commission. City won their second Premier League title in 2013-14, overtaking Liverpool during the run-in to finish two points above the Reds. Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher, who retired in 2013, said: "I feel for the players... they'll almost feel like a lot of their career is going to have an asterisk, or a lot of people will be calling it a sham. "The players were told everything was fine. What the [City] hierarchy are coming out with now, they're just gaslighting. "I think the titles should be taken off their list. Whether other clubs get them is probably slightly different. City have not just hurt their own players." The 2013-14 season was the closest that Carragher's long-time team-mate Steven Gerrard came to winning the Premier League title. "Those players will never get that feeling and it was robbed by Man City," Carragher added on Sky Sports News. "No-one remembers the medal. Giving trophies or medals back, it doesn't mean anything. It's not about medals, it's about feelings." £1.2bn on transfers with £830m inflated in accounts - Man City's 'asterisk era' The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League Latest Manchester City news, analysis and fan views Ask about Man City - what do you want to know? title: Singapore launches matchmaking service for government workers
description: The launch of FirstDate comes as the ageing nation wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.
body: FirstDate launched this week for government workers in Singapore aged 21 to 35 Singapore has rolled out a matchmaking service for its government workers, an initiative that comes as the country wrestles with a record-low fertility rate. FirstDate, which launched this week for those aged 21 to 35, boasts "a different approach to dating", where it uses a Nobel-winning algorithm to match participants to one date at a time. "Swipe fatigue ends here," its website reads. Participants sign in using the national digital identity system and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values. FirstDate's launch drew mixed responses among Singaporeans, with some describing it as "dystopian" and others saying they would be keen to give it a shot. On its website, FirstDate highlights the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm which powers the programme. The mathematical framework pairs two equally sized groups of people based on their preferences. The late mathematician Lloyd Shapley was awarded the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences for discovering the algorithm, which has been used in public school admissions, medical residency matching, and dating apps, among other things. "At the end of the day, I think the experience of meeting someone through an application doesn't change much across the [different types of] applications," Elizabeth, a 29-year-old who works in Singapore's defence ministry and is keen on trying FirstDate out told the BBC. "But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower. We're all public servants looking for a partner, right?" But some social media users say the initiative, which is currently in its pilot phase, discriminates against those not working in government. Others criticised the age limit. "They are only doing this to raise the total fertility rate. They don't actually [care] about whether we find a partner otherwise. "Since there are higher risks involved in having kids at 35 and older, the government just writes [the older singles] off," wrote another Reddit user. It is not clear if the pilot programme will be available to the wider public in future. The BBC has reached out to GovTech, the statutory board behind the pilot, for comment. The pilot launch comes as Singapore's birth rate has slumped to historic lows. For the first time in the past 60 years, fewer than 30,000 babies were born in 2025. The number of deaths meanwhile have been rising steadily in the greying nation, hitting about 26,500 in 2025. In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to better support families and to encourage couples to have children, including almost S$70,000 ($54,000; £41,000) in financial support for every child by the time they turn 17. The launch of FirstDate comes as the ageing nation wrestles with a record-low fertility rate FirstDate is not the first time the citystate is trying to play Cupid to its citizens. In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit (SDU) tasked with organising social events to encourage graduate singles to mingle. Its exclusive target audience of university graduates was criticised as being elitist, but authorities justified the approach saying non-graduates did not seem to have difficulty finding partners. The SDU was eventually phased out. The next year, the government set up another agency to promote marriages among non-graduates. The idea of a government-run dating service is not unique to Singapore. In September 2024, Tokyo's metropolitan government launched an AI-powered dating app in an effort to combat the country's declining birth rate. The app, which is open to single residents in the city, resulted in 265 couples getting married, according to government data released in July this year. title: Young minds develop ideas to tackle climate change
description: Sixteen teenagers take part in a hackathon to devise ways to combat issues such as light pollution.
body: Baveen and Shanice focused on ideas to combat light pollution at the hackathon A group of young people have developed ideas to tackle the effects of climate change as part of a free touring exhibition. On Tuesday 16 young people took part in a hackathon - a timed event where people work together to build creative solutions to problems - where they devised posters with ways to combat light pollution, wild fires, damage to oceans and poor water quality. The event was hosted by Seeds of Hope and Change, an organisation run by the Soka Gakkai International and the UN Earth Charter, at the Jerwood Dancehouse in Ipswich. Maryanne, 16, took part in the project and said: "We just want people to be aware of what's going on, especially with major issues such as ocean pollution." Maryanne and Hannah discussed the challenge of pollution in seas and oceans Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions. This year's summer was the UK's hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office. The Met Office said the heat experienced this summer was made about 130 times more likely by human-induced climate change. Baveen, 17, said "We wanted to talk about the cities and the sky and how it affects people and also wildlife." The poster her group produced included ideas for using low-intensity bulbs and motion sensors in street lights so that they were not continuously left on. Each group at the hackathon put their ideas on big posters The exhibition, which is free and runs until 4 October, includes 24 pop-up panels that share information and environmental case studies from around the world on the impact of climate change. The hackathon for young people was run by ambassadors from the youth-led campaigning organisation #iWill. Alex Harrison, one of the #iWill ambassadors, said: "The main purpose is reminding young people that in the face of something really scary like climate change, there's a lot that you can do personally to make a real change." title: What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation
description: The woman alleges she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house at the university two years ago.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Why an investigation into alleged frat house gang rape is reopening New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house at the university. She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. The men have been dubbed the "Cornell Seven" and the woman was identified as Jane Doe in court filings. Cornell has said it supported presenting the case to a grand jury, while rejecting as "false" claims that it failed to punish those involved. Here's what we know about the case. Cornell in Ithaca, New York, is an elite US university In a 101-page civil lawsuit, the woman alleged that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine. She was a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate at the time. Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and incapable of providing consent. She says she left her sorority sisters after drinking that night and "stumbled alone" to the Chi Phi fraternity house in the city of Ithaca to see a male friend. The lawsuit alleges sexual assault and battery, negligence, breach of contract and violations of New York's Human Rights Law. It was filed against the university, fraternity sorority and men involved in the alleged attack. The lawsuit contains an image purported to be from a fraternity group chat in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe. Her lawyer has said she was "traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened" in the days after the assault, which she reported to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024. The outrage in recent weeks grew when Jane Doe alleged in her lawsuit that the men were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays". Doe's lawyer has said two of those involved were expelled. The university newspaper's editorial board published the names of the defendants in the lawsuit on 21 September in a piece titled "Cornell Won't, We Will", fuelling a social media outcry. Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity house in September 2026 The Cornell University Police Department provided an image of the Snapchat group, titled Chi Phi Actives, to prosecutors as evidence in November 2024, the university said. The members are named in the chat and discuss a "free" sexual encounter with Jane Doe, using coarse language, just before 02:00 local time on 20 October 2024. CBS News New York has also published excerpts of additional text messages reportedly exchanged between one of the defendants and a woman who appears to be the person who made the allegations. The messages were reportedly sent two days after the alleged assault. In one of the messages, one of the men appeared to apologise for "how things went down". He said his memory was "kinda fuzzy", and that he and another man felt bad for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand". The woman in the text chain replied saying her memory was "super clouded too" and that they were all intoxicated. She also wrote that "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal", that she liked being with him and another man. Doe suggested they smoke together again, but leave out "the extra 5 billion men and ketamine". The woman said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police two weeks after it took place. Shortly after, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house". It said that the campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students". Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law, which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities. Following the new lawsuit, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators. The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell". Cornell did not deny that the punishment for some of those involved included writing an essay. But it said: "None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement." In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell said "temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures" were issued when the conduct was reported. It also said the events that took place on its campus in 2024 "were appalling then and remain so now". "We are doing all we can to foster a culture where sexual misconduct is never tolerated," it said. The Xi Chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus. US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University The county's top prosecutor said on Monday that his office would reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape. Once appropriate charges were determined, the case would be prosecuted "in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, said Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten. In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges. title: Israel-bound flight diverted after fight between pilots
description: Despite a brief emergency alert signalling a hijacking, the Israeli prime minister's office confirmed this had been ruled out.
body: The Flydubai plane took off early on Wednesday morning (Stock photo) A flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was unexpectedly diverted to Saudi Arabia after a fight between the pilots, Israeli officials told local media. The Flydubai plane - which took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates early on Wednesday morning - signalled an emergency code two hours into the journey, flight tracking website Flightradar24 said. Minutes later it switched to a code used to report a hijacking, but was later turned back to the general emergency signal, it added. The Israeli prime minister's office said the incident was not believed to have been a hijacking. Passengers told local media they feared or their lives as the plane started to drop during the incident. The emergency signal is thought to be issued following an altercation between the pilot and co-pilot, local media reported citing Israeli defence officials. Flight FZ1073 - carrying around 150 people, most of whom are Israeli - was due to land at Ben-Gurion Airport but instead landed at Tabuk Airport in northeastern Saudi Arabia. A Flydubai spokesperson confirmed the flight "experienced an incident while en route", and that updates will be issued as further details become available. "Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities," it added. Data from Flightrader24 shows a rapid descent for the plane over Saudi Arabia, just two hours after take-off, descending more than 17,000 feet (over 5000 m) in less than two minutes just after 05:21 UTC (06:21 BST). At 05:40, the flight briefly entered Jordanian airspace before looping back into Saudi Arabia minutes later, where it then began its descent for landing. The Israeli air force dispatched fighter jets in response to the incident and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held urgent consultations on the incident. title: US actor Chad Lowe 'heartbroken' by death of daughter Fiona aged 13
description: Lowe and his wife Kim Painter announce the death of their daughter, who "was the light of our lives".
body: US actor Chad Lowe and his wife, producer Kim Painter, have said they are "deeply heartbroken" following the death of their "beloved" 13-year-old daughter Fiona. "She was a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance," the family said in a statement to Page Six, external and People, external. "She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives. "Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time." The statement concluded: "If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988." Chad Lowe, the brother of fellow actor Rob Lowe, won an Emmy Award in 1993 for TV show Life Goes On and has appeared in other programmes including Pretty Little Liars and Supergirl. He and Painter are also parents to daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, 10. title: Greggs to shut four factories and cut 740 jobs
description: The company says it needs to "keep evolving alongside changing customer expectations".
body: Greggs said proposals would not affect its shops High street bakery brand Greggs has announced plans to shut four of its factories and cut 740 jobs. It plans to close manufacturing sites at North Lakes near Penrith, Cumbria, Pettigrews in Kelso, Scotland, Seaham in County Durham and Enfield, Greater London, though distribution operations would continue to run from the latter. The proposals will also impact manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will also continue as a distribution centre for the business. The chain, which has headquarters in Newcastle, said its retail shops would not be affected by the proposed changes. The changes would take place over the next two-and-a-half years, with parts of Greggs' manufacturing processes relocating, the firm said. The range of products manufactured at its Clydesmill Glasgow and Manchester locations would be reduced and production of tinned bread at Gosforth would be stopped. Some products would also be sourced from specialist suppliers. Chief executive Roisin Currie said the company needed to "keep evolving alongside changing customer expectations". She said: "Greggs manufacturing and logistics network remains a key strength of the business, and these proposals are intended to strengthen our manufacturing network, improve efficiency and ensure we remain well placed for the future while continuing to deliver the quality, value and service our customers expect." The firm employs 33,000 people in the UK, the majority working in its stores. A consultation with staff is expected to start soon and the company said "no final decisions" had been made yet. The shake-up is expected to cost the firm about £60m, including disruption costs and redundancy payments. It said the plans would save it about £20m across the 2028 and 2029 financial years. The retail business said its sales grew by 7.7% in the three months to September 26, compared with the same period a year earlier. It said this represented progress in the face of "challenging market conditions", as consumer finances continued to come under pressure. The company said positive trading and continued cost control meant it expected a "modestly improved outcome" for 2026. Greggs opened 95 new shops and closed 38 in the year to date, taking its overall estate to 2,796 shops. title: 'He will never walk free': Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
description: In the emotional letter, the judge describes the survivor as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".
body: More than 69,000 cases of child sexual abuse were recorded in India in 2024 alone (representative image) An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India. Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen". The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274). At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage". "When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor. "Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added. Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth". "The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again. "The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again." Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage". Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims. It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him. Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money. Tensions in Indian state after 11-year-old raped and murdered The child abuse survivor fighting to save others India media storm over 10-year-old pregnant rape victim The emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge. Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven. The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external. And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities. Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life. In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child. After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child. title: Africa's richest man to launch Kenya oil refinery despite land protests
description: The Kenya refinery is part of Dangote's ambitious bid to expand and help industralise Africa by 2030.
body: Aliko Dangote made his fortune in cement before branching into oil Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto are set to break ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast. Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity. Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery. Speaking to the BBC, Dangote dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned. The Lamu refinery is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway. East Africa does not currently have any oil refineries. In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available. "To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests. At the height of construction, Dangote, who is Africa's richest man, said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project. "Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said. Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline. But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region. "Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said. Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example. "Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said. This video can not be played Dangote speaks to the BBC about his new oil refinery in Kenya The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant. Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally. He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand. In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area. "The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said. Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump. The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria, with construction due to begin on 1 November. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day. Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1b earlier this month. title: More talks over Drumcree dispute as stalemate continues
description: Lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition issued a fresh legal bid on Tuesday to try to prevent the march from going ahead.
body: Portadown District Lodge made their way from Drumcree Church and were stopped by police officers on Tuesday night The Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, is planning further talks on Wednesday over the the controversial Drumcree march. It comes after lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition issued a fresh legal bid to try to prevent the march from going ahead. Members of the Orange Order are still waiting to begin their permitted parade, which was due to take place on Sunday, and walk down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown. The residents' appeal will be the latest challenge to the march, which was given the go ahead after three separate legal hearings over the course of 13 hours late on Saturday and into the early hours of Sunday morning. A group of protesters remain at the Garvaghy Road. Members of the Orange Order left Drumcree Church overnight - for the first time since the stand off began - but Deputy District Master Alastair Power returned on Wednesday morning. He said other members would also be there throughout the day. There was another attempt by Portadown District Lodge to walk the route at 22:10 BST on Tuesday. Accompanied by DUP MP Carla Lockhart, Power asked the police if they could facilitate their parade. The answer was no. Members of the Orange Order started to return to Drumcree Church on Wednesday The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in almost 30 years after a series of legal challenges. Since 1998, the Orange Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes. The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation, while the area where it wants to walk - specifically along the Garvaghy Road - is largely Catholic and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists. Both the Orange Order and members of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition met Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle again on Tuesday. Speaking on his way into the talks, Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, said "reroute the sectarian parade, that's it". Speaking after a separate meeting with the secretary of state, Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said the talks had been "positive and constructive". Later, hundreds of people attended a meeting beside St John the Baptist Church on the Garvaghy Road for an update on the talks process. Speaking to the media outside the hall, Mac Cionnaith said the only person the residents had left to meet was PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher. He said he will be waiting for Boutcher to let him know when the meeting would happen, adding: "Or is he going to hide behind a wall of uniforms of police in riot gear?" A police Land Rover remains on the road on Wednesday morning Meanwhile, the Portadown district master told hundreds of supporters at an outdoor rally in the town that unionist leaders needed to keep pressure on the secretary of state and chief constable and that the law must be "respected and applied". Nigel Dawson said: "Tonight, my position, our position, is very, very clear. The chief constable, who is responsible for ensuring the law is complied in this country, must apply the law. "He must respect the High Court judgement and he must deliver us safely and securely back to Carleton Street Orange Hall via the Garvaghy Road because that's what the Parade's Commission said and that is what a High Court has said. "He needs to deliver that now." Sinn Féin have called on the Irish government to intervene in the dispute. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Parading, policing and power sharing collide amid Drumcree dispute Drumcree parade resolution not going to be easy - NI secretary The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident. However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas. The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. The row sparked some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history and was linked to several murders. The row reemerged after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission - the organisation formed during the Drumcree dispute to decide on contentious marches during Northern Ireland's parading season - was overturned. On Friday, following 28 years of unsuccessful applications, the commission decided the march could go ahead with restrictions in place. Rather than start at 13:00 on Sunday as intended, the commission said it could begin no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. However that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go ahead just hours before it was due to take place. Protesters spent more than a day along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of points The Drumcree dispute was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes during the 1990s, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders across Northern Ireland. title: Tumultuous summer ends in success - what next for Stokes?
description: After concluding the county summer with Durham and the end of his England central contract, what is in store for Ben Stokes?
body: Ben Stokes took 25 wickets in seven Championship matches in 2026 As cricket prepares to go into hibernation for the winter after the usual summer slog, Ben Stokes' playing diary is a lot quieter than previously. For the first time since 2014, there will be no central contract from the England and Wales Cricket Board as he begins the next chapter of his career. The 35-year-old caused one of the sporting stories of the year when he announced in the middle of a Test decider against New Zealand that he was walking away from the England captaincy and international cricket as a whole. Initial sanctuary has come at his own county, Durham, where he has been a wholehearted and willing contributor to their Division Two title success. But it is a long six months before whites will be seen around English grounds again, and it means one of the greatest all-rounders the game has ever seen - and arguably the game's best player over the past decade - is now open to offers. So what next for Stokes? Tough chats and Three Peaks - Durham's road to the title Campbell moves to Durham director of cricket role As England's Test team start focusing on a Christmas tour to South Africa, Stokes is heading to Australia for the festive period. That's because he has signed to play in the Big Bash for Adelaide Strikers as he plays in the T20 competition for the first time since 2015. From there, Stokes has a variety of options as the gates of the franchise world are open to him. But there are also complications. A global superstar like him would surely be of interest in India, but he did not take part in the IPL's mega auction in 2025 because of England commitments. Overseas players who have previously played in the IPL - as Stokes has done for Chennai Super Kings, Rajasthan Royals and Rising Pune Supergiant - must register for the mega-auction that takes place every three years, or miss the subsequent two mini-auctions. As things stand, that makes him ineligible until the 2028 edition. South Africa's SA 20 begins just before the Big Bash finishes, while the Pakistan Super League, which is expected to run concurrently with the IPL in the spring, would love a headliner like Stokes to bring some stardust and eyeballs to their tournament. Head into the summer and there is Major League Cricket in the United States. But this is where another complication may arise. If Stokes wants to play for Durham, or signs a contract that includes any white-ball cricket in the T20 Blast or One-Day Cup, he would need a special No-Objection Certificate (NOC) from the ECB to play in a franchise league that clashes with domestic competitions for which they are contracted. And the ECB has previously refused NOCs to former England players who have wanted to pursue freelance T20 careers. Retirement the best thing for me - Stokes England captain Ben Stokes announces retirement 12 Dec 2026 - 26 Jan 2027: Big Bash (Australia) 17 Jan - 21 Feb: SA T20 (South Africa) 14 Mar - 30 May: IPL (India) Apr - May: PSL (Pakistan) Mid-June - mid-July: Major League Cricket (USA) Stokes played all 10 of Durham's matches in the One-Day Cup And then there is his boyhood club, Durham. It is where Stokes has wholeheartedly thrown himself into things away from the England spotlight. After a family holiday, he returned to play in all 10 of their One-Day Cup games as they reached the semi-finals, before turning out in four of their remaining six Championship matches as the side romped to the Division Two title by 47 points, going unbeaten in the process. There were plenty of highlights, too. He smashed an unbeaten 108 away to Derbyshire in his first game away from the international spotlight in the 50-over competition in July. In the Championship, he hit four half-centuries in 10 innings and averaged 47.88 but it was with the ball in hand that the fireworks happened. His rapid burst of 5-17 blew away Derbyshire again last month and, in a dead rubber at home to Worcestershire in the penultimate game, with the title already secured, Stokes produced one of his marathon spells to finish with 6-94 off 31.3 overs - the most wickets and overs of any bowler in the team. His 25 wickets this season came at average of 20.36 and he demonstrated once again that he remains a fearsome and competitive animal when the match is on the line. But Durham now need to discuss with Stokes how next summer will look, and it will be one of the first tasks for Ryan Campbell in his new role as director of cricket. The Australian has spent the past four seasons as head coach, and enjoyed having Stokes in the dressing room and part of his team, and he believes that the all-rounder is keen to continue playing county cricket - and the red-ball stuff in particular. "Yes, I do, I honestly do," Campbell told BBC Sport in an interview before his new role was announced. "His love of the game, he talks about his bowling run-up and stuff that he can adapt to county cricket so he can bowl more. The playing, the batting, where he wants to bat, this sort of stuff, he's all-in I would have thought for the next couple of years at least." When Stokes was suspended by the ECB for the second Test in June, it was Durham where he rediscovered his love of the game after the troubles of the Ashes in Australia last winter and the broken curfew post-Lords. Being in and around the Riverside, singing the Blaydon Races after team victories and helping academy youngsters with practice is something that has not gone unnoticed. "Ben's England through-and-through, but he is Durham through-and-through," said Campbell. "He loves the club. The proudest thing I've ever had in relation to our work was when he said, 'I want to go back and play at Durham because the time there has been so amazing'. That's a big rap for our club and our environment that we've created." Stokes last played in the IPL in 2023 for Chennai Super Kings But as Stokes contemplates his fu

title: Somali pirates killed oil tanker crew before rescue, official tells BBC
description: Piracy off the Somali coast has increased in recent years after dropping when international naval operations began in 2011.
body: Security forces from Puntland have stepped up patrols amid increasing pirate attacks off the coast of Somalia Five crew members of an oil tanker seized by pirates off the coast of Somalia were killed before local security forces retook the vessel, a senior regional official has told the BBC. Puntland Deputy Information Minister Bile Qabowsade said the five were killed by pirates before regional forces boarded MT Hoarner 25. He said the dead included three Pakistani nationals, one Indian and one national of Myanmar. Four other crew members were injured, including three Pakistanis and one Indian. The tanker, which was carrying about 18,500 barrels of oil destined for the Somali capital, Mogadishu, was seized in April by six armed men while sailing off the coast of Somalia. Sixteen suspected pirates have been arrested, while others escaped and were being pursued, officials said. Qabowsade rejected suggestions that forces from Puntland, a semi-autonomous region of Somalia, had helped some of the pirates escape. The authorities have not given further details how the five crew members were killed or how the pirates took control of the vessel. The hijacked tanker was anchored near the Somali coast between the fishing towns of Xaafun and Bander Beyla. In April, officials had said there were 17 crew members on board when the vessel was hijacked. They included 10 Pakistanis, four Indonesians, one Indian, one Sri Lankan and a Myanmar national. Piracy off the Somali coast fell sharply after 2011 following international naval operations, but attacks and hijackings have increased again in recent years. title: The Premier League footballers studying to become sporting directors
description: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Taiwo Awoniyi and others have been juggling education with a football career - even studying on the team bus during away trips.
body: Steve Cook and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall are among those looking at football careers beyond their playing days The scene resembles an Oxbridge graduation ceremony, but those gathered in caps and gowns are in fact Premier League footballers or former players who have won major honours in Europe and around the world. The 2026 cohort of graduates from the PFA Business School includes Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Coventry City striker Taiwo Awoniyi and a host of well-known figures. In the event at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, Cesar Azpilicueta tells the group how studying on the morning of the 2021 Champions League final helped take his mind off the occasion before he captained Chelsea to a 1-0 win over Manchester City in Porto. Dewsbury-Hall, 28, travelled by train from Merseyside to London to attend the ceremony and, despite being in the best form of his career, explains why he had completed a postgraduate diploma in global football sport directorship. The former Leicester City and Chelsea player tells BBC Sport: "I hope I've got a long time left in football. But as a person, I'm always trying to learn and develop away from the pitch. I don't want to stop playing and then just sit around doing nothing. "This was something that genuinely interested me. Whether I use it in the future, we'll see, but it's always good to do it now rather than wait until you've finished playing. "If the time ever comes when an opportunity presents itself, luckily I've got something that can help me." The assembled players are potential leaders in football's future. Awoniyi, 29, joined Coventry from Nottingham Forest during the summer, and he remains part of Nigeria's squad as they attempt to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations. The striker has also continued his studies throughout his playing career. "I've got a degree in business management and another diploma, so this is my third qualification," he says. Awoniyi's father, Solomon, has previously spoken about his strict approach to education. At times it almost prevented his son from pursuing a career in football, but Awoniyi progressed from the Imperial Soccer Academy to Liverpool before making his name in German football with Union Berlin. "I say to people I am a quiet dreamer," says Awoniyi, who was born in Ilorin, Nigeria. "I always felt education was important. It was a promise I made to my dad that if I played football, I would keep studying. "That's what I have done and I am proud of it." Awoniyi says footballers have plenty of time available to study, but understands it is not for everyone Awoniyi points to the "ups and downs" he has experienced as a footballer, referencing the serious injury he suffered in May 2025 when he was placed in a medically induced coma after rupturing an intestine in a collision with a goalpost when playing for Nottingham Forest against Leicester City. To him, it is important to keep improving and to recognise there is more to life than football, which is where the Professional Footballers' Association course comes in. Awoniyi says: "It's not like a 9-5 job in football. We go in and sometimes finish quite early and, although it's challenging, I think every footballer has time in the evening for something like this business school. "Of course, it demands a lot from you and it's all about how willing you are to do it. I say to people there are a lot of things that are bigger than football. "Yes, football is our passion, but we are normal human beings as well and maybe that's something the world doesn't always see." The graduates certainly appear no different from anyone else celebrating an academic achievement, exhibiting their pride. Awoniyi has brought members of his extended family to the ceremony, while Dewsbury-Hall seeks out former Everton midfielder Tim Cahill, now working in Qatari football, to discuss the art of scoring goals. "Obviously there are stereotypes around footballers," Dewsbury-Hall says. "But in every industry there are smart people and there are people who aren't so smart. You'd be surprised how many intelligent people there are in football. "Maybe some players just don't want to do things like this, but they easily could. It's just not their passion. "I'm not saying this is my passion, but it's something I've done to show that footballers can complete these kinds of courses while they're still playing. Who knows where it will lead?" The course is designed to run alongside a football career. Seminars are scheduled to minimise clashes with matches and training sessions. Players can study in their own time, although Dewsbury-Hall says he has had some "weird looks" while studying on an iPad during journeys home from away games. Every graduate has a different story. For Wycombe Wanderers defender Steve Cook, who captained Bournemouth in the Premier League earlier in his career, the course marked a return to formal education for the first time since his school days. Having already obtained coaching badges, he knows he is approaching the end of his playing career. Some may not actively use their newly gained expertise for many years. All will benefit in some way, though, believes Azpilicueta. "It's not only about preparing for life after football. It's about becoming a better version of yourself in your football career as well," the former Spain defender, who retired from playing at the end of last season, tells BBC Sport. Education has been part of his life and is what helped him become a leader on and off the pitch. Azpilicueta built a career after turning professional with hometown club Osasuna at the age of 17. He had continued studying until that point and, after abandoning his degree when he became a professional footballer, he later returned to complete an MBA at Harvard University in the United States during his nine-year spell at Chelsea. title: Orionid meteor shower to streak across night sky this week
description: The Orionid meteor shower peaks in October as Earth passes through debris left behind by Halley’s Comet.
body: One of the best-known meteor showers of the year is returning to our skies this week, as the Earth passes through debris left behind by Halley's Comet. The Orionid meteor shower is active from 2 October until 7 November and will peak overnight from 21 to 22 October. The display occurs at around the same time each year as the Earth passes through a trail of dust and debris left behind by Halley's Comet. The best time to spot the meteors will be between midnight and dawn, when the sky is at its darkest. As tiny particles from the comet enter the Earth's atmosphere at high speed, they heat up and produce streaks of light across the night sky that we see as meteors. The Orionids are particularly fast, entering the atmosphere at around 41 miles per second and can leave glowing trails which remain visible for several seconds. Halley's Comet is one of the most famous comets in our Solar System and has been observed from Earth for centuries. It takes around 76 years to complete one orbit of the Sun and was last seen from Earth in 1986. But while the comet itself is a rare visitor, the Earth encounters material left behind by it twice a year, resulting in the Eta Aquariid meteor shower in May and the Orionids in October. Halley's Comet is not expected to be visible from Earth again until 2061, but its debris will continue to produce meteor showers each year Under ideal conditions, around 10 to 20 meteors can be seen each hour at the shower's peak. The meteors appear to radiate from the constellation of Orion, which is where the shower gets its name, but they can appear anywhere across the night sky. For the best chance of seeing them, find a dark location away from street lights and with as wide a view of the sky as possible. Allow around 15 to 20 minutes for your eyes to adjust. You won't need binoculars or a telescope; the shower is best viewed with the naked eye. Viewing prospects will be rather mixed with the best conditions likely to be across southern and eastern parts of England - where there should be long clear spells, albeit with a few areas of cloud drifting across the sky from time-to-time. In Wales, the Midlands and Northern England it may be more of a struggle to see the meteor shower, with a slow-moving weather front providing cloud and outbreaks of rain. The rain is likely to turn patchier later in the night with a few cloud breaks likely to develop. For Scotland and Northern Ireland it will be a story of clear periods, patchy cloud and a few showers - and if the gaps between the showers are long enough you should get a view for at least some of the time. The Moon could also affect how many meteors are visible at the peak of the Orionids later in October, as it will be in its waxing gibbous phase, meaning its light could make some of the fainter meteors more difficult to see. Brighter meteors however should still be visible, particularly from darker locations away from artificial light. title: Man City charges leave football fans questioning legitimacy of team's achievements
description: BBC Sport analyses Manchester City's dominance of English football during the period in which they were breaching financial rules.
body: This video can not be played Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts & misleading accounts Outside Manchester City's Etihad Stadium is a lustrous silver statue of Sergio Aguero - mouth agape in ecstasy, kit swirling over his head - depicting his goal celebration after securing the club's first Premier League title. It is the immortalisation of the most famous goal in English league football history, when City snatched the trophy away from Manchester United in the dying seconds of the 2011-12 season. But what if the goal never happened? What if Aguero had never played for the club? What if City had opted to abide by football's financial rules instead of purposefully breaking them through a "disguised funding scheme"? The revelation that the club has been found guilty of the charges brought against it by the Premier League three and a half years ago has left football fans around the world questioning the legitimacy of City's achievements between 2009 and 2018, when they were the most successful club in English football and cemented themselves among the global game's elite. Some fans are referring to it as the asterisk era, and there is a possibility City could be retroactively stripped of the honours they earned during the period, with some clubs seeking legal advice over potential financial compensation. So how exactly did City's "hugely overstated" income impact their actions in the transfer market, how key were the players who were brought in, and what does it all mean for both the past and the future? Long-time captain Vincent Kompany joined Manchester City before the era in which they breached financial rules, but stars such as Kevin de Bruyne, Sergio Aguero, Fernandinho and David Silva were signed during it Manchester City spent about £1.2bn on new players in the transfer windows between summer 2009 and January 2018. In that time, the club won seven major trophies - three Premier Leagues, one FA Cup, and three EFL Cups - having previously gone without a significant honour since 1970. The players they purchased during that time included some of the world's best, in all areas of the pitch. Multiple were signed for figures in the tens of millions every summer and made a huge contribution to the club's consistent success. The graphic below demonstrates how much City spent in each summer and across the whole time period, and contrasts it with the amount of money that the commission which has found the club guilty determined had been falsely pumped into the club by its owners, under the guise of sponsorship income. City did not only generate revenue from sponsorship funds in that time. And income is also spent on many things other than transfers, including player wages, utilities, insurance, infrastructure, marketing, foundations and more. But the figures underline the fact that City would simply not have been able to purchase the quantity and quality of players they signed during their era of domination had they not been conducting what the commission described as a "concerted campaign to falsify" their financial accounts. If City's financial power had been slashed by the extra £830m the commission says they falsely added to their books, their transfer spend would surely have been massively reduced. Chop the amount in half, say, and maybe they would only have brought in half the amount of players. Or the same amount, but heavily reduced in quality. Which potentially means no Aguero, no David Silva, no Yaya Toure, no Kevin de Bruyne, or at least a significant reduction in the number or ability of the less glamorous players who were key cogs in the trophy-winning machine. Would those successes have been achieved had the rule breaking not been going on in tandem? And what would the impact have been on all the other clubs who have played in the Premier League during that time? Nobody will ever know. The seasons cannot be replayed. And so the outcomes exist in a kind of mixed reality where the world watched them happen, but isn't sure if they're really 'real'. The era provided the foundation for City's ongoing success, too, meaning more trophies and TV income, and the chaos of the situation has also unleashed doubt about the present and future. A quick quiz question - what do The Wizard of Oz, Super Mario Bros 2 and the ninth season of Dallas all have in common? Feel free to grab yourself a hot drink and mull it over for a moment. If you figured out that the plots of all three never really happened - because in their endings it was revealed that they existed only in the dreams of one of the lead characters - then very well done indeed. So do the guilty verdicts mean the Premier League seasons between 2009-10 and 2017-18 should now be considered a figment of our collective imaginations too? City have until Friday to mount an appeal. If that appeal is unsuccessful, then, at some point, the club will be given some sort of punishment. Whether sanctions will retcon the past in any way is unknown. And about moving forwards? Right now football fans, both of City and other clubs across the country, do not know whether the football they are watching is 'real' or not. Are City actually top of the league and in a title challenge, or will they be docked points later in the season? If they are linked with another team's star player, could that transfer happen or will they be unable to make deals at some point? Will they be in the Premier League next season or will they be expelled and will there need to be a quite significant rejigging of the pyramid to accommodate them somewhere else? And then there are questions about what comes later down the line. Is anybody else breaking rules right now, which fans will only find out about in the future? title: Watch: Burnham says UK could go 'all the way' towards rejoining EU
description: Andy Burnham says rejoining the EU is among options the government could look at - telling the BBC the current Brexit settlement has caused "more harm than good".
body: This video can not be played Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told the BBC that rejoining the EU is among options the government could look at. Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme after delivering his first Labour conference speech as PM on Tuesday, Burnham said he would try to "find consensus" in the country on one option to clarify the UK's long-term position. "There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each," he added. Asked what the options might look like, Burnham said "we could stay as we are, that's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay." Read more about Andy Burnham's comments. title: The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row
description: You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won four League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
body: The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley? You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first. Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football. The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot. And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success. Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge. It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports. His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit. After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat. Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history. "It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport. "But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do. "Then the lads wanted to do it again." Ian Chandler played for Barnsley, Stockport and Aldershot before a successful non-league career Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning. "There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says. "The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised." Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park. After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide. "We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001. "When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other." A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'. Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013. Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park. "He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches." And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work. "Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says. Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion. "Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields. "But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league." Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign. Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not. "One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2. "By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand." Paul Robinson scored the fifth goal in Whitley Bay's 6-1 win over Wroxham in the 2010 FA Vase final Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast. And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals. They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street. "There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson

title: Move to rejoin EU among options for UK, says Burnham
description: The prime minister tells the BBC the current Brexit settlement has caused "more harm than good".
body: This video can not be played Watch: Andy Burnham tells Today programme that UK could go 'all the way' towards rejoining EU Andy Burnham has suggested rejoining the EU is among options the government could examine to reshape the UK's long-term relationship with Europe. The prime minister told the BBC the current Brexit settlement had caused "more harm than good" and he wanted to look at "what is doable" to repair relations. It comes after he pledged in his Labour conference speech on Tuesday to explore closer ties with the bloc at a delayed summit later this year. The move could set up a huge dividing line at the next general election, with the Conservatives accusing him of trying to "reopen old wounds by restarting the battles of the Brexit years". Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care Chris Mason: Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market Last week, Burnham left the door open to campaigning at the next general election for a mandate to rejoin the EU. As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, he had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU". But his latest comments are the clearest indication yet he could make a decisive break from Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which pledged to "make Brexit work" whilst ruling out rejoining either its customs union or single market. Predecessor Sir Keir Starmer had instead tried to carve out a more limited reset in relations, including aligning with EU food standards, a youth visa deal and relinking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime. Sir Keir's departure from office delayed a summer summit with the EU until later this year, at which time Burnham has also said he wants to publish a 10-year plan to transform the UK economy. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Burnham said he did not want to leave the question of the EU relationship "hanging" and he wanted to be clear on "where we want Britain to go in the next decade". Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, he replied that he wanted to "look at the options". He added he had previously advocated such a move within his lifetime, whilst acknowledging it was "not necessarily the case that that is now". "We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay," he told the programme. "We could look at what [former Chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way." "So there are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each," he added. In his conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham blamed Brexit for a loss of control over both immigration and the economy, telling delegates he did not believe the current relationship was "good enough". He told activists he wanted to use the rescheduled summit later this year to lay out "different options" for the UK's long-term relationship with Europe. He promised to "find consensus" on an option to clarify the UK's position, although did not offer further detail of how this would be measured. In response to Burnham's conference speech, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "Labour cannot pin the blame for their disastrous economic decisions on a vote that happened over a decade ago. "Besides, they are already dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset." title: The Irish international rugby 'trailblazer' and her legacy of cancer awareness
description: Rosie Stewart played for Ireland and was a founding member of Ulster Women's Rugby but died after being diagnosed with breast cancer.
body: Rosie Stewart passed away in 2003 aged 33 They gathered to remember "a girl like no other" - a trailblazing rugby player whose exploits on the pitch were cruelly cut short by her death at just 33. Last Saturday, on a sunny September afternoon two teams from two different corners of Northern Ireland came to City of Derry to contest the Rosie Stewart Memorial Bowl. Stewart, from Londonderry, won four caps for Ireland between 1999 and 2000 and was a founding member of Ulster Women's Rugby but, in 2004, she died after being diagnosed with breast cancer. The memorial match is held every year in her memory and also to promote female health, a cause her sister Colette Risely said would have been close to Stewart's heart. Kelly Gormley plays for the City of Derry women's rugby club "I think the more we do the talking, the more lives we will save," she said. "Rosie would be the one to promote the awareness too if she could." On Saturday, Stewart's former club Cooke, which contest the memorial match every year, took on Enniskillen in Stewart's home city, watched on by the likes of Collette, her father John Gallagher and husband Adrian, who said his wife was a "girl like no other". But what was going on off the pitch was just as important, with a women's health discussion held before the match hosted by the Western Trust's Jacinta McCool and fitness coach Claire O'Hagan. O'Hagan's spoke on female strength and conditioning and the impact of the menstrual cycle on athletic performance, while McCool focused on breast and cervical cancer awareness. It was a "poignant" event for City of Derry player Kelly Gormley, who said a number of squad members have been affected by or had breast cancer. Jacinta McCool works at a midwife for the Western Trust "It's at the forefront of our minds," she said. "I think when you are delivering information and awareness, it's information you're taking to 20 or 30 girls." Jacinta McCool, whose message of early detection of breast or cervical cancer leads to better cure rates, said it was important to raise that awareness. "Hopefully anybody that hears one thing, they go off and tell three or four of their friends, then we are reaching a much bigger audience." For Gormley, Stewart was a "pioneering" player in her efforts to grow the women's game. "Why not celebrate someone from Derry who started the movement in women's rugby?" she said. "She started a change for women to play rugby and so we are just marking that at our own club." Speaking about the increase of women playing rugby in Northern Ireland, Gormley said she thinks Stewart would not be surprised about the growth. "She was knocking down doors before people even knew about women's rugby, these rugby teams are growing really fast and it is a result of decisions she made and took," she said.
