title: 'They disgust me': The fight for smaller breasts
description: Charlotte Howard has been turned down for breast reduction surgery by the NHS, despite daily pain.
body: Charlotte Howard says "I'm basically carrying half a stone off my neck and shoulders" Back pain, rashes, harassment and a bad smell. These are just some of the reasons why Charlotte Howard, 52, from West Lavington, says she is "disgusted" by her own breasts. Once measuring at a 32B, they soon grew to a 40GG when she started the menopause. "I find them intolerable. I'm basically carrying half a stone off my neck and shoulders. I can't look at myself without clothes on," she says. "I dream of cutting them off with a pair of scissors." One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself Thousands of South West students get free MenB jab RAF Fairford incident involves 'foreign actor', says Rubio Howard says her breasts are now so large, she has to use medicated talc under them to prevent rashes, also washing them "two or three times a day" because they smell. Like many others, Howard, who works as a horticulturist, says because of her breasts she also finds exercise painful and uncomfortable, making it difficult to stay active. When she is out and about in public, she says she is regularly harassed because of them. "I get fat-shamed in the street, people shout stupid jokes, lewd comments about them," she describes. Finding the pain and discomfort too much, Howard says she visited her GP to ask about breast reduction surgery, but was told there was "no chance" she would qualify. She is now considering private breast reduction surgery, but says the estimated £6,000 - £9,000 cost is daunting. Charlotte Howard used to work as a Marilyn Monroe impersonator The exact criteria for having breast reduction surgery on the NHS depends on where you live but may be possible if other options, which include wearing professionally fitted bras, have not worked. According to the NHS, external, health problems caused by having very large breasts are also considered, along with the size of your breasts, your weight, your general health and if you smoke. Not being able to take part in sport or exercise Grooves on shoulders from bra straps Skin irritation under the breasts Back, shoulder or neck pain Those who want the surgery to change their appearance, rather than for health reasons, will need to pay for it privately. Simon Hawkins, a consultant breast surgeon in Wiltshire, treating both NHS and private patients, says he has seen an increase in women requesting the surgery privately over the last 15 years. "It's always been very difficult to get approved for breast reduction surgery on the NHS," he says. "It's generally regarded as a cosmetic treatment." According to the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, there were 4,673 private breast reduction procedures carried out in the UK in 2025, a 2% rise on the year before. "It's not just a cosmetic operation where you have body confidence benefits, you might also be able to do activities and exercise more. There's also the potential impact on back and neck issues," says Hawkins. Charlotte Howard in 1999, aged 25 It is the role of integrated care boards (ICBs) to manage local NHS budgets and commission care and services, including surgeries such as breast reduction. A spokesperson for the NHS Bath and North East Somerset, Swindon and Wiltshire, NHS Dorset and NHS Somerset ICB say while "breast reduction surgery is not routinely commissioned for all patients" in the area, decisions "about treatment are made on an individual clinical basis". They say the person's circumstances are taken into account, including "the evidence of likely benefit". "The policy is designed to ensure that NHS resources are used fairly," they add. Howard says she was not given a clear reason why she would not receive further support from the NHS. The NHS declined to comment on Howard's individual case when approached by the BBC. "I'm just exhausted really, it's a fight to get heard, to be listened to," she says. "The lack of support feels isolating," she says. "If you're a woman of a certain age and you have anything wrong with you they say 'lose some weight dear', or its the menopause," she adds. Meanwhile Hawkins says more women are also looking to get cheaper surgery abroad, with travel packages available in Lithuania, Turkey and Prague among other places. The NHS warns "safety standards may not be as high" in those countries as in the UK. "It's certainly is a lot cheaper but we're seeing quite a few patients who present to NHS services with problems and complications after surgery performed abroad," Hawkins adds. title: Drop in donations puts community pantry at risk
description: St Paul's Pantry in Norton Lees say things are looking "pretty grim" without support.
body: St Paul's Pantry in Norton Lees has had to expand into the church building to accommodate all the people that use the food bank Volunteers at a community pantry say they fear they may have to close unless they can bring in additional donations of money and food. Tina Sampson-Smith from St Paul's community pantry, in Norton Lees, Sheffield, said a drop off in donations and a rise in demand had left them in a precarious situation. Asked how the coming weeks and months looked she replied: "They look pretty grim at the moment." According to the Trussell Trust more than 2.2m food parcels were given out in England in 2025, a 56% rise on 2019. Sampson-Smith said: "I looked at our freezers yesterday and the majority of them are off because we do not have the food stock in them. "It's always tough from September to November, but this year is tougher than ever." She said, in recent weeks, one day the pantry had 204 people turn up in need of support. "Food poverty is really, really high at the moment and it's a never-ending battle to get food because our supermarkets haven't got the stock to give us," she said. Co-founder Jay Judge said: "It's a day to day battle "[There's] more and more people in food poverty, those that you see and those that you don't see. "For every person that turns up at the pantry there's a family behind that. "We might be seeing over 200 people coming through the door but it's feeding a lot more people than that." Sampson-Smith added: "We provided school lunches during the school holidays, but at this point in time we've nothing in our freezers to do that for half term." The community pantry welcomed 204 people one Wednesday morning Jenny Farrall‑Bird, area manager for charity the Trussel Trust, said this time of year was especially demanding for food banks. She said some families on the lowest incomes were going to have to make decisions such as whether to "prioritise feeding their children over themselves", skipping meals and choosing not to heat their homes. "Food banks are really a lifeline for people in financial crisis," she said. The rising cost of food has also led to a significant drop in donations over recent years, she added. "Food banks are having to do more fundraising and to get income to buy food stock so they can pass that on to people." Sampson-Smith said, as well as providing food parcels and meals, the community pantry also provide a space for people to speak with a cost of living worker and family hub workers. Appealing for support she said: "We really want to continue. We don't want to stop what we're doing." title: South Korea demands apology from Pyongyang for landmine blasts that injured three
description: Blasts in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) injured three South Korean personnel earlier this month.
body: Explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) earlier this month have set off a war of words between North and South Korea South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month. Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September. South Korea said on Tuesday that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, were "highly likely" from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what it said was a violation of a decades-old armistice. North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation". Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea. Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making." South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border. South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War. That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5mi) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas. In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ. In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied. Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now. Ties between Pyongyang and Seoul have only deteriorated since 2015, raising the risk of friction when such incidents happen. Christopher Green, a senior consultant with Crisis Group, tells the BBC that "The North Koreans have been wilfully attempting to harden the border [and] eliminate inter-Korean relations". As a result, he adds, the two Koreas no longer have the "same low-level communication" that they shared in 2015. "Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he says. The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms". "UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said. title: Endometriosis trial gives hope to millions of women in pain like me
description: A £2.3m study will look at whether a personalised pain management plan can improve the quality of life of women who have the debilitating condition.
body: Charlotte McCann said the trial gave her hope for the future Charlotte McCann has been dealing with severe pain from endometriosis since she was 14. It became so intolerable as an adult she had to leave her chosen career. She would wake up in the night vomiting, and on some days Charlotte found she could not stand or get out of bed. It is a myth that endometriosis is a painful period condition - rather, it is a system-wide inflammatory disease where cells, similar to those which line the womb, start to grow in other parts of the body. This can be on the bowel or in the lungs - and the cells multiply, creating raw and angry sores. Those affected can wait years for diagnosis, and there is no cure - meaning women are left grappling with debilitating pain that can affect their relationships, work, education and mental health. Now age 27, Charlotte hopes a new pain management programme for the condition, which is being trialled as part of a £2.3m study, might help others in her position. The UK-wide study, led by the University of Aberdeen and NHS Grampian, will include pain medication alongside other treatments such as physiotherapy, and will investigate whether a personalised plan can improve quality of life. Women can wait years for an endometriosis diagnosis. New tech could change that Emma Barnett: We can't ignore this disease that leaves one in 10 women like me in agony Charlotte, from Huntly in Aberdeenshire, is currently living with stage 4 endometriosis, external. She had to abandon her career in corporate finance due to the pain, and now works as a freelance pet-sitter when she can. "I would wake up in the night vomiting and I was always worried that maybe my appendix had burst or I had a kidney infection or something like that," she recalled. "The pain would come on so strong, I wouldn't be able to even sit up straight, I wouldn't be able to stand up. "It was heavily disrupting my life. I couldn't focus on anything, and I couldn't sleep or eat because of the pain. "There's no way I could continue my nine-to-five job when I could barely sit up." Charlotte said she had years of not knowing what was wrong, until an MRI scan confirmed endometriosis. More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds It affected her bladder, and has spread to other parts of her body. "I am now on very strong opioid painkillers to try to get on top of the pain, but they make me feel very sick, to the point I can't eat, so I have lost a lot of weight now as well," she said. Charlotte described being in so much pain that there are days when she cannot get out of bed. She also has to use walking aids to get around due to the pain in her back brought on by her endometriosis symptoms. She tried surgery to remove the tissue in question, but the symptoms returned. Asked about the new trial, Charlotte said she was optimistic. "Endometriosis has had a huge impact on my life, and I am delighted to hear that they are looking at new ways to help the millions of women who are suffering with this every single day." Preparatory work has now begun for the five-year study, which is being funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR). Once participants are recruited, they will take part in a 12-week personalised programme - called an endometriosis-specific pain management programme (e-PMP). The project will evaluate whether this strategy can offer more effective treatment for women who find their pain is not adequately controlled by surgery or medication. It includes cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)-informed psychotherapy, specialist physiotherapy, guidance on relationships, intimacy and communication, and medication to reduce side effects. Pre-menopausal women will either receive the new programme alongside existing standard care, or existing standard care alone, with the results of each approach then compared. Eligible participants will be recruited to the study by their specialist. Consultant gynaecologist Dr Lucky Saraswat, an honorary senior lecturer at the university, and lead for Aberdeen Endometriosis Centre at NHS Grampian, is heading the study. Dr Lucky Saraswat is leading the new study "Endometriosis is one of the most common yet under researched causes of chronic pain," she said. "Many women continue to suffer even after surgery or medication. "This study will help us understand whether a tailored, interdisciplinary pain management programme can offer meaningful, long term improvements in quality of life. "If effective, e-PMP could become a vital new treatment option, particularly for women who wish to avoid repeated surgery or hormonal therapies, or who are planning a pregnancy." Alongside the clinical results, the study will also aim to assess cost effectiveness. Prof Anthony Gordon, director of NIHR's health technology assessment programme, said many women could face years of "agonising" symptoms with few long-term options. "High-quality research is essential to break this cycle and deliver treatment that addresses the full, complex impact of endometriosis," he said. "By evaluating tailored, non-surgical pain management, this trial could revolutionise care - providing desperately needed support, improving daily lives, and offering long-term relief when standard treatments haven't worked." Emma Cox, chief executive of Endometriosis UK, added: "Symptoms of endometriosis including chronic pelvic pain can have a significant impact on someone's physical and mental health, and research is vital to helping improve management and treatment options. "We welcome this much-needed research and look forward to working with the team to see how an endometriosis specific pain management programme could support those with the disease in the future." title: 'He was deeply loved': Tribute to former UK school pupil killed in Ukraine
description: Arkadii Petrov, who attended Kirkcudbright Academy, was killed after returning to Ukraine to fight.
body: Arkadii Petrov was a former pupil of Kirkcudbright Academy A former pupil at a Scottish high school has been killed in action on the frontline in Ukraine. Arkadii Petrov and his family moved to Dumfries and Galloway when he was a teenager, following Russia's invasion in 2022. He attended Kirkcudbright Academy before returning to Ukraine to fight and was killed in action in the east of the country. His mother, Liudmyla, said he was "funny, bright, very charismatic and full of life" and had been an "incredibly loving brother" to his younger sisters and brother. Arkadii studied for a year in Edinburgh before heading back to Ukraine She said the family had been told on 22 September that her eldest son had been killed in a combat mission on 18 September - just two days before he would have turned 21. As well as attending Kirkcudbright Academy, he also went to the University of Edinburgh for a year before interrupting his studies to return to Ukraine. "Ukraine was the country he loved more than anything," said his mother. "As the war continued, I could see him becoming more serious. "He followed everything that was happening in Ukraine very closely and felt that he could not simply continue his normal life while other Ukrainians were defending the country where he was born." The young soldier was killed two days before his 21st birthday He worked as a combat medic and drone operator and was wounded on a number of occasions in battle. "Arkadii was sincere, brave and very honest - he had no falseness in him," said Liudmyla. "But to us he was never only a soldier or his call sign, Arka. "He was our Arkadii - my son, a brother, a grandson, a young man with books, music, jokes, dreams and an entire life that should have been ahead of him." She said he adored his sisters, Avrora and Kapitolina, and his younger brother Aaron. "Wherever he was, he carried his family with him," added his mother. The tiny chapel offering Ukraine a helping hand After his death, the family travelled from Scotland to Ukraine to arrange his funeral. "The hardest thing for me is knowing that I will never again see his living face, hear his voice or hold him," said Liudmyla. "I also grieve for the future he was meant to have - his dreams, his family one day, the children he might have had." However, she said she was also "enormously proud" of her son. "He loved Ukraine more than anything, and he gave his life defending its freedom," she said. "I want people to remember not simply that another young soldier died in Ukraine, but that Arkadii was a whole person, deeply loved, with a family, a childhood, a future and dreams. "He was our son, our pride, and I want his name and his life to be remembered." Arkadii's mother said she wanted his name to be remembered Peter Kormylo, archivist at the Ukrainian Prisoner of War chapel in Lockerbie where Petrov attended services, said the whole community was upset by the death of a young man. He described Arkadii as a "very pleasant young man" who had arrived in Scotland with his mother and three younger siblings - one brother and two sisters. However, he said he had always been keen to go back to Ukraine and fight. "All I can say about the boy is, having met him on a few occasions, he was a very courteous young man and quite a serious young man," he said. "The last time I remember him being at the chapel I found him, when everyone had gone, sitting in the chapel writing a couple of what looked like letters - but in actual fact were prayers. "He was a deep thinker and obviously felt the need to do what many Ukrainians are doing and that's fulfill their patriotic duty." Petrov regularly attended services at the Ukrainian chapel near Lockerbie Kormylo said Arkadii's death was sad news for the wider Ukrainian community in the south of Scotland. "He came here, at 16 or 17 years old with his mother, they were refugees," he said. "They didn't know what the future would bring, but he did believe in Ukraine's eventual victory. "He was a teenager maturing here and obviously gathered his own thoughts and decided to make a very adult decision. "So the community is quite upset, as you would guess, everyone feels this pain." More stories from South Scotland Anthony Tuffery, rector at Arkadii's old school, said everyone at Kirkcudbright Academy was saddened to hear of his death. "Although he was only at the school for one year to complete his S6 studies, he was a polite, respectful and hardworking young man," he said. "We would like to pass on our deepest sympathies to his family and friends and our thoughts are with them at this incredibly difficult time." title: Miami-inspired London house features on Grand Designs
description: Architect Peter Morris spent about a decade developing the homes, which feature duck-egg blue metalwork.
body: This video can not be played A pair of pale-pink homes known as The Cloud House has been completed in Gospel Oak, north London. Architect Peter Morris spent about a decade developing the homes, which feature sweeping arches and duck-egg blue metalwork. The semi-detached homes have separate owners, but were built by the same architect and contractor to an agreed exterior design. Morris said nearby St Martin's Church and Miami's Art Deco architecture inspired the project, featured on Channel 4's Grand Designs. Miami-inspired London house features on Grand Designs. title: Dead animals found in canal where children row
description: Residents in Brentford raise concerns about sewage flowing into the local canal network.
body: One of the animals Paul Keane says his rowing groups passed in the same spot day after day Residents in Brentford have raised concerns about sewage flowing into the local canal network, with dead animals washing up over the summer. Paul Keane, general manager of watersports charity Brentford Community Boathouse, told the Brentford and Syon Area Forum that the problem had been worsened by the "epidemic of heat" this summer. The animals were mostly found in the Brentford Lock basin, where the Grand Union Canal meets the River Thames. "We saw dead foxes, dead ducks and there was a dead cat," Keane told BBC London. Keane says the water has to be hygienic if children are going to keep rowing on it "Because of the stagnant water and the fact that the water wasn't travelling anywhere, we were going past them every day in exactly the same spot." Brentford Community Boathouse events officer Kelly Everden, who volunteered on a clean-up operation organised by Keane, said the children who used the canal were worst affected. "It's really upsetting on behalf of the children, because that's not anything that they should ever be faced with, especially with a pet cat," she said. Keane said the problem was at least partly down to misconnections, where plumbing from housing developments is wrongly linked to surface water drains rather than sewers, sending untreated waste into waterways. "The big fly in the ointment is sewage coming into the canal," he said. "That gets worse in the summer when the water is moving slowly, and some of that is historic, but also a contemporary misdirecting of sewage into storm drains." He said he did not believe this was Hounslow Council's fault, but that it needed attention "if we do want to develop usage of the canal, particularly for children on the water". Ben Morris set up Clean Up the River Brent to deal with the misconnections sending waste into the water He added: "The water has to be hygienic, and there are times when it simply isn't. It's a very difficult issue, but it needs an overall strategy." Keane said the animals were predominantly found with E. coli and botulism, and that the most stagnant stretch was within the locks around Boston Manor Park. Warm, still water holds less oxygen, creating the conditions in which botulism thrives and speeding up the growth of E. coli. Hounslow councillor Katherine Dunne said officers in Ealing and Brent were examining misconnections through a River Brent catchment group, and committee chair councillor Dan Bowring urged residents to contact their ward councillors. "All councillors in Brentford will be concerned about this," he said. The Canal and River Trust said it aimed to remove any dead animal as quickly as possible. Aquatic weed has been a particular problem at Brentford, it said, because both of its west London weed clearance boats were out of action at the same time. Thames Water said the area was known to have issues with misconnections and that, while it was not responsible for third-party drainage, it was working with property owners and councils. The Environment Agency said the area remained in drought, which can affect river health, and that it would continue investigating reports of pollution. title: Risks being taken with heating oil orders, firm says
description: Customers in Berkshire and Hampshire are leaving it late to refill their tanks, an oil firm says.
body: Supplier Dave Marsh said customers might be leaving it too late to refill their tanks Heating oil customers who are worried about the cost are taking risks by delaying orders in the hope of a price fall, a firm has warned. Marsh Fuels, which supplies heating oil in Berkshire and Hampshire, said its sales were lower than expected as colder weather approaches. However, the firm said customers could run out of oil or expose themselves to even higher bills by waiting. UK heating oil prices have risen by about 75% since the start of the Iran conflict on 28 February, according to the BoilerJuice website, external. Dave Marsh from the Newbury-based firm said: "We're coming into autumn and we would expect to be busier than we are. "And so we've made the assumption that customers are hanging on, trying to eke out that little bit of oil they've still got left in the bottom of their tank, hoping for the price to dip. "The problem is that can be quite risky. If we get a cold snap and the customers are lower than they think they are, they may suddenly be urgent." Andrew Illingworth said heating oil orders had fallen in his village Andrew Illingworth, who buys oil on behalf of residents in Broughton, Hampshire, said he was handling fewer orders than normal for the time of year. "A lot of them are holding off at the moment," he said. "They're hoping that it's going to go back down again, but who knows at the moment." Chris Wheeler, from Bucklebury, Berkshire, said the price volatility, including surges and dips, was "frustrating". "You never know what's going to happen," he said. "Except at the moment all you can expect is that the price is going to go up. "So we're trying to manage our purchases so that we can buy it when it's at its cheapest." Chris Wheeler said he planned to buy oil when the price dropped Ellen Fraser, energy expert at the Baringa consultancy, said she would buy oil now. She told the Money Box programme on BBC Radio 4: "We're expecting those prices to stay high until at least April and May, which is obviously far too late to fill the tank." The Fuel Distribution Association (UKIFDA) previously said customers should prepare for periods of increased demand, severe weather or unexpected delivery delays. Chief executive Ken Mackness said: "The events we saw earlier this year demonstrated how quickly international developments can affect wholesale energy markets." In March, the government announced a £50m emergency fund, external to help struggling families with heating oil costs. title: Girl, 12, campaigns for healthier hospital food
description: Audrina, 12, launched a petition after spending time in hospital with cancer.
body: Audrina is asking for hospital food to be improved A 12-year-old girl who spent time in hospital battling an aggressive form of cancer has launched a petition calling for improvements to the food dished up to patients. Audrina, from Derby, said despite receiving excellent care from doctors and nurses during her treatment, the food she was served often left her disappointed. She described the meals as tasteless and lacking in important nutrients she believes patients need while recovering. Now she is urging the UK government to take action to raise standards. The Department for Health and Social Care said it welcomed ideas from campaigners like Audrina on how hospital food can be improved. Audrina spent time in hospital being treated for cancer Audrina was diagnosed with neuroblastoma in 2018 but is now cancer-free after completing her treatment. However, despite being given the all-clear at the age of five, she has spent further time in hospital with another condition, cyclic vomiting syndrome. In this time, she says she feels hospital meals have not improved. "The food is often lacking nutrition and it's important that patients have something to look forward to when they're going through a really tough time," she said. "If you don't have the vitamins, minerals and proteins your body needs, it's going to slow your recovery down. "I remember having a shepherd's pie and the mash was brown and burnt - and it was just served in the plastic pot it had been microwaved in." Audrina's mum says her daughter has always hated hospital food Her mother, Gemma, says Audrina has always hated hospital food and is determined to bring about change. "We're just over 500 signatures but she's got to get to 100,000 [to be considered for Parliamentary debate] so there's a really long way to go yet," she said. Audrina has also launched a new series on Instagram called £1 meals. Gemma said: "She's going to be showing examples of meals which are healthy and tasty as well, so that hospitals can see they don't necessarily need to spend more money to get decent food." Audrina hopes the videos will help with her campaign. "It's alright saying you can do this, but sometimes you need the proof. This will achieve that proof and that evidence," she said. Audrina believes hospitals could make better use of locally-sourced produce and community support. She has also suggested growing fruit and vegetables at hospital sites as one possible way of providing fresher food. Audrina's local MP Jonathan Davies is backing the campaign The petition has grabbed the attention of Jonathan Davies, Labour MP for Mid Derbyshire, who said he found out about it while knocking on his constituents' doors. "I was really inspired by Audrina's energy and enthusiasm, informed by her personal experience of spending quite long period's of time in hospital," he said. "I said I'd get behind her campaign and make sure ministers heard what she had to say." Audrina has already visited the Houses of Parliament as part of her work and is hoping Davies can help her speak to the prime minster about the campaign. A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "We want every hospital patient to receive food that is appetising and supports their recovery. "Hospital food in England is already subject to national standards, covering nutrition, safety and quality and we welcome ideas from campaigners like Audrina on how hospital food - especially for young people - can be improved." title: Girl has multiple surgeries to control infections after strike in Gaza
description: Witnesses say Raseel's tent was hit by an Israeli helicopter strike. Israel’s military says it has no record of the attack.
body: This video can not be played Six-year-old Raseel al-Balawi in Gaza has had more than 20 surgeries since an Israeli air strike injured her in late July. Witnesses say her tent in al-Mawasi camp was hit by a strike from an Israeli helicopter, and she now has to have frequent surgeries to try and control infections in her wounds. Israel's military says it has no record of the attack and that it "regrets any harm to civilians". BBC Eye Investigations has spent time with Raseel across the summer, as the ceasefire falters and bombardment continues, to see the challenges doctors are facing in Gaza. The BBC World Service has been filming across the summer in Gaza to reveal how children there are coping amid the near-total destruction of the infrastructure they rely on to survive. You can watch the full film on iPlayer. Girl has multiple surgeries to control infections after strike in Gaza. title: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner
description: "Backpack" defeated a bear known only as "910" in the final round of the annual competition.
body: Backpack, the winning bear, after months of eating to gain weight ahead of hibernating in winter. A brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing". Backpack's wideness narrowly defeated a bear known only as 910, earning 103,344 votes to 910's 98,253 in the final round of the competition, which is run by the Katmai National Park in Alaska. The National Parks Service thanked the 16 bears who "involuntarily participated" in the competition, now in its thirteenth year. Backpack, who was described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months. His mother Holly was the 2019 Fat Bear Week winner. Backpack's name derives not from what another supporter described as the "light bulb shape" of his body, but his habit, as a cub, of climbing onto Holly's back when she waded through the park's salmon-filled Brooks River. Another supporter described him as being a "big fuzzy boy". But Backpack was not without his detractors. One person said she felt that Bear 910, a female who raised both her biological cub and an adopted niece, was a "larger bear all around. Backpack just has a bigger booty". "I just feel like 910 really put in the work this year," another 910 fan wrote on the park's Facebook page, while a voter commented, "She round, she thick my girl 910 got my vote." This video can not be played Fat Bear Week: Which bear has put on the most weight? The finalists' latest weights have not yet been revealed. But adult male brown bears average up to 408kg in mid-summer and often pack on the equivalent of 25% of their body weight by autumn. The largest males can weigh more than 540kg. Females are smaller but can reach weights of over 300kg. Cubs are born weighing roughly half a kilogram. "During hibernation, bears do not eat or drink and lose one-third of their body weight. Their winter survival depends on accumulating ample fat reserves before entering the den," organisers wrote. From June until mid October, the bears gorge on food, including salmon caught with their jaws or paws. Backpack's biography says his "quiet toughness has allowed him to find his niche alongside the biggest bears at Brooks River". Last year, over 1.7 million votes were cast from more than 100 countries to crown the competition's heavyweight champion. Fat Bear Week 2026: What is it? title: Police criticised for telling family with mental health fears to call locksmith
description: A force should have flagged mental health services after a family called about their son, IOPC says.
body: Mark and Roberta Harrison say Hobie was funny and mischievous The police watchdog has criticised a force after call handlers told a family raising mental health concerns to ring a locksmith. On 6 August 2025, Hobie Harrison's parents called Norfolk Police to request a welfare check after he failed to respond to them. He was found dead the next day. The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said the force's 101 call handlers should have referred the family to mental health services, but instead suggested they contacted a locksmith. Norfolk Police said it was reviewing the findings and it had been following the force's Right Care, Right Person (RCRP) policy, external, which limits officer attendance at welfare calls to cases involving "immediate risk to life". The IOPC said the call handlers should have asked more probing questions to assess Hobie's level of risk and there should have been a better explanation to his parents about why officers were not sent under its RCRP guidelines. Hobie's parents, Mark and Roberta Harrison, made a second request for a welfare check for their son to Norfolk Police the following day. Officers attended and found the 30-year-old dead in his flat in Norwich. The couple say they were left unsure where to turn after being told their concerns for their son did not meet the threshold for a police response In October 2025, the family made a complaint to Norfolk Police over its handling of their call. In its report, the IOPC criticised Norfolk Police's response to that complaint after the force told the parents officers should not have attended either call, including the second one that led to Hobie's body being found. The IOPC called that reply "unnecessary and insensitive". Hobie had previously threatened suicide and Mark said: "We'll never know whether he was still alive when we first called and whether something could have been done. "He might already have been dead, but we'll never know." More stories on Right Care, Right Person: Senior officer defends new mental health approach Costessey deaths: Norfolk police must improve call handling Bedfordshire Police to focus on crime over mental health calls New mental health policy 'saves police officer time' In its findings, the IOPC said it was concerned Norfolk Police may not fully understand the risks of the policy. David Ford, the watchdog's director of oversight and casework, said: "We have raised our concerns with the force around its interpretation of RCRP and monitoring of the initiative. "As a result... the force has said it will undertake a review to examine whether there are any organisational learnings." Norfolk Police said it could not comment further because an inquest has yet to take place, which is due to happen in November. Hobie's parents say the 30-year-old loved music and enjoyed gardening Hobie had schizophrenia and developmental trauma and was under the care of the Norfolk and Suffolk Foundation Trust Community Mental Health Team. His parents said he had a history of drug use. The couple adopted Hobie as a child and said he had been in "good spirits" the last time they saw him before his death. In August 2025, the family said they became concerned he had not spoken to them for more than 24 hours as he usually contacted them "several times a day". "The non-contact was just... it didn't happen. So, it was very, very unusual," said Roberta. The couple went to Hobie's flat but could not use their key to get inside because his key was still in the lock on the inside of the door. "We were 100% certain he was in there and he wasn't responding, so we knew there was something seriously wrong," said Mark. If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, you can visit the BBC Action Line for support and information Unsure whether they had legal authority to break in, they called Norfolk Police and told call handlers that their son had a history of self-harm and suicidal threats. After consulting a supervisor, the staff member told them the situation did not meet the threshold for a police response and suggested they consider contacting a locksmith. "We didn't know how to make a decision at that point or what to do quite frankly," said Roberta. The following morning, after a second call to police, officers attended the flat and found Hobie's body. "If the police are no longer going to come, then it has to be very clear who's got the responsibility," Roberta added. The Harrisons say regular calls, walks, shopping trips and meals together formed part of their daily routine with Hobie RCRP was first developed by Humberside Police in 2019 and has since been adopted by forces across England and Wales. The policy is intended to reduce police involvement in welfare and mental health-related incidents so officers can focus on crime and immediate threats to life. Norfolk Police said the approach, which it introduced in 2024, had reduced officer attendance at welfare-related incidents, from 11,831 in the year before the policy was introduced to 9,229 by its second year. The force said there was "no defined response" to welfare concerns and the appropriate pathway depended on the circumstances. His family say Hobie enjoyed riding his bike when he felt well enough to get out and about The Norfolk and Suffolk Integrated Care Board said support could involve health, social care, ambulance or police services. A 2024 national agreement on the policy, external said people experiencing mental health crises should not be left without support. Some coroners have raised concerns about RCRP. A Prevention of Future Deaths report into the death of Sophie Cotton in County Durham, external said the policy appeared to overlook that mental health teams could not enter locked premises. title: Facing the future without the 'bank of mum and dad'
description: Young people struggling to make ends meet respond to the government's Your First Home scheme.
body: Chari said she was having to use the money she had saved for the future to survive now The prime minister used the plight of young people unable to rely on the "bank of mum and dad" as a curtain-raiser for Labour's annual conference. The Your First Home scheme will offer a government-backed loan of 20% of the purchase price - with a minimum deposit of 2.5%. But how tough are things at the moment for young people who have left school and want to make their way in the world? Chari said choosing financial stability over pursuing a dream was "heartbreaking" Chari, 19, from Hertfordshire, spent some of her childhood in care but has just started at university and has ambitions to qualify as a doctor of psychology. The challenge at the moment is just getting through the next few years, she says. "I receive universal credit and that's usually what I would use to pay for my housing in Hertfordshire, but they've cut it off this month because I'm moving to university and they think SFE [the student loan] will cover it. "SFE is delayed, so I have no money this month whatsoever - I'm three days in and already I'm in debt." She added: "I'm dipping into savings I had planned to afford a future for myself just to get by now. "As a care leaver, you don't really get that chance to save money for your future or make future plans." Chari believes her dream of a doctorate may have to be put on hold while she pursues a career - and a salary - in banking. "It's heart-breaking," she said, adding: "I don't think somebody should have to choose financial stability over pursuing their dream." Elliot does not believe they will ever earn enough money to own a house Elliot, 18, is also from Hertfordshire and is living with their parents, but wants to move on. "I've been looking for places because I'm in college and I plan on going to uni, but it's just that things keep rising and the bills keep getting more and more," they said. "I don't think I've ever expected to be able to buy a house at all. It would be nice to own my own place, but will I actually earn enough to be able to?" As they turn 19 within a couple of months, Elliot believes they will have to pay for their studies. "It's about £1,500 to £2,000 just for the course and I've got to get there and back every day," they said. "In the area that I live, one of the main things is if you don't have the education, you're probably not going to get out of the place. "It's quite a low-income area. I would like to go to uni but I think 'can I afford it?'" The government said the Your First Home scheme would "help tackle the deposit barrier for first-time buyers who would be unable to afford their first home otherwise, building on the government's existing work to help more young people and families onto the housing ladder". The Conservatives warned that the policy could leave first-time buyers taking on more debt and risked "pushing up the price of new homes". But the prime minister said it would aim to help those who did not have support from the "bank of mum and dad". Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own. "So we will step in to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder." Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Village gets 1990s makeover for Harry Potter shoot
description: Period cars line the streets and a fete is staged on the village green.
body: This video can not be played A Buckinghamshire village has been transported back to the 1990s for filming connected to the new Harry Potter television series. Residents of Latimer were told earlier this month that Plum Jam Productions, a subsidiary of Warner Bros. Discovery, would be filming a major HBO series there over three days. Local permit-holding residents could briefly pass through the village on Monday evening, where period cars lined the streets and a fete was staged on the village green. Only emergency vehicles were permitted access on Tuesday, while the set is due to be dismantled on Wednesday. Some villagers said they had been "cut off", with traffic diverted along a narrow, unlit country road that becomes easily congested. title: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
description: The owner said he chose the name because he wanted to run the "best Chinese restaurant" in South Korea.
body: Surveillance footage show a group of masked men spraying lacquer across the restaurant in South Korea's Seongnam A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say. Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer. The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent". The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported. The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said. "People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent." In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues. The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400). Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery. Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province. Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition. Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars. title: Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal amid floods
description: The municipality building in Baglung was left teetering on an unstable ledge due to floods before it fell into a river.
body: This video can not be played Massive flooding left a government building in western Nepal teetering on the edge of an unstable ledge before it fell into the Daram River. Witnesses captured the moment that the building in Baglung collapsed on Sunday, 27 September. Officials removed important documents and computers from the building before it fell, local ward chair Tej Thapa confirmed to the BBC. No one was injured. Landslides and floods have killed at least 27 people over recent days, according to Nepal's national disaster agency, only weeks after a flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border killed 1,400 people and left thousands more missing. title: Student: Uni strikes 'not what we signed up for'
description: The University of Nottingham said it was "disappointed" by the timing of industrial action.
body: The University of Nottingham said it was "disappointed" by the timing of industrial action A student has said she feels "shorthanded" as staff at University of Nottingham are to go on strike for three months. The University and College Union (UCU) said its members would strike on Wednesday and Thursday and would then carry out "sustained strike action" from 5 October to 11 December over the Future Nottingham restructuring plans. A spokesperson for the University of Nottingham said it was "disappointed" by the timing of industrial action, adding many students would be "unaffected" by the strikes. Zoe Monroe, who studies English literature with creative writing, told the BBC the strikes were not what students had signed up for. The university said previously the proposals could involve programme closures and academic restructure. It added it had reviewed and considered all Future Nottingham counterproposals, which would now go to the University Council for a decision. The university had suspended music and language courses and planned hundreds of job cuts earlier this year to deal with "significant financial challenges". Union members from UCU, Unison and Unite voted in July in favour of a motion of no confidence in the vice-chancellor and other senior leaders after a "complete breakdown of trust". The first two days of action have been planned to coincide with the university's council meeting at which the final business case for cuts will be considered. The strike will also include action short of a strike, such as only working to contract and not covering for absent colleagues, the UCU said. Monroe said strikes have affected her learning in previous years Monroe said the strikes announcement had left her feeling shortchanged by the teaching she had received during her three years in Nottingham. "[The strikes are] going to be highly disruptive," said the 20-year-old. "It's not what we've paid and signed up for. It's awful because I don't know what else we can do about it other than just raise awareness. "I feel quite shorthanded because it is a lot of money and I've come to university to to learn. It's very disappointing." The third year student fears the strikes will damage the university's reputation, which she feels could affect her chances of securing a job in the future. "I'm going to learn less, and the reputation of the university is going to most likely go downhill after this," she said. "People will be less likely to accept University of Nottingham students and feel as if we are less qualified and we are going to be offered less opportunities." Isaac Wood, a third year politics and international relations student, said he supported the strikes, however he also added: "I'm not really sure about their approach to the strikes with going on for so long because I think that's a big ask of a lot of their members to do it for that long and to sustain it. "I support them and I wish them all the best but it is starting to become a little strenuous," the 20-year-old said. Students and staff formed a picket line outside the university in May in protests over job losses Nick Clare, UCU branch president, said: "We don't want to strike, but staff will not stand by while colleagues lose their jobs and whole areas of teaching and research are dismantled unnecessarily." He said the dispute could still be resolved, adding the union were "open" to meaningful talks with management to resolve the issue ahead of the new academic year. The union said it was calling on the university to rule out compulsory redundancies, the closure of full departments, protect teaching and research, and "engage seriously" with the alternative proposals put forward by staff. A spokesperson for the university said they continued to engage in "meaningful discussions" with trade union colleagues. They added: "While we know many of our students will be unaffected by this action, the timing of this to deliberately disrupt the start of the new academic year for our students is particularly disappointing. "We want to reassure them we have clear procedures and support in place to minimise any disruption and ensure they get the most from their university experience." title: Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
description: The president also signed an executive order requiring his government to refer to AI as Super Intelligence.
body: Trump met with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AI US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age". The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry. The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI and a slowdown in developing the technology, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity. Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House. Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson and top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting. The president told reporters that the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. Under the agreement, which Trump posted on social media, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues, the document said. They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways." The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. "It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president." Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board. The president has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks, dismissing them as a "hoax". He has said the only "guardrails" the industry needs is a "smart" president. OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent weeks called for tighter oversight of the industry and foe a slowdown of development of the technology. On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns. The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation. Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI. The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the country over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on from communities. Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November. A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas. Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters. Trump previously said on social media that the only reason communities in the US should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor". "The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame," he said. Huang from Nvidia, which produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories". These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added. Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of term artificial intelligence. SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch," the order said. "As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said. During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake". Some tech leaders and other people close to the president have already started to use the term. Zuckerberg said on social media on Monday: "We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses." On Wednesday, Musk reposted a clip of tech executives gathered around Trump at the White House, with the words: "Super Intelligence." But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction in the industry because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems. title: The Papers: 'Burnham's triple shock' and 'City face expulsion'
description: Every front page on Wednesday is dominated by Prime Minister Andy Burnham's speech at the Labour Party conference.
body: Every front page on Wednesday is dominated by Prime Minister Andy Burnham's speech at the Labour Party conference. The Daily Mail describes it as "the most Left-wing speech by a PM since 1970s", after Burnham vowed to axe the state pensions triple lock by 2030 as part of his plan to help fund a new national care service. "Burnham's triple shock" declares the paper. "Triple lock scrapped by 2030" reads the headline of the Daily Telegraph, which reports Burnham's pensions plan would replace the triple lock with a double lock. This means the state pension would increase by either inflation or a minimum of 2.5% - the link with wage growth will be scrapped. The front page also includes a story about Manchester City football club, which has been found guilty of charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules."City face expulsion over £1bn cheating scandal," it says. The Times says Burnham is staking his future on "free care for all", adding that in his speech, the prime minister admitted there would be a "political price" to pay but "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off". Describing the 70-minute speech as a "high-stakes gamble to win Labour a second term in power", the paper adds that it also saw Burnham pledge to reopen the Brexit deal with Europe and reform the voting system. Burnham's own words lead the Daily Mirror, which reads: "I will build a Britain my dad would be proud of." The paper says that the "emotional PM's rousing message" was a "moment of hope" for Britons. The Metro calls it "Andy's rallying cry", pointing to a moment during the speech which saw Burnham shed a tear as he vowed to make Britain "unstoppable". It came as the prime minister paid tribute to his father, Roy, whom he lost to Alzheimer's earlier this month. The Express has taken a more skeptical view of Burnham's address to the Labour Party conference, launching a "crusade" to save the triple lock. The paper says he is betraying pensioners by getting rid of it, and betraying Brexit by seeking closer ties with the EU. "It's a crying shame for our nation," it writes. Similarly, the Sun deems the prime minister's speech a "Locky horror show". The i Paper includes the key details from Burnham's "extraordinary" speech, which it says saw cabinet ministers in tears. It adds that "billions are expected to be saved" by adjusting the way pensions are calculated. "Burnham picks the lock" says the Daily Star, with the front page also dedicated to the prime minister's "plan for a 'new Britain'". Burnham is pictured against a backdrop that reads "Hope again" on the front page of the Financial Times, which says the most unexpected part of Burnham's speech was when he suggested that Labour's three "red lines" on Europe could be "up for grabs" at the next general election. It says that the prime minister wanted to start a national debate about "options" for the UK's future relations with Europe - although the paper notes that it is "far from clear what outcome he favours". title: How AI is creating a UK super-museum and revealing our planet's history
description: More than 70 million specimens from 100 UK collections will be put into an online digital museum
body: Beetles that look as if they are gold plated are among the millions of specimens that will be available to view online Researchers are using AI to create a vast digital museum of millions of specimens from collections across the UK that they say could "supercharge" our understanding of the natural world. People will eventually be able to see around 70 million animals, plants, fossils and rocks from their phones and computers. Robots and AI are being used to scan and analyse the specimens - some collected centuries ago - speeding up the digitisation process from hundreds of years to a decade. The new digital museum will enable researchers to understand how the UK has changed over the entire history of our planet and predict future changes to the climate, food supplies and species loss. The resource will be something that the public can access and enjoy too, says Dr Joanna Dunster, who is an associate director of the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) - part of the UK Research and Innovation Agency which is funding the project. "I'm looking forward to exploring the resource with my four-year-old son, whose knowledge of science is little, but enthusiasm is great," she told BBC News. Some specimens are already searchable on the database, but they represent only a fraction of the country's collections, mostly from a handful of large institutions such as the Natural History Museum and the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. New funding will open drawers and cupboards in institutions across the UK to include millions more plants, animals and fossils. "We need to make these collections openly accessible instead of sitting where they can rarely be reached," Dunster said. The public and researchers will be able to see the full diversity of the natural world, from the unusual - like the blind tripod fish that props itself on the seafloor, to the historical - a horse tooth recovered by Charles Darwin around 1833 from northeast Argentina. The resource is called the Distributed System of Scientific Collections, external (DiSSCo UK). Many specimens have scientific labels handwritten decades ago which can now be read more easily and digitally captured There are over 35 million pinned insect specimens at the Natural History Museum alone - digitising these helps scientists track insect decline and monitor changing pest populations A red algae species called sea beech, collected in 1969 off the coast of Dorset and preserved in the Natural History Museum Some specimens like this seahorse have already been digitised - researchers can analyse internal bone structures remotely without dissecting or damaging specimens From rocks and minerals to fossils, UK collections preserve millions of geological specimens Scanning the specimens is not a trivial process. Not only does each one need to be photographed, but the tiny labels containing important scientific information, often handwritten, sometimes centuries ago, also have to be recorded. The team involved calculated that it would have taken hundreds of years to do this manually, but using robots and AI this process can now be done in a decade, according to Sarah Addezio, the DiSSCo UK's programme delivery director. "What we're able to do now is connect and analyse that information at a scale that's unprecedented and has not been possible before." One hundred museums, botanic gardens, universities and other organisations are involved in the project. The specimens to go under the cameras will not be the big beasties: there are no whales or dinosaurs in the opening phase, which begins in Wales and Scotland. Beetles, butterflies, moths, flies, pressed flowers and ferns will go first - the small, less glamorous material that actually hold the best record of how the country around them has changed. In Cardiff, the team will scan around half a million insect and plant specimens, from large, showy butterflies down to flies you could lose on a fingertip, which turn out to be among the most sensitive indicators of a healthy landscape. In Scotland, the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh and National Museums Scotland hold 13 million specimens between them, the UK's second-largest natural science collection. Together with 50 smaller Scottish collections, the collections span from sea level to the tops of mountains - two centuries of change in the plants and insects of every kind of Scottish landscape. Jenny Geroni, who is the head of Natural Sciences and Research at the Amgueddfa Cymru - Museum Wales, said it will be a chance to showcase material from across the country. "Each collection is unique. We have a lot of Welsh material that is not held anywhere else. "By taking material from across the UK, it also allows us to build a good picture of what is going on across the whole country. And everyone adding their world collections will build a much stronger picture of what is going on elsewhere," Geroni told BBC News. Britain's pressed plants and flowers collected over hundreds of years will form an important part of the new digital museum Every specimen in a museum is a snapshot of the past. A large part of natural history is the detective story of piecing these clues together from tens of millions of these jigsaw pieces to recreate a vivid and detailed picture of how our world has changed. The new initiative will make that much easier by bringing millions of specimens together along with powerful AI tools to search the information. Dr Vince Smith said the digital museum will accelerate research into the natural world Dr Vincent Smith, a research leader at the Natural History Museum in London, says it will "supercharge" research into the natural world. "Natural history collections record long periods of change, often through really fundamental periods, such as the Industrial Revolution. title: Hidden habits that make your social anxiety worse - and how to break them
description: Social anxiety is more common than many think. Here's what you need to know about the condition.
body: Overcoming social anxiety can be tricky but experts have shared some tips to try and make it easier It was during her teenage years that Mary began to become anxious in social situations. It got so bad she developed depression and had to have time off school. By the time she started university, she avoided group settings altogether. "I didn't join clubs and societies like others did," says Mary (not her real name). "I just thought nobody would want to get to know me. I didn't really make a single friend during my whole degree." Mary's social anxiety was so bad that she was diagnosed as having social anxiety disorder - something that affects up to 12% of people, external at some point in their lives. But plenty more report struggling more generally. As students return to uni, we asked experts how to overcome these feelings whether in your first, or final year. This video can not be played What makes you socially anxious? A study by the University of Chichester found , externalmore than a fifth of university students face some kind of social anxiety during their studies – and it is linked to lower grades, poorer relationships and isolation. For many, university marks the first time they have moved out of home – and the expectation is that they will quickly make friends. Mary, who went to the University of Exeter, says she did try. "When I first got there I went to one society, but everybody was talking to each other and I had a sudden fear come over me. I felt I wouldn't fit in and I went home." Mary describes her social anxiety as like an out of body experience. When she was talking to new people, heat would rise in her face and her hands would begin to tingle. "I'd almost feel myself separating from my body. I forgot how to form words," says Mary, who is now 25. "After social situations I was often left with the sense that I'd done something awful. I had an all-consuming feel of shame. I kept thinking there was something fundamentally flawed in me." Neil Greening, chair of the Social Anxiety Alliance UK, says this is a typical characteristic of people with social anxiety. "People think they have a personality flaw. They internalise it rather than seeing it as a recognisable condition that they can get help for." The key thing to remember: It's fairly normal to feel a little shy or anxious when meeting new people, being in new situations or going for a job interview. Social anxiety is when it actually stops people doing things, Greening says. For those with a clinical diagnosis it can have a debilitating impact like it did for Mary. "It can be hard to admit to any form of social anxiety in a world where extrovertism and social confidence is generally admired. Many people try to hide their social anxiety or use safety behaviours." Signs someone may be socially anxious: Playing with a phone to avoid interacting Always staying close to someone or staying on the edges of a group Sticking to safe subjects of conversation like work Greening says there is some evidence social anxiety is getting worse and that increased use of smartphones and remote working is contributing by "leading to less social interactions and increased levels of anxiety". Mary, who has moved on to do a postgraduate course, is now managing her social anxiety better. After her undergraduate degree she got support from the NHS in the form of a talking therapy called CBT. It is considered the gold standard treatment for social anxiety and encourages people to re-frame their thoughts and change their behaviours. Prof David Clark, a psychologist at the University of Oxford, says he would like to see more people come forward for therapy but says people can also take steps to help themselves. The first step, he says, is to stop obsessive self-focus. "People with social anxiety often monitor themselves constantly during social situations. Am I blushing? Do I sound stupid? Do I look nervous? "Focus outwardly on the conversation, other person or your surroundings." He says you also need to test your fears with behavioural experiments by asking a question in a meeting or saying something in a group and noticing what happens. "People with social anxiety often assume negative outcomes – that they will embarrass themselves or think others will find them boring. Testing that can help people break that. It's frightening, but it can really help." He also says they need to drop safety behaviours, such as rehearing every sentence, avoiding eye contact or sticking close to one particular person. And finally, Clark adds, try to avoid post-event rumination. "It's so easy to distort what actually happened." This is something Mary can empathise with. "I used to play things over constantly in my mind. What I've learnt is that dealing with social anxiety is a gradual process. The therapy really helped me, but so did something a friend said to me a couple of years ago. "When I said I didn't want to join her in meeting some of her friends, citing my poor social skills, she said she'd never thought that about me and that I shouldn't undersell myself. I was overcome with emotion. "I'm now pushing myself to engage more. It helps that in my postgrad course we're in smaller groups, but I've also joined an astronomy group. It's still difficult and it doesn't always go how I want it to, but I'm learning to manage it." title: Antisemitism on the rise at universities, charity warns
description: The Community Security Trust says reported incidents are "substantially higher" than before the war in Gaza began.
body: Cases of antisemitism affecting university students and staff in the UK increased in the last academic year, according to a charity that monitors antisemitic incidents. The Community Security Trust (CST) said it had recorded 95 "university-related" incidents in the 2025-26 academic year - up from 83 the year before. It said the number had fallen from its peak in the year after Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza began, but remains "substantially higher" than before that point. Universities UK (UUK) represents more than 140 institutions and said its members needed to "protect Jewish students and staff", adding that the findings were a "serious concern". Lucy Powell, education secretary in England, said the findings in the CST report were "deeply troubling". "We expect universities to take a zero-tolerance approach to antisemitism, and are providing training to help university staff identify and respond to incidents swiftly," she said. The CST defines an antisemitic incident as "university-related" if it concerns a student, member of staff or academic at a UK university "in their academic or student capacity" - including on campus and online. In 2022-23, the last academic year before the 7 October attack, the CST recorded 53 incidents. That grew to 272 in 2023-24. A report from the charity examining the past two academic years says reported incidents fell in 2024-25 and but grew again in 2025-26. The most common type of incident recorded by CST over both years was abusive behaviour, including verbal abuse, comments made in person or online and antisemitic graffiti. Its report said that, for the first time, there were two occurrences of extreme violence in 2024-25. It said there were six reported assaults across both years, eight incidents of damage and desecration to Jewish property - five of which were in student accommodation - and ten threats. Around two-thirds of reported incidents involved antisemitic language or targeting alongside references to Israel, Gaza, Hamas, the 7 October attack, and the subsequent conflicts in the Middle East. The war in Gaza was triggered by the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage. Israel launched a mass military offensive on Gaza in response which has killed around 74,000 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. The CST report said: "While criticism of Israel and Zionism is not inherently antisemitic, the data in this report continue to demonstrate that anti-Zionist language is frequently deployed in conjunction with hostility towards Jews and Jewish organisations." Mark Gardner, CST's chief executive, said "Jews are still facing a very serious campus antisemitism problem" and it was "particularly troubling that a growing proportion of the anti-Jewish actions involve university staff". He added that universities had "a duty to ensure that Jewish students and staff can study, work and participate on campus the same as anyone else". Raphi Leon, president of the Union of Jewish Students, said the report "must be a shot in the arm to boost action to support Jewish students and tackle antisemitism". Vivienne Stern, chief executive of UUK, said: "The rise in antisemitic incidents in the UK, including on university campuses, is a serious concern. "Universities have a responsibility to protect Jewish students and staff from abuse, and to ensure that students and staff clearly understand where the expression of a strongly held view becomes antisemitism and harassment." She said UUK had worked with organisations including the CST on guidance for universities, but added there was "more to do, particularly in building confidence in the effectiveness of disciplinary processes".
