title: Village team triumphs in FA Cup row replay
description: The controversial replay follows the FA ruling a referee had made a mistake in the initial match.
body: The FA Cup replay in Norfolk drew hundreds more fans than a normal game Village football club Mulbarton Wanderers saw off lower league rivals Woodford Town to settle a controversial FA Cup replay. The first meeting of the teams made international headlines after the Football Association (FA) made the rare decision to order a replay due to a referee's error. A record crowd of 806 people attended the match in Norfolk this evening, with Wanderers sealing progress thanks to a 2-0 win. The victory brings with it £3,375 from the FA Cup prize fund and a home tie against Gloucester City in the third qualifying round of the world's oldest football competition. Mulbarton Wanderers in blue saw off Woodford Town in yellow Mulbarton had to introduce advance ticketing because of "unprecedented demand" due to the attention. That followed a surprise decision by the FA to rule that the game should be replayed and switched to Norfolk. London club Woodford, who play in a league below Mulbarton, lodged an appeal due to the laws of the game being applied incorrectly during the initial game, which Wanderers had won 2-1. With the match still at 0-0 in the first half, Woodford had a penalty disallowed for their players encroaching into the penalty area. However, the game was restarted with Mulbarton being awarded a free-kick, instead of Woodford being able to retake the penalty. Danny Self, joint first team manager at Mulbarton Wanderers, was frustrated by the decision Speaking before the game, Danny Self, joint first team manager at Mulbarton, said: "There's all the emotions, you ask questions and you're frustrated. "Then you ask can we appeal this and you're told you can't. "Whether we agree or disagree, we are where we are and we've just got to prepare for it." Dan Robathan, a retired Premier League and FIFA referee, defended the original matchday official. He said: "There's a misconception that when we make a decision, that we don't care which is so far from the truth. "It hits you quite personally and you don't want to have a negative effect on a game. "But you're trying to process all that at once and I can only assume he's got confused with the law in that moment." The village club, around six miles (10km) south of Norwich, has risen through local leagues in recent years and is competing at step four of the non-league pyramid for the first time this season. The tie against Gloucester in the next round is scheduled for the weekend of Saturday 3 October. Gloucester play at step three of non-league, in Southern League Premier Division South. The winner will claim £5,625 in winnings and the losers £1,875. Despite losing tonight's tie, Woodford also collect £1,125 from the prize fund. title: Former American Idol contestant and pastor found guilty of murdering wife
description: Caleb Flynn weeps in court as he is convicted of shooting his wife, Ashley, dead in their Ohio home.
body: A former Ohio music pastor who once appeared on the TV talent show American Idol has been found guilty of murdering his wife. Caleb Flynn, 40, fatally shot Ashley Flynn twice in the back of the head while she was asleep in bed at their Ohio home on 16 February this year, then tried to claim that burglars had shot her. Flynn wept in court after the jury delivered its verdict following less than three hours of deliberations. He was also found guilty of the other eight charges against him, which included aggravated murder and tampering with evidence. He faces life in prison without parole. Closing arguments ended on Tuesday in Flynn's trial, wrapping up eight days of testimony that included a song played in court that prosecutors say he wrote and dedicated to the woman with whom he was having an affair. Throughout the trial, the prosecution presented evidence including police body camera footage, and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch around the time of the murder. They also called dozens of witnesses, including his former mistress Alleigha Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church. Some of their 100,000 exchanged text messages were read aloud in court. The defence called no witnesses. "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail," Flynn wrote in a message to Botner, 24, in August 2025. In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone." Testifying in court, Botner said she now hates Flynn "because I believe that he murdered his wife". During closing arguments on Tuesday, prosecuting attorney Paul Watkins leaned heavily into Flynn's text exchanges, which he said demonstrated the defendant's "hatred" for his wife. An emotional Flynn was seen in court at times sniffling and wiping tears from his eyes. Watkins also said that when police arrived at the family home in Tipp City in the early hours on 16 February, Flynn told police he had been lying in his daughters' bedroom when he heard gunfire. Flynn said he found his 37-year-old wife dead in the bedroom, after noticing the garage side door was open. Watkins said Flynn later told investigators he had not been to the garage, contradicting his earlier statement. Flynn's defence lawyer Patrick Mulligan, meanwhile, told the court there was no concrete evidence, saying: "Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn't solve the case." Mulligan said the issue was not whether Flynn was a good husband and that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder. "They can't find the gun, therefore they blame it on him?" Mulligan questioned, referring to the charge of tampering with evidence that Flynn also faced. Flynn's gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has remained missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open. Earlier in the trial, Botner took the stand as a witness for two days, offering testimony about her nearly 18-month relationship with Flynn. In addition to reading some of their text exchanges, she also explained the lyrics line by line from an AI-generated song. Video of the jury's reaction to the song, including what looked like laughter, went viral. Prosecutors also called Joseph Wilhelm, a special agent from Ohio's Bureau of Criminal Investigations, as a witness. He said multiple apps had been uninstalled from Flynn's phone before his wife's death, including Instagram and an AI-music generating app. The music-generating app, Wilhelm said, "related to his relationship with Alleigha Botner". Flynn appeared in 2013 on the 12th series of American Idol. He was featured in televised auditions, and was given a "golden ticket" to go to Hollywood, but he never reached the main competition. "Music is all I know, it's what I live to do and I love to sing, so that's why I auditioned," he said in videos shown on the programme. "Maybe my wife kinda nudged me a little, too." He is due to be sentenced on 5 October. title: Who continues to show how important they are? - England player ratings
description: How the England players rated following their Nations League match.
body: Anthony Gordon scored for the second England game in a row. England got their first win in the Nations League as Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane scored to beat the Czech Republic 2-0. Here's how BBC Sport England reporter Alex Howell rated the players. You can see how you scored them below. What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? James Trafford: Made a good save in the second half. Trafford was very calm with the ball at his feet and showed his passing range which pleased Tuchel throughout. 6 Trent Alexander-Arnold: Started his first England game for nearly two years. Not much to do defensively but put in a great ball for the England opener. 7 Trevoh Chalobah: A shaky start from the centre back who lost possession a couple of times and lost out in challenges which frustrated manager Thomas Tuchel. But Chalobah settled and ensured England kept a clean sheet against 10-man Czech Republic. 6 Marc Guehi: The usual reliable performance from Guehi. England didn't have much defending to do but he put in a couple of important blocks. 6 Lewis Hall: The left-back combined well with Anthony Gordon and offered a good outlet for England. Hall was a threat going forward and should have scored in the second half. 7 Elliot Anderson: Dominated the midfield, kept the ball ticking for England and won possession back the few times that the Czech Republic ventured forward. A mature performance. 7 Myles Lewis-Skelly: Started the game well and was given a lot of responsibility in England's build up play. However, Lewis-Skelly was booked for a mis-timed tackle and then taken off at half time. 6 Morgan Rogers: Played Bukayo Saka through with a nice pass early on and hit the post twice. Not given much room by a Czech side who defended very deep. 6 Bukayo Saka: Not much of note to mark for Saka in what was a cagey match as England laboured when breaking down the Czech defence before Gordon's goal. 6 Anthony Gordon: A constant threat in behind and put in a dangerous cross in the first half that deserved to end up with a goal. Scored the opener and continues to show why he is becoming so important for the Three Lions. 8 Harry Kane: A quieter night for Kane who dropped deep and went looking for the ball but the England captain still got on the score sheet with a good finish inside the area in the second half. 7 Eberechi Eze (on 46, Lewis-Skelly): Added a spark to midfield. 6 Jude Bellingham (on 70, Kane): Took the captains armband and led the line. 6 Alex Scott (on 70, Anderson): Made his England debut. 6 Rio Ngumoha (on 71, Saka): His first thought was to go forward. 6 Morgan Gibbs-White (on 81, Gordon): Subs not used: Pickford, Steele, Konsa, Branthwaite, Garner, Calvert-Lewin, Quansah After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: How Lindsay Clancy's return to court after mistrial unfolded
description: The BBC's Ione Wells describes what happened in court, as the US mother's defence for the first time argued there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children.
body: This video can not be played Lindsay Clancy has appeared in court for the first time since her murder trial fell apart, with lawyers on both sides arguing how to proceed with the case. Her defence argued that the judge should use his power to declare her not guilty. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, also brought a new defence forward arguing there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children. Posecutors say the state "met its burden" in proving Clancy's guilt. During court, both sides also resisted the judge's request to decide a potential retrial date, arguing that important legal questions still need to be decided first. The BBC's Ione Wells breaks down how Lindsay Clancy's first court appearance went after her 4 September mistrial. How Lindsay Clancy's return to court after mistrial unfolded. title: Three teenagers die after car enters River Wear
description: The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water, police say.
body: Three teenagers have died after a car went into the River Wear Three teenagers have died after a car entered the River Wear. Northumbria Police said just before 13:30 BST a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and entered the water. Four people were in the car at the time and a 17-year-old boy managed to reach safety. He is currently in hospital with non-serious injuries, and has subsequently been arrested in connection with the incident, the force said. The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water. No other vehicles are believed to have been involved. Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said it was "a truly tragic incident". "Our thoughts are with their families, friends and all those impacted by what has happened," he said. He added the investigation was at an early stage and the force was working to establish the circumstances. The RNLI assisted with rescue efforts Members of the public have been asked to continue to avoid the area. Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service, the North East Ambulance Service and RNLI teams were in attendance earlier helping with the rescue efforts. A spokesperson for Sunderland AFC posted on social media: "At a deeply difficult time for our city, our thoughts are with the families and friends of those who have lost their lives, and everyone affected by this tragedy. "We also pay tribute to the emergency services and all those who have responded at the scene." Earlier, North East mayor, Kim McGuinness, said she had asked the incident commander to keep her updated. Meanwhile Labour MP for Sunderland Central, Lewis Atkinson, said on X: "My thoughts are with everyone involved and their families, and with the emergency services responding to the scene." A large number of emergency services attended the scene in Sunderland Follow BBC Sunderland on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen on BBC Sounds. title: Could changing the pension triple lock pay for Burnham's big social care plan?
description: Burnham said he wants to change the pensions triple lock from 2030 to pay for his social care reform, but analysts have questioned whether it will raise enough money.
body: In his Labour conference speech, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would "adjust" the triple lock on the state pension to help pay for a new "national care service" in England from 2030. While his proposed reform is likely to reduce public spending on pensions, analysts say it would be unlikely to save enough money between 2030 and 2040 to pay for comprehensive social care reform. BBC Verify has looked at the key figures. Since it was introduced by the coalition government in 2011, the triple lock has guaranteed that the UK state pension rises each year in line with whichever is the highest of inflation, average wages, or 2.5%. Burnham said that from April 2030, instead, it would only rise in line with the highest of inflation or 2.5%. The prime minister added that "it will hold its value relative to earnings over time". We are still awaiting full details from the government, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think tank, external says the new proposed system would ensure that the state pension rises by whichever is highest of: average earnings over time rather than every year The IFS says the key change is that the state pension will not automatically jump up with average wage increases every year, but only broadly track them over a longer period of time. That is important because in some years the triple lock has meant the state pension has risen faster than earnings. "The removal of this permanent ratchet is to be welcomed and marks a substantial step towards a more sustainable and predictable state pension system," the IFS says. The IFS estimates that the present triple lock will increase annual state pension expenditure by £16bn a year by 2026–27, compared with if it had risen in line with average earnings growth since 2011. It says that if the new lock had been in place instead, spending would be £9bn a year lower than it currently is. There is considerable uncertainty about future savings though because the cost of the triple lock is linked to the future volatility of people's earnings and inflation, which are impossible to confidently forecast. Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care Faisal Islam: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options? What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it? Moreover, analysts think it could take more than a decade for the reform to deliver major savings. Earlier this year, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) - the government's official forecaster - analysed how much , externalshifting to just an earnings-linked state pension in 2030 would cost relative to keeping the triple lock. This is similar to what Burnham is proposing. The OBR did not identify any significant savings for the government from such a shift until 2034. And by 2040 the annual saving was estimated by the OBR to be 0.2% of GDP, equivalent to £6bn a year in today's money. Downing Street has said the planned change will save £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s, but did not provide detail on how it reached that figure. Different social care reforms come with different price tags. The Health Foundation think tank has estimated that imposing a lifetime cap on an individual's care costs of around £86,000 in England, as proposed by the official report for the coalition government by Andrew Dilnot in 2011, would cost the government around £4bn a year. The think tank estimates that introducing a Scotland-style system of "free personal care" - which does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs - would amount to around £7.5bn a year. And the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system , externalin England would be around £18.5bn a year extra by 2036. The government has not set out the full details of how the "national care system" will work, but has clarified that while an individual's direct care costs would be covered, their accommodation costs in a residential or nursing home would not be. Nevertheless, if it implemented a universal and comprehensive social care system then the expected revenues from the proposed reform could fall short. Jonathan Cribb of the IFS said the pension reform "will not be the answer to funding universal social care". This could put pressure on a future government to raise revenues from other sources - either from tax rises or spending cuts elsewhere - to pay for a comprehensive social care service in England. title: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?
description: Detectives are entering a vital stage of the investigation, with a number of options still open, the BBC's Daniel Sandford writes.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What's next for the RAF Fairford counter-terror investigation? On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford. Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force. One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard. They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol. What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on? The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor." But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary". He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump. Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy". This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation. A resident of Whelford took this photo of five men sitting on the ground, handcuffed In truth, once it became clear that the military remote-controlled robots that were used found no explosives in the vans, only petrol, the investigation inevitably changed. It left detectives with five men from London in their 20s in police custody who had simply been found parked up near the air base in the middle of the night in suspicious circumstances and with some petrol - but little other usable concrete evidence. It might have been hard to persuade a senior officer or a magistrate to extend the suspects' detention without something more definite. The men were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE), not the Terrorism Act (TACT). This meant detectives had the option to use police bail with strict conditions, but could not hold the men for 14 days, which they could have done if TACT had been used. What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe More questions than answers after major incident near RAF Fairford For a while it was unclear whether the men were already being watched by undercover surveillance teams when they were spotted by villagers in the dead of night, or whether the villagers really were the first people to alert the police. Taylor has now given some assistance on this, saying the response on Sunday morning was "due to a range of information that we received", suggesting the police had some other intelligence Certainly security had been visibly stepped up at the base in the preceding days, so certainly there had been some intelligence about a possible attack. Elite firearms officers were very quick to respond to the villagers' 999 calls. Both counter-terrorism and military sources have told me that this story is still quite near the beginning, raising the possibility that detectives are trying to identify some kind of "controlling hand" behind the presence of the suspects in Whelford with their petrol. That leaves a number of options open: The men could be entirely innocent and able to give a good explanation for being in Whelford on Sunday They could have been paid or tricked into moving the vehicles and the petrol, but unaware of who they were working for Or they could have been part of a plot which was interrupted before it reached a more dangerous phase That is why the next bit of the counter-terrorism investigation is so vital. By examining mobile phones and computers, tracking vehicles, searching addresses, and using the covert techniques of MI5, GCHQ and US intelligence, detectives are trying to build a clearer picture. On that critical investigation rests the decision over whether to arrest anyone else, whether to charge the five men, and whether we ever find out the true story of the mysterious RAF Fairford plot. body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations The latest two minute news summary from BBC World Service. How a Chinese AI model was persuaded to ignore its rules and give dangerous advice. From Mongolia to Texas, record numbers of lithium-ion batteries are being added to the world's electricity grids - helping to provide more reliable power and speeding up the transition to renewable energy sources such as wind and solar. China is installing over half of these new batteries, often in giant battery farms, followed by the United States and Europe. And with prices dropping fast, the trend is likely to continue and spread to more developing countries. But is battery development moving fast enough to help us meet our climate goals? And what about alternatives to lithium-ion technology like using air, water or even sand? Could these types of batteries help us with other energy problems such as storing heat over the winter. In this edition of The Climate Question, Hosts Graihagh Jackson talk to Akshat Rathi, senior climate reporter at Bloomberg news and host of Bloomberg Green's Zero podcast. title: OpenAI agents get rebrand - as 'dots' - while safety worries delay new model
description: Sam Altman spoke in San Francisco during OpenAI’s yearly event for tech developers.
body: Sam Altman has spoken repeatedly in recent weeks about the risks posed by AI agents. OpenAI has chosen to rename new versions of artificial intelligence tools widely known as agents. They are now being called "dots." Company boss Sam Altman, speaking in San Francisco on Tuesday during OpenAI's yearly event for technology developers, referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of." OpenAI in recent months has come under intense scrutiny as internal tests of its AI agents have revealed often unexpected and occasionally harmful actions, leading to more public and government fears. Dots, however, were pitched as brightly colored cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives. The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of." A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children. Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously. "You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added. The day prior to OpenAI's Tuesday event, the company said it was delaying the launch of its latest model due to certain safety issues that showed up during internal testing. Since July, the company has been dealing with a series of issues with its AI agents acting improperly. It has faced unprompted hacking into the AI platform Hugging Face, posting to third-party websites images that AI agents took from ChatGPT user chats, and accessing non-public information maintained by the Australian government. OpenAI, as well as rival AI firm Anthropic, previously delayed public release of certain AI models due to potential risks, mostly pertaining to cybersecurity or hacking concerns. Both companies also expect to be listed on the public stock market in the coming months. Anthropic likely will do so this year, while OpenAI is poised for 2027. And both companies have lately been clear that they believe AI poses a genuine risk on a large scale, be it to public infrastructure or public safety. Speaking last week to the UN, Altman pleaded for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, told the UN that if the speeding development of AI was not properly managed and overseen, future versions of the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole." title: Chris Mason: Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
description: The key thing to understand about Andy Burnham's speech is these were the words and the delivery of both a new prime minister and a grieving son, the BBC's political editor writes.
body: The key thing to understand about Andy Burnham's speech is these were the words and the delivery of both a new prime minister and a grieving son. Burnham is living through two life-shaping, even life-defining moments right now – becoming and adjusting to being prime minister during the final weeks of his dad Roy's life, and preparing his speech while dealing with the grief of his loss. The funeral will take place in a few days' time. Reflections on his dad's life and influence formed the personal spine to this deeply political speech, which ranged far and wide. Labour figures are enthused that they now have a leader with what they see as a clear sense of purpose that can be easily articulated. The tacit, unflattering comparison with former PM Sir Keir Starmer is obvious. Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system Burnham says public body will invest in electricity grid What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years. The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation. Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election. The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like – the idea being that the argument is won in advance. Let's see. The debate is only just beginning. The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage. The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest. But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage. Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock – note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals – it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many. Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and – after a review to come – the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union. How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know. And from the longer term stuff to the here and now – including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid. There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead. His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into. It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour. The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver? And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable? You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters. Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward. Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety
description: A former chef contacted Hackney Council after complaining to managers at the members' club.
body: Shoreditch House is one of 10 Soho House locations in London A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and out-of-date food allegedly being served. The former staff member told BBC News he was pressured replace labels on prepared food if it was not sold at the end of the day and said he regularly saw rats at the venue. His contract was terminated two months after he first raised concerns, but Soho House said this was unrelated to his complaints. It added that the food incident was isolated and re-labelling unsold food was not company policy, but it did not comment on the rats claim. Hackney Council has confirmed it is investigating food safety and hygiene at Soho House's Shoreditch location. Soho House is a popular haunt for A-list celebrities. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle reportedly had their first date at one of its London venues. The former staff member at Shoreditch House, Kamran Khan, first raised concerns informally about the alleged re-labelling practice before formally filing a complaint with Soho House. Khan was on probation at the venue when he raised the concerns in July, and his employment was terminated earlier in September. Following his formal complaint, the company investigated and told Khan on 24 August there was evidence to support his claim and steps were being taken to address the matter. Khan claimed the practice continued despite the assurances he was allegedly offered, leading him to complain to Hackney Council instead. A spokesperson for the council said: "We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation." Speaking to BBC News, Khan said he was told in a probation meeting to continue the practice. The 30-year-old, who told BBC News he has had several jobs in catering and hospitality said he was told "if I don't change labels on my own initiative, [they] would take that as a performance concern". He said he felt compelled to raise the issue because he saw a lot of children and pregnant women at the restaurant. "I told them that I don't want to be held personally liable for anyone that gets injured," he said. Food served in a restaurant must legally be labelled with information including the best-before or use-by date. Khan also said there had been rats at the venue for a long time and that cleaners were told to check daily for rat droppings. A spokesperson for Soho House apologised for the incident, saying: "This is not how we expect our houses to operate and it is not company policy." They said an external, independent investigation and audit was conducted. "Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us," they added. "For clarity, the former employee's contract was terminated for reasons entirely unrelated to food labelling." Soho House membership starts from £291.67 monthly or £204.17 for under-27s. The group opened its first club in London in 1995, and now has 46 Soho Houses in Europe, North America and Asia, as well a string of other up-market hospitality businesses. The company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, but its share price dropped sharply in the following years as it struggled to make a profit and fought accusations it was losing its exclusivity. It was bought by a consortium of investors last year, with actor Ashton Kutcher joining the company's board. title: Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts
description: The Premier League confirms that Manchester City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.
body: This video can not be played Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts & misleading accounts Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of its commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m, the Premier League says. The League confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged the "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs". The club continues to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal. News broke last week that City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, but on Tuesday the Premier League published a redacted version of the commission's report. The commission's report said the charges "concerned well over 100 alleged individual breaches of Premier League Rules across four broad charge categories". It also found the club guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation and said that "a number of important Club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence". The sham commercial deals were described as being part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m. City recorded £360m in sponsor fees in the three seasons they won the Premier League - 2011-12, 2013-14, and 2017-18. Only £43m of it was legitimate - the rest came from their owners and was disguised. "The relevant sponsorship agreements were found to be shams, or at minimum did not reflect their economic substance," the commission said. It also describes "deliberate or reckless conduct intended to circumvent the Premier League rules" and that the "sham" scheme devised by City allowed the club "to avoid recording what would otherwise have been the largest single-season loss in Premier League history in 2009-10". The commission highlighted the scale of evidence it had to consider by pointing out that the index alone ran to more than 750 pages, while the core bundle of documents "ran to many tens of thousands of pages". City are owned by the Abu Dhabi United Group, who took over the club in 2008 and are referred to as "ADUG" in the commission's report. Live reaction - Man City guilty: 'Sham' contracts and £830m overstated income revealed This video can not be played Man City CEO refuses to answer questions on guilty verdict Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, said: "The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade. "It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently. "It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously." The Premier League also said that City's sanction "will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission". The League's rules state that the hearing must remain private and confidential. Lisa Nandy MP, the Culture, Media & Sport secretary, told the BBC: "It's incredibly serious, the Premier League report is incredibly stark. "This is causing a lot of concern for Man City fans and all fans of Premier League football." This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City In its own statement, the club said: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today. "The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums. "The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe. "The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence. "The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete." November 2018: Football Leaks allegations emerge with Der Spiegel publishing claims Manchester City breached financial fair play rules. March 2019: Uefa launches a formal investigation off the back of Der Spiegel's findings. May 2019: City criticise the investigation and launch an appeal process. November 2019: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) deems City's appeal inadmissible. February 2020: Uefa announces a two-year ban for City from European competitions and a €30m fine. July 2020: City's European ban is overturned after an appeal to Cas. July 2021: City lose a jurisdiction ruling that allows the media to report the Premier League is continuing to investigate the champions for alleged financial breaches. April 2022: Der Spiegel publishes a fresh report claiming the Premier League has been investigating the club for three years, providing detailed claims. title: 'Quantity of petrol' but no explosives found in three vehicles near RAF Fairford
description: Police say the decision to release five men on bail is one "grounded in experience and strategy".
body: A quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the three vans near RAF Fairford in the west of England, counter-terror police have said. Five men, all UK nationals in their 20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after the vehicles were spotted in the early hours of Sunday, sparking a major security incident around the base which is operated by the US military. They were released on bail the following day in what police described as an "investigative decision" which was "grounded in experience and strategy". It comes after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved. Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said the police response on Sunday morning was due to "a range of information", including a call from a member of public about "several vehicles acting suspiciously" close to the base. He added that he hoped to close the "investigative scenes" by Wednesday. title: Hull conference to discuss training space workers
description: The event will bring together leaders from industry, education and the space sector.
body: The conference will discuss training for the space sector Hull College is hosting a conference on training people for the space industry. The event on 8 October will "bring together leaders from industry, education and the space sector," according to a college spokesperson. Speakers will talk about the skills the sector will need over the next five to 10 years, with a focus how to develop a more diverse workforce. Hull College principal Debra Gray said: "When people hear 'space', they still tend to think of astronauts, scientists and rockets. But there is a much bigger workforce beneath that – the people who will build, operate, maintain and support the technology and infrastructure the sector needs." She added: "There is a huge amount of ambition around the growth of the UK space sector, but ultimately that ambition can only be realised if we have the people with the skills to deliver it." "Further Education has the scale, reach and technical expertise to make a significant contribution. Talent is everywhere, but opportunity isn't, and we want to make sure people from every background can see that there could be a place for them in this industry." title: Fury & Joshua in London for news conference as doubts ease
description: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua arrive in London for Wednesday’s launch news conference, with their December fight now expected to take place as scheduled.
body: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are two of the biggest names in British boxing but have never shared the ring in a professional fight Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have both arrived in London before Wednesday's launch news conference for their fight. It appears the all-British heavyweight contest - more than a decade in the making - remains on for 11 December at Cardiff's Principality Stadium following several days of uncertainty. Fury, 38, has travelled back from the United States, where he had been at Walt Disney World Resort with his family, while Joshua, 36, has flown in from his training camp in Dubai. Fury-Joshua was officially announced on Thursday by Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh, but doubts emerged 24 hours later amid a dispute over the role of UFC chief Dana White in the promotion. Broadcaster Netflix said Alalshikh's The Ring and White would collaborate to promote the event, but Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn said his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role. White said on Saturday night he did not know whether the fight - or Wednesday's news conference - would happen. BBC Sport now understands he will not attend the launch. A further potential hurdle emerged late on Monday over Fury's enrolment in the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association (Vada) testing programme. Fury's manager Spencer Brown has since said Fury is now enrolled with Vada, appearing to resolve another issue before the launch. Fury and Joshua have never fought despite several previous attempts to make the all-British contest. Wednesday's event at the British Airways ARC in Olympia will be the first time the pair have come face-to-face since the fight was officially announced, with a limited number of tickets also being made available to the public. Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua in Cardiff is expected to take place in the early hours to suit US audiences and will be broadcast globally on Netflix There was at least something reassuring about seeing both men step out of cars in London on Tuesday, ready for Wednesday's launch. But a Fury-Joshua fight being 'on' has now been announced so many times it is hard to keep count. And that is part of the problem. We have been here before and there is no way to dress up the past few days as anything other than a desperately poor look for boxing. The majority of supporters felt Fury-Joshua had arrived too late, with both men now former champions and far from the peak of their powers. Yet within 48 hours of the long-awaited announcement, even some of those still excited by the contest had been turned into cynics. Instead of discussing how Fury and Joshua match up, the conversation became about promoters, contractual clauses, competing egos and whether the fight would happen at all. That is remarkable for a shared purse reported to be worth close to $200m (£151m), backed by some of the most powerful figures in the sport. Hearn has alleged contractual terms around White's involvement have not been adhered to. White has publicly attacked Hearn. Fury accused Joshua's camp of trying to pull out. All of it created unnecessary uncertainty around a fight boxing has spent years failing to deliver. With all that said, Wednesday offers an opportunity to change the mood quickly. If Fury and Joshua both walk on stage and produce the kind of fireworks their rivalry had long-promised, some - though not all - of the noise of the past few days could fade. title: Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care
description: The PM was at times emotional during his conference speech in which he outlined his long-term plan for the UK.
body: Andy Burnham has set out his plan to transform Britain, including by ending the existing state pension triple lock from 2030 to help fund a new national care service. In his first Labour Party conference speech as prime minister, Burnham also said he wants to pave the way for greater public control over housing, water and energy services, and potentially reform the UK's electoral system. After days of questions over how to fund his social care reforms in England, Burnham pointed to changing the triple lock to generate "significant savings". His plans would see the state pension increase every year at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. Andy Burnham: Northern PM's long journey to power In front of a packed hall and watched on by family and friends, Burnham spoke for more than an hour - at times pausing and appearing to hold back tears as he referred to his father, Roy, who died earlier this month. Arriving on stage to the sound of "All Together Now" by Liverpool band The Farm, Burnham made the song title a theme of his speech. He said he wanted to "draw a line on a decade of division" and to "stop doomscrolling on posts running Britain down". Burnham also told conference that he wants to "put the country on a new path" and recalled his family's "working-class aspiration" and how the government wanted to "unlock" this for others. There was an expectation that Burnham's time in Liverpool for his party's conference would see him flesh out his vision for the future of the country. In the conference hall, he offered more details albeit with some of the proposals relating to the content of the Labour manifesto at the next general election rather than delivering immediate action. Burnham's plan to offer free at the point of use social care in England is among those being developed so it can be put before voters in 2029. He said it would be "fully funded and not through borrowing". Explaining his long-held ambition to make changes, he raised his family's experiences - including how his grandmother Kitty's engagement ring was "ripped from her finger and stolen in a care home". He argued a national care service was a "landmark" policy that would be "as significant as the creation of the NHS itself and utterly essential to securing its future". Before turning to the pension triple lock changes, Burnham accepted he may "pay a political price" by trying to make the reforms but argued "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off". The triple lock was introduced in 2010 by the coalition government and designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people. It means the state pension rates rise every April by either inflation, earnings growth or 2.5% - whichever is the highest. Burnham said this will stay in place until 2030, at which point he would like to "adjust it". He said: "The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%. And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation. "But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service. "Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care changes today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen." Officials have suggested the change could save £15bn a year by 2040. Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said savings "are likely to be relatively small in the first few years, but rise substantially over time". He also said "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament". Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, told the BBC she believed the government should have "pulled another lever", such as a wealth tax, rather than making changes to the triple lock. The political backlash was immediate. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "more tax rises are inevitable" under Labour's plan, while Reform UK's Nigel Farage accused the PM of "launching an offensive against our elderly". Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said families "cannot wait until after another election and it can't be funded from the pockets of our poorest pensioners". Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel greet delegates in the audience after he delivered his keynote speech Elsewhere in his speech, Burnham said he wanted to repeal "Margaret Thatcher's ideological ban on public ownership of water companies". The PM said legislation will be put before Parliament, adding the changes will "start a 10-year journey to a very different water system", which includes new powers for mayors to hold "companies to account". Burnham said it will be made easier for councils to acquire private rented homes in poor condition if landlords refuse to take action after being issued warnings. He said the government will change the law "if necessary". Burnham also told delegates that "Brexit has done more harm than good" before he indicated he wanted to explore closer UK-EU ties. Ahead of talks expected later this year with EU chiefs, Burnham said he would set out the "different options" for Britain's "long-term relationship" with the bloc. He said: "I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in." To cheers in the hall, Burnham announced a national commission on electoral reform, which could result in changes to the current voting system for UK parliamentary elections. He asked all political parties to contribute to the work of the commission, adding: "We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment

title: Prince William and Catherine's surprise visit to Kevin Sinfield's charity run
description: The rugby league star is on the third day of his endurance challenge to raise funds for Motor Neurone Disease charities.
body: Prince William and Catherine made an unexpected appearance to meet Sir Kevin The Prince and Princess of Wales made a surprise visit to support rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield, on the third day of his endurance challenge to raise funds for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities. "What you're doing is so inspiring – the unity that you're building," Catherine told Sir Kevin. Prince William and Catherine caught up with Sir Kevin in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, as he carries out what he says will be his final fundraising challenge. Sir Kevin is aiming to complete seven ultra marathons in seven days, running between Hull and Manchester, in a challenge inspired by his former teammate Rob Burrow, who died from MND in 2024. Prince William and Catherine met young people at the Leeds Rhinos rugby league club Catherine applauded Sir Kevin's charity fundraising, which has raised more than £11m for MND causes The rugby star's gruelling mission will end on Saturday at Old Trafford in Manchester, when Sir Kevin arrives ahead of the Super League Grand Final. "Make sure you hold yourself together for another few days," Prince William told him. Sir Kevin replied that he had been dreaming of an ice bath all day. Since his first challenge in 2020, Sir Kevin has raised more than £11m for MND causes - and Prince William and Catherine made a private donation to the charity effort. Before meeting Sir Kevin, the royal couple talked to families facing the impact of MND and heard how fundraising projects had helped them. Earlier on Tuesday, Prince William and Catherine visited the home ground of Rob Burrow's rugby league team, Leeds Rhinos, and met some young players. The royal visitors heard how the club's charitable foundation was working to help health, education and well-being projects in the Leeds area. Jamie Jones-Buchanan, a former teammate of Rob Burrow, described the team's ethos in good and bad times: "We went through success and adversity, but we always came out on the other side together." Sir Kevin Sinfield began his running endurance test on Saturday Prince William and Catherine have previously supported Sir Kevin's efforts for MND charities - and the prince had presented Sir Kevin and Rob Burrow with their CBEs at the Leeds Rhinos ground in Headingley in January 2024. Rob Burrow died in June that year, aged 41, with Prince William among those paying tribute. This was the second royal endorsement this week for Sir Kevin's charity run - with Princess Anne having shown her support for him on Monday at the University of York. Although Princess Anne observed that the term "fun run" was a contradiction in terms. "I can run but I don't do it for fun. I'm past that stage," she told Sir Kevin. The knighthood awarded to Sir Kevin this year was among the first for a rugby league player. There had been accusations that the honours system had been ignoring rugby league out of snobbishness. But in June 2025, Sir Billy Boston became a rugby league knight - the first in the sport's 130-year history. title: Lindsay Clancy appears in court as her lawyer pushes for murder case dismissal
description: Clancy's defence lawyer wants her to be cleared of murdering her three children in 2023 but prosecutors say the state proved guilt.
body: This video can not be played Watch: How Lindsay Clancy's return to court after mistrial unfolded Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, has appeared in court for the first time since her murder trial fell apart earlier this month. Her defence team on Tuesday argued the judge should dismiss her case but prosecutors said the state had "met its burden" in proving her guilt. Clancy, 36, does not deny killing her three children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional. It is still not clear if she will face a retrial. The request to dismiss the case is among those that will be discussed at a hearing on 2 November, Judge William Sullivan said. One of the motions addressed on Tuesday was from Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, who asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts motion that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not argue their case effectively. Reddington also brought a new defence forward arguing there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children. "This entire case is based on speculation," he said. It was a change of argument from the defence lawyer, who during the trial focused on Clancy's mental health - urging the jury to find her not criminally responsible because of it. Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called Reddington's argument "laughable". She said state prosecutors had presented numerous pieces of evidence showing Clancy was in a healthy mental state at the time of the murders during the trial. "The Commonwealth met its burden," Buckingham said. She argued Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months, in their Massachusetts home. This video can not be played How the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apart Judge Sullivan pushed back when both Reddington and Buckingham refused to agree to his suggestion that they might agree to a possible retrial date now ahead of the hearing, saying he wanted to "get this thing moving". He asked both sides to be prepared to discuss possible trial dates at the November hearing. Reddington said he would be unable to go to trial until at least June if the case is retried. District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters outside after court that prosecutors have not yet decided if they are going to retry Clancy on murder charges. "We're doing our due diligence, we're going to continue doing that," he said. "We're going to do what we can for the children. That's what this case is about." Following a week of deliberations earlier this month, a Massachusetts jury told Sullivan they could not reach a verdict because of a lone holdout juror and a mistrial was declared on 4 September. title: Oura pulls $15bn stock market listing days after announcement
description: The wearable technology company had been expected to list its shares in the US.
body: Oura's chief executive Tom Hale wears one of the company's smart rings Oura has pulled its plan to sell shares in its business on the US stock market, in a move which would have valued the firm at $15bn (£11.3bn), just days after announcing it. The maker of smart rings which track their owners' health said it would postpone its flotation "due to uncertainty in the Initial Public Offering (IPO) market" and did not say when it might go ahead. Oura had filed official documents setting out plans to raise up to $2.2bn by offering shares in the business to investors just over a week ago. The tech firm has become the latest business to delay its public listing, with experts saying the IPO market is getting more challenging. Oura's chief executive Tom Hale said "an IPO is just one step in our journey", adding that "we have the luxury of choosing our moment". Earlier this month, US nuclear technology firm Holtec International also postponed its flotation. It blamed an "unusual confluence of developments that has impaired investor confidence in the market for new public offerings". In particular, it cited rising energy costs, military conflicts, global trade tensions and concerns about inflation which have led to central banks including the US Federal Reserve raising benchmark interest rates. This week, the yield – or interest rate – on US debt repayable in 10 years' time hit the highest level since 2007. Samuel Kerr, global head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said: "What is now clear is we are in a very different IPO market to the one we envisaged just a few weeks ago." Oura had planned to sell shares priced at between $40 and $44 on the Nasdaq stock market index, giving the company an implied market value of $15bn. In its last full financial year, ending 30 September 2025, Oura made a pre-tax profit of $23.5m on sales $907.8m. That compares to a $6.2m pre-tax profit in the previous year. Its most recent figures for the nine months to 30 June this year show pre-tax income of $70m on sales of $1.2bn. Oura, founded in Finland in 2013, has its global headquarters in San Francisco and makes smart rings – costing upwards of $300 – which monitor things such as its owner's heartbeat and sleep patterns which are analysed and presented on an app. The company is the subject of a class action lawsuit which accused it of false advertising by claiming its rings can accurately track a person's sleep activity and patterns. The lawsuit, filed by the Clarkson Law Firm in August, claimed: "Oura rings cannot measure one's sleep or cycles. That's because sleep happens in the brain, not on one's finger." It is understood that Oura's decision to delay an IPO is not connected to the lawsuit. In a statement, a spokesperson for Oura said: "We stand behind our science, research and accuracy claims." They added: "Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature." title: First female prime minister named in Morocco after winning elections
description: Her appointment by the king makes her only the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world.
body: A lawyer by training, 50-year-old Fatima Zahra El Mansouri has been the mayor of Marrakesh for a number of years Fatima Zahra El Mansouri has been named Morocco's first female prime minister, after her centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in last week's parliamentary elections. Her appointment makes her only the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden. She was named by King Mohammed VI, who chose her as prime minister over the country's football chief Fouzi Lekjaa, a top politician from the same party. El Mansouri, 50, has been the mayor of Marrakesh for a number of years and also served as a minister in the previous coalition government. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy but most power remains in the hands of the king. How Ceuta, football and Israel shaped Morocco's election At a victory press conference, prior to her announcement as prime minister, El Mansouri was asked whether the state would need to make changes to accommodate her in Muslim religious ceremonies attended by the king, including Friday and Eid prayers, where men and women pray in separate sections. She did not directly answer the question, instead praising the king as "the biggest advocate for women" in the country. "His Majesty is the holder of wisdom… If I am entrusted with the responsibility of head of government, it will be a great honour," she said. El Mansouri is one of Morocco's most prominent female politicians. A lawyer by training, she studied at Mohammed V University in the capital, Rabat, before continuing her education in France and the US, specialising in business and corporate law. She entered politics after Pam was founded in 2008 and became the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh in 2009. She returned to the post after the 2021 elections. In the past five years, she served as a minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under former Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch. In February 2024, she became the co-ordinator of Pam's leadership coalition. El Mansouri has rejected her portrayal as an "iron woman", telling Pam's magazine in 2021: "I am neither a woman of steel nor iron... I am a free activist." During her political career, El Mansouri has rarely spoken publicly about women's rights or gender inequality, despite ongoing debates in Morocco over issues such as whether polygamy should be banned and whether men and women should have equal inheritance rights. As prime minister, El Mansouri (R) now needs to negotiate a coalition with other parties to govern Under Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the party that comes first in elections to the House of Representatives. Pam has been led by a collective leadership since February 2024, rather than a single secretary general. After the results were announced last week, El Mansouri said the decision was ultimately up to the king to choose between her and Lekjaa. In the past, the appointment was largely a formality, as most Moroccan parties were led by a single secretary general, making it clear who would be nominated to head the government. With 97 seats, Pam does not have a majority and will need to form a coalition to reach the 198 seats required for an absolute majority in the 395-member parliament. It is not clear which party it will work with as it has fallen out with the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which led the outgoing government in which Pam was a junior partner. The Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) ⁠rebounded with 54 seats, from only 13 in the previous election - buoyed by the return of party leader Abdelilah Benkirane, a former prime minister. After the vote, Benkirane said the party would stay in opposition, refusing a partnership with Pam. title: Michael Sheen says being an actor will be a disadvantage on Celebrity Traitors
description: The Hollywood actor says he is a big fan of the BBC reality show, which he will now try and win.
body: The winning celeb will scoop £100,000 for their chosen charity Michael Sheen has said he thinks being an actor will be a disadvantage while he is on Celebrity Traitors. The 57-year-old is among the stars who will go head to head in the second series of the BBC reality game spin-off. A total of 21 presenters, comedians, actors and musicians will try their hand at being traitors and faithfuls in the show, which airs on 1 October. The Hollywood actor from Port Talbot said he wanted to participate because he is a "big fan" of the show and wanted to be in the castle after previously filming in the area. Speaking about how his public persona may affect how others perceive and treat him on the show, the actor said: "Well, I do think it's a disadvantage to be an actor because people immediately go, 'oh well, he pretends for a living'. "I don't think that is the case, because the whole point of acting is that you have to trick yourself into believing that what you're doing is true. If you are consciously aware that you're pretending or you're saying things that aren't true, then it's bad acting. It's just bad. "Just for me being an actor, I think that's a disadvantage because people are already suspicious of that. "Beyond being an actor, just my persona, I don't really know what people think about me. So, I don't know if it'll help or not." Michael Sheen starred as Prince Andrew in A Very Royal Scandal Sheen portrayed the disgraced Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in the 2024 Prime Video series, A Very Royal Scandal. It was based on the 2019 BBC Newsnight interview conducted by Emily Maitlis with Mountbatten-Windsor regarding his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, and became a defining moment in modern royal and media history. Sheen has also starred in films including Frost/Nixon, The Damned United and The Special Relationship. Sheen said: "I knew the area a bit [where Traitors is filmed in Scotland], and it is stunningly beautiful. It's a lovely place to be and the game is just fascinating. "I think for a show to be so popular and to grab the cultural imagination so much, it has to have the ability to go beyond what its genre is. "It somehow speaks to something a bit deeper, maybe. People get so absorbed in it." This video can not be played Watch: The Celebrity Traitors series 2 line up is revealed The first series of The Celebrity Traitors aired on the BBC last autumn, with its nail-biting finale hitting a peak of 15.4 million viewers, and Alan Carr emerging victorious. Bringing in an average audience of 14.9 million people during its run, it received the biggest TV audience of 2025. Fronted by Claudia Winkleman, the game is set in a Scottish castle in the Highlands, and follows the contestants - the majority of whom are known as faithfuls - as they try to seek out the murderous traitors among them, who kill off players in the middle of the night. The celebrities will use their skills and experience to convince the other players that they are faithfuls as they try and win £100,000 for a charity of their choice. The second celebrity version of the show will consist of 10 hour-long episodes. Those taking part alongside Sheen include comedians Joe Lycett and Romesh Ranganathan, actors Miranda Hart and Richard E. Grant, and singer James Blunt. The latest regular series was broadcast in January, attracting more than 12 million viewers per episode. The Celebrity Traitors returns to BBC One and iPlayer on 1 October. title: Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit
description: The company that runs the Eiffel Tower said the removal of female staff during the visit earlier this month was "unacceptable".
body: A delegation of BAPS Hindu monks visited the Eiffel Tower as part of a visit to Paris to open a new temple earlier this month The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group. Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, will leave his job at the end of the year, the company SETE said in a statement. It said an internal investigation found that "operational flaws and shortcomings" in organising the visit led to the "unacceptable" removal of female staff. They were replaced by male colleagues as a delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the Eiffel Tower earlier this month. BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances. At the time, SETE said the Hindu delegation had requested that the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted". A staff union representative said "women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated". Staff at the monument said female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present". The visit led to the closure of the tower as staff went on strike to show their outrage and politicians condemned the incident. Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said after the visit: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors." The Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Gregoire, called it an "absurd, unjust and unacceptable decision" and ordered two separate investigations. SETE chair Ariel Weil said on Tuesday that he had requested measures and training programmes promoting gender equality to be implemented. "The coming months will allow us to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions," he said. The tower closed as staff went on strike to show their outrage BAPS apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused" earlier this month, adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service". On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values. It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney. It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation. BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory. title: Faisal Islam: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble
description: I had expected him to try to forge a political consensus on this thorny issue at this stage, but he has gone further than that.
body: It was a significant announcement from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on his plans for the triple lock after the general election. It will reverberate well beyond the hall. For months, I have heard suggestions that Andy Burnham was warm to suggestions that the triple lock as we know it had to go. I had expected him to try to forge a political consensus on this thorny issue at this stage, but he has gone further than that. He has tried to take the sting out of the politics of his decision by tying it to funding a new national social care service. The government calls it an "adjusted triple lock" as it is keen that pensioners are reassured. It is more like a double lock plus. The sensitivity over this political gamble is clear. Under Burnham's plans, the state pension will go up by either the pace of price rises or 2.5%, whichever is higher. So, it will still keep up with inflation and go up every year. The link to rises in yearly average earnings, which is the factor currently setting the rise under the triple lock, will be gone on an annual basis and instead be reflected over time. The policy would be to maintain the state pension as a share of earnings at the record level it is due to reach in 2030. This change is sharper than expected. Not a review or a consultation. Ministers and MPs will have to back the plans in interviews and, at some point, MPs will have to vote on changing the historic annual earnings link to the state pension. It seems far more significant than a mere "adjustment". This will save many billions in the coming decades, but not so much in the next few years. The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank says that, had Burnham's tweak been in place since 2011, it would have more than halved the annual £16bn cost of the triple lock, a £9bn saving every year. Government sources said the decision to make the change now will save around £15bn a year by 2040. The prime minister was repeatedly advised that bond markets would show some appreciation for a UK government capable of taking tough decisions. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves might have imagined the same reward for her decision to scrap the winter fuel allowance, which was one of her first acts and later reversed. Part of the UK premium in bond markets has been an understandable perception that UK politics cannot have long-term debates. And the triple lock is only one of those debates started by today's speech – with significant further moves on energy and post-Brexit policy expected – that the prime minister and chancellor need the markets as well as the country to get behind. title: What did Andy Burnham promise at Labour conference?

title: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
description: The US president continues to push back on calls to establish guardrails around artificial intelligence, arguing it will stifle growth.
body: Trump was speaking at the launch of America.gov, an AI-powered web portal for US government services US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival. Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern. Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November. The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents. During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US is "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and does not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors. "If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China." Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remains steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology. "Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way". Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder AI governance. Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place. A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity. A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused. The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".
