title: Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech
description: Big policy announcements and emotional moments as the prime minister delivers a speech to Labour's conference.
body: Andy Burnham has delivered his first speech to the Labour conference as party leader and prime minister. Here is what stood out. It was no surprise to see Andy Burnham tieless and roaming the conference stage in Liverpool, unanchored by the traditional leader's speech podium. But despite the relaxed TED talk vibe, this was sober and serious speech. He set out major new policies - not always a given on these occasions - and spoke with real emotion about his family and working class roots. There were few jokes - and in stark contrast to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's speech last year, he did not mention Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch once. But he also avoided mention of some of the trickier issues he faces, such as welfare reform and how his government will pay for promised increases in defence spending. Follow live: Reaction and analysis of Burnham's speech Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care Much of his speech was aimed at the party faithful, with a promise to "break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path", and bring back traditional Labour values. It went down extremely well in the hall. We counted 11 standing ovations in just over an hour. The first came when he vowed to overturn Margaret Thatcher's 1980s reforms to give the public greater control over housing, water and energy. The new part was a plan to legislate later this year to repeal Thatcher's "ideological ban on public ownership of water companies". He said this would put the UK on a 10-year path to a "very different water system" - although there was not an explicit commitment to renationalisation. The run up to the speech was dominated by speculation about whether Burnham would scrap the state pension triple lock, which guarantees increases in line with the highest of inflation, earnings or 2.5%. In the end, it was a bit more nuanced than that. He said he would "honour" Labour's commitment to keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament. But from April 2030, the state pension would rise every year by inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, under Burnham's plans - and it will be increased in some years if needed to keep pace with average worker earnings. The change, he said, would "generate significant savings" to fund his long-held ambition of creating a National Care Service in England. "I accept I may pay a political price," he told the conference. "But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off." Burnham has made no secret of his desire to scrap Westminster's first-past-the-post voting system. And his announcement of a national commission on electoral reform went down very well with many in the hall, who have been calling for it. "We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard," he said to cheers. As he neared the end of his speech, Burnham appeared overcome by emotion and it looked for a brief moment as though he could not carry on. He was speaking about his father Roy, who he lost to Alzheimer's earlier this month. "If only, if only he had been able to appreciate that moment of the family in Downing Street," Burnham said of his first day in his new role. "The son of a man who failed his 11-plus becoming prime minister." The longest ovation of all came when he pledged to "use this job to build the kind of Britain my dad wanted to see – and fight with everything I've got to keep it together". title: Saracens face fines over 'wine consultant' Venter's media no-shows
description: Saracens are facing fines from Prem Rugby for director of rugby Brendan Venter's failure to fulfil media commitments.
body: Brendan Venter returned to Saracens as director of rugby this summer Saracens are set to receive a series of fines from Prem Rugby due to director of rugby Brendan Venter's failure to fulfil media commitments. It is understood the club have already been handed a £5,000 sanction after Venter was not present at the Prem's pre-season launch day. The South African also did not speak to the media before, during or after the opening-weekend victory at Leicester. The Daily Telegraph reported earlier on Tuesday, external that Venter "resigned" as director of rugby last month and took up a new role of "head of rugby culture and wine consultant", with head coach Joe Shaw assuming responsibility for media commitments. The report also claims Saracens asked permission in July for Shaw to front the club's media commitments. However, none of this has been confirmed by the club nor Prem Rugby. It is also thought a change of job title would not preclude Venter from his contractual responsibilities. Saracens announced in January that Venter would be returning to the club as director of rugby and have yet to confirm any change to his day-to-day responsibilities. He succeeded Mark McCall, who stepped down at the end of last season after 15 trophy-laden years in the job. Venter's first spell as Sarries' director of rugby, which began in 2009, also included clashes with authorities over media commitments. In September 2010, the club apologised to European Rugby Cup (ERC) officials for then-captain Steve Borthwick's failure to attend the Heineken Cup launch at Cardiff's Millennium Stadium. Borthwick, now England head coach, was the only missing representative from the coaches and captains of 12 English, Welsh and Scottish clubs attending the event. He had been told by Saracens to instead attend a team bonding session at a beer festival in Munich. In December 2010, Venter himself was warned by European Rugby Cup officials for a post-match interview after his side's 24-21 Heineken Cup loss to Racing Metro, in which he repeatedly gave short answers, agreeing with whatever was being asked. He later said it was inspired by a scene in the football mockumentary film, Mike Bassett: England Manager. Venter left his full-time role at Saracens halfway through the 2010–11 season, to be replaced by McCall. title: No 'deliberate' contact to stop car in A66 crash
description: No stinger was used by police before the fatal A66 crash, an initial investigation reveals.
body: PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in the collision No evidence of "tactical contact" or the use of a stinger has been found before the A66 crash which killed five young men and two police officers, an initial investigation has revealed. The crash between a Volkswagen Passat and a marked Cleveland Police vehicle happened at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August and followed a police pursuit which was abandoned. The initial investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said there was no evidence police had initiated contact with the Passat. However, director of engagement, Emily Barry, said it will take the IOPC months to conclude its full investigation due to the amount of information to review. PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who had not been following the Passat, were killed. The five people in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy. The five who died in the Passat were Jakub Matusiak, Makai Saddington, Theo Rae, Michael Robert Cahill and Cole Robert Worthy The IOPC said the pursuit began at 03.33 BST and six minutes and 12 seconds later, the Passat slowed as it approached the A66, turned right and headed the wrong way down the dual carriageway. The pursuing police driver did not follow the Passat along the wrong carriageway, turned off the blue warning lights and headed along the A66 on the right side of the road, the watchdog said. The Passat and the car PC Clough and PC Blades were in collided around 17 seconds later. A forensic collision investigator is still working to ascertain the speed of both vehicles at the point of collision. Barry said: "We continue to recognise the devastating and long-lasting impact this incident has had on the families and those in the force, the policing community, and the wider local community. "We are aware there is speculation regarding how the collision occurred. "There is no suggestion the collision was a result of any direct police contact, nor was a stinger used by the police in an attempt to stop the Passat." A stinger is a portable spike strip used to puncture the tyres of a vehicle. The IOPC has commissioned two expert reports, with one considering the collision reconstruction and another assessing the relevant policies and procedures that are in place for officers during pursuits. title: Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
description: The prime minister says he wants other parties to take part in a national commission on electoral reform.
body: Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system. In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform. He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard". He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come". Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years. Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024. Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester. In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less 30% of the vote or less." He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times." Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work. Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029. However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled. Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging after Burnham's speech that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it. Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available. At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections. Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament. Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system. title: Dutch police arrest suspected member of group that claimed FBI hack
description: The suspect, 24, was arrested before the alleged cyber attack took place.
body: Dutch police have arrested a suspected member of the ShinyHunters cyber-crime group that claimed to have stolen sensitive information on all FBI bureau staff - around 38,000 people. After the alleged attack last week, the group claimed to have every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address and phone numbers. In a statement, Dutch police said it had arrested a 24-year-old man from Amsterdam on suspicion of being part of the group, which has also claimed other hacks. The suspect was arrested on 15 September, before the alleged FBI attack. He is also suspected of attempted incitement to commit two murders, police said. Police said they seized his devices and found a "large amount of information" on his laptop, including "details about two murders that were to be committed abroad" that they suspect he may have ordered. The suspect has been held since his arrest. Dutch officials have not ruled out further arrests. Stan Duijf, who leads Dutch investigations into cybercrime, said in a statement: "The ShinyHunters group is responsible for a large number of national and international victims. "It is good that we have been able to arrest a suspect in the investigation into this group." Taking to X, FBI director Kash Patel thanked Dutch partners and said: "As we speak, FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest." Following the arrest, Brett Leatherman, assistant director of FBI Cyber, urged members of the group to hand themselves in "while the choice is still yours". He added: "Other groups believed anonymity or their friends would protect them... but arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk. "The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you, you know how to find us, we know how to find you." ShinyHunters claimed to have breached the FBI's servers on 21 September and began contacting reporters the next day sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data. The BBC has seen a small portion of the data, which appears to be genuine. ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May. The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records, and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information. In its message on the dark web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money. Instead, the cyber-criminals asked the agency to retract an advisory that it issued in May about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation. The public service announcement, external, which is still up on the FBI's website, described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims". "They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said. title: Watch: How did Burnham's speech go down in the conference hall?
description: The PM received a standing ovation as he spoke about his late dad while setting out reforms to social care.
body: This video can not be played Andy Burnham has said the government will end the pensions "triple lock" in an emotional speech at his first Labour conference as prime minister. Reflecting on the recent death of his father, Burnham set how he was determined to honour his memory by creating a new national care service funded by savings from pensions from 2030. He also announced a plan to end the ban on water companies being owned publicly and a proposal to change the UK's electoral system. The BBC's Jack Fenwick explains how the big announcements were received by Labour MPs and members in Liverpool. Watch: How did Burnham's speech go down in the conference hall? title: Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's eviction
description: The ban is part of a number of proposals that must be approved in parliament within 30 days.
body: Protests have taken place in Madrid, Barcelona, Seville, Malaga and Cadiz in response to the housing crisis Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last week. Ministers met on Tuesday to discuss the proposals, which include a ban on evictions until 2030, Health Minister Mónica García said. She said the measures would bring relief to more than five million people - but opposition politician Míriam Nogueras said the agreement left "small landlords out in the cold". The proposals - which have been presented in the form of two decrees - come into effect immediately, but must be approved by Congress within a month, although the government hopes to hold the vote as soon as this Friday. Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government lacks a majority in parliament and has struggled to get right-leaning parties to approve previous decrees. In April, a decree seeking to roll over rental contracts was blocked by right-leaning parties. García said other measures agreed upon on Tuesday included the rolling over of contracts until 2028; stricter regulation of short-term and room rentals; and banning the purchase of housing by investment firms. "It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," García said. Referencing the protests, she added: "Thanks to the mobilisations and the encampments. Without you, this would not have been possible." But Nogueras, spokeswoman for the centre-right Catalan nationalists of Junts party, said: "We all agreed that evictions - where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros - obviously need to be stopped. "Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property - putting them all in the same basket - is a mistake," she told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE. The minority government, which is made up of the Sánchez's ruling Socialists and junior partner the Sumar alliance, has 30 days from the decrees' publication to reach an agreement in parliament. Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez urged political parties to support the decrees after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week. "We all have our eyes on the text, on the small print, to make sure this is the Maricarmen decree," said Alicia del Río, spokeswoman for the Sindicato de Inquilinas, the organisation which has been leading housing protests. Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her apartment in Madrid on a stretcher on Wednesday The two decrees approved by the cabinet contain enough to at least suggest that the government has been listening carefully to the demands of the activists who have been protesting in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere in recent days. The temporary ban on evictions, the rolling over of rental contracts and the ban on investment firms - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property are all the kinds of policies that have been on the lips of housing activists in recent days. Pablo Bustinduy, minister of social rights, described the measures approved by the cabinet as "a first step towards the economic and social transformation of the country". Bustinduy and his Sumar alliance had entered the negotiations with Sánchez's Socialists determined to take a stand on this issue, which is one they feel strongly about. Sumar's tough stance was a major reason why talks between the coalition partners on the decrees went down to the wire ahead of Tuesday's cabinet meeting. While the relatively bold new measures may please many on the left, they have raised the hackles of the Junts, whose support is again likely to be needed to approve them. Junts and other parties on the right tend to be reluctant to intervene in the housing market, particularly if it means tipping the balance of the law in favour of tenants and against landlords, many of who are their natural electorate. The question now is whether the social momentum generated by the Maricarmen Abascal case will override such reservations and manage to ensure this package of measures becomes law. The hard men removing squatters in Spain 'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic Ahead of the government's announcement on Tuesday, the lawyer for Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing crisis, said she would be allowed to return to her home after reaching a deal with the company that owns it on Monday. Abascal, who was admitted to hospital after being forcibly removed from the apartment on a stretcher, was unable to attend the meeting and is yet to sign the deal. In the north-eastern city of Zaragoza, another woman's eviction was temporarily suspended on Tuesday, the European Pressphoto Agency reported. Esmeralda Tejero, 51, has lived in a flat in the city for eight years with her 11-year-old daughter, but stopped paying her rent some time ago as she could not afford it on top of her daily living costs, she told Catalan newspaper el Periódico on Monday. Protests calling for housing relief measures broke out last week in Madrid and have spread to other cities including Barcelona, Seville, Malaga and Cadiz. Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday demanding stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents. They have warned that they would continue to protest if the government does not meet their demands. The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE. The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista,

title: National museums to stay free for all visitors
description: It follows discussions about whether charging tourists could boost museums' finances.
body: Egyptian sculptures are among the collection at the British Museum in London Overseas visitors will not be charged to enter England's national museums after ministers decided against changing the universal free admission policy. It comes after months of discussions between the government, museums, the tourism sector and local leaders to examine whether making tourists from abroad pay could boost the institutions' finances. In March, the government said it would explore charging international visitors to enter national museums as it looks for ways to tackle funding pressures. But the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has now said this could deter domestic visitors and that any benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector. The UK's 15 national museums, including 12 in London, have been free for all to enter since 2001. But a review published last year by former Labour minister Baroness Margaret Hodge suggested that a charging model for international tourists "would align the UK with other countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore". On Tuesday, DCMS confirmed free admission to these museums would remain in place for everyone. "The government believes that charging overseas visitors could deter domestic visitors and that the impacts and benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector and therefore will not introduce charges for overseas visitors," a spokesperson said. Culture secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Our museums are the places that light up the world. "That's why they must be free, forever, for everyone to access." The DCMS said national museums contribute more than £1bn a year to the economy and attract visitors from around the world, with the Natural History Museum and the British Museum drawing 7.1 million and 6.4 million visitors respectively in 2025. The Natural History Museum's director Dr Doug Gurr said although his museum would have benefitted from charging, the sector would have lost out overall. "Free museums aren't a cost to the economy - they're a key reason the economy benefits from tourism in the first place," he said. "So, we're delighted to remain free but given the visitors we bring there's a strong case for reinvesting a share of any tourism revenues in the institutions that help attract them." Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, said: "When the British Museum was founded as the world's first public national museum in 1753 it was to be free for 'all persons'. "So, we are delighted by the government's announcement that free entry for all will be maintained. "This will allow everyone to enjoy and have access to our great museums across the nation as one of the things this country does so brilliantly." The government also pointed to £760m in funding for museums through its £1.5bn Arts Everywhere Fund, as well as £600m in infrastructure funding for national museums. It said the £13.6m museum transformation programme would help organisations move towards more sustainable business models, while ministers would work with the Arts Council and the sector on a long-term strategic plan for museums, with further details to be announced. title: Watch: US journalist Evan Gershkovich describes being detained by Russian agents
description: He was arrested in Russia in 2023 and later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges.
body: This video can not be played US journalist Evan Gershkovich has told the BBC's Today programme about the 16 months when he was detained in Russia. In his first UK broadcast interview, the Wall Street Journal correspondent said he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in March 2023, and arrested him. He was later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges, but released in 2024 as part of a high-profile prisoner exchange. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false, and following his arrest, then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home. Read more on this story. title: Booker Prize nominee praises his school teachers
description: Luke Kennard, who grew up in Chard, is shortlisted for the award for his novel Black Bag.
body: Luke Kennard attended Holyrood Academy in Chard An author whose latest book has been nominated for the prestigious Booker Prize said childhood boredom inspired his creativity. Luke Kennard, who grew up in Chard in Somerset, has been shortlisted for Black Bag, which is based on an experiment involving an actor sitting in a bin bag at the back of a lecture hall. He said, as a child, he had "quite a lot of time to practice" his creative passions. Kennard also praised his teachers at the town's Holyrood Academy and said: "It just can't be exaggerated how much difference a teacher can make when they find a kid who has a passion for their subjects." Key mistakes to avoid when buying Glastonbury tickets Winter Olympian swapping bobsleigh for comedy Sir Ranulph Fiennes family tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him Kennard said growing up in a quiet town had an impact on his "creative impulse". "You stay in your room playing the clarinet or writing a poem - there's a certain virtue to being a little bit bored sometimes, and just having to amuse yourself." Kennard attended Holyrood Academy from 1992 to 1999 and studied both GCSE and A-level English Literature. He added: "It was the teachers that I had who really encouraged my writing- that's quite foundational." Kennard said the former head of English, Paul Coffman, would read his short stories during break times, and leave him notes and suggestions. "He was the first person who really got me to take my writing seriously." Luke Kennard says his teachers supported his writing Holyrood Academy said it was "thrilled" with Kennard's nomination. It added his praise of Coffman "is a moving reminder of the lasting impact teachers can have on the lives and achievements of their students". "This remarkable accomplishment is a testament to Luke's talent, dedication and love of literature. The winner of the 2026 Booker Prize will be announced on 9 November. title: Amputee, nine, tells Catherine of Three Peaks success
description: Albie-Junior Thomas had his foot removed as a child but has since scaled the UK's highest mountains.
body: Albie-Junior attended the event celebrating people who had completed the Three Peaks Challenge A nine-year-old amputee who completed the Three Peaks challenge alongside his dad has met Catherine, Princess of Wales to celebrate his success. Albie-Junior Thomas, from Holywell, Flintshire, was invited for a tea party at Windsor Castle after his father sent a letter describing how he had climbed the highest mountains in Wales, Scotland and England. Dad Daniel said he thought the message would resonate with the princess, after she completed her own Three Peaks challenge earlier this year, in aid of the hospital where she was treated for cancer. In a post on X, the princess said it was a "pleasure" to hear the stories of "resilience, determination and hope" shared by each person she met. Princess Catherine welcomed a group of people at Windsor Castle The youngster from Holywell, Flintshire, was born without a fibula in his left leg and his foot was removed at 15 months. Despite this, at four he became the youngest amputee to scale Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, Wales' highest peak. Albie-Junior and his father have since embarked on several climbing challenges together raising thousands for their local football club in the process. In August, he finished the Three Peaks Challenge in 22 hours and 30 minutes alongside his dad, powered by ham and cheese sandwiches, sour sweets and four months' training. This included conquering Ben Nevis in Scotland and Scafell Pike in England as well as Yr Wyddfa. Daniel described the moment they received a phone call inviting them to Windsor Castle as "unbelievable". Once they arrived, Daniel said he stayed in the background, letting Albie-Junior enjoy the experience as "it was his thing". "For him it was just like a chat to a lady, you know, just the innocence of it," he said. "It's like a mother talking to a son." He said the conversation stood out to him because of how "pleasant" it was and said Catherine made him like they were "both equals". In a post on X, the princess said: "Listening to their experiences of the challenge and their reasons for taking it on was a powerful reminder that recovery is rarely a journey we make alone, and of the importance of the people who walk alongside us along the way." Daniel and Albie-Junior completed the Three Peaks Challenge in 22 hours and 30 minutes Despite getting millions of view on their social media channels, Daniel said his son is still as humble as ever, and he reminds him all he has done is "walk up a few mountains". "To him, it's he's just doing what boys should do. Getting out and having fun," added Daniel. "It's not like it's for the fame or nothing like that." Talking about his sons experiences with the princess, he said: "As long as you're nice with someone else and they're nice back, you know that's the way it should be." Daniel said they are planning to tackle Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, and are gathering up ten others to climb it with them in August next year. He added: "When there's a challenge set you want to get it done, but it's not just about that because you have to acclimatise and get the safety right." Daniel said he intends to contact Guinness World Records as Albie-Junior could become the youngest amputee to climb the mountain. "Yeah I'm determined to get him in it," he added. title: Nowak killer given leave to appeal against sentence
description: The Court of Appeal will decide in November whether to reduce or lengthen the 21-year minimum term.
body: Vickrum Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum of 21 years for Henry Nowak's murder The man who murdered student Henry Nowak is being allowed to appeal against the length of his sentence. Vickrum Digwa stabbed 18-year-old Henry Nowak to death in Southampton in December 2025. In June, he was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years. He has now been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the Court of Appeal on 5 November. The court will also decide on a referral by the Attorney General's office, which argued the sentence was too lenient. Digwa has also applied to appeal against his conviction for murder, which will be decided separately. The 23-year-old was also sentenced for possessing a knife in public, despite claiming in court that the 21cm (8in) blade was being carried as part of his Sikh faith. Henry Nowak was a student at the University of Southampton After stabbing Nowak, who came from Chafford Hundred in Essex, Digwa lied to police that he was the victim of a racist attack. The case later sparked protests after police body-worn footage was released showing officers failing to give Nowak first aid and instead handcuffing him as he lay dying, despite him telling officers he could not breathe. The Independent Office for Police Conduct previously said it was investigating two officers for potential gross misconduct. Twelve police officers and a police dog were injured during the protests in Southampton on 2 June. Demonstrators gathered outside the city centre police station before moving to an area near the Digwa family home and the murder scene. More than 30 people have so far been charged with violent disorder following the incident. On 15 June, former Solicitor General Ellie Reeves KC referred the case to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme. Sikh leaders have reported a "backlash" and increase in "hate crime" against their community following the case. Do you have a story BBC Hampshire & Isle of Wight should cover? title: Close-up look at Turner's '£50m' Rome painting on show in the city
description: Turner’s early 19th century painting - Rome, from Mount Aventine - will be on display in the Italian capital for the first time ahead of an auction in London in December.
body: This video can not be played A renowned painting by British landscape artist JMW Turner has returned to the city that inspired it nearly two centuries ago. Rome, from Mount Aventine features a panoramic view of the Italian capital and will be on display at the Palazzo Rondinini for three days. Dating back to the 19th century, the masterpiece was based on sketches made in Rome. The work of art is remarkably well preserved and is believed to have never been restored. It even features traces of fingerprints and brush hairs are still visible. The painting has only been to auction once before, selling for more than £30 million. Sotheby's now expects it could fetch around £50 million when it goes under the hammer in London this December. The BBC's Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Sarah Rainsford, had a close-up look at the painting in Rome. Close-up look at Turner's '£50m' Rome painting on show in the city. title: Why Salisbury are 'bigger than many Premier League teams' in Kuwait
description: Sixth-tier Salisbury FC have a unique relationship with Kuwait, where they are regarded as "bigger than many Premier League" clubs.
body: Salisbury will be in Kuwait for five days before playing in the FA Cup qualifying round on Saturday As with every home game, the Salisbury FC players and coaching staff went to embrace the fans in the Andrews Terrace at The Ray Mac Stadium after Saturday's 2-0 win against Folkestone Invicta. Alongside the normal applause and cheers, they were greeted with a chant that isn't a regular from the songbook. "Kuwait away ole, ole," sang fans of the National League South outfit. The players clapped back with an extra buzz - within 24 hours they would be travelling to the Middle East. "Straight away we all said, 'yeah, we're all in," explains Salisbury player Luke Russe. "It's a unique opportunity and as players, we are so thankful to everybody involved in making this trip happen. I've been involved in this level for a long time now and I've never had an experience like it." The five-day trip involves the club facing one of Kuwait's most successful teams on Wednesday, Al Qadsia, who have won more than 50 trophies, before returning on Thursday to play Saturday's FA Cup third qualifying round against Dulwich Hamlet. It comes as part of the club's continued link with Kuwait through their owner Ali Alhamad, who purchased the club in 2025. The club hopes the trip will offer significant commercial growth and, for the players, an opportunity to experience football in a new environment and culture. The Mohammad Al-Hamad Stadium holds 22,000 spectators, more than five times that of Salisbury's The Ray Mac. "We'd love to win the game," says Russe. "But at the same time I think it's more about the experience and about the club as a whole, going over there, living that way of life and experiencing the game. "We've got a very young group, so for them to experience that and kind of experience cultures and differences is great. "It'll be a fantastic opportunity for us players, for the staff, and I think it'll bring the whole club even closer to what we are now." Ali Alhamad is a Kuwait businessman who owns Salisbury FC The players will get to visit local restaurants, try local food and coffee, visit schools and universities, and hold a question and answer session for locals to understand how an English football club operates from the perspective of owner Alhamad. "It will help the players themselves with opening up their horizons into different cultures, different countries, experiencing other footballing nations and other styles of football," he says. The country's interest in Salisbury is evident. Four of the club's sponsors are from Kuwait, including the front of shirt sponsor for a company that created the country's first Sharia-compliant digital bank, and the training kit represents a popular Acai company that can only be bought in Kuwait. On Instagram the official Arabic account of Salisbury FC has more than 14,000 followers - only slightly fewer than their official English profile. When the squad arrived in Kuwait they were greeted by a small group of fans, while school children interacted with them as if they were Premier League players. "I would even go further than saying that Salisbury in Kuwait is bigger than many of the Premier League teams in the UK," says Alhamad. "So I am not exaggerating when I do say that it is a huge name in Kuwait but what's more important than the size is we are contributing a lot to the local community here in Kuwait and to the children and the future of the football in Kuwait. "Salisbury really is an integral part of opening those avenues and helping the youth here to be better in all the aspects we're looking for." Four of Salisbury's sponsors are from Kuwait The eagerness the players showed shocked Alhamad, with all of the squad, except Jaiden Bartolo who is on international duty, agreeing to go within an hour. Along with the cultural experience, the club is also using this as a way to grow financially, with all ticket sales and advertisement money going to Salisbury. Meanwhile, Salisbury have set up a summer camp in the country and ran a trial session where the top three players trained with the first team during pre-season. "It's quite simple in my mind. If you do what other people do, you'll just get the same results everyone else does," says Alhamad. "Football in England, especially in the non-league, is a brutal business. So just throwing in money to the football club with the aim of getting promotion is fool's gold, in my opinion. "The right way to do it is to build it properly all the way from the bottom and if you just limit yourself to one market, which is the city or town that you are in, that is pretty limited. "With social media and the avenues we have, such as being in Kuwait and the Gulf and Arab regions. That's a huge untapped market that is thirsty for English football." People in Kuwait are avid watchers of the Premier League but non-league is still very much an unknown commodity in the country. "People are not properly educated in the fact that the non-league is actually a really high quality and that is also an indirect goal of mine with this match," he adds. "We're here to show them, you're belittling, playing the sixth tier of English football, the second step of the English non-league. "We'll show you what we have and you never know, maybe the sixth tier of English football will beat the top tier on the biggest team in Kuwait. Al Qadsia are one of the most successful teams in Kuwait, winning a continental tournament in 2014. This growth in Kuwait will offer Salisbury FC an important opportunity that is rare for a National League South team. But ensuring The Whites remain strongly embedded within the local community in the city will also be vital, with the FA Cup on Saturday the first test on their return. title: Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence company supplying Ukraine
description: Russia has been accused of launching sabotage attacks across a number of European Nato countries which have been helping Ukraine.
body: Estonian company Milrem Robotics makes unmanned military vehicles such as this one Russia was behind an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in the capital Tallinn last month, authorities say. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack on Milrem Robotics - which supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles - was ordered by Russian special services, but gave no details. Moscow has been accused of launching sabotage attacks in a number of Nato countries that have been helping Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022. Russia denies such allegations and has been quick to reject the Estonian accusation, too. But EU countries have rushed to Estonia's support, adding such attacks will not deter them from helping Ukraine. The attack on Milrem Robotics occurred on the night of 14-15 August. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that, based on information collected by the country's Internal Security Service, "we can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation". Security service chief Margo Palloson told broadcaster ERR that Russia was "constantly planning, looking for opportunities, trying to find people who would carry out attacks", but that last month's arson attack was its first successful attack this year. The foreign minister said the perpetrators had been arrested and Palloson said they were Latvians who had been living in Russia and taken part in previous attacks. Three suspects were arrested in Latvia and extradited to Estonia earlier this month. Margus Tsahkna said that "this act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine". French President Emmanuel Macron responded to Estonia's assessment, saying "the multiplication of these hostile acts represents a dangerous escalation by Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end". He mentioned the incident at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near Ukrainian cargo planes. "Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron added. An EU spokesman said the 27-member bloc would not cease supporting Ukraine. Nato chief Mark Rutte urged European governments to stay calm and continue supporting Ukraine. "Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte said. Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack Inside the Russian explosives plot that sent incendiary parcels to the UK In August alone, Russia was either accused or suspected of the Leipzig airport attack in Germany, a major fire at a warehouse of a defence firm in Bulgaria, a large explosion at a munitions factory outside Rome in Italy, an attempted arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer in Slovakia, and two suspicious fires in Poland - the latest in a country which has reported several such attacks. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms that tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. Estonia's internal security service, known as Kapo, said Russia was continuing to look for further opportunities for either sabotage or other hostile acts. "Individuals recruited for such operations may be misled or manipulated and may be given false or fabricated justifications for their actions in an effort to conceal the involvement of the Russian state," Kapo head Palloson said, external. Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said "such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning". "We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Dmitry Peskov said. title: Man charged over AI image of crocodile in Singapore reservoir
description: The defendant could face jail or a fine after the image sparked a search operation in the city’s largest reservoir.
body: The authorities alerted the public to the possible danger of an estuarine crocodile (non-AI file photo) Police in Singapore have charged a man who is accused of posting an AI-generated image of a saltwater crocodile in a popular reservoir. Ye Lin was charged with communicating a false message and obstructing the course of justice for allegedly deleting the picture and the application he used. The fake image caused public concern, authorities allege. The national water agency suspended its work at the city-state's largest reservoir for two days last month after receiving information that a crocodile had been spotted. Ye Lin, who is from Myanmar, told the court through an interpreter that he intended to plead guilty, according to local media reports. The Pandan Reservoir is a popular jogging and kayaking spot west of the city centre The national water agency said it was alerted to a crocodile sighting in Pandan Reservoir on 20 August. Agency officials and national parks staff conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were told the suspend their activities. But the following day, the water agency confirmed that the crocodile image was fake and reported it to the police. The case will return to court in November and Ye Lin could face a prison sentence and a large fine if he is found guilty. In Singapore, sending a false message is punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about US$7,800; £5,900), or both. Obstructing justice carries up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both. Police allege that Ye Lin created the photo of the crocodile using artificial intelligence before sending it to a colleague. "The man subsequently deleted the image and the related application in an attempt to conceal his actions," the police statement said. It is not clear how the national water agency was notified of the false photo that Ye Lin sent to his colleague. title: Rayner announces crackdown on 'cowboy' leasehold property agents
description: The housing secretary used her Labour conference speech to announce protections for leaseholders facing 'injustice'.
body: Angela Rayner took aim at the 'injustice' of leasehold in her conference speech Leaseholders will be given extra protections from "cowboy" property agents and hidden fees, Angela Rayner has announced. The housing secretary told Labour's annual conference the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap "rip off" administrative fees. The changes would cover the estimated five million leaseholders in England and Wales who can be forced to pay a landlord for simple changes to their home, despite having bought it. Rayner told party activists she had heard of leaseholders being charged £250 for permission to own a pet and £400 to change their front door. She said people in these situations were "powerless against the vested interests that only take, while giving nothing back in return". The government is already legislating, external to ban new leasehold flats, described in Labour's 2024 election manifesto as a "feudal" system where people own the right to occupy a property via a lease for a limited number of years from a freeholder, or landlord, who owns the land. Through the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, ministers want a commonhold system where residents collectively own and manage their buildings. Now, Rayner is taking aim at the web of management companies that operate between leaseholders and their effective landlords. She said the sector had many decent businesses which were "undermined by far too many cowboys, crooks and con artists". People excited at buying their own homes are "tricked" into using in-house services, meaning that "with no transparency or accountability, vultures can take advantage", Rayner added. "We will legislate for an independent regulation to rein these cowboys in," she said, announcing legislation for an independent watchdog of property agents. This includes estate agents, managing agents and estate managers. This regulator would be able to set codes of practice, such as standards of conduct and proper complaint handling for those they regulate, and property agents will be required to obtain a licence. If they fall foul of the required standards, the regulator would have the power to take their licenses away, the government added. The government said it wanted to bring forward the changes "as soon as possible". Rayner also said new legislation would create the power for caps on permission and administration fees leaseholders pay to landlords. These caps would cover freehold estates and privately managed estates where people can face additional fees for making cosmetic changes to their properties and requesting documents like building safety certificates. A public consultation will be launched to help decide the rate of caps. It comes in addition to an already-announced £250 cap on yearly ground rents paid by leaseholders in England and Wales, which had stalled during the change of prime minister over the summer. The government has said it expects the limit on ground rents - an annual fee paid by leaseholders to their freeholder - to come into force in late 2028, but MPs have called for this to be brought forward to late 2027. Rayner said she was "capping and then scrapping" ground rents, indicating she may try to go further than a cap. In her speech, Rayner did not mention the government's housing target of building 1.5m homes in England by the next election. She admitted earlier this month there was only a "slim chance" of hitting it. Last week, ministers announced a new Your First Home policy to help first-time homebuyers in England with a deposit of 2.5%, similar to the Help To Buy scheme introduced under the Conservatives in 2013. Rayner also said she plans to strengthen council powers to take over empty homes to meet the need for council houses and tackle homelessness. But this was criticised by the Tories as a "desperate" attempt by Labour to try to hit its housing target. title: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
description: The US journalist says he realised he was a "a pawn in a greater game" when he was not interrogated or tortured by FSB agents.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Evan Gershkovich describes the moment he was detained by masked men US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy. In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him. "I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game". Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal. Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false. On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story. They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place". The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service. "It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned." What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd. Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state. "I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years." That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap. "I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right. Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home. The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov, an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany. "They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically." This video can not be played Watch: Freed prisoners Evan Gershkovich and Paul Whelan met by Biden and Harris Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace. He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space. "That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine." Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright. "I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to." Evan Gershkovich said he smiled at the cameras during his court appearances to show he was doing ok But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently." Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed. Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long". When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again." Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions. He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped. And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. title: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home
description: Two homes belonging to the al-Tubasi family were set on fire and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Videos show the al-Tubasi family's homes on fire and damage inside one of them before it was set ablaze More than 100 Israeli settlers have carried out attacks in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank, stopping a family escorted by the Israeli military from returning to their homes, which had been seized weeks ago by settlers. Two houses belonging to the al-Tubasi family in Jalud, south of Nablus, were set on fire in the raid on Monday night and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers. Human rights groups say the events show how Israeli authorities are failing to take effective action against settler violence. "It was extremely terrifying, beyond words. It's hard to imagine the situation," Mahmoud al-Tubasi told the BBC. "My feeling now is that I am happy to have escaped death. I genuinely expected they were going to kill us." Al-Tubasi, 60, his wife Aida, 51, and their 33-year-old son, Wael, had returned to their properties accompanied by Israeli forces after Israel's High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed to go back. Mahmoud al-Tubasi said he thought settlers were going to kill him and his family The family was forced to leave this summer after weeks of settler harassment and attacks. Extremist settlers had set up an illegal outpost close to Jalud and besieged three houses, including two belonging to the al-Tubasis' sons who are married with young daughters. Al-Tubasi said that he was called at about midnight and told that there was coordination with Israel's military for his family to go back to their houses. He received a message from Israeli officials saying that if he wanted to reclaim his property he had to go immediately with the army and Israeli border police. By torchlight, the family inspected one home. A video shared with the BBC shows that the settlers had already extensively damaged it - smashing holes through doors, tearing out electrical fittings, ripping up tiles, breaking windows and leaving rubbish strewn about. The toilet was smashed and appeared to be full of human waste. A large number of extremist settlers arrived in Jalud after alerts were posted in WhatsApp groups they use to coordinate action, saying that the Palestinian family they had forced out was returning and should be stopped. "As soon as we entered the house, which had already been completely destroyed, settlers started throwing stones at us. The army responded by firing tear gas at them, but there were so many settlers, more than 150, that the army could no longer control them," al-Tubasi told the BBC. Israel's High Court has ruled that the al-Tubasi family must be allowed to return to their homes The grandfather says that a group of Israeli soldiers protected his family from the settlers who tried to approach them, using pepper spray to force them back. Settlers slashed the tyres of a military van they were put in and then they were transferred to an armoured military vehicle. As the family was being driven away, the settlers set fire to their car and both of their houses. Video shot from a distance shows smoke billowing from them. Al-Tubasi says that the Israeli security forces "essentially formed a barrier, took us out safely and got us away from there. But they did not take any action against the settlers themselves." An Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said that "more than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire, and throwing stones at security forces." The Israeli military said that three police officers were lightly injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged. It described the Tubasi family as victims of "nationalist crime" adding that "due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed." The head of the local council in Jalud told reporters that residents had confronted the settlers leading to clashes which even spread to a nearby village, where a Palestinian woman was assaulted by settlers and her house set ablaze. Israel's prime minister called on law enforcement authorities to prosecute those he called "rioters" One month ago, Aida al-Tubasi was attacked by masked Israeli settlers and injured along with American journalists who were interviewing her in Jalud. The high court decision, which criticised Israeli authorities for failing to crack down on settler violence, ruled that the family should be safely returned home by 20 September - more than a week ago. The legal ruling was strongly worded describing Israeli settlers' actions as "a completely unacceptable phenomenon that stands in contrast to the basic values and moral principles of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he strongly condemned the attacks on security forces, calling on law enforcement, "to prosecute the rioters to the fullest extent of the law." Israeli police said that they had arrested three people suspected of being involved in the attacks. Speaking at the UN General Assembly last week, Netanyahu dismissed international concerns about settler violence. He accused the media of ignoring attacks on Jewish Israelis and covering "a handful of juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires." According to the Israeli human rights group, Yesh Din, fewer than three per cent of police investigations into settler violence over the last two decades have led to a conviction. Ziv Stahl, its executive director, said the lack of effective law enforcement was because, "the violence is part of a systematic government policy aimed at pushing Palestinians out of the area and expanding Israeli control over land in the West Bank". Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank claiming biblical and legal rights to the land. Some ministe

title: French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism
description: National Rally President Jordan Bardella says he will sue for libel over comments he is accused of making as a young activist.
body: Jordan Bardella, 31, would probably be prime minister if Marine Le Pen wins next year's presidential election The president of France's hard-right National Rally (RN), Jordan Bardella, has said he will sue for libel after a report published antisemitic comments that it alleged he had made as a young activist. The Mediapart website released what it said was the result of "several months" of investigation into "dozens of written conversations" Bardella allegedly had in 2013. With seven months to go before France's presidential elections, Bardella condemned "the beginnings of a total war" aimed at destabilising his party, and RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said she had total confidence in him. The alleged remarks included blatantly antisemitic tropes, and Bardella said they were an attempt to destroy his political career. Mediapart did not produce screen-grabs of any of the alleged remarks. It said it had "independently authenticated" the conversations, which came from "a bigger documentary base corroborated by witness statements". But Bardella, 31 – who is a likely prime minister if Le Pen wins the presidential election – said the allegations were a fabrication aimed at derailing the RN's increasingly confident bid for power. "Everything is going to be done to destabilise the campaign," he told CNews television on Monday night. "Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties. "Of course I have instructed my lawyer to sue for libel." Le Pen said the alleged remarks "seem so weird that they can only be a forgery – one of those dirty tricks for which Mediapart appears to hold the secret". Among the statements that Mediapart alleges Bardella made when he was 17 or 18 are: "All the banks are owned by Jews"; "The Jew has to dominate other people, crush them and rob them"; and "What they want is a new world order dominated by Israel, with of course Jerusalem as its capital." Mediapart is an avowedly leftwing website which has exposed a number of scandals over the years, though its targets have been politicians of all stripes. The French hard right is riding higher than ever in pre-election polls, with the latest this week, from Toluna-Harris, showing Le Pen a clear victor over whatever rival she faces in the crucial second round in May. Marine Le Pen (R) is now favourite to win the second round of next year's presidential elections According to the survey, Le Pen would pick up 35-36% of the vote in the multi-candidate first round. Her likely opponent in the two-way run-off would be Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical left who she would eradicate with 69% of the vote. But in a stark warning for the political establishment, the poll showed that she would also easily beat the most popular centrist candidate Edouard Philippe, with a score of 57%. On Sunday the RN received another boost when results of a partial election for the upper house of parliament, the Senate, produced for the first time enough seats for the party to form an official group. Under Marine Le Pen, daughter of the historic party founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, the RN has made huge efforts to distance itself from the French far-right's antisemitic roots. Last year Bardella was the first senior figure from the party to be invited to Israel, for a conference on antisemitism. Today the party regards militant Islam as a pre-eminent threat – a position it shares with many Jews. The RN even styles itself as a "shield for the Jewish community". The alleged comments from Bardella throw back to a current of far-right thinking that Mediapart says has never been eradicated but only covered up in the new-look party. Leftwing politicians called on Bardella to resign, and the head of the Jewish umbrella organisation Crif, Yonathan Arfi, said the alleged comments "were an illustration of the limits of the RN's clean-up act". But RN deputy Jean-Philippe Tanguy said the source of the allegations was disaffected members of the party who had been expelled years ago because of their antisemitic ideas. "From what I know, it is the antisemitic rabble that were so bravely purged by Marine Le Pen. At the start of the 2010s, they were numerous and well-organised, but they were defeated. These people have always had it in for us." title: South West Water fined almost £8m for sewage spills
description: South West Water previously entered guilty pleas to pollution offences spanning six years.
body: South West Water has been fined almost £8m for untreated sewage spills including at Harlyn in Cornwall A water company has been fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years. South West Water pleaded guilty at Plymouth Magistrates' Court after an investigation by the Environment Agency into incidents between 2015 and 2021 in Bodmin, Harlyn, Playing Place, and Polperro in Cornwall, and Plymouth in Devon. Sentencing, Judge Jo Matson described the pollution as "horrendous" and "very significant". The water company said in a statement after sentencing: "We apologise for what happened in the past." Of the 18 charges, 17 were for illegal discharge activities including sewage discharges and one is for failing to take reasonable remedial measures following a failure at a sewage pumping station. The firm was fined £7,867,733 ordered to pay £329,993 in costs. It is the latest to be imposed on South West Water after it was fined £1.8m over a parasite outbreak in July and fined more than £2.1 after admitting causing pollution in the region in 2023. Should you take the plunge? How to tell how clean the sea is South West Water has sharpest rise in complaints Residents demand action over 'Plymouth pongs' Judge Matson said she had made clear in the 2023 case "incidents of pollution by water companies will not be tolerated and must be taken very seriously by these courts". "I have taken into account that these incidents pre-date that sentence and I have also taken into account the changes that South West Water have made since then," she said. "Only time will tell if those changes are successful, I certainly hope that will be the case." She noted the water company had adopted wording that said "one pollution is too many". "It goes without saying that must be the case," she said. "However, in this case there were hundreds of incidents of sewage spills on to our beaches and into our waterways and sea and untreated sewage gushed through the harbour wall into the harbour at Polperro on a bank holiday weekend." The firm needed to make sure "horrendous, very significant incidents of pollution such as these never happen again", she added. Clarissa Newell, from the Environment Agency, welcomed the fine imposed on South West Water The fine is the the largest to be imposed on South West Water in a case pursued by the Environment Agency, it said. Clarissa Newell, environment manager for Devon and Cornwall, said: "There's been a clear message today to show that pollution will not be tolerated. "Today we've seen offences where alarms have not been responded to and data has been collected but not thought through." She said it had "taken a long time for these offences to come to court" due to the nature of the investigation. "We will get challenged by South West Water every step of the way so every piece of science we use has to be done with calibrated instruments and with qualified people," she said. South West Water said the case related to "historic matters between 2015 and 2021" and the majority of spills involved "the use of overflows in storm conditions". "We're investing £760m to tackle storm overflows and have reduced spills by 17% in the last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%," the company said. It added "significant improvements" had been made at the sites where pollution occurred. "We remain focused on the future as we deliver record levels of investment to achieve cleaner rivers and seas across the South West by 2040, a decade ahead of national targets," it said. title: Body of newborn baby found on shoreline in Wales as police search for mother
description: The body of the newborn was found near Siliwen Road near the Menai Strait on Sunday.
body: The body of a newborn baby has been found along a shoreline in north Wales. North Wales Police have appealed for the mother who maybe "extremely vulnerable" to come forward. A member of the public found the remains on the Menai Strait shoreline near Siliwen Road on Sunday shortly before 17:00 BST. During a press conference, Director of Midwifery and Women's Services for Betsi Cadwaladr health board Fiona Giraud has appealed directly to the mother to come forward. "I want you to know that our immediate concern is for your health, safety and wellbeing. We recognise that you may be feeling frightened, overwhelmed or unsure about what to do next," she said. Giraud said they "have real concerns for the health of the mother". "We recognise that she is likely to be extremely vulnerable. She may be fearful of seeking the support she needs through fear of identifying herself. Speaking directly to the mother, she added: "You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone. "We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe, and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need. "I am asking you personally, to please get in touch with us. You can speak to a healthcare professional, approach a police officer or attend a police station. "If you are watching or listening to this appeal, please know that we want to hear from you. Please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you." title: Gisele Pelicot rape case to be told in London play
description: Thirty actors will take part in the documentary-style performance based on documents from the trial.
body: Gisèle Pelicot was hailed around the world for her courage in publicly confronting her rapists A play telling the "harrowing" story of the Gisele Pelicot rape case will be performed in London at a one-off event at London County Hall, on the South Bank. Ms Pelicot's ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious, in abuse that lasted nearly a decade. The 73-year-old, who waived her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse, said shame should fall on her abusers, not her. Thirty actors and public figures will take part in the "documentary theatre" style performance, created from documents from the trial and psychiatric reports of the 51 men who were prosecuted. The story of Gisèle Pelicot will be told over a four-hour performance The Pelicot Rape Trial created by Swiss director and playwright Milo Rau started as a stand-alone piece as part of the Festival d'Avignon, an arts festival in the town where the crimes took place. The performance then travelled across cities in Europe, with only one show per location. Milo Rau said: "It's about disentangling the story from the couple Gisèle and Dominique Pelicot – turning it into a story that belongs to all of us and at the same time to none of us." In London, the piece is being put on at London County Hall, by the Young Vic Theatre, on 30 November. The theatre's website said the performance is a "profoundly affecting piece of documentary theatre, comprised of testimonies and written accounts from the trial, (which) pays tribute to the ordinary woman who opened the way to change". It added: "The Pelicot trial is undoubtedly the most publicised, discussed, and symbolic of our time. "As a sociological study it shows that in a typical Western European city – the small town of Mazan in the south of France – perfectly ordinary men from all social classes and age groups are capable of perhaps the most extreme crime: the repeated rape of an unconscious woman." Fifty men were found guilty of rape or sexual offences after a three-and-a-half-month trial. Young Vic Theatre's artistic director and chief executive, Nadia Fall said: "Milo Rau's extraordinary testimonial piece The Pelicot Trial breaks out beyond our theatre walls to County Hall; a piece of confronting event-theatre which bears witness to the harrowing story of Gisèle Pelicot."
