title: Toone and Kelly miss out on Lionesses squad
description: Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone misses out on selection for England's Women's World Cup qualifying matches this month.
body: Chloe Kelly and Ella Toone have 136 England appearances between them England manager Sarina Wiegman says Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly have "not been playing to their potential" and that is why they have missed out on selection. The Lionesses face Greece in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off matches in October. Manchester United midfielder Toone, 27, and Arsenal forward Kelly, 28 have had inconsistent starts to the season. They both had crucial involvements at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025 as the Lionesses won back-to-back titles, but Wiegman is "convinced they can be better". "Of course, I still believe in these players. They are really good and have shown so much for us," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live. "But that is also why I didn't pick them this time, because they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks. "I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and of course, they want to work on that." On reports suggesting Kelly's absence may have been linked to an injury, Wiegman added in her media conference: "I had the conversation with Chloe and for me, it was just what I saw on the pitch. I kept that with football with her." In addition, Chelsea forward Aggie Beever-Jones and Arsenal duo Lotte Wubben-Moy and Taylor Hinds have not made the 23-player squad. Captain Leah Williamson returns having missed June's 4-0 defeat by Spain and 3-0 win over Ukraine. "I think she's played really well in the last few weeks and at the start of the season. She is happy and you can see," added Wiegman. Could Potter be England's next breakthrough star? All you need to know about 2027 Women's World Cup Meanwhile, there is a first senior call-up for Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter, 20, who has impressed alongside England's Keira Walsh in the Women's Super League. She has started three of Chelsea's opening four matches and was a standout performer in their 1-0 win over Arsenal on Sunday. "Her performances were just really good. We started following her closely last season and she got minutes over time," said Wiegman. "She plays with a lot of courage, a lot of understanding and her decision-making is really good. Her technical ability, we have seen, is really good too. "What I've seen is that no matter who she plays against, like last Sunday [against Arsenal], it looks like it doesn't bother her at all and she will just play football. "She played against very high-level players, international players, and she just played. She looked very comfortable. I hope she shows that with us too." There is also a return to the squad for uncapped midfielder Erica Meg Parkinson, 18, who has excelled since joining North Carolina Courage in the summer. Manchester City full-back Niamh Charles made her return from injury as a substitute in their 1-0 win over Charlton Athletic on Saturday and is included. London City Lionesses forward Freya Godfrey and Liverpool defender Grace Fisk are the other two uncapped players named. England play a double-header against Greece, first in Crete on Friday, 9 October (17:30 BST) and then in Leicester on Tuesday, 13 October (19:30 BST). If they win the two-legged tie, they progress to round two of the play-offs where they can compete for a place in next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil. title: Taylor Swift dominated the VMAs, but do music videos still matter?
description: Cinematographer Melissa Cofie says their purpose has evolved with the growth of platforms like TikTok.
body: Taylor Swift became the most successful artist in the history of the VMAs on Sunday We're far from the days of blockbuster music videos playing back-to-back on TV channels like MTV. Catchy hooks and sleek dance routines now dominate social media feeds, each hoping to stop people in their tracks long enough for them to give a new song a chance. The evolution of this landscape was cemented last year when MTV axed five music channels in the UK after almost 40 years of rolling footage. But despite the broadcaster reacting to the changes in viewing habits, its Video Music Awards (VMAs) still appear to hold power over music A-listers. Pop music heavyweights, including Taylor Swift, Madonna and Charli XCX, were among those who turned up on Sunday to accept prizes and deliver dramatic performances. Cinematographer Melissa Cofie tells BBC Newsbeat that while these award shows "may seem very performative to others", they are "so important" to those in the music industry. "The sleepless nights, the months, the weeks that it takes to put together a music video, it's almost as much work as you would put into a film itself," she says. But do music videos still hold the same importance for fans as they once did? Graham Norton and Domhnall Gleeson were among the stars who featured in Taylor Swift's Opalite video Cofie, who has directed music videos, feels their purpose has evolved over the last couple of decades. For her, they're more of a way to "connect with artists" and for them to express their vision, rather than a crucial part of their press run like they were in the 2000s. Pop stars like Swift, Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Rodrigo are among those who still lean on videos heavily to build out the visual world for each of their albums' eras. Swift, who broke the record for most MTV VMA wins ever last weekend, is known for big budget productions which fans trawl through for Easter eggs - clues that could point to something else she has planned. She also often enlists the help of her star-studded contact book, with her recent video for Opalite jam-packed with famous faces, including Graham Norton, Lewis Capaldi, Cillian Murphy, Domhnall Gleeson and Jodie Turner-Smith. However, the music video was released exclusively on Spotify and Apple Music in February, and did not appear on YouTube until 48 hours later. Industry analysts speculated at the time that the exclusivity period was due to a change in the US chart rules, where songs streamed on YouTube will no longer count towards the Top 100. This change came into place in January, with YouTube saying it was ending its decade-long partnership with Billboard, external as it claimed the chart uses an "outdated formula that weights subscription-supported streams higher than ad-supported". "This doesn't reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don't have a subscription," it added. And while most artists don't have Swift-level budgets to start with, this change may have further discouraged US artists' to throw a lot of money into creating elaborate music videos. K-Pop superstars like BTS often release multiple music videos for one song However, in international markets like the world of K-Pop, creating visually aesthetic music videos featuring polished choreography has become essential when promoting the act to a global audience. The genre's superstars like BTS and Blackpink often also release dance practice videos and behind-the-scenes clips alongside traditional music videos. These variations offer them more content to clip up for social media, and also helps drive up their streaming numbers and global chart positions. Cofie feels the rise of platforms like TikTok, Instagram and YouTube has "100%" changed the way videos are consumed and therefore, how they are created. But she doesn't see this as a "blow" to the industry and isn't "discouraged that things are changing so quickly". "It kind of pushes us to think: 'Okay, how can each scene, each still be the one that captures people's attention?'," she says. "We don't have five minutes anymore. We've actually got two minutes, sometimes less. "I think it pushes us as creatives to think how can we get the point across quickly in the best way possible." Cinematographer Melissa Cofie isn't "discouraged that things are changing so quickly" Gener8ion and Swedish rapper Yung Lean's cinematic music video for their collaboration track Storm is a testament to how a short mesmerising visual moment can make a song go viral online. The scene from within the full video sees Lean, acting as a teenage bully, stand amongst a group of dancers who are also dressed in school uniforms as they perform hypnotic, synchronised choreography, external. They recreated the routine at the VMAs, and while it lost out on the coveted video of the year award to Swift's The Fate of Ophelia, clips of the performance once again have flooded social media. Cofie admits it has been "really tough" to come up with "new creative ideas" like this since short clips have boomed post-pandemic, but says she is continually inspired by new music videos. And her advice to artists and crews who still want to create music videos? "It's cliche, but just to continue being creative and just exploring every corner of your mind, any idea that you have, just do it," she says. "Don't worry that it's already been done and it's not original because each and every person's interpretation or perspective is different." title: RAF Fairford incident involves 'foreign actor', says Rubio
description: In a television interview the US Secretary of State mentioned Iran, which has denied any involvement
body: This video can not be played Watch: What we do and don't know about the incident near RAF Fairford US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor". In an interview with Fox News on Monday, Rubio said "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally". He did not provide evidence or further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. A major incident was declared at the weekend after "suspicious vehicles" were seen near the RAF base in Gloucestershire, which has been used by US forces to carry out strikes against Iran. Dozens of homes were evacuated after the three vehicles were reported to police in the early hours of Sunday morning. Five men, who are all UK nationals in their 20s, were arrested on suspicion of terror offences, and later released on bail. On Monday Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), said officers are considering all angles, including that "this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state". In his comments to Fox News, Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation." He added: "There's a lot more news that'll come out on this in the days to come, but there's only so much I can say right now at this point about it." The Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident. The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what the government calls defensive strikes on Iran. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". According to CTP, the five men - aged between 23 and 25 and from London - remain under investigation, and their release is "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others". Speaking at the White House earlier on Monday, Donald Trump said "I will tell you, I would have said 'Don't let them have bail'. I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that." Prime Minister Andy Burnham meanwhile chaired a Cobra meeting on Monday and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts". On Tuesday a heavily guarded police cordon remained in place around the RAF base at Fairford. Residents of the nearby village of Whelford have been told they can move home. One local told the BBC most people had returned home, but had been told by police to stay inside and not take any photos. "I haven't gone home as I want to wait until I know more about what the hell happened, as it feels super dodge to me," she said. Local councillor Tristan Wilkinson said the mood among residents is a mixture of "confusion" and "weariness". "I don't think there's going to be anything normal about Whelford for quite a considerable amount of time," he told BBC local radio. In the village of Fairford meanwhile, butcher Andrew Butler said "people are worried, a bit panicky". "Any suspicious vehicle that people aren't sure about, they think could potentially be a problem," he said. title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott jailed for seven years for child sex abuse
description: The 49-year-old was found guilty of two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.
body: Graeme Dott was sentenced to seven years in jail at the High Court in Edinburgh Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years after being convicted of child sexual abuse. Judge Lord Harrower said Dott robbed his victims of "a significant part of their childhood" and said his behaviour bore the hallmarks of grooming. Dott had denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010 but was found guilty following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The 49-year-old Scot, who won the world snooker title in 2006, showed no emotion as he was sentenced, only nodding to someone in the public gallery as he was led away. This video can not be played Former snooker champion Graeme Dott jailed for child sexual abuse Lord Harrower told the High Court in Edinburgh that each of Dott's victims were vulnerable for reasons beyond their age. He said Dott rewarded the victims with treats and disguised his abuse as being part of a game. The former snooker champion was 16 or 17 when he abused the girl, who was about nine when her ordeal began. Dott's abuse of the second victim - a boy aged about eight - began about 10 years later. The court heard that he warned them they would not be believed if they told anyone about his actions. As it happened: Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott sentenced The judge added Dott's victims had experienced "overwhelming emotions of fear, shame and anger" as a result of the abuse, affecting their mental health into adulthood. Dott's behaviour towards the children "involved a gross violation of trust". As Lord Harrower addressed him, Dott repeatedly shook his head in apparent disbelief. The judge added social work reports have deemed Dott poses a "below average risk of reoffending", but as he still maintains his innocence, Lord Harrower could not take into account any remorse from Dott. Graeme Dott abused a girl and a boy between 2006 and 2010 The court also heard that Dott has already been the subject of threats in prison, and moved to a different jail as a result. Euan Dow, representing Dott, told the court the father-of-two was now separated from his wife but "continues to enjoy the support of his family and friends". He added Dott suffers from "long-standing mental health issues" and that his personal and professional reputations had been destroyed. The sentence of seven years has been backdated to 24 August, which is when the 49-year-old was remanded in custody. He will spend the rest of his life on the sex offenders register. Procurator Fiscal Faye Cook, of the Crown Office, said: "Graeme Dott achieved success and public admiration but, in private, he exploited the trust of two children to abuse and coerce them. "Dott's criminal behaviour has been his downfall and he now faces the consequences of his actions." She added that "justice has no time limit" and encouraged any victims of historical abuse to report it. Dott was found guilty after a trial at the High Court in Glasgow in August During the trial, the court heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010. Dott called the allegations made against him "disgusting". The girl, now a woman in her 40s, said Dott had "caressed" her bottom while giving her a piggyback and that, on another occasion, he had exposed himself to her. On another occasion, she said Dott, of Glasgow, suggested she "take her trousers down" and lifted her top and began kissing her stomach after asking if she wanted to "play a guessing game". The victim said Dott would kiss her, touch her inappropriately and carried out a sexual act that would, if committed now, amount to rape. She said she recalled the "smell" of creams Dott used for a skin condition after he kissed her and that the actions left her "shocked and scared". The court heard that Dott bought her a teddy bear with a love heart on it in the course of the abuse. Police previously contacted Dott about the allegations in 2001, but no charges were brought. The woman gave a new statement to police in 2025. Dott won the world championship title in 2006 During his evidence, Dott's male victim said the abuse began shortly after Dott defeated Peter Ebdon to win his sole world title at The Crucible in Sheffield in 2006. The boy, now a man in his 20s, said he was about eight years old when Dott molested him in a shower at a home in South Lanarkshire. He told the court that Dott "rewarded" him with crisps and fizzy drinks and once handed him a £50 note, only to accuse the boy of stealing it when his parents found out he had the money. He also said he was abused in a car on a number of occasions and "inappropriately touched" while Dott played online poker. Dott was convicted of lewd and libidinous practices, which refer to any sexual crimes against children committed prior to 1 December 2010. The offence was abolished in 2009, but is still used for crimes carried out before then. Following his conviction in August, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association said it had permanently revoked Dott's membership with immediate effect. Dott was previously suspended from all professional snooker activities on 9 April 2025 pending the outcome of his trial. He was subsequently relegated from the professional ranking list at the conclusion of the 2025/26 season. Dott has two previous convictions for minor road traffic offences in 2013 and 2015. title: What happens next in the RAF Fairford investigation?
description: BBC correspondent Daniel Sandford explains where the investigation goes from here.
body: This video can not be played Five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near RAF Fairford, Gloucestershire, have been bailed. The men, all UK nationals in their 20s, were initially detained on suspicion of terror offences near the base, which is used by the US military. Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that the incident "clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor". BBC correspondent Daniel Sandford explains where the investigation goes from here. What angles are the police exploring and what evidence will they be collecting? title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage
description: Daniel Thomas is remanded in custody after appearing at Portsmouth Crown Court.
body: Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared in court via videolink (file photo) Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel. Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared via videolink at Portsmouth Crown Court accused of criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at the boat with a knife. The 37-year-old, whose address was withheld by the court at a previous hearing, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone. He has been remanded in custody, with a provisional trial date set for 1 March. The defendant, wearing a grey t-shirt and holding a copy of the Bible, did not enter a plea during the hearing but previously pleaded not guilty to both charges at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Friday. This video can not be played Police had been examining livestream footage appearing to show Daniel Thomas slashing at a migrant boat Thomas is alleged to have used his social media platform to livestream himself from the English Channel at around 16:30 BST on 22 September, broadcasting to a large audience, the court heard. He is accused of slashing a boat that had been used by migrants, which was adrift in the sea, while a rescue crew member was on board. He is also alleged to have said "this is what needs to happen" and "this is England, this isn't France any more". Simon Pentol KC, defending, had proposed a "package of bail conditions" as an alternative to Thomas being remanded in custody and described the allegation against his client as "politically charged and fundamentally flawed". On his decision to refuse bail, the Judge James Newton-Price KC, said: "I am not concerned with the political issues or motivations in this matter and I put them aside in deciding this matter." A handful of supporters waited outside the court to hear the outcome of the hearing. title: Bank cash machines ripped out and taken away on a horsebox
description: Two cash machines are taken away in a horsebox from the Royal Bank of Scotland in Peebles.
body: The bank was targeted in the early hours of the morning Two cash machines have been ripped out of the walls of a bank in southern Scotland and taken away on a horsebox in an early morning raid. Peebles High Street has been closed to vehicles after the Royal Bank of Scotland branch on the town's Eastgate was targeted at about 03:00. A telescopic forklift, used to ram the building, was left abandoned in the street. Police Scotland has appealed for any witnesses to what it described as a "planned series of crimes involving stolen vehicles". Rubble was left strewn across the pavement following the incident Police said a grey Audi saloon car, grey Isuzu D-Max pick-up towing a horsebox and a Manitou telehandler had entered the Eastgate area in the early hours of the morning. After ramming the building, the forklift was used to remove two cash machines before they were loaded onto the horsebox. The pick-up and horsebox had been reported stolen while the vehicle used to smash into the bank, which is also believed to be stolen, was left at the scene. The road was closed to traffic following the raid Three men, all wearing dark clothing, were seen leaving the area in the Audi and pick-up heading in the direction of Northgate. Det Insp Keith Sinclair said: "This was clearly a planned series of crimes, involving stolen vehicles, to target the cash machines. "Extensive inquiries are ongoing to trace the suspects and officers are working through CCTV from the area and speaking to witnesses." He appealed to anyone with information or anyone who saw any of the vehicles to get in touch. Anyone with information about the incident has been asked to contact police Footage posted on social media shows the machines being dragged out of the badly damaged building. One person dressed all in black is standing outside the bank while the forklift pulls the cash machines away. It can then be seen lifting one of them up into the air before it is lowered carefully onto the back of the horsebox. The figure outside the bank then runs towards the back of the vehicle with arms waving before appearing to signal for the forklift to be raised back up after dropping the first ATM into position. Borders Buses has said it will not be able to serve the nearby bus stop until further notice. title: 'I still feel as fast as anybody' - Alonso on why he's staying in F1
description: Fernando Alonso commits to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year. - and explains why to BBC Sport.
body: Fernando Alonso made his Formula 1 debut at the 2001 Australian Grand Prix, before eight current F1 drivers were born Fernando Alonso has committed to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year - and says the biggest single reason for his decision is because he "still feels fast". The 45-year-old Spaniard has been weighing up his future all year. And while, like Max Verstappen, he has been outspoken in his criticism of the new hybrid engines introduced in 2026, his love for the sport has won out. "First, this is my life," Alonso told BBC Sport in his only English language interview about his decision, which was announced on Tuesday., external "I have this in my blood and I keep racing and I keep enjoying and this is a way of life, in a way. "Probably for me the biggest, or the clearest thing to keep racing is I still feel self-confidence that I have something extra. "And when I think about stepping down or taking a different role in the team or not driving the car or whatever, in a way I feel it should not be like that because I still feel as fast as anybody. So let's have another go." His own personal performance was only one factor at play in Alonso's decision, he explained in an extensive and open conversation. Alonso also considered the new rules, and the competitiveness of his team, which has been close to rock bottom for most of this season. Alonso's most recent podium in F1 came at the 2023 Sao Paulo Grand Prix. Alonso is regarded as one of the all-time F1 greats, and has created an iconic status over a career that dates back to 2001. And he continues to reject any suggestion that he has lost any of his ability. "When I jump in the car, in free practice, I will see some people braking late in a corner, locking up the front tyres here or there, making mistakes there," Alonso says. "I feel that I'm OK. Or, I'm faster than them. "So when I get changed and I go back home, even if I'm P18, in a way I feel some satisfaction and pride inside, even if it should not be the case because we are not competitive. "How will I be in the living room, watching TV, thinking that I can do better? That will be my feeling now. When that changes, if I see that I lost abilities, I lost speed, I lost reflexes, I lost something, then I will be happy to watch from my living room the race. "At the moment, I feel it was not the time because I'm better than that guy. I'm better than that other guy. I will think like that. And I cannot stop racing if I still think like that." Alonso has only had a couple of chances this year to prove his point that he's still as good as he ever was. One was at the Dutch Grand Prix, when he finished ninth, holding at bay the faster cars of Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint. I suggest to him that it was a typical Alonso drive, proof to those who doubted that he still has it. But he says it will have had no impact on the audience. "You only prove to people when you are in the podium or you are on TV," he says. "That's where eyes are open, and people remember suddenly that you're still on the grid. "So now I'm at peace with this period of time that I'm anonymous, and no one knows that we're still there and we're still fast. "We are preparing ourselves for the moment of truth and that will be a surprise for everybody again." Along with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Alonso has been one of the drivers most critical of the 2026 rules. Drivers feel the new hybrid engines, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have diminished F1's challenge. The key problems are the fact the cars run out of half their energy long before some corners, a process known as "derating", and that some of the sport's most demanding corners have been neutered because they are used to charge the batteries. Alonso, as is his way, has produced some particularly pithy turns of phrase this season to express his unhappiness. He has called F1 the "battery world championship". He has described fast corners as "the charging station for the car" and said that "the chef could drive the car" in a particular corner in Bahrain that used to be a major challenge. And he's been dismissive of the increased number of overtaking moves created by offsets in energy levels between cars, calling them "avoidance actions". How did he square all that with deciding to keep racing these cars he dislikes so much? "That's a good question," he says, "because that was the hardest thing for me." He says he hopes the changes being made to change the power ratio to 60-40 in two steps by 2028 "will make things a little bit easier". "This year, there have been some good races and some bad races," Alonso says. "Maybe some of the shorter circuits that you had the battery until the braking point are changing the way you perceive the driving. "And some of the circuits like Silverstone, Spa, Suzuka, they were very bad, you know, because they derate and things like that. "Maybe even for next year they can tweak a little bit the battery power to have a little bit maybe less battery for longer or something like that because F1 at the moment is not natural driving. "Reaching the top speed in the middle of the straight, it goes against the driver instinct of braking late and going on power earlier. It seems that if you want to drive these cars fast, you ended up going slower and that's not the way it should be." Alonso says that, as something of an elder statesman, he "feels some responsibility also in this regard to help the sport" make the right decisions for the future. And the willingness of governing body the FIA and commercial rights holder F1 to accept there is a problem and make changes to address it has also been a reassurance. title: Rank the biggest scandals in Test cricket history
description: As memories of sandpapergate are rekindled by Australia's upcoming tour of South Africa, rank the biggest scandals in Test cricket's history.
body: Australia's first Test tour of South Africa since the sandpapergate scandal begins on 9 October Australia are due to play their first Test in South Africa since the sandpapergate scandal rocked the cricketing world eight years ago. To mark one of the biggest controversies the game has ever seen, Test Match Special is asking which is Test cricket's biggest scandal. Ten of the most famous scandals in Test cricket have been picked out by a TMS panel and we are asking you to rank them in order of how big they were. Results of the vote will be revealed on the TMS podcast and you can read more about each scandal below the following vote. Harold Larwood strikes Australian wicketkeeper Bert Oldfield in the head with a bouncer during the third day of the the Third Test at the Adelaide Oval in 1933 On the 1932-33 tour of Australia, England needed a plan to stop the great Donald Bradman. Douglas Jardine, England's charismatic captain, came up with a tactic that would change the game forever: Bodyline. Jardine instructed his fast bowlers, Harold Larwood and Bill Voce, to bowl hostile, short-pitched deliveries at the Australians. In an era when batters wore no upper-body protection, England's method was criticised as unsporting and against the spirit of cricket. The bad blood between the two teams escalated to the administrators of the game in each country and even turned into a diplomatic incident, threatening to strain relationships between governments. England won the series 4-1, a result almost lost in the infamy of the entire episode. Basil D'Oliveira played 44 Tests for England In 1968, England were due to tour South Africa, a country then operating under a system of racial segregation known as apartheid. In line for selection was Basil D'Oliveira, a mixed-race all-rounder born in South Africa, who had emigrated to and qualified to play for England. Despite scoring 158 in the final Test of the summer against Australia, D'Oliveira was initially left out of the England squad, only to then be called in as a replacement for the injured Tom Cartwright. His inclusion was criticised in South Africa and the tour was called off little more than a week later. South Africa played one more Test series – at home to Australia the following year – then spent two decades out of international cricket. In the intervening time, a number of rebel tours to South Africa took place, with huge consequences for the players involved. Sporting Witness: The D'Oliveira Affair Australia's Ian Chappell (left) and England captain Tony Greig examine the damaged Headingley wicket in 1975 Australia were defending the Ashes in England in 1975. The series was shortened to four Tests because of the inaugural men's World Cup earlier in the summer. At 1-0 down, England had a huge chance to level the series in the third Test at Headingley. At the close of the fourth day, Australia had reached 220-3 in pursuit of 445. A thrilling finish was in prospect. Overnight, the pitch was vandalised. Holes were dug and oil was poured on the surface. The damage was caused by supporters of George Davis, who had been jailed for armed robbery the previous year. "George Davis is innocent" was written on the wall around the ground. The Test was abandoned as a draw, meaning Australia retained the urn and ruining the prospect of a decider at The Oval. Davis was released in 1976 when his conviction was adjudged to be unsafe, and it was overturned entirely on appeal in 2011. George Davis appeal win sparks Headingley Ashes memories West Indies players sit on a balcony during World Series Cricket In the mid-1970s, Kerry Packer, one of the richest men in Australia, wanted to boost the ratings of his Channel Nine TV network with live sport. He approached the Australian Cricket Board with a lucrative offer, one that was rejected in favour of keeping live cricket on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. So, Packer created his own product: World Series Cricket. The plan was simple – Packer recruited the best players in the world to stage his own matches. Most significant was the signing of England captain Tony Greig, who effectively acted as an agent. Greig was stripped of the captaincy and Australia's 1977 Ashes tour of England was overshadowed by the emergence of Packer's outfit. World Series Cricket lasted for two seasons – 1977-78 and 1978-79 – comprising one-day matches and 'SuperTests' between teams representing Australia, West Indies and a World XI. Meanwhile, traditional cricket rolled on. In 1978-79, England embarked on Ashes tour they won 5-1, beating an Australia side decimated by Packer defections. Later in 1979, a truce between Packer and the board was brokered, and Nine earned TV rights to the game in Australia. Many of the innovations of WSC – coloured clothing and day-night cricket among them – shaped the game as we know it today. Sporting Witness: Kerry Packer's cricket revolution Mike Gatting, centre, later said he regretted the Shakoor Rana incident England had already been frustrated by the decisions of a home umpire in losing the first Test on their tour of Pakistan in late 1987. Shakoor Rana was appointed to stand in the second Test, much to England's displeasure. Rana had previously clashed with New Zealand skipper Jeremy Coney. On the second day in Faisalabad, Rana was at square leg when he appeared to halt the game to object to one of England captain Mike Gatting's field placements. Gatting was furious, confronting the official in footage that has been replayed over and over. The following day, Rana refused to take the field, leaving England waiting in the middle for play that did not get under way. The match eventually resumed on the fourth day and the cancellation of the tour was narrowly avoided, but mistrust and ill-feeling between England and Pakistan lingered for years later. title: Met Police officer charged after BBC Charing Cross investigation
description: The police watchdog began an investigation into alleged misconduct at Charing Cross police station in London as a result of a BBC Panorama investigation.
body: A Metropolitan Police officer has become the first person to be charged as a result of a BBC Panorama investigation into alleged misconduct at Charing Cross police station in London. Sgt Sadiq Al-Hasani, 37, has been charged with perverting the course of justice. He will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. In a statement, the Met Police said the charge related to an allegation Sgt Al-Hasani, who was attached to Central West Command Unit, "deliberately sought to discourage another officer from making a statement to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC)". The IOPC had begun an investigation following the broadcast on 1 October 2025 of BBC Panorama – Undercover in the Police. As part of the programme, a BBC journalist went undercover working in the custody suite, secretly filming a number of officers making racist comments and bragging about violence used against suspects. Al-Hasani was charged on 13 August in relation to an incident on 2 October 2025. In a statement, the IOPC said Sgt Al-Hasani allegedly approached a junior officer, who was a potential key witness in the wider Charing Cross investigation, with the intention to obstruct or interfere with the probe. He remains suspended from duty, the Met said. The IOPC began its investigation after a mandatory conduct referral from the Met on 3 October. As part of this, the IOPC reviewed footage gathered as part of the programme which was not broadcast. Its investigation finished in June, at which point it decided to refer a file of evidence to the Crown Prosecution Service. According to the IOPC, 15 officers have been found to have committed gross misconduct. All except one of the 15, a former PC, have been barred from policing. Investigations continue into the conduct of a further 14 officers or police staff. title: Celine Dion kicks off Paris Fashion Week with surprise performance
description: The singer appeared at the end of L'Oreal's annual show as the French fashion bonanza kicked off.
body: Celine Dion has opened Paris Fashion Week with a surprise performance of her 2002 hit I'm Alive, underneath the city's famous Eiffel Tower. The Canadian star, who was diagnosed with a rare neurological disease called stiff person syndrome in 2022, took to the runway at the end of L'Oreal's annual show. The singer, who wore a ruched full-length velvet black gown, was later joined by famous ambassadors for the French brand, including Viola Davis, Simone Ashley, Aja Naomi King and Eva Longoria. Dion recently performed a comeback show in the city earlier this month, her first since her 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. Paris Fashion Week, showcasing women's spring/summer collections, runs until 6 October. Actress Viola Davis was feeling the love from the crowd as she joined Dion under the stars in the French capital. Actress Eva Longoria was also pleased to see Dion on the runway Kendall Jenner also modelled at the show, wearing a sheer black halterneck dress with thigh split and an ivory corset underneath. Supermodel Cara Delavingne, meanwhile, walked the runway in a sparkling red sheer dress with train. Pop star Rihanna brought her usual fashion credentials to Paris on day one, with a shimmering, glamorous copper two-piece worn over sheer black lingerie. She was on the front row of the Matières Fécales fashion show - the label behind Zendaya's angel wings dress at The Odyssey premiere in New York this summer. Wicked star Cynthia Erivo was also in the French capital at a Tiffany and M.A.D - Musée des Arts Décoratifs - event. Other labels showing in Paris over the next week include Louis Vuitton, Tom Ford, Schiaparelli, Givenchy, Jean Paul Gaultier, Balenciaga and Loewe. The fashion world is keeping a particularly close eye on Dior and Chanel, after both signed up new artistic directors last year. Matthieu Blazy took over as Chanel's creative director in early 2025, while Jonathan Anderson began the same role at Dior last summer. This week should see the pair continue to solidify their strategies for the two brands. Expect some serious aesthetic rivalry on the runways. title: Chris Mason: Burnham opens debate on huge issue of social care reform
description: The pitch from Andy Burnham is that there needs to be a willingness to say "the things politicians usually avoid", the BBC's political editor writes.
body: Conference speech day is always a big day for a prime minister, and perhaps no bigger than when it is your first one in the role. The pitch from Andy Burnham is that "hope comes from honesty," there needs to be "less drift and more direction" and there needs to be a willingness to say "the things politicians usually avoid." On Sunday, he told the BBC he wants to shake up social care in England, but would only be able to do so after a general election given he was committed to the tax promises Sir Keir Starmer made at the last general election. This prompted a flurry of chat about how his social care plan could be paid for - and in particular the future of what is known as the triple lock, the promise to increase the state pension in line with wages, prices or 2.5%, whichever is the highest. This was a policy introduced in 2010 by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government to try to address pensioner poverty. But plenty of politicians, in multiple parties, have long privately fretted that its cost is ballooning and will continue to do so, but would bemoan how politically difficult it would be to drop it. It's a tricky one for the prime minister: he has the leader of the Unite union, Sharon Graham, saying it could be "electoral suicide" to ditch the triple lock. Meanwhile the markets - which determine the cost of borrowing for the government - are keeping a keen eye on whether Burnham's promises appear to be financially credible. In other words, he has to be able to point to things where money won't be spent, as well as where it will be. No10 are being pretty coy about precisely what Andy Burnham will or won't say on all this later on. They really don't want to overcook it or overdo it, instead suggesting it is others who have been getting carried away. But ministers are well aware that a hare is running about it all - and given that, it would be extraordinary if there was no mention of it all, given that promise about "honesty," candour and trade offs. Sufficiently extraordinary that his critics would pounce on what they'd see as a precise lack of the very thing he is promising - candour. Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid Folk I am hearing from this morning suggest, as one figure put it, "people will be surprised on the upside" about how much Burnham will be willing to lean into the options that could be explored as part of Labour's offer at the next general election. He will be explicit it will be retained, as promised, until the election. Instead, it would appear Burnham will seek to seed a conversation about all of the above, without nailing down the details. His allies see this as a different approach to politics – being open about options, starting a debate but not crudely or abruptly shifting policy. There is an implicit comparison with Sir Keir Starmer's ditching of the Winter Fuel Payment – which appeared to come from nowhere and had a near immediate impact. But that didn't stop Graham likening the two approaches – claiming "the danger of doing it" is that Labour could "waste" a second hearing which it now has under Andy Burnham. And so the debate begins. In the round, though, ministers I speak to are relishing what they see as a return to big arguments, about generational issues with a prime minister willing to wrestle with them in public. This afternoon we will get a fuller sense of the scope and scale of that – on social care, pensions and much else. title: Andy Burnham: Northern PM's long journey to power
description: The former mayor of Greater Manchester has had designs on the top job since 2010 when he first ran to be Labour leader.
body: Andy Burnham might be a new face at No 10, after ousting Sir Keir Starmer in July, but his rise to power has been decades in the making. The 56-year-old started out as a special adviser and then an MP in Tony Blair's New Labour government. He first stood to be Labour leader back in 2010 and then again in 2015, when he came a distant second to Jeremy Corbyn, before turning his back on Westminster and re-inventing himself as the King of the North. As the first Mayor of Greater Manchester, he built a powerful political brand - affable, down-to-earth and, above all, proudly Northern. When asked by the website Mumsnet to name his favourite biscuit, the new prime minister replied that he did not have a sweet tooth and preferred "beer and chips and gravy". This video can not be played Watch: Who is Andy Burnham?.. in 90 seconds Andy Burnham: Who is the new PM? From Manchester mayor to prime minister; what is his record and what does he stand for? Born in Liverpool in 1970, Burnham grew up in Culcheth, a quiet commuter belt village in Cheshire, near Warrington. His father, a BT engineer, and his mother, a GP receptionist, were both staunch Labour supporters and he developed an early interest in politics. Burnham has described how he was inspired to join the Labour Party at the age of 14, after being moved by the BBC TV drama, Boys from the Blackstuff, about life on the dole in Liverpool. A lifelong Everton fan, his friends remember Burnham as a competitive, sports-mad child, who was a fast bowler for Lancashire schoolboys cricket team. At school, the local Roman Catholic comprehensive, his English teacher recalls how he stood to be a Labour candidate in mock elections - and won by a landslide. Burnham credits his working-class Catholic upbringing for having a big impact on his politics, particularly teachings around social justice. He has described himself as "Catholic by upbringing" although "not particularly religious", but he was sworn in to Parliament over a Bible and will be the UK's first prime minister to enter Downing Street as a Catholic. While Burnham told the Times his mother would be "wearing her rosary beads out" to mark him becoming prime minister, his father, Roy, will unfortunately be unaware of his son's achievement due to his dementia. He told The Times: "That's a sadness because he would be (proud). The way I look at it, it's his achievement as well. "A whole family achievement although he doesn't know it." Burnham and his two brothers were the first in their family to go to university, with Andy studying English at Cambridge. In his book, Head North, Burnham wrote that he "struggled to feel part of things" at university and felt like an "imposter". However, the music-lover - who is a fan of Manchester indie bands like The Smiths and The Stone Roses - said his "growing interest in Manchester music gave me an identity and an advantage". Burnham appeared alongside Sir Keir Starmer during a visit by the PM to Ashton-under-Lyne in April After graduating, he started out in journalism, working for trade magazines including Tank World and Passenger World Management. In his early 20s, he got his first break in politics, working as a researcher for the late Tessa Jowell, then MP for Dulwich and West Norwood, who would go on to be a minister under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. Burnham rose quickly through the ranks, becoming a special adviser to Culture Secretary Chris Smith before being elected as the MP for his hometown of Leigh, in Greater Manchester, in 2001. He first served as a junior minister under Blair, but joined the cabinet as chief secretary to the Treasury, and later culture secretary and health secretary, under Brown. It was as secretary of state for culture, media and sport that Burnham was heckled at a memorial service marking the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster. Ninety-seven Liverpool fans were killed in the stadium crush of 1989. The heckling spurred Burnham on to raise the issue in cabinet, contributing to the launch of a second inquiry into the disaster. A keen footballer, Burnham was a regular feature in the annual Labour MPs vs political journalists match In 2010, after Brown resigned following Labour's general election defeat, Burnham ran to become the party's leader. He came fourth out of the five contenders, losing to Ed Miliband, but spent the next five years building up his appeal with the party's grassroots. In 2015 he tried again, beaten this time by Jeremy Corbyn. Burnham's critics have branded him a weather vane, whose views have blown with the political winds to give him the best chance of success. He served in Corbyn's shadow cabinet, as shadow home secretary, despite being seen as on the Blairite centre-right of the party. Burnham's views have moved increasingly to the left, backing the nationalisation of water and energy. He was not one of those who resigned in protest at Corbyn's leadership in 2016. Instead he stood down in 2017 to run to be the first mayor of Greater Manchester. Burnham won the contest with more than 60% of the vote and was re-elected by an even bigger margin in 2021. Burnham gave a speech in 2014 at Anfield Stadium to mark the 25th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster As mayor, he has drawn praise for his transformation of the region's transport system. Under his leadership, Greater Manchester was the first area in England outside London to bring bus services back under public control, while integrating them with other modes of transport under the branding of the "Bee Network". Other bold pledges included ending rough sleeping in the region by 2020 - although the target was missed. His profile rose further during the Covid pandemic, when he accused the Conservative government of treating the north of England with "contempt" over regional lockdown restrictions. title: Watch: Luxury units uncovered inside an Indonesian prison
description: A surprise inspection at the prison revealed apartment-like units appearing to house inmates, equipped with televisions, a gym and fridges stocked with alcohol.
body: This video can not be played A surprise inspection by the Indonesian Ombudsman at Cibinong Prison in Bogor, West Java, revealed apartment-like units located just outside the main detention blocks. Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff. The BBC's Liza Tambunan explains what they found inside. title: Life bright for Gilmour after baseball and World Cup heartache
description: Scotland midfielder Billy Gilmour opens up on the pain of missing out of this summer's World Cup.
body: Billy Gilmour was Scotland's star player against Slovenia Billy Gilmour sits at Lesser Hampden, a beaming smile bursting across his face. The topic of conversation is revolving around him missing the World Cup in the summer, something that could have been defined by harrowing disappointment and regret. Instead, the Napoli midfielder's face lights up when asked about a night at the baseball in Miami, where the injured Scotland ace was asked to hobble on to the field and hurl the ceremonial first pitch. "I was nervous," Gilmour tells BBC Scotland, recollecting the evening at the Miami Marlins against the Texas Rangers. "I was just so happy it wasn't a crap throw, or it was bouncing. It was some experience." How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents Listen: Can Scotland shock the Swiss at Hampden? Pocognoli has no concern over Scotland's lack of goals The maturity and level-headedness of the 25-year-old defies his years. Just days before he was due to jet off to the United States with the Scotland squad for the first men's World Cup the nation had experienced since before he was born, a crushing blow. In the farewell game at Hampden against Curacao, he suffered a knee injury that would mean he was left behind. While a body blow to Steve Clarke, his squad and the country, it would have been devastating to a young man with the world stage at his feet. He admits those initial days were difficult as reality set in, but Gilmour seized the chance to become a supporter across Boston and Miami with his family around him. "The boys fell on top of me and I've heard something straight away," he said of the injury. "Typical, try to run it off, make sure it was okay. "It was tough. You have to take yourself away for a couple of days and I did. "I got to go away for a bit, just kind of switch off and it happened, so I had to deal with it. When you're there around the squad, you try to be as best as you can, as positive as you can. "When you think of it, how lucky you still are to get to go there and watch the games and be with family and family holiday also." Gilmour added: "I would be with the team some nights, but the squad and Robbo [captain Andy Robertson] and the gaffer, Steve Clarke, at the time, he basically said: 'Look, if it's too much to come in, don't come in. Stay as much time with the family. Go and experience it with the fans'." Billy Gilmour made a guest appearance with Miami Marlins Gilmour was still in Miami when news broke of Clarke's resignation as Scotland head coach. He's a man the Napoli midfielder acknowledges he owes so much to after giving him his debut in 2001. Now, however, it's the Sebastien Pocognoli era and the former Rangers, Chelsea and Brighton & Hove Albion man seems central to it. In the 0-0 draw in Slovenia on Saturday, it was Gilmour who caught the attention during a resurgent second half for the Scots. He is often seen as more of a deep-lying central midfielder, but there was a different dynamic to his game with the absence of club-mate Scott McTominay, who is recovering from a heart procedure. "When I was younger, I really liked playing higher up, trying to be among it," Gilmour, who is set to feature at Hampden on Tuesday against Switzerland - live on the BBC, said. "Whenever I get asked to play on the pitch, as long as I'm on the pitch, I'm happy. I just want to play football and enjoy it." Now 25, there is plenty time to make new memories in a Scotland shirt. Yet, with so many young faces coming into the squad, the Ayrshire man is probably now a senior figure in the group. It's something he says he embraces, although Gilmour is coy about the prospect of maybe taking on the armband whenever current captain Robertson decides to pass it on. "For me, it's everyone's dream to be a captain at a club or a country," he said. "Of course I'd be really proud to, but Robbo's my captain and he's a really good captain as well. "What he's done for Scotland is incredible and he's very close on the record [most caps held by Kenny Dalglish] and I'm sure he'll get it." title: 'Period of deception' - Pochettino on Man City verdict
description: Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino says it is "impossible to turn back time" after Manchester City being found guilty of financial breaches.
body: Mauricio Pochettino has managed three clubs in England Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino says "we have lived through a period of deception" after Manchester City were found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges brought against them by the Premier League. An independent panel found City to be guilty of a wide range of financial rule breaches, with the Athletic, external reporting on Friday that 114 of the 115 charges against them have been upheld. Sanctions are yet to be announced, but City plan on appealing against the decision. The charges relate to a period from 2009-10 to 2017-18, while they were accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between December 2018 to February 2023. United States manager Pochettino managed three clubs in the Premier League during that time, with the 54-year-old spending 15 months at Southampton, five years at Tottenham and a single season with Chelsea. "Whatever punishment [they choose], it's impossible to turn back time," said Pochettino. "It's done a lot of damage. Many clubs followed the rules and some didn't. "Maybe they thought that the punishment [wouldn't come for a lot of years] - what are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points? It's really hard. "It is a huge sadness. We get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn't that real, what seemed good maybe wasn't so good, what didn't look good maybe was good but couldn't be good because of what happened. "We went through something where sporting fairness didn't exist. So, how do you repair everything that was damaged because of that, if it's true all of the 114 rules that were broken, we've lived through a period of deception." Man City CEO defiant over Premier League charges Spurs should be awarded 2016-17 title - Pochettino Man City rule breaches not my concern - Mancini Earlier this month, Pochettino said Chelsea should be stripped of the 2016-17 Premier League title after being found guilty of historical rule breaches and that it should be "awarded" to his Tottenham side, who finished runners-up. Sources have told BBC Sport that other top flight clubs are seeking legal advice over possible compensation claims following the decision against City. City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation. The club were referred to an independent commission. A behind-closed-doors hearing began in September 2024 and ran for about 12 weeks. "Where were the controls?" said Pochettino on City being found guilty. "That's what gets my attention. Where were the controls? "If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham - I remember building [the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months. "I think we were the only team in the history of the Premier League with 18 months without [making a transfer]. "Tottenham was fighting for titles with those above us and every year in the top four, getting to the semi-finals of the Champions League without being able to do a transfer for 18 months, all because we needed to get used to the [Premier League financial controls]? "They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that's why I say: it's all very strange." title: Scrapping pensions triple lock 'morally wrong', says union boss
description: Andy Burnham wants to outline his ideas for a free-at-the-point-of-use social care system in his first speech to Labour conference as prime minister.
body: Union boss Sharon Graham has been an outspoken critic of Labour governments in the past Unite the Union general secretary Sharon Graham has warned the prime minister that scrapping the pensions triple lock would be "morally wrong", as Andy Burnham prepares to deliver his first speech to Labour conference as PM. Burnham told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that he wants to use his speech to set out his "vision" to introduce an NHS-style social care system, free at the point of use. There is growing speculation about how such a care system could be funded, including removing the pensions triple lock in the future. Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell told BBC Breakfast the party is committed to the triple lock, which was in the party's 2024 manifesto. The triple lock, which has been in place for 16 years, means state pensions rise every April by at least 2.5% or in line with the highest of prices or earnings. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Graham said axing the triple lock risked repeating the unpopular removal of the Winter Fuel Allowance under previous prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. "Instead of going to try and pick the pocket of pensioners, we need to move over to the other side of the equation and think about things like wealth taxes way before we try to stop something like the triple lock," she said. "Going to a group of people who are getting around £12,500 a year in order to pay for it [social care], to take away their security, is wrong - I think its morally wrong," she added, highlighting how current pensions are the lowest of the G7 countries. On Tuesday morning, Powell said the lock was a manifesto commitment, and asked whether it would stay in place until the next election, she said: "I can absolutely assure your viewers watching this that we are committed to the triple lock, it's in our manifesto. "The triple lock is really delivering for pensioners right now: over the course of this parliament it's set to increase the value of the state pension by around about £2,000 a year - significant uplifts to the state pension." Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister who is currently leading an independent review into young people and work for the government, has said scrapping the triple lock to fund social care is "the sort of call" the prime minister is "prepared to make". In the BBC's Political Thinking podcast, Milburn was asked if Burnham's new social care plans could be funded by getting rid of the triple lock, he responded that Burnham was "exactly the sort of person who can take the big decisions". He said: "Andy is absolutely right about this - the social care system is broken... That is going to be a really big call. "But it's the sort of call that I've got no doubt - from everything, and every conversation I've been in with him - it's the sort of call that he is prepared to make." title: All in the Mind
description: Plus, we reveal the All in the Mind Awards judging panel.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·29 Sep 2026,·28 mins Available for over a year Claudia Hammond chats to All in the Mind Awards judge, writer and former doctor Adam Kay. Adam shares his mental health first aid kit, the importance of saying thank you and why you should nominate someone for an Award. Plus, how do you judge another person’s emotions? New research suggests that children and adults use different information to reach a conclusion on how someone is feeling. And Claudia is joined by Kavita Vedhara, professor of health psychology at Cardiff University. Kavita shares how stress can scramble your internal GPS and how the brain may have evolved from two separate systems. You’ll find the terms and conditions and the privacy notice on the website, and you must be over 18 to send in a nomination. You have until 1pm on Friday the 8th of January 2027 to enter. title: Mistakes to avoid when buying Glastonbury tickets
description: Tips and expert advice to ensure you have the best success when buying Glastonbury 2027 tickets.
body: There are mistakes that people repeatedly make when attempting to purchase a ticket Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for the 2027 event will go on sale later this week. After taking a year off in 2026, thousands of festival-goers are preparing to secure a place at next year's five-day event. Coach and ticket packages are due to go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday and general admission tickets a few days later at 09:00 on Sunday. The festival has introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of the sale. But for those anxious about securing a place, we have rounded up some hardened festival-goers' advice on the biggest pitfalls to avoid. Works begins on new £12m urgent treatment centre 'Easier to get Glastonbury tickets than farm fund' Theatre to close over 'serious financial constraints' Some may think using multiple devices to secure tickets may give you better odds, however the website can mistake this for an error and kick you out of the queue at any point. It may also ban you from re-entering the site. Having multiple tabs open might mean the website decides you're a bot and blocks you. Joining the waiting room earlier than the advertised time may give you a better chance in the queue, even if it is randomised. However, joining late will place you at the back of the queue, which lessens your chance due to the amount of people already waiting. As you have a strict time limit to secure your tickets, having your payment information written down or saved on your browser to auto-fill will make getting tickets an easier and speedier process. You will need to enter your card information, billing address and contact information within five minutes. Make sure that you, and those in your group, have enough funds to place a deposit on every ticket. Have your phone at the ready to authenticate payments on banking apps and two-factor authentication through text, email and call. Paul Farrugia, the writer of the 100% unofficial Glastonbury Festival Guidebook , external, has shared his tips as someone who has been to Glastonbury 10 times. He said Glastonbury tickets are connected through See Tickets so it is a good idea to ensure the company is a trusted merchant for your banking group before the sale or your payment may not be authorised. He also advised applying with friends in the same house as you could harm your chances as your IP address will be the same. However, he said heading into offices together could be a bonus as the WiFi speeds tend to be faster. SJ Smallpage, founder of 'Glastonbury Festival Fans' Facebook group and admin of 'Glasto Girls' Facebook group, has advice about what to do if you have completed the first hurdle of getting through the "green line of doom", but then your page crashes. SJ advises not to refresh the page as this will send you to the back of the queue, lessening your chances of ever getting through again. Instead their key advice is to "click the back button once, cool and patiently". If you are unsuccessful with tickets in October, there is the April resale just around the corner. The April resale allows for one registration to secure four tickets, giving you another chance of success. But if you're not successful and still want the Glastonbury experience, SJ recommends Shindig Festival and quotes Emily Eavis, who described it as a "pint-sized Glasto." This could also be a good choice for people wanting to go to Glastonbury for the first time or those who are anxious of the big crowds and space. title: 'We don't know where he is': Relatives of the explorer speak to BBC
description: Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.
body: This video can not be played Family and friends of British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said they have not been able to visit or contact him for months. His former sister-in-law Arabella Pepper told BBC Newsnight that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him. "All his friends and family want to see him and take him Toblerones and cheer him up, but we don't know where is," she said. It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes. Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, said he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind". Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment. Read more about Sir Ranulph Fiennes. title: Aston Villa sack boss Arroyo after winless WSL start
description: Aston Villa manager Natalia Arroyo is sacked following two defeats and two draws in their opening four matches of the Women's Super League season.
body: Natalia Arroyo played for Barcelona and Spain before retiring in 2009 Aston Villa manager Natalia Arroyo has been sacked following a disappointing start to the Women's Super League season. Villa are yet to win this season, drawing two and losing two of their opening four matches and BBC Sport is told that led to the club’s decision. They suffered a 4-0 defeat by Tottenham on Sunday in the WSL and are due to play Newcastle in the Women's League Cup on Wednesday (19:30 BST). Spaniard Arroyo joined Villa in January 2025 and had another two years remaining on her contract. She becomes the first managerial departure this season, though former Manchester United boss Marc Skinner and ex-Brighton head coach Dario Vidosic both stepped down earlier this year. The club informed Arroyo of their decision on Monday evening and players were told on Tuesday morning. Former Everton manager Brian Sorensen, who is now Villa’s women’s technical advisor, has been placed in interim charge. Since Arroyo's arrival, Villa have shown flashes of potential and she initially steadied the ship as they toyed with relegation in her first six months at the club. But despite investment in the transfer window, Villa lacked consistency and were underwhelming last season. There was pressure on them to perform in 2026-27 and while they earned a draw on the opening weekend against Chelsea, they have looked dangerously open at the back and chaotic out of possession. Their latest defeat by Spurs was a worrying display and appears to have been enough to lead to Arroyo's sacking. title: Ex-England captain Dallaglio to sell World Cup winner's medal
description: Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio is set to sell his 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal after being declared bankrupt.
body: Lawrence Dallaglio (middle) made 326 appearances for Wasps during his club career Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio is set to sell his 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal after being declared bankrupt. The 54-year-old has put a number of items from his illustrious career up for auction including medals, trophies and caps. The World Cup medal is expected to raise between £50,000 and £80,000 while in total the collection has an estimated value of £180,000. Dallaglio was one of the stars of the England side that won the World Cup in dramatic fashion against Australia 23 years ago. Other items up for sale include a British and Irish Lions cap, his 1993 World Cup Sevens winner's medal and a 2003 Six Nations Championship winner's medal. During an appearance on The High Performance podcast, external earlier this month, Dallaglio spoke about his bankrupcy. He said: "As a result of getting divorced, I was made bankrupt. "I had some financial problems - I could've done things a lot better." He also said he sought therapy after his divorce and bankruptcy left him wallowing in "self-pity". The auction at Budd's, external in Northamptonshire takes place on 13 October. title: Raids on suspected organised crime see 17 arrested
description: Searches continue at a number of properties and there is expected to be an ongoing police presence.
body: Police investigating a suspected organised crime group have arrested 17 people in dawn raids at 24 properties in London, Essex, Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Suffolk. More than 800 officers took part in the arrest operations in the early hours of Tuesday. Searches are ongoing at a number of the properties and there is expected to be a police presence for some days, the Metropolitan Police said. An officer taking part in the operation in Cockfosters, Barnet, was stabbed in the leg while carrying out a warrant - his injuries are non-life changing. The arrests were part of an investigation by the Met along with His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The Met said the FCA has "disrupted" seven businesses and is "actively pursuing" another 30. A spokesperson said: "These arrests mark a significant point in this investigation. "Those arrested are suspected of leading or being involved at a senior level in serious and organised crime and related financial offending." In total, 15 men aged between 26 and 65 were arrested, and two women aged 31 and 41. They are being held on suspicion of participating in the activities of an organised crime group, money laundering, cheating the public revenue, false accounting, and conspiracy to commit GBH. A 56-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of GBH over the stabbing. title: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels
description: Police are trying to verify whether a female student was raped at Lovely Professional University (LPU).
body: Some violent protesters allegedly torched police cars parked on the highway on Sunday One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence. Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation. Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack. But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad. Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus. Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised. By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed. University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home. Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate. Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier. The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed. BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered. Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge. Behind the gates, students described a night of fear. "We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here." Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here." Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence That the police open a case and investigate the allegation was among the protesters' central demands. "The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC. Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred. Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room. "As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said. But they are continuing to examine the footage. "The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this." Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself. There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university. "We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield." Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played. Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own. On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them. The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations. Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the rece
