title: Burkina Faso's junta leader opens major gold refinery to keep mining profits at home
description: Junta leader Ibrahim Traoré wants the country to profit more from its mineral wealth.
body: Captain Ibrahim Traoré has insisted on state control over Burkina Faso's natural resources Burkina Faso has opened its first gold refinery as the military-led government seeks to process more of the country's mineral wealth at home and tighten its control over one of its most important industries. Junta leader Ibrahim Traoré said the move was part of a wider effort to end the country's reliance on exporting raw materials for processing abroad. "We want to refine all our metals on site... we want to have the entire value chain on site," he said at the plant's inauguration in the capital, Ouagadougou, on Monday. Burkina Faso is one of Africa's biggest gold producers but the authorities have struggled to regulate the informal mining sector, which has been blighted by jihadist violence. Traoré's government hopes the new facility can turn the landlocked country into a regional gold-refining hub. Why Burkina Faso's junta leader has captured hearts and minds around the world How 'blood gold' is fuelling conflict in West Africa With gold production on the rise, Traoré's government set up a state-owned mining company two years ago. Foreign mining firms are now required to give the state a 15% stake in their operations and train local workers. The World Gold Council said output rose by 17% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, helped by increased production at several mines. But successive governments have struggled to regulate the country's extensive artisanal and small-scale mining industry, where smuggling and informal trading have made it difficult for the authorities to account for all the gold produced. The government has also alleged that some illegally traded gold helps finance the Islamist insurgency that has engulfed much of the country. Burkina Faso has been fighting armed Islamist groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State for years, with large areas outside full government control. The new refinery, known as Raffinor-BF, cost more than 11bn CFA francs ($19m; £14m), according to the presidency. It said the project was financed by the state, including through the National Precious Metals Company (Sonasp), in partnership with Burkina Faso's private sector. The plant will initially be capable of refining 164 tonnes of gold a year, significantly more than the country's current annual production. The government says its eventual capacity could rise to 515 tonnes, suggesting it also wants the refinery to process gold from elsewhere in the region. "This is the day we take back the keys to our own house," Mines Minister Yacouba Zabré Gouba said at the opening. "Our gold will no longer be used to create added value for others while our people remain in need." The plant will initially be capable of refining 164 tonnes of gold a year, presidency says The refinery is the latest element of Capt Traoré's drive to increase state control over Burkina Faso's natural resources and reduce its economic dependence on foreign companies and former Western partners. Since taking power in a coup in September 2022, the 38-year-old army captain has promoted a nationalist economic agenda centred on domestic production and greater control of strategic industries. His government has increased state involvement in the mining sector and has sought to reorganise the trade in artisanal gold. The authorities suspended exports of gold produced by artisanal and semi-mechanised mines in 2024, saying the move was intended to better regulate the sector. Capt Traoré has previously accused smugglers of taking large quantities of gold out of Burkina Faso illegally and said some of the proceeds were helping finance militant groups. The refinery also forms part of a broader government campaign to process more commodities domestically rather than exporting them in raw form. Traoré has presented such projects as evidence of Burkina Faso becoming more economically self-reliant, alongside investments in industries including cotton, textiles and food processing. His policies have coincided with historically high international gold prices and increased global production. Worldwide mine output reached an estimated record 3,672 tonnes in 2025, according to the World Gold Council. Burkina Faso's government says the new plant should eventually be capable of refining all the gold produced by both its industrial mines and artisanal miners. Several West African countries are also seeking to process more of their gold at home. Guinea and Ghana have restricted exports of unrefined gold, while Mali is building its first refinery with help of a Russian firm. Ivory Coast also plans to open a refinery next year. title: Fifa accuses Uefa of 'misinformation campaign'
description: Uefa's suggestions that Fifa president Gianni Infantino "violated any law or ethical principle are categorically without merit" says world football's governing body.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Fifa has accused Uefa of a "misinformation campaign" and attempting to influence the race for its presidential campaign in new court documents. They also described Uefa's conduct as "in bad faith and for the purpose of harassment". Last month European football's governing body filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland. Uefa accused Fifa president Gianni Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" and "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by [him] for his own benefit" over the now-shelved Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme. In its response on Monday night, world governing body Fifa said Uefa's filing contained "numerous false or misleading statements about Fifa and Infantino". "With no basis whatsoever, Uefa suggests that Mr Infantino sought to profit personally from the FFE proposal," Fifa said in a filing in the Southern District of Florida, opposing Uefa's motion for discovery. "Uefa's suggestions that Mr Infantino violated any law or ethical principle are categorically without merit." It also described Uefa's filing as "farcically overbroad" saying "districts faced with similar requests have outright rejected such applications". BBC Sport has contacted Uefa for comment. BBC Sport has been told insiders believe that if Fifa has nothing to hide, it should disclose the documents and speed up the legal process. Uefa has led the rebellion against the Fifa president, who is facing calls to stand down from three confederations. Fifa's FFE plan proposed selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, sparking a major backlash. Infantino faced calls for his resignation but claimed the project had been intended to generate additional money for the game. Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE. Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. title: Inside Liverpool's increasing global investment in youth
description: Liverpool are becoming increasingly proactive in their search for global young talent. BBC Sport takes a closer look.
body: Mor Talla Ndiaye made the move to Liverpool after the U17 World Cup Liverpool may have made three signings worth more than £100m each over the past two summers in Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola, but internally there is a realisation that after a significant amount of young talent was sold last summer, the club need to replenish that talent pool. Since 2020, Liverpool have made more than £230m from selling players who have represented them at youth level and that has been a major part of owner Fenway Sports Group's self-sustaining business model, with the funds reinvested into the club. Since Brexit, there is a 'premium' on young English players and it is why Liverpool's global talent department, led by Matt Newberry since the winter of 2024, now have a major role to play. Fifa rules state that international transfers of players are only permitted if the player is over 18 and, since Brexit, Premier League clubs are no longer permitted to sign players under 18 from European countries. Newberry's team is responsible for deciding which young talents from overseas should be targeted for a move. Using their wealth of contacts across the world, including dedicated regional scouts, Liverpool are becoming increasingly aggressive in the space. It helps that new sporting director Julian Ward is well known for his global network. "Any player we sign, the first intention is that we want them to play in the first team and there's a belief that there's a chance for everyone that signs here," Alex Inglethorpe, Liverpool Academy director told BBC Sport. "That really is no different since the impact of Brexit on the English market, which is quite significant. There's now a premium on young English players. Time will tell if that premium is worthwhile but it's definitely a change. "So it's fairly natural for a club like Liverpool to look within Merseyside in the first instance then broaden that out - national recruitment happens at 14 and after that you look globally, which is what we've done." Mor Talla Ndiaye's journey began in the Senegalese village of Sandiara where he played football in the streets. He progressed through the ranks playing for Bousports Academy in the town of Thiadiaye before joining Amitie Football Club in the city of Thies. Come January this year, Liverpool fended off interest from other European clubs and signed the 18-year-old for about £1m plus add-ons. "You have access to certain talent based on points accrued from playing homegrown players. We had a couple of ESC (elite significant contribution) spots to explore the wider market and that's something which, even prior to Brexit, was a fairly normal thing," Inglethorpe adds. Ndiaye is a left-footed centre-half who played for Liverpool in pre-season under Andoni Iraola and was an unused substitute in three games in the second half of last season under Arne Slot. "He's an incredible story, isn't he? From where he's come from to where he is - and he's such a humble kid. He's an unbelievable lad to work with," Rob Page, Liverpool's U21 boss, told BBC Sport. "There's exciting times ahead but he's got a lot of work to do. He's nowhere near the finished article but he's on the right path. His attitude is spot on and he's at the club that will definitely help him develop." At Liverpool, there is an optimism regarding Ndiaye and a genuine belief that if he makes it to the top, it could be one of the great football stories. Liverpool opened discussions with his academy and his agency, Sport Cover, after scouts spotted his performances at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last winter and several video calls were arranged before the club's representatives travelled to Senegal. Once there, they visited where Ndiaye trained, as well as meeting the people that supported his development before presenting their vision to him directly. A round-table meeting was organised with his family to help understand his environment, the story and the context in which he grew up. Ultimately, Ndiaye chose Liverpool because they offered the clearest pathway and their approach in getting to know him stood out. Ndiaye isn't the only player to have been identified and recruited by Liverpool's global talent team. After the U17 World Cup, Liverpool also made a £2.6m move for another centre-half, Ifeanyi Ndukwe. Ndukwe was impressive in pre-season and the 18-year-old Austrian has gone on loan to Levante in La Liga as he looks to obtain a UK work permit. The list doesn't stop there. Samuel Martinez, the 17-year-old Colombian midfielder, will join next summer after having "30 offers from around the world, external", according to his father. It doesn't always work. Arsenal beat Liverpool to the signing of Andria Bartishvili from Georgia last month and the 17-year-old will join the Gunners next summer when he is 18. But the moves for Martinez and Ndiaye showcase Liverpool's willingness to spread beyond Europe and into areas they may not have explored before. Given the inevitability of other top clubs circling emerging talent, the idea of selling the pathway that Liverpool offers is imperative. Since arriving, Ndiaye has settled in with a host family - which is normal when players aren't from the area - that are used to working with Liverpool. "Players come from varying parts of the world and, when someone comes in and doesn't speak much English at the start, you have to help with that and help understand culturally the differences in food, the weather and even the pitches you play on," Inglethorpe said. "There's a lot of understanding in terms of the level of support that's needed and the most important thing you can give a young player is the time. title: How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents
description: Aston Villa's summer signing Johan Manzambi has been nominated for the best young player at the Ballon d'Or ceremony. BBC Sport looks at his rise.
body: Johan Manzambi scored his first Aston Villa against Tottenham earlier in September In just two years Johan Manzambi has gone from being an unknown teenager to a European star. The 20-year-old could be named young talent of the year at the Ballon d'Or ceremony next month having only made his senior debut for Freiburg in 2024. A breakout season in Germany last term convinced Villa to pay more than £50m for a player with just 47 club starts. Manzambi scored on his full Villa debut to help secure a first Premier League win of the season and now faces Scotland with Switzerland in the Nations League on Tuesday looking to continue his progression. Vega hails Yakin and Manzambi as Swiss head for Hampden Villa complete club record Manzambi signing Manzambi is already in the discussion with fellow nominees Lamine Yamal of Barcelona, Real Madrid's Yan Diomande and new Manchester City midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi for the best young player in the world award. He scored three goals in four games for Switzerland at the World Cup before a knee injury ended his tournament, only a year after making his full international debut. It is a rapid rise for a player who used to return to Freiburg's academy to do his washing. Bernhard Weis, who gave Manzambi his debut for Freiburg Under-19s, told BBC Sport: "He is playing for the professionals and he comes to us at the academy and brings some dirty clothes. "He didn't have a washing machine so he comes here and washes some clothes. "I would speak with him and then he would pick up some young guys from the under-13s, under-14s and take them to the train station. "He would see the guys and say, 'come with me, I'll take you to the station', so they could get home. That's Johan Manzambi." As for his profile, though, Weis did not expect a Ballon d'Or nomination coming so quickly. He added: "I didn't see that. I saw something for the first team, for us, but this way, no chance. "The first half year at Freiburg it was not so easy for him, he's not so strong and he's not so stable. He put on five kilos and then he thought, 'now I go, it's the right moment, I will be faster and stronger'. Massimo Lombardo, Servette's academy director agreed. He first worked with Manzambi when he was 15 and oversaw his early development before he moved to Freiburg as a 17-year-old in 2023. "It is a real surprise for many people, that he can do something special so quickly," he told BBC Sport. "For me, the difference he can make is because of his mentality, personality, enthusiasm and courage. He has the technical skills and tactical skills and the physical possibility now to perform in England. Why Newcastle target Manzambi is in demand Manzambi made his senior Switzerland debut against Mexico in June 2025 "Mentally he was always a player who, when he came into the training session and games, always wanted to do something important. You can see that as a player who starts with Freiburg, he took his chance. "I can remember his second game with Switzerland, against the USA and he scored. It was always important for him to come into the game and to do something." Last season Manzambi was named the Europa League's Young Player of the Season, as Freiburg lost the final to Villa in May. He scored 12 goals in 61 appearances and Weis, now Freiburg II boss, has watched him develop, with Manzambi also learning German in three months. It helped him swiftly move from the academy to the first team, making his debut against Heidenheim a year after joining. Weis described him a "difference maker" and, among players in the Bundesliga in his position last season, Manzambi ranked first for 10-plus metre progressive carries (116), shot-ending carries (13) and fouls won (78). Villa knew he would move this summer so it was a case of now or never for Emery. Had he gone to Newcastle instead they believed his next move would put him out of their financial reach. The Magpies were always wary of being hijacked, having previously lost Victor Munoz to Liverpool and, while they agreed a deal with Freiburg, they never got a yes from Manzambi. Villa then turned the versatile forward into the most expensive Swiss player in history - surpassing Granit Xhaka's £38.25m move from Borussia Mönchengladbach to Arsenal 10 years ago. Yet, despite signing a five-year deal, Weis backed him to make the next step quickly. "I think Aston Villa is the right club for him. He will play every time when he is fit and that's the right way. Then I think he plays two seasons at Villa and then he goes to the next step," he added. "After the World Cup I said he must go to the Premier League. Bayern Munich were mentioned, he didn't go to [Borussia] Dortmund, [Bayer] Leverkusen. It's the right way." Freiburg have made light of Manzambi's absence and went into the international break unbeaten and sitting third, having topped the Bundesliga after three straight opening wins. Without him they have won six of their seven games in all competitions, scoring 24 goals, and boss Julian Schuster said earlier this month he had hoped to keep the player. It was the same for Lombardo at Servette, who fought to keep their young talent, but the former Switzerland international admitted Manzambi had made the right decisions. "We wanted him to stay with us, we gave him a contract but he wouldn't sign and history would say it's a good way, he came to Freiburg and played with the under-19s and was always improving," said the ex-Perugia midfielder. "Then Johan came into the first team and performed so well he started to play from the beginning and the coach couldn't move him from the starting XI. "With us he was incredible, he wanted to stay on the pitch to improve, to stay in the games and he had a lot of personality at 15. title: Drumcree stalemate continues as protesters remain overnight
description: Talks to resolve the issue took place on Monday as members of the Orange Order waited to begin their permitted parade.
body: Protesters remained on the Garvaghy Road overnight as the Drumcree parade dispute continues. The main parties involved in the dispute in Northern Ireland are still in a stalemate, following a day of political talks and heated exchanges at Stormont. Talks to resolve the issue took place on Monday as members of the Orange Order waited to begin their permitted parade, which was due to take place on Sunday morning, and walk down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown. Orangemen also maintained a presence at Drumcree church overnight, but were smaller in number than previous nights. Members of the Orange Order have tried a number of times to march from Drumcree church They spoke to officers at the police line near the church in an attempt to walk down the Garvaghy Road. However, there did not appear to be any serious expectation that would happen. Parading, policing and power sharing collide amid Drumcree dispute Christopher Nelson, who was 11 when his mother, the solicitor Rosemary Nelson, was murdered by loyalists in 1999, said the current situation had brought back memories of that time. Rosemary Nelson represented Garvaghy Road Residents Association. Nelson said he "dreaded the summer holidays approaching" because he knew his mother "would be spending a lot of time on the Garvaghy Road". "With that came the worry about what was going to happen her when she was out there. Is mum coming home tonight and if she is, is she going to be okay?" Chris Nelson urged politicians to "think about the children on both sides" He said his mother spoke to her children about her job a lot and told them she was "helping families like our own". "She tried her best to make you feel safe even though there was uncertainty in the back of your head," he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme. Nelson has never spoken publicly about his mother's death. He feels now is the time to do so because "if she were here she would want me to be here and she would be standing on that road". Lurgan solicitor Rosemary Nelson was murdered in 1999 Now a father-of-two himself, and married to Sinn Féin councillor Catherine Nelson, he said he did not want any child "worrying or concerned" and said it was like it was "happening all over again". He said his message to representatives was to "think about the children on both sides". "This comes from a child who went through it, who experienced it, whose life it impacted. Do whatever needs to be done to protect them," he said. He added that he was "very worried" about the current situation as "I know how badly it escalated and what the repercussions were in many cases". 'Is mum coming home tonight?' Christopher Nelson, whose mother was murdered by loyalists in 1999, says the current situation has brought back memories. The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in 30 years after a series of legal challenges. Since 1998, the Orange Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes. The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation, while the area where it wants to walk - specifically along the Garvaghy Road - is largely Catholic and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Protesters blocked the road over the weekend, and after a meeting with the Northern Ireland secretary, a representative of the road's residents said the Orange Order should focus on a different route. On Sunday, protesters on the Garvaghy Road were joined by members of Sinn Féin, including First Minister Michelle O'Neill, and the Social Democratic Labour Party. The Democratic Unionist Party subsequently accused O'Neill of acting unlawfully. Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant said "nobody should be attending an unlawful protest", but he added it was not his job "to decide whether somebody has or hasn't broken the law". Speaking in the Northern Ireland Assembly on Monday, O'Neill said she was proud to protest with the residents. Protesters, pictured on Monday afternoon, continued to maintain a presence on the Garvaghy Road People continued to gather at the Garvaghy Road, with a crowd of up to 400 people at one point on Monday night - and a group of Orangemen tried to begin their parade a number of times. Police scaled back their operation with only two police cars and one Land Rover in place. The road was not blocked. The two most senior members of Portadown Orange Order met Sir Chris at Hillsborough Castle. They described the hour-long talks as "constructive". Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, also met the secretary of state. He said the Orange Order should use their outward route to Drumcree Church as their return route, rather than the Garvaghy Road. The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident. However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas. The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. The row sparked some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history and was linked to several murders. The row reemerged after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission - the organisation formed during the Drumcree dispute to decide on contentious marches during Northern Ireland's parading season - was overturned. On Friday, following 28 years of unsuccessful applications, the commission decided the march could go ahead with restrictions in place

title: Lives 'will be lost' unless UK does more to combat wildfires, committee chairwoman says
description: Baroness Brown says there must be better training and planning, after a record year for wildfires in England and Wales.
body: The aftermath of a wildfire in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk, during the summer Lives "will be lost" unless more is done to combat the increasing risk of wildfires, the chairwoman of the UK's Climate Change Committee (CCC) has said after a record number of blazes this summer. Baroness Brown told BBC File on 4 Investigates "not enough action" had been taken in light of predictions the UK is facing longer, drier summers because of global warming. Earlier this year, one man died in a wildfire in Gloucestershire, while 19 homes were destroyed in Stourbridge, near Birmingham, and villagers were evacuated in the Cairngorms. The government said it was investing nearly £100m to improve national resilience capabilities, which includes piloting specially trained firefighting teams. As far back as 2012, the independent CCC warned of "more frequent wildfires due to warmer and drier conditions". File on 4 Investigates has seen figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council showing that 2026 set a new all-time high, with 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales, up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024. Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025. Baroness Brown said the CCC, formed in 2008, has been telling the government for years that the UK is "not prepared for the changing climate". She continued: "The warnings have been there and not enough action has been taken. "I fear that lives will be lost. We need to be doing much more education and preparation." She said that included investing in specialist teams and equipment, but also "planning our woodlands, thinking about fire breaks" and early warning systems. By 2050, she said the risk of wildfires could be doubled across much of the UK. Tinderbox Britain - Are we ready for more wildfires? File on 4 Investigates looks at whether the country is prepared for the growing threat, and if the emergency services have the resources to cope. Uttam and Sandy Shiralkar are still coming to terms with the loss of their family home in Stourbridge after it was engulfed by a wildfire in August. Sandy, a surgeon, said: "We saw the complete destruction of the house. There was no roof, no floorboards. Nothing. No-one should have this experience." Uttam and Sandy Shiralkar are now living in temporary accommodation after losing their family home in a wildfire... ... their home was one of 19 destroyed in Stourbridge The fires started accidentally in fields in Stourbridge, where farming machinery was in use on the hottest day of the year. The couple are now living in temporary accommodation. Uttam said: "Every loss is painful, but losing a house has got a different dimension. Coming back to normality is going to take a long time." While the risk of wildfires is on the rise, the number of firefighters has been in decline. Steve Wright, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union, which represents firefighters, said more than a fifth of firefighter and control room posts across the UK – some 12,000 jobs - had been cut since 2010, which left crews dangerously overstretched over the summer. "We had firefighters from London being mobilised to Yorkshire, firefighters from Merseyside being mobilised to Dorset," he said. "The effect, when you have wildfires happening at the same time across the UK, is there's just not enough firefighters on the ground to be able to deal with them." There are calls for more specialist training on how to tackle wildfires Phil Garrigan, chairman of the National Fire Chiefs Council, which represents senior managers of the UK's fire and rescue services, said he welcomed the £97m investment to provide six specialist firefighting teams to work across the UK. But he insisted more money was needed to boost aerial firefighting capability and improve specialist equipment for firefighters. He said: "The money has to be there, otherwise we'll be going into 2027 and 2028 with a likely occurrence that we'll see what we've seen in 2026, which is 50 plus homes lost and families devastated by the impacts of wildfire. We've got to get ahead of that." State-of-the-art equipment such as dedicated off-road vehicles will be bought as part of the £97m investment, which the government said was funding the biggest upgrade to national resilience for 20 years. What can be done to reduce risk of wildfires? description: As sellers waded through floodwaters to sell produce like fish and vegetables from floating platforms and foam boxes, buyers walked or paddled between the makeshift stalls to buy their groceries.
body: This video can not be played Locals in Bangkok have transformed a flooded street in front of a shopping mall into a temporary floating market during flooding in the city. Bangkok was declared a disaster-affected zone after continuous heavy rains caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital. As sellers waded through floodwaters to sell produce like fish and vegetables from floating platforms and foam boxes, buyers walked or paddled between the makeshift stalls to buy their groceries. title: Does Horner have a chance of Ferrari job? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
body: Christian Horner was Red Bull's team principal from 2005 to 2025 Mercedes' George Russell took his first victory since June by holding off Max Verstappen to win the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar completed the podium on his return after missing three races with a broken wrist. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished fifth in Baku, meaning his advantage over team-mate Russell has narrowed to 66 points. This weekend, Formula 1 heads to Malaysia, the host of the Bahrain Grand Prix - an event originally due to take place in April but which was postponed because of the war in the Middle East. Before the race in Sepang, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions. Does Christian Horner really want the team principal job at Ferrari, or even have a shot at it? - Ben This topic has become a subject for conversation in recent days following an interview Horner did with the Times, external as he promotes his new book. Horner said: "At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership." Asked whether he would take a job there, he replied: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1." Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur made his views about Horner's intervention pretty plain after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix when he said: "Mr Horner is looking for a job - that, everybody knows - everywhere." Vasseur said the speculation surrounding the team meant Ferrari were "not working in the perfect serenity". Horner's comments seem to make it clear that he would consider a job offer from Ferrari. But the key questions are under what conditions he might accept it, and whether he would be offered it in the first place. Horner has made it very clear over the years that he believes an F1 team needs one person in charge and in overall control. It's highly unlikely he would get that at Ferrari, where chairman John Elkann and chief executive officer Benedetto Vigna will always have more authority than any team principal. Even at Red Bull, where Horner had theoretical leadership at the F1 team, he was ultimately answerable to headquarters in Austria and that is what led to his removal in the end. It's hard to imagine how Elkann and Vigna could or would countenance any situation where they were removed from any input into the F1 team. And it's even harder to imagine a situation where that was not the de facto position even if a team boss had been given assurances they would be left alone. Then there is the question of whether Ferrari would want Horner. Horner comes with baggage. All of the above for a start, and on top of that there is the cloud under which he left Red Bull. There is no doubt that he was a remarkably successful team principal there, the team winning eight drivers' titles, six constructors' championships and 124 grands prix in his two-decade tenure. However, the team unravelled in his final 18 months in charge, in the wake of the accusations of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour that were made against him by a female employee. Red Bull dismissed those allegations after two internal investigations led by external lawyers. But they were a key factor in Adrian Newey leaving his position as chief technical officer - along with internal politics in which Newey felt his role had been diminished by Horner. Newey was followed out of the door by long-time sporting director Jonathan Wheatley and head of strategy Will Courtenay. Horner was finally dismissed following a slump in form which Red Bull bosses concluded the team did not appear to be capable of arresting under his leadership. In the Times interview, Horner says that the only justification he was given by Red Bull for his sacking was "it was more Christian Horner Racing than Red Bull Racing". He adds at other points in the interview: "I am a bit of a Marmite character. I know I'm not everybody's cup of tea. It's impossible to be." And: "I'm the cure and the problem." Clearly, any decision as to whether Horner is the person you want to lead your F1 team would need careful consideration. It's also worth mentioning that Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton has made it pretty clear over the past few years that he has little time for Horner. Why hasn't the FIA made a decision on the final two races of the season? They've cancelled the final rounds of the World Rally Championship and World Endurance Championship because of the Middle East conflict. Surely they should be confirming the changes in the calendar now? - Nigel To start with a point of order, it is Formula 1 that decides the calendar - as in, the commercial rights holder - not the FIA, the governing body. The FIA's role is effectively only to rubber-stamp F1's decision. As things stand, F1 is planning to end the season as the calendar was originally scheduled - with Las Vegas followed by Qatar and then Abu Dhabi, external over the last two weekends in November and the first in December. Although the war continues between the US/Israel and Iran, the advice F1 has been getting is that the situation in those two countries is stable, and there is not a high risk of attacks on civilian infrastructure. The UK Foreign Office, for example, does not advise against travel to Qatar and Abu Dhabi., external It simply says the situation there "remains unpredictable" and that "there is a risk of more attacks and unforeseen escalation in the region". And the two countries consider themselves open for business. However, F1 has a contingency plan. Imola in Italy is preparing to host a race on the weekend of Abu Dhabi. If the two Middle Eastern races cannot happen as a result of an escalation of the situation in the Gulf, Imola would step in and hold the season finale on 4-6 December. But u

title: Malaysia begins controversial repatriation of asylum seekers to Myanmar
description: Human rights groups say some 5,000 returnees could face violence, persecution and forced conscription.
body: The repatriation represents a striking shift in Malaysia's attitude towards the refugees The Malaysian government has started repatriating around 5,000 asylum seekers from Myanmar, under a controversial deal agreed with Myanmar's military ruler Min Aung Hlaing. Three ships from the Myanmar navy are scheduled to leave Malaysia later today carrying the first 1,476 returnees. Human rights groups have condemned the repatriation, saying the returnees face violence, persecution and forced conscription into the Myanmar army. Malaysia has described the repatriation as voluntary, but has barred the UN refugee agency from seeing or screening the returnees, who have been kept in detention centres. According to Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, these returnees will include Rohingyas: a persecuted Muslim minority who have sought sanctuary in Malaysia in large numbers after being driven out of Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens. Anwar, whose popularity has fallen sharply this year, says he is responding to growing public hostility towards the large Rohingya population in Malaysia and has no choice but to negotiate with the Myanmar government over their return. But the move signals a striking shift in attitude. Anwar, a former political prisoner, has previously presented himself as a defender of human rights and freedom, and called for more to be done to help the Rohingyas. Under him, Malaysia has refused to recognise Min Aung Hlaing's regime, and has been one of the strongest voices in South East Asia pushing for a negotiated end to Myanmar's civil war. Two things. First, increased economic strain on lower-income Malaysians since the Covid pandemic, which has stirred resentment of the Rohingyas. Second, the febrile state of Malaysian politics since 2018, when a historic election unseated the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the ethnic Malay party which had monopolised power for more than 60 years, leading to a revolving door of unstable coalition governments. For many years there was strong public sympathy among Malaysians for their fellow Muslims in Myanmar. In August 2017, a brutal campaign by the Myanmar military drove three quarters of a million Rohingyas out of their homes in Rakhine State and into neighbouring Bangladesh. In the years since, dire conditions in Bangladeshi refugee camps have driven those with enough money to make the perilous sea journey to Malaysia in search of sanctuary and work. While the Malaysian navy and coastguard have long tried to block Rohingya boats from landing in Malaysia, many gotten in via other routes, and for a long time were tolerated. More than 200,000 are now believed to live there, most eking out basic livings from manual labour. Sentiment among Malaysians started to shift during the pandemic, which hit the country's economy hard. At a time of heightened public fear over the new coronavirus, accusations against Rohingya migrants spread on social media, with demands for their deportation. In response, the then-government hardened its attitude, saying Malaysia could accept no more refugees and ordering raids on communities believed to be harbouring illegal immigrants. Much the same has happened in 2026. In May, an online complaint claimed that Rohingyas had failed to dispose of animal waste properly after the Muslim Eid al Adha festival, igniting a viral social media campaign falsely accusing Rohingya leaders of demanding land and citizenship in Malaysia. Shortly thereafter, an online petition on Change.org calling for Rohingyas to be kicked out of Malaysia received more than 400,000 signatures, before being taken down. Given Anwar's one-time reputation as a champion of liberal values, he might have been expected to push back against this wave of hate and disinformation. He has said the Rohingyas should be treated humanely. "We can arrest them, but do not beat, intimidate or humiliate them," he said in a recent podcast interview - although this is exactly what human rights groups have accused Malaysian officials of doing in immigration detention centres. Nonetheless, Anwar insists that the Rohingya must be expelled. "They have clearly become a burden," he said in the same interview. "A security burden, an economic burden and a source of hostility among the people." Some of his former supporters have accused him of betraying his principles. The former head of the Malaysian Anti Corruption Commission, Latheefa Koya, says his decision is "disgraceful, amoral, and shames the nation in the eyes of the international community". Anwar says Rohingya refugees have become a burden for Malaysia Anwar, though, is under great political pressure. Once described as a perpetual prime minister-in-waiting, he finally got the top job in 2022, but only by forming an uneasy coalition with his one-time adversaries UMNO. Since then he has seen his own popularity plunge and his party lose seats in recent local elections. He must call a general election by early 2028. "He is in a corner, at his weakest point", says Tricia Yeoh, Director of the Asian Institute for Policy and Engagement at the University of Nottingham Malaysia. "He has been forced to make concessions to his UMNO partners... There have been several corruption scandals, and his own party is divided. And after four years of telling voters this is what is required to maintain his fragile coalition, they are no longer willing to go along with that narrative." Instead, Yeoh says, ethnic Malays, who make up more than half of the electorate, are responding to the well-trodden UMNO narrative that they need special support and protection from the state - the kind of racial politics which she says feeds fear and resentment of outsiders. "It's the same narrative you hear in the rest of the world, about immigrants taking jobs, that we should not be spending our public funds on facilities for them." However, it is not clear how any Rohingyas can be repatriated to Myan

title: Rights group accuses Vietnam of abducting Australian and Norwegian activists
description: Vietnam says the men entered the country illegally and accused them of planning terrorist activities.
body: Nguyen Duc Thuan (left) and Tran Hiep have been detained in Vietnam in what a pro-democracy group has called an act of "transnational repression" A pro-democracy group has accused the Vietnamese government of abducting two of its members, an Australian and a Norwegian citizen, in Cambodia and taking them back across the border. Vietnamese authorities confirmed that they had arrested Tran Hiep and Nguyen Duc Thuan, but say they had entered the country using forged documents and planned to carry out terrorist activities. It said the men had admitted to being members of Viet Tan, which Vietnam sees as a terrorist organisation. Viet Tan called their arrest a "blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam". The group, which has members in Vietnam and abroad, said the two men had been travelling in the southern border district of Kaoh Andaet in Cambodia when they went missing and had not been heard from since 18 September. Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, told Australian media he had been meeting pro-democracy activists in Cambodia and had no intention of travelling to Vietnam. He was meant to meet her in Bangkok to board a return flight to Australia but never turned up, she said. "He always knew there was a risk doing human rights work, but we never thought that this would happen," she told the ABC. According to a Vietnamese state media report published on Monday, Tran and Nguyen were detained with a third man at the border in Tay Ninh province on 18 September. The trio "confessed to being members of the terrorist organisation 'Viet Tan,' [and] carrying forged documents to illegally enter Vietnam in order to carry out terrorist and sabotage activities," the report said. They were charged on Monday with membership of a terrorist organisation while an investigation continued "to clarify the criminal acts of the suspects in order to handle them according to the law", it said. "A state orchestrating the abduction of individuals abroad and forcibly taking them to its territory is a serious act of transnational repression," said Viet Tan. "It violates Cambodia's sovereignty and the fundamental principles of international law." The Viet Tan statement did not mention the third man, who was named by authorities as Thai Cong Truong Son. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consular support was being provided to Tran's family. "That's what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we'll continue to engage directly with the family." "Vietnam authorities' confirmation that they detained [these] activists... demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia," Phil Robertson, Director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates said in a statement. "This latest act is an unacceptable outrage." The Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities have been contacted for comment. title: Food waste charity gets grant for rising costs
description: The charity received a £60,000 grant, over three years, from Shrewsbury Town Council.
body: Volunteers at the charity never know how much will come to a foodshare beforehand A charity that is helping tackle the issue of food waste has received a funding grant from the council. Shrewsbury Food Hub collects surplus food from supermarkets, manufacturers and farms, and shares it with 90 community groups and 13 weekly food shares. Earlier this month, it was announced the charity received a £60,000 grant, over three years, from Shrewsbury Town Council. The charity's fundraiser, Cherry Teearu, said: "It is a lot of money. It sounds fantastic and we are so so grateful." She added: "It will go a long way to helping us to continue [to cover our extra] costs that we have got. With the cost of living crisis all of our costs are going up." Teearu said the organisation is having to spend thousands to fuel its vans and depot and covering covering staff costs, with spending reaching nearly £500,000 every year. Shrewsbury Food Hub started in 2016, after a local homeless charity contacted it's co-founders because it had been offered surplus food by a supermarket, but they didn't have volunteers to collect it. The group says that over the last year alone they have rescued 272 tonnes of food from the bin – enough for over 649,000 meals. John Hughes is in charge of the logistics at the charity Community engagement officer and head of logistics, John Hughes, is often in charge of the deliveries. "It operates seven days a week, all year round, bar Christmas Day, and so its a seven day a week operation," he said. "We start early doors and then work right the way through. Then at the end of the day we are preparing for the next day ahead. He added: "We have a lot of overheads, all of that costs money just to keep the wheels turning before we do anything, so this grant is hugely important to us and just gives us sort of hope and sustainability [to keep] going forward." Self-described conservationist, Peter Hampton, said he attends the Food Hub to help the environment and help his budget. "I brought my grandchildren along and they were gobsmacked that food was going to waste," he said. "They ended up going back to their junior school and told the teacher, and the teacher did a lesson on it. "When you realise how much is being saved and how much it helps the community in different parts of the community, be it mothers and toddlers groups, schools, people on lower incomes, its great." title: Brothers who both had meningitis within a year lucky to be alive
description: Saul and Drew Darlington learnt they had a rare condition which meant they were susceptible to meningitis.
body: Saul and Drew had meningitis as teenagers Two brothers who contracted meningitis within a year of each other say they are lucky to be alive. Saul and Drew Darlington from Wrexham, now 29 and 26, initially thought it was a "weird" coincidence they both caught the illness as teenagers but later learnt they had a rare condition which meant they were susceptible to it. "The day I had it, if I had gone to sleep that night, I'd have probably died," said Saul who, along with his brother, now wants to raise awareness of the symptoms of meningitis, particularly among young people. Nearly 20,000 young people have been vaccinated in Wales through catch-up clinics, following a deadly outbreak of meningitis B in Kent earlier this year. Drew spent two weeks in hospital with regular visits from family members including his other brother Joel, pictured beside him Saul was 17 and on a school trip when he first started feeling cold and experiencing sensitivity to light, but when a purple rash developed, the family went to A&E. "It all happened very fast," said Saul. "When my mum used the word meningitis, I could see how worried she was. It was really concerning - it was all so alien to us." Saul spent a week in hospital and said the experience was "really scary", especially as he was so young. Almost exactly a year later, his then 16-year-old brother Drew began to feel unwell as he was studying for his GCSEs with a high temperature but no other obvious symptoms. Things escalated quickly following a trip to the GP. "When I left the house I had no rashes on me at all. When the doctor lifted up my top, I had a big rash all over my chest and belly," he said, adding that purple dots on the roof of his mouth had also developed. Drew spent two weeks on the children's ward at Wrexham Maelor hospital. "I did think it's a bit weird isn't it really that we've both caught it, what are the odds of that?" said Saul. It was touch and go for the first 48 hours before Drew slowly began to recover, but he lost a lot of weight and it would be months before he felt completely well. "I'm really thankful the doctor called the ambulance straight away when he noticed the rash - those quick decisions potentially saved our lives," said Drew. Drew and Saul are planning to take on an Ironman challenge next year to support meningitis charities Saul and Drew have both since recovered but take daily antibiotics after tests revealed they both had properdin deficiency - a rare immunodeficiency which means they are more susceptible to infections such as meningitis. They enjoy hiking and running, with Saul taking on the London Marathon in 2025 to support the charity Meningitis Research Foundation and to raise awareness of the illness. "A lot of the symptoms just display themselves as being a bit tired or hungover, and it's so much more than that," said Saul. "You've just got to be vigilant," added Drew. "You don't have much time when dealing with meningitis and every hour counts in potentially saving your life." Symptoms, external can develop suddenly and can include: a rash that doesn't fade when pressed with a glass sudden onset of high fever very cold hands and feet Meningitis is an infection of the protective membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord. It can affect anyone but is most common in babies, young children, teenagers and young adults. It can be very serious if not treated quickly. The cause of the infection - either certain bacteria or viruses - can be determined by tests. Bacterial meningitis is rarer but more serious than viral meningitis. It can lead to blood poisoning or sepsis, and can affect the brain. "We know that young people can be at increased risk of meningitis for a number of reasons," said Caroline Hughes from the Meningitis Research Foundation. "The bacteria spreads more easily in that group, it's lots of people mixing together, and more independence as people move away from parents." She said it was important to be aware of the signs and symptoms, and to have all the vaccines available to you. The deadly outbreak of meningitis B in Kent earlier this year sparked a vaccination catch-up campaign across Wales and England aimed at young people starting further or higher education in September 2026, and who hadn't had protection against the most prevalent strain. Public Health Wales said 19,700 young people have had their first dose through the programme, with 14,459 also having a second dose, which needs to be given four weeks apart. Clinics are being put on at universities across the country during the first few weeks of term. Vaccination nurse Dalia Nassr says students needed to remember to get two doses of the vaccine for full protection "We had one student come in who had a friend who died of meningitis just last year, so she was really appreciative that we were here," said Dalia Nassr, one of the vaccination nurses for the Cardiff and Vale University Health Board visiting universities in the area. "We know students are very busy, they are trying to find their way around campus, and most haven't registered with a GP yet - so by coming here we just give them the opportunity to just walk in at any time," she said. title: Apprentice star tells PM why pie shop is closing
description: Paul Bowen says a rise in employer's National Insurance was "the tipping edge" to him closing a pie shop.
body: Paul Bowen took part in The Apprentice in 2024 A pie shop owner who starred in The Apprentice has told Prime Minister Andy Burnham he is closing one of his three shops because of rising business costs. In a social media post directed at the prime minister, Paul Bowen, who owns Bowen Pies in Chorley, Lancashire, said the increase in employers' National Insurance was "the tipping edge" to him shutting the shop on Market Street, despite it taking £100,000 a year. "We were already trying to cover everything else going up. Then the government made it more expensive to employ people," he wrote. In response, Burnham said: "I am listening and I'm sorry it has got to the point that you need to close your doors." Bowen, who took part in The Apprentice in 2024, said: "Look around Chorley or your home town. How many shops have "To Let" signs in the windows?" "Years ago, this shop would tick over and pay its way. Now, with employer's National Insurance, energy bills, business rates, wages and everything else, there just isn't enough left." On energy prices, he asked Burnham: "What are you actually doing to bring those down?". He also asked the government to "scrap or significantly reduce employer's National Insurance for small businesses, reduce business rates, ease the VAT burden and get business energy costs down". "Let us grow. Let us take people on. Let us have something left to put back into the business," he said. Paul Bowen is closing one of his three pie shops Burnham replied: "You're right that what you are seeing in Chorley is happening across the country." He added: "Empty shops, family businesses closing, and buildings that have been left neglected for too long. "We've all walked past them and thought: 'Someone should do something about that.' "That's why, yesterday, I announced that we're investing £210 million to help bring neglected high street buildings back into use - turning empty spaces into community hubs, health centres, shared workspaces, cafés and the local services people actually want to see." He added: "I know people don't measure growth on a spreadsheet, they measure it on their high street. "I'm determined to restore that pride." title: Czech Republic ready for Wembley 30 years after Euro '96
description: The Czech Republic are returning to Wembley for a Nations League game with England, just over 30 years after their Euro '96 heartbreak there.
body: Patrik Berger's penalty had the Czech Republic just over 30 minutes away from winning Euro '96 The Czech Republic will return to the north London site that staged one of the biggest days in their history during this international break - as they head back to Wembley. They face England twice in Nations League Group A3 - in Prague on Tuesday (19:45 BST) and London on 6 October. The Czechs have been to Wembley since losing the Euro '96 final to Germany under the old stadium's twin towers, but this visit marks the 30-year anniversary of that remarkable summer in England. Germany's golden goal ended the Czech dreams in the Euro '96 final Euro '96 was the first European Championship staged after Czechoslovakia separated - forming the Czech Republic and Slovakia. But nobody expected the Czech team to have much impact at the tournament, including the country's own players. They were outsiders, and most of the squad were still based in their domestic league. Several had booked their holidays for straight after the group stage - which involved Germany, Italy and Russia - and Vladimir Smicer was even due to get married. Midfielder Patrik Berger says his then Borussia Dortmund team-mate Jurgen Kohler did not even know the Czechs were at the Euros... and the defender was in the Germany squad. Berger, speaking to the BBC Sporting Witness podcast earlier this year, said of Kohler: "He was asking me what my plans were for the summer. I said 'I'm going to the Euros' and he said 'to watch games?' "I said 'no, we're playing you guys the first game of the group stages and then we will play in the final' - and he was laughing." The Czechs lost their opening game 2-0 to Germany at Old Trafford before beating Italy 2-1 at Anfield. Smicer's late equaliser in a 3-3 draw against Russia - at his future home of Anfield - was enough to see them through because Italy failed to beat Germany in the other game, finishing 0-0. "We knew we were still in it, but we didn't know what the other result is," said Berger, who would go on to play for Liverpool with Smicer. "One minute we're not qualifying, the next it was we qualified, so we didn't really know. "After the final whistle it took a few minutes before we realised we qualified for the quarter-finals." In the quarters came one of the most memorable European Championship goals ever, with Karel Poborsky scooping the ball over Vitor Baia from the edge of the box to give the Czech Republic a 1-0 win over Portugal at Villa Park. And, after a goalless draw against France in the semis at Old Trafford, the Czechs would win 6-5 on penalties. Their spot-kicks were netted by players including future Ballon d'Or winner Pavel Nedved, Berger and Poborsky, who was back at the ground weeks later as a newly signed Manchester United player. "You don't want to go there," said Berger of taking a penalty in a shootout. "If someone says something different they're lying. Nobody wants to take that penalty." He said the team "couldn't believe" they had beaten France. "We were living the dream," Berger said. "It was an amazing feeling. An amazing moment for the country. "To get to the final was kind of like a miracle for everyone." Two days before the final, Smicer returned to Prague to get married. Thousands of Czech fans turned out in the city centre for the occasion, but Smicer had to return to England the same day. The Czech Republic faced Germany in the final at Wembley - and led after 59 minutes through Berger's drilled penalty. He revealed he was not even meant to be the penalty taker but "could see nobody really wanted to take the ball". "The only thing in my mind was hit it as hard as possible on target," he said. Sadly for the Czechs, Oliver Bierhoff equalised 14 minutes later - and then scored the first ever golden goal in a major tournament final to give Germany the win. "It wasn't meant to be," said Berger. "I'd love to be European champion, but silver for us was like a gold because it opened doors to so many of us. And it opened doors to the generation after us. I have no regrets. "Thanks to Euro 96, because it was played in England, I caught the eye of Liverpool. "There were 100,000 waiting for us in Prague celebrating. Even silver felt like winning the tournament for us." This video can not be played Mokoena's late penalty earns South Africa draw against Czech Republic As Czechoslovakia, the country won the European Championship in 1976 - and lost two World Cup finals (1934 and 1962). But the Czech Republic's first tournament as a separate nation remains the last time they reached a final. They have, however, enjoyed other memorable European Championships - having reached the 2004 semi-finals and the quarters in 2012 and 2021. The 2004 squad had a mix of youth - such as Petr Cech, Milan Baros and Tomas Rosicky - and experience with Smicer, Berger and Poborsky. They lost to eventual winners Greece in the last four. Ondrej Zlamal, a Prague-based football journalist, says that team and their performances "were even better" than in 1996. "This generation with Nedved and others culminated in 2004 and we had a feeling we should have won the Euros. We played better football than in 1996," Zlamal said. "It was the second highlight of the golden generation." Their only two World Cups since then - 2006 and 2026 - have ended in group stage exits. Zlamal said: "The performance this summer was really disappointing. "There is a simple answer to why [the team have not lived up to the heights of the past] – we don't have such talented footballers as we had. "We don't have enough players in the top teams like we used to. "When I was six I watched the 1976 final which Czechoslovakia won, and my father told me 'remember this because you won't see it any more'. title: Old US warship deliberately sunk during training off Scotland
description: The 43-year-old decommissioned frigate was used for target practice off the Outer Hebrides.
body: This video can not be played The decommissioned USS Klakring was sunk at the Ministry of Defence's Hebrides range A decommissioned US warship has been sunk off Scotland's west coast during a training exercise. USS Klakring was hit by a missile and a torpedo before sinking in the North Atlantic about 170 miles (274km) off the Outer Hebrides last Monday. The US Navy said the ship went a through "rigorous" cleaning process first, and personnel checked for the presence of whales and dolphins before the live-firing exercise started. Other warships, including an aircraft carrier in 2006, have been deliberately sunk at sea by the US as part of training and to create artificial reefs for marine life. A 43-year-old frigate was used for target practice USS Klakring was sunk during Exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026, which involved US and UK armed forces. The former guided missile frigate was fired on by a missile from USS Paul Ignatius and a torpedo from USS Massachusetts. The UK's Royal Navy also tested "ship-busting" weapons during the exercise. USS Klakring entered service in 1983 and was decommissioned in 2013. It was named for Rear Adm Thomas B Klakring, who was awarded three US Navy Crosses as the commander of a submarine during World War Two. USS Klakring was hit by a missile and torpedo during Exercise Atlantic Thunder The US Navy said sinking exercises were prepared in strict compliance with environmental regulations. A spokesperson said: "The extensive preparations for the exercise include putting the hulk through a rigorous cleaning process to remove contaminants and old equipment, thereby assuring that the environmental impact of the exercise is minimal. "Sinking ex-navy vessels, which are specially prepared as targets, provides a practicable method for conducting large scale exercises of this type, to train at the high level required by the armed forces." title: Proposed budget 'a step in the right direction'
description: The government releases its proposed budget with "targeted measures" to help families.
body: Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said the proposed budget sought to "target the resources we had available to those most in need" Jersey's government has released its budget for 2027 to 2030, with a number of targeted measures designed to help families with the cost of living. These include increasing the number of free hours of nursery care for two to three-year-olds from 15 hours to 20 hours, and doubling the parental grant, external to £1,800 for families with newborns or those adopting a child. The funding for the Health Department has increased again, from £381m in 2026 to £406m. Last year, the Fiscal Policy Panel , externalsaid Jersey was spending more than it was earning, but Treasury Minister Alan Maclean told the BBC the planned new budget was "a step in the right direction" towards correcting that. In his foreword to the budget, Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham wrote: "For many households, the cost of living remains the most immediate concern. "Housing, childcare and everyday living costs continue to put pressure on family budgets. Businesses are also dealing with higher costs and an increasingly competitive environment. "We are providing practical support to help put more money back into islanders' pockets, particularly for families facing the greatest pressures." The measures targeted to help families with the cost of living include: Free nursery care for two to three-year-olds increasing from 15 hours a week to 20 hours The parental grant, external rising from £887.25 to £1,800 for families with newborns or adopting a child A £250 family support payment for each school-aged child in low to middle-income households in 2027 Free school meals extended to secondary school pupils on the Jersey Premium funding scheme, external When asked if he thought these measures helped islanders in a meaningful way, Maclean said: "I hope so. It's a step in the right direction. "Obviously a lot more needs to be done, but what we've sought to do is target the resources we had available to those most in need." He also explained it was not just families measures were targeted at. He said: "You will have the seen that the pension has been uprated by 4.7%, and we've also got the community cost bonus which helps people not in families who are typically just above the income threshold levels." Health's spending is due to increase by £25m. In the previous budget, the Health Department's funding was increased by £60m, something former Treasury Minister Elaine Millar said was "concerning". While the planned increase in health funding was less, Maclean said it was the "largest spending department by a significant way". "We need to do some proper forensic analysis and make certain that the right money is invested to deliver the correct result for islanders," he said. The minister also said revenues from Pillar Two, a global rate of corporation tax for multinational companies with revenues of €750m (£631m) or more, would pay towards the building of the new acute hospital. Maclean said: "We're very fortunate to have that and we will be targeting that money at the cost of building the hospital at Overdale. "That will reduce our need to borrow more money and it will reduce our need to use reserves." Maclean said the budget was a "small step in the right direction" to addressing concerns by the Fiscal Policy Panel that Jersey had been spending more than it was earning. He said: "In recent years, the government has been at an operating level of spending more than it's been receiving in income in terms of taxes and charges. "That's not sustainable and we do need to address that. "So we've started with this budget, but the key is I describe this as a transitional budget. "The 2028-2030 budgetary period is where we're going to need to make structural changes to make certain that as we move forward public finances are sustainable for the long term." States members are due to debate and vote on the budget in December. Follow BBC Jersey on X, external and Facebook, external. Send your story ideas to channel.islands@bbc.co.uk, external. title: Channel Islands fuel prices set to rise again
description: The increases could mean mean diesel costing more than £2 per litre.
body: Rubis says global fuel market prices increases are beginning to filter through to the local market Fuel prices are set to rise in a move which will likely see diesel cost more than £2 per litre. Nick Crolla, head of marketing for Channel Islands supplier Rubis, said: "We have seen global fuel market prices increase by nearly 30% since the end of August. These increases are now beginning to filter through to the local market and will be reflected at forecourts over coming weeks." He added: "While these factors are outside our control, we are doing everything possible to keep prices as low as possible." With the war still ongoing in the Middle East, fuel prices have increased across the UK, with diesel prices hitting an all-time high, according to the RAC motoring organisation. Rubis said its focus still remains ensuring that the Channel Islands continue to benefit from secure fuel supplies when global fuel supply chains remain under significant pressure. In Guernsey, Dave Beausire, chairman of Le Mont Saint Garage highlighted that, in the last 12-month period, wholesale fuel prices had gone up 30p a litre on unleaded petrol and 42p a litre on diesel. Also in Guernsey, Mike Lucas, manager of Vale Garage, said: "We have recently seen more price increases, so I was expecting it. "I think the States need to look at fuel duty, otherwise it's going to have a knock-on effect for everyone." There are more electric vehicles operating on Guernsey, but many companies and people still operate petrol and diesel vehicles, including staff and volunteers for the Guernsey Voluntary Service (GVS). Its meals on wheels and social clubs rely on volunteers and their vehicles. GVS service manager Mandy Le Bachelet said: "It's not ideal, but it's important that our priority is our clients and nothing is going to stop us delivering those services. "We'll absorb the cost and continue how we operate. We have had to do this when prices have risen previously." Follow BBC Guernsey on X, external and Facebook, external. title: Former farmland to be restored to boost wildlife
description: The 30-year project aims to enhance existing grassland with specialist wildflower and herb mixes.
body: The project will restore woodland and scrub in the area to enhance existing grassland with specialist wildflower and herb seed mixes Arable land farmed by a family for about 80 years is to be restored to an orchard and wildlife area. A 30-year project will be undertaken on a 70-acre (28 hectareS) site at Pipers Hill, Great Gaddesden, close to Hemel Hempstead in Hertfordshire and aims to enhance existing grassland with specialist wildflower and herb seed mixes. Work is due to start later this year and will be undertaken by landowners Naturum. Animals expected to benefit include native British species such as brown hares, hedgehogs, great crested newts, common toads and the Small Heath butterfly, a spokesperson for the company said. Pipers Hill sits within the Chilterns National Character Area, and is about three miles (5km) from Hemel Hempstead The company, which buys land to restore it to nature, said a traditional orchard "that once stood on the land but was lost over a century ago" would be reinstated. It sits within a "wildlife corridor" adjoining Highpark Wood, an ancient woodland, and the Great Gaddesden Water Meadows, home to the River Gade, a rare chalk stream, otters and water voles, it added. The farming family will remain as long-term land managers and local children will be able to visit. Giles Perry, co-founder of the company, said: "This land has been farmed by the same family for the best part of 80 years, and it means a great deal to us to be working alongside them as we start to bring nature back to it. "Species like brown hares, hedgehogs and great crested newts are all found nearby, but decades of arable farming have made it harder for them to continue making their habitats here. "Giving them the space to come back is really what this project is about." River Gade runs through the site The work is part of the Hertfordshire Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS), which identified the area as a priority location for woodland, scrub and grassland recovery. It is hoped it will "ease pressure on the River Gade which, like chalk streams nationally, has been put under stress by modern farming practices," the spokesperson added. title: Family of British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes say they don't know where he is
description: It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names.
body: Sir Ranulph is seen here in 2022 Family and friends of renowned British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said they have not been able to visit or contact him for months. His former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him. It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes. Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment. Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care. They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns". Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease. He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by The Guinness Book of Records as "the world's greatest living explorer". Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who have "have fully his best interests in mind". "He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said. Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer. He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather. Arabella Pepper, the younger sister of Sir Ranulph's late first wife Ginny, told BBC Newsnight that she had not been able to see her former brother-in-law for over a year. "All his friends and family want to see him and take him Toblerones and cheer him up, but we don't know where is, and he's not available, he's not accessible - that's what worries us," she said. She alleges that she was only able to see him in July 2025 after she admitted herself to a care home where she had been told he was staying. "The first thing I said to him, apart from the usual greetings, was that everybody was worried about him, was looking for him, was longing to see him," Pepper told the BBC. "The relief on his face was very obvious, and he said, send a message to everybody, send them my love, tell them I love them and tell them I'm longing to see them." title: US ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy comes into effect as trade war drags on
description: It is the latest escalation in the Canada-US trade war after negotiations collapsed in late August, with no word on when talks may resume.
body: About 90% of all Canadian alcohol exports were bound for the US in 2025, with most coming from Ontario A US ban on several Canadian imports, including alcohol, dairy and motorcycles, has come into effect as a trade war between the two neighbours drags on. The latest measure by the Trump administration is in response to Canada's implementation of tariffs on a range of US goods earlier this month following a breakdown in trade talks. Canada is not expected to retaliate further, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying earlier this month that the impact the import bans will have on Canada's economy is "modest". Trade talks remain on ice, with US trade representative Jamieson Greer telling CNBC recently that President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with his current relationship with Canada. "They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side," Greer said of relations with Canada in an interview with the US network last week. Tuesday's trade ban applies to nearly C$1bn ($710m; £530m) worth of Canadian liquor exported to the US, as well as whey products used in protein powder. Motorcycle exports to the US will also be impacted, though Canada only sent about 5,000 motorcycles south of the border in 2025 that were worth about C$120m, according to national data by Statistics Canada, meaning the impact would be limited. The import bans were first announced by Trump in a series of executive orders signed on 8 September. In them, Trump said the measures are in response to "continued discrimination" by Canada on US dairy, automotives and alcohol. Speaking to reports on Monday, he accused Canada of "treating the United States very unfairly". "They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world," Trump said. The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? Carney said earlier this month that the bans "are relatively modest measures" when compared to other trade actions the US has imposed on Canada. He acknowledged, however, that the bans will hurt certain businesses and sectors that are directly targeted. Derek Holt, an economist with Canadian bank Scotiabank, wrote in an analysis that "these actions are face-saving by the US administration, not substantive in nature and that's a positive". About 93% of all Canadian liquor exports in 2025 were sold to the US. Spirits Canada, a group representing Canadian liquor producers, has said the consequences to the industry "could be significant"., external Economists and businesses have also warned that the bans will add uncertainty to the future of Canada's trade relationship with the US, its largest trade partner. In addition to these latest import bans, the US has imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, including dairy, alcohol, steel and aluminium products, as well as 25% tariffs on Canadian-built cars. Canada in return has placed retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on more than 700 US products, as well as a 25% levy on certain steel and aluminium products. Most Canadian provinces have also stopped selling US liquor. Tariffs - taxes paid on imported goods - are central to Trump's economic agenda, who argues that they raise government revenue and encourage consumers to buy American-made goods. Economists, however, argue that they have raised prices of everyday goods for consumers and have disrupted the global economy.
