title: Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration
description: President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project to be scrapped.
body: Argentina's president has threatened to launch a legal challenge against the British government unless it halts oil exploration work off the coast of the Falkland Islands. In a social media post, President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies, to be scrapped. The companies insist they have valid licences issued by Britain. The comments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the archipelago, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982. Milei said that if the two-week deadline was not met, he had "instructed the Foreign Ministry and legal teams to initiate international arbitration" against the UK over what he called "the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project". He continued to warn the UK that if the "illegitimate exploitation" of the region didn't end within two weeks, Argentina would take the matter before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The International Tribunal is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea. The move comes soon after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats". Since then, the UK Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said that Argentina "lacks the ability" to take back the Falklands by force. Milei had previously said the Sea Lion oilfield was a "clear and present danger". The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil. Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years. Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands. In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against. Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them. The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel. title: Blue Lights: The police drama hitting home in Northern Ireland
description: As the award winning series returns, it highlights tensions between police and communities in Northern Ireland.
body: Katherine Devlin's first major role was in Blue Lights as Constable Annie Conlon "Whether it's your friends or your family, everybody has their own relationships with, and viewpoints on, the police," says Dearbháile McKinney, star of BBC drama Blue Lights. The Londonderry actress and her co-star Katherine Devlin, who also grew up in Northern Ireland, say relationships between police and communities there were at the forefront of their minds as they prepared for filming. The Bafta-winning series follows police officers working at the fictional Blackthorn Station in Belfast. But, for many watching, the drama feels all too real. The difficulty police in Northern Ireland still face was thrown into focus this weekend by the long-running dispute over the controversial Garvaghy Road parade route when officers had to prevent a march by Protestant Orangemen through a largely Catholic area. Many scenes in Blue Lights highlight the distrust of, and hostility towards, the police in some communities. Warning: This article includes spoilers for the first three seasons of Blue Lights. Annie Conlon (Katherine Devlin), Grace Ellis (Siân Brooke) and Tommy Foster (Nathan Braniff) join as new recruits in the first series Devlin plays Annie Conlon, whose storyline deals with her having to move away from home as a result of death threats because she's from a Catholic family. "We do have similarities - she comes from a Catholic background and so do I," Devlin tells BBC Newsbeat. "I know girls like Annie. "But I've realised we're different in a lot of ways. Mainly, to be honest with you, I wouldn't go into the police." Devlin says that forming Annie's character was about trying to understand why she decided to become an officer and "for that to be the crux of her story". "I think a huge thing with this season is the idea of home and what home means to her," she says. "Just battling that inner dialogue that she has with 'is it all worth it?' "Especially her being a Catholic and the intricacies of that and the politics of that. "It's heavy stuff and she has to really think about it." Blue Lights won Best Drama Series at the BAFTAs in 2025 The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) had its lowest number of Catholic applicants in more than a decade earlier this year, with some pointing to "fear and apprehension" in those communities putting them off joining the police. One of the force's aims when it was founded in 2001 was to build broader community support and increase Catholic officers. At the time, only 8% of the force was from that background. It's now at 32%. In a statement sent to Newsbeat, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said the PSNI was "totally committed to being more representative of the communities we serve". "I am deeply concerned at persistent and often unjustified criticism and the outdated and unsupported views of dissident paramilitaries remaining as barriers to people seeing themselves having a career in the police," he said. Boutcher said he "absolutely" accepted the PSNI needed to do more to diversify its recruitment but could only do so if "people in all communities in Northern Ireland see policing as a career for them." He said the force planned to launch a new student officer recruitment campaign "in the coming weeks". The storyline following the strain on Aisling's relationship with fellow officer Tommy continues in the new series Blue Lights is filmed locally and on set in east Belfast you can spot the attention to detail, right down to the information leaflets at a police station reception area and case folders on officers' desks. "It's really lovely just to see the amount of people who see themselves in the characters," Devlin says. "And [mention] how complex the characters are. How real and human they are". It's something McKinney considered in how she plays Aisling Byrne. Aisling struggled with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in the last series, something Dearbháile says she spoke to real-life officers about. "They've had to witness some horrific things and been left with PTSD and trauma that they just have to learn to live with," she says. "It's the reality here. It would be ignorant to not think about that." Aisling's condition puts a strain on her relationship with Tommy Foster, played by Nathan Braniff, who is then faced with the decision whether to report her to their bosses so she can get help. And while Braniff says Blue Lights often deals with heavy themes, he believes it does a good job at showing what Northern Ireland is really like. "It shows that Northern Ireland's moving forward and changing all the time." Frank Blake had plenty of practice with his Belfast accent after roles in Trespasses and Say Nothing. One thing that's changed for the fourth series is the public interest when the actors are filming scenes in Belfast city centre. "After having lived here my whole life, it's funny walking down the streets of Belfast and bumping into people that I know wearing my full police costume," Braniff says. "The support for the show here is unmatched." Frank Blake, who plays Shane Bradley, is one of the few actors who isn't from Northern Ireland but he says he felt the same welcome, thanks mainly to a scene where his character opens up about his love of a certain Westlife song. "We were shooting in town, and someone drove past blaring World of Our Own out of the speakers," he tells Newsbeat. "I've long been a Westlife fan and it was great craic. It's so funny seeing how it really took off." Series four of Blue Lights starts on BBC One at 21:00 BST on BBC One and is available to watch on iPlayer. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: Tennessee governor declines to halt execution of state's lone woman on death row
description: If the execution proceeds, Pike would be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
body: If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike would be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has denied a clemency request from death row inmate Christa Pike, who is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection on Wednesday. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. She may have one last chance at halting her execution as her attorneys have filed a petition with the US Supreme Court hoping for a last-minute reprieve. If it proceeds, Pike would be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men. Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim too "After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike's request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene," Governor Lee said in a statement. Pike's legal team had filed the clemency petition earlier this month, requesting that her death sentence be commuted to life in prison. Moving ahead with Pike's execution puts Tennessee "on singular footing", her attorneys said, as she would be the first person the state "executes in the modern death penalty era who was a teenager at the time of the offence". Attorneys Stephen Ferrell, Kelly Gleason and Randy Spivey said the governor's decision "leaves unanswered vital questions about Tennessee's execution protocol". "With this decision, the State of Tennessee is ignoring what both science and our legal system have decided: an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain, and 18 is too young to face execution," they said in a statement on Monday. The murder of Colleen Slemmer created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the 19-year-old was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest. Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull. A year later, she was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, while then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp- who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. At the time of her incarceration, the 21-year-old was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections. Pike is scheduled to be executed on 30 September after years of failed appeals. Colleen's mother has insisted she wants Pike's execution to move forward so that her daughter "finally can be resting". Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence. "The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," her attorneys said. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women." In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider. title: Delays in fitting electronic tags putting victims at risk, report finds
description: The reports says some criminals are waiting up to five months to be fitted with an electronic tag.
body: Almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements are not fitted on time, with significant delays putting victims in England and Wales at risk, a report has found. The report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) says some criminals are waiting up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders. Only 55% of GPS and radio frequency tags were fitted on time, while 60% of alcohol monitoring tags were fitted promptly, according to the report's findings. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said the government was delivering the "biggest expansion of tagging in British history" with £100 million in funding. Electronic monitoring is used by the Probation Service to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order. A total of 27,847 people were given tagging orders with equipment in England and Wales as of June 2026. "There is a real danger that electronic monitoring creates a false sense of assurance if the technology is not matched by effective professional practice," said Martin Jones CBE, HM Chief Inspector of Probation. "Expanding tagging programmes without addressing their weaknesses risks overpromising and underdelivering on public protection," he added. In some cases, there were waits of more than two weeks for the equipment while one in 10 people waited five months to be tagged after the required time. Some of the reasons for tags not being fitted on time included individuals not making themselves available. Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman OBE said victims needed to "know immediately" if tagging was delayed because this could give a "false sense of security". She said a "robust response" was required in the event of breaches but there were "real concerns" over how "overstretched" probation services would be able to handle this. Data from the tags was often found to be underused with major violations raised and explored in just 46% of relevant cases, the report also found. Inspectors discovered little evidence that electronic monitoring was being used consistently to promote behaviour change. There are three types of tags: They include strict controls of an offender's punishment to manage risk, safeguarding and the protection of victims. Those who breach their orders either immediately return to prison, are given a court order or a formal warning. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "public protection" was the government's priority. They said: "That's why we are delivering the biggest expansion of tagging in British history, backed by £100 million in funding, with tag install rates up by nearly 50% since 2024. "This is part of our record £700 million investment in probation and community services, recruiting 2,300 trainee officers over the last two years and a further 1,300 this year – ensuring dangerous offenders are kept under closer surveillance than ever before." Plans to significantly expand electronic monitoring were announced earlier this year as part of the Sentencing Act 2026, which aims to ease prison pressures by managing more offenders in the community. Thousands more prisoners will be released early from October as part of the new law. Most will require tagging. title: OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns
description: The firm also issued an update on incidents in which its models accessed Australian government systems.
body: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman OpenAI will not release its new AI model - GPT-6.1 Astra - due to safety concerns, the ChatGPT-maker confirmed on Tuesday. The AI system - which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself - "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI, said. On Tuesday, OpenAI also issued an update on incidents - that occurred in June but were not made public until last week - in which its models accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorisation. Those incidents and similar breaches by models developed by major AI firms have in recent weeks intensified the debate around the risks posed by the technology. In recent weeks, top AI leaders including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic boss Dario Amodei have urged the industry to slow the pace of development due to concerns about risks associated with the technology. OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns. The latest model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said. "We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added. The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets". The announcement came a day before OpenAI is set to hold its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco, where it is expected to make several announcements. It is unclear if a new version of Astra will be among them. The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology. Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into government websites and systems in June in what experts said was the first known case of its kind in the world. Albanese criticised OpenAI for notifying the Australian government through a generic email address rather than making direct contact with officials. OpenAI said in a statement on Tuesday that it was sorry for the incident and that it "should have handled our response better". Services Australia, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare were all affected, OpenAI clarified. The firm said it launched investigations into the incidents as soon as it became aware of them in mid-August and notified the affected organisations between 10 and 24 September. "Our aim was to give affected agencies a detailed account once our investigation was complete," OpenAI said, adding that it should have shared early findings more promptly and kept Australian authorities updated. Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first OpenAI bots meddled with multiple US government agency sites OpenAI added that it will develop "practical approaches" to how developers and governments identify and disclose future AI incidents. The company will fund cyber security measures, offer dedicated support to impacted agencies and set up a taskforce to manage the risks from increasingly advanced AI agents. The also said a top OpenAI executive will be in Australia to attend a Joint Select Committee hearing on AI on 6 October. In July, OpenAI said its AI systems had accessed the internet and hacked into open-source developer hub Hugging Face, prompting researchers and officials to call for tighter controls over the technology. On Monday, AI chip giant Nvidia released a set of software safety tools for autonomous AI platforms - called agents - that it said could have prevented the Hugging Face hack. One of the new tools uses hardware features in Nvidia's chips to contain agents. Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has largely dismissed calls for tighter AI regulations, arguing that rogue agents are an engineering problem that can be solved. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9bn (£9.74bn) earlier this month. Pope Leo XIV said on Monday during his visit to France that the technology "should be taken seriously" and expressed scepticism over Huang's views. This video can not be played Watch: Pope Leo XIV arrives in Paris for four-day visit The pontiff said he had read that Nvidia CEO had announced there could be a way to insert guardrails ‌into certain AI models. "He's the same one, however, ⁠that says there should ⁠be no limits placed and no government regulation," said the Pope. "This is a problem that I think we need to sit down and talk about," added Pope Leo, who has previously warned about "losing our humanity" to machines. US President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are set to host tech executives at the White House later on Tuesday to discuss regulations around AI. Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks as a "hoax", arguing that the US has sufficient laws in place and that the only "guardrails" the technology needs is a "strong and smart" president. title: Lost songs from iconic Australian rockstar found in garage
description: Divinyls frontwoman Chrissy Amphlett recorded the songs with Split Enz's Tim Finn in 1998.
body: Three songs recorded by Chrissy Amphlett in 1998 will be released on Friday More than a decade after her death, the voice of Australian rock icon Chrissy Amphlett will be heard like never before after three lost songs were discovered in a garage. The trailblazing frontwoman of rock band Divinyls, Amphlett's trademark husky voice and charismatic stage presence brought the world the 1990 number one track I Touch Myself as well as earlier hits Pleasure and Pain (1985) and Boys in Town (1981). Years before her 2013 death, Amphlett recorded three songs with Tim Finn, former lead singer of New Zealand's Split Enz, in 1998. The tracks were thought to be lost until Finn found them in his garage in 2023. On Friday, the songs will be released on an EP titled Some Times. In an interview with Australian Story, a documentary programme by national broadcaster ABC, Finn recalled the 1998 recording session with Amphlett in Sydney. "It was a good time for us to meet because she was looking for something new, something different in her life musically," Finn said. Around that time, Amphlett had split from fellow band member, guitarist Mark McEntee after a tumultuous relationship and was growing close to drummer Charley Drayton, according to the documentary. The pair would later marry. Over several days, Finn and Amphlett wrote a trio of songs and headed into the studio to record them, with Drayton on the drums. "She was so focused," Finn said. "She just wanted to get it right... I was in the presence of great talent, great charisma." In a social media post on Monday about the 1998 session, Finn said he had reached out to Amphlett having been a great admirer of her work. "We hadn't met previously but instantly felt a bond, a camaraderie of shared history as ex-lead singers of two brilliant bands," Finn wrote on Monday. When the session wrapped up, Finn took the recordings home and planned to work on it, but "they were never fully realised". In 2023, Drayton contacted Finn, about the 1998 recordings. "I thought they were lost to the universe but remarkably found the two-inch tape in my garage," Finn wrote in the post, describing the songs as "incredibly important to me, Charley and those close to Chrissy". "It was still in perfect condition and we are now able to share these songs with you." title: Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says
description: The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, 87, prompted large-scale protests across Spain.
body: The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal prompted large-scale protests across Spain An evicted elderly disabled woman, who became symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her lawyer. Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September. She was admitted to hospital after the eviction. The eviction led to widespread anger across Spain, and prime minister Pedro Sanchez has promised housing relief measures when his cabinet meets on Tuesday. Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told a press conference there had been "goodwill from both parties" and that she would pay a similar amount of rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike. Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. Investment firm Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020). The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 however she was still unable to pay this with her monthly pension of €1,350. Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts. Her case triggered nationwide protests and tens of thousands of people to march through the Spanish capital on Saturday to object to the eviction and to demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents. This video can not be played Watch: Spain’s housing crisis in focus after eviction of 87-year-old woman Duro said the agreement, yet to be signed, was the "result of the social mobilisation". She added that Abascal, who is being treated for exhaustion, would sign the deal when she feels better. Supporters called it a victory but promised to continue their fight to prevent similar evictions, and to press for more affordable housing. The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. Pedro Sanchez's Socialist Party, which lacks a majority in Parliament, is hoping to pass a law to appease public outrage. title: Are Trump's US government funded ads illegal?
description: President Trump has faced criticism after fronting adverts which were paid for by the US government.
body: This video can not be played President Trump has faced criticism after fronting television ads paid for by the US government. There are laws against federal funds being used in the US for political advertising. The White House has said they are public service announcements, rather than publicity or propaganda. BBC Verify's Jake Horton examined the ads and spoke to legal experts about their legality. Produced by Krystal Campos. Graphics by Sally Nicholls. Are Trump's US government funded ads illegal? title: The Papers: 'Labour split on triple lock' and 'Plot's going on, PM?'
description: A number of the papers preview a speech from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Tuesday.
body: A number of the papers preview a speech from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Tuesday, where the Times says he will pledge to have an "honest conversation" with voters over "difficult issues" that have been ignored for "far too long by Westminster". Ahead of the speech, the paper highlights ongoing questions around reforming the triple lock, under which pensions rise each year by the highest of inflation, average earnings or 2.5%. It writes that the issue has "exposed deep splits" among senior Labour figures. "Burnham signals end of triple lock" declares the Daily Telegraph, which says the prime minister will address ending the triple lock in Tuesday's speech. The paper reports Burnham will "tell Labour that the triple lock does not work in its current form" and suggest it be reviewed in the party's next manifesto, but "stop short of a pledge to scrap it all together". It adds that the prime minister is "under pressure" to scrap the policy in order to fund his "multi-billion-pound" social care plans. A union source tells the i Paper that the triple lock in its current form is "completely unsustainable" in the long term, reiterating that scrapping it could fund social care. The paper takes a similar view to the Telegraph, writing that the chances of the triple lock being dropped from the next manifesto have increased as "trade unions soften their position". The Daily Express warns Burnham he will face "voter revolt" if he scraps the triple lock, with activists suggesting that "such a betrayal" would see him "kicked out of office". Though the Daily Mail also previews Burnham's speech on Tuesday, it focuses on the prime minister's intention to set out plans for greater state control of water, energy and housing. The paper says it will be "the most left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister", adding that he is also expected to make a "renewed push" to move the UK back into the orbit of the European Union. The Mirror also considers what it calls the "PM's energy prices pledge", and says Tuesday will see Burnham promise to fix Britain's "broken" energy market and bring bills down. In his speech, the prime minister will announce the Great British Grid, the paper reports, which it says will "reverse decades of decline since Tory privitisation". The speech will be Burnham's first to his party conference since becoming the Labour leader in July, the Financial Times notes. It says the prime minister will say he had planned to deliver a "tub-thumping speech" but instead decided to use the address to show he is ready to "take on tough problems" and break with "politics as usual". The release on police bail of five men arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences near RAF Fairford is the main story for the Sun, which asks: "Plot's going on, PM?" It points to an "emergency Cobra meeting" chaired by Burnham on Monday afternoon, and adds Donald Trump has said he is "surprised" by the release. Similarly, the front page of the Daily Star reads "Trump 'surprise' at release of RAF plot suspects". It notes that the five men released on bail are all UK nationals from London. The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident, adding that these would "serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK". The details of the "alleged plot to bomb an RAF base" lead the Metro, which summarises the incident in its headline "Something very odd is going on". title: From Amazon retreats to clinical research: The rise of psychedelic therapy
description: Could hallucinogenic drugs become part of mainstream NHS care to treat depression?
body: Claire Torpey attended retreats in Central and South America where participants legally take psychedelics as part of guided therapeutic programmes From retreats in the Amazon to clinical trials in Newcastle, psychedelic therapy is attracting growing attention as a possible treatment for depression. Could hallucinogenic drugs one day become part of mainstream NHS care? Claire Torpey had tried traditional forms of mental health support, including counselling. But she says there was still something she could not shake. "There was a deep sadness. I was living in chronic anxiety," she says. Claire, from Tynemouth, North Tyneside, spent part of her childhood in care and says the challenges she faced growing up were compounded by the deaths of her father and grandmother in consecutive years. "There wasn't anything that was really moving the needle from my internal state. I was deeply sad and I didn't want to be here." Ayahuasca is a traditional Amazonian brew containing the psychedelic compound DMT Seeking alternatives, Claire travelled to South and Central America to attend retreats where participants legally take psychedelics as part of guided therapeutic programmes. The retreats involved psilocybin, the psychoactive compound found in magic mushrooms, and ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian brew containing the psychedelic compound DMT. Psychedelic tourism has grown in popularity, but experts warn that unethical and unregulated practices can pose serious risks. There have been reports of participants dying after attending retreats and ceremonies abroad. For Claire, however, she says the experience was transformative. "It wasn't until I started taking these medicines that it started to lift," she says. "I started to find a place of peace and happiness. It took me on a journey of forgiveness. "I don't believe that normal talk therapies would have got me there." In the UK, psilocybin and DMT are Class A drugs and are classified as Schedule 1 substances, meaning they are considered to have no recognised medicinal use. Yet interest in psychedelic-assisted therapy is growing. At Newcastle's Care Pathway Enhancement (CaPE) Clinic, run by Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust, researchers are investigating whether psilocybin could help treat conditions including depression. Participants to the clinical trial are given psilocybin in capsule form The theory is that, when used in a controlled setting, psychedelics can help people process difficult thoughts and emotions. Some researchers liken the mind to a snow globe: the drugs temporarily disrupt established thought patterns, allowing thoughts and feelings to settle differently and providing new perspectives on past experiences. Consultant psychiatrist Dr Mourad Wahba, who leads the research, says participants often report significant shifts in how they view themselves and their experiences. "The idea is that through having this experience, people can change their behaviours and patterns of thinking," he says. Lead researcher Dr Mourad Wahba says obtaining licences to work with Schedule 1 substances can significantly delay studies The treatment involves extensive preparation and support before and after dosing sessions. Clinical psychologist Tom Sharp helps facilitate the trials. Participants receive psilocybin in capsule form before spending up to eight hours in a specially designed dosing room under the supervision of therapists. "People can develop a sense of what might have caused their depression," he says. Researchers are keen to temper expectations. "This type of work isn't some silver bullet," says Sharp. "It doesn't turn off depression." Wahba agrees. While early findings are encouraging, he says larger studies are still needed to establish how effective the treatments are and whether any benefits can be sustained in the longer term. Participants can spend up to eight hours in a specially designed dosing room under the supervision of therapists The Royal College of Psychiatrists has backed further research into psychedelic-assisted therapy. Dr David Cousins, chair of its psychopharmacology committee, said: "The College supports further research into psychedelics such as psilocybin, which have the potential to help in the treatment of people with conditions such as depression, including those who are less responsive to other forms of care." Some researchers believe psychedelic-assisted therapy may offer longer-lasting benefits for certain patients by helping them address underlying thoughts, emotions and behaviours rather than simply managing symptoms. However, Cousins cautioned against seeking treatment outside regulated settings. "We strongly advise against people self-medicating or seeking access to unregulated treatments as there are risks in doing so." Supporters stress that psychedelic therapy is very different from recreational drug use. In clinical settings, participants are screened, monitored and supported before, during and after treatment. Some UK charities and organisations are also helping people access psychedelic therapy overseas. Keith John Abraham, founder of Heroic Hearts Project UK, helps former military personnel attend retreats involving ayahuasca to support conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder. "Most people come out of this and feel like they've got a renewed sense of energy and purpose," he says. Abraham, an army veteran, turned to psychedelic therapy after struggling with the effects of military service. "Afghanistan came at a great personal cost to me. "I went down the traditional avenues and I found they didn't work for me and became quite desperate." title: Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state
description: A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra is raising questions about faith, choice and freedom.
body: A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra has sparked fears among Christians Some churches in and around India's financial capital Mumbai have begun asking worshippers to give a declaration in writing - "I came here to pray of my own free will." Visitors write down their names, sometimes add an ID card number, and sign to say that nobody forced or enticed them to attend church. The forms, a copy of which the BBC has seen, have no official standing. Churches keep them in case a prayer meeting is challenged and its organisers are accused of trying to convert those inside. The practice began at some churches in late August, just before a new law against religious conversion took effect in Maharashtra state, of which Mumbai is the capital. The law prohibits religious conversions brought about by force, fraud, coercion or inducement. It also requires people who want to convert voluntarily to notify authorities in advance. An unlawful conversion can lead to a prison sentence of up to seven years, rising to 10 for a repeat offence. Maharashtra's government says the law protects people, particularly those who are socially or economically vulnerable, from being forced or deceived into changing their religion. But critics say its broad definitions, severe penalties and scrutiny of even voluntary conversions risk drawing the state and the police into one of the most private decisions a person can make. The state government did not respond to the BBC's repeated requests for comment. While the law applies to all religions, the anxiety is being felt most deeply at places where minorities, especially Christians, worship. At the heart of the debate is a long-running tension over allegations, usually made by right-wing groups, about people being coerced or induced to change their religion for benefits. Devdan Tribhuvan has seen some of that anxiety up close. A fourth-generation Christian in Vasai, a suburb of Mumbai, he is part of an organisation that provides legal aid to Christians in and around the city. In recent months, he says, people have increasingly approached him not about court cases, but with accounts of disrupted prayer meetings and questions about what they are still free to do. Some have described strangers walking into churches and questioning those inside: "What is your name? Why are you here? Has anyone offered you something?" People from all religions visit the famous Mount Mary Church in Mumbai The questions can become more pointed, Tribhuvan said, when a worshipper has a name that does not sound Christian: "Has anyone forced you to come? Has anyone offered you an inducement?" Many who contact him are not looking to take legal action. They want to know whether simply gathering to pray could leave them vulnerable to an accusation of conversion. In July, an investigation by The Indian Express, external documented five disruptions of Christian prayer meetings around Mumbai between April and July. Nine police cases followed - seven against worshippers or prayer organisers, and two against members of the Hindu nationalist group Bajrang Dal. Police did not respond to detailed questions about the cases or the action taken. "Is gathering for prayer itself conversion?" Tribhuvan asks. In Mumbai, Tribhuvan's question carries particular weight. The city grew by drawing people from across India and beyond, bringing their gods and rituals with them. A church bell can sound within earshot of a mosque's call to prayer; a shrine belonging to one faith can draw followers of another. People of many faiths make their way to the Muslim shrine Haji Ali. Hindus light candles at Mount Mary, a Catholic basilica overlooking the city. Crowds fill the streets around Lalbaug during the Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi and stream to Siddhivinayak temple throughout the year. Maharashtra is the latest of more than a dozen states to restrict religious conversion. The laws differ, but their reach has expanded in recent years, particularly in states governed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. Several are being challenged before the Supreme Court. Behind that expansion lie claims long made by Hindu nationalist groups, that Christians use money, schooling or medical care to draw poor and tribal communities away from Hinduism, and that Muslim men court Hindu women to convert them - an alleged conspiracy they call "love jihad." A bunch of anti-conversion laws in Indian states have made interfaith marriages more challenging Critics say such accusations have fuelled harassment of Christian prayer meetings and interfaith couples, and that the laws give those making them a way to draw the police into questions of prayer, marriage and belief. Maharashtra's government says the new law leaves people free to convert by choice, while addressing what it says is a rise in forced conversions that existing laws have failed to curb. Critics question where it draws the line between force and choice. "We do not support forceful conversions, if any," said Samsuddin Tamboli, president of the Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal (Muslim Truth-seeking Society), a reformist organisation. His concern is what the law counts as inducement. Its definition of "allurement" includes employment, free education at a religious institution, a promise of marriage, a "better lifestyle" and "divine healing". Even glorifying one religion over another can fall within it. "The definition has been kept so vague that almost any benefit accruing to a person can be considered or argued to be an allurement," said Abhay Thipsay, a retired Bombay High Court judge. "If a person receives some benefit and consciously chooses to convert for that reason, why should it be considered wrong?" The law also allows parents, siblings and other relatives to complain to police about an allegedly unlawful conversion, leaving the person accused of causing or assisting it to prove that it was lawful. title: Migrants using longer, more dangerous routes across Channel
description: The government says it is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings.
body: Smugglers have launched small boats from beaches much further from Calais and Dunkirk A growing number of migrants are trying to cross the Channel on small boats using longer routes from beaches further south and west of Calais and Dunkirk, French authorities say. Last week one boat set off from Normandy and spent more than 30 hours at sea, before being intercepted and taken to Dover by Border Force. Although attempts from Normandy have been rare, authorities in neighbouring Seine-Maritime say there have already been 58 attempts this year, up from 30 last year. The government says it is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings, with figures showing a sharp drop in arrivals this year. Despite overall crossings dropping, the stretch of coastline used for smuggling appears to be widening. Earlier this month another migrant boat was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight having set off from the Cherbourg area. These locations are nearly 80 miles (128 km) from the beaches where many of the small boats have crossed in recent years, with those on board spending longer at sea. Recent attempted crossings have started in parts of Normandy and the Dieppe area in Seine-Maritime Audrey Baconnais-Rosez, the local government representative in Seine-Maritime, said: "The number of attempts to cross the Channel has increased in number and it is getting further and further from the north of France." She added that authorities were "managing to stop half of them". The number of gendarmes patrolling the coast within Dieppe and further to nearly the Le Havre area have been increased, she said. "Nowadays it's about 50 gendarmes on the coast and we have nearly 20 police officers in Dieppe and the surrounding [area] to try to stop them," she said. Baconnais-Rosez also said some smugglers were still attempting to use ferries to Newhaven in Sussex. "We are still intercepting them and we are bringing them to justice as well," she added. Audrey Baconnais-Rosez, the local government representative in Dieppe, says police patrols have been increased Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, says it is highly plausible that the new routes are due to police disrupting boat launches in northern France. "It's not at all optimal for these boats to set off so far away from their intended destination," he said. "Some of these journeys would not be 20 miles (32km) but 50 miles (80km) or even more, which substantially increases the danger of course on board the boats." David McFarlane, a marine safety consultant, said the longer the voyage, the more risk of encountering hazardous sea conditions. "If a low pressure system is developing over the Atlantic, it can mean that in advance of the winds picking up, a swell will start to increase, with the increased likelihood of sea sickness for some, which can lead to dehydration," he said. "The wind of course can pick up very quickly and waves can get up to 3.5m (11ft) in height in the Channel. "This increases the risk of the boat being swamped by sea water, with the obvious danger to human life by drowning or exposure." Between 1 January and 27 September 2026, a total of 19,135 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 28 September 2025 to 27 September 2026 carried an average of 67 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. So far, 2026 has seen 19,135 people make the Channel crossing, compared to 32,188 during the same period in 2025. However, the Home Secretary ordered a review last week after two migrant vessels reached the Kent coast unintercepted. A total of 781 migrants arrived in 10 small boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day this year, according to Home Office figures. Tony Smith, the former director general of Border Force, said the smugglers would continue to adapt. "We've seen the Normandy crossings and the undetected crossings," he said. "They're not going to give up as long as the business model continues to exist and there's a market to bring migrants over from France. "Every successful landing is a message to the next migrant waiting on a French beach that it's worth a try." title: Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
description: Kijanangoma is being crowned amid a dispute over a young heir whom the royal clan does not recognise.
body: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo II, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country. For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster. But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country. Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant. Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34. The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned. A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast. He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king. But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward. According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne. But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma. The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son. Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected. However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions. The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome. The late King Oyo's mother has expressed her pain over the succession row Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family". "As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay". The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute". "No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X. But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind". While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan". A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources. Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965. Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs. According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities. After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development. "I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said. President Museveni (left), who restored the traditional kingdoms in the 1990s, was pictured with Tooro's King Oyo (right) in 2010 Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead. The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala. The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s. The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty. Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him. The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend. The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X. Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage. His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, wh

title: Egyptian officials convicted of kidnapping Cambridge student found dead in 2016
description: Giulio Regeni's tortured body was found days after he went missing on a research trip to Egypt in 2016, while studying at Cambridge University.
body: Three members of the Egyptian security forces have been convicted by a Rome court for being involved in kidnapping Italian student Giulio Regeni Three Egyptian security officials have been convicted by a Rome court over the kidnapping of an Italian student whose tortured body was found in Cairo a decade ago. The men, who were tried in absentia, denied the charges. On Monday they were sentenced to 10 years in prison on charges of aggravated kidnapping. A fourth Egyptian defendant was acquitted. Giulio Regeni, 28, was studying for a doctorate at Cambridge University when he went missing while on a research trip in Egypt in 2016. Days later, his mutilated body was found in a ditch near Cairo. An autopsy later revealed he had been tortured. Italian and Egyptian prosecutors originally investigated the case together, but reached opposing conclusions. Egyptian authorities argued criminal gangsters were to blame for Regeni's murder and suggested various other explanations for his death, including a car accident, failed drug deal, or botched robbery. They also denied any state involvement in Regeni's disappearance or death. But prosecutors in Rome concluded that the Egyptian national security agency was involved in the crime. The four defendants were Gen Tariq Sabir, Col Usham Helmi, Col Athar Kamel Mohamed Ibrahim and Maj Magdi Ibrahim Abdelal Sharif. Sabir was acquitted. Rome's chief prosecutor and a lawyer for Regeni's family welcomed the verdict. "From today, people around the world can feel safer," Alessandra Ballerini, the family's lawyer, said. "Impunity can be defeated and democracies can place limits on arbitrary power." Regeni's family have campaigned throughout the decade for justice. As the verdict was read out, there was silence from family members and supporters in court who wore yellow t-shirts and badges, the colour of their campaign, AFP reported. Regeni's parents, Claudio and Paola Regeni and his sister Irene Regeni react after the verdict in the trial on Monday Regeni was abducted on 25 January 2016 while carrying out research for his PhD at Cambridge University on Egypt's independent trade unions - a politically controversial topic in Egypt. His mother told the Italian parliament in 2018 that her son's body was so disfigured that she was only able to identify him by the tip of his nose. Prosecutors said he sustained injuries that showed he was beaten with "kicks, fists, sticks and clubs", and that he died from a broken neck. The verdict was the end of a years-long effort by Italy to prosecute the security officials. The trial, initially scheduled for 2021, was suspended due to concerns prosecutors had been unable to track down the defendants to issue the charges. However, in September 2023, Italy's Constitutional Court allowed the trial to go ahead. While extradition remains unlikely, the convictions could renew diplomatic tensions between Italy and Egypt. title: Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid
description: The prime minister will say he wants to reduce energy costs in his first conference speech as Labour leader.
body: Andy Burnham is expected to announce a new government body to invest in Britain's electricity grid in his first party conference speech as Labour leader on Tuesday. The prime minister will tell party activists in Liverpool that the new publicly owned company, branded Great British Grid, will speed up grid hook-ups by driving up competition for connection projects. He is expected to put the proposals at the heart of a new goal to bring UK energy costs in line with other nations in Europe within ten years. He has also promised to use the address to give details of how he intends to pay for the new NHS-style social care system for England he announced over the weekend. Burnham is expected to bill the creation of the GB Grid as the first significant move in his ambition to provide greater public control of utilities, which he put at the centre of his pitch for power over the summer. He is expected to say that faster connections to the electricity grid could help fix a "cost crisis" in energy that has proved "crippling for businesses". Full details of the new body are yet to be set out, but Labour said it would invest in and compete for transmission connection projects alongside the three private companies that currently own and manage the grid in Britain. The party said it would also make it easier for firms waiting to be connected to the grid to finance connection infrastructure themselves, with GB Grid supporting and potentially co-investing in projects alongside them. Labour has said that funding for the new body will be found within the existing budget of GB Energy, the public green investment company set up by Labour last year and which is now headquartered in Aberdeen. Faster grid hook-ups planned for some green energy projects Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge The transition of electricity generation from large fossil fuel stations to the more remote locations used for renewables, such as offshore windfarms, will require Britain's ageing transmission grid to undergo extensive rewiring in coming years. Energy regulator Ofgem has estimated that £70bn of investment is required in the grid between 2025 and 2031, quadrupling the current rate of investment. But in a report earlier this month, the National Audit Office warned that the number of projects waiting to connect to the grid had grown "significantly" whilst delays to projects were also increasing. In his speech on Tuesday afternoon, Burnham is expected to say that GB Grid will "work with the private sector and network companies" to "reform a broken energy market". He will add: "It will increase competition to drive down costs and speed up delivery so businesses can connect faster and grow quicker. "This is what more public control can do." Burnham's speech will see him promise an "honest conversation" with voters about difficult subjects, alongside the overall message of "hope" that he has made the theme of the four-day gathering. He is expected to say that he initially wanted to "give the usual tub-thumping conference speech" but that "the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed". It comes ahead of a tricky Budget at the end of next month, where the room for manoeuvre facing the prime minister has been narrowed by recent rises to the cost of UK borrowing. Ahead of the speech, the prime minister has promised to reveal details of how he intends to fund his plans to provide free social care services to everyone in England. He has said he wants to put his his plans before voters at the next general election, which legally must be held by August 2029 at the latest, before aiming to roll out the new system from 2030. There has been speculation that in his efforts to free up future funding for his social care plans, the prime minister could signal his willingness to review the "triple lock" uprating policy for the state pension. The policy - under which pension payments rise annually by the highest of 2.5%, inflation, or average wage rises - is expected to add billions to the cost of pensions in future years because of the UK's ageing population. On Monday, Chancellor John Healey declined to guarantee the promise - which has featured in every Labour manifesto since 2015 - would feature in the party's blueprint for voters at the next election. "The manifesto will be the manifesto at the time, I'm not going to do that now," he told BBC Radio 5 Live. title: Temperatures to hit 25C in burst of late September warmth
description: Temperatures are expected to rise well above the late September average on Tuesday with a very warm night to follow, as Simon King explains.
body: Temperatures could reach as high as 25C in parts of the UK on Tuesday in a burst of late September warmth. The warmest locations will be across the south-east of England, though temperatures will widely reach into the 20s Celsius across England and the high teens elsewhere. This will be around 3 to 6 degrees above the average for the time of year. Tuesday night will also be unusually warm with the temperature in some locations not falling much below 20C. The boost in temperatures will come as a strong southerly airflow develops into Tuesday. With unusually hot air across France and Spain - where temperatures have widely been in excess of 30C - the southerly wind will bring some of this warmth to the UK. Temperatures across England will exceed 20C widely with the highest temperatures in south-east England where it will get into the mid-20s Celsius. Average temperatures across England in late September are around 16 to 19C. While there could be a lot of cloud with a few showers on Tuesday morning, sunny spells will develop over England and Wales. It will also be warmer than average across Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland with maximum temperatures on Tuesday of 17 to 22C. However, after starting sunny here, cloud will increase during the day. The southerly winds will strengthen with gusts up to 50mph expected in Northern Ireland and western Scotland. This is linked to a large and deep area of low pressure moving north in the eastern Atlantic toward Iceland. The warm southerly winds will continue overnight into Wednesday with minimum temperatures more typical of a summer's night than early autumn. Widely, it will be around 15 to 19C. In parts of south-east England, it is not out of the question that temperatures won't dip below 20C overnight. Overnight temperatures in late September are typically around 7 to 11C, so this will make for an unusually warm night. Every month of 2026 has been warmer than average, according to data from the Central England Temperature record September will mark another month where average temperatures will come in well above normal. Up to 26 September, the Central England Temperature (CET) - the world's longest running temperature record, which tracks the average temperature across various locations in England - is 2.6 degrees Celsius above normal. Every month this calendar year has seen the average mean CET above average. It is also 2.6C higher than normal for the year to date. It would need to be much colder than normal during the rest of the year for 2026 to not be one the warmest on record for the UK. The Met Office's latest three-month outlook, spanning October to December, suggests higher-than-normal chances of a mild autumn and start to winter. Just how hot and dry was your summer? title: Warning more homes will be uninsurable due to flood risk
description: Aviva boss Amanda Blanc said England was "for sure" building homes that might be uninsurable at some point in the future.
body: This video can not be played Aviva boss says it 'doesn't make sense' to be building homes in flood zones as risk increases Homes are being built today that could become uninsurable in the future due to the risk of flooding, the boss of insurance giant Aviva has said. Amanda Blanc said the risk of flooding is "absolutely increasing", but based on current building patterns 115,000 new homes will be built in flood zones in the next decade. "That doesn't seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built," she told the BBC. About 6.3 million homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency, and Aviva research found one in nine homes built between 2022 and 2024 are at medium to high risk of flooding. Blanc told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that England was "for sure" building homes that might be uninsurable at some point in the future. "It's very well known where these flooding areas are. Let's think very carefully about homes that are being built." Blanc said construction that borders those flood zones also needs a different approach. "You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood," she said. According to Aviva's research, nearly a third of new homes built in 2024 will be at risk of some flooding by 2050, and one in seven would be at medium to high risk of flooding as extreme weather becomes more acute. Earlier this year the Met Office estimated that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters like the one experienced in the UK in 2023-2024 have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events. The BBC has approached the government for comment. Homes in Loughborough were hit by floods in January last year In a wide-ranging interview, Blanc urged the government to avoid policy "kite flying" ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on 28 October. Aviva is a major UK private pension provider, and Blanc said speculation over the last couple of Budgets about changes to pensions led to a significant increase in withdrawals. "Effectively we saw in the last year 30 times the normal withdrawal from pensions that we would normally see, which is clearly something which customers may regret afterwards because once you take your tax-free lump sum out, you can't put it back in," she said. "So we would say be very, very thoughtful about the things that you are testing, thinking about." The few policy announcements ahead of the Budget so far have included a scheme to help first-time buyers get on to the property ladder, and a commitment from Healey to deliver a "new age of industrialisation" for the UK. Big Boss Interview: Aviva's Amanda Blanc Amanda Blanc tells Sean Farrington that we are building homes that could become uninsurable in the future due to the risk of flooding - and talks about how she approaches leading a company. Blanc said Aviva was "ready with capital" to invest in infrastructure, pointing out that the company already invests more than £100bn in the UK, £35bn of which goes into infrastructure, from hospitals to schools to windfarms. "We've got that capital. We want to invest, we're a big UK employer. We want to invest in UK infrastructure. It provides good returns for our pension holders and for the members of those pension schemes," she said, but added detail was needed to turn it into reality. Asked about the current debate about the pension triple lock, which means the state pension rises by the highest of either average wage increases, inflation or 2.5%, and whether the government is looking to change that, Blanc said it was not for her to say what should happen. But potential lower annual increases to pensions if the triple lock is changed would have knock-on effects, she added. "If you've got a lower state pension then you need a higher private pension, don't you? So you need to think about that balance," Blanc said. title: Unis are offering degrees in content creation for £30,000. But are they worth it?
description: Content creation degrees aim to help people make money from their social media posts.
body: Destiny McGowan is now earning money as a content creator As university courses go it may raise a few eyebrows, but Destiny McGowan has no doubt that hers was very useful. In July the 21-year-old graduated from Nottingham Trent University with a degree in content creation. As well as teaching how to best make videos and posts for Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, the course also focused on how to build audiences, engage with brands and monetise your content. "I always wanted to be an entrepreneur, so for me the course was about the transferable skills that I believed I would gain," says Destiny, pointing to both the social media and business aspects she was taught. It's early on in her career, and Destiny refuses to disclose precisely what she is earning, but says she's already making money. In addition to posting about fashion on her own accounts, she makes videos for others, and has also been hired as a TikTok live selling host, presenting products for sale on camera. She says the course gave her access to equipment, technology and industry contacts. "The incredible people I've met through panels that the university hosted would take someone five to 10 years to get to that place," she explains. Nottingham Trent says its content creation degree, which it launched in 2022, provides "hands-on experience". Several universities in the UK now offer such courses. The University of Brighton says it teaches students how to create "content that cuts through the noise". Meanwhile in the US, Arizona State University say its similar qualification allows students to "turn your creativity into content that connects with audiences". Yet you'd be paying a lot of money for this. The three-year degrees at Nottingham Trent and Brighton both currently cost £9,790 per year for UK students, while the standard annual fee at Arizona State is $14,724 (£11,000) for a resident of that state. More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024 So are such degrees worth it? Knightenator, a UK-based, full-time content creator, isn't sure. "I don't think I would have taken the course," she says. The 31-year-old, who doesn't reveal her real name, has been posting videos about gaming and travel on social media since 2015. She now has 65,000 followers on Twitch, and more than 100,000 on TikTok. It is her full-time job, and while she won't reveal how much money she makes, she says she gets most of her income from deals with brands that she promotes. "Honestly, from my experience, I don't think companies would care too much if you had a content creator degree," she says. She adds that the internet is saturated with free advice on how to get started. "If you have the drive to want to become a content creator, the tips are out there, and you don't need to commit to a three-year degree." Her advice is to watch other people's content and find your own niche. "I honestly think that you don't need much in this day and age at this moment to be able to do it." Knightenator doesn't see the point of content creation degrees But fellow content creator Aiesha Beasley from Phoenix, Arizona disagrees. The 36-year-old, who posts about food, fashion and lifestyle, says she would have enrolled on one of these courses if they had been available when she first started blogging on Tumblr in the early 2010s. She believes a degree would have given her a "clearer pathway", particularly when it comes to how to earn a living. "You really do have to have a business mindset on: how can I transition this from a hobby into something that makes me money?" says Aiesha. She adds that such courses are "ahead of the curve" in recognising that content creation is increasingly an important part of marketing. "Now you have to have a digital presence," she explains, "whether you are a business owner or an entrepreneur or building a personal brand." The degrees by the likes of Nottingham Trent and Arizona State come as the content creator economy booms on both sides of the Atlantic. YouTube content creators alone contribute £2.2bn to the UK economy, according to one report last year. Meanwhile, one in three people aged between 18 and 30 in the US wish to become an influencer, a 2024 survey suggests. , external Aiesha Beasley says she would have done a content creation degree if they had existed when she started However, Jacky Gurr, course leader and senior lecturer for content creation at Nottingham Trent University, points out that the majority of people on the course are not actually aspiring to become influencers. For Gurr, content creation is a professional skill that organisations increasingly need, whether someone runs their own business, works in-house, joins an agency or works freelance across multiple clients. "Those skills absolutely can be taught. Students learn how to plan and produce video content, develop campaigns, understand audiences, analyse performance data and adapt strategies based on that data." She adds that the business side of content creation "is an important part of the degree", where they discuss monetisation and the commercial side of the industry. But for anyone who thinks a university degree will lead to overnight success as an influencer, Jacky Gurr has these words of caution: "So much of being a successful influencer is about luck, and we can't teach luck or personality." title: Littler stunned by Waterhouse at World Grand Prix
description: World champion Luke Littler's hopes of defending his World Grand Prix title are dashed as he falls to a shock shock first-round defeat by Luke Woodhouse in Leicester.
body: Luke Littler averaged 82.41 against Luke Woodhouse World champion Luke Littler's hopes of defending his World Grand Prix title were dashed as he fell to a shock first-round defeat by Luke Woodhouse in Leicester. Littler, 19, had been looking to bounce back from his quarter-final exit to Jonny Clayton at the World Series of Darts Finals just over a week ago. But despite taking the first set, he was distinctly below par throughout the best-of-three encounter, averaging just 82.41. That allowed Woodhouse to level the match and deliver a checkout of 75 to win the deciding set 3-1 in legs. Woodhouse will face 2022 runner-up Nathan Aspinall in the last 16, who edged past Dutch debutant Kevin Doets 2-1. Earlier on Monday, six-time winner Michael van Gerwen lost five legs out of the last six as 2024 semi-finalist Ryan Joyce fought back to win 2-1. England's Joyce will play Dutchman Danny Noppert, who advanced past Germany's Niko Springer by the same scoreline. Elsewhere, Wales' Gerwyn Price only lost a single leg as he comfortably beat Poland's Sebastian Bialecki 2-0 to set up a meeting with England's Ross Smith, who came from behind to triumph 2-1 against Scotland's Cameron Menzies. Welshman Clayton edged past Krzysztof Ratajski 2-1, and he will take on the Netherlands' Wessel Nijman, who overcame 2018 world champion Rob Cross in straight sets. title: Infantino makes bigger cash pledge to Fifa members
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino indicates more money could be distributed to the governing body's members from its cash reserves.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Gianni Infantino has indicated a greater amount of money could be distributed to Fifa members from its estimated £4.4bn cash reserves. In a letter seen by BBC Sport, and sent to the governing body's six continental confederations on Monday, Fifa president Infantino said he would support "the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered". Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan, which proposed selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, sparking a major backlash. His letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m (£7.5m) to all 211 members from its reserves. The proposal will be considered by the Fifa Council when they meet on 15 October. "I will not prejudge the amount," Infantino said in the letter. "A single figure can begin the discussion, but it cannot complete a global policy." Infantino issued his latest defence of the failed proposal to sell a slice of the World Cup commercial rights that brought calls for his resignation, again claiming it had been intended to generate additional money for the game. "The recent commercial proposal, now withdrawn, was intended to enable Fifa to invest more in football," wrote the Swiss-Italian. Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE. Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.
