title: Stroke patient, 80, could be placed in care 100 miles from home
description: John Russell's wife, Teresa, wants to look after him at home with some help - but because he needs 24-hour care he could be placed in a care home in Edinburgh.
body: John Russell was admitted to hospital in April last year The family of a man stuck in hospital for 16 months have been told he could be placed in a care home 100 miles away. John Russell, from Oban, was admitted to the town's Lorn & Islands Hospital last year after he suffered a stroke. His wife Teresa, 79, said she was prepared to care for him at home with some help, but his discharge from hospital was delayed and his health has deteriorated. Teresa, who uses a wheelchair and a walking frame, said she had been told that because John needs 24-hour care he could be moved to a home in Edinburgh - which is about 93 miles away by train or 122 miles by road. Argyll and Bute Health and Social Care Partnership (ABHSCP) said it could be challenging to arrange care at home or find a suitable care home place in remote and rural communities, particularly for people who needed 24-hour support. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Teresa, a former nurse, said Oban had been the couple's home for 50 years and they marked their golden wedding anniversary in hospital. "When you've been married for 50 years you don't want your husband in Edinburgh and you in Oban," she said. She said local care homes were full and there were waiting lists for places. "This talk about putting him in a nursing home in Edinburgh just wouldn't work for me," said Teresa. "I would need to take two trains, taking my Zimmer frame and everything else I need. It just frightens me." She added: "I just want to know he can stay in Oban somehow, even if that is in hospital." The Russells have been married for 50 years John was admitted to hospital in April last year. Teresa said his condition had deteriorated since then and he was having difficulty walking and, due to a feeding tube, struggles to talk. "I think he is mentally deteriorating. He must be fed up." Teresa said the situation was taking a toll on her. "I'm beginning to feel the 16 months. That sounds selfish, but I'm tired and I miss John," she said. "People forget he was my carer, so it's role reversal, although I'm not really looking after him. I'm just trying to keep his spirits up." Teresa had nothing but praise for the hospital's staff, but described the care system as "broken". Teresa hopes her husband can continue to be cared for close to home Teresa said she had written to politicians in frustration, asking for help. Scottish Conservative Highlands and Islands MSP, Tim Eagle, hopes to raise the case at Holyrood. He said: "This is a desperately sad situation for John and Teresa to find themselves in through no fault of their own and it is completely unacceptable that it has gone on for so long. "It is inconceivable that they should be asked to move away from the community they have lived in for over 50 years, all because local health bosses can't arrange a home care package for John." ABHSCP said it understood how distressing a long stay in hospital was for patients and their families. It said patient confidentiality meant it could not discuss specific cases publicly. A spokesperson said: "When someone is ready to leave hospital, our aim is to support them to return home or, where that is not possible, to move to a care setting that meets their needs as close to home and family as we can. "In remote and rural communities, arranging care at home or finding a suitable care home place, particularly for people who need 24-hour support, can be challenging as some needs that are specific in nature can only be met in certain establishments. "Where no local option is available, alternatives are discussed with the person and their family." The spokesperson added that ABHSCP welcomed the opportunity to meet any family with concerns about a discharge plan to talk through the options available. Sadly, stories like John's are not uncommon. The latest data tells us that in July, just over 2,000 people were stuck in hospital that were medically well enough to leave. Hundreds of them had been there for more than three months. Two thousand patients is almost twice the capacity of Scotland's biggest hospital - so those beds could be used much more effectively. And being stuck in a hospital bed is not good for a patient, often leading to a decline in physical health rather than aiding their recovery. But finding appropriate social care or space in a care home is challenging, particularly in rural areas. Ask anyone in healthcare, and they will say if you improve social care it would take the pressure of hospitals and allow people a better quality of life. But attracting staff into a profession where pay does not match that of NHS workers is a big barrier for the sector. Experts and politicians agree that social care needs fundamental reform, but efforts to create a National Care Service for Scotland fell apart last year. It's partly because the delivery of care is so fragmented and complicated, with local authorities and the NHS working alongside charities and private companies. Now Scottish ministers are starting a consultation process to simplify the delivery of social care, with the NHS taking the lead. But with so many bodies involved such negotiations will never be straight forward. title: French PM warns against escalation of school protests after 164 arrested
description: Students are protesting over issues such as overcrowded classes, but the prime minister has condemned reports of violence.
body: Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned reported violence during school blockades France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", following the arrests of 164 people on Monday. The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockading their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers." But a French union that defends the interests of high school students said the protests were a "legitimate response" to the conditions they face. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 12 members of the security forces, 12 students and three school staff were injured on Monday, while 180 schools were affected. He did not provide further details on those who had been arrested. The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris. Incidents of vandalism were reported, along with fireworks being aimed at police, and the protests have now spread to other regions in France. According to the AFP news agency, four high schools were reported to have been blockaded in the southern regions of Alpes-Maritimes and Var. Protests have also been reported in Marseille, the northern Lille area and Sedan in the north-eastern Ardennes. The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, defended the protests in a post on social media. "Lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classes, stress caused by Parcoursup [the web platform used in France for students to apply to the first year of higher education]... These issues are by no means inevitable, but simply the result of 10 years of Macron's policies and the lack of resources in the national education system," it said. It called on students to blockade schools on Tuesday in defence of "their rights and against budget austerity". On the same day, unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants also called for a day of walkouts to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions. In response to the student movement, Lecornu said "the difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed", but that "violence must be condemned unequivocally, and its perpetrators must answer for their actions". The prime minister also accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of urging students to expand the movement. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, LFI's leader, blamed the Lecornu government for having "ordered the crackdown" on the protest, adding that the high school students taking part were "harmless". But Nuñez said the demonstrations and blockades were "not very typical protest movements". "It is much more like urban violence, with a number of individuals who were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes, equipped with projectiles, who clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces," he said. "It wasn't about making demands; it was really violence in its purest form." Since the protests began, several incidents involving violence between students and police officers have been reported. In one incident, a police officer reportedly fired a round from a grenade launcher used for crowd control, injuring a high school student, according to France's BFMTV. Investigations have been launched into these incidents, the broadcaster added. title: Parading, policing and power sharing collide amid Drumcree dispute
description: Divisions that had been dormant over Drumcree have flowed angrily again between Stormont parties.
body: Orangemen were blocked by police outside Drumcree church on Sunday Politics in Northern Ireland is often accused of going nowhere fast but right now it more resembles a time warp taking us back three decades. Divisions that had been dormant over Drumcree flowed angrily again between the parties over the weekend, spilling over into Monday when MLAs returned to the chamber. Less than 24 hours after the secretary of state called on Stormont's leaders to "double down on compromise", what unfolded in the assembly was all double down, no compromise. Tempers and emotions flared - despite a warning from the Speaker, Edwin Poots, to mind their manners - amid shouting across the packed benches. Stormont is known for its theatrics but was what unfolded simply more performative politics or the warm-up for a dramatic act over devolution's future? Soon after, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson appeared to provide the answer as he gave a press conference on his party's next steps. He'd already warned that power sharing was in "difficult territory", as he hit out at First Minister Michelle O'Neill and other Sinn Féin politicians for taking part in the Garvaghy Road protest, and called for them to face prosecution. While saying then that it could not be "business as usual" at Stormont any more, the DUP leader went on to say he was not prepared to be reckless. From that we can take it to mean power sharing is going to carry on, for now. DUP leader Gavin Robinson has hit out at Sinn Féin vice president Michelle O'Neill for taking part in the Garvaghy Road protest But what Robinson is prepared to do first is explore tabling censure motions against Sinn Féin ministers, as well as reporting them to Stormont's standards commissioner for alleged breaches of the ministerial code. None of those mechanisms will have any hard or immediate effect and O'Neill can only be forcibly removed as first minister, if DUP deputy first minister Emma Little-Pengelly resigns her post, as neither can hold office without the other. Despite some calls from unionist rivals for the DUP to walk out of the executive, party insiders say they are embarking on a "pathway" of graduated responses, rather than merely opting to pull the emergency lever and halt power-sharing. Robinson has also pulled out of attending a Stormont committee on Tuesday that is coincidentally looking at the issue of reforming the institutions. More steps may soon follow. Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald joined O'Neill at the Garvaghy Road on Sunday While the hope is that time and space may allow for rising tempers and rhetoric to be dialled down in a bid to find a resolution, don't expect to see O'Neill and Little-Pengelly standing side-by-side at joint photo opportunities any time soon. Instead on Monday, it was notable that the two women spoke from their respective backbenches as Little-Pengelly accused the first minister of "running from scrutiny", while O'Neill maintained that she was "proud to stand up" for the Garvaghy Road residents. A cynic might say the assembly election slogans are already being formed as Sinn Féin politicians said there can be "no going back", while DUP MLAs have been referring to their power-sharing partners as "law breakers not law makers". Relations between the parties were already in tough terrain, but this unexpected bump in the road over parading has steered things further off course. All parties know that suddenly stepping off the precipice of devolution is one thing but as recent history tells us, trying to get back up over it never happens as quickly. Crowds have gathered on the Garvaghy Road in recent days Already there is disruption on the hill but with the stand off between the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents still going, Stormont's future will likely be linked to whatever the final outcome is at Drumcree. Not for the first time parading, policing and power-sharing are colliding and finding the route out of this row isn't yet obvious. title: New York Times executive fatally shot allegedly by elderly in-laws
description: Jonathan McKinsey's in-laws, who are both 77 years old, face multiple charges including first-degree murder.
body: A New York Times executive was fatally shot in California, allegedly by his wife's elderly parents who have been arrested on suspicion of murder. Jonathan McKinsey, 40, the newspaper's director of engineering for games player experience, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in a car park in Dublin - 35 miles (56km) west of San Francisco - on Saturday afternoon, police said. Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, his parents-in-law who are both 77 years old, are facing multiple charges, including first-degree murder. It was unclear whether the couple have a lawyer, and they are due to appear in court to formally face the charges on Wednesday. McKinsey's death was confirmed by The New York Times. His body was found at 15:00 (23:00 GMT) on Thursday afternoon outside the Dublin Sports Grounds. Witnesses told KGO-TV in San Francisco that they heard a flurry of gunshots, before seeing the victim on the ground. "I saw the guy drop to the floor: head bloody and chest bloody," witness Assad Razawi told the news outlet. His daughter added that her father saw the couple "walking together and then casually walk away from the shooting". The couple were arrested several minutes later by an officer passing by the scene. They had remained in the area after the attack, a witness said. McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police. Police have not disclosed any motive for his killing. The elderly couple are being held at the Santa Rita jail. They also face charges of felony conspiracy, wilful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence, and child endangerment. title: Stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan
description: Turkish comedian Deniz Göktaş also faces a travel ban but has been released due to time served.
body: The comedian's supporters gathered outside the courthouse in Istanbul on Monday with signs that translate to "Deniz Göktaş not alone" An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but ordered his release due to time served. It has also placed him under a travel ban, preventing him from travelling outside Turkey. A final decision in the case will come from the court of appeals. Deniz Göktaş - who denied the charges - has already spent nearly 90 days in prison. Prosecutors had asked for up to 12 years. His case comes amid a wave of arrests in Turkey that human rights groups say is aimed at crushing dissent. His stand-up routine went viral on YouTube, attracting more than 15 million views. Prosecutors had singled out a line in which the comedian called the Turkish leader "a shy dictator", but Göktaş insisted there was "no criminal element" in his comments. "Dictator is not an insult," he said, "it is a political characterisation." But angering the president in Turkey is not funny. Göktaş was arrested and handcuffed at Istanbul airport in July when he returned from a holiday. During his court appearance on Monday, it was clear he did not lose his sense of humour during his 88 days in solitary confinement. "Three months have been taken away from my life," he said on the stand. "But I quit smoking, so I'll add another three months to my life." That drew laughter and loud applause in court. Outside, supporters like Firat Aksal – a fellow comedian – were very pleasantly surprised by the verdict. "We hardly know what to do with our happiness," he said. "We are thrilled. To be honest we weren't hopeful of getting a fair trial. " Göktaş was released at 21:45 local time (18:45 GMT) and greeted by well-wishers, including his parents who he was seen hugging, outside a prison facility. Aksal said Göktaş would now rest for a few days, and see his family, and then return to the stage. After his release, Göktaş told reporters: "I'm very happy to be reunited with my family, mother, father, and friends." But he added: "There are thousands of other people in prisons across Turkey. Some, like me, are being held in pre-trial detention, while others have been convicted because of their views. "So, of course, it's wonderful to be out. I've missed it very much. But there is not much difference between inside and outside. I hope the day comes when we can all regain our freedom together." Many others remain behind bars, including journalists, human rights campaigners, student protesters, LGBTQ activists, and the elected Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu. Prisons are full in Turkey these days. Erdogan and his party in the past have denied arrests, such as that of Imamoglu, have been politically motivated, insisting that Turkey's judiciary is independent. title: Watch: RAF Fairford suspects are bailed, what happens now?
description: The men were all UK nationals in their 20s who live in London and were arrested under the Explosives Act and on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.
body: This video can not be played The five men arrested on suspicion of terror offences near RAF Fairford on Sunday have been released on bail, according to the head of UK counter terrorism policing. The men, UK nationals in their 20s, were arrested under the Explosives Act and on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Speaking to the press on Monday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the investigation was not over as police are considering numerous angles, including if proxies working on behalf of a foreign state could have been involved. The BBC's Daniel Sandford explains what authorities said they would be looking at next. Watch: RAF Fairford suspects are bailed, what happens now? title: Hart trusts Man City chair Al Mubarak over ruling
description: Former Manchester City goalkeeper Joe Hart believes club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak's claims they are innocent of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.
body: Joe Hart was capped 75 times by England Former Manchester City goalkeeper Joe Hart believes club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak's claims they are innocent of breaking financial rules. City have been found guilty of the majority of 115 breaches of financial rules they had been accused of by the Premier League, although they are set to appeal against the ruling. Al Mubarak said he is still committed to "proving the club's innocence" and the "process still has a long way to run". Hart, who made 348 appearances for City in all competitions between 2006 and 2016, told BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club Al Mubarak was someone who has "led the club brilliantly" and is a person to "trust". "I've heard everyone else go down every single rabbit hole, every single wormhole, every single discussion," Hart said. "My honest opinion is I've got no reason not to trust Khaldoon. What he said is enough for me. "I loved how he spoke. I loved the letter because that was from someone who cared about the club." Man City CEO defiant over Premier League charges The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City The four 'what next?' scenarios for Premier League after Man City ruling Manchester City vs The Premier League Hart twice won the Premier League (2011-12 and 2013-14) and League Cup (2013-14 and 2015-16) as well as the FA Cup (2010-11) during his time at City. The 39-year-old said because there was "nothing concrete", it was matter of allowing things to "play out" and none of his achievements are in any way tarnished. Hart added: "If Man City are found guilty, which I don't think they are because of what Khaldoon said, then there's conversations to be had. "But right now I'm very confident and very, very calm. I'm very proud of what I've achieved and what I did with Manchester City and what we achieved as a team. And that doesn't change. That doesn't change until you tell me." City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centering around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations. Hart said it hadn't "crossed my mind" to talk about the news with his former City team-mates because he "can't get involved in the ifs, buts and maybes". "I did what I did. I lined up 11 v 11 and had it out on the pitch. I won some games, lost some games, drew some games, and I shook hands and I walked off," he said. "I know what I did, I know what we did, and I know how it happened. It didn't feel like we were scheming or plotting." title: Five men arrested in RAF Fairford incident released on police bail
description: Police are exploring whether proxies or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state are involved.
body: Five men who were arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences near RAF Fairford are being released on police bail, counter-terror police have said. A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of Sunday morning. Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said officers were exploring "multiple lines of inquiry", including whether proxies or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state were involved. The five men are all UK nationals in their 20s from London. They were initially detained on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. Counter-terror police said they remained under investigation and their release was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others". Three of the men live in Westminster, one in Camden and another in Willesden, police said, and they are aged between 23 and 25. A farmer who called 999 to report the three white vans in the village of Whelford, which lies directly east of the base, told the BBC it was "pure luck" that she spotted them. The woman, who wished to remain anonymous, said she arrived home to find the driveway and road blocked and saw a "large group of hooded and masked men". "When they saw me they ran ahead of me - some into the field and some towards the neighbouring village of Kempsford. I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. She said that she called the Ministry of Defence police at RAF Fairford but received no answer. She then rang 999 at 01:36 BST and said "within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police". "I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she added. This video can not be played I saw masked men, farmer who called 999 says Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said on Monday afternoon that the three "suspicious vehicles" had been "subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts". Officers were considering the incident "from every possible angle", including that "this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state", he added. Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting on Monday afternoon and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts". The Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident, adding that these would "serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK". The embassy said Iran "reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives". The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". Speaking at the Oval Office on Monday, US President Donald Trump said he wouldn't have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released. "We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this. A large cordon remains in place near the base, while 85 households who were evacuated on Sunday have now been told by Gloucestershire Police that they can return home. But police have said a cordon will remain around the three vehicles. Gloucestershire Constabulary's Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth said the last 48 hours had thrown "our usually quiet and peaceful communities under the spotlight of the international media". Airspace restrictions have also been put in place above the base - nobody can fly within a five mile (8km) zone encircling it without permission. Banned items include balloons, kites, parachutes and paragliders. Watch: Were the RAF Fairford arrests 'pure luck'? title: Russian foreign minister questions 'what will become of UK' and future of 'the Celts'
description: In response, Plaid Cymru said Wales' future was "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit".
body: Sergey Lavrov is Russia's foreign minister Russia's foreign minister has questioned the future of the UK, suggesting it looks uncertain with "the Celts" looking to hold independence referendums. Sergey Lavrov made the comments at a youth conference where he said he did "not know what will become of the country called Great Britain", according to The Times, external. The comments come weeks after the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland declared "Westminster's time is coming to an end" and signed an agreement to say it had no right to "block democracy". In response to Lavrov's comments, Plaid Cymru said Wales' constitutional future was "a matter for the people of Wales", and "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit". In the conference, Lavrov also suggested the west had too much influence in the UN Security Council, external - the five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK, and the US. According to The Times, he said: "The Celts — Wales, Ireland, Scotland — are now seeking to hold referenda. "We do not advocate the expulsion of any of the permanent members of the security council. Although, of course, the scale of the British Empire, when it first took its seat in the UN security council at the organisation's founding, has, naturally, diminished to the utmost degree." For the first time since devolution began Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have a leader who wants to leave the UK Plaid Cymru won a historic Senedd election victory in May, which means for the first time the biggest party in each devolved parliament is pro-independence. First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has declined to give a timetable for a referendum. Former diplomat Craig Murray, who was jailed over blog posts he wrote about the trial of Alex Salmond in 2021, attended the international youth festival in Yekaterinburg after revealing he had been flown to the city by the Russian state. In his blog, he said the meeting between the first ministers had been "featured with striking prominence" in Russian media. The leaders of the three nations met for a summit at the Senedd earlier this month Ap Iorwerth said last weekend there was "no turning back" on the independence journey, as he became the first leader of Wales to attend a Yes Cymru march. In response to Lavrov's comments, a Plaid spokesman described Russia as an "existential threat to modern democracy". "Plaid Cymru believes firmly in the right of nations to determine their own future through democratic means. That applies to Wales, and it applies to Ukraine," the spokesman said, referring to Russia's full-scale invasion of the country in 2022. They said the memorandum with the SNP and Sinn Féin was about "strengthening democracy, cooperation, and standing up for the interests of our nations and communities". "Wales' constitutional future is a matter for the people of Wales, and it is not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit," the statement added. Stephen Gethins, the SNP's external affairs minister who had sanctions imposed on him by Russia, said: "The Scottish Government is committed to ensuring the people of Scotland have the democratic right to decide their constitutional future, just as we support the people of Ukraine and elsewhere in democratic Europe determining their future too." Sinn Féin has been asked to comment. title: Man City CEO defiant over Premier League charges
description: Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano issues a defiant message to the executives of other teams about the club being found guilty of a majority of Premier League charges, BBC Sport has been told.
body: This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano has issued a defiant message to the executives of other teams about the club being found guilty of a majority of Premier League charges, BBC Sport has been told. He was speaking at a board meeting of European Football Clubs (formerly the ECA) in Copenhagen before its general assembly on Tuesday. Soriano was said to have vowed to fight the charges and the process had a long way to run, reiterating what the club's chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a letter to fans. The Press Association reported Soriano told the executives "it's taken eight years to get here and it's going to take a lot more time", referring to the start of the Premier League's investigation in 2018. He then left the meeting without answering any questions from the media. The report added Manchester United's chief of international football relations Jean-Claude Blanc and Everton owner Dan Friedkin - there in his capacity as owner of Roma - were among those to attend. City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centering around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations. On Friday, it emerged they had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them. Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal. Sanctions are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the top flight or a huge fine. The Premier League has declined to comment, while City released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality". Chairman Al Mubarak told supporters on Saturday he was confident the club would prove their innocence. "The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began," he said. "There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. "But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies." title: Stuck between superpowers: How Australia navigates the China-US rivalry
description: Australia is increasingly concerned about China's military might - but Beijing is also its biggest trade partner.
body: China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 2024. Relations between the two countries have been rocky in recent years Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead. Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might. " We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan. "Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important." War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation. With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower. But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner. Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan says Australia is rehearsing for "the worst type of war" It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight. "We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is. The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific. "We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says. And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500. A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing. "Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said. "China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects." The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers. But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties. The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer. The Southern Jackaroo exercises are aimed at improving defence cooperation in the Indo-Pacific But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US. "Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll. "Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States." While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China. Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner. Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer. Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015. The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs. And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up. A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years. Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges. In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement. China is Australia's biggest export market Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China inves

title: What a US diesel export ban could mean for you
description: The threatened proposal aims to protect US consumers from rising costs, but it could trigger major economic waves if it were to happen.
body: US President Donald Trump has said he would back a ban on diesel producers selling overseas as surging fuel prices hit drivers ahead of the midterm elections. Diesel prices are hovering near a record $6.45 per gallon on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), due to the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran and tight global supplies. Trump and his backers say a US diesel export ban would protect domestic consumers from those rising costs, but experts say it could trigger major economic waves both at home and across the world if it were to happen. The US is one of the world's leading energy producers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels of diesel every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA). Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that daily output. Refiners export the remaining1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market. Between 60% and 70% of this exported fuel goes to Latin America. Nations like Mexico, Brazil, Chile, and Ecuador depend heavily on American shipments to power their transport, farming, and factory sectors. Significant volumes also head across the Atlantic to European countries like France, the Netherlands, and the UK, as buyers search for alternatives to Middle Eastern supplies. US diesel prices have climbed to a record high of over $6.50 per gallon – up nearly 70% year-on-year. The spike has been driven by broader energy market shocks tied to ongoing conflict with Iran, which has restricted critical shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway south of Iran through which one fifth of the world's oil and gas usually flows. Diesel primarily fuels commercial vehicles in the US – such as freight trucks, farm machinery, and cargo trains – which are used for transporting goods and construction. This means higher diesel prices can drive up the price of food, building projects, and many other things. Outside the US, diesel is used in both commercial and consumer vehicles, but the effects of higher prices are similar. In the UK, diesel prices at the pump have hit an all-time high, prompting warnings about logistics costs and household budgets. UK Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News that the UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential diesel export ban and has started preparing for it. Meanwhile, in France and across continental Europe, governments are struggling with similar cost-of-living pressures because of rising fuel prices. Trump suggested over the weekend that restricting or outright banning US diesel exports could keep fuel in the domestic market and drive down prices for American consumers. The president said on Sunday that the administration was "thinking about it very seriously". His comments mirror remarks made on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, where he stated that he had called to "not send out the diesel". Trump argues that keeping those extra barrels in the US would lower pump prices, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections. Supporters, including key Republican lawmakers like Congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Senator Dan Sullivan, view the strategy as an effective way to shield the domestic economy from foreign shocks, arguing that American energy should serve American workers first. For the US economy, a ban could deliver short-term relief at the pump by flooding the domestic market with excess supply. However, energy analysts warn it could backfire. David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, notes that cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket. That would push up global freight, food, and industrial costs, ultimately "feeding inflation back into the global economy". "At a stroke, the US's reputation as a reliable supplier of energy to the world would be shot," Fyfe added. Removing more than a million barrels of daily American supply would trigger a fierce bidding war among importing nations in Latin America and Europe. Sarah Raffoul, analytics manager at Argus Media, noted that while higher international prices would eventually curb demand, the immediate gap would severely strain trade relationships and accelerate global inflation. title: US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University
description: It comes after the woman filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Why an investigation into alleged frat house gang rape is reopening New York state prosecutors say they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman filed a civil lawsuit on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house at the university. "Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said Monday. Cornell University said that while it supported the case being brought before a grand jury, "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false". The woman, referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in her lawsuit that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine. Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and was incapable of providing consent. She said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024. The lawsuit also contains an image purported to be from a Snapchat fraternity group chat, in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe. Van Houten said on Monday that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from her statement to authorities did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges. He said he reached out to Jane Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury. In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges. In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Jane Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack. He noted the statement differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit. "Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday. "On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual." Van Houten added that Jane Doe's lawyers had never been in touch with him to say her original statement was inaccurate or to ask him to reconsider his decision not to bring charges. He later acknowledged "the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them". The BBC has contacted Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. In a statement on Monday obtained by CBS, the BBC's US partner, he said: "In the days following the assault, [Jane Doe] was traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode." Giuffra said Jane Doe never spoke to anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint, adding: "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations." "The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognise that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them," he said. Jane Doe also alleged in her civil lawsuit that Cornell did not protect her nor adequately punish the men involved, alleging they were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays". Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the incident and the university's handling, the suit states, adding that news of the incident quickly circulated through the school. In November 2024, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house", saying its campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students." Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law - which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities. On Monday, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators. The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell". "None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," Cornell said. Jeremy Saland, an attorney for one of the men named in the lawsuit, denied the allegations. Saland acknowledged his client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat", but "did nothing else." Saland denied his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine". The case has received national attention following Doe's lawsuit and the announcement the case would be reopened. Several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, have spoken out about it. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide., external A list of UK organisations that can help is available here. title: Mahmood signals rethink on migrants' right to remain
description: The home secretary has been under pressure to water down the proposals from some Labour MPs, including Angela Rayner.
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is willing to rethink plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK. The home secretary has been under pressure to water down the proposals from a significant number of Labour MPs, including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, and trade unions. In a speech to Labour's annual conference, Mahmood acknowledged "some have said elements of these reforms are not fair". And she said the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country". Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. Mahmood suggested doubling the time it takes for most migrants to qualify for the right from five to 10 years. Under the proposals, people who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years. Earlier this year, when Rayner was a backbench MP, she accused the government of "moving the goalposts", branding Mahmood's plans "un-British" - and then stuck with her criticisms when she re-joined the cabinet. Andrea Egan, general secretary of Unison, said the proposed changes would unfairly penalise overseas care workers. Home Office sources insist no final decision on changes to the immigration rules have been taken, and Mahmood was setting out the principles that would guide her in her conference speech. The home secretary told delegates: "As we restore control and fairness to our asylum system, we must do the same for legal migration too. "Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did, and fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young. "That same principle underpins my reforms to the right to live here indefinitely, ensuring settled status is earned by those who have shown a consistent commitment to this country." And she vowed to come up with a policy that was fair to those who "came here legally" and to British citizens. A Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain. "This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants." Speaking earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham denied Mahmood had been forced to ditch the plans because Rayner viewed them as "un-British", saying the reforms would need to "strike the right balance". Asked whether he was "Team Shabana" or "Team Angela," he told LBC: "I'm both of them, I'm Team Angela and Shabana. "But it just reflects that there's a consultation, there's different not just opinions from politicians, but obviously there's a range of views that have gone into that consultation, so we're in the process now of looking at that." title: Aldi boss says some of rivals' loyalty discounts 'dupe' customers
description: Aldi is the only major supermarket chain that doesn't operate a loyalty scheme, which are hugely popular and used by millions of shoppers.
body: Aldi's UK boss has accused rival supermarket chains of duping customers in some cases with loyalty discounts that start with "unrealistically high prices" and then drop. Chief executive Giles Hurley said discounts are helpful "when they're real and when they show realistic reductions", but hit out at what he said were unrealistic reductions which "dupe customers". Aldi is the only major supermarket chain that doesn't operate a loyalty scheme, which are used by millions of shoppers. The UK's official competition watchdog investigated supermarkets' loyalty pricing schemes in 2024 and concluded shoppers "almost always make a genuine saving". Former Asda buyer and retail consultant Ged Futter told the BBC Hurley's comments were a "a distraction from the fact is that Aldi is under pressure in the UK". He said Aldi was "on a meteoric rise until about two years ago" but that it is "now growing behind the main supermarket pack". "The price gap isn't as clear as it once was," he added. Hurely, who has made similar comments on discount schemes in the past, was speaking as Aldi reported a 5% increase in sales to £19bn for 2025 from 2024. However, operating profits had fallen slightly over the same period, which the retailer said was due to higher staff pay as well as investments in infrastructure and prices. Hurley said the business was attracting new customers despite fierce competition across the sector. "We are the only retailer where the price of your weekly shop is actually cheaper this summer than last summer," said Hurley He said the business was focussed on "everyday low prices, not short-lived offers that disappear the following week". "Promotions can supplement every day low prices when they're meaningful, when they're real and when they show realistic reductions. "However, when promotions start with unrealistically high prices – and come down to prices which aren't that competitive and dupe customers – we would view that as loyalty that isn't supportive, that isn't transparent and doesn't help customers plan and budget." Aldi said it had spent £340m this year on cutting prices. The German-owned chain also announced plans to open 40 new stores next year as part of a £900m investment programme and expand long-term agreements with British suppliers. Hurley said recent droughts and global events had highlighted vulnerabilities in food supply chains, arguing that boosting domestic production should be a national strategic priority, helping to reduce the UK's exposure to shocks that can push up food prices. title: Leicestershire get partial points reprieve but stay in limbo
description: Leicestershire have eight points of their 27-point County Championship deduction reinstated but their Division One status remains in limbo.
body: Leicestershire's Division One points total has risen from 111 to 119 as a result of the amended sanction Leicestershire have had eight points of their 27-point County Championship deduction reinstated but their Division One status remains in limbo. The original penalty for breaching pitch regulations, relating to their win against Glamorgan in August, was announced on 16 September. The amendment to the punishment comes after the Cricket Regulator raised with the Cricket Discipline Panel (CDP) whether the 19-point penalty imposed under the County Championship's playing conditions had been taken into account when making its original decision. The Cricket Regulator said it had "raised this issue with the CDP and Leicestershire CCC in the interests of fairness and transparency". A section of the County Championship's playing conditions state that teams charged with producing a pitch rated as poor or below average, and the CDP upholding the charge, would receive zero points from the fixture in question. Leicestershire took 19 points from the match against Glamorgan - 16 for winning and three bonus points - which were removed but remain the subject of appeal. The CDP had applied an additional eight-point deduction, a further eight-point penalty suspended for a year, plus a £5,000 fine. The latter two sanctions remain part of the amended decision but the eight-point deduction for this season has been waived. Without the 27 points being docked, Leicestershire would have finished two points above the relegation zone. After the eight-point reinstatement but with the 19-point penalty still in place, the Foxes are 17 points behind Essex and will be relegated if their appeal is unsuccessful. Leicestershire had already stated their intention to appeal against the panel's decision and a statement by chief executive Emma White said the club's position is "unchanged" by the amendment. Leicestershire to appeal against 27-point penalty Leics on brink of relegation after points deduction County Championship Division One table Leicestershire's Ian Holland reacts during the defeat against Warwickshire that has left the Foxes facing relegation In its amended decision, the panel said that "in a 162-page bundle prepared by the Cricket Regulator for the tribunal in advance of the original hearing on 12 September, there was no reference by the Cricket Regulator to the County Championship playing conditions and specifically no reference at all to Playing Condition 16.2.6". It added that its "clear view" was that "eight points is the appropriate deduction and no more". Confirming it was removing the immediate eight-point sanction, the panel said: "Regrettably that is the limit of this tribunal's powers given that, as both parties agree, it has no power to interfere in any way with the applicability of Playing Condition 16.2.6. "If it had the power to do so, this tribunal makes it plain that it would have reduced the points deduction to the eight points it imposed in its original decision." In a statement,, external the Cricket Regulator said: "Following the initial hearing on 11 September and the decision of 15 September, a question arose as to whether the separate 19-point deduction imposed under the Playing Conditions should have been taken into account by the CDP when considering the proportionality of the sanction imposed under the Pitch Regulations. "In the interests of fairness and transparency, the Cricket Regulator raised this issue with the CDP and Leicestershire CCC. The CDP has now considered this issue and adjusted their decision on the sanction accordingly. "The amended decision only adjusts the sanction imposed by the CDP in relation to the Pitch Regulations. It does not impact the finding that the charge for a breach of the Pitch Regulations was upheld, and it does not impact the 19-points deduction imposed as a result of the Playing Conditions." White's statement on Leicestershire's website, external said: "The panel made clear that the latest hearing and amended decision, which relates to the sanction alone, were not appeal proceedings. "Our position on the charge is therefore unchanged. We continue to believe it should not have been upheld and that we ought not to have suffered the points deduction we have. "We therefore still intend to appeal, focusing upon the process and resultant evidential position upon which the panel was caused to decide the case." Both the Cricket Regulator and Leicestershire said it would not comment further while the appeal process is ongoing. title: Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
description: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa says the murders are a "stain on our national conscience".
body: The discovery of 12 bodies in an area east of Johannesburg has sparked alarm in South Africa Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months. The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police. Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer. The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa. Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties. Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed. Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026. The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park. No arrests have been made so far. Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park. Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises. No arrests have been made. Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear. No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made. Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area. Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death. Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park. Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case. This video can not be played Women held a memorial run in Johannesburg after the discovery of Moselakgomo's body Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed. No arrests have been made. The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive. Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni. She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case. The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni. According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence. The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice. The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body. This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death. A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge. The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni. The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area. The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared. No arrests have been made. Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken. Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand. Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies. While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September. The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg. It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni. President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience". South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day. Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests. title: Iran court upholds lashes sentence for singer who performed without hijab
description: Parastoo Ahmadi was convicted of "offending public decency" after singing while wearing a sleeveless dress during a livestreamed concert.
body: Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024 An appeals court in Iran has confirmed a sentence of 74 lashes handed to a prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab, lawyers say. Parastoo Ahmadi sang while wearing a sleeveless dress during a concert livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024, external. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing. Iran's judiciary launched proceedings against the 29-year-old after the video went viral, gaining millions of views, saying the performance was "in violation of the country's legal and cultural regulations". In June, a criminal court in Qom reportedly found Ahmadi and eight members of her band and production team guilty of charges including "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material". In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years. On Friday, the defendants' appeal was "rejected" by a higher court without a hearing, according to their lawyers. "In our view, holding the concert was not a crime at all," one of the lawyers told the BBC. "The trial court imposed one of the harshest punishments for these charges, although fines and less severe penalties were also available." "The Court of Appeal, despite having the option of holding a hearing, did not hold a hearing and upheld the judgment. It appears that the main reason for issuing this judgment was to deter the recurrence of similar events." News of the initial sentence sparked widespread reaction among Iranians on social media. "May these dark days come to an end, and may women regain the freedom to choose how they live and dress, and may artistic expression once again flourish in our precious homeland," exiled singer Googoosh wrote on Instagram at the time. Musician Hossein Alizadeh meanwhile said he was "willing to take 70 lashes in Parastoo Ahmadi's place". Human rights activists also condemned the sentence, with Amnesty International warning that "flogging constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violates the absolute prohibition on torture and other ill treatment". In January 2024, Kurdish-Iranian activist Roya Heshmati was flogged 74 times after being convicted of "violating public morals" over a photo on social media that showed her without the hijab. She said a female officer forcibly placed a scarf on her head at a prosecutor's office in Tehran before a male officer whipped her shoulders, back, hips and legs, according to Kurdish rights group Hengaw, external. Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures. In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly". Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces. Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures. When discussing hijab enforcement earlier this month, conservative politician and Expediency Council member Gholamali Haddad‑Adel - who is also the father-in-law of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei - said that Iran's war with the US and Israel meant authorities "cannot engage on this front as much as we should for the time being". The war began at the end of February, only weeks after Iranian security forces had violently repressed another wave of mass protests sparked by the country's economic crisis, killing thousands of people. title: People escape historic Kyiv building hit by Russian drone
description: The BBC's Paul Adams reports from the scene of the strike on Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences.
body: This video can not be played Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences has been hit by a Russian drone strike, killing one person and leaving three injured, according to city's mayor Vitaliy Klitschko. Footage showed people leaning out of windows as they evacuated the burning building. Firefighters helped people evacuate through the windows as a plume a black smoke billowed out of the building. The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Paul Adams was at the scene as emergency services attempted to stop the raging fire. People escape historic Kyiv building hit by Russian drone. title: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
description: John Healey said the government is in talks with the US over Donald Trump's threat to stop exports.
body: The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News. Diesel prices in the UK reached a new high on Monday due to supply pressures springing from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. Fuel prices are rising globally and US President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports, stating at the weekend: "We're thinking about it very seriously." Healey, who admitted that UK diesel prices are "extreme", said the government was in discussions with the US, adding: "We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK." Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Healey said: "We work very closely with the Americans. "In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran." The UK depends on the US for around a third of its diesel imports and a ban would send prices even higher. US sources suggest that Trump is considering a ban to attempt to bring down prices for domestic consumers ahead of the critical midterm elections. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. In the UK, the average price for a litre of diesel reached 199.18p, according to the RAC motoring organisation, surpassing a previous high of 191.5p in June 2022 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.13p. Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge. The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away". Healey said he was "very aware" of these cost of living pressures as he prepared what he called a "breathing space" Budget on 28 October. A freeze on fuel duty, first implemented by the Conservative government in 2022, is due to expire at the end of the year. Duty is scheduled to increase by 3p in January and a further 2p in March. Healey said: "Fundamentally, what we need is a settlement in the Middle East. We need an easing of the pressure of costs on business, the costs on households and on ordinary families that we see at the pumps in the most extreme level today for diesel." title: Slipknot fans hit back after Marilyn Manson announced as support act for UK show
description: The heavy metal band will be joined by the US rock musician during their London show.
body: The heavy metal band will be joined by the US rock musician during their London and some South American shows Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act. The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour. Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old. Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him. Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed. While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing". Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance. One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets." Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending. However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act". US rock musician Marilyn Manson has always strongly denied any allegations against him Manson was publicly accused of abuse by actress Evan Rachel Wood, who was in a three-year relationship with the singer from 2007. Posting in 2021, she alleged he "horrifically abused" and "manipulated" her and said she had spoken out to warn others about "a dangerous man". Manson said the claims were "horrible distortions of reality" and his "intimate relationships had always been entirely consensual". Several other women came forward on social media at the time with similar statements accusing Manson of abuse. Wood featured in a 2022 documentary series, Phoenix Rising, which focused on her allegations against Manson. He sued Wood and another woman for defamation, accusing them of impersonating FBI agents and forging federal documents. A judge dismissed some of Manson's claims, and he eventually settled the case and agreed to pay Woods' legal fees in 2024. Last year, prosecutors in Los Angeles said they would not bring criminal charges against Manson, external after a four-year investigation into accusations of domestic abuse and sexual assault involving multiple women. The district attorney's office said the domestic abuse charges fell "outside of the statute of limitations" and it was unable to "prove charges of sexual assault beyond a reasonable doubt." BBC Newsbeat has approached Marilyn Manson's representatives and gig promoters Live Nation UK for a response. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.
