title: UK needs plan in case of 'unprecedented' AI job losses, says minister
description: Kanishka Narayan says one of his top priorities is to have a plan in place if job losses are as bad as some fear.
body: Kanishka Narayan was appointed AI minister by Andy Burnham in July The government must "take seriously the possibility of an unprecedented impact on the jobs market" caused by artificial intelligence (AI), a UK minister has said. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said there was no evidence so far of an overall reduction in jobs as a result of AI, but one of his priorities was to have a contingency plan in place for worst case scenarios. "If it's going to hit us in a big way, you are going to want to be as ahead of the curve as possible," he told a fringe meeting at the Labour Party conference. Carsten Jung, of the IPPR think tank, said: "In a worst case scenario you could have about 8 million jobs being negatively affected by this." Jung said the think tank was working on a "pandemic preparedness" report on AI labour market disruption. The level of AI adoption by industry was not that high so far and it might not ultimately lead to massive job losses, he said, but he claimed it was still going to have a bigger impact on the labour market than the industrial revolution. He also admitted that "stark scenarios" the IPPR had produced in 2024 were "to some extent" wrong but, he argued, AI had evolved rapidly since then from doing "boring" tasks to "more high-level reasoning and creative tasks". "We are not preparing enough for something quite big that's coming," he told the meeting. According to Jung, about 11% of UK jobs are "highly exposed" to being replaced by AI chatbots, "led by secretarial and administrative occupations". But with the rise of more sophisticated agentic AI, he argued that the proportion "could rise to about 60% of tasks across the UK economy". The government needed to be ready to help retrain service sector workers, he argued, but also to bring in measures to "slow down the transition slightly" to keep people in their jobs. That could involve redesigning tax structures to "make it a bit more attractive to hold on to workers than automating them," he said. But he warned that "a lot of the policies we might want to do in a really severe disruption scenario will cost a lot of money," particularly as the UK is more of a service-based economy than other G7 nations. He also said that women were "40% more exposed than men" to the threat of AI because a higher proportion worked in service jobs. Narayan told the meeting that the impact of AI might have been under-estimated because of the "silent adoption" of the technology by workers, which did not show up in industry surveys. UK firms had said there was "no aggregate impact in the overall labour market today," the AI minister added, but one tech firm had told him they had hired fewer people because tasks had been automated "so the actual net impact might not be fully captured". The minister said he was determined that workers would have a voice in the transition to AI, and promised "much better transparency when AI and technology is adopted" so that any productivity gains could be measured. And he said one of his top priorities was "thinking through what you would do in contingency" if the job losses were as bad as some were predicting. This could involve changes to "labour market policy" and "even where we might go on some aspects of regulation," he added. Mike Clancy, general secretary of the Prospect trade union, welcomed the government's commitment to giving workers more of a say, but warned against "creating the conditions in which working people become victims" of AI. Ed Miliband took aim at tech firms in his conference speech Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has, meanwhile, used his conference speech to fire a warning shot at "tech titans" he said could not be relied on to manage the safety risks posed by AI alone. He said that while some tech companies were "calling for us to act", others "are saying we should leave it all to them". But he argued that the "lesson of history is that we cannot leave it to corporations to put in place the guardrails to serve the public interest". "It is neither their purpose nor their motive, theirs is to maximise profits. We cannot and will not allow that to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity," he continued. He said that while the "technological progress" from AI was "inspiring", the "threat it poses according to its own inventors is daunting". He said the UK would confront those "urgent risks", including by using its G20 presidency next year to "lead the efforts to manage AI so we keep our country and our world safe". description: The mission was supposed to last 10 hours, but SpaceX announced it was ending after 90 minutes.
body: This video can not be played SpaceX's Starship splashed down in the Pacific Ocean after completing about three hours of orbital flight. The mission was supposed to last 10 hours, but SpaceX announced it was ending early after 90 minutes. During the trip, the ship deployed 26 "next generation" Starlink V3 satellites, joining the existing constellation which deliver broadband internet on Earth. title: Remains of dozens of suspected kidnap victims found in Nigerian forests
description: Investigations are ongoing to establish the identities of at least 28 people whose remains were recovered by police.
body: Human skulls and bones were found by police in the Umuaku and Nneato forests The skulls and bones of at least 28 people have been recovered from suspected criminal camps in Nigerian forests. Police in the south-eastern state of Abia are investigating the identities of the remains found in the Umuaku and Nneato forests on Saturday after a security operation was carried out in the Umunneochi area. Police spokeswoman Maureen Chinaka said the suspects fled when police arrived. The discovery is likely to revive concerns about kidnapping gangs operating in remote forests across parts of south-eastern Nigeria, where criminal groups have frequently targeted motorists, travellers and residents for ransom. According to Abia State Police Command, the raids were launched following intelligence reports about suspected criminal activity in the forests. Officers suspect the remains belong to kidnapping victims, although forensic and other investigations are ongoing to establish their identities and the circumstances surrounding their deaths. "Upon arrival of the Command's tactical operatives at the camps, the suspects fled. The criminal camps were subsequently dismantled. A total of twenty-eight human skulls and bones, suspected to be kidnap victims, were recovered," Chinaka said in a statement. Police said surveillance had been intensified in the area as officers sought to track down those who fled. Abia state police commissioner Wilfred Afolabi said the operation was part of an ongoing campaign to dismantle criminal hideouts in the state. Police have appealed to residents to report suspicious activity and security concerns as efforts continue to identify the victims and determine whether the remains are connected to unresolved kidnapping cases in the region. Authorities have previously discovered decomposing bodies believed to be linked to kidnapping activities during security raids in Umunneochi. Separately over the weekend, more than 80 people, mostly women, were seized in separate mass kidnappings in two states in the country's north. In an attack on Sunday, nearly 50 farmers were abducted by gunmen in Niger State. On Sunday, about 40 other women were kidnapped in the neighbouring state of Zamfara, according to two security reports seen by AFP and a local source. Abductions for ransom have become a key source of income for criminals, including bandits and militant Islamists, in northern Nigeria. title: Women protest in the streets of Delhi after string of sexual assaults
description: BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri reports from Delhi, where hundreds of women are protesting.
body: This video can not be played Hundreds of women have come together in Delhi to protest against the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old near Delhi university's campus. This is one of multiple protests that have been taking place in the capital over the past week, after a string of sexual assaults and rape cases have made headlines. BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri has been speaking to women at one of the protests who have told her they simply haven't felt safe for years. title: Fossil found on Welsh beach ends 'confusion' over 200-million-year-old fish teeth
description: Fossilised teeth across Europe had been wrongly identified until the latest find in south Wales.
body: Jonathan Bow, pictured with his son at Lavernock, says he was happy to have "contributed to science" An amateur fossil hunter's discovery of a 200-million-year-old fish jawbone has helped solve two centuries of "confusion" over the origins of fossils across Europe, palaeontologists say. Fossilised teeth found in rock around the Bristol Channel, along with other examples around Europe, had previously been grouped together as one type of large ancient fish called Severnichthys. But the bone found on the Welsh side of the channel by Jonathan Bow turned out to be the first found there to belong to a different type. It has helped experts discover that fossils in museums across the continent had been wrongly grouped and were actually made up of two different species - Saurichthys and Birgeria. The Saurichthys bone discovered at Lavernock by Bow, and which helped experts make their breakthrough, will go on display at National Museum Cardiff later in 2026. The jaw on the beach before Bow removed it Bow, from Bridgend, said he had been walking along the beach in the Vale of Glamorgan at low tide in the spring of 2012 when he had spotted "what looked to be a jaw". He said it "was like nothing I'd ever spotted on the beach before", having been a fossil hunter for about 10 years. "I was super excited because I thought it was going to be a miniature crocodile, something brand new," he said. For many years he had no idea what it was as experts were unsure, but in 2022 University of Bristol lead researcher Jacob Quinn came to see Bow's collection and went on to research the jaw. While a fish jaw was not what Bow had hoped for, he said "it felt good" to have been part of the team that had "contributed to science". "I've been collecting for quite some time over the years and it was interesting," he said. It is now believed the teeth come from two Triassic era fishes, the Birgeria (top) and the Saurichthys Researchers from Amgueddfa Cymru - Museum Wales worked with State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart and the University of Bristol, where the fossil had been sent for detailed inspection. They discovered it belonged to a Saurichthys - a predator fish that lived in shallow tropical seas during the Late Triassic period. "Many teeth from Saurichthys were once mistaken for those of an amphibian, and that misunderstanding continued well into the 20th Century," said Museum Wales curator Cindy Howells. "This lovely little jaw caused great confusion when it was first found as it bore no resemblance to any known species," she said. Quinn said the fossils found in the Bristol Channel had come from storms that had happened 200 million years ago. "It is remarkable that such a delicate fossil survived," she said. "Although British Triassic fossils have been studied for over 200 years, this is the first bone from Saurichthys ever found in these rocks." The discovery led to the publication of a scientific paper, external that compared the fossil with those across Europe. By comparing the new snout with museum specimens from Britain and Europe, it provided clear evidence that fossils originally thought to be Severnichthys were actually a combination of two separate species. The name Severnichthys had been used for individual teeth and a few small bones that existed in many museum collections. These were even thought to be from amphibians well into the 20th Century, rather than the fish that experts now know they were. "These predators lived in a shallow tropical sea filled with small limestone islands," paper co-author Dr David Whiteside said of the two species. "Saurichthys was probably a fast and agile hunter, while Birgeria was larger and more powerful, likely feeding on a wider variety of prey." Another co-author, Dr Sam Cooper, said: "These fish have a remarkably complicated history. "It's amazing that a single fossil, found by Jonathan Bow during a spring tide, has helped clear up nearly 200 years of confusion." title: Nigerian attempts to break world record by dancing non-stop for seven days
description: Crowds have gathered in Lagos to watch Ben Dancer, who says he will carry on dancing until Tuesday morning.
body: Ben Dancer is due to reach his target early on Tuesday morning A Nigerian dancer is attempting to dance non-stop for seven days in order to set a new world record. Benjamin Daniel, known as Ben Dancer, is aiming to dance for 168 hours - 41 hours longer than the current record for the longest individual dance marathon. Guinness World Records has yet to confirm whether the attempt qualifies as an official record. The BBC has contacted the organisation for comment. Young people have been gathering in recent days to cheer him on at Freedom Park in Lagos, filming his every move and dancing along from behind the barriers. "It's a beautiful moment. Seeing how far he has come and witnessing him achieve this feat made me incredibly proud and grateful to God," Uche Anumudu, one of those watching, told the BBC. The current record is 127 hours, set by Indian dancer Srushti Sudhir Jagtap in 2023, when she was 16. Her performance focused mainly on kathak, one of India's major classical dance forms. Ben Dancer, 33, has been dancing professionally for 18 years. His attempt began on Tuesday 22 September and, if he completes the planned 168 hours, he is due to reach his target early on Tuesday morning. For much of the marathon, Ben Dancer has drawn on Nigeria's rich dance traditions as well as its fast-changing internet culture. Afrobeats has been a constant presence, alongside genres including fuji, jazz and zouk. Crowds of people have gathered to watch the performance At times, he has swapped his dance clothes for traditional Nigerian outfits, including the flowing agbada and dashiki. Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, with a wide range of cultural traditions. Ben Dancer's team says the performance is intended to reflect that diversity, rather than simply test his physical endurance. His team says he underwent intensive fitness training before the attempt, changing his diet and focusing on carbohydrates and cardiovascular conditioning. During the marathon, he has been eating lightly and drinking fluids while taking the permitted five minutes of rest for every continuous hour of activity. Ben Dancer has chosen to dance for several hours at a time before taking his accumulated rest. A medical team has also been present at Freedom Park to provide assistance when needed. Ben Dancer is allowed to rest for five minutes every hour The scene around him has become something of a street party. Crowds of young people have gathered to cheer him on. Videos from the attempt have gone viral across social media platforms, drawing more people to the venue. Moronumubo Akodu, who has repeatedly visited to support Ben Dancer, said she was impressed by his determination but worried about the physical toll. "It is actually insane but I am so proud of him," she told the BBC. Emmanuel Ulelu, who visited the performance twice, said he noticed a striking change in the dancer's energy. "On day two, you could see the stress," he said. "Even after just three hours of dancing at the location myself, I wondered how he would keep going." But when he returned 16 hours into day five, he said Ben Dancer appeared more energetic than before. "It reminded me that we're capable of doing unbelievable things when how badly we want something matches and surpasses the difficulty of achieving it," he said. Nigeria has also developed a strong relationship with Guinness World Records, particularly in entertainment. In 2023, Nigerian chef Hilda Baci cooked continuously for 93 hours and 11 minutes in Lagos, which Guinness officially recognised as a new record. Her achievement sparked a surge of interest in record attempts in Nigeria, even though others have since surpassed her. Guinness says it received more than 1,500 new applications from the country within two months of her cook-a-thon, including events such as reading, singing, and crocheting. title: Ferguson retains Rangers dream but Bologna exit never close
description: Lewis Ferguson reveals "nothing was ever that close" on a move away from Bologna this summer amid reports of interest from Rangers but he does harbour ambitions of a return to his boyhood club.
body: This video can not be played 'Rangers was a dream - that has not changed' Lewis Ferguson says he was never close to leaving Bologna this summer amid reports of interest from boyhood club Rangers. But the Scotland midfielder, 27, does retain aspirations of an Ibrox return at some stage in his career. Ferguson was released by Rangers at 14 and made his way to Serie A in 2022, via Hamilton Academical and Aberdeen. He has captained Bologna since 2023 and led them to their first Coppa Italia in over 50 years in 2025. However, starts became sparse last term under Vincenzo Italiano, making just 17 in the league. Asked about links to Rangers, Ferguson said: "I had a long think after the World Cup about my future and I was a little bit unsure but nothing was ever that close." Pocognoli has no concern over Scotland's lack of goals From shaky start to statement wins - 100 days of McInnes at Rangers And he added: "When I went back for pre-season, we had a new manager [Domenico Tedesco] and it was like a fresh start. "We changed again since [with Raffaele Palladino], so I've had three new managers in the last two months [including Sebastien Pocognoli with Scotland]. "I had a long think about what my future was going to look like and in the end it was still at Bologna. "I've loved every moment that I've had there. It was just about continuing that journey and seeing where it takes me." Ferguson, who is under contract until 2028 with the option of a further year, has played every minute of Bologna's five Serie A games so far this season. His father, Derek, and uncle, Barry, both played for Rangers with the latter captaining and at one stage managing at Ibrox. In July, newly-installed Rangers manager Derek McInnes spoke of an "obvious link" with Ferguson, having worked with the player at Aberdeen. On his bond with Rangers, Ferguson said: "It's no secret that I grew up a fan and my family is involved in the club. "It was a dream of mine as a kid and that's not changed but I don't want to speak about that while I'm a player at Bologna. "In the future, you never know. It might happen, it might not, but it's always been something in the back of mind." title: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
description: John Healey's speech comes ahead of next month's Budget, as he faces pressure to bring down government borrowing costs.
body: John Healey and cabinet ministers from the other great offices of state gave speeches at Labour Party conference on Monday The chancellor has warned against allowing Britain's benefits bill to balloon while not offering young people opportunities. John Healey told Labour's annual conference in Liverpool that cutting welfare spending was "more than an economic must - it's a moral duty". "The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage," he said. He announced the expansion of a Local Apprenticeships Service for mayors in England, which he said would deliver thousands more apprenticeships for young people. Healey's speech comes as he faces pressure to cut public spending or raise taxes ahead of next month's Budget to bring down government borrowing costs. In an attempt to reassure the markets, he said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" with him and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "united on meeting the fiscal rules". Fiscal rules are the government's self-imposed constraints to manage decisions on spending and tax. The Budget would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space", the chancellor said. And he admitted that "the money New Labour had in the '90s is simply not there now". Healey blamed the Conservative Party's time in government for leaving Britain spending more on debt than on the Home Office, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Justice combined. Tory shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said in response to the speech that "Labour MPs will never support cutting the out-of-control welfare bill" and "with Labour, it's always more taxes if you work and more benefits if you don't". Healey praised young people as "digital natives, whip-smart, questioning, ambitious, brave" who could move from "generation jeopardy to generation hope". But he pointed to the million young people not in education, employment or training - known as Neets - which he said created a necessity to make benefits a bridge into work, rather than a "trap". "It is not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill, and a system which offers an income but doesn't offer a future," he said. The Local Apprenticeships Service was initially planned as a pilot in a limited number of areas but would now be available to any English mayor who wants it, he said. Through the scheme, which the Treasury says will roll out across England from March 2027, local teams plan to match young people with employers, including small businesses that have never taken on a trainee. The department said an extra £100m was going into the scheme, "fully funded" by savings from the Department for Work and Pensions' crackdown on fraud. Powers to implement the scheme will rest with mayors because "they know which firms are hiring, which colleges are delivering, which estates have been left behind," Healey said. It comes as the final instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the one in eight people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are Neets in the coming weeks. Healey said these young people had been "signed off, written off" which the Labour government would address. Helen Miller, director of the Institute for fiscal studies think tank, told the BBC that sticking to fiscal rules alone would not be enough to reduce debt because it is "basically a promise to get down debt tomorrow". She suggested that reducing the benefits bill, including removing support from some people, could be one way of cutting the national debt sooner. Elsewhere in his speech, Healey repeated his promises to re-industrialise the country and said Rolls Royce would invest £300m more into its British factories in Derby, Bristol, Glasgow and Rotherham. He also said he was bringing back the Union Learning Fund in England, established in 1998 and abolished by the Tories, to help working people gain more skills in an age of artificial intelligence. It was initially unclear how this would be funded. Healey did not set out a pathway for greater defence spending in his speech, another area of pressure for ministers. And he declined to commit to the pensions triple lock being in Labour's next manifesto, when asked several times by BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley, after speculation it may be dropped to help fund a new social care system. title: Seoul summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row
description: Last week Zelensky revealed Ukraine had sent two captured North Koreans to South Korea - which Seoul says was meant to be a secret.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky made an announcement concerning the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war last week - which South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has called "greatly disappointing" South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador after President Volodymyr Zelensky last week announced his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo lodged a formal complaint with Andrii Vieshkin and expressed "strong regret" that Zelensky had revealed the transfer, which Seoul says was supposed to be a secret. The two North Koreans, who were among thousands of soldiers supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. President Lee Jae Myung called the disclosure "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. Ukraine's foreign ministry declined to comment when approached by the BBC. In early 2025, Ukraine said its forces had captured two North Korean soldiers as prisoners of war in Russia's Kursk Oblast. After more than a year of negotiations between Seoul and Kyiv, Zelensky announced they had been transferred to South Korea at the UN General Assembly last Wednesday - adding they had not been "easy to capture alive". Seoul confirmed the news but sharply criticised Zelensky for allegedly breaking an agreement to keep the transfer a secret. This was partly to protect the North Koreans' families, President Lee's office said in a statement, which added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. Seoul demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. Lee faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure. The South Korean opposition accused him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. Lee, whose party takes a conciliatory approach to the North, has been making efforts to reopen peace talks, with little success. Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. "When North Korea actively participates in a war in Europe, South Korea cannot remain a distant observer," said Mykhailo Podolyak, a senior adviser to Zelensky. "The transfer of defence technologies and capabilities from Seoul to Kyiv is not just about helping Ukraine; it is about South Korea protecting its own long-term security interests by containing the expansion of an aggressive totalitarian axis." This July, Seoul announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang. title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
description: Chancellor John Healey will set out his plans for UK taxes in October.
body: Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October. He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs". But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited. Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT. In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes. Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs. The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future. The run-up to the Budget typically sees speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year. Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules. The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are: Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk. Analysts at KPMG believe it could have fallen to £12bn, mainly due to the rise in government borrowing costs this year. However, one option that has been floated is Healey potentially accepting a smaller buffer, reducing the need to increase taxes in the Budget. Further details on the "Your First Home" scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget. The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase. There has been speculation that Capital Gains Tax - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the Mansion Tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028. However, reports have suggested the government is considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. Banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions to increase taxes on the sector. But banks have pushed back, suggesting heavier levies would undermine the government's aim to boost growth and make the UK less competitive. In the first three months of the year, the UK's economy grew by 0.6%, although it slowed to 0.4% in the April-to-June period. The Office for National Statistics said that figure was "relatively robust", with the UK growing faster than other G7 countries. The most recent data showed the economy grew by 0.4% in July, which was much stronger than expected. Analysts say the UK economy is proving resilient in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran. The conflict has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and gas trade. This caused a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices. Economists expect UK growth to slow in the months ahead as those costs continue to weigh on households and businesses. Prices for goods and services are still rising faster than wanted. Inflation hit 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months, and above the Bank of England's 2% target, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% for the sixth time in a row in September, but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist. The Budget speech usually starts at about 12:30 UK time - after Prime Minister's Questions - and lasts about an hour. It will be broadcast live on the BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website. The Leader of the Opposition, Conservative MP Kemi Badenoch, will respond to the speech in the House of Commons. MPs debate the measures for four days, before voting on them. If approved by MPs, tax changes can come into effect immediately. However, the government must pass a finance bill to make them permanent. title: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
description: The regulator Ofgem says the price cap increases by 4% in October for millions of households.
body: Typical annual energy bills are rising by £60 to £1,723 at the start of October, under regulator Ofgem's latest energy price cap. The increase of around 4% in the cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran. It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, and - with forecasts of significant increases in bills to come - prepare for a more expensive winter. The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used. It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months, external. It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways. Most of the increase in the energy price cap is driven by higher gas prices. Gas bills are rising by 8%, which means households that do not use gas will see an energy bill increase of less than 1%. The government's decision to remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has also affected the new price cap - Ofgem says the typical annual bill would have been £45 higher without that cut. While Ofgem's director general for markets Neil Kenward said the price rise for October to December was technically 3.6%, Ofgem always rounds the number which is why it publicised the 4% figure. The typical annual usage figure applies to the first category: dual-fuel households on a standard variable tariff which pay by direct debit. But customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy used and how they pay for it. For the roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs, they will not be affected by this increase. Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system. Although the price cap sets the unit prices for gas and electricity, your household's actual bill depends on the overall amount of energy you use, and how you pay for it. Where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference. The Ofgem cap is based on "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit. The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year. In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved. Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year. Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate. This is especially important when prices go up. Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically. How high could UK petrol and diesel prices go? Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region, external and payment method. Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers will be 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas. The electricity charge is lower than the amount charged in the previous three-month period, while the gas charge is largely unchanged. Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. In response, Ofgem said it wants all energy firms to offer at least one tariff that has a low standing charge but higher cost per unit of energy to give some customers more choice and control. Charities, campaigners and the suppliers' trade body criticised the proposal for just shifting the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it. Energy standing charge plans could backfire, MPs told Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price. You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind. Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal. Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills. Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households. However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising. In December 2025, Ofgem approved a £28bn investment to improve the electricity and gas grids in Great Britain to strengthen energy supplies and protect customers against volatile energy prices. It will also reduce Britain's dependence on gas. Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional £108 added to energy bills by 2031. These charges started to appear from April 2026, adding about £6 a month to the bill for a typical household covered by the energy cap. Analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise sharply in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months. title: Bulger killer's parole hearing to be held in private
description: James Bulger's mother Denise Fergus had demanded that the hearing be held in public.
body: Jon Venables has been jailed twice since he was released for the 1993 murder of James Bulger Child killer Jon Venables will have his latest parole bid heard in private despite a plea from his victim's mother for it to be public, the Parole Board has decided. Venables tortured and murdered two-year-old James Bulger in 1993. The 44-year-old will have his case heard by parole chiefs at an oral hearing more than two years after his last appeal. James's mother Denise Fergus had demanded that the hearing be held in public to help combat "misinformation" about the case which had a "retraumatising impact" on her. Parole Board hearings are usually held in private but they can be made public "in the interests of justice". Various media organisations also applied for a public hearing. In reaching its decision, the Parole Board said a public hearing would make it "very difficult for Jon Venables to give evidence" because he could be "being listened to by people who are seeking to get information so that they can kill him". In 2023, the Parole Board rejected the bid and found he still posed a danger to children and could go on to offend again. James Bulger was abducted and killed by Jon Venables and Robert Thompson Venables was jailed alongside Robert Thompson after the pair of then 10-year-olds snatched James from a shopping centre in Bootle, Merseyside, in February 1993. Venables was released on licence in July 2001 and recalled to prison in February 2010 after indecent images of children were found on his computer. He was once again freed in August 2013 and then called back in November 2017 for the same offence, with parole judges considering his case again in September 2020. A spokeswoman for Denise Fergus previously said her application to observe the hearing had been granted. Victims have been able to attend parole hearings held in private under reforms rolled out nationally in April as part of efforts to boost confidence in the justice system. title: Council dropped initial investigation into sex abuse teacher
description: Martin Gallacher was convicted last week of sexually abusing a dozen youngsters at a Paisley school over an 11-year period.
body: Martin Gallacher was found to have sexually abused a dozen youngsters at a Paisley school A council has launched an investigation into how it handled sex assault allegations against a teacher later found to have abused 12 boys. The probe will examine why police were not called in after it emerged computing teacher Martin Gallacher had assaulted a teenager at a school in Paisley. The boy told the school what had happened to him in 2024 but an internal investigation was dropped due to "insufficient evidence". Gallacher was eventually arrested and charged, before being convicted last week of sexually abusing pupils at the Renfrewshire school over 11 years. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland It has now emerged that Renfrewshire Council did not inform authorities about the original complaint and Gallacher was allowed to remain teaching. The trial at Paisley Sheriff Court heard the initial complainer left the school as he had not been believed and Gallacher remained in his post. But as news of the attack spread around the school and the town, other victims came forward. The court heard Gallacher had been grooming and abusing vulnerable youngsters for more than a decade, targeting them in his classes and at lunch, badminton and football clubs he ran within the school. The 46-year-old is now facing a lengthy prison sentence after being convicted of 14 charges. Renfrewshire Council said it was now commissioning an independent learning review into the case. A spokesperson for the local authority said it was sorry for the impact his behaviour had on his victims. They added: "The safety and wellbeing of our pupils is of the utmost importance to us. Wellbeing support is being offered to everyone affected by his actions." The spokesperson confirmed a complaint about Gallacher's contact was received in October 2024. They continued: "There was an investigation into that complaint and no action was taken due to insufficient evidence at that time." They said that following the court decision it had commissioned a review which would involve police, health and multi-agency partners. Giving evidence in Gallacher's defence, a fellow teacher described him as "the perfect teacher". She added he had also been recognised with a "best teacher" award. Gallacher denied any wrongdoing, and claimed that he had touched boys innocently through his roles as a teacher, club organiser or football coach. But the court heard he targeted victims in lessons or when they were alone. He also contacted some on messaging and gaming platforms, and handed out gifts and money. The court heard he rubbed children on the body and touched them inappropriately. Gallacher, who said he suffers from "mild cerebral palsy", agreed that he had touched boys on their shoulders or legs but added that it was "definitely not in a sexual fashion". He claimed sometimes he had touched their shoulders as he was "steadying himself" due to being unsteady on his feet because of his condition. After Gallacher was convicted last week, prosecutor Jason Stark asked Sheriff Eoin McGinty to consider imposing a sexual harm prevention order, which would place limitations on the sex offender's activities. He also asked the sheriff to impose non-harassment orders, banning Gallacher from having any contact with his victims. Sheriff McGinty said the teacher had taken advantage of the vulnerability of his victims and behaved in a manipulative and predatory way. Gallacher was remanded in custody and will be sentenced next month. title: Watch: SpaceX launches Starship rocket into orbit for first time
description: Until now, all Starship flights have been suborbital, meaning the capsules did not complete a loop around the Earth.
body: This video can not be played SpaceX describes Starship as "the world's most powerful launch vehicle ever developed" and says it will eventually carry crew and cargo "to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond". The aim of the spacecraft - which will undergo its 14th test flight today - is to be able to carry up to 100 people on "long-duration, inter-planetary flights". The rocket is aiming to make six orbits of Earth for the first time during a 10-hour flight, before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean to the west of Chile. Until now, all Starship flights have been suborbital, meaning the capsules were high enough to reach space, but did not travel fast enough or long enough to complete a loop around the Earth. Most of the previous flights were about one hour. Read more on the launch Watch: SpaceX launches Starship rocket into orbit for first time. title: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options?
description: Andy Burnham has said social care in England should be reformed - what are the possible options?
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants major reform of social care in England to create "a system that works on NHS principles" and where "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". "There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same", he told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg. The prime minister has asked Baroness Casey to conduct a review on the "best way of doing it" and she has been asked to report by April 2027. Casey will also look at how to pay for any reforms. BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching social care reform and how much they could cost. Some people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life. It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than £100,000. One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold. In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000. Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between £1.3bn and £2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population. The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations. But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances. In 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care. This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes. It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan. The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped. In England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than £23,250. This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings. Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support. Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to £100,000. The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been £1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified. The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down. An alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use. This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home. Scotland has implemented such a system. However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet. But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing. The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost £7.5bn a year by 2036. Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay. Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers. Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses. Some have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS. This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria. The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around £19bn a year extra by 2036. When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service. It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died. But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further. In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded. And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028. It's worth bearing in mind that the four approaches above are not mutually exclusive. Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test. Burnham told the BBC that any changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse". One option - suggested by former Labour Treasury minister Darren Jones - is to get rid of the triple lock on the state pension. This guarantees that the pension rises every year by whichever is the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%, to pay for a new system of social care. title: Forest Green allow Savage to talk to another club
description: Forest Green give manager Robbie Savage permission to speak to another club, amid speculation linking him to Peterborough United.
body: The Forest Green job is Robbie Savage's first managerial role in the top five tiers of English football Forest Green Rovers have given manager Robbie Savage permission to speak to another club, amid speculation linking him to the vacant role at Peterborough United. The National League side added that Savage would not be in the dugout for Tuesday night's game at home to Wealdstone. Asked on Saturday whether he had any contact from Posh, Savage did not deny the speculation but said he did not know if there had been contact from the club. "I don't know, I've got a game to prepare for and I'm really excited to watch my team," he told BBC Radio Gloucestershire. Former Wales international Savage was appointed at Forest Green on 1 July 2025, having previously managed non-league Macclesfield Town. The 51-year-old, who played as a midfielder for clubs including Derby County, Birmingham City, Leicester City and Blackburn Rovers, guided Forest Green to seventh in the table last season but they were beaten in the play-off eliminators. This season they sit 12th after 10 matches, with four wins, two draws and four defeats. Peterborough are looking for a new manager after sacking Luke Williams on 19 September following a poor start to the season. They are currently 23rd in League One with just one win in eight league games. title: Konsa and O'Reilly doubts to face Czech Republic
description: Ezri Konsa and Nico O'Reilly are both doubts to play in England's Nations League match against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night.
body: Konsa and O'Reilly helped England reach the semi-finals of the 2026 World Cup Ezri Konsa and Nico O'Reilly are both doubts to play in England's Nations League match against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night. The pair were the only two members of the England squad to miss training on Monday morning, with the players following their own individual programmes. Both played the full 90 minutes in England's 3-2 loss to Spain on Saturday. Manchester City's O'Reilly started at left-back, a position he made his own during the World Cup, and his absence would open an opportunity for Lewis Hall to play. It was O'Reilly's mistake which led to Alex Baena drawing Spain level at 2-2 at Wembley before the World Cup winners went on to claim victory. Arsenal centre-back Konsa has become one of Tuchel's most trusted players and started seven of the eight matches at the World Cup. Central defender Jarrad Branthwaite came on for Marc Guehi late on against Spain and could be a contender to start if Konsa is unavailable. England play four matches in this international window and, after the loss to Spain, take on the Czech Republic both home and away, either side of travelling to Rijeka to play Croatia. title: Mahmood to reopen scheme to resettle refugees in the UK
description: Around 25% of arrivals under the UK Resettlement Scheme are expected to be Afghan women and girls and Palestinians.
body: Shabana Mahmood sent officials to Denmark to study its immigration system Shabana Mahmood will announce the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK, as she hopes that offering "safe and legal" routes will deter small boat crossings. The home secretary will say the UK wants to "live up to our international obligations" by helping those who are fleeing war and persecution, but the process must be "capped and controlled". The Home Office said the UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will reopen immediately and expects that around 25% of arrivals will be Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Mahmood was making a "desperate attempt to appease" people within Labour who have been critical of her asylum reforms. Hundreds of people are expected to arrive under the UKRS, which stopped taking new applicants in December 2024, and three new sponsorship routes. The latter will involve communities, universities and companies hosting refugees from next year. The Home Office expects arrivals to increase to the "low thousands" as levels of illegal migration fall. A cap will be set for each year although details of the number have yet to be provided. People arriving in Britain under the safe and legal routes will be be put on a five-year path to permanent settlement. Mahmood is expected to tell the Labour Party conference on Monday that "fairness" is behind her approach, limits are needed and communities "must be ready and able to welcome those who come here". She will also say: "This is what we can do and who we can be as we restore control to our borders, bear down on the small boat crossings, and unlock the inherent generosity of this country." More than 18,500 people have crossed the Channel in small boats this year compared to more than 32,000 than the same period in 2025. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "not obligated to take in more migrants", adding if his party was in power then those arriving under Labour's schemes would "not be able to stay". He said: "If Labour are so sure the public wants their open borders policies, they'd call a general election to get a mandate." In expressing his criticism, Farage also referenced a report in The Sunday Times, external about a former bodyguard to the leader of Hamas securing asylum and citizenship in the UK before "plotting" an attack against Jewish people in Europe. The newspaper reported the man moved to the UK more than a decade ago and now faces extradition to Germany. Jon Featonby, chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, welcomed the government's new proposals but said it came after a "drastic reduction in safe routes over the last year". He said: "Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people smugglers' business model, but they only work if they operate at scale. "The government has to show ambition and commitment, and that means thousands of places, not hundreds. "Alongside any new schemes, the government must also reopen refugee family reunion without delay." Rayner criticises visa rule proposals ahead of Labour conference UK suspends refugee family reunion applications Thousands of Afghans were moved to UK in secret scheme after data breach Safe and legal routes run, external to bring refugees from other countries to the UK have included schemes helping Afghans following the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan, Ukrainians affected after Russia launched its full-scale invasion and British National (Overseas) passport holders from Hong Kong. More than 39,000 people arrived under the Afghan Resettlement Programme and in July 2025 the government confirmed the schemes were either closed to new applicants or discontinued. A scheme allowing refugees to bring their family members to the UK was paused in September 2025. Government statistics show the UKRS resettled 4,589 refugees after its launch in 2021. Flora Alexander, executive director of the International Rescue Committee UK, said she welcomed the government prioritising Afghan women and girls and Palestinians under the UKRS. She described the UKRS as a "well-established safe route" to support people to "rebuild their lives in the UK", adding: "But it needs to be scaled up if it is to make a real difference." For the Conservatives, Philp said: "We shouldn't be shipping in any more migrants or asylum seekers, no matter how deserving, until illegal immigration has been reduced to close to zero. "Shabana Mahmood is running scared of Angela Rayner and the Labour left. She is opening up our borders even more in a desperate attempt to appease them." Rayner, the housing secretary, renewed her criticism of Mahmood's planned changes to the asylum system on the eve of Labour's conference in Liverpool. The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years. Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules. Settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. title: Four ways to keep your energy bills down
description: Household energy bills are due to rise again in October but there are ways to keep a lid on your expenditure.
body: Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and drinking hot drinks can help reduce heating bills Energy prices are rising to a three-year high at the start of October and forecasts suggest there will also be a hefty increase in costs in January. Regulator Ofgem's price cap affects millions of people on variable or default tariffs, but those on a range of tariffs may use more energy - and so pay more - if it proves to be a cold winter. So what can you do to keep a check on rising bills? The energy regulator, Ofgem, is advising people to consider fixing - so that the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use. The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment. Should energy prices rise sharply, then those who have fixed already have the certainty of what they will pay for each unit of energy. That price may well be lower than the forecast price in January. However, if events in the Gulf region settle down, and a peace deal in the Iran war leads to lower international gas prices, then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap. So consumer group Which? also recommends keeping an eye on any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum. Before you fix, consumer website Money Saving Expert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering. Energy price cap: How much gas and electricity does a typical household use? Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months. For some that's because they do not want their supplier to estimate their usage in case they are overcharged. Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem. Moreover, paying by direct debit costs less per unit than by so-called standard credit. You will usually - although not always - need to switch to direct debit if you want to take advantage of the fixed deals on offer. Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate. There are also a range of pricing schemes offering cheaper off-peak electricity, for example if they are charging an electric car overnight. Changing habits when using household appliances can also help, for example reducing washing machine temperatures There are a range of ways people on low incomes can access support. This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill. Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help. Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment, external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment, after political pressure forced the government to U-turn on its plan to restrict it to the poorest pensioners. Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme, external can help you repay energy debt. You can get more advice from Ofgem, external, Citizens Advice, external, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes, external. People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like. But if you are hunting round for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes. Once the temperature outside starts to fall again, it is important to stay warm, especially for the very young, old, and those with health conditions or reduced mobility. But there are plenty of ways you can keep bills lower without letting the temperature in your home fall below the recommended 18C minimum. You may already have hung thicker curtains and blocked the draughts over the last couple of winters, but do not forget to switch off radiators in rooms you are not using and wrap up. Money Saving Expert advises to "heat the human not the home". Turning down the flow rate on a combi boiler can save you money as often the water is being heated higher than it needs to be. Batch cooking and using an air fryer or microwave rather than heating up the oven for a small item can save energy. Take shorter showers and wash clothes at 30C rather than 40C. Dry clothes outdoors if you can, rather than using a tumble dryer, or hang clothes indoors but ventilate well or use a dehumidifier to avoid damp. If you are thinking about moving home, or undertaking renovations, it is worth thinking through how to reduce bills. When it comes to white goods, look for energy-efficient appliances. title: Faslane dry docks and research ship to be built in UK, says chancellor
description: John Healey says orders worth £6bn will be placed with a UK-based shipbuilder as part of a "new age of industrialisation".
body: The new dry docks will significantly enhance capacity at the Faslane naval base in the Firth of Clyde Orders for three floating dry docks, worth £6bn, to maintain the Royal Navy's nuclear-powered submarine fleet at Faslane will go to a UK-based shipbuilder, the chancellor has confirmed. John Healey told the Labour conference the facilities were vital to national security and would support domestic shipbuilding as part of a "new age of industrialisation". A UK-only bidding competition will decide who builds the floating docks but Navantia UK, which owns sites in Fife and Belfast, is seen as a frontrunner. Healey has also pledged £115m for construction in the UK of a new marine research vessel to replace Cefas Endeavour, built by the Ferguson shipyard on the Clyde more than 20 years ago. He told delegates in Liverpool: "I want to confirm today that we, this government will commit to £6bn of contracts for our British shipyards. "They'll build the new docks for the submarines that will defend us all for decades to come, built in Britain by British workers because of the decisions of this Labour government." Submarines are currently hoisted clear of the water inside the shiplift building at Faslane The investment is part of a wider £15bn upgrade of the Faslane site, on the eastern side of Gare Loch, over the coming decade. Floating dry docks are structures that can be submerged to allow a ship or submarine to enter. They are then raised and emptied of water, enabling inspections, maintenance and repair. Unlike their land-based equivalents, their ability to float means they can be towed to different locations. The last floating dry dock to be manufactured in the UK is believed to be Admiralty Dock 60, built in the 1960s and based at HMNB Clyde at Faslane until the late 1990s when it was sold for commercial use. Currently the base has to rely on a single shiplift, an elevator-type device which hoists submarines out of the water inside a large maintenance building. Harland & Wolff, prior to its takeover by Navantia, issued visualisations of construction of the dry docks taking place at Methil in Fife The Spanish state-owned shipbuilder Navantia has been lobbying hard to build the new floating docks for Faslane, through its UK division. The company owns the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast, along with fabrication sites at Arnish on the Isle of Lewis, Methil in Fife and Appledore in Devon. The GMB union has previously written to Healey, external asking for the work to be shared between the Methil site and Belfast. Other possible contenders include the Cammell Laird shipyard in Merseyside, now owned by Balaena, and Babcock which has facilities at Rosyth. A new ship will be ordered to replace the research vessel Cefas Endeavour Healey has also confirmed funding for a ship to replace Cefas Endeavour, the UK government's main fisheries and marine science research ship. Operated by the Centre of Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas) the ship is based at Lowestoft in Suffolk. Cefas Endeavour was launched in 2002 by the now nationalised Ferguson shipyard in Port Glasgow on the Clyde, and entered service the following year. The firm could potentially bid to build the replacement as its size - expected to be up to 85m (279ft) - is well-suited to the yard's capabilities. But Ferguson's is likely to face competition from other commercial yards such as Navantia and Cammell Laird. Cefas Endeavour was a technically challenging ship, with exacting specifications for noise and vibration so that it would not disturb fish during survey work. Still in active service after 20 years, its replacement is expected to be delivered in the early 2030s. Healey also used his speech to announce that Rolls-Royce will invest an extra £300m into its British factories in Derby, in Bristol, in Glasgow and in Rotherham. title: Watch: Were the arrests near RAF Fairford 'pure luck'?
description: A farmer who called 999 when she saw a group of "masked men" near RAF Fairford early on Sunday believes she "foiled" their plans by "pure luck".
body: This video can not be played A farmer who called 999 when she saw a group of "masked men" near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday believes she "foiled" their plans by "pure luck". But she only has a "partial picture" of what happened, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said. The RAF base is used by the US military, and President Donald Trump has stated that the US had the five men "under view for a long time". So what really happened? BBC Security Correspondent Frank Gardner has this analysis. More on the RAF Fairford incident. Watch: Were the arrests near RAF Fairford 'pure luck'? title: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back
description: Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment".
body: A sign campaigning against the centre displayed outside a home in a Sydney suburb Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners. The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area. The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners. The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres. With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction. However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities. The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it. According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application, external. In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation". "During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said. It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development. The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres. The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy. In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community". "This is a common-sense win for our community," he said. "This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward. "Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind." AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost? title: Lithium-ion battery caused fire that killed mum and 3 children
description: Elisha Brabin, 36, and three of her children, died after a blaze at their home in Bootle, Merseyside.
body: (l-r) Elisha Brabin (with Prudence) and three of her children: Ellis, Prudence and Leo died in the house fire A fatal house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery, the fire service has said. Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of 22 September. Following an investigation with Merseyside Police, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said the fire was caused by an electrical event linked to a lithium-ion battery, which are used in e-bikes and e-scooters. Kev Johnson, of MFRS, said: "This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire." Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property, at 03:45 BST last Tuesday. MFRS said four people "showing no signs of life" had been found in an upstairs bedroom. A fifth casualty was taken to hospital suffering from burns. Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze "This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of the mother and children who lost their lives and those who were injured," said Johnson, head of prevention at the fire service. He commended the efforts of staff and NWAS colleagues "who made every effort to provide a different outcome". "Sadly this was not the case due to the speed and intensity of the fire". MFRS has not confirmed what the battery was being used for, but they are often found in e-bikes and e-scooters. The fire service said there had been 150 fires linked to lithium-ion batteries in Merseyside between April 2023 and August 2026, and five fatalities linked to the batteries. Johnson said: "We're urging people to follow the manufacturer's instructions - only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk. "It's also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge, or is smoking, please stop using immediately."
