title: New NHS-style social care system could take decades, Dilnot says
description: Sir Andrew Dilnot, who proposed reforms 15 years ago, says the cost of such a scheme would be "very substantial".
body: A new NHS-style social care system for England could take decades to be implemented, economist Sir Andrew Dilnot has told the BBC. Sir Andrew, who led a commission proposing reform of the system 15 years ago, said Prime Minister Andy Burnham appeared to want social care to be completely free, including residential costs. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the cost of such a scheme would be "very substantial". And with Burnham promising to put his plans before voters at the next general election, Sir Andrew said change "is now further away". Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home. However, unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use in England, leaving some people facing huge bills. In an interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Burnham suggested his proposals for social care would mean "everyone contributes, everyone is covered" and refused to rule out tax rises to fund such a system. He promised to set out more details of his vision in his conference speech on Tuesday. However, he suggested any proposals would not be implemented before the next general election, as he wanted to stick to the commitments in Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which included a promise not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT. Labour MP and former minister Darren Jones told Laura Kuenssberg that scrapping the pensions triple lock was an "option that the government should consider alongside others" in order to fund social care reforms. The triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest - and keeping it in place is also a Labour manifesto pledge. But Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said scrapping the triple lock would not be enough to pay for social care and tax rises would also probably be needed. The next general election is not due until August 2029, although Burnham could choose to call one earlier. Sir Andrew told the BBC change on social care "is now further away" than had been implied when Burnham first promised a new national care service for England in a speech in July, shortly after he became prime minister. He pointed out that if proposals are included in Labour's 2029 election manifesto, that would be 30 years after Sir Tony Blair launched a royal commission on social care and more than 15 years since his own commission reported back. Social care reform could mean big risks and big rewards for Burnham Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge By promising an NHS-style system for social care, Sir Andrew said the PM was implying it would be "entirely free". In England and Northern Ireland, people with assets worth more than £23,250 - including their home - are not currently entitled to help with care costs from their council. In Wales, social care is also means-tested. In Scotland, state-funded personal care is offered to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing. However, this does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs, which are subject to means testing. Sir Andrew said a Scottish-style system would still leave people in residential care facing "very substantial bills", which Burnham has said he wants to avoid. The Health Foundation has estimated a universal social care system in England, with the government funding all support, could cost around £18.5bn a year. On Sunday, Burnham said he believed the costs would be lower than this but he has not set out how he would fund his plans. Sir Andrew said he believed an NHS-style social care system could costs "well in excess of £18bn", although a Scottish model could cost half this figure. He added: "I also think that there was an indication in what [Burnham] said that he's imagining something that could take many years, even many decades before it came to fruition." Sir Andrew said he would "love to see such a scheme", where all social care is government-funded, but "the cost would become very, very large". He added that a system where the amount people must pay towards their care is capped, "could still work well for elderly people". Sir Andrew's own commission proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000. The report's recommendations were accepted by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron. However, the implementation of the cap was delayed to 2020, with Cameron blaming pressure on the public finances, and the idea was eventually dropped by subsequent Conservative governments. Other proposals to reform the system have also failed, with Theresa May's Conservative government scrapping plans to make people receiving care at home pay the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000, after this was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents. Meanwhile, when he was health secretary in Gordon Brown's government, Burnham's plan for a national care service suggested this could be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they die. The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election. title: Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt
description: A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women were on board the boat - which was carrying 105 people.
body: Rescuees were taken back to the port in Calais after disembarking A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women have died after a small boat that was attempting to cross the English Channel got into difficulty off the northern coast of France, local authorities have said. Officials responded to a distress call from the boat, which was carrying 105 people, after it departed from the Blériot Plage in Sangatte on Monday morning. Three passengers were treated on board but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter, the French Maritime Prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said. Pas-de-Calais prefecture said its initial findings suggested the deaths were caused by trampling but an investigation has been launched to determine the exact cause. Of the 102 other people on board, nine were treated by emergency services upon their arrival in the port of Calais, the prefecture said. François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, blamed the incident on smuggling networks, which he said expose vulnerable people, including children, to the deadly risks of crossings. The prefecture described the boat as a taxi-boat, which requires migrants to wade out onto the water to board. Three other people died after similar taxi-boat departures last week, French authorities said. Monday's deaths take the total number of migrants who have died so far this year to 20, according to Pas-de-Calais prefecture. For the same period last year, it said the number was 21. Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey from France to the UK every year. In doing so, they cross one of the most dangerous and busiest shipping lanes in the world. More people attempt the route in the summer months when the weather is warmer and when seas are calmer. The UK recorded the highest number of migrant arrivals so far this year on Wednesday - with a total of 781 arriving in 10 small boats, according to Home Office figures. Two boats also reached UK shores last week without being intercepted by UK authorities, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent. In July last year, France and the UK agreed on a "one in, one out" returns deal, which was designed as a deterrent to stop boats from crossing the Channel. The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain. In August the UK government said it was making progress in tackling small boats, with the percentage who had made the journey in 2026 much lower than for the same period in 2025 but added it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade". So far, 2026 has seen 18,609 people successfully make the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats. 781 migrants arrive in small boats in 2026 record Channel smuggling gangs resort to 'mega-dinghies' as crackdown limits small boat supply Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC Five men arrested near RAF Fairford on suspicion of terror offences were UK nationals from London, police say Watch: Were the RAF Fairford arrests 'pure luck'? title: Comebacks, fly-hacks and cornrows - Prem talking points
description: Old names, new looks and some stunning scores marked the return of the Prem for another season.
body: Brendan Venter's Saracens, Santi Carreras' Bath and Henry Pollock's Northampton all made winning starts to their Prem seasons At the start of pre-season, at their St Albans training ground, Brendan Venter made a speech to his Saracens squad. "I don't want to be competitive in this league," the returning director of rugby said. "I want to dominate." Sunday was a good start. Sarries were short of domination - the lead swapped hands four times in the final half hour of a blockbuster - but victory away at Leicester was a fine statement of intent. Hobbled by an injury to Olly Hartley in the first half and then reduced to 14 men by Nick Isiekwe's 20-minute red card in the second, the visitors nonetheless dug deep and silenced the baying Tigers fans with an extraordinary 40-38 win. "We've worked a lot more on our mental game, our ability to deal with setbacks, to keep sticking to our process when things don't go our way," Ben Earl, who was initially deployed in the centres in a rejigged backline, told BBC Radio 5 Live afterwards. "Maybe a different Sarries team from the last couple of years would probably have dropped away in different points in that, but we kept fighting away and finding a way." Since their return from the Championship, no club has racked up more regular-season Prem points over the last five campaigns than Saracens. They haven't felt as consistent as that stat suggests though. They narrowly missed out on the play-offs in each of the past two seasons. This year, they have been strengthened by signings; Tomos Williams crackled with cunning at scrum-half. But they also have a hugely promising generation of talent coming through. Second row Olamide Sodeke, 21, came on and played his part in a massive front-five final-quarter effort. Twenty-two year-old Nathan Michelow, part of the England's 2024 under-20 World Cup winning side, is pushing hard for a starting spot in a stacked back row. If Venter can marry young, new and superstar existing talent, while rallying the squad around his belligerent belief, they will be hard to stop. Saracens edge out Leicester despite Isiekwe red Taking care to stay in play, Carreras gathers his own kick ahead to score a crucial try for Bath You probably have seen it already. If you haven't, you really should., external The try of the round came 32 minutes into Bath's win at Harlequins on Friday night. The hosts, only four points down at that stage, had a clear two-on-one 30m out down the left wing. Quins' Tyrone Green made what he thought would be a scoring pass to Oscar Beard, only for Bath full-back Santi Carreras to lunge foot-first between the two. The ball cannoned upwards, Carreras chased, gathered one-handed and raced in under the sticks at the other end. An outrageous score, with an outrageous slice of luck presuming Carreras was gambling to get anything on the ball, rather than plotting that particular flightpath. It is unlikely many will repeat Carreras's exact play. But more may start sticking a boot into the passing lane in similar situations, given the stakes involved. Had Carreras gone with a hand and knocked on, he was likely looking at a penalty try and a sin-binning, given the lack of cover behind. All that was at risk by going for a volleyed fly-hack was looking very silly had Green hung on to the ball. Carreras magic lights up Bath win over Harlequins Will Joseph leaves Immanuel Feyi-Waboso in his wake en route to a solo score Gloucester's pre-season was not all forward-facing. Brett Deacon and Joel Tomkins, brought in from Leicester and Catalan Dragons, as new forwards and defence coach respectively also used a bit of nostalgia to inspire their new charges. Mike Teague, part of a gnarly 1980s Cherry-and-White pack, was among the club legends they channelled to explain the hard-nosed approach they wanted. In winning away to Exeter, there was plenty of that grit on show. As there should be when you look down the teamsheet Val Rapava Ruskin is one of the top-flight's best scrummaging loose-heads. He packed down alongside Dewi Lake, who put in a player-of-the-match performance on debut, and England prospect Afolabi Fasogbon. The second row consisted of Springbok Rugby World Cup winner Jean Kleyn and Arthur Clark, one of the league's best young locks. Add in the energy and bravery of Jac Morgan, typically topping the turnover and tackle charts, Freddie Thomas's industry and Will Trenholm's old-school go-forward and there is a foundation there to build on. Out the back there is a rat-pack set of bright young English-qualified things. Seb Atkinson was immense. Will Joseph scorched past Immanuel Feyi-Waboso for a superb score. Ben Redshaw at full-back is eye-wateringly rapid. Fly-half Charlie Atkinson, all clever kicks and keen eye for a gap, has looked the part since switching back into 10 from full-back halfway though last season. All are 24 or under. Chris Boyd, newly appointed as the club's technical director, previously moulded something special from Northampton's raw, local talent. You would forgive some in the Shed for dreaming big. "The important thing is that it's not one and done for us," said Lake afterwards. Quins at home on Saturday is next up and expectations have been raised. Gloucester wanted to lay down marker - Lake Gloucester shock Exeter for superb victory Wales team-mates Tomos Williams and Aaron Wainwright collide as Saracens take on Leicester With the upheaval and restructuring in Welsh rugby, the perennial talking point of turning the Prem into an Anglo-Welsh league reared its head over the summer. Rob Baxter, Pat Lam and George Skivington, bosses of Exeter, Bristol and Gloucester respectively, are all positive on the idea. title: Watch: Were the RAF Fairford arrests 'pure luck'?
description: Five men have been arrested on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences after a major incident was declared at an airbase in the west of England.
body: This video can not be played A farmer who called 999 when she saw a group of "masked men" near RAF Fairford early on Sunday believes she "foiled" their plans by "pure luck". But she only has a "partial picture" of what happened, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said. The RAF base is used by the US military, and President Donald Trump said the US had the five men "under view for a long time". More on the RAF Fairford incident. title: Apple ordered to pay $5.7bn after losing vibration tech patent suit
description: Audio firm Taction Technology claimed Apple infringed its patents for tech used to power device vibrations.
body: Apple has been ordered to pay $5.7bn (£4.3bn) in damages after a US jury found it had used another firm's tech without permission. Audio firm Taction Technology claimed in 2021 that Apple had infringed two of its patents for haptics systems, which enable vibrations for actions such as receiving a message or pressing a button. This tech is built into devices like the iPhone and Apple Watch. Apple has been approached for comment. In a statement given to news outlets including CNBC, external, the company said it had not used Taction's vibration tech and would appeal the verdict. "While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts," Apple said. "Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial." Haptics allow people to interact with devices by simulating the sense of touch or feel through vibrations. They have become a hallmark of modern devices, with smartphones, watches and video game controllers among those containing small motors that move in response to specific electronic signals. Apple's "Taptic Engine" system - enabling haptic feedback in its devices - first debuted with the Apple Watch in 2014. Since then, it has improved its underlying system, and with that expanded haptics in its devices. Taction, which makes headphones and gaming headsets, claimed in 2021 that these improvements infringed patents it was issued in 2020. It wrote in its complaint, external that by producing better haptic vibrations in its devices, Apple had been able to improve its overall user experience. As such, the tech giant had been "capitalising on Taction's innovation and success by selling devices that infringe [its] patents", Taction said. It also accused Apple of using its inventions "without license or authority". A San Diego judge ruled in 2023 that Apple did not infringe upon Taction's patents. However, an appeal was subsequently taken up by a federal appeal circuit - resulting in a September jury trial at the US District Court for the Southern District of California which found in its favour. In Friday's verdict, external, jurors did not find that Apple had infringed the patents in question willingly. It marks one of many similar lawsuits the tech giant has defended itself against in recent years. In November 2025 a judge ordered Apple to pay $634m, external to medical tech firm Masimo after a jury found it had infringed a patent for blood-oxygen reading tech. title: Judge imposes £100,000 bail condition on Rwanda genocide accused
description: Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He denies wrongdoing.
body: Dr Vincent Brown was allegedly a "leader" or "supervisor" of violent acts carried out by others A man accused of offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide will remain in custody unless he pays the court a £100,000 guarantee. Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, was allegedly a "leader" or "supervisor" of violent acts carried out by others and is the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide. At the Old Bailey on Monday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC granted conditional bail with stricter conditions than at a previous hearing, including the increased surety and electronic monitoring. Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He denies wrongdoing. Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son between April 6 and 13. The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime. Brown, of Islington, north London, was charged following a seven-year British investigation into the killings. An estimated 800,000 Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were killed during the 1994 Rwanda genocide which lasted for 100 days. On Wednesday the judge imposed a £100,000 bail condition on Brown's release. This is up from an earlier £25,000 security imposed by magistrates. Brown was also ordered to surrender his passport and any national identity cards, not to apply for international travel documents and was told he must abide by a curfew to live and sleep at his London address. He would also be electronically monitored and have to report daily to police. Lucraft said that until the £100,000 condition was met, the defendant would remain in custody. Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son. In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda. He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government. Brown is next due to appear at the Old Bailey on 9 October. Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda. title: Mexico's Pacific coast braces for Hurricane Polo
description: The category-four storm is approaching the state of Baja California Sur, on Mexico's northern Pacific coast.
body: Lifeguards raised red flags on the beaches of Baja California Sur to alert holidaymakers of the hazardous sea conditions People living on the northern Pacific coast of Mexico are bracing for the arrival of Hurricane Polo, which is forecast to make landfall later on Monday or early on Tuesday. The category three storm, with maximum sustained winds near 115 mph (185 km/h), is expected to move over the state Baja California Sur, a region popular with tourists and home to the resort destination of Los Cabos. Meteorologists at the US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) have warned of heavy rainfall which could lead to life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain. Residents on Sunday stocked up on essentials such as drinking water and food as the storm approached. The NHC warned of the storm surge Hurricane Polo could unleash, which it said could be accompanied by large and destructive waves. In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, the authorities restricted access to the beaches. Some restaurants also closed in the town, which acts as a base for sport fishers and whale watchers. The Arch was created by the tides and the erosion of the wind over thousands of years The regional government of Baja California Sur has ordered schools to remain closed on Monday as a preventive measure. Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said temporary shelters had been opened should residents need to be evacuated. The federal authorities have also deployed thousands of members of the navy and the army along with specialised machinery. Polo has been slowly moving towards Mexico's coast line. Meteorologists said it was being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon. title: Offshore wind plant to bring jobs boost to Montrose
description: The new facility will manufacture parts for offshore wind farms in Scottish waters and for overseas markets.
body: The Port of Montrose has also been selected as the preferred base for a major offshore windfarm project An offshore wind turbine facility is to be created at the Port of Montrose, supporting about 80 jobs. The factory, which will make components for off-shore wind turbines, is to be run by engineering firm Subsea Micropiles following a £5m investment. A further £6.7m is being provided by the state-owned Scottish National Investment Bank, with Scottish Enterprise also pledging £1.45m. First Minister John Swinney, during a visit to the site in Angus, said it would help ensure "benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland". He also welcomed an announcement from SSE that the Port of Montrose is its preferred location for an operations base for the Berwick Bank B offshore wind farm, which is expected to create a further 100 jobs. The Berwick project, set to be one of the largest offshore wind farms in the world, will see up to 307 turbines generating enough electricity to power up to six million homes. Subsea Micropiles, which has offices in Ireland and Aberdeenshire, already has an operations base at the Port of Montrose. The firm's new facility is expected to make parts for wind turbines in Scottish waters, and for international markets. Chief executive Derek Robertson said: "Scotland has become an important base for our growth. "We rely on the deep pool of talent, skills and offshore experience here to develop our technology, services and expand into a global market. He added that the company's products "can be manufactured locally, with the potential to retain significant economic benefit in Scotland through engineering, vessel services and offshore supply chain". Swinney said: "Scotland is already recognised as being at the forefront of floating offshore wind development. "The investment behind today's announcements is a strong vote of confidence in the sector and in the skilled workforce, innovation and expertise that exists here. "Subsea Micropiles' commitment to expand at the Port of Montrose will help ensure more of the economic benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland, creating high-quality jobs in Angus and the North East, supporting local businesses and strengthening our industrial capabilities." He added that SSE's selection of Montrose as its preferred location for the Berwick project would strengthen "Scotland's offshore wind supply chain" and create "more jobs as well as investment in skills, infrastructure and local communities". title: Buttler out of tri-series while England prepare central contracts
description: Wicketkeeper Jos Buttler will miss England's 50-over tri-series in Pakistan next month, with Jordan Cox set to be given another chance to impress in his place.
body: Buttler raced to 67 not out before injuring his hamstring against Sri Lanka at Headingley. He returned after retiring hurt but was dismissed for 69 from 49 balls Wicketkeeper Jos Buttler will miss England's 50-over tri-series in Pakistan next month, with Jordan Cox set to be given another chance to impress in his place. Buttler, 36, has been ruled out with the hamstring injury suffered while batting in Thursday's second one-day international against Sri Lanka at Headingley. Coach Brendon McCullum said it is "hard to judge" how long Buttler will be out for and confirmed Cox will take his place for the series against Pakistan and Sri Lanka, which begins on 20 October. "We know Jos is an incredible athlete, we know he is supremely fit and is an ultra-professional," McCullum said. "He will do everything he can to be back as soon as possible." England also tour Australia for white-ball matches in November - where they are considering playing warm-up matches - as they look to add to their six series wins in limited-overs cricket this year and build towards next year's 50-over World Cup. They will finalise their squads on Monday with the latest batch of central contracts also set to be announced in the coming days. Durham opener Emilio Gay is in line for a first deal after his debut Test summer, putting him in line to tour South Africa this winter, while Cox, Tom Banton, who scored his first international century on Sunday, and all-rounder Dan Lawrence could also feature. Contracts held by former captain Ben Stokes and Mark Wood are set to end after their international retirements. Ollie Pope, Zak Crawley, Matthew Potts and Luke Wood are all out of favour and their one-year deals are due to run out. Spinner Shoaib Bashir is another intriguing name in that category. He played two Tests against New Zealand and was picked in the Test squad to play Pakistan but did not make an XI as England preferred a four-man pace attack. England are learning - these are the World Cup issues they need to solve In a breakout international summer, Cox impressed by scoring fifties in all three Tests when picked to bat number three against Pakistan. He also hit 76 against Sri Lanka when deputising for Buttler in the third ODI at The Oval on Sunday. "I thought it was quite a Jos Buttler innings," McCullum said. "He has done really well domestically for a number of years and has been unlucky with injuries. "For him to have the type of summer he has had and be in the position he is in, he deserves it. "He is a phenomenal talent, is very well liked in dressing room as well and seems to be one of those guys who is good at everything he does, which will be incredibly annoying." England will also make a decision on whether to pick bowler Brydon Carse to tour Pakistan. He has not been selected since being arrested then de-arrested on a night out in Derby in August. After a police investigation ended without action, he is now subject to a Cricket Regulator investigation and, while he remains available for selection, white-ball captain Harry Brook said last week he needs time away from the international scene. McCullum, who began the summer as England's coach across the three formats before being sacked from the Test role in July, dismissed any suggestion of regret at the end of the English season. "I loved coaching all three formats," he said. "Things move on, times change. I am biased but I genuinely think [new Test coach] Stephen Fleming will do an unbelievable job with the red-ball side. "With the extra bit of time it probably does allow you to drill down on a few aspects you have identified you need to improve or shape things differently to get to where you want to." title: Passports needed for ferry passengers travelling between UK and Ireland
description: Previously, passengers were able to use other forms of ID, such as driving licences and national identity cards.
body: The changes are being brought in to comply with UK Border Force rules Passengers travelling on ferries between the UK and the Republic of Ireland will need to show their passport from Monday. Ferry operator Irish Ferries said the new requirement applies to their Dublin to Holyhead and Rosslare to Pembroke routes, in both directions. Stena Line said all passengers travelling from Dublin, Holyhead, Fishguard or Rosslare ports would also be required to present a valid passport at check-in. Previously, passengers were able to use other forms of ID, such as driving licences and national identity cards - but the changes are being brought in to comply with UK Border Force rules. In a statement on its website, Stena Line said the change would meet UK Border Force requirements "in relation to the accuracy and integrity of passenger data before boarding". Irish Ferries said the requirement would apply to all passengers, including Irish and UK citizens, adding that from Monday, driving licences, national identity cards and other forms of photographic identification would no longer be accepted on the two routes in question. Irish Ferries said passengers who were not British or Irish citizens and were visiting for a short stay of up to six months in the UK may need an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA), which allows travel to the UK, Jersey, Guernsey or the Isle of Man for up to six months. Passport cards will also be accepted by both operators. title: Norris apologises to Colapinto for ban comments
description: World champion Lando Norris apologises to Franco Colapinto for saying the Argentine should be banned for causing an accident at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
body: Franco Colapinto's lock-up in Turn One took out his Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly as well as McLaren's Lando Norris Lando Norris has apologised to Franco Colapinto for saying the Argentine should be banned for causing an accident at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Colapinto locked up at the restart after a safety-car period and slid into Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly, who then hit McLaren driver Norris, in an incident which resulted in all three retiring from the race. Colapinto said he was "sorry" for his "big mistake" but Norris, speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, said: "Give him a ban. It's quite simple." In a message on Instagram, world champion Norris said he was sorry for his comments on Saturday. "Tough weekend overall in Baku and of course a disappointing and early end to the race," he said. "After the race, I sent Franco a message apologising for the comments I made that I simply should not have said. "I know better and emotions were running high but that is not an excuse, it was wrong of me. "I've made mistakes of my own over the years and I know this is very much a part of racing and fighting on the limit. "Me and Franco came to a good understanding, are still good friends and are both excited to get back racing this weekend." Colapinto was given a 10-second penalty during the race, but as he was already retired this has been converted into a five-place grid drop, which he will serve at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia this weekend. title: UK diesel price hits all-time high, RAC says
description: The US-Israel war with Iran has caused fuel prices to soar.
body: Diesel prices have hit an all-time high of 199.18p per litre, according to the motoring organisation RAC, as the war in the Middle East continues to push up the cost of fuel. Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.13p. Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge. RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away". The cost of diesel has now risen by 59p a litre, or just under 40%, since the conflict between the USA and Iran erupted at the end of February. The previous record was 199.09p in June 2022. The increase means the cost of filling an average family car with diesel is now £110, £31 more than at the start of the conflict. Petrol prices are now 41p per litre more than at the start of the conflict, but still well below a 2022 peak. The RAC data is based on the average price of diesel at a range of supermarkets, motorway service stations and independent retailers. Simon Williams, RAC's head of policy, said the diesel record "spells pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans". "Undoubtedly these increased costs will be passed on to consumers," he said. Williams said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days". The price of Brent crude, a benchmark for global oil used to make petrol, diesel and other fuel products, rose over the weekend and is now hovering at around $108 per barrel. Before the US invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73. Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets. Russia, which is also a major producer, has also implemented an export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand. The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs. UK diesel price hits all-time high There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before. There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million. title: Man City rule breaches not my concern - Mancini
description: Roberto Mancini says an alleged "double contract" during his time as Manchester City manager is "not my concern".
body: Roberto Mancini managed Manchester City from December 2009 until May 2013 Roberto Mancini says an alleged "double contract" during his time as Manchester City manager is "not my concern" after the club were found guilty of breaking the majority of the financial rules they were accused of breaching. The 115 charges brought by the Premier League against City included 14 instances of failing to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from 2009-10 to 2017-18. That period covered Mancini's three and a half years in charge, during which he won the FA Cup in 2011 and City's first top-flight title for 44 years in 2012. Mancini, the current Italy manager, was asked during a news conference before Monday's Nations League game against Turkey about the allegations relating to his remuneration as City manager. "Found guilty of what?" he said. "It's not an issue that concerns me. It's nothing new because this matter has been discussed for the last four or five years. "Manchester City has not been found guilty, and the alleged double contract is not my concern. It's their issue, not mine." This video can not be played Mancini 'not concerned' by City charges German newspaper Der Spiegel had previously accused City of paying a "significant portion" of Mancini's compensation "by way of a fictitious consultancy contract". It alleged that Mancini was paid more by City for his role as a consultant to Abu Dhabi club Al Jazira than he was getting from his role as City manager, excluding bonuses and incentives. On Friday it emerged that an independent panel had found City guilty of all but one count of charges brought against them by the Premier League, although sanctions have yet to be determined. The Premier League declined to comment, while City released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality". It added: "The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence." Other Premier League clubs are believed to have been informed about the decision and have sought legal advice over possible compensation claims. City were charged with more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules following a four-year investigation in February 2023. The club was referred to an independent commission. A behind-closed-doors hearing began in September 2024 and ran for about 12 weeks. title: FAI unclear over possible sanctions if game not played
description: Republic of Ireland could have faced "undetermined" sanctions had they not played their Nations League match against Israel on Sunday, according to FAI president Paul Cooke.
body: Paul Cooke was speaking after the Republic of Ireland's win in Hungary Republic of Ireland could have faced "undetermined" sanctions had they not played their Nations League match against Israel on Sunday, according to FAI president Paul Cooke. The players did not shake hands with each other and the Republic of Ireland squad bowed their heads when Israel's anthem was played before their 3-0 win in Hungary. The two Nations League fixtures, being played at neutral venues, have been embroiled in controversy since February when the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3. The Republic of Ireland players have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace. There was also no exchange of pennants between Republic of Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel skipper Manor Solomon, who did not shake hands. Cooke added that along with standard punishments for not fulfilling a fixture, there was were also possible "undetermined" extras. "No," he told RTE Sport when asked is Uefa threatened additional sanctions if one or both of the matches were not fulfilled. "The rules are clear. It specifies if we don't fulfil the fixtures what the sanctions are and then there's reference to other sanctions undetermined. "I think it depends on Uefa and what sanctions they levy on somebody as a result of it. We saw a recent thing in England and Southampton, the levies that were levied on them [expelled from the English Championship play-offs after admitting spying on opponents]." Republic of Ireland 'raised awareness worldwide' in Israel game Republic of Ireland defeat Israel in Debrecen Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place with players locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding. The FAI later confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game - the second match between the sides will take place on 4 October in the Serbian town of Backa Topola. Cooke, who praised the players and manager Heimir Hallgrimsson after the victory, defended how the FAI dealt with the build-up to the controversial match. "Some people think it was quite well handled. "We said all along that we would play the game. That was mandated through us by our members, through the board, and we've fulfilled one of the fixtures now thanks to the courage of those players who played tonight and togged out." Cooke was also asked about Uefa's response to an FAI letter sent last November which proposed Israel's expulsion from international and club competitions. "Their response was that they'd consider it and they're still considering it," he said. Cooke has spoken to the the two other countries in the group - Austria and Kosovo - asking if would they back sanctions against Israel. "I've certainly spoken to the other countries in our group and they reaffirmed their decisions to play the games." title: British chess prodigy, 11, becomes youngest woman grandmaster
description: The 11-year-old has broken another chess record after a remarkable performance representing England.
body: Bodhana first took up chess during the Covid pandemic A British child chess prodigy has become the youngest player in history to earn the woman grandmaster (WGM) title. Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, from north-west London, secured her third and final WGM norm - a certified title-level performance - while representing England at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the International Chess Federation (FIDE) confirmed. Speaking to FIDE, Sivanandan said she was happy about the achievement but wanted to "keep making history". It is the latest milestone in a remarkable rise for the schoolgirl, who has already become Britain's youngest women's chess champion and the youngest person to represent England internationally in any sport. Sivanandan, from Harrow, played all 11 rounds on England's top board - a position assigned to the team's top player - and finished the tournament with eight points. She had already passed the 2300 rating threshold required for the WGM title before securing her third and final norm. She told Fide in an interview on Sunday about making history: "I'm happy to do it, but I want to keep going and keep making history as well, instead of just stopping here." Kateryna Lagno, who has represented both Russia and Ukraine, previously held the age record for the WGM title, having achieved it aged 12. Hou Yifan, from China, also achieved the title at 12 and remains the youngest woman to have earned the higher, open grandmaster (GM) title, which she achieved aged 14. Woman grandmaster is the highest woman only title a female player can attain and the rank is held for life. Sivanandan's success in Samarkand also earned her a second International Master (IM) norm, taking her another step towards the higher title. Players normally need three qualifying norms and a rating of at least 2400 to become an international master. Sivanandan now has two IM norms. The international master title, open to both sexes, ranks higher than Sivanandan's current accolades - the woman grandmaster and woman international master titles. Speaking to Fide about her love of the game, she added: "I like travelling and also because I do full-time school as well, it links to loads of school subjects, so it's really useful there as well." Bodhana Sivanandan attends school full-time whilst playing international chess Her father Siva previously told the BBC he had no idea where his daughter got her talent from as neither he or his wife, both engineering graduates, are any good at chess. Her rise through chess has been rapid. After teaching herself to play during the coronavirus lockdown, she entered her first tournament at Harrow Chess Club in July 2021. A year later, aged seven, she won all 24 of her games at the European Schools Championship. In 2023, she became the youngest person to avoid defeat against a grandmaster in a competitive game at the European Rapid and Blitz championship in Croatia. The following year, aged nine, she was selected to represent England at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest. The English Chess Federation said that selection, when she was nine, made her the youngest person to represent England internationally in any sport. Last year, aged 10, Sivanandan became the youngest female player to defeat a grandmaster when she beat Peter Wells at the British Chess Championships. In July this year, she earned her first IM norm at the Dole Open in France, becoming the youngest girl to achieve one, aged 11 years and four months. She also defeated grandmaster Marc'Andria Maurizzi, becoming the youngest girl known to beat a player rated above 2600 in a classical game. title: Childminder facing 'severe financial burden' as heating oil costs rise
description: The war in Iran is having a practical impact on people across the island as energy prices continue to climb.
body: Many households across Northern Ireland continue to be hit with high prices for home heating oil, with one woman saying there is a "severe" financial burden on childminders. The war in Iran is having a practical impact on people across the island as energy prices continue to climb. On 24 September, the average price of 500 litres of home heating oil in Northern Ireland was £561.83, according to the Consumer Council NI (CCNI), external. "It's a severe financial and operational burden on all registered childminders because as well as the prices of the oil, there's massive increases in the food bills, the insurance," Rachel Jeffers, from Stewartstown, County Tyrone said. "That's all increased massively and a lot of the parents are saying if we're increasing our rates it's a financial burden on them." Almost two-thirds of homes (62.5%) in Northern Ireland use oil for heating, the highest proportion of the UK nations. Unlike gas or electricity the heating oil market is unregulated, so global price rises are rapidly passed through to consumers. Childminder Rachel Jeffers says the cost of home heating is "always on the back of your mind" Alongside her six-year-old daughter and seven-year-old son, Jeffers minds one child after school hours and three children under school age all day. She told BBC News NI the cost of her home heating oil had "doubled" since last year. Last week, she purchased 500 litres of oil for £560. Jeffers said her tank was "not even near filled", but the price is currently too high to fill it completely. Jeffers said she had found herself turning off her heating sooner in the day than she usually would. During the winter months, Jeffers said she had to run the heating all day to keep the house warm for the young children. "Through the summer we were still using it because our hot water runs off our heating oil," she said. Jeffers has not yet had to increase her childminding fees, but it is something she has been "discussing". "The guilt is there also because whenever you start minding, the families nearly become an extension of your family, so you're feeling for them." She said the cost of home heating was "always on the back of your mind". In terms of the knock-on impact the high costs are having on her own family, Jeffers said she has had to rethink whether to send her children to after school activities. "They do piano, they do football, and you're sitting and questioning is it worth going to these? "And then that's impacting on them and they're out and they feel like they're missing out because they're seeing their friends still going to it, but you obviously then can't afford to do everything," she said. The CCNI's weekly oil price checker, external shows typical oil prices for 300, 500 and 900 litres and is updated every Thursday. Raymond Gormley, head of energy at the CCNI, told BBC News NI that the cost of home heating oil was "about 80% more expensive than it was just before the war with Iran started". "At the minute, 300 litres is about £347 and before the war began it was £202. That just shows you, that's £146 of a difference for 300 litres," Gormley said. "It's really hard for people to find that 80% increase in such a short space of time because, as we know, budgets are hard pressed as it is," he said. In short, Gormley said it "all depends on what happens in the Middle East". "If there is peace discussions and there is sort of a truce, you'll see prices coming down, slowly be that, but they'll come down. If not, if war continues, prices will only go one way," he said. He added that the oil prices were "really headline driven". He said prices had "come down slightly in a week". However, he added: "As you know, prices go up a lot quicker than they come down." Gormley is suggesting that people keep an eye on the daily oil prices. "If you're going to wait and see if your price is going to come down, well then keep an eye on the daily prices," he said. "And then you get to a point where you think you're going to buy, price around a few oil suppliers because there is a bit of variancy on prices there." Applications for a Stormont scheme to give eligible households a £100 voucher towards home heating oil costs opened on 9 September. About 340,000 lower-income households were expected to qualify for the payment which was first announced in March. As of midday on 23 September, a total of 123,987 applications had been received by the Department for Communities. Successful applicants for the Home Heating Oil Support Scheme, external expected to receive a payment card within 10 working days of applying. The scheme will be open for applications until 31 March 2027. It is open to households with a combined income of £30,000 or less, or those on certain benefits including pension credit and PIP. It is expected that 75% or more of applications will be processed automatically. However, some people will have to provide additional information to show they qualify. £100 home heating oil support scheme opens Consumers face another sharp rise in energy prices Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC Farmer who called 999 saw 'large group of hooded and masked men' near RAF Fairford, she tells BBC What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe Police block Orange Order from controversial parade route You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die Feather or foam? title: Award-winner to fourth choice - what has gone wrong for Ramsdale?
description: From challenging for the Premier League with Arsenal and playing for England, Aaron Ramsdale is now Southampton's fourth-choice goalkeeper.
body: Aaron Ramsdale has not played a competitive game of football for five months In April 2023, Aaron Ramsdale was within touching distance of winning the Premier League with Arsenal. But the goalkeeper made a costly error for the Gunners to give away the opening goal in a 3-3 draw with Southampton at Emirates Stadium which contributed to the demise of Arsenal's 2022-23 title bid. If Arsenal had won that game, the title would have been in their hands. Instead, the draw handed the initiative to Manchester City, who took full advantage. It was a mistake which perhaps also signalled the beginning of the end for Ramsdale under Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta. Four months later, the north London club brought in David Raya from Brentford and the Spaniard quickly claimed the number one spot. And in a somewhat unfortunate poetic twist, it is the Saints where Ramsdale finds himself completely out of favour three years on as the fourth-choice goalkeeper at a Championship club. From an England international on the cusp of greatness, Ramsdale is now in the almost unthinkable situation of being without senior football this season in the prime of his career at the age of 28. So why has Ramsdale had such a fall from grace and where have things gone wrong? Aaron Ramsdale made 89 appearances for Arsenal and kept 32 clean sheets Questions were raised among the Arsenal fanbase when the club paid £24m to sign Ramsdale from Sheffield United in August 2021 after the Blades had been relegated from the top flight. But he quickly won supporters over by producing a string of excellent saves in his debut season, perhaps most notably against Leicester City when he denied a James Maddison free-kick at full stretch - a save which Peter Schmeichel described at the time as "the best I've seen for years". After ousting Bernd Leno, his efforts helped Arsenal finish fifth in 2021-22, improving on an eighth-placed finish the previous year. The following season, Ramsdale was a vital cog in Arsenal's spine as they launched a surprise title challenge, only to be outdone by an imperious Manchester City side. Despite his blunder in the draw with Southampton - which was one of several results that dented Arsenal's title hopes - Ramsdale made the Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) team of the year and was also named goalkeeper of the year at the London Football Awards. But Ramsdale quickly fell behind Raya in the pecking order in 2023-24 and lost his starting berth after just four league games. And in one of the only two other Premier League matches he did play that season against Raya's then parent club Brentford, Ramsdale made another mistake to allow Yoane Wissa to put the Bees ahead. Arsenal recovered to win that game 2-1 in March 2024. But Ramsdale never played for the club again. He was sold to Southampton for £25m in August 2024 after returning from Euro 2024 with England, having been an unused sub throughout the competition in Germany. Clubs have paid a combined £74m in transfer fees for Aaron Ramsdale, who has five England caps At the time of Ramsdale's signing, he looked to be the perfect goalkeeper and a coup for Southampton. Russell Martin's side had just won promotion and were hoping to implement a style of play in the Premier League that had brought them such success the previous season. Ramsdale ticked all the boxes as a goalkeeper who had ability with his feet to complement Martin's preference to build up from the back. His previous spells at Sheffield United and Bournemouth also justified his addition as someone whose stock had continued to rise despite being involved in relegations. Ultimately, though, the move to Southampton did not work out as planned. He made 30 league appearances for a Saints side which finished bottom of the Premier League with just 12 points - the second-lowest ever points tally in the competition - and conceded more goals (66) than any other goalkeeper in 2024-25. That is not to say Ramsdale was to blame in a Southampton side which performed poorly across the board, with some fans at the time in fact praising him for keeping the score down in games. It would, however, be the fourth relegation Ramsdale had suffered, having already done so with Chesterfield, while on loan in 2017-18, the Cherries in 2019-20 - although he was named player of the year for Bournemouth that season - and then the Blades. Aaron Ramsdale and Asmir Begovic both signed for Bournemouth in 2017 After signing from Sheffield United in 2017, Ramsdale was an understudy to experienced goalkeeper Asmir Begovic at the Vitality Stadium for two years before his breakthrough. "First of all, Aaron's a fantastic goalkeeper," Begovic told BBC Sport. "We first worked together about nine years ago and since then he's been on an incredible ride where he's performed at the highest level. "I remember my remit when I came into Bournemouth was to mentor and set a tone for some of the younger goalkeepers, one of which was Aaron Ramsdale. "There's many different factors that go into it but I think it's been unfortunate that maybe a few things haven't aligned for him [at Southampton]." Southampton's relegation prompted Ramsdale to seek top flight football once more and he moved to Newcastle United on loan for the 2025-26 campaign. But again, what was supposed to be a move to help re-establish his career at the highest level did not come to pass. Ramsdale kept just two clean sheets in 23 appearances in all competitions for the Magpies, featuring only 12 times in the Premier League - and neither he nor Nick Pope could make the number one spot permanently their own. He also had the unfortunate experience of letting in seven goals in one game in a 7-2 defeat by Barcelona in the Champions League last-16 - the most he has ever conceded in a single game. title: Angela Scanlon takes over Sara Cox's drivetime slot on Radio 2
description: The station also announces a new presenter for its country show after Bob Harris's departure.
body: Angela Scanlon (left) was among the hosts who tried out over the summer to be Sara Cox's replacement Angela Scanlon is to take over BBC Radio 2's drivetime show after Sara Cox moved to the breakfast slot. The Irish personality said it was "properly exciting" to be hosting the station's 16:00-19:00 show every weekday from November. She said: "Millions of people, all having completely different days, piling into the same conversation for a few hours - what a strange and lovely thing!" Scanlon, who hosted a Sunday early morning programme on the station from 2018 to 2021, was among a number of people who filled in after Cox vacated the drivetime slot in May, including Joel Dommett, Jason Manford, Ellie Taylor, Alex Jones and Gary Davies. Scanlon is also known for The One Show, This Morning, Your Home Made Perfect, The Apprentice: Unfinished Business, and for taking part in Strictly Come Dancing in 2023. Scanlon appeared on Cox's breakfast show on Monday to announce the news "Every weekday, I'll be in your ears, your cars and your kitchens - on the school run, on the way home, or standing at the hob wondering what on earth to feed a small but hungry mob," she said. "I want all of it: the stories, the opinions, the chaos, the tiny triumphs and the things you probably shouldn't admit on national radio." Radio 2 controller Helen Thomas described Scanlon as "incredibly warm and quick witted and proved to be extremely popular with the Radio 2 audience this summer". She added: "Drivetime is such an important show in terms of ensuring people get home and start their evenings in a positive and upbeat mood, and I'm delighted Angela will be taking up the reins in November. "I'd like to extend my thanks to all the hosts who have presented in this slot since our Sara moved on up to Breakfast." Scanlon also hosted the Virgin Radio weekend breakfast show after Graham Norton's departure in 2024, and co-hosts the Get A Grip podcast. Earle (right) has presented a show on Absolute Radio Country, pictured interviewing Robert Plant in 2021 Meanwhile, Radio 2 has also announced that Ben Earle will present the station's weekly country music programme following the departure of longtime host Bob Harris. "Whispering" Bob, who presented the show for 27 years, announced his departure in June, weeks after revealing his prostate cancer has spread to his spine. Earle, one half of British country group The Shires, has also fronted a weekly show on Absolute Radio Country for the past five years. Thomas said: "His knowledge, passion and enthusiasm for the genre, coupled with his years as a musician plus experience presenting on the radio, make him the ideal person to pick up the reins from the legendary Bob Harris. Like Bob, I hope Ben hosts the show for decades to come." title: A 31-year wait for success - but can Everton fans still celebrate?
description: Is supporting Everton a life of misery, or are there still reasons to celebrate? Chief football writer Phil McNulty seeks the answer.
body: Everton fans have experienced highs and lows since the turn of the century Everton's unbeaten start to the Premier League season and progress in the Carabao Cup has prompted a minor outbreak of something rarely felt among their fanbase in recent times - optimism. Guarded optimism, understandably, but the mood has shifted somewhat since the fury that followed a badly botched transfer window, typified by a shambolic final day that left manager David Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players. A move for AS Monaco striker Falorin Balogun fell through when he walked away from the deal after problems with the medical, while Iliman Ndiaye, arguably Everton's best player, was sold to Manchester City for £65m. It is against this backdrop that Moyes seeks to end Everton's 31-year search for success that has saddled them with an unwanted record. Since the turn of the century, Everton are the only club in English football's current top four tiers who have not won a trophy - their last being the 1995 FA Cup triumph against Manchester United at the old Wembley - or been promoted. Of course, to the enjoy the rush of promotion, Everton would first have to suffer the pain of relegation. It nearly happened this millennium as Everton - last relegated in 1951 - stayed up by beating Bournemouth on the final day of the 2022-23 season. They had only guaranteed safety in the previous campaign by coming from two goals down to beat Crystal Palace in their penultimate game on a night of thunderous sporting theatre at Goodison Park. So is supporting Everton a life of unrelenting sporting misery? Or is there still joy and celebration to be had following of one the grand old English football institutions? Former player Leon Osman, who made 433 appearances for Everton between 2003 and 2016, scoring 58 goals, says: "Yes, there have been disappointments and those years without trophies, but let me tell you this - I wouldn't swap being an Evertonian for anything in the world." And prominent Everton fan Dr. David France, who calculates he has travelled two million miles - the equivalent of going to the moon and back four times - to watch his beloved club from his home in the United States, told BBC Sport: "I can explain what I celebrate, even if we haven't had tangible success for so long. I celebrate being an Evertonian." Others who also celebrate supporting Everton include Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canada counterpart Mark Carney, who recently both attended the 1-0 EFL Cup win against Wolverhampton Wanderers at Hill Dickinson Stadium that set up a last-16 home tie with Newcastle United. Moyes demands more from Everton - but don't mention Europe Everton fans Andy Burnham and Mark Carney celebrate the winner against Wolves The statistics that pile pain on Everton and their fans reflect those occasional highs and more regular lows - but always accompanied by fiercely passionate, loyal support and sold-out games, at Goodison Park and the magnificent new Hill Dickinson Stadium. And Everton remain one of only six Premier League originals, along with Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur, who have never dropped out of the top tier. Elsewhere, Everton's tale of the tape is not so flattering. Since 2000, they have lost two FA Cup semi-finals, winning a third against Manchester United on penalties in 2009, only to lose to Chelsea in the final. Everton have been knocked out eight times at the first time of asking in the third round. In the EFL Cup, they have only reached the semi-finals twice, in 2008 and 2016, losing both. In the league since 2000, Everton have failed to win at Chelsea in 27 attempts, won only twice at Manchester United, once at Arsenal and Liverpool and five times at Manchester City. Everton did win an FA Cup fourth-round replay at Stamford Bridge in 2011. In the 53 Merseyside derbies in the Premier League in this time, Everton have won only five and lost 28. Their ledger is balanced by a dramatic FA Cup fourth-round replay win against Liverpool in 2009, secured with Dan Gosling's last-minute goal in extra-time, as well as a crucial 1-0 derby win that was part of their finest season in this fallow period. In 2004-05, Everton manager David Moyes performed what then Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger described as "a miracle" when, after selling Wayne Rooney to Manchester United, he guided them to fourth place and into the Champions League. It was a campaign that contained another of Everton's celebratory moments, when Duncan Ferguson tormented Sir Alex Ferguson's Manchester United, scoring the winner with a trademark header from Mikel Arteta's free-kick on another memorable Goodison night. Leon Osman made more than 400 appearances in a 13-year Everton first-team career Sadly, Everton's journey into the Champions League qualifying round ended in heartbreak and controversy when, after losing the first leg 2-1 at home to eventual semi-finalists Villarreal, referee Pierluigi Collina mysteriously ruled out a late Ferguson header that would have sent the tie into extra-time. They eventually went out 4-2 on aggregate following a decision that still rankles today. So is it really as bad as all that? Osman is well qualified to answer, having enjoyed a distinguished first-team career at Everton stretching between 2003 and 2016. He told BBC Sport: "We've had some disappointments in those times, certainly in terms of not winning anything, but we've had some good days along the way, good moments. "We've reached semi-finals, an FA Cup final, some great celebrations. We had some great trips in Europe - I think about us winning in Nuremberg in the Uefa Cup with thousands of our fans there to enjoy it. "I certainly don't feel it's been 26 years of misery. I would argue very strongly against that. When we qualified for the Champions League in 2005, that was an incredible achievement, given the clubs we were up a

title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
description: The most revealing thing about the summit in Washington may be what the two leaders did not say - and what we still don't know.
body: Xi and Trump's talks in Washington yielded no joint statements and few major breakthroughs On Monday, China released more information of what was agreed at the talks between Xi Jinping and Donald Tump last week, shedding light on a handful of concrete outcomes. But there were no joint statements and few major breakthroughs. Instead, both governments issued separate accounts of the meeting - perhaps a sign that despite the White House tours and promise of warmer ties, Washington and Beijing remain wary of each other. Here are four things we now know - and still don't - about what transpired at the talks. Beijing says it has agreed with Washington to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for the end of November. As both countries race to develop advanced artificial intelligence, the move suggests they see a need for some guardrails around a technology that is increasingly being used in everything from business to military planning. They have also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents, aimed at preventing misunderstandings or unexpected developments from turning into a broader confrontation. The meeting was being closely watched for any developments or agreements in relation to AI - especially in the wake of calls by US companies like Anthropic to slow down developments, and revelations that Open AI had gained unauthorised access to government websites in countries like Australia and had "meddled" with multiple US government agency sites. Huge data centres rise at 'China speed' to power its AI ambitions Trump and Xi come face-to-face as US and China battle to win the AI race Trump wants AI to be rebranded as super intelligence. Will it work? Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January. The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year. Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December. It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently. But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough. China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing. Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs. The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028. What is striking is what was left out. There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased. Chinese toys heading to American stores will benefit from the lower tariffs The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping. According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution. After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack. He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue. This time, Trump disclosed far less. "We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend. "Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel." That silence may be significant. Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months. Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit. The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so. Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The issue of Taiwan was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations. The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it. Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed. Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen. And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans. Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention. So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place. This summit produced more dialogue - but very little decision change for now. The most contentious issues from advanced technology to Taiwan remain unresolved.

title: Taylor Swift breaks record for most MTV VMAs as Madonna also wins
description: Swift took home the big award for video of the year on a night when the original Queen of Pop performed.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Madonna and Taylor Swift win big at the MTV VMAs Taylor Swift took home the video of the year award as she became the most successful artist in the history of the MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday. The singer went into the night tied with Beyoncé on 30 wins, and went on to score the night's top award for the visuals for her track The Fate of Ophelia, taken from her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl. The original Queen of Pop, Madonna, won artist of the year, best dance and best collaboration alongside Sabrina Carpenter for their dancefloor-filler Bring Your Love, which was the lead single from Madonna's 2026 album Confessions II. Swift also received the inaugural award for artist director, having written and directed the glitzy and theatrical Ophelia music video herself. Taylor Swift and Madonna were the two big winners on the night She dedicated her new award to the "ultimate showgirl", saying: "I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time". The 36-year-old also debuted the music video for her new song Patient Zero - starring actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson - during the Los Angeles ceremony, hosted by rapper Snoop Dogg. The dark gothic thriller is her first music video since marrying NFL player Travis Kelce. The song is one of four new tracks on The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, which dropped last week. In a ceremony that largely awarded female artists, Madonna went into the night with the most nominations - 13. And her team also won best cinematography and choreography both for Confessions II, the film. "Most of you were probably not born when I performed at the very first VMAs 43 years ago," the 68-year-old said after winning artist of the year. She went on to recall how she had fallen over and exposed her backside, an accident which had threatened to end her fledgling career. Reflecting on more recent times, she added: "I spent the last year and a half finding myself, believing in myself and really making the music that I wanted to make." This video can not be played Sabrina Carpenter’s team didn't respond straight away to Madonna collab Madonna's performance - her first VMAs show since her infamous onstage kiss with Britney Spears in 2003 - included a duet with Carpenter and an appearance from British Brat star Charli XCX. While accepting the award for best collab, Madonna noted how Carpenter's team had taken five days to respond. "When five days passed and I still didn't get connected with Sabrina and didn't hear back from her about whether she wanted to do a song with me - five days - I DM'd [direct messaged] her," said the star. "She answered me back and... within weeks we were in the studio together," she continued. "It was fabulous." Carpenter, who grimaced slightly at the thought of her team having kept the pop icon waiting, clarified: "My team replies. Just so everybody knows, they do respond to people. "But I respond faster. So direct line to me is always the best way to get in contact." This video can not be played Watch: Taylor Swift, Charli XCX among stars to light up VMAs red carpet Swift, Charli XCX and Lisa from K-pop group Blackpink were among the celebrities walking the blue carpet ahead of the event. Lisa became the first Asian solo artist to win the best pop category for her song Dream, which featured Japanese actor Kentaro Sakaguchi in its music video. The Thai rapper-singer fended off competition from some of pop music's biggest names, including Swift, Ariana Grande, Olivia Rodrigo. Lisa, whose real name is Lalisa Manoba, was visibly moved as she accepted her award. Addressing her fans, known as Lillies, the 29-year-old said she "wouldn't be here without you guys". Lisa from K-pop group Blackpink became the first Asian solo artist to win the best pop category at the VMAs British singers Raye and Sienna Spiro, who won best new artist, also performed on the night, where there were tributes to the late Parton and George Michael. Another Brit, PinkPantheress won best art direction alongside Sweden's Zara Larsson for Stateside. BTS picked up best group and song of the year for Swim, Olivia Rodrigo's The Cure won best alternative and Nirvana were honoured with the Video Vanguard award.
