title: Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge
description: Andy Burnham said that he would make tough decisions to fund a new national care service.
body: The prime minister's Sunday morning BBC interview set hares running when it comes to the future of a policy once seen as politically untouchable. The timing of the PM's new social care plan sparked suggestions the government could be about to signal the death knell to the state pension triple lock after 16 years. Andy Burnham said he will put forward tough decisions to fund a new national care service as part of Labour's next general election manifesto, seeking a mandate to make the changes next Parliament. The triple lock, which in theory expires at the end of this Parliament, means state pensions rise every April by at least 2.5%, or in line with the highest of prices or earnings. Earlier this month, BBC News put this precise question about changing the triple lock in the next Parliament to Chancellor John Healey, who replied "the PM has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs". It was a non-denial reflecting the fact that the PM has been besieged with advice, including from some of his favourite economists, that scrapping the triple lock, or even signalling it is a future possibility, is a golden opportunity for Britain's economic policy at a tricky moment in the bond markets for all heavily indebted nations. The UK specifically is seen as a place where successive governments have shirked tough long-term decisions. Could this be Burnham and Healey's attempt to shift that perception, even in the slightly wild markets for government borrowing? The politics are trickier. Reform's leaders see the policy as a key potential dividing line with Labour. Many in Westminster privately agree the Osborne-era policy is unsustainable economically, but argue it is politically impossible to unpick. Many pensions campaigners point to the fact that even after increases, the UK's state pension is not generous by international standards, though other countries have very different systems and rates of private provision. Former ministers point out that the quid pro quo of redeploying the pension cash savings towards an in kind care service could shift the argument. The lock is costing £15.5bn a year, treble original estimates of the 2030 cost, especially because of the volatility of prices and earnings. Reverting to an earnings link could save tens of billions of pounds a year in the long run. It is the sort of saving that could plausibly fund some form of national care service, potentially with cash left over as a buffer in a volatile world - but that depends on the ambition of the care plan, the generosity of any replacement for the triple lock, and how volatile prices are in the long term. It had been deemed politically unthinkable, but the government now seems to be thinking about it, at least for the future. title: Broncos deny Rams and Seahawks lose - five things from NFL week three
description: The NFL produced another thrilling day of action with a shock for the defending Super Bowl champions and several tight finishes.
body: The Washington Commanders have a 1-2 record, while the Baltimore Ravens are 2-1 The NFL produced another thrilling day of action on Sunday with a shock for the defending champions as five teams maintained their unbeaten record this season. There were several nail-biting finishes as 12 of the 14 games were decided by eight points or fewer, tying the NFL record for the most one-score games in a day. One of those took place in Brazil, where the NFL staged the second of a record nine international games to be played this season. But they saved the best for last as the two teams that went within one win of last season's Super Bowl traded blows in a gripping primetime clash. The Denver Broncos and the Los Angeles Rams remain potential Super Bowl contenders after losing last season's Conference Championship games. Both teams had an underwhelming season opener before bouncing back last week, and Sunday's game in Denver gave them an opportunity to show their title credentials. The Rams dominated the first half and led 16-0 at the interval, but the Broncos regrouped to draw level in the third quarter. That set up a fascinating finish, with three lead changes in the final five minutes, beginning with an interception by Denver safety Talanoa Hufanga which he ran back for a 66-yard touchdown. In just over a minute, last season's Most Valuable Player Matt Stafford led the Rams down the field, culminating in a 48-yard touchdown for receiver Konata Mumpfield to regain the lead. The Broncos replied with quarterback Bo Nix reaching into the endzone after another long drive to put the hosts back in front. That left Stafford 47 seconds to get into a game-winning position and he did just that. With two seconds left, he had a shot at the endzone from 19 yards, but Hufanga intercepted for a second time to clinch a 30-26 Broncos win. Talanoa Hufanga claimed more than one interception in a game for the first time in his six-year NFL career The Washington Commanders' hopes of getting back in the play-offs were dealt a huge blow last week as quarterback Jayden Daniels dislocated his left elbow. But Daniels could be back inside three weeks and, although the Commanders hosted defending champions the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, they led 24-10 after experienced back-up Marcus Mariota threw his third touchdown pass. The Seahawks drew level in the fourth quarter, but Sam Darnold, who returned from a game out for Seattle, then threw his second interception, and it was returned by linebacker Kain Medrano for a 50-yard score. That proved enough for Washington to clinch a 33-31 win and halt a 12-game win streak by Seattle, which included last season's Super Bowl run. The New England Patriots were their opponents in the Super Bowl, but their quarterback Drake Maye has struggled since. After having only 11 turnovers last year, he already has seven this season after another three against the Jacksonville Jaguars, and he was benched as the Jags romped to a 35-6 home win. After playing in Sao Paulo the past two seasons, the NFL returned to Brazil for its first game in Rio de Janeiro. There had been concerns about the condition of the field at the iconic Maracana stadium, but there were no issues. The NFL picked a mouth-watering match-up for Rio and it delivered, with the Baltimore Ravens and the Dallas Cowboys producing a thriller. Two Derrick Henry touchdowns helped the Ravens into a 24-13 lead in the third quarter before Dallas, playing only their second international game, fought back. The lead changed hands twice in the fourth quarter and the game looked set for overtime when a Cowboys field goal levelled the score with seven seconds left. But Lamar Jackson then completed a 27-yard pass down the middle to get the Ravens within field-goal range and Tyler Loop made a 56-yard kick as time expired to win the game 34-31. That sparked wild celebrations at the Maracana and means all four AFC North teams have a 2-1 record this season. Brazil footballer Neymar was at the Maracana, while Ricky Martin and Brazilian singer Pedro Sampaio performed the half-time show Some Cleveland Browns fans cheered when quarterback Deshaun Watson suffered a season-ending injury in 2024. Some booed as he returned to action in pre-season, but could Watson finally be winning over the 'Dawg Pound'? The 31-year-old led the Browns to a comeback win at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last week and repeated the feat as Cleveland beat the Carolina Panthers 21-18 in their home opener. Watson held his nerve to step out of the pocket and fire a 14-yard touchdown pass to tight end Harold Fannin Jr to cap a game-winning 65-yard drive. "The past is the past," said Watson. "I know we've been through some ups and downs. But if we look forward, build off this win, come back Thursday night and get another big one, we can make something special for this city." The Browns are at home again on Thursday against divisional rivals the Pittsburgh Steelers, who enjoyed a morale-boosting victory in another AFC North match-up on Sunday. After only one offensive touchdown in their opening two games, Aaron Rodgers got the Steelers firing, throwing three touchdown passes before Derrick Harmon pulled off a strip-sack on Joe Burrow to seal a 30-27 win at home to the Cincinnati Bengals. Three of the teams who remain unbeaten are regular play-off contenders. The Buffalo Bills came from 10-0 down to beat the Los Angeles Chargers 24-16, with quarterback Josh Allen barging over for two touchdowns. Travis Kelce scored as the Kansas City Chiefs won 24-10 at the Miami Dolphins, while Brock Purdy threw four touchdown passes in the San Francisco 49ers' 36-30 win at home to the Arizona Cardinals. Few expected the Minnesota Vikings to be 3-0, though. They won 23-16 at Tampa Bay despite losing receiver Justin Jefferson to an early ankle injury. And the biggest surprise has been the Las Vegas Raiders. They have now won as many games as they did last season,

title: Is Premier League possession football on the way out?
description: Only 36% of teams with more than 60% possession have won this season in the Premier League. BBC Sport looks at why?
body: In the early 2000s, Premier League defences tried to make the pitch as small as possible, giving their opposition less space to score in. Coaches therefore encouraged their attackers to play quickly, taking advantage of open space that saw them face fewer defenders. Logically, this made total sense. It was Pep Guardiola's influence that, in part, flipped this logic on its head over the last decade. His Manchester City sides looked to force teams back into a compact defence, a challenge that in theory should be harder to break down. The counter logic was that they were forcing opponents to give them a familiar challenge they were prepared for. City's defenders also had big spaces to cover, often standing at the halfway line. But for Guardiola, those spaces were less worrying if the ball stayed near the opposition's goal for as long as possible. After all, if you have the ball, the opposition cannot score. So why now are teams that dominate the ball dropping points? Across this season's opening 50 Premier League matches, teams recording at least 60% possession have won only 36.4% of those games, while in 2023-24, the figure was 53.5%. Does this suggest possession football is on the way out? Well, the answer isn't that simple. Are teams winning because of their low possession, or having less possession because they have taken the lead early? There could be some truth in both answers. Let's use Xabi Alonso's Chelsea as a case study. They won their opening games against Fulham and Brighton - 3-2 and 4-3 respectively - with the minority of possession, then drew 2-2 with Hull and lost 3-0 to Brentford despite having considerably more of the ball. Against Brighton, Chelsea's 25.6% possession and 146 successful passes were their lowest recorded figures in a Premier League match, with records beginning in 2003-04. And yet, the Blues scored four goals. For three of them, accelerating play from throw-ins and counter-attacks allowed their direct attackers to find space against fewer defenders. This dynamic can partly be explained by Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton wanting to dominate the ball - with only Manchester City averaging more possession than the Seagulls this season - which played into Chelsea's hands. Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto and Morgan Rogers boast skillsets suited to transition-heavy football, and the low possession against Brighton helped them play to their strengths. By breaking quickly, Chelsea scored their third against Brighton in what became a two-against-two situation. Counter-attacking comes with a stigma. It is more accepted underdogs like newly promoted Hull will play this way. For bigger teams, there is an expectation to eventually control the game with the ball. This makes a low-possession approach harder to sell long term, even if the players might look better conceding possession. And that disconnect between players' skillsets and tactics could help explain some dropped points. Alongside Chelsea, Manchester United have also suffered in this way. Under Michael Carrick, they have averaged 1.5 points per game with more than 50% possession. With less, that rises to 2.6. Clubs without the same expectation, like Brentford, Leeds and Hull, can concede possession and have built squads for that style. With impressive box defenders, dangerous counter-attackers and set-piece specialists, their tactics can align with their players' strengths, helping them compete against more less aligned opponents, irrespective of their wealth gap. In recent seasons, there has been a rise in man-to-man pressure that has made building out from the back challenging. Teams, as a result, have looked to play long over the press or past its first line into space for players to drive with the ball - think the likes of City's Nico O'Reilly or Arsenal's Declan Rice. Both of these have been great solutions to the initial problem, but it does mean that teams full of physical athletes, focused on bringing down long passes or driving with the ball over distance, could be less suited to the intricate play required to unlock stubborn defences - a situation commonly faced by teams who have more of the ball. To dominate in 2026 likely requires a squad that has enough solutions in small spaces as well as big ones. In this example we see Liverpool look to press Manchester City high. City play the ball through the pressure into Nico O'Reilly behind Liverpool's first line of pressure. O'Reilly then uses his ball-carrying ability to take advantage of the big space ahead of him. Opponents have used man-to-man defending closer to goal too, making it harder to find the unmarked player, a key attacking principle used in Guardiola's positional play. With players marked, attacks can then depend on winning one-against-one situations, requiring individual quality often in the form of dribbling. Given the way teams have been built over the last few years, certain sides may lack this type of problem solver. It is important to note possession is an average across a match, which can hide how the scoreline changes a team's approach. Chelsea scored within seven minutes in each of their opening four league games after which opponents pushed forward looking for a goal. The Blues dropped deeper, defending their lead and attacking the space left behind. Across their opening five matches, Chelsea averaged 51.4% possession when level, 34.5% when ahead and 67.2% when behind - highlighting how much their possession has varied with the score. Interestingly, protecting a lead created favourable opportunities for Chelsea's attackers to play intuitively, carry the ball and attack space. When chasing a goal, they had more possession but appeared to lack solutions against compact defences. Arsenal show the value of being able to do both parts well when needed. title: Police block Orange Order from controversial parade route
description: They had been unable to make the permitted parade on Sunday morning because protesters had gathered on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road.
body: Orangemen tried a number of times throughout Sunday and overnight to walk down Garvaghy Road The police prevented the Orange Order from making a controversial parade down a road which had been previously been blocked by protesters. A group of men tried to march from Drumcree Church down the Garvaghy Road in Portadown in the early hours of Monday but a line of police Land Rovers stood in the way. They had been unable to make the permitted parade on Sunday morning because protesters had gathered on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road. The stand-off continued throughout Sunday, with the Orangemen waiting at the church, around a mile from the road, for the go-ahead from police. Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined the protest, prompting Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson to accuse her of acting unlawfully. Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant called for "compromise". Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents Coaltion, said he was meeting the secretary of state and chief constable on Monday and that he would not prejudge those conversations The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident. However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas. The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. The row sparked some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history and was linked to several murders. This was the scene on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday afternoon as hundreds of people protested The row reemerged after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission - the organisation formed during the Drumcree dispute to decide on contentious marches during Northern Ireland's parading season - was overturned. On Friday, following 28 years of unsuccessful applications, the commission decided the march could go ahead with restrictions in place. Rather than start at 13:00 on Sunday as intended, the commission said it could begin no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. However that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go ahead just hours before it was due to take place. The Drumcree parade sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history. Protesters started gathering on the Garvaghy Road in the early hours of Sunday, after the final court decision. Dozens of armoured police vehicles arrived in the town, calling on them to clear the route while members of the Portadown District Lodge waited in a hall at Drumcree Parish Church. At one point Orangemen began walking down Drumcree Road before stopping and turning back. On Sunday evening, a large group of people joined the Orange Order, and police blocked the road with Land Rovers. The Orange Order was warned that they were breaking the terms of the determination by having more than 35 people here, but loyalist activists argued they had not asked for a crowd. Police Land Rovers blocked the road outside Drumcree Parish Church on Sunday evening For most of Sunday, police maintained a sterile zone between the two sides, while officers repeatedly called on protesters to disperse. At Garvaghy Road, protesters were joined by members the Social Democratic Labour Party (SDLP) and Sinn Féin, with First Minister Michelle O'Neill urging the crowd to "stay the course" to "at least" midnight. Meanwhile other political leaders engaged with the Northern Ireland Secretary. Sir Chris Bryant, who returned from the Labour Party conference for talks, urged both sides to "double down on compromise" and said "nobody should be attending an unlawful protest". However, he added, it was not his job "to decide whether somebody has or hasn't broken the law". This video can not be played DUP leader accuses Sinn Féin first minister of breaking the law Earlier, the first minister said the decision to permit the march "brings into question how the peace process works". DUP leader Gavin Robinson accused O'Neill and other Sinn Féin politicians at the protest of being "lawmakers acting as lawbreakers". After meeting Sir Chris at Hillsborough Castle, Robinson said the stakes for Stormont were high and "could get higher" if the Orange Order was unable to complete the parade, and there needed to be consequences for politicians he accused of breaking the law. His party colleague, Carla Lockhart MP, warned of "profound" consequences if the Parade Commission's determination was not upheld. This video can not be played 'There must be no march' - Sinn Féin leaders on Garvaghy Road SDLP leader Claire Hanna, who also attended the protest, called for de-escalation and said: "Whatever the legalities, it was never politically right or morally right to do this." Following talks at Hillsborough, her party called for an international mediator to help resolve the dispute, with Sir Chris saying he is "giving consideration to anything that anybody comes up with". He said he is determined to keep on working and talking with people, but added that "we haven't got a solution yet". Also speaking after the meeting, UUP leader Jon Burrows said the rule of law needed to apply to "everyone", and that Stormont has been "put under threat". "It is vital that everyone obeys the law. I don't care who that is. I don't care how senior you are. The law applies to everyone. It cannot be enforced basically on the basis of it might be politically inconvenient," he added. Justice Minister Naomi Long described the stand-off as an "entirely avoidable conflict" and said politicians risked delivering "misery" to the people of Northern Ireland. title: Nature spaces 'need to be next to where people live'
description: Campaigners are pushing for more wildlife-rich green spaces to be created within urban communities.
body: Longhorn cattle graze at a former open-cast coal mine on the edge of Salford People should not have to travel far to experience the joys of nature, conservationists have said, as campaigners push for more wildlife-rich green spaces in urban areas. From Greater Manchester to north London, organisations and volunteers are transforming former industrial land and neglected parks into habitats for wildlife and places for people to enjoy. Research suggests many people do not have access to parks, woodlands or wetlands within a 15-minute walk of their home, despite evidence that time spent in nature can improve health and wellbeing. Stephen Cartwright, from the Lancashire Wildlife Trust, said: "We need the places right next to where people live, that are scrappy bits of land." Cutacre Nature Reserve, near Salford, offers access to nature for people who may not otherwise visit a reserve If wildlife is to thrive alongside growing communities, campaigners said access to nature must become a bigger priority for policymakers and planners. The Wildlife Trusts - a federation of 47 independent wildlife conservation charities covering the UK - has called on the government to improve people's access to nature. Meanwhile a coalition led by the Horticultural Trades Association and the Gardens Trust wants trees, plants, gardens and parks to be recognised as essential infrastructure backed by long-term investment. In the Tottenham area of north London, residents have led the transformation of the Lordship Recreation Ground Across the country, projects have already demonstrated how green spaces can be brought closer to people. At Cutacre, a former open-cast coal mine on the edge of Salford in Greater Manchester, the Lancashire Wildlife Trust has created meadows, wetlands, ponds and grazing areas with longhorn cattle. The reserve is home to species including grey partridge, lapwing, skylark, grasshopper warbler and willow tit. Conservationists have also reintroduced dyer's greenweed to Greater Manchester after the plant became functionally extinct in the area. Cutacre Nature Reserve's location is said to be a very important asset Cartwright said the reserve's location was one of its most important features. Bordered by a housing estate, industrial units and communities in and around Salford, Bolton, Wigan and Manchester, the site offers nearby access to nature for people who may not otherwise visit a reserve. "If you're a child growing up in a school over there, the majority of them won't travel to nature reserves," he said. "We need to bring reserves to them." Cartwright's colleague Alan Wright, added: "We want to engage people in nature and the best way to do it is do things next to where they live. This is a perfect example." Lordship Recreation Ground features woodland, meadows, an orchard, food-growing areas, sports facilities and a restored watercourse More than 150 miles (241km) away in Tottenham, local residents have led the transformation of the Lordship Recreation Ground. When the Friends of Lordship Rec group formed in 2001, chairman David Morris said the park was a neglected and unsafe space with derelict buildings and little biodiversity. Today, supported by £7m in lottery and other funding, it features woodland, meadows, an orchard, food-growing areas, sports facilities and a restored watercourse. The community group co-manages the park with Haringey Council and has helped secure its designation as a site of importance for nature conservation. Lordship Recreation Ground has been designated as a site of importance for nature conservation Morris said green spaces benefited both wildlife and residents. "Being in nature has an amazing positive effect, immediate effect," he said. He also called for increased funding for parks, adding: "Every neighbourhood should have access to a public green space." The site now attracts volunteers of all ages and hosts activities including bat walks, birdwatching groups and events with schoolchildren aimed at encouraging a lifelong connection with nature. title: England are learning - these are the World Cup issues they need to solve
description: Who are England's openers? Which spinner supports Adil Rashid? Which seamers get nod when Sam Curran returns?
body: This video can not be played Banton stars as England win Sri Lanka ODI series The most surprising moment of England's thumping win over Sri Lanka at The Oval was not Jofra Archer's direct hit run-out, nor Tom Banton's first international century. It came in an answer that coach Brendon McCullum gave afterwards. "We are also trying to include a number of warm-up games as well," McCullum told BBC Test Match Special of his winter plans. That is McCullum, the coach whose side had only one in-house warm-up before last winter's Ashes, talking about arranging 50-over practice matches - something England have not had on a tour outside World Cups for six years in the longest white-ball format. "A lot of these guys just haven't played a lot of white-ball cricket," McCullum said. It was an eyebrow-raising, yet encouraging, answer which hints at a change in McCullum, who has also had a beefed-up backroom staff this summer and spoke on more than one occasion about fitness in the Oval aftermath. And a team that lost six of seven ODI series between their final match of a dismal 2023 World Cup and the end of last year - exiting the Champions Trophy without winning a game in between - have won all three of their 50-over series this year. With the next World Cup a year away, England may not be the best 50-over side in the world, but they are no longer the format's biggest underachievers. "I think they might be in with a shout, with a bit of luck on their side," said former England spinner Phil Tufnell. There is hope again, albeit with some issues to solve… England win series as Banton delivers on potential Banton blasts England to series win This video can not be played 'Brilliant' Banton scores maiden ODI century for England In the most bizarre of cricketing summers, Ben Duckett has had a bizarre summer of his own. The only Englishman to compile a Test ton, and the scorer of 141 against India in a one-day international at Lord's, ends with nine scores below 20 from his other 15 innings. He was talked about as the world's best all-format batter after his 149 against India last summer but has averaged 27.15 since then across formats. It is right that England are reticent to drop a batter who has hit such highs, especially as a senior player and one with significant List A experience - a total of 111 matches - behind him in a squad still lacking in 50-over matches. Duckett and Jacob Bethell also shared an opening stand of 192 in the series decider against India at Lord's. But, unlike the Test side where Emilio Gay's place as Duckett's partner is not fully secure, never mind a replacement waiting in the wings, Tom Banton and Bethell have shown there could be another world without the diminutive left-hander. Bethell, who scored 91 in the third ODI against India before missing the Sri Lanka series with a knee injury, is talked of as a senior player in the group, despite still being just 22, while Banton's first England century on Sunday was superb. The way Banton hits the ball at the top of the bounce looks suited to the bouncy pitches of South Africa, where the majority of the World Cup will be played. Duckett, in contrast, averages 23.4 on surfaces deemed as 'high bouncing' since the start of 2023. This winter's Test series in South Africa may shed some more light. This was supposed to be the series Rehan Ahmed got his long-awaited chance as England's leg-spinner with Adil Rashid injured. That the 22-year-old was dropped for the series decider is of obvious concern. Ahmed bowled better than figures of 1-46 suggested in the first ODI, but was flattered by a return of 2-48 from eight overs in the second. In his place at The Oval, Liam Dawson - 14 years his senior - took 3-26. Dawson was helped by the combination of turn and bounce on offer from the surface, something Ahmed was not afforded earlier in the series. But he also landed 39% of deliveries on a spinner's 'good' length, compared to the 22% from Ahmed in the previous two games. Ahmed is clearly talented but has not progressed as an international cricketer. A sloppy run-out in Durham and a five-ball duck in the Headingley chase did not help his cause. It leaves Rashid, who will be 39 at the World Cup, as important as ever. While the alarming statistics that England have won only one of their past nine ODIs in which neither captain Harry Brook nor number three Joe Root made fifty remains, Sunday's win was significant given the key contributions from other names. Banton laid the platform of their 355-7 and Jordan Cox's 52-ball 76 pushed the game beyond Sri Lanka. Cox's opportunity came after an injury to Jos Buttler in the second ODI. The way he took down the Sri Lanka bowling was an ideal imitation of England's greatest white-ball player. Buttler is facing a spell on the sidelines with his hamstring injury but on this evidence England have a capable understudy. Again, experience will come into the equation if Cox's form suggests a more drastic decision must be made. Buttler's brilliant boundary-hitting before being cut down by injury in the second ODI showed his best days are not necessarily all behind him. Equally, the 36-year-old's injury reminded no-one can go on forever. With Cox having made a breakout summer across formats and Banton likely to get more opportunities before Bethell returns, England are beginning to build promising depth. The impending return of Sam Curran from a groin injury - who remains important as a left-handed batter and seam-bowling option in the top seven - could also create a squeeze for places. At his best, the all-rounder would improve the balance which was slightly bowling-heavy in this series but would likely leave England needing to leave out two of Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Jamie Overton, Josh Tongue and Sonny Baker from their first-choice XI. title: Carer at home investigated by BBC struck off for threatening elderly man
description: Amina Sani, who is Nigerian, was found to have threatened the 81-year-old with police and threatened to hit him.
body: Amina Sani was secretly filmed threatening and distressing the 81-year-old A carer who was secretly filmed mocking and threatening an elderly bedbound man with dementia has been struck off. Amina Sani was found to have threatened the 81-year-old with police and threatened to hit him when he became distressed and lashed out at the prospect of being showered against his will. The Nigerian worker went on to carry out the man's intimate personal care while a cleaner held his arms down. The incidents at Castlehill Care Home in Inverness on 10 April last year came to light after the resident's daughter installed a secret camera in his room due to concerns over his care. The footage was later featured in a BBC documentary into care standards at Castlehill, in which families accused the home of "cruelty" and "neglect". Sani's legal representative told a Scottish Social Services Council misconduct hearing that she had not been trained properly in what was her first job in the UK. Worker at care home in BBC investigation faces being struck off Care home in BBC probe making progress on improvements, says watchdog I went undercover as a cleaner at a failing care home. Here's what I witnessed Namatirai Chipere said her client was a victim of problems in the social care system herself. However, hearing chairman Iain Burke said the incidents were a "significant abuse of trust and power" for which she had shown no insight or remorse. He said her attitude and behaviour were "fundamentally incompatible" with registration as a social care worker. In a statement, the home's owner - Morar Living - said it acted promptly when concerns were brought to its attention. It said there was "no truth" in Sani's claim that she was not trained properly. Castlehill, now renamed Morar Highland, was graded "good" in its most recent care inspection. The panel was shown video footage covering a period of more than 20 minutes, in which Sani repeatedly tells the bed man that he was to be showered. He can be heard screaming "no" and "leave me alone", before swearing at Sani and another carer. The pair can be seen laughing during the encounter. During evidence at the hearing, the man's daughter Su Christie, said her father, a former merchant navy crewman, had a lifelong fear of showers due to a childhood trauma. Following the judgement, she said: "You could tell by the things he was doing, the things he was saying, that his distress was growing and growing throughout that interaction and there was no attempt to bring him down or de-escalate him whatsoever. "He didn't know what was going on. He's a confused 81-year-old man living with dementia. He was frightened. "It was devastating, utterly devastating. I was in shock because, although I knew there were issues, I didn't expect to see that. It was very distressing to watch." Su Christie secretly filmed what was being done to her father The panel ruled Sani told Christie's father: "We will call the police and they will take you to court" and, referring to a male cleaner, "do you think that man is going to hit you?" or words to that effect. She also pulled his duvet off without any warning, causing him to become distressed and agitated. Delivering the panel's judgment, the chairman said: "We agree with your solicitor's submissions that you were let down by your employer, and there is little doubt that there was institutional failure. "None of the failures you have highlighted absolve you from your personal responsibility as a registered social care worker. "It is clear throughout the video clips that you did not show any kindness or compassion to the resident. At one point you and your colleague can be seen laughing in response to something the resident says or does. "It does not appear to us to be laughing with the resident, but it appears more disrespectful in nature. We find that the resident suffered harm and you did not respect his dignity." Burke added that the panel felt Sani's treatment of the man was "not something that could be remediated with training" as it reflected her attitude. It also noted she failed to use any de-escalation techniques. In closing submissions, Sani's legal representative said her client wished to apologise to the family. Christie, who moved her father into a new home shortly after the incident, said: "I think it was the right decision. "Whilst the panel did comment on institutional failures, this hearing is about her own personal accountability. And I think it sends the message that personal accountability matters. "In a care setting, people living this dementia, like my father, should be treated with respect, dignity, and patience and courtesy. They should be treated as human beings and that's all I was asking for." This video can not be played Su Christie said it was "incredibly upsetting" to see the footage of how her father had been treated. A hearing to decide sanctions over the behaviour of carer Oluwabunmi Salami, involving the same man, continues. Earlier in the hearing, Salami admitted allegations that she raised and lowered the man's bed without warning, causing him distress. A spokesperson for Morar Living said: "There is no truth in Amina Sani's claim that she was not trained properly by Morar. "When concerns were brought to our attention, Morar Highland acted promptly, including suspending employees where appropriate, undertaking formal investigations and taking action in line with the findings. "We made the relevant referrals to the Scottish Social Services Council (SSSC) and, where required, to the Protecting Vulnerable Groups (PVG) Scheme. "The safety, dignity and wellbeing of our residents remains our priority, and all concerns regarding staff conduct are taken seriously and acted upon appropriately." title: How waste food helps families through the week
description: The scheme runs in schools across the West Midlands, including Birmingham and Walsall.
body: Families attend a weekly community meal where surplus supermarket food is turned into free dinners and grocery bags to take home Food that would otherwise be thrown away by supermarkets is helping to feed hundreds of families and schoolchildren through a community meal scheme. Charity FoodCycle said its programme turns surplus supermarket produce into free meals and groceries for families, helping to cut waste while easing household costs. Among the schools taking part is Ark Tindal Academy in Balsall Heath, Birmingham, where families go to a weekly community meal and children take part in activities before dinner is served. Families are given a free vegetarian meal as well as groceries to take home. "It's a free meal in the week, and then they get a bag of groceries to take home with them, which some parents have said has been really helpful," said FoodCycle's Sophie Aoun. She said the meals were also designed to introduce children to a wider range of fruit and vegetables. Volunteers use surplus supermarket produce to create meals and reduce food waste Teacher Amy Henderson, from the academy, said the scheme had helped ease pressure on families facing rising household bills. "With the cost of living, we know how expensive things are today, and it really does take pressure off the families," she said. "It's really heart-warming to know that they have had a good meal." Henderson said the sessions also helped parents, children, school staff and volunteers build relationships. "It's a really lovely social event," she added. FoodCycle collects surplus produce from supermarkets and uses it to prepare meals and provide groceries for families. The initiative runs at schools across the West Midlands including Windsor Olympic Academy in Birmingham and Goldsmiths Primary Academy in Walsall. "Our hope is that by turning surplus food into these free community meals we're doing more than just filling plates for an evening," Aoun said. title: House up for auction for £17k - but it doesn't have a roof
description: It's been home to north Wales' strongest man Dewi Arfon near Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon.
body: The ruined stone house comes with "lovely walks in all directions" You can walk from the house to the top of Yr Wyddfa without crossing a public road, Auction House says The property includes several other ruined buildings The house has intact walls to eaves level The A-frame roof and other original timber have been preserved by the owners With property prices soaring in recent years, the idea of buying your own home for £17,000 might seem like a dream come true. But there's a catch - it doesn't have a roof. The "ruined shell" of 400-year-old Ty Du near Llanberis, Gwynedd, lies in the wooded foothills of Wales' highest mountain, Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon. It dates from the 13th Century, and once belonged to the Goodman family of Ruthin. In 1650 Godfrey Goodman - the Bishop of Gloucester - was banished there by Oliver Cromwell for his religious beliefs. Over the years, it has also been home to north Wales' strongest man, and in the 19th Century, a poet called Dewi Arfon, according to Auction House. The house is thought to have begun as a platform house, being rebuilt in the 17th Century as a storied house. Auction House said it was listed in the Inventory of the Royal Commission as an important domestic building in the parish. The auctioneers said the ruined property has intact walls to eaves level, as well as two ruined cottages, a smithy and old shop. The owners on Anglesey, they added, have preserved the A-frame roof and other timbers. At the back of the house there is an old pack horse trail that once connected Llanberis to Caernarfon. title: Uni student living at home 'wasn't ready' to move away
description: A third of students starting courses are living at home, the University of Gloucestershire says.
body: Ofelia Bines says lots of her friends are also living at home A university says a third of students starting courses this year are living at home or commuting to lectures so they can be "financially better off". The University of Gloucestershire said it had expanded support for students with flexible accommodation available for them to use, discounted travel and that it had created new facilities designed specifically for commuters. Communications and media student Ofelia Bines grew up in Gloucester and, while she said she wanted to leave the city one day, she explained she "wasn't ready" yet. "I know I'm better off financially compared to a lot of people living in halls," she said, adding "loads of people" were doing the same thing. "Most people that I went to school with have stayed in the local area and gone to uni. "For me, it just didn't make any sense to pay money for accommodation when I'm staying so close and still able to have friends and find that university experience is the best of both worlds," she added. "I also couldn't leave my dog behind and being close to family is so important". Artist explores 'beautiful mess' of motherhood Estate to build 'UK's largest beaver enclosure' Greengrocer sent good wishes ahead of retirement Taylor Barker, who has started her second year studying forensic psychology, makes a 40-minute commute to lectures at the university's City Campus in Gloucester. She said studying from home was "a bonus" and financially it worked "out better to commute". "My family are really important to me, I don't want to lose that connection from moving away," she said. "It was quite scary, the thought of having to move." She said she went to look at "a couple of universities a bit further away and I just didn't like it". "It hasn't stopped me from being independent. You're meeting people in lectures, most of the time you'll find someone similar who commutes from either similar distances, or actually lives quite near you. "It's just different ways of meeting people." The former Debenhams building has been transformed into a £75m University of Gloucestershire City Campus Stewart Dove, director of student experience at the university, said it was "sad" people were having to make decisions based around the cost of living, but commuting could help "manage the cost of university" and allow students to "continue with a part-time job or stay close to family and friends". He added: "Our flexible accommodation at Pittville [campus] means students don't necessarily have to choose between moving away or commuting every day, they can live at home but have the option to stay close to campus for up to three nights a week. "We hope that these options mean that commuter students are supported to easily access everything that the university can offer." title: Getting river pollution investigated like 'pulling teeth'
description: Bristol residents say an oil-like substance has been bubbling up for years and killing wildlife.
body: Nicola Irvine and Toby White have been reporting an oily substance bubbling up in the river for more than a year An oil-like substance has been bubbling up in the River Avon in Bristol for years and killing wildlife, according to local residents who have made regular reports to the Environment Agency (EA). Nicola Irvine, who lives in Crews Hole, said it had been like "pulling teeth" getting the EA to investigate the pollution since she contacted them in July 2025. Her partner, Toby White, said: "It's hard to describe how bad the smell is - at times it's like you're living on a petrol station and you start getting headaches." The EA said it had already visited the site and was "continuing to investigate the source of contamination and its damage to the environment". An EA spokesperson added: "While minor impacts have been found where the contamination has entered the watercourse, we have not found wider environmental effects downstream. "We continue to work with landowners, the local authority and partner organisations to take action to protect the local environment." Body found in search for missing teenager 'Batch cooking saves my family of eight a fortune' Why saunas are becoming the new dating hotspot Nearby is a popular swimming spot at Conham River Park where there has been years of campaigning to protect the Avon from pollution, most recently with a charter of rights for the river. Irvine said she first noticed the oily substance leaving a rainbow film on the river's surface and a strong acrid smell in early 2025. She reported it to the EA in July that year when she believed it was bubbling up rather than coming from boats. The EA first dismissed the substance as surface run-off but, after Irvine continued sending photos, including of dead wildlife, the investigation reopened in May this year. "This stretch of the Avon used to regularly have 30 to 40 ducks, but now it's unusual to see more than a handful," she said. "I have personally found dead fish, ducks and ducklings. I know we can't prove it, but there has to be a link with the pollution." One of the many photos of dead fish Irvine has sent to the Environment Agency The EA's investigations so far suggest a likely cause is contamination linked to pollution from the former tar works that operated in the area from the mid 19th Century up to the 1980s, but further work is needed. Irvine said the issue had been even worse during this summer's heatwaves, which had led to her being prescribed medication for migraines. "It would all bubble up, the smell would be so strong, it would surround the whole house," she said. The EA said the pollution was a category three pollution incident because impacts were limited to the area where contamination enters the watercourse. "I cant believe that even with all the health concerns and the fact there are otters in this river as well, it's still deemed minor," Irvine said. In 2022, a leaked internal EA report told staff to ignore lower-impact category three and four pollution reports because of limited funding to investigate. "I've been so frustrated with the EA," Irvine said. "It feels like pulling teeth trying to get any action from them." The EA is also investigating another incident nearby at Brislington Brook, where dead fish and eels, foam on the water and "an intense chemical smell" were reported by volunteers. The oily substance on the River Avon's surface in August 2025 Dominic Linnell, who walks his dog along the river every day, said he first noticed the issue more than two years ago. "Two or three times a week, there's an awful chemical smell, and I see a huge oil slick that seems to bubble up from the bottom of the river," he said. "I've seen fish floating dead and ducks. There's a lot of wildlife along there, you get herons, so it's a real shame. "We all really care about the river, it's definitely killing wildlife and it's very unpleasant," he said. Another local resident, Tristan Dhalla, said he had noticed the pollution ever since he moved to the area five years ago, and neighbours had even claimed the problem went back as far as a decade. Wessex Water said their investigation had found "no issues" with any of their assets, while the substance did not pass through their sewerage network. A Bristol City Council spokesperson said it was supporting the EA's investigation by providing information and records, while officers had visited the site last week. title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
description: Illegal registration plates are far too easy to get hold of and are putting the public at risk, BBC is told.
body: This video can not be played Watch: What is a ghost plate? Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal. These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones, as well as track criminals. Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor. We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved. Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks. The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it. The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition. Ghost Plates: Drivers Cheating the Law How cloned and ghost number plates are leaving innocent motorists facing fines, debt collection threats and years of stress. Watch on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One (BBC Two in Northern Ireland) at 20:00 on Monday 28 September. These tactics include deliberately using false plates that clone the number of another vehicle - and so-called "ghost plates", where special plastic is used to make all or part of the registration number unreadable by most motorway cameras. One of the main providers of ANPR technology, MAV Systems, has been testing a new camera capable of identifying and reading ghost plates. At one test site, just outside London near the Dartford Crossing, it has recorded an average of more than 1,000 of the ghost plates a day over several months. Two other sites have been running for almost two years. At one, near the M25, detections have risen from 1,000 a day to nearly 2,000 a day - while at the other, near the Eurotunnel at Folkestone, the system is flagging more than 400 a day. Sharon Gannon's son, Jason Wallis, died in a crash where hidden registration plates were involved. She believes being invisible to ANPR cameras emboldens drivers to take deadly risks. Wallis was killed in Buckinghamshire in 2023. He and his brother-in-law, Lewis Baker, had been riding their motorbikes at high speed when they both crashed into a car. The car driver was not hurt. Baker survived and was later jailed for 15 months for dangerous driving. In court, he admitted using a device to hide his number plate from public view. He also said he and Wallis had ridden at high speed more than 100 times. "It has broken us all," Sharon Gannon says of the effect the crash has had on her family. In another case, from 2025, 81-year-old Graham Slinn was killed on a pedestrian crossing when a car with cloned plates hit him at high speed. Graham Slinn was killed in a crash involving a driver using illegal plates The 20-year-old driver, Cain Byrne, who was driving without a licence or insurance, had also inhaled nitrous oxide minutes before the collision. He was identified after police trawled through hours of CCTV footage. One camera even caught the moment he had put the illegal plates on his car. Byrne was jailed for 11 years and six months for causing death by dangerous driving, driving while disqualified and driving without insurance. The victim's daughter, Nicola Timmis, says cloned plates are like a "gateway drug" which allow drivers to take more dangerous risks. "It seems like it's harmless, but then one thing leads to another, leads to another, and before you know it, it's somebody dead," she tells Panorama. "It is not a victimless crime." Both cloned and ghost plates look like normal vehicle registration plates when viewed by the naked eye. In the case of cloned ones, at least two vehicles are on the road with the same letters and numbers - with only one of them being legal. Ghost plates, on the other hand, show correct details for the vehicle - but they are made up of reflective materials which are difficult or impossible for most ANPR cameras to read. Cloned and ghost plates undermine the police's ability to track organised criminals, says Tony Porter, a former senior counter-terrorism officer who has advised the government on surveillance cameras. "The police need an effective ANPR system that doesn't have weaknesses [and] doesn't put the public at risk," he says. While passports have security features such as watermarks and electronic ID chips, Porter says, "we tolerate a £10 number plate with no security mechanism on it". In the UK, there are more than 34,000 businesses registered with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) to supply number plates. Anyone can currently become a registered number-plate supplier by filling in a quick form and paying a one-off fee. Panorama secretly filmed at a market in Essex to find out how easy it is to buy a plate in breach of the rules. Two out of three businesses we approached there offered ghost plates which they said could help avoid cameras policing London's Ultra-Low Emission Zone (Ulez) cameras. One of them allowed us to buy a plate without asking for either ID or proof that we were allowed to use the registration - both of which are required by law. In the UK it is easy to set up as a supplier of registered number plates Instead, we handed over £40 in cash and, eight minutes later, we had a brand new number plate. Buying a ghost plate is not illegal in itself, but it would be against the law to put it on a vehicle and drive with it. Just two number plate suppliers have been prosecuted and forcibly removed f

title: Felled Sycamore Gap stump has 'encouraging' growth
description: A thick layer of growth surrounds the stump three years after the landmark was illegally felled.
body: The tree stump on Hadrian's Wall has been surrounded by a fence to protect it The stump of the iconic Sycamore Gap tree is showing "encouraging" signs with a thick ring of new shoots growing around it, three years on from its illegal felling. The landmark on Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland was targeted on 28 September 2023 by Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers, who travelled during a storm from their homes in Cumbria to cut it down. Their actions sparked widespread outrage and the pair were later jailed for criminal damage to the Victorian-planted tree and Roman wall. Site owners the National Trust fenced off the stump to see if it would recover, with general manager Andrew Poad saying he is "filled with hope by the way nature is taking its course". He said: "These flourishing shoots are really encouraging and show the special measures we've taken, including reducing soil compaction around the roots and limiting human disturbance, are paying off." Poad said the trust was grateful to visitors supporting their efforts to give the tree "the best possible chance to thrive". He added: "We're monitoring the tree closely and, over time, our rangers will manage it depending on how it develops." A thick layer of new shoots now surrounds the Sycamore Gap stump After the tree was felled, seedlings were kept in a secret National Trust centre to help preserve the legacy of the much-photographed landmark. Saplings were then donated to community groups and charities around the country, with art projects launched to highlight nature's importance and condemn the illegal felling. The Sycamore Gap tree was a landmark of Northumberland and northern England Graham and Carruthers were jailed for four years and three months in July 2025 for their roles in chopping down the tree with a chainsaw. The pair, who were 39 and 32 at the time of their conviction, filmed themselves in the act and took a wedge of trunk away as a trophy. Graham, a groundworker from near Carlisle, and Carruthers, a mechanic from Wigton, never explained the motive for what prosecutors called a "moronic mission", but sought to blame each other during the trial. The site is looked after by the National Trust and Northumberland National Park The tree was planted in the late 1800s and became a much-loved visitor destination and landmark at the former frontier of the Roman Empire. It found global fame after featuring in a scene of the 1991 film Robin Hood Prince of Thieves, starring Kevin Costner, and was popular with photographers and artists. title: 'All options' considered for Banksy's flag statue
description: Westminster City Council says it is the statue's custodian and is responsible for its safety.
body: The statue appeared on a plinth in Waterloo Place in April Westminster City Council has said it is "exploring all options" for the future of Banksy's Blinded by the Flag statue in central London. The street artist erected the statue of a man marching off a plinth with his face covered by a flag at Waterloo Place on 29 April. Discussions about the artwork's future were held in the summer, but no decision was made. It will be discussed at an upcoming cabinet meeting, the Local Democracy Reporting Service understands. The council has described itself as the statue's custodian and said it had been in contact with the street artist's team. Banksy owns the copyright but the council is responsible for the cost of keeping the statue safe. A council spokesperson said: "Over the summer the council has been exploring all options for the Banksy Statue in Waterloo Place. No formal decision has been made about its long-term future." The spokesperson did not state what options were being considered. The statue is located just off the Mall and is near the statue of Florence Nightingale and Crimean War Memorial. In August the council said it had spent almost £60,000 on protecting the statue Critics interpreted the statue as a commentary on the consequences of blind allegiance to symbols. In response to a Freedom of Information request from the BBC in August, the council said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and for a security guard to keep watch over it. The artwork is largely undisturbed however its plinth has been defaced with a spray-painted tag. title: British wrestler Benjamin Satterley, known as Pac, dies aged 40
description: His death was confirmed just a day after he participated in an AEW match in Chicago.
body: British wrestler Benjamin Satterley, known as Pac, has died, his representatives have confirmed. All Elite Wrestling (AEW) said it was "saddened to announce the passing" of Satterley, 40, who they said had signed with them in 2019. The wrestler's death was confirmed just a day after he participated in AEW's "All Out" event at an arena in Chicago on Saturday evening. "A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability," AEW said in a statement. No cause of death has been provided. Satterley held multiple AEW Championships, and the organisation said he had competed in "some of the most memorable matches in AEW history". Prior to his partnership with AEW, he also performed in World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), New Japan Pro-Wrestling and Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre in Mexico. He had a number of different personas during his career including Pac, Adrian Neville and "The Man that Gravity Forgot". The latter was in reference to a signature finishing move which saw him spin 360 degrees from the top rope of the wrestling ring and land on his opponent. Many of the tributes paid to Satterley have expressed shock at his death. WWE Hall of Famer Paul Heyman described it as a "truly terrible loss" and said he was a "tremendous talent and even finer human being". AEW President Tony Khan said he "defined excellence" as a husband, friend and in his wrestling knowledge, skill and "unprecedented athleticism". "The greatest export from our country. Also the greatest human being," fellow British wrestler Will Ospreay wrote on X, sharing a photo of the pair in the ring together. "I am in shock. This is heartbreaking," AEW wrestler Evil Uno said. "We have lost another great person, a great soul, a true professional." title: Avanti West Coast main line to be nationalised
description: The move is part of a plan to improve rail infrastructure, cut train delays and improve experiences for passengers.
body: Avanti West Coast train services will be nationalised from March next year, the government has announced. "For years, we've heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price. Enough is enough," Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said. The move is part of a government plan to improve rail infrastructure, cut train delays and improve experiences for passengers. Avanti West Coast's contract was due to come to an end on 7 March. In a post on social media, Prime Minister Andy Burnham echoed Alexander's comments. "For years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti's cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again," he said. "We're proud of what we've achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before," Andy Mellors, managing director at Avanti West Coast, said. "Over the coming months, we'll work closely with the government to ensure a seamless transition into public ownership while remaining focused on delivering for our customers and communities," he added. In May, Avanti West Coast said one-in-seven rail services will be cut on its busiest routes following a government request to reduce spending. Avanti West Coast - a joint venture between FirstGroup (70%) and Italian state operator Trenitalia (30%) - predicted the move would cause minimum disruption to passengers and not reduce revenues. Companies such as Avanti West Coast have their finances heavily influenced by the Department for Transport (DfT) due to contracts introduced in March 2020 at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. All train services operated under DfT contracts are being transferred to public ownership. Great Western Railway - which is owned by FirstGroup - is to be brought under public ownership in December. Several rail firms around the country are already publicly owned, including Great Anglia and South Western Railway. Welsh services were nationalised in 2021 and Scotland took trains into public ownership the following year. title: Late September warmth before wind and rain returns this week
description: Temperatures remain above the average at the start of the week but wetter conditions are on the way for some
body: A vast area of low pressure in the Atlantic is set to draw warm south to south-easterly winds across the UK early this week, but for some rain will not be far behind. Tuesday looks as if it will be the warmest day and after that temperatures will generally return closer to the September average. Much of the UK can also expect a spell of wetter and windier weather from the approaching depression, with the most unsettled conditions likely to affect Scotland, Northern Ireland and western parts of England and Wales. However, many central, southern and eastern areas of England, which have been affected by drought, may see far less rain. Warm southerly winds ahead of Atlantic weather fronts Last week saw the autumn equinox, so our nights are now longer than our days. This means that despite the warmth in the September sun, we are getting some cooler nights under clear skies. So it will be notably chilly on Monday morning, perhaps with some fog patches to be aware of for the commute. Once the fog clears a brighter day will follow for many, with high pressure allowing sunny spells and just a few scattered showers. South-east England may see some welcome rain throughout the afternoon and evening, but it is by no means guaranteed. Temperatures will range from the mid to high teens, with some southern areas reaching 20C. The weather outlook for the week ahead On Tuesday a strengthening southerly wind will bring a much warmer day. Temperatures in the high teens are forecast in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and between 20 to 26 C for England and Wales. However rain will move into Northern Ireland during the afternoon and then trek slowly eastwards throughout the evening and night. It may become persistent and occasionally heavy, with strong winds and gales for exposed coasts and hills. Further east, drier and brighter conditions may remain before the rain arrives on Wednesday - it could possibly linger overnight. Behind the rain it is back to sunny spells and scattered showers, and still windy in the west on Wednesday. By Thursday, we are expecting high pressure to build, so it should be calmer and drier, and by Friday the north-west becomes the focus for any showers. Of course the caveat is that forecast details may change, so you can stay up-to-date with the short term forecast for your area here. Rainfall so far this September compared to the average Following the UK's hottest summer on record, September has been another notably warm month for many. But it has also highlighted a stark north-west to south-east contrast. While Scotland and other western areas have seen frequent Atlantic weather systems bearing rain and wind, much of central, southern and eastern England has remained largely dry with plenty of sunshine. As a result, rainfall totals have varied dramatically. Some drought-affected parts of England have received very little, while parts of north-west Scotland have been very wet. Some parts - including Kirkwall and Prestwick - have already had nearly one-and-a-half times their average September rainfall. At Achnagart in the Highlands, rain has been recorded every day for the past 27 days. Parts of Northern Ireland and Wales have had their average rainfall, whilst north-east England has seen some of the lowest amounts so far. title: Watch: Shipwreck uncovered on Nantucket island during nor'easter storm
description: The so-called nor'easter storm has washed up what may be a shipwreck from the 19th century in Massachusetts, local media says.
body: This video can not be played A powerful nor'easter storm has washed up what may be a shipwreck from the 19th century in Massachusetts, local media said. The wreckage discovered on a beach on Sunday is believed to be part of the "Warren Sawyer" – which ran aground near Nantucket in 1884, according to the Nantucket Current. Fragments of the wooden ship were also discovered in 2022 and 2023. Heavy rainfall and dangerous coastal flooding have hit parts of north-eastern US, with more than 160,000 households experiencing power cuts. title: The Papers: 'Iran link to RAF bomb plot' and 'Tax rise talks at No 10'
description: Almost every front page on Monday is dominated by the what the Telegraph suggests is an "Iran link" to a "bomb plot" at RAF Fairford.
body: Almost every front page is dominated by what the Telegraph suggests is an "Iran link to RAF bomb plot". It reports five men have been arrested for "terror and explosive offences" after three suspicious vans were reported travelling towards RAF Fairford. Counter terrorism police are now leading the investigation into the incident at the base, according to the paper. It says that in July, Iran threatened to attack the base, on the basis that anywhere used to launch strikes on Iran was a "legitimate target". Following the incident on Sunday morning, the paper reports that RAF Fairford is on its highest state of alert, and RAF Lakenheath, which also hosts US troops, has had its threat level increased. The Sun adds that it was a "hero farmer" who thwarted the potential attack, after she spotted people in balaclavas near the base on her way home from a party in the early hours of Sunday morning. "999 call foils 'terror plot'" reads the Mirror, which says the "heroic" woman's 00:45 call to police could have saved a lot of lives. Police are probing any links to Iran, the paper says. The Daily Mail declares "'Iran bomb plot' at RAF base foiled by farmer's 999 call". The paper says RAF Fairford has been used by US military to launch airstrikes against Iran, and quotes US President Donald Trump, who said the suspects "were looking to do big damage to our fort". The US president is also quoted in the headline of the Daily Star, which says: "They were looking to do big damage". The Daily Express is one of many papers that carries a photograph it says shows the five men being arrested near the RAF base. The paper reports bomb disposal teams have examined devices found across three vans, and adds that some 85 families from nearby homes have been evacuated. The same image is front and centre of the Times, which reports the "apparently sophisticated nature of the plot" caught police and security services by surprise. Although intelligence has led to increased security at military bases across the UK, the paper writes, police only launched a "last-minute" intervention at RAF Fairford after receiving the 999 call in the early hours of Sunday morning. Sources confirmed to the paper that the arrests were neither "pre-planned nor intelligence-led". "Let's be Apping you" says the Metro, which suggests that the suspected "terror plot" was foiled by a village WhatsApp group. The i Paper says Andy Burnham has signalled that major tax hikes may be required to fund a free NHS-style National Care Service in England. The prime minister has vowed to put free social care in Labour's next general election manifesto, the paper says, calling it a "major political gamble" from Burnham. Labour insiders have told the outlet that Burnham could present free social care as part of a "grand bargain" that includes ditching the state pension triple lock. Private equity has become an important target on the campaign trail for the US midterms, says the Financial Times. The paper has analysed campaign language in competitive congressional races over the past decade, and found that negative comments about private equity and corporate landlords have risen "sharply" this year. title: Protesters disperse after blocking contentious Orange Order parade
description: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant, who returned from the Labour Party conference for talks, urged both sides of the dispute to "double down on compromise".
body: Orange Order members and supporters gathered near Drumcree Parish church on Sunday, as police vehicles were stationed nearby Hundreds of protesters blocked a road in Portadown on Sunday after a contentious Orange Order parade was given late-night clearance to march down it for the first time in almost 30 years. Following a series of legal challenges, a ruling by the Parades Commission permitting the Drumcree parade down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road was upheld in an "unprecedented" sitting of the High Court in Belfast. Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined the protesters, while members of the Orange Order and Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politicians gathered about a mile away, waiting for the road to clear. DUP leader Gavin Robinson said O'Neill was breaking the law by protesting. He said the first minister had "broken her pledge of office". Orangemen were waiting in the Drumcree church hall for the go-ahead to proceed down the Garvaghy Road "It is shameful that we see on the streets of Portadown, a first minister, a collection of ministers and series of elected representatives who are participating in an unlawful protest, who are blocking the road and who are giving two fingers to the police, the courts and the rule of law," Robinson added. Sinn Féin has been contacted for comment. Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant, who returned from the Labour Party conference for talks, urged both sides to "double down on compromise" and said "nobody should be attending an unlawful protest", but he added it was not his job "to decide whether somebody has or hasn't broken the law". In the 1990s, the Drumcree parade sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history. Breandán Mac Cionnaith addressed protesters on Sunday night Addressing protesters as they cleared the area on Sunday night, Breandán Mac Cionnaith from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition said he would be meeting the chief constable and Northern Ireland Secretary on Monday. "The last 48 have been a long 48 hours for everybody," he said. "We said they weren't getting down and we stopped them getting down." Having "stopped them once", Mac Cionnaith said the process now "is to make sure we stop them permanently". Residents are "not going in to deals", and they "aren't going back", he said but warned the dispute is going to "drag on for a while". Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has said he is determined to keep on working and talking with people Sir Chris met politicians from the DUP, the Alliance Party, the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) in relation to the Drumcree dispute on Sunday evening, but Sinn Féin said, while they had agreed to meet, the form did not suit the secretary of state. Sir Chris said he had been in discussions with Michelle O'Neill on Sunday evening in relation to the dispute. On Sunday night, Sir Chris responded to the SDLP's call for an international mediator in relation to the dispute, and said he is "giving consideration to anything that anybody comes up with". He confirmed he has had discussions with all the main political parties in a bid to get a resolution to the Drumcree dispute, but added that "we haven't got a solution yet". Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson speaking on his phone as Orange Order members and supporters gathered near Drumcree Parish Church He said he is determined to keep on working and talking with people. "There's a few ideas around about things we might be able to do and I'm happy to explore those and I'll continue those conversations tomorrow," he added. Earlier, on the Garvaghy Road, First Minister Michelle O'Neill urged protesters to stay on the road until at least midnight. "The reason the parade has not come down this road thus far is because you are here, and we need you to stay the course, we need you to stay here to 12 o'clock tonight at least," she said. The crowd on Garvaghy Road had started to disperse on Sunday evening Orange Order march row goes to heart of ongoing divisions in Northern Ireland What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident. However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas. The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders across Northern Ireland. In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision upheld until Friday. Hundreds of people had blocked the Garvaghy Road earlier in the day Protesters started gathering on the Garvaghy Road in the early hours of Sunday, after the final court decision. Police are monitoring the situation and dozens of armoured vehicles arrived in the town. They have called on protesters to clear the route. The march was meant to begin no later than 08:00 BST, but police told the Orange Order that the road was not clear. Members of the Portadown District Lodge are waiting in a hall at Drumcree Parish Church. They intend to walk from there down the Garvaghy Road to Carleton Street Orange Hall in the town, where supporters are waiting for them to arrive. Nigel Dawson, Portadown District Master of the Orange Order, said on Sunday night that they are waiting patiently "for the police to fulfil their legal obligations" in relation to the parade.
