title: 'I take my pillow everywhere': An expert's guide to finding your perfect match
description: Dr Chris McCarthy talks through the four considerations you need to make before buying your pillow.
body: Dr Chris McCarthy says the pillow that's best for you depends on the way you sleep (branding has been obscured) "I am one of those people," says Dr Chris McCarthy. "I do take my pillow with me." You may have seen those people at the airport - a pillow stuffed under an arm as they drag their suitcases to check-in. Or you might be one yourself - attached to a pillow that's soft enough to settle into but robust enough that it's not bunched into a ball by morning. McCarthy insists he's not being fussy. He's a top physiotherapist and knows the wrong pillow can be a pain in the neck. He doesn't take his abroad, but as soon as he gets to his hotel he starts "faffing about" with the pillows - and he's got a tried and tested trick to make even the most lacklustre one fit for sleep. Here's his guide to choosing the perfect pillow for you. What makes the perfect pillow? One advertised for your sleeping position? Soft or firm? Feathers, foam or fibre? Sliced Bread separates science fact from the marketing fiction. McCarthy, an associate professor at the Manchester School of Physiotherapy, says the right pillow will depend on what position you sleep in. He tells the BBC's Sliced Bread podcast that most people fall into one of three categories of sleeper: side, back or front. McCarthy discourages front sleeping as your neck is turned one way for a long period of time. "Inevitably a muscle or ligament gets stretched and a bit irritated," he says. "If there's one thing there's a really good consensus on... in the physiotherapy world about treating spinal pain, it's don't sleep on your front." When choosing a pillow, back sleepers should consider the flexion at the top of their spine, a curving that increases naturally in many people as they age. If you have a bigger bend "it means you need a slightly thicker pillow than someone who's got a very flat back," says McCarthy. For side sleepers the key measurement is the width of your shoulders. In general, the broader you are the thicker the pillow you will need. But you also need to consider your mattress. McCarthy says how much you sink into your mattress "makes a huge difference in the subsequent height you then need from the pillow". "Broad shoulders need a thick pillow [if] you're on a very firm mattress," he explains. "If you're on a softer mattress, then you need a thinner pillow because your shoulder sinks into the mattress [more]." This is less of an issue for back sleepers as they don't sink into the mattress as much as side sleepers do. If your pillow feels too flat, McCarthy suggests placing a folded towel underneath and changing the number of folds to adjust the height. Then you can make a rough measurement to help you pick a new one. Specialist pillows are often advertised as contoured, ergonomic or orthopaedic - but McCarthy says their effectiveness isn't completely proven. "There is a little bit of fairly scrappy evidence to suggest that having a little bit of a higher front of the pillow, which goes into the neck area... does help [side sleepers]." To see if a higher front helps you sleep better, you can try McCarthy's towel trick by rolling it and placing it underneath your pillow. He urges side sleepers to pick a position that keeps their back straight. For back sleepers, some manufacturers advertise a pillow with a dip in the middle that is raised at the sides. It does put people into a good sleeping position, says McCarthy, but some of his patients have found them "a bit claustrophobic". Someone who has a large and heavy head also needs a thicker and firmer pillow, he adds. Feather and down can keep you cool on warm nights because they wick away heat from your head, says McCarthy. But they can change shape during the night, particularly if the sleeper moves around a lot and the pillow can end up bunched towards the headboard. "What starts off as a nice, flat, supported surface becomes a wedge and so your neck is then kinked up." Hollow fibre and microfibre fillings can hold shape better though they generally don't wick away heat as well, says McCarthy. Some are made with a firmer material in the lower half of the pillow, which help retain the shape during the night. This article contains content provided by Instagram. You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. McCarthy bought his foam pillow, which has tubular spaces for ventilation, five years ago for about £50. As a side sleeper, he adjusts its height using a folded towel laid underneath it. He says choosing the right pillow is very much "horses for courses" and encourages people to utilise the trial period some manufacturers offer customers. "There just isn't a one-off design that is perfect for everybody or every position, I'm afraid," he says. "You really have to personalise it." title: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day boss
description: World News Day aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.
body: More than 1,000 news providers around the world have signed up to support World News Day on Monday, which aims to promote the role of journalism at a time when organisers say the industry faces an "existential threat". Participating media organisations, including the New York Times, Reuters and the Kyiv Independent, are sharing editorials, ads and cartoons to highlight the value of "trusted journalism". Trust in news dropped to a new low globally in 2026, according to the Reuters Institute's latest Digital News Report, which noted that people are increasingly turning to social media and AI chatbots for news. Branko Brkic, co-organiser of World News Day, said media organisations that were once rivals must work together, adding: "If we do not change the game, we are just not going to exist." World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events. It comes against a backdrop of what the recent Reuters Institute report described as "anxiety, disengagement, and cynicism" towards news among the public, "but also openness to new sources and formats, and continued belief in what news at its best can offer". Social media and video networks overtook news organisations' own websites and apps as the main source of online news last year, but are trusted less, the report said. In another report, published earlier this month, UK media regulator Ofcom, external also said people now get news from a wider variety of sources, with YouTube "growing rapidly" and 20% of people using AI tools to access news. But growing choice has gone hand-in-hand with greater uncertainty about who and what to believe, and traditional providers are still seen as more trustworthy, accurate and impartial than online platforms, Ofcom said. Brkic, who founded South Africa's Daily Maverick, accepts that the media landscape has changed, and said established news organisations must respond. "The old days are not coming back. We need to form a new equilibrium, and the only way we can do it is that if we actually join forces," he said. "If we continue like this, we're just going to be weak individual players waiting to be taken out. If we don't change something pretty fundamentally and pretty urgently, we're just going to be roadkill." Brkic said the mainstream media has "committed mistakes", but professional and reliable journalists play a vital role in society. "We need to talk to our audiences and explain to them, it's not in your interest not to choose truth and trust," he said. "We cannot function without a thing called the truth, without facts." The definition of "the truth" is often contested, however, as seen in US President Donald Trump's long-running battle with what he labels the "fake news media". Brkic added: "This is the information-based society. We are the infrastructure for that information-based society. And that society is actually going to really struggle without us." title: You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to do it
description: Here are four ways you can put money aside to save enough for a deposit on your first home.
body: This video can not be played How much is in your savings account? If buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the money to get there is a marathon. The "Your First Home" scheme, announced on Saturday, aims to help first-time buyers in England get on the housing ladder with a small deposit. Currently a 5% deposit on the current average UK house price of £272,000 plus moving costs and legal fees - will set you back about £16,850, according to financial information service Moneyfacts. That's daunting, but here are four ways that experts say you can at least make a start on saving for a deposit. Depositing an amount you can afford into a regular savers account the day after you are paid is a good way to start, suggests Anna Bowes, savings expert at financial advisers The Private Office. "It becomes like another bill, but one that you can benefit from in the future," she says. The type of account that's suitable depends on your circumstances. Some of the ones which pay the highest interest are only accessible if you hold a current account with the provider, she says. Other considerations are whether you can lock the money away for longer, to receive a better savings rate. If you don't have a buffer of other savings, then experts say an easy access account gives you the chance to dip into the money to pay an unexpected bill. You can save up to £4,000 a year in a Lifetime Individual Savings Account (LISA) and the government guarantees a 25% bonus. So, if you put the full amount in then the government will add £1,000 a year. But there is a catch, that has left some people out of pocket. Money saved in a LISA can only be used to buy a first home up to the value of £450,000 - a threshold that has not changed since 2017. The only other time you can withdraw the money is after the age of 60 or in the exceptional case that you are terminally ill with less than 12 months to live. Withdrawal under any other circumstances means you get hit with a penalty - so you could get back less than you put in. Ministers are planning to replace the LISA with a new First Time Buyer ISA, but there are no clear details yet about how it will work. 'I lost thousands in savings and my partner's money is in limbo' The earlier you start saving the more you can build up thanks to the magic of compound interest. In short, interest is added on a larger and larger pot as time goes by. Bowes says that saving £50 a month from the age of 20 would give you about £41,000 in 30 years' time when you hit 50, assuming interest of 5% is paid a year. Start 10 years later, and you'd need to save more than double - £101 a month - to have the same amount at the age of 50. Investing in stocks and shares is another option, but the value of investments can go down as well as up. Watch: What is compound interest? An increasing number of lenders are offering mortgage deals with little or no deposit required. David Hollingworth, from L&C, points to mortgages that have deposits starting from £5,000 and allow people to borrow up to 98% or 99% of the property purchase price. They might not always be the best option, and not everyone will be eligible. And, of course, some first-time buyers turn to their parents for help. Again that's not available to all, but a survey by the Nationwide Building Society suggests that more than half of parents who charge their adult children rent are putting some or all of the money towards helping their child save to buy their own home. title: My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die
description: Aberdeen is launching an ambitious bid to revive its struggling centre. Could it offer lessons for other high streets?
body: My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die The empty building that used to be the home of Marks & Spencer in Aberdeen is one of the first things you see when you arrive off the train and come into the city centre. The sign has gone, though the shape of the lettering can still be made out; the windows are blacked out and the doors boarded up. This is my hometown. As a teenager, I spent hours on Union Street, its main thoroughfare, nicknamed the Granite Mile after the local silver-grey stone. It was the place to try on all the latest fashions from the likes of Clockhouse and Chelsea Girl. The street used to be packed with shoppers from across the north-east of Scotland. Now, it's pockmarked with empty shops. "I come to Union Street to take a bus somewhere else... there's nothing to shop for now… it's horrendous," complains Marie Sim, a lifelong Aberdeen resident. It's a similar story across the country: High Streets, once bursting with shops, hit first by the rise of out-of-town retail centres and then by online commerce. But Aberdeen is in the thick of an ambitious turnaround plan. The port city has essentially declared war on its empty shop problem, taking an unusually hands-on approach to filling vacant units and bringing long-neglected upper floors of buildings into use. The Marks & Spencer flagship store in Aberdeen closed in August, 80 years after it opened there On top of that, the council is pouring tens of millions into trying to make the city centre a destination again. Like many other places, it's leaning into the "experience economy", with a new indoor food and drink market and a major redevelopment of the seafront. High Streets are integral to how we feel about where we live. The sight of vacant shops and graffiti can quickly become a vicious circle, deterring shoppers, discouraging investment and leading to anti-social behaviour. Politicians of all stripes have been trying for years to breathe new life into town centres - and Andy Burnham, who has made a focus on "place" part of his political identity, is the latest. He argues they should become "symbols of Britain's renaissance". But can it be achieved? And if they're to survive, do town centres need a fundamental rethink? One in eight properties on British High Streets are currently vacant, according to Green Street, the property and retail analytics company, a number that's stayed stubbornly high for years. "If there was a silver bullet, it would have been fired years ago," says Jackie Sadek, a former government adviser on urban regeneration, who has spent nearly four decades working in town centre renewal. One of the biggest obstacles is fractured ownership. Shops and buildings are often owned by dozens of different landlords, sometimes through offshore companies or complex structures, each with their own interests and priorities. That can slow decision-making and make large-scale regeneration difficult. But even with empty units that are available, you need to find someone willing to take them on. Many units are old and need modernising. One in eight properties on British High Streets are currently vacant The cost of running a High Street business has also risen; employment costs are higher, and there's the burden of business rates. Firms need customers. Footfall on many High Streets has been in long-term decline as shopping and services move online, and this enormous structural shift has yet to play out fully. Two-thirds of town centre experts think there is still 20% to 40% too much retail space, according to a survey by retail body Revo and real estate consultancy Lambert Smith Hampton. In Aberdeen's boom years of North Sea oil, from the late 1970s through to the early 2010s, it didn't have to work hard to fill its hotels and restaurants and get the cash tills ringing because of the wealth the energy industry brought to the city. I remember weekends with friends as a teenager, spending whatever cash we had in the fashion chains and shoe shops. Later came the pubs and bar-hopping, and trips to the art deco Capitol Theatre (now office space), where I saw Duran Duran. But by the end of 2022, Union Street had hit rock bottom. Aberdonians had long deserted the High Street for a shopping centre, which opened in 2009 next to the railway station. "They'd fallen out of love with their city," says Bob Keiller, head of Our Union Street coalition, a community-led group formed after an emergency summit to reverse the decline. The first thing it did was listen to what residents wanted, receiving thousands of submissions. Restoring a bit of civic pride and filling empty units became the focus. It's been a co-ordinated effort, involving letting agents, the council, landlords, businesses and a big team of volunteers, led by Keiller, a former FTSE 100 CEO, who isn't getting paid. He has a map on his office wall, detailing the status of every property, unit by unit, with colour-coded Post-it notes. They audited the street, tracking down absent landlords, and logging what was empty and why. Volunteers offered to give the empty properties a clean and a lick of paint, to make them more attractive to let. They also spruced up the streets, picking litter, weeding, and painting bins. A small team still goes out once a fortnight. Bob Keiller heads a community-led group set up to help revive Aberdeen's Union Street There's a website where all the available properties are collated; crucially, all of the financial incentives are also listed. These can include council fit-out grants (where a new business gets money to decorate premises), and a two-year discount from business rates. In 2023, 57 of the 198 units on Union Street were empty. As of today, 33 have been filled, with a further 14 in the process of being let. But it can feel like a game of whack-a-mole because since the initiative started, another 20 units have become vacant. title: Healey to promise 'new age of industrialisation' for UK in conference speech
description: The chancellor will unveil policies aimed at boosting British shipbuilding in his speech to Labour's annual conference on Monday.
body: John Healey will promise "a new age of industrialisation" for the UK, when he delivers his first Labour conference speech as chancellor on Monday. Healey will tell delegates "our coal mines are not coming back", but that Labour will remake Britain's industrial past "for the modern age" by backing advanced manufacturing. He will also announce plans to boost Britain's shipbuilding industry, with new orders for Royal Navy floating docks and a maritime research vessel. With just a month to go until his first Budget, the chancellor is under pressure to cut spending or raise taxes to tackle the ballooning cost of government borrowing. But he is not expected to reveal any details about his Budget plans in his speech at Labour's annual conference in Liverpool. Instead, he will attempt to set out a positive vision for the future of British industry, based around what he will call a "new confidence in Britain". The former defence secretary will announce that three new floating docks at HM Royal Naval Base Clyde, at Faslane, will be built in the UK, rather than put out to international tender. Plans for the new docks were first set out in 2023 and are expected to upgrade Faslane's facilities for the next generation of British submarines. The docks form part of a wider £15bn upgrade programme for the Royal Navy's shipyards and are expected to come into service in the early 2030s. First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said in a speech on Sunday that the government would also commission a new marine research vessel as part of plans for a "new era of reindustrialisation". The chancellor is expected to announce £115m in funding for the ship, which is also set to come into service in the early 2030s. Ahead of his speech, Healey said: "By backing British shipyards, we are not only boosting national security but also securing resilience in the industries that will drive growth today while building the capabilities the country needs for the future." Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the plans were "reheated announcements" with "no clarity on where the money is coming from". He added: "Labour are running scared of making the tough choices needed to pay for Britain's defence. "All they can offer is reannounced docks and more hot air from Healey. Only the Conservatives will cut the welfare bill to fund defence." Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, national secretary of the GMB union, which has campaigned for the move, said it would be a "massive boost" for the UK's shipbuilding sector. "For too long juicy contracts have been sent to overseas - often subsidised - yards. "This policy could reinvigorate UK yards and the communities that depend on them," he added. Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who is due to deliver his big conference speech on Tuesday - has previously spoken about his ambition to "reindustrialise" Britain, including in talks last week with US President Donald Trump. But in a survey to be published on Monday, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) will highlight falling economic activity across key sectors such as retail and services in the three months to September, with manufacturing declining more moderately. CBI deputy chief economist Alpesh Paleja said rising energy and employment costs combined with weak demand were continuing to put pressure on profit margins. He added: "Uncertainty ahead of next month's Budget is also holding back activity in some sectors. "Against the backdrop of renewed fiscal pressures, the Budget must draw a clear red line under any more rises in the cost of hiring, investing and doing business." The chancellor is also under pressure from some of Labour's trade union backers to do more to tackle the cost of living. Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, has called on Healey to "do something for workers and the working class" in his Budget. She urged him to unfreeze income tax thresholds "to put money back into people's pockets" and take further action on energy bills. In his conference speech, Healey will also announce plans to bring back a training scheme run by trade unions, to help workers in England gain new skills and adapt as technology, including AI, changes the workplace. The Union Learning Fund will get £15m in taxpayers' money, taken from existing government budgets. Employees do not need to be union members to benefit, with support options ranging from essential English, maths and digital skills, to training for jobs in growing industries, such as advanced manufacturing. title: Why some Indian civil servants become heroes for doing their jobs
description: In a system often marked by red tape and exhausting delays, officers seen to be following the rules get adulation.
body: Tukaram Mundhe has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few years. Tukaram Mundhe, 51, is one of them. The commissioner of Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, he has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May. His teams have inspected restaurants and other food businesses, uncovering pest infestations, poor hygiene and expired food. He has also highlighted large gaps between what hospitals pay for common medical supplies and what patients are charged. These actions have made Mundhe a social-media celebrity, with videos and images from inspections widely shared online. Hundreds of people have commented that they wished officers like him could be sent to fix food safety concerns in their state. Mundhe is not alone. In Gurugram, a suburb of Delhi, district town planner RS Batth has won praise for acting against illegal construction and encroachments. But why are these officials treated like heroes for doing their jobs? In India, civil servants are responsible for many services people rely on every day, from issuing documents to policing, food safety and healthcare. But many are also accused of delays, bribes and making people run from pillar to post. So when an official appears to cut through the red tape, the response can be surprisingly enthusiastic. "What should have been normal has become exceptional," says retired civil servant Kamal Kant Jaswal. For many citizens, delays, bureaucratic hurdles and indifferent treatment have become so familiar that efficient governance now stands out as an exception, he adds. Many Indians associate government offices with lengthy procedures, repeated visits and an often-unresponsive bureaucracy Mundhe is not the first official to gain recognition for doing exactly that. One of the most prominent examples is TN Seshan, who became a household name as India's chief election commissioner in the 1990s for fearlessly enforcing rules. Kiran Bedi, the first woman to join the officer ranks of the Indian Police Service, was nicknamed "Crane Bedi" in the early 1980s after it was widely reported that she got an illegally parked car belonging to then prime minister Indira Gandhi towed away (it was removed by a sub-inspector who reported to her, who said years later that she supported, external his decision). Ashok Khemka became nationally known after intervening in a controversial land transaction in 2012, while police officer Neeraj Jadaun was praised for confronting a mob during deadly religious violence in Delhi in 2020. These stories have made the idea of the "honest" or "no-nonsense" bureaucrat both familiar and rare. Jaswal, however, points out that thousands of officials in India do their jobs without attracting public attention. "Their work may not involve much direct contact with citizens, or may simply be less visible." For ordinary people, however, a visit to a government office is often seen as an exhausting process. Rajesh Singh, 43, who works at a finance company in Delhi, says he has experienced long waits to get his work done and even longer processes to solve complaints. "What is supposed to take 24 hours, I have personally experienced being stretched to six months with no guarantee of a positive outcome even then," he says. But an officer praised for enforcing rules can also face criticism for applying them too rigidly without taking into account ground realities. Kiran Bedi, India's first woman IPS officer, became known for her strict approach to law enforcement Mundhe has been criticised by sections of the food and hospitality industry over his enforcement drives. He has rejected allegations of selective or unlawful action, saying inspections are evidence-driven and licences are suspended only in serious cases. Batth, too, has faced flak for acting against illegal encroachments, with critics alleging his enforcement is selective and disproportionately affects vulnerable people. In several viral videos, he has said his actions are carried out strictly under town-planning rules. Jaswal explains a street vendor's stall may be an unauthorised structure in the eyes of the law, but could be a family's only source of income. And in a country where millions migrate to cities in search of work, unsanctioned living spaces could be the only way to find a place to stay. This tension between the law and economics helps explain why the same enforcement action can be viewed as both lawful and harsh. Bureaucrats also face challenges of their own while carrying out their duties. Pushpa Sundar, who briefly served as a civil servant and has written extensively on development issues, says officers can face political pressure and transfers when they refuse to comply with demands. "They too have families, careers and financial responsibilities and it needs extraordinary courage to risk those things in order to act independently," she says. She argues that officers need stronger institutional support when they refuse to do something illegal or improper. Jaswal remembers facing such pressure himself. In 1974, when he was district magistrate of Uttarkashi in what was then undivided Uttar Pradesh, a senior minister was contesting the state legislature election. He says he had to turn down a number of demands from the minister as they were against the rules. The minister won the election and Jaswal says he got his "marching orders soon after". But when he left for his next assignment, people stood in the summer heat for several kilometres on his way to say goodbye. The relationship between politicians and civil servants, he says, is rarely straightforward. Many civil servants who seek desirable postings or rely on political support choose the path of least resistance, while standing up to political pressure entails certain costs, he says. title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
description: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts report "This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack." The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away. Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed. It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz. Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war. We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close. Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting. It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire. "Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line. Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goats He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals. "I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway." He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too. At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach. "We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said. Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled. The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region. Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions. Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha. We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based. About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side. As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle. We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city. An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing the Yemeni government with weapons Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons. Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line. "It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said. The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces. Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. title: Tourism tax needs to be more flexible in Wales, warns expert
description: Anglesey, Conwy and Gwynedd councils have all put a pause on introducing the nightly tourist tax.
body: Gwynedd and Conwy have both postponed making any decisions on introducing a tourism tax Wales' tourism tax needs to be more flexible, an expert has said. Last week, Anglesey council rejected introducing the visitor levy for now, over concerns for its tourism industry, while Gwynedd and Conwy councils both postponed making any decision on the nightly fee. It is down to local authorities to decide whether they want to introduce the Welsh government legislation, which means that from 2027 a fixed price can be charged per person, per night, external, and applies to both adults and children. The Welsh government said the legislation allowed for decisions to be taken at a local level, with councils able to introduce the levy "to support investment in tourism services and facilities". A tourism tax, or levy, is a charge which would need to be paid by anyone staying overnight in any area which introduces it. The idea is that it covers, or contributes to, the costs which authorities face as a result of the tourism industry. Anglesy council says it will not be bringing in the levy at the moment, over concerns about the inpact on the tourism sector If a local authority decides to introduce the tourism tax, fees for people staying in hostels, shared rooms and tent pitches would be 75p + VAT per person per night, while most other types of accommodation would be charged at £1.30 + VAT. But according to Dr Linda Osti, senior tourism lecturer at Bangor University, decisions on how much is charged, and how a levy is brought in, should be made on a more local level instead of a one-size-fits-all approach. "It's one legislation for every county and and it's applied at county level, when we should think about sub-county level," she said. "Geographically, if we think about Gwynedd....we cannot have the same levy on Eryri or Porthmadog. The same legislation cannot work for Cardiff, or in Anglesey, on the coast. "There are different visitors, there are also different conditions." Osti also suggested there was a "mistrust" from tourism businesses on how local authorities would spend money generated from tourism tax, compared to places like the Italian alps where decisions are made through smaller co-operatives. Dr Linda Osti believes a levy in specific areas would work in Wales Earlier this month, it was announced that regional mayors in England would gain new powers to charge an uncapped levy on overnight stays for visitors. Osti, who co-authored a 2024 report for the Welsh government studying how visitor levies worked in other countries, external, said: "If we compare what we know from England, which is very little at the moment, it appears to be much more flexible. "So local authorities can decide the percentage to charge and whether to introduce exemptions, and it seems they may also decide for how many nights, and whether to charge children or not. "I wish Wales would go back and think about flexibility and revisit the legislation." On Thursday, Anglesey council confirmed it would not introduce the so-called tourism tax for now, "given the challenges already facing its tourism industry". It said a public consultation received more than 2,000 responses, including from residents, businesses and tourism stakeholders, with concerns voiced about increased costs for visitors, and the island's "competitiveness" as a holiday destination. Meanwhile, Cyngor Gywnedd agreed to delay its decision over the levy so more analysis could be done of almost 7,000 responses to its consultation - a number it said was "much higher" than other areas. The local authority said initial figures showed a mixed reaction to the proposals, with more support from residents but higher levels of opposition from visitors and businesses. In Conwy, council members also chose to defer a decision on implementing the levy until "further evidence and practical experience are available". It said concerns from consultations included fears over reduced bookings, shorter stays and reduced visitor spend at a time when local businesses are facing economic pressures. Bethan Evans says roads get blocked and car parks become full in tourist season Bethan Evans, of family-run business Dolgamedd caravan park in Dolgellau, Gwynedd, is one of those in support of introducing a tourism tax in the county to help areas cope with busy roads and car parks at peak times. She said she was "disappointed" that councils appeared to be "scared of a noisy, selfish minority" opposing the fee, and described the 75p per night levy for people camping as "nothing" compared to the rubbish that some visitors left behind at the site. "You get people [with] brand new tents who can't be bothered to put a wet tent back in the car so they try and dump them in our bins, which we pay for," she said. "There is such a lot of that happening, and the amount of food waste is just incredible. So it's ridiculous saying they can't afford it, oh yes they can." But she added: "Some people are wonderful, and those people are happy to pay the tax. We want people who respect the area, who are willing to pay the tax, so that's the kind of tourist I'd like." Gwynedd saw almost 7,000 responses to its consultation on introducing a tourism tax Nicky Williamson, of the Professional Association of Self-Caterers (PASC) UK Cymru, described the pause on introducing the levy across the three counties as a "welcome victory for common sense and for listening to the evidence". She said: "Tourism businesses across Wales have been clear about the pressures they are already facing, and the response to these consultations shows the strength of concern about adding another cost to Welsh holidays. "This is simply the wrong time to introduce another cost for either businesses or visitors. We welcome councils listening to the evidence and urge others to do the same before taking decisions that could have long-term consequences for Wales' visitor economy." So far, Cardiff

title: McNulty first US world road race winner in 33 years
description: Brandon McNulty becomes the first American winner of the men's road race world title in 33 years with a stunning victory in Montreal.
body: Brandon McNulty also won the Montreal Grand Prix in 2025 Brandon McNulty became the first American winner of the men's road race world title in 33 years with a stunning victory in Montreal. The 28-year-old put his hands on his head in disbelief as he crossed the line 13 seconds clear of the chasing pack, completing the gruelling 273.4km course in six hours and 17 minutes. Australian Michael Matthews was second, with former winner Mathieu van der Poel, of the Netherlands, in third. The last American winner of the race was Lance Armstrong in 1993. "Until the last 800m I didn't believe, I was so tired," said McNulty. "I'm at a loss for words. I knew something could happen but it would take a miracle and I guess today a miracle happened". He launched an attack going into the final 30km and was 50 seconds clear going into the last lap. McNulty visibly began to tire on the final climb and his lead was cut to just 10 seconds, but the chasing pack were unable to reel him in. Britain's Tom Pidcock finished seventh, with Ireland's Ben Healy 10th and Remco Evenepoel of Belgium in 12th place. Even without injured riding legend Tadej Pogacar, Montreal 2026 was still full of favourites who were expected to dictate the shape of this monumentally long race. Van der poel, Evenepoel, Wout van Aert, Paul Seixas and Pidcock were all there, all animating and pushing to breakaway from one another under gradually yellowing Canadian maples. But timing, not power or race craft, proved crucial. Such was the distance all attacked far too early, and it was McNulty - a time triallist and domestique to Pogacar by trade - who took off and emptied himself. The unassuming and, at times, seemingly timid American is a very popular winner of what was unquestionably one of the best races of a long season. title: Watch: The ups and downs of SpaceX's 13 Starship test flights
description: The BBC's Ricky Boleto looks how previous SpaceX test flights went.
body: This video can not be played SpaceX is planning to carry out its 14th Starship rocket test flight on Monday. If successful, it will be the first Starship to go in orbit around the Earth and the furthest one has ever flown. The mission is set to complete approximately six orbits around the planet over a 10-hour flight. But as the BBC's Ricky Boleto reports, there have been many ups and downs along the way. title: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections
description: Aleksandar Vučić's administration has been dogged by prolonged protests over allegations of corruption.
body: Aleksandar Vučić's resignation comes years after more than a year of protests over allegations of government corruption Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption. Aleksandar Vučić said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade. He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Vučić cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution. The pro-Russian populist's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting. It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof, killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024. Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed. Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress. A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality. Vučić's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation. This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year. Vučić said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands. He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics. Parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected. Vučić used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS. The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit Vučić's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia. Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade, becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017. He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment. title: More than 50 arrested at Palestine Action support rally
description: More than 250 protesters sat outside Labour's party conference in Liverpool to support the banned group.
body: Merseyside Police said more than 50 protesters had been arrested More than 50 demonstrators have been arrested outside the Labour Party conference in Liverpool during a protest in support of the banned Palestine Action group, police have said. More than 250 protesters sat outside the conference centre earlier, many holding home-made banners which read: "I support Palestine Action". Scores of police officers stood by before moving in to start making arrests, warning protesters they were illegally holding signs supporting a proscribed organisation. After asking them if they were going to continue to do so, officers led some of the protesters away, telling them they had been arrested under the Terrorism Act. Merseyside Police said more than 50 people had so far been detained at the Defend Our Juries event and that officers were in the process of making arrests on suspicion of wearing/carrying an article supporting a proscribed organisation. A force spokesperson said it respected everyone's rights to protest lawfully while also aiming to keep the peace and ensure public safety. The force said it made "detailed and co-ordinated plans ahead of such events to ensure it can apply this consistently, fairly and proportionately". The spokesperson said not everyone present at the protest had been committing a criminal offence. The arrests were criticised by Amnesty International, which called them a "shameful attack on freedom of speech". One of those detained was human rights barrister Margaret Owen, 94. A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries said: "We had hoped the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, would do the sensible thing and bin the ban on Palestine Action given the weight of public pressure to do so and the escalating amount of resources required in enforcing it. "Continuing the charade of the proscription of Palestine Action is illogical, unsustainable and immoral." Protesters gathered outside court in July to call for the Palestine Action ban to be lifted Demonstrators in Liverpool cheered every time someone was carried away by police. Kerry Moscogiuri, chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: "Protesting is one of the most effective tools we have to make our leaders listen to us, but we have seen consecutive governments crack down on our right to do it. "The arrests of grandparents, teenagers and everyone in between for holding placards outside the Labour Party conference are a truly shameful attack on freedom of speech. "The new prime minister can reform our laws so that communities are protected in coming together and demonstrating on the issues they care about. Will he do so?" In July it was confirmed that Palestine Action's proscription would be reviewed by the Supreme Court. The court said it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban, which came into force in July 2025. In a statement issued shortly afterwards, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the government would "robustly defend this appeal". The Home Office has repeatedly said that the ban of the group has nothing to do with protest in support of Palestinian causes - and was necessary because it was causing significant criminal damage to legitimate businesses. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal have ruled that Palestine Action's activities include criminal acts - although they were divided on whether those incidents justified turning to terrorism laws. BBC News has asked the Ministry of Justice to comment. title: Chelsea restore resilience - are they title contenders again?
description: Doubt crept in at Chelsea last season when they lost their Women's Super League crown - but early signs in this campaign suggest they have regained their spark for another challenge.
body: Katie McCabe (right) joined Chelsea from Arsenal in the summer Doubt crept in at Chelsea last season when they lost their Women's Super League crown - but early signs in this campaign suggest they have regained their spark. A crucial 1-0 victory over rivals Arsenal on Sunday meant they extended their WSL unbeaten run to 12 games and sit just two points off leaders Manchester City. They showed a different side - one that was willing to dig deep, control the game without the ball and defend with composure while Arsenal put pressure on. It may have been the missing ingredient as Chelsea look revitalised and refreshed. Could they win the WSL title this year? It would be foolish to say they can't. Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed Sonia Bompastor led Chelsea to an unbeaten domestic treble in her first season in charge, but it did not go to plan in 2025-26 as their six-year stranglehold on the WSL ended. City overtook them at the top and many believed Arsenal would be the main challengers this season after a strong summer's recruitment. Perhaps written off, Chelsea started the season tamely, drawing 1-1 with Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge despite a dominant performance. The same issues were rife as they lacked ruthlessness in front of goal and a mistake at the back gifted Villa an opportunity. But since then, Chelsea have turned dominant performances into results, winning three matches in a row, capping it off with a well-rounded display against Arsenal, who are seven points behind City in seventh spot. Bompastor said her side were prepared to "mentally fight" and able to "adjust" to Arsenal's pressure in a way perhaps they didn't last season. It was a defensive masterclass and they delivered Bompastor's gameplan perfectly, capping off victory with a third successive clean sheet - a run of 315 minutes without conceding a goal. "In this league, you have so many different opponents and you have to be able to adjust and do something different," said the Blues boss. "I've been talking a lot about that, to be strong and to be together, I always want to see a group of players who are together in those high and low moments. "We came into this game well prepared. We knew we would have moments in the game where we were not in control. We prepared for those moments. "We knew exactly where we wanted them to take the ball and where to leave some spaces. We were really strong mentally and physically." It is a result that could be the catalyst Chelsea needed to push on and put pressure on Manchester City, who face Arsenal next in the WSL (Sunday, 16:30 BST). Chelsea's match-winner Alyssa Thompson said their victory over the Gunners was "amazing for team morale". Even Bompastor admitted Chelsea are "a different team from last season" and there are tangible examples of their improvements. England midfielder Keira Walsh was a standout performer against Arsenal and it was her strike which was parried into the path of Thompson for the only goal. Her new parternship with 20-year-old Lexi Potter is flourishing and has allowed Walsh to get further up the pitch and play with more freedom. Bompastor said the 29-year-old was "a boss on the pitch" when she reaches those levels and it helps the team have "better foundations". Goalscorer Thompson has consistently delivered up front, while the arrival of summer signing Melvine Malard from Manchester United has given them an outlet. The French striker missed their opening two matches with a minor injury but scored on her debut against Birmingham City and caused havoc against Arsenal. "She's massive for us. She puts in work off the ball and sets off the press," said team-mate Walsh. "Her awareness of people around her and her ability... She's an incredible striker and she will be very good for us." That press, led by Malard, has moved higher up and teams have struggled to break through, while full-back Ellie Carpenter continues to overlap dangerously. Katie McCabe, who switched from Arsenal to Chelsea this summer, has brought leadership and bite - an aggression that was lacking at times last season. Most of all, the Blues look like a team who believe they should be champions and are willing to work for it. It was in contrast to toothless Arsenal, who have one victory in their first four WSL games and scored just twice. "We've got both sides to our game and we showed that tonight in spells. Everyone was fighting for each other. Every first and second ball was ours," added Walsh. title: More questions than answers after major incident near RAF Fairford
description: The vital US launchpad in England has long been a possible target, writes diplomatic correspondent James Landale.
body: A major incident was declared and five men arrested near the base after "suspicious vehicles" were seen driving towards it, police said RAF Fairford is a slice of America in the heart of England; a forward operating base for the US Air Force since the Cold War. Its two-mile runway is so long it was once an emergency backup for the US space shuttle programme. Now it is a vital launchpad for the vast, lumbering bombers President Donald Trump uses to strike Iran, the only airbase with such capabilities available to the US in Europe. And that – by definition – has long made it a potential target. What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe Five arrested as counter-terror police investigate major incident near RAF Fairford In July, Iran's foreign ministry accused the UK of being complicit in war crimes for allowing the US to use Fairford as a staging post for defensive strikes in its war against Tehran. And it warned "any party that, in any manner, participates in military aggression against Iran will bear responsibility for the consequences and repercussions of its decision". That was seen as an explicit threat. There is also a stalemate in diplomatic efforts to end the war. That has given rise to speculation Iran could seek to step up pressure on the US, perhaps with an attack outside the Middle East, to try to shift the dial ahead of the US midterm elections in November. When Ed Miliband met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations last week, the foreign secretary explicitly warned of the UK's "unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups" and said it would not tolerate any "hostile activity" on UK soil. A major response was mounted near the base in Gloucestershire on Sunday But some eyes, too, have turned to Moscow. Danish intelligence warned last week Russia could in the coming months launch a limited military attack on a Nato country. Germany has already formally accused Russia of using a drone carrying explosives in an attempted attack on Leipzig in August. Over the summer, the Russian embassy in London warned the UK against allowing Ukraine to use British drones deep inside Russian territory: "The deeper [the UK's] involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv's terrorist machinery, the higher price it will pay." That, too, was seen as a direct threat. There are also possibilities of some kind of Islamist attack, or even an incident of direct action by a group opposed to both the US-Israeli war on Iran or the use of UK bases to launch strikes. One central question is whether the authorities were prepared for such an attack. The US handles security within the base; the UK is responsible all threats outside the perimeter. What did the authorities know? President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation "for a long time". But there are also suggestions the incident was foiled only because a passing driver reported strange vans to the police. At the time of the explicit Iranian threat against the UK, a spokesman for the Ministry of Defence said: "Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it's on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself." So for now, there remain more questions that facts. Was a hostile foreign state involved, or were proxies acting on its behalf? What was intended and what was the potential risk to local people? One thing is clear: the threat from conflicts involving the UK will not always stay overseas. title: Bellamy 'hurting' as Denmark outclass Wales
description: Craig Bellamy says he is "hurting" on the back of Wales' 2-0 Nations League A defeat away to Denmark, but feels his side will continue to improve.
body: This video can not be played Craig Bellamy says he is "hurting" after admitting Denmark were worthy winners against his Wales side in Copenhagen. A Ben Davies own goal along with Gustav Isaksen's strike earned Brian Riemer's men a 2-0 victory over Wales at Parken Stadium. It leaves Bellamy's team winless in six matches in 2026 and without a point from their away Nations League A double-header with Portugal and the Danes. Despite the loss, Bellamy remains confident his side will improve by playing against Europe's elite on a consistent basis. "I'm really hurting. When you see an athletic team run over you a little bit... but then, will we improve? I think we will," said the Wales head coach. "This team will get better, these players will keep improving. There are young ones coming in well after I'm gone. "For me now it's just focus, two more games to go. How can I help you improve for the next two games but also how can I improve? "I'm probably more loving when I'm losing, I'm probably more of a pain in the backside when I'm winning." This video can not be played Wales must be ready 'when the heat comes' Denmark dominated early on and Mikkel Damsgaard fired against the post shortly after Isaksen had a goal disallowed for offside. Despite an improvement from Wales after the opening half an hour, they were ultimately undone from two set-pieces. "I said to the players before the game, 'this is going to be tougher than Portugal'," Bellamy added. "It was a different challenge but a very difficult one. The best team won overall. "As disappointed as I am with that, the result I probably think was fair." Nations League: Wales well beaten by Denmark - reaction 'Workhorse' Koumas growing with Wales Defeat - which came just three days after a 1-0 loss to Portugal in Lisbon - has left Wales with plenty of work to do. They will at least have home advantage at Cardiff City Stadium as they prepare for the remainder of the current international break, with matches against Norway on Thursday, 1 October, and then Denmark the following Sunday. Captain Davies felt Wales were being taught some harsh lessons in what is their second stint in the top tier of the Nations League. "It was a tough game. They are a good team and made it a hard game for us," the Spurs defender told BBC Match of the Day Wales. "It was really frustrating to concede from two set-pieces. The Nations League games are against the best teams in Europe, it was always going to be tough. "If you're not at 100% then you are going to get punished at this level. We have to regroup and go again on Thursday." Despite the setback in the Danish capital, winger Sorba Thomas echoed Bellamy's sentiments. "Thankfully we've got two games at home still to come. We'll have home advantage so we need to show a reaction," he told BBC Match of the Day Wales. "We are just going to get better. We are a small nation but we've got big hearts and beliefs and for us it's about showing that more on the pitch." title: No handshakes between Republic of Ireland and Israel
description: The Republic of Ireland and Israel players do not shake hands with each other before or after Sunday's controversial Uefa Nations League game in Hungary.
body: The Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during Israel's national anthem The Republic of Ireland and Israel players did not shake hands with each other before or after Sunday's controversial Uefa Nations League game in Hungary. After walking on to the pitch at Nagyerdei Stadion, the Republic of Ireland squad stood for their national anthem and bowed their heads before Israel's anthem. Following the anthems, the two teams did not line up for the traditional handshakes. There was also no exchange of pennants between Republic of Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel skipper Manor Solomon, who did not shake hands. The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since February when the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3. The Republic of Ireland players have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace. However, the players voted to fulfil the fixture during a lengthy meeting at the team's hotel in Debrecen on Saturday. Later on Saturday, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu confirmed he had withdrawn from the squad, saying he felt it "would be wrong to participate" in Sunday's game and the return fixture in the Serbian town of Backa Topola on 4 October. The Irish players wore black armbands, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said on Saturday was a gesture "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict". After scoring the Republic of Ireland's third goal in a 3-0 win, Jack Moylan removed his armband and kissed it before kissing his team's badge. The Republic of Ireland players were jeered by the small number of Israel fans in attendance when they emerged for their pre-game warm-up. While the FAI confirmed no tickets would be sold to Republic of Ireland supporters, a handful of fans were spotted inside the stadium. Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious Speaking to RTE prior to kick-off, Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke about the impact the intense scrutiny on the games have had on him and his squad. "It's been one of the most challenging weeks for me as a coach and I guess it is the same for most of the players. It is situations we haven't been in before," said Hallgrimsson. "When we are in these positions we hope we take more right decisions than wrong but you never get everything correct. "I feel for the players, a lot of young players in this squad that we need to take good care of. Honestly, there are a lot of players who have mixed emotions for this game and it is our job to protect all of them." Hallgrimsson added: "As you can expect, the preparation has been probably as bad as it can be so I just hope the players come and do a good performance. We are here to play football, they are footballers and I hope they can enjoy that at least." Jack Moylan kissed his black armband after scoring against Israel During a dramatic day on Saturday, doubts emerged over whether the game would take place after the Republic of Ireland's pre-match news conference was postponed because of the squad meeting. When the news conference commended at 14:30 BST on Saturday - more than five hours later than planned - Courell said a players' vote on whether to play the game passed by a "significant majority". Courell added that the Republic of Ireland would not engage in pre-match formalities such as handshakes. In 2024, the Ireland women's basketball team chose not to shake hands with Israel players or stand on court for the anthems before a EuroBasket qualifier in Riga, but the teams did exchange handshakes when they met again last year. The Republic of Ireland have faced calls to boycott the matches since the Nations League draw in February. Last November, the FAI approved a motion calling for Uefa to suspend Israel from Uefa competitions. In May, the team's friendly against Qatar was interrupted after fans threw tennis balls featuring the Palestinian flag onto the pitch. In June, the FAI confirmed their home fixture would be played behind closed doors in Backa Topola instead of Dublin's Aviva Stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil". At an extraordinary general meeting in July, delegates backed an FAI motion to proceed with the games amid concerns that boycotting the fixtures would cause "significant and lasting harm" for the association. Calls for the Republic of Ireland to boycott the games have intensified in recent weeks. Earlier this week, more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by Irish Sport for Palestine group urging the team not to play. Courell also said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the Republic of Ireland and Israel to be kept apart in future competition draws. Tensions between the teams were raised this week when the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" after the coach said, "we're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide". Speaking on Saturday, Hallgrimsson said it was "a wrong word for me to use", while Israel FA head of communications Shlomi Barzel said he would not apologise for his association's response but said he would "take back the word stupidity". The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Israel has repeatedly denied that it has committed genocide, as well as war crimes and crimes against humanity. It says its military operations in Gaza have been

title: What we know about RAF base counter-terror investigation
description: Five men have been arrested as counter-terror police lead an investigation into a major incident near the airbase.
body: Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching two stationary white vans in a wooded area Five men have been arrested on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences after a major incident was declared at an airbase in the west of England. Bomb disposal teams have been examining a number of vehicles near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire and dozens of homes in the surrounding area have been evacuated. Here is a summary of what we know so far. RAF Fairford is located in the Cotswolds, about four miles (6.4km) south of the town of Fairford, which sits along the River Coln. The base shares a long history with the American military, and has recently been used by US warplanes as a staging post for defensive strikes on Iran. Follow live updates on this story Local police said they received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on Sunday. Five men were later arrested by armed officers near Whelford, a village around two miles (3.2km) south-east of the base. A bomb disposal team was also deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles, police said, around which a 400m (1,312ft) cordon has been placed. Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching two stationary white vans in a wooded area, though its use has not been confirmed by police. There has been large emergency service presence in the area since the early hours of Sunday, which Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said would remain "for some time". Ocone told a news conference on Sunday afternoon that "work to establish the full nature of the incident is ongoing". Counter Terrorism Policing is now leading the investigation. Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said officers were "working closely" with partners to "understand the circumstances of the incident". This video can not be played Watch: What we know about the counter-terrorism operation near RAF Fairford The five men were initially detained on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. The men, who remain in custody, have not been named. Police have not said where they are being held. US President Donald Trump said those arrested were "looking to do big damage", adding: "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them." This image has been circulating following the arrests of five men near RAF Fairford BBC Your Voice has since received an image purporting to show the moment five men were arrested. It showed detained men in Whelford, about 350m (1148ft) from runway access at Crash Gate 6A at RAF Fairford. The BBC has been unable to verify the original source but BBC Verify has geolocated the image and confirmed it appeared to be authentic. Eighty-five households have been evacuated and residents have been urged to shelter at a nearby leisure centre. Several people have told the BBC they were woken by police in the middle of the night and ordered to leave their homes. "We just had to throw our clothes on and come. We didn't know anything," one resident, who named herself only as Jo, said. Another resident, Jason, said: "It all happened very quickly. We just packed our stuff up and came here." Several people in the leisure centre are still wearing their pyjamas, according to a BBC reporter there. Gloucestershire County Councillor Paul Hodgkinson has told PA news agency there is a chance that the evacuated residents may have to stay overnight while the area around their homes is made safe. A unnamed resident of Whelford told the PA news agency she called police after she saw three vans "blocking the road" and a "large group of hooded and 'balaclava'd' men". The resident said she was driving home in the early hours of Sunday morning when she saw people in the road. "They would have seen the bright headlights," she said. "They probably thought we were the police (and) panicked." She added: "It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they were planning." Another resident described the moment he said he saw police apprehend the suspects. Jeff told the BBC he heard "shouting outside his front door", although he could not be sure where it came from. He said he then looked out of his window and saw "people being held by police outside". This video can not be played Watch: Police told us to leave our home immediately, says local resident Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was "deeply concerning" and the government would "always take every step necessary" to protect people. His defence secretary, Wes Streeting, declined to comment on a live operation but said he had been in contact with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth. Asked at a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool whether there was any Iranian involvement, he said it was "far too early to comment or speculate, and it would be irresponsible for me to do so". RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. The base was occupied by USAF Strategic Air Command during the Cold War and later the first Gulf War in 1991. B-52 bombers were also deployed by USAF from RAF Fairford on raids to Iraq in 2003. It was most recently used on 1 March, following a decision by former UK prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to allow the US to use UK bases - including RAF Fairford - for "defensive" strikes on Iranian capabilities. Conflict was sparked across the Middle East after the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states in the Gulf. title: England win series as Banton delivers on potential
description: Tom Banton delivers on all of his potential by crashing a brilliant first international century as England wrapped up their summer with an ODI series win over Sri Lanka.
body: This video can not be played Banton stars as England win Sri Lanka ODI series Third Metro Bank one-day international, Kia Oval England 355-7 (50 overs): Banton 126, Brook 77, Cox 76 Sri Lanka 132 (29.1 overs): Kusal 35; Dawson 3-26 England won by 223 runs Tom Banton delivered on all of his potential by crashing a brilliant first international century as England wrapped up their summer with an ODI series win over Sri Lanka. The 27-year-old right-hander was once the rising star of English cricket when handed a debut in 2019 but afterwards fell out of love with the game after losing his way. After reaching his hundred in 95 balls in the third one-day international at The Oval, he stood with arms wide and looked to the sky - all of that disappointment seemingly behind him. "My fiance, Lilly, was here and all of her family," Banton said. "Unfortunately, my mum, dad and brother weren't here because whenever my mum seems to come I don't do that well. "Bless her, she is not banned from coming, but she avoids coming now." The opener went on to make 126 from 105 deliveries, perfectly countering tricky early conditions - conditions in which Joe Root struggled uncharacteristically for 18 from 37 balls - and going on to share an increasingly aggressive stand of 150 in 117 balls with captain Harry Brook. "To score a hundred for England is just the best feeling on earth," Banton said. "I don't think anything is going to beat it." Brook made 77 and Jordan Cox, picked in the place of the injured Jos Buttler, added a 52-ball 76 to lift England to 355-7. That always appeared a match-winning total on a surface offering bounce for the pace bowlers and turn for the spinners. Sri Lanka crumbled to 132 all out in 29.1 overs, giving England a 223-run win and their biggest ODI victory against the tourists. It meant England signed off their summer, one that included off-field issues, the end of Bazball, Ben Stokes' retirement and Root's surprise return as Test skipper, with a fifth successive series win amid the madness across formats. Banton blasts England to series win England thrash Sri Lanka by 223 runs to win ODI series - reaction, analysis & clips This video can not be played 'Brilliant' Banton scores maiden ODI century for England Banton's success is heartwarming. When, fresh out of Second XI cricket, he made his debut as a 20-year-old in 2019 he was seen as England's next big thing. He was in the same England Under-19 team as Brook but, rather than the Yorkshireman who is now captain, it was the Somerset product who was given the opportunity when Eoin Morgan's World Cup-winning side needed a fresh face on its journey forward. Tougher times followed, resulting in almost five years out of the 50-over side and only occasional T20 appearances. During that time Kevin Pietersen, now an England mentor, said Banton "has all the talent but, at the moment, he is wasting it". It was comparisons to Pietersen which Banton struggled with. Last week, Banton said remains "in awe" of the iconic England batter. With thrilling reverse sweeps here, he showed the invention that drew those comparisons. He was also vicious on the pull, hit classically through the covers and, when Ben Duckett was bowled in the second over and Root faced 13 dot balls in a row, did not panic. By the time he was dismissed he had hit 16 fours and five sixes. When he walked off he turned and raised his bat amid a standing ovation from The Oval crowd – as Pietersen famously did 21 years ago. Banton's wagonwheel shows he hit all around the ground but was particularly strong through the covers Banton only has the opportunity as opener here because of Jacob Bethell's injury. He may find himself out of the XI when England begin a tri-series in Pakistan - a series that also involves Sri Lanka - on 20 October. The tourists, impressive in setting up this decider on Thursday, were poor here. They had already dropped Root before he was dismissed and wicketkeeper and captain Kusal Mendis spilled a thick edge when Brook had seven. Afterwards the England captain started slowly but he kicked it into life from a position of 108-2 after 25 overs. Also encouraging was the performance of Cox, whose knock also built on a slow start and followed an impressive run in the Test side against Pakistan. Sonny Baker, recalled for his second ODI in place of Josh Tongue, nicked off Pathum Nissanka with a quick, swinging and rising delivery two balls into the second over, after which Sri Lanka did not recover. Left-arm spinner Liam Dawson also repaid the faith for his inclusion over Rehan Ahmed with figures of 3-26. This summer has provided so many issues for England, including the end of Brendon McCullum's reign as Test coach. Still his ODI side now has momentum - a third series win a row - as it builds towards next year's World Cup. Series in Pakistan, Australia and South Africa are to come this winter.
