title: Woman charged with stealing from patients and staff at hospitals across Ontario
description: The 34-year-old is under investigation for incidents that began in February 2024 up until as recently as last month.
body: Items seized from the suspect by police Police in Ontario, Canada, have charged a woman with 65 offences including fraud and theft for allegedly stealing from patients and staff at several healthcare centres in the province. Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) identified the suspect as Nassim Eronn, 34, from Burlington, a city 56km (34 miles) south of Toronto. "The investigation was initiated following multiple reports of theft and fraud involving patients and staff members within healthcare facilities," police said in a statement to BBC News. They say the incidents under investigation began in February 2024 and continued until as recently as last month. The suspect worked at health centres across the province. The suspect faces charges including 34 counts of fraud under $5,000 (£3,800), 13 counts of theft under $5,000 and seven counts of disobeying a court order, according to police. Other charges include breach of trust and impersonation. OPP began investigating the woman in May after a report of theft when she worked at Orillia Soldiers' Memorial Hospital, about 130km north of Toronto. "This investigation was prompted by several complaints of theft and fraud from patients and staff within the hospital," police said at the time. The investigation was expanded to cover more hospitals where further incidents were uncovered. "Multiple search warrants were executed where significant amounts of property were seized," police said. Items seized as part of the investigation It is unclear what were the suspect's specific duties at the hospitals. Investigators believe there may be more victims and have urged the public to come forward with relevant information after reviewing their financial records for suspicious transactions. Five healthcare facilities are covered by the investigation: Orillia Soldiers' Memorial Hospital (Orillia, ON) - between April 2025 and March 2026 Headwaters Health Care Centre (Orangeville, ON) - between August 2026 and September 2026 Trillium Health Partners, Mississauga Hospital (Mississauga, ON) - between August 2025 and July 2026 St Joseph's Health Centre (Toronto, ON) - between July 2024 and January 2025 West Park Health Care Centre (Toronto, ON) - between February 2024 and April 2024 Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC Dozens of residents to be displaced overnight as counter-terror police continue RAF Fairford probe What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses? title: Father and son crowned Sheep Dog World Trial champions
description: David and Jack Howells say they "never in million years" thought they would win the double.
body: David and Jack Howells returned home to celebrate their victory with their dogs The first father and son to both be crowned champions at the Sheep Dog World Trial said they "never in million years" thought they would win the double. Farmer David Howells and his son, Jack, 19, from Cymmer, Neath Port Talbot, travelled to the trials in Scotland last weekend. David took the world title with his Border Collie dog, Wyverne Pip, in a field of about 300 competitors from 34 different countries. Meanwhile his son, Jack, won the Young Handler world title with his dog, Cydros Boss. "I feel upside down. I didn't expect to win. I can't quite believe it, to be honest," said David. Speaking on BBC Radio Wales on Wednesday, he added it was a "crazy" experience to win alongside his son and pick up the trophies. It marks the first time that a parent and child have won both titles at the same world trial. "We both live on a farm, and it's a hill farm with lots of sheep, so we need the sheep dogs as every day work," he said. "Then we've got into trials as well. To do a job that you enjoy, and then get to do a hobby alongside it, is extra special." David said he was "proud" that his son had followed in his footsteps. "He's grown up on the farm, and he started with the sheep dogs when he was about 10. "During the Covid years, when he wasn't in school, he got more involved because he was home. He caught the bug, and he was mad on the sheep dogs." It is the first time a parent and child have both won at the same world trial The pair travelled to Lauder in Scotland over the weekend to compete, and Jack said the victory "still hasn't sunk in yet". "It's unbelievable actually," he said. "My mam, sister and the girlfriend all flew up to Edinburgh and came to watch. My uncle, my grandpa, were all watching from home." David explained there were competitors from tens of countries, and that his son was in the final with two other young men from Belgium and Uruguay. "The dog has to run up the field, picks up five sheep, and they're brought down to a set of gates," he said. "Then, they have to drive up through a set of gates, across to another set of gates, and the sheep have to be split apart, and then they have to be put in the pen. That's the qualifying stages. "In the final then, there's more sheep involved and it all gets a bit more technical. "There's an element of luck involved as well because your dog's got to perform, the sheep have got to behave - they don't always. And you've got to get everything right yourself. "So, for the two of us to achieve it, it was just extra special." Jack said he would "stick at it" and looked forward to the International Championship next year. "That's with the four British countries," he said. title: Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
description: The initiative would have prevented the nation from imposing sanctions unless approved by the UN.
body: Russia openly backed the initiative, which would have required Switzerland to seek UN approval for sanctions Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality. More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed. The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment. Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties. Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia. "People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility". While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference". He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace". Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe. This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv. Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees. Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s. Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda. title: Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow
description: A slew of dissidents being released from long-term detention comes days after the nation's interim leader met the US president.
body: Prisoner releases and free elections were two key pledges made to the US by the new administration Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York. Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President Nicolás Maduro. Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday. Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure. However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end". Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president. Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres. Rights groups critical as Venezuela prisoner release scheme 'coming to an end' US lifts sanctions on Venezuelan interim leader Delcy Rodríguez Venezuelan prison director sacked as inmates allege mistreatment Foro Penal confirmed the release of Miguel Castillo Cedeño, who it said had been arbitrarily detained since June 2019. Also released was Frank Cabañas, who rights groups say had been held in prison for nine years after being linked to the death of a police officer. Foro Penal said he was the only suspect who remained detained, despite family members reporting that he was suffering health problems last year. Opposition and human rights groups have said Maduro's government used the detention of political prisoners to stamp out dissent and silence critics for years. Rodriguez has sought to frame her interim government as more permissive of political dissent while currying favour with the US. The prisoner release scheme was a key concession by her administration to the US. However, her decision to end the scheme attracted criticism from opposition and rights groups. Foro Penal said it was stopped with less than half of the nation's political prisoners released. Rodriguez's government continues to deny dissidents are jailed. It has cast the release of prisoners as a gesture of goodwill and reconciliation. Delcy Rodríguez's meeting with Donald Trump in New York has brought renewed calls for elections in Venezuela Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a minister closely associated with Maduro's authoritarian rule, called the interim president's meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace". But opposition voices expressed their disapproval over the meeting, viewing it as a snub of their calls – that the US has previously endorsed – for swift elections. Pedro Mario Burelli, a former Venezuelan state oil company executive and opposition commentator, called the two world leaders "the shameless puppet and her unscrupulous and undignified puppet-master", adding: "Little has changed in Venezuela under Washington's clumsy and selective oversight." Venezuela's last elections, held in 2024, in which Maduro was declared the winner, were widely disputed as rigged. Opposition tallies suggested their candidate, who stood after Machado was barred from running, had won by 70% of the vote. Despite this, the Trump administration backed Rodriguez, Maduro's former vice-president, as his successor rather than opposition leader María Corina Machado after Maduro was seized and put on trial on drug charges in January. Analysts at the time cast this decision as the US choosing short-term stability in Venezuela until elections could be held. Rodriguez used her UN General Assembly speech on Thursday to reiterate that there "will be elections in Venezuela", without specifying when. title: Social care reform could mean big risks and big rewards for Burnham
description: The state of the social care system in England is a topic that's made Andy Burnham angry for decades - but will his plans for reform work?
body: The state of the social care system in England is a topic that's made Andy Burnham angry for decades. As Gordon Brown's health secretary he proposed a compulsory levy collected from people's estates – an idea the Conservatives dubbed the "death tax". He repeatedly returned to the issue when making interventions as the Mayor of Greater Manchester, and in his first major interview as prime minister back in July, Burnham pledged to put "whatever political capital I have into fixing broken social care". We now have the first outline about how he hopes to do that. But there are a host of unanswered questions about how the government would fund and deliver what could be an eye-wateringly expensive and politically perilous idea. The prime minister told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that he will go into the next election proposing a free-to-use, universally funded national care system. Past governments have looked at how to reform social care and balked at the potential costs. The Health Foundation has previously estimated that a free system could end up costing the taxpayer around £18bn a year. Burnham denied that figure but conceded that tackling the issue could make him "unpopular" with some. He stressed that the current system comes with hidden costs for individuals and the state, such as people losing their houses to pay for costs and spending time in A&E because their home care isn't adequate. But it's difficult to deny that this idea would come with a staggering up front cost and one the prime minister would have to lay out a far more detailed funding plan for, if he went into an election with this as his flagship proposal. The last prime minister to attempt a substantial overhaul of social care was Theresa May, whose 2017 plans unfurled when they were nicknamed the "dementia tax". Burnham said the manifesto that Labour was elected on at the last general election would make it "hard" to achieve his goal. That's a clear hint that he could well go into the next election pledging to increase tax in order to fund social care. The manifesto that Burnham is currently bound by pledged not to hike income tax, VAT or National Insurance. This video can not be played 'Broken social care will in the end break the NHS,' says Burnham Other funding options are not being taken off the table, including a return to Burnham's old plan to make some people pay out of their inheritance. He could also get some political cover, in the form of an ongoing review by the longtime policy guru Baroness Casey. She's been heading a commission into adult social care since April last year and Burnham said her findings would influence what he proposes. It's understood she's been asked to find a "sustainable" solution, and it would be within her remit to recommend tax changes and cuts to other areas of spending, to raise the money needed. The prime minister wouldn't engage with the question of what areas he might cut but did promise more meat on the bones of his social care plans when he makes his speech to the Labour Party conference on Tuesday. Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options? Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC Darren Jones, who was Sir Keir Starmer's chief secretary, and has assumed the mantle of an internal Burnham critic, warned against taxing, spending and borrowing, without making cuts. He suggested that if Burnham wanted to prioritise social care, he may need to look at scrapping the triple lock for pensioners, which Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged to keep. The Conservatives have already criticised the potential for increasing the tax burden and Reform have described Burnham's plan as another "death tax". Some Labour MPs would undoubtedly be uncomfortable at the prospect of having to sell controversial decisions like tax rises or changes to the triple lock, on the doorstep at the next election. But there's been a general trend in recent years among both the Conservative and Labour parties, of backbenchers grumbling about party leaders being unwilling – perhaps not brave enough – to make forthright political arguments. Burnham hasn't yet revealed the finer details, but for now, at least, he's confident enough in his own ability to win the argument. Those around the PM believe there are enormous plaudits to be won for whoever manages to adequately fix the system. History would suggest, though, that prime ministers who fail to convince the public on social care reforms don't last long in the job. It may be an issue he's talked about for years, but on social care, Andy Burnham is taking a big swing. title: Police get more time to quiz suspects in alleged plot against Jewish community
description: Two men - both in the 30s - were arrested under the 2000 Terrorism Act in Manchester on 20 September.
body: The men can now be detained up until 4 October Detectives have been granted an extra week to question two men arrested as part of an investigation into an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester. The extension means the men - both in the 30s - can now be detained until 4 October. The men were arrested in the Northern Quarter area of Manchester on 20 September - the eve of Yom Kippur, when thousands of British Jews were in synagogues. A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police, which is leading the investigation, said their work was "ongoing and officers continue to pursue a number of lines of enquiry". The two men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, the force said on Tuesday. Sources told the BBC that the suspected plot was "fairly imminent" and in the later stages of planning. Police said searches at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford had also taken place. Yom Kippur is considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. A spokesperson for the Community Security Trust, which coordinates security for Jewish communities in the UK, said on Tuesday that the suspected plot was "utterly chilling coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year". They added: "[This] is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time." title: Why Premier League faces uncertainty and chaos after Man City ruling
description: It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been made on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City. Here's what it means.
body: This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City If you were getting the impression that the saga over Manchester City's 115 charges was almost over, think again. Two years and 10 days since the hearing began, and 1,329 days after City were charged, we now know a verdict has been reached, with the club guilty of the majority of financial rule breaches. That is not because the Premier League or Manchester City have told us - it is thanks to the Athletic finding out and breaking the story., external BBC Sport was later told the verdict was sent during the week to club executives, who had to sign a non-disclosure agreement to open the file. A process can appear to be completely watertight, as this one certainly had been, but when the circle of trust is expanded, the chance of information getting out increases. Despite this, public silence from the Premier League continues. City did not address whether they had been found guilty in a statement making it clear - with an appeal expected - that the "process remains ongoing" from their point of view. It all points to the suggestion that the long-awaited decision of the independent panel was not a case of this process nearing an end, but perhaps instead reaching the end of the beginning. It appears the chaos and uncertainty is only going to increase now. City fans, and the rest of football, are left to guess what the punishment might be. And when this all might reach a definitive conclusion. The charges are so serious that some form of points deduction now appears inevitable, subject to the appeal by City, who have always insisted they have done nothing wrong. When and how any punishment is applied will be crucial not just for City, but the Premier League as a whole. And that's before we get to the prospect of clubs suing City for compensation. Enzo Maresca's side go to Liverpool on 11 October when the Premier League resumes after the international break. They could go six points clear at the top. But is that now rendered meaningless? Let's look at possible scenarios - none of which are particularly appealing. No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains Deciding the punishment should be quicker than ascertaining guilt, but nothing is certain in this case. As the charges have been denied, it will have to go to a sanction hearing convened by the independent panel. BBC Sport has been told this hearing could still be months away, and the result may not be published until the appeal is completed. At the hearing, everything will be on the table. Fines, points deductions and even demotion. This differs from Chelsea's case earlier this year, as the Stamford Bridge club self-reported and admitted guilt. That allowed them to negotiate with the Premier League and reach a sanctioning agreement. It is possible that City could decide to hold their hands up and try to agree a deal - which would be better for the league - though that seems unlikely given the club's consistently strong denials over many years. The panel will have to comb through the hundreds of pages of evidence and determine the punishment. Remember, Everton were docked six points, reduced from 10 on appeal, and then two points in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR). Nottingham Forest were deducted four points. These were considered to be minor breaches, while City faced seven separate charges on PSR breaches in the Premier League alone, as well as a further five related to Uefa competitions. This aspect alone suggests a large points penalty. That is before you get into the inflated sponsorship revenue allegedly channelled through the companies' accounts as a means of meeting financial fair play rules, payments to players and managers, and a failure to comply with investigations. Take all this into account, and it places an asterisk against the Premier League between 2009 and 2018. Chelsea and Manchester City, two of the competition's most successful clubs, have been part of that. While Chelsea admitted effectively cheating, City have been found guilty. They got around the financial rules to put them in a position to be able to sign more expensive players than their finances should have permitted. And if this season passes with no decision on the sanction while it is known City were guilty of the majority of counts, what does that mean for the integrity of the competition? Could a penalty be backdated to this season when finally awarded? Unlikely. So what if Manchester City win the league? Coventry are third from bottom right now. What if they finish in that position, are relegated, but would have stayed up had City's punishment come this season? This inertia is terrible news for the Premier League as a competition. There's a strong argument that a sanctioning agreement is the cleanest way out of this. But that may not be palatable to the league as they would have to negotiate with City, who would presumably want a lesser punishment. Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict Man City legal fight could spiral out of control - Purslow The usual process when any points penalty is handed down is that it is applied immediately, subject to appeal. It could be a points deduction so large that it is effectively a relegation. Alternatively, if City's membership of the Premier League was revoked, it is unclear how that might be applied mid-season. It could also be that the punishment is a huge fine, although that would seem unlikely given points deductions to other clubs. The question would be how soon we hear, and how long after the appeal is heard. Usually, the league asks for an expedited process from the independent arbitration company which handles disciplinary cases. title: Orange Order march row goes to heart of ongoing divisions in Northern Ireland
description: The dispute over the controversial parade is a reminder that the peace process is not over.
body: Hundreds of protesters blocked the parade route after it was given clearance for the first time in almost 30 years History shows that when the politics of Northern Ireland are wrapped up in a street dispute, friction is seldom far away. Bitter rows in the Stormont chamber between unionists and nationalists happen almost every week, but ground-level arguments are rare these days. The Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown is a clash of political cultures. The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation. The area where it wants to walk is largely Catholic, and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists. This dispute over a piece of road is not just a local problem. It has the potential to affect other parts of Northern Ireland and the power-sharing arrangements at Stormont. "What happens at Drumcree never stays at Drumcree," was how one retired politician put it. Follow live updates on this story What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? When the parade dispute first erupted into violence in the mid-1990s, the disorder spread to other places - and almost derailed the peace process. But while it was never fully resolved, the dispute faded over the next 30 years. Its sudden re-emergence has caught most people by surprise, including many politicians. What happened was that a legal case was brought to court over the dispute early this summer, re-opening the debate. The two largest parties in Northern Ireland, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), have been on opposite sides of the argument. Sinn Féin are firmly behind the residents. The DUP fully supports the Orange Order. They may be partners in the devolved government at Stormont, but when it comes to Drumcree they could not be further apart. As always in Northern Ireland, the historical context is important. Orangemen waited in the Drumcree church hall for the go-ahead to proceed down the Garvaghy Road Although there has been an uneasy calm in Portadown over the parading issue in recent years, the Orange Order regards the march as unfinished business. In 1998, it was banned from completing its Drumcree march - which includes the Garvaghy Road - and has been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route ever since. It has applied and been turned down more than 1,000 times in the past three decades. It says it is being denied a traditional walk which dates back to the early 1800s. A Parades Commission was set up in the late 1990s to adjudicate on marching disputes and, until now, it has consistently ruled against the route. The Orange Order's legal challenge to a ruling in June this year succeeded on procedural grounds. The order subsequently re-applied for permission to carry out the parade, albeit a scaled-back version with only 35 participants rather than 400 - and was successful. Nationalist residents on the Garvaghy Road were left shocked and angry. For them, the parade is triumphalist and unwelcome in the area. Rather than being about tradition, they see the parade as an act of supremacy and say it re-opens old community wounds. During a last-minute legal battle over the march, a judge appealed for all sides of the dispute to find common ground and come to an agreement. Nobody was surprised when that did not happen. Feelings are running high on the issue on all sides, including among the political parties. Relations in the power-sharing executive are now dangerously close to breaking point. There is a Stormont election next year which means parties tend to dig in, rather than search for compromises. The Drumcree dispute goes to the heart of the divisions which remain in Northern Ireland. Events of recent days are a reminder that the peace process is not over, it is ongoing - and there is still work to be done on the ground and at Stormont. title: Currently
description: Russia's super-rich once ruled the country - could they restore their political influence?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·27 Sep 2026,·28 mins Available for over a year Russia's super-rich once ruled the country, holding deep influence over the country's politicians in the years immediately after the collapse of the Soviet Union. They then gradually saw their power decline under the rise of Vladimir Putin, but could they - and would they - ever seek to restore their political influence? Russia Editor at BBC Monitoring, Vitaly Shevchenko, traces the origin story of Russia’s oligarchs and why the party is now over for Russia’s wealthiest men. From the chaotic post-Soviet days of the 1990s when they amassed vast fortunes and wielded immense power to today where their number has reached an all-time high - while their political influence has virtually disappeared. Vitaly asks what, if anything, might lead them to restore their political clout? If four and a half years of sanctions fuelled by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine can’t convince them, then what does that say about their relationship with President Putin today?

title: Ten climbers missing after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
description: The Nepali team was preparing to take overseas climbers up the Himlung Himal peak.
body: The avalanche struck Himlung Himal, a mountain popular with overseas climbers At least 10 Nepalese climbers who were preparing to lead an expedition in the Himalayas are missing after an avalanche hit a base camp on Sunday morning. The climb's organisers said the local guides were at a staging point close to the Himlung Himal peak in Manang district when the avalanche struck. Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet. Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams unable to reach the site. Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP: "Eight members of our expedition team and two more from another company have been reported missing." The Nepali team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain. Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry. Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches. The latest death of Nepali climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja. Extreme weather further south in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said. It comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August. More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements. title: Your pictures of the Harvest Moon shimmering across the UK sky
description: The full Moon put on a stunning display over the skies of UK on Saturday night and here are some of your photographs.
body: A beautiful sight from both the plane and on the ground in Buckinghamshire September's full Moon glowed across the UK sky on Saturday and many people seemed to have perfect conditions for viewing it. It's also known as the Harvest Moon because of its association with the time of year people traditionally gather crops. The Moon reached its fullest point at 17:49 BST on Saturday but it was later, when the sky got darker, that it made its biggest impact. BBC Weather Watchers have been submitting the photos they took and here are a few of our favourites of those submitted so far. A runaway Moon? title: Four men down - but Australia still beat South Africa
description: Australia are reduced to 11 men but dig in for a remarkable win against a much-changed South Africa side as they beat the world champions 42-38 in Perth.
body: Australia will open the 2027 World Cup against Hong Kong in Perth Tries: Ikitau 2, Donaldson, Wilson, Jorgensen Cons: Lonergan 4 Pens: Lonergan 3 Tries: Grobbelaar, van der Merwe, penalty try, van den Berg, Nche Cons: Pollard 2, Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Pollard Australia were reduced to 11 men but dug in for an extraordinary win against a much-changed South Africa side as they beat the world champions 42-38 in Perth. The Wallabies excelled with some vibrant attacking rugby, scoring five tries against the back-to-back World Cup winners to lead by 25 points with 16 minutes left. But then a manic spell of four yellow cards in nine minutes left the hosts overrun, with South Africa mounting a comeback that ultimately fell just short. The visitors made 13 changes after beating New Zealand in Baltimore but still fielded a strong starting XV, which boasted 240 caps in the second row alone. But a year out from hosting the World Cup, and a year on from being soundly beaten on home soil by the Lions, it was the home side who impressed before their bizarre late collapse. The teams traded early penalties before Springboks hooker Johan Grobbelaar drove over for the first try of the match after a powerful maul. Australia responded well with a wave of pressure which was rewarded when centre Len Ikitau drove over from a metre out. Ikitau then flew over for his second after the Boks made a mess of a high ball kicked through, but the lead lasted just three minutes. South Africa played the ball quickly and flung it out wide with Edwill van der Merwe on the end of a stunning break to score in the corner. The high level continued as the hosts took the lead again before the break. After 14 patient but quick phases, the Wallabies whipped the ball from right to left to find fly-half Ben Donaldson free to score in the corner. The Springboks had strength in depth to call on, and coach Rassie Erasmus made all eight changes early in the second half with his side down by 10 points. But it was Australia who continued to dominate. Captain Harry Wilson was denied a try as his foot was in touch but just seconds later he did burrow over the line close to the posts. Wing Max Jorgensen then sprinted the length of the pitch to score a stunning solo score after South Africa fumbled the ball to make it 42-17. Wilson was then sin-binned and South Africa finally got their first score of the second half with a penalty try, with Ryan Lonergan yellow carded as well. The Wallabies were down to 13 and a crossfield kick found Van der Merwe in the corner but the wing dropped the ball before he could ground it. Australia wing Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i was then sin-binned as well to leave Australia three men down and replacement scrum-half Morne van den Berg scrambled in to cut the lead to 11 points. Remarkably Australia then appeared to have scored again as Tom Wright intercepted a pass to run in - only for the try to be ruled out and Hunter Paisami shown a fourth yellow card for a dangerous tackle in the build-up. South Africa had so much space and scored again through Ox Nche to cut the lead to four but time ran out. title: Horner a distraction for Ferrari says Vasseur
description: Christian Horner is proving a distraction for Ferrari by "looking for a job", team principal Frederic Vasseur says.
body: Horner's remarks about Ferrari have been a distraction, Vasseur (right) says Christian Horner is proving a distraction for Ferrari by "looking for a job", team principal Frederic Vasseur says. Horner, dismissed as Red Bull team principal in July 2025, used an interview with the Times this week to say that Ferrari are the only Formula 1 team he would work for without being given a shareholding, describing it as "the dream", external. Vasseur outlined his frustration with Horner following Saturday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix - at which Charles Leclerc finished fourth and his Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton was sixth. He said: "We are not working in the perfect serenity. "For me, first, but for everybody in the team, for the media, for 50% of the questions [to be] about this, it's a bit of a frustrating situation. "We are fighting for P3 [third place] in the championship, and at the end of the day, we are all speaking a lot about this, and even for the guys in the garage, to discuss about this, it's the best discussion that we can have. "But it is what it is, it's not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job - that everybody knows - everywhere. But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team, to rise them to be motivated, focus on what is better today." Vasseur was asked whether he was joking about Horner, and replied: "I was very serious." And asked whether he would consider working with Horner, he replied: "This you have to ask my assistant." That remark appears to be a reference to the circumstances surrounding Horner's departure from Red Bull in July 2025. Horner was accused of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour by a female employee. The allegation became public in February 2024 but the accusations were dismissed by Red Bull following two internal investigations. Horner was fired from his role as chief executive officer and team principal by Red Bull after the 2025 British Grand Prix. That decision followed a tumultuous 18 months in the wake of the employee's allegations, during which a number of senior team figures left - including chief technical officer Adrian Newey - and there was a slump in form. Red Bull have never given a public explanation for Horner's dismissal. The two parties agreed on a settlement said by sources to be worth 60m euros (£51.5m). Ferrari entered this season hoping to be title contenders following the introduction of new chassis and engine rules in F1. But while their car was acknowledged as the best in the corners as the season began, their engine has lacked performance compared to those of Mercedes and Red Bull. This lack of power was exposed on the long straights of the Baku circuit, as Leclerc slipped back in the race after qualifying second. Vasseur said on Saturday: "With the situation that we are in the engine, we are losing one position per lap, and then we lose the path of the race. "Honestly we were surprised to be in the first row, because Baku is the most demanding in terms of engine, and was not expecting to do so. But we knew even starting from the first row that the opening laps, or in case of restarting safety car and so, it would be difficult. And it was." Asked whether he was still committed to his position at Ferrari, Vasseur said: "Motorsport is my life, it's my business. I'm trying to do my best. I'm there to do my job. I have the best job in the world, heh. But, it is like it is. We have still seven races to go, and I will push until the last corner." Ferrari have not won a world championship since 2008, and have rarely had a fully competitive car since then. Horner said in his interview: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1." title: Pope says 'scourge' of abuse must be rooted out as he visits Lourdes
description: Pope Leo spoke to bishops before leading a service attended by thousands of worshippers in France.
body: Hundreds of thousands of people have gathered to hear the Pope speak during a four-day visit to France Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, telling them to "maintain the greatest vigilance", ahead of a meeting with abuse survivors. The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France. A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years. The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes, before he was scheduled to meet survivors of abuse privately later. Before giving Mass the Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context. "It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance." The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters. The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak. Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile. On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron. Pope Leo greeted people from his popemobile at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed". The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church". "How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said. The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000. The Pope said Mass at the Meadow of the Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025. Later on Sunday the Pope will meet staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, before taking part in a torchlight procession in the evening. It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic church in May 2025. Pope's have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots. Why is the Pope in France? title: Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow
description: Andy Burnham said he would wait for the results of a consultation on a scheme estimated to cost £33bn
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to say whether he backs a third runway at Heathrow after it emerged that the expansion of the London airport could be delayed by up to four years. Burnham - who, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, opposed the project - told Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg: "I think principally, it's a matter for London and Londoners." He added: "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation." Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had championed the runway to boost the economy, with a schedule to open by 2035 but Heathrow indicated on Saturday it may not be operational before 2039. As Manchester's mayor, Burnham had been against the project over concerns that it would delay investment in transport for the north. When he took office, he said he was "open-minded" about the scheme. As he prepared for his first annual Labour Party conference as prime minister, Burnham said: "There's a consultion but there are different views and you have to take those views seriously in coming to a decision." In response, Heathrow said: "We agree with the prime minister that local voices must be heard. We know from consistent polling over the last decade that communities support our plans for expansion and support is only growing over time." The project, estimated to cost £33bn, has attracted opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups as well as Mayor of London Sadiq Khan. A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers and rerouting a section of the M25 motorway through a tunnel. But it is estimated it would create 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the UK economy. The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000, or nearly 2,000 a day on average. A new runway has been backed by the unions Unite and the GMB. Sharon Graham, Unite's general secretary said: "A third runway at Heathrow is essential and we need to get going with it. "This is more than just infrastructure. It's about investing in the workforce, securing the future of good, unionised jobs and a guaranteed market for UK steel." Earlier this weekend, Heathrow conceded that meeting the original deadline would be increasingly difficult without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade". The Department for Transport said the timeline had "always been ambitious" and it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter. title: Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
description: The prime minister told the BBC that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare".
body: This video can not be played 'Broken social care will in the end break the NHS,' says Burnham Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election. The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some. Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it". Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this. Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month. While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded. Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home. Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council. In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility. Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work. "There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush." Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing. Burnham said the changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse". But he said that "nothing is off the table at this moment in time" in terms of how the proposals would be funded. When he was told it had been estimated that a system for everyone in England that is free at the point of use could cost taxpayers £18bn a year, Burnham replied: "It's not that high." He said people already face a "huge cost" at the moment and that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out". Burnham added there is also a cost to the NHS due to the "huge number" of people in hospitals across England who cannot be discharged home "because the social care isn't there". Asked whether everyone will have to contribute to his proposed system, Burnham replied: "It will be a system of that kind – so everyone contributes, everyone is covered but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS." He said the details developed by Baroness Casey would be subject to cross-party talks in a bid to "build consensus". Baroness Casey was originally tasked by former PM Sir Keir Starmer to deliver her review of social care in 2028, but Burnham asked her to bring that forward to next summer. On the timeline, Burnham added: "I'm going to say that we stick to the manifesto because I have to keep people's trust, and there are commitments in the manifesto that would make it hard to do in this Parliament." The Labour manifesto in 2024 made clear commitments on tax, including not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT. Burnham added: "I don't think you can reform this system without consensus. I will develop a very clear plan and I will put that plan to the public at a general election and that will be where the plan gets tested and people will then be able to decide." Philp said tax increases would be a "red line" for the Conservatives and they would "not under any circumstances" support more of them. He said the country is "already taxed too highly", telling the BBC: "If more money is needed, for example, for social care or indeed for defence we would find that money through savings elsewhere, particularly in the welfare budget." Labour MP Darren Jones, who served as a cabinet minister in Sir Keir's government, said Burnham was being "very bold and brave" on social care. He said: "Politics is about prioritisation and these things do cost money and so we'll need to see the detail of that policy." Jones added if the PM "can land it in the right way, that'd be a huge achievement" for him and the government. Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Andy Burnham refuses to rule out his universal death tax. "He's too weak to cut the benefits bill so he's coming for your home instead." Burnham accused previous generations of politicians of "cowardice" for failing to reform social care, although his push for change is not without jeopardy. He previously produced a plan for a national care service while serving as health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government. It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution, including from people's estates after they had died. The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election. At the 2017 general election, then-Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May was accused of trying to introduce a "dementia tax" by proposing that people receiving care at home pay for the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000. The policy sparked a political outcry and the Conservatives lost their majority in the House of Commons at the election. Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options? title: USA's new breakout star? Sullivan living up to Premier League promise
description: Cavan Sullivan made his United States debut on Saturday aged just 16 - and produced a performance to show just why Manchester City moved to sign him.
body: Cavan Sullivan made his MLS debut at the age of 14 With a little over a year to go before he can officially join Manchester City, United States wonderkid Cavan Sullivan has taken his next step towards the big time. At 16 years and 363 days, the Philadelphia Union midfielder became the fourth youngest player to play for the USA - starting Saturday's 4-1 friendly win over Peru. Ever since City moved to secure the future signing of a then 14-year-old Sullivan back in 2024, there has been plenty of intrigue around his progress, and hype to go with it. It led to a level of expectation rarely seen around a young American player - reinforcing the sense that he might be the real deal. Manchester City saw something in him and were willing to wait for that potential to be realised at senior level. His MLS team, Philadelphia Union, have also shown patience as they gradually introduced him to senior football. His first run of regular starts for Union came as the 2026 MLS season resumed post-World Cup, and that first international call-up soon followed. There is one complication, though - the ongoing news around his future club. He made his international debut the day after City were found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching. The club are expected to appeal. His performances, goals, and assists since the World Cup put him up there with the MLS's top individual stars, including Lionel Messi, Antoine Griezmann and Luis Suarez. Few players beyond those mentioned can match Sullivan's goal contribution rate in MLS since the World Cup, and there is a strong argument to say the youngster has been the best player in the league during that time. The numbers speak for themselves. They speak of a player who has performed a key role in his team's rise up the league table in the past few months, and of one who has the output in front of goal to go with the minutes on the pitch. The facts need no extra hype or sensational Messi comparisons. Sullivan has seven goals and five assists in MLS this season. Six of those goals and four of those assists have come during August and September. Sullivan has scored six goals in the past six games, and has been named in the league's Team of the Matchday a total of seven times, including for the past three consecutive matchdays. Is he the breakout soccer star that the United States have long been desperate for? He is about to become a big part of that conversation. As the expectation rises, there has to be caution when discussing a player who only turns 17 this month. "It's well known that Americans are drawn to stars in sports, and as the World Cup showed, that applies to soccer too," Jonathan Tannenwald, chief soccer correspondent for the Philadelphia Inquirer, told the BBC. "So it's no surprise that the country hopes for a star in men's soccer to match the many it has had in women's soccer. "I'm not going to say today that Cavan Sullivan is going to be that player. It's too early to know for certain, and I've seen plenty of names not make the grade. "Freddy Adu is among the infamous, but there are others, such as Gedion Zelalem at Arsenal. Christian Pulisic has come closest, but isn't really there and had a worse World Cup than hoped for. Gio Reyna has never measured up to his talent. "What I will say about Sullivan is he has the work ethic to go with the talent. As his current manager at the Philadelphia Union, Ryan Richter, said recently, external: 'His outstanding quality is the mentality that he has, and the way that he approaches every game and every day, and that's what pushes him to get better and better.'" Sullivan's full-time introduction to the Philadelphia Union team has coincided with a turnaround in their season, led by interim coach Richter, who took over before this post-World Cup run-in. They are unbeaten in 11 games, winning nine. This is in stark contrast to the beginning of the season when they only won one game in 15. Sullivan has played a key part in this improvement. During this time, Sullivan has been playing in a right-sided attacking midfield role, but with the freedom to drift as a central number 10 might and cut inside on his stronger left foot. He has a good all-round game, and also has good strength relative to his age. He is not quite at the level an emerging Wayne Rooney was as a teenager at Everton, but his physicality that means he can more than hold his own in a robust league such as MLS. Rather than struggle with the weight of expectation, his performances have improved as the spotlight on him has brightened. It appears he is already outgrowing the North American league, but it might be wise to allow him to play at this level, in his hometown, with his family around him (his brother Quinn, 22, also plays for the Union) for a little while longer, regardless of the other options open to him pre-City. "I find him to be handling the pressure of everything pretty well," added Tannenwald. "Talk with him for long enough, and you'll know he's still a teenager, still finding his way with some things as any teen would. "Yes, he can come across as cocky, but he's well grounded, not just by Richter, but by having his oldest brother there in the locker room with him. "Away from the stadium, Sullivan has a strong family at home. Both of his parents, Brendan and Heike, played soccer, and grandfather Larry went from a player in the 1960s to one of the most famous coaches in the Philadelphia region. "They all keep Cavan grounded too, even as they know he is the best of all of them." title: Our Friends in the North still relevant - writer
description: Peter Flannery says a new stage version of the classic TV show will resonate with modern audiences.
body: A new set of local actors have been cast in a theatre production of Our Friends in the North The writer of acclaimed 1990s BBC TV drama Our Friends in the North has said a new stage version will resonate with modern audiences, even if he had once thought its themes would become irrelevant. Peter Flannery, who was born and raised in Jarrow, said he had hoped the corruption and poverty the original show explored in the North East would fade away. But in an interview ahead of a new stage adaptation in Newcastle, he said he was expecting the 21st Century audience to recognise the same problems today. "If you asked me 30 years ago, would things be as bad as they are now, I'd probably have said no. I'd have said things are sure to get better and we would do something about inequality, corruption, greed, deprivation in pockets of the UK." "So the fact it's got worse wasn't me being prescient. I didn't know it was going to get worse, it just has." Flannery has adapted two episodes from the original nine-part series into a play that will open at Newcastle's Theatre Royal on 15 October. It covers the years between Margaret Thatcher becoming prime minister in 1979 and the miners' strike of 1984, showing the impact of events on "friends" Nicky, Mary, Geordie and Tosker – and the North East. Flannery added: "I wish, in my political heart, it was all now irrelevant. But with my vanity and my desire to be listened to as a writer, I do feel validated." Peter Flannery with Christopher Eccleston who played Nicky in the TV series But he said as well as exploring problems the drama offered hope. "Through the characters, it shows the enduring nature of love and friendship, and that, even though all this stuff is going on, people survive." The TV series launched the careers of the four main actors, Daniel Craig, Christopher Eccleston, Gina McKee and Mark Strong. And the new stage play also features a cast that is hoping it will have an impact on their futures as well as the audience. Ryan Nolan, 30, from Newcastle, was born in the week the TV series first aired. He is Nicky Hutchinson, the role originally played by Christopher Eccleston. He said: "I've worked as an actor for 10 years, but I've never had more people want to talk to me since being cast. Saying they're coming to see it, saying they love the original, saying they can't wait to see what I do with it. But Scott Turnbull, 45, from Stockton, who plays Geordie, is not expecting his career to follow the path of original cast member Daniel Craig, who ended up as a buff James Bond, emerging from the sea when he debuted in the role in Casino Royale. "What I would say is don't expect me to enter Act Two in a pair of Speedos looking absolutely ripped. I think the bird on the James Bond ticket might have already flown!" Sam Neale and Ryan Nolan play Mary and Nicky in the theatre production The cast agree that the drama will appeal to both fans of the original and audiences encountering it for the first time. Sam Neale, 41, from Newcastle, who plays Mary said: "At the centre of it you've got inadequate social housing, mistrust of the police and mass unemployment. "All issues we are still dealing with. If younger audiences are coming in and have no point of reference to the miners' strike, they will relate to and understand a lack of opportunity or the difficulty getting a house." And Jack Robertson, from Whitley Bay, who plays Tosker said it will also give younger audiences an insight into how the region was impacted by the 1980s. "A lot of what we are doing is showing the loss of community back in those days. Even if you knew jobs were under threat, there was still this sense of people knowing each other and that family feel. "That's such a highlight of the show and by virtue of comparison, it shows how divided we are now." The original TV production of Our Friends in the North dramatised clashes between police and miners in a pit village Flannery is not taking part in rehearsals but is looking forward to seeing it on stage, though he did have doubts about returning to Our Friends in the North. "When I see it I think I'll have moments of elation and moments of thinking why did you do this Peter, why didn't you just stop? "But actually I think it will be a success. And I hope it will tour the country next." Our Friends in the North – The Thatcher Years runs at Newcastle's Theatre Royal between 15 and 24 October. title: Murder probe as cyclist dies following moped crash
description: It is believed the moped had been pursuing the e-bike cyclist prior to the crash, the Met Police says.
body: Police are appealing for witnesses who may have seen the crash and the events leading up to it A murder inquiry has begun after an e-bike cyclist died following a collision with a moped in west London. Emergency services were called to North Pole Road, North Kensington, at about 01:20 BST on Friday where the seriously injured 24-year-old man was found. He was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after. Police said the investigation was at an early stage but it was believed the moped had been pursuing the e-bike cyclist prior to the crash. Dt Ch Insp Neil John said detectives were "pursuing a number of lines of inquiry, including efforts to identify and trace the rider of the moped". "Our thoughts are with the victim's family at what is a very difficult time," he added. "We have launched a full investigation and are working hard to get answers and establish exactly what happened. "As part of this, we're urging anyone who was in the area at the time and may have seen the e-bike or the moped to get in touch with us as soon as possible. If you have any information that could help, please come forward." Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. title: 'Broken social care will in the end break the NHS,' says Burnham
description: Andy Burnham said the proposed care service would be laid out in detail and put on the ballot at the next general election.
body: This video can not be played UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed a national care service, free at the point of use, to tackle England's "threadbare" social care services. In an interview with BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said "broken social care will in the end break the NHS" and that he would not look in the other direction. Burnham went on to say that he will develop a clear plan for a new national care service that is then put to the public at the next general election. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp, who also spoke to Kuenssberg, warned that "more tax rises" are likely planned to fund the scheme, which is a "red line" for the Conservatives 'Broken social care will in the end break the NHS,' says Burnham. title: Men held in major incident near RAF base as homes evacuated
description: A major incident is declared and villagers have been evacuated from their homes in Whelford near RAF Fairford.
body: Police said several men were arrested A major incident has been declared and homes have been evacuated in a village near an RAF base which hosts the United States Air Force. Several men have been arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, Gloucestershire police said. An army explosive ordnance disposal team is currently examining a number of vehicles. Residents in Whelford, near RAF Fairford, have been taken to a leisure centre while investigations continue, police said. A cordon is currently in place in the area and officers say they believe the incident is contained. The base has been recently used to deploy American bombers since the country's conflict in Iran began on 28 February. Live updates on this story In March this year, after then prime minister Sir Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from UK bases, four American bombers landed at RAF Fairford and the US started using British bases for "specific defensive operations". The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team is currently examining a number of vehicles A large emergency services presence has been seen in the area, including a Hazardous Area Response Team. Gloucestershire Police said: "A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. "We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place." Police said the men were arrested early on Sunday morning. A spokesperson for the US Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford "remain vigilant". They said: "For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures. "The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families. "We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families." Did you witness what happened? title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back
description: Big Bang played London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, marking a long-awaited return for the group that helped build the blueprint for modern K-pop.
body: Taeyang, G-Dragon and Daesung of BigBang perform during the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean. An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back. Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour. Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert; they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history. As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming. For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia. Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia. The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal. Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking. Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio , comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community. By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging. The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful. G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung on stage with dancers In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards. When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours. They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible. Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List. "When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool. "Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds. "Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be." G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung celebrating their 20th anniversary during the XX: Cosmos World Tour Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies. But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre. For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live. "They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore. "They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me." The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS. Fans arrived kitted out with Big Bang merchandise And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong. In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks. But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise. "Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology." The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow. Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years. Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, coordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances. Fans exchanging handmade gifts outside the stadium Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success. South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus. In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group. Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal. title: Thousands without water and roads closed after burst pipe
description: Southern Water says it is investigating the burst pipe which happened on Sunday morning.
body: Areas of Crawley are flooded and about 9,000 homes have water supply issues Thousands of homes in parts of Crawley have water supply issues and a number of roads have flooded after what police are describing as a "significant" leak. Roads around the Southgate Roundabout in Crawley have been closed on Sunday morning due to the burst water pipe, Sussex Police said. Southern Water said around 9,000 customers were impacted and it was setting up bottled water stations. A company spokesperson said: "Our teams are on site and working as quickly and safely as possible to repair the burst and restore supplies." The company said customers were experiencing a loss of water supply or low pressure in the following areas - Woolborough Road, Holmcroft, Southgate, Tilgate and Furnace Green. The Southern Water spokesperson added: "Restoring water to customers as quickly as possible remains our highest priority." Southgate Avenue, Crawley Avenue and part of the A23 are currently closed, according to the company. Sussex Police has asked that people avoid the area while emergency services manage the situation safely. The water main burst in the early hours of Sunday morning causing extensive flooding Martin Lawrence was making deliveries in the area at 05:00 BST. He told BBC Radio Sussex: "I came across this massive flood going across the road. "There was a large amount of water going from one side of the roundabout to the other and going into an underpass. "I've never seen so much water in my life." Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
description: The two attacks hours apart come as the country struggles to stop high levels of gang-related armed violence.
body: Gunmen torched vehicles as they fled the scene of a mass shooting at bar near Johannesburg Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country. Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured. In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks. In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing. Police said thirteen men and four women were killed, adding that the motive was not clear. In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital. No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning. The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township. Armed security forces were deployed to the scene of a mass shooting in Cape Town on Sunday morning Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million. But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining. In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development". Earlier this year the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence. title: Dog rescued from cliff ledge at landmark waterfall
description: Eight-year-old Labrador Penny was stranded on a narrow ledge in Ingleton, rescue services say.
body: Volunteers from Cave Rescue Organisation helped to reunite Penny with her owners A dog stranded on a narrow ledge at the bottom of a 40ft (12m) cliff next to a waterfall has been safely retrieved thanks to the efforts of a volunteer-run rescue team. Yorkshire Dales charity Cave Rescue Organisation (CRO) and North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue responded to the incident at the well-known Pecca Falls, in Ingleton, after 15:15 BST on Saturday. Eight-year-old Labrador Penny had fallen into the river before becoming stuck after climbing up to a rocky outcrop 6.5ft (2m) above the water. Using a rope system, a volunteer was lowered to the ledge to reach the dog before she was "hauled back up the gorge where she was reunited with her owners". The fire service's Ripon swiftwater rescue team provided support downstream from where Penny was stranded. The incident happened yesterday at Pecca Falls, in Ingleton CRO is based in Clapham and provides services across the Yorkshire Dales National Park, extending into Lancashire and Cumbria. Formed in 1935, it currently has more than 80 volunteers who regularly attend mountain and cave rescues, as well as assisting in other public service incidents. Penny isn't the first pet the charity has saved after a tumble at Pecca Falls, which features five falls dropping a total of more than 30m (98ft). In March this year, the team used a similar rope pulley system to rescue a dog that had fallen 26.2ft (8m) and also become stuck on a narrow ledge.
