title: Marra to claim Holyrood 'hoarding power' in conference speech
description: The new Scottish Labour leader will address the UK Labour conference in Liverpool.
body: Michael Marra will give his first conference speech as Scottish Labour leader in Liverpool Michael Marra is set to call for the Scottish government to decentralise power from Holyrood in his first conference speech as Scottish Labour leader. Marra will claim the Scottish Parliament has "hoarded money and control" in Edinburgh and demand skills policy is devolved to Scotland's regions. The MSP for North East Scotland, who defeated Joe Fagan in a vote to replace Anas Sarwar just over a week ago, will address the first day of the UK Labour conference in Liverpool. He is expected to call on the Scottish government to put "power and money" in the hands of local people to grow regional economies. Marra will say: "Had our regions grown at the same pace as Manchester in the last decade, the Scottish economy would be £30bn larger. "Too much power is centralised in Scotland. The Scottish Parliament has hoarded money and control at the expense of Scotland's communities." Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader Who is new Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra? Marra took over as leader of Scottish Labour following Sarwar's decision to stand down in order to take up a role in the House of Lords as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government. That decision came a few months after the party's worst ever Holyrood election result in May. Their return of 17 MSPs saw them tied with Reform UK as the second-largest party in the Scottish Parliament. Marra, who first joined Labour as a teenager, previously called for a redistribution of "power, wealth and opportunity" across Scotland. He will use his conference speech to highlight Scotland's shipbuilding history as an example of what he will call a "staggering failure" in the government's skills policy. Marra will say that Scotland has a reliance on foreign workers, due to a lack of available, skilled Scottish equivalents. "We have welders from the Philippines and South Africa working on the next generation of Scottish warships because not enough Scottish workers have the skills," Marra is expected to say. "Shipbuilding – Scotland is famous for it. We're world class at it. There should be a sense of national pride that the ships being built in Scotland are providing opportunity and security for Scottish workers. "So, my message to Bute House is put control and money in the hands of the councils, colleges and industries who know what their local economies need better than any bureaucrat in Edinburgh." title: Baby bank's urgent appeal as demand for help grows
description: The founder of Leeds Baby Bank says the charity has seen a "massive" increase in referrals recently.
body: Chantal Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 and the charity marks its first decade in January The founder of a charity which provides essentials like Moses baskets, prams, nappies and clothes to struggling families across Leeds has said it urgently needs more donations to help keep up with demand. Chantal Nogbou said there had been a "massive increase" in the number of people referred by health and social care professionals to Leeds Baby Bank in recent months. Nogbou said staff had helped an "unprecedented" 550 families in Leeds since the start of June, and were expecting numbers to rise as winter loomed. "We get even more people needing help then because they want to put the heating on, but they still need to buy nappies and feed and clothe their child," she said. Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 when she was a single parent of four children, including twins, and she realised how many other families were struggling. More families than ever have been referred to Leeds Baby Bank for help since the start of June, according to the charity The charity will be 10 years old in January and Nogbou said that staff had seen a change in the families who needed their support over time. "When we started, pre-Covid, maybe one in five children in Leeds lived in relative poverty," she explained. "Now, you're looking at one in two children in some parts, and that's just a shocking number that really shouldn't be happening." Nogbou said that about 70% of the children they helped had a parent who was working and she said many were "not managing to manage the bills with energy and fuel prices going up". According to government statistics, 27% of children in the Yorkshire and Humber region lived in relative low income families - the joint highest proportion, alongside the West Midlands, in the country. A relative low income family is one living on less than 60% of the median national household income for that year. Chantal Nogbou said people did not realise how far a small financial donation could go Nogbou said the rise in referrals meant more financial challenges for the charity, especially after moving from a city centre office to a larger and more accessible building in Armley which could now provide more services. "All that has cost money and obviously bills for us have also gone up when it comes to the utilities, so it's definitely a scary thing as a charity," she said. She added that it was the donations of items and money from the community that had kept the charity going. "It's the people that, instead of buying a coffee every day, set up a direct debit and send £5 to Leeds Baby Bank every month," she said. "That £5 can buy something like a brand new mattress for a Moses basket." Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. title: From turgid to thrusting - mixed start for new Scotland
description: BBC Sport Scotland's Tom English reviews a mixed start to life as Scotland head coach for Sebastien Pocognoli as his side open their Nations League campaign with a goalless draw in Slovenia.
body: This video can not be played For 45 turgid minutes in Slovenia, some in the Tartan Army might have reimagined the Steve Clarke years as a time of plenty, the halcyon era of ambitious football when Scotland were an all-electric thrill-fest. The opening half of the Sebastien Pocognoli regime was, as expected, disjointed. It was also, rather unexpectedly, devoid of anything remotely related to what Pocognoli laid out as his non-negotiables - front-foot pressing, high intensity, speed of thought and mind, goal threat. They had no shot on target and lost so many aerial duels that you stopped counting beyond the half-hour mark. They took 38 minutes to touch the ball in Slovenia's penalty area. It wasn't like they were under major pressure - the hosts are a pretty toothless side - but neither were they accurate or energetic. Everybody who preached patience in the new era gulped hard. This was not good. We didn't expect champagne, but this was stale beer. And then it changed, not so completely that Scotland roared and won the game, but they certainly cleared their throats as an attacking force. Gilmour catalyst, impressive Welsh, but same issue for Scotland? Scotland begin Pocognoli era with encouraging Slovenia draw From being impotent, they became thrusting. That second half was as big a 0-0 rout as you're likely to see. Frustrating, but encouraging at the same time. It will be agonising for Oli McBurnie that he's still without an international goal - he said he wouldn't sleep after failing to convert a one-on-one with Jan Oblak - but his second-half performance was full of good things; efforts on goal, link-up play, presence and danger. Robbie Ure hit a post, Kieron Bowie had a terrific chance, but missed. The three strikers drew a blank, but as far as 0-0s go, it offered hope that more productive days may lay ahead with these guys. There are two ways of looking at the draw. All 10 starting outfield players had a shot on goal, the first time that's happened since June 2022, against Armenia. Scotland had 17 shots, their most attempts in a competitive game in more than 14 years. The flipside is that they have now failed to score in three tournament games in a row for the first time in almost 22 years. After the break, Pocognoli dropped McBurnie a little deeper, in a pocket just behind Robbie Ure and then Bowie when he came on. He got Billy Gilmour to sit lower in midfield, where he had time to dictate, which he absolutely did. Gilmour tied it all together in the second half. Pocognoli called it "two games in one game" and he was right. The subtle shift in McBurnie's and Gilmour's positioning brought Scotland alive. It was an impressive watch; ambition, relentlessness, belief. No cherry on top but enough there to leave most folk happy about day one and motivated ahead of day two, against Switzerland on Tuesday night at Hampden. This video can not be played 'I'm not going to be able to sleep thinking about those chances' - McBurnie McBurnie, not so much the prodigal son but now the forgiven one, had that big chance six minutes into the new half - the one he would have dreamed about. He created it for himself, winning possession and getting into a wonderful position right in front of an isolated Oblak. He could have dinked it as the goalkeeper committed himself, he could have slid it home to Oblak's left or through his legs. Instead, he went for the flourish, trying to take it round the Slovenian and marking his return to the side after 2,005 days in the wilderness with a first goal on his 17th appearance. Oblak won the duel. Painful, for sure, but a prelude to a stirring second half from the striker and his new-old team-mates. McBurnie played a slick one-two with the increasingly dominant Gilmour, who had his shot saved. Oblak was by a million miles Slovenia's best player. McBurnie had a header fly over, Aaron Hickey had a header just wide, Bowie came on and had an immediate impact. He had three chances in eight minutes - a tame shot, a clipped attempt and then the big one - played in by Gilmour but pulled wide. In that moment, he joined McBurnie and Ure (after hitting a post late in the first half) in the torture chamber. In the midst of all of that, McBurnie powered a header on goal, but Oblak was equal to it. That was Scotland's ninth consecutive crack without reply. They were utterly dominant but achingly goalless. So much encouraging stuff and yet just one point to show for it when it really should have been three. Pocognoli said he was heartened by that second half. Scotland fans should be buoyed by the new head coach recognising the problems in his team and then fixing them. With such a small track record to feed off, the subject of his tactical acumen was always going to be an interesting one - the ownership of the second 45 minutes showed that he's no slouch in identifying and changing the things that need to be changed. Going with McBurnie and Ure up front was something of a surprise, but it sent a signal out that Scotland are here to go on the offensive rather than just defend their way to decent outcomes. That didn't materialise in the first half, but it clicked in the second. It's a touch surreal that, at the end of another game when Scotland failed to score, there is a lot to be hopeful about in the men who are there to supply the goals. McBurnie, Ure and Bowie are an exciting trio. When others are fit, there's Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland, Tommy Conway and Ross Stewart. Young James Wilson will have his moment at some point. New blood has joined the old guard and things should be better when everything settles down. For Pocognoli, the next test is the biggest one. Switzerland, ranked 14th in the world, are missing some serious operators, but they are brilliantly coached by Murat Yakin and they're settled and formidable. Their whole is greater than the sum of their parts. This will be

title: Man charged with murdering woman in Darlington
description: Andrew Bell, 44 and from Darlington, is due to appear before magistrates on Monday.
body: Leanne Park was pronounced dead at the scene in Darlington A man has been charged with murdering a woman who was found dead by police. Andrew Bell, 44, of Darlington, is accused of killing Leanne Park, 44, in the town on Wednesday. Durham Police said she was pronounced dead at an address in Parkgate at about 21:15 BST. Her family said she was the "best mam, nana, daughter and friend we could wish for". Bell is due to appear at Newton Aycliffe Magistrates' Court on Monday. A 27-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender has been released on bail, the force said. A spokesperson said crime scene investigators would continue to work at the scene and a police cordon was "expected to remain in place for some time". Anyone with information about the murder is urged to contact detectives. Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds. title: Man City? I feel cheated - when do Stoke City get our FA Cup?
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains what he and all Stoke fans are thinking after Manchester City are found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced.
body: When do we get our FA Cup? That is what all Stoke City fans have been asking me since the news broke on Friday that Manchester City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they have been accused of breaching. I thought exactly the same. While the process is far from over because Manchester City are expected to appeal, I have to say this verdict and the whole situation has left a very sour taste in my mouth. Taking my Stoke side to the 2011 FA Cup final was one of the highlights - if not THE highlight - of my 50 years in football as a player and manager. That day in May will also live long in the memory of all Stoke fans who followed their team to Wembley dreaming that they would win the greatest club cup competition in world football for the first time in their long history. The club we were playing, Manchester City, were on their way to dominating English football. At that time they had not won a major trophy for 35 years but they were a team that, in transfer fees and wages, cost well above anything Stoke City could ever aspire to. Think back now, and I can still picture walking out before kick-off to see our end of the ground decked in red and white and hear the amazing rendition of Delilah from our supporters. Many of those fans had come from all corners of the world, and had spent or borrowed fortunes to make it, just to say: "I was there." For me, experiencing that game and occasion with Stoke City's owners, the Coates family, was really touching too. Continuously, over many decades, they have helped to finance their own community's local professional team. For Peter, Denise, John and all the family and friends who in good times and bad found the money and spirit to back the club, it was their one day in the sun. It was the same for all of us connected with Stoke. This was our day, that day that many smaller clubs and their fans pray for. Although we lost 1-0, our players were fantastic and gave, as always, a fully committed performance against the odds. Yaya Toure, who scored the winning goal, was reportedly earning 10 times what we were paying any of our players and, on his own, had cost more than our entire starting 11 when they had signed him from Barcelona in 2010. Yaya Toure scored Manchester City's winner against Stoke at Wembley. He had joined City for around £24m in July 2010 After the game, my disappointment was buried in the fact we had played a team full of superstars, and faced an elite coach in Roberto Mancini, and had just fallen short. Today, I feel very differently, as I am sure people connected with the other clubs affected by City's successes in the same period, between 2009 and 2018, do too. We lost, but to a team that have been found guilty of breaking the financial rules set out by the Premier League. In doing so, they did not just beat Stoke in an FA Cup final, they collected a stack of titles and went on to completely dominate English football for more than a decade. So, with those rules having been broken, what will the punishment be? This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City Well, I know all Stoke supporters will be demanding that City pass the trophy over and every club that has been affected by their actions will be considering their legal options. I don't expect Manchester City to phone me or the club up and offer back the 2011 FA Cup and the winners' medals their players received. I don't seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either. A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely. But I still feel cheated. Whatever happens next, we won't ever get that day back and the chance to celebrate around Stoke-on-Trent with the cup and medals we so honestly fought for. After breaking the rules, Manchester City got to do that instead. Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan. title: Why families are being urged to look closer on autumn walks
description: Experts urge families to spot, photograph and enjoy autumn fungi on their doorstep.
body: James Benwell says searching for fungi can turn an ordinary family walk into an outdoor adventure From fairytale toadstools to fungi that look like birds' nests, experts say some of Britain's most unusual mushrooms are beginning to emerge as autumn arrives. Hidden in parks, woodlands and nature reserves, species ranging from the bright-red fly agaric to the rare red cage fungus can be found by anyone willing to slow down and take a closer look. For James Benwell, of the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, searching for fungi has become a way to explore the outdoors with his young son. He said mushroom spotting can transform an ordinary walk into an adventure, revealing colourful and unusual species that many people pass by without noticing. Across the West Midlands, fungi enthusiasts have recorded everything from tiny bird's nest fungi in Birmingham city centre, to fly agaric mushrooms growing beneath woodland birch trees and a rare red cage fungus discovered in Cannon Hill Park. Many species can go unnoticed among fallen leaves, rotting wood and the bases of trees, but Benwell said taking the time to look more closely opens up a hidden world. "Every walk becomes interesting and exciting if you're exploring and if you're looking for new things," he said. Magpie inkcap mushrooms get their name from their black-and-white appearance, Benwell said With more than 15,000 species of fungi found in the UK, experts are encouraging people to photograph and record what they find, rather than pick them. Interest in fungi has grown in recent years, according to Lucas Large, chairman of the West Midlands Fungus Group, who said the organisation regularly attracted newcomers to its activities and fungi forays. Benwell added one of the attractions was the variety of shapes, colours and forms that can be discovered throughout autumn. "Sometimes you've just got to look through the leaf litter a bit, and you'd be amazed at the colours and different shapes and sizes of mushrooms you can find when you do look," he said. The fly agaric's distinctive red cap and white spots have made it one of the world's most recognisable mushrooms Among the most recognisable species is the fly agaric,, external the striking red mushroom covered in white spots that has become closely associated with folklore and popular culture. Benwell described it as "the mushroom of fairy tales". "It's in Alice in Wonderland, it's in Super Mario Brothers... It's everywhere as part of fairy tales and folklore," he said. "But there are still adults who've never seen it." The bright-red cage fungus attracts flies with its distinctive smell Other species offer equally unusual sights. Bird's nest fungi resemble miniature nests complete with tiny eggs, while the rare red cage fungus forms a vivid crimson lattice structure. The latter was spotted in Birmingham's Cannon Hill Park last year, in what Benwell said was only the second recorded sighting of the species in Birmingham and the Black Country. "UK-wide, you're only talking hundreds of records ever. It's not a common species at all," he said. Large said the red cage fungus also had another notable characteristic. "It smells horrible," he said, explaining the fungus attracts flies which help spread its spores. After more than a decade studying fungi, Large said the rarest species he had seen in the region was the coral tooth fungus. "It formed this enormous kind of white, coraloid fruiting body," he said. Bird's nest fungi get their name from their resemblance to tiny nests filled with eggs While the colourful displays may encourage people to learn more about fungi, experts are warning against assuming wild mushrooms are safe to eat. Several species found in the UK can cause severe illness or death if consumed, including the death cap mushroom, which the Woodland Trust says is responsible for most fungus-related fatalities., external Large said there was no foolproof shortcut to determining whether a mushroom was poisonous. "The only way to do it is to know which one it is, or be sort of certain that you've got a particular species," he said. Benwell agreed and said people without specialist knowledge should avoid picking wild mushrooms. "There are mushrooms that will harm you, that will make you sick or even kill you in this country," he said. "The best place to get your mushrooms if you want to eat them is the supermarket." Lucas Large describes the coral tooth fungus as one of the rarest species he has seen in the region Instead, people are encouraged to enjoy fungi where they are found, whether in Birmingham city parks, the woodlands of Cannock Chase, Sutton Park or the Wyre Forest. When searching with his son, the pair follow a simple rule. "No licking, no picking, no kicking." For Benwell, that approach allows families to enjoy the excitement of discovery while ensuring the region's remarkable fungi can be appreciated by everyone who passes by. title: 'I was angry at my husband - I didn't know he had dementia'
description: Helen Beaumont was told her husband was depressed. In fact he had young onset dementia.
body: Helen said she thought her husband was "just being a grumpy middle-aged man" Helen Beaumont spent years arguing with her husband before realising he had a terminal illness. Helen, who lives in Manchester, married Clive when she was 21 and the couple had their two children two decades later. While she expected parenthood to change things - when elements of Clive's personality appeared to shift she spent years frustrated. She wondered why he had stopped listening, had become unreliable, was unable to get a job and had been diagnosed with depression. About five years later, when Clive was 46, he was diagnosed with young onset dementia. He died aged 51. Helen, now 75, said if Clive had received an earlier diagnosis they could have had "at least two years when we weren't fighting all the time". Clive Beaumont spent more than two decades working for the army before developing young onset dementia Since Clive's death in 1999, Helen has been working as a dementia researcher, raising awareness of his condition and continuing his legacy through her charity, The Clive Project. She continues to tell her story because there is still "more to be done" to help dementia patients and their families, she said. Helen described her late-husband as a calm, level-headed and "very active guy" who used to run marathons, even "before it was popular". "Clive was unflappable," she said. "He reckoned he failed if he lost his temper." But as Clive approached his 40s things began to change. "You can't really tell at what stage somebody's behaviour changes," she said. "Younger people in particular are always going to be difficult to diagnose. "And he covered up some things. He never admitted to me that he was having problems with reading and writing." While Helen had never before heard of dementia in younger people, she said she "knew there was something wrong". "I would make plans and he would forget he was looking after the children," she said. "We had very many arguments about it. "He said, 'I'm just growing old' - and he was early forties then." Clive first went to the GP about his symptoms at age 40 and he was diagnosed with depression Clive was made redundant when he was 44 and after taking on odd jobs, he struggled to get another permanent role. "I had to fill in his job application forms," Helen recalled. "He couldn't do it." Helen said Clive's symptoms began to lead to tensions between them. "He went shopping, he bought things like cream and chocolates instead of fish fingers and bread," she said. "And I just couldn't understand it. "I was cross with him - really cross with him for quite a lot of the time. "We could have a conversation and then it was like it had never happened." "I didn't know it was dementia. "With hindsight you think, 'How could I have been so silly?'. "But I talked to a medic friend and I said, 'I think there's something wrong. He might have something like dementia'. "And she said he couldn't possibly - not at his age." Clive's diagnosis came six years after he first went to his GP presenting symptoms Finally, when Clive was 46, he was sent for neurological tests. "Clive was never depressed," Helen said. "The symptoms had been confused. "For a long time they refused to admit that a healthy man in his early 40s could have dementia. "Eventually he got to see a neurologist and six months later I was told over a telephone call that he was very sorry to say my husband had pre-senile dementia, [as it was then referred to]. "There was no treatment and very little support." Dementia is associated with an ongoing decline of brain functioning Symptoms can include memory loss, slower thinking speed, and lower levels of understanding, judgement and mood, according to the NHS, external The condition is often associated with old age, but according to Dementia UK, external, 7.5% of people with dementia in the UK have young onset dementia, meaning their symptoms began below the age of 65 Young onset dementia often develops in people between the ages of 45 and 65 but can affect people of any age Helen said caring for Clive was like having a third child For about a year Helen balanced her job with raising her then three and four-year-old children - while also caring for Clive. "I just had three children," she said. "Two of them I could pick up when I wanted them somewhere where they weren't. And Clive, I had to cajole along." Helen said the family were able to do normal activities like going to the park or the cinema for some time - but then Clive became more difficult to care for. "There was a time where we were on the M14 and he tried to get out of the car," she said. "And in he last couple of years he could be quite aggressive." She said when he left the house and went missing she knew he would need full-time care in a residential home. "Fortunately, somebody noticed how uncomfortable he was walking and asked him in for a cup of tea and then got in touch with the police," she said. Clive in 1996 , three years before he died Helen said she felt "fortunate" that the NHS had covered the costs of social care for Clive. Nonetheless, finding care for Clive was not easy. "He was moved three times," Helen said. "And as he got worse, it got more difficult for them to manage him. "Looking after somebody like Clive counts as social care - not medical care." Five years after his initial diagnosis, Clive died in a residential home in 1999, aged 51. After Clive died, Helen said: "I was very depressed. "I kept going. It took me a long time to get back to having some joy in my life" In 2008, at the age of 58, Helen made a big change. "My daughter and son had left home to go to university and I moved from Oxford to Manchester to pursue a new career as a dementia researcher," she said. She did a PhD in 2015 and specialised in using magnetic resonance imaging to investigate brain changes in people with dementia with the aim

title: Traitors star burgled after sharing holiday photos
description: Paul Gorton urges people to think twice before sharing holiday pictures before they are back home.
body: Paul Gorton believes he was targeted after sharing his holiday snaps on social media Traitors star Paul Gorton did not think twice about sharing photographs on social media while enjoying a family holiday with his wife and two young children. But when he returned home he discovered that his house in Cheshire had been burgled just days earlier. "The eerie bit is at 21:10 BST I posted that me and Kate were by the side of the pool, we've got full bellies, the kids are in bed, we're actually having our little bit of the holiday," he said. "About 20 minutes later, little did we know, our house has been broken into." Paul's bike as well as several sentimental items including an irreplaceable ring from Kate's grandmother were stolen in the burglary on 28 August. The perpetrators managed to break in through the bi-fold doors at the back of the house by using a technique known as lock snapping before cutting the broadband connection. Paul's home in Cheshire was targeted while he was on holiday Paul, who was a contestant on the second series of the popular BBC series, said he reported the burglary to Cheshire Police, with the force describing it as a "one-off hit". As a result, Paul believes it was a "targeted attack". "They said they normally see people come in from far and wide and they [target] a couple of houses in a night but this isn't the case," said Paul, who is originally from St Helens. "This makes me suspect that it could be someone that follows me. "They've seen that I've posted that I was away and then thought 'let's go in the house and see if we can get ourselves some goodies'." Paul said he hoped other people would learn from his misfortune. "I think the key message is for people to be a little bit smarter, more conscientious when they're posting and post when they're back at home. "Hopefully people can learn from my mistakes. "I guess the aim is the worst thing that's happened to us could be the best thing that will happen to you because you can protect yourself moving forward and that's the whole reason behind the campaign." Following the burglary, Paul has joined forces with Compare the Market, which commissioned a licensed private investigator to examine the publicly available digital footprints of nine volunteers. They were able to identify seven home addresses by using publicly available information. The fastest home address was identified in 15 minutes, with the first lead found in only 50 seconds. "It's not just about social media," said Paul. "I've learned to think about the whole picture with locks, alarms, lights, what you're posting online and whether you're accidentally advertising that nobody's home." Cheshire Police confirmed investigations were ongoing into the burglary but no arrests had been made. title: Alcaraz wins after saving match points as Europe lead Laver Cup
description: Carlos Alcaraz narrowly avoids back-to-back singles defeats for the first time in 18 months as Team Europe lead Team World at the Laver Cup.
body: Carlos Alcaraz has struggled with a wrist injury this year Two-time Wimbledon champion Carlos Alcaraz narrowly avoided back-to-back singles defeats for the first time in 18 months as Team Europe took a 7-5 lead over Team World at the Laver Cup. The world number three saved two match points before overcoming Taylor Fritz 6-3 4-6 13-11 in a dramatic deciding tie-break at London's O2 Arena. It was Alcaraz's first singles outing since his late-night quarter-final exit to Ben Shelton at the US Open. "The drop shot is part of my game," Alcaraz said after sealing victory with a trademark touch. "In those really close and important moments, I tried to use it because it was a really good weapon for me in this match." American Fritz, whose only previous victory against the Spaniard came during Team World's triumph in last year's competition, kept errors to a minimum. However, Alcaraz struck 42 winners to Fritz's 20, bringing an audience that included Roger Federer and Andy Murray to their feet. Facing match point at 8-9 down in the tie break, Alcaraz fired an ace before leaning on a drop shot to stave off a second. He converted his third match point when Fritz failed to retrieve another delicate drop shot over the net. Earlier on Saturday, Andre Agassi's Team World had threatened to run away with things. Alex de Minaur fought back from a set down to shock Alexander Zverev 2-6 7-6 (7-5) 11-9, while American debutant Learner Tien edged Italy's Flavio Cobolli 6-3 2-6 10-7. Following Alcaraz's singles heroics, Zverev returned to the court alongside Casper Ruud to secure an important 6-4 7-6 (9-7) doubles victory over Alexander Bublik and Brandon Nakashima, keeping Europe ahead going into the final day. Match wins are worth three points on Sunday, with the first team to reach 13 points lifting the trophy. Europe are chasing their sixth Laver Cup title, while holders Team World are aiming for their third. title: Bumblebee project seeking to help rare species
description: The programme to help the Moss carder species will focus on Cornwall, Kent and the North Pennines.
body: The project will focus on Cornwall, Kent and the North Pennines A project is under way to try and help one of the UK's "most threatened" species of bumblebee. The Bumblebee Conservation Trust is leading a £907,000 three-year scheme alongside the University of Cambridge to recover the Moss carder species. It said the initiative would focus on landscapes across Cornwall's coastal grasslands, dunes and heathland as well as grazing marshes and sea walls in Kent and the upland fringe landscape of the North Pennines. During the project, the trust said it would work with landowners to trial "small-scale habitat interventions" to identify those which work well while gaining a better understanding of the species' behaviour and needs. More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall Moss carder bumblebees are largely found in small, fragmented populations, according to the trust. It said it was distinctive with a velvety covering of ginger-yellow hairs across its body and no black hairs. The trust said habitat loss and fragmentation were likely to have a bigger impact on the Moss carder than many other species as it typically foraged closer to its nest than most other bumblebees. Amy Plowman, head of conservation and science at the trust, said: "This is a hugely exciting and ambitious three-year project that gives us a real opportunity to turn the tide for one of the UK's rarest bumblebees." Moss carder bumblebees are largely found in small, fragmented populations Funding worth more than £530,000 has been provided to the project by Natural England's Species Recovery Programme. Tylan Berry, Natural England's species and nature recovery networks senior officer, said the Species Recovery Programme was helping "take practical action to halt species decline and support nature recovery across England". Berry said the Moss carder was "one of England's most threatened pollinators". "Projects like this demonstrate how targeted investment can support practical conservation action on the ground," he added. title: Investigation launched as NHS trust apologises for Noah Woods data breach
description: East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust has apologised to the family for "extra anguish" caused.
body: Noah's family paid tribute to a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy An NHS trust has apologised to the family of three-year-old Noah Woods for the "extra anguish" caused after a data breach of his medical records. Launching an "urgent" investigation, Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said that any unauthorised access of patient data was "completely unacceptable". Disciplinary action will be taken if needed, the statement from the trust added. A major search for Noah was carried out in the village of Brantham, Suffolk, after the child went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in nearby water by police divers. In the statement issued on Sunday,, external Dr Mansfield said of the data breach: "Immediate steps were also taken to secure the records and prevent further access that was not for a legitimate, clinical reason. "We have reported the matter to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), and we will continue to keep Noah's family informed as our investigation progresses." At least 1,300 people helped in the search for Noah in the 24 hours before he was found. A tribute issued by his family called him a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy who loved to laugh. His mother urged other parents to "hold their children a little tighter and cherish every moment". An inquest last week heard that the three-year-old had left a play area "through a gap in the fence". Assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said it was a "very sad and tragic death" as she opened and adjourned the inquest in Ipswich. title: White casts doubt on Fury-Joshua after 24 hours of chaos
description: There is fresh uncertainty around the proposed Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua fight - after Dana White said he did not know whether it would happen.
body: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury were officially announced to fight in Cardiff on 11 December but fresh uncertainty has emerged over the contest Two days after the announcement British boxing had waited a decade for, Dana White - the UFC president and Zuffa Boxing chief named as one of the figures promoting Tyson Fury against Anthony Joshua - was asked whether the fight would actually happen. "I don't know," he said. White was speaking at London's Copper Box on Saturday, where British heavyweight Johnny Fisher beat Michael Pirotton on his Zuffa Boxing debut. But for much of the media in attendance another heavyweight fight dominated the evening. Asked whether Wednesday's scheduled Fury-Joshua news conference in London would take place, White added: "I have no idea." On Thursday, Fury and Joshua were officially announced to meet at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December, live globally on Netflix. By Friday, that certainty had unravelled. A dispute over who is entitled to promote the event led to claims of contractual breaches, talk of possible replacement fights and another flurry of cryptic social-media posts. Even by boxing's recent standards, the past 24 hours have been extraordinary - and not a particularly flattering look for the sport. White (right) has become increasingly involved in Turki Alalshikh's boxing plans, with the pair working together through Zuffa Boxing Netflix and Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's fight announcement was striking for who it included - and who it did not. The event was presented as a collaboration involving Alalshikh's The Ring and White. There was no mention of Matchroom's Eddie Hearn, who has promoted Joshua throughout his professional career, or Queensberry's Frank Warren, Fury's long-time promoter. White's involvement was not entirely unexpected. The Zuffa Boxing promoter has been saying for weeks he would be involved in Fury-Joshua. Hearn has been equally adamant he would not. After Thursday's announcement, Hearn said Joshua's contract specifically prevented White and American sports entertainment company TKO from having a promotional role, claiming Netflix had not been made aware of that provision. Hearn said there had been breaches of the agreement which needed to be resolved and cast doubt on whether Wednesday's news conference would go ahead. Fury says a similar restriction originally appeared in his own contract but was removed because he wanted White involved. Warren has taken a more pragmatic position. Speaking to BBC Sport before the latest dispute escalated, he said his understanding was White had helped secure the Netflix deal and compromises had been necessary to get the fight made. On Saturday, White was generally non-committal on the future of the contest but much clearer in his criticism of Hearn. "The guy who is supposed to be helping the fight has been hurting the fight," White said. "He hasn't done the fight any favours." This video can not be played 'None of this is unusual' - Warren on AJ v Fury fight timings The uncertainty intensified on Friday evening. Reports emerged that Fury-Joshua could be in jeopardy and alternative fights for 11 December were being discussed, including Ryan Garcia against the recently retired three-weight undisputed champion Terence Crawford. Crawford appeared as surprised as anyone, publicly questioning the suggestion he could be fighting Garcia. In a video posted on social media, he claimed Joshua and Hearn were "trying to pull out" and blamed the dispute largely on Hearn's objection to White. There has been no announcement from Joshua saying he intends to withdraw. On Instagram, Alalshikh posted pictures of himself with White and later shared a cryptic message in Arabic about somebody attempting to "stab you where you told them it hurts", although he made no explicit reference to Fury-Joshua. Hearn, meanwhile, posted a picture with a shushing emoji and the message: "Bet against me." For a fight negotiated so publicly for so many years, the familiar mix of claims, counter-claims and cryptic posts had returned almost immediately. Among the media in east London on Saturday, much of the conversation centred around Fury-Joshua. Who had heard what? Was the fight genuinely in danger? Would Wednesday's news conference happen? And, with White in the building, would he provide any clarity afterwards? Instead, his post-fight comments only underlined the uncertainty. White has been openly critical of Hearn, while the precise nature of his own role in Fury-Joshua remains at the heart of the dispute. That distinction could prove significant when lawyers examine exactly what Joshua's contract permits. During Saturday's US broadcast of the Zuffa Boxing card, it was suggested White was helping Alalshikh on a personal level rather than acting as a promoter. White rejected that interpretation. "I don't know where that came from," he said. "That was weird." And White offered another tease when asked whether he would attend Wednesday's news conference if it does go ahead. "I guess I'll leave that as a surprise," he said. This video can not be played 'I think Tyson will knock Joshua out' As of Saturday night, Netflix continued to list Fury against Joshua at the Principality Stadium on 11 December and said the fighters would attend Wednesday's news conference. But the contractual disagreement remains unresolved. The unusual position is that, little more than 48 hours after the fight was officially announced, one of the central figures in its promotion cannot say whether it will happen - or whether its first major launch event will go ahead. There is too much money, time and work invested in Fury-Joshua for anyone involved to walk away lightly. But if the past decade has taught boxing anything, an agreement does not necessarily mean the fight is safe. Fury-Joshua is once again wait

title: Gaming pays me double what I earned as a teacher
description: Jarvs Tasker says it would have taken her 20 years as a teacher to make what she earns now.
body: Jarvs Tasker is the director and founder of Jarvs Indie Insights and left her teaching career behind seven years ago In 2019, Jarvs Tasker was forced to give up her teaching career due to chronic illness when she was just 28. Fast forward seven years, and she earns double her former annual salary, running Jarvs Indie Insights, which provides communication and marketing within the gaming industry. She visited the University of Suffolk's e-sport building in Ipswich to celebrate independent game developers and studios on Wednesday. "I can comfortably say it probably would have taken me about 20 years in teaching to earn what I make now," she said. When Tasker left teaching, she initially started volunteering for PlayStation's YouTube channel, but she said there was lots of crossover between the two industries. "Managing a community is very similar to managing a class of kids, so there's a lot of crossover skills there, but actually, video games is one of those industries where a lot of people come into it later on in life." Tasker, who lives in Exeter, believed young people might not know the "many pathways" available in the industry. "The video games community is very strong, and they will champion people that love what they do, but they'll also notice if you're in it just for the money," she continued. "Passion is the most important thing." Asked about the impact of AI, she said she believed the industry was doing a "really great job" at rejecting it, because players hated it. "I think as an industry we should be really proud of the fact that we're still championing human creativity and that the audience is also on board with that," she added. Mark Backler of Game Anglia says the group works to raise awareness about careers in the gaming industry Tasker had been in Suffolk as part of an event hosted by Game Anglia to showcase the growing independent gaming industry in the East of England. Mark Backler from Game Anglia said the industry was now one of the biggest in the UK, and while he agreed it was competitive, it was "more possible than ever to develop and release your own independent games". "It's like being a content creator - it's tricky to be one of the standout ones, but it is doable," he said. He added it was difficult to tell how AI would change things, but a lot of players were against its use. Developer Sam Read-Graves says the industry is growing in the East of England Sam Read-Graves is a developer at Read Graves and works specifically in the East. At the event, he said the gaming industry had "grown massively in the past 10 years". "Because of schemes like Game Anglia across Suffolk, Essex, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk, there are really great clusters of a lot of students and a lot of developers, and I like to think that this has started to bring in studios who could make the big games. "When it comes to those games like Call of Duty or FIFA, those at the minute aren't going to come out of the East of England because we don't have big studios. "But when it comes to independent developers, there's no reason those games can't financially be as big." Abbygale Dunn studied game design and programming at university Abbygale Dunn, 22, is the founder and director of Astral Forge, an independent game development company based in Essex. She said there was "so much space for women" in the industry today. "It's obviously daunting. When I studied, there were only about three women in my course," she said. "Everyone is so kind; it's really not as bad as it seems, especially nowadays. "As a programmer myself, which is more rare for women to be in, I've never felt out of place." Game scout Omar Khalil says it can be hard to create the next big game Omar Khalil is game scout lead at Entity and said there was "no shortage of talent in the UK", but it was challenging to create the next big game. "There are so many games out there right now, and it's not like there aren't enough good games; it's how do you get visibility on those games?" he explained. "I think that's the biggest challenge." title: Child's hidden letter found after 44 years
description: Michelle Harwood had not been born when the letter was written and did not expect to find the writer.
body: The letter would have been written before Michelle Harwood was born A letter written by a 10-year-old girl in the 1980s and hidden in the cavity of the stairs at her home has been found 44 years later. The house in Hockley, Essex, was undergoing renovation work when a worker found the scrap of paper and passed it to Michelle Harwood, who now lives there. Filled with curiosity, the 36-year-old charity worker examined it - noting "really neat" handwriting for a child - and posted on her local Facebook community group on Thursday morning to track down the author. Within an hour, multiple people had found and tagged Rachel Miles, now a 54-year- old teacher in Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire. And she responded. The BBC contacted Miles almost half a century after she wrote the letter. She explained that time capsules were popular in the 1980s because of the influence of Blue Peter, and recalled writing the letter after her dad found a cavity behind the stairs. "I just thought it would be quite nice to basically post a letter for the future and I'm obviously quite delighted to see that someone had found it," she said. Harwood said she had "goosebumps" when she read the words Miles said it was "lovely" reliving her Essex childhood and "really nice" to see how many people remembered her, despite her moving out of the county. "It's nice to hear familiar names that I knew and to be reconnected with the area," she said. She added it amused her that, out of her whole family, she had only named her cat, Kizzy, who was a "legend of those parts". Harwood described the moment she saw the letter. "[Reading] 'to the finder' just immediately gave me goosebumps," she said. "I couldn't believe that note had been there longer than I've been alive." "I couldn't really believe my handwriting", said Miles The letter is dated 12 August 1982, eight years before Harwood was born. While the Harwoods have lived at Betts Farm Estate for 11 years, Miles said her family were there when it was just a building site that she and her friends would play on. The letter is now stuck to the Harwood family fridge Harwood noticed parallels between her own life and that of Miles. Miles was born in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, near where Harwood's husband, Jonathan, lived as a child. They also both owned cats while living at the house, which explained why a catflap was already at the back door when the Harwoods arrived. Harwood said in her social media post that it was "a long shot" and she had no expectations of finding the writer at all, let alone in the same morning. "I think social media is great for things like that, because so many people are connected," she said Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below. title: Four killed in helicopter crash near Montreal
description: The victims of the crash have not yet been identified, Quebec provincial police told the BBC.
body: A file photo of a black and white helicopter Four people have died after a helicopter crashed in a small town 50km (31 miles) from Montreal, Quebec's provincial police have told the BBC. Emergency services were called to Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville shortly after 14:30 local time (19:30 BST) on Saturday afternoon, where they found the aircraft on fire and declared its occupants dead at the scene. The victims have not yet been identified but the aircraft appeared to be a private helicopter, Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said. An investigation into the crash is being led by the Major Crime Unit of the Sûreté du Québec, working alongside crime scene technicians as well as investigators from the Transportation Safety Board of Canada. The crash site is located near the Rang des Écossais road off Highway 10, according to Bilodeau. In an emergency call, police were notified of a helicopter in distress that may have crashed and caught fire. An hour after the call, the fire at the site had been brought under control though officials were still working at the crash site just before 22:00 local time (03:00 GMT). The victims have not yet been identified and Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said this process may "take a few days." title: Iran says it will wait for official US response after Trump rejects Strait of Hormuz proposal
description: The US president earlier said that Tehran only made the proposal to open the strait within seven days because "they're losing so badly".
body: Iran has said it will wait for an official response from US negotiators after President Donald Trump rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within seven days. In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but accused the president of previously making contradictory statements. Earlier, Trump told reporters at the White House that Tehran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that they wanted to make a deal to open the strait immediately because "they're losing so badly". On Friday at the UN, Araghchi told reporters that an agreement could be reached if "necessary conditions are met" between the two countries. Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran that was signed in June. Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week. The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February. "I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it. Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently". "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi said. Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis. Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway. Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by the US ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker. Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage". "President Trump's right to reject it," he said. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic pressure from the US was taking a toll on Tehran. Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran. The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran as "Operation Economic Outcast", and is using sanctions to pressure Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners. These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran. title: The Papers: 'Noel's crying his heart out' and 'global IVF disaster'
description: A couple of the papers feature more reaction to the Manchester City drama, after the club was found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.
body: The Premier League drama, after Manchester City was found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, features again on the front page of some of Sunday's papers. Oasis's Noel Gallagher is "crying his heart out" over the news, the Daily Star reports, as the musician says he is "sad for City fans" "True Blue Noel Gallagher" is on the cover of the Sunday People, saying he is "gutted for fans" over the Man City financial rule "breaches". Manchester City have always denied wrongdoing and plan to appeal Andy Burnham's "social care mission" was inspired by "seeing his dad Roy suffer with Alzheimer's", the Sunday Mirror reports. Burnham's father died earlier this month. Ahead of Labour's annual conference, the prime minister said "I won't leave office without having grasped this nettle," the paper reports The Independent leads with an image of Prime Minister Andy Burnham, with his wife, arriving at a Labour conference at Liverpool on Saturday. Elsewhere, the paper reports on dozens of patients losing thousands of pounds in savings in a "global IVF disaster". The paper says an international clinic filed for insolvency "leaving many in limbo mid-treatment". Investors in the company that runs the clinic said claims for prepaid treatment can be registered with the insolvency administrator The Telegraph leads again on the pleas from the family of retired explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes. In recent days the paper has reported on allegations regarding the care of Sir Ranulph, who has been open about his battle with Parkinson's disease The Sunday Express headlines on the deaths of people crossing the Channel on small boats, asking the government: "When will you stop this tragedy?" The government has previously said its "progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable" A former bodyguard to the leader of Hamas secured asylum and citizenship in the UK before "plotting" an attack in Europe ahead of the second anniversary of the 7 October attacks, the Sunday Times reports. The man, who isn't named for legal reasons, moved to the UK more than a decade ago, according to the paper - and now faces extradition to Germany Meanwhile, the Observer splashes on who it calls the "most powerful woman in Britain" - Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state. Haigh, "Burnham's de facto deputy" has brought her "Sheffield steel to Westminster", the paper says And as dancers take to the Stricly Come Dancing ballroom for the first time, the Sun on Sunday has a "Strictly warning" to head judge Shirley Ballas from her new partner's ex-fiance Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Internationals hold three-point Presidents Cup lead over US
description: The Internationals team could secure a first President's Cup in 28 years on Sunday after holding off a United States fightback on day three in Medinah.
body: Canada's Corey Conners (centre) saved par on the 18th The International team need five points on the final day to secure a first Presidents Cup in 28 years after holding off a United States fightback on day three in Medinah. The Internationals were behind in every match at one stage but will go into Sunday's singles holding a 10-5-7.5 lead. The hosts had the better of the morning session, winning two and tying one of the four-balls. But the teams split the afternoon foursomes, with Canada's Corey Conners saving par at the 18th to win the final match on the course and preserve the Internationals' three-point lead. The International team have only won the President's Cup once since its inception in 1994 and never on American soil. "We were down in every match, and to come back and get one and a half points out of this morning, we felt that was a little victory because we were down everywhere," said team captain Geoff Ogilvy. "This afternoon, the same thing happened. Team USA played so well all day. They played some really high-level foursomes, especially this afternoon. "For the boys to somehow come back and pinch two points out of that and split the session was amazing." Sunday sees 12 singles games take place, with each side needing 15.5 points to seal victory. title: Pickford or Trafford? The battle to be England's number one is now on
description: Jordan Pickford has been England's number one for a long time. But does he now have a rival in James Trafford?
body: James Trafford has made three appearances for England You have to go back 10 years to find a major tournament where Jordan Pickford was not starting in goal for England. The Everton goalkeeper has pretty much been England's number one since making his debut in 2017 - until now. Saturday's 3-2 Nations League loss to Spain saw Leeds' James Trafford make his competitive debut for the Three Lions as manager Thomas Tuchel signalled the battle to be number one is on. Pickford became England's highest appearance maker at World Cups, overtaking Peter Shilton when he started in England's 2026 quarter-final win over Norway. During Gareth Southgate's tenure there was not a natural goalkeeper to rival Pickford, and that looked to continue under Tuchel as Pickford started all but one of England's World Cup qualifiers and then every game in the summer. But it looks as though Pickford has finally got a rival in Trafford, with Tuchel saying that the pair get "two consecutive matches each" during this international break. Trafford has impressed since making his move to Leeds for a deal worth up to £45m. Against Spain, the 23-year-old showed his quality with the ball at his feet and made an impressive save to deny Ferran Torres in the first half. But he was beaten three times as England lost their Nations League opener to the world champions. "I think he deserved to get the two matches, that's why we gave him two matches," Tuchel said. "He started the Premier League season well and gets minutes as number one at Leeds. "Jordan [Pickford] did absolutely nothing wrong but we wanted to use this competition to see how far actually James is." Trafford's form this season has helped Leeds to fifth in the Premier League table. He has kept two clean sheets and now has his chance to stake his claim as England's future number one over two matches. Trafford had only played 32 top-flight games before moving to Leeds following time at Burnley and Manchester City. He came through City's academy and joined Burnley for an initial fee of £15m in the summer of 2023. However, he conceded 67 goals in only 28 matches before losing his place towards the end of the 2023-24 season. But after starring in Burnley's successful promotion in 2024-25 and the Clarets conceding just 16 goals, Trafford returned to City for £27m last summer with the hope of being Pep Guardiola's number one. City brought in one of the best goalkeepers in the world in Gianluigi Donnarumma, just four weeks after Trafford's arrival and he became second choice. Despite it being a frustrating campaign, Trafford did get vital experience and started both the FA Cup final and Carabao Cup final for City before his move to Leeds. He has been part of England success too, winning the U21 European Championship in 2023 and saving a stoppage-time penalty as Lee Carsley's side beat Spain in the final. Pickford has kept 46 clean sheets in his 91 appearances for England and has been a huge part of the Three Lions' recent success at major tournaments. "I think Jordan Pickford will be very disappointed," former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said on BBC Radio 5 Live. "Putting myself in that place, he will be questioning why he is not in that place. If he is number one, then why is he not playing against the world champions? "You wonder whether this is the next generation coming through for Thomas Tuchel." Pickford put in an excellent performance as England beat Mexico in the World Cup to progress to the quarter-finals, but it was not the goalkeeper's best tournament. "Jordan Pickford has never let England down," Ian Dennis said. "You have opposition against the Czech Republic and Croatia where you could give James Trafford an opportunity then. I do find the decision quite strange. "Pickford against the world champions - you would back him to play in this game." Pickford is in current possession of the number one shirt and played every minute of the World Cup until he was rested for England's third-place play-off win over France, with Dean Henderson starting. The 32-year-old, who will be 34 at Euro 2028, has 91 England caps and has saved four of the 14 penalties he has faced in major tournament shootouts. In the Premier League Pickford's overall numbers dwarf Trafford's. Since the start of the 2024-25 season no-one has prevented more expected goals than the Everton stopper. But there is very little between the two this campaign with Pickford preventing more goals but Trafford having a higher save percentage and better passing accuracy. Pickford has been fantastic for England but he didn't have the best World Cup, with a couple conceded that arguably he should've saved and a few nervy moments playing out from the back. Now seems as good a time as any to try James Trafford. James Trafford deserves to start, he's going to be England's next number one and why not start him against Spain or would you rather he only played against third-rate nations? James Trafford deserves his shot! Jordan Pickford has been quality for 10 years! Time feels right to test who could be next. Finding the next Harry Kane is going to be the problem! Jordan Pickford is paying the price for those mistakes creeping in during the World Cup. Could he have stopped the goals v Croatia, DR Congo and Fernandez v Argentina? Prime Pickford does. title: Christa Pike to be first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years - but her defence say she's a victim too
description: Lawyers for Pike, who killed a fellow student in 1995, say she should get clemency and would not be sentenced to death if the crime happened today.
body: Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee. Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says. Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest. Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull. A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men. Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting". Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence. In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider. "It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence. "Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness." Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parents In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened. But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge. In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since. Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her. "Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says. Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation." Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable." Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution. A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy. Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021. Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.
