title: Can you eat ultra-processed foods and still be healthy? A dietitian analysed my weekly shop
description: UPFs are linked to a range of health problems. But no-one seems to be able to agree why.
body: Going to the supermarket has become a minefield. I'm in aisle 15, reading long lists of ingredients and worrying if what's in my trolley is good for me or not. There's growing evidence, external that a hefty proportion of the food we consume could be damaging to our health, with ultra-processed foods (UPFs) linked to a range of health problems. But I've had enough of second-guessing myself and panicking I'm poisoning my child if I feed him chicken nuggets, so I've given my shopping list to a dietitian to analyse. Even the most chemical-sounding ingredients in chicken nuggets are tested and approved under UK food laws First things first, what is a UPF? It depends who you ask. A basic rule of thumb is that to be ultra-processed a product needs more than five ingredients, with at least one not normally found in your kitchen - things like emulsifiers, additives and flavourings. There is a large and growing body of evidence that shows UPFs are linked to obesity, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders such as diabetes, as well as mental health problems and even premature death. But scientists, doctors and dietitians can't agree on why. Is it purely down to the high fat, sugar, salt and calorie content? Or is the ultra-processing also a factor? Studies show more than half the calories we consume in the UK come from ultra-processed food, external. Dr Chris van Tulleken has written books and made documentaries about how bad these foods can be, and he tells me they're "almost impossible to avoid" - even his own family's diet includes a few. And my shopping list isn't UPF-free either. Maeve Hanan, a member of the British Dietetic Association, pauses as she scans through some of my weekly shopping list (there was more fruit and veg, honest) and points to a box of bran flakes. "This is ultra-processed, but I often buy this for my family. It's got so many health benefits." Hanan says there's a "growing hysteria" about UPFs. "Mainly because the messaging around them is so black and white," she says. "This food is good. This food is bad. "It just fuels fear - and fear around food is never good." A snapshot of my shopping list So what is her verdict on my grocery shopping? Not as bad as I expected, I'm relieved to learn. While there are UPFs in there, that doesn't necessarily make it an unhealthy food shop. In fact, Hanan says, "there's a good mix of foods which cover each food group". Just because some products have a long ingredient list, it doesn't make them "inherently bad", she explains, with the nutritional value "far more important". What about foods that contain ingredients I can barely pronounce, never mind recognise? Hanan takes my son's chicken nuggets as an example. "There are mandatory vitamins and minerals which manufacturers in the UK are required to add to white wheat flour such as calcium carbonate, niacin and thiamin," she says. Raising agents, such as disodium diphosphate, are used alongside sodium bicarbonate (baking powder) to make the batter crisp and light. Hanan says even the most chemical-sounding ingredients will have been tested and approved under UK food laws. "But while chicken nuggets are a good source of protein," she warns, "they are higher in fat and salt than a plain chicken breast, so I would eat them in moderation as part of a balanced diet." I tell Hanan my son usually eats them with raw carrot sticks and pasta. "One food does not make your diet healthy or unhealthy," she says, "it's about getting that balance over time." Megan Bamford believes cutting out UPFs from her diet has helped her manage irritable bowel syndrome and chronic pain. But now, as a mum to two young children, cooking from scratch is not always viable. Her eldest, seven-year-old Ella, has struggled on and off with food since she was little. "It's not always easy to feed your children what you think they should eat," Megan says. "Ella has been poorly in the past because of her severe picky eating - we had no choice but to give her ultra-processed food from a packet." Megan cut out ultra-processed foods to help manage her health, but focuses on choosing the healthiest options available for her children So Megan's kitchen is still full of fruit, vegetables, seeds and oats but there are now also breakfast cereals, crisps, biscuits and other processed foods too. She looks for food with five ingredients or fewer. "Most of the snacks, pizzas, and cereal I buy are not ultra-processed," she says. "I'm happy with that. I feed my children in the best way I can, I choose the healthiest options I can find." Ultra-processed food is global health threat, experts warn Pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein - how Italian children became so overweight Struggling to focus? What you eat might be affecting your brain While many UPFs are high in fat, sugar and salt, which we know cause a whole range of health problems, some scientists say there is not as much understanding about what the act of processing does to our food. Author and food scientist Prof David Julian McClements says the "ultra-processed food idea is not very well defined". "Focussing on the processing element is a bit of red herring," he says, "I don't think that's the main problem here." Some studies suggest, external the more processed food is, the easier it is to overeat it. Others link UPFs to changes in our gut microbiome. But McClements says there is no conclusive evidence to say this alone inherently damages our health. But given he works in the food industry, does he have a vested interest? "Any successful food scientist works a lot with the food industry," McClements says, "and I think trying to get rid of UPFs is holding back innovation." So many of us lead busy lives, he says, convenience is a major part of society. "What I want to do is to redesign processed foods to make them healthier," he says. Experts are calling for clearer

title: The young women guiding tourists through India's night sky
description: Astronomy tourism is giving young women in Hanle income, confidence and a new role in their community.
body: Padma Chamchot, Tsering Yangdol, Tsering Dolker and Palzes Angmo (left to right) - Hanle's astro-ambassadors, trained to guide visitors through the night sky It's 10pm and bitterly cold in Hanle. Strong winds sweep across this remote village in India's Himalayan Ladakh region, but no one seems to mind. Dinner is over, yet, instead of bed, many people are gathering outside. The reason is above them. At 14,764ft (4,500m) above sea level, Hanle is known for its exceptionally clear, dark skies. Wrapped in thick jackets, woollen caps and gloves, tourists and visitors gather to see the Milky Way and look through telescopes at planets, the Moon and distant stars. Among them are four young women: Palzes Angmo, Tsering Dolker, Tsering Yangdol and Padma Chamchot. They are Hanle's astro-ambassadors, trained to guide visitors through the night sky. By day, they cook meals, clean rooms and look after guests at their family-run homestays. By night, they set up telescopes, trace constellations with laser pointers and explain what visitors are seeing in the dark skies. These women - all in their late 20s - grew up watching these stars, but it was only a few years ago that they learnt to study them through a telescope. "The sky here has always been twinkling like this," 28-year-old Dolker says. The difference today is that people travel hundreds of kilometres to see what locals have long regarded as an ordinary part of life. The Indian Astronomical Observatory is one of the world's highest sites for astronomical observation Hanle's remote, high-altitude location, dry air and lack of light pollution make its skies prized by astronomers. The cold desert offers suitable observing conditions on around 260 nights a year. Hanle is also home to the Indian Astronomical Observatory, run by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, and is a major centre for astronomical research. In 2022, it became India's first Dark Sky Reserve, helping protect its pristine skies from artificial light and putting Hanle on the astronomy tourism map. Visitor numbers have since surged: from about 3,000 a year five years ago to nearly 30,000 in 2024-25, according to government figures. As visitors grew, so did opportunities for locals. In 2022, the Ladakh administration and Indian Institute of Astrophysics trained 24 young people from Hanle and nearby villages in astronomy. These four women were among them. Over 15 days, they learnt to identify stars, planets and constellations, navigate the night sky, operate telescopes and photograph the Milky Way on their phones. Becoming astronomy guides was never part of their plans. They were nervous when they first handled the equipment, fearing they might break something. Gradually, they learnt how it worked and grew confident using it. Hanle was designated as India's first dark sky reserve in 2022 Four years on, they are confident astronomers, with evenings beginning around 9pm. They position telescopes for the night's planets and constellations before guiding visitors from local homestays. They show them the Moon's craters, Saturn's rings, Vega - the brightest star in the night sky - and other planets, using laser pointers to trace constellations and objects visible to the naked eye. Then comes the Milky Way. At 11pm each night, the village switches off its lights, plunging Hanle into darkness as visitors scramble to photograph the now-brilliant galaxy. "When people look through the telescope and capture a photo alongside the Milky Way, they experience immense joy. We also help them with their mobile phone settings so they can capture the Milky Way," Padma Chamchot says. It often starts with helping one visitor take a picture and ends with a long queue. The women take pictures for their own social media too, comparing notes on the stars and other sights they captured that night. The women also point laser at the sky to help visitors spot stars visible to the naked eye But by day, life is more ordinary. Hanle has few hotels and no resorts, so visitors mostly stay in family-run homestays, often extensions of their homes. Chamchot's family runs one too. "Taking care of guests, cooking meals, cleaning rooms, and managing household chores fills our day," she says. "From nine in the evening, we begin setting up the telescopes for the night's stargazing sessions." Their families' homestays remain the main income source, but the women earn about 25,000 rupees ($260; £193) a month from astronomy, charging 200 rupees a session. Income dips during the harsh winter, when few tourists visit, but the earnings have given them greater financial independence: they no longer need to ask their parents for money. "We can save our earnings and spend them on things we want - including new phones," Padma says. For the astro-ambassadors, the transformation has been personal as much as financial. "Before taking on this work, we lacked confidence," they say. However, the growing popularity of Hanle comes with risks. The same tourism that supports local livelihoods could also threaten the darkness that makes Hanle unique. Rapid construction and rising tourism also poses a threat to Hanle's dark skies Visitor numbers have surged, fuelled partly by social media posts about Hanle's night skies and its location on the route to Umling La, which is among the world's highest motorable mountain passes. But more tourists also mean more traffic, construction and artificial light - all threats to the darkness they come to see. Sonam Jorphail, a senior engineer and head of outreach at the IAO, says tourism is creating jobs and driving development in Hanle, but growth must be managed to protect its dark skies. "They bridge the gap between the science community and common people - locals and visitors," Jorphail adds. But longtime residents say Hanle's night sky is already changing. title: Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses?
description: The reality TV game show returns on Thursday, with 21 stars vying to win £100,000 for their chosen charity.
body: The winning celeb will score £100,000 for their chosen charity Celebrity Traitors returns next week for a second round of deception and amateur detective work. Hosted by Claudia Winkleman, the Traitors castle will welcome 21 new celebrities on Thursday, as a group of famous "faithfuls" attempts to work out which among them are - and perhaps, always have been - "traitors", secretly murdering contestants each night. Last year's show provided Bafta's most memorable TV moment - an award voted for by the British public - when traitor Alan Carr broke down in tears at the end of the final having bluffed his way to a win by hiding in plain sight. Let's have a stab in the dark, then, at who might follow in Jonathan Ross's footsteps as this year's "big dog", and who, like singer Cat Burns, could fly under the radar? If Carr was the star of last year's show, then perhaps his fellow TV funnymen could be the ones to watch this time around. Naturally good readers of a room and skilled at misdirection, comedians can inject some comic relief into those tense roundtable moments. It worked for Carr, who was considered to be less of a threat and more out of his depth by the other sleuths. This time around, stand-up star Joe Lycett, 38, is one of the leading candidates for the role of class clown. Known for his quick wit and political stunts, Lycett told the BBC he asked Carr for advice on "how to spot a rotten little traitor like you". Last year's winner replied: "Just anyone that's sweating and giggling." With his brightly coloured outfits, Lycett will bring some glamour to the castle, if and when he's not donning the famous dark cloak. "There's a lot of variety and silly stuff that I might not get to wear at all if I end up doing a Paloma," he noted, with reference to Paloma Faith, who was brutally killed off early doors last year by her supposed friend, Carr. If laughing all the way to the winning line is to work again, then it's hard to look beyond James Acaster. Anyone who has seen his Netflix special Repertoire or heard his podcast Off Menu will know his deadpan, absurdist humour and whimsical flights of fancy could make it difficult to tell whether he is telling the truth or not. A "huge fan" of the show since the first non-celebrity edition in 2022, Acaster, 41, said he would prefer to be a faithful as he wasn't good at lying - though Carr did previously say something similar... Romesh Ranganathan's dry humour and wry presenting style saw him succeed Anne Robinson as the host of The Weakest Link revival in 2021. Could it help him to become a more believable traitor or faithful? The former maths teacher and now comedy podcaster, 48, blamed his youngest son, who was "desperate for me to come on", for his reluctant participation this year. One of his best friends on the comedy circuit, Parenting Hell podcaster Rob Beckett, is another of this year's funniest contestants. A decade's worth of friendship with the 8 Out of 10 Cats and Mock the Week panellist could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said. He believes Beckett, 40, is "just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity". One of the nation's other most celebrated comics, Miranda Hart will no doubt be a big personality among the group. In her self-titled sitcom, she starred as an awkward, accident-prone shopkeeper. Her apparent clumsiness and warm, self-deprecating persona might make her seem more trustworthy (rightly or wrongly). After a spell of ill-health, Hart, 53, hopes "the joy of mucking about on television again will hopefully outweigh some of the challenges". Irish comedian Joanne McNally, 43, could also be the joker of the pack this year. Her popular podcast My Therapist Ghosted Me is full of gossip, oversharing and comic bickering - music to the ears of the Traitors producers, no doubt. Her stand-up is confessional and brutally honest. But honesty gets you nowhere in this game - or does it? The "Big Dog Theory" was a piece of gameplay logic proposed by ex-rugby union star Joe Marler during roundtable discussions last year. His reasoning was that one of the most famous contestants, AKA the big dogs, would have been chosen as a traitor to cause mass confusion (and, presumably, strong viewing figures). Marler wondered out loud whether the big dog traitor in question was Sir Stephen Fry (no) or Jonathan Ross (yes). For the new series, a glut of huge names and personalities from across the worlds of film, TV, music, modelling and broadcasting have also been selected. Michael Sheen, the award-winning Welsh actor and campaigner, is perhaps the biggest dog in the fight, so will come under real scrutiny. Sheen, 57, is acclaimed for his ability to convincingly portray a range of different personalities on screen, from Tony Blair to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor via Brian Clough. But in real life, he's seen more as a loveable golden retriever than a Rottweiler, despite his success. Which version of him we shall see on the show remains to be seen. Fellow big screen charmer Richard E. Grant, 69, who starred in films such as Withnail and I, may also leave some of the less well-known celebrities star-struck at first, as might American-British supermodel/actress Jerry Hall. Hall, 70, shares four children with ex-partner Mick Jagger and has also been married to media mogul Rupert Murdoch. Love Island presenter Maya Jama, 32, and University Challenge host, journalist and YouTuber Amol Rajan are also powerhouses in the world of broadcasting. Speaking ahead of the show, 43-year-old Rajan, who is in it to win it, said : "I don't want to go in there and at round table number one be Mr Forensic Investigator! "However, I do interview politicians for a living, and I really have to pursue answers to questions." He's conscious of putting "a target" on his back too soon, so plans to form alliances. "To begin

title: Faisal Islam: The two big calls the chancellor has to make ahead of the Budget
description: He must consider the longevity of Iran war economic pressures and how to sustain modest optimism, writes the BBC's Faisal Islam.
body: "It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering? "Conflicts, uncertainty, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates. But we've got great strengths. We've got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain," he insisted. The new scheme to try and help young people get on the property ladder, announced on Saturday, was aimed at boosting confidence in the economy. But the chancellor is now facing two big decisions before his inaugural Budget on 28 October. Firstly, about the longevity of the economic pressures caused by the Iran War, and then about how to sustain a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits, through yet more global turbulence. In his first weeks as chancellor the oil price fell as low as $75 a barrel while the yield - the effective interest rate - on 10-year government bonds was 4.9%. Just over two months later oil has largely traded above $100 and the 10-year yield is at around 5.4%. It is the ultimate double whammy for a chancellor facing his first Budget. Yet there is something unusual about this energy shock. It could quickly reverse, as illustrated earlier in the summer when assumptions about a deescalation in the US Iran conflict led to sharp falls in energy prices and yields. In New York this week both President Trump and his Iranian counterpart President Pezeshkian suggested November's US midterm elections were connected to when the war might end. The Iranians would wait until after the elections to seek peace because the war's impact on the cost of living - particularly soaring diesel costs - could damage him electorally, the US president told the UN General Assembly. The Iranian president said his nation "didn't want it to get to the midterms". Both sides in this war are feeling the economic squeeze of conflict. The 3 November vote is six days after the Budget. No one could rely on there being a settlement by then, but it is plausible. So the Budget tax, spend and borrowing forecasts could be based on a prolonged conflict, which is actually on the cusp of ending, or even already ended. The chancellor has to therefore decide whether to plan for the worst, and make some painful permanent tax and spend decisions, or buy some time. One option is to let borrowing take some of the strain, by tolerating a reduction in the £24bn of headroom - room for manoeuvre against its self-imposed borrowing rules - left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves. This year's headroom will be judged in three years rather than four, so there is some rationale as to why a smaller number over a closer target might be appropriate. And while higher inflation means higher interest costs, it also means higher cash tax receipts, at a time when thresholds continue to be frozen. There is a second consideration. The hopeful optimism "vibes" strategy of the Burnham administration appears to have had some impact. The longest running UK consumer confidence survey has hit a two-year high. Among younger people it has not been this high since before Brexit. Some data companies call it a "Burnham bounce", although the weather and World Cup were also factors. There is evidence, more mixed, that business optimism has also perked up in recent months, possibly because of earlier falls in energy prices, though this has been clouded by anticipation of possible tax rises. Business group, the Institute of Directors said this was despite, rather than because of, the new government. While no one should get too carried away with these turnarounds, they do stand in contrast to the admitted mistake of the Starmer government in talking up consumer pain, two years ago. The question for the chancellor is whether better consumer and business spirits can be reconciled with the need for a "challenging" Budget? Indeed, it's important to determine how much of the summer global bond market shock is solely down to the impact of the Iran war and how much is more structural. Governments are facing new and intense competition in bond markets from the world's biggest AI businesses. In addition, the UK has had recent, prominent political and economic uncertainty. Right now the bond markets are like a pack of wolves stalking red deer, probing for weaknesses. "At times like this you don't want to be at the back of the herd," said one very senior former Treasury adviser. UK and US warned to take action on spiralling debt costs by IMF Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor Government borrowing, bonds and yields explained In response, the Treasury has pointed to the UK having the highest growth and the fastest falling borrowing of the major G7 countries so far this year and our overall energy prices starting to decouple from high and volatile gas prices. However, the IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva this week dismissed the idea that advanced nations could pause their fiscal homework, while the Gulf situation calmed. "Bring debt levels down, make fiscal consolidation as a priority… it is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary," Georgieva told me, acknowledging the UK's "fairly consistent, credible" plans. Then there is the curious conundrum of British productivity. Last year, the government's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded the UK's productivity peformance, leading to a notable hit to the public finances. Now the UK's productivity record has been upgraded materially by the Office for National Statistics, although this is because of fewer hours worked. There could therefore be an argument to reverse some of that downgrade. Separately, the new chair of the OBR Jonathan Haskel is known for his argument that official statistics understate investment in intangibles like software and data. title: Tuchel rues 'big mistakes' - did Man City charges have impact?
description: England's loss to Spain was decided by uncharacteristic mistakes, with two Man City players making errors - so did club news affect performances for country?
body: Rodri and Nico O'Reilly were Manchester City team-mates last season It was a match full of world-class players - but England's loss to Spain was ultimately decided by uncharacteristic mistakes. Just a day after Manchester City were found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules, two errors by City players - Nico O'Reilly and Marc Guehi - gifted world champions Spain two goals. And former City midfielder Rodri, who moved to Barcelona in the summer, also gave away a penalty in Spain's 3-2 win on Saturday. Pundit Roy Keane was among those left to wonder whether news of the verdict had affected players with City ties. Asked if it was a distraction after his side's loss at Wembley, England boss Thomas Tuchel said: "Not for me but I can imagine for the Manchester City players. "For the players who have more time than me, for sure I can imagine they talk about it." Speaking to ITV Sport former Manchester United captain Keane said: "In top level football you want to be focused and they certainly would have been affected. "To see so many top-class players make so many mistakes - it has certainly affected them." Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered Man City chairman confident club will prove innocence Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict Manchester City vs The Premier League This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City Three City players - Elliot Anderson, Guehi and O'Reilly - started for England, while Rodri, who spent seven years at the club, was in Spain's XI. And three of those four players made significant errors at Wembley. First Guehi was tackled by Lamine Yamal on the edge of his own box, allowing the Spain winger to drive towards goal and slot in his side's opener. In the second half Rodri's late challenge on Jude Bellingham led to an England penalty, which Harry Kane struck against the crossbar after slipping. And then O'Reilly had a pass intercepted deep in his own half which led to Alex Baena's equaliser at 2-2. On Friday, sources told BBC Sport City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching. After a four-year investigation, the club were accused of a wide range of rule breaches centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial rules between 2009 and 2018. Sanctions are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine. BBC Sport understands Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about potential compensation. England captain Kane played down any links between the charges and player mistakes, telling ITV Sport after Saturday's game: "There was a discussion, but at the end of the day when we're with England we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week." This video can not be played What do Man City charges mean and what happens next? A few hours before kick-off at Wembley, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak told supporters he was still confident of proving the club's innocence and the "Premier League process still has a long way to run". Spain captain Rodri had also stressed his belief in the club's innocence in a news conference on Friday. "They always express the confidence that they never did something wrong and we believe in that," he said. "Until the moment they are proved wrong, we will believe the club. They always tell us the confidence they have on the innocence." The charges cover the managerial tenures of Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini, and the first two years under Pep Guardiola, who left the club after 10 seasons at the end of the 2025-26 campaign. City won the Premier League and EFL Cup three times and FA Cup once between 2009 and 2018. Guehi, Rodri and O'Reilly all made their City debuts after the period in question. title: England embrace the chaos - but control also needed to win big prizes
description: England embrace the chaos, but superb Spain show it will never win big prizes, says chief football writer Phil McNulty.
body: England captain Harry Kane missed a second-half penalty in the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley Thomas Tuchel talked about England having to "embrace the chaos" as they embarked on recovery from the crushing disappointment of World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina. As England took those first steps on the road to rehabilitation against reigning world and European champions Spain in the Nations League at Wembley, head coach Tuchel learned the brutal lesson that chaos without control is a loser's strategy at elite level. Spain do control, not chaos. And this is why they are serial winners and England remain a nearly team without a major men's success since the 1966 World Cup. England delivered moments to admire in the 3-2 defeat, even embracing those chaotic spells in an enthralling encounter, but ultimately they came up short once more against this summer's World Cup winners, who are now unbeaten in 39 games. Once Tuchel's England stopped playing themselves into trouble by mimicking Spain's passing style without having anywhere near the quality of their opponents and followed their own "DNA", to use the buzz-phrase of the moment, they actually threatened with power and pace. Quite how England reached the 36th minute only one goal down was a mystery to everyone inside Wembley, Marc Guehi's inexplicable turn into trouble gifting Lamine Yamal an opener inside two minutes. Ferran Torres saw a goal ruled out for offside, was denied by a fine stop by England goalkeeper James Trafford, then rolled an effort wide of the post when clean through. Tuchel was managing England in their first game since the World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina England took advantage of those reprieves to somehow be ahead by the break, through star performer Anthony Gordon's composed finish and Harry Kane's deflected header. Kane's penalty miss just after the break was a turning point, hitting the bar after slipping and touching the ball twice, before England once again paid the price for errors. Nico O'Reilly coughed up possession in the build-up to Alex Baena's equaliser before another substitute in Mikel Oyarzabal, who scored the winner in the Euro 2024 final against England in Berlin, settled matters after 74 minutes. If it was a bad night for Manchester City defensive duo Guehi and O'Reilly, it was not much better for Jarell Quansah, who was given the nod ahead of the recalled Trent Alexander-Arnold. He was uncertain throughout and does not look a natural right-back - perhaps because he is not a natural right-back. Of course, it could have been different had Kane scored his penalty. He did not and it was not. Kane said: "On another day we could have won." This was not another day and England did not win. England's bolder approach after a shaky opening 25 minutes offered up the prospect of a landmark victory, but shambolic defending saw Guehi and O'Reilly present gifts Spain were happy to accept. As against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final in Atlanta, England led by a Gordon goal and lost, but at least here they went down swinging and not by going into cowering retreat. It was a small mercy appreciated by the home support, but the gulf in class when it mattered was still evident as Spain's smooth, unhurried style cut a sharp contrast to England's often frantic efforts. Tuchel's defence looked horribly vulnerable and easy to slice through, although keeper Trafford – given two games before first-choice Jordan Pickford returns – was blameless and will have created a good impression as he tries to create greater competition in that department. They have now shipped 13 goals in their last six matches in all competitions, after conceding only seven in their first 17 games under Tuchel. Ironically, it was two players now plying their trade in Spain, Gordon at Barcelona and Jude Bellingham at Real Madrid, who were England's standout performers. Gordon was in electrifying form, while Bellingham was relentless in driving England forward, even in a losing cause. As for the chaos, Tuchel begged to differ. He told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm not sure there was a lot of chaos. We had an incredible amount of high-ball recoveries in the opponent's half. I think 15 more than Spain. Overall, I think 15 in total in the first half. That only goes against a team like Spain if we play man to man, so we were very brave." Gordon was England's outstanding performer and brought them back into match at Wembley with a fine goal Tuchel added: "The defending and the deep block were excellent, except for the third goal where we got cut open through the middle. This normally should not happen. "Offensively, I think we played in a clear structure. We tried to switch sides a lot. We tried to put the full-backs up to make the difference and they did. A lot of good stuff but unfortunately not the result." On the gap between the sides, Tuchel said: "We saw no gap except for the technical execution. In the last 20 metres, they were superior than us." Tuchel's comments are questionable here, ignoring the fact that if Spain's own technical execution was better they could easily have been four goals up before England scored, but he was correct to point out the improvement after Gordon drew them level. England captain Kane said: "I spoke before that we reached good levels at the World Cup but didn't quite put a full 90 minutes together. It was probably similar again here. We had a couple of good moments though, that period was as good as we've played in a long, long time and that's the standard we know we can reach. "We're playing against the world champions, the European champions, and we went toe-to-toe. On another day for sure we'd have won that game." England certainly embrace the chaos, as Tuchel suggested, but chaos alone does not claim big prizes and never has. At least this is a lesson Tuchel did not have to w

title: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
description: China's economy and tech have developed at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z.
body: Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing country "A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol". Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation. And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it. China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up. "The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home. "People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me." She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting". Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media. About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently In Sinapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better. These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times". "Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore. "But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it." He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia. Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it. China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development". Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air. "The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected. This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful." Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us." Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things." Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation. Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money." And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says. Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them. They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job. title: Are claims of a white genocide in South Africa real?
description: Thousands of white crosses have been displayed in Washington by an Afrikaner lobby group But South Africa's new ambassador Roelf Meyer says there is not a genocide.
body: This video can not be played An Afrikaner lobby group has displayed thousands of white crosses on the National Mall in Washington DC, saying they represent the victims of a genocide of white people in South Africa. But South Africa's new ambassador to the US, Roelf Meyer, says that the notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday. The BBC's North America correspondent Ione Wells explains what role the US has played in the claim of a genocide. Are claims of a white genocide in South Africa real? title: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
description: Christy Spivey tells the BBC she only has more questions now police think Tasia Fortune's body was put in the tree after her death.
body: Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree in August Warning: This story contains distressing details The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene. Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August. The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree. "I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC. The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged". Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging. Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black. "I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way. "Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?" Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes. But the latest developments have created more confusion. Christy Spivey told the BBC she was upset at how the police had handled the investigation Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought. "When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people." When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down". Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs. Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction. "Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said. "If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does." She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes. Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted. title: The ecstasy of buying our first home was short-lived after we found 150 faults
description: Getting the keys to a new home felt like a dream come true, until this couple found 150 faults.
body: Charles and Georgina bought a new build home in February 2026 It was the day Georgina and Charles Barnes had waited three years for - collecting the keys to their first home. But when the brand new property was inspected just days later by a Welsh snagging company - the final quality check by independent inspectors - they identified 150 defects, including incorrectly installed fire barriers, signs of a previous leak and what they called "exceptionally poor" workmanship. Swansea-based New Home Quality Control was set up by John Cooper after he became fed up of being asked to hide things from customers on building sites. It is the responsibility of developers to make sure new-builds meet regulations, according to the National House Building Council, external (NHBC). The couple are far from alone when it comes to issues with new houses. Written evidence submitted by the New Homes Ombudsman Service said the Home Builders Federation national new homes customer satisfaction survey, published in March 2025, showed 93.7% of new-build buyers reporting defects or snags to their developer after moving in, external. Just over a quarter of buyers also found more than 15 problems in their new-build home. Charles and Georgina were excited to move into their new home "We just wouldn't have known," said Georgina. "If there had been a fire, that's one thing that could have happened and been very detrimental." Georgina, 36, and her husband saved for three years to buy a house, before falling in love with the development in south Leicestershire. As moving day approached, social media began serving her a steady stream of new-build horror stories After paying £299,995 for the house, she said getting it snagged was "non-negotiable". "It just felt unbelievable that we'd finally done it," she added. "We actually finally got our own place. This is ours. This is ours to do what we want with. It just felt great." But the report also identified improperly roofing defects, low water pressure and what inspectors described as "exceptionally poor" installation of the gas meter cabinet and gas pipe. More than a dozen of additional cosmetic and finishing defects were also recorded throughout the property As they had a two-year warranty from the developer, it meant they fixed the issues. This video can not be played "I quit my job to find badly built new homes" "I would say for any new-build buyer, 100% no doubt, I recommend a snagger," Georgina said. Vistry, responsible for the housing developer Countryside, which built Charles and Georgina's house, said it supported "appropriately conducted independent inspections as an additional source of reassurance about build quality". It said each home is checked by its teams and independent inspections take place and, two to three weeks after customers move in, the build team meets to discuss and agree any snagging work. Such issues are not new to John Cooper, 50, co-founder of New Home Quality Control. He said, while working as a contracts manager in 2018: "The site manager asked me to hide something from a customer that was moving in the next day." This was the tip of the iceberg after he had seen poor quality workmanship over about six years. "From that moment on, I thought to myself 'I've got to make a change in this industry somehow. This can't continue'," he said. Cooper spoke to his supervisor at the time, Lee Challenger, 42, and the two men quit their jobs and started New Homes Quality Control. "We've never inspected a house and found absolutely nothing wrong with it," he said. John Cooper was asked to hide issues in new build homes so he created a company to fight back The most common defects involve brickwork, carpentry and roofing, he said. "It's always going to be carpentry issues and bricklaying issues. "I just think that there's not enough quality bricklayers to build the amount of properties that the developers are building across the UK on a yearly basis." The team also regularly identifies missing or incorrectly installed weep vents - which are installed in exterior walls to let moisture escape. Cooper said some developments had even featured "fake" weep vents, where decorative plastic pieces had been fitted instead of functioning openings. "They thought they could get away with it," he said. Cooper said before new owners get the keys, the NHBC inspects the property and sign it off. "I'm sick of hearing every property being signed off, because if that was the case, then we wouldn't have a company," he said. Many of Cooper's clients get emotional when they see how many issues there are with their new houses. "We've had people cry," he said. "There were some quite serious issues in their new property and they had spent all their life savings on it." Cooper said his long-term goal was for every new-build home to undergo an independent inspection before its owners moved in. "If someone's spending their life savings on a house, they deserve to get what they paid for," he said. The inspections take between two and four hours, depending on the size of the house, and cost about £349-£499. Among the arsenal of tools the snaggers use are drones, GoPro cameras, cavity cameras, thermal imaging equipment and laser levels. But not everyone can afford their services as they spend all their money on the house. "Money is tight for a lot of people." Georgina and Charles' home had 150 issues when they moved in NHBC said it is the responsibility of the builders to ensure they meet building regulations and homeowners must raise any issues with the house builder within two years - if they are not fixed can seek resolution via NHBC. The organisation said it carries out inspections at "key stages of the build" and "provide feedback" on the quality. title: Who made an uncharacteristic error? England player ratings v Spain
description: England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - here's how BBC Sport rated the Three Lions' players.
body: Alex Baena curled in Spain's second goal England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - the Three Lions' first match since this summer's World Cup. Lamine Yamal gave Spain the lead before goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put England ahead. Kane then missed a penalty before Alex Baena curled in to level the score, with Mikel Oyarzabal scoring the winner. Here's how we rated England's players - and you can have your say in the comments at the bottom. James Trafford: Showed early on his ability to play with the ball at his feet but conceded after just two minutes when Guehi gifted the ball to Lamine Yamal. An important save stopped Torres making it 2-0 in the first half. 6 Jarell Quansah: Continued at right-back after showing what he could do in the position at the World Cup. A physically dominant performance and had a chance to score but headed over. 6 Ezri Konsa: Some shaky moments for Konsa and England's back four but the centre-back regrouped and got better as the game went on. 6 Marc Guehi: An uncharacteristic error gifted the ball - and the opening goal - to Lamine Yamal. 5 Nico O'Reilly: Put in the cross for Kane's goal as England took the lead in the first half. Did a good job of trying to deal with Lamine Yamal. However he gave the ball away for Spain's second goal. 6 Elliot Anderson: Nearly punished for giving the ball away in a dangerous position in the first half but Ferran Torres rolled his shot wide. Anderson and midfield partner Lewis-Skelly took some time to settle in what was a tough night in the middle of the pitch against a Spain side who moved the ball so well. 6 Myles Lewis-Skelly: A first England start in centre midfield for Lewis-Skelly after shining for Arsenal. Given the tough task of trying to shut off the supply to Spain's conductor, Rodri. A solid performance. Replaced after 70 minutes. 6 Jude Bellingham: The Real Madrid midfielder produced another dominant display and was unlucky to be on the losing side. He provided an assist for England's equaliser and won a penalty which Kane hit against the bar after slipping. Stung Simon's palms with a drive in stoppage time. 8 Bukayo Saka: Won a couple of free-kicks around the box and shot over from the edge of the area in the first half. Curled just wide with the score level but a quiet night for the winger. 6 Anthony Gordon: The Barcelona winger scored an excellent goal on the counter-attack. He kept calm when played through on goal by Bellingham when his pace put him clear. A dangerous cross in the first half after England went behind and a threat in behind all night. 8 Harry Kane: Started dropping deep in the first half in search of the ball after England went behind. Scored the second with a deflected header to put England in the lead but missed a penalty when they had the chance to add a third in the second half. 7 James Garner (on 70, Lewis-Skelly): Took on Lewis-Skelly's role of trying to keep Rodri quiet. 6 Morgan Rogers (on 70, Gordon): Did not get much of the ball in his 20 minutes on the pitch. 6 Morgan Gibbs-White (on 83, Saka): Came on and played on the left wing. 6 Calvert-Lewin (on 83, Kane): Not much time to impact the play. 6 Jarrad Branthwaite, (on 89, Guehi): A late change for Guehi in the England backline. No time to make an impression. 6 Subs not used: Pickford, Steele, Alexander-Arnold, Scott, Chalobah, Hall, Eze. title: Vollering wins women's road race world title
description: Demi Vollering continues her remarkable season with a thrilling victory in the women's road race in Montreal.
body: Demi Vollering won her second Tour de France Femmes title this year, adding to her 2023 triumph Demi Vollering continued her remarkable season with a thrilling victory to win the women's road race world title in Montreal. The Dutchwoman held off a late challenge from Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney to add another title to her collection, following wins at the Tour de France Femmes, Giro d'Italia Women and World Championships. The 29-year-old also won a string of one-day classics in the spring, including the Tour of Flanders and Liege-Bastogne-Liege. "I can still not believe it. I worked so hard towards this goal, and it takes guts to truly believe in it with your whole heart," she said. Italian Elisa Longo Borghini edged out world time-trial champion Marlen Reusser to take bronze. Great Britain's Flora Perkins was among 15 riders to crash while speeding downhill early in the race. Defending champion Magdeleine Vallieres, Mauritius' Kimberley Le Court and Spain's Paula Blasi were also involved and eventually had to withdraw. Vollering launched her initial attack with about 40km to go only to be reeled in by the chasing pack over the final two laps. Poland's Niewiadoma-Phinney stayed on her wheel in the closing stages but was beaten to the line, with Vollering claiming victory in four hours 45 minutes nine seconds. "There were so many moments I thought I went too early," Vollering said. "I didn't dare to turn around and look back because I felt like they were almost on my wheel already. "I just dared, tried again and never gave up to the finish line." title: 'Pipe dream' to reality? Wakefield reach Grand Final
description: Wakefield Trinity were playing in rugby league's second tier in 2024. Two years on, they are one win away from becoming Super League champions.
body: This video can not be played Wakefield stun Wigan to reach first Grand Final "It's something I've dreamed about for years and it used to be a bit of a pipe dream," said Tom Johnstone, when asked about the prospect of Wakefield Trinity winning a Super League Grand Final. That dream could become a reality for the England winger on 3 October, after Wakefield shocked treble-chasing Wigan Warriors 33-6 in Saturday's play-off semi-final to secure their place in the Old Trafford showpiece for the first time. Wakefield, who will play Warrington Wolves in the title decider, have been a club transformed in recent seasons. So often competing at the wrong end of the Super League table, they lost their top-flight status in 2023 - but that proved to be the beginning of the club's reinvigoration, sparked by the completion of a takeover by kitchen magnate Matt Ellis. His financial support, along with the leadership and experience of head coach Daryl Powell, have led Wakefield up from the Championship and now to within 80 minutes of becoming Super League champions. Johnstone, 31, began his career with Wakefield and was back for Trinity's return to the top division at the start of 2025 after a two-year spell with Catalans Dragons. "I went to Matt's kitchen factory with my agent and we had a chat about everything they want to achieve and everything they promised to do," Johnstone, who scored two of Wakefield's five tries against Wigan, told BBC Two. "We left and said: 'If they do any of that, it's going to be something special.' I couldn't say no." Wakefield have risen from the Championship to the top end of Super League under the ownership of Matt Ellis Powell, who was appointed shortly after Wakefield had dropped into the second tier, added: "The journey's been an interesting one. "We got relegated but it was probably good for us. It allowed us to stabilise the team, get our staff in and sign some players that got us out of the Championship. "We started to sign high-quality players like Mike [McMeeken] and Tom, and some of the guys we signed the year before have really grown and prospered." Wakefield shock Wigan to reach first Grand Final Warrington edge past Leeds to reach Grand Final Prior to the semi-final, many viewed Wakefield - who finished fourth in Super League - as second favourites against a Wigan team that had won 16 successive matches and were seeking a second domestic treble in the space of three seasons. But Trinity responded brilliantly to falling behind early on and took full advantage of Adam Keighran's second-half yellow card, seizing control of the contest and winning it with 33 unanswered points. Ex-England half-back Kevin Brown, working as a BBC pundit, described Wakefield's display against Wigan as "definitely their best ever performance in Super League", adding: "It's been an incredible story where we're at right now and we're going to run out of superlatives if they go and win it." Captain McMeeken has played in three previous Grand Finals with Castleford and Catalans, while he was also part of the England side that played in a World Cup semi-final on home soil in 2022 - but the significance of Saturday's achievement was not lost on him, either. "To take in an experience like this is up there as one of the best moments of my career so far," he said. Daryl Powell has led a team into a Super League Grand Final before - his Castleford side lost to Leeds at Old Trafford in 2017 At Old Trafford, Powell will come up against the club he coached for a season and a half before his exit midway through the 2023 campaign. He said: "It's not about me or my journey, it's about the players and how they're writing different scripts every time we take the field." Whoever is victorious will be a first-time Super League champion and Powell added: "It'll be awesome for the game. I think it's awesome that we're there in particular, Warrington have been there before. "For us, it's about not getting too ahead of ourselves, playing the game as it is like we did tonight, and if we do that, we've got a great chance." title: Radio 2 presenter to take on 'greatest ever distance' in Children in Need challenge
description: Owain Wyn Evans will cycle almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff.
body: BBC Radio 2 host Owain Wyn Evans will ride through the UK's four nations Radio presenter Owain Wyn Evans will cycle through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need. The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show will travel almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff. The five-day challenge will start on Monday, 9 November, and finish on Friday, 13 November - when the fundraiser will be broadcast. The only member of the annual TV fundraiser's hosting team for 2026 to be revealed so far is fellow Welsh presenter, One Show host Alex Jones. The BBC said Evans' challenge would be the "greatest ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity. Evans, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, said: "When I said yes to this challenge, I knew it would push me well outside my comfort zone. "It's going to be tough, demanding and probably a little daunting at times, but I'm ready to give it absolutely everything I've got." Alex Jones is among the presenting team for the BBC's flagship fundraiser He said fellow BBC presenters Sara Cox, Paddy McGuinness and Vernon Kay had previously achieved "extraordinary things" for Children in Need, adding: "I've got a lot to live up to." Sports scientist Prof Greg Whyte will be offering support to him throughout the journey. He previously helped Sara Cox when she jogged, walked and ran 135 miles through Northumberland, Durham, North Yorkshire and West Yorkshire. BBC Radio 2 boss Helen Thomas said: "Thank you to Owain for picking up the Pudsey backpack baton from Sara on behalf of the many thousands of children who will benefit." title: England embrace growing competitiveness of women's game
description: England edge past New Zealand with a last-gasp try by Zoe Harrison as they embrace the growing competitiveness of women's rugby.
body: This video can not be played England secure win over New Zealand with last-gasp try Winning had been the only currency known to John Mitchell's Red Roses. From his arrival midway through the 2023 WXV1 campaign to winning the Women's Rugby World Cup for the first time in 11 years, England won every single game. However, their record 39-game run of victories was finally halted by Canada, last year's World Cup finalists, in a thrilling 26-26 draw at Sandy Park last week. Welcoming New Zealand, unbeaten under new head coach Whitney Hansen, to Allianz Stadium brought a feeling of jeopardy that had not been felt for a very long time. Despite Mitchell openly stating that the WXV Global Series, with no trophy at the end of it, would provide new opportunities, losing in front of a 59,871 crowd at the home of English rugby would not have been part of the long-term development plan. When Braxton Sorensen-McGee, with less than 10 minutes remaining, landed a tough conversion to bring the Black Ferns level at 19-19, the Red Roses once again found themselves in a sticky situation. Unlike last week, they came up clutch as Zoe Harrison redeemed herself for a late penalty miss by snatching victory with an intercept try in the final play. Given the clock was in overtime, England do have to count themselves lucky that New Zealand attempted to run from deep and gifted them a winning score. However, a win is a win. "We couldn't have a repeat of what happened against Canada last week. A draw wasn't good enough, so we had to get the points somehow," Harrison told BBC Radio 5 Live. "It's massive - it goes back to that World Cup final [in 2022] for me - beating them on home soil was fantastic and it being such a close game is great for women's rugby." Rugby Union Weekly: Harrison's last-gasp try seals dramatic England win This video can not be played Late try seals dramatic win for England over New Zealand New Zealand, the world's second-ranked side, remain the last team to defeat the Red Roses at the World Cup final in 2022. Leading 12-7 at half-time, ending that unbeaten run looked a real possibility. This campaign, England have lacked the same clinical edge that saw them become world champions. Their defence, now supported by coaching legend Shaun Edwards, has also been leaky. But they are without a number of key players, including World Cup-winning captain Zoe Stratford. "To put it into context, the Red Roses don't play New Zealand and Canada often - it's important to learn how to win tight Test matches," Mitchell said. "The message at half-time was that this game will turn - we will get some possession and let's attack it. "The girls took the handbrake off and tried to go to space, even from deep, and were still tenacious without the ball, which was awesome." Running from 2026 to 2028, the new WXV Global Series features the world's top 12 teams and is designed to provide more competitive matches before the 2029 World Cup. England have already faced the world's second and third-ranked sides and now travel to Canada to complete their three-Test series against the World Cup runners-up. "The game is getting better and better and we are just trying to make that gap bigger," Red Roses captain Meg Jones said. "We know there are going to be close games and we will compete as hard as we can." This video can not be played Kildunne gets round the back of NZ defence to put England back in front New Zealand have beaten England in five World Cup finals and were once the undisputed number one team in the world. That dominance has faded in recent years, particularly after their failure to reach last year's World Cup final. Despite a fourth straight defeat by the Red Roses, it is clear under Hansen that the Black Ferns are trending in the right direction. That comes after increased investment in the domestic game, with Super Rugby Aupiki operating as a fully professional, full-time competition for the first time this year. "We didn't want a draw," New Zealand head coach Whitney Hansen said. "After watching last week [against Canada], we knew we were going to fight to the death, so I love that she threw that pass. "I think for us, win or lose, we're about our performance. We've talked heaps about what does great look like - where have we achieved that and where haven't we?" Next year, the British and Irish Lions women's team will tour New Zealand for the first time. A competitive series is essential to the success of the tour. Prior to last year's epic finale at Allianz Stadium, England - likely to make up a large portion of the Lions squad - comfortably beat New Zealand 49-31 in their most recent meeting in 2024. "People are starting to realise the context we are in. Even if we had lost, we were right up there," Mitchell added. "New Zealand are in a really great position for the Lions series and heading in the right direction for the [2027] World Cup. We are also evolving [as a team]." Blowing away every team comfortably or being pushed to the limit to win a Test - which would England prefer? "This is what living feels like," Jones declared. Games in October against Toronto and Ottawa, with the series perfectly poised at 1-1, should give them those feelings again. This was only the third game of the season for Mitchell's players, but being pushed all the way is something that he and his side are loving and embracing. Despite all that, an undefeated run spanning four years has been extended further. title: Tenth woman's body found in South Africa suburb as police probe killings
description: The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country.
body: File photo of South African Police Service officers in Johannesburg Police in South Africa say that they have discovered another body in a Johannesburg suburb, bringing the number of women found dead there in recent months to ten. The body was found on Saturday morning and was identified by the friend with whom she had been at a bar the previous evening. The local police commissioner said his force could not rule out the possibility that there was a serial killer on the loose, noting similarities across the 10 deaths in Ekurhuleni, as well as another in Soweto. The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world. The latest body was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg. Police issued a statement a short while later saying crime scene investigators were at the scene gathering evidence. Officials have yet to publicly identify the victim. The woman's friend told national broadcaster SABC that she recognised her friend's clothes from the previous night when shown a picture of the body. "I don't know what I'm going to say to her children," she said while wiping away tears. "It's painful." Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said that, at this early stage in the investigation, it was too soon to say whether the woman's death was linked to the others. He told reporters that the other bodies shared a "similar victimology" that indicated a shared "modus operandi" of killing, which would allow police to determine whether this latest death was linked to the others. "For now, it's not something which we can overrule to say there's a serial killer, but we cannot conclusively indicate as such," Lt Gen Mthombeni said. South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. But it is the nature of the recent killings around Johannesburg that has left many women there reeling from the growing death toll. The 10 other bodies have been found in similar circumstances to one another since July. Most of them were found in Kempton Park, one neighbourhood over from Tembisa. Many of the bodies were those of young women and almost all had suffered extreme violence prior to their deaths. The deaths have increased pressure on the national government less than a year after ministers declared gender-based violence a national disaster. While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year. Three men appeared in court earlier this week accused of being involved in one of the nine murders, with police working to track down others who may have been involved. title: Watch: Thousands turn out to see Pope during Lourdes and Paris visit
description: The BBC's religion editor Aleem Maqbool explains what Pope Leo's visit means for France.
body: This video can not be played Pope Leo XIV gave a mass in central Paris on Saturday, as the city turned into a "huge open air cathedral," BBC religion editor Aleem Maqbool reports. An estimated 700,000 people gathered for the Mass celebrated by the Pope from a special altar on the Place de la Concorde, on the second day of his four-day visit to France. The Pope then travelled to Lourdes, where he prayed in the grotto where the Virgin Mary was believed to have appeared in the 19th century. He will give Mass there on Sunday. President Emmanuel Macron met Pope Leo on Friday, but did not attend Saturday's events, largely to avoid appearing to breach France's strict rules on the separation of Church and state. title: Nor'easter storm brings coastal flooding, as New York and New Jersey declare emergency
description: Tens of millions of people from Maine to Virginia are in the path of the powerful storm.
body: Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm this weekend, which has already brought coastal flooding, power outages, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events. Peaking on Saturday, the so-called nor'easter will "bring dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds, and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, the latter of which is already facing a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine. Ed Sheeran's much-awaited Boston concert was among events called off. Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood The nor'easter is already causing widespread power outages. Nearly 150,000 households have so far lost electricity, according to poweroutageus. The Federal Aviation Administration recommended flyers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 1,100 flights have been delayed and another 400 grounded, according to FlightAware. Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal inundations. Streets and homes were flooded on Saturday in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan. "I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert, and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said. Flights have been cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power outages. "Don't travel if you don't have to," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater." In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs from Sunday afternoon game to next Friday. Waves pound the coast in Massachusetts A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. Nor is the Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, going ahead. Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston-area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.
