title: 'Mr Saturday' Russell 'comes through other side after real tough period'
description: George Russell described the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as "the most dominant weekend I've had in my career" after a win that felt like vindication.
body: George Russell's victory in Azerbaijan was his third of the 2026 season For George Russell, this one felt like vindication, proof that he had "come through the other side" and was back to his best after what he acknowledged was a "real tough period" during this Formula 1 season. The Mercedes driver's victory in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, holding off Red Bull's Max Verstappen in one of the closest finishes in history, was his first since the end of June - seven races ago. In that time, team-mate Kimi Antonelli has won three times, to take his tally of victories to eight for the season. So Russell needed this, his third victory, in a year that he started as championship favourite. Instead, Antonelli has taken the season by the throat and all but crushed the life out of Russell's hopes. Now, though, a glimmer of hope still exists for Russell, even if he is too realistic to think too much about it for now. His win, combined with Antonelli's fifth place after what the Italian admitted was his "worst weekend of the year in terms of performance", has cut the points gap between them to 66. That's still huge, with either seven or eight races still to go, and 25 points for a win. But it's a lot better than the 81-point margin Russell faced before Baku. "My team-mate's had an incredible season," Russell said. "He's been pretty flawless throughout, but now we're getting to crunch time. "But I'm just going to focus on myself. You know, if I continue delivering performances like I've done this weekend, no matter what happens towards the end of the season, I'll be happy." With the grand prix brought forward 24 hours from the usual Sunday slot, it was an appropriate result for a man whose prowess in qualifying has earned him the nickname 'Mr Saturday'. Russell wins despite late Verstappen challenge Russell faultless and Hadjar excellent on return - driver ratings Russell has been through the mill in 2026. He dominated the intra-team battle last year, but the tables have turned dramatically this season, as Antonelli felt immediately at home in the new Mercedes after the biggest rule changes in F1 history, and the Briton very much did not. For Russell, the blows have kept coming. Every apparent revival was met with another setback. Every time he felt he had made progress, Antonelli's apparently effortless way of extracting that little bit more from the car chastened him. No experience was more painful than the Italian Grand Prix at Monza two races ago, when Russell started from the front row, and Antonelli 19th after a grid penalty. Russell knew it was a golden opportunity to make up ground. Instead, it was Antonelli who won the race, with what will go down as one of the greatest drives in history. Russell looked on the verge of tears after that one. But he kept the belief, and in Baku it all came together. Kimi Antonelli finished off the podium for the first time since the British Grand Prix Russell was a man on a mission all weekend, fastest from the moment he took to the track, while Antonelli, after losing half the two hours of practice on the first day, lost his cool. He made a mistake in qualifying, took a wheel off on an inside wall, and started 16th. There was to be no repeat of Monza, even if fifth was a very creditable comeback result. "I felt always a step behind," Antonelli said, "and especially with the mistake in qualifying the confidence level was not high and today was about damage limitation. "Just probably also the mindset was not in the best place. I wasn't there. I wasn't really present, especially with what happened so early on and just didn't take the same risks, especially after qualifying. "Today was more damage-safe mode instead of full attack. I just make sure next weekend we get back in the right level." If he does, this will go down as a blip in an otherwise stunningly impressive breakthrough season by a potential future great. But the parallels with last year are unavoidable. In 2025, McLaren's Oscar Piastri arrived in Azerbaijan apparently in control of the championship, and possessing a big lead over team-mate Lando Norris, albeit less than half what Antonelli's is now. But Piastri had some kind of meltdown on the streets of Baku, what he described after arriving back in the city this week as "the worst race of my career". And after that, the wheels came off for the Australian, and he was overtaken by the end of the year not only by Norris, but also by Verstappen. There is no reason to believe Antonelli will suffer the same fate. But he still has something to process in the few days before taking to the track again in Malaysia on Friday. Russell led from start to finish in Azerbaijan This was the first time Russell has produced a weekend like this all year, when he was simply superior. Before, even when he won, Antonelli was right there with him, sometimes even faster. How did Russell do this? It has taken hard work and analysis on his part and with his engineers. He hasn't been comfortable in this year's car, feeling it does not suit his driving style, so he has had to put in the effort to make the driving feel natural. And he feels he is finally getting somewhere. Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "He had some difficult moments before the summer break, some soul-searching as well at points, and he's come back really strong, focused on the driving, focusing on the essentials of what he needs to do to put his weekends together step by step." Russell said: "I'm very proud of the resilience that I and my close group of engineers have shown during the tough periods this year because there's been a lot of hard work to overcome some of the challenges, to adapt my driving style to suit this new car better. "And F1 is so tough, you don't get opportunities to practise this, and finally it's coming to me a bit more intuitively than it once

title: Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder
description: The prime minister says he wants people without support from the "bank of mum and dad" to receive help.
body: The prime minister announced the scheme on the eve of the Labour Party conference in Liverpool Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to introduce a new scheme to try to help young people get on the property ladder. The "Your First Home" scheme would be open to first-time buyers in England with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their new build property's value to help pay for the purchase. Burnham said people who do not have support from the "bank of mum and dad" are among those the scheme would aim to help. Labour said there would be an initial interest-free period for the equity loan. Further details on the scheme are expected in next month's Budget and pre-registration will open before the end of the year. Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own. "So we will step in to help more first-time buyers onto the housing ladder." The PM added he believes the scheme will give builders the "confidence to deliver the high-quality new homes the country needs". Funding for the scheme is expected to come from reprioritising existing budgets; but housing developers will pay towards the running costs. Ministers have not yet confirmed whether there is an age restriction on the scheme, or a cap on the price on the value of the property. The announcement came as Burnham arrived in Liverpool ahead of his first Labour Party conference since becoming prime minister. The policy is similar to initiatives from previous governments, including the coalition's Help To Buy scheme, introduced in 2013 by then-Chancellor George Osborne. It expanded a previous scheme, known as FirstBuy, which was aimed solely at first-time buyers. Help to Buy initially enabled all purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home. Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said Your First Home would "build on the lessons learned from previous schemes, while retaining the benefits". "We're delivering a new generation of equity loans in a Labour way, targeting support to those first-time buyers who need support the most," she said. Rayner told the BBC earlier this month that there was only a "slim chance" the government would meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England by the next election, but said she was "not giving it up". Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic. BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives. title: England's Harrison scores last-gasp try to beat Black Ferns
description: Zoe Harrison scores last-gasp try as England defeat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium to avoid a second successive draw in the WXV Global Series.
body: This video can not be played England secure win over New Zealand with last-gasp try Tries: Moloney-MacDonald, Kildunne, Breach, Harrison Cons: Harrison 3 Tries: Du Plessis, Leti-I'iga, Paul Cons: Sorensen-McGee 2 Zoe Harrison scored a last-gasp try as England defeated New Zealand at Allianz Stadium to avoid a second successive draw in the WXV Global Series. With the scores level at 19-19 in the 81st minute and having missed a penalty moments earlier, Harrison intercepted a pass as the Black Ferns tried to counter-attack, the fly-half diving over the line and piled up on by celebrating team-mates. The world champions' record 39-game winning run came to an end last weekend in the 26-26 draw with Canada, but this week they were able to find a dramatic path to victory, much to the delight of the 59,871 crowd. New Zealand, the last team to beat England in the World Cup final in 2022, suffered their first defeat under new head coach Whitney Hansen. The Black Ferns had taken a deserved lead at half-time after tries from Amy du Plessis and Ayesha Leti-I'iga ruled out Claudia Moloney-MacDonald's opening score. Tries by Ellie Kildunne and Jess Breach restored John Mitchell's side's lead, before Mererangi Paul's converted try drew the game level on 70 minutes. England now travel to Canada to complete their three-Test series against the World Cup finalists in Toronto and Ottawa, while the Black Ferns play France in Hamilton. Video clips and reaction after England score overtime try to beat New Zealand This video can not be played 'Absolutely brilliant' - Moloney-MacDonald try puts Red Roses in front The Black Ferns have beaten the Red Roses in all five World Cup final meetings they have contested. Canada outclassed New Zealand in last year's World Cup semi-final to deny a repeat of what is one of rugby's great rivalries. Under Hansen, who took over as head coach after last year's disappointing World Cup, the Black Ferns were unbeaten and have defeated Canada and France this year. The world's second-ranked side spent a large chunk of the first half deep in England's 22, and an opportunistic kick found unmarked space for Du Plessis to dot down for a deserved try. England comfortably beat New Zealand 49-31 in their most recent meeting in 2024, winning all three encounters since their 2022 World Cup final defeat, which has opened the door for Canada to become the Red Roses' toughest contest. However, the years were rolled back in Twickenham as Hansen's side brought a fearsome level of physicality and speed to challenge the Red Roses. Leti-I'iga, who had an opening try ruled out, caused havoc throughout the first half and finally crossed after Tyla King broke clear, before a poorly judged cross-field kick, with another try beckoning, let Mitchell's side off the hook. This video can not be played King splits defence with 'brilliant dummy' to set up Leti-I'iga try England have not led at half-time in any of their Global WXV Series games. Given their season only began two weeks ago against Australia, Mitchell has been quick to defend his side's rustiness. Individual magic from Kildunne, who spotted a gap on the wing for her try, and a yellow card for a high shot by Veisinia Mahutariki-Fakalelu, presented Mitchell with an opportunity to empty his bench with momentum behind his side. Breach's simple finish came in the next play as any fears of a first loss in four years began to dissolve. But the Black Ferns refused to go away and continued to trouble England's defence, which is now being influenced by coaching consultant Shaun Edwards. Mitchell's side were criticised for turning down a kickable penalty late in the game against Canada. The opportunity again presented itself, and Harrison took it on from distance, but the ball came up well short. Canada opted to kick the ball out and accept the draw last week, which is not in the DNA of New Zealand, and they attacked from distance in an attempt to inflict England's first loss on home soil since 2016. That proved to be the wrong decision, as a pass was picked off deep inside the visitors' 22, and instead the Red Roses won their 14th straight game at Allianz Stadium. title: Mayfair club shuts as Met investigates weapon claim
description: Popular celebrity venue Maison Estelle is temporarily closed and has had its alcohol licence suspended.
body: The venue's alcohol licence was suspended with immediate effect following a private hearing A private members' club popular with celebrities has temporarily closed while police investigate allegations of threatening behaviour and whether a weapon was brandished in a nearby street. The Metropolitan Police said it asked Westminster City Council to review Maison Estelle's alcohol licence as the premises was "allegedly associated with serious crime, or serious disorder, or both". It related to an incident on 19 September, the force said. No injuries were reported. Councillors suspended the licence at a private hearing on Thursday. The Mayfair venue, which has hosted Princess Beatrice, Idris Elba and Kim Kardashian, said it would be closed for "a few weeks" while investigations took place. "A further hearing will be held in due course," a Met spokesperson said. "The circumstances remain under investigation, including whether a firearm – or imitation firearm – was involved." Westminster City Council said councillors, on consideration of the application and the relevant representations, suspended the licence "in the interest of public safety". Maison Estelle did not oppose the Met's application at the hearing, the council said. "The safety of our staff, our members and their guests will always come first," a spokesperson for the club said. "We are continuing to work closely with Westminster City Council and the police as we review our licence conditions and procedures." Councillors will review the licence at a full hearing due to take place within 28 days. Located within a Georgian townhouse, the seven-floor venue has four dining rooms, 11 bars and two floors of "nightlife spaces", according to the Maison Estelle website. Membership to the club costs £5,950 a year. Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: German town bans 'stumbling stone' memorials to Nazi victims
description: Germany's education minister has branded the ban on the small brass memorial plaques a "scandal".
body: "Stumbling stone" memorials - like the one pictured in the Netherlands - are often placed in memory of Jews and other victims of the Holocaust There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis. Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal". Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria, have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities. The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations. But now councillors from the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones in their town. The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects. The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate. Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated. Stumbling stones placed near the Reichstag in Berlin However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision. "Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild. She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision. Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach". She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD". Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance – which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance. In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings. As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location. Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen". The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects. Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. title: Watch: Bangkok declared flood disaster zone
description: Heavy rain over the last two days has overwhelmed Bangkok's water systems, with more rain forecast on Sunday.
body: This video can not be played The whole of Bangkok has been declared a flood disaster zone as authorities try to pump days of floodwater into the sea. Heavy rain over the last two days has overwhelmed Bangkok's water systems, with more rain forecast on Sunday. People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors. title: 'No turning back' in independence journey, says first minister at rally
description: It is the first time the first minister of Wales has attended a Yes Cymru march.
body: Rhun ap Iorwerth told the crowd "equality with Scotland" is the next step for Wales Wales' first minister has said there is "no turning back" on the journey to independence for the country, as he attended a rally on Saturday. In a speech addressing the crowd gathered in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, Rhun ap Iorwerth said the "next step" for Wales had to be "equality with Scotland, as a minimum". Thousands were in attendance, with the event organisers, campaign group Yes Cymru, saying it estimated the march attracted between 8,000 and 9,000 people. "[Wales is] on a journey, and there's no turning back," ap Iorwerth said. Since 2019, thousands have taken part in independence marches across Wales, including in Cardiff, Swansea, Wrexham, Merthyr Tydfil, Rhyl and Barry. But this was the first time the first minister of Wales had attended a Yes Cymru march. A Reform Cymru Member of the Senedd (MS) said he was "disappointed" by the first minister's decision to attend, while a Welsh Conservative MS said it would be "better for him to be behind his desk in Cathays sorting the problems he said he would sort out". Thousands of people attended the event in Aberystwyth on Saturday Following the march, a rally in Castle Gardens featured speeches, including from the fiest minister, as well as Yes Cymru's chairman Rob Hughes and Elwyn Vaughan, Plaid Cymru MS for Gwynedd Maldwyn. It was the first march since the pro-independence party Plaid Cymru came into government in Wales following the Senedd elections in May. Ap Iorwerth said: "We are standing up for Wales, pursuing the investment and greater powers we need from Westminster now, so we can make a real difference to people's lives as the next step in our constitutional journey." In his speech, the Plaid Cymru MS for Bangor Conwy Môn referenced Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments yesterday, ruling out the handing of powers to hold a referendum on independence to the Welsh government. "The right to self-determination is not a right that the UK government is willing to acknowledge," ap Iorwerth said. This week, the Senedd narrowly rejected a Reform motion declaring Wales should remain part of the United Kingdom. The vote was initially tied, with 45 members backing the motion and 45 opposed, requiring Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies to cast the deciding vote against the proposal in line with parliamentary convention. Rhun ap Iorwerth made a speech at the rally held in Castle Gardens, Aberystwyth Reform MS Joe Martin said the first minister's attendance at the event was "disappointing to see, especially so early in the term, given that Plaid Cymru campaigned on a platform where independence wasn't on the table for the Senedd term". "It's not where their priorities and their attention should be," he told Politics Wales. "If there was a clear and overwhelming majority of people in Wales who wanted independence then obviously that would change things, but there isn't, there's a clear and overwhelming majority of people who don't want independence." It was the first pro-independence march since Plaid Cymru came into power in Wales in May Andrew RT Davies MS from the Welsh Conservatives added that "waiting times have gone up, and we've had the Pisa results that shows we've fallen further behind, external other parts of the United Kingdom. So instead of marching in Aberystwyth, [the first minister would] better off behind his desk in Cathays sorting the problems that he said he would sort out". Welsh Labour declined to comment. Responding to the opposition parties' criticism, a spokesperson for Plaid Cymru said: "We are getting on with the priorities facing Wales right now - reducing NHS waiting times, improving literacy and numeracy, supporting jobs and businesses, and tackling the cost of living - while also standing up for Wales and being ambitious for our nation's future." title: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
description: The indpendent report also says Kirk's aides insisted he speak outdoors, overriding concerns from campus officials.
body: Kirk's Utah Valley University event was held in a courtyard surrounded by tall buildings An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year. The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA. It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers. The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025. Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed. University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says. "But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds. Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note. They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team. A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said. The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures. However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety. Charlie Kirk was addressing about 3,000 people when he was shot in the neck Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action. The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones. "The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day." When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement. The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events. UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations". It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures now common practice at high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors. Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead. His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. title: Norris says Colapinto should be banned after accident
description: World champion Lando Norris calls for Alpine's Franco Colapinto to be banned for causing an accident at a restart at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
body: Franco Colapinto's lock-up in Turn One took out his team-mate Pierre Gasly as well as world champion Lando Norris World champion Lando Norris has called for Alpine's Franco Colapinto to be banned for causing an accident at a restart at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. McLaren's Norris was taken out in a chain reaction when the Argentine locked up his brakes and slid into team-mate Pierre Gasly, who then hit Norris. All three cars retired as a result of the incident. Norris told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Give him a ban. It's quite simple." Colapinto said: "I can be sorry to everyone. It's been a big mistake, of course. I just locked up and then I was very out of control." Briton Norris said he believed governing body the FIA should take such incidents more seriously because of the impact it has on other drivers who are blameless, and the cost in terms of damaged parts. "The FIA should be more strict and start handing out bans for this kind of stuff," Norris said. "It's careless from people. It costs a lot of money. All my parts are in the bin now, so people should just get banned for this kind of driving. (They) don't deserve to be in Formula 1. "If you cause a crash on a restart like this, yeah, you should have at least a one-race ban." Russell wins despite late Verstappen challenge However, race winner George Russell and Max Verstappen, who took second, both said a ban would be too severe. Mercedes' Russell said: "That's too harsh. Safety car restarts, cold tyres, a very small mistake can have big consequences. And from what I saw today, that's what it looked like. It was a small error that had a big consequence. Race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless." Red Bull's Verstappen added: "As long as the driver that caused it is aware of what he did, right, and apologised... It's not nice. Not nice for anyone involved, right? But like George said, a race ban probably is a bit much." Colapinto was given a 10-second penalty in the race, but as he was already retired this will be converted into a grid drop at the next race, the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, next weekend. The size of the grid penalty has not been confirmed, but it is likely to be in the order of five places. Both Alpine drivers were in with a chance of scoring points in the race, and were running seventh and 10th before the incident. Most galling for the team was that Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad finished seventh and that has extended their gap over Alpine in their fight for fifth place in the constructors' championship to 15 points. Gasly said he was "crushed" by the incident. "We're all very disappointed with the outcome after such a strong weekend, strong race," the Frenchman said. "It's still difficult to process what just happened." A McLaren spokesperson said it was too early to say whether the incident would mean Norris would not be able to use the upgraded parts the team debuted in Baku at the race in Malaysia. title: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
description: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Uefa Nations League B3 game in Debrecen, Hungary, after confirming they will proceed with the fixture.
body: FAI chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the Republic of Ireland squad in protest Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Uefa Nations League B3 game against Israel in Debrecen, Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture. Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the game. But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing. As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia. The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other. Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace. "One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference. "They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict. "There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]." This video can not be played FAI CEO David Courell delivers a statement ahead of the Israel game There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place. A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed. The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, believed to be goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding. Around 13:00 BST, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow. More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game. "This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell confirmed. "This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive. "There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion." This video can not be played 'It's a situation you can't win' - Heimir Hallgrimsson Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures. The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game". "All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed. "The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead. "We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage." Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games. Asked whether the far from ideal build-up to tomorrow's game will affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see". "Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," he continued. "There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland. "We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win." title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
description: The UK's busiest airport cautions it may miss the government target of 2035 as ministers say the deadline has "always been ambitious".
body: The UK's busiest airport, Heathrow serves 80 million travellers a year with its two runways and four passenger terminals in west London Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues. The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost £49bn, would open by 2035. But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade". The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter. The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission. It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove policy and regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace". Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office. Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups from neighbouring areas, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy. The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. The number of flights from the airport, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average. London Mayor Sadiq Khan has always opposed the project, warning of the impact on noise, air pollution and climate change. A consultation on the expansion was published in June this year. Once finalised, it then needs to be put to a parliamentary vote, which could reportedly be delayed until 2027. An artist's impression showing three runways at Heathrow Airport A DfT spokesperson said: "There is currently no live planning application for a third runway, and we cannot comment on ongoing consultation processes or prejudice them in a way that will only delay progress. "The timeline has always been ambitious. We'll continue to work with promoters, including Heathrow, and all other stakeholders at pace to ensure the right framework is in place for which a planning application for a third runway could be considered." A spokesperson for Heathrow said: "It's right that ambitious targets were set; the sooner expansion begins, the sooner the whole UK will benefit." They said the benefits would involve "at least 108,000 new jobs and billions of pounds invested in supply chains in every part of the country". "This is a national project, 100% privately financed which will support growth today and secure the UK's position in the global economy once the runway opens." Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. What's the plan for a third runway at Heathrow Airport? title: WW2 sailor and SBS member dies aged 101
description: The decorated veteran of the Royal Marines and SBS carried out missions behind enemy lines.
body: Friends described Henry Francis as a "remarkable" person who "gave everything" for our freedom One of the West of England's last surviving veterans from World War Two has passed away aged 101. Harry Francis, from South Gloucestershire, joined the Royal Navy in 1942 at 16, having lied about his age to serve. He went on to join the Royal Marines and became one of the first men to join the Special Boat Service (SBS), carrying out covert operations in Italy, Lebanon and Burma, where he was wounded. South Gloucestershire Armed Forces Day put out a tribute on social media where organisers said: "His quiet bravery and his remarkable life will not be forgotten." Estate to build 'UK's largest beaver enclosure' Greengrocer sent good wishes ahead of retirement 'Hefty school fines' and 'new bellringers sought' "Harry belonged to a generation that gave everything so that we could live in freedom. His quiet bravery, and his remarkable life, will not be forgotten," they said. "Our thoughts are with his wife Gwen, his children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and all who knew and loved H." The organisation went on to say how Francis celebrated his centenary last year surrounded by family and friends. Relatives said Francis' covert missions during WW2 remain largely untold due to his oath of secrecy He was also visited by the Royal Marines Reserve Bristol, whose personnel delivered a personal message from the First Sea Lord and Chief of the Naval Staff General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, recognising him for his extraordinary courage. His daughter Teresa Betton previously told the BBC: "What he gave for this country, all the friends that he lost... I'm so proud of him. "He tells the stories, but not all of them. He signed the [Official] Secrets Act and has stuck by it." A selection of Mr Francis' wartime medals alongside his military cap In a tribute on Facebook, Charlie Liston said, when she was younger, they were neighbours and remembered how Francis had helped her with a school project about the war. "Sat in his dining room with a cup of tea Gwen had made, Harry told me just a small portion of his many many experiences whilst fighting in Burma," Liston said. "These stories made me very moved, both with tears and laughter. "Harry was a very special person, not just as a public figure, but as a mentor, a neighbour, as a friend. He will be missed dearly." title: No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains
description: After being found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges for breaching Premier League, could Manchester city really be stripped of eight trophies?
body: Manchester City won the Premier League title three times in the period covered by the investigation It is one of the biggest talking points from the Manchester City case. Should City be stripped of the eight trophies they won between 2009 and 2018, the period in which they were accused of breaking Premier League financial rules? Judging by social media, many fans of rival clubs are now hoping for such an outcome. However BBC Sport has been told there has been little appetite from within the Premier League - both the organisation and clubs - for past titles to be stripped from City Does that put an end to it? Not quite, as the decision will be made by an independent panel which is yet to hold a "sanction hearing". That means it cannot be ruled out, although a points deduction, huge fine or possibly even expulsion from the Premier League are thought to be more likely. Here, BBC Sport analyses this difficult issue and decision the panel is now facing. Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City "I think we still have a chance to win that league… and then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal." It was almost two years ago that Jose Mourinho mischievously raised the possibility that his former club Manchester United could be handed the 2018 Premier League title held by Manchester City. Under Mourinho, United finished second to City by 19 points in 2018, his final full campaign in charge at Old Trafford. City have always denied wrongdoing. But now we know they have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges, was Mourinho right? Premier League rules do not directly make reference to such a sanction, with a fine, points deduction or expulsion listed as possible punishments. However, they also allow for a disciplinary commission panel to impose a penalty "as it shall think fit". That theoretically could include retrospectively-applied points deductions, or the stripping of titles. Many will argue that if upheld after any appeal, the nature and scale of the wrongdoing City have been found guilty of warrants such as sanction on the basis that titles were won unfairly, and any misrepresentation of revenue and costs gave them a crucial competitive advantage. City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules. So with a cloud hanging over the trophy-laden era City have enjoyed since the takeover of the club by Abu Dhabi billionaire Sheikh Mansour in 2008, could asterisks now be applied to the titles City won during the period in which they have been found to have broken the rules? Could they be left blank? Or, as implied by Mourinho, reallocated to those teams who finished runners-up to City? Such a move would threaten to open the proverbial can of worms, raising questions over other accomplishments. For instance, there is now scepticism towards the various trophies Chelsea won in the 2010s, after the club were found to have made a catalogue of secret payments to agents over transfers, between 2011 and 2018. Some will ask that if retrospective action is applied to City, should the same not happen to Chelsea? This video can not be played What do Man City charges mean and what happens next? It is impossible to know exactly to what extent City benefited on the field from their rule breaches. And which players they may not have been able to afford if they had adhered to the regulations. And what about the period between December 2018 and February 2023, when City stand accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations? Should retrospective action be applied then too? Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City twice during that time, by a single point in both 2019 and 2022. Last year, the German coach joked he would host a party in his garden if his former club were suddenly awarded those titles. Some will conclude that the rule breaches between 2009 and 2018 helped City to lay the foundations on which Guardiola built on to achieve so much success, culminating in the Treble triumph of 2023. Does that era come into scope? Where does it end? For some, the mass reallocation of titles over such a long period would risk making a mockery of Premier League history, jeopardising its reputation and commercial viability. Others would argue that some 17 years after the first alleged breach, and with City accused of distorting the competition over multiple seasons, serious damage has already been done to the league's standing. And while there is no Premier League precedent, such concerns have not prevented such punishments being applied before in football. Juventus had the Serie A titles they won in 2005 and 2006 revoked as a result of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal - when five Italians teams were penalised for attempting to influence results by picking certain referees. The first title was left blank by authorities, with the second reallocated to Inter Milan. There is also a British precedent. Elgin City won the 1992-93 Highland League, but were later stripped of the title after having been found to have fielded ineligible players. There are examples in other sports too. In 2012, Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven Tour de France titles by the UCI, cycling's governing body, for doping. And the reallocation of medals has become commonplace in athletics as a result of positive drugs tests that can emerge long after events have taken place. In cases such as City's, involving financial rule breaches, the argument for such a punishment is more complicated. title: Huge crowds greet Pope in Paris for open-air Mass
description: More than half a million people are expected to attend the event in the heart of the French capital.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Huge crowds greeted the Pope as he travelled down the Champs-Élysées Hundreds of thousands of people have greeted Pope Leo XIV in the centre of Paris for a giant open-air Mass. Crowds cheered as the pontiff moved down the Champs-Élysées Avenue beneath the Arc de Triomphe, waving to crowds from his popemobile. The head of the Catholic Church blessed several babies as he stopped at different stages along the avenue as chants of "Leo, Leo" rang out. More than half a million people are expected to attend the event in the heart of the French capital on Saturday and a special altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde for the ceremony. French President Emmanuel Macron, who met Leo for an hour of talks on Friday, will not be at any of the Pope's Masses during his four-day visit to France, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion. But the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by Macron's wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also expected to attend. Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally party and conservative Bruno Retailleau were both pictured at the Place de la Concorde ahead of the event, while centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal are also due to be there. Mayor of Le Havre and former French Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and former Prime Minister Francois Fillon were both also seen at the Place de la Concorde. Thousands have gathered along Champs-Elysees Avenue ahead of Pope Leo's open-air Mass Earlier on Saturday, the Pope met migrants as he visited the Maison Bakhita centre, an association supporting refugees, and praised the organisation for inviting "us to see those who are invisible". During the visit Leo said it was "possible to encounter one another and to live together in dignity and peace". He also stressed the "the fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love". The Pope also issued a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of his visit to France on Friday. Leo cautioned against "losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines" in wide-ranging remarks to Church and state officials at the Élysée Palace. This video can not be played Why is the Pope in France? Large crowds are expected throughout the pontiff's trip, which the Church believes reflects a growing spirituality among the French and other Europeans. On Sunday, 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes. The Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, on Monday where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification. Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name. His paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later, she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden name. title: Russell wins despite late Verstappen challenge
description: Mercedes' George Russell holds off a late challenge from Red Bull's Max Verstappen to win an Azerbaijan Grand Prix enlivened by two late safety car periods.
body: George Russell crosses the finish line with Max Verstappen less than two tenths of a second behind Mercedes' George Russell held off a late challenge from Red Bull's Max Verstappen to win an Azerbaijan Grand Prix enlivened late on by two safety car periods. Russell dominated the first part of the race while Verstappen was climbing up from eighth place on the grid before becoming stuck behind McLaren's Oscar Piastri. But two safety cars in quick succession put the Red Bull on Russell's tail for an 11-lap chase to the flag. Russell could never break free of Verstappen but the four-time world champion was not quite able to get close enough to try an overtaking move. After an issue with energy deployment, Russell was scared Verstappen would pass him on the run to the line, but held on to win by just under 0.2 seconds. Russell's victory meant he cut the championship lead of team-mate Kimi Antonelli - who recovered from 16th on the grid to finish fifth - to 66 points. "It's amazing to be back on the top step of the podium. I do want to say a big thanks to my team because they've continued to believe in me through a tough moment, helped me come through it," the Briton said. "I'm really proud to have had this weekend." Behind the top two, Red Bull's Isack Hadjar drove a strong race to the final podium position on his return after missing three races with a broken wrist. The key stories of an initially soporific and then dramatic and tense grand prix were: Russell's accomplished drive to his first win since the Austrian Grand Prix in June Verstappen's superb fightback from a difficult qualifying Mid-race chaos with a first safety car triggering a second almost immediately, as so often happens McLaren's race unravelling after a promising start Russell appeared on course for a comfortable win as the race unfolded with few incidents of note in the opening stages. Piastri moved up from third on the grid to second by passing Ferrari's Charles Leclerc at the start but the Australian lacked the pace to chase Russell, who edged away into a comfortable lead. Behind, Piastri soon found himself holding off Hadjar, who won an early battle with McLaren's Lando Norris and then passed Leclerc to challenge the McLaren. Meanwhile, Verstappen was making his way up from eighth place after a qualifying session in which a cascade of problems had prevented him qualifying second to Russell. By lap seven, he was past Hadjar into third place after the Frenchman did not fight him. The three cars circulated together in a stalemate, with no-one able to pass and the teams all waiting for the expected accident that would lead to a safety car and a cheap pit stop. That happened on lap 30, when Williams' Alex Albon crashed at Turn Five. Norris says Colapinto should be banned after accident On the restart, six laps later, Verstappen passed Piastri into Turn One to move into second place. But the race was almost immediately put back under caution after a pile-up at the first corner caused by Alpine's Franco Colapinto, who cannoned into team-mate Pierre Gasly, who in turn clattered into Norris. Behind them, the two Racing Bulls also came together, Arvid Lindblad tipping Liam Lawson into a spin, leading to a sarcastic response from the New Zealander on the radio. That put Verstappen on to Russell's tail for another restart but the Briton handled the situation coolly, accelerating early and catching the Dutchman somewhat unawares. He was unable to shake Verstappen, who was always about 0.5secs behind but never quite close enough to try a move into Turn One, the only significant overtaking place. There was one last chance for Verstappen on the final lap. Valtteri Bottas crashed his Cadillac at Turn 15, and after backing off for the yellow flags, Russell lost his turbo which in turn cost him electrical boost. Verstappen closed in and there was just 0.196secs between them as they crossed the line, the closest green-flag finish since the 2002 United States Grand Prix. Russell has now finished on the podium in three of the four races since the summer break. Asked what has changed for him since then, he said: "I think it's just having more experience with this new driving style I've adopted and every race since the break I feel like I've gone from strength to strength. I feel more like myself again." The incident that led to the retirement of McLaren's Lando Norris and both Alpines immediately after the first safety car restart Antonelli only just missed out on passing Leclerc for fourth, crossing the line 0.3secs adrift of the Ferrari. Leclerc's team-mate Lewis Hamilton was sixth after a quiet race, while Lindblad made amends for hitting Lawson with a strong final 10 laps to move up to seventh place. McLaren were left licking their wounds after a strong first part of the race in which Piastri was looking on course for a potential podium. The first issue came when Norris locked up into Turn One, which dropped him from seventh place behind Gasly and Antonelli. Then at the first restart, Norris was trying to pass Gasly around the outside of Turn One when Colapinto locked up on the inside and slid into Gasly, who was knocked into Norris. The Frenchman and the world champion retired on the spot, while Colapinto limped around the lap to stop in the pits, where his race also came to an end. Norris told BBC Radio 5 Live the Argentine should be hit with a race ban for his driving. Piastri at that point was still in podium contention, but his race unravelled soon after. He lost second to Verstappen at the first restart and then at the end of the first racing lap after the second, he made the same mistake as Norris had earlier, a lock-up at Turn One sending him into the escape road. Because the field was still so tightly bunched, the error dropped him to 14th place, where he finished. 2. Max Verstappen (Red Bull) 3. Isack Hadjar (Red Bull)

title: Watch: Prince Harry says 'kids are happy' in British school after six years in US
description: He says his children are “happy in school” and the family returned to the UK for "lots of reasons".
body: This video can not be played The Duke of Sussex spoke to Canadian TV (CTV) after completing a charity skydive near Toronto The Duke of Sussex has said it feels "great" to be back in Britain after spending six years living in California. He told Canadian network CTV: "It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil. The kids are happy in school and it gives me a chance to be able to really focus on the Invictus Games in Birmingham in July next year." Prince Harry and Meghan stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020, before returning to live in Britain last month. It is thought the family are basing themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area. The couple's children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, had to be moved to a different school only days after they started over security concerns about the school run. It is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had raised concerns about the distance and heavy traffic on the route to the school. Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has been marked by tensions with the Royal Family. Meghan previously shared a glimpse of family life back in England to Instagram Meghan has largely stayed out of the public eye, with few public appearances. Harry has carried out several public engagements linked to his work with the Invictus Games. Last week, he visited a school in Birmingham to launch an education programme inspired by the games, where he played pickleball with pupils and took part in a science lesson on prosthetic design. The games will take place in Birmingham from 10 to 17 July next year, with 550 wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans from 25 nations expected to compete in 12 adaptive sports. Harry spoke to CTV after completing a skydive in Toronto to honour a promise to a 102-year-old World War Two veteran and raise awareness of military charities. Asked what had prompted the family's return to the UK, Harry said there were "lots of reasons" but did not elaborate. The couple were reportedly surprised by a letter authorised by the King which reiterated that they are private citizens and set out guidance to senior government and military figures on how they should be treated. Prince Harry and King Charles have had a strained relationship since the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped down as senior working royals and moved to the US. Meanwhile, the Sussexes are waiting to hear whether they will receive taxpayer-funded security in the UK. The committee which oversees royal and VIP security, Ravec, is set to reconsider the family's level of police protection now that they are full-time residents rather than visitors. title: Met to re-examine CCTV from Jill Dando murder case
description: Police are reviewing footage of a man at Putney Bridge station after the Crimewatch presenter was shot in 1999.
body: The BBC TV presenter was shot on the doorstep of her Fulham house in April 1999 The Met Police has confirmed it will re-examine CCTV footage relating to the unsolved murder of Jill Dando, 27 years ago. The BBC presenter and journalist was shot dead with a single bullet on her doorstep in Fulham in April 1999. Despite one of the biggest and most high-profile murder investigations in British history, the case remains unsolved. A Met spokesperson said recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology had "provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station". The CCTV includes an unidentified man who was seen sprinting near the scene of the shooting, 20 minutes after the event. The Met said in the 27 years since Dando's death, the investigation had been "subject to numerous reviews", aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics. It warned this latest review was part of "ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter". Good News Rooms a 'brilliant' Jill Dando legacy Jill Dando good news initiative aims to go global Young people mark 25th anniversary of Jill Dando's death The TV presenter and newsreader was 37 when she died on the doorstep of her home on Gowan Avenue. Barry George, a local man, was convicted of her murder and spent eight years in jail before being acquitted at a retrial in 2008. Her killing was the subject of a Netflix documentary Who Killed Jill Dando? in 2023. title: Hundreds of wildflowers to be planted at meadow
description: Friends of the Lake District wants to reintroduce species lost to some farming practices.
body: Friends of the Lake District wants to plant 1,500 wildflower plants at land at Mazonwath A project to preserve vulnerable vegetation and wildlife will see hundreds of wildflower plants introduced to an upland hay meadow. Friends of the Lake District (Fold) wants to plant 1,500 wildflowers on land at Mazonwath, in Little Asby, Cumbria, to help reintroduce many native species lost through some farming practices. A spokesperson for the environmental charity said plant roots were good for moisture retention and soil health, with their texture playing a part in slowing the flow of overland water. They added: "Conservation work like this is really important to help our insects and birds have a home into the future." Fold is calling for volunteers to help join the planting efforts on 13 October and more information on how to join is available on the charity's website. The charity will be planting great burnet, bird's foot trefoil, black knapweed, cranesbills, oxeye daisy and vetches. The organisation is working with Cumbria Wildlife Trust as part of the Cumbria Seed Bank Project, which aims to reverse the decline of grassland habitats in the county. Volunteers are needed for a planting event at Mazonwath next month The two-year project in partnership with Kew Millennium Seed Bank, aims to collect, store and sow seed from rare and declining grassland species that are found in Cumbria. A Fold spokesperson said: "The aim is not only to introduce harder-to-establish plants that are missing from grasslands, but to also use this project to inform future work to safeguard vulnerable populations of plant species in Cumbria, so that these wildflower species are not lost forever." title: How long can Labour's feel-good factor last?
description: The party’s spirits have been transformed since Burnham became PM, but what's coming down the tracks, asks Laura Kuenssberg.
body: How long can Labour's feel-good factor last? "He just loves being prime minister," a government insider observes. Andy Burnham might not yet have delivered his all-important conference speech, but he has been preparing for this moment for years. He'll lap up the inevitable whoops and cheers – not just as Labour's leader, but the kind of leader who chimes with the party's rank and file, who puts social justice at the top of his list, who is not averse to cranking up the greatest hits – whether taking a pop at Mrs Thatcher, privatisation, or the divides between north and south. Speaking to MPs, ministers and advisers inside the party, there is no doubt whatsoever that Labour is in a much, much happier place than this time last year. There is a very simple reason, according to one cabinet minister, fans of Sir Keir Starmer, look away now, "people like the new prime minister more than they liked the old one – that's the truth of it". Another minister tells me: "There is no appetite for destruction – very little naysaying." But Labour is in a position that's been all too rare for all our political parties in the last few years – there are no whispers about chucking out the leader, no-one stirring revolt. And even those who don't like the direction of travel are labelling their opinions as a desire to be helpful, they're not trying to criticise the boss. "The mood's good – everyone is going into conference with their ears open," one MP said, keen to hear more from the prime minister. The feel-good factor is also driven by the party inching up a little in the polls – one senior figure says: "We're all witnessing the Burnham bounce – whether that's how you feel when you see the polls, or how we all feel when we have meetings together." And those who work inside government also credit a more effective political operation around the prime minister. "The system's better, you get clearer decisions, better steers when you need them," says a minister. Another government source also credits the new Downing Street operation but notes wryly, "it's unfair to compare the end of a regime which is always pretty nasty, with the arrival of a new one which is always more hopeful… these things can change". There are whispers of announcements in the next few days on housing and defence. Some MPs also want to hear Burnham expand on themes they, and the country, have heard plenty about but that aren't specifically defined – "public control" and "re-industrialisation". And frankly, the happy prime minister would likely be only too glad to talk for as long as necessary about those favourite subjects. But however much he loves being PM there are also less tempting realities he'll have to confront. "It's a new front man," says a minister, "but the song hasn't changed." And the soundtrack to this autumn might prove to be downright miserable. While Andy Burnham will be pressing the flesh at dozens of party events in the next few days, his Chancellor John Healey will be spending a lot of time holed up in his hotel room making decisions about the Budget which is only a month away. The pressure on public cash is intense as the budget approaches – the choice for the chancellor doing the rounds is, "10 billion of cuts or 10 billion of tax rises," according to a well-connected senior figure. Treasury sources say they don't recognise that simple number. However the figures shake down, the increasing cost of paying the interest on the country's debts weighs heavily. Don't forget the rising welfare bill, demands for more defence spending. It's unusual that a party conference is happening with a budget just weeks away, and it looms over the conference, just as the state of the economy looms over Labour's current feel-good factor. The UK can't force the US and Iran to find peace, to get traffic flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz, to bring the oil price down. Nor can the prime minister make Putin bring his war on Ukraine to an end, with pressure on European gas supply as we enter another winter. There are already predictions of our annual energy bills going up by £500 early next year. You know the script – higher energy costs raise the spectre of price rises everywhere. "We're really suffering at the hands of energy prices," says an insider. One influential figure predicts an array of grim economic consequences, unconvinced that Burnham and his team have grasped what might be coming down the track and planned accordingly. "The big economic challenges coming – rising housing costs, rising inflation, downward pressure on public spending because of the cost of borrowing, 500 quid on energy from January - I just don't see what the game plan is." And there are nerves about whether the new No 10 is concentrating on getting the economy growing. Many of Burham's priorities so far are about spending money, not helping people make it. One of his own advisors publicly described the administration as a "traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok". Ouch. Now, the former business secretary, Peter Kyle, has very politely, but firmly, expressed concern that Burnham and his team are not thinking hard enough about helping the country make money, perhaps more focused on how to spend it. You can read more about his comments here. He told me: "We must act with more urgency, and we must feel the need for economic growth as acutely as we do about tackling things like rough sleeping and about social care, and some of the social reforms that we want because they are inextricably linked." Kyle is not the only person in the Labour Party who worries Burnham and Healey are more interested in spending money than helping business generate it. title: Survey to show 'vital insight' of children's lives
description: Statistics Jersey says the 2026 Children and Young People’s Survey will open in October.
body: The chief statistician said the survey provided a "vital insight" into the lives of young people A survey for young people on topics including health, wellbeing, school life and social media is set to open in October. Statistics Jersey said the survey would be offered to students from Year 4 to Year 12 and would run from 5 to 16 October. It said the 2026 Children and Young People's Survey was voluntary, anonymous and could be completed online. Officials said it would be the first time the survey would ask participants about social media apps and generative AI tools, including how often they use them. Chief statistician Ian Cope said it provided a "vital insight" into the lives of children and young people on the island. Statistics Jersey said it would explore whether young people had caring responsibilities and enough food for each day. It said the results would be used across the Government of Jersey to inform policy and improve services. "We have worked directly with students this year to help shape the content, ensuring it reflects the issues that matter most to them," Cope added. "New questions on social media, generative AI, caring responsibilities and food security will help build a more complete picture of the opportunities and challenges facing young people today." The final report is due to be published in Spring 2027, officials said, alongside a child-friendly version for schools. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Statistics Jersey said the last survey, carried out in 2024, achieved strong participation. Response rates were 87% for Years 4 and 8, 84% for Years 6 and 10, and 78% for Year 12, with 4,360 children taking part, it said. Follow BBC Jersey on X, external and Facebook, external. title: PM pledges £210m to regenerate UK's high streets
description: Burnham said the fund would would support communities to transform derelict buildings and keep businesses open
body: The prime minister said money would be allocated to rescue buildings at risk of closure The prime minister has announced a £210m package to regenerate the UK's communities and high streets. Empty spaces will be put back into use, Andy Burnham said, turning them into "community hubs, health centres, shared workspaces, cafés and the local services that people actually want to see." The scheme is part of funding earmarked by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government for high street support and regeneration. It comes ahead of Burnham's first Labour Party conference as prime minister, where he is set to emphasise his plans for the UK will have "making life more affordable" at its core. As part of Burnham's high streets scheme, a £125 million derelict buildings fund will be available to transform mothballed and dilapidated buildings. And an £85m pot will enable communities to take over neglected spaces including pubs, clubs and shops, the government said. There will also be £65m allocated to rescuing businesses and buildings at risk of closure, and a further £20m allocated to help communities set up co-operative businesses and let out empty units. The prime minister said: "People don't measure growth by looking at a spreadsheet. They measure it by looking at their local high street. Are shops opening or are the shutters down? Does the place feel like it's moving forward or being left behind? "Today's funding will help put power back into the hands of locals who know their area best." Communities Secretary Angela Rayner said the scheme showed the government would mean communities see "boarded-up buildings that have been left to rack and ruin turned into places people are proud to visit again". Meanwhile First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said the investment would give local people the resources they need to make change, adding: "This is what devolution means in practice". The move follows Burnham's announcement in the summer that pubs, clubs and social venues would see 20% cuts to business rates from April. But Peter Kyle, business secretary to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, suggested Burnham needs to act with "more urgency" to boost growth, as the PM arrives in Liverpool for Labour's party conference this weekend. The Conservatives' own plan for "stronger high streets" would abolish business rates for thousands of businesses, and would "defend key pillars of the community such as post offices, pubs and pharmacies", according to the party. title: Butterfly populations 'could crash' due to weather
description: More than 77,000 butterflies were recorded in Devon while 47,000 were spotted in Cornwall this July.
body: The Gatekeeper species was the most-spotted butterfly across the counties Butterfly and day-flying moth numbers recorded across Devon and Cornwall this summer have been "very good" - but experts fear prolonged hot and dry weather could lead to a decline. Nearly 5,000 people took part in the Butterfly Conservation's 2026 big butterfly count in Devon, recording 77,151 insects during the three-week count. It said nearly 3,000 people took part in Cornwall, spotting 47,712. Professor Richard Fox, head of science at the conservation, said adult butterflies loved hot weather, but warned they could be on course "for a population crash". "The extreme droughts in 1976 and 1995 had severe impacts on butterfly populations, with some species never fully recovering," he said. One of the standout species was the Painted Lady More news stories for Devon Listen to the latest news for Devon The charity said strong butterfly numbers were "likely" down to favourable conditions for caterpillars in spring, followed by the hot, sunny weather enjoyed by adult butterflies during the summer months. However, it said previous drought conditions across much of the UK may have caused food plants used by caterpillars to wither before they had finished feeding. The charity said it feared the full impact may not become clear until next year. Fox said many species were already under pressure, with 80% of the UK's butterfly populations having declined since the 1970s. "So many are already struggling for survival without these extreme weather pressures," Fox said. He added: "With increasingly hot, dry summers and droughts predicted to become more and more frequent due to climate breakdown, degraded habitats and already depleted butterfly populations, some species may be pushed further and faster towards extinction, which is a very sombre thought. "They are, quite simply, less resilient to these events, which means we could be looking at very difficult years ahead." The charity has urged people to help wildlife recover by planting more trees and shrubs, installing water butts to store rainwater and leaving areas of grass uncut. The gatekeeper was the most commonly spotted butterfly in Devon and Cornwall. The meadow brown took the second spot in Devon, followed by the red admiral. In Cornwall, the red admiral took second spot, followed by the painted lady. Butterfly Conservation said the painted lady was one of the standout species with 6,955 recorded in Devon and 6,033 in Cornwall. The migratory butterfly enjoyed a strong year nationally. Painted ladies undertake one of the world's most remarkable insect migrations, travelling from Africa to the UK over several generations, crossing the Sahara Desert and Mediterranean Sea.
