title: Man City legal fight could spiral out of control, former Premier League club executive warns
description: Christian Purslow's comments come after Manchester City was found guilty of dozens of financial rule charges brought by the Premier League.
body: This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City Manchester City's legal fight with the Premier League has the potential to "spiral out of control", a former top club executive has warned. Christian Purslow, a former Liverpool managing director and Aston Villa chief executive, who also held a senior role at Chelsea, said the case could begin a chain of events that would be "appalling for the game". City have been found guilty of the vast majority of 115 charges brought forward by the Premier League. The club were accused of a wide range of rule breaches which centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules. Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told that City will appeal. Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine. Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Purslow appeared alongside football law expert Paul Gilroy KC, who described the case as a "seismic moment for world football". Purslow said: "It's a sort of 'where does this end?' because if you look at every single season - the nine seasons which we now know Manchester City breached rules - then all of their 19 Premier League rivals in that season, to differing extents, suffered easy-to-compute loss. Whether it was a place in the Premier League - every place was worth £3m. "Teams that came fifth who didn't make the Champions League maybe lost tens of millions of pounds - and of course teams that were relegated. Let's say the team that finished 18th would've finished 17th if Manchester City weren't there. And they, of course, suffered huge loss. "If you add all those claims up, over nine years, and that's just in the Premier League, you can see that the potential here for this to spiral out of control is huge. "I really hope that common sense prevails here and that there is a comprehensive solution between the authorities and Manchester City that looks at all these issues and tries to draw a line in the sand. "Because a never-ending waterfall of legal claims and uncertainties for another four or five years would be absolutely appalling for the game." Gilroy added that, so far, four clubs have put in protective claims "reserving the right to claim compensation if City are found guilty". Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict Everton told to pay Burnley £35m over PSR breach The news, broken by the Athletic,, external came 1,327 days after City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation, and 22 months after a hearing by an independent commission concluded. No official announcement has been made by the Premier League, which has declined to comment. Manchester City declined to comment on whether they had been found guilty, instead providing a statement which read: "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. "The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence." Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has urged the Premier League to come to a quick resolution. She told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think most football fans will be feeling that this is not a good moment for football as a whole and I think Manchester City fans will be feeling very, very anxious about what happens next. "It's very unsettling for football fans and I hope that it can be resolved as swiftly as possible. "I will obviously look very closely as what comes out of this but we can't apply those rules for the Premier League. They have got to do it themselves and are going to have to resolve this as swiftly as possible - not just for the sake of Manchester City but for the sake of football." This video can not be played What do Man City charges mean and what happens next? City won eight trophies in the period covered by the case, including three Premier League titles, three EFL Cups, one Community Shield and one FA Cup. The charges cover the managerial tenures of Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini, and the first two years under Pep Guardiola, who left the club at the end of last season after 10 years in charge. David Bernstein, who was Manchester City chairman from 1998-2003, told Times Radio he felt "absolutely awful" on hearing the news of City being found guilty - but admitted any punishment would have to be "more drastic" than a fine. "To see all this tarnished in this way is very sad," he said. "I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who've stayed with the club through thick and thin. "This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process now has to be done quickly because you've got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it's just not viable. "The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster, not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial." He continued: "I can't give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty. "All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that." Meanwhile, singer-songwriter Noel Gallagher says he is "shocked" at the news and it is "quite sad" for players and fans. "A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges,"

title: Republic of Ireland news conference delayed before controversial Israel game
description: The Republic of Ireland delay the pre-match news conference planned for Sunday's Uefa Nations League game against Israel in Hungary - a fixture campaigners have called on them to boycott.
body: The top table remained empty at the appointed time The Republic of Ireland have delayed the pre-match news conference planned for Sunday's Uefa Nations League game against Israel in Hungary - a fixture campaigners have called on them to boycott. Heimir Hallgrimsson's team are scheduled to meet Israel in Debrecen at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October. They have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace. Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott. However, there are also Irish supporters, perhaps less vocal, who have always believed that the match should be played with supporters in attendance. Following Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo, midfielder Jason Knight opined he didn't think "the game should be going ahead", while winger Chiedozie Ogbene urged the public to not "put the pressure on us" regarding their approach to the scheduled game. Hallgrimsson and a player were scheduled to meet the media at 09:15 BST (10.15 local time), before training, but the conference was delayed shortly beforehand. A Uefa official entered the room to inform waiting media teams that the press conference was postponed until after training, which would have been about 11:30 BST (12.30 local time). But shortly afterwards, the Uefa official returned to the media room to announce that the Republic of Ireland's training session had also been postponed, with no time given for when it might take place. There is also no confirmed time for the news conference. Reporters have now gathered out side the Republic of Ireland team hotel The fixture has been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3. A team meeting took place on Friday for players to air their views on Sunday's game and the return fixture in Serbia. The players were expected to release a statement at Saturday's news conference, but the delay has added further uncertainty, with some reports of at least one player wishing to withdraw from the squad. It has since emerged the news conference, scheduled to take place at the stadium, is now set to be staged at the team hotel, with Uefa unable to provide information regarding the delay. The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. title: Rayner criticises visa rule proposals ahead of Labour conference
description: The housing secretary says the government's plans to change wait times for permanent residency are unfair because they "change the goalposts".
body: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said she is concerned about Labour's proposals to change visa rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK. In an interview with the Times, external ahead of Labour's annual conference, Rayner questioned Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's plans, saying they are unfair because they "change the goalposts". Under the proposals, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for residency - instead of the current five - while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait. Mahmood said the government would make a decision on the immigration overhaul by the end of the year. Speaking to the Times, Rayner said she was concerned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules. She described the potential rule change as "very disruptive" and added: "I do have concerns about that." During her interview with the Times, she said that the changes would impact foreign care workers who "moved their lives here to look after our loved ones". Her remarks represent direct criticism of a policy inherited by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. Rayner previously served as deputy prime minister under Sir Keir, and was brought back into cabinet by Burnham in July. It is significant that a serving cabinet minister feels able to criticise an existing government proposal on the eve of Labour's conference, albeit one inherited from the Starmer era. It is part of a growing head of steam from some parts of the party to quash the retrospective elements of these plans. Rayner has previously criticised the measures. In June, she said proposals to retrospectively alter the rules for migrants already working in the UK would be "wrong". Rayner said she believed that Mahmood was aware of her position, telling the Times she has "not changed [her] view" since re-entering the cabinet. Burnham not doing enough to boost growth, says former business secretary I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say". Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary. She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship. In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British". Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas." Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in". Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right". The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK. She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in." Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here. But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly. But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight. The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this week. Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement. She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement." title: Ngumoha not in England squad to face Spain
description: Liverpool teenager Rio Ngumoha is not named in England's matchday squad for Saturday's Nations League opener against Spain.
body: Rio Ngumoha received his first England call-up earlier this month Liverpool teenager Rio Ngumoha has not been named in England's matchday squad for Saturday's Nations League opener against Spain. The forward, 18, was named in a full squad for the first time by boss Thomas Tuchel earlier this month but he will miss out on the party that will play against the reigning world and European champions at Wembley (19:45 BST). Ngumoha was one of the five supplementary players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Florida in the summer. This video can not be played He was unexpectedly handed his debut in a 1-0 friendly win against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo and becoming the fifth youngest player to represent the Three Lions. Ngumoha has enjoyed a rapid rise since becoming the youngest player in Liverpool's history to start a first-team match when he made his debut as a 16-year-old in the FA Cup against Accrington Stanley during the 2024-25 season. He then marked his Premier League debut by scoring a stunning late winner in the Reds' 3-2 win at Newcastle last season. He has made three league appearances for Andoni Iraola's Liverpool this season but only one of them has come as a starter. Do England have a problem against top-10 teams? title: At least two dead after explosion destroys building close to Acropolis in Athens
description: Local media report the property included a holiday rental, with US tourists and a UK national among the missing.
body: The explosion happened in the central Plaka district of the Greek capital At least two people have died, with a British national among four more missing, after an explosion destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens. The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis. An American man and woman have died, with two more US tourists missing, AFP news agency reported citing local officials. A Greek national and UK national who lived in the building are also said to be missing. Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast. The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with a Greek fire official later telling reporters the body of a man had also been found. The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster." The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road. Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated. Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors. The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus. A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are aware of a suspected explosion in Athens and are in touch with the local authorities." title: Memorial unveiled at school where boys were experimented on with contaminated blood
description: During the 1970s and 1980s pupils received medical treatments using contaminated blood products.
body: The memorial has been installed at the college, near Alton, Hampshire A memorial has been created at a school where boys were experimented on and infected with HIV and hepatitis. During the 1970s and 1980s, the Lord Mayor Treloar School and College in Hampshire offered specialist care for children with haemophilia but pupils received medical treatments using contaminated blood products. Of the 122 pupils with haemophilia that attended the school, only about 30 were still alive when the Infected Blood Public Inquiry published its report into the scandal in 2024. It highlighted how "very few" of the pupils with haemophilia that attended the school between 1970 and 1987 "escaped being infected". It said children were treated as "objects for research" and were experimented on without their knowledge by NHS clinicians, who knew the dangers it posed. Survivors Richard Warwick, Adrian Goodyear, Steve Nicholls and Gary Webster attended the unveiling of the memorial The memorial installed at the college, near Alton, Hampshire, depicts two pupils, one with a sling and and another holding a cane, embracing each other. Adrian Goodyear, 55, who first attended Treloar's when he was nine, said: "We couldn't believe the place we were looking at. Rolling country hills, swimming pools, canoes, a Jacobian mansion. It was just remarkable at first. "We left school with death sentences." Goodyear was infected with hepatitis and HIV while at the school. "In 1985, a doctor tearfully said that I had two to three years to live," he explained. "I was told this with five other boys and the doctor went round the room and said: 'You have… you haven't… you have… you haven't… you have got HIV'." He said the memorial was important to keep the scandal "in the public consciousness" and to honour those who died. He added: "When we were here we made promises… they died in front of us, one winter we lost five boys. "I made promises to them, as did the other lads here today, that we would never give up. We would find out what happened." If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line. The plaque features a quote from Sir Brian Langstaff, chairman of the public inquiry Gary Webster, 61, who was infected with HIV and hepatitis C when he attended between 1975 and 1983, was called to the doctor's office one dinnertime as a child, and told he had two years to live. He said that the memorial was important "to remember what happened and to make sure it never happens again". Steve Nicholls, 59, who attended the school from 1976 to 1983, said the memorial "represents me 50 years ago, it represents the boys 50 years ago, it's what we were". "It resembles the comradeship and the bonds that were formed at the college at the time," he continued. "I have known the majority of these boys for 50 years. I went to school with them for eight years. We played together, we slept in the same dormitories as each other and we were treated together. So, we became like brothers. "We were often referred to as blood brothers and we've stayed in contact throughout the years. He added: "We feel incredibly guilty for surviving it and getting through it when many of our friends didn't." Richard Warwick, who attended the school between 1976 and 1982, said the memorial was a "symbol of comradeship, friendship and support". Former pupils of the Lord Mayor Treloar School and College took their case to the High Court The inquiry found that medical research was carried out at Treloar's "to an extent which appears unparalleled elsewhere". In his report Sir Brian Langstaff said it had "left long scars, not only in this Hampshire community but across the UK". Des Collins, senior partner of Collins Solicitors, said: "Today is about remembering the real-life consequences of responsibilities, at a local and state level." Former pupils have sought legal action against the school's trust in the High Court. Reading a statement on the trust's behalf at the time, Toby Riley-Smith KC said it was "so sorry" that many former pupils were among the affected. "It is so sorry that as a result, they and their loved ones have suffered so much, and for so long. "It is so sorry that they have been victims of this tragedy, which Sir Brian Langstaff has described as the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS, a tragedy that has been compounded by the fact that it has taken so long for their plight to be recognised." More than £2bn has now been paid in compensation to victims across the UK of the infected blood scandal. Do you have a story BBC Hampshire & Isle of Wight should cover? title: Weekend of mixed UK weather with sunshine before showers arrive for some on Sunday
description: Expect a dry and pleasant Saturday with rain for northern and western areas on Sunday, ahead of some strong wind and rain early next week.
body: A deep area of low pressure is forecast to approach from the Atlantic next week bringing a spell of windy weather. This potential storm may also bring heavy rain to places, especially in the west, whilst some places further east could stay dry. Many drought affected parts of England and Wales - where significant rainfall is still needed - may stay largely dry throughout the next week. Before the arrival of wind and rain, though, some bursts of warmth will lift temperatures above average, possibly reaching the low-20s Celsius at times in south-east England. It will be a day of warm sunshine for many on Saturday with rain for some on Sunday After some unseasonable warmth over the past week, especially in the south, a weak weather front ushered in cooler air to Scotland and Northern Ireland on Friday, whilst warm and humid air stayed put in southern England and south Wales. Into the weekend it does look as though most places will return to more typically late September conditions, with UK temperatures ranging between roughly 15 to 21C north to south.. Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out Summer 2026 was UK's hottest on record, Met Office says Temperatures will again be close to the seasonal average through the weekend and it should feel pleasantly warm in the sunny spells. Saturday will bring the chance of further showers to many western areas, while on Sunday spells of rain will sweep most areas at some point. As we head into next week and the final days of September there are currently no signs of any significant bouts of unseasonable warmth. Some pleasantly warm and sunny days are still possible during the first half of the week, but forecasts show a very changeable pattern overall. As well as occasional rain for most, northern and western areas could see much windier conditions at times. Expected rainfall over the next five days will be focused on northern and western parts of the UK. Some places in central and eastern England may stay completely dry September rainfall so far has been very mixed across the UK. In parts of north-west Scotland, there has already been 146% of expected September rainfall. At Achnagart in Highland, it has rained for the past 27 days. In contrast, it has been very dry in parts of eastern England, with Bridlington in East Yorkshire seeing just 11% of expected September rainfall. Low pressure systems will bring some rain over the next week or so. However, the bulk of the rain will fall in Scotland, Northern Ireland and western parts of England and Wales, with no significant or useful forecast further south and east. title: Joshua fight at risk over promoter row, says Fury
description: Tyson Fury says his long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in December is in jeopardy.
body: Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua are former two-time heavyweight champions Tyson Fury says his long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in December is in jeopardy because of a row between rival promoters. The bout was announced earlier this week following years of failed negotiations, with the pair set to fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December. The event, which will be broadcast on Netflix, was confirmed as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC president Dana White, but this appears to be the sticking point. Eddie Hearn, Joshua's promoter, has been at odds with White in recent months, and says the UFC head's involvement is a breach of their contract. Fury says Matchroom promoter Hearn's reluctance to work with White is putting the fight in doubt. "Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight. They're saying they're not going to fight now," Fury posted on Instagram. "It's mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego. He's making up a million different things and threatening we're not going to fight. "Now you've got Turki Alalshikh finding alternative real men who will fight at the drop of a hand. Eddie Hearn has cost us the biggest fight in boxing history." Hearn has been publicly feuding with UFC president White since the launch of Zuffa Boxing earlier this year. Speaking to IFL TV, Hearn said White's involvement in the promotion of the Fury and Joshua fight "ain't happening", despite Netflix's news release. "Dana White cannot be involved with this fight promotion. Netflix clearly didn't get the memo. No-one talks to each other," said Hearn. "Then Netflix say the fight is in conjunction with Dana White. Now we have to go through that process and deal with it. It's a little bit annoying but as I've shown through the UK battle that we won, we stand by our contracts." Fury's promoter Frank Warren said White was influential in securing the deal with Netflix after the fight was confirmed. Fury's claim the bout could be off follows his post on social media earlier this month suggesting that Joshua, 36, was backing out of the fight, before calling for a third match-up with Oleksandr Usyk. There was no official statement from Hearn or Warren in the news release sent out by Netflix to announce the fight. BBC Sport has contacted Matchroom, Warren's company Queensberry Promotions, The Ring and Netflix for comment. The dispute between Hearn and White is the latest stumbling block following years of failed negotiations around the fight. In 2020, the two camps agreed the basis of a two-fight deal. In 2021, contracts were signed for an undisputed heavyweight contest, only for Deontay Wilder's successful arbitration case to force Fury into a third fight with the American. Then, in 2022, Joshua accepted a 60-40 split to challenge Fury, but that attempt also fell apart. Fury and Joshua finally signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, with the date and venue confirmed this week. title: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
description: An emergency has been declared across the capital of Thailand as days of heavy rain leave the city inundated.
body: This video can not be played Disaster declared as heavy rain sparks Bangkok flooding A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after 48 hours of heavy rain left roads in the Thai capital submerged. People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors. Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested. The rain is expected to continue into Sunday, raising fears that more canals could burst their banks. Canals across the Thai capital have burst their banks, leaving roads under water Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now. "I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now." She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding. Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding. The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand. All 50 of Bangkok's districts have been declared emergency zones. Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported. He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled." title: The MMA fighter helping Brighton - and filling stadiums
description: From helping Brighton with set pieces to fighting in front of nearly 60,000 people - meet MMA star Christian Eckerlin, who competes at Oktagon 94 in Frankfurt on Saturday.
body: Christian Eckerlin has won 18 of his 26 professional fights Christian Eckerlin laughs modestly when asked if he feels he has contributed to Brighton's success. Last season, the 39-year-old MMA fighter was brought in by the Premier League club to help with their training for set-pieces. Eckerlin was a professional footballer in Germany before transitioning to MMA, and says he taught Brighton players "wrestling, head control, hip control, and how to push back against opponents". Days before this interview with Eckerlin took place, the Seagulls moved up to third in the Premier League after beating champions and set-piece kings Arsenal 3-0. Eckerlin is quick to play down the impact of his advice for the Brighton players, but admits his training "opened doors" for them. "The Premier League is more physical, more aggressive, and they don't know how to use their body," Eckerlin told BBC Sport. "Brighton sent me videos of how they defend, and they did nothing with their hips and arms. "I taught them first in the weightlifting room, then the pitch, and it worked. This is what I did, I opened doors for them." Eckerlin was a professional footballer from 2005 to 2009, playing for SV Darmstadt in the third tier of German football at the peak of his career. As a youngster, Eckerlin always wanted to play for the team he supports, Eintracht Frankfurt, but believed his dream was over when he left the sport. Little did he know that MMA, and specifically European promotion Oktagon, would help make his dream of performing there come true. In 2024, Eckerlin beat fellow German Christian Jungwirth at Frankfurt's Deutsche Bank Park in front of nearly 60,000 fans in the most-attended MMA event of the year. On Saturday, Eckerlin returns to the stadium also known as the Waldstadion for a second time to face the Czech Republic's David Kozma at Oktagon 94 with nearly 60,000 expected once again. "It was my first dream, when I was in the Waldstadion when I was six or seven with my uncle. It was the dream for me to play there but I thought the fire went out," says Eckerlin. "I cannot tell you in words what this means to me. The biggest thing in my career. And now for the second time... crazy. "I'm at the end of my career, I'm 39, so this is maybe my last fight. There's no better way to stop fighting in my backyard, you know." 'My promise to my late son is what keeps me alive' Eckerlin grew up in a small town outside Frankfurt called Erbach and says football "was his first passion". During his youth career he played against stars such as Bastian Schweinsteiger and Mats Hummels, but ended up leaving football at the age of 20 after a disagreement with his coaches. "I got a little bit crazy and partied with friends. But my popularity went down with the coaches," said Eckerlin. "They said 'you cannot do this'. But I was young, nobody was on my side to say 'calm down and do your thing'. So I said 'OK, I'm going'." Eckerlin played at left-back but admits he "wasn't a technical guy" before joking he was more of a fighter on the pitch. He knows Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler through a friend who used to play with him in Munich. It was Hurzeler who invited Eckerlin over to Brighton, where he spent three days with the players. Eckerlin says all the players did well learning the MMA techniques he taught them, but Danny Welbeck, James Milner and Lewis Dunk "had the feeling for it". Football remains the most popular sport in Germany, but Eckerlin says he helped grow his following after switching to MMA via his YouTube channel. He says the fanfare in Frankfurt is "crazy", with fans always wanting to take pictures with him, but adds he is equally as well known in large cities such as Berlin and Hamburg. With nearly 60,000 fans expected again for his fight on Saturday, the show is likely to be the most well-attended MMA event of the year once again. Before what Eckerlin describes as probably the final fight of his 26-fight career, he takes a moment to reflect on the impact he's had on MMA in Germany. "I love this sport, and I push the sport more than everybody or anybody before in this country," says Eckerlin. "After my career, when I look back, I think then I will realise, what I do for the sport, or for MMA in Germany. But now I'm fully focused, and there's no time to think about the things in the past." title: Do England have a problem against top-10 teams?
description: As England prepare to take on Spain in their opening Nations League match, BBC Sport takes a look at whether they have a problem when faced with teams in the world top 10.
body: The last time England faced Spain was the Euro 2024 final, which Spain won When England take on Spain in their opening Nations League match on Saturday, it will be tinged with a feeling of 'what could have been' for Three Lions fans. The Wembley match comes three months after England agonisingly missed out on the chance to face La Roja in the World Cup final, having lost to Argentina in the last four. That would have been a repeat of the 2024 Euros final, which England also lost. In fact, their record against top-10 sides leaves much to be desired. In their past 15 matches against sides ranked in the top 10 in the world - according to Fifa's rankings - England have won six matches. Three of those wins were at major tournaments - the Euros semi-finals in 2021 and 2024 against Denmark and the Netherlands, and the bronze-medal match against France at this summer's World Cup. The victory over Les Bleus to take third place was Thomas Tuchel's first win as England boss over a top-10 opponent. And his first win over opposition ranked inside the top 20 came in their opening group game at the tournament against Croatia. So do England have a problem against top-10 opposition? Six wins in their past 15 games against top-10 opponents are not the kind of numbers an England team with the ambition of winning major tournaments can be happy with. Two of those wins meant the Three Lions advanced to the Euro finals of 2020 and 2024. One was in the World Cup match no one wants to play in, two were Euro qualifying matches against an Italy side already on a sharp decline and one came against Belgium in a Nations League match six years ago. To put it simply, when faced with really elite opposition, England continue to stumble. Particularly at the World Cup. England have been eliminated every time they have faced a top-10 ranked nation in the knockout stages of the World Cup since 1998 - seven times out of seven. In their past 10 World Cup games against sides ranked in the top 10, their sole win came in the 2002 group stage against Argentina. When faced with the defending world champions at the World Cup, they have lost on all four occasions. 1954 - Uruguay 4-2 England 1962 - Brazil 3-1 England 2022 - England 1-2 France 2026 - England 1-2 Argentina England have fared better at the Euros, overcoming top-10 opponents in Denmark and the Netherlands to reach the final at the past two tournaments but ultimately falling at the final hurdle on both occasions against Spain (2024) and Italy (2020). Meanwhile, their lowest possession in their last 15 games against top-10 opponents came in the semi-final against Argentina (35.8%) at this summer's World Cup and in those Euros finals against Spain (34.9%) and Italy (42.1%). England's all-time top scorer Kane, with 85 goals, was asked which missing ingredient was needed to get them over the line. "I think it's just in those biggest moments, still being ourselves," he told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The Argentina game was so hard to take, because we had a mindset of going to win the tournament, win in our way and our style, and if we lose trying to do that then we will take that. "The Argentina game was maybe the first game we tried 'not to lose' in the last 30 minutes and then we ended up losing anyway." Kane has scored 152 goals in 154 games for Bayern, winning two Bundesliga titles. "I have experienced it at Bayern Munich for example, you don't fear anyone," the 33-year-old said. "You go and be yourself, if a team beats you, shake their hand after and say well done. "You have an identity that you keep throughout. "I think with England now that is where we need to look. "We are very close, we have been very close but ultimately, we don't need to fear anyone. "We just need to be ourselves in the biggest moments and hopefully get over the line." England have been getting closer to major tournament glory over a number of years but the same question remains - can they dominate the ball and beat elite opposition? At Euro 2020, the last-16 win over Germany was huge - beating one of the historic footballing powers. But that was a German side in transition who were, at the time, ranked outside the world's top 10. England were then beaten by Italy in the final after taking the lead, dropping deep and giving up possession before losing on penalties. At the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, the Three Lions started the tournament with a free-flowing 6-2 win over Iran. Although this was not top opposition, the change in mentality from previous tournaments was notable. But yet again the same issues resurfaced. Despite largely being the better team against France, a Harry Kane missed penalty and Les Bleus' know-how put England out at the quarter-final stage. This video can not be played Argentina shatter England's World Cup dreams in semi-final Euro 2024 proved to be one tournament too far for Gareth Southgate and that team did not play anywhere near their best, relying on individual quality to get them through. A last-gasp Ollie Watkins strike was needed to beat the Netherlands in the semis while Kane was not at full fitness and without him at his best, the team never troubled a formidable Spain side. After a flawless 2026 World Cup qualifying campaign and a new elite coach in Tuchel, many thought this was England's time for glory. But, despite showing a huge amount of togetherness and grit in the last-16 win over Mexico, the same old problems once again sunk England. The Three Lions cannot seem to translate world class talent into ball possession and control of the game, with Tuchel saying he may have to embrace the chaos, and Anthony Gordon adding that England should lean on their traditional direct style. Perhaps that is what is needed to finally end their long wait for a trophy. title: Fuel costs putting off meal delivery driver applicants
description: Maureen Bougeard says some prospective volunteers do not respond after learning about expenses.
body: The service delivers meals to about 100 people, four days a week A delivery service offering meals to people in need has spoken about the challenges of recruiting new volunteers due to rising fuel costs. Maureen Bougeard said Meals on Wheels Jersey had received £38,000 from the Jersey Community Foundation to fund work supplying hot meals to islanders who are unable to prepare meals themselves. She said the service packed and delivered meals to about 100 people, four days a week - but added fuel costs were having an impact. "Very often volunteers say, you know, 'the petrol's getting expensive'," she said. "We're looking for new volunteers and I send the information out which says 'you drive your car at your own expense' and I don't hear from them again." The secretary said the organisation had more than 200 volunteers. "Our complete organisation is run by volunteers," Bougeard said. "We don't have any paid staff at all." Bougeard said some of the voluntary meal delivery drivers drove the length of the island twice in a day, adding most volunteers were retired people. "I'm not saying everyone has a poor pension, not everyone is on the basic pension, but some are and they still manage to come and volunteer, which is absolutely fabulous," she said. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey The service said people who receive the meals currently pay a cost price of £5. It said the grant from Jersey Community Foundation covered the charge to the government of Jersey's health and community services, which supply and facilitate the preparation of the meals. The service said the grant had been offered for 2026 and 2027. Meals on Wheels said it hoped to renegotiate the service level agreement with the government to allow it to continue. title: Bangkok declares disaster as heavy rains spark flooding
description: Days of near continuous downpours have caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital.
body: This video can not be played Days of almost continuous heavy rains have caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital, with the city's governor declaring it a disaster-affected zone. Almost 300 millimetres (11.8 inches) has fallen over the period, and more is expected in the coming days, according to Governor Chadchart Sittipunt. Videos from Bangkok show cars trying to navigate roads that have been entirely submerged by the floodwaters, with some vehicles appearing stranded. title: 'Agony aunt' with months to live tackles bucket list
description: More than £3,000 is raised by customers and friends to help Claire Bailey make lasting memories.
body: Claire Bailey (far left) - who has terminal lung cancer - has enjoyed train journeys, hotel stays and visits to places she has always wanted to see A shopkeeper given months to live after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer said "unbelievable" support from her community had allowed her to tick off almost all the items on her bucket list. Claire Bailey, who runs the Sun newsagents in Shepshed, Leicestershire, was told in April she had six to nine months to live. A fundraising appeal - launched to help Claire make memories with her husband, Rob Lord - raised £3,000 and has since reached nearly £6,000. Since then, Bailey has enjoyed train journeys, hotel stays and visits to places she had always wanted to see. Of receiving her diagnosis, Claire said: "For a split second it was like 'wow'. "But after that I thought there's no point being depressed about it. It's not going to make me better. "Just carry on as normal. It is what it is." Claire, who has worked in the shop for almost three decades, said she was overwhelmed by the response from customers. "I thought I'd get about £50 or £60," she said. "Within a week, I'd got about £2,500 and it was unbelievable." The fundraising has help finance the majority of Claire's bucket list items Claire said people had also come into the shop with cards containing money, while others had given her cash for meals when they met her around Shepshed. "Honestly, I've never known anything like it. You just do your job and don't think anything of it, but it's humbling," she said. The fundraising page was originally set up by one of her regular customers, Tereza Lingard. Lingard described Bailey as an "agony aunt" for the town, someone who "listened to everyone's problems" but rarely took time away from the shop. Tereza Lingard's fundraising page has generated nearly £6,000 The fundraising efforts have paid for many of Claire's trips and stays, with the 52-year-old able to enjoy the experiences with her family and friends. Claire said one of the items she was most keen to tick off was a visit to nearby East Midlands Airport. A lifelong aviation enthusiast, she said she had always wanted to visit the airport's air traffic control tower, and described the experience as one of the highlights of her bucket list. "The last two flights of stairs were up a spiral staircase," she said. "Whether I had to climb up on my hands and knees... I was getting to the top of that control tower." After supporters contacted the airport, Claire was given a tour of the tower before travelling the length of the runway and staying overnight in a hotel room overlooking the airfield. "I've always been obsessed with planes," she added. "That was amazing. Money can't buy it." A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Claire was desperate to visit the East Midlands Airport control tower Claire has also travelled on the world-famous Flying Scotsman train twice with her husband. "We went down to Portsmouth the first time," she said. "And the second time, I went on it to Eastbourne to watch the air show, which they have over the sea on the beach." She said one week, the couple had so many trips planned, they did not bother unpacking their suitcase. Claire added: "It was like 'right, we're here for two days, then there for three days, then somewhere else for another night'. "It was like a whirlwind." She said another memorable moment was when she was strapped up with firefighters and went up a 131ft (40m) ladder, thanks to an invitation from the local fire service after lobbying from her friends. She said her husband did not go up, and instead "stood at the bottom filming" during the summer. Claire experienced being inside a crane at about 131ft (40m) alongside members of Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Service One of Claire's favourite places is a converted railway carriage near Ely in Cambridgeshire, which she has visited three times. The accommodation has a Jacuzzi hot tub. Claire described it as her "little piece of heaven". She said since her terminal diagnosis, the owner had planted a rose - named Claire - in the garden. "A little piece of me is always going to be at that carriage," she said. "That's coming from somebody who was a stranger and who I've only met three times. That's what nice people are." Claire has visited the converted railway carriage three times Claire said only two items from her bucket list remained: A two-night stay at the Burleigh House hotel in Loughborough, and afternoon tea at Belvoir Castle. Despite her diagnosis, Claire said she remained determined to enjoy life. "I'm still all right, touch wood," she said. "I'm just struggling to walk a little bit more, but I can cope with that." Her message to others facing similarly difficult circumstances was "never, ever give up". "Even if they tell you devastating news that can smash people's lives into smithereens, you're still here, you're still breathing," Claire said. "There is always someone worse off than you. "Just keep smiling. That's what I'm known for in Shepshed." title: Woman pregnant years after life-saving transplant
description: Keeleigh John says her pregnancy would not be possible without her childhood organ donor.
body: Keeleigh John was told she might not be able to have children A woman who received a double organ transplant as a child says becoming pregnant would not have been possible without the family of her donor. Keeleigh John, from Bridgwater in Somerset, was diagnosed with chronic renal failure and underwent life-saving surgery to receive a new liver and kidneys when she was 12 years old. Keeleigh, now 28, said doctors had told her family it was unlikely she would ever have children. After recovering from four bouts of sepsis this year, she discovered she was pregnant on the day she returned home from hospital. Keeleigh said she "owes it all" to the donor family who made a decision at probably "the most difficult time in their life". 'Hefty school fines' and 'new bellringers sought' Olympic champion 'living out a dream' on Strictly Coastal path sign that sent millions on their way up for auction "We're at the 14-week point now. Baby looks healthy, I'm doing really well," she said. "They've done all the tests and they've said it's almost impossible for any sort of condition that I have to transfer over to baby." Keeleigh's mother, Tracy John, said doctors had warned the family that her daughter was unlikely to have children. "Me and my husband were told years ago we'd be lucky to see her survive to eight, and then it was to 12. "Then she received a transplant and now she's flying all over the world and having her own children. It's just something we never dreamed of." Keeleigh and her partner Sam Longman are looking forward to the arrival of their baby Keeleigh now campaigns for organ donation and has competed in the British Transplant Games and international events, winning gold medals in events including shot put, archery and discus. She is due to find out this week whether she has been selected for the 2027 World Transplant Games in Belgium. "I'm hoping I'll be on that plane to Belgium next year, hopefully with a tiny little baby." She said she hoped her achievements would make both her family and her donor's family proud. Keeleigh's mother, Tracy John, said doctors had warned the family her daughter was unlikely to have children Keeleigh actively advocates for the NHS Organ Donor Register, saying: "If you are prepared to accept an organ, you should be prepared to donate one." Recently, the NHS launched its first "urgent response plan" to address the drop in the number of organs being donated. NHS Blood and Transplant figures show deceased donation rates are 9% lower than at the same point last year, while the UK transplant waiting list has reached a record high. Keeleigh hopes to be selected for the 2027 World Transplant Games in Belgium Keeleigh said the life she has now, including her pregnancy, was only possible because her donor's family agreed to donation at a difficult time. "Not only would my life not have been possible, but also now I'm creating a life which also wouldn't have been possible. We never thought it would be possible." Her mother said the family remained grateful to the donor. "Without the donor family, for one, I wouldn't have my baby here, and she wouldn't have had the chance to have her own baby," she said. title: Coroner appeals to families linked to jailed surgeon
description: Surgeon Ian Paterson is serving a 20-year sentence for his botched and unnecessary operations.
body: Ian Paterson was given a 20-year prison sentence after being convicted of wounding patients through his operations A coroner investigating the deaths of people treated by the jailed breast surgeon Ian Paterson has appealed for 106 more patients' families to make contact. Inquests are currently being heard into the deaths of 70 women, to see if Paterson's treatment or care caused an unnatural death. Paterson was jailed in 2017 after being convicted of wounding patients by way of botched and unnecessary operations and given a 20-year prison sentence. The inquests' coroner, Judge Richard Foster, said he was recently notified of the deaths of a further 106 patients who were in their lifetime treated by Paterson for breast cancer, but he said he had not been told of their medical cause of death. The list of 106 names, including six men, appears on the investigation website, external asking next of kin to contact the solicitors to the inquests Higgs LLP. The law firm told the BBC: "We are simply seeking cause of death information to assess whether the deaths of these former patients of Mr Paterson will be investigated." The disgraced breast surgeon worked with cancer patients at NHS and private hospitals in the West Midlands over 14 years. At his trial the court heard that Paterson's technique involved leaving some breast tissue behind, preserving patients' cleavages, which breached national guidelines. Investigations have so far found 106 patients died between 1995 and July 2026. His unregulated "cleavage-sparing" mastectomies meant the disease returned in many of his patients. Others had surgery they did not need - some even finding out years later they did not have cancer. The surgeries caused serious lasting physical and physiological harm to all the victims. One woman was unable to breast feed her baby as a result. Paterson is due to be automatically released halfway through his sentence in 2027, before the inquests in Birmingham are due to conclude. title: Seahorse habitats 'healing' thanks to eco-moorings
description: Scars in Studland Bay's seagrass meadows, caused by boat anchor chains, are healing, a study finds.
body: The research was carried out by Kira Dunn of Southampton University Scars caused to rare seahorse habitats by boat anchors off the Dorset coast are starting to heal, thanks to the installation of new moorings. In 2021, Studland Bay Marine Partnership began installing the first of dozens of eco-moorings in a bid to reverse damage to delicate seagrass meadows. A new scientific study has now provided the first evidence that eco-moorings can help restore seagrass, with some scars shrinking by more than 90% over four years. David Brown, chair of the partnership steering group, called the results "incredibly exciting", adding: "The impact has been beyond our expectations." Seagrass habitats store carbon, support biodiversity and help protect coastlines from erosion, but are declining globally due to pollution, development, disturbance and climate change. The research, conducted by Kira Dunn as part of her MSc in Marine Biology with Oceanography at the University of Southampton, analysed monitoring data collected since the first eco-moorings were installed. Studland Bay is home to protected spiny seahorses Using sonar surveys, historical satellite imagery and five years of monitoring data, the study tracked recovery across 39 damaged areas of seabed. In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed in 2021, the size of bare patches in the seagrass decreased by an average of 93.6% between 2021 and 2025, shrinking by around 57 sq m each year. In a second study area, where traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, the scars reduced by 65.4%, around 15.9 sq m a year. Studland Bay has been a designated a Marine Conservation Zone since 2019 and is home to one of the UK's largest seagrass meadows, supporting species such as the protected spiny seahorse and short-snouted seahorse. The bay also became a voluntary no-anchor zone in 2021. Dunn, who graduated this year, said the research project had been "rewarding and positive". She said: "It's incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity." Traditional boat anchors cause damage to delicate seagrass Dr Ken Collins, of the University of Southampton, who supervised the study, said: "Studland Bay is becoming a powerful example of how practical conservation measures can reverse habitat damage and deliver measurable environmental improvements." Brown, who is also lead ecologist for the National Trust, said: "These results are incredibly exciting, and a huge encouragement to all the organisations and individuals who have given so much time and support to the partnership. "The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it." Studland Bay Marine Partnership is made up of conservation charities, boating organisations, academics, statutory bodies, community groups and businesses, with the aim of restoring Studland's seagrass. Partners include Dorset Wildlife Trust, Natural England, the National Trust, the Seahorse Trust and the University of Southampton. title: 'Our wedding present left us gutted': Couple join dozens in car seller dispute
description: Thirty-four customers battling for refunds on faulty cars as Trading Standards investigates.
body: Just two weeks after tying the knot Amber and Nathan Cooper were left with a nightmare Newlyweds Amber and Nathan Cooper spent all their wedding present money on a £7,000 Citroen C4 to take them on their dream honeymoon. But as they made their way to Cornwall in August 2025, it lost power and began to roll backwards leaving them stranded on the A30, near the Jamaica Inn in Bodmin Moor, they told the BBC. When they returned it to Trade Centre UK two weeks later, they discovered it needed a new engine, clutch and gearbox. But a year on, they are still fighting for an apology and their money back. The used car dealership said it 'works hard to resolve problems when they arise' They are among 34 customers who told the BBC that they also bought cars from Trade Centre UK branches in Coventry, Rochdale, Rotherham and Wales but are still locked in a battle for refunds. Customers say they have been left with loud noises from the engine, suspension and clutch problems. The company insists problems are "rare". They have said that when they rejected the vehicle under the Consumer Rights Act, the process through Trade Centre UK was complicated, lengthy and their claims were often refused. Amber said: "It's gutted us mentally, emotionally, physically, financially, I don't know what we can do apart from get this story out and have people learn from our mistake." Trade Centre UK has said it takes concerns raised "very seriously" and recognises that "problems can sometimes occur". A statement from the company said: "On these rare occasions, our teams work with customers to investigate the issue and identify an appropriate resolution, which can include repairs, replacement vehicles or, where appropriate, accepting rejection of a vehicle." Amber Cooper says she and her husband are still in debt The couple from Wolverhampton said they have been left in debt and emotional turmoil as they spent a year having to hire and borrow cars before taking out a loan to replace what they lost. Amber added: "People are coming to us and asking are you enjoying your wedding present? "We have to say, 'No, it's sitting in the Trade Centre's car park'. We're having to apologise to people who turned up to our wedding and kindly gave us money. "My husband works in Telford, which is a 60-mile round trip every day, and without a car he has had to miss work which means we've lost even more money. "We're still in debt, trying to pay off this loan and now I can't save for a house, start a family and move on with my life." Connor and Danielle Johnson-Bray say their car ended up back on the forecourt for sale despite the plethora of problems they experienced Connor and Danielle Johnson-Bray from Stoke-on-Trent also bought their car from the Wednesbury branch last September. They say it broke down within two days, so they were offered a different one, which subsequently broke down three times in eight months. Connor explained: "We spent £2,200 on repairs, courtesy cars, and just the initial getting the car, trying to get it back on the road." After being refused a refund, they took their case to the small claims court against the finance company they had bought the car through, who agreed to settle. Danielle added: "We did accept that [settlement], and it meant that we did lose a lot of money as well. We didn't have any more fight left in us. "It had drained us, we were very stressed, we were tired, I wasn't sleeping." Michelle Chancellor, whose new car broke down two weeks after she bought it, has since recieved a refund As part of a BBC Investigation in July, Michelle Chancellor, from Stourport-on-Severn, Worcestershire, shared that she bought her Vauxhall from the Wednesbury branch of The Trade Centre UK but soon heard loud noises coming from the engine. After appearing in BBC coverage she was contacted by the used car dealer, who told her that the refund was accepted. However, it took weeks to be processed. She said: "It was another two to three weeks until my refund came through and I was able to buy a new car, which meant I was still losing out on income after signing the rejection papers. "I think that the financial loss will affect me for a while yet, especially as I'm a self-employed mature student that lives alone." Sandwell Council Trading Standards has confirmed it has launched an investigation into the complaints and has urged anyone with issues to report concerns via the Citizens Advice Consumer Service. Consumer expert Stuart Masson explained that it is worrying when multiple customers feel they have no option but to pursue disputes because they believe a dealership is failing to cooperate. "It's enormously frustrating, the Consumer Rights Act has to be fair to both parties when it comes to buying used cars," he said. "It should be easy, especially within the first month. After six months it becomes more complicated. But it sounds like a lot of these problems are happening within the first few weeks." Trade Centre UK's statement added: "We are committed to meeting our responsibilities to our customers and continue to invest in our vehicle preparation, aftersales and customer service operations. "We are proud to have been in operation across the UK for over 20 years and to have served hundreds of thousands of customers during that time." title: Chadwick says driving F1 car 'top of bucket list'
description: Jamie Chadwick says testing a Formula 1 car is the highlight of her motorsport career.
body: Chadwick won all three seasons of the all-female W Series One of the world's most decorated female racing drivers, Jamie Chadwick has described testing a Formula 1 car as the highlight of her motorsport career. Britain's Chadwick joins an exclusive list of women to have driven an F1 car, after taking part in 32 laps at the Portimao circuit in Portugal, which will be on the F1 calendar in 2027. The 28-year-old first joined Formula 1 team Williams in 2019 as a development driver and has gone on to win all three seasons of the all-female W Series, as well as being the first female driver to win a road race in IndyCar's feeder series. She told BBC Sport: "In terms of a dream or a bucket list item, it's definitely the top. "It was pretty surreal. It's kind of everything I imagined, but more. The feeling you get from a car like that is pretty incredible. And then at a track like Portimao, it's a proper rollercoaster." This video can not be played Chadwick says driving F1 car is 'highlight' of career She practised in a simulator beforehand and took part in a detailed programme of gym work, which included neck strengthening sessions, with some of the drivers on the F1 grid. "I train my neck anyway for what I do, but it's that times 10. Just the sheer level of strength that's required in the neck is huge," she said. "I can't really put it into words the G-force and the feeling on your neck. As soon as you accelerate out of the pit-lane, your head hits the back of the headrest because it's so aggressive. "You wake up the next morning like you've been in a fight with Mike Tyson. It feels like you've been beaten about a bit, but it's an incredible feeling." There are now 13 women who have driven an F1 car. Five of those have officially entered a F1 Grand Prix weekend, and only two have gone on to actually take part in a race. Maria Teresa de Filippis made history as the first female in 1958 when she took part in the Belgium Grand Prix, finishing 10th. It took 15 years to see the next woman in an F1 car. The legendary Lella Lombardi took part in a record 17 grands prix, including the Spanish GP in 1975, where she finished sixth, becoming the first and so far only woman to score points. In 2014, Susie Wolff made the first female appearance in an official F1 session for more than two decades, when she drove a Williams car at the British Grand Prix. Wolff, who is now the managing director of the all-female series F1 Academy, has been instrumental in helping more females get into the sport and was one of the "inspirations" behind Chadwick wanting to drive an F1 car. Chadwick is not the only woman to have driven an F1 car this year. Doriane Pin, who won the F1 Academy title in 2025, became the first female to drive a Mercedes in April. But despite the progress, no woman has started an F1 race since Lombardi, 50 years ago. Chadwick believed that women are "capable of competing in Formula 1", but that there "shouldn't be a timeline on it". "I definitely believe the talent is out there," she said, adding: "And I'm excited. "Me doing this test and Williams giving opportunities to female drivers for example, will hopefully lead to a race seat one day." But with only 22 seats in F1, it is extremely tough for any driver to break into. Chadwick said: "You're looking at F2, F3 champions not getting seats and you realise that there's more talent than there are seats often available. Then you narrow it down to a female driver and it's even tougher and an even smaller talent pool. "But I genuinely believe with everything that we're doing now to support female talent it's only going to lead in a positive direction." title: Friends embark on 20-year board game battle
description: James Purcell and Andy Taeger are confident their friendship will survive the test.
body: James Purcell and Andy Taeger will officially start Campaign for North Africa on 30 October Two friends from Newcastle have set themselves the challenge of completing a board game which has never officially been completed. They expect it will take 20 years as they battle to fit it around their everyday lives - but while games can often put friendships to the test, the pair are determined to see it through, no matter how different life will look. What would you be willing to commit 1,500 hours of your life doing? Playing a game about a week during World War Two in North Africa might not be top of your list - but James Purcell, 29, and Andy Taeger, 30, decided to do just that. The pair met about a decade ago at a house party and became fast friends after duetting to a James Blunt song. They have spent every week since playing Dungeons and Dragons together. "One day we were playing and this friend just mentioned off-handedly that there was a game that supposedly had never been finished and takes up to 1,500 hours," Purcell says. "We had a bit of a laugh about it, thought nothing of it, and then a few weeks later we were at the pub and one of us said 'have you been thinking about that board game a lot?'" They spent the next few hours in the pub discussing it and left committed to playing Campaign for North Africa in its entirety. That was in October 2024. And for Purcell and Taeger, there's no going back. The strategic board wargame was released in 1978 and simulates the entire North African campaign of World War Two. Purcell says there has been no evidenced play of the full game and theirs would be the first occasion. "The game was never fully playtested by the designers either," he adds. Now two years on from their original commitment, the pair have managed a six-turn practice run to get to grips with the rules before jumping into the full game, which is 111 turns. Every turn simulates a real week during World War Two in North Africa. Purcell is playing as the Axis forces - Germany, Italy, Japan - while Taeger is playing as the Commonwealth. While 10 players are suggested, they are making do with just two. Through spreadsheets they have to keep track of things like ammunition, food, fuel, water, even down to the rate at which water evaporates depending on the heat. A practice run took more than a year to complete The practice ended in a draw and took 18 months to complete alongside their jobs and everyday lives. Purcell works in mental health services while Taeger is a software developer. "It feels sometimes like a job as well, we're filling out spreadsheets more so than playing a game, so a lot of the time it doesn't feel like fun, it feels like admin," Purcell says. To hold themselves accountable, they set up a podcast, War With A Mate, which has already had more than 90 episodes. And it has a good following already, with Purcell joking it is nice not having to bribe his friends and family to listen along. But board games are known to get tense, even more so if you are at war with one another, and the friends are mindful of that. "We're trying to keep it fairly chill, but sometimes it'll come down to a single dice roll and someone gets unlucky and there has been a bit of, not quite throwing pieces around because the board's too big, but there have been moments of frustration and tension," Taeger says. Purcell adds: "I've had a few hissy fits, just with the rules being so complicated. "I've been a bit annoyed when we've been so far in and I've realised I've done something wrong and had to make new plans based on that. "Because to finish a single turn, it takes us months at a time." But their podcast has a segment called Common Ground which forces the pair to try and agree on something from the episode, no matter how ridiculous. They are hopeful it will stop them fighting. The friends are now gearing up to starting their official Campaign for North Africa on 30 October, which will coincide with the podcast's 100th episode. "I think when we start the full game, it'll be exciting," Purcell says. "And then from there we've got the sort of void of 20 plus years that it'll take to finish the game. "So I'm kind of worried that the excitement might wear off and then we're just locked into this thing for two decades." War With A Mate already has listeners from around the globe, many of whom are happy they get to experience the game without having to do hundreds of hours of legwork. "I think at certain times it'll be our biggest regret starting it and sometimes it'll be some real highs," Taeger says. "But I think it'll be part people listening along to our deteriorating mental state." It is certain the pair's lives will look different after 20 years, when they hope to have completed the game. Purcell says: "It's sort of weird knowing that we'll be 20 years older. "We can have any sort of different living circumstance, careers, so it's strange that this game is going to be a constant through that and it already has for two years. "So it'll be interesting to see how it maps across." Follow BBC Newcastle on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.
