title: The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City
description: BBC Sport travelled to Portugal to find out more about Rui Pinto - the computer hacker who sparked the Manchester City investigation.
body: The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City Mention Rui Pinto's name to Manchester City fans outside Etihad Stadium, and you mostly get blank faces. But while they might not know his name, they are more than familiar with his work. Pinto is the Portuguese computer hacker who tried to bring down City. Through his website Football Leaks, he published a cache of confidential club documents, including internal emails about sponsorship deals and payments. That ultimately led to the Premier League charges for breaching of financial rules and Friday's news that the club had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 counts. For some, 37-year-old Pinto is no more than a criminal who stole information with sinister intentions. To others, though, he is a bastion of truth who has shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game. BBC Sport has been on a journey across Europe to find out more about the mysterious figure who was the catalyst for so much controversy. We spoke to one of Pinto's former teachers, a Portuguese politician fighting for him to be protected as a whistleblower, journalists who published the leaks, and a former financial adviser at Manchester City. And we sat just a few feet from Pinto in the latest of his court cases. This video can not be played With his cherubic face and spiky hair, Pinto is instantly recognisable. And it seems he hasn't changed. It is how Mario Falcao, his former geography teacher, remembers him. In a small courtyard garden in Portugal, we got a glimpse of what Pinto was like as a boy. "Rui was a perfectly normal pupil. He was nice, with his spiky hair, he was quite sociable but not extrovert," Falcao said. "He had a good relationship with the teachers, although he did miss these classes quite often. His father was always on top of things, so in the end he passed quite easily." Did he spot a strong interest in computers in a young Pinto? "Certainly he was very good in computers. All the work that he did for various courses were very good, when he put his mind to it," his former teacher explained. The now-retired Falcao speaks fondly of Pinto, who he says behaved just like his friends and would "go to the gym, go to McDonald's". Pinto had a modest upbringing. He grew up in an area called Vila Nova de Gaia, just across the Douro River from Porto, Portugal's second-largest city. We visited the road where he used to live, which featured tile-fronted houses with terracotta roofs. His school, Escola Secundaria Almeida Garrett, was well-regarded and was known by locals as 'the university'. His father, Francisco, worked in a shoe factory and later as an antiques dealer. His mother had died when he was 11. Falcao said he never predicted what was to come of his former pupil. "We were very surprised," he said of the moment Pinto was named as the founder of Football Leaks in 2019. "We weren't imagining anything like this could happen, that he could have problems with justice. "I certainly wouldn't wish him and his family to be in this situation. Perhaps it was a question of the excesses of youth, his ability with computers, and maybe an excess of club-ism." "So, you know, the fact that he supported FC Porto prompted him to commit some acts, but maybe he also felt the need for justice that young people very often do feel." Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City We visited the street where Rui Pinto grew up in Portugal Pinto set up Football Leaks in 2015, to - in his words - expose "the hidden side of football". Antonio Varela remembers the website's launch like it was yesterday. The Portuguese journalist was the first person contacted by Pinto, whose real identity would not be known for years to come, and was initially known by the pseudonym "John". "It was a common day of September 2015. I was at the news room at [Portuguese sports newspaper] Record and I got an email from Football Leaks. It was strange. Then I immediately go to the site, and I can't believe there is lots of information that you never heard or read. We made the conclusion this is very, very important." Re-publishing what had been leaked by Pinto brought legal and ethical conundrums. "We realised that [Football Leaks] got the information illegally. But since the moment they publish the information on the site, that's public information," said Varela. "You can't ignore that. Ethically, it's complicated, but the public interest is more relevant than the ethical issue. That was the conclusion." It wasn't just eight-time Premier League champions Manchester City that Pinto targeted. The early revelations on Football Leaks focused on matters closer to home, with leaks around Benfica and even the side he supported, FC Porto. Later, there were leaked documents and communications relating to some of the world's most famous players, clubs and agents, including Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Neymar. Pinto agreed to meet a journalist, Rafael Buschmann from the German magazine Der Spiegel. Once he knew he could trust him, he shared tens of millions of documents with him. It was then up to a team of journalists in the Der Spiegel headquarters in Hamburg to meticulously go through it all, producing some of the most explosive articles the football world has ever seen. Christoph Winterbach, a data journalist, was part of that team. "In the beginning it was very much a fascinating feeling of like a child in a candy store," he said. "If you're a football fan, if you're a sports journalist, it was amazing to see the actual documents, to see those emails where things are negotiated and to get a real look behind the curtain, how things work. "It's very important when you have this type of documents, this type of data, that you make a lot of cross checks, that you use some software which we did that can put it all into context a

title: Liam Neeson involved in new movie revealing story behind Tuam babies
description: The Lost Children of Tuam, co-produced by Liam Neeson, is now in cinemas.
body: Catherine Corless is played by English actor Monica Dolan in the film The story of the amateur historian whose research helped uncover the Tuam babies scandal is being brought to the big screen, with the help of actor Liam Neeson. The Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home institution for unmarried mothers and their children was in operation from 1925 until 1961. It came to international attention in 2014, after local historian Catherine Corless discovered there were 796 death certificates for children and babies who died there, but no burial records. A 2017 article in the New York Times, external about Corless' journey left Neeson in a "quiet rage", he told RTÉ's Late Late Show, external, prompting him to use his standing in the film industry to bring the story to life, and be a co-producer. "I thought if my standing in the film business is anything at all I'd love this to become a film so more people could see it and we could share this atrocity," Neeson said. Irish filmmaker Frank Berry, Monica Dolan and Liam Neeson at the Toronto Film Festival From there, Corless said she received a call from the New York Times writer Dan Barry, who said: "Listen, Liam Neeson may be giving you a call and he'd like to speak to you and get permission to do the film." Nine years later, the film - The Lost Children of Tuam - is now in cinemas. The film tells of the story of how Corless began researching a former institution for unmarried mothers and their children in Tuam, County Galway, and uncovers the hidden history of neglect and loss. It examines how Corless was faced with the silence of church and state as she embarked on a campaign for justice. Catherine Corless discovered there were 796 death certificates for children and babies who died at the institution "The way the film is done, it's just true to life," Corless told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme, describing it as "fantastic". Corless said the film's director, Frank Berry, "really wanted" the film "to be true and they stuck to the truth". "It shows the diversity between people in power and ordinary people like myself struggling to get a story out there that I knew was true, I had all the evidence," she said. A team is currently excavating the site of the former institution. In June, it was reported that they had found a further eight sets of infant remains, bringing the total number recovered to 77. "I really had to fight for it to come to this stage, not for the film exactly, also the excavation in Tuam is going ahead and the exhumation. I fought years with the denial from authorities that anything wrong happened," Corless said. "It's something I had to keep working on and that's portrayed very, very well in the film." English actor Dolan had to develop a Galway accent for the role Catherine Corless is played by English actor Monica Dolan in the film. Corless noted that Dolan had to develop a Galway accent for the role, which she said the actress did "very well". "She wanted to actually become me, to get into the knitty gritty of the efforts that I had to put in," Corless said of Dolan. "She portrayed me just as myself. I was amazed at what she was able to do," she said. "She went to the extremes, really, to get the feeling and the emotion I went through and the struggle." Corless added: "She did it so, so well, I must say that, she really did." The film was awarded Best Irish Film Award at the 38th Galway Film Fleadh in July. The Lost Children of Tuam opened in cinemas in Ireland on 25 September and it is scheduled for UK release on 9 October. title: White House bars CNN from travelling with Trump on Air Force One
description: CNN was scheduled to fly with US President Donald Trump for his trip to Tennessee on Saturday.
body: CNN had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One US broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday. The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the media after it was forced to lift its ban on some news outlets. CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule. The BBC has requested comment from the White House. CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule. Last week Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. All three media outlets said they were pursuing legal action, and accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press. Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage along with CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets. The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the United General Assembly in New York. A federal judge has since ruled Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and the administration had to let them back in, at least for now. However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday. A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call". Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after White House officials allowed reporters entry. The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday on Saturday. title: Burnham not doing enough to boost growth, says Starmer ally
description: Ex-Business Secretary Peter Kyle calls for more urgency on the economy, as Labour members head to the party's annual conference.
body: Peter Kyle served as business secretary during Sir Keir Starmer's premiership A cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer has said Andy Burnham's government is not focused enough on boosting economic growth and needs to act with "more urgency". Speaking to the BBC two months after being sacked in Burnham's cabinet reshuffle upon entering office, Peter Kyle said he wasn't making a "criticism" but "pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government". "If the destination means prosperity, it means freedom for people to do new things, and it means security for people and families, then why wouldn't we put our foot down and get there quicker," the former business secretary said. It comes as Labour prepares to gather in Liverpool for its annual conference. Burnham will address the conference on Tuesday and has said his speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role." He has previously said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him "a clear theory of growth" stressing his belief in the importance of devolving powers to local areas. Giving regions and nations more control would, he has argued, create the conditions for "good growth in every postcode". Kyle served as science secretary and later business secretary in the Starmer government, but has now returned to the backbenches as the MP for Hove and Portslade. In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said the government should be willing to take decisions that involve "short-term" pain in order to deliver economic growth, suggesting a delay to expanding workers' rights. "We might need to look and have honest conversations with unions about how we sequence some of the rights going forward in order to make sure that we get growth into the economy in the shorter term," he said. The government's Employment Rights Act was passed in December 2025 but some of the changes are not due to come into force until next year. The former minister also suggested introducing a "tax growth test" which would measure the impact of each tax on the economy and asking government experts to review "obstacles" to growth. Asked if there was enough focus on growth in the government, Kyle replied: "I don't think there is and that isn't a criticism - it is pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government. "I think we need to up our ambition, I think that we need to act with more urgency when it comes to economic growth." Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October, but faces rising debt costs and warnings of slower economic growth. According to the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the UK economy is expected to grow by 1%, slightly less than the 1.1% previously forecast. Henry Zeffman: Andy Burnham and his chancellor have a battle on their hands as the Budget approaches Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost? Earlier this week, Starmer ally Darren Jones told the New Statesman, external he thought Sir Keir should have been given more time in office and criticised "this modern approach of getting queasy and then just changing [leader] too rapidly". "In the past it was normal for governments to be unpopular midterm because you've got to take difficult structural long-term decisions." The former chief secretary to the prime minister added: "Irrespective of what's happened and how, we want it to be successful, and we have a collective responsibility to help make that the case. "We, as backbenchers in the PLP [Parliamentary Labour Party], are looking to… Andy and his team to get that right. We want them to get it right." title: Profile
description: German co-leader of the AfD.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·26 Sep 2026,·14 mins Available for over a year Mark Coles profiles Alice Weidel, the some say, unlikely joint leader and public face of the far right, nationalist AfD - the Alternative for Germany party. Weidel's a right wing populist and a self confessed fan of Margaret Thatcher. Yet in some respects, particularly when it comes to her private life is seemingly at odds with, almost the antithesis of what her party stands for. Her supporters don't seem to mind. Weidel and the AfD have notched up a series of big win in local elections this month, including Saxony Anhalt, causing huge headaches for beleaguered German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s, Christian Democratic Union. With the AfD currently topping opinion polls, many are now wondering out loud if Weidel could become Germany’s first far right leader since the Second World War. title: Brazil's Lula bans online gambling ahead of presidential election
description: Lula, who is currently in a tight presidential race against Flávio Bolsonaro, said the industry was a "cancer" that he must "remove".
body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva announcing new economic measures in São Paulo Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has announced a ban on online gambling, just days before an election in which he is seeking a fourth term as the country's leader. Lula, who is running against the son of the incarcerated former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, signed a provisional order on Friday that "prohibits all sports betting and online casinos". The online gambling industry in Brazil was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction. Lula described the industry as a "cancer" in his announcement, adding "either we remove the tumour, or it kills us". The move comes just over a week before the first round of voting in Brazil's presidential election. Recent polls have the 80-year-old leader almost neck-and-neck with Flávio Bolsonaro. The new measures must receive congressional approval within 120 days to remain in force. Lula acknowledged online betting was created under the former President Michel Temer's administration but that it "grew without regulation under Bolsonaro's management", in a statement on X . He said that there were "no restrictions" particularly for preventing children and adolescents from accessing online betting. "We won't allow betting companies to profit at the expense of Brazilian families' income and lives," the president added. The president described how he had heard from families who had sold everything in their houses because of their gambling addictions. Separate to the online betting order, Lula also signed a bill to penalise criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting. Earlier this week, at the United Nations General Assembly, Lula accused the industry of "transforming addiction into profit". But Flávio Bolsonaro called the gambling crackdown "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday, according to Reuters. Most types of gambling, such as casinos and slot machines, are illegal in Brazil, but ever since online betting was legalised in 2018, it has exploded in popularity. About 59.9% of Brazilian adults support banning internet betting, a survey by Atlas and Bloomberg published this week has found. title: UK ticket holder wins £111m EuroMillions jackpot
description: It is the third time a UK-based player has scooped the EuroMillions jackpot this year, National Lottery operator Allwyn said.
body: A UK ticket holder has won Friday's £111m EuroMillions jackpot, National Lottery operator Allwyn has confirmed. One mystery player matched all five numbers – 11, 12, 15, 38, 49 – plus the two Lucky Star numbers – 10 and 12 – to scoop the major prize. Allwyn's senior winners' adviser Andy Carter said it was "fantastic news for a UK EuroMillions player" who has secured the "life-changing" sum. It marks the third time a UK winner has claimed the jackpot this year. On 10 March, one UK winner took home a £181m jackpot - the third-largest in UK National Lottery history - while two UK-based winners shared a £125m jackpot with a French player in April. "Be sure to check your tickets and get in touch if you think you might be tonight's lucky winner," Carter urged. The record for the largest EuroMillions prize for a UK player currently stands at £195m - won by an anonymous player in 2022. EuroMillions draws are held every Tuesday and Friday night across nine European countries. Tuesday's jackpot now stands at an estimated £14m. title: Two men jailed for 2022 murder of Argentine rugby player
description: Loik Le Priol, 32, a former soldier who fired the fatal shots, was sentenced to 26 years in jail.
body: Federico Martin Ambaru was shot dead in Paris in March 2022 Two men with links to the far-right have been jailed over the fatal shooting of a former Argentine international rugby player in the streets of Paris four years ago. Federico Martin Aramburu, who played more than twenty matches for Argentina, was killed in a drive-by shooting in 2022 after an early-morning fight broke out in a bar near Boulevard Saint-Germain. Loik Le Priol, 32, a former soldier who fired the fatal shots, was sentenced to 26 years in jail. Romain Bouvier, 35, who opened fire initially, was sentenced to 19 years in jail. In a Paris court on Friday, Le Priol asked Aramburu's family for forgiveness as the trial concluded. "I'm Christian like you, the pope is here today" he said, referring to Pope Leo XIV's visit to France. "I don't know if it's a sign... [I] hope one day you can find the strength to forgive me," Le Priol continued. Former rugby star Aramburu was 42 when he was killed. He played for Argentina 22 times, including at the 2007 World Cup in France where he scored a try against the hosts to help his country finish third. The player also had spells at French clubs Perpignan, Biarritz and Dax before joining Glasgow Warriors in 2010. CCTV footage reviewed during the investigation showed Aramburu and his former rugby teammate, Shaun Hegarty, sitting at a bar opposite the former soldier, Le Priol, and his friend Bouvier on 19 March 2022. Le Priol and Bouvier were both linked to a far-right extremist group at the time, which has since dissolved. An altercation broke out between the two groups of men, the CCTV footage showed. As the two former Rugby players walked off towards their hotel, Le Priol and Bouvier drove around to find them and opened fire. Aramburu died at the scene, Reuters reported. Le Priol was subsequently arrested in Hungary while attempting to cross the border ⁠into ​Ukraine. He told Hungarian police at the time he was going to Ukraine to fight. The defence cited post-traumatic stress disorder in Le Priol's case and childhood trauma in Bouvier's case. But in court, Le Priol was described as "animated by the will to kill". "The narcissistic, intrusive and uncontrollable rage of Loik Le Priol ultimately led to the gratuitous killing of Mr. Aramburu," the presiding judge said. Meanwhile, Aramburu's widow Maria asked for a verdict that would allow her and Aramburu's three children "to build their lives as adults". title: The Papers: 'Verdicts that rocked football' and 'Burnham bottles it'
description: Manchester City being found guilty of financial breaches and the prime minister ruling out an early general election leads Saturday's papers.
body: Premier League side Manchester City being found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching leads a number of Saturday's papers. "The 114 guilty verdicts that rocked football," is how the i Weekend describes it. The paper calls the verdicts a "warning to foreign owners", quoting Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy as saying "investment is welcome, undue influence is not". The club's punishment has not yet been decided and it denies the charges, the i Weekend adds The Manchester City logo dominates the front page of the Sun, with the paper asking: "Going down?". It says the club "could face Prem drop" following the verdict, with charges "covering the trophy-laden period from 2009 and 2018". Bosses at Manchester City, which currently boats "superstars including Erling Haaland", are poised to appeal, according to the paper "Ban City" is the Daily Star's take. The paper says "calls for a ban" have reached "fever pitch" - and it pictures former manager Pep Guardiola kissing the Premier League trophy The FT Weekend says the findings "will send shockwaves through European football". Meanwhile, the paper has a feature on how "a global effort to tax tourists is picking up steam". It says cash-strapped areas are seeking "voter-friendly ways to raise revenues and exert some control over a travel boom that keeps breaking records" The Guardian also leads on the Manchester City verdict, saying the Premier League is now in "turmoil". It says the "most serious" charges relate to "claims that the club failed to provide 'accurate financial information' to the league". Elsewhere, the paper reports on Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying he "will not call a snap general election before 2029", during a round of broadcast interviews with regional media "Burnham bottles it!" is the headline leading the Daily Mail. The paper says he ruled out a snap election "after poll shows he'd lose majority". It adds that aides of the prime minister had "flirted with the idea" of an early election, but Burnham has now moved "kill off speculation" he might send the country to the polls on the eve of Labour's autumn conference The Times leads on a "cabinet rift", reporting Housing Secretary Angela Rayner criticising Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's visa reforms plan that would "make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK". Rayner tells the paper the plan would "hit" foreign care workers who had "moved their lives here to look after our loved ones". The Times describes it as "significant public criticism by a senior cabinet minister of a policy that Burnham inherited from Sir Keir Starmer" The Daily Telegraph leads with pleas from the family of retired explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes who "have demanded an urgent investigation into his care arrangements". The family accuses the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG) of "ignoring repeated requests to look into the explorer's welfare after his wife, Louise Millington-Cotes, stopped him from receiving visitors", the paper says. Millington-Cotes hasn't responded to requests for comment, and the OPG has been contacted for comment, the paper adds The Daily Mirror reports that detectives are "looking again at CCTV evidence which could point to Jill Dando's killer" The Independent leads on comments by Labour Party Chair Bridget Phillipson, who accuses Reform UK and the Tories of having "weaponised" violence against women for "political point-scoring". A source close to Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch describes it as a "spiteful and absurd attack", the paper reports, while Reform UK did not respond to a request for comment The Daily Express reports that the prime minister "[blaming] Brexit for the Channel boats crisis", after Burnham said a "loss of collaboration" with European neighbours "had made it harder to stop illegal Channel crossings". It follows what the paper describes as a "bruising" week for the Home Office "bruising week for the Home Office", with more than 700 migrants reaching the UK via small boats on Wednesday Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: TikTok to pay $100m and limit daily child usage in Alabama settlement
description: Alabama was set to take TikTok to trial over claims that it intentionally addicted young users.
body: TikTok has become one of the most popular social media platforms in the world. TikTok and its parent company ByteDance will pay the US state of Alabama $100m (£754.5m) and make a series of changes to restrict children's usage in the state as part of a lawsuit settlement. The deal was reached just before a jury trial was set to begin on Monday. It ends a lawsuit alleging TikTok is intentionally designed to addict children to its features, mirroring a host of lawsuits against social media platforms. The company is now required to install a number of new safety features, including a two-hour daily usage limit for children as well as overnight and school-hour restrictions. The changes will only apply in Alabama. It marks the platform's first settlement with a US state. "We're very pleased," said Katherine Robertson, chief counsel in the Alabama Attorney General's office in an interview with the BBC. She added that the state had been engaged in mediation with TikTok in the run-up to trial and that the deal they have now reached was the state's final offer. "This is very restrictive injunctive relief that's going to require them to change a lot of the policies that we had identified as the culprits in what we call the war on childhood," Robertson said. The new time limits and usage blocks are due to take effect immediately. However, TikTok has up to a year to implement other changes included as part of the settlement, such as the establishment of age verification measures. Many of the measures follow a framework established by an August settlement struck between social media rival Meta and 52 state Attorneys General. TikTok has agreed to pay up to $300m to Alabama if conditions of the new settlement are not met. The $100m payment is due to the state within 45 days. Other safety features demanded as part of the deal include a host of measures to allow parents to heavily moderate usage by their children, along with restrictions on some content, and new ways to verify the age of young users. TikTok will also limit children's accounts being discovered by adults, and notify parents to any "suspicious interactions" between teen users and adult users. A blanket ban on all cosmetic filters for children will also be put in place. "TikTok's priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community," a spokesperson for TikTok USDS said. "This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens." Earlier this year, TikTok split its business ownership, with a new group of investors taking control of operations in the US. The remainder of the business is operated out of China. ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok in China, was also part of Friday's settlement as ByteDance remains a minority owner of the US joint venture. title: OpenAI investigating 'dozens' of instances of agents acting improperly
description: OpenAI agents tried to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through extreme means that sometimes curbed security controls, the company said.
body: OpenAI has been at the center of new concerns over uncontrolled AI activity. OpenAI said Friday it had alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been impacted by its AI agents acting improperly. OpenAI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through sometimes extreme means, the company said. While some of the activity was simply due to the tools working to find "authoritative sources of public information," some went beyond that. Like an AI agent taking and transferring data when it should not have, OpenAI said. Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere. The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had allowed OpenAI to train models using their data. Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted, "This is not an appropriate use of this data". It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed. The new disclosures came just days after Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme, Medicare. Since August, public fears have grown around the potentially serious, even life threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control. Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog. In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools, essentially AI bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, "bypassed" security controls of some websites. In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended. OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details. "Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said. Not all of the instances involved in this incident are being considered a significant security breach, the company noted. "Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address." The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet. OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after and incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being prompted to do so. Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later. Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, said Wednesday during a United Nations Security Council session on AI: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to close this attack publicly." "Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added. During that same UN meeting, Sam Altman, head of OpenAI, and Dario Amodei, head of rival AI firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to form global standards for AI safety and ways to monitor and report such incidents. While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as the BBC reported. OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred. "Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete." title: Smoke rises from burning Greek cargo ship near Mykonos
description: All 29 people aboard the ship were safely evacuated using lifeboats, the Hellenic Coastguard said.
body: This video can not be played A fire broke out on the deck of a truck ferry sailing north of Mykonos on September 25. According to the Hellenic Coastguard, the blaze required an "extensive firefighting operation", but it is not clear how it started. All 28 staff and the single passenger on board were safely evacuated using lifeboats, they added. Watch: Smoke rises from burning Greek cargo ship near Mykonos. title: Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
description: Exploring the issues behind the escalation of tensions between the TPLF and the national army.
body: Tigrayan forces have been patrolling the streets of Tigray's capital, Mekelle, this week Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army. Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict. There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted. This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago. It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray. The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions. This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting. This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation. The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray. For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government. It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades. At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population. When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence. Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century. The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine. An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022. There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray. The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army. Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991. When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa. The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum. People have been reportedly rushing to buy food, panicking that a full-blown war will start For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms. The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy. But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy. This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions. A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies. Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army. Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power. So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside. TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated. Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests. As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country. It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies. During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out. Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports. Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force. title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
description: Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC "constructive discussions" were taking place through mediators.
body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week. Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June. "The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar. Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump threatened to "annihilate the Islamic Republic". The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices. It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November. "If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters. He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU". "I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added. A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush". This video can not be played Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached The MOU between the US and Iran, signed on 18 June, was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including the end of a US naval blockade and sanctions relief. It also said Iran would "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait and hold talks with Oman over future shipping arrangements. But it fell apart a short time later when both sides resumed strikes. Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation. The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy. Trump since has claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with daily numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm cited by Reuters. However, Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting oil exports from Saudi Arabia via the Red Sea on the other side of the Arabian peninsula. The group seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping. The situation has been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations. US media has reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has requested military support from Trump. During his speech at the UN General Assembly this week, Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" On Friday, Araghchi said Iran did not accept "coercion, threats or intimidation" and added that "peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation". title: Indie and punk music made me feel I was betraying my race
description: Big Joanie's Stephanie Phillips sets out the history of black people and alternative music.
body: A new book by musician and author Stephanie Phillips sets out the history of black people and alternative music Growing up in Wolverhampton, Stephanie Phillips says she was initially pretty much into the same chart music as her friends. But alongside TLC, Aaliyah and Destiny's Child, she developed a passion for rock, indie and punk. "It was music that meant a lot to me as someone who was very shy and needed an outlet," she said. Yet she felt compelled to keep that passion hidden. "There was always this idea that black people weren't really into alternative music, or punk," the musician, journalist and author told the BBC. "When I first got into alternative music I felt like I was betraying my race, and had to keep my love of rock practically secret," she writes in her new book. "There was a particular way that I was supposed to move through the world and being super into this genre was seen as something that wasn't for black people." Big Joanie was set up as a black feminist punk band, says the author and journalist In We Were Here, the Big Joanie singer and guitarist charts the role of black artists in creating, shaping and transforming rock 'n' roll, punk and alternative music. Phillips argues black artists never disappeared from the scene but were often forgotten, overlooked or deliberately excluded. "There was this insinuation that we weren't really part of those histories," she said, "but when you look back, there was so much there." She says the phrase "black weirdo" captures both how she felt and how others viewed her involvement in the punk scene. The lead singer of ska and 2 Tone group The Selecter, Pauline Black, agrees. The pair are set to take part in an event together as part of Black History Month, in Coventry. "Although what I do still comes from the genre of black music, I was one of those weirdos in a way because I come from a folk background, and you can't get much whiter than that," said Black. "Certainly when I was growing up if you weren't into Tamla, you weren't into soul - which I am, but didn't particularly want to do music like that - then nobody really understands. "If you want to be a punk, and are black and a woman it's very difficult." The book explores figures including Sister Rosetta Tharpe and Jimi Hendrix before moving through later genres, from heavy rock to pioneering punk acts such as Bad Brains and Pure Hell. "We've always known that black people were essential to the creation of rock and roll," Phillips said. "They're also essential to the creation and continuation of so many different genres that came off of that." Gospel singer Sister Rosetta Tharpe played a significant role in the creation of rock'n'roll, music experts say Tharpe, whose guitar work helped shape artists including Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley and Little Richard, was "pivotal" to the emergence of rock'n'roll, Phillips said. Yet she was largely forgotten after her death in 1973 before being rediscovered decades later. Phillips argues these histories were often overlooked as music journalism grew more influential. Publications such as Rolling Stone helped define the archetypal rock star, she argues, often favouring white male artists while overlooking many groundbreaking black performers. Segregation also shaped the music industry and charts until the mid-1960s. "The threat of the colour line being breached was terrifying in America," she said. "It wasn't just in schools or public spaces, it was in culture too." Punk band Bad Brains "changed what hardcore could be", the author says Pioneering black punk bands such as Bad Brains were frequently under-recognised despite their influence, Phillips said. "They completely changed what hardcore could be. They had the technical proficiency to play harder, to play faster," she added. "People think black people haven't been there. It's like, well, we probably have been, the question is whether it was documented properly." The band Skunk Anansie were seen as "outsiders" by the industry, says Phillips After moving to London, Phillips became involved in the independent DIY punk scene, which she said was welcoming to women, non-binary and trans people. But despite the city's diversity, there were still only a handful of black people involved. "It still made me feel a bit of an outsider," she said. In response she co-founded Big Joanie, describing the group as a black feminist punk band. "It was exciting creating a space where black women could exist outside all those expectations," she said. Bloc Party frontman Kele Okereke was interviewed for the book about his experiences in the indie scene The book also examines how black artists within alternative music have faced hostile or distorted media coverage. She points to Skunk Anansie's Skin, who was often portrayed through the lens of her appearance rather than her music. "The only way they would speak about her is either that they found her scary or they couldn't take their eyes off her," she explained. "They were seen as outsiders and their music wasn't really as well championed as other artists." Bloc Party frontman Kele Okereke experienced similar treatment, including being outed by a music magazine. Interviewing him for the book, Phillips said it was clear the experience had remained painful. "The shyness and vulnerability of one of the few black men in the indie world was often being interpreted as hostility," she said. title: Inside iconic horror game Silent Hill's Scottish makeover
description: One of gaming's biggest horror franchises has come to the UK. Can it live up to the original?
body: This video can not be played Watch: Take a look at clips from Silent Hill: Townfall As I creep through the heavy fog of Silent Hill: Townfall, I'm met by an oddly familiar sight amid the terror - a sign for a Sunday roast. For the first time, one of gaming's biggest horror franchises - created in Japan but traditionally set in the US - has come to the UK, set on a fictional Scottish island. Jon McKellan, director at Glaswegian developers Screen Burn, told me taking on the mega brand was an "absolutely terrifying" prospect for the relatively small team. As a fan of the games, I was keen to find out what one of the most iconic survival horror series looks like in Scotland - and whether it can live up to its legacy. Sadly there's no option to go inside The Mariner, have a nice cold pint, and wait for all this to blow over I played Silent Hill: Townfall, which was released on Thursday, on my PlayStation 5, and it ran well, though there have been some reports, external from others of performance issues. Set in 1996, the game follows the plight of an American man called Simon Ordell, who washes up on St Amelia with a red hospital ID band around his wrist and an IV drip in his arm. As is to be expected from the Silent Hill games, the real reasons why you're there and what's going on are teased as you progress through the story in a typically vague fashion. Simon Ordell arrives on the island of St Amelia, with no memory of who he is or why he's there The team took inspiration for the setting from the tiny fishing village of St Monans in Fife. For those concerned the game might lean into any typical Scottish stereotypes, McKellan told me he wanted it to feel "authentic and natural". "It's not tartan everywhere, but if you grew up in a working-class town in the 90s, you will get a lot of the references," he said. In Townfall I walked past film-quality models of red pillar boxes, 20 mph speed limit signs and charity collection boxes shaped like guide dogs. Not since 2006, when I had to storm Manchester Cathedral in Resistance: Fall of Man, have I felt an oddly patriotic attachment to game areas or objects. To save the game, I had to use a phone, which often meant stepping inside a "coins and card" telephone box - a sight instantly familiar to anyone old enough to remember them on British streets. Meanwhile, a level set in a council estate leans into the concrete starkness of the area's looming grey buildings. While some may question why the main character is American rather than Scottish given the setting, there are narrative reasons why Simon is more of an outsider to this community, which are slowly drip-fed into cutscenes and in-game documents. For the most part I was intrigued by the story, which, like many of the previous games, explores themes of trauma and guilt sensitively. This edition also touches on ideas around the impact of big corporations on small communities, which brought added relevance to the setting of an isolated seaside town. Even everyday objects like electricity meters appear as part of the game's puzzles and missions I soon had to face the island's monsters - gnarled, fleshy beings with axe-like heads or mangled faces. While St Amelia's inhabitants might not quite live up to the heights of Silent Hill 2's mannequins for sudden frights, their speed and general nastiness were still enough to make me want to run away as fast as possible. Even when I picked up weapons such as a plank of wood or a steel pipe, a series staple, there was never much sense that I had the upper hand. These all degrade over time, and though I did eventually get a gun, bullets are scarce, meaning I still had to sneak around rather than face threats head-on. If you do end up going the wrong way down a one-way street, the game has a few weapons you can use, like this plank "We don't do jump scares, really," said McKellan - although I can think of a few alarming times playing the game I vehemently disagreed with that statement. The fear is dialled up an extra notch by Byron Bullock's rich sound design, with the music swelling almost unbearably intensely when spluttering nasties stumbled closer. Composer Pilotpriest, also known as Anthony Scott Burns, deserves recognition too for his hauntingly bleak soundtrack. I think it says a lot that I closed every door I opened behind me in the game, in the naive hope it might stop monsters following - even at moments when there were none around. The CRT monitor is just one example of the retro tech used to avoid getting attacked Simon soon picks up a handheld CRT device to help with sneaking - a clever updated version of another staple of the Silent Hill series: the crackling radio. This piece of retro tech - basically a small portable TV - gives you a fuzzy image of nearby monsters on its screen, so you have some idea of where they are in order to avoid them, though it can get a little fiddly if there are several nearby. "I think it lends itself well to horror when the technology is a bit frail, a bit outdated," said McKellan. "You don't feel safe when those kinds of things are fragile." Later sections where you rely on even cruder tech to spot enemies ratchet up the tension further, at the expense of making the gameplay much slower. Thankfully, there are often other cues as to the whereabouts of your fleshy foes, such as flickering lights and their awful, gurgling cries. Reviews of the game have championed its atmosphere, with IGN's Tristan Ogilvie calling it "oppressively ominous". Silent Hill: Townfall has three difficulty settings for combat - easy, normal and nightmare (there are also two settings for puzzles, with one giving more hints). I played on normal, though there were one or two sections with a new, super-strong and fast single enemy where I considered changing to easy. These were the most aggravating parts of the game for me, despite having played and loved Alien: Isolatio

title: How the bare nails trend became a class issue
description: Bare nails - or nails that appear that way - are a growing trend. But is it as innocent as it seems?
body: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all. "It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says. These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on." Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails. In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury". But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful. Paloma Buddemeier has seen a shift in what customers are looking for at her London nail salon Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say. "That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC. "They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty." For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine. Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue. For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore. Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail. "It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair." Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth. "I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.' "And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'." Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein. Angela Scanlon recently decided to abandon her manicure habit Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new. But beauty magazines have declared "All The Cool Girls Are Quietly Quitting Manicures, external", that "Bare Nails Are the New Status Symbol, external" of "Polished Women" and that "Manicures Are No Longer Classy, external". And now, there's a never-ending stream of posts on Insta and TikTok promoting shiny, natural-looking nails, and detailing how you can get them yourself. The look has become so hyped some have gone full circle, booking in salon appointments to mimic it. At the Wumman Spa nail salon, some of Buddemeier's clients sit in the chair for hours, as nail artists build them hyper-realistic fake nails in sheer, glossy neutrals, à la Zoe Kravitz and Zendaya. Londoner Khadija says she was once a fan of elaborate nail art but pivoted to bare nails earlier this year. "It's just really chic. And I love less is more, I love minimalism... less consumerism and just self-care things that you could probably do at home." Reluctantly joining the bandwagon thanks to the rising cost of living is her friend Emmanuella. "It's just too expensive now," she says. "I think getting [your] nails done is tacky now, because who's got an hour to waste?" one 25-year-old tells the BBC, adding, "also, I lift weights in the gym, so I don't want to snap a nail and waste money." But there are those who think the trend - or the way it's being discussed by some - belies something more sinister. Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro. "Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC. Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour. A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman. And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement. But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say. title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
description: Roelf Meyer tells the BBC that being a white Afrikaner gives him legitimacy to challenge Trump's claim of a genocide.
body: This video can not be played Are claims of a white genocide in South Africa real? South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself. "Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it. His response to the US president's claim is blunt. The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so. Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted. In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from. Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners. Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African. Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas. Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property. "Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said. She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside". President Trump confronted South African counterpart Cyril Ramaphosa over widely discredited claims that genocide was being committed against white people The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday. In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa. "While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart." SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme. Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms". "There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says. SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, alleges there's a "political drive towards killing white people" Race policies or Israel - what's really driving Trump's fury with South Africa? Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? Do Afrikaners want to take Trump up on his South African refugee offer? An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks". Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners. "I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind." Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject. The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party. He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner". "But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says. Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue. Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country. While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution". Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home". He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing. Rudi Swanepoel says it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too. "Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Ru

title: Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?
description: Employees and recruiters weigh into the online debate around interview etiquette.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Is it OK to take an iced coffee to a job interview? Would you bring an iced coffee to a job interview? The question on the internet's lips this week started life, as many do, in a TikTok video. "Don't waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee, it just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand," said US recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen. It's what her Gen Z job candidates are doing, she said, warning it makes it look like the interview is "just a stop on your list of errands for the day". The post has started what Wehniainen calls the Great Iced Coffee Debate of 2026. Some believe turning up with an iced matcha latte in hand is a cardinal sin. They say it's unprofessional, too informal, and a distraction. Others feel this is an overreaction - distracting from how difficult it is to secure a job - or even just get an interview in the first place. In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Wehniainen says she "was never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate. "My point was simply about avoiding distractions." Hanad, 28, works for an energy supplier in London. He likes iced coffee but wouldn't bring one to an interview. "A job interview is all about first impressions," he says. "Anything can deter the employer from employing you. "Iced coffee is something a lot of teens drink… it would look immature and too informal." Hanad says he wouldn't take an iced coffee to an interview He would never bring along an energy drink for the same reasons. But he says water or a hot coffee would be okay. His colleague Tsvetina, 24, thinks a potential employee shouldn't be judged by what they bring to the interview, nor their dress code. "I think we should be moving away from these traditional corporate stigmas. What matters is what the person is actually communicating during the interview." Aisha, 28, says she would take along an iced coffee. "I think it shows that I have come early enough to get iced coffee." She wouldn't bring a fizzy drink, however. In general, she thinks a lot of employers like to see personality in a candidate. "It makes you stand out from other people who are coming [applying] for the job." Katy feels there is a sexist element to the controversary around Wehniainen's post Katy, 25, a personal assistant in events, says she personally wouldn't turn up to a job interview with an iced coffee. But she sees the controversy around Wehniainen's post as "a bit sexist, because it's usually girls who drink iced coffee". "If it was a hot coffee, which is more masculine, there wouldn't be a discourse about that." Young people trying to land their first job are facing multiple challenges. The number of graduate vacancies in the UK has almost halved in the past year, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs. Around one in eight people aged 16-24 are not in education, employment or training - so called Neets. Young workers in the US are also struggling with a tight jobs market, external as hiring slows. Lucy Cooper is the founder of Spark, a design and branding recruitment company in London. She says her industry - marketing - is really tough right now, and she doesn't know of any Gen Z candidates who would risk turning up to an interview with an iced coffee. You could "seem too relaxed and a little bit flippant, like you're not taking it seriously enough, or you are interviewing the employer rather than the other way round". "I think people at junior level are very conscious about not doing anything that could jeopardise their chances," she says. She adds that it would be fine to accept a coffee offered by the employer, however, or drink one on a video interview. The one thing you need to do to succeed - according to top bosses I changed jobs 10 times in 10 years to get the career I wanted I've spent 30 years in recruitment - this is how to get a job Dan Craddock, director at Hays, says employers shouldn't rely on "snap judgements". "It's important not to read too much into a single item a candidate brings to an interview. "Whether that's an iced coffee, a bottle of water or a notebook, employers are ultimately assessing the skills, experience and behaviours that will make someone successful in the role." Chris Mason, co-founder of Intelligent People - a specialist recruitment agency for the tech industry, says focusing on ice coffees alone "does seem to be an overreaction on the US recruiter's part". He advises candidates to "try to do everything possible to project the right image and attitude". He warns bringing snacks or specialist drinks may undermine the impression candidates will want to give - that they're "serious and focused on the interview". He says the main issue they see with some younger candidates is a lack of preparation, not being punctual, and not researching the role, organisation or interviewer.
